*Second Series*

## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

# Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, Entire, Uniform, Convenient, Economical, of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III

A chronological reprint of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the Church’s first twelve centuries, carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text and with headings at the upper margin of each page distinguishing and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal that nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one weighs the clearness of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient form of the volumes, uniformly maintained throughout the course of the work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# [The Complete Works of Alcuin]

## Third Part of the Works of Blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, Teacher of Charlemagne

# Dogmatic Treatises

[Col. 0009]

## First Treatise

### On the Faith of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, in Three Books, Addressed to the Glorious Emperor Charlemagne, Devoted to God

## 701–702. Preliminary Notice

[Col. 0009A]

Alcuin wrote the present little work in the monastery at Tours, toward the end of his life, and at precisely the time which he himself indicates in his dedicatory letter to the emperor Charlemagne: the time “when the peoples whom military effort in earlier times had been unable to subdue for himself were coming in voluntary submission”; and when “the most celebrated assembly, at which the priests of God and the Christian preachers of the people were gathered together by imperial command,” was being held. I believe these statements should be understood of the year 802.

For the Moissac Annals, in Bouquet, volume V of the *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum et Francicarum*, p. 80, record the following under that year:

> “In the month of October the emperor Charlemagne assembled a universal synod at Aachen. There he ordered all the canons received by the holy synod, and the decrees of the pontiffs, to be read again to the bishops, priests, and deacons, and ordered them to be fully handed down in the presence of all the bishops, priests, and deacons. Likewise, at that synod he gathered all the abbots and monks who were present there, etc.”

The same synod is also mentioned under that year in the *Brief Chronicle*, composed in the year of Christ 810, in the same Bouquet, cited work, p. 29, and in Chesnius, volume III of the *Scriptores Francici*, p. 125.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] See also Baluzius, in his notes to the *Capitularia*, volume II, p. 1059.]

In that same year the peoples—especially the Saxons, who had resisted Charlemagne for thirty years—were negotiating with that emperor concerning their submission, until finally, in the following year, 803, peace was established between both sides in such a way that the Franks and Saxons

> … might become one people in concord,
>
> and alike obey one king forever.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] The Saxon Poet under the year 803, in Bouquet, cited above, p. 167.]

I have no doubt that this little work, sent to Charlemagne, was proposed and commended by that same king to the Fathers assembled in council, in accordance with Alcuin’s wish. Certainly thereafter it was approved and praised by the most distinguished men of that age.

For Teganus—whom I believe to be the same man who wrote the *Life of the Emperor Louis the Pious*—sent this work of Alcuin as a gift to Hatto, or Hetto, apparently bishop of Basel, and judged it worthy “for that bishop to exercise his holy intellect.” “For this reason,” he says, “I have sent you this volume, because Saint Alcuin, the supreme master of learning, gathered it into one work from various books of Saint Augustine and presented it to the most skilled and noble emperor Charles. It treats, as the greatest need of mortals requires, of the divine Nature and Essence; of the eternal Begetting of God the Father; of the eternal Birth of the Son of God; of the eternal Procession of the Holy Spirit; of the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and of how there is one Triune God and one God who is Triune, as true faith commands us to believe, etc.”

Thus Teganus writes in his letter to Hatto, published by D. Martène in volume I of the *Amplissima Collectio*, p. 84. Aeneas, likewise, bishop of Paris, who flourished under the emperor Charles the Bald, cites numerous testimonies from this writing of Alcuin in his book *Against the Greeks*, as may be seen in that work from chapter 79 through chapter 89, in D. d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, new edition, volume I, pp. 130–131.

Indeed, the present little work is almost a system and compendium of the theology that prevailed in that age. It contains a thoroughly sound doctrine, free from every error, and was therefore considered a classic book of the greatest usefulness both for teaching and for preaching.

[Col. 0010B] It is consequently not surprising that, after the book became known through the commendation of the most wise emperor, the Fathers of the Council of Aachen, Teganus, Aeneas of Paris, and others, it was eagerly sought out and copied many times, and that even today copies of it are preserved in all the older libraries.

Nor did the esteem in which the work was held diminish in more recent times. After the fortunate invention of printing, it deserved to be brought into the public light in various forms—sometimes separately, sometimes together with other collections.

As far as we have been able to discover, it first appeared in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, printed at Basel by Nicolaus Kessler in 1498, on the tenth day before the Nones of August. From that edition, different readings were collected with the greatest fidelity and painstaking labor and communicated to us by the most cultivated man, D. Christian Frederick Temler, secretary of letters to the king of Denmark.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Title: “The Book of the Levite Alcuin: On the Faith of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, sent and written to the glorious emperor Charles, devoted to God.”]

Afterward it passed into other homiliaries of the Fathers, printed frequently in the sixteenth century.

Among separate editions, the oldest known to us—and an exceedingly rare one—is that printed in 1509 in the celebrated and ancient monastery of Ottobeuren of the Order of Saint Benedict, as the first specimen of the printing workshop established by the Reverend Abbot Leonardo. At the end of it the place and year of printing are recorded in these words:

> “The present little work was printed in the monastery of Uttinpurrha, of the holy martyrs Alexander and Theodore, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the year 1509, on the Kalends of September.”

The letter which the aforementioned abbot placed before the little work, addressed to the future members of that monastery, is reported by the celebrated D. Schelhornius in the *Ecclesiastical and Literary Pleasures*, volume II, p. 603.

This edition is now so rare that we have been unable to find it either in the monastery mentioned above or anywhere else. Nevertheless, a manuscript codex still remains at Ottobeuren, according to which the same work was printed, and which we have had in our hands.

Another old separate edition appeared at Strasbourg, from the press of Peter Schœffer and John Apronianus, his associates, on the Kalends of March 1530, in octavo. The editor added these words to the title in commendation of the work:

> “In these books many things are defined with certainty and clarity which, especially in this century, are being called into question, not without insult to the faith.”

We likewise had this edition at hand for recording variant readings, through the kindness of a man born for the good of the republic of letters and praised above, D. Schelhornius, in whose library it is preserved.

That distinguished man also reports another separate edition, prepared with the commentary of Lucas Lossius at Frankfurt in 1554, in octavo, in Book I of his *Latin Library*, p. 136. In the Thuane Library, however, the date of that edition is given as 1555, while the commentary is attributed to Leonardo Lessius, although he scarcely saw the light of day in that year.

Finally, we received a third edition of these books—one deserving to be counted among the older and rarer editions—from the exceedingly rich Electoral Library of Munich, through the distinguished D. Felix Oefelius, its most industrious curator and a man of great reputation and merit among scholars.

It appeared at Constance from the printing house of Nicolaus Kalt in 1596 under the following title:

> *A little book on the Most Holy Trinity, addressed to the most serene and powerful king and august emperor Charles the Great, by the very reverend Father Friar Alcuin Albinus, formerly abbot of Saint Martin of Tours. First found and copied from an ancient codex in the celebrated monastery of men dedicated to divine worship called Rich Abbey, and now at last published in print through the industry of Nicolaus Kalt.*

The editor’s dedicatory letter is addressed to the Reverend, Noble, and Magnificent Lord D. John George von Hallwyl, dean and canon of the cathedral church of Constance.

The distinguished Andreas Quercetanus published these books, corrected with the aid of ancient and recent exemplars, and enlarged with an invocation of the Holy Trinity and the Creed, on p. 701 and following.

In order to improve this last edition further, besides the various older editions just reviewed, we had the assistance of very ancient manuscript codices: two from our library of Saint Emmeram; and four others from the library of Vienna, the illustrious cathedral chapter of Freising, the celebrated monastery of Tegernsee, and finally the renowned canonry of Beyerberg.

We later received other corrections from the distinguished D. Catelinot, a member of the Benedictine Congregation of Lorraine, noted from the manuscript codices of Saint-Viton and Saint Michael in the diocese of Verdun. Still other corrections were carefully copied from the Basel edition of 1498 by the distinguished D. Christian Frederick Temler, praised above.

Accordingly, we have had the passages missing from D. Quercetanus’s edition supplied from these codices, and have inserted into the text, within brackets, the variant readings that deserved to be recorded.

# Dedicatory Letter

To the glorious, most august, and most Christian emperor Charles, the humble levite Alcuin sends, in the Lord God, health in present prosperity and perpetual blessedness.

Since imperial dignity, ordained by God, appears to have been exalted for no other purpose than to rule over and benefit the people, let power and wisdom therefore be granted by God to his chosen ones: power, so that it may crush the proud and defend the humble from the wicked; wisdom, so that it may govern and teach its subjects with pious care.

With these two gifts, holy emperor, divine grace has incomparably exalted and honored your subtlety [Manuscript: sublimity], together with the predecessors who bore the same name and served the same divine purpose. It has spread the terror of your power among all peoples everywhere, so that those whom military effort in earlier times could not subdue for you now come to you in voluntary submission.

What, then, is to be done by your most God-devoted concern in a time of serenity and peace, when, released from the belt of military labor, the whole people hastens in peaceful quiet to gather at the proclamation of your command, and, attentive, to stand before the throne of your grace [other reading: glory], awaiting what your authority may wish to command and to whom—unless it should also assign what is just to every dignity, command what is binding, and admonish what is holy, so that each person may joyfully return home with the commandment of perpetual salvation?

[Col. 0012B] So that the zeal of my devotion in the Lord, languishing in idleness, might not fail to assist you in preaching the Catholic faith, I have sent to your most holy authority, in the form of a small handbook, a discourse on the faith of the holy and undivided Trinity, so that the praise and faith of divine wisdom might be tested by the judgment of the wisest of men.

I considered no wisdom worthy of another gift from your imperial majesty, nor did I think anyone else equally worthy of receiving so excellent a gift, since it is well known that the ruler of the Christian people must know and proclaim everything that pleases God.

For no one is more fittingly required to know either better or more than the emperor, whose teaching ought to benefit all his subjects.

I do not say this because I imagined that anything concerning knowledge of the Catholic faith was unknown or insufficiently understood by you, unconquered and most wise emperor, resplendent ruler. Rather, I wished to display the office of my name, by which I am called by some “teacher,” though not deservedly; and also to refute those who thought it of little use for your noble purpose to wish to learn the principles of dialectical discipline—principles which Father Augustine judged especially necessary in his books *On the Holy Trinity*, when he proved that the deepest questions concerning the Holy Trinity could be explained only through the subtlety [Manuscript: sublimity] of the categories.

The devout and faithful seeker will readily find this also in the work of that same Father mentioned above, if he does not neglect to acquire knowledge of philosophy through study.

Considering all these things with the devoted attention of my mind, at the time of the most celebrated assembly at which the priests of God and the Christian preachers of the people gathered together by imperial command, I brought to your most excellent authority—not, as I believe, an idle burden of resources—an exposition of the Catholic faith, if the Lord, who had given me the will to speak, illuminated my heart by the spirit of grace in the knowledge of the truth, as I trust in his mercy.

My devotion was unable to find anything that it could offer more freely, nor could I think of anything that royal benevolence would receive more graciously.

What should properly result from this awaits the judgment of your approval [Manuscripts: “What I might accomplish from this,” omitting “properly”], if this labor of mine is worthy to proceed to priestly ears.

Therefore, since the right hand of your dignity grants permission for it to be read, no one can justly despise my words, because the authority of one who approves is valued more highly than the devotion of the writer.

All the faithful have abundant reason to glory in your piety, since your clemency possesses, as is fitting, priestly vigor in preaching the word of God, perfect knowledge of the Catholic faith, and the holiest devotion for the salvation of human beings [Manuscripts: all].

Therefore, the prayers of all the faithful should desire that your empire be extended through every glory, so that the Catholic faith—which alone gives life to the human race and alone sanctifies it—may truly be fixed in the hearts of all in one confession; so that, by the gracious gift of the supreme King, the same unity of holy peace and perfect charity may everywhere rule and guard everyone.

Nor is any gift proved more pleasing to almighty God than the charity of divine concord in the Catholic faith [Manuscript: the concord of charity], so that all may be one in Christ, who died for all; through him all who believe in him may become children of eternal blessedness.

> O King, most worthy of august honor,
>
> Both leader, teacher, and glory of the empire,
>
> May the Father, the Father’s Offspring, and the gracious Spirit
>
> Protect, exalt, save, honor, and love you.
>
> May your pious mind continually compel peoples,
>
> Lands, kingdoms, and cities to love God.

# 705–706. Book One

## Preface  
### [In the edition, chapter I]

[Col. 0013B]

In the name of the Holy Trinity.

Although, as the most just punishment for original sin, we have been cast down from the joy [other reading: from joy] of blessed happiness into the miserable blindness of this exile, we have not been so completely cut off and torn away from it that, even amid these changeable and temporal things, we do not know or desire to seek eternity, truth, and blessedness.

This is clear from the fact that we do not wish either to die, to be deceived, or to be miserable.

Accordingly, by this natural instinct, the desire to be blessed is common to all human beings, although the desire for blessedness takes different forms in the minds of individuals. [of all people]

Some, indeed, thought [other reading: think] that blessedness consisted in possessing an earthly kingdom; others, in abounding in riches; others, in being exalted by honors. Some rejoice in being famous for praise; others gape after carnal pleasures. Yet true blessedness can by no means be found amid the instability of this life.

Therefore the entire sequence of the holy Scriptures urges us to rise from earthly things to heavenly things, where blessedness is true and everlasting. It is absolutely certain that no one can attain it except through faith in Catholic peace, with the cooperation of love of God and neighbor.

## 707. Chapter I  
### [In the edition, chapter II]

### No one can attain true blessedness except through Catholic faith

[Col. 0013D]

Finally, for those who wish to attain true blessedness, faith is necessary before all else, as apostolic authority teaches when it says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

It is therefore certain that no one can attain true blessedness unless he pleases God, and that no one can please God except through faith.

For faith [is] the foundation of all good things. Faith is the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can attain fellowship with the children of God, because without it no one in this world obtains the grace of justification, nor will anyone possess eternal life in the world to come.

And if anyone here does not walk by faith, he will not attain the visible presence of the blessed vision of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore every rational soul, at a suitable age, should learn the Catholic faith, especially the Christian preachers of the people and the teachers of the churches of God, so that they may resist those who contradict the truth and benefit those who love Catholic peace.

How will anyone teach what he has not learned? Or how can he be a shepherd if he does not know how to feed the flock entrusted to him with the bread of life?

Let the person who does not know not be ashamed to learn what he does not know, nor let the person who knows be slow to teach what he has learned.

Let each understand that he will have to render an account to his Lord of the money entrusted to him.

Then the faithful servant will hear the desired voice of the Lord saying:

> “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord God” (Matthew 25:21).

## Chapter II  
### [In the edition, chapter III]

[Note: [Col. 0013] Other readings: “What is true faith?” “That God is one—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and yet the divine persons are distinct from one another, coeternal and coessential.”]

# On the Unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of Unity

[Col. 0014D]

Thus every divinely inspired Scripture of the Old and New Testament, if it is understood in a Catholic manner, makes known that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, of the same substance and one essence, inseparably united in divinity.

Therefore there are not three gods, but one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Although the Father has begotten the Son, and therefore the Son is not the one who is the Father; and although the Son has been begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the one who is the Son; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but solely the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also equal to the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity.

And this Trinity is one God, from whom all things exist [“through whom are all things, in whom are all things”], as the blessed apostle Paul bears witness when he says:

> “For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory for ever and ever” (Romans 11:36).

[In the manuscripts this is the beginning of chapter 3.]

Let us therefore hold most firmly that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God. Yet the Father is not himself the one who is the Son; the Son is not himself the one who is the Father; and the Holy Spirit is not himself the one who is the Father or the Son.

For there is one essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In that essence the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

This is shown to us most clearly at the very beginning of the holy Scriptures, where God says:

> “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

When he said “image” in the singular, he showed that there is one nature according to whose image man was to be made. But when he says “our” in the plural, he showed that the God according to whose image man was made is not one person.

If that one essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one person, he would not have said “in our image,” but “in my image”; nor would he have said “Let us make,” but “Let me make.”

If, on the other hand, three substances were to be understood or believed in those three persons, he would not have said “in our image,” but “in our images.”

But man is said to have been made according to the one image of the one God, so that the essential divinity of the Holy Trinity might be indicated.

The prophet Isaiah also did not remain silent about this Trinity of persons and unity of nature revealed to him, when he says that he saw the Seraphim crying out:

> “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah 6).

In the fact that “Holy” is said three times, we recognize the Trinity of persons; in the fact that “Lord God of Sabaoth” is said once, we recognize the unity of the divine nature.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] In the manuscripts chapter 4 begins here: “That God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one.”]

It must plainly be believed, without any doubt, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one Lord [other reading: God], omnipotent, eternal, and immutable.

Each of them individually is God; and all together are one God. Each individually is a full, perfect, and eternal substance [and all together are one substance].

For whatever the Father is insofar as he is God, insofar as he is substance, and insofar as he is eternity, the Son and the Holy Spirit are likewise.

Similarly, whatever the Son is insofar as he is God, insofar as he is substance, and insofar as he is eternity, the Father [Col. 0015D] and the Holy Spirit are likewise.

And whatever the Holy Spirit is insofar as he is God, insofar as he is substance, and insofar as he is eternity, the Father and the Son are likewise: one divinity in three, one essence, one omnipotence, and whatever can be said substantially of God.

If you are asked about the Father alone, “What is the Father?” answer, “God.”

If you are asked about the Son, answer, “God.”

If you are asked about the Holy Spirit, answer, “God.”

If you are asked about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together, answer not “gods,” but “one God,” omnipotent and immutable.

# Chapter III  
### [In the edition, chapter IV; in the manuscripts, chapter V]

## That Some Things Are Said Substantially of God and Some Relatively

[Col. 0016A]

It must be understood that some things are said substantially of God, such as “God is great,” “omnipotent,” and whatever is said with reference to himself—that is, whatever signifies the substance of divinity.

Some things, then, are said relatively, such as the Father in relation to the Son, the Son in relation to the Father, and the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father and the Son.

With reference to himself, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are said substantially to be God.

Thus the Father, insofar as he is God, is by that very fact substance. Since the Son [and the Holy Spirit] are unquestionably of the same substance, the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God.

But God is said relatively insofar as he is Father, because “Father” is not the name of a substance but is referred to the Son.

[Col. 0016B] We do not say that the Son is the Father in the same way that we say that the Son is God. Nor do we say that the Father is the Son in the same way that we say that he is God, because “God” is said substantially, whereas “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are said relatively.

# Chapter IV  
### [In the edition, chapter V; in the manuscripts, chapter VI]

## That the Holy Spirit Is Said Relatively to the Father and the Son [but not in the same way as the Father and the Son are said relatively to each other]

[Note: [Col. 0015D] The words enclosed in brackets are omitted in the manuscripts.]

The Holy Spirit also is certainly said relatively to the Father and the Son, but not in the same way as the Father and the Son are said relatively to one another.

For just as the Father and the Son are said relatively, so the Holy Spirit also is said in a certain manner relatively to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

But the relation of the Holy Spirit cannot be converted reciprocally in the same way as that of the Father and the Son.

For the Father is called the Father of the Son, and the Son is called the Son of the Father.

The Holy Spirit, however, is spoken of uniformly in relation to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

We say “the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Father,” but we do not say conversely “the Father of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Holy Spirit be understood to be his son.

Likewise, we say “the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Son,” but we do not say “the Son of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Holy Spirit be understood to be his father.

The same Spirit [Holy Spirit] is also called the gift of God, because God is the giver of his gift.

In these names the rule of relation can be turned around reciprocally, so that we may say “the giver of the gift” and “the gift of the giver.”

For in these terms the customary reciprocal relation belonging to the category called “relation” can be found.

# 709

[Note: [Col. 0016D] Aeneas of Paris cites this chapter in his book *Against the Greeks*, chapter 79.]

# Chapter V  
### [In the edition, chapter VI; in the manuscripts, chapter VII]

## That the Holy Spirit Is the Common Spirit of the Father and the Son

This gift of God, therefore—that is, the Holy Spirit, who proceeds equally from the Father and the Son—is an ineffable communion of the Father and the Son.

Perhaps this is why he is called by this name: because the same designation can apply to the Father and the Son. For he is properly called what they are commonly called, since the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit; and the Father is rightly called holy, and the Son holy.

Therefore, so that the communion of both persons might be properly signified by names that separately apply to each person, he is called the Holy Spirit. He is the third person in the Holy Trinity, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with them.

And this Trinity is one God: alone good, great, eternal, and omnipotent.

The unity, divinity, greatness, goodness, omnipotence, and everything that is said substantially with reference to himself belong to him alone.

The same must not be understood or said of relative terms. For it cannot be said that the Father is Father to himself, or that the Son is Son to himself, or that the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit to himself. These relative terms must unquestionably be referred to another person.

# Chapter VI  
### [In the edition, chapter VII; in the manuscript, chapter VIII]

[Note: [Col. 0017] Alcuin: “What cannot be said of the Father and the Son, that can be said of the one concerning the other.” Manuscripts: “What can be said of the Father and the Son, that can be said of the one concerning the other.”]

## What Should Be Said of the Father and the Son According to Substance or According to Relation

Whatever is said with reference to themselves of the Father and the Son is not said of one without the other—that is, whatever is said of them that displays their substance is said of both together.

If this is so, then the Father is not God without the Son, nor the Son God without the Father. That is, the Father is not called God as though the Son were not God; nor is the Son called God as though the Father were not God. Rather, both together are God, and also one God.

Accordingly, whatever can be said of them according to substance or eternity belongs to both together.

Although the Son is called “God from God” and “light from light,” both together are God and both together are light. Yet the Father is not “God from God” or “light from light”; rather, the Son is God from God and light from light.

Nevertheless, both together, and always together, [other reading: are] one God and one light.

The same should be said of the other designations that are spoken according to substance—that is, of what both are together: omnipotent, great, good, eternal, and the rest of what is said with reference to themselves.

If this is so, the only thing that cannot be said of them is “the one from the other” when the designation belongs to both together.

Thus “Word from Word” cannot be said, because both together are not Word, but only the Son is Word. Nor can “image from image” be said, because both together are not image, but only the Son is image. Nor can “Son from Son” be said, because both together are not Son. Nor can “Father from Father” be said, because both together are not Father.

[Col. 0017D] And therefore, when the Evangelist says, “And the Word was with God,” it is important that it be understood in this way: the Word, who is the Son alone, was with God, who is not the Father alone [Manuscript of Vienna: “not that which is the Father alone”], but the Father and the Son together are God.

Here it is perfectly understood that the begetter did not precede what he begot, and also what he himself says in the Gospel:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

He says, “We are one,” that is, what he is, I also am according to essence, not according to relation [other reading: relationship].

When we say “light from light,” we must not understand two lights or a separation of light. Rather, it must be understood that the Son is the eternal radiance of eternal light, just as the image of an eternal substance is an eternal image.

# Chapter VII  
### [In the edition, chapter VIII; in the manuscript, chapter IX]

## That It Is Necessary to Distinguish What Is Said of God Substantially from What Is Said Relatively
For example, if you ask what Abraham is according to substance, the answer is: a human being. If you ask of Abraham why he is a father, the answer is given relatively: because he has a son, Isaac. If you ask of Isaac why he is a son, the answer is given relatively: because he has a father [Abraham]. Every relation, moreover, refers to something else. This rule of relation is to be understood with respect to the persons of the holy Trinity.

If, then, you are asked about God why he is called Father, answer relatively: because he has a Son. [Col. 0018B] Likewise, concerning the Son, answer relatively that he is the Son because he has a Father. If, then, it is said to you concerning God, “How is the Father that which the Son is, or the Son that which the Father is?” answer: according to substance, the Son is that which the Father is, and the Father that which the Son is, because the Father and the Son are one God and one substance. For God is spoken of substantially with reference to himself; the Father is spoken of relatively with reference to the Son, and the Son with reference to the Father. According to the distinct property of the person, the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father. According to the unity of substance, the Father is that which the Son is—that is, one almighty God.

Whatever God is said to be with reference to himself is said of each of the persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and likewise of the Trinity itself—not in the plural, [Col. 0018C] but in the singular. For it is not one thing for God to be, and another for him to be great; nor one thing for him to be, and another for him to be good; rather, being, being great, and being good are the same thing in him. Therefore, just as we do not say three gods or three essences, so we do not say three greatnesses or three goodnesses; but one God, one essence, one greatness, and one goodness.

## CHAPTER VIII (EDITED CHAPTER IX; IN THE MANUSCRIPT X). That the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, spoken of together, are not something greater than any one of them

It must, without any doubt, be believed that the Father is fully and perfectly God, the Son is fully and perfectly God, and the Holy Spirit is fully [Col. 0018D] and perfectly God; yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one full and perfect God. Nor are the three spoken of together—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—something greater than any one of them, whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit; for the greatness that exists when each person is named individually is the same as that which exists when the three persons are named together.

We cannot say that the same is possible among human beings: Abraham is a complete human being, Isaac a complete human being, and Jacob a complete human being, and all three are of one substance insofar as human nature is concerned. Yet these three are not one human being, but in every respect three human beings; and something greater is recognized in the three than in any one of them. Likewise, Abraham is one human being, yet there are not three persons in him, as there are three full and perfect persons in the one God; rather, there is one person in Abraham, as there ordinarily is in one human being. [Col. 0019A]

## CHAPTER IX (EDITED CHAPTER X; IN THE MANUSCRIPT XI). That nothing is said of God according to accident

In God, nothing is said according to accident, because nothing in him [Alt.: “in God”] is mutable. Yet not everything said of God is said according to substance, as we stated above. Although the Father is spoken of with reference to the Son, and the Son with reference to the Father, according to relation, it is nevertheless not accidental to the Father to be Father, nor to the Son to be Son, because the one is always Father and the other always Son. For eternity [Col. 0019B] and immutability exclude the instability of any accident in God: every accident can, according to time, either be or not be, and could or may likewise be so; but the Father is never not Father, and the Son is never not Son. Nor did the Father ever begin to be Father, nor the Son to be Son. If the Father had at some time begun to be Father, or the Son to be Son, or if either had ceased to be what he was, the Father or the Son would be spoken of according to accident.

But if what is called “Father” were said with reference to himself, not to the Son, and what is called “Son” were said with reference to himself, not to the Father, they would be spoken of according to substance. The Father, however, is called Father only because he has a Son, and the Son is called Son only because he has a Father; [Col. 0019C] not according to substance, as was said earlier, because these terms are not said of either with reference to himself, but with reference to one another and reciprocally; nor according to accident, because what is called Father and what is called Son are eternal and immutable for them.

## CHAPTER X (EDITED XI; IN THE MANUSCRIPT XII). That it is not a difference in substance to be called Father or Son [Alt.: to call Father or Son]

Although the Father is one and the Son another, the substance of the Father and the Son is not different. For they are not called by these names according to substance, but according to the relative [Alt.: relation]; yet this relation is not an accident, because it is not mutable.

Since the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, God must in no way be called “threefold,” because nothing can be added to the perfection of the supreme Trinity. The Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit is perfect; and God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is perfect. Therefore it is more appropriate to speak of the Trinity than of a threefold God. [Col. 0019D]

## CHAPTER XI (EDITED XII; IN THE MANUSCRIPT XIII). What is proper to each person in the holy Trinity

[Col. 0020A]

Each of the persons in the holy Trinity therefore has something proper to it, by which, in inseparable equality, it displays a certain property within itself. The Father alone is Father, the Son alone is Son, and the Holy Spirit alone [is] Holy Spirit. The Father has this as his proper characteristic: of all that exists, he alone is the one who is not from another. Accordingly, he alone exists in the person of fatherhood, not alone in the essence of divinity.

The only-begotten Son of God has this as his proper characteristic: of the one alone—that is, the Father—he alone is begotten consubstantially and coessentially; and in this lies the property of his person.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, has this as his proper characteristic: he proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, and is the Spirit of both, of the same substance and eternity as the Father and the Son. [Note: [Col. 0019D] Aeneas of Paris cites the following, chapter 80.]

Yet these three are truly three, and ineffably three, and essentially three, possessing their own properties. And these three are one, truly one; and this one is three—but not three Fathers, nor three Sons, [Col. 0020B] nor three Holy Spirits, but three persons: one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit. And these three—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are one in nature, omnipotence, and eternity.

But this must also be held with the utmost firmness: nothing said of the holy Trinity with reference to itself is to be expressed in the plural number, because that simple nature of supreme divinity must be designated in the singular, not the plural. Therefore it is not permissible to speak in God of three gods, three almighty beings, three good beings, three great beings, or three essences. Although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, they nevertheless have one name of nature, which is called God, substance, essence, omnipotence, or many other names that are said of God substantially, not relatively. [Col. 0020C]

## CHAPTER XII (EDITED CHAPTER XIII; IN THE MANUSCRIPT XIV). That certain works of the holy Trinity properly belong to certain persons

We must undoubtedly believe that the holy Trinity itself is of inseparable substance and essence, and that it operates inseparably whatever we read as having been performed by the individual persons.

Although it is absolutely certain that the Father alone is the one who said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and that the Son alone is the one over whom that voice [of the Father alone] sounded when he was baptized as a man in the Jordan—the same only-begotten God who alone assumed flesh; and although the Holy Spirit alone, belonging to the Father and the Son, is the one who descended in the form of a dove upon that same baptized man as he rose from the water [Col. 0020D] (Matthew 3:16), and who, on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, came upon the faithful gathered in one place and filled them in the appearance of tongues of fire (Acts 2:3–4);

nevertheless, we must most truly believe that the voice by which God the Father alone spoke, the flesh by which the only-begotten God alone became human, the dove in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ, and the fiery tongues in whose appearance he filled the faithful gathered in one place, are works of the whole holy Trinity—that is, of the one God who made visible and invisible things in heaven and on earth.

## CHAPTER XIII (EDITED CHAPTER XIV; IN THE MANUSCRIPTS XV). That the holy Trinity is not to be said to be separable either in nature or in persons

[Col. 0021A]

God, therefore, through the immensity of his nature, both fills and contains his entire creation; consequently, the Father fills all that exists, the Son all that exists, and the Holy Spirit all that exists. Thus [Mss.: “Because the Father”] the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God. The unity of nature, therefore, being inseparable, cannot have separable persons.

This nature of the supreme Trinity and undivided unity, which alone is wholly everywhere, just as it possesses everywhere an inseparable unity of nature and operation, so it cannot admit a separation of persons. Those persons are sometimes named individually; but God the Trinity itself willed to show itself inseparable in the persons in such a way that no name occurring in any one person would not, according to the rule of relation, be referred to another [Alt.: “is not referred”]—as the Father is truly referred to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son. [Col. 0021B]

Those names, however, that signify the substance, power, or essence of God, or anything that is properly said of God with reference to himself, belong equally to all the persons: great God, good God, eternal God, almighty God, and everything else that is said naturally of God. There is therefore no name of nature [Alt.: *non potest igitur dici*, “therefore it cannot be said”] that can belong to the Father in such a way that it cannot belong equally to the Son or the Holy Spirit. For the Father is naturally God, but the Son is naturally God, and the Holy Spirit is naturally God. [Col. 0021C] Yet they are not three gods, but naturally one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For this reason the holy Trinity must be understood as inseparable in its persons, although in speech it has names that are separable [Alt.: inseparable], because the names of nature admit no plural number whatsoever. This shows that the persons cannot be divided in the holy Trinity, because the name of each person always looks toward another person. If you say “Father,” you point to the Son; if you name the Son, you proclaim the Father; if you call him the Holy Spirit, you must understand that he is the Spirit of someone—that is, of the Father and the Son.

We must also hold this rule: all names of the divine nature or essence, just as they are spoken in the singular of one person, must likewise always be spoken in the singular of the three. [Col. 0021D] But if someone is insufficiently practiced in such mysteries of the supreme Trinity, let him ask God in prayer to understand the things of God; he will not complain against me [Alt.: “with complaints”] for having written what I read in the writings of the holy teachers.

## CHAPTER XIV (EDITED CHAPTER XV; IN THE MANUSCRIPTS XVI). What is the difference between “unbegotten” and “Father,” and that the Son alone is begotten, while the Holy Spirit is neither unbegotten nor begotten

It must be understood that saying “Father” and saying “unbegotten” are not entirely the same. Even if he had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent him from being called unbegotten, because when someone is called unbegotten, it signifies not what he is but what he is not—the one of whom you say “unbegotten.” [Col. 0022A]

Thus “Father” is said according to affirmation, while “unbegotten” is said according to negation. The one of whom this is said is denied to be begotten; yet, when he is called unbegotten, it is not signified that he has begotten anything.

When we call him Father, however, we signify that he has begotten the Son, because the Son is properly called begotten for the reason that he has a Father who begot him. But there is no division or cleaving between the Father and the Son, because one is in the other, as we read the Lord himself saying in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

One begotten from one, perfect from perfect, the fullness of divinity in both, with one in no way differing from the other: life is from the living one [Alt.: from life], the Son from the Father. As he himself says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26)—that is, he begot such a Son that he would have life in himself.

[Note: [Col. 0021] The following material is cited by Aeneas of Paris, chapter 81.]

The Holy Spirit, indeed, is said nowhere to be either unbegotten or begotten. If he were called unbegotten like the Father, two Fathers would be understood to exist in the holy Trinity; or if he were called begotten like the Son, two Sons would likewise be thought to exist in that holy Trinity. He must therefore be said, without prejudice to the faith, merely to proceed from the Father and the Son.

Yet he does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation, as some, misunderstanding the matter, thought it necessary to believe. Rather, he proceeds from both together, because the Father begot the Son in such a way that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father.

## CHAPTER XV (EDITED CHAPTER XVI; IN THE MANUSCRIPTS XVII). How the expressions of the categories are to be understood concerning God

[Col. 0022C]

There are ten kinds of human expression by which people ordinarily communicate their thoughts to one another. I do not mean those that grammarians call the parts of speech, but those that philosophers customarily call *categories* in Greek and *praedicamenta*—“predicaments”—in Latin. They are named by them as follows: substance, quantity, quality, relation—namely, the kind of expression called relative—along with possession, position, time, place, doing, and undergoing.

These, then, are the bases of our speech. For we speak either about the substance of some thing, or about quantity—that is, magnitude—or about quality, in which category of expression we call good those who are good; or about relation, that is, when persons are compared with one another, so that “master” is not said unless “servant” is understood, nor “servant” unless it looks toward “master.” We also speak about the condition of the mind or body; about position, in which standing, sitting, or lying is considered; about place and time—that is, what is done, and in what place or at what time it is done. Our speech also frequently indicates who does what, or what someone undergoes. [Col. 0022D]

Holy Scripture commonly speaks of God in all these ways, but in some cases properly, in others figuratively, and in others relatively.

Properly, God is called one substance, supreme and ineffable, which is always what it is and into which no accident or incidental property can enter. [Col. 0023A] He is always what he is because he is always immutable. God is also called great, not with any greatness other than that by which he himself is great and immense. He is therefore great by the greatness that he himself is; and he is good by the goodness that he himself is [goodness]. For God, being is not one thing, being great another, and being good another; rather, by what he is, he is great and good. Therefore it is not permissible to speak of three substances, three great beings, or three good beings in God.

That God is said to “do” is said of him most truly, because through him all things that exist were made, as the Lord says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). These things are said properly of God in the categories named above, provided that anything can be said properly of him by human speech.

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are therefore spoken of relatively concerning God, as we have explained at length above. Position, possession, places, times, and undergoing are not said properly of God, but figuratively through likenesses. Thus he is said to sit above the cherubim (Psalm 79:2), which pertains to position; to be clothed with the deep as with a garment (Psalm 104:6), which pertains to possession; and, “your years will not [Col. 0024A] fail” (Psalm 102:28), which pertains to time. “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm 139:8) pertains to place.

It is also said of God, “It repents me that I made man” (Genesis 6:7), and, “I have labored while enduring.” Yet God undergoes nothing insofar as the substance of God is concerned, because, as God, he is an immutable and impassible substance; whereas all other substances admit accidents by which some change, whether great or of whatever degree, may occur in them. Nothing of this kind can happen to God. Therefore the only immutable substance or essence is God.

To him, assuredly, being itself—whence he is called “essence”—belongs most fully and truly. To him alone the name expressed by the Greeks as *ὤν* and by the Latins as *est*—“is” or “being”—corresponds perfectly, as the Apostle says: “There is not in him ‘yes and no,’ but in him is ‘yes.’”

Now the loftiness of this very arduous discussion urges the speaker to breathe for a little while, so that he may enter upon and explain what follows with a freer mind. [Col. 0024B]

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0023]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0023B]

The entire authority of the holy books works with us toward this end: that we should believe rightly concerning God and love him with the whole intention of our soul. But the sight of the human mind is too weak to behold the most excellent light of the divine majesty unless, by God’s gracious gift, it is illumined by the splendor of the righteousness of faith and love.

Therefore divine grace must be sought with every prayer, so that the eye of the heart may be cleansed to see how properly the Trinity is one, and the one and only true God, and how rightly the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said, believed, and understood to be of one and the same substance or essence. No one can attain the vision of this most sacred blessedness except with a heart cleansed through faith, as Truth itself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

This vision must not be thought capable of being perceived by bodily eyes; rather, it must be contemplated by the gaze of a pure mind, insofar as the grace of the Holy Spirit deigns to illumine the sight of our mind. [Col. 0023D]

## CHAPTER I. That God is the cause of all things that exist

God is the cause of those things that exist, have existed, or are to exist, and he is their giver and creator. Nor must it be said that the things to which he gave existence are himself [Alt.: that he himself is that which they are]. Nor did he give any creature a part of his substance; and, although he himself is immutable, he created mutable things without undergoing mutability himself.

Therefore, in that praiseworthy hymn which, after the mystical meal, the Son of God sang before his disciples in praise of the Father, he did not say concerning his faithful, “that they may be one [Col. 0024B] with us,” but “that they may be one in us” (John 17:21), because the substance of the creator and that of the creature are different.

Nor did he say, “I and they are one [we are one],” although, because he is the head of the Church and the [Col. 0024C] Church is his body, he could say, “I and they”—not “one” in the neuter, but “one” in the masculine—because the head and the body are one Christ. But showing that his divinity is consubstantial with the Father, he said: “That they may be one, just as we are one” (ibid., 23). [Col. 0024C]

He therefore wishes his own to be one, but in him, because they cannot be one in themselves, being separated from one another by differing wills. Since the holy Trinity is one and only God—one in substance, three in persons—when he willed many things to exist, he did not will them to be that which he himself is; for the things he willed to exist have an origin, whereas his being is without origin.

## CHAPTER II. That God is above all things

We believe that God exists above all existence, above all life, and above all understanding. He is supreme existence, supreme understanding, and supreme life, from whom come all life, all understanding, and all existence. For in God, power, substance, and divinity are the same thing; all these are one, and this one is simple. [Col. 0024D]

## CHAPTER III. That it is better to speak of equality than of likeness concerning God

Concerning the Son of God, the distinguished teacher, the blessed apostle Paul, says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider himself to be equal with God a robbery” (Philippians 2:6).

Accordingly, it seems better to speak of equality concerning the divine persons than of likeness, although both expressions are found. For one substance, insofar as it is substance, is not another substance, so that it might be similar to another. In the holy Trinity, substance is not similar to substance, but is one substance; and that same substance belongs to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

There are not three similar substances, but one substance equally possessed by the three. The Father is not prior to the Son, nor is the Son later than the Father, as the Arians wished. For although Abraham and Isaac are of one substance according to their humanity, Abraham is earlier in time and Isaac later. Although they are of similar substance, that similarity of substance in Isaac the son is later in time. It is impious to believe that anything in God is earlier or later, because God did not begin to be Father in time; rather, just as he is always God, so he is always Father, always having the Son whom he begot *simul* (“at once/together”) [Alt.: *semel*, “once”; Alt.: *solus*, “alone”] from his own nature, equal to himself. [Col. 0025B]

The dialecticians also add that everything similar can admit dissimilarity: two human beings, although they may be of similar substance [Alt.: “although they may be similar in substance”], can nevertheless be dissimilar in character. Therefore they cannot rightly be called equal in every respect, and in them there are two substances divided, each one a complete human being in its own substance.

In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, however, substance is not similar to substance, but one substance, equal in every respect. Therefore the correct term is *ὁμοούσιος*—that is, “of one substance”—not *ὁμοιούσιος*—that is, “of similar substance”—as the heretics wished. [Col. 0025C]

## CHAPTER IV. On the immensity of God’s omnipotence

Whatever exists in the nature of creatures is God’s creature, and his omnipotence governs, rules, and fills what he has created. We do not say that God fills all things so that they contain him, but rather so that they themselves are contained by him.

God does not fill all things in parts; nor should it in any way be thought that God is in all things in such a way that each thing receives him according to the magnitude of its position [Alt.: in proportion to the magnitude of its portion]—that is, the greatest thing receives more and the smallest less. Rather, he himself is wholly in all things, or all things are in him, whose omnipotence encompasses everything.

No one can find a means of escaping his power. Whoever does not have him appeased will certainly not escape him when he is angry. The immensity of the divine greatness is such that we understand him to be within all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not excluded. He is therefore inward, so that he may contain all things; outward, so that by the immensity of his unbounded greatness he may encompass all things.

By being outward, he is shown to be the creator; by being inward, he is demonstrated to govern all things. And so that created things might not exist without God, God is within all things; but so that they might not exist outside God, God is outward, so that all things may be encompassed by him—not by local magnitude, but by the presence of his power, because he is present everywhere and all things are present to him.

Although some understand this and others do not—for the sun is absent to a blind person, although the blind person is in the sun and the sun is present to him—no one should form or entertain any thought about such statements concerning God in terms of human, local, or temporal mutability. [Col. 0025D]

## CHAPTER V. Why God is said to dwell more in heaven than on earth

[Col. 0026A]

What is said in the Lord’s Prayer, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9), or what is read in the Psalms, “To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 123:1), is not to be understood bodily but spiritually, because God is not contained by the extent of places.

The heavens are indeed the most excellent bodies of the world, and they cannot exist except in a place. But if God’s place is believed to be in the heavens, as in the higher regions of the world, then birds, whose life is closer to God, would have the better merit. Yet it is not written, “The Lord is near to lofty people,” or to those who live in the mountains; rather, it is written: “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted” (Isaiah 57:15), which pertains more to humility. [Col. 0026B]

But just as the sinner was called “earth” when it was said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19), so, conversely, the righteous can be called “heaven.” For it is said to the righteous: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

Therefore, if God dwells in his temple because the saints are his temple, it is rightly said, “who are in heaven”—that is, “in the saints.” This is a most fitting likeness, so that spiritually there appears to be as much difference between the righteous and sinners as there is bodily between heaven and earth.

To signify this, when we stand for prayer, we turn toward the east, from which the heaven rises and the light arises—not as though God dwelt there and had abandoned the other parts of the world, since he is present everywhere, not by the extent of places but by the power of his majesty, but so that the mind may be reminded to turn toward the more excellent nature, that is, toward God, who is the true light enlightening every person coming into this world (John 1), while a human being turns his own body, which is earthly, toward a more excellent body, that is, the heavenly body.

For if we understand this bodily heaven, which we see with our eyes, to be the dwelling place of God, God’s dwelling place will pass away: “For heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35) [Source: singular *transibit*; Alt.: plural *transibunt*]. Furthermore, before God made heaven and earth, where did he dwell?

Someone may then say: “And before God made the saints, where did he dwell?” The answer is: he dwelt in himself, he dwelt with himself, and God is with himself and remains in himself.

He is therefore said to dwell in heaven because there is a greater knowledge [Alt.: recognition] of that supreme majesty and essence in the angels in heaven, or in the holy souls of the saints, than among the saints who dwell on earth, because of the burden [Alt.: weight] of bodily dwelling, which scarcely permits the soul to fly away [Alt.: rise away] to the pure light of truth. Thus it is said: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9:15).

When, therefore, the soul has been stripped of this mortal dwelling and is restored to perpetual serenity, it will see face to face what it now considers through a mirror in an enigma (1 Corinthians 13:12).

## CHAPTER VI. Although Scripture speaks of God in human fashion, there is nevertheless no change in God

[Col. 0027A]

The sacred Scriptures, divinely supplied to us through the holy teachers for the knowledge of God, raise us from an earthly and human understanding to a divine and heavenly one, yet they descend to the words used by human custom. Thus they also ascribe to God the movements, passions, or affections of the human mind, saying that God is jealous, becomes angry, or repents, and that at some time he wills or does not will something. These are instabilities of the human mind, not changes in the divine serenity, which is always the same.

When God is therefore said to become angry, this is not a movement of a disturbed mind, because God’s anger is not subject to passion as human anger is. God becomes angry, then, without any passibility, disturbance, or change in his simple nature. For it is said of him: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wisdom 12:18). What is tranquil is not disturbed. [Col. 0027B]

They also ascribe to God the limbs of the human body, as in: “Your hands made me” (Psalm 119:73); and again: “I will walk among them”; and again: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Psalm 34:16). Yet the human mind must in every respect not think of anything such or bodily concerning God.

God has so mercifully accommodated himself to human weakness that, since we cannot know him as he is, he wished to make himself known to us according to the custom of our speech, so that through what is ours he might draw us toward what is his. While, through his goodness, he condescends to our weakness, we may ascend through the purity of understanding toward him, according to the gift of his grace. [Col. 0027C]

## CHAPTER VII. That God is wholly everywhere by his natural power

This above all we must understand: the one and same nature of the holy Trinity fills everything in such a way that there is nothing where it is not. It is reported that when a philosopher asked a certain Christian where God is, the Christian answered most astutely: “You tell me first, philosopher, where he is not.”

The whole divinity, therefore, is wholly everywhere, and is contained by no place, because God is not local. He is wholly in each spiritual and bodily thing, and wholly at once in all creatures. [Col. 0027D]

We are not yet speaking of grace, by which, through the free gift of his mercy, he offers himself for the salvation of human beings, but of the nature by which God both fills and contains everything he has made, according to which he says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24).

And according to this nature blessed David says to God himself: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). Concerning Christ, who is the wisdom of God, it is said: “He reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1).

Holy Scripture also speaks in this way of the Holy Spirit: “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7). The Trinity, therefore, which is the one, true, good, eternal, and immutable God, is wholly everywhere according to its natural immensity and omnipotence, although it does not dwell in all things according to the abundance of grace. [Col. 0028A]

## CHAPTER VIII. That God is present in the saints in one way and rules sinners in another

God therefore draws near to the good both by nature and by grace: by nature, through which he makes them human beings; by grace, through which he justifies those same sinners.

[Nature, by which he causes them to be born from human beings; grace, by which he gives them power to become children of God.]

Nature, by which he causes them to live; grace, by which he causes them to live temperately [justly and piously]. Nature, by which he causes them to remain for a short time in this world; grace, by which he causes them to reign in heaven without end.

Among the wicked, however, there is only the natural immensity and omnipotence of God, by which he causes them to exist, live, and perceive, to be rational, and also to possess freedom of will—but free, not liberated. By nature, free choice remains even now in human beings [Alt.: all people]. God deigns to liberate it by grace in those whom he chooses, so that they may not have an evil will.

Ever since the first human being was sold under sin by free choice, human freedom began to be evil, because the goodness of the will was taken away from free choice. From that time no one could possess it from himself unless, aided by the grace of divine mercy, he received it; without that aid, free choice can neither be converted to God nor make progress in God.

We must believe both realities: the grace of God and the free choice of the human being. If there is no grace of God, how is the world saved? And if there is no free choice, how will the world be judged?

## CHAPTER IX. On the diversity of things that exist
Everything that exists either always existed and did not begin to exist, or did not always exist and began to exist. Whatever, therefore, did not begin to exist but always existed is God alone: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Whatever began to exist is the whole of creation. Thus, in the natures of things there are only these two: Creator and creature.

But what always existed and always exists is either unbegotten, begotten, or neither unbegotten nor begotten. These are eternally three. [Note: [Col. 0027D] Aeneas of Paris, chapter 82.] The unbegotten is the Father alone, because he derives his being from no one but himself; the begotten is the Son, whose being comes from the Father; and what is neither unbegotten nor begotten is the Holy Spirit, whose being consists in proceeding from the Father and the Son. These three constitute the true Trinity, consubstantial and coeternal.

Since, therefore, begetting is one thing and being born another, and proceeding is something other than begetting or being born, it is clear that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. The Trinity, then, refers to the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; unity pertains to the nature of the eternal Godhead.

Moreover, among the things that were made and began in time there is found a very great diversity. Some are spiritual, others bodily; some invisible, others visible. Thus one thing is said to have been made and not born, such as heaven, earth, and many things in creation. Another is said to have been made and born, but insensibly, such as trees and plants from the earth. Another was made and born in a sentient manner, such as human beings and animals.

Something was also made, born, and reborn: the human being, made by God, born from parents, and reborn by God’s grace through the ministry [Al., mystery] of baptism. This regeneration is found in the human being alone, though not in every human being.

Among things that have been made, something is rational and mortal, such as that same human being. This is found in the human being alone, but in every human being. Something else is rational but not mortal, such as an angel; and this likewise is found in the angelic nature alone, and in every angel. Yet among these—that is, among the angels—some are eternally miserable and some eternally blessed. Likewise among human beings, some will be punished because of the merits of their wickedness, while others, together with the angels who kept their original rank, will be eternally blessed through the grace of God.

But these diversities and mutabilities of creatures were created by the one immutable God, who without any doubt made everything in heaven and on earth just as he willed. This also must be known: every substance that is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God.

## CHAPTER X. That a wondrous union of the Creator with the creature took place.

[Col. 0029C]

Among this wondrous and beautiful variety of creatures—[variety from which] the most beautiful universe of formed things consists—of which it is said, “And all things were very good” (Gen. 1:31), human beings alone are read to have been created in the image and likeness of their Creator. They were appointed inhabitants of the most blessed garden called paradise and were forbidden the enjoyment of only one fruit, so that, by the easy observance of the commandment, they might merit heavenly blessedness.

But through the envy of the angel who had fallen from his blessedness, the human being became a transgressor of this commandment and, as the Creator had threatened him, was cast down into the sorrowful misery of this exile and subjected to the penal condition of death (Gen. 2).

But the most merciful Creator, unwilling that the work made in his image should perish eternally, sent his only-begotten Son, God, through whom he created the human being, so that the human being might be redeemed by the very one through whom he was created. Taking flesh from a virgin, he was so united to human nature that the same one was both human and God, and God and human; for that was the kind of assumption that made God human and the human being God. There is no personal separation in this union of the two natures, namely divinity and humanity.

Therefore, because the form of God received the form of a servant, he is both wholly God and wholly human: wholly God because of the one who receives, and wholly human because of the human being who was received. Yet by that assumption neither of them was converted or changed into the other. Divinity was not changed into a creature, so as to cease to be divinity; nor was the creature changed into divinity, so as to cease to be a creature.

One of these natures, however, shone forth in miracles, while the other submitted to insults. Yet it was by no means one person who shone forth in miracles and another who was wearied by insults. It was one and the same person: consubstantial with the Father in the form of God, consubstantial with his mother in the form of a servant, and fully human in soul and flesh.

## CHAPTER XI. Whether Christ’s soul possesses full knowledge of its divinity.

[Col. 0030B]

We confidently and unhesitatingly declare concerning the holy angels and holy human beings that, although any one of them may be called “God” nominally through the grace of adoption, nevertheless none can in any way naturally be called the God of angels or the God of the saints, as Christ is called: “And let all the angels of God worship him” (Ps. 96:8); and, “You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Heb. 2:8; Ps. 8:8). In saying that he subjected all things, he left nothing that was not subject to him.

However distinguished any saint might be through the indwelling of divine grace [Al., through the grace of indwelling], none of them was chosen to be one person with divinity except Christ, God and human being. For Christ’s soul and flesh are one Christ and one Son with the Word.

It is exceedingly difficult, and entirely alien to the soundness [Al., firmness] of faith, to say that Christ’s soul does not possess full knowledge of its own divinity [Al., of the divinity within it], with which it is believed to have naturally one person. Hence John the Baptist said that the abundance of the Spirit had been given to Christ uniquely and without measure: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34). He gives to human beings by measure; he did not give to the only Son by measure, because the whole fullness of divinity dwells in him.

He is the one who gives to the saints, and he is the one who received; and because he is powerful enough to give by measure, he ought not to have received by measure. Remaining in the form of God, he gives the Spirit; receiving the form of a servant, he received the Spirit. For he received the very one whom he gives by measure, and received him in his entirety.

He gives by measure to many sons; but he did not receive by measure, because he is the only Son. For he is naturally true human being in such a way that he is also naturally true God.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Aeneas of Paris, chapter 83.] In Christ, according to the truth of the catholic faith, we confess both divinity and a rational soul and flesh in the unity of one person. Yet divinity could not receive the Spirit, because according to divinity the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

The divinity of the Son, therefore, could not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, and is given by the Son just as he is given by the Father. It remains, then, that Christ’s soul received the Spirit, though it did not receive him by measure, because it received him in his entirety.

Where measure is said not to exist, the fullness of perfection and the perfection of fullness are found. Through this fullness it is also clear that Christ’s soul possesses the fullness of divine knowledge. To the extent that the Spirit is given to any saint, to that extent knowledge of the Godhead is received by that saint.

It must not be thought that Christ’s soul lacks in any respect the full knowledge of divinity, since it is one person with the Word. Wisdom assumed it in such a way that, together with its own divinity, it is one person in the Trinity: Christ crucified, whom the Apostle Paul proclaims to be “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

## CHAPTER XII. If Christ’s soul possesses full knowledge of divinity, how is the Son said in the Gospel not to know the day of judgment? (Mark 13:32)

[Col. 0031B]

In the sacred Scriptures there is a kind of expression which grammarians call metonymy: that is, what is effected is designated through the one who effects it.

By this kind of expression God is said not to know because he makes people not know; and God is also said to know because he makes people know. Thus it is written: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Exod. 16:4; Deut. 13:3). This is not to be understood as though God does not know whether those of whom this is said love him. Rather, it means that they themselves may know how far they have progressed in the love of the Lord [Al., might progress]. Without the temptations that occur, this is not fully recognized by human beings. The expression “he tests” itself stands for “he permits to be tested.”

Similarly, when God is said not to know, the expression may mean that he does not approve, as when he will say to the wicked, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Or it may mean that he usefully makes them not know; or even that the time for knowing has not arrived, as it is said in the Gospel: “No one knows the day and hour, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father” (Matt. 13:32).

By this kind of expression the Son is said not to know because he made them not know—something it was useful for them not to know—that is, he did not know it in such a way as to make them know it. For it was more useful for them not to know the day of judgment than to know it, so that they might always be ready and watchful, and so that, at whatever hour the day of the Lord might come like a thief, it would find them prepared.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Father and the Son have one work.

[Col. 0031D]

The Father works through the Son, through whom he made all things, and he always works, as it is said: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3); and again: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). This does not indicate a diversity of work, since the Father and the Son have one work, but it manifests the distinct property of the persons.

The very operation of God—that is, of the holy Trinity—is God’s will; and God’s will is simple and always at rest in blessedness. For God, working is not one thing and willing another: willing and working are the same for him, because God’s will is effective power. Nor is being one thing and willing another for God, but they are one and the same.

And all of this is simple, all Unity, all Trinity, all ὁμοούσιον [consubstantial], because substantial being is one in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and their action is one, just as their will is one.

All things existed eternally in God. Through operation—that is, through the power of God, who is the Son—all things appeared and were made as he willed, when he willed, and in the manner he willed, he who made all things; but he himself was not made, through whom all things were made.

The Son of God, therefore, was born eternal from eternity, God from God, light from light, as we have very often said and shall always say.

## CHAPTER XIV. That all things were made through Christ, but that he himself was born, not made.

[Col. 0032B]

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), that is, God made them in Christ, who is the Son of God, the Word of God, the power and wisdom of God, as it is said in the Psalm: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 104:24).

But this same Son was before all things, is always God, and is always in God. Therefore the Father and the Son are ὁμοούσιον [consubstantial]. In that he is called and is the Son, he was begotten, not made. Although the Apostle said, “who was made for us wisdom from God” (1 Cor. 1:30), this does not mean that he was made in his substance in order to exist. Rather, he was made Lord of all the things that were made, once there were things of which he could be Lord.
