God therefore made creatures through the Son, but he did not make the Son through whom he made all things. He begot him from his own substance, equal to himself. Christ, therefore, was born, not made.

Whenever he is said to have been made, this is said after the first generation, which is eternal [Al., which is everlasting], one, holy, and ineffable. It is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Therefore let the whole house of Israel know with certainty that God made this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). The Apostle says: “who was made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4); and the evangelist says: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14).

All these statements refer not to his existence or substance, but to his actions and to the ministry of his power and might.

When the Apostle calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), this is not to be understood as meaning that the Father cannot be called power or wisdom, any more than he can be called Son or Word. “Son” and “Word” are relative names, as was said above; “power” and “wisdom,” however, are substantial names.

Therefore the Father is power and wisdom, the Son is power and wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is power and wisdom. Yet there are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; just as there is one substance, one omnipotence, and the other things said concerning the substance of divinity.

The Son is therefore to be understood as the wisdom of the Father in the same way that he is called the light of the Father: just as light is from light and both are one light, so wisdom is from wisdom and both are one wisdom. For in the simplicity of the divine nature, knowing is not other than being, nor being other than being able, nor being able other than living.

There the same thing is wisdom as essence, the same thing is power as essence, and the same thing is life as essence; and all these are one, and there is one God.

## CHAPTER XV. That just as the Father is life, so also the Son is life.

“As the Father gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:26). Yet the Father does not give life to some and the Son to others, or in different ways. Rather, the Son gives life to the same people whom the Father gives life.

Nor is the Holy Spirit to be separated from this giving of life, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one work, just as they have one substance and essence.

For just as the living Father is life, so also the Son is life. The Father remains life; the Son [also] remains life. The Father is life in himself, from no other; the Son is life in himself, but from the Father, who begot him such that he would have life in himself.

For it was said, as the Son himself says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26)—that is, he begot the Son as one who has life in himself.

The only difference is that the Father is life without being born, while the Son is [life] by being born. The Father is from no father; the Son is from God the Father. The Father is Father because of the Son; the Son is Son because of the Father, and what he is, he is from the Father, and from life he is life.

The Father, who is life in himself, begot the Son, who would be life in himself. Therefore the Son himself says: “As the Father lives, so I live because of the Father” (John 6:58).

This was not said as though the Son did not possess life proper to himself, but had life by participation in the Father’s life—like a bodily eye that receives light by participating in another light, which it does not have in itself unless it borrows it from elsewhere.

But the Son was begotten by the Father precisely as one who would live in himself. Just as the Father does not need life, so the Son does not need another life [Al., does not need another life]. The Father is life; the Son is life. Yet both are one life, not two, because there is one God, not two gods.

The world lives in this life and will live as long as it obeys this life. Hence Peter says: “You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:69)—that is, whoever obeys you has eternal life.

And the Lord himself says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25).

What does “will hear” mean except “will obey,” that is, “will be obedient”? As far as the hearing of the ear is concerned, not all who hear will live. Many hear but do not believe, or do not do what they believe. By hearing and not believing they do not obey; by not obeying they will not live.

Thus, “those who hear” means nothing other than “those who obey.” Therefore those who obey will live.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the substance of divinity is altogether invisible and incomprehensible to creatures in its nature.

Just as God is altogether immutable, so also he is invisible in the nature of his greatness. Although it is often read that God appeared to various patriarchs in the Old Testament, he appeared to them through a created thing placed beneath him, in whatever form he wished and in whatever manner he wished.

No one has ever seen him in the substance of his divinity, which is altogether invisible and immutable.

The most blessed and great prophet Moses understood this when he said to God—with whom he is said to have spoken face to face, as a friend speaks with a friend—“If I have found favor before you, show me yourself” (Exod. 33:13).

If he had perceived God’s nature and substance, he would by no means have said, “Show me yourself.” God therefore appeared to him in the form he had chosen; he did not appear to him in his own nature, which Moses desired to see.

Moses clearly knew that whatever he saw bodily, he saw bodily; and spiritually he sought a true vision of God. For that speech, which took place through voices, was shaped as though it were a friend speaking to a friend.

The evangelist confirms that God’s nature is altogether invisible when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), because no one has seen with the eyes the fullness of divinity that is in God, and no one has comprehended it with the mind.

Nor is God comprehensible to the angelic nature, since he is truly said to be incomprehensible. But according to the measure of God’s gift, angels and the souls of the saints understand God.

Therefore, although after the resurrection human nature may advance to angelic equality and rise glorified to contemplate God, it nevertheless cannot fully see his essence. His glory will be manifested to each of the saints according to the sufficiency of that saint’s blessedness.

## CHAPTER XVII. That those visions which are read to have appeared to the patriarchs in the Old Testament were chiefly effected through angelic ministries.

That all the things seen by the patriarchs at appropriate times and places, according to God’s dispensation, occurred through angelic ministries [Al., were angelic ministries], is shown most clearly by the distinguished Teacher of the world, who was caught up to the third heaven and heard certain secret words of God’s mysteries. He says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for ministry, for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

He wants it understood that all those things read in the ancient figures were not only done through angels but also done for our sake.

A little later, when he says, “For if the word spoken through angels was made firm,” he shows that everything given or spoken to the former people was ministered through angels. But the origin and fullness of our salvation he demonstrates in the subsequent words of the same epistle to have been ministered through the very Son of God.

And the blessed Stephen, the first martyr, asserted that an angel spoke to Moses in the flame of fire, in the speech he delivered against those who stoned him (Acts 7). Yet in the same vision the Lord is said to have appeared to Moses. Angels appeared and spoke in the person of the one who had sent them (Exod. 3).

But one may ask why Scripture does not say, “An angel appeared,” or “An angel spoke to one of the patriarchs.” Although a herald conveys the words of a judge, the records do not say, “The herald said or did this,” but, “The judge said or did this.”

For this reason, it may reasonably be held that, before Christ’s incarnation, angels appeared or spoke to our patriarchs under the person of the Lord. Nor should it be believed that they appeared in their own substance, but in a created thing assumed by them at the appropriate time for the ministry of their office.

Just as the human soul is invisible, so it is entirely certain that the angelic nature is invisible to bodily eyes.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That “who alone does great wonders” is not to be understood of the Father alone.

[Col. 0035B]

Wherever “God alone” is read in sacred Scripture, it is not to be understood of any one person in the holy Trinity, but of the whole holy Trinity, which works equally whatever it judges ought to be done.

Therefore, where it is said in the Psalms, “Who alone does great wonders” (Ps. 72:18), and “who alone made the great lights” (Ps. 136:7), this is not to be understood of the Father alone, as the adversaries wish, but of the whole holy Trinity, which is one and only God.

Similarly, what the Apostle says is not to be understood of the Father alone: “Blessed and only sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:15–16).

In these words neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is specifically named. Rather, “blessed and only sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords” refers to the one, only, blessed, powerful, invisible, true God: the Trinity itself, which is equally blessed and equally powerful—indeed omnipotent, and even “unipotent,” because the whole holy Trinity has one power.

Nor, because the Son himself elsewhere, speaking with the voice of Wisdom—for he is the wisdom of God—says, “I alone have traversed the circuit of heaven” (Eccl. 24:8), did he separate the Father from himself.

How much less, then, is it necessary to understand as referring to the Father alone, apart from the Son or the Holy Spirit, what is said: “He alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light”?

## CHAPTER XIX. On the unity of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0035D]

[Note: [Col. 0035D] Aeneas of Paris, chapter 84.] The Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is full and perfect God; indeed, he is one God with the Father and the Son, and one substance with them, as we have mentioned above.

For he is the Holy Spirit who in Scripture is called the Spirit of God, or the Spirit of Christ, or the Spirit of the Father, or the Spirit Paraclete, and also the Spirit of truth; likewise the Spirit of life. He proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, and is equally worshiped with the Father and the Son, because he is equally God.

He is wholly the Spirit of the Father and wholly the Spirit of the Son, because naturally there is one Spirit of both the Father and the Son. Therefore he proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son; he remains wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son, because he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains.

Hence, by nature, he possesses with the Father and the Son this fullness of unity and unity of fullness, so that he possesses the whole Father and the whole Son; and he himself is possessed wholly by the Father and wholly by the Son.

He is also given equally by the Father and the Son—indeed, he is given by himself as well, as the Son says of him: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8).

He spoke in the prophets. Through him the Apostles bore testimony concerning Christ without fear of worldly powers, because he was speaking in them (Acts 2, 4, 6, 18), as the Lord himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

In him all the faithful have the forgiveness of sins, whether in baptism or in penance. He is called the love of God, although the Father and the Son are also love.

For just as the Son is called the wisdom of God, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom, so the Spirit himself is called the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter, because, while distributing the gifts of the sacraments, he truly gives consolation to the soul.

Through him the love of God is poured into our hearts, and through that love the whole Trinity dwells in us.

Therefore, since the Holy Spirit is God, he is rightly also called the gift of God. What is this gift properly understood to be, if not love [Al., what is to be understood as this gift, if not love]? Love leads to God, and without it no other virtue of good works leads to God.

## CHAPTER XX. Therefore we must not understand anything temporal in the Holy Spirit when he is called the gift of God.

[Col. 0036C]

This gift of God, which is the Holy Spirit, is coeternal and consubstantial with the giver. A gift capable of being given can exist even when there is no one to whom it may be given.

This gift—that is, the Holy Spirit—does not proceed in time but from eternity. Yet because he proceeded in such a way that he could be given, he was already a gift before there was anyone to whom he could be given.

For “gift” is understood in one way when it means a gift, and in another way when it means something given. A gift can exist before it is given; but something given cannot be called “given” unless it has been given to someone.

This gift of God, then, was hidden eternally in the Father and the Son, to be manifested at the appropriate time, when there would be those to whom it ought to be manifested.

This gift—that is, the Holy Spirit—exists in the same unity of substance and equality with the Father and the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0036D] The same, chapter 85.] Whether he is the unity of both, or holiness, or love; whether he is unity because he is love, and love because he is holiness, he is in no respect less than those from whom he proceeds.

This is the supreme love: that the one begotten is loved by the one who begets, and loves the one who begets him; and therefore there are no more than three: one who loves him who is from him; one who loves him from whom he is; and love itself, of which it is said that God is love.

This supreme and ineffable Trinity should not be called the God of one person, but one God.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why was the same Holy Spirit given twice by God Christ?

[Col. 0037A]

[Note: [Col. 0037C] Aeneas of Paris, chapter 86.] Without doubt the Holy Spirit was given twice so that the two commandments of love might be commended. There are two commandments, but there is one love; likewise there is one Spirit and two givings.

The love that loves one’s neighbor is not different from the love that loves God. The Spirit is given on earth so that one may love one’s neighbor; he is given from heaven so that one may love God.

Although God and one’s neighbor are different, God and one’s neighbor are to be loved with one love. The lover should love God more than himself, and his neighbor as himself.

On earth Christ gave the Spirit, but what he gave was from heaven. For the one who descended from heaven gave him. Here he found someone to whom he could give; from there he brought what he was to give.

But this love is held only in the unity of Christ’s Church, and those who divide themselves from the unity of catholic peace do not possess it.

## CHAPTER XXII. Although the gifts of God are diverse in the saints, each receives a particular gift from the one and same Spirit.

The gifts of the Holy Spirit are divided individually among the members of the Church, and particular gifts are assigned to particular persons.

In Christ alone there is the fullness of gifts, because the whole fullness of divinity dwells in him. Hence the evangelist proclaims him full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

In the Holy Spirit the whole grace of gifts consists [Al., exists]. He bestows the graces of gifts as he wills, giving to some the word of wisdom, to others knowledge, and to others faith. Thus to each person grace is given through the power of the Holy Spirit according to the will of the giver, and the same Spirit is possessed in all, just as one and the same Spirit spoke in the prophets (1 Cor. 12:4 ff.).

He also teaches ineffable things which human speech cannot express. For the Apostle says that he pleads for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8:26). He is said to plead because he makes us plead with an ineffable groaning of the heart.

But the gifts of the Holy Spirit are not now in human beings as they once were. Formerly, among the people of Israel, the gifts of the Holy Spirit shone forth in a few through various signs or prophecies. Now, however, the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out among the whole multitude of believers, according to the will of the Spirit who distributes [Al., of God].

This is what is said in the Gospel: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” [Al., clarified] (John 7:39).

Just as the members of one body have different functions, though one soul operates and governs them all, assigning to each member what it should do—to the eye, that it may see; to the hand, that it may work; to the foot, that it may walk; to the ear, that it may hear—so the faithful also have different gifts distributed to each according to the proper measure.

Although there are different graces of gifts throughout the whole multitude of the faithful, the Church is nevertheless one body through one Spirit, joined and bound together by the one bond of love.

May that Spirit deign to inspire the spirit of my humility with what must next be said concerning the ineffable Nativity of Christ Jesus our Lord, of whom the Prophet says, “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). I think it better that this should be begun from another starting point.

# BOOK THREE

## PROLOGUE

The Creator made two rational creatures: one heavenly and the other earthly. He ennobled both with the power of free choice, so that they might voluntarily and happily remain perpetually in the love of God and the praise of divine power.

But because the first of these—that is, the angelic creature, though not the whole of it—delighting in its own power, withdrew from the love of the highest good and fell into itself, becoming the murderer of itself, it experienced the sorrowful and penal eternity of its impiety.

Therefore, burning with envy against the human being, lest the human being possess the heavenly seat of blessedness, it incited him to sin, making him a companion of its own misery—as though it would be some consolation for it to suffer punishment together with many others—or even so that an injury might be inflicted upon the Creator, if the creature made in his image, having lost the name and power of its dignity [Al., having lost its name forever in the fire of its own impiety], were subjected to the angel’s impiety.

The merciful Creator did not permit this. Taking pity on the human being and wishing to restore him to the nobility of his former dignity, he sent his only Son to assume humanity, so that the one who was God from God might be human from a human being, and, being immortal, might have something from which he could die.

The Son of God therefore assumed from our mortality that by which, without endangering his immortality, he might be mortal [Al., might be able to die]. Thus he conquered the devil, the victor over humanity, more by justice than by power, to show both the perpetual justice of his equity and the mercy of his eternal goodness.

He showed justice in the angel who had murdered himself and humanity; but in humanity, which the same angel had destroyed, he showed mercy, since he wished to redeem it by the gratuitous gift of his great compassion.

By God’s gracious gift, we shall speak of this in what follows.

## CHAPTER I. On the grace of God by which God became human.

[Col. 0038D]

This also clearly commends the fact that the Holy Spirit is the gift of God, as we showed above, when the Symbol of the catholic faith says that Christ was conceived from the Holy Spirit and born from the Virgin Mary.

Since he was born differently from him and from her—from him not as from a father, but from her as from a mother—why is the Holy Spirit mentioned here, unless to commend the great grace of God?

For what did human nature merit in the human being Christ, that it should be uniquely assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will? What devotion to a good purpose? What good works preceded this, by which this human being might merit becoming one person with God—or rather, that the human being himself might be God?

Certainly, from the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and that Son was the only, only-begotten, proper Son. And because of the Word of God, which became flesh, he was indeed God.

Thus, just as every human being is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, Word and flesh [Al., flesh and Word].

Whence did such glory come to human nature, without any preceding merits, undoubtedly as a gratuitous gift, unless it is because here, for those who consider faithfully and soberly, the great and unique grace of God is clearly displayed? It is displayed so that human beings may understand that through the same grace they can be justified from sins through which it came about that the human being Christ could have no sin.

Thus the holy Virgin, the mother of the Son of God, was greeted by the angel when he announced to her the birth that was to come: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace”; and shortly afterward: “You have found grace,” he said, “with God” (Luke 1:28, 30).

She is called full of grace and said to have found grace with God so that, while preserving her virginity, she might be the mother of her Lord—indeed, of the Lord of all.

## CHAPTER II. To commend the same grace, the blessed evangelist says that Christ was full of grace and truth.

John the evangelist, having said of the Lord himself, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” added: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). What he says, “The Word became flesh,” means “full of grace”; what he says, “glory as of the only-begotten from the Father,” means “full of truth.” For Truth itself is the only-begotten Son of God—not by grace, but by nature. By grace he assumed humanity in so great a unity of person that the very one who was the one, only-begotten Son of God was also the son of man. In that one God and man, the fullness of humanity by grace and the fullness of divinity in truth are recognized: this fullness of divinity in itself possesses the fullness of grace by which all humanity is in its divinity; and the fullness of grace in itself possesses the fullness of truth by which all divinity is in its humanity. Thus the fullness of truth contains within itself the fullness of grace, and the fullness of grace contains within itself the fullness of truth. [Thus Christ is full of grace and truth,] so that, just as the fullness of humanity was assumed by the divinity, so in his humanity there is the fullness of divinity, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

## CHAPTER III. How Christ is not the Son of the Holy Spirit, although the Creed says that he was born of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary

It may cause perplexity how Christ is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, since in no way is the Son the son of the Holy Spirit. Is he therefore said to have been born of the Holy Spirit because the Spirit caused him to be born of the Virgin? For this whole wonderful work was accomplished by God’s gift [Al., “a gift”], and God’s gift is properly called the Holy Spirit. Indeed, although God made this world, it is not lawful to call the world God’s son; one ought not to say that it was born of God, but that it was made, or created, or formed, or established by him, or whatever similar expression we may correctly use. Nor, therefore, must we grant that whatever is born from something must immediately be called the son of that same thing. To give one example among many, surely no one would rightly call those who are born of water and the Holy Spirit children of water or of the Holy Spirit; rather, they are plainly called children of God the Father and of Mother Church. Thus the Son of God the Father was born of the Holy Spirit, but was not the son of the Holy Spirit. For if Christ were called the son of the Holy Spirit according to his humanity, there would be two Fathers in the holy Trinity, and God who became man would have had two fathers, one with respect to his divinity and another with respect to his humanity. But who would dare say this?

## CHAPTER IV. How the Son’s mission from the Father is to be understood

We must ask how the Son’s mission is to be understood. For the Father alone is nowhere read to have been sent; concerning the Son, the Apostle writes: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4). When he says, “God sent his Son, made of a woman,” he clearly shows that the Son was sent precisely when he was made of a woman. Therefore, insofar as he was born of God, the Son of God was in this world, as the evangelist says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:10); but insofar as he was born of the Virgin Mary, he came sent into this world. For the Lord himself also says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28). [Therefore, to come forth from the Father and to come into this world] is to be sent.

What, then, is the meaning of what that same evangelist says about him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10); and then adds: “He came into his own”? [Note: [Col. 0039D] See Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book II, nos. 7 and 8.] He was certainly sent there where he came. But if he was sent into this world, he was sent there where he already was. He was in the world, and he was sent into the world. Nevertheless, no Catholic should doubt that this mission is the work of the holy Trinity.

## CHAPTER V. How the mission of the Holy Spirit is to be understood

[Note: [Col. 0040D] Aeneas of Paris, chapter 87.]

For just as the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father, so also by the Son; both are read in the Gospel, when the Lord himself says: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). And concerning himself: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, whom I will send in the name of my Father.” But this mission took place for a time through certain visible creatures. For a kind of created form came into being in time, in which the Holy Spirit might be visibly manifested, whether when he descended in bodily form as a dove upon the baptized Lord (Matthew 3:16), or when he was also seen to descend upon the apostles in bodily form, in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). This operation, visibly expressed and presented to mortal eyes, is called the mission of the Holy Spirit—not because his very substance appeared, since he too is invisible and unchangeable, like the Father and the Son, but so that, through outward sights, human hearts might be stirred [Al., “moved”] by the temporal manifestation of him who was coming, and turned toward the hidden eternity of him who is always present.

## CHAPTER VI. Why the Father is not read to have been sent

[Col. 0041B]

The Father is not read to have been sent because he is not believed to have been incarnate. The one who appeared in the flesh is appropriately said to have been sent [“to have sent” the one who did not appear in it]. That assumed form of man, therefore, belongs to the person of the Son, not also to the Father. Accordingly, the invisible Father, together with the Son who is invisible with him, is said to have sent that same Son by making him visible. He accepted the form of a servant in such a way that the unchangeable form of God remained. Whatever appeared to bodily eyes in the Son was accomplished by the invisible holy Trinity [as in the case of Abraham, Moses, John the Baptist, and the three disciples on the mountain].

[Note: [Col. 0041C]

In Codex Vindobonensis Theol. 433, of the twelfth century, chapter 7 of this book differs from the preceding one and reads as follows:

“By what distinction is the Son now equal to the Father and now lesser than the Father to be understood?

“Therefore, once this rule for understanding the Scriptures concerning the Son of God is known—namely, that we distinguish what in them sounds according to the form of God, in which he exists and is equal to the Father, from what is according to the form of a servant, which he assumed and in which he is lesser than the Father—we will not be disturbed as though by contradictory and conflicting statements of the holy books. For according to the form of God, both the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, since neither of them is a creature, as we have already shown. But according to the form of a servant he is lesser than the Father, because he himself said: ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28). He is lesser than himself, because it was said of him: ‘He emptied himself’ (Philippians 2:7). He is lesser than the Holy Spirit, because he himself said: ‘Whoever speaks blasphemy against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven’ (Matthew 12:32). And through him he performed mighty works, saying: ‘If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you’ (Luke 11:20). And in Isaiah he says—reading the passage himself in the synagogue and showing without any hesitation that it had been fulfilled concerning him—‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives,’ and so forth (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1). He says that he was sent to do these things because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him.

“According to the form of God, all things were made through him; according to the form of a servant, he himself was made of a woman, made under the law. According to the form of God, he and the Father are one; according to the form of a servant, he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him. According to the form of God, just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself (John 5:26); according to the form of a servant: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death’; and, he says, ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’ (Matthew 26:38–39). According to the form of God, he is the true God and eternal life; according to the form of a servant, he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). According to the form of God, everything the Father has belongs to him: ‘All that is yours is mine, and mine is yours,’ he says (John 17:10); according to the form of a servant, the teaching is not his own, but that of the one who sent him.”]

## CHAPTER VII. Why the Son is sometimes said to be equal to the Father and sometimes lesser than the Father

[Col. 0041C]

From one statement of the Apostle, two natures in the Son of God are understood: one in which he is wholly equal to the Father, and another in which he is lesser than the Father. He says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized [Al., “as equal”], but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6). Accordingly, certain things are spoken in the holy Scriptures in such a way that the Son is understood to be lesser, as he himself says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); but certain things are spoken in such a way that he is shown to be equal to the Father, as when [there] he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—“one” because of the unity of substance, “are” because of the distinctness of the persons.

The prudent reader must consider this most carefully [Al., “most wisely”:] what is said with respect to which form. Yet in the form of a servant and in the form of God, it is the very same Son, one and only-begotten of God the Father: in the form of God, equal to the Father; in the form of a servant, lesser than the Father. Therefore Scripture rightly says both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The former is understood with reference to the form of God; the latter with reference to the form of a servant, without any distinction of person [Al., “without any confusion of nature”].

In the form of God, “In the beginning was the Word”; in the form of a servant, “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), that is, God became man. In the former, he is eternally equal [to the Father]; in the latter, lesser in time. In the form in which he is equal to the Father, he made man; in the form in which he is lesser than the Father, he became man.

Accordingly, catholic faith has firmly established, without any doubt, that the man whom the Wisdom of God assumed from the virginal womb lacked nothing that other human beings possess, insofar as concerns the integrity of human nature in which man was created, and that he possessed nothing at all of what the deceiver introduced into man. But with regard to the excellence of his person, he is altogether different from other human beings, because that same man was made one person with the Word of God.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why the Holy Spirit is nowhere read to be lesser than the Father

[Col. 0042C]

[Note: [Col. 0042D] See Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XI, no. 11.]

It is nowhere written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is lesser than God the Father, because the dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed by the Holy Spirit into the unity of a divine person, nor was the fire in which he descended upon the apostles so assumed, as humanity was assumed by the Son of God from the Virgin Mary into the unity of his divine person. For the Holy Spirit did not bless the dove [Col. 0043A] [or] that breath or that fire, nor join it to himself and to his person in unity and permanent possession. Rather, these things appeared as they appropriately had to appear: a creature serving its Creator and, at the command of him who remains unchangeably in himself, being changed and transformed in order to signify and manifest him, as it was necessary for him to be signified and manifested to mortals.

Although the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove or of fire, we nevertheless cannot call the Holy Spirit God-and-dove or God-and-fire, as we call the Son God-and-man. Therefore, because of these bodily forms in which the Holy Spirit appeared, he is said to have been sent; but because of them he cannot be called lesser than the Father, as the Son can because of the form of a servant. For that form of a servant adhered to him in the unity of person perpetually, whereas those bodily appearances—the dove and the fire—appeared for a time in order to manifest what was necessary, and afterward ceased to exist.

## CHAPTER IX. That “the Word became flesh” is to be understood differently from “the Word of God” in any of the saints

The God-speaking Paul says that God spoke in many ways to the fathers through the prophets, but in these last days spoke to us in his Son [Al., “but finally”] (Hebrews 1:1). And so that it might be understood with complete certainty which Son he meant, he immediately added: “Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (ibid., 2). Through the one through whom he created all things—that is, Christ, the Son of God—he spoke in the last times of the age to his saints, although God is read [Al., “we read that God”] to have spoken in the prophets. Thus it is said, “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea” (Hosea 1:2); or likewise, “The word of the Lord came to” a particular prophet, as we read: “The word of the Lord came to Isaiah the prophet” (Isaiah 38:4).

Christ, therefore, did not have the Word of God within himself in the way that other saints did; rather, he himself is the Word of God. For “the Word in flesh” is one thing, and “the Word become flesh” another; “God in man” is one thing, and “God-man” another.

Therefore the Son of God is believed and proclaimed by all Catholics to be true God not only according to the true divinity which he has by nature from God the Father, but also according to the flesh which he truly possesses by nature from the body of the blessed Mother. For the Son’s eternal divinity together with his full humanity, and that same full humanity of the Son together with his eternal divinity, are one person in the holy Trinity—and this person is not adoptive, but proper and perfect. He himself, wholly in his divinity and humanity, is the only-begotten and true Son of God, the same one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one true God, not merely titularly so, as the impious Spanish heresy has presumptuously dared to affirm by asserting that the Son of God is true God in his divine nature but titularly God in his human nature, and likewise that he is the proper Son of God in his divine nature but an adoptive son in his human nature. With Nestorius, this heresy divides the one person of the Son of God into two persons—that is, the person of the true Son of God and that of the adoptive son [Al., “of the true Son and the adoptive son”].

Yet it is utterly certain that, in the person whom he eternally possessed by being begotten from the Father, the Son of God assumed a human nature. No Catholic, confirmed in the faith, has dared to say that this nature is adoptive. The Son of God assumed human nature, not a human person, receiving the temporal substance of humanity into the eternal person of his divinity. Man passed into God—not by a change of nature, but because of the unity of the divine person. Therefore there are not two Christs or two Sons, but one Christ and one Son, God-man.

## CHAPTER X. That neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, was incarnate

[Col. 0044B]

Although the nature of the holy Trinity is one, the whole Trinity was not incarnate; only the person of the Son mercifully assumed human nature. Yet the Son of God was not incarnate in such a way that the nature of divinity and the nature of flesh were one in him. For in Christ divinity could not be what flesh is, nor flesh what divinity is, because each nature—that is, divinity and humanity—remained in its own property.

Therefore we confess that human nature, that is, flesh and a rational soul, was assumed not by the whole Trinity but by the Son alone—not into a unity of nature, but into a unity of person. Certainly the person of the Son is not the same as that of the Father or of the Holy Spirit. Thus the unity of person, while the property of each substance remained intact, just as did not make Christ’s person double, likewise did not make the assumption of human nature common to the holy Trinity.

That assumption of the form of a servant belongs only to the person of the Word of God. Yet the assumption of humanity took nothing away from the fullness of divinity and deprived Christ of none of his dominion. Hence, in one and the same Christ, the reality of human nature was revealed and the unchangeability of divine nature remained eternal.

Nevertheless, this must be understood: the whole Trinity made this form of a servant, which the Son of God alone assumed. Although it was certainly made by the whole holy Trinity, it belongs to the person of the Son of God alone. For neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but only the Son, so that the one who was the Son in the divinity of God the Father might himself become the son in the humanity of the virgin mother, lest the name “Son” pass to another person who would not be a son by birth.

Thus the Son of God became the son of man: born according to the truth of nature from God, the Son of God, and according to the truth of nature from man, the son of man, in both natures—not merely by designation or adoption, but in truth the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Word of God was conceived in the Virgin’s womb through the conception of his flesh

The Son alone, as we have said, assumed flesh so that he could be seen with bodily eyes and touched with bodily hands. He alone assumed human nature in such a way as to make it his own, and through it mercifully to pour into human beings knowledge of his divinity [Al., “to convey it to them”].

Nevertheless, it must in no way be believed that Christ’s flesh was conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before it was assumed by the Word. Rather, the very Word, God, was conceived through the assumption of his flesh; the flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word of God; and the Son of God truly possessed that same flesh of human nature, through which the Word, God, was born from the Virgin.

The divinity of the Word did not therefore come to the blessed Virgin by local movement, but by the manifestation of its ineffable power; as one to be born, he filled his mother’s womb, yet he did not leave the Father when he came to the Virgin. He is wholly everywhere and perfect everywhere. The fullness of divinity cannot be divided, but the whole Son is in the Father, the whole Son is in the Virgin’s womb, and the whole Son, assuming flesh from that same blessed Virgin, is in the flesh in which he was crucified and buried, in which he rose again and ascended into heaven, and in which he sits at the right hand of God; in that flesh also he will come to judge the living and the dead. In it all the tribes of the earth will see him—not in the humility in which he is judged [Al., “was judged”], but in the glory in which he will judge the whole world.

## CHAPTER XII. On the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ

No one will be able to possess true peace with God except through the mediator, the Lord Christ, who in two natures is true God and true man, one Christ, at once priest and sacrifice. He comes to us to offer on our behalf what he took from us, so that he might remove from us what he found in us—that is, sins. [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book IV, no. 13.]

For just as the devil is a mediator toward death, who in his pride led the proud human being to death, so Christ is a mediator toward life, who in humility led the obedient human being back to life. For just as the former, lifted up, fell and cast down the one who consented to him, so the latter, humbled, rose and raised up the one who believed.

He is therefore the mediator because he is the same true God and man, possessing with the Father the same divine nature and with his mother the same substance of humility. From us he possesses, even unto death, the penalty of our iniquity; from God the Father he possesses unchangeable righteousness. On account of our iniquity he died in time; on account of his righteousness he is himself always living—he who was crucified because of our weakness, but lives by his own power (2 Corinthians 13).

## CHAPTER XIII. That in Christ there is distinction of natures, not of person; and in the holy Trinity distinction of persons, not of nature

The Son of God, eternal God from the Father, did not abandon God the Father, although he became man from his mother. Rather, the very one who carried out on earth the things belonging to man also carried out in heaven the things belonging to God. As he himself says in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). The Son of Man was speaking these words on earth, yet that same Son of Man was in heaven.

Although he appeared to have been hidden within the narrow confines of one small body, he nevertheless governed the breadth of all creatures. The one through whom all things were created is not another from the one who was created as man; the same one is both Creator and creature: Creator in his divinity, creature in his humanity. He is not another person, but another thing, because there is not one nature in him but, in every respect, one person.

This must not be said or understood in the same way of the holy Trinity. For it is not lawful to say *aliud* (“another thing”) of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because their nature is one; rather, *alius* (“another person”), because there is distinction of persons among them. In Christ, therefore, there is not distinction of persons but of natures. For this reason he should not be called *alius* (“another person”), but *aliud* (“another thing”) [Al., “[another] concerning God”].

Accordingly, in every respect he is one and the same, mortal and immortal, capable of suffering and incapable of suffering. Therefore the Apostle said that the Lord of glory was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), although only his humanity was subject to suffering. The Son of God was therefore crucified, but according to the flesh, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians 1:23); but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God [Al., “the truth of God”].

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Virgin Mary and the incarnation of the Word of God

The blessed evangelist, in order to show the property of the one person in Christ, said: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). The Word that was with God before the world existed, through which the world was made; the Word that did not lose its eternity, although in time it wished to become man by assuming flesh from a virginal womb.

By his omnipotence, the Word willed that this man whom he assumed should become in time what he himself had always been without time—that is, the proper Son of God—so that two Sons of God could not be said to exist, one begotten before the ages and another born in time, but only one proper and perfect Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Blessed Mary the Virgin, preserving the integrity of her body, gave birth to him as God and man. She was the purest wool, most radiant in virginity, and incomparable among all the virgins beneath heaven. She was such and so great that she alone was made worthy to receive the divinity of the Son of God within herself.

For just as wool receives the blood of the shellfish so that purple made from that wool may become worthy only of imperial majesty, and no one except one endowed with august dignity may wear it, so the Holy Spirit, coming upon the blessed Virgin, and the power of the Most High overshadowing her, made her like wool dyed purple with divinity, supremely worthy to be clothed by the eternal Emperor alone.

Thus the most blessed Virgin Mary became *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”), just as she was also *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος, “Christ-bearer”). For before her there were other *Christotokoi* (Χριστοτόκοι) among the people—that is, mothers of christs—but they were not virgins, nor were they overshadowed by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, so as to be found worthy to give birth to God.

She, however, was both *Christotokos* and the only *Theotokos*, and the only virgin who conceived from the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, and was so glorified that she gave birth to God the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father.

A virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth: for it was fitting that, when God was born, the merit of chastity should increase, lest his coming violate what was intact, since he came to heal what was corrupted. Nor did the Ruler of heaven disdain the narrow confines of a virginal womb, he who fills the breadth of all creatures, and at whose birth the army of angels came to sing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

[Note: [Col. 0047D] This chapter is omitted in Codex Vindobonensis.]

## CHAPTER XV. What is proper to each nature in Christ

[Col. 0047B]

We must believe with the utmost firmness that, under the property of one person, there are in Christ the distinguishing characteristics of two natures—not so that we divide the one Christ, but so that in the one Son of God and one Christ we distinguish two substances: one that had its beginning from the virginal womb, and another that is coeternal with God the Father without beginning; one that advanced in age and wisdom (Luke 2:52), and another that is the eternal power and wisdom of God.

To say a little from among many examples: one nature slept in the boat and was awakened by the disciples, while the other commanded the winds and the waves (Matthew 8); one nature wept for the dead friend, while the other, by its voice alone, called him from the tomb and restored him to life (John 11); one nature was sorrowful unto death (Matthew 26), while the other freed the saints from sorrow and gave them the joy of eternal life; one nature ascended into heaven in the sight of the apostles (Acts 1) and sits at the Father’s right hand, while the other never departed from the Father’s bosom but was always with the Father and in the Father, and does not cease to be so.

While the property of each nature remained intact and the two came together in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, and mortality by eternity. To accomplish the work of human salvation, unchangeable nature was united to a nature capable of suffering, so that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, could die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.

Because of the identity of the one person, both glory and insult are attributed in common to God and man. Accordingly, the operations of both natures are found together in the one Christ in such a way that, although Christ is not divided in his powers or weaknesses, nevertheless something in his activity is not common to both natures. Whatever was done in Christ, however, was done by one Christ, not by two Christs. In the operations, the property of the natures is distinguished; in the power, the unity of the person is understood.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the divinity never abandoned the man whom it assumed

In none of the properties of action that distinguish the natures in Christ did the divinity abandon the humanity—not even in the passion itself. To make this easier to understand, faith should be strengthened by examples.

For example, if you strike a tree with an axe and at the same time strike the sunlight shining upon it, you inflict a wound upon the tree, but you leave the sun—whose light and warmth you strike at the same time—unaffected. If the sun does not abandon the tree struck by the axe, how much more did the Son of God, who is the Word, not abandon his holy humanity in the passion, although divinity itself always remains impassible in its own nature.

Just as, when Moses was leading the people of God, the bush had flame, so Christ’s humanity truly suffered; and just as the bush truly was not consumed, so the divinity truly did not suffer. Nevertheless, from the moment the divinity assumed the humanity into the unity of its person, it never abandoned it anywhere.

Indeed, the same God-man came forth from his mother’s womb; the same God-man hung upon the cross; and the same God-man lay in the tomb. But in the tomb the same God-man lay according to the flesh alone, and into hell he descended according to the soul alone.

No Catholic should doubt that whatever is read to have been done in Christ was done by one Christ and by one Son of God. Christ himself, whole and entire in his person, graciously undertook all these things. For he is found to have brought about his own sufferings, since he had nothing that he suffered unwillingly. He is himself both the work and the author of the work.

Now, since Christ at one and the same time lay in the tomb and descended into hell, who would not see the inseparable operation of both natures? And who, in that one and inseparable work, would not clearly recognize what properly belongs to the flesh, the soul, and the divinity?

For in order that Christ should lie in the tomb according to the flesh, did the whole Christ accomplish this? Yet by nature only the flesh was capable of burial. Likewise, in order that Christ should descend into hell according to the soul, the operation of both natures—that is, divine and human—was one; but that descent was natural to the soul alone.

At the same time Christ continued to work, wholly in heaven and on earth. It belonged to the divinity alone both not to be confined by place and to carry out with the Father, naturally and equally, those things pertaining to the governance of the universe.

For this reason, in all those works of passion and death, apostolic authority assigns to the one person who acted what Christ accomplished wholly in himself, while unmistakably showing what belongs to each nature. Blessed Paul says of one and the same Christ: “Although he was crucified because of weakness, he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

And blessed Peter expressed the prophetic word from the Psalms in such a way that he said of Christ’s soul—which he knew had descended into hell—that it was not abandoned in hell (Acts 2:27; Psalm 15:10). When it returned from the underworld to the flesh on the third day, the same God, according to the flesh in which he had lain in the tomb, rose from the tomb.

On the fortieth day after the resurrection, the same God, having become man, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God; from there, at the end of the age, he will come to judge the living and the dead.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Christ’s baptism, and that everything done in Christ was done for the sake of our salvation

The evangelist says that Christ answered the blessed Baptist when he came to his baptism: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). What else does “to fulfill all righteousness” mean except that he wished to show in himself the order of our whole life, as he also demonstrates elsewhere when he says: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12)?

Christ was therefore baptized not so that any iniquity of his might be washed away—for he had none at all—but so that his great humility might be commended. Thus baptism found in him nothing to wash away, just as death found nothing to punish. He alone could be born in such a way that he had no need to be reborn; for those who were baptized with John’s baptism, by which he himself was also baptized, were not being reborn.

Accordingly, Christ’s baptism was not in water alone, like John’s, but in the Holy Spirit, for the remission of sins. He says elsewhere: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Thus those who believe in Christ, regenerated by the Holy Spirit, may have remission of all sins. Christ, who was generated by that Spirit, had no need of regeneration.

When he was baptized, the Holy Spirit was seen to descend upon him in the form of a dove. It must not be believed that he then first received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, since from his first conception he had always been full of the Holy Spirit [Al., “is full of the Holy Spirit”]. Rather, this occurred so that the mystery of the holy and undivided Trinity might be manifested in baptism.

The Son of God is baptized in the man; the Spirit of God descends in the dove; God the Father is present in the voice. Without the invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, of the holy Trinity—no baptism can be beneficial.

Therefore the Son of God himself first wished personally to show in his baptism that the whole Trinity was present, since he was about to command the ministers of his sacraments to teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:15).

Whatever was done at Christ’s cross, in his burial, in his resurrection on the third day, in his ascension into heaven, and in his sitting at the right hand of God the Father, was done so that the Christian life lived here might be conformed to these events—not merely by symbolic statements but also by deeds.

With reference to his cross it was said: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5:24). With reference to his burial: “You were buried with Christ through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4). With reference to his resurrection: “Just as Christ rose from the dead into the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life.” With reference to his ascension into heaven and his sitting at the Father’s right hand: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:1).

## CHAPTER XVIII. That God the Father performs some works through the Son, who is coeternal with him in the form of God, and some through that same Son in the form of a servant, the Son of Man
For the Lord himself, concerning the authority which he possesses from eternity with the Father, and concerning the authority which he received in time in the form of a servant, says this: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself, and he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:26). Therefore God the Father begot the Son possessing life and authority in himself. For he gave that same Son authority to execute judgment—the one who was made man in the form of a servant.

God the Father works through the two natures in Christ: through one, which he shares with God the Father, insofar as he is God; through the other, by which he was made man from the Virgin Mary. Through these two natures in the one Son of God, God the Father brings about two resurrections of the human race, namely, of souls and of bodies.

For souls too have their own death in impiety and sins, according to which death they have died. Concerning them the same Lord says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60), so that the dead in soul might bury the dead in body. The death of the soul occurs when God abandons it because of the greatness of its sins; the death of the body occurs when it is abandoned by the soul.

We therefore say that those raised from these two kinds of death have two resurrections. Now the resurrection of souls takes place in the Church through the Son of God, the Word of God, when, made alive by the grace of God, they will rise from the death of iniquity. [Alternative: “they rise.”] This is the first resurrection; those who possess it will rise blessedly in the second, which is the resurrection of bodies.

The Son of Man, however, received authority to execute judgment. That judgment will take place at the end of the age, and there will not be a resurrection of souls but of bodies. Therefore the Lord himself indicates these two resurrections in the same passage: the resurrection of souls, when he says, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God” (John 5:25); and that of bodies: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice” (ibid., 28).

The hour is now here for the dead to rise; the hour will come at the end of the age for the dead to rise. They rise now in mind, but then in the flesh; they rise now in mind through the Word of God, the Son of God; then they will rise in the flesh through the Word of God made flesh, the Son of Man.

God therefore now raises souls through the Word, the Son of God, so that they may live in Christ; at the end of the age God raises bodies through that same Son of Man, so that they may live eternally with Christ.

For the Father himself will not come to judge the living and the dead; yet the Father does not depart from the Son. How, then, will he himself not come? Because he himself did not put on the form of a servant, and he will not be seen in the judgment. For “the wicked will see him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). That form will be the judge which stood beneath the judge; that form will judge which was judged. For it was judged unjustly, but it will judge justly. The judge will appear such as he can be seen both by those whom he will crown and by those whom he will condemn.

The form of a servant, therefore, will be seen; hidden will be the form of God, which is promised to the righteous alone as their eternal reward of blessedness.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Final Times of the Age

Certain signs which the Lord himself foretold in the Gospel as destined to occur before the end of the world are read as having already taken place; others, which are imminent, are perceived daily. Some, therefore, have not yet occurred, but are most certainly believed to be future: namely, the faith of the Israelite people, concerning which the Apostle says, “When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26); and the kingdom of Antichrist and his cruelty toward the saints.

For this will be the final persecution, with the final judgment impending, which the holy Church will suffer throughout the whole world: the entire city of Christ from the entire city of the devil, insofar as each of them will exist upon the earth. There is no doubt that the same Antichrist will be the author of this persecution. The Apostle called him the son of perdition and the apostate—certainly an apostate from the Lord God—“who will exalt himself above everything that is called God or is worshiped, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

The holy Church is indeed called God.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] This passage is corrupt and could not be corrected with the aid of the manuscripts. The Reich manuscripts read: “Above everything that is called God or is worshiped, the holy Church, which is called God.” [Col. 0052D]]

Therefore only the holy Trinity, God, is rightly worshiped, and that most impious apostate will presume to claim this honor for himself. He will entice some by flatteries, others by terrors, and others by signs, so that they may worship him in place of God. His persecution is foretold in the Apocalypse as raging upon the earth for three and a half years (Revelation 11:12).

But lest so monstrous and cruel a persecution, coming unexpectedly, overwhelm everyone while they are insufficiently prepared, the Church believes that Elijah and Enoch, the greatest prophets, will come. Through their teaching the Israelite people will be converted to the faith. After they themselves have preached for three and a half years, they will, in that same persecution, together with the other faithful of Christ, be crowned with glorious martyrdom.

When that son of perdition, the most impious teacher of all iniquity, has been struck down by the Lord himself—as the Apostle says, “whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8)—one must not suppose that the day of judgment will immediately follow. Thus will be fulfilled what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matthew 24:36). We explained earlier, in the appropriate place, how these words of the Lord are to be understood.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Resurrection of Bodies on the Last Day

The Lord himself, Jesus Christ, in the resurrection of his flesh—which he raised from the tomb on the third day—showed us the true resurrection of our flesh. We must believe this most firmly, without any doubt, so that each person may rise in the same flesh in which he lived here in this present life.

Nor should it seem incredible to anyone that divine power can raise our bodies from the corruption of whatever condition they may have undergone.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] See Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 20.]

Far be it from our faith to doubt that the bodies which are to be raised and restored to life can be completely recalled by the omnipotence of the Creator—whether a beast or fire has consumed them, whether they have collapsed into dust and ashes, whether they have been dissolved into moisture, or whether they have been lifted into the air. [Alternative: “that omnipotence cannot recall …”; alternatives: “collapsed,” “dissolved,” “lifted.”]

Far be it from us to suppose that any recess or secret place of nature can receive something withdrawn from our senses in such a way that it either escapes the knowledge of the Creator of all things or eludes his power.

The bodies of the saints will indeed rise to glory, without any defect or deformity; in them there will be as much felicity as blessedness [alternative reading: *facilitas*, “ease,” for the first *felicitas*]. For although their bodies in this present life may possess some deformity, greater or lesser, and may have less beauty than the beauty appropriate to human nature, they will have nothing of the sort in that perfection of everlasting blessedness. They will possess the measure and dignity which they would have had if they had died before attaining the beauty of perfect maturity, or which they had possessed before the years of declining age began to turn toward weakness, with the beauty of all their members preserved in fitting harmony, so that they will have nothing incongruous in any part of the body, because the body will be spiritual, not carnal.

Although it will be flesh and not spirit, it will nevertheless not be subject to carnal vices, concerning which the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). All weakness, all deformity, all sluggishness, all corruption, all poverty, all need, and whatever else is unworthy of the kingdom of the supreme King will be far from them—in that kingdom where the children of the resurrection and of the promise will be equal to the angels of God (Matthew 22:30).

Therefore whatever has perished from living bodies, or after death from corpses, and has escaped human sight—whether it has been consumed by beasts or fire, reduced to dust and ashes, dissolved into moisture, or scattered into the air—will rise together with what remained in the graves, transformed from the old condition of the animal body into the newness of a spiritual body and clothed in incorruption and immortality. [Alternative: “in the new state.”]

The wicked too will each rise with his own flesh, so that they may be punished with the devil and his angels. Whether they will rise with the vices and deformities of their bodies, retaining whatever defective and deformed members they bore, why should we trouble ourselves by investigating this? Their condition or beauty is uncertain, but their condemnation will be certain and everlasting; therefore it should not exhaust us.

This must be known with complete certainty: no one will be saved except by the undeserved mercy of God, and no one will be condemned except by his deserved judgment. Then the saints will understand more fully what good grace has conferred upon them, and what they would have attained if divine mercy had not chosen them by a gratuitous gift; and they will understand how true is what is sung in the Psalm: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Reward of the Righteous and the Punishment of Sinners

Concerning the fire of the day of judgment the Apostle says: “The fire will disclose what sort of work each person’s work is” (1 Corinthians 3:13). There is no doubt that he spoke here of purgatorial fire. The wicked will experience that fire in one way, the saints in another, and the righteous in another.

The wicked, from the torment of that fire, will be thrust down into the everlasting flames of fire. But the saints, who will rise in their bodies without any stain of sin, and who built gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation which is Christ, will fly through that fire with as much ease as was the integrity of faith and love for Christ with which they kept his commandments in this life.

For them that fire of the day of judgment will be as the Babylonian furnace was for the three youths, who, without any injury from the flames, summoned all the beauty of creatures to the Lord’s praises.

There are therefore certain righteous people subject to certain minor sins, because they built hay, wood, and straw upon the foundation which is Christ. These materials are purified by the heat of that fire, and once cleansed from them, they will be made worthy of the glory of eternal blessedness.

When that transitory fire and the entire judgment of the final day have been completed, two assemblies will be divided: that of the saints and that of the wicked; one belonging to Christ, the other to the devil; one of the good, the other of the evil—each consisting of angels and human beings.

For the former there will be no will to sin; for the latter, no ability to sin, and neither group will possess any condition of dying: the former will live truly and happily in eternal life, while the latter will endure unhappily in eternal torments, without the power to die.

For the winnowing fan of the final judgment will separate the grain from the chaff. Each person will be either condemned or crowned according to the measure of his merits. Some, according to the character of their sins, will be tormented more mildly because they are weighed down by a lesser burden of crimes.

The merits of the saints too will be diverse, and each will receive the rewards of eternal blessedness according to the greatness of his merits. The Lord himself signified this in the Gospel when he said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). Yet no one among them will feel any diminution of joy or blessedness, because what each receives will be sufficient for him; for Christ will be “all in all” (Colossians 3:11).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Eternal Blessedness of the Saints

What the saints will do in that supreme rest of blessedness, the Psalmist explained when he said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 84:5). The Lord himself demonstrated it even more explicitly in the Gospel, where he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8).

This is the blessed peace of God, without any disturbance, which surpasses all understanding; in it the God of gods will be seen in Zion, that is, in the mirror of perpetual rest. For all the members and inward parts of the incorruptible body, which we now see distributed among the functions of necessity, will then advance the praises of God, because there will be no necessity of laboring for them, no distress of any need, but complete and certain security, everlasting blessedness, and unfailing joy.

How ineffable will that blessedness be, where there will be no evil and no good will be lacking! There will be leisure for the praises of God, who will be every good in all things. There will be one love for all, one harmony among everyone, true honor, denied to no one who is worthy and bestowed upon no one who is unworthy.

No unworthy person will reach that place, where no one is permitted to exist except the worthy; where there is peace; where no one will suffer anything hostile either from himself or from anyone else. The reward of virtue will itself be the one who gave virtue; and he who promised himself—than whom nothing better or greater can exist—will be blessed satiety for all. The Prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit, foresaw this and expressed it as a desire: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI, 15).

Then God himself will be the satiety of the saints, the delight of the blessed, and everything that they can rightly desire: life, salvation, virtue [alternative: *victus*, “sustenance”], abundance, glory, honor, peace, eternal blessedness, and blessed eternity. He will be the perfection of our desires. He will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue.

Then alone there will be true immortality, where no one can die. The first condition of humanity was the ability not to die [to which, because of the punishment of sin, there came the inability not to die]. In that blessedness there remains the third condition: the inability to die.

Then free choice will fully exist. It was first given to the human being as the ability not to sin; but it will be more blessed when it is such that one cannot sin.

Then the sabbath-rest [Alternative: “the most complete sabbath”] of eternal repose will be the day of all the saints. There he will be seen who will be loved, and he who will be loved will be praised.

Now, therefore, may he who was the beginning and cause of this discourse also be its perfection and end. For love of him, we beseech those who read to intercede for us before his mercy, so that, through his compassion, we may deserve to attain with them that kingdom which has no end. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] This title is absent from the other manuscript codices. The invocation itself to the Holy Trinity is also omitted here in the Tegernsee manuscript and in some printed editions; but the creed beginning “We believe,” as below, is placed immediately at the end of this final chapter.]

## INVOCATION TO THE HOLY TRINITY AND ITS CREED

Be present, true Light, Father, almighty God.

[Col. 0055A] Be present, Light from Light, Word and Son of God, almighty God.

Be present, Holy Spirit, concord of the Father and the Son, almighty God.

Be present, one almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Teach faith, awaken hope, pour in love.

The will lies near at hand for me, but this is not from me, but from you:

I desire to leave the world and the earth and seek heaven.

But my feather is weak: desiring without your help.

Give wings to faith, so that I may fly upward to you.

This faith I confess in you, through you, and concerning you.

I confess you as one in substance and three in persons.

I confess that you are always the same, living, and understanding.

[Col. 0055B] I confess that the three are one and the one is three.

Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, O blessed Trinity.

God, Lord, Paraclete, O blessed Trinity.

Love, grace, communion, O blessed Trinity.

Love is God, grace is Christ, communion is the Holy Spirit, O blessed Trinity.

Begetter, begotten, regenerating, O blessed Trinity.

True Light, true Light from Light, true illumination, O blessed Trinity.

Invisible invisibly, visible invisibly, invisible visibly, O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 0055C] Fountain, river, irrigation, O blessed Trinity.

From one are all things, through one are all things, in one are all things, O blessed Trinity.

From whom, through whom, in whom are all things, O blessed Trinity.

Living Life, life from the living one, vivifier of the living, O blessed Trinity.

One from himself, one from one, one from both, O blessed Trinity.

Ὤν (“the One who is”) from himself, ὤν (“the One who is”) from the other, ὤν (“the One who is”) from both, O blessed Trinity.

Every ὤν (“One who is”) is always in the three, and every ὤν is equally in each, O blessed Trinity.

Truthful Father, Truth the Son, Truth the Spirit, O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 0055D] The Father, the Word (λογός), and the Paraclete are therefore one substance, O blessed Trinity.

One essence, one power, one goodness, O blessed Trinity.

God, blessedness, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are blessed are blessed, O blessed Trinity.

[Col. 0056A] God, true and supreme life, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that truly and supremely live have life, O blessed Trinity.

God, the good and beautiful one, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are good and beautiful are good and beautiful, O blessed Trinity.

God, whom faith awakens us to seek, hope raises us toward, and love joins us to, O blessed Trinity.

God, who commands us to ask, causes us to find, and opens to those who knock, O blessed Trinity.

God, above whom there is nothing, outside whom there is nothing, without whom there is nothing, O blessed Trinity.

God, beneath whom is everything, in whom is everything, with whom is everything, O blessed Trinity.

We invoke you, we adore you, we praise you, O blessed Trinity.

Hear us, hear us, hear us, O blessed Trinity.

Our hope, our salvation, our honor, O blessed Trinity.

Increase faith in us, increase hope, increase love, O blessed Trinity.

[Page 738] Deliver us, save us, justify us, O blessed Trinity.

Have mercy, Lord, because your mercy has delivered us, O blessed Trinity.

Have mercy, Lord, because by your mercy we believe in you, O blessed Trinity.

Have mercy, Lord, because by your mercy we have known you, O blessed Trinity.

Have mercy, Lord, because by your mercy we hope in you, O blessed Trinity.

Have mercy, Lord, because by your mercy we love you, O blessed Trinity.

We all adore you as the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, O blessed Trinity.

Grant forgiveness of sins, bestow eternal life, give peace and glory, O blessed Trinity.

O blessed, and blessed, and glorious Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [O blessed Trinity].

O blessed, blessed, glorious Unity, Father, Son, Holy Spirit [O blessed Trinity].

O true, supreme, eternal Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [O blessed Trinity].

O true, supreme, eternal Unity, Father, Son, Holy Spirit [O blessed Trinity].

[Col. 0056D] Have mercy on us, have mercy on us, have mercy on us, O blessed Trinity.

To you be praise, to you glory, to you thanksgiving throughout everlasting ages, O blessed Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] Cited by Aeneas of Paris, chapter 88.]

[Note: [Col. 0055D] In the Basel edition of the *Homiliarium* of 1496, the invocation of the Holy Trinity is omitted, and the following creed appears under the title “Recapitulation.” In the Vienna manuscript it is entitled “Confession concerning the Holy Trinity.” In the manuscript of the Library of Saint-Germain in Paris it bears this heading: “Readings concerning the Holy Trinity,” that is, readings customarily read on the feast of the Holy Trinity.

The beginning of this creed is praised under the name of Alcuin by Aeneas, bishop of Paris, who flourished under Emperor Charles the Bald, in his book against the Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, in d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, volume I of the new edition, page 131.

John Leuclavius found a Greek copy of it in the library of Sambucus under the name of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; he translated it into Latin in his own style and published it at Basel in 1578 as a new work of Saint Hilary.
