D. Coustant and the Veronese scholars subsequently relegated it to the appendix of Saint Hilary’s works and attributed it to Alcuin. Here we provide the genuine text, corrected from several manuscript codices.]

We believe in the most holy Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0057A] one almighty God, of one substance, one essence, and one power, creator of all creatures: from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

[We believe in] the Father from himself, not from another; the Son begotten from the Father, true God from true God, true Light from true Light; yet not two Lights, but one Light.

The Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son; he is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The Father is fully God in himself; the Son is fully God, begotten from the Father; the Holy Spirit is fully God, proceeding from the Father and the Son. Yet we do not call them three gods, but one almighty, eternal, invisible, unchangeable God, who is wholly everywhere and wholly present everywhere—not divided into parts, but wholly in all things, not locally but in power.

[Col. 0057B] Without communicating himself, he created mutable things and governs what he created, always remaining what he is. Nothing accidental can occur in him, because nothing can be added to or taken away from the simple nature of divinity. For he always is what he is; for him it is proper, everlasting, and identical to be, to live, and to understand.

These three are one God, and one God is these three: the same God and Lord [Saint-Germain manuscript: “These three are one God and one Lord; these three are the same God and Lord, etc.”], true and eternal Trinity in persons, true and eternal Unity in substance, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance.

This holy Trinity is no greater in the three persons named together than in any one person named once, because each person is full substance [Col. 0057C] in himself. Yet there are not three substances, but one God, one substance, one power, one essence, one eternity, one greatness, and one goodness: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Nor is the Father anything different in nature from the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor are the Son and the Holy Spirit anything different in nature from the Father, since they have one nature. But the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person.

In the Father is eternity [Saint-Germain manuscript: “In the Father eternity remains”]; in the Son equality; in the Holy Spirit the joining together of eternity and equality. All are one in substance, essence, omnipotence, and divinity.

[Page 739] [Note: [Col. 0057] From Saint Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, chapter 5.]

For just as the same holy Trinity is inseparable in substance, so it is inseparable [Col. 0057D] in its works, although certain works of God are specially appropriate to certain persons. Thus, the voice which sounded from heaven over Christ when he was baptized is associated with the Father; the assumption of humanity pertains solely to the person of the Son; and the dove, in whose form the same Holy Spirit descended upon that same Son of God baptized according to his humanity, properly belongs to the person of the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, without any doubt, the whole holy Trinity brought about that voice, that dove, and Christ’s humanity, for its works are inseparable.

We believe that the same Son of God, the Word of God, was eternally born from the Father, consubstantial with the Father in all things, and was born in time from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever-virgin [the word “ever” is omitted in some editions]. He had two births: one eternal, from the Father; the other temporal, from his mother.

This Son of God was also conceived through the conception of his flesh and born through the birth of his flesh. We confess that God was conceived and true God was born—the same true God and true man, one Christ, one only-begotten Son of God, proper and perfect in two natures, in the singularity of one person.

Impassible and passible, mortal and immortal, crucified in our weakness, yet always living in his own power. He died by the death of his flesh and was buried; then, returning from the underworld after condemning and stripping the ruler of all iniquity, he rose on the third day and, with the triumph of glory, ascended into heaven in the sight of his disciples, sitting at the right hand of the Father, that is, in the majesty of his divinity.

From there he will now come to judge the living and the dead. The wicked will see him judging in the form in which he was crucified—not in the humiliation in which he was unjustly judged, but in the glory in which he will justly judge the world. The vision of his majesty will be the eternal blessedness and glory of all the saints.

May grace and peace from God the Father and from his Son Jesus Christ our Lord be with the one who confesses this throughout all ages of ages.

From manuscripts and editions.

[Explicit: Book III on the Holy Trinity, which Alcuin excerpted from the books of Saint Augustine.]

# THE TWENTY-EIGHT QUESTIONS OF MASTER ALBINUS FLACCUS ALCUIN CONCERNING THE TRINITY, ADDRESSED TO FREDEGISUS

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057D] Albinus sends greetings to his most beloved son Fredegisus.

It pleased your prudence, dearest son, to propose to me certain questions concerning the most holy Trinity for me to solve—questions by which, perhaps, you think that the ears of your wisdom may be troubled. Yet I do not at all suppose that you have understood less than you should concerning such matters, or that you are deficient in learning or purity of Catholic faith. Rather, with divine grace especially at work, from the beginning of the vigor of your mature understanding I have pursued this with you, so that you might appear to be a strong preacher and an unconquerable teacher in the faith of the most holy Trinity. We have learned that there have always been opponents of this faith, in accordance with apostolic prophecy, and that there are such opponents also in our own times.

Nevertheless, I gladly receive the devotion of anyone who asks about these matters; indeed, I praise even more the earnestness of one who teaches, because devotion to learning accomplishes little without zeal for teaching, according to Solomon’s saying: “An unseen treasure and hidden wisdom—what use are either of them?” (Ecclesiasticus 41:17).

Therefore one who understands well must devote his whole care to teaching, lest he labor in learning in vain. For it is written in the Prophet: “Those who instruct many will shine like the brightness of the firmament in perpetual splendor” (Daniel 12:3).

### Question 1

How is God truly Unity and truly Trinity?

**Answer.** Unity in substance, Trinity in persons.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] Aeneas of Paris, chapter 89.]

### Question 2

What is proper to each person in the holy Trinity?

**Answer.** It is proper to the Father that he alone is Father and that he is from no other but himself. It is proper to the Son that he is begotten from the Father, alone from the alone, coeternal and consubstantial with the Begetter. It is proper to the Holy Spirit that he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds equally from the Father and the Son.

### Question 3

Why should the Holy Spirit not be called unbegotten or begotten?

**Answer.** Because if he were called unbegotten like the Father, there could be thought to be two Fathers; if begotten, two Sons in the holy Trinity.

### Question 4

Should the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone be called fully God and perfect in himself?

**Answer.** Certainly the Father in himself is fully God; likewise, the Son, if named alone, is fully God; and the Holy Spirit is believed to be fully God.

### Question 5

If each person can individually be called fully God, why do we not call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three gods?

**Answer.** Because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, not three substances. Therefore the unity of substance prevents us from calling or believing them to be three gods.

### Question 6

Since we call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three persons, why is it not permissible to call them three gods, three almighty beings, three great beings, or three good beings?

**Answer.** Because “God,” “almighty,” “great,” “good,” and “eternal” are substantial names and are said absolutely. Therefore they may not be expressed in the plural but in the singular. Every name that signifies God’s substance or essence must always be expressed in the singular.

“Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are relative names, and therefore they are rightly called three persons.

### Question 7

In what sense are they relative?

**Answer.** According to dialectic, relative names are those that refer to something else, such as “lord” to “servant,” “servant” to “lord,” “father” to “son,” and “son” to “father.”

When I say “Father,” I signify the Son at the same time, because there is no Father unless there is a Son of whom he is Father. Likewise, there is no Son unless there is a Father whose Son he is.

### Question 8

Is the Holy Spirit spoken of relatively or substantially?

**Answer.** Relatively, certainly, because the Spirit is the Spirit of someone; but the rule of relation does not apply to him in the same way as to the Father and the Son.

### Question 9

Why does the Holy Spirit not have an equal rule of relation, as do the Father and the Son?

**Answer.** Because the names “Father” and “Son” can be mutually related: we can say “Father of the Son” and “Son of the Father.” But a double reciprocal relation cannot be found in the name “Holy Spirit.”

### Question 10

By what necessity does the relation of the Holy Spirit not permit this reciprocal form?

**Answer.** We can rightly say “the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son,” but in the reverse order we cannot say “Father of the Holy Spirit,” as we say “Father of the Son,” lest two Sons be understood in the holy Trinity.

Likewise, we cannot say “Son of the Holy Spirit,” as we say “Son of the Father,” lest two Fathers be understood in the holy Trinity. We therefore say “the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son,” without reciprocal reversal of the relative names.

### Question 11

Are the works of the holy Trinity inseparable?

**Answer.** Whatever God works, the whole holy Trinity works inseparably as the same works, because the operation of the holy Trinity is one, just as its substance, essence, and will are one.

### Question 12

Since the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, should the holy Trinity be called separable or inseparable in persons?

**Answer.** Truly, the Father is one person and the Son another, just as the Son is one person and the Father another, and the Holy Spirit is another person from the Father and the Son.

Yet neither of them is different from the other in nature, divinity, or essence. For you cannot say “Father” without understanding the Son; nor can you say “Son” without understanding the Father; nor can you say “Holy Spirit” without understanding whose Spirit he is.

Therefore the holy Trinity must be called wholly inseparable in persons, just as it is inseparable in works.

### Question 13

Does the statement “who alone does great wonders” (Psalm 72:18), and the Apostle’s statement “who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), pertain only to the person of the Father?

**Answer.** It does not pertain at all to the person of the Father alone. Whenever it is said in either the New or the Old Testament that God alone possesses or does this or that, it pertains to the whole holy Trinity, which is one almighty God, doing all things that are in heaven and on earth.

### Question 14

How can the blessed evangelist John say, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), while the Lord himself says elsewhere, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8), and the Apostle calls God invisible (1 Timothy 1:17)?

**Answer.** God can be seen—that is, understood—according to the gift of his grace, whether by angels or by the souls of the saints. But no angel, nor any of the saints, will be able to understand the fullness of the divine nature perfectly. Therefore God is called incomprehensible.

### Question 15

When the supreme reward, the eternal vision of God, is promised to the saints, will they all see or understand him equally?

[Note: [Col. 0061D] The Salmasian manuscript and others read: “Question 15. What supreme reward is promised to the saints?—Answer: The eternal vision of God.—Question: Will they see or understand equally?”]

**Answer.** Not at all will all angels or all souls of the saints see or understand God equally, either now or after the resurrection. Rather, they will do so according to the dispensation of the giver and the quality of their merits.

Nevertheless, each will possess sufficient blessedness in his vision of God according to his merits. No one will desire more than he possesses, nor will he grieve at possessing less than he wishes.

### Question 16

Is there any distinction in God between being, living, understanding, and being able?

**Answer.** In God, being is not one thing, living another, understanding another, or being able another. For by the very fact that God is, he lives; by the fact that he lives, he understands; by the fact that he understands, he is able; and by the fact that he is able, he is.

Because the nature of divinity is simple, it has one being, lives, understands, and can do all things. It is not so with us, since in our nature living is one thing, understanding another, and being able another. In God, however, all these are one and the same.

## Retained apparatus and source boundaries

The supplied textual readings are retained with their associations: *Dei* (“of God”) is omitted in the alternate form after “Son”; *qui* (“who”) for *quam* (“which”); *vindicare* (“to claim/vindicate”) for *vendicare*; *habeant* (“may have”), *subjacebit* (“will be subject”), *quod illud* (“that which”), *novitate* (“newness”), and *consecuturi* (“about to obtain”); in Chapter XXI, *qui* (“who”), *minorum* (“of lesser things”), and *discernet* (“will distinguish”); in Chapter XXII, *est* (“is”), *victus* (“sustenance”), and *sabbatissimus* (“most sabbatical/restful”); in the Creed, *sancta* (“holy”) for *sanctissima* (“most holy”); and *verum* (“true”) for *vero* (“indeed”), together with the Saint-Germain form concerning “impassible and passibly mortal.” The introduction and Questions 1–16 retain their supplied manuscript alternatives rather than silently normalizing them.

Source boundaries retained: [Col. 0050B] [Col. 0050C] [Col. 0050D] [Col. 0051A] [Col. 0051B] [Col. 0051C] [Col. 0051D] [Col. 0052A] [Col. 0052B] [Col. 0052C] [Col. 0052D] [Col. 0053A] [Col. 0053B] [Col. 0053C] [Col. 0053D] [Col. 0054A] [Col. 0054B] [Col. 0054C] [Col. 0054D] [Col. 0058D] [Col. 0059A] [Col. 0059B] [Col. 0059C] [Col. 0059D] [Col. 0060A] [Col. 0060B] [Col. 0060C] [Col. 0060D] [Col. 0061A] [Col. 0061B].

### Question 17

Can it be said of the Son of God, just as it is said “light from light” and “God from God,” that he is “almighty from the Almighty,” “good from the Good,” “great from the Great,” and so forth?

**Answer.** As a general rule, we must hold that all the names of the nature which can be said equally of the Son as of the Father can all be said in this way of him. Therefore, just as it is said “God from God” and “light from light,” so it must be said “almighty from the Almighty,” “good from the Good,” and “great from the Great”; but not so with relative terms.

### Question 18

But how should one speak in the case of relative names?

**Answer.** We cannot say “Word from Word,” because “Word” is a relative name, and the Word is the Son alone; whereas we say “God from God,” which does not refer to the Son alone. Nor can we say “image from image,” because the Son alone is the Image; whereas we say “light from light,” since “light” does not refer to the Son alone, because “light” is a substantial name.

### Question 19

Is the Father one light and the Son another?

**Answer.** By no means are they different; the Father and the Son are one light, just as they are one substance. Therefore it is rightly said “light from light,” just as “God from God.” Just as the Father and the Son are one God, so they are one light.

### Question 20

We read the Apostle saying that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Here, as always, we understand “God” to mean the Father and “Christ” to mean the Son. Does the Father not possess wisdom or power in himself except in the Son, whom the Apostle called the wisdom of God and the power of God?

**Answer.** Very many people destroy the Arian impiety in this way, saying that it is impious to believe that God the Father was ever without his wisdom or without his power. But it is better to understand the Father as wisdom and power, just as the Son is wisdom and power [rather, also the Holy Spirit is wisdom and power]; not, however, three powers or three wisdoms, because “wisdom” is a substantial name, as is “power.” Nor is it one thing for God to be, another to be wise, and another to be able; rather, for God, being, being wise, and being able are one and the same.

### Question 21

Does it belong exclusively to the person of the Holy Spirit when the Apostle says, “God is love” (1 John 4:8), although this love is read to be that of the Father and the Son?

**Answer.** The Holy Spirit is by no means understood as love in such a way that the Father and the Son are not also love. Just as the Holy Spirit is love, so the Father is love [and the Son is love]; yet there are not three loves, but one love. But because the Holy Spirit is properly called the gift of God, and no gift of God is greater than love—indeed, without it no gift can lead a human being to everlasting blessedness—the Holy Spirit is therefore properly called love.

### Question 22

Do the impious possess the gifts of God?

**Answer.** They do [indeed], through him who enlightens every human being coming into this world, “in whom we are, and move, and live” (Acts 17:28). For the gifts of God are good for those who use them well. Therefore love is a singular gift among the saints, by which the children of God are distinguished from the children of impiety.

### Question 23

If God is wholly everywhere, why is he said to dwell more in heaven than on earth?

**Answer.** Because the knowledge of the divinity is greater among the holy angels and the souls of the saints, when they are with God in heaven, than on earth. For just as in this mortal body some understand the divine substance more and others less, so God is said to be more in heaven than on earth because the inhabitants of heaven understand that substance more fully than the dwellers on earth.

### Question 24

If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one substance, why is the Son alone said to have become incarnate?

**Answer.** Because the person of the Son is one, the person of the Father another, and the person of the Holy Spirit another. The person of the Son alone was indeed incarnate; yet the whole Holy Trinity effected the same incarnation, whose works are inseparable.

### Question 25

Since it is customary to sing in the Catholic Creed that the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, why is he not called the Son of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0062D], as he is called the Son of the blessed Virgin?

**Answer.** The Son of God was not born from him in the same way as from her. From her—that is, from the holy Virgin—the Son of God was born as from a mother; not from him—that is, from the Holy Spirit—as from a father, lest two fathers be said to exist in the Holy Trinity.

### Question 26

If the Father and the Son have one nature, and the incarnate Son is fully and perfect God, how was the Father not incarnate?

**Answer.** The Son is fully and perfect God; he alone was incarnate and became human. For fire has one substance, but heat does one thing in fire and light another: light illuminates, while heat warms [Al., “makes hot”]. Yet one nature of fire produces both, heat and light.

[Note: [Col. 0063] This question is omitted in the *Orthodoxographia*.]

### Question 27

Was the divinity conceived, born, and subjected to suffering together with the flesh, and so forth—things known to belong properly to humanity?

**Answer.** Indeed, the divinity was conceived in the conception of its flesh and was born in its birth; through participation in human feeling it experienced the death which it had freely undertaken, without losing the power of its own nature, through which it gives life to all things. He is himself both the author and the work of the author. The same is the author, because if he was born willingly, he also suffered willingly. The same is the work, because one and the same person endured both—not under compulsion from another, but alone himself—while the impassibility of the divinity remained unharmed.

### Question 28

From which nature did he say, “I have power to lay down my life”?

**Answer.** The authority of all the works performed in Christ comes from the divinity; nevertheless, it belongs to the flesh to say, “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10:18), not to the divinity. The divinity did not abandon the soul after assuming it in the Virgin’s womb. The flesh abandoned it when Christ released his spirit on the cross.

[Col. 0063]

## 743. SECOND LITTLE WORK, OR BOOKLET, ON THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. TO CHARLES THE GREAT. (G)*

### Preliminary Notice

[Col. 0063B]

We received the booklet published here from the distinguished and learned D. Ildephonsus Catelinot, librarian of the monastery of Saint Michael in Lorraine while he lived. The celebrated Bernard de Montfaucon first discovered it and listed it among the manuscripts of the library of Laon in his distinguished work *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, volume II, page 1297. D. Catelinot obtained the same work, copied from that same very ancient manuscript, through the kindness of the lord abbot of Hédouville, canon of the cathedral church of Laon, and through the work of D. Breton, professor of the Premonstratensian abbey.

Dido, bishop of Laon, gave the manuscript from which this booklet was copied to the aforementioned church, as the inscription at the beginning of the manuscript demonstrates. It reads as follows:

> “The lord Bishop Dido gave this booklet to God and to Saint Mary’s church of Laon. Whoever removes it shall incur the offense of God and of Saint Mary.”

Bishop Dido presided over the church of Laon around the end of the ninth century. He died in 891 [Note: [Col. 0063D] San-Marthani, *Gallia Christiana*.]. The manuscript is therefore almost contemporary with the life of Alcuin.

The title of the little work, which the distinguished Montfaucon also noted at the cited place, is: “Alcuin, On the Procession of the Holy Spirit.” Although none of those who catalogue the writings of blessed Alcuin mentions this little work, and although this controversy concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son first began to be debated more vigorously after Alcuin’s death—namely, in the year 809, at the Council of Aachen—and although the style of the letter to Charles Augustus differs in some respects from the style Alcuin used in his other letters to the same man, we nevertheless judge that we are not at liberty to depart from the testimony of the ancient manuscript and from the testimony of Bishop Dido, who was almost contemporary with Alcuin, and to relegate this booklet among his doubtful or spurious works. Indeed, a slight difference in style is not so significant that a work should be denied to an author if other, weightier arguments support its attribution [Col. 0063D]. Moreover, this controversy had already arisen in Gaul before the year 809, namely in 767 at the Council of Gentilly. Since it was therefore already growing while Alcuin was alive, it can scarcely be doubted that Charles the Great, being especially concerned to settle or remove such disputes from the Church, consulted the master of his palace and charged him to express his judgment.

[Col. 0064B] We therefore present the text here from a certified copy, as it is called, sent to us by the same D. Catelinot, whose subscription is as follows:

> “The present treatise of Alcuin on the Holy Spirit, together with the explanation of the divine Augustine on the mystery of the most Holy Trinity, was excerpted from an old manuscript written on parchment, which D. D. Dido, bishop of the church of Laon, donated to the library of the cathedral church; and it was transmitted to me through the special kindness of the distinguished canons of that same cathedral church. Done at Premonstratensian Abbey on 13 March 1747. — F. BRETON, written with my own hand. Canon of Premonstratensian Abbey.”

See what the distinguished and learned men D. Rivet, *Literary History of France*, volume VIII, Preliminary Notice, section 2, page X, and D. Ceillier, *History of the Sacred Authors*, volume XVIII, page 297, have written about this work. The distinguished Sirmond also saw this treatise somewhere; he lists its title, entirely like ours but under the name of an unknown author, in volume II of his works, page 695, among the notes. From the same work he also cites the testimony of Saint Athanasius, as we have noted below in section 9.

This little work is divided into three parts. In the first it is shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; in the second, that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son; in the third, that the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son.

## 744. IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY TRINITY BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES COLLECTED FROM THE SACRED BOOKS, IN WHICH IT IS CLEARLY SHOWN THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT PROCEEDS FROM THE FATHER AND THE SON, AND THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS RIGHTLY CALLED THE SPIRIT OF THE FATHER AND THE SON

Health, peace, strength, life, and victory to the most serene Augustus Charles.

Sacred and most serene Augustus, the Christian multitude established under the glorious rule of your dominion, commending your empire to divine protection on behalf of you and of the condition of your entire kingdom, offers its prayers to the almighty Lord, who is the governor of your kingdom. It also gives him immense thanks because throughout the universal Church, which flourishes under the most excellent rule of your dominion, there is the most tranquil peace and quiet for all worshipers of God.

For they are protected not only from the attacks of the pagans and of all the enemies of the Christian name, whom, with the Lord’s favor, your Sublimity restrains and prostrates, but also, through the excellence of your rule and wisdom, innumerable peoples are being brought from the worship of idols to the recognition of the Catholic faith and divine worship. Each day the number of those who believe in Christ increases, and the house of God, throughout all the boundaries of your kingdom, rejoices as it is filled with divine worship and sacred prayers offered on your behalf.

It also rejoices to see, through the providence of your government, the Christian multitude receiving immense daily increase, while the perverse doctrines of heretics, together with their faithless authors, are condemned, and Christ, who possesses your heart, triumphs through you over them. Among the other most glorious gifts he has bestowed upon you, he has enriched you with the most excellent and incomparable gift of divine and human knowledge, so that not only those who are daily granted the freedom to behold your most serene countenance may be refreshed by the purest fountain of your wisdom, but also those who are kept far and wide from your presence may be illuminated by your fame-spreading character and by the supreme light of your learning.

For this reason, from the various regions and peoples of the world, innumerable nations daily hasten to you, most serene Augustus, summoned also by your piety. Your royal kindness receives them into its broadest and most glorious embrace and never ceases to instruct them in spiritual and liberal knowledge. Therefore the title of your most glorious and tranquil rule will remain in the universal Church, erased by neither age nor antiquity, because under the most just rule of your dominion no fraud and no suggestion of perverse doctrine can remain hidden within it. Rather, all the orthodox, instructed by your brilliant admonition, are called [perhaps “devote themselves”] to divine worship as they follow and defend the holy Catholic and apostolic faith.

Among them I, the least and last of your servants, have written, according to the command of your Sublimity, this small booklet—following the authority of the holy Gospel and of the blessed Fathers—concerning the procession and sending of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, and concerning the fact that in the sacred books the same Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

### CHAPTER ONE  
### On the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son

For it is clearly declared in the words of the holy Gospel, in the synodal letters of the blessed Fathers, and in many books by men learned in spiritual knowledge, that the Holy Spirit, who is of one and the same substance with the Father and the Son, proceeds from and is sent by both.

## 745

For blessed Luke the Evangelist testifies in the fourteenth chapter [now chapter 6:19] of his Gospel that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the only-begotten Son of God, who is the Word of the Father, saying:

> “The whole crowd was seeking to touch him, because power was going out from him [Manuscript: ‘was repeatedly going out’], and he healed them all.”

In this chapter he therefore declares that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son when he says, “because power was going out from him.” For the Holy Spirit is that very power which is said in this chapter to go out from the Son of God, just as blessed Augustine affirms in Book XV *On the Trinity*. We shall also give below his words concerning the explanation of this passage.

The holy Evangelist John likewise reports at the end of his Gospel, that is, in chapter 214 [now 20:21 ff.], that on the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ had risen—that is, on the Lord’s Day—he entered to his apostles while the doors were shut and said to them a second time, “Peace be with you,” and added, “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed on them and said:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.”

We read in the Acts of the Apostles that what he promised was fulfilled:

> “For they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4).

The same blessed Evangelist John, in his Epistle which he wrote concerning love of God and neighbor, testifies in chapter 12 [now 1 John 3:23–24] that the only-begotten Son of God gave the Holy Spirit to his apostles, so that he himself might remain in them and they in him, as the same Apostle John says:

> “This is God’s commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, as he gave us commandment. And whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him; and by this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us.”

Pope Leo, most reverend pontiff of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0065D] Pope Leo at the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV of Coleti’s *Collection*, page 1223], likewise testifies in the synodal letter which he wrote to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, that our Lord Jesus Christ gave the Holy Spirit proceeding from him, through his own breath, to the apostles, as blessed John reports in the aforementioned chapter of his Gospel. He says:

> “After his resurrection, our Lord Jesus Christ entered to his disciples while the doors were shut, and by his breath gave them the Holy Spirit; and, having bestowed the light of understanding, he disclosed the hidden things of the sacred Scriptures.”

Blessed Gregory Nazianzen, or perhaps Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, a most learned investigator of the divine books [Note: [Col. 0066D] Perhaps Saint Gregory Nazianzen, from Oration 44, section 17], likewise explained the same Gospel passage in the same sense as Pope Leo. In the homily which he composed concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, he says that our Savior gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles by breathing upon their faces.

Hence Gregory himself says:

> “The Holy Spirit was present with Christ’s disciples not only by cooperating, but also by administering all things through the power and authority of the divinity. He was therefore present with them a third time, insofar as they were able to receive him, with the distinctions of the times also preserved: namely, before Christ’s Passion, again after his resurrection, and a third time after his Ascension into heaven. The power of his first presence is indicated by the graces of healings and by the cleansing and expulsion of demons from human beings, which the apostles certainly did not accomplish without the Holy Spirit. Then, after the resurrection, the Savior clearly said to his disciples, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ and he breathed upon their faces (John 20:22). At the third time he was present in tongues of fire.”

Saint Jerome, an excellent interpreter of the divine law and an astute disciple of the aforementioned Father Gregory [Note: [Col. 0067D] Saint Jerome, Letter 120, chapter 9], likewise explains the aforementioned passage in the Gospel according to John in the same sense. He testifies that our Savior, after his resurrection, gave the Holy Spirit proceeding from him to the apostles through his breath, just as he affirms in the letter concerning twelve questions which he wrote to Hedibia. In the eighth chapter he says:

> “How does our Savior, according to John, breathe the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, while according to Luke he says that he will send him after the Ascension? The solution to this question is very easy if, following the teaching of the Apostle Paul, we recognize the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. For he wrote in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: ‘There are divisions of gifts, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is beneficial. To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another the gift of healings in one Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of words. All these things the one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills’ (1 Cor. 12:4 ff.).

> “Therefore, after his resurrection, according to Luke’s Gospel, the Lord had said: ‘I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’ (Luke 24:49). And according to that same evangelist, in the Acts of the Apostles he said to them: ‘He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which you have heard, he said, from my mouth. For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now’ (Acts 1:5).

> “Again, at the end of the Gospel according to John, on the day on which he had risen—that is, on the Lord’s Day—he is reported to have entered to the apostles while the doors were shut and said to them a second time, ‘Peace be with you,’ and added: ‘As the Father sent me, so I send you.’ When he had said this, he breathed on them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained’ (John 20:21–23).

> “On the first day of his resurrection, therefore, they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they were to forgive sins, baptize, make people children of God, and bestow the spirit of adoption on believers, as the Savior himself said: ‘Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.’ On the day of Pentecost, however, it was promised to them more fully that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and clothed with the power by which they would preach Christ’s Gospel to all nations, according to what we read in Psalm 67: ‘The Lord will give a word to those who evangelize with great power’ [Read: ‘with great strength’] (Psalm 77:12), so that they would have the working of powers and the grace of healings, and, because they were to preach to many nations, would receive various kinds of tongues.”

[Col. 0068B] Blessed and venerable Bishop Augustine [Note: [Col. 0068D] From Saint Augustine, Tractate 121 on John, section 45], whom we mentioned shortly before, likewise affirms that Saint John, in the passage where he said, “He breathed,” and “Receive the Holy Spirit,” clearly declares the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, as he testifies in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

> “‘As the Father sent me, so I send you’: here he indicates the mediating relationship when he says, ‘He sent me, and I send you.’ He breathed and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:21). By breathing he signified that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but also his own [Augustine: ‘also his own’]. ‘Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.’ The love of the Church, which is poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit, forgives the sins of those who share in it; but it retains the sins of those who do not share in it.”

The same Augustine, explaining the aforementioned passage in Book IV *On the Trinity*, chapter 21, testifies that the only-begotten Son of God declares that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him by breathing upon the apostles and saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Hence Saint Augustine says:

> “Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit does not also proceed from the Son; for the same Spirit is not called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son without reason. Nor do I see what else he wished to signify when, breathing, he said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22). For that bodily breath, proceeding from the body and physically touching the senses, was not the substance of the Holy Spirit; rather, through an appropriate sign it certainly demonstrated that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son. For what utterly insane person would say that the Holy Spirit whom he gave by breathing was one Spirit, and the one whom he sent after his Ascension another? There is one Spirit: the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit, who works all things in all.

> “When the Lord therefore says, ‘whom I will send to you from the Father,’ he shows that the Spirit belongs to both the Father and the Son. For when he had said, ‘whom the Father will send,’ he added, ‘in my name’; yet he did not say, ‘whom the Father will send from me,’ as he said, ‘whom I will send to you from the Father.’ In this he evidently showed that the Father is the source of the whole divinity—or, if it is better said, of the Godhead. Therefore, since the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he is referred to him from whom the Son was born.”

## 747

The same distinguished teacher Augustine [Note: [Col. 0069D] From Saint Augustine, Book XV *On the Trinity*, chapter 26], following the authority of the holy Evangelists Luke and John, likewise testifies in Book XV *On the Trinity*, chapter 26, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, saying:

> “In that supreme Trinity which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown—or even sought—whether the Son was first born from the Father and the Holy Spirit afterward proceeded from both, because Holy Scripture calls him the Spirit of both. For he is the one of whom the Apostle says: ‘Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Gal. 4:6). And he is the one of whom the same Son says: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matt. 10:20). Many other testimonies of the divine utterances also prove that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who is properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity.

> “The Son himself also says of him: ‘whom I will send to you from the Father’ (John 15:26), and elsewhere: ‘whom the Father will send in my name’ (John 14:26). But that he proceeds from both is taught as follows: the Son himself says, ‘He proceeds from the Father’; and when he had risen from the dead and appeared to his disciples, ‘he breathed and said, Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22), so that he might also show that the Spirit proceeds from himself. And he is that power which went out from him, as we read in the Gospel according to Luke and which healed all.”

[Col. 0069C] In Luke’s passage, where we read in the Gospel, “I knew that power had gone out from me” (Luke 6:19), “power” may be understood as the effect of divine healing, as blessed Fulgentius explained. Augustine, however, says that Luke indicates the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son in the aforementioned passage when he says, “because power was going out from him.”

In the foregoing words of the holy Gospel according to Luke and John, and in the Epistle of that same John, which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles, it is clearly shown that the Holy Spirit, who is coequal and coeternal with the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son, just as the aforementioned Fathers—namely Pope Leo, Gregory Nazianzen, Jerome, and Augustine—testified by faithfully investigating the words of the holy Gospel.

[Col. 0069D] Thus far concerning the Gospel; now begins the section concerning the canons of the holy Fathers.

The most blessed and most reverend pontiffs who presided over the holy and distinguished councils of the blessed Fathers, whose canons and decrees the universal Church follows—namely Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, who appears to have presided over two hundred bishops at the Council of Ephesus, and Leo, venerable pontiff of the apostolic see, whose authority was followed by the six hundred and thirty Fathers assembled at Chalcedon—testified in their synodal letters, which the aforementioned pontiffs themselves wrote, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the only-begotten Son of God, who is the Word of the Father. These letters were read and approved in the presence of the entire Council of Ephesus and of Chalcedon, as well as at the Fifth Council, held at Constantinople under Pope Vigilius and the emperor Justinian.

The Council of Chalcedon considered their authority correct and credible, expressed through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and harmonious with the exposition made by the holy Council of Nicaea and with the faith and rules expounded by the holy and great Council of Ephesus, saying:

> “We have learned to follow the holy Fathers. For our Fathers who assembled at Nicaea did not speak from themselves what they spoke, but what the Holy Spirit dictated. Likewise, the most holy and God-loving blessed Cyril spoke and taught from the Holy Spirit what belongs to the holy Fathers.”

And shortly afterward the same aforementioned council says:

> “Having read the exposition of the holy Fathers read by the holy council, and having read the letters of the most holy and God-worthy former bishop Cyril, and having examined the rules and the faith expounded by the holy and great Council of Ephesus, we found all things harmonious.”

Therefore I too believe and confess in this way, and I judge anyone who thinks otherwise to be alien from the holy Catholic Church and from the right faith of believers.

Blessed Cyril [Note: [Col. 0069D] Saint Cyril at the Council of Ephesus, volume III of Coleti’s *Councils*, page 955, section 10], in the aforementioned canonical letter which he wrote to Nestorius, likewise testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, saying:

> “Although the Spirit exists in a distinct subsistence—for he is understood in himself insofar as he is Spirit and not the Son—he is nevertheless not alien to him. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is truth, and he flows forth from him, as from God and the Father.”

The same Saint Cyril [Note: [Col. 0070D] Cyril again at the Council of Ephesus, volume III] expressed a similar judgment concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in another canonical letter which he wrote to John of Antioch, saying:

> “For we remember the words: ‘Do not move the ancient boundaries which your fathers established’ (Prov. 22:28). For it was not they who spoke, but the Spirit of God the Father, who indeed proceeds from him. Yet he is not alien from the Son according to the principle of the one essence, and the words of the holy teachers of these mysteries confirm this. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘They attempted to go into Bithynia when they had come to Asia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them’ (Acts 16:7) [Manuscript: ‘Bythia’]. Likewise the admirable Paul writes: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him’ (Rom. 8:8–9).”

Everything, therefore, which Saint Cyril and the two hundred holy Fathers gathered at the Council of Ephesus decreed concerning the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical institutions, the most blessed Pope Celestine confirmed by apostolic authority and judged that it must be believed and followed by the universal Church. He said as follows:

> “Bishop Celestine [Note: [Col. 0070D] The written instructions given to legates traveling abroad are called *commonitoria*, says Severinus Binius in his notes on chapter 3 of the Sixth Council of Carthage. The *Commonitorium* of Pope Celestine I is published in volume I of D. Coustant’s *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, page 1152, and in volume IV of D. Mansi’s new edition of the Councils, page 556.]—Instructions to the bishops and priests going to the East. When, with our God as author, as we believe and hope, your charity arrives at the places appointed for you, refer every matter to our brother and fellow bishop Cyril; whatever you see to be his judgment, you shall do, and we command that the authority of the apostolic see be preserved.”

Thus far concerning the authority of the Council of Ephesus. Now begins the section concerning the authority of the Council of Chalcedon.

The most blessed and most reverend Leo, pontiff of the apostolic see, by whose authority and judgment the Council of Chalcedon was approved and confirmed, and who, as the words of that council testify, had foreseen matters by the Spirit and deliberated as though with brothers, appearing to them through the presence of his representatives—this aforementioned Saint Leo confirms the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son in the synodal letter mentioned shortly before, which he wrote to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople. He says:

[Note: [Col. 0072D] Pope Leo at the Council of Chalcedon, volume III of Coleti’s *Councils*, page 1223.]

> “After the Lord’s resurrection—which was certainly the resurrection of a true body, since someone other than the one who had been crucified and died was not raised—what else was accomplished during the interval of forty days except that the integrity of our faith might be cleansed of every darkness? For he conversed with his disciples, lived with them, ate with them, and allowed himself to be examined by careful and inquisitive touch by those whom doubt had affected. Therefore he also entered to his disciples while the doors were shut, and by his breath gave them the Holy Spirit; and, having bestowed the light of understanding, he disclosed the hidden things of the sacred Scriptures.”

After the reading of the aforementioned letter of the most reverend bishop, the bishops cried out:

> “This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the apostles. We all believe thus, we orthodox all believe thus. Let him be anathema who does not believe thus. Peter has spoken thus through Leo; the apostles taught thus; Leo taught piously and truly; Cyril taught thus. Eternal memory to Cyril. Leo and Cyril taught the same. Anathema to anyone who does not believe thus. This is the true faith; this is how we Catholics think. This is the faith of the Fathers.”

The same most holy Pope Leo likewise testifies, in agreement with the words of the aforementioned canonical letter, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son in a letter which he wrote to Turbius [Read: Turribius], bishop of Astorga:

[Note: [Col. 0072D] Pope Leo, Letter 15, chapter 1.]

> “The first chapter demonstrates how impiously they think about the divine Trinity who assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as though the same God were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit; as though the one who begot, the one who was begotten, and the one who proceeded from both were not distinct . . . . For the Catholic faith confesses the Trinity of the Godhead as consubstantial, believing that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are undivided without confusion, eternal without time, and equal without difference; because unity in the Trinity is fulfilled not by the same person but by the same essence.”

Thus far concerning the letters of Pope Leo and the authority of the Council of Chalcedon. Now begins the section concerning the confirmation of the Council of Constantinople.

The holy synod of Constantinople likewise believes and professes that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, just as Cyril established and confirmed in the presence of the universal Council of Ephesus. In the book of that same Constantinopolitan synod, this is contained in a comparison agreeing with the words of Saint Cyril, as follows:

“When the Son says concerning the Spirit, ‘He will glorify me’ (John 16:14), understanding this correctly, we do not say that Christ and the Son receive glory from the Holy Spirit as though they needed another’s glory, for the Spirit is neither greater than he nor above him. Since, however, he used his own Spirit to demonstrate his divinity, he says that he has been glorified by him through a great work, just as a man might perhaps say of a strength or some discipline implanted in him, ‘They will glorify me.’ Although the Spirit has a distinct subsistence and is understood separately insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien to him. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is truth; and he is poured forth from him, as from God and the Father.”

The holy synod of Constantinople therefore confirms and testifies that whatever the most holy Pope Leo and the most blessed Cyril taught and decreed concerning the catholic faith and the other ecclesiastical institutions agrees and accords with the decrees and traditions of the four principal councils—that is, the Councils of Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and Constantinople—as is contained in the book of the aforesaid synod in these words:

[Note: Likewise, in the Council of Constantinople, collation 6, p. 168 of volume VI of Colet’s Collection.]

“Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, a most reverend presbyter, legates of the Apostolic See, said through Paschasinus:

“It is manifest, and cannot be doubted, that the one faith of the most blessed Pope Leo, ruler of the Apostolic See, agrees and accords with the faith of the 318 Fathers assembled at Nicaea. Likewise, it does not in the least disagree with the decrees of the 150 bishops assembled at Constantinople, who confirmed that same faith; nor with those of Cyril, a man of holy memory, at Ephesus, when Nestorius was condemned for his error. Therefore, the letter of the most blessed pope, which is known to have expounded that same faith on account of the error of Eutyches, is seen to be united with that faith in one meaning and one spirit.”

The same Constantinopolitan synod also confirms that the authority and tradition of the aforesaid Fathers and of other distinguished teachers are to be received by the universal Church, saying:

“We wish you to know that we shall preserve and defend what was expounded and defined concerning one and the same faith by the four holy councils—the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon—and what was regularly established concerning ecclesiastical order. We follow these teachings, and we receive and embrace everything that agrees with them. Whatever does not agree with them, or whatever is found written by any person against what the four holy councils, or one of them, defined concerning one and the same faith, we utterly reject as foreign to piety.

“We follow in all things the holy Fathers and teachers of the holy Church of God: Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, Gregory the Theologian and Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Theophilus, John of Constantinople, Cyril, Augustine, Proclus, and Leo. We receive everything written and expounded by them concerning the true faith and the condemnation of heretics. Remaining, therefore, in all the matters mentioned above, we receive those Fathers and bishops who preserve and preach in the holy Church of God what was expounded concerning the faith by the four holy councils and preached by the holy Fathers named above.”

[750] The most blessed and most reverend pontiff of the city of Rome, Gelasius, likewise brought forward words agreeing with the decrees of the aforesaid Council of Constantinople concerning the books of all the orthodox, which are to be received and read. In his Decretal Letter, written concerning the authority of the divine books and concerning those books that are not to be received in the Church, he says:

[Note: Pope Gelasius, volume V of the Councils, p. 387.]

“We decree that the little works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in that communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read.”

The blessed Athanasius, most reverend bishop of the city of Alexandria, who had served at Nicaea as the devoted assistant of Alexander, the chief bishop of that city and also his own teacher, declares the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in the Exposition of the Catholic Faith, which that distinguished teacher himself composed and which the universal Church confesses. He says:

“The Father was made by no one, neither created nor begotten. The Son is from the Father alone, not made nor created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.”

[Note: Alcuin believed that the Creed from which these words are quoted had Saint Athanasius as its author, although modern critics disagree.]

The holy bishop Hilary, likewise, a man distinguished in divine worship, whose authority Pope Gelasius in the aforesaid decretal letter and the Constantinopolitan synod confirm is to be received by the catholic Church, testifies in Book VIII of On the Trinity that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. He says (no. 20):

“The Holy Spirit receives from the Son; he is also sent by him, and proceeds from the Father. And I ask whether ‘to receive from the Son’ is the same as ‘to proceed from the Father.’ [If it is believed that there is no difference between receiving from the Son and proceeding from the Father], then it will certainly be considered to be the same and one thing: receiving from the Son and receiving from the Father. For the Lord himself says: ‘Because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said: He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (John 16:14–15). Whatever he receives—whether power, strength, or teaching—the Son said that it must be received from him.”

The same distinguished teacher says in Book XII of On the Trinity, in prayer to God:

“Preserve, I pray, this undefiled devotion of my faith, and grant me, until the departure of my spirit, this voice of my conscience: that I may always retain what I professed when I was baptized in the Creed of my regeneration, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; namely, that I may worship you as our Father, and your Son together with you, and that I may merit the Holy Spirit, who is from you through your Only-Begotten, since he is a reliable witness to the faith for me, saying: ‘Father, all that is mine is yours, and yours is mine’” (John 17:10).

The most reverend pontiff Ambrose, whose faith and sound tradition the aforementioned Pope Gelasius and the aforesaid Constantinopolitan synod likewise decreed were to be received by the universal Church, confirms in Book VI of the works he wrote on the faith for the emperor Gratian that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. He says:

[Note: Saint Ambrose, On the Holy Spirit, Book I, chapter 1.]

“Therefore,” he says, “the Spirit is not sent as though from one place, nor does he proceed as though from one place when he proceeds from the Son. Just as the Son himself, when he says, ‘I proceeded from the Father and came’ (John 16:28), destroyed all opinions that can be applied to movement from place to place, as they can in the case of certain bodies.

“Similarly, when we read that God is within or outside, we do not thereby enclose God within some body or separate him from some body; rather, weighing the matter with profound and indescribable consideration, we understand the mystery of the divine nature. In the same way, Wisdom says that she proceeded from the mouth of the Most High (Ecclesiasticus 24:5), yet she is not outside the Father but with the Father, because ‘the Word was with God’ (John 1:1); and not only with the Father, but also in the Father, for he says: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (John 14:10).

“Yet when he goes out from the Father, he does not depart from a place or become separated like one body from another; nor, when he is in the Father, is he enclosed in him as one body in another body. Likewise, when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he is not separated from the Father, nor is he separated from the Son.

“For how can he be separated from the Father who is the Spirit of his mouth (Psalm 32:6), a phrase that expresses the sign of eternity and the unity of divinity? He therefore exists and always remains the Spirit of his mouth; but he appears to descend when we receive him, so that he may dwell in us and we may not be estranged from his grace. He appears to descend for us—not because he ascends, but because our spirit ascends to him.”

[Note: In Saint Ambrose: “Not because he descends, but because our spirit ascends to him.”]

[Col. 0075A] The blessed Augustine likewise, whose authority and teaching Pope Gelasius, by apostolic authority, and the aforesaid Council of Constantinople decreed were to be received and followed by the universal Church, testifies in Book XV of On the Holy Trinity, chapter 26, that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. He says (no. 47):

“Whoever can understand the generation of the Son from the Father without time should understand the procession of the Holy Spirit from both without time. Whoever can understand, in what the Son says—‘Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself’ (John 5:26)—that the Father did not give life to the Son as though he already existed without life, but begot him without time in such a way that the life which the Father gave the Son by begetting him is coeternal with the life of the Father who gave it, should understand that, just as the Father has in himself that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, so he gave the Son that the same Holy Spirit should proceed from him—and both without time.

“Thus, when the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, it should be understood that he also proceeds from the Son, and that, in proceeding from the Father, he is from the Father for the Son. For if everything the Son has he has from the Father, then surely he has from the Father that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him.

“But no temporal sequence should be imagined there, involving an earlier and a later, because there is absolutely no such sequence there. For just as generation from the Father gives the Son his essence without any beginning of time and without any change of nature, so procession from both gives the Holy Spirit his essence without any beginning of time and without any change of nature.

“For this reason, although we do not call the Holy Spirit begotten, we nevertheless do not dare to call him unbegotten, lest anyone should suppose from this term either two Fathers in that Trinity or two who are not from another. For the Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten—not indeed in the Scriptures, but in the customary language of disputants, who produce whatever expression they wish [Augustine: ‘are able’] in speaking about so great a matter. The Son, however, was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and, with the Father giving without any interval of time, proceeds jointly from both.”

Again, in the same book he says:

“From the one from whom the Son has that he is God—for he is God from God—from that one he has also that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. Consequently, the Holy Spirit’s proceeding also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father, is something he has from the Father himself.”

The blessed Pope Gregory likewise testifies in the homily he wrote on the Gospel reading beginning, “When evening had come,” that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. He says:

[Note: Pope Gregory, Homily 26, no. 2.]

“The sending of the Son may also be understood according to the nature of his divinity. For the Son is said to be sent by the Father precisely insofar as he is begotten by the Father. The Son himself also declares that he sends the Holy Spirit, who is coequal with the Father and the Son, although he was not incarnate, saying: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father’ (John 15:26). If being sent were to be understood only as becoming incarnate, then assuredly the Holy Spirit could in no way be said to be sent, since he was not incarnate.

“But his sending is itself his procession, by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore, just as the Spirit is said to be sent because he proceeds, so the Son is not improperly said to be sent because he is begotten.”

Gennadius, bishop of Massilia, likewise, in the little book he composed On Ecclesiastical Dogma, setting forth the form of the Creed in its first chapter, expressed concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son a judgment similar to that of the aforementioned teachers. He says:

“We believe that there is one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the Father, because he has a Son; the Son, because he has a Father; the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Father, therefore, is the beginning of the Godhead. Just as he was never anything but God, so he was never anything but Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit was not born, because he is not the Son, nor is he unbegotten, because he is not the Father. Nor was the Holy Spirit made, because he is not from nothing, but proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son.”

Isidore likewise, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, following the Fathers mentioned above, says in Book VII of the Etymologies, chapter 3:

“The Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, and possesses his substance. For he could not proceed from the Father in any other way than as that which the Father himself is.”

Boethius, a man learned not only in divine writings but also in philosophical works, testifies in the book he composed on the unity of the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, imitating the men mentioned above in the rule of the catholic faith, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. He says:

“Nor can it be said that anything was added to God by which he became Father. For he never began to be Father, since the production of the Son is consubstantial with him, whereas the predication of Father is relational. If we remember all the foregoing statements about God, let us think in this way: God the Son proceeded from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both. Since these are incorporeal, they are in no way separated by place.

“Since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and since God has no differences by which he differs from God, none of them differs from any other. Where differences are absent, plurality is absent; where plurality is absent, unity is present. Nothing else could be begotten from God except God.”

Paschasius likewise, in the little book he composed On the Holy Spirit, testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the only-begotten Son of God, who is the Word of the Father.

[Note: Paschasius, Book I, chapter 10.]

Therefore, those who try to deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son because our Savior, as we read in the Gospel according to John, declares concerning the Holy Spirit, saying, “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26), should hear what the blessed Augustine says when explaining these words of the holy Gospel in Book XV of On the Trinity, chapter 26. He says (no. 38):

“Since in that coeternal, equal, incorporeal, ineffably immutable, and inseparable Trinity it is extremely difficult to distinguish generation from procession, let it suffice for the time being for those who are unable to extend their understanding further what we said in a certain sermon delivered to the ears of the Christian people and committed to writing.

“Among other things, after I had shown through the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures that the Spirit proceeds from both, I said: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, why does the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’? Why do you think, except because he customarily refers to him what is his own, from whom he himself also is? Hence comes the statement: ‘My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 7:16). If here the teaching is understood to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more must it be understood there that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from him, where he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’?

“For from the one from whom, as we have said, the Son has that he is God—for he is God from God—from that one he has that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him. Consequently, the Holy Spirit’s proceeding also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father, is something he has from the Father himself.”

That same Holy Spirit, who is of one and the same substance with the Father and the Son, is called in one place the Spirit of God the Father and in another the Spirit of Christ, and is said to proceed from both and to be sent by both. We have shown this on the basis both of the authority of divine Scripture and of the tradition of learned men in the sacred writings, because of the unity of his substance with the Father and the Son and because of the inseparable nature, will, power, and operation of the holy Trinity.

Nevertheless, he is true God, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, eternity, and substance. Concerning him Gregory of Nazianzus says in the aforesaid homily:

[Note: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 44, nos. 13–14.]

“The Holy Spirit is life and life-giving, light and illuminating, good and goodness; the upright Spirit, the princely Spirit, who is Lord of all, sending apostles, assigning ministers to himself, establishing temples for himself; inspiring where he wills; distributing gifts; the Spirit of truth, the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, knowledge, piety, counsel, strength, and the fear of God; through whom the Father is recognized and the Son glorified, and who himself is known by the Father and the Son alone.

“One order, one worship, one veneration, one power, one perfection and sanctification. And what need is there of many words? Everything that the Father is, the Son is, except that the Father is unborn; everything that the Son is, the Holy Spirit is, except that the Son is born. Yet these distinctions do not separate the substance; they are distinctions in relation to the substance.”

As for what our same Savior declares concerning that same Holy Spirit, as we read in the same Gospel according to John, saying, “He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak,” and because “he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:13–14), we most certainly believe that this was said to demonstrate the one substance and will of the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For the Holy Spirit does not speak from himself in such a way as to demonstrate the Godhead of the one nature, yet so that what he speaks may be believed to be his and not another’s. Luke testifies about the apostles, saying: “They began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4). And in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

He therefore possesses his own authority to speak, who freely grants to others the ability to speak. Yet he cannot be separated from the operation, power, and goodness of the Father and the Son, since he possesses unity of Godhead substantially with the Father and the Son, although he has a distinct person in his own property.

## CHAPTER II. That the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son in the divine books

[Col. 0078B]

The Holy Spirit, who is coequal and coeternal with the Father and the Son, is called in some passages of Scripture the Spirit of the Father; in others, because of the unity of the will, power, eternity, and substance of the holy Trinity, he is called the Spirit of Christ.

The blessed Peter, demonstrating that the same Holy Spirit is Christ’s, speaks in his First Letter, written to those who had believed from the circumcision, concerning the prophets as follows:

“Rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy as you receive the goal of your faith, the salvation of souls, concerning which salvation the prophets sought and searched carefully. They prophesied of the future grace of God in you, searching into what time or what circumstances the Spirit of Christ who was in them was indicating” (1 Peter 1:8–11).

The blessed Paul likewise says in his Letter to the Romans, chapter 18: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Romans 8:9). Again, that distinguished Teacher of the Gentiles testifies in his Letter to the Galatians, chapter 18, that the same Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the only-begotten Son of God, saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6).

Pope Leo likewise, in the homily he wrote on the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, expressed a judgment agreeing with the words of the blessed Peter concerning the same Holy Spirit. He says:

[Note: Pope Leo, Sermon 75, chapter 3; Sermon 76, chapter 2; Letter 16, chapter 3 at the end.]

“The Only-Begotten is indeed from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.”

The same pope also says in a second homily:

“The Son’s being begotten timelessly from the Father is eternal; likewise, it is eternal for the Holy Spirit to be the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.”

The same venerable Pope Leo also testifies in the decretal letter he composed concerning the mystery of baptism that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, that is, the Spirit of Christ, saying:

“When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). Since Christ is truth and the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of truth, and since the name Paraclete is proper to both, the celebration is not dissimilar where there is one sacrament.”

[754] The blessed Augustine likewise says in a statement he delivered in disputing against Eusebius concerning the Holy Spirit:

“The Holy Spirit knows the mysteries of God only through substance. For one substance has one understanding and one will. He speaks concerning God, who is always one and immutable, whether in the Son or in the Holy Spirit. What the Father wills, the Son wills; and what the Son wills, the Holy Spirit wills. For this reason he is sometimes called the Spirit of God, and sometimes the Spirit of Christ, who, as he says, ‘proceeds from God and will receive from what is mine’ (John 16:15).”

The same distinguished teacher Augustine, in his Exposition of the Gospel according to John, testifies that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is the Spirit of the Son. He says:

[Note: Saint Augustine, Tractate 99 on John, no. 7.]

“There are many testimonies by which it is clearly shown that the Spirit called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity belongs both to the Father and to the Son. Why, then, should we not believe that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, since he is himself the Spirit of the Son? For what else does that breathing signify, and what else does he mean when he says to the woman, ‘Someone touched me, for I perceived power go out from me’ (Luke 8:46)? The Holy Spirit is called by the name of power, as in the words: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’ (Luke 1:35). What else does this mean except that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him?”

The blessed Ambrose likewise says:

“He is breathed forth by Christ, so that you may believe that he is the Spirit of Christ, and so that you may believe that the Spirit is from God. For God alone forgives sins.”

Isidore likewise says in Book XV of the work he composed On the Nature of Things:

[Note: In Petavius, volume II of Theological Dogmas, Book VII, chapter 11, no. 16, this passage of Isidore is cited from Book I of the Sentences, chapter 17.]

“The Holy Spirit is creator, just as the Father and the Word, as we read in the Book of Blessed Job: ‘The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life’ (Job 33:4). The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son; and the Father and the Son are one for this reason: that the Father has nothing which the Son does not have. For one thing, consubstantial with two, could not proceed from them and be present in them simultaneously unless those from whom it proceeds were one.”

The holy bishop Fulgentius likewise, in the little book he composed concerning the Holy Spirit, testifies that the same Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, saying:

[Note: I think this little book is the still-undiscovered Short Memorandum on the Holy Spirit, written by Saint Fulgentius in response to the questions of the presbyter Abragila. The author of the Life of Saint Fulgentius mentions it in chapter 24.]

“When it is asked which Holy Spirit the angel announced to the Virgin, we say that it is certainly the same Spirit who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, without whom the flesh of Christ could neither be formed nor baptized, nor even be raised from the dead.”

Again, in the same book he says:

“When it is asked which Spirit spoke through the prophets, no other should be understood except the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of Christ.”

Having thus briefly explained, both from divine Scripture and from the tradition of the holy Fathers, the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, and the fact that the same Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son, we must now say a little concerning the sending of the Son by the Father and of the Holy Spirit by both—that is, by the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER III. The sending of the Son by the Father and of the Holy Spirit by both

The Only-Begotten Son of God, who is coequal and coeternal with the Father, is said to be sent by that same Father. Hence our same Savior, as we read in the Gospel according to John, chapter 214 at the end, says to his disciples:

“As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21).

Our same Savior, who is the Word of the Father, testifies that he sends the Holy Spirit and that he is sent by the Father in his own name. For, as we read in the Gospel according to John, chapter 142, he says to his disciples:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

Again, in the same Gospel, chapter 147, the same Savior says:

“I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7).

A little later in the same book he adds:

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said to you that he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:12–15).

Our same Savior, after his resurrection, as we read in the Gospel according to Luke, chapter 342, spoke words agreeing with those above, saying:

“I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49).

According to the same evangelist, he also said in the Acts of the Apostles:

“He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which you have heard from my mouth. For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:4–5).

Again, at the end of the Gospel according to John, on the day on which he had risen—that is, on the Lord’s Day—he is reported to have entered to the apostles while the doors were closed and to have said to them a second time, “Peace be with you,” and then added:

“As the Father sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:21–23).

Thus, we read in the Acts of the Apostles that what he promised was fulfilled:

“For they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4).
