The blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, in the same homily he composed on the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, says concerning the sending of that same Holy Spirit:

“The Holy Spirit came as Lord in power, but he is sent as one who is not opposed to God. These expressions do not separate the nature but teach concord. For this reason, after Christ’s ascension, he is said to be sent to us as another Paraclete, so that you may recognize the equality of nature and power.”

The holy Augustine likewise testifies in Book IV of On the Trinity, chapter 21, that the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father according to the unity of substance, although they are said to be sent by him. He says:

“Just as the Father begot and the Son was begotten, so the Father sent and the Son was sent. But just as the one who begot and the one who was begotten are one, so the one who sent and the one who was sent are one, because the Father and the Son are one. Thus also the Holy Spirit is one with them, because these three are one.”

Again, in Book II, chapter 3, he says:

“Just as it does not follow that the Son is lesser because he said, ‘The Son can do nothing of himself, but only what he sees the Father doing’ (John 5:19)—for he did not say this according to the form of a servant but according to the form of God, as we have already shown; and these words do not indicate that he is lesser, but that he is from the Father—so it does not follow that the Holy Spirit is lesser because it was said of him: ‘He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak’ (John 16:13).”

Here the holy and venerable Father Athanasius, in the disputation he held with the heretic Arius, says that the Holy Spirit, who is of one and the same substance with the Father and the Son, says and speaks what is common to the Father and the Son. He says:

[Note: Learned editors of the works of Saint Athanasius, volume II, p. 205, demonstrate by weighty arguments that this book was falsely attributed to Saint Athanasius. See Ceillier, General History of Sacred Authors, volume V, p. 283.]

“This makes it much more evident that the Holy Spirit is not alien to the substance of the Father and the Son, since he does not speak from himself as an alien and outsider, but, as a companion of one and the same nature, says and speaks what is common to the Father and the Son. For if he spoke from his own things, he would unquestionably be regarded not only as alien to the Father but also as deceitful and deceptive, since, as the Son says, ‘Everyone who speaks falsehood speaks from his own things’ (John 8:44). Therefore he speaks the truth because he does not speak from his own things—that is, not from himself—but speaks what belongs to the Father and the Son and what they have to be spoken.

“‘He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (John 16:14). To show that receiving from himself is the same as having received from the Father, he says: ‘Therefore I said, He will receive from what is mine, because everything that the Father has is mine.’ You see, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is not separate from the Father and the Son, since he speaks what is known to belong properly to the Father and the Son.”

[756] Therefore, although the Only-Begotten Son of God and the Holy Spirit are said to be sent by the Father on account of the unity of substance of the holy Trinity, as we have stated, they are nevertheless equal in every respect to the Father in will, power, eternity, and substance.

For, as the holy Jerome testifies in the Creed composed by that distinguished teacher, there is in this supreme and ineffable Trinity no degree, nothing that can be called lower or higher; rather, the whole Godhead is equal in its perfection. Thus, apart from the names that indicate the properties of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most properly be understood of all three.

[Note: Consult volume II of the works of Saint Athanasius, pp. 719 ff.]

“For, as the blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, testifies: As is the Father, so also is the Son, and so also is the Holy Spirit. For in this Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, but all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another. Thus, in every respect, as has already been said above, both the unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in the unity are to be venerated. Therefore, whoever wishes to be saved must think this way concerning the Trinity.”

With this belief, therefore, neither do we confuse the Trinity nor separate the unity of substance. Rather, we confess and follow the firm and immutable rule of the catholic faith, through which the blessed apostles and martyrs, and all men devoted to religion and endowed with holiness, were found worthy to possess divine grace, obtained the hope of eternal life, and received the everlasting blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

## THE EXPLANATION OF THE MYSTERY OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY BY THE LORD AUGUSTINE

[Note: Thus in the manuscript.]

Certainly Christ is life. And if Christ is true life, why did life die? The same Lord Jesus Christ could both die in one respect and not die in another. Seek death: it could never exist in the Word. Seek death: it was never in the soul, because there was a true death. The one and same Christ is he who wholly endured injury while the power of his divinity remained unharmed, and who was cast into the depths without being submerged.

**Question:** Is he himself the Father who is the Son?

**Answer:** Far be it! He is not himself the Father who is the Son; nor is the Holy Spirit himself the one who is the Father.

**Question:** How so—because in persons one is the Father, another the Son, another the Holy Spirit? And not indeed something else, but someone else.

**Question:** Is the Father the same thing as the Son?

**Answer:** The same.

**Question:** Is this the Father which is the Son?

**Answer:** This is.

Interrogation: Is he the Father who is the Son? Response: God forbid: he is not the Father who is the Son, but the Father is that which the Son is.

[Col. 0082D] Interrogation: Is God the Father, who is before the ages and unto the end of the age, himself born of the Virgin? Response: God forbid: God the Father, who is before the ages and unto the end of the age, is not himself born of the Virgin; the Lord the Son himself was born of the Virgin.

Interrogation: Does the Father have anything in common with the Son? Response: He does.

Interrogation: What does he have? Response: Eternity and divinity.

Interrogation: Does the Father have anything proper to himself that the Son does not have? Response: He does.

Interrogation: What does he have? Response: Eternity without birth, because he is unbegotten.

[Col. 0083A] Interrogation: Does the Son have anything proper to himself that the Father does not have? Response: He does.

Interrogation: What does he have? Response: Birth together with eternity, because he is begotten.

Interrogation: Does the Holy Spirit have anything proper to himself that neither the Father nor the Son has? Response: He does.

Interrogation: What does he have? Response: Procession, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Interrogation: Can the Father alone be called the Trinity, or how is this so? Response: He can.

Interrogation: How can he? Response: Because the Son and the Holy Spirit proceeded from him. The Son cannot be called the Trinity, because the Father did not proceed from him, but only the Spirit; for if we call the Holy Spirit unbegotten, we affirm two Fathers, and if begotten, we acknowledge two Sons. But for this reason we call him neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son; and there is a Trinity in one person of the Godhead.

Interrogation: Is there essence in the Father? Response: There is.

Interrogation: How? Response: Because he always is, and is in himself.

Interrogation: Did the whole Trinity act in the Virgin’s womb, or how? Response: The whole Trinity acted, but the person of the Son alone assumed flesh, and willed the Word itself to be called his Son. But do not be afraid to call the Word the Son of God, since God the Father is the Father of his Word; and where the Word of God is, there is God, because the Word of God is from God. Moses and the Prophet bear witness: “God made all things by the word” (Ps. XXXII, 6). And again it is said in the Psalms: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established”; and again: “Your word remains forever, throughout the age and generation” (ibid. CXVIII, 89). And again Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14).

Interrogation: Is Christ, the Son of God, himself God? Response: He is himself.

Interrogation: Was he himself born of the Virgin? Response: He was himself.

Interrogation: Was he himself hung upon the cross? Response: He was himself.

Interrogation: Did he himself descend into hell? Response: He did himself.

Interrogation: Was he himself dead? Response: He died for our sins, and rose again on the third day by his own power.

Interrogation: Therefore, was the true God dead? Response: He was dead.

Interrogation: How was he dead? Response: In the flesh.

Interrogation: He died in the flesh and descended in the soul [Col. 0084B] into hell—he who was in heaven? Response: The divinity reigned everywhere.

757 THIRD WORK, OR THE WRITINGS OF BLESSED ALCUIN AGAINST FELIX OF URGELL AND ELIPANDUS OF TOLEDO

[Col. 0083]

PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0083C] The first and principal undertaking that occupied blessed Alcuin, summoned by Charlemagne from England to Francia, was the attack upon the new sect of the Adoptionists, which had then arisen in Spain and had begun to spread into Francia as well. These were the men who said that Christ the Lord, insofar as he was man, was not the proper Son of God but an adoptive son; not true God but nominally so. The authors and leaders of this error were Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of Urgell. For the origin and development of this error, if you please, consult our dissertation at the end of this work. Blessed Alcuin performed excellently the commission entrusted to him by the most Christian and truly Catholic king: at one time urging the erring to repentance through letters full both of Christian doctrine and charity; at another confirming the household of the faith in the truth by word and written letters; at another supplying teachers of the faith, preachers of the Gospel, and bishops with arguments by which they might resist [Col. 0083D] the creeping poison; at another engaging the very authors of the error in public assemblies; and finally refuting their errors learnedly and forcefully in several books. All this succeeded so happily that it must be attributed above all to his own industry that at last, in the Council of Aachen of the year 799, an end was put to these disturbances, which had afflicted the Church for many years. Thus our blessed Alcuin could rightly glory and say: “By God’s mercy I made Felix a Catholic” (Book I against Elipandus, no. 8).

We therefore collect here, in this arrangement, all these writings, filled with excellent fruit and once so salutary and beneficial to the universal Church, and still especially useful for demonstrating the antiquity and consistent truth of Catholic doctrine. First we present a booklet hitherto desired, which Alcuin had sent to the abbots and monks of Gothia while he was still occupied in refuting the letter addressed to him by Felix of Urgell. He himself also mentions it in Letter 132, writing to the same abbots and monks: “As was partly done in the booklet which we sent to you through Blessed Benedict, for the consolation and confirmation of the Catholic faith,” etc. This booklet was discovered by the most learned man, D. Peter Francis Fogginius, in manuscript 290 of the Palatine-Vatican Library, whose custody he holds, to his great credit and with much praise. He had already prepared it for the press and was about to issue it into public light with a learned preface. But after the eminent Cardinal Passionei, while he lived the greatest patron of our labors, opportunely informed him that I was preparing a new and complete edition of the works of Blessed Flavius Alcuin, the distinguished scholar abandoned his undertaking and most kindly furnished me with this booklet, together with the preface in which the booklet is defended as belonging to Alcuin by solid arguments. We have therefore prefixed it to the work, judging that it will not be unwelcome to learned readers.

[Col. 0084D] In the second place we present the seven books of blessed Alcuin against Felix of Urgell, according to the edition of D. Quercetanus, who restored them to their author, although they had once been published under another name, namely that of St. Paulinus of Aquileia. Before them, however, we place, first, the letter of Albinus to Felix the heretic, hitherto unpublished, which we transcribed from a very ancient and almost contemporary manuscript preserved, together with other truly precious and little-known relics of antiquity, in the library of the illustrious metropolitan chapter of Salzburg. This is that exhortatory letter which Alcuin, arriving from England in Gaul in the year 793, “took care to send to Felix with the pen of charity, not the goad of contention; with a desire for fraternal salvation, not with the biting style of correction, so that he might join the Catholic unity.” Felix, however, opposed to it a booklet “not concise in the brevity of a letter, but extended in a sequence of discourses, in which he opened all the hiding places of his perfidy,” as Alcuin himself writes at the beginning of Book I against Felix and in Book I against Elipandus, no. 16.

758 Secondly, before these same seven books we place two letters of blessed Alcuin to Charlemagne. In the first he submits his books to the examination and approval of the most Christian king; in the second, having corrected them, he dedicates them to the honors of that same king and commends them to his authority. We owe both letters, unknown to the distinguished Quercetanus, to the industry of the celebrated Stephen Baluze, who first brought them into public light from a manuscript of the Colbert Library in Book IV of the *Miscellanea*, pp. 413–415.

Moreover, since the text in the earlier editions of these books is riddled with many errors—so that, because of inept punctuation and other grosser mistakes, the meaning often becomes obscure and many times appears wholly corrupted—and since we have been unable anywhere to investigate an old manuscript exemplar that might assist us in restoring the true reading, we have therefore judged that not merely liberty but necessity was imposed upon us to remove those errors and defects by ingenuity and probable conjecture. Nevertheless, we always maintain that we have acted genuinely and in accordance with the requirements of the text itself, as learned men will discover who have both the opportunity and the leisure to compare the two editions with one another. We have marked with their own notes the opinions of the holy Fathers, which are cited abundantly in these books, adding, for the convenience of readers, citations from the latest editions of their works.

We have done the same in the four books that follow, written against Elipandus, which the distinguished Quercetanus published from a manuscript of the church of Saint Mary of Rheims, supplied to him by the very learned Jacobus Sirmundus. We have arranged these books in the order in which they were once arranged and bound by blessed Alcuin himself, when he sent them to Laidradus and his companions in Spain to quell the disturbances that had arisen there on account of the new doctrine and that they were about to visit again. First, therefore, comes Alcuin’s letter to Laidradus, bishop of Lyons, Nefridius of Narbonne, [Col. 0086A] and Benedict the abbot, as well as to all the bishops, abbots, and brothers of the province of Gothia. To this we attach another letter, which the distinguished Quercetanus exhibited at the end of the said books, and thus out of order. In it Alcuin informs Laidradus and his companions what is contained in the entire bundle he had sent and in what order he had arranged the same materials in separate gatherings, as will become clear to readers of this second letter, or supplement to the first. After these almost dedicatory letters follows Alcuin’s exhortatory letter to Elipandus concerning the Catholic faith. To it is appended Elipandus’s letter to Albinus, containing his replies to the earlier letter; Alcuin endeavors to weaken these in the two books that we append. In the two books that follow, he confirms in plain speech the truth of the Catholic faith concerning Christ. At the end of these books Alcuin himself added Elipandus’s letter to Felix, now converted, together with Felix’s Confession, by which he condemns his errors and vigorously exhorts his followers to repentance.

Finally, the entire series of these writings is closed by the Letter to a daughter most dear in Christ, in which he supplies easier arguments by which the errors and deceptive sophistries of the Adoptionists may be resisted.

I think that no learned person will now miss anything that has been reported anywhere as having been written by Alcuin against the error of the Spaniards concerning the Adoption of Christ as Son of God. From all these little works, as well as from the letters of Elipandus and of the bishops of Spain to the bishops of Gaul and Germany, which we have relegated to an appendix, the whole history of this controversy is brought fully into the light, to the considerable advantage of the ecclesiastical history of those times. We shall endeavor to shed light upon it in two dissertations to be added at the end.

[Col. 0085]

759 BOOKLET OF BLESSED ALCUIN AGAINST THE HERESY OF FELIX, SENT TO THE ABBOTS AND MONKS OF GOTHIA

From manuscript 290 of the Vatican-Palatine Library.

A SPECIMEN OF A PREFACE BY THE MOST DISTINGUISHED D. PETER F. FOGGINIUS, CUSTODIAN OF THE VATICAN LIBRARY, TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0085C]

When Adrian I occupied the Roman see, a kind of offshoot of the Nestorian heresy, already almost entirely eradicated, began to grow in Spain through the efforts of Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of Urgell. For they taught that Christ Jesus, insofar as he was man, was not the natural but the adoptive Son of God. This impious and sacrilegious opinion was condemned not only by several synods and by the Roman pontiff Adrian in a peremptory decree, but was also attacked by many distinguished men, among whom must be numbered Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, most dear to Charlemagne and the restorer of learning in Gaul. Through his doctrine and holiness of life he was at that time a great support and ornament of the Church. He conducted the affair both through private letters sent to the heretical bishops and through public writings: for he rebuked and refuted Felix in seven books, and Elipandus in a two-part work, each part consisting of two books.

These writings had already been published in print more than once; but what had until then been regarded as lost—that is, the work he had written before all the others against Felix—became known to us from Alcuin’s letter addressed to the abbots and monks of Gothia, published by Baluze from manuscripts of the Colbert Library. In that letter (Letter 132), after he had set forth the Catholic position against what Felix taught, he adds:

“This can be confirmed by many evangelical and apostolic testimonies, and also by the traditions of the holy Fathers, as was partly done in the booklet which we sent to you through Blessed Benedict, for the consolation and confirmation of the Catholic faith. But at present we have a larger work in hand for other reasons, which we read in the booklet of the venerable Felix; and, God willing, we shall send it to you after it has been read and approved by our bishops and by the lord king.”

Since, therefore, I found this booklet in manuscript 290 of the Vatican-Palatine Library, bearing an age of eight hundred years, I thought that I would please men of letters by bringing it into public light. Indeed, Alcuin’s singular merit seems in a certain sense to demand that no work written by him should remain unpublished. Nor will it be difficult to understand that this booklet is Alcuin’s first treatise written against the heresy of Felix, since this is immediately clear from its opening, and since the whole work consists of evangelical and patristic testimonies. This corresponds perfectly with the description of it found in the aforementioned letter.

But the recent authors of the *Literary History of Gaul* (vol. IV, p. 338, no. 7) have mistakenly persuaded themselves that the work mentioned in the passage I cited from the letter to the monks of Gothia is the same work Alcuin mentions in the first book of those he published against Elipandus.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] [ [Col. 0087] This note appears at the foot of column 87, but the callout number (c) has not been printed in the text.] This title is found in the manuscript itself, previously mentioned.]

[Col. 0087A] In these passages the discussion concerns an exhortatory letter, apparently a private one, sent to Felix.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Certainly the letter that we shall present shortly, which was still unknown to D. Fogginius. FROBEN.]

But in the letter to the monks of Gothia the subject is a polemical treatise, issued for the public good so that the Catholic faith might have it as a shield against the heresy of Felix. Such indeed is the treatise we are publishing: there is nothing in it that suggests an exhortatory letter or indicates that it was sent to Felix. Here are Alcuin’s words in the first of the seven books written against Felix:

“I previously wrote a letter to Bishop Felix with the pen of charity, not the goad of contention; with a desire for fraternal salvation, not with the biting style of correction, wishing to correct him in the love of Christ, etc. But, as I recognize, he did not receive my little letter with that charitable duty or humble service with which anyone who reads my letter with a view to my piety will recognize that I wrote it.”

760 These statements agree with what is read around the middle of the first book against Elipandus:

“To him”—that is, to Felix—“upon coming into these regions, I took care to send an exhortatory letter with the pen of charity, so that he might join the Catholic unity. He attempted to reply to it, not with the brevity of a letter but with the length of a booklet. We replied to his booklet with seven booklets of our devotion, emptying out all the doctrines of your depravity.”

Moreover, the aforementioned authors of the *Literary History of Gaul* assert that evidence for a booklet published by Alcuin against Felix before he wrote those seven books is also found in a letter Alcuin sent to King Charles.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] The letter prefixed below to the seven books.]

In it he asks him to examine the seven books before they are brought into public light. But here too, at most, some evidence concerning that same exhortatory letter appears. Indeed, we reach this conclusion only by conjecture: from the passages cited, it is clear that the booklet of Felix, against which the seven books were directed, was preceded by another writing—namely, the exhortatory letter—which furnished Alcuin with the occasion.

The words of the letter to King Charles are these:

“Your authority, which must be despised by no one, commanded our devotion to write something against the new inventions of heretical depravity and to reply to the booklet that a certain bishop Felix sent against us to your authority.”

Thus far D. Fogginius.

THE BOOK OF ALBINUS BEGINS, WHICH HE PUBLISHED AGAINST THE HERESY OF FELIX

I. We read in the histories of secular literature that certain men skilled in the medical art, when they heard that some cities had been infected by the plague, out of love for their fellow citizens devised with prudent care some kind of medicine by which they might protect their fellow citizens against the assault of the raging disease, lest the impending danger unexpectedly destroy part of the related population. The same thing must apparently be done by our devotion against the pestilence of heretical depravity, whose doctrine spreads like a cancer, is poured in like a virus, and, like poison taken in through a serpent’s tooth, tears apart and kills those whom it attacks. Our concern for the integrity of souls in the truth of the Catholic faith ought not to be less than the concern for bodily health that the ancients are shown to have possessed in their own science.

II. Behold, a certain part of the world has been infected with the poison of heretical depravity, asserting that Christ Jesus is not the true Son of God the Father, nor his proper Son but an adoptive son. And the Nestorian heresy, revived after a long exile from the East—where it had been condemned by the synodal authority of two hundred Fathers—

[Note: [Col. 0087D] The author is speaking of the Synod of Ephesus, held in the year of salvation 431. Vincent of Lérins likewise testifies in the *Commonitorium*, § 42, that two hundred Fathers assembled there. But in the Acts of the First Council, after the subscriptions of the bishops, [Col. 0088D] the following is added: “After all these men had subscribed to the deposition of Nestorius, other bishops approached the holy synod, and they too subscribed to the condemnation that had been issued. The bishops who deposed Nestorius were therefore more than two hundred; for some took the place of other bishops who had been unable to come to the metropolitan city of Ephesus.” FOGGINIUS.]

—returned after a long exile and secretly fled into the West, so that where the visible sun hides itself from human eyes, there the sun of righteousness might withdraw from the hearts of the unbelieving [perhaps, the faithful]. Nestorius impiously asserts that the most blessed Virgin Mary is not the mother of God but only of a man. Similarly, these men, deceived by the same depravity, deny that she is truly the mother of the Son of God, but make her the mother of some adoptive [Col. 0088B] son. They wish Christ, God-with-us, to be adoptive, through whom we have been made adoptive sons of God the Father.

Abhorring this pestilential disease, I took care to search through the apothecaries’ chambers of the ancient Fathers; or rather, I hastened to traverse the flowering meadows of the venerable teachers of later times, so that I might prepare some kind of medicine for my fellow citizens—that is, for the children of holy Church—by which, with the help of divine grace, they might protect themselves against the contagion of this pestilence. I gathered ingredients, as it were, from the paternal treasuries of spices and flowers, attaching the names of their individual authors, so that the preparation might be more wholesome and secure, since it would be drawn from the treasures of the wisdom and holiness of the most distinguished men.

First of all, let us set forth what the evangelical light, brighter than every sun, reveals for the illumination of the true faith. No one with sound eyes dares resist the brightness of this light; but, just as a blind man wanders in the sunlight, and although the sun is present to him, the sun nevertheless proves to be absent from him, so the one who does not assent to evangelical truth wanders from the way until he falls into the final pit of perdition. You, however, children of the holy Church of God, repay this devotion of mine on your behalf with the support of your holy prayers; and if our present industry benefits you in anything, may your perpetual intercession benefit us.

III. Let us believe the testimony of the Lord God the Father, where, with a magnificent voice, he bears witness over the baptized Son, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III, 17). And lest anyone doubt that this was spoken of another, the Holy Spirit also, in the form of a dove, confirms by his presence that this is the Son of God who is baptized by John in the Jordan. Although the Son’s proper status is clearer than daylight from the authority of the Father’s voice, we must nevertheless listen to the venerable thoughts of the holy Fathers and Catholic teachers, to learn what they understood by this truthful profession of the Father’s testimony.

[Col. 0089A] IV. For Hilary, that remarkable teacher of the Church’s faith, says in Book VI, which he wrote on the Holy Trinity, after other statements agreeing with the Catholic faith:

[Note: [Col. 0089D] St. Hilary, vol. X of Migne’s *Patrologia*, col. 174, nos. 22–24.]

“It is known and taught in many ways that our Lord Jesus Christ is truly God’s only-begotten Son: the Father bears witness concerning him; he himself professes it concerning himself; the apostles preach it; the devout believe it; the demons confess it; the Jews deny it; the nations recognize it in his passion. For what is said concerning the faith of his proper status does not arise merely from a shared designation. And since everything that Christ the Lord either did or taught surpasses everything belonging to those who are called sons, and since among all these things that are pre-eminent in Christ this is taught above all: that he is the Son of God, he does not possess the title of son merely through a general relationship. I do not corrupt the faith of the truth in asserting this with my words. Let the Father speak, as he so often does, of his only-begotten Son, lest Jesus Christ be unknowable through his body under the sacrament of the completion of baptism: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matt. III, 17). I ask: in what respect does the truth perish, and in what respect is the faith of the profession weak? The birth announced by an angel, from the Holy Spirit and of a virgin; the star as guide to the Magi; the honor of his adoration in the cradle; and the power of the one being baptized at the profession of the Baptist—are these not thought sufficient to demonstrate his majesty? The Father speaks from heaven, and this is how he speaks: ‘This is my Son.’ What does the faith of pronouns, not of titles, mean? Titles are added to names; pronouns, however, possess within themselves the force of names. The indication of proper status is present where we hear both ‘this’ and ‘my’ being said. Understand, then, what the truth and reason of these words are. You had read: ‘I have begotten and raised sons’ (Isa. I, 2). But you had not read: ‘my sons’; for he had begotten them for himself through the division of the nations and the people of his inheritance as sons. Therefore, lest through the sharing of adoptive inheritance a title be added to God’s only-begotten Son, the truth of his nature was shown through the indication of proper status.

Let this name of shared sonship indeed be assigned to Christ, if it is found to have been said of anyone: ‘This is my Son.’ But if the statement is proper and unique to him—‘This is my Son’—what accusation against God the Father concerning the professed proper status of the Son are we bringing? Do you not see that in the words ‘this is’ it is signified that others have indeed been given titles as sons by him, but ‘this is my Son’: I have given the name of adoption to many, but this one is my Son? Do not seek another; do not fail to believe that this is he. I point to him, as it were, with the finger and indication of the word when I say: ‘he is mine,’ ‘this is he,’ and ‘he is the Son.’ What room for understanding can remain after this, so that he should not be believed to be what he is?

The significance of the Father’s voice was given so that no one would remain ignorant of what he was who was to be baptized in order to fulfill all righteousness, but so that the man who was seen for the sacrament of our salvation might be recognized, by God’s voice, as the Son of God. And since the life of believers would consist in confessing this faith—for there is no other life of eternity than to know that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God, is the Son of God—the voice from heaven is heard again, repeated by the apostles, so that what it would be death not to believe might be believed more firmly unto life.

For when the Lord had stood upon the mountain in the form of his majesty, with Moses and Elijah standing beside him, and three pillars of the Churches had been taken as witnesses to the vision and the voice, this paternal voice came from heaven: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him’” (Matt. XVII, 5).

V. The same writer, after many truthful statements concerning the natural proper status of the Son of God, concludes as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0089D] St. Hilary, cited above, col. 179, no. 27.]

“What slander is brought forward today—that adoption is merely a name, that God is a liar, that names are empty? The Father has borne witness concerning the Son; by his works the Son makes the Father’s testimony equal to itself. Why should the same truth of the Son not be seen in him, since it is both taught [variant: said] and proved? The name of Son in Christ does not come from God the Father by adoption [variant: from the adoption of goodness]; nor did he earn this name through holiness, as many become sons of God after confessing the faith. For there is no indication of proper status in them; rather, there is only a gracious bestowal of the name, as is fitting for God. One thing is ‘this is,’ ‘he is mine,’ and ‘listen to him’: in this there is truth, nature, and faith.”

VI. Again, in what follows in the same Book VI:

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Ibid., col. 181, no. 30.]

“To all for whom God the Father is Father through faith, he is Father by that faith by which we confess Jesus Christ to be the Son of God. But what faith is there in confessing the Son according to the general name of the saints, so that we say, ‘He is one of the sons’? Are the others not also sons in the weakness of their created nature? In what, then, does faith confessing Jesus Christ as the Son of God surpass them, when, in relation to the sons, sonship in him is not nature but merely a name? This unbelief does not love Christ.”

VII. Again, in what follows in the same book:

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Ibid., col. 183, no. 32.]

“Indeed, according to the order of the response we proposed, this is a most appropriate place for us now to teach, thirdly, that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was believed by the apostles not by designation but by nature, not by adoption but by birth.”

[Col. 0090D] VIII. Again, in what follows:

[Note: [Col. 0090D] Ibid., col. 186, no. 36.]

“It is not evangelical and apostolic faith to believe that he is the Son of God by name rather than by nature [variant: to have believed]. For if this designation is one of adoption, and he is not the Son for the reason that he has come forth from God, I ask from where blessed Simon Bar-Jonah confessed: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (Matt. XVI, 16). Or, since through the sacrament of regeneration everyone has the power to be born as a son of God, if Christ the Son of God is such according to this designation, what, I ask, is meant by the fact that it was not flesh and blood that revealed this to Peter, but the Father who is in heaven?” [Col. 0091A]

IX. Again, from the same book:

[Note: [Col. 0091D] St. Hilary, cited above, col. 190, no. 41.]

“Certainly the evangelist, when writing, ought to have supplied the reason for writing, so that we might see what he was indicating when he said: ‘But these things are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God’ (John XX, 31). In writing the Gospels [variant: of the Gospel], therefore, he put forward no other reason than that all should believe Jesus to be the Christ, the Son of God. If it is sufficient for salvation to believe in Christ, why did he add ‘the Son of God’? But if believing in Christ is finally that faith which means believing not merely in Christ but in Christ the Son of God, then the name of Son in Christ, the only-begotten God, does not arise from the customary practice of adoption.”

[Col. 0091B] X. Let us also see what testimony blessed John the Baptist gave concerning him after the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him in the form of a dove: “And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I, 34). Concerning this testimony blessed Augustine says in Homily VII on the Evangelist John:

[Note: [Col. 0091D] St. Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, Tractate VII, no. 4, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 1439.]

“John bore witness because he saw. What testimony did he bear? That he is the Son of God. Therefore it was necessary that he should baptize who is the only Son of God, not an adopted son. Adopted sons are ministers of the only Son; the only Son has authority, the adopted have ministry.”

XI. Again, in the same homily (no. 13):

“Messiah in Hebrew, Christ in Greek, Anointed in Latin. For he is called [Christ] from anointing, and *chrisma* means anointing. Thus in Greek, Christ means Anointed. He is singularly anointed, especially anointed; from him all Christians are anointed, but he is especially so. Hear how he says in the Psalm: ‘Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions’ (Ps. XLIV, 8). All the saints are his companions, but he alone is singularly the Holy of Holies, singularly anointed, singularly Christ.”

[Col. 0091C] XII. Why is it necessary to amplify the profession of Nathanael, who declared in these words: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel” (John I, 49), concerning whom Truth itself gave such a praiseworthy testimony, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (ibid., 47)?

“For this Nathanael,” as Augustine says (no. 20), “uttered the words ‘You are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel’ in the same manner as Peter did much later, when the Lord said to him: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. XVI, 17). There he named the rock and praised the foundation of the Church. In this faith Nathanael now says: ‘You are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel.’”

Again, in the eighth homily of the same work, the aforesaid Father speaks as follows concerning the unity of the Son of God (no. 4):

“Now the Lord, dying securely, gave his blood for her whom, rising again, he would have, whom he had already joined to himself in the Virgin’s womb.

[Col. 0092A] [ [Note: [Col. 0091D] Restored from the printed editions, where it was omitted in the manuscript.] For the bridegroom is the Word and the bride is human flesh, and both are one Son of God and the same Son of Man, where he was made the head of the Church. That Virgin’s womb was Mary’s bridal chamber; from there he came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber.”

XIII. Therefore, if the Lord Christ is an adoptive Son according to the flesh, as certain men babble in their wicked faith, he is by no means one Son, because a proper Son and an adoptive son can in no way be one Son, since one is recognized as true and the other not true. Why do we attempt, with wicked presumption, to constrain the omnipotence of God by the limits of our own necessity? He is not bound by the law of our mortality; for the Lord does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth (Ps. CXIII, 3). But if he wished to create for himself a proper Son from a virginal womb, who would dare say that he was unable to do so? Who can resist his power (Rom. IX, 19)? Why does anyone dare investigate the secrets of his will or power? Or why ought we not to believe his testimony concerning his Son, whom he so often called his own in the Gospel and not another’s? The Son himself also frequently called him Father.

Let us see what he answered the blind man who asked who the Son of God was, so that he might believe in him. He replied: “You have seen him, and he who speaks with you is he” (John IX, 37). For that blind man had not yet understood spiritually who the Son of God was; nevertheless, he heard from him: “You have seen him.” Whom, if not the Son of God? “And he who speaks with you is he.” Who, if not the Son of God? He displayed the unity of the person of humanity and divinity, so that it might be believed that that man who had been seen was truly the Son of God.

Strengthened by these testimonies of the truth, O man, do not judge your judge, but adore your God reigning in heaven, whom the Magus adored while he was crying [manuscript: whimpering] in the cradle. Honor him seated upon the throne of majesty, whom his mother, after his birth, placed in the manger of hospitality; and do not injure your Creator, as blessed Augustine says in a homily on the Nativity of the Lord:

[Note: [Col. 0092D] We did not find this text in the sermons on the Nativity of the Lord attributed to St. Augustine.]

“Why is it now thought an injury, when God mercifully and wondrously received in himself what he himself had made, and wished truly to be seen in the man in whom he had previously wished to be seen figuratively, and granted that he himself should be the reality who had earlier accepted the likeness?”

Let us also enter the aromatic chambers of other holy Fathers [Col. 0092D] and draw from them something for the salvation of readers and the completion of our work.

### XIV

Let us see what blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, whose teachings against Nestorius became especially prominent at the Sixth Council, thought about this question. For in a Letter which he wrote jointly to the ecclesiastical orders, he says, among other things [Note: St. Cyril of Alexandria, Letter 1, volume V of the Paris edition of his Works, 1638, part II, p. 12]:

> “For when,” he says, “he brings the Firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him’ (Heb. 1:6). But although we have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, are enriched with the grace of adoption, and are even called gods [that is, “gods”], let us not fail to recognize the measure of our nature: for we are on earth and dwell among servants. But he is not what we are; rather, by nature and truly he is Son and Lord of all.”

### XV

The same author, in the same Letter, shortly afterward:

> “Accordingly, Emmanuel is unquestionably from two things, divinity and humanity. Nevertheless, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and one true Son, God and man together; not a man made God by an equality with those who are so by grace, but rather the true God appearing in human form for our sake. The divine-speaking Paul also gives us faith in this, saying: ‘When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, that we might receive adoption as sons of God’” (Gal. 4:4–5).

### XVI

And not long afterward in the same Letter:

> “How, then, was Christ named the proper Son of God, who was also handed over by God and the Father for the salvation and life of all? For he was handed over because of our sins, and he himself bore the iniquities of many in his body upon the wood, according to the prophet’s utterance. It is therefore evident that the thing assumed by the union necessarily declared him to be the proper Son of God, who is from the holy Virgin. For the body is not, according to our understanding, that of some other person, but rather the proper body of the Word who exists from the Father, born from her.”

### XVII

It must also be considered what blessed Athanasius said in his Letter to Epictetus concerning the firmness of the catholic faith [Note: St. Athanasius, volume I of the Paris edition of his Works, part II, pp. 902, 903, 906]:

> “How, then,” he says, “do those who are called Christians dare even to doubt whether [for *an*, ‘whether’], he who proceeded from Mary is God, the Son in substance and nature of God, but according to the flesh from the seed of David and, according to the flesh, from holy Mary? What do you think? Have they become so reckless as to say that Christ, who suffered in the flesh and was crucified, is not the Lord and Savior, God, and the Son of the Father? Or how can those wish to be called Christians who say that the Word came into a holy man, as into one of the prophets, and not that he became man by taking a body from Mary, but that Christ is one person and the Word of God another, the Word who existed as the Son of the Father before Mary and before the ages? Or how can they be Christians who say that the Son is one person and the Word of God another? These things did not happen by adoption—far be it!—as certain people have thought. Rather, as the truth is, when the Savior became man, the salvation of the whole human race was accomplished. For if the Word was present in the body by adoption, according to their view (and what is called adoption is an illusion), then the salvation and resurrection of human beings would also be found to be merely supposed and imaginary, as the most impious Manichaean teaching maintains. But our salvation is not an illusion; nor was salvation accomplished merely of the body, but truly of the whole human being, soul and body. What came from Mary according to the divine Scriptures was human by nature, and was the true [body] of the Savior.”

### XVIII

Likewise Julius, most holy bishop of Rome, says this in his Letter to Prosdocimus [Note: See this authority in the Acts of the First Council of Ephesus, Coleti’s edition, vol. III, col. 1055]:

> “For, for the fullness of faith, the Son of God is preached as incarnate from the virgin Mary and as having dwelt among human beings; he does not operate in a man. For this is found in the prophets and in the apostles: [perfect God in the flesh, and perfect man [Note: These words are restored from the printed editions.]] in the Spirit—not two sons, one properly the Son who assumed a man, and another a mortal man assumed by God, but one Only-Begotten in heaven, the Only-Begotten God on earth.”

### XIX

Likewise, the confirmation of the sacred faith sent by Felix, most blessed [Note: The manuscript incorrectly reads *Felicissimi*, through the carelessness of the copyist, instead of *Felicis sanctissimi*. This authority belongs to Felix I, pope, in the place of the Council of Ephesus cited immediately below.], bishop of Rome and martyr, to Maximus, bishop, and the clergy of Alexandria:

> “Concerning the Incarnation of the Word and the faith, we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, because he himself is the everlasting Son and Word of God, and not a man assumed by God so that there might be another besides him. For the Son of God did not assume a man so that there might be another besides himself; rather, while existing as perfect God, he became at the same time perfect man, incarnate from the Virgin.”

### XX

Likewise blessed Gregory of Nazianzus:

> “Let people neither deceive nor be deceived by thoughtlessly accepting the Lord’s man, as they themselves say; rather, let them accept our Lord and God. For we do not divide the man from the divinity, but confess one and the same person: formerly not a man, but God and the Son alone, existing before the ages and not mingled with the body or with anything belonging to the body; but at the end, a man assumed for our salvation, passible in the flesh and impassible in divinity, circumscribed in body and uncircumscribed in divinity, the same earthly and heavenly, visible and intelligible, comprehensible and incomprehensible, so that in the whole and same man who is also God, the whole human being who had fallen under sin might be restored.

> “If anyone does not regard Mary as the Mother of God, he is separated from the divinity. If anyone says that he passed through the Virgin as through a channel, and was not formed within her, in a manner at once divine and human—the divine because without a man, the human because according to the law of childbirth—let him be anathema. If anyone says that a man was formed and that God subsequently entered him, let him be condemned; for this is not God’s birth, but an evasion of birth. If anyone introduces two sons, one from God the Father and another, newly made, from Mary, he cuts himself off from the adoption promised to those who rightly believe. For there are two natures, God and man, just as there are soul and body; but there are not two Sons, nor two Gods.

> “Nor are there here two men, although Paul has called the inner man and the outer man, and, if one must speak more briefly, one thing and another, from which the Savior is composed—for the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless the same as what is subject to time—but they are not one person and another, far be it! Both belong to the supreme union in a mutual blending: God made human, and man made divine.”

### XXI

Likewise Atticus, bishop of Constantinople [Note: In the cited passage of the Council of Ephesus, where this text is quoted as belonging to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium]:

> “For unless he had been born bodily, you would not have been reborn spiritually. Unless he had endured the form of a servant, you would not have gained the dignity of adoption. For this reason the heavenly one came to earth, so that you, an earthly one, might be preserved in heaven. For this reason Christ emptied himself, so that we all might receive from his fullness. His death became your immortality.”

### XXII

Likewise Theodotus, bishop of Cyprus, in a sermon on the Lord’s Nativity, among other things also said the following [Note: The homily of Theodotus, bishop of Ancyra, was read at the Synod of Ephesus and is found in Coleti’s *Councils*, vol. III, col. 1531, near the end]:

> “What, then? God, while remaining God, came to human beings, not moving from one place to another, but showing the invisible nature as visible; he was seen as a man and appeared as related to human beings, just as the evangelist also proclaims, saying that the Word became flesh. You ask how it is possible for God the Word to become man, and demand from us an account of God’s miracle. If what is incomprehensible in speech were comprehensible to us, it would not be a miracle but a matter of nature. But if what has happened is a miracle and a sign, yield the explanation to the Lord who performs miracles. I want you to know that it has happened, and from what has happened to gain the fruit of faith. Yield to the one who is at work.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Creator of miracles accomplished this, drawing nature toward his own will, and nature obeyed the command. Do not, then, fall into the weakness of human nature. Do not say, ‘How did the nature of man begin God? How did God become man? How did God the Word become visible flesh?’ Rather, because it has happened, believe; but yield the manner and explanation to the Creator.”

### XXIII

Let us also hear what blessed Gregory, pope and teacher of the apostolic see, wondrous in his teaching, says in the first book of his most excellent work, the *Moralia* [Note: St. Gregory, *Moralia*, book I, chapter 18, on Job 1:3]:

> “‘And that man was great among all the Orientals’ (Job 1:3). That our Redeemer is called the Orient, the Prophet confirms when he says: ‘Behold, the man whose name is Orient’ (Zech. 6:12). Therefore all who stand in the faith of this Orient are rightly called Orientals. But because all other human beings are merely human, while he is the Orient, God and man, it is rightly said: ‘He was great among all the Orientals.’ It is as though it were plainly said: He surpasses all who are born to God in faith, because adoption does not exalt him, as it does the others, but the nature of divinity; and although in humanity he appeared similar to the others, in divinity he remained uniquely above all.”

### XXIV

Likewise, in the eighteenth book of the same work, blessed Gregory, marveling at the excellence of Christ’s birth and at how greatly he differs from us, says [Note: The same work, book XVIII, chapter 52, on Job 28:19]:

> “‘The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be compared with it’ (Job 28:19). What should we understand Ethiopia to be except the present world, which by the blackness of its color represents the sinful people, the foulness of their merits? Sometimes, however, the name Ethiopia customarily designates the Gentiles in particular, formerly black with the sins of unbelief. When the Lord came, the prophet Habakkuk saw them terrified with fear and said: ‘The tents of the Ethiopians shall tremble; the tents of the land of Midian’ (Hab. 3:7).

> “The prophet David also, seeing that the Lord would come to redeem Judea, but that the Gentiles would believe before Judea followed, as it is written, ‘until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved’ (Rom. 11:25), says: ‘Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God’ (Ps. 67:32); that is, before Judea believes, the Gentiles, black with sins, offer themselves to the almighty Lord to be saved.

> “The topaz, however, is a precious stone; and because in the Greek language *pân* (πᾶν) means ‘all,’ since the topaz shines with every color, it is called, as it were, *topandium*. When the Gentiles, converted to God, believed, many among them were enriched by the gift of the Spirit so that they shone with many virtues, as though with many colors.

> “But so that no one might be exalted because of the virtues received, the holy man now says: ‘The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be compared with it.’ It is as though he plainly said: No saint, however full of virtues, gathered nevertheless from this blackness of the world, can be compared with him of whom it was said: ‘That which shall be born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God’ (Luke 1:35).

> “We become holy, but we are not born holy, because we are constrained by the very condition of corruptible nature, so that with the prophet we say: ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth’ (Ps. 50:7). He alone was truly born holy who, in order to overcome the very condition of nature, was not conceived through the mingling of carnal intercourse.

> “A certain heresiarch wished to compare himself with him in wisdom as though with a topaz of Ethiopia when he said: ‘I do not envy Christ, who was made God; if I wish, I too can become one.’ He regarded our Lord Jesus not as God through the mystery of conception, but through an advancement of grace, asserting by perverse reasoning that he was born a small man but advanced through merit so as to be God. For this reason he thought that both he and any others who become sons of God by grace could be made equal to him. He did not understand or consider that ‘the topaz of Ethiopia shall not be compared with it.’

> “For it is one thing for a man who has been born to receive the grace of adoption; it is another for one uniquely to emerge as God, through the power of divinity, from the very moment of conception. The glory of the Only-Begotten, possessed by nature, cannot be equated with what others receive by grace.

> “The mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is not, as this heretic foolishly imagines, one person in humanity and another in divinity. He was not conceived and born as a mere man, and afterward received, through merit, what would make him God. Rather, when the angel announced and the Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb, immediately within the womb the Word was flesh; and while the essence that he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit remained unchangeable and coeternal, he assumed flesh within the Virgin’s womb. There the impassible one could suffer, the immortal one die, and the eternal one who existed before the ages become temporal at the end of the ages.

> “Through this ineffable mystery, by a holy conception and an inviolate birth, one Son of God was born according to the truth of both natures, so that the same virgin might be both the handmaid of the Lord and his mother. Thus Elizabeth says to her: ‘And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ (Luke 1:43). And the virgin herself, conceiving, says: ‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word’ (Luke 1:38).

> “Although he is one thing from the Father and another from the virgin, he is not one person from the Father and another from the virgin. Rather, he is himself eternal from the Father and himself temporal from his mother; himself the one who made, and himself the one who was made; himself beautiful beyond the sons of men in form according to divinity (Ps. 44:3), and himself the one of whom it was said: ‘We saw him, and there was no appearance in him, nor beauty or comeliness’ according to humanity (Isa. 53:2); himself before the ages from the Father without a mother, and himself at the end of the ages from the mother without a father.”

### XXV

Likewise blessed Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, writing to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, in a Letter which he composed on behalf of the catholic faith, after an appropriate preface adds the following [Note: It was not Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, writing to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, as this passage perhaps carelessly written by the copyist states; rather, the latter wrote these things to the former. This Letter, with the text cited here, is found in Theodoret, book I, chapter 4]:

> “Moreover, his creatures, human beings and angels, received blessings as they strove to advance in virtue and in lawful commandments, so that they might not sin. But our Lord, existing naturally as the Son of the Father, is worshiped by all. They, laying aside the spirit of slavery through good works and advancement, receive the Spirit of sonship and are made righteous through the natural Son; they too become sons by adoption.

> “Paul also made this Son’s own and natural and pre-eminent sonship clear when he says of God: ‘He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us’ (Rom. 8:32)—that is, for us who are not sons by nature. For the sake of distinction from those who are not his own, he called him his own Son. In the Gospel he says: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matt. 3:17).”

### XXVI

Likewise Chromatius, prelate of the holy Roman Church, in the little book which he wrote on the Eight Beatitudes, says this [Note: This passage is found not in the little book on the Eight Beatitudes, but in a fragment of Chromatius on Matt. 3:4, volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Chromatius was bishop of Aquileia, not of Rome, although in the manuscripts containing his writings he is also called, in an uncertain sense, a Roman bishop. Perhaps the copyists were misled because St. Jerome calls him “holy pope” in Letter 81 to Rufinus, volume I, and in book II *Against Rufinus*, volume II. See D. Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. XI, p. 534, and D. Ceillier, *Histoire générale des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. X, p. 82.]:

> “For in the mystery of baptism, the Son is seen in the body [Others add: ‘remaining’], and the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice is heard from heaven, so that the unity of the Trinity may be declared, because neither can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Son known without the Holy Spirit.

> “See [Another reading: ‘Whence’], therefore, what kind of testimony the Father gives concerning the Son when he says: ‘This is my Son.’ His own, certainly—not by the adoption of grace, nor through the religious status of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the particularity of his lineage and the truth of his nature.

> “Many saints are called and are sons of God, but this one, without comparison [Another reading: ‘without compassion’], is the one Only-Begotten, true, and proper Son of God the Father, born from no other than the Father; for the Father is as truly Father as he is truly God; likewise, he is a true son [Other readings: *tam*, ‘as’; *Filius*, ‘Son’] as he is true Lord.

> “The perfect faith of the Trinity has therefore been manifested, since the Father testifies that Christ our Lord and God is his Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Paraclete—is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a sacrament of faith that we do not hesitate to believe in a true Father, a true Son, and a true Holy Spirit, three persons but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance.”

### XXVII

But blessed Augustine confirms the truth of this faith with many testimonies, which appear scattered throughout his little works to readers and students. For the treasures of truth are disclosed not to those sleeping [read: *dormientibus*, ‘to those sleeping’] in unbelief, but to those devoted to wisdom. Hence Wisdom itself said in the Gospel: “Wisdom is justified by her children” (Matt. 11:19).

Accordingly, in the work of Homilies mentioned above, under the fourteenth title, the same Father offered the following testimony [Note: St. Augustine, Tractate XIV on John, no. 11]:

> “Hear also what follows, since he had said concerning the Son: ‘For God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand’ (John 3:34–35). He adds: ‘He has given all things into his hand,’ so that here too you might recognize how distinctly it was said: ‘The Father loves the Son.’

> “Why? Does the Father not love John? And yet he has not given all things into his hand. Does the Father not love Paul? And yet he has not given all things into his hand. ‘The Father loves the Son’—but as a father loves the Son, not as a lord loves a servant; as the only Son, not as one adopted.”

### XXVIII

Likewise, in Sermon XXII [Note: The same author, Tractate XXV, no. 11]:

> “And truly, brothers, I think that since it is right that he humbled himself for us, we should glorify him. For the Son of man did not exist for his own sake, but for ours. Thus he was the Son of man in that manner when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

> “Therefore God the Father sealed him. What does ‘to seal’ mean except to place something proper? To seal means to place something by which he is not confused with the others. To seal means to place a mark upon him. Whatever thing you mark, you mark it so that it may not previously have been confused with other things and remain unrecognized.

> “The Father therefore sealed him. What does ‘he sealed him’ mean? He gave him something proper, so that he would not be compared with the other human beings. Therefore it is said: ‘God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions’ (Ps. 44:8). What, then, does ‘to seal’ mean? It means to hold him as exceptional, above his companions.”

### XXIX

Likewise, in Sermon XXIV of the same work [Note: Tractate XXVII on John, no. 4]:

> “‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven’ (John 3:13). He had not said, ‘The Son of man who was in heaven’ [Edition: ‘He did not say “was,” but “the Son of man who is in heaven”’]. He was speaking on earth and said that he was in heaven.

> “And he did not say in this way: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man’ [Edition: ‘the Son of God’] ‘who is in heaven.’ What does this concern except that we should understand what I also commended to your charity in my earlier sermon: that Christ God and man is one person, not two, lest our faith be not a Trinity but a Quaternity?

> “Christ is therefore one: Word, soul, and flesh, one Christ; Son of God and Son of man, one Christ; Son of God always, Son of man in time, yet one Christ according to the unity of person.

> “He was in heaven when he spoke on earth. Thus the Son of man was in heaven in the same way that the Son of God was on earth: the Son of God on earth through the flesh he assumed; the Son of man in heaven through the unity of person.”

### XXX

See how this venerable Father confronts the recently introduced name of adoption! How would there not be four persons, if [perhaps: ‘namely’] Father, Holy Spirit, proper Son, and adopted son are counted? For, as we have often said, everyone who thinks soundly understands that the proper and the adopted are two things, just as the true and the non-true are two things.

And how impious it is to say that there are two sons, one proper and the other adopted! Against this impiety the profession of the holy faith in the creed composed by blessed Isidore in his *Etymologies* openly contends, saying [Note: We do not find this text in the *Etymologies*. It may be seen in the work *On the Teaching and Faith of Church Doctrine*, chapter 2]:

> “Therefore the Son of God became the Son of man: born according to the truth of nature from God as the Son of God, and according to the truth of nature from man as the Son of man, so that the truth of the Only-Begotten [Edition: ‘begotten’] might possess the name of Son by being born in both births—not through adoption, nor merely by designation [Edition: ‘appearance’]—so that one Son might be true God and true man.”

Therefore there are not two Christs or two Sons, but one Son, God and man, whom for this reason we call the Only-Begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of his nature has bestowed upon him.

### XXXI

Likewise the aforementioned Father Augustine says in Homily XXVI, in the passage where he explains the Lord’s saying, “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18) [Note: Tractate XXIX, no. 8]:

> “What ought you, a human being, to do, when, whenever you do something good, you seek your own glory, but whenever you do something evil, you devise a slander against God? Pay attention to yourself: you are a creature; acknowledge the Creator. You are a servant; do not despise God. You have been adopted, but not through your own merits. Seek the glory of him from whom you have this grace, you adopted human being; his glory was sought by the one who was born from him as the only Son.

> “But the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him” (John 7:18).

### XXXII

The same aforementioned Father also says in Homily XXXIII, in explaining the saying which Truth itself gave in response to the Jews who were slandering him: “If I judge, my judgment is true” (John 8:16) [Note: Tractate XXXV, no. 7]:

> “How, then, is his judgment true, unless because he is the true Son?”

See: he called him the true Son, not an adopted son; and he called him truly so, because the difference between a true Son and an adopted son is as great as that between the true and the non-true. How can anything be found in Christ except truth, when he says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)? And the Apostle says: “Christ is the truth” (1 John 5:6).

### XXXIII

Likewise, in Homily XXXVIII, where he discussed the excellence of Truth itself, he says [Note: Tractate XLI, no. 1]:

> “Truth itself is the Word of God, God with God, the Only-Begotten Son. For our sake this Truth put on flesh, so that he might be born from the virgin Mary and the prophecy might be fulfilled: ‘Truth has sprung from the earth’ (Ps. 84:12).

> “When this Truth was speaking with the Jews, he was hidden in the flesh. He was hidden, not so that he might be denied, but so that the time might be postponed; postponed so that he might suffer in the flesh; suffer in the flesh so that sinful flesh might be redeemed.

> “Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, standing visibly according to the weakness of the flesh and hidden according to the majesty of divinity, said to those who believed in him while he was saying these things: ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples’ (John 8:31); for ‘whoever perseveres to the end will be saved’ (Matt. 10:22); ‘and you will know the truth,’ which now lies hidden from you and speaks to you, ‘and the truth will set you free’ (ibid. 8:32).

> “For nothing else properly liberates except making free, just as nothing else saves except making safe. Nothing else enriches except making rich; so liberating is nothing other than making free.”

Who else liberates us except Christ, who is the Truth, the true Son, and the true Liberator? Concerning him the evangelist John himself says: “Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into his hands” (John 13:3). If he had not granted him to be the true Son, he had not given all things into his hands—that is, into his power—and what so great an evangelist says would be false, which it is most impious to think.

For the Lord Christ himself says: “My judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (John 8:16), as though he were saying: “Therefore my judgment is true because I am the true Son of God, because I speak the truth, because I myself am the Truth.”

### XXXIV

To confirm this interpretation, the same Father speaks in Homily XXXVI concerning what Christ says: “I have many things to say and judge concerning you, but he who sent me is truthful” (John 8:26) [Note: Tractate XXXIX, no. 7]:

> “As though he were saying: ‘Therefore I speak the truth because I am the Truth, the Son of the truthful One; the Father is truthful, the Son is Truth.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “For the Lord himself says most openly: ‘I am the way and the truth and the life.’ Therefore, if the Son is Truth, what is the Father except what Truth says: ‘He who sent me is truthful’? The Son is Truth, the Father is truthful. I ask what is greater, but I find equality.”

The evangelist John himself bears witness to this truth in his Letter, saying: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ, who is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

Likewise, in his Gospel, the same God Christ, raising his eyes to heaven, said to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

### XXXV

“The order of the words, however, is as blessed Augustine says: ‘This is eternal life: that they know you and Jesus Christ, the only true God.’”

This sending is Christ’s Incarnation. In this passage he called Christ the true God, and elsewhere, as we have said, the true Son; and in both passages he declared that eternal life consists in the knowledge of him by faith. If eternal life consists in knowing and believing Jesus Christ as true God and true Son, whether in the glory of majesty or in the assumption of humility, then it follows that whoever does not possess faith in this truth concerning Christ will never have eternal life.

John himself says this: “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard how [another reading: ‘that’] he is coming, and he is now already in the world” (1 John 4:3).

What is it to dissolve Jesus except not to believe that in each nature he is both true God and true Son of God—he who is one God, one Son, and one Christ in the substance of divinity and humanity?

It is not as certain people, through wicked blindness, assert: that in divinity he is the proper Son of God the Father, but in humanity the adopted son of that same God the Father. If this were so, there would altogether be two Sons, because, as we have already said, one person cannot in any way exist in a proper Son and an adopted son, since one of them is the true Son and the other therefore is not the true Son.

Who would fail to recognize that the true and the non-true are different, unless he were suffering from the disease of lethargy and madness?

For blessed Ambrose says in the first book of his *Catholic Faith* [Note: St. Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book I, chapter 17, no. 111]:

> “The adopted and the true are not one; nor would the Son say, ‘We are one,’ if he himself, who was true, were comparing himself with one who was not true.”

### XXXVI

I ask you, profane advocate of error: the rational soul that is in you, which gives life, vitality, and movement to your entire body, and which, as the holy Fathers maintain, is not generated from the origin of the body [The text lacks: “not”], but is created from nothing elsewhere and placed in the body—would it not be an adopted daughter of your father, while the flesh alone is his proper daughter? Or are you, whole and entire, soul and body, one proper son of your father?

If a human being can have a proper and true son from a substance that is not generated from itself but is joined to the body, why do you think God is incapable of having a proper and true Son, born from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary?

Will you impose laws upon him who does everything whatsoever he wishes, in heaven and on earth? In heaven he willed eternally to have from his own substance a Son equal to himself in all things. On earth, from a virgin’s womb, could he not also have a proper Son—lesser in the form of a servant, yet equal in the form of divinity?

What a lawgiver you are, who think that you can bind God by your laws, while the Apostle rebukes you: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” And elsewhere: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34).

You have come late as God’s counselor, as though without you he could not do what he wished. You seem ungrateful to me for his benefits: when you did not exist, he created you in his image, and when you were lost, he restored you to that same image through his own Son with greater dignity.

And do you assert that you are equal in adoption to the one who made you an adopted son? You wish the Liberator and the liberated to be bound by one equal designation of sonship, while Truth itself says: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

But in your heart, with the pen of unbelief, although you had not read it in the Gospel writings, you have written: “If the adopted son sets you free, you will truly be free.” And you secretly leave to your readers the implication of the corrupt Arian faith. For if God and man are one person and one Son, and the man is an adopted son, it is necessary that God also be an adopted son.

Would it not be far more fitting that the subject nature should be glorified into the proper sonship of the dominant nature?

### XXXVII

Erase, I beg you, from your heart this name of adoption in Christ God, so that you may be in the true Son of God and have eternal life in him.

Alas, blind perversity! While it strives to appear wise, it reveals itself as foolish; and while it presumptuously dares to scrutinize the lofty mysteries of divinity, although Scripture says, “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Ecclus. 3:22), it falls headlong into a deep pit of error.

For the same man, the Son of the Virgin, conceived by the Holy Spirit, was conceived as true God from the beginning of his conception, and at the appointed time was born as true God.

Behold: God the Father willed true God to be born, so that there would be one person of God and man, and one Son of God, God and man. How could he not have wished him to be the true Son whom he wished to be true God? Or could he do the one but not the other?

Where now is the omnipotence of God, whose will no one resists? If he could do it but did not wish to do it, why did he begrudge him the truth of sonship, to whom he did not begrudge the truth of divinity?

And what is the meaning of the Father’s voice: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”? And again on the mountain: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

The devil doubts whether the one whom he saw was the Son of God, and therefore in his temptation he always acted so as to discover whether he was the Son of God. But these advocates of adoption, with greater presumption than the devil, publicly deny that he is the true Son of God, yet do not fear to affirm that he shares in our adoption.

The Lord himself, when the high priest adjured him by the name of the living God and asked whether he was the Son of God, answered: “I am” (Mark 14:62).

But these people say: “He is not,” refusing to accept either the testimony of the Father’s voice or the testimony of Christ himself, who says elsewhere: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going” (John 8:14). And again: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (ibid. 18).

Let whoever reads these things understand them as he wishes. Let us return to gathering examples from the holy Fathers.

### XXXVIII

For Saint Augustine, in the forty-sixth Homily of the work so often mentioned, says as follows [Note: Saint Augustine, Tractate XLIX on chapter 11 of John, no. 18]:

> “He groaned in spirit, troubled himself, and said, ‘Where have you laid him?’ (John 11:33). By groaning in spirit and troubling himself, he indicated something mysterious to us. For who could trouble him except himself? Therefore, my brothers, first attend here to his power, and then inquire into the meaning. You are troubled unwillingly; Christ is troubled because he willed it. Jesus hungered—it is true, because he willed it. Jesus slept—it is true, because he willed it. Jesus was sorrowful—it is true, but because he willed it. Jesus died—it is true, because he willed it. It was in his power to be affected in this way or that, or not to be affected.
>
> “He assumed, he says, a true soul and flesh, fitting the nature of the whole man to himself in the unity of his person. For the apostle’s soul too was illumined by the Word; Paul’s soul and Peter’s soul were illumined by the Word; the souls of the other apostles and of the holy prophets were illumined by the Word. But of none of them was it said: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). The soul of Christ and the flesh of Christ are one person with the Word of God; there is one Christ. Therefore, where supreme power is concerned, weakness is troubled according to the inclination of the will: that is, he troubled himself [Manuscript: ‘he will trouble himself’].”

### XXXIX

Let us also consider what Pope Leo of Rome, a man most trustworthy in the Catholic faith and most distinguished in eloquence, explains concerning the union in Christ of the divine and human natures. For in the homily that he wrote on the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ he says [Note: Pope Saint Leo, Sermon 27, chapters 1–2]:

> “It is true what blessed John, filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.’ Likewise, it is true what the same preacher added: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.’
>
> “Therefore, in each nature the same Son of God receives what is ours without losing what is his own; in man he renews man, while remaining immutable in himself. For the divinity that is shared there with the Father [perhaps: “with him”] suffered no diminution of omnipotence, nor did the form of a servant violate the form of God. The supreme and everlasting essence, which inclined itself toward the salvation of the human race, transferred us indeed into its glory, but did not cease to be what it was.
>
