> “Hence, when the only-begotten Son of God confesses himself lesser than the Father, to whom he declares himself equal, he demonstrates in himself the truth of both forms: inequality proves the human nature, equality declares the divine. Thus bodily birth neither took anything from nor added anything to the majesty of the Son of God, because the immutable substance could neither be diminished nor increased.
>
> “For the statement ‘the Word became flesh’ does not mean that the nature of God was changed into flesh, but that flesh was assumed by the Word into the unity of his person. In the name of flesh, the whole man is certainly understood; with him, within the womb of the virgin made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and destined never to lose her virginity, the Son of God was united so inseparably that he who was timelessly begotten from the essence of the Father was himself born in time from the virgin’s womb.”

### XL

Likewise, in another homily [Note: The same author, Sermon 30, chapter 4]:

> “It must certainly be recognized, beloved, and confessed with all our heart, that this generation, by which the Word and flesh—that is, God and man—become one Son of God and one Christ, surpasses every origin of human creation.”

A little later in the same homily:

> “The nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ surpasses all understanding and transcends every example; nor can it be compared with anything, since among all things it is unique.”

### XLI

Let us see what such a great Father and so illustrious a teacher declares: that the nativity of Christ surpasses all understanding. What do these new investigators of God’s mysteries imagine that they understand, when the ancient Fathers and Catholic teachers professed that they did not know them? The prophet Isaiah likewise testifies that the mystery of his birth is ineffable, and he does so in the passage where he spoke of the injuries to his humanity that he was to suffer for our salvation:

> “Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent; and he did not open his mouth. From anguish and judgment he was taken away. Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:7–8).

### XLII

The same Leo confirms this in another homily [Note: The same author, Sermon 29, chapter 1]:

> “The greatness of the divine work,” he says, “far exceeds and greatly rises above the capacity of human speech; hence arises the difficulty of speaking, from the very source where there is reason not to remain silent. For in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, what was spoken through the prophet—‘Who will declare his generation?’—pertains [Manuscript: “pertain”; edition: “pertains”] not only to the divine essence but also to the human nature.
>
> “Unless faith believes that both substances have come together in one person, speech cannot explain it. Therefore the material for praise never fails, because the speaker’s capacity for praise is never sufficient. Let us rejoice, then, that we are unequal to expressing so great a mystery of mercy; and since we cannot set forth the height of our salvation, let us recognize that it is good for us to be overcome.”

A little later, the same Father says in the same homily [Note: Ibid., Sermon 30, chapters 5–7]:

> “Let the monstrous opinions of the heretics and the sacrileges of their insane falsehoods withdraw far away, and let them withdraw into their own darkness [Edition: ‘let them go’]. Let the exulting multitude of heaven praise God; let the shepherds, instructed by angels, teach us that, having recognized the evidences of both natures, we should adore both the Word in Christ the man and Christ the man in the Word.
>
> “For if, as the Apostle says, ‘the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit’ (1 Corinthians 6:17), how much more is the Word made flesh one Christ? In him there is nothing belonging to the one nature [in the dispensation of our salvation] [Note: This clause is omitted in Saint Leo’s edition] that does not belong to both.
>
> “For let us not grow weak [Edition: “therefore”] in the purpose of God’s mercy, which restores us both to innocence and to life; nor, because in our Savior we plainly recognize the twofold signs of nature [Correction: ‘of the two natures’], let us doubt either the truth of the flesh in the glory of God or the majesty of the Godhead in the humility of man.
>
> “The same man is in the form of God who received the form of a servant [Edition omits ‘man’]. The same remains incorporeal and assumes a body. The same is inviolable in his own power and passible in our weakness. The same is undivided from the Father’s throne and crucified by the impious on the wood. The same, victorious over death, ascends above the heights of heaven and does not abandon the universal Church until the consummation of the age.
>
> “Finally, the same one who will come in the same flesh in which he ascended will, just as he endured the judgment of the impious, judge the deeds of all mortals.
>
> “Therefore, not to linger over many testimonies, it is enough to adduce one from the Gospel of Saint John, in which our Lord himself says: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man’ (John 5:25).
>
> “Thus, in a single statement, it is shown that the same one is both the Son of God and the Son of Man. Hence it is clear how we ought to believe Christ the Lord in the unity of his person: although he is the Son of God, through whom we were made, he also became the Son of Man through the assumption of flesh, so that he might die, as the Apostle says, ‘for our offenses,’ and rise again ‘for our justification’ (Romans 4:25).
>
> “This confession, beloved, fears no contradiction and yields to no error. For we recognize the mercy of God promised from the beginning and prepared before the ages, through which alone the bonds of human captivity could be loosed—bonds with which the deceitfully persuaded author had bound the first man and all his posterity, claiming the enslaved race for himself under the sentence of original guilt.
>
> “Since, therefore, what principally assists in justifying human beings is that the only-begotten Son of God deigned also to be the son of man, so that, as God he was ὁμοούσιος [homoousios] with the Father—that is, of one substance—and as true man he existed according to the flesh, consubstantial with his mother, we rejoice in both, because we are saved only through both. We divide nothing: neither the visible from the invisible, nor the corporeal from the incorporeal, nor the passible from the impassible, nor the form of a servant from the form of God. For although one remains from eternity and the other began in time, these nevertheless came together in unity and can have neither separation nor end. The exalter and the exalted, the glorifier and the glorified, cling [Edition: “clung”] so closely to one another that, whether in omnipotence or in humiliation, neither the divine in Christ is without the human, nor the human without the divine.
>
> “Believing this, beloved, we are Christians, true Israelites, and truly adopted into fellowship with the sons of God. For all the saints who preceded the times of our Savior were justified by this faith and through this mystery became the body of Christ.”

### XLIII

Pope Leo likewise says in another homily [Note: Ibid., Sermon 28, chapter 6]:

> “Knowing that the eternal divinity of the Son received no increase with the Father, understand carefully that to the same nature to which it was said in Adam, ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3:19), it is said in Christ, ‘Sit at my right hand’ (Psalm 109:1).
>
> “According to that nature by which Christ is equal to the Father, the only-begotten Son was never lower than the sublimity of his Begetter. His glory with the Father is not temporal, since he is at the very right hand of the Father [Edition: ‘which is the very right hand of the Father’], of which it is sung in Exodus: ‘Your right hand, Lord, has been glorified in power’ (Exodus 15:6); and in Isaiah: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” (Isaiah 53:1).

A little later:

> “The man assumed into the Son of God was received into the unity of Christ’s person from his very bodily beginnings [supplied], so that he was neither conceived without divinity [nor born without divinity, nor nourished without divinity].”

### XLIV

Likewise, in another homily [Note: Ibid., Sermon 25, chapter 3]:

> “Having therefore repudiated and cast far away all the opinions of the impious, for whom the cross of Christ is either foolishness or a stumbling block, let the faith of right-minded people rejoice and understand the one true Son of God not only according to his divinity, by which he was begotten from the Father, but also according to his humanity, by which he was born from a virgin mother. He is the same one in our humility who is in divine majesty, true God and true man.”

### XLV

The same venerable Father says in his homily on the Epiphany [Note: Ibid., Sermon 36, chapter 1]:

> “If we wish to consider attentively how that threefold kind of gift is also brought by all who come to Christ with the step of faith [Edition: ‘offered’], is not the same offering celebrated in the hearts of right believers [Edition: ‘celebrated’]?
>
> “For the one who recognizes Christ as King of the universe brings forth gold from the treasure of his soul. The one who believes that the only-begotten Son of God has united to himself the true nature of man offers myrrh. And the one who confesses that he is in no respect unequal to the Father’s majesty [Edition: ‘to the majesty of the Father’] venerates him with a kind of frankincense.”

### XLVI

Blessed Augustine also, in a homily to the people on the day of the Purification of holy Mary, testified in these words concerning the unity of the person of God and man and the unity of the Churches of Christ [Note: I do not know which homily of Augustine this is, nor is it found among the published works of Saint Augustine. The rest, however, which we have enclosed in quotation marks, is not by Saint Augustine but by Pope Saint Leo, drawn from Epistle 165, chapter 6]:

> “Therefore, out of the love that is in Christ, I write these things, seeking you as brothers and testifying before Christ and the elect angels that the peace of the Churches may be preserved and that the bond of concord and charity may remain indissoluble among the priests of God. For great is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed on in this world, and taken up in glory (1 Timothy 3:16)—while that immutable essence of the Word, which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit and which is timeless and coeternal with them, remained unchanged; yet, through an ineffable mystery, the Word became flesh within the virgin’s womb, so that by one conception and one birth the same virgin was, according to the truth of both natures, both the handmaid of the Lord and a mother.”

A little later in the same homily:

> “Although, therefore, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and man, there is one person of the Word and flesh, which inseparably and indivisibly possesses their common actions, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood, and by the contemplation of sincere faith it must be discerned to what the humility of the flesh is raised and toward what the loftiness of the divinity inclines.”

### XLVII

The aforementioned Leo likewise says in his homily on the Passion [Note: Ibid., Sermon 65, chapter 5]:

> “Therefore, beloved, embracing the pledge of Christian hope [Manuscript: “of a Christian”], let us not be torn away from the structure of the body of Christ, in whom, as the Apostle says, ‘the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him’ (Colossians 2:9–10). For since the substance of God is incorporeal, how does it dwell bodily in Christ, unless the flesh of our race has become the flesh of divinity?”

### XLVIII

What shall I say? Is there anything more worthy of wonder—or pity—than the blindness of unbelief, which on the one hand believes in God’s omnipotence and on the other detracts from it? He was able to make man beget God, yet was unable to make a virgin beget for herself God’s own Son. For what is more difficult: that man should beget God, or that man should beget for God his own Son? Both are impossible for human beings, but both are possible for God.

He who was able to make a virgin the mother of the Son of God was able to make the virgin’s son truly the Son of God. For, as Saint Ambrose says in the book he wrote on the Incarnation of Christ, “nothing is imperfect in Christ.” An adopted son cannot attain the nobility of a proper son.

Are we to say that Christ is imperfect in some respect? And if Christ is an adopted son, then he is imperfect—yet the whole Catholic Church believes him to be perfect God and perfect man. For how is he imperfect in sonship alone, when in one person God and man are one Son, one Christ, and one Savior of all who believe in him?

Let us return again to the examples of the holy teachers and crush the unbelieving head of heretical perversity under the great weight of their testimonies, so that perhaps it may be awakened from the sleep of unbelief and attain, at least to some degree, the light of the Catholic faith through the inner eye of the mind.

### XLIX

Let us hear the testimony of John Chrysostom concerning the majesty of Christ the Son of God. For in his second homily, where he expounded the blessed Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, he says [Note: Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 2 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, from the translation of Mutianus Scholasticus]:

> “‘Having become so much superior to the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name’ (Hebrews 1:4). In the statement ‘having become,’ understand ‘having been assumed,’ as if he had said, ‘he was assumed in a manner superior to the angels.’
>
> “And from what does he establish this? From the name itself. Do you observe that the name ‘son’ ordinarily indicates the distinctiveness of relationship [Edition: ‘knowledge’]? Indeed, unless he were a proper son—and a proper son is nothing other than one begotten from him—how can this also assert the greatness of his honor?
>
> “For if he were a son by grace, he would differ not only from himself [the editions read: “from the Father”], but would also be lower than the angels. How so, you ask? Because righteous human beings too have been called sons. Therefore, unless the name ‘son’ indicates distinctiveness, it cannot demonstrate the difference between creatures and the Creator.
>
> “Notice, then, what he said: ‘To which of the angels did he ever say, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”’ (Hebrews 1:5)? [Some material omitted here, which is present in the printed editions.] It manifests nothing other than that he was begotten from the very essence of the Father.
>
> “For just as ‘to be’ is spoken of in the present tense, so indeed it is more fitting for this to be said of God. ‘You are my Son,’ he says, ‘today I have begotten you.’ The word ‘today’ belongs to the present time; yet this statement can also be understood according to the flesh. For when he has named the flesh, he speaks without any fear of perverse suspicion. Indeed, the flesh shares in what is higher, just as the divinity has deigned to share itself with human beings [Edition: ‘the humble’].”

### L

Blessed Jerome, interpreter of sacred history and the greatest teacher and defender of the Catholic faith, discussed the natural sonship of Christ as God and our adoption in his Tractate on the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Ephesians as follows [Note: Saint Jerome on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, verse 5]:

> “‘It must also be added,’ he says, ‘that although God predestines or foreordains us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, nevertheless we cannot be sons before we receive faith in and understanding of his Son Jesus Christ. He is Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He was never not the Son; we, before we existed, were predestined, and we received the spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.’”

### LI

The same holy author, writing to Euprepia on the harmony of the Evangelists, says among other things concerning this passage [Note: No one has edited Saint Jerome’s Tractate on the Harmony of the Evangelists. Euprepia is unknown, and the tractate cited below is likewise unknown]:

> “We say these things not because we believe that there is one God and another man, making two persons in the one Son of God, as the new heresy falsely accuses us, but because the one and the same is both the Son of God and the son of man. Whatever he says, we refer one part to his divine glory and another to our salvation, for which he did not consider it [OCR uncertain: *copinam*] to be equal to God, but ‘emptied himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross’ (Philippians 2:6–8); and ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14).”

Likewise, from the Tractate of the same holy author on the Nativity of the Lord:

> “Today the true sun has risen upon the world; today light has gone forth into the darkness of the ages. God became man, so that man might become God. The Lord took the form of a servant, so that the servant might be transformed in the Lord. The inhabitant and creator of the heavens dwelt on earth, so that man, the tenant of the earth, might migrate to heaven.”

### LII

Leporius, a Gallican priest, discussed the unity of the person of the Son of God in the little book that he published on the Confession of the True Faith [Note: Sirmond was the first to publish this little book of Leporius. The passage transcribed here is found in volume I of his Works, page 205. It was also cited by Cassian, book I of On the Incarnation, chapter 11; John II, in his letter to Avienus; and Facundus of Hermiane, book I, chapter 4]:

> “Therefore Jesus Christ, God-man and Son of God, is properly born for us from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin. Thus the Word and flesh become one in one another, while each substance remains naturally in its own perfection, so that without prejudice to itself the divine may share in humanity and the human participate in divinity.
>
> “There is not one God and another man, but the same one is God who is also man, and conversely man who is also God: Jesus Christ is both named and truly is one Son of God. Therefore we must always act and believe in such a way that we do not deny Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to be true God—the God whom we confess to have always been with the Father and equal to the Father before the ages—to have become, from the time when he assumed flesh, God-man.”

A little later:

> “But because the Word, God, graciously descended to assume man, and through the assumption of God man ascended into God the Word, the whole Word God became the whole man. For it was not God the Father who became man, nor the Holy Spirit, but the only-begotten Son of the Father.
>
> “Therefore one person of flesh and Word must be acknowledged, so that we may faithfully and without any doubt believe that the one and same Son of God is always inseparable in his twofold substance. He was even called a giant in the days of his flesh, and truly always accomplished everything that belongs to man and truly always possessed everything that belongs to God. For although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God.”

Again, after some intervening material, he added at an appropriate place:

> “We preach Christ, and him crucified—certainly the power of God and the wisdom of God—because what is foolishness in God is wiser than men, and what is weakness in God is stronger than men.
>
> “For what appears so foolish and so weak to unbelieving men as this: when they hear that God, the Son of God, was crucified? But it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. For our faith consists especially in this: that we believe the unique Son of God, not adopted but proper, not imaginary but true, not temporary but eternal, endured everything according to the flesh for us, and did not undergo agony for himself but for us; and that he, in his mercy, came down from the heights to the depths for our sake, who were lying prostrate.”

### LIII

Victor, bishop of Capua, likewise wrote in his explanation of the apostolic statement, “who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3) [Note: No other ancient or modern author remembers Victor of Capua as having written anything similar. It would therefore be worthwhile to investigate this work of Victor more carefully]:

> “Nevertheless, this entire passage is directed against the Manichaeans, where it says that even before the Gospel he was thus near, through God’s prophets and in the holy Scriptures; and that Christ, according to the flesh, was created from David’s stock—that is, from the virgin Mary—in accordance with what Isaiah had foretold.
>
> “Many are sons by grace; here, by nature. His birth according to the flesh is also found to be unlike that of others. By adding ‘according to the flesh,’ he destroyed Photinus and Arius alike. For if he was made according to the flesh, then according to the substance of the Word he was certainly not made. Thus, in all things, he holds primacy according to the spirit of sanctification, having been predestined to rise first of all through the power of incorruptibility and to open the way of resurrection as the Son of God. These are the ones of whom he himself says that they are sons of God, since they are sons of resurrection—not of all who rise, but of those who belong to Christ.”

### LIV

Origen also disclosed his understanding of the distinctiveness of the Son of God in the seventh book of his Tractate on the Epistle to the Romans, saying:

> “He further gives the greatest indication of God’s immense love for us, who loved us so greatly, he says, ‘that he did not spare his own Son but handed him over to suffering for us all’ (Romans 8:32).
>
> “And to bind us with even greater wonder, he added words conscious of a great mystery, saying that ‘he did not spare his own Son.’ For earlier he had said that we too, who have received the spirit of adoption, are sons of God (ibid., verse 15). Therefore, lest anyone suppose that, by this common designation of sons, he had handed over one of those who seemed to have been admitted among the sons, he added ‘his own Son,’ so that he might show that he had handed over the one who alone is begotten from God himself by an ineffable birth. Therefore, for us all he handed him over.”

### LV

Jerome likewise said in his Tractate on Ephesians, book two:

> “This too can therefore be said: because God the Father is Father of our Lord Jesus Christ according to substance, the only-begotten is not Son by adoption but by nature. The other creatures have merited the name of fatherhood by adoption.
>
> “Whatever we say about the Father and the Son, we should know that the same has been said about the Holy Spirit. Our Savior too knows himself to be the Father, saying: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven you’ (Mark 2:5); and, ‘Daughter, your faith has saved you’ (Matthew 9:22); and, ‘My little children, I am with you a little while longer’ (John 13:13). Through the Holy Spirit, all the righteous are adopted as sons.”

### LVI

Ambrose, archbishop of the city of Milan, also says in the book addressed to the Emperor Gratian [Note: Saint Ambrose, On the Faith, book V, chapter 1, nos. 20 and following]:

> “I ask [Edition: “I inquire”], then, [why] they do not understand and infer from what precedes that, since he had mentioned the one true God the Father, we should also understand Jesus Christ to be the one true God? It could not otherwise have been expressed without seeming to say that there were two. For we do not say that there are two Gods, and we confess that the Son is of the same divinity [supplied] as the Father.
>
> “Let us therefore ask in what way they think a distinction of divinity has been made here. Do they deny that Christ is God? They cannot deny it. Or [Edition: “And”] do they deny that he is true God? But if they deny that he is true, let them say whether they judge him to be a false or a titular God. For according to the Scriptures, he is either true God, titular God, or false god: true, as the Father; titular, as the saints; false, as demons and idols.
>
> “Let them therefore say by what confession they designate the Son of God: whether they think that the name of God was falsely seized [or, alternatively, presumptuously assumed], or is true; or whether, as though he were a titular god, they think that he possesses only an inspiration of divinity.
>
> “I do not think they would say that the name was falsely seized, lest they entangle themselves in a more manifest crime of impiety by revealing that they secretly attribute to Christ a false name of God, as to demons and idols. But if they think he was called God because he possessed an inspiration of divinity, like many holy men—for Scripture called those to whom the word of God was addressed ‘gods’—then they do not place him above men, but consider him comparable to men, thinking him to be merely what he himself bestowed upon men.”

The same author adds a little later:

> “When he reads [Edition: “read”] in the second psalm the Father saying to the Son, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’ (Psalm 2:7), he noted the word ‘today,’ referring it to the eternity of the divine generation, whereas what was remembered concerned the assumption of flesh.
>
> “Therefore the Apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, in order to overthrow that violence, says: ‘Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever’ (Hebrews 13:8). ‘Yesterday,’ because of eternity; ‘today,’ because of the assumption of the body. Christ therefore is, and he always is; for whoever is, always is.”

### LVII

Likewise, in a Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord [Note: This sermon of Saint Ambrose is unknown; nor is this text found among the sermons on the Nativity of the Lord falsely attributed to that holy Father]:

> “Let those who ask who it is who was born from Mary hear: ‘She will bear a Son,’ says the angel, ‘and you shall call his name Jesus’ (Luke 1:31). Why Jesus? Let the Apostle answer: ‘At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth’ (Philippians 2:10).
>
> “And you, deceitful investigator, ask what Jesus is. Every tongue now confesses that ‘the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father’ (ibid., verse 11). And you still wickedly scrutinize what he is.
>
> “Hear further what Jesus is: ‘You will bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins.’ He will not save another’s people [Addition: “people”]. From what? From their sins.
>
> “If you do not believe Christians that the one who forgives sins is God, believe, most unbelieving one, at least the Jews, who say: ‘Although you are a man, you make yourself God’; and, ‘No one can forgive sins except God alone’ (John 10:33; Mark 2:7).
>
> “They deny him to be God because, while he forgave sins, they did not believe. You believe that sins are forgiven by him, yet hesitate to confess him as God.
>
> “The Word became flesh so that fleshly man might be advanced into the glory of God, not so that God might be changed into flesh, as the Apostle says: ‘The one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit.’”

Likewise, in another homily [Note: We have likewise been unable to find this homily among the works of Saint Ambrose]:

> “Man is soul and flesh; so Christ is God and man. The same is God who is man, and the same man is God—not by confusion of nature but by unity of person.
>
> “Finally, the one who was eternally coeternal with the Father as Son of God by generation, the same began to be the Son of Man from the virgin. Thus humanity was also added to the divinity of the Son, and yet a quaternity of persons did not arise; the Trinity remains.
>
> “Therefore, let the opinion of certain insufficiently attentive people not steal upon us, whether against the rule of faith or against the oracles of the divine Scriptures. For they say: ‘The one who is the son of man became the Son of God; but the one who is the Son of God did not become the son of man.’
>
> “In saying this, they failed to attend to what is true and did not wish to speak the truth. What did they attend to except that a certain human nature could be changed for the better, whereas the divine nature could not be changed for the worse? This is true. But even so, without the divinity being changed for the worse, the Word nevertheless became flesh.
>
> “For the Gospel does not say, ‘Flesh became the Word,’ but ‘the Word became flesh.’ If, therefore, the Word is God and flesh is man, what else is meant by ‘the Word became flesh’ except that he who was God became man, and that, in addition to being the Son of God, he became the son of man?”

### LVIII

Athanasius likewise says in his Exposition of his Faith [Note: Saint Athanasius, On the Incarnation of the Word of God, volume II of the Works, page 1; this work is there listed among the doubtful writings]:

> “If anyone teaches against the divine Scriptures, saying that one is the Son of God and another is the man who was adopted from the virgin Mary according to grace, as we too are, as though there were two sons—one according to nature, who is from God, and one according to grace, who is from Mary—or teaches that the divinity was changed into and confused with flesh, or that the Lord’s divinity was alienated or passible, or that it is not to be adored in the flesh of his Son, let him be anathema from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church.”

### LIX

Augustine likewise says in the fourth book of On Holy Divinity [Thus the manuscript reads; the correct title is On the Trinity] [Note: Saint Augustine, On the Trinity, book IV, chapter 20, no. 27, at the end]:

> “When the fullness of time came, she was sent—not to fill the angels, nor to be an angel, except insofar as she announced the Father’s plan, which was also her own; nor to be with men or in men, for this had already occurred in the patriarchs and prophets; but so that the Word himself might become flesh, that is, become man.”

The same author also says in his exposition of the Gospel of John, in the seventh homily [Note: Through the carelessness of the copyist, the following text was undoubtedly omitted in the manuscript, with only the final two words, ‘the ministry of adoption’ [Correction: ‘of the adopted,’] remaining. Blessed Alcuin supplied the complete passage above, no. 10]:

> “John bore witness because he saw. What testimony did he bear? That he is the Son of God (John 1:34). Therefore it was necessary that the one who baptized should be the only Son of God, not an adopted son. The adopted sons are ministers of the only Son. The only Son has the authority; the adopted have the ministry.”

### LX

Blessed Augustine, in his homily on the octave of Holy Easter [Note: Saint Augustine, Tractate LI on John, no. 11]:

> “‘If anyone ministers to me, my Father will honor him’ (John 12:26). With what honor, unless that he should be with his Son? For when he said earlier, ‘Where I am, there also will my minister be,’ he explained this when he said, ‘My Father will honor him.’ For what greater honor can an adopted son receive than to be where the only Son is?”

### LXI

Likewise, blessed Athanasius, in his letter to Bishop Potamius, says among other things [Note: I confess that I do not know this letter of Athanasius, which perhaps perished along with many others. There does exist a letter of the same Potamius to Athanasius, which the distinguished D. Lucas d’Achery published from the manuscript of the Abbey of Saint-Evroul in volume III of the new edition of the *Spicilegium*, page 299]:

> “I ask you, then, whoever you are who investigates this mystery: how did God establish all things from nothing? How did one rib of a man produce a complete man? How did he turn the waters of the Egyptians into blood? How did he bring forth liquid streams from the hardest rock? How did the very one whom you regard as a creature become flesh from a virgin?
>
> “How was he able to satisfy five thousand men with five loaves, or enter among the disciples with his body while the doors were shut?
>
> “Or, if you admit that these things exceed the powers of your understanding and concede that they ought rather to be believed than explained, what could be more unjust than for me simply to refuse to believe what I read, while presumptuously wishing to believe what I do not read?”

### LXII

Likewise, in a letter of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus addressed to Cledonius:

> “If anyone says that, on the basis of the perfection of his works, or after baptism, or after rising from the dead, the Redeemer earned the adoption by which he became the Son of God—as the pagans introduce it from the inscription—let him be anathema.”

### LXIII

The holy and venerable Father Capreolus, bishop of the city of Carthage, in his reply to Vitalis and Constantius [Note: [Col. 0113D] Sirmond first published Capreolus’s letter to Vitalis and Constantine; this passage appears in volume I of Sirmond’s Works.], writes:

> “For what he says, ‘I ascend to my Father,’ appears to pertain to the Only-Begotten Son; but what he says, ‘to my God,’ appears to pertain to the one who was made human. Yet in Christ Jesus neither can he be called a created man, nor can the human being who was born be denied to be the Son and the Only-Begotten God. And therefore this utterance is proved to belong neither solely to God nor solely to man, since the one and unique Son himself, who is both God and man, entrusted it to his disciples to be conveyed with an altogether inseparable and indivisible affection.”

### LXIV

Blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0114D] St. Augustine, *On the Presence of God*, or Letter 187 to Dardanus, chapter 13, no. 40.] writes:

> “No saint, however eminent in the excellence of grace, received the name ‘Only-Begotten,’ so that what the Word of God is before the ages might be said, together with the humanity assumed, to be the same person. That assumption, therefore, is unique, and in no way can it be shared with any holy men, however outstanding in wisdom and holiness.”

It is therefore certain that the judgment of the holy Fathers agrees with the heavenly Scriptures. These Scriptures most clearly testify [perhaps plural *contestantur*]—and proclaim to us under divine inspiration—that, according to the will of the giver, a share in the knowledge and wisdom of divinity is infused by grace into all who are adopted; but that Christ—that is, his soul—possesses the full knowledge of the whole divinity.

### 779. LXV

Ambrose likewise [Note: [Col. 0114D] We were unable to find this text in St. Ambrose, nor in Cassian, to whom the following passages belong.] writes:

> “The Father begot his own Son from his own nature, and made him from the nature of the virgin. Whatever he made, however, he made with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Father alone begot his Son, but did not make him alone. In the begotten Son there is the Father’s eternal generation alone; and in that same Son who was made there is the one operation of the entire Trinity.”

The same author, in the same book [Note: [Col. 0114D] These words are found not in St. Ambrose but in Cassian, *On the Incarnation of Christ*, book II, chapter 6.], writes:

> “Therefore the virgin Mary, about to give birth to God [Edition: ‘the Lord’], conceived when the Holy Spirit descended upon her and the power of the Most High cooperated. Hence you understand that the origin of our Lord and Savior is from the same source as his conception; and since he was born with the fullness of all virginity descending into the virgin [Edition: ‘of all divinity’], he could not be the son of man unless he had first been the Son of God. Therefore, when the angel of God, [sent] to announce the birth of the sacred origin, had first spoken with the mystery [Edition: ‘sacrament’] of the conception, he gave the child its name, saying: ‘Therefore also what shall be born from you will be called the Son of God’ (Luke 1:35)—that is, he will be called the Son of him who both begets and is begotten [Edition: ‘by whom he has been begotten’]. Therefore Jesus Christ is the Son of God, because he was conceived from divinity [and begotten from divinity]; but if he is the Son of God, then unquestionably he is God.”

The same author, in book III [Note: [Col. 0114D] Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book III, chapter 1.], writes:

> “ ‘From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever’ (Romans 9:5). He says that Christ was born from them according to the flesh, yet that he is God over all. You do not deny that Christ was born from them according to the flesh; but the same one who was born from them is God. Why do you go around the matter? Why do you evade it? The Apostle says that Christ, born from Israel according to the flesh, is God; you show when he was not. ‘From whom is Christ according to the flesh,’ he says, ‘who is God over all.’ ”

The same author, in the same book [Note: [Col. 0114D] Ibid., chapter 2.], writes:

> “When it is said of our God and Lord Jesus Christ, ‘who is God over all, blessed forever,’ the matter is immediately proved in the word, and the reality of the word is demonstrated in the name, because the name ‘God’ in the Son of God is not a designation of an adoption that has been granted, but the truth and proper character of his nature.”

In a homily of blessed John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0115D] It is unknown whose homily this is. Perhaps it is by St. Augustine, whose statements in *Treatise on John* XIV, no. 10, agree with it.], we read:

> “He gives to many sons according to measure, but the Only Son receives not according to measure, because he is truly man in such a way that he is also truly God.”

### LXVI

Blessed Cassian, in his book *On the Incarnation of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 0115D] Cassian, book II cited above, chapter 1.], writes:

> “Therefore the Word, the Son, descended; the majesty of the Holy Spirit was present; the power of the Father overshadowed—all this so that, in the mystery of the sacred conception, there might be the cooperation of the entire Trinity. ‘Therefore also what shall be born in you’ [Edition: ‘from you’] ‘will be called holy, the Son of God’ (Luke 1). He rightly added ‘therefore,’ clearly to show that these things would follow because those preceding things had occurred: and because God had come upon her in the conception, therefore he would be God [Manuscript: ‘would make God’] in the birth. Thus he gave the uninformed maiden an explanation of so great a matter, saying that the Holy Spirit would come upon her [Edition: ‘will come upon her’] and that the power of the Most High would overshadow her; therefore what would be born holy would be called the Son of God. This is what he means: ‘Do not fail to understand,’ he says, ‘the preparation for so great a matter’ [alternative: ‘this sacrament of so great a mystery’]; ‘therefore the whole majesty will come upon you, because from you the true Son of God will be born.’ What more can be doubted here, what more can be said? He said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born.”

The same author, in the same work [Note: [Col. 0116D] The same author, book III, chapter 12.], writes:

> “What, then, did Peter say? ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (Matthew 16:16). Tell me, I ask you, heretic: who was the one to whom Peter replied in this way? You cannot deny that he was Christ. Therefore I ask: which Christ do you call him—the man or God? Clearly, man; for this is the foundation of your entire heresy, that you deny this Christ to be the true Son of God.… What, then, did Peter answer to these things? ‘You are,’ he says, ‘the Son of the living God.’ This Christ, whom you assert to be merely the son of man, Peter testifies to be the Son of God. Whom should we believe—you or Peter? I suppose you are not so shameless as to dare to put yourself before the first of the apostles. But what is there you would not dare, since you have been able to deny the Son of God? ‘You are therefore,’ he says, ‘the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ Does this contain anything uncertain or obscure? It is a simple and open confession, proclaiming Christ to be the Son of God” [Edition: “proclaims”].

But if, as you customarily do, seeking hiding places, you say that this is said in an appropriative or adoptive sense, what will you say about the testimony of many others, all bearing witness together and even crying out: “Truly you are the Son of God” (Matthew 14:33)? They point to the man whom they saw present. What, moreover, will you answer the centurion, who, seeing the man Christ die on the cross, cried out: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew 27:54)? Yet he knew nothing of the mystery of Christ’s divinity; he saw only that he could die, and nevertheless testified that he was the Son of God.

### LXVII

From a sermon of Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 0116D] St. Augustine, *Treatise on John* LXXII, no. 1.]:

> “What the Lord means, and how we should understand what he says—‘Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do’ (John 14:12)—is not easy to comprehend. And since this is very difficult to understand, he added something still more difficult: ‘and he will do greater works than these.’ What does this mean? We could not find anyone who would do the works Christ did; are we going to find someone who will also do greater works? But in the preceding sermon we had said that it was a greater work when the disciples healed the sick through the passing of their shadow than when the Lord himself healed them by the touch of his garment’s fringe; and because more believed through the apostles than through the Lord himself preaching with his own mouth, these works were to be understood as greater—not because the disciple was greater than the teacher, or the servant greater than the Lord, or the adopted one greater than the Only-Begotten, or man greater than God, but because he himself, who says to them elsewhere, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5), deigned to perform those greater works through them.”

### LXVIII

The same author, in Sermon XXI [Note: [Col. 0116D] St. Augustine, *Treatise on John* LXXV, no. 1.]:

> “After the promise of the Holy Spirit, lest anyone should think that the Lord would give him in such a way that he would be present with them only in his place, and not himself also be with them, he added and said: ‘I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you’ (John 14:18). Orphans are the same as fatherless children; the former is the Greek name for the same thing, the latter the Latin. For in the Psalm, where we read, ‘You will be the helper of the orphan’ (Psalm 10:14), the Greek has *orphanō*. Therefore, although the Son of God adopted us as sons for his Father, and wished us to have as Father by grace the one who is his Father by nature [Manuscript: ‘of the fathers’], nevertheless he himself also shows toward us, in a certain manner, a fatherly affection when he says: ‘I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.’ Hence he also calls us the children of the bridegroom when he says: ‘The hour will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then the children of the bridegroom will fast’ (Matthew 9:15).”

### LXIX

The cause of this heresy appears to lie in the minds of those who err: those who assert that Christ is adoptive think that he assumed and adopted something as one entity. We have answered this error sufficiently in its proper place. They also regard grace and adoption as one and the same, although the Apostle is read to say: “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9). Yet the Apostle did not say, “By adoption he tasted death for everyone,” because in many passages grace [Manuscript: “glory”] and adoption are very different.

In certain passages grace precedes adoption. Thus, when we were by nature children of wrath, the grace of God made us children of God through adoption. Grace went before us so that we might become adoptive children. But Christ was not first made man and afterward made an adoptive Son of God through grace; rather, immediately in the virgin’s womb the true God and God-man was conceived; and from the virgin’s womb the true God and true man was born. Saint Augustine bears this out most clearly in the book he chose to call the *Enchiridion*, saying [Note: [Col. 0117] St. Augustine, *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, chapters 36 and following.]:

> “Here the grace of God is commended in a wholly profound and evident manner. For what did human nature deserve in the man Christ, that it should be singularly assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will, what zeal for a good purpose, what good works preceded him, by which this man might merit becoming one person with God? Was he previously a man, and was this singular benefit then granted to him, when by singular merit he had deserved God? Surely, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this the Only-Begotten. And because of the Word of God, who, having assumed him, became flesh, he was certainly God; so that, just as every human being is one person—namely, rational soul and flesh—so Christ might be one person, Word and man. Whence did human nature receive such glory, without any preceding merits, freely and without doubt, except that here the great and unique grace of God is clearly displayed to those who consider it faithfully and soberly, so that they may understand that human beings are justified from sins by the same grace through which it came about that the man Christ could have no sin?”

### LXX

Augustine did not say that Christ was first conceived or born as a man and then received adoption by grace so that he might be the Son of God. Rather, he said that immediately in the conception itself and in the birth itself the true God and true man was born, the true Son, true God [perhaps ‘of God’]—and this Son was the Only-Begotten.

Why the Only-Begotten, if he is adoptive, as we are? Clearly, because he is the Son of God by a greater proper relation than we are, who are adoptive sons of God through preceding grace.

Then the same Father continues in the same chapter:

> “Thus also the angel greeted his mother when he announced to her the birth that was to come: ‘Hail,’ he said, ‘full of grace.’ And shortly afterward: ‘You have found grace,’ he says, ‘with God’ (Luke 1:28, 30). She is said to be full of grace and to have found grace with God so that she might be the mother of her Lord—indeed, of the Lord of all. But concerning Christ himself, when the Evangelist John had said, ‘And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,’ he added, ‘and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth’ (John 1:14). What he says, ‘The Word became flesh,’ means ‘full of grace.’ What he says, ‘the glory of the Only-Begotten from the Father,’ is full of truth. For the truth itself, the Only-Begotten Son of God, is not Son by grace but by nature. By grace he assumes man in such a unity of person that the same one is also the Son of man. The same Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten Son of God, the one Lord, was born from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary. The Holy Spirit is indeed the gift of God, and yet the gift itself is equal to the giver; therefore the Holy Spirit too is God, not inferior to the Father and the Son. From the fact, therefore, that Christ’s birth according to humanity is from the Holy Spirit, what else is demonstrated than grace itself? For when the virgin asked the angel how what he announced would happen, since she did not know man, the angel replied: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore what will be born from you will be called holy, the Son of God’ (Luke 1:35).”

And shortly afterward, in the same chapter:

> “Accordingly, as we confess, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God from God, but was born as man from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, is of both substances, divine namely and human. He is the Only Son of God the almighty Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds.”

Soon afterward, speaking further about the same grace, he says:

> “And thus, in the assumption of human nature, grace itself would in a certain sense become natural to that man—a grace incapable of admitting any sin. This grace had to be signified through the Holy Spirit because he is properly God in such a way that he is also called the gift of God.”

### LXXI

Therefore, if the Holy Spirit, as this most holy Father declares, is the gift of God, and if our Lord Jesus Christ was born from this gift of the virgin Mary—Christ whom the Apostle did not hesitate to call the grace of God—how can adoption enter the matter, when he who was conceived from God was advancing into God?

Since the Holy Spirit is God, this one person in the holy Trinity is equal and consubstantial in every respect with the Father and the Son. That man did not exist before God, so that he could be adopted as the Son of God; just as we first were children of wrath and, when divine grace preceded us, became children of God through adoption. Rather, this man was immediately conceived as the Son of God in both natures, as the doctor mentioned above testified with the utmost clarity.

Thus it is most certainly understood that not everything which comes through grace is adopted as a son, and that grace and adoption are not identical in every respect. Any man who has two sons can by grace make one of them his heir; yet he cannot make the son who is naturally his own into an adoptive son. Saint David had many natural sons, but through singular grace he made Solomon alone his heir to the kingdom—not an adoptive son, since Solomon was his own son.

Likewise, any man can have one own son, and this son can be his only-begotten; but he can have many adoptive sons. He can make the one who is his only and unique son his heir by a certain natural appointment and grace, but not by adoption, as with the others.

Thus the almighty Father has our Lord Jesus Christ as his one and Only-Begotten Son, his proper heir. To him it was said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8). But us he made co-heirs with his Only-Begotten, as the Apostle says: “Heirs of God, and co-heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

The Apostle also says in another passage: “For the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with us all” (2 Corinthians 13:13). In this passage he most clearly assigns the persons of the holy Trinity: he joins grace to the person of the Son, assigns love to the person of the Father, and attributes communion to the Holy Spirit [Col. 0119A] [Reading perhaps: “the persons are designated”].

If, on account of grace, they think that God the man according to his humanity is adoptive, and if the Apostle assigns grace to the person of the Son, then that man who was born from the virgin, as belonging to the person of the Son, is adoptive. Who would dare to say or believe this? Therefore, on account of the grace of the assumption [variant: “of adoption”] the Son of the virgin cannot be adoptive.

What, then, must be maintained except that he is wholly the proper Son of God the Father in both natures? Just as he is true God, who was born from the virgin, so also he is the true Son of God the Father in both natures, human no less than divine.

### LXXII

Blessed Augustine likewise, in a certain homily, confesses Christ to be wholly the most high God according to true faith, not only according to his divinity but also according to his humanity:

> “The mother Zion will say: ‘A man and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her’ ” (Psalm 86:5).

And indeed, who would dare deny that he is the Most High?

The same author, in his *Exposition on John* [Note: [Col. 0119B] See above, no. 64.], writes:

> “No saint, however eminent in the excellence of grace, received the name ‘Only-Begotten,’ so that what the Word of God himself is before the ages might be said and truly be the same together with the man assumed. That assumption, therefore, is unique, and in no way can it be shared with holy men, however outstanding in wisdom and holiness.”

---

## 783. The Seven Books of Blessed Alcuin Against Felix, Bishop of Urgell

[Note: [Col. 0119D] This is the title of this letter in the Salzburg manuscript, hitherto unpublished. See the preliminary notice above.]

### Letter of Albinus to Felix the Heretic

*(In the year 793.)* He urges Felix to abandon the novelty of his doctrine and follow the teaching of the universal Church and of the holy Fathers.

To the venerable and dearly desired bishop Felix, in the love of Christ, Alcuin, the humble levite, sends greetings.

### I

Concern for a brother’s salvation must not be considered a small matter. As long as the spirit rules these limbs, no one’s conversion should be despaired of, with divine grace going before it. Since these things are so, and no one can justly contradict them, those present must always be admonished by an exchange of words, and those absent exhorted through the devotion of letters, so that in one way the duty of charity may show its devotion, and in the other the humility of common brotherhood may demonstrate its obedience.

To one person holy Scripture cries: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’ ”; to another the authority of the Gospel resounds: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16). “The Spirit blows where it wills.” Thus Saul the persecutor became Paul the preacher.

### II

Long ago, when I heard the very celebrated report of your holiness from a presbyter from your region, I took care to commend myself to your most sacred [supply: intercessions; the manuscript has “cess.”] … [Note: [Col. 0120D] See Letter 4, to Bishop Felix.] I had then eagerly desired to love you merely on the basis of reputation; now, in the love of Christ and the unity of Catholic peace, I dare to love you more ardently, wishing for you the glory of eternal blessedness, which can in no way come to anyone without the peace and concord of the universal Church.

For this reason, venerable Father and beloved brother, I have taken care to send these little letters of supplication to your praiseworthy wisdom with great humility and charity—not dragging along a contentious rope of disputation, but drawing the threefold cord of Christ’s charity, which saved the spies of Jesus son of Nave [manuscript: “Jesus our Lord,” incorrectly] from the destruction of Jericho [the place is Jericho]. I humbly and urgently exhort us both to flee from its destruction and to desire nothing from its anathema.

For whatever teachings are found outside the walls of ecclesiastical faith and apostolic teaching must be handed over to the anathema of Jericho’s destruction. Therefore, dearest brother, I humbly beseech you by the blood of our salvation to take diligent care that no spoils of the ruined city be found among you, lest part of the people of God, because of the wickedness of one man—even if he is from the tribe of Judah—flee from the battles of the Lord and fall before their enemies [F.: “fall,” subjunctive].

Gather yourself and your companions into the camp of the heavenly King. If you have stumbled anywhere with an unsteady foot, restore your step, stand in your proper rank, and fight the battles of the Lord bravely. Behold, Jesus raises his shield before you. Turn back, and do not cease slaughtering your pursuing enemies until you reach the palm of victory.

### III

No one is a heretic except through contention. Do not contend fruitlessly. The teaching of the Gospel is clear throughout the whole world; let us hold it unanimously and preach it faithfully.

What could we little men, at the end of the age, when the charity of many has grown cold, devise better than to follow with the whole intention of our minds the apostolic and evangelical teaching in complete firmness and truth of faith? Let us not invent new names; let us not introduce something unfamiliar; let us not sing vain praise to our own name through the novelty of any doctrine, lest we be found blameworthy where we wished to be praiseworthy.

Turn in hope to the most holy mercy of the Lord your God, and implore him day and night to turn the final days of your life toward the way of truth and the peace of the Catholic faith, lest, if the holiness of the universal Church rejects you here, it refuse to have you there in eternal peace.

Remember the judgment of the Lord God Christ and the privilege of the great authority that he granted to his holy Church when he said: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth—the rest” (Matthew 18:18).

Behold the authority of the holy Church of God; behold the terror awaiting those who withdraw from it. For we know that there is one holy Church of God, concerning which we customarily sing in the Catholic Creed: “One holy catholic and apostolic Church.” Concerning it the Bridegroom himself also sang: “My dove, my perfect one, my undefiled one, is one; she is the chosen one of her mother. The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed” (Song of Songs 6:8).

### IV

Behold, schismatic error tears away a part from her and stains the unity of charity. Therefore the Church has remained either among us or among you. There are two parties, and there is no concord of unity.

With the whole world as witness, we proclaim that Christ is truly the Son of God. John, the disciple beloved of God, after the many testimonies that he customarily offers in his Gospel concerning the birth of the Only-Begotten according to the flesh, added this:

> “Jesus also performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God” [supply: “is”], “and so that, believing, you may have life in his name” (John 20:30–31).

After such thunder, why do you hesitate, inventing for his birth [F.: ‘after his birth’] the new name of adoption, which is found nowhere in the whole series of the Old and New Testaments?

Know, brothers, how little it is for Christ God to have no elect in this world except as few as you, and to have no Church broader than the one confined within the limits of your narrowness.

Where is the power given to Peter, the prince of the apostles: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” and the rest up to “of heaven” (Matthew 16:18)? Has this power been taken away from him and handed over to you, so that at the end of the age and in a corner of the world a new Church, contrary to apostolic traditions, may be built upon you?

Take diligent care, venerable brother, lest this building of yours be erected upon sand and your labor be in another’s house. Arise, son, arise, and return to your Father and to the bosom of holy Mother Church. She is a devoted mother. Gather yourself again, and gather with you into Christ’s sheepfold the sheep whom Christ himself, for the glory of Peter’s threefold confession, entrusted to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to feed.

“Will the one who sleeps not add to rising again?” (Psalm 40:9). Do not be ashamed to turn back; do not despise the souls of all the children whom you have begotten, brother.

The whole authority of the Gospel cries out, all the sayings of the apostles testify, the breadth of the world believes, and the Roman Church proclaims that Christ Jesus is truly and properly the Son of God. Why do you wish to impose upon him the name “adoptive”?

What is an adoptive son except a false son? And if Christ Jesus is a false Son to God the Father, then—and it is impious to say this—he is also a false God, and the whole dispensation of our salvation is false. For if he is an adoptive son in his humanity, then that God-man who was born from the Virgin is adoptive.

What, then, is the meaning of what the Psalmist sings: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84:12)? Who is the one who sits at God’s right hand and will come in glory to judge the living and the dead?

O, by how many examples of the holy Fathers could I have proved this faith: that Christ Jesus is truly the Son of God the Father, and that immediately from the conception in the virgin womb he was truly conceived as God, and was truly born as God.

But my purpose was, compelled by charity and concerned for your salvation and that of your people, to send these little letters of supplication to your holiness.

### V

I have found many things in your writings that are just and true. Take care lest, in this name “adoption” alone [Manuscript: “in this age,” incorrectly], you dissent from the understanding of the holy Fathers. Do not be a lover of your own opinion with the few, but an advocate of truth with the many.

You will have in me, in the love of Christ, a faithful fellow worker for your salvation, insofar as I am able. And if I were speaking with you, I would not disdain to learn with you what is true and consistent with the Catholic faith.

I would not wish you to lose the labor of your religious life, which you have endured for Christ’s name from your earliest years, lest it be said to you, “You suffered so much without cause.” Come, brother, come; Christ calls you. The Church longs for you; all the saints desire you as a fellow citizen.

### VI

Although I had not intended to deal with you by examples but by prayers, I shall nevertheless offer a few from among the many, so that, if you are not bent by the letters of my smallness, you may be led into the way of truth by the Catholic understanding of the holy Fathers.

Blessed Hilary, a remarkable teacher and praiseworthy throughout the Church of God, in book VI of his beautiful work which he published on the profession of the Catholic faith, after many testimonies to the truth, added the following [*On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 23]:

> “Let this name of communion in Christ be assigned so that he may be a son, if we find it said of someone: ‘This is my Son’ (Matthew 3:17). But if the statement ‘This is my Son’ is proper and unique to him, why do we bring an accusation against God the Father concerning the Son’s proper identity? Does it not appear to you that in what is said, ‘This is,’ this meaning is conveyed? Others have indeed been called sons by him, but ‘this one is my Son.’ I have granted the name of adoption to many, but ‘this one is my Son.’ Do not seek another; do not believe that he is not this one. I touch this one as with a fitting pointing finger and with the meaning of the word when I say: ‘He is mine, and he is this one; he is the Son.’ What room for understanding could remain after this, so that he should not be believed to be what he is?” [Hilary: “of understanding”]

The same author in the same book [ibid., no. 36]:

> “What merit does a general confession possess, or what glory of revelation, if he is a son by adoption? Or whence does there arise in blessed Peter a confession concerning this Son, presenting him as different from what is common to the saints?” [Manuscript: “what merit whatsoever”; Hilary: “presenting”]

### VII

Blessed Athanasius likewise, in his Letter to Epictetus, chapter 5, says:

> “How, then, do certain Christians dare to doubt that the one who came forth from Mary is the Son of God, who is from the substance and nature of God, but according to the flesh from the seed of David and according to the flesh from holy Mary? Others have become still more reckless, saying that Christ, who suffered in the flesh and was crucified, is not the Lord and Savior, and the divine Son of the Father. Or how do those who say that the Word came into a holy man, as into one of the prophets, wish to be called Christians, and not that he himself became man, taking a body from Mary?”

The same author, shortly afterward in the same letter, chapter 6, writes:

> “[Note: [Col. 0123D] In the editions the text reads: ‘These things, however, did not happen by fiction, as some have thought—far from it—but when the Savior truly became man, the salvation of the whole man followed from this. For if the Word was only fictitiously in the body, as they assert, and if what is said to be fictitious is a phantom, it follows that, according to the most impious Manichaean doctrine, the salvation and resurrection of human beings are said to take place only in appearance.’ See what the distinguished Madrisius critically and learnedly observes concerning this passage of St. Athanasius, which was also reproduced by St. Paulinus of Aquileia, *Works of St. Paulinus*, p. 164, note (Patrologia, volume XCIX, col. 459).]  
> These things did not happen through adoption—far from it, as they supposed—but, as the truth is, when the Savior became man, the salvation of the whole man was accomplished. For if, according to their view, the Word was in the body by adoption, and if what is called adoption is a phantom, then salvation too is found to be merely apparent.”

### VIII

Blessed Cyril likewise, in a letter addressed to the monks against the Nestorian heresy, says among many other things:

> “For it was said to him, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’ (Psalm 109); and let the multitude of the heavenly spirits also worship him. For when, he says, he introduces the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him’ (Hebrews 3:6). But although we have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, we are enriched by the grace of adoption and are even called gods; nevertheless, let us not fail to recognize the measure of our nature. We are from the earth and dwell among servants; but he is not as we are. He is by nature the true Son and Lord of all.”

### IX

The most blessed Augustine likewise, in his *Exposition of the Psalms*, on Psalm 88:

> “Who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord, or who will be like God among the sons of God? He is one and Only-Begotten; we are many. He is one, and in him we are one. He was born; we were adopted. He was begotten from eternity by nature; we were made in time by grace. He was without any sin; through him we were freed from sin.”

The same author, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, homily 7, no. 4, says:

> “For it was necessary that the one who baptized should be the Only Son of God, not an adoptive son; the adoptive sons, however, are ministers of the Only Son. For the Only Son possesses the power of adoption” [Augustine: “the ministry of adoption”].

The same author, in the same work, homily 14 [*Treatise* XIV, no. 11], says:

> “The Father loves the Son, and has given everything into his hand. The Father loves the Son—but as the Father loves the Son, not as the Lord loves a servant; as the Only-Begotten, not as an adopted son.”

### X

Blessed Gregory likewise says in book XVIII of the *Moralia* (chapter 52, no. 85):

> “For it is one thing for human beings, once born, to receive the grace of adoption; it is another for one person, uniquely, to have proceeded from the very conception as God through the power of divinity. No glory possessed by the Only-Begotten through nature can be equated with another glory received through grace.”

The same author in book I (chapter 18):

> “For even if an adoptive son progresses toward receiving divinity, he certainly did not naturally receive divinity in order to be God.”

The same author in the same book:

> “He surpasses all who are born to God in faith, because adoption did not exalt him, as it does the others; rather, the nature of divinity exalted him.”

The same author says in his homily on Pentecost (Homily 30, no. 9):

> “Consider, dearest brothers, what kind of solemnity today’s feast of the coming of the Holy Spirit is, after the birth of the Only-Begotten Son. For just as that feast is honorable, so also is this one. There God, by creating, assumed man into himself; here human beings received God, who came from above. There God naturally became man; here human beings became gods through adoption.”

Finally, hear what blessed Gregory said in the same book of Homilies when treating the paschal lamb:

> “You shall not eat anything from it raw, nor cooked in water” (Exodus 12:9).

Shortly afterward he added (Homily 22, no. 8):

> “Our Redeemer must not be considered a mere man, nor should anyone reason according to human wisdom about how God could have become incarnate.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, whoever desires to celebrate the feast of paschal joy should neither cook the lamb in water nor eat it raw; that is, he should neither, through undisciplined speculation, attempt to understand how God could have become incarnate, nor believe in him as though he were merely a man” [Note: [Col. 0124D] Edition: “So that he neither seeks, through human wisdom, to penetrate the depth of his incarnation, nor believes in him as though he were merely a man.”]

### XI

Likewise Chromatius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, says in the little book that he wrote on the Eight Beatitudes:

> “For in the mystery of baptism both the Son is seen remaining in the body, and the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, while the voice of the Father is heard from heaven, so that the unity of the Trinity may be declared; for neither can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Son be known without the Holy Spirit. Consider, therefore, what kind of testimony the Father gives concerning the Son when he says: ‘This is my Son.’ Certainly, he is his own Son not through adoption by grace, nor through the creature’s religious devotion, as the heretics wish, but by the distinctiveness of his own lineage and the truth of his nature. For many of the saints are called sons of God, and are so; but this one, without comparison [the text reads “with compassion”; the editor corrects it to “without comparison”], is the one and only Son of God the Father, only-begotten, true, and proper—not born from anywhere other than the Father—for the true Father is as truly Father as he is true God. Just as the true Son is as truly Son as he is true Lord. Thus the perfect faith of the Trinity has been revealed, since the Father testifies that Christ our Lord and God is his Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Paraclete—is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a mystery of faith, so that we might believe in the true Father, the true Son, and also the true Holy Spirit: three persons, but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance.”

[Note: [Column 0124D] See also this passage transcribed above, column 97, no. 26, with the note added there.]

### XII

We think it impious not to believe these and similar venerable statements of the holy Fathers. No sober person thinks against the truth; no Catholic thinks against the teachers of the holy and unique Church; no devout person thinks against the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. Learn the things that pertain to the salvation of your souls, and walk with the full step of Catholic faith along the royal road trodden by the apostles, frequented by the Fathers, and chosen from the breadth of the world.

Exhort your venerable brother, the bishop whom I name with affection [the manuscript reads *nomina*; read *nomino*], Elipandus, to ascend with you and with the innumerable multitude of the saints to the gate of the eternal city. Do not destroy the flock of Christ that you have received to pasture, but save it.

[Note: “In one … word of adoption.” Alcuin later understood this differently, after reading the little book sent against him by Felix. For he writes in Letter 83 to the lord king: “Recently a little book was sent to me by Felix the unhappy. As I skimmed through a few pages of it out of curiosity, I found worse heresies—or rather, blasphemies—than I had previously read in his writings.”]

You disagree with the holy and apostolic Church in only one word of adoption. With the help of divine grace, it is easy for you to change this word and to use evangelical and apostolic words. How beautiful, praiseworthy, and salutary your conversion to the unity of peace and faith would be, and how great a glory you would have with God and his saints!

Would that my lowliness might read and see, amid peace and progress, the letters of your Beatitude, so that I might joyfully understand whether the prayers of my devotion and charity, which I have for you in Christ, have accomplished anything. Humble yourselves under the hand of almighty God, so that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation (1 Pet. 5:6); and do not be lovers of your own wisdom with the few, but be defenders of the truth with the many.

“Turn to me, and I will return to you,” says the Lord (Zech. 1:3). May divine grace in the Paraclete precede you, so that you may understand and proclaim the truth of the faith, and may you deserve, undefiled and crowned, to hear before the tribunal of the supreme Judge: “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. 25:34). The rest follows.

## LETTER

[Note: We received this letter from Baluze, who first brought it to light in *Miscellanea*, vol. IV, pp. 413–415, from MS 3953 of the Colbert Library.]

### OF THE BLESSED ALCUIN TO CHARLEMAGNE

*(In the year 800.)*

He commends seven books against Felix of Urgell to the king’s examination and approval.

### [Column 0126A]

To the most mighty and unconquered triumphant victor, and most merciful ruler of kingdoms, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Alcuin, humble Levite, sends greetings.

The praiseworthy goodness and incomparable graciousness of your Excellence have given my lowliness the confidence to write something concerning ecclesiastical matters or scholastic disciplines. I would in no way do this unless I hoped that, protected by the shield of your good will, my little letters of obedience might be defended from the tongues of the envious; for some people’s cleverness is more concerned with gnawing secretly at the words of others than with bringing their own words into public. Solomon compared their knowledge to a serpent biting in secret (Eccl. 10:11).

Your authority, which no one may despise, has nevertheless commanded my devotion to write something against new inventions of heretical depravity and to answer the little book that a certain bishop Felix sent against us to your authority. In it I find many things written not in a Catholic style, but empty labor expended against the truth of the apostolic faith. I willingly submitted to this labor, encouraged more by the command of your piety than relying on the assistance of my own ability.

Although no one can justly excuse himself from defending the Catholic faith, nevertheless the command of your holy will made my devoted pen especially indebted to this work, which awaits above all the judgment of your most excellent wisdom as to whether it is worthy to be opened to ecclesiastical ears.

For I had this little book with me during the disputation that took place in your venerable presence between Felix and myself.

[Note: “In disputation.” “From this passage we learn,” say the authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 311, “what we read nowhere else: that the seven books against Felix had been completed before this disputation with him. Thus they must have met after he had relapsed into his earlier error and before Alcuin published these books.” We find nowhere that Alcuin disputed with Felix before Charlemagne except at the Council of Aachen, held about the end of 799. Therefore, only after that council had ended did he send the books to Charles for approval; and only in the following year, 800, after they had long remained under review, did he publish them.]

But since it has not yet been read before your wisdom [Note: On this matter he treats again in Letters 100 and 101.], nor approved by you, for whom it was chiefly labored over, I considered it proper not to bring it before public ears. Now let your authority decide what it wishes to be done with it. I ask only that it not be cast aside or brought into public before it has first been read in its entirety and examined by persons close to your authority.

For in many places it seems to proceed through a less orderly disputation, often repeating what has already been said and seeming to repeat propositions already resolved; since it was necessary to answer the questions proposed at every point, lest the adversary boast that his propositions remained unexamined at some point and that I, as though defeated, had nothing to answer.

Accordingly, the disputant mentioned above has taken care to gather numerous examples of the holy Fathers in abundant but unscholarly language. Some of these seem greatly to contradict one another; some are understood to lend no support at all to his position; and some he endeavors to interpret with a perverse meaning, differently from how they were set down by their authors. The multitude of his statements is woven together in these three ways.

In truth, it would have been much better for him to remain forever silent than for the teaching of evil perversity to make his name more widely known and for him to involve himself in unnecessary questions. For what benefit does it bring the Church of God to call Christ an adopted son or a titular God? What Catholic ears, instructed in the faith, willingly tolerate hearing these names applied to our Lord Jesus Christ, almighty God and the true Son of God, who is the third person in the holy Trinity [Note: “Third person”: not in order, but in number, as one of three; for in strict theological order the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, is called third.] and will come as judge of the living and the dead?

We proclaim one substance in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and three persons. But we believe one person and two substances in Christ our God and Lord: the same one wholly almighty God and the true and proper Son of God. Whoever neither believes this faith in his heart nor confesses it with his mouth is in no way to be regarded as Catholic, but as a schismatic.

May your holy will and God-ordained power everywhere defend the Catholic and apostolic faith; and just as you strive vigorously to extend the Christian Empire by arms, so may you strive to defend, teach, and propagate the truth of the apostolic faith, with the help of him in whose power are all the kingdoms of the earth, so that with the reward of manifold labor you may deserve to attain the blessedness of the eternal kingdom.

May almighty God, for the exaltation and defense of his holy Church and for the peace and prosperity of the Christian Empire, deign in eternal mercy to increase, protect, and preserve the power of your royal glory, most desired and most blessed lord.

[Note: We also owe this preface to Baluze, in the work cited, p. 416.]

## PREFACE TO THE SEVEN BOOKS AGAINST FELIX
