### TO CHARLEMAGNE

### [Column 0128A]

I have sent these five loaves and two fish, consecrated together by the number seven and brought forth from the purse of the apostolic faith, to your most holy authority, my lord David, so that, multiplied by the blessing of the God Christ, they may through you be Catholicly distributed to satiety for the hungry people dwelling in desert places.

[Note: He alludes to the five barley loaves and two fish of the Gospel of St. John, chapter 6, with which he compares his seven books against Felix.]

[Note: “I have sent.” Through Candidus, as he says in the letter to his daughter below, at the end of this little work.]

In this little work I have endeavored to prove the truth of the Catholic faith by the most certain testimonies of the holy Fathers: namely, those of the blessed Jerome; Saint Augustine; Gregory, pope of Rome; Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; Pope Leo; Bishop Fulgentius; and Ambrose, bishop of Milan; as well as those of the most valiant soldier against Nestorius, the blessed Cyril; Peter, bishop of Ravenna; the blessed presbyter Bede; Gregory of Nazianzus; and also Isidore of Hispalis and Juvencus, a scholar of that same province.

If anyone therefore wishes to criticize me or to gnaw at my opinions with an evil tooth, once overcome by the testimonies of these holy Fathers, he will necessarily have to submit to the truth; nor should the person who remains within the camp of the Catholic faith with such men be thought to be in error.

I have also included certain examples from Origen and Cassian, although in some passages of their writings they may appear to deviate from the faith. I have included, however, those passages in which they are shown to have spoken in agreement with the teachers named above, following the example of the most blessed teacher Jerome, who was accustomed to insert many testimonies from Origen into his own little works and did not shrink from adopting statements of other teachers, although they are marked as having erred in certain opinions.

For even the blessed Paul, the vessel of election and teacher of the nations, is shown to have brought forth certain testimonies from pagan books, considering it acceptable to take gold from dung, wash it, and bring it into the Lord’s treasuries. Following his example, nearly all the holy teachers inserted many passages from the books of pagan philosophers and poets into their own little works.

*Here ends.*

# BOOK ONE

### [Column 0127]

### I

I previously wrote a letter to Bishop Felix with the pen of charity, not the goad of contention; out of a desire for fraternal salvation, not in the style of biting criticism. I wished to correct him in the love of Christ, since he is known to have departed from Christ and from the unity of Catholic peace over a certain novelty of terminology.

But, as I recognize, he did not receive my little letter with that charitable duty or humble compliance which the person who reads my letter with a pious regard for me would recognize as the reason for my writing. For the aforesaid Felix soon took pains to send us a little book not compressed into the brevity of a letter, but extended in a long series of discourses.

At its beginning I read certain statements from the Catholic understanding of the holy Fathers, well expressed by him concerning the confession of the true faith. But shortly afterward he attempted in many ways to confirm his former error; and he undertook not merely to leave the old errors standing, but also to add certain new ones, worse than those that came before.

For just as the fables relate that the hydra, with one neck, sprouted a hundred heads, so from the error of one serpentine head a multitude of a wicked doctrine’s harvest bristled forth. Nor was it enough for him merely to deny that Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is the proper Son of God; he also refuses to admit that this same one is true God. Rather, he does not fear to call him, under a new and unheard-of name in the holy Church of God, a titular God, dividing Christ into two sons: one whom he calls proper, the other adopted; and into two gods: one true God, the other a titular God.

To confirm this error he collected, with a perverse interpretation, many testimonies that the teachers of the New and Old Testaments brought forth, under the direction of the Holy Spirit, for the recognition of the true faith.

### II

I hoped, following the judgment of the wisest Solomon, to give him an occasion for wisdom through letters of entreaty. Solomon says: “Give an occasion to the wise man, and he will become wiser” (Prov. 9:9). A little later: “Reprove the wise man, and he will become wiser.” But, as I fear, what follows in that same passage may be more applicable to his disposition: “Reprove,” he says, “a fool, and he will hate you.”

This too may justly be said of such a presumptuous man: “It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool confident in his folly” (Prov. 17:12). And again: “Though you should pound a fool in a mortar, as one pounding groats from above with a pestle, his folly will not be taken away from him” (Prov. 27:22).

It is great folly for a man to trust solely in his own opinion and to despise the Catholic understanding of the holy Fathers or of the whole Church. Was this not the cause of the ruin of all heretics: that they preferred to be lovers of their own opinion rather than of the truth?

If he had been willing to consider only this with a wise mind or humble understanding, it ought to have recalled the aforesaid man Felix from his error: that the whole Church of Christ, from the beginning of apostolic preaching, has never possessed or preached the name of adoption in Christ or of titular divinity.

These names are found neither in the Gospels nor in the Epistles of the apostles, indeed nowhere in the prophetic writings of the entire Old Testament. Nor are they found in the books of any of the holy Fathers or ecclesiastical teachers, in the Apostles’ Creed, in the Creed of the Council of Nicaea, in any declaration of a synod, or in any authoritative statement of the Catholic faith.

It is astonishing that such teachers are not afraid to introduce new things, unknown in ancient times, when the distinguished teacher of the nations firmly forbids any Catholic to receive all novelties of language and newly invented sects (1 Tim. 6:20). Indeed, he did not hesitate to pronounce an anathema even upon angels and upon any human being who preached differently from what he had preached (Gal. 1:8).

Yet in his preaching we find that Christ, who was handed over by God the Father to suffering for us (Rom. 8:32), is called the proper Son of God, and nowhere adopted; and that he who was born from the Father is “God blessed above all” (Rom. 9:5), and nowhere a titular God.

Does he not preach otherwise than that great apostle preached—Christ speaking in him—when he who calls Christ God and man, whom the apostle named the proper Son of God, asserts him to be adopted? Or when he affirms that the blessed God, conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the blessed Virgin Mary, is a titular God?

Let whoever preaches this know with certainty that he is subject to the apostolic anathema. Whoever does not fear the censure of this apostolic authority must be judged to be not asleep but utterly dead.

Nevertheless, he who called the four-day dead man from the tomb to life is able to raise him also. For he himself says: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die forever” (John 11:25–26). Who is the one who lives, except the one of whom the Apostle says: “He who lives in faith is the Son of God”?

### III

There are two things in human error that are exceedingly difficult to tolerate: presumption before the truth has been revealed, and, once it has been revealed, the defense of presumed falsehood. From these two muddy streams all the perversity of the heretics has flowed.

If God, as I pray and hope, defends and fortifies me with the shield of his good will and assists me by the grace of his mercy, I will not be sluggish in seeking the firmness of truth with those who seek it, and in defending the holiness of the Catholic faith with those who defend it—against these vices, which are especially hostile to the discovery of truth and to the investigation or consideration of the holy Scriptures.

Nor will I hesitate to put forward my opinion, in which I will prefer to be examined by the upright rather than fear being gnawed by the perverse. For no critic is to be feared by a lover of truth.

Is the critic an enemy or a friend? If an enemy insults, he must be endured; but if a friend is in error, he must be instructed; if he teaches what is right, he must be heard. Most beautiful and modest charity gladly receives the dove’s eye; cautious humility either avoids the dog’s tooth or the most solid truth blunts it.

### IV

But it is time for us to examine the statements of the aforesaid man and to show that the saints understood differently the passages of holy Scripture whose testimony he strives to draw toward his own meaning.

At the beginning of his little book he explained the unity of the holy Church very well. Would that he had preserved in what followed the same harmony that he took such pains to exalt at the beginning with such great praise! But, as I see, he conceals a sword coated with honey, so that he may more easily deceive those who carelessly read through the sequence of his little book.

### [Column 0130D]

He says:

> “We believe and confess the holy Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world through the preaching of the apostles, founded in Christ the Lord like a solid rock. Outside it we believe that no one can be saved, and that no one is saved except the one who remains steadfastly within the boundaries of its faith and in the harmony of charity until the appointed end: namely, one Church, not divided; simple, not torn apart; existing among Catholics, not among heretics; among the faithful joined together by charity, not among schismatics.”

He very elegantly asserts the outstanding unity of the holy Church of God, spread throughout the whole world. But he gives too little consideration to himself and his followers, who in one corner of the earth whisper, with a few followers, certain unheard-of names concerning Christ God—while praising the Church’s breadth.

Therefore, if the holy Church of God is spread throughout the whole world, then it is certainly not among them, because they are not throughout the whole world. But if it is among them, then even in that case it is not throughout the whole world, because they invent names contrary to the whole world concerning the humanity of Christ our God, who is the head of the Church.

As for us, we stand firmly within the boundaries of apostolic teaching and of the holy Roman Church, following the most approved authority of the Fathers and adhering to their most holy teachings. We introduce nothing new and accept nothing except what is found in their Catholic writings.

Who should be judged a heretic: the person who follows the Catholic understanding of the holy Fathers and of the whole Church from its beginning, or the person who, at the end of the world, invents concerning the humanity or divinity of Christ the Lord—he who was born of the Virgin—certain new names unheard of in ancient times?

We have read the Eastern synods gathered by the holy Fathers at different times against various heresiarchs, and nowhere do we find one saying or affirming that Christ is an adopted son or a titular God. We have likewise examined the Western synods and found nothing of this kind in them. Nor have we found these names, which recent presumption has newly brought forth, in any of the synods promulgated in Spain, Gaul, or these regions.

But everywhere, throughout all the synods and little books of the holy teachers, we have always read that one proper Son of God and one true God are preached in two natures; and one Christ, not two Christs; nor two gods, one true and the other titular; nor two sons, one proper and the other adopted. Rather, we have always read of one proper Son of God the Father, who is also the true God. In what follows, with divine assistance, we shall take care to prove this from evangelical and apostolic teachings and from the testimonies of the holy Fathers.

For we do not, as you say, move stones—that is, Catholic understandings—from the stability of God’s Church. Rather, we choose that stone which, cut from the mountain without hands, filled the whole world. Upon this stone we build and place it as the cornerstone at the summit of our structure. Your presumption rejects it, together with the Jews, detracting from its power and refusing to fall upon it so that it might break the hardness of your hearts. Instead, you wait until it falls upon you in judgment and crushes your audacity.

You spoke with the voice of truth: “It is necessary that scandals come,” but you were silent about what follows in that saying: “Yet woe to the person through whom the scandals come” (Matt. 18:7). Let each person beware lest scandals of dissension and schismatic error arise through him.

In our time the holy Church of God was resting in quiet and peace, until you disturbed it and, according to your opinion, made it wane like the moon. But our unanimity, insofar as it has strength and God’s grace assists us, labors so that it may grow and advance toward the perfect day. Concerning this you added further, when you compared it to the splendor of the full moon, saying:

### V

> “The holy Church, whenever peace and tranquility have been granted to it throughout the whole world by the gift of divine grace, in all the cities and places of the faithful, through the unity of faith and the harmony of charity, because there is no one who tempts it, appears in such a way that anyone who does not see it present everywhere is judged exceedingly blind and to be groping with his hands.”

You say, “because there is no one who tempts it.” Consider, then, I beg you, whether you yourselves may perhaps be its tempters, tearing the tunic of Christ, which the soldiers at his Passion did not dare to divide.

And you rightly added: “so that anyone who does not see it present everywhere is judged exceedingly blind and to be groping with his hands.” For it appears absent because of your blindness.

And if it is everywhere, then act through prayers before God and humility before human beings, so that what shines and advances throughout the whole world, although dispersed, may also be among you. Do not become exiles from its light and strangers to the brightness of the fullness of eternal light.

Do not grow proud and think that its kingdom belongs to you few alone. Of it is said: “And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8). And shortly afterward: “All the kings of the earth will adore him; all nations will serve him” (ibid., v. 7).

This was most certainly prophesied concerning the one whose divine power your presumption attempts to diminish. Concerning his divine humanity and human divinity, with his own gift, we shall speak more fully below.

### VI

According to the continuation of your disputation and your discourse, you say:

> “Sometimes, however, the Church is in small numbers, but it is not confined to one corner of the earth, nor to one province, people, or kingdom, but is spread throughout the whole world.”

Are you not yourselves in one corner of the earth and among one people? Why do you not understand, according to your own statement, that the Church of Christ is not among you, since you are in one corner of the earth and among one people?

Or, if it is among you, you must indicate among what other people, nation, or kingdom it exists, and who agrees with you in the names “adoption” or “nuncupation” concerning Christ.

Or, if you cannot find throughout the whole world associates who share your opinion, recognize by your own judgment that you are heretics, and let it please you to be saved with the many rather than perish with the few.

Observe, as the apostle James says, where the origin of your wisdom lies. For he says:

> “If you have bitter zeal and contention in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. Where zeal and contention are, there are instability and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, persuadable, agreeing with what is good” (James 3:14–17).

Do you see that your wisdom is not peaceable, not persuadable, and not in agreement with what is good? Therefore understand fully that it has not been given by God, but invented through a certain cunning of demonic fraud.

You say that we have not spoken the truth in saying that the whole world—that is, the universal Church of Christ—agrees with us, except for you alone. Prove, if you can, that what you say is true. Show us even one nation, one city, or the holy Roman Church, which is the head of the Churches; or Constantinople; or Jerusalem, consecrated by the presence of the Lord himself; or Antioch, in which [Querc.: “into which”] the holy name of Christianity is first recorded as having arisen; or Alexandria; or any Church in all Italy, Germany, Gaul, Aquitaine, or even Britain, that agrees with you in this assertion of yours. Thus prove that you have some associates who share your opinion.

And if you cannot do this, believe that you think contrary to the holy Church of God. Beware of the sword of apostolic authority, and fear the anathema of the holy universal Church, unless you correct your opinion and return to the unity of apostolic teaching.

### VII

You also proposed the example of two litigants: “Which of them would defend himself more fairly—the one who first brought the case, or the one who attempted to defend himself from the other’s persecution?”

You proposed this well, but you did not understand truthfully who has caused this scandal, how [F.: “what has now”] it is being conducted between our party and yours.

Was not the whole Church of Christ, after the heresies of Eutyches and Nestorius had been condemned, resting everywhere in Catholic peace and in the unity of the apostolic faith, with no one disturbing it, for a long time—until this new sect, unheard of in ancient times, suddenly broke out through your insolence?

Accordingly, it seems more just to regard as the heretic the other person (*alium*; F.: *illum*) who dares to introduce new sects than the person who, nourished and instructed by the traditions of the Fathers, stands manfully in the defenses of his city and strives vigorously to defend himself and his fellow citizens. He has the armor of which the bride herself sings in the Song of Songs:

> “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with defenses; a thousand shields hang upon it, the whole armor of the strong” (Song of Songs 4:4).

Who is David, king of Jerusalem, except Christ our Lord, the strong and true king, who rose like a flower from the rod that came forth from the root of Jesse? His city is the holy and universal Church, part of which reigns crowned with him in heaven, while part of it labors for him as a pilgrim on earth, until it too is crowned and reaches its homeland.

The defenses of this city are the holy Scriptures and the examples of the preceding Fathers, by which it has been fortified against every adversity. This is the armor of the strong—that is, of the holy teachers—who by these weapons have emerged victorious against every heretical perversity.

Armed with these weapons, according to the measure of our strength, and with divine grace assisting us, we stand manfully [against] all novelties and unheard-of questions, defending the apostolic traditions and the faith that we have drunk from their breasts.

### VIII

You say that a certain blessed abbot and his disciple, Bishop Hitherius, were the first to oppose this sect of yours. We praise them insofar as they attempted to defend the truth.

But if it is true that, as you said, they confuse Christ’s two natures into one, like wine and water, we in no way agree with this; rather, if it is true, we judge them to be greatly blameworthy in this respect.

For the Catholic faith, which we defend, preach, and love, holds that in Christ there are two proper and perfect natures: the divine, by which he was born consubstantially from God the Father before all ages; and the human, by which, in the fullness of time, this same Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin and became true man. He is the true Son of God, wholly in what is his own, as blessed Pope Leo says, and wholly in what is ours—the same in both, not one in what is his own and another in what is ours.

Because the Word was united with flesh in so ineffable a manner that we may say that the very Word of whom blessed John the evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), was made flesh, just as the same evangelist says, “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” that is, with us, although that Word was not changed into flesh; and that flesh is called God, although it was not changed into the nature of deity. There is one Son, God, and one God, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Because of this unity, the Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven, and the Lord of glory to have been crucified. Thus, without suffering in his divine nature, the Word of God suffered; the Son of Man wondrously descended from heaven; the hands of the one who created heaven and earth were fastened with nails to the cross; and the blood of the one through whom all things were created was poured out for the salvation of all, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The blood of the Son of God redeemed us” (1 John 4:7).

All these things we ought to venerate more by faith than examine by reason, because where reason fails, faith is necessary.

### IX

It is contrary to nature that a staff, dry for many days, blossomed in the tabernacle. It is contrary to nature that a virgin should bear a son without union with a man. But the creator of natures did not make anything impossible for himself, so that he could not bring about from any nature whatever he wished.

Could he or could he not beget for himself his proper Son from the flesh of the Virgin? If he could not, he is not almighty. But if he could and did not wish to do so, you must give the reason why he did not wish it. And if you can explain this, then the will of the Most High God is comprehensible to the human mind, and what the Apostle says—that God is incomprehensible—is false.

Is there not greater dignity in a proper son than in an adopted one? But he willed that we should have adopted sons in the second degree through the one who, in the first degree, was made his proper Son from the Virgin, who conceived through the Holy Spirit.

What could be born from God except true God? For the Spirit is God, and the entire Catholic Church sings, believes, and proclaims, after confessing the Father’s majesty, these words concerning the one and only-begotten Son in the Creed:

> “We believe also in Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended from heaven, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became man. He was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried; and he rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.”

### X

Turn back upon yourselves the eyes of your heart, and understand the sequence of this most solid creed. It always speaks of one only-begotten Son of God, and of two natures in one Son of God; it says that the same one was born from the Father, God from God, and that the same one was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, suffered and was buried, and rose again on the third day.

Why do you divide him into two sons: one born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, whom you assert to be adopted; the other from God the Father, whom you call the true Son? For it is certain that the Lord Jesus Christ, according to the catholic faith and the proclamations of Scripture, has two births: one from the Father, without time; the other from his mother, without sexual union. These two births have their own proper natures: that of God, by which he was born from the Father, and that of man, by which he was begotten from his mother. He is one and the same God, one and the same man, one and the same Son, Jesus Christ.

For a double birth gave one Christ a double nature. He who is God from the Father is that same God-man from his mother. The Apostle calls these natures, which he possesses from both parents, two forms, saying of him: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

You see that, in the one person of Christ, the mystery of both forms and both natures is contained: the same one is subject to suffering and beyond suffering, mortal and immortal—not one and another, but the same one and one person in two natures. Just as one man is mortal and immortal—mortal in flesh, immortal in soul—yet he is one man and not another, so Christ is one in divinity and humanity, not one and another. And according to the Evangelist, if the Word is God and the Word became flesh, then the flesh is God because of the Word, and the Word is man because of the flesh. Jesus Christ is both God and man, the one only-begotten Son of God the Father in one person, as we have often said and shall always say.

The blessed Augustine also discussed these two forms in the first book of his work *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter 7, saying [Col. 0135D]:

> “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. For he did not take the form of a servant in such a way as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father. Thus the form of a servant was taken without the form of God being lost, since, in the form of a servant and in the form of God, the very same one is the Son of the Virgin and of God the Father” [Note: See the complete text at the place cited].

And shortly afterward:

> “Accordingly, in the form of God he made man; in the form of a servant he became man. For if the Father alone, without the Son, had made man, it would not have been written: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Gen. 1:28). Therefore, because the form of God took the form of a servant, both are God and both are man: both are God because of the one who took the servant’s form, and both are man because of the one who was taken” [Col. 0136A].

### XI

We follow neither the Nestorian division, which wished to introduce two persons in Christ because of the two natures, nor the confusion of Eutyches, who wished to introduce one nature in Christ because of the one person. Both deviated from the catholic faith and were equal in impiety, because they did not hold the right faith; yet they differed in their error, because one confuses while the other divides.

But in order to refute these impious and detestable errors with catholic understanding, let us discuss the distinct property of each nature and the mystery of the one person. Christ is one: the same God and the same man. In his names and actions he possesses one thing that properly belongs to his human nature and another that properly belongs to his divine nature, although both together pertain to his one person, to the one identity of the Son, and to the one dignity of the Godhead [Col. 0136B].

Thus, just as Nestorian impiety divides Christ into two persons because of the two natures—which the Truth himself, who is Christ, openly manifests in himself when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), with reference to the substance of divinity, and again, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:20), with reference to the nature of humanity—so your unlearned rashness divides him into two sons, one proper and the other adopted.

But if Christ is the proper Son of God the Father and an adopted son, then he is one and another. Similarly, if in divinity he is true God but in humanity only called God, then he is one and another. Those who think in this way can in no manner avoid the impiety of Nestorian teaching. For what Nestorius divides into two persons because of two natures, you divide into two sons and two gods through the language of adoption and appellation [Col. 0136C].

Understand, then, your error, humble yourselves under the hand of almighty God, and learn the doctrine of truth, lest you become teachers of error. While you seem to avoid the pit of Eutyches and to guard against the mingling [Querc.: *impermixtionem*, “non-mingling”] of the two natures, you fall improperly into the abyss of Nestorius by dividing him—though with different wording, yet with an equivalent confession. For what he made one and another in persons, you make one and another both in two sons and in a diversity of divinity. You cannot in any way unite into one person the one who said to Moses his servant from the bush, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Gen. 28:13), with the one who said, “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1) [Col. 0136D].

Hence the blessed Gregory, in a homily on the prophet Ezekiel (*Homily 8 on Ezekiel*, no. 3), testifies that Christ possesses divinity by nature, not merely by appellation. In discussing the designation “God,” he says:

> “In Sacred Scripture, God is sometimes spoken of by appellation, but at other times essentially. He is called God by appellation, as it was said to Moses: ‘Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh.’ Again, Moses says: ‘If someone does this or that, bring him before the gods,’ that is, before the priests (Exod. 22:8). And as the Psalmist says: ‘God has stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges among the gods’ (Ps. 81:1) [Col. 0137A].
>
> “God is spoken of essentially, however, as he himself says to Moses: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’ (Exod. 3:6). Therefore the apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the name ‘God’ by appellation from God essentially so called, says: ‘Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever’ (Rom. 9:5). God by appellation is among all things, whereas God essentially is over all things. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, he did not merely call him God, but remembered that he is God over all things. For any just person is also called god, but only among all things, since he is God by appellation; Christ, however, is God over all things, because he is God by nature.”

Accordingly, the sons of the patriarch Jacob—Judah, who was begotten for him as a proper son, and Ephraim, whom the patriarch himself adopted as his son—do not possess an equal relationship of sonship [Col. 0137B]. And although a royal line arose from both grandsons, Christ nevertheless preferred to be born from the grandson who was a proper son rather than from the one whom the patriarch had adopted as his son.

### XII

As for what you say [Note: See below, book III, no. 1]—that “Christ has two fathers, almighty God and King David, and that a proper son cannot have two fathers”—who among human beings does not, after his proper father, have another father in the manner in which David was the father of Christ?

The blessed Virgin herself could have not merely one but several fathers, from whose genealogy she arose, from the father who begot her down to David, or even down to Adam [Col. 0137C]. Although, by a special privilege of royal dignity because of Christ, she ought to be called the daughter of David, Joseph himself is likewise called the son of David, to whom the angel said: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matt. 1:20). For the most holy Virgin Mary arose from the seed of David, and from her Christ assumed flesh for himself.

Now, according to your view, David’s fatherhood in Christ is more honorable than the fatherhood of God the Father. And what will you say about Joseph himself, of whom the Evangelist says: “His father and mother were marveling at what was said about him” (Luke 2:33), and about the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2:48)? To her he himself, the Son, replied: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke 2:49) [Col. 0137D]. He thus showed that God was his Father rather than Joseph.

Nevertheless, as Saint Augustine says, Christ is more truly the son of Joseph than he would be if Joseph had adopted him from elsewhere, because he was born from Joseph’s wife. Therefore I should like you to answer whether Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin, is more truly the son of God the Father or the son of Joseph. You certainly do not dare, I think, to place Joseph’s fatherhood above that of God the Father in Christ Jesus, lest you involve yourselves in manifest blasphemy. For everywhere [F.: *ubique*, “everywhere”] in the holy Gospels that same God Christ habitually names almighty God as his Father; anyone who reads them frequently can find this without needing examples. The Father himself also called him his Son, as we read at his holy baptism, where he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17) [Col. 0138A].

Likewise, on the holy mountain, in the hearing of the apostles who were with him, he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5). Therefore the Father’s voice did not create a division between one Son and another, because the one whom he begot as his proper Son from eternity he also wished to have as his proper Son from his mother.

The blessed presbyter Bede also made the following reference to this testimony of the Father’s voice in his exposition of the Song of Songs:

> “‘My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands’ (Song 5:10): white because he is without sin; ruddy because he redeemed us with his own blood; chosen out of thousands because, from the whole human race, the one mediator between God and human beings, through whom the world is reconciled, was taken up by God. He alone among mortals was worthy to hear from God in heaven: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matt. 17:5)” [Col. 0138B].

### XIII

Who is so contentious and so treacherous that he does not believe the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son? The aforementioned teacher says that this testimony came upon the one who was mortal. Where, then, does your contention have any place in denying that he is the proper Son of God, when the supreme Father himself testified by his own testimony that he is his proper and beloved Son?

I do not know by what blindness you have been led astray, as though the one born from the Virgin could not be the proper Son of God. And why does the holy Church of God customarily call the blessed Virgin “Mother of God” unless because the one who was born from her flesh is the proper Son of God, and the one born from the substance of God the Father is the proper Son of the Virgin? Thus in both generations there is proper sonship, not adoption; truth, not mere appellation.

As we read in the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, after the catholic confession of the Holy Trinity, the following is appropriately inserted, in accordance with apostolic traditions, concerning the Son’s proper sonship in both natures [Note: Included among the appendices to the works of Saint Augustine]:

> “The Father did not assume flesh, nor did the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might himself become, as man, the Son of man. Thus the name ‘Son’ would not pass to another who was not a Son by birth. The Son of God therefore became the Son of man: born according to the truth of nature from God as the Son of God, so that according to the truth of nature he might be the Son of man from man. Thus the truth of the begotten one would possess the name ‘Son’ by being born—not by adoption or appellation—in both births, and he would be true God and true man, one Son.  
>
> “Therefore there are not two Christs or two sons, but one Son who is God and man. For this reason we also call him the only-begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of created reality has established: the natures are not confused or mixed, as the Timothians wish, but united in fellowship [Col. 0139A].  
>
> “God therefore assumed man, and man passed into God—not by a changeability of nature, but by God’s gracious condescension. Thus God was not changed into human substance by assuming man, nor man into divine, although he was glorified in God.”

For if Christ must be the adopted son of God the Father because he was not born from his substance according to the flesh, how is the Virgin’s son not likewise the adopted son of the Virgin, since he was born from God and was not formed from that Virgin’s substance? Therefore, if a man born from the Virgin and the son of the Virgin must by adoption be the Son of God, then in the same way it is necessary that God, the Son of God, should by adoption be the son of the Virgin, because the substance of God the Father, from which the Son of God was born essentially, is one substance, while the Virgin’s is another, from which Christ was born bodily [Col. 0139B].

Or, if you do not dare to say this because you bear the Christian name, so that the blessed Virgin is not properly the Mother of God but only by adoption, then you should likewise not dare to affirm that the Virgin’s son is by adoption the Son of God the Father. What, then, remains except that Jesus Christ, the true and perfect Son of both parents in two substances, is wholly the proper Son of God the Father and wholly the proper Son of the Virgin mother, so that he is one Christ, one Son, and one God?

### XIV

Let us hear what the blessed Augustine says in his letter to Hilary and Prosper concerning this wondrous and singular birth of Christ [Note: The letter is unknown]:

> “Let it be answered: the man who was assumed by the coeternal Word into the unity of person so as to be the only-begotten Son of God—from where did human nature merit this, that it should attain such ineffable excellence? Did not that very man, from the moment he began to exist, begin to be the one Son of God through the action and assumption of the Word? Did not that woman, full of grace, conceive the one Son of God? Was not the one Son of God born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—not through the desire of the flesh, but through the singular gift of God?” [Col. 0139C]

What ambiguity, then, is there in the testimony of so great a Father? Behold, he did not hesitate to name and believe the one born from the Virgin to be the only-begotten and unique Son of God. Can one Son of one Father be both only-begotten and adopted? Or is anyone among the saints ever called the only-begotten Son of God, except Christ alone, who was born from the Virgin?

### XV

And if you place little faith in the testimonies of the holy Fathers, believe the Son of God himself when he gives testimony about himself [Col. 0139D]. For he says in the Gospel: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16).

Who, then, was given for the salvation of the world? Certainly the one who alone trod the winepress and whose garments were made red by the shedding of blood. You contend that he is in every respect like us, except for the law of sin, as is shown in the sequence of your little book. Let us set down your own words as you wrote them there:

> “Not in the glory of divinity, in which he is in every respect like the Father and unlike every creature, but only in humanity, in which he was made in every respect like us, except for the law of sin—like us in nature, although no one is like or equal to him in glory. In this respect we believe him to be adopted by the Father, in which according to the flesh he is the son of David; not, however, in the respect in which he exists as Lord” [Col. 0140A].

We say that he is like us in many respects and unlike us in more: like us in nature, as you say, but unlike us in glory. Is he unlike us if he is an adopted son and a God only by appellation? Take care lest you contradict yourselves. The one whom you assert to be in every respect like us in nature, you call that same one unlike us in glory.

We call him unlike us in this respect: he was not born merely a pure human being, as we were, but God-man as well. He is like us in what the Apostle says: “Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death” (Heb. 2:14). But he is unlike us in that he accepted the same death not through miserable necessity but through merciful will, as he himself testifies: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). We die by necessity, not by will, as the Apostle says: “For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4).

He is also unlike us in that his flesh, which he took from the Virgin, is the flesh of the Son of God because of the union with the Word that became flesh.

Concerning the surpassing glory of this man, who was born from the Virgin, and whose glory is incomparable with that of all the saints—in other words, concerning the one who came from the Virgin and is truly the only-begotten Son of God—the aforementioned Father Augustine discoursed wonderfully and sublimely in the book that he wrote to Dardanus, *On the Presence of God*, section 40 [Col. 0140C]:

> “What, then, is the difference? Do we think that the distinction between the head and the other members consists in this: that, although divinity dwells in any member, however distinguished—in some great prophet or apostle, for example—it does not dwell there as in the head, which is Christ, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells? For in our body there is sensation in each of the members, but not as much as in the head, where all five senses are entirely present. There are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; in the other members there is touch alone.
>
> “Or, beyond the fact that the whole fullness of divinity dwells in that body as in a temple, is there another distinction between that head and the excellence of any member? Certainly there is: by a singular assumption of that man, one person was made with the Word. For of none of the saints could it be said, or can it be said, or will it be said: ‘The Word became flesh.’ No saint, however outstanding in grace, received the name ‘only-begotten,’ so that what the Word of God itself was before the ages might be said, together with the assumed man, of that same person.
>
> “That assumption is singular, and it cannot in any way be shared with any holy human beings, however great in wisdom and holiness. In it the evidence of divine grace is sufficiently clear and manifest. Who could be so sacrilegious as to dare to assert that any soul could, through the merit of free will, make another Christ? For in order that it might belong to the person of the only-begotten Word, how could one soul, through free will—a gift common and naturally given to all—have merited this, unless singular grace had bestowed it? That grace it is lawful to proclaim, but impious to presume to judge” [Col. 0140D–0141A].

The same Father also speaks sublimely in the aforementioned letter to Hilary and Prosper about the excellence of that man who was born from the Virgin. There he argues at length against adversaries who claim to be equal to Christ in grace because they share the same nature. He first presents the adversaries’ words in this way:

> “Let a human being answer God, if he dares, and say: ‘Why not I also?’ And if he hears: ‘O man, who are you to answer God?’ let him not even then restrain himself, but increase his insolence and say: ‘How do I hear, “Who are you, O man?” when I am what I hear—that is, a man, as is the one of whom I speak? Why should I not be what he is?’
>
> “‘But he is such a great one by grace.’ Why is grace different where nature is common? Certainly there is no partiality with God. Who—not merely a Christian, but even a sane person—would say such things?
>
> “Let the fountain of grace itself therefore appear to us in our head, from which he pours grace, according to the measure of each, over all his members. By that grace any human being becomes a Christian from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that man became Christ from the beginning. This one is reborn from the same Spirit from whom that one was born” [Col. 0141B].

In another way, as Saint Augustine wishes it to be understood, the fullness of the fountain flows forth, while the measure of the streams runs from the fountain. The blessed Baptist testifies to this: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34–35). “For the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” [Col. 0141C]. The Apostle testifies concerning the measure of the streams: “Grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7).

### XVI

Since shortly before you mentioned David, I should like you to say whom the Truth himself was asking when he questioned the Jews, saying: “Whose son is Christ?” They answered: “David’s” (Matt. 22:42).

He then put this question to them: how was it said, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand”? If he is David’s son, how is he his Lord? (Ibid., vv. 44–45).

To which nature was the command “Sit at my right hand” addressed, divine or human? Clearly to the human nature, as the creed sings: “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.” Hence Mark the Evangelist says at the end of his Gospel: “And the Lord God [Jesus], after he had spoken, was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19) [Col. 0141D].

To the nature to which it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:19), it was also said, “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

> “Christ said this,” as the blessed Jerome explained in his exposition of this psalm [Note: Saint Jerome’s work in the *Breviary on the Psalter*, which Alcuin attributed to this holy Father; learned men of our time, however, reject it among the works spuriously attributed to him], “to the Pharisees, who confessed Christ to be simply David’s son: ‘If he is David’s son, how does he call his own son Lord?’” [Col. 0142A]

And shortly afterward the same author says:

> “See, then, what he says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord.’ Is this one [perhaps: *huic*, ‘to this one’], to whom the command to sit is given, God? God does not sit; the assumed body sits. Therefore the command to sit is given to this one, because it is the man who was assumed [Jerome reads *qui*, ‘who,’ for *quia*, ‘because’].”

Of him the Apostle also says: “He is Lord of all” (Rom. 10:12). And if he is Lord of all, he is certainly also Lord of David, from whose seed he was born according to the flesh. Christ, who is God, asked this question with such subtlety precisely so that it might be understood that the one who is David’s Lord is also his son.

### XVII

And if the testimony of so great a Father seems insufficient to your unbelief—that the one born from David’s seed is Lord—then, Felix, advocate of this novelty, whom I address particularly through the testimony of the angelic voice, hear also the angel of God speaking to the shepherds about the birth of God:

> “Today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:11).

He added the name of God and of Savior so that you would not understand Christ merely as a man, but, recognizing him as Savior, would not doubt that he is God. Since the power to save belongs only to divine authority, you should have no doubt that the power in him is divine, in whom you have learned that the power of salvation exists.

But perhaps even this seems insufficient to your unbelief, because the angel of the Lord called him Savior rather than God or Son of God. Yet you deny God most impiously while confessing him to be Savior, although the blessed teacher of the nations did not hesitate to call him Savior repeatedly, saying to Titus: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared” (Titus 2:11).

Hear also the archangel Gabriel proclaiming to the Virgin Mary:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born in you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35) [Col. 0142C].

You see how, when he was about to announce the birth of God, he first mentioned the works of divinity: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Speaking most beautifully, the angel explained the majesty of the divine work through the excellence of his words.

What need was there for such great preparation for the birth of a mere little child, as you would have it, an adopted one? The Father overshadowed, the Holy Spirit impregnated, and the Son was incarnate, while every heavenly and earthly creature was made by the mere word of the one commanding, as it is written in the psalm: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5).

Why was the command of the one speaking not enough for the generation of one human being, as it was for all other creatures, if he was merely a pure man and not God, or even the true Son of God? All those works of angelic powers and of all creatures were accomplished by God’s command. The birth of the Son of God, however, could not take place except through the coming and operation of the Holy Trinity. For God could not be conceived by a human being unless he gave himself, nor born unless he entered into her.

Therefore the archangel revealed the sacred majesty that was to come upon the Virgin. Since such a great matter could not be accomplished by human agency, he declared that the majesty itself would be present at the conception, just as it was destined to be present at the birth. And because God came upon her at the conception, God would therefore be present at the birth.

And what could be born from God except God? “God is Spirit” (John 4:24), as the Apostle says; and from that Spirit, as we sing in the creed, the Son of God was born from the Virgin Mary.

The archangel also added to the Virgin when she asked:

> “Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35) [Col. 0143A].

This means: “Do not fail to understand this preparation for so great a matter, this sacrament of so great a mystery. The majesty of God will come upon you for this reason: the Son of God will be born from you.”

What further doubt can there be, or what more can be said? He said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. Ask now, if you wish, how he is the Son of God—or how he is not the Son of God, since he was born—or, if he is the Son of God, how he is not God.

### XVIII

But if you do not believe even the testimony of the archangels, believe at least that of God the Father himself, who said, when Christ was transfigured on the holy mountain, as we stated earlier: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3:17) [Col. 0143B].

He commanded the apostles to keep this vision silent until the Son of Man had risen from the dead, lest, while the glory of his majesty was proclaimed, the mystery of the cross be impeded.

For if he had said this concerning the divine nature of the Son of God—“This is my beloved Son”—why was silence commanded, when Christ so often openly revealed himself and proclaimed that he was the Son of God? For example, he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); again: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9); and again: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19). There are many similar passages in which he did not conceal that he was altogether equal to the Father in divine substance and that he was the Father’s Son [Col. 0143C].

But this voice of the Father was made at the baptism over the Son of Man for the purpose that it might be recognized and believed that the man who was formed from the substance of the blessed Virgin is the true Son of God.

### XIX

But perhaps the judgment of my insignificance is insufficient for you to accept that these testimonies of the Father were spoken concerning Christ who was born from the Virgin. Hear also how our fathers, men who were truly catholic, answered your predecessors, who refused to believe Christ to be either the Son of God or true God. Let us set down the very words found in the book of the blessed Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book 3, chapters 15–16 [Col. 0143D]:

> “Or believe the divine testimony in this way, from the heavenly signs that appeared at Christ’s baptism.”

These are the words of the catholic faith:

> “What, then, did the apostle Thomas touch when he approached in order to touch God? Clearly Christ, without any doubt. What did he exclaim? ‘My Lord and my God!’ (John 20:28).
>
> “Now, if you can, separate Christ from God and alter this statement, if you are able. Bring dialectical argument, bring worldly prudence, bring that foolish wisdom through wordy cleverness. Turn yourselves into every shape and draw together whatever you can accomplish either by intelligence or by skill. Say whatever you wish and do whatever you wish: you have no way out of this except by confessing that the one whom the apostle touched is God.
>
> “Indeed, if you could somehow do so, you might wish to alter the proclamation of the Gospel narrative, so that the apostle Thomas would read neither that he had touched the Lord’s body nor that he had called Christ the Lord God [Cassian reads *legeretur*, “it would be read,” for *legeret*, “he would read”]. But what has been written in God’s Gospel cannot be altered: ‘Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of God will not pass away’ (Matt. 24:35) [Col. 0144A].
>
> “For behold, even now that same Thomas, who then bore witness, cries out to you: ‘Jesus, whom I touched, is God; God is the one whose limbs I handled. I did not hold incorporeal things, nor attempt things that cannot be handled [Cass.: handle].’ I did not touch the Spirit with my hand, so that I might be thought to have said only of him, ‘He is God.’ According to my Lord’s statement, the Spirit does not have flesh and bones (Luke 24:39).
>
> “I touched the body of my Lord; I handled flesh and bones; I placed my fingers in the places of the wounds; and concerning Christ my Lord, whom I had handled, I proclaimed: ‘My Lord and my God!’ I do not know how to create a distinction between Christ and God. I do not wish to insert sacrilegious opinions between Jesus and God. I do not know how to tear my Lord away from himself [Col. 0144B].
>
> “Let whoever thinks or speaks differently from me be separate from me. I know Christ as nothing other than God. This I have held with my fellow apostles; this I have handed down to the churches; this I have proclaimed to the nations; this I also cry out to you: Christ is God, Christ is God.
>
> “A sound mind does not perceive anything else; a sound faith does not speak anything else. Divinity cannot be torn away from itself. And since whatever Christ is, he is God, nothing other than God can be found in God.”

## XX

What do you say now, heretic? Are these testimonies sufficient even for the highest infidelity, or must something further be added? And what could be added either after the prophets or after the apostles, unless perhaps, just as the Jews once demanded a sign from heaven for themselves, you too should demand that one be given to you? But when you make this request, the answer given to them then must necessarily be given to you: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. 16:4). Indeed, this sign ought to have sufficed for you, even together with the Jews who crucified him, so that, instructed by this one matter alone, you might believe in our Lord, who is God—him in whom even those who had persecuted him believed.

Yet, since we have mentioned a heavenly sign, I shall show you a sign from heaven, and one such that demons have never contradicted it. Compelled by the very necessity of truth, although they perceived Jesus to be bodily, they nevertheless proclaimed that he was God, as he was. What, then, does the evangelist say about the Lord Jesus Christ?

“He was baptized,” he says, “and immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit descending like a dove and coming upon him; and behold, a voice from the heavens said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3:16–17).

What do you say to this now, heretic? Do you dislike the saying, or the person who spoke it? The meaning of the address certainly needs no interpretation, nor does the dignity of the one addressing him need commendation. It is God the Father who spoke; what was said is clear. Will you be able to utter so shameless or sacrilegious a statement as to say that the only-begotten Son of God is not to be believed even by God the Father?

“This is,” he says, “my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” But perhaps, in your madness, you will try to say that this was spoken of the Word, not of Christ. Tell me, then: who was being baptized, the Word or Christ? Who was baptized in the Jordan, flesh or Spirit? You cannot deny that it was Christ.

That man, therefore, born from a human being and from God, conceived when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and thus the Son of man and of God—that man, whom you cannot deny, was baptized. If he was baptized, then he was also named; for the one who was named was certainly the one who was baptized: “This is,” he says, “my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

Could anything be said more meaningfully or more explicitly? Christ was baptized; Christ came up from the water; when Christ was baptized, the heavens were opened; the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in bodily form; the Father addressed Christ [Cass., “because of Christ the dove descended; the Holy Spirit stood over Christ in bodily form; the Father addressed Christ”].

If you dare deny that this was spoken of Christ, it remains for you to assert that Christ was not baptized, that the Spirit did not descend, and that the Father did not speak. But truth itself presses and constrains you, so that even if you refuse to confess it, you cannot deny it.

For what does the evangelist say? “Now when he had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water.” Who was baptized? Christ, certainly. “And behold,” he says, “the heavens were opened.” To whom, unless to the one who was baptized—to Christ, certainly? “And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.” Who saw? Christ, obviously—or John [Cass., omits “or John”]. Upon whom did it descend? Upon Christ, certainly. “And a voice came from heaven, saying.” Concerning whom? Concerning Christ, obviously; for what follows? “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

So that everything might be shown to have occurred for the sake of the one for whom it was done, the voice followed, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” This is to say: “This is the one for whom all these things happened; this is my Son. For his sake the heavens were opened; for his sake my Spirit came; for his sake my voice was heard. This is my Son.”

When he said, “This is my Son,” whom was he designating? The one whom the dove touched, certainly. Whom, then, did the dove touch? Christ, obviously. Therefore Christ is the Son of God.

I think my promise has been fulfilled. You see, then, heretic, that a sign has indeed been given you from heaven—and not one sign only, but many, and extraordinary ones. You have one in the opening of heaven, another in the descent of the Spirit, and a third in the Father’s voice. All these plainly declare that Christ is God: the opening of the heavens indicates him to be God; the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him proves him to be God; and the Father’s address confirms that he is God.

For neither would heaven have opened except for the honor of its Lord; nor would the Spirit have descended in bodily form except upon the Son of God; nor would the Father have declared the Son except as truly Son—especially since these signs of divine birth not only confirmed the truth of pious faith but also excluded the perversity of impious opinion.

With the ineffable majesty of the divine utterance, after the Father had said clearly and emphatically, “This is my Son,” he added what followed: “beloved,” namely, and “in whom I am well pleased.” Just as through prophecy he had already proclaimed him “the mighty God and the great God” (Isa. 9:6), so here, saying “my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” he added to the name of his proper Son also the designation “beloved” and “the Son in whom he was well pleased” [Cass., “he added, moreover, the name of his proper Son,” etc.]. Thus the addition of these names signified the distinctiveness of the divine nature; and what belonged uniquely to the honor of the Son of God was something that had happened to no human being at all.

Accordingly, just as these things were proper and unique to the person of our Lord Jesus Christ—that the heavens were opened, that God the Father touched him before everyone’s eyes through the approaching and witnessing dove, as though with his own hand, and, as if pointing with a finger, showed him by saying, “This is my Son”—so too this was proper and unique to him: that he is called particularly beloved and particularly pleasing to the Father. The distinctive additions thus displayed the distinctive significance of his nature, and the distinctiveness of these additional titles confirmed the distinctiveness of the only-begotten Son, which the honor of the preceding signs had already established.

But let this little book now come to an end. For this saying of God the Father can neither be increased nor equaled by human speech. Concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, the Father himself is a sufficient witness, saying: “This is my Son.” If you think that these words of God the Father must be contradicted, then you must contradict the one who wished the whole world to recognize, by the clearest declaration, that he was his Son.

[Note: Up to this point the text is from Cassian.]

# LIBER SECUNDUS

## Book Two

[Col. 0145]

### I

The reader should not charge me with a somewhat confused and disordered argument, because I am compelled to follow the disputant’s footsteps—not as one proceeding along a straight path, but as one whose speech turns in a circular whirl of verbosity. The respondent’s speech must follow the order in which the proposer’s argument has unfolded.

Nor is it surprising that I proceed along a different path in my speech, since he too advances through the very broad fields of sacred Scripture with varying meanings and, in some places, with meanings inconsistent with himself. He does not seek the truth of the catholic faith, but strives to produce testimonies for his error, although that error is greatly self-contradictory [Deest: “to find,” or something similar], following the practice of all heretics, who strive to interpret the sayings of divine eloquence perversely in support of their own error.

### II

You say, then, that the new man ought to have a new name. Tell me, I ask, what new name did the Spirit sound in your ears? Perhaps God was speaking with you in the whirlwind, as once with his servant Job; or perhaps on the Pyrenean hills, amid thunder and the sound of a trumpet, as when he spoke with his servant Moses on Mount Sinai; or perhaps you saw the Lord with the prophet Isaiah sitting upon a throne, and a seraph was sent with a burning coal to cleanse your lips, so that you might proclaim to the world names unheard through the ages; or perhaps, like the Apostle, you were caught up to the third heaven and there heard unspeakable words; or perhaps, with the blessed evangelist, you saw and read the book sealed with seven seals, which no one could open except the Lion of the tribe of Judah—whose authority Felix unhappily does not fear to diminish!

Nevertheless, bring us what God spoke with you either in the whirlwind or on the Pyrenean hills. Tell us those unspeakable words that you heard, or show us from the sealed book the testimonies concerning the new name that you have imposed upon the new man.

I believe that another spirit spoke to you, telling you that Christ is adopted, while another inspired the prophet Isaiah when he said: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14); or again, as he says elsewhere: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isa. 9:6).

And another spirit dictated to you that Christ is a titular God, while another inspired the words of the other prophet: “Does a man fasten his God to the cross, because you fasten me to the cross?” (Mal. 3:8).

Could this not have been Christ’s voice when he was led to the cross, as though he were saying: “Why, I ask, do you not recognize your Redeemer? Why do you not know God clothed in flesh for your sake? You are preparing death for your Savior. You are leading the Author of life to death. I am your God, whom you are hanging; your God, whom you are crucifying.”

What error, I ask, or what madness is this? “Does a man fasten his God to the cross, because you fasten me to the cross?” You see how this voice is, in a manner of speaking, the voice of the very things that happened. Are you seeking anything more explicit or clearer?

You see how the sacred testimonies followed the Lord Jesus Christ, born in the flesh, from something like his very cradle all the way to the cross that he endured. Isaiah proclaimed that the Lord would be born in the flesh; here the prophet sees God fastened to the cross. Therefore, at the place where he was born, God is called God by the prophet, and at the place where he was crucified, God is most clearly named God.

Certainly, one angel appeared to you sleeping in a dream, and another to Joseph, the husband of Mary; one revealed one name to you and another to him. Or perhaps someone other than Gabriel, some unknown messenger, stood beside you while you were awake, whispering in your ear: “Remember to call this child, who was born of the Virgin, adopted.”

But another stood beside the most blessed Virgin—no ordinary messenger, but the archangel Gabriel—proclaiming in a clear voice: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

If Gabriel himself, who is called “the strength of God,” had found you praying in the temple, he would have condemned your unbelieving mouth not to nine months of silence but to perpetual silence. For the one whom he, sent by God and conscious of the divine will, foretold would be born of the Virgin—Jesus, that is, the Savior—and whom he showed to be great, the Son of the Most High, holy, and destined to reign forever—you do not fear to testify to be little, adopted, and a conditional servant.

### III

First, then, I ask you this: do you say that the Lord Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin Mary, is merely the son of man, or also the Son of God? But it is unnecessary to ask you this, since it is obvious that you think and, although vainly, confirm at length that the one born of the Virgin is merely the son of man and not the Son of God except by adoption.

We, however—that is, the faith of all Catholics—we, I say, both believe and understand, know and confess both: that he is the son of man, because he was born from a human being, and the Son of God, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

Do you therefore assert that he is both—the Son of God and the son of man—or only the son of man? If only the son of man, the apostles protest against you, the prophets protest, and finally the Holy Spirit himself, through whom the conception occurred, protests.

Your most shameless mouth is overwhelmed by all the testimonies of the divine writings; it is overwhelmed by the sacred books and holy witnesses; finally, it is overwhelmed by the very Gospel of God, as though by the divine hand, in many places, especially by the paternal voice from heaven, and by the testimony of the one about whom we are now speaking.

The archangel himself also condemns the unbelieving voice within you—the one whose words closed the unbelieving mouth of Zechariah. How much more does he condemn you, since you refuse to agree with the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son, with apostolic teachings, prophetic foretellings, or angelic announcements, and yet, after all these testimonies to the truth, you presume, together with a few men of Spain—not doctors of the truth, I say, but deserters from it—to impose a new name upon the Son of God.

At last, turn back to the harmony of catholic unity. While you still have the light, run, lest darkness overtake you, so that through him you may be found worthy of adoption as sons—him who is the true Son of God, who was born in the fullness of divinity as perfect God and perfect man: wholly God, wholly man; wholly Son of God, and wholly son of man.

Hold firmly, believe, and proclaim the name that the angel foretold to the Virgin when she conceived: namely, the Son of God. For Jesus Christ is the Son of God, begotten from divinity and conceived from divinity.

But if he is the Son of God, then he is undoubtedly God; and if he is God, he is certainly full of all truth, because “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Therefore all grace, all truth, all virtue, all power, all divinity, and finally the entire fullness of his divinity and majesty were always with him and in him—whether in heaven, on earth, in the womb, or at his birth.

Nothing was ever lacking to God from God; for deity was always with God, and the distinctiveness of the divine nature was always in the Son. The same one who was in the lowliness of man was also in the majesty of God.

Therefore the Apostle rightly, when naming the grace of Christ, named the grace of God, because Christ was everything that God is. At the very conception of the man, all the power of God, all divinity, and the entire fullness of divinity had come upon him. His perfection of divinity came from the same source as his origin.

For that man had never been without God, since he had begun to be what he was from God. This first point, then, whether you wish it or not, you cannot deny: that the Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of God, since the archangel proclaimed: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Once this has been established, know that whatever you read about Christ, you read about the Son of God; whatever you read about the Lord or Jesus pertains to the Son of God. All these names demonstrate the Son of God, and therefore, in everything you hear, you will recognize the name of divinity.

All these titles cry out that he is the Son of God, so that in all of them you must understand that he is the Son of God. Argue, if you wish, how you can separate God from the Son of God. For the Son of God would not be named so many times throughout the pages of the holy Gospels if the one born from the Virgin according to the flesh were not properly the Son of God.

What is sufficient for you, if the testimonies of the Gospels [are not] sufficient? Or whose testimony will you believe, if you are unbelieving even toward the testimony of the Father himself?

### IV

It is also read in the text of your little book:

“In that one, namely, in which, according to the substance of the flesh, all his faithful are his members; not in that one—that is, in his divinity—in which he has not members but a temple.”

How can it be that Christ, who is God, does not have members but does have a temple? Is not the body that he took from the Virgin the temple of God? As the evangelist says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

And if he has a body, then certainly he also has members, as the Apostle testifies: “You are the body of Christ and members individually” (1 Cor. 12:27).

We know that the divine nature is not divided into parts as a body is divided into members. Nevertheless, since you have said that the same nature has a temple, if it has a temple—that is, a body—it certainly also has members, because a temple cannot exist without members.

For the same divine nature, which had no members before the incarnation, had members when it became man—members in which it was fastened to the cross. It also testifies after the resurrection that it still has them, when it says to the apostles: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39). He showed them his members and his side, demonstrating the reality of his body after the resurrection in human members.

There was no diminution of divinity in the assumption of humanity, but an exaltation of humanity through participation in divinity, as the blessed doctor Augustine often said in his book *On the Baptism of Infants* [Note: St. Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book I, chapter 31, where see the complete text]:

“Through the unity of person, because [Aug., ‘by which’] the two substances are one Christ, the Son of God walked on earth, and that same Son of man remained in heaven. Thus faith in incredible things arises from things believed that are more incredible [Aug., ‘faith in more credible things arises from things believed that are more credible’]. For if the divine substance, so much farther removed and exalted by an incomparable difference, could on our behalf receive human substance in such a way that one person was formed, and thus the Son of man, who was on earth through the weakness of the flesh, should himself also be in heaven through divinity shared with the flesh [Note: The text is mutilated].”

### V

You also objected, and said that we had said among other things:

“After such a thunderclap, why do you hesitate, inventing for his birth a new name of adoption, which is nowhere found concerning Christ in the entire sequence of the Old and New Testament?”

To this objection, you say, I also reply: “A new man can rightly have a new name.”

I too shall speak: it is astonishing that this new name has become known to you alone, and only in the final age of Christianity, as something that ought to be said of Christ—if indeed this name of adoption is so new that it did not previously exist in the world, but arrived only with the birth of Christ.

Did not Pharaoh’s daughter adopt Moses as her son? Likewise, the patriarch Jacob adopted his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh as sons.

The prophets did not foretell this concerning Christ; the law did not contain it in its figures of sacrifice; the evangelists did not write it; the apostles did not preach it; all their successors were ignorant of it—except you alone.

The Holy Spirit also foretold six names concerning him through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah: “And his name,” he says, “shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6).

Therefore the blessed Jerome, in his exposition of this prophecy, said:

“Although from what he had said above, ‘Emmanuel,’ that is, ‘God with us,’ it was shown that he was God [Jer., ‘he had shown him to be God’], yet now he says that his rule has been placed upon his shoulder [Quercet., erroneously, ‘God has now been made his rule’], either because he himself had carried his cross, or because by the shoulder he indicates the strength of the arm.”

The blessed Cassian also explained the meaning of this same prophecy against heretical perversity in this way (*On the Incarnation*, Book II, chapter 3):

“Without doubt, the divine Spirit, foreseeing this perversity of blaspheming heretics, demonstrated to the whole world by the very names of the things that he who was being born was God, so that even if a heretic sought to blaspheme, he would have no place at all in which to do so. ‘A Son,’ he says, ‘has been born to us; a child has been given to us; whose rule is upon his shoulder. And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace’ (Isa. 9:6).

“He taught that this child who was born was Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come, and Mighty God. What room, then, is there for evasion? This child who was born cannot be separated from the God who was born in him. For the one whom he said was born, he named Father of the age to come and foretold to be Mighty God.”

Concerning him the same prophet also says above: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). The evangelist Matthew, explaining this, says: “Which is interpreted, ‘God with us’” (Matt. 1:23).

The angel Gabriel, sent by God to the Virgin, also said: “Behold, you will conceive and bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:31).

Concerning this name the Apostle also says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–11).

The holy Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, says concerning him in his letter to the Armenians:

“If Christ is someone other than the true God, Christ must be merely a man. And how do the heavenly armies honor him beyond the merit of nature, and bend the knee to him who is inferior?”

What is this glory of the Father in which Christ is, if he is not the true Son of God the Father but adopted, like all of us? And if this is so, his name is not above every name but among all names—that is, adopted—for “adopted” is a common name of all the saints.

Concerning the name Jesus, it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And they were baptized in the name of Jesus” (Acts 19:5). That name, Jesus, was foretold by the angel to the Virgin, so that the one who would be born from her would be called Jesus.

If Jesus were not God, how were they baptized in the name of Jesus?

The blessed Father Cassian also says concerning this name, in the same discussion mentioned above:

“Can you raise any objection based on the ambiguity of names, so that you say that Christ is one thing and God another, separating the Savior from the majesty of his name and distinguishing God from his divinity? Behold, this vessel of God [Cass., ‘this man of God’] speaks from God and bears witness by the clearest proclamation that the grace of God appeared from Mary.
