“And lest perhaps you should say that God did not appear from Mary [‘the name of the Savior was immediately added’], namely, so that you might believe that God was born from Mary, whom you could not deny was born as Savior, the blessed Apostle says: ‘Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ’ (Titus 2:13).

“That teacher of divine wisdom clearly saw that simple instruction alone was insufficient against the crafty devices of the devil’s deception unless he armed the holy proclamation of faith with the protection of caution.

“Therefore, after he had earlier used the name ‘God the Savior,’ he added here ‘Jesus Christ.’ Granted [Cass., ‘Clearly’], lest perhaps you should think that the name ‘Savior’ alone was sufficient to signify the Lord Jesus Christ, and would not understand that the same Jesus Christ whom you knew to be God the Savior was God.

“What, then, does he say? ‘Awaiting,’ he says, ‘the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.’ Nothing concerning the names of our Lord is absent here. Here you see God, Savior, Jesus, and Christ; but when you see all these, you perceive that all are in God.

“You heard ‘God,’ but also ‘Savior’; you heard ‘God,’ but also ‘Jesus’; you heard that he is God, but also ‘Christ.’ What divinity has joined in unity cannot be separated by the diversity of its appellations.

“Yet whatever you inquire about among these, you will find the same thing: Savior is God, Jesus is God, Christ is God. All that you hear is plural in designation but one in power. Since Savior is God, Jesus is God, and Christ is God, it is clear that all these are distinguished by appellation but joined in majesty.

“And when you hear most clearly that one God is named in each case, you can plainly understand that one God is present in all. Why do you hesitate, new teachers, to call the one born from the Virgin the true and proper Son of God, when the settled reasoning of the catholic faith establishes that the God who is Jesus is the same God who is Christ, the same God who suffered for the salvation of the world?”

### VI

But if you do not wish to believe the other teachers of the world, at least believe your own most learned men.

The presbyter Juvencus, a most learned scholar of Spain, sang in his evangelical poem (*Evangelical History*, Book I) as follows:

> For by heavenly command your womb will conceive a child,  
>
> whom God rejoices and commands to reign over all things in every particular [F., “through all the ages”]  
>
> and to be believed his own offspring;  
>
> when you have brought him [Hunc; Huic, “him/to him”] into the light, let him be Jesus by name [nomine; nomen, “name”; Iesus, “Jesus”].

This man flourished in the time of the emperor Constantine. You see plainly that this heresy of adoption or titular designation did not yet exist in Spain. Either judge this man, who stands among you as a most learned teacher, to be a heretic because he says that the one born from the Virgin is God and the proper Son of God; or, if you wish to accept him, condemn your own opinion—or rather correct it according to his understanding, since he offers testimonies consistent with the holy Fathers who flourished in different places throughout the world.

### VII

The distinguished Spanish doctor, the blessed Isidore, also appears to agree with us rather than with you. In his writings, insofar as his statements have come down to us, he used everywhere concerning Christ those names that we believe and confess, whether they are proper or descriptive. Nowhere have I found him calling Christ an adopted son or a titular God.

Are you therefore more learned than he, either in the divine Scriptures or in secular disciplines, so that the world ought to believe you, so few in number and appearing so late?

### VIII

Origen says concerning the divinity of Christ’s flesh, in the fifth homily on the prophet Isaiah:

> “Who raised up the righteous one from the East? He called him to his feet” (Isa. 41:2). The Father called him Son; or, to speak truly, God called the man righteous—or righteousness—to his feet, that is, the incarnation of his Son. Therefore let them also worship the footstool of his feet, because he is holy [Origen, “because it is holy”]. The flesh of the Lord, however, assumed the honor of divinity.

### IX

In the fourth book *On the Incarnation of Christ*, which Cassian published against Nestorius at the command of Pope Leo, we also find the following written (Book IV, chapter 5):

> “Whoever believes that Jesus is the Son of God has God dwelling in him, and the love of God is perfected in him” (1 John 4:12); he proclaims that person to be a believer, and asserts that person to be full of divine love, who believes Jesus to be the Son of God. He testifies that the Son of God is the Word of God; and therefore he wishes the only-begotten Word of God and Jesus Christ the Son of God to be understood as wholly one and the same.

Does not the one who has not believed Jesus to be the true Son of God empty this fullness of love? For such a great apostle and evangelist says that the one who has believed and known the Son of God to be true is the one who came into this world [Note: Something is missing].

Concerning him the distinguished preacher also says: “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15).

And concerning him he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs” (Heb. 1:4). He introduced an argument for his excellence from the distinctiveness of the name. For when he said, “Having become as much superior to the angels,” there is no doubt that this is said of the assumed man, who is superior to the angels to the same degree that a proper son is more excellent than a ministering servant.

The distinctiveness of the son, therefore, in the paternal inheritance is placed above the subjection of servants.

### X

The blessed Augustine likewise says in his book against the heretic Maximinus [Note: I do not know which book Alcuin intends here by Augustine’s book against Maximinus. This text is not found in the two books that St. Augustine wrote against the heretic Maximinus. Perhaps Alcuin copied it from the book *Against the Maximianists*, written against the Donatists, or from the *Admonition to the Donatists Concerning the Maximianists*. St. Augustine mentions both in Book II of the *Retractations*, chapters 29 and 35; but neither work now survives]:

> “Do you wish to know more fully that, although Christ was truly born as man from a human being according to the flesh, nevertheless, because of the ineffable unity of the mystery by which the man is united with God, there is absolutely no distinction between Christ and the Word? Hear the Lord’s Gospel—or rather, hear him himself speaking of himself as God: ‘This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent’” (John 17:3).
>
> “Above, you heard that the Word of God was sent to heal human beings; here you hear that the one who was sent is Jesus Christ. Separate these, if you can, when you see such great unity between Christ and the Word that it is said not only that the Word was united with Christ, but, because of that very unity, Christ is already called the Word.”

Concerning this same testimony of truth, the same Father Augustine says in a certain homily on the exposition of the Gospel [Note: The same, *Tractate* 105 on John, no. 3]:

> “The order of the words is: ‘that they know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, the only true God.’”

For, as he testified in the books that he composed on the Holy Trinity, this sending of the Son of God is his incarnation. If, therefore, his incarnation is his sending, and the one who was sent—Jesus Christ—is the true God, no room for doubt will remain that Jesus Christ is true God and the true Son of God who was sent, that is, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

Tell me, introducer of this new sect: when Jesus was born from the Virgin, what do you wish him to have been—a man or God? If God alone, then you have dissolved Jesus, since you deny that a man was united to him [Forte, “to whom a man was united”]. But if man alone, you have likewise dissolved him, since you blasphemously maintain that only a man was born.

This, therefore, is the only catholic and true faith: that we do not hesitate to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be God as well as man, and man as well as God. For “everyone who dissolves Jesus is not from God” (1 John 4:3). To dissolve him means to wish to tear apart what was united in Jesus and to separate what is indivisible.

What, then, is united and indivisible in Jesus? Man and God, certainly, so that there is one Son, God and man, and one Son of man who was born from the Virgin—not one adopted son and another proper son, nor one titular God and another true God.

### XI

The following occurs in the aforementioned little book of Felix:

> “Why do you elicit [perhaps: reject] this name? What more excellent, more honorable, or holier gift can be conferred by God upon human nature than this gift, by which that same creature is known to have been reconciled to God after man’s transgression?”

He says this concerning the name of adoption, and he speaks truly in saying that it is our greatest dignity to be called adopted sons of God—but through him who is the true Son of God. Thus, in us this name is exceedingly honorable, but in Christ it is of little worth, because it is a greater dignity to be the true Son of God than an adopted son.

We have discussed more fully the basis of this adoption in another little book [Note: “In another little book.” Perhaps the one he wrote against Felix for the monks of Gothia, presented above], against the same Felix, in our reply to the letter which he published on this very subject. There are found there many authoritative testimonies of the holy Fathers, from which anyone who reads and considers the matter with reverence will be able to understand most clearly that Christ is truly the Son of God in both natures, while we are adopted through him, by whose grace we have been saved.

In the Gospel, always and everywhere, he is called the true Son of God—by angels, apostles, and other saints, and sometimes even by demons, as well as by the pagan centurion. For whom else did that centurion see hanging upon the cross except the one whom he saw dying? Yet he confessed that this man was the true Son of God.

But you, sons of the Church—even if in name only—join the Jews in reproaching Christ because he said that he was the Son of God, and because he now reigns in the seat of his Father’s majesty and sits upon the throne of heavenly glory, worshiped by the entire host of angels, while thousands upon thousands minister to him, whose authority is eternal and whose kingdom will have no end. Nevertheless, you do not fear, in your continuing blasphemies, to deny that he is the proper Son and true God.

For this reason also your predecessors, the Jews, wished to stone Christ, because he said:

> “I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works do you wish to stone me?”

They answered:

> “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God” (John 10:32–33).

Likewise, when Christ said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you,” the envious Jews said among themselves:

> “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2:5–7).

Christ then showed them by deed as well as by word that he was God and also the Son of Man, saying:

> “Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise and walk” (ibid., 9–10).

And immediately the man was healed.

Thus we are, as he says—or rather, as the Apostle says—bone from his bones and flesh from his flesh: not fashioned bodily like Eve, our first mother, from the man’s rib, but specially through the blood of Christ, which was poured out from his side. We have indeed been redeemed at the great price of the Son of God, not of some adopted son.

Therefore the Apostle also says:

> “This mystery is great” (Ephesians 5:32).

He called the event that took place in Adam and Eve a mystery, because it has been spiritually enacted in us. That is why he—the true Son of God, whose blood was poured out for us—was made [the text leaves the predicate unstated], so that through him we might become adopted sons.

### XII

You also propose an argument of this kind, saying:

> “But if our Redeemer, in his flesh—which he assumed from the Virgin’s womb, from the very moment of conception—was not adopted by the Father but was his true and proper Son, what remains except that this same flesh of his was not created and made from the mass of the human race or from his mother’s flesh, but from the substance of the Father, just as his divinity was generated from it?”

I shall propose an argument to you in return. If the man whom the Son of God assumed is adopted, then the one who assumed him is adopted, because there is one person in the man and in God, and there is altogether one son, not two sons.

But how can one son be both the proper son and the adopted son of one father? If he is adopted, he cannot be proper; if he is proper, he cannot be adopted by that same father. It is utterly impious to believe that Christ has two sons, one proper and the other adopted.

The Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin, but he did not lose the proper status that he possessed under the name of Son. Even though after his birth from the Virgin he possessed two natures, he nevertheless firmly retained one proper status in the person of the Son. Humanity was added to the unity of the person of the Son of God, and the same proper status remained in the two natures under the name of Son, which previously existed in one substance.

In the assumption of flesh by God, the person of the man perishes, not his nature. In us there is the person of adoption, but not in the Son of God, because that one man, conceived from God and assumed into God, possesses uniquely the status of being the Son of God—a status which all the saints possess through the adoption of God’s grace. He was found in human form as man, but in divinity as God.

Nor in that assumption is one God and another man, or one the Son of God and another the son of the Virgin. Rather, the same is the Son of God who is the son of the Virgin, and the same is the son of the Virgin who is the Son of God, so that there is one Son, both proper and perfect, in the two natures of God and man.

Concerning Christ’s human form, blessed Augustine says [Note: St. Augustine, *On Various Questions*, question 73, no. 2]:

> “Thus the man was assumed so that he might advance [Augustine: ‘be transformed’] for the better and be formed by him ineffably more excellently and more closely than a garment is when it is put on by a man. By this name ‘garb’ the Apostle sufficiently indicated in what sense he said, ‘made in the likeness of men’ (Philippians 2:7): for he was made not by transformation into a man, but by garb, when he was clothed with the man whom, adapting to himself [Augustine: ‘uniting’] and in a manner conforming, he made a companion of immortality and eternity.”

### XIII

I do not sufficiently understand what relevance you assign to the body of Christ, which hung upon the cross for us, when you say that the Apostle declares:

> “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin” (Romans 6:6).

Christ was never the old man and never possessed a body of sin. From the beginning of his conception he was conceived and born as true God and the true Son of God, without any sin.

But all of us were old men in Adam’s sins. Through Christ Jesus we have been changed into new men, adopted, and predestined as sons of adoption by grace. You assert that Christ had this predestination equally with us, failing to notice that the Apostle testifies that Christ was predestined in one way and we in another.

He says that Christ was predestined to be the Son of God, as he states:

> “Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power” (Romans 1:4).

In what power, if not that of divinity? But he says that we were predestined through him for adoption as sons. We have predestination through him, not he through us (Romans 8:29).

### XIV

You also put forward an argument from the saying of that same distinguished preacher, where he says:

> “We must know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

And you say:

> “Adopted members must have an adopted head. Therefore, if Christ, who is the head of all of us, is adopted on account of his adopted members, which we are, do you not see that for the same reason God the Father can be called adopted, since he is the head of Christ? For the head is a member in the body; and since he is the head of the head, how, on account of the adoption of the head, which is Christ, will that principal head itself not also be adopted?”

Everyone of sound understanding recognizes how impious and absurd this is.

Therefore this apostolic statement must be understood spiritually, not carnally. Flesh is born from flesh in one way, and spirit from spirit in another, as Truth itself says in the Gospel:

> “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).

Because God is Spirit, the gift is given from God. Spiritual birth makes us members of Christ, not carnal birth. This will remain so until the creature of our body itself is freed from slavery to corruption and renewed in the adoption of the sons of God, until hostile death is destroyed, this mortal nature is clothed with immortality, and God is all in all.

### XV

After this, the aforementioned Felix runs—not with a straight step, but with a limping gait—through the fields of Holy Scripture, putting forward many testimonies that do not suit his arguments, as though he had lengthened his discourse until he reached the waters of the Jordan, in order to impose upon Christ, once baptized, the name of adoption.

Yet he still does not know how to remain silent, terrified by the Father’s heavenly voice. That voice, too, bore witness to the baptized Christ in the hearing of blessed John the Baptist, crying out:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

We have spoken more fully above concerning this testimony [Note: See above, Book I, nos. 12 and 18]. For the present, I wish only to ask here whether this paternal voice referred to one person of Christ.

If it referred to one, then that one person to whom the voice was addressed is wholly the beloved Son of God, although in two natures. But if it referred only to the divinity, then the divinity was baptized there and not the humanity, because the voice was spoken over the one who was baptized.

The man who was baptized was proclaimed by God the Father to be the Son of God; and over him the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove. Thus the paternal voice and the descent of the Holy Spirit demonstrated that the one who was baptized was the Son of God.

The Baptist himself, inspired by the one who sent him to baptize, also offered testimony agreeing with the Father’s voice, saying:

> “And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:34).

### XVI

Why, then, O remarkable teacher, do you still impose the name of adoption upon Christ? You even assert that he needed the washing of baptism [Supplement: “you assert,” or something similar], and a second birth, just as we sinners, already born through carnal generation, were born as sons of wrath [Col. 0157D], as can plainly be understood from your words. For among other things you say:

> “Just as in the first generation, through which we are born according to the flesh, no human being can have an origin elsewhere than from that first Adam, who was created from virgin earth, so in this second spiritual generation, in which we are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, no one can obtain the grace of adoption except him who received it [the text is corrupt: ‘in eam in Christo, created and born from the flesh of the Virgin’], who is the second Adam. This Redeemer of ours, according to the man, embraced and contains in himself these two generations: the first, namely, the one according to the flesh, which he assumed by being born from the Virgin; and the second, namely, the spiritual one, which he inaugurated in the washing by rising from the dead.”

You endeavor to confirm this by the genealogies read in the Gospel, one according to Matthew and the other according to Luke. All these statements, as you have set them forth, produce more weariness than benefit for readers, until at last you arrive at this conclusion:

> “But if anyone wishes to deny to Christ according to the man this spiritual generation, which takes place through adoption, he must first completely cut off from him that generation which is according to the flesh. For if he does not share with us in this spiritual generation, plainly he does not share with us in that which is carnal.”

### XVII

Let anyone who reads examine these statements of the aforementioned teacher. First, the sentence is wrapped in a kind of discordance among the parts of speech and obscurity of meaning, so that its sense does not come to light.

What does he mean when he says, “He inaugurated it by rising from the dead”? From what dead did Christ rise in baptism? Did he have sins, so that he might rise from the death of sins, as we, born in sins because of the transgression of our first parents, are born—and are not freed from them except in Christ Jesus through the second generation, in which sons of wrath are made sons of God?

On the contrary, Christ Jesus, conceived and born without any sin, came to baptism to display an example of humility and to sanctify the waters by his baptism—not in order to be sanctified in the waters, since he possessed no sin from which he needed to be cleansed through baptism.

Therefore blessed John the Baptist himself said to the Son of God when he came to him:

> “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14).

It was as though he had said: “In me there is what must be cleansed by you; in you there is nothing that must be cleansed by me.”

But this must be understood: in John’s baptism, in which Christ was baptized, there was no regeneration, but a certain preliminary signification of Christ’s baptism. Thus in the Acts of the Apostles we read that blessed Paul the Apostle rebaptized those who had been baptized with John’s baptism (Acts 19:5).

No one could receive the adoption of the sons of God in John’s baptism. How much less, then, was Christ adopted as Son by God the Father in that baptism, in which no one could receive the grace of adoption? For no one could obtain forgiveness of sins in that baptism; they were baptized only for repentance, so that they might believe in him, as that same Apostle says: “the one who was to come,” that is, in Jesus.

Observe, reader, that he says “to believe in Jesus.” If Jesus, who was born from the Virgin, were not God and the Son of God, the Apostle would never have spoken in such terms that they ought to believe in Jesus, because Catholic faith alone teaches that one must believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, in the Holy Trinity.

In other professions of the Catholic faith, ecclesiastical teachers do not wish to place the preposition *in*, but only to say: “We believe the holy Church, and the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the dead,” and the other things contained in the holy Creed.

Concerning the distinction between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism, blessed Augustine says in the book *Enchiridion* [Note: St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 48]:

> “That one sin, however, which was committed in a place and condition of such great happiness, was so great that in one man, originally and, so to speak, radically, the whole human race was condemned [it is not dissolved and destroyed]—unless by the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who alone could be born in such a way that he did not need to be reborn. For those who were baptized with John’s baptism, by which he himself was also baptized [Augustine omits the word ‘John’], were not reborn; rather, they were prepared by a certain preliminary ministry of the one who said, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord’ (Matthew 3:3), where the one thing by which alone they could be reborn was being prepared. His baptism [Quercetanus: ‘baptism’] is not merely in water, as John’s was, but also in the Holy Spirit, so that whoever believes in Christ may be regenerated by that Spirit from whom Christ was begotten [Augustine: ‘generated’], though Christ did not need regeneration.”

And shortly afterward in the same book:

> “Therefore he wished to be baptized in water by John, not so that any iniquity of his might be washed away, but so that great humility might be commended. Thus baptism found nothing in him to wash away, just as death found nothing to punish, so that the devil, overcome and defeated by the truth of justice rather than by force of power—since he had most unjustly killed the one in whom there was no guilt of sin—might most justly lose through him what [Augustine: ‘those whom’] he held on account of the merit of sin. Both things, therefore—that is, baptism and death—were received by him for the sake of a definite dispensation, not through pitiable necessity but rather through merciful will, so that one might take away the sin of the world, just as one brought sin into the world, that is, into the whole human race, as the Apostle testifies: ‘For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive’ (1 Corinthians 15:22).”

### XVIII

How blatant is this blasphemy—that he says Christ needed a second birth! The one whom he repeatedly affirms to be without sin he now suddenly insists needed regeneration as though he were a sinner. The one whom he shortly before declared to be God and born from a virgin’s womb he now suddenly pronounces to be like a mere man, requiring purification through the washing; and he says that the one who was conceived and born the Son of God was adopted as the Son of God in imitation of us.

He undertakes to confirm these two generations in Christ by the two genealogies of Christ that are read in the Gospel: one by which Christ descended, and the other by which he ascended—as though he were a sinner in his descent and cleansed in the ascent of adoption.

Pay attention, reader, to this new interpreter of evangelical history. He mentions two genealogies of Christ with the evangelists. According to Matthew, Christ descended not only through righteous people but also through sinful women, and needed baptism in that generation which is given according to Matthew. According to Luke, after baptism he ascended and was made the Son of God through the grace of adoption.

And lest you think that I am falsely representing him, listen to the words of this new interpreter himself:

> “Matthew, at the beginning of his Gospel, counts out and traces the sequence of the generation according to the flesh that descends to Christ, beginning with David or Abraham and continuing to Joseph, the husband of Mary, through kings and the other successive members of the tribe of Judah. In this fleshly generation four women are introduced: three from the nations, and the fourth the woman with whom David sinned. Thus it might clearly appear that our Redeemer assumed true flesh from the Virgin not only from the Jews but also from the nations, and not only from the righteous but also from sinners.
>
> “Luke, however, constructs the sequence of generation that is through adoption, not through a genealogy of the flesh as Matthew does. Beginning with Christ himself at the baptism in which Christ was baptized in the Jordan, he traces it not through the tribe of Judah, as the former does, but through the priestly tribe; not by descending downward, as the other does, but upward. He traces it not through Solomon, who was born from Bathsheba, but through Nathan, rejoining him to David, and carries it all the way to Adam and to God, repeating the head back to the Head.”

### XIX

Nor is there any need for me here to elaborate words in response, since the truth of the Gospel shows that Christ was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, not as a sinner but truly as the Son of God, indeed as God.

Did not an angel appear in a dream to Joseph, the husband of Mary, when he was in doubt, saying:

> “Do not fear, son of David, to take Mary your wife, For that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will give birth to a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus. All this took place so that what had been spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘She will give birth to a Son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel’” (Matthew 1:20–23).

And lest there be ignorance concerning the name, the evangelist added: “which is interpreted, ‘God with us.’”

The one who is called Emmanuel in Matthew is called the Son of the Most High in Luke. And lest there be any doubt about who the Most High is, he immediately added:

> “And the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:32–35).

Felix asserts that the genealogy according to Luke ascends through adoption, as though all those counted in it were adopted—something which anyone who reads the sacred histories of Holy Scripture recognizes to be entirely otherwise.

He adds also the most atrocious poison of his error:

> “But if anyone,” he says, “wishes to deny to Christ according to the man this spiritual generation, which takes place through adoption, he must first completely cut off from him that which is according to the flesh.”

Listen, listen, you who read and understand, how blatant this blasphemy is. Either he wants Christ, insofar as he is man, to have two generations, or else none at all—as though it were necessary that after a carnal generation he should also have a spiritual one through adoption, so that what Truth itself says concerning us might be understood to have been said equally concerning him:

> “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

As we showed above (no. 17), there was absolutely no regeneration of anyone in John’s baptism, but only a demonstration of a greater mystery.

Nor, when Christ rose from the water, was there his anointing there—that is, sanctification by the Holy Spirit descending upon him. Rather, it was a demonstration of who he was and a figure of our anointing and adoption, by which we are sanctified in baptism as sons of God, as blessed Bede the presbyter shows in his exposition of the preaching of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, by which he instructed Cornelius and many others in the faith [Note: Venerable Bede, on Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10]:

> “Jesus was therefore anointed,” he says, “not with invisible oil [Bede: ‘visible oil’], but with the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized. Yet he was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit, when the Spirit descended upon him in the likeness of a dove. For at that time he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which the baptized principally receive the Holy Spirit.
>
> “Rather, he must be understood to have been anointed with that mystical and invisible anointing when the Word of God became flesh—that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to God the Word in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person. For this reason we confess that he was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”

### XX

Concerning Christ’s genealogies, we think that this should instead be understood: the genealogy narrated by Matthew signifies the Lord Christ’s assumption of our sins, for which he was suspended upon the cross. In Luke’s generations, which ascend to God, the abolition of our sins is signified through the same one who was crucified for our sins.

Therefore one evangelist narrates them as a descent and the other as an ascent: Christ descended to free us, but ascended to justify us; he descended to die for us, but ascended so that we might live in him.

When the Apostle says:

> “God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3),

this refers to the assumption of sins. But when he says:

> “In order that, through sin, he might condemn sin in the flesh” (ibid.),

this refers to the expiation of sins.

Thus Matthew descends from David through Solomon, whose mother was the woman with whom David sinned; but Luke ascends to David through Nathan, the prophet through whom God expiated his sin.

Christ descended through the royal line and ascended through the priestly line, since he became priest and sacrifice for us. For he is both king and priest and the Lord who brings reconciliation.

It must be held most firmly that Christ’s flesh was propagated from both lines, namely the royal and the priestly. Among that Hebrew people, a mystical anointing was also prefigured in these persons, namely the chrism, from which the name “Christ” shines forth, foretold so long beforehand with the clearest significance.

But we cry out with a free voice, together with the whole Church of Christ, that Christ neither had sin to be expiated nor needed a second birth, since he was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit as true God and the true Son of God.

For if Christ needed a second birth, then he was a sinner. And if he was a sinner, what does the Lord himself mean when he says:

> “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30)?

If the ruler of this world—that is, the devil—had nothing in him, why did he need to be reborn?

We, however, are not born sons of God but are reborn as such. He was conceived and born immediately as the Son of God. Therefore he did not need adoption in order to be the Son of God, since he was born the Son of God.

If, then, the one who was born from the Virgin was made the Son of God through adoption, the blessed Virgin was not the Mother of God but merely the mother of a man who, after birth, was adopted as the Son of God. How impious this is to believe—and how much more impious to say!

### XXI

But let this be the end of this discussion, so that the discourse may begin more freely from another starting point concerning the matters that remain to be said. For the end of a little book offers some refreshment to the reader, just as a harbor does to a sailor, especially when the language of the respondent’s disputation has been laboring through rough stretches.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0161]

### I

The argumentation of one proposing new things requires a new beginning for the little book, lest the confused sequence of the discourse weary the reader and it be less clear what belongs to which part if the text does not begin its discourse elsewhere, at appropriate points.

Therefore the oft-mentioned sophist suddenly returns from Christ’s baptism to his birth. He wants the one whom he understands to have been adopted as the Son of God through a second generation to be testified as more truly the son of King David than of God the Father.

To present his own words, he says:

> “Certainly our Redeemer himself, in the form of humanity, is, as the sacred writings testify, the son of David and the Son of God. Both statements are true. Yet it is not unreasonable to ask how both can apply to him. For it cannot happen that one son can naturally have two fathers; but it is entirely possible for him to have one father by nature and another by adoption.”

You have unquestionably received above, in accordance with the requirements of the discussion, an answer concerning this double fatherhood in Christ Jesus—namely, that of God the Father and that of King David [Note: See above, Book I, no. 12].

Unless perhaps this should be added: nowhere in Holy Scripture will you find it written that David said of Christ, “You are my beloved Son,” as we read that God the Father uttered a voice over Christ, saying:

> “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

But the one whom the paternal voice testified to be his beloved Son is the same one whom David is read to have called his Lord through the prophetic Spirit.

Therefore, according to human custom, David should be counted among Christ’s grandfathers or great-grandfathers, rather than being called his father—perhaps [possibly: “his own father”].

For if God the Father is not Christ’s proper Father, then he has no proper father at all, since the blessed Virgin conceived from no man’s seed but was impregnated by the Holy Spirit.

If you think the testimony of God the Father should be believed, believe that Christ is the Son of God. Or if you judge it right to believe the testimony of David himself through the prophetic Spirit, believe that the same one who is called David’s Son is David’s Lord.

### II

You say, then, that one man cannot have two natural fathers, but can have one natural father and another adoptive father.

I too shall say that no father can have one son who is both natural and adoptive with respect to him, because that one son cannot be divided so that he is both the father’s natural and adoptive son; nor can one part of the son be adopted and another natural in the dignity of sonship, as though one hand were adopted and the other proper, or the soul were adopted while the flesh possessed the status of sonship.

Although the soul does not come from the father’s seed as the flesh does, the son is one in soul and flesh, wholly adopted or wholly proper, according to what the condition of the name or nature entails.

In one person, however, there can be both passibility and impassibility, mortality and immortality, just as man is immortal in soul but mortal in flesh. So also Christ is impassible in divinity but passible in flesh. Yet wholly and altogether he is one and the same God and man: one Christ in the form of God and one Christ in the form of a servant; one Christ equal to the Father and one Christ lesser than the Father; the same God, the same man, one Son of God the Father wholly proper and the Virgin Mother’s wholly proper son.

Blessed Leo, pope of Rome, clearly testifies to this in his letter to Flavian [Note: St. Leo, pope, Letter 165 to Emperor Leo, chapter 8]:

> “Since, therefore, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him there is altogether one and the same person of true divinity and true humanity, we understand that the exaltation by which, as the Teacher of the Nations says, God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9) belongs to that same form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification.
>
> “For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction of essence and no diversity in majesty. Through the mystery of the Incarnation nothing had departed from the Word that would be restored to him as a gift from the Father.
>
> “The form of a servant, however, through which the impassible divinity fulfilled the sacrament of great piety, is human humility. Raised into the glory of divine power, it was joined in such unity from the very conception in the Virgin that divinity and humanity were so united that neither divine things were done without man nor human things without God.”

Do not suppose, therefore, O Felix, that you can investigate by human reasoning the birth of the Word of God by which he became flesh. You must not measure the omnipotence of divinity by human possibility.

He himself, who is the law of natures, is subject to no law of another nature. He who is incomprehensible cannot be comprehended by the feeble little calculations of human conjecture.

Therefore cease reducing the birth of the only-begotten God, whether divine or human, to the impossibility of our mortality. Do not attempt to prejudge by human definitions the one who was born beyond the conception of human origin—how he could be born or how he could be the proper Son of God while being born.

If you acknowledge that all things are possible for God, know that this too is possible for him: that he could create from the Virgin and possess as his proper Son the one who was born from her.

### III

You say:

> “What could be born from a slave woman except a slave?”

Your predecessor Pelagius once said this too, though in different words but with the same meaning, asserting that Christ was a solitary man. From this source Nestorius also established his heresy, by which he wished two persons to be understood in Christ.

Explain, then, how living creatures such as bees are born from flowers—that is, from insensible things—or expound the wondrous nature of bees and the exceedingly well-ordered arrangement of the commonwealth in their administration.

Perhaps you will say that this is because such a nature was established in them by the Creator. Consider and understand: the one who could create these miracles in the least of creatures—things that cannot be understood or narrated by man—could create for himself a free Son from a virgin womb.

Consider the height of heaven, the stability of the earth, the depth of the waters, and the diversity of all living things. Explain, if you can, the principles of all these things. And if you confess that this is impossible, why do you presumptuously intrude upon the ineffable miracle of Christ’s birth—how God could become man, man God, or the Son of God the son of man?

For the mystery of this birth, and also of the union of God and man, is greater than the creation of all creatures.

Grant, then, that God can do something which human weakness cannot comprehend. Let us not by our reasoning impose a law upon eternal majesty concerning what it can do, since the one who is omnipotent can do all things.

Nor is his power defective in this one birth of Christ, as though the one who is omnipotent could not create for himself as his proper or natural Son the man who was born from the Virgin.

Understand at last to what end and to how great a blasphemy this assertion of yours leads. Either confess Christ to be the proper and true Son of God the Father, in accordance with the omnipotence of his ineffable will; or, if you contend that this could not happen, acknowledge that God is powerless to accomplish his will. It is utterly impious to believe or say this.

Therefore, on the basis of this consideration, clothe yourself in the better faith. Recognize your own weakness and confess that God can do everything he wills, while you cannot understand everything the Creator wills to bring about.

## IV.

For many of the saints have professed that they neither understood nor could explain this wondrous generation of Christ. Among them was Isaiah, who, after foretelling the weaknesses, reproaches, scourges, and spittings that Christ suffered for our salvation, added this as well: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Blessed John the Baptist likewise testified that he was unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal (Mark 1:7). Blessed Gregory explained this in his homilies as follows [Note: [Col. 0165D] Saint Gregory, Homily 7 on the Gospels.]:

> “But the mystery of this incarnation,” he says, “the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate. For it cannot in any way investigate how the Word became embodied, how the highest and life-giving Spirit was made alive within a mother’s womb, or how he who has no beginning both exists and is conceived. The strap of the sandal, therefore, is the bond of the mystery. John cannot loosen the strap of his sandal, because even he who recognized this mystery through the spirit of prophecy is not sufficient to investigate the mystery of the incarnation. What, then, does it mean to say, ‘I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal,’ except openly and humbly to confess his ignorance? It is as though he plainly said: ‘What wonder if he is preferred to me, whom I perceive to have been born after me, but whose birth I do not comprehend?’”

## V.

Jerome too, a teacher honored throughout the Church of Christ, did not blush to confess in his exposition of Psalm 98 (Psalm 98:15) that he was entirely ignorant of this generation of Christ [Note: [Col. 0165D] Saint Jerome, on Psalm 98. The words that Alcuin cites here are not found in the commonly published Breviary of Saint Jerome. They are, however, found in the oldest ninth-century manuscript of our monastery’s library, Saint Emmeram’s, marked number 134. It contains a treatise on the Psalter under Saint Jerome’s name, differing in many places from the printed editions.]:

> “See,” he says, “what I dare to say: I so greatly adore [Ms., ‘adore’] the footstool, which once existed, just as I adore the throne. For although we knew Christ according to the flesh, [‘yet now we know him no longer according to the flesh’ (2 Corinthians 5:16)], he may have had a footstool before his death, before his resurrection, when he ate, when he drank, when he endured our human emotions. But after he rose and ascended victoriously into heaven, I do not understand one person sitting and another footstool; rather, the whole of Christ is the throne. He asks and says: ‘Why, or for what reason?’ I do not know how it is, and yet I believe that it is. I would be astonished if I were ignorant of the mystery of divinity, since I do not understand even myself. You ask me how it is that divinity and incarnation are one [Ms., ‘how divinity and incarnation are one’], while I do not know how I live. To have understood God is to have believed; to know God is to honor him. It is enough for me to know what is written; it is enough for me to know what I believe [Col. 0165D]. Beyond this I neither want nor desire anything. For if I wish to know, I begin to lose even what I believe. We are called faithful, not rational [Ms., ‘reasoning’]. Finally, the Lord himself says: ‘Do you believe that I can do this?’ And he says to the woman: ‘Your faith has saved you’ (Matthew 9:22)—not reasoning, not inquiry, not asking why or how it happened. She believed that it would happen, and it happened [Ms., ‘and it happened because she believed’].”

## VI.

In a similar manner, the aforementioned Father Gregory, in his Paschal homily, restrained presumptuous inquiry into Christ’s birth in these words [Note: [Col. 0166D] Saint Gregory the Great, Homily 22 on the Gospels, no. 8.]:

> “Whoever, therefore,” he says, “desires to celebrate the solemnity of Paschal joy must neither cook the lamb in water nor eat it raw: he must neither seek, through human wisdom, to penetrate the depth of its incarnation, nor believe in him as though he were merely a man; rather, he must eat the flesh roasted by fire, so that he may know that all things are administered through the power of the Holy Spirit.”

And shortly afterward:

> “And whatever remains of it you shall burn with fire” (Exodus 12:10). We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit whatever we cannot understand or penetrate concerning the mystery of his incarnation, so that no one may presumptuously dare either to despise or to condemn what he does not understand, but may entrust it to the fire and reserve it with the Holy Spirit [Saint Gregory: “entrusts it to the fire”].

By these and similar testimonies of the holy Fathers, human humility should restrain itself within the limits of its own measure. It should cease to assess the wondrous birth of our Savior by human reasoning, and should not seek to understand more than it ought to understand. Let it hear the counsel of the wisest Solomon, who says: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too deep for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22). Let it also set before itself another statement of the same author, by which he terrified the presumption of human weakness: “It is not good for him who eats much honey, and he who is an investigator of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Proverbs 25:16).

If we patiently remain ignorant of the birth of our own origin—how the soul gives life in the mother’s womb to the tender substance of our flesh—how much more must we confess that we can in no way comprehend or understand the ineffable union of almighty God and human nature?

God came into the world as he wished, when he wished, and from whom he wished. Neither time, nor person, nor human custom, nor the examples of created things prejudiced his will or prevented it from being accomplished. For the law of created things could not oppose him who himself is the creator of all. It was always ready for him to do what he wished, because power accompanied his will. “O man, who are you to answer God?” Will you impose a law upon him who is the law of the universe, since every creature is subject to his will?

## VII.

But you say, as it is written in your letter: “It must in no way be believed that almighty God the Father, who is spirit, generates flesh from himself.”

Tell me, I ask, whether you know that you have a soul. Surely you are not so ignorant that you do not know that you have a soul. You also know that you had a carnal father, from whose flesh the soul within you was neither produced nor generated, as the catholic faith holds. How, then, can it be that you yourself are wholly the proper and true son of your father, from whose flesh your soul was not generated?

But if you agree that you are your father’s proper son, with soul and body, although only your flesh was produced from the substance of your father and mother, then consider with the eyes of your heart all the more carefully, so that you may understand that Jesus Christ can become the proper and true Son of God the Father in both substances.

Or is his power powerless in this respect, so that he cannot accomplish in his Son what he causes to occur in all human beings? Or is your father more powerful than God in this matter, so that he could possess you as his proper son in soul and body, although the soul was introduced into the body from elsewhere?

But if no one can be a proper and true son unless he was born wholly from the substance of his father, then among all human beings no father has a proper and true son except from the flesh alone. Do you see into what folly this opinion of yours descends, and how contrary to all reason and to the whole human race your assertion is?

Therefore, using your own example and considering yourself, recognize that the sonship you assert in yourself can exist in the Son of God. You do not wish to divide yourself, on account of soul and flesh, into two sons—one proper and one adopted. By the same reasoning, do not attempt to divide Christ into two sons on account of the nature of his perfect divinity and perfect humanity, because our mediator Jesus Christ is one.

## VIII.

Your pamphlet continues as follows:

> “Therefore, you say, if we cannot find the name of adoption applied to Christ the Lord according to the flesh, in clear and explicit language in either Testament, as you maintain, nevertheless all the other things that belong to the word ‘adoption’ are plainly and openly found in many ways in the divine books. For what, I ask, is adoption for any son, except election, grace, will, assumption, reception, approval, or affiliation? None of these can in any way belong to a proper and true son. But if anyone wishes to deny the grace of adoption in Christ’s humanity, let him likewise strive to deny in him all the things that you have said belong to this adoption.”

What of these things that you have proposed, I ask, cannot occur in a proper son? Did not King David, with greater grace, choose Solomon, his proper son, as his successor to the kingdom than his other proper sons whom he had? Behold, there was greater grace, greater will, and greater choice in his case than in the case of his other sons, although they too were proper sons.

Nor can every assumption be adoption. The Son of God assumed flesh from the virgin’s womb into the unity of his person—not being changed into flesh, but so that he might be the proper Son of God in two substances, namely, of God and man. Just as previously, in one nature, he was the proper Son of God, losing nothing that he was, although he assumed what he was not. He made neither division in the propriety of the person nor mixture in the union of the natures.

But if, on account of assumption or reception, Christ who was born of the Virgin is an adopted son, to which person of the Holy Trinity must he be said to be adopted? Clearly, to the person of the Son. He himself assumed the man, or received him.

If this is so, Christ is the Father’s grandson according to his humanity, because the man was assumed by the Son of God—or, as you wish, adopted. Therefore, not every assumption is adoption.

It is read in the Gospel that the devil assumed him and set him on the pinnacle of the temple (Matthew 4:5). In this assumption by the devil there can be no adoption, but only wicked temptation.

Who does not know that approval can exist in many matters and not only in adoption? The same is true of affiliation. For we often read in histories: “That commander or that commander brought his camp up to this or that city.” If affiliation is adoption, then he adopted the city as his son, when in fact he came to conquer it.

## IX.

Here too your blind folly and unlearned presumption appear, by which you do not understand how contrary and opposed to all reason are the things you propose and affirm. You add even this: “So that because of the name ‘servant’ he is also adopted,” not understanding that among the former people, who were subjected to the harsh servitude of the Law, Christ was called by the prophets a servant on account of the great mystery of humility and the dispensation of true humanity.

We read in some places. For among the sons of grace—that is, among the new people—he is everywhere called the Son. These terms are plainly distinguished in one passage by the prophet Isaiah, who says: “A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6).

He who was a child or servant among the synagogue serving in the shadow is the Son among Christians living in the light of freedom. The Lord himself also seems to designate this distinction between son and servant in the Gospel, where he says: “A servant does not remain in the house forever, but the Son remains forever.” Immediately he adds: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:35–36).

Among unbelievers he is the son of a craftsman and a servant; among believers he is the Son of God and true God.

## X.

I do not know with what face, O new teacher, you profess yourself a priest of Christ while denying that Christ is God. The Jews closed the ears of their bodies so that they would not hear the Apostle Paul preaching that Christ is God. You close the eyes of your heart so that you will not understand that he is God.

Of him that outstanding preacher says: “But we preach Christ crucified, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). And indeed, the wisdom and power of God is certainly the Lord [The passage is corrupt. Perhaps: “And what is the wisdom and power of God? The Lord, certainly.”].

“We preach Christ crucified,” he says, “to the Jews a stumbling-block, and to the Gentiles foolishness.” For the cross of the Lord, which was foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling-block to the Jews, is both to you. There is no greater foolishness than refusing to believe the truth, nor a greater stumbling-block than refusing to hear what is true.

It seemed foolishness to the Gentiles that the Lord should be crucified; and to the Jews it was a stumbling-block that the Son of God should die. Your impiety might perhaps seem equal to that of the Jews, except that your crime is greater in this respect: they denied that he was God while his suffering still displayed his humanity; you deny that he is God after his resurrection has proved him to be God.

Thus they persecuted him on earth, while you persecute him even in heaven, refusing to preach as God the one reigning in heaven whose ministry you exercise in the Church.

## XI.

After listing the names by which you endeavor to establish that Christ is adopted, you add this:

> “Whoever decides to deny any one of these things, since one cannot stand without the other—or rather, whoever he may be, compelled by the truth of reason, whether he wishes it or not—will deny that he is a true man.”

But we confess truthfully and confidently that Christ is a true man and that he assumed true flesh from the Virgin. Nor is this statement of yours true: “He who strives to deny one of these things, because the others cannot stand,” namely, that because of assumption the man born of the Virgin must necessarily be the adopted Son of God the Father, as we proved above.

And if this one thing cannot stand, then according to your opinion all the others must likewise be rejected, because this one thing certainly cannot stand: that Christ is the adopted Son of God the Father because of his assumption of flesh.

## XII.

You say: “The name ‘adoption’ belongs to an elect creature, not to a reprobate one.”

Everyone who knows understands how true this is. For evil people too can have adopted sons, just as good people can, and this name is common to good and evil because it is found among both.

Anyone who reads secular histories will find that the custom of adoption exists even among pagans. Nor is adoption necessarily present everywhere that grace is present. It is said that Joseph found favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison (Genesis 39:21); this does not mean that the keeper adopted him as a son.

In many passages too one will find “favor” named in other senses, not always referring to adoption. The same is true of “election,” “assumption,” and the other names that you have contentiously gathered together in order to assert that Christ must be adopted because of these names. Anyone who carefully reads either sacred or secular writings understands that this is entirely untrue.

## XIII.

You say—and rightly say:

> “Christ is truth, he is justice, he is equity, he is piety, he is mercy; he does not wish anything to be believed or proclaimed about himself other than what he is.”

If Christ is truth, there is certainly no fiction in him. And if there is no fiction in him, he is certainly a true son and cannot be called adopted, since adoption is a kind of expression of will, not the truth of birth. The one who adopts a son from someone else wishes to possess in name one whom he does not possess by nature as his own.

According to the Psalmist, however, “truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12): clearly the true Son of God, who arose from the earth of our nature—that is, from virginal flesh—and was born true God and true man. We therefore believe of him what he is: truth.

It was fitting—truly fitting—that there should be in the Son of God the nobility, truth, and dignity of propriety, not adoption’s fellowship with the rest, nor the weakness of mere naming among others. For no fiction of designation could arise in Christ, who is truth and in whom all the fullness of divinity exists, as the Apostle testifies:

> “For Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was preached among you through us, through me [lacuna], was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but ‘Yes’ was in him. For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in him” (2 Corinthians 1:19–20).

## XIV.

This, then, is the substance of our disputation. I say—and I am not alone in saying it, for the entire harmony of the catholic Church testifies with devout faith—that Christ is God and the true Son of God, indeed true God, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

You say that he is an adopted son and a God only by designation.

Therefore I desire to hear from you whether you wish to worship as God the one who was crucified, died, and rose again on the third day [Perhaps: “whether you wish him to be worshiped”]. If you say that he must be worshiped, then you must consequently confess that the one whom you worship is God, lest that divine testimony condemn you by which the devil, terrified, withdrew from Christ when he heard him say: “Get behind me, Satan; it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve’” (Mark 8:33).

But if you judge that God who was crucified is not to be worshiped, then the angelic powers must be condemned, since they are shown to worship that same one seated upon the throne of the Father’s majesty. The Apostle testifies:

> “When he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him’” (Hebrews 1:6).

John, the expositor of this epistle, affirms in the homilies that he composed on the same epistle, in which this statement is found, that this was said of the man who was assumed [Note: [Col. 0169D] Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, no. 1, from the translation of Mutianus the Scholastic.]:

> “Whenever,” he says, “he is about to say something great and lofty, he first prepares the way and makes it receptive. Earlier he had said that God did not speak to us through prophets, but through him, and that the Son is greater than the angels, an argument he derived from the name itself. Here he wishes to derive arguments from another matter. From what matter? From worship, clearly. For he shows him to be as much greater as the Lord is known to be greater than servants. It is as though someone brought a person into a certain house and immediately ordered all the leaders of that house to worship him together, bowing down. So also he commanded all the angels to worship Christ according to the flesh, saying: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him.’”

In a passage of the following homily he repeats the same meaning, saying [Note: [Col. 0170D] The same author, Homily 5, no. 1.]:

> “Truly it is a great, wondrous, and astonishing thing that our flesh should sit above and be worshiped by angels, archangels, cherubim, and seraphim. Turning this over frequently in my mind, I am overcome with amazement, and I imagine greater things concerning the human race. For I see greater and glorious beginnings, with God hastening greatly [Chrysostom: ‘with God hastening much’] on account of our nature.”

## XV.

Learn, then, from the angels to believe that Christ is God and to worship him, lest you unhappily begin to doubt with the devil—or, worse, deny him in whom the devil doubted.

The devil said, “If you are the Son of God”; you say, “He is not the Son of God.” What the devil asked doubtfully, you deny emphatically. No one has yet been found, apart from the founders of this sect, who has surpassed the devil’s impiety in this respect: what he confessed could be true of the Lord, you do not believe could have been true.

Even if the devil departed from Christ after being driven away by the strongest testimonies of Holy Scripture, nevertheless every suspicion of his divinity remained in him right up to the cross. Nor did he then cease to regard him as the Son of God, after he discovered that Christ had allowed his persecutors such power over him.

But the cunning enemy attempted, even amid Christ’s bodily sufferings, to reach the recognition of his divinity, even at the very moment of his death. He spoke through those who had crucified him: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 27:42). They intended, of course, that the Lord, moved by the insults of their words, should abandon the mystery of human salvation by becoming angry at the injury.

But the great patience of God our Savior reserved the dispensation of his triumph and the mystery of our redemption for the glory of the resurrection. For it was a greater miracle that the dead man rose from the tomb to life than that the living man should have descended from the cross.

## XVI.

Your letter also continues:

> “Just as we believe and praise the things about him that are exalted and glorious, so we must in no way despise his humility and all the things unworthy of him that he mercifully wished to assume for our sake.”

You therefore say that the one who created us when we did not yet exist suffered all these unworthy things for us. We know who it is that created us: the proper Son of God.

How can both of these things be true—that the one who created us suffered these unworthy things for us, if the one who created us is the proper Son of God while the one who suffered is adopted? You cannot divide the Creator from him who suffered these things for us, as the very sequence of your argument proves.

But if there is one person, there is also one sonship, because, as has often been said, a proper son and an adopted son are two persons. The God and man who was assumed are one person. It is therefore necessary that there be one sonship in one person, so that the whole person is either a proper son or an adopted son. One person compels you to confess one sonship in two natures.

## XVII.

You set out the words of our letter [Note: See Alcuin’s letter to Felix above, column 121, no. 4.], where, after a suitable exhortation in our argument, we said:

> “O by how many examples of the holy Fathers we could prove this faith: that Christ Jesus is the true Son of God the Father, and that immediately from the conception in the virginal womb he was truly conceived as God and truly born as God.”

To this you replied [the text has “you reply”]:

> “These are the statements of your belief concerning the two natures in Christ, which you so confuse into the singularity of one person that you assert there is no difference between God and man, between the Word and flesh, between creator and creature, or between the one who assumes and the one who is assumed.”

In saying that we confuse the two natures into the singularity of one person, you speak partly truly, but partly, according to your usual custom, you falsely accuse us.

For we believe and confess, with the catholic Church, that the two natures in the one person of Christ are joined ineffably—not, as you say, confused with Eutyches—in such a way that the propriety of each nature remains, and, so to speak, the integrity of both is preserved. The divine things communicate with the human, and the human with the divine.

In this holy and wondrous union there is not a conversion of divinity, but an exaltation of humanity: not God changed into man, but man glorified in God. The divine nature did not cease to be what it was—that is, God—but the human nature began to be what it was not.

Thus, as we have often said and will always say, Christ is one, from two natures wondrously and ineffably united, wholly one and the true Son of God. Accordingly, in two natures he is both named and truly is one true God.

For almighty God never wishes anything to be said of him that is not true; this is wholly alien to the catholic faith. Rather, as we have said, the Son of God assumed the man in such a way that he lost nothing he possessed. With the assumption of man he remained the true Son of God, as he always is. His divinity was not diminished on account of man, nor was it changed into man.

Nor did man depart from the nature of humanity so as to cease to be man. The nature of humanity preserved the propriety of its nature, and the substance of divinity did not lose the propriety of divinity.

Nevertheless, Christ is man-God, and God became man, so that what the blessed Evangelist said might be true: “The Word became flesh.” In the name “Word” he signifies God, and in the name “flesh” he demonstrates man.

Blessed Jerome says of this against Jovinianus [Note: [Col. 0172D] Saint Jerome, Book II Against Jovinianus, no. 29.]:

> “The Word became flesh so that we might pass from flesh into the Word. The Word did not cease to be what it had been, nor did man lose what he was born to be. Glory was increased; nature was not changed.”

Blessed Augustine likewise says in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0172D] Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 34.]:

> “It would take a long time to say as much about this mediator as is worthy of him, although nothing worthy of him can be said by man. For who could explain in fitting words this one thing: that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), so that we might believe in the only-begotten Son of almighty God, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary?
>
> “Thus the Word became flesh, with flesh assumed into divinity [Augustine: ‘from divinity’], but with divinity not changed into flesh. Here we must understand ‘flesh’ as meaning man, the whole being signified by a part, just as it is said: ‘By works of the law no flesh will be justified’ (Romans 3:10), that is, no human being.
>
> “For it is not lawful to say that anything belonging to human nature was absent from that assumption, except that it was a nature entirely free from every bond of sin. It was not the nature born from both sexes through the desire of the flesh, with the guilt of sin attached, whose guilt is dissolved by regeneration; it was the nature that ought to be born from a virgin, whom the faith of his mother, not lust, had conceived.”

To that man, therefore, who was born of the Virgin, it was granted by a singular gift above all the other saints that, from the very moment he began to become man in the Virgin’s womb, he was also God. Hence that same glorious ever-virgin Mary must rightly be believed and confessed to be not only the mother of man but also the Mother of God.

## XVIII.

Among the other testimonies that you gather from Holy Scripture, you, often-mentioned Felix, set forth an evangelical and an apostolic statement. These most completely destroy the impiety of your evil belief. The Savior himself, lifting his eyes to the Father, says:

> “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

And again, from the letter of blessed John the Evangelist, where he says:

> “He assumed us and gave us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

If, therefore, “God,” as the angel foretold to the blessed Virgin Mary, is the name of the humanity assumed by the Son of God, and if Christ, because of his royal dignity, is truly and altogether—as the same Evangelist testifies, whether in the Gospel where Truth itself speaks or in his letter—the very one called Jesus Christ, who is true God and the true Son of God, then either these names must be removed from the humanity of the Son of God, or, if these names belong properly to the one who was born of the Virgin [Supplement: “or something similar”], then that man who was born of the Virgin and is called by these names is true God and the true Son of God.

But because more seems to need to be said about this very question, we have decided to bring the present pamphlet to an end here, so that what follows may be reserved for discussion in the next pamphlet.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0173]

## I.

There follows in the pamphlet of the aforementioned teacher an argument of the worst and, since the beginning of the world, unheard-of blasphemy, by which, with utterly impious presumption, he contradicts the divinity of Christ God. It seems necessary to destroy this argument by the many testimonies of the holy Fathers.

Therefore I beseech the reader not to criticize me for being too lengthy in this series of argument. True faith can be presented in simple speech to devout listeners; but an assertion of impiety must be dissolved by the authority of many testimonies. Thus, even if he regards the judgment of our smallness as contemptible, he may at least be overcome by the manifold authority of catholic teachers and corrected by the gift and merciful clemency of Christ God.

## II.

He sets out words of this kind:

> “In the second manner, however,” he says, “God is called by designation, as was said above of the holy preachers, concerning whom the Savior said to the Jews: ‘If he called them gods to whom the word of God came’ (John 10:35). They were called gods under him, not by nature as God, but because they had been made gods by the grace of God by him who is the true God.
>
> “In this order the Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer, according to his humanity, shares with them most truly, just as in nature so also in name, although he was chosen more excellently than all of them. He shares with them also in all the other things—that is, in predestination, election, grace, reception, assumption, the assumption of the name of servant, affiliation, and other things similar to these—so that the same one who is essentially true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of divinity might himself, in the form of humanity, be made God with his elect through the grace of adoption, and be God by designation.”

A little earlier you called him true God, on the authority of the Gospel and of the Evangelist himself. How, then, do you now call him God by designation?

You must either agree with the authority of the Gospel and with the testimony of Truth itself that you cited, where it says: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), and with what the same Evangelist says: “That we may know the true God and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 5:20); or you must confirm your opinion by some other testimony greater than that of Truth itself, or of so great an Apostle and Evangelist who reclined upon the Lord’s breast.

If you dare not do this—indeed, because you cannot—then what remains is for you, condemning your own opinion, to erase from your heart this name of designated divinity in Christ, a name invented by man, not by God, and composed by human invention, not by divine authority.

### III.

Let the blessed Apostle say what he thinks about this, or of whom he spoke that statement which you too have cited: “Who is over all, God blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). He says, therefore, with Christ speaking in him:

“I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; to them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Rom. 9:3–5).

Understand the sequence of the Apostle’s words. He testifies concerning the Israelites, as though wishing to excuse himself for not observing their law—not because of envy, but because, having understood the truth, he preferred to obey the truth. He speaks of their promises, that is, of the Israelites, whose fathers were the patriarchs, and from whom—that is, from those patriarchs—Christ was born according to the flesh. He did not hesitate to call him also “God blessed forever”: God, I say, he called the one who was born carnally from the lineage of the Fathers blessed—not merely a titular God.

Concerning this statement, the blessed Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, says in his letter to the Armenians [Note: The letter of Blessed Proclus and this passage are found in *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VI.]:

> “The Apostle called him Christ, in order to show that he truly became man as God. He called him ‘the one who is,’ in order to declare that he is without beginning. He called him ‘over all,’ in order to proclaim him Lord of all creation. He called him ‘blessed,’ so that we may humbly adore him as almighty, and not attack him with accusations as though he were our fellow servant.”

Likewise Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, on the unity of person and the distinct character of the two natures of the Son of God [Note: St. Cyril of Alexandria, in the *Scholia*, vol. V; the second testimony, however, is lacking there shortly afterward. Cyril has nearly identical material in the cited work, chapter 17.]:

> “There is therefore one,” he says, “who is God before the incarnation [Cyril: ‘true God’], and who remained in humanity, in whom was what he was [Cyril: ‘that which he was’], and is, and will be. We do not therefore divide the one Lord Jesus Christ by distinguishing a man separately and God separately; rather, we say that he is one and the same Jesus Christ. We do not disregard the differences of the natures, but preserve them unconfused with one another [Cyril: ‘setting them’].”

And shortly afterward [Note: St. Cyril does not say “shortly afterward” in that place, but in another passage, namely in the *Letter to Nestorius*, vol. IV of the Council of Mansi, p. 890, and vol. V, p. 497; and in vol. V, part II of St. Cyril’s works, Letter 6, p. 24. In all these places, however, the interpretation of the Greek text differs in wording from Alcuin’s version.]:

> “We confess Christ as one God and Lord, not worshiping a man together with the Word, lest some appearance of division be introduced, but worshiping one and the same, because his body is not alien to the Word, with which he himself also sits at the Father’s side [Quercet.: *adsedet*, ‘sits beside’]. We do not say this as though two sons were sitting beside him, but as one with the flesh through unity. For if, wishing to evade such a union effected according to substance as either impossible or insufficiently seemly, we are deceived, we fall into saying that there are two sons. For [Reading from Cyril: ‘For it is necessary’] we must not distinguish and teach that a separate man was honored merely by the title of Son, and again that the Word who is from God is by name and in truth the Son of God; rather, we must not divide into two sons the one Lord Jesus Christ.”

Likewise the blessed Hilary, in the ninth book of the Catholic faith [Note: St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IX, section 3]:

> “This, then, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess the Word and the flesh. We must neither fail to recognize that God is also man, nor fail to recognize that the flesh is the Word.”

The blessed Cassian also puts forward statements consistent with the Gospel testimonies, apostolic teachings, and the understanding of the holy Fathers, in that book which he wrote against the sect of heretical depravity [Note: I do not know which book Cassian wrote against the sect of heretical depravity, or concerning the mystery of Christ’s passion, and so on. I have not been able to find these passages, cited here, in the books *On the Incarnation of the Lord*.]:

> “The Old Testament,” he says, “has sung in harmony with the New; let David yield to John.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The same one whom David calls true man—because Mother Zion says, ‘A man, and a man was born in her’—John knows as true God and proclaims him as such, because ‘the Most High himself founded her’ (Ps. 86:5). The same one whom John knows as true man when he hears him say, ‘You seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you’ (John 8:40), he shows to be true God when he says, ‘This is the true God and eternal life’ (1 John 5:20).
