He recognizes Christ as true man because ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’; and he shows him to be the same true God because ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’”

And shortly afterward the same Cassian, in the third book concerning the mystery of Christ’s passion and the unity of the Son of God, says:

> “Thus the true and supreme God wholly received the entire man into himself, and thus the fullness of divinity, while the truth of the divine and human substance remained unconfused, fully joined himself to man, so that thereafter, with the unity of person remaining forever, neither Christ the man could be separated from his divinity, nor the same Christ God from his humanity. Yet one and the same Christ, through the reality of human suffering, restored what had been ours, and through the reality of the divine, impassible nature, bestowed what had been his. Thus the unconfused truth of both natures endured, so that neither man could be torn away from God, nor God separated from the man he had assumed.”

Concerning this unity, the distinguished teacher, the blessed Augustine, says in the first book of *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter thirteen, among many other statements agreeing with the Catholic faith [Note: St. Augustine, cited work, section 26]:

> “Unless the same one were also the Son of Man because of the form of a servant which he received, who is the Son of God because of the form of God in which he exists, the Apostle Paul would not have said concerning the rulers of this age: ‘For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Cor. 2:8). He was crucified according to the form of a servant, and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. Such indeed was that assumption which made God man and man God.”

Likewise in the same book, chapter seven [Note: The same work, chapter 7, section 14]:

> “For he did not receive the form of a servant in such a way as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father.”

### IV.

If, then, the form of a servant was assumed without the form of God being lost, and if in both the form of a servant and the form of God the same one is the only-begotten Son of God the Father, then the one whom your rashness declares adoptive the blessed Augustine did not hesitate to call only-begotten. Where there is an only-begotten son, there is no place for an adoptive one.

Nor, according to your assertion, is he only-begotten merely in the divine nature and firstborn in the human, since the blessed Virgin bore no other than the true and only-begotten Son of God the Father and her own son. He is firstborn in humanity, as the Evangelist says: “Until she bore her firstborn son” (Matt. 1:25); but in the divine birth, as the Apostle says: “The firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:15). He himself is before all things, and all things subsist in him. According to the form of a servant, he himself is the head of the body, the Church.

Regarding the statement of the teacher of the nations which we said above that the blessed Augustine expounded—“For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory”—the outstanding teacher Cyril says in his second letter to Successus [Note: Cyril, vol. V, part II]:

> “The blessed Paul affirms that not only the Lord of glory but also God, blessed over all forever, had his own body of the Word fastened to the wood.”

Peter, bishop of Ravenna, also confirms in his sermon this holy faith: that Jesus, who was born from the Virgin, is true God. Among other testimonies to the Catholic faith, he says [Note: Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 114, p. 956, vol. VII of *Bibliotheca Patrum*]:

> “You will conceive in your womb,” the angel says, “and bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:31). In Hebrew, *Jesus*; in Greek, σωτήρ (*sōtēr*), “Savior”; in Latin, *Salvator*, “Savior.” Rightly, therefore, all things are safe for the Virgin who bore the Savior. “You will call his name Jesus,” because in this name the whole majesty of divinity is worshiped: all who dwell in heaven, all who inhabit the earth, and all who are held in the depths of hell prostrate themselves before this name and worship it. Hear the Apostle saying: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10).

> This is the name that gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, movement to the lame, speech to the mute, and life to the dead; and by the power of this name it drove out the whole power of the devil from possessed bodies. If it is only a name, how great is its power? But who is the one called by this name? Let the Angel say: “He will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32). You see that what the Virgin conceived was not born from earthly seed but from a heavenly conception; the Virgin bore him, but God received the Son [Note: The printed edition reads: “It is not an earthly seed, but a heavenly one; the Virgin bore him, but God received the Son.”].

> Therefore, whoever argues about this birth in merely human terms aims at every possible insult against so great a parent.

### V.

Understand, O unlearned rashness, what room for titular designation or adoption in Christ can remain after the testimonies of so many Fathers. The Truth itself says: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). God joined himself to human nature, so that there might be one God in two natures and one Son of God. Who can separate what Jesus made one, or divide what God joined together?

For if, because of the manifest blasphemy, you fear confessing two persons in one Christ, nevertheless you do not fear confirming in your confession everything that must belong to two persons. Are there not two, then: the one who is true God and the one who is titular God? Are there not also two: the one who is the adoptive Son and the one who is the true Son? One person belongs to the true God and another to the titular god; one person belongs to the true Son of God and another to the adoptive son.

Anyone who reads the Gospel history can understand that *Jesus* and *Christ* are names of the humanity in the Son of God. And if Jesus Christ, who was born from the Virgin, is not true God, how does the universal Church throughout the world, in its common custom—and, I think, you yourselves—in all the prayers sung during the solemnities of Mass, habitually say:

> “Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever”?

He himself also said to his apostles—the one who suffered and rose again: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 18:18). To whom was authority given, if not to the one who was born from the Virgin? For, as you said shortly before:

> “The Son of God, born substantially from God, essentially possessed all authority with the Father and the Holy Spirit; but this authority was given to the Son of the Virgin.”

And if he possesses all authority, how can he not be altogether true God and the true Son of God? Moses was a titular god, yet all authority was not given to him; therefore he struck the rock a second time to draw out water. Whatever miracles Christ performed in the world while he lived among human beings in visible presence, he did by his own power, as the powerful and true God.

Could any of the saints, by himself, do anything apart from him who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)? Say, then, from where the apostles performed such great works in the name of Jesus, if Jesus himself did not possess his own power but only a titular power. Tell me also, I ask you, who contradict the divinity of Jesus and refuse to acknowledge in him his own power, but call it another’s gift: how did his name possess such great power that he himself, whose name it is—and whom you blaspheme—needed it? How were demons cast out, the weak healed, and the dead raised in his name?

For the Apostle Peter said to the lame man who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). Again, in the city of Joppa, he said to Aeneas, who had lain paralyzed in bed for eight years: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed” (Acts 9:34). Paul likewise said to the spirit of Python: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ, come out of her.” And the demon came out (Acts 15:16).

Understand, therefore, how far this weakness was from the Lord: even those who were weak were not weak when they were able to do such things through his name, which he himself powerfully exercised through his own name. For we know that, after God’s resurrection, no demons or illnesses resisted any of the apostles. Was he weak in himself whose faith reigned over all things even through others?

What does it mean, moreover, that he himself, whose power you diminish, said to his disciples: “In my name cast out demons”? Did he need another’s name in order to exercise power, when he made his own name itself power? But what more is added? “Behold,” he says, “I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19).

The Apostle, writing to Titus, did not hesitate to call the one whom you call a titular god “the great God”:

> “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, training us to renounce impiety and worldly desires and to live temperately, justly, and devoutly in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:11–13).

The blessed Jerome explained the meaning of this statement in his commentary on the same Epistle:

> “Where is Arius, that serpent? Where is Eunomius, that snake? Jesus Christ the great God is called Savior—not ‘the firstborn of all creation,’ not ‘the Word of God and Wisdom’ [which are titles of divine generation; Note: These words are absent from Jerome]—but Jesus and Christ, which are names of the assumed man. Nor do we say that there is one Jesus Christ and another Word, as the new heresy slanders us; rather, we say that he is the same one both before the ages [St. Jerome adds: ‘and after the ages’], and before the world and after Mary. Indeed, from Mary we call Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, our great God and Savior.”

### VI.

Who, then, is the one who will judge the world: merely a solitary man, or God the Son of Man? You are not so hostile to the truth that you would dare contradict the testimony of Truth itself, which says: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19:28).

The Apostle Paul likewise unequivocally affirmed that the same one who will judge the world is God, saying to the Romans: “Otherwise, how will God judge this world?” (Rom. 3:6). Unless, perhaps, because in one Epistle the Apostle says that we shall be revealed before the tribunal of Christ (2 Cor. 5:10), and in another, before the tribunal of God (Rom. 14:10)? [Note: Something is missing.]

Love life; love your salvation; love the one through whom you were redeemed; fear the one by whom you will be judged. Whether you wish it or not, you will be revealed before the tribunal of Christ. Set aside the blasphemy of impiety and the chant of unbelieving words. If you think that the tribunal of God is something other than Christ’s, come before the tribunal of Christ, and you will discover from both testimonies, by an inexplicable proof, that the tribunal of God is the same as Christ’s, and that the whole power of divinity and the majesty of God the Father are in the one Son, Jesus Christ.

The same preacher of the nations, writing to the Corinthians and showing that Christ possesses both the dispensation of the flesh and the true sublimity of divinity, says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). In these very few words he demonstrates the great mystery of Christ’s incarnation.

The blessed Cassian, explaining these words in a Catholic sense (*On the Incarnation*, book III, chapter 3), says:

> “The preaching of apostolic teaching therefore rose, as it were, to a higher level; and although the meaning in both passages agrees, it confirms the mystery of perfect faith in a more explicit statement, saying: ‘Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer.’ This means that previously we knew him both as man and as God, but now only as God [Quercet.: ‘as God to be worshiped’]. With the weakness of the flesh having ceased, we now know nothing in him except the power of divinity; for everything in God is the power of divine majesty, where the weakness of human frailty has ceased to exist.

> “Thus he has wholly explained by this testimony the mystery both of the assumed flesh and of perfect divinity. In saying, ‘Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh,’ he spoke of the mystery of God born in the flesh. By adding, ‘Now we know him no longer,’ he expressed the force of the weakness that had been laid aside [Cassian: ‘he explained’]. Accordingly, knowledge of that flesh refers to the signification of man, while ignorance refers to the honor of divinity.

> “This is what he means: ‘We knew Christ according to the flesh’ for as long as that which was to be known according to the flesh existed; ‘now we know him no longer,’ after it ceased to exist [Cassian: ‘after it ceased’]. For the nature of the flesh has been transferred into spiritual substance, and what was once human has become wholly divine. Therefore we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, because, with bodily weakness absorbed by divine majesty, nothing remains in the sacred body from which the weakness of the flesh in him can be recognized.

> “Accordingly, whatever had previously been of two substances has become of one power. There can be no doubt that Christ, who was crucified through our weakness, lives wholly through divine majesty.”

And shortly afterward, in chapter 5:

> “The Apostle therefore rightly proclaimed that he had been sent both by God the Father and by God the Son, and immediately added the confession of the Lord’s incarnation, saying: ‘Who raised him from the dead’ (Gal. 1:1). He thus taught that the true body of God incarnate had been raised from the dead, in accordance with the statement: ‘Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh,’ rightly adding, ‘but now we know him no longer.’

> “For he says that we know him according to the flesh in that he was raised from the dead; but that we no longer know him according to the flesh in that, with the frailty of the flesh having ceased, we know him only as existing in the power of God.”

### VII.

Hear, then, what the same Apostle says about Christ, and whether he wished him to be understood as man or also as God: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

Here I want you to explain to me, O Felix, whether this one whom the Apostle says speaks within him is man or God. If man, how could the body of another speak in his heart? If God, then Christ is not man but God—for since Christ spoke in the Apostle, and only God could speak in him, Christ God spoke in him.

You see, therefore, that nothing can now be said here against this. No separation or division can be made between Christ and God, because God is wholly in Christ and Christ wholly in God. No separation, no division can be admitted here. There is only one simple and sound confession: to adore, love, and worship Christ God.

The blessed Jerome also agrees with the views of the Fathers cited above: that the man assumed by the Word of God was glorified by the power of divinity and that one God, with an undivided majesty, is to be worshiped in Christ. He expresses the same meaning more explicitly in the third book of his *Commentaries on the Prophet Jeremiah*, where he says, on chapter 17:

> “If the man who trusts in man is accursed (Jer. 17:5), then those who confess Jesus to be merely man will be accursed. If it is objected to us that we too believe in the one who says, ‘But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God; Abraham did not do this, but you do the works of your father’ (John 8:40), we shall answer with the apostolic statement: ‘Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer.’

> “Finally, the same Apostle writes at the beginning of his Epistle to the Galatians: ‘Paul, an Apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me’ (Gal. 1:1–2). If death has been swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54), why should the lowliness of the flesh, assumed for human salvation, not have passed into the majesty of divinity, so that the two might become one?”

Here the blessed Jerome does not indicate a confusion of the two natures, but a unity of power, so that we may believe in one divine power in Christ the Lord our God, lest a duality of majesty be asserted in Christ, in whom there is the indivisible unity of person.

Likewise the same author, in the same work and context:

> “From these things we also learn that God alone knows the thoughts of human beings. If it is said of the Savior, ‘Jesus saw their thoughts’ (Luke 11:17), and no one can see thoughts except God alone, then Christ too is God [is], the one who searches hearts and will repay each person according to his works.”

Likewise in his third book on the prophet Amos:

> “Then also the firstborn people of God, Israel [Jerome: ‘the firstborn Son of God, the people Israel’], who had laid hands upon the only-begotten and truly Son of God, were delivered over to eternal mourning, and their final days—or those who were with them—were filled with bitterness.”

Likewise in his first book on Zechariah:

> “Nor is it surprising,” he says, “if Christ is called almighty, to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (Matt. 24:18), and who says, ‘Everything that belongs to the Father is mine’ (John 17:10).”

### VIII.

How can someone be considered Catholic who neither believes the testimonies of so many teachers, nor is moved to belief by apostolic authority, nor agrees with the divine truth expressed throughout the Gospel pages?

The whole of sacred Scripture therefore shines with the radiance of this faithful Catholic confession, like stars gleaming in the heavens. No designation of divinity is ascribed to Christ in them without the power of truth [F.: *sine*, ‘without,’ for *sive*]; rather, all the benefits of healing and miracles of signs that he performed are testified to have been accomplished by his own power.

There is no doubt that he himself, by his own authority, did everything marvelous that is read about him. We must be exceedingly careful not to think that anything in Christ was done through deceptive imitation. Rather, we must believe that everything read about him, whether in names or deeds, was done and spoken in complete reality, because in truth no shadow of fiction can be found.

He who will always be true God in God the Father is true God also in the man. He who is truly the Son of Man is also that same true Son of God; and the same one is man-God because of God, and God-man because of man, just as in every human being there are soul and body.

This unity and truth in Christ did not begin after the Virgin’s childbirth, but was joined and united in the Virgin’s womb itself. We must take careful precautions, therefore, to confess Christ not merely as one after baptism or resurrection, but as always one from the moment he was conceived in the virginal womb. For it is intolerable blasphemy to grant that he is now one while nevertheless maintaining that at some time he was not one but two.

Thus this Felix, with his followers, also seems to think in the following passage of his writings:

> “If, as you wish, a man assumed by the Son of God was, immediately from the conception in the virginal womb, truly conceived as God, and was truly born God, how does the Son of God himself, speaking through the voice of the servant-form, bear witness about himself to the prophecy of the Old Testament, that he was formed as a servant from his mother’s womb? He says through the prophet Isaiah: ‘And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself, to bring Jacob back to him, and Israel will not be gathered’ [Isa. 49:5; the printed text includes *non*, ‘not’].”

Consider carefully, reader, what he wishes to be understood about Christ when he reproaches us for wanting the same one who came forth from the virginal womb like a bridegroom from his chamber to be true God, conceived [Supply: “conceived”] and born. For he says, “if, as you wish.” It is clear that he does not want what he charges us with wanting. He tries to affirm his own position by prophetic testimony, so that Christ might be considered more a servant formed from the womb than God—the one whom the entire Catholic Church, from the very beginning of his sacred conception, confesses and proclaims to be true God, since it holds as certain from the Gospel testimony that he was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

For what ought to have been born from God except God?

### IX.

This Felix also frequently insists that Christ is a conditional servant, not understanding that he was called a servant according to the mystery of the divine dispensation—not by the condition of due servitude, as we said above, but through voluntary obedience in fulfilling the Father’s will for the salvation of humanity.

For everything done in Christ was a matter of will, not necessity. As the Apostle testifies, he “humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8). Voluntary humility is one thing; servile necessity is another.

Some things are said of Christ according to the property of his nature, such as “the way, the truth, and the life.” Other things were proclaimed about him by the prophets through a signification of the things that were to be accomplished through him. It is according to this manner of speaking that Christ must be understood to be called a servant by the prophets.

For immediately after the prophet gave this testimony about him, he added: “I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6). And lest the honor of so great a light appear insignificant, he added:

> “Kings shall see and arise; princes shall prostrate themselves, because of the Lord, for he is faithful, and because of the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you” (Isa. 49:7).

But if he is a servant, how is he worshiped by kings and princes?

Shortly before, the same prophet, speaking in the person of the one whom he prophetically called a servant, says: “He made me like an arrow.”

“Christ,” however, as the blessed Jerome says in his commentary on Isaiah 49, “is one chosen arrow from among many arrows and many sons, and is the only-begotten Son. To him the Father’s voice immediately replied: ‘You are my servant, Israel, because in you I shall be glorified’ (Isa. 49:3). He is a servant because, although he existed in the form of God, he graciously deigned to assume the form of a servant; and he is Israel because he was born from the seed of the Jews. What cannot be understood of any other servants is then added: ‘because in you I shall be glorified.’ For he himself says in the Gospel: ‘Father, glorify your name’ (John 12:28); and in the Psalm he speaks to the Son: ‘Rise up, my glory, psaltery and lyre’ (Ps. 56:9), that is, the chorus of all virtues.”

Thus the aforesaid Father Jerome, separating Christ from the servitude of our conditional necessity, speaks of him. From this it is understood that Christ is not called a servant according to the common condition of humanity, but must be understood according to a higher mystery.

If Christ is a servant, how did he make so many free, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “We are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom by which Christ did not set us free” (Gal. 4:31). The Truth itself also says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

For if all the saints are free according to the word of the Truth, who is Christ, how did he alone remain a servant—the one who makes free all who believe in him? Concerning them he says elsewhere: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15). And in the same Gospel: “A servant does not remain in the house forever, but the Son remains” (John 8:35).

The Lord, however, as the holy Augustine says, was not a servant in the form of a servant, but was Lord in the form of a servant.

### X.

That true God was conceived at the very origin of Christ’s most holy incarnation can be affirmed by the testimonies of many Catholic Fathers. We have chosen to set down a few of them here, because the matter under discussion is so clear and well known that it does not require many witnesses; its witnesses are as numerous as the faithful.

The blessed Augustine therefore says in the often-mentioned book *Enchiridion*, chapter 36:

> “Was he previously a man, and was this singular benefit bestowed upon him by which he might singularly merit God? Indeed, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God. And this was uniquely because of God the Word, who, having assumed him, became flesh—and was certainly God. Just as every human being is one person, consisting, namely, of rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, consisting of the Word and man.”

Likewise Fulgentius, in the book *On the Catholic Faith* (*On Faith to Peter*, chapter 18):

> “Hold this most firmly,” he says, “and do not doubt in any way: it was not the flesh of Christ that was conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before being assumed by the Word; rather, the Word of God himself was conceived through the assumption of his flesh, and that flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word of God.”

It is not surprising that a heretic dares to assert that Christ, who was born from the Virgin, is a titular god, when he insists in every way, through prophetic testimonies not understood in the Catholic sense, that the same Christ is a servant, and reproaches us as though it were a fault to proclaim the one born from the Virgin to be true God.

From this his entire error seems to have arisen: that, out of some servant, he might make an adoptive son or a titular god. For he affirms three things concerning Christ: that he is a conditional servant, that he is an adoptive son, and that he is a titular god.

Conversely, he denies three things: that true God was born from the Virgin; that the one who was born is the true Son of God; and that it is in any way possible for one who was born a servant not to require the regeneration of baptism.

But now it is time for him who is overshadowed by the darkness of impious error to be overwhelmed by a cloud of witnesses.

## XI

Hilary, illustrious in every virtue and adornment, and distinguished in eloquence as well as in life, says in the second book on the faith (*On the Trinity*, Book II, §§25 and 27; Book IX, §5):

> “The one and only-begotten God, inserted in the womb of the holy Virgin in the form of a little human body [Hilary: ‘into the form’], and adhering [Hilary: ‘growing’], who contains all things and within whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth.”

Again, in the same book:

> “The angel is witness: God is with us, he who is born.”

Likewise, in his ninth book:

> “The one and only-begotten God, therefore, born from a human being [Hilary: ‘from the Virgin’] as a human being, will, in the fullness of time, advance God in himself as a human being [Hilary: ‘will advance into God the human being’]. He consistently maintained this manner of evangelical speech, so that he might teach that he should be believed to be the Son of God and admonish that he should be proclaimed as the Son of man [Hilary: ‘believed … proclaimed’]: speaking and acting as a human being in all that belongs to God, and then speaking and acting as God in all that belongs to the human being.”

In the preface to his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew, he likewise says:

> “For it was first necessary for us that the one God should be recognized as having been born a human being for our sake.”

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Saint Hilary. This preface, which Saint Jerome nevertheless mentions in his *Catalogue of the Works of Saint Hilary*, and which Cassian likewise cites in Book VII *On the Incarnation*, is now lost. The text in Cassian reads as follows: “For it was first necessary for us that the only-begotten God should, for our sake, be generated as a human being, something he was not at that time.”]

Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, also offered the following testimony concerning Christ’s birth in his Paschal Letter:

> “The one Son of the Father and our mediator neither lost his equality with him nor was separated from our fellowship: invisible God [Note: [Col. 0184D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Theophilus.] [and visible God: invisible human being] and visible human being, hidden in the form of a servant and acknowledged by the confession of believers as the Lord of glory. For the Father did not deprive him of the name of his nature after he had become poor as a human being for our sake; nor, when he was baptized in the Jordan River, did he call him by another name, but ‘only-begotten Son’: ‘You are,’ he says, ‘my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matthew 3:17).”

Ambrose, the outstanding priest of God, recalls the following in his book addressed to virgins:

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Saint Ambrose; more probably the uncertain author of Sermon 111, *On the Nativity of the Lord*, §4, among the works of Saint Augustine.]

> “Glorious virginity and splendid fruitfulness! The Lord of the world is born, and there is no groaning of the woman giving birth, because it was fitting that, when God was born, the merit of chastity should increase.”

Jerome, the most renowned teacher of the catholic faith, says in his book addressed to the virgin Eustochium (*Letter 22*, §29):

> “The Son of God became the son of a human being for our salvation. He waits ten months [Others: nine months] in the womb in order to be born … and he whose grasp encloses the world is confined within the narrowness of a manger [Jerome: ‘and he, enclosing the world in his fist, is confined within the narrowness of a manger’].”

[Note: [Col. 0185D] “Ten months.” Martianaeus also read this way. All the other printed editions, according to the most learned Vallarsi in the latest edition of Saint Jerome’s works, and our manuscript codices, have “nine.” Although elsewhere we know that ten months are counted—not only by Jerome but also by other ancient writers—as the period during which infants are carried in the womb, Baluzius indicates more than twenty authors who support this view in his notes on Cyprian’s letter to Fortunatus. We could cite many more who count only nine. See also the learned annotation on this passage by the most learned Gazaeus in Cassian’s Book VII *On the Incarnation*, chapter 36.]

The same author says in his commentary on Isaiah (on Isaiah 7:14):

> “For the Lord of hosts, who is the King of glory, himself descended into the virginal womb, and entered and departed through the eastern gate.”

Augustine, whom we have mentioned so often above, says (*Sermon 5, On the Nativity of the Lord*):

> “But in order that human beings might be born from God, God was first of all born from among human beings. For Christ is God, and Christ was born from a human being. He who already had a Father in heaven sought only a mother on earth. Born from God, through whom we were made; born from the Virgin, through whom we would be restored.”

The same author says in his letter to Volusianus (*Letter 137*, chapter 4):

> “Moses himself and the other prophets most truly prophesied the Lord Christ and bestowed great glory upon him. They foretold that he would come not as their Father [Augustine: ‘as their equal’], nor as one superior in the same power of miracles, but fully [Augustine: *plane*, ‘plainly’] as the Lord and God of all, and as a human being made for the sake of human beings.”

Gregory Nazianzen says likewise (*Oration 38, On the Nativity of Christ*):

> “When God, therefore, had proceeded from the Virgin in the human nature which he had assumed—one being composed of two mutually opposed elements, flesh and spirit—one element is taken up into God, while the other bestows the grace of divinity.”

Blessed Cyril, in his letter against Nestorius (*Letter 4 to Nestorius*), says:

> “For a common human being was not first born from the holy Virgin, and only afterward did the Word dwell in him; rather, in the very womb and virginal uterus he united himself with the flesh and underwent a carnal generation of his own flesh [Others: ‘making his own birth belong to the flesh’].”

Peter, bishop of Ravenna, says in the same letter from which we cited an example shortly before:

[Note: [Col. 0186D] See above, column 177.]

> “The Word became flesh so that the human being might be advanced through flesh into the glory of God, not so that God might be changed into the dishonor of flesh. As the Apostle says: ‘Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit’ (1 Corinthians 6:17). And how could it be otherwise, when God joins himself to the human being? There is one God.”

A little later:

> “Heretic! Stop judging your judge; instead, adore in heaven the God whom the magus adored on earth.”

Blessed Bede the presbyter says in his exposition of the apostolic exhortation to the bishops of Ephesus (Bede, on Acts 20):

> “‘The Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood’ (Acts 20:28). He did not hesitate to speak of the blood of God because of the union of person in the two natures of the same Jesus Christ. Because of this union, he is also called the Son of man who is in heaven. Let Nestorius, therefore, cease separating the Son of man from the Son of God and making two Christs for himself.”

Let us say the same to Felix: let him cease dividing Christ into two sons or two gods, lest he become a participant in Nestorian unbelief. For what Nestorius appears to do with the number of persons, Felix appears to do with the number of sons: making one adoptive and another proper, and dividing the Son of God—through the one divinity of his majesty—into two powers, one proper and the other merely nominal.

Did all these men, as though once inspired by a prophetic spirit, not say these things to refute your blasphemies? You confess that our Lord and Savior is Christ, but you deny that he is God. Nor are you satisfied with this alone, unless you also assert that he is a conditional servant. Yet all those whom we have named, and many other catholic men far more numerous than these, proclaimed Christ the Lord to be the true God. They affirm that the blessed Virgin Mary is the Mother of God; whereas you appear, in impious novelty, to believe and proclaim her to be not only the mother of the human being whom you call Christ, but the mother of a certain servant.

## XII

Furthermore, you demand from us the authority by which it can be believed that the human being born from the virginal womb is the true God. For you say:

> “By what authority is that same lordly human being proclaimed by us to have been conceived as the true God from his mother’s womb, and born as the true God, when he is by nature a true human being and in all things subject to God?”

If you seek authority for why we proclaim as the true God the one who was born from the Virgin, you have in the preceding pages the weighty authority of the many Fathers whom we cited. Nevertheless, if you refuse to believe their authority, believe at least the authority of the Holy Spirit himself, through whom and from whom that wondrous conception of the Son of God took place in the virginal womb.

When the Virgin asked how the things announced to her by the angel could come to pass, the archangel Gabriel, sent by God, foretold them to her. Could the angel have announced anything other than what had been commanded him by almighty God? What does the angel say?

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Earlier the angel had said:

> “For he will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32).

Now he says, “the Son of God,” so that the one whom he had previously called “the Most High” he might now show to be God.

Of John the same angel says:

> “He will be great before God” (Luke 1:15).

Here John is called great by way of distinction from the other: “and the Son of the Most High,” so that you might understand that John is called great in one way, and Jesus—who was announced by the angel—in another. John is a great human being; this one is the great God.

Therefore, the same Son of the Most High who was conceived and born in the virginal womb is the same human being created in time from his mother who is God, born before time from the Father.

If, then, the same one is human who is God, and the same one is God who is human, let every heretical perversity cease—whether its belief that this human being is a mere human being, its proclamation that he is a conditional servant, or its division of the one whom the angelic announcement declared to be the one Son of God into two sons.

As we read in the treatise of the aforementioned presbyter Bede, which he wrote on the Gospel according to Luke:

> “The human being assumed into God was glorified with the glory which the Word of God had with the Father before the world existed, so that the same name of Son might belong to the same person of Christ, the human being who is God, full of grace and truth” [Bede: “the human being with God”].

Again, in the same treatise:

> “‘Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.’ In distinction from our holiness, Jesus is asserted to be uniquely holy by birth. For although we may become holy, we are not born holy. He alone is truly holy who, in order to overcome the conception itself of corruptible nature, was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse. ‘He will be called holy, the Son of God.’ What do you say here, Nestorian, who, by denying that blessed Mary is the Mother of God, strive to attack the manifest truth? Behold: he said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. How, then, is the Son of God not God? Or how can she who gave birth to God not be θεοτόκος—that is, the Mother of God?”

## XIII

Supported by the authority of these and similar testimonies, we believe and proclaim nothing concerning Christ except what the most holy teachers of the Churches of God have handed down to us. Together with them we curse every novelty and oppose every doctrine that attempts to overthrow this faith concerning Christ Jesus, promulgated by the holy Fathers. We seek no praise for ourselves, but defend the catholic faith, ready, insofar as divine grace grants us the ability, to give an account of our faith to everyone who asks it. We believe the testimonies of the holy Fathers and the authority of the Gospel, subjecting our own judgments to them. We proclaim that Christ, the Son of God, was conceived and born as the true God.

The holy Council of Chalcedon says:

> “Let us follow the judgments of our Fathers, confessing one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, and teaching consistently that the same one is perfect in divinity and the same one is perfect as the incarnate God. For the Truth itself says in the Gospel that he is both the Son of God and the son of man. To the blind man he said: ‘Do you believe in the Son of God?’ And when he asked who he was, he replied: ‘You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he’ (John 9:35–36). Likewise, he says: ‘When the Son of man comes in his majesty’ (Luke 9:26).”

We confess two natures in Christ and two operations, but one divinity, not two. For just as, when we say “the human being saw,” the whole human being did not see, but only the eyes, so when we say “God suffered,” he suffered in the flesh alone.

The works of the head in the human body are one thing, and those of the feet another. Each member has its own particular work, but there is one body and one human being in whom the head and the feet operate, with the soul directing and giving life. The body senses a bruise in one way, and the mind a harsh word in another; nevertheless, the human being is one.

So there is one God who suffered and did not suffer: he suffered in his humanity and did not suffer in his divinity. Therefore, one Son of God in one person and two natures must rightly and devoutly be confessed.

Without separation from God the Word, the nature of the flesh was not conceived in the virginal womb. Rather, the Word of God was ineffably united to the flesh, so that he might truly and without confusion become a perfect human being. Hence we confess him to be at once human and God, possessing in himself both: the nature of the Word, by which he is God, and the nature of the flesh, by which the same God is human.

The whole and perfect God is in the human being, and the perfect human being is in God: one God and one human being, and also one Christ. Whoever attempts to oppose this faith must in no way be considered catholic, but schismatic.

# BOOK FIVE

## I

After passing over many matters found in your little book by which you strive to assert that our Lord Jesus Christ is not the true God—matters to which, insofar as divine grace had granted us the ability, we responded—we have finally reached the point at which you destroy what you built and confess what you denied.

I do not know whether your earlier statements should be believed more readily, in which you attempted to attack the truth through arguments of many kinds, or whether, terrified by fear of the devil, you unwillingly confess Christ to be the Son of God. The Truth itself everywhere refuses to accept his testimony and commands him to be silent, since the Son of God has disdained to be proclaimed by such an advocate.

For you say that the same one is the Son of God who is also the son of man, and that the son of man is the Son of God, as could be understood from your words:

> “He united and joined that one to himself from his mother’s womb, that is, from the very conception, in the singularity of his person, so that the Son of God might be the son of man—not by a change of nature, but by condescension; and likewise so that the son of man might be the Son of God—not by a change of substance, but so that in the Son of God there might be a true Son.”

It is not surprising that you are found to disagree with others in the catholic confession, since you appear at intervals to disagree with yourself. In this statement you could have been regarded as catholic, had you not first displayed yourself in the perversity of your error.

You say, then, that there might be a Son in the true Son of God. If there is a Son in the true Son of God, who is Christ, then he is also the true Son, because in what is true there can be nothing other than truth. Adoption has no place in the birth of truth.

Christ, therefore, is one Son of God, true and perfect God and human being, as has often been said.

You add: “There are not two gods”—which plainly shows that you are fighting against yourself. For if there are not two gods, then he is not both the true God and a merely nominal god; rather, he is one true God, because God is truth, and there is no pretense in him, but the whole fountain of truth.

## II

Another statement follows in your little book that does not agree with your earlier words:

> “We believe him to be the true and proper Son of God and the true God, who, according to the form of God, was born twice: first, from the Father without flesh and without a mother; second, from his mother with flesh and without a father. We believe that this true God was ineffably generated from both parents, to whom the Father speaks through David: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.’”

Shortly before, you said that Christ had two fathers: David, namely, as his natural father, and God the Father by adoption. Here, however, having forgotten these words, you say: “second, from his mother without a father.”

Both statements cannot be true: Christ cannot, insofar as he is human, have two fathers and no father. If, according to your statement, the true Son of God was born twice, and is the true Son of God in both births, paternal and maternal, how can it be that two sons were not born from the mother—one whom you assert, in catholic language, to be the true Son of God, and another whom your perversity declares not to be the true Son of God?

The true and the non-true cannot in any way be one. Likewise, a true son and a non-true son cannot in any way be one son. Nor can the true God and a merely nominal god be one, because the truth of divinity is entirely one thing, and a bare naming of deity is another, as we showed above from Moses and the other saints.

But both cannot in any way exist in one person, because the dignity of truth is one thing and the generosity of mere naming another. Whoever attempts to assert this pretense of nominal or titular divinity in Christ’s humanity will in no way be able to escape the pit of Nestorian impiety.

## III

To make it appear that you wish to avoid this duality of person in Christ, you give as an example a human being who is one son of his parents from soul and body:

> “Although God from God and human being from human being, in the singularity of his person, is one and the same Christ of God, just as every human being, from a soul created from nothing and flesh formed from both parents, is one son of both parents, namely, the son of his father and mother.”

This example, if you understood it correctly, and if you carefully considered yourself, could destroy in you the whole treachery of your error and recall your understanding to the recognition of truth.

From this root, as it seems, the thorns of your entire unbelief have grown: it appears impossible to you for a son to be proper in any other way than by being born wholly from the nature of his parents. You do not understand that you yourself are the proper son of your father and mother, although the more noble nature that is in you—your soul—was not generated from their nature but, as you assert, created from nothing.

What blindness of mind, contrary to all reason, is this, when you insist that something cannot exist in the one and proper Son of God which you cannot possibly deny exists in yourself? If, then, from soul and flesh you are wholly the proper and true son of your parents, why do you not much more believe that almighty God could have a true and proper Son, born from the Virgin as God and human being in two substances?

Is God incapable of accomplishing in himself what he is capable of accomplishing in the birth of every human being? Either divide yourself into two sons—one proper, from the flesh, and one adoptive, from the soul—for your parents; or, if this seems absurd to you, grant that God the Father could, by the same law or by an even more powerful one, have a proper and truly begotten Son born from the Virgin, just as you wish to be the proper son of your parents.

Nevertheless, you cannot compare that ineffable birth of God and human being in one person with the ordinary conditions and conventions of human birth.

Either deny, then, that you are a natural son through the substance of the soul of your parents, or grant to God that he could have a proper Son from the virginal womb—especially since the union of God and the human being is such that there is one person of God and human being, although what was mortal properly belongs to the human being, and what always existed to the divinity.

And just as you do not deny that you yourself are mortal and immortal, so Christ was immortal in his divinity but mortal in the flesh alone. Yet that flesh, having conquered death according to the true and catholic faith, is now also placed at the right hand of the Father and glorified in the power of divinity, reigning unchangeably in heaven.

I know that I have already discussed these matters more fully above. Nevertheless, because of the relevance of this statement, I thought it better to respond to something here in the present place. Since the adversary repeats what he previously set forth, it is necessary that a repetition of my response also be supplied, lest he perhaps repeat [F.: suppose] that there is nothing to say against him.

## IV

Thus, running through the very broad fields of Holy Scripture, as though repenting of some things he had earlier stated correctly, he searches for statements of sacred Scripture by which he might affirm the doctrine of his former error. But because he cannot find what he seeks, he does not cease interpreting the statements of Holy Scripture according to the sense of his perversity. This can be understood from three statements supported by the authority of the Apostle.

He sets forth the following interpretation of the wondrous confession of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, which was praised by the Truth himself, as can be seen from his words:

> “For blessed Peter the apostle confessed particularly in him, by divine revelation, two natures in one person, saying: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (Matthew 16:16). In saying, ‘You are the Christ,’ he refers to his humanity, in which he was joined [Perhaps: ‘anointed’]; what he added, ‘the Son of the living God,’ refers to his divinity, in which he is essentially the true Son of God.”

He also produces the words of that same blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, from the Acts of the Apostles, where he preached the word of God to Cornelius and those who were with him:

> “Again, as the Acts of the Apostles records, the same apostle, speaking specifically of his humanity, said among other things while evangelizing Cornelius and his companions: ‘Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him’ (Acts 10:38). He does not say, ‘God himself was he,’ but, ‘God was with him.’ For if that assumed human being were the true God according to the true confession, so great an apostle would never have dared to say, ‘God was with him,’ but rather, ‘He himself was God.’”

He also brings forward a third statement from blessed Paul, that outstanding preacher:

> “Because God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

He does not say, “Christ was God,” but “God was in Christ”—not because Christ, namely the assumed human being, is not God, but because he is God not by nature but by grace and by naming.

Look, look, readers, at this new interpreter of Holy Scripture, who strives to separate God from the human being assumed, and from the one God, our Redeemer, to make two gods: one true and the other nominal. Christ, whom the whole Church worships and adores as God—not only the Church that labors on earth in hope, but also the Church that rightly rejoices in heaven—this new interpreter wishes to be believed to be a solitary human being, according to Nestorian or Pelagian perversity.

If it is true that Christ possesses only the pretense of a name, not the reality of divinity, how is he the true Redeemer of the human race? If there is only an imagined power in the head, whence is there the reality of salvation in the body?

One response, therefore, can be made to these three statements, which he has interpreted according to one and the same perversity [F.: *interpretatae*, ‘interpreted’]. If Christ is not God because Scripture says, “God was in Christ,” and likewise, “God was with him,” how is the Son of God to be understood as God when he says:

> “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”?

If he is not God because the Father is in the Son, then the Father himself is not God either, because the Son is said to be in the Father. For “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” means the same as if he had said, “The Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father.”

But if it is true that the Son is God and the Father is God, then, even though the Truth himself said, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” Christ is also God, even though the Apostle said, “God was in Christ.”

Therefore, if, according to Felix’s confession, Christ is not [supplied: God] because the Apostle says, “God was in Christ,” there are altogether two beings, God and Christ, and a fourth person is introduced. May the one of whom we speak—Jesus Christ our Lord, the one true and supreme God—turn this away from every Christian heart.

## V

Although we possess an abundance of thoroughly proven interpretations by the holy Fathers, who understood these statements otherwise, let us nevertheless present a few from among the many.

Concerning the confession of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so excellently praised by the Truth himself, we respond with what Cassian (*On the Incarnation*, Book III, chapters 12–13) said in reply to Nestorius, this Felix’s predecessor:

> “The first of the apostles, Peter, answered, certainly one on behalf of all; for the answer of one contained the faith of all. But it was fitting that the first should answer, so that the order of the response might correspond to the order of honor, and that the one who preceded in age should also precede in confession. What, then, did he say? ‘You are,’ he says, ‘the Son of the living God.’”

> “I must use a simple question to refute you, heretic. Tell me, please: who was the one to whom Peter gave this answer? You cannot deny that he was Christ. I ask, therefore: was the Christ whom you call a human being or God? A human being, without doubt—for this is the source of your entire heresy, that you deny Christ to be the Son of God. For this reason you also say that Mary is Christotokos, not Theotokos—that she is the mother of Christ, not the mother of God.”

> “What, then, did Peter answer concerning these things? ‘You are,’ he says, ‘the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ The one whom you assert to be merely the son of a human being, Peter testifies to be the Son of God. Whom do you wish us to believe, you or Peter? I suppose you are not so shameless as to dare to put yourself before the first of the apostles. Yet what would you not dare, or how would you not despise an apostle, when you have not feared to deny God?”

> “‘You are,’ therefore, he says, ‘the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ Does this contain anything doubtful or obscure? It is simply an open confession: it proclaims Christ to be the Son of God.”

A little later he says:

> “Let us see how the one whom he confessed approved his confession, since it is far more than the Apostle said if God himself praised his statement. When the apostle said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,’ what did the Lord and Savior answer? ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’”

> “If you dislike using the testimony of the apostle, use that of God. By praising what had been said, God added his own authority to the apostolic statement. Thus, although that statement proceeded from the apostle’s mouth, God made it his own by approving it.”

> “‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but the Spirit of my Father who is in heaven’ (Matthew 16:17). Therefore, in the apostle’s statement you see the testimony of the Holy Spirit, of the Son who was present, and of God the Father. What more, or what similar testimony, do you seek? The Son of man praised it, the Father was present, and the Spirit revealed it.”

> “The apostle’s statement is therefore the testimony of the whole divinity, because this statement must possess the authority of the one by whose authority [Cassian: ‘by whose agency’] it proceeded. ‘Blessed are you,’ he says, ‘Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but the Spirit of my Father who is in heaven.’”

> “Therefore, if [flesh and blood] did not reveal these things to Peter or inspire them, you now understand who inspired you. If the Spirit of God taught the one who confessed Christ to be the Son of God, you see that you have been taught by the spirit of the devil, since you were able to deny it.”

## VI

Blessed Bede the presbyter also explains in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 10) the statement “God was with him” as follows:

> “‘God was with him’ means the Father was with the Son. For it is better to understand it in this way than to take it as signifying that the divinity of the Son dwelt together with the human being whom he assumed, lest we double Christ’s person and fall into the Nestorian doctrine.”

Concerning the Apostle’s statement, “God was in Christ,” Victor, bishop of Capua, says in *The Book of the Betrothed*, chapter 24:

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Victor of Capua’s *Book of the Betrothed* is unknown.]

> “‘God was in Christ,’ namely, the Father was in the Son, because in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell. In the other saints, apostles, patriarchs, and prophets there was grace; but in Christ the whole divinity dwelt, that is, the whole fullness of divinity bodily.”

The same bishop Victor, drawing from Cyril’s work, says in his *Book Addressed to the Augustae*, which begins, “Those who proclaim the divine and heavenly mystery”:

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Saint Cyril’s *Oration to the Augustae* survives in volume IV of Mansi’s *Councils*, p. 803. No one else mentions Victor’s work referred to here.]

> “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, that is, substantially—not by participation, nor by grace, which is granted to adoptive sons, but bodily, that is, substantially, just as a person’s spirit is said to dwell in a human being, although the human being and his spirit are not two different beings.”

The same teacher, Cassian, whom we also cited above, discusses the inseparable operation of divinity and humanity and the wondrous sharing of actions in Christ, for the most blessed truth of the catholic faith:

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Cassian, Book I *On the Incarnation*, chapter 5, drawing from the confession of Leporius.]

> “Confessing both substances, of the flesh and of the Word, as one and the same human being, inseparable from the beginning of his conception, we receive him in the devout belief of faith. From the time when the flesh was assumed, we say that everything belonging to God passed into the human being, so that everything belonging to the human being came into God. In this understanding the Word became flesh—not because by any change or mutability he began to be what he was not, but so that, by the power of the divine dispensation, the Word of the Father, never departing from the Father, might deign to become properly incarnate as a human being.”

[Note: [Col. 0194D] These words differ somewhat in Cassian.]

> “I will not say that the human being was born together with God in such a way that I assign separately what belongs to God to God alone and separately what belongs to the human being to the human being alone, and thus begin to make not one but two Christs from the one Son of God—something from which the Lord and God Christ himself now turn us away.”

> “Rather, the Word and flesh become one with each other in such a way that, while each substance remains naturally perfect without injury to itself, the divine shares with the human and the human participates in the divine. There is not one who is God and another who is human; rather, the same one is God who is also human, and conversely the human being who is also God: Jesus Christ, one God.”

## VII

But overcome, Felix, by these and similar, most powerful testimonies of the holy Fathers, you did not cease to flee to other hiding places for your error. From there, hissing the poisons of a serpent’s mouth, you seek ways by which you may destroy yourself—for by the very things rightly uttered from which discerning sons of acquisition are saved, sons of perdition are condemned when they do not fear to interpret well-spoken words in the holy Scriptures wrongly. Accordingly, you put forward a statement from the Epistle of the Evangelist, where he says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1). You assert that it is to be understood by you as follows:

> “An advocate,” you say, “is the same as a mediator, who intercedes with the Father on behalf of sinners because of their offenses; this is to be understood not of the true God, but of the man who was assumed.”

Why, however, do you not understand that the Evangelist calls the same one both propitiator and advocate, when he says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins”? In naming him advocate, he designates the man; in calling him propitiator, he shows that he is God. But understand from the testimonies of the holy Fathers how he who is God is an advocate. Augustine—for whom we so often make mention—says concerning this intercession in his book Against Arius [Note: [Col. 0194D] “St. Augustine. Where? I do not know. The book of Augustine Against Arius is likewise unknown. Perhaps Alcuin intended to convey Augustine’s meaning rather than his words, from Book Against the Arian Sermon, chapters 19 and 25.]:

> “The Arians are accustomed, plainly, to raise a slander from the cause of intercession, saying that the one who is interceded with is greater than the one interceding. They must be answered that God does not suffer forgetfulness, so that he must continually be reminded on behalf of those whom he himself has chosen; but he intercedes with him in this respect: he continually shows and offers to the Father the man whom he assumed, as our pledge, as the true and eternal high priest.”

Hear also how blessed Bede the presbyter (On 1 John, chapter 2) agrees with this interpretation in his exposition of the same apostolic statement:

> “For the only-begotten Son’s interceding for man is to show himself to the coeternal Father; and his asking on behalf of human nature is to have assumed that same nature into the exalted state of his divinity. The Lord therefore intercedes for us not by voice but by mercy.”

It must truly be understood that the intercession of Christ, now seated at the right hand of the Father, should in no way be understood as being like that of a man, when someone intercedes with a judge in humble words on another’s behalf. Rather, the dispensation of humanity in the Son of God to God the Father [text corrupt] is an intercession for the human race. For it is also written of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” [Col. 0194D] (Rom. 8:26). The Holy Spirit does not groan; but, using a figurative expression, the Apostle signifies that the Holy Spirit makes us groan. Thus he is said to plead for the saints because he makes the saints plead. In the same way, what is said of Christ—that he is an advocate—is to be understood in a higher mystical sense [Perhaps, “mystery”] than the human practice of interceding among human beings ordinarily permits.

## VIII

Then, turning back to the Gospel, you put forward the following statement [Col. 0195A]. For you say:

> “Nowhere in the Gospel is the Son of God read to have been delivered up for us, but only the Son of Man.”

You have evidently forgotten that the Son of God himself had spoken of his being delivered up:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16).

The only-begotten Son of God, therefore, is the Son who was given for the salvation of the world. But what is “given” except “delivered up”? The Apostle also confirms this, saying:

> “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

The same Apostle likewise says of this Son of God:

> “He who delivered himself up for us” (Eph. 5:2).

Blessed Peter also, preaching to the Jews, did not hesitate to testify that he was the Son of God, saying:

> “The God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed delivered up and denied before Pilate’s face, when he was judging that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One and asked that a murderer be given to you. You killed the author of life, whom God raised from the dead on the third day” (Acts 3:13–15).

What room for doubt can there be in these words of apostolic authority? He testified that the one who was delivered up, who died, and indeed who was raised again, was the Son of God. He added, “the author of life.” Who, then, is the author of life except the Son of God, who is said to have been delivered up for the salvation of the world either by God the Father or by himself?

It is also read that he was delivered up by his betrayer, Judas Iscariot, and by the Jews. Blessed Peter says:

> “He delivered himself to the one who judges unjustly” (1 Pet. 2:23),

although he was delivered up in one way by God the Father, in another by Judas the betrayer, in another by himself, and in another by the Jews: by God the Father for the salvation of the human race; by the betrayer, to satisfy the desire of his greed; by himself, to accomplish the effect of the Father’s will; and by the Jews, to display the wickedness of their treachery.

Therefore, the Son of Man can in no way be divided from the Son of God, nor the Son of God separated from the Son of Man, because there is one Son of God, God and man, who was delivered up to death on account of our sins. Blessed Cassianus truthfully demonstrates this in the book from which we cited testimonies above [Note: [Col. 0195D] Cassianus, Book VI On the Incarnation, chapter 22, where the text reads: “Nor in time can anyone so distinguish the man from God in the passion, or God from man, etc.”]:

> “Nor, in respect of time, can anyone distinguish the man from God in the passion, or God from man. For if you look to time, you will always find the Son of Man with the Son of God; [ [Note: [Col. 0196D] The words enclosed in brackets have been supplied from Cassianus.] and if you look to the passion, you will always find the Son of God with the Son of Man]. Thus Christ, the Son of Man and the Son of God, is so united and undivided in himself that, as far as the wording of Scripture is concerned, neither can the man be separated from God in time, nor God wholly from man in the passion.”

We plainly confess this also in the symbol of the catholic faith: that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, suffered for human salvation. No Catholic, therefore, ought to doubt that the Son of God was delivered up for the salvation of the world. Whoever denies that the Son of God was delivered up to the passion can in no way be Catholic; rather, by remaining in this obstinacy, he must be judged alien from the profession of the catholic faith.

## IX

Then you proceed, seeking what is said specifically of Christ’s humanity and what of his divinity in the holy Scriptures. At last you came to the point where the same Lord speaks of the day of the final judgment. You strive to deny Christ knowledge of that day insofar as he is man, as can be recognized from your words:

> “He is the one who, according to the foreknowledge of his divinity, foretold the day of judgment through the Prophet: ‘The day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my redemption has come’ (Isa. 63:4). Nevertheless, because of the nature of his humanity, he is the one who declares in the Gospel according to Mark: ‘But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone’ (Mark 13:32).”

The holy Fathers understood this statement, in which Mark the Evangelist said that the Son did not know the day of judgment, very differently from the way you assert that it should be understood. Blessed Jerome, in his Commentary on Matthew (chapter 24, verse 36), and Bede the presbyter, in his treatise on the Evangelist Mark (chapter 13), explained the meaning of this statement as follows:

> “The reason must therefore be given why he is said not to know. The Apostle wrote of the Savior: ‘In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge’ (Col. 2:3). Therefore all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. Why are they hidden? When he was questioned by the apostles after the resurrection about the day of judgment, he answered more clearly: ‘It is not for you to know times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority’ (Acts 1:7). When he says, ‘It is not for you,’ he shows that he himself knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on that day.”

If he does not know the day of judgment, how is it true that he earlier said: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Luke 10:22)? If knowledge of the final day was not handed over to him, then all things have not been handed over to him by the Father.

Saint Augustine, in Book XII of On the Holy Trinity (no. 23), explains the meaning of these words of Christ through the figure called by grammarians metonymy:

> “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father. For he does not know this in the sense that he makes those who do not know it; that is, he did not know it in such a way as then to disclose it to the disciples, just as it was said to Abraham: ‘Now I know that you fear God’ (Gen. 22:12)—that is, now I have made you know it, because he too came to know himself through having been tested in that temptation.””

Tell me, I ask, how can it be that the Judge of all does not know the day of judgment, and that the one who is to judge the merits of each person is ignorant of the time of that judgment? His judicial power was proclaimed long beforehand in the Psalms:

> “Our God, says the Prophet, will come manifestly; our God will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him. He summoned heaven above and the earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. 49:3–4).

And lest you be ignorant of whom he had spoken, the same prophet had prefaced this shortly before:

> “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken” (ibid., 1).

Who is that God who is God of gods, that is, Lord of the saints? Truly and entirely, Christ, who will judge the living and the dead.

Blessed Cassiodorus explains this passage of prophecy (On Psalm 49:1, 3) as follows:

> “Lest anyone think that Christ’s incarnation should be assessed with an ordinary judgment, his power is proclaimed beforehand, so that every perversity of unbelief may be removed. Those are called gods who receive the grace of the heavenly majesty through good conduct, as he says in another Psalm: ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’ (Ps. 81:6). Thus they are called sons, just as they are called gods; both are granted by grace, not by nature. Christ, however, is God of gods.”

A little later he says:

> “The God of Christians is himself the God of gods, who will come manifestly and will not be silent. For now he is silent, while this world is being carried on: when, with the severity of his judgment, he does not condemn blasphemies and sacrilegious words, but endures sinners for the medicine of conversion. Then he will not be silent, when he says to the wicked: ‘Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matt. 25:41).”

Let the one who now dares to blaspheme Christ, who will judge the world, as a merely titular and not a true God fear this saying. Titular designation does not consist in the truth of power, but only in the dignity of a name. He who will summon heaven and earth to judgment possesses not merely the name of deity but also the power of divinity.

And lest you perhaps object that he is the Son of Man who possesses the power of judging, hear what that same one said about his power:

> “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 25:31).

He testifies that the Son of Man will sit and judge in his own majesty, not in another’s, and will give the kingdom of his Father to the saints.

And elsewhere:

> “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

A little later:

> “As the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself, and he has given him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:23, 26–27).

And lest any doubt remain for anyone about who it is who will be seen by all at the judgment, blessed John the Evangelist foretold that the prophetic testimony concerning him would be fulfilled. He says:

> “All this happened so that what had been written might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him.’ And again another Scripture says: ‘They shall look upon him whom they pierced’” (John 19:36).

The wounds of the true body will therefore reveal the true Son of Man, who will judge the world. That form will be the judge in which he stood before the judge. He will appear as judge in a form that can be seen by those whom he will crown and by those whom he will condemn.

The angels also foretold this very thing to the apostles as Christ ascended:

> “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11),

that is, he will come to judge in the same form and substance of flesh.

The Apostle did not hesitate to call this same Son of Man, who will judge the world, God. For he says:

> “Otherwise, how will God judge this world?” (Rom. 3:6)

And elsewhere:

> “Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God” (Titus 2:13).

## X

In what follows, you also set forth the words of Truth himself, with which he replied to a certain rich man who called him a good teacher: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19). You join the words, Felix, very inappropriately as far as the logic of the interpretation is concerned:

> “He who, essentially, is alone good with the Father and the Holy Spirit is God; he himself, although he is good in the man, nevertheless does not become good naturally from himself.”

How can what you say stand—that he himself is good, and yet he himself is not naturally good in himself? If he is good in himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit, then he is likewise good in the man who was assumed, not with an alien goodness but naturally, because “he himself” and “he himself” signify one person, and one is not in the Father and another in the man.

It is astonishing that you wish to become a teacher of the catholic faith while you do not understand the meaning of the words by which the faith is expressed. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). What is rightly believed in the heart must therefore be brought forth in words appropriate to the true faith.

But from your preceding professions of faith a certain suspicion arises in these words: you seem indeed to wish to assert that the Son of God, who assumed man, is naturally good, but that the man whom he assumed is not good by natural goodness. This interpretation of yours is destroyed by many testimonies of holy Scripture.

First, it is read in Genesis that God created all things good. Scripture says concerning each day: “God saw that it was good.” And when all things had been created as God pleased, it was said: “And all things were very good” (Gen. 1). How, then, was that man alone—not merely any man, but the one whom the Son of God himself, through whom all things were made, assumed to the unity of his person in the virginal womb—not naturally good?

What sin was there in that wondrous conception and birth from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, so that the one who was born and joined to the Son of God in the unity of his person from the very beginning of the incarnation would not be naturally good?

Every rational creature is either good or evil. For the holy Scriptures speak of a good angel and an evil angel, and likewise of a good man and an evil man, as Truth himself testifies:

> “The good man, from the good treasure of his heart, brings forth good things” (although all that God created was very good), “and the evil man, from the evil treasure of his heart, brings forth evil things” (Luke 6:45).

But all things that are good are naturally good, through the activity of God’s grace; those that are evil become evil through their own fault.

How, then, is Christ not naturally good, through whom all who are good are made good? For just as he is [perhaps, “properly”] the Son of God through whom all the saints have been made sons of God, so he is naturally good, without whom no one can naturally be good.

Blessed Jerome the presbyter wished the words of Christ’s reply to be understood very differently from the way you assert, as is read in the Commentary cited above, from which we set forth testimonies shortly before [Note: [Col. 0199] St. Jerome on Matthew 19; from this we chiefly corrected the text, which was badly corrupt in the earlier edition.]:

> “‘Why do you ask me about the good?’ he says. ‘There is one who is good, God’ (Matt. 19:17; Luke 18:19). Since he had called him good teacher and had not confessed him to be [God] or the Son of God, he says that any holy man, in comparison with God, is not good. Of him it is said: ‘Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good’ (Ps. 105:1). But lest anyone suppose that, when the Lord [Jerome: “God”] is called good, the Son of God is excluded from goodness, we read elsewhere: ‘The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep’ (John 10:11). And in the Prophet: ‘Your good Spirit, and good land’ (Ps. 142:10).”

The Lord therefore does not deny that he is good, but signifies that he is God. He does not testify that he is not a good teacher, but that no teacher is good apart from God.

## XI

You add also, when you discuss the two natures in Christ:

> “Impassible in his own nature, passible in what is alien.”

What do you call alien to the Son of God in that assumption of humanity which was taken into such a great and wondrous union with the Son of God that he was one, not two? He is the same in the glory of divinity as in the weakness of humanity; the same Son of God as Son of Man, and the same Son of Man as Son of God.

For what could be alien in this conjunction, when it is certain that all the acts of both natures in Christ belong to one proper person, as blessed Pope Leo says [Note: [Col. 0199C] St. Leo, Sermon 54, chapters 1–2]:

> “With the proper character of the natures preserved, the things that belong to God passed into man, and all the things that belong to man passed into God, so that the divine acts were performed neither without man nor the human acts without God.
