For this is what the catholic faith transmits, this is what it requires: that I acknowledge [Leo: “we acknowledge”] that two natures came together in our Redeemer, and that, while their properties remained, such a great unity of both substances was brought about that, from the time when, as the cause of the human race required, the Word became flesh in the womb of the blessed Virgin, it is not permitted to think of him as God without what he is as man, or as man without what he is as God.

> “Each nature indeed shows [Leo: “expresses”] its reality through distinct actions, but neither separates itself from the conjunction of the other. Nothing there is mutually alien. For divinity was not absent from the soul as it grieved before the passion, nor did he abandon his own flesh in the passion. The whole of humility is in majesty, and the whole of majesty is in humility. Therefore the insult belongs to the same one to whom the glory belongs. He is the same one in weakness as in power; the same one capable of death and victorious over death.

> “God therefore assumed the whole man and so joined himself to him and him to himself through mercy and power that each nature was present in the other, while neither passed over from its own property into the other. Thus, in his own flesh, the impassible God suffered, so that, because he willed it, he might experience true suffering in true flesh, while remaining wholly impassible in divinity. Nor did another deign to hand himself over to death than the one who, by dying, was able to conquer death in such a way that he could not experience death in death.

> “But we must know with complete certainty that whatever violence and suffering the fury of the wicked inflicted was endured not from necessity but assumed by will”—

just as he also bore willingly, not by necessity, everything belonging to human weakness: hunger, thirst, weariness, sleep, mockeries, the cross, and death itself. Thus the one who died by his own will also rose by his own power, as he foretold:

> “I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (Luke 10:18).

But lest the longer sequence of this little book produce weariness in reading, let this be the end of this discourse, so that speech may more freely take its beginning from another.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0199]

## I

The sublimity of apostolic authority ought to have terrified these advocates of adoption or titular designation in Christ, so that they would remain silent, since it has forbidden all innovations of expression to all the sons of the catholic faith under threat of anathema. But an obstinate mind, softened by no terrors, is not restrained from its perseverance in perversity; nor does it take care to correct itself by the example of those whose condemnation occurred in former times, when they attempted to introduce new sects contrary to apostolic traditions.

Thus these men also, who strive to insert the introduction of this novelty into the catholic faith, do not seek, through a pious consideration of humility, to recall themselves into the fold of the universal Church by the unity of apostolic faith. They not only refuse to correct their badly expressed statements by a healthier interpretation, but also strive to entangle themselves again in worse errors.

Hence this Felix, with still more unhappy boldness, attempts, together with the other followers of his perversity, to impose upon Christ a due servitude, conditional service, and necessary subjection, although all the pages of the Gospel and the apostolic Scriptures most openly testify that Christ is truly the Lord God and the Son of God.

No saint possessed such breadth of wisdom or such abundance of eloquence that he could adequately recount the praise and glory of Christ God. The greatness of this mystery surpasses all the understanding of rational creation: the Son of God deigned to assume human nature into the unity of his person and to live among human beings as the God-man, while he is worshiped by angels in heaven. Yet the wretched rashness of these men does not fear to call our Redeemer Christ, true God, King of kings, and Lord of lords a debtor to servitude or a conditional servant, and dares to impose upon him the lowest of names.

## II

Since you contend, then, that Christ is bound by the necessity of due servitude, tell me, I ask, in what was Christ Jesus a debtor? Did he have sins, so that he was a debtor because of the remission of sins? For in the Lord’s Prayer debts are set in place of sins, as we are accustomed daily to sing at the command of Truth himself:

> “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

Immediately afterward a summary of this petition is added, so that it might be understood what debts he had meant. The Lord himself says in what follows:

> “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses” (ibid., 14).

And where one Evangelist says “our debts,” another places “sins” for debts (Luke 11:4).

If a debtor is also a sinner, as the truth of the Gospel shows, was Christ therefore a sinner, so that he ought to be called a debtor? Unless perhaps you wish to understand “debtor” in another sense, namely, as one who repays a previously received benefit. But what does this have to do with Christ? Was he first a man and afterward chosen by a singular benefit to be the Son of God, so that he should be called a debtor for so great a benefit?

Was not the true God and true Son of God conceived at the very conception, and was not the union of two natures made in one person in the virginal womb, in such unity of person that this whole one who was born of the Virgin must undoubtedly be called and believed to be one true Son of God?

Elsewhere in the Gospel it is said of debtors:

> “There were two debtors to a certain creditor” (Luke 7:41).

Who are to be understood here as debtors except those bound by the obligation of some agreement to the creditor’s legal claim? Pious belief permits nothing of this kind to be said of Christ.

But when you say that he is a conditional servant, what Catholic ears could patiently endure this great blasphemy—that Christ, the Son of God, is by a worthless condition and harsh necessity a servant of God the Father?

What, then, do you say about Adam? Was he created with free dignity or in servile condition? If he was formed as a conditional servant, how is he the image of God? Or where was his free will? Or what did he lose by sinning? But if he was free, how much more must Christ—in whom all divinity dwelt bodily—be believed to have been born from the Virgin of royal nobility with free dignity, not in conditional servitude?

Blessed Augustine says of this in his letter to Consentius (Epistle 205, no. 12):

> “He assumed the form of a servant without changing the nature of the Lord; imparting the Lord’s grace, not retaining servile disgrace.”

If human nobility is to be regarded as possessing any importance or dignity, who was nobler than King David himself? From his seed, as from the nobility of royal excellence rather than the ignobility of servile condition, Christ willed to be born in the world.

If you consider the glory of divinity, who can be compared with the Son of God, who was one and the same in two natures, to whom none of the saints could or can be equal in nobility, freedom, or the privilege of power?

## III

But as for what you say—“Because of the ignobility of the blessed Virgin, who humbly declares in a lowly voice that she is God’s handmaid, he is a conditional servant”—

if, according to your rashness, the most holy Virgin Mary is a conditional handmaid, then Sarah is nobler according to apostolic authority. Concerning her the teacher of the nations himself says:

> “It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, whereas the one by the free woman was born through promise” (Gal. 4:22–23).

And shortly afterward:

> “But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman’” (ibid., 30).

Perhaps Isaac is also nobler in your view than Christ: Isaac was born, according to the apostolic testimony, from a free woman, while Christ, as you assert, was born from a slave woman. And all the adoptive sons of God are nobler than Christ, concerning whom Truth himself says:

> “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15).

Concerning them the preacher to the nations also says:

> “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore he is no longer a servant but a son. And if a son, then also an heir through God” (Gal. 4:6–7).

You say: “What could be born from a slave woman except a servant?”

Where is your understanding, when you do not consider that many kinds of animals were created from the earth and numerous varieties of fish from the waters? How, then, could a living creature be created from an insensible nature, that is, from the nature of earth or water? Or how do trees arise from dust, and flowers and fruits from trees? Why should only dust be born from dust, as you say that nothing could have been born from a slave woman except a servant?

For the moment, let us not deny that the blessed Virgin may be called a handmaid. Nevertheless, grant to divine omnipotence that from a handmaid it could create whatever pleased its ineffable will. Unless perhaps you wish to resist God and say: “I do not want anything other than a servant to be made from a handmaid.”

But truly Christ alone, as the Prophet foretold concerning him, was found “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:5). Concerning this glorious freedom of his, blessed Cassiodorus says in his exposition of Psalm 87:

> “He alone was free among the dead, who also broke the very barriers of death. His death alone was free, because it was voluntary; he had power to lay down his life and to take it up again” (John 10:18). “Yet although he was free among the dead, he was nevertheless regarded by the foolish as one of the wounded who sleep. Truly the Lord was called free, who deigned to free the human race.”

Perhaps you slander him as being a conditional servant for this reason: that by the benevolent submission of his obedience he made the human race free.

But blessed Gregory is proved to have understood this liberation of which we speak very differently in the twenty-third book of the Moralia [Note: [Col. 0201D] St. Gregory, Book XXIV of the Moralia, chapter 3]:

> “The mediator between God and men, Jesus [Gregory: ‘the man Christ Jesus’], has mercy on man insofar as he assumed the form of man. By this mercy, having redeemed man [Gregory: ‘for redeemed man’], he says to the Father: ‘Deliver him, so that he may not descend into corruption’ (Job 33:24). As we said above, for him to say, ‘Deliver that man,’ is to show that human nature has been made free through the assumption of human nature. For from the flesh that he assumed he also showed that this flesh, which he redeemed, was free. We are that redeemed flesh: we are bound by the knowledge of our guilt, but we are freed by the justice of so great a mediator, as he himself says: ‘If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free’” (John 8:36).

You therefore appear exceedingly ungrateful to the liberator of the human race, since you so often say not only that he is called a servant absolutely, but also testify that he is a conditional servant, whereas “condition” indicates harsh necessity, not the gift of voluntary obedience.

[Col. 0203B] **IV.** But among the other consequences to which the wandering course of your discourse has led you, you have also reached the point of saying that there are two kinds of servitude among creatures—voluntary and conditional—because, as you say, every creature serves God either willingly or necessarily, by condition. It is plainly evident to everyone that conditional servitude is a lower kind than voluntary servitude; yet, with impious presumption, you do not fear to reckon Christ under this inferior degree, as we have already shown from your own words.

You have even placed the devil himself in this degree of conditional servitude, saying: “Indeed, in sacred Scripture the devil is called the Lord’s servant by condition.” Do you see where your blasphemy has led you—that you reckon Christ and the devil under one kind of servitude, and do not allow Christ himself to serve God the Father by voluntary obedience in the days of his flesh, but by conditional necessity, like the devil?

Surely all Christian service in the religion of holiness ought to be voluntary toward God rather than necessary, to such an extent that a good will is counted as the deed, even when some necessity of action impedes one’s ability to perform it?

You add the following words concerning Christ’s conditional servitude: “Can it be,” you say, “that he who is truly God should become God’s servant by condition, as Christ the Lord is in the form of a servant—he who, by many methods and many proofs, is shown most truly to be not only a servant because of obedience, as most people think, but also by nature a servant of the Father and his maidservant’s son?”

No one who is pious is unaware how absurd and inappropriate it is to believe this about God, the Son of God, and true God. Among the many people whom you say believe that Christ serves God through obedience, one is certainly blessed Paul, the apostle and teacher of the nations, who says: “Christ, obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross; for this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II, 8–9).

A conditional servant is not above every name, but is beneath the name of sons. For the name “sons” has been commonly bestowed upon all the saints by God’s gracious favor. What, then, is that name more excellent than all other names which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, is said to have been given to Christ by God the Father, because of the wonderful mystery of his obedience? It is plainly the name which he himself adds, saying:

[Col. 0204A] “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

If Jesus is now Lord and is in the glory of God the Father—that is, in the majesty of divinity—then he is not subject to the yoke of conditional servitude. Rather, as blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, says: “He has gone into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers subjected to him” (I Pet. III, 22).

The Psalmist also foretold this long beforehand: “You made him a little lower [than the angels]; you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII, 6).

O glorious obedience, worthy of every praise, which has been raised to such greatness of divine power that he was set over all the works of God!

Again, the Apostle says elsewhere: “He handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice” (Eph. V, 2). In saying, “He handed himself over,” he shows the disposition of one who gives himself voluntarily, not of one who serves conditionally.

David himself also says in the person of the saints: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. LIII, 8). If the sacrifices of the saints, which are customarily offered to God, were plainly voluntary, how do you slander this one sacrifice alone—in which lies the redemption of the whole world—as having been made by necessity and not by the will of one who freely offered himself? Thus the same prophet says elsewhere: “In the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will; my God, I have willed it, and your law is in the midst of my heart” (Ps. XXXIX, 8).

“I have willed it,” he says—not, as you customarily say, “I was obliged” to be subject to God the Father (for you assert that it was a servitude owed to him). This supposed debt and conditional servitude is recognized as wholly alien to the truth of ecclesiastical faith.

For Catholic truth believes and confesses that, in one and the same Christ, according to the true substance of the flesh, Christ possessed all the infirmities of that flesh which he assumed voluntarily, whenever he willed. He possessed a voluntary and genuine hunger when, hungry, he came to the fig tree; a voluntary and genuine weariness when, tired from his journey, he sat beside the well; a voluntary and genuine wound when the soldier’s spear struck his side; a voluntary and genuine death when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit on the cross; and a voluntary and genuine burial when Joseph and Nicodemus placed him in the tomb after taking him down from the wood.

[Col. 0204D] Christ possessed all these infirmities of the flesh voluntarily, but truly, because he assumed the nature of human flesh not in appearance but in reality. He therefore possessed these sufferings voluntarily in the flesh so that, through the truth of the flesh, divine power—which could never suffer or die—might conquer infirmity and death and raise his flesh to perpetual life and power. Yet you strive to oppress him under the servitude of eternal subjection.

**V.** For you say: “Or in what form will he be eternally subject to the Father, if we believe that there will be no difference and no inequality between his divinity and humanity?”

We therefore say that in Christ God there are two proper natures: one of divinity, the other of humanity. But we believe that the glory of divinity is truly in him, lest the mere designation of divinity, recently introduced by you and separated from the nature of divinity in the human nature, divide the profession of our faith into two gods. We confess one God under the particular properties of two natures.

He will judge the world in the form in which he can be seen by all—a form which you assert to be conditionally subject to God the Father. You understand the subjection of that form in one way; the holy Fathers, inspired by the Holy Spirit, were able to contemplate the divine mysteries in another and deeper sense.

It is enough, however, to set forth the sense of blessed Hilary, that most renowned teacher, who completed the eleventh book of *On the Trinity* chiefly in discussion of this subjection:

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book II, chapter 27. Learned critics still disagree about the correct reading of this text in Saint Hilary, since the ancient manuscripts differ; this is not the place for a lengthy discussion.]

“First,” he says (*On the Trinity*, Book XI, no. 30), “I ask common understanding whether we should now understand subjection as servitude to lordship, weakness to strength, or dishonor to honor, so that, by subjecting contrary qualities [Hilary: ‘we subject’], the Son according to these things might be cast down beneath God the Father as one of a different nature [Hilary: ‘subjected’]? … Therefore the meaning of subjection is now nothing other than the manifestation of the mystery.”

And later (no. 40):

“Thus there is no other reason for subjection than that God may be all in all, with no part of an earthly body remaining in him, so that whereas formerly he contained two things in himself, now he may be God alone—not because the body has been cast away, but because through subjection it has been transformed; nor because it has been destroyed through dissolution, but because it has been changed through glorification. He acquires man for himself [Hilary: ‘God rather acquires man’], rather than losing God through man. He is subjected for this reason: not that he may cease to exist, but that God may be all in all.”

A little later he speaks of the glorification of the Lord himself, by which he testifies in the Gospel that he was to be glorified, where he says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John XIII, 31).

“He glorified him,” he says (no. 42), “in himself, so that, since he now reigns in the glory which proceeds from God’s glory, he might thereafter pass into the glory of God. For God glorified him in himself—that is, in the nature in which he is what God is—in order that God might be all in all.”

A little later (no. 43):

“And in this,” he says, “how great is the folly of heretical madness: to despair of this concerning God—that he might be flattered by his human hopes [the printed text reads ‘feet’; proposed reading: *spebus*]; and that God, who is powerful in man, should be weak in himself by accomplishing this. Neither speech nor reason capable of understanding such a thing says that God, being subject by some natural necessity to care for us, can bring himself no blessedness—not because he needs advancement, since he possesses an unshaken nature and power, but because, through the dispensation and mystery of great piety, he who is God, and is great [Hilary: ‘and is man’], is powerless for himself—that is, unable to bestow fully what he is as God—although he will unquestionably grant us also to be what we are not.

“For the end of human life and death is resurrection, and the surest reward of our warfare is incorruptible eternity, not remaining for the continuance of punishment but enduring for the fruit and delight of everlasting glory. Therefore, when the origin of our earthly bodies surpasses the condition of nature in the form of a higher nature and becomes conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body, God, found in the form of a servant [another reading: ‘perpetual’], although already glorified in the body, nevertheless, insofar as he is in the form of a servant, will not be conformed to God. Thus he who grants us the form of his glorified body [Hilary: ‘will grant’] will himself be able to bestow upon his body nothing beyond what he is to us and to himself in common.”

Let these testimonies of the holy Father Hilary concerning the subjection of the Son—which you assert to be owed and eternal—and also concerning the glorification in divine glory of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin, suffice.

**VI.** It is now worthwhile to bring forward some testimonies from the books of the holy teachers, which you also strive to twist into an opposite meaning in confirmation of your party, although they will be understood to be wholly opposed to you and thoroughly contrary to the sect of your error.

Moreover, you deceitfully suppress certain things which seem to condemn your heresy; and with your customary craft you do not fear to alter others, as you appear to have done in the books of blessed Hilary. There, that eminent and Catholic teacher says: “The power of dignity is not lost,” whereas you, in a thoroughly perverse manner, say: “It is adopted.” Where blessed Hilary says “it is adored,” you say “it is adopted.”

The humility of the flesh was indeed adored by the Magi and honored by the symbolic kinds of gifts; it was not adopted. This can be clearly understood from the preceding words of the same teacher, where he says—as you yourself have quoted—that “God is still adored in swaddling clothes.”

He himself, who lay in the cradle, is proclaimed by the angels as Christ the Lord and adored by the Magi as God; he is not adopted by the Father as a son. In this passage the same Father Hilary is most certainly discussing the adoration of the Magi, not paternal adoption, which you wickedly attempt to insert into the passage.

Moreover, when you quoted a testimony from the disputation that blessed Augustine held with Felician, an Arian bishop, you deliberately omitted certain words in the middle of the sentence [Note: See this disputation among the appendices to the works of blessed Augustine. It is there attributed to Vigilius of Thapsus.], words which seem contrary to your position. He says there (chapter 6):

“For some sons are adoptive, others natural: those who are begotten are sons from the beginning and proper sons; the others are first strangers, then sons [another reading: ‘a son’], when they appear to be received into the family through adoption.”

But the other words that you quoted in that passage were spoken by blessed Augustine from the standpoint of the heretic, not from his own, since he was conducting a disputation about the Catholic faith with him. You did not understand from whose person he had spoken the words you quoted. For he says:

“What then? You say, I suppose, that the Son could not have been born from the substance of the Father, lest we seem, through the generation of the Son, to divide the unbegotten Father?”

—and the rest of the passage, which plainly corresponds to the heretic’s position, not to that of Saint Augustine.

You also altered, with your customary perversity, another statement in the same book (the work cited, chapter 10). The text reads: “impassible in his own nature, passible in ours,” but you write: “impassible in his own nature, having suffered in what was alien”—as though his own body, which the Son of God made his own, were alien to him.

By introducing the word “alien,” you therefore set both assertions against yourself, for both cannot be true: Christ’s flesh cannot be alien and adoptive to the Son of God. For once it is adopted as a son, it can in no way remain alien to the one who adopted it as a son; having been assumed into the dignity of the Son, it ceases to be alien.

Christ’s humanity, however—neither soul nor body—was never alien to his divinity. From the beginning of conception and birth it was assumed into the possession of one person, so that the Son of God might be true and proper in two substances.

Why, then, did you suppress what is read in the same book concerning the glorification of Christ’s body and the unity of divinity? There the same aforesaid teacher says (the work cited immediately above):

“Therefore, when the flesh has been glorified by majesty, majesty is taught as humbled [Augustine: ‘having been humbled’] in the flesh. But we are certain that both statements concern not two Christs, as you suppose, but one and the same Christ, whom after the Virgin’s childbirth we know and proclaim to be God and man.”

And a little later (the work cited, chapter 11):

“One and the same Christ is he who wholly [Augustine: ‘so often’] endured insults and, having been led into the depths [Augustine: ‘in the deep’], was not overwhelmed. Accordingly, in the Mediator between God and human beings, we confess that the Godhead suffered injury through the body that was assumed, just as we know the flesh to have been glorified by the majesty of divinity.”

But all these things which the Savior of the world suffered for human salvation he suffered, as the same Father testifies in the same book, not—as you wish—by an obligation of necessity, but by free will. He says, among other things (chapter 14):

“Therefore,” he says, “the divinity of Christ experienced death through participation in the human affection which he had voluntarily assumed; it did not lose the power of its own nature, through which it gives life to all things. Thus, by dying, he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb, just as by being born he formed it in the Virgin’s womb. In both cases he freely willed to be born and to die, not compelled by the other, so that it is clear that he suffered what he himself had done. Nor is he therefore not suffering because he himself was acting; nor is he therefore not acting because another was not enduring it.”

Let the human mind also believe, without investigating, this marvelous and ineffable unity of natures in the Son of God, in one person and power, as is read in the same book. The same teacher says (chapter 8):

“For just as, without precedent, a mother bore her own creator, so the Father must be believed to have ineffably begotten the coeternal one. He was born from a mother, yet he already existed; from the Father, who was never without him. Let faith believe this; let understanding not investigate it, lest it either judge what it has not found to be unbelievable or, having found it, fail to believe it unique.”

If a mother bore her creator, and he was born from a mother who existed from the Father, how do you, with reckless audacity, habitually deny that he who was born from the Virgin is true God? Or how does what follows not terrify you: that, because this cannot be investigated by reason, “faith should believe it and understanding should not investigate it”? For this is a unique and unprecedented mystery.

**VII.** You also say that the humanity of the Son of God was made externally, as though it were alien—or rather, that the Son of God himself was made externally, as we read in your writing:

“These are the opinions of the aforesaid and outstanding teacher Augustine—not concerning the humanity of the Son of God, in which he was made externally, not subsisting from the substance of the Father, but born from the flesh of his mother.”

How is he the Son of God if he was made externally? The Son of God was eternally born from the Father, whom you here say was made externally. If you wish this to be understood of his humanity, then you are saying, together with us, that he who was born from the Virgin is the Son of God.

Nevertheless, Saint Cyril in no way agrees that Christ as man was made externally as though he were alien, like some garment of divinity. Rather, affirming that he is the proper and perfect Son of God in two natures, he says in the little book he wrote against Theodoret:

“We do not say that a man was assumed by God the Word and joined to him according to an externally devised manner, but rather we determine that he himself became man.”

Again, in the same author, from the passage cited above:

“Although we are called temples possessing God who dwells within us through the Spirit [Cyril: ‘temples of God, since we have God dwelling within us through the Spirit’], nevertheless we recognize another mode of the mystery according to Christ. For we assert that the flesh was united in truth to God the Word, together with a rational soul.”

Again, in the same work (Cyril, *Explanation*, chapter XII):

“Those who therefore divide the subsistences after the union and posit each separately—that is, man and God—understanding that the joining between them is according to dignity alone, establish two sons in every respect, whereas divinely inspired Scripture speaks of one Son and Lord.

“Accordingly, after the ineffable union, whether you call him God, we understand Emmanuel, incarnate and made God, to be the Word from God the Father; or whether you call him man, we nevertheless understand him as having participated dispensationally in human conditions [Cyril: ‘whether you name Emmanuel, incarnate and made human, God, we receive him as the Word of God the Father; or if you call him man, we likewise recognize that very one—the Word of God—who lowered himself through the dispensation to the measures of humanity’].

“We say that he who is intangible became tangible, and that he who is invisible became visible. For the body united to him was not foreign to him; we also say that it is tangible and visible.”

Again, after a little further on:

“The Only-Begotten became man not without will, but willingly. He did not, as you say, assume a man, granting him union with himself according to an arrangement and crowning him with the grace of sonship, as he has done with us.”

And shortly afterward:

“Once united, it is not safe to divide them, nor to split them into two sons—one Christ, Son, and Lord.”

**VIII.** Do you not divide Christ—not only contrary to the statements of this holy Father, but also contrary to the universal and apostolic practice of the holy Church of God—into two gods, namely a titular god and a true God, and into two sons, an adoptive son and a proper son, thereby heaping upon your own head the terrible anathema which is read in the same book of the aforesaid Father?

“If anyone presumes to say that Christ is a man bearing God, and not rather truly God, as one natural Son, according to the Word having become flesh and having shared with us in flesh and blood, let him be anathema.”

And later:

“For Christ himself also said concerning the holy prophets, or the holy men who existed before: ‘If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came—him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world—you say that he blasphemes because I said, I am the Son of God’” (John X, 36–37).

“But God does not dwell in Christ as he dwells in us. For he was God by nature, appearing according to our condition, and was one and only Son, even when he became flesh. Therefore those who presume to call him a man bearing God, rather than God made human, necessarily fall under the proposed anathema.”

Again, that same author, in a letter addressed to monks:

“For when it is proved that he who was born from the holy Virgin is God according to nature, no one should be slow to understand and declare that she must be called the Mother of God” [F.: ‘I think’].

And again:

“Nevertheless, there is one Lord Jesus Christ and one true Son, at once God and man; not a man made God [Cyril: ‘deified’] on equal terms with those who are so by grace, but rather true God appearing in human form for our sake.”

And later in the same letter:

“Come, let us demonstrate from the sacred writings themselves that he is God according to nature, even though he united his own flesh to himself; once this is shown [Cyril: ‘once this is revealed’], we call the holy Virgin the Mother of God, and with ample justification.”

Again, in the same letter:

“How, then, was Christ named the proper Son of God, he who was also handed over by God the Father for the salvation and life of all? For he was handed over because of our sins, and he himself bore the sins of many in his body upon the wood, according to the prophet’s word” (Isa. LIII, 12).

“It is therefore clear that the united thing assumed necessarily declared him to be the proper Son of God, who is from the holy Virgin” [Cyril: “It is clear that, looking to the union of the natures, he defines Emmanuel, who arose from the holy Virgin, as the Son of God”]. “For the body was not, according to our condition, that of anyone else, but rather was the proper body of the Word existing from the Father, born from her.”

Whence, O Felix, after such clear testimonies of the holy Fathers, has such hostile recklessness crept into you that you dare deny Christ to be the proper Son of God, or the true Lord, or that he suffered in his own body for the sake of our salvation?

Would it not be safer for you to keep yourself within the wall of the Catholic faith than to wander through the byways of unbelief? What should be thought of the sheep when the shepherd himself is shown to be wandering, and the one who ought to have been a guide to salvation has become a teacher leading to destruction?

Concerning the avoidance of such people, Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. It is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should be cast into Gehenna” (Matt. V, 29).

**IX.** Arnobius [Arnonius], a man of keen intellect, also brings forth, in the dispute he held with Serapion concerning the nobility of holy Mary, the Mother of God, and her incomparable holiness among all women, as well as concerning the divinity of the Son of God who was born from her, testimonies consistent with those of the holy Fathers, whose statements we have quoted abundantly. He says:

“While we confess two natures and two substances in the Only-Begotten,” he says, “it is objected that we are saying that one is the Son of God and the other the son of man. But we, by the authority of the Apostle, say: ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself’” (II Cor. V, 19).

“If he reconciled the world so that, by believing in him, he made human beings sons of God—although by nature they were servants, and in conduct guilty, and through the transgression of the first man subject to the enemy of the human race—nevertheless, through his grace he made them sons of God. [If, then, he made others sons of God,] how is he himself not the Son of God, united with the Word who is read to have become flesh?”

And shortly afterward:

“By his omnipotence, therefore, when he willed, he caused this man whom he assumed to do this, assuming in time what he himself always was beyond time, so that two sons of God could not be said to exist—one before time and another born in time—but one Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ.

“This is why it was said by the Apostle: ‘Although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him’” (II Cor. V, 16). It is as though he were saying: “Even if we once knew wool before it became purple through the admixture of the blood of the sea-snail, yet now we no longer know wool but purple, which no one among human beings may use unless he has been endowed with the dignity of an Augustus” [Arnobius: “of Augustus”].

“An objection is raised here: Was Jesus therefore previously worthless wool, and did the divinity that came upon him make him purple? We do not say this. But before the Holy Spirit came upon Mary, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and she conceived that which was to be called holy, the Son of God” (Luke I, 35–36), “before this, I say, Mary’s womb, although it was free from sin and holy, nevertheless, by the lowliness of humanity, was like the finest and incomparable wool among all the virgins beneath heaven. It was such and so great that it could fittingly receive within itself the divinity of the Son of God, just as wool receives the blood of the sea-snail; and it ceased to be wool, becoming true purple through the aforementioned blood.

“For it is not worthless wool but precious wool that is capable of receiving this blood. If this blood, through its admixture, exalted wool with such majesty that no one may use it except one endowed with royal dignity, how much more, when the Holy Spirit came upon Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, did he make that which was born from her from the seed of David according to the flesh, holy [Arnobius: ‘with himself’], the Son of God?

“Thus Mary was *Christotokos*—Mother of Christ—just as she was *Theotokos*—Mother of God. For before Mary there were other mothers of Christ, but they were neither virgins nor overshadowed by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High.

“She, however, is both Mother of Christ and the only Mother of God; she alone is a virgin, conceiving through the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High.”

[Note: “For what reason?” This and the following material are absent from the printed editions. They seem to belong to another holy Father. See Sermon 7, *On the Nativity of the Lord*, in the appendices to the works of Saint Augustine, no. 2.]

What, then, is there to investigate by human reasoning in a matter proved to have been accomplished by the miracle of divine power? A virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, and a virgin remained a virgin. With the majesty of the Father overshadowing her and the Holy Spirit impregnating her womb, she conceived God and gave birth to the Son of God. The archangel infused the word into her ears; God joined himself to human limbs. Faith received him whom chastity brought forth; the ancient curse was erased by a new blessing.

For it was said to Eve: “In pain and sorrow you shall give birth, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III, 16). By these three evils the first mother of the human race was punished: pain, sorrow, and servitude.

In contrast, the blessed Virgin Mary was honored by three most glorious goods: the angelic greeting, divine blessing, and fullness of grace.

For the first man was formed from virgin earth by the counsel of the Holy Trinity, when the Lord said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 23). The second Adam, that is, Christ, was created from the earth through the operation of the same Holy Trinity in the virgin womb—not merely truly human in every respect, but also perfect God in every respect.

“And, in order to discharge the debt of our condition, inviolable nature was united to passible nature, so that what was fitting for our remedies might be accomplished: one and the same Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, could die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.

“Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of the true man, true God was born, wholly in what was his own and wholly in what was ours. We call ‘ours’ those things which the Creator established in us from the beginning and undertook to restore. But those things which the deceiver introduced and the deceived man admitted left no trace in the Savior …

“He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, increasing what was human without diminishing what was divine” (Saint Leo, Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 3).

One and the same person is the Son of God in the conjunction of two natures, not by the grace of adoption but by the proper identity of the person. One is both the Only-Begotten and the First-Born—not one Only-Begotten and another First-Born (ibid., chapter 5).

“Therefore we all confess in the Creed that the Only-Begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, according to the Apostle’s testimony: ‘If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory and majesty’” (I Cor. II, 8).

Therefore the Lord of glory and the God of powers possessed in himself that by which he could be crucified and die. It was not one who was crucified for the salvation of the world and another who is the life of all living things, but one and the same—undivided by adoption and united by proper identity.

“The Word became flesh so that flesh as man might be advanced into the glory of God, not so that God might be changed into the dishonor of flesh,” as the Apostle says:

[Col. 0212A] “He who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17).

**X.** And when God joined himself to man, how is he not one God? Saint Augustine says in a certain homily on the Lord’s Nativity:

“The Son assumed flesh and did not abandon the Father, nor did he divide himself from the Father. The Son assumed flesh, I say—or as his own property [F.: ‘into a property’?]. Yet the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty, divinity, and equality; in the flesh alone there was the Son’s proper identity.”

With what confidence do you believe in adoption in Christ’s flesh, in which so great a teacher, and one so persuasive to all the faithful everywhere, unquestionably asserted the Son’s proper identity? Proper identity and adoption cannot be one and the same.

Whatever the Gospel history relates to have occurred in the conception and birth of Christ from the Virgin must unquestionably be believed to have been accomplished through miracles of divine power and through a dispensation beyond human investigation.

For the Virgin conceived and gave birth with her womb closed; and he who was born from her is the Son of God, true and perfect, one from the flesh of one woman. He who is God from God proceeded as man from man, like a bridegroom from the bridal chamber, a giant of twofold substance, wholly the proper Son of God the Father and wholly the proper Son of the virgin mother, inseparable in the unity of the person, one in the proper identity of the Son, and possessing in himself the power by which he would live eternally and by which he would die in time.

By his power he created us when we did not exist; by his goodness he redeemed us when we were lost; his praise is our salvation, as he himself says through the Prophet: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me; there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX, 23).

Whoever reads this verse faithfully should understand truthfully that it is better for every human being to praise his goodness than to scrutinize his power; to obey his commands humbly rather than stubbornly investigate his mysteries; and to venerate him lovingly rather than presumptuously reason about him.

In comparison with him, as the prophet says, “all the nations are like a drop from a bucket” (Isa. XL, 15). He is great and fearsome above all who surround him.

If he is great and fearsome even to the angelic orders and the spirits of the righteous, how do we, who dwell in houses of clay, presume to judge or discern the greatness or power of his faith?

When he willed, he made the world; and as he willed, he came into the world. As the Evangelist says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become sons of God” (John I, 10, 12).

Since he gave others the power to be sons of God, how can it be that he did not have the power to make himself the proper Son of God? Or how could he, although existing in two natures—divinity and humanity—be the proper Son of man and yet be unable to be wholly, in both natures, the proper Son of God?

Therefore, if he who was born from the Virgin is wholly the proper son of the Virgin, it is fitting that we believe him to be likewise the proper Son of God the Father.

For no nature resists the Creator of natures, so that he could not make from it what he willed—he who was able to create all things from nothing whenever he willed. From created things, therefore, he could much more accomplish whatever pleased his omnipotence.

Human reason cannot investigate how he who made all things was himself made among all things.

Many things could be said about this. Is there anyone whose holiness of life and grace of the Holy Spirit are such that he can say anything worthy of him? But let us pause here for a little while, so that, with divine grace assisting us, we may answer with a sharper pen the arguments which you strive to multiply either against the holy Church or even as a reproach against our name.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0213]

[Col. 0213A] **I.** It is said that blessed Jerome, that most vigorous champion of the Church of Christ against heretical perversities, declared that he applied himself with every effort so that the enemies of Christ might also be his enemies. Not only he, but all defenders of the Catholic faith, regarded this as a gift granted to them by God and as the highest praise.

Therefore I too, a very small servant of the Church of Christ, patiently endure the insults directed against my name, because, in the measure of my smallness, it is greatly delightful to me and a complete joy to have common enemies with my Lord Jesus Christ.

To love him is the highest wisdom; to praise him is perfect blessedness; to know him is eternal life. Conversely, not to love him is the deepest folly; to wish to take anything away from his glory is the final misery; and to be ignorant of him is the peril of perpetual death.

## II.

You therefore object that I said—and I confess that it is true—that Jesus Christ is true God and the true Son of God: because I have already said this, and I shall continue to say it. Not I alone, but also the entire holy Church of God, together with the apostles and all catholic teachers, says, believes, and confidently proclaims this throughout the celebration of the orthodox faith.

Nor is it enough for you to say such words once: “For if,” you say, “our same Redeemer, in the form of a servant, as you wish, is the true Son of God.” Why do you repeat this very thing again and again? So that it may be clearly understood that you do not wish to understand what you criticize us for wishing to affirm.

If, then, that man who was conceived and born through the divine operation of the Holy Spirit and the glorious chastity of the blessed Virgin is not, as you assert, the true Son of God, nor true God, what remains except that the blessed Virgin is in no way the true mother of God, but only a titular one? For if he who was born from her is a titular God, she who bore him is likewise titular, not the true mother of God. How impious it is to say this is most plainly demonstrated throughout the whole extent of the world in which Christ reigns and is worshiped.

This very charge was also made by heretics against the blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria: namely, that the blessed Virgin was not the mother of God but merely so called. In the same way, you now customarily say that Jesus Christ is not the true Lord and Son of God, but merely called such, as though he were only titular. Thus a certain Nestorian, arguing against the catholic faith, said:

> “He who exists before the ages is God; but, fashioning for himself a temple in the virgin womb, he was present with the one who was conceived and formed. For this reason we call that holy Virgin the mother of God—not as though she gave birth to God, but as though she gave birth to a man united to God, who fashioned him.”

[Note: These are the words of Theodoret in his refutation of the First Anathema of Cyril.]

But what else are you saying when you claim that the Word of God dwelt in the assumed man as in a kind of temple, rather than, as the evangelist says, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14)? “According to the Lord’s command,” you say, “he bore divinity, and he is the inhabitant of his own temple.”

But it is one thing for God to dwell in the saints, and another for God himself to have become man, and for God and man to be one person from two substances. “For,” as the blessed Cyril says, “we do not receive Christ’s common flesh as do sanctified men joined to the Word, nor as though he possessed a divine indwelling; rather, it is truly life-giving and has become the proper flesh of the Word himself, who is life by nature and God.”

And elsewhere:

> “Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt as in an ordinary man who was born from the holy Virgin, lest Christ the man be believed to possess God as an inhabitant. Although the Word dwelt in us, and it was said, ‘In Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily’ (Colossians 2:9), nevertheless we understand that, because he became flesh, he is not said to dwell as in the saints; nor do we attempt to define that such an indwelling occurred in him. Rather, being one according to nature and not changed into flesh, he made for himself such an indwelling as the soul is believed to have in its own body.”

(Saint Cyril, Letter to Nestorius on Excommunication.)

Christ our Lord and Son is therefore one, not as though by some conjunction or unity of dignity and authority a man possessed God—whom you are accustomed to call joined to God or adopted, and to say that he also bore divinity, even using, I do not know what unusual word, the expression “to line” divinity. For in common usage *liniare* means to draw or outline painted or sculpted images, or to represent the forms of any work. But I do not understand how this relates to the divinity or humanity of the Son of God.

Since, as we said above, you say that he bore divinity, hear what reward you receive for this from the holy and catholic men who were accustomed to argue extensively against this heresy of yours. Saint Cyril says:

> “If anyone dares to say that Christ the man is a God-bearing man, and not rather truly God according to nature as the only Son, in accordance with the fact that the Word became flesh and came near to share flesh and blood with us, let him be anathema.”

(Saint Cyril, Anathema V.)

This, then, is the reward for your labor here and now. What the reward will be in the future from that very one whom you strive so greatly to abase, attempting to deprive him of all the truth of sonship and all the power of divinity, you yourself will discover when you stand to be judged before his tribunal.

The aforesaid Fathers also add the following concerning the same matter:

> “God does not dwell in Christ as he dwells in us. For he himself was God, naturally appearing among us as one and the only Son, even when he became flesh. Therefore those who dare to say that he is a God-bearing man, and not rather God incarnate, necessarily fall under anathema.”

## III.

I am astonished that you are not afraid to introduce a new name of titular status into Christ, since your heretical predecessors were separated from communion with the Church for employing this very expression. For the blessed Cyril says:

> “Let us therefore beware of saying concerning Christ: ‘Because of the one who assumed, I venerate the one who was assumed; and because of the invisible one, I adore the visible one.’”

Yet you add something even more dreadful to this:

> “The one who was received is called God together with the one who received him.”

Whoever says this divides the one Christ into two Christs, establishing the man separately on one side and God likewise separately on the other; for he plainly divides the unity. Thus one is not co-adored or co-called God together with another. Rather, Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, is understood to be one, to be venerated with a single service together with his own flesh. For where there is bare titular language, there is denial of solid truth.

In truth, we say that the only-begotten Son of God became incarnate through that secret mystery known to him alone. It is ours to believe; it is his to know. But you, entirely forgetting this, attempt to investigate by reason what you ought to have revered by faith. It was yours to believe that God the Word, the Son of God, receiving all that belongs to man, became true man, and that the humanity he assumed, receiving all that belongs to God, cannot be anything other than God.

## IV.

You also accuse me of having misunderstood concerning which nature the blessed Gregory was speaking when he said:

> “It is one thing for human beings who are born to receive the grace of adoption; it is another for one singularly to have proceeded as God, through the power of divinity, from conception itself.”

[Note: Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 52, cited by Alcuin in his letter to Felix, no. 10, above, column 124.]

You give thanks that you understood the same sentence better, and you affirm that it was spoken of divinity, not humanity. But recognize who it is that was conceived as God through the power of divinity. For how can it be said of the divine divinity of the Son of God that he proceeded from conception? God begot his only-begotten Son—not from the conception of someone else; and the holy Virgin conceived that same Son from the Holy Spirit. From her the Son of God himself proceeded, as a bridegroom from the bridal chamber.

Or what nature was made what it is through the power of God? Was it the nature through which all things were made, or that nature which in the last times was conceived as being made from the Virgin?

You boast that you are an interpreter of the words of others, although you have scarcely ever been able to express your own correctly. You also reproach me—when I am rightly reproved, I do not refuse correction but rather desire and greatly welcome it. Yet there are many who, while eager to criticize others, merely display their own ignorance, which might have remained hidden had they kept silent, as it is written: “If a fool keeps silent, he will be considered wise” (Proverbs 17:28).

It is great foolishness to wish to produce testimony which is manifestly altogether against yourself. For three kinds of testimony are found in your writings. Some seem neither to harm nor to favor you, and do not pertain at all to the matter of the present dispute; this is a most certain indication of ignorance. Others are set forth by you in such a way that they nevertheless support us and are proved by clear truth to oppose you; as we said above, this is no small folly—to provide weapons for your adversary. Still others you have produced in such a way that, unless you corrupted them, they would in no manner appear to help you; this is recognized as the fault of an altogether malicious conscience.

In the first case you showed yourself ignorant, in the second unlearned, and in the third malicious. It is therefore astonishing—or rather, lamentable—that you dare to corrupt and alter the clearest testimonies of the holy Fathers and transfer them to a meaning different from the one in which those who wrote them set them down, as we have proved you did shortly before and as can be found in many places in your letters.

## V.

You presented a testimony from Saint Athanasius which most completely destroys your sect. Perhaps you understood that certain words in his testimonies were contrary to your views, and so you omitted what he said in the middle, lest you might appear to speak against yourself.

Let us therefore set out his complete statement, so that it may be recognized how maliciously you removed what you understood to have been placed most firmly against you:

> “How, then,” he says, “do those who are called Christians dare to doubt whether he who proceeded from Mary is God, the Son according to the nature and substance of God, but according to the flesh from the seed of David and, according to the flesh, from holy Mary?”

(Saint Athanasius, Letter to Epictetus, no. 2.)

But you kept silent about what follows, which most firmly contradicts your sect:

> “What do you think? Were they not rash when they said that Christ, who suffered and was crucified in the flesh, is not the Lord and Savior, God, and Son of the Father? Or how can they wish to be called Christians, who say that the Word came into [a holy man, just as into one of the prophets, and that he himself was not made man], taking a body from Mary, but that Christ is one and the Word of God another—the Word who existed as the Son of the Father before Mary and before the ages? Or how can they be Christians who say that one is the Son and another the Word of God?”

You kept silent about this and took the following words of the same statement as support for yourself, although they too are understood to be strongly contrary to you. You set down the words of the same Father Athanasius:

> “These things did not happen through adoption—far from it, as some have thought—but, as the truth is, when the Savior became man, the salvation of the whole human race was accomplished. For if, according to them, the Word was in the body by adoption, then what is called adoption is fantasy, and salvation too is found to be merely imaginary.”

(Athanasius, same work.)

Do you see how this most proven soldier of the catholic faith batters down the wall of your falsehood with the strongest battering ram? He says:

> “What do you think? Were they not rash when they said that Christ, who suffered and was crucified in the flesh, is not the Lord and Savior, God, and Son of the Father?”

Clearly he regards as rash those who deny that the one who was crucified is Lord, Savior, God, and Son of the Father. Nor does he consider those Christians who contradict this faith. He most truthfully affirms that everything accomplished in Christ happened without adoption, since he calls adoption fantasy and not truth.

How impious it is for someone who calls himself a Christian to believe that Christ is the Son of God merely by fantasy! This most truthful teacher of the catholic faith therefore said that these things occurred in Christ’s humanity, because it is not permissible to say or believe that anything was made in the eternal generation of the Word of God. He was generated eternally from the Father, not made in time.

What testimony against yourself could you have found more truthful and stronger than that which this most holy and truthful teacher of the Church asserts—he who most firmly affirms that everything accomplished in Christ’s conception, birth, passion, and resurrection occurred in truth and not through adoption, since he calls adoption fantasy?

## VI.

You also set down words of Saint Augustine from his homily on John, where he says:

> “The Father loves the Son—but how does the Father love the Son? Not as a lord loves a servant; as the unique one, not as an adopted one.”

(Saint Augustine, *Tractate XIV on John*, no. 11; Saint Augustine has “adopted” in place of “adoptive.”)

But you added words expressing your own meaning to Saint Augustine’s words, saying:

> “And if he thinks that this was said in the same way of both natures, let him first teach, if he can, how the Son of God in the form of a servant is not the servant of the Father, just as in his divinity he is believed and proclaimed not to be a servant but a Son, and not an adopted son but truly his own Son.”

We, however, taught by the most holy voice of God the Father, say that in both natures Jesus Christ is truly one Son of God, and that he is wholly loved by God the Father—not, as you suppose, partly as Son and partly as servant, which is entirely ridiculous to say. Rather, we say that the Father loves him wholly as his own and unique Son.

Over whom, I ask, did the voice sound at the baptism and on the holy mountain: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17; 17:5)? Was it over his divinity alone and not over his humanity? It is impious to believe this and presumptuous to say that the Father does not love the Son in the nature of the humanity he assumed. He is manifestly united from two substances in such a way that he is one only-begotten Son, not two sons—one only-begotten and the other adopted.

For this reason the Gospel says, a testimony that you frequently employ:

> “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

And you say that “grace pertains to the humanity, but truth to the divinity.” Nevertheless, the same evangelist called him one and only-begotten, in whom, according to your understanding, grace and truth exist—that is, the wondrous union of two natures, as we confess and believe, in one person and in one love of the Son of God.

## VII.

You also presented another evangelical statement with the exposition of the blessed Augustine, saying:

> “And you loved them,” he says, “as you loved me. For the Father loves us in the Son, because in him he chose us before the foundation of the world. Whoever loves the only-begotten Son certainly also loves his members, whom he adopted in him and through him.”

(Saint Augustine, *Tractate CX on John*, no. 5.)

But you kept silent about what follows in the same exposition, where the same teacher says:

> “Nor are we therefore equal to the only-begotten Son, through whom we were created and recreated, because it was said, ‘You loved them as you loved me’” (John 17:23).

He calls him the only-begotten through whom we were created and recreated: one only-begotten, not two only-begotten ones—a creator and a recreator. If he is only-begotten, he cannot be adopted.

> “For to say this means nothing other than: ‘You loved them because you loved me.’ For he who loves the Son would not fail to love his members. Or is there any other reason for loving his members than that he loves him? But he loves the Son according to his divinity, because he begot him equal to himself; he also loves him according to that in which he is man, because that same only-begotten Word became flesh, and because of the Word the flesh of the Word is dear to him. But he loves us because we are his members; for this reason he loved us before we existed. Therefore incomprehensible is the love with which God loves, and it is not changeable.”

Something more distinctive must be understood in the love of his Son than the poverty of our understanding can grasp. For this reason the same teacher, in another place in the same work, indicated that there is a particular property of love toward the Son of God according to the fact that he became man. He says:

> “For the Father sealed him” (John 6:27). “What does ‘to seal’ mean except to place something proper? For to seal means to put something by which he is not confused with others. To seal is to place a mark upon him [F.: “upon a thing”]. Whatever thing you mark, you mark it so that, because it is not confused with others, it can be recognized by you. Therefore the Father sealed him: he gave him something proper, so that he would not be compared with other men. Therefore it was said to him: ‘God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions’ (Psalm 44:8). To seal, then, means to hold as distinguished, that is, ‘above your companions.’ Therefore do not despise me,” he says, “because I am the Son of Man, and seek from me food—not food that perishes, but food that endures to eternal life.”

(Saint Augustine, *Tractate XXV on John*, no. 11.)

You also set down a statement from the books of the blessed Ambrose, which he composed on the Christian faith:

> “Others arise who say that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one nature. What underworlds have spewed forth such sacrilege?”

(Saint Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 6, no. 49.)

I do not know why you said this. What catholic believes that the divinity and flesh are one nature? But why did you keep silent about the beginning of the same statement, where the same teacher says:

> “Of no prophet was it said that the Word became flesh. No prophet took away the sins of the world. Of no other was it said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matthew 3:17). Of no prophet do we read that he is the Lord of majesty, which the Apostle said concerning Christ, whom the Jews crucified.”

The same teacher, in the same work, also gives the following words concerning the distinction [F.: “vision”] between Christ, Moses, and Elijah, who appeared with him on the mountain:

> “On the mountain Peter saw Moses and Elijah with the Son of God. He did not err concerning nature, nor did he err concerning glory. Finally, he asked not them but Christ what he should do. For although he was preparing service for three, he nevertheless awaited the command of one. But since he simply thought that three should be honored by the number (*numero* [variant: *numerum*]) of tents, he was corrected by the authority of God the Father, who said: ‘This is my beloved Son; listen to him’ (Matthew 17:5)—that is, ‘Why do you associate your fellow servants with your Lord? This is my Son: not Moses the son, but this one is the Son.’ The apostle perceived the correction; he fell on his face, terrified by the Father’s voice and the Son’s splendor. But he was raised up by the Son, who is accustomed to lift up those lying prostrate, and he saw one, he saw only the Son of God. For the servants withdrew, so that the Lord alone, who alone was designated as Son, might be seen.”

(Saint Ambrose, Book I *On the Faith*, chapter 13, no. 81.)

## VIII.

Thus, while reviewing and bringing forward many testimonies of the holy Fathers in which no genuine support for your side is found—and while we have shown most clearly that some of them are plainly contrary to you and are certainly understood to affirm the truth of the catholic faith—you suddenly came to the prophet Zechariah, to whom Jesus the priest was shown by the angel in filthy garments (Zechariah 3).

You assert that the blessed Jerome explained this vision or prophecy in one way, whereas we read that he wrote about the same prophet in another way. For you say that this interpreter of sacred history gives the following words:

> “And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments”—that is, filthy from transgression, from the flesh of sin which he deigned to put on. Hence he is seen wrapped in cloths and bearing the rent garments of the human race, since he took those things upon himself, until he was covered by the tunic of innocence through the ray of the cross. “Is this not,” he says, “a brand snatched from the fire?” A brand snatched from the fire is shown to have been half-burned, not consumed. The Lord put on that body of the human race which had been scorched by the transgression of the first-formed ancestors and by the flame of crimes; and, like a half-burned brand, he freed it from the fire of Gehenna.

In what book or work the blessed Jerome said this, we have not found. Therefore, in his treatise on the same prophet, which that outstanding teacher composed either from the Hebrew truth or from the catholic interpretation of the holy Fathers, as we have said, this meaning is nowhere found.

You certainly say: “filthy from transgression, from the flesh of sin which he deigned to put on.” But Jesus, the eternal priest according to the order of Melchizedek, did not have sinful flesh, because there was no transgression in his flesh, but only the likeness of sinful flesh. No scorching of sin appeared in his body. Rather, like wool, pure and unstained by any sin, and like a most radiant jewel, more precious than the entire world, the most holy body of Christ shone translucent, entirely free from the filth of transgression.

The same outstanding teacher explained the meaning of this vision in the treatise on the work mentioned above in two ways. According to the Hebrew interpretation, he asserted that it ought to be understood of Jesus son of Jehozadak, the high priest. That priest of God had filthy garments because of the foreign woman whom he had taken as his wife, or because of the sins of the people, or because of the squalor of the captivity from which he had recently been rescued, like a half-burned brand. For this reason Satan stood at his right hand, because he had a true accusation against him.

But the devil never stood at the right hand of our Jesus, because he never found a true accusation in him. Defeated in every temptation, he withdrew from him like a fleeing thief and a frightened warrior. Or how is it fitting to say of God Jesus that the angel said to him, “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity,” when he had no iniquity? Nor was any angel stronger than he, so that he would need to cleanse him from sin, since our Jesus—the angel of great counsel—was sent from the Father’s throne to cleanse the sins of the whole world.

The same teacher also sets forth, not as confirmation but as an exposition, the opinions of certain people who wished to understand these things of Christ. Concerning the brand snatched from the fire, he says that Jesus was not consumed in the Babylonian fire [According to Saint Jerome’s meaning: not consumed by Babylonian fire], that is, he was not scorched by the blackness of sins, nor touched by the flame of this age—that is, he was touched by no flame of vices, or at least touched—but was free from all filth of sins, shining like gold tested in fire.

Yet they say that the meaning of this prophecy can better be understood of Christ where it says:

> “Hear, Jesus the great priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men who signify portents. Behold, I will bring my servant the Rising One; for behold, the stone which I have set before Jesus has seven eyes” (Zechariah 3:8).

The one of whom it is written, “Behold, a man whose name is the Rising One” (Zechariah 6:12), was promised to Jesus and his friends, who are men signifying portents—that is, to the prophets and the Jewish priesthood. And in the Gospel: “In which the Rising One from on high visited us” (Luke 1:78). He is also the cornerstone, cut without hands from the mountain, which crushed all the kingdoms of the world (Matthew 21:44).

Upon this stone are seven eyes—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are read in Isaiah (Isaiah 11:1) as resting upon the flower that sprang from the branch of the root of Jesse. Concerning him it is also written in the Song of Songs:

> “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1).

Concerning this stone it is immediately added:

> “I will carve its carving,” says the Lord of hosts, “and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day” (Zechariah 3:9).

> “I will cause this stone, which was said to be before Jesus, to be wounded by the nails of the cross and the soldier’s lance; and in his passion I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day, of which it is written: ‘This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it’” (Psalm 117:24).

(Saint Jerome, on the cited passage.)

We have therefore explained the meaning of this prophecy more fully, so that it might be understood how differently the blessed Jerome set forth the meaning or interpretation of this vision in his treatise on the prophecy.

## IX.

You also set forth sayings of the blessed Ambrose, but you disturb the meaning of his sentence by adding a single pronoun. That outstanding teacher says:

> “To the holy patriarch David, the Lord is Lord according to his glory; according to the sequence of bodily descent, he is Son—not failing to be himself, but acquiring for himself the right of our adoption.”

(Saint Ambrose, Book V *On the Faith*, no. 107.)

But you altered his words. Where he said “descent,” you wrote “reception”; and where he said “acquiring for himself the right of our adoption”—which makes no sense at all—you repeated this same sentence twice in your little book, delighting, I suppose, in the word “adoption.” Yet here it is placed entirely concerning us, not concerning Christ, who is said to acquire the right of our adoption—that is, the power of adoption.

I do not know whether, according to your customary practice, you altered his words through ill will or through ignorance. If through ill will you attempt to alter the pure meanings of the holy Fathers, why are you not afraid of Scripture, which says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11)? If through ignorance, I am astonished that you are not ashamed of your stupidity; for while you wish to appear wise, you appear foolish. According to Solomon, you could have been considered wise if you had kept silent.

You also take the testimony of the most blessed Pope Leo as assistance for your sect, although it is plainly recognized as very much contrary to your views. He says:

> “For he who is true God is true man, and there is no falsehood in this unity, since in one another there are both the lowliness of man and the height of divinity.”

But you divide this unity into two sons, one proper and the other adopted. The height of divinity descended to the lowliness of humanity, and the lowliness of humanity ascended to the height of divinity—not by a change of nature, but by the condescension of honor.

You also set forth a testimony from the book of the blessed Augustine which he himself called the *Enchiridion*. In a certain earlier letter of yours, you greatly defiled the words of the same holy Father in that book by inserting things he never said. So too in this testimony you say things that he in no way said and that make no sense according to any rational interpretation.

He says:

> “Because that man, without any preceding merits, at the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, was joined to the Word of God in such a unity of person that the very same one was both the Son of God and the son of man, and the son of man was the Son of God.”

(Saint Augustine, chapter 40.)

But you say: “without any preceding males.” What do you wish to signify by “males,” except perhaps husbands? This cannot stand at all according to the rules of Latin eloquence. If you wished to refer to males, you ought to have said *maribus*, not *maris*. But the eloquence of your singular expertise is accustomed to use such words, which in no way accord either with the rules of correct speech or with the meaning of the catholic faith.

Perhaps you were afraid to say “without any preceding merits,” because immediately afterward, in the statements displaying your learning, you are found to have said:

> “That which,” you say, “he spoke concerning the humanity of the Son of God, in which, having been born a man, he merited through the grace of adoption to be what he is and to receive what he has.”

You say, together with your predecessors Pelagius and Nestorius, that Christ merited to be what he is, whereas Saint Augustine and all catholic teachers testify that, without any preceding merits, that same one was conceived and born as God at the very beginning of Christ’s humanity.

And how do you assert that there are different sons in Christ because of the two natures, when this most holy teacher, in the testimony—*quem* [variant: *quod*]—that you yourself presented, says that the Son of God is the same one as the son of man, and the son of man the same one as the Son of God? If the son of man is the same as the Son of God, there is altogether one truth and one name of Son in Christ. For the unity of person rejects a duality of sonship in Christ; adoption has no place where proper sonship has preceded. Nor is divinity held bound by human prejudices, since it works all things according to the proper power of its will—he who said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

## X.

What is this? With a presumptuous mind and foolish recklessness, you are not afraid to probe matters higher than yourself, and you attempt to insert yourself between the divinity and humanity of the Son of God. You strive to scrutinize by human reasoning the ineffable mystery of divine goodness.

You do not know how to set a limit to your opinion, although you cannot even discern yourself or adequately explain how your soul was placed in the most delicate beginnings of your formation in your mother’s womb. Without you, the Son of God did what he willed. The Wisdom of God knew how, without diminution of himself, to pour himself into human nature and, through an ineffable unity, to become in time the son of man who had always been, before all times, the Son of God through whom times were made.

But, filled with carnal thinking, you do not believe that the power of God could have a proper Son unless he underwent something like what the substance of flesh undergoes when it gives birth to flesh. This seems incredible to the foolish, although all things are rightly believed possible for God by the wise, since Truth itself says:

> “This is impossible with human beings, but with God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26).

It is therefore also recognized as possible for God that he could have a proper Son from the Virgin. The same Son of God made for himself the time in which he would become man. From his mother he assumed that by which he could die, while he remained immortal forever. Yet he was one and the same—[possibly missing: mortal and] immortal, impassible and passible—not one and another.

He who is life-giving life dies by his own will, when he willed to do so, just as the Lord spoke through Moses in the Book of Exodus:

> “You shall see your life hanging upon a tree, and you shall not believe your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66).

Learn from his own testimony in the Gospel that Christ is God and life, when he says:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

For this reason the blessed Peter, preaching to the people in the Acts of the Apostles, said:

> “But you asked for a murderer to be released for you, while you killed the author of life” (Acts 3:15).

Concerning him the blessed Cyprian also says:

> “He who will judge is judged, and the Word of God is led silently to the sacrifice.”

Gregory of Nazianzus likewise says:

> “We needed God incarnate and put to death, so that we might live. It was an old thing for man to die; but, lest this should always happen in man, a new thing occurred: God died. Yet he died in the flesh, not in divinity.”

### XI
