Nor do we in any way confuse the natures in Christ, as you claim that we have done; but, while preserving the property of each nature—namely, the divine and the human—we confess one God, Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of God, in two natures, but in one person and one dignity of Sonship. For just as the soul shares in the body’s pains, although the soul remains immortal, while the body cannot suffer without the soul’s sharing in its suffering—because soul and body are one man, and the feelings of soul and body, whether sorrowful or joyful, are shared, since it is one man who simultaneously suffers or rejoices—so the Son of God suffered in his own flesh. It was not one who was passible in the body and another who was impassible in divinity, but one in both.

Nor again do we divide Christ into two sons, or two gods, or two persons with Nestorius. Although he did not openly speak of two persons, he nevertheless professes in his statement everything that must necessarily belong to two persons. In the same way, although you avoid the words “two persons,” we find you professing in your letters everything that must necessarily belong to two persons.

For who does not know that, in the case of one Father, the person of an adopted son is one thing and that of a proper son another? No father, according to the usage of human custom, could adopt his own proper son for himself as though he were a stranger; nor could he make his own proper son the one whom he adopts as a son, since paternity belonging to another made that one a stranger to him. Adoption is made from someone else; a proper son, however, remains in the truth of his own property.

There is one God the Father, and he has one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. In both substances, moreover—the substance of divinity and of humanity—the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is one and the same: just as he is true God, so also true man, as the Apostle bears witness, saying: “From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). And elsewhere: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (John 2:5).

Thus, from these and other apostolic declarations, we prove that our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ is both true God and true man. Although he possesses with the Father equal impassibility and immortality, nevertheless, for our salvation, he assumed a passible human nature without losing the majesty of impassible divinity—not so that divinity might be changed into humanity, but so that humanity might be preserved in divinity.

Accordingly, in accordance with the truth of this man, the Son of God was born of the Virgin and of the Holy Spirit for our redemption. Thus the angel speaks to Mary in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

If anyone despises this confession of the true faith, or considers it insufficiently catholic, let him read the words of Saint Augustine, which he composed in his explanation of the Catholic Creed [Note: [Col. 0223D] Saint Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*], and he will find that I most certainly follow that doctor’s understanding. Everywhere he is shown to be a most pure and truthful teacher in the Catholic faith.

For, as that same Saint Augustine says, Sacred Scripture speaks of Christ in three ways. The first is when, according to that supreme divinity which is equal and coeternal with the Father, it calls him so before the assumption of flesh. The second is when, after the flesh has been assumed, the same God is man and the same man is God; he is read and understood according to a certain human excellence [Possibly: dignity] of his, by which he is not equal to other men but is mediator and head of the Church. The third is when, in a certain manner, the whole Christ is understood in the fullness of the Church—that is, the head and the body, according to the fullness of a certain perfect man, in whom we have become members—and is preached to believers and presented as recognizable to the discerning.

The present discussion is chiefly concerned with the second manner. In it, with a public confession, in catholic peace, and strengthened by the most approved testimonies of all the holy teachers, we profess our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ to be true God and true man. We do not say that he is true God in part and titular God in part, as your unlearned novelty is accustomed to assert when it says: “Christ is God according to divinity, and the true Son of God; but according to humanity he is a titular God and an adopted son”—as though truth belonged to the divine part, while the human part had only a title and not pure truth.

Hear, therefore, how blessed Augustine responds to your division in his disputation against the heretic Maximinus. He says (Book II, chapter 10, no. 2):

> “Christ is one person of a twofold substance, because he is both God and man. Yet God cannot be called a part of his person; otherwise the Son of God, God, before he assumed the form of a servant, would not have been whole, and he would have grown when humanity was added to his divinity—something that would be said most absurdly in one person, because God cannot be a part of anything.”

### XII

Blessed Cyril also agrees with this most holy Father—Cyril, whose testimonies you yourself frequently employ—binding under the bond of anathema those who dare to offer unequal [Possibly: inappropriate] veneration to God’s Son Jesus Christ: one veneration, as though for the true Word of God, and another, as though under the title of the man who was assumed.

He says, therefore [Note: [Col. 0225D] The texts of Saint Cyril are presented here with considerable corruption. Alcuin copied them partly from the *Explanation of the Twelve Chapters*, which appears in volume VI of Saint Cyril’s works, p. 154, and partly from the *Apologetic Epistle against the Objections of Theodoret to the Twelve Chapters*. The first passage is Cyril’s Eighth Anathema, which reads as follows: “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be worshiped and glorified together with the Word of God, and that God should be jointly named with the other as though he were another— for this is the meaning that the particle ‘with,’ when added, invariably and necessarily conveys—and does not rather honor Emmanuel with one worship and assign him one glorification, insofar as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”]:

> “If anyone says that the man who was assumed ought to be worshiped together with God the Word, and glorified as one [being] in another, and does not rather honor Emmanuel with one worship and call one glorification his, according to the fact that he became flesh, let him be anathema. For the syllable *co-* prefixed to the word compels this meaning: that one is, as it were, another in another.”

And below [Note: [Col. 0225D] This second text appears in the declaration of the aforesaid Eighth Anathema, where it is given as follows: “If anyone therefore says that he should be worshiped together with God the Father’s Word as a man separately, as though he were another apart from him, and does not unite him according to the true union into one Christ, Son, and Lord, honoring him with one worship, he is justly subjected to the force of this Anathema.”]:

> “If anyone therefore says that he should be worshiped together as a man separately, with God the Word existing as another apart from him, and does not unite him according to the true unity into one Christ, Son, and Lord, glorifying him with one worship, he is justly subjected to the force of the anathema.”

And again [Note: [Col. 0226D] This third passage is found in the defense of this Anathema against Theodoret’s objection, in the work cited above, p. 226, and there reads as follows: “For if he himself, God and man at the same time, is worshiped as one with one worship, and is not worshiped together with another and jointly called God, lest Emmanuel be believed to be a mere and ordinary man like us, sharing by grace in divine glory, but rather we confess him to be God in the flesh for our sake—that is, truly made man—not through a change of nature by alteration and conversion, but through the dispensation of union.”]:

> “For if he is the same God and man at the same time, he is rather worshiped as one with one worship, and is not worshiped together with another or jointly called God, so that Emmanuel may not be believed to be merely an ordinary man, and, like us, to have received a share in divine glory by grace; rather, we confess that he was made truly man for our sake, God in the flesh—not through a transition of nature by change and conversion, but through the dispensation of unity.”

In the aforesaid book against Maximinus, blessed Augustine also most truthfully testifies that the Son of God became man and was truly exalted, according to the apostolic word, above every name that is in heaven or on earth (Phil. 2:9).

> “This,” he says (chapter 2), “was granted to him as man, according to whom he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; yet he himself, the Son of God, God born of God, equal to the Father, already possessed it.”

If, therefore, in the dispensation of the flesh, this was granted to him which he already possessed in the nature of divinity, it follows that the same true Son of God, born of the Virgin, must be believed and confessed.

You say, then, that he is God, but not the true Son—[“whom you do not deny to exist”] [Note: [Col. 0226D] The words enclosed in brackets appear to be superfluous]—but an adopted and not a true son. What is this novel introduction of sonship in Christ? You say that he is God, but not true God. What fruit is there in such a title when truth is diminished? And how is all truth in Christ if, according to your opinion, that which above all must be confessed is not to be believed true?

You have attempted to refute the most certain truth by saying that Christ was called God because he was joined and attached to God—not because he is truly God or the Son of God, but on account of him, as you are accustomed to say, by whom he was assumed—plainly considering the one who assumes to be one and the one assumed to be another.

For if the one who assumes is true God, while the one assumed is not true God and not the true Son, it necessarily follows that you are trying to introduce two persons into one Christ, though by a false confession; for there are altogether two: the true and the non-true.

But if the blessed Virgin did not give birth to the true God, the Son of God, how is she rightly venerated and believed by all who believe correctly throughout the universal Church of the whole world as the Mother of God? Or, if you are not ashamed to deny that she is the Mother of God, lest you openly and plainly reveal yourself as a public enemy of the Church, you are necessarily compelled to admit that she gave birth to two gods, one true [Possibly supplement: and the other titular].

Or, if this seems as absurd to you as it does to us, confess with us that he is truly called and truly is the true God—not fictitiously called God, and called what he is not. For it is incongruous and utterly foolish to call God something that he is not, just as it is known to be impious and detestable to deny what he is.

### XIII

After the testimonies of the holy Fathers—many of them, and some of them indeed rightly set forth by you, though wholly favoring the catholic rather than the heretical position—you introduce the bishops of Spain, whom you call orthodox. In the speeches you have presented, they are unmistakably shown to be heretics.

Unless, perhaps, you have corrupted their statements, as you were accustomed to do with the others: namely, so that what they said well, you might dare to change into support for your error and substitute one thing for another. For some of those Fathers [Possibly: passages] assert that, where you said “adoption” or “adopted man,” they said “assumption,” and where you said “adopted,” they said “assumed.” In this too your malicious obstinacy is exposed.

For if you were confident in your position as though it were the truth, you would by no means change what others had said well into a perverse meaning; for truth, wherever it exists, defends itself.

But whether you have altered these testimonies, or set them down as they were spoken by them, it is not a matter of great concern. We desire to be supported more by Roman than by Spanish authority, by the truth of our assertion and faith; although we do not reject the Spanish testimonies when they speak in a catholic manner.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] See below, in the letter to Elipandus, no. 11.]

Let everyone know that he must be refuted on the point in which he disagrees with the universal Church.

The Roman Church, therefore, which is shown to be the one to be followed by Catholics and by those who believe correctly, customarily confesses in the true Son of God, both in the solemn celebration of the Mass and in all its other writings and letters, him who deigned to become man for our salvation and to undergo the torment of the cross [Possibly: to have undergone it].

In the Mass for the human Nativity of this same Lord of ours, we customarily sing:

> “Grant that we may joyfully receive your Only-Begotten as our Redeemer and confidently behold him also as the coming Judge.”

We confess that he who redeemed us by his blood and is to judge the world at his coming is the only-begotten Son of God. This was unquestionably said concerning his humanity.

Likewise, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that the new birth of your Only-Begotten according to the flesh may free us.”

And elsewhere:

> “O God, who by the precious blood of your Only-Begotten…”

Likewise, on the Wednesday before Easter:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we may be freed through the passion of your Only-Begotten.”

And in another prayer:

> “Bestow, almighty God, that through the temporal death of your Son, which the venerable mysteries attest…”

This is found so frequently that examples are unnecessary: namely, that he himself who suffered death for us is called the one and true Son of God, just as he truly is.

We have therefore chosen to follow such authorities, in whom the more correct faith and the more manifest truth are evident.

### XIV

What you earnestly requested, I believe, has been fulfilled by us. For you say:

> “If anyone wishes to make us depart from our confession, let him produce equally suitable witnesses who affirm that the true God was conceived from his mother’s womb and that he is the true Son of God.”

As we said above, all the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church customarily employed arguments of this kind, so that they might undoubtedly confess Jesus Christ our Savior to be the only-begotten Son of God.

It is not surprising, however, that those who are recognized as seeking the Truth itself in their prayers improperly and foolishly should wander far from the path of truth. Or how can someone be thought capable of recognizing the Truth when he attacks that same Truth in his words and writings?

You also ask me to show how the true God was conceived and born. Throughout the whole course of this present work we have dealt with you on this point: that the only-begotten Son of God, the Word of the Father, became flesh.

For if he who was conceived and born of the Virgin Mary is not the true Son of God, then what John says is not true: “The Word became flesh.” What does the statement “The Word became flesh” mean except that the Son of God, having assumed human flesh, became man?

But if the true God and true Son of God was not conceived, then the true Son of God was not born of the Virgin. And if this is so, he was born a mere man and without divinity; how contrary this is to the Catholic faith, every correct believer understands.

According to the Catholic faith, therefore, the same true Son of God was conceived and born of the Virgin who, before all ages, was born of the Father. For the assumed nature of humanity did not make him who was born of the Virgin someone other than him who was begotten of the Father before time; rather, it plainly shows that the very same one became what he had not previously been.

### XV

But because it would be lengthy to examine all the arguments of your perversity, it is sufficient for the present to answer you concerning this point: you especially attempt to deny that the Son of God, having become man, is true God because he is read to have prayed for himself just as he prayed for us.

Where you read that the Son of God prayed for himself as well as for us, I certainly do not know—namely, “that the Son of God prayed for himself as he did for us.” For what could he not provide for himself, to whom the Father gave all things into his hands (John 3:55)? Or for what sin should he be thought to ask forgiveness from God, who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found (Isa. 53:9; 1 Pet. 2:22)?

We, who are commanded to pray to God without ceasing, unquestionably have something that must be forgiven us by him. But what would Christ ask to have forgiven him, when he never did anything that could have been forgiven him?

He must therefore be believed to have prayed for us—that is, for his body, which is the Church—and he knows that it still frequently sins while placed in the frailty of the flesh. He does this even today, as the Apostle bears witness, saying: “Who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34).

As we said above, he is said to pray for us in this sense: he presents to God the Father the flesh that he assumed for us and in which he also suffered. This is his intercession for us: by displaying the sufferings that he innocently endured for us, he in a certain way reminds God the Father to have mercy on us—not because that fountain of wisdom and fullness of knowledge could be ignorant of anything, but because, through the nature of the flesh assumed from us, he accomplishes what he always knows and desires and knows ought to be accomplished for our benefit. That is, he causes the Father to acknowledge those who believe in him, hope in him, and love him.

Your predecessor Nestorius himself was accustomed to say this very thing: namely, that Christ had offered sacrifice for himself and for the race of his body. What you say—that he prayed for himself—Nestorius, intending the same meaning, said that he had offered himself for himself and for his race.

Hear what blessed Cyril opposed to this blasphemy. He says:

> “If anyone says that Christ offered an offering for himself, and not rather for us alone, let him be anathema.”

And elsewhere:

> “For he offered his own body, not for himself, but for us. For what offering or sacrifice would he need for himself, who exists as God, free from every sin? Whoever says that he offered himself both for himself and for us will in no way escape the charge of impiety.”

The same Cyril also says:

> “The heretics say that Christ offered himself not only for us but also for himself; this is foreign to the right and undefiled faith.”

That he is therefore said to have prayed, to have spent the night in prayer, and to have supplicated with such earnestness that his sweat ran down upon the ground like drops of blood (Luke 21:44), must all be understood to have happened so that he might show the truth of the humanity he had assumed, which could have tears and sweat; and so that he might show that the Father’s hearing is accessible to our prayers, so that we may take care not to waste away in temptations through sluggish sleep, but rather exercise ourselves vigilantly in the persistence of prayer.

This is what is signified by the fact that, when he is read to have prayed, he is said to have done so frequently at night: he was indicating, through the darkness of night, the storms of temptations.

His prayer also especially suggests that the earth had to be washed by his innocent sweat, since it had been polluted by the harmful sweat of the one to whom it was said: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19).

For that nature propagated from Adam, the first man, would never have tasted its bread, by which it might be nourished unto eternal life, if the Son of God had not deigned to assume that same nature as living bread and the bread of angels.

The Evangelist’s statement that his sweat was like drops of blood falling upon the earth also seems to signify that the first homicide had to be cleansed by Christ’s blood, concerning which it is said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4:10).

That blood of Christ cries more powerfully to God the Father, having been poured out upon the earth for the salvation of us all—whether when our Lord himself prayed for us, or when, hanging on the cross for us, he endured the wounds inflicted by the striking soldier.

But let this suffice concerning these matters.

### XVI

The statement of the Apostle James, which you brought forward as an example in place of the term “adoption,” is customarily explained quite differently by the holy Fathers than by you, as is also the passage you cited from Solomon:

> “By denying,” you say, “the name of adoption in Christ’s flesh—one word, as I think, spreads itself into how many snares of offense!—as it is written in Solomon: ‘Whoever sins in one thing will lose many good things’ (Eccl. 9:18). And in the Apostle James: ‘If anyone keeps the whole law but offends in one point, he has become guilty of all’ (James 2:10).”

But who does not know that these testimonies ought properly to be brought forward against you yourself? For what else have you done than sin in that one matter in which you have lost many good things?

There is one supreme and first commandment: charity, which alone is known to be true in the Catholic Church. Since you have placed yourself outside the Catholic Church, what else have you done than sin against that commandment of charity? Whoever sins against it, even if he keeps the whole law, has become guilty of all.

This was therefore not said about adoption being denied in Christ, but about the unity of charity being broken: whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all.

For, as the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3), and so forth—the other things said there in praise of charity.

Strive, therefore, to reach more quickly the bosom of this charity. Outside it, all other things, even if they appear to be rightly done, can profit nothing; nor should those deeds be called good deeds which are performed without the perfection of charity.

Let it be enough for you that you have sinned until now. Do not think it a lesser danger to divide the unity of the Catholic Church by making a schism, and by teaching perversely to separate Christ’s members from his body, than to commit murder by killing yourself. Indeed, it is clearly a greater loss to destroy so many by leading them astray than for one person alone to perish.

### XVII

Return, then, at last to yourself, repenting of what you have done—you who have poured yourself out so far from yourself by examining what you ought not to have examined.

Let it be enough for you, as I have frequently urged and still do not cease urging, that the holy and universal Church of God has always believed and taught concerning Christ from the beginning, and will not cease teaching until the end of the age wherever the Catholic Church of God exists. This fulfills the word of our Lord Jesus Christ [Read: “the Lord”], who promised that he would remain with his faithful until the end of the age.

Let it be enough, I say, for you to believe that Christ, the Son of God, is true God and the true Son of G—[Note: [Col. 0229D] In the royal manuscript codex no. 2848, the words here are so obliterated, as Quercetanus noted at this point, that they can scarcely, if at all, be read. The distinguished Mr. Lieble, librarian of the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris, who examined the same codex, nevertheless believes that the words “in two natures” can be read here.]

And do not labor to investigate more concerning the mystery of the incarnation of this same God of ours than what you have read in the Gospels and found written in the apostles’ teachings.

Whatever agrees with these, hold firmly and believe truly; but whatever you see to be contrary to and inconsistent with them, flee as the plague of deadly poison.

Praise and adore Christ, the King of all ages, and strive to remove from your heart and mouth the term “conditional servitude.” For the fact that he willed to be called or to be a servant for your sake is the gift of voluntary obedience, not—[Note: [Col. 0230D] The cited Mr. Lieble writes that the reading should be: “not the punishment of a necessary condition.”] nor the punishment of a condition.

> “For this reason,” says blessed Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 56 (no. 5, 10), “he became man: because he is merciful—not so that he might be born by the necessity of a condition, but so that he might free us from the condition of necessity.”

A little later he adds:

> “The angelic creature serves Christ. The angels were instructed to render obedience; they could be sent for service, not for assistance, as it is written: ‘The angels ministered to him’ (Matt. 4:11)—not as though they were ministering to one in need, but as subjects to the Almighty.” [Possibly: Augustine reads “merciful” instead of “ministering”; the manuscripts have “could be sent,” while Augustine may read “could be dispatched.”]

If, therefore, every angelic creature is subject to him [and], as though to God, worships him, and every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows to him, what then are you, who alone remain among all? . . . .

Adore him, then, with us: the King of heaven, Lord of all, the true Son of God the Father, our true God and Savior, to whom belong eternal honor, unfailing power, and perpetual praise forever and ever. Amen.

### 860. Four Books of Blessed Alcuin against the Letter Sent to Him by Elipandus

In these he refutes that man’s erroneous assertions.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] This is the title of this letter in the Vatican Codex, from which we corrected it.]

### Letter of Albinus to Laidradus and Nefridius, Bishops, and Benedict, Abbot

*(A.D. 800.)*

To the venerable and most beloved lords in the charity of Christ: Laidradus, bishop of Lyons; Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne; Benedict, abbot; and likewise to the most holy and highly honored bishops, abbots, and brothers of the province of Gothia, Albinus, the most humble son of the holy Church, sends greetings.

I know that I am indebted to all the sons of the devout mother Church in the service of holy charity, in preaching and defending the truth of the Catholic faith. I desire, by God’s gracious gift, to be able to accomplish this as effectively as I willingly confess that I devote my service to this most pious labor [Quercetanus: “or, to accomplish it”].

Above all, however, I consider it right that my mind should labor in this grace for your most holy love, according to the unfailing gift of the Giver, lest the neighboring plague of Spanish error be able to stain the minds of some among you.

That land, as one reads in the ancient histories, was formerly prolific in tyrants who often used to tear apart the Roman Empire. But now it is attempting to weary the most sacred ears of the Christian Empire with innovations of schismatic perversity, much worse than before—as your inviolable faith and renowned holiness know very well. With the help of divine mercy, you formerly undertook to disperse this clouded sect of impiety by the clear light of truth [Note: [Col. 0232D] In the year 799. See below, the historical dissertation], and, with Christ God’s gift, you have also completed much of the work of preaching that was begun.

We have heard that, at the command of the glorious prince and most devout man in every virtue, King Charles, you are again going to undertake the venerable work of this most pious preaching [Note: [Col. 0232D] In the year 800].

Therefore I took up the labor of a few days, as a consolation for your most holy journey, so that you might have in your hands pious and most necessary responses to a certain letter addressed to me by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo. This was so that the minds of some might not be stained by reading that letter, since we heard that the same letter had reached the hands of others before it was returned to us, to whom it had been sent.

This was the reason why the aforesaid Father wished to send me the written document of his unbelief. For, when some brothers of our community told us about him, I learned that Elipandus was first among those people both in dignity and in the evil of his perfidy.

Accordingly, in peaceful charity, I sent him letters of exhortation, wishing to counsel his old age and to recall, through fraternal affection and humble admonition, to the way of Catholic truth a man burdened with advanced years and long famous for his religious life.

But when he received the little letter of my devotion, he immediately blazed up in the flames of anger. Gathering the whole intention of his mind into rage, he did not even look at my words with that consideration of piety with which, as Christ is my witness, I know that I sent them to him. Instead, he immediately burst into words of cursing, armed himself entirely in defense of his sect, and took care to inform us by letter what he thought and what he taught his disciples to believe.

He called me a falsifier and at times a heretic, at times a subverter, and also considered me a persecutor of Christians. He omitted scarcely any kind of curse or perfidy with which he did not brand my name, showing what he himself was and how impatiently he endured anyone’s attempt to oppose the error of his impiety.

He brought forward many testimonies from the series of the holy Scriptures and introduced many statements of Catholic teachers, almost all of which he did not fear to stain with a most perverse interpretation.

I took care to answer those little letters of his madness in two brief books, emptying out all his assertions and most perverse interpretations through the most truthful understandings of the holy Fathers.

To those two books I added two others, which in plain language bear witness to the truth concerning Christ God according to the Catholic faith and confirm it most abundantly with the testimonies of the holy Fathers. I believe that your piety will rejoice in reading them, since I was glad to dedicate the whole work to your name and sent it first of all to you for examination and correction.

I am content only with the judgment of your authority and holiness, and I do not wish those little letters of my devotion to proceed to public ears unless they have first been examined by the judgment of your authority and confirmed by the reading of the brotherly congregation. I consider it sufficient for them to be examined by the judgment of those whose love I have specially chosen as the motive for my labor.

I did not answer his curses with curses, as though vindicating my own injuries. Rather, as the testimony of truth required, I answered in some places with harsher words, while in others I mixed in gentle admonitions [Vatican Codex: “interspersed”], lest either the bitterness of my words should exasperate his most hostile soul or, conversely, the sweetness of honey should irritate his savage mind.

Nor did I labor solely, as I said, for his salvation. I fear that, because of his decrepit old age, he may perhaps have been taken more quickly by death [Quercetanus: “more urgently”], or that, because of the dissensions among the peoples, my words may not reach him, since he is not present. Rather, I labored also for the assistance of your most pious preaching and for the consolation of men and women living in the neighboring regions of Spain.

The same aforesaid Father reproached me for the abundance of my wealth and for the number of my servants, up to twenty thousand, not knowing with what disposition a person may possess the world.

It is one thing to possess the world, another to be possessed by the world. There is one who has riches and does not have them; there is one who does not have them and yet has them.

I have never placed a human being in service to me. Rather, with devoted charity, I desire to serve all the servants of Christ my God. For the opportunity to perform that service, I came—by divine providence, as I believe, directing it—to the glorious ruler and king of this realm, Charles, worthy to be named with every honor.

A certain most holy man, endowed with the spirit of prophecy, had foretold to me in my homeland that this was God’s will. Likewise, a venerable man, wholly devoted to God and my teacher, gave me this instruction: if I heard that new sects had arisen anywhere, contrary to apostolic teachings, I should immediately devote my entire self to defending the Catholic faith.

Although, because of the unskilled smallness of my ability, I carry this out less suitably than I should, nevertheless, with the readiest mind, insofar as divine grace assists me, I strive to devote myself to this most necessary work together with my betters, the excellent teachers of Christ’s Church. Their good abundance is found throughout the various Churches of Christ in this present kingdom.

Nor should I remain silent for this reason, even though the Church of God has teachers and defenders of the Catholic faith better than I. Each person will give an account for himself, and whoever labors more will receive the greater reward.

Therefore, most holy Fathers and most beloved brothers, labor with diligent attention and unfailing exertion in preaching the word of God and bearing witness to the truth, according to the grace given to you by God.

Present yourselves in religious conduct as an example to all; in the office of piety, as fathers to all; in the admonition of fraternal love, as brothers to all; in the administration of true humility, as sons to all. Become all things to all, so that, by God’s gift, the salvation and progress of all in eternal blessedness may make you worthy of a manifold reward.

May divine grace preserve your holiness safe and advancing in the preaching of God’s word, most holy brothers.

### 862. Another Letter to the Same Persons

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Quercetanus presented this letter, or addition to the preceding one, at the end of these books against Elipandus. We gave above, in the preliminary notice, around the middle, the reason for the order changed by us, drawn from the actual wording of this addition.]

[Col. 0234A]

It seemed fitting to place before this little work of ours the letter that I formerly sent to Father Elipandus through your holy devotion and God-pleasing charity [Note: In the year 799, when they were first going to Spain], appending to it the replies to his letters, which he took care to address in my name, so that whoever reads may understand with what charity I wrote to his venerable dignity, and with what disposition I received the service of fraternal affection. Thereafter I decided to append the Catholic responses that I gathered from the sayings of the holy Fathers against his impious profession. We completed this work in four books.

Then we took care to add Elipandus’s letter to Felix, formerly a defender of that sect but now, by God’s gift, a preacher of the Christian faith, together with the letter concerning his conversion to the Catholic faith, so that from all these things the devout reader might examine himself and beware, with the help of divine grace, lest he be caught in the snare of the Spanish error. And, as I see it, the chief origin of this perfidy proceeded from the city of Córdoba, as may be understood from Elipandus’s letter addressed to the aforementioned Felix, when he believed that Felix was still bound by the chains of his error. But since God, in his better providence, arranged something else concerning him, his heart returned, recognizing the light of truth, to the bosom of holy Mother Church, giving glory to God, who does not abandon those who hope in him. This is clearly evident in the letters that he wrote and that I wished to append to this little work for the praise of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and the salvation of readers, provided that anyone takes care to read those letters with sound judgment. Thus, if anyone should doubt the principles of the Catholic faith, let him, instructed by the example of that religious man, a person of great reputation among his own people, praise and proclaim without hesitation the mercy of almighty God, who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live (Ezek. 33:11), following the concord of the universal Church.

But you, dearest brothers, read all these things carefully before allowing the sequence of this letter to come before the public ear. For my part, because of the urgency of your journey, I dictated these pages—whatever their worth—in haste, so that I had no suitable time to reread or correct them; I am content merely with your charity’s reading and correction. If it seems worthy of your consideration, show it to the fraternal assembly [Leg., to the assembly]; but if not, hide it beneath the protection of your most devout charity until, by common counsel, we determine what should be done with this work. Nevertheless, follow firmly and without any doubt the footsteps of the holy Fathers, and hold and proclaim the Catholic faith, which you see strengthened by many testimonies. Do not consider so much my slowness in an unskilled tongue as the truth of the Catholic faith in the testimonies of the Fathers.

Also consider whether it may seem useful to you to send this little letter to the brothers in Spain, should a suitable carrier happen to appear. Nor should it seem burdensome to you, before you leave the city, to order these quires to be tied and wrapped and arranged in the form of a single body, lest, if torn apart and scattered, they be dispersed through the hands of readers—or perhaps of those envious of my name. Rather, keep all these things arranged together as one codex; and if you wish to send any portion elsewhere, let it be copied and dispatched. Let this part remain with you until, God willing, you return to us.

These letters can also speak on my behalf to fraternal ears, if your prudence should decide that they ought to be shown or made public. Whatever you find in them strengthened by the support of truth is God’s gift; if you see anything otherwise—which God forbid—recognize it as the error of an ignorant mind. In the former, praise the giver of all goodness; in the latter, correct the writer with a brotherly eraser. For devout charity must patiently endure a dove’s eye, just as prudence requires that it avoid the serpent’s tooth. Everywhere, with every exertion, we must seek the salvation of our fellow servants, whether through the preaching of those present or the exhortation of letters sent to those absent, so that none of those who belong to us may lack the affection of our devotion, in the hope of perpetual prosperity and salvation.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript the title is: “Letter of Albinus, abbot of Tours, to Elipandus, bishop of Toledo.” In the Paris manuscript: “Letter of Albinus to Elipandus, archbishop—or rather arch-heretic—of Toledo.” The letter has been corrected with the aid of both manuscripts.]

## LETTER OF ALBINUS THE MASTER TO ELIPANDUS, BISHOP OF TOLEDO

An exhortation concerning the Catholic faith.

To the venerable Father Elipandus, bishop, beloved in the charity of Christ, Albinus the Levite, son of ecclesiastical peace, sends greetings.

### I

The perfection of fraternal charity rejoices to gather many friends into the bosom of peaceful [Cod. Paris., “into the bosom of peace and”] unity [Ibid., “rejoices harmoniously”], and considers it a kind of loss to itself if it does not strive to commend itself more widely to men of famous name and praised piety, so that there may be spiritual unanimity in true love, even though there is some bodily separation from one another’s sight.

Considering these things more carefully, my smallness, venerable man, has striven with many prayers to commend myself more diligently to the sacred prayers of your blessedness. I desire [Cod. Paris., “desiring”], with the help of your most holy affection [Ibid., “with God’s help”], to advance toward the salvation of my soul, so that your reward may be increased by my progress and my diligence in good will may contribute something to you in the service of charity; so that our Lord God Jesus Christ may be pleased with the participation of your humility in fraternal love, and the devotion of my smallness may be acceptable in the salvation of many.

A great reward before God and abundant praise among human beings await your affection if you do not disdain to receive the benefit of fraternal counsel concerning ecclesiastical peace [Cod. Vat., “It is certain, then”]. Therefore the most holy devotion of the very poor widow was praised by God himself, the Son of God, in the offering of two small coins. I am not bringing two small coins into a Roman temple destined to perish in fire; rather, I offer two great commandments of charity in the temple of the living God—that is, a soul endowed with priestly dignity [Possibly, “and furnished with priestly prerogative”]. It is not right to despise the poverty [Editor’s edition, “usefulness”] of the one who offers, but to consider the greatness of the gift.

For you, most holy bishop, are a city set upon a mountain, which cannot in any way be hidden. Its wall must not be pierced anywhere by the treacherous tunnels of any perfidy, but must be surrounded on every side by the strongest defense of the Catholic faith, so that it may remain everywhere unconquerable for the salvation of the whole people who rejoice in you and look to the command of your mouth.

Nor is there between you and me, Father most excellent, in this little writing of my smallness any lofty disputation, but a humble supplication. I earnestly beg you to strive with the whole intention of your mind to attain apostolic teaching in Catholic unity and peace, and to be a standard-bearer for the people entrusted to you toward the prosperity of eternal blessedness.

Do not permit any new names to be inserted into the traditions of the Fathers. Whatever evangelical authority, apostolic dignity, paternal holiness, and Catholic unity urge you to say about Christ or to call Christ, may it please your holiness to love, proclaim, and believe. Do not permit the new name of adoption in Christ—unheard of in the world from the beginning of apostolic preaching—to be sounded, read, or preached into Christian ears.

### II

For we read in the letters of the blessed Felix, a man outstanding in religious life and distinguished for holiness, that—if he wishes to love and proclaim the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical unity, without which no one can please God—he says “that Christ is adoptive because of the assumption,” failing to consider sufficiently that not every assumption is adoption, although every adoption is a kind of assumption.

In the Gospel we read that the apostle Peter took Christ aside and rebuked him (Matt. 16:22); yet it is not right for that reason to think that he adopted him as his son, because he is said to have taken him aside. Likewise it is written in the Gospel: “And the devil took him into the holy city” (Matt. 4:5). You see, dearest and most holy Father, how far assumption in this passage is from adoption.

And if Christ must be adoptive because of assumption, to which person of the Holy Trinity is he adoptive? To the Son, certainly, because the person of the Son assumed a human being in the virginal womb and united him to himself in one person, so that he might be one Son of God. And if he is adoptive, then he is adoptive in relation to the Son who assumed the human being; and God would have a grandson of the Father, and there would be a quaternity rather than a Trinity in almighty God, because an adoptive son and a proper son absolutely cannot in every respect be one and the same, as the reading of many books proves.

Therefore the Son of God assumed the form of a servant without diminishing the form of God, so that there might be one Son of God in two natures, with the proper character of each nature preserved in the unity of the person; so that in two natures there might be one Son, one Christ, and also one God.

In the Holy Trinity, namely, the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; but there is not something else in nature, substance, glory, essence, or eternity. In Christ, however, there is one thing in divinity and another in humanity; not one person and another person, but one and the same true God and true man, one person, one Son of God, one Christ. This can be proved by many testimonies.

But it is superfluous to add anything to the testimony of the eternal Father, who with a divine voice said at Christ’s baptism, or on the mountain where Christ was transfigured: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5).

### III

Likewise, in the letters of the aforementioned Father we find: “Christ, who was born from the Virgin, is not truly God but nominally God.” The Catholic faith utterly rejects this, because just as a proper son and an adoptive son cannot be one and the same, so a true God and a nominal God cannot in any way be one and the same.

Is he the true God who will judge the world? And who is the one who will judge the world? Clearly, he who was born from the Virgin, as Truth itself testifies: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father.” And shortly afterward: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself, and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:22ff.).

Likewise the blessed apostle Paul says: “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ” (2 Cor. 5:8). And in another place: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God” (Rom. 14:13). I would have you believe, most holy Father, that the one who now denies him to be true God will then, once judged, recognize and prove him to be true God. The manifestation of power will be the proof of truth.

How is he not true God of whom we read in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 25:31)? Of him it was foretold long before: “Let all the angels of God worship him” (Ps. 96:8).

If he is not true God, why is he worshiped by the angels? And if the Son of God is not true, why does he sit at the right hand of God the Father?

Therefore the Psalmist also testifies that this Christ is God [Cod. Vat., “testifies”]: “God has gone up amid shouts of joy, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet” (Ps. 46:6). Again: “Our God will come manifestly, our God will not be silent; fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him. He summoned heaven above and the earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. 50:3–4).

Of him the same Psalmist had shortly before said, distinguishing him from others who are called gods: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth. From the rising of the sun to its setting, from Zion comes the splendor of his beauty” (ibid. 50:1–2). Concerning his preaching the Prophet says: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3).

### IV

The same venerable man Felix also says: “He is in every respect equal to us, except only that he was born without sin.”

There is a certain inequality between his death and ours. His death redeemed us all from eternal death, whereas the death of none of us can free even himself without him. There is also a certain inequality in that he is true God and true man, while we are merely human beings, born in sins and saved by his grace—not by our merits, but by his mercy.

For in many respects he is like us, but in more respects unlike us. Hence it is said of him in the Psalms: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Ps. 45:3).

### V

He also reports that Christ “needed baptism,” apparently wishing him to be adopted as Son in baptism, just as we are. No one with sound judgment is unaware how great an infidelity it is for any Christian to believe this.

Our Lord Jesus Christ alone could be born in such a way that he did not need a second regeneration. Therefore he willed to be baptized in John’s baptism through a definite dispensation of mercy, because John’s baptism was not regeneration but a certain preliminary signification of Christ’s baptism. In that baptism alone, through the Holy Spirit, is there true remission of sins for believers, so that we might be reborn in that Spirit in which he was born from the Virgin Mary.

He willed to be baptized by John in water, not so that any iniquity of his might be washed away, but so that his great humility might be commended. Thus baptism found nothing in him to cleanse, just as death found nothing to punish, so that the devil might be conquered by the truth of justice rather than crushed by force of power. Both baptism and death were received not from pitiable necessity, but rather from merciful will.

Many other things are also found in his writings that do not accord with the understanding of the Catholic Fathers. The narrowness of a letter now prevents me from discussing or explaining them, and I do not know when or how your holiness and the good will that you possess in Christ may wish to receive these words of my smallness.

### VI

I ask only, by that charity with which Christ loved us, that you deign kindly to read through these lines of mine, and that your most holy humility not disdain to receive what fraternal charity compelled me to send to your excellence.

Since I have often heard a good reputation of your religious life, I was therefore moved by love of fraternal affection to commend myself to your charity and to that of your faithful servants of God in those regions. I also begged you to act with greater care concerning the salvation of your soul and that of your subjects.

Although the aforementioned servant of God Felix lives a praiseworthy life before human beings, nevertheless, as it appears, in many matters he does not entirely follow the judgment of the Fathers in his profession of the Catholic faith. Do not trust in the appearance of his goodness, for “cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17:5).

Rather, place your hope in almighty God and beseech him day and night that your labor may not be vain in his sight, and that you may hold a firm faith approved by the whole Church of Christ. It seems fitting that, through the common prayer of all your fellow servants, you should turn yourself wholly to the Lord and beseech his clemency, so that he may confirm your hearts in right faith, that you may not be deceived by any error and that no one belonging to you may wander from the way of truth.

You will have a very great reward before almighty God if you correct those who err, if you consent to the truth [consenseris], if you read humbly the sequence of the holy Scriptures, desiring more truly to obey the truth than stubbornly to establish your own judgment or that of anyone else. For the mercy of almighty God is ready to receive your prayers if you pour them out from love of knowing the truth.

### VII

I could prove by many testimonies of the holy Scriptures and by the writings of Catholic teachers that Jesus Christ our Lord, who was born from the Virgin, is true God and the proper Son of God. But knowing that a few things suffice for the wise, and believing that you attend more to the truth of meanings than delight in a multiplication of words, I trust that the most merciful goodness of our Lord Jesus Christ will make you understand the truth, if you humbly persist in seeking it, because “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11), and by the steps of humility one reaches the height of the heavenly kingdom.

The Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world, ought to be one in faith and charity. There are only two possibilities: either the Church of Christ is founded upon the rock throughout the whole world, as we believe and confess, or it exists only in Felix and his few followers [Possibly, “or in Felix alone”]. The latter is utterly unworthy of Christ our God: that he should have no more in his sheepfold than those few who hide in the mountains with Felix.

But you, man chosen and beloved by God, join yourself and your companions to the universal Church of Christ, so that you may be an honorable member of that head who did not disdain to pour out his blood for you. Consider how great will be the joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance. I do not call you a sinner, but a preacher; a confessor of Christ, not an enemy of the faith; a lamp placed upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house of God.

### VIII

I also considered it right to urge your most holy will more insistently on this matter: strive through your holy prayers and sweetest counsels to convert that same venerable man Felix to the unity and truth of the Catholic faith.

God is faithful, pious, and merciful; he will certainly not forget Felix’s many good qualities, his religious life, and the labors through which he toils day and night with tireless devotion. Consider and reflect carefully how great will be your glory and reward before God and his saints in the salvation of your brother, and of so great a man and servant of Christ, so distinguished in dignity and holiness.

Always remember the saying of the Apostle, who says: “Avoid profane novelties of words” (1 Tim. 6:20). Behold what sort of novelty it is to proclaim and call Christ, who was born from the Virgin, an adoptive son, or a nominal God, and not to believe the clearest testimonies of apostolic authority, but rather to reject them. The Apostle says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32). Could the Apostle have said “who did not spare his adoptive son,” if he had wished us to believe that the one delivered for our salvation was adoptive?

Likewise Truth itself says in the Gospel: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16). Concerning him it had shortly before said: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” [the citation in the source reads “Rom. 9:5”].

And what is it that the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Their fathers, and from them is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (ibid. 9:5)? Could he not here also have said “who is nominally God forever”? For in Christ, unlike any ordinary human being, there is not one kind of generation: every ordinary human being is born a child of wrath, but afterward, in baptism, is adopted as a son of God by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Christ, however, was the Son of God from the very conception itself, and, born at the appointed time, was the true Son of God.

Likewise the majesty of divinity is not in Christ as an episcopal dignity is in an ordinary human being. The apostle Peter was not born an apostle, but was afterward chosen by God; just as no bishop is born a bishop, but after the proper time of birth is chosen and ordained to the episcopate. Christ, however, was born as true God and the proper Son of God from the very moment of conception and birth—not an adoptive son and not a nominal God.

It must be believed and proclaimed firmly and without any doubt that the one born from the Virgin is true God in two natures and the true Son of God, so that there is one Christ, one God, one Son of God, one king, and one Savior of the whole world: consubstantial with the Father in divinity and consubstantial with his mother in humanity, so that he is the same true God and true man in the unity of one person.

At the time of his passion, when adjured by the high priest, he himself confessed that he was the Son of God. We also have many similar testimonies in the holy Gospel, which everywhere testify that he is the Son of God [Cod. Vat., “and we have many other testimonies”].

Go through all the pages of evangelical authority, the apostolic sentences of the dignity of the epistles, and the whole sequence of the holy Scriptures. Whatever you find in them, proclaim faithfully. Let your understanding rest and rejoice in these things, so that you may deserve to receive in eternal blessedness a reward worthy of Catholic faith and preaching.

### IX

I humbly beseech you, by the blood of our redemption and by the terrible judgment of the last day, that, if the meaning and words of this little letter reach the hands of your blessedness, you deign to send it through the holy priests of Christ and the exalted lights of the Church who are in the regions of Spain.

By this it will be known whether you possess love of the truth and communion with the universal Church: whether you desire faithfully to open these writings—whatever their worth—to the ears of your fellow servants, and to confirm them in the unity of Catholic peace.

I shall say it again, and I shall say it with all humility, repeating it often: Let us awake, brother-men, at the trumpet of the whole world. Behold, the chosen vessel, the preacher to the nations, the secretary of heaven, cries out against all novelties of words, saying: “But even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8–9).

See how great is the confidence of the preacher of the world in his preaching: he not only pronounced an anathema upon human beings if they preached otherwise than he had preached, but also threatened angels with anathema [Cod. Vat., “anathematized them”] if they introduced anything new into the preaching of apostolic authority. He testifies that he learned this preaching of evangelical truth not from human beings but from our Lord Jesus Christ himself, saying: “For I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (ibid. 1:12).

He preaches otherwise who calls Christ the adoptive Son of God, whereas the Apostle called him the proper Son of God. He preaches otherwise who calls Christ Jesus a nominal God, whereas the Apostle called him God blessed above all things. And whoever preaches otherwise should fear the anathema of apostolic authority—not only of the Apostle, but also of God Christ, who, he testifies, speaks in him: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

How does anyone dare, with reckless presumption, to call our Lord Jesus Christ the adoptive Son of God, whom so great a preacher, as we have said, called the proper Son of God when he said: “Who did not spare his own Son” (Rom. 8:32)? Or with what audacity does anyone presume to call the same Lord and our God a nominal God, whom the same Apostle did not hesitate to confess and call aloud the God blessed above all things, and even the great God?

Thus he says to Titus: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity” (Titus 2:13–14). He certainly called him the great God, the one who will come to judge the living and the dead—not some little god, as the new presumption of certain people invents.

If anyone doubts of whom the Apostle was speaking, let him read the treatise of the blessed Jerome [Note: St. Jerome, on the cited passage of the Epistle to Titus: “The great God is called Jesus Christ the Savior, not the firstborn of every creature, not the Word of God and Wisdom, but Jesus Christ: these terms belong to the assumed man.”], which he composed on this Epistle.

### X

It must be considered more carefully and grasped with an understanding of all piety what that wondrous evangelist says: “The Word became flesh,” that is, God became man.

By the name “flesh,” therefore, he signifies the whole human being, as is understood in the passage: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6), that is, every human being. This does not mean that the nature of divinity was changed into humanity; rather, humanity was assumed while divine majesty remained intact. Divinity was not diminished, but humanity was honored, while the proper character of human nature remained, so that the very one who was eternally born from God the Father might be temporally born from his Virgin mother. Thus what so great an Evangelist says is true: “The Word became flesh.”

If God became man, then certainly man became God, because of the unity of the person, so that there may be complete truth in Christ Jesus our Lord. If, therefore, the man who was assumed by the Word of God is a nominal God because the nature of humanity is one thing and the nature of divinity another, it follows that the God who assumed the man is a nominal man; and what the Evangelist says, “The Word became flesh,” cannot stand.

The same must likewise be understood in reverse concerning adoption. If the man who was assumed is for that reason an adoptive son of God, because the nature of humanity is one thing and the nature of divinity another, it follows necessarily that God, who was born from the Virgin, is an adoptive God. The blessed Virgin, according to Nestorian impiety, would not be the true Mother of God, but, if such a thing were possible, a mother of God by a certain adoption.

Anyone who thinks piously about Christ recognizes how wicked, impious, and alien from all truth this is.

But cast away these novelties of words entirely, dearest men of most distinguished dignity, and believe and proclaim what accords with the evangelical pages and apostolic traditions. Understand that some names in Christ God are proper and others are descriptive, and distinguish what belongs to each thing.

The proper names in Christ are: Only-Begotten, Firstborn, God, Son of God, and one Jesus Christ [Cod. Vat., “and Lord”]. Descriptive names are those arising from certain actions completed in him: lion, stone, sheep, calf, worm, and very many others of this kind, which must be distinguished by reason.

### XI

The aforementioned venerable Felix says that “the teachers of Spain have been accustomed to call Christ adoptive.” But we have not read those teachers, nor have their writings reached us. And if they did say this, perhaps simple ignorance protects them from the sword of anathema; but a stubborn defense of error is struck by the sword of excommunication [Cod. Vat., “the sword”].

The authority of the teachers of the whole world ought also to be greater than that of the few in Spain. Therefore the blessed Isidore, than whom Spain had no more illustrious man, sets forth many names for Christ God in his *Etymologies* and in his other writings. Yet nowhere do we find that he called Christ the adoptive or nominal God, or the adoptive Son of God. Rather, we always find him agreeing in the Catholic faith with the universal holy Church of God.

### XII

If your piety and the good will that you possess in the charity of Christ takes care to read through this letter, and if our sharing in the holy faith pleases you, as does the desire that we should more often make familiar conversation with one another, then, with Christ the true God and proper Son of God showing mercy, we shall take care to send you more concerning the principles of orthodox faith, ecclesiastical peace, and holy unity.

For now we have dictated these few things from the fountain of charity, wishing you to advance everywhere in complete holiness and peaceful unity before God and human beings.

But I jointly beseech you at the end of this letter, most sacred lights of Spain, to deign to remember us in your most holy prayers.

And you, most holy Fathers, whom God has appointed rulers of his people, we wish to see you advance through the gifts of the Holy Spirit in all the wisdom of Catholic peace and in the charity of Christ God, dearest Fathers, Brothers, and Sons in Christ our Lord.

Farewell forever. May whoever reads, read happily; understand truly; and faithfully believe what has been said, so that he may deserve to reign eternally with him of whom we are speaking, our Savior, the true and living God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

## LETTER OF ELIPANDUS TO ALBINUS

Containing replies to the preceding letter.

This letter may be found among the works of Elipandus, in volume 96 of this *Patrologia*, column 870.

## 876. BOOK ONE AGAINST ELIPANDUS OF TOLEDO

### I

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8): ready, by the inspiration of divine grace, to set forth the teaching of truth; ready to resist the errors of falsehood; ready, Lord Jesus, to love, praise, and proclaim you; ready to understand you as true God and true Son of God, with the blessed Evangelist, who, drawing faith in Catholic truth from the most sacred fullness of your breast, says: “These things have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31).

Immediately showing the perpetual reward of this faith, he added: “And that, believing, you may have eternal life in his name.” By evangelical authority he proclaims as the Son of God the same one whom the archangel Gabriel, before he was conceived, foretold to the blessed Virgin would be called Jesus and Son of the Most High.

No one doubts that the name Jesus belonged to his human nature. In that name, as the blessed teacher of the nations testifies, every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10).

The blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, also demonstrated the power of this name in healing the lame man who lay at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, saying: “In the name of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). Immediately healed, he leaped up, walked, and praised God.

The same blessed Apostle added to the excellence of this name when the apostles were forbidden by the Jews to preach in that name, saying: “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

### II

This same matter, by God’s mercy, is my reason for writing against you and destroying your infidelities, Father Elipandus. It was also the holy reason that moved the blessed John the Evangelist to write his Gospel: so that by the authority of the holy Scriptures and the truth of the Catholic faith I might show that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God—not only in the nature that was eternally begotten from God the Father, but also in that which was temporally made from the Virgin mother [Possibly, “in that which was temporally made from the mother”]—lest the one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, be divided into two sons, a proper son and an adoptive son. Such a division is without doubt understood to be a division into two persons…

### III

Just as it must not be denied that it was possible for God, when he willed, to make the Son of Man perfect and proper to himself, so one must not contradict God’s ability to exalt the human nature—which he assumed into the dignity of his own person—into the property of the Son, so that the person in union with the assumed man might be the same person in the Son’s own right as had existed before all ages in the substance of the Godhead.

Therefore, throughout the entire sequence of the holy Scriptures, Christ is never read to have been given the name “adoption”; rather, they testify that through him we have received the grace of adoption. Concerning this adoption bestowed upon us, the aforementioned evangelist says:

> He came to what was his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God (John 1:11).

This power of adoption was not conferred upon the saints by some adopted person, but by him whom the same evangelist immediately afterward testifies to be, as it were, the only-begotten one, full of grace and truth. A little later he says:

> From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (ibid., 16).

And the Apostle says:

> In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2:9).

If there is adoption in Christ, then the whole fullness of nobility is not in him, since adoption ordinarily means that someone is taken from an unrelated person and assumed into the name of a son. Nor did any of the apostles, who are the lights and teachers of the whole world, wish to add “adoption” to the name of Jesus.

Indeed, blessed Augustine distinguished between adopted and natural sons in a disputation he held with a certain Felicianus, a defender of the Arian sect, saying:

> For some sons are adopted, while others are natural. The latter, because they were begotten from the beginning, are always sons and proper sons; the former are initially outsiders and afterward sons, when they appear to be received into a family through adoption.

[Note: This passage is rather from Vigilius of Thapsus, *On the Unity of the Trinity*, chapter 6, in volume 8 of the works of St. Augustine, Appendix.]

When Christ the man was born from the Virgin, was he an outsider to God the Father, so that from being some kind of outsider he might be received by adoption into the name of a son? Was not, at the very conception itself, through the working of the Holy Spirit, true God and the true Son of God conceived from the blessed Virgin, and then born at the appointed time?

But if he was never an outsider, then he was never adopted, since, as blessed Augustine says, an adopted son is ordinarily made from someone who is an outsider. It follows, therefore, that Christ became the proper Son of God immediately from his conception, because he was never an outsider. He was never an outsider because he was never the old man, although in your error, contrary to the Catholic faith, Christ the man is called the old man.

### IV

For blessed Jerome says in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> What was not new in the man who was assumed by our Savior? His conception, birth, delivery, infancy, teaching, life, virtues; and finally the cross and passion, which stripped the principalities and opposing powers and exposed them to public view. Likewise his resurrection and ascension into heaven. This one, therefore, was truly created in righteousness and the holiness of truth, because he was true God and truly the Son of God, and all religion and righteousness in him was completed in the truth of God.

You see with what confidence this eminent teacher in the Church of God proclaimed that Christ was always the new man, and that true God and the true Son of God were truly created, affirming that in him all righteousness was completed in the truth of God.

This one statement, if it is read confidently and understood truthfully, empties out the worst assertions of your error, when you say that Christ is the old man, a nominal God, and an adopted son. But this most noble teacher testifies without any doubt that our Savior was created as the new man, true God, and truly the Son of God.

### V

Behold, a certain zeal for bearing witness to the truth has carried me away from the order of my response. Let us begin, however, to examine, before me [perhaps: “before”], the statements of your little book. Let those who read understand whether the pages written to your reverence, Father Elipandus, with the pen of pious exhortation and charity—or rather the pages of impious cursing that you tried to direct insolently against my name with your poisonous mouth—reveal the spirit from which you wished to utter, at the very outset of your letter, words of the harshest malediction.

I directed to your reverence the prayers of my devotion with wholly sincere charity, desiring that your old age might be saved through Christ and recalled to the harmony of Catholic peace, without which nothing—not even the glory of martyrdom—is acceptable to God, as the blessed Apostle Paul declares.

[Codex Parisinus: “not even the glory of martyrdom itself is acceptable.”]

You, on the contrary, burst forth into words of abominable abuse, in accordance with Solomon’s truthful saying:

> In the mouth of a fool are weapons and a sword (Prov. 22:5).

And again:

> Rebuke a fool, and he will hate you (ibid., 9:7).

Thus you opposed a curse to my blessing, revealing what you held in your heart and what spirit entirely possessed you. But may the Lord, who enlightens the blind and heals the brokenhearted, illuminate the darkness of your ignorance, heal the wounds of unbelief in your heart, and make you a shepherd of his people—prudent, devout, peaceful, and Catholic.

### VI

What is this, brother, that you have imposed upon my person so many names of heretics, whose images and powers the Lord God once reduced to nothing in their own city? Do you not remember what the Psalmist sings concerning men like you?

> The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness (Ps. 13:3).

And Truth itself, reproaching the Jews in the Gospel for their curses in return for his good deeds, says:

> You brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

And again:

> The good person brings good things out of the good treasure of the heart, and the evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure (Matt. 12:34–35).

A curse is evil [read: “If a curse is evil”]; it has plainly proceeded from an evil treasure of the heart. A curse is altogether evil, since the Apostle forbids it:

> Do not curse (Rom. 12:14).

Therefore the one who curses brings forth a curse from the evil treasure of the heart.

If you thought that I was in error, ought you not to have corrected me according to the apostolic command, in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted?

> Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. 6:2).

From the words of the blessed Apostle James it is easy to recognize what sort of wisdom is yours. When he was discussing the gentleness of true wisdom and the bitterness of impious rivalry, he said:

> But if you have bitter jealousy and strife in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth (James 3:14).

> This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where jealousy and strife exist, there is disorder and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, agreeing with what is good, full of mercy and good fruits (ibid., 16–17).

### VII

I carried an olive branch in a dove’s mouth, wishing to heal the wound of your heart [Note: Here and frequently below there are allusions to Elipandus’s letter to Alcuin]. You, on the contrary, vomited deadly poison with a serpent’s tongue, more ready to curse than to bless.

I do not extinguish wedding torches with Nicolas, to whom you compared me; rather, with blessed Stephen the protomartyr, in the vision of my mind I see Jesus standing at the right hand of God and assisting those who contend for the nobility of his name.

I am not, with the wicked Datianus, a persecutor of the renowned martyr Vincent; rather, with God’s help, I am a devoted eradicator of heretical depravity, according to the measure of my strength.

I did not, with Rufinus, make blessed Felix a martyr; rather, by God’s mercy I made Felix, once an accomplice of your error, a Catholic. In him I persecuted the impious doubt of the one who, testing the Son of God, had said:

> If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread (Matt. 4:3).

And again, through the Jews, while he himself hung upon the cross, he cried out:

> If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe in him (Matt. 27:42).

Is your unbelief not worse than the devil’s doubt? The devil wished to test whether he was the Son of God, whom he saw hungering, thirsting, and growing weary; but you do not fear to deny that the one reigning in heaven is the true Son of God, surpassing the devil’s unbelief by your own unbelief.

That Felix, whom you assert to be outstanding in charity, chaste, and adorned with good conduct, we have in the camp of Christ. Would that you too, together with your followers, instructed by his example, might attain knowledge of the true faith through the favor of the one whom we proclaim to be true God and the proper Son of God.

### VIII

You say:

> “A fool speaks foolishly.”

Does the person who preaches the truth speak foolishly, or is the one who asserts falsehood rather the fool? You also cite the Apostle’s statement:

> The natural person does not perceive the things that are of God’s Spirit (1 Cor. 2:14),

wishing to understand me as natural and yourself as spiritual.

Let whoever reads our letters see to whom this statement more truly applies: whether to me, who, strengthened by evangelical, apostolic, and also patristic testimonies, proclaim Christ to be true God and the true Son of God; or perhaps to you, who, corrupted by the Spanish error, do not fear to bark with canine madness against the Catholic faith, refusing Christ the true nobility of sonship and asserting that only an external, nominal nobility exists in him.

When he was adjured by the Jewish pontiff in the name of the Most High God whether he was the Son of God, he plainly replied:

> I am.

And when the man healed of blindness asked who the Son of God was, so that he might believe in him, he said:

> You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he (John 9:37).

What did that man, now illuminated, see? Without doubt, the nature of humanity, not the substance of divinity, which cannot be seen by bodily eyes.

The Lord said two things to him: “You have seen him,” and “the one speaking with you.” These are properly understood as pertaining to the human nature. Yet he confessed that the very nature which could be seen and heard speaking was the Son of God.

You also say, from a verse of the Psalmist, that I am a defender and an enemy. Perhaps, unwillingly, you have offered true testimony about me. For I confess that I am a defender of the Catholic faith and an enemy of the enemies of Christ, who strive to deprive him of the honor of divinity and the nobility of dignity—him whom the pagan centurion, seeing him die and terrified by the transformation of the elements, confessed to be the true Son of God, saying:

> Truly this man was the Son of God (Matt. 27:54; Mark 3:11–12).

Indeed, the demonic powers, as we read in the Gospel, cried out from the bodies of the possessed and confessed Christ to be the Son of God.

I do not say this because I need their testimony, since I have the pages of the whole of sacred Scripture as witnesses; rather, to expose your unbelief, I set their faith before you, since you alone are so perverse in faith that the confession of demons can rightly be preferred to yours.

### IX
