As for your assertion that I deny true humanity in Christ, it is entirely false. Nor will you be able to prove, throughout the whole sequence of my writings, that I have said or believed this.

But in him, without any doubt or hesitation, I confess two perfect and complete natures—namely, divinity and humanity—in one person and under one name, that of the Son of God. You can clearly understand this if you are willing to read and understand, with sober judgment, the words of piety that I wrote to your reverence and for your salvation in the service of charity.

Know with absolute certainty that, as I said above, I confess two natures and one person in Christ. For it must be firmly believed and proclaimed, without any doubt, that the one born from the Virgin is true God in two natures and the true Son of God. Thus there is one Christ, one God, one Son of God, one king, and one Savior of the whole world: in divinity consubstantial with the Father, and in humanity consubstantial with his mother. He is therefore the same true God and true man in the unity of one person.

You, without doubt, divide him with Nestorius into two sons and two persons, according to property and adoption.

It is not, therefore, found that your teacher Nestorius openly professed two persons in Christ, insofar as his writings have reached us. Rather, he is found to have brought forward concerning Christ everything that necessarily belongs to two persons, assigning adoption to the humanity, as you do, and designating the property of sonship as belonging to the divinity.

### X

But you, brother Elipandus, a natural man, understanding the generation of the Son of God in the manner of natural beings and giving little consideration to yourself, should ask whether you are wholly the proper son of your father and mother in both soul and body.

It is certain that only the flesh was produced from the union of your parents, while the soul is a creature created from nothing by God’s power. The forming flesh in the mother’s womb was joined to life-giving power, so that a living, rational, and mortal soul might be born.

You see this taking place in every human being, yet you hesitate to confess that the same could take place in the Son of God through the working of the Holy Spirit. You hesitate to admit that the almighty God, who does everything he wills in heaven and on earth, could not—against your will—have caused his proper Son to be born from a virginal womb.

Either deny that you yourself are your parents’ proper son except according to the flesh alone, or, if that seems absurd to you, you must confess that this property can exist in the Son of God, even though one nature is eternal divinity and the other is humanity made in time—a property that you do not deny exists in yourself, indeed in every human being.

### XI

You order me to remember that the Lord said:

> Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it (Matt. 7:13–14)!

You too should remember that the Prophet said:

> The lambs will feed in a spacious place (Hos. 4:16).

And long before, the Psalmist prophesied concerning the power of the one about whom we are speaking:

> He will rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth (Ps. 71:8).

And when he ascended into heaven in triumph and glory, he gave his apostles the command to teach all nations, saying:

> Go, teach all nations (Matt. 28:19).

Once God was known only in Judea (Ps. 75:2); now Christ is one voice among all nations. Yet you think that he has not reigned within the Pyrenean passes, but has lain hidden there as a captive.

### XII

You produce another testimony from the Gospel, where Truth itself speaks of the fellowship of the saints in charity:

> Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them (Matt. 18:20).

And you believe that this was said only about Felix and his accomplices, such as Felix once was when he was bound together with you by the chains of your error. But now, by God’s mercy, he has been overcome by rational argument, released from your error, and restored to the unanimity of Catholic peace.

You once had him as a kind of shield for your perfidy; now the Church has him as a powerful and sharp arrow, with coals of desolation (Ps. 119:4).

You, in whom charity has grown cold, gather in the name of the adopted son, in the name of the captive servant, in the name of the nominal God. We gather in the name of the only-begotten Son of God, the Savior of the world; in the name of Christ the Lord, whose birth the angel proclaimed to the shepherds, saying:

> Today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David (Luke 2:11).

You bend your knees in the name of the adopted one; we bend our knees with the angels and archangels and the whole heavenly host in the name of Jesus, concerning whom it is said:

> Let all the angels of God adore him (Heb. 1:6).

### XIII

At last you have come to God’s promise made to David:

> When you sleep, God says, with your fathers, I will raise up from your loins one who will sit upon the throne of Israel. I will be his Father, and he will be my Son (2 Sam. 7:12, 14).

O Father Elipandus, where have you lost your eyes? Why have you set forth such a powerful testimony against yourself? Perhaps, because of the dignity of the priesthood, you uttered it like Caiaphas, without recognizing the truth.

It is a paternal promise and a paternal testimony, as you yourself said: “I will be his Father, and he will be my Son.” Nothing concerning adoption is found in these words of the paternal promise.

There is a great difference between “I will be” and “I am called.” The former is true in itself, without any imagining; the adopted one is called so not according to truth, but according to the imagination of a willing mind.

There is a great difference between your lies and God’s promises. He said, “He will be my Son”; you say, “He is merely called so, but is not properly so.”

You also brought forward Isaiah’s prophecy concerning Christ, where he says:

> The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples; the nations will seek him, and his tomb will be glorious (Isa. 11:10).

For which peoples does he stand as a sign, and which nations will seek him, if only a very few murmurers in Spain seek him in a Catholic manner? Certainly, he receives no one’s prayers unless they are offered in the charity of Catholic peace.

The Prophet also foretold that the tomb of the one whom you call ignoble would be glorious. If his tomb is glorious, how much more glorious is the one who slept in the tomb, of whose person the Prophet once sang:

> I slept and fell into slumber, and I rose again (Ps. 3:6).

You also add the Catholic statement of the Fathers:

> “Wholly in what is ours, and wholly in what is his,”

adding from your own understanding:

> “Why should he not be called adopted, who is wholly in what is ours just as he is wholly in what is his, except for sin?”

Would that you had understood the words of the holy teachers better! “Wholly in what is ours” means wholly the Son of Man; “wholly in what is his” means wholly the Son of God—full and perfect in both (*in utraque*; Codex Parisinus: *in utroque*).

But you wish him to be the Son of God only in part, truly in one part and merely nominally in another.

Answer me this, please: Is Christ wholly and truly, properly speaking, in both natures the Son of the most blessed Virgin? Or, if holy Mary truly gave birth to God, as all Catholics believe and confess her to be the Mother of God, is the eternal Son of God truly the Son of the blessed Virgin, or adopted?

If you say “adopted,” then the most holy Virgin Mary was in no way truly the Mother of God. But if you wish, with a Catholic mouth, to confess her truly to be the Mother of God, what remains except that, in that same truth, Christ is wholly the true Son of God in two natures, in which he is truly the Son of the most blessed Virgin in two natures?

But if his humanity is adopted by God the Father, it appears to follow that his divinity is adopted by the Virgin Mother. No believer is unaware how impious it is to say this.

### XIV

You demand that I provide witnesses “that there is no adoption in the flesh of Christ.” At the proper time, when the Holy Spirit inspires Catholic convictions in our heart, I will do so; and anyone who does not disdain to read my little writings understands that I have done so abundantly in other letters of ours that I published against your error.

[Note: In the seven books against Felix—or rather, in the little book sent to the monks of Gothia.]

As for what you ask me to prove—“that there is no true humanity in Christ”—I will not give you witnesses for this, because I am a Catholic, born and raised in the Catholic Church. Instead, I will give you the series of my writings as witnesses, if you deign to read them: they confess true divinity and true humanity in Christ God.

And I wonder why you wish to charge me with something you have never read me saying.

You urge me not to be an Arian, who stained the hearts of many through his perversity so that they would not believe rightly. By the glory of God Jesus, I have never fallen into Arius’s abyss. But either you will be proved to be an Arian, or you will be forced to condemn your own position, since you assert that the one and only, only-begotten Son of God, undoubtedly one person, is adopted.

Do you not affirm that adoption exists in the very person whom Arius once asserted, with detestable impiety, to be adopted? Or, if you strive to avoid this blasphemy, you immediately fall into the snare of Nestorius, dividing Christ into two persons, one proper and the other adopted.

For Nestorius did not openly name two persons in Christ; nevertheless, with a perverse understanding, he affirmed in Christ everything that must belong to two persons—that is, the property and adoption of the Son.

In his writings, without doubt, the name of adoption is found in connection with Christ. After obscure meanings, shadowy statements, and impious unbeliefs concerning Christ’s humanity, his words are as follows. He says:

[Note: Nestorius, cited by Agobard in *Book against Felix*, chapter 7. The complete text is therefore restored as follows: “this, [Col. 0251D] which, participating in the union and lordship of the Word of God.”]

> Hence, according to blessed Paul, many are called sons, but he alone has this prerogative, that … participates in the adoption of the Word’s union.

### XV

See, brethren, see your danger, and at last recover your senses from the error of unbelief, avoiding the doctrine of duality concerning our Redeemer.

But if you refuse to correct your position according to the Catholic preaching of the holy Fathers, then correct it according to the impious unbelief and just condemnation of Nestorius. You affirm the same adoption in Christ’s humanity that your persistent ignorance strives to affirm, as you can hear in his words.

For the Prophet says:

> May the Lord destroy him [perhaps: “him”], the teacher and disciple teaching such things (Mal. 2:12).

The angel of the Lord also brandishes the sword of vengeance over your head, so that he may divide you, if you divide Christ into a proper son and an adopted son, and place your portion with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

And you, venerable Father Elipandus, beware lest younger men insult your age and say with Daniel:

> You have grown old in evil days; now your sins have come upon you, which you committed previously (Dan. 13:52),

overturning the paths of the innocent and not preaching rightly concerning the Savior of the world.

We have heard from the letter that you sent to the aforementioned Felix that you are eighty years old.

[Note: See this letter in *Patrologia Latina*, volume 96, column 880.]

Hear Christ crying out to you:

> There is still a little light in you. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you; for the one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be children of light (John 12:35–36).

Whatever you have produced in your letter from the dark understanding of your heart is recognized as having flowed entirely from the gall of cursing or falsehood.

But perhaps, in ignorance of the truth, you uttered falsehood. Learn first, and afterward teach, lest you become a teacher of error. The humility of learning is better than the rashness of teaching.

Do not become arrogant in your knowledge.

> Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up (1 Cor. 8:1).

And:

> Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Matt. 23:12).

### XVI

You admonish me, as it seems, not with a pious spirit but with a severe rebuke, not to corrupt the glorious king Charles.

I did not come to France to corrupt him—he cannot be corrupted—but to assist him in the Catholic faith in which he was nurtured from his earliest age and excellently instructed by his most Christian parents and Catholic teachers.

It is impossible for anyone to corrupt him, because he is Catholic in faith, a king in power, a pontiff in preaching, a judge in equity, a philosopher in liberal studies, renowned in character, and outstanding in every kind of honorable conduct.

Before I came to France at the command of that most wise king Charles, this same sect of your error, while the same glorious prince presided and Felix was present—Felix, whom you are accustomed to praise greatly and who at that time defended your party—was debated at a very distinguished place called Regensburg. By the synodal authority of the priests of Christ, who had gathered from different parts of the Christian empire, it was condemned with an eternal anathema.

Indeed, it was utterly eradicated by Pope Adrian of blessed memory, who at that time governed the see of the holy Roman Church with apostolic authority.

Then Felix, unhappily fleeing back to your party, intended, at your urging, to revive the smoldering ashes of unbelief. When I came into these regions, I took care to send him a letter of exhortation, written with the pen of charity, urging him to join the Catholic unity.

He attempted to answer not with the brevity of a letter but with the length of a little book, and in it he opened up most fully all the hiding places of your perfidy, asserting that Christ was the old man, a nominal God, an adopted son, and in need of a second regeneration, together with many other things incompatible with ecclesiastical teaching.

We answered his little book with seven little books of our devotion, emptying out all the doctrines of your depravity. These writings of our devotion were also read and approved in the presence of our lord the king and the priests of Christ.

Moreover, in the thirty-second year of the aforementioned glorious ruler, Felix was summoned and willingly came to the Palace at Aachen. There, in the presence of our lord the king, his nobles, and the priests of God, he was rationally examined and truly convicted. Giving glory to God and confessing the true faith, he returned to the peace of Catholic unanimity with his disciples who were present there at that time.

I urge you, venerable Father, to follow his humility together with your disciples.

### XVII

Gather yourself and the sheep entrusted to you into the sheepfold of Christian charity, through him who says:

> I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out (John 10:9).

You must carefully and watchfully take heed lest you be among those concerning whom Truth itself added in the same passage:

> All who came are thieves and robbers (ibid., 8).

He says “who came,” not “who were sent.” And the Apostle says:

> How will they preach unless they are sent? (Rom. 10:15).

Who sent you, Father Elipandus, to preach adoption in Christ the Son of God? Therefore, if you came and preached through yourself, with no one sending you, you are proved to be a thief and a robber.

The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. Let your disciples beware lest through you they be killed and perish. It would be better for them to pluck out their right eye than, with their whole body intact, to be cast into the gehenna of fire.

> If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit (Matt. 15:14).

Hear also the blessed Apostle distinguishing Moses and Christ, whom you assert to be alike, when he places the excellence of Christ’s majesty above his servant Moses:

> Moses was faithful as a servant in his whole house, but Christ as a Son in his house (Heb. 3:5–6).

He calls Moses a servant and Christ the Son. As great as the difference between a servant of the master of a household and a son is, so great is the difference between Moses and Christ.

The same Apostle never says this of Moses, but of Christ:

> Made higher than the heavens (Heb. 7:26).

At the beginning of the same Epistle he did not hesitate to place him above the angels:

> Having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son; today I have begotten you? And again: I will be his Father, and he will be my Son. And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: Let all the angels of God adore him (Heb. 1:4–6).

He says, “You are my Son,” of the one to whom, in the following verse, he adds—as you yourself brought forward shortly before:

> Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance (Ps. 2:8).

He says, “You are my Son,” to the one to whom he says, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations.”

The blessed Gregory, also, an outstanding teacher and acceptable to all the churches of Christ, distinguishing between the saints’ divinity and Christ’s divinity, said the following in a homily on the first part of the prophet Ezekiel, when he was discussing the nominal power of the saints and Christ’s proper divinity:

[Note: St. Gregory, *Homily 8 on Ezekiel*, section 3.]

> Hence, says the Apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the nominal name “God” from the essential one, spoke of our Redeemer, saying: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). For the one who is called God nominally is among all things; but the one who is God essentially is above all things. Thus, in order to show that Christ is God by nature, he remembered that he is not merely God but God above all things. For each of the elect, as we have said before, may be called God when he is set in a position of preeminence as an example of righteousness; but he is among all things, since he is God nominally. Christ, however, is God above all things, because he is God by nature.

He did not hesitate to affirm that he was God by nature whom the teacher of the nations testified to have been born, according to the flesh, from the seed of the holy Fathers.

### XVIII

When the testimonies of God’s prophets that suited your error failed you, you invented for yourself a new prophet who supposedly said:

> Have mercy, Lord, upon your people over whom your name has been invoked, and upon Israel, whom you have made equal to your firstborn (Sirach 36:14).

You also added this interpretation of the statement:

> “This equality,” you say, “is not in divinity but only in humanity, and in the adopted flesh which he received from the Virgin.”

Behold falsehood in the name of the prophet! Behold perversity in the interpretation of the statement! It was not without reason that a new teacher needed to find a new prophet for himself.

Just as King Jeroboam, turning away from the worship of the true God, invented new gods for himself, so that, having been ruined, he might ruin the people subject to him—concerning whom it had been foretold long before in the Song of Deuteronomy:

> He abandoned God his maker and departed from God his Savior (Deut. 32:16)—

so you, turning away from the true God and the proper Son of God, invent for yourself a nominal God and an adopted son as redeemer, whom our fathers did not know.

You have abandoned the God who freed you and forgotten God your Redeemer.

The aforementioned statement is found in the book of Jesus son of Sirach. Blessed Jerome and Isidore unequivocally testify that this book was counted among the apocrypha—that is, doubtful Scriptures.

[Note: Alcuin clearly hesitated over whether the book of Sirach should be counted among the sacred Scriptures, although he himself sometimes uses its testimonies. In a poem that we numbered 6, he included that book, together with the Book of Wisdom, in the catalogue of sacred books, in these words:

> And the three little works of the peaceful king Solomon.

> To these are joined Wisdom, and likewise the little book of Jesus.

In another poem bearing the same number, however, he asserts that these two little books are joined to the other sacred books only by way of comparison, in the following verses:

> The marvelous author Solomon produced three books.

> Two books are joined to these by comparison.

> The first of them is called nourishing Wisdom;

> The latter is designated by the name of Jesus.

Perhaps *τὸ per paradigma* should not be understood to mean that the two aforementioned little books are listed among the sacred Scriptures solely because of some similarity to them, but rather that they are joined to Solomon’s first three books because of the similarity of their subject matter and statements, even though they are not considered to have the same author. Whatever the case may be, in our own age there can certainly be no doubt about the authenticity of the aforementioned books, Wisdom and Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, on account of the definition of the Catholic Church at the Council of Trent.]

That book, moreover, was written not in the time of the prophets but of the priests, under Simon the high priest, during the reign of Ptolemy Euergetes. It appears to present not so much prophecies as moral instruction and praise of wisdom.

The firstborn mentioned here can better be understood as the people of God led out of Egypt. Concerning them the Lord gave Moses his servant this command to Pharaoh:

> Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Let my firstborn son go, so that he may serve me; and you refused to let him go. Therefore, behold, I will kill your firstborn son (Exod. 4:22–23).

I think that the man who composed these words of the prayer wished the people of the two tribes, who had not long before been brought out of Babylonian captivity by God’s mercy, to be understood as having been made equal to this people. It is not thought that these words prophesied anything about Christ, as you assert with your novel interpretation.

## XIX

Then, wandering about in your customary manner, you go searching throughout the breadth of Holy Scripture for what pertains to Christ’s divinity and what pertains to his humanity—as though any one of us appeared to deny true humanity and true divinity in Christ.

First you present the Son of God as saying, according to his divinity: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18), paying insufficient attention to what blessed Augustine understood by this statement. In his Gospel homilies he wished to interpret the Lord’s words as follows:

> “Who lays down,” he says, “his life, and again takes up his life? Does Christ lay down his life and again take it up insofar as he is the Word? Or insofar as he is a human soul, does the soul itself lay itself down and again take itself up? Or insofar as he is flesh, does flesh lay down the soul and again take it up? I have proposed three possibilities; let us examine them all and choose what accords with the rule of truth. For if we say that the Word of God laid down his soul and again took it up, we must fear lest some perverse thought intrude and someone say to us: ‘Therefore that soul was at some time separated from the Word, and at some time that Word, who had assumed that soul, was without a soul.’

> “I see that the Word was without a human soul; but this was when ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.’ Once, however, ‘the Word was made flesh, that he might dwell among us,’ and humanity—that is, the whole human being, soul and flesh—was assumed by the Word, what did suffering accomplish, what did death accomplish, except to separate the body from the soul while not separating the soul from the Word? For if the Lord died—indeed, because the Lord died, for he died for us on the cross—without doubt his flesh breathed out its soul; for a brief time the soul abandoned the flesh, and when the soul returned, he rose again. But I do not say that the soul was separated from the Word . . . . .

> “All human beings, when they die, lay down their souls; but not all lay them down for Christ. And no one has the power to take back what he has laid down. Christ, however, both laid down his soul for us, and laid it down when he willed, and took it up when he willed. To lay down the soul, therefore, is to die. Thus Peter said to the Lord: ‘I will lay down my life for you’ (John 13:37), that is, ‘I will die in the flesh’ [the word *flesh* is absent in Augustine].”

A little later he says:

> “How did Christ lay down his soul? Was Christ not flesh? Certainly Christ was flesh, and Christ was soul, and Christ was the Word; yet these three are not three Christs, but one Christ,”

and one only-begotten God and man.

Did not a perverse thought enter you, O new interpreter of the Holy Scriptures—that Christ’s soul had been separated from the Word—when you say that the Lord uttered these same words according to his divinity? This distinguished teacher, with rational reverence, warned you that this was something greatly to be feared.

[Editorial note: Augustine, *Tractates on John* 47.10–12. At the beginning, the text reads: “Who lays down the soul and takes it up again? Does Christ, insofar as he is the Word, lay down the soul and take it up again? Or, insofar as he is a human soul, does the soul itself lay itself down and itself take itself up again? Or, insofar as he is flesh, does flesh lay down the soul and again take it up?” Augustine reads “for once the Word was made flesh” and “was to rise again”; the word *flesh* is absent from Augustine’s wording of Peter’s saying.]

## XX

With similar perversity you also wish to divide Christ in the voice which the Father uttered on the holy mountain in the hearing of the disciples, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5), as though this had been spoken only of his divinity and not rather also of his humanity.

If, therefore, you think that this was uttered only of his divinity, you wish to divide Christ and to make the Son only the nature of divinity. No Catholic is unaware how perverse this is. This voice of the Father came from heaven concerning one Son, and of that one Son it says: “This is my beloved Son.” Whatever exists in Christ and bears the name of Son is called “my beloved Son” by the testimony of the Father himself—not, as you assert, “adoptive.”

Three things, moreover, were heard in the paternal voice: “Son,” “my,” and “beloved.” And he added: “In whom I am well pleased.” The voice of the Father from heaven cries, “my”; you cry from earth, “not yours.” What salvation can you hope for if you do not believe the testimony of God?

Nor is any opportunity for separation given you here. He spoke of one Son and showed one, as though he had said: “Seek no other, and do not believe that this one is not the Son.” Or, if perhaps you have doubts whether these words were spoken of Christ’s human nature, read the interpretation of blessed Gregory, the aforementioned Father, in his homilies on Ezekiel concerning this paternal voice. After discussing many mysteries of Christ’s humanity and of the prophetic vision, he introduces the excellence of this paternal voice, saying:

> “A voice,” he says, “was made above the firmament, which sounded from heaven over the baptized Lord, saying: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased’ (Luke 3:22); or, as it is said through another Evangelist: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matthew 3:17).

And shortly afterward:

> “In our only-begotten Lord God Jesus Christ alone was he well pleased, because he did not repent of having created him as man among human beings, in whom he found absolutely no sin, as it is said of him through the Psalmist: ‘The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Psalm 109:4).

> “In our Redeemer alone, therefore, is the Father well pleased, because in him alone he found no fault.”

Again, in the same homily:

> “Since the voice,” he says, “is above the firmament, the living creatures stand and lower their wings, because, whenever the saints see even the only-begotten one himself scourged in this world, they lay aside whatever they presume upon concerning their own merits.”

This outstanding teacher most certainly understood that this voice had been uttered over the baptized Lord. Without doubt, humanity could be baptized, not divinity; and he did not fear to call him only-begotten who came without sin and endured scourges for our sins. If he is only-begotten, he is by no means adoptive.

[Editorial note: Gregory the Great, *Homilies on Ezekiel* 8.21–22.]

## XXI

We know that blessed Isidore says of Christ:

> “Only-begotten in divinity, firstborn in humanity. Yet we do not read that he contradicts the claim that he was also firstborn in divinity and only-begotten in humanity, lest he himself appear to affirm something contrary to the Holy Scriptures. Our Lord Jesus Christ was both only-begotten and firstborn in both natures.

> “Only-begotten in divinity, because he alone was begotten from the unbegotten Father; likewise, in that same nature, firstborn, as the Apostle says: ‘The firstborn of every creature’ (Colossians 1:15). Likewise, from his Virgin Mother he was firstborn and only-begotten: firstborn because the blessed Virgin had no son before him; only-begotten because she bore no son after him.

> “And he who was born from the Virgin is the only-begotten Son of God the Father, as the Lord himself said of himself in the Gospel: ‘For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son’ (John 3:16). He who was given over to suffering is called only-begotten, just as the prophet Zechariah foretold long ago: ‘They shall look upon me whom they pierced, and they shall mourn for him with a mourning as for an only-begotten son; and they shall grieve over him as one grieves over the death of a firstborn’ (Zechariah 12:10).

> “Him whom the prophet and the Evangelist called only-begotten, the Apostle, teacher of the nations, wished without hesitation to call his own Son, saying: ‘He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all’ (Romans 8:32). ‘Given’ and ‘handed over’ signify the same thing. The only-begotten Son was given for the salvation of the world, and the own Son was handed over to death.

> “The same one is both only-begotten and own Son, both passible and impassible, both God and man, one Son and one Christ in one person.”

[Editorial note: Isidore, *Differentiae*, book 2, distinction 5.]

## XXII

Speak, speak, O hearer of the words of God, who, though you have eyes open like Balaam, do not see, and though you have a rational heart, do not understand what the person of the Son of God, eternally born from God the Father, is—whether own or adoptive.

I do not think you are so turned away from the faith that you would dare to say that the person of the eternal birth of the only-begotten Son of God is adoptive, lest the whole world condemn you with Arius.

Know with absolute certainty and believe with complete truth that the Son of God assumed human nature into precisely that person which he had before the ages, so that the whole was one person, own and perfect in the dignity of the Son, possessing nothing adoptive either in divinity or in humanity: one Son of one Father.

He cannot be both own and adoptive. Either he is wholly own or wholly adoptive. Either you must confess that Christ is two sons in two persons, one of ownership and one of adoption, according to the impiety of Nestorius; or, if you agree that Christ is one, the own Son in one person with Catholics, you must necessarily confess the whole Son of God to be own in one person of supreme truth, because all truth is in him and there is nothing imaginary, as there ordinarily is in adopted sons.

He assumed the truth of our nature, not the person of our adoption. He did not change the nature of our humanity into the nature of his divinity; rather, he changed the person of our adoption into the person of his own sonship, diminishing nothing of his own but increasing what was ours. He remained what he was while assuming what he was not.

If, on account of the assumption, you consider humanity adoptive, as we heard from Felix when he persisted in defending your unbelief, then he who assumed humanity is adoptive, and is the Father’s grandson through the adoption of the Son. No one among you, I think, is unaware how impious it is to think this.

But lest the length of my discourse create weariness for the reader, let us here bring this little book to an end; and, having regained strength through God’s grace, let us begin more freely, from another starting point, what must be said.

# BOOK TWO

## I

Once, therefore, there were holy prophets among the people of God, in whom and through whom the Spirit of God spoke. There were also false prophets, who prophesied falsely under the influence of a possessing spirit. Their likeness is borne today by the teachers of new sects, who assume an appearance of piety but deny its power.

They tear apart the tunic of Christ, woven from above, and, like the soldiers who crucified the Son of God, they do not know how to cast lots over it to determine whose it should be. Rather, with impious audacity, as schismatics they strive to tear apart the sacred unity of Christ’s body with the claws of error. In wishing to divide the author of life into two persons—namely, one of ownership and one of adoption—they strive to sever themselves from Catholic peace, without which nothing can be pleasing to God. They understand neither what they read nor what is read [Paris Codex: “nor what they say”; perhaps the correct reading is “nor what they speak”].

For them it would be better, in accordance with the words of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, not to recognize the way of truth than, after recognizing it, to turn back. It would have been better for Judas the traitor never to have possessed the apostolic name than to have sold the Son of God into the impious hands of the Jews. Likewise, it would be better for perverse teachers never to have possessed the name of honor or the teacher’s seat in the Church than to have destroyed themselves, together with the people subject to them, through the dogmas of a perverse faith.

It is therefore clear to readers of our little writings and of theirs which of us follows the Catholic understanding of the holy Fathers in the divine Scriptures, and which of us presumes to divert the statements of the Holy Scriptures from the path of the Catholic faith.

Let us see, then, how this new interpreter interprets the prophetic words concerning Christ.

## II

After running through many passages in his search, you suddenly stumbled upon a verse of Psalm 67, in which the Prophet, singing the glory of the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Psalm 67:19).

You add from your own understanding: “Behold, he is said to be captive; why, then, should he not be called adoptive according to the flesh?”

The holy Fathers interpreted the meaning of this verse quite differently. Blessed Augustine explained the verse as follows [Editorial note: Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm* 67, verse 19; Alcuin here reports Augustine’s sense more than his exact words]:

> “What does he mean when he says, ‘You have taken captivity captive,’ except that those who were held captive under the devil were set free from him?”

Likewise blessed Jerome says [Editorial note: Jerome, *Breviary on the Psalter*]:

> “You ascended into heaven,” he says; “you took us captive, who were being held captive by the devil. He who once descended upon Sinai and distributed the law to the people now, in the holy one—that is, in the man he assumed, concerning whom the angel said to Mary, ‘The holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God’ (Luke 1:35)—freed those who were held in the devil’s captivity and, having led them after himself like captives, restored them to eternal life.”

Cassiodorus says:

> “For Jesus, our Lord and God, crucified, descended to the underworld, and brought to heaven the souls freed from the captivity of the devil.”

The one whom you, brother Elipandus, dare in your perverse mind to call captive, the Psalmist testifies through words spoken in his own person to be free, when he says: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:6). Again, in another psalm: “The Lord, God of vengeance, the God of vengeance has acted freely” (Psalm 93:1). And the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

What is our freedom if our liberator is thought to be captive? He is held captive in the worst captivity who believes Christ to be captive, on whose garments the Apostle saw written: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15).

Even Adam, the first-created man, was not created captive but free and noble, since he was made according to the image and likeness of God. Nor should he be believed to have been captive before he is read to have been deceived by the devil.

And how can Christ be called captive when he himself says in the Gospel: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30)? If the ancient enemy could find nothing in Christ that belonged to him, by what means could he hold him captive?

Rather, the one who was overcome and bound by Christ is the one who, displaying his strength—which had overcome him—in the Gospel parable, says:

> “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, his possessions are at peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all the armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11:21–22).

Christ, however, the victor, ascending into heaven in the glory of his triumph, took captive by his strength the souls of the saints, long held in exile and excluded from the joys of paradise, and brought them with him into the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

## III

You also brought forward another verse of the Psalmist, constructing it in these words:

> “To him,” you say, “the Son of God, the Father’s voice says: ‘Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth’” (Psalm 2:8).

And shortly afterward you add:

> “To ask and to give are not the same. To ask belongs to a servant; to give belongs to a lord.”

Have you not forgotten the name of adoption in this passage, while plainly confessing him to be the Son of God to whom this paternal voice was addressed: “Ask, and I will give you the nations”? According to your own position, surely the one who asks is himself the Son of God.

Here, unwillingly, you entered upon the way of truth, from which you immediately wandered off; and soon, by a rough path, you fell again into the pit of your error. Under the influence of a possessing spirit, you began to interpret two statements of the prophet Isaiah concerning Christ—statements which Catholic interpreters altogether refuse to acknowledge as prophecies about him—and prefaced them with these words:

> “Of him,” you say, “the Father’s voice says: ‘Behold, I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth.’ And again: ‘Behold, I will walk before you, and I will make the mountains level, and I will break the doors of bronze, and I will give you hidden treasures, so that you may know that I am the Lord your God’” (Isaiah 45:2–3).

You also add your interpretation of these words:

> “Behold,” you say, “to whom the Father says, ‘I am your God.’ He does not say this to him—that is, to the Word—who was begotten from the Father before the ages; rather, he says it to him who at the end of time was made man from the Virgin Mary.”

How do you fail to understand that in these words you affirm two persons in Christ when you say “to him” and “to that one”? It is as though the one begotten from God the Father were one person and the one made from the Virgin Mother another, although the Evangelist says: “The Word was made flesh.”

But those words of the prophet Isaiah, which you think were prophesied about Christ, were spoken beforehand about Cyrus, king of the Persians, who sent God’s people home from Babylonian captivity—not about Christ, as you suppose. This can easily be understood from the words immediately surrounding the passage, where he says: “I girded you, and you did not know me” (Isaiah 45:5). This certainly cannot be said of Christ.

The testimony of Jerome also proves that this prophecy does not in any way pertain to Christ. He says:

> “I know that in this chapter very many, not only among the Latins but also among the Greeks, greatly err, thinking that it was written about the Lord Christ, because *Κυρίῳ*—that is, ‘to the Lord’—is being read, and not about Cyrus.”

And again, shortly afterward:

> “‘I girded you, and you did not know me.’ ‘You did not know me,’ that is, you worshiped idols, not God. ‘I girded you with strength,’ that is, I made you victorious over many nations, and you did not recognize your helper.”

> “In this passage I cannot sufficiently marvel at the foolishness of readers, who refer these words to Christ, through whom the world was reconciled to God.”

If Jerome, the most learned teacher of Greek, Latin, and indeed Hebrew letters, considered it astonishing foolishness to interpret these words of Christ, how do you fail to understand your own foolishness, when you are shown to differ so greatly from his Catholic understanding?

## IV

You also followed with another statement of the same prophet, prescribing it according to your own understanding and saying:

> “God himself, the Son of God, according to his divinity, in which he and the Father are one, says: ‘I will not give my glory to another’” (Isaiah 42:8).

As I see it, you wish “another” to be understood as one person who speaks these words and another as the one about whom they are spoken—that is, Christ’s humanity. You would never have introduced this statement unless you had wanted it understood in this way.

You err, brother Elipandus; you err, and you err badly, in interpreting this statement. Arius once also erred in this, understanding there to be two persons: the one who spoke these words and the one to whom they were spoken—as though God the Father had said of the Son, “I will not give my glory to another.” From the word “another,” he wished to understand that the Son was lesser than the Father.

But while you attempted to leap over this pit of impiety, you fell with an unwary foot into the abyss of Nestorius, thinking that the Son of God was proclaiming these words from the substance of his divinity concerning the nature of his humanity, which he assumed from the blessed Virgin.

But holy Jerome, the most distinguished teacher in the Church of Christ, strongly resists both of you with the Catholic interpretation of this statement. In his exposition of the same prophet, through whom these words sounded in our ears, he judged that they should be understood as follows:

> “I am the Lord,” he says; “this is my name: ‘I will not give my glory to another.’ He does not exclude the Son, who, when he said in the Gospel, ‘Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed,’ received this answer from him: ‘I have glorified you, and I will glorify you.’ For he did not say, ‘I will give my glory to no one’; if he had said that, he would have excluded the Son. Rather, he said, ‘I will not give my glory to another,’ because of you, to whom I have given it and to whom I will give it.”

By these words he condemned the impiety of the Arian understanding. In what follows he immediately crushed the head of your error with a most powerful hammer:

> “But so that we may know that by this statement the Son, not idols, is not excluded, the following words testify: ‘and my praise to graven images’; for which the Septuagint has: ‘nor my powers to images.’ Since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he contains all the powers of the Father in himself.”

“Sidon, be ashamed,” said the sea (Isaiah 23:4). Be ashamed, brother Elipandus, let the children of Catholic learning say. Either explain the statements of the Holy Scriptures better, or place your finger upon your mouth, because if a fool keeps silent, he may be considered wise.

Do not, to bring shame upon your name, send your writings beyond the borders of Spain into the ears of the Churches of Christ, unless perhaps, instructed by the example of Felix—once yours, but now ours—you wish to repent of your former error and erase the syllables of your unbelief with Catholic writings, so that the holy Church of God may receive you into the lap of a mother’s affection and have as a most beloved son in the harmony of charity the one whom it had as a most savage enemy in the dogma of perversity.

You said: “He is nearest to God who knows how to be silent rationally.” Correct yourself by this statement of your own and keep silent, because it is better to be silent than to speak harmful things; the one who turns many away from the way of truth is guilty of the blood of many.

## V

Therefore, you strive not only to defile the inviolable mystery of Holy Scripture through perverse interpretation, but also in many places to corrupt the Catholic meanings of the holy Fathers and to draw them into support of your error [Paris Codex: “you strive to corrupt . . . and to enlist them as support”]. In your wandering you have descended into such a darkness of ignorance that you think you can enlist on your side even those things which are undoubtedly contrary to your own views.

Wherever the blind ignorance of your mind has been able to find the name of adoption, you strive to refer it to Christ with the pen of perverse interpretation, as can be shown by two testimonies of holy and exalted teachers—namely, by the words of blessed Ambrose and of Saint Augustine.

How impiously and how far from their meaning you interpret what they left written for us in their letters with Catholic pen! Blessed Ambrose says [Editorial note: Ambrose, *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, ch. 8, no. 87. Paulinus of Aquileia charges Felix with corrupting Ambrose’s text by writing “he himself by our usage” in place of “by that very usage”]:

> “By our very usage he is adoptive and an own Son.”

Your most unlearned rashness appears to think that this was said about Christ. But the context of the reading proves to readers who understand it properly that it was said with an entirely different meaning.

That remarkable teacher is understood here to be speaking only about the distinction between sons according to human custom, and to be saying nothing about the incomparable and ineffable birth of Christ’s humanity. Rather, in order to destroy the impious teaching of Arius, he inserted these words in the appropriate place within the sequence of his writing.

As for the passage from a homily of Saint Augustine, a doctor wholly Catholic, of the keenest understanding, and a most vigorous fighter against heretical perversities, you quoted it as follows:

> “According to humanity he says, ‘an adopted man,’ whose glory he sought, who was born uniquely from him.”

You impiously interpret these words as though he were speaking of Christ’s two natures—as though Christ were both adopted and uniquely born. That is entirely false, as can be proved from an understanding of the preceding words in the same passage.

Among the many words of sacred exhortation which blessed Augustine composed concerning the Lord’s saying, “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18), he added these words of pious admonition [Editorial note: Augustine, *Tractates on John* 29.8; Augustine reads “Take heed to yourself”]:

> “What ought you to do, O man,” he says, “who, whenever you do something good, seek your own glory, but whenever you do something evil, contemplate accusing God? Pay attention to yourself [Augustine: ‘Take heed to yourself’]. You are a creature; acknowledge the Creator. You are a servant; do not despise the Lord. You have been adopted, but not through your own merits. Seek the glory of him from whom you have this grace, the adopted man whose glory was sought by him who was uniquely born from him.”

As the text of his discourse plainly shows, he speaks of “the adopted man” with reference to any human being who boasts of his good works and accuses God concerning his evil works—not of Christ, who did no evil and who, as we read in this passage, did not accuse God but rather praised and glorified him:

> “But he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.”

Regarding Christ, however, the aforementioned teacher said without any doubt: “whose glory he sought, who was uniquely born from him.” This strongly supports our position, not your unbelief, by which you strive to make the God-Christ equal to us through adoption.

He who was uniquely born can in no way be adoptive. Christ is rightly believed and proclaimed to be both the only and unique Son of God the Father and of the blessed Virgin Mary, the one only-begotten Son of God, as is read in the letter of blessed Pope Leo, which he sent to Leo Augustus against the teaching of Eutychian perversity, written in Catholic and splendid language.

You wished to introduce almost the whole of this letter into your own writings, as though bringing light into a dark place. Would that you would show yourself to believe as you have shown yourself to read in the writings of that most blessed teacher!

Among other things, that distinguished teacher says in the same letter, speaking with marvelous eloquence and commendable purity of faith concerning the distinct properties of the two natures in Christ [Editorial note: Leo the Great, Epistle 165, ch. 6; the Paris Codex reads “purity”]: 

> “Although, therefore, in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and true son of man, there is one person of the Word and flesh, which possesses inseparably and indivisibly common actions, and so forth.”

Does not this Catholic teacher, whom you yourself introduced, affirm by these words, against the impiety of your error, that he is one and the same true Son of God and true Son of man?

And shortly afterward:

> “Since,” he says, “the Catholic faith accepts both and defends both, according to the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, it believes one Christ, the Son of the living God, both man and Word.”

Consider yourself, correct your understanding from these words, and do not divide Christ into two sons, one adoptive and the other own. Rather, with blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and according to the understanding of this most holy Father, believe in one Christ and one Son of the living God, and proclaim him as both Word and man.

Among the other exhortations to the Catholic faith he also added this:

> “The form of a servant, through which the impassible Deity fulfilled the mystery of great piety, is human lowliness, which has been raised into the glory of divine power. It has been joined to the Deity and unity in such an indivisible unity from the very conception in the Virgin that neither the divine acts without the human nor the human acts without God.”

It is impossible not to find in your writings that you either failed to understand these words or did not believe them to be true. Does he not testify that human lowliness has been raised into divine power, which you did not shrink from calling captive?

And shortly afterward:

> “With the unity of the person remaining inseparable, one and the same is wholly Son of man because of the flesh and wholly Son of God because of his one divinity with the Father.”

Blessed Leo, the Catholic teacher, did not fear to make entirely clear in this passage that Christ is wholly Son of God and wholly Son of man. Yet you do not fear to separate him, affirming that one part of him possesses the dignity of an own Son and another part possesses adoption, which ordinarily comes from an extraneous person.

It is utterly incongruous to believe this of Christ: that he was ever extraneous to God the Father and was therefore adopted as a son.

The universal holy Church of God everywhere most certainly rejects and condemns this division or separation of your error concerning the divinity and humanity of our Redeemer. With confidence, together with blessed Leo, its distinguished teacher, it proclaims Christ wholly Son of God and wholly Son of man, wholly own Son and wholly perfect God.

Again and again, be ashamed, Elipandus, and at last recognize your errors—you who do not believe the testimonies of those whom you wished to summon in support of your sect.

It is entirely clear that you do not understand what you read and therefore do not believe as you ought. Yet although a dark gloom holds your minds, where the visible and invisible sun has set, the holy Church of God still has sons of Catholic learning through whom, with divine grace assisting, the light of truth shines most brightly. The tents of the Ethiopians and the tents of the land of Midian will tremble before them. They will go forth in the light of God’s arrows, prepared to strike the adversaries of the Catholic faith with the flashing thrust of the spear (Habakkuk 3:7, 11).

They are the sixty mighty men, chosen from the mightiest of Israel, who surround the bed of the true Solomon, all holding the sword of the word of God and most ready for battle; each one’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night (Song of Songs 3:7 and following).

To them the Bridegroom cries from his heavenly chamber:

> “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed” (Song of Songs 2:15).

Through them the mouth of all who speak wickedness will be stopped (Psalm 62:12). In harmony of one voice and one faith they cry with the Prophet:

> “Blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Psalm 143:1).

> “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are exhausted. I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand” (Psalm 17:38–39).

Lying lips, which speak iniquity and arrogance against the righteous, are made mute (Psalm 30:19).

## VI

You are greatly astonished that Christ could be born from David, who was adoptive, and yet not be adoptive; but you are not astonished that Christ could be born from David, a sinner, and yet be without sin.

By the same power by which he could be conceived and born without sin, through the strength of divine will and the operation of the Holy Spirit, he could be conceived and born from one who was adoptive without being adoptive.

Just as a son can be born from a weak father, or from one deprived of the integrity of some bodily member, with the complete perfection of his members intact, so Christ, from the integrity of human nature, became true man and true Son of God. He had no taint of oldness or defect, drawing from nature its beauty rather than the deformity of its faults.

He received what God created in man, not what man added through the deception of the devil’s suggestion.

Just as flowers of various colors grow from green plants, as the rose from thorns and the dazzling white lily from the green reed, so the fruits of all trees produce one thing in their fruit while displaying another in their root.

The whole world is full of miracles wrought by him who alone performs great wonders (Psalm 135:4), yet an unbelieving mind still doubts whether he could produce for himself an own Son from a virginal womb—he whose power is omnipotent and whose will is perfect goodness.

He who can make adopted sons for himself from the children of the devil through water and the Spirit could much more, through the ineffable power of his goodness, produce from a virginal womb an own Son for his most holy Fatherhood, so that he would be God and man in one person—entirely own, not adoptive.

### VII

Since your unbelief lacked witnesses from other doctors of the Churches of Christ, venerable brother, you suddenly produced, as you say, the venerable Fathers of Toledo and summoned their prayers from the solemn celebrations of the Masses to aid your sect. You say that in their sacramental prayers at the Lord’s Supper there is such a prayer:

> “Who, through the passion of the adopted man, while not sparing his own body, finally—that is, again—not spared ours.”

The words of this petition do not cohere at all, and it appears that *adopted* was put by certain corrupters in place of *assumed* man. What follows—“and finally, that is, again, did not spare ours”—is plainly meaningless, nor is it sufficiently clear what the composer of these words intended to signify by them in his prayer to God.

You give another prayer:

> “Look, Lord,” you say, “upon the multitude of your faithful, whom by the grace of adoption you have deigned to make coheirs with your Son.”

Here too the term “adoption” plainly refers to the multitude of the faithful, whom God by the grace of adoption made coheirs with his Son, not to the person of Christ, the Son of God.

Similarly, when you say in another prayer:

> “The gift came beforehand in adoption, but judgment still remains in conduct,”

here too “adoption” refers entirely to the faithful, who are to be judged, not to him who will judge.

In the Preface, moreover, where you say:

> “And to Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, who through the passion of the adopted man …”

perhaps in the more ancient copies *assumed man* was written there, but it was subsequently corrupted. What, however, is meant by what follows—“When he did not go forth from heaven, he displayed [himself] in triumph”? It is obscurely expressed, if indeed a meaning worthy of the words can be found in them.

[Note: See Cardinal Bona, *Rerum Liturgicarum*, book I, chapter 11, § 2, note 2, and § 5, note 3.]

Likewise, where you say:

> “Today our Savior, after the adoption of the flesh, reclaimed the seat of the Godhead,”

it is much more appropriate here to say “the assumption of the flesh” than “the adoption,” because the Son of God assumed flesh; he did not adopt it.

And what follows:

> “He exalted in the heavens the one whom he had humbled in the lower regions”—

what humiliation of Christ was there among the dead? Had he not bound the strong man, distributed his spoils, triumphantly taken captivity captive, and carried it with him in the triumph of glory into the heavens? This appears to be glorification rather than humiliation, since Christ was exalted in victory and the devil condemned in misery.

As for what you say occurs in the Mass of Saint Speratus the Martyr:

> “You did not shrink from taking upon yourself the garment of flesh belonging to an adopted man,”

the expression “the garment of flesh belonging to an adopted man” is unsuitable. Nevertheless, it can better be understood to mean that Christ assumed the garment of our adoption—that is, our flesh—not that he possessed an adopted garment.

For you are so pleased by the term “adoption” that wherever you find it written, you strive to refer it to our Redeemer without any reverence or consideration, failing to understand what you read.

[Note: See above, book VII against Felix, no. 13.]

Moreover, you are striving to make heretics of your own fathers and forebears in Christ, whom the Church of God has accepted down to your own times. How impious and dishonorable this is, scarcely anyone, learned or unlearned, is unaware. Many writings of theirs have reached us, worthy of reverence for their Catholic faith and consistent with the greatest doctors of the holy Church of God.

### VIII

Stop, brothers; stop, and do not attribute the blasphemy of your error to your fathers. They had their own times, and they left us glorious traces of their labor in holy conduct. We praise and love them—but such as we have recognized them in their writings, not as you report them to be.

We have read very many short works of the blessed Isidore, that most renowned doctor—not only of Spain but also of all the Churches of Latin eloquence—and we hold them in great veneration. Yet nowhere in them have we found the term “adoption” written concerning the humanity of our Redeemer.

We also examined the verses of Juvencus the presbyter and excellent scholar, whom blessed Jerome praises, [or, perhaps, “we examined carefully”] the poems of his *Evangelical History*. In one of his verses he did not hesitate, with Catholic speech, to call Christ the proper Son of God. For he says:

[Note: Juvencus, *Evangelical History*, book I, in volume XIX of Migne’s *Patrologia Latina*.]

> For [perhaps: Not] your womb shall conceive, at heaven’s command,  
>   
> the Son whom God rejoices and commands  
>   
> to reign through all ages and be believed  
>   
> to be his own offspring.  
>   
> When you have given him under the law [Juvencus: “under the light”],  
>   
> let his name be Jesus.

We also considered the *Prognostics* of Julian Pomerius, [Note: Julian Pomerius, unquestionably the archbishop of Toledo, whom certain other ancient writers also called Pomerius; his *Prognostics* are published in volume XCVI of Migne’s *Patrologia Latina*.] collected from the flowers of the holy Fathers, and we found nothing there depicting this sect of yours.

The synodal decrees of the venerable Fathers at Toledo have also reached us. In their letters we recognized nothing new or contrary to the ancient Fathers, but everything written in a Catholic style.

It is therefore more likely that certain younger men, bound by the chains of this new unbelief, are corrupting the sayings of the holy doctors to their own destruction and staining the name of their parents by their most evil obstinacy. Nothing could be more wicked or more atrocious than such audacity.

This appears all the more probable because we have recognized that you either interpret perversely the Catholic judgments of doctors of the Church of Christ who are highly approved and acceptable to all, or alter them with faithless rashness—as we have demonstrated in certain passages, when several little letters expressing your error were brought to us by Felix, formerly yours but now our fellow soldier.

### IX

But you should know that the blessed Gregory, a venerable and most approved doctor in the Catholic faith, composed many prayers in various places for the celebration and observances of the Mass, in order to implore God’s mercy for us. He never hesitated to call the one through whose adoption your priests offer their prayers to God “the Only-Begotten,” using this holy and distinctive name with perpetual veneration.

For in a prayer at the Mass for Palm Sunday he says:

[Note: Saint Gregory, *Book of the Sacraments*.]

> Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who fail amid so many adversities because of our weakness may recover through the passion of your Only-Begotten Son.

Likewise, on the Wednesday of that same week:

> Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who are continually afflicted by our transgressions may be freed through the passion of your Only-Begotten Son.

Likewise, at the Ascension of the Lord:

> Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who believe that today your Only-Begotten, our Redeemer, ascended into heaven [Paris manuscript: “has ascended”] …

Likewise, at the Exaltation of the Holy Cross:

[Note: Ibid. The prayer, however, reads as follows: “O God, who in your mercy deigned to redeem the human race by the precious blood of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord, grant graciously that those who come to adore his life-giving cross …”]

> O God, who willed to sanctify the standard of the life-giving cross by the precious blood of your Only-Begotten Son;

calling the same one—that is, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who suffered and redeemed the world with his own blood—“the Only-Begotten” by this beloved and distinctive name, so that almighty God might have mercy on those who cry out to him in singular love for the one who alone is the unique and Only-Begotten Son of God the Father.

But let these examples suffice. Let us now examine what follows in the rugged style of your letters.

### X

Thus, just as we proved a little earlier that you suddenly introduced new prophets, so you fabricate new letters under the names of the holy Fathers, so that you might be able to affirm your error from their statements.

Nor is this surprising. If Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light, pseudodoctors may also disguise their own sayings as writings of reputable doctors.

For with a deceitful breath you fabricate certain letters as though blessed Jerome or Saint Augustine had written them. In them we have observed the term “adoption” inserted repeatedly, as though those most holy and most approved doctors had said concerning that often-mentioned adoption things which they never said, which are found nowhere in their writings, and which do not breathe their pious and venerable eloquence. Rather, they seek [Paris manuscript: “are able”] to resemble the letters and syllables of your ignorance. Indeed, copies of those letters are found nowhere in Catholic archives.

We have read such extensive and lengthy works of Saint Jerome and blessed Augustine, and almost innumerable letters, in which nowhere have we found either of them calling Christ “adopted” or “God merely by name.” Instead, without any doubt, they have always called and proclaimed Christ the true God and the true Son of God. With God’s help, we shall demonstrate this at the appropriate place.

### XI

Nevertheless, let us set down some statements from those deceitful letters which you sent us in your little book, so that the reader may recognize how inappropriately the parts of speech have been arranged in them and how impious a sense is suggested by the corrupt composition of the words.

First, let us bring forward the statement which you perversely claim to be that of blessed Jerome. You thought—or rather, wished us to think—that he said:

> “The Son of man,” he says, “is deemed worthy through the Son of God to be in the Son of God; and adoption is not separated from nature, but nature is joined with adoption.”

What do you mean by saying, “Adoption is joined with nature”? Consider and understand whether adoption is natural to us. What purpose would the sacrament of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit serve if we were born from our parents with adoption?

Why does blessed David say, though born of lawful parents:

> “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother brought me forth in sins” (Psalm 50:7)?

Do you not appear, in your first three words, to invent sons—one son of man and two sons of God—when you say:

> “This son of man is deemed worthy through the Son of God to be in the Son of God”?

You also used the verb “is deemed worthy” in the present tense, as though the son of man were now deemed worthy by his own merits, through the Son of God, to be in the Son of God. The holy and Catholic faith most firmly contradicts the claim that, by any preceding merits, the man assumed by the Word of God had merited that he should be the Son of God. I consider this sufficiently proved by the testimony of blessed Augustine alone.

For after other doctrines of the Catholic faith he says in the book called the *Enchiridion* (chapter 36):

> “What, then, did human nature in the man Christ merit, that it should be singularly assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will, what devotion to a good purpose, what good works preceded, by which this man might merit to become one person with God? Was he previously a man, and was this singular benefit granted to him so that he might singularly merit God? Surely, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this Son, the Only-Begotten.”

What uncertainty remains here as to whether Christ is one and only Son of God in both natures? For just as this outstanding doctor applied the name “Only-Begotten Son” to the divine nature, so also to the human nature, when he said: “From the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this Son, the Only-Begotten.”

And shortly afterward he adds concerning Christ:

> “The man,” he says, “without any preceding merits, at the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, was joined to the Word of God in such unity of person that the very same one was the Son of God who was the son of man, and the son of man who was the Son of God.”

I repeatedly impress this upon your charity, so that these words of this most learned Father may admonish you that the very one who is wholly the proper son of the blessed Virgin is also wholly the Son of God the Father.

This is also entirely clear to anyone who reads faithfully and understands truthfully from the reciprocal relation of these words, since this holy doctor affirms that the one who is the Son of God is the same as the one who is the son of man, and that the son of man is the same as the Son of God.

### XII

Let us also examine the words which, with your customary cunning, you write as belonging to Augustine in a certain letter to Evodius, reporting that he said (*Letter* 169, chapter 2):

> “The Father in the voice that sounded, ‘You are my Son,’ and the Son in the adopted man whom he received from the Virgin, and the Holy Spirit in bodily form as a dove.”

These words, whoever the falsifier was, secretly snatched with a single [Paris manuscript: “hooked”] hand from the sermons of Saint Augustine and added what he never said: “in the adopted man.”

We find that he expressed the same meaning differently when he discussed the operation of the individual persons:

[Note: Saint Augustine, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapter 15.]

> “The works of the individual persons,” he says, “are said to be those which are manifested as belonging to each one of them. Thus, the one born of the Virgin is none other than the Son of God; and the voice from the cloud, ‘You are my beloved Son’ (Matthew 3:17), pertains to the person of the Father alone; and in bodily form, like a dove, the Holy Spirit alone appeared. Yet the holy Trinity brought about both that flesh belonging to the Son alone, that voice belonging to the Father alone, and that appearance of the dove belonging to the Holy Spirit alone.”

These are Catholic words; these are the words that the aforementioned Father uttered. He added nothing about the adoption of Christ’s flesh, which [Paris manuscript: “that”] your rashness most perversely inserted into his sayings.

Without doubt, we find the same thing in other statements which you have presented under the name of this same Father from that false letter: following your customary falsification, the term “adoption” has been added, although that pious doctor in no way used it.

For example, where we read that he said:

> “He suffered this according to the flesh,”

you, following the practice of your perversity, added:

> “adopted flesh.”

Likewise, in another passage you say that he said:

> “He is immutable and coeternal with the Father, but in the Word alone; the Son of God suffered, but in the adopted man alone; and the Son of God was buried, but in adopted flesh alone.”

We find that in a certain homily, where he discussed the distinct properties of the natures in Christ and the fact that there is one Son of God, namely Christ, he said (*Letter* 169):

> “The Son of God is immutable,” he says, “but in the Word alone; the Son of God suffered, but in the assumed man; and the Son of God was buried, but in the flesh alone.”

Likewise, in another homily on evangelical preaching:

[Note: Treatise 78 on John, no. 3.]

> “For just as there is one man in a rational soul [Augustine: *anima rationalis*, ‘a rational soul’] and flesh, so there is one Christ, God and man. Therefore Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all things and Christ in each thing. Who, then, is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant.”

Likewise, in the same work:

> “Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone. Who lay for three days in the tomb, destined to rise again? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone. Thus Christ is spoken of in each of these particulars; yet all these things are not two or three, but one Christ. Therefore he said: ‘If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father’” (John 14:28).

Likewise, when he was bringing forward from Christ the meanings prefigured in the ancient Law, among other things he said:

> “Christ was the rock, because the rock signified Christ.”

Neither here nor in the passages cited above did he add anything about adoption, which the unbelief of those who fabricate such things has endeavored to add in opposition to the apostolic faith.

### XIII

You also set down another statement, which up to now I have tried [perhaps, “postponed”] to discuss, written in a most perverse hand and allegedly taken from the same letter:

> “And thus,” you say, “the Son of God is called adopted together with the man, and the son of man is called adopted together with the Word.”

In the rest of your unbelieving mind and impious judgment, you erred only concerning Christ’s humanity. Now, however, you have proceeded from impiety to the most atrocious impiety, affirming that the Son of God is adopted together with the man.

Immediately repeating the same meaning in a perverse reversal, you said:

> “And the son of man is called adopted together with the Word.”

What could be said or imagined more wicked or impious than that the Son of God—that is, the Word of God—should be called adopted together with the man he assumed?

Perhaps you sensed that, with Nestorius, you were dividing Christ into two persons: one the proper Son, the other an adopted son. In wishing to avoid this snare, you fell into the prison of Arian perversity.

These words never belonged to Saint Augustine, nor to any Catholic doctor or disciple. Long ago an Arian hand wrote them with a poisonous pen and ink of black gall. For them he was condemned and perished by an impious death together with Judas the betrayer, struck by eternal anathema and handed over to Satan with all his accomplices, so that in the torments of the devil he might experience what he had refused to confess in the Churches of Christ.

### XIV

Erase, brother, these words from your heart, and wherever you find the little sheet containing this writing, immediately commit it to the devouring flames of fire. It is far better for these syllables of an impious doctrine to be burned than for your soul to burn in everlasting torments.

Believe me: even if you clothe yourself in sheep’s garments; even if, adorned with priestly honor, you go forth before the people; even if you shave your beard every day—if you do not change this opinion, willingly or unwillingly you will be counted among the goats and assigned among the shepherds who seem to pasture young goats in the tents of Kedar, who are to stand on the left.

Erase, erase more quickly, pious Father, this opinion from the secret chamber of your heart, lest your Lord, who appointed you to give the measure of wheat to his household, find it written upon the tablets of your heart and say to you:

> “I do not recognize these letters; I reject these syllables. Those whom I said, ‘Go, teach all nations’ (Matthew 28:19), did not teach these words.”

Perhaps the demands of pastoral care and the affliction caused by the impious people prevented you from considering more carefully what you were writing. But, wrongly trusting your juniors, you regarded as true what they had written or persuaded your old age to accept—something proved beyond all doubt to be false and heretical.

### XV

But now I humbly ask the charity of those who read these little letters of my devotion not to charge me [Paris manuscript: *imputent*, plural, ‘that they not charge me’] with impatience, because in certain harsher passages I answered the pious Father with more severe words.

The cause itself answered the cause, and truth confronted falsehood. Readers should consider what was said rather than who said it. No one should seek praise in his own name [perhaps: *suo nomini*, ‘for his own name’] in questions of this kind; instead, with the full understanding of the heart and the peaceful service of the mouth, he should seek praise and glory for Christ, the true God and true Son of God.

But now, having reached the harbor of our desired rest, let us lower our sails for a little while and grant the body its due repose. Then, when the dawn of the following day arrives with new light, let us begin the third little book with a new beginning.

---

## Two Little Books of the Same Albinus on the Incarnation of Christ and on the Two Natures in Him, and Also a Book on the Truth of the One Person: Book One, Which Is Also the Third, Against Elipandus

### I

While, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the vessel of our discourse was passing from the rugged places of disputation to the harbor of free expression [Paris manuscript: “passed”], and the rose-colored dawn shone upon our eyes with heavenly light, while meadows of varied color appeared to us upon the flower-bearing hills of the riverbanks, let us go through the most beautiful estates of the holy Fathers to gather flowers, in order to compose a crown of ecclesiastical truth for our head—that is, for Christ Jesus.

First of all, with humble heart, attentive ear, and bowed neck, let us kiss the most holy footprints of our Savior along the delightful banks of the Jordan countryside and proceed step by step to hear the testimony of the Father’s voice concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, who was baptized by the blessed forerunner John in the waves of that most pure stream.

### II

Luke, one of the four living creatures formerly ordained to write the miracles of our Redeemer, reports that after all the people had been baptized, and Jesus himself had been baptized, as he was coming up from the water and praying, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, and the voice of the eternal Father came to him from heaven:

> “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22).

And lest there be any doubt among the many who were present there at that time concerning whom this voice had been spoken, let the most blessed Baptist himself say what he had seen and heard. He saw Jesus coming toward him and said:
