> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world. This is he of whom I said to you: ‘After me comes a man’” (John 1:29–30).

He called him the Lamb; he called him a man; and he bore witness concerning him:

> “For I saw the Spirit of God descending upon him.”

He also added how he knew who it was concerning whom he had borne witness:

> “I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God” (ibid., verses 31–34).

Behold the Father’s testimony concerning the one who was baptized:

> “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.”

Behold the testimony of blessed John:

> “I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

The one whom he called the Lamb of God and the man, this same one, under the inspiration of the one who sent him to baptize, he unquestionably proclaimed to be the Son of God.

### III

Having heard these things upon the hills of the Jordan River, let us follow, even if from a distance, the footsteps of the blessed apostles who ascended with Christ to the summit of the most holy mountain, and let us observe what they report to us when they return—what they saw and what they heard.

But while they were descending, they were given orders to conceal what they had seen and heard until the Son of Man should rise from the dead (Matthew 17). So great was the glory of the vision and the majesty of the Father’s voice that the world was not permitted to proclaim these things until the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished.

Now Christ, having completed the entire dispensation of our salvation, sits at the right hand of God. Let the apostles say with free voice and public proclamation what they heard and saw.

> “We saw,” says blessed John, one of the sons of thunder, “his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14);

thereby signifying one person, in whom is all the fullness of truth and grace, upon whom this voice of the Father’s testimony was uttered.

Let us also consider what the same blessed evangelist, who reclined upon Christ’s breast, thought concerning this same voice in his Epistle. After many other testimonies of truth that he brought forward concerning Christ, he says:

> “If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God, which is greater: that he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself” (1 John 5:9–10).

Great is the testimony of the Forerunner, who was sent to bear witness concerning the light, so that all might believe through him. When he saw the Holy Spirit descending upon Jesus who had been baptized and heard the voice of the Father’s majesty, he said:

> “I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:34).

But much greater is God’s testimony, which he gave concerning his Son when, addressing him from heaven, he said:

> “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.”

Let us also hear how the same evangelist terrified those who did not believe the truth in the Son of God. He adds words of this kind, full of dread:

> “Whoever does not believe in the Son of God makes God a liar, because he does not believe in the testimony that God has given concerning his Son” (1 John 5:10).

What is more impious, what more wicked, what worse than every evil, than not to believe God’s testimony and to refuse to acknowledge as the true Son of God the one concerning whom the Father’s voice says:

> “You are my beloved Son”?

Blessed John repeats and reinforces this:

> “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ” (ibid., verse 20).

What could have been said more plainly, more sweetly, or more powerfully against all heresies than these words?

Christ is the true Son of God, and all truth is in him, just as he himself says in the Gospel:

> “I am the truth and the life” (John 14:6).

The same writer testifies repeatedly concerning the truth of Christ our God. In the Epistle mentioned above he says in one place:

> “It is the Spirit who testifies, because Christ is the truth” (1 John 5:6).

Likewise:

> “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God” (1 John 4:15).

The Holy Spirit therefore proclaims him to be the truth; the Baptist recognized him as the true Son of God; and the evangelist repeatedly calls him the truth. Let us believe firmly and hold fast that all truth is in Christ Jesus.

Let the blasphemers be silent, those who deny that he is the true God or the true Son of God. May the memory of those who write and have written iniquity perish from the earth, seeking to turn the hearts of the innocent from the way of truth, not fearing the terrible judgment of God that will come upon those who resist the truth but believe the lie.

### IV

We have now heard what the eminent evangelist, the son indeed of thunder, understood concerning this voice of the Father’s testimony. Let us also question his fellow apostle, blessed Peter: to which nature does this voice of the Father most properly belong?

In his most holy Epistle, after writing much about the dispensation of our salvation and the glory of the Savior, he says:

> “We did not make known to you the power of our Lord Jesus Christ by following cleverly devised myths, but having become eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received honor and glory from God the Father, when a voice such as this came to him from the magnificent glory: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ And we heard this voice brought from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain, and we have the prophetic word made firmer” (2 Peter 1:16 and following).

What, then, brothers, is that prophetic word which, from this testimony of God, received the foundation of holy authority, except what is read in the Psalm, as the holy interpreters understood it:

> “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7)?

Paul also, preaching to the Jews with apostolic authority, testified that this prophetic testimony had been uttered concerning Christ’s humanity:

> “We announce to you the promise made to our fathers, because God has fulfilled it for our children by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13:32–33).

Our Savior was raised in that nature which was assumed from the Virgin.

And so that we may know more certainly concerning which nature the Father’s voice had sounded—

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”—

the blessed apostle Peter first said:

> “For he received honor and glory from God the Father.”

Without doubt, the human nature received the honor and glory which the divinity of the Son of God had eternally possessed with God the Father and the Holy Spirit.

### V

Jesus Christ, who became man from the blessed virgin Mary, can be proved to be the true Son of God by many testimonies from the authority of the holy Scriptures. But if these testimonies of the most high God the Father are insufficient for anyone, I do not know what could suffice for him.

This voice was spoken over that nature which was transfigured before the eyes of the apostles, so that those who heard might know what distinction there was between him and Moses and Elijah, who appeared with him on the mountain, and whom they ought to believe and proclaim to the world.

There was therefore no mere appearance—*imaginatio*—either in the name of the Son or in Christ’s dispensation of our salvation. Rather, there was complete truth, the fullness of divine power, and the complete perfection and consummation of our salvation.

A kind of appearance may exist in adopted sons, but not the integrity of truth; and it is impious to believe such a thing concerning Christ. Instead, all truth and the fullness of truth must be believed to be in him.

What is the person of the Son of God, and what do we signify when we speak of the third person in the Trinity, the person of the Son of God, unless we are demonstrating the Only-Begotten, unique, proper, and true Son of God?

Into the excellence and proper character of this person the nature of our humanity was assumed from the blessed Virgin, so that it might be with God, the Son of God, in the proper person of the Only-Begotten, unique, proper, and true Son of God, and so that, with the one who assumes, all these things might be in the one who is assumed.

If any one of these things is lacking in Christ’s humanity, the complete person of the Son of God is not in the one who is the Only-Begotten, true, proper, and perfect Son of God in his own person.

Human nature was exalted into the proper character of this person, as we have said, so that it might be one and the same, the Only-Begotten, proper, and true Son of God, possessing nothing of adoption or division in the dignity of the person.

That nature to which it was said:

> “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19),

and which, because of the first man’s sins, was made one with the devil in a single concord, was joined in one person with the proper, not adoptive, Son of God.

The nature that was subjected to the devil because of sin was exalted above the angels because of Christ’s triumph, and it heard from God the Father:

> “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109:1).

For everything accomplished in that wondrous and ineffable union of divinity and humanity in our Savior was carried out with complete and perfect truth, so that our liberation might be true, as he himself says in the Gospel:

> “If the truth sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

## VI

Since all truth is in Christ, how can he not be true God, or the true Son of God? Does not the whole holy Church of God habitually sing in the Catholic Creed that the only-begotten Son of God suffered, was buried, and rose again on the third day, although these things were done in the form of a servant, not in the glory of eternal divinity, which is entirely impassible and immortal? Yet the unity of person is so great that the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, and the only-begotten Son to have been given over to suffering, as the evangelist mentioned above says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16). The one whom John calls “only-begotten,” blessed Paul the apostle calls “his own Son,” where he says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The evangelist says that he was given over to suffering; the Apostle shows that this same one was delivered up for us.

But Jesus Christ is one Son of God, and without any doubt one person [Col. 0275A]. It must be understood that unity cannot be divided into parts: if it is divided, it will not be unity. For one cannot in any way be divided, and personal union has never admitted separation by any possible rational principle. Therefore, if the Son of God is proper in divinity and adoptive in humanity, there are two; for the inseparable mystery of unity in him would then likewise be divided by the number two—which absolutely cannot happen. For divinity was so tempered with humanity, and humanity so joined to divinity, that neither confusion of the natures nor separation of the natures should occur in the person of the one Son of God; rather, with the proper character of each substance preserved—namely, the divine and the human—in one person of God and man, God should never be believed to exist without man, nor man without God.

This wondrous and immeasurable union in the Son of God took place immediately in the very conception within the Virgin’s womb, through the activity of the Holy Spirit. From the bridal chamber of heavenly childbirth he came forth in magnificent, giant-like course, like the rising sun: the Son of God. Much more could be said of him, if the human mouth could utter anything worthy of such majesty. For “the peace of Christ surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7), and in it heavenly and earthly things have been reconciled and restored to one harmony.

Such excellence was bestowed upon human nature in Christ that it was raised into the one person of perpetual divinity. Everything whatsoever that was accomplished in him within the great mystery of piety was, beyond doubt, accomplished by this one and the same God, the Son of God. Although in some words he displayed divine excellence and in others demonstrated human frailty [Col. 0275C], it is nevertheless one who speaks, and one who manifests both through the clearest signs in himself—namely, the power of divinity and the weakness of humanity.

For example, it is one man who distinguishes colors with his eyes between white and black, and who separates justice from iniquity in his mind; yet there is one person and one man in whom there are spiritual understanding and bodily perception. Do we not have five senses distributed throughout one body, each of which has its own proper activity? The eye sees and the ear hears; the eye does not hear, nor the ear see. Yet hearing and sight are in one body, and there is one man in whom these activities occur at suitable times and places.

So, likewise, God and man are one person; Christ is one, and the Son of God is one. In him divinity shone forth through miracles, while flesh submitted to injuries: the true and only-begotten—indeed, the only—Son of God in both.

## VII

He also habitually called God his Father throughout the entire text of the holy Gospel, everywhere, by a special designation; this is found so often that examples need hardly be supplied. Nor did he ever call the Father his own together with us by a common designation, because he knew that God was his Father in an entirely different way from ours. This is evident in the familiar and thoroughly mystery-filled discourse that he held with his disciples on the night when he was delivered up, speaking to them privately; in it he also frequently called the Father “my Father” by the private pronoun.

Although in one passage he had said, “The Father is greater than I,” he nevertheless specifically said “my Father,” not distinguishing in the name “Son” between the nature that he eternally received from the Father and that which he temporally took from the Virgin Mother. He named himself uniformly “Son” according to the rule of unity, as in the sacred prayer that he addressed to God the Father with raised hands, saying: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1).

“My” and “your” are singular pronouns on both sides. He wished to use them many times amid the most sacred words in order to show the proper intimacy between Father and Son, lest he designate the Father for himself merely by an empty title, or show himself equal to us through an adoptive fellowship.

Therefore, appearing to Mary Magdalene after the resurrection, he gave her this command: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go, tell my brothers, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father’” (John 20:17). If he wished us to understand that God was Father to him and to us in the same way, why did he not say, “I am ascending to our Father,” but speak of himself with the special pronoun “my Father,” and of the disciples with the general expression “your Father”? What other distinction can there be there except that the Father is his by nature, but ours by grace?

## VIII

With these matters thus briefly set forth, let us consider what the prophetic and apostolic utterances think about Jesus Christ, true God and true Son of God. Although it might reasonably seem superfluous to summon other witnesses in addition to the testimonies of the Father’s truth that we presented shortly before, or to the words of the Son of God himself that we have just cited, nevertheless, so that the impious mouth and unbelieving heart may be stopped by the testimonies of the prophets and apostles, as well as by those of the venerable Fathers who flourished in preaching the Catholic faith throughout different parts of the world, let the tongue of iniquity at last learn to keep prudent silence—though it has never learned to speak wisely.

## IX

First of all, let Isaiah be brought forward, whose lips the heavenly seraph purified with a coal from the altar. Let us hear, then, what he announces to our ears with cleansed lips and with a mouth almost more evangelical than prophetic concerning Christ’s human birth:

“Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he will be accounted exalted.”

He admonishes the people to cease from the blood of Christ, although, since he breathes as a man, he will nevertheless be accounted exalted. From where is he exalted, unless because he will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, as the archangel foretold to the blessed Virgin (Luke 1:32)? And so that it might be understood more certainly of which nature he had spoken when he said, “He will be called Son of the Most High,” the angel continued: “And the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (ibid. 35). He used the neuter term “holy,” that is, “the holy body”: the holy body that will be born from you will be called the Son of God.

The prophet mentioned above showed the excellence of this birth when he said: “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). The evangelist Matthew supplied a fitting interpretation of this name, saying that it means “God with us” [Col. 0277A] (Matthew 1:23).

Again, the same Prophet added several names under the perfection of the number six, saying: “A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6). And lest anyone should be uncertain of whom he was speaking, he added: “And the government has been placed upon his shoulder,” plainly signifying our Savior, who, hastening toward the place of his passion, deigned to carry the standard of the holy Cross upon his shoulder.

Immediately he gave this child, distinctly, the following proper names: “And his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come.” He added nothing of adoption or titular designation to these names; rather, the one whom he had foretold as the child born and the Son given to us, this same one he called God—and not merely God, but mighty God [Col. 0277B].

Likewise, after many marks of divine praise, he foretold that the same one whom he knew would come as Redeemer would be called Lord of hosts and God of the whole earth. He was speaking words of great consolation to her who once sat in the sorrow of widowhood, adding: “For he who made you will rule over you; the Lord of hosts is his name. And your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, will be called God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:5).

## X

The Psalmist also sang in harmony with these names: “Who is this,” he sings, “the King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” And he added, as we stated earlier: “The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (Psalm 23:8–10).

And elsewhere: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8:6 and following). When the Apostle wished to use this example, he added: “For in saying, ‘You subjected all things beneath his feet,’ he left nothing that was not subject to him” (Hebrews 2:8).

Should we believe that everything was subjected to some adoptive son or titular god, rather than to the one who alone is the only-begotten and proper Son of God in the union of two natures?

Concerning him, after the praiseworthy completion of the triumph of our salvation, the Psalmist said: “God has ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 46:6). He said, “God has ascended,” and “the Lord will come.” Corresponding to this verse, as Christ ascended, an angelic voice sounded in the apostles’ ears, saying: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

The Psalm-writer also displays the manifestation and terror of his coming, saying: “God will come openly; our God will not keep silence” (Psalm 49:3). He is therefore God himself who is also the Son of Man. Before the throne of his majesty all nations will be gathered, and he will separate them as a shepherd separates the flock, placing the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left.

And so that on that day we may fear him more as King than despise him as a servant, he himself says: “Then the King will say to those who are at his right hand”—and so forth, as the passage continues concerning the separation of the two groups, namely, the righteous and the impious (Matthew 25:34). He concluded the final separation of that judgment with this sentence: “Then these”—that is, the impious—“will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (ibid. 46).

The teacher of the nations also spoke of this judgment: “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). In another passage he called this tribunal of Christ the tribunal of God, showing that Christ is God, and also great God, where he says: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13).

The evangelist John likewise says of him: “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). Empty titular designation has no place there, where the truth of divine power is present. Christ himself demonstrated that this truth of divine power exists in the Son of Man through the healing of the paralytic. When the Jews were reasoning among themselves, “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” he replied: “So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” and then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Matthew 9:6). Immediately the paralytic’s healing followed the voice of the one commanding.

## XI

And lest anyone perhaps be able to doubt whether the one who suffered possesses the glory of divinity, let him read in Daniel the mystery of that most exalted vision, in which he saw the Son of Man brought before the Ancient of Days:

“I was watching in the night vision, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He reached the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. He gave him power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him. His power is an eternal power, which will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13–14).

Blessed John the evangelist testifies in his revelations that he saw things very similar concerning Christ, who was slain:

“I saw,” he says, “and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Revelation 5:6).

A little later he records that the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders sang: “You are worthy, Lord God, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood” (ibid. 8–9).

The entire army of heaven bears witness to this victory, saying: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive glory, honor, divinity, strength, and power” (ibid. 12).

Behold, the slain Lamb has seven horns, that is, the kingdoms of the whole world; he has seven eyes, that is, the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, which Isaiah specifically foretold would rest upon the flower arising from the root of Jesse. Behold, the Lord God is said to have been slain; he redeemed us with his blood and made us a kingdom and priests for himself forever.

All the angelic powers testify that the Son of God who was slain received all these things according to the nature of his humanity. Did not that same one—that is, Christ—affirm the truth of this prophetic and apostolic vision after the glory of the resurrection, when he said to his disciples: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18)?

Alas! What sorrow! Unhappy soul that is unbelieving toward all these witnesses and does not correct itself so as to believe the testimonies of such splendid authority!

## XII

But you, brothers, wake up at last, and wash from your hearts with the tears of repentance the letters that you wrote there with the black gall of unbelief, if you wish to have a dwelling in the house of that Father to whom all power in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld has been given.

Until now you have withdrawn into a distant land from the house of paternal compassion and, under the spirit that bound you in its wings, have fed swine. But rise, rise from the filth of your former unbelief, remembering the most kindly mercy of the compassionate Father. Return to him and say in a humble voice: “Father, we have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:21), so that you may be deemed worthy to put on the robe of the Catholic faith.

“Wisdom of God,” Scripture says, “will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1:4). Do not be contentious, loving your own opinion. Have the humility to learn and the desire for ecclesiastical truth, knowing with complete certainty that without communion with this Church—which is journeying as a pilgrim on earth—the Church that reigns with Christ in heaven will never receive you into the peace of eternal blessedness.

## XIII

Since that often-mentioned Father, Elipandus, a man venerable in dignity—would that he were also honorable in Catholic faith—was demanding other witnesses, let us seek, in concise speech, testimonies from the short works of the holy Fathers, a few from among many. He listed their names in his little letters, asserting that he had believed, or would believe [the manuscript reading is uncertain: *credidisse* / *crediturum*], our error on the basis of their statements; and it is strange that he should wish to say that he believed any error [the printed correction suggests *cuilibet* for *quolibet*].

Nevertheless, from their most sacred writings I shall prove that I have not erred, and I shall show that I wish to correct him. He requested testimonies from blessed Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Isidore. I shall add others as suitable witnesses in support of the truth: Jerome, that most chaste teacher of the faith and the most learned master of Hebrew, Greek, and Latin literature; Gregory, pontiff of the apostolic see and in every respect a man of the purest faith; Cyril, the most vigorous destroyer of the Nestorian sect; and Fulgentius [the manuscript/editorial variant reads *Fulgentianum* / *Fulgentium*], a teacher of brilliant speech and tested faith. By the sacred doctrines of all these men, may he acknowledge that he has long been in error.

## XIV

Hilary, a teacher of no small authority in the Church of Christ and a most vigorous combatant against Arian perfidy, set forth highly persuasive testimonies concerning Christ in the books that he wrote in Catholic style on behalf of the apostolic faith. I judge it fitting to offer a brief selection from them.

In Book Eight of *On the Trinity*, among other things, he says [Note: St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VIII, nos. 27–28]:

> “Christ cannot be anything different from what God is; therefore Christ is God.”

And again:

> “If Christ is your Lord by the nature of God, you will have the Holy Spirit. But if he is Lord here by an adoptive name, then, lacking the Holy Spirit, you are animated by the spirit of error.”

Likewise, from Book Nine:

> “Therefore Christ Jesus the man, God the only-begotten, through flesh and Word, is both the Son of Man and the Son of God.”

This most approved teacher declares Christ Jesus the man to be the only-begotten God. “Just as he is the Son of Man,” he says, “so also he is the Son of God.” If our Savior is the proper Son of Man, then, according to the faith of this most holy Father, he is likewise the proper Son of God.

Again, in Book Ten:

> “The apostolic faith does not allow Jesus Christ to be such that Jesus is not himself the Christ, nor does it distinguish the Son of Man from the Son of God.”

Does not the one who proclaims the Son of Man adoptive and the Son of God truly a son distinguish the Son of Man from the Son of God?

In Book Twelve:

> “For God glorified him in himself—that is, in the nature in which he is God—so that God may be all in all.”

He speaks of the human nature, which was glorified, so that God might be all in all.

## XV

Likewise, blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a most vigorous warrior against heretical depravity, clearly affirms that Christ, according to that in which he is man, is the proper Son of God, as is read in the exposition that he composed on the Gospel of Luke:

> “He”—that is, Christ—“confesses him truly to be the proper Son of God, and declares him to be the one whom the Father’s voice proclaimed according to his humanity.”

This is also said concerning the verse found in the second Psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7):

> “Nor, therefore,” he says, “is permission given you to refute this in your customary manner, as though it had been spoken solely of the divine generation before the ages, although it could also suitably be understood of that generation. Nevertheless, from the circumstances of what precedes and follows, it is rightly understood as having been spoken of the second birth, which he did not reject from taking upon himself temporally for our sake. For the words, ‘But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain’ (ibid. 6), and ‘Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,’ plainly belong to the great mystery of piety that appeared in the world through the dispensation of the flesh.”

“Who,” Ambrose says [Note: St. Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, Book III, no. 9], “is that proper Son of God except the one to whom the Father’s voice said: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?”

In Book Six of *On the Incarnation of Christ* [Note: More properly, *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*, chapter 5, no. 35], concerning the fact that Christ is the true Son of God, he says:

> “This is the general faith against all heresies: that Christ is the Son of God, eternal from the Father and of this day from the Virgin” [Ambrose: “and born of the Virgin Mary”].

A little later:

> “Although the Lord [Ambrose: ‘God’] was always eternal, he received the mysteries of the incarnation, not divided but one; because one is both, and one in both—that is, whether in divinity or in body.”

**Editorial note:** The preceding extended excerpts are not Ambrose’s, but belong to Paulinus of Aquileia, *Against Felix*, Book III, chapter 21. We do not know by what error they were transferred here by Alcuin under the name of St. Ambrose [Col. 0280D].

## XVI

We also have the testimony of Athanasius—not such as your unbelief seeks, but such as agrees with the Catholic faith—as we read it written in the letter that ecclesiastical style composed for Epictetus. After expressing many things about Christ’s incarnation with great elegance, he adds the following [Note: St. Athanasius, volume I of the works, part II. See Madrisius’s note in the works of St. Paulinus of Aquileia, p. 164]:

> “These things,” he says, “did not happen through adoption—far from it, as some have thought—but, as the truth is, when the Savior became man, the salvation of the whole man was accomplished. For if, according to them, the Word was in the body by adoption—and what is said to be by adoption is a phantom—then salvation too is found to be merely apparent.”

What could have been said better or more truly than what this most noble teacher said: that the things read concerning Christ’s dispensation did not happen through adoption, but that all these things were accomplished in truth?

These words are shown to have been spoken with reference to his humanity. By saying “these things happened,” he does not mean that divinity was made, but humanity, which this devout Father affirms was not made through adoption.

The same man, in the little book of his faith, which he judged best to compose in the form of a dialogue against heretical depravity, adds the following at the appropriate point after many declarations of sacred doctrine [Note: Athanasius, *On His Faith*, volume II of the works. The editors, however, count this work among the spurious writings; Paulinus also cites the same passage under Athanasius’s name]:

> “The only-begotten was incarnate in that secret mystery which he himself knows. It is ours to believe; it is his to know. And so God the Word himself, taking up everything that belongs to man, becomes man [Athanasius: ‘may be man’]; and the man who was assumed, by receiving everything that belongs to God, could not be anything other than God” [the same: “cannot be”].

Therefore, if the man received everything that belongs to God, he received it so that he might be true God and the true Son of God, the only-begotten, the only, and the proper Son. All this was in the Son of God before all the ages. It was proper to the Son of Man, whom in the fullness of time he assumed from the Virgin’s womb, from the very beginning of his conception, that he should be the only, only-begotten, true, and proper Son of God.

## XVII

Let us also inquire what the most acute and most truthful teacher in the Catholic faith, blessed Augustine, says, so that, if you are unwilling to believe the testimonies of the teachers mentioned above, you may at least believe the one whom you falsely imagine to support your sect more than others.

If any learned reader with sound understanding examines the many books of his writings, he will find that Augustine writes, believes, and proclaims concerning Christ in agreement with us, not with you. From his many statements, let us touch briefly upon a few examples, lest a great multitude of words burden the mind of a fastidious reader more than it edifies him. Let us not revisit what we cited shortly before from the *Enchiridion*, but pass on to other defenses of his teaching.

For in the first and second books of *Predestination* (chapter 15, no. 30), he openly declares concerning the proper character that exists in Christ:

> “Did not the Word, by making and assuming, cause that very man, from the moment he began to exist, to begin to be the only Son of God? Did not that woman, full of grace, conceive the only Son of God? Was not the only Son of God born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary?”

Likewise, in the second book of the same work [Note: St. Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 67. For why this book is called the second book *On Predestination*, consult the admonition prefixed to this work]:

> “The faithful person,” I say, “who believes and confesses that the true human nature in him is human—that is, ours—although, through the singular assumption by the Lord [Augustine: ‘God’] the Word, it was exalted into the only Son of God, so that the one who assumes and that which he assumed might be one person in the Trinity” [Paris manuscript: “was exalted”].

Blessed Augustine, a truthful and credible witness of the truth, calls him the only Son of God who, only-begotten, came forth from the womb like a bridegroom from the bridal chamber into our land. “Only” and “only-begotten” are names of proper identity, not of fellowship with adoptive sons.

In his treatise on Psalm 99, you find the following (no. 15):

> “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Psalm 99:3). “Who,” he says, “does not know that the Lord himself is God? Let that Lord not seem insignificant to you: you crucified him, scourged him, smeared him with spittle, crowned him with thorns, and so forth; you placed guards at the tomb—he himself is God. ‘Know that the Lord himself is God.’”

Thus, also in Psalm 109, he clearly proves that the human nature in our Redeemer, which arose from the seed of David through a long succession of ancestors, is itself both the Lord of David and the Son of David. He proves this from the verse that the Savior himself proposed to the Jews as a question: how could he be both the Son of David and the Lord of David? He said: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Psalm 109:1).

If he is the Son, how is he the Lord? Blessed Augustine explained this in his exposition of the same Psalm (no. 7):

> “We know that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father after the resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven. It has already happened; we did not see it, but we believe it. We read it in the books, heard it proclaimed, and hold it by faith. Thus, precisely because Christ was the Son of David, he became the Lord of David. For that which was born from the seed of David was so honored that it became also the Lord of David.”

He repeats this again and again, lest anyone perhaps be uncertain of which nature is meant by the words, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’” He therefore adds these words:

> “Precisely because Christ received flesh, because he died in that flesh, because he rose again in that same flesh, because in that same flesh he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; and in that very flesh, so honored, so glorified, so changed into a heavenly form, he is both the Son of David and the Lord of David.”

He also took care to clarify this meaning by apostolic authority:

> “According to this dispensation of Christ’s passage, the Apostle also says: ‘Therefore he exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth’” (Philippians 2:10).

“He gave him a name,” he says—that is, a name above every name. He gave this name to Christ according to his humanity, to Christ according to the flesh, who died, rose, and ascended; he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

“Where will David be, so that Christ will not be his Lord? Let him be in heaven, on earth, or under the earth: his Lord will be the one who is Lord of heavenly, earthly, and infernal things. Let David therefore rejoice with us, honored by the birth of his son and freed from servitude; and rejoicing, let him say so that the rejoicing may hear: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.’”

Where is there a frivolous titular designation of divinity when the dominion of power is so great? Where is there an adoption equal to ours in the Son of David when his dominion is so excellent above all heavenly powers?

I say this because I remember having read among the other absurdities of this new sect that Christ is Lord of David only according to his divine nature, not according to the human nature through which he took his origin from David’s seed. For this reason I have set forth at this point the words of Saint Augustine at greater length.

Likewise, on Psalm 52 (no. 3):

> “When he appeared on earth in the form of a servant, those who crucified him said: ‘He is not God.’ Since he was the Son of God, he was certainly God, the proper and true Son of God; but those who said, ‘He is not God,’ became corrupt and detestable. Let us kill him.”

Behold: he confesses that the proper and true Son of God was crucified by the Jews, just as he is consistently recognized as confessing.

Likewise, concerning the unity of power in the Son of God, blessed Pope Leo stated the matter more explicitly in a homily to be read on the day of the Epiphany (Sermon 31, chapter 2):

> “We venerate the divine and human nature knowingly in the unity, because what was proper in the substances was not different in power.”

## XVIII

But let us now pass to the beautiful work of the Father mentioned above, namely, his *Homilies on the Gospel of the blessed evangelist John*, and examine what he thinks about Christ in them.

Among other things, concerning the testimony of John the Baptist, he says (Tractate 7, no. 4):

> “In no way can those who divide the Trinity say that they have charity” [Augustine: “those who divide unity”]. “These words have now been spoken; let us examine what follows. John bore witness because he saw. What testimony did he bear? That he is the Son of God. Therefore it was necessary that the one who baptized should be the only Son of God, not an adopted son. Adopted sons are ministers of the only Son. The only Son has power; adopted sons have ministry.”

In these words he clearly shows that Christ is the only Son, while we are adopted. Those who wish to divide the unity of the Son plainly do not possess charity, as this teacher mentioned above testifies. By dividing Christ into a proper and an adoptive son, however, such a person divides himself from the unity of Catholic peace.

Again, when John says of Christ, “He must increase, but I must decrease,” Augustine says:

> “Whoever receives his testimony has certified that God is true.”

He then continues: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:30, 33–34). Concerning this, the same teacher says in the same discourse (Tractate 14, no. 10):

> “Hear the Apostle saying: ‘According to the measure of Christ’s gift’” (Ephesians 4:7). “He gives to human beings by measure; to the only Son he does not give by measure.”

Concerning the statement here, “He certified that God is true,” and also concerning what the Truth himself says elsewhere, “For this one the Father, God, has sealed” (John 6:27), Augustine offered the following interpretation (Tractate 25, no. 11):

> “This one is the Son of Man and the Son of God; this man is also God.”

A little later:

> “For this reason God the Father sealed him. What does ‘to seal’ mean except to place something proper [the text is uncertain: perhaps ‘to place something’]? For this is what sealing is: to impose something. To whatever thing you place a seal, you place it so that, because it is not confused with other things, it may be recognized by you. Therefore the Father sealed him. What does ‘he sealed him’ mean? He gave him something proper, so that he would not be compared with the other human beings. Therefore it was said of him: ‘God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions’” (Psalm 44:8).

Blessed Augustine, together with the Prophet, understood something more excellent in Christ’s anointing than these new investigators of divine matters can understand with their darkened hearts of unbelief. He was inspired by the same Spirit in bearing witness to the truth by which Christ was anointed in the Virgin’s womb.

Our Savior was anointed above his companions because we all first existed as sinful human beings and were afterward sanctified through the anointing of the Holy Spirit. He, however, existing as God before the ages, was conceived as man by the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb at the end of the ages. There he was anointed by the same Spirit where he was conceived; he was not conceived first and anointed afterward. But this very conception by the Holy Spirit and the Virgin’s flesh was itself anointing by the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle also understood that he was anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—more abundantly than all the saints. Moses was anointed, like the other saints, into an adoptive son; Christ was anointed in the Virgin’s womb into the proper Son of God.

Blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, also agrees with these words, saying: “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power.”

In the same passage he says:

> “God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed delivered up and denied before the face of Pilate, when he judged that he should be released” (Acts 10:38).

He calls him “his Son,” not an adoptive son, using the familiar pronoun “his,” that is, “proper,” the one who was delivered up by the Jews.

But what does blessed Augustine say about the one whom the Jews insulted as he hung upon the cross? Let us consider whether he believes him to be the true Son of God, to whom they said: “You are the Son of God; come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40):

> “Why, then,” he says, “did he not show those who insulted him that he was himself the Son of God, so that, if he allowed himself to be lifted upon the cross, at least when they said, ‘If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross,’ he might then have come down and shown them that he truly was the Son of God whom they had dared to mock? He did not wish to. Why did he not wish to? Was it because he could not? Certainly he could. For what is greater: to come down from the cross, or to rise from the tomb?”

## XIX

With all the Fathers mentioned above, blessed Isidore, the light of Spain, is recognized as agreeing concerning the unity of person and the distinct properties of the natures of our Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0285B] St. Isidore, *Book I of the Sentences*, chapter 16]:

> “The man Christ Jesus,” he says, “although one thing is from the Father and another from the Virgin, is nevertheless not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin; rather, the same person is eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Remaining one from both and in both natures, neither confused by the joining of the natures nor doubled by the distinction of the natures.”

Why, then, contrary to the confession of your excellent teacher, do you divide Christ into a true and a non-true Son of God? Just as “adoptive” cannot be said of the true Son, so “true son” cannot be said of the adoptive one [Note: [Col. 0285B] We restore the genuine reading from the Paris manuscript. In the printed editions it was erroneously read as follows: “Just as a son from the womb cannot be called adoptive, so an adoptive one cannot be called a true son.”]. From this reciprocal formulation it necessarily follows that there are two persons: a proper son and an adoptive son.

## XX

Come now, Elipandus—venerable in age, noble in character, exalted in rank—fulfill what you promised; do as you said. It is entirely fitting that your long experience should be truthful. Recall that you are bound by your own words: you said that, if I produced for you the testimonies of the Fathers whom we have named concerning the truth in Christ, you would wish to pass over—not, as you say, to the sect of our error, but, as we most certainly know and prove most truly, to the truth of the Catholic faith. I have set before you, abundantly, as I think, the opinions of those whom you yourself chose as witnesses, opinions agreeing with the Catholic faith. Do not depart from the unity of those whose authority pleased you. Let us also present to you, although I fear that you will be an ungrateful hearer, the acceptable confession in holy faith of other teachers of great renown, universally acknowledged by the Church: so that either, ashamed to find yourself alone opposed to all these men, you may correct your opinion; or—God forbid—if you persist in unbelief, you may be struck down by the apostolic sword together with them all. But I judge that this must begin with the opening of another discourse.

# BOOK TWO, ALSO THE FOURTH AGAINST ELIPANDUS

[Col. 0285]

### I

Although the unjust men who have withdrawn from ecclesiastical peace are known to have erred in different ways, nevertheless the origin of nearly all the diverse sects has boiled up from one spring of proud arrogance: each of them preferred to be a defender of his own opinion rather than a follower of the truth. From the very source from which he strove to acquire glory for his name, he became deservedly reprehensible and hateful to everyone.

For this is the worst hinge and origin of the evils that have produced from themselves the occasions of every impiety: when the wisdom of heavenly teachers, violated by the rashness of those who misunderstand it, is not weighed according to its proper meaning, but is diverted into alien meanings according to the reader’s judgment and will, contrary to the rule of truth. Anyone who understands the holy Scriptures correctly can easily detect this in the inventions of all heretics. For the perversity of the ungodly not only misunderstood the Catholic interpretations of the spiritual teachers in the holy Scriptures, but also, with impious rashness or perverse blindness, did not fear to draw the most sacred words of the divine books into conformity with their own error. Most unhappily, they have continued to err especially concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom alone the salvation and life of each person consist, as blessed Peter, the chief of the Apostles, testifies, saying:

> “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

### II

What is more miserable than for someone, by his own will, to turn into the cause of destruction and everlasting ruin what was given to everyone for salvation? If you, Father Elipandus, would take care to consider this kind of impiety and misery with a prudent mind or humble inquiry, you would never have fallen into the pit of this error by withdrawing from the unity of Catholic peace.

Where did this name of adoption or designation concerning Christ lie hidden or sleep when, in the city of Nicaea, the Catholic faith was confirmed by three hundred and eighteen bishops, excluding every impious sect, while the Holy Spirit spoke in their hearts? Perhaps this glory of a new doctrine was reserved for your times, so that you might discover something new by which to exalt your name throughout the world. Behold, it has happened: knowledge of your name has become very famous—but not with the praise of charity [Possibly, “clarity”], but with the contempt of execration; not with the blessing of which Solomon says, “The name of the righteous will be blessed” (Proverbs 10:7). Beware lest what follows be applied more appropriately to your name: “But the name of the wicked,” he says, “rots.”

There were also many synodal assemblies after the authority of this Council of Nicaea, summoned in various parts of the world by the imperial decrees of Christian rulers, as the cause or defense of the Catholic faith against heretical impieties required. In none of them has anything like this ever been heard, nor has anything of this kind been found committed to writing concerning Christ, such as your recent ingenuity—or rather, your insolence—has suddenly brought to Christian ears.

What an unusual and wholly irrational arrogance of mind is yours, that you alone, together with your few muttering companions—not teachers—should reject the faith of the universal Church, while everyone everywhere proclaims with one voice that Christ is the true God and the true Son of God; yet you alone, crying out with the Jews, say: “He deserves to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (Matthew 26:64, 66). And you pursue me, his little servant, with curses, although I, instructed by the authority of all the holy Scriptures and strengthened by apostolic preaching, confess and testify to the whole truth in Christ, just as apostolic teaching has handed it down to the whole world and the holy Church everywhere believes and proclaims it.

But you alone oppose all these things; you alone have arrogated to yourself the singular title of teacher, while you alone have lost the holy and universal creed of the Catholic faith.

It is reported in the histories of secular literature that a certain impious young man burned the temple of Diana, which was held in great renown among the Ephesians. When he was asked why he had wanted to do this, he replied: “Since I could not become known for good through outstanding deeds performed by the living, I wanted my name to become known through some kind of wickedness.” Thus, thus, we have learned that you too have acted, brother Elipandus. Since you possessed neither the ornament of eloquence nor the splendor of wisdom, you took care to spread your name by some unusual sect. No path of salvation remains for you except that, with ready hand, you erase the document of iniquity that you wrote on the small secret page of your heart, and begin to overshadow the characters of your former unbelief with the new syllables of the Catholic faith.

It is read in the writings of those who have written about the nature of stones that the hardness of the adamant stone cannot be broken by any blow of hammers or dissolved by the heat of any fire; but that this exceptionally hard natural substance yields only to the blood of a goat. If the hardness of your heart cannot be crushed by the weight of any testimonies, let it soften and dissolve through the blood of the true God, our Lord Jesus Christ, which was poured out for your salvation. He is truly God, who redeemed you with his own blood; and he is truly the Son of God, who rose from the tomb.

Strike [Paris manuscript: “Fall”] upon the stone that was rejected by the builders, so that the obstinacy of your heart may be shattered (Matthew 21:44). Do not wait for it to fall upon you from heaven and crush you [Paris manuscript: “crush”]. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the almighty God (Hebrews 10:31).

### III

I made this preface to so lengthy a discourse because I wished to rouse your sluggishness, so that you might recognize the concern of our will for your salvation. But it is time, mindful of our promise, that I begin to call other witnesses for you.

Gregory, bishop of the Roman See, a man of noble eloquence and a most pure teacher in the Catholic faith, testifies in many places in his writings that our Redeemer is the only-begotten and true Son of God. For in the first book of the *Moralia* he says this about the Son of God (chapter 23):

> “For although each adoptive son may advance toward receiving divinity [Gregory: ‘advances’], nevertheless he does not receive it so as to be God by nature.”

Again, in the same book, among other things, he says that Christ Jesus is not a son by adoption (chapter 28):

> “He surpasses all who are born to God through faith, because adoption does not exalt him as it does the others; rather, the nature of divinity exalts him.”

Here, without doubt, this holy man, filled with God, teaches that Christ, born as a man from the Virgin, was exalted as the Son of God not through an adoption granted as to the other sons of God, but through the nature of divinity.

The same point appears in Book 26 [Book 27, chapter 2]:

> “Our Redeemer, being a man without sin, is a son without adoption.”

Just as it belongs to divine power that a man should be born without sin from a virgin’s womb, so it belongs to divine power that the man who could be born without sin should uniquely be the Son of God without adoption.

The same most holy Father demonstrates this in Book 18, saying (chapter 52):

> “For it is one thing for human beings who are born to receive the grace of adoption; it is another for one person uniquely, through the power of divinity, to have proceeded as God from the very conception. The glory possessed by the only-begotten through nature cannot be equated with what others receive through grace” [Gregory: “the glory received”; “another”].

Understand concerning which nature he said that God proceeded from the very conception.

Again, concerning what the adversaries believe most helps their case—that Christ is an advocate for us before the Father—this holy Father made clear by a most illustrious proclamation what it means for him to be an advocate, saying in Book 22 (chapter 17):

> “For the only-begotten Son of God to intercede for a human being means that before the co-eternal Father he demonstrates himself to be human; and to have pleaded for human nature means that he has assumed that same nature into the height of his divinity” [Gregory: “has demonstrated himself to be human”].

Recognize that the only-begotten cannot be called such unless he is the true Son. No adoptive son can be called the only-begotten, because there are many of them. Nor has anyone from among the adoptive sons been assumed into unity of person with the Son of God or exalted to the glory of divinity. Indeed, he cannot properly be called the only one either, as we showed shortly before through the most proven testimonies of blessed Augustine, where we demonstrated that Christ was called this; and we also showed above that blessed Gregory placed this designation in the holy prayers of the Masses and of the Church.

### IV

Therefore blessed Jerome also agrees in his interpretation of that verse in which the Prophet says:

> “Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor” (Psalm 24:16).

[Note: [Col. 0287D] St. Jerome, *Brief Commentary on the Psalter*.]

> “He rightly calls himself alone, because he is the only-begotten of the Father, born in the flesh.”

Whoever denies that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified for the salvation of the world, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, and rose again on the third day is wholly opposed to the Catholic creed of the universal Church, in which it is most truly sung that all these things took place in the only-begotten Son of God.

Blessed Fulgentius, a brilliant writer on the Catholic faith, demonstrated this in the letter he addressed to Peter the Deacon, showing that the one who suffered, died, and rose again is the true Son of God. After presenting many proofs of the Catholic faith, he expressed the following judgment concerning Christ [Note: [Col. 0288D] St. Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, sections 10–11, and shortly below, sections 16–17]:

> “For the Word of God was born from the Father; the Word made flesh was born from the mother. Therefore the one and the same Son of God, God, was born before the ages and was born in the world, and both births belong to one Son of God. Indeed, the same God-man came forth from his mother’s womb, and the same God-man lay in the tomb, and the same God-man rose from the dead on the third day.”

Again, in the same letter:

> “By what words can the singular excellence of that flesh be explained, whose person is divine from the very moment of its conception?”

Pay attention to what he says: “Whose person is divine from the very moment of its conception.” Does anyone dare to say that there is adoption in the divine person of the Son of God? The divine person preserved in itself the whole distinct property it possessed before the ages, even though humanity was joined to the divine person of the Son of God.

And shortly afterward:

> “The only-begotten God, when he was conceived, received the reality of flesh from the Virgin. For this is why God became the son of the virgin Mary, and the virgin Mary became the mother of the only-begotten God.”

Blessed Mary bore one and the same person, the only-begotten God—not two: one true God and another titular or nominal god, as your perversity habitually asserts.

Again, in the same letter [Note: [Col. 0289D] St. Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 9, section 52. The complete text reads: “He alone is the Son over whom the voice of the one Father resounded when the only-begotten God was baptized in the Jordan according to the flesh”]:

> “When the only-begotten God was baptized in the Jordan according to the flesh.”

Behold, blessed Fulgentius confesses that the one who was baptized in the Jordan according to the flesh—the one over whom the Father’s voice thundered and upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove—is the only-begotten God.

Again, the same author, in Book Three, called *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion*, says that because our Redeemer is the author of life, the Apostle Peter teaches that he must be believed without hesitation to be the true God, not a titular or nominal one; and after many other statements he adds the following [Note: [Col. 0290D] The same author, *To King Thrasamund*, chapter 12]:

> “Since, then, the God who is the author of life assumed a man into unity of person, from that moment that man obtained the name of the author of life” [Alternative: “from that time”].

Who can be the author of life except the true God? Blessed Peter plainly testifies to this in the sermon he delivered to the Jews. After other excellent statements, he added:

> “But you denied the holy and righteous one before the face of Pilate, when he had decided to release him, and you asked that a murderous man be granted to you. But you killed the author of life, hanging him on a tree” (Acts 3:14).

Long ago Moses, worthy of divine prophetic speech, foretold through the Spirit that this would happen, saying:

> “You shall see your life hanging before you, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66).

### V

I want you, you men and brothers who assert this adoption in Christ, to know most certainly that whatever blessed Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, replied to the impious Nestorius with synodal authority, you must know beyond doubt was replied to you as well; for the impiety of the same error must be destroyed by replies concerning the same truth.

Your sect of perfidy differs in no respect from the unbelief of Nestorius, except that he erred concerning the Virgin Mother, whereas you err concerning Christ the Son. He asserted that the blessed Virgin was not the Mother of God; you, however, affirm that the one born from the virgin womb is neither the true God nor truly the Son of God.

He thought that holy Mary was merely the mother of a man, holding the one born from the Father before all ages to be other than the one who, in the fullness of time, was made man in the flesh from the Virgin.

You, indeed, deceived by no lesser impiety, want the one born from the Father before the ages to be the true Son of God, but the one born from the Virgin to be the adoptive son of God. You add still another kind of impiety to this unbelief of yours, saying that the one born from God is true God, while that man who was made from the Virgin is a titular or nominal god. Over and above these names of duality—that is, of truth and designation, of proper sonship [and] adoption—you have a heart darkened by excessive blindness. You say that there is one God and one Son, while by your many and varied statements you repeatedly divide the one whom you call true God and nominal god, proper son and adoptive son, into two gods and two sons. You reject the name of duality only in persons, while firmly displaying the reality of duality in your own faith.

Read the synodal letters of blessed Bishop Cyril more carefully, so that you may recognize the origin of your error boiling up from the poisonous abyss of Nestorius. Correct yourselves through the writings of that most holy Father, blessed Cyril, following the example of your former dearest Felix, who is now ours. Once he recognized the way of truth, he was not ashamed to confess his ignorance of his error and to join himself through the Catholic faith to the unity of the Church of Christ.

Nevertheless, let us set forth a few testimonies from the writing of that previously named Father, so that by reading them you may understand what he wishes to establish concerning “the man” throughout the sequence of his writings [Paris manuscript: “through the whole sequence”].

### VI

In the letter that he sent to Nestorius himself, among other things he says:

> “Therefore we confess one Christ and Lord, not worshiping a man together with the Word, lest some form of division be introduced, but worshiping one and the same Son.”

Again, in the synod of celebrated authority that was assembled in the city of Ephesus against Nestorius himself, Cyril testifies concerning Christ in this way (*Letter 1 to the Monks of Egypt*):

> “We do not confess two Christs, a man and the Word—one exalted and the other subordinate—but we confess one and the same Christ, God and man.”

Does he not confess two Christs—one exalted and another subordinate—who says that one Christ is true God and another nominal god, or one Lord and another servant?

And shortly afterward:

> “For we ourselves are called gods by the grace of God; nevertheless the Son of God is not so, but rather by nature and truth, although he became flesh.”

And in what follows he says:

> “We too have been anointed with the Holy Spirit; we have been enriched with the grace of adoption and are even called gods. But let us not fail to recognize the measure of our nature. For we are from earth and dwell among servants. But he is not as we are: he is truly the Son by nature and Lord of all.”

Pay careful attention to how he distinguishes between the dignity of our adoption and the natural truth in Christ, the Son of God, who was born from the Virgin. He soon takes care to show this even more clearly:

> “Therefore, it is beyond doubt that Emmanuel consists of two things, divinity and humanity. Nevertheless there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and one true Son, God at once and man—not a man made God on the level of those who exist by grace, but rather the true God.”

See, reader, how confidently he affirms Christ in two natures, asserting that he is one and is both Son and truly God—not according to grace, as we are.

Pay attention to what he says next:

> “Therefore it is evident that the assumed reality of the union necessarily declared him to be the proper Son of God, who is from the holy Virgin.”

Again, in order to refute the statements of the adversaries, he set forth an argument in opposition:

> “But if Christ is neither truly Son nor naturally God, but a mere man according to our condition and an instrument of divinity, then we have been saved not in God, in some sense, but rather in one like ourselves, who died for us and was raised by another’s powers.”

And at the end of the same discourses:

> “But we worship not a mere man—far from it!—but rather God by nature, without failing to recognize his glory, although he became man.”

### VII

What need is there to extract more testimonies from the same writing, when in the city of Ephesus a gathering of Christ’s priests, assembled from different parts of the world, came together precisely to destroy this sect of iniquity, in which there is no doubt that you are entangled together with Nestorius? You can recognize this with complete certainty by reading the letters of that synod, if any fragment of rational creaturehood remains in you.

This single remedy remains for you: that with the utmost eagerness of mind you abandon the unbelief of that Nestorius and your own, which undoubtedly proceeded from the impiety of one and the same root. But if this does not please your obstinacy, know with complete certainty that by the judgment of ecclesiastical authority you will be condemned eternally together with him—the man who darkened the brightness of the Catholic faith throughout many eastern regions of the world with the clouds of his perfidy and was therefore, by a just judgment, handed over by that same universal Church to Satan for everlasting destruction.

### VIII

But so that you may know that we neither divide Christ into two persons with Nestorius and your unbelief, nor confuse Christ into one nature with Eutyches, we confess with Catholic mouth and heart two distinct and perfect natures and one person.

In him Christ is one—or perhaps, “the same” [possibly *idem*]—God and man. The Apostle named the two natures that are in him “two forms” when he said:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6).

Again, to show that Christ has one person, he says elsewhere:

> “And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

[Note: [Col. 0291D] St. Leo, Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 4.]

> “Each form acted in communion with the other,” as blessed Leo says, “the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles; the other submits to insults. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father’s glory, so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race. For one and the same person, as must often be said, is truly the Son of God and truly the son of man.”

Do you see that blessed Leo, the outstanding teacher of the Catholic faith, confesses Christ as the true Son of God and the true son of man? Where did you find that he is an adoptive and not a true son in his human nature, except through the rashness of Nestorian or your own impiety?

Again, Leo himself, in the same letter addressed to Bishop Flavian, from which we drew his earlier statements, says:

> “For the one who is true God is the same one who is true man, and there is no falsehood in this unity, since the humility of man and the loftiness of divinity are mutually present.”

Again, in the same homily on the Nativity of the Lord he says (chapter 8):

> “Some, however, were so entangled in perfidy that they thought Christ should be believed to be a greater God and a lesser god.”

Does not your new unbelief fabricate two gods, one greater and another lesser, when it asserts that Christ is true God according to divinity—that is, the greater God—but a nominal god according to humanity—that is, the lesser god? Nor can there be a true unity of person where the inequality of power is so divided.

### IX

Vigilius also, in his *Opuscula*, which he composed with a truthful pen against the impiety of Nestorius and Eutyches, holds views similar to those of this most holy Pope Leo concerning the two natures in Christ and the unity of person. In them he explained very admirably many things concerning the distinct properties of the natures in Christ and the singularity of the one person.

If you would deign to read these writings of the Catholic faith with a devout mind, perhaps, through God’s mercy, you will reach the path of ecclesiastical peace. Among other things that he clearly set forth concerning Christ, he says [Note: [Col. 0292D] Vigilius of Tapsus, Book II against Eutyches, volume VIII of *The Fathers*, section 7]:

> “But let the Word, because of his flesh, be man, and let the flesh, because of the Word, be God; and whatever is proper to the Word, let it be shared with the flesh, and whatever is proper to the flesh, let it be shared with the Word, because the Word and the flesh are one Christ and one person.”

Many other statements can be found in the writings of the same Father by those who read them and understand them devoutly—concerning the truth that is in Christ, the distinct properties of the two natures, and the singularity of one person.

In addition to these aforementioned Fathers, the distinguished rhetor Victorinus also incorporated very similar arguments into his discussions. He had advanced from the school of Tullian rhetoric to ecclesiastical battles and became as strong a defender of the faith as he had been renowned among rhetors.

For in the first book of his Catholic faith he wrote concerning Christ as follows [Note: [Col. 0293D] Marius Victorinus Afer, *Reply to Candidus the Arian*]:

> “We say that God is our Father, and especially so. For this reason, and according to this, God predestined us in love for adoption through Christ. Does God also have Christ as a Son by adoption? No one has dared to say so.”

And in what follows [Note: [Col. 0294D] The same author, Book I against Arius, *The Fathers*, volume IV]:

> “Christ is therefore the Son of God, and we are sons; but we are sons through adoption, we through Jesus Christ, we as sons scattered abroad” [Victorinus: “you as scattered sons”]. “Is Christ also Son in this way? Therefore Jesus is Son by nature, while we are sons by adoption. That he is Son by nature, he himself often says: ‘Father, I thank you that you have heard me’ (John 11:41), and, ‘Father, save me from this hour’” (John 12:27).

### X

Therefore, trusting in the authority of all these witnesses whom we have enumerated, stand firm, brothers, and correct yourselves through their most sacred writings. Join yourselves in the confession of the Catholic faith to the universal Church of Christ, remembering what the outstanding preacher to the Gentiles added when writing to the Hebrew people, after enumerating a great multitude of holy witnesses:

> “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and let us run with perseverance the race set before us” (Hebrews 12:1).

Lay aside, brothers—lay aside this weight of the worst unbelief and the little bundles of perverse doctrine, and the sin of unbelief that surrounds the small doors of your hearts. Return—return to the light of serene truth and to the unity of Catholic peace.

Again and again recall whom I have set before you as witnesses, and believe their most thoroughly proven testimonies rather than the utterly empty little arguments of your rashness. What greater blasphemy can there be than not to believe the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son, whom he testified by heavenly voice, once and again, to be his own and also his beloved? What kind of impiety is it not to believe the authority of the Gospel, to despise the divine statements of the Old and New Testaments? What perversity is it to contradict the prophetic and apostolic pages? What a wicked and impious rashness it is to resist the preaching of the teachers of the whole world? Or what miserable unhappiness is it to sever the unity of the holy Church of God through any perversity and to separate oneself from the fellowship of charity, without whose association, the Apostle testifies, nothing is pleasing to God?

[Col. 0293D] 911

### XI

Therefore I have collected very many testimonies from the works of the holy Fathers, and I could have collected many more if the work had not become excessively long. I also know that these are sufficient—or rather, more than sufficient—for the person whose heart God opens to belief. But for the one who trusts in his own obstinacy with his heart closed, nothing is sufficient, because he will become a son of Gehenna. The Lord knows those who are his, and he recognizes their ways.

Know with certainty that your ignorance will not be able to excuse you, because “the one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38). Learn much more from the one who says:

> “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29),

who also habitually said to those being healed:

> “Your faith has saved you” (Mark 10:52).

For without faith it is impossible to please God; indeed, we must approach God by believing [Paris manuscript: “approach the Lord”]. The Apostle says:

> “Let all your proper things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

And elsewhere in holy Scripture it is said:

> “Set your love in order within me” (Song of Songs 2:4).

Ordered love consists first in believing about God what is read in the divine books, and after faith in applying devotion to understanding. But you, as has been shown, wish to approach God in an inverted order, placing the frivolous little arguments of human conjecture before the solidity of the Catholic faith, wanting first to understand and to believe only afterward.

The Prophet prohibited this when he said:

> “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint),

signifying that faith must first be offered to the divine miracles and that afterward the gifts of understanding must be sought from God.

Therefore your knowledge labors in vain when you wish first to understand and then to believe, since the proper order is first to believe and afterward to understand. Blessed Peter, the chief of the Apostles, knew this. When the apostles were questioned by Christ, God himself, about what they thought concerning him, or whether they wished to depart like the others who had abandoned him, Peter answered, one for all—or rather, all in one:

> “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and have known that you are the Christ, the Son of God” (John 6:69–70).

Explaining these words of the apostolic confession, holy Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0294D] St. Augustine, *Treatise 27 on John*, section 9]:

> “Lord, to whom shall we go? You drive us away from yourself; give us another self. To whom shall we go? [If we depart from you, to whom shall we go?] You have the words of eternal life. See how Peter, with God giving and the Holy Spirit restoring him, understood. From where, unless because he believed? You have the words of eternal life [Augustine: ‘From where, unless because he believed? You have the words of eternal life’]. For you have eternal life in the ministry of your body and blood. And we have believed and have known—not ‘we have known and believed,’ but ‘we have believed and have known’ [Augustine: ‘we have known’]. For we believed in order that we might know. For if we wished first to know and then to believe, we would be able neither to know nor to believe. What have we believed, and what have we known? That you are the Christ, the Son of God—that is, that you yourself are eternal life.”

Having learned this confession of apostolic authority, follow this rule and maintain this order of confession, so that you may reach recognition of the truth.

Abstain from conversations of foolishness. Do not pursue investigations of investigations, lest you fail in your own effectiveness, thinking yourselves wise when you are found to have become foolish. Do not be high-minded, but associate with the humble (Romans 12:16). “It is not good for one who eats much honey,” and “the one who searches into majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Proverbs 25:27).

But a mind made fat and entangled in carnal habit cannot in any way behold the pure light of truth unless the Spirit of God illumines it. Therefore nothing impedes your understanding of the true faith concerning Christ our Lord and God more than carnal habit. For what you understand cannot happen among human sons, who are generated by carnal union [Note: [Col. 0295D] The true reading is restored from the Paris manuscript in the words enclosed in brackets.], you judge cannot happen at all in the Son of God.

Without doubt, every carnal thought must be driven completely from your hearts if you wish to know the truth of the divine and human generation in Christ the Son of God. Have faith in the pages of the holy Scriptures, and do not transgress the boundaries established by the Fathers of ecclesiastical rank.

They are the ones to whom the sweetest promise of God Christ was spoken as he ascended into heaven:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

In them the same Spirit speaks daily who formerly spoke in the prophets, who proclaimed that Christ would come into the world. They preach daily in Christ that all the things foretold by the prophets have been fulfilled. In them true peace and charity remain through the Holy Spirit, just as the Truth itself testifies, saying:

> “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27),

that is, “I leave you in peace; I will find you in peace.”

Of these people it is said elsewhere:

> “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).
