They too are the chosen sons of God who remain in peace and in the unity of ecclesiastical harmony and who believe in their hearts and proclaim with their mouths that Christ our Lord is true God and the true Son of God, because:

> “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

## XII

It must be known with absolute certainty “that the greatness of the divine work,” as blessed Pope Leo says,[1] “greatly surpasses and rises above the capacity of human speech. Hence arises the difficulty of speaking, and hence also the reason for not remaining silent: for what was said through the Prophet—‘Who shall recount his generation?’ (Isaiah 53:8)—pertains not only to the divine essence but also to the human nature of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Unless faith believes that both substances meet in one person, speech cannot explain it; and therefore the subject of praise never fails, because the abundance of the one who praises is never sufficient.”

[1] [Col. 0296D] Saint Pope Leo, *Sermon 9, On the Nativity of the Lord*, chapter 1.

And so that the unity of person in Christ, and the distinct property of the two natures, may more easily be understood by our simpler brothers, let us offer an example, following the customary practice of the holy teachers, drawing upon visible things to understand invisible ones—although nothing can worthily be compared with such excellence and with the ineffable union that took place in Christ.

If a cup is fashioned from gold and silver for the service of the holy altar, where the sacraments of our salvation are prepared through spiritual blessing, in such a way that the gold retains the radiance of its own nature and the silver, in the appropriate places, surrounds the brightness of the gold with its own whiteness [Codex Parisinus: “encloses” the brightness of the gold], is it not nevertheless one cup, although made from two metals, indeed fashioned by skilled workmanship for the service of one ministry? Who could rightly say that, on account of the incomparable beauty of the gold, it is truly a cup? The gold alone shines for you, and only in the part where the silver surrounds the gold is it a merely nominal (*nuncupativum*) cup; indeed, it is one and the same cup, chosen for the dignity of one ministry.

Let this example be understood as referring to the unity of person and to the ministry of one dispensation, which was completed in Christ—not so that anyone should suppose that the substance of the divinity, which I have represented by the gold, was created. Just as light is hidden inside a glass vessel and shines outward through the glass, so through the most pure flesh the glory of the divinity shone forth, through miracles, to those who looked outward and believed, as he who was hidden within willed and was pleased.

## XIII

Hear me, I beg you patiently, scholastic assembly of Spain, as I speak to you—you who always desire to hear or proclaim something new, not content with the apostolic traditions or with the catholic faith of the universal Church, unless you yourselves discover something by which to celebrate your name throughout the world.

Tell me, tell me, holy nation, people of acquisition, royal race (1 Peter 2:9): what has Christ done to you? In what has he sinned against you, that he should have become so worthless in your heart? Why has his glory been so diminished in your mind? Why are you indignant at glorifying him whom the paternal voice glorified from heaven? Why do you disdain to adore him as the true God and true Son of God, whom the angels adore in heaven?

Is he not the one who left the ninety-nine sheep in heaven in order to seek you, who were lost, on earth (Matthew 18:12)? Is he not the one who saw you lying beneath the fig tree before Philip called you, and descended to set you free (John 1:48)? Why do you not say with Nathanael, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John 1:40)?

Did he not find you half-dead, stripped and wounded by robbers, when you had descended from Jerusalem to Jericho; and, taking pity on you, place you upon his own beast, lead you into an inn, and give the innkeeper two denarii for you, ordering him to care for you (Luke 10:30 ff.)?

Is he not the one who, for the sake of your salvation, was led like a sheep to the sacrifice, bound, scourged, spat upon, crowned with thorns, and finally lifted up upon the cross, dying and being buried; but on the third day rising again and ascending to heaven in the triumph of glory, seated at the right hand of God the Father, and destined to come as judge of the living and the dead?

Do you not hear him crying out to you from heaven: “My people, what have I done to you?” (Micah 6:3). “Did I not lead you out of the house of slavery and free you from the hands of my enemies [Codex Parisinus: ‘your enemies’], overwhelm in the waters of the saving fountain all who sought your life [perhaps: ‘wash them’], protect your journey with the dew-bearing cloud of the Holy Spirit, feed you with the heavenly bread of my body, and give you to drink the water and blood that flowed from my side when it was pierced by the soldier? Above all these things, I prepared for you a dwelling of perpetual blessedness in my Father’s house.

“You, ungrateful for all these benefits of mine, dare to blaspheme me as an ignoble son of the Father’s majesty, and strive to degrade me into conditional servitude with you. You regard me as one of yourselves, scarcely worthy of adoption in the person of a son.

“What were you before my mercy looked upon you, before I assumed your nature into the person of my own property—glorifying you, not diminishing myself? Did I not find you lying in your own blood, wrapped, I say, in your own blood? Your umbilical cord was not cut, nor were your limbs rubbed with salt (Ezekiel 16:4). Did I not find you bound with the harshest chains of diabolical cruelty, and do you now disdain to confess me as the true God or the true Son of God?

“Do you at least fear to call me your King, Redeemer, and Savior; yet you do not hesitate to call me, or even to believe me, an adoptive son, in every respect like yourself, a conditional servant, or one marked by the name of captivity. The testimony of the paternal voice has departed from your mind: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’ (Psalm 2:7). And lest you doubt of what nature he had spoken, he immediately adds: ‘Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance’ (ibid., 8).

“You have consigned to oblivion the words of the same prophet in Psalm 23, where he did not fear to proclaim me five times as the King of glory, adding, so that you might know of whom he spoke: ‘The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.’ He adds this as well: ‘The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory’ (Psalm 23:8, 10). Likewise, in another psalm: ‘O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son’ (Psalm 71:1); and that same Prophet repeatedly testifies, in various declarations, that I reign.

“Moreover, so that you might know with absolute certainty of what nature he had spoken, he says in one place: ‘The Lord has reigned from the wood’ (Psalm 95:10), so that you might not doubt that the one whom you saw hanging upon the wood has reigned eternally.”

## XIV

But I also see that you, Elipandus, are forgetful of my benefits. Was it not I who took you from your father’s house and appointed you to shepherd the flock of my people? I anointed you with my holy oil, so that you might be a leader in my Father’s house. I chose you to be a faithful and prudent servant, and appointed you over my household, to give it its measure of wheat at the proper time and distribute provisions to my maidservants.

But you rejected and despised me, and secretly sowed, with the hand of treachery, weeds among the wheat of the purest faith. You threw me behind your back in order to make a name for yourself. You disregarded all my counsel. What will you do when I come to demand the money that I gave you to multiply, not to hide beneath the dust of the earth?

You were therefore not merely slow to multiply it, failing to give it to the money-changers so that I might receive back what was mine with interest; you also marked it with counterfeit coin under my name and tried to mix dross into silver purified sevenfold, having become a treacherous money-dealer—not a prudent and faithful servant, but a wicked and faithless servant, who was accustomed to call me not merely a harsh master but a captive servant.

What will you answer to these charges, preacher of adoption and defender of the designation of Christ, God the Son of God, when these and many other things are brought against you to your face?

Why did you not first consider what benefit this preaching of adoption, or this designation by name, would bring to the Church of Christ? If this novelty of names were necessary for the Christian people, why did the apostles not preach it, nor leave it written for us in their letters?

Without doubt, one spirit is preaching through you Christ as an adoptive son and a designated God, but another spirit, through the apostles, preaches Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, the true God and the proper Son of God. We wholeheartedly agree with the apostles’ preaching, adding or subtracting nothing whatsoever from the most sacred doctrine, the universal creed, or ecclesiastical custom. Firmly establishing ourselves within the bounds of the paternal tradition and the truth of the catholic faith, we believe without hesitation and proclaim confidently whatever is read in their most holy writings, knowing with absolute certainty that the mysteries of God are to be praised, not scrutinized by reason: “For his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:33–34).

Divine providence willed only that as much should be written down in the authoritative record of the Gospel and in the credible writings of the holy Fathers as it judged sufficient for our salvation. Let us use those names for Christ that are found written in the Old and New Testaments. Let the teaching of apostolic authority and the faith tested over a long period by the catholic Fathers be sufficient for us. Whatever they said about Christ, let us also say—or rather, let us hold with devout faith whatever we find has been handed down to us by others as sacred doctrine.

The Jews, who wandered in the shadow of the law and stumbled over the stone of offense, judged concerning the Redeemer of the world in one way; we, walking in the light of evangelical splendor, must understand in another. To them a child was born; to us a son was given. If to them a servant was promised in the enigmatic language of the prophets, to us came the Lord and Son of God, rising like the sun and bringing forth the eternal day. They crucified the one in whom they did not believe; let us glorify the one in whom we believe. Let us sing to him with the entire heavenly host: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14), so that his most merciful goodness may grant us peace and good will on earth.

## XV

Let us therefore believe that he is truly the Son of God, and confess that he was born of the Virgin, true God and true man, one Son of God, proper and perfect, true and living forever; and let us praise his mercies and venerate his power, because he is the King of glory, the King of kings, the Lord of lords, the God of gods, the great God, almighty God, and true Son of God.

Through him all things were created; through him all things that are in heaven and on earth were restored. He created man when man did not exist; he reformed him when he was lost. He is the summit of all power; he is the treasure of virtues, the fountain of life, the beauty of peace. He is the flower of paradise who rose from the branch of the root of Jesse into our world. He is the banquet of angels, the festival of the saints, the salvation of the sick. He is the true friend, the counselor of our salvation, the diadem of the eternal kingdom.

This is the life of believers, the resurrection of the dead, the redemption of captives, the unfailing light. He is the angel of peace, the minister of life. He is eternal blessedness; he is blessed eternity. He is the Word coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, through whom all things were made.

He became flesh, was born of the Virgin, foretold by the prophets, pointed out by a star, adored by the Magi, made known by the shepherds, called Emmanuel, and declared to be the true Son of God. He was made subject to human rule on earth, although he himself is the ruler of the angels in heaven.

He restored the first robe to the sons of Adam, opened paradise, displayed the realm of life, and opened the gate of freedom. Moreover, he showed to all believers the kingdom of heaven, which Adam did not possess. For the fact that the gates of paradise and the heavenly kingdom stand open is Christ’s victory.

Let us therefore believe every truth in him. Indeed, the blessed Virgin Mary conceived Christ by believing, and let us reach him by believing. Let us believe that he reigns in heaven, the one who was born for us on earth; the one whose first birth alone was not defiled, so that he might cleanse us by a second birth.

Through him we have been freed from the yoke of slavery; through him we have been reconciled to God the Father—not through the glory of merits, but through the grace of mercy. He is our mediator unto life and our rewarder unto glory: Jesus Christ, true God and true Son of God, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

[Col. 0299]

## ADDITION BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR

### A Remarkable Testimony of Saint Augustine on Psalm 54

[Col. 0299B] When that treatise was being read to me at table, these words suddenly came to my ears:

“If Christ does not come to your mind, he is sleeping; awaken Christ, recall the faith. Christ sleeps in you if you deny that he is truly the Son of God, if you have forgotten his passion. Christ keeps watch in you if you remember the passion of Christ.”

In the present dispute, if the occasion arises to exchange arguments with anyone concerning the adoption and proper status that they say exist in Christ, he must be asked: What is the person of the Son of God in the eternal birth? Is he, in that person, the Only-begotten, the true and proper Son of God?

If the questioner [perhaps: “the person questioned,” or “the one examined”] answers, “He is certainly the Only-begotten in that person, the true and proper Son of God,” you must immediately answer and catch him by his own words: If he is the Only-begotten in the person that he possessed eternally, then surely he assumed true humanity into that person, so that he might be the Only-begotten, proper, and true Son of God; and adoption has no place in that person. We are in the person of adoption; he is, just as he was before the assumption of humanity, wholly in the person of proper sonship.

If he is adoptive in his humanity and Only-begotten in his divinity, then without any doubt he has two persons—namely, ours, who are adoptive sons of God, and his own, which he possessed eternally.

He must also be asked whether the most blessed Virgin is truly called the Mother of God, and whether Christ is the proper son of that same Virgin in both the divine and human nature.

If the questioner answers, “For this reason Christ in his entirety is properly, in both natures, the Son of God the Father: just as the divinity humbled itself so that he might be a son of man [perhaps: ‘so that he might be one among men’; something appears to be missing], so humanity was exalted so that he might be the true Son of God,” then: If humanity is adoptive with respect to God the Father, divinity is adoptive with respect to the Virgin mother, because divinity is one substance and humanity another, and conversely humanity is one thing and divinity another. The former—that is, divinity—is, on account of man, true man and true son of man; the latter, on account of God, is true God and true Son of God.

Likewise, if, on account of the assumption, he is adoptive in his humanity, as they customarily say, then the one who assumed man is adoptive—namely, the Son of God. For only the person of the Son assumed man, that is, the Son of God.

[Col. 0299]

## LETTER OF ALCUIN TO A DAUGHTER IN CHRIST

*(In the year 800.) He instructs his daughter in doctrine against the Adoptionists.*

[Col. 0299D] [921] To his most beloved daughter in Christ, her devoted father in the faith sends greetings.

I would write more often to your thoroughly approved charity if your affection gave me the opportunity, whether through words of peaceful greeting or through the sweetness of familiar letters. Yet urged on by that charity which hopes all things, I do not cease, in the service of my office, to address your affection in a few syllables and to touch briefly upon the sweetness of our familiar relationship in a few written lines, lest anyone should mark me as forgetful of your goodness—which can never be forgotten, but always remains perpetually rooted in our heart.

And while continually commending the prosperity of your salvation to the Lord in my prayers, I ask that he grant you joy not only in present happiness but also in eternal blessedness. I desire that your nobility shine in excellent conduct, that your power become radiant through the sweetness of piety, and that your exalted position be loved and your dignity praised.

I beg that this confidence of our faith never depart from your thoughts, because I know that the ancients expressed this proverbial saying: “Charity that can be abandoned was never true.” I also read this statement attributed to Jerome: “A friend is sought for a long time, scarcely found, and preserved with difficulty.” And I carefully consider, with a vigilant mind, what the Apostle testifies when he says: “It is impossible to please God without faith” (Hebrews 11:6).

Indeed, every friendship that people customarily preserve among themselves without faith is undoubtedly empty—or rather, no friendship at all. Therefore faith must be joined to the duty of charity, so that the concord of brotherhood, once begun, may be nourished perpetually by watchful unanimity.

I sent your Candidus [1], at the command of my lord David, together with a little book written against those who assert adoption in Christ, not knowing whether perhaps something new had sprouted somewhere from the roots of the earlier perversity.

[1] [Col. 0301D] See letter 129, note.

You, however, should remain with an inviolable mind in the catholic faith, always having ready answers by which the adversary may be defeated. And, to speak playfully for a moment with your wisdom—for everyone is especially accustomed to use examples from his own art—the sailor compares misfortunes and joys with storm and calm; the soldier discusses weapons; the grammarian uses the resources of his own art.

You, however, should produce from your grammar its natural rules, showing that certain things called “proper” do not belong to the same substance as that of which they are said to be proper. For we call names proper not because they are of our substance, but because they have a particular signification of our substance.

We also customarily call possessions of lands “proper” to us when they come to us by hereditary right, although they are nevertheless of a substance altogether different from ours. This can also be confirmed by the Gospel example, where the evangelist says of the Son of God: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11).

Although the people of whom this was said are not of the same nature as God, the evangelist nevertheless designated them by the term “proper,” on account of their knowledge of God, which in ancient days had been granted to this people alone, as the Psalmist says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75:2).

Since so many things in human affairs are called “proper,” why can this property not exist in the Son of God alone, so that he may be the proper Son of God who was born of the Virgin? Among all the sons of God, he alone possessed this as his own: that he should be one person with him, because he was eternally begotten from God the Father—not one and another, but one and one, although not one thing and one thing, because the divinity is of one substance and the humanity of another.

Yet in his entirety he is one and proper Son, God-man for God’s sake and man-God for man’s sake, in both generations the proper and perfect Son of God. Let your venerable faith hold this belief firmly and proclaim it confidently.

Because I know that your prudence has been excellently trained in dialectical subtleties, I have decided to append a few questions from the discipline of dialectic to this little letter, by which the assertion of adoption or designation in Christ may be emptied of force.

It must be asked whether every man, who consists of soul and body, is the proper son of his father. If he says, “Proper,” he must next be asked whether the soul was sown from the father in the same way as the flesh. If he says, “No,” it must be inferred: How is he a proper son in respect of the soul, if the soul is not from the father in the same way as the flesh? It must also be inferred why he does not believe in Christ, the son of the Virgin, the property of sonship that must necessarily be believed in every man.

It must be asked whether the dignity of a proper son is greater than that of an adoptive son. If he says, “Of a proper son,” it must be inferred: Why does he believe Christ to be a son of the second rank?

It must be asked whether one son of one father can be both proper and adoptive. If he says that this is impossible, it must be inferred that Christ likewise cannot in any way be believed to be both, although he is certainly one person, the proper and adoptive Son of God the Father.

It must be asked whether adoption is made from one’s own son or from another’s son. If he says, “From another’s,” it must be inferred: When was Christ alien to God the Father, so that he might be adopted as a son from another’s son? Was not the true and proper Son conceived and born as God in the very conception and birth?

It must be asked whether the true Son of God is the son of the Virgin. If he says, “True and proper,” it must be inferred: How is he true, when the divinity is of one nature and the humanity of another?

It must be asked: Since the Son of God, according to the catholic faith, is truly the son of the Virgin, how can the son of the Virgin not be the true Son of God? Or, if the son of the Virgin is adoptive with respect to God the Father, it seems to follow that the Son of God, who is the son of the Virgin, is adoptive. Therefore, if the Son of God is truly the son of the Virgin, the son of the Virgin is also truly the Son of God; and in neither generation does the name of adoption have a place.

It must be asked whether a designated God is to be adored. If he says, “No,” it must be inferred: How is Christ adored by the angels in heaven, concerning whom the Apostle says: “When he brings the firstborn into the world, let all the angels of God adore him” (Hebrews 1:6)?

It must be asked: If Christ is designated God in the same way as Peter, why is Christ not read to have forbidden himself to be adored as God, while Peter forbade Cornelius to adore him? If it is said, “Because Peter was a mere man, whereas Christ is God and man,” it must be inferred: If God and man are one person, then one person is true God, and there is no place for designation in either nature.

It must be asked what lies between the true and the non-true. If he says, “Nothing,” it must be inferred: Therefore Christ, insofar as he is man, is either true God or not true God. But it is exceedingly absurd to say that he is God but not true God. Or, if the adversary is ashamed to say this, let him state what lies between the true and the non-true.

According to the art of dialectic, it must be asked whether one person can be a true man and a painted man, who is not a true man. If he says that this is impossible, it must be inferred that in Christ, who is one person in two natures, there can likewise be nothing true and non-true; rather, whatever is in him is true, because he is wholly God, wholly the true Son of God, and the whole truth is in him, with nothing fictitious in him.

It must be asked whether anything should be adored or worshiped by us except the true God. If he says that nothing should be, it must be inferred: How will you adore the son of the Virgin, if he is not true God?

It must be asked whether a designated God is to be adored. If he says that he is not, it must be inferred: Therefore Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is not to be adored, because he is not true God; and there are two gods, Christ God and Christ man—one to be adored and the other not to be adored.

But may God turn this understanding away from every catholic heart, because the whole Christ is one God and is to be venerated with one act of adoration.

It must be asked: If he who is the son of David is not God, by what power did he illumine the blind man who cried out to him, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark 10:47–48)? Who can give light from him [perhaps: ‘give light to the blind’] except God? And if he is God who illumined the blind man, then the son of David is certainly God.

It must be asked whether the blessed Virgin gave birth to one God or two. If he says, “One,” he must again be asked: True or non-true? If he says, “True,” it must be inferred: Therefore the whole son of the Virgin is one God and true God. For if she gave birth to a true and a designated God, she undoubtedly gave birth to two gods, one true and the other designated.

Likewise, it must be asked whether she gave birth to two sons or one. If he says, “One,” it must be inferred: Proper or adoptive? If he says, “Both,” it must be inferred: Therefore the blessed Virgin gave birth to two sons, one the proper son of God the Father and the other an adoptive son, because property is incompatible with adoption.

These matters having thus been confirmed through questions and answers, what remains except that Christ Jesus should be believed to be true, full God, and that he should be believed to be one proper Son, perfectly adored and praised by every creature, as the Psalmist says: “Let heaven and earth praise him, the sea and everything in them” (Psalm 68:35).

[Col. 0303]

## 923 — HISTORICAL DISSERTATION ON THE HERESY OF ELIPANDUS OF TOLEDO AND FELIX OF URGELL

In which matters that had hitherto been obscure are illuminated from recently discovered documents and from the writings of Blessed Alcuin.

### I. The State of the Controversy

That controversy—whether Christ, the Son of God, could or should be called adoptive, and in what sense—had once been raised and long debated in the Church by the Arians, Bonosians, and Nestorians. It was finally revived in Spain in the eighth Christian century and spread also into the provinces of the Frankish kingdom.

Certain bishops, whose leaders were Elipandus, bishop of the Church of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of the Church of Urgell, maintained that Christ, at least according to his human nature, not only could but also ought to be called the adoptive rather than the proper Son of God, and, according to that same nature, a designated rather than a true God.

### II. What Is to Be Expected in This Dissertation?

After several earlier writers, the most learned men of our age have admirably clarified the history of this controversy, which arose and became greatly inflamed in the Church through this new doctrine: the Reverend Giovanni Francesco Madrisius of Udine, a priest of the Oratory, in a historical-chronological dissertation composed by him and inserted on page 212 of the new edition of the works of Saint Paulinus of Aquileia (volume 99 of the *Patrology*, column 557); and after him the Reverend Christoph Wilhelm Franz Walch, professor at Göttingen, in a separate booklet, *On the History of the Adoptionists*. To these may be added the celebrated Jacques Basnage, volume 2 of Canisius’s *Thesaurus of Monuments*, page 284 and following.

It might therefore seem superfluous to bring this same history once more to the anvil. Nevertheless, in the judgment of the learned it ought not to be considered superfluous if several people contribute their observations toward clarifying the history of the Middle Ages, which is still shrouded in much darkness and in which many documents remain hidden, while all hope of discovering them has not perished.

I have in fact been fortunate enough that, after finding and obtaining the documents hitherto lacking, a new light may be kindled upon this obscure matter. We have presented some of these documents in the preceding writings of Blessed Alcuin; we shall present others in Appendix II.

In the present Dissertation, therefore, we shall touch briefly upon those matters that have been sufficiently clarified elsewhere by the distinguished writers mentioned above, and shall dwell at somewhat greater length only on those that concern our Alcuin, who constitutes the largest part of this history, and in which we have detected certain arguments that love of truth commands us to use in dissenting from those learned men.

### III. Who Was the First Author of the Controversy?

The common voice and judgment of historians is that the first author of the error concerning Christ’s adoption into the Sonship of God according to his human nature was Felix, bishop of Urgell. It is said that Elipandus, archbishop of the Church of Toledo, was either instructed in or confirmed in the error by Felix’s counsel and writings.

“Felix,” writes Einhard in his *Annals* under the year 792, “a Spaniard by nationality, when consulted by letter by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, about what he ought to think concerning the humanity of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ—whether, according to that by which he is man, he should be believed and called the proper or adoptive Son of God—very rashly and inconsiderately, and contrary to the ancient teaching of the catholic Church, not only declared him adoptive, but also most stubbornly endeavored, in books written to the aforesaid bishop, to defend the perversity of his opinion.”

The Saxon poet agrees with Einhard, as he usually does, under the same year, as does Jonas of Orléans in Book I of *On the Worship of Images*.

### IV. Felix or Elipandus?

If these things are so, it is certainly surprising that none of those who wrote against Felix with great zeal and examined his errors with every effort should nevertheless have seen, or even mentioned in passing, the books written by him to Elipandus in defense of his heresy, which the annalists cited above recalled.

It is surprising that Blessed Paulinus of Aquileia, and Alcuin himself, should have been unaware of what Einhard knew. For at the beginning of the booklet called the *Sacrosyllabus*, Paulinus explicitly calls Elipandus, not Felix, the author of the criminal error. And Alcuin seems to imply the same thing fairly clearly in a letter written to Laidradus, Nefridius, and Benedict, in these words (column 231 of this volume):

“For when certain brothers of our fellowship reported these things to me, I recognized that Elipandus was first in those regions both in dignity and in the evil of perfidy.”

It is also surprising that Elipandus, who endured most impatiently being instructed by others, and who therefore rebuked Etherius and Beatus in his letter to Abbot Fidelis below, in Appendix II, “because they did not wish to question him as though he were ignorant, but to teach him,” and who says, “It has never been heard that the people of Libana should teach those of Toledo,” should nevertheless have sought counsel from Felix with such humility.

Finally, it is surprising that Pope Hadrian, when he accused Elipandus of error in his letter to the bishops of Spain, volume 13 of Mansi’s *Councils*, page 865 (volume 96 of the *Patrology*, column 1208), did not mention Felix in a single word as the author of all the evil, as they maintain.

Whatever the truth may be, this much must certainly be granted to those ancient and contemporary writers of annals: Elipandus inquired by letter of Felix what his opinion was concerning this doctrine, and received from him an answer that pleased him. Whether this occurred before or after the disturbances raised by Elipandus cannot be clearly understood from Einhard’s account or from those of other writers of that period.

### V. The Year in Which the Schism Broke Out Is Debated

Leaving this matter in its uncertainty, we must now inquire into the year in which that dispute concerning Christ’s adoption into the Sonship of God publicly broke out among the Spaniards.

The only testimony from which anything certain can be extracted is that of Bishop Etherius and Abbot Beatus, who begin their books against Elipandus as follows, below in Appendix II:

“We read the letter of your prudence, sent this present year—not to us, but secretly under seal to Abbot Fidelis in the month of October, in the Spanish era 823—and we heard from report that it had arrived, but we did not see it until the sixth day before the Kalends of December. When devotion to the religious lady Adosinda brought us to our brother Fidelis—not compulsion from that letter—we heard that the little book against us and our faith had been publicly circulated throughout all Asturias. And while our faith was one and indissoluble, the little boat began to toss among the rocks, and two parties had been formed.”

For a further clarification of this obscure matter, the words of Elipandus from his letter to Abbot Fidelis, preserved in the same work of Etherius and Beatus, must be added. There he writes, in the place cited above:

“They do not question me, but seek to teach me . . . Sometimes by saying the opposite, sometimes treating me as though I were ignorant, they did not wish to question me about what was right, but to teach me. Therefore God knows that, although they had written arrogantly, nevertheless, if they had spoken the truth, I ought gratefully to have obeyed.”

It should further be noted that the Spanish era 823, according to the calculation of all chronologists, falls in the year 785 of the Incarnation, because the Spanish era exceeds the Christian era by a full thirty-eight years.

### VI

From these facts it is now clear, first, that around this time Elipandus made his error concerning Christ’s adoption into the Son of God manifest, whether by writing, teaching, or discussing it with others; and that Etherius and Beatus confronted that same perverse and emerging doctrine in this same year 785, or earlier, with a sharper pen—although, as Elipandus says, “they had written arrogantly.”

Second, it is clear that Elipandus bore this rebuke or contradiction from his opponents unjustly, and therefore wrote to Abbot Fidelis, who was perhaps attached to him and to his opinion, inciting him against the heresy that he calls “Beatian.”

Third, it is clear that, when Etherius and Beatus encountered it, Elipandus’s letter had been “circulated throughout all Asturias,” so that already at that time two questions had arisen in the Asturian Church:

“One party of the bishops said that Jesus Christ is adoptive in his humanity and in no way adoptive in his divinity; the other party said that unless, from both natures, he is the one proper Son of God the Father, he is not adoptive.”

So speak Etherius and Beatus; their words may be read below in Appendix II, at the place cited.

It must therefore be concluded that the origin of the Elipandian heresy—namely, the point at which it burst into public disturbances—must be placed in the year of Christ 785.

### VII. The rumor of this dissension spreads

In this very year the rumor of this dissension “was spread not only throughout Asturias, but throughout all Spain and as far as France” (in the passage cited). Beyond doubt it also reached Rome at the same time, penetrating to the Apostolic See. Stirred by it, Pope Adrian I, in the following year—or, as seems to me, somewhat later, but certainly before the Council of Narbonne of 788, discussed below—wrote a letter of exhortation and refutation to the bishops residing throughout “Spain,” especially to Elipandus and Ascaricus, “[Col. 0306B] together with those who agree with them in the heresy or blasphemy of calling the Son of God adoptive,” and so forth, as the heading of Letter 83 of the *Codex Carolinus* states (new edition by D. Gaetano Cenni, vol. I, p. 442 [*Patrologia*, vol. XCVIII, col. 373]).

D. Basnage, *Lect. Antiq. Canisii*, vol. II, p. 284, and, with him, D. Gaetano Cenni, *Monumentorum dominationis pontificiae*, vol. I, p. 443 (*Patrologia*, as above), agree with this opinion of ours. Therefore, although in some earlier years the question concerning this doctrine may perhaps have been debated in private discussions among certain ecclesiastics, I nevertheless think that the year of Christ 785 must be assigned as the year in which this controversy became especially heated among the bishops of the region and other men holding ecclesiastical office, and broke out into public view.

### VIII. Those who first opposed the new doctrine

The most distinguished champions who fought for the Catholic doctrine were the men whom we have already praised, Etherius and Beatus. Etherius was indeed bishop of Uxama; for this reason Beatus, although—if we believe Elipandus—he had been Etherius’s teacher, called him “Father” at the end of his commentary on the Apocalypse, as reported by the most learned Caspar Ibáñez in *Praedicatio beati Jacobi in Hispania*, chap. 22, fol. 128. D. Majansius cites him below in Appendix II, no. 9. Elipandus, however, calls him “brother” in his letter to Fidelis.

Beatus, on the other hand, is called by Alvarus of Córdoba, in Letter 18 to Aurelius Flavius John, preserved in Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XI, p. 120 and p. 127, a priest of Libana, not an abbot or monk. Alcuin nevertheless calls him an abbot, though in the sense of “priest,” as the most learned D. Gregorius Majansius believes in his letter to D. Pluer, no. 4, below in Appendix II. This opinion of that most learned man—may I say so without offending him—is novel, and it is very doubtful whether, just as the title “abbot” is now used in Galicia for parish priests, and *abadía* or *abbatia* in the kingdom of Valencia denotes a parish priest’s residence, this usage already prevailed there in those ancient times.

It is indeed established that in former times priests were often called abbots; it is not equally established that priests who were not monks were designated by the name “abbot.” Consult Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, fourth century, part II, p. 733. Whether the documents cited by him should be regarded as fabricated, as D. Majansius suggests, is not a matter to investigate here.

### IX. The zeal of Beatus and Etherius

After Etherius and Beatus had gained a sufficiently clear understanding of the error of Elipandus and those who agreed with him, both from the creed publicly issued by them and from the letter written to the abbot Fidelis, they, animated by zeal for incorrupt faith and the defense of Catholic truth, once again sharpened their pens. In two books filled with remarkable learning, considering the character of that age, they attempted to lead those who had gone astray back to the path of truth.

You may consult the published editions of these books in Basnage’s edition of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. II, p. 280ff. (*Patrologia*, vol. XCVI, col. 893). I particularly wish you to read what the frequently cited D. Gregorius Majansius has written with great learning about their editions, and especially about the manuscripts in which they are still preserved, in the letter edited by me below in Appendix II, no. 10ff. Nevertheless, I cannot accept the judgment of this most illustrious man when, in another letter written to me (ibid.), he asserts that Etherius and Beatus, in these books, attacked the letter written by Elipandus to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and Austria, which was condemned by the Council of Frankfurt, and which we have received from the same D. Majansius, previously unpublished, and present below.

It seems much more likely to me that those books were composed not against that letter of Elipandus—for it is nowhere mentioned in them—but against his creed, publicly issued in the year 785, and against the letter written to the abbot Fidelis. Etherius and Beatus inserted both writings into their books for this very reason. They composed the books several years before Elipandus and the bishops who agreed with him sent their letters to Charlemagne and to the bishops of his kingdom; not long afterward, in the year 794, those bishops convened a council against them [Col. 0307B] and condemned the aforementioned letters.

### X. Elipandus’s response to this second grave reproof

It is not known from the writers of that period whom we have so far encountered with what disposition Elipandus received this second grave reproof directed against him by Etherius and Beatus, whether he himself made any reply to it in writing, or whether the controversy between them continued, and for how long. Nevertheless, the fact that the error and disturbances in those regions did not cease on account of those books, but that, through the impatience of the erroneous, they began daily to gain greater strength, is demonstrated by what happened afterward.

### XI. Elipandus’s efforts

Elipandus made every effort to draw more people over to his side and to incite them against his opponents. First, since his archiepiscopal dignity gave him great authority, he bound several men of Córdoba to himself, as Alvarus of Córdoba testifies in D. Majansius below, Appendix II, no. 4. He subsequently drew Ascaricus, bishop of the Church of Braga, as some hold, into his nets. Elipandus appeals to him in his letter to the abbot Fidelis, and Pope Adrian also mentions him in the letter cited above by us, Letter 83 of the *Codex Carolinus*.

He had, however, another opponent in Spain, namely Theodula, bishop of Seville, who struck his error with an anathema, as Alvarus of Córdoba reports in his letter to John of Seville, in Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XI, no. 27, p. 123. See also Majansius in the passage cited.

### XII. The error spreads through Septimania and is opposed by the Council of Narbonne in 788

Afterward Elipandus’s error advanced even into the border provinces of Spain and found a defender in Felix, bishop of Urgel, who supported the same error with great determination. Felix propagated it through Septimania just as Elipandus propagated it through Asturias and Galicia, as Jonah of Orléans testifies in Book I of *On the Worship of Images*.

As this evil spread so widely, it made the supreme and most vigilant rulers of the flock of the Lord and of the Christian people anxious: Adrian I, pontiff of the Roman Church, and Charles, king of the Franks. The pontiff by letters, and the king through his envoy Desiderius, urged the Catholic bishops to seek and provide a remedy for the evil through a solemn assembly or synod to be held in the provinces of Gaul bordering on Spain.

For this reason, and also because of other ecclesiastical matters that arose at the same time, twenty-five bishops of Narbonensis, Tarraconensis, and the neighboring provinces assembled at Narbonne in the year 788. At that time the metropolitan jurisdiction of Narbonne also included the province of Tarraconensis, together with the bishopric of Urgel, which was united to and subject to it. See Peter de Marca, *De Concordia Sacerdotii et Imperii*, Book VI, chap. 25, Roboreti edition, pp. 380–381, and *Marca Hispanica*, Book IV, p. 343.

This is attested by a very ancient parchment, first published by Guillem Catel, senator of Toulouse, from Book V of the register of the archbishop of Narbonne in Daniel, archbishop of Narbonne, and subsequently, from another ancient parchment in a more accurate form, by Stephanus Baluzius [Col. 0308A] in his additions to the cited chapter 25 of Book VI of *De Concordia Sacerdotii et Imperii*. It is useful to transcribe and consider here the beginning of this document, which reads as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 788, in the twelfth indiction, while the most glorious lord Emperor Charles was reigning in the twenty-third year of his reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, when, at the urging of the apostolic lord Adrian through letters expressing his authority, and of the lord Emperor through his envoy named Desiderius, we had assembled in the city of Narbonne for many and various ecclesiastical matters, and especially for the pestiferous doctrine of Felix, bishop of the see of Urgel … among the other matters that were settled with truthful speech, a question arose before all of us concerning the parish of Narbonne, and so forth.”

### XIII. Whether this council was ever held is doubted by some

I am certainly not unaware of the many defects that appear in the beginning and end of this document, so that some learned men suspect it of being false. For neither the number of the twelfth indiction nor the twenty-third year of Charles’s reign in Francia agrees with the year 788. The eleventh indiction belongs to that year, and it was only the twentieth year of Charlemagne’s reign, since he began to rule the Franks after the death of his father Pippin, which occurred on 24 September 768.

A second defect in this document is that Charles the Great is said there, in that year, to have been emperor not once but four times, although he did not receive the imperial dignity until twelve years later.

Third, the same document seems suspicious to some because it states that the bishops were summoned to proscribe Felix’s pestiferous doctrine, whereas it records that nothing concerning him was done at this assembly. Yet it is established from the annalists of that period that Felix’s doctrine was condemned first at Regensburg, then at Rome in the year 792, and third at Frankfurt in the year 794. “The Felician heresy,” as the Loiselian Annals and others state under the year 792, “was first heard and condemned at Regensburg”; and under the year 794: “There [at Frankfurt] the Felician heresy was condemned for the third time.”

Both statements would be false if the same heresy had existed at an earlier time—namely, in the year 788—and had either been condemned or abjured by some council or by Felix himself, who is found to have subscribed to that Council of Narbonne. Finally, Pagius, under the year 788, no. 11, also thinks that the document does not deserve credence because it lists as subscribers archbishops and bishops of other provinces who were in no way subject to the authority of the archbishop of Narbonne.

### XIV. The objections are answered

These difficulties raised against the Council of Narbonne are certainly of no little importance. Nevertheless, they are not, in my judgment, so weighty that they can deprive the ancient parchment of all credibility. The celebrated Baluzius, a just judge of such matters, testifies that it is “either nearly contemporary with the age of Charlemagne, or certainly not far removed from it.”

Just as the celebrated Pagius, in the passage cited, recognizes three decrees of this council concerning the boundaries of the parish of Narbonne as genuine on account of the antiquity of the parchment, so credibility cannot be denied to the same document because of the additions mentioned above, since it reports that the bishops were summoned by the authority of the pontiff and the emperor or king “for many and various ecclesiastical matters, but especially for Felix’s pestiferous doctrine.”

It is certain that the copyist made errors in the chronological notices. Yet it must be considered that the documents possessed by Catel and Baluzius cannot be regarded as autographs, but may perhaps have been copied carelessly and incompetently by a third, fourth, or fifth hand, as is frequently found in ancient writings. It could therefore easily have happened that less attentive scribes added one line to the true number of the indiction and three lines to the number of Charles’s regnal year, and thus wrote XII instead of XI and XXIII instead of XX.

The eleventh indiction and the twentieth year of Charles’s reign agree with the year of the Incarnation 788, which I think must be retained. An error in the note of the Incarnation is less likely to have been made by copyists than one in the year of the indiction or reign, because even the simplest people are not ignorant of it.

The other defect, arising from the title “emperor,” which is attributed to Charles thirteen years before he was proclaimed emperor, is very skillfully explained by the celebrated Baluzius:

> “For the kings of the Franks, although they did not yet possess the Roman Empire, were nevertheless sometimes called emperors, because they succeeded emperors in the kingdom.”

The learned man then demonstrates this with several examples. I add that the documents of Catel and Baluzius may perhaps have been written after Charlemagne had already been proclaimed emperor. In that case it could easily have happened that an unskilled scribe considered it improper not to attribute to Charles, already emperor, this appropriate title of praise.

The third difficulty is not equally easy to remove. D. Madrisius, *Opera sancti Paulini Aquileiensis*, p. 216, no. 27 (*Patrologia*, vol. XCIX), thinks that one should say that “Felix’s heresy was first condemned at the Council of Regensburg, that is, by name and solemnly.” He nevertheless believes that it was also dealt with at the Council of Narbonne, but only by discussion, without any definition.

The learned man, I think, failed to notice that in the conciliar decree the doctrine of Felix is called “pestiferous.” Therefore it was rejected and condemned there by the bishops. The only remaining way to escape this difficulty is to say either that the word “pestiferous” was afterward inserted by the writer of the document, or that the Frankish annalists were unaware of the proceedings of the Spanish council. I would more readily believe the latter than that the document, which preserved the memory of those proceedings, is wholly false and wantonly fabricated.

The final difficulty, inferred from the subscription of bishops independent of the metropolitan see of Narbonne, and from Felix’s subscription to the condemnation of his own doctrine, should deter no one. The matter at issue was sufficiently serious: namely, the integrity of the faith and doctrine of the Catholic Church. The evil was spreading in the neighborhood of those bishoprics, most of which were subject to the authority of the Frankish kingdom, and it had already seized the very heart of the Church—that is, the Church of Urgel.

There can be no doubt that the shepherds of Christ’s sheep, threatened by the wolf, even though they were not subject to the archbishop of Narbonne, themselves considered how a remedy might be applied to the evil; that they brought the danger before the head of the Church and the ruler of the land; and that, in accordance with the practice of the Church when heresy arose, they were summoned by these authorities to a council to be held at Narbonne, the chief see of that region.

Moreover, Felix’s subscription to the condemnation of his own doctrine can no more damage the truth of that conciliar document than his treachery can render suspect the confession he later made at Regensburg and Rome, and finally at Aachen. Therefore, notwithstanding the difficulties found in it, that conciliar document must be regarded as genuine because of the antiquity of its writing and the sincere traces of ancient usage that it contains. Consequently, we must hold that at that time a council was held at Narbonne concerning Felix’s doctrine, and that it was there rejected as pestiferous.

### XV. The growing error, promoted by Felix of Urgel, is opposed at Regensburg in 792

When the Council of Narbonne had ended, the dispute and controversy had not ended. Rather, the evil grew daily stronger, so that not only the Gauls but also the Italians and Germans seriously considered measures for driving back this plague.

King Charles, truly “the Great” and most Christian, wishing by his authority to aid the wavering Church, convened a synod of bishops at Regensburg in 792, where he then spent the winter and celebrated Easter. All the Frankish annalists unanimously testify to this under that year, in Bouquet, vol. V of the *Scriptores Rerum Francicarum*.

Alcuin himself also gives a clear account of it in Book I against Elipandus, no. 16, in these words:

> “Before I … had come to Francia, this same sect of your error was debated, with that glorious prince presiding, in the presence of Felix, whom you are accustomed to praise greatly, then the defender of your party, in the very famous place called Regensburg; and by the synodal authority of the priests of Christ, who had assembled from various parts of the Christian Empire, it was condemned with an eternal anathema.”

The passage of time has preserved for us no acts or canons of this council. Nevertheless, the following facts are known about it from the annalists and writers of that period:

1. The time of the council, namely the year 792, is known, and all unanimously designate that year.

2. It is known that King Charlemagne himself was present and presided over the council, as Alcuin testifies in the words just cited.

3. According to the same testimony, priests of Christ assembled from various parts of the Christian Empire. Among them was Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, as D. Madrisius demonstrates exceptionally well from his own words in *Opera sancti Paulini*, Dissertation IV, no. 33.

There appears to be no reason to doubt that all the bishops of Bavaria were present at that assembly: Adalwin of Regensburg, Arno of Salzburg—then not yet archbishop—Atto of Freising, and Walderic of Passau. Which bishops came from other provinces is not recorded in the sources.

4. It is known that Felix himself, accused of error, was brought before the same assembly and was granted the opportunity to defend himself. When he had been convicted of error, he abjured it after touching the most holy Gospels, as Saint Paulinus testifies in Book I against Felix, chap. 5. His heresy, however, was condemned with an eternal anathema, as Alcuin says in the passage cited.

The Fulda Annalist gives the same testimony under this year:

> “The Felician heresy was first condemned at Regensburg, with its author himself denying it.”

### XVI. And at Rome by Pope Adrian

Although Felix had abjured the heresy and had solemnly promised “that he would remain perpetually and unchangeably in the rule of faith to which he had then assented,” as Paulinus testifies in the passage cited, King Charles, who was exceedingly zealous for the integrity of the Catholic faith, nevertheless did not think that the doctrine had been sufficiently confirmed by this council unless the acts performed there, in the absence of legates of the Apostolic See, were confirmed by the authority of that See.

Therefore, by order of the most Christian prince, Felix was brought to Rome to Pope Adrian by the abbot Angilbert, as the Frankish annalists and Pope Leo III testify in the Roman Council of 799. The purpose was that his case might also be judged in the chair of Saint Peter, for the instruction of the entire Catholic world.

### XVII. The reason for which Felix was sent from Regensburg to Rome, as invented by D. Walchius, is rejected; the true reason is shown

The most learned D. Walchius gives another reason why Charles took this course in his *History of the Adoptianists*, chap. 2, section 1, no. 15, p. 115. He writes:

> “It does not seem far from the truth if one says that Felix, although he had declared at Regensburg that he had abandoned his error, nevertheless was not steadfast; and that for this reason Charles did not wish to send him back to Spain, but ordered him to proceed to Rome, so that Adrian might move him to change his opinion. To prevent him from pretending to undertake the journey or from securing his own safety by flight, Charles gave him Angilbert as a companion, a man of the greatest influence with Charles. When he arrived at Rome, he was thrown into prison; and I cannot but believe that this happened after he had embraced his former error again. But he was easily induced by his desire for freedom to pretend that he thought otherwise and, in a solemn formula, to reject what he had previously taught. The Romans persuaded themselves that he had done everything sincerely and allowed him, after being released, to return to Urgel.”

Thus far D. Walchius.

### XVIII. Walchius’s conjecture is rejected

I do not approve of this conjecture of the learned man. It rests on no historical evidence, but only on the possibility of the matter, which in historical affairs has no weight. It occurred to this non-Catholic writer—as I interpret his mind from the connection of his words—that the papal party might draw from this event an argument in defense of the authority of the Apostolic See in confirming the doctrinal decrees of councils. He therefore had to invent another reason why Felix had been sent from the Council of Regensburg to Rome for a definitive judgment.

Indeed, if Felix had revealed his inconsistency at Regensburg shortly after abjuring the heresy there, it would certainly seem strange that no writer of that period and no opponent of Felix should have reproached him for it. On the contrary, all testify that Felix’s inconsistency and treachery first became known after he returned to Urgel.

“And afterward,” says Pope Leo III in the Roman Council cited above, no. 17, “having transgressed the law of God, he fled among the pagans and became a perjurer.”

And if Felix at Regensburg had professed his conversion deceitfully out of fear of the king who was present, who would believe that, while the cause of his fear remained unchanged, he would have wished to expose his earlier deception there?

### XIX. The true reason for Felix’s being sent to Rome

I therefore prefer to believe that Felix, having been convicted of error in the synod of Regensburg, was sent by King Charles to Adrian, the Roman pontiff, because of the prerogative of the First See, so that the controversy might be settled by his judgment, not for one nation alone but for the universal Church.

This could not have been accomplished through the Council of Regensburg, which was merely national and perhaps did not even include all the bishops of that nation. For Spain and the other kingdoms outside Frankish rule, its authority would consequently not have been especially weighty, particularly since no legates of the Apostolic See were present.

No one versed in ancient discipline will deny that this opinion of mine conforms at least to the customs and practice of that age. Certainly the bishops of Italy, in the *Sacrosyllabus* against Elipandus, later published and approved at the Council of Frankfurt, strike the heresy and its adherents with an anathema while nevertheless wishing to preserve the right of the supreme See, even though apostolic legates were present there:

> “The privilege of the jurisdiction of the supreme pontiff and of our Father Adrian, the most blessed pope of the First See, being reserved in every respect.”

See vol. XIII of Mansi’s *Councils*, p. 882, near the end.

The Fathers gathered at Frankfurt—nearly the same men who had assembled at Regensburg two years earlier—therefore believed that the final judgment in matters of faith must be referred to the Roman Pontiff.

This, then, must be regarded as the true reason why Felix was brought from Regensburg to Rome. A companion was assigned to him so that he might reach Rome more securely and might not perhaps escape by flight before the judgment had been completed.

When he was committed to prison at Rome, what happened was what ordinarily happens with defendants who are handed over to custody so that they may neither escape the punishment they deserve nor spread more widely the evil that is still feared.

### XX. Felix makes a profession of faith at Rome

When Felix had been brought before Adrian, the supreme pontiff, at Rome, he again made the profession of faith that he had made at Regensburg. While in chains, he also composed an orthodox statement, under the pontiff’s instruction—or, as I interpret it, at the pontiff’s dictation of the formula. In it he renounced his former heresy and condemned it twice under oath: once over the most holy mysteries, and again over the body of the apostle Saint Peter, thereby providing a perpetual testimony to his conversion.

We have a witness to this act beyond all exception in Pope Leo III. It is useful to quote his words from the Roman Council held near the beginning of the year 799. They read as follows in session 2, in vol. XIII of Mansi’s *Councils*, p. 1031:

> “Under our predecessor of holy memory, the lord Pope Adrian, that most wretched, unhappy, heretical bishop, sent by the lord Charles, the glorious and great king, and instructed by that gracious pontiff, composed while in chains that orthodox statement, anathematizing and affirming among other things that the Son of God is by no means adoptive, as he had said; rather, I confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the proper and true Son of God. Accordingly, placing his orthodox statement upon the most holy mysteries of God in our Patriarchium, he swore that he would hold and confess it thus. Again, placing his orthodox statement in his confession upon the body of the blessed apostle Peter, he likewise swore there that he would in no way dare to call him adoptive, but that he held and confessed him to be the proper and beloved Son of God.”

### XXI. Felix was released at Rome but was nevertheless not restored to his see

After making this twofold confession of Catholic doctrine and confirming his renunciation of his former error so many times by oath, Pope Adrian, believing that all this proceeded from sincere conviction, released Felix from his chains and allowed him to depart.

“After this,” says the writer of the annals commonly attributed to Einhard, “he returned to his own city.”

Whether Felix was then also restored to his own see, or to the honor of his episcopate, is unclear. The Saxon Annalist does indeed seem to suggest this quite plainly under the year 792, where he writes:

> … and he deserved to return  
> To retain once more the honor of his own see.

Nevertheless, among the other annalists and writers of that period I know of no one who expressly affirms it. Certainly the other bishops of Spain, together with Elipandus, were unaware of this restoration when, in the year 794, before the Council of Frankfurt, they wrote their letter to Charles, asking “that he restore Felix to his proper honor and restore a shepherd to the flock scattered by rapacious wolves.” See below in Appendix I.

No one will doubt that these men, as Felix’s associates and contemporaries, deserve greater credence than an outsider poet, who perhaps imagined in his mind that this had happened.

### XXII. Was Felix corrected at Rome in some council of bishops?

The same poet—and he alone—reports that Felix was corrected at Rome “in the celebrated assembly of pontiffs,” that is, in some solemn council of bishops convened for this purpose. He sings in the passage cited:

> In Adrian’s presence, corrected in the temple of blessed Peter,  
> Before the sacred and distinguished assembly of pontiffs,  
> Felix condemned …

No other writer of that period says this. Rather, all report only that Felix was sent from Regensburg to Rome, that he again condemned his heresy before the pontiff, and that afterward, fleeing to his own people, he became a perjurer, as Pope Leo says in the passage cited.

Pope Adrian had examined the acts of the Council of Regensburg and discussed them with his clergy—or perhaps with certain bishops who happened to be present at Rome for other reasons. He therefore judged that there was no need to summon a new council and investigate the doctrine further. Instead, he wished to conclude the matter through the accused man’s renewed confession and his own confirmation of the acts of Regensburg.

“Indeed,” says Alcuin in Book I against Elipandus, no. 16, “this sect of your error was utterly exterminated also by Pope Adrian of blessed memory, who at that time governed the See of the holy Roman Church with apostolic authority”—not, as he had previously said of the Council of Regensburg, “by synodal authority.”

### XXIII. Pope Adrian’s letter to the Spanish bishops came not from the Roman Council of 792, but from another council in 794

For this reason the celebrated Madrisius is mistaken—if I may say so with due respect for such a learned man—when, in the cited dissertation, no. 35, he writes:

> “Adrian collected into one letter or statement what had been defined in this Roman Council, namely that of the present year 792, and sent it to the bishops of Spain against Elipandus.”

In that letter or statement, however, the pontiff does not mention even in a single word any decrees previously made in a council convened against Felix. He says nothing about Felix’s confession or about the condemnation of his error at Rome or Regensburg. He merely explains his own mind and the doctrine and faith of the Church; refutes the letters written by the bishops of Spain to the bishops of Gaul and Germany and to Charlemagne; and condemns the doctrine contained in those letters, together with its authors, unless they repent.

For this reason D. Mansi, vol. XIII of the *Councils*, p. 860, column D, accuses the Venetian editor of the *Councils* of error for supposing that Adrian’s letters proceeded from the Roman Council of 792. Mansi proves that they should instead be attributed to another Roman Council, held in 794. He also asserts, as we do, that it is not sufficiently clear whether Felix abjured his heresy at Rome in any council.

“This alone,” he says, “is certain: after being convicted at Regensburg, he abjured his heresy at Rome before the shrine (*confessio*) of Saint Peter.”

Nor can I grant D. Madrisius’s further claim, in the same place, no. 36, that Felix wrote to Elipandus from Rome in that year, 792, and that while still residing at Rome he received a reply from Elipandus toward the end of that year or at the beginning of the next—namely, the letter presented above. We shall show below, in no. 50 of this dissertation, that this occurred later.

### XXIV. Felix revives his error in Spain

Felix’s conversion at that time was therefore fabricated and feigned, as he himself later openly declared and wrote at the Council of Aachen:

> “We returned with our whole heart, not with any pretense or veil of falsehood, as formerly”—namely, at Regensburg and Rome.

Thus freed by this trick, Felix treacherously returned to Urgel and at the same time to his former error.

“Afterward, having transgressed the law of God,” says Pope Leo in the passage cited above, no. 21, “he fled to his pagan sympathizers and became a perjurer.”

Alcuin gives the same testimony in the passage cited above, no. 22, writing:

> “Until that same Felix, unhappily fleeing to your regions, intended, at your urging, to revive the smoldering ashes of infidelity.”

### XXV. King Charles recalls Blessed Alcuin and several companions from Britain

Felix’s treachery did not long remain hidden from the most vigilant King Charles, who was deeply concerned for the purity of religion and the peace of the Church. Since the efforts employed up to that time had accomplished nothing toward extinguishing the error, the most Christian prince had to consider new remedies by which the evil might finally be driven entirely from his kingdoms and from the Church.

The prince remembered the extraordinary sacred learning that he had long experienced in Alcuin, the master of his court. At that time Alcuin was absent from Francia. He had departed for his homeland in the year 790, either to seek permission from his own king and bishop to leave England and the Church to which he was attached and thereafter remain in Francia—as the writer of his Life suggests, no. 12—or, as Mabillon thinks in *Annales Benedictini*, Book XXVI, no. 10, to settle certain disputes that had arisen at that time between Charles and Offa, king of the Mercians, as is suggested in Alcuin’s Letter 3 to Colcu, the reader—or for both reasons together.

Charlemagne therefore judged that Alcuin was exceptionally well suited to combat the errors of the Spaniards. He urged him not to delay his return any longer, but to devote his services to aiding the affairs of the Church in his kingdom.

Alcuin himself testifies more than once that this was the reason for his return from England. In the preface to his books against Elipandus, cited above, he says:

> “By divine providence, as I believe, commanding it, I came, summoned, to Charles, the glorious prince and king of this kingdom, worthy to be named with every honor.”

D. Walchius, in the passage cited, no. 17, p. 121, thinks that by these words Alcuin did not mean “that he had been summoned by Charles from England to undertake the struggle against Felix and Elipandus,” but rather that it was a sign of the divine will that he should come to Francia at the time when his counsel and learning were needed to refute those errors.

But Alcuin means both: he came from England by divine providence and because he had been summoned. He says this more clearly above, in Book I against Elipandus, no. 16:

> “Before I came to Francia at the command of that same most wise king, this same sect of your error … was debated.”

Afterward King Charles “also summoned other men trained in ecclesiastical discipline from the regions of Britain” to celebrate the Council of Frankfurt, as he himself says in his letter to Elipandus, inserted into the acts of that council and republished by us in Appendix II.

### XXVI. Blessed Alcuin obeys the royal summons

Alcuin therefore returned from England toward the end of the year 792 or at the beginning of the following year, as Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 304; Cointius, *Annales Ecclesiastici Franciae*, p. 496; Pagius, *Critica Baronii*, under the year 793, no. 7; and others correctly judge.

Certainly, in that same year 793 he was already residing in Francia, as is clear from his letters written that year to the people of York and to others; see our annotations there.

### XXVII. He writes an exhortatory letter to Felix, now published for the first time

After his arrival in Gaul, Alcuin approached Bishop Felix calmly and amicably by letter (I remain uncertain whether this occurred before or after the Council of Frankfurt in 794), trying to determine whether he could move him toward better things by fraternal admonitions and friendly exhortation. “To him,” he says in Book I Against Elipandus, [Col. 0314B] “upon coming into these regions, I took care to send an exhortatory letter with the pen of charity, so that he might join the Catholic unity.” And again, in Book I Against Felix: “I wrote some time ago,” he says, “to Bishop Felix with the pen of charity, not with the goad of contention; with a desire for fraternal salvation, not with the stylus of biting criticism; wishing to correct in the love of Christ the man who is known to have withdrawn from the unity of Catholic peace concerning Christ because of the novelty of a certain name.”

Until now learned men had desired this exhortatory letter, and D. Walch had entirely despaired of its ever being brought to light. In no. 18, p. 129, of his *History of the Adoptionists*, he declared that “it is certain that these letters of Alcuin, together with Felix’s little book, were lost and destroyed by the injury of time.” Yet the learned man ought to have remembered that not everything should be considered lost merely because it still lies hidden from antiquity. Indeed, we have now happily drawn this letter of Alcuin from a very ancient manuscript codex of Salzburg [Col. 0314C], and, having faithfully transcribed it, have placed it above his seven books Against Felix as his first attempt to bring about Felix’s conversion.

### XXVIII. Felix had already written something in defense of his error before receiving this letter of Alcuin

From this letter of Alcuin to Felix we learn that this bishop of Urgell had already written certain things that were sound and true, and that at that time he had gone astray only in the name of adoption. “Very many things,” says Alcuin, no. 5, “in your writings are found to be sound and true; take care not to dissent from the understanding of the holy Fathers in this one matter of the name ‘adoption.’”

I believe that those writings were none other than his response to Elipandus, who had wished to learn from him what he thought about Christ’s adoption as the Son of God, together with the books written to that same man, in which Felix took the greatest pains to defend the perversity of his opinion, as Einhard relates in the *Annals* attributed to him under the year 792; or else the letter that Alcuin undertook to refute in the little book which he sent through the blessed Benedict [Col. 0314D] to the monks of Gothia. We shall say something about this below, no. 36.

For the rest, Felix’s writings listed in the *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 431, are later than this letter of Alcuin to Felix, as will become clear in the course of this dissertation. Thus, in the writings that Alcuin had then read, nothing contrary to Catholic truth was contained except the name “adoption,” which Felix attributed to Christ contrary to the understanding of the holy Fathers. Afterwards, however, he introduced several other heresies and blasphemies into his little book, which he set against this letter of Alcuin. “When I ran through a few pages of this little book,” says Alcuin in Letter 83, “I found worse heresies, or greater blasphemies, than I had previously read in his writings.”

Leo III confirms the same thing in almost the same words in excerpts from the proceedings of the Roman Council of 799, where we read: “And, as it seemed to us, we found there worse heresies or greater blasphemies than we had ever before heard in his writings or statements.” And a little [Col. 0315A] farther on: “As a dog has returned to his vomit—Felix, as you have heard, through his blasphemous little book, which he sent to the venerable man Albinus, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin—he has descended into worse barking than before.” The same is also sufficiently clear from various passages of Alcuin’s books Against Felix and from his letter to Elipandus.

### XXIX. He answers Alcuin’s letter at length, but not before the Council of Frankfurt

After Felix had received this letter from Alcuin, although it was written with great moderation and more as a stimulus of charity than of contention, he nevertheless “soon endeavored to send him a little book not compressed into the brevity of a letter, but extended at length in a continuous sequence of discourse,” as Alcuin writes at the beginning of Book I Against Felix; or, as he expresses it elsewhere, in Book I Against Elipandus: “He tried to answer not with the brevity of a letter, but with the length of a little book.” Learned men are uncertain about the year in which Felix published that little book. What seems more probable to us we shall present below, no. 36. Meanwhile, [Col. 0315B] against D. Walch, in the place cited, p. 129, it is enough to observe that Felix’s little book did not reach Alcuin before the Council of Frankfurt in 794; otherwise he would undoubtedly have presented it to the Fathers assembled there, just as he later caused it to be circulated by King Charles among the Roman pontiff and certain bishops.

### XXX. Around the year 794, Elipandus and the bishops allied with him send letters to King Charles and to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and Austrasia

In the year 794, or around the end of the preceding year, Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain who adhered to him—having presumably been informed by Felix, who had returned to their region, of everything that had been done at Rome and Regensburg against their position—sent letters to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and Austrasia. They added special letters to the most Christian king himself, Charles, in which they disclosed their profession of faith and attempted to explain their doctrine. They denounced the blessed Beatus as the author of heresy and worse than all earlier heretics, and accused him in addition of abominable crimes. [Col. 0315C] They solemnly adjured King Charles, in the name of everything sacred, to sit as judge himself and to pronounce an equitable judgment between Felix, the defender of their party—whom they praised as steadfast in God’s service from the beginning of his life—and those who slandered Beatus as sacrilegious and fattened by carnal vice. They urged him to abolish from his kingdom Beatus’s doctrine, which they opposed to their own, and to restore Felix to his former honor.

Finally, they did not shrink from charging the most just and most Christian king openly, and with the grossest slander based on mere rumor, with overcoming his enemies more by the terror of his power than by justice, and with denying, in the manner of the pagans, that Christ is the Son of God the Father. This, indeed, is the custom of heretics: when they know very well that their cause is wavering, they try to strengthen it by slanders and lies, and thus impose it upon the ignorant populace—even upon rulers themselves.

### XXXI. These recently discovered letters are now published for the first time

[Col. 0315D] This is a brief synopsis of those letters, which for a long time eluded the eager eyes of scholars. We can now satisfy their curiosity, and shall present the letters below in Appendix II, where we shall also recount the occasion and the means by which they came into our possession. Here we note only one point that will be useful elsewhere: in these letters the style of the Spanish bishops is directed exclusively against the abbot Beatus, with no mention of Alcuin. This provides a fairly clear indication that, at the time when those bishops’ letters were written to the bishops of Gaul and to Charlemagne, they had no knowledge either of Alcuin’s exhortatory letter to Felix, of his other letter to Elipandus, or of any other writing of Alcuin concerning this controversy. Had they known of those writings, they would certainly not have left them entirely untouched.

### XXXII. In response to those Spanish complaints, King Charles caused a council to assemble at Frankfurt in 794, summoning bishops from every direction
