After receiving these letters from Spain, King Charles devoted his efforts to providing a remedy for their complaints [Col. 0316A], so that a new council of bishops, Catholic Fathers, and teachers might be assembled in his kingdom. “Therefore,” as he himself says in his responses to the Spaniards below in Appendix II, no. 5, “he ordered a synodal council of the holy Fathers to be assembled from all the churches under his authority” (in the year 794, as all the historical records of that period testify); “but above all he sent his messengers three and four times to the most blessed pontiff of the Apostolic See, Adrian, wishing to learn what the holy Roman Church, instructed by the apostolic traditions, might wish to answer concerning this inquiry. He also summoned certain men skilled in ecclesiastical discipline from the regions of Britain.”

The place at which the assembly was convened was the famous city of Frankfurt, still situated on the Main, where King Charles celebrated Easter that year and where the kingdom’s assemblies were also to be held. That this meeting took place at the beginning of summer is testified by the *Annals* bearing Einhard’s name [Col. 0316B], and indeed before the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, as D. Mansi proves in vol. XIII of the latest edition of the *Councils*, p. 860. The ancient annalists and all the records then published unanimously testify to the year, place, and purpose of this Council of Frankfurt.

### XXXIII. Thomas Reinesius’s doubt concerning this council is answered

It is surprising that Thomas Reinesius, in a letter to Johann Tobias Maius (published as Letter 251 among the letters of distinguished men from the library of Marquard Gude, edited by Peter Burmann in Utrecht in 1697, p. 312), should object that Paulinus says that Elipandus’s letter to Charles was examined and scrutinized at the council, while not naming the place where the council was held; that Alcuin nowhere mentions this synod, nor does the author of his *Life*, nor Elipandus or Felix themselves.

But even if these points were true, they should in no way render suspect the testimony of so many witnesses, who attest the same matter in words that are by no means obscure. The silence [Col. 0316C] of the author of Alcuin’s *Life* is not decisive, because, as he himself admits in no. 13, he wrote only what everyone now knows. He could easily have omitted matters that did not pertain specifically to Alcuin, such as his presence at the Council of Frankfurt.

Elipandus sent to the king and the bishops the letter that had been examined at Frankfurt, although he did not know to what place they were to be summoned. In his other letters to Alcuin and Felix, however, he prudently refrained from mentioning that council, at which his errors had been condemned. Moreover, Alcuin would have appealed in vain to the Council of Frankfurt in his books Against Felix and Elipandus, since they did not acknowledge its authority and, indeed, later continued to cling to their errors while despising the council.

Finally, as regards Paulinus of Aquileia, the same explanation applies to his silence as to Alcuin’s. Furthermore, Reinesius seems either not to have known or not to have read the brief preface prefixed to Paulinus’s little book, which was produced and approved at the Council of Frankfurt. There [Col. 0316D] the council is explicitly named as having been held because of Elipandus:

“Here begins the sacred syllabus, salutarily composed in Catholic style, issued at the council held in the suburbs of Mainz, in the celebrated place called Frankfurt. It therefore pleased the holy council that this little book, concerning the cause of the faith, should be sent to the provinces of Gaul and Spain, and especially to Elipandus, and so forth.”

No one should suppose that this title was perhaps added later by some ignorant person, for it is found in the very ancient and excellently preserved manuscript codex of our monastery of St. Emmeram, written around the sixteenth year of the ninth century.

### XXXIV. Not only Alcuin but also other Britons, invited by the king, attended this council, contrary to D. Walch’s view

Alcuin too is believed to have attended this assembly at Frankfurt, as seems possible to infer from its final canon. For King Charles “admonished”—for that is how the canon reads in Baluze, vol. I of the *Capitularies*, p. 270—“that the holy synod itself should deign to receive Alcuin, who was certainly present, into its fellowship, or in its prayers, because he was a man learned in ecclesiastical teachings [Col. 0317A]. Accordingly, the whole synod, in accordance with the king’s admonition, agreed and received him into their fellowship, or in their prayers.”

Because of these words, the most learned Walch, in the frequently cited *History of the Adoptionists*, chap. 2, no. 28, p. 164, inclines to the opinion that “Alcuin was perhaps the only Englishman among the members of the council, and that they hesitated to admit him to their number because he was neither German, nor Gaul, nor Italian, and that Charles’s exhortation was therefore necessary.”

Yet it is clearly evident from the testimony of King Charles himself—which is surprising that D. Walch did not notice, although he cites it once and again in his own little book—that several Englishmen, or Britons, skilled in ecclesiastical discipline were not only invited to the aforesaid council but were also present at it. King Charles writes in his letter to the Spaniards, sent after the council had ended [Col. 0317B], below in Appendix II, no. 5, that he had “summoned several men skilled in ecclesiastical discipline from the regions of Britain.” He also asserts that they took part in the decisions made against the Spanish letters:

“The third little book,” he says in the same place, no. 8, “contains the faith of the orthodox holy Fathers, bishops, and venerable men who serve God in worthy offices in the regions of Germany, Gaul, Aquitaine, and BRITAIN, and so forth.”

D. Walch rightly interprets this as referring to transmarine Britain, that most fortunate island of Europe, following Mabillon in vol. II of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 311, no. 30; nor does he believe that anyone has understood it otherwise. Alcuin therefore did not need the king’s commendation because he was neither German, nor Gaul, nor Italian.

I therefore believe that Charles commended Alcuin to the assembled Fathers because, during that synod, they had sufficiently experienced his learning in divine and ecclesiastical matters, so that they might consider him worthy of their fellowship and regard him as a fellow-countryman, since he was to be retained permanently thereafter in the king’s realm [Col. 0317C]. Hence that admonition, or commendation, is placed last among the council’s decrees. It signifies quite clearly that, although Alcuin was foreign by nation, once the synod had ended he was received into fellowship by the Germans, Gauls, and Italians not merely for that occasion but also for future ecclesiastical affairs.

### XXXV. The blessed Benedict of Aniane also attended, together with the abbots and monks of Gothia

Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, also attended this Council of Frankfurt, together with the other abbots and religious monks of Gothia, as the ancient *Annals of the Franks*, published in vol. V of Martène and Durand’s *Collection of Ancient Monuments*, p. 902, testify in these words:

“Among them [the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt] was also the venerable and most holy abbot Benedict, who is called Vitiza, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, from the regions of Gothia, together with the religious monks Bede and Ardo, who is also called Smaragdus, and all their brothers and disciples. These are Ingeila, Aimo, [Col. 0317D] Rabanus, and Georgius, with the other brothers.”

On this occasion, I think, Alcuin formed a close association and friendship with the same blessed Benedict, which was afterward continued through their mutual exchange of letters, as is recorded in the *Life of Saint Benedict the Abbot* in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fourth century, part I, p. 203, no. 36.

### XXXVI. Benedict, returning to his own people, carries to the monks of Gothia Alcuin’s little book, by which they may be fortified against the Spanish errors; it is now published for the first time

After the synod had ended, unless my conjecture deceives me, when the blessed Benedict was about to return to his homeland with the other bishops and monks of Gothia, or Septimania, Alcuin, grieving with the monks of that province over the affliction arising from the unhappy schism and fearing for their danger from the nearby poison of heresy, gathered into a brief little book arguments by which they could defend themselves against the heretics. He entrusted this book to the aforementioned blessed Benedict to [Col. 0318A] carry to them. It is the book of which Alcuin speaks in his letter to the abbots and brothers of Gothia, sent in the year 800 and numbered 132:

“This can be demonstrated by many evangelical testimonies” (namely, that Christ is the proper Son of God, not an adoptive son), “as has been done in part in the little book that we sent to you through the blessed Benedict, for your consolation and the confirmation of the faith.”

This little book, long sought and considered entirely lost, remained so until the most distinguished D. Pietro Francesco Foggini discovered it in the Vatican-Palatine Library, codex 290, a manuscript more than eight hundred years old, and, through the generosity of the eminent Cardinal Passionei of the Holy Roman Church, shared it with me. I have related the matter more fully in the preliminary notice to the same little work, placed before the seven books Against Felix.

I suspect that this is the very book with which Alcuin answered one of Felix’s letters—perhaps one written to Elipandus, in which certain sound and true statements may have been contained; see [Col. 0318B] above, no. 28—and which he himself mentions in Book II Against Felix, no. 11, where he says:

“Concerning his doctrine of adoption, we have spoken more fully against the same Felix in another little book, answering [perhaps read: ‘a certain’] his letter which he composed on this very subject. There are found there many testimonies of the holy Fathers, from which anyone who reads and considers the matter with a pious mind will be able to understand most clearly that Christ is truly God’s Son in both natures, while we are adoptive sons through him, by whose grace we have been saved.”

These words certainly agree with the aforesaid little book, which is composed entirely of testimonies gathered from the holy Fathers.

### XXXVII. In what year was that little book written?

When I said shortly above that this little book was written after the Council of Frankfurt had ended and entrusted to the abbot Saint Benedict as he departed for his homeland, I did not intend to assign it so firmly to the year 794 that it could not have occurred in a later year. Benedict often afterward visited Alcuin even for the sake of counsel, as the author of his *Life* testifies in no. 17:

“The venerable man Benedict also often hastened from the regions of Gothia to obtain counsel for his own salvation and that of his people.”

Nevertheless, [Col. 0318C] it must be maintained that this little book was written by Alcuin before he received Felix’s response to his exhortatory letter. For the letter of Felix to which Alcuin replied in the little book sent through the blessed Benedict of Aniane to the abbots and monks of Gothia is different from, and earlier than, the other letter of Felix, whose refutation Alcuin was still pursuing when he wrote Letter 132 to those same abbots and monks. I ask the reader to consider what we shall say below, no. 40, concerning the year in which Felix’s later letter to Alcuin was sent.

### XXXVIII. Felix, summoned to the Council of Frankfurt together with other bishops, did not appear

There can be no doubt that Bishop Felix of Urgell, since he was situated within the dominion [Col. 0318D] of Charles, king of the Franks, was summoned to that Council of Frankfurt. “We ordered,” says the king in the frequently cited letter to the Spaniards, below in Appendix II, no. 5, “a synodal council of the holy Fathers to be assembled from all the churches everywhere under our authority.”

The attendance of the bishops of Gothia and Galicia—provinces of Spain subject to Charles, within which the city of Urgell was situated—is also testified by the *Annals of Moissac*, in the royal codex, published in Bouquet, *Writers of the History of Gaul*, vol. V, p. 47, note. Why, then, would Charles have wished to pass over Felix, whose case was moreover at issue? I do not see.

Yet the silence of the writings on this matter—though it is a matter worth mentioning—persuades us that Felix did not appear on this occasion. The heretic, already terrified at Regensburg and Rome, evidently shrank from a new judgment convened to put to death the heresy that he had treacherously swallowed again.

### XXXIX. After that council ended, another was convened at Rome in the same year on the same matter, from which Pope Adrian’s letter to the Spaniards proceeded

Before we leave the proceedings of the Council of Frankfurt, we must mention [Col. 0319A] the Roman Council of the same year, 794, which was held to confirm the Frankfurt synod. At it Pope Adrian’s letter to the bishops of Spain and Galicia was issued. Sent to Charlemagne, it was afterward forwarded by him to those same bishops, and it is customarily prefixed to the acts of that council, evidently out of reverence for the supreme see.

Until now, everyone has assigned the publication of this letter to another Roman council of the year 792, at which Felix is thought to have been condemned. D. Mansi has shown very convincingly that they were mistaken in the latest Florentine edition of the *Councils*, vol. XIII, p. 859, on the basis of the *Annals of Moissac*, edited by Fathers Martène and Durand in vol. V of the *Collection of Ancient Monuments*, p. 904. There [Col. 0319B] we read:

“It pleased the universal council [of Frankfurt] that, out of reverence for the holy apostolic Adrian, pope of the city of Rome, the writings” (which had evidently been issued there) “should be sent, with every privilege of jurisdiction reserved to the supreme pontiff” (the Italian bishops also used these words in the sacred syllabus near its conclusion); “and that the aforesaid pope, with a council of bishops of the whole Church convened again, should likewise condemn Elipandus and Felix, arch-heretics of all perfidy, and their followers, as the holy council” (of Frankfurt) “had done. The aforesaid pope also sent a consolatory letter to all the bishops and churches in the regions of Spain and Galicia; whoever reads and believes it will find it sufficiently filled throughout, from the New and Old Testaments, for advancing along the path of faith.”

But it is now time to continue the remaining sequence of events begun above in no. 29.

### XL. In what year Felix’s response reached Alcuin

Felix soon began to consider what answer he should make to the exhortatory letter he had received from Alcuin. Yet he did not send the little book by which he tried briefly to weaken Alcuin’s arguments directed against him and to defend his own error; Alcuin scarcely received it before the year 799 [Col. 0319C]. For in his letter to Bishop Aquila, or Arno, written in the year 800—if our conjecture does not deceive us—and numbered 159, Alcuin expressly says that Felix sent his little book to him in the preceding year. See the notes to that letter.

To conceal nothing, however, at the beginning of Book I Against Felix Alcuin speaks in such a way that one might think Felix delayed not at all in answering. “Felix,” he says, “soon endeavored to send us a little book.” Yet that word “soon” seems to signify nothing other than that Felix immediately undertook the effort to reply, not that the little book itself was sent at once: “He soon endeavored to send it,” he says. The following events will make this clearer.

### XLI. Felix first submitted his little book to Elipandus for examination, and sent it not to Alcuin but to King Charles

It seems very probable to me that Felix did not wish to publish his little book, or his responses to Alcuin’s letter [Col. 0319D], before they had been read and approved by Elipandus and the others who adhered to him; this may also have been the cause of the delayed publication. I believe that Elipandus had this little book in mind when he wrote to Felix in these words:

“I sent your letter to the brethren at Córdoba, who think rightly about God. But I sent it to be reread by that heresiarch himself, Albinus’s master [read: ‘master’], Antiphrasius Beatus [read: ‘Antiphrasius Beatus’]. But send that writing to your faithful, glorious prince, to the king himself, before it comes to that son of perdition, Albinus, who does not believe in the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God.”

Felix therefore gave his little book against Alcuin to Elipandus to be read and approved. Elipandus, for the same purpose, sent it to the brothers at Córdoba and also to the abbot Beatus—not with the same intention, but in order to criticize the man whom he calls a heresiarch, or, as he flatteringly imagined, to teach him better things. At the same time, he advised Felix to send the writing not to his adversary Albinus himself [Col. 0320A] but to his own king, Charles, whom he trusted would be more equitable.

I infer that Felix followed this advice of Elipandus from Alcuin’s letter prefixed to his seven books Against Felix. There Alcuin writes that Felix sent his little book to the royal authority:

“Your authority, which must be despised by no one, has entrusted to our devotion the task of answering the little book which a certain bishop Felix sent against us to your authority.”

### XLII. King Charles entrusted Alcuin with the refutation of Felix’s little book

King Charles therefore sent the little book received from Felix to Alcuin, as we have learned from the passage just cited, with an order that he should answer the book and write against the new inventions of heretical depravity. But the humble man, distrustful of his own strength, appeals to the king in Letter 83:

“I alone,” he says, “am not sufficient to answer. Let your holy piety provide suitable assistants for this task, so difficult and so [Col. 0320B] necessary, so that this impious heresy may be completely extinguished before it spreads more widely throughout the world of the Christian empire, which divine piety has entrusted to you and your sons to rule and govern.”

He then earnestly exhorts the king: “Rise,” he says, “man chosen by God; rise, son of God; rise, soldier of Christ, and defend the bride of the Lord your God, and so forth.”

Moved by these admonitions and by consideration of the new danger threatening the Church through the aforesaid little book, Charles accepted Alcuin’s advice and promised that he would take care of the matter—namely, of appointing coadjutors who would contribute their efforts to refuting the heresy.

### XLIII. He gave him Pope Leo and Paulinus as assistants

Accordingly, in another letter to the king, Alcuin suggested those whom he judged suitable for this contest: Leo, then pontiff of the Roman See—not Adrian, as many believe, as we shall soon demonstrate—Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, and the bishops Richbod of Trier and Theodulf of Orléans [Col. 0320C].

Thus Alcuin writes to the king in Letter 84:

“I am very pleased that your most holy will and devotion has taken care of answering the little book of the unhappy man, not a teacher but a subverter, in defense of the Catholic faith. But I beg you to send a copy of that little book to the apostolic lord, and another to the patriarch Paulinus, and likewise to Richbod and Bishop Theodulf, teachers and masters, so that each may answer on his own behalf.”

The king followed this advice of Alcuin as well, sending a copy of Felix’s little book to Leo, the Roman pontiff, and another to Paulinus of Aquileia.

As regards Leo, this is established partly by the Roman Council held around the beginning of the year 799, on April 25, when the most holy pontiff was blinded by the Romans. That council was held against “the blasphemous little book which Felix sent to the venerable man Albinus, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin,” as is recorded in the second session of that council. It is established partly by Felix’s confession sent to the people of Urgell, where he says:

“A synod was recently convened at Rome [Col. 0320D] against my letter, which I had written some time ago to the venerable man Albinus, abbot of the Church of Tours.”

I have no doubt that Paulinus also received the aforesaid book from the king for the refutation of its errors. Certainly Paulinus himself, when he completed his books Against Felix and sent them to the king, declares in his dedicatory letter that he undertook the labor at the king’s command:

“Therefore, prompted by the most salutary commands of your venerable letters, I do not refuse to write, in whatever style, for the cause of the faith against the objections of pestilential and perverse invention.”

Nor do I see any other occasion on which Paulinus, who had already vigorously completed his task at the Council of Frankfurt in defense of Catholic doctrine, could have been summoned to a new battle, except on the occasion of that little book of Felix set against Alcuin.

Paulinus also wished his books to be sent by the king to Alcuin, since he did not have sufficient leisure to send them to him himself in a single volume. For in a fragment of a letter published at the end of Paulinus’s third book by Madrisius, p. 168 [Col. 0321A], he asks the king that this “little gift”—namely, the three books mentioned above—“be delivered into the hands of the most reverend man, most learned and distinguished in divine matters, Albinus, that eminent champion of religion and your foremost orator.”

Paulinus certainly wanted this, not because he believed Alcuin needed his work for his own defense, “but so that it might be understood more clearly,” he says in the same place, “how the sweetness of the love that fills my heart with affection and friendship toward him, sweetly lulled to rest, may make sweet his breast.”

Alcuin in fact also received those books, undoubtedly by the king’s order, as Paulinus had requested. He praises them in Letter 108, to Aquila, which we shall discuss below, no. 47. Whether copies of the aforementioned book of Felix were also sent by the king to Richbod and Theodulf [Col. 0321B], as Alcuin had requested, and whether they took up their pens to refute it, is unknown. We have said in the notes to Letter 108 that Mabillon was deceived by a mutilated letter in his conjecture concerning Richbod.

### XLIV. Alcuin promptly devotes himself to the assigned work and completes it before the Council of Aachen

After Alcuin had informed the king whom he wished to have as assistants, he himself set about refuting Felix’s little book. At the same time, in the aforementioned Letter 84, he asked the king “to grant him time, so that he might quietly and diligently consider with his boys”—certainly his disciples, who were now also teachers of others—the Fathers’ understanding, and what each one had said concerning the propositions that the aforesaid subverter had set forth in his little book. “At the time fixed by you,” he says, “let the responses of each be brought to your authority.”

From the time he received Felix’s little book, he devoted himself to this labor with the utmost diligence, so that before he entered into public disputation with Felix at the Council of Aachen, he had already completed the entire work. He himself testifies to this in the letter prefixed to his books addressed to Charles, in these words [Col. 0321C]:

“For I had this little book present at the disputation that took place in your venerable presence with Felix.” [Col. 0321C]

### XLV. Alcuin disputes with Felix at the aforesaid council

The author of Alcuin’s *Life*, no. 13, also affirms that the same disputation lasted almost an entire week. “From the second,” he says, “until the seventh day of the week scarcely anything else was done.”

This cannot be understood except of the disputation held at the Council of Aachen in 799. At the preceding councils Felix and Alcuin never met: Felix was present at the Council of Regensburg and the Roman Council of 792, while Alcuin was absent; at the Council of Frankfurt in 794, Alcuin was present and Felix absent.

The disputation between them therefore took place at the Council of Aachen, which both attended, and to which both were summoned by the king for mutual debate, as the author of Alcuin’s *Life*, no. 13, writes:

“For King Charles summoned his teacher from Tours [Col. 0321D] and the wretched Felix, the supporter of this heresy, from the regions of Spain, and convened a great synod of bishops in the imperial palace at Aachen. Sitting among them himself, he ordered Felix, although strongly resisting, to engage in rational disputation with the most learned Albinus concerning the nature of the Son of God according to the flesh.”

Alcuin himself affirms the same thing in two letters. In one, Letter 91, to his own Aquila, or Archbishop Arno, he writes:

“By the middle of May, if God brings it to completion, I expect to be at the palace, as our lord the king has commanded us. And Felix, the defender of novelty, has sworn to come to the lord king to give an account of his faith. I, a native servant of the holy Church of God, must stand with you [that is, at the council], and I labor and speak with the unanimity of Christ’s priests in what they believe and proclaim; and for the children of the holy Church of God I shall open my mouth, and so forth.”

In the other letter to the same Aquila, Letter 159, he relates how that disputation proceeded [Col. 0322A]:

“With the heretic Felix,” he says, “we had a great contest in the presence of the lord king and the holy Fathers. But he, long hardened, consents to no authority except that of the follower of his own sect, believing himself wiser than everyone. Yet when divine clemency finally visited his heart, he confessed that he had been deceived by a false opinion and acknowledged that he firmly held the Catholic faith.”

XLVI. Alcuin published his books against Felix only later.—From what we have related thus far, it is indeed clear that Alcuin’s books against Felix had been completed, at least for the most part, before the aforementioned Council of Aachen. Nevertheless, we must believe that they were not published until after the council had ended and were first brought into public circulation in the following year. For this man, who distrusted his own expertise with the greatest humility, did not dare to release his writings publicly unless they had first been examined by several persons, submitted to their correction, and approved by the king himself. [Col. 0322B] Accordingly, after the disputation at Aachen had ended, he sent his books, revised once more by himself and arranged in proper order, to King Charles for examination and approval. For he writes in the letter that he attached to those books:

> “Since this little book has not yet been read through before your wisdom, nor approved by you, for whom it labored most intensely, I have judged that it should not be brought before the public ear. Now, however, let your authority decide what it wishes to be done with it. I ask only that it not in any way be rejected or brought into public circulation before it has been read through in its entirety and examined by your authority among persons close to you.”

Here I should like attentive and devout readers to observe how cautiously the ancient Fathers who were truly Catholic acted when combating newly arising doctrines and establishing the doctrines of the faith, which cannot be new. They attributed almost nothing to their private studies or insights unless these agreed with the teaching of the Fathers and of the Church. Would that this had always been observed by everyone in the Church.

XLVII. Only after obtaining the approval of the king and the bishops.—[Col. 0322C] King Charles himself examined these books, as Alcuin desired, and submitted them to the examination of others. This required some considerable delay, so that they could not be returned to Alcuin as quickly as he wished. He complains somewhat of this delay in Letter 100, written to the king “after the errors of the schisms had been quieted,” that is, after the Council of Aachen:

> “Thus you wished to summon the devotion of my littleness to a kind of inward battle. I willingly submitted to the toil of that contest, as may be recognized in the little book that I recently sent to your piety, although I have not yet learned that the same text of the little book has been confirmed by the seal of your authority; and I think this was caused either by the slowness of the bearer or by the shortness of time.”

He was still awaiting this approval of the king and the bishops when, in the year 800, he wrote Letter 132 to the abbots and monks of Gothia. He promises them that he will send his little book against Felix “after it has,” as he says, “been read and approved by [Col. 0322D] our bishops and by our lord the king.”

XLVIII. And first, around the beginning of the year 800.—After, therefore, Alcuin’s entire work had long been under review, for at least a month or two, King Charles returned it to Alcuin after the beginning of the year 800 so that he could correct certain errors that the king had ordered to be marked. These did not concern Catholic meaning or doctrine, but letters and punctuation, which had slipped in contrary to the rules of grammar through the speed of dictation or writing. Alcuin himself explains this in Letter 101:

> “We give thanks that you ordered the errors in that [little book] to be marked and sent it back for correction … Yet you did somewhat less than the full duty of charity required, since you likewise did not wish to mark passages whose meaning was not expressed learnedly or written in a Catholic manner … But where the letters or punctuation do not proceed as scholastically as the order and rule of the grammatical art require, this is often caused by the speed of the mind, when the reader’s intention hastens [Col. 0323A] ahead of the work of the eyes. Nor can I, exhausted by pain in my head, examine what suddenly flies from the mouth of the dictator.”

I think that this letter was written to the king in the year mentioned above, while he was still staying at Aachen. He finally departed from there in mid-March to inspect the shores of the Ocean and prepare a fleet against the pirates, as is recorded in the Loiselian Annals, in Einhard’s Annals, and in others for that same year.

XLIX. When all these matters have been duly considered, we confidently believe that we have clearly demonstrated: (1) that Felix’s little book, opposed to Alcuin’s charitable letter, reached Alcuin only around the beginning of the year 799, nos. 36 and 37; (2) that this same little book was sent by King Charles, in accordance with Alcuin’s wish, not to Hadrian I, as had hitherto been believed, but to Leo III, who was then exercising the apostolic office, no. 38; (3) that Alcuin completed his books against the aforesaid little book within the walls of his chamber before the Council of Aachen, no. 39; and (4) that he did not publish them until the following year, 800, after receiving royal [Col. 0323B] and episcopal approval.

But let us now continue with what happened afterward in the case of Felix.

L. King Charles, fearing Felix’s steadfastness, entrusts him to the custody of Laidrad, bishop of Lyons.—At the Council of Aachen Felix appeared to have been overcome by the force of the arguments and convicted by the authority of the holy Fathers, and he seemed seriously to detest his error and submit to the council’s decrees. Since, however, he had already several times elsewhere violated his pledged faith, the king, lest the Catholic cause should through Felix’s inconstancy be thrown into still more dangerous disturbances, did not permit him to return to Urgell. Instead, he ordered that Felix be handed over to one of the bishops of his kingdom, by whom he could be kept in secure custody.

At first he intended to give Felix for safekeeping and correction to Riculf, archbishop of Mainz, while entrusting Felix’s presbyter—who had proved worse than his master—to the care of Arno of Salzburg. Later, however, it seemed and was arranged otherwise: Felix was entrusted [Col. 0323C] to the care of Laidrad, bishop of Lyons, who was to keep him and test whether what he claimed to have believed was true, “and whether he was willing through his letters to condemn his former error,” as Alcuin reports to his own Aquila in Letter 159.

935

LI. In that place he composed and published his confession of faith.—Felix, therefore, while under Laidrad’s custody and, without doubt, at his urging, as may be inferred from the words of Alcuin soon to be quoted, wrote the confession of faith that we presented above to the priests, clergy, and other faithful of his diocese.

First, he declares that at the Council of Aachen he had been convicted not by any coercion but by the authority of the holy Fathers and of the supreme see, and that he had returned to the universal Church not hypocritically, as formerly, but with true belief of heart and confession of mouth. Second, he explains the Catholic doctrine that he now embraces after rejecting his former errors, and for the first time expressly condemns Nestorius, urging his own people to do the same. Third, [Col. 0323D] he confirms this profession by the opinions of certain holy Fathers.

LII. Alcuin boasts of this confession and conversion of Felix.—After this confession had been published, no one any longer doubted Felix’s faith and sincerity. Alcuin repeatedly boasts of his conversion, which he considered chiefly his own achievement, and proposes it as an example for Elipandus to follow.

“I,” he says in Book I *Against Elipandus*, no. 7, “by God’s mercy made Felix, formerly a partner in your error, a Catholic.”

A little later he says:

> “That Felix whom you assert to be outstanding in charity, chaste, and adorned with moral virtue, we have in the camp of Christ.”

Again, in no. 12, he writes of him:

> “Felix, formerly bound with you by the chains of your error, has now, by God’s mercy, been convicted through rational disputation … and has been brought back into the unanimity of Catholic peace. He whom you once possessed as though he were a shield of your unbelief, the Church now possesses as a powerful and sharp arrow, together with [Col. 0324A] desolating coals.”

In no. 16 he relates that Felix, after being rationally heard and truly convicted at the aforesaid Council of Aachen in the presence of the lord king, his nobles, and the bishops, “confessed the true faith, giving glory to God, and returned with his disciples to the peace of Catholic unanimity.” He urges Elipandus to follow Felix’s humility. Again, in Book IV, no. 5, he exhorts Elipandus and his followers in these words:

> “Follow, dearest ones, the example of your former Felix, now ours, who, having recognized the way of truth, was not ashamed to confess his ignorance of his error and to join himself through the Catholic faith to the unity of the Church of Christ.”

Alcuin, therefore, subsequently had no doubt whatever about the sincerity of Felix’s confession, especially because he experienced Felix returning to friendship with him and his hatred being changed into love. Thus he writes to his own Aquila in Letter 108, p. 36:

> “Felix has now been at Saint [Col. 0324B] Martin’s with our aforesaid son [Laidrad], and he loves me greatly; all the hatred that he had for me has been changed into the sweetness of charity.”

LIII. Yet this too was feigned, and Felix remained attached to his errors until his death, which is believed to have occurred in 818.—But, alas, the outcome showed that this friendship had been disguised and that his conversion had been feigned. While Laidrad and Alcuin were still alive, no report of Felix’s infidelity came to light. Only Agobard, who succeeded Laidrad in the see of Lyons, where Felix was being held in exile, reports in his book *Against Felix*, chapter 5, that Felix, while still alive, taught certain people that Christ, according to the flesh, had not known the tomb of Lazarus; that he had been ignorant of the day of judgment; that he had likewise been ignorant of what the disciples, as they went to Emmaus, were discussing with one another; and whether Christ was loved more by Peter than by the other disciples.

For this reason Agobard, who did not yet possess episcopal authority, once reproved Felix privately before his own companions, when Felix was trying to persuade them of [Col. 0324C] these errors, and admonished him to think more correctly.

That Felix remained attached to his former errors to the end of his life was revealed by a written note left by Felix himself, as Agobard likewise testifies in the passage cited, chapters 5, 6, and 9. Felix is believed to have died around the year 818. See Madrisius, p. 224, no. 77 (*Patrologia*, vol. XCIX, col. 586); *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 431.

LIV. Alcuin’s second struggle with Elipandus.—The second struggle that Alcuin undertook for Catholic truth was with Elipandus himself, archbishop of Toledo, the principal author or promoter of the error. The occasion of the contest was Alcuin’s letter to Elipandus and Elipandus’s reply to it; both letters are given above.

Before we proceed further in recounting this struggle, however, certain chronological questions that some people customarily raise concerning it must be resolved, so that the light of truth may shine more clearly once the clouds have been dispersed.

The first concerns the date [Col. 0324D] of the journey on which Laidrad, Nefridius, and Benedict, abbot of Aniane, went to Spain to bring Felix back and suppress his error. The second concerns the year in which Alcuin’s exhortatory letter to Elipandus and Elipandus’s reply to it were written. The third concerns the year in which Elipandus’s letter to Felix was written. We shall settle these matters briefly.

## DOUBT THE FIRST. CONCERNING THE TWO JOURNEYS OF LAIDRAD AND HIS COMPANIONS TO SPAIN.

LV. Laidrad was sent to Spain with his companions twice.—We are informed that Laidrad, bishop of Lyons, with certain companions—specifically Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne, and Benedict, abbot of Aniane—went twice, at the command of Charlemagne, into the regions of Spain then subject to the Franks, especially to Urgell. This is shown both by Felix’s own confession of the Catholic faith and by Alcuin’s letter written to those same [Col. 0325A] apostolic men as they were preparing to go to Spain again, that is, for a second time, as will soon become clear.

LVI. Once before the Council of Aachen in 799 and again after it had ended.—Felix mentions the first journey, which took place before the Council of Aachen in 799 and, as we are justified in believing, during that same year, at the beginning of his confession of faith:

> “After I had been brought into the presence of our lord, the most pious and glorious King Charles, and presented before him, we received from him permission—just as the venerable lord Laidrad, bishop, had promised us at Urgell—to present our opinions in his presence, before the bishops whom the decree of our glorious prince had caused to assemble at Aachen …”

From this we understand that Laidrad had been at Urgell before the celebration of the aforesaid council, 936 and had moved Felix so that he would not fear appearing at that council. The same is also clear from the words [Col. 0325B] of Alcuin, who writes to Laidrad and his companions:

> “By the support of divine mercy you formerly strove to disperse this cloudy sect of impiety with the clear light of truth, and, with Christ granting it, you have also accomplished a large part of the work of preaching that you began.”

Felix, as I interpret it, had thereby been brought to the point “that in the presence of the lord king and his nobles or priests … giving glory to God and confessing the true faith, he returned with his disciples, who were then present [namely, at the Council of Aachen], to the peace of Catholic unanimity,” as Alcuin says in Book I *Against Elipandus*, no. 16.

Alcuin must be understood as referring to the second journey when, in the same letter to Laidrad and the others, mentioned above, he writes:

> “We have heard that, at the command of the glorious prince and most devoted king Charles, you are going again to undertake the work of that most pious preaching.”

Alcuin wrote this after Felix had just returned at Aachen to Catholic unity and, while under Laidrad’s custody, had published his confession of faith (see above, no. [Col. 0325C] 51). For Alcuin attached this confession to his books against Elipandus, which he sent to Laidrad and his companions as they were preparing to depart again, or for the second time, for Spain. This is stated in another letter to them, given above, where he calls the confession the letter of Felix’s conversion.

This second journey, therefore, was undertaken after the Council of Aachen had ended shortly before the Christmas holidays of 799, and not before the year 800. In this view we are joined by the celebrated scholars Charles Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, vol. VI, p. 693; Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 335; Pagius, *Criticism of Baronius*, vol. III, p. 311; and others.

LVII. The contrary opinion of the distinguished D. Madrisius is refuted.—The distinguished D. Madrisius, in his historical dissertation on the heresy of Felix and Elipandus, *Works of Saint Paulinus*, nos. 62 and following, takes an entirely different view. He does indeed admit, in nos. 64 and 65, that Laidrad went to Spain twice. But he thinks that the first journey was the one [Col. 0325D] on which Alcuin sent that little book through Benedict of Aniane to the abbots and monks of Gothia in the year 797 or the following year, “for their consolation and the confirmation of the Catholic faith,” as we discussed above, no. 36.

The learned man likewise believes that the second journey preceded the Council of Aachen in 799, and he does not allow that any other journey to Spain was undertaken by Laidrad and his companions after that year. D. Walch, *History of Adoptionism*, chapter 2, section I, no. 40, attributes a greater appearance of truth to this opinion of Madrisius than to the common opinion. But when the arguments by which Madrisius hopes to establish his singular view are examined, they will appear to be of little weight.

LVIII. D. Madrisius derives his first argument, in nos. 64 and 65, from Alcuin’s Letter 132 to the abbots and monks of Gothia. He believes that this letter was written in the year 797 or 798, at the time when Alcuin had in hand his larger work, namely [Col. 0326A] the seven books against Felix. In that letter Alcuin informs the Goths that he had previously sent them, through Benedict of Aniane, a little book that would serve them for consolation and confirmation of the Catholic faith.

From this D. Madrisius concludes that Benedict, accompanied, of course, by Laidrad and Nefridius, went to Spain at that time for the first time in connection with the Felix controversy, and brought that little book to the Goths:

> “The first journey,” says D. Madrisius in the cited work, no. 64 at the end, “took place before Alcuin published his books against Felix; and on that first occasion he sent through Abbot Benedict the little book that would be their consolation.”

Here, however, Madrisius assumes two things that do not seem proven to us. The first is that Alcuin already had the seven books against Felix in hand in the years 797 or 798. In fact, it is far more likely that Felix’s reply, which Alcuin refutes in the seven books, did not reach him [Col. 0326B] before the year 799, as we said above, no. 40.

The second assumption of Madrisius is equally unstable: namely, that the first embassy of Laidrad and his companions to Spain occurred when Alcuin gave Abbot Benedict what were, as it were, his first lines against the heresy of Adoptionism—or the little book against Felix’s heresy that we edited above—to carry to the monks of Gothia.

But Benedict of Aniane took part in the Council of Frankfurt, as we said above, no. 35. Afterward he was often and for long periods at court or near it because of various needs of the Church for which he was employed. When his business was concluded, he returned again to his own people in Septimania, without a royal commission. On these occasions Alcuin could have entrusted the aforesaid little book to Benedict, either when he was setting out on a journey or while he was remaining at home, so that he might carry it to the other abbots and monks of Gothia.

Nothing, therefore, can be concluded from the cited letter of Alcuin to the monks of Gothia concerning the date of the first embassy to Spain in the matter of the Felix controversy.

[Col. 0326C] LIX. The second argument by which D. Madrisius attempts to prove that the second journey of Laidrad and his companions likewise preceded the Council of Aachen in 799 is suggested in these words of no. 66:

> “Because a second journey to Urgell may appear superfluous after Felix’s conversion, for the sake of which it was to have been undertaken.”

The answer is easy. The second journey was undertaken not for Felix’s conversion but for the preaching of Catholic truth against the disturbances that Elipandus continued to cause. We learn this from Alcuin’s Letter 108 to Arno, in which he writes:

> “But something still remains to be done [although Felix has already been converted]. For a certain Elipandus, a bishop of the city of Toledo in name, not in dignity, remains in a condemned heresy. Yet let your affection know that our son Laidrad, your brother in the episcopate, has, by God’s gift, accomplished much in those regions, and continues to do so every day; etc.”

It was chiefly for this purpose, therefore, that Laidrad and his companions were sent to Spain a second time: [Col. 0326D] to bring Elipandus and his followers back to better things, or at least to cleanse or preserve from the poison of heretical depravity the province that was subject to Charles’s rule.

For this same purpose Alcuin gave them pious and necessary replies to the letter addressed to him by Elipandus—that is, the four books against Elipandus himself. Alcuin again teaches us this in the letter prefixed to those books, where he says:

> “Therefore 937 I undertook the labor of a few days, for the consolation of your most holy journey, so that you might have in your hands pious and entirely necessary replies to a certain letter addressed to me by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo,” etc.

LX. But the distinguished Madrisius thinks that the pious and necessary [Col. 0327A] replies of which Alcuin speaks there, and which he calls the labor of a few days, were a different work from the four books opposed to Elipandus, which were certainly written only after Felix’s conversion in the year 800.

> “We suspect,” he says in no. 66, “that Alcuin composed some brief writing over a few days—for example, a compendium and summary of the arguments and replies, by which he might satisfy, so to speak, the objections that arose ex tempore. For the four books, written expressly for this purpose, ought not to be called a work of a few days, since they could not have been completed by labor of only a few days.”

LXI. This suspicion of the distinguished man might not be considered entirely without plausibility, were it not evident from the context of the previously cited letter that the pious and necessary replies given to Laidrad and his companions as they were again setting out for Spain were the very four books written against Elipandus’s letter.

For at the beginning of that letter Alcuin continues:

> “I took care to answer those little letters of his madness in brief speech with two little books, refuting all his assertions and most perverse interpretations by means of the most truthful opinions of the holy Fathers. To those two little books I also added two others, written in plain speech, bearing witness to the truth of the Catholic faith concerning Christ [Col. 0327B] God and confirming it most abundantly with the testimonies of the holy Fathers. I think that your piety will rejoice in reading them, because I was glad to dedicate the whole work to your name, and I sent it first of all to you for examination and correction.”

There it is clear that what he had previously called pious and necessary replies, completed by the labor of a few days, were not some compendium or summary of arguments, but those very four little books that he opposed to Elipandus’s madness and gave to the envoys as a consolation for their journey to Spain, submitting them to their correction or approval.

Who can say in what sense Alcuin called those four books the labor of a few days? I think that Alcuin wished he had been permitted to devote more time to a work of such great importance than the impending journey of the envoys to Spain allowed him. For that reason the days that he was able to give to this labor seemed few to him—few, I say, not because [Col. 0327C] they were insufficient to accomplish what he actually accomplished, since he already had most of the arguments prepared against Felix, but because they were insufficient to polish and complete the work as he desired.

LXII. But the distinguished Madrisius still refuses to yield. He argues further, in no. 67, that even if those four books were included under the name of the replies sent to Laidrad and his companions, “it still has not been proved,” he says, “that the second departure of Laidrad and his companions took place in the year 800, in which year the books are said to have been published after Felix’s conversion. … Alcuin could therefore have sent them only a work outlined and sketched in its first lines, as it were, while Laidrad and his companions were departing, intending afterward to publish it, once it had been examined and approved—for he had submitted it to their examination and approval—at a more convenient time. This is what he did in the year 800, inserting, when he put the final hand [Col. 0327D] to the work, the fact that Felix’s conversion had already taken place, and dedicating the work to the aforesaid men by adding a recent preface, after the work had been completed with polished labor.”

LXIII. I am astonished that this learned man is looking for a knot in a rush. In both letters, or dedicatory prefaces, Alcuin submits his work to the examination and correction of Laidrad and his companions. In both he humbly confesses that, because of the haste with which he had to complete it, the work was imperfect.

In the second preface he says:

> “But you, dearest brothers, read through all these things with diligent devotion before you cause this series of writings to proceed into public circulation. For I dictated these things, whatever they may be, in the urgency caused by the haste of your journey, so that I did not have suitable time to read them over or correct them.”

From this it is clear that Alcuin did not append this second preface or letter to Laidrad and his companions to a work that had been revised a second time [Col. 0328A] and previously examined and approved, adding only at that point a mention of Felix’s conversion, as Madrisius supposed.

LXIV. Alcuin completed the four books against Elipandus in the year 800, when Laidrad and his companions were sent again to Spain.—“But why,” you ask, “did Alcuin prefix two prefaces to the same books?” I shall state what I think, and what I believe can be drawn from those two prefaces themselves.

In the first letter Alcuin speaks of his principal work, namely the four books that he composed against the errors of Elipandus. In the second, which should be regarded as an appendix to the first, he instructs Laidrad and his companions in what order the remaining writings belonging to the whole sequence of the controversy, which he had added in separate gatherings, should be arranged and combined with the principal work in the form of a single codex.

“It seemed fitting to me,” he says, “to place before this little work of ours”—namely, the four books [Col. 0328B] of which he had spoken in the first letter—“the letter that I formerly sent to Father Elipandus as a duty of charity,” etc.

And below:

> “Nor should it seem burdensome to you, before you leave the city, to order these gatherings to be bound and wrapped together and composed in the form of a single body, lest, if they are taken up separately, they perhaps be scattered among the hands of readers.”

There can therefore be no doubt that Alcuin completed the four books against Elipandus at the time when Laidrad and his companions were preparing to depart for Spain again, specifically in the year 800, after the Council of Aachen had ended—the council at which he compelled Felix to confess Catholic doctrine.

We have D. Basnage agreeing with this opinion in volume II of Canisius’s *Monuments*, p. 296, where he writes:

> “In this year 800 the Emperor Charles sent the bishops Laidrad and the others praised earlier; Alcuin entrusted his books against the bishop of Toledo to them, so that they might use them.”

LXV. Laidrad came to Tours with Felix.—Alcuin himself teaches us in Letters 87 and 92 that Laidrad came to Tours, to Saint Martin’s, together with Felix [Col. 0328C] around the time of the Lenten fast in the year 800, and that there he consulted with Alcuin about whether to continue his preaching in Spain or interrupt it because his bodily strength had been worn down.

In the first letter, written around Lent and before Easter, he warns Arno to write to him “what he wishes to entrust to Laidrad. For,” he says, “he scarcely lives if he will not see our faces as well. He has been very ill throughout the whole year, and, with his spirit weakened, he wishes to consult with us. He has accomplished many good things in those regions, glory to God! But he doubts whether it is better to labor in the ministry of preaching or to lead a quiet life.”

In the other letter, written later, after Laidrad had returned to Spain to continue his apostolic labors there, Alcuin tells Arno that Felix had been “at Saint Martin’s, with our aforesaid son,” namely Laidrad, concerning whose progress in those regions he was speaking there.

From these [Col. 0328D] passages I infer that Felix came with Laidrad, to whose care and custody the king had entrusted him at the Council of Aachen (see above, no. 50), to Tours and to Saint Martin’s, certainly in the company of Alcuin, who was returning from that council. Laidrad remained there for some time, perhaps because of an illness contracted through the labors of the preceding year and the long journey. Finally, once his strength had been restored, perhaps at the king’s insistence and Alcuin’s urging, or even stimulated by his own zeal, he went again to Spain around Easter of the year 800 or after Easter had ended, in order to complete his ministry of preaching.

## DOUBT THE SECOND. IN WHAT YEAR ALCUIN’S LETTER TO ELIPANDUS AND ELIPANDUS’S REPLY TO IT WERE WRITTEN.

LXVI. Alcuin wrote his exhortatory letter to Elipandus not before the Council of Frankfurt in 794, [Col. 0329A] nor immediately after it had ended, but in the year 799.—There are various scholarly opinions concerning the date of the exhortatory letter from Alcuin to Elipandus that we presented above. Some, such as D. Ceillier, *History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. XVIII, p. 307, no. 17, and D. Rivet, *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 312, no. 14, believe that it was written before the Council of Frankfurt in 794. They argue that Alcuin makes no mention in it of what was done at that synod against Elipandus’s errors.

D. Madrisius, by contrast, in his frequently cited historical dissertation on the heresy of Felix and Elipandus, nos. 51 and 52, thinks that the letter was written immediately after the Council of Frankfurt, which was celebrated at the beginning of summer, according to Einhard. Elipandus received it at the end of July, as is clear from his reply. See the beginning of Elipandus’s letter above.

LXVII. We cannot adopt either of these opinions. On the testimony of Alcuin himself, we are persuaded [Col. 0329B] that the exhortatory letter to Elipandus must be assigned to the year 799, in which, as we showed above in no. 56, Laidrad and his companions first went to Spain.

For in another letter to those envoys, which we said above could have been written only in the year 800, Alcuin reminds them that he had formerly entrusted to them a letter to be delivered to Elipandus—namely, the letter now under discussion, to which Elipandus afterward opposed his replies.

“It seemed fitting to me,” he says there, above, p. 862, “to place before this little work of ours”—the books against Elipandus—“the letter that I formerly sent to Father Elipandus as a duty of charity through your holy devotion,” etc.

Alcuin therefore wrote his letter to Elipandus neither before the Council of Frankfurt, as the Benedictine writers cited above believe, nor on the occasion provided by that council’s celebration, as D. Madrisius thought, but on the occasion of the journey that Laidrad and his companions were undertaking for the first time to Spain.

Perhaps Alcuin did not mention the Council of Frankfurt in his letter [Col. 0329C] because he wished to discover Elipandus’s own position in this controversy—namely, whether he truly agreed with the other Spanish bishops and with Felix—and to admonish him not to assent to the aforesaid error.

For this reason he did not wish in his letter to refute either Elipandus or the other bishops of Spain. While he wished to draw Elipandus, who surpassed the others in dignity, back from error by charity, he avoided provoking him further by attacking him. He therefore mentions Felix alone and briefly touches upon his errors. To do this he had no need of the authority of the Council of Frankfurt, which had been wholly occupied in refuting the error of the other Spanish bishops and had made no mention of Felix.

In any event, D. Ceillier’s reason for thinking that Alcuin’s letter was written before the Council of Frankfurt is not compelling. Just as Alcuin makes no mention in his letter of that council, so Elipandus in his letters to Charlemagne and the bishops [Col. 0329D] of Gaul does not mention Alcuin’s letter to him even once.

If, therefore, Alcuin’s silence could allow us to infer that his letter to Elipandus had been written before the aforesaid council, it would much more strongly allow us to infer from Elipandus’s silence that the letter had not been sent to Elipandus before that same council, or at least had not reached him. For Elipandus, together with his followers, would not have left it untouched in his letters; rather, he would have marked it with the same black mark that he used against the books of Beatus and Etherius.

But let us now apply our pen to the discussion of the third doubt.

## DOUBT THE THIRD. IN WHAT YEAR ELIPANDUS’S LETTER TO FELIX WAS WRITTEN.

LXVIII. The distinguished D. Madrisius argues that Elipandus’s letter to Felix was written toward the end of the year 792.—The letter that Elipandus wrote to Felix, bishop of Urgell, and that we presented above is assigned to the year [Col. 0330A] 799 by the celebrated scholars D. Antonius Pagius, in his *Critical Remarks on Baronius’s Annals* for that year, no. 16, and D. Jacobus Basnagius, in his historical observations on the Felixian heresy, *Treasury of Monuments*, vol. II, part I, p. 295 at the end. Most recently, the highly learned D. Gregory Majansius has joined them in the letter that we present in Appendix II. Neither of these men, however, explains sufficiently the arguments by which this opinion might be established.

The distinguished D. Madrisius, in the dissertation cited so frequently, nos. 36 and 68, argues that Elipandus wrote to Felix toward the end of the year 792 or the beginning of the following year, when Felix, after the Council of Regensburg, had been brought to Rome by Angilbert the abbot to be judged again by [939] the apostolic see.

The learned man places almost the sole foundation of this opinion, in the cited no. 68, in these words of Elipandus’s letter:

> “Certify me, you who have been placed in Rome.”

“Until it has been shown,” he says, “that Felix was in Rome in the year 799, to whom those words could [Col. 0330B] truthfully have been written, we must not depart from Elipandus’s perfectly clear words … Hence, since in the year 792 we have Felix brought to Rome by Abbot Angilbert, we cannot remove the letter from that year. For it is not established that Felix was in Rome in any other year.”

D. Walch, in preference to the opinion of Pagius and Basnage, praises this view of D. Madrisius in his *History of Adoptionism*, chapter 2, section I, no. 16, though he prefers to leave the matter doubtful. “For,” he says, “Madrisius’s opinion is not without difficulty. There is reason to doubt that Alcuin was fighting against Elipandus at that time.”

But it seems to us that D. Madrisius’s opinion is not merely difficult; it also rests upon a weak foundation, as we shall now show.

### LXIX. Its principal foundation is refuted, and it is demonstrated that that letter was written around November 799

The sole foundation, then, as we have said, which D. Madrisius took up was found in the cited words of Elipandus’s letter: “Inform me, you who are placed in Rome.” But these words certainly convey no suitable meaning [Col. 0330C], an evident indication that an error lies in them. For if those words were to be understood as D. Madrisius thinks—“You who now reside in Rome, inform me”—Elipandus would have had to add what he wished to be informed about; for the words cited stand between sentences with which they are in no way connected. It would have been easy, however, for some inept or inattentive copyist, the transcriber of the letter, whose negligence he reveals elsewhere more than once, to have written *qui* in place of *quod* or *si*. It should therefore be read, so that the meaning emerges: “Inform me, whether or if you are placed in Rome”; that is, “Let me know whether, if you have perhaps been brought to Rome, you are still residing there.”

The rumor had evidently reached Elipandus—or perhaps he had learned the matter itself from Felix by letter—that, by order of King Charles, Felix had again been summoned to the royal palace to render an account of his faith or perfidy. Elipandus therefore believed that Felix, just as after the Council of Regensburg, was now again to be brought to Rome and judged once more by the apostolic [Col. 0330D] see. Elipandus consequently wished to be informed about that event and about what was being done with Felix in Rome. This interpretation of the obscure and corrupted text of Elipandus’s letter is certainly not without plausibility; and therefore it is wrongly inferred from that corrupt text that Elipandus’s letter to Felix must be assigned to the year 792.

### LXX. The principal and sole foundation of D. Madrisius’s opinion having therefore tottered, we must adhere to better, indeed certain, arguments

These arguments are drawn from that very letter and from Alcuin’s own words, by which it is unmistakably proved that Elipandus wrote to Felix after the month of August, or perhaps around November, of the year 799.

### LXXI. First argument

The first argument for this position is drawn from the cited letter of Elipandus, in which he tells Felix that, after replying in the following month of August to a certain writing of Felix’s which he had received in July, and after that reply had accidentally been consumed by fire [Col. 0331A], he resumed his labor for forty days and thus wrote around November “to that heretic, the pitch-black Albinus, as much as,” he says, “I was able to write for his confusion.”

This writing of Elipandus against Alcuin was unquestionably that letter in which he attempts to answer Alcuin’s exhortatory letter brought to Spain by Laidradus in the year 799 (above, nos. 65 and 66). For no document or testimony informs us that Elipandus engaged Alcuin in controversy in any other writing. Elipandus therefore could not have mentioned this letter, first written in the year just specified, in his letter to Felix if that letter had already been composed fully seven years earlier, in 792, as Madrisius prefers to believe. Elipandus consequently wrote that letter to Felix in the same year in which he wrote against Alcuin’s exhortatory letter—that is, in the year 799.

### LXXII. Second argument

A second argument for our position is supplied by Alcuin’s second dedicatory letter to Laidradus and his companions (above), in which he says that he had added to his four books [Col. 0331B] “Elipandus’s letter to Felix, formerly the defender of his sect, but now, by God’s gift, a preacher of the Christian faith.” A little farther below he says that the letter was “addressed to Felix” while “Elipandus still supposed him to be bound by the chains of his error.”

### LXXIII. D. Madrisius’s response is answered and our position confirmed

D. Madrisius wishes to interpret Alcuin’s earlier words in this way, so that the meaning is: “Elipandus wrote to Felix when Felix had formerly been a defender of his sect, but who now, at the time when I am writing this, is a preacher of the faith. Nor could Alcuin then have spoken otherwise, since Felix had in fact been converted by the time Alcuin completed his books.”

The learned author proceeds further and says that the word “still” in Alcuin’s later words refers to the time when Elipandus’s letter was written, at which time Felix truly was bound by errors; and that the sense is: “Elipandus wrote to Felix at the time when he supposed him still to be bound” [Col. 0331C]—as he truly was—“by his errors, though he was later released.”

### LXXIV. Madrisius’s interpretation rejected

But this interpretation by D. Madrisius of the words of Alcuin’s letter is entirely novel and arbitrary, not to say forced. The learned man was compelled to devise it after he had claimed that, from the mutilated words “Inform me, you who are placed in Rome,” it had been most clearly demonstrated that Felix was actually in Rome at the time the letter was delivered.

Since, however, we showed above in no. 69 that no determinate meaning can be extracted from those truncated words, and since it is moreover sufficiently clear from no. 71 that Elipandus sent his letter to Felix in the same year in which he wrote the other letter to Alcuin—that is, in 799—the far better interpretation of the words of Alcuin now under discussion will be apparent if they are explained as follows: Elipandus’s letter was addressed or delivered to Felix at a time when Felix had already become a preacher of the Catholic faith, and when Elipandus “supposed” him—mistakenly, of course—still to be “bound by the chains of his error” [Col. 0331D].

By the word “supposed,” Alcuin evidently wished to signify that Elipandus was then unaware that Felix had been released from the chains of his error at the Council of Aachen. For if he had wished to signify that Elipandus had written to Felix while Felix was still unconverted, Alcuin would not have said that the letter had been addressed to Felix while Elipandus supposed him to be bound by the chains of his error; rather, he would have said: “at the time when Felix was still bound by the chains of his error.”

### LXXV. Further confirmation

For confirmation of what has been said, I shall add the following conjecture. I believe that Alcuin received Elipandus’s letter to Felix, together with Felix’s confession of faith, addressed to the clergy formerly subject to him, from Felix himself after Felix had become joined to him in friendship; indeed, this very act of communication was no minor sign of their friendship.

By what other means could that letter have become known to Alcuin if it had been addressed to him already in 792? For it is scarcely credible that Felix, while he still adhered to Elipandus and his teaching, would have wished prematurely to disclose Elipandus’s private letters concerning so delicate a matter, which ought to have been handled clandestinely and secretly, or to guard them less carefully [Col. 0332A].

Alcuin therefore did not receive that frequently mentioned letter before Felix’s conversion and before Felix entered into friendship with him. Alcuin—something which D. Madrisius does not deny—accordingly added this heading to the letter: “Letter to Felix, recently converted.” He would have added another heading if it had been written to Felix while Felix still adhered to Elipandus’s party, namely this or something similar: “To Felix, not yet converted.”

Now that those three doubts have been resolved, we may proceed more freely with the account, begun above in no. 54, of Alcuin’s struggle with Elipandus.

### LXXVI. Alcuin’s exhortatory letter is brought to Spain by Laidradus in 799

While Alcuin was occupied with refuting Felix’s pamphlet and was burning with great zeal to uproot the harmful error completely, he began to consider whether he should also test by letter the mind [Col. 0332B] of Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, whose authority he knew to carry great weight among the other Spaniards: whether Elipandus still obstinately adhered to the same error, already so often condemned by councils and by the apostolic see, or whether he might be moved to better things by exhortations of charity.

He therefore wrote him a letter which everywhere breathes humility and charity:

> “Nor is my dispute with you, most excellent Father, in this little writing of mine a lofty controversy, but a humble supplication, earnestly entreating you to strive with the whole intention of your mind to attain apostolic doctrine within Catholic unity and peace,” etc.

Out of the same spirit of charity, Alcuin attacks only Felix and his errors, while entirely passing over Elipandus’s own errors, so that, if I judge correctly, he might remove every shadow from which Elipandus could take occasion for offense or be moved to indignation. Alcuin sent this letter to Elipandus by Laidradus in the year 799, as we showed above in the resolution of the second doubt, no. 67 [Col. 0332C].

### LXXVII. In the same year Elipandus received from Felix the pamphlet which Felix opposed to Alcuin’s letter

In that same year, 799, at the end of July, Elipandus received Felix’s letter, about which he himself writes in his response to Felix, who had already been converted contrary to his expectations:

> “Lord Felix, I make known to you that at the end of July I received your writing.”

A little farther below:

> “When, at the end of July, I received your letter as though it had descended upon me from heaven, I gave immense thanks to my God with outstretched arms, who made me rejoice with your words.”

That writing, or letter, was unquestionably the very pamphlet which Felix opposed to Alcuin’s exhortatory letter and which is now regarded as lost, apart from what Alcuin preserved against it in his books. Elipandus was extraordinarily delighted with it and promptly sent it to the Corduban brothers who adhered to his sect, and also to the man whom he calls “the teacher of Albinus, the Antiphrasian Beatus.” At the same time he urged Felix to ensure that the same letter, or pamphlet, was delivered not to Alcuin but to his own king, Charles:

> “I have sent your letter,” he says in the cited passage, “to the brothers at Córdoba who think rightly concerning God. But I have also sent it to the very heresiarch, the teacher of Albinus, the Antiphrasian Beatus, to be read. You, however, send that writing on behalf of your faithful and glorious prince, before it comes to that son of perdition, Albinus,” etc. [Col. 0332D]

### LXXVIII. On the same occasion Elipandus received from Felix, together with this pamphlet, Alcuin’s letter addressed to him

On the same occasion, and apparently through Felix himself, Elipandus received the exhortatory letter of Alcuin brought by Laidradus, which Laidradus may perhaps have entrusted to Felix so that Felix would arrange for it to be delivered to Elipandus.

For after Elipandus informed Felix that he had received Felix’s letter at the end of July, he added:

> “But also”—for I think that this word *also* should be supplied so that the meaning may emerge—“I received [understand: ‘I received also’] the most foul letter concerning the son of the gehenna of fire, Albinus, the new Arius.”

This appears more clearly from the beginning of Elipandus’s letter to Albinus, which reads:

> “We received your letter, deviating from the path of the true faith, at the end of July,” etc. [Col. 0333A]

### LXXIX. Elipandus writes against Alcuin’s letter

After receiving Alcuin’s letter, Elipandus, impatient of being instructed by others, burst into the most violent anger; and in his answering letter he loaded Alcuin with many insults and slanders, as he himself boasts in the letter to Felix cited above, where he says:

> “I wrote to that heretic, the pitch-black Albinus, as much as I was able to write for his confusion.”

Alcuin complains about these injuries in his letter to Laidradus and his companions, writing:

> “At once Elipandus glowed with the flames of anger, gathering the whole intention of his mind into rage. . . . Immediately he burst into words of cursing, armed his whole self for the defense of his sect, and took care to communicate to us by letter what he thought and what he taught his disciples to believe; calling me a falsifier, at times reckoning me a heretic, at times a subverter, and also a persecutor of Christians. He omitted scarcely any kind of curse or perfidy that he did not stamp upon our name,” etc. [Col. 0333B]

And indeed, no one who has read these and the other things contained in his responses will deny that Alcuin had cause to complain about Elipandus’s insolence.

### LXXX. By what means Alcuin received Elipandus’s writing

It is uncertain by what means Alcuin received these letters of Elipandus. Elipandus entrusted them to Felix so that Felix would arrange for them, together with certain writings of the Corduban brothers, to be delivered first to the king himself and only afterward to Alcuin; for Elipandus hoped that the king, not yet forestalled by Alcuin, would be more favorable to him.

I understand the following words of Elipandus’s letter to refer to these writings:

> “You, however, send that writing”—which shortly before he had called the reply against Alcuin’s letter, “confirmed by the opinions of the orthodox and Catholic”—[Col. 0333C] “on behalf of your faithful and glorious prince, before it comes to that son of perdition, Albinus, who does not believe in the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God.”

It is exceedingly probable that, just as Felix did not receive the aforementioned letter of Elipandus until after he had once again abjured his error at the Council of Aachen in the year 799, with all the sincerity he professed, and had entered into friendship with Alcuin, as we saw above in nos. 71 and following, so Felix at that same time handed Elipandus’s reply against Alcuin to his new friend, together with the letter addressed to Felix himself.

### LXXXI. Alcuin takes up his pen against Elipandus’s responses

From Elipandus’s letter opposing his exhortatory letter, Alcuin learned that the old man had become so deeply rooted and hardened in his error that he could not even tolerate fraternal correction or admonition proceeding from pure charity. Therefore, despairing of being able to break his obstinacy, he did not wish to continue any further exchange of letters with him.

Nevertheless, in defense of his own honor and of Catholic doctrine, he took up his pen [Col. 0333D]:

> “Lest perhaps,” he says in his letter to Laidradus and his companions (above), “the minds of some be stained by reading that letter, since we heard that the same writings had first fallen into the hands of others before they were returned to us, to whom they had been sent.”

### LXXXII. Alcuin entrusts his books to Laidradus and his companions, who were again setting out for Spain, as an aid to their preaching

The renewed embassy which Laidradus and his companions were to undertake in Spain gave Alcuin an opportunity—perhaps sooner than he would have wished—to write against Elipandus’s aforesaid letters. Just as, when they first set out for that same region, Alcuin had given them an exhortatory letter to deliver to Elipandus, so now he overturned the arguments which Elipandus had employed in his responses in defense of his error in two books [Col. 0334A], and in two other books he most abundantly defended and confirmed Catholic truth. He entrusted those books to these apostolic preachers as a consolation for their journey, an aid to their preaching, and a strengthening of the Christians who lived near heretical depravity and were exposed to the danger of perversion.

### LXXXIII. Aided by these resources, those apostolic men brought many from error back to the truth

Alcuin did not sow this evangelical seed in the Lord’s field in vain, for it produced a hundredfold harvest, indeed a thousandfold and more. Aided by Alcuin’s labors, those apostolic men brought some twenty thousand people of various conditions to faith and repentance, as Alcuin himself writes in Letter 108 to Aquila, in these words:

> “Let your affection know, however, that our son Laidradus, your brother and bishop, by God’s gift has accomplished, and accomplishes daily, great progress in those regions, as religious and truthful men from those regions have truthfully reported, up to twenty thousand have been converted—among bishops, priests, monks, the people, men and women—mourning their former error and rejoicing, daily giving thanks to God in the knowledge of the truth and in the firmness of the Catholic faith.” [Col. 0334B]

### LXXXIV. Whether Elipandus repented of his error

There is, however, serious reason to doubt Elipandus’s conversion. Certainly, in the year 800, when Alcuin wrote to Aquila, or Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, about the conversion of so many bishops, priests, monks, and others, which we shall soon report, Elipandus himself still obstinately adhered to his error.

“But something still remains to be done,” says Alcuin shortly before the words just quoted, “for a certain Elipandus, bishop in name but not in dignity of the city of Toledo, remains in the heresy condemned by synodal authority and apostolic censure.”

Accordingly, no credence is due to the Annals of Julian and Liutprand—which Nicolaus Antonius of Seville shows to be full of fables, *Bibliotheca Hispana*, vol. I, book VI, chapter 2, no. 42; in D. Madrisius’s edition [Col. 0334C] of the works of St. Paulinus of Aquileia, p. 224, no. 75 and following [*Patrologia*, vol. XCIX, col. 585]—nor to the writer of the *Life of St. Beatus the Abbot* [Note: [Col. 0333] For the judgment passed by D.
