Gregorius Majansius on the *Acts of Beatus the Abbot*, see below in Appendix II, no. 5, in the letter to D. Pluer.], in Mabillon, *Acta Ordinis S. Benedicti*, fourth century, p. 737, no. 7 [*Patrologia*, vol. XCVI, col. 887]. They report that Elipandus:

> “returned to the mind and true sense of the Church through the letters of Pope Adrian and Charlemagne”—namely, those which they wrote to the bishops of Spain on the occasion of the Council of Frankfurt in 794—“indeed, that he convened an assembly of bishops at Toledo, where, repentant, he offered a written confession in which, with humble profession, he declared the only-begotten Son to be consubstantial with the Father, not adoptive but natural; and that he was received by the Fathers with an outpouring of tears and received the benefit of reconciliation. [Col. 0334D] Thereafter he kindly welcomed Beatus and Etherius, having laid aside the malevolence of their former dispute, and addressed them, not without tears and sobs, as defenders of the faith and patrons of Catholic truth.”

The man whom Alcuin reports to have remained in error even in the year 800, those writers say had returned to the unity of the Church six full years earlier, after the Council of Frankfurt had ended, through the letters of Pope Adrian and King Charles, and had been reconciled with the Fathers at some Council of Toledo of which there is otherwise no record anywhere.

Yet no one will fail to judge that greater credence ought to be given to our Alcuin than to those writers, whom all men distinguished for learning in our own age reject. Nevertheless, from the time when Laidradus and his companions gathered so abundant a harvest in the Lord’s field during their second embassy to the Spaniards, Elipandus remained silent, and the storm which he himself had raised and nurtured for so long also subsided. During that period of peace it could have happened that the decrepit old man, soon to be examined by God’s judgment, moved by the example of so many other bishops and priests, at last adopted a sounder mind [Col. 0335A] and repented before his death.

If this happened—which I wish were established by better testimony—it must certainly be attributed solely to the infinite mercy which exalts itself above justice. Yet who would not, after such prolonged obstinacy, still fear the divine judgment?

### LXXXV. In what year he died

This famous archbishop of Toledo died in the year 809 or the following year, after nearly thirty years of episcopal governance, which he had obtained around the year 780, as the distinguished D. Madrisius demonstrates with considerable plausibility in the frequently cited historical dissertation, no. 81.

We are nevertheless compelled to disagree with the highly praised author concerning the year of Elipandus’s birth and concerning his age. In our opinion, Elipandus’s letter to Felix [942], in which he asserts that he had entered his eighty-second year, was written not in 792, as D. Madrisius believed, but seven years later, namely after Felix’s conversion, which took place in 799, as we showed in nos. 68 and following.

Elipandus was therefore born not in 710 [Col. 0335B], but in 717, and he died not at the age of ninety-nine, but at approximately ninety-two.

### LXXXVI. St. Paulinus wrote against Felix not in 796 but later, and not before the year 800

Before we conclude the present Dissertation, in which we have chiefly attempted to elucidate the history of the controversy of blessed Alcuin against Felix and Elipandus, we have undertaken to resolve another question, namely the time at which St. Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, who was joined to Alcuin by the closest friendship and had shared his labors in refuting the errors of the Adoptionists, composed and published his books against Felix of Urgell, which the distinguished D. Madrisius published again.

No one before the distinguished author just mentioned had determined this date. In his notes to St. Paulinus’s letter to Charles, prefixed to his books, p. 98, he assigns them to the year 796, using the following reasoning.

The aforesaid dedicatory letter to Charles was written in a year in which 366 full days were being counted; Paulinus repeats this twice there, although he could not have been unaware that an ordinary year consists of only 365 days, together with some hours and minutes. Therefore the year in which the aforesaid letter was written was a leap year.

“They were written,” he says, “together with the letter after the Council of Frankfurt of 794 and before the year 799, as will be stated in the Dissertation on the Felician heresy. No other year between these limits was a leap year except 796. Therefore it must be held that the letter was written in that year.” [Col. 0335C]

### LXXXVII. Madrisius’s conjecture rejected

D. Walchius considers that this conjecture of D. Madrisius ought to be counted among the most felicitous, *History of Adoptionism*, chapter 2, section I, no. 33. To us, however, the opposite appears more probable.

No one, perhaps not even [Col. 0335D] Madrisius himself, will doubt that St. Paulinus wrote those books against Felix’s pamphlet, in which Felix replied to Alcuin’s exhortatory letter and which King Charles, at Alcuin’s request, entrusted to St. Paulinus for refutation. See what we said above in no. 26.

But we demonstrated above in no. 35, by sufficiently firm arguments, that Felix’s pamphlet did not reach Alcuin, the king, or—still less—Paulinus before the year 798. Paulinus therefore could not have refuted it before that year, or, as D. Madrisius wishes, as early as 796.

Indeed, [Col. 0336A] that these books of St. Paulinus appeared later—when Felix had already been converted at the Council of Aachen—can, unless we are greatly mistaken, be inferred from Paulinus’s own dedicatory letter to the king. There St. Paulinus asks pardon because, owing to intervening business, his labor in carrying out the king’s commands had proceeded more slowly than it should have. He nevertheless hoped, he says, that although that labor might no longer be necessary for Felix’s conversion, it might still prove very useful in the future, if the error should again be revived either by Felix himself—whose inconstancy was still feared—or by his accomplices.

This is how I interpret the following words of the aforesaid letter:

> “Finally, probable judgments concerning events compel us to suspect that, at some other time—Felix now having been converted—either Felix himself, if life should be granted him, or his accomplices, if he should by God’s just judgment be taken from this light, may attempt to plant anew in a rejuvenated shoot the branch of this violent stock. Hence, because the fault of my tardiness in replying arose from an intervening necessary cause, the hope of seeking pardon will not hesitate to entrust itself to the petitioner, whose expectation of negligence has been frustrated by sloth. Therefore, taking precautions for the future, I thought it not inappropriate to oppose, with the testimonies of Scripture, each of the points inserted in his letters”—namely, Felix’s letters against Alcuin—“which are seen to conflict with the rule of the Catholic faith.” [Col. 0336B]

### LXXXVIII. Alcuin’s Letter 108 to Aquila

The same conclusion is supported finally by Alcuin’s Letter 108 to Aquila, which now appears for the first time in full. In D. Madrisius’s judgment, p. 251, note, it was sent in May or June of 799; in our judgment, it was sent in the following year. We read there:

> “If you happen to see Patriarch Paulinus, greet him a thousand thousand times. As for the pamphlet of the Catholic faith which he sent to the lord king, I was reading it, and it pleased me greatly. . . . Thus I thought that nothing needed to be added to these matters concerning the questions recently debated between us and the Felician party at the Council of Aachen. But something still remains to be done. For a certain Elipandus. . . . remains in the heresy condemned by synodal authority and apostolic censure,” etc. [Col. 0336C]

From these words we learn clearly that St. Paulinus’s books to King Charles, and through the king—just as Paulinus had requested in a fragment of a letter preserved by Madrisius, p. 168—to Alcuin, first arrived after the controversy in Gaul concerning the adoption of Christ had been settled and concluded with Felix, and nothing remained except for Elipandus and his followers also to be restored to Catholic unity through the renewed preaching of Laidradus, undertaken in the year 800.

We must therefore hold that St. Paulinus’s books were not written or completed before that year.

### LXXXIX. D. Madrisius’s argument is answered

We grant, therefore, to the distinguished D. Madrisius that St. Paulinus sent his books, with the letter prefixed to Charles, in some year that was a leap year; we grant that they were written and published after the Council of Frankfurt of 794 [Col. 0336D]. But we cannot grant that this occurred before the year 799, something which the same distinguished author nowhere proved in his otherwise most learned Dissertation on the heresy of Felix.

We, for our part, have thus far shown by sufficiently firm arguments, unless we are greatly mistaken, that those books first became known or appeared in the year 800, which was itself also a leap year.

[Col. 0337]

## 944. DOGMATIC-HISTORICAL DISSERTATION DEMONSTRATING THAT, AGAINST CHRISTIAN WALCH, FELIX AND ELIPANDUS, THE ASSERTORS OF ADOPTION IN THE MAN CHRIST, WERE RIGHTLY CHARGED BY ALCUIN WITH NESTORIANISM

By D. JOANNES BAPTISTA ENHUEBER, Prior of St. Emmeram

[Col. 0337A] Among all Alcuin’s scholarly works, those which he directed against the errors of the Adoptionists plainly deserve the foremost place. This is demonstrated by the dignity of the subject, the treasury of ecclesiastical learning, and the weight of the arguments. For the primary mystery of our religion is treated there, namely the incarnation of the divine Word, and the faith of the Church is strengthened not only by the richest testimonies of the ancient Fathers but also by the force of theological reasoning.

Nevertheless, there have been men who attempted greatly to diminish the excellence of the work. Among them Christian Wilhelm Franz Walch, doctor and professor of theology, is especially prominent. In his *History of the Adoptionists*, published at Göttingen in the year 1755, he seems to have aimed at nothing other than demonstrating that Elipandus and Felix had thought quite differently from what Alcuin attributed to them, and consequently that Alcuin had argued badly against his adversaries in the books mentioned above.

Walch does not accuse Alcuin alone. He also asserts that Adrian I, Supreme Pontiff; Paulinus of Aquileia; the Fathers of Frankfurt [Col. 0337B]; and all who contributed their support in that controversy with the Adoptionists failed to understand the mind of their opponents.

All of these men, he says, argued that Felix and Elipandus were guilty of Nestorianism and affirmed that the doctrine of adoption in Christ could not be defended without positing two persons in him. Later writers, including those of the more recent age, interpreted this assertion concerning the adoptive son in the same way, with the exception of Gabriel Vasquez and Cardinal Aguirre among our own writers, and a few others from the Protestant body whom Walch cites in the place mentioned in support of his position, merely to increase their number.

Walch maintains that the Spanish bishops, although they did not think rightly in every respect and were indeed guilty of the gravest error concerning Christ’s regeneration, nevertheless defended adoption in a sense which, just as it was utterly foreign to Nestorius’s mind, did not in any way abolish the unity of person.

Jacob Basnage went still further [Col. 0337C], declaring the Spaniards free from every suspicion of error and confidently asserting that the entire controversy between them and the Franks and Germans concerned nothing but words.

> “We openly admit,” he says, “that it was merely a dispute about words, such as often occurs among theologians.”

*Thesaurus Monumentorum Ecclesiasticorum*, vol. II, fol. 288, no. 5.

There were also others who agreed with Basnage; they may again be seen cited by Walch.

More moderate than these, Mabillon, in the preface to the fourth Benedictine century, part I, § 1, reports that Felix and Elipandus were accused of the Nestorian heresy in such a way that he himself might plainly be thought to have reached the same judgment concerning those bishops.

Yet because he knew that the matter was still disputed among scholars, when he presented at the end of his work, in the treatise *On Monastic Studies*, a list [Col. 0338A] of the principal difficulties encountered in reading the councils, the Fathers, and ecclesiastical history which still require fuller explanation, he included the following among the questions concerning the eighth century, as the final item:

> “Were Felix and Elipandus, whose heresy was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt, Nestorians?”

The distinguished Joannes Franciscus Madrisius later treated this question more carefully than the others and answered it affirmatively in his *Dogmatic Dissertation on the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*. He appended this work, as the third dissertation, to the works of St. Paulinus of Aquileia, which he himself published at Venice in 1737 [*Patrologia*, vol. XCIX]. He demonstrated from the testimonies both of Felix’s age and of our own, as well as from theological arguments, that the doctrine of adoption in Christ [945] was imbued with Nestorianism.

Walch nevertheless attaches little importance even to these arguments, and perhaps is not far from approving and making his own the conjecture of Basnage just reported.

[Col. 0338B] We have therefore considered it worthwhile that, in this newest edition of the works of Alcuin, by far the most important of all who fought against the Adoptionists, the matter should be subjected to a new examination. We wish to demonstrate both the affinity of Adoptionism with the errors concerning two persons in Christ by irrefutable arguments—drawn not so much from theological reasoning as from the history of those times themselves—and to vindicate our author by showing that, when he attacked Felix and Elipandus as followers of Nestorius, he fought well against his adversaries.

This is contrary to Walch’s judgment. Walch believes that Felix and Elipandus spoke orthodoxly concerning the hypostatic union in Christ, but calls Alcuin “a fickle and inconsistent man, saying now this and now that, and not knowing what is certain.” He makes many other assertions throughout his *History* which, if they were consistent with the truth, would considerably diminish the praise and authority of this otherwise most celebrated writer.

[Col. 0338C] We think, moreover, that we shall attain our proposed end more securely and certainly if we demonstrate that the Adoptionists arose from the same origins as the Nestorians, rested upon the same principles, and were finally defeated by the same weapons. To accomplish this more accurately, we divide the entire Dissertation into three chapters: in the first we shall discuss the genesis, in the second the assertions, and in the third the refutation of both errors.

## § I. — ON THE GENESIS OF NESTORIANISM AND ADOPTIONISM

### I. The difficulty of detecting the genesis of heresies

The considerable difficulty involved in detecting the genesis of heresies was recognized long ago by the distinguished D. Bernard de [Col. 0339A] Montfaucon in his edition of the works of St. Athanasius. He says in vol. I, part II, fol. 648, in a note on the first letter to Serapion:

> “The beginnings of such ‘light-shunning ones’”—that is, heretics—“are more obscure than would allow a certain and indubitable judgment to be formed concerning them. Moreover, it is remarkable how great a variety of opinions arises concerning the beginnings of heresies, as different people grasp different things and draw different conclusions from the same principles. For it is characteristic of heretics that, once they have lost the path of truth, they wander here and there and cannot remain consistent even with themselves. Indeed:
>
> *Πάντη μαινόμενος, καὶ ἀμήχανος, ἀμφαλάληται.*”

That is:

> “Raving in every direction, helpless, he babbles wildly.”

### II. A later heresy is generally born from an earlier one

Indeed, if we consider hundreds of formulas of faith, the continually new methods of explaining earlier assertions, and the errors added to errors—especially with regard to the heresies of the earlier centuries, Arian, Nestorian, Eutychian, and so forth—such dense darkness is at first presented to the eyes that one might almost despair of its being dispelled [Col. 0339B].

Yet there is something amid these shadows that kindles a little light. This consists chiefly in the fact that, when the principal heresies are considered, the later one has usually found its origin in the bosom of the earlier, either directly or indirectly.

Directly, when some added another doctrine to a perverse dogma. Thus Macedonius, certainly to be numbered among the chief leaders of the Arians, as Father Montfaucon says in the cited passage, after declaring the divine Son to be a creature, eventually went so far as to deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit also. Hence the common and familiar judgment of all is that the Pneumatomachi originated from the Arians.

Indirectly, when others, through a less prudent zeal, attacked errors arising in the Church in such a way that they fell into opposite errors. Thus, again, it is clear that Eutyches confused the natures in Christ because he defended the unity of person against Nestorius without sufficient caution.

### III. The origin of the Nestorian heresy

The same thing also seems to have happened with regard to the errors of which we are speaking. This may be inferred from what ecclesiastical men argued against them or what historians committed to writing. We may therefore reasonably hope to uncover, at least to some extent, the genesis of both heresies—namely, the Nestorian and the Adoptionist.

## IV. Concerning the former, Nestorius, indeed, was patriarch of Constantinople, whose obstinate pride had spread far and wide throughout the Christian world the error concerning the virgin mother—that she ought to be called not *Theotokos* (“Bearer of God”), but *Christotokos* (“Bearer of Christ”)—and, as followed from that premise, the error concerning two persons. Yet it is universally known that there were men before him who had laid the foundations of this heresy. Among these Theodorus, bishop of Mopsuestia, certainly stands out. Nestorius is commonly said to have drawn his perverse doctrine from him, and for this principal reason his writings were afterward condemned by the Fifth Synod among those famous Three Chapters [Col. 0339D].

But Theodorus too is said by some to have had a forerunner, another teacher of his in literature—namely Diodorus of Tarsus. Diodorus was joined in friendship to men of great holiness and was highly commended by many both for his zeal for the faith and for the vigorous struggle he undertook against the Arians. By others, however, he was also called into suspicion of error. Among these, Saint Cyril of Alexandria especially deserves to be heard. In his letter to Successus he writes:

> “A certain Diodorus, formerly, as they say, an opponent of the Holy Spirit, entered into communion with the orthodox Church. Having, as he supposed, laid aside the stain of the Macedonian heresy, he fell into the power of another disease. For he perceived and wrote that the one born from David’s seed, from the holy Virgin and Mother of God, was one son separately, while that which was from God the Father, the Word, was another Son privately and separately.”

*Volume V, part II, Paris edition, 1638, folio 135.*

And in his letter to Acacius, bishop of Melitene, folio 197:

> “Since, however, it was necessary that written refutations should also be brought against them, after examining the books of Theodorus and Diodorus—which they wrote not about the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten, but rather against the Incarnation—I set down some chapters and contradicted them as best I could, declaring everywhere that their sect was full of abomination.” [Col. 0340A]

We can scarcely avoid judging that full credence ought to be given to these testimonies of Saint Cyril. He not only lived very near the time of Diodorus, who died around the year 390 or 392—for Cyril himself was consecrated bishop of Alexandria in 412—but also refuted the errors of Diodorus and Theodorus in a special treatise, now lamented by scholars as lost, and therefore examined their writings with exceptional care and diligence. This was not done by the Fathers who preceded Cyril, who were content to praise Diodorus’s zeal in refuting Arianism and Apollinarianism. Nor was it done by Diodorus’s defenders after Cyril—namely Theodoret, the lord of Antioch, Facundus of Hermiane, and the deacon Liberatus—who, carried away by partisan zeal, thought it advantageous to commend and excuse Diodorus [Col. 0340B]. The first of these remained devoted to Nestorius right up to the Council of Chalcedon; the second, namely the lord of Antioch, was of uncertain faith; and the remaining two died obstinate in their defense of the Three Chapters. Consequently, their testimonies on this point are rightly regarded as suspect.

Nevertheless, we do not on that account think that Diodorus himself ought to be condemned for heresy, or that he fought against the Arians and Apollinarists in such a way as knowingly to establish two persons in Christ. Rather, we think that in that struggle he asserted these things in the best of faith, perhaps, and that from them, by an easy consequence, there flowed what Nestorius afterward defended obstinately.

For more on this controversy—which is not precisely our own subject—see Tillemont, volume VIII, page 565, and Ceillier, *Histoire générale des auteurs sacrés*, etc., volume VII, pages 705 and following.

All these men had, finally, been anticipated by Saint Athanasius, who had both mentioned and refuted the assertions concerning a double son in Christ in his letter [Col. 0340C] to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth. He noted that in his own time there were certain people who said that Christ, who suffered and was crucified in the flesh, was not the Lord and Savior, nor the Son of the Father. Likewise: that one was the Son and another the Word of God, and so forth. We shall examine these matters more accurately a little below.

## V. The occasion of the Nestorian error was the struggle against the Arians and Apollinarists

The whole question now comes down to this: what was the occasion and what was the cause of these assertions? Leontius of Byzantium seems to have discovered the answer in what he wrote about Diodorus of Tarsus and Theodorus of Mopsuestia. Although his words are rather lengthy, it is useful to set them down in full, since they appear likely to shed much light on the question before us:

> “In those times”—namely, the times of Apollinaris, who is being discussed there—“there arose two great men, Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, and Theodorus of Mopsuestia, who fought against the Arians, Macedonius, and Apollinaris, and illumined all the sacred Scriptures with commentaries. They were held in honor and died without anyone, while they were alive, censuring any of their statements. Indeed, many celebrated them in written encomia. Basil and John Chrysostom—for he was a disciple of Diodorus of Tarsus—also praise them. But afterward, when the Nestorian doctrine had arisen, Cyril, who had himself previously praised them, was compelled to write against their works, because Nestorius used them to confirm his doctrine. For when they had published their sacred commentaries, they did not remain within proper bounds; rather, when they wished to distribute the sayings of sacred Scripture, assigning some to the divinity and others to the human nature, they were found to introduce two hypostases of Christ and a certain division.” [Col. 0340D]

*Volume IX of the Lyons Library of the Fathers, On the Sects, Act VI, folio 666.*

Saint Cyril had given the same testimony long before, in the letter to Successus cited above, where he writes concerning Nestorius:

> “Accordingly, he distinguishes the sayings concerning Christ found in the evangelical and apostolic proclamations, asserting that some are to be attributed to the man—namely, that they are human—while others belong peculiarly to God the Word—namely, that they are divine. Since he divides them in many ways and sets them apart, placing as one person, properly and separately, the one born from the holy Virgin, and likewise, properly and separately, that Word who is the Son from God the Father, he consequently asserts that the holy Virgin is not the Mother of God, but rather the mother of a man.” [Col. 0341A]

## VI. Behold, then, the occasion of the error

When these men, and others with them, were fighting against Arius, Macedonius, and Apollinaris, and “wished to distribute the sayings of sacred Scripture, assigning some to the divinity and others to the human nature,” they did this in such a way that they simultaneously fell into a division of the persons.

The struggle, therefore, especially against the Arians and Apollinaris, provided an opening for the error. This is also gathered quite clearly from the fact that Nestorius, in his letters, judged that the doctrine opposed to him could not be defended without someone falling into the heresy of Arius or Apollinaris:

> “To ascribe birth, as he says in his letter to Cyril (*Tomi IV Conciliorum*, Mansi edition), to the divine Word—passion, death, and the other properties of the flesh—this, my brother, is either the work of a mind truly in error after the manner of the pagans, or certainly of one suffering from the disease of the mad Apollinaris or Arius, or of some other yet more serious disorder.”

And in his letter to Pope Celestine:

> “For this is no small disease, but one akin to the rottenness of Apollinaris and Arius.”

And still more openly in another letter to Celestine:

> “For we too are engaged in much labor here, as we strive to root out the most filthy impiety of the worst opinion of Apollinaris and Arius.” [Col. 0341B]

We must now investigate more carefully, in due order, by what process they deviated from this struggle, undertaken insufficiently cautiously against both heresies, into opinions alien to the Church’s doctrine.

## VII. The Arians said that the Word was the adoptive Son of the Father

It is universally known that the chief error of the Arians consisted in their placing the divine Word among creatures and denying that he was *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος, “of the same substance”) with the Father. From this they concluded that the Word could be nothing other than God’s adoptive Son—God in name only and the Father’s servant—as Saint Athanasius expressly reports in various places.

First, in his *Book on the Synods*, volume I, part II, folio 728, he recounts the blasphemies of Arius from the *Thalia* as follows:

> “We worship the Eternal himself”—that is, God the Father—“because of him who was born in time. The One without beginning established the Son as the beginning of creatures; he brought him forth and adopted him as a son for himself: ‘having made this one a son for himself by adoption’” (Εἰς Υἱὸν ἑαυτῷ τόνδε τεκνοποιήσας).

Likewise, on folio 767, number 54, Athanasius argues as follows:

> “For it must be considered and carefully observed that, when we say that he is unlike in substance, we by no means signify a true Son, but one of the creatures, a son received by adoption, which is what the heretics believe” (Καὶ τὸν ἐποιητὸν καὶ θέσει υἱόν, ὅπερ τοῖς αἱρετικοῖς δόκει). [Col. 0341D]

And in his *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, volume I, part I, folio 258, number 23, he introduces the following words as those of Arius:

> “The Word is not proper to the Father, but there is another word in God. This one, however, the Lord, is foreign and alien to the Father’s substance, and is called the Word only according to a mode of thought; he is not, according to nature, the true Son of God. Rather, by adoption (κατὰ θέσιν), this one too is called Son.”

We omit, for the sake of brevity, the other testimonies that could still be brought forward on this matter, since it is abundantly clear from these that the Arians attributed adoption to the Word himself. In support of this error they pressed especially those passages of Scripture in which the divine Word is called “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), “the firstborn from the dead” (ibid., verse 18), and “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). All these passages may be seen in Saint Athanasius, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, volume I, part I, folio 531, number 63 and following.

## VIII. Likewise, a titular God

The Arians also held an erroneous view concerning the designation “God,” as is again evident from various assertions reported by Athanasius. Thus, in his letter to the bishops of Egypt and Libya, number 12, folio 281, volume I, part I, he cites the following among other blasphemies of Arius:

> “They say, therefore, that Christ is not the true God, but that he, like all the others, is called God by participation.”

And in *Oration 1 against the Arians*, in the same volume, folio 409, number 6:

> “Moreover, he dared to say that the Word is not the true God. For although he is called God, he says, nevertheless he is not the true God; rather, having been made a participant in grace no differently from all the others, he too is called God in name only.”

They placed the principal foundation of this perverse assertion in the words of Psalm 81:6:

> “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

Or rather, they based it on the argument that Christ himself derived from this passage in John 10:34. When the Jews accused him of blasphemy because he had said that he was the Son of God, he replied:

> “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said: You are gods’? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” [Col. 0342B]

## IX. Thirdly, they called him the Father’s servant

Finally, they also attributed an unworthy servitude to the Word and frequently called him the Father’s servant. Again they contended from those passages of Scripture in which Christ is called by the prophets a servant, an elected child, and so forth, or in which he himself said that he was less than the Father.

In the work *On the Synods*, folio 745, Athanasius records the following words of the Arians from their seventh formula of faith:

> “No one is unaware that it is catholic teaching that there are two persons, those of the Father and the Son: the Father is greater, and the Son is subject, together with all those things which the Father subjected to him.”

Moreover, in *Oration 2 against the Arians*, folio 471, numbers 3 and 4, the same holy Father devotes himself entirely to proving that, although the Word is sometimes called a servant in Scripture, he is nevertheless the genuine and true Son of the Father. From this it is clear that the Arians asserted servitude concerning the Word in a perverse sense. [Col. 0342C]

## X. The Arians maintained that the Word took the place of the soul in the assumed man

The Arians added yet another error to these earlier ones, apparently arising from them. Saint Athanasius reports it in *Book II against Apollinaris*, number 3, in these words:

> “Arius confesses only flesh, for the concealment of the divinity; but in place of our inner man, that is, the soul, he says that the Word existed in the flesh, daring to attribute passion and resurrection from the dead to the divinity.”

They therefore held that the Word fulfilled the role of the soul in Christ. They believed this both because the sufferings, death, and other weaknesses of human nature were frequently attributed to the Son of God in Scripture, and because, as Athanasius notes in his letter to Adelphius, number 1, Christ could not be worshiped as man if he were a perfect man; and finally because two perfect things could not become one. This was subsequently made their own argument by the Apollinarists, who taught the same doctrine. [Col. 0342D]

## XI. Some opposed these errors in such a way that they appeared to establish two sons in Christ

While Athanasius was crushing all these errors in his writings with the greatest weight of argument, assigning the divine things in Christ to the divine nature and the human things to the human nature, he also repeatedly protested that no double Son, nor any separation of the Word from the humanity assumed by him with respect to hypostasis, should thereby be inferred.

This provides a sufficiently clear indication that already at that time there were some who, in order not to be compelled to attribute human weaknesses to the divine Word and thus to succumb to the Arians’ sophistries, separated this Word from the son of the blessed Virgin.

They incautiously distributed “the sayings of sacred Scripture, assigning some to the divinity and others to the human nature.” When Christ was called “the firstborn of all creation” or “the firstborn among many brothers,” and the Arians therefore asserted that the Word was an adoptive Son among adoptive sons [Col. 0343A], they maintained that these expressions were to be understood not of the Word insofar as he is the eternal Son of the eternal Father, but insofar as he is the Son born from David’s seed and from the flesh of Saint Mary.

## XII. Marius Victorinus says that Christ, insofar as he is man, is an adoptive son. The author of the Disputation against Arius does likewise

A trace of this appears to remain in the first book of Marius Victorinus against Arius, *Library of the Fathers of Lyons*, volume IV, folio 256, where he writes:

> “The Son, then, is equal to the Father, and therefore the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son, and both are one. But enough of that for now. Let us examine those words of John. The Savior himself says: ‘I am the resurrection,’ because he himself is life. But who is this one? Martha says: ‘For you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into the world.’ He is not a Son in the same way as we are. We are sons by adoption; he by nature. He is also, in a certain adoption, Son and Christ, but according to the flesh.”

I know, to be sure, that many defend Marius Victorinus from this sort of error and claim that by this adoption according to the flesh he understood nothing other than the assumption of the flesh itself, or of the human nature, into the unity of the person.

Indeed, Alcuin also uses Victorinus’s authority against the Adoptianists. In book IV against Elipandus, number 9, he quotes the following words from Victorinus’s response to the Arian Candidus, in Mabillon, *Analecta*, page 22, Paris edition, 1723:

> “We say that God is our Father, and above all. For this reason, and according to this, God predestined us in love to adoption through Christ. Does God also have Christ as an adoptive Son? No one has dared to say so.”

And in what follows:

> “Christ, therefore, is the Son of God, and we are sons also; but we through adoption, we through Jesus Christ, we as dispersed sons. Is Christ a Son in this way too? Jesus, therefore, is Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. That he is Son by nature, he often says himself: ‘Father, I thank you because you have heard me.’ And: ‘Father, save me from this hour.’”

These latter words are found in Victorinus in the already cited first book against Arius, and are added after a short interval to those which we quoted above from the same work as our first passage [Col. 0343C]. It is therefore surprising to us that Alcuin left them entirely untouched. The reason may perhaps have been either that they were missing from the copy used by Alcuin or that, even if they were present there, our author interpreted them in the same way—as referring to the assumption of human nature.

But if we consider the purpose Victorinus set for himself in both works—namely, to blunt the Arian perfidy, which attributed adoption to the Word himself—it seems clear that he was speaking not of the assumption of the flesh, but of a genuine adoption that would apply to Christ insofar as he is man.

Victorinus admits adoption with respect to Christ’s humanity, although against the Arians he had denied adoption with respect to Christ’s divine nature. In explicit terms he says that Christ is Son by nature insofar as he is the Father’s Word—this was the only subject under discussion with the Arians—but at the same time he maintains that Christ is also Son in a certain adoption, namely according to the flesh.

Thus D. Ceillier, *Histoire générale*, etc., volume VI, chapter 4, number 5, page 29, after explaining how Marius Victorinus defended the divinity of the Word against the Arians, adds:

> “Nevertheless, he admits that one may say that Jesus Christ is God’s adoptive Son, but according to the human nature; for according to his divinity he is the Son of God by nature.”

Here, perhaps not inappropriately, we should also place the author of the *Disputation against Arius*, once spuriously attributed to Saint Athanasius. When Arius asked him, “Is there another Son?” he replied:

> “There is indeed one true Son of God, the Word and God. Yet there is, as it were, another adopted Son through the temple of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, as the divine Apostle says: ‘For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, Abba, Father.’” (*Volume II of the Works of Saint Athanasius*, folio 219.)

Here again adoption with respect to the humanity seems to be admitted, and indeed because of the occasion supplied by the refutation of Arianism, although two Sons are not expressly said to exist, but only: “there is, as it were, another Son.” [Col. 0344A]

## XIII. Some asserted that Christ, as man, was a titular God

As regards the designation “God,” which Arius granted only in name, and likewise the servitude by which he maintained that the same Word was subject to the Father, as we saw above, some appear to have used the distinction mentioned earlier between Christ insofar as he is the eternal Son of the eternal Father and Christ insofar as he is man, in order to dissolve the Arians’ arguments.

Among these we may perhaps name Phoebadius, whom Saint Jerome calls “Soebadius” in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. He was bishop of Agen in Gaul. In his book against the Arians (*Library of the Fathers*, volume IV, folio 300), he notes that Ursacius, Valens, and Potamius, with heretical subtlety, confess one God, by which name they understand the Father alone, while nevertheless granting the Word the name “God,” though in a deceitful sense, in order to mislead the simple.

It is necessary to quote his words in full, because they serve our purpose remarkably well, not only concerning this external designation but also concerning the servitude that the Arians assigned to the Word:

> “Throughout the whole body of their profession, the Arians do not deny our Lord in such a way as to destroy him as God—that is, they say that he is Lord in name only, by which name we too are accustomed to be called. ‘I said,’ he says, ‘You are gods.’ Moses too was previously honored by this name: ‘I will make you,’ he says, ‘a god to Pharaoh.’ Let no one, therefore, think that the catholic confession is completed by these words, if we both confess one God, the Father, and do not deny God the Son. For God the Father can be called one God in such a way that he is one Father, not one God. The Son too can be called God in such a way that he is not God . . . . .

> “Immediately, when they deny two gods, they add: ‘For God himself says: I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ By this definition of an evil interpretation, the Son is so separated from the Father and placed beneath almighty God that the condition of his birth and the weakness of his humanity are made common to us. Finally they add: ‘The God of all is one God,’ by which statement the Lord is not absolutely denied to be God. For he is subjected to God the Father not under the name of Son, but under the condition of a creature.

> “And I believe that apostolic authority will be claimed at this point, so that Christ may be called God rather than actually be God, because it says: ‘And God gave him the name that is above every name.’ But you will also hear the Lord himself denying that he is the true God when he says: ‘This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only and true God’; and: ‘Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God.’ You will still hear: ‘Why do you not seek honor from the one and only God?’ And concerning the day and hour, no one knows except the Father alone, and so forth.”

After reviewing all these sophistries of the Arians, drawn for the most part from passages of Scripture, Phoebadius exclaims:

> “O blind leaders! O men deceived by the ambition of the age! You do not distinguish the two states of the Lord’s power, each differing in its own property, and whatever has been said of his humanity you apply to God, so that God himself may be made to share in human weakness.” [Col. 0344D]

Phoebadius therefore judged that one must distinguish “the two states of the Lord’s power.” When the Arians inferred from the passages they cited that the Word was “a titular God and the Father’s servant,” he believed that these passages were to be interpreted not of the Word himself, but of the nature assumed by him, or of Christ insofar as he is man.

## XIV. Some taught these things in good faith

I would not say that the writers cited above defended adoption, the external designation “God,” or servitude in Christ insofar as he is man in such a way that they thereby inferred two persons in the Nestorian sense.

Victorinus certainly teaches the hypostatic union with sufficient clarity when he says:

> “Let the disciples of Marcellus and Photinus depart. For we say that the Word himself was in the flesh; that the Word is not one thing and the man another, in whom they say Christ exists, but that the *Logos* (Λόγος, “Word”) himself put on flesh. For they say that there are God, the *Logos*, and the Spirit. But the fourth is the Son, that is, the man who is from Mary, whom the *Logos* assumed and governed as a servant; and for this man, they say, a seat was prepared. Thus they have fallen away from the Trinity.”

Nevertheless, it is clear from these things how, through the incautious refutation of Arianism and the distribution of the sacred expressions, a path was laid toward the division of the persons. Whatever seemed in any way unworthy of the Word was immediately and without discrimination referred to the human nature. Some, it is rightly judged, did this perhaps with a heretical spirit; others did it even in good faith, because, while the matter had not yet been fully clarified and discussed, they did not perceive the danger.

## XV. The preceding points are confirmed by Saint Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius

This argument is confirmed by what Saint Gregory of Nyssa writes in his letter [Col. 0345B] to Theophilus of Alexandria, *Works*, volume II, Paris edition of 1615, and volume I of Basnage’s *Thesaurus Monumentorum Ecclesiasticorum*, folio 192:

> “Those who defend the doctrines of Apollinaris try to confirm their own position by accusing us, making the Word and the Author of the ages—the Son of Man, I mean—fleshly, and making the Son’s divinity mortal. For they produce it as though certain people, in accordance with the Catholic Church, professed in their doctrine a double son: one by nature, the other by position—or adoption—‘the one existing by nature, the other subsequently added by position’” (τὸν μὲν κατὰ φύσιν ὄντα, τὸν δὲ κατὰ θέσιν ὕστερον προσγενόμενον).

Gregory indeed adds these words:

> “I do not know from whom they heard this, nor against whom they are fighting. For I have not yet understood who falsely said these things.”

Yet although Gregory knew no one who openly professed two sons, it is not without reason that some people are said to have given the Apollinarists an occasion to level this accusation against Catholics by their distinction between a natural and an adoptive Son.

That this charge against Catholics concerning the assertion of a double son had become very widespread may also be gathered from what Athanasius writes in book I against the Apollinarists, after listing the errors of the heretics:

> “You too”—he is addressing the Apollinarists—“like false accusers, say that we admit two sons, or you call us worshipers of a man and accuse us of sin.” [Col. 0345C]

Among the errors of Arius already mentioned was this as well, as we noted above: he confessed “only flesh, for the concealment of the divinity,” and said that “the Word existed in the flesh in place of our inner man, that is, the soul,” daring “to attribute passion and resurrection from the dead to the divinity.”

So says Athanasius. The Catholics denied this, maintaining that the Word had assumed a complete human nature consisting of body and soul. From this Apollinaris, following the Arians’ tracks at least in the respect that he held “a heavenly mind to have been in Christ in place of our inner man,” took occasion, according to Athanasius in the passage cited, to attribute that error concerning a double son to the Catholics. He was led to this by the reasoning that “two perfect things cannot be one.” *Athanasius, cited passage.*

Whether this accusation was false—as we readily grant concerning most of the persons involved—or whether, with respect to some who fought less cautiously, it was true, it certainly teaches that the refutation of Arianism provided an occasion for thinking and writing about a double son in Christ, or at least for asserting propositions from which that double son could rightly be inferred. [Col. 0345D]

## XVI. The Arians themselves provided the occasion for the doctrine of a double son

Indeed, the Arians themselves, while being carried in different directions by a spirit of confusion and continually varying and disagreeing in the exposition of their doctrine, laid the foundation for this error, as can be drawn from Saint Athanasius’s *Oration 4 against the Arians*.

There the holy Father reports the absurd opinion of certain people according to which unity was said to be expanded into the Trinity. After rejecting it, he continues:

> “When those who think in this way dare to divide the Word and the Son, and contend that the Word is one and the Son another” (ἀλλὸν μὲν εἶναι τὸν Λόγον, ἕτερον δὲ τὸν Υἱόν), “the Word first and then the Son, come, if it pleases you, let us examine this as well. Their rashness, however, is varied. Some wish the man whom the Savior assumed to be the Son; others think that both—the man and the Word—became the Son when they were joined to one another. Others believe that the Word himself became the Son when he became man; for, they say, from the Word was made the Son, who previously was not Son but only Word.”

There were therefore certain Arians who had divided the Word from the Son, or who asserted that the Word became the Son only when he became man.

The author of the book against the *Synousiasts* (Συνουσιασταί), whom some cite under the name of Diodorus of Tarsus and others under that of Theodorus of Mopsuestia, appears to refute this error when he says, in Leontius of Byzantium, *On the Sects*, Act IV, *Library of the Fathers of Lyons*, volume IX, folio 704:

> “By grace the Son is the man born from Mary; by nature, God the Word. The former is so by grace and not by nature; the latter by nature and not by grace. It is enough for the body, from our human stock, to have sonship according to grace, glory, immortality, and the fact that it was made the temple of God. Let it not be raised above nature, and let God the Word not be insulted instead of receiving the thanksgiving that we owe him. And what is the insult? To join him with the body and to suppose that he needed the body for perfect sonship.”

This author therefore denies that the Word needed the assumption of human nature for perfect sonship, an idea which, as we reported from Athanasius, certain Arians had defended. He says that the Word had already been the Son from eternity by his own nature, while the assumed man was so by grace—that is, by adoption.

Who does not see here a direct occasion, arising from the refutation of Arian perfidy, for establishing a double Son, one natural and the other adoptive? [Col. 0346C]

## XVII. Diodorus of Tarsus opposed the Arians. Theodorus of Mopsuestia did the same

It is indeed true that the book from which this passage is taken is directed not directly against the Arians, but against the Synousiasts, or Apollinarists.

Yet if it is to be attributed to Diodorus of Tarsus, it is established that this bishop opposed not only the Apollinarists but also the Arians, or Eunomians, as Fabricius reports concerning him, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, volume VIII, pages 358 and following. Fabricius further says there, number 23, that Diodorus wrote various arguments on the Holy Spirit, apparently directed against the Macedonians, in which, as Fabricius notes, he had anticipated Nestorius. Photius, codex 102, had read those writings in the same volume in which the book of Gelasius of Caesarea against the Eunomians was contained.

It is therefore not surprising if, even in his book against the Synousiasts, he mentioned the Eunomian or Arian error and attempted to defeat it again [Col. 0346D], although, because he used weapons less suited to the matter, he did not accomplish it very successfully.

If, however, the aforementioned book has Theodorus of Mopsuestia as its author, he too fought the same battle, as is gathered from his words reported by Facundus of Hermiane, book X, chapter 1, *Works of Sirmond*, volume II, Venice, 1728, column 513, from his book *On Apollinaris and His Heresy*:

> “More than thirty years ago [Note: [Col. 0345] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book V, part V, page 157, gives: around the year of Christ 385] we composed a book on the Incarnation extending to fifteen thousand lines, in which throughout the work we examined the errors of Arius and Eunomius on this matter, as well as the vain presumption of Apollinaris.”

These heretics had agreed, as we said above, in holding that the Word had taken the place of the soul in Christ. Theodorus therefore refuted them all at once. Moreover, as Facundus reports in the cited passage, Theodorus complained that he was falsely accused of saying that there were two sons. From this complaint it may be inferred that, in the struggle undertaken against the assertions of Eunomius and Apollinaris, Theodorus let fall statements from which some people were already then led to conclude that he admitted two sons. [Col. 0347A]

Finally, history also makes clear concerning Nestorius that he fought against the Arians to excess. We have already quoted several passages from his letters which show that this struggle against the Arians provided an occasion for the error concerning a double son—namely, one natural and the other adoptive.

This is stated in the clearest terms in the letter of John of Antioch and certain Easterners who had been sent to Constantinople, addressed to Rufus of Thessalonica, *Volume IV of the Councils*, Mansi, column 1415. There they complain against Cyril of Alexandria as follows:

> “In addition, he curses those who distinguish the evangelical and apostolic sayings concerning Christ the Lord, assigning the humble expressions to the humanity and the divine expressions to Christ’s divinity. For the Arians and Eunomians, thinking in this way, and referring the humble expressions of the dispensation to the divinity, did not hesitate to assert that God the Word was a creature and a work, of another substance, and unequal to the Father.” [Col. 0347B]

## XVIII. The Nestorian error made further progress through the refutation of Apollinarianism

This error nevertheless made still greater progress through the struggle undertaken against the Apollinarians—or against the Synousiasts, who emerged from their circle. We have already noted more than once that the Arians themselves also fell into the error of maintaining that the divine Word had taken the place of the soul in the assumed man, so that passion, death, and the other weaknesses fell upon the Word itself; consequently, the Word had to be called a creature rather than God.

Apollinaris later adopted this error. He did not, indeed, deny the divinity of the Word, as the Arians did, but he altogether denied that Christ possessed a human soul, or at least a human mind. He maintained that he—that is, the Son of God, or the Word—had used the surrounding body as an instrument, since, he claimed, a perfect man could not exist. For wherever there is a perfect man, there is sin; and two perfect things cannot be united into one, and so forth. Athanasius, *On the Incarnation, against Apollinaris*, book I, no. 2.

Apollinaris is believed to have drawn this error from the sources of Platonic philosophy, as Bishop Nemesius of Emesa testifies at the beginning of his book *On the Nature of Man*:

> “Some,” he says, “among whom is Plotinus, maintaining that the soul is one thing and the intellect another, wish man to consist of three things: body, soul, and intellect. Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea, followed them as well; for, having laid this foundation of his opinion, he built the remainder in accordance with his doctrine.”

Volume VIII of the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, folio 619.

Besides the reasons already assigned for asserting such things—namely, that Apollinaris feared Christ would be subject to sin, or would have to be divided into two sons, if he were said to possess a human mind—it is reasonably conjectured that there were further considerations.

Although the Arians wished the Word to be a created thing, they nevertheless worshiped it. Hence Athanasius repeatedly reproaches them for worshiping and serving a created thing. The further question was whether it was also lawful to worship the Word made man. The Arians thought that they were right to do so because, as they mistakenly believed, the Word itself occupied the place of the soul. Conversely, they denied that Christ was to be worshiped as a man if, according to the Catholic position, he were a perfect man. This is how we should understand what Athanasius says in his *Letter to Adelphius*, no. 7: namely, that the Arians did not wish to worship the Lord as one existing in the flesh as in a temple.

To avoid, at least in appearance, the difficulty raised by the Arians, and to prove that even Christ’s body itself ought to be worshiped, Apollinaris agreed with the Arians to this extent: he maintained that the Word had supplied the place of the soul. Thus he decided that one perfect entity had been formed, as it were, from the divine Word and an imperfect human nature, and that this entity, in its single state, was to be worshiped with a single act of worship.

See the notes of D. Bernard de Montfaucon prefixed to the letter of Saint Athanasius to Adelphius, volume I, part II of the *Works*, folio 910.

From this error, others seem to have proceeded—those whom Athanasius lists in his *Letter to Epictetus*, no. 2. Their position was that the body born from Mary was consubstantial with the divinity of the Word; that the Word had been changed into flesh, bones, hair, and the entire body, and had departed from its own nature; that the Word had formed for itself a passible body not from Mary but from its own substance; and that the very divinity, consubstantial with the Father, had been circumcised and fastened to the cross, and so forth.

I would certainly not say that Apollinaris himself adhered to these absurd opinions. Indeed, the contrary is inferred from the first volume of Leontius of Byzantium’s *Readings*, in the Basnage edition, folio 600, where he reports a fragment of Apollinaris’s letter to Serapion in these words:

> “We have condemned as sheer madness the opinion of those who say that the flesh is consubstantial with God.”

Likewise, a fragment from another letter of his to Dionysius:

> “That no one can charge us with these things, which were said against certain persons, is clear from what we have always written: neither that the Savior’s flesh is from heaven, nor that his flesh is of the same substance as God insofar as it is flesh and not God; but it is God insofar as it has been united with the divinity in one person.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let him therefore be anathema who does not say that the flesh is from Mary, and who says that this flesh is of an uncreated nature and *homoousios* [ὁμοούσιον, consubstantial] with God; indeed, let him also be anathema who says that the divinity is passible and that the passions of the soul arise from it.”

Even if Apollinaris himself was free from these perverse doctrines, proponents of them nevertheless emerged from his school. Among them, the more famous were those who defended the claim that Christ’s flesh was consubstantial with the Word. They were therefore called Synousiasts [Συνουσίασται, “those of one substance”], or those who asserted that the Word had been converted into flesh, bones, hair, sinews, and the entire body. In this respect they had already anticipated Eutyches by abolishing the distinction of natures in Christ.

## XIX. Some improperly attack the Apollinarians

Several of the holy Fathers rose against these errors; but if anyone did so, certainly Saint Athanasius refuted them with the strongest arguments in his letter to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth. Nevertheless, others again, stirred to the contest by a less prudent zeal, failed—as we have often observed from Saint Cyril and Leontius of Byzantium—to divide the Scriptural expressions against the Synousiasts with sufficient precision. They consequently fell into a division of persons and made the error concerning an adoptive son with respect to the humanity their own particular doctrine.

Saint Athanasius had already noted this in the letter first cited. After listing the errors of the Apollinarians, he continues as follows in no. 2, folio 902:

> “How, then, could men who are called Christians even dare to doubt whether the Lord who was born from Mary is, according to his own substance and nature, the Son of God, while according to the flesh he is from the seed of David and born from the flesh of holy Mary? Who, indeed, were so rash as to say that Christ, who suffered and was crucified in the flesh, is not the Lord and Savior, God, and the Son of the Father? Or how can those wish to be called Christians who say that the Word came into a holy man, just as into one of the prophets, and that he himself did not become man by assuming a body from Mary, but that Christ is one person and the Word of God another—the Word who was the Father’s Son before Mary and before the ages? Or by what reasoning, I ask, could those be Christians who say that one is the Son and another the Word of God?”

That these assertions arose from the refutation of the earlier positions is clearly gathered from what Athanasius immediately adds in no. 3:

> “These things,” he says, “were found in the commentaries, expressed in different words, but containing one and the same meaning and force directed toward impiety. On account of them those who boast of the confession of the Fathers at Nicaea disputed and contended with one another.”

## XX. The opponents of the Apollinarians call Christ the man an adoptive son and also a titular God

Everything becomes still clearer if we examine the writings of those who are commonly called the parents of the Nestorian heresy. The first to appear is the author of the book against the Synousiasts. Garnerius, in his edition of the works of Marius Mercator, Paris 1673, part II, folio 317, *Dissertation on the Heresy and Books of Nestorius*, section 8, considers this author to have been Diodore of Tarsus, and calls him the parent of Theodore and the grandfather of Nestorius.

That he called Christ the Lord, insofar as he is man, a Son by grace or adoption is sufficiently and abundantly clear from the words quoted above. That he reached this position through his struggle against the Synousiasts, who confused the natures in Christ, will become evident from what follows.

After the followers of Apollinaris had foolishly asserted that the flesh was consubstantial with the Word, or that the Word had passed into the flesh, they consequently called the Word itself, as such, the son of David—or rather, they misused the passages of Scripture in which the divine Son is called the son of David, employing them in defense of their error.

The author of the aforementioned book argues against this and says:

> “If anyone wishes improperly to call the Son of God, God the Word, the son of David because the temple of God the Word is from David, and to call the one who is from the seed of David the Son of God by grace, not by nature—without being ignorant of the natural Fathers, overturning the order, or also calling the incorporeal one a body.”

In Garnerius, at the place cited.

A short while later he plainly shows that he wrote these things to avoid the confusion of the natures, saying:

> “Let us confess the natures, and let us not deny the dispensations.”

Again, when the Synousiasts pressed the Evangelist’s words, “The Word became flesh,” and also other passages of Scripture in which the Son of God is called the son of man, and conversely the son of man is called the Son of God, the aforementioned author replies:

> “When the matter concerns the saving dispensation, God is called man—not because he became this, but because he assumed this; and man is called God, not as though he had become uncircumscribed or omnipresent. For he was a body, tangible even after the resurrection, and such a body was received into heaven; and so he will come, just as he was received.”

Here we plainly find both the doctrine of the adoptive Son and that of a titular God; and they arose from no other source than that struggle against the Synousiasts, undertaken with insufficient caution.

## XXI. Theodore of Mopsuestia teaches the same thing

Theodore of Mopsuestia also discusses similar matters in his writings, almost all of which he directed against the Apollinarians. Several fragments from them are cited in the Fifth General Synod, volume IX of the *Councils*, Mansi edition, column 219, where his writings were individually examined and subsequently condemned. Among other passages, no. 46 cites the following from his interpretation of the Letter to the Hebrews:

> “They will therefore now cease from their shameless struggle; they will desist from their empty contention, being put to shame by the evidence of the foregoing statements. For he says that he is bringing many sons into glory. Here, then, the apostle appears in the matter of sonship to be numbering the assumed man among the others—not according to the way in which he is likewise a participant in sonship with them, but according to the way in which he likewise assumed sonship by grace, while the Godhead alone possesses natural sonship.”

Since the Apollinarians called the assumed man the natural Son of God while at the same time confusing the natures, because they had asserted either that the Word itself had been changed into flesh or that this flesh was consubstantial with the Word, Theodore attempts to defend against them the distinction of the natures. He calls the assumed man a Son only by adoption, and calls the Word alone, by nature, the Father’s Only-Begotten.

He reasoned in the same way concerning the name “God,” which he wished to apply to the son of man. For in number 34 of the first book of his interpretation of the Gospel according to John, we read:

> “He himself was also certain that he was speaking of the Son of God not according to the birth of his divinity, but according to the fact that he was familiar with God; and for this reason men who, through their virtue, had been made familiar with God were meanwhile called sons of God.”

According to Theodore, therefore, Christ himself was not God; nevertheless, he was more familiar with God than other men. And just as other holy men are called sons of God, so he too, because of the familiarity he possesses with God, was called God by Nathanael, with whom he was speaking. Pope Vigilius reasons in nearly the same way in his reply to the words of Theodore cited above, at the place mentioned, column 83.

## XXII. Nestorius

All these assertions arose from no other source than the fact that these men proceeded against the Apollinarians without sufficient prudence and divided the Scriptural expressions carelessly, as is abundantly clear to anyone who considers the matter.

And what else, finally, did Nestorius himself intend—the immediate parent of the error concerning two sons—when in his letter to Cyril, volume IV of the *Councils*, column 894, no. 1, he writes:

> “Observe here how, laying down the Lord, Jesus, Christ, the Only-Begotten, and the Son—names, certainly, which belong equally to the human and divine natures—as certain foundations, the holy Fathers (to whom he there appeals against Cyril) immediately append and build upon them the tradition of the Incarnation, death, and resurrection. They do this by setting forth certain common signs belonging to both natures, so that neither the things that belong to sonship and lordship may be divided, nor again the things that belong to the natures be brought into danger of confusion because of the singularity of sonship.”

To avoid the confusion of the Apollinarians, Nestorius therefore asserts that the names belonging to the natures in Christ must be divided; and in fact he divided them in such a way that he also divided the persons.

> “Nestorius,” says Vincent of Lérins, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume VII, folio 254, “through the disease opposed to that of Apollinaris, while pretending to distinguish two substances in Christ, suddenly introduces two persons, and, with unprecedented wickedness, wishes there to be two sons of God, two Christs: one God, the other man; one from the Father, the other begotten from the mother.”

If we consider, then, the evidence so far brought forward, no doubt remains that the Nestorian heresy arose from an insufficiently cautious refutation of both errors—namely, the Arian error and the other error taught by Apollinaris and his disciples. The proper order therefore requires us to prove that the Adoptianist doctrine also had the same origins, and that from this circumstance the two heresies—those of Nestorius and those of Elipandus and Felix—were closely related. This work will be aided both by what the historians of Spain have recorded for us and by the surviving fragments or letters of Felix and Elipandus, as well as by the works of Alcuin, whose authority we shall always invoke.

## XXIII. Remnants of the Arian heresy in Spain down to the eighth century

Although Arian depravity was almost suppressed in Spain around the year 587 through the labor and diligence of Saint Leander and the piety of King Reccared, historical documents of various kinds relate that it repeatedly sprouted again there as time passed and that, even in the eighth century—toward the end of which the controversy concerning the adoptive Son began to be debated more vigorously—it disturbed the churches of that kingdom.

When Reccared died in 601 and left his son Liuba as heir to the kingdom, Vitericus immediately afterward, in the year 603, murdered this prince, who was only twenty-two years old and had wholly inherited his father’s character. With the assistance of the Arians, as Mariana writes, he ascended the throne. Mariana, volume I, folio 199, edition of The Hague, 1733; at folio 206 the same Mariana says:

> “Under King Suinthila, around the year 627, John, bishop of Zaragoza, is celebrated. … Vincent and Ramirus were John’s contemporaries. Vincent, while serving as abbot of Saint Claudius of León, shed his blood in defense of the religion when the sect of the Arians, which had seemed to be dormant, rose again.”

The Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year 633, immediately proposes in its first chapter, with sufficient care, that the faithful must believe the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father. The same occurs in the Sixth Council of Toledo in 638.

The Eighth Council of Toledo, in 653, again condemns Arius along with other heretics; and King Flavius Recesvintus himself, in his address to the Fathers of the synod, professes the faith according to the definition of Nicaea and of the other councils. From all this it is not obscurely inferred that remnants of Arianism still existed in Spain, which the bishops attempted to suppress through their vigilance, their repeated conciliar decrees, and their professions of faith.

Such professions of faith occur in nearly all the Spanish councils of those times, as in the Council of Mérida in 666 and the Fourth Council of Braga in 675. There the Fathers indeed boast of their agreement in the faith; nevertheless, to eradicate errors that perhaps were spreading among others, they encourage one another and for this purpose publicly profess the faith from the Nicene Creed.

The preface of the Ninth Council of Toledo in 675 makes it still more clearly evident that neither the people nor even the pastors or ecclesiastical men of Spain had been free from every error. The assembled Fathers lament there as follows:

> “Until now we have been unstable through the collusion of the declining age, because the long succession of the years, deprived of the light of councils, increased vices less than it implanted ignorance, the mother of all errors, in idle minds. For until now roaring boars have devastated the Lord’s flourishing vineyard. The deceitful contrivance of heretics has attempted to spit upon and pollute the bride of Christ, whom he won through the pouring out of his most precious blood; to divide the Lord’s seamless garment; to sever the unity of faith; to remove the supports of charity; and, stubbornly wishing to cling to its own opinion, it profanes the purity of sacred Scripture by an understanding dictated by its own depravity.”

That is, eighteen years had passed since the Tenth Council of Toledo, held in the era 694—that is, in the year 656—as the Fathers expressly complain in the preface cited. During so long a period, since no synod had been held, various errors had again disturbed the people, among them Arianism as well, as can easily be inferred from the fact that the Fathers labored there to expound the doctrine of the divinity of the Word so clearly and at such length.

## XXIV. The mystery of the Holy Trinity was long debated in Spain

Moreover, it can sufficiently be gathered from the acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in 688 that many matters concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the Incarnation were debated in Spain during those times. It may reasonably be presumed that certain errors still spreading here and there at that time provided the occasion for these debates.

Mariana relates, volume I, folio 234, that the Fathers of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo approved the acts of the Sixth General Council against the Monothelites, and that the bishops of Spain sent to the Roman pontiff, through a certain Peter, a regional official of the Roman Church, an apology against the heretics containing the principal points of Catholic religion. It was the work of Julian, bishop of Toledo, who enjoyed an outstanding reputation for learning.

> “In this work,” Mariana continues, “while Leo II had meanwhile died, Benedict, Leo’s successor, judged certain things worthy of censure. Among them were statements made in discussing the sacred Trinity: that wisdom proceeds from wisdom and will from will, just as the Catholic Church says, ‘God from God, light from light.’ The pontiff argued that these expressions should not be extended. He was also offended by the claim that Christ the Savior was composed of three substances. While these controversies were being debated in Spain …”

That is, around the year 684.

Speaking afterward of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, folio 236, Mariana says:

> “Furthermore, the accusations and blemishes of Pope Benedict, with which he had branded the acts of the preceding council, were removed by a new debate. In a new apology, it was established by the words of Julian and the authority of the Fathers that he who had said that will proceeds from will in God appeared to commit nothing against Christian piety, and likewise that Christ God is composed of three substances, and so forth.”

See the acts of the aforementioned council, where these controversies are treated at considerable length.

At the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, in 693, King Flavius Egica exhorted the Fathers:

> “First of all, let the rectitude of the holy faith, which through true belief is diffused and extended throughout the whole world, be proclaimed by the words of your deliberation.”

Likewise:

> “Let the various affairs of the peoples and the other deeds of wicked men contrary to the holy faith be brought to an end, according to the canons and the law, through the examination of your judgment.”

The most religious king plainly seems to assume in these words that there were then certain people opposed to the true faith. Hence the Fathers also say that they wished to provide “salutary defenses without interruption for sound joints of the body” and to apply “suitable medicines to weakened limbs, wounded as they were by various injuries of disease,” so that “the old ulcers might more easily be torn out by the roots and remedies of the desired health obtained.”

To achieve this end, they added an extensive exposition of the faith, in which they again dealt chiefly with the Holy Trinity, the divinity of the Word, and his Incarnation.

At the Seventeenth Council of Toledo in 694, the same king admonished the bishops to debate the mystery of the faith and to proclaim “the doctrine of the apostolic order through spiritual edicts,” so that “the hearts of the faithful, illumined by an incomparable star, and also the breasts of unbelievers, converted by the steps of the mind from darkness to light, might pass onward.”

Thus stimulated, the Fathers again prefixed the symbol of faith to their decrees. Moreover, in the first chapter they established that during the first three days of the council the mystery of the Holy Trinity should chiefly be discussed. This plainly indicates that there were then certain people who either attacked this mystery or at least did not sufficiently acknowledge it.

Finally, it is clearly inferred from what Roderic Santius relates in part III of his *History of Spain*, chapter 3, concerning Alfonso the Catholic, that traces of the Arian heresy appeared in Spain even in the eighth century:

> “For just as,” he says, “through the faith and work of Constantine the Great—that is, Constantine Pogonatus—the heresy of the Manichaeans [read: Monothelites] was cut down in the East at the Sixth Synod, so in the West Alfonso, through the same religion and faith, uprooted the Arian heresy. … He began to reign in the year of the Lord 731.”

Volume I of the *Illustrious Writers of Spain*, folio 156, Frankfurt edition, 1603.

Franciscus Tarapha, canon of Barcelona, relates similar things in his book *On the Origin and Deeds of the Kings of Spain*, under Alfonso:

> “Alfonso,” he says, “obtained the kingdom in the year of human salvation 739. … He uprooted the Arian heresy, which had again sprouted in Spain.”

Ibid., folio 547.

There is indeed a difference between these authors concerning the beginning of Alfonso’s reign. This, however, concerns us little, since in the account relevant to our purpose both agree.

## XXV. The Spaniards debated the adoption of Christ long ago

It should also be noted that the Spaniards had debated the adoption of Christ long before this time.

Saint Isidore writes in his treatise *On Illustrious Writers*, especially those of Spain, volume II of the *Illustrious Spanish Writers*, folio 4 of the edition cited:

> “Justinian, a Spaniard and bishop of the Church of Valencia. Of four brothers who were bishops and born of the same mother, one also wrote a book of responses to a certain Rusticus concerning questions that had been asked. The first question concerns the Holy Spirit; the second is against the Bonosians, who say that Christ is adoptive and not proper … The fifth response states that the Son, like the Father, is invisible. He flourished in Spain during the time of Theudis, prince of the Goths.”

According to Roderic of Toledo, Theudis began to reign in the era 570, that is, in the year of Christ 532, and was killed in the era 587, that is, in the year 549. Mariana relates the same account in volume I of *Spanish Affairs*, folio 171.

At that time it was not surprising that some people accepted this adoption in Christ, since the Arian heresy still held broad sway over Spain. It is reasonably said that the errors of Bonosus had formerly arisen from that source, whether we suppose that Bonosus asserted adoption in Christ according to Photinian principles or according to Arian principles. The matter has not yet been settled among historians, although Elipandus later held this opinion concerning Bonosus, as we shall immediately see.

This error revived afterward in the seventh century, after Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, had died in 636. “The most blessed Isidore,” writes Lucas of Tuy, *Chronicle of the World*, book III, volume IV of the *Illustrious Spanish Writers*, page 53, “was succeeded by Theodiscus, a Greek by nationality. … He was found to be an unbeliever and was judged erroneous in the articles of faith; by a synod he was degraded from the archiepiscopal dignity. For he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was not one God but rather adoptive. After being deprived of the honor of the priesthood, he went over to the Arabs, adhered to the sect of the false prophet Muhammad, and taught many detestable things under the emperor Heraclius.”

Other historians of Spanish affairs also report that Theodiscus taught errors, including John Vasaeus, volume I of the *Spanish Writers*, folio 687, no. 643, in his *Chronicle of Spain*; Roderic Ximénez, archbishop of Toledo, *On Spanish Affairs*, book II, chapter 21, volume II of the *Illustrated History of Spain*, folios 51 and 52; and Mariana, folio 214 of the edition cited.

They do not, however, specify his errors, and they also differ from Lucas of Tuy in claiming that Theodiscus did not immediately succeed Saint Isidore, but succeeded Honoratus, who had subscribed to the Sixth Council of Toledo in 638. They likewise assert that he was deprived of his dignity not under Heraclius, who according to Fleury died on March 11, 641, but somewhat later, during the reign of Cindaswinth, who began to govern Spain in 642.
