That remnants of this error still remained in Spain after Theodiscus’s departure is inferred from the fact that the Eleventh Council of Toledo, in 675, after stating in its profession of faith that the Son is *homoousios* [ὁμοούσίον, consubstantial] with the Father, carefully adds:

> “This Son is also Son by nature, not by adoption; and God the Father must not be believed to have begotten him either by will or by necessity, because no necessity falls upon God, nor does will precede wisdom.”

## XXVI. Arian errors strengthened in Spain through the invasion of the barbarians

From all these considerations it is already abundantly clear that traces of Arianism were found for a long time, even into the eighth century, in Spain. We reasonably suspect that they became still more widespread after the invasion of the barbarians, when the royal city had been occupied by the Arabs, and the clergy and other Christians lived under servitude. They were permitted to live according to the law and ecclesiastical institutions and to have bishops and evangelical priests only under restrictive conditions. Among them, as the cited Roderic Ximénez says, the offices of Isidore and Leander continued to flourish.

Amid these disturbances, ecclesiastical learning began to languish among those very bishops and priests. As a result, they did not always fight against the enemies of the faith with the weapons by which their obstinacy could properly have been defeated.

> “Peter Pulcer,” it is said in the *Treatise on the Primacy of the Church of Toledo*, volume X of Mansi’s *Councils*, column 513, section 4, “had Elipandus as his successor, after certain others. He discharged so great an office entrusted to him not merely negligently but also most unjustly. For, through frequent intercourse with the Moors, since he was far removed from the good fortune of those times in which sound ecclesiastical teaching flourished, and since he was insufficiently versed in the sacred writings, he fell arrogantly and ignorantly into the heresy concerning the adoption of Christ our Savior.”

We readily concede that Elipandus, whom we consider to have been the principal parent in that age of the error concerning Christ’s adoption insofar as he is man, initially did this through ignorance and carelessness. He became a heretic only afterward, when, having been warned about the error, he arrogantly and stubbornly defended what he had spread ignorantly at the beginning.

We do not rashly judge, however, that the refutation of Arian doctrine provided Elipandus with the occasion for going astray in the opposite direction; this can be drawn from various testimonies of writers.

Christian Walchius willingly grants this point in the cited *History of the Adoptianists*, chapter 2, section 1, page 77, where he writes:

> “Nor am I unwilling to admit that it appears probable to me that the doctrine of Christ’s adoption was brought into Spain by the Bonosians and preserved from that time by clandestine plans; and that it was finally corrected by Felix, who referred to Christ the man those things which they had said concerning Christ God.”

Walchius himself defends the position that the Bonosians transmitted the same doctrine as the Arians in his *Dissertation on Bonosus the Heretic*, published at Göttingen in 1754, page 21.

Again, in the aforementioned *History of the Adoptianists*, page 211, Walchius says that the Fathers of Frankfurt wrongly reproached the Felicians for making no mention of Nestorius in their letter and for not condemning him together with the other heretics. He thinks that the Spanish bishops were silent about Nestorius because they were concerned only with condemning errors concerning Christ’s divine nature, not those concerning his human nature.

Although we shall shortly show that those bishops debated not only Christ’s divine nature but also his human nature, Walchius’s own admission nevertheless makes it clear that Elipandus, Felix, and their associates contended most fiercely concerning the divinity of the Word and, in the heat of this dispute, slipped into that perverse opinion concerning adoption.

The distinguished Majansius supports us in this matter in his letter to Carolus Christophorus Pluer, no. 4 of this edition, volume II, folio 590, no. 2, writing as follows:

> “The affairs of Elipandus, a Goth by nation, as his name indicates, and metropolitan of Toledo, are so well known that it is better to remain silent about them than to say little. His error was that Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, was not the proper Son of God but an adoptive son. That he had Felix, bishop of Urgell—truly an unfortunate man—as his follower is testified by Jonas of Orléans at the beginning of his books against Claudius of Turin. But both of them received a burning and smoking brand from the Bonosian heretics, against whom Justinian, bishop of the Church of Valencia, expressly wrote, and so forth.””

[Col. 0354C] **XXVII. The Spaniards, in attacking Arianism, slide into the doctrine of adoption concerning Christ as man.**—There are, in fact, weighty considerations from contemporary writers—and even from the writings of Elipandus and Felix themselves—by which this conjecture may be strongly confirmed. Thus, in Book II *Against Elipandus*, no. 4, Alcuin seems to indicate that this archbishop deviated into the doctrine of adoption while intending to avoid the errors of Arius. “You also followed and set down another statement of the same prophet,” Alcuin says, “which, prescribing it from your own understanding, you said: ‘He himself, God the Son of God, according to his divinity, in which he and the Father are one, says: I will not give my glory to another.’ You evidently wish one person who says these things and another concerning whom they were said to be understood—that is, concerning Christ’s humanity. You would never have set down this statement unless you had been pleased to understand it in this way. You are mistaken, Brother Elipandus; you are mistaken, and grievously mistaken, in interpreting this statement, [Col. 0354D] in which Arius also once erred, understanding two persons: namely, the one who spoke these words and the one to whom they were spoken—as though God the Father had said of the Son, ‘I will not give my glory to another.’ From the word ‘another,’ he wished to understand the Son as inferior to the Father. But you, while attempting to leap over this pit of impiety, have fallen with an unwary foot into the abyss of Nestorius, supposing that the Son of God, from the substance of his divinity, foretold these things concerning the nature of his humanity, which he assumed from the blessed Virgin.”

Similar statements are found in Paulinus, who addresses Felix as follows in Book I: “The almighty Father marked his beloved Son; but you, O unhappy man, conferred upon him nothing more than upon a mere man. Moreover, while mockingly calling him a God by appellation and a wished-for Son, what else do you bestow than the common honor belonging to any one of the elect, when you ought to have displayed to him alone, and more gloriously, the glory of the wings of power? But because you know that Arius was for this reason condemned by the holy Fathers with an eternal anathema, you labor by a dismal objection to defraud the Catholic faith; and while you pretend, with an itching ear, to reject the viperous hissings—without doubt those of the Arians—you are disgraced and killed by a deadly breath, like that of the asp and the basilisk.” [Col. 0355A]

Elipandus himself also adds full force to our opinion when he frequently calls Alcuin “a new Arius” in his writings, believing that adoption cannot be denied without denying the divinity of the Word. Moreover, in his letter to Abbot Fidelis he says: “Bonosus and Beatus were condemned for the same error. The former believed him adopted from his mother, and not begotten from the Father before the ages; and not adopted temporally from his mother.”

From all this it follows that Elipandus was especially concerned to avoid and suppress the heresy of Arius and of Bonosus, who agreed with Arius in attributing adoption to the divine Word itself; and that for this reason he once again called to his aid the distinction—already employed in earlier times by certain persons, as we have seen—between a natural Son with respect to divinity and an adopted Son with respect to humanity.

[Col. 0355B] Indeed, the Spanish bishops of the eighth century were laboring in their exposition of the same biblical passages. We have already said that the Arians had abused these passages from the beginning in order to defend adoption, an external designation as God, and servitude in the very Word, and that certain people who attempted to blunt their attacks had explained them improperly. Thus, with regard to adoption, the letter of the bishops of Spain to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and others cites nearly all the testimonies of sacred Scripture in which the name “Firstborn” is attributed to the divine Son, and says that it must be understood of Christ not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is man.

As for the external name “God,” Alcuin, in Book IV *Against Felix*, no. 2, reports these words of Felix: “In a second manner he is called God by designation, as was said above concerning the holy preachers, of whom the Savior says to the Jews: ‘If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came’ 955; yet they are called gods under him who is the true God—not gods by nature as God is, but deified by God’s grace. In this order, indeed, the Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer, according to his humanity, although chosen above all more excellently, nevertheless shares with them most truly, both in nature and in name, and likewise in all other things: namely, in predestination, election, grace, reception, assumption of the name of servant, and application, or other like things. Thus he who is essentially the true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of deity became, in the form of his humanity, deified with his elect by the grace of adoption, and became God by designation.”

Finally, speaking of the servitude which Felix and Elipandus, in a perverse sense, attributed to the Savior’s humanity, they themselves also abuse the words of the Prophet in asserting it: “Behold, my servant shall understand” (Isaiah 52:13); and, “Behold my servant, I will receive him; my elect, my soul has been pleased with him” (Isaiah 42:1). See again the previously cited letter of the bishops of Spain.

[Col. 0355D] **XXVIII. The struggle against Migetius.**—Nevertheless, the immediate occasion for adopting such a view of Christ may perhaps have been that fierce struggle which Elipandus had shortly before waged against a certain heretic named Migetius. It will not be useless briefly to examine his history, which is still shrouded in considerable darkness, and to bring it into the light as far as possible.

Pope Adrian first mentions him in a letter addressed to the bishops of Spain, in which he reproves Egila, a bishop of that kingdom, for having followed certain errors of his teacher Migetius; but he does not determine what those errors were. In the already mentioned letter of the Spanish bishops to the bishops of Gaul and others, they accuse Abbot Beatus of resembling Migetius, but provide only obscure indications of the latter’s errors.

In his letter to Fidelis, a fragment of which Beatus [Col. 0356A] and Etherius preserved for us in their work written against the error of the Adoptionists, Elipandus boasts repeatedly of having suppressed the Migetian heresy through his own efforts, without explaining even a word of its doctrines. Meanwhile, he speaks somewhat more openly about it in a letter addressed to Migetius himself, which the distinguished Floresius published not long ago in volume V of *Hispania Sacra*, page 543. From it we learn that Migetius’s principal error consisted in positing three corporeal persons in the Godhead, saying that the person of the Father was David, that of the Son Jesus of Nazareth, and that of the Holy Spirit the Apostle Paul.

This error certainly seems too crude for us to believe that his assertions are to be taken literally, so that, in Migetius’s view, these corporeal persons would have to be attributed to the divinity itself. Hence we reasonably suspect that another meaning lies concealed beneath them, especially if we consider that Migetius had elsewhere been regarded as orthodox by the common people, and even by Elipandus himself, as appears from no. 2 of the cited letter; and, furthermore, that [Col. 0356B] Egila had also adhered to certain errors of this man, although Wulcharius, bishop of Gaul, had previously praised Egila highly before Adrian for his Catholic faith, morals, and conduct, and Adrian himself had proclaimed his faith in glowing terms, as is explicitly read in three letters of that pontiff written concerning the present matter.

But to discover what error or heresy lies hidden in those assertions is the task—and the difficulty—before us. It is truly regrettable that Migetius’s letter, adapted to the form of a little book, as Elipandus says in no. 1, and later called by him in no. 3 “a most fetid sheet,” has either perished through the ravages of time or perhaps still lies hidden somewhere in obscurity. From it, no doubt, every difficulty could easily be removed and every controversy settled.

In the absence of this document, however, we may at least offer conjectures, whose foundation we seem to find in the very writings we have just mentioned. In his first letter to Egila, Pope Adrian indeed notes that heretics existed in [Col. 0356C] Spain at that time; but he reports none of their other errors except that they differed from the observance of the Roman Church concerning fasting on Friday and Saturday.

In another letter to the aforesaid Egila and to the presbyter John, he speaks of errors concerning the celebration of Easter, the eating of blood and of strangled animals, predestination, communion with Jews, and the marriage of priests—all of which Egila and John themselves had brought before the Apostolic See. He then adds: “And many other matters, as you have stated, which would take too long to recount. Why should I write out for you individually the various heresies? For it is long since they have been filled with the doctrine of Priscillian.”

Finally, he concludes as follows: “Your charity must therefore be on guard, and must forbid with the greatest diligence that, through such men, scandals long since extinguished should be revived, and that from the formerly cut-down doctrine some shoot of the same evil should arise in that province, which would not only grow from its roots but would also infect the offspring of the holy Church with the poison of its odor.”

From these words it may be inferred that, besides the errors already mentioned, other disturbances still troubled Spain in that age—errors of the kind that had once been condemned in Priscillianism, and whose revival Pope Adrian feared.

[Col. 0356D] **XXIX. The errors of the Priscillianists revived by Migetius.**—The principal errors of the Priscillianists, as we learn them from the letter of Saint Leo to Turibius of Astorga, were the following.

First, they asserted with Sabellius that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one and the same person. His disciples, Saint Leo says in the cited passage, chapter 1, “are rightly also called Patripassians, because if the Son is himself the Father, the cross of the Son is the suffering of the Father; and whatever the Son endured in the form of a servant by obeying the Father, the Father himself entirely assumed.”

Second, they maintained that certain powers proceeded from God, which he began to have and which he himself, in his essence, preceded. “In this,” Saint Leo again says, “they support the error of the Arians, who say that the Father is prior to the Son because he once existed without the Son and began to be Father when he begot the Son.”

[Col. 0357A] Third, they said that the Son of God was called “only-begotten” for this reason: because he alone had been born from a virgin. “They would certainly not dare say this,” Saint Leo writes, “unless they had drunk in the poison of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who said that our Lord Jesus Christ did not exist before he was born from the Virgin Mary. But if these men wish something else to be understood from their meaning, and do not assign Christ’s beginning to his mother, they must necessarily assert that there is not one Son of God but others also begotten from the supreme Father, of whom this one alone was born from a woman and is therefore called ‘only-begotten,’ because none of the other Sons of God received this condition of birth.”

Moreover, in chapter 17 of the same letter, Saint Leo testifies that the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, with sacrilegious understanding, [Col. 0357B] 956 pretended to confess Christ in such a way that they removed the truth of his incarnation, death, and resurrection.

**XXX.** If we consider what was shortly before quoted from Adrian’s letter, the conjecture is not unfounded that these errors were revived by Migetius. Elipandus accused him of fabricating three corporeal persons in the Godhead; from this, unless we are greatly mistaken, it may be inferred that Migetius denied the true Trinity of persons in the one substance of the Godhead, and that he interpreted the words of Christ the Lord, who frequently speaks of the Father and the Holy Spirit, as referring to David, his father according to the flesh, and to Paul, who says that he is an apostle “not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Galatians 1:1). Thus, in the end, Migetius admitted only some sort of metaphorical Trinity in this sense.

This is confirmed by the letter of the Spanish bishops to the bishops of Gaul and others already cited, in which the following is read: “And again, to whom shall we say that the antiphrasist [antiphrasium], Beatus, is similar, unless to Migetius, who in our times arose as the teacher of the Casiani and Salibani, and who, while being cauterized on the head by a physician in the manner of a madman, considered himself similar to Christ and chose twelve apostles for himself? Seeing a certain little woman standing before him [perhaps *cernuae*, as the distinguished Majansius thinks], and grieving over her [perhaps ‘over him’; or ‘while grieving’], he is said to have said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise.’”

In this passage it is useful first to note the apparent error which seems to have entered the wording, either through ignorance of Latin or through the carelessness of scribes. Instead of *magistro nostris temporibus exorto* (“the teacher who arose in our times”), the text has *magistrum . . . exortum*. These words belong not to Beatus but to Migetius, who is therefore called by the bishops the teacher of the Casiani and Salibani. This is sufficiently clear from what immediately follows, since it can refer to no one other than the aforesaid Migetius, as becomes evident to anyone who reads the context.

[Col. 0357D] **XXXI. Migetius, teacher of the Sabellians.**—With this note prefixed, what especially serves our purpose is that Migetius is called the teacher of the Casiani and Salibani. The distinguished Majansius thinks that *Sabellianorum* (“of the Sabellians”) should be read instead of *Salibanorum*, a view strengthened considerably by the fact that, at the end of their letter, those bishops pronounce a special anathema against Sabellius, evidently for no other reason than that in those times there were people who had revived the same errors concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity.

Why he is also called the teacher of the Casiani, or who these heretics were, cannot be determined, since, so far as I know, this name occurs nowhere else, whether among ancient or modern writers—unless perhaps the Donatists are intended. Their author and leader, Donatus, had been bishop of the Casae Nigrae in Africa, and the bishops may therefore have called them Casiani as a term of contempt.

Certainly, it may be inferred from the letter of Bishop Saul to Alvarus of Córdoba, [Col. 0358A] which is found in volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*, no. 12, page 165, that Migetius adopted some portion of their errors. There Saul seems to touch upon the error of the Donatists who denied that evil ministers validly administer the sacraments; he had refuted this at greater length in Letter 10, and finally writes in the aforesaid Letter 12: “But plainly I do not know whom you represent as salt-encrusted and designate as Donatists and Luciferians, nearly Migetians.”

Elipandus likewise charged Migetius with something of this kind, saying: “But concerning priests, when you assert that they are sinners, why do they proclaim themselves saints? Or, if they certainly confess that they are sinners, why do they presume to approach the ministry, since the Lord himself says: ‘Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy’?”

Furthermore, in no. 12 he seems to indicate that Migetius confined the Church to the city of Rome alone. In this way of thinking he may again have shared something of the Donatist system, since the Donatists loudly proclaimed that the true Church remained only in Africa and in the party of Donatus.

But whatever the matter may be—for it is of little concern to us—it seems certain that Migetius erred concerning the Trinity with Sabellius and Priscillian.

[Col. 0358B] **XXXII. Migetius appears to have denied the divinity of the Word.**—Moreover, he did not acknowledge any other person of the divine Son, at least if Elipandus is to be believed, than the one who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. Hence, like the Priscillianists—or in accordance with the assertions of Paul of Samosata and Photinus—he either denied that Christ existed before the Virgin his mother, or, following the Arians, admitted several sons or powers proceeding from God and inferior to him. In either case, he could regard Christ never as the true Son of God, but only as an adopted son.

These, then, were the errors which Elipandus undertook to refute in Migetius, and whose suppression he boasted of so greatly, as we have said. This may be gathered from his creed, which Beatus and Etherius preserved for us in the work cited above. In it his entire concern was to expound the doctrine of the Trinity of persons, [Col. 0358C] the divinity of the Son, and his incarnation. It is also most clearly apparent that Elipandus deviated into the doctrine of adoption precisely when he was striving to vindicate the Son’s divinity and to establish the distinction between the two natures in Christ.

Perhaps more could still be found in the books on the Trinity which he wrote. Beatus and Etherius preserved only the memory of these works in the frequently mentioned treatise, since either the ravages of time destroyed them or fortune has not yet granted us access to them, if they still lie hidden somewhere.

The refutation of the Arian and Bonosian heresies, and of the Migetian heresy—which in certain respects was identical with them—provided Elipandus with the occasion for his Adoptionist error. It was exceedingly easy for him to turn toward that distinction between divinity and humanity when he was acting against a heretic who acknowledged Christ only as an adopted Son of God and not as the true Son, just as we have recalled that this happened earlier to the opponents of the Arians.

And just as, according to [Col. 0358D] Leontius of Byzantium, the beginning of the Nestorian heresy was nothing other than the careless distribution by certain people of the words of sacred Scripture, some being referred to the divinity and others to the humanity, so the arguments presented thus far prove that Elipandus likewise proceeded along the same path into the error of adoption in Christ. This can be drawn quite clearly from nos. 4 and 7 of his letter to Migetius, where he makes a very careful effort to divide between the two natures the biblical texts which Migetius had perhaps brought against him.

Hence, in his letter to Alcuin, new edition, volume I, folio 876, where he exerts all his strength in establishing his position, he appeals to the words of Saint Isidore, who says: “For there are some who think perversely about the Son of God, transferring to his divinity what was said of him according to his humanity, and changing to his humanity what was said of his divinity.”

Elipandus’s purpose, therefore, was to distribute the words of sacred Scripture in such a way that each would correspond to its own nature: whatever had been said of the humanity would be asserted of the humanity alone, and whatever had been said of the divinity would likewise be ascribed to the divinity alone. By the former distinction the Arians were repelled, since they transferred the weaknesses of the human nature to the divinity and thereby denied the consubstantiality of the Word; by the latter, the Eutychians were refuted, for some of them, by ascribing the attributes of divinity also to the flesh, and others, conversely, by attributing the sufferings of the flesh after the union to the divinity, had thereby introduced a confusion of the natures.

[Col. 0359A] **XXXIII. The Eutychian heresy also long survived in Spain.**—In fact, it was not only the refutation of Arian depravity that paved the way for Elipandus to assert adoption in Christ; it was also the refutation of Eutychianism. That traces of this heresy persisted in Spain down to those times can readily be proved from the same considerations by which we previously inferred that Arianism had survived for so long.

Certainly, in all the councils of Spain cited shortly before, the doctrine concerning the incarnate Word is explained with great care. Several historians testify that, at the beginning [Col. 0359B] of the seventh century, serious disturbances arose in Spain through the followers of the Eutychian heresy, disturbances which had to be suppressed by a special synod held at Seville.

Joannes Vasaeus writes in his *Chronicle of Spain*, volume I of *Illustrious Spanish Writers*, folio 682 of the cited edition: “In the seventh year of Sisebut’s reign, in the month of December, the second council of Seville was celebrated by eight bishops, under the presidency of Saint Isidore, against the Acephalous heretics, who denied the distinctive properties of the two natures in Christ. They were so called because no founder could be found from whom they [Col. 0359C] originated. A certain Syrian bishop, a most zealous defender of the aforesaid heresy, was present at this synod. After stubborn disputation, he was overcome by the arguments of Saint Isidore and the other holy Fathers and was converted to the true and orthodox faith, as is clear from chapter twelve of that council.”

This historian is somewhat mistaken in saying that the Acephalous heretics received that name because no founder could be found from whom they originated. The reason for the name is entirely different, as is clear to anyone acquainted with the history of Eutychianism. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that he wrote what is substantially true, since precisely the same account is found in the other writers of Spanish history.

“A gathering of eight bishops was held at Seville,” Mariana says, “in the seventh year of Sisebut’s reign, with Isidore presiding. At that gathering the sect of the Acephali was rejected. It had formerly been suppressed in the East but had begun to rise again in Spain through the efforts and deceptions of a certain Syrian bishop, and so forth.”

The acts of this council of Seville, the second of that name, also place the matter beyond all controversy. In chapter twelve they narrate in explicit terms the events just mentioned, while in chapter thirteen they expound at length the doctrine of the two natures in Christ.

In the councils that followed, especially the Eleventh and Fourteenth Councils of Toledo, the same doctrine is repeatedly inculcated. We have already noted that Pope Benedict was offended because the Spaniards said that there were three substances in Christ, until they showed at the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, in the year 688, that they had asserted this in a Catholic sense and proved that they had used such language only to combat more effectively the heresies of Apollinaris and Eutyches.

From this, once again, it may be inferred that much was still being debated in Spain in those times concerning the mystery of the incarnation, and that not a few people survived against whom it was necessary to employ such weapons in defense of Catholic truth.

[Col. 0359D] **XXXIV. Migetius was infected with the same heresy; Elipandus attacks it again.**—That these errors had by then been completely defeated is all the less plausible because it is clear how great a confusion arose not long afterward, at the beginning of the eighth century, in the churches of Spain through the invasion of the Saracens. Christians lived there under barbarian domination, and councils in which the doctrine of the faith might be explained were rare—or rather, entirely absent.

Indeed, in the very errors of Migetius, which Elipandus had attacked with such fervor, something akin to [Col. 0360A] Eutychian doctrine lay concealed. This gave him an occasion to dispute not only about the divinity of the Word but also about its incarnation.

As for the doctrine of Eutyches, Liberatus describes it in the following words in chapter 11 of his *Brief Account of the Cause of Nestorianism and Eutychianism*: “Eutyches, urged on by Satan, preached that our Lord Jesus Christ was not consubstantial with us according to the flesh, but had a body from heaven; and again, changing his statement, he said: ‘Before the union there were two natures in Christ, but after the union they became one.’”

Eutyches therefore denied that true flesh had been assumed by the Word; and as a consequence of his doctrine he also had to deny it, once he asserted that the human nature had been absorbed by the divine after the union.

The Priscillianists, whose doctrines Migetius followed according to what was mentioned above, likewise taught something similar. This is evident from the previously cited Saint Leo. For, in chapter 17 of his letter to Turibius of Astorga, once more presenting a summary of the [Col. 0360B] Priscillianists’ errors at the end, he says: “The Son of God is proclaimed only-begotten because he was born from the Virgin, not because he was begotten from the Father; therefore neither a true offspring of God nor a true birth is asserted, so that through a false passion and death there may be a false resurrection of the flesh taken again from the tomb.”

Although there was a notable difference between the two heretics, Priscillian and Eutyches—for the former denied that the Son born from the Virgin was consubstantial with the eternal Father and true God, whereas the latter held an orthodox view concerning the divinity of the Word—nevertheless, both appear to have agreed in denying the reality of the assumed flesh. Thus, after vindicating the Son’s consubstantiality, Elipandus found it necessary also to defend the Church’s doctrine concerning his true incarnation from the womb of the blessed Virgin.

He defended it, as his writings clearly show, with particular zeal. In his creed preserved by Beatus, he describes the mystery of the incarnation with great precision in its individual [Col. 0360C] properties and says: “The one whom sacred Scripture testifies to have been made man for the salvation of the human race, with his divinity emptied, was circumcised, baptized, scourged, crucified, dead, buried, a servant, 958 a captive, and so forth.”

Hence, in his letter to Alcuin he says: “You are recognized as both an enemy and a defender, because, while you appear to vindicate the divinity of the Son of God, begotten from the Father before the ages, you seem to deny his humanity, assumed from the Virgin’s womb at the end of time.”

And in no. 7: “For with my own ears I heard the wicked presbyter say, following the doctrine of the wicked Beatus: ‘Christ Jesus, assuming flesh in his mother’s womb, did not draw it from his mother’s womb, but made new flesh for himself.’”

The same point appears in both letters of the Spanish bishops to the bishops of Gaul and others, and in the letter addressed to Charlemagne. In the former they say: “A grievous and mournful opinion has come to our knowledge ... concerning the wicked Beatus, presbyter of Astorga ... [Col. 0360D] because he asserts that the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, according to the form of human servitude, did not exist at all, and that he did not assume a true visible form from the Virgin.”

And farther below: “It remains that whoever denies that adoption ... is without doubt unable to affirm that a true man ... was born.”

In the latter they say: “The wicked presbyter and false prophet asserts that the Son of God, in the form of a servant, with his divinity emptied, did not at all assume flesh from the Virgin’s womb.”

And again: “Therefore we likewise ask that you eradicate from your kingdom the doctrine of the most fetid antiphrasis Beatus, who denies that the Son of God assumed from the Virgin true flesh like ours, except for sin.”

**XXXV. Felix likewise.**—Felix of Urgell also brought similar charges against the Catholics, as is plainly evident from his words reported by Alcuin in Book II. He says: “But if our Redeemer, in his flesh which he assumed from the Virgin’s womb—from the very moment of conception, namely [Col. 0361A]—was not an adopted son before the Father but a true and proper Son, what remains except that this same flesh was not created and made from the mass of the human race or from his mother’s flesh, but from the substance of the Father, just as his divinity was generated from it?”

Paulinus of Aquileia reports the following objection of Felix in chapter 27: “You, Felix, argue: ‘Whoever denies,’ you say, ‘that he is the adopted Son of God according to his humanity must necessarily deny that he was truly man.’”

The same statements occur frequently elsewhere in the writings of Felix and Elipandus. They seem to have devoted themselves entirely to avoiding the mixture or confusion of the natures introduced by the Apollinarists and Eutychians.

Therefore Alcuin says in Book I *Against Felix*: “Thus, just as Nestorian impiety divides Christ into two persons because of the two [Col. 0361B] natures ... so your ignorant rashness divides him into two sons, one proper and the other adopted. You cannot in any way, by thinking in this manner, avoid the impiety of Nestorian doctrine. For the one whom Nestorius divides into two persons on account of the two natures, you divide into two sons and two gods through the names ‘adoption’ and ‘designation.’ Recognize, then, this error of yours, humble yourselves beneath the hand of almighty God, and learn the doctrine of truth, lest you become teachers of error; lest, while you appear to avoid the pit of Eutyches and to guard against the mixture of the two natures, you fall improperly into the abyss of Nestorius by dividing him.”

Here Alcuin clearly indicates that Felix and his followers were extremely concerned to defend the two natures in Christ as unconfused against Eutyches. Because they proceeded incautiously, however, it eventually happened that, just as Nestorius divided Christ into persons on account of the two natures which he had undertaken to defend against the Apollinarists and the forerunners of Eutyches, so Elipandus and Felix divided him into two sons, a true son and an adopted son, in order to vindicate in him the existence of two unmixed natures.

**XXXVI. The same origin of the Nestorian and Adoptionist errors.**—It is therefore not unreasonable to say that the Nestorian and Adoptionist heresies had the same [Col. 0361C] origin. Just as Nestorianism owed its origin to an imprudent attack upon Arianism and Apollinarianism, as appears from the documents cited above, so Adoptionism must likewise be traced to those disputes in which the aforementioned Spanish bishops, with insufficiently purified zeal, contended concerning the divinity of the Word and its incarnation against the defenders and revivers of Arian and Eutychian depravity—which in this respect is the same as Apollinarianism.

From this alone, then, the affinity between the two errors—Nestorianism and Adoptionism—already becomes clear. Consequently, Alcuin had sufficient reason for counting the Adoptionists among the Nestorians, since their origins were precisely the same, as we have amply seen in this section. Indeed, their doctrines and principles also amounted to exactly the same thing, as we shall attempt to make clear in the following section from their own writings and from the testimony of others.

**§ II.—ON THE PRINCIPLES AND ASSERTIONS OF NESTORIANISM AND ADOPTIONISM**

[Col. 0361D] **I. How the mind of heretics may be discerned.**—If the opinions of heretics are to be known accurately, either their own writings must be examined, or, if these have perhaps perished entirely or at least for the greater part, the works of those who deliberately defended the Church’s doctrine against the efforts of innovators must be consulted. Such writers examined the assertions of their adversaries more thoroughly for this very reason.

We therefore cannot sufficiently wonder at the method proposed by the distinguished Walchius for detecting the Adoptionists’ opinion. In chapter 2, section 2, no. 7, page 216 of the cited *History*, he writes: “First, the testimonies of historians who, with their minds free from the desire to contradict, usually narrate events as they occurred must be placed before the eyes of readers. Next, the surviving testimonies of Elipandus and Felix must be collected and distributed into categories. Finally, when these are compared with one another, their true opinion and the coherence of their various [Col. 0362A] doctrines with one another may be more easily determined. The writings left to us by learned men who publicly fought against them—Felix and Elipandus—must, I think, be entirely disregarded, since it is abundantly clear that they were accustomed to commit to writing not what Elipandus and Felix actually thought, but what they believed those men to have thought.”

Walchius therefore considers greater trust to be owed to annalists, who sometimes narrate events in two words, than to men whom he himself calls learned; to men who devoted all their efforts to explaining the doctrine of the Church; and who examined and refuted the positions of their adversaries in extensive works.

Does Walchius consider greater trust to be owed to two bishops raised amid the barbarism oppressing Spain than to entire councils, convened not once but repeatedly, summoned from the whole Frankish empire as far as it then extended, and even from England, 959 and laboring diligently to elucidate the doctrine both of the Church and of the heretics? Let the learned [Col. 0362B] world judge whether this manner of forming an opinion conforms to sound rules of criticism.

We certainly believe that Walchius adopted this method of writing for a very different reason, as anyone may readily perceive by considering that he belonged to a group whose interest it is to detract from the authority of councils, the Fathers, and especially the Roman pontiff in matters of faith. Walchius pursued this aim, as it were, through underground passages, although he knew very well that, by the judgment of all these authorities, the Adoptionists had been condemned as Nestorians on more than one occasion.

But whatever his motive may have been in writing this, the aforementioned author should not otherwise be deprived of the praise of his learning. We trust that discerning critics will readily grant that there are no other sources to which one should turn in order to discover the opinions of heretics than those we have just indicated. We do not, however, deny that annalists and historians also possess authority; we ourselves shall often appeal to their testimony, and shall show shortly below that the Adoptionists are not so acquitted by the historians whom Walchius considers suitable for determining [Col. 0362C] this controversy that they are freed from the stain of Nestorianism. Rather, those same historians condemn them for the very same error.

To proceed once more in an orderly manner, we divide this section into two parts. In the first we shall discuss the assertions of the Nestorians; in the second, the positions of the Adoptionists. From their comparison, the intimate affinity of the two heresies will become almost visibly apparent.

## II. The Principles of the Nestorians

The errors concerning the incarnate Son of God that Nestorius and, before him, his teachers had long cherished in their hearts finally burst into public view in the sacrilegious sermons delivered by the presbyter Anastasius and the bishop Dorotheus from the sacred pulpits of Constantinople. Their principal purpose was to persuade people that the most blessed Virgin should not be called Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), or “God-bearer,” but Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*), that is, “Christ-bearer,” contrary to the faith of earlier times.

It is impossible to express how greatly the people of the imperial city were saddened by these assertions, by which the honor of the divine [Col. 0362D] Mother was attacked—especially when they saw that the most shameless mouths of these preachers were not merely left unclosed by their bishop, but were opened still more widely by him for the confirmation of impious doctrines. For without delay Nestorius undertook the defense of his most intimate friend Anastasius; he deemed that treacherous betrayer of the sacred deposit, Dorotheus, worthy of communion in the mysteries; he harassed the defenders of sound faith with terrible persecutions; and finally he arranged that his own sermons, filled everywhere with insults against the Virgin Θεοτόκος, should be circulated.

Nor should it be considered surprising that Nestorius and his supporters deviated into this opinion concerning the Mother of the incarnate Word, if we consider those principles that Nestorius himself had long conceived concerning the οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*, “dispensation”) of the Savior and later openly advanced in defense of his doctrine, or that his predecessors had formerly handed down concerning the same mystery. For these principles were such that they plainly introduced two sons in Christ, and were even believed by the entire Catholic world to introduce two sons [Col. 0363A]—something that Walchius himself does not deny was done legitimately and without injury to those men.

Once this had been granted, the consequence was exceedingly obvious: the most blessed Virgin would be called not Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), but ἀνθρωποτόκος (*anthropotokos*, “man-bearer”), since according to these principles she had given birth not to the Word himself, but only to a man assumed by the Word.

It is useful to report these matters in order, so that a closer comparison may subsequently be made with those doctrines that Felix and Elipandus later attempted to defend with such persistence in Spain.

## III. According to the Nestorians, the Man Assumed by the Word Was an Adoptive Son

That the author of the book against the Synusiasts regarded Christ, insofar as he is man, as merely an adoptive son is sufficiently clear from his words cited above in § 1, nos. 16 and 20; we therefore consider it unnecessary to repeat them here. Likewise, in no. 21 we cited words of Theodore of Mopsuestia filled with the same error; here we wish to add only a few things.

In vol. IX of the Councils, cited edition, col. 208, no. 13, the following appears in his interpretation of the Gospel according to John:

> “Concerning this expression, ‘My Father and your Father, my God and your God,’ no one is so insane as to say that it applies to someone else, except to the temple of the Word of God, that is, to the man assumed for our salvation—who also died, rose again, and was about to ascend into heaven; who assigned the Father to himself together with the Lord’s disciples; who himself, having merited adoption by grace, calls him his God, because he received existence in the same way as the other human beings. Therefore, because of the community of nature, he says, ‘My Father and your Father,’ and ‘my God and your God’; but again he distinguished his person from theirs, signifying the special grace by which, because of his union with the Word of God, he is honored by all human beings in the place of the true Son.”

And in no. 48, from the twelfth book *On the Incarnation*:

> “Therefore he is shown not only to call him a son, separating him from the Word of God, but also to number him, according to the principle of sonship, among the other participants in sonship; for he too participated in sonship by grace, not having been born naturally from the Father, yet possessing superiority over the others because, through union with him, he possesses sonship, which grants him a firmer participation in the reality itself.”

Nestorius also taught the same thing. For in the first session of the Council of Ephesus, the following words are cited from his *Quaternion* 17:

> “The Word of God was indeed God, and Son, and coexisting with the Father before the incarnation; but in the last times he also assumed the form of a servant. Yet although he was already the Son and was called the Son, after assuming the flesh he should not separately and by himself be called by the name ‘Son,’ lest we appear to introduce two sons. But because he was united to him who was the Son in the beginning, and joined to him, he cannot fail to receive a division with respect to the dignity of sonship, though not with respect to the natures. I speak of a division according to the dignity of sonship, not according to the natures. Hence the Word of God is also called Christ, because he has an everlasting union with Christ.”

Vol. IV of Mansi’s *Councils*, col. 1202.

Thus Nestorius considered the man assumed by the Word to be a Son only by dignity and grace—or, what is the same thing, by adoption—not by nature. This is even clearer from Cyril’s *Commonitorium*, where he describes the errors of Nestorius as follows:

> “The faith, or rather the heresy, of Nestorius is as follows. ‘The Word of God,’ he says, ‘having foreknown that the one born of the blessed Virgin would be holy and great, therefore chose him and caused him to be born of a virgin without a man; moreover, he bestowed upon him this grace, that he should be called by his own names and thus be called Son, Lord, and Christ.’”

Ibid., col. 547.

And in his book to Theodosius:

> “They dared to write concerning the Word in this manner: ‘This one’—namely, the Word of God the Father—‘is the true and natural Son; but that one’—namely, the one born of the Virgin—is called the Son of God equivocally.’ And shortly afterward again: ‘Certainly the Word of God is not man, but assumed a man. For the Only-begotten has from the beginning been the Son of God, the maker of all things; but the man whom he assumed, since he is not God by nature, is called by the same name as he, because of the one by whom he was assumed, who is the true Son of God.”

Col. 626.

Finally, in his book to the *Queens*, col. 609, no. 8 at the end, he says:

> “For they think that the glory both of sonship and of lordship came to the man born in our likeness from the holy Virgin by a certain mode of grace and through a process of development.”

## IV. The Reasons for This Assertion: Neither the Word Was Begotten from Mary, Nor the Man from the Eternal Father

Moreover, in order to confirm these assertions concerning a Son by adoption and grace, the Nestorians employed various arguments and testimonies from Scripture, the more important of which we consider it entirely necessary to present here.

First of all, they relied chiefly on the claim that neither the divinity had been born from the Virgin nor the humanity from the eternal Father. From this they inferred that the Word alone was the natural Son of God, while the man assumed was a son only by grace and adoption; consequently, the most holy Virgin ought to be called not the Mother of the Word, but the mother of the man.

The author of the book against the Synusiasts says:

> “And it is fitting for those who look carefully, since we seek natural fathers, neither to call the Word of God the son of David or of Abraham, but their maker; nor to say that the body existed before the ages from the Father, but that the seed of Abraham and David was born from Mary. When the question concerns births according to nature, let God the Word not be thought to be the son of Mary: for a mortal begets a mortal according to nature, and a body begets a body like itself. The Word of God did not undergo two births, one before the ages and the other in later times; rather, he was born from the Father according to nature, while the temple that was born from Mary he fashioned for himself from her very womb.”

And again:

> “We raise you up to a careful and cautious examination of doctrines; we labor for your sake, lest we have to render an account to the Lord for our silence. The perfect Son before the ages assumed the perfect one who is shown to be from David: the Son of God assumed the son of David. You will therefore say to me: ‘You preach two sons.’ I do not say two sons of David. Have I asserted that God is the son of David? Nor do I say two sons according to substance. Do I assert two sons begotten from the substance of God before the ages? I say that the Word of God dwelt in the one who is shown to be from the seed of David.”

In Garnerius’s edition of the works of Marius Mercator, cited above in § 1, no. 20.

Theodore argued in the same manner. In his book to the baptized the following is found:

> “For when he says, ‘concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh,’ it is certain that here he calls the one who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh a son, but does not call God the Word a son; rather, he speaks of the assumed form of a servant. For God is not according to the flesh; nor was God made from the seed of David, but a man assumed for us, whom the blessed Apostle plainly calls a son.”

Vol. IX of the Councils, col. 217, no. 35.

And in his book against Apollinarius:

> “The one who consists of the substance of the Virgin was born from the Virgin; God the Word was not born from Mary. The one who is from the seed of David was born from Mary. God the Word was not born from a woman, but the one who was fashioned in her by the power of the Holy Spirit was born from a woman. The one born from the mother is not consubstantial with the Father; for, according to the word of the blessed Paul, he is without a mother. Rather, the one who in later times was fashioned in the maternal womb by the power of the Holy Spirit was called without a father for this reason.”

Finally, in the twelfth book *On the Incarnation*, he explicitly says that the man assumed is not the proper Son of God, but merely an adoptive son, because he was not begotten from the eternal Father. These are his words, already cited in the preceding number:

> “Therefore he is shown not only to call him a son, separating him from the Word of God, but also to number him, according to the principle of sonship, among the other participants in sonship; for he too participated in sonship by grace, not having been born naturally from the Father, yet possessing superiority over the others because, through union with him, he possesses sonship, which grants him a firmer participation in the reality itself.”

Nestorius also denied on this basis that the blessed Virgin should be called Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), as appears from several of his writings:

> “Observe what follows, heretic,” he says in *Quaternion* 21, vol. IV of the Councils, col. 1198. “I do not begrudge the Virgin Christ-bearer her title. For I acknowledge that she is worthy of veneration, she who received God, through whom the Lord of all proceeded, through whom the Sun of righteousness shone forth. But again I regard the applause with suspicion: how have you understood the phrase ‘he proceeded’? I do not interpret ‘he proceeded’ and ‘he was begotten’ as the same thing. For we do not so quickly forget ourselves: I have indeed learned from divine Scripture that God proceeded from the Virgin Christ-bearer; but I have nowhere found it written that God was born from her.”

And shortly before, in *Quaternion* 17:

> “When Scripture explains the generation from the Virgin to us, it does not say, ‘God sent his Word,’ but says, ‘God sent his Son.’ For it takes the name that signifies both natures. Since the Son is simultaneously God and man, it therefore says, ‘God sent his Son, made from a woman’; so that when you hear ‘made from a woman’ and then see the name that denotes both natures placed before the birth from the holy Virgin, you hear the expressions concerning the Son—for the Virgin Christ-bearer also gave birth to the Son of God—yet, because the Son of God exists with a double nature, she gave birth not to the Son of God but to the humanity, which is a son because of the Son joined to it.”

Nestorius therefore held as his foundation that not the divine Word but only a man was born from the Virgin; and since this man was not begotten from the eternal Father, he was called the Son of God not by nature but only by grace or adoption, and indeed in a wholly singular and eminent manner, because of his singular union with the Word. Consequently, the Virgin was to be called not Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), but Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*).

## V. Other Nestorian Arguments Based on the Anointing of the Man Assumed

Furthermore, they maintained that the Son born from Mary was the Son of God by adoption alone because he had been anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit in the same manner as the other human beings, sanctified by baptism, and raised to this dignity as if through a process of development.

Theodore explains his view in his commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “For he says of Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power. Now whoever is anointed by the Spirit has certainly received something. But what madman would say that the divine nature received something from the Spirit and was also made a participant? For he calls those who themselves have been anointed his participants. Those who have been anointed, and who have rightly been made participants in him by this fact, cannot be said to share in the anointing in any other way than by sharing in the one who was assumed. This too is demonstrated by the fact that he received a just reward. For, he says, ‘because you loved righteousness and hated iniquity, for this reason you received an anointing surpassing that of your companions.’”

Vol. IX of the Councils, col. 216, no. 32.

And in book III against Apollinarius, col. 206, no. 7:

> “Let the wisest of all tell us: If, as they say, divinity had been made for the Lord Christ according to the flesh, what need did Christ have of the cooperation of the Holy Spirit for these things? For the divinity of the Only-begotten did not need the Spirit for justification; it did not need the Spirit for conquering the devil [lacuna]. But now he says that the very one was anointed by the Spirit, that the Spirit dwelt in him and assisted him in all his undertakings, that from it he received doctrine and power, that from it he obtained justification, and that by it he was made immaculate.”

And in no. 39, from the book to the baptized, col. 218:

> “For he says: ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Spirit and with power’; having merited his anointing, he was made immaculate in every respect and merited union with the divine nature. Nor would he have received that union unless he had first been made immaculate, so that he might thus be worthy of its unity.”

Theodore would certainly not have erred if, in refuting the errors of Apollinarius, he had demonstrated from this that Christ possessed a human soul, since he is said to have been anointed by the Holy Spirit, whereas this anointing cannot apply to the divine Word. For it must be regarded as entirely true that Christ received this anointing only insofar as he is man.

Nevertheless, the bishop mentioned above departed from the doctrine of the Church in judging that the frequently mentioned anointing was not owed to the assumed nature from the hypostatic union itself, but was first acquired by merit through actions by which he loved righteousness and hated iniquity, in a manner common to other human beings; and that by its power Christ the man was finally counted among the adoptive sons.

Nor was Nestorius foreign to this way of thinking. He attributed the name Christ, or “anointed,” to the man assumed by the Word, as we learn from Saint Cyril, who writes in his book to the *Queens*, no. 12:

> “Moreover, concerning this name ‘Christ,’ certain people—I do not know how—assert that it applies also to the Word of God the Father separately and by himself, that is, as he is conceived in the mind as existing outside the flesh; then they maintain that it applies similarly to the one born from the holy Virgin, insofar as he too is considered to subsist separately and by himself; finally, they teach that it is equally appropriate to both together as to one, on account of what they call their conjunction, which gathers them into one person. For they take no account among themselves of the true and natural conjunction, although they have before them this one way of the mystery, clear and safe from every error. And this feigned confession is not sincere, but full of the deception of black poison. For when divine Scripture names Christ and simply attributes all divine things to him—for it knows, yes, it knows, that the Word of God appeared in human form and became flesh—the purpose and design of those who think otherwise is to persuade us that the one born from a woman is some one man who, through growth and through his own, that is, human, power, showed himself worthy to obtain also the honor of connection with the Word of God and to be chosen by an extraordinary predestination.”

And in fact Nestorius thought that the name Christ was common to both natures, as appears from another of his letters to Cyril:

> “Here”—he is speaking of Saint Paul—“having mentioned the incarnation of God and immediately intending to add what concerned the passion, he first uses that name ‘Christ,’ as I said shortly before, as common to both natures; then he proceeds in such a way that the expression is appropriate to both natures, and so forth.”

They attributed the designation Christ to the Word because the Holy Spirit, to whom the anointing is ascribed, was proper to him and proceeded from the Father and the Son as of the same nature. But they called the assumed man “anointed,” just as each of the saints uses the power of the Holy Spirit as something external to himself.

All these points are gathered from Theodoret’s criticism of the ninth anathema of Saint Cyril and from Cyril’s defense against him, vol. V of the Councils, cols. 122 and 23; likewise from Saint Cyril’s letter to the Egyptian monks, nos. 15 and 16, vol. IV of the Councils, col. 602 and following.

## VI. The Argument for Adoption from Christ’s Baptism

Moreover, the adherents of the Nestorian system asserted in more than one place that the man whom the divine Word joined to himself in the last times had been sanctified by baptism and adopted as the Son of God, or at least had first been manifested to human beings as such. They thought that it was thereby conclusively proved that he was God’s adoptive Son, since he had received the sacrament of adoption.

Let us hear Theodore arguing in this way in book XIII *On the Incarnation*:

> “The Apostle also says consistently: ‘And manifestly great is the mystery of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit.’ In saying that he was justified in the Spirit, he means either that before baptism he kept the law with appropriate exactness, or that after baptism he also completed his way of life in grace with great exactness through the cooperation of the Spirit.”

Vol. IX of the Councils, col. 221, no. 53.

And in book III against Apollinarius, col. 205, no. 6:

> “When the Evangelist had said that he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, he clearly demonstrated that for this reason he received the indwelling of the Holy Spirit at baptism, so that from it he might receive the power he had undertaken to exercise. Therefore he was led by the Spirit to that contest which he was about to undertake against the devil for our sake.”

Finally, in book VIII against the Incarnation, in Leontius of Byzantium, vol. IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, fol. 701:

> “‘And the glory that you gave me I have given them.’ What glory? Namely, participation in adoption. For he himself received this according to his humanity when he was first baptized in the Jordan, in which our baptism was symbolically represented and regeneration confirmed by the testimony of the voice of the one who said, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ And the Spirit descended and remained upon him, as was to happen so that we too might participate in this Spirit in him. The Spirit came upon him more excellently than upon us through his union with the Word, while he participated in those things that belong to a son according to nature.”

Nestorius also agrees with these views, as we learn from the protest presented by the clergy of Constantinople in the church, accusing Nestorius of holding the same opinion as Paul of Samosata. There it says:

> “Paul says: ‘Yet he is superior to us in every respect, for he is from the Holy Spirit and was brought forth through divine promises, and according to Scripture grace was given to him.’ Nestorius says: ‘I saw the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, and also imparting to him the power of ascension; for, having chosen the apostles, he was taken up through the Holy Spirit. This, then, is the one who bestowed such great glory upon Christ.’”

Vol. IV of the Councils, cols. 1007 and 10.

## VII. The Argument from Progressive Development

Finally, Theodore and his disciple Nestorius consistently taught that the man assumed by the Word was raised to the dignity of the Son as if through a process of development.

Theodore says in book III against Apollinarius, in a fragment cited in Vigilius’s *Constitutum* concerning the Three Chapters:

> “Thus, he says, you also teach us to possess the most accurate understanding of Christ: that he had the Holy Spirit, who supplied some power to his understanding and granted him prudence for everything that had to be done. As we demonstrated earlier, he was led by the Spirit itself into the desert for the contests against the devil; he received from it his anointing, knowledge, and power concerning the things that had to be done. Having become its participant, he not only performed miracles, but also knew precisely how miracles ought to be used, so that he might make piety known to the nations, suffer the infirmities of those who were suffering, and thus bring his will to accomplishment. By this means he was justified and shown to be immaculate, whether through the restoration of worse things, the preservation of better things, or even through gradual advances toward better things.”

And in Leontius of Byzantium, in the place cited, fol. 701, from book VII against the Incarnation:

> “Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings. He advanced in age through the passage of time; in wisdom, acquiring understanding according to the progress of time; and in grace, receiving a power corresponding to his understanding and knowledge. Thereafter the grace that he possessed before God received addition and increase. In all these things he advanced before God and human beings. Human beings saw his progress; God not only saw it but approved it by his testimony and cooperated in the things that were done. It is therefore also evident that he carried out virtue with so much greater perfection and ease than the other human beings could achieve, as God, who had united him to himself at the very beginning of his formation, gave him greater cooperation from himself to accomplish the things necessary for the salvation of all. He governed all his actions, urged him toward greater perfection, and lightened to a greater extent his labors, whether they concerned soul or body. Thus the completion of virtue was established in him as greater and easier.”

Nestorius taught similar things, as is evident from his words reported in the first session of the Council of Ephesus, vol. IV of the Councils, col. 1203, from *Quaternion* 6, where he speaks about Christ:

> “He was sent to preach release to the captives and restoration of sight to the blind. And, as the Apostle adds, he says: ‘This is the one who was made a faithful high priest to God.’ For he was made one who had not pre-existed from eternity. This, heretic, is the one who was gradually raised to priestly dignity. Hear a voice that thunders this more clearly to you: ‘In the days of his flesh,’ it says, ‘he offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, and he was heard because of his reverence’; and although he was a son, ‘he learned obedience from the things he suffered,’ and, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him. But that which gradually advances is brought to perfection, heretic. Therefore John also cries out in the Gospels: ‘Jesus,’ he says, ‘advanced in age, wisdom, and grace.’”

Theodoret agrees in his criticism of Saint Cyril’s tenth anathema, where he says:

> “[Lacuna.] Then, showing the weakness of the assumed nature, he says: ‘In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, and he was heard because of his reverence,’ and so forth. Who, then, is the one who was made perfect through labors of virtue and does not exist perfect by nature? Who is the one who learned obedience, having been ignorant of it before experience? Who lived with reverence and offered supplications with a loud cry and tears, and was unable to save himself, but asked the one who could save him and sought deliverance from death? Not God the Word [lacuna], but the one assumed from the seed of David.”

Vol. V of the Councils, col. 126.

Proclus, bishop of Cyzicus, also sets the following statement against the Nestorians in his homily, no. 4:

> “Nor did Christ become God through successive increases in virtues—far be it from us.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, col. 582.

From these things it is clear that the common opinion of those heretics was that the man assumed by the Word successively attained the dignity of the Son, or grew into it as if by progressing. Indeed, it can also be gathered without ambiguity from another letter of Cyril to Nestorius that some held the opinion that the human nature had not been united to the Word from the first moment of conception, but had acquired this union later, first by its own merits:

> “For,” says Cyril, “it was not the case that first an ordinary man arose from the Virgin and that the Word of God subsequently descended upon him.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, col. 890.

The words of Theodore cited above in no. 5 from the book to the baptized also appear to refer to this error, although in other places he teaches the contrary.

These, then, were the reasons why Theodore, Nestorius, and their other fellow soldiers counted the man assumed among the adoptive sons, going further and inferring that the Virgin who had borne him should be called merely ἀνθρωποτόκος (*anthropotokos*, “man-bearer”).

## VIII. Christ as a God Named by Extrinsic Designation

Just as they defended the position that Christ, insofar as he is man, was an adoptive, not a natural or proper, Son of God, so they stubbornly maintained that, with respect to his humanity, he too should be believed to be God only by an extrinsic designation.

There are again many testimonies of theirs concerning this matter, of which it will be sufficient to recite only some. We already mentioned the words of Theodore and the judgment of Pope Vigilius concerning them in § I, no. 21. Here we do not wish to add anything except what is found in his creed, reported in session IV of the fifth council.

There it says:

> “We do not say two sons, nor two lords, because one Son according to substance is God the Word, the only-begotten Son of the Father, to whom this one is joined and in communion with whom he shares the name and honor of Son; and one Lord according to substance is God the Word, with whom this one is joined and with whom he shares the honor. Therefore we do not say two sons or two lords, because, once the Lord and Son have been established according to nature, the one assumed for our salvation, having an inseparable union with him, shares with him the honor and designation of son and lord, and so forth.”

According to Theodore, therefore, the assumed man, because of his union with the Word, possesses with him “the honor and designation of son and lord”; or, what amounts to the same thing, Christ, insofar as he is man, can be called God and Lord by designation alone, not in the reality of the thing.

Hence Leontius of Byzantium attacks Theodore in book III against the Nestorians and Eutychians with these words:

> “For you do not teach that God became man, but that worship should be offered eternally to a man honored by the designation of God.”

Vol. IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, fol. 697.

Nestorius had adopted the same opinion as his own, saying:

> “Thus we call the one who is Christ according to the flesh God because he is joined to the Word of God, although we are not unaware that the man who appeared was a man. Hear Paul preaching both: ‘From the Jews,’ he says, ‘is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all.’ First he confesses that he is a man; then, because of the fellowship that he has obtained with God, he calls that man God, lest anyone should suspect that Christians worship a man.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, col. 1199, from *Quaternion* 15, in the dogmatic statement.

And again in *Quaternion* 16, where he speaks about Christ:

> “That which was formed in the womb is not God by itself and according to itself; that which was formed by the work of the Holy Spirit is not God by itself and according to itself; that which was laid in the tomb is not God by itself and according to itself. For otherwise we would plainly be worshipers of dead human beings. But because God exists in the man assumed, the assumed one is called God because he is joined to the one who assumes him.”

Ibid., col. 1203.

Cyril also reports this error of Nestorius in his *Commonitorium*, saying:

> “Therefore he does not confess that he himself”—namely, the man assumed—“is the true God, but that he was called so because of God’s benevolent will; and although he was called Lord, he again wishes him to be Lord in such a way that God the Word granted him by grace to be called so.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, col. 550.

## IX. The Reasons by Which the Nestorians Supported the Extrinsic Designation of God: From the Scriptural Passages in Which Human Beings Are Called Gods

Furthermore, the defenders of that view of a God named only by designation attempted to establish it by various arguments drawn both from Scripture and from elsewhere. They thought they could extract a sufficiently firm foundation from those passages of Scripture in which the name of God is also attributed to human beings, namely by an extrinsic designation alone. From this they concluded that Christ, insofar as he is man, likewise shares in this designation, since according to his human nature he must be considered entirely different from the divine Word and, on the other hand, of the same condition as the other human beings.

Theodore appears to have used this method of argument in his commentary on the Gospel of Saint Luke, when he says:

> “For this expression, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,’ demonstrates adoption in baptism according to the analogy of Jewish adoption, since it had also been said to them: ‘I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High,’ and so forth.”

Nestorius affirms that Christ the man was called God for the same reason that Moses was called the god of Pharaoh:

> “Indeed, just as we call the maker of all things God,” he says, “and again call Moses God—for he says, ‘I have appointed you God over Pharaoh’—and Israel the Son of God—for he says, ‘Israel is my firstborn son’—and just as Saul is called Christ—for he says, ‘I will not lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s Christ’—and likewise it is said concerning Cyrus, ‘Thus says the Lord to my Christ, Cyrus’—and concerning the holy Babylonians, ‘For I will command them; for they have been sanctified, and I will lead them’; so also we call Christ Lord, God, Son, holy, and Christ.”

*Quaternion* 27, vol. IV of the Councils, col. 1199.

Cyril, in his explanation of the fifth anathema, by which he had established that Christ was not a God-bearing man (*Deiferum*) but the true God, writes:

> “But they affirm”—the Nestorians—“that the only-begotten Word of God dwelt in the man born from the holy Virgin just as in one of the saints, so that it is no longer necessary to confess that there is one Christ, Son, and Lord, who is to be worshiped; rather, that, considered as a man in himself and separately, he should, on account merely of the conjunction in a unity of dignity, be honored by being worshiped and glorified together with the Word. ‘The God of all dwells in us through the Holy Spirit,’ and so forth.”

He then adduces certain passages of Scripture that the Nestorians had abused. Among these he also includes the following passage from the Gospel of Saint John 10:34, saying:

> “Christ himself said of his holy prophets, or of the saints who had gone before: ‘If he called those gods to whom the word of God came, do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, “You blaspheme,” because I said, “I am the Son of God”?’ But God does not dwell in Christ in the same way as in us. For he was God by nature, made like us, one and the only Son even when he became flesh.”

Vol. V of the Councils, col. 11.

In these and similar words, therefore, the Nestorians placed their defense, attempting to prove that the man assumed was God only in name, whereas the Synusiasts had affirmed that after the union he had become of the same nature as the Word.

For since the Arians, as we noted already in § I, had maintained that the very Word of the Father was God only by designation, while the Synusiasts said that the human nature, or flesh, was also consubstantial with the Word, the Nestorians—believing that they were proceeding by a middle path—attributed to Christ the truth of divine nature insofar as he is the Son begotten eternally from the Father, but the external dignity of the divine name insofar as he is man and of the same nature as us.

## X. The Nestorians’ Argument from the Statement that the Word Dwelt in Us, or that God Was in Christ

There were nevertheless other texts on which they still relied, among which the principal ones were those in which God, or the Word, is said to have dwelt in the assumed man. Hence they appeal very frequently to the Evangelist’s words: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Likewise to Paul’s words: “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9); “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

Accordingly, the following expressions were also familiar to them: that Christ’s humanity was a temple inhabited by the Word; that Christ was a man who bore God, *homo Deifer*, a man belonging to the Lord, *homo Dominicus*; and therefore that he was God not by nature or in truth, but by mere designation.

The author of the book *Against the Synusiasts* (*κατὰ Συνουσιαστῶν*), in the frequently cited passage, says:

> “I say, then, that the Word of God dwelt in him who is shown to be from David’s seed.”

And again:

> “Let it suffice for the body that is from us, according to grace, to have sonship, glory, and immortality, because it has been made the temple of the Word of God.”

And:

> “The Word was begotten from the Father by nature; but the temple, which was born from Mary, he fashioned for himself from the womb itself.”

Theodore, in the third book *Against Apollinarius*, addresses this heretic as follows:

> “How, then, can you, to whom above all it is most fitting to exercise the governance of minds, say that he who was born from the Virgin is God and is regarded as consubstantial with the Father from God—unless, perhaps, you command us to attribute his creation to the Holy Spirit? But who is God from God and consubstantial with the Father? The very one who was born from the Virgin, astonishingly enough!—the one who was fashioned by the Holy Spirit according to the divine Scriptures and received his formation in a woman’s womb? Perhaps he was present immediately after he had been fashioned, and received this status so that he might be the temple of God. Yet we must not think that God was born from the Virgin—unless perhaps we must likewise regard as identical what was born, what is the temple in the one who was born, and God the Word who is in the temple.”

Volume IX of the Councils, column 203, no. 1.

Nestorius, in his second letter to Cyril, no. 2, praises this holy teacher for having been exceedingly careful to avoid confusion of the natures in Christ; then he continues:

> “The one whom previously you had proclaimed neither passible nor capable of a second generation, you now assert to be passible and, recently and somehow inexplicably, to have been produced—as though those things that naturally belong to the Word had been abolished by the conjunction with the temple; or as though that temple, never polluted by any sin and inseparable from the divine nature, ought to be considered of little account among human beings because it was both born and died for the sake of our sins; or finally as though one ought not to believe the Lord when he addresses the Jews with this utterance: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ Notice that he does not say, ‘Destroy my divinity,’ but, ‘Destroy this temple.’”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 895.

Theodoret, in his refutation of the first anathema of Saint Cyril, expresses his mind in these words:

> “Therefore God the Word did not become flesh, but assumed living and rational flesh; he himself was not naturally born from the Virgin . . . but, forming a temple for himself in the virginal womb, he was with the one who had been formed and born.”

And shortly afterward:
