> “Since [the form of a servant] was not bare of the form of God, but was the temple of the God Word who inhabited it, according to Paul’s saying—for he says, ‘In him it pleased the whole fullness of deity to dwell bodily’—we call the Virgin not the mother of a man but the Mother of God, assigning the former designation to the molding, formation, and conception, and the latter to the union.”

Volume V of the Councils, column 87.

That the Nestorians also abused the Apostle’s words, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” in order to prove that the assumed man was God only by an external designation, is manifest from a second discourse of Saint Cyril, addressed to the most religious queens on the right faith. The holy teacher argues there as follows:

> “He also subjects the whole race of mortals, otherwise unbridled and prone to rebellion, to the scepters of the divinity through him, since, as the most wise Paul admonishes us, ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.’ Yet we most certainly do not assert what certain less instructed persons do: that another Christ, distinct from him whom the holy Virgin brought forth, dwelt in a man and reconciled the world to himself.”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 866.

Since the Nestorians consistently asserted that the assumed man was the temple of the divine Word, they very frequently employed the following expressions: namely, that Christ was God’s household member, a man belonging to the Lord, or a man who bore God. It will therefore be useful to adduce one or two testimonies concerning this matter.

Theodore, in the first book of his interpretation of the Gospel according to John, commenting on the words, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel,” says:

> “This means: You are the one who was proclaimed from afar as the Christ. For this is what he hoped concerning Christ, since he had been constituted, above all others, a member of God’s household.”

Volume IX of the Councils, column 217, no. 33.

Immediately afterward, in the following number, he says:

> “He himself was indeed certain, when speaking of the Son of God, that he did not mean birth according to deity, but according to the fact that he was a member of God’s household; by this designation the sons of God—human beings who, through the virtue of being members of God’s household, had been constituted such—were meanwhile called.”

Here Theodore calls the human Christ “God” and “Son of God” because, through the assumption, he had been made a member of God’s household; but he does so only in the same manner in which other human beings, through the virtue of belonging to God’s household, are honored with the same titles.

That Nestorius and his followers called Christ a man who bore God is testified by Saint Cyril. In his letter of excommunication to Nestorius, no. 4, he writes:

> “Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt in the Son of the holy Virgin as in some ordinary man, lest Christ be understood as a man who bears God.”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 1074.

Accordingly, he formulated his fifth anathema in these words:

> “If anyone dares to say that Christ is a man who bears God, and not rather the true God, as the one and natural Son—insofar, namely, as the Word, having become flesh, shared in flesh and blood just as we do—let him be anathema.”

Theodoret, however, in his refutation of this anathema, says:

> “Therefore, using the term ‘sharing,’ we worship one Son, both him who assumed and that which was assumed; yet we acknowledge the distinction of the natures, and we do not avoid calling him a man who bears God, as he has been called by many holy Fathers . . . We call him a man who bears God, not because he received some particular divine grace, but because he possesses the entire deity of the Son united to him.”

Volume V of the Councils, column 111.

Cyril then responds to these words:

> “For we say that Christ ought not to be called by anyone a man who bears God, lest he be understood as one of the saints, but rather as the true God, the Word of God himself, who became man and was incarnate.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Why, then, does he not cease disturbing the right and entirely unperverted rule of faith? At one time he calls Christ and Son and Lord one and the same, God and man together; at another, granting him the measure of the prophets, he calls him a man who bears God. Perhaps he does not realize that by this he makes him equal to us. For if he is not truly God but rather a temple, inasmuch as God the Word dwells in him, just as he does in us . . .”

The same place.

## XI. The Nestorians’ Argument from Christ’s Priestly Office and Prayer

The Nestorians constructed a third argument from the priestly dignity that Scripture everywhere ascribes to Christ, and from the prayer that he is said to have poured out to the Father in more than one passage. They thought that neither of these belonged to the true God, but only to the man who, like others, although called God by a singular privilege, possessed them.

Nestorius teaches this in the clearest terms when he says:

> “Since, then, this one is our high priest, compassionate, related to us, and steadfast, do not depart from the faith that is in him. For he was sent to us from the seed of Abraham according to the promised blessing, offering sacrifice as though on behalf of himself and of the race related to him.”

But notice that, while he admits that every high priest needs a sacrifice, he exempts Christ as though he had not needed one; nevertheless, he asserts that Christ offered sacrifice both on his own behalf and on behalf of the race related to him.

Quaternio 17, volume IV of the Councils, column 1206. See also what we cited above, no. 7, from Nestorius’s quaternio 6.

Cyril likewise reports these words of his in book III *Against Nestorius*:

> “When they hear the name ‘apostle,’ they understand the Word of God himself as an apostle. When they read the designation ‘high priest,’ they imagine the divinity itself to be a high priest, in a new form of madness. For who, upon learning of the office of an apostle, would not immediately understand that a man is indicated? Who, hearing the designation ‘high priest,’ would regard the divine essence itself as the high priest? For if the divinity itself is the high priest, who is the one honored by the office of high priesthood? If it is God who offers, there is no one to whom he offers. For what is worthy of divinity, that it should offer as an inferior to one greater?”

Volume VI of the Works of Saint Cyril, folio 64, Paris edition, 1638.

Therefore Cyril opposed these erroneous assertions with his tenth anathema, saying:

> “Divine Scripture teaches that Christ has been made the high priest and apostle of our confession, and that he also offered himself for us to God and the Father as a fragrant offering. If anyone therefore says that our high priest and apostle is not the Word of God himself, after he became flesh and a man like us, but that man born of a woman, as though he were someone else distinct from him; or if anyone says that he offered sacrifice also for himself and not rather for us alone—for he had no need of an offering, since he knew no sin—let him be anathema.”

In his explanation of this anathema he says:

> “I do not know how those who think otherwise contend that it was not the Word of God himself, made man, who became the apostle and high priest of our confession, but rather some other man, separately born from the holy Virgin, who was called an apostle and high priest and was raised to this dignity by making progress; nor do they say that he offered himself as a sacrifice to God and the Father for us alone, but also for himself. This is wholly alien to the right and blameless faith, for he had committed no sin.”

Volume V of the Councils, column 18.

Theodoret, in his refutation of the same anathema, writes:

> “The unchangeable nature was not transformed into the nature of flesh; rather, it assumed human nature and set it above ordinary high priests, as blessed Paul teaches when he says: ‘Every high priest taken from among human beings,’ and so forth.”

After quoting the Apostle’s words at length from chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, he continues: “Who, then, is he?” and so forth. See above, no. 7.

## XII. The Nestorians’ Argument from the Fact that the True God Cannot Suffer

Finally, they also denied that Christ, insofar as he is man, is the true God because, once this assertion was admitted, death, suffering, and other things would have to be ascribed to God or the Word which in fact belonged only to human nature. Hence their common opinion was that it was not this Word but only the assumed man who endured the suffering of death in himself, and that no passage occurred in Scripture in which God himself was affirmed to have died or to have been handed over for us.

The author of the book *Against the Synusiasts* consistently impressed upon his opponents that suffering was to be attributed not to the Word but only to the flesh, only to the assumed man. When they objected to the miracles that occurred at the Savior’s death—miracles that certainly would not have taken place if a mere man, and not the very Word of the Father, had suffered—he answers the objection as follows:

> “But if it was flesh that was crucified,” he says, “how did the sun turn away its rays, darkness cover the whole earth, earthquakes occur, rocks split apart, and the dead rise? What, then, will they say about the darkness that occurred in Egypt in the time of Moses—not for three hours but for three days? What will they say about the other miracles performed through Moses, and those performed through Joshua, who made the sun stand still? The sun also turned backward contrary to nature in the time of King Hezekiah. And what of the remains of Elisha, which raised a dead man? If they demonstrate that God the Word suffered from what took place on the cross, and do not allow that these things occurred on account of the man, did not the things that occurred in the time of Moses occur on account of the race of Abraham, and those in the time of Joshua, and those in the time of King Hezekiah? But if those things were miraculously done for the people of the Jews, how could the things that occurred on the cross not have occurred all the more for the temple of God the Word?”

Garner, in the place cited.

In the work addressed *To the Baptized*, Theodore attributes the passion solely to the assumed man, saying:

> “In order to show great care for him [that is, the assumed man], he made everything belonging to him his own and endured all his sufferings, leading him through all the passions by which he perfected him according to his virtue. He did not withdraw from the dead according to the law of his own nature, but by his presence, operation, and grace he both freed him from death and from the evils that arise from it, raised him from the dead, and brought him to a better end.”

Volume IX of the Councils, column 217, no. 37.

In the immediately following number he speaks more explicitly:

> “Then, showing for whose sake he suffered, he introduces the abasement: that, apart from God, he might taste death for all; because, the divine nature so willing, it having been separated, he himself by himself tasted death for the benefit of all. And he shows that the deity was indeed separated from him who suffered with respect to the experience of death—for it was impossible for it to undergo the experience of death—yet was not absent from him who suffered with respect to its care.”

Nestorius, in his second letter to Cyril, no. 3, argues in this way:

> “There are countless other statements which make it evident to the human race that the divinity was neither recently born nor capable of bodily suffering, but that it was the flesh itself which was joined to the divine nature. Hence Christ himself also calls David his Lord and his Son: ‘What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?’ They say to him, ‘David.’ Jesus answered and said to them, ‘How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand”?’ He is plainly the son of David according to the flesh, but according to divinity he is David’s Lord.

> “It is therefore right and consistent with evangelical tradition that we confess Christ’s body to be the temple of the divinity, and that it was joined to the divinity by so lofty, divine, and wondrous a bond that we say that the divine nature appropriates to itself things that otherwise belong properly to the body. But to ascribe to the divine Word, on account of this appropriation, birth, suffering, death, and the other properties of the flesh—that, my brother, is the thinking either of a truly misguided mind in the manner of the pagans, or of the insane Apollinarius, or of one suffering from the disease of Arius and the other heretics, or from some even more serious illness, and so forth.”

Volume IV of the Councils, columns 895 and 98.

Elsewhere, namely in quaternio 16, he says:

> “And in general, if you carefully search the whole of the New Testament together, nowhere in it will you find death ascribed to God, but rather to Christ, or the Lord, or the Son. When these expressions—Christ, Son, and Lord—are attributed to the Only-Begotten in the Scriptures, they serve as indicators of the two natures. At one time they express the divinity, at another the humanity, and at times both together.

> “For example, when the Apostle Paul proclaims in his Epistle, ‘When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son,’ he clearly indicates the humanity of the Son. But when he again says to the Hebrews, ‘God has spoken to us in the Son, through whom he made the ages,’ he indicates the divinity of the Son. For the flesh did not create the ages, since it was formed only after many ages.

> “And below: The deity did not have Jacob as a brother, nor do we proclaim the death of the Word of God while we are refreshed by the Lord’s body and blood.”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 1206.

For this reason they also denied that the proper Son of God had been handed over or had suffered for us. Saint Cyril censures this error in his book *On the Faith to the Queens*, writing:

> “If God the Father gave his proper Son—that is, the very one who originated from his substance—for us, then the body that endured death belonged to the one who suffered according to the flesh. For according to the account of his divinity he could not suffer. Thus he who in himself cannot suffer endured death economically, according to the dispensation.

> “Therefore those who divide the one into two plainly bind themselves under the charge of impiety. For if there is a man by himself and in himself, separately, and not the very Word of God clothed in flesh, then the Father is not found to have given his proper Son for us.”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 770.

He pursues this error further in his twelfth anathema:

> “If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh and was crucified in the flesh, and that he tasted death in the flesh, and that he became the firstborn from the dead—insofar as, being God, he is life and life-giving—let him be anathema.”

Theodoret responded to this in an erroneous manner:

> “Sufferings belong to the passible nature; for the impassible is too exalted to be able to suffer. Therefore the form of a servant suffered, while the form of God was attached to it and permitted it to suffer for the sake of the salvation brought about through suffering; yet, because of the union, it claimed the sufferings for itself. Therefore it was not Christ who suffered, but the man from among us who was assumed by the Word.”

Volume V of the Councils, column 138.

## XIII. Christ, as Man, the Servant of God in the Perverse Sense According to the Nestorians

Since, as is clear from what has been said thus far, the Nestorians said that Christ, as man, was a son only by adoption and God only by designation, it is not surprising that they likewise made the servitude frequently attributed by Scripture to the divine Son belong exclusively to human nature, and called Christ, insofar as he is man, a servant.

This seems to be gathered without difficulty from what Nestorius wrote on Paul’s words in Philippians 2:3, “Have this mind among yourselves,” and so forth:

> “He did not say, ‘Have this mind among yourselves, which was also in the Word God, who, although he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant.’ Rather, by accepting the word ‘Christ’ as encompassing the notion of both natures, he safely asserts both that he took the form of a servant and calls him God, distributing the force of the statements without injury between the duality of the natures.”

This is confirmed by Saint Cyril’s sixth anathema, which reads:

> “If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that he is at once God and man, the same person, insofar as the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.”

The Nestorians therefore said that the Word of the Father was the Lord of the assumed man, and that the latter was his servant. The eternal Son united the form of the servant to himself; and by uniting himself to that form, or by dwelling in it, he emptied himself, as they understood the matter. Saint Cyril reports this again in his letter to the Monks of Egypt, no. 14, volume IV of the Councils, column 602:

> “Let him answer whether the one who by nature and in truth was the Son, free, and the Word of the Father, who existed in the form of the Begetter and was equal to him, dwelt in the man whom the woman brought forth; and whether everything that is transmitted anywhere concerning emptying, humiliation, or assumption of the form of a servant tends toward this.
>
> “But tell me, whoever you are: Do you think that the mere indwelling of the divine Word in the man is sufficient to establish that emptying? Do you consider it harmless if the Word is said, on this single basis, to have assumed the form of a servant and endured such a manner of humiliation?”

In no. 13 of the same letter he relates that there were certain persons among Nestorius’s followers who attributed this emptying, or assumption of the form of a servant, not to the Word himself but solely to the man whom the Word had united to himself. From this it follows that, in explaining Paul’s words, they differed somewhat from one another in the customary manner of heretics; yet they were especially united in thinking that Christ, as man, was truly the servant of the Father and even of the Word who had assumed him.

Let us hear Theodore further. In his refutation of the first anathema cited above, he reasons as follows:

> “Blessed Paul calls what was assumed by God the Word the form of a servant. But since the assumption preceded the union, and since, in discussing the assumption, the same blessed Paul called the assumed nature the form of a servant, the name of servitude no longer has a place once the union has taken place.
>
> “For if the same Apostle, writing to those who had believed in him, said, ‘Therefore you are no longer a servant but a son,’ and if the Lord said to the disciples, ‘I will no longer call you servants but friends,’ much more has the firstfruits of our nature, through whom we too have obtained the gift of adoption, been freed from the designation of servant.
>
> “We therefore confess that the very form of a servant is God, and we believe the Prophet when he calls Emmanuel a child, and the child born ‘the angel of great counsel,’ ‘Wonderful Counselor,’ ‘Mighty God,’ ‘the one who has authority,’ ‘the Prince of Peace,’ and ‘the Father of the age to come.’”

Nevertheless, the same Prophet, even after the union, when proclaiming the nature of the assumed one, calls him a servant who is from the seed of Abraham, saying: “You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified” (Isaiah 49). And again: “Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as his servant,” and so forth.

Theodoret indeed admits here that the assumed man ought not to be called a servant once the union has taken place, since by reason of this union he is honored with the designation of God and Son. Nevertheless, if Christ is considered precisely as man, he thinks that he must still be called a servant; and he believes that he found the foundation of this opinion in the words of Isaiah, without considering that two persons must necessarily follow in Christ if true and properly understood servitude is ascribed to him as man.

## XIV. The Nestorians Established These Principles Above All to Avoid Confusion of the Natures in Christ

These, finally, were the more important principles of the Nestorians and their more notable assertions. They adopted them all the more readily because they seemed to themselves thereby to restrain the attack of the Apollinarists with greater security and strength.

Although, in the earlier struggle against the Arians, some had already fallen into similar distinctions between the divine and human natures, their more immediate conflict was then against the Synusiasts, who had arisen within the circle of Apollinarius. Since these men wished the flesh to be consubstantial with the Word, thereby introducing a confusion of the natures, the distinction between them had to be defended with every force of argument even after the union.

This was also the principal aim of the writers whom we have cited from the company of the Nestorians in the course of this paragraph, although, by hurling their arguments imprudently, they went beyond that aim.

The author of the book *Against the Synusiasts* indicates this plainly enough when, in the passage cited several times, he says:

> “We raise you to a careful and prudent examination of doctrines. The perfect Son before the ages assumed the perfect one who is shown to be from David: the Son of God assumed the son of David.”

And shortly afterward:

> “I say, then, that the Word of God dwelt in him who is shown to be from David’s seed.”

And again:

> “If anyone wishes, abusively, to call the Son of God, God the Word, the son of David, let him do so on account of the temple of the Word of God, which is from David; and let him call him who is from David’s seed the Son of God by grace, not by nature.”

Here there is an evident distinction between “this one” and “that one,” between the Son of God and the son of David.

Theodore argues similarly in his interpretation of Psalm 8:

> “Therefore the Psalm shows us so great a difference between God the Word and the man who was received. These matters are divided in the New Testament: the Lord takes up the beginning of the Psalm, in which it says that he is the creator of creation, that he possesses magnificence exalted above the heavens, and that he is made wondrous in all the earth; whereas the Apostle takes up the second part, the things concerning the man who received so great a benefit, in Jesus.
>
> “How is it not manifest that divine Scripture clearly teaches us that the one is God the Word and the other is a man, and shows us that there is a great difference between them? For the one remembers, whereas the other is worthy to be remembered; the one visits, whereas the other, when he is deemed worthy of visitation, is called blessed; the one, by granting a benefit, makes him a little lower than the angels, whereas the other received a benefit through such abasement; the one crowns with glory and honor, whereas the other is crowned and is called blessed for these things; the one establishes him over all the works of his hands and subjects everything beneath his feet, whereas the other was deemed worthy to rule over those things over which he previously had no authority.”

Volume IX of the Councils, column 211, no. 19.

## XV. The Nestorians’ Distinctive Distinctions between “This One” and “That One” in Christ

Further, in order, as they thought, to express this difference of natures more clearly, they everywhere employed the following modes of speech: “this one and that one,” “the one who assumed,” “the one who was assumed,” and so forth. For this reason Saint Cyril rightly reproves them for dividing the persons, when in his book *On the Faith to Theodosius*, no. 6, he says:

> “For they separate the one Christ into two, and, introducing a certain gross separation between this one and that one, maintain that each stands separately and, as it were, by himself.”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 626.

The author of the book *Against the Synusiasts* opposed his adversaries by this line of argument, writing in the passage cited:

> “We raise you to a careful and prudent examination of doctrines. The perfect Son before the ages assumed the perfect one who is shown to be from David: the Son of God assumed the son of David.”

And shortly afterward:

> “I say, then, that the Word of God dwelt in him who is shown to be from David’s seed.”

And again:

> “If anyone wishes, abusively, to call the Son of God, God the Word, the son of David, let him do so on account of the temple of the Word of God, which is from David; and let him call him who is from David’s seed the Son of God by grace, not by nature.”

Here is a manifest distinction between this one and that one, between the Son of God and the son of David.

Theodore argues thus in his interpretation of Psalm 8:

> “Therefore the Psalm shows us so great a difference between God the Word and the man who was received. These matters are divided in the New Testament: the Lord takes up the beginning of the Psalm, in which he is said to be the creator of creation, to possess magnificence exalted above the heavens, and to be made wondrous in all the earth; whereas the Apostle takes up in Jesus the second part, concerning the man who received so great a benefit. How is it not manifest that divine Scripture clearly teaches us that the one is God the Word and the other a man, and shows us that there is a great difference between them? For the one remembers, whereas the other is worthy to be remembered; the one visits, whereas the other, when he is deemed worthy of visitation, is called blessed; the one, by granting a benefit, makes him a little lower than the angels, whereas the other received a benefit through such abasement; the one crowns with glory and honor, whereas the other is crowned and is called blessed for these things; the one establishes him over all the works of his hands and subjects everything beneath his feet, whereas the other was deemed worthy to rule over those things over which he previously had no authority.”

Volume IX of the Councils, column 211, no. 19.

Nestorius also held views entirely consistent with these. In quaternio 15, cited above in no. 8, he says:

> “Thus we also call him who is Christ according to the flesh God, because he is joined to God the Word, not being unaware that the one who appeared was a man. Hear Paul proclaiming both: ‘From the Jews is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all.’ First he confesses him to be a man; then, on account of the fellowship that he received with God, he calls that man God.”

Nestorius carefully distinguishes between God the Word and that man. He does the same when he calls one the assumer and the other the assumed, the bearer and the borne:

> “Because of the bearer,” he says, “I venerate the borne; because of the one who is hidden, I adore the one who is visible. God is inseparable from the visible; therefore I do not separate the honor of the one who is not separated.”

Volume IV of the Councils, column 1202, quaternio 16.

Moreover, the Fifth Synod, in its criticism of Theodoret’s refutation of Saint Cyril’s first anathema, censures him in the following words:

> “It is therefore certain from what has been said that the form of God, without being changed into the form of a servant, while remaining what it was, took the form of a servant. If, then, God the Word did not become flesh but assumed living and rational flesh, it was not he who by nature was born from the Virgin, conceived, formed together, and molded, receiving from that point a beginning of existence—he who is before the ages, is God, is with God, is with the Father, and is known and worshiped with the Father. Rather, when he formed a temple for himself in the virginal womb, he was with the one who had been formed together, conceived, formed, and born.
>
> “Therefore we call that holy Virgin Mother of God, not because she naturally gave birth to God, but because she gave birth to a man united to God, who had formed him.”

Volume IX of the Councils, column 290.

## XVI. The Nestorians Admit That There Is One Person in Christ

Here, then, is the whole system of Nestorian doctrine—a system which the Church repeatedly judged incapable of being defended without thereby entailing two persons in Christ [Col. 0378B]—although its advocates occasionally admitted the unity of person and even protested against such a division, as may still be demonstrated by several of their testimonies.

The author of the book *Against the Synusiasts*, in the passage often cited, says:

> “By grace, the son who is from Mary is man; by nature, however, God the Word. But what is according to grace is not according to nature, and what is according to nature is not according to grace: not two sons, and so forth.”

Theodore speaks still more plainly in his creed:

> “And therefore we do not say two sons, nor two lords; for, once the Lord and Son according to nature has been clearly established, since he has an inseparable union with him who was assumed for our salvation, he possesses with him the honor and designation of son and lord—not as though each were a son subsisting separately in his own right (whence, according to blessed Paul, we are called many sons), but because he alone possesses this distinctive privilege: that, through his union with God the Word, he shares both sonship and lordship, cutting off every conception of two sons and two lords.”  
> *Tom. IX Conc.*, col. 228.

Nestorius explains himself in the second letter to Cyril, no. 1:

> “Because he was going to mention death, lest anyone should infer from this that God the Word was passible, he adds the name ‘Christ,’ which denotes both natures—the passible, I mean, and the impassible—in one person.”

And in no. 2:

> “I praise you, however, for proclaiming the distinction of the natures according to the account of divinity and humanity, and their conjunction in one person.”  
> *Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 894.

Likewise, in quaternio 27:

> “You may learn,” he says, “how extraordinary that union of divinity was, even when the Lord’s flesh was seen in the infant. For he himself was both an infant and the lord of the infant. You have praised the statement; but beware of applauding it rashly and without examination. For I said: He was altogether the same infant and inhabitant of the infant.”

Ibid., col. 1202.

To Cyril, however, he speaks as follows:

> “Therefore I want you to hold firmly and carefully to this: there is no division of conjunction, dignity, or sonship. That very thing which is Christ suffers no division; but there is a division of deity and humanity. Christ, insofar as he is Christ, is indivisible. For we do not have two Christs, nor two sons; there is not among us a first and a second, nor one and another, nor again one son and another son. Rather, that one himself is twofold—not in dignity, but in nature.”  
> Book II *Against Nestorius*, vol. VI of Cyril’s works, fol. 44.

Theodoret, too, in his refutation of Cyril’s third anathema, confesses one person in Christ, saying:

> “If, therefore, each nature possesses perfection, and both have come together into one—namely, the form of God receiving the form of a servant—it is pious to confess one person, one Son, and one Christ.”  
> *Tom. V Conc.*, col. 98.

Nevertheless, although by these and other statements they might appear to support the Catholic doctrine concerning one person in Christ, the Church consistently held them guilty of the opposite error. Nor was there ever anyone who defended Nestorius, or his precursors or followers, from this censure on the grounds that in certain passages they seemed to speak soundly of the unity of person in the mystery of the Incarnation. For elsewhere they either expressly declared that by this unity nothing other than unity of affection was to be understood, or at least established principles which, once posited, made it impossible for the unity of person—properly so called and in the sense of the Church—to remain.

But the same fate befell Felix and Elipandus. It will become obvious that Alcuin rightly counted them among the Nestorians when, in due order, we report their assertions and show that these possess complete affinity with those which we have so far related as characteristic of the Nestorians.

## XVII. Christ, as Man, Was Not Begotten by the Eternal Father, According to the Bishops of Spain; Hence He Is Not the Proper Son

It was plainly the principal assertion of Elipandus and Felix that Christ, as man, was not God’s proper son but only his adoptive son. There is no need to prove this at length, since it is clear both from their own writings and from the accounts of historians that their principal dispute was concentrated on this point [Col. 0379B].

Felix says in Alcuin, book I, no. 15, fol. 797:

> “Not in the glory of his divinity, in which he is altogether like the Father but unlike every creature; rather, only in his humanity, in which he was made altogether like us, except for the law of sin. He is indeed like us in nature, although no one is like or equal to him in glory. In this respect we believe him to be adoptive with the Father: insofar as, according to the flesh, he is David’s son—not, however, insofar as he is Lord.”

Elipandus reasons in the following manner in his letter to the same Alcuin, fol. 870:

> “Behold Joachim, whose daughter is recognized as the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God: he is believed to be adoptive [perhaps *adoptiva*, ‘adoptive,’ though the masculine form is expected]. Why, then, should the Lord Jesus, born from her, not be called adoptive?”

And in his creed, preserved in the work of Beatus and Etherius:

> “Through this Son of God and man, adoptive in humanity and in no way adoptive in divinity, he redeemed the world.”

Vol. II of the *Ancient Lessons* of Henry Canisius, 969 edition of Basnage, fol. 310.

The bishops of Spain express themselves in the same way in their letter to the bishops of Gaul, and so forth, when they say:

> “For the salvation of the human race, at the end of time, proceeding from that intimate and ineffable substance of the Father, yet not departing from the Father, seeking the lowest things of this world, appearing publicly to the human race, he who is invisible assuming a visible body, ineffably brought forth from the intact virginity of his mother according to the tradition of the Fathers, we confess that he was made from a woman, made under the law, not by generation but by adoption the Son of God, and not by nature but by grace.”

Historians likewise report these things to us—everyone who wrote about those times. We do not wish to adduce their testimonies concerning a matter otherwise certain to everyone; instead, we shall now briefly examine the arguments by which the bishops mentioned above attempted to establish this adoption in Christ as man.

## XVIII. The Argument That the Man Assumed by the Word Was Not the Proper or Natural Son

We said above that the Nestorians, while defending the adoption of the man assumed by the Word, placed the primary argument for this opinion in the claim that neither divinity had been generated from the Virgin nor humanity from the eternal Father, and consequently that that man could not be called God’s proper or natural Son. Elipandus, Felix, and other Spanish bishops later made the very same argument.

Felix says in Alcuin:

> “But if our same Redeemer, in his flesh—which he received from the Virgin’s womb, from the very moment of conception—is not adoptive with the Father, but is the true and proper Son, what remains except that this same flesh was not created and made from the mass of the human race or from his mother’s flesh, but was generated from the substance of the Father, just as his divinity was?”

Book II *Against Felix*.

Accordingly, just as the author of the book *Against the Synusiasts* had formerly said that God the Word did not undergo two generations, Felix likewise insisted that one son could not naturally have two fathers.

> “For certainly,” he says, “our same Redeemer, in the form of humanity, as the sacred writings testify, is David’s son and the Son of God. Both statements are true; yet it is not absurd to ask how both apply to him. For it cannot happen that one son can naturally have two fathers; nevertheless, he can certainly have one by nature and another by adoption.”

Book III *Against Felix*, no. 1.

Again Felix says:

> “If anyone wishes to depart from our confession, let him produce equally suitable witnesses who affirm that a true God was conceived from the womb and that he is the true Son of God.”

And elsewhere:

> “There is no way we should believe that the omnipotent God the Father, who is spirit, generates flesh from himself.”

## XIX. The Adoptionists Argue from Christ’s Anointing

Again, just as we said concerning the Nestorians, Elipandus and his associates sought a defense of their error in the anointing attributed to Christ in Scripture, in the baptism which he received, and in the progress which he is said to have made in grace and wisdom.

Felix says:

> “For blessed Peter the Apostle, uniquely confessing in him two natures simultaneously in one person, God having revealed this to him, said: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ For in what he says, ‘You are the Christ,’ this pertains to his humanity, in which he was anointed; what he added, ‘the Son of the living God,’ pertains to his divinity, in which he is essentially the true Son of God.”

In Alcuin, book IV *Against Felix*.

Here he appears to profess one person in Christ—a thing which we shall not deny he frequently did elsewhere as well—while merely observing for the present that, according to his position, Christ is not, insofar as he is man, the proper Son of God because he is said to have been anointed with respect to his humanity.

The bishops of Spain argued in the same way in their letter to the bishops of Gaul, and so forth, where the following is found:

> “We confess the only-begotten in nature, the firstborn in adoption and grace. Concerning him the Apostle says: ‘For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.’ Brothers, namely, those of whom the Psalmist says: ‘I will declare your name to my brothers.’ Whence are they brothers, except from the adoption of the flesh alone, through which he deigned to have brothers, concerning whom the Holy Spirit spoke through David: ‘God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.’ His companions are those of whom the Apostle John says: ‘Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be, when we see him as he is.’ They are like him in the adoption of the flesh, but not like him in divinity.

> “We believe that the anointing of the Holy Spirit—through which, especially in the Son of God according to his humanity, it took place more abundantly than in his elect, by the grace of the sevenfold spiritual gifts—is that of which Isaiah speaks when he says: ‘The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him,’ and so forth. We believe that this fullness of anointing exists in the one adoptive and firstborn Son of God; but in the other saints such grace was given according to measure. Concerning the only-begotten Son, however, and the one without adoption, the Father’s voice says: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,’ and so forth.”

## XX. Likewise from Christ’s Baptism

It is certain that the Adoptionists also drew an argument for their opinion from Christ’s baptism; and Walchius himself—otherwise so friendly toward Felix and Elipandus—admits that their error concerning Christ’s regeneration was most serious. *History of Adoptionism*, chapter 2, section 2, no. 8, p. 233.

Let us hear Felix’s words as Alcuin reports them in book II, no. 16:

> “If anyone wishes to deny to Christ according to man this spiritual generation which takes place through adoption, he must first completely sever from him that generation which is according to the flesh. For if he does not share with us in the former, which is spiritual, unquestionably he does not share in the latter, which is carnal.”

Accordingly, in the same place, no. 15, Alcuin says:

> “After this, the aforementioned Felix runs through the fields of Holy Scripture—not with a steady step, but with a limping gait—offering many testimonies which do not suit his position, so as to make his speech longer, until he arrived at the waters of the Jordan, in order to impose the name of adoption upon Christ when he had been baptized.”

And in no. 18:

> “The man whom he repeatedly affirms to be without sin he now suddenly claims, as though he were a sinner, to have needed regeneration. The one whom shortly before he asserted to be God and to have been born from a virginal womb he now suddenly declares, as though he were a mere man, to have needed cleansing by the washing of baptism; and he says that the one who had been conceived and born as the Son of God was adopted as the Son of God in our likeness.”

Beatus and Etherius had already reproved the same teachings in Elipandus when they set the following words against him:

> “Christ was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit when the Spirit descended upon him after he had been baptized in the form of a dove. For then he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which we who are baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit. Rather, he is to be understood as having been anointed by that mystical and invisible anointing when the Word of God became flesh—that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to God the Word in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person . . . . . For it is utterly absurd to believe that, when he was already thirty years old and was baptized by John, he received the Holy Spirit.”

In the cited passage, fol. 300.

Finally, Paulinus of Aquileia writes of Felix:

> “In this way he hastens, through arguments of various kinds, to carry his figure of speech to such a point that, with a ruined mouth, he defines him as both the adoptive Son of God and a titular God—as though he were a mere ordinary man, to whom the privilege of faith is freely granted, and to whom, through the washing of regeneration, power is given by that same Son of God, so that by a gratuitous gift he may be the adoptive Son of God and may become a titular God through the progress of religious devotion, by the divine grace which has gone before.”

Book I *Against Felix*, chapter 9.

And in chapter 44:

> “Because, with your mind deceived by vain talk, you think Christ the man an adoptive son, as though it were necessary for him to be born again, from both his mother’s womb and the womb of the font, like the other human beings who are baptized for the remission of sins.”

## XXI. Likewise from His Successive Progress

As regards successive progress in grace, the Adoptionists certainly taught such things that it can plainly be inferred that they attributed this progress to Christ as man and sought from it a defense of their error concerning the adoptive son.

It will suffice to adduce a single testimony, all the more so because it appears stronger, since it flowed from the pen of almost all those who supported the doctrine of adoption in Christ. The bishops of Spain, namely, in their frequently mentioned letter to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and others, had publicly professed their faith in the following words:

> “We confess and believe that he was made from a woman, made under the law, not by generation but by adoption the Son of God, and not by nature but by grace.”

They then proceed to argue from Scripture in confirmation of their position:

> “The same Lord himself bears witness to this when he says: ‘The Father is greater than I’; and the Evangelist says of him: ‘But the child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was in him.’”

As we saw above, no. 7, Theodore and Nestorius likewise used these words of the Gospel to defend successive progress in Christ as man and his adoption. They further taught that this progress—or the foreseen merits of the assumed man—had prepared the way for him to be admitted by the divine Word into participation in the dignity both of son and of lord. See the words of Saint Cyril cited in no. 3.

Felix later reasons in conformity with this, as Alcuin testifies in book VII, addressing his opponent as follows:

> “Immediately afterward, in the following statements of your learning, you are found to have said: ‘What he,’ you say, ‘merited through the grace of adoption in the humanity of the Son of God, in which he was born a man, was to be what he is and to receive what he has.’ You say, along with your predecessors Pelagius and Nestorius, that Christ merited becoming what he is; whereas Saint Augustine and all Catholic teachers testify that the same God was conceived and born in the very beginning of Christ’s humanity without any preceding merits.”

How precisely Elipandus and Felix agree in their arguments with the Nestorians, asserting that the man assumed is a son only by grace or by adoption alone! Once this is considered, it must surely seem remarkable that Walchius labored with such zeal to vindicate those Spanish bishops from the stain of this heresy. We shall immediately demonstrate that, even in the external designation of God—which alone they granted to Christ as man—they were altogether of the same mind.

## XXII. Christ, as Man, Is a Titular God According to Elipandus and Felix

This was plainly the other principal error which Alcuin, and all who with him defended the sound doctrine of the Church, reproached in his opponents.

Felix speaks as follows in Alcuin, book IV:

> “In a second manner, God is called ‘God’ titularly, as was said above concerning the holy preachers, of whom the Savior says to the Jews: ‘If he called them gods to whom the word of God came’—although they are not gods by nature as God is, but, having been deified by the grace of God by him who is the true God, they were called gods by him. In this respect the Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer, according to his humanity, just as he is like them in nature, so also in name—although he was chosen more excellently than all—nevertheless most truly shares with them, as he does in all other things as well: in predestination, in election, in grace, in reception, in assumption, in the taking upon himself of the name of servant, and in application, or in other matters similar to these. Thus the same one who, essentially with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is the true God in the unity of the Godhead, in the form of humanity became deified with his elect through the grace of adoption and became a titular God.”

Alcuin reports the same error concerning Felix in book I, writing:

> “Nor was it enough for him merely to deny that Christ, who was born from the Virgin, is the proper Son of God. He also refuses to acknowledge this same one as the true God; rather, he is not afraid to call him by a new and unheard-of name in the holy Church of God, ‘a titular God,’ dividing Christ into two sons—calling one proper and the other adoptive—and into two gods—one the true God and the other a titular God.”

Paulinus of Aquileia agrees, as will be evident to anyone reading chapters 30, 40, and 41 of book I *Against Felix*.

Beatus and Etherius also testify that Elipandus held the same opinion in the work mentioned above, where they express their faith against this bishop as follows:

> “Therefore we must not say: ‘That one is God and this one is man.’ We have and adore one God, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit—not a man, introducing a fourth person—but, together with the flesh itself, let us adore one Christ, the Son of God and God, according to the true confession of faith of the Council of Ephesus, which says: ‘We beware of saying of Christ: Because of the one who assumed, I venerate the one assumed; and because of the invisible one, I adore the visible one.’ It is horrifying, moreover, to say this as well: ‘The one who was received is co-called God together with the one who received him.’ For whoever says these things again divides into two Christs the one who is one, establishing the man separately on one side and God likewise separately on the other. For he evidently denies the unity according to which one is not co-adored and co-called with the other, and so forth.”

The cited place, fol. 303.

We consider it superfluous to adduce more testimonies of this kind. We shall instead examine the arguments by which Elipandus and Felix labored to support this opinion also; and it will become clear that these arguments are the same as those of the Nestorians.

## XXIII. From the Scriptural Passages That Sometimes Call Human Beings Gods

The fact that the Adoptionists also drew an argument from those passages of Scripture in which human beings are sometimes called gods, on the ground that this name applies in the same way to Christ as man, is clearly shown by the words of Felix cited in the preceding section:

> “In a second manner,” he says, “he is called God titularly, as was said above concerning the holy preachers, of whom the Savior says to the Jews: ‘If he called them gods to whom the word of God came,’ and so forth.”

The manner in which Felix and his followers commonly reasoned on this point is so plainly evident from this passage that we think we may dispense entirely with their other statements, lest repeated citation weary the reader.

## XXIV. From the Claim That the Word Dwelt in Us and That God Was in Christ: Felix’s Words

Just as in this matter, so also in their other arguments Felix and Elipandus followed the Nestorians. They too frequently employed the passages of Scripture:

> “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I);

> “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II, 9);

> “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Corinthians V, 19).

They also very frequently used expressions such as “the Word dwelt in the man who was assumed,” and “Christ is a man who bears God, or a man belonging to the Lord,” and so forth.

Felix says:

> “In that nature in which, according to the substance of the flesh, all his faithful are his members; not in that one—that is, in his divinity—in which he has not members but a temple.”

In Alcuin, book II.

In book VII Alcuin likewise reports Theodore’s words:

> “He who exists before the ages is God; but, fashioning a temple for himself in the virginal womb, he was with the one who was conceived and formed, and so forth.”

Then he addresses Felix as follows:

> “What else is it that you too say, when you claim that the Word of God dwelt in the man who was assumed, as in a kind of temple, rather than as the Evangelist says: ‘The Word became flesh’? ‘According to the Lord’s command,’ you say, ‘he bore divinity, and he is the inhabitant of his temple.’”

Paulinus makes the same reproach against Felix in book I, chapter 15, and book II, chapter 10, where he says:

> “For immediately forgetting the profession of the purest faith, you strive with anxious breath to make him God by titular designation and son by adoption. You are seen to be so enveloped in the densest smoke of such obscure darkness that you assert the true God to dwell in a titular god, and the proper Son to dwell in an adoptive son.”

They attempted to prove this indwelling from the Apostle’s words cited above, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” and from other similar passages, as Alcuin again relates in book V. He says:

> “Felix produces the words of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, from the Acts of the Apostles, where he preached the Word of God to Cornelius and those who were with him. He says: ‘Again, concerning this humanity of his, the same Apostle, preaching among other things to Cornelius and his companions, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, said: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.”’ He does not say, ‘He himself was God,’ but, ‘God was with him.’ For if, according to the true confession, that man assumed by the Word were true God, so great an Apostle would never have dared to say, ‘God was with him,’ but rather, ‘He himself was God.’”

He also presents a third statement of blessed Paul, that distinguished preacher, where he says: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

> “He did not say, ‘Christ was God,’ but, ‘God was in Christ’—not because Christ, namely the man assumed, is not God, but because he is God not by nature but by grace and titular designation.”

Similar statements are also found in Paulinus of Aquileia, who argues as follows:

> “Since, therefore, O marvelous teacher”—he is speaking of the holy Paul—“you had often taught that he was the instrument of Christ, uttering the blessed sound of the one who spoke in you, and that through his Holy Spirit the world had been reconciled to God, you said: ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.’ From this passage, fortified with the weapons of impiety, this heretic does not cease to contradict the truth that Christ is God, with the utterly false assertion that you are being accused of having said, ‘God was in Christ,’ and not ‘Christ was God.’ As is his custom, he is not ashamed here either to distort the testimony, just as elsewhere he distorts the Scriptures—as though one were the God in Christ and another were Christ the man in whom God was, whereas Christ Jesus is one, God and man.”

Since the Adoptionists pressed these arguments concerning the Word’s indwelling in the man assumed and said that he was God only in name, they also very commonly used expressions such as “Christ is a man who bears God,” or “a man belonging to the Lord,” and so forth, just as we noted above concerning the Nestorians.

Felix says in the passage cited shortly before:

> “According to the Lord’s command, he bore divinity.”

And elsewhere:

> “By what authority is that same man belonging to the Lord proclaimed by us to have been conceived as true God from his mother’s womb and born as true God, when by nature he is a true man and altogether subject to God?”

In Alcuin, book IV.

This is even more clearly gathered from Alcuin’s response to Felix in the earlier passage:

> “There is therefore one Christ, the Son and our Lord—not as though by some kind of conjunction, unity of dignity, or authority of a man who possesses a relationship to God, whom you are accustomed to call joined to God or adopted, and to say also that he bears divinity; and, using some unusual word, you say that he ‘lines’ divinity. For among ordinary people, to ‘line’ means to depict or carve images, or to express the forms of any work. But I do not understand what this has to do with the divinity or humanity of the Son of God. As for your saying, as we mentioned earlier, that he bears divinity, hear what reward you receive for this from the holy and Catholic men who were accustomed to argue at length against your heresy.”

There follows Cyril’s fifth anathema, in which that holy teacher denied against the Nestorians that Christ as man should be called “one who bears God,” or, which is the same thing, that he bears or carries divinity or God.

Elipandus wrote similarly in his letter to Alcuin, no. 13:

> “I do not mean,” he says, “the Son of God, God, begotten before the ages from the Father, through whom visible and invisible things, spiritual and corporeal things, were made—whom I believe to be a Son not by adoption but by generation, not by grace but by nature. Rather, I mean what blessed Isidore says: ‘There are some who think wrongly about the Son of God, transferring to divinity what was said of him according to his humanity, and changing to humanity what they have altered from divinity.’ Yet our Julian says: ‘The man belonging to the Lord, and God made human.’”

Elipandus calls Christ “the man belonging to the Lord,” having indeed adopted Julian’s words, but not his mind, since Julian was entirely orthodox.

See also Paulinus, book I, chapter 9, and elsewhere.

## XXV. The Argument from Christ’s Office as Advocate and from His Prayer

Again, from the fact that Christ is said in Scripture to be our advocate with the Father and to have poured out prayers to him, the Adoptionists inferred that he was a titular God—certainly after the manner of the Nestorians, who had drawn the same conclusion from Christ’s priestly dignity and his prayer to the Father.

Alcuin says of Felix in book V:

> “He therefore sets forth a statement from the Evangelist’s epistle, where it says: ‘We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins,’ which you assert must be understood by you in this way: ‘An advocate,’ you say, ‘who is also mediator, who intercedes with the Father on behalf of the sins of those who offend. This is to be understood not of the true God but of the man assumed.’”

Agobard also testifies that Felix said that Christ the Lord “in his humanity alone was an apostle and a priest.” Book *Against Felix*, chapter 31, *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIV, fol. 252.

This manner of argument is plainly related to that of the Nestorians, who denied that Christ as man was the true God because he is called our priest, who must certainly be different from the God to whom sacrifice is offered.

See also Paulinus, book I, chapters 23 and 24, and especially chapter 25, where he devotes himself entirely to proving that Christ had no need of redemption. From this it follows that Felix was not far removed from the opinion of Nestorius, who asserted that Christ as man, our priest, also offered sacrifice to God the Father for himself.

Moreover, in more than one passage Felix maintains that Christ prayed for himself as well. Since this is incompatible with the true God, he attributes to him, with respect to his humanity, the dignity of a titular God.

Alcuin testifies to this in book VII, no. 15:

> “But because it would be lengthy to examine all the arguments of your depravity, let it suffice for the present to answer you concerning this: that you endeavor above all, on this account, to deny that the Son of God made man is the true God, because he is read to have prayed for himself just as he did for us. Where you read that the Son of God prayed for himself as he did for us, I altogether do not know . . . . . For your predecessor Nestorius himself also used to say that Christ had offered sacrifice for himself and for the race of his body. What you say—that he prayed for himself—he, wishing the same thing to be understood, said that he offered sacrifice for himself and for his race. Hear what blessed Cyril opposed to this blasphemy. He says: ‘If anyone says that Christ offered an oblation for himself, and not rather for us alone, let him be anathema.’”

Cyril, anathema 10.

We learn similar things from Paulinus, who reproves Felix in book I, chapter 30:

> “You, therefore, were not ashamed, with your bile-filled throat, to explain that he is not the true God and the true Son of God because, not only for others but necessarily also for himself, he spent the night in prayer and supplication to God. You take an apostolic testimony that is sufficiently clear and evident, but according to the meaning of your unbelief you corrupt it most badly and obscurely.”

In the immediately following chapter he indicates which testimony of the Apostle Felix had misunderstood, writing:

> “You endeavor to support the assertions of your false conjectural objections with the testimony of Paul that is mentioned, because in the epistle entitled ‘To the Hebrews’ he wrote concerning the mediator of God and human beings that, in the days of his flesh, he offered prayers and supplications with tears and a loud cry for himself to the one who could save him from death. You are unaware that one thing must be gathered from another, and that the force of a statement which you cannot grasp from one passage may be competently tested by comparing many very similar passages.”

An egg is not more like an egg than this argument of Felix is like that of the Nestorians, which we related above in no. 11.

## XXVI. The Adoptionists Argue from the Fact That the Word Could Not Suffer

Moreover, Felix and Elipandus constantly accused the Catholics of saying that the Word was passible, whereas they themselves attributed suffering and the other properties of human nature solely to the man assumed.

Felix says in the clearest terms:

> “Nowhere in the Gospel is the Son of God said to have been delivered up for us, but only the son of man.”

In Alcuin, book V, no. 8.

The same Alcuin responds to this in that place:

> “Therefore the Son of Man can in no way be divided from the Son of God, nor can the Son of God be separated from the Son of Man, because there is one Son of God, God and man, who was delivered up to death on account of our sins . . . . . We also clearly confess in the creed of the Catholic faith that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, suffered for the salvation of the human race. Therefore no Catholic ought to doubt that the Son of God was delivered up for the salvation of the world. For whoever denies that the Son of God was delivered up to suffering can in no way be Catholic; rather, by persisting in this obstinacy, he must be judged alien to the profession of the Catholic faith.”

Felix therefore denied that Christ, insofar as he is man, is the true God, on the grounds that he endured the suffering of death, since suffering is not compatible with God. Consequently, together with the Nestorians, he denied that the Word had suffered.

For this reason Paulinus sets the following against Felix in book I, chapter 17:

> “Because we are taught by apostolic testimonies that the flesh assumed by the Word is the Word’s own flesh, and that the invisible one can be seen, the impassible one can suffer, and the immortal one can die in his own flesh. The first shepherd of the Church says: ‘Christ suffered in the flesh’—in the flesh, certainly, not with the divinity suffering along with the flesh, since the divinity is established in every respect outside suffering. But because it was the Word’s own flesh that suffered, that one is said to have suffered and died whose own flesh is declared to have suffered and died. After the mystery of the assumption, his impassible and unchangeable divinity is never proclaimed to have been separated from that flesh. Accordingly, Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is truly declared, according to the Scriptures, to have suffered, died, been buried, and risen again.”

From this we truly learn that Felix maintained the contrary position—that is, he denied that the Father’s Word had suffered—and from this derived his opinion concerning a titular God. From the same premises he further inferred that Christ had suffered not willingly but by necessity, and therefore had asked the Father that the cup be taken away from him. Paulinus again bears witness to this in book III, chapter 4, and frequently elsewhere.

### XXVII. Christ, as Man, a Servant According to the Adoptianists

Finally, the Adoptianists also preached servitude of Christ as man, just as we have recalled above that the Nestorians did. “Can it possibly be,” says Felix, “that he who is the true God should by condition be God’s servant, as Christ the Lord is in the form of a servant—he who is most truly shown by many arguments and many proofs to be not only a servant because of obedience, as most people hold, but also by nature a servant [973] of the Father and the son of his handmaid?” In Alcuin, book VI, no. 4.

Elsewhere he says: “For if, as you maintain, the man assumed [Col. 0386B] by the Son of God was, from the moment of conception in the virgin womb, truly conceived as God and truly born as God, how does the Son of God himself, speaking through the designation ‘form of a servant,’ bear witness concerning himself to the prophecy of the Old Testament—that he was formed as a servant from his mother’s womb? For through the prophet Isaiah he says: ‘And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself, that I might bring Jacob back to him, and Israel shall be gathered.’”

From these words we further learn the foundation on which Felix relied when he called Christ, as man, the Father’s servant: namely, Isaiah’s prophecy, in which, as we noted shortly before from Theodoret, the Nestorians also sought refuge. Felix therefore asserted that the man assumed by the Word was a servant by condition and necessity, not by free will. Alcuin also expressly reproaches him for this in book VI, no. 4:

“But among other things,” he says, “the progression of your wandering discourse has led you to this point also: you have said that there are two kinds of servitude among creatures, [Col. 0386C] voluntary and conditional. For, you say, every creature serves God either voluntarily or by necessity, through condition. It is plainly evident to everyone that conditional servitude is a lower kind than voluntary servitude; yet, under this lower degree, you do not fear impiously to rank Christ, as we have already shown from your own words.”

Beatus and Etherius also noted this error in Elipandus, when they wrote at the cited place, folio 301:

“Why have we said all this, unless to establish firmly that Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is true God and the true, proper Son of God, and with open face to deny that he is God among gods, an adopted son among adopted sons, a little one among little ones, and a servant among servants, as the heretics blaspheme?”

Finally, the bishops of Spain declared their position in a letter to the bishops of Gaul, writing with one voice:

“For this reason, therefore, we have brought forward the judgments of the teachers in our defense: so that we might believe the only-begotten Son of God to have been begotten timelessly from the Father—not [Col. 0386D] by adoption but by generation, not by grace but by nature. At the end of time, however, for the salvation of the human race, by assuming flesh from the Virgin in the form of a servant, according to the Apostle, he became the firstborn among brothers, in one and the same person of God and man—not by generation but by adoption, not by nature but by grace; in that form in which he is equal to his mother, not in that in which he is equal to the Father. For in the form of a servant he is a servant, and therefore adopted; but in the form of the Lord, he is the Lord of the servant. Concerning this form of servitude God the Father speaks through the Prophet, saying: ‘Behold, my servant shall understand.’ And again: ‘Behold my servant; I shall receive him, my chosen one, in whom my soul has been well pleased.’”

Here these bishops openly profess that Christ, in the form of the Lord—that is, in the divine nature—is the Lord of the servant, namely, of the man assumed. Yet they obstinately affirmed that this man ought to be called a servant by condition or by nature. The holy Cyril had long before reproved this error so sharply in the sixth anathema, declaring:

[Col. 0387A] “If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is Christ’s God or Lord … let him be anathema.”

### XXVIII. The Adoptianists Asserted These Things in Order to Refute the Arians, Especially the Eutychians

Felix and Elipandus employed all these principles for no other purpose than to ward off the attacks of the heretics whose remnants, as we said in the first paragraph, had survived in Spain down to those times—namely, the Arians and Eutychians. Against the former they vindicated the divine Word from the weaknesses of human nature; against the latter they defended the distinctions between the two natures by maintaining their respective differences.

Indeed, they appear to have been especially concerned with the latter doctrine, namely, the distinction between each of the two natures in Christ after the union, since they more frequently charged their adversaries, Beatus, Etherius, and Alcuin, with the crime of Eutychian heresy, that is, with confusing the natures. To confirm this point, it will be useful to cite several of their statements.

[Col. 0387B] Alcuin, in book I *Against Felix*, no. 8, expressly notes that Beatus and Etherius, the opponents of Elipandus, were accused of this confusion of the natures:

“But as for your saying that a certain blessed abbot and his disciple, the bishop Etherius, were the first to oppose your sect, we praise them for having attempted to defend the truth. But if it is true, as you have said, that they confuse the two natures in Christ into one, like wine and water, we in no way agree with this.”

Felix later made the same objection to Alcuin, saying:

“These are the statements of your faith concerning the two natures in Christ, which you confuse into the singularity of one person, so that you assert there to be no difference between God and man, between the Word and flesh, between the Creator and the creature, or between the one who assumes and the one assumed.”

In Alcuin, book III, and likewise book VI, he asks:

“Or in what form will he be subject to the Father forever, if it is believed that there will be no difference or inequality between his divinity and his humanity?”

[Col. 0387C] Alcuin protests against this accusation in book VII, no. 11, writing:

“We in no way confuse the natures in Christ, as you claim that we have done. Rather, preserving the proper character of both natures, divine and human, we confess one God, Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of God, in two natures, but in one person and one dignity of sonship.”

### XXIX. They Distinguish “The One” and “The Other” in Christ

From these statements it is plainly evident how concerned Felix and Elipandus were to preserve the distinction of the natures in Christ. To express this more effectively, they too employed formulas of speech which, as we said above in no. 15, were familiar to the Nestorians: namely, “the one and the other”; “the one who assumed” and “the one who was assumed.”

“Did he create visible and invisible things through the one who was born of the Virgin,” says Elipandus at the cited place in Beatus and Etherius, folio 312, “or through the one who was not a son by adoption but by generation, and who created all things not by grace but by nature? And through this [Col. 0387D] Son of God and man, the Word made flesh—adopted in his humanity but in no way adopted in his divinity—he redeemed the world.”

Again, in his letter to Alcuin, no. 10:

“Behold, to whom does the Father say, ‘I am your God’? Not to him—that is, not to the Word—who was begotten from the Father before the ages, but to the one who at the end of time became man from the Virgin Mary, of whom the Apostle says: ‘Born of a woman, born under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law.’”

It is likewise evident from the statements cited above concerning Felix’s interpretation of the words, “God was in Christ; God was with him,” that this manner of speaking was also customary with Felix. For when Felix argued that the Apostle had not said, “God was he,” what else was he expressing than “the one and the other”: that one who was God and dwelt within, and that man in whom this God dwelt?

The following words of Felix, reported by Alcuin in book V, have the same implication:

“He” (namely, the eternal Son of the eternal Father, or the divine Word) “united and joined that one to himself from his mother’s womb—that is, from the very [Col. 0388A] conception—in the singularity of his person, in such a way that the Son of God was the son of man, not by a change of nature but by condescension; and likewise the son of man was the Son of God, not by a transformation of substance, but because in the Son of God he was a true son. He united that one to himself in such a way that in the Son of God he was a true son.”

According to Felix, therefore, that one, so united in the Word who unites, is the true Son; or, which is the same thing, in Christ the one who assumes and the one who is assumed must be distinguished as “the one and the other.”

### XXX. The Adoptianists Confess One Person in Christ

Nor should it trouble us that Felix appears, in the words just cited, to admit the unity of person, saying, “He united him in the singularity of his person.” For he himself, Elipandus, and all their followers repeatedly confessed this elsewhere, and even protested against every division.

“The inner man,” it is said in the creed of Elipandus preserved by Beatus and Etherius, folio 310, is “[Col. 0388B] joined together in one and the same person of God and man,” and clothed in the garment of flesh.

And in his letter to Alcuin he says:

“For the Prophet also says: ‘Have mercy, Lord, upon your people, over whom your name has been invoked, and upon Israel, whom you have made equal to your firstborn.’ This equality is not in divinity, but solely in humanity and in the adoption of flesh, which that one and the same God and man received from the Virgin. In two natures and one person, preserving his divinity, he removed the destruction of death.”

Felix declares himself in the following words at the cited place, no. 3:

“Although God from God and man from the Virgin are one and the same Christ of God in the singularity of person, just as any man formed from a soul created out of nothing and flesh formed from both parents is one person belonging to both parents, namely, the son of his father and mother.”

Felix might appear to have expressed in these words the very doctrine of the Catholic Church, unless he had adopted other principles which cannot possibly be reconciled with them. [Col. 0388C] Hence, after reporting this assertion of Felix, Alcuin continues:

“If you had understood this example well, and if you had carefully considered yourself, it could have destroyed in you all the treachery of error and restored your understanding to the recognition of truth. From this root, surely, the thorns of all your unbelief seem to have grown: that it appears impossible to your understanding for a son to be a proper son in any other way than by being born wholly from the nature of his parents. You do not understand that you yourself are the proper son of your father and mother, although the nobler nature within you—namely, your soul—was not generated from their nature, but was created from nothing, as you assert. What blindness of mind, opposed to all reason, is this—that you contend that what you cannot deny exists in yourself cannot exist in the only and proper Son of God the Father?”

[Col. 0388D] We also learn from the same Alcuin that Felix protested against the division of persons in Christ. His words in book VII, no. 11, are:

“Nor do we divide Christ into two sons, or two gods, or two persons, with Nestorius. Although he did not openly say ‘two persons,’ he nevertheless professes in his confession everything that must belong to two persons. In the same way, although you avoid the words ‘two persons,’ we find you professing in your writings everything that must belong to two persons.”

To conceal nothing, the bishops of Spain also proclaim this unity of person in their letter to the bishops of Gaul, expressing their faith as follows:

“Having set forth these judgments of the holy Fathers and strengthened our assertions by them, we have jointly resolved in no way to depart from their decrees, but carefully to obey their instructions, so that in one and the same Son of God and man, in one person, there may also be two complete and perfect natures, of God and man, of Lord and servant, of the visible and invisible; and likewise three substances, namely, of the Word, soul, and body. Thus it is to be believed that in one and the same person of God and man there is both a man made divine and God made human, and so forth.”

[Col. 0389A]

### XXXI. Profession of One Person Does Not Justify the Adoptianists. Felix Confesses That He Agreed with Nestorius

In former times, the Nestorians’ similar profession of one person in Christ could scarcely justify them against the opposing error, because, as Alcuin says, they admitted everything that necessarily belongs to two persons. In the same way, Elipandus and Felix could scarcely later be excused from the same heresy, since they too approved and established principles which are certainly identical with those of the Nestorians and cannot be reconciled with the unity of person.

Indeed, the very profession of one person made by the Adoptianists entirely agrees with that which is consistently found in Nestorian writings. Those writings assert that the unity was merely moral, so that the Father’s Word was called the son of man, and conversely the man assumed was called the Son of God, not in reality but solely by condescension. Felix expressed precisely the same doctrine in the passage cited by us in the preceding section:

“So that the Son of God might be the son of man, not by a change of nature but by [Col. 0389B] condescension; and likewise the son of man might be the Son of God, not by a transformation of substance, but because in the Son of God he was a true son.”

Therefore, by the common judgment of the Church and its teachers, they were condemned as guilty of Nestorian heresy. Nor does Felix himself, in the confession of faith which he issued after rejecting his error, deny that he had previously been deceived by Nestorius’s errors. He says:

“Since we all, thinking alike with the universal Church, which is known to be spread throughout the whole world, anathematize in the same way the position that arose some time ago—namely, the adoption of the flesh, or the naming of the Son of God as adopted in his humanity—we retain, as I have said, peace and unity of faith with all the faithful of the Church, without any pretense and with unwavering faith, lest, agreeing with the impiety of Nestorius, who believed Christ the Lord to be a mere man, we should henceforth in any way go astray.”

[Col. 0389C] After he had quoted the creed which Marius Mercator and the Emperor Justinian attribute to Theodore of Mopsuestia, and which is also brought forward under Theodore’s name at the Fifth Synod—a creed in which the doctrine of “nominal God” and “adopted son” is plainly contained—he continues:

“This is the opinion of the heretic Nestorius, who impiously asserted that a mere man was born from the Virgin’s womb without God. He shamelessly preached that, after the birth of this man who had been produced and born from the same holy Virgin, the Word of God—that is, the divinity of the Son of God—descended upon him and dwelt in him above all the other saints. For this reason, just as he claimed two natures in Christ, so also he wickedly endeavored to vindicate two persons in him.
