But we, anathematizing his impiety, have selected certain testimonies from the books of the holy Fathers, whom the Church venerably receives, and appended them to this letter. Through these testimonies, having returned to the way of truth after our former error, we have sent you what is written below, by which you too can more fully recognize the truth of the faith concerning the position in question and return to the right path of faith. Whoever disagrees with these judgments of the Fathers, wishes to believe or teach otherwise than they instruct us, and presumes to believe or preach adoption and nominal sonship in the flesh of the Savior, let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0389D] Walchius could not conceal the fact that Felix appears here to speak of his own opinion in such a way as to concede that it was Nestorian. Nevertheless, in defending him, he continues:

“But whoever examines his words with a freer mind will easily understand that he does not confess this at all. For he did not know what Nestorius believed. ‘Let us retain,’ he says, ‘peace and unity of faith with all the faithful of the Church, without any pretense and with unwavering faith, lest, agreeing with the impiety of Nestorius, who believed Christ the Lord to be a mere man, we should henceforth in any way go astray.’ Later, indeed, he explained Nestorius’s position more accurately and confessed that he had been moved to change his mind by the arguments of Christian teachers who opposed Nestorius; but he never said that he had established the same doctrines as Nestorius.”

[Col. 0390A] This is plainly a gross evasion. First, Walchius says that Felix did not know what Nestorius believed; then, immediately afterward, he says that this same Felix explained Nestorius’s position more accurately. Felix did in fact explain his doctrine, and therefore understood it well, since from Theodore’s creed—which Felix himself calls by the name of Nestorius—he recites the errors concerning the adopted son and the nominal God, and confesses that these had formerly been his own errors in the words immediately preceding, which Walchius has deliberately omitted. For this reason Felix now anathematizes them, lest he should henceforth go astray by agreeing with the impiety of Nestorius.

We plainly do not see what clearer confession could have been demanded from Felix by which he might openly have shown that he had formerly held the same doctrines as Nestorius. But even if Felix had not confessed this charge, neither he nor Elipandus nor the other bishops of Spain could nevertheless be defended, since it is clear from what has been said that they adopted the same principles as the Nestorians and employed the same arguments against their [Col. 0390B] adversaries. Learned men who publicly disputed with them, examining their opinions not from their own imagination but from the writings of their opponents—writings which were then still in everyone’s hands—had rightly accused them, together with the whole Church assembled in so many synods, of reviving the Nestorian heresy.

Walchius himself does not deny this. On page 208 of his *History* he writes:

“At the time when this controversy was being disputed, everyone agreed that the doctrines of Nestorius were, so to speak, being brought back into the light.”

### XXXII. The Testimonies of the Historians to Whom Walchius Appeals Are Examined

[Col. 0390C] Walchius appeals to historians who were supposedly free from any desire to contradict, and he judges that their testimonies entirely absolve Elipandus and Felix from this charge. But even granting that this controversy could be settled from annalists who merely touch upon the matter superficially—a claim which we rightly denied at the beginning of this paragraph—he plainly would not have found them supporting the cause undertaken for the Spanish bishops if he himself had been free from any desire to contradict.

To establish the truth of this assertion, there is no need to produce other writers than those whom Walchius himself pointed out to us in the cited place. The first is Einhard—or whoever may ultimately have been the author of the annals—who writes under the year 792:

“Urgell is a city situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees. Its bishop, named Felix, a Spaniard by nation, was consulted by letter by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, as to what he ought to think and say concerning the humanity of our Savior, God and Lord Jesus Christ: whether, according to that in which he is man, he should be believed and called the proper or adopted Son of God. Felix answered very carelessly and thoughtlessly, and contrary to the ancient doctrine of the Catholic Church, not only pronounced him adopted, but also obstinately endeavored to defend his depraved opinion in books written to the aforesaid bishop. For this reason he was brought to the royal palace, where the king was then residing at Regensburg, [Col. 0390D] a city of Bavaria in which he had also wintered. There, after a council of bishops had been assembled, Felix was heard and convicted of error. He was sent to Rome to the presence of Pope Adrian, where, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he also confessed the heresy before the pope himself and renounced it. After this he returned to his own city.”

Concerning these words we note that not even a syllable appears in them by which Felix could be absolved from the charge of Nestorian error. On the contrary, he is expressly said to have been convicted of heresy both at Regensburg and at Rome, and, after judgment had been rendered in both places—especially by Pope Adrian, who had long before declared that the very poison of Nestorian doctrine was being administered anew in Felix’s teaching—he was compelled to renounce it.

The author of the Annals certainly knew of this judgment. He did not omit to add it expressly to his history for any other reason than that it was then commonly known. Thus, under the year 794, he writes:

[Col. 0391A] “At the beginning of summer, when he also held a general assembly of his people, the king gathered a council of bishops from all the provinces of his kingdom in the same place, namely, Frankfurt, to condemn the Felician heresy. The legates of the Roman pontiff were also present at that synod: Theophylact and Stephen, bishops serving as representatives of the Roman pontiff Adrian, by whom they had been sent. At that council the aforesaid heresy was condemned, and a book was composed against it by the common authority of the bishops, to which all subscribed.”

Volume V of the *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum et Francicarum*, folio 210.

Thus this author reports that all subscribed both to the Council of Frankfurt and to the book composed against the Felician heresy. Since the Felician heresy is regarded as Nestorian both in the acts of the council and in the aforementioned book, should we not consider our historian to have tacitly reported the same thing? He would undoubtedly have expressed his judgment more clearly if he himself had held a different opinion on the matter, or had known that some others held one.

The same arguments may be drawn from the account of the Saxon Poet and from the Annals of Moissac.

[Col. 0391B] As for Jonah of Orléans, we cannot sufficiently wonder that Walchius could have named him here in confirmation of his opinion, since shortly before he himself had quoted words of Jonah which were so hostile to Felix. Let us hear the writer’s complete text, and we shall see that Walchius has in a way forgotten himself:

“To omit the others,” he says, “there arose from that same Spain, in the time of Charles, the most pious and invincible emperor of holy memory, a certain Felix by name but unhappy in conduct, bishop of the city of Urgell. He dared, together with his most wicked associate in error, Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, to preach that according to his humanity Christ was not the proper Son of God but an adopted son.”

A little later he continues:

“Against this mad doctrine the soldiers of Christ, equipped with invincible arms, raised their defense. By order of that same ruler they assembled in one place, with the authority of the holy Roman Church also present, and condemned Felix himself; indeed, together with the author of his error, Nestorius, whom he imitated, they [Col. 0391C] consigned him to perpetual anathema.”

Volume XIV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

With what confidence, I ask, could Walchius appeal to this writer, when he reports Felix’s error concerning adoption in Christ in such a way that he simultaneously calls Nestorius the author of that error and explicitly says that Felix followed in Nestorius’s footsteps?

But this is what generally happens when we are carried away by prejudices: we no longer form our arguments from the monuments of antiquity, but instead twist those monuments to fit our arguments.

Nor was this judgment concerning Elipandus and Felix held only by foreign writers. The same judgment was held by Spanish writers themselves, as will be clear to anyone who reads the letters of Alvarus of Córdoba, who flourished around the middle of the ninth century. There this author attacks the error concerning the often-mentioned adoption in such a way that he simultaneously asserts that it had been condemned in Nestorius by the Council of Ephesus and that two persons in Christ followed from it more than once. See Flórez, *Hispania Sacra*, volume XI, pages 119 and following.

[Col. 0391D]

### XXXIII. Walchius’s Evasions Are Answered

Walchius’s evasions are no less empty when he attempts to justify the statements of Felix and Elipandus against this error. To conceal nothing, it is useful briefly to review their principal arguments here and weaken them with the appropriate replies.

First, on page 221 he says:

“We certainly do not deny that there are some statements of Elipandus and Felix which, by a strained interpretation, can be explained in such a way that they appear to signify a distinction between the two natures of the kind that abolishes the hypostatic union (*unionem hypostaticam*). But if we examine the matter with a freer mind, everyone will understand that they present no difficulty. For they were spoken not of Christ, who is man, but of Christ [Col. 0392A] insofar as he is man.”

These words were plainly spoken to excuse excuses for sins. Walchius therefore admits that Elipandus and Felix uttered statements which appear to abolish the hypostatic union, yet he urges that they should be examined with a freer mind and, once so examined, judges them free of error.

But is the interpretation strained if one says that a natural son cannot be the same as an adopted son? Is not Walchius’s explanation of the words of Elipandus and Felix even more strained, when he says that they were spoken not of Christ who is man, but of Christ insofar as he is man? What distinction is there between these two expressions: “Christ who is man” and “Christ insofar as he is man”?

If, in Walchius’s understanding, the words of those bishops are taken of Christ who is man, they abolish the hypostatic union, because that Christ who is man is the natural Son of God. But must not that Christ also who is man, and indeed—what is the central point of the question—who is this man, be called the natural Son of God? Certainly he must. For insofar as he is this man, there is no other supposit in him except the divine one; therefore, insofar as he is this man, he must also be called the natural Son of God.

Or if he is said to be adopted insofar as he is this man, then a human supposit must also be admitted in him insofar as he is this man. Unless, finally, one wishes to consider human nature as though it had been [Col. 0392B] divided from union with the Word and separated by an abstraction of the mind. But everyone sees how absurd this would be, since the question then being discussed was what should be believed concerning the Word actually incarnate and the humanity actually assumed by the Word, precisely as it had been assumed.

The entire dispute concerned the mystery of the Incarnation as it had actually been accomplished and as it actually existed: human nature as it was actually united to the Word. It is therefore said to no purpose by Walchius that Elipandus and Felix considered humanity as though it had been set apart from the Word. No dispute then concerned humanity considered in that way, but rather the complete supposit in which two natures, divine and human, were present.

[Col. 0392C] Again, on the same page Walchius says:

“I would not have the reader offended by the word ‘adopted,’ since we have not yet agreed among ourselves concerning the meaning which Elipandus assigns to it.”

But why dispute about the meaning of the word “adopted,” which Elipandus did not invent in the first place, but received in the sense which it bears among everyone, precisely because he nowhere explained it otherwise?

Furthermore, after Walchius had touched upon the distinction mentioned above between “the one” and “the other” in Christ from the creed of Elipandus exhibited by Beatus and Etherius, he writes:

“We point out that Elipandus, if he ever uttered these statements, clearly enough showed that he was speaking of a distinction of natures, not of persons.”

We readily concede this. Yet no one is unaware that the Nestorians too, while wholly occupied with preserving the distinction of the natures against the Apollinarians, did this in such a way that they simultaneously divided the persons.

On page 224 Walchius admits that Felix had indeed carelessly asserted that nowhere in the Gospel is the Son of God said to have been delivered up for us, but only the son of man. He then adds:

[Col. 0392D] “Felix seems to have conceived better things in his mind than he expressed in words.”

Who does not see here a desire to quibble? Do words not express the meaning of the mind? Certainly, if this method of conjecture were accepted, no ancient heretic—whether Arian, Nestorian, Eutychian, or anyone else—could fail to be excused from his false doctrine, on the presumption that he had conceived better things in his mind than he had expressed in words.

Walchius continues:

“For I think Felix meant nothing other than what the theologians of purer doctrine teach: that, for the various functions of the mediatorship to be properly performed by Christ, each nature contributed distinctly what properly belongs to it. The concrete being of the divine nature could not die; therefore the Son of God joined to himself a human nature, so that he could die. Hence Felix was not wrong to say that the son of man, not the Son of God, died. But he would have been wrong to say that the son of man died without the Son of God, or to deny that the Son of God, who is the son of man, died.”

This is altogether an empty subtlety devised as a defense for heretics. For to say, “The son of man, not the Son of God, died,” is the same as saying, “The son of man died without the Son of God.” It is just as saying, “Peter, not John, entered the tomb,” is the same [Col. 0393A] as saying, “Peter entered the tomb without John.”

Whoever says, “The son of man, not the Son of God, died,” plainly denies that the one who died is the Son of God. He also denies that the Son of God is the one who died as the son of man.

No doubt therefore remains for us that the bishops so often mentioned—Elipandus and Felix—were altogether of the same mind as Nestorius. Throughout this paragraph we have seen that their principles and assertions led precisely to the same conclusion as those of the Nestorians. Alcuin therefore cannot at all be reproached on this account for branding his adversaries with the censure of Nestorian heresy.

Nothing remains except to justify the manner in which our writer attacked those heretics, a manner in which Walchius believed that there were so many matters deserving of criticism.

## § III. On the Manner in Which Saint Cyril Fought Against the Nestorians and Alcuin Against the Adoptianists

[Col. 0393B]

## I. Cyril’s manner of proceeding against Nestorius briefly vindicated

We are by no means unaware how greatly Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, was censured for the manner in which he attacked his adversaries—or rather, the Catholic Church’s adversaries—not only by those whom Nestorius counted among his particular friends in his own time, but also by certain more recent writers, among whom Peter Bayle is by no means the least, in the *Dictionnaire critique et historique*, vol. III, under “Nestorius.” Bayle supposed, first, that Cyril, out of private hatred and envy toward Nestorius, had disregarded the laws of equity in judging his doctrine and had precipitately imposed his sentence at the Council of Ephesus without any regard for legal procedure; and, next, that the controversy between them had been nothing more than an empty *λογομαχία*—a dispute about words—that both had in reality held orthodox opinions, and that they had argued so vehemently with one another for no other reason than that neither had properly penetrated the other’s meaning. [Col. 0393C]

Nevertheless, these and other charges brought against Cyril do not delay us from believing that Alcuin’s method of arguing against the Adoptianists may be justified on this ground alone: that it agrees exceedingly well with Cyril’s method against the Nestorians. Learned men long ago vindicated Cyril from these cavils, and we judge that no other defense is necessary than the judgment of the universal Church, which publicly declared that the dispute between him and Nestorius concerned not merely words but the very doctrine itself; that Nestorius’s assertions abolished the hypostatic union in Christ, whereas Cyril’s arguments fully established it—not only at the Council of Ephesus, but also at the Councils of Chalcedon and Constantinople II.

Moreover, the emperor Theodosius himself, although initially more severe toward Cyril, after learning of the frauds and machinations of his courtiers and of others who favored Nestorius’s person more than was proper, approved by public edict Cyril’s manner of proceeding against that heresiarch and ordered Nestorius himself to be deported into exile. [Col. 0393D]

There is, however, another difficulty that must still be briefly resolved before we approach our main subject. It was raised by Walch, who, in chapter 1 of his *History*, p. 49, did not hesitate to include our Cyril among the defenders of adoption in Christ, led by words found in dialogue 3 of this holy doctor’s work *On the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity*, vol. V of the *Works*, part I, fol. 486. They are as follows:

> “It is therefore clear, and according to the opinion of those who think rightly, that the name which is above every name was certainly given to the Son when, after taking our form as one of us, he was enrolled as the Son of God, adopted with us (*θετὸς μεθ’ ἡμῶν*), and, because of us, he who is the true and genuine one (*ὁ γνήσιος*), so that we too, because of him, might be sons and partakers of supernatural glory.”

But if these words are examined more carefully, they certainly appear foreign to the meaning that Walch believed he had discovered in them. For it must be understood that Cyril is there arguing against the Arians and refuting their reasoning from words taken from Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians, chapter II. Their argument was framed as follows: God the Father exalted his Son, or the Word, after the emptying, and bestowed upon him the name that is above every name, so that thereafter every knee should bow to him; therefore, he had received the designation “Son of God” and “God” not by nature but only by grace, and as such was worshiped by all.

Cyril further concedes that this is not to be understood of the Word before the incarnation, but that this name, which is above every name, was given to him only when, after assuming human nature, he as it were emptied himself. Accordingly, those words, “he was enrolled as the Son of God, adopted with us,” signify nothing other than the Son’s external glorification; and the adoption of which Cyril speaks in the cited passage is quite different from that about which he argued against the Nestorians.

For adoption, in a broader and less proper sense—the sense in which several of the Fathers also took it—may mean an assumption to glory; but in a narrower and more proper sense it means the assumption of an extraneous person as a son. Now everyone can see that the Word, hypostatically united to humanity—that is, united into one person—could not strictly be adopted; yet the Word clothed with humanity could be assumed, or, to use that term, adopted, into an external glory that he had not previously possessed. [Col. 0394A]

Finally, the holy doctor carefully distinguishes between the glorification of the Son, “the genuine one” (*τοῦ γνησίου*), and our glorification, since he calls us, because of him, sons—that is, strictly adopted sons of God.

It is further evident from other passages of Cyril how foreign he was to this way of thinking. There he denies that adoption, or sonship resembling ours—that is, proceeding from grace and not from nature—can be asserted of Christ the man without thereby producing two sons in the incarnate Word. Thus, in the dialogue *That Christ Is One*, he says:

> “But if, while confessing one Son and Lord, the Word from God the Father, they say that a mere man from the seed of David is associated with him in sonship and therefore also in glory, it will be fitting for us, grieving on behalf of those who think thus, out of the compassion that we owe to one another, to cry out: ‘Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, and I will weep for my people day and night’ (Jeremiah IX, 1)? For they have been delivered over to a depraved mind, denying the Lord who redeemed them. They establish a duality of sons of unequal nature, attributing divine glory to a servant and adorning some spurious one with equal excellence of honor, alongside the natural and true Son, although God plainly says: ‘I will not give my glory to another’ (Isaiah XLII, 8). For how can he not be different, separately from the natural and true Son, who has been adorned with a slight and merely apparent conjunction, assumed in the place of a servant, and who, adopted as we ourselves are (*καὶ ἀξιωθεὶς υἱότητος, καθὰ καὶ ἡμεῖς αὐτοί*), has been made a partaker of glory from another and has attained this by gift and grace?”

Vol. V of the *Works*, part I, fols. 734–735. A little further on, fol. 737, [Col. 0394D] he says:

> “Their discourse therefore undoubtedly preaches to us two sons and two Christs.”

He then introduces his interlocutor as replying:

> “Not at all two. They say that one is the Son according to nature, the Word from God the Father; but that the one who was assumed is indeed by nature a man of David, yet is the Son of God because he was assumed by the Word of God and, because the Word of God dwelt in him, obtained the same dignity and is a son by grace.”

Cyril answers:

> “But how can those who maintain this not be out of their minds? Or how do they not make two sons by separating man and God from one another? For according to their opinion, one is by nature and truly a Son, while the other possesses the same dignity by adoption, since the Word dwells in him (*ὅδε χάριτι τὴν υἱοθεσίαν ἔχων*).”

These passages clearly indicate that Cyril regarded as establishing a duality of sons in Christ those who confessed the Word as the natural Son of God but wished the assumed man to have been raised, like one of us, to the dignity of sonship—or, which is the same thing, to have been adopted. It must therefore be considered truly astonishing that Walch could also count Cyril among the defenders of adoption in Christ, since Cyril devoted himself entirely to demonstrating that not only the Word himself but also the man united to him is the proper Son of God.

Having briefly disposed of these matters, we now descend to the arguments themselves by which Cyril attacked the Nestorian assertions. We shall next examine Alcuin’s arguments against the Adoptianists, and shall see that these were wholly consonant with Cyril’s, so that our author too must be said to have fought his contest well, just as the entire orthodox world long ago proclaimed of Cyril.

For since, as we saw in the preceding paragraph, the principles or assertions of the Adoptianists were exactly the same as those of the Nestorians, they likewise had to be beaten back by the same weapons—that is, arguments and lines of reasoning—with which Cyril, and other defenders of Catholic doctrine together with him, refuted the Nestorians. If we show that Alcuin did this accurately in every detail, we shall consider the whole matter accomplished. [Col. 0395B]

## II. Cyril argues that two persons in Christ follow from the Nestorian doctrine

The general argument that Cyril opposed to nearly all the assertions of the Nestorians was this: from their teaching there followed two persons and two sons in Christ, and consequently the hypostatic union—which was certain not only from the faith of the universal Church but was verbally admitted at least by the heretics themselves—was abolished.

He pressed this argument with particular care against the assertion of adoption in Christ, and first of all refuted his adversaries by saying that their doctrine was new, hitherto unheard of in the Church, and for that reason to be rejected. For in the dialogue repeatedly cited, *That Christ Is One*, after he had said through his interlocutor:

> “We shall therefore reject this opinion as erroneous: that a man is united to God the Word, made a partaker of glory with him, and possesses adoption as a son by grace (*καὶ ἐν τάξει χάριτος τὴν υἱοθεσίαν ἔχειν*).”

He replies:

> “Certainly. For it cannot be proved from the sacred writings; rather, it is an invention of a weak and lax mind, eager for novelty.”

Folio 744 of the cited volume V, part I.

He then shows more forcefully how the hypostatic union is overturned by the assertion of this new doctrine. We already cited testimonies to this argument in the preceding section and shall recall one or two more.

In the frequently cited dialogue, fol. 739, he reports through his interlocutor the opinion of the Nestorians in these words:

> “We do not say, they reply, that the man is the Son of God, lest we establish two sons by nature. For just as the Word who descended from heaven is not by nature the son of David, so neither is he who is from the seed of David the Son of God according to nature.”

He then answers:

> “Will they therefore be divided into two sons, and will both be found falsely so called? Someone might say that the mystery of Christ is an empty and vain imposture if matters stand as these demented heretics wish. What, then, will the unity be? Or for what reason will they say that it was made?”

And in his second letter to Nestorius he says:

> “But if we reject the union according to hypostasis as incomprehensible and unfitting, we fall into saying that there are two sons. For it is necessary to distinguish one as a man in himself, honored with the title of son, and the other as the Word of God in himself and separately, who possesses both the name and the reality of sonship according to nature.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, col. 890.

For Cyril, therefore, to call Christ a man who was a son by grace, or adoptive, and to grant natural sonship to the Word alone, was the same as rejecting the union according to hypostasis, or distinguishing one from the other in Christ.

The holy doctor knew that the name “adoptive son” never properly belongs to a nature but is a designation of a person; and that not the nature of an extraneous person but the person himself, previously existing in his own right, is adopted as a son, since adoption is a kind of imitation of natural sonship, whereas a person, not a nature, is said to be begotten.

Hence he so consistently argues that persons are multiplied in Christ by the assertion of adoption, since every adoption presupposes an extraneous person—such a person as Catholic faith certainly cannot admit in Christ.

This argument was not Cyril’s alone, but also belonged to others, whether earlier or later than he, all of whom declared with one voice that two persons in Christ followed from the doctrine of adoption.

Thus Leporius, in his *Book of Correction*, says:

> “Our faith consists especially in this: that we believe in one sole Son of God, not an adoptive but a proper Son.”

Here this man, after returning from error to Catholic truth, proclaims one Son and calls him proper, not adoptive. He therefore believed that this unity was abolished precisely by establishing adoption in Christ.

Moreover, we already related above, in § I, no. 15, from Saint Gregory of Nyssa, that certain people had been accused of the error of a double son solely because they admitted adoption in the Word clothed with flesh. [Col. 0396B]

The words also deserve notice that are found in Cyril’s defense against the opposition raised by the Easterners to his eighth anathema, vol. V of the Councils, col. 50, and likewise in the book *To the Queens*, vol. IV of the Councils, cols. 690–691, where they are presented under the name of Athanasius from the book *On the Incarnation*:

> “We also confess that he is the Son of God and God according to the Spirit, and the Son of man according to the flesh . . . and not two sons: one the true and worshiped Son of God, the other a man from Mary, not to be worshiped—that is, made Son of God by grace, as human beings also are (*κατὰ χάριν δὲ Υἱὸν Θεοῦ γενόμενον, ὡς καὶ ἄνθρωποι*).”

And after a little more:

> “Therefore he who was born from the Virgin Mary is by nature the Son of God and true God, and not, by grace and participation, according to the flesh alone, a man from Mary, while according to the Spirit he himself is the Son of God and God.”

And again:

> “But if anyone teaches from the divine Scriptures anything contrary to this, saying that one is the Son of God and another, from Mary, is an adopted son by grace, as we are (*καὶ ἕτερον ἐκ τῆς Μαρίας κατὰ χάριν υἱοποιηθέντα, ὡς ἡμεῖς*), so that there are two sons—one according to nature, the Son of God who is from God, and one according to grace, a man from Mary . . . let the holy and Catholic Church anathematize him, etc.”

We certainly know that the book *On the Incarnation*, from which these passages were taken, is listed among the doubtful works of Athanasius because of expressions occurring in it that seem to favor the error of the Eutychians, or at least were not otherwise familiar to Athanasius. Hence there is no slight suspicion that this little work is an invention of the Eutychians or of other heretics, and that the quoted words were inserted under Athanasius’s name into Cyril’s writings after his death, either by Dioscorus of Alexandria or by another Eutychian heretic, as some think.

Or at least, if that work already existed before Cyril’s time, it may have been falsely attributed to Athanasius; yet Cyril, who perhaps interpreted certain harsher expressions more favorably, recognized it as a genuine work of Athanasius and therefore cited it as testimony to Catholic truth. Unless, perhaps, one may say that the statements which appear to reproduce the Eutychian error were appended only after Cyril’s death by the aforementioned Dioscorus or another heretic to a work genuinely composed by Athanasius. [Col. 0396D]

Whatever may be decided about this matter, whether the book *On the Incarnation* was written before or after Cyril’s death, it is at least clear that its author rejected adoption in Christ on the basis that it cannot be defended without division of persons.

Pope Vigilius shortly afterward likewise used the same argument in his *Constitutum on the Three Chapters*. Regarding chapter 19 of Theodore, he says:

> “In the aforementioned nineteenth chapter, where the Gospel according to Luke appears to be explained with reference to Christ’s baptism, there are two objections: one, that a duality of sons is introduced when Christ is called the Son of God by adoption; the other, that he himself is also said to have been baptized in the name of the Trinity, by which a quaternity is without doubt displayed.”

Vol. IX of the Councils, col. 76.

And regarding chapter 47:

> “In the aforementioned forty-seventh chapter, when the Apostle’s statement is explained—‘who had brought many sons to glory’ (Hebrews II, 10)—it is said that the holy Apostle counts the assumed man among the others because he likewise received the grace of sonship, while the deity alone possesses natural sonship. These words, as was stated above, introduce two sons: one by grace, the other by nature.”

Vol. IX of the Councils, col. 88.

Cyril, therefore, was not the only one who inferred a duality of sons from the doctrine of adoption; rather, all of them agreed with him in this line of reasoning. We have noted this so that none of the more recent adversaries of this holy doctor may object to his manner of attacking the enemies of the Church and of the faith as wholly singular or insufficiently accurate. We shall now present the arguments by which he refuted the reasoning employed by the Nestorians to establish that adoption.

## III. To the Nestorian argument that neither divinity was born from the Virgin Mother nor humanity from the eternal Father, Cyril replies that a man is nevertheless called the whole son of his parents, even if his soul did not arise from his mother’s flesh

We stated in the preceding paragraph, no. 5, that the Nestorians based themselves chiefly on the claim that neither divinity was born from the Virgin nor humanity from the eternal Father; and consequently that the most blessed Virgin should not be called *Deipara*, nor the man born from her the natural Son of God, but only an adoptive son.

Against this inference Cyril replies by appealing to human mothers. Although they do not generate the principal part of their offspring—namely, the soul—they are nevertheless mothers of the whole man; and a man is, and must be, called the son of his mother in respect of all his parts.

> “But perhaps here you will ask,” he says in his *Letter to the Egyptian Monks*, no. 12, “whether, tell me, the Virgin was the mother of divinity. To this we say that the living and subsisting Word of God was truly, beyond all controversy, begotten from the very essence of God and the Father. . . . But in the last times of this age he became incarnate—that is, he was united to a body formed by an intelligent soul—and according to the flesh also was born from a woman.

> “The mystery of the incarnate Word has a kinship with human birth. For the mothers of earthly human beings, serving nature in generation, carry in the womb flesh which gradually grows denser through intervals of time and, slowly receiving increase through certain hidden operations of the Creator, is brought to perfection and finally reaches human form. God, however, in a manner known to himself, infuses the spirit. . . .

> “The relation of the flesh is one thing, and that of the soul another. Yet although those women become mothers only of earthly bodies, they are nevertheless said to give birth not to one part but to the whole, which is composed of soul and body. For no one, to make the matter clear by an example, would say that Elizabeth gave birth only to flesh and not also to a soul; she gave birth to the Baptist as an animated man, one being constituted from two things—flesh, I mean, and soul.

> “Let us therefore think that the same thing occurred in the birth of Emmanuel. For, as I have said, his only-begotten Word was born from the substance of God the Father; but after assuming flesh, which he made his own, and taking on our nature, he became the Son of man. Without any absurdity, indeed with necessary and fitting reason, he is believed and proclaimed according to the flesh to have been born from a woman.

> “In the same way, although the human soul is understood to differ by nature from the body that it informs and exists in its own proper mode, it nevertheless arises together with its body and is regarded as one thing with it. If anyone should insist that the mother of someone ought not to be called a giver of soul but only a giver of flesh, he would plainly reveal himself as an absurd babbler. For although what the woman gives birth to is composed of two unlike things harmoniously fitted together, she nevertheless gives birth to one animal and one man, with each part retaining its own nature and, as it were, entering into a natural union, so that these two are mingled with each other and each makes common to the other what properly belongs to itself.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, cols. 598–599.

In no. 17 he addresses the charge of the Nestorians, who accused Catholics as though they said that the flesh itself had been begotten from the eternal Father. He says:

> “Nor do we, who have resolved to think rightly, say that God became the father of the flesh, nor again that the nature of divinity was born from a woman before it had assumed human nature. Rather, bringing together into unity the Word who is by nature from God and the man who was perfectly born into this world from the holy Virgin, we shall worship one Lord and Christ Jesus. Thus we shall not cast this one outside the bounds of divinity because of the assumed flesh; nor, because of the likeness which he shares with us, enclose him within the limits of human nature alone.”

Ibid., col. 606.

For when the Nestorians argued that Christ, in respect of his humanity, was not begotten from the Father and therefore had to be called a son only by grace or adoption—and consequently that his mother, who had borne humanity alone and not divinity, should be called *Christotokos* (*Χριστοτόκος*), not *Theotokos* (*Θεοτόκος*)—Cyril replied that although Christ was not begotten from the eternal Father according to the flesh, he was nevertheless, even in this respect, the Father’s natural Son, because after the union the flesh had become proper to the Word.

He argued by analogy that parents who produce only a man’s flesh are nevertheless called the parents of the whole man and therefore also in respect of the soul, although God alone infuses the soul, because after its infusion the soul is regarded as belonging to the flesh that the mother had brought forth. Similarly, although the blessed Virgin did not herself generate divinity, she nevertheless exists as the mother of Christ the Lord even in respect of his divinity, since she bore the human nature that the eternal Son had intimately united to himself.

Thus, in the same place, no. 20, col. 610, after reporting the Apostle’s words, “who did not spare his own Son, etc.” (Romans VIII, 32), he continues:

> “I now ask you: how is he who was born from the holy Virgin called the proper Son of God? Just as it is rightly said to be proper to a man, or to any other living creature, whatever naturally proceeds from it, so that also is deservedly regarded and called proper to God which is generated from his substance. How, then, is Christ called God’s proper Son, who is also proclaimed as having been offered by God, the Father of all, for the sake of salvation and life? . . . It is clear that, with regard to the union of the natures, he defines Emmanuel, who arose from the holy Virgin, as the Son of God, since the body born from her belonged not to some other man like us, but to the very Word who was born from the Father.”

Nestorius himself perhaps provided the occasion for this argument when he had abused it in support of his error. According to Cyril, he says:

> “An infant is formed in the womb, but until it has received its shape it does not yet have a soul; once it has been formed, however, the soul is fashioned by God. Thus, just as a woman gives birth to the body, while God grants the soul, and therefore she is not called the mother of the soul because she gave birth to an ensouled being, but rather the mother of the man, so also the blessed Virgin, although she gave birth to a man, is not for that reason the Mother of God, since the Word of God passed through with him.”

Book I *Against Nestorius*, vol. VI, fol. 17.

Cyril answers there, fol. 18:

> “Flesh is undoubtedly begotten from flesh, and the maker of all things causes it, in a manner and by a method known to himself, to be animated. Yet the woman who gave birth, although she is the source only of the flesh, is nevertheless believed to have brought forth the whole man, consisting, I mean, of soul and body, although she contributed nothing of herself to the soul’s existence. But whoever said ‘man’ thereby signified the soul united with the body.

> “Therefore, just as a woman, although she has given birth only to the body, is said to have brought forth one composed of soul and body, without this in any way harming the account of the soul—as though it had received from the flesh the beginning of its existence—so also is the case with the blessed Virgin. For although she is the mother of that holy flesh, she nevertheless truly gave birth to the God Word who came from God and was united to it. Nor, if anyone calls her the Mother of God, does he thereby immediately impose novelty upon the Word of God or define that he derived the beginning of his existence from the flesh, etc.”

Cyril develops this argument at greater length in the same place and finally also dissolves Nestorius’s reasoning by which he denied that Christ the man was the natural Son of God, on the ground that if this were admitted, two generations would fall upon the divine Word, something that he did not think could be conceded.

> “I rejoice,” Nestorius says in the cited passage, fol. 21, “to see your zeal. From this it can plainly be shown what shameful things have been spoken by the wretched man. For those who have two generations must necessarily have two sons; but the Church acknowledges one Son, the Lord Christ.”

Cyril replies that either two generations must altogether be admitted in Christ, or the mystery of the Incarnation must be denied. Here are his words. Although they are rather lengthy, we give them in full, since they display the remarkable and precise power of reasoning that the holy doctor employed against the heretics:

> “He therefore judged that two generations should by no means be admitted. He asserts that we must confess one birth, lest we understand there to be two sons, as though it were necessary, if there are altogether two generations, to infer two sons as well. Let him therefore come forward and teach which generation he prefers to admit: that from the Father before the ages, through which God the Word was not yet incarnate, or this recent one, from a woman.

> “For if he says that only the former is to be admitted—the one, I mean, before the ages and from the Father—then that one, and that one alone, will certainly be the Son who was born from him according to nature before he shared in flesh and blood. But the mystery of the Incarnation is then asserted rashly and vainly; he did not empty himself in any way, nor did he assume the form of a servant, but remained as he was and continued to reject a true union with flesh.

> “If, on the other hand, he who was born from a woman in the last times is said to be the Son, and if we admit only this generation from a woman, then the Word from God the Father has necessarily been lost, so that he is no longer the Son according to nature.

> “But the man who loves God clearly sees how absurd these positions are and how greatly they tend toward impiety. Therefore, to walk along the royal road, we say that there were two births but one Son in both: the Word from God before he was in the flesh, and the same Word afterward incarnate, who for our sake underwent a second generation.

> “If he had said that among human beings, whenever we speak of two generations, there must necessarily be two sons, he would have spoken rightly and truly. But since the mystery of Christ and the nature of the Incarnation follow another path, and since the matter is not seen in the same way in our affairs, why, after examining the custom that prevails among us, does he then turn his mind toward things marvelous and beyond reason only to fall openly into weak and foolish unbelief?

> “What I find astonishing is this: although in these words he had confessed that the Church acknowledges one Son and had added that this one is the Lord Christ himself, he nowhere afterward retained the one, but distinguished the united realities from one another and set each separately, without investigating what the Word is according to nature and what the flesh is, but combining man and God as though by an equality of glory alone, as he supposes. This is neither believable to anyone nor possible, and it drives the explanation of so great a mystery into absurdity.”

## IV. He demonstrates that the anointing belonged to Christ the man from the hypostatic union itself, and did not first come to him through merits

Cyril no less soundly refutes the arguments of the Nestorians drawn from the anointing of the Holy Spirit received by Christ, from his baptism, and from his progressive advancement in grace and wisdom. [Col. 0400A]

When they said that Christ the man had acquired this anointing through his merits and then inferred from it that he had been adopted as the Son of God by grace alone, Cyril replies that this anointing did not first come to the assumed nature through merits or progress in virtues, but was owed to it by virtue of the hypostatic union itself. This could not be denied without abolishing that union and making Christ a mere man.

It will not be unwelcome to repeat here Cyril’s words, already quoted above in § 2, no. 5:

> “Some people, I do not know how, assert that this name ‘Christ’ belongs also separately and in itself to the Word of God the Father—that is, when it is conceived mentally as existing outside the flesh—and then contend that it likewise belongs to him who was born from the holy Virgin, considered as existing in himself and separately. Finally, they say that it belongs equally to both together as to one, on account of the conjunction, as they themselves express it, which brings them together into one person. (For among them the true and natural union receives no consideration, although it offers a single path through this mystery, plain and safe from every error.) Their simulated confession is not sincere but full of dark poison and deceit.

> “For when Holy Scripture, naming Christ, simply ascribes everything divine to him—for it knows, it knows, I say, that the Word of God appeared in human form and became flesh—the purpose and aim of those who think differently is to persuade us that he who was born from a woman is some single man who, through gradual development, as I have said, and through his own, that is, human, virtue, showed himself worthy of obtaining the honor of conjunction with the Word of God and of being chosen by an eminent predestination.”

Vol. IV of the Councils, col. 698.

In the immediately following section he then shows that the name “Christ,” or “anointed,” belongs not precisely to the Word alone but to the humanity, and to both together because of the hypostatic union:

> “For this reason they assert that this name ‘Christ’ belongs also to the Word alone, who arose from God the Father, when he is considered as existing separately and in himself. But we have by no means learned to think or speak in this way. For we say that the Word first received the designation ‘Jesus Christ’ when he became flesh, since he is called Christ because he was anointed by God the Father with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit.

> “That this anointing belongs to him in respect of the assumed humanity is not questioned among those who think rightly. For if the Word of God is God, he certainly has no need of anointing. No one has ever taught that the Word of God was anointed or sanctified by the Holy Spirit, as though the Spirit were by nature different from him, superior and more excellent. For the lesser is always blessed without contradiction by the better (Hebrews VII, 7).

> “Since sanctification and anointing therefore correspond to the lowliness of human nature, it necessarily follows that the Word of God was not given the name ‘Christ’ when he was still naked—that is, not yet incarnate—but only when, having become man in our manner, he was anointed according to human nature. . . .

> “If Christ is named absolutely anywhere, understand him at once as incarnate; and if you hear the word after the Incarnation has been accomplished, do not forget the flesh united to him. To suppose, however, or to say that this word ‘Christ’ belongs separately to one and separately again to the other is utterly foolish, indeed impious and profane. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, not divided, not cut apart, etc.”

Cyril therefore believed that the anointing was to be attributed not to the merits of the assumed man but to the assumption itself, or to the hypostatic union. From this he proved that Christ, even insofar as he is man, must be called the natural Son of God, since from his very birth he possessed the right to the Father’s inheritance and all his goods. Consequently, adoption in Christ could not be proved from that anointing unless one wished to say that he was a mere man. [Col. 0401A]

Pope Vigilius afterward employed the same line of reasoning in his responses to Theodore’s chapters. In his response to chapter 32, whose words we saw above in § 2, no. 5, he says:

> “In the aforementioned thirty-second chapter, in the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Peter’s statement is introduced: ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power.’ It is then inferred: ‘Whoever has been anointed with the Spirit of God has in every respect received something from him’; and it is added: ‘Who, being in his right mind, would say that the divine nature received something from the Spirit?’

> “By these words Christ is presented as a mere man who, through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, became a partaker of the divine nature, as others did; and, in the name of a just reward, because he loved righteousness and hated iniquity, obtained an everlasting anointing. Whoever thinks, believes, or preaches in this way, let him be anathema.”

Vol. IX of the Councils, col. 82.

You will read similar statements in the responses to chapters 7 and 39.

[Col. 0401B] **V. He gives the same answer to the argument drawn from Christ’s baptism, and says that at least imperfections would have to be admitted in him if he is said to have needed baptism.**—Cyril resolves the Nestorians’ argument drawn from Christ’s baptism with virtually the same reply, saying that Christ received, not first at the bank of the Jordan on account of the merit of his actions, but in the womb and from the first instant of conception, the fullness of the Holy Spirit that was due to him by virtue of the hypostatic union. Nor can the contrary be maintained—namely, that the Savior needed baptism and that through this washing he was adopted—without dividing him into two sons: one said to be coeternal with the Father and equal to him in every kind of perfection; the other a mere man, either altogether subject at the beginning to certain imperfections and subsequently justified from them in baptism, or at least first endowed in baptism, on account of a preceding exercise of virtue, with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“But I am astonished” (he says in the fragments against Theodore reported in the [Col. 0401C] fifth collation of the Fifth Synod) “that the adversary wrote that Jesus would never have merited union with God the Word unless he had first been made immaculate through anointing. For first he plainly separates and clearly distinguishes two sons. Then let him say when, as he claims, he was made immaculate and merited union with God the Word: whether from the womb itself, or when he was thirty years old. He did indeed come to the Jordan, and he also sought John’s baptism. If he was holy from the womb, was he made holy, and did he thereby become something he was not? For whenever something is said to be made, it is altogether necessary to understand that what was made did not previously exist. But if he was always holy, and was not made so in time, how does he say that the Spirit descended upon him, demonstrated him worthy of union, and added to him what was lacking? What, indeed, was lacking to him from the womb for sanctification—indeed, even before his birth according to the flesh—to him who was holy and immaculate and sanctifying the creature? Since, therefore, he says that Jesus would not have merited union with God the Word unless he had first been made immaculate, he simultaneously writes many accusations against his own empty chatter. First, he improperly says ‘merited’; then he separates off another son, the one descended from David, whom he shamelessly insists on calling Jesus alone and separately. Moreover, to say that he was made immaculate, as though he had at some point not possessed this quality, contains the greatest blasphemy. For God the Word, united with his flesh from the womb itself, was one with it; and thus he was also the immaculate Son, the Holy of Holies, giving from his own fullness not only to human beings but also to the rational powers above and in heaven.” *Tom. IX Concil.*, col. 238.

Cyril consequently held that the Holy Spirit was proper to the assumed man also by virtue of the hypostatic union, and that the Spirit was not first bestowed in baptism by grace or merely by the benevolent will of the one assuming him. Hence, in Book [Col. 0402A] IV against Nestorius, after reporting the words of that heresiarch—“The descending Spirit procured the glory of the assumed man; the Father commended the baptized man,” and so forth—he argues as follows:

“Without doubt he was glorified, the Spirit effecting divine signs—not as though he were a deified man who received that gift from an external and superior nature, as happens to us, but using the Spirit as his own. For he was God by nature, and therefore his Spirit was not alien to him. We do not, then, say that the Spirit’s power was given to him from outside or acquired elsewhere, as it was given to us ourselves or certainly to the holy apostles. For Christ gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they might cast them out; he also commanded them to heal every sickness and every disease among the people. His Spirit, therefore, is within him and from him. A clear proof of this is that he can also give the Spirit to others, and not according to measure, as the blessed Evangelist says. For that God of all does indeed grant the grace of the Holy Spirit to holy men according to measure: to one he gave the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the gift of healings. Is this not, as I suppose, what those who possess the power mean when they say ‘according to measure’? But our Lord Jesus Christ, pouring forth the Spirit from his own fullness, just as the Father does, does not give him according to measure to those who are worthy to receive him. Why, then, excellent sir, do you place among those who possess the Spirit in measured fashion the one who gives the Spirit not according to measure, when you say that he acquired glory from his Spirit and was rather subject to that Spirit’s power, receiving cooperation from it as a grace, like one of us, than effecting divine signs by his own Spirit?” *Tom. VI oper.*, fols. 98–99.

A little farther on he speaks even more explicitly about baptism, showing that Christ himself is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit—that is, that the Holy Spirit is infused into human beings when they are baptized in Christ’s name. Christ therefore did not need baptism in order to receive an increase or fullness of sanctification, since the Holy Spirit was already proper to him from his first conception and his gifts were due to him from another source.

“Accordingly,” Cyril says, “let us examine the rest of his [Nestorius’s] statements, if you please. ‘The Father commended him,’ he says. I cannot understand what ‘commended’ means here, for the expression is taken from the marketplace and is full of vulgar speech and common foolishness. Yet I suppose it means ‘deposited’ or, for example, ‘gave testimony.’ How, then, I ask you, did the Father commend a man who had been deemed worthy of divine indwelling? Or did he not rather demonstrate that the proper Son had become man while remaining in the flesh what he was, is, and will be—namely, God? For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

“Come, then, let us investigate the statements made about him. What does the Evangelist say? ‘And John bore witness, saying: I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and he remained upon him. This is he who baptizes in the Spirit. And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God’ (John 1:32–33).

“Our Lord Jesus Christ proceeded according to the economy in order to sanctify the Jordan, and he deigned to be baptized with us so that he might carry out, in ways appropriate to it, the mystery of that dispensation according to the flesh. For it was necessary that the Word who was from God the Father should be recognized as having become man. He was baptized as man, but he baptized as God in the Holy Spirit. Nor do we say that he supplied a participation in the Holy Spirit either as one who serves another or as though receiving it from someone else; rather, as God by nature, he poured forth from his fullness and made the sanctified holy.

“Why, then, do you disregard straightforward words and propositions and assert that indwelling in a man was effected by the Word himself, although many holy men have had him dwelling within them, while no one among them baptized anyone in his own Spirit, or dwelt in anyone in the divine manner, or was said to have done so? Christ himself dwells in us through the Spirit, who is also his own, just as he is undoubtedly the Spirit of God and the Father.” *Ibid.*, fol. 101.

Pope Vigilius likewise refutes Theodore’s errors by similar reasoning. In response to chapter 54 he says:

“In the aforementioned fifty-fourth chapter, the statement of the Apostle—‘He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit’ (1 Tim. 3:16)—is expounded as asserting that Christ was justified, either because before baptism he observed the law with appropriate exactness, or because after it he likewise completed a life of grace through the cooperation of the Spirit with great exactness. Since these words likewise demonstrate that a mere man, Christ, needed justification, if anyone thinks thus . . . and does not rather believe that he, as true God consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, justifies the ungodly through faith, let him be anathema.” *Tom. IX Conc.*, col. 90.

And in response to chapter 6:

“In the aforementioned sixth chapter, he is again presented as a mere man, led to everything by the Spirit whose presence he is said to have received after baptism, strengthened and taught like the other human beings, concerning whom the Apostle appears here to say: ‘All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God’ (Rom. 8:14). If anyone thinks thus . . . and does not believe, confess, and preach that Christ is one—the incarnate Word of God—let him be anathema.” *Ibid.*, col. 69.

See also the response to Theodore’s chapter 19, reported shortly before in section 2.

**VI. He gives a similar reply to the argument that the Nestorians had constructed from the supposed successive progress in wisdom and grace attributed to Christ in the Gospels.**—With regard to the successive progress in virtue that the Nestorians attributed to Christ as man, Cyril replied in the passage first cited that nothing of perfection or holiness was ever lacking in him, since from the first instant of conception he received all the fullness of grace that was properly due to him. The progress in wisdom and grace mentioned by the Evangelists concerning Christ meant nothing other than an outward manifestation by which, in proportion to his age, he was increasingly glorified before human beings.

But if anyone should maintain that Christ truly acquired this perfection only gradually over time, Cyril held that such an opinion destroyed the mystery of the Incarnation and established Christ, successively adorned with virtues, as a mere man and a person distinct from the divine Word.

“How, then,” he says in Book III against Nestorius, “are you not ashamed to bring forward, in order to prove what you have said, the words of blessed Luke: ‘Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace’ (Luke 2:52)? You say that he increased in wisdom—yet how could that not be foolish? We believe that Emmanuel himself came forth from the womb and the virgin womb as man, although he was God, undoubtedly full of wisdom and grace, which were inherent in him by nature. What increase, then, could he receive who contains all the treasures of wisdom and, together with God the Father, is the dispenser of heavenly grace? How, then, is he said to advance? In my judgment, because God the Word measured out the manifestation of those divine goods inherent in him according to the increase and age of his body.

“Let us consider that, although he had already become a man like us, he initially sought to remain hidden, quietly and without disturbance gradually arranging the force of the mystery. God and the Father will be our ample guarantor of this, when he says: ‘Jacob is my servant; I will receive him. Israel is my chosen one; my soul has received him. I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring judgment to the nations. He will not cry out or raise his voice, nor will his voice be heard outside. He will not break a bruised reed, nor extinguish a smoldering wick’ (Isa. 42; Matt. 12). He also rebuked the holy apostles themselves, lest they make him known.

“Thus it would have been something new and extraordinary, requiring closer investigation, if while still an infant he had displayed the appearance of divine wisdom. But since he gradually enlarged it in proportion to the age of his body and made it evident to all, he may quite appropriately be said to have advanced.” *Tom. VI Oper.*, fol. 86.

You will find similar statements in the second *Oration on the Right Faith to the Queens*, no. 16, *Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 819.

In his defense against the fourth anathema proposed by the Easterners he says:

“But since at the beginning of their discourse they included only a small portion of our letter and threaten that they will refute us in due course, as though we had committed no ordinary offense against the Word from God the Father by foolishly attributing to his nature the increase and progress that belong to the flesh, let us say what is appropriate here as well, adding the entire passage of the letter . . . It reads as follows: ‘And if you hear that Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace, do not suppose that the wise Word of God became wise through progress. Rather, I will recall what the divine Paul wrote: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (1 Cor. 1:24).

“Nor should you again foolishly dare to say that we attribute progress in age, wisdom, and grace to the man. For this, in my judgment, means nothing other than dividing the one Christ into two. Rather, as I said shortly before, the Son who exists before the ages is said to have been predestined as Son of God in the final times of the age, appropriating the birth of his flesh to himself according to the economy. Thus, although he exists as the Wisdom of the one who begot him and is most perfect, being God, he is said to advance in wisdom, since he appropriately assumed the properties of humanity through the supreme union.” *Tom. V Conc.*, col. 47.

Finally, Pope Vigilius, in his response to Theodore’s chapter 12, where this successive progress is asserted concerning Christ as man, says:

“In the aforementioned twelfth chapter, the same things that appear to be expounded in the seventh chapter are again asserted: namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ was instructed in everything through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit and reached the perfection of his anointing over time with the Spirit’s assistance. Therefore, if anyone believes, teaches, or preaches that he was not perfected by his own deity but, as a mere man in need of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, was assisted by it, let him be anathema.” *Tom. IX Conc.*, col. 72.

From these statements anyone can easily see that all the arguments of Cyril and of the others who fought against the Nestorians were directed chiefly toward demonstrating that, on the principles of their adversaries—namely, the doctrine of adoption in Christ and the arguments by which they attempted to establish it—the hypostatic union, and consequently the very mystery of the Incarnation, were abolished. The divine Word would, in reality, not have assumed human nature or become flesh; Christ would have to be regarded as a mere man, distinguished from the rest only in that, on account of the singular conjunction—an expression which the Nestorians used as a kind of watchword while consistently rejecting the term “union”—he had been admitted into communion of dignity and names with the Word.

[Col. 0404D] **VII. He shows that if Christ as man is only a titular God, there are two persons, and that we possess the same dignity as the man assumed by the Word. The words of Nestorius.**—By the same kind of arguments Cyril and the others also attacked another chief error of Nestorianism: the claim that Christ as man was merely a titular God, as we saw above in section 8 of the preceding paragraph.

Saint Cyril specifically opposed this assertion in the eighth anathema, formulated in these words:

“If anyone dares to say that the assumed man must be worshiped and glorified together with the Word of God, and that the assumed man must be jointly called God with the Word, as one with another—for this is the meaning that the particle ‘with,’ when added, perpetually and necessarily conveys—and does not rather honor Emmanuel with one worship and attribute to him one glorification, insofar as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”

In defense of this anathema, responding to the objection of the Easterners, he says:

“To say that a man is worshiped with God and jointly called God is altogether to confess that there are two who must be worshiped, or even two who must be jointly called.”” *Tom. V Conc.*, col. 54.

In his response to Theodore’s criticism he teaches that, if the assumed man is called God together with the Word, or is so only titularly, it plainly follows that the Word did not properly unite human nature to himself and that Emmanuel is a mere man like us.

“For,” he says, “the one who is himself God and man is worshiped as one with one worship, not co-worshiped, and is at the same time called God—not so that Emmanuel may be believed to be simply an ordinary man like us and a participant in divine glory by grace, but so that we may confess him rather as God in the flesh for our sake, that is, truly made man, not by a change of nature through alteration or transformation, but by the economy of union.” *Ibid.*, cols. 119 and 22.

Finally, when Nestorius says in Book II against Nestorius: “That which was formed in the womb is not God in itself; . . . but because God is in the one assumed, the one assumed is called God together with the one assuming, as joined to the one assuming,” Cyril replies that human nature was indeed made proper to the Word through the assumption, and that after the Incarnation it can no more be conceived separately from him than, when one speaks of a man, his soul can be considered separated from his body. Thus Christ, even insofar as he is man, must be called true God and not a titular god.

He then says that to assert that the assumed man is called God in the same way as the rest of human beings is to assert that there are two persons in Christ and two Gods. It further entails that we possess exactly the same dignity as that man, whom the Word nevertheless united to himself in a wholly ineffable manner.

Cyril’s words are so profound that they seem to exhaust the entire subject:

“For who would dare to say such a thing? Or who has ever been unaware that what was born of flesh is flesh? Yet it was proper to the Word, and is understood as one with it, just as, without doubt, we said above, the soul of a man is one with his body.

“If, then, someone wished to say of us also that the body itself is not a man in isolation, would he not rightly be called excessively pedantic and foolish in his speech? No one will deny that the body by itself is not a man, but is rather called the body of a man. Yet no one, dividing the two parts and setting soul and body apart, has ever said that the body is called by the same name as the soul in order to signify one man. Such speech would not be appropriate but full of ignorance. When, however, he joins both according to their natural union into the constitution of one man, then at last he calls him a man, and he will not seem to speak ineptly or absurdly.

“Therefore, if he was in any way wise and skillful, he ought to have said that the body was from a woman and, in addition, confessed that, through unity according to hypostasis, it had been joined to the Word, which had constituted one Christ, Son, and Lord, at once God and man.

“But now, omitting this, he proceeds along a perverse path, departing from the right one, and preaches two Gods to us: one according to nature and truth, namely, the Word from God the Father; and another besides him, who is called God together with him. For just as no one of our kind is said to associate with himself and himself alone, but associates with another, and just as anyone who said that he reigned with himself would rightly be laughed at and would be speaking foolishly, since he would state and pronounce of one alone as though it were said of two, so it would be exceedingly foolish to suppose that the phrase ‘called together’ could be said of one alone. There will therefore be two altogether: one God according to nature, and the other, who has nothing except that he is called God together with the former, and that externally and as something acquired, has newly become a god for us.

“If this is so, how do we worship Christ, and how shall every knee bow to him? How do you also confess that you venerate him, while nevertheless fearing, as you said, lest you appear to be a worshiper of a man? Yet he has, as he supposes, a clever answer to this: ‘He is called God together with the one assuming, as one joined to him.’ Explain how he was assumed, or in what manner he was joined. If you mean according to a true union—the union according to hypostasis—I say, then stop dividing what has been united. And appropriately we too shall say to you, who divide what is indivisible: ‘What God has joined together, let man not divide’ (Matt. 19).

“But if you say that the assumption or conjunction is external and relative, how do you fail to see that God is also in us, that we too are joined to him relatively, and that we have become participants in his divine nature?

“Therefore, according to your opinion, we too shall be gods by nature together with him who is God by nature, and shall be called gods together with him; and every knee shall bow to us,” and so forth. *Tom. VI Oper.*, fols. 58–59.

**VIII. When the Nestorians abused scriptural passages in which human beings are sometimes called gods, as Moses was called the god of Pharaoh, Cyril gives substantially the same answer.**—Cyril says in Book II against Nestorius:

“What are you saying? What sort of speech are you spewing from your heart, not from the mouth of the Lord, as it is written? ‘No one says “Anathema to Jesus” except in Beelzebub.’ As Moses himself is understood or called God by us, is Christ also so called? Tell me, then: is the Son likewise comparable to Israel? O supreme impiety! O words that are not even afraid to diminish the glory of our Savior!

“For blessed Moses was a man, by nature like us, and nothing more. But when God said, ‘Come, I will send you to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and you will bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt’ (Exod. 7), he put forward the weakness of his speech as an excuse for refusing, alleging that he was not eloquent from yesterday or the day before. Therefore he heard God say: ‘Behold, I have given you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your interpreter’ (ibid.).

“For the law is weak when it comes to liberating anyone from the slavery of the devil. Yet this too was accomplished through Christ the mediator, just as at that time in Egypt Israel was liberated from slavery when Aaron himself had been joined to blessed Moses. But because in the course of time Christ was destined to come even under the law, since he was like us and a man, Aaron was placed second after Moses.

“This, then, is the meaning of the mystery. Yet if anyone should also wish to say that Moses, that great man, was honored by this designation of God, in accordance with the common saying spoken of us through God’s grace and magnificence, ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’—is Christ God in this way as well? How could this not be madness and the empty product of a foolish mind?

“For that man, as I have already said, was honored with a bare and simple title, since he was by nature a man. But this one is truly God—for the Word was God—preserving intact, in human form, the excellence of his nature by which he surpasses all things. For the divine nature can never be corrupted for the worse because it descended to share in flesh and blood. Thus, even when he appeared as man, he is nevertheless recognized as God. The Gospels contain clear evidence of this concerning him.

“For blessed John said: ‘When he was in Jerusalem during the feast, many believed in his name, seeing the signs that he performed. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all things, and because he had no need for anyone to testify about man; for he himself knew what was in man’ (John 2).

“Yet to be able to look into the human heart and know hidden things belongs neither to any man who is like us nor to any other creature, but only to him who is also said to have formed our hearts one by one (Ps. 32). If this is so, how was Emmanuel honored by a mere and simple title, so that he would be called God just as Moses was, rather than truly being what he is called?” *Tom.* [Col. 0407A] *VI Oper.*, fols. 41–42.

The whole of Cyril’s argument comes down to this: the designation “God” cannot be merely external, nor can it apply to the Word, since through the Incarnation he did not fall away from the excellence of his nature; nor can it apply to the assumed nature, since Christ, even insofar as he is man, possesses prerogatives that properly belong to God. From this Cyril seems further to infer that Christ, even as such, must either be true God or, if that is denied, a mere man and an entirely different person from the Word who assumes him.

### IX. He denies that the assumed nature is the temple of the assuming Word in the Nestorian sense, since by this manner of understanding the mystery of the Incarnation is overturned

In response to the Nestorians’ argument drawn from the words of Scripture saying that the Word dwelt among us, and likewise that the whole fullness of divinity dwelt in Christ, and so forth—words from which they inferred that the man assumed was the temple of the divine Word and therefore ought not to be called true God—Cyril again replies that by this explanation his opponents completely overturn the whole mystery of the Incarnation. On this interpretation, he says, they would likewise have to hold that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate, since they too are said to dwell in holy men; and in this sense the mystery of the Incarnation would still be renewed every day.

Let us hear Cyril’s words, in Book I *Against Nestorius*:

> “We readily acknowledge that what he says—that a change of the divine nature into flesh is both impossible and in no way appropriate to it—has been said most correctly. We should praise him for wishing to speak rightly on this point. For I confess that it remains unshaken and is in no way changed into anything different from what it is believed to be. But I shall try to show that his words have wandered far from what is fitting and from the truth itself, in asserting that humanization is the same thing as indwelling in a man.
>
> “For if he asserts that this is true in one and only one Emmanuel, let him explain the reason for it; for I cannot understand it. Otherwise, certainly, no one will tolerate this determiner and legislator of whatever he has rashly chosen to say. But the force of this definition does not extend to one alone, nor will there be any objection even if it applies to all. Therefore we shall find that God became man not once but often—indeed, not only the Word from God the Father, but, I add, the Father himself as well, and furthermore the Holy Spirit.
>
> “For through one of the holy prophets he said concerning men justified by faith: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people’ (1 Cor. VI). Christ himself also said: ‘If anyone hears me, my Father and I will come, and we will make our dwelling with him, and we will abide in him’ (John XIV). Blessed Paul also wrote: ‘Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his house, whose house we are’ (Heb. III, 5–6). And even concerning the Holy Spirit: ‘Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?’ (1 Cor. III).
>
> “Therefore, if it is permissible to call that very thing which the Lord of all is said to do—namely, to dwell in certain persons—humanization or incarnation, then it may also be said of each participant in the divine nature, and of each who has him dwelling within, that he has both become man and been incarnated. If this has happened, and if it is admitted as true, then nothing prevents the Word from God from being said to have become flesh more than once; for he still dwells in many who worship him.”

He then presents the genuine meaning of the words by which the Nestorians were attempting to confirm their error, and continues:

> “But, he says, it is written concerning the Word: ‘He dwelt among us.’ Blessed Paul also said concerning Christ, the Savior of all: ‘In him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily’ (Col. II, 9). I confess that he dwelt among us—for so it is written—and I will not contradict you when you say that he dwelt in him also. But I would rather examine these theological expressions.
>
> “For when the blessed Evangelist had first said, ‘The Word became flesh,’ he appropriately added: ‘And he dwelt among us,’ so that through both statements he might hand down to us a complete knowledge of Christ’s mystery. The Word from God the Father clearly indicated that he had been united to flesh according to hypostasis when he said that he himself had become flesh.
