That he became flesh without passing over into the nature of flesh, and without undergoing change into what he was not, but remained what he was while united with that which had become like us, is again made clear by the words ‘He dwelt among us,’ which he added to the preceding statement.
>
> “Blessed Paul says that the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in Christ so that no one might suspect a simple or relational habitation [Greek: σχετικήν], but a true habitation, as I have just said, and one according to hypostasis. For that man, filled with the Spirit of God, was not ignorant that the Word of God is incorporeal and intangible. But because it was necessary that the explanation of the mystery should appear in no respect deficient, and should convey the truth so accurately and distinctly, according to the proper rule, that it surpassed every marvel, he presses the force of the sequence of the things and, I might almost say, neglects what is appropriate to that incorporeal and supreme nature. For he added the word ‘bodily,’ since he had no other way to speak than one that our understanding and language could grasp.”

Volume VI of the Works, folios 26 and 27.

The statements which Cyril writes on this same Pauline text in his second discourse *On the Right Faith to the Queens* are entirely in agreement with these:

> “Believing, therefore,” he says, “that the Word dwelt among us not through any change or alteration of himself, but through the true union of his own temple—that is, of a body complete with a human soul—we affirm this piously and rightly. When the great Paul writes that the whole fullness of divinity dwelt in him, he did not mean by participation, or relation (ἤ σχετικῶς), or communication of grace, but ‘bodily,’ that is, essentially. By that indwelling he wished to intimate nothing other than the true and natural union of the Word with the sacred flesh.
>
> “Just as the human spirit is said to dwell in a man, yet is not judged to be another or different from him, so it happens that, by a figure of speech, the relation of two persons is sometimes presented to us concerning one person; nevertheless, the truth is in no respect harmed. Thus, for example, divine Scripture says of God: ‘Who forms the spirit of man within him’ (Zech. XII). Yet it is clear to everyone that the spirit of man formed within him is not something other than the man himself.
>
> “To this also belongs what blessed David says: ‘During the night I exercised myself with my heart, and my spirit was troubled’ (Ps. LXXVI, 7). Who, I ask, was it that exercised himself with his heart and had his own spirit troubled? We must therefore not scrutinize the forms of expression with excessive anxiety, but rather contemplate the natures of the things themselves and, guided by them, strive toward the truth itself.”

Volume IV of the Councils, col. 827 and 30.

As for the Apostle’s text, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. V, 19), the perverse interpretation which the Nestorians had given it implied that this reconciliation had to be attributed to someone other than him whom the holy Virgin had borne. Cyril judged that such an assertion removed the truth of the reconciliation, and said that the divine Son himself, in the assumed nature, reconciled the world both to himself and to the Father.

> “We by no means assert,” he says in the second discourse to the Queens cited above, “what certain less instructed persons do: that a Christ other than he whom the holy Virgin brought forth dwelt in the man and reconciled the world to himself. Rather, it was God himself and the Father who reconciled the world to himself in Christ.
>
> “For after assuming human nature, the Son became mediator and, in a certain manner, reconciler for the attainment of peace—not reconciling obedience in the world to someone else, but, in his own person, to God the Father. For when we are reconciled to Christ, through him and in him we are also reconciled to God, the Savior of all.
>
> “Hence the saying: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matt. XI, 2). That those who attach themselves to him are reconciled not to someone else but to the true and natural God, he himself makes clear in these words: ‘Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me’ (John XII, 44); and, ‘Whoever sees me sees him who sent me’ (John XIV). And again: ‘Believe in God, and believe in me.’”

Volume IV of the Councils, col. 866.

Thus Cyril taught from the right faith that the same one whom the holy Virgin bore accomplished this reconciliation of the world. Yet this could not be said if, according to the Nestorian interpretation, the Word had merely dwelt in the assumed man and had not truly and hypostatically united him to himself. For, considered separately, neither the Word nor the assumed man would have been capable of making satisfaction or reconciling the world.

Finally, Cyril also responds to those modes of speaking by which his opponents had called the man born from Mary “God-bearing” or “Lordly” (Dominicus). He again proves that division of persons follows from such expressions, and that, if Christ is called God-bearing, he must be regarded as a mere man, while the true incarnation of the Word must at the same time be denied.

He opposed this error with the fifth anathema, condemning those who dare to say that Christ is a God-bearing man and not rather true God, since he is the one and natural Son. He later explained this more fully in his declaration of the anathema, saying:

> “The inventors of impious doctrines, Nestorius and those who follow him or think with him, pretend to confess the expression ‘incarnation’; nevertheless, they deny that the Word of God was truly incarnate—that is, that, while remaining what he was, he became a man like us.
>
> “They assert that the only-begotten Word of God dwelt in the man born from the holy Virgin just as he dwells in one of the saints, so that it is no longer necessary to confess that there is one Christ, Son, Lord, and object of worship. Instead, he is worshiped and glorified together with the Word as a man understood independently and separately, honored solely because of a conjunction in dignity.
>
> “The God of all does indeed dwell in us through the Holy Spirit. For long ago he said through one of the holy prophets: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they shall be my people’ (Lev. XXVI, 12; 2 Cor. VI, 16). Blessed Paul also writes: ‘Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?’ (2 Cor. III). Christ himself, speaking of his holy prophets, or of the saints who had preceded him, said: ‘If he called them gods, to whom the word of God camedo you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, “You are blaspheming,” because I said, “I am the Son of God”?’ (John X, 35).
>
> “But God does not dwell in Christ in the same way as he dwells in us. Christ was God by nature, made like us, and was one and only Son even when he became flesh. Therefore, whoever dares to say that he is a God-bearing man and not rather God made man necessarily falls under the anathema proposed.”

Volume V of the Councils, col. 11.

In his defense against Theodorets’ criticism he says:

> “For we say that Christ ought not to be called by anyone a God-bearing man, so that he may not be understood as one of the saints, but rather as the true God, the Word of God who became man and was incarnate.”

After several intervening matters, he adds:

> “I am astonished that, although he everywhere affirms Emmanuel to be God, he is nevertheless found here attributing to him the measure of a prophet. He calls him a God-bearing man, so that he may appear like us, who through the Holy Spirit have the God of all dwelling within us. He dwells in our hearts, and we are temples of the living God.
>
> “Yet it is not the same thing to say that the Word became man and to suppose that God dwells in a man. For even if blessed Paul’s statement is true—that it pleased God that the whole fullness of divinity should dwell in him bodily, that is, not relationally—he nevertheless says that there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist.
>
> “Moreover, someone might say that his spirit also dwells in a man; hence it is written concerning certain persons: ‘Those who dwell in houses of clay’ (Job IV, 19), since we too are made from the same clay. Yet one man is understood, and one man exists according to his constitution, consisting of flesh and a rational soul dwelling within it.
>
> “Why, then, does he not cease disturbing the correct and entirely sound rule of faith? At one time he says that Christ, Son, and Lord are one, the same God and man; at another, giving him the measure of the prophets, he calls him a God-bearing man—perhaps unaware that he thereby makes him our equal, since he is not truly God but rather a temple in which God the Word dwells as he does in us.””

The same work, cols. 111 and 114.

### X. He says that, if Christ is called our high priest precisely insofar as he is man, the merit of our redemption is taken away. And if it is asserted that he also sacrificed for himself, he proves that Christ too would have been subject to sin

Cyril rejects the argument which the Nestorians had drawn from Christ’s priestly dignity and his sacrifice. He says that it would no longer be true that God redeemed the world through his Son, and that the entire merit of the sacrifice offered for us would be destroyed, if the assumed man alone, rather than the Word himself in the nature united to him, were called the high priest and apostle of our confession. Furthermore, if that man is held to have sacrificed also for himself, it follows that he was subject to sin along with other men, contrary to what Scripture teaches about him.

> “But you foolishly fear,” he says to Nestorius in Book III, “and I do not know why you are ashamed to attribute to him [the Word] both the name and the reality of apostleship and priesthood. Do you think that this is appropriate to that man born from a woman, as though he were distinct from the Word, possessing a simple conjunction, as you suppose, and equality of dignity alone?
>
> “How, then, is the Word himself, who was God, seen to have helped our condition, if we have also been brought to God the Father through another? We have no longer had access through him himself; rather, our mediator was a man like us, possessing an invented name of divinity.”

Volume VI of the Works, folio 64.

On folio 93 he argues as follows:

> “Whoever is held guilty of sin needs a sacrifice for his own offenses. Christ offered himself for the race according to the flesh—that is, for us—but not for himself, since he was superior to sin, being God. For if he was sacrificed for himself, then according to the Scriptures it is not we alone who were purchased by his blood; he too, together with us, will have been redeemed. Nor, according to Isaiah’s words, did ‘the Lord deliver him over for our sins’ (Isa. LIII), but he was delivered also for his own.
>
> “For wherever there is a sacrifice and offering, there is plainly remission of sins. Blessed Paul therefore deceived the whole world when he wrote of him: ‘Such a high priest was fitting for us, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; one who has no need daily, as those priests do, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered himself’ (Heb. VII, 26).
>
> “The Law appoints men as priests who have infirmity, but the word of the oath, which came after the Law, appoints the Son, perfected forever (Heb. VII, 28). How, then, is Christ a holy high priest? Or how is he innocent and undefiled, if he needs a sacrifice together with us for sins to be forgiven, and if he was offered in order to justify sinners? How is he separated from sinners, if he is justified together with them, since a sacrifice is offered for no other reason than for those very persons?”

When Nestorius and his Oriental supporters objected that, if God the Word were the high priest, there would then be no one greater to whom he could offer sacrifice; and likewise that the high priest, tempted in every respect as we are, had been specially called to priestly dignity, glorified through it, and placed in the same order as Melchizedek—all of which, they claimed, could not apply to the Word himself—Cyril responds in this manner:

> “Believe that although he was God by nature and the Son in the form of the Father, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. If he became man and also took the form of a servant, how can it be considered trivial or inconsistent with the principles of the economy that he should be called and be an apostle and high priest? And he who did not disdain the measure of our humanity—how could he regard human things as something to be rejected?”

A little later he continues:

> “Therefore, if they say that there is one Son, in no way dividing him into two—one from the seed of David and another, the Word from God the Father—how do they not injure the sacrament by dividing the economy between God and man? Why do they not rather say that the same one is God and man, so that everything belongs to him, both the divine and the human?
>
> “Whenever something that is most appropriate to God is said of him, we affirm that it is altogether true, for we know that he himself is God. And if something human is said, we shall also admit this. For we confess that God is in flesh and blood, and through human things we recognize the measure of his humanity.
>
> “Thousands upon thousands of holy angels minister to him, and seraphim surround his divine throne. But when he became man, he was also called high priest—not because he offered sacrifice to a God greater than himself, but because he secured the confession of our faith for himself and for the Father.
>
> “Are you ashamed that he is called a priest because of his humanity? How, then, did you not marvel that he did not offer the manner of sacrifice according to the custom of priests to someone else, but rather to himself and to the Father, as I have said? When you say that it is unworthy of God to sacrifice, I agree with you. But if the Word were alone and without flesh, you would speak correctly. Since, however, he became flesh, behold the one who sacrifices because of his humanity, and who, in dignity, is beyond creation as God; for he sits with God the Father.
>
> “Therefore behold him sacrificing according to his humanity, but sitting as God. For what does blessed Paul say? ‘We have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens’ (Heb. VIII).
>
> “Knowing, therefore, that he became man while he was God—and that the Son is one and the same—we shall attribute everything to him as one person. We shall not be ignorant of the modes of the economy, but shall always turn the force of our thought wisely and carefully toward obedience to him.”

Volume V of the Councils, col. 66.

### XI. He says that it is false that the Word is passible in his own nature if he is held to have suffered in the assumed nature. Indeed, he says that it is altogether necessary to assert that the Word himself died for us, since otherwise the merit of satisfaction cannot stand

When the Nestorians persisted and claimed that, according to the doctrine which establishes Christ as true God even as man, passion, death, and the other weaknesses or imperfections of human nature would be attributed to divinity, and that the divine Word would thereby be called passible, Cyril replied that Scripture everywhere says that the heavenly Father handed over his own Son, eternally begotten from him, to all these things and made him subject to them. He further maintained that the truth of the Incarnation and the merit of redemption are denied unless it is admitted that the divine Word endured these things in the body which, through union, he made his own. Nevertheless, from this it cannot follow that he should be considered mortal any more than the soul is mortal, although it suffers death in the body.

> “To make what is being said clearer,” he writes in his letter to the Egyptian monks, no. 24, “let us inquire also into our own death and consider its nature carefully. Does anyone of sound mind believe that, when this earthly body is extinguished, the soul itself is extinguished along with it? I do not think that even one person among all mankind is persuaded of this. Yet, as commonly happens, it is called not the death of the body but the death of the man.
>
> “In the same way, then, you may form your judgment concerning Emmanuel. The Word was in that which had been received from a woman as in his own body. He delivered this body to death at the appointed time, while his own nature suffered no harm. For he himself is life and gives life to all other things. Nevertheless, by making the things of the flesh his own, he is said—having suffered death and risen again, as one who died for all—to have purified the human race by his own blood, and to have acquired for God the Father all who dwell throughout the world.”

Then, in no. 25, he shows that the merit of redemption derives solely from the fact that the Son himself, the eternal Son of the eternal Father, endured death in his own flesh:

> “One, therefore, surpassing all in dignity, laid down his soul for all, and, according to a certain economy, allowed the flesh to be humbled somewhat through death. But according to his own nature, upon which no pain or suffering falls, he in turn destroyed that same death, so that in this way corruption might be weakened in all bodies and the dominion of death dissolved.
>
> “For just as all die in Adam, so conversely all are given life in Christ. He would not have accomplished what contributes to our salvation according to the divine nature if he had not suffered death for our sake according to the human nature. For he is handed over as having first undergone death as man; then, through that which he is by nature—God—he returned to life again.
>
> “If, therefore, according to the Scriptures he did not suffer death in the body, neither was he made alive in spirit nor did he rise again. But if he did not rise to life, our faith is vain and we still lie buried in our sins. For, according to the teaching of blessed Paul, we were baptized into his death, and through his blood we obtained the remission of sins.”

He presses the same point in no. 26, saying that death has in no respect been destroyed—or, which is the same thing, that full satisfaction for our sins has not been made—unless it is held that the divine Word himself endured death for us in the assumed flesh. Here are his words:

> “Moreover, if Christ is neither the true Son of God nor God by nature, but is no more than a man like us, or an instrument of divinity, then we have obtained salvation not through God but through one who, being like us, died for our sake and was raised by the power and authority of another.
>
> “How, then, is death said to have been conquered through Christ? I hear Christ himself declaring concerning his soul: ‘No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord; for I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again’ (John X, 18).
>
> “He who did not know death cast himself, according to his own flesh, into the death common to all, so that we too might rise to life together with him. He came to life again after despoiling the underworld, not as a man of our condition, but as God in the flesh, with us and above us. In him as the head he secured incorruption. Death too was crushed when it attacked with hostility the body that belonged to life itself. For just as death conquered through Adam, so through Christ it was defeated and fell.”

Volume IV of the Councils, cols. 614 and 615.

Further, from the Apostle’s words to the Philippians—“Although he was in the form of God … he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross”—he proves that the Son, or divine Word, endured death in the form united to him and became obedient to the Father even unto the cross.

> “Consider, then,” he says in Book V *Against Nestorius*, “how he who was in the form of God and of the Father, being God, the very character and image of his substance, and in no way inferior, since he is and is understood to be equal in all things, emptied himself and willingly brought himself down into humility.
>
> “Explain now the manner of his emptying: how was he also humbled, taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross? Is it not evident to everyone that what is exalted is humbled, not what is submissive and humble inwardly and by nature? Is it not, if I am not mistaken, what is full and needs nothing that is emptied? Is it not what was free by nature before taking the form of a servant that also took that form? Is it not the man who was not such before he was found that is said to have been found as man?
>
> “Who, then, is that one who is exalted by nature and cast himself down to humility? Who is full, so that he may be understood to have been emptied? Who is beyond the measure of servitude, so that he may be said to have taken the form of a servant? Who, since he was not previously a man like us, is said to have been found as such?
>
> “It would be foolish and truly full of the utmost madness to dare to attribute these things to an ordinary man from our number; but they fit most aptly the supreme nature. That Word of God, moved by extraordinary benevolence and mercy toward us, offered his own body for us, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to God the Father unto death. Nor did he judge it necessary to shrink from being willing to suffer in the flesh for us, although as God he was impassible by nature.
>
> “This man, however, foolishly blushes at his divine purposes on our behalf and, while thinking that he honors him, inflicts an injury upon him. For he exempts him from suffering, although no one says that he suffered in his own nature. He does not perceive that he thereby prevents us from confessing him as the Savior and Redeemer of all, if the one through whom we were saved and through whose venerable cross we were redeemed is another Son and Lord, properly and separately distinct from him.
>
> “If he is a simple man, and the Word from God the Father did not himself appear in human form, let him come forward and show that he is in the form and equality of the Father—for he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized—and, in addition, that he took the form of a servant, as though he had not possessed it at some time, and that he was emptied, although by nature he possessed fullness.”

Volume VI of the Works, folio 127.

Again, from the words of the same Apostle in Romans VIII—“He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all”—he proves the same truth, arguing as follows:

> “If God the Father gave his own Son for us, namely the very one who originated from his substance, then the body which endured death belonged to him who suffered according to the flesh—for according to the nature of divinity he could not suffer. Thus he who cannot suffer according to himself endured death according to the economy.
>
> “Therefore those who divide the one into two plainly bind themselves under the charge of impiety. For if there is a man in himself and by himself, divided and separate, and not the Word of God himself clothed in flesh, then the Father is not found to have given his own Son for us.”

In the *Book to the Queens*, Volume IV of the Councils, col. 770.

### XII. He shows that the Word himself is called the Father’s servant because of the form he assumed. The words of Nestorius

Finally, against the assertion of the Nestorians that Christ, insofar as he is man, is called God’s servant—so that the form of a servant which the Son of God is said to have assumed would once again apply only to the assumed man—Cyril objects that this interpretation is wholly foreign to Paul’s meaning. Paul testifies that the same one who had eternally been in the form of God assumed the form of a servant at the end of the ages. Therefore the Word himself, in the nature united to him, must be called the Father’s servant, unless one wishes once again to divide Christ into two and consequently abolish the truth of the Incarnation and the emptying.

> “The only-begotten Son,” he says in his defense of the sixth anathema against Theodorets’ criticism, “who is in the form of God the Father, equal to him in every measure, of equal glory, and free, was called brother, after assuming the form of a servant, of those who were under the yoke of servitude—that is, our brother.
>
> “Thus, as one of us, he paid the two-drachma tax to those who demanded the tribute, and, as man, became subject to the Law, although as God he is the Lawgiver. He taught his disciples that he is truly the Son and that, because of the flesh, he is in the form of a servant, although according to his own nature he is free, being God and from God.
>
> “Nevertheless, because he possessed the proper form of a servant in accordance with the measure of his emptying, he was subject to the collectors of tribute. Therefore, if anyone says that he was called a servant in the words of the holy prophets, there is no reason for offense. Through the Holy Spirit who revealed these things to them, they knew that the Word who is from God the Father, having become man, was indeed free as the Son, yet did not reject the measure of his wise emptying, being conformed to us who are subject to the yoke of servitude.
>
> “Thus he also calls the Father his God, although he existed as God by nature and was from him, in no way inferior to the excellence of the one who begot him.

“When Nestorius writes of Christ as follows: ‘And so the suffering high priest is merciful, but not the God who gives life to the one who suffered,’ and calls the Word of God ‘the God of Christ,’ adding, ‘He himself was also an infant, and the Lord of the infant,’ we assert that these statements are not only improper but profoundly impious.

“For if the Word who is from God the Father is Christ’s God, there will unquestionably and indubitably be two in every respect. But how can the same person be both an infant and the Lord of the infant? Emmanuel, then, will not be called the God and Lord of himself, since he himself is simultaneously God and man, after the Word of God became man and was incarnate.

“Who could doubt that divinity is one thing according to its own nature and humanity another according to its own nature? Nevertheless, there is one Christ from both natures, divinity and humanity, according to the union of the economy.”

Volume V of the Councils, col. 115.

### XIII. He Removes the Charge of Having Introduced a Confusion of the Natures in Christ by Accurately Explaining the Nature of the Incarnation

Since the Nestorians thought that the principles they had established were altogether necessary in order to preserve the distinction of the natures in Christ, and therefore also accused Cyril of having introduced a confusion and revived Apollinarianism, the holy teacher shows that this consequence is in no way to be feared from his own doctrine—or rather, from that of the Church—by clearly explaining the nature, or essence, of the Incarnation in several places. He says that the human nature necessarily had to be joined to the person of the Word, since otherwise neither a true incarnation nor the union of both natures could subsist [Col. 0414C]; nevertheless, no confusion or transformation of divinity into flesh, or of flesh into divinity, can thereby be inferred.

In his defense of the first anathema, he responds to Theodoret in these words:

> “But the wise and clever expositor, omitting what ought to have been said and what was necessary, and giving no thought at all to such matters, takes another course. Immediately he turns to establishing that the Word of God is above transformation and has not been transformed into the nature of flesh—as though the anathema confirmed and wished to demonstrate this. Let him therefore hear one who in no way knows how to answer the things he contradicts: you speak superfluously, man, and you oppose a judgment hateful even among us. For we know that the divine and supreme nature does not permit itself to endure the appearance of transformation; nor, while ceasing to be what it is—the Word of God—did it pass into the nature of flesh. But since he says that the form of a servant was assumed from the form of God, let him come forward and show whether the forms alone, without subsistences, met one another. But I think he will immediately refute himself. For it was not mere non-subsisting likenesses and forms that met one another through an economic union; rather, there was a coming together of realities, or substances, so that the account of the humanization may truly be believed to have taken place.

> “Therefore, if we say that the Word became flesh, we are not saying that any confusion, mixture, transformation, or alteration occurred in it; rather, we say that it was ineffably and indescribably united to a body possessing an intellectual soul. That which is said to be united is not immediately confused, but rather assumes the other. We therefore affirm that the Word who is from God the Father assumed holy and animate flesh and, having been truly united without confusion, came forth from the womb itself as man, while even thus remaining true God.”

*Tom. V Conc.*, col. 90.

Nor, we think, should we pass over what Cyril wrote on this subject in his letters to Succensus, bishop of Diocaesarea in the province of Isauria. There he explains the mystery of the Incarnation with singular learning and vigorously answers his accusers:

> “Since, however,” he writes in his first letter to the aforementioned bishop, “some charge us with the errors of Apollinarius and say: ‘If you declare that the one Son, according to a perfect and compounded union, the Word from God the Father, became man and was incarnate, you have surely decided and judged that a mixture, confusion, or compounding of the Word with the body took place, or at least that the body was transformed into the nature of divinity’—for this reason, in order very wisely to repel the slander, we say that the Word of God the Father united to himself, in a manner that can neither be understood nor expressed in words, a body animated by an intellectual soul, and came forth as man from a woman—not by a transformation of nature, but rather by an economic will, having been made like us. For he willed to become man without losing that which he was by nature, God. Although he descended to our condition [Col. 0415B] and assumed the form of a servant, he nevertheless remained in the excellence of his divinity and in his natural lordship . . .

> “Considering, then, as I have said, the manner of the humanization, we understand that two natures came together in an indissoluble union, without confusion or any alteration. For flesh is flesh and not divinity, even though it became the flesh of God; likewise, the Word is God and not flesh, although by an economic arrangement he made flesh his own. Therefore, when we consider this, we do not violate that coming together into unity by saying that he was made from two natures. After the union we do not divide the natures from one another, nor do we cut the one indivisible one into two sons; rather, we affirm one Son and, as the holy Fathers said, one incarnate nature of the Word of God.

> “Thus, so far as consideration and the contemplation of the mind’s eye are concerned, we say that two natures were united, insofar as we consider how the Only-Begotten became man; but we affirm one Christ, one Son, and one Lord, the Word of God the Father, who became man and was incarnate. If you wish, let us take this very composition of ours, by which we are human beings, as an example. We are composed of soul and body, and we contemplate two natures, one of the body and the other of the soul; yet one human being consists of the union of both. Nor, because a human being is composed of two natures, should we think that there are two human beings in the one who is one; rather, he is one and the same through the composition, as I have said, consisting of soul and body.

> “For if we deny that Christ is one and alone from two different natures, incapable of being divided after the union, those who fight against the right faith will say: ‘If there is one nature altogether, how was he made man, and what flesh did he make his own?’ and so forth.”

*Tom. V, part II*, fol. 536 and following.

Since certain people were offended because Cyril had said “one incarnate nature,” he explains his meaning more openly in a second letter to Succensus, saying:

> “Again they are ignorant who pervert what is right: that there truly is one incarnate nature of the Word. For if there is one Son—naturally and truly the one ineffably begotten Word from God the Father—who afterward, through the assumption of flesh, not lifeless but endowed with an intellectual soul, came forth as man from a woman, he will not on that account be divided into two persons and two sons, since he has remained one—not, however, without flesh or outside the body, but possessing his own body through a union that can in no way be broken.

> “The one who says this does not in any way whatsoever signify a mixture, confusion, or anything of that kind; nor will such a consequence follow in any way as a matter of necessity. For even though we call the Only-Begotten Son of God incarnate and made man, he was not therefore mixed, as they suppose; nor did the nature of the Word pass into the nature of flesh, nor the nature of flesh into the nature of the Word. Rather, while each remains and is contemplated in its own natural property, having been ineffably and inexplicably united according to the account given shortly before, it displays to us one nature of the Son—but, as we said, an incarnate nature.

> “For ‘one’ is not truly said only of things that are simple according to nature, but also of things joined through composition, such as a human being consisting of soul and body. Although things of this kind belong to different species and are by no means of the same essence as one another, when they are united they complete one human nature, even though a difference exists in the constitution of the composition according to the nature of the things coming together into unity.

> “It is therefore pointless for those who assert that, if there is one incarnate nature of the Word, it necessarily follows that a mixture and confusion have occurred, with the human nature evidently diminished and taken away. For it has neither been diminished nor taken away, as they claim. To declare fully what it means that he became man, it is enough to confess that he was incarnate. If we were silent about this, their slanders would have some place; but since it is necessarily added that he was incarnate, where is any room left for diminution or subtraction?”

*Ibid.*, fols. 142 and 43.

### XIV. He Demonstrates That Two Persons Necessarily Follow from the Modes of Speech Used by the Nestorians

#### The Words of the Nestorians

As for the modes of speech used by the Nestorians to express the distinction of the natures more effectively—namely, their habitual distinction, when speaking of the Incarnation of the Word, between “this one” and “that one”—Cyril rightly reproaches them for having said nothing by which the unity of the person in Christ could be more plainly destroyed, as is in fact evident to anyone who considers the matter even superficially.

> “Since,” he says in his book *On the Faith to Theodosius*, “they separate the one Christ into two, introducing a crude division between ‘this one’ and ‘that one,’ and insist that each stands separately and, as it were, by himself, they call one—the one born from the Virgin—a perfect man, and again call the other the Word of God the Father. They do not distinguish what difference there is between the nature of God and that of flesh, nor do they remain within the limits of the differing natures alone; for in that case they would not have strayed from the truth. The nature of flesh is one thing, and the nature of the Word another. But these men establish one separately and by himself as a mere man, while they name the other a true and natural God . . .

> “They even dared to write the following: ‘This one’—namely, the Word of God the Father—‘is the true and natural Son; that one’—meaning the one born from the Virgin—‘is called the Son of God equivocally.’ And shortly afterward again: ‘Certainly the Word of God is not man, but assumed a man. For from the beginning the Only-Begotten is in himself the Son of God, the maker of all; but the man whom he received, since he is not God by nature, is called by the same name as the one from whom he was assumed, who is the true Son of God.’”

*Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 626.

With complete justice Cyril said that these modes of speech introduced a crude separation—namely, through the distinction between “this one” and “that one”—since everyone can see that the pronouns “this one” and “that one” must be understood not of the natures but plainly of the persons. Consequently, if there is a “this one” and a “that one” in the incarnate Word, two persons must also be admitted in him; or rather, the true Incarnation of the Word is being denied, as Cyril repeatedly warns elsewhere.

Hence Pope Vigilius, in his response to Theodore’s twentieth chapter, where Theodore likewise distinguishes between “that one” and “that one,” as we saw above in § 2, no. 15, says:

> “In the aforementioned twentieth chapter, where the eighth psalm appears to be expounded, Christ is asserted to be a bare man—as has already been said in the other passages—and is shown to be divided from the Word; a duality of persons is introduced.”

And since Vigilius too considered that a true Incarnation could not subsist in Theodore’s view, he continues:

> “If anyone thinks in this way . . . and does not understand the two natures in Christ the Lord as indivisibly and without confusion united, so that, while the distinction of those natures remains, he himself is one and the same true Son of God and true Son of man, let him be anathema.”

*Tom. IX Conc.*, col. 76.

### XV. Why He Considers Their Profession Concerning the Unity of the Person to Be Specious

Cyril also judges that Nestorius and the others cannot be excused from this error, although they repeatedly proclaimed the unity of the person in Christ. He demonstrates most solidly that they did so only verbally, and that such a profession was utterly foreign to the principles they had always adopted elsewhere.

> “We say,” he states in Book II *Against Nestorius*, “that the Word itself, substantially born from God the Father, was made like us, became incarnate, and became man—that is, that he took a body from the holy Virgin and made it his own. For in this way the Lord Jesus Christ truly becomes one; in this way we shall worship him as one, if we do not set man and God apart from one another, but believe that he is one and the same in divinity and humanity—that is, God and man at the same time.

> “But this recent inventor of impiety, although he pretends to say that Christ is one, nevertheless everywhere divides the natures and places each separately. He asserts that they did not truly come together, but conceals excuses and pretexts in sins, as it is written, and devises a certain mode of conjunction—namely, one according only to equality of dignity, as we shall plainly demonstrate from his own words. He makes the Word from God, as though in a man who possesses nothing above the others, inhabit him by participation, and divides the sayings found in the Gospels in such a way that he attributes certain ones at one time to the Word alone and properly, and at another time separately to the one born from a woman.”

*Tom. VI*, fols. 30 and 31.

Shortly afterward he quotes the words of Nestorius reported by us above in § 2, no. 16. In those words that heretic seemed to admit the unity of the person and said that there was no division of conjunction, dignity, or sonship; that Christ suffered no division; that Christ was indivisible; that there were not two Christs, not two sons, not a first and a second, and not “one and another,” but that the one himself was double—not in dignity, but in nature.

Cyril immediately proves that this manner of speaking is deceptive, saying:

> “Explain to me again what you mean by an indivisible conjunction. Do you mean the unity according to hypostasis—the unity that we proclaim when we contend for the truth of the doctrines—or do you mean that which is understood according to an attachment and the proximity of one thing to another? . . .

> “But we do not say that the union in Christ took place in this manner. For he was not joined to another, for example, by a harmony of will or by bodily proximity, as one person may be joined to another. Rather, as I have often said, he made the body assumed from the holy Virgin his own, and we say that the Word from God the Father was truly united to flesh that was not lifeless.

> “Therefore, if the force of conjunction, as he calls it, signifies the unity that we understand—namely, the unity according to hypostasis—then he rightly said that there is no division of Christ, insofar as Christ is Christ. For there is not ‘another and another,’ nor ‘son and son,’ nor ‘one and another,’ nor a first and a second; rather, he is one, both before the flesh and after the flesh. Thus he will be, as you say, indivisible in dignity and also in power—indeed, the same.

> “If this is so, how can you say that he is both indivisible and double, and that he is so not in dignity but in nature? Because the Word of God the Father came forth as man, having assumed flesh and having been made like us, he should not for that reason be called double. For he is one, and not without flesh, although according to his own nature he is outside flesh and blood.

> “Thus, if someone had killed a man like us, he would rightly be accused not of having violated two men, but one alone, even though the man may perhaps be considered as consisting of soul and body, and although the things that happen to either part do not belong to one and the same nature but to different natures. So it must likewise be understood in Christ. He is not double, but one and alone, the Lord and Son, the Word from God the Father, not without flesh.

> “I too acknowledge that there is a very great difference, or distance, between humanity and divinity. For the things signified by these names are different in respect of the account of essence, and they seem to have nothing similar to one another. But when the mystery of Christ is set before us, the account of that union does not indeed disregard the difference, but excludes division—not because it confuses or mixes the natures, but because the Word of God himself, having become a partaker of flesh and blood, is understood and called in this way also one Son.

> “But while you say that two Christs ought not to be called, and again refuse to confess two Sons, pretending to hold the correct doctrine, you are nevertheless convicted of saying that there are two Christs. You distinguish God and man into their proper difference and attempt to show that one is summoned to perform the work while the other summons him to the work.”

*Ibid.*, fol. 44.

Cyril clearly knew that his opponents had never admitted a true, or hypostatic, union, but only a moral union, or one according to will. They explained this by the unity of a man and a woman, who are said to be “one flesh.” By this reasoning, two persons plainly followed in Christ, just as it is perfectly clear that the man and the woman are in reality two persons, even though they are morally called one flesh.

Hence Pope Vigilius, in his response to Theodore’s thirtieth chapter, where Theodore had explained the union of the Word with human nature in the aforementioned manner, says:

> “In the aforementioned thirtieth chapter an exceedingly bad example is used in an attempt to show how the one person of Christ may be understood: namely, just as it is read concerning a man and a woman coming together, so also in Christ, with the natures distinguished, there is supposedly one person. It then follows that the nature of the Word of God is perfect, and the person perfect, and the nature and person of the man perfect; and likewise: hence it is apparent that, both from the example of the man and woman, where there are two persons, and from what follows, although the number is not stated, two persons are introduced as one person of Christ.”

*Tom. IX Conc.*, col. 81.

These, finally, were the weapons and arguments with which Cyril attacked each individual head of the errors. Anyone who, setting aside prejudices, investigates the inner nature of the mystery of the Incarnation from the principles of sound theology and right faith can easily perceive that he attacked them successfully.

### XVI. Alcuin Also Responds with the Same Reasoning to Felix and Elipandus concerning Their Assertion of Adoption in Christ

It remains now to examine the arguments with which Alcuin opposed the assertions of Felix and Elipandus. Since those arguments rested upon the same foundations, he will certainly be free from the accusations of Walch, who thought he had uncovered so many matters deserving censure in Alcuin’s struggle against these bishops.

We do not intend here to report every argument with which Alcuin fought against his opponents. That would be too long and entirely foreign to our purpose, since, as we have often stated, our sole intention is to vindicate this writer on the ground that he himself used against the Spanish bishops the arguments and authorities that Cyril had rightly employed against the Nestorians according to the judgment of the entire Catholic world—using them, as we saw in the preceding paragraph, against men who taught the same doctrines.

Alcuin himself suggests that no other weapons ought to be brought against his opponents than those once used by Cyril in refuting Nestorianism. Thus, in Book IV *Against Elipandus*, no. 5, he writes:

> “I wish you to know with complete certainty, O men and brothers who assert this adoption in Christ, that whatever the blessed Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, answered the impious Nestorius by synodal authority, you should know beyond doubt has been answered to you. For the impiety of the same error must be destroyed by the answers of the same truth.”

The first argument Alcuin uses with Cyril is therefore a negative one: namely, that the doctrine handed down by Felix and Elipandus was new, founded nowhere in Scripture, and previously unheard of in the Church, and for that reason alone ought to be rejected.

> “If he had been willing,” he says in Book I *Against Felix*, no. 2, “to consider this one point with a wise mind or humble understanding, it ought to have recalled the aforementioned Felix from error: from the beginning of the apostolic preaching, the whole Church of Christ has never possessed or proclaimed the term ‘adoption in Christ’ or ‘titular divinity.’ These terms are found nowhere in the Gospels, nor in the Epistles of the apostles, nor indeed anywhere in the prophetic writings of the whole Old Testament; nor are they found in the books of any of the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical teachers, or in the Apostles’ Creed, or the Creed of the Council of Nicaea, or in the affirmation of any synod, or in any authority of the Catholic faith.

> “It is astonishing that such teachers are not afraid to introduce novelties, things unknown in ancient times, when the distinguished teacher of the nations strictly forbids any Catholic to accept every novelty of language and newly invented sect—so much so that he did not hesitate to pronounce an anathema even upon angels and every human being if he preached otherwise than he himself had preached.”

Alcuin was not alone in accusing Felix and Elipandus of novelty in doctrine, since Beatus and Etherius, as well as the Synod of Frankfurt, censured the same thing in these bishops.

They say in Book II *Against Elipandus*:

> “The Church throughout the whole world has not learned this faith of yours, nor has it been accustomed to believe in the one born from the Virgin as the one through whom visible and invisible things were made; rather, it believes this only of the one who is not a son by adoption but by generation. Nor is it accustomed to say: ‘I believe in God the Father almighty, and in his Son, who emptied his divinity and appeared in the world under the form of a subject creature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to Abraham in the heat of the day; who is adoptive in humanity and by no means adoptive in divinity.’ This is your faith. For it does not exist throughout the whole world,” and so forth.

*Tom. II Thesaur. Monum. Eccl.*, Basnage edition, fol. 348.

The Fathers of Frankfurt write in their letter to the bishops of Spain:

> “But you, whoever you are who preach Christ as adoptive, I would like to know from where this opinion of yours arose; show where you learned this name. The patriarchs did not know it, the prophets did not say it, the apostles did not preach it, the holy interpreters remained silent about it, and the teachers of our faith did not teach it,” and so forth.

*Tom. IX Conc.*, Coleti edition, col. 87.

Next, Alcuin everywhere presses the unity of the person in Christ and proves by the strongest arguments that it is destroyed by the assertions of Felix and Elipandus. In particular, he employs this argument against the new doctrine of the adoptive son, saying in his booklet *To the Abbots and Monks of Gothia*, no. 13:

> “Therefore, if the Lord Christ according to the flesh is, as some men of wicked faith babble, an adoptive son, he is by no means one Son, since a proper son and an adoptive son can in no way be one son: one is recognized as true and the other not true.”

In no. 35 he argues in the same way. After quoting the following words from 1 John 4—“Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God,” and so forth—he continues:

> “What is it to dissolve Jesus except not to believe that he is either true God or true Son of God in both natures, he who is one God, one Son, and one Christ in the substance of divinity and humanity? It is not as certain men, in wicked blindness, affirm him to be the proper Son of God the Father in divinity but the adoptive son of that same God the Father in humanity. If this were so, there would altogether be two sons, since, as we have said, there can in no way be one person in a proper son and an adoptive son: one of them is a true son, and the other therefore is not true. Who would fail to recognize that they are different, one true and the other not true, unless he were suffering from a lethargic and frenzied disease?”

Alcuin knew, of course, that adoption applies to a person—and indeed to an external person—to whom the right of inheritance from the father does not belong by birth. Since this was not the case with Christ—for the Father’s goods were owed to him from the hypostatic union itself and therefore from the first instant of conception—he certainly cannot be called an adoptive son even according to his human nature; or, if he is so called, he must without question be divided into two persons.

Thus, in Book III *Against Felix*, no. 13, he describes adoption as follows:

> “Adoption is a certain indication of the will, not the reality of birth. For the one who adopts wishes to have in name as his son someone from outside, whom he does not possess as his own by nature.”

In his booklet *To the Monks of Gothia*, no. 70, he says that we were born first and only afterward received the benefit of adoption through grace, whereas Christ, from the very moment when his humanity was united to the Word, became the Son of God and consequently must be called not adoptive but natural, by right of birth.

Alcuin’s words are these:

> “The cause of this heresy appears to lie in the minds of those who err: those who assert that Christ is adoptive think that there is one who assumed something and adopted it. We have answered this error sufficiently in its proper place. They consider grace and adoption to be one and the same, whereas the Apostle is read to say: ‘By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone’ (Heb. 2:9). Yet the Apostle did not say, ‘By adoption he tasted death for everyone,’ because grace is one thing in many passages, and adoption another. In some passages grace precedes adoption. Grace went before us so that we might be adopted; but Christ was not first made man and then, through grace, made an adoptive Son of God. Rather, immediately in the Virgin’s womb, true God and man was conceived; and from the Virgin’s womb true God and true man was born.”

After quoting blessed Augustine’s testimony on this matter from the *Enchiridion*, he continues:

> “He did not say that Christ was first conceived or born and then received adoption through grace, so that he might be the Son of God; rather, at the very conception and at the very birth, he was born true God and true Son of God [perhaps, ‘true Son of God’], and this one and unique Son. Why unique, if he is adoptive as we are? Certainly because he is the Son of God in a far more proper sense than we are, who are adoptive sons of God through preceding grace.”

*Tom. I.*

You will find similar statements in the same book, no. 71, and also in Book I *Against Elipandus*, no. 3. See also the booklet *Sacrosyllabum*, published at the Council of Frankfurt, *Tom. IX Conc.*, Coleti, cols. 69–70.

### XVII. On the Argument That Christ, as Man, Was Not Begotten of the Eternal Father

#### The Words of Felix

But Felix and Elipandus also sought support for their assertion in the claim that Christ, as man, was not begotten of the eternal Father and therefore, as such, cannot be called his natural Son. Alcuin answers this argument with Cyril: it is not necessary that Christ’s humanity be from God’s substance in order that he be the natural Son of God even as man; it is enough that Christ’s whole person is begotten from the Father’s substance. Thus the whole Felix was the proper and natural son of his father, although his soul was not from his father’s seed.

> “I ask you,” he says in the aforementioned booklet *To the Monks of Gothia*, no. 36, “you assertor of profane error: is not the rational soul that is in you, which gives life, growth, and motion to your whole body—and which, as the holy Fathers hold, is not sown from the bodily origin but is created from nothing and infused into the body from elsewhere—an adoptive daughter to your father, while the flesh alone is his proper daughter? Or are you, whole in soul and body, one and proper son to your father? If a man, joined to a body from a substance not generated from himself, can have a proper and true son, why do you think God unable to have as his proper and true Son one born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary?”

Likewise, in Book II *Against Felix*, he says:

> “But you say, as is read in your letters, that one must in no way believe that almighty God the Father, who is spirit, generates flesh from his own seed. Tell me, I ask: do you know that you have a soul, or not? Such is your ignorance that you do not know that you have a soul. You also know that you had a carnal father, from whose flesh the soul that is in you was neither produced nor generated, as the Catholic faith maintains. How, then, can you yourself, whole in soul and flesh, be the proper and true son of your father, from whose flesh your soul was not generated? But if you acknowledge that you are the proper son of your father in soul and flesh, although the flesh alone was produced from the substance of father and mother, consider still more carefully, so that you may understand that Jesus Christ can become the proper and true Son of God the Father in both substances . . . If, indeed, no son can be proper and true unless he is born wholly from his father’s substance, then in the whole human race no father has a proper and true son except with respect to flesh alone . . . Using, therefore, the example of your own self, and considering yourself, recognize that the sonship which you assert in yourself can occur in the Son of God; and since you do not wish to divide yourself, because of soul and flesh, into two sons, one proper and one adoptive, do not in the same way attempt to divide Christ into two sons because of the natures of perfect divinity and perfect humanity, for our mediator Jesus Christ is one.”

This is certainly the very same line of argument used by Cyril, who, as we saw above in no. 3, shows from comparison with human generation that Christ, even insofar as he is man, is by nature the Son of the eternal Father, and that the most blessed Virgin is truly called Mother of God, although neither the heavenly Father begot the humanity nor the Virgin Mother the divinity. For the body borne by the Virgin became, through the hypostatic union, proper to the Son begotten of the Father; hence the Word of the Father, made man in the Virgin’s womb, is rightly called the natural Son of both in both natures.

Alcuin further proves that, if Christ as man is only the adoptive Son of God because he was not begotten of the Father with respect to his humanity, then the most blessed Virgin cannot in reality be called Mother of God—although the Church had long since both acknowledged and defined this in public judgments against the Nestorians.

> “If,” he says in Book I *Against Felix*, no. 13, “Christ must be the adoptive Son of God the Father because according to the flesh he was not born from his substance, how is he not the adoptive son of the Virgin who was born from God, since he was not created from that Virgin’s substance? Therefore, if the man born from the Virgin, and the Virgin’s Son, must be the adoptive Son of God, then in the same way the Son of God must necessarily be the adoptive son of the Virgin, because the substance of God the Father, from which the Son of God was essentially born, is one thing, and the substance of the Virgin, from which Christ was bodily born, another. Or, if you do not dare to say this, because you bear the Christian name, so that the blessed Virgin is not properly Mother of God but only by adoption, it is fair that you should not dare to affirm that the Son of the Virgin is the adoptive Son of God the Father.”

This is a very strict argument, from which it appears how little the doctrine of Felix and Elipandus can be defended from the charge of Nestorianism. They also tried to confirm their error from the assertion “that one son cannot naturally have two fathers,” just as the Nestorians had denied that the divine Word underwent two generations. Alcuin first says, in Book III *Against Felix*, no. 2:

> “You say, therefore, that one man cannot have two natural fathers, but may have one natural father and another adoptive father. I too say that no father can have one son who is both natural and adoptive to him, because that one son cannot be divided so that he is both natural and adoptive son of the father; nor can one part of the son be adoptive and the other natural in the dignity of sonship, or the soul adoptive and the flesh in the status of a proper son, and so forth.”

He then indicates that the mystery of the Incarnation altogether requires that Christ, one and the same Son, be said to have had two natural fathers: the eternal Father through eternal generation, and the temporal father, David, from whose lineage the Word assumed flesh through generation in time.

> “It is certain,” he says in Book I *Against Felix*, no. 10, “that according to the Catholic faith and the proclamations of Scripture the Lord Jesus Christ has two births: one from the Father without time, the other from the Mother without a man’s union; and that these two births have their proper natures, that of God, insofar as he was born of the Father, and that of man, insofar as he was born of the Mother: one and the same God, one and the same man, one and the same Son, Jesus Christ. For the twofold birth gave to the one Christ a twofold nature. He who is God from the Father is the same God and man from the Mother, and so forth.”

Accordingly, in the cited Book III *Against Felix*, no. 2, Alcuin carefully describes the essence of the Incarnation from the 165th letter of Saint Leo to the Emperor Leo, and finally concludes:

> “Therefore, Felix, do not think that you can investigate by human reasoning the birth of the Word of God by which he became flesh. You must not measure the omnipotence of divinity by human possibility. He who is the law of natures is subject to no law of another nature, nor can he who is incomprehensible be comprehended by the feeble little reasonings of human conjecture. Therefore cease to reduce either the divine or the human birth of the Only-Begotten God to the impossibility of our mortality; nor attempt to prejudge by human definitions how he could have been born, or how he could be the proper Son of God, while he was born.”

He therefore holds that in the incarnate Word two births and two fathers, eternal and temporal, must be admitted in the sense indicated above; yet he forbids an overly curious investigation of this mystery, lest it be overthrown rather than confirmed by the weakness of human reason.

### XVIII. On the arguments drawn from the anointing of the Holy Spirit, baptism, and Christ’s successive development

Alcuin again overturns the arguments of Felix and Elipandus from the anointing of the Holy Spirit mentioned in Scripture as having taken place in Christ, from his baptism, and from his successive progress in wisdom and grace, by the same replies with which Cyril formerly answered similar arguments. Namely, Christ as man, being hypostatically united to the Word from the first instant of his conception—and therefore not only being utterly remote from every sin or imperfection, but already adorned, by virtue of that union, with the fullness of grace and holiness—had no need either of regeneration, that is, baptism, or of having first acquired that anointing and increase of virtues by his own merits over the course of time [Col. 0422C].

First, concerning the anointing of the Holy Spirit, Alcuin says that Christ did not first obtain it through merits, but that it was owed to him by virtue of the aforesaid union. “In no way,” he writes in Book II *Against Felix*, no. 19, “as we showed above, was there a regeneration of anyone in baptism, but a manifestation of a greater mystery. Nor, when Christ rose from the water, was his anointing there—that is, his sanctification by the Holy Spirit descending upon him—but rather a manifestation of who he was, and a representation of our anointing and adoption, by which in baptism we are sanctified as sons of God.”

Alcuin then adds the exposition which the Venerable Bede had given on chapter 10 of Acts, and makes it his own in these words:

“As the blessed priest Bede demonstrates in his exposition of the preaching of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, by which he instructed Cornelius together with many others in the faith: ‘Jesus, therefore, was anointed,’ he says, ‘not with invisible oil’ [Bede: *visible*], ‘but with the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints those who have been baptized. Yet he was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit, when the Spirit descended upon him in the likeness of a dove. For then he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which especially those who are baptized receive the Holy Spirit. Rather, by that mystical and invisible anointing he is to be understood as having been anointed when the Word of God became flesh—that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person.’”

And in Book III *Against Elipandus*, no. 18, after introducing the words of Augustine from *Tractate XXV on John*, no. 11, he says:

“The blessed Augustine, together with the prophet, understood something more excellent in the anointing of Christ than these recent investigators of divine matters can understand with the darkness of their unbelieving hearts. He was inspired by the same Spirit in bearing witness to the truth by which Christ was anointed in the Virgin’s womb. For our Savior was anointed above his companions, because we all first existed as sinful human beings and afterward are sanctified through the anointing of the Holy Spirit; but he, existing as God before the ages, was conceived as man through the Holy Spirit in the fullness of time. There he was anointed by the same Spirit where he was conceived; he was not first conceived and afterward anointed. Rather, the very fact that he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and the Virgin’s flesh was his being anointed by the Holy Spirit. The Apostle also understood that he was anointed more abundantly than all the saints with the oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Spirit. Moses was anointed, like the other saints, for adoption as a son; Christ was anointed in the Virgin’s womb as the proper Son of God. In these words the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, also agrees, saying: ‘God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power’” (Acts 10:38).

### XIX. On the argument drawn from Christ’s baptism

By nearly the same reasoning Alcuin also refutes the argument of Felix and Elipandus drawn from Christ’s baptism. He says that it is the gravest blasphemy if anyone asserts that Christ needed a second generation, since this cannot be maintained without supposing that the man assumed by the Word was subject to sin [Col. 0423B].

“But what is meant,” he argues in Book II *Against Felix*, “by what he [Felix] says: ‘He initiated by rising from the dead’? From what dead did Christ rise in baptism? Did he have sins, so that he might rise from the death of sins, as we were born in sins because of the transgression of our first parents, and were not freed from them except in Christ Jesus through a second generation, in which the children of wrath are made children of God?

“On the contrary, Christ Jesus, conceived and born without any sin, came to baptism to display an example of humility and to sanctify the waters by his baptism—not so that he himself might be sanctified in the waters, since he had no sin in himself from which he needed to be cleansed through baptism. Therefore the blessed Baptist himself said to the Son of God who came to him: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?’ (Matt. 3:14). It was as though he had said: ‘In me there is that which must be cleansed by you; in you there is nothing that must be cleansed by me.’”

In these words Alcuin notes three things together with Cyril: first, that Christ was holy from the womb itself, or from the first instant of his conception; second, that he therefore had no need whatsoever of the washing of regeneration, unless one wishes to declare him guilty of sin—a declaration by which, however, the hypostatic union with the Word would necessarily be abolished; third, that the reason why he wished to be baptized by John was not that he might be adopted with us as a son of God, but solely to give us an example of humility and to sanctify the waters of baptism.

He says nearly the same in his letter to Elipandus, no. 5:

“Elipandus also reports that he needed baptism, apparently wishing him to be adopted in baptism as a son, just as we are. No one who thinks soundly can fail to recognize what unbelief it is for any Christian to believe this. Our Lord Jesus Christ alone could be born in such a way that he did not need a second regeneration. Therefore, in the baptism of John he wished to be baptized by a definite dispensation of mercy, because John’s baptism was not regeneration, but a certain preliminary signification of Christ’s baptism. In that baptism alone there is true remission of sins for believers through the Holy Spirit, so that we might be reborn in the Spirit in whom he was born of the Virgin Mary.

“He wished to be baptized by John in water, not so that any iniquity of his might be washed away, but so that his great humility might be commended. Thus baptism found nothing in him that it could wash away, just as death found nothing that it could punish; so that the devil might be conquered by the truth of justice, rather than crushed by an exercise of power. Both baptism and death were undertaken not from pitiable necessity, but rather from merciful will.”

These statements agree with what Paulinus of Aquileia writes in Book I *Against Felix*, chapter 44, and with what we cited above in § 2, no. 20, from the work of Beatus and Etherius *Against Elipandus*.

### XX. On Christ’s having no merit by which he successively advanced to become the Son of God

Alcuin consistently maintains that no merit can be admitted in Christ by which he progressively advanced to become the Son of God. Otherwise it would have to be said that the man assumed by the Word was previously subject to certain imperfections and first laid them aside through the progress of time [Col. 0424A]—something that, given the hypostatic union with the Word, has no place whatsoever.

This is clear from his words, which we cited in the preceding section, no. 21. Moreover, in Book IV *Against Felix*, no. 10, he says:

“That the true God was conceived at the very origin of Christ’s most holy incarnation can be affirmed by the testimonies of many Catholic Fathers, a few of which we have decided to set down here.”

He then adduces, in confirmation of his assertion, the words of the blessed Augustine from the *Enchiridion*, chapter 31:

“Was he previously a man, and was this singular benefit bestowed upon him by which he might singularly merit God? Certainly, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—the only-begotten, and certainly God because of God the Word, which, having assumed him, became flesh—so that, just as every human being is one person, namely, rational soul and flesh, so Christ might be one person, the Word and man.”

He likewise adduces the testimony of Saint Fulgentius from Book *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 18:

“Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that Christ’s flesh was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before it was assumed by the Word; rather, the Word of God himself was conceived through the assumption of his flesh, and that flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word of God.”

Alcuin rightly judged, then, that either it must be admitted that Christ as man was truly the Son of God from the womb itself and was not first advanced to this dignity by his own merits, or else it must be denied that the divine Word united human nature to himself at the very conception of the flesh and already then existed as one person with the man whom he assumed.

Hence he reproaches Felix as being supremely erroneous because he denied that the true God was born of the Virgin, or that the one who was born was the true Son of God. He therefore wished it to be believed not that the man assumed had grown progressively in holiness, but that he had been conceived in the fullness of holiness. This he confirms with Bede’s words on chapter 1 of Luke:

“Therefore also what will be born holy from you will be called the Son of God. To distinguish our holiness from his, Jesus is asserted to be born uniquely holy. For although we are made holy, we are not nevertheless born holy. He alone is truly holy, who, in order to overcome the very conception of corruptible nature, was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse.”

The same work, no. 12.

It is already clear from these passages how accurately Alcuin, in accordance with the mind of Cyril—or rather of the Church, which had long before approved the arguments of this holy teacher against the same Nestorian quibbles by its judgment—answered what Felix and Elipandus had borrowed from those heretics in defense of adoption in Christ as man.

But he refuted no less solidly the doctrine and reasoning by which they maintained that Christ, insofar as he is man, was not the true God but only God in name. We shall see this immediately from the writings of the same author.

### XXI. On extrinsic designation as God

We noted above, in no. 7 of this paragraph, that Cyril demonstrated chiefly from this point the falsity of the assertion concerning a merely titular God: if it were maintained, it would follow that the Word had not properly united human nature to himself and that Emmanuel was a mere man like us.

Alcuin likewise uses this argument repeatedly to blunt the attacks of his adversaries. “But also the matter which you ask me to explain,” he says in Book VII *Against Felix*, no. 14, “namely, how the true God was conceived and born, has been treated with you throughout the whole course of the present work: that the only-begotten Son of God, the Word of the Father, became flesh.

“For if the one conceived and born of the Virgin Mary is not the true Son of God, then what John says is not true: ‘The Word became flesh.’ For what does this statement mean—‘The Word became flesh’—unless that the Son of God, by assuming human flesh, became man? But if the true God and true Son of God was not conceived, then the true Son of God was not born of the Virgin. And if that is so, he was a mere man and was born without divinity. Every right-believing person understands how contrary this is to the Catholic faith.

“According to the Catholic faith, therefore, the true Son of God was conceived and born of the Virgin—the very one who was born of the Father before all ages. For the nature of humanity that he assumed did not make the one born of the Virgin someone other than the one begotten of the Father before time; rather, it plainly demonstrates that the very same one became what he had not previously been.”

You will find the same argument in his Letter to Elipandus, no. 10.

Alcuin also presses Cyril’s reasoning more frequently: human nature, after its assumption, certainly became proper to the Word, so that Christ, even insofar as he is man, must either be called the true God or be divided into two persons.

“If in divinity he is the true God,” he says in Book I *Against Felix*, no. 11, “and in humanity a titular God, then he is one and another; and you who think this way can in no manner escape the impiety of Nestorian doctrine. For the one whom Nestorius divides into two persons on account of the two natures, you divide into two sons and two gods by the name of adoption and designation.

“Whom he makes one and another in persons, you make one and another in two sons and in a diversity of divinity, because you can in no way join into one person him who said to Moses his servant in the bush, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,’ and him who said, ‘I have appointed you god of Pharaoh.’”

Finally, he indicates that from this doctrine of his adversaries it would follow that we, who are sometimes called gods, would have the same dignity as Christ as man. He shows that this is contrary both to Scripture and to the Fathers, citing the testimony of Pope Gregory, whose words from Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 11, he quotes there:

“In Sacred Scripture God is sometimes called God by designation, and sometimes God essentially. He is called God by designation, as it was said to Moses: ‘Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh’ (Exod. 22:8). Again, as Moses says: ‘If one man does this or that, bring him before the gods,’ that is, before the priests; and as the Psalmist says: ‘God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes gods’ (Ps. 81:1).

“But God is called God essentially, as he himself says to Moses: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’ (Exod. 3:6). Therefore the Apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the name ‘God’ by designation from God essentially, says: ‘Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever’ (Rom. 9:5). A titular god is among all things; the essential God is over all. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, he mentioned not merely this God but God over all: for every just person is a god, but Christ is God over all because he is God by nature.”

And in the same book, no. 15, he says:

“For it could not, cannot, and will never be said of any of the saints: ‘The Word became flesh.’ No saint, however great his excellence in grace, received the name of only-begotten, so that what the Word of God is before the ages might be said to be the same together with the man whom he assumed. That assumption is unique; it cannot in any manner be shared with any holy human beings, however distinguished by wisdom and holiness. There the exceedingly evident and clear proof of divine grace is found.”

After he had shown from a certain letter of Saint Augustine, hitherto unknown, how great the difference is between us and the man assumed by the Word, he concludes as follows:

“According to what Saint Augustine wishes to be understood, the fullness of the fountain flows in one way, while the measure of the streams runs from the fountain in another way. The blessed Baptist bears witness to this: ‘For God does not give the Spirit by measure,’ he says. ‘The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand’ (John 3:34–35). The Apostle testifies concerning the measure of the streams: ‘To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift’ (Eph. 4:7).”

Certainly the entire force of this argument tends to show that there is the greatest possible distinction between us and the human nature hypostatically united to the divine Word. Such a distinction would plainly not exist if Christ, with respect to his humanity, were merely a titular god in the same way that we are sometimes called gods in Scripture.

See also Book IV *Against Elipandus*, no. 6, where Alcuin argues in the same way from Saint Cyril and other Fathers.

### XXII. On the argument drawn from passages of Scripture in which human beings are called gods. The words of Felix

This also contains the response to the argument of the Adoptionists drawn from Christ’s words (John 10:34) and from other passages of Scripture in which human beings are called gods. Alcuin says that these passages cannot be applied to Christ as man unless we are willing to admit that he was a mere man, distinct in hypostasis from the Word who assumed him.

In Book IV, at the very beginning of which he examines the assertions of Felix presented by us above in § 2, no. 23, and based on the aforementioned testimonies of Scripture, he argues in no. 5 as follows:

“Are there not two: the one who is the true God and the one who is a titular god? For the person of the true God is one, and the person of the titular god another.

“Everyone who reads the Gospel history can understand that ‘Jesus’ and ‘Christ’ are names of the humanity in the Son of God.
