And if Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is not the true God, how does the universal Church throughout the whole world, including you also, as I suppose, customarily say in all the prayers sung during the solemn celebrations of Mass: ‘Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever’?

“He himself also said to his apostles, he who suffered and rose again: ‘All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth’ (Matt. 28:18). To whom was power given except to the one born of the Virgin? For, as you said shortly before, the Son of God, substantially born from God, essentially possessed all power with the Father and the Holy Spirit; but this power was given to the Son of the Virgin. And if he possesses all power, how can it be that he is not altogether the true God and the true Son of God?

“Moses was a titular god, yet all power was not given to him; therefore he struck the rock a second time to bring forth water. But whatever miracles Christ performed in the world while he dwelt among human beings in visible presence, he performed by his own power, as the powerful and true God. Could any of the saints, by himself, do anything apart from him who said, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5)? Tell me, then, from where the apostles performed such mighty works in the name of Jesus, if Jesus himself did not possess his own power but only titular power?”

This mode of argument certainly agrees closely with that of the blessed Cyril. As we saw above, no. 8, Cyril likewise established the difference between Moses and Christ as man from the power of performing miracles in one’s own name.

And just as this holy teacher further confirmed the Church’s doctrine by observing that Jesus is said by John to have known what was in man—a power that can belong not to a titular god, or man, but only to the true God—so Alcuin later set against his adversaries a similar testimony of Scripture, namely that of the Apostle Paul: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

From this Alcuin argues in Book IV *Against Felix*, no. 7:

“I want you to explain to me, Felix, whether this one whom the Apostle says speaks within him is man or God. If he is man, how could the body of another speak in his heart? If he is God, then Christ is not man but God. For since Christ has spoken in the Apostle, and could not speak in him unless he were God, Christ God has spoken in him.

“You see, therefore, that nothing can now be said here against this, nor can any separation or division be made between Christ and God, because God is wholly in Christ and Christ wholly in God. No separation can be admitted here, no division.”

He then adduces the words of the blessed Jerome on chapter 17 of Jeremiah:

“From this too we learn that God alone knows the thoughts of human beings. But if it is said of the Savior, ‘Jesus, seeing their thoughts’ (Luke 11:17), and no one can see thoughts except God alone, then Christ too is God, who searches hearts and will repay each person according to his works.”

Finally, in no. 8, he concludes:

“He who will always be the true God in God the Father is true and God in man as well. And he who is truly the Son of man is himself also truly the Son of God. The same one is man-God because of God, and the same one is God-man because of man, just as in any human being there are soul and body.

“This unity and truth in Christ did not begin after the Virgin’s delivery; rather, it was joined and united in the Virgin’s womb itself, and so forth.”

### XXIII. On the inept interpretation of the words by which the Word is said to have dwelt in us or in the assumed nature. The words of Felix

With no less skill Alcuin refuted another argument of the Adoptionists, by which they attempted to prove that Christ as man was God only in name. This argument was drawn from the statement that the divine Word dwelt in us and that all the fullness of divinity dwelt in Christ.

As we said above concerning Cyril, Alcuin demonstrates that, if the interpretation of these words handed down by Felix and Elipandus were true, the divine Word would not have been incarnate precisely in the man Christ, but would also be incarnated daily in the other righteous human beings in whom it is said to dwell by its grace—or rather, in reality, it would never have assumed human nature and would not properly have become flesh.

This is certainly the point of what he writes in Book VII *Against Felix*, no. 2. There, citing Theodoret’s words from his critique of Cyril’s first anathema, volume VI of the works, folio 204, which read as follows—

“He who exists before the ages is God; but fashioning a temple for himself in the Virgin’s womb, he was present with the one conceived and formed. For this reason we call that holy virgin Mother of God—not as though she gave birth to God, but as though she gave birth to a man united to God, who fashioned him”—

Alcuin continues:

“What else is it that you too say, when you claim that the Word of God dwelt in the man assumed as in a certain temple, rather than as the Evangelist says: ‘The Word became flesh’? ‘According to the Lord’s command,’ you say, ‘he bore divinity and is the inhabitant of his temple.’

“But it is one thing for God to have dwelt in the saints, and another for God himself to have become man, and from two substances to be one person, God and man.”

He then adds the words of Cyril in his Letter to Nestorius, volume V of the works, part II:

“Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt as in an ordinary man who was born of the holy Virgin, lest Christ the man be believed to possess God as an inhabitant. For although the Word dwelt in us, and it was said that ‘all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ,’ we understand that he became flesh, not in the manner in which he is said to dwell in the saints; nor do we attempt to define that such a dwelling took place in him. Rather, being one according to nature and not changed into flesh, he made for himself such a dwelling as the soul of a human being is believed to have in its own body.”

From these passages Alcuin concludes:

“Christ our God is therefore the unique Son, not through some kind of conjunction, unity of dignity, or authority of a man who possesses a relation to God—whom you customarily call joined to God or adopted—and who also bears divinity, and so forth.”

Alcuin explains the text from Paul’s Letter to the Colossians 2:9 in Book V *Against Felix*, no. 6, simply in the words of Saint Cyril. According to Cyril, the statement that all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ signifies a true and substantial dwelling, and indeed one according to the entire fullness of divinity. This implies that the divine Word truly and properly assumed the whole of human nature into the unity of his person, and did not dwell in it merely through participation in grace, as he is said to dwell in other saints.

For this reason Alcuin also cites in the same place the words of Victor of Capua from his hitherto unknown book *Of the Betrothed*:

“God was in Christ—certainly the Father in the Son—because it pleased him that all the fullness of divinity should dwell in him. In the other saints, apostles, patriarchs, and prophets there was grace; but in Christ the whole divinity dwelt, that is, the whole fullness of divinity bodily.”

Then, just as Cyril rejected the erroneous interpretation of Paul’s words, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19), on the ground that the truth of redemption would thereby be abolished, Alcuin uses the same reasoning in Book V *Against Felix*, no. 4:

“He also sets down a third statement of the blessed Paul, the distinguished preacher, where he says: ‘For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.’”

Felix’s argument from this passage of Scripture then follows, formulated as follows:

“He does not say, ‘Christ was God,’ but ‘God was in Christ.’ This does not mean that Christ—the man who was assumed—is not God, but that he is God not by nature, but by grace and designation.”

Alcuin replies:

“Look, readers, at this new interpreter of Sacred Scripture, who attempts to separate God from the man assumed and to make two gods from our one God and Redeemer, one true and the other titular. This new interpreter wants Christ, whom the whole Church worships and adores—not only the Church which labors on earth in hope, but also the Church which rightly rejoices in heaven—to be believed to be a solitary man, in accordance with Nestorian or Pelagian perversity.

“But if this is true, so that there is only an appearance of the name ‘God’ in Christ and not the reality of divinity, how is he the true Redeemer of the human race? If there is only an imagined exercise of power in the head, whence is there truth of salvation in the body?”

Finally, together with Cyril, Alcuin rejects the expressions “Christ the God-bearing man” and “the Lordly man,” because division of persons would follow from them, and Christ would be a mere man while the Word would not truly have been incarnate.

In Book VI *Against Felix*, no. 8, he cites the testimonies by which Cyril insisted on the unity of person against these modes of speech so familiar to the Nestorians.

In Book VII, no. 2, he touches on another argument of this holy teacher: namely, that through these expressions the truth of the incarnation is overturned and Christ must be regarded as a mere man. He therefore says:

“But since, as we have said, you claim that he ‘bears divinity,’ hear what reward you receive for this from the holy and Catholic men who were accustomed to argue at length against your heresy:

“‘If anyone presumes to say that Christ is a God-bearing man, rather than truly God, as the only Son by nature, according to the fact that the Word became flesh and immediately shared with us in blood and flesh, let him be anathema.’

“For this is the reward of your labor here and now. What the future reward will be from that very one whom you strive so greatly to humble, attempting to deprive him of the whole truth of sonship and the power of divinity, you yourself will discover when you stand to be judged before his tribunal.

“The aforementioned Fathers also add, speaking of the same matter:

“‘Christ is not as God dwells in us. For he himself was God, appearing naturally according to our condition, one and the only Son, both when he became flesh and thereafter. Those who therefore presume to say that he is a God-bearing man rather than God incarnate necessarily fall under anathema.’”

### XXIV. On the assertion that Christ, only insofar as he is man, is our high priest or advocate, and that he also prayed for himself. The words of Felix

Alcuin also answers, together with Cyril, another argument which the Adoptionists had drawn from Christ’s office as high priest and advocate, as well as from Christ’s prayer, in order to prove that Christ as man was only a titular god.

He first says that the name “propitiator” presupposes the true God. By this reasoning he indicates that a mere man would not possess sufficient merit to make satisfaction for our sins, and that therefore all the merit of the sacrifice offered for us on the cross would be nullified unless the very Word had performed it in the assumed nature.

Here are his words from Book V *Against Felix*, no. 7:

“Felix therefore proposes a statement from the Apostle’s letter, where he says: ‘We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2:1). You assert that this is to be understood by you as follows: ‘Advocate,’ you say, ‘is the same as mediator, who intercedes with the Father on behalf of the offenses of sinners.’ But this must not be understood of the true God, but of the man assumed.

“Why do you not understand that the Evangelist calls the same one propitiator whom he calls advocate, when he says: ‘We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins’? In calling him advocate, he designates the man; in calling him propitiator, he demonstrates the God.”

By these words Alcuin certainly implies that the passion, death, and other actions of the human nature assumed by the Word are, considered in themselves, offerings or sacrifices presented to the Father for our redemption. Yet this sacrifice is not brought to completion unless they receive from the person of the Word a price or merit proportionate both to the cancellation of infinite debts and to the attainment of eternal glory. Thus not the man alone who was assumed, but the eternal Son of the eternal Father himself, in the nature united to him, must be regarded as our high priest, advocate, and mediator [Col. 0429B].

Moreover, in the preceding section we already noted that Alcuin rightly judged Christ not to be our Redeemer in reality unless he is also the true God.

As for the assertion by which Felix and Elipandus maintained that Christ also prayed or sacrificed for himself, Alcuin argues that this necessarily implies that Christ was subject to sin and other defects.

“But since it would take too long,” he argues in Book VII *Against Felix*, no. 15, “to examine all the arguments of your perversity, let it suffice to answer you at present concerning this point: you chiefly attempt to deny that the Son of God, having become man, is the true God because he is said to have prayed for himself, just as he prayed for us.

“Where you read that, I utterly do not know—namely, that the Son of God prayed for himself as he did for us. For what could he himself provide for himself, to whom the Father gave all things into his hands (John 3:35)? Or for what sin should he be thought to have asked forgiveness from God, when he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (Isa. 53:9; 1 Pet. 2:22)?

“For we, who are commanded to pray to God without ceasing, undoubtedly have something that we may ask him to forgive us. But what would Christ have asked to be forgiven him, since he never did anything that could have been forgiven him?”

Paulinus of Aquileia argues in the same way in Book I *Against Felix*, chapter 30:

“Moreover, if he prayed for himself, then he was born, suffered, died, and was buried for himself and for his own sake; for himself also he shed his own blood. Therefore, if he prayed for himself under the compulsion of necessity, he had nothing more than a mere man.

“Thus you too argue that, according to the flesh, he was certainly not—as he himself testifies through the prophet—‘free among the dead,’ nor was he born exempt from that mass of perdition and law of sin. May divine mercy turn such a suspicion far away from every heart.”

## XXV. On the Argument Derived from the Passion [Cols. 0429D–0432B]

From almost the same principle Alcuin answers his adversaries when they said that Christ was God only in name, and merely nominally so, because the true God cannot suffer. First of all, he shows that the entire merit of the reconciliation of the human race, accomplished through the blood and death of Jesus Christ, rests upon the fact that the divine Word himself endured all these things in the nature he had assumed. To this he certainly referred when, in Book VI against Felix, no. 9, he quoted the words of Saint Leo, who says in Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 3, that it was altogether necessary for the redemption of the human race that the divine Son himself should appear in the flesh and, although impassible in himself, should suffer in it:

> “And in order to discharge the debt of our condition” (these are the words of Saint Leo), “an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that what was suited to our remedies might be accomplished by one and the same mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus: from the one nature he could die, and from the other he could not die. Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, the true God was born, wholly in what was his own, wholly in what was ours. By ‘ours’ we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and undertook to restore, etc.”

Alcuin then continues:

> “The Son of God is one and the same in the conjunction of the two natures—not by the grace of adoption, but as one person by propriety. He is one only-begotten and firstborn Son, not one only-begotten and another firstborn.”

To this he adds a passage under the name of Saint Augustine, although it is not clear from where he took it. It reads as follows:

> “Accordingly, in the Creed also we all confess that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s testimony: ‘For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory and majesty.’”

Finally he concludes:

> “Therefore the Lord of glory and the God of hosts had within himself that by which he could be crucified and die. It was not one who was crucified for the salvation of the world and another who is the life of all living beings, but one and the same—not divided by adoption, but united by propriety. The Word became flesh so that flesh might be exalted into the glory of God, not so that God might be changed into the dishonor of flesh.”

Accordingly, in order to discharge the debt of our condition—or, what amounts to the same thing, in order to offer adequate satisfaction for our sins—Alcuin, with Saint Leo, judged it necessary that the impassible God himself should suffer in a passible nature. He judged it necessary that the very one who is the life of all living beings should be crucified for the salvation of the world. By this manner of argument he clearly implies that the merit of human redemption is utterly destroyed by those adversaries who say that not the divine Son himself, not the true God, but merely the assumed human being—the titular God—endured the pains of death.

For the same purpose, in Book IV against Elipandus, no. 6, he cites the words of Cyril from his letter to the Egyptian monks:

> “But if Christ,” he says, “is neither truly Son nor naturally God, but a mere human being like us and an instrument of divinity, then we have indeed been saved not somehow in God, but in one who, more according to our condition, died for us and was raised again by another’s powers.”

By means of the absurd consequence, Alcuin, together with Cyril, attempts to demonstrate the absurdity of the primary assertion itself. He teaches that it must necessarily be admitted that God himself suffered for us in the flesh, since, if a human being alone had endured death, a human being alone would also have redeemed us—something which anyone of sound mind understands to be wholly impossible.

But since the Adoptionists were also afraid that this doctrine would imply that the Word of God the Father himself was passible or mortal, Alcuin demonstrates that they were troubled by a groundless fear, and that this conclusion follows from it no more than the mortality of the human soul follows from the common statement that the whole human being dies, although only the flesh is dissolved by death.

> “The Apostle calls these two natures,” he says in Book I against Felix, no. 10, “which he possesses from both parents, two forms, when he says of him: ‘Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.’ You see that in the one person of Christ both the mystery of the two forms and of the two natures is contained: the same one is passible and impassible, the same one mortal and immortal—not one and another, but the same one in two natures. Just as one human being is mortal and immortal—mortal in the flesh, immortal in the soul—yet is one human being and not another.”

Thus, just as the whole human being is said to die, although only the flesh perishes, because through union the flesh has become proper to the spirit, which is immortal in itself, so the Word is rightly said to suffer and die in his flesh, because by assuming it he made it his own. Hence, in the same book, no. 8, he says:

> “Because the Word was united with the flesh in such an ineffable manner that we call the very Word of whom blessed John the Evangelist says, ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,’ made flesh, just as that same Evangelist says, ‘And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,’ that is, with us—although that Word was not changed into flesh, and that flesh is called God although it was not changed into the nature of divinity—there is one Son, God, and one God, the Lord Jesus Christ. On account of this unity the Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven, and the Lord of glory to have been crucified. Thus, without suffering in himself, the Word of God suffered; the Son of Man wondrously descended from heaven; and the hands of the one who created heaven and earth were fastened to the cross with nails. His blood, through which all things were created, was poured out for the salvation of all, as the Apostle testifies when he says: ‘And the blood of the Son of God redeemed us’ (1 John I, 7).”

In Book VI, no. 6, he accuses Felix of corrupting a passage of Saint Augustine. Where this holy Father had said of the Son of God, “Impassible in what is his own, passible in what is ours,” Felix had instead written, “Impassible in what is his own, passible in what is another’s.” Alcuin then continues:

> “As though his own body, which the Son of God made proper to himself, were alien to him.”

A little later he adds the words of the same Saint Augustine—or rather of Vigilius of Thapsus, from his Disputation with the Arian Bishop Felicianus, volume VIII of the Appendix, chapter 11:

> “It is one and the same Christ who endured insults wholly, yet was not submerged when led into the depths. Accordingly, in the mediator between God and human beings, we confess that the divinity experienced the dishonor of the assumed body, just as we know that the flesh was glorified by the majesty of divinity.”

Alcuin inserted these statements solely to show that, on account of the supreme—namely, hypostatic—union between the Word and human nature, divine things are ascribed to the human being and human things to God, and therefore suffering and death are rightly ascribed to the Word.

He had also touched upon this point in Book V, no. 11, where he addresses Felix as follows:

> “You also add, when you discuss the two natures in Christ: ‘Impassible in what is his own, passible in what is another’s.’ What do you mean by saying that what is another’s belongs to the Son of God in that assumption of humanity which was united to the Son of God in so great and wondrous a unity that he was one, not two? He is the same in the glory of divinity as in the weakness of humanity; the same Son of God who is also the Son of Man, and the same Son of Man who is also the Son of God. For what could be alien in this union, when it is certain that all the actions of both natures in Christ belong to one proper person?”

Alcuin also confirms his doctrine by testimonies from Scripture, and above all presses those passages in which the only-begotten Son of God, the proper Son of God, is said to have been given and delivered up for us.

Felix himself had provided the occasion for a fuller discussion of these texts when he said that nowhere in the Gospel was it written that the Son of God had been delivered up for us. To this Alcuin replies in Book V, no. 8:

> “You have forgotten that the Son of God himself spoke of his being delivered up: ‘For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son’ (John III, 16). Therefore the only-begotten Son of God is the Son who was given for the salvation of the world. But what does ‘given’ mean except ‘delivered up’? The Apostle also confirms this when he says: ‘He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all’ (Romans VIII, 32). Again, concerning the same Son of God, the same Apostle says: ‘He delivered himself up for us’ (Ephesians V, 2).

> “Blessed Peter also, preaching to the Jews, did not hesitate to testify that he was the Son of God, saying: ‘The God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed delivered up and denied before Pilate, when he was judging that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One and asked that a murderer be given to you. You killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead on the third day’ (Acts III, 13–15).

> “What room for doubt can there be in these words of apostolic authority? He testified that the Son of God was the one who was delivered up, who died, and indeed who was raised again. He added: ‘The Author of life.’ Who, then, is the Author of life except the Son of God, who is said to have been delivered up for the salvation of the world either by God the Father or by himself? ...

> “Therefore the Son of Man can in no way be divided from the Son of God, nor the Son of God separated from the Son of Man, because the Son of God is one—God and human being—who was delivered up to death for our offenses. ...

> “We also openly confess this in the Creed of the Catholic faith: that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, suffered for human salvation. Therefore no Catholic ought to doubt that the Son of God was delivered up for the salvation of the world. For whoever denies that the Son of God was delivered up to suffering can in no way be a Catholic; rather, by persisting in this obstinacy, he must be judged alien to the profession of the Catholic faith.”

He further appeals, in Book VI against Felix, to the words of Saint Cyril:

> “How, then, was Christ named the proper Son of God, who was also delivered up by God the Father for the salvation and life of all? For he was delivered up on account of our sins, and he himself bore the sins of many in his body upon the tree, according to the prophet’s word. It is therefore evident that the assumed reality, once united, necessarily showed that he who is from the holy Virgin is God’s proper Son. For the body was not, according to our condition, that of some other person, but rather the proper body of the Word existing from the Father, born from her.”

Alcuin adds:

> “After so many and such clear testimonies of the holy Fathers, how, Felix, did such hostile rashness creep into you that you dare deny Christ to be the proper Son of God, or the true Lord, or that he endured sufferings in his own body for the sake of our salvation?”

## XXVI. On the Opinion by Which Felix and Elipandus Asserted That Christ, as a Human Being, Was the Father’s Conditional Servant [Cols. 0432C–0433B]

Finally, since the Adoptionists also wished the servitude attributed to Christ in Scripture to be understood not of the Word but precisely of the assumed human being alone, and since they maintained that Christ, insofar as he is human, was the Father’s servant by condition or necessity rather than by free will, Alcuin appeals to the same testimony of Paul in the Letter to the Philippians II, 8, which we noted above that Cyril had used. He replies that the Word himself is called the Father’s servant dispensationally, in the assumed nature, and that the contrary cannot be maintained: Christ cannot be called a conditional servant as a human being without abolishing the hypostatic union in the mystery of the Incarnation.

> “This Felix,” he says in Book IV, no. 9, “frequently asserts that Christ is a conditional servant, failing to understand that he is called a servant according to the mystery of the divine dispensation: not by a condition of due servitude, as we said above, but by voluntary obedience in fulfilling the Father’s will for human salvation. For in Christ everything that was done was an act of will, not of necessity; for, as the Apostle testifies, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross.

> “Voluntary humility is one thing; servile necessity is another. Certain things are said of Christ according to the propriety of his nature, such as ‘the way, the truth, and the life.’ Others were proclaimed about him by the prophets through expressions signifying the things that were to be accomplished through him. It is in this kind of language that Christ must be understood to have been called a servant by the prophets.”

Thus Alcuin says that the one who had been in the form of God assumed the form of a servant, and that in this form he voluntarily served the Father in order to bring the work of human salvation to completion. For this reason alone, he says, the prophets called him a servant.

When Felix attempted to support his assertion concerning Christ’s servitude as a human being by the previously cited words of Paul, Alcuin replies as follows:

> “Among the many whom you say believe that Christ serves God through obedience is blessed Paul the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, who says: ‘Christ was obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross; therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.’ A conditional servant does not possess a name above every name, but one lower than the name of sons. The name ‘sons’ has been granted by God’s favor to all the saints in common. What, then, is that name more excellent than all others which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, was given to Christ by God the Father on account of the wondrous mystery of his obedience? It is the name which he himself immediately adds: ‘That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.’

> “If Jesus is now Lord and is in the glory of God the Father—that is, in the majesty of divinity—then he is not subject to the yoke of conditional servitude.”

Accordingly, Alcuin judged that no conditional or necessary servitude could be admitted in Christ, since the same one who is said by the Apostle to have been obedient unto death is also mentioned as Lord and as being in the glory of the Father. The Word assumed human nature into the unity of his person, and therefore it must be held that he offered obedience to the Father for the salvation of our race in the flesh united to him by the freest and most gracious will.

Alcuin considers this all the more certain because the division of persons is more evident in the opinion of his adversaries. Thus, when Felix objected and asked:

> “In what form will he be subject to the Father, if it is believed that there is no difference or inequality between his divinity and his humanity?”

Alcuin replies:

> “We therefore say that in Christ God there are two proper natures, one of divinity and the other of humanity. But we believe in him the true glory of divinity, lest the mere naming of divinity, recently introduced by you and separated in human nature from the nature of divinity, should divide the profession of our faith into two gods. Rather, we confess one God under the propriety of two natures, who will judge the world in the form in which he can be seen by all, which you assert to be conditionally subject to God the Father.”

In Book IV against Elipandus, no. 6, he also appeals to the words of Saint Cyril in his Letter to the Egyptian Monks, volume V, part II:

> “We do not confess two Christs, a human being and the Word, one exalted and the other subject, but one and the same Christ, God and human being.”

He adds:

> “Does he not confess two Christs, one exalted and the other subject, who says that one Christ is the true God and the other titular, or one Lord and the other servant?”

## XXVII. He Proves That His Opinion in No Way Entails a Confusion of the Natures [Cols. 0433C–0434A]

Alcuin also refutes the charge made by Felix and Elipandus, who everywhere accused the Catholics of confusing the natures, in the same way that Saint Cyril formerly refuted the similar charge of the Nestorians: by carefully explaining the mystery of the Incarnation and showing that the intimate union of the Word with human nature in one person was altogether necessary if he was truly to be called made flesh, without its following that he had undergone any change or that the two natures had been mixed, or confused through some sort of blending, as the Nestorians expressed it.

We shall cite only one testimony on this subject from Book III against Felix, no. 17. After Alcuin had reported the words with which that bishop accused him of confusing the natures—words cited above in § 2, no. 28—he replies as follows:

> “What do you mean by saying that we confuse two natures into the singularity of one person? In part you speak truly; in part, according to your usual manner, you falsely slander us. For we believe and confess, with the Catholic Church, that the two natures in the one person of Christ are not confused, as you say, with Eutyches, but are joined together in such an ineffable manner that, while the propriety of each nature remains—and, so to speak, the integrity of both is preserved—divine things communicate with human things and human things with divine things.

> “In this holy and wondrous union there would be not a conversion of divinity but an exaltation of humanity: that is, not God changed into a human being, but a human being glorified into God. Nor would the divine nature have ceased to be what it was, namely God; rather, human nature would begin to be what it had not been. Thus, as we have often said and shall always say, there is one Christ from two natures wondrously and ineffably united, wholly one and true Son of God.

> “Accordingly, in two natures one true God is both named and truly is. For almighty God never wishes anything to be said of him that is not true; this is altogether alien to the Catholic faith. Rather, as we have said, the Son of God assumed a human being in such a way that he lost nothing of what he possessed. With the assumption of the human being he remained the true Son of God, as he always is. Nor was divinity diminished on account of the human being, nor changed into a human being. Likewise, the human being did not depart from the nature of humanity so as to cease to be human; rather, the nature of humanity preserved the propriety of its nature, and the substance of divinity did not lose the propriety of divinity.

> “Nevertheless, Christ is a human being who is God, and God became a human being, so that what the blessed Evangelist says might be true: ‘The Word became flesh,’ with the name ‘Word’ designating God and the name ‘flesh’ indicating the human being.”

In this passage Alcuin describes the essence of the Incarnation with great care and precision. He says that it was necessary for human things to be attributed to God, or to the Word, and divine things to the assumed human being; that the two natures should come together in the unity of the person, yet without any confusion or mixture; and that in this way the Evangelist’s statement, “The Word became flesh,” would finally be true. We plainly cannot see how Alcuin could have expressed himself more clearly in removing from himself the charge of confusing the natures in Christ.

## XXVIII. He Proves That the Expressions Used by Felix and Elipandus Introduce a Division of Persons [Cols. 0434B–0434D]

With much greater justification Alcuin, together with Cyril, attacks his adversaries for Nestorianism—that is, the error of a double person—on the basis of the expressions they had made especially familiar, constantly distinguishing one from another in Christ.

Thus, in Book II against Elipandus, while arguing against the words of that bishop in a letter addressed to him:

> “Behold, to whom the Father says, ‘I am your God’? Not to him—that is, to the Word who was begotten from the Father before the ages—but to him who at the end of time was made human from the Virgin Mary, etc.,”

he says:

> “How do you fail to understand that in these words of yours you affirm two persons in Christ, when you say ‘to him’ and ‘to that one,’ as though the one begotten from God the Father were someone other than the one made from the virgin mother, although the Evangelist says: ‘The Word became flesh’?”

Here again Alcuin refers to the Evangelist’s testimony, implying that the truth of the Incarnation is destroyed if Christ is said to consist of “that one” and “the other.” Such pronouns designate not nature but person; therefore, when the pronoun is doubled, the person itself must also be considered double, contrary to the faith of the Incarnation, which declares that the Word took human nature to himself in one hypostasis.

Beatus and Etherius also reasoned in the same way as Alcuin in their work against Elipandus. In Book I, from the Apostle’s words, “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God” (1 John IV, 1), they construct the following argument against the words of Elipandus:

> “What does it mean to dissolve Jesus except to preach God separately and the human being separately? Without doubt he dissolves Jesus who preaches to the people, saying: ‘Did he create visible and invisible things through HIM who was born of the Virgin, or through HIM who is not adopted but begotten, not by grace but by nature, and created all things?’ And therefore without doubt he created all things through HIM whom he begot equal to himself and without adoption. And through this same Son of God and human being, adoptive in humanity and in no way adoptive in divinity, he redeemed the world.

> “See the spirit that dissolves Jesus. Open your eyes: the matter is clear. The spirit of error dictated this. The spirit of Antichrist inspired this.”

*Cited edition*, volume II, folio 310.

They therefore judged that Jesus was being dissolved—that is, that the persons in Christ were being divided—by these expressions customarily used by Elipandus, “that one” and “the other.” Consequently, they judged that the mystery of the Incarnation was overthrown as well, since in what follows they very carefully establish that mystery from the Apostle.

## XXIX. Hence He Says That the Profession of One Person Made by the Adoptionists in Words Alone Was Not Sincere. The Words of Felix [Cols. 0435A–0436A]

For this reason Alcuin did not think that the adversaries were helped by their frequent explicit confession of the unity of Christ’s person, since they had adopted principles and language that could in no way be reconciled with that confession.

> “We do not divide Christ,” he says in Book VII against Felix, no. 11, “into two sons, or two gods, or two persons with Nestorius. Although he did not openly say ‘two persons,’ he nevertheless admits in his profession everything that must necessarily belong to two persons. In the same way, although you avoid the words ‘two persons,’ we find you professing in your writings everything that must necessarily belong to two persons.

> “For who does not know that, with one father, the person of an adopted son is one thing and that of a proper son another? According to ordinary human custom, no father could adopt his own son as though he were another’s; nor could he make proper to himself the one whom he adopts as a son, since the paternity of another had made him alien. Adoption is made from what is alien, whereas a proper son remains in the truth of propriety.”

Accordingly, in Book V, no. 1, he also proves that Felix contradicts himself, since he verbally admitted the singularity or unity of the person but in reality denied it:

> “At last we have reached the point where you destroy what you built and confess what you denied. I no longer know whether greater credence ought to have been given to your earlier statements as a crafty pretense, by which you are shown to attack the truth with manifold argumentation, or to your unwilling confession, like the devil’s when terrified by fear, that Christ is the Son of God—the devil’s testimony the Truth herself everywhere refuses to accept, commanding him to be silent, because the Son of God disdained to be proclaimed by such a praiser.

> “For you say that the same one is the Son of God who is also the Son of Man, and that the Son of Man is the Son of God, as could be understood from your words. You say that he united and joined him to himself from his mother’s womb, that is, from the very conception, in the singularity of his person, so that the Son of God would be the Son of Man, not by a change of nature but by gracious condescension; and similarly, so that the Son of Man would be the Son of God, not by a changeability of substance, but that in the Son of God he would be a true son.

> “It is not surprising that you are shown to disagree with others in your Catholic profession, since you appear to disagree with yourself in turn. In this opinion of yours you might have been considered Catholic if you had not previously shown yourself to be in the perversity of your error.

> “You say, then, that in the true Son of God there would be a son. If the Son, who is Christ, is in the true Son of God, then he is also a true Son, because in what is true there can be nothing but truth. Adoption has no place in the birth of truth. Christ, the Son of God, is therefore one: true and perfect God and human being, as has often been said.

> “You also add that there are not two gods, which plainly means that you are fighting against yourself. For if there are not two gods, then there is not in him a true God and a titular god, but one true God, because God is truth. There is no pretense in him, but he is the source of all truth.”

He also reproaches Elipandus with the same matter in Book I, no. 9, writing:

> “It must be firmly believed and proclaimed, without any doubt, that the one born from the Virgin is the true God in two natures and the true Son of God: so that there is one Christ, one God, one Son of God, one king, and one Savior of the whole world, consubstantial with the Father in divinity and consubstantial with his mother in humanity, so that the same one is true God and true human being in the unity of person.

> “You undoubtedly divide him, together with Nestorius, into two sons and two persons, by propriety and adoption. Your teacher Nestorius is therefore not found to have openly professed two persons in Christ, at least insofar as his writings have reached us; but he is found to have put forward everything that must necessarily belong to two persons, ascribing adoption to the humanity, as you do, and designating the propriety of sonship in the divinity.”

A little later, in no. 14, he says:

> “You urge me not to be an Arian, who stained the hearts of many by his perversity so that they did not believe rightly. By the glory of God Jesus, I have never fallen into Arius’s abyss. But you will either be proved to be an Arian or be forced to condemn your own opinion, since you assert that the one Son of God, the only-begotten Son, and undoubtedly one person, is adoptive.

> “Do you not affirm adoption in the same person which Arius once asserted, with detestable impiety, to be adoptive? Or, if you strive to avoid this blasphemy, you immediately fall into the snare of Nestorius, dividing Christ into two persons, one proper and the other adoptive.

> “For Nestorius did not openly name two persons in Christ, but nevertheless, in a perverse sense, he affirmed everything that must belong to two persons—namely, the propriety and adoption of the Son—in Christ, etc.”

### XXX. The Dissertation Concludes, and Certain Further Sophistries of Walch Are Refuted

Whoever now weighs with an unprejudiced mind these arguments by which Alcuin attempted to overthrow each individual head of error in Felix and Elipandus will certainly find nothing for which our author can rightly be censured. For they agree exceedingly well both with the principles of sounder theology and with the method of reasoning employed by the ancient Fathers, whose works Alcuin was certainly most diligent in studying; and, to say everything in a few words, they are precisely the same arguments which the Church formerly employed and, as it were, consecrated in Cyril, and therefore they were most appropriately used against heretics whose origin and manner of thinking we have shown at length, throughout the first and second paragraphs, to have been identical with those of the Nestorians.

Nor should these arguments be judged any less suitable because Alcuin’s efforts did not produce the desired result in the conversion of his opponents, and because none of those whom he had attacked with such zeal withdrew from their pernicious doctrine. On this point, at least, Walch censures the Synod of Regensburg and the Roman judges, believing, together with Bunavius, p. 123, that those who undertook at both places to recall Felix to a sounder opinion concerning Christ did not employ a legitimate method, nor refute his errors with arguments that were just and appropriate to the matter—because those measures lacked the expected outcome and ultimately achieved only this: that Felix declared, falsely and hypocritically, that the opinions he had conceived in his mind were erroneous.

A fine conclusion indeed, if heaven permits, would this be: Felix did not sincerely abjure his heresy either at Regensburg or at Rome; therefore the arguments by which the defenders of the true faith tried to lead him back from error were inept and insufficiently coherent. For were the Fathers of the first four councils not reasoning soundly, even though the heresiarchs whom they undertook to refute did not turn away from the destructive doctrine? We consider Walch’s censure less than just when, on p. 70, he accuses Alcuin of flattery for writing to Elipandus as follows:

> “For you, most holy bishop, are a city set upon a mountain, which can in no way be hidden; its wall must by no means be pierced anywhere by the treacherous tunnels of any faithlessness, but must be surrounded on every side by the strongest rampart of the Catholic faith, so that it may remain everywhere unconquerable for the salvation of the people who rejoice in you and heed the command of your mouth.”

Certainly anyone who is a fair judge of matters sees that this praise is directed not to Elipandus’s person but to his office, and that Alcuin means nothing other than to show his opponent how great a crime it is if a bishop who has been placed upon a lampstand so that he may shine in the house of God before all should be darkened by the shadows of error and lose the flock he ought to have fed. Accordingly, Alcuin should be regarded as having admonished Elipandus concerning his duty by these praises, rather than having soothed him with empty flattery, as will also be clear to anyone reading the context of the cited letter.

Finally, we attribute solely to partisan zeal the fact that, on p. 62 of his history, Walch calls Alcuin “a fickle and inconsistent man, saying now this and now that, and not knowing what is actually certain.” The occasion for writing this was Alcuin’s reply to arguments which the Spanish bishops who supported the doctrine of adoption in Christ had repeatedly drawn from their liturgies in favor of the doctrine in question. They appealed to the authority of Eugenius, Ildephonsus, and Julian, bishops of the see of Toledo, and said that the term “adoption” had long ago been used and, as it were, consecrated by these men.

Alcuin replied in this manner:

> “You also introduce the bishops of Spain, whom you call orthodox; in the prayers you have set forth they are unmistakably shown to be heretics. Unless, perhaps, you have corrupted their statements, as you were accustomed to do in other matters—namely, if you have dared to alter what they said correctly into support for your error, and to put one thing in place of another. For some of those fathers [or, perhaps, ‘parties’ should be read] assert that where you said ‘adoption’ or ‘adopted man,’ they said ‘assumption’ or ‘assumed man’; and in this too your malicious obstinacy is exposed. . . . But whether you have presented these same testimonies in altered form or exactly as they were spoken by them, it is not greatly important. For we desire that the truth of our assertion and faith be supported more by Roman than by Spanish authority; although we do not reject the latter either in matters that are stated in a Catholic manner.”

*Book VII against Felix*, no. 13.

Yet we plainly do not see what fickleness, ignorance, or inconsistency appears in this reply. We gather from this passage, and further from Alcuin’s letter to Elipandus, no. 11, that when he wrote these words he had not yet obtained or examined copies of the Spanish Liturgy. No one, however, could rightly reproach him for that.

Thus he answered quite properly: either those bishops whose testimonies Felix and Elipandus were attempting to use in support of their position had themselves been contaminated by the same heresy, unless—as he says in the letter mentioned above—“perhaps simple ignorance defended them from the sword of anathema, and not a stubborn defense of error struck them with the sword of excommunication”; or their writings had been corrupted by his opponent. This conjecture certainly does him no injury, since elsewhere he had repeatedly convicted both Felix and Elipandus of similar treachery in corrupting the texts of the ancient Fathers.

He judges the latter explanation more probable than the former, saying in Book II *against Elipandus*, no. 10:

> “It must therefore rather be judged that certain younger men, bound in the chains of this new infidelity, corrupt the sayings of the holy teachers to their own destruction and stain, through their most wicked obstinacy, the name of their forefathers. Nothing more criminal or atrocious than such audacity could exist. This appears likely to be true because we have recognized that you either interpret perversely the Catholic opinions of the most approved teachers in the Church of Christ, acceptable to everyone, or alter them through treacherous rashness—for example, as we have established in certain places, when several little letters concerning your error reached us through Felix, formerly your fellow-soldier and now ours.”

We think, however, that we should pass over these and the other sophistries which may be read against Alcuin in the frequently mentioned *History of the Adoptionists*. For, as we confidently believe, we have sufficiently and more than sufficiently removed the principal charges of criticism from this author, whom Walch himself does not deny to have flourished in his time with the highest distinction for every kind of learning and therefore to have been honored by Charlemagne with notable benefits. We have shown that he rightly accused the Spaniards of Nestorianism and argued against them by a legitimate method. He therefore deserves praise rather than blame, as an exceedingly keen and diligent defender of sound faith.

We should consequently judge it rashness, not prudence, if, after more than nine hundred years, certain individuals should dare to oppose, on the basis of a few monuments that have survived for us, the judgment of men whom we know to have been present at the controversy itself, to have frequently disputed face to face with their opponents, to have understood their minds either from their own mouths or at least from writings that were then still in everyone’s hands, and to have attacked their errors in such a way that no one of that age detected anything in this struggle deserving censure.

Or, if Felix and Elipandus truly believed that they had been slandered, why did they not complain of it? Why did they not expressly condemn Nestorius, when they had explicitly mentioned other heretics and anathematized their opinions? Why did they not charge their opponent Alcuin with an unsound method of argument or with incompetence, when elsewhere they were excessively eager to criticize his life? Therefore one must either say that what Walch wrote in defense of these bishops against Alcuin lacks foundation, or finally that there is no ancient heretic whose condemnation could not be attributed to the ignorance and imprudence of the Fathers.

Many of Walch’s party will perhaps readily grant the latter point, paying no attention to the fact that partisan zeal and preconceived opinions sometimes carry them so far that, in judging events and controversies of ancient times, they transgress even the rules of sounder criticism.

May heaven grant that these prejudices, so hostile to peace and truth, may at last be dispersed—and, something even more desirable, that an end may be put to the corrupted disposition of the human mind and to its unrestrained desire to investigate hidden matters lying beyond the powers of our understanding. For from this alone Walch judged that the controversy concerning Adoption in Christ had been revived in the eighth century.

This author rightly seemed to himself to have discovered an excellent remedy for such an evil in that wisdom-filled admonition which Charlemagne transcribed to the bishops of Spain, who were disputing so fiercely about the adopted Son; and we append it here as a concluding passage. We give it in full, because Walch deliberately omitted the earlier words in which Charlemagne commends to those bishops the authority of the Church and of the Catholic Fathers—undoubtedly because they were contrary to his system.

Thus the most Christian king speaks:

> “Again and again I appeal to you to remain firmly with us in peaceful unanimity and in the profession of the Catholic faith; and do not consider yourselves wiser than the universal holy Church of God. Hold fast the faith which the orthodox Fathers left written for us in their creeds. ‘Do not be wise beyond what is fitting, but be wise with sober judgment’ (Rom. 12:3); and do not imagine that by reasoning with human ingenuity you can investigate the divine mysteries. Rather, by believing, honor those things which human frailty cannot discover by rash scrutiny.”

*Letter of Charlemagne to Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain*, no. 15, *Patrologia*, vol. 98, col. 899.

[Note: In Frobenius’s edition, the second volume begins here. EDITOR.]

# BEATI FLACCI ALBINI SEU ALCUINI, CAROLI MAGNI MAGISTRI, OPERUM PARS QUARTA  
## THE FOURTH PART OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, TEACHER OF CHARLEMAGNE

### LITURGICAL AND MORAL WORKS

[Col. 0439]

## 1. Preliminary Notice

Our original intention was to attach these liturgical and moral booklets to the first volume of this collection of works. It became necessary, however, to change our plan when we observed that this volume had already grown so greatly in bulk that it could not be enlarged further without inconveniencing readers.

We therefore begin the second volume of this edition with those works that concern the liturgy, various formulas of prayer, and, finally, moral instruction. For blessed Alcuin did not devote his studies solely to knowledge of Sacred Scripture, to the explanation and defense of sacred doctrines, or to the secular sciences of the liberal arts. He also burned with great zeal and desire for the worship of God, for exercises of piety and devotion, and for the formation of excellent morals, so that, as teacher of an entire nation, he might form not merely learned but also pious and well-behaved men, and overcome all the barbarism that in his time occupied the hearts and minds of everyone.

The letters of this most religious and devout man are full of such instruction. In them he strives with the greatest zeal to teach the emperor himself, kings, queens, leading nobles, bishops, monks, and nuns, and to instill in them the worship of God, piety, faith, religion, and every virtue. It would be inappropriate to repeat those things here; they can easily be consulted in the letters themselves.

Only a few works of this kind, arranged according to a distinctive and doctrinal method, survive from blessed Alcuin. We present them here in such an order that the first place is given to those concerning the liturgy and the second to those that expound the doctrine of Christian morals.

We consider the following works to belong to the liturgy, or the order of divine worship: first, the *Book of Sacraments*; second, the *Book on the Use of the Psalms*; third, the *Offices for the Weekdays*; fourth, the *Letter to Oduin the Priest on the Ceremonies of Baptism*. We relegate another letter on a similar subject, together with the *Book on the Divine Office* and certain other fragments found under Alcuin’s name in a manuscript of the Vatican library, to the doubtful and spurious works, for the reasons to be given there.

Among the moral works we count: first, the *Book on Virtues and Vices for Count Wido*; second, the *Letter to the Boys of St. Martin on the Confession of Sins*; third, the *Letter to Eulalia on the Nature of the Soul*. Some homilies and moral exhortations would justly claim a place here if it were certain that they flowed from blessed Alcuin’s pen. Since this cannot by any means be proved, however, we judge that some must be wholly rejected and others inserted among the doubtful works.

Among the liturgical works, therefore, the first place belongs to the *Book of Sacraments*, which is composed of the Mass prayers distributed among the days of the week: collects, secrets, prefaces, and postcommunions, together with the beginnings of the appropriate Epistles and Gospels.

Blessed Alcuin himself speaks of this Sacramentary, or of one plainly similar to it, in Letter 51, to the monks of Vedast, and in Letter 142, to the monks of Fulda. In the former he writes as follows:

> “I have also taken certain Masses from our Missal for the daily and ecclesiastical offices: first, in honor of the Most Holy Trinity; then, for imploring the intercession of the saints and also seeking the assistance of the angels, which is greatly necessary for those laboring in this pilgrimage. Afterward we added a Mass of holy Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, to be sung on several days if anyone should wish it, and also we composed a Mass of St. Vedast . . . We have likewise added prayers for sins and for those who give alms.”

In the other letter, to the monks of Fulda, recently recovered from a manuscript of the Harley Library in England, he writes in a similar manner:

> “I have sent you a little Mass-book . . . so that you may have [it] for each day on which anyone may wish to direct prayers to God: sometimes in honor of the Holy Trinity, sometimes concerning the love of wisdom, sometimes concerning tears of repentance, sometimes concerning perfect charity, or sometimes when anyone wishes to seek the assistance of the angels or to petition any of the saints. Or if someone wishes to offer prayers for his sins, or for any living friend, or even for many friends, or for brethren departing from this world; or if someone especially wishes to implore the intercession of blessed Mary, the perpetual virgin and Mother of God; or if anyone wishes to sing in honor of your most holy father Boniface and call upon his most devout presence through prayers.”

The Masses of St. Vedast and St. Boniface are missing from our present booklet, having evidently been omitted by scribes who copied Alcuin’s Sacramentary for the use of other churches whose patrons were different. The prayers for those who give alms are also absent, although blessed Alcuin mentions them in his letter to the monks of Vedast.

Conversely, this Book of Sacraments contains other Masses and prayers of which blessed Alcuin makes no mention in the letters cited above: a Mass for asking the grace of the Holy Spirit; a Mass for temptations of thought; a Mass for asking humility; a Mass against temptations of the flesh; a Mass of the Holy Cross; another concerning tribulation and necessity; Masses in honor of the holy apostles, martyrs, and saints who rest in the church or whose relics are deposited there; a Mass for enemies; a Mass for one confessing his sins; and finally blessings, which are added here together with various other prayers.

It may be gathered from the words of the letter to the monks of Vedast that blessed Alcuin did not compose these Masses anew, but took them from the Missal of his monastery—of Tours, I believe—and distributed them among the individual days of the week. It is not so certain, however, that he arranged them in the order in which they now appear in our Sacramentary.

The author of the *Micrologus*, in his *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 60, describes a copy of this Alcuinian Sacramentary that differs from ours both in number and in order. He speaks as follows:

> “It should be known that a certain master Alboin, teacher of the Emperor Charles, is said to have composed, at the request of Archbishop Boniface, Mass prayers of the Holy Trinity; for Monday, of wisdom; for Tuesday, of the Holy Spirit; for Wednesday, of charity; for Thursday, of the angels; for Friday, of the cross; and for Saturday, of holy Mary.”

I suspect that this book was altered and enlarged in various ways by different people after blessed Alcuin’s lifetime. Certainly the Masses placed under the name of St. Augustine for each day were added through the industry of someone else and were undoubtedly falsely attributed to that holy Father. Even highly distinguished scholars have suffered ordinary human error in this matter: namely, the author of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. 4, p. 314, no. 18, and D. Ceillier, *History of the Sacred Authors*, vol. 18, p. 313, who assert that those Masses were composed by blessed Alcuin in honor of St. Augustine. Neither the text of those prayers nor their title supports that assertion.

The author of the *Micrologus*, cited above and much later than Alcuin, departed still further from the truth when he wrote in the same place that blessed Alcuin composed that book “at the request of St. Boniface, archbishop”—that is, of Mainz—“so that, as he says, the priests of that time, newly converted to the faith, not yet instructed in ecclesiastical offices and not yet provided with a sufficient supply of books, might at least have something with which they could perform their office on any day.”

No learned person is unaware of how far this is from the truth. Nowhere do we read that blessed Alcuin ever had any association with St. Boniface. Moreover, in the year 754, when that holy archbishop received the crown of martyrdom, Alcuin had not yet attained such age or prominence of name that the apostolic man could either have entrusted or wished to entrust such a commission to him.

The letter to the monks of Fulda quoted shortly before makes clear that Alcuin composed a Mass in honor of St. Boniface, but not at his request. The aforementioned author of the *Micrologus*, having drawn this error from the report of others, compounds it by adding the reason for the composition:

> “So that, as he says, the priests of that time”—that is, the time when St. Boniface labored in his apostolic office—“newly converted to the faith, etc., might at least have something with which they could perform their office on any day.”

Blessed Alcuin did not collect this Book of Sacraments for such public use or for the convenience of newly converted priests, but for the private use and devotion of priests, monks, and churches that were no longer novices in ecclesiastical matters.

The same writer later, again relying on the report of others, attributes another work of no little importance in the Holy Church to Albinus:

> “For he is said to have collected Gregorian prayers in the Book of Sacraments, inserting a few others, which he nevertheless indicated should be marked with an obelus. Then he collected other prayers or prefaces which, although not Gregorian, were nevertheless suitable for ecclesiastical celebration, as the prologue testifies—a prologue that he placed in the middle of the same book after the Gregorian prayers.”

“These words,” says Hugo Menardus in the preface to the *Book of Sacraments of St. Gregory*, vol. 3 of this saintly pontiff’s works, p. 12 [*Patrologia*, vol. 78, col. 24], “indicate that Albinus wrote a Book of Sacraments similar to the codices of Rodradus and Grimoldus.” In those books, plainly, there is a similar preface placed between the Gregorian prayers and those added by others.

Nor, says the aforementioned Menardus, can it be a scribal error, as Pamelius maintains, that “Albinus” was written in place of “Grimoldus,” and so forth, in the same passage.

In the library of the monastery of Centula there existed in the year 831 a book bearing this title: *Gregorian and Gelasian Missal, arranged by Albinus in modern times*. D. d’Achery wished to publish this book [Note: See *Spicilegium* of D. Luc d’Achery, vol. 2, p. 311, Paris edition of 1723, or vol. 13 of the first old edition, p. 13]. Later he shared it with D. de Voisin, who wished to enrich his treatise on the Mass from it. Since that time, its whereabouts have again become unknown, as the author of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. 4, p. 338, no. 6, reports.

The *Book of Sacraments* that we have caused to be printed here from Quercetanus’s edition first appeared through the care of Jacobus Pamelius among the liturgical works he collected, at Cologne in the years 1561, 1571, and 1609, vol. 2. We were unable to consult that edition, which is exceedingly rare among us and found nowhere else.

We assign the second place among blessed Alcuin’s liturgical booklets to the *Book on the Use of the Psalms*. D. Quercetanus had it reprinted on p. 123 according to what he calls the Douai edition of 1571, which we have not seen. We did, however, have at hand another edition of the same year, prepared at Cologne by Adrian Aerntspergius and granted for our use, from the extremely well-stocked electoral library of Munich, through the kindness of the distinguished man and most learned scholar D. Felix Oefelius.

Its title is: *Alcuin on the Use of the Psalms Adapted to the Daily Arising Needs of Human Beings, Together with Various Forms of Prayer; Newly Published by Adrian Aerntspergius*. The booklet is dedicated to the honor of the most illustrious prince, D. Georg, Baron of Graveneck and abbot of the imperial monastery of Kempten. In commendation of this little book and in praise of blessed Alcuin, the editor prefaces it as follows:

> “That this Alcuin is indeed the same man”—namely, the teacher of Charlemagne in the liberal arts, and therefore a founder of public schools and religious houses because of his exceptional devotion both to the arts and to virtue—“and not some spurious other, can easily be recognized from this little book, just as a lion is recognized from its claws: everywhere it breathes a simple purity joined with sincere piety and plainly reveals the character of the man. For it is everywhere devout, everywhere learned, concise, mature, serious, and more than any other worthy always to be carried in the hands, so that the vanity of worldly things may be brought to light and the hearts of mortals may be inflamed more ardently from unstable cares toward heavenly love.”

Aerntspergius then recounts the difficulties that had to be endured in bringing this little book to light and correcting it, because of the poor condition of the manuscript he used, the obscurity of its characters, and their joining and separation.

To the corruption of this manuscript must undoubtedly also be attributed the fact that certain formulas of prayer were placed outside their proper order and that, since they belonged to the first part according to the author’s arrangement, they were subsequently cast into the second through the scribe’s carelessness. The editor himself, or perhaps the scribe of the manuscript, noticed this when he attempted to indicate the order with numerals, though in a very obscure fashion, and when he again suggested, with considerable confusion, where the first part ought to end.

For this reason we believed that we had been left free to restore everything to its proper order as far as seemed possible. We therefore removed from the second part of the earlier edition the formulas that genuinely instruct concerning the use of the psalms in various circumstances and restored them to the first part. We began the second part with the prayer for singing psalms on one’s own behalf. Learned men will not disapprove of this.

We believe that the manuscript’s corruption, or some other error, also caused the preface to be placed before this booklet, although the text itself suggests that it belongs rather to the other work entitled *Offices for the Weekdays*. For that other booklet contains the psalms whose use for various necessities the author prescribes in this Prologue. Thus the title *On the Use of the Psalms* seems more appropriate to the later booklet than to the earlier one. Nevertheless, lacking the support of manuscript copies, we judged that its title should not be changed.

A poem of two verses is placed before the preface, in which Alcuin indicates that he dedicated this work to the honor of his lord—surely Charlemagne? Later, however, different scribes added other prayers according to their individual devotion, or especially for the use of monks, such as appear in this edition.

For this reason the learned author of the *Literary History of France* (vol. 4, p. 304) judged that this booklet had not been written for the use of one particular person but for the common benefit. D. Cave, however, in the latest edition of his *Literary History*, vol. 1, p. 638, reports that the book was written to Fredegisus, a disciple. No trace of this appears in the book, and therefore it is unknown from where Cave learned it.

We assign the third place among the liturgical works to the booklet entitled by D. Quercetanus *Offices for the Weekdays*. That editor first brought it to light from a manuscript belonging to the most illustrious man D. Jacques-Auguste de Thou, counselor in the king’s supreme court. In that manuscript the work is undoubtedly attributed to our Alcuin, and the common voice and judgment of scholars likewise truly assign it to him.

Unless we are greatly mistaken, this is the booklet which the author of Alcuin’s *Life* says was written by Alcuin for Charlemagne’s use under the title *On the Method of Prayer*. He speaks in these words:

> “He taught him”—Charles—“throughout the whole course of his life which psalms of repentance he should sing with the litany, prayers, and petitions; which he should use for making special prayer; which in praise of God; which for every kind of tribulation; and which he should sing in order to exercise himself in divine praises. Whoever wishes to know this should read his booklet *On the Method of Prayer*.”

All these matters are found in our booklet.

The Englishman John Bale likewise lists among Alcuin’s writings: “One book for Charles’s prayer”—which I think should be read as “to Charles, on Prayer.” He reports that it begins: “Our Lord and teacher.” That beginning is now lost; perhaps it could have been supplied from the deficiencies of the Thuan manuscript, as Quercetanus noted.

A manuscript booklet of this kind, on the various times of daily prayers, exists under the name of Master Albinus in the Royal Library of Paris, no. 2731, letter A. It differs considerably from ours and begins as follows: “In the name of the Most High God begins the writing of Master Albinus to the emperor Charles. Blessed David, etc.”

I owe knowledge of this work to the most learned and devout D. Lieble, librarian of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, who kindly arranged to send us this preface to Charles together with certain variant readings. We have inserted all these materials in their proper places.

This booklet was later cast into various forms for the use and benefit of the kings and emperors who succeeded Charles. An example of this exists in the celebrated electoral library of Munich, where a prayer-book for the use of the young Charles the Bald is preserved. It was first written in letters of gold and then printed at Ingolstadt in Bavaria in 1583, under the care of F. Felicianus, bishop of Scala, and dedicated to the honor of the most serene prince Maximilian, the firstborn son of the most serene D. William. This extremely rare edition is in our hands [Note: On this booklet, see Mabillon, *Annals*, Book 34, no. 97; Baluzius, *Capitularies*, vol. 2, p. 1276 and pp. 1486–1488; *Literary History of France*, vol. 5, p. 514].

The prologue of this booklet is identical with Alcuin’s, transcribed from the aforementioned royal manuscript in Paris, although it is incomplete at the end. The psalms and prayers for various necessities are arranged there not according to the weekdays but according to occasion or devotion. The prayers and confessions composed by Alcuin himself are presented under his name, as we have noted in their proper places.

Finally, in the fourth place we present the *Letter to Oduin the Priest on the Ceremonies of Baptism*. The most learned author of the *Literary History of France*, vol. 4, p. 313, no. 16, preferred to place this letter among the other letters of blessed Alcuin.

Since it expressly instructs a novice priest concerning the administration of baptism and describes only the rites to be employed in it, it may rightly also be counted among the liturgical works. The author of a brief treatise *On Baptism*, published by D. Martene in *On the Rites of the Church*, vol. 1, pp. 161–162, used this letter. It is also found in the uncertain *Book on Divine Offices*, attributed to Alcuin, chapter 19.

We have collated it with several manuscripts of excellent quality and have recorded the variant readings.

We append the moral works to the liturgical booklets because they are few and do not equal the size of a separate section. Other writings of blessed Alcuin, especially his letters, are full—as we have said—of teachings concerning good and Christian conduct, but those teachings are inserted only incidentally. The works we present now, however, are arranged so that the first booklet is a complete treatise on virtues and vices, while the two letters deliberately provide instruction: one on making confession of sins, the other on the necessity of loving God, demonstrated from the very nature of the soul, as well as on controlling the passions and pursuing true wisdom.

Although certain learned men may perhaps judge that these letters could more suitably have been placed among the others, they will nevertheless readily grant that they occupy an appropriate place here, especially since the distinguished Quercetanus himself removed them from the number of the remaining letters.

We therefore assign the first place among the moral works to the *Book on Virtues and Vices for Count Wido*. This is undoubtedly the count “who,” as the Loiselian Annals report under the year 799, “was in charge of the March of Brittany”—the cismarine Brittany, in which the city and monastery of Tours are situated—“and entered Brittany together with his fellow counts, traversed the whole region, and received it into submission.”

Unless we are greatly mistaken, this is the same man to whose testimony, as “a perfect man, an incorruptible judge, and a faithful envoy,” Alcuin appeals in Letter 166 in the dispute between the bishop of Orléans and the monks of Tours.

Wido had asked Alcuin to gather into a brief booklet teachings suited to Christian life and to his own condition and station, so that amid secular affairs he might have a handbook by which he could constantly examine his actions and stir himself to pursue eternal blessedness, as Alcuin says in the dedicatory letter to the same count.

As far as we have been able to determine, this treatise first appeared in the appendix to the Bignaean edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, although it was greatly defective at the end. Canisius later supplied the missing portion from a manuscript of St. Gall in volume 6 of the *Ancient Readings*.

Quercetanus, however, restored, corrected, and enlarged the same treatise, previously divided into two parts, with the aid of a manuscript belonging to the distinguished man Jacques-Auguste de Thou.

Yet Quercetanus’s distinguished edition is not so complete and free from corruption that a better reading could not be restored in some places—or indeed in many places—that variant readings could not be noted, and that some errors could not be filled out. We have done this here with the aid of several manuscripts of great antiquity and excellent quality. The principal ones are two belonging to our library of St. Emmeram and one belonging to the renowned monastery of St. James of the Scots in our city of Regensburg. The last supplied certain unusual supplements, as we note in their proper places.

This book was also held in such high esteem by ecclesiastical men that many moral sermons were drawn from it. Later, because some did not know the true author—perhaps designated only by the initial letter A, a practice not uncommon among medieval scribes—these sermons were attributed to St. Augustine because of their excellence. The most recent editors of St. Augustine’s works relegated them to the appendix and restored them to Alcuin. We identify them in their respective chapters.

This treatise is followed by the *Letter to Eulalia the Virgin on the Nature of the Soul*. We discovered who this virgin was from Letter 125, recently recovered from the Harley Library. Her true name was Gundrada, the sister of St. Adalhard, abbot of Corbie; Eulalia was her cognomen, as we have already noted in connection with this letter.

The author of Alcuin’s *Life* also calls Gundrada a virgin, to whom Alcuin wrote this letter:

> “He wrote to Gundrada on the nature of the soul.”

Quercetanus transcribed this letter from the Cologne edition of 1598. We have corrected it from manuscripts and, from one belonging to the library of the celebrated monastery of Tegernsee, have added the poem *What the Palms Customarily Carried in the Hands Signify Mystically*, which appears to us to have been written to the same virgin.

Some material from this letter was incorporated into the treatise *On the Spirit and the Soul*, at one time attributed to St. Augustine in the appendix to his works.

Finally, this section is closed by the Letter to the boys of Saint Martin on the confession of sins, in which he teaches the usefulness and necessity of doing penance and confessing one’s sins to priests. He later also sent this letter to the people of Salzburg at the request and insistence of Arno; see Letters 152 and 153. On the necessity of confession, read much more in Letter 134, to the brothers in the province of the Goths. He prescribes formulas of confession below in the little book *On the Use of the Psalms*, no. 9. From this we learn, against our modern innovators, the antiquity of the law and practice of auricular confession and its constant observance in the Church. See Mabillon, preface to Part I of the third century of the Benedictines, p. 9. Canisius was the first to extract this letter from a manuscript of Saint Gall and publish it, vol. VI, pp. 323–328, from which Quercetanus copied it. Here, with the aid of several manuscript codices, we supply certain deficiencies and add variant readings.

[Col. 0445]

## 6. FIRST OPUSCULUM. BOOK OF SACRAMENTS

### CHAPTER I. Sunday: Mass of the Holy Trinity [Saint Gregory, on the Octave of Pentecost]

[Col. 0445B]
