Grant that we may be preserved through your protection as the kinds of people you, most high Creator, granted us to become through the water of regeneration.

Since we began to belong to you, let us know no other God. We have been redeemed by your grace; with your gift, let us perform your commandments. If you abandon us, the deceiver attacks. Tireless and shameless, he is always present, counting his gains [Col. 0612B] in human ruin. He flatters in order to deceive; he incites in order to destroy. Above all, he deceives souls through our body, and so diffuses himself through human desires, which are so unstable, that he is scarcely perceived by any foresight or prior deliberation.

It would take too long to go through each matter. Who could resist such an enemy, unless you, Lord, have determined to oppose him? For what could he do to us, when he dared to tempt you in our body through deceitful machinations? Hear us, O guardian of humankind. Here, by your forgiveness, free us from him who strives to drag us to Gehenna. Let us not share his lot, so that we may share yours, Lord. Vindicate your creation from him who destroys it. May he rule over others, if he does so [F., “if he does so”], he who condemned himself; but rather let him perish with his own, who hastens to destroy everything [Col. 0612C] . . . . . The remainder is lacking.

## Prayer of Lord Alcuin at Night [Note: [Col. 0611C] This poem exists under Alcuin’s name in the Book of Prayers of Charles the Bald, written in a manuscript in golden letters and once richly ornamented, preserved in the Electoral Library at Munich. It was printed by F. Felician, Bishop of Scaldis, at Ingolstadt in 1583, in octavo.]

He who was taking sleep in a tranquil heart in the calm vessel,

rising, commands the winds and the sea.

Although here my weary limbs rest

after heavy labor,

may my watchful heart yield itself to you.

Lamb of God, who took away

all the sins of the world,

kindly preserve my rest

from the enemy.

[Col. 0611]

## 127. FOURTH OPUSCULUM. ALcuin’s Letter to Oduinus the Presbyter on the Ceremonies of Baptism (G)*

[Col. 0611D] Albinus the teacher sends greetings to his dearest son, Oduinus [Ms. Einsidl., Oduuino; Ms. Reg. Paris., Adoino], the presbyter.

Because, by the gift of divine grace and through prolonged labor, I have brought you to the point that you are considered worthy of priestly honor [Ms. Einsidl., “of priestly honor”]—and would that you might administer that office in the house of God as elegantly as I have carefully instructed you through God’s gift—I wished to write to you briefly, so that you may learn the rational order of sacred baptism, concerning the ministries [Ms. Einsidl., mysteries] of the entire rite, and may understand how necessary it is to omit nothing in that office that has been taken from the holy Fathers [Mss., “laid down”; Al., “established”].

[Col. 0613A] [Note: [Col. 0613] See, among the spurious works, the book On Divine Offices, chapter 19, and letter 90.]

First the pagan becomes a catechumen; approaching baptism, he renounces the evil spirit and all his harmful works and [Al. omits “and”] spectacles. He is also breathed upon, so that, once the devil has been driven away, an entrance may be prepared for Christ the Lord [Al., God]. He is exorcised—that is, the evil spirit is adjured—to depart and withdraw, giving place to the true God. He receives the salt of the catechumens [Ms. Fris., “the catechumen”], so that his rotten and fleeting sins may be cleansed by the salt of wisdom, through the divine gift.

Then the faith of the Apostles’ Creed is handed over to him, so that the empty house, abandoned by its former inhabitant, may be adorned with faith, and so that a dwelling place may be prepared for God [Ms. Reg., “of God”]. Then scrutinies are conducted, so that it may be examined whether, after renouncing Satan, the servant has firmly fixed the sacred words of the faith that was given in his heart [Mss., “whether he is examined more often than firmly”].

His nostrils are also touched, so that, as long as he draws breath through his nostrils, he may remain steadfast in the faith he has received. His breast is likewise anointed with oil [Ms. Fris., “on him”], so that access to him may be closed to the devil by the sign of the holy cross. His shoulders are also signed, so that he may be fortified on every side. Likewise, in the anointing of the breast and shoulders, the firmness of faith and perseverance in good works are signified.

And thus he is baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity by a threefold immersion [Col. 0614A]. Rightly so: a human being, created in the image of the Holy Trinity, is renewed to that same image through invocation of the Holy Trinity. And because he fell into death through the third stage of sin—that is, consent—so may he, raised three times from the font, rise through grace to life [Ms. Reg., “will rise”].

Then he is clothed in white garments, on account of the joy of regeneration, the purity of life, and the beauty of angelic splendor. Then his head is anointed [Ms., “thoroughly anointed”] with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he will bear the diadem of the dignity of kingship and priesthood, according to the Apostle: “You are a royal and priestly race, offering yourselves to the Lord as a holy and pleasing sacrifice” [Ms., “to the living God”] (I Peter II, 9; Romans XII, 1).

Thus he is confirmed with the Lord’s body and blood, so that he may be a member of that head who suffered and rose again for him [Al., “for us”]. Finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief Priest, he receives the Spirit of sevenfold grace, so that he may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others—he who in baptism was given the grace of eternal life [Al., “life . . . eternal”].

[Col. 0613]

## 128. [Note: [Col. 0613D] See what we prefaced about this opusculum in the Preliminary Notice. The material presented here in brackets [Col. 0614D] has been drawn from various manuscript codices.] FIFTH OPUSCULUM. BOOK ON VIRTUES AND VICES, TO COUNT WIDO

### Dedication Letter

[Col. 0613C]

The humble levite Alcuin sends greetings to his most beloved son, Count Wido [Al., Huito].

I remember your request and my promise, by which you earnestly begged me to compose in a brief discourse some exhortations for your occupation—which, as we know, you have in military affairs—so that you might always have at hand sentences of paternal admonition [Al., “in your hands”], in which you ought to consider yourself and be stirred to pursue eternal blessedness. I gladly confess that I have assented to this honorable request, hoping that the lines of my devotion may contribute to your perpetual salvation.

Although you may see them composed with less eloquence [Col. 0613D] [Al., “although they may seem to be composed”], nevertheless know with complete certainty that they have been dictated by the power of holy charity. I have divided the sequence of this discourse into individual chapters, so that these words of mine might more easily remain in the memory of your devotion [Al., “your devotion”], knowing that you are occupied with many thoughts of worldly affairs.

Therefore I ask the holy desire for your salvation to return often, as to a kind of consolation, to the reading of these [Col. 0614C] writings, so that your mind, wearied by external troubles, may return to itself and have something in which to rejoice, and may understand toward what it ought especially to hasten.

Just as you diligently requested from me these little letters of pious exhortation [Al., “just as I requested these from myself”], so I humbly ask you to deign to reread them often. For this reason, dearest son, I earnestly beseech your love to strive with tireless will to prepare for yourself a dwelling in heavenly glory through abundant generosity in almsgiving, through the equity of judges and judgments, and through constant mercy [Al., “the best almsgiving for yourself”]. In this work and desire may divine clemency always deign to assist you everywhere [dearest son].

## 129. CHAPTER ONE [Note: [Col. 0614D] This chapter is part of Sermon 303 of Saint Augustine.] On Wisdom

[Col. 0614D]

Above all, a human being must seek what true knowledge and true wisdom are, because the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God (I Corinthians III, 19). True knowledge is to withdraw from the service of the devil, which consists in sins; and perfect wisdom is to worship God according to the truth of his commandments. For blessed life is acquired in these two things, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm XXXIII, 15).

It is not enough for anyone not to do evil unless he also does good; nor is it enough to do good unless he also refrains from committing evil [Al., “unless he also abandons evil]. Therefore everyone who is wise in this way will undoubtedly be blessed forever. For the knowledge of divinity is blessed [life]; and the knowledge of divinity is the virtue of good action; the virtue of good action is the fruit of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Faith

But this knowledge of divinity and knowledge of truth must be learned through the Catholic faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews XI, 6). Truly blessed is the one who both lives well by believing rightly and, by living well, preserves right faith.

Therefore, just as faith is useless without [good] works, so good works accomplish nothing without right faith. Hence blessed James the Apostle also said: “What good will it do, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works [Mss., ‘if he has’]? Can faith save him? Faith without works is dead [Mss., ‘useless’]. For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James II, 14 ff.).

To discuss its excellence belongs to another time, because the brief summary that you requested me to compose for you in a concise discourse concerning the commandments of God [Note: [Col. 0615D] Ms. of St. James of the Scots: “Since the summary that we have resolved to write concerning the commandments of God will not be able to explain the deepest reasons of the Catholic faith, etc.”] will not be able to explain the deepest reasons of the Catholic faith [Edit., “discourses,” erroneously].

## CHAPTER THREE. On Charity

[Col. 0615C]

Among the commandments of God, charity holds the chief place. The Apostle Paul testifies that without its perfection nothing can please God (I Corinthians XIII); he shows that neither martyrdom, nor contempt of the world, nor generosity in almsgiving can accomplish anything without the duty of charity [Al., “be of any benefit”].

Therefore, when a certain scribe asked the Lord what the greatest commandment was, he replied: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” He added: “And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself; on these two commandments depend the whole Law and [Col. 0615D] the Prophets” (Matthew XXII, 36 ff.).

When he says “with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind,” this means that God is to be loved with the whole understanding, the whole will, and the whole memory. The love of God consists entirely in the observance of his commandments, as he says elsewhere: “If anyone loves me, he keeps my words” (John XIV, 23).

Hence Truth itself says elsewhere: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid., XIII, 35). The Apostle likewise says: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans XIII, 10). The evangelist John likewise says: “We have this commandment from the Lord [Al., God]: whoever loves the Lord [Al., God] must also love his neighbor” (I John IV, 21).

If anyone should ask who one’s neighbor is, let him know that every Christian is rightly called a neighbor, because in baptism we are all sanctified as children of God, so that spiritually we may be brothers in perfect charity. Spiritual generation is nobler than bodily generation. Concerning it Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again [Al., ‘born’] of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5).

Let a person learn what God’s commandments are and keep them as far as he is able; and in this way let him know that he possesses the love of God. I will take care to set some of them out by name for your devotion, dearest son, so that, once a few have been understood [Al., “examined”], you may more easily be able to understand the virtues of the others [Note: [Col. 0615D] In the manuscript of St. James, the final sentence is expressed as follows: [Col. 0616D] “It is worthy briefly to demonstrate some of them, so that the other virtues may more easily be understood.”]

## 130. CHAPTER FOUR. On Hope

[Col. 0616B]

The distinguished teacher of the nations set before our soul three necessary things, saying: “Hope, faith, charity—these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (I Corinthians XIII, 13).

Therefore no one, even if he is weighed down by an immense burden of sins, ought to despair of the goodness of divine mercy; rather, with hope in his certain mercy [Ms., “certain”], let him beg forgiveness for himself with daily tears. They can rightly hope for it if they cease from evil action.

Therefore we must neither sin persistently because of hope for pardon, nor despair of pardon because God justly punishes sins; but, avoiding both dangers, let us turn away from evil and hope for pardon from God’s mercy.

Likewise, in every distress of tribulation, we must run through hope for the consolation of heavenly mercy, because in God alone all hope and salvation unquestionably consist, as the Prophet says: “In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God” (Psalm LXI, 8).

## CHAPTER FIVE [Note: [Col. 0616D] This chapter 5 is part of Sermon 302 of Saint Augustine.] On Devotion to Reading

The reading of the Holy Scriptures is knowledge of divine blessedness. In them, as in a certain mirror, a person can contemplate himself: what he is and toward what he is tending. Constant reading purifies the soul, instills fear of Gehenna, and stirs the heart of the reader toward heavenly joys [Col. 0616D].

Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray [frequently] and to read. For when we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us. The reading of the Holy Scriptures confers a twofold gift: both because it trains the understanding of the mind and because, drawing a person away from worldly vanities, it leads him to the love of God.

The labor of reading [study] is honorable and contributes greatly to the cleansing of the soul. For just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine utterances, as the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat [Col. 0617A], Lord! They are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm CXVIII, 103).

But the one who, while reading the divine Scriptures, turns words into deeds is supremely blessed. Clearly, all Holy Scripture was written for our salvation, so that we may advance through it in the knowledge of truth. A blind person stumbles more often than one who sees; likewise, one who is ignorant of God’s law sins in ignorance more often than one who knows it. Just as a blind person without a guide, so a human being without a teacher scarcely walks along the right path.

## CHAPTER SIX. On Peace

When the Savior was returning to the Father, he gave the disciples the commandments of peace as a special gift, saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV, 27). “In peace I leave you; in peace I shall find you.” As he departed, he wished to give what he desired to find in all when he returned.

Elsewhere he wonderfully displayed the adornments of this peace, saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V, 9). Behold, the Son of God begins to be called the one who has already begun to be a peacemaker. He does not wish to be called a son of God who refuses to embrace peace. He denies God as his Father who scorns being a peacemaker.

But this peace is to be maintained with the good and with those who keep God’s commandments, not with the wicked and criminal, who have peace among themselves in their sins. Christ’s peace advances toward eternal salvation. The peace that exists in the devil reaches [Al., “leads to”] everlasting destruction. There must always be peace with the good and war against vices.

The evils of impious people are to be hated [Col. 0617C], not the people themselves, although they are evil, because they are God’s creatures. The peace that exists in us [Al., “in the good”] joins together the harmony of brothers and the charity of neighbors. Peace especially merits the Spirit of God. Peace is the mother of love. Peace is a sign of holiness, concerning which God says through the prophet: “Love peace and truth” (Zechariah VIII, 19).

Peace is the health of the people, the glory of the priest, the joy of the homeland, and the terror of enemies, whether visible or invisible. [131] Peace must be guarded with all one’s strength, because it always remains in God.

Whoever remains in holy peace remains with God’s saints. It is the priest’s responsibility, in peace, to admonish God’s people concerning what they ought to do; it is the people’s responsibility to listen humbly to what the priest teaches. Whatever is not permitted, it is the shepherd’s responsibility to forbid, so that it may not be done; it is the people’s responsibility to listen, so that they may not do it.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] This chapter 7 is part of Sermon 304 of Saint Augustine.] ## CHAPTER SEVEN. On Mercy

[Col. 0617D]

## Sedulius hymn: retained textual apparatus and source boundaries

The following printed forms are retained with their English distinctions: *quos* (“those whom”) / Al. *quod* (“what”); *clausae* (“closed,” feminine plural) / Al. *clausa* (“closed,” neuter singular); *Enixa est puerpera* (“the mother has given birth”) / Al. *Enixa jam puerpera est* (“the mother has now given birth”); *non eripit* (“does not take away”) / Al. *non abripit* (“does not snatch away”); *munere* (“by a gift”) / Al. *lumine* (“by light”); *aqua* (“water”) / Al. *aquae* (“waters”); *ambul at* (“walks”) / Al. *ambulans* (“walking”); *levatus* (“lifted”) / Al. *levatur* (“is lifted”); *Conjunctus est* (“was joined”) / Al. *conjungitur* (“is joined”); *Xyro* / Al. *Xero*, perhaps *Xro* (“Christ”); and *compares* (“female companions”) / Al. *corpori* (“to the body”).

Printed boundaries retained for the hymn: [Col. 0609C] [Col. 0610A] [Col. 0610B] [Col. 0610C] [Col. 0610D] [Col. 0611A] [Col. 0611B].

The chief good is mercy, concerning which the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). A sinner cannot hope for mercy from God if he does not show mercy to those who sin against him. Therefore, let a person forgive a temporal debt, so that he may deserve to receive an eternal good. If we desire our souls to be cleansed from the filth of sins, let us not deny mercy to those who sin against us, so that on the day of recompense we may be helped by works of mercy to obtain God’s mercy. How does one who is cruel toward his fellow servants expect mercy from God [Ms., “hope for mercy”]? Just as someone desires God to have mercy on him, so also let him have mercy on his debtors. He may most certainly expect forgiveness [Ms., “hope for forgiveness”] who knows how to forgive others.

The Lord strengthened us toward the work of mercy by an excellent example in the Gospel, where he says: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Luke 6:36). Every act of mercy will make room for each person according to the merit of his works. Whoever shows mercy offers God a propitiatory sacrifice of salvation [Ms., “sufficiently pleasing”]. In a judge there ought to be both mercy and discipline, because one cannot properly exist without the other [Ms., “will not be able to exist”]. For if there is mercy alone, it gives those subject to judgment license to sin. Again, if discipline alone is always present, the mind of the offender is turned toward despair, and the judge will not deserve mercy from God. But a person ought to begin this mercy with himself. How can someone be merciful toward others who is cruel toward himself? He is cruel toward himself who prepares eternal flames for himself through his sins. He is truly merciful who begins with himself and carefully guards himself, lest he be punished with the devil, and thus gives others what he recognizes to be good for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0618D] This chapter 8 is the second part of Sermon 304 of St. Augustine.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Forgiveness

[Col. 0618C]

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” Likewise: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14–15). This saying of the Lord expresses great mercy [Ms., “clemency”] toward those who are able to understand it rightly. Therefore God judges us according to our own judgment, and in a certain sense it lies within our power how we shall be judged by God the Judge. If we judge mercifully those who sin against us, God will judge mercifully those who sin against him. Let us heed the example of that one, as the Teacher of the Gentiles says: “Forgive one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as God forgives you in Christ [Ms., forgave you], so also do you” (Col. 3:13).

Just as God forgave us our sins in Christ, so let us also forgive those who sin against us. Likewise: “Returning evil for evil to no one.” And elsewhere: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12:17, 21). We must know with absolute certainty that each person will receive from God the kind of forgiveness that he himself has given to his neighbor. That prayer for our sins will quickly reach the ears of almighty God if the prayers of those who have sinned against us are acceptable in our ears. Whoever knows how to pardon sinners mercifully will most certainly receive the merciful kindness of divine compassion. [Col. 0619A] For we shall be forgiven in the same way as we have forgiven those who have harmed us by any sort of wickedness.

## CHAPTER IX. On Patience

“In your patience,” it is said in the Gospel, “you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). For patience is necessary throughout every human life. Just as we must patiently endure injuries inflicted upon us by others, so it is also necessary patiently to endure the tribulations that come upon us. Very often in this world the good suffer tribulations from the reprobate. Therefore, if someone suffers tribulations after good works, he ought not say in his thoughts: “I have lost the good works I was doing.” For whoever says this is shown to have done a good work not out of love for God, [Col. 0619B] but for the reward of the happiness of this life or for human praise.

A person will be tested by God’s scourges, to determine with what intention he does good or with what strength he endures the temptations that come upon him. “God is testing you,” the Apostle says, “to discover whether you love him.” Indeed, tribulation produces patience, while patience is a perfected work. “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him” (James 1:3–4). No one is truly wise who does not have patience. “He who rules (dominator; Ms., domitor, ‘tamer’) his spirit is stronger than he who captures cities” (Prov. 16:32).

In patience one must seek the ability to forgive, not the opportunity for revenge. There are some who endure injuries patiently at the time they occur so that afterward they may more easily take revenge. These do not possess true patience. True patience is courageously enduring injuries face-to-face and not seeking vengeance in the future, but forgiving from the heart. Without sword or flames we can be martyrs if we truly preserve patience in our hearts toward our neighbors. It is more praiseworthy to avoid an injury by remaining silent than to overcome it by answering back. Whoever patiently endures evils will deserve an everlasting crown in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] This chapter 10 is part of Sermon 297 of St. Augustine.]

## CHAPTER X. On Humility

The greatness of the virtue of true humility is easily recognized from the words of the Lord, who, in condemning the pride of the Pharisees, said: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 23:12). [Col. 0619D] By the steps of humility one ascends to the heights of heaven, because the exalted God is reached not through pride but through humility. Concerning this it is said: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Hence it is also said in the Psalms: “The Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble, but he knows the proud from afar” (Ps. 137:6). He used “the exalted” for the proud, and “the humble” for the humble [Al., for the gentle]. He regards the humble in order to raise them up; he knows the exalted—that is, the proud—in order to cast them down.

Let us therefore learn humility, through which we shall be able to draw near to God, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). Through pride the wondrous creature of the angels fell from heaven; through humility [of God], the frailty of human nature ascended to heaven.

The practice of humility is honorable among human beings, as Solomon says: “Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace; but where there is humility, there is wisdom” (Prov. 11:2). Another Wise Man likewise says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Sir. 3:20). The Lord also says through the prophet: “To whom shall I look, except to the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Whoever is not humble and quiet cannot have the grace of the Holy Spirit dwelling in him.

God became humble for the sake of our salvation, so that the proud person might be ashamed to be proud. To the degree that the heart is bent downward through humility, to that degree it advances upward. For whoever is humble [Col. 0620B] will be exalted in glory [Al., whoever is humble here on earth . . . in future glory]. The first step of humility is to hear the word of truth humbly, retain it faithfully, and willingly carry it out. For [truth] flees the mind in which it does not find humility. The humbler a person is regarding himself, the greater he will be in the sight of God. But the prouder he appears among human beings, the more cast down he will be before God.

For whoever performs good works without humility carries dust into the wind. Why does earth and ashes boast, while what it seems to gather through fasts and almsgiving is scattered by the wind of pride? Do not boast, O human being, in your virtues, because you will have another judge, not yourself; and in his sight you must humble yourself in your heart, so that he may exalt you at the time of your recompense. Descend so that you may ascend; humble yourself so that you may be exalted, lest, once exalted, you be humbled. Whoever is contemptible in his own eyes is great before God [Al., beautiful]; and whoever is displeasing to himself is pleasing to God [Al., and those who please themselves are displeasing to God]. Be small in your own eyes, therefore, so that you may be great in the eyes of the Lord. You will be more precious before God the more despised you are in your own eyes. In the highest honor, let humility be held highest by you. Honor is the praise of humility; humility is its virtue.

## CHAPTER XI. On Compunction of Heart

Compunction of heart arises from the virtue of humility; from compunction comes confession of sins; from confession, penance; and from true penance comes the forgiveness of offenses. Compunction of heart is humility of mind accompanied by tears, remembrance of sins, and fear of judgment.

Tears customarily flow from the twofold fountain of compunction: one source is the careful consideration of the merits of one’s works [Ms., while the mind more carefully considers its evils]; the other is the sighing of desire for eternal life. Hence the Prophet says: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:3–4). Likewise: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” And: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83:3). [Col. 0621A]

There are four kinds of affections [Ms., afflictions] by which the thought of the just person is pierced with salutary sorrow: namely, remembrance of past crimes; recollection of future punishments; consideration of one’s pilgrimage in the misery of this present life; and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may be able to reach it as quickly as possible.

When these things take place in a person’s heart, one must know that God is then present to the human heart through his grace. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “I declared my life to you, O God; I placed my tears in your sight, as also in your promise” (Ps. 55:9) [Ms., “you placed”]. The promise of forgiveness that we have from God arouses tears of repentance in our heart. The sweetness of compunction is a desirable treasure in the human heart. The soul of a person who is pierced with compunction in prayer greatly advances toward salvation. When compunction is poured out through prayer, there is no doubt that the presence of the Holy Spirit is with our hearts.

## CHAPTER XII. On Confession

Scripture frequently urges us to flee to the remedy of confession—not because God needs our confession, since everything we think, say, or do is present to him, but because we cannot otherwise be saved unless, in repentance, we confess what we have wickedly done through negligence.

Whoever accuses himself of his sins leaves the devil nothing further with which to accuse him on the day of judgment—provided that, by confessing and repenting, he washes away what he has done and does not again renew what he committed [Ms., “recall what he laments”]. “Confess your sins to one another,” the Apostle James says, “and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Likewise blessed Paul the Apostle: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Solomon also said concerning confession of sins: “Whoever hides his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13) [Ms., “crimes”]. It is a great remedy of salvation not to repeat what we have done wrongly [Ms., wickedly], nor to reopen the scars of former wounds.

Thus the evangelist John said: “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he may forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:9). Likewise the Psalmist says: “I said: I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Ps. 31:5) [Ms., “the wickedness of my sin”].

While alive, let the sinner confess what he has done, because confession is not fruitful in hell, nor is repentance effective for salvation. “Behold, now is the time of salvation; behold, now is the acceptable time before God” (2 Cor. 6:2). Now is the time of forgiveness for those who repent; but after death there will be a time of vengeance for those who neglected to confess their crimes.

All the wicked have bitter repentance amid torments, but their repentance does not benefit them for salvation [Ms., forgiveness]; rather, their conscience torments them, increasing the punishments they suffer. They could have guarded themselves against the enormity of torments through confession, but they neglected to do so. Thus they are tortured outwardly by flames and inwardly in their own conscience.

How can a physician heal a wound that the sick person is ashamed to show? God desires our confession so that he may have a just reason for forgiving. Whoever conceals his sins and is ashamed to confess them for his healing has God as his witness now, and will again have him as his avenger. A person judges himself most wisely in this life, so that he will not be judged by God with everlasting condemnation.

Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he did not do good, or because through boldness he committed evil. He failed to do what ought to have been done, and did what ought not to have been done. Confession justifies; confession grants pardon for sins. All hope of forgiveness rests in confession. Confession is a work of mercy; [Col. 0622B] together with repentance, it is the sole remedy for the sick person’s weaknesses [Probably, “vices”].

[Note: [Col. 0621] From chapters 12 and 13, Sermon 254 of St. Augustine is shown to have been formed.]

## CHAPTER XIII. On Penance

The Savior himself displayed the virtue of penance in the Gospel, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. 3:2). John the Baptist also says: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:8). A fruit worthy of repentance is to mourn sins already committed and not commit them again, as Scripture says: “Do not add sin upon sin” (Sir. 5:5).

“Wash yourselves,” the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah, “and be clean” (Isa. 1:16). Therefore the person who laments past sins and does not again admit what must be lamented is washed and clean [Al., “does not again commit them”]. The person who laments what he has done but does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats the things over which he had wept, is washed but not clean.

Concerning those who return after their tears to worse offenses [Al., former offenses], blessed Peter says terrifyingly: “The dog returns to its own vomit” (2 Pet. 2:22). “Son, you have sinned,” it is said in Holy Scripture; “do not add to it again, but pray for forgiveness concerning your former sins, and they will be forgiven you” (Sir. 21:1).

True penance is not measured by the number of years but by the bitterness of the heart. Hence blessed Peter immediately received forgiveness from the Lord, because he wept most bitterly over the guilt of his threefold denial. Penance, even if it lasts only a short time, is not despised before God the just Judge if it is performed with the innermost bitterness of heart. For God does not require so much the length of time as he weighs the sincerity of the penitent’s affection [supplied].

Whoever trusts in Christ with his whole mind lives forever by his faith, even if he dies amid many sins, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25). He spoke of the death of the soul, because it comes upon a person through the sickness of sins [Al., “which occurs because of sickness”].

But God is merciful by nature. He is ready to save through mercy those whom he will not come to save through justice [Ms., “will not find”]; he desires all to be saved and none to perish (1 Tim. 2:4). Through the prophet he says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 18:21). However sinful and impious someone may be, if he turns to penance, he should not doubt that through God’s mercy he can obtain forgiveness.

In this world God’s mercy assists those who practice penance. In the future, however, penance is of no benefit; rather, we shall give an account of our works. In this life alone freedom is open to the penitent [Ms., to penance]; after death there is no opportunity for correction.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Not Delaying Conversion to God  
[Al., On Conversion to the Lord]

It is read in the divinely inspired writings: “[Col. 0623B] Son, do not delay turning to God [Ms., the Lord], for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth” (Sir. 5:8). Whoever delays conversion endangers his soul, because death does not delay (Sir. 14:12). If death finds him delaying conversion, it leads him away to torments.

It is a disordered and paralyzed [Ms., dangerous] thought to think about conversion tomorrow while neglecting it today. Why do you, sinner, put off [turning] and not fear that sudden death may steal from you the day of conversion? Do people not die suddenly? If it is good to abandon sins and turn to God, let it be done quickly. God promises you forgiveness when you turn from sins; he has not promised you the security of living for a long time. [Read the prophets; read the Apostle, and see whether an hour or a day has been promised you.]

Therefore let each person turn more quickly to God, and when he has found him, let the impious person abandon his way. If the final day suddenly enters, delay perishes and condemnation remains. You do not wish to perish? Return to God, and you will live. Do not despair of forgiveness for sins [Ms., “hope by sinning”], nor trust in a longer life. Turn, therefore, and do penance.

“You will say, ‘Tomorrow I shall turn.’” Why not today? “What harm is there,” you say, “if I say tomorrow?” What harm is there if today? Perhaps you say: “My life will be long.” I say: if it is long, let it be good; if it is short, let it also be good. Who could endure a long evil? You do not want a long meal to be bad, yet you want a long life to be bad? You buy an estate and desire it to be good. You wish to marry a wife and seek a good one. You wish children to be born to you and hope that they will be good. And, to speak even of the most worthless things, you buy shoes and do not want bad ones; yet you love a bad life? What has offended you about your life, that you alone wish it to be bad, so that amid all your good things [supplied] you alone may be evil?

“Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Sir. 5:8). These are the words of God, not mine. You did not hear these things from me, but I hear them with you from the Lord. Perhaps you answer: “Tomorrow, tomorrow.” O raven-like voice! The raven does not return to the ark; the dove returns.

If you wish to do penance only when you can no longer sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them. He is sufficiently alien from the faith who waits for old age before undertaking penance. One must fear that, while hoping for mercy, he may fall into judgment. For then he will not find forgiveness who has now lost the time suitable for forgiveness. There, before God, he cannot merit what he asks who here refused to heed what God commanded. Whoever neglects the time of penance granted to him pours out prayers in vain before the tribunal of Christ.

Everyone must hurry to turn to God while he can, lest, if he does not wish to do so while he can, he may be unable to do so when at last he wishes.

[Note: [Col. 0623] This chapter 15 is part of Sermon 97 of St. Augustine, Appendix.]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Fear of the Lord

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). It is a great safeguard against sin always to fear God’s presence [Ms., the presence of God]. Whoever perfectly fears God carefully guards himself from sins. “It will be well with the one who fears God at the end, and his reward remains forever” (Sir. 1:13). Whoever is ashamed to sin in the sight of a human being ought to be much more ashamed to commit iniquity in the sight of God, who considers not only deeds but also hearts.

Those who fear God with holy fear seek the good things that are pleasing to him. There is one kind of fear among sons and another among servants. Servants fear their masters because of torments, but sons fear their fathers because of love. If we are sons of God, let us fear him from the sweetness of charity, not from the bitterness of fear.

The wise person fears the Lord in all his works, knowing that he can never flee from his presence, as the Psalmist says to God: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 138:7). Again: “For neither from the East nor from the West” (Ps. 74:7), with the unspoken conclusion that no place for fleeing from God is open.

Whoever fears God will receive his instruction, and those who watch over his commandments will find everlasting blessing (Sir. 32:18). The soul that fears God is blessed (Sir. 34:17), and remains safe from diabolical temptation. “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14), and to whom it has been granted always to have the fear of God before his eyes.

Whoever fears the Lord turns away from the wicked path and directs his ways toward the path of virtue. The fear of the Lord drives away sins and adds virtues. Fear makes a person cautious and vigilant, lest he sin. But where the fear of the Lord is absent, there is disorder of life.

Whoever does not fear God in prosperity should flee to him in adversity [Ms., “at least”]—to him who scourges in order to heal. “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly desires his commandments” (Ps. 111:1). The fear of God casts out the fear of hell. Let us therefore fear God in such a way that we love him, because perfect love casts out servile fear (1 John 4:18).

## CHAPTER XVI. On Fasting

Fasting is perfect when it is practiced with almsgiving and prayer. It passes through the heavens [Al., “with prayers into heaven”] and reaches the throne of the Most High God. For then, when a person has become spiritual, he is joined to the angels and more freely united to God, if abstinence from the flesh is lifted up by prayers.

Through fasts and prayers the hidden mysteries of heavenly things are revealed, and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed. As long as Adam abstained, he remained in paradise; he ate, and he was expelled. Fasts are powerful weapons against the temptations of demons, for through abstinence they are quickly overcome.

Hence our Lord and Savior also teaches us to overcome their assaults by fasts and prayers, saying: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:20; Mark 9:28). Unclean spirits thrust themselves into places where they see feasting and drunkenness frequently practiced. Abstinence weakens the body, but the heart grows fat [Ms., “strengthens the heart”]. It weakens the flesh, but strengthens the soul.

It must be known, however, that fasts are most acceptable to God when accompanied by good works. Those who abstain from food but act wickedly imitate demons, who have no bodily nourishment but always possess spiritual wickedness. For the person abstains properly from food who also fasts from acts of malice and from the ambitions of the world. It is better to nourish the mind perpetually with the banquet of holy preaching [and the food of the word of God] than to fill the belly of deadly flesh [with earthly bread and] luxurious feasts.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Almsgiving

It must be understood that it is a work of piety for us, from the things that our heavenly Father has mercifully bestowed upon us, also to help others. There are very many who possess no share in fields, no share in vineyards, and no share in the riches of this world. We ought to relieve their poverty from the abundance that the Lord has given us, so that they too may bless God with us for the fertility of the earth and rejoice that the things given to those who possess them have also been made common to the poor and to strangers.

Happy is that granary, and most worthy of the multiplication of all fruits, from which the hunger of the needy, the weak, and strangers is satisfied. God has permitted these people to labor under various afflictions so that he might crown the miserable for their patience and the merciful for their benevolence.

For almsgiving and fasting are an exceedingly effective plea for sins, and prayer lifted up by such supports swiftly ascends to the divine ears, since it is written: “The merciful man does good to his own soul” (Prov. 11:17). A portion of bodily possessions that is supplied to the needy passes into eternal riches for the one who gives it.

Thus we merit God’s mercy and forgiveness for our sins through compassion toward the poor and through almsgiving, because whoever does not turn his heart away from the needy quickly turns the Lord’s hearing toward himself, as the Lord says: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

Let human generosity confidently spend and distribute what Truth promises it will repay. Be steadfast, Christian giver: give what you may receive; sow what you may reap; scatter what you may gather. Do not fear loss; do not sigh over uncertain gain. When your substance is well distributed, it increases. Your Rewarder wants you to be generous. He who gives so that you may possess commands you to give, saying: “Give, and it will be given to you.”

O miser, if you love gold or the riches of the world, give, lest you lose them. If you keep them, you will undoubtedly lose them; if you distribute them, you will possess them eternally, as Truth itself says: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6:29).

Certainly, by wisely dispensing temporal things you will acquire eternal things. Do not be timid in giving, lest you be needy in receiving your reward, because “whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6). “Whoever has mercy on the poor will be blessed” (Prov. 14:21). “The redemption of a man’s soul is his wealth” (Prov. 13:8). Whoever has mercy on the poor honors God.

“Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor,” Holy Scripture says, “and it will pray for you” (Sir. 29:15). Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. “Do not despise a hungry soul, and do not provoke the poor in his distress” (Sir. 4:2). Whoever turns his ear away from the cry of the poor will not deserve the mercy of God [Ms., “does not deserve”].

In your lifetime, do good to your soul by giving alms to the wretched, because after death you have no power to do good. Let the poor eat at your banquets, and let Christ be present in them.

There are three kinds of almsgiving: the first is bodily, to give the needy whatever you are able; the second is spiritual, to forgive the person by whom you have been injured; the third is to correct the offender and bring those who have gone astray back to the way of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0625] Sermon 91 of St. Augustine was formed from this chapter 18.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Chastity

Chastity is an angelic way of life. Chastity together with humility will deserve the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, whom the impurity of lusts drives away, as Scripture says: “The Holy Spirit will flee the body subjected to sins” (Wis. 1:5). Our members ought to be dedicated to God, not to fornication.

Let a person set the flames of eternal torments against the desire of his flesh. Let a young man become accustomed to chastity, so that he may be worthy of the wisdom of God. Where there is bodily impurity, there is the dwelling of the diabolical spirit, which especially rejoices in the defilement of our flesh. All impurities displease God, and especially those that are unnatural.

Holy Scripture therefore admonishes us, saying: “Do not follow your lusts, and turn away from your desire. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Sir. 18:30–31). The most wise Solomon likewise offered judgments concerning the avoidance of bodily impurity, saying: “The lips of a prostitute drip honey, and her throat is smoother than oil. But her end is bitter as wormwood, and sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet descend to death, and her steps penetrate to the underworld. They do not walk along the path of life; her steps wander, and they cannot be traced. Now therefore, my son, hear me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not approach the doors of her house” (Prov. 5:3–8).

He said this not only concerning the impurity of prostitutes but also concerning every desire of the flesh that urges the soul to consent to its cravings. But the reason of the mind ought to restrain the impulses of the flesh and bridle its unlawful pleasures.

The same man mentioned above, forbidding cohabitation with women, says to young men: “Can a man hide fire in his bosom without burning his garments? Or can he walk upon burning coals without scorching the soles of his feet? So is it with the one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife: he will not be clean when he has touched her” (Prov. 6:27–29).

Likewise blessed Paul the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7:1), as though danger arose immediately from the touch. The chastity of young people is beautiful, pleasing to God, and useful for every good thing.

Whoever has spiritual or bodily children should nurture them in chastity for God, not in fornication for the devil. What benefit is it for a person to have, nurture, and love a son if he will nurture him for eternal torments?

Those who live in chastity have an angelic manner of life on earth. Chastity joins a person to heaven and makes him a fellow citizen with the angels. Whoever has a lawful wife should use her lawfully at appropriate times, so that he may deserve to receive from God the blessing of children.

Let no one say that he is unable to guard himself from fornication. “God is faithful,” blessed Paul the Apostle says, “and will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear [Ms. omits ‘not’], but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape” (1 Cor. 10:13). Each person receives a temptation—whether in the desire of the flesh, in worldly ambition, or in any other trouble of temptation—such as he will be able either to conquer with praise or to succumb to with disgrace.

Chastity is always necessary for everyone, but especially for the ministers of Christ’s altar, whose life ought to be instruction for others and an unceasing proclamation of salvation. For the Lord ought to have such ministers, men who are corrupted by no contamination of the flesh [Ms., “by no . . . contamination”], but who rather shine through the restraint of chastity and glow among the people as examples of complete integrity.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Avoiding Fraud

The Lord himself, who urges us to be kind from our substance toward the poor and wretched, forbids us every form of greed and unjust acquisition of money. [Col. 0627D] He who says, “Give alms from your just labors” (Tob. 4:7), himself exhorts us through his Apostle, saying: “Do not commit fraud against one another” (Mark 10:19) [Ms., “do not defraud one another”].

Whoever acquires anything by any fraud loses justice and equity [Ms., “the equity of justice”]. Tell me, miser; tell me, greedy man; tell me, criminal: what have you acquired? Perhaps you say: “I acquired gold,” and you speak the truth. Behold, you acquired gold through fraud, and you lost faith through injustice. If you were to find faith for sale in the marketplace, if you were a good person, how would you purchase it [Ms., “how would you buy it”]? Why are you not afraid of losing what God wanted you to have in your heart [Ms., “losing the thing which”]?

You have gold or silver, or something else more precious, in your chest; but you have loss in your heart. You have lost riches better than all these things: faith, justice, and love of God and neighbor. You consider your profit but do not consider your loss. If you rejoice in this profit, why do you not mourn those things that have been lost? Therefore you have lost more than you acquired.

O rich man, through power you seize what you desire to possess, and through injustice you lose what God wants you to possess—that is, everlasting blessedness. If every thief or robber had lost the light of his eyes during the theft or robbery, would he afterward have committed theft or robbery? Yet he does not know that in such a sin he loses the light of the heart, which is better than all bodily light.

Rather, miser, give to the poor what you have, so that you may find in heaven what you gave on earth. Why do you fear losing your money and do not fear being utterly lost? For the sake of acquiring money you give false testimony, lie, and seize what belongs to others. You swear and perjure yourself, things which the law forbids. When you do all these things, why are you not afraid that you may burn entirely forever?

Why, miser, do you love gold more than your soul? “For what will it profit you if you gain the whole world but suffer the loss of your soul?” (Matt. 16:26). The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses” (Luke 12:15).

Do the rich not die in the same way as the poor? Riches cannot help on the day of vengeance, nor will they free those who use them badly [Al., “those who live badly by means of them”] from everlasting punishments. Nothing is more wicked than a miser, who has placed his soul up for sale because of his desire for riches.

Greed knows no limit, and although it devours everything, it never knows how to be satisfied [Ms., “to be filled”]. It is always hungry and needy. The miser is like hell, which is never filled.

## CHAPTER XX. On Judges
Everyone who judges rightly carries a balance in his hand. In both senses [Ms., *pensu*] he bears justice and mercy: so that, in accordance with justice, he may pronounce sentence on sins, and in accordance with mercy temper the punishment of sin. Some matters, however, are to be corrected by a good judge through equity, while others are to be pardoned through mercy.

Judgments must be rendered without respect of persons. For nothing is more unjust than accepting gifts in judgments, because gifts blind the hearts [Ms., eyes] of the prudent [Col. 0628D] and subvert the hearts [Ms., words] of the righteous (Deut. XVI, 19). “With whatever judgment,” says the Lord, “you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. VII, 2). Therefore let a judge fear God the judge, lest, when God judges, he himself be condemned. Whoever condemns the innocent or justifies the impious for gifts, or judges unjustly through love or hatred of any person, will endure vengeance in God’s judgment.

No ruler ought to appoint foolish or wicked judges. For the fool, through indolence, is ignorant of justice, while the wicked, through greed, overturns the very truth he has learned. The poor are torn apart by evil judges almost more grievously than by the bloodiest enemies. For no plunderer is so greedy for another’s possessions as an unjust judge is for those of his own people. Unjust judges are worse than enemies. Enemies can often be avoided by flight; but judges, because of their power, cannot be escaped—judges who strive to amass wealth through the oppression of their fellow citizens.

Sometimes good judges have rapacious officials; and they are stained by the crime of these men if they do not restrain their rapacity. Such men perish through the sins of others, because, as the distinguished teacher of the world says, not only those who commit such deeds, but also those who consent to them, are worthy of everlasting death (Rom. I, 32).

Often wicked judges, for the sake of greed, either delay or pervert legal proceedings. They do not bring cases to an end until their lifetime has run its course. For when they judge, they consider not the cases but the gifts. Wicked judges, according to the Prophet’s word, are “like wolves in the evening; they leave nothing for the morning” (Zeph. III, 3)—that is, they think only about the advantage of the present life [Col. 0629B] and nothing about the future, snatching everything like wolves and scarcely leaving the poor a few scraps.

An angry judge cannot fully examine the matter before the court, because, blinded by the darkness of rage, he does not see the clarity of justice. In judgment, one must consider not the person but the case. For it is written: “You shall not show partiality in judgment” (Deut. I, 17). Unjust judges go astray in their verdict concerning the truth when they attend to the rank of the person; and they often harm the just when they wickedly defend the impious. Accepting gifts in judgments is a betrayal of the truth. Those who judge justly in the fear of God will receive eternal rewards from the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXI. On False Witnesses

“A false witness,” says Solomon, “will not go unpunished” (Prov. XIX, 9). Whoever gives false testimony against his neighbor will have his lamp extinguished on the last day. Whoever conceals the truth through fear of any power provokes God’s anger against himself, because he fears a human being more than God.

A lying witness is liable to three persons: first, to God, whose presence he disregards; next, to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; finally, to the innocent person whom he injures by false testimony. If false witnesses are separated, they are immediately found to be liars. Both are equally guilty: the one who conceals the truth and the one who tells a lie, because the former refuses to be of help, while the latter desires to cause harm.

Blessed is the person whose testimony is found acceptable in God’s sight. Justice is overturned in judgments in four ways: [Col. 0629D] through fear, greed, hatred, and affection. Through fear, when anyone is afraid to speak or judge the truth because of fear of some powerful person; through greed, when a judge is corrupted by the reward of a gift; through hatred, when someone wishes to harm another because of hostility toward him; through affection, when a powerful person defends friends or relatives against justice.

By these four means the equity of judgment is often overturned and innocence is injured. Those who oppress the poor are more deserving of grief than those who suffer injustice. For those who are oppressed quickly bring their temporal misery to an end [Al., pass through it]; but those who oppress them unjustly will be assigned to eternal flames. Here the good are often judged by the wicked; but in the future life the wicked [Col. 0630A] will be judged by the good. Often, even here, the good are unhappy and wretched in the eyes of human beings, while the wicked are happy. In that eternal recompense, therefore, the good will always be happy, and the wicked will always be wretched. Those to whom things go well in this age should strive above all not to lose eternal goods; and those who suffer hardships should endure them bravely, so that they may be found worthy of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Envy

“Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). When he begrudged heaven to the earthly human being, he sought a way to destroy him through transgression of the command that the Creator had set for humanity. [Col. 0630B]

Nothing can be more wicked than envy, which is tormented by the goods of others and begrudges others having what it itself does not possess. Envy is hostile to every good. Where envy is, charity cannot be; and where charity is not, there can be nothing good.

Whoever envies is like the devil, who through envy cast humanity down from the happiness of paradise. Great is the person who overcomes envy through humility and destroys discord through charity. What is more wretched for a person than to have made another’s good his own punishment? Every envious person is tormented in spirit. Therefore, from the very source from which a good person prospers, the envious person withers.

It is better to imitate the examples of good people than to goad them with the spur of envy. Envy bites the senses, burns the breast, and afflicts the mind. Let no one grieve over another person’s good, or be distressed by another’s happiness [Col. 0630C]. A person can make another’s good his own, when he loves in another what he does not do in himself [Ms., “what he himself does not do”].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Pride

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6; 1 Peter V, 5). The greatest sin of the devil was pride. Therefore pride is worse than every vice [Ms., “worse than all evils”]. It often arises even from good deeds, when a person becomes proud of his good works; and through pride he loses what he had acquired through charity.

Pride is the last of all the vices, when a person is adorned with virtues and begins to become proud in them [Ms., “has become proud”; Al., “desires”]. Pride is also the beginning of every sin [Col. 0630D] (Eccl. X, 15), when the soul despises the Creator’s commands and immediately falls into the pit of some sin.

The more pride raises itself on high, the more deeply it lies below. And the higher it is lifted, the more deeply it falls. For whoever is exalted through his own pride is condemned by God’s justice. Before a person’s ruin, his spirit is exalted.

Nothing must be avoided more by a Christian than pride, which provokes God’s anger. For pride made demons from angels, while humility makes human beings like the holy angels. The proud desire to be praised for things they do not do; the humble shrink from having whatever good they do recognized.

Let no one exalt himself in his goodness or seek praise for himself, even if he does something good; but let him desire to praise God in his gifts [Col. 0631A] [Ms., “to be praised”], because he does no good thing [Ms., “did no good thing”] except what God has granted him to do.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Anger

The distinguished Preacher of the world says: “Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you” (Eph. IV, 31). For “the anger of man cannot accomplish the justice of God” (James I, 20).

Anger without restraint is devoid of reason. A gentle answer calms anger; a harsh word arouses fury. An angry person, as Solomon says, provokes quarrels; “the patient person calms what has been aroused” (Prov. XV, 18). But who can endure a person whose spirit is easily stirred to anger [Col. 0631B] (Prov. XVIII, 14)?

Anger has no mercy, nor does erupting fury know when to end its vengeance (Prov. XXVII, 4). If anger overtakes you, O human being, calm it. That anger is evil which disturbs the mind so that it loses sound counsel. Anger is just and necessary when a person becomes angry with his own sins and is indignant with himself when he acts wrongly. For the prophet says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5). He allowed what belongs to nature and removed what belongs to guilt.

Let your patience smooth away another person’s anger. “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Rom. XII, 21). Let another person’s sin become your reward. Does another person’s anger displease you? What displeases you in another should also displease you in yourself. Do not stain the tranquility of your mind with another person’s disturbance.

Do not make yourself equal to a fool, because “anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. VII, 10). If you become angry with him, there will be two evil persons—you and he. It is better for you to be good, even though he is wicked [Ms., “it would be better”]. Why should you become wicked because of another person’s wickedness?

## CHAPTER XXV. On Not Seeking Human Praise

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI, 1)—that is, do not do good deeds with the intention of receiving empty praise from human beings; rather, whatever good a person does, let him do it for the love of God, for the salvation of his soul, and in brotherly charity.

Therefore the Lord himself spoke of certain people who give alms, or pray and fast, in order to receive praise from human beings: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). Whoever does any good thing in order to be praised by human beings has this as the reward he sought and has no recompense to hope for from God, because he did not act for God’s love but for the empty boasting of human praise, as hypocrites are accustomed to do.

The Lord Jesus Christ greatly detests this vice of seeking to please human beings through good works. He repeatedly strikes the Pharisees, who were such people in Judea, with a terrible curse, saying: “Woe to you, hypocrites” [Col. 0632A] (Matt. XXIII, 13)! [“But let us not imitate them,”] rather, according to the Apostle: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. I, 31).

Whoever does not desire praise is not disturbed by insult. Nor should a person therefore consider himself good merely because someone else praises him, since God is the examiner of the heart. For what does it profit an evil person to be proclaimed good? What a person does is truly good when he desires to please God, from whom he has whatever good he possesses or does.

Whoever appears to do good deeds but through them desires to please not God but human beings labors in vain and sows into the wind. Let each person strive to be great in his works, but let him not seek human approval for his greatness, lest he lose what he possessed and become small [Ms., “and be made small”]. For whatever good a person does [Col. 0632B], let him know that he has it not from himself but from God.

Blessed Paul the Apostle rebukes those who boast in their good deeds, saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV, 7). Whoever turns some gift of God that he has received into his own praise unquestionably turns virtue into vice, and the good he has done into sin.

For when a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting, even the work of mercy itself is turned into sin. Whatever good a person does, let him seek praise from God, not for himself, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Perseverance in Good Works [Ms., “in a good work”]

[Col. 0632C]

In a Christian, the beginning of a good work is not sought but its end, because each person will be judged according to his end. There are some who begin their way of life well but finish it badly, like Judas, at first an apostle and afterward the Lord’s betrayer; conscious of his deed, he hanged himself with a noose (Acts I).

Saul [Al., Paul] began badly but finished well: first a persecutor, afterward a preacher. The virtue of a good work is perseverance, as the Lord himself says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). Therefore it is not the person who begins what is good, but the person who perseveres in goodness, who will be saved.

Our manner of life pleases God when we complete with a persevering end the good that we begin [Col. 0632D] [Ms., “complete”]. To have perfected the good, then—not merely to have begun it—is virtue. The reward is not promised to those who begin, but is given to those who persevere.

The end of every human life is always examined: what sort of end a person has at the final time of his life. For each person is either justified or condemned according to his end. Therefore let everyone strive with the utmost eagerness to complete the good things he has begun, so that he may deserve to receive an everlasting reward from the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] Some make a separate second book from the following chapters and divide it from what precedes. But the sequence and subject matter of these chapters refute this, and the testimony of the manuscript codices, together with the author’s intention, clearly protests against it. QUERCETANUS.—In Vatican Codex 650, quarto, eleventh century, the following chapters are divided into two treatises. The first is entitled *Alcuin’s Dicta on the Eight Principal Vices*; the second, *On the Four Virtues*.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Eight Principal Vices, and First on Pride

There are eight principal or original vices, the roots from which, as it were, all the vices of a corrupted mind or an unchaste body and the various forms of iniquity put forth their shoots [Col. 0633A]. We have decided to say a few words about them, or about the roots from which the branches of vicious growth appear to arise, so that each person may know that, once the roots have been torn out, he can more easily cut off the branches.

The first vice is spiritual: pride. Of it is said, “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccl. X, 15). It is the queen of all evils, through which the angels fell from heaven, and it arises from contempt for God’s commandments. It also arises when the mind is lifted up because of good works and considers itself better than others, while in the very respect in which it thinks itself better it is worse than others.

Pride also arises through obstinacy, when people disdain obeying their elders. From it, in turn, arise all disobedience, all presumption, all stubbornness, quarrels, heresies, and arrogance: [In speech, clamor; in silence, bitterness; laughter excessive and uncontrolled in merriment; unreasonable sadness in tranquility; rancor in reply; falsehood in speech. Words bursting forth everywhere without any seriousness of heart; boldness in inflicting insults; cowardice in enduring them.]

All these evils true humility, as a servant of God, will be able very easily to overcome [Ms., “to remedy”]. [True humility is, as we have said, to hear the word of truth humbly, retain it faithfully, and carry it out willingly.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Gluttony

[Col. 0633C]

The first bodily sin is gluttony, that is, an immoderate pleasure in food or drink. Through it the first parents of the human race lost the happiness of paradise and were cast into the misery [of this wretched life]; in it every human being is born through sin, lives through labor, and dies through suffering.

Gluttony appears to rule in a person in three ways: when someone desires, for the sake of gluttony, to anticipate the canonical and appointed hour; when he orders more exquisite foods to be prepared for himself than the need of his body or the dignity of his person requires; or when, through the desire of his intemperance, he takes more in eating or drinking than benefits his salvation.

From this gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, frivolity, empty talk, bodily uncleanness, instability of mind, drunkenness, [Col. 0633D] and lust. For lust of the body is accumulated from the fullness of the belly; it is best conquered through fasting and abstinence and through continual application to any kind of work. [For this is the common rule for all religious persons, healthy and sick: never to fill the belly completely with any kind of food.]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Fornication

Fornication is every bodily uncleanness that ordinarily arises from lack of restraint in lust and from weakness of soul, when the soul consents to its flesh’s sinning. For the soul ought to be mistress and command the flesh, while the flesh ought to be the servant and obey its mistress, that is, the rational soul.

This fornication occurs through the joining of the flesh with any woman, or also through any other uncleanness for the satisfaction of the heat of lust. From this [fornication] arise blindness of mind, instability of the eyes, or immoderate love of the whole body; often danger to life, wantonness, jesting, insolence, and every kind of lack of restraint; hatred of God’s commandments, enervation of the mind, and unjust desires; neglect of the future life and delight in the present [Ms., “love of the present”].

It is conquered through habitual chastity and continence, through remembrance of the eternal fire, and through fear of the presence of the everlasting God [who sees us and our deeds everywhere].

## CHAPTER XXX. On Greed

[Col. 0634B]

Greed is an excessive desire to acquire, possess, or retain riches; it is an insatiable plague. Like a dropsical person, who the more he drinks, the more his thirst increases [Ms., “the increase is added”], so greed, the more it possesses, the more it desires [to possess]. And since it has no limit in possessing, it will have no limit in desiring.

Its offspring [Ms., “germs”] are envy, theft, robbery, murder, lies, perjury, plunder, violence, restlessness, unjust judgments, contempt for truth, forgetfulness of future blessedness, and hardness of heart. Greed is contrary to mercy, to almsgiving for the poor, and to all compassion toward the wretched. It is conquered through fear of God [Col. 0634C], through brotherly charity, through works of mercy, through almsgiving to the poor, and through hope of future blessedness, when the true riches of future blessedness overcome the false riches of this age.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Anger

Anger is one of the eight principal vices. If it is not governed by reason, it turns into fury, so that a person becomes powerless over his own spirit [Ms., “becomes”] and does what is unfitting.

If anger takes up residence in the heart [Ms., “settles in”], it removes from it all foresight regarding one’s actions. A person will be unable to seek the judgment of right guidance [Ms., “discernment”], to possess the virtue of honorable contemplation, or to have mature counsel; rather, he appears to do everything through a kind of precipitousness [Col. 0634D].

From it—that is, from anger—arise swelling of mind, quarrels and insults, clamor, indignation, presumption, blasphemies, shedding of blood, murders, desire for vengeance, and remembrance of injuries. It is conquered through patience and long-suffering, through the intellectual reason that God implants in human minds, and through remembrance [of the injuries and sufferings that Christ unjustly endured for us, and through remembrance] of the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Acedia

[Col. 0635A]

Acedia is a plague that is shown to do great harm to those who serve God. An idle person grows sluggish in carnal desires; he does not rejoice in spiritual work, does not delight in the salvation [Ms., “health”] of his soul, and does not become cheerful in assisting his brother’s labor. Instead, he merely lusts and desires, and his idle mind wanders everywhere.

This is what most of all drives monks from the cell into the world and casts them from the regular way of life into the precipices of vice. When it besieges a pitiable mind, it infects it with many miseries and teaches it many evils.

From it arise sleepiness, laziness in good work, instability of place, wandering from one place to another, lukewarmness in labor, weariness of heart, [Col. 0635B] grumbling, and empty talk [Al., “grandiloquent talk”]. It is conquered through devotion to reading, through constant good work, through desire for the future rewards of blessedness, through confession of the temptation one has in mind, through stability of place and purpose, and through exercise in any craft or labor, or through persistence in prayers and vigils, so that the servant of God may never be found idle.

The devil finds a place for tempting with greater difficulty in a person whom he finds engaged in good work than in one whom he finds idle and doing nothing good.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Sadness

There are two kinds of sadness: one salutary, the other deadly [Col. 0635C]. Salutary sadness occurs when the sinner’s spirit is grieved over its sins and is so grieved that it seeks to make confession and do penance and desires to turn itself toward God.

The other is the sadness of this world, which produces death for the soul. It is unable to make progress in any good work, disturbs the mind, and often casts it into despair, taking away hope of future good things [Ms., “removing”]. From it arise wickedness, rancor, weakness of spirit, bitterness, and despair. Often there is also no delight in the present life.

It is conquered through spiritual joy, hope of future things, the consolation of the Scriptures, and brotherly conversation [in spiritual gladness].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Cenodoxia, That Is, Vain Glory

[Col. 0635D]

Vain glory occurs when a person desires to be praised for his good deeds and does not give honor to God [but to himself; nor] attribute to divine grace whatever good he does, but [as though] he possessed from himself either the dignity of secular honor or the beauty of spiritual wisdom—although no one can possess anything good without God’s grace or help, as Truth itself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

Therefore, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord,” because no one can possess anything good without God’s gift. From the root of this vice many shoots of wickedness appear to grow: boasting, arrogance, indignation, [Col. 0636A] discord, desire for vain glory, and hypocrisy—that is, the pretence of a good work, when a person wishes to be praised for doing something he does not know how to do.

Indeed, he performs almost everything in such a way that he may be praised by human beings; of such people the Lord himself says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). [ [Note: [Col. 0635] The passages enclosed in brackets are found only in the manuscript codex of St. James.]

This plague, that is, vain glory, is a many-formed greed, and it confronts the soldier fighting against vices—and even the victor over vices—from every side. For it tries to wound Christ’s soldier in clothing and bodily appearance, in gait, in voice, in work, in vigils, in fasts, in prayer, in withdrawal, in reading, in knowledge, in silence, in obedience, in humility, and in patient endurance; and, like a most destructive reef hidden beneath swelling waves, when it is not guarded against, it brings sudden and pitiable shipwreck upon those sailing prosperously.

For when it could not produce cenodoxia in someone under the guise of beautiful and shining clothing, it attempts to implant it through clothing that is filthy, neglected, and more humble. Whom it could not overthrow through honor, it trips up through humility; whom it could not elevate through the adornment of knowledge and eloquence, it crushes through the gravity of silence.

If he fasts publicly, he is struck by the glory of vanity; if he conceals the fast for the sake of despising glory, the person is inwardly crushed within himself by the same vice of elation. To avoid being stained by the contagion of vain glory, he avoids celebrating lengthy prayers in the sight of the brothers, yet even when he practices them secretly he does not escape the barbs of vanity.

It tries to exalt one person because he is extremely patient in work and labor, another because he is most ready to obey, another because he surpasses the others in humility. One is tempted through knowledge, another through devotion to reading, another through the length of his vigils. Thus this disease strives to wound a person not only through worldly works but also through his virtues.]
