The medicine for this disease is remembrance of divine goodness, through which all the good things that we appear to possess have been bestowed on us; and also the perpetual love of God himself, in whose praise we ought to do everything good that we accomplish in this world. We should desire more to be praised by God on the day of eternal recompense than by any human being during the conduct of this passing life.

[Thus also we shall be able to escape this beast, if we think upon that Davidic verse: “The Lord will scatter the bones of those who please human beings” (Ps. LII, 6). First, let us do nothing for the sake of vain glory; then let us guard with similar vigilance whatever we have done with a good beginning, lest the disease of vain glory, creeping in afterward, empty out the fruit of all our labors. Whatever in the conduct of the brothers the common custom does not at all accept, let us reject with every effort and avoid as though devoted to boasting; and let us avoid whatever might make us conspicuous among the others, as though praise among human beings were to be sought only by those who do such things.]

These are the eight leaders of all ungodliness, with their armies, and the strongest fighters of diabolical deceit against the human race. [Therefore whoever possesses one of these vices and dies without confession and penance is condemned to eternal punishment. Hence John says in his Epistle: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John V, 15). These fighters, however,] with God’s help, are very easily conquered by Christ’s soldiers through holy virtues.

Pride is conquered by humility; gluttony by abstinence; fornication by chastity; greed by abstinence [Ms. St. James, “generosity and contempt for the world”]; anger by patience; acedia by persistence in good work; evil sadness by spiritual joy; vain glory by the love of God [Al., “by wisdom”] [“is conquered”].

Therefore, among these leaders of the Christian religion whom we have set against the fighters of diabolical wickedness, four most glorious leaders preside [“whose names are these”]: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Four Virtues

[Col. 0637B]

First, one must know what virtue is. Virtue is a habit of the soul, the adornment of nature, a way of life, the devotion of moral conduct, the worship of divinity, the honor of the human being, and the reward of eternal blessedness.

Its parts, as we have said, are four principal ones: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

Prudence is knowledge of divine and human matters, insofar as it has been granted to a human being. In it one must understand what a person ought to avoid and what he ought to do; and this is what is read in the Psalm: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII, 15).

Justice is nobility of soul, assigning to each thing its proper dignity. In it the worship of divinity, the rights of humanity, just judgments, and the equity [Col. 0637C] of the whole of life are preserved.

Fortitude is great patience and long-suffering of spirit, perseverance in good works, and victory over every kind of vice [Ms., “all vices”].

Temperance is the proper measure of the whole of life, so that a person neither loves nor hates anything excessively, but moderates all the changes of this life with carefully considered diligence.

To those who observe these things in faith and charity, the Truth himself, Christ Jesus, promises the rewards of eternal glory. There is no better wisdom than that by which God is understood and feared according to the measure of the human mind [Ms., “understood and loved”], and his future judgment is believed.

For what is more just than to love God and keep his commandments, through whom we were created when we did not exist [Col. 0637D] [and through whom, when we were lost, we were recreated], and liberated from the slavery of the devil, who forgave us all the good things we possess?

And what fortitude is better than to conquer the devil, overcome all his suggestions, and endure courageously, for God’s name, all the adversities of the world?

Temperance is a very noble virtue, through which all the honor of this life among human beings is established, so that in every matter a person thinks, speaks, and acts temperately, with counsel for his salvation.

These things are light and sweet to the person who loves God, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” [Col. 0638A] (Matt. XI, 29).

Is it not better and more blessed to love God, who is eternal beauty, eternal fragrance, eternal joy, eternal sweetness, eternal delight, perpetual honor, and unfailing happiness, than to love the vanities and false insanities of this age (Ps. XXXIX, 5), beautiful appearances [Al., “superfluous beauty”], sweet flavors, pleasant sounds, fragrant odors, delightful touches, and the transient honors and happiness of this world? All these things withdraw and pass away like a fleeting shadow; they deceive the one who loves them and send him into everlasting misery.

But whoever faithfully loves God and the Lord, worships him without ceasing, and steadfastly fulfills his commandments will be made worthy to possess everlasting glory with God’s angels forever.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0637D] In the manuscript of St. Gall it reads: “Superscription.” In the others it is absent, and the chapter is not numbered.] Conclusion of the Work

[Col. 0638B]

I have dictated these words for you, dearest son [Wido], in a brief discourse, as you requested, so that you may have them every day before you like a little handbook, in which you can examine yourself concerning what you ought to avoid or what you ought to do, and through the various prosperities and adversities of this life exhort yourself concerning how you ought to ascend to the summit of perfection.

Nor should the condition of a lay habit or secular way of life frighten you, as though, in such a state, you could not enter the gates of the heavenly life. Therefore, just as the blessedness of the kingdom of God has been proclaimed equally to all, so entry into the kingdom of God is equally open to every sex, age, and person according to the dignity of their merits.

There there is no distinction between who in this world was lay or cleric, rich or poor, younger or older, servant or master; rather, each person will be crowned with everlasting glory according to the merit of his good work. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] These passages are absent from the manuscript codices. Quercetanus added them from volume VI of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*.]

Solomon said:

“Sweet speech multiplies friends and calms enemies; and a gracious tongue will abound in a good person. Let many be at peace with you, and let one out of a thousand be your counselor. If you possess a friend, possess him in temptation, and do not easily trust him. For there is a friend according to his appointed time, and he will not remain on the day of distress. There is a friend who goes forth to friendship [Vulg., ‘who turns toward enmity . . .’]. But there is a friend who is a companion at table and does not remain on the day of need.

“If a friend remains steadfast, he will be your equal, and attend to your household affairs [Vulg., ‘he will act confidently . . .’]. A faithful friend is a strong protection; whoever finds him has found a treasure. Nothing compares with a faithful friend, and gold and silver are not worth weighing against the goodness of his fidelity. A faithful friend is a medicine of life and immortality; and those who fear the Lord find him.

“Whoever fears the Lord will likewise have good friendship, because his friend will be like him. Son, receive instruction from your youth, and until your gray hairs you will find wisdom. Approach it like one who plows and sows, and endure its good fruits; for you will labor little in its work.”

[Col. 0639]

# SIXTH OPUSCULUM

[Note: [Col. 0639D] See St. Augustine, *Book On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 13, volume XL of Migne’s *Patrologia*, column 784.]

## BOOK ON THE NATURE OF THE SOUL, TO EULALIA THE VIRGIN

[Col. 0639A] 146

To Eulalia, a virgin, most beloved sister in the charity of Christ [Note: [Col. 0640D] Eulalia or Gundrada. See the Preliminary Notice and the letters cited there], Albinus sends greetings in the Lord.

### I.

Your holy concern and praiseworthy devotion to God were pleased to ask that I write something concerning the nature of the soul, because of certain questions, as you say, discussed among you in the past year. I would gladly have done so if I knew myself to be endowed with such great talent that I could confidently expound such difficult matters worthily.

Yet in one respect it seems unworthy to say that I do not know myself. What am I, except soul and flesh? What flesh is, is known to everyone who knows that he is human; but to know the nature of the soul fully belongs to very few. Nor is there anything more necessary for a human being living in this mortality to know [Col. 0639B] than God and the soul.

For to the extent that anyone recognizes God, to that extent he loves him; whoever recognizes him less loves him less. Therefore it is natural for every human being to love God. If it is natural for every human being to love the good, it is also natural to love God, because God is the highest good, without which no one can possess anything good.

He is unfailing goodness, complete beauty, and the abundance of all happiness. But love of this good can exist only in the soul; and this is the soul’s supreme good: to love that good in which alone, and from which, and through which, whatever good exists in any creature is good.

II. And the soul alone is noble if it loves him from whom it has what it is: he created it in such a way that it bears within itself the imprint of his own image and likeness, and is worthy to be God’s dwelling, according to the manner in which any creature can possess its Creator within itself. It was ordered so that it should love with complete devotion what is superior to it—namely, God—and govern with complete diligence what is inferior to it—namely, the flesh. Since, therefore, the soul is the better part of the human being, it is fitting that it should be mistress and, as though from the seat of royal majesty, command what its members should do, by what means, when, where, and how; and carefully consider what it commands each member to perform and what it permits each member to desire according to its nature. It must discern all these things with the rational gaze of the mind, lest anything improper occur anywhere in the service of its flesh.

### III

For, as the philosophers maintain, the soul has a threefold nature: one part in it is appetitive, another rational, and a third spirited or irascible. Two of these parts—appetite and anger—we share with beasts and animals. Human beings alone among mortals flourish through reason, possess deliberative judgment, and excel in understanding. But reason, which belongs properly to the mind, ought to command these two powers, appetite and anger. Its superior virtues are plainly four: prudence, by which it distinguishes what should and should not be done; justice, by which God is worshiped and loved, and life is rightly conducted among fellow souls; temperance, which governs appetite and anger so that they do not transgress the fixed bounds of moral goodness; and fortitude, by which it endures with steadfast spirit whatever adversities of this life may occur.

### IV

If these four virtues are produced in the soul through perfect charity, they make it close to God. For there is nothing else that is the human being’s highest good, to which it is supremely blessed to cling, except God; and we cannot cling to him except through love. Therefore these four virtues are adorned with the single diadem of charity.

What is true wisdom except understanding that God is to be loved? What is justice except worshiping him from whom one exists and from whom one has whatever good one possesses? What is temperance except presenting oneself whole in the perfection of life to the one whom one loves? What is fortitude except bravely enduring every adversity for the love of God?

For if God is the highest good of the human being—and this cannot be denied—it follows that to desire the highest good is to live well, so that living well is nothing other than loving with all one’s heart, soul, and mind God, from whom one exists. Thus the person lives in an ordered way who considers what he is and toward what he is hastening, if he governs the affections of his soul and the movements of the flesh with prudent reason.

For if either appetite or anger conquers reason, and either of them rules in the soul, a perverted order will hurl the one who consents to it into worse things. Anger, if it is immoderate, or unrestrained appetite will occupy the throne of reason. From these three roots, if they are corrupted, almost all the diseases of vice sprout.

Appetite was given to human beings so that they might desire what is useful and what advances them toward eternal salvation. But if it is corrupted, gluttony, fornication, and avarice arise from it. Anger was given for restraining vices, so that a human being would not serve the impious—namely, sins—as masters, for according to the Lord’s word, “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). When anger is corrupted, sadness and acedia proceed from it.

Reason was given, as we have said, to direct and govern the whole of human life. When it is corrupted, pride and vainglory arise from it. From these trees, as it were, many small branches of vices grow to the soul’s destruction; to discuss them in the limited space of this letter would be lengthy and not especially necessary.

### V

The soul is also exceedingly ennobled, in its chief part—which is called the mind—by the image and likeness of its Creator. This image is at last clear and beautiful in it if it is bound by the whole desire of its being to God its Creator. Although, when it withdraws from God, it becomes base and deformed, nevertheless, if it possesses reason or perceives through understanding, a certain dignity of its nature remains in it.

Concerning such a soul, withdrawing from love of its Creator, divine Scripture says:

> Although a human being walks in the image of God, he is nevertheless troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.  
> (Psalm 38:7)

This shows that such vanity cannot remove from the soul the image of God. Although human nature is indeed great, it can nevertheless be corrupted, because it is not the highest nature. Yet because it is the image of the highest nature—that is, of the divine nature—it is great and noble.

It was created noble by its Creator but made ignoble by its own fault, namely, when it turns away from God’s service, wishing to use its own power. This is the first evil in every rational creature.

The soul therefore lives in an ordered way if it loves the one who is above it, namely God, and wisely governs what it ought to govern, namely the bodily senses. Thus there are four things that the soul ought to love: what is above it, what is beside it, what it itself is, and what is beneath it. Of two of these, Scripture contains a commandment: the love of God and of one’s neighbor. No commandments have been established concerning love of oneself and of one’s flesh, because these two are understood to be contained in the first two. Whoever perfectly loves God or a neighbor cannot neglect himself.

For this is the soul’s supreme blessedness: to love the one from whom it exists, and to love the souls that share its blessedness, benefiting them either through the service of the flesh or through the gift of the mind—wishing good for them and doing whatever lies within its power.

### VI

The soul therefore has, as we have said, in its nature an image of the holy Trinity, in that it possesses understanding, will, and memory. There is one soul, which is called the mind, one life, and one substance, and it possesses these three within itself. Yet these three are not three lives but one life, nor three minds but one mind; consequently, they are not three substances but one substance.

When the soul or mind is called “life” or “substance,” this is said in relation to itself. But when it is called “memory,” “understanding,” or “will,” it is spoken of relationally, in relation to something else. Therefore these three are one insofar as they are one life, one mind, and one substance; and whatever else is said of each in relation to itself is likewise spoken, even when taken together, not plurally but singularly. They are three insofar as they are related to one another.

For memory is memory of something, understanding is understanding of something, and will is will of something; and these are related to one another. Yet there is a certain unity in these three:

I understand that I understand, will, and remember; and I will that I understand, remember, and will; and I remember that I understand, will, and remember.

Thus each of the three is grasped within each of the others. But concerning these matters elsewhere.

### VII

Now let us consider the soul’s marvelous speed in forming the things it perceives through the bodily senses. Through these senses, as through messengers, it perceives whatever sensible things—known or unknown—it encounters; then, with ineffable speed, it immediately forms their images within itself and stores the formed images in the treasury of its memory.

For just as someone who has seen Rome forms Rome in his mind and represents what it is like, so, when he hears the name or remembers Rome, his mind immediately returns to the memory where it has stored the image of Rome, and there recognizes what it previously deposited there.

More marvelous still is the fact that, if unknown things are read or heard with the ears, the soul immediately forms an image of the unknown thing. Thus perhaps one of us has formed Jerusalem in his soul, imagining what it is like, although it is very different from the way the soul imagines it when it is pictured.

Similarly, in the case of a human being—for example, Abraham—a person forms in his soul an image of what Abraham might have been. From the other human beings he has seen, he imagines all Abraham’s limbs in the same way as he recognizes them in others or in himself.

He does not imagine walls, houses, and streets in Abraham as he does in Jerusalem. Rather, whatever he has seen in other cities known to him, he imagines could exist in Jerusalem. From familiar forms he imagines the unfamiliar. For in imagining the city of Jerusalem he does not imagine human limbs, but buildings customary in cities.

The human mind does this with everything: from what is known it imagines what is unknown, possessing all these forms within itself. Whenever it wishes to think of one particular thing, it thinks of it at once. The soul does not leave its seat in order to learn something; it remains within itself and recognizes within itself the image that it previously formed with marvelous speed.

This explains why, if the soul suddenly forgets something and then remembers it again, it does not find, at the moment when it forgets, the little place—or place—where it has stored what it is seeking and later remembers, whether by attending to the matter or not attending to it.

### VIII

From this speed of the soul—by which it forms within itself everything heard, seen, sensed, smelled, or tasted, and recognizes again what it has found—the marvelous power of God and the efficacy of nature may in some measure be understood.

When I am thinking about Jerusalem, at that moment I cannot think about Rome. When I am thinking about any one thing, I cannot at that same moment think about several things; only the one thing that I am then thinking about is present to me in my soul, until that thought departs, sooner or later, and another takes its place.

But to the nature and ineffable knowledge of almighty God all things are present simultaneously, always present, and never departing. This is what is meant when it is said that God is wholly everywhere: all things that exist, that have existed, or that will exist, he possesses as present simultaneously—not once only, but always.

No one can adequately marvel at the fact that this living and heavenly sense, which is called the mind or *animus*, is so mobile that it does not rest even when it is asleep; and so swift that in a single instant of time it may illuminate the heavens, fly across the seas if it wishes, and traverse lands and cities. In thought it can set before itself everything it desires, however far away and widely separated those things may be.

Yet someone wonders whether God’s divine mind has all the parts of the world simultaneously and always present to it, since it governs everything, present everywhere and wholly everywhere, even though the power and force of the human mind, enclosed within a mortal body, are so great that not even the barriers of this heavy and sluggish body, to which it is bound, can in any way restrain it from possessing the free power of thought, restless as it is in its desire for repose.

### IX

We must know with complete certainty that, if the soul had remained in the nobility in which it was created by the Creator, it would be wholly immortal, as the souls of the saints are. But when it was corrupted through free choice, at the instigation of the evil spirit, it became partly mortal from immortal, though not entirely so.

As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. When the soul leaves the body, the body dies and is rightly called dead, because it is without sensation. Yet the body remains a certain corruption arising from the nature of the flesh, although it is not vivified by the soul.

The soul’s death, however, occurs when God abandons it by withdrawing the gift of his grace on account of the magnitude of its crimes; it dies in the better part of itself.

The Creator glorified the soul in its nature with two dignities: eternity and blessedness. The soul’s blessedness is, plainly, to have God within itself.

How does it have him? By being just, because God is just; merciful, because God is merciful; good, because God is good; holy, because God is holy; and by possessing charity, because “God is charity” (1 John 4:8).

Whoever possesses these qualities most abundantly within himself has within himself the greater likeness and image of God. But whoever does not possess these qualities in the soul, together with others like them that the Apostle called the fruits of the Spirit, will become unworthy of God’s dwelling and will be half-alive, as the robbers stripped and wounded the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho and left him half-alive (Luke 10:30).

The soul will be half-alive if, because of vices and iniquities, it loses the blessedness of seeing and possessing God. Yet it cannot lose the eternity for which it was created. Its blessedness will indeed be changed into misery because of its sins. This will happen if appetite or anger rules in a human being more than reason, in which alone the human being excels the animals.

Therefore it was said of such a person in the Psalm:

> When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them.  
> (Psalm 48:13)

Just as speech makes the flesh superior to the other animals, so the soul is nobler than they through reason alone. As mistress and queen, it ought to govern and moderate all bodily appetites and movements of the spirit from the lofty seat of equity.

### X

The soul may be defined in accordance with the property of its nature as follows: the soul or spirit is an intellectual, rational spirit, always in motion, always living, capable of good and evil will; ennobled by free choice according to the Creator’s kindness, but corrupted by its own will; liberated by God’s grace [in those matters in which God himself willed it]; created to govern the movements of the flesh; invisible, incorporeal, without weight, without color, bounded, yet wholly present in each of the members of its flesh. In it the image of its Creator was spiritually impressed at the first creation, as we showed above.

Although it is wretched when it falls away from its Creator into itself, it cannot lose eternity or the image of its dignity. It does not possess the power to leave the flesh and return to it, but this depends on the will of the one who made it and placed it in the flesh.

It will leave the flesh, even unwillingly, to be brought before God’s judgment; and when God has judged, it will enter the place corresponding to its merits, awaiting the judgment of the last day, so that it may receive the flesh in which it lived in this world.

This spirit is sometimes troubled by cares, sometimes grieves over bodily pains, sometimes rejoices in happiness, sometimes recalls what it knows, and sometimes seeks to know what it does not know. It wills some things and does not will others. Love is naturally present in it, because love must be discerned by understanding and restrained by reason from unlawful pleasures, so that it may love what ought to be loved.

### XI

According to the function of its activity, the soul is now called by various names. It is “soul” when it gives life; “spirit” when it contemplates; “sense” when it perceives; “animus” when it is wise; “mind” when it understands; “reason” when it distinguishes; “will” when it consents; and “memory” when it remembers.

These names are not divided in the substance as they are in the terminology, because all of them designate one soul.

A distinction of this kind may be made between spirit and soul: every soul is spirit, but not every spirit is soul. The blessed Apostle Paul also wonderfully distinguishes between spirit and mind when he says: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:15).

He sings with the spirit who utters things with his mouth without understanding their obscure meanings; he sings with the mind who understands those same meanings through the power of the mind. For the spirit of King Nebuchadnezzar had been shaped so that he might see future things, but his mind had not been illuminated so that he might understand what he saw.

Then a prophet came, illuminated by the divine Spirit, who both understood what the king saw and explained what it signified (Daniel 2).

### XII

This must therefore be known without doubt: the soul’s beauty is virtue, and its ugliness is vice. If it desires to contemplate God, itself, or anything spiritual, it turns away from the bodily senses so that they may not hinder it while it searches out spiritual things.

Often it becomes so absorbed in some thought that, although its eyes are open, it does not see what is present; it does not understand a voice that is sounding, nor feel a body that is touching it [alternatively: “it did not see, did not understand, did not feel”].

For it governs the body through the five senses, although it is none of these things. When we think about the soul, we must think of nothing corporeal. Just as God surpasses every creature, so the soul surpasses every corporeal creature in the dignity of its nature.

It also governs its body through light and air, which are the more excellent bodies of the world. The light of the soul announces the forms of all things; the soul receives these forms within itself, gives them their particular shape, and stores them after they have been shaped.

When some afflictions befall the body, the soul is offended because it lacks the means of maintaining the balance required for carrying out what it wishes; this offense is called pain. But if it is deprived of the service of its members to such an extent that it has nothing to do through them, it departs, as though angered at its dwelling.

There is no better way to say what the soul is than to call it the spirit of life—not the life that exists in animals without a rational mind, but a life now lower than that of the angels and destined to become angelic in the future, if here it lives according to the command of its Creator.

### XIII

The origin of souls must be left to the knowledge of God alone. How many vain theories philosophers have fabricated about it, and how many opinions Christian teachers have advanced, leaving almost nothing certain.

[Note: Augustine’s opinion on the origin of the soul may be found in his Letter 166.]

Accordingly, the blessed Augustine wrote and sent to the blessed Jerome concerning the origin of the soul, wishing to know what so great a teacher affirmed about its origin. If that book is found with you, read it and learn what that most acute investigator of natural matters said concerning the soul’s origin.

In that discussion he set forth, as I believe, four opinions, to which the blessed Jerome replied in a very brief—but extremely penetrating—letter. We read that little work in our homeland, but it is not found here with us; nor is the letter of reply to it.

The same teacher also composed, as is read in his books of *Retractions*, other little works on the nature of the soul: one book *On the Quantity of the Soul*; one book *On the Immortality of the Soul*; one book *On Two Souls*; and four books *On the Immortality and Origin of the Soul*, which we have not yet found.

If they should be found in the imperial library, seek them out, read them, and send them to us, united by the fellowship of charity, so that we may read them.

For all Catholic writers agree on this: the soul was created by God. It is not part of God’s nature, because if it had been taken from God’s nature, it could not sin. Nor is it a tangible or visible body. Nor can it die in such a way that it ceases to exist. Nor can it be freed from the guilt of the first transgression except through the grace and mystery of the mediator between God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, who assumed the full nature of our humanity, without any sin, into the person of his divinity.

For the whole human being sinned, and the whole human being had to be liberated, according to the dispensation of eternal mercy in God. The whole human being had to be assumed—namely, soul and flesh. His soul, that is, the soul of our Redeemer, possesses such holiness and justification that through him the souls of all who believe in him can be sanctified and justified. His flesh possesses such purity and freedom from sin that, through divine grace working in it, the flesh of all who trust in him can be cleansed and liberated.

For the blood that flowed from that same flesh, wounded by the soldier’s lance, is the price of human salvation. Through its outpouring, that flaming guardian of paradise was extinguished, and the way was opened for the faithful to the tree of life, planted beside the streams of living waters (Psalm 1:3).

The most wise Solomon remembered this tree when, after saying many things in praise of wisdom, he spoke as follows:

> Blessed is the person who has found wisdom and who abounds in prudence.  
> And shortly afterward:  
> Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful. She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds her.  
> (Proverbs 3:13, 17)

### XIV

The beauty and adornment of the human soul is the pursuit of wisdom—not that wisdom which is usually occupied with earthly affairs, but rather that by which God is worshiped and loved.

Devote yourself wholly to this, most noble Virgin, with the full attention of your mind, because in it is a life blessed with complete tranquility; in it the image of that highest Trinity is happily perfected.

Here is the desirable treasure that rests in the mouth of the prudent and abounds in the heart of the wise. It will not be found in the lying fictions of Virgil, but it is found abundantly in evangelical truth.

Of true wisdom it is said: “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Sirach 1:1). Whatever is rightly understood and loved through wisdom is God’s gift. Therefore everyone who is wise according to God is blessed.

Hence it is said in Job: “The wisdom of a human being is piety, and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28), wishing, under the single name “piety,” to designate the worship of the whole divine religion.

What is more blessed for the soul than to love the highest good, which is God? What is happier than to prepare itself to be worthy of eternal blessedness, since it knows with complete truth that it is immortal?

Do not think that it is enough for you merely to know what you ought to do unless you also fulfill in action what you know. Very many consider themselves wise and boast that they know the way of truth, but they are not truly wise if they do not possess the strength of spirit to advance—or perfect—in action what they understand.

True wisdom, therefore, is knowing what you ought to do and accomplishing what you know. Accordingly, the soul does not perfectly possess any of the four virtues of the soul that we mentioned above unless it possesses them all, because all of them aim at the one commandment of charity. Charity alone, in the truth of the Catholic faith, will make the soul worthy of the dwelling of the holy Trinity, in whose image we showed above that it was created.

Concerning its nature and character, as you requested, we have touched briefly on these matters, insofar as the narrow limits of a letter allowed. It may seem strange, in a way, to students that you wished to be considered more familiar to me than to yourself. For from what do you live, or through what do you possess reason, except in the substance of the soul? I saw you only very rarely with my eyes, and through them I could not behold the nature of your soul.

Nevertheless, in accordance with the Lord’s common commandment, I love you; and because of the excellent reputation of your studies, which I have often heard from others, I wish you always to advance and to please God, so that you may become worthy to know the nature and character of the soul and may see with perfect knowledge in future blessedness what you now see in a riddle.

Therefore, dearest daughter, I wish you to pursue with undivided will the happiness of the eternal homeland, which I know you wisely desire as your wisdom. May no ambition of this world turn you away from desiring it, nor the pleasure of any temporal thing. The days of this life are few, but the recompense of merits has no end.

True wisdom is to love true life with all one’s heart and to strive with all one’s strength to reach it, so that the one who appears to profess most truly in words that he loves it may deserve to attain it. For the kingdom of God is not merely in speech, but in the power of the Holy Spirit and in the perfect splendor of holy merits.

[Note: In the Tegernsee manuscript the title is: “A Poem on the Noble and Subtle Nature of the Soul.”]

## ELEGIAC POEM

He who created the sea, who created the earth, who created the lofty heaven,

who governs all created things by his command,

had ordained that human beings should rule over the things beneath the stars,

for he alone among living creatures flourishes through sense and reason;

for among living beings he is able to recognize the Creator of the world,

and already to know him in the citadel of the mind.

Created by the Eternal, so that he might be eternally blessed,

he alone is indeed the wondrous image of the great God.

Hence noble is the nature of the subtle soul,

and powerful to perceive all things through its own understanding.

It traverses the sea, the lands, and the lofty heaven,

although it is enclosed in the prison of its own flesh.

Just as the eye of the body directs its sight toward the stars,

although it remains fixed in one place in the citadel of the flesh,

so the soul is the immortal glory and golden light of this life,

worthy always to possess its God within itself.

If it is good, wise, and adorns itself with the love of Christ,

it is able to live happily in the citadel of heaven,

and after the labors of this life,

through the ages, to behold him forever in the heavenly kingdom.

God is eternal light; to him belong praise and glory, and he is the reward,

if the soul has lived well and worthily for God.

Let it now be holy; let it be chaste and pure through pious merits;

let it always flourish everywhere in sacred studies.

Let it govern itself and its bodily acts with vigor,

as a powerful queen, according to heavenly laws.

Let it desire nothing evil within itself, wish for nothing unjust,

harm no one, and neither wish for, do, nor love anything harmful.

Let it not darken the time of life given to it by stains upon itself.

Let it be pious in serving God, holy, and at peace.

Let it now live honorably within itself through excellent conduct,

so that, thus disciplined, it may please its pious bridegroom.

The soul is spirit, already wholly present everywhere in its members,

living through its own members and made to love God.

Let it praise without end its kindly Creator,

who has granted it openly to know him.

Prudent in worship, let it venerate him with gracious devotion;

this alone is the soul’s salvation, glory, and life.

Therefore let it adorn itself with heavenly actions,

before the eyes of its own Lord, night and day,

who sees all the secrets of the heart with heavenly light,

and whom no will can conceal anything.

For this reason it is necessary that we apply ourselves earnestly,

so that the mind, worthy of God, may handle sacred matters well,

in order that it may look only toward heavenly things,

its breast already filled with the holy love of God.

This is truly the soul’s true glory above all our possessions,

its nobility and blessed rest.

Remember now to exercise yourself in this pursuit,

woman renowned, so that you may please God as a distinguished bride.

## ANOTHER ADONIC POEM

May the human being praise you,

kindly Creator,

with heart and mind,

in love of peace;

not merely because he is

a small part of the world,

but because for you, Holy Creator,

he alone is a great image

of the mind,

in the citadel of the heart,

while he lives piously

with a pure breast.

O God and light,

may your praise always

fill hearts and mouths,

so that we may always love you,

holy everywhere.

Guard these pious words,

faithful Virgin,

with watchful speech [the reading *cavelo* is uncertain],

so that gentle Christ

may wholly govern

your times.

Direct to him your chaste

temple in body and mind,

sweet friend,

and always fare well

without end.

May he alone,

I pray, always be for you

light, love,

and the form of salvation,

everlasting life,

perpetual glory.

I have sung this poem to you in the noble senary meter, a meter that is most perfect in its parts, wishing you to be perfect in your understanding. The wisest emperor can very easily explain the principles of this meter, as well as of the others, to your discernment. His mind’s nobility is marvelous: amid so many cares of the palace and affairs of the kingdom, he took care to learn fully the mysteries of the philosophers—something that scarcely anyone else today, sluggish with leisure, attempts to understand.

Nor is it necessary for you to seek from us the causes of things or the hidden principles of physical knowledge, since you daily make use of his most illustrious wisdom and behold his venerable face. Nor must you visit Jerusalem from Ethiopia by a long and arduous journey in order to see Solomon disputing about the natures of things.

Behold, he is beside you—the one whom the queen of the South sought through so many difficulties of the earth. But with the same celebrated praise you must be told:

> Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants, who always stand before you and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God, who has taken pleasure in you and set you upon the throne of your people, because the Lord loved his people forever.  
> (1 Kings 10:1 and following)

O daughters of Jerusalem, behold our Solomon shining in the diadem of wisdom. Imitate his most noble conduct; turn away from vices and cultivate virtues.

A great necessity for living excellently rests upon you, if you do not wish to disregard it, since you are daily in his company—in the company of one in whom you possess an example of every kind of goodness. Thus, through his present and most sacred conduct, may you deserve to reach with him that presence of which Wisdom herself sang:

> King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its back of gold, and its ascent of purple; he paved its center with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.  
> (Song of Songs 3:9–10)

## LITANY OR PRAYER TO CHRIST

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ.

You are my mercy; have mercy on me.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that I may believe in you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that I may know you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that I may love you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that I may hope in you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that my soul may live in you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that my flesh may rejoice in you.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, so that my life may advance in you.

Have mercy, Lord God the Father, my glory, my life.

Have mercy, Christ the Savior, my salvation, my strength.

Have mercy, Holy Spirit the Paraclete, my consolation, my illumination.

Have mercy, Lord, God who are Trinity and Unity.

I praise you, I adore you, I confess you.

My peace, my hope, my praise, my light.

My beauty, my blessedness.

To you be praise, to you glory, to you thanksgiving, always and everywhere, throughout everlasting ages.

[Note: From the Tegernsee manuscript.]

## POEM: WHAT THE PALMS CUSTOMARILY CARRIED IN THE HANDS SIGNIFY MYSTICALLY

White, they shine like lilies among flower-bearing fields;

so may the pious Virgin shine in sacred merits.

[Note: In the Saint Gall manuscript used by Canisius (*Thesaurus Monumentorum*, vol. II, Basnage’s edition, p. 377), other verses followed the preceding couplet. It is rightly uncertain whether they belong to Eulalia or to the letter written to her, since they seem rather to be inscriptions from various places. They run as follows:

While you sit joyfully as possessor in a beautiful hall,

remember then that wretched people are standing outside.

So that [lacuna] he who gave you this enduring [thing],

and now a dwelling, merciful Christ, in the citadel of heaven.

Let whoever flees the cold come to warm his limbs here;

let the chilled traveler come rejoicing to me.

The sacred cross of God shines with the blood of the Most High;

may it graciously protect us and our dwelling together.

May this door always stand open to dear friends,

who seek the father with joyful heart.

Here rests the abbot rejoicing; may he rise again in health—

may your right hand preserve him, powerful Christ.

May Christ be your love, your drink, your food—Christ everything:

light, way, life, salvation, praise, venerable Father.]

In verse I shall briefly explain, dear friend, what the palm signifies,

which we shall all carry in our hands.

[Note: Perhaps read *amicae*: “I shall explain to my female friend.”]

Palm, great King Christ, is the sign of your triumph.

The palm teaches us to conquer our own flesh.

The palm is the heavenly sign of the reward to come.

This palm urges us to hope for the life to come.

The first victory is the victory of Christ hanging upon the cross.

To conquer ourselves is no small victory.

Conquer yourself, I beg you; always conquer yourself, my friend,

and may Christ be the reward and end of your labor.

## SEVENTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE CONFESSION OF SINS, TO THE BOYS OF SAINT MARTIN

## LETTER

[Note: In the manuscript of Saint Emmeram the title is: “Letter and Admonition of Albinus to the Boys and Young Men,” that is, “On Confession.” Canisius conjectures that this letter is the same as the book *On Auricular Confession*, which Balaeus lists among Alcuin’s works; perhaps rightly. Nevertheless, the manuscript codices consistently bear the title prefixed here. BASNAGE.—Concerning boys, their offering in monasteries, their studies, and their discipline, consult D. Edmond Martène, *Commentary on Chapter 59 of the Rule of Saint Benedict*.]

To the most beloved sons in Christ, young men of good hope, who appear to serve the Lord Jesus in the church of the supreme pontiff and great protector, the blessed Martin, and who are instructed by ecclesiastical teachers in the Lord God [manuscript: “in the house of God”:] I, Albinus [Saint Emmeram manuscript: *Alchuuinus*], desiring the good of your salvation, send greetings in Christ the Lord and wishes for your eternal prosperity [alternative: “the prosperity of your salvation”].

[Textual apparatus: II: *quem* (“which”) has the alternative *quo* (“by which”); *Deus* has the variant accusative *Deum*; twice, *quid cuique* (“what to each member”) has *quid cui*. III: *rationalis* (“rational”) has *rationabilis* (“reasonable”); *qua* has *quae*. IV: *nihil* has *aliud* (“else”); *tenebit* has *tenet* (“holds”); *phylargiria* has *philargeria* (both “avarice”). V: *vincta est* (“is bound”) has *juncta est* (“is joined”). VII: at both occurrences *enim fingit* (“indeed forms”) is perhaps *etiam fingit* (“also forms”); the supplied *sed* is editorially supplied. VIII: *efficacia* has *efficientia* (“efficacy”). IX: *ad quam* has the manuscript reading *sed tamen ad quam* (“but nevertheless, for which”). X: *spectare* (“to look toward”) has *exspectare* (“to await”). XI: *obscuras* (“obscure”) is editorially supplied. XII: the reading “Just as God surpasses every creature, so the soul surpasses every corporeal creature” is supplied as *creaturam, sic anima omnem*. XIII: *brevissima* has *parvissima* (“very small”); *per eum* (“through him”) has *per eam* (“through it/her”); *possint* has *queunt* (“are able”); and *possint* has *possunt* (“are able”). XIV: *se dignum* has *se dignam* (“herself worthy”); *proficiendum* (“advancing”) has *perficiendum* (“perfecting”); *videatur* has *videtur* (“appears”); in the elegiac poem *sic moderata* has the added *mens* (“mind”); *incubuit* (“has pressed upon”) has *incumbit* (“presses upon”); and *per praesentes illius ... mores* has *per praesentis illius ... mores* (“through the conduct of his presence”).]

I. Desiring you, dearest sons, to advance toward the salvation of your souls, I have therefore endeavored, with paternal affection, to address you certain admonitions in gentle speech, so that through them you may merit to possess the prosperity of the present life and, God having mercy, the blessedness of the future, and so that, instructed in God’s service, you may bring the frail years of your age to the perfect day of old age. You also, holy Fathers, lights of this fraternal congregation, teachers and guides of the young in every virtue, I beseech you to admonish them—that is, your disciples—to learn diligently what pleases God [Al., may please] and pertains to the salvation of their souls, so that from their progress and prosperity you may have an everlasting reward with the Lord [Al., with God]. Exhort them to serve God soberly, chastely, modestly, with all humility and obedience, in good conduct, holy behavior, religious purity, and especially concerning confession of their sins, because many are the snares of diabolical deceit laid against adolescents in carnal desire and the other vices of youth.

II. Yet, by God’s gift, the devil gains nothing from his wickedness if the young wish to make a pure confession and perform worthy works of repentance—that is, if they do not add wounds to wounds or reopen wounds that have been healed. For it is a saving remedy of repentance not to commit again the things of which one must repent. For it is written: “God has given penitents a portion of justice” [Vulg., “the way of justice”] (Ecclus. XVII, 20). Therefore, repentant, confess [Cod. Vat., *confiteri*, “to confess”] your own crimes; disclose through confession the secret of your iniquity. God knows what you have done in secret; if the tongue does not speak of it, conscience will not be able to conceal it. In vain do you suppose [Mss., *aestimas*, “you suppose,” for *aestimes*] that your crimes can be hidden within walls. Everything you think hidden is open [Cod. Vat., *pate*, “be open,” for *patet*] to God; and even if you can escape the eyes of human beings in your sins, whatever you have done in secret can in no way escape God’s sight.

[Col. 0651D] Tell your sins in confession before you experience the anger of the Judge. Believe me: everything you have sinned will become venial if you are not ashamed to confess and take care to cleanse yourself through repentance [Cod. S. Em., “if you take care”; Al., “if you do not cease to cleanse yourself through repentance”], as the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘I will confess my iniquities against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. XXXI, 5). The Lord awaits from us the sacrifice of confession, so that he may grant us the pleasing gift of forgiveness—he who wills all human beings to be saved and none to perish—[Col. 0652A] as he says elsewhere in Scripture: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12, 15).

O singular benefit of the most merciful Judge! O magnificent treasure of divine compassion! For this reason he wishes to receive the gift of confession from sinners, so that he may find nothing requiring punishment. Let us not be ungrateful for so great a kindness of our Redeemer, who wishes rather [Cod. Vat., “prefers”] to forgive than to punish, rather to save than to destroy. What is not punished in the servant is acquired for the Lord; and much is contributed to the author if one assigned to punishment is pardoned. Nor does he desire to avenge who is ready to show mercy, saying of himself through the Prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” [ibid., 11]. Behold the true author of life, who does not [Col. 0652B] desire the death of the sinner, but the life of the one who turns [Al., “of the one who has turned]. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “So there will be joy in heaven before your Father and his angels over one sinner [Mss., *super unum peccatorem*, rather than *super uno peccatore*] who repents” (Luke XV, 7); and in the Prophet: “Tell your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 26).

Behold the gracious giver of forgiveness, who grants the joy of eternity in exchange for temporal gain [Ms., *luctu*, “grief,” for *lucru*], saying: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5); and elsewhere: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). For, as we have said, he says: “Tell your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” [Vulg., “Tell me if you have anything, so that you may be justified”], and not condemned, so that the reward of repentance, [Col. 0652C] not the punishment of sins, may remain in you.

III. Does God, as though ignorant, exhort us to confess our sins, though he knew them before they were committed, and though all hidden things lie open to his providence? You will then be able to obtain the perfect benefit of healing if you do not conceal the wounds of your conscience from the physician. For I think that, unless the physician is called in, the sick person is not healed. Your confession is the medicine of your wounds and the surest support of your salvation. A sick person seeks medicine from a physician, who often toils with uncertain effort over the patient. God, however, heals without toil and grants the medicines of forgiveness without delay, if repentance, devoted and written with tears, is read in the ears of his mercy [Ms., “if repentance is read”].

No one restores you, O human being, better than the one who made you; nor does anyone else heal except the one who both scourges and cures. For he alone knows the frailty of his own work, and he awaits only this: that you confess. There will be no delay before you are healed. Through the prophet Ezekiel he says: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII).

IV. The most kindly Judge grants us an opportunity to accuse ourselves of our sins before God’s priest, so that the devil may not again accuse us of them before Christ the Judge. He wishes them to be forgiven [in this age], so that they may not be punished in the future. Therefore the merciful Father, [Col. 0653A] when he sees us condemning our sins through repentance, rejoices to show mercy and desires to exercise his proper ministry of mercy toward penitents, as he testifies through the prophet Isaiah: “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. XLIII, 25); and again: “Turn back to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and gracious, patient and rich in mercy” (Joel II, 13).

Knowing this, blessed David says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities” (Ps. XXXI, 5). Conversely, if the sin that a person has committed is denied [read: “covered”], the punishment of guilt is increased, because obstinacy is punished in the denial of the crime. But perhaps you say: “The magnitude of my sins terrifies me.” On the contrary, all the more must you, O sinner, persist in the medicine of confession, lest you perish in the rottenness of your wounds because you are ashamed to open the many pains of your ulcers to the physician. The abundance of divine clemency can in no way be overcome by the number of your sins.

“Do not delay from day to day to turn back,” Scripture says, “because you do not know what the coming day may bring” [Cod. S. Em., “what the day will bring forth”] (Ecclus. V, 8). For whatever the final day finds you to be, such will you be judged [Ms., *judicaberis*, rather than *judicaris*]. Nor did God wish you to know that day beforehand, so that you might always be prepared. As you wish to stand before the Judge, so prepare yourself while you have time to act. Be a devoted merchant. Buy for yourself the kingdom of God with the profits of repentance, remembering the Lord’s words: “Do penance, and the kingdom of God will draw near to you” (Matt. II, 3).

V. Therefore, O young man, God became human for your sake, [Col. 0653C] to redeem you, and handed himself over to death, to save you for life. Why do you lie in the death of crimes? Rise and say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven” (Luke XV). Bring forward for yourself a faithful witness to your repentance. You wish to have clean clothing; why do you not much more seek to have a clean soul? You do not wish to appear filthy in the sight of human beings; why do you not much more fear to appear filthy with sins [Al., “to proceed, filthy with sins”] in the sight of God? Wash yourself in the fountain of tears, lest anything in you offend the eyes of his majesty.

Who, I ask, when he falls does not seek to rise? Who becomes ill and does not desire to recover? Who is in danger and does not wish to escape? Later you will regret your delay if you do not consider what benefits your soul toward salvation. Rise, son, rise; appease by repentance the Father whom you have offended by your crime. Confess your fault, so that you may be healed by the physician. Be concerned for your salvation. If you yourself do not care for yourself, who will be able to help you toward salvation? Or who will be faithful to you if you yourself prove faithless to yourself [Cod. S. Em., *probaris*, “if you are proved”]? 

It is great faithlessness [for you] not to care for your salvation; not to raise yourself, through repentance, when you are dying in sins. The farther you have withdrawn from God because of the magnitude of your crimes, the more earnestly you should strive to draw near through repentance. The merciful Father is ready to receive you if you do not delay in returning. Conversion seems harsh to you, because it requires you to abandon carnal desires; but much harsher is the condition of burning in eternal flames and being handed over to everlasting punishments for a brief period of luxury. How many now assigned to infernal torments would have wished to turn back, if time for conversion had been given them! All the hardships of this age appear light and, in a certain sense, pleasant when compared with the torments of hell.

You served the devil in luxury; serve [Mss., *servi*] Christ in chastity. Consider the end of each. Luxury sends a person into the flames. Chastity joined to charity leads us into the kingdom of God. Return to the way from which you wandered. The body is afflicted by fasts [Mss., “let the body be afflicted”], but the beauty of the soul is produced [Mss., “restored”]. Let the adornment of the body be cheap; the adornment of holiness itself is of the highest value. Constant vigils in prayers and in the praise of God are an imitation of angelic [Col. 0654B] life. Sparse food is nourishment for the soul.

If you have the means, extend your hand to the poor [Cod. S. Em., “so that you may be able to extend your hand to the poor”], because the poor person’s hand is Christ’s treasury. Nor will you be able rightly to excuse yourself from the work of mercy, since even a cup of cold water will be repaid with an eternal reward. To visit the sick, console the sorrowful, welcome guests, and refresh those suffering from hunger or thirst is possession of the kingdom of God in heaven, as is read in the Gospel (Matt. XXV). In the performance of such works, O son, forgiveness of sins is bestowed [Cod. Vat., “in the excuse,” incorrectly]; moreover, entry into everlasting blessedness is granted.

VI. Do not be of a degenerate spirit. You have been consecrated in baptism as a son of God; but such exalted nobility [Col. 0654C] can be preserved only by the great dignity of good conduct. The heavenly Father—indeed, the Lord of all—disdains to have those subject to sins as his sons. Shake from your neck the yoke of diabolical captivity. Return to the compassion of your Father’s love. Return to the Lord [Al., “to God”], son; return, and come back to life from death, and be restored from being lost.

The good shepherd seeks the wandering sheep and rejoices more over the one found than over the one not lost, carrying it back on his shoulders amid the angelic hosts (Luke XV). Consider the most merciful sentence of the Lord’s compassion, when he says: “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX, 13), to repentance. The Lord therefore calls sinners to repentance, because he desires rather to save than to condemn, and prefers that we rejoice with the saints rather than be punished with the devil.

[Col. 0654D] He calls us through himself; he calls us through the holy Scriptures; he also calls us through catholic teachers, so that we may return to him, who is ready to receive us if we are not too sluggish to come to him. Let us hear blessed John the Evangelist exhorting us to repentance. For he says in his Epistle: “If we say that we have no sins [Al., ‘no sin’], we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he may forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John I, 8).

If no one is without sin, who is there who does not need repentance, which can scarcely be fruitful without confession? Let us consider the command of blessed James the Apostle, who says: “Confess your sins to one another” [Col. 0655A] (James V, 16). Let us remember that our Redeemer preferred the sinful publican who confessed himself to the Pharisee who praised himself for his own righteousness. For our Creator knows the frailty of our nature; therefore he has granted the medicines of repentance for our wounds. Let us say with the Prophet: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed.” Likewise: “Lord, heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Jer. XVII).

VII. Therefore, dearest sons, hasten to the medicine of confession. Open your wounds in confession, so that the medicines of salvation may be effective in you. The days of this life are passing, and the hour is uncertain for each of us at which [Cod. Vat., *quia*, “because”] dust will return to dust and the spirit will return to the Lord who gave it, so that it may be judged according to its works. [Col. 0655B] Then the soul will hear whatever it did here in secret while joined to the flesh. If it is now ashamed to confess its sins and be cleansed [Mss., “corrected”] through repentance, the malignant accuser will stand against it—he who once suggested that it sin—if we neglect to go before the face of the Judge through confessions [Mss., “through confession”].

For whatever we humbly confess concerning our sins, the devil has no power to bring any of it against us in that fearful judgment of our life. Act now, young men, adolescents, and boys; free yourselves from diabolical servitude. Through repentance hasten together to the most merciful compassion of almighty God. Do not lose, through the desires of your flesh, the joys of heaven and the blessedness of the eternal kingdom among the angelic hosts. Rather, strengthen yourselves and fight manfully [“act and”] against your adversary, so that you may deservedly be crowned faithfully [Ms., “happily”] with God’s saints and possess everlasting glory with them.

And you, most holy teachers and fathers of this household, teach your sons to live piously, soberly, and chastely before God, in all humility, obedience, and holiness; teach them to make a pure confession of their sins to Christ’s priests and to wash away the filth of the flesh’s luxury with the tears of repentance, and not to repeat those sins, because later wounds are worse than earlier ones. Know that you yourselves have an everlasting reward with the Lord for the salvation of your sons, so that, for those whose services you employ on earth, you may possess in heaven the perpetual reward of their prosperity.

THE FIFTH PART OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, TEACHER OF CHARLES THE GREAT.—HAGIOGRAPHICAL WORKS.

[Col. 0655]

157 PRELIMINARY NOTICE.

[Col. 0655C] Just as blessed Alcuin repeatedly bears witness, in many places and in various monuments that can be read in these works, that he was always especially devoted to the veneration of the saints—those crowned in heaven with the glory of their merits and rejoicing eternally in the intuitive vision of God—so too he declined no task demanded of him by friends: whether compiling anew the Lives of certain holy men, correcting those that were crude, abridging longer works for easier use, or finally reducing them to the form of a sermon that could be presented to the people for their edification.

He himself makes sufficiently clear in his letters or prefaces what occasion led him to write or embellish the Lives of Saints Vedast, Richarius, and Willibrord. But the brief writing on the Life of Saint Martin, which is divided into two parts, as if into two sermons, lacks a preface; and the first part was published by Quercetanus from an earlier Paris edition of the year 1610 [Note: [Col. 0655D] At the end of the History of Saint Gregory of Tours] and from two manuscript codices. The other was taken from a manuscript codex of the Putean brothers. Both end with the same epilogue and nearly the same words. Hence, following the distinguished author of the *History of France’s Literature*, vol. IV, p. 318, no. 24, we suspect that the two writings originally formed a single work, later divided into two sermons, with the epilogue of the whole work also attached to the first part.

Saint Odilo the Abbot testifies (Cluniac Library, p. 204) that Alcuin elucidated the Life of Saint Martin written by Sulpicius Severus with fuller expressions. But since no such fuller Life appears anywhere, and the author of Alcuin’s Life makes no mention of it, I believe that in Saint Odilo “fuller expressions” should be read as “clearer expressions.” This is aptly understood of these two writings, composed in a shorter and clearer style than the work of Sulpicius Severus and borrowed from it.

Alcuin was not the first author of the Life of Saint Vedast, but its corrector, as he states in the opening of his dedicatory letter to Abbot Radon. What that earlier Life may have been is not sufficiently certain. André du Chesne, in volume I of the *Historical Writers of France*, considers it to be the work from which the author excerpted certain material for embellishing the deeds of King Clovis I, and which Godefridus Henschenius later published, under the title of the *Shorter Life*, from manuscripts of Vedast in volume I of the February volume.

But this Life differs so greatly from the one written by Alcuin that it may be considered not corrected but wholly transformed into another work. Hence Henschenius thinks it not improbable [Col. 0657A] that some other, more extensive Life existed, which Alcuin corrected. Lambecius, *Vienna Imperial Library*, vol. II, pp. 409–415, believed that the Life corrected by Alcuin—at the same time adding what is read in printed editions concerning the translation of Saint Vedast’s body by Autbert and Saint Audomar—was the one preserved in a codex written in Alcuin’s age in the library of the Imperial Vienna; but in that codex the letter to Abbot Radon is also absent, and nothing is said about the aforementioned translation.

Whatever the case may be, here we present the Life that appears under Alcuin’s name both in printed and manuscript codices, in the form in which, compared with manuscript codices, it has been published in volume I of the February *Acts of the Saints* of the Bollandists, with variant readings and notes added by Henschenius. There is also, from the same edition, an *Exhortation to Imitate the Virtues of Saint Vedast*, described in the *Acts* and by the same Alcuin. This is undoubtedly the work that he promised in Letter 51 to the monks of Vedast.

[Col. 0657B] Next follows the Life of the most blessed Father Richarius, a title that Alcuin himself wished it to bear in his preface, or letter, to Charles Augustus. Before Alcuin described the deeds of this blessed man, another Life of him had already existed, arranged in a simpler style, together with a larger book of miracles. At the request of blessed Angilbert, Abbot of Centula, and with the authority of Charles the Great also involved, Alcuin polished this Life, leaving the book of miracles untouched. That book, together with the original writing or Life, is believed to have perished.

Moreover, according to Hariulf in book II, chapter 11 of the *Chronicle of Centula* (vol. IV of Achery’s *Spicilegium*), Alcuin wrote “antiphons, responsories, or hymns concerning the same saint, so that the feast of the great Father might seem to lack no fitting office.” It should be noted that in one hymn, addressing and praising Richarius himself, he says:

“You built a monastery near the place of Argubium,

and another at Centula; both endure in everlasting merit.”

[Col. 0657C] What Argubium may be is unknown, says Mabillon in the preliminary observations to this Life. It was undoubtedly a place near the forest of Crisciacum, in which the monastery called Forestis Cella (Forest-Monstier) was built by Saint Richarius, as is related below in chapter 2, no. 12. In a letter of Guido, bishop of Amiens, in book IV of the *Chronicle of Centula*, chapter 22, the altars of the villages of Argubium and Mons Elisius are mentioned.

The antiphons, responsories, and hymns composed by Alcuin in honor of Saint Richarius appear nowhere. But concerning the epitaph, which the cited author of the *Chronicle of Centula* reports there, we judge—not rashly—that Alcuin was not its author, because those verses proclaim that Saint Richarius was descended from a lofty lineage, shone with the world’s highest honors, and possessed great wealth; whereas Alcuin recalls at the beginning of the Life that he was born of parents who were not especially noble and, while living a rural life, displayed signs of his future holiness. These claims can scarcely be reconciled. We therefore relegate that poem at least to the category of doubtful works.

Here we present the Life of Saint Richarius divided into three chapters, corrected according to the editions of the most distinguished scholars [Col. 0658B] [Note: [Col. 0657C] Mabillon, *Benedictine Acts*, second century, part I, p. 189; Bollandist *Acts of the Saints*, vol. III, April, p. 441, Venetian edition; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXVI, no. 51], with the notes by which those same celebrated writers illuminated this Life.

Finally, we present the Life of Saint Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine, contained in two books, one in prose and the other in verse. Alcuin devoted himself to composing it around the year 796, more than fifty years after the holy man’s death, at the request, as is reported, of Beornred or Beornrad, formerly abbot of Echternach and later archbishop of Sens. At the end of the prose Life there is added a homily to be preached to the people on the feast of Saint Willibrord; at the end of the metrical Life an elegy on Saint Wilgis, the father of Saint Willibrord, has been added.

We have transcribed all these works from Quercetanus’s edition, which we nevertheless compared with the other editions of Canisius [Note: [Col. 0658C] Canisius, Basnage’s edition, vol. II, part I, pp. 458–471] and Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0658C] Mabillon, *Benedictine Acts*, third century, part I, p. 603], also borrowing their notes. Christian Daumius likewise inserted the metrical Life, together with its appended Elegy, into his collection of other poems, published at Zwickau in 1662 and 1672, as the author of the *History of Gallic Literature*, vol. IV, p. 321, reports. We have never seen that collection.

[Col. 0657]

159 FIRST WORK WRITTEN ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIN OF TOURS [Note: [Col. 0657D] In Vatican Codex 6074, of the eleventh century, p. 233, the following title is prefixed: “Homily on the feast of Saint Martin, by Albinus the teacher.” In other Vatican codices of the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries, it is noted in the margin that it was read [Col. 0658D] on the Octave of the feast of Saint Martin], in which his virtues are briefly and wonderfully expounded.

[Col. 0657D] I. After our Lord Jesus Christ the triumphant had ascended to the heights of heaven, and God had taken his seat in the Father’s majesty, he granted many lights of teachers to the ages, so that, dispelling the darkness of ignorance, he might turn peoples everywhere to recognition of the true light [Al., “so that they might turn”]. Just as the stars shine in different regions of the sky, so holy teachers might shine throughout the various regions of the world, so that the way of salvation might be open to all and the light of truth might shine forth.

Therefore he led the most blessed Martin into the regions of Gaul, so that he might illuminate with the light of truth peoples lying inert in foul darkness, draw many nations from the jaws of the ancient enemy, and insert them into the most sacred body of Christ.

II. The holy man’s homeland and military service. He loves to follow Christ’s warfare. As a catechumen, he clothes a poor man.—[Note: [Col. 0658D] See Sulpicius Severus’s *Life of Saint Martin* and also the *Dialogues*. Many passages in this work appear to have been taken from them here and there.]

Therefore the most blessed man was born to pagan parents in the region of Pannonia, in the town of Sabaria; but he was raised at Ticinum in Italy and, in accordance with the nobility of his parents, was assigned to military service by the governor [Al., “by the treacherous”] Julian. But the holy man chose rather to serve the heavenly God than to serve under an earthly emperor. He was specially chosen to carry the standard of the holy cross into the western regions of the world and to exchange the military oath for the commands of the Gospel: not to contend for the Roman kingdom with worldly arms, but to extend the Christian empire through distinctive teachings; not to subject fierce peoples under the harsh law of the Romans, but to place Christ’s gentle yoke upon the necks of many nations.

After the mystery of sacred baptism, he became renowned throughout the world for great miracles and shone far and wide through his teachings. The following was his first notable deed. While he was still a catechumen, in the winter cold he clothed a poor man with half of his cloak. In the same half [Col. 0659B] of his cloak, on the following night, divinely illumined, he saw the Lord Jesus clothed amid the angelic hosts, so that he might understand as true what the Lord Jesus himself proclaims in the pages of the Gospel: “As long as you did it for one of these least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

III. As a young man he remains at Milan and resists the Arians. He withdraws to Gaul and joins Saint Hilary.—This man passed the flower of his youth in the city of Milan, which at that time, with Auxentius favoring it, was greatly stained by Arian perfidy. Saint Martin, as a strong athlete of Christ, bravely resisted it and fearlessly taught the true faith of the Holy Trinity.

But driven from there by the ferocity of the Arian leaders, he withdrew into the regions of Gaul and joined the venerable bishop of the city of Poitiers, Hilary, who at that time stood praised by all as an exceedingly firm pillar of the faith. And just as Lucifer shines brighter than the other stars in heaven, so that holy man shone more excellently than all in Christ’s Church through the greatness of his reputation, the holiness of his life, and the truth of his sacred teachings [Forte, “and just as Lucifer…”].

Saint Martin attached himself to his instruction after abandoning military service, so that, instructed by the example of so great a man, he might advance more strongly into the Christian battle, armed with the helmet of faith and girded with the breastplate of righteousness, armed with the sword of God’s word, and fearlessly fortified against all the weapons of the Evil One.

IV. Visiting his parents, he converts his mother to the faith. Likewise a robber.—[Col. 0659D] The same holy man, instructed by a divine oracle, converted his parents [Note: [Col. 0659D] “His parents,” etc. Sulpicius Severus says in chapter 4 that it was only his mother, while his father remained in evil] to the profession of the holy faith; and he himself regenerated in Christ the mother who had given him birth in the world.

On this journey he also suffered the ambush of robbers. When he was handed over to one of them for custody, he converted the robber to Christ by preaching the Gospel; and the man to whom he had been handed over for punishment became, for him, an instrument of salvation.

160 V. He returns to Gaul. He builds a cell. He raises three dead men. He heals a mute girl.—From there, on his return, he encountered an evil spirit, who promised the holy man that he would be his companion wherever he went. Fearlessly he answered him: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear your threats.”

But after enduring many tribulations from the Arians, he returned again to Gaul and joined Saint Hilary of Poitiers. Near the city he built himself a small cell, in which he might more freely enjoy the fruits of contemplation. A certain catechumen attached himself to him but, while the holy man was absent, was suddenly carried off by death. The man of God restored him to life through abundant prayers and, after returning him to life, baptized him; he lived for many years afterward.

He also restored to life through sacred prayers another man who had been hanged by a noose in the field of a certain Lupicinus [Note: [Col. 0660D] Lupicinus. Sulpicius calls him, in the passage cited, a distinguished man according to worldly standards]. A third time, in the town of Chartres, the same holy man restored to life by prayer alone, before the eyes of the people, the weeping son of a certain woman. When many of the people saw this miracle, they believed in Christ. In due course, in the same town, he healed by anointing with blessed oil a girl who had been mute from infancy.

VI. He is chosen bishop of Tours. He excelled in every virtue.—But lest the Lord’s lamp remain hidden beneath a bushel, he was taken from his beloved retreats, and, bound by the prayers of many, was chosen bishop of the city of Tours. There he performed many notable holy virtues and spread abroad many teachings of heavenly life, yet he did not lose the continence of private life amid the crowds of the people.

Humble in dress, pleasant in speech, devoted in preaching, truthful in judgment, venerable in conduct, ever-watchful in prayer, constant in reading, steadfast in countenance, compassionate in feeling, honorable in priestly ministry, tireless [Col. 0660C] as a sower of God’s word, diligent in multiplying the money entrusted to him by his Lord; rejoicing with those who rejoiced, mourning with those who mourned, becoming all things to all people so that he might win all for Christ; distinguished in virtues, praiseworthy in goodness, beloved for his compassion, shining with many virtues in his episcopate.

VII. Miracles.—For he bound a crowd of pagans, tumultuous in pagan ritual while accompanying a certain corpse, to one place by the word of prayer; then, releasing them, he allowed them to direct their steps as they wished. When a pine tree was falling upon him, he turned it aside by opposing the sign of the cross, and caused the astonished crowd to believe in Christ.

He placed himself on the roof of a certain house against the flames, so that the fire—which had set fire to a shrine of idolatry—would not harm the innocent buildings. He also overthrew another temple dedicated to demons according to an ancient error, when human hands could not do so, supported by angelic assistance.

In another place, while he was overthrowing the sacred rites of the pagans, a certain pagan attacked him with a sword. He exposed his bare neck to the blow of the attacker; but the impious man, falling backward and recognizing his own wickedness, asked forgiveness from the holy man. When another man was about to strike the saint’s head, the iron slipped from his hands.

At Trier he restored a paralyzed girl, whose limbs had all been rendered powerless, to her former health by the sacred application of blessed oil, with the people standing by. By the laying on of hands he freed a servant of Tetradius, a proconsular man, from a demon. As a result, Tetradius himself, with his entire household, was converted to the Christian profession.

He also drove out an exceedingly savage demon from the son of a certain head of household who had been seized by it, inserting his fingers into the boy’s mouth and forcing the evil spirit to leave through the patient’s privy parts. At the gate of the city of Paris he saved a leper from the deformity of his body by a single kiss; and it was also discovered that the fringes of his clothing and the threads of his hair shirt healed many diseases.

The daughter of Arborius the prefect was freed from severe fevers through the imposition of a letter from Saint Martin. He healed Paulinus’s eye [Note: [Col. 0661D] Paulinus, bishop of Nola. See Baronius, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 23, no. 17] of pain and darkness by laying a small cloth upon it.
