VIII. He is visited by angels, the Blessed Virgin, and other saints. He shone with the spirit of prophecy.—The same holy Martin, after falling down some steps and suffering almost total and severe bruising of his limbs, was restored to complete health during the night by an angel. He also frequently enjoyed angelic visitations [Col. 0661B] and familiar conversation.

On one day the man of God was honored and strengthened by a visitation from the most blessed Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, from the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and also from the holy virgins Thecla and Agnes. For he feared nothing—neither the phantoms of demons nor terrifying appearances in various forms—and he could not be deceived by any of their tricks.

He shone with the spirit of the prophets so greatly that he foretold many future events to many people. Thus he foretold victory in Italy to the emperor Maximus and his death at Aquileia. And while that blessed man was celebrating the holy mystery at the altar, a globe of fire suddenly shone from the crown of his head.

A certain sick man, Evantius, received his health before Saint Martin, who was hurrying to him, entered the house. In that same house he rescued a boy bitten by a serpent from the danger of death by the touch of his holy fingers.

IX. The holy man’s patience. He drives out demons, and so forth.—The man of God possessed such great patience that he did not grieve at insults or feel reproaches. Indeed, he calmly endured the blows of certain peasants, and by a single word he freed their animals, which had been fixed to the ground. He did not flatter anyone; to no ruler did he withhold words of truth, always having recourse to the familiar assistance of prayers.

Therefore, if secular power refused him anything, divine mercy immediately provided it. A certain girl seized by a demonic spirit was freed from the enemy’s power by the straw on which Saint Martin sat. He freed not only human beings but also animals from the power of demons and ordered them, once tamed, to return to their own herd.

[Col. 0661D] He also possessed such great compassion that he commanded the dogs pursuing a hare to stop, and rescued the wretched little creature from immediate death. A certain estate in the region of Sens, repeatedly devastated by hailstorms, was freed for many years at the prayers of Saint Martin. A woman was healed of a flow of blood by touching his clothing.

X. He died.—By such miracles the chosen priest of God also shone before the world; perfect in all his life and conduct, distinguished in every piety and religious observance, pleasant in all goodness and kindness, he was called to the heavenly kingdoms in the eighty-first year of his age and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate, mature in years and merits, so that he might receive from Christ the Lord an everlasting crown together with the manifold reward of his labor.

But, having learned long beforehand the day of his death and having foretold it to some of his brothers, as the hour approached he was struck by the pain of fever. Joyful in the praise of God, amid the words of divine preaching and the voices of angelic heavenly hymns, with his disciples standing around him, he returned his holy soul to God and Christ.

### XI. He Is Buried at Tours

When his holy body was carried to the city of Tours by the clergy of the cities and by crowds of the people, amid praises and hymns, it was buried there [Col. 0662B] in the public cemetery. Later, the blessed bishop Perpetuus [Note: [Col. 0661D] Perpetuus was the fifth bishop of Tours after Saint Martin. He built a basilica at the tomb of this holy pontiff, whose appearance is described by Saint Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 14.] constructed there, in a praiseworthy work and with venerable adornment, a church worthy of so great a Father’s merits. In it, even to this day, many signs of miracles, very numerous acts of healing, consolations for the sorrowful, and acts of kindness toward the joyful regularly take place, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father [ [Note: [Col. 0662D] The words enclosed in brackets have been taken from a twelfth-century manuscript from Reims.] and the Holy Spirit, in the unity of divine majesty, forever].  

[Note: [Col. 0662D] From the manuscript of the Putean brothers.] **A SERMON OF THE SAME ALCUIN ON THE PASSING OF SAINT MARTIN**

### XII. Saint Martin’s Holiness, Miracles, and Gift of Prophecy

It is fitting for us all to rejoice with one accord, dearest brothers, and faithfully to venerate the illustrious day of Saint Martin’s death; but especially for those faithful to Christ who live in the western regions of the world, since they were enlightened alike by his teachings and by his example: for whatever he preached in words, he demonstrated by his works. In all his life and conduct he was perfect, distinguished in all piety and religion, pleasing in all goodness and kindness, praiseworthy to everyone and beloved by everyone: a virgin among choirs of virgins, an outstanding priest, an imitator of the apostles, and a preacher of Christ.

The Lord deigned to choose him with apostolic grace, as it is written concerning him: “This is Martin, the chosen bishop of God, to whom the Lord deigned, after the apostles, to grant such great grace that, through the power of the holy and divine Trinity, he deserved to become a renowned raiser of three dead persons” [Col. 0662D]. In imitation of the Lord, he raised three dead persons; he also foresaw many things by the spirit of prophecy before they happened. For he was full of the spirit of prophecy, and therefore, by divine inspiration, he foresaw his own death and revealed to certain of the brothers that the dissolution of his body was approaching.

### XIII. He Restores Peace among Quarrelling Clerics. He Commands the Birds

[Note: [Col. 0662D] From a letter of Severus to Basula, with a few alterations.]

At that time an occasion arose for him that made it necessary to visit a village of his diocese at Condat, in order to restore peace among the clerics of that church, who were quarrelling with one another [Col. 0663A]. Although he was not unaware that the end of his days had arrived, he nevertheless did not refuse to set out for this reason, remembering the Gospel saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God”; and wishing to leave peace to everyone, in imitation of the Lord, who on the day of his ascension said to the apostles: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace. I left you in peace; in peace I shall find you.”

As he was traveling for this purpose with a close company of his disciples, he saw cormorants on the river catching a multitude of fish and said: “This is the form of demons.” Then, by the powerful force of his words, he commanded them to leave that whirlpool and seek dry, deserted places. Immediately, in a marvelous manner, they all gathered into a single flock [Col. 0663B] and, abandoning the river, made for the mountains and forests. Those who were present together marveled that such power existed in Martin, so that, by the grace of God, he could command even birds—or demons.

### XIV. He Falls Ill and Refuses to Have a Softer Bed Prepared for Him

After he had stayed for a few days in the village to which he had gone, and peace had been restored among the clerics, he was now considering returning to the monastery when his bodily strength suddenly began to fail. He summoned his disciples and told them that the time had come for his spirit to be released from the body.

Then there arose the grief and sorrow of everyone, one common voice of mourners saying: “Why are you abandoning us, Father, or to whom are you leaving us in our desolation? For ravenous wolves will attack your flock. And who will defend us from their rapacity when you depart? We know [Col. 0663C] that you desire Christ, but your rewards are secure and will not be diminished by delay; have pity on us instead.”

Moved by their tears, he is said to have wept; then, turning to the Lord, he said in a submissive voice: “Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor; let your will be done.” Clearly, he did not know which he preferred: for he wished neither to abandon them nor to remain separated from Christ any longer. Putting nothing of his own desire forward, he left everything to God’s judgment, saying: “Lord, if you still wish me to remain in the body, I do not refuse the labor; and if you spare my old age, it is good for me; let your will be done. But guard these people themselves, for whom I am afraid.”

O ineffable man, defeated neither by labor [Col. 0664A] nor to be overcome by death; one who neither feared dying nor refused to live. When his disciples asked that bedding be placed beneath him, since he had been suffering from the violence of fevers for several days, he said: “It is not fitting, sons, it is not fitting for a Christian to die except in ashes and sackcloth; for if I have left you any other example, I myself have sinned.”

When the priests who had come to visit him in his illness again asked that he ease his body by turning onto his side, he said: “Allow me, brothers, allow me rather to see heaven than earth, so that my spirit, already about to depart to the Lord, may be directed upon its journey.”

### XV. He Gives Up His Spirit amid Angelic Hymns

In the eighty-first year of his age and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate, mature in years and conduct, he happily departed from this world in the village of his diocese at Condat, as we have said. [Col. 0664B] But amid the words of sacred preaching, together with the angelic voices of heavenly hymns, while his disciples stood around him, full of grace and holiness, he delivered his holy soul to Jesus Christ.

Many heard, at his passing, the voices of angels praising Saint Martin. The great multitude that gathered for his funeral cannot be told. Many came in tears from the neighboring cities, monasteries, and villages, mourning Saint Martin with one voice. O how great was the grief of everyone! How especially great were the laments of the monks and virgins, who said that it is pious to rejoice over Martin, and pious to weep for Martin. For it was pious that he lived, and pious also that he died, because in his life he had pleased God.

### XVI. He Is Buried at Tours

[Note: [Col. 0663] This conclusion is the same as that of the preceding text, above, no. 11.]

His body [Col. 0664C] was carried to the city of Tours by the clergy of the cities and by crowds of the people, amid praises and hymns, and was buried there with great veneration. A heavenly crowd accompanied him, with heavenly hymns, as far as the place of burial. Later, at that place, the blessed bishop Perpetuus constructed a new church in a praiseworthy work, worthy in its merits of so great a patron and such a man. In it, even to this day, many signs of miracles, very numerous acts of healing, consolations for the sorrowful, and acts of kindness toward the joyful regularly take place, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns in the unity of majesty, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0663]

## 163. SECOND LITTLE WORK. THE LIFE OF SAINT VEDASTUS, BISHOP OF ARRAS

Written around the year 800.

[Col. 0663D] To Radon, the sweetest son of [my] affection [Note: [Col. 0663D] *Radoni.* Surius has *Rodani*. He became abbot of the monastery of Vedast in 795 and restored the monastery, church, and worship of Saint Vedastus at enormous expense; he died in 815, as is read in the Chronicle of Vedast, in Locrius and François Le Bar’s manuscript monuments.], Albinus, a humble deacon, sends greetings.

### I

Following the venerable command of your affection, I have worked to revise the Life of Saint Vedastus, your Father and our intercessor [Col. 0665A] [Note: [Col. 0665D] “I have worked to revise.” We discussed this in the preliminary Notice.]; not because I had been capable of producing anything worthy of his most excellent merits, but because I considered it an established duty to refuse nothing commanded by your reverence. Therefore, the praise or blame of these writings belongs chiefly to you [Boll., *maxime*, “especially”]. Would that they please you and the brothers, whatever they may be.

I ask that you deign to repay my labor with the comfort of your prayers, and that I may deserve to be one of yours in the fellowship of charity, always mindful of the command of him who said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XV, 12). For in this command the salvation of all consists; it is clearly most necessary to everyone, and especially to those who accept the task of governing Christ’s flock.

Therefore, dearest one, diligently strive to instruct in fraternal love the flock that you have received to govern, and hasten to lead it through the pastures of life by holy admonitions. You have Christ as your helper in every good work, and Saint Vedastus as your intercessor. Just as you have adorned the house of God exceedingly well through great labor and decorated it with the most generous gifts, so strive that those subject to you be adorned with good morals [Boll., *tibi*, “you”], and make them persevere in divine praise; and let the brothers continually do in the churches what the angels always do in heaven.

It is yours to command; theirs to obey. It is yours to go before; theirs to follow. Therefore, all should have one will in the service of God, so that there may be one reward in the kingdom of God.

### II

Let no one withdraw from the divine praises at the canonical hours, lest through anyone’s negligence some place be found vacant in the sight of God. Let the words of God be uttered in the churches with the innermost affection of the heart, and let the offices of almighty God be celebrated with great reverence [and let every ministry of Christ be fulfilled humbly and devoutly]. Everywhere let all faithfully and energetically perform obedience in the needs of this world [Note: [Col. 0665D] Bollandus: “Therefore let all obedience in the needs of this world be performed faithfully and energetically.”].

Let there be among all the most harmonious peace, and the most holy charity [and devotion to the regular life]. Let the elders instruct the younger by good examples and constant admonition, and love them as sons; and let the younger honor the elders as fathers and obey their commands with complete eagerness.

But your conduct, venerable son, must be an example of salvation to everyone. Take care that no one, however insignificant, is scandalized by your life, but rather that each person is built up and strengthened in the way of truth; for an eternal reward will be judged yours on account of their salvation. Gray hairs announce that the final day is hastening. Therefore be ready at every hour to meet the Lord your God.

Brotherly love, almsgiving to the needy, and chastity of life prepare for you the steps to heaven. Work diligently to secure eternal days of happiness for yourself. May the secular honor that you possess abound for you in spiritual glory.

### III

On feast days, when the people come to church, have the word of God preached to them [Note: [Col. 0666D] “Have the Word of God preached to them.” This indicates that by that time the office of preaching had already existed in monastic churches. Mabillon, volume II of the *Annals*, page 322.]. Wherever you go, let the clerics fully perform the service of God; let them go with you, adorned with sobriety and unaccustomed to drunkenness, so that the integrity of their lives may be a doctrine of salvation for others 164. Everywhere take particular care of the poor, widows, and orphans, so that on the dreadful day you may hear from Christ the Lord, together with the others who give alms: “Inasmuch as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me” (Matthew XV, 40).

Be a father to the wretched, carefully examine the case of those who cry out to you, and be lenient toward those who sin against you, so that God may pardon your sins. Be just in judgments and merciful toward debtors. Be a teacher of virtues, honorable in conduct, pleasant in speech, praiseworthy in life, and devoted to every work of God.

Also exhort the brothers to read the holy Scriptures most diligently. Let them not trust in knowledge of the tongue, but in understanding of the truth, so that they may be able to resist those who contradict the truth. These are dangerous times, as the apostles foretold, because many false teachers will arise, introducing new sects, who will strive to stain the purity of the catholic faith with impious assertions (2 Timothy III, 1; 2 Peter II, 1). Therefore the Church must have many defenders, able to defend the camp of God manfully not only by the holiness of their lives but also by the teaching of truth.

### IV

I have sent these little letters of pious admonition not as though you were ignorant, but to show the faith of true charity in my heart. What does a friend accomplish if he does not reveal himself in words? If the rich do not disdain the little gifts of the poor, why should the streams of our understanding be rejected by the rivers of your wisdom? For even great rivers are enlarged by flowing streams, and the Lord himself praised the widow’s two small coins, which, from the poverty of her want, she offered to God with a generous hand—everything she had (Luke XXI, 2).

And I, although poor in knowledge, have nevertheless sent these little gifts to your piety in faithful affection [Boll., “faithful in fraternal love,”], asking that you deign to regard them with the humble consideration of brotherhood, just as we have endeavored to send them to you with the devout charity of our affection. May almighty God cause you and your [dearest] brothers to advance in every good work and grant you to attain the blessedness of eternal glory.

## CHAPTER ONE. Christian Doctrine Explained to King Chlodovech by Saint Vedastus

### V

After God and our Lord Jesus Christ had come from heaven into this world through a virginal womb to seek the lost sheep [Col. 0666D] (Luke XV, 4), and, having completed the whole fullness of his dispensation and our salvation, had returned in triumphal glory to the seat of the Father’s majesty [he returned], he distributed throughout the whole world many lights of holy teachers, shining with the light of evangelical preaching, so that he might drive away everywhere the murky [Al., “dark”] shadows of ignorance.

Just as heaven is adorned with shining stars, all of which are nevertheless illuminated by one sun, so the broad expanses of the earth might shine with holy teachers. Yet these teachers, illuminated by the eternal sun and preceded by divine grace, would illumine the blind [Col. 0667A] darkness of ignorance with the radiance of true faith [and] the glorious name of Christ, so that, through their ministry, the long hunger for eternal life that had existed from the beginning of the world might be satisfied with the banquets of eternal life.

Among their number was Vedastus, a holy priest of God and an outstanding preacher. In the time of the most powerful king of the Franks, Clodovech [Note: [Col. 0667D] Clodovech reigned from the end of 479 until 509, when he died on November 27. Bollandus.], divine grace directed him to these regions for the salvation of many, so that, supported by the aid of heavenly mercy, he might lead a people deceived by the devil’s fraud and held captive in the snares of error into the way of eternal salvation and restore them to the true freedom that is in Christ.

But so that this might happen at an acceptable time, according to the Apostle, who says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians VI, 2), the Lord Jesus, who “wills all people to be saved” (1 Timothy II, 4), was preparing for his servant an appropriate occasion by which he might reach the ministry of God’s word at the proper time.

### VI

It happened that the aforementioned king of the Franks, Clodovech, made war against the Alemanni [Boll., “war” singular] [Note: [Col. 0667D] “To make war against the Alemanni.” Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 30; Aimoinus, Book I, chapter 15; Hincmar and other writers discuss this war of Clodovech with the Alemanni. It took place in the thirteenth year of his reign, in the year 494 of Christ. More recent writers assign this battle to Tolbiac, commonly called Zülpich, but others more correctly believe that the Alemanni were defeated near Strasbourg. See Bollandus on this passage.], who at that time possessed their own kingdom independently. But he did not attack them so unprepared as he wished. For, having gathered a very strong force, they met the king near the banks of the Rhine River 165, united in defending their homeland by military valor or in dying freely for their country. The battle was fiercely contested on both sides: these fought lest they lose the glory of triumph, those lest they lose [Al., “betray”] their homeland’s freedom, as they fell into mutual slaughter.

The king, therefore, overcome by great terror when he saw the enemy fighting bravely and his own men almost defeated to the point of destruction, began to despair more of safety than to hope for victory. Although he had not yet been reborn in Christ by his will, necessity compelled him to flee for help to Christ. Since he had a religious queen, initiated into the sacraments of baptism, named Clotildis [Note: [Col. 0668D] *Clotilden.* Saint Clotildis, also called Chlotildis, Crotildis, Hlotild, Rothilt, and Rothildis, is commemorated on June 3.], he raised his eyes to heaven and said:

“O God of unique power and supreme majesty, whom Queen Clotildis worships, confesses, and adores: grant me victory over my enemies today. From this day forward you alone shall be my God and my revered power. Grant me triumph, and I promise you everlasting service.”

At once, through the working of divine mercy, the Alemanni turned their backs, and victory passed to the king and the Franks. O marvelous clemency of almighty God! O ineffable goodness, who so hears those who hope in him and never abandons them [Col. 0667D]! With how great faith should Christians invoke his mercy, when a pagan king, through the fulfillment of a single prayer, deserved so great a victory!

To whom among the ancient examples of this divine mercy should we compare the aid that he received, since, on account of the tears of a single moment, God granted such a celebrated triumph to his future servant, except to King Hezekiah? In the distress of his tribulation, by one brief petition alone he deserved not only that his city be defended by heavenly protection from its present devastation, but also, on that very night when he had poured out his prayers into the divine ears, to see 185,000 enemies slain, while he remained joyful and delivered (2 Kings XIX).

### VII

This victory, of which we spoke earlier, became for the king and his people the cause of eternal salvation. Thus the lamp—that is, Saint Vedastus—would not remain hidden beneath a bushel, but, placed upon a lampstand, would shine in the house of God through examples and preaching, leading many from the error of idolatry and the darkness of ignorance into the way of truth.

After conquering his enemies, restoring peace, and bringing the Alemanni under his authority, the king returned joyfully to his homeland amid the praise of triumph. To show himself a faithful sponsor of so great a glory granted to him, he hastened to be imbued with the sacred preaching of Christ’s servants and washed in the sacraments of holy baptism.

He came to the town of Toul [Note: [Col. 0668D] “He came to the town of Toul.” Toul is an episcopal city on the Moselle, where the king recognized Saint Vedastus and took him as a companion on his journey, says Aimoinus, Book I, chapter 16.], where he recognized that Saint Vedastus was serving God alone in praiseworthy devotion and gathering the sweetest fruits of the contemplative life. He took him with himself as a companion to Saint Remigius, the most illustrious priest of Christ, as he hurried toward the city of Reims, so that at every step of his journey he might be instructed by him in the most salutary teachings and initiated into the firm foundations of the catholic faith. Thus, prepared by faith and knowledge of virtues, he might be washed by so great a bishop in the spiritual bath and strengthened by him with heavenly gifts, while what had begun through this man’s evangelical preaching had first been preceded by divine grace [Al., “mercy”].

The one led the king as he hastened toward the fountain of life; the other washed him as he came to the fountain of eternal salvation. Both acted with nearly equal paternal devotion [Perhaps, “fathers”]: the former through the doctrine of faith, the latter through the water of baptism. Both offered a temporal king as an acceptable gift to the eternal King.

These are the two olive trees and the two shining lampstands (Zechariah IV, 3). Through them the aforementioned king, instructed in the way of God, entered, by God’s mercy, the gate of perpetual light and believed in Christ together with the mighty nation of the Franks. Thus the nation became “a holy people, a people for possession” (1 Peter II, 9), so that in it the virtues of him who called them from darkness into his marvelous light might be proclaimed.

## CHAPTER II. The Miracles and Virtues of Saint Vedastus. The Baptism of King Chlodovech

[Col. 0668D]

### VIII

The sacred history of evangelical authority relates that, as the Lord Jesus was traveling toward Jericho to strengthen the hearts of the people present in faith in his majesty, he restored the light of his eyes to a certain blind man who cried out to him (Luke XVIII), so that, through the bodily light of that one blind man, the hearts of many might be spiritually illumined.

So too Saint Vedastus, by the gift of Christ God, confirmed in the king’s heart by the illumination of a certain blind man the faith that he preached in words. Thus the king himself might understand that the light of the heart was as necessary to him as the illumination of the eyes was to the blind man. What divine grace accomplished through the prayers of its servant in the eyes punished with the darkness of blindness, the same power would accomplish through the words of that servant, by the understanding of spiritual light, in the king’s heart.

For, while the royal majesty was traveling with a suitable retinue and a very great multitude [of people], they came to a certain district that, according to the custom of the inhabitants of that land, is called Vungise [Note: [Col. 0669D] “The district of Vungise.” Elsewhere it is written *Vongise* and *Vungisus*. In the Itinerary of Antoninus, *Vongus* is a village. In the capitulary of Charles the Bald for the year 853, where the districts are described as organized by royal envoys, it is *Vonziso*. In a charter of Louis for the Church of Reims, *the fortress of Vonzense*; and in Flodoard, *the municipality of Vongum*. Commonly Vouzy, which gave its name to the district or territory subject to it. Bollandus.], near the estate of Reguliacum [Note: [Col. 0669D] “Near the estate of Reguliacum.” Elsewhere *Rilugiacum*. It is a village on the Aisne, called Rilly, between Attigny and Vongum.], situated on the flower-bearing banks of the river Aisne.

And behold, as the king crossed the bridge of that same river with the multitude of the people, a certain blind man, long deprived of the light of the sun, met him. Perhaps he had not been blinded through any fault of his own, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him and, through his illumination, the hearts of many who were present might be spiritually illumined.

When he learned from passers-by that Saint Vedastus, the servant of Christ, was traveling in the same company, he cried out: “Holy Vedastus, chosen by God, have mercy on me, and earnestly seek heavenly power with a pious heart, so that it may come to the aid of my misery. I ask for neither gold nor silver, but that, through the prayers of your holiness, he restore the light of my eyes to me.”

The man of God therefore perceived that heavenly power was present with him—not merely for the sake of that blind man, but even more for the salvation of the people present [Al., “of the present age”]. He poured himself entirely into sacred prayers, trusting in divine mercy, and placed his right hand, with the sign of the cross, upon the blind man’s eyes, saying:

“Lord Jesus, who are the true light, who opened the eyes of the man born blind when he cried out to you, open the eyes of this man also, so that this people present may understand that you alone are God, doing wonders in heaven and on earth.”

Immediately the blind man, having received his sight, went on his way rejoicing. Later, a church was built at that place by devout men as a testimony to this miracle. In it, even to this day, divine benefits are granted to those who pray and believe [Note: [Col. 0670D] “Even to this day.” Balderic testifies that the church constructed as a testimony to this miracle still existed in his own time, that is, in the eleventh century of Christ. Bollandus.].

### IX

The king, thoroughly instructed by the man of God in evangelical teachings and firmly strengthened in the faith by this recent miracle, did not linger on the road and did not waver in faith. With great eagerness of spirit and great haste in his journey, he hurried to see the most holy bishop Remigius, so that, through his most sacred ministry and by the working of the Holy Spirit, he might be washed in the living font of catholic baptism for the remission of sins and the hope of eternal life.

He stayed with him for several days, in order to satisfy the ecclesiastical regulations and first to be washed by tears of repentance according to the apostolic command, as blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, says: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts II, 38), and then receive baptism, the heavenly mystery, in the name of the holy Trinity.

Since the blessed bishop knew that the Apostle Paul said, “Let all your things be done honorably and in order” (1 Corinthians XIV, 40), he set the day [Note: [Col. 0670D] “He set the day.” “On which the world received from heaven the Lord born for its redemption, and on which Christ was born into the world,” says Saint Avitus in his Letter to King Chlodovech. “Hence,” he adds, “the sacred night now finds us secure concerning you, on which he is said to have been baptized.” Bollandus.] on which the king would enter the church to receive the sacraments of divine mercy.

What joy there was then among God’s saints! What gladness in the Church of Christ, when they saw the king of Nineveh descend from his throne of majesty at Jonah’s preaching, sit in the ashes of repentance, and bow the head of his excellence beneath the pious hand of God’s priest (Jonah III)!

The king was then baptized together with his nobles and the people, who, through the prevenient grace of God, rejoiced to receive the sacrament of the saving bath.

### X

Having obtained his desire both for victory over his enemies and for his own salvation, he returned to govern the kingdom and entrusted Saint Vedastus to the blessed bishop Remigius.

While Vedastus remained there, he became renowned for the merits of his life and the examples of his virtues, and was made beloved and venerable by everyone. He was religious in the dignity of his conduct, outstanding in charity, pleasing in brotherly love, exceptional in humble piety, constant in the vigilance of his prayers, restrained in speech, chaste in body, sober in fasting, and a consoler of the sorrowful. He did not think about the next day, but always trusted in God’s mercy; he nourished everyone who came to him with the food of eternal life.

He despised no one in distress, but refreshed the sorrowful with a word of pious consolation. He harmed no one even by a word, but strove to benefit everyone through brotherly love. Hence very many distinguished men visited him, either to receive consolation from his sacred conversation in the sadness of any anxiety, or to hear from him the pure truth in the religious practice of the Church.

Through his pious devotion [Al., “admonition”], many were freed from the snares of the devil and, with the aid of heavenly mercy, entered the ways of eternal life. Indeed, as we said above, many nobles and commoners regularly visited the man of God because of the very celebrated reputation of his holiness, so that they might be consoled by the grace that abounded on his lips. Since “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matthew XII, 34), and since he loved everyone with brotherly love, he showed himself approachable to all.

Regarding the salvation of others as his own gain, he did not bury the Lord’s talent [Col. 0670D] of money [Col. 0671A] in the ground through sloth, but strove to multiply it by the daily sweat of charity, lest, when his Lord returned, he should appear empty-handed in his presence [Al., “be found so”].

### XI

Among others, a certain noble and devout man came to visit the servant of Christ, so that he might be refreshed by him with the honey of heavenly teaching. While the conversation of their most sweet fellowship was prolonged and the sun, crossing the midpoint of the sky, lengthened the shadows, the man of God did not wish to dismiss his guest without the provision of charity for the journey.

He ordered a boy that, if any wine remained, he should bring cups to his dear friend, so that, refreshed in both soul and body, he might return home strengthened. But because of the continual presence of guests and the generous munificence of the man of God toward everyone, the boy found the vessel in which the wine was usually kept dry—not because the Father’s charity was dry. At once, sadly and with a quiet murmur, the boy reported this to his father’s ears.

The man of God, suffused with the blush of embarrassment yet rich in the sweetness of charity in his heart, trusted in divine assistance. He silently poured out prayers to God for a little while, doubting nothing about divine aid and hesitating not at all concerning the fulfillment of his request. He trusted entirely in the mercy of him who brought forth from a dry rock a spring of living water for his thirsty people (Exodus XVII; Numbers XX), and who changed water into the marvelous taste of wine at Cana of Galilee [Al., “turned it into wine”] (John II).

He said to the boy: “Go, trusting in God’s goodness, and whatever you find in the vessel, do not hesitate to bring it to us.”

The boy, swift and obedient to his father’s command, ran and found the vessel overflowing with excellent wine. Giving thanks to God, he poured it out with a joyful spirit for the friend who was coming and for his companions. Strengthened by this double charity, the man returned to his home.

But the servant of Christ, lest he be celebrated by empty words of boasting or by the noisy praise of the people, strictly charged the boy to keep this miracle secret throughout all the days of his life. He wished to be known more by God alone than by human beings, knowing for certain that the true safeguard of every virtue lies in humility, and that humility is what ascends by the steps of charity to the highest kingdoms of heaven, as the Truth himself says: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew XXIII, 12).

## CHAPTER III. Saint Vedastus’s Bishopric of Arras

[Col. 0671D]

### XII

As the very celebrated reputation of the man of God spread, and his generosity in charity, the religious character of his life, and his zeal for the word of God were praised everywhere far and wide [Al., “grew more and more”], the most blessed bishop Remigius judged that so distinguished a lamp of Christ ought rather to be placed upon a lampstand, so that, through the splendid radiance of his holiness, it might shine more broadly for the salvation of many, rather than remain almost hidden beneath the sides [Boll., “in the hiding places”] of a single place.

Therefore, by divine providence and the salutary counsel of the priests, he ordained him bishop and sent him to the city of Arras to preach the word of life 168, so that a people lying for a long time in the ancient errors of evil custom might, with God’s help, be led by him, through the continual zeal of sacred preaching, into the way of truth and the knowledge of the Son of God.

After receiving the rank of bishop and the office of preaching, he hastened to set out for the aforementioned city. But, as a sign of future prosperity and salvation, God revealed his entrance to the citizens through the testimony of a certain miracle.

### XIII

At the very gate of the city, two needy and sick men met him: a blind man and a lame man, asking alms from the man of God with a pitiable voice. The priest of Christ immediately took pity on their misery and considered what consolation he could provide for them.

Since the apostolic preacher knew that he had no money in his purse, he trusted in divine mercy and, strengthened by the example of the holy apostles Peter and John, said: “I have neither gold nor silver with me; but what I have—that is, acts of charity and the piety of prayer [Al., “a prayer of piety”] to God—I do not delay in giving you” (Acts III, 6).

After these words, the man of God poured out tears from the depths of his heart over their misery, and with purity of faith sought divine aid for them, both for the healing of their bodies and for the spiritual salvation of the people present.

Nor could such pious and necessary prayers be ineffective. Rather, from him who says through the prophet Isaiah, “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah XLIX, 8), both men immediately received the desired health in the sight of the multitude: one enriched with the brightness of sight, the other rejoicing in the swiftness of his feet.

Both, giving thanks to heavenly mercy and carrying home gifts greater than they had hoped for, returned home. This miracle of healing in them also became for many a cause of eternal salvation. For when they saw heavenly power accompanying the words of God’s priest, they abandoned the filth of idolatry, believed in Christ, and were cleansed in the living fountain of holy baptism.

### XIV

Strengthened by the favor of the people through the testimony of the aforementioned miracle, the man of God traveled through the individual districts of the city and searched among the ruins of the buildings to see whether any sign of a church could be found. For he recognized that in ancient times the worship of the holy faith had flourished in those places; but because of the sins of the inhabitants of that land, by the hidden yet most just judgment of God, it had been handed over, together with the other cities of Gaul and Germany, to the pagan and treacherous king of the Huns, Attila [Note: [Col. 0671D] *Attila.* In the year of Christ 450 and the following year. Concerning Attila, Sidonius Apollinaris sings in the *Panegyric on Avitus*, poem VII, line 327:

[Col. 0672D]

“And already Attila had spread himself with his terrifying hordes.”]

Into your fields, O Belga. BOLL.] That city too was to be plundered: for, because of the savagery of his spirit, he knew neither how to show honor to the priests of God nor how to pay reverence to the churches of Christ, but laid everything waste with sword and fire, like a most savage storm. Then, in a likeness to the devastation of Jerusalem inflicted by the impious king of Babylon, nations entered the inheritance of God [Col. 0673A] and, with polluted hands, profaned the sanctuaries of Christ, shedding the blood of God’s servants around the altars of the Most High King (IV Kings XXV). It was not the strength of the pagans that brought this about, but the sins of the Christian people deserved it.

But the servant of Christ found the ruins of an ancient church, and amid the fragments of the walls he saw dense thickets of brambles growing. Where once there had been choirs singing psalms, there were now lairs and hiding places of wild beasts; everything was full of dung and filth, so that scarcely any trace of the walls remained. Seeing this, he groaned in the deepest sorrow of his heart, saying:

“O Lord, all these things have come upon us because we sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly and committed iniquity. But you, Lord, remember your mercy, spare our sins, and do not forget your poor forever” (Psalm CV, 6).

## XV

While he was thus murmuring these tearful laments, suddenly a bear sprang out from the ruined caves. The man of God indignantly commanded it to withdraw into deserted places, to seek a suitable dwelling for itself among the dense forests, and never again to cross the banks of that river. Terrified at once by this threat, it fled and was never afterward seen in those regions.

O wondrous power of almighty God in his saints, whom the fiercest beasts know how to obey! O pitiable boldness of human beings, who do not fear to scorn the words of saving instruction spoken by holy teachers! The irrational beast, in obeying the commands of the saints, uses human reason, so to speak; but the human being, created in the image of God [Col. 0673C] and endowed with reason, failing to understand his own honor, has been compared to senseless beasts and made like them (Psalm XLVIII, 13).

## XVI

When the man of God discovered that the churches of Christ were deserted and that the heart of the people was infected with the errors of idolatry and blinded by the darkness of ignorance, he devoted himself to a twofold labor of piety. With constant diligence he led the people to recognition of the true light; he raised the churches to the height of the highest honor; and he appointed priests and deacons to assist him in various places belonging to the churches. Where previously there had been caves of robbers, there he built houses of prayer, and he took greater care to adorn them with divine praises than to decorate them with the worldly riches of pomp.

He was generous to the poor and approachable toward the rich, so that he might lead everyone onto the way of truth either by the generosity of his gifts [Col. 0673D] or by the pleasantness of his words. Knowing, therefore, that the proud necks of the powerful could in no way be bent [Boll., turned or inclined] toward the humility of Christian religion except through the gentlest admonitions of piety, and instructed by the apostolic example, he became all things to all people, that he might win them all (I Cor. IX, 12). He anticipated his elders with honor, admonished the younger with fatherly affection, and everywhere, through the duties of charity, sought not his own interests but the things of God. Following in the footsteps of Christ, he did not avoid the banquets of the powerful—not for the sake of luxury, but for the purpose of preaching—so that, through the harmony of familiarity [Boll., the concord of familiarity], he might more easily pour the word of God into the hearts of those dining.

## XVII

A certain noble Frank, distinguished by his power, named Ocinus, invited King Clotarius [Note: [Col. 0673D] King Clotarius. After Clovis died on 27 November 509, his four sons succeeded him; among them the first was Clotarius, who established his seat at Soissons and ruled the Atrebates.]—the son of the aforementioned King Clovis, who at that time governed the scepter of the kingdom nobly [Boll., held the scepter]—to a meal that he had prepared with great ceremony in his house for the king and his leading men [Note: [Col. 0673D] Leading men. That several of these were pagans, and that cups consecrated by pagan superstition were set before them, is indicated by another Life of Saint Vedast. ID.].

Saint Vedast was also invited to the banquet. Entering the house, as was his customary practice, he extended his right hand and marked everything with the sign of the holy cross. Certain vessels stood there filled with beer, but they had been wickedly infected with demonic incantations through pagan error [Col. 0674B]. At once, through the power of the holy cross, they burst apart and broke, pouring onto the ground whatever liquid they contained.

The king and his leading men were terrified by the sight of this miracle and asked the bishop about the cause of the sudden portent. The holy bishop replied:

“Through certain incantations of sorcerers, demonic power lay hidden in these liquids in order to deceive the souls of the guests. But, terrified by the power of Christ’s cross, it has invisibly fled from the house in the same way that you have visibly seen the liquid poured onto the ground.”

This event brought salvation to many. For many, released from the hidden chains of demonic deception, rejected the vanity of omens, abandoned the practice of incantations, and advanced toward the purity of true religion [Col. 0674C] [Boll., hastened toward it], understanding that the efficacy of divine power manifested signs in its servant [Boll., that he performed signs through divine power], and that the schemes of the ancient serpent had no power against his holiness. What that one had prepared for the destruction of some, the grace of Christ turned toward the redemption of many.

# CHAPTER IV. The Death and Burial of Saint Vedast

## XVIII

The aforesaid priest of God therefore governed the Church of Christ, with divine grace assisting him, for approximately forty years [Note: [Col. 0674D] Approximately forty years. From about the year 500 to 540; see Bollandus, Preliminary Commentary, § 3], with great devotion to evangelical preaching and great love of piety. During that time he converted a multitude of people to the holiness of the Christian faith through Catholic teaching.

[Col. 0674D] Everywhere knowledge of the divine law flourished; the most holy name of Christ was heard on the lips of all; the integrity of a most chaste life blossomed in their conduct; love of the heavenly homeland burned in the hearts of each one; the people flocked to church on appointed days; the feasts of our Savior were celebrated on the proper days with great joy; alms were distributed most abundantly to the poor around the houses; the word of God was preached daily to the people in every place; and in the churches the choir sang hymns of praise to God at the canonical hours [Col. 0675A].

“They called the people blessed to whom these things belong: blessed the people whose Lord is their God” (Psalm CXLIII, 15). For everyone rested in the beauty of peace, rejoiced in the knowledge of truth, and was glad in the holiness of Christian religion.

## XIX

When the devout preacher and holy priest of God, mature in merits and years, was destined to receive the rewards of his labor, by God’s dispensation he was struck in that same city of Arras by a severe fever. Divine mercy foresaw that, having labored greatly in God’s service in that place, he might from there attain the palm of eternal blessedness and, amid the hands of his dearly beloved sons, return his soul to its Creator.

To indicate the death of his servant, God caused a very bright column of light to be seen one night, standing from the roof of the house in which the holy priest lay all the way to the summit of heaven, for nearly two hours. When this was reported to the man of God, he immediately understood that the sign announced his death. He therefore summoned his sons to him, so that through their prayers he might commend his soul to the faithful Creator.

After sweet admonitions of fatherly piety and final words of charity, strengthened by the most holy viaticum of the body and blood of Christ, he gave up his spirit amid the hands of those who wept.

O day most joyful for the holy priest, but most sorrowful for the whole people, whom so great a shepherd suddenly left in bodily life, though he never abandons them in spiritual intercession, if they do not cease to follow the words of his sacred admonition [Col. 0675C] and the traces of his most exemplary life!

## XX

The clergy and a large crowd of people therefore gathered for the final funeral rites of the venerable man, together with priests, presbyters, and deacons from other churches. But, wondrously, amid the voices of those weeping on earth, a company of singing persons was reportedly heard by certain devout men in heaven. And while the bier on which the body lay stood prepared in the midst with the fitting honor, those who approached could not move it.

They were uncertain what to do and did not know where to turn. They asked Scopilio [Al., Saint Phyleon], an archpresbyter and indeed a religious man, who had been the secretary of the holy man’s sermons, whether he remembered that Vedast had ever testified anything about his burial. They feared that this had perhaps happened because they intended to bury him within the walls of the same city.

He replied that he had often heard him say that no one ought to be buried within [Al., below the walls] the walls of a city, because every city ought to be a place for the living, not for the dead [Note: [Col. 0675D] In the Marchian manuscript and that of Saint Maximinus, as found among the Bollandists, the work continues as follows, and the Life ends after the remainder has been omitted:

“Having received this advice from him, they were to bury the Father outside the city, in the oratory that he himself had prepared. At once they lifted the bier with great ease and carried the holy body with lights, praises, and hymns to the place he had chosen, burying him with great honor beside the altar of that oratory and committing to the earth a noble treasure. At that place, by the divine favor of God, miracles are customarily performed even to this day; they are reported more by the mouths of those who see them than written by the pen of one who records them.

“After some time had passed, the house in which the beloved of God died was seized by flames and began to burn. But while a religious woman named Abita was watching, Saint Vedast came and drove the flames away from the house. It thus remained unharmed, together with the little bed on which the venerable man had sent his holy soul to the heavenly kingdoms, so that all might recognize how great was the blessedness in heaven of the one whose bedchamber could not be burned on earth. Because of the holiness of his merits, through the working of divine mercy, either ancient miracles are reported daily or new ones are seen.

“Happy indeed is the city of Arras, fortified by so excellent a patron! Though it grows poor through the ruins of its walls, it shines through the nobility of his merits. Therefore let the whole people rejoice in the intercession of his holiness and offer eternal praises to almighty God, who bestowed upon them so illustrious a teacher. Through his preaching it recognized the way of truth; through his prayers, if it remains firm in faith and holy in life, it will remain secure from every adversity and attain the perfect glory of blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

(For the clause that follows, see below, no. 24, at the end.)]

For they wished to bury him in the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, where he had presided in the episcopal chair. But it is known that he had arranged for the place of his burial to be in the oratory that he had built near the bank of the little river Criention [Note: [Col. 0676D] The little river Criention. In other sources Triention; now commonly called the Crinchon], at modest expense—that is, of wooden boards. Although he himself had wished this to be done out of the humility that he had always practiced, everyone who was present, considering the distinction of his merits, thought it unworthy that the body of so great a man should be buried in a humble place [Col. 0676B], especially since the place itself was unsuitable for so great a monument and, being covered by marshland, was inaccessible to the people.

## XXI

While they were discussing such matters among themselves, the venerable Scopilio, trained by the power of prayer, believed that he should have recourse to his customary weapons: namely, that the prayer of faith should obtain what the strength of many people could not accomplish. Therefore, exhorting everyone to pray, he himself first began to weep and, bending over the most sacred body in prayer, burst forth in these words, moved by the sorrow of his heart:

“Alas for me,” he said, “O most blessed Father! What do you wish me to do? The day is already declining toward evening, and all who have gathered for your funeral are hastening to return to their homes [Col. 0676C]. Permit us, I beg you, to carry you to the place that the care of your sons has prepared for you.”

After he had said this, they took hold of the bier on which the lifeless body of the holy man lay. Feeling no burden, they carried him eagerly on their shoulders to the place of burial. They buried him in the already mentioned church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God, on the right side of the altar, where he had once exercised the office of the episcopal chair, concealing in the earth a noble treasure.

He lay there for some time, until, by the Lord’s revelation, he was transferred in a fortunate change by the holy bishops Autbert [Col. 0677A] and Audomar to the place where his memory now shines.

## XXII

Now let what was seen as worthy of remembrance concerning the same bishop after his departure be related. After some time had passed, the little house in which the beloved of God died was seized by flames and began to burn. But while a certain religious woman named Abita was watching, Saint Vedast came and drove the flames away from the house. Thus it remained unharmed, together with the bed on which the man of God had sent his holy soul to the heavenly kingdoms, so that all might recognize how great was his blessedness in heaven, whose bedchamber could not burn on earth.

# CHAPTER V. The Translation of the Body of Saint Vedast

## XXIII

He lay in that same place until the time of blessed Autbert, who was the seventh bishop to succeed him in the episcopal seat. As we have learned from the report of our predecessors, as is repeated by the mouths of countless people, and as we also establish by what was done before our eyes, one day, after the morning hymns, while he was among men [Boll., in the fortifications; Fulbert, in the Life of Saint Autbert, “standing on the walls”], gazing eastward as dawn reddened, he saw at a distance, across the little river called the Crienton, a radiant man holding a staff in his hand and measuring out the site of a basilica.

Seeing this, and by God’s revelation, he recognized the vision as angelic. It was shown to him that, with Christ’s approval, blessed Vedast was undoubtedly to be transferred there. Made certain by this revelation, he invited blessed Audomar to undertake so great a work. At that time Audomar was bishop of Tarvanna, the city of the Morini, and was considered eminent in the things of God.

Although he was already weighed down by old age and appeared weakened by the loss of his sight, he nevertheless had a spirit stretched toward spiritual endeavor like a bow. Immediately, ready and with Christ covering his steps, he hastened to the venerable Autbert. Autbert then told him what he had in mind and what had been divinely shown to him. With equal desire and common counsel, amid the great joy of the people who had flocked together from every direction, they transferred the most blessed Vedast to the designated place.

During this translation, blessed Audomar is said to have received the light of his eyes, but immediately, through his prayers, to have obtained again the blindness that he had willingly borne. For he regarded the light of bodily eyes as of little account, having earned the light of the heavenly citizens [Note: [Col. 0677D] Bollandus, in his Preliminary Commentary, no. 36, suspects that what is related in the following number 24 was added after Alcuin’s death, because of these words found there: “Moreover, the miracles that were performed then [at the translation] and those that have now [since that time] been performed for nearly one hundred sixty years through the merits of blessed Vedast, etc.” Those years, says Bollandus, do not elapse between that translation, which took place in the year 667, and the year 804, when Alcuin died. Nor can the same years be counted from the death of Saint Vedast, since two hundred sixty years had elapsed from the year 540 by the time the year 800 was reached, around which time this Life appears to have been revised.].

[Col. 0678A] 172

## XXIV

Moreover, the miracles that are reported to have taken place then, and those that have now been performed for nearly one hundred sixty years through the merits of blessed Vedast, have not been committed to writing in any record, except that the following antiphon is sung by the voices of the chanters:

“This is blessed Vedast, for whom the angels commanded that a temple be built by human beings.”

That place itself is not far from the same city. Because of its distinction it was first called Nobiliacus [Note: [Col. 0677D] Nobiliacus. This monastery of Nobiliacus was afterward distinguished by the name of Saint Vedast and remains most famous even today. We shall provide its inscriptions among other poems of blessed Alcuin.]. But as time went on it became so distinguished that it came to be called a city, although it had almost become obscure through repeated ruin.

It has been exalted by the generosity of the faithful and filled with a company of monks and a throng of other people devoted to God [Note: [Col. 0678D] And a throng of other devoted people. Namely, in addition to the monks. These words of Alcuin are noteworthy, as Mabillon observes, volume I of the Annals, book XV, no. 49; by this expression he understands religious men of a second order, such as afterward were the oblates or donates, who were by no means counted among the monks.]. There divine praises are celebrated continually every day, and heavenly deeds have frequently occurred and continue to occur as signs of miracles [Col. 0678B], which are now reported more by the mouths of those who see them than written by the pen of one who records them.

Happy indeed is the city of Arras, fortified by so excellent a patron! Though it grows poor through the ruins of its walls, it nevertheless shines through the nobility of his merits. Let the whole people rejoice in the intercession of his holiness and offer eternal praises to almighty God, who bestowed upon them so illustrious a teacher, through whose preaching it recognized the way of truth. Through his prayers, if it remains firm in faith and holy in life, it will remain secure from every adversity and attain the perfect glory of blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] In Bollandus, this Life ends as follows: “will attain it. The same priest of Christ, Vedast, died on the eighth day before the Ides of February, while our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning,” etc., as above.]

[Note: [Col. 0678D] In the Vienna manuscript, in Lambecius’s new edition, volume I of the Annals, page 634, the title is: “Homily to be delivered to the people on the birthday of Saint Vedast, bishop.”]

# Exhortation to Imitate the Virtues of Saint Vedast Described in the Acts, by the Same Alcuin

From the Vedastine and Antwerp manuscripts.

[Col. 0678C]

## I

Rejoice, beloved brothers in the Lord, who have gathered for the solemn feast of our most holy Father and protector, namely Saint Vedast. Rejoice with spiritual gladness, and from the inmost affection of your hearts praise together the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned, through the preaching of this holy priest, to lead us from the errors of idolatry to recognition of his holy name.

Let us all follow the footsteps of so holy a teacher. Let us not be degenerate sons of so great a Father, but imitate the holiness of his life through nobility of conduct. Let us cast away from ourselves the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day, because the night of ignorance has withdrawn and the light of true knowledge has shone upon us, so that we may walk as children of light in all chastity and piety.

Let there be no hidden seeds of wickedness or malice in our hearts, because human beings look upon the face, but God examines the hearts, and nothing can be hidden from the eyes of his omnipotence. Let us prepare ourselves in every goodness, so that our distinguished bishop and devout preacher Vedast may joyfully lead us before the tribunal of the supreme Judge on the last day [Col. 0679A], so that, increased by the multitude of his sons, we may be filled with glory and, with him, deserve to hear the desired sentence:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

From the heavenly homeland he does not cease daily to aid our struggle through devout prayers, desiring that we, his dearest sons whom he begot in Christ with fatherly devotion, come to the glory of everlasting blessedness. Therefore, dearest brothers, let each person, in his own order and according to the capacity of his strength, resist the devil’s suggestions courageously, so that he may be made worthy to receive with our devout parent the eternal crown of triumph.

“For the sufferings of this present time,” as the Apostle says, “are not worthy of the glory to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII, 18). Therefore divine mercy has willed that the time of our labor be brief, the reward of our struggle eternal, and that for temporal tribulation we rejoice in the recompense of abiding glory [Col. 0679C].

## II

When the Life of the priest beloved of God was read, we heard how great was his devotion in every goodness, how through the strictness of abstinence he disciplined his body, and how through the duties of charity he strove to benefit everyone. Let us advance with complete eagerness of mind and the full strength of our ability along the footsteps of his life, so that we may deserve to become participants in the blessedness in which he reigns with Christ.

Let no carnal desire and no worldly ambition hinder our journey. Let us run through works of piety to the gates of the heavenly homeland. The citizens of the eternal city await us, and the King himself, who wishes all people to be saved, greatly desires our salvation together with his saints.

For it is fitting that we should be his fellow workers in our salvation [Col. 0679D], since he loved us so greatly that he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all. Let us love him, because he first loved us; let us do his will, because his will is our happiness.

Let us always keep in mind what Truth itself answered a certain rich man in the Gospel: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments” (Matthew XIX, 17). What are the commandments except love of God and love of neighbor? On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

Love of neighbor is therefore demonstrated in works of mercy: whoever possesses the substance of the world should help the one who does not possess it. Whoever possesses knowledge of doctrine should correct the one who is wandering, as the Apostle James says: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way has covered a multitude of his sins” (James V, 20).

We must know, dearest brothers, that as many souls as anyone wins for God, so many rewards he will receive from God. How great do you suppose is the glory that Saint Vedast possesses in the heavenly kingdom with Christ, since through diligent preaching he acquired for Christ so innumerable a people on earth? Or how great do you hope the glory of his soul is among the angels, since his body enjoys such great honor among human beings? Or what can he not obtain in heaven through prayers of piety, who shone in the world through such great miracles?

Yet greater than all miracles is the urgency of evangelical preaching and the fragrance of holy charity in the heart. For he labored very manfully to multiply the talents of the Lord’s money entrusted to him. Therefore he will joyfully hear the Lord say to him:

“Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew XXV, 23).

The goods of the present life are small in comparison with future goods. But whoever labors faithfully in the former will rest faithfully in the latter [Col. 0680B].

## III

This is the saint whose feast you have wished to celebrate together. He labored for the salvation of many, and therefore he will receive the rewards of many on the day of judgment. He mortified himself through the rigor of abstinence and benefited others through the diligence of his preaching; therefore he stands forth as worthy of praise to all, according to the saying of the wisest Solomon:

“The memory of the just is with praises, and the name of the impious will rot” (Proverbs X, 7).

While the life of the just is praised, the wickedness of the impious is detested by all like dung. What is happier than to earn from God the glory of perpetual blessedness through a good way of life and to be praised by everyone’s mouth?

Let us consider daily with what confidence we shall come before the tribunal of the supreme Judge and what good work we shall bring with us. His justice will show partiality toward no one, but will repay each according to his works. Whoever labors more in the work of God will receive more reward in the kingdom of God.

Let each person work manfully for his salvation in the vocation to which he has been called. The door of the heavenly kingdom stands open to all [Col. 0680D], but the quality of merits brings one person in and drives another out. How wretched it is for a human being to be excluded from the glory of the saints and assigned to eternal flames with the devil! The burden of sins plunges the soul into Tartarus; an abundance of righteousness raises it to heavenly glory.

Let us frequent the church of Christ more often; let us listen more attentively there to the words of God; and what we receive with our ears, let us retain in our hearts, so that we may bear the fruit of good works in patience and each person may strive to help the other with brotherly love.

We have abundant and distinguished examples of our most holy Father in every duty of charity, in the ardor of faith, in the perseverance of hope, and in his perseverance in every goodness. Let us whom we celebrate with such great praise and love with such great affection follow his footsteps with the full attention of our minds in every holy way of life, so that, running along the path of his life, we may deserve to receive with him the glory of eternal blessedness, with the help of our eternal King, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father [Col. 0681A] and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# Verses to Radon, the Abbot

Do not, I beg you, Father, disdain our little gifts:

Though you see them as small, great affection sends them.

# Alcuin’s Hymn on Saint Vedast

(From Lambecius, cited work, page 413.)

Christ, Savior of humankind from the mouth

of the ancient enemy who overcomes Adam,

graciously, Lord, we beseech you:

receive our vows.

You have wrought many gifts through the merits of your own;

you bestowed gifts proper to Vedast.

We, your servants, Christ, ask for your abundant gifts

with all our heart.

The land of the Franks had dreadful

darkness; the transmitted text continues, “he removed the rays of salvation / our inmost parts”; its sense is uncertain.

Through the Father’s mercy,

Christ, shine forth.

[Note: [Col. 0681B] Thus indeed it is written in the manuscript, but I am not yet sufficiently certain about the authentic reading of this passage. [Col. 0682B] LAMBECIUS. Perhaps it should read: *Miserans nostri* (“having pity on us”).]

Moved by pity for blind faces,

the holy man himself gave them bright eyes;

that fiery one made dark hearts

luminous.

He restored the weak crowds to health,

with his accustomed healing, before the people’s eyes;

with the Lord’s favor, he courageously performed

many glorious deeds.

The deadly bear withdrew in fear,

at Vedast’s forbidding voice,

not to cross beyond the prescribed dread boundary

throughout all ages.

With a pure heart he poured holy, true words

into the ears of the faithful people;

thereby he increased the number of the devout

in the heavenly dwellings.

A radiant column came to meet him,

accompanied by the splendid host of heaven,

when the Lord called his pure spirit

to its blessed end.

With the Devil conquered through faith and labor [Note: [Col. 0682B] *Zabulo* is used by the ancients for “devil.” See Lambecius], the warrior-soldier

entered the stars;

he receives worthy rewards with due honor

in the King’s palace.

May the glory of praise resound in the mouth

of all; and may it alike resound in everlasting praise

of the Father, the begotten Son,

and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0681]

175

# THIRD OPUSCULE. THE LIFE OF THE MOST BLESSED RICHARIUS, THE PRIEST

## Preface to the Emperor Charles

[Col. 0681C]

To the ever-venerable and ever-desirable lord, the most devout protector of the holy Church, Charles, by the grace of God ever Augustus, Albinus, the perpetual friend of your well-being.

While the piety of Your Excellence was lingering in the holy and deservedly venerable place of Centula [Note: [Col. 0681D] Charlemagne’s arrival at the monastery of Centula, and his celebration of Easter there in the year 800, are attested by the Annals of Einhard, the Tilian Annals, the Loiselian Annals, and many other writers. But he may have been there afterward, when he had already been crowned Augustus Caesar], and while I too, as a servant of Your Glory, was following the footsteps of your piety there and staying for a little while, the great man in Christ, the lord and venerable abbot Angilbert [Note: [Col. 0681D] Abbot Angilbert. His Life was treated by Bollandus on 18 February and by Mabillon in the Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, century IV. Angilbert attended Charlemagne’s coronation in the year 800, on the Nativity of Christ, and passed to heaven in the year 814], had asked my humble self to revise in a more polished style a certain little book, composed in a simpler manner, concerning the life of the most holy and truly magnificent confessor Richarius, to the praise of the Creator, who always appears wondrous in his chosen ones.

When I had at once complied with his prayers—for they are known to be heard and dear to the divine Majesty—and asked that the same little book be shown to me, I was not a little surprised that a confessor of so great a name, who was known to be a worker of such great virtues and whom ancient fame reported to have been surpassed by scarcely anyone after the apostles in the performance of miracles, possessed so small a volume of deeds.

While I was wondering at this, the aforementioned illustrious man Angilbert and the spiritual brothers of that holy place informed me that they possessed, and indeed that various churches also possessed, another larger codex [Note: [Col. 0682D] Another codex. This codex has been lost; it contained the deeds of Saint Richarius, arranged in a rougher style, together with the book of miracles. BOLLANDUS. MABILLON.], in which those miracles were read by which all Gaul rightly exalted the holy confessor of Christ.

Because its simple and less polished diction seemed more suitable to the brothers for recitation before the people [Al., clearer for recitation to the people], they agreed that this same account was sufficient for them. And while I was already applying my mind to setting down the matters they requested, suddenly I was summoned by a messenger from Your Piety, so that I might write what I was undertaking in such a way that it would truly be presented to the ears of Your Wisdom.

Therefore, after summoning a notary and setting the aforementioned little book before my eyes, we arranged, in a very concise dictation, what it seemed to report about his conversion, his conduct, his continence and truly incomparable holiness, as well as his glorious passing to Christ and the transfer of his precious body back to its former place [Col. 0683A], under the title The Life of the Most Blessed Richarius, the Noble Father [Al., The Life of the Most Blessed Father Richarius]. Unless I am deceived by my own incompetence, we humbly and most devotedly commend it to Your Most Prudent Wisdom like precious gold [Al., refined gold], for adorning the diadem of Christian philosophy.

And because we know that the glory of Christ and the honor of his saints reign in the chamber of your heart, we dedicate this preface of our little work, so blessed in its subject, to your blessed honor in the Lord.

# History of the Life

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Deeds of the priest. Mabillon asserts that this distich is not by Alcuin; nevertheless, the Bollandists consider the matter doubtful.]

This little book contains the deeds of the great priest Richarius,

whose body Centula holds.

176

# CHAPTER I. His Birth, Conversion to a Pious Life, Priesthood, Aid to His Neighbor, and Also to the Britons

[Col. 0683B]

I.

In the days [Al., *tempore*, “at the time”; text, *temporibus*, “in the times”] of the most glorious king of the Franks, Dagobert, who shone forth distinguished both by secular power and by Christian religion—for he exalted his nobles with dignities and honored the servants of God with honors [Al., “raised them to high positions”]—in those days, I say, very many monasteries began everywhere to be built by holy Fathers, and many religious men were also found among those of lay dress.

Among these, a certain Richarius, born in the village of Centula [Note: “In the village of Centula.” The region of Ponthieu—commonly called le Ponthieu—was a district of Picardy within the boundaries of the Ambians, Morini, and Neustrians. Its chief town was Abbeville, from which the town of Centula, or Centulum, lay two leagues to the east; there stood the monastery of Centula, both now bearing the name of Saint-Riquier, on the Scarduon, the river of the Cardoons. Mabillon, *Observations preliminary*, no. 6.], in the province of Ponthieu [le Ponthieu], shone forth like the morning star rising amid shadows, born not of parents especially noble according to the standards of the world [Note: “Not of especially noble parents.” Those, therefore, are not to be approved who derive the blessed Richarius’s family lineage from Raganarius, brother of Clovis the Great. Mabillon calls this genealogy fabulous and rejects it. Hence I am also inclined to believe that the epitaph of Saint Richarius, in which the holy man is said to have been “born of exalted lineage” [Col. 0684D], was not written by Alcuin, although the author of the *Chronicle of Centula* seems to attribute it to him.], but honorable in character and most devoted to every virtue; so that, while still living a rustic life, he bore certain signs foretelling his future holiness [Quercet., “Thus he”].

It happened at that time that two priests distinguished by holiness and shining with the merits of their virtues arrived in the regions of Ponthieu from the parts of Ireland. The first was called Caidocus, the other Frichorius [Note: “The other was Frichorius.” This is omitted by Quercetanus, and, according to Mabillon, the name Frichorius is lacking in most manuscripts. Saint Angilbert wrote the epitaphs of Caidocus and Frichorius; they are extant in the *Chronicle of Centula*, book I, chapter 11, and in Mabillon at the end of this Life of Saint Richarius. Gervinus, abbot of the holy confessor Caidocus and his companion, raised their bodies from the earth and, placing their relics more suitably, judged them worthy of veneration by the faithful, says Hariulfus in the cited *Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 33. See the Acts of both saints in the Bollandists under 30 May.].

But the peasants and local inhabitants of that place, because of the unusualness of their conduct, did not receive them, nor treat them with honor worthy of their holiness. Rather, after afflicting them with injuries and chastising them with insults, they began to drive them from their borders.

The future servant of God, Richarius, opposed their violence and criminal presumption. He rescued Christ’s servants from the hands of the wicked and, escorting them with all kindness to his own house, obtained—by God’s providence—that they should be protected and that he himself should be saved [Al., “he escorted them”; Mab., “to escort them”].

Nor could the lamp of God’s grace, once kindled, remain hidden for long. The light of holiness and preaching, when revealed, shone far and wide for the salvation of many [Al., “but when the light of holiness was revealed, it spread far and wide”]. He cared for his guests, whom he had welcomed, with great charity, and listened to them as they preached the word of God to him with complete humility and attentiveness.

The seed of God’s word was not scattered upon the ground in vain. What he heard with his ears he retained deeply in his heart, and it produced a hundredfold fruit in Christ’s granaries—as later became clearer than daylight through his holiness and the manifestation of his miracles.

### II. Conversion and ascetic discipline

Therefore, pierced by the preaching of God’s servants and by the inspiration of divine grace, he turned to tears, confessed his sins, and, earnestly seeking pardon in the sight of almighty God, washed away with tears what he had sinned through ignorance amid the enticements of youth. He who, through hospitality, had received the Lord in His servants was himself received by the Lord in mercy and compassion [Al., “in the mercy of repentance,” or “in merciful compassion”].

From that time [Note: “The beginning of sacred religion.” The author of the *Chronicle of Centula*, book I, chapter 6, writes: “he assumed the religious habit.”] he took up the beginning of sacred religion and daily strove to climb, by steps of humility, toward the higher heights of piety. Having once undertaken the path of life, he tried to travel it with the steps of faith; forgetting what lay behind, he stretched forward with the Apostle toward what lay ahead (Philippians 3:13), remembering at every step that verse: “The saints shall go from strength to strength, until they reach [text, *perveniant*, “they may reach”; Al., *perveniret*, “he might reach”] what follows: the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Psalm 83:8).

Thus, from the very beginning of his conversion, he bound himself with such harsh discipline that, after long and prolonged fasts, he restored his weary little body with barley bread mixed with ashes and water tempered with tears. [Thereafter, throughout his life, he admitted no more luxurious food;] and sustained by this nourishment [taken only twice a week, namely on Sunday and Thursday], the devoted athlete of Christ served the Lord day and night in vigils and prayers—not striking the air, but chastising his body, lest the future preacher of Christ should be found reprobate in anything.
