### III. Priesthood and preaching

By these and similar degrees of virtue, and by the conduct of his most holy life, he became acceptable to God and reached the priestly dignity through worthy advancement, so that the one who possessed devotion to preaching should not lack the dignity of office.

As a servant of God, he adorned that office with great humility, cultivated it with true charity, and enlarged it through the preaching of God’s word. Like a good farmer, he uprooted the thorns of sins from the Lord’s evangelical field with the plow, and irrigated arid hearts with the heavenly dew of eternal salvation.

After his irrigation, divine mercy also gave this people abundant growth in faith. Thus the aforesaid man of God, Richarius, became honored and beloved by all, because what he preached with his mouth he demonstrated by his example, and the way of life that he pointed out to others in speech he himself first traversed in action.

### IV. Charity toward the poor and afflicted

Whatever the people willingly offered him as compensation for his preaching, he hastened to distribute entirely among the poor. He considered it unworthy to think about the morrow of this present life when he longed to receive the riches of eternal life. Therefore he distributed what everyone offered, so that he might receive what God had promised.

A blessed exchange: he who cheerfully distributed small and transitory things was destined happily to receive great and eternal ones.

He was an exceptionally devoted comforter of the poor, a receiver of strangers, a defender of widows, and a father to the fatherless and orphans, so that the testimony of holy Job could most truly have been spoken of him:

> “I was an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, and a father to the orphan; and the cause I did not know I investigated most diligently” (Job 29:15).

Therefore the sick flocked to him from every direction. He welcomed them with a joyful spirit and offered them the healing of consolation through holy prayers.

He did not shrink from lepers or those suffering from elephantiasis, but embraced them as brothers and warmed their wounded limbs in baths. He entered those same baths after them, cleansing them by his compassion more than defiling himself, not deaf to the prophetic saying:

> “Bring the poor and the homeless into your house; cover the naked with your garments, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah 58:7).

### V. Preaching, correction, and redemption

He not only nourished those who came to him with bodily food; he also continually refreshed them with the spiritual consolation of holy preaching.

And just as he was everywhere an able consoler of the wretched, so he did not fear to be a stern chastiser of the proud. He raised the former by the clemency of compassion; he humbled the latter by the censure of severe rebuke.

He did not fear the anger of earthly power [Al., “anger from outside”], because inward fear of divine power strengthened him completely. He despised the threats of the wealthy, so that he might stand forth as a herald of truth.

He was not a reed shaken by the wind, so that any breath of human praise or disparagement might disturb him. Standing upon the stronghold of solid truth, he refused to be judged by human speech [Al., “by human day”], according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 4:3). Walking along the royal road, he turned neither to the right because of the terrors of the powerful nor to the left because of the flatteries of sycophants.

Therefore he won a great people for the Lord their God in that present province and earned perpetual honor for himself. When his people saw his religious devotion in Christ, they began to honor him more attentively and to bring him many gifts for distribution as alms.

He, being filled with love of God and neighbor, distributed all of them as aid to the poor, and spent the greatest part upon the redemption of captives. Some, bound by the spiritual chains of sins through the devil’s deceit, he released through the earnest encouragement of his preaching; others, oppressed by secular captivity, he redeemed by the distribution of money. Thus the former, spiritually freed, rejoiced in the Lord, while the latter, liberated from bodily servitude, were converted to God.

### VI. Mission in Britain

Nor did the aforesaid man of the Lord shine forth only in these regions through works of compassion and the light of preaching. As Lucifer, leaping across the level fields of the Ocean, scatters the shadows of night by his rising as the herald of daylight, so Richarius spread the light of truth by his arrival in the overseas regions of Britain, to drive away the darkness of ignorance.

There, as here, he liberated some from demonic servitude and others from bodily captivity. To the former he imparted the word of God; for the latter he paid the price of charity, so that they might receive eternal freedom in exchange for temporal redemption.

Thus, as a good merchant of the Lord’s money, he strove to multiply the two talents of the single [Al., “double”] charity of God and neighbor, so that, with the abundant fruit of his labor, he might meet his Lord and hear that most joyful voice:

> “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:21).

### VII. The liberation of his own servants

It is reported that, while he remained in Britain for a considerable time on account of preaching, it suddenly came to his mind that he had left some people belonging to him in servitude in Gaul.

Struck with grief, he said to his companions:

> “Alas! We have left our own people in servitude in our homeland, while we came here to liberate others—and I know especially that they are soon to die. Go, therefore, in haste, board a ship, and make them free before they die.”

They promptly obeyed their father’s command and came to the homeland. They found the aforesaid servants of the man of God safe and unharmed, and, freeing them as they had been ordered, made them free persons. Not long afterward, just as the holy man of God had foretold, they died.

O how great is the clemency of Christ God, who implanted in His servant a compassionate affection and revealed to him the future death of his servants, so that the reward of mercy might not be lost to him on account of his own people, nor the yoke of servitude burden those who were dying!

He had not feared to undertake the danger of so great a journey in order to liberate strangers. From that time onward he wished to retain no one belonging to him under the yoke of servitude, but everywhere granted full freedom to all under his authority, lest he should appear harsher toward his own than he desired to appear gentle toward others, and lest he should accumulate for himself from his own people the reward that he had gathered from others.

## Chapter II. Deeds involving Saint Rictrude and King Dagobert; retreat into the Crisciac forest

### VIII. Return from Britain and spiritual warfare

When he had completed his preaching ministry in Britain, he returned to his homeland with abundant fruit of the word of God, lest, while seeking a reward in another’s harvest, he should lose it in his own.

He subjected himself to God’s service all the more ardently as he sensed the day of recompense drawing nearer. He afflicted himself with daily fasts, bound himself by mortification of the flesh, tormented himself with vigils, fortified himself with prayers, strengthened himself with charity, strengthened himself with hope, and armed himself with faith. He returned evil to no one for evil, flattered no one, and despised no one, so that he might himself first walk the way of truth that he had shown to others by preaching.

Thus the man of God put on the helmet of salvation [Al., “having put on”], girded himself with the sword of God’s word, was surrounded on every side by the breastplate of righteousness, armed with the shield of faith, and shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace (Ephesians 6). He advanced into open battle against the ancient enemy, repelling all his fiery darts with the strongest boss of faith. By daily triumphs he carried away abundant spoils after conquering the enemy.

In the Church [text, *Ecclesia*, “in the Church”; Al., *Ecclesiam*, “into the Church”] of Christ he was as fearsome to the enemy of the human race as he was necessary to the human race, since he sought the salvation not only of himself but of many.

It is therefore just that he should be praised in Christ by many mouths, and called the redeemer of many for Christ [Al., “through Christ”]. It is not so important to recount the miracles he performed as to recognize the power of those miracles, by which he gained many people for the heavenly King during his lifetime.

There is no doubt that the ministry of preaching is greater than the display of all signs, although, as circumstances and the times required, the divine clemency did not fail to perform signs through him.

### IX. The miracle of Rictrude’s son

At a certain time, a temptation by an evil spirit befell the man of God as a source of embarrassment, but by God’s mercy it was permitted to occur for his glory.

He visited on horseback a woman devoted to God, named Rictrude [Note: Rictrude. She is commemorated on 12 May. The Bollandists. Mabillon discusses whether she is the same as Saint Rictrude, abbess of Marchiennes, in the Life of Rictrude itself, *Acts of the Saints*, second century, part I, p. 946.].

After the sweet fare of life and salutary conversation, when the man of God had mounted his horse and was preparing to return home, the woman mentioned above, according to custom, followed the footsteps of the Father as he rode, holding her son [text, *filium*, “son”; Al., *filiolum*, “little son”] in her arms [Note: “Holding her son in her arms.” This was Saint Maurontus, commemorated on 5 May. Hucbald, a monk of Elnone, writes in the Life of Saint Rictrude that he was regenerated through holy baptism by Saint Richarius. He is different from Marontus, the king’s forest-keeper at that time, who is mentioned shortly below in section 11. The Bollandists.], so that the child too might be strengthened by the blessing of the man of God, who had himself previously regenerated him through holy baptism.

When the venerable horseman took the infant, either to bless him or to kiss him, the ancient enemy, hostile to every good thing, infused ferocity into the horse. Gnashing its teeth, kicking with its feet, and raging with its whole body, it began to race across the field with an unfamiliar violence.

Seeing this in terror, the mother turned her eyes away lest she see her son dying, while the servant of God held him in his hand amid the horse’s fury. The household did not cease to raise an uproar, lament, and howl, fearing the child’s death or the man of God’s fall.

But the right hand of Christ, which lifted up trembling Peter so that he would not sink in the waves, raised up the falling child so that he would not be dashed upon the ground. After the servant of God had prayed, the child reached the earth unharmed, like a little bird, and the horse was restored to its gentleness.

The mother received her son in her arms, safe and laughing, upon the ground. From that time onward, however, the priest of God wished to travel not on a horse but on a most gentle little donkey.

Thus, by God’s mercy, the temptation of the evil enemy was turned for him into an honor of praise, and the horse’s pride became a lesson and occasion of humility. He had not forgotten that the Lord Christ, when hastening toward the redemption of the human race, traveled on a donkey, not on a horse (Matthew 21). So too, for the sake of salutary preaching, while hastening daily through many places, he judged a donkey sufficient to carry him.

Wherever he traveled, either psalms resounded from his mouth or preaching of salvation was heard from it. Nor is it surprising that he always preached Christ with his tongue, since he always carried Him in his heart. Through Christ he was a gracious consoler to the wretched and a stern rebuker of the powerful, relieving the poverty of the former with compassionate mercy and restraining the pride of the latter with severe correction.

### X. King Dagobert’s visit

At a certain time, the most powerful King Dagobert, at the request of the illustrious Gislemarus, came into those same regions [Al., “came”], and happened to visit the man of God in order to commend himself to his holy prayers.

The servant of God both strengthened him by the blessing of his holiness and rebuked him with priestly authority in an unrestrained voice. He warned him not to take pride in secular power, not to place his hope in fleeting riches, not to be lifted up by the empty reports of flatterers, and not to rejoice in perishable honors. Rather, he should fear God’s power and praise His immeasurable glory; he should consider human power and glory as nothing, since they suddenly withdraw like a fleeting shadow and, like foam upon water, vanish when the wind of temptation blows.

He urged him instead to fearfully consider that “the mighty shall be mightily tested” (Wisdom 6:7), and that “from the one to whom more has been given, more will be demanded” (Luke 12:48).

He who scarcely suffices to render an account to God for himself alone on the day of judgment—what will he do for the many thousands of people entrusted to him [Al., “how will he be able to bear rendering an account for so many thousands of people entrusted to him”]?

For this reason, each person may have greater cause to fear presiding than being subject. One who is subject will render an account to God for himself alone; those who preside will render an account for all who have been placed under their authority.

The king, being most wise, received this rebuke graciously. Rejoicing in the priest’s frank confidence in the truth, he invited the priest of Christ to accompany him to a banquet.

Strengthened by Christ’s example, who did not reject secular banquets, and seeking an opportunity for preaching, he went with the king to his table. Throughout that entire day and night, amid the festivities of the meal, he served the word of God—the food of salvation—to his guests.

The aforesaid king, delighted by his steadfast character and persistence in preaching, began to love and honor him sincerely, to such an extent that on that very day he donated something from his revenues for the lamps of the house of God [Note: “For the lamps of the house of God.” Namely, the church that he had founded in the village of Centula, as is said in the following section. In the *Chronicle of Centula*, book IV, chapter 21, Dagobert is said to have donated land called Campania.].

He considered it right that, just as he himself had been enlightened by the invisible light of Richarius’s preaching, so the house of the Lord should be illuminated by visible light through him; and that what shone within him in faith should shine outwardly in the Church. He remembered the Lord’s command:

> “Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Likewise, in the Psalm:

> “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10);

that is, in the light of faith that shines in the mind, an outward light sparkles and shines forth in action.

### XI. Retreat into the Crisciac forest

Since the servant of God was honored by human beings, he began to contemplate fleeing from human beings, so that by avoiding temporal honors he might receive eternal honors.

He longed for the wilderness, so that he might devote himself more freely to God alone and enjoy the fruits of contemplation, whereas up to that time he had labored diligently amid active works. He knew that the Lord had spoken of Mary, sitting at His feet and listening attentively to the word of life:

> “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

Remembering this saying, he sought the monastic life [that is, the eremitical life], so that in greater seclusion he might investigate heavenly things with his mind alone. He entrusted the governance of the Church [Note: “To another.” Namely, Ocialdus, mentioned below in section 14, whom Hariulfus, book I, chapter 19, calls “a man of perfect and proven holiness.”] to another—the Church he himself had founded for Christ in the village of Centula.

Gislemarus, an illustrious man and devoted lover of the Christian religion, together with Maurontus, a certain nobleman and keeper of the lands and forests belonging to the king, provided him with a place to stay [Note: “In the Crisciac forest.” This forest lies ten thousand paces west of Centula. In the printed editions it was corruptly read as “the Tristiac forest”; the earlier reading, according to Mabillon, is found in all the copies. Hence Malbrancus should be corrected: in book III *On the Morini*, chapter 39, on the basis of that corrupt reading he imagined here a Nepian forest beside the river Lys, where Richarius, at the urging of the illustrious Maurontus, built the monastery of Broile and eventually ended his life. Mabillon.] in the Crisciac forest [printed edition: Tristiac].

Maurontus himself later laid aside his secular dress and became a monk in that same place. After preparing a solitary dwelling for the man of God, he began to build a monastery for Christ [Note: “He began to construct a monastery.” This is now the monastery of Foreste, commonly called Forest-Montier. Although it possesses little revenue and is greatly worn down, it has its own abbot and a very few monks of the Order of Saint Benedict. The same editor.].

### XII. Life in the wilderness

The man of God therefore entered that dwelling [Note: “With only one companion.” This was Sigobardus, to whom the holy man appeared after his death and who arranged his funeral. See below, sections 13 and 14. Hariulfus, the Centulan chronicler, calls this Sygobardus “resplendent with the highest nobility.”] with only one companion, content with a small hut made by the poorest workmanship, so that the dwelling might correspond to the life. He considered it excessive for one who despised the world to possess or behold any of the world’s luxuries [Al., “to wish to possess”; perhaps “or wish to possess”].

There he chastised himself with such great mortification of the flesh and afflicted himself with such constant fasting and vigils that scarcely did his dry bones cling together through their loosened joints, and he could move his trembling footsteps only with difficulty, guided by a staff.

Already greater in mind than the world, he thought continually of heavenly things alone. The more alien he was to the world, the closer he was to God. Each day in the wilderness he conquered the one by whom Adam was once conquered in paradise. He walked upon the asp and the basilisk, crushed daily the head of the ancient serpent, despised temporal things, sighed only for eternal ones, ascended at every hour Jacob’s ladder of dreams, and proceeded along the narrow way that leads to life, fortifying his journey with continual prayers.

Yet the narrow enclosure of the wilderness could not conceal the pillar of light. Rather, by the rays of its brilliance, it became known more widely and more conspicuously.

Therefore people worn down by various illnesses flocked to the man of God from every direction. He healed them through the remedies of holy prayers, and caused all who came to him afflicted by whatever disease or oppressed by the bitterness of any grief to return home healthy and joyful.

Disease could not remain long in the house of healing. The nearer it came, the more swiftly it withdrew.

My purpose, however, is not to recount individually and by name every kind of his virtue, but to touch upon the holiness of his life in a few words, lest the abundance of the fame of the signs performed through him be obscured rather than praised by the slowness of my speech.

## Chapter III. Pious death; translation of the body to Centula; miracles

### XIII. Richarius’s death

Leaving those matters to the learned [Al., “leaving them”], it is enough for me alone to say with what end that holy soul departed this present world.

Thus, foreknowing—through the Holy Spirit, by whom he had always been quickened—the day of his summons, on which he was to receive the happiness he had long desired, so that he might be forever joined to Christ, whom he had always loved, he called to himself his companion Sigobardus and said to him:

> “I know, my son, I know that my end is not far off, and I shall soon see my King, whom I have long desired. Would that I might see Him, His servant, as gracious toward me as He is desirable to His saints.
>
> “But you, my son, prepare a little vessel for my body, in which it may be placed—not with superfluous effort but for necessary use—so that it may be preserved there until the day when this corruption shall be changed into incorruption and this mortal body shall put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53).
>
> “And prepare yourself with every care, dearest son, so that when that day, which is now approaching me, comes for you, it may find you ready.
>
> “I am entering the way of all flesh. May the Savior of the world be merciful to me; may He now defend me from the enemy who once redeemed me from the enemy; and may I find Him who was my consoler in this present life to be my giver of eternal life.”

Hearing these words from his father, the disciple was covered with tears. Nevertheless, he followed the command. Finding a piece of wood, he split it, hollowed it out, and fitted it for his father’s body. He watered what he had made with pious tears, almost filling it with bitter tears before filling it with his father’s limbs. As best he could, he placed the fitted sarcophagus in the spot designated by his father.

Meanwhile, while the son was sorrowfully preparing his father’s burial service [Al., “while he was preparing the sad burial service”], a stronger illness was consuming the father. In his cold little body scarcely any breath remained. Yet he did not cease from the duty of prayer or the service of divine praise.

After strengthening his journey with the life-giving viaticum of Christ’s body and blood, he gave up his spirit amid thanksgiving and words of prayer, on 26 April [Note: “He gave up his spirit.” In the year of the Christian era 645, as Mabillon proves in the cited work, p. 196.]. His disciple placed him in the tomb at the spot he had himself commanded.

### XIV. The vision of Sigobardus and the translation of the body

It is marvelous to relate that, during his father’s funeral rites, the disciple was suddenly overcome by sleep and saw in a vision—as though he had been snatched away into a most splendid hall, exceedingly beautiful and brighter even than the light of the sun.

There he saw blessed Richarius dwelling with a radiant and joyful countenance and speaking to him:

> “Behold, brother Sigobardus, what sort of dwelling God has prepared for me: in place of the wretched one I had on earth, a most beautiful one in heaven; in place of the contemptible one, a glorious one; in place of the dark one, one most full of light; and in place of the smoky one, one radiant with every delight.”

When Sigobardus awoke, he completed the funeral work more joyfully, God providing that the son should be consoled and that his father’s glory should be shown to him.

Thus the soldier of Christ was buried, as I have said, where he had served his King with the greatest devotion.

Not long afterward [Note: “Not long afterward.” After a period of five months and twelve days, that is, from 26 April until 9 October. The Bollandist, from other interpolated Acts.], the brothers from the monastery of Centula, with their abbot Ocialdus, a religious man and the saint’s successor, came and carried away the body of Saint Richarius [Note: “The body of Saint Richarius.” Free from every corruption, just as his heart had been free from every love of the world. The same editor, in the same place.]. They placed it in the spot where it still rests, with great glory for his merits.

There, by God’s favor, new miracles are frequently heard to be performed through the relics of His servant [Al., “to be brought about”], so that the faith of those who pray may be made manifest, the merits of the holy man displayed, and Christ praised in His servant, as it is said:

> “Praise the Lord in His saints” (Psalm 150:1).

### XV. Healings at the tomb

A certain man, crippled and physically weak but strong in faith, frequently visited the tomb of the holy man of God in prayer. When he suddenly received the health he desired, he gave glory to God because he had come ill and departed healthy.

In memory of this miracle, the supports of his former infirmity hang in the church of Saint Richarius to this day.

Likewise, demoniacs, often brought to the body of the holy man of God by the service of their companions, are freed from the torment of the evil spirit by divine mercy.

At a certain time, some people bound with fetters and chains were being led through the public street beside the church of blessed Richarius. When they approached the temple of the man of God from a distance, they began to cry out in a loud voice:

> “Saint Richarius, save us!”

At once their bonds broke, and they were released.

### XVI. Deliverance from the plague

There was also a great pestilence, which they call the poisonous lizard, that killed the inhabitants of the land far and wide with bitter death; scarcely anyone touched by it escaped alive.

One of the brothers of Saint Richarius was struck by this plague. Although he feared death because of the pestilence, he did not despair of life because of his patron.

Therefore, accompanied by the brothers as though seeking certain aid, he ran to the tomb of the man of God. After they had prayed there together, he himself was freed from death, and all the others were protected from the plague. None of those brothers was struck by the deadly devastation of that pestilence.

Nor were they alone delivered. If anyone came from far away, touched by the pestilential plague, and fled in faith to the aid of Saint Richarius, he too escaped the danger of death even amid the devastation.

### XVII. Exhortation to imitate the saint

From this it may be understood how great a power he possesses with God to intercede for our sins, if we cry out in faith to one endowed with such power to drive away diseases from those who come to him in faith.

The miracles make clear what he is by his merits, and his life already lived shines forth in the works that followed, so that there is no need to doubt his holiness when he is so powerful in virtue.

Understand from this, dearest brothers, what riches he now possesses with Christ who wished to be poor for Christ, and how gloriously he reigns among the angels who desired to be despised among human beings, now possessing most happily in heaven the honor he fled on earth.

Therefore it is fitting that he should be honored by all, since he always loved the Lord of all—and especially by us, who serve at his body [Note: Alcuin says this in the person of the monks of Centula.]—so that those whom he begot through instruction he may possess as worthy heirs in merits.

Our praise benefits him less than his imitation benefits us. A devoted imitator pleases him more than an idle praiser.

Therefore, dearest brothers, most holy Fathers, most joyful sons, and people of the entire holy congregation who have gathered for the feast of so great a patron, make yourselves worthy, so that almighty God, through his intercessions, may hear your prayers.

Adorn yourselves with spiritual beauty, with the glory of surpassing charity, with the strength of victorious faith, and with the sweetest hope in Christ’s goodness. Always follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers, so that, walking by their examples, you may be made worthy of their fellowship.

And, according to the Apostle, let us deny impiety and worldly desires and live soberly, justly, and piously in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for us so that He might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for Himself a people acceptable to Him, devoted to good works (Titus 2:12), to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Fourth Work: Two Books on the Life of Saint Willibrord, Bishop of Utrecht

### 183 Prologue

To the distinguished lord, venerable and praiseworthy Archbishop Beornradus [Note: Beornradus. Also called Beornredus or Berneradus. In the list of abbots of Echternach, John Bertelius, abbot of that place, and Gabriel Bucelinus count him third, after Willibrord and Albert, and assert that he was archbishop of Sens. He must therefore have been the same man whom Saint-Marthanus calls Berardus and who is said to have died in 795, although Bertelius places Beornradus’s death in 796.], the humble deacon Alcuin sends greetings.

Letters from Your Excellency were brought to us, in which, recognizing your devotion to the Lord and your long-standing meditation upon his law, I confess that I was filled with great joy. Yet I considered myself far unequal to your request, since I possess no distinction of eloquence with which to accomplish what you commanded [Mab., “what you commanded”]: and unless charity urged me on—which is accustomed to refuse no one [Id., “which is accustomed to refuse no one”]—I would not have dared to undertake a task beyond the strength of my poverty [Id., “smallness”].

Nevertheless, with divine grace granted in answer to your prayers, and with the most holy Father Willibrord interceding, whose life, conduct, and miracles you so earnestly ask me to write [Id., “whom you asked with pious zeal”], I have obeyed your commands, holy Father, and composed two little books. One proceeds in prose, and could be read publicly to the brothers in church, if it should seem worthy of your wisdom; the other runs in the foot of Pierian verse and ought to be pondered only in private chambers among your students. Yet both were dictated amid the occupations of the day, in stolen little vigils of the night; and they require your defense all the more because they have received so little polishing from their own author.

It was my part not to despise the authority of the one commanding; it is yours to defend the ignorance of the obedient. I have also added to the first little book a homily, which I wish were worthy to be proclaimed to the people by your venerable mouth. Likewise, I appended to the second work an elegiac poem concerning the venerable man Wilgis, namely the father of the most holy bishop Willibrord, whose body rests in a certain maritime cell [Note: “In a certain maritime cell.” There were two maritime cells over which Alcuin presided. One was situated in the promontories nearest the Ocean Sea and the River Humber, and indeed in the province of Northumbria, therefore in the present-day county of York. There the holy Wilgis, father of Saint Willibrord, was buried, as is said in the following chapter, chapter 1. The other is called Saint-Josse and is situated among the Morini on the shore of the Gallic Ocean, far removed from the former; it is otherwise called Wicus and today Saint-Josse-sur-Mer. See letters 39, 96, and 115. Mabillon observes that Alcuin is speaking here of the former cell, contrary to the opinion of the Sancta-Marthani. Perhaps this was the first which Alcuin received to govern by legitimate succession, as he himself says here and below in chapter 1 of the Life, and in letter 226.] where I, although unworthy, serve by legitimate succession, granted by God.

But everything that I have dictated, whether moving in prose or running in verse, belongs to the judgment of Your Holiness: whether it is worthy of remembrance or ought to be scraped away with the harsh pumice [Id. adds: “whether it should be”]. It will not proceed into public unless strengthened by your examination.

# BOOK ONE

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN

### CHAPTER I. Wilgis first embraces the monastic life, then the solitary life. He becomes renowned for miracles. He builds a church from the donations of kings and nobles. Alcuin becomes his successor by legitimate inheritance.

There was in the island of Britain, in the province of Northumbria, a certain householder of Saxon race named Wilgis, who, with his wife and his entire household, was leading a religious life in Christ, as was later revealed by signs. For, abandoning secular dress, he chose the monastic way of life; and not long afterward, as the ardor of the spiritual life increased in him, he devoted himself with stricter zeal of mind to solitary discipline [Mab., “to solitary discipline”] in the promontories enclosed by the Ocean Sea and the River Humber.

There, for a long time, serving God in fasts, prayers, and vigils in a certain small oratory dedicated to the name of Saint Andrew, apostle of Christ, he also became renowned for signs of miracles [Mab., “so that he became renowned”], and his name became famous. Nor did he cease to exhort the crowds who gathered to him with the most pleasing admonition of the word of God.

He also became honored by the king and nobles of that people, to such an extent that they granted him, as a perpetual gift, certain small properties adjoining those promontories, for the building of a church to God. In it the devout father gathered a modest but honorable community of servants of God. After many struggles of holy labor, he rests there in body, crowned by God, and his descendants possess it to this day through the tradition of his holiness.

I, last both in merit and in succession among them, received that same cell to govern by legitimate succession. At your command, most blessed bishop Beornrad, I have written this history of the most holy Father and supreme priest Willibrord. According to the grace given you by God, you have proved the worthiest heir of so great a Father—in the dignity of the supreme priesthood, in descent from his family, and in the guardianship of the holy places known to have been built by him in honor of God.

### CHAPTER II. The wondrous conception of Saint Willibrord. His mother’s vision. Interpretation of the vision.

And in order to retrace more deeply the origin of the birth of that same holy Father Willibrord, and then the signs of divine election in his mother’s womb, I shall return to the point from which I departed. For just as the blessed John the Baptist, most holy forerunner of our Lord Jesus Christ, sanctified to God from his mother’s womb and born of religious parents, as the Gospel history relates (Luke I), was born as a morning star preceding Christ, like the sun, destined to benefit many for salvation, so Saint Willibrord is recognized as having been born of religious parents for the salvation of many.

For the venerable man Wilgis, of whom we spoke shortly before, entered marriage by God’s predestination for this sole purpose: that from him offspring might be born for the advancement of many peoples. Accordingly, his wife—the mother, that is, of the blessed Father Willibrord—during the deepest stillness of the night saw a heavenly vision in sleep (*orama*, ὅραμα, that is, “a vision”). She seemed to see a new moon in the sky, growing until it appeared to be full. As she gazed at it more attentively, it suddenly slipped downward and fell into her mouth. After she had swallowed it, her inward parts were suffused with its brightness.

When she awoke, terrified by fear, she related the dream to a certain religious priest. He asked her whether, on the night in which the vision had appeared to her, she had united with her husband according to her customary practice. After she confessed that this had occurred, he replied:

“The moon which you saw grow from small to great [Mab., ‘from small to great’] is the son whom you conceived that night. He will disperse the dark errors of shadows by the light of truth; and wherever he goes, with the splendor of heavenly light accompanying him, he will display the full sphere of his perfection. As the brightness of his renown and the beauty of his conduct shine forth, he will attract the gaze of many.”

The truth of events followed upon the interpretation of this dream.

### CHAPTER III. The birth and baptism of Saint Willibrord. He becomes a cleric and a monk.

After the passage of the appointed days, the woman gave birth to a son. Having been reborn in the sacred baptismal font, the child was given the name Willibrord by his mother; and as soon as he had been weaned, his father handed the infant over to the brothers of the Ripon church [Note: “Of the Ripon church.” Mabillon teaches that this monastery was founded by Alcfrid, king of the Northumbrians, in the year 651, in the second century of the Benedictine era, in the Life of Saint Cuthbert, chapter 7], to be trained in religious studies and sacred letters, so that his more fragile age might grow strong through stronger disciplines, seeing nothing except what was honorable and hearing nothing except what was holy.

Divine grace soon granted that from early childhood he should advance in understanding and excel in conduct, as is appropriate to such years, so that in our own times you might have thought a new Samuel had been born, of whom it is said: “Now the boy Samuel progressed and grew, and was pleasing both to God and to men” (1 Kings II, 26).

There, in the aforesaid monastery, the boy, destined to benefit many, received the tonsure of the clerical state, and by a devout profession made himself a monk. He was raised among the other youths of that most holy monastery, but inferior to none in eagerness, second to none in the duty of humility, and surpassed by none in devotion to reading. Thus the boy of good character advanced daily, so that he surpassed the tender years of childhood in the gravity of his conduct. He became advanced in understanding, though his body was small and frail.

### CHAPTER IV. He sets out for Ireland.

Thus, as the blessed youth advanced in sacred learning, in every form of sobriety, and in uprightness of conduct until his twentieth year, he was kindled by an ardor for a stricter life and urged on by love of pilgrimage. Having heard that scholarly learning flourished in Ireland, he was also encouraged by the reported way of life of certain holy men, especially the most blessed Father and bishop Egbert [Note: “Bishop Egbert.” Mabillon doubts whether this bishop was a bishop or archbishop, in the third century of the Benedictine era, part I, in his Eulogy, no. 6, p. 490, because of the silence of the Venerable Bede, who nowhere calls him a prelate or bishop, but only a priest. Accordingly, the pseudo-Marcellinus is not to be heeded in the fanciful Acts of Saint Suidbert, where he calls Egbert archbishop of York, evidently confusing him with Ecgbert, prelate of that see, who, in the third year after this Egbert’s death, succeeded to the place of the younger Wilfrid, archbishop of York], who was called “the Saint,” and also of Wicbert, a venerable man and priest of God.

Both of these, for love of their heavenly homeland, had abandoned home, country, and family and withdrawn to Ireland. There, stripped of the world and filled with God, they daily drew the sweetest fruits of heavenly contemplation from a solitary way of life.

Wishing to imitate the holiness of these men, the blessed youth, with the consent of his abbot and brothers, hastened to Ireland [Mab., “went to Ireland”], joining himself to the familiarity of the aforesaid Fathers, so that, like a most prudent bee, he might gather honey-sweet flowers of devotion from their nearness and construct the sweetest honeycombs of virtues in the hive of his heart.

There, for twelve years, among outstanding teachers alike of holy religion and sacred learning, he was instructed to become a preacher of many peoples, until he attained a perfect man and the measure of the fullness of Christ.

### CHAPTER V. He burns with the desire to convert the pagans.

In the thirty-third year of his life, the flame of faith grew greater in the breast of this excellent man, so that it seemed little to him to have labored only for himself in the holiness of religion, unless he also benefited others through the truth of preaching. He heard that in the northern parts of the world there was indeed a great harvest, but few laborers.

But, so that the truth of the dream might be fulfilled according to God’s providence—the dream which his mother once testified that she had seen concerning him [Mab., “testified that she had seen”]—and conscious of his own desire, though still unaware of the divine dispensation, he planned to sail toward those regions, so that, if it were God’s will, he might enlighten peoples numbed by long unbelief with the brilliant light of evangelical preaching.

Taking twelve brothers with him [Mab., “eleven”], armed with the same fervor of faith as himself, he boarded ship. Some of them were later crowned with martyrdom because of their persistence in evangelical preaching; others, receiving the rank of bishop, rested in peace after the labors of holy preaching.

### CHAPTER VI. He comes to Traiectum with twelve companions. Leaving there, he makes for Francia and is honorably received by Pippin. At Pippin’s urging he goes to Rome to be ordained bishop.

Accordingly, as we said, the man of God sailed with his companions to Frisia [Note: “He sailed to Frisia.” In the thirty-third year of his life, as Alcuin related shortly before, and in the year 690 of the Incarnation, as John of Beka, canon of Traiectum, attests along with all the others in his Chronicle; indeed Saint Willibrord himself says so in an ancient calendar preserved in the monastery of Echternach, with the following words written in the margin, apparently by the holy man himself: “In the name of the Lord, Clemens Willibrord came across the sea to Francia in the year 690 from the Incarnation of Christ,” and so forth. See Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. III, Chronological Lists, p. 99], until with a favorable voyage he lowered his sails at the mouths of the Rhine.

There they recovered their strength at the desired landing-place, and soon reached the fortress of Traiectum, situated on the very bank of the river. After some time, by God’s gift and as the word of faith grew, the same holy Willibrord also had the seat of his episcopate there.

But because the same people of the Frisians, among whom that fortress had been built, were still defiled by pagan rites together with their king Radbod [Mab., “were still being defiled”], the man of God decided to make for Francia and approach their leader Pippin, a vigorous man, renowned for his triumphs and upright in conduct. He received him with every honor, but, unwilling to deprive himself or his people of so great a teacher, he identified suitable places for him within the boundaries of his kingdom, where he could uproot the thorns of idolatry and scatter the purest seeds of the word of God more abundantly across newly plowed fields, fulfilling the prophetic command: “Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jeremiah IV, 3).

When the man of God had traveled most diligently through the individual regions and carried out the desired work of evangelization, and when the seeds of life, watered by the dew of heavenly grace, had sprung up most abundantly far and wide in the fields of many hearts in response to his preaching, the aforesaid leader of the Franks rejoiced in his most holy devotion [Mab., “rejoicing through his most holy devotion”] and in the glorious multiplication of the word of God.

Considering the opportunity for greater advancement, he wisely planned to send him to Rome, so that he might be ordained by the apostolic lord Sergius, a most holy man at that time, to the honor of the supreme priesthood. Thus, having received apostolic blessing and command, he could return to the work of the Gospel, sent by him with greater confidence and strengthened by authority, in accordance with the apostolic saying: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans X, 15).

When he tried to persuade the man of God of this, he initially refused and declared that he was not worthy of so great an honor of authority. He enumerated the precepts of apostolic sanction and asserted that he was far inferior to the catalogue of virtues which the distinguished preacher of the world judged necessary for a bishop when instructing his son Timothy (1 Timothy III).

But the leader earnestly argued the opposite, while the man of God modestly denied it. At last, overcome by the unanimous agreement of all—and, what is more, compelled by God’s providence—he consented, preferring humbly to obey the counsel of many rather than stubbornly defend his own will.

And so he was sent to Rome with an honorable embassy and gifts worthy of apostolic authority [Note: “He was sent to Rome.” The Venerable Bede, book V, chapter 12, distinguishes two Roman journeys of Saint Willibrord: one in the early period of his arrival in Frisia, when he received from Pope Sergius permission and blessing to preach to the nations, together with relics to be used in the dedication of churches, in the year 692 of the Incarnation, as Mabillon proves in his notes here; the other after he had taught the people in Frisia for several years, when he was sent to Rome by Pippin so that he might be ordained there by that same Pope Sergius as archbishop of the Frisian people. Bede says that this occurred in the year 696].

### CHAPTER VII. An angelic vision. He is ordained archbishop and called Clemens.

But four days before he arrived there, the most blessed apostolic was warned in sleep by an angelic answer that he should receive him with the greatest honor; that he had been chosen by God and was destined to be the illuminator of many souls; and that he had come for this purpose, to receive from him the honor of the supreme priesthood. Nothing was to be denied him, whatever he might ask [Mab., “whatever he might have asked”].

Having been made certain by this apostolic warning, he received him with great joy and the highest honor. When he recognized in him the fervor of faith, the devotion of religion, and fullness of wisdom, on the appointed day, when the people had assembled and venerable priests had been called to share in the ministry, he ordained him publicly in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with great dignity and according to apostolic custom, as archbishop [Note: “In the church of Saint Peter.” The Venerable Bede nevertheless says in the place cited that Saint Willibrord was ordained in the church of Saint Cecilia the martyr, on her feast day].

After ordaining him, he gave him the name Clemens; he clothed him in his own priestly garments; and he confirmed him with the glory of the mantle of dignity, like the breastpiece of Aaron, and with the splendor of the vestment [Mab., “with the garment of glory”]. Whatever he desired or was able to obtain [Mab., “whatever he requested,”] whether among the patronages of the saints or in ecclesiastical affairs, he handed over to him with complete eagerness of mind. Having established him by blessing and enriched him with gifts, he sent him back again to the work of the Gospel with salutary instructions.

### CHAPTER VIII. He returns to Francia and devotes himself to the work of the Gospel with abundant fruit.

Having received the blessing of apostolic authority, the devoted preacher of the word of God returned to the aforesaid leader of the Franks with greater confidence. The leader received him with the utmost magnificence of honor and, by command of his own authority, sent him to the work of the Gospel, especially in the northern regions of his kingdom, where until then the flame of faith had shone less brightly because of the scarcity of teachers or the hardness of the inhabitants.

The more urgently the man of God scattered the seeds of life in those regions, the more clearly he perceived the necessity of driving away the ancient hunger of ignorance. The people who remain to this day throughout the cities, villages, and fortresses are witnesses to the fruit which, with the help of divine grace, he produced among those inhabitants, leading them by pious admonition to the recognition of truth and to the worship of the one almighty God.

The churches which he built in the various places are also witnesses; and so are the communities of servants of God which he gathered together in certain places [Mab., “which he assembled”].

### CHAPTER IX. He preaches Christ in Frisia, and also in Denmark; from there he leads thirty boys to Francia.

The same man of God also attempted to channel the streams of heavenly teaching beyond the boundaries of the Frankish kingdom. At that time he did not fear approaching the king of the Frisians, Radbod, with his people, though they were pagan; and wherever he went, he spoke the word of God with complete confidence.

But although the aforesaid king of the Frisians kindly received the man of God because of his humility, his stony heart could not be softened by any encouragement to a better life. When the man of God realized that he could not bear fruit with him [Note: “Realized.” The Compendian manuscript, as Mabillon reports, inserts here: “For at that time there was in his company a venerable man, worthy in life and name, Vulframnus, who had come as bishop from the city of Sens, burning with the same ardent desire, namely, to win some souls for the Lord.” See the Life of Saint Vulframnus under the year 720, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, third century, part I, p. 355 and following] [Mab., “recognized”], he turned the work of evangelization toward the fiercest peoples of the Danes.

At that time, it is said, Ungendus ruled there [Note: “Ungendus.” This king is not known to the Danes themselves, nor does Eric, king of Denmark, mention him in the history of the Danish people which he wrote. MABILLON.] [Surius, “Ongendus”], a man more savage than any wild beast and harder than any stone. Nevertheless, by God’s command, he treated the herald of truth honorably.

When the holy man found him hardened in conduct, devoted to idolatry, and offering no hope of a better life, he took thirty boys of that country and hastened to return to the peoples of the Frankish kingdom chosen by God. During that very journey he washed those boys, after catechizing them, in the fountain of life [Mab., “in a saving fountain”], lest they should suffer any harm because of the dangers of the very long voyage [Mab., “the longer journey”] or through the snares of the fiercest inhabitants of that land. He wished to anticipate the cunning of the ancient enemy and fortify the souls he had acquired with the sacraments of the Lord.

### CHAPTER X. He despises the superstition of a barbarian people. One of his companions is killed and becomes a martyr. With great confidence he announces Christ to the king. The king sends him back to Pippin.

As the pious preacher of the word of God was traveling, he reached, on the boundary between the Frisians and the Danes, a certain island called Fositesland by the inhabitants, after one of their gods, Fosite [Note: “Fositesland.” Adam of Bremen, book IV of his *History*, says that Fositesland is the same as the island of Farria, which lies hidden at a long distance within the mouth of the River Elbe and is situated on the boundary between the Danes and Frisians. The same island is said to have been made habitable by the archbishop and distinguished by the monastery of Heiligen. MABILLON.].

The island was so greatly revered by the pagans because temples of that god had been built there that none of the heathen dared touch anything on it—not even the animals grazing there or any other object. Nor did anyone presume to draw water from the spring which bubbled there unless he remained silent.

When the man of God was driven there by a storm, he remained for several days, until the storms had subsided and a suitable time for sailing arrived. But disregarding the foolish religion of the place and the ferocious temper of the king, who habitually condemned violators of its sacred rites to a most atrocious death, he baptized three men in that spring with invocation of the Holy Trinity. He also ordered animals grazing on that land to be slaughtered for food.

When the pagans saw this, they thought that the men would either be driven mad or die a swift death. But when they saw that nothing bad happened to them, they, enraged with fury, reported to King Radbod what they had witnessed.

The king, inflamed by immense anger, planned to avenge upon the priest of the living God the injury done to his gods. For days [Mab., “for three days”], three times each day according to his custom, he cast lots; yet, while the true God defended his servants, the lot of the condemned could never fall upon the servant of God or any of his men. Only one of his companions was indicated by the lot and crowned with martyrdom.

The holy man was summoned before the king and severely rebuked for violating his sacred rites and insulting his god. The herald of truth answered him with steadfast courage:

“Your god is not God, but the devil, who keeps you deceived in the worst error, O king, so that he may deliver your soul to eternal flames” [Note: The words enclosed here and below in brackets are absent from Mabillon.]. “For there is no God except the one who created heaven and earth and everything that is in them. Whoever worships him with true faith will have everlasting life. I, his servant, testify to you today so that at last you may recover from the vanity of the ancient error which your fathers worshiped, and, believing in the one almighty God [‘our Lord Jesus Christ’], and washed in the fountain of life, you may cleanse all your sins. Having cast away every iniquity and injustice, may you henceforth live as a new man in complete sobriety, justice, and holiness.

“If you do this, you will possess everlasting glory with God and his saints. But if you despise me, who am showing you the way of salvation, know with absolute certainty that you will suffer eternal punishments and the flames of hell with the devil, whom you obey.”

The king, astonished at this, replied:

“I see that you have not feared our threats and that your words are like your deeds.”

Although he was unwilling to believe the preacher of truth, he nevertheless sent him back honorably to Pippin, the leader of the Franks.

### CHAPTER XI. In Francia he preaches the Gospel with greater fervor. From the gifts offered, he builds churches, appointing priests everywhere.

Pippin rejoiced at his arrival and urged him to devote himself to the work of the word of God entrusted to him, uprooting the thorns of idolatry and diligently sowing the word of God throughout the various places.

The pious preacher also strove earnestly to fulfill this command. He traveled through all the regions of that land, through cities, villages, and fortresses where he had previously preached [Mab., “where he was preaching”], exhorting everyone to remain with a good purpose firmly established in the true faith.

As the number of the faithful increased day by day and a greater crowd of believers gathered to learn the word of God, many, moved by the fervor of faith, began to offer their ancestral properties to the man of God. After receiving these, he immediately ordered churches to be built on them. He appointed individual priests in them, as fellow workers with him in the word of God, so that the new people of God would have places where they could assemble on feast days, hear salutary admonitions, receive the gifts of sacred baptism, and learn the writings [Surius and Mabillon, “rules”] of the Christian religion.

Thus, by the gift of divine grace, the man of God advanced more and more from day to day.

### CHAPTER XII. Charles Martel conquers many peoples. Saint Willibrord becomes bishop of Traiectum.

It happened that Pippin, leader of the Franks, died, and his son Charles took possession of his father’s kingdom. He added many peoples to the Frankish scepter, among them Frisia, which he added to his paternal empire with the glory of triumph after defeating Radbod.

Saint Willibrord was then established as preacher among that people and was assigned the episcopal see at the fortress of Traiectum [Note: “He was assigned the fortress of Traiectum.” Mabillon thinks Bede should rather be followed, for Bede states in book V, chapter 12, that Willibrord was placed in charge as bishop of Traiectum by Pippin. Read Mabillon’s note here].

Having received a greater opportunity for evangelization, he attempted to wash in holy baptism the people recently acquired by the sword. He allowed none of the ancient error, nor any darkness [Surius, “nor any darkness”; Mab., “the darkness and ignorance of ancient error”] of ignorance to remain hidden in them, but immediately flooded the whole people with evangelical light, so that the prophetic testimony might suddenly be fulfilled among them:

“And it shall come to pass that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘Sons of the living God’” (Hosea I, 10).

Divine power also performed very many miracles through its servant. Although the ministry of evangelical preaching must be preferred to every working of miracles and display of signs, nevertheless I judge that the deeds which are reported should not be left unmentioned for the glory of the God who grants them; rather, they should be bound to the written page, lest what is known to have happened in ancient times perish for later generations.

### CHAPTER XIII. He smashes an idol. Struck with a sword, he is unharmed. Divine vengeance falls upon the striker.

At a certain time, while the venerable man was traveling in the customary manner to evangelize, he came to a certain village called Walachrum [Note: “To a certain village called Walachrum.” Mabillon: “To a certain island.” Walacra or Walacria is one of the five islands of Zealand and has a famous basilica subject to the monastery of Echternach. Browerus, book XII of the *Annals of Trier*], in which an idol of the ancient error remained [“to which, at the appointed time, the entire people gathered, worshiping it with the greatest reverence”].

When the man of God, burning with zeal, attempted to smash it [“and erase its name from beneath the heavens”], its custodian was present. Inflamed with overwhelming fury, as though he were avenging an injury done to his god, he struck the head of Christ’s priest with a sword in a fit of mad rage. But while God defended his servant, he suffered no wound from the blow of the striker [Mab., “he received no injury”].

When his companions saw this, they rushed to avenge the wicked presumption of the impious man [“by death”]. But the accused was freed from their hands and released by the man of God in a spirit of piety. Nevertheless, on that same day he was seized by a demonic spirit, and on the third day he ended his wretched life miserably.

Because the man of God, according to the Lord’s command, refused to avenge his own injuries, he was nevertheless swiftly avenged by the Lord, according to the saying: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans XII, 19).

### CHAPTER XIV. A man who had cursed the servant of God perishes the following day.

At another time, while the blessed man was traveling to a certain cell under his jurisdiction called Suestra, after the stream flowing past it [Note: “Suestra.” The monastery of Susteren, once a monastery of monks and now a celebrated collegiate church of noble canonesses, lies in the region of the Meuse, in the duchy of Jülich; it was named after the stream flowing past it], he entered by way of a shortcut a narrow path through the fields of a certain rich man.

When the keeper of those fields saw this, swollen with immense anger, he began to blaspheme the man of God. When his companions, who were with him, wished to avenge the insults he was inflicting upon the man of God, the servant of God restrained them with a gentle spirit, unwilling that anyone should perish on his account, since he desired the salvation of all [Mab., “when they wished to avenge him, the man of God restrained them, unwilling,” etc.].

But when he was unable in any way to calm the madman’s spirit, he gave way to his anger and returned by the road on which he had come. On the following day, however, the wretched man who had not shrunk from hurling insults at the servant of God [Mab., “from insulting the man of God”] died suddenly in the same place, in the sight of many.

### CHAPTER XV. He draws fresh water from a rock.

When the man full of God was traveling through the maritime regions because of the urgency of evangelical preaching, he suffered from a shortage of fresh water in those same places. Seeing his fellow soldiers suffering severely from the heat of thirst, he summoned one of them and ordered him to dig a small pit inside his tent, where he secretly prayed to God on bended knees, asking that the one who had brought water from a rock in the desert for his people (Exodus XVII; Numbers XX) might, by the same mercy, bring water from the sandy earth for his servants.

He was immediately heard, for suddenly a spring of exceedingly sweet taste filled the pit [Note: “A pit of exceedingly sweet taste.” “That same cistern,” says John Beka in his *Chronicle*, “is now plainly shown in the territory of Heylingen; the inhabitants living there in our own time call it the Well of Saint Willibrord.” MABILLON.].

When his men saw this, they gave thanks to almighty God, who had magnified his saint and had deigned to hear him. They drank until satisfied and took care to carry with them, for the needs of the journey ordained for them, as much as seemed sufficient.

### CHAPTER XVI. He multiplies wine.

Again, the holy priest of God, traveling through a certain place, saw twelve poor beggars together, asking passersby to give them some comfort. Since he was most gentle, he looked upon them with a kindly spirit and ordered one of his men to take his own flask and pour it out for the poor in the name of Christ [“pour it out” rather than “mix it”].

All twelve drank from it until they were satisfied. And, wonderfully, when they had departed, the flask of excellent wine from which so many men had drunk was found by the servant to be full, as before.

When this became known, they all blessed the Lord our God [Mab., “the Lord Jesus”], saying:

“Truly fulfilled in us is what is said in the Gospel: ‘Give, and it will be given to you’” (Luke VI, 38).

### CHAPTER XVII. Again he multiplies wine.

The holy man also came to his monastery to visit it. After prayers to God, greetings to the brothers, and peaceful admonitions, he went around the individual dwellings of the brothers, wishing, as a pious shepherd, to investigate whether anything in them needed correction.

He also entered the cellar [Mab., “then it happened that he entered”], where he found a small amount of wine in a vessel [Id., “in a single cask”]. With prayer, he placed his staff into it for the sake of blessing and departed.

That same night the wine began to increase in the vessel itself and to overflow the rim of the vessel [Id., “so that it overflowed the rim of the vessel”]. When the cellarer saw this, he was astonished at the unexpected abundance and did not dare conceal what he recognized had been brought about by divine mercy through the blessing of God’s servant.

The following morning he ran to the holy Father, prostrated himself at his feet, and confessed what he had seen. As was his custom, the saint gave thanks to God; and, mindful of the Lord’s command to his disciples that they should tell no one of the glory of his transfiguration before the day of his resurrection, he ordered the cellarer not to disclose to anyone the miracle he had seen [Mab., “the miracle he was seeing”] before the day of his death.

## Chapter XVIII [Mabillon, XIX]. A Similar Miracle

But God Christ also performed, through his blessing, another miracle similar to this one. The servant of God, arriving with his companions at the house of a certain friend and wishing for a little while to ease the lengthy labor of the journey by refreshment in the beloved man’s house, discovered that the head of the household had no wine. He therefore ordered four small flasks to be brought—the only ones his companions had carried with them as a provision for the journey—and blessed them in the name of him who at the wedding feast changed water into wine (John II). [Mabillon: “who in Cana of Galilee changed waters into the taste of wine.”] [Col. 0704B] After the blessing [Mabillon: “after the grace of the blessing”], marvelously, nearly forty men drank from those little flasks to satiety, and with great thanksgiving they said to one another with joyful hearts:

“Truly the Lord Jesus has here fulfilled what he promised in the Gospel, saying: ‘Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these’” (John XIV, 12).

[Note: “Small flasks.” In Mabillon the reading is *modicas*, feminine, the gender in which the word *flasco* is always used there. Is this from Alcuin himself, or from the carelessness of a copyist? The manuscripts certainly differ, as is evident from this edition of Quercetanus. See this word in D. Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]

## Chapter XIX [Mabillon, XX]. A Man Who Insulted the Servant of God Is Punished by Divine Judgment, but Is Freed When He Repents

At a certain time the same holy preacher proceeded, as usual, to Frisia in haste for the sake of evangelizing. Because of the labor of the journey, he wished to refresh his tired horses for a little while in the meadows of a certain rich man. When that wealthy man saw them grazing in his meadows, he began, moved by a spirit of pride, to beat the horses and drive them from the pasture.

The man of God addressed him in the gentlest words, saying:

“Stop doing us an injury, [brother]. We did not wish to rest for a time in these pastures because of any harm to you, but because of our own necessity. The work of God that we must accomplish presses upon us. You too may receive its reward if, so far as it concerns you, you help us with a [kindly] disposition, remembering that most sweet promise of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me’ (Matthew X, 40). Rather, with a peaceful mind, refresh yourself with us as with a friend: drink a little, and when we have continued the journey we have begun, return to your house blessed by God.”

But he remained obstinate in his wickedness, unwilling to heed the peaceful words of the man of God. He repeated insults and hurled reproaches:

“You urge me to drink and to make peace with you. Know with absolute certainty that I consider drinking with you worthless.”

The man of God seized this word from his mouth and said:

“If you do not wish to drink with me, then do not drink.”

He immediately prepared his companions and continued on his way.

The other, however, still defiant, hurried toward his house, but suddenly began to burn entirely with thirst. Wishing to cool his burning stomach with wine, he could not receive a drink of wine with the mouth that had inflicted insults upon the man of God. [Mabillon: “he was unwilling.”] And he who deliberately refused peace with the servant of God [necessarily endured the punishment in himself].

Physicians were summoned to relieve his thirst or to provide the sick man with the ability to drink. His inward parts were parched, but no one could pour even a drop of wine into his fevered lungs. At last [Mabillon: “Late at last”], moved by repentance, he came to himself and recognized that the holy Willibrord was the man whom he had offended. With labored breath he longed for his return.

The following year Willibrord returned by the same road. When the sick man had learned beforehand of his arrival, he hurried to meet him [Mabillon: “the sick man arrived”], confessing his fault, revealing the punishment he was suffering, and begging that, for the love of Christ, he might be released from it.

Moved by mercy, the man of God absolved him and, with a blessing, gave him something to drink from his own cup. Immediately released, he drank and returned home in good health.

## Chapter XX [Mabillon, XXI]. He Frees Nuns from a Pestilence

In the city of Trier there is a monastery of women which, during the episcopate of blessed Willibrord, was attacked by a very severe pestilence. Because of its violence, many of the servants of God were dying [Mabillon: “died”]; some lay sick in bed through prolonged suffering; and the rest, shaken by excessive terror, feared death as though it were already present.

Since the monastery of the holy man, called Esternachus, was near the aforementioned city, and since the holy man still rests there in body, while his successors are known to hold it by the lawful tradition of their Father and through the piety of most devout kings, the women of the aforementioned monastery, hearing that the holy man was coming there, immediately sent messengers, asking him not to delay his arrival.

He, instructed by the gentlest example of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, who came from Joppa to Lydda at the request of Christ’s widows in order to raise the holy Tabitha (Acts IX), came hastily to them when he heard the desire of Christ’s servants. [Mabillon: “he did not hesitate to come to them.”]

Upon arriving, he immediately celebrated Mass in the same monastery for the sick. He blessed water, ordered their houses to be sprinkled with it, and sent it to the sick to drink. By the mercy of God, they soon recovered, and thereafter none in that monastery died of the pestilence mentioned above.

[Note: “The monastery of women.” Browerus interprets this passage as referring to the monastery of Horreum, situated within the city of Trier, in *Annals of Trier*, book VII. Mabillon doubts whether it should instead be understood as the monastery of Palatiolum, formerly a monastery of virgins and now a collegiate church. But Palatiolum—today Pfalzel—is one hour from the city, on the left bank of the Moselle, and is not situated within the city itself, as the distinguished D. de Hontheim testifies in *History of Trier*, volume I, page 23. Browerus’s interpretation is therefore more probable.]

[Note: “Which is called Esternachus.” Today the monastery of Echternach. Concerning its origin, rights and acquisitions, secularization, and restoration to the Benedictines, consult the distinguished D. ab Hontheim, *History of Trier*, volume I.]

## Chapter XXI [Mabillon, XXII]. A Malignant Spirit Is Driven from a House by Blessed Water

A certain head of a household and his family suffered a dreadful temptation of demonic illusion, so that it was plainly recognized that an evil spirit dwelt in his house through its horrors and harmful acts. For suddenly it would seize food, clothing, or other necessities of the household and throw them into the fire. [Mabillon: “it would throw them.”] It even took a little child who was resting in its parents’ embrace while they slept and threw him into the fire.

Awakened by the infant’s cries [Mabillon: “roused”], the parents scarcely rescued the child from the flames, and the same family suffered many terrible things from the wicked spirit. It could not be driven out by any priest until the holy man Willibrord, asked by the head of the household, sent them blessed water. He ordered all the household furnishings to be carried outside and sprinkled with that water, foreseeing in spirit that the house would be consumed by flames.

When this had been done, fire invaded the empty house from the place where the bed had stood and consumed it entirely. Another house was built in that place, with the sanctification of blessed water, and thereafter they suffered nothing there from their former affliction. Instead, they lived in complete tranquility and peace, giving thanks to the Lord, who had deigned to redeem them through his servant.

## Chapter XXII [Mabillon, XXIII]. He Baptizes Pippin and Foretells His Future Elevation

The same man, beloved by God, had also foretold certain things in a prophetic spirit, which later events proved true. He baptized Pippin, son of Charles, the strongest leader of the Franks, and father of this most noble Charles, who now governs the empire of the Franks with the greatest triumphs and every distinction in the highest glory.

Concerning this Pippin, his father, the same holy man, with prophetic voice, foretold the following oracle before his disciples:

“Know that this child will be very exalted and glorious, and greater than all the preceding leaders of the Franks.”

The truth of this prophecy has been proved in our own times, and there is no need to establish by testimony what the authority of the entire kingdom acknowledges. For the whole people recognizes how the most noble victor is celebrated in triumphs; how far he extended the boundaries of our empire [Mabillon: “the boundaries of our imperial rule”]; how devoutly he established Christian religion in his kingdom; and what he accomplished among foreign peoples for the defense of God’s holy Church. All these things can be demonstrated more effectively to the eyes than explained in words.

[Note: “Our empire.” From these words it seems possible to understand that Alcuin wrote this life while residing in Francia.]

## Chapter XXIII [Mabillon, XXIV]. His Endowments and Virtues. His Death. His Burial at Echternach. A Distinguished Miracle

This holy man was distinguished by every excellence: he was of pleasing stature, honorable in appearance, handsome in face, joyful in heart, wise in counsel, pleasant in speech, composed in conduct, and energetic in every work of God.

How patient he was is shown by the deeds related above. How great his diligence was in preaching the Gospel of Christ, and how divine grace assisted him in the work of preaching, need not be described by our pen, since it is confirmed by the testimony of the entire people. How great his diligence was in preaching the Gospel of Christ [Mabillon: “or how great it had been”], and how divine grace assisted him in the work of preaching, need not be described by our pen, since it is confirmed by the testimony of the entire people. His private life of vigilance and prayer, fasting and psalmody, is revealed by the holiness of his life and the manifestation of signs. His charity, certainly, was shown by the constant labor he endured every day for the name of Christ.

Finally, the holy man, advancing in the divine work throughout all the days of his life, beloved by God and pleasing to all the people [Mabillon: “agreeable”], in the time of Charles the ancient, strongest leader of the Franks, in old age and full of days in every perfection, was gathered to his fathers, destined to receive from God the manifold fruit of his labor. Leaving this age [Mabillon: “putting off the human being together with the age”], he was to possess heaven and see Christ without end in eternal glory. In love for him he had never ceased to labor as long as he lived among us.

[Note: “Full of days.” That is, having passed beyond eighty-one years, as Alcuin himself writes below in book II, or in the metrical Life, chapter 24, where he sings:

“Twice eight lustrums the devout priest completed,

three times four, and months; and now, on the eighth Ides

of the month of November, he passed to the court of heaven.”

Because of the words in the last verse, *Idibus octenis* (“on the eighth Ides”), Mabillon judges that the reading in the Quercetan edition should be corrected where it reads, “On the seventh day of November,” that is, the seventh Ides. Rather, on the authority of the manuscript books, it should read: “On the sixth day of November,” that is, the eighth Ides. Hrabanus supports this reading in his Martyrology, although other martyrologists—Wandelbert, Usuard, Ado, the Roman and Benedictine Martyrologies, and ecclesiastical calendars—record Saint Willibrord’s feast-day as the seventh Ides of November.]

On the seventh day of November, that is, the seventh day before the Ides [Mabillon: “on the sixth day of November, that is, the eighth day before the Ides”], he departed from this pilgrimage to his everlasting homeland.

[Note: “He departed to his everlasting homeland.” Saint Willibrord crossed into Frisia in the thirty-third year of his life, in the year of Christ 690, as stated above. It is certain from letter 97 of Saint Boniface to Pope Stephen, where it says, “After preaching for fifty years, he converted most of the aforementioned people of the Frisians to the faith,” that he devoted fifty years to preaching in Frisia. If fifty is added to 690, the year 740 results, and the year of Saint Willibrord’s death should accordingly be placed there. Mabillon, in his notes on this life of Saint Willibrord, assigned his death to the year 739, following Theofrid, abbot of Echternach, who lived in the eleventh century. He later corrected this opinion in volume II of the *Benedictine Annals*, book XXI, number 64, where he assigned the holy man’s death to the year 741 or the preceding year. The distinguished scholar believes that Alcuin does not agree well with Saint Boniface: “For if Alcuin’s reckoning is accepted,” he says, “only forty-eight years remain for Saint Willibrord’s preaching. For if the thirty-three years of age at which he came to Frisia are subtracted from eighty-one years of life, only forty-eight remain for preaching.”

“But I think there is no discrepancy here if, according to Alcuin’s intention, the thirty-third year of his life, in which he came to Frisia, is counted together with the years of preaching, and the year of his death is taken as the eighty-second year, begun but not yet completed. Let us therefore suppose that when Saint Willibrord began preaching in Frisia, thirty-two complete years of his life had passed; the year in which, after completely fulfilling eighty-one years, he died was his eighty-second. Thus, when the thirty-two years before his arrival are subtracted from the eighty-two years of the year of his death, fifty years of preaching remain. Alcuin’s reckoning therefore agrees perfectly with Saint Boniface’s statement.”]

He was buried in the monastery of Echternach, which, as we have said, he himself had built for God. There, through the mercy of God, signs and healings continue to occur to this day at the relics of the holy priest of God. We have judged that some of them should be appended to our history of him, for the glory and praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has often deigned to perform these things through the protection of his servant.

[Mabillon, Chapter XXV.] His venerable body was placed in a marble sarcophagus, which was initially found to be about half a foot shorter than the entire body of the servant of God. The brothers were therefore greatly saddened and repeatedly deliberated [Mabillon: “were repeatedly in suspense”] where they might find a suitable resting place for the holy body. But, through the marvelous favor of God, a sarcophagus was suddenly found longer than the body of the man of God by exactly as much as the former had appeared too short.
