They placed the body of the man of God in it with hymns, psalms, and every honor, and buried it in the church of the aforementioned monastery, which that supreme priest of God had built and dedicated in honor of the Holy Trinity. Moreover, a fragrance of marvelous sweetness filled everyone’s nostrils, so that it was clearly understood that an angelic ministry had come to the funeral of the holy man.

## Chapter XXIV [Mabillon, XXVI]. His Soul Is Carried to Heaven by Angels. Miracles at the Holy Man’s Body

The death of the holy man was also revealed to a certain religious disciple of his who was living at a distance and keeping vigil in prayer. He testified that he had seen the soul of his most holy father carried by angelic hosts into the kingdom of heaven, with great brightness of light and the harmonious praise of singers.

Many of the brothers also testified that they had often seen a marvelous light over the bed on which he had surrendered his blessed soul to its Creator, and had sensed the sweetest fragrance of a delightful odor. These signs led them altogether to believe that the citizens of heaven frequently visited [Mabillon: “frequently visit”] the place where the holy soul had departed to the Lord [Mabillon: “to Christ”].

[Mabillon, Chapter XXVII.] Many sick people were also healed through the anointing with the oil that habitually shone above the saint’s body, by God’s gift and with the cooperation of their faith. Penitents who often came to the same church, bound in the customary manner with iron rings, suddenly felt their bonds loosen when the rings broke. [Mabillon: “For the penitents … the bonds were loosened.”] The rings still hanging in the church are witnesses to this event.

## Chapter XXV [Mabillon, XXVIII]. A Paralytic Woman Is Healed

A certain paralytic woman, tormented by severe pains for seven years [Mabillon: “for many years”], was so afflicted by the same daily illness that, deprived of the use of all her limbs, she depended on the service of another. With only her little breast still faintly breathing, her spirit could scarcely draw its weary sighs.

Her relatives carried her to the church where the holy man of God rests and placed her near the shrine of his relics [Mabillon: “and, having been placed there”]. There, shedding abundant tears, she prayed that through the intercession of his holy servant the divine mercy might have compassion on her [Mabillon: “that divine mercy might assist her”]. She was heard by the Lord God and immediately freed from every illness. Restored to health, she joyfully gave thanks to God and ran home on her own feet—she who had previously been carried by others.

## Chapter XXVI [Mabillon, XXIX]. A Sick Man Is Restored to Health

A certain sick young man was carried by the hands of his friends to the body of the blessed bishop. All his limbs trembled. He could not even raise his head by himself; as though it were not fixed to his neck, it fell and rolled from side to side. At times he became so lifeless that he seemed entirely dead.

As we have said, his companions placed him near the body of the holy man. But, by God’s merciful gift, before the eyes of all who were present he suddenly became so completely well that nothing of his former illness or earlier pain remained in him.

## Chapter XXVII [Mabillon, XXX]. A Sacrilegious Thief Is Exposed

A certain man who was a deacon by office, though not by merit, did not shrink from stealing [Mabillon: “snatching away”] in the church of the holy man a golden cross that the saint used to carry with him on journeys, together with other church money, in a most wretched theft. The brothers were troubled by this matter [Mabillon: “the brothers being troubled concerning this”], since they did not know who had committed the impious crime. Yet, trusting in the prayers of the holy man of God, they believed that so wicked a crime could not remain hidden. At the same time, in brotherly compassion, they tried to call the man back to repentance, not wishing to destroy him.

But the man who had committed this crime, with a hardened heart, despised his salvation, like the wicked man of whom Solomon says: “When he has come into the depths of sins, he despises” (Proverbs XVIII, 3).

The wretch thought that he could remain hidden, because he knew that he had done this secretly, without the eyes of others; but he could not remain hidden from the eye of God, to whom all things are open, and who often does not delay to avenge injuries done to his servants.

For that miserable man, who had not shrunk from committing this crime, was suddenly seized by a miserable death and perished. At the very end of his life he revealed the guilt of his crime to some of the brothers; and, when he had shown it, he indicated what he had carried away by theft.

You see, brothers, by how terrible a judgment he was condemned who did not fear to violate the Church of God’s saint by theft. Therefore I beg you to maintain a chaste conduct in this place, so that through the prayers of the holy Clement, the apostolic man, divine mercy may deign to hear you in every honorable petition, just as, as we said earlier, it granted the prayers of the sick in this same [variant: “this”] church and allowed them to return home with the health they had long desired.

There should, of course, be no doubt that just as Christ deigned visibly to heal their bodily illnesses, so also, with his saint who rests here bodily interceding for us, he does not cease to heal the hidden diseases of our souls. We believe him to be spiritually present; and if with firm faith and true confession we pour out our hearts with tears in this place before the sight of his mercy, then in his divine clemency he is ready [Mabillon: “disposed”] to forgive, provided that we are not slow to pray.

To him be praise and glory forever and ever.

[Note: “Who rests here bodily.” One might say that Alcuin was then living at the monastery of Echternach as a resident. But he writes these and similar words in the name of the monks of Echternach, who were to recite them in the divine offices. The same should be said of the homily on the feast of this saint, authored by Alcuin and intended to be recited. Mabillon.]

## Chapter XXVIII. Through a Miracle, Wine Increases While It Is Being Drunk

It remains now to speak of blessed Wilgis, the father of this holy man, as we said earlier, so that the final chapter of this history may end with the man from whom its first chapter began.

The anniversary of the blessed Wilgis’s holy departure returned. On that day the pious abbot Albert [Alcuin: “Alcbertus”], successor of the venerable archbishop in the governance of the monastery of Echternach, after the most sacred solemnities of Mass and the honor due to God, began to feast and rejoice with the brothers.

[Note: “Abbot Albert.” [Alcuin: “Alcbertus”], successor of Saint Willibrord in the governance of the monastery of Echternach. A charter of King Pippin addressed to him is preserved in Browerus, *Annals of Trier*, book VII.]

But in that monastery no more wine was found than two small flasks. One of them was emptied at the hour of dinner [Mabillon: “was drunk”]; the other was kept for the hour of supper. Therefore, after the evening hymn, the brothers returned to the refectory out of reverence for that day. After the sacred readings, the aforementioned abbot addressed the brothers, saying:

“It is fitting for us, venerable fathers, to celebrate the feast days of our venerable fathers with spiritual joy, allowing our bodies a little more indulgence than usual, relaxing our customary strictness [perhaps: “our customary loosened strictness”]—not for luxury, but for the sake of charity. I certainly would not have concealed from you that I had anything more in this monastery than this one flask, which remained for us after dinner. Yet God is powerful: through the prayers of his saints he can make this same flask abundant for us, honor them, gladden us, and show us, though unworthy, the miracles of his mercy. Through the blessing of Saint Willibrord, our father, he once deigned to satisfy forty men from four flasks. Let us therefore drink with thanksgiving in hope of what we have.”

All the brothers drank once and then a second time from the same flask, and the minister found it just as full as before. When the abbot heard this, he and the brothers earnestly gave thanks to God. That night they drank as much as they wished, praising the divine mercy [Mabillon: “rejoicing in the divine mercy”], with sobriety and joy.

O happy father, who begot such a son, and who was judged worthy by God of such an heir! In him is fulfilled the blessing written in Deuteronomy:

“Blessed are you, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Deuteronomy XVIII, 3, 4).

Amen.

# The Homily of the Same Alcuin on the Feast of Saint Willibrord, Archbishop

[Note: Mabillon has: “Here begins the sermon for his feast, to be recited before the congregation.”]

## I. The More Celebrated Protections of the Saints Are Enumerated

Although throughout the churches of the entire world it is fitting for all Christian people to celebrate the feasts of the saints, praise their victories [variant: “imitate their life”], and, since their sound has gone out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, praise them throughout the earth with the harmonious voice of all who live, nevertheless, in each place, because of the familiarity of living together with any one of them and because of the presence of the holy relics granted for the consolation of particular inhabitants, they are honored among their own citizens with a certain special veneration.

Thus the city of Rome, the head of the world, rejoices in a special way in the most glorious triumphs of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore peoples and nations come to it every day with devout service of the heart, so that, with greater compunction of faith before the blessed apostles, they may either lament their sins or ask that an entrance be opened for them through a more abundant hope of heavenly life.

Milan, once an imperial city, rejoices in Saint Ambrose as its defender. The Acunumia Alps [variant: “Agaunian”] are raised more gloriously by the fortunate blood of the Thebans than by their snowy height.

[Note: “The Acunumia Alps,” that is, the Pennine Alps, near Sion, where the monastery of Agaunum is adorned with the relics of the holy Theban martyrs. Mabillon.]

Fertile Poitiers rejoices more blessedly in the relics of the blessed bishop Hilary than in the disputes of buying and selling, in which injustice is often involved.

What shall I say of you, city of Tours, small and contemptible in your walls, but great and praiseworthy through the protection of Saint Martin? Who would approach you for your own sake? Do not crowds of Christians flow to you because of his most certain assistance?

All the suburbs of the city of Paris rejoice in the magnificent aid of Saint Denis or Saint Germanus, and celebrate their feast days with a greater gathering of peoples.

[Note: Adrian Valesius noted this passage in his discussion *On Basilicas*, chapter 8, against Jean Launoy, who maintained that the basilica of Saint Denis, famous for its tomb, was originally built within the walls of the city of Paris.]

All Campania with its peoples praises the venerable preacher Remigius and hastens to the city of Rheims, bringing their vows before him as though he were a patron present there.

Thus divine mercy provided for the whole world, giving each province or people a particular patron in whom they might rejoice.

## II. The Apostolic Labors of Saint Willibrord

But to us he granted no lowly assistance through the most holy Willibrord; rather, he bestowed splendid and glorious aid. Let us rejoice in the Lord, beloved brothers, and be glad with spiritual joy, because he granted us such a teacher of life, an instructor in justice, and the founder of our unity—one who gathered us into this most sacred fold and instructed us by the teaching of piety.

Let all the people who have gathered today for the feast of the most holy Father rejoice with us. They have sought, with devout dedication, to take part in the vigils of the apostolic man and to stand in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, the holy angels, and the most blessed bishop.

Let no one, I beg you, doubt in faith, hesitate concerning the abundance of forgiveness, or doubt the fruit and fulfillment of devout prayer, since he has granted us such a patron. Through his prayers he grants that we may be heard; for the more confidently we pray, the more quickly we shall be heard.

All things are obtained through faith, as we have the most certain examples before our eyes in this most holy man whose feast we celebrate today. From his earliest childhood he strove through faith to please God. For, inflamed by faith, he abandoned his homeland, family, and friends for the love of God; he despised earthly things in order to acquire heavenly ones.

Therefore he found the great fruit of his labor. He converted many crowds of peoples to Christ, turned very many pagans away from the wickedness of error, and, with divine grace cooperating, made children of wrath into children of mercy. He shut hell and opened heaven; he traveled through many peoples so that he might lead them all into the way of truth. He spared not even himself. He approached fierce peoples, hoping perhaps to find the purple crowns of martyrdom.

God preserved him for the salvation of many, so that he might be honored with the greater glory of preaching rather than crowned with martyrdom alone. He rested in peace because he labored in hope. He found eternal life because he left temporal life; taken from us, he was joined to the angels.

## III. The Protection and Glory of Saint Willibrord

O most blessed priest of Christ, do not abandon us laboring on earth, but never cease to help us from heaven through your prayers. Your life among human beings was always approved before God; may your prayers before God always be directed toward human beings.

Your meditation was on the law of the Lord day and night; therefore you flourished like a palm tree in the house of the Lord. Like a cedar of Lebanon, you multiplied your children, who cry out to you with the full devotion of their minds. Deign to help them through your pious intercession.

May we feel that your aid [supplied reading: “to be”] most mercifully present to us, we who most devoutly persist in your service.

O happy soul, who left behind the labors of the world and entered heavenly rest with the fruit of your manifold toil! You multiplied the talents entrusted to you and received the promised rewards. You were faithful over a little on earth; now, set over many things, you rejoice in heaven.

You, Father, we pursue with continual praises; aid us with unceasing prayers. We believe that in the presence of the Lord your God you can obtain everything that you ask, since through his grace you were able to perform so many miracles in our presence.

Now you are a citizen of the angels, a companion of the saints, and joyful with them you sing the new song:

“As we have heard, so have we seen” (Psalm XLVII, 9).

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII, 5).

“And the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (ibid. 8).

The blessed vision of him is complete happiness, as the Truth himself testifies in the Gospel, saying:

“Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

This saint lived in the world in the sweetest love of him; therefore he rejoices in heaven in his presence.

## IV. He Is to Be Imitated by Us

See, dearest brothers, how great is the glory of following God. For the love of Christ this man despised his homeland, chose pilgrimage, considered the riches of the world of little worth, and voluntarily loved poverty.

We have learned what honor he afterward possessed among human beings, but better is the glory that he possesses eternally among the angels. May the examples of this most holy teacher rouse us from the torpor of sloth, so that what we preach about him we may fulfill in ourselves.

We praise the struggles of his labor; let us correct our ways according to his footsteps, so that we who follow the examples of his holiness may also receive the rewards of blessedness, through him who crowned him and will help us, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns in everlasting glory.

Amen.

Here ends the first book, proceeding in prose discourse, concerning the life, virtues, and death of Saint Willibrord, archbishop.

# Book Two, Which Alcuin Composed in Verse

## Preface

Behold, revered priest, my heart burns with true love

for your small requests.

[As I swiftly pass through the famous deeds

of the great bishop and gracious prelate Willibrord,]

my speech, though inferior and murmuring with a hoarse sound,

resounds for the sake of his distinguished merits.

Willibrord, priest, our faith, small and humble though it is,

has brought your [reading uncertain: *vestrum*] to the temple of Christ.

I beg you to receive them kindly, with a gracious mind,

and, I pray, ask forgiveness for my offenses.

My gifts, prelate, are not worthy of your merits,

for you reign rich in the citadel of the highest heaven—

unless the merciful God in the temple praised

the widow who brought her small coins and gave her offering.

These are two small coins of different weight;

holy Father, I bring them humbly to your temples.

The first of these still bears its coin-image in plain figures [Alcuin: “bronze”],

but the second already gleams with Pierian brightness.

There are people whom the sacred Law commands

to bring hairs and goatskins as an offering to God’s holy dwelling.

Yet the holy Law of the Thunderer did not command these things to be despised,

but instructed that whatever a devout mind has brought

should be gratefully received.

Thus, best Father, you do not seek grandiloquent treasures [variant: “thanks”],

but my heart warmed by true love.

## The Narrative Begins

### Chapter I. How Blessed Willibrord Came from Britain or Ireland to Francia

A certain man had come from the western regions of the world,

a man powerful in virtue and full of divine love,

wise in speech, vigilant in mind, and fervent in action,

to you, happy Francia, in the time of Pippin.

Productive Britain, his mother, had already given him to you,

and learned Ireland had nourished him in sacred studies.

His name was Willibrord, gracious in his vigorous merits.

Seeking foreign lands, led by the love of the Lord,

and desiring to scatter the heavenly seeds

of everlasting life where previously the Word had had few adherents,

he came.

Then honorable Pippin, ruler of the Franks,

received him and ordered him to water the thirsty countryside

throughout its various regions with heavenly dew,

strengthening the servant of God with worthy assistance.

### Chapter II. How the Same Man of God Advanced in the Work of Preaching

That man, full of God—of Christ, Light from Light—,

wherever he traveled with pious steps—

through cities, fortresses, cottages, or crossroads—

everywhere scattered rays of evangelical light through human hearts.

At length the devout flame of faith shone in many,

and that blind night departed far from the land [Mabillon: “from that world”].

Every day the profane temples of idols collapsed,

and Christ resounded in the mouths of the faithful people.

### Chapter III. How Pippin, Duke of the Franks, Sent the Same Servant of Christ to Rome to Be Ordained Archbishop

When renowned Pippin saw the Church of Christ growing,

a venerable gift of faith,

he rejoiced greatly in such a teacher of salvation

and judged it better to send to Rome without delay

the chief herald of the faith,

so that the apostolic shepherd might establish him in the highest rank,

that he might be bishop of the Church and its supreme priest.

### Chapter IV. How It Was Shown in a Vision to the Most Blessed Apostolic Pope Sergius That Blessed Willibrord Had Come to Rome, and How He Was to Receive Him with Every Honor

The summit of the episcopate, most worthy heir of Peter,

Saint Sergius then held the apostolic court,

a good and prudent man, second to none in piety.

On the fourth night before the illustrious man came to Rome to him, a vision occurred to him.

An angel coming from heaven foretold this to him:

“Behold, one dear to God is hastening to this city as a guest,

sent by the duke of the Franks with a generous gift.

Remember to receive him, at least, with a devout mind,

and soon you shall consecrate him as bishop with the highest honor.

Let the priest receive whatever gifts he requests from you.

This man joins many thousands of peoples to God.”

After speaking these words, the angel returned to heaven.

## CHAPTER V. How the same blessed pope treated him honorably, gave him the name Clement when he ordained him, and enriched him with gifts

[Col. 0715A]

The blessed pope at once obeyed the angelic commands  
and treated God’s servant with a kindly mind.  
Promptly, as he had been ordered, he completed everything,  
and consecrated him pope with great honor.  
He ordered him to be called Clement by his native [Mab., paternal] name,  
and whatever the holy man asked for himself, he gave him,  
presenting him with very many gifts of the holy and devout.

## CHAPTER VI. How the man of God returned to Francia and earnestly preached Christ’s Gospel to all

[Col. 0715B]

When these things had been done, the Lord’s servant returned to the land  
of the Franks, strengthened by the highest gift.  
Then the whole people, rejoicing, received him,  
eager to drink in the honey-flowing streams of salvation  
that the excellent Father freely bestowed on all,  
watering the hearts of all Christ’s people with heavenly dew.  
And wherever the devout priest came,  
with God’s help he gathered pleasant fruits.

[Until he had filled the cities, villages, towns, and countryside  
with knowledge of the Catholic faith and of God.]

## CHAPTER VII. How he attempted to preach to the Frisians and Danes

Not content with these boundaries of Francia,  
he nevertheless attempted to scatter the seeds of the divine word  
among the peoples of the Frisians, captured by ancient error,  
and among the Danes, a people very fierce through the ages.  
At that time he could not convert them to the gift of faith  
because, as it happened, they had wicked kings.

[Col. 0715C]

## CHAPTER VIII. How he baptized some of them on the way, performed certain signs, and returned to Francia

But almighty God had granted him souls  
from among those very peoples, and through his servant  
he performed certain wonders. Then he returned in peace,  
looking toward the Lord’s people in those regions,  
while Christ opened the perpetual door of salvation  
through his devout exhortations. Yet everywhere and always  
he strengthened all; and Pippin, completing the course of his present life,  
left his kingdoms to Charles.

## CHAPTER IX. How Charles, duke of the Franks, subjected the Frisian people to himself

[Col. 0715D]

He soon nobly governed the royal reins,  
enlarging his boundaries and overcoming foreign peoples  
with triumphs. He also conquered the Frisians in war  
and subdued them with iron-clad wagons,  
taking from their hands the reins of tribute as well.

## CHAPTER X. How Willibrord returned to preach to the Frisians and converted them to the faith of Christ

[Col. 0716A]

Then the evangelist Willibrord returned to them,  
bringing words of life, and bathed them in holy baptism—  
those whom the holy man had first imbued with the gracious gifts of faith.  
And light arose for the people who had long been dwelling  
in the shadow of death. The true sun, Christ,  
shone everywhere, as the dark shadows suddenly withdrew.

## CHAPTER XI. How an episcopal see was given to him in the fortress of Traiectum, and how he appointed priests throughout the various places

Then a seat was given to the bishop in the city of Traiectum,  
and the entire people of the Frisians was subjected to him,  
so that it might learn the lessons of faith from the great minister.

[Col. 0716B]

Soon temples, built for God, flourished perpetually,  
and throughout the regions many faithful teachers were appointed  
to govern the people, to teach the words of life,  
to administer baptism, and to feed them with heaven’s bread—  
so that the hungry populace would not return from them unfed,  
but that Christ might be abundant drink and food for all.

198

## CHAPTER XII. How he hastened most devotedly to preach the word of God everywhere

This was always the work of the illustrious bishop:  
to bring the Thunderer the greatest harvest of souls,  
and to go out willingly to meet the Lord returning to his servants,  
bringing talents multiplied in both hands.

Therefore, vigilant under this protection, he went around the folds  
[Note: [Col. 0715D] That is, monasteries; Mabillon and Du Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.]

in order to enlarge Christ’s sheepfold through worthy names.

[Col. 0716C]

And wherever the devout herald of salvation went,  
the grace of the high-enthroned One always preceded him,  
granting effect to the deeds and words of the teacher.

## CHAPTER XIII. How not everything that the same bishop did could be recounted in verse

Through his servant God performed very many miracles,  
all of which I have not now wished to run through in verse.  
Rather, hastening, I touch upon a few with my plectrum,  
and attach brief titles to his deeds in song,  
then send my reader to my prose work.  
There he will find all his deeds more fully:  
the zeal of the great bishop, the teacher’s instructions,  
his lineage, his life, his customs, and his kindly minds  
[Mab., his kindly mind],  
and his heart, always devoted to God at every hour,

[Col. 0716D]

meditating on the sacred laws night and day.

## CHAPTER XIV. How, while the servant of God was demolishing a certain shrine, he was struck on the head with a sword by a certain man (a temple attendant), but, protected by God, felt no injury from the blow

Behold, at a certain time the bishop, dear to God,  
was himself attempting to demolish a certain shrine.  
Seeing this, the guardian of the idol [Note: [Col. 0715D] “The guardian of the idol.” By the poetic license of medieval Latin, the first two syllables in *idoli* are shortened, although they ought to be lengthened. Prudentius and Walafrid Strabo likewise used *idola* with the second syllable shortened. Many other things in the poems of Alcuin and of other writers of that age would also deserve correction if one wished to bring everything back under the laws of stricter prosody. The observation of Scaliger in book II, chapter 21, of his commentary on Ausonius is relevant here: “Latin poets had the peculiar habit,” he says, “not only of neglecting Greek declensions in Greek words, but also of so overturning quantity that they measured it solely by accent.”]

inflamed with anger,  
struck the bishop’s head with a sharp sword.

[Col. 0717A]

But the eminent man neither felt it nor suffered even a slight wound.  
His companions wished to kill the attacker immediately;  
nevertheless, the gentle priest rescued him from death.  
The man who had been seized soon paid a wretched, slight penalty,  
and after three days ended his bitter life.  
Thus Christ willingly avenges his saints.

## CHAPTER XV. How a certain man who had cursed the servant of God perished the following day

Once the venerable traveler was making a journey.  
The path led him and his companions nearer through the crops—  
crops which a rich miser had enclosed.  
The guardian of the grain wished to bar the way,  
shouting many insults at the holy man,  
and adding outrage to outrage through dreadful actions.

[Col. 0717B]

The saint turned aside onto the road where the public way appeared.  
The unhappy mocker soon perished on the following day,  
because he had not feared to curse Christ’s servant.

## CHAPTER XVI. How, by praying, he brought forth a spring from dry earth

While the devout heavenly inhabitant was hastening  
to scatter the divine seeds of life through many lands,  
he reached a place where nothing grows except barren sands.  
The soil was unfruitful near the shores of the sea,  
and no sweet stream of water could be found for the thirsty.

The holy man, wishing to help his exhausted companions,  
ordered them to dig a pit inside the tents  
[Mab., *tentoria*, “tents”; the text reads *tectoria*, “coverings” or “roofs”].

[Col. 0717C]

When this had been done, the bishop shut himself alone within,  
and, fixed upon his knees, poured out bitter tears  
before God. Soon they deserved sweet water:  
the previously dry earth suddenly produced a spring,  
from which his companions drank and carried water with them,  
as much as the journey begun through the barren fields required.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, through his blessing, a flask of wine sufficed for twelve poor men

Twelve miserable men, dressed in rags  
and lacking bread, came to meet God’s servant.  
When the devout priest saw them, moved by compassion,  
he said: “Bring my flask; bring it, servants,  
and mix it for the men. I believe that Christ’s blessing  
will make it most abundantly sufficient for them all.”

[Col. 0717D]

The crowd drank eagerly as much as each desired,  
yet the flask had been full of the finest Falernian wine.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Likewise, how through his blessing wine increased in a cask

A venerable guest had come to a certain cell.  
After he had duly completed all the Church’s affairs  
and greeted the brothers with the customary greeting,  
he inspected all the seats of the sacred cell.

Entering the storeroom as well with a few companions,  
he found that a single cask scarcely held a little wine.

[Col. 0718A]

The servant of Christ blessed it with the staff  
which the holy man always used to carry in his hands.  
On the following night the watchman, remaining alone in the building,  
saw the wine increase—wonderful to tell!—  
until the cask was filled with honey-flowing nectar.

He joyfully reported this to the venerable Father, who kept silent  
[Mab., silently],  
for the devout bishop had given him orders to remain silent  
until the day of his death, unwilling to seek glory for himself.

## CHAPTER XIX. Likewise, how through the blessing of the same man of God forty men drank their fill from four small flasks

There was in the people a hospitable man, generous toward strangers,  
whose lodging the excellent bishop often used to enter  
when he came into those parts.

Behold, one day the bishop arrived,  
and the man had no foreknowledge of his coming.  
Therefore, when the dear master suddenly arrived,  
he had no cups of wine.

The Father, recognizing this, ordered him to bring four flasks,  
which the boys customarily carried with them from place to place,  
small flasks all alike. He blessed them and said:

“Now mix them for us. I believe that Christ’s blessing,  
in kindly compassion, will increase the wine.”

And so it happened. Behold, twice twenty men  
were the guests, drinking the wine together.  
Through Christ’s gift, the drink sufficed for them all.

## CHAPTER XX. Of a certain insolent rich man who refused to drink with God’s servant and afterward wished to do so but could not until he had been absolved by him

[Col. 0718C]

Weary from his journey, the Lord’s servant was making his beloved way,  
wishing to water the broad fields with heavenly rains.  
The devout bishop entered the meadows of a certain rich man  
with his companions, in order to rest for a short time.

The rich man began to strike the horses with rods  
and drive them out of the meadows. The devout priest addressed him  
in gentle speech:

“Stop, I beg you, driving us from your meadows now.  
Instead, come as a guest to our meal,  
and drink with us; let us always be friends.”

The rich man, proud in his furious mind, replied:

“I do not want your meal; I refuse to drink with you.”

The bishop immediately took the words from the speaker’s mouth:

“If you refuse to drink with me now, then do not drink, I beg you.”

After saying this, the Lord’s servant continued on his way,  
and the wicked rich man returned home.  
Suddenly, excessive thirst inflamed him with fierce heat.  
In his frenzy he ordered his servants to mix wine for him,  
and, taking the cup, he was unable to swallow anything.

[Col. 0718D]

His stomach burned with thirst, but it rejected the cups of Bacchus,  
and his whole body burned with panting flames.  
No physician could relieve his suffering  
until the wretched man himself recognized his wicked offense  
and paid the penalty for his torment, in accordance with the servant of God’s word.

Therefore he longed for the return of the gracious bishop.  
The old man came when another year had passed.  
The wretched man met him and confessed his bitter punishment.  
The devout bishop forgave whatever he had committed against him,

[Col. 0719A]

199

and with his own hand offered him a drink.  
Immediately healed, and abandoning his long loathing,  
the man took the cup and washed himself with a full mouthful.

## CHAPTER XXI. How, by praying in the city of Trier, he removed an impending plague from Christ’s maidservants

[Col. 0719A]

Trier is an ancient city, broad, powerful with walls and towers,  
and surrounded by sacred cells.  
In them a united crowd of devout people  
keeps watch in the praises of the Lord night and day.

Among these there was a cell of sacred sisters,  
whom a grievous plague suddenly shook with excessive force.  
It carried many away from this life by the final death;  
some lay half-dead in prolonged suffering.  
The terror of death was immense, and the same terror affected all.

[Col. 0719B]

Their hope was in Christ’s servant, and he was summoned  
to come more swiftly, with weary tears, to their aid.  
But the devout Father fulfilled the sisters’ prayers.  
When he arrived, their blessed hope did not fail them;  
rather, through the saint’s prayers the grievous plague soon withdrew,  
and they rendered praise to the Lord for their preserved lives.

## CHAPTER XXII. How he freed the entire household of the same head of a family from a most severe demonic temptation [Mab., “had freed”]

For a long time the roofs of a certain father’s house  
were repeatedly troubled by the attacks of the black demon.  
The dreadful spirit tormented it with various terrors,  
and no longer only with an empty apparition.

[Col. 0719C]

It did great harm openly through manifest deeds:  
many times it snatched clothing and food with its hands  
and threw them into the flames. One night, while an infant lay sleeping,  
the dreadful force carried him off from between his parents’ embraces;  
it was seen to carry the crying child into a blazing fire,  
but the child was scarcely rescued from the hands of death.

No priest could heal this affliction,  
until God’s servant himself, asked by the father,  
cleansed the plague through holy prayers  
and sent him water blessed in Christ’s name.

The bishop, who knew beforehand what would happen, also foretold to him  
that the old house would first be consumed by flames through the enemy.  
“Therefore, I beg you, do not let the fire terrify you.  
Build for yourself a better dwelling of the desired salvation,  
and remember to fortify it quickly with blessed water.

[Col. 0719D]

Afterward, by God’s gift, you will be free from the serpent’s plague,  
and your whole beloved household will rejoice with you.”

Soon everything the Father had said was fulfilled in order.  
From then on no such temptation touched the house,  
and its inhabitant remained safely secure within it.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the man of God baptized Pippin, son of Charles, duke of the Franks, and foretold that he would one day reign

This holy man of God had foretold future things beforehand,  
which later events proved true as they occurred.  
When Pippin, the son of Duke Charles, was born,  
he baptized him in the sacred baptismal rite, as the Father desired.  
Concerning him the prophet foretold the following to his disciples:

“This child will be higher than all the other Frankish dukes  
whom the long ages have brought forth.

[Col. 0720A]

He will happily govern this fortunate empire,  
enlarging its boundaries with great triumphs on every side.”

There is no need for our Muses to display that fact,  
which is celebrated by truthful speech throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the character and death of the holy Father

This man of God was patient, moderate, honorable,  
excellent in character and vigorous in every action,  
devout in heart, gentle toward the humble and stern toward the proud,  
a comforter of the wretched, poor for himself and rich toward the needy.

After he had been perfected through the merits of his life,  
the devout priest completed eight times two lustral periods—  
and three times four months, with the month of November already at hand.

[Col. 0720B]

On the eighth Ides he migrated to heaven’s court,  
joined to the angelic assemblies,  
and, blessed forever without end, praised Christ  
with heavenly hymns.

## CHAPTER XXV. How, when the brothers were burying the Father in a sarcophagus that was too short for his body, it suddenly lengthened to a suitable measure

The brothers took care to bury him with holy devotion,  
with psalms, hymns, and great honor of praise.  
But the sarcophagus was shorter than the Father’s body,  
and the brothers then wished to place the body in it.

They became exceedingly sad. But, wonderful to tell,  
behold, suddenly the stone of the little coffin  
began to extend itself and adapted itself  
to the form of the gracious body.

## CHAPTER XXVI. And how the fragrance of a marvelous scent spread throughout the whole church

[Col. 0720C]

During the funeral rites, the fragrance of a marvelous scent  
filled the entire church with ambrosial nectar,  
clearly showing that an angelic host had come  
to perform the service for the gracious Father  
with joyful harmonies.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How, through God’s working, signs continue to be performed up to the present where the holy man rests in body

This holy Father, pastor, patriarch, and priest,  
rests happily in his own cell at Aster­nacum,  
which he himself had built for the praise of the Lord.  
There God continues even now to perform signs of salvation.

[Col. 0720D]

Many sick people are healed by the touch of the oil,  
which customarily shines beside the body of the great patron.  
The bonds of their sins are broken of themselves for those who hurry there;  
they come with tears to lament their evil offenses,  
and return joyfully, released by Christ’s gift.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How a light is often seen above the little bed where Saint Willibrord died

At the place of the saintly Father, where the sacred bed stands,  
a heavenly light is often seen to have appeared.  
For there, leaving the prison-house of the flesh,  
his spirit seeks the lofty stars through its life-giving merits,  
to enjoy everlasting light with Christ and the saints.  
That light is frequently seen there as a sign.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How there too the fragrance of a marvelous scent is perceived from time to time

[Col. 0721A]

In that place, many times, a sweet fragrance  
breathes forth with heavenly nectar, sweeter than every perfume.  
Many witnesses prove that this truly occurs,  
and their chaste lives contended to give credibility to their account.

What blessed rest do you suppose that soul possesses,  
while such signs are performed on earth  
through the holy relics of so great a father?  
He can relieve our pains  
if we pour out tears there with devout hearts,  
where the excellent Father rests in his consecrated body.

## CHAPTER XXX. How a certain paralytic woman was suddenly healed while praying at the holy man’s body

[Col. 0721B]

Meanwhile a woman, paralytic in all her limbs,  
had languished continuously for seven full years.  
Her limbs could not move themselves in any way.  
She was scarcely drawing her final, dying breaths from her heart  
when she was carried and laid before the body of the holy man of God,  
pouring out warm tears with an exhausted voice.

Only faith remained strong: she could hope for salvation  
through Christ’s servant, and that hope did not deceive her.  
Behold, suddenly health ran lightly through her limbs;  
a fiery color breathed through her open veins,  
and renowned strength returned to all her bones and nerves.

The woman immediately rose, sound in her whole body,

[Col. 0721C]

and joyfully ran home on her own feet—  
she who previously, weakened, had been carried  
in another person’s arms.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How a certain young man was healed of a dreadful illness at his body

A certain young man had suffered from a severe illness  
for many years. Alas! His nerves scarcely clung to his bones,  
and the limbs of his afflicted body trembled together.  
You would have thought you saw a head torn away  
whirled this way and that, to the right and left,  
from its highest crown.

Often he also lay as though about to die for a long time.  
Such a wretched man, with a heart firm in faith,  
came to the church, led by friends by the hands,  
where the devout body of the great bishop rests.

[Col. 0721D]

He poured out bitter tears for his salvation.  
The grace of compassionate Christ soon heard him,  
and renewed health ran everywhere through his limbs.  
The man’s supple array of sinews recovered,  
and strength crept into [*irrepit*; Al., *repit*, “creeps into”] all his bones, with power into his marrow.

In the presence of the assembled people, with everyone looking on,  
he was suddenly made sound and strong in vigor.  
He went away healed, wherever his prayers were leading him,  
always giving thanks to almighty God for the gifts of salvation:

“Thanks to Christ; praise to Christ; glory always.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning a certain deacon who perished by a wretched death because of the theft he had committed in the church of the man of God

[Col. 0722A]

A young minister of the altar, corrupted in mind,  
secretly carried off certain offerings from the holy temple.  
A certain golden cross was taken in a savage theft,  
which the servant of Christ used to carry with him  
when, with Christ accompanying him, he traveled devoutly,  
because he kept many relics enclosed within it.

The wicked thief soon paid the torments of his crime.  
Just vengeance follows an ungodly offense,  
and the unhappy man perished, struck down by a cruel plague.

At the moment of death, however, he revealed his impious thefts  
and showed where everything he had taken was hidden.  
When he died, great trembling increased among the brothers and the people,

[Col. 0722B]

who saw that Christ was guarding and preserving  
everything that had belonged to his servant.

## THE ELEGY OF THE SAME ALCUIN, ON SAINT WILGILS, FATHER OF SAINT WILLIBRORD

### CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Wilgils, father of Bishop Willibrord, and his honorable life in secular dress

This priest was noble, descended from a great people,  
but much nobler through his great merits.  
As I sang earlier, fertile Britain,  
the homeland of the Scots, was his glorious teacher.

But fortunate Francia seized him, revered him, and possessed him,  
and to this day holds his buried remains.  
The renowned Wilgils begot him in his own age:

[Col. 0722C]

a holy man, wise, and upright in piety.  
Of him I may play with my poetic plectrum,  
reader, so that you may recognize what he himself was like,  
and from what holy root of his parents’ lineage  
this servant of God was born.

There was among the people a man worthy of the name Wilgils,  
living among a noble people in Trans-Humbria  
[Note: [Col. 0721D] Mabillon corrects the earlier editions, in which the text was most corruptly read: “Living among us in Trans-Humbria.” The Utrecht manuscript reads: “Living in the strong people of Trans-Humbria.”]

He was greatly loved by all the people for his excellent character.  
His life with his chaste wife was sufficiently exemplary;  
she had already been subjected in devout mind to her husband,  
as Sarah once was to her own husband.

### CHAPTER XXXIV. And how his wife saw dreams, how he abandoned the world, how he lived in solitude, and where he rests in body

[Col. 0722D]

She perceived future things in her mind, with God revealing them  
[Mab., “disclosing them”],  
as she lay in bed and saw true dreams.

For she thought that she had seen a new moon,  
with its horns raised, as a new moon normally is.  
It began to grow and gradually to fill out its horns,  
until full light shone for it throughout its orb.

Suddenly that moon fell into the mouth of one who swallowed it,  
and its light shone through the person’s entrails.  
Awakening from sleep, the woman pondered these things in her mind,  
wondering what what she saw might signify.

She disclosed everything to a certain priest,  
whose life in the Church had been proven.

[Col. 0723A]

When the aforementioned priest considered these things,  
he inferred heavenly visions from the strange events.  
At last the prophet answered the woman in these words,  
with God inspiring his truthful speech:

“You, woman, saw the moon growing small  
and its horns entirely filled with new light.  
Perhaps on that night you had lain with a man,  
and you are to give birth to a new light throughout the world.

A little child is born to you, woman, from the womb;  
he will grow great through honorable merits.  
He will be an outstanding teacher and a future bishop;  
a new morning star will shine in our world.

And the peoples whom blind darkness previously held  
he will illuminate with the light from the highest heaven.”

Everything foretold was fulfilled in order,  
and the outcome of events proved the dreams true.

The child was born to his mother, and after he had been washed in baptism,  
his father gave him the name Willibrord.  
His life, faith, character, and teaching  
were once celebrated by the Muses with praise.

Soon the excellent father left behind the world’s evil pleasures,  
desiring with mind and hand to serve God.  
Seizing heavenly life in all its sweetness,  
he gave himself to a sacred monastery.

Joined to the brothers, he lived as a brother without fault,  
patient, humble, and ready for every good.  
After this, the holy servant, pursuing greater things,  
began to seek alone the contemplative way,  
among the headlands of the resounding sea,  
where he found places suited to his heart:

[Col. 0723C]

places where he could pluck heavenly flowers  
and remain free from the world’s evil cares.

Here, alone, he passed the whole period of his life,  
advancing in great merits night and day.  
He suffered many battles from the wicked serpent,  
who habitually turns his weapons against the saints.

[Col. 0724A]

But almighty God, who rightly triumphs over the saints’ enemies,  
granted bright trophies to his servant  
[Mab., “granted the servant bright trophies”].

Through him also the compassion of Christ accomplished certain things,  
wondrous signs indeed through his servant.  
Nor was it fitting that so bright a lamp should be hidden under a bowl,  
nor that it should be placed beneath a bed.

Rather, it should be set above the roof’s foothold,  
so that it might scatter its holy light more widely.  
Yet I have not wished, with my hastening plectrum,  
to touch upon these things or disclose the illustrious signs in my songs.

It is nevertheless enough to know this about the father’s life  
[the word *vitam*, “life,” is supplied in the text],  
that it is everywhere and always pleasing to the Most High.

The life of God’s servant offered many examples of salvation,  
and his whole heart was a witness to them.  
Kings serve this servant of Christ, and throughout the land  
the entire people honors him with love.

[Col. 0724B]

This man of God was patient, moderate, honorable,  
excellent in character, gentle, and devout in speech.  
After he had earned many gifts through perfected labor,  
with Christ bringing his work to completion,  
soon filled with merits, years, and complete piety,  
he finally rested joyfully in tranquil peace.

His spirit happily migrated to heaven’s court,  
already holding joys with the saints without end.  
The brothers took care to bury his body in the church,  
which stands built near the shores of the sea.

And the most glorious Mother of God, Christ’s holy bearer,  
shines there in your name, Virgin Mary.  
We rightly believe that you will be present there  
as our aid, powerful always in honor.

[Col. 0724C]

You, eternal Virgin, gave birth in the lodging of your womb  
to the life of the world, to joy throughout all ages,  
to the King of heaven, the Lord and God.  
Help us by your prayers.

The unlearned poet Alcuin sang these verses.  
Whoever reads them, I beg you, say: “God, have mercy.”

# PART SIX OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, TEACHER OF CHARLEMAGNE—POEMS

[Col. 0723]

201

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0723D]

The poems of blessed Alcuin that we present here are of various kinds, namely inscriptions, epigrams, epitaphs, riddles, salutations, and similar pieces.

“Our poet does not sing,” as the learned Dom Catelinot prefaced this section in his manuscript, “of the burning of Troy, nor of the Argonauts, nor of the boar’s head; nor of famous Hercules or Ulysses, as Homer does; nor of Aeneas, as Virgil does; nor of the wars and brave deeds of the ancient heroes, as Lucan does; nor of how the earth is joined to the sea in most fitting structure, as Lucretius does; nor of the splendor of gems; nor of the courses of the heavenly spheres, as Manilius does; nor of furious loves, as Seneca does; nor of the exceptional beauty of young men gently striking the lyre with their first fingers, as Gregory Nazianzen said of himself; nor does he attack morals in satirical verses, as Plautus, Persius, and Juvenal do.

Rather, he sang of the great God and the light of the Trinity, and of the choirs of angels. He sings the praises of the saints, the sufferings of the martyrs, the deeds and immortal glory of men distinguished by piety. If these poems are compared with the epics and with Pindar’s victory odes, which he entitled *Olympian*, *Nemean*, and *Pythian*, everyone will see how much those works savor of mere trifles and foolishness in comparison with those divine and most delightful praises with which the minds of young people ought to be imbued”—so says Possevinus in *Bibliotheca selecta*, book XVII, p. 411—“before they are filled with the false fables and dreams of poets and leave either the narrowest possible place or no place at all for the heavenly mysteries that raise and nourish the soul most exaltedly.”

This excellent man, together with the celebrated Possevinus, speaks admirably, devoutly, and truly, if we attend to the nature of the subject treated in most of these poems. Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that if the poetry of blessed Alcuin is compared with that of the ancients for elegance of style, fervor of genius, nobility, and natural charm, it is far inferior. Everyone will judge that this is to be attributed more to the conditions of that age—when one should look for the beginnings of the liberal arts rather than for the mature development that flourished among the Romans in their golden age—than to the author’s talent.

Indeed, several of Alcuin’s poems clearly demonstrate that he was not wholly unacquainted with poetic elegance, since sparks of poetic fire are sometimes scattered through them. Moreover, if anyone wishes to know the condition of the poetic art as it existed in the eighth century, let him read what the learned writer of the *Histoire littéraire de la France* discusses with great erudition, volume IV, p. 21, no. 34 and following. Among other things, he says that neither Alcuin nor anyone else of that age laid down precepts or rules concerning the poetic art itself.

But did this very learned man not at least remember the book *On the Art of Meter* by the Venerable Bede, which appears among his works? There also survives in a manuscript of the Vatican Royal Library, no. 1587, *Verses of Albinus the Teacher on the Praise of the Metrical Art*. In them certain rules of prosody are transmitted, and certain words are listed whose syllables should be lengthened or shortened.

It appears, however, that these verses have been torn from some more extensive work and are very corrupt. Nor can a certain conclusion be drawn from them as to which Albinus they should be attributed: whether our Albinus, to whom Trithemius, in book II, chapter 26, of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, attributes two short works, one *On the Poetic Art* and the other *On Meters*; or an older writer who composed a work on the feet of verses, or on a hundred meters [Note: [Col. 0725D] See Elias Putschius, *Grammar*, book IV, chapter 7].

It is pleasing to copy them here, [Col. 0725D] so that the reader may judge what seems fair.

## VERSES OF ALBINUS THE TEACHER ON THE PRAISE OF THE METRICAL ART

Light is the world’s honor, the heaven’s burning majesty.  
Whatever lacks these is rightly shortened in every syllable.  
The sailor, skilled, utters the short sound of Xerses from the shore.  
“Peace” is always *xis*, but kingdoms and slander are far away.  
Muse, necklace, adornment, consul, man, teacher, origin,  
horn, watchman, roof, song, honey—the sense of the corrupt reading *album* is uncertain.  
These run short in the nominative case.

Sun, *allectanaquil*, *fruginam*: these have long quantity.  
Salt, animal, Caesar, spelt, murmur, thief, father, and spring;  
lawsuit, strong, simple—the disyllable is long. But not  
long are day, temple, wall, foot, syllable, wage,  
soldier, and the white field: in speech they are shortened.

*Os oris*—“mouth”—is long, but *os ossis*—“bone”—is short.  
*Compotis* and *compos* are short, but *nepotis* is long.  
*Virtus*, *virtutis*—“virtue”—is long, except *palus* alone  
has a short *a*; but *pectus*, *vulgus*, with *pectore*, *vulgi*—

[Col. 0726A]

are spoken with their proper quantities.

Certain verbs sound short in the present tense,  
but in the completed tense they make long delays in time.  
These are collected below and marked together.

Now I read, now I see, I throw, I favor, and I vow;  
so I help, so I dig, I beware, I warm, I sow—it runs.  
Soon I buy, soon I allow, soon I hollow out, soon I wash, and I hate.  
But I did, I saw, I made; when I shall have made, I favored.

And I sat, I helped, I dug; when I shall have dug, I hollowed out.  
This I bought, sowed, allowed; when I shall have allowed, I hollowed.  
This I hated, warmed, washed; when I shall have washed, I joined.

[Col. 0726B]

Here ends. Thanks be to God.

Quercetanus first collected Alcuin’s poems and published them divided into 272 numbers from an ancient manuscript of the library of Saint Bertin, which he was able to use through the aid and good will of the distinguished man Jacques Sirmond.

Among them some pieces are falsely attributed, some of doubtful authenticity, and some, although different from one another, are confused into a single work. Some that ought to be connected are separated. Nor is there any order of the poems in that edition; everything is mixed together according to the way the old writer happened to collect it onto the page, without titles and without connection.

We have therefore, we think with permissible freedom, brought everything under general titles according to the diversity of its subject: inscriptions of the sacred Scriptures, churches, altars, and other places; epitaphs; riddles; salutations to friends. We have also supplied each poem with an individual title and added brief notes wherever something suitable occurred or seemed necessary.

We separated what had been confused and joined what had been divided. Finally, pieces about which it could reasonably be doubted whether blessed Alcuin was their author were assigned to the doubtful works; those that certainly reveal other authors were relegated to the spurious works. Finally, some pieces drawn from other editions, or newly discovered by us, have been inserted in their proper places. In the notes appended throughout, or in the preliminary notices, we explain the reasons for all these decisions.

[Col. 0726]

## [POEMS.(C)*]

203

## NIGHT PRAYERS

### I

Fountain of light, light and source of light,  
favor our prayers in your goodness;  
and, when the darkness of sin has been driven away,

[Col. 0726D]

may the holy power that created humanity  
and condemned it by justice,  
but redeemed it through mercy,  
seek us with gracious light.  
May you be compassionate and just in all things,  
almighty One.

What awakens us is the power of faith;  
the glory of hope in the future raises us;  
charity joins us, destined to have no end  
through all time.

May the gracious guide of this life  
grant both labor and rest;  
and while they succeed one another in turn,  
may we be renewed.

[Col. 0727A]

Behold, the day’s labor has been completed,  
and, with your assent, we are safe under your protection.  
To you we give perpetual thanks  
for all time.

The sun’s departure has brought back darkness.  
May that radiant sun shine upon us,  
the sun that cherishes with golden light  
the holy hosts of angels.

Pour back from heaven your shining light,  
and drive away the darkness of our sluggish mind.  
May we be kindled, as vessels of light,  
by a spiritual torch.

Whatever sins this present day has covered,  
merciful and gentle Christ, erase them.  
And let the heart shine with pure brightness  
during the night.

[Col. 0727B]

Let luxury be far away, and every honor far away,  
as well as phantom and beautiful appearance.  
But may the unarmed mind be able  
to see the citizens above.

While ever watchful, may it seek you, God;  
freed from every care, may it think upon you,  
so that in all its deeds it may be able  
to please you, supreme King.

May the divine word and the trophy of the cross  
protect the forehead, the places, and the heart’s  
[F., the hearts’] regions,  
and drive away the demons’ crafty winding paths  
and their attacks.

May the limbs that we shall entrust to the chaste bed  
rise ready for the work of day,  
the limbs that the gracious Spirit comes to make  
his pure temple—

[Col. 0727C]

that he may inhabit it entirely for all ages.  
May neither sin nor disease offend him;  
rather, may the integrity of life call him,  
and may it become a pleasing dwelling.

May we complete the course of this age  
by a straight path: a discerning way, a strong way, a narrow way,  
a just or skillful way, well governed.

For six days we perform righteous works;  
on the seventh let our minds receive rest.  
On the eighth, may the joys of life  
be renewed for us.

[Col. 0727D]

May the fullness of devotion be the praise of glory  
to the Father alone [F., “to the Son”], to you, Holy Spirit,  
who alone bear the gracious scepters  
in the threefold Name.

## INSCRIPTIONS OF THE SACRED CODEX

### II. Inscription of the Vallicellian sacred codex, from volume IX of Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 778

[Note: [Col. 0727D] These verses appear at the end of the biblical codex of the Vallicellian Library. It contains the whole of divine Scripture, copied, reviewed, and corrected by Alcuin from older and more reliable sources, and subsequently presented by him to Charlemagne. See Baronius, cited work.]

Remember to call this sacred book  
by its proper name, *Pandect*,  
reader, with your mouth.

[Col. 0728A]

It is now called a “Library” by many:

Not by its proper name, as the Pelasgian language teaches.

And within this are stored the mystical things of the supreme God, concerning which the illustrious prophet sings with his lips (Psalm 118):

> The law of the Lord is sweeter to me than all honey,  
> and dearer than many thousands of pieces of gold.

The diligent servant of the Lord will guard this citadel, for an everlasting heavenly reward awaits him in the citadel.

For all the little letters depicted in various forms throughout the sacred body of that book, may King Charles, who ordered it to be written, receive rewards throughout the ages, with Christ granting them.

Christ, eternal giver of all good things, accept these holy gifts from your own gifts.

These King Charles, suppliant with devoted heart, has offered to you here for the praise of your name.

May your right hand preserve him through unending days, so that he may live happily with you in the citadel of heaven.

### Another poem in the same place

May this divine Scripture, we pray, please you, honorable reader, in both your understanding and your eyes.

The Holy Spirit dictated it from the citadel of heaven, where true faith shines and gracious salvation.

### Another

Whoever you are who read these verses, remember to pray for me.

I am called Alcuin. Farewell forever!

### Another

Those who bring great gifts to God’s great temple, whom the devout people praised with rejoicing lips—

yet the Lord places the widow’s two small coins above the gifts of the noble, according to the truthful saying.

I do not bring you, O ruler, small gifts to your treasures, although my person may be small.

But I bring you, excellent king, with full hands, gifts renowned in the heavenly kingdoms of the Lord.

For indeed the pious words of both the New and Old Law are enclosed in this sacred body.

I gladly bring these to the holy sanctuary of the temple, which your gracious mind has newly founded for God.

So that this book may always be present there for Christ’s praises, resounding with the heavenly words of God.

### 204. Another

The inexperienced sailor, rescued from the sea’s savage waves and arriving in harbor, holds a joyful heart.

So may the weary scribe, laying down his pen at the end of his labor, possess a sufficiently joyful heart.

Let him give thanks to God for his life preserved, and for the fruits and rest of his labor.

### Another

Go forth, sacred little book, more splendid than all songs; prosper now in peace, through God’s mercy.

And seek the splendid palace of the splendid King, so that you may always remain in Christ’s holy dwelling.

Bring gifts of peace to all God’s servants, whom the Lord’s right hand protects and guides.

I honor them in my heart, in faith, and always with holy love, desiring with tears that they may flourish and remain strong.

## III. On the Ten Canons of Eusebius, or the Harmony of the Four Evangelists

How splendid above all is the four-horse chariot: man, lion, calf, and eagle, speaking of equal things through seventy-one chapters.

In the second, man and lion immediately follow, and the calf speaks, in which the number nineteen is set out in orderly fashion.

Then, third in order, man, beast, and ox speak with the winged creature; their number corresponds to the ancient letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

In the fourth place they speak equal things: man, lion, and eagle together.

Speaking with one mouth, they have twenty-six chapters of the word of the Most High.

For the fifth time they agree in speech: the prudent man and the gentle victim.

The believing hosts of Juda, imitating Jesus Christ, without the Savior [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

Behold, in the sixth place, the son of Adam sounds forth to the father with a cry, together with the roaring lion.

The towns handed over as a gift, counted in honor of the priests.

Behold, in the seventh, man and bird speak seven times, in harmony concerning the Lord.

In the eighth, now the lion’s cub, whose words are reckoned with the addition of the apostle Paul.

The ninth order, in which the calf and the winged creature speak together, utter spiritually inspired words in a simple threefold form.

Man, then, utters his own word, numbering forty-two,

and the roaring lion, boldly and alone, exactly nineteen times.

You will find the ox speaking alone seventy-two times, the word of God [Note: The passage is corrupt. Perhaps: “the word of God seventy-two times.”]

You will find the one flying upward to the stars speaking ninety-seven times.

## IV. On the Codex Written at the Order of Bishop Gerfrid

### [Col. 0729D]

This sacred codex contains within a single body

all the mysteries of the New and Old Law.

Here is the fountain of life; here are the precepts of salvation.

The saints wrote this for the ages, with God dictating it.

This is the holy faith; from here comes its heavenly origin.

Whatever that pious Lawgiver had once written concerning things to come,

whatever the holy prophets of the Hebrew people had sung,

whatever history had accomplished,

whatever David had sung in hymnic or mystical praise,

whatever the apostolic assembly had taught throughout the ages,

and whatever the Savior, when he came, had already done in the world—

this single codex contains all these things together.

The bishop Gerfrid [Note: The distinguished Cathelinot conjectured in his manuscript that this Gerfrid was Saint Ludger’s nephew through his sister, who died in 809, and later succeeded him both in the bishopric of Münster and in the abbacy of Werden. But Alcuin died five years before Gerfrid could have succeeded Saint Ludger, and yet this poem styles Gerfrid a bishop. Was he, while Alcuin still lived, bishop or abbot of some other church?] ordered this volume to be written

for the praise of Christ, his mother, and that gracious church,

so that it might be present in the church for those who read.

In it, whoever reads the Lord’s sweetest words

should remember its author, the one who ordered it to be written.

And let him say with devout lips: “Christ, protect Gerfrid;

may he live happily forever and ever.”

And farewell, reader. I beg that you take the greatest care, as you read,

to sound forth Christ’s heavenly words with a right understanding;

a great reward will remain for you.

[Note: The verses that follow concern not the codex but the inscriptions of a church restored by Gerfrid. We have nevertheless not wished to separate them from this passage, since they concern the same Gerfrid.]

This gracious house of God, Christ’s venerable hall,

had long lain dishonored, demolished by ruins.

But when Gerfrid, the bishop and priest [Note: The passage is corrupt. Perhaps: “when Gerfrid, bishop and priest together”],

had assumed the governance of this gracious church,

moved by the love of God, he renewed the whole building [Note: The aforementioned Cathelinot interprets this as the basilica of the Savior in the monastery of Werden on the Ruhr; but that church could not have fallen into ruin through age during Alcuin’s lifetime, since Saint Ludger, Alcuin’s disciple, had first built it. See Mabillon’s preliminary observations on the Life of Saint Ludger, part I, century IV, p. 15, nos. 6–7; *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 323, no. 52, and p. 385, no. 69.]

with walls, roofs, paintings, and columns,

with vestments and vessels, and with the sacred order of the clergy,

sparing none of his own resources. For whatever he possessed,

he distributed with generous mind among Christ’s offerings,

devoting all his strength to adorning the temple on every side.

So that the Lord’s outstanding beauty might shine forth in honor,

and the hall might resound with divine praises as well,

he had it done, as they say, throughout the seven hours [Alternative: “so that it might belong to the Lord”].

Receive graciously, merciful Christ God, all these things,

and from the hands of your servant receive, we pray, these vows [Alternative: “these vows, we pray”].

And you, most holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God,

assist the prayers of your servants, O Virgin.

Since these temples have been consecrated in your name,

may praise, worship, and honor remain here for Christ throughout the ages.

Say, I beg you, reader: “Christ, protect Albinus.”

### 205. V. On the Sacred Codex Written at Ava’s Order

### [Col. 0730D]

This servant of God, Ava [Note: The printed editions read *Aula* here, certainly in error. The editor restores the true reading, also recognized by the celebrated Mabillon, from an old Salzburg manuscript. Ava appears to be none other than the sister of Gisla whom Alcuin mentions in Epistle 127; see Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 327.], had already ordered this little book

to be written, led by great fear of the Lord [Note: The printed edition reads “led by love,” but the manuscript reading is “led by fear”],

for the glory of the Church and at once for her own salvation.

It sets forth all the beginnings of the flower-bearing world [Note: The printed edition reads *simul geri*, which makes no sense.],

and likewise the events of the ages through long periods of time—

the things that the Almighty gave to humankind, and the precepts of salvation,

all the miracles of Christ enthroned on high,

and also the hope of everlasting life after these ages.

This codex alone contains all these things;

therefore let it always be held in great honor.

Grant, I beg you, powerful Christ, the rewards of eternal life,

and grant them to your servant, who ordered this to be written,

so that after this life she may deserve to possess

everlasting rest, joined forever to the company of the saints.

## VI. On the Sacred Codex Written through the Care of Rado, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Vedast

[Note: This poem is printed by the distinguished Lambecius from a very ancient manuscript belonging to the age of Charlemagne and indeed of Alcuin himself, preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna; see *Commentary on the Imperial Library*, vol. II, p. 403 of the old edition, or vol. I, p. 618 of the new. It bears the title: “Verses at the head of the library edited by Alcuin”; the plural noun “verses” must unquestionably be understood. By “library” here is meant the complete body of all sacred Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament.]

In this codex are preserved the five books of Moses,

the wars of the commander Joshua, and the times of the elders and fathers.

Ruth, Job, and the four books of Kings;

also the sixteen sacred books of the Prophets;

the hymnic songs of David, the renowned father of Christ,

and the three works of the peaceful king Solomon.

Joined to these are the Wisdom of Jesus and the book of Sirach,

and also the two books of Chronicles.

Then the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and Judith,

and the two books containing the wars of the Maccabees.

The book of Matthew, of Mark, of Luke, and of John,

containing the famous deeds of Christ, the Savior of the ages.

The holy Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles.

Paul’s fourteen teachings are written throughout the pages,

together with the devout words of James, Peter, Jude, and John.

The book of John stands at the end of the sequence.

Read them all, fortunate reader, happily,

for Christ’s praise and your own salvation through the ages.

### Another poem by the same Alcuin, appended there without any new title

When the first man had been driven from the beautiful garden

into this wretched day of death and sorrow,

and had groaned under the fitting punishment of his unspeakable deed,

destitute of salvation together with all his offspring,

nevertheless the goodness of the Almighty had not abandoned

every work of his great mercy toward the wretched.

Rather, in his goodness, the gentle one brought from heaven

very many consolations for our tears,

so that his mercy might always be praised and loved

in the heart, mind, and hand of everyone.

Whatever good a conscience aware of righteousness could possess,

all of it the highest grace bestowed.

Among these gifts, indeed, the greatest are books,

which sing of the sequence and times of all things,

and, with God dictating, preserve the world’s beginnings,

and proclaim beforehand the gracious Christ through the ages.

In them a sure understanding is also given to humanity

of how to worship God himself—the true way, life, and salvation.

Let whoever wishes to live with Christ, forever in heaven’s citadel,

read and hold these books dear with a pure heart.

They are seventy-two in number [Note: That is, seventy-two],

and no one may now doubt this.

This venerable number is present among us in Christ,

for it was mystically consecrated to the disciples.

These books too possess a heavenly origin,

because the Spirit himself, God, dictated them.

This codex contains all of them together

within one sacred body, the great gifts of God—

all the pious words of the New and Old Law.

Do not doubt, devout reader, that you have them all here.

Here is the fountain of life; here is true wisdom;

here are the riches of everlasting salvation.

Whoever desires will find the sacred Scriptures recited here [Manuscript: “learned”],

the venerable words of the holy Fathers.

That pious Lawgiver had once written whatever concerned

the beginning of the world and of created things:

how the Almighty established all natures,

so far as the human mind is able to know.

Here too one reads of the creation of the human being,

and how he afterward fled as an exile from the sacred presence,

or how the wicked brother, deprived of piety,

stained his murderous hand with fraternal blood.

Afterward it preserves the numbers and names of the Fathers,

through whom the succession of the ages proceeded in triumph.

Then Noah, the repose of the gracious world, came into being,

in whose time the cataclysm occurred,

while God’s ark floated upon the sea, a second hope of the whole world,

filled at once with the offspring of the age.

Condemnable pride builds a vast tower,

because of which the harmonious speech of humankind is divided.

Then Father Abraham, well taught by the stars of heaven,

to whom the very Son of God had been promised.

From there the long exiles of Isaac and Jacob are recounted,

and through twelve fathers the origin of the holy nation.

From there Joseph is sold into Egypt through his brothers’ crime

and carried away, while his pious father grieves;

he is suddenly made ruler of the kingdom from prison,

and brings his aged father with his offspring into the fields [Manuscript: “Gesen”].

The first book, Genesis, contains all these things together,

up to the bitter day of Joseph’s death.

After his death another impious king, Pharaoh,

imposed harsh bonds upon God’s servants.

Then Exodus contains the glorious times of Moses,

who, at God’s command, was leader of the people,

bravely leading them out from the wicked nation of Egypt

through the ten plagues, the holy hosts of God.

Thus the people traveled with dry feet across the waters,

singing songs of joy to the Lord.

### 206

Then the Law was given from Sinai’s lofty summit,

written on tablets by the holy finger of God.

Descending from the mountain, the pious Lawgiver himself,

with horned face, brought it back to the crowds.

For a long time, indeed, he instructed the people wandering with difficulty through the deserts [Note: Perhaps: “the people”],

ordering them to build holy courts for God,

with the tent, vessels, tablets, and lamps,

and the Holy of Holies, where God’s ark was.

Then the third book describes in order the worship of the priests,

and of the Levites,

the recurring times of the holy feast days,

and Aaron’s vestments and sacred offspring.

In the fourth, Numbers, the mystical order is written,

the total of God’s people arranged by tribes and companies.

But the mystical words of Balaam, the ancient prophet,

singing the truth, foretold very many things.

Then for forty years, amid the vast silences of the world,

the faithless people wandered, thirsting, against God.

The leader renews the gracious Law with biting words [Note: *Deuteronomy.*],

as he sensed that the day of his death was approaching.

This the fifth little book holds in its noble discourse,

recalling God’s gifts to the people.

The wicked crowd perishes because it denied the Lord in the desert,

and the gracious Lawgiver dies at God’s command [Note: That is, Moses].

Joshua arose, a renowned leader in arms,

bringing into their homeland the crowds whom God himself had given.

He waged many wars with glorious triumphs,

scattering the Canaanite peoples by the sword [Manuscript: “destroying”];

through tribes and lots, through the illustrious names of their ancestors,

he distributed the renowned kingdoms to God’s people.

The sixth volume in order contains his deeds,

and is indeed titled by his name.

After his death, the people were governed for a long time,

up to the days of Saul, by Judges.

That seventh book recounts their deeds, lineage, times, places,

wars, triumphs, and names;

and the *paticus* book proceeds into this one [Note: The correction of this error was unknown to Lambecius. It should unquestionably be read *Eptaticus* or *Heptaticus*, equivalent to *Heptateuchus*: the first volume of the sacred Bible, containing the Pentateuch, the five books of Moses, and the two following books, Joshua and Judges. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, s.v. “Heptaticus.”]

Ruth, a woman of sufficient renown, follows it.

Then comes Job, the fearless warrior of faith,

prefiguring the sacred times of Christ, God.

Then the deeds of the prophet Samuel are written,

and Saul, who perished by the Philistine’s savage sword.

The powerful Israelite, chosen from his earliest years,

after whom David held the blessed kingdom,

the prophet who sang the hymnic songs of the Psalms,

proclaiming the times, deeds, and day of Christ.

From his royal line came the blessed

gracious Mother of God, the Virgin Mary.

After him the peaceful Solomon ruled the kingdom [Manuscript adds: “king”],

who joyfully built consecrated temples for God.

In his son the kingdom is divided,

and King Rehoboam held only Judah.

Jeroboam, small in stature, assumed the royal line of Samaria [Perhaps: “wicked”],

and was the first of the kings to worship calves.

From then on the two kingdoms were always opposed,

and the brothers were guilty of wars among themselves.

Thus the succession of kings continued through long periods,

burdened with very many crimes of wickedness,

until the people, together with their prince,

were led among foreign nations and began to suffer their punishments.

These times of the Kings are enclosed in four books.

The holy city perishes, together with king and people.

Then the splendid volumes of the Prophets stand forth,

who sang of the days of Christ yet to come;

there are sixteen books, each under its own name.

Then come Jeremiah’s lamentations for Joshua and the people.

The Psalter is a hymnic volume consisting of songs

which King David himself, the father of Christ, sang.

The wondrous author Solomon produced three books;

two books are joined to these in the form of a parallel work.

The first of them is called gracious Wisdom;

the second is designated by the name of Jesus.

Then there is the sacred book of Chronicles,

which is called the epitome of the Old Law.

Then come the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Judith, and Esther;

then the piety, angel, deeds, and journey of Tobit.

The famous wars of the Maccabees are written in two books,

with peoples and nations defeated.

This is indeed the sacred Scripture of the Ancient Law,

fragrant throughout with divine titles.

From the time of John the Baptist onward,

the holy dignity of the Gospel is celebrated.
