In it the deeds of the sacred books, long concealed,

are now revealed and laid open at Christ’s coming.

When God came into the world as the glorious light,

the darkness of the shadows immediately departed far away.

Then God’s four-horse chariot shines forth, accompanied by the cherub,

proclaiming the sacred times of Christ in the world:

Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John together,

writing the sacred deeds of Christ, God.

The holy Luke had described the Acts of the Apostles,

their teachings, labors, and course of toil.

Paul wrote fourteen letters in sequence

to disciples, cities, and peoples—

chosen by the Lord as a special teacher in the world,

bringing sacred teachings to countless nations.

Then James, Peter, Jude, and John

wrote mystical words under sacred titles.

Here too is the gracious one who reclined upon the divine breast,

pious in exile, expelled from the human world,

seeing many things that were to come in future ages:

what punishment awaits the wicked, and what glory the good.

This final book is inscribed as part of gracious Scripture,

entirely fragrant with divine mysteries [Note: Revelation].

These are the gifts of God, renowned in heavenly treasures;

in them are life, salvation, glory, and riches.

Without them no one can know God,

or the commandments of God, or heaven’s blessed kingdoms.

In them alone true wisdom shines,

in them the praise, reward, life, and salvation of humankind.

Without them false knowledge leads the mind astray,

because it does not care to learn the sacred words of God—

in which is the true wisdom of eternal life,

glory, light, piety, and God himself made known.

Let every reader in the church

read the books in this sacred body,

the heavenly words of God.

### 207

Let him distinguish aloud their meanings, titles, cola, and commas,

and speak [Alternative: “learn”] so that he knows how to sound the accents with his mouth.

Let the *vinula* voice resound far through the ears of the church [Note: “*Vinnolata* voice is light, soft, and flexible; it is called *vinnolata* from *vinno*, that is, ‘a curl,’ softly bent.” So Isidore, *Origins*, book III, ch. 19],

so that every hearer may praise God from his mouth.

To Christ, King of kingdoms and Lord of lords,

glory, light, power, praise, honor, and salvation—

to him who rules earth, sea, and sky by his command,

who willed that his name be known throughout the world,

and who, dying in the flesh upon the cross,

joyfully redeemed the human race from the malignant enemy.

May he govern King Charles with his customary mercy,

and protect and guide him forever and ever.

And let the whole multitude of peoples throughout the world say, “Amen.”

May gracious Christ grant this from heaven’s citadel,

so that he may live happily for many years,

and afterward possess God’s blessed kingdoms.

When the sacred codices had been consumed by hostile destruction,

the zealous Rado restored this work [Note: Rado was abbot of the celebrated Benedictine monastery of Saint Vedast at Arras; he obtained the abbacy in the year 795. See the editor’s notes on Rado above, column 663.]

For this work draws you away from the black flames,

O reader, if you read it with love of peace.

# VARIOUS HISTORIES OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT

## VII. On Christ the Savior

The lofty Creator is born from human flesh,

so that through a human being the human being may ascend to God among the stars.

Behold the lion, born from Judah’s stock,

frees the world and triumphantly celebrates his scepters amid joy [Alternative: “among the dead”].

Christ, the supreme Victim of the Father, with precious blood,

cleansing the world, calls it beneath the heavenly realms.

Christ, taking up the eagle’s wings, seeks the ether,

and reigns forever with the Father in heaven’s citadel.

## VIII. The Appearance of an Angel to Saint Joseph

The angel, through dreams, urges Joseph to preserve

the inviolate marriage with Mary; here, wisely [Alternative: “as a dowry”],

the Spirit, filled with this, blazes with the Savior’s honor [Note: Perhaps: “the pregnant woman is saved with honor”].

## IX. On Saint John the Baptist

You reveal Christ to the peoples, John the Baptist:

“Behold the Lamb, and behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

## X. The Centurion’s Faith

“For me too, the Savior—my servant longs to be saved.

I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof;

but you can heal by a word, for you are sufficient even when absent.”

## XI. The Changing of Water into Wine at the Wedding

The elements of once tasteless liquid took on

the flavor of fiery wine; for the provident author

made it a gift of joy, the beginning of miracles.

## XII. The Feeding of the People in the Desert

Here he feeds four thousand peoples with seven loaves,

and a few fish fill the banquets [Alternative: “may fill”];

for the fragments filled seven remaining baskets [Note: Perhaps: “the fragments filled them”].

## XIII. The Miraculous Healing of the Sick

He gives his right hand to the wretched and, in pity, raises from the ground

those whom the distant faults of their illness had bent down.

“Rise with upright faith; the devout mind cleanses the believer.”

## XIV. On the Sisters Mary and Martha

Martha reproves her companion with undeserved complaints,

because she is free from service; to her the truthful judge says:

“The care of the household is useful, but that which is always regarded as better…”

## XV. On the Calling of Zacchaeus

The sweet honor of the Lord shone upon his friend Zacchaeus.

Resounding with majesty: “Today you proceed as my guest

to greater things; descend, leaving these branches behind.”

## XVI. On Judas the Traitor

A dreadful hunger for money compels Judas to sell

the royal head; the impious mind conducts the commerce

of such great blood for a small profit.

## XVII. To Christ Hanging on the Cross

He bears what must be borne by all … the illustrious king set upon [Note: Perhaps: “the illustrious cross bears the king honored by all”].

Those whom he may … be victims hanging for the world,

so that a single death may restore salvation to the wretched.

## XVIII. On the Good Thief

Through the pleasant green places of the Lord’s sacred grove [Note: Perhaps: “through the pleasant green places, with the Lord as guide”],

the fortunate thief, under the guide, merits a dwelling of life.

A faith that has been made gracious conquers so many crimes of life.

## XIX. On Eve’s Sin

The envious one prepares Eve by serpent-craft

to pluck the forbidden fruit; and, tested and unaware of the deception,

the unhappy woman believed, destined to perish with her sacred husband [Alternative: “with her companion”].

## XX. On the Punishment of the First Parents

Girded with skins and bearing the signs of sin,

servants of punishment, they leave the blessed kingdoms.

The hall, always friendly to the devout, rejects sinners.

## XXI. On Noah’s Ark and Saint Peter’s Vision at Joppa

Here Noah gathers birds, cattle, men, and every kind of wild beast,

so that the violent force of the flood may not destroy all things [Note: Perhaps: “the violence of the flood”],

and he encloses one creation in the ark.

Of reptiles, cattle, and every kind of bird … the dish contains them all,

and the Father orders Peter to eat all these things,

judging nothing common that is created by the author of the world.

## XXII. The Confusion and Gift of Languages

Pride builds a tower with immense resources,

but it confounds the highest speech of the peoples [Note: Perhaps: “the foolish speech of the foolish people”],

so that the foolish hand might not plan anything beyond its rights.

Preaching pours forth harmonious but diverse languages [Note: Perhaps: “spreads them abroad”];

every foreign nation recognizes its own speech,

which the holy Spirit utters beforehand through a human mouth.

## XXIII. The Sale of Joseph

Here consuming jealousy compels the brothers

to conspire to sell their brother; contrary things benefit the righteous.

This deed belongs to grace, so that the one who sold him may worship [Note: The middle vowel of *vendidit* has been lengthened].

## XXIV. On the Manna in the Desert

Here quail, sent as food, nourish those greedy for flesh,

and heavenly abundance fills undeserving tables [Alternative: “the tables”];

for it gives manna its flavor to whomever it wishes among the worthy.

## XXV. On the Law Given through Moses

Moses opens the inner chambers of the truthful Law:

that there is one supreme reader [Note: Perhaps: “ruler”] and the same for all,

and that the world is not governed by divided powers, but by one sole authority.

## XXVI. On the Same Subject

[Note: Perhaps this should be understood of Christ’s sermon on the mount.]

Seated in the valley of the mountain [Note: Perhaps: “bidding farewell from the mountain”], he proclaims

great and unchangeable truth [Note: Perhaps: “word”] and pious precepts of justice to the peoples,

and shows what wisdom may accomplish within itself [Note: Perhaps: “may proceed within itself”].

## XXVII. On the Sacrifice of Isaac

The victim bears the wood for its own untried slaughter [Note: Perhaps: “the untried victim bears the wood of his own…”],

for he is prepared to sacrifice his beloved obedient pledge.

Abraham leads the merit of faith: he does not spare his son.

# VARIOUS INSCRIPTIONS OF CHURCHES, ALTARS, TOMBS, ETC.

## I. In a Church of a Certain Monastery, Perhaps Elnone

[Note: Mabillon believes that the following inscriptions, through number XL, belong to the monastery of Saint Amandus at Elnone.]

### XXVIII. For the Church and Tomb of Saint Amandus

This is God’s hall, the house of forgiveness, the hall of salvation;

here is Christ’s worship, here the honor of piety.

Here the people who come are accustomed to ask forgiveness;

here God is believed always to be present.

Here God hears the vows of his servants;

here he generously wipes the tears from their faces.

Here the father and shepherd, the bishop Amandus, rests,

a man powerful in virtue and good in piety.

He assists the prayers of the people crying to the stars,

he who always stands beside the Lord in heaven’s citadel.

### XXIX. For the Temple of Saint Michael Restored by Arnonus

When the river, swelling more and more, had flooded

the sacred thresholds of the present temple and was heaped up in a torrent [Note: On “the river,” Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 306, no. 71, interprets this as referring to an overflowing of the bed of the Scarpe, the stream near the monastery of Elnone],

the priest Arnonus could not endure the temples’ being defiled [Note: Arnonus was abbot of Elnone and later bishop of Salzburg, while retaining some responsibility for that place; Mabillon, *loc. cit.*],

so the bishop ordered all these things to be renewed for the better,

so that this crypt might be made wider and loftier,

supporting it with firm arches, four times three in number,

so that the mystical keystone might strengthen the entire hall.

He consecrated the little roofed building to the exalted minister

Michael, who attends upon Christ in heaven’s citadel,

and offers prayers to the King of heaven.

Here too, we ask, may he carry our vows to the Thunderer,

and defend us everywhere with pious aid.

Hlotharius, the guardian, made this at his master’s command.

May Christ preserve both of them forever and ever.

Whoever reads these verses, let him say, I beg, with a pure heart:

“Christ, we pray, grant Alcuin forgiveness of his sins.”

[Note: Mabillon interprets this epigram by Alcuin as referring to the second elevation of Saint Amandus’s body, which Milo the monk and the Annals of Elnone say took place in 809. Hence he considers it more probable that these verses are not by Alcuin, but by another poet, his disciple, who prayed for Alcuin’s soul out of affection for Bishop Arnonus. The editor disagrees because of the final four verses, in which the poet wishes good things both for Arnonus and Hlotharius, while asking the reader to pray Christ for forgiveness on his own behalf. It is difficult to see how anyone other than the author himself would have written in this way. Nor is Milo’s reckoning secure, since, as Mabillon himself observes in his notes on the Life of Saint Amandus, he often goes astray.]

### XXX. Prayer to Saint Amandus

Bishop Amandus, worthy of such a name before God,

assist the vows of your servants, Father,

and defend, through pious prayers, both the servants and the house.

### XXXI. For the Altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr

This altar shines with the merits of Stephen the protomartyr,

who, amid stones, saw God in the citadel of heaven.

He who asked forgiveness for his enemies at the very moment of death

can certainly ask forgiveness for his servants.

The renowned and illustrious beloved of Christ, Amandus,

is both an ornament and shepherd, a sweet love to his own.

### XXXII. For the Church Door

This is heaven’s gate; this is the door of eternal life.

It leads its traveler to the stars.

Entering this, he has penetrated the gate of Olympus [Alternative: “will penetrate”];

may hope and faith accompany him together.

Here forgiveness is sought [The passage is corrupt. Perhaps: “Here forgiveness is sought”]; therefore, traveler,

with devoted heart, let him often pass through on his own feet.

### 209

Here too may the sinner wash away his wicked deeds,

and wash the sacred threshold with his own tears.

Cleansed by tears poured forth in humble devotion,

may he come more worthy to the holy places of God.

I believe that gracious Jesus forgives his faults,

if he comes sorrowful so that he may return more joyful.

### XXXIII. For the Altar of Saint Lawrence

May Lawrence, God’s Levite, preserve this entire hall,

since this altar has been dedicated to him.

A man strong in virtue and faith, he conquered the flames of fire,

and conquered every torment through the love of God.

Giving to the poor whatever he possessed in the world,

so that he might receive Christ’s riches in heaven.

### XXXIV. For the Church of Saint Martin

Martin, worthy through his merits of the Lord’s love,

rules this church consecrated to him.

An outstanding bishop, renowned throughout the whole world,

a pious shepherd resting at Tours [Printed edition: “in the world”].

This gracious house was first founded for God the Thunderer,

before the other precincts of the sacred monastery.

The honor of these places grew, through the Lord’s gift,

and a larger house was built for the Lord.

While the holy bishop Amandus dwelt here,

the Father’s honor grew, and this place grew as well.

[Note: The distinguished Cathelinot interprets this poem as referring to the basilica at Tours, where Saint Amandus, as his Life relates, cut the hair of his head after attaining clerical rank. It seems more probable to me that it refers to the first church at Elnone built in honor of Saint Martin and later enlarged by Saint Amandus: now the parish church of the town of Saint-Amand, under the patronage of Saint Martin, according to Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, century IV, part I, p. 65.]

### XXXV. For the Oratory of Saint Andrew the Apostle

Andrew was the first among the apostles to recognize Christ;

he calls his own brother as well.

Through his merits he now guards this consecrated building,

so that the enemy may flee far from his dwelling.

### XXXVI. For the Oratory of Saint Peter the Apostle

Peter, apostolic prince and faithful shepherd,

now of the heavenly flock, now the glory of the Church,

who holds the keys of the eternal kingdom through the ages,

able by a single word either to loose or to bind—

in whose sacred honor this hall is now dedicated—

may he protect and guide his flock.

And may he deign, through an everlasting gift,

to open the heavenly gates to his sheep, we pray.

### XXXVII. For the Altar of Saint Michael the Archangel

Michael, heavenly prince and first teacher

of the eternal kingdom, supreme in heaven’s citadel,

may he preserve with life-giving gifts this altar,

which shines as consecrated in his name.

And before the eyes of the supreme God, in the secret places of heaven,

may he offer our service [Note: Perhaps: “our services”] and prayers.

### XXXVIII. For the Altar of Saints Hilary and Victor

Father Bishop Hilary adorns this altar,

a pious teacher known far and wide throughout the world.

Victor is commemorated at this altar through his great merits,

an illustrious soldier, powerful in glorious arms.

### XXXIX. For the Tomb of Saint Amandus, Renewed by Arnonus

[Note: See above, nos. XXVIII and XXIX.]

Arnonus, a humble bishop of the Lord and devoted to his honor,

renewed the tomb of Saint Amandus,

sparing no resources; for whatever he possessed

he had distributed to the wretched, and the priest adorned Christ’s holy temples.

Therefore, whoever you are who read these verses, remember to pray.

### XL. On Saint Amandus, Bishop of Tongeren

Here the great father and shepherd, Christ’s priest,

Saint Amandus, died—he who always loved Christ.

During his life he performed many miracles through his merits [Alternative: “coming through his merits”].

His life was the teaching and salvation of his people.

He had now despised the riches of the world,

so that he might gain Christ’s eternal riches in heaven’s hall.

The teacher of souls multiplied riches everywhere,
Forming [him] by examples, and a master with [Christ as] teacher.

[Note: [Col. 0740D] Perhaps: “with Christ as teacher.”]

This excellent father founded this fold for Christ,

and afterward, throughout the world, scattered the seeds of the everlasting kingdom

among peoples, far and wide.

After the fruits of the word, and after the savage battles of the world,

here he was pleased to gather contemplative fruits.

And, resting, to serve God alone,

a shepherd perfect in merits and full of days,

borne by Christ into the heavenly palace among the angelic choirs,

he rests buried bodily here with us in holiness.

For whose merits, Christ, protect us here;

may praise, glory, and power be yours forever and ever,

you most merciful King, who had given us such a father.

## II. In the Church of Saint Vedast

[Note: We judge that the following poems, through no. 65, belong to the church of Saint Vedast because mention of Radon, abbot of that monastery, occurs not only at the beginning but also in the middle.]

### XLI. On the church of Saint Vedast, renovated by Abbot Radon

[Note: [Col. 0741D] We have corrected this poem from the edition of the celebrated Lambecius, vol. II of the *Commentary on the Imperial Library*, p. 414; new edition, vol. I, p. 643. In the Vienna manuscript these verses bear the heading: “To be written on the wall in the church of Saint Vedast.” Lambecius observes that it says here not *scriptum* (“written”) but *scribendum* (“to be written”), because that very ancient Imperial manuscript was copied before this epigram was inscribed on the wall of the church of Saint Vedast.]

This gracious [Henschenius: “lofty”] house of God once burned amid crackling flames

and was entirely reduced to ashes [Lamb., “collapsed”];

but, with God taking pity, the venerable [Quercetanus: “wretched”] abbot Radon

built it better and restored it.

[Note: See the note to poem 6.]

Providing the present house with very many ornaments,

he adorned it completely with sacred gifts.

He wished to clothe the altars with metal grilles,

fashioning a sarcophagus for Father Vedast.

He hung coverings on the walls and lamps,

adding them so that sacred light might shine in the church.

He also made consecrated vessels for the Lord’s services,

entirely of silver and also of gold.

He clothed the ministers of the altar in a beautiful vestment,

so that there might always and everywhere be splendid adornment.

Restoring all the works for the better,

the holy man, devoted to Christ’s honey-sweet love,

for this reason, whoever you are who read these inscriptions, remember to pray

that God’s supreme grace may aid him.

[Notes: [Col. 0742D] Lambecius reads *cancellos* (“metal grilles”) for *cancellis*; Quercetanus reads *opere* for *opera* (“works”), and *cogitare* (“to think”) for *rogitare* (“to pray”).]

### XLII. At the body of Saint Vedast

Here rests in bodily form the excellent Father Vedast,

by whose sacred honor this gracious house shines.

Through the ages it is upheld by the merits of so great a patron,

through whom God works many signs of salvation.

While alive, he followed the sacred footsteps of Christ, enthroned on high,

with tongue, mind, and hand.

He multiplied his resources, perhaps by twice ten talents,

and did not idly bind up the profits entrusted to his purse.

[Note: “He did not idly bind up” is the true reading of this passage, says Lambecius in the cited work; it is the genuine reading, not, as in Quercetanus’s edition, “he bound up profits as wealth,” nor, as in the manuscripts used by Fathers Bollandus and Henschenius, “he transferred profits as wealth.”]

Therefore he will soon hear the voice of the gracious Judge:

“Enter now into the holy joys of your Lord.”

### XLIII. At the altar of Saint Vedast

Vedast the holy Father himself, the summit of pontifical dignity,

with living merits, rules this altar.

The humble abbot Radon clothed it with metal,

moved by love for the Lord the Father.

### XLIV. At the altar of Saint Martin

This altar of God the illustrious priest Martin

everywhere preserves through his merits.

May he wash away the sins of the weeping people,

seeking merciful pardon with a powerful voice.

### XLV. At the altar of Saint Denis

May Bishop Denis, through the blood of martyrdom,

adorn this altar together with his companions—

the magnificent teacher who scattered the seeds of the word,

watering the dry furrow with heavenly rains.

### XLVI. At the altar of Saints Landibert the Martyr and Richarius the Abbot

Landibert holds this altar, and Richarius likewise;

the one was a confessor, the other a holy martyr.

Both fathers, dear to God and weighty in merits,

carried very great profits to their Lord.

[Note: On Saint Landisbert the martyr, see Mabillon, vol. II of the *Annals of the Benedictines*, p. 18.]

### XLVII. At the altar of Saints Remedius and Audoin

The illustrious teacher of the Franks, Remedius, holds this altar,

and Audoin, lover of goodness, holds it with him.

Therefore, traveler, while passing through these holy places,

go piously because of their merits; may sure salvation be yours.

### XLVIII. To Saints Gregory and Jerome

Bishop Gregory and the gracious teacher Jerome:

the former was a father of the Church, the latter its teacher.

May they likewise bear our vows in prayer to the Thunderer,

so that God may always preserve us everywhere.

### XLIX. At the altar of Saints Benedict and Scholastica

On this altar the excellent Father Benedict is honored,

who himself wrote a holy life for monks.

His illustrious sister, the virgin Scholastica,

is joined here to her noble brother.

### L. At the altar of Saints Cosmas and Damian

On this altar the two brothers Cosmas and Damian

are likewise inscribed by the hand of the poet.

How good it is for brothers always to dwell together—

as the Psalmist sings, behold, a delightful love.

### LI. At the altar of the holy women Cecilia, Agatha, Agnes, and Lucy

The virgin Cecilia, Agatha, Agnes, and Lucy:

this altar, consecrated to them together, shines.

Lilies together with roses gleam upon their crowns,

and a lamp likewise glows with perpetual light.

### LII. At the altar of the holy Cross and Saints Crispin and Crispinian

This is the altar consecrated to the triumphs of the holy Cross,

on which the life and salvation of the world now suffer.

It shines with the sacred names

of the excellent martyrs Crispin and Crispinian.

### LIII. At the altar of the Blessed Virgin and Saint Clement

May the pious Virgin Mary, Mother of God,

look upon this altar of God with her customary, powerful compassion.

[The following source phrase, *tua intacta Tonantis*, is defective or corrupt: “[you], the inviolate [virgin] of the Thunderer.”]

May Clement, the summit of pontifical dignity and blessed successor of Peter,

increase it through his illustrious merits.

### LIV. At the altar of Saints John and Matthew

May John hold this altar of God on the left,

and may Matthew adorn it with his own merits!

These men indeed wrote the sacred deeds of Christ the Thunderer;

therefore this altar holds the two together.

### LV. At the altar of Saints Platonius and George

May the martyr Platonius and the victorious George

hold this altar here, both through holy merits.

They conquered the battles of the world for God’s peace

and earned the sacred heaven through their reddened blood.

### LVI. At the altar of Saints John, Paul, and Laurence

May John, Paul together, and Laurence

preserve this altar, by God’s mercy.

This one was a deacon, while those two, having shed their blood,

hold the blessed kingdoms: all through martyrdom [variant: *forti*, “bravely,” for *toti*, “all”].

### LVII. At the church of Saint Peter the Apostle

The heavenly key-bearer, who guards the kingdoms of heaven,

being powerful to loose whatever he wishes and to bind,

once a fisherman, now the gracious doorkeeper of heaven,

prince of the Church and himself a good shepherd—

to whom Christ entrusted his own flock to guard

when he returned to the blessed kingdoms of his Father.

O exceedingly happy man, whom the whole world loves!

Christ gave him the name Peter.

May he, in his kindness, surround this temple on every side,

and protect and govern it by his coming.

May he, its protector, bring assistance to his servants

and be present everywhere to their prayers.

Radon had also renewed this place, destroyed by flames;

I pray that Peter himself may repay him with a reward.

[Note: See poem 41 above.]

### LVIII. At the altar of the same Saint Peter

The Church’s prince, himself wholly God’s,

the temple’s savior, will also protect this altar.

May he aid those here who offer vows to Christ God,

so that we may always rejoice in his merits.

### LIX. At the altar of Saint Paul the Apostle

This altar here is indeed consecrated in Paul’s name,

who led the peoples of the world to the stars of heaven.

Chosen by the Lord, he was everywhere a teacher

to nations and peoples, kingdoms and cities.

### LX. At the altar of Saint Andrew the Apostle

The apostolic teacher—whom this gracious voice, John,

had sent to Christ, saying, “Behold, the Lamb of God,

coming from the Father’s heavenly court, so that he might always follow him”—

Andrew: may he guard his altar from the enemy.

[Note: Perhaps *Joannis*, “of John.”]

### LXI. At the altar of Saint John the Baptist

This altar is held by Saint John the Baptist,

Christ’s Forerunner, great throughout the world and belonging to God.

He alone pointed out Christ’s presence with his finger.

May he, I pray, aid our prayers through his own.

### LXII. At the altar of Saint Germanus

A great altar has been dedicated to Bishop Germanus,

which you now see, joyful traveler!

[Note: Perhaps *haec*, “this,” should be supplied.]

### LXIII. At the altar of Saint Amandus

May Amandus, the illustrious lover of Christ,

always defend this altar from the enemy through his merits.

### LXIV. At the altar of Saint Quintinus and Saint Michael the Archangel

This altar of the excellent martyr Quintinus

shines with triumphs; here he brings aid to the people.

Among wing-bearing companions and supreme ministers,

Michael, the prince, first in heaven’s citadel,

may preserve these places with the great piety of the Thunderer,

and, coming, may himself ask pardon for himself.

### LXV. To Saint Genevieve

Consecrated virgin, illustrious for heavenly gifts,

may Genevieve here rejoice in your vows.

## III. In a Certain Monastery, Perhaps at Tours

### LXVI. On the school and the students

Here let the boys learn from the mouth of their elder teacher

so that they may be able to resound hymnic praises.

Let the tender mouth devoutly draw up the waters of salvation,

lest the elder be silent in the church.

The years of youth are suited to learning anything;

the practice of the ancient Church requires it.

Let the teacher instruct the boys in their studies while the time is favorable,

for the years flee like flowing water.

An aged oak in the woods is scarcely ever bent

[Note: [Col. 0744D] Perhaps *annosa in sylvis*, “an aged [oak] in the woods.”]

but the powerful hand of a mighty man breaks it.

[Note: [Col. 0744D] The following passage is corrupt.]

Nor will an old man, accustomed to many plunderings,

ever submit his strong neck beneath the yoke.

For an old man will not be able to learn well,

when his white beard falls into the lap of the man cutting [his hair].

[Manuscript variant: “nor will he be able to learn after the white beard falls into the lap of the shearer.”]

Be pious, and be a teacher devoted to the boys;

boys, always love your fathers.

May the Father’s sweet blessing remain with us,

and may it not be [corrupt text: “lest, since born, he holds two in mind”].

### LXVII. At the library of those writing books

Here let those who write the words of the sacred law sit,

and also the consecrated sayings of the holy Fathers.

Let them beware of inserting their own trivialities among these words,

and let the hand itself not wander through frivolity [perhaps *properans*, “hastening,” rather than *propter*, “because of”].

Let them diligently seek corrected books for themselves,

so that the flying pen may travel along the straight path.

Let them distinguish their proper senses by cola and commas,

and place the points, each in its proper order.

Lest the reader in the Church either read something false

or suddenly fall silent before the pious brothers.

It is an excellent work to write sacred books,

and the scribe himself does not lack his reward.

It is better to write books than to dig vines:

the one serves his belly, the other his soul.

Anyone who reads can bring forth many new or old things—

sacred sayings of the Fathers.

### LXVIII. The raising of the mind from earthly palaces to the heavenly dwelling

Whoever, reading these verses, runs through the lofty palaces,

always keep the name of God in your mouth.

And while your tongue resounds with pious praises in song,

let your breast burn with love for him.

While you climb the beautiful floors of the house with your feet,

do not forget to climb heaven in your mind.

The radiant sun brightens the lofty houses with its rays;

Christ, with perpetual light, shines in heaven’s citadel.

As the sun, wholly resplendent, illuminates the world,

so the saints always shine in the Father’s citadel.

The lofty houses are called *solaria* from the sun;

likewise, we have a holy name from Christ.

If you delight in a dwelling made by hands,

seek all the more for yourself a house not made by hands.

Whatever the hand of man has ever built in the city—

all things perish and fall into ashes.

Whatever honor the saints possess amid the joys of heaven,

they can always possess together with Christ.

Wherever love leads, seizes, and draws you at every hour,

carry me away with you also, I beg, through your prayers.

May Christ be protector, ruler, light, way, life, and salvation

for you and for me as we hasten there.

### LXIX. At the dormitory

[Note: I wish to note beforehand that the following two poems have been corrected from the manuscript of Salzburg and that their titles have been added.]

May he who restrains the force of winds and calms the waves of the sea,

who preserves Israel and never sleeps through any age,

grant sweet rest to the brothers in this hall,

and may the merciful, powerful hand of the Lord restrain

the black force that sends fears into those whom it casts into sleep.

He who appointed labor for man by day in the light,

and granted rest at night to the weary body,

will also make the healthy rise to his praise.

### LXX. At the latrine

Reader, recognize the gluttony of the devouring belly,

you who smell its putrid excrement with your nose.

Flee the belly’s greed; therefore let your life be sober

at a fixed time and in your mouth.

[Manuscript: *luxorium*, “luxury-house,” rather than *luxuriam*, “gluttony.”]

### LXXI. Admonition to the religious young men to shake off sleep

It is indeed a marvelous thing, which the poet wishes to tell you:

the Lethean branch struck the temples of the young men,

so that, as a guest, it might open when the temple’s door was closed.

Everyone can see this better with blind sight,

and utter words better with the senses asleep,

since it can fashion various unknown shapes.

He is seen and heard, although he had existed at no time:

young man, beware of him throughout the night with your whole heart.

He overthrows the senses and closes both eyes

[Note: [Col. 0746D] Thus I read *binos* (“two”), in place of *bonos* (“good”).]

lest you see the splendid lights of the starry heaven.

Or lest your ear now drink in the teacher’s voice,

or your foot run to the church during the night.

Strike his head, I beg, with a powerful fist,

lest, while you are seeing, the guest blind your eyes,

or evil torpor overthrow all your senses.

But pour into your sight the eye-salve of salvation,

so that you may be able to hear the voice of the ringing bell,

which surely calls you to sing the praises of the Thunderer.

Join your hands; remember to sleep only a little,

and do not let sudden, overwhelming need come upon you,

as Solomon advises readers in his excellent saying.

[Note: The manuscript reads “strike him.”]

### LXXII. On the way to the choir

I beg you, do not let the brothers’ path seem hard to you;

it leads you, as you hasten, to the church.

Let no crowd of people sound [manuscript: *sonet*, “may sound”] here, no tumult either;

let no outsider walk among you here.

May this way lead you all together with harmonious hearts,

intent upon praises, to the holy praise of God [manuscript: *ad pia templa*, “to the holy shrines”].

Let one love—Christ—and one path be ours;

he is certain salvation, hope, honor, and charity.

Do not go through it drowsy with torpor,

but let the gracious praise of God always sound in your mouth,

so that an angel may run with you from the heavenly citadel

when he sees you resounding with God’s praises.

May he also join you to the saints’ joyful heart,

as you rejoice with Christ’s assembly in the church,

where many relics of theirs are buried,

a holy gift surpassing a thousand talents.

Therefore hope and faith together were likewise

a sure means of salvation with you in these porticoes.

For every footprint you place while running with your feet,

you are able, brother, to possess the whole reward [manuscript: *tot tu mercedes*, “so many rewards”].

Therefore do not think this path long:

through it the passable gate of heaven lies open.

For blessed is the day on which it receives you;

there, together with Christ, you will hold blessed kingdoms.

Run, young men, hastening into Christ’s palace;

run, young men, to Christ’s praise.

With one mind together praise the heavenly King,

and always love God with one mind together.

If you cannot run with your feet, elder, I beg you, run in your heart;

climb heaven in your mind if you cannot do so with your feet.

### LXXIII. Exhortation to praise God

With your thumb, brother, shake off sleep from your sluggish eyes,

and strive first to enter beneath God’s roof [manuscript: *tecta*, “roofs,” for *mente*, “in mind”].

Enter the temple first, but leave later;

may Christ’s love lead you and bring you back.

Remember to praise the Lord seven times a day,

as the Psalmist sings from David’s mouth concerning God.

## IV. In a Certain Monastery, Perhaps at Nobiliacum

### LXXIV. To the church of Saints Lambert and Cecilia in the monastery of Nobiliacum

The excellent martyr, bishop, and faithful servant of Christ,

the holy Lambert, possesses these illustrious places.

The virgin Cecilia is joined equally to this Father,

powerful in virginity and likewise in martyrdom.

For he had been a great shepherd of the Church,

while she was the everlasting bride of Christ the King.

The humble abbot Ato had built this church;

may Christ grant him gifts in heaven’s citadel.

[Note: Ato was abbot and restorer of the monastery of Nobiliacum among the Pictones in the year 793. On him, see Mabillon, vol. II of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 307.]

### LXXV. At the altar of Saints Quintinus and Denis the Martyrs

May the martyr Quintinus and Father Denis

always preserve this altar from the enemy through their prayers,

both teachers of life through their living merits,

who, through rosy blood, possess the blessed kingdoms.

### LXXVI. At the altar of Saints Philibert and Agatha

The excellent Father Philibert shall possess this altar,

who built many holy places for God.

The most renowned martyr Agatha is also joined to him,

the virgin who came into heaven’s bridal chamber through blood.

[Note: Philibert was abbot of Jumièges in the seventh century. He built the monasteries of Jumièges—Saint Mary’s, or Saint Peter’s—in the diocese of Rouen, and of Her, or Noirmoutier, among the Pictones.]

### LXXVII. At the altar of Saint Michael the Archangel

May the great archangel Michael from heaven’s citadel

always preserve this church from the enemy through holy prayers.

Whoever you are who read these verses, remember to pray for him,

so that, for brief labor, he may receive long rewards.

### LXXVIII. At the altar of Saints Sulpicius and Columba

May Sulpicius, bishop, shepherd, and faithful patriarch,

bring us holy aid here.

And may the illustrious virgin Columba, likewise through martyrdom,

defend the sacred dwelling dedicated to God by her prayers.

### LXXIX. At the altar of Saints Amandus and Agatha

Behold, your honor, Bishop Amandus, is now worshiped on this altar;

help us, Father.

The virgin Agatha, consecrated to God, is also venerated;

may she defend the sacred dwelling through her prayers.

### LXXX. Desire to dwell in the house of God

How beloved your temples are to me, O God of hosts,

Lord of powers, my King and my God!

You, gracious Father, my heart seeks; my flesh seeks you everywhere;

you, living God, are my great joys.

Those who dwell in your houses are exceedingly blessed,

and they resound with perpetual praises to you.

Grant me a home here, I beg, most merciful shepherd,

so that here I may sing your praises without end.

### LXXXI. At the oratory of Saint Laurence the Martyr

May Laurence, God’s illustrious deacon,

adorn this house through his merits, now full of love for the Lord;

he whom neither devouring flame nor chains nor iron conquered,

and who, through swords and fires, ascended into the heights of heaven.

Behold, he always performs intercession for God’s servants,

and, we believe, aids his own worshipers from there.

### LXXXII. At the church of Saints Eligius the Bishop and Leonius

Here also rest the bodies of two holy Fathers:

Elidius, bishop, the glory of the people of Pictavium,

and the enclosed Father Leonius, rich in merits.

The brother Arnulfus had renovated this church;

may Christ grant him rewards through the ages of salvation.

### LXXXIII. At the church consecrated to Saint Peter the Apostle

May Peter, the pious apostolic prince, aid us here,

in whose sacred honor these buildings stand dedicated.

May he, as shepherd, preserve the flock entrusted to him,

protect and govern it with heavenly gifts,

and open for us the everlasting gates of Olympus.

### LXXXIV. At the guesthouse

May this place freely lie open to guests who come [perhaps *venientibus*, “to those arriving”],

for Christ will always be received in the guest.

May the joyful servant be ready to serve the weary traveler,

and may he rejoice to wash the feet of pilgrims.

Christ, lover of compassion, gave these examples:

he first washed the feet of his disciples.

By doing this, may the brother hope that great rewards

will be granted to him in heaven, as he follows Christ’s commands.

Always love God, brothers, and love one another;

the true lover of his brother is the one who loves God.

### LXXXV. At the oratory of Saints Martin and Gelasius

The illustrious pontiff, the renowned priest throughout the world,

Martin, greatest author through his merits of virtue,

may this patron defend the sacred dwelling dedicated to him.

May he aid our prayers in his love of compassion,

so that almighty God may fulfill the vows of his servants

and increase them with heavenly gifts.

May that excellent King be kind and merciful to us.

Here also now rests the gracious bishop Gelasius,

a renowned father in the present city and an honorable teacher,

outstanding in merits and vigorous in speech that brings salvation.

For Gundun had already restored this hall,

moved by love for the Fathers;

may Christ grant him rewards,

gentle, in the blessed seat of heaven forever.

[Note: *Gundun*. See poem 101 below. The edition has it corruptly as *Gununmepribus*.]

### LXXXVI. At the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Nobiliacum

These places which you see, reader, belonging to the parts of the venerable church,

were once a church.

But the suppliant Father and shepherd Ato raised up these structures,

because he loved them exceedingly with an earthly love.

Virgin Mary, Mother of God, your untouched one of the Thunderer,

you, Queen of heaven, greatest hope of our life:

may worship and memorable honor be rendered to you here.

And may you, in your accustomed compassion, look upon those who pray.

Here, most gentle Virgin, be graciously present always

to our prayers for the servants and handmaids of God.

And always rule our days everywhere by your prayers,

so that the gracious grace of Jesus Christ may preserve us.

[Note: Ato; see poem 74 above. Mabillon likewise thinks this poem can be explained as referring to the Nobiliacum basilica, once distinguished by the title of the Most Blessed Virgin Mother of God, as is clear from various charters in which it is called the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Junianus, although now it commonly retains only the name of Saint Junianus. See further Mabillon in the cited place.]

### LXXXVII. At the refectory

Christ God, bless the meals of our table,

and whatever gifts you, most merciful, have given to your servants,

may they indeed be blessed through you. You are the gracious giver;

you had given us everything; whatever we have now

is truly your good, because you, being good, create all things.

You also, diners, I beg you, speak praises to Christ;

let words of peace and salvation always sound in your mouths.

Christ always loves peace, who himself had said:

“I give you peace, and I leave you peace.”

May our hand also always be most generous to the wretched;

whatever you give to the poor, Christ receives,

and he does not delay in repaying you with a great reward.

### LXXXVIII. At the dormitory

[Note: [Col. 0749D] In the manuscript the heading is: “At the heated room where the abbot sleeps.”]

You had given rest to the night [manuscript: *ad requiem noctem*, “for the night’s rest”] and light to labor,

preserving your servants prosperously through nights and days.

May the heart remain awake toward you if sleep closes the eyes;

may labor and rest praise you at every hour.

### LXXXIX. At the hypocaust

A cold winter traveler [manuscript: *frigidus e verno*, “cold from spring”] coming from the mountain,

I beg you, do not disdain [manuscript: *despiciat*, “look down upon”] my hospitable roof.

If, rainy traveler, you desire my gifts,

behold, give yours first; thus take mine for yourself.

### XC. At the dining hall

This is a holy house, a place of peace, a hall of salvation;

may Christ’s blessing always remain above it.

In it may the generous one multiply [edition: *multiplici et*] the banquets of the brothers—

he who once, rich in heavenly generosity,

satisfied five thousand people with five loaves.

### XCI. At the altar of Saints Cosmas and Damian

Here the two brothers Cosmas and Damian

are joined on the altar, in equal honor.

One mother bore them on earth from a single womb;

as equal brothers, she bore them to martyrdom and heaven.

### XCII. At the tombs of Saint John the Bishop and Abbot Aper

[Note: Mabillon gave this poem in corrected form in book XXVI of vol. II of the *Annals*, p. 307. According to the same interpreter, it is an epitaph of John, bishop of Pictavium, and Aper, abbot. Because their tombs were being trampled by passersby, Ato, successor of Aper in office and restorer of the monastery of Nobiliacum, enclosed them with a wall, placing a cross together with an altar on which a sacred victim might be offered to God for the dead Fathers. This is an excellent testimony in favor of the Catholic doctrine of sacrifice for the dead.]

Here rests the illustrious bishop of this city,

John by name, a pious and good man.

Here rests Aper, the venerable abbot of this church,

a shepherd ready for every good work.

But the tombs had been trampled by the feet of the people,

and no wall enclosed them as befitted the Fathers.

Ato, the successor in Aper’s office, does not tolerate this:

that the sacred bodies of the Fathers should be trampled by feet.

Therefore he decided to surround the monuments with a short wall,

lest the tombs remain accessible to the people’s feet.

He immediately added the holy signs of our salvation,

the sign in which the Savior returns victorious from the enemy.

Moreover, he established a venerable altar for Christ,

on which a sacred victim might be offered for the Fathers,

so that almighty God might grant them rest

together with the saints, forever in heaven’s citadel.

### XCIII. At the altar of Saints Gervasius and Protasius the Martyrs

The martyr Gervasius and the gracious Protasius,

these two brothers, are likewise venerated on this altar.

One day carried them from earth, and one day likewise to heaven;

they were alike in martyrdom and alike in the fervor of faith.

### XCIV. At the gate of the Nobiliacum basilica

[Note: On the various restoration of the monastery of Nobiliacum carried out by Abbot Ato in the year 793, see poems 74, 86, and 92 above.]

This is the gate of the Lord’s house and the royal gate of heaven;

it opens for you the way and the shrines of the holy temple,

where you will soon find the great Fathers resting.

May the splendid hope of salvation through their prayers be yours,

if, with pious heart and prostrate body, you ask,

sinner, Christ for forgiveness of your sins.

Enter without hesitation upon the thresholds of the sacred temple;

Christ’s gracious grace provides everything for the believer.

A pious abbot, servant of the altar, made these doors,

as Ato, the venerable abbot of the brothers, had commanded.

As you enter the temple, traveler, intercede for him,

so that almighty God may preserve him everywhere.

### XCV. At the oratory of Saint Andrew the Apostle

Andrew, Christ’s true disciple and first follower,

may he govern this sacred dwelling dedicated to him.

May the inhabitant of Olympus bring us aid,

so that our tears may reach Christ.

May Christ from his heavenly citadel, being gracious,

deign always to hear his servants.

### XCVI. Epitaph of Fortunatus, the Christian poet

In this present hall also rests the bishop Fortunatus,

a man who was the Church’s glory,

who composed very many poems of the saints in meter,

celebrating the saints with hymnic praises.

He was polished in speech and faithful in understanding,

ardent in talent and ready in his utterance.

### XCVII. At the altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr

Here the noble Stephen, the protomartyr, is honored on the altar,

forcing heaven while he first seeks the stars.

From earth to heaven, a ladder made of a hailstorm of stones

was this for him, so that he might behold Christ in heaven’s citadel.

### XCVIII. At the altar of Saint John the Evangelist

John holds this altar on Christ’s left,

he who reclines above upon the holy breast at the supper.

He who drank the secrets of heaven from the sacred fountain—

may he protect this whole house through his prayers.

### XCIX. At the altar of the holy virgin martyrs

This altar is dedicated to the sacred virgins,

whose bodies were temples of God.

They will possess heaven’s kingdoms through rosy blood

and wage strong battles in fragile sex.

### C. At the altar of the holy martyrs

This present altar shines dedicated

to all the martyrs who conquered the world through triumphs.

Through swords, fires, tortures, and scourges,

with fearless minds they seek the blessed kingdoms.

### CI. Epitaph of the priest Gunvinus

The priest Gunvinus renovated these ruined temples,

moved by great love of God.

A cultivator of justice, a lover of a better life,

prudent in talent, cautious in speech—

may Christ, who gives rewards, repay his love forever.

His body rests here in this tomb.

[Note: Gunvinus—whether he is the same man who above, in poem 85, is called Gundun, we know nothing about either of them. The manuscript has *Gunduinus*.]

## V. In the Monastery of Fleury

Corrected from the manuscript of Salzburg.

### CII. On Abbot Magnulf

[Note: Mabillon, vol. II of the *Annals*, p. 243, understands this poem and the following one, now published in more corrected form from the Salzburg manuscript, as referring to Magulf, or, as he is otherwise called, Magnulf, abbot of Fleury. He is praised here for building a chamber for the use of the reading brothers, with an oratory attached in which he could devote himself privately to prayer.]

The humble abbot Magnulf [Salzburg manuscript: *Magulf*] had built this chamber,

so that it might become a sweet dwelling for the holy Fathers,

whom Christ might grant to serve Benedict forever [edition: *duret benedictio*, “may the blessing endure”],

so that this place might now [variant: *jamque*, “and now”] be suitable for readers.

He foresaw that shining light would radiate into it,

and that a house of prayer would be made very near to Christ,

in which, alone and in private,

he could lie before the altar and pour out sweet tears.

Now [perhaps *tunc*, “then”], holy shepherd of this flock, I beg you,

that, among the words of those praying in remembrance [edition: *ut quae*, “that which”],

you commend the soul of Magnulf especially [*maxime*] to Christ.

[He] had built such a dwelling for you to inhabit

[Edition: “which he had built for habitation”].

You too, live happily for God through long ages;

correct the life of the brothers according to the rule,

so that Christ, enthroned on high, may grant you gracious rewards

together with the holy Father Benedict forever.

[Note: The phrase “you, shepherd of this flock” led the learned Mabillon to think that Magnulf was still alive when Alcuin composed these poems. But it is perfectly clear from this passage that Alcuin is exhorting a successor of Magnulf to remember him in his prayers. Therefore Alcuin composed this and the following poem after Magnulf’s death, which occurred in 794. They were addressed either to Fultrad, who governed the abbacy for only a year and a half, or to Theodulf, then also bishop of Orléans. See Mabillon in the cited work, p. 314.]

### CIII. On the same Abbot Magnulf

The venerable abbot Magnulf had purchased this table—

[In the Salzburg manuscript, *mansam* occurs instead of *mensam*; perhaps “this estate” should be read.]

and, having purchased it, he handed it over to Father Benedict,

so that it might be a reward for the purchaser with the Father forever.

Nevertheless, he had ordered this church to be consecrated

to Peter, the great prince who holds the keys of heaven,

and likewise in the name of the pious Father Benedict,

so that by their prayers they might govern its life through the ages

and both might ask [edition: *cogitassent*, “might have thought,” for *rogitassent*, “might ask”] for everlasting rest for its soul.

[Note: “Wicked death snatched away the Father.” From this passage Meurisse’s chronology is refuted: he extended Angilramnus’s episcopate and life to the year 808, long after the death of Alcuin, the author of this epitaph.]

You also, whoever recite the inscription, remember to pray—

I beg [Salzburg manuscript: *obsecra*, “pray,” for *obsecro*, “I beg”] you, friendly reader—for Father Magnulf.

May Christ’s mercy also always preserve you.

May Christ mercifully protect and govern these places.

May praise, honor, and power always be here and there.

[Salzburg manuscript: *et cultus*, “and worship,” instead of *et virtus*, “and power.”]

## VI. In the Monastery of Saint Nabor

### CIV. On the tomb of Saint Nabor, begun to be adorned by Bishop Angilramnus and completed by Abbot Vasco

The pontifical summit, shepherd, patriarch, and priest,

Angilramnus, rejoicing and relying upon piety as his guide,

moved by love of the excellent martyr Nabor,

had begun, with attention, to clothe the sacred [perhaps *sacrum*] tomb,

with gifts, aided by the pious King Charles.

But wicked death seized the Father before he completed the work.

Afterward the humble deacon Vasco [the text has *vas*; note: “read *Vasco*”] completed it.

You who read both verses, commend them to Christ,

so that whoever comes here to fulfill his vows

may remember the disciple together with the Father in kindly words.

The former begins it, but this latter has completed it.

It is one work belonging to both: may Christ preserve them both.

And you, holy martyr of God, unconquered in triumphs,

aid your servants, excellent shepherd and Father.

[Note: Angilramnus was bishop of Metz. He died in the year 791 and was buried in the monastery of Saint Nabor, otherwise called Nova-Cella.]

### CV. A poem added to the preceding one, addressed to Vasco

Vasco, I sent you twice seven verses,

because you sent two pairs of *butristae* as well.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] Perhaps one should read *buttistas*: the word seems to mean wine-vessels holding seven cups, or seven fixed measures, each; see Watcher’s Glossary under *Butte*, and Du Cange under *Butro* and *Butristas*.]

Perhaps twice seven cups [the text has *caliges*; perhaps *calices*], already holding their measure,

and through the poems may you have twice seven thanks.

But I beg you, remember us in your prayers, and our parents also,

whose written names you see here in this seat.

May you flourish forever in eternity … [lacuna] poems, vessels. [Note: [Col. 0753D] Perhaps “Vasco.”]

[Col. 0754A] Fel [Note: [Col. 0754C] The passage is corrupt.] has come to Flaccus; may the mouth of Maro bless me,

Today, if it pleases you, Virgilian boy.

## VII. IN THE CORMARICAN MONASTERY

### CVI. [Note: [Col. 0754C] We follow the illustrious Mabillon, who likewise thinks that this epigram should be understood as referring to the cell at Cormaric, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 176.] On the excellence of the Cormarican cell in comparison with great cities

The distinguished cities, whose new summits rise

And whose renowned praises fly above the stars,

Which the books of ancient prophets celebrate in song,

Do not number their manifold riches of gold.

Yet this little rural cell, which you see,

Built beneath a woodland roof in the wilderness,

Is nobler.

[216] It flourishes in sacred studies and reads through

The wise [Note: [Col. 0754D] The edition has *esophica*; Mabillon, *theosophica*.] laws,

And examines in secret the sayings of the elders.

There the merchant and the elders roll out a thousand lies,

So that by evil fraud he may ensnare his companion:

Here the sacred truth is sought through syllogistic [Note: [Col. 0754D] The edition has *Singulogistica*.] reasoning,

Within cloisters, by varied methods and peaceful speech.

There, drunkenness too often destroys the mind;

And the master is scarcely carried by the servant’s hands.

Here evening [Note: [Col. 0754D] Perhaps *vesper*, “evening.”] beholds the long fasts of those who read,

And soberly feed their hearts with sacred banquets.

To you, Christ, most gentle, may our prayers come;

To us, Christ, may your grace come. [Note: [Col. 0754D] Here I judged that poem 198 in Quercetanus’s edition should be broken off, since what follows does not at all cohere with what precedes, and the customary closing formula of the poem appears here. The poem appended there is an enigma about a furnace; see below among the other riddles, nos. 221 and 222.]

## VIII. IN A CERTAIN MONASTERY OVER WHICH ALCUIN PRESIDED

### CVII. [Note: [Col. 0754D] This is the title of the poem in the Salzburg manuscript, which we used. The following two poems lack titles in the same manuscript, but are separated from the preceding poem; in Quercetanus’s edition they run together as no. 203.] Where the books are kept

Little roofs contain the heavenly gifts of wisdom,

Which you, rejoicing reader, learn with a devout heart.

Wisdom is better than all the gifts of every treasure;

The one who follows it will have the path of light.

### CVIII. To the bell

May this little bell always and forever produce only

Poems; but may the good cooks’ bell resound for us.

### CIX. To the place from which the reading is given at table

From the lofty seat let good reading resound for the brothers [Note: [Col. 0754D] The manuscript has *sacra*, “sacred”],

Always exhorting their minds to meditate on things above.

While the hungry body is fed with food,

Let the devout mind be fed with heavenly words.

And may full praise of God be sung throughout the hall [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has *cantetur*, “be sung.”],

Which provides dishes filled with food for his servants [Note: [Col. 0755D] The manuscript has *qui*, “who.”].

And likewise has fed the mind with heavenly bread.

### CX. [Note: [Col. 0755D] This is how the poem is titled in the Salzburg manuscript.] At table

May devout Christ bless our dishes in the hall,

And graciously multiply his gifts for his servants [Note: [Col. 0755D] Thus the poem ends in the same manuscript; in Quercetanus’s edition it continues.].

He who sent manna to the heavenly people in the rain,

And likewise poured rivers from the rocks for the thirsty,

Who satisfied five thousand with five loaves,

Who changed water into wine of wondrous flavor—

May he, in his mercy, bless us and our dishes together,

[Col. 0755B] And preserve his servants in tranquil peace,

And make them stand healthy in his praises.

Brothers, always love peaceful ways,

For the King of heaven himself always loves peace.

Behold, the lovers of peace are born of the Thunderer.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] What follows seems to belong not to the table, but to the place where the brothers customarily went to choir, to conversations, and to school.]

Here likewise let the brothers of the Lord enter with praises,

Whose praise and glory to Christ always sound from their mouths.

This is the sacred way; this path is open to the brothers’ feet.

Let only the joyful friend pass over it with his feet.

Let no stranger tread it with wicked feet—

No thief, no liar, no one of malicious mind—

But let fraternal love accompany those who go together.

And let peace, faith, piety, and sacred concord,

Together with divine praise, always resound in the mouth.

Run, young men of Christ, quickly to the hall,

[Col. 0755C] And with attentive minds hear the heavenly voices.

Let the deceptive sweetness of amusements not deceive you,

Nor carnal love, games, wantonness, or laughter.

While the body is vigorous and strong with its warm blood,

Learn sacred wisdom in the flowering season of life,

For time always flees like flowing water.

### CXI. To the altar of Saint John the Baptist

The great Baptist John, the Lord’s forerunner,

Adorns this holy hall with sublime merits.

He was the venerable herald of human salvation;

Here may he bring us aid through heavenly power.

### CXII. To the altar of Saint Salvius the martyr

Here Salvius, a bishop honored for his merits and a martyr,

Is remembered at the altar by sacred vows.

### CXIII. To the altar of Saint Bavo

May the venerable priest Bavo sanctify these places,

A disciple worthy in life of Father Amandus.

### CXIV. To the church of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr [Note: [Col. 0756D] We have likewise compared this and the following poem with the Salzburg manuscript.]

[Col. 0756A]

In this hall the great protomartyr Stephen is honored,

A man distinguished in merits and renowned in name.

Among the stones he saw Christ in the citadel,

Standing at God’s right hand above the lofty summits

Of heaven, and bearing great aid through his martyrdom.

In his devout honor Ambrosius built this church,

So that by his gracious prayers he might merit pardon [Note: [Col. 0756D] The Salzburg manuscript has *meretur*, “he merits.”].

Therefore, whoever reads this inscription, remember to pray

That Christ preserve his servant forever.

### CXV. To the altar of Saint Peter the apostle

King Charles, devoted to Christ with great love,

[Col. 0756B] Ordered this altar to be clothed with sacred metals,

For the glory of the Church and his own salvation.

Peter, first prince in the apostolic company,

May govern this altar and likewise protect this temple;

May he also aid the prayers of his servants.

This work was completed at the king’s command

By Hildibaldus [Note: [Col. 0756D] Hildibaldus: Hildebaldus or Hildeboldus, archbishop of Cologne and chief chaplain of the palace; he died in 819.], the rejoicing bishop in the city of Agrippina.

[217] Here, Fathers, offer pious gifts to Christ for the king,

That heavenly grace may always preserve him.

This gracious house has been strengthened by gifts from above.

May the Almighty govern it together with the great prince Peter.

May certain salvation, hope of pardon, and the gate of life be yours,

Whoever with a devout heart pours out tears in this hall.

### CXVI. To the repository of the holy relics

[Col. 0756C]

This little house, reader, which you see prepared,

Is known to have been established for the sacred relics,

So that this clean place might contain holy intercession.

Albinus the poet ordered this roof to be prepared,

So that a servant of Christ might come and pray here;

Therefore, whoever sees the inscription, remember to pray for him.

### CXVII. On the chastisement of the peasants

The unhappy rural crowd had come in fear,

Whom the unloved Amandus oppresses among the workmen [Note: [Col. 0756D] The meaning is obscure.].

What are the wretches to do? Let their backs be broken by whips.

Let the peasants’ property alone remain safe.

### CXVIII. On the sacred buildings restored by Alcuin

[Col. 0756D]

Albinus the poet came from a foreign land,

Whom illustrious Britain sent to these lands.

Charles, the renowned king of this world, received him,

Both because of his love of sacred wisdom and because of affection.

He ordered the long-ruined vaulted roofs,

[Col. 0757A] As you see, reader, to be entirely renewed throughout the hall [Note: [Col. 0757D] Mabillon understands this as referring to the vaulted chapels of the basilica of Tours, *Annals*, vol. II, book XXVII, p. 361.].

Here he established places most suitable for the sacred relics,

So that the saints’ resting place might receive its proper honors,

As befits the veneration on earth of the holy ones,

Whom God wished to reign forever in heaven.

## IX. IN THE MONASTERIES OF SAINT PETER AT SALZBURG AND SAINT AMANDUS AT ELNO

### CXIX. [Note: [Col. 0757D] In Quercetanus’s edition this poem is joined to the following one; we separated it because of the difference in subject matter, following the Salzburg manuscript, which does not contain these verses.] On the twofold road to the school and the tavern

Here, traveler, stop as you go along the road,

And read these few verses with an eager mind.

The road you see is divided into two honorable paths:

One leads to the tavern for the one who wishes to drink [Note: [Col. 0757D] The edition has *portare*, “to carry.” A second verse about the road to the school seems to be missing.].

Choose now, traveler, whichever path pleases you:

Either drink with me, or learn the sacred books.

If you wish to drink, you will have to pay money;

But if you desire to learn, you will have what you seek for free.

### CXX. [Note: [Col. 0757D] This poem and the following ten occur in the Salzburg manuscript, from which we have corrected them in some places and supplied titles for each.] To the church of Saint Peter

The heavenly key-bearer, who opens the gates of Olympus,

Peter, foremost prince in the apostolic company [Note: [Col. 0757D] The edition has *maxime*, “greatest.”],

May he protect this hall forever, by Christ’s gift,

Which the excellent Father Hrodbertus [Note: [Col. 0757D] Hrodbertus: namely, Saint Rupert, the first bishop of Salzburg and founder of the monastery of Saint Peter there.] once built,

So that praise and glory might always be given there to the Most High,

Where the brothers gather seven times each day

To sing praises to Christ together, with devout hearts.

You all, when the signals sound, hasten together [Note: [Col. 0758D] The manuscript has *prumptim*, “promptly,”],

Come with bowed heads and devout minds.

For the angelic host watches you in the hall,

[Col. 0757C] And God brings aid to the one who prays with a humble heart [Note: [Col. 0758D] The manuscript has *humilis est*, “is humble.”].

Therefore pour out bitter tears before God’s altar,

Together with sweet-sounding praise to the Thunderer,

That he may preserve you all through paternal love.

### CXXI. To the altar of the blessed Virgin Mary

By your prayers aid the servants of the eternal King,

Holy Virgin Mary, Queen of heaven.

Since this altar is dedicated in your name,

Drive away sorrows and grant us prosperity [Note: [Col. 0758D] The edition has *donis*, “with gifts.”].

### CXXII. To Saint Andrew

May Andrew, Christ’s servant, defend this altar from the enemy

By his merits—he who despised the nets of the world,

Following Christ with all his strength,

And, blessed, ascended from the sacred cross to Olympus [Note: [Col. 0758D] The edition has *concessit*, “granted.”].

### CXXIII. To Saint Paul

[Col. 0758A]

The renowned teacher throughout the world, Paul,

Counted among the apostolic order of teachers,

The chosen vessel of wisdom, the heavenly herald of salvation,

Who with rosy blood entered the citadel of heaven [Note: [Col. 0758D] The edition has *in arce*, “in the citadel.”],

Holds these holy places.

### CXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0758D] According to Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Benedictines*, fourth century, part I, p. 63, this poem is to be understood as referring to the oratory of Saint Peter at Elnon, which Arno restored and intended to be a *polyandrum*, that is, a cemetery, under the patronage of Saint Michael and Saint Amandus. See above, poem 29.] In the cemetery

This renowned house, once leveled to the ground, had fallen into disrepair.

The humble bishop Arno, devoted to Christ’s honor,

Could not endure this appearance; he began to restore

The fallen structure and rebuilt the entire house better,

Consecrating it to the greatest intercessors:

First in honor of the illustrious prince Michael,

Then under the name of Peter, prince of the Church;

And also of the illustrious prince of the brothers, Father Amandus;

For he wished it to be a holy cemetery for the brothers.

Dear brothers, rest here in God’s peace,

Until the devout angel cries from the heavenly citadel:

Rise now, brothers, promptly [Note: [Col. 0758D] The manuscript has *prumptim*, “promptly,”] from the dust of the earth;

The judge who comes from heaven’s summit calls you:

Take up your souls with your own merits;

Now stand before the great tribunal of God Christ,

That each may receive rewards worthy of his deeds.

And fear that day, I beg you, at every hour,

[218] You who read the verses of this work while you have time,

So that when that light comes, it may find you prepared [Note: [Col. 0758D] The edition has *pacatos*, “peaceful.”].

And, remembering me, I humbly ask you always to say with your mouth:

“Be gracious forever, Christ, to your servant” [Note: [Col. 0758D] The edition has “say perpetually.”].

I am called Alcuin [Note: [Col. 0758D] The manuscript has *Alchuine*.]; now farewell forever.

### CXXV. To Saint Mary

This house is regarded as a mother among other churches;

Therefore in it the Virgin, Mother of God and Christ,

Is honored with Christ. We ask that she always and everywhere

Preserve this flock from the enemy through her pious prayers.

### CXXVI. To Saint John the Baptist

May the powerful Baptist John hold this altar,

And the excellent martyr, the gracious Anastasius.

The confessor Maximilianus likewise shall possess it;

May Christ’s holy right hand protect us through the prayers of these men.

### CXXVII. To Saint Paul

[Col. 0758D]

Paul, teacher of the world, and Benedict are honored at this altar,

And Father Columba [Note: [Col. 0759D] In the Salzburg manuscript, with *Pater* omitted, the name is written *Columbanus*.] with great honor [Note: [Col. 0759D] The edition has *in ore*, “in the mouth.”].

May the piety of these men likewise aid us here through their prayers,

So that Christ may grant us the good gifts [Note: [Col. 0759D] The edition has *vera*, “true.”] of salvation.

### CXXVIII. To Saint Florian

Florianus, renowned for great triumphs in the world [Note: [Col. 0759D] Supplied from the Salzburg manuscript.],

And the boy Cyriacus, together with his own mother Julitta,

Are honored together in this hall of Christ.

May he be your petitioner for pardon, your certain hope of salvation.

### CXXIX. Also to Saint John the Baptist

The great Baptist John, the Lord’s forerunner,

And the devout bishop Martin likewise, are joined here

By their sacred names upon this altar.

Before their feet, traveler, pour out your tears [Note: [Col. 0759D] This is the end of the epigram in the Salzburg manuscript. The remaining verses, which are joined to it in the printed editions, are absent there and likewise belong to another subject, as follows.].

### CXXX. On Saint Vergilius, bishop of Salzburg

[Col. 0759B]

The renowned building which you see as you approach, reader, [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0760D] This seems to refer to the cathedral basilica at Salzburg erected by Vergilius, although he also built other churches on a splendid scale. See his epitaph in Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 527.]

Vergilius built, led by love of the Lord—

An excellent bishop in merits and gracious in character—

Whom his mother Ireland first brought forth,

Instructed, taught, nurtured, and [lacuna] loved.

But seeking foreign lands now for love of Christ,

He scorned the world’s delights and his beloved homeland.

Across sea and land he came to these regions,

Striving with all his strength to multiply his talent,

And to scatter among the peoples the seeds of doctrine and life.

A pious and prudent man, second to none in piety.

The greatest prince of the Church and key-bearer of the heavenly hall,

Christ entrusted his own lambs to him [Note: [Col. 0760D] Perhaps *cui*, “to whom.”].

[Col. 0759C] May Peter, together with the saints whose bodies rest here,

Graciously govern this place in the heavenly name;

May they protect Christ’s people here with friendly prayers,

And ask for us prosperous times in this present life,

As well as the joys of the eternal kingdom.

## OTHER INSCRIPTIONS OF SACRED PLACES

### CXXXI. To the altar of Saints Andrew, Laurence, and Hippolytus

The devout Andrew will protect this altar by his merits,

And likewise the victorious deacon Laurence, martyr of the fire;

Third is Hippolytus, who subdued his neck to the sword.

May their prayers grant us their aid [Note: [Col. 0760D] Perhaps, “I pray that they grant us their aid.”].

### CXXXII. To the altar of Saints Paul, Silvester, and Leo

May Paul adorn this altar with his living merits,

And likewise Silvester, the glory of the Roman people,

And Pope Leo, most dear, wise in eloquence [Note: [Col. 0760D] Perhaps *clarissimus*, “most illustrious.”];

May they favor us from the citadel of the heavenly kingdom.

### CXXXIII. To the altar of Saint James the apostle, etc.

[Col. 0760A]

James, the son of Zebedee, rejoices at this altar;

And Dionysius, together with his holy companions;

And Gregory, who had been a teacher for Rome throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0760D] Perhaps *urbe*, “city.”].

I beseech these Fathers to defend our life.

### CXXXIV. To the altar of the blessed Virgin and the other saints

Here is the devout Virgin Mary, Queen and Mother of God;

Here also the sacred virgin Agatha is honored with you;

Attend, with your magnificent name, to the prayers of those who pray.

And Petronilla, the illustrious daughter of Peter her father;

Sulpitius, the renowned bishop in the city of Bourges;

And you, Leutgarius, both martyr and priest;

And the excellent presbyter Gislarius—

May they always defend this urn through their present prayers.

### CXXXV. To the altar of Saints John the Evangelist, Jerome, and Maurice

This altar holds John, at Christ’s left hand,

The presbyter Jerome, most renowned teacher of the world,

And likewise that wonderful martyr Maurice.

I beg them to offer our vows here to the heavenly Thunderer.

### CXXXVI. To the altar of Saints Thomas the apostle, Anianus, and Athanasius

Here Thomas is honored, he who touched Christ’s wounds;

And Anianus, the devout bishop of the city of Orléans;

And the gracious Athanasius, likewise a soldier of the Church.

May they together protect Christ’s people from the enemy.

### CXXXVII. To the altar of Saints James, Germanus, and Vedastus

Here James, the brother of the Lord, is venerated at the altar,

As is the beloved bishop Germanus of Christ.

The third joined to them is the gracious bishop Vedastus.

May their intercession always aid us.

### CXXXVIII. To the altar of Saints Hrodherotus, Berto, and Ansfridus

This altar holds three supreme Fathers together,

Great in the weight of their merits:

Hrodherotus, renowned in name,

The distinguished bishop named Berto,

And Ansfridus, joined to these as the third gracious saint.

### CXXXIX. To the altar of Saints Philip, Marcellus, and Medard

May this altar hold Philip, Christ’s disciple,

And likewise the holy Marcellus and Medard,

Both distinguished bishops in holy virtues.

By their twofold aid may the gifts of salvation be ours here.

### CXL. To the altar of Saints Bartholomew, Gervasius, and Protasius

Bartholomew the apostle, who converted the dark Indians

To the light of faith, possesses this altar here.

Gervasius and likewise the gracious Protasius, brothers both in martyrdom and in parents [Note: [Col. 0761A] The transmitted text is syntactically obscure.].

### CXLI. To the altar of Saints Matthew, Cornelius, and Cyprian

Matthew, the evangelical writer, may preserve this altar;

Cornelius, bishop and martyr in the city of Rome;

And Cyprian, the glory of the Africans, himself also a martyr.

Brothers, pour out tears of hope before their feet.

### CXLII. To the altar of Saints Simon, Hilary, and Remedius

[Col. 0761B] Simon, the brother of James and an apostle, adorns this altar,

As does the gracious bishop Hilary, by his merits,

And likewise Remedius, the beloved teacher of the Franks.

May these men, through the help of their piety, offer us intercession.

### CXLIII. To the altar of Saints Thaddeus, Felix, and Samson

Thaddeus, distinguished [lacuna], teacher and minister;

And the presbyter Felix, rightly called by that name;

And Samson, the mighty glory of honorable faith—

May they protect this altar and these buildings together by their merits.

### CXLIV. To the altar of Saints Apollinaris, Gregory, and Pancratius

Those who conquered the battles of the world through the peace of the Thunderer,

Great martyrs, are joined at this table:

The teacher Apollinaris and the gracious martyr Gregory,

And the boy Pancratius of the Roman city [lacuna].

### CXLV. To the altar of Saint Patrick and other Scots

Patrick, Ciarán, the glory of the Scottish people,

And Columbanus, Congallus, and Adomnanus,

Illustrious Fathers, teachers of conduct and life—

May the piety of these men aid us all here through their prayers.

### CXLVI. To the altar of the holy virgins of Scotland

This altar here is dedicated to the sacred virgins,

Whose life was renowned throughout the cities of the Scots.

Holy Brigid, a woman faithful to Christ in this way as well—

May she provide us salvation through her holy intercession.

### CXLVII. To the altar of the holy cross

[Col. 0761D]

Look, reader, upon the devout signs of our salvation,

In the middle of the Church, a wondrous gift [lacuna];

For the life of the world, the Life of the world once hung;

For his servants the Lord dies—may he whom holy will made a servant

Always be with his servant through his blood.

Remember this when you see the cross standing in the light [Note: [Col. 0761D] The passage is corrupt.],

And at once pray happily before the face of God.

Prostrate your body upon the ground, but ascend to heaven in your heart,

And pour out hot tears for your sins;

[Col. 0762A] May you have the certain salvation of hope [Note: [Col. 0761D] Perhaps “the hope of salvation.”] through everlasting piety—

He who, with immaculate blood, redeems the whole world,

And who in his mercy forgives the sins of his servants.

Here too may we have great hope of sacred salvation,

For this altar shines with the apostolic company,

And likewise with the vigorous merits of holy Helena,

Who is said to have found the wondrous wood of the cross,

On which Christ, the honor, praise, and life of the world, hung,

While the Most High endured such things for us.

What, then, must we servants do for love of him,

Except now give ourselves wholly to him as well?

May that God be our love and our entire will [Note: [Col. 0761D] Perhaps *voluptas*, “delight.”];

Praise, honor, strength, drink, food—may Christ be everything.

### CXLVIII. To the church of Saints Martin, Brictius, and Christopher

[Col. 0762B] Martin, a bishop revered throughout the whole world,

Brictius, Christ’s devout servant and priest,

And Christopher, [lacuna], are honored as martyrs in this hall.

May they protect those entering the church from the enemy through their prayers.

### CXLIX. On the threshold of the church of the blessed Virgin, Saint Michael, and Saint Stephen

Here, weary traveler, stop first as you arrive,

And then adore the King of heaven, prostrate in body.

Seek the saints’ aid in prayer,

That they may receive you into the embrace of their goodness:

The merciful and holy Virgin, Mother of God, the gracious one;

Michael, who stands before God in heaven’s citadel;

The deacon Stephen, the great protomartyr in the world.

May they lead you to the threshold of the greater church,

[Col. 0762C] And carry your prayers with them; ask this always and everywhere;

May they guide you prosperously to the gates and bring you back prosperously.

And you, rejoicing traveler, remember to praise Christ,

That Christ may preserve you wherever you go.

### CL. To the church of Christ the Savior

Christ, the Savior of the world, is honored in this hall,

He who rules the sea, the earth, and the heavens by his command.

May he himself govern all the places of this monastery,

Protect, enlarge, and preserve them at every hour.

### CLI. [Note: [Col. 0762D] This poem was published among the poems of Walahfrid Strabo, like many other poems by Alcuin (Quercetanus, poem 2).] On the church and in praise of the blessed Virgin Mary
