This hall of the Lord is protected by Mary’s guardianship,

To whom the venerable roofs of the newly built church are consecrated,

And new banners rise in sacred triumphs.

[Col. 0762D] In this hall the honor of the holy Mother is celebrated,

She who gave birth to the true Light from the Father’s Light,

Whom the prophets proclaim as the Titan [sun] with holy breath.

Most powerful woman, sacred Virgin who gave birth,

Hear mercifully the vows of the peoples who pray,

Who moisten their withered faces with flowing showers,

And beat the earth with their knees bent:

While they earn pardon by pouring forth a fountain of tears,

And erase the sins of life with frequent prayers.

This Virgin, I say, pregnant with a heavenly pledge,

Brought forth from her womb the King who saves the ages,

Who alone governs the empire of the world by right,

[Col. 0763A] As the maiden learned long ago from the angelic message,

When the loud-voiced Father had sent Gabriel from the stars.

This was the one whom the excellent poet foretold in song,

Who once ruled richly over the fields of Jerusalem:

[220] A garden enclosed, blooming upon a flowering height.

A sealed fountain too, powerful with a heavenly flood;

And also the trembling turtledove. To her the prophetic

Angel said: “Behold, virgin, you will bear an everlasting offspring,

And, giving birth, you who are to bear a child will bring forth a son;

Let him be called forever the blessed Son of the Most High.

The most holy Spirit will come upon you from heaven;

Behold, power grants a shadowy shelter to your heart.

The lofty power of the Father will overshadow you, Virgin.”

At these words the mother’s womb swelled with the fetus,

Who, once born, freed the world from its pitiable stain,

[Col. 0763B] And, crucified, wiped away its polluted sins.

### CLII. [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Of Saint Liutger”; that is, concerning the church of Saint Boniface built by Saint Liudger. This poem is recorded by Altfrid, author of the *Life of Saint Liudger*, first bishop of Mimigernaford among the Westphalians. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Benedictines*, fourth century, part I, p. 24.] Alcuin’s verses on the church of Saint Liutger

Here the excellent Father Boniface, with his gracious merits,

Together with his companions, poured out a stream of blood,

Receiving the illustrious marks of sacred martyrdom.

O exceedingly blessed land, rich in the blood of the saints!

From here the victorious soldier flies to the rewards of heaven,

Leaving his final footprints upon these stretches of earth.

Therefore I urge you: with bent knee, humbly,

Whoever you are who read, press kisses upon this earth.

Let great hope arise in you that your tears have been able

To ascend from here to heaven, supported by these patrons [Note: [Col. 0763D] *Patronibus*, from *patron* or *patrones*. See Cange’s Glossary under this word.].

Here that blood remains, more precious than all gold,

And here the limbs, drenched with heavenly dew, rest.

[Col. 0763C] From here Paul the teacher aids us, from there Boniface,

Since this hall is known to have been dedicated to them together.

### CLIII. [Note: [Col. 0763D] This poem was published with the following eleven among the poems of Strabo. Quercetanus, poem 4.] On the basilicas of Saint Peter and the holy apostles

Peter, the heavenly key-bearer who opens the gate in heaven,

The doorkeeper who unlocks the thresholds of eternal life,

Crowns this apse [Note: [Col. 0763D] “This apse of Peter.” Perhaps the church at Thanet in England, which Abbess Eadburga built at almost the same time in honor of the prince of the apostles. [Col. 0764D] Cathelinot in the manuscript. I do not agree with this otherwise most learned man, since there is no basis for the conjecture; nor do the following poems about the other apostles, which are certainly by the same author, seem to belong to that place.] of the saints by lot.

Here throughout the world he arranged a twofold teaching,

Which is properly set down in two books [Note: [Col. 0764D] “Properly in books”: he means the two canonical Epistles of the apostle Peter, which contain Christ’s commands and the doctrines of faith.],

So that those with open hearts might receive Christ’s commands.

As earlier he rightly captured the watery crowds,

Stretching a line of nets among the scaly schools,

So he leads the troops of human beings, snatched from the world’s abyss,

To the eternal kingdom with a heavenly oarsman;

[Col. 0763D] Just as the Savior promised you with truthful voice

When he called the fisherman from his open boat.

He who walked on the blue waters of the green sea,

But the sea did not swallow him, though he was sinking amid its swelling waves,

While Christ’s right hand pressed the heaving marble-like waters,

[Col. 0764A] Whose shadow offered healing to the sick,

As they returned healthy again to the light of life,

Although earlier they had passed through the thresholds of black death.

Here too, relying on the power of the Thunderer,

He restores the lame man in both knees and feet,

And quickly commands the healed man to go on his feet—

The man whom previously a relative had carried, perhaps, to the nearby temple.

Here too he punished two wicked men with death,

Who had fraudulently concealed the price of the property.

Moreover, he utterly emptied the magical phantom of the false Simon,

Driving it down into the dark shadows;

He released the Roman people from their ancient error—

The man who, untrained, climbed the lofty heights of a tower,

And, crowned with laurel foliage, flew away,

But soon, dropping through the fruitful air,

Headfirst to the ground, with both bones broken,

He fell, and Peter won the victory in the contest.

He, nailed to the cross, gladly paid the penalty of torment,

Destined to suffer the dreadful wounds of the cruel iron.

God, the almighty Judge, adorned him by right with eternal triumphs

And raised him to the summits of heaven.

### CLIV. Saint Paul the apostle

Saul, who had imprisoned the holy crowds,

Became a believer, his name changed to Paul,

Scattering many seeds through fruitful words;

From him the sacred harvest of the world grew in the field.

God called him from the citadel of heaven while he was an unbeliever:

“Why are you persecuting me, resisting with a hard heel?”

[Col. 0764C] Therefore, plunged day and night beneath the depths of the sea,

He earned great visions of heavenly realities.

Carried up, he climbed to the third heights of heaven,

And with his mind saw the hosts of the princes of the sky.

The insolent pythoness called out with a presumptuous voice;

The spirit departed when Paul purified the girl,

And, fleeing far away, vanished into the empty air.

He raised a young boy who had fallen into death’s underworld,

As the soul entered his marrow.

Did he not rightly deprive the magician of both eyes,

So that he would never see Phoebus shining with light?

He restores in legs and shins the lame and sick man,

Whom fortune had previously deprived of the ability to walk.

Likewise he quickly cured the father of Publius [Note: [Col. 0764D] Read *Publii*, “of Publius.”],

Whom breathless fever tormented,

And scorching heat, together with wintry cold [Note: [Col. 0764D] Perhaps *frigus et*, “and cold.”], was consuming.

And he also quickly healed [lacuna] many [lacuna] shameful punishment [Note: [Col. 0764D] The passage is corrupt.].

When Paul had first gathered branches for the fire,

To drive away the excessive cold of winter.

A dreadful viper bit his hand with a deadly tooth,

[Col. 0765A] But Paul did not feel the icy venom in the wound,

Nor could the cruel poison harm the holy man.

Finally, he handed over to the dark flames to be burned

The serpent [Note: [Col. 0765D] Perhaps *colubrum*, “snake”] covered with scaly skin.

After he had completed the span of his mortal life,

[221] He sought sacred martyrdom in red blood,

And purple blood flowed from the fountain of his veins. [Note: [Col. 0765D] “And purple blood”: the author of Sermon 11 in the Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, p. 141, and the author of Sermon 30, vol. VI of the works of Saint Chrysostom, p. 267, write that the severed head of Saint Paul poured milk instead of blood. But this is supported by no ancient author, and Alcuin, as this passage proves, was unaware of the story. See Tillemont, *Memoirs*, vol. I, note 80 on Saint Paul, p. 538, Paris edition, 1701.]

Although the earth now covers his bones beneath the mass of a tomb,

His spirit nevertheless ascended to the lofty citadels,

Led through the misty heavens among angelic assemblies.

### CLV. Saint Andrew the apostle

Here Andrew likewise will protect the altar of the church,

Peter’s brother, who once endured the dreadful death-punishment

And hung upon the sacred wood in the flesh;

God summoned him from heaven as he traversed the ocean’s waves

In a little boat [Note: [Col. 0765D] *Frustra* should be read *flustra*, “waves,” as below in poem 163. *Flustrum* means water or rippling wave, and is derived from *fluo, fluis*. Cange, *Glossary*, under *Flustrum*.],

Walking along the shores of the sea.

At once Andrew, pierced by the Thunderer’s voice,

Believed in the eternal King who saves the ages,

Despising the hanging nets of the rejected catch,

And very quickly carried out Christ’s commands.

Who can count the towns filled with populous crowds

Which, through his eloquence, were rubbing away their profane temples,

Opening their trusting hearts to Christ the King?

Indeed, he repaid the Lord’s favor with a bloody heel,

While hanging as a martyr upon the cross’s outstretched stake;

He closed the final breath of mortal life,

Receiving purple crowns while Christ reigned.

### CLVI. Saint James the apostle

[Col. 0765C] Here too James, born of an ancient father,

Defends the lofty shrine with a sacred covering.

When Christ, in his devotion, called from the shore of the sea,

He was leaving his own father in the open boat.

He first converted the Spanish [Note: [Col. 0766D] The edition has *Spanas*.] peoples by his teaching,

Converting barbarian bands with divine words—

Peoples who had long worshiped ancient rites and gloomy shrines,

Deceived by the fraud of the dreadful demon.

Here this astonishing bishop performed many signs,

Which are now properly written on squared tablets.

Cruel Herod, the tyrant tetrarch, killed him,

Struck down by a cruel sword;

But the exalted Father, who rightly crowns the saints with triumph,

Raised him to the heavenly citadels by his shining merits.

### CLVII. Saint John the apostle and evangelist

[Col. 0765D]

Meanwhile let the virgin John [Note: [Col. 0766A] The grammatical form is corrupt or unusual.] likewise be gathered here,

Whom brotherly concord joined together with Christ,

When he left the open boat with his aged father,

A boat enclosing sea-born prey in its nets,

He who earlier swept the blue waters with seaweed-covered oars,

Setting traps for fish beneath the depths of the sea.

But when God called from the shore of the struggling waters,

He left the net-bearing boat with his dear brother,

And followed the Lord, who reigns in heaven’s citadel.

He was the distinguished disciple of the reigning Christ,

Before all the others, loved with great affection,

Whom the king who ruled at Rome,

Having carried him across the blue waters in a small boat,

Thrust into exile.

Placed in exile, he grew in ecstasy,

Supported by divine power, seeing many spectacles of the world [Note: [Col. 0766D] Perhaps *crevit a cerno*, “he saw.”],

Which are now read throughout the world, written on parchment.

And the aforesaid bishop rests at Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0766D] The edition has *effoeto*.] in body,

To receive his rewards when the trumpet sounds [Note: [Col. 0766D] *Salpix*: “trumpet.” See this word frequently in Cange’s *Glossary*],

While the final ages slip away into ancient time.

### CLVIII. Saint Thomas the apostle

Here Thomas Didymus, who received a Greek name,

Guards the sacred temple beneath a sound roof;

He who, touching the wounds made by the cruel spear,

Immediately believed in the monarch who saves the ages,

Although previously he had been incredulous toward his gracious companions

And carried doubtful faith in a troubled heart,

While the Redeemer, rising from death,

Was leaving the infernal chaos closed up, with a vast throng accompanying him.

But soon the red scar converted the doubter,

When the disciple touched the little wounds of the cruel iron,

As, with the doors closed, Christ the Savior, bringer of peace,

Entered the hall where the trembling crowd was hiding.

Therefore this venerable offspring of the Thunderer sent him,
To convert the Eastern peoples with kindly books [Note: Edition: “Billis.”],  
performing many signs with magnificent triumphs.

Then India, devoted to pagan rites, worshiped unholy images,  
instructed by the foolish teachings of its ancestors;  
but, confounded by faith as Thomas won salvation,  
it believed in Christ, who governs heaven’s scepters.

Finally, when the time of this present life had passed,  
Thomas immediately surveyed the heavenly Olympus.  
The priest and keeper of an ancient shrine  
pierced him, dripping with blood, with a hard sword,  
as he awaited his rewards, when the earth will open of its own accord  
and all bodies will rise from their ancient tombs.

### CLIX. Of Saint James the Apostle

[Col. 0766D]

James also, born of Christ’s maternal aunt  
[Note: “Matertera” (maternal aunt). Here Alcuin follows Saint Jerome, the Venerable Bede, and others, who believed that Mary of Cleophas, mother of James the Less, was the true sister of the Blessed Virgin, taking John 19:25 literally. See critics who treat the matter more fully, especially Tillemont, cited above, note 2 on the Blessed Virgin, p. 458.]  
and relying on the fortunate name of cousin,  
[Col. 0767A] guards this house of the Lord from high Olympus.  
The Jewish people, raging in savage tumult,  
killed him after casting him down from the pinnacle, with a fuller’s club,  
because, ascending the heights of the temple,  
he frequently preached Christ to the people in the language of a priest.

On his knees, a hardened skin is said to have formed,  
as he repeatedly prayed aloud to the Thunderer,  
striking the pavement of the shrine with bent knees.

He rejected woolen coverings of shaggy cloth,  
taking linen towels against the wintry drafts.  
Likewise, scorning fragrant nard upon his body,  
he utterly disregarded the luxury of baths upon his breast.  
He did not cut the curls of his head with an iron shear,  
nor did a knife shave his cheeks of their covering of hair.

222 [Col. 0767B] Such great praises of his virtues remain  
that the vengeance for his death, which he paid by a dreadful death,  
became the destruction of Jerusalem and the ruin of its people  
[Note: A description of the destruction of Jerusalem, which may be read in Josephus, *The Jewish War*.].

While Caesar Titus, accompanied by a dense host,  
besieged the broad city with iron-bearing armies,  
together with his father, born to the Roman citadel,  
until dire famine consumed the multitudes—  
those shut in by the walls and enclosed in the prison of the ramparts.

At that time a woman slaughtered her tender child  
and even pierced it with sharp spits for roasting;  
when it had been cooked, the cruel mother ate it by her household hearth,  
utterly dissolving the laws of human nature.  
I shudder to relate it: the bitter death of the young man.

Thus vengeance for the cross punished the wicked with disaster;  
thus also the suffering of James punished the guilty.

[Col. 0767C] Eleven times a hundred thousand are said to have fallen  
in the wretched city, its citizens dying.  
Moreover, a hundred thousand were sold everywhere—  
those whom the neglected sword-point of iron had spared—  
and those spared by the sword’s point perished from hunger through scant sustenance.

### CLX. Of Saint Philip the Apostle

Here too the metrical poem commemorates Philip,  
whom pious Christ enriched with heavenly grace.  
He taught barbarian hosts sacred doctrines,  
throughout Scythia, to believe in Christ, the Savior of the ages—  
those who had long lain numb in the grim shadow of death,  
denying the Author of light with darkened hearts  
[Col. 0767D] and serving the creature in an inverted order.

Until they drank in apostolic speech with their ears,  
beholding the clear lights of the everlasting Sun.  
All eagerly plunge into the sacred flood,  
cleansing the pollution of sin in the water of the font.

From there he hastens to Asia, to convert it with sacred books,  
for it had long worshiped idols, deceived by fraud.  
But Asia, attentive—or, according to another reading, credulous—  
quickly opens its inmost heart to Christ,  
as it receives the splendid words of the speaking disciple.

Yet he happily converts the kingdom of Asia by his teaching,  
in which, after his death, he rests by fateful decree,  
[Col. 0768A] whose sacred altar [another reading: “ark”] will guard this temple.

### CLXI. Of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle

The farthest and most powerful India is known to exist,  
which the writings of books divide into three parts,  
devoted to pagan rites in which it worshiped idols.

But Bartholomew destroyed the lurid shrines,  
rightly shattering the images of the ancient gods.  
The Hebrew tongue calls him the son  
of him who hangs up the waters in the dark clouds,  
while the heavens drip with drops from rain-filled skies;  
the one whom the heavenly gift of the heights marks out,  
as the Psalmist once sang in verse:

[Col. 0768B] “Behold, liquid drips from the dark clouds of the air.”

After this he purchases the bloodstained wreath of martyrdom  
and follows the Lord, marked with Christ’s stigmata,  
whose venerable altar will guard this temple.

### CLXII. Of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist

Matthew, describing the glorious doctrine of salvation,  
arranged the Hebrew sayings in a single little book,  
relating many miracles for the holy ages [Note: Another reading: “wondrous”],  
which the four-sided Scripture now proclaims throughout the world.

The river Pishon, overflowing from the fountain of paradise,  
foretelling and unfolding the figurative mysteries of things,  
rightly signifies the figure of the Savior,  
from whom four rivers flow in four channels.

As once, at the origin of the newborn world,  
four clear rivers flowed through the broad earth,  
watering red flowers and meadows green with turf  
with pure currents and bluish dew,  
so the teaching of God flowed from a fourfold source,  
sprinkling dry hearts with divine streams.

Matthew, the truthful writer, once expressed this teaching.  
The prophet of God, filled with holy inspiration,  
saw him once marked in human form,  
because he was to enumerate Christ’s fathers  
and the ancestors of his ancestors—  
from whom our Savior had received the sacred cradle—  
[Col. 0768D] the remaining text is corrupt: *sacrata piacula demens* (“consecrated expiations, mad”), with variants *scelerata* (“wicked”) and *clemens* (“merciful”).

### CLXIII. Of Saint Simon the Apostle

[Col. 0768D]

Simon the Zealot, also called the Cananaean,  
held the name of Peter among the apostles  
[Note: Another reading has “relied upon.”].  
He taught the Gentile assembly the heavenly doctrine,  
so that they might seek the lofty kingdom by a heavenly path.

His altar will be preserved in this sacred hall  
when heaven and earth, and the waves of the sea, fall apart;  
until the ages glitter with their final ashes,  
and the mass of the world, its mountains and hills, melt,  
and creation, like wax flowing away,  
collapses throughout the universe as the crackling flame consumes it.

### CLXIV. Of Saint Jude Thaddeus the Apostle

[Col. 0769A]

Kindly Thaddeus completes the final number.  
His illustrious surname was once Bibleus [Libbeus],  
who, they say, brought a letter of Christ to the world [Note: Read *scedam*, “a letter.”]  
[Note: “They say he brought.” Saint Jerome also believed that, after Christ’s Ascension, Jude Thaddeus was sent to Edessa to King Abgar (in his commentary on Matthew 10:4). Other writers, however, think that Saint Jerome did not properly distinguish between the apostle Thaddeus and another Thaddeus, one of the seventy disciples. Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* I.13; II.1) records that this other Thaddeus was sent by the apostle Thomas shortly after Christ’s Ascension into heaven and came to Edessa to King Abgar. Tillemont, cited above, note 5 on Saint Thomas, p. 613.]  
to Abgar, who once ruled the scepters of the kingdom.

After Christ condemned the Tartarean tyrant by death  
and joyfully emerged from the dark caverns of Erebus,  
Christ then ascended to the starry Olympus.

He is also called Jude by the common name,  
whose praises are now celebrated in this hall.  
With eloquent speech he published for us a twofold book  
[Note: “A twofold book”—that is, two books. Only one writing of the apostle Jude survives, namely the canonical Epistle addressed to all the faithful, beloved in God the Father and called by Jesus Christ; no other writing is accepted by the Church. For Pope Gelasius rejected the *Pseudo-Gospel* falsely attributed to Saint Jude. It is surprising if this escaped Alcuin’s notice.],  
proclaiming ancient sayings with his mouth,

[Col. 0769B] 223 which the prophet Enoch described in ancient time,  
before the predatory world was lashed by the sea with waves,  
saying: “Behold, the Lord comes with kindly thousands  
to pass judgment on all who inhabit the world,”  
whom he compares to clouds lacking drops of water,  
which cold winds scatter with swift blasts;  
and likewise to trees born from barren stock,  
which lose their fruit at autumn’s season.

So too he compares them to the foaming waves of the waters,  
calling the wandering stars of heaven guilty,  
for whom punishment remains stored in dark storms.

Indeed, Jude had bent savage peoples  
and the barbarian kingdoms of the sea toward the Lord  
with kindly teachings.  
His body, lulled to rest by death in Armenia,  
awaits resurrection at the fateful end;  
[Col. 0769C] yet his spirit has surveyed the heavenly citadels.

### CLXV. The Poet’s Prayer to the Twelve Apostles Praised Above

I have now set forth twice six names of the Fathers,  
through whom the world, converted, believed in the Most High Thunderer.

I venerate these men with frequent prayers  
[Note: Perhaps “I honor”], and with a devoted heart,  
so that they may mercifully lighten the burden of my sins  
and, granting forgiveness, release the offenses committed;  
so that, relying on divine grace  
[Note: The correction reads “by divine gift.”],  
I may enter last through the heavens, with Christ fighting on my behalf.

### CLXVI. Of Saint Matthias the Apostle

This holy shrine honors kindly Matthias,  
who is said to have been one of the seventy  
[Col. 0769D] disciples of the Lord who taught the sacred doctrine.

God marked him out as chosen by heavenly lot,  
when Judas Iscariot, deceived by wicked trickery,  
lost the lofty dignity of the apostolic honor  
and poured out his foul entrails together with his stinking viscera,  
when, suspended from above by a noose, his middle burst open.

[Col. 0770A] He sold the Lord of light, who redeemed the ages with his blood,  
so that, in his greed, he might obtain the gleaming coin.

Therefore Matthias, rejecting the wicked traitor,  
and relying on the Lord, filled up the same number;  
joined to the apostolic triumphs, he rightly rejoices.

### CLXVII. To the Holy Cross

Faithful one, venerate the lofty banner of the cross;  
whoever arms himself with it fears no sorrow.  
Blessed the cross, shining where the Lord hung in the flesh,  
and by his death closed the path of the mind [F.: “of death”].

Here the Author of life destroyed death by dying,  
healing our wounds with his own wounds.

### CLXVIII. To the Church of Saint Michael the Archangel

[Col. 0770B]

Happy Michael, before the throne of the eternal King  
who reigns forever, you serve in the highest citadel;  
among winged companions who remain throughout the ages  
of abiding light, you sing the blessed kingdoms of peace.

Protect this hall, which on earth we have rightly dedicated to you,  
as we pray to ascend to the stars through your prayers.  
And, so that the fiery arrows of the hostile dragon may not harm us,  
mercifully extend continual aid to the weak,  
so that, when the struggle of this present warfare is complete,  
your right hand may raise us to the palm of life.

### CLXIX. On the Chains of Saint Peter the Apostle

By these chains, Rome, your faith was made firm;  
by these chains he has now rightly granted Simplicius himself to hold sacred office.

You will always be free. For what could bonds not accomplish  
which were touched by him who can release all things?  
His unconquered hand, or his walls made victorious  
by religion, will not be shaken at all by any enemy.

He closes the way to wars who opens the gate in the heavens.

### CLXX. Intercession of Saint Paul the Apostle

Almighty Father, who pour forth upon all peoples  
the kindly radiance of the distinguished Paul’s mouth,  
grant us, through his prayers, the joys and kingdoms  
whose heights you command us to seek by his admonitions.

### CLXXI. To the Church of Saint Paul the Apostle

You who, armed with the cross, overcome the savage battles of the world  
and victoriously lead blessed choirs to the stars,  
Paul, preserve the venerable shrines of your temple  
[printed reading: “savage,” rather than “preserve”],  
lest the plundering thief ravage your sheepfold.

### CLXXII. To the Church of the Holy Martyrs Stephen and Laurence

Behold, Stephen endures stones, Laurence fires,  
[Col. 0771A] and by the narrow path they seek the blessed kingdoms.

The hall of the Levites rightly flashes with a radiant color;  
precious death calls them to the palm of life.

### CLXXIII. To the Altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary

Virgin Mother of God, queen of our salvation,  
here aid your servants through your prayers.

Since this altar is venerable through your vows,  
you are praise, honor, and salvation to sacred virgins.

### CLXXIV. To the Church and Altar of the Blessed Virgin

This holy house is holy for you, most holy Virgin,  
Virgin Mary, undefiled Mother of God the Thunderer.

As a virgin you gave birth to everlasting salvation for the world;  
therefore the whole world praises you everywhere.

[Col. 0771B] Behold, I, your servant, praise you with the Muses;  
you are my sweet love, my honor, and my great hope of salvation.

Aid your servant, most illustrious Virgin;  
my voice strikes you with tears, and my mind burns with love.  
Also heed here the prayers of all the brothers  
who cry to you: “Virgin, full of grace,  
through you may the grace of Christ always preserve us.”

Whoever reads these verses, say: “Christ, protect the poet.”

This table too has been consecrated in your name, Virgin;  
you are queen of heaven, flower of the field, lily of the world,  
enclosed garden, fountain of life, and spring of salvation.

Kindly receive the vows of your servants,  
and, in humble prayer, I beg you to return them to Christ God.

### CLXXV. To the Altar of Saint Martin

[Col. 0771C]

This altar is evidently dedicated to you, Martin,  
great in the world for your pious merits as a confessor.

### CLXXVI. To Saint John the Baptist

O powerful Baptist, you baptized Christ in the Jordan;  
here wash away our sins through your prayers.

224 ### CLXXVII. To the Altar of Saint Anianus

On this sacred altar the pious Anianus is commemorated,  
the holy confessor of Christ in the mouth of his people.

### CLXXVIII. To the Church and Altar of Saint Medard

This is indeed the venerable hall of Saint Medard;  
it is no less clear that this altar belongs to him.

[Col. 0771D] Whoever comes here in faith to mourn his sins  
will receive forgiveness here through the merit of the saint.

### CLXXIX. To the Altar of Saints Quintinus and Dionysius

On this altar two illustrious Fathers are venerated:  
Quintinus, certainly, and Saint Dionysius.  
The one was a confessor of Christ, but the other a martyr;  
may their intercession benefit us before the Lord.

### CLXXX. To the Altar of Saints Salvius and Amandus

Salvius embraces this altar, and likewise the great—[lacuna]—Amandus  
[Note: Perhaps “the great Saint Amandus also.”].  
For both embrace it with their minds  
[Note: Perhaps “both with their own pious [minds].”],  
both flourishing in virtues, and both, we believe,  
[Col. 0772A] remaining in the everlasting kingdom of heaven.

### CLXXXI. To the Church and Altar of Saint Mauritius

He returns victorious from the enemy, glorious by divine favor,  
while with his sacred legion he returns victorious from the enemy  
[variant: “when he returns”].

Mauritius overcame arduous battles through God’s peace,  
surpassing the battles of the world through God’s peace.

Behold, this holy house is marked with his name;  
may this house also shine with his merits.  
In whose honor this sacred dedicated altar gleams,  
and in whose sacred honor may the people rejoice.

### CLXXXII. To the Altar of Saint John the Baptist

This altar dedicated to you shines, John the Baptist;  
always remember that it must be honored with worthy praises.

[Col. 0772B] You who were worthy to baptize the Lord in sacred waters,  
O blessed one, wash away our sins here through your prayers.

### CLXXXIII. To the Chapel of Saint Martin

Defend this chapel with your prayers, holy Martin,  
and, when entreated, kindly deign also  
to hear our prayers, Father, and suppress the various waves  
of the heart, so that we may be able to seize eternal life.

### CLXXXIV. To the Church of Saint Stephen the Martyr

This eternal house shines for the great protomartyr Stephen,  
who asks forgiveness for those stoning him—perhaps, according to a conjecture, “pardon for the unworthy”—  
and followed Christ’s sacred example.

Behold, the martyr helps his friends even more through his prayers.

### CLXXXV. To the Church of Saint Peter the Apostle

[Col. 0772C]

May Peter, illustrious prince, always preserve  
the roof consecrated to him under the apostolic name.

He who carries the key of heaven in honorable hands  
may open for us the merciful way to the stars.

### CLXXXVI. To the Altar of the Holy Archangels

May the angel Michael, almighty, govern this altar;  
through him that treacherous dragon was defeated  
and cast far away from heaven’s lofty summit—  
he who always seeks to accuse the pious with his mouth.

Gabriel, venerable companion, is joined to this altar,  
who shines by holy power in the citadel of heaven.

[Col. 0772D] From whose sacred mouth the eternal Virgin Mary  
learned to bring forth the God who is the world’s salvation.

Raphael is added to these, who perhaps healed Tobias’s eyes  
and also led his son.

We pray that these three may stand here beside our prayers,  
so that Christ may hear his servants from the citadel.

### CLXXXVII. To the Altar of Saint John the Baptist

This powerful Baptist will protect this altar by his merits,  
he who baptized the Lord Christ in the sacred river.

He was chosen from his mother’s womb;  
he was the voice of the Thunderer’s Word and the herald of our salvation.

He was the distinguished sponsor of Christ in the world;  
he showed with the finger of God that the Lamb was present,  
who bore away all the sins of the world with his blood.

### CLXXXVIII. To the Altar of Saints Stephen and Paul the Apostle

On this altar the great protomartyr Stephen is worshiped,  
who through a hail of stones sought the blessed kingdoms.

And through whose prayers—most wondrous to say—  
Saul suddenly became Paul among the pious in the world.

A ravenous beast in the morning, one that handles spoils in the evening,  
let this man himself assist our prayers through his own.

### CLXXXIX. To the Altar of Saint Laurence the Martyr

Laurence, whom no devouring flame overcame,  
preserve this altar, I beg, with the blood of martyrdom.

He fulfilled the commandments of Christ God through love,  
giving to the poor whatever he possessed in his poverty.

He scorned the wealth of the fleeting age  
so that he might possess Christ’s everlasting riches in heaven.

### CXC. To the Altar of Saint Quintinus and His Fellow Martyrs

May pious Quintinus preserve this altar from the enemy,  
he who through sacred blood sought the blessed kingdoms.

Joined to him is also a crowd of devout laymen,  
who sought heaven through the blood of martyrdom.

### CXCI. To Saints Mauritius and His Fellow Martyrs

May Mauritius adorn these places with his living merits,  
the distinguished martyr together with his legion.

Their wonderful faith of heart and wonderful steadfastness  
earned them pious praises forever in the world.

### CXCII. To the Altar of Saint Dionysius and His Fellow Martyrs

May Dionysius, the pontifical summit, preserve this altar,  
I ask, together with his fellow martyrs and the others.

Their little books the heavenly scribe holds in the citadel,  
with their names forever before the face of God.

### CXCIII. To the Altar of Saint Germanus and Others

Germanus, a confessor renowned for the merits  
and name of faith, a bishop and himself a pious shepherd—  
with the company of confessors joined to him on this altar—  
may God preserve us everywhere through their prayers.

### CXCIV. To the Altar of Saint Martin and Others

[Col. 0773D] Here the love—or, according to another reading, honor—of Martin shines, consecrated on the altar,  
him whom Europe worships and whom the world likewise loves.

Sacred companies of saints are joined to him  
with great honor, through the pious vows of faith.

225 ### CXCV. To the Altar of Saint Remedius and Others

The distinguished Father and teacher Remedius  
preserves this altar everywhere with his companions in life.

He who raised this table and dedicated it together fed them there with pious care.

### CXCVI. To the Church of Saint Benedict the Abbot

These roofs remain dedicated to you, Benedict,  
pious abbot and monk, your confessor.

[Col. 0774A] A holy crowd of monks throughout the world celebrates you,  
whose life was written through your speech.

Here too the holy company of brothers specially  
praises, honors, and loves you with continual prayers.  
This hall is always open to them at night;  
here it teaches them to pray, and here to pour forth tears.

Holy Father, be ever present here through their prayers.

### CXCVII. To the Altar of Saint Jerome and Others

Jerome, the wondrous teacher of the whole world,  
together with his companions, occupies these holy places.

Whoever reads the names written out in the titles of the pious,  
ask them humbly in prayer to be present to you.

### CXCVIII. To the Altar of Saint Gregory the Pope

[Col. 0774B]

Gregory, teacher, shepherd, patriarch, and priest,  
once a pious bishop in the city of Rome—  
I pray that here he may carry the pious vows of the brothers  
to the Thunderer, together with the Fathers whose names  
you see written here.

### CXCIX. To the Church Where the Relics of the Saints Are Venerated

Whoever desires to enter heaven’s open gates  
should enter this place frequently on his own feet.

This is the gate of everlasting salvation for the one who comes;  
this is the path of light and now the way of forgiveness.

This is the kindly house of God; here are the treasures of the Thunderer,  
the many relics of the holy Fathers.

Therefore, traveler, when you enter, with devoted mind  
stretch your limbs upon the ground and embrace heaven in your heart.

[Col. 0774C] Here is God, here are the saints, here is hope for you,  
here is the land of salvation; let firm faith be joined to your heart.

### CC. To Saint Michael the Archangel

Here may Michael the archangel stand beside our prayers,  
the great prince in heaven’s citadel and Christ’s minister  
[printed reading: “master”].

May he always assist the prayers of the saints everywhere;  
may he preserve us here from the enemy through his prayers;  
and may he make us watch there in the praises of God.

### CCI. To a Certain Altar

Here God the Judge, the image of the Father, sits enthroned.  
Here the seraphim shine, burning beneath the love of the Lord.  
Here, among the cherubim, the mysteries of the Thunderer fly.

[Col. 0774D] Here likewise five wise maidens shine,  
carrying lamps with everlasting light in their hands.

### CCII. To the Altar of Saint Peter the Apostle

The heavenly key-bearer, Peter the Apostle,  
who guards the gates of Olympus, prince and shepherd of the flock,

this altar has been roofed and dedicated to the everlasting King himself;  
may he preserve it for all ages through continual prayers.

### CCIII. To the Altar of the Blessed Virgin

Virgin Mary, Mother of God, most chaste Virgin,  
light and star of the sea, queen of our salvation,

may she always adorn this altar with living merits,  
which stands consecrated in its fitting honor.

### CCIV. To the Altar of Saint Paul the Apostle

[Col. 0775A]

For in your name, most illustrious teacher of the world,  
Paul, called from heaven on high by Christ God,

this present altar will be consecrated by its inscriptions of life;  
on it great salvation has come, a sure hope of salvation.

### CCV. On the Dedication of the Church of Gorze

This house was dedicated to the Lord Christ and the saints  
on the fifth Ides of fiery July [edition: “indibus”] in former times.

The pious archfather, the glory of the people of Metz,  
Bishop Hrogandus, consecrated it with great honor  
[Note: Hrogandus—that is, Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, who dedicated the church of the monastery at Gorze and placed there the relics of Saint Nazarius on the fifth Ides of July in the year 765. See Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 208, no. 6.].

### CCVI. Prayer to Christ

Grant us your help always, O High-Throned One,  
Christ, to hear the prayers of your servants,

who offer you vows of praise with devoted hearts,  
granting everlasting life by your merciful gift.

Whoever pours out tears to God at this altar [lacuna],  
remember me, who sang these verses to Christ.

Hear the prayers of your servants, Christ,  
who offer you praise at this present altar,  
and grant us the holy gifts of heavenly salvation.

Reader, I beg you, remember Alcuin, the author of this poem.

You, my sweet love, illustrious sister, farewell always;  
in your prayers remember your brother.

Learn to scorn with mind, hand, and tongue  
the pleasures, pomp, and fleeting treasures of the age.

Let Christ be your love, your strength, your praise; let Christ be everything.  
May he remain [lacuna] and always resound upon your lips.

### CCVII. To the Altar Adorned by Hildebold

Led by your great love, most gentle Christ,  
and likewise by yours, most holy Virgin Mary,  
and by yours, illustrious in merits, priest Medard,

Hildebold, rejoicing, humble father and priest,  
ordered this altar to be adorned with beautiful metals  
[Note: Hildebold was certainly the bishop of Cologne from whom Charlemagne requested the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, to confirm his departure when he was on the point of death; he died the following day. Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 407, no. 14. See also poem 115 above.].

For him, readers of this inscription, we ask you to pray.

### CCVIII. To the Paintings of the Patriarchs Adam, Noah, and Abraham

[Note: We extracted this inscription from the longer epigram 199 of Quercetanus’s edition, since it has no connection there either with the preceding or following verses, and since it was joined to them only through the carelessness of the scribe.]

Here almighty God fashions Adam from dust;  
here Adam is first made an inhabitant of paradise.

“Give names to all living creatures, Father Adam.”

When the man slept, Adam brought forth the mother from his rib.

Here the woman was deceived, and Adam was deceived also.

“Guard these blessed gates with flames, cherubim.”

“Go forth, Adam, and leave the happy kingdoms.”

“Let the earth produce thorns for you, Adam, because of your crime.”

The devouring envy that struck the righteous Abel, his brother  
[Note: The edition reads, “the devouring envy that struck Adam, the righteous one.”].

Here Noah, beloved of the Lord, builds an ark for himself.

Behold, the ark floats upon the waters with the citizens of the world.

[Col. 0776A] Behold, the pious dove brings you an olive branch of peace;  
the white dove returns while the little black raven perishes.

“Go forth, and lead out all the animals with you.”

Here is Father Abram, ordered to leave his homeland.

Here Sarai, hiding behind the doors of the hut, laughed.

### CCIX. On a Certain Church

May he who rules the sea, the earth, and heaven by his command  
himself govern this hall with his heavenly gifts,

in which the worship, honor, praises, and glory of Christ  
may always remain forever through love of piety.

### CCX. On Christ the Savior of the World

[Note: From the manuscript of Salzburg.]

The Virgin Mary shines, with no one violating her modesty;  
after the birth of the Child, the Virgin Mary shines.

[Col. 0776B] Here the Son of Man becomes the world’s greatest question;  
here the Son of Man is God with us.

This man, who is God, is the ancient hope of those who came before;  
this man, who is God, is hope for the pious at the end.

The harsh death of the people ran forth, led down upon the wood;  
the harsh death of the people is removed upon the wood.

The vast Tartarus perceived that the light of God was present;  
and human beings do not believe that the light of God is present.

Fierce death subjected the world to itself through miserable humanity;  
subjected, fierce death groaned through humanity.

Behold, that earthly father begets the race for death;  
behold, Christ raises the race to life.

# EXHORTATIONS, OR MORAL VERSES

[Col. 0776C]

### CCXI. Exhortation to Nocturnal Praises

Rise, brothers, and sing praises to Christ;  
this house is suitable for you at night.

Now devote yourselves vigilantly to sacred prayers;  
we believe that angelic choirs, who guard the hours of night,  
grant help here to those who ask  
and kindly carry the pious vows of the brothers to Christ.

May they always find you honorably wakeful here,  
and praising the heavenly King with pious minds.

### CCXII. Exhortation to Shake Off Sleep

Rise, I beg you, young man, while your body is healthy and strong,  
and open for yourself through prayers the way to the kingdoms of heaven.

Do not, I beg, give your senses entirely to sleep throughout the night.

Constant sleep is an image of cold death;  
long rest will make the grave your destiny.

For the ancient enemy possesses a thousand arts of harming.

Therefore, remain awake and store up a great triumph for yourself,  
so that Christ’s pious right hand may always preserve you.

### CCXIII. Remembrance of Death

[Col. 0777A]

O mortal human being, remember the fate of death.

You differ in nothing from a beast if you seek only prosperity.

All the joys of the various things you see  
withdraw like a thin shadow with swift completion.

Take care lest an unhappy end, while you neither know nor hear it,  
shake you and dissolve you in a sudden whirlwind.

Give food to the one who asks, or cover the naked,  
and after death such deeds will bless you.

### CCXIV. On Despising Wealth

Love poverty; avoid biting treasures,  
for after the sweetness of the flesh they bring flames to the greedy.

Although you shine transparently with gold and jewels,  
you will go poor, insignificant, and naked to the shades.

Only that will remain with you after the fate of death  
which you yourself have done well, justly, and rightly.

### CCXV. On Entreating Divine Mercy

[Note: This poem too was copied from a very ancient manuscript of Salzburg, where it is likewise attributed to Alcuin.]

God is certainly not to be blamed for these punishments,  
but our life must quickly be brought to better things.

His pious mercy must be bent by our prayers,  
so that he himself may remove the blows from us  
and, in his mercy, grant consolations to his servants,  
bestowing upon them every favorable season.

So that with joyful minds we may sing hymnic praises  
always and everywhere to the High-Throned One.

To him be praise, worship, honor, strength, blessing, and song;  
always and forever, great glory to God!

# INSCRIPTIONS OF VARIOUS PLACES

[Col. 0777C]

### CCXVI. In the Refectory of the Brothers

Here let the pious patriarch and high priest sit,  
one whose hand is generous, whose heart is peaceful, whose words are serene;

through his right hand may the right hand of Christ bless  
whatever is brought for the brothers to eat.

### CCXVII. In the Same Place

This is a holy house, a place of peace, a hall of salvation;  
O may Christ’s blessing always remain above it.

Here may he generously multiply the banquets of the brothers  
who once, rich through heavenly gift,  
satisfied five thousand of the people with five loaves.

### CCXVIII. In the Same Place

Let brotherly love always exist among you, brothers;  
let there be peace, pure faith in Christ, and sweet harmony.

Let Christ resound in your mouth, and let Christ dwell in your heart;  
let Christ be food and drink, life and salvation.

### CCXIX. In the Same Place

[Col. 0778A]

Here let fathers and brothers enter with the praises of the Lord  
[Note: The manuscript reads, “Here likewise let the brothers enter.”].

May the Lord preserve them all together forever;  
may he likewise feed them with the shining bread of salvation,  
and likewise grant them the dishes of heavenly life.

227 ### CCXX. In the Same Place

He who gave food from dew and drink from the rock,  
who changed liquid waters into Falernian wines,  
who walked over the waves of the sea with dry feet,  
may he himself kindly increase his gifts for his servants.

### CCXXI. To the Oven

[Note: In Quercetanus’s edition this poem concludes poem 198, to which it is in no way connected. We have therefore given it here under a separate title. See poem 106 above.]

If, rainy traveler, you desire my gifts,  
behold, first give yours, and then take mine.

I have a greedy belly, fed by hot fire;  
from beneath my square crown a smoky odor rises.

The guest flees to me at once in the cold rain of December,  
and from me he flees into the flowering fields in August.

### CCXXII. To the Oven Again

[Note: In Quercetanus’s edition this poem begins poem 199, but it has no connection with the following verses; we have therefore detached it here and placed it under this title. See poem 208 above and poem 260 below.]

Behold, I am beautiful outside, but more useful within;  
my belly is hot while my crown is struck by cold.

The eager guest loves me in the cold season of winter,  
but in the warm summer he refuses to come near me.

I have a mouth in my belly and nostrils in my square throat;  
it breathes smoke while the hearth within is hot.

# VERSES TO VARIOUS PERSONS

[Col. 0778C]

### CCXXIII. To Pope Leo III

May you prosper forever and ever, most holy pope,  
you Leo, victorious, beloved offspring of God.

Pious teacher in the world, most illustrious trumpet of Christ  
—that is, trumpet—  
and head of the Church, its light, honor, and father.

Cultivator of justice and lover of true piety,  
renowned among the poor for [lacuna] pious honor.

Known far and wide in the world, beautiful in the praise of your merits,  
bearing the name of love in the titles of your virtues.

Be pious and gentle, shepherd, for Christ’s sake,  
of the angelic riches—or, according to another reading, the sheep—  
which your right hand governs.

[Col. 0778D] May eternal God keep you healthy through long years  
and exalt you with good prosperity;

and may he grant you everlasting life in heaven’s citadel,  
a kingdom with the saints. Now farewell without end!

### CCXXIV. Pious Vows for the City of Rome and Pope Leo

[Note: Different readings from the Salzburg manuscript have been noted.]

Hail, mighty Rome, glory of the world, illustrious mother,  
and may your children prosper with you through the ages.

And, honor and head of the world, great Pope Leo—  
the Salzburg manuscript reads “great” rather than “great [vocative]”—  
fare well.

May you too, scepter of justice, light of the seat  
[the manuscript reads “law”], honor,  
prosper in perpetual triumphs, with Christ granting it  
[the manuscript reads “in perpetual triumphs”].

May the heavenly key-bearer, also the illustrious teacher of the world,  
preserve you always and everywhere through prayers.

And may the saints, through holy prayers, likewise protect everywhere  
those whom Rome holds within its surrounding walls.

O Fathers, people, glory of the Roman race,  
fare well always and forever, with the Lord showing mercy!

### CCXXV. To Leo, Apostolic Head of the See

[Note: Thus Quercetanus.]

[Col. 0779B]

Pontifical summit, prince, patriarch, priest,  
bishop beloved of God, holy teacher of the saints,  
apostolic shepherd, great Pope Leo, farewell.

Light and glory of the Church, glory of the Roman people,  
and great hope of salvation for the ancestral people of the fatherland;

distinguished teacher, renowned in merits and name,  
illustrious throughout the world in the titles of your virtues.

May eternal God, the gentlest creator of the world,  
the Savior of the human race, the greatest heir,  
protect and govern you, sound, for many years;  
and may he mercifully grant you happy times.

May he increase the number of the people through the doctrines of the word,  
so that, rejoicing in the manifold reward of your labor,  
you may see forever the blessed face of the High-Throned One,

joined forever to the apostolic prince Peter,  
joyful in the heavenly citadel with Christ in kindly praises.

Rule the kingdoms throughout the world with teachings—  
“worldly glory,” perhaps, according to the note  
[Note: The passage is corrupt. Perhaps “rule the worldly kingdoms with teachings.”].

May your letter travel, sealed in the sacred name,  
through land, sea, regions, kingdoms, and cities,  
exhorting all who read it with holy speech.

May the tares of death not stain the seeds of life;  
may the shining harvest of heaven grow from your mouth,  
so that all God’s people may live happily.

May it rejoice and possess the heavenly kingdoms with you  
always and forever, with the Supreme Thunderer granting it.

Live happily for God, and live happily forever,  
golden light of the world, salt of the earth, gate of salvation,  
and glory of the Church, shining with a crown of jewels.

Remember Albinus, and may Christ’s grace remember you,  
[Col. 0779D] and preserve you always, most holy bishop.

### CCXXVI. To Leo, Apostolic Bishop of the City of Rome

Pontifical summit and first priest in the world,  
apostolic shepherd, Pope Leo, farewell.

Holy Father, summit of the illustrious fatherland and of honor,  
worthy in the sacred city, learned far throughout the world,

cultivator of justice and lover of holy piety,  
steadfast in duties and truthful in speech.

You are the glory of the Church, the praise of the world, the glory of the clergy,

an example of life, a model of salvation’s aid.

[Col. 0780A] May the eternal God graciously grant you many years,

so that you may multiply the sacred flock.

May praise and reward remain for you, holy priest,

through all time, in peace throughout the sacred world.

May the teachings of the divine law be renewed everywhere

through you and through your devotion, holy Father.

This work the ancient Fathers accomplished throughout the world,

whose sayings the sacred page now sings,

and whose honor in virtue is celebrated throughout the wide world;

their names the heavenly book preserves,

and the world continually chants their praise in song:

the Church was built upon such leaders.

This is the work, this the devotion, of a great shepherd in the world:

namely, to multiply the talents entrusted to him.

228 The whole hour indeed hastens toward the world [Note: [Col. 0779D] The verse is corrupt.] . . . .

[Col. 0780B] as the holy prophets once foretold.

And the heavenly Judge keeps watch over the deeds of human beings,

to judge everyone according to his own merits.

Then the faithful servant will receive the gifts of his merits,

and joyfully enter into the highest joys of God.

You too, holy Father, will have praise among these,

a citizen of the saints, glorious in the realm of heaven.

So that then you may deserve to be happy among the good in . . . .

Now let no labor in the world be harsh for you.

The saints despised every kind of punishment,

so that they might receive the blessed kingdoms of heaven with Christ.

As a happy shepherd, following their holy footsteps,

with the teachings of the mind joined to sacred devotion,

may the glory of heaven receive and keep you

with Christ and the saints, in everlasting gifts.

[Col. 0780C] The lover of your piety, Bishop Eantbaldus [Note: [Col. 0780D] Bishop Eantbaldus. Perhaps Eanbaldus, bishop of York, who is mentioned several times elsewhere?], sent this boy,

bearing these small gifts.

May your goodness kindly receive him, I beg,

and [is] your servant, and both his son and mine.

To the great pope and shepherd of the Church, Leo,

your servant Albinus has sent this letter.

## CCXXVII. To Charlemagne.

For your servant Homer was coming to us [Note: [Col. 0780D] That is, Angilbertus.],

bringing joyful messages from David’s mouth.

He had also made your Flaccus rejoice in his heart,

and [brought news] of your well-being and of your offspring.

O sweet love to me, sweet presence of Christ,

sweet your devotion, and sweet the sound from your mouth.

May you and your friends together endure

[Col. 0780D] and flourish forever through the ages; David, fare well everywhere.

I have sent this boy back to you through your piety,

so that he may serve us [F., you] in song, heart, and hand.

## CCXXVIII. To the same, concerning studies at the royal court.

Letters from your piety have come from the court,

O David, dearest to God, sweetest to Flaccus,

bringing us the pious gifts of your salvation,

which, I pray, almighty God may always increase.

You are the praise and hope of your people, their joy throughout the whole kingdom;

you are the glory of the Church, its ruler, defender, and lover.

[Col. 0781A] Indeed, you have sent worthy ministers by lot

to the sacred orders, now throughout the known regions of the chapel.

Behold, Christ’s priests will uphold their rights;

let the ministers rightly preserve [they preserve] their official dignity,

and rejoice beneath their own sure prince, Nathan.

The physicians quickly hasten to the Hippocratic halls:

one pours out veins, another mixes herbs in a pot;

one cooks porridge, another offers cups;

and yet, O physicians, show thanks to all [F., freely],

so that Christ’s blessing may attend your hands.

All these things please me; this is a praiseworthy order.

Why has Maro the versifier alone done wrong at court?

Was he not already a father worthy to have a teacher

who would give the boys excellent songs throughout the halls?

[Col. 0781B] What will Beleel do, learned in the Heliac songs [reading uncertain]?

Why, I ask, did he not maintain a school in his father’s name?

What will the sluggish Drances do, with his gray-crowned head,

strong in counsel, though his right hand is as cold in war?

Little Zacchaeus climbed a tall tree,

so that he might see the crowd of writers running about;

with little letters and papers he offers solace to the wretched.

Let him beware lest the boys’ basket touch his right hand.

Now each person in the order properly holds his own teacher.

An excellent presbyter, filled throughout his breast,

governs these priests by deeds and by voice,

walking before them, a most radiant image of salvation.

The order of ministers follows you, Jesse, their teacher.

Perhaps a mighty, bull-like voice of Christ sounds through the court,

as befits one reading pious words to the people from on high.

[Col. 0781C] White-robed Sulpicius, a reader, draws the ranks behind you;

let him govern and teach them, so that they do not err in their exact accents.

He instructs the boys with Idithun’s sacred melody,

so that they may sing sweet sounds with ringing voice.

Let them learn on how many feet, with what measures and rhythm, music stands.

At night let my daughter contemplate the stars of heaven,

and accustom herself always to praise almighty God,

who adorned heaven with stars and the earth with grass,

who made all the world’s wonders by his word.

Then Flaccus’s pipe will make its proper song for you, Homer,

when you have returned to the sacred court.

May Thyrsis and Menalcas together prosper forever;

let Menalcas himself chastise the cooks in the dark court,

so that Flaccus may have hot porridge throughout the dishes.

And let Nemias pour his cups of Bacchus for Groco,

[Col. 0781D] who is accustomed always to carry a tunna with him [Note: [Col. 0781D] *Tunna*. A *tunna* is a vessel capable of holding water, wine, beer, or another liquid . . . . By these words Alcuin indicates the royal cupbearer. Du Cange, *Glossarium*, s.v. “Tunna.”].

## CCXXIX. To the same [Note: [Col. 0781D] In Quercetanus’s edition, these preceding verses—which may perhaps be part of the preceding poem 228—are followed by a poem in a different meter and on a wholly different subject, namely, the *Description of the Hermitage and School of Cormaric*; it is uncertain whether this is rightly attributed to Alcuin. For that reason we have separated it at this point and rejected it among the poems of doubtful authorship.].

May gracious salvation be with all boys and girls,

may the royal offspring prosper through long ages;

may Christ grant him to live happily for many years,

bestowing also the joys of the eternal kingdom.

Christ, salvation of the world, praise, glory, life, Redeemer,

through all times, years, and every hour,

[Col. 0782A] preserve beloved David for many ages,

so that he may live happily and prosperously reign.

Let all the people everywhere answer together: Amen!

In your clemency, gentle one, have mercy on the wretched people:

they are indeed your flock, and you are their kindly shepherd;

Christ will grant you your reward throughout the ages.

Now prosper again, and prosper forever through the ages!

## CCXXX. To the same.

While the radiant charioteer gleams with rosy four-horse teams,

flooding the shining sea with new light,

with his thumb he scatters the night’s sleep from our eyes,

and soon the old man himself leaps from his bed,

running into the fields of the ancients to pluck flowers

that speak rightly, so that he might scatter them in play for the boys:

[Col. 0782B] these he offered to you, sweet love, most glorious consul David,

so that your piety might approve them.

229 If, as judge, you should deem them worthy to be entrusted to the boys,

O glory of wisdom, to store in your heart for your own people,

defend, I beg, the poet who joyfully directed these few gifts to you.

There are indeed many who wish to pluck another’s sayings

more often than to bring their own things out:

thinking themselves wise in this pursuit,

they are able to stain the melody of their children.

May your wisdom, rich king, confront such men,

defending the few sayings of the old Flaccus.

Let them remember Father Entellus and the young Dares,

lest the very praise they seek diminish it still more.

[Col. 0782C] May Christ’s grace fill you with eternal gifts,

O praise and glory, king: fare well without end!

## CCXXXI. To the same and to Angilbertus.

Sweet Homer, farewell; may your life prosper forever;

always, through eternity, sweet Homer, farewell!

May sweet love prosper in our hearts;

may Christ prosper in our hearts.

May Christ, the light, the way, the life, and salvation of all, be loved;

may Christ be for us light, way, life, and salvation.

Always and everywhere fare well—speak, speak, sweetest David;

David, love of Flaccus, always and everywhere fare well!

O sweet love to me, David, fare well through the ages;

how I would always wish to have you present,

[Col. 0782D] so that I might play with you in Pierian verse,

or climb with you to the lofty stars of the highest heaven,

or learn with you the beautiful forms of numbers,

or enter into the wondrous sayings of the ancient Fathers,

or handle the sacred teachings of eternal salvation,

by which path you might carry me with you above the stars.

This alone is salvation; this is true wisdom.

Whoever loves this . . . . loves it, him salvation itself loves.

May he who gave earthly things grant heavenly kingdoms,

so that you may always live happily in the citadel of heaven.

[Col. 0783A] May Christ himself, the pious one, please us above all,

and protect and govern our days.

## CCXXXII. [Note: [Col. 0783D] Alcuin wrote this poem for Charlemagne when, having already left the court, he was residing in his monastery at Tours and Charlemagne was departing for Rome to settle disputes there, as the context shows; namely, in the year 800.] To the same Charlemagne.

May my pipe make songs for beloved David;

David, worthy of laurel-bearing song, will be praised.

David, love of the people, David, praise and glory of the populace,

the glory of the kingdom and the hope and crown of his people.

Go through the cities of the West, Muses, with your harmonies,

crying out: “David, always and everywhere, fare well!”

Let earth, heaven, and sea resound with this ringing voice,

and let the world say: “Honor to him who is life and salvation.”

May the holy hosts of heaven together desire this in their prayers;

may merciful Christ grant it from heaven’s citadel.

[Col. 0783B] May he live and reign happily for many years,

the pious David, to the praise of the people in the world.

And when the time of this present life has happily passed,

may he possess the blessed kingdoms of heaven with Christ.

Now let my pipe carry its voices to you, David—

voices which, I beg, you may read with your customary piety.

My mind follows you, and the song of love follows as well;

together, night and day, it sings and praises you.

And, prostrate in devotion before Father Martin’s altar,

behold, with tears it asks for every prosperity for me [F., you].

May mercy always go with you, holy Father,

and the glory of justice and love of piety.

May the people rejoice throughout the cities when you come,

all together everywhere, the young with the old.

[Col. 0783C] May your goodness reach here, best father of the realm [F., “to this place”],

so that your praise, honor, and glory may remain.

You are the father of your country, an illustrious shepherd of the flock;

let the wicked fear you, and let every pious person love you.

May the wicked will of certain men not steal you away,

men who perhaps desire what is theirs, not what is yours or the Lord’s.

Rome, head of the world and summit of the highest honor,

in which the sacred treasures lie hidden,

which now, after its offspring has been torn apart, mourns its own entrails—

may you quickly heal its wounded members [Note: [Col. 0783D] Perhaps: “may they be healed”],

so that father and people may be governed in harmonious peace,

so that those whom one faith possesses may become of one mind,

those whom Peter, the heavenly key-bearer, pious throughout the world,

has begotten for Christ while confessing Christ’s love.

May the troubled river’s water not flow throughout the world,

from which pure water once used to pour.

For many things must indeed be corrected throughout the world by you,

O king, O ruler, O glory of the Church!

The simoniacal plague is indeed flourishing wickedly throughout the world;

the mystical gifts of God are bestowed for money,

although the eternal God commanded them to be given freely to all,

so that the giver himself receives them freely.

Judgment also stands under the payment of the one who gives;

a gift turns justice aside in the mouth of the old man.

[Col. 0784A] With gifts given, witnesses come to the cups,

and impious drunkenness now acquits the guilty man.

The savage power of certain men also crushes the wretched,

so that the rich man may fill his own sacks from his mouth.

Thieves who commit thefts roam about with impunity;

even the associates of criminals are avengers of crimes.

May your venerable power, O king, restrain such things;

God appointed you ruler of the kingdom.

The people are indeed your flock, and you are the noble shepherd

of an excellent flock, a great father in the world.

As your nobility does, so may your wisdom,

virtue, praise, honor, and glory surpass all others.

The prayers of your servants look toward you,

awaiting what your pious mind may command.

Rome itself, the head of the world, looks to you as its patron,

[Col. 0784B] together with the Father and the people, in devoted love of peace—

those whom your holy will should strive to recall

to the gift of peace through the pious words of God.

Raise up those laid low, and now bring down the proud,

so that sacred peace and piety may reign everywhere.

May the apostolic shepherd, now the first priest in the world,

rejoice through you with the people.

May the Church’s ruler likewise be properly governed through you, O king;

and may the almighty right hand of the Lord guide you,

so that you may live happily, ruler throughout the wide world,

and prosper while doing everything pleasing to God.

May an angel come from the heavenly citadel,

and remain with you night and day together,

always prosperously leading you, O king, as you go,

and protecting and guiding the journey of your return.

[Col. 0784C] 230 May joyful Francia receive you as victor,

and come to meet you with outstretched, palm-bearing hands.

May Christ, the gentlest creator of the world, grant this,

so that, beloved David, you may come quickly.

May the almighty clemency of Christ grant me this:

that I may joyfully see your face in the world.

O father, shepherd, ruler, gracious hope of your people,

may you have life and salvation; farewell without end!

## CCXXXII bis. [Note: [Col. 0784D] We have restored this poem here, although Frobenius placed it among the *ADDENDA*. EDIT.] To the same [Note: [Col. 0784D] This is the poem’s title in the manuscript itself; throughout it he directs his wishes for prosperity to the entire court.].

Rise, my pipe; make sweet verses for my lord.

David loves verses; rise, pipe, and make verses.

David loves poets; David is the glory of poets.

Therefore, poets, all come together,

and sing sweet songs to my David.

David loves poets, etc., as above.

David’s sweet love inspires the hearts of singers;

may his love make odes in our hearts.

The poet Homer loves David; make verses, pipe.

David loves poets, etc., as above.

Illustrious flute, do not remain silent with your sweet-sounding plectrum;

let David’s name resound in your mouth through songs,

and let love for him fill your breast.

David loves poets, etc., as above.

David loves to know the sacred meanings of the ancients,

[Col. 0785A] and to traverse the riches of the old men with discerning mind,

and eagerly to search out the secrets of sacred wisdom.

David loves poets, etc., as above.

David desires to have wise teachers in mind,

for the honor and praise of every art at court,

so that by studious thought he may renew the wisdom of the ancients.

David loves poets, etc., as above.

He also lays the foundations high upon the rock,

so that the gracious house may remain most firm for God and Christ.

Thus, happily, he laid the stones . . . first with his right hand,

so that glorious temples might be made for the Thunderer enthroned on high.

May Christ’s clemency assist the holy work!

May the heavenly ministers assist the work, I beg,

and may the company of the saints likewise help it.

David loves Christ; Christ is David’s glory.

[Col. 0785B] Rise, my dear ones; make sweet verses, pipe.

Illustrious youth, why should I be silent about you, Charles, in my songs? [Note: [Col. 0785D] Charles, the eldest son of Charlemagne; Rotrud and Berta were his daughters.]

You too are worthy offspring of great parents;

you are the glory of the court, the hope of the kingdom, of gracious character.

Therefore every poets’ pipe praises you.

Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

You too, sacred virgin of God, illustrious sister of David,

Gisla, fare well now in our perpetual song.

I know that Christ, the glory of heaven, loves you as his bride,

since you have dedicated your members always to him alone.

Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Rotthrud loves song, the most brilliant virgin in mind.

A very beautiful virgin, and a virgin illustrious in character.

Run through the shining fields and gather flowers;

from the meadows of the ancients unfold a beautiful crown for yourself.

[Col. 0785C] Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Now sing the praises of the excellent virgin Berta,

Pierian Muses, with me; may our songs please her.

The girl is worthy of the songs of the Muses . . . .

Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Now let our flute praise you together, girls,

delicate in years, mature in gracious character;

honor has already surpassed your exceedingly beautiful appearance.

Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Why should I not remember you, Primicerius of the great court [Note: [Col. 0785D] Perhaps Angilbertus?],

for in you Aaron, once the great priest under Moses,

suddenly comes to life again in our court.

You bear the ephod, the sacred fire for the altars;

with your mouth you bear the key of heaven, and with your hands the chapel.

You always defend the people from the enemy with prayers.

[Col. 0785D] Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Thyrsis loves verses; let us sing songs to Thyrsis,

for lofty faith shines in his gray-crowned head.

Therefore Thyrsis’s love shines in our breast.

Gracious faith will also make Thyrsis dear to David.

Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Vidus [*madidus*, “wet”] Menalcas will come from the rain-bearing mountain,

[Col. 0786A] so that he, worthy of the court’s love, may read these verses.

Worthy love glows in the poet’s heart [Note: [Col. 0785D] Perhaps “of the poets,” as above.] of Menalcas.

Rise, my dear ones, etc., as above.

Now run, little letter, through David’s sacred palace,

and humbly carry greetings to all my dear ones,

always giving kisses to friends with sweet effort,

and, prostrate at the feet of my David,

quickly unfold your songs; say ten times a thousand greetings,

and give sweet kisses to the sacred toes of his feet.

Thus turn yourself to bring greetings to my dear ones,

and run through the chambers of the girls while singing,

and seek out the most illustrious camp of young Julius . . . [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Julius*. So the manuscript reads; perhaps Charles’s or Pippin’s. Poem 256, col. 796, is addressed to Julius and Lucia.],

and proclaim to the youth manifold praises in song.

And then hasten to the sacred chapel,

so that you may carry peaceful greetings in your mouth to all.

[Col. 0786B] And whoever faithful person meets you on the roads—

man, father, or perhaps brother, young or old—

always carry the consecrated olive of peace in your mouth.

Say: “Homer loves your salvation through the ages.

May almighty God always preserve you everywhere.

May Christ also preserve you, David, forever.

David, our love, David, dear above all,

David loves poets; David is the glory of poets.

David loves Christ; Christ is David’s glory.”

After this, run quickly through the pleasant gardens,

where Homer once lived with the boys.

Look at the life-giving flowers from the beautiful grass;

see whether they are doing well, whether they are growing with joyful shoots,

unless the devouring enemy breaks them with hostile hand.

Let them be surrounded everywhere by the firmest hedges.

[Col. 0786C] If the house, the boys, and the roofs of the houses flourish,

you will offer joyful praises to God, if you find everything prosperous,

and say to the boys: “Guard the camp faithfully, I beg,

until the poet Homer comes to you.

May neither devouring flame nor thief destroy anything

within these fences, with the highest Thunderer showing mercy.”

And you, my boys, fare well, dear beloved ones of the poet,

and carry my songs to my sweet David.

David loves poets, and the rest as above.

David loves Christ, as above.

## CCXXXIII. Complaint to the same because lodging was refused.

[Col. 0786D] Snow falls from heaven, and icy rain rushes down as well.

There was no one for Albinus in the city who would say, “Wait [Note: [Col. 0786D] The sense is: “who might have said: Wait a little, etc.”] a little,”

and, when he had said so, “until the rain passes,”

“restore your breast with the warm front of paradise” [Note: [Col. 0786D] The passage is corrupt.].

The saddened old poet departs with an empty stomach,

and the sad boys mourned Flaccus in song.

Therefore let the cold pipe keep its song to itself;

let it merely stammer these few songs with its mouth:

“David does not care for songs, nor does Delia care” [Note: [Col. 0786D] *Delia*. He seems to address the daughter by this name in the following poem.].

[Col. 0787A] When Phoebus’s good warm seasons return again,

Flaccus’s former strength quickly returns to his song;

then he will rush more joyfully upon David in the songs of the Muses.

Now there is peace, life, and salvation for David; then there will be battles for the Muses.

## CCXXXIV. Perhaps to Charlemagne’s daughter.

Nor did you, daughter, care for your own Flaccus:

behold, your poet departs trembling throughout his whole body,

barely sounding a verse of Virgil in silent song:

“About me are a powerful wind, snow, and storm everywhere.”

Nevertheless, you will be able to purge this injury by praying.

If the master Regenberctus can serve [Note: [Col. 0787D] Perhaps: “if you can preserve”] [Note: [Col. 0787D] *Regenberctus*. Mabillon reports that a teacher of this name, *Regimbertus*, existed at the beginning of the ninth century in the monastery of St. Gall, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 284.],

preserve him—thus, for your patron and great bishop—

with strength and hands, with axe, trowel, and shovel;

then let the rest of his company proceed at once against the people [Note: [Col. 0787D] Perhaps: “of the people.”],

[Col. 0787B] while he alone attends to the work with his gray-crowned head.

May you always prosper, my Delia, in accomplishing this, I ask.

## CCXXXV. To the same.

Whatever you desire may come, take care that you do not come [with] the letter,

lest the dire *sospita* [reading and sense uncertain] drown your Muses.

When Moses divided the sea with a blow of the staff,

say once or twice if he himself strikes his breast.

Albinus has added gifts to David’s gifts;

may Christ add gifts to him as well.

May he add two songs to his songs;

may good God always increase all his gifts for him.

And may he make you, my daughter, flourish with gifts,

and flourish eternally, dearest of David’s offspring, with gifts:

may all you faithful ones flourish.

Now greetings, farewell, prosper, and hail—farewell!

## CCXXXVI. Prayers for the royal family.

May Delia, with her learned-sounding grammatical plectrum [Note: [Col. 0787D] The sense is incomplete.],

flourish, so that your heart may flourish everywhere in studies.

Life and salvation to all girls, with the Lord’s gift,

and may something perpetual [Note: [Col. 0788D] Something is missing.] endure for long ages.

Happy indeed is the Father who produced such flowers,

offspring bearing the world’s distinguished titles.

May the right hand of the highest Father preserve equally

the daughters, sons, and father, and protect and guide them.

## CCXXXVII. Address to the Muses on behalf of a royal boy [Note: [Col. 0788D] Perhaps Pippin or another son of Charlemagne.].

[Col. 0787D] Go on, Pierian Muses, and with your musical thumb pluck flowers

that grow beside the clear-flowing streams,

so that you may make garlands of salvation for the royal youth.

As he shines throughout with various virtues,

renowned for ancestral nobility and praiseworthy throughout the world,

so run through the flower-bearing meadows of honor.

Crown his youthful head with a Castalian garland;

let the crown of virtue shine with rosy honor.

There too, gathering lilies of wisdom, let it shine.

[Col. 0788A] Let the brilliance of justice vary across his temples like violets,

and let modesty, golden-yellow and bashful, gleam upon his face.

Adorn the youth with such garlands, Camenae.

Behold, most illustrious of young men, I have wished to touch your ears

a little with my versifying plectrum,

and to entrust you to the Muses’ perpetual greeting.

Would that you might flourish through the ages with flower-bearing scepters,

and, joined to God, possess the heavenly kingdoms.

## CCXXXVIII. Concerning Richbodo, to Angilbertus.

The little servant Richbodo [Note: [Col. 0788D] *Richbodo*. Surnamed Macarius, to whom Alcuin wrote letters 169, 170, 171, and 172. As we have already noted elsewhere, Angilbertus is also addressed by the name Homer.] offered to the high-throned One the small gifts

which you see, reader, in the sacred church,

for forgiveness of sins and for love of the heavenly life.

For him, whoever you are who read, pour out prayers to the Lord;

for you and yours, beloved brother, may you pour out the prayers,

[Col. 0788B] so that, when you come to the sacred threshold of the house,

merciful Christ may hear you from the heavenly citadel,

making you, reader, return home in heart.

I beg you, holy Father, humbly through our songs:

remember us; I beg you, holy Father—

sweet Homer, remember the poet Flaccus;

remember him, sweet Homer, I beg, as Samuel did.

Assist the old man through our friends, I ask you;

there is a place, *insenos* . . . assist the old man [Note: [Col. 0788D] The word is corrupt; perhaps *insenes* (“old men”) or *non senes* (“not old men”).]

I have certain faith in you, dearest brother,

that with Christ and the saints salvation is certain for you.

Dying for the world, here hung the life of the world;

the wave of this blood washed away every sin.

While you bow your head, he raises the world above and lifts it to the stars,

and, wondrous to the ages, your death was life.

The sacred Lamb who led the people through the sea

now more fully saves his own world from the enemy.

Behold the bronze serpent that heals the wounds of the people;

now look upon the sinner with a devout mind.

## CCXXXVIII bis. Flaccus to Homer [Angilbertus].

While the swan is accustomed to preserve its customary songs,

and the cuckoo knows how to have its own sounds,

while the sea, while the fountains, while the stars each preserve

their proper course under God’s guidance,

why should Flaccus suddenly keep his songs silent for Homer?

Why should the son suddenly be silent toward the father?

Alas, why are mouths now mute, deprived of voice,

mouths that once sang honey-sweet sounds?

Venerable love joined us through the bonds of peace;

may our God perfect and strengthen that peace.

God adopts those who make peace into the number of his offspring;

whoever loves peace is himself a son of God.

Bitter resentment, begone; sweet harmony, return.

Let the former perish in flight; let the latter remain, holding its ground.

O sweet love, where shall I now seek you,
