when a son could hate his own father?

[Col. 0789A] But let him return quickly, who can drive away hatred;

let the son himself be joined to his father.

Then Flaccus will be able to compose sweet songs for Homer

in verse, though now he sings only a few.

May Christ God from on high join our love together.

May you, my son, prosper, my sweet Homer.

## CCXXXIX. To Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia.

Dip your reeds, O love, in Christ’s deep waters,

and fill my breast with heavenly songs,

so that I may be able to offer worthy thanks to Paulinus,

who filled our ears with honey-sweet Muses,

and, remembering his like-minded friend after a long time,

repeats in sacred songs: “Albinus, farewell.”

231 How joyful the day was when the page for us

[Col. 0789B] was happy [Note: [Col. 0789D] Salzburg manuscript: “read.”] with the inscriptions of the desired greeting!

All his words flowed for me with the honey of love.

Wherever the joyful eye of the reader turned,

it saw everywhere new joys of its own mind,

especially now rejoicing in paternal prosperity—

may God preserve him healthy forever.

O light of Ausonia, glory of your country, illustrious author,

cultivator of justice, lover of sacred piety,

my mind, bound by sacred chains, burns for you;

it loves, seeks, embraces, attracts, and surrounds you,

and will place you in the eternal archive of its heart.

[Note: [Col. 0789D] The following two poems are joined to the preceding one without division in the Salzburg manuscript, from which we have also corrected several errors.]

## CCXL. [Note: [Col. 0789D] The distinguished Catelinot judged this poem to be Paulinus’s epitaph. A different conclusion is required if these verses are part of the preceding poem, as they are in the cited Salzburg manuscript. Accordingly, I interpret “Here,” “this resting place,” and “this temple” as referring to the archive of the heart, in which he says that he has stored Paulinus in the final verse of the preceding poem. The distinguished Madrisius, in his work on Saint Paulinus, *Life*, chapter 13, no. 11, p. XXXVIII, interprets these verses as meaning: “Would that Paulinus rest here—that is, in the Martinian church—and choose burial there, so that, buried in that same basilica, he might await the resurrection with Alcuin.” Dreams!] To the same Paulinus.

Here may Paulinus rest joyfully through all ages,

and may the worthy Father deign to have this resting place.

[Col. 0789C] May an envious enemy never pass through this temple,

lest he suddenly separate dear friends in spirit,

friends whom Christ’s love joined as dear friends.

## CCXLI. To the same.

O Father Paulinus, shepherd, patriarch, priest,

the better part of life, the illustrious part of our life!

Remember Albinus as you stand at the sacred altars,

and amid sweet tears flowing over your face,

say: “Merciful God, have mercy on our friend,

and graciously grant forgiveness for his sins,

so that he may be permitted to praise you with the saints forever.”

The almighty power of the Father, Christ the Wisdom,

I, poor man, humbly beg you with my whole heart:

[Col. 0789D] may your right hand always preserve Paulinus,

protect and guide him, and adorn him with flowers of virtue.

[Col. 0790A] And you, Mary, Mother of God, most holy Virgin,

ask every prosperity for my Paulinus, we pray,

so that, filled with Christ’s love, he may prosper and flourish.

You too, beloved company of the saints of the Thunderer [Note: [Col. 0790D] Salzburg manuscript: “of the Thunderer”],

who always kept your ears, thirsting for heavenly instruction,

open, Fathers of the Church,

and now possess the heavenly kingdoms with Christ,

pour out prayers, I ask, for the salvation of my Paulinus,

with devotion to the King supreme above all.

May he prosper and flourish, following Christ’s commands.

And you, most holy offspring of the holy Church,

I pray collectively, with body prostrate upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0790D] The edition reads: “with body prostrate, healthy,”],

[May you care for my Paulinus forever [Note: [Col. 0790D] We restore this verse from the Salzburg manuscript; in the printed editions it was corruptly written: “May you have the dear face of angelic Paulinus forever.”]],

and commend his life to Christ in your prayers,

so that he may prosper and flourish, healthy for a long time.

[Col. 0790B] You who behold the gracious face of the angelic assembly

always in the heavenly summit of the eternal Father,

with outstretched hands, but humble in heart, I ask:

you too defend Paulinus in your prayers,

so that he may rejoice and reign, joined to your honor,

and be present with you in the eternal praises of God,

holding the blessed kingdoms of heaven, happy without end.

I ask you, best Father, to keep these little verses with you,

so that your mind may remember your son through the joyful song [Note: [Col. 0790D] The edition reads: “your inclination.”].

May Christ be your love, your strength, your glory—may everything be Christ;

may he be your way, life, salvation, hope, praise, and everlasting glory.

May he always sound in your mouth and always remain in your heart,

so that with the saints he may grant you the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore remember your son; ask for yourself through him,

the one who may lead you forever into heaven’s court.

[Col. 0790C] And now and always, my, my Paulinus, farewell.

Here we shall end the poem with tears arising [Note: [Col. 0790D] The edition reads: “with tears loved.”],

but we shall never end our sacred love.

## CCXLII. To the same.

Hurry, letter, and carry greetings to Father Paulinus;

say, “Father Paulinus, sweet friend, farewell.”

There is indeed a small door, and a small inhabitant in the house.

Reader, do not despise the nard, small in body;

the nard already gives off a strong scent with its spiked grass.

A remarkable stone bears me to you in a small body.

A small thing, indeed, is the pupil of the eye; look at it:

yet it governs by command the actions of the living body.

Thus little Nardulus himself governs this whole thing for himself.

“Nardulus” [Note: [Col. 0790D] Perhaps “Nardule.”], say, reader as you proceed, “you little one, farewell.”

## CCXLIII. To Theophylactus [Note: [Col. 0791D] This poem appears in the Salzburg manuscript, whose variant readings we have recorded. I find two Theophylacti who lived in Alcuin’s time: one was bishop of Todi, a legate of Pope Hadrian I, who presided over the Council of Calchuth in 788 and was also sent to the Council of Frankfurt in 794. The other was a notary of the Apostolic See, who wrote the letter by which Pope Paschal I granted the pallium to Bernard, bishop of Vienne, in 817; concerning him see Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 441, no. 71, and *Appendix to the fourth Benedictine century*, p. 566. The present poem seems especially to suit this latter man, whom Alcuin compares to the learned scribe by whom the little book of life is written under the apostolic name.].

[Col. 0791A]

Father Theophylactus, honorable teacher of wisdom,

famous throughout the distant world for your excellent praises.

You appear great in the kingdom, renowned throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0791D] Salzburg manuscript: “you appear as the heavenly scribe.”];

the gifts of your heart are new or old.

The greatest city, Rome, head of the world, has you as its teacher;

you always have words of salvation in your mouth.

You are gentle toward all, a teacher of holy piety,

which is accustomed to inhabit your excellent heart.

Into its bosom of love, I beg, receive me also as your friend [Note: [Col. 0791D] Salzburg manuscript: *amictum*, “clothed”],

though I may be unknown, holy man, so that I may belong to you.

For Scripture sings true sacred examples [Note: [Col. 0792D] Salzburg manuscript: “in a true example”]

in song, celebrating the praises of wisdom.

[Col. 0791B] Thus, as new wine, the friend will grow old with you [Note: [Col. 0792D] Edition: “so that our . . . may grow old.”],

and so, because you drink sweetly today, he will be a sweet friend.

Paul, that most renowned teacher of the world, had said:

“Test everything first, and hold fast to what is good.”

I humbly beg you in spirit: do not despise me,

but test me, your brother, with your customary piety.

Indeed, Christ’s generous love is accustomed to exist throughout the world;

it gathers many into its embrace.

Whoever remains in love bears Christ in his breast;

true love is almighty God.

A friend who can be useful is not to be despised;

the one able to be useful is another’s friend.

Thus Christ helped the one groaning from dreadful wounds,

bringing two coins for his care.

With this piety, I beg, receive me as your brother,

for grace has made us brothers in Christ.

[We are illustrious brothers, begotten by one faith.]

I advise you, most illustrious teacher of the world,

to let teaching flow from your sacred mouth.

Let the little book of life be written and sent everywhere,

bearing the pious apostolic name as its title.

Thus your praise increases; thus a great reward will remain

for the supreme shepherd of the Apostolic See.

For his pious love, commend me, brother, I beg [Note: [Col. 0792D] Salzburg manuscript: “we ask you to commend me.”],

so that the Father may commend me to Christ with his own mouth.

Fathers, fare well together always, without end;

may Christ’s right hand protect and guide you.

## CCXLIV. [Note: [Col. 0792D] We present this poem to Archbishop Arno of Salzburg, whom Alcuin customarily calls “Aquila,” as we have seen in the letters, from a manuscript codex of our library at St. Emmeram. The distinguished Mabillon also copied it from there and included it among the *Vetera Analecta*, p. 348 of the later edition.] To Aquila (Arno), bishop of Salzburg.

[Col. 0791D] Across mountains and fields, seek out Aquila, my little letter,

the pontiff of great name and merit;

[Col. 0792A] when you have found him, sing a thousand verses so that he may prosper,

and bid him everlasting farewell on Albinus’s behalf [Note: Ms. reads “on behalf of Albino, his son.”].

Say: “Always remember your own teacher, loving Father,

in your sacred prayers, amid the holy places of the Fathers.”

Say also—say, suppliant, say, I ask you [Note: Ms. reads “say with tears.”—] holy priest:

“Always pursue justice in your speech.”

Let neither worldly flattery nor empty pleasure [Note: Ms. reads “will.”],

nor fear or terror, fall into the chambers of your heart;

but may complete confidence in the life-giving word

possess your heart, filled with love of God.

May your tongue, priest, utter righteous judgment,

so that whatever sounds from your mouth may please Christ.

May the Spirit coming from heaven, O bishop,

make your heart glad, dwell in it, sanctify it, and fill it.

The eternal power of God and Christ is more greatly to be feared

than earthly power, which flies away like a shadow.

May the almighty Judge, who grants rewards to the righteous,

give you words of holy peace in your mouth.

The times are now exceedingly full of various dangers,

which the holy Fathers once foretold.

The ages of men, their morals and actions, are changing,

and life will quickly flee like passing moments.

The day itself does not return, nor the month, night, hour, or year,

but, fleeing, it will flee like flowing water from a spring.

Grievous times mingle with our joys;

and as night and day take their turns,

joys now come, and sorrows immediately come as well:

no one remains as he was; every person will pass away.

O Father, therefore, while you have time,

do with mind, hand, and tongue whatever pleases God.

[Col. 0792C] Let your mouth sound the praises of Christ and speak the truth,

and let your whole heart be fragrant with love of God.

Let all the actions of your body now attend to good things,

and let your limbs, night and day alike, please God.

May you please Christ, the great Judge, in your entirety,

so that God may preserve you always and everywhere.

I ask you, illustrious bishop, remember your teacher [Note: “Your teacher” … From this it may be conjectured that Arno was Alcuin’s disciple.],

in your prayers and tears, amid the holy places [Note: Ms. reads “the holy places of the Fathers.”],

so that the merciful Christ may grant forgiveness from his throne

for the wicked deeds of his sinful life, I pray.

Farewell without end, shepherd, patriarch, priest;

may Christ be your love, light, way, life, and salvation!

### CCXLIV bis. To Aquila.

[Col. 0792D] Dip your pen once, Charity, in Christ’s flood,

and make a few verses for my Aquila,

[Col. 0793A] whose whole heart burns with love of the Father,

and whose name sounds from his mouth at every hour.

May God grant him eternal salvation through the ages,

protect him, exalt him, make him fruitful, and give him vigor.

My mind burns, bound by sacred chains,

and surrounds, seeks, loves, and remembers him.

May a third Albinus be joined to you as a friend,

and let him echo sacred tears in his mouth.

For a threefold cord is not easily broken,

and so firm love flourishes among three.

Where three are gathered together in Christ’s name,

there Christ himself, merciful, stands among them.

Remember this, men, and fare well through all ages;

may I soon see you joyful, if God has mercy.

Then all the hairs of body and head

shall sing joyful songs with a Pierian plectrum.

Neither Orpheus nor Linus, nor Maro, surpasses me in songs,

while I clasp your breasts with my hands.

### CCXLV. To a certain bishop.

May Christ, most dear bishop, preserve you safe for me,

mercifully always and everywhere, I pray.

You are my sweet love, you are the song in my heart and mouth;

remember me, and farewell without end!

### CCXLVI. To a certain bishop.

Let no hand unbind … [Note: Perhaps “unfasten the letter.”] except yours, O bishop.

Hail [Note: Perhaps “Unseal.”], holy Father, and read it happily.

Let him who desires to know hidden things unfasten what is bound [Note: “Bound,” that is, the letter. I think this is related to what Blessed Alcuin cited in Letter 187 concerning “the Bound One” from Epictetus.],

yet no right hand except yours, holy Father.

### CCXLVII. To Bishop Macarius [Note: This Macarius is Richbod, bishop of Trier; see above.].

These gifts I have devoted to you, shepherd Macarius;

with Christ and the saints, farewell without end!

Remember Albinus, and may Christ’s grace remember you;

and you, my black one [Note: “My black one.” Alcuin also calls Adalbert “the Black,” but simultaneously “the Great,” in Letter 91.], be white before God.

Why are you silent, my black one? Of you now I know something … [Note: Perhaps “anything.”]

Or, behold, let God be all love for you [Note: Edition reads “lover.”].

May “potus dippeus” be to you, O king, life and salvation [Note: The sense is corrupt.];

may his praise always resound in your mouth.

As I instructed you, instruct our people of Berg [Note: Berg. In the district of the Meuse, on the Roer River, where it joins the Meuse at Roermond, there was a monastery called Berg, mentioned by Brower in book eight of his *Trier Antiquities*. There it is said that King Lothair gave this place to Hunger, bishop of Utrecht, in the third year of his reign. Mabillon conjectures that Alcuin is referring here to this monastery, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, book XXVI, p. 323, no. 52.],

and let the one who greatly pleases you learn with you.

### 233

These ten commandments, which the little letter sings to you [Note: “The little letter.” This has been lost, unless it is the work *On the Ten Words of the Law* above, vol. C, col. 567],

hold night and day with devout heart, I pray,

and, often remembering us, say:

“Christ, remember your poor Albinus.”

### CCXLVIII. To a certain bishop.

[Col. 0794A]

Beloved bishop, I ask you, traveler, turn aside here;

as a beloved bishop, remember Albinus, I ask you.

O my dear house, sweet and beloved dwelling,

may you always be happy, O my dear house.

Holy wisdom of the Fathers is preserved within these walls;

in you may the holy wisdom of the Fathers be learned.

May you always prosper and flourish, illustrious in these gifts [supplied],

and in the cultivation of wisdom may you prosper and flourish.

May no rustic crowd ever dwell beneath your roof;

may the rustic crowd remain far from your house.

May the grace of Christ always protect and govern you,

and, together with your companions, protect and govern you.

### CCXLIX. Perhaps to the same person.

[Col. 0794B]

Beloved bishop, I ask you, let this little letter go with you;

as a beloved bishop, remember the Father, I ask you.

You are my sweet love, my son; farewell through the ages;

may Christ be your sweet love forever.

May holy words of salvation always resound in your mouth;

may praise of Christ always resound in your mouth.

Give consolation to the afflicted with heart, mind, and hand;

always love Christ with heart, mind, and hand.

Be father, shepherd, patriarch, and priest to all;

be father to the poor, the afflicted, and everyone.

Be the glory of the Church and a model of salvation to all;

be its head and guardian, its glory.

May the highest grace of God accompany you everywhere,

and may the highest grace of God increase through your merits.

[Col. 0794C] Say, I ask you: “Everlasting greeting to the boys, illustrious boy”;

and also say everlasting farewell to Albinus [Note: Perhaps “to Albino.”].

May a joyful day come to us under our name,

and may an eternal joyful day come to you.

Care for me; may Christ care for you everywhere;

I care for you; may you care for me.

### CCL. To Maurus.

These songs, holy boy of Benedict, Maurus [Note: “Boy of Benedict.” Alcuin’s Letter 150 is likewise addressed: “To Benedict, boy of Saint Benedict, Maurus.” Rabanus Maurus also calls himself this in his poem to Saint Martin, the third among his poems, vol. VI, p. 202.],

the poet Albinus has sung to you in little verses,

earnestly desiring in faithful spirit every prosperity for you,

that you may always live happily for God.

For him pour out prayers, with your customary devotion, to the Thunderer,

that Christ may preserve his servant from the enemy.

### CCLI. To a certain friend.

[Col. 0794D]

You too, not because of your merits, but because you are bald with curled hair,

may you prosper and flourish for all time, I pray.

While you pour out tears to the Lord in Benedict’s hall,

remember your own Albinus, sweet friend.

### CCLII. To another friend.

You too, Nave [Note: Perhaps “son.”], farewell, great in faithful mind;

amid sacred words, I ask you, remember me.

Small and insignificant, the limbs of books minister no harm,

if an elevated mind seeks great things through love of God.

### CCLIII. To several friends.

And you, men, brothers, and faithful Fathers, farewell;

may almighty God protect and govern you.

Preserve the commandments of all the ancient Fathers

with every strength, in heart, mind, and hand, I ask.

I beseech you, commend me to Christ in your devout prayers [Note: Elsewhere often “commend”],

so that he may grant me forgiveness for my sins everywhere.

### CCLIV. To Saint Benedict.

O Benedict, greatest shepherd of monks,

rule by your prayers those whom you beget by your words.

Before the Judge’s throne each company of teachers

will lead its own people, whom it begot for the Lord;

then you too will lead your monks before the tribunal

of the high-throned King, loving Father, your own sons.

Therefore assist your people everywhere with your prayers;

may your flock increase in number, beloved shepherd.

The shepherd’s glory now grows from the number of his flock;

behold, preserve your servants by your merits.

### CCLV. To a certain friend.

[Col. 0795C]

The flame of love has penetrated our heart …

and love continually burns with new heat.

Neither sea nor land, mountains nor forest nor Alps,

can obstruct it or impede its way,

so that, loving Father, it may not continually lick your heart,

or wash your beloved breast with tears.

Why, sweet love, do you produce bitter tears,

and why do bitter cups flow from holy honey [Note: Edition reads “bonds”]?

Thus, world, your sweet things are already mingled with bitter ones;

all prosperity quickly alternates with adversity.

All joys are changed into grief that brings sorrow;

nothing is perpetual; everything can perish.

Therefore let us flee you now with all our heart;

and you too, world doomed to perish, flee from us.

Let us seek with all heart, mind, and hand

the delights of heaven and kingdoms that endure forever.

The blessed hall of heaven never separates a friend;

it always possesses what the heart, warm with love, loves.

Father, I beg you, hasten me there with you by your prayers,

where our love will never be separated.

Look with rejoicing, grateful heart, I pray,

upon the little gifts that great love has sent.

For the master had praised two coins,

which the destitute widow cast into the temple treasury.

[Col. 0796A] Holy love is better than all gifts,

and firm faith, which flourishes and endures.

May divine gifts follow you, dearest Father,

and always everywhere go before you together. Farewell!

### CCLVI. To Julius and Lucia.

May almighty God preserve you always and everywhere,

Julius, young man, hope, love, and glory!

Lucia, most illustrious virgin, live happily for God;

forever and eternally, Lucia the virgin, farewell.

### 234

And may my *Mathematica*, a woman mighty in speech, prosper through sweet verses;

you, farewell without end.

### CCLVII. To a departing friend.

[Col. 0796B] May an angel coming from heaven accompany the departing one [Note: Perhaps “the departing man”]

always; go on your ways, sweet friend.

My mind follows you with great love of heart,

earnestly wishing every prosperity for you.

May Christ, who granted you to me as a friend, brother,

preserve you safe for me everywhere,

bringing it about that child and parent alike

may rejoice together in good prosperity.

Because I have not now seen you, you, dearest brother,

I truly confess that my heart grieves exceedingly.

How near you remained, I did not know, as we looked upon you;

now no one has told me except in joy [Note: The passage is corrupt.].

Yet behold, I beg you, always consider me present,

as I shall always consider you present, Father.

May God be present to you and to me at every hour;

may he be merciful and kind, glory, life, and salvation.

May he join together joyfully in heaven

those friends whom holy love joined on earth.

Brother and friend, carry these little verses with you, I ask;

always remember your Albinus, friend.

As you travel across fields, hills, forests, and rivers,

may Christ protect your journey always;

farewell forever through the prayers of the saints,

now and always, sweet friend, farewell!

### CCLVIII. Perhaps to the same person.

Run, brother, along the narrow path, beautiful through its track [Note: Ms. reads “narrow”],

which leads you beneath the Lord’s roof into his hall.

Perhaps your feet will not be splashed with filthy mud,

nor will the blue rain pour upon your hair.

[Col. 0796D] The force of winds does not disturb you, nor hail in storms;

nor fear, nor robbers at your throat who would strip away your garments,

nor lion nor tiger … nor a boar: both are seen [lacuna];

nor does a serpent or basilisk or snake strike down the traveler.

But you will be able to run safely along the road.

Therefore let divine praise resound in your mouth,

and carry Christ in your peaceful heart as a devout man.

May he govern your steps, thoughts, and words;

may he be your guide, path, ruler, love, and protector everywhere.

May he lead you safely and bring you back as you travel.

### CCLIX. [Note: From a manuscript codex of Salzburg.] Sighs for an absent friend.

[Col. 0797A]

Sweet love mourns the absent friend with tears,

whom a distant land denies to my eyes.

The rarity of human faith has made dear friends;

many thousands stir within the heart; he alone will remain.

He shines better than silver, more precious than refined gold,

and brighter than all treasures.

My whole desire of mind longs for and seeks him,

to have him, hold him, love him, and honor him.

Behold, you will be joined to me by great love;

you are the rest of my mind, you are my sweet love.

May God preserve you forever through eternal time;

always and everywhere remember Albinus, and farewell.

### CCLX. [Note: In Quercetanus’s edition these verses were previously given separately above as nos. 208 and 222; see our annotation there. They seem to belong to the year 781, when he was prefect of the Palatine school. See the notes to Letter 162.] To the Brothers at York.

[Col. 0797B]

Now the cuckoo has resounded also in the high branches;

the flower-covered, many-colored earth will soon put forth its shoots.

The vine that bears Bacchus’s fruit puts forth buds from its branch [Note: Ms. reads “pushes forth”],

and the tireless nightingale rouses our minds

with varied melody among the shining thorns.

The sun crosses the middle of the star-bearing sphere,

and Phoebus, shining, has overcome the realms of darkness;

and, floating across the waters of the great sea toward you,

a letter from Father Albinus brings greeting.

You sacred youth dwelling within the walls of York,

therefore, I think, it is permitted to summon the plectrum of Maro,

and suddenly awaken the sleep-bringing songs from your mouth [Note: Ms. reads “rouse”],

[Col. 0797C] and fill the bridled ships with sacred songs [Note: Ms. reads “of the Frisians.”].

For such gifts please your Father,

who now sounds forth noble arts in royal ears

and leads the following Fathers through the meadows,

reigning beneath the splendid crown of lofty wisdom.

You too, youth greatly beloved by the Father,

offspring of life, every glory and honor of your homeland,

happily make use of the heavenly gifts of wisdom,

so that reward and glory may always remain yours.

May drunken Bacchus not cast chains upon you,

nor the baneful one erase the arts inscribed upon your minds;

nor may that wicked boy from Crete, armed with sharp goads,

drive you away from the citadel of salvation.

Nor may the wandering world snatch you through empty things,

submerging your life-giving hearts in a black whirlpool;

[Col. 0797D] but, mindful of the commandments of holy salvation, preserve them,

always sounding Christ forth in your sweet-speaking mouths.

May he be your food, drink, song, praise, and glory, I ask,

he who grants you blessed kingdoms

and forever joins you to his saints through the heavens.

### CCLXI. [Note: We have added variant readings from the Salzburg manuscript. The learned Catelinot wishes these verses to be understood of the Saxons, converted to the faith after a war lasting thirty-three years, though he offers no reason. It seems to me much more likely that Alcuin wrote to the peoples of the province of Gothia, neighboring the Saracens and conquered by Charlemagne, and encouraged them against their nearby enemies.] To the nation of the Goths.

[Col. 0798A]

Holy nation of the Goths, holy [Note: Salzburg Ms. reads “Good nation of the Goths, always”], farewell without end;

chosen people of the Lord, illustrious nation, hail.

You have conquered many nations, especially in victorious wars [Note: Salzburg Ms. reads “splendid nations”;]

now conquer the enemies of Christ

by the shield of faith and the strong weapons of salvation.

The merciful God will be your helper everywhere,

if firm faith now dwells within your hearts,

and noble works follow the good gifts of faith.

Read through these little letters, I ask, with peaceful understanding,

which holy love has now sent to you.

May God of Olympus grant every prosperity to the Goths,

granting all the good joys of the eternal kingdom;

and, mindful in your devout prayers, we ask,

remember Albinus, who wrote such things to you.

### 235

May almighty God preserve you wholly for eternity,

granting you an eternal kingdom through the ages [Note: Edition reads “will grant.”].

### CCLXII. [Note: Perhaps to Osulf, whose unhappy fall he laments in Letters 206, 207, and 208.] To an exiled son.

Why, I ask, son, are you angry with your loving father,

as you now undertake the long-desired journey?

You depart sadly and leave your father sorrowful,

as though guilty; behold, I am judged the culprit.

I said nothing in an angry, heated heart;

I instructed you to speak peaceful words.

Use those possessions happily as your own;

for mine are yours—may yours, I ask, be mine.

### CCLXIII. To a disciple.

[Col. 0798C] Behold, your Albinus, rescued from savage waves,

has come, with God of the high throne now showing mercy,

desiring you—“apel-peregrinus-lare,” a corrupt and uncertain reading—with the Muses,

O Corion, Corion, exceedingly sweet friend.

Whatever you fly through the great palaces of kings,

like a winged creature playing over the sounding sea,

you who in your earliest years sucked the books of wisdom

with your milk, and the sacred breasts with your lips,

while, as your age grew greater through the years,

you became accustomed to take solid food into your heart.

You drank strong Falernian wine from the treasures of the ancients,

and everything was accessible to your understanding.

Whatever the Fathers had discovered in ancient times,

your noble and comprehensive intellect opened up to you;

[Col. 0798D] and divine Scripture became clear through your speech,

while your voice resounded in the sacred halls.

Why should I now recall your scholarly songs as a poet,

when you were able to surpass all old men?

Your whole inward being and your hair sang;

now your tongue is silent. Why is your tongue silent?

[Col. 0799A] Perhaps your tongue is no longer able to sing songs?

And, I think, your tongue sleeps, Corion.

My Corydon himself, once a scholar, also sleeps,

lulled by Bacchus. Woe to you, Father Bacchus!

For you seek to overturn sacred understanding,

and make my Corydon silent with his mouth.

Drunk, Corydon wanders through palatial halls,

remembering neither Albinus nor himself.

He sent no welcoming songs to the Father as he came,

to sing “hail”; yet to you, behold, farewell!

“Corydon is rustic,” perhaps the prophet Virgil once said—

“Corydon is rustic.”

But another poet, Naso, said it better [Note: Edition reads “Nassa”]:

“Corydon is a presbyter; may he always receive greeting!”

### CCLXIV. [Note: From a Salzburg manuscript codex.] To another disciple.

[Col. 0799B]

Now in a two-footed poem

we shall sing sweet praises

to you, my trusting,

dear son,

with a faithful heart.

Farewell with certainty!

Always and everywhere

may Christ be for you

peace, way, and strength.

Be full

of his love,

behold, we pray.

May he also always

protect you

at every hour

and moment,

so that no one

may be able to harm you.

[Col. 0799C] Curved old age

certainly draws near,

and the crown of your head

shows white signs;

perhaps your final destiny

is now at hand.

Be ready,

behold, we pray,

to go forth

to meet the Almighty,

rejoicing in heart.

Peace be always with you,

[Col. 0799B] dear faithful one,

trusting son,

first in love

and in the fatherly

sweet love

of discipleship.

And you, sacred treasury

of wisdom,

ark of faith,

and trumpet of life,

herald of salvation,

first in the hall—

may your voice

open to the people

the highest gates

of Olympus,

and the temple of light,

where blessed praise

resounds to Christ.

[Col. 0799C] Sing this poem, I ask, with your mouth;

hold it in your mind,

and remember

the Father, I beseech you;

and may you be blessed

forever and ever.

May Christ’s grace,

the glory of heaven,

perpetual life,

and peace

always accompany you.

## EPITAPHS

### CCLXV. [Note: Gislebert, abbot of Elnon or Saint-Amand, became bishop of Tournai and Noyon and seems also to have retained the administration of the aforesaid monastery, as was then customary for abbots elevated to the episcopate, as Mabillon notes, vol. II of the *Benedictine Annals*, book XXV, no. 31. He died in 782, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the church of Saint Peter on the right side of the presbytery. Bouquet, *Writings of the History of the Franks*, vol. V, p. 410.] Epitaph of Bishop Gislebert.

Here Gislebert, the bishop, rests buried.

[Col. 0799D] Earth covers his body; his spirit seeks the stars.

[Col. 0800A] A man powerful in piety, humble, modest, and honorable,

an exceedingly devoted shepherd, in honor of God.

Here this devout man built the church of Saint Amand,

and, renewing everything, restored the monastery’s entire cloister.

### CCLXVI. [Note: Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis near Paris, died in 784. His body was buried in the church of Saint-Denis and then transferred to the cell of Lebrah, or Lièvre. Bouquet, *Writings of Gallic History*, vol. V, p. 410.] Epitaph of Abbot Fulrad.

An outstanding and highly venerable presbyter and abbot,

energetic in action and work, devout in heart and mind.

Fulrad rests in this tomb in body,

known far throughout the world, our Father in the world.

This illustrious man was pastor of the sacred chapel [Note: “Pastor.” Mabillon, vol. II of the *Benedictine Annals*, book XXV, no. 43, reads “guardian,” which is better; for Fulrad was chaplain to King Pippin and his sons. Read more about him in the same author.];

here he was the Church’s glory, ready for every good.

### 236

This holy house of God was renewed with great splendor,

as you see, reader, in its own time.

[Col. 0800B] He loved the devout Fathers with great love,

whose relics this holy house contains.

Therefore we believe that he was joined to them in heaven,

since on earth he always loved them.

### CCLXVII. Epitaph of Abbot Maginarius.

May your rest now be beneath the feet of your master, Maginarius [Note: “Master.” The sense is: “Here, Maginarius, may your rest be beneath the feet of your master Fulrad.” Maginarius was Fulrad’s disciple and later succeeded him in governing the monastery of Saint-Denis; after a short period, he died in 793, after eight years, and obtained rest or a tomb beneath his master’s feet. Mabillon, vol. II of the *Benedictine Annals*, book XXV, no. 43, p. 270.],

when sacred rest has already overtaken worldly times.

That devout Father nourished you from tender years;

you too were his successor in honor.

Alas, for a short time you governed this flock;

evil death carried you away amid the flowers.

But he whom Christ loves will be harmed by no death;

after death he lives better in heaven’s citadel.

Therefore live for Christ in your morals [Note: Read “in holy things.”],

I beg you who wish to read these verses of ours [Note: Ms. adds “these”].

I beseech you, commend me to Christ in devout prayers,

so that I may deserve to be a citizen [the place has “citizen” instead of “citizens”] of God’s city.

### CCLXVIII. [Note: Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XXVI, p. 321, calls this epitaph very rough. Nothing is known about this monk Paul beyond what is related here.] Epitaph of Paul, monk of Saint Martin at Tours.

Whoever you are, traveler, who wish to know the resting places of the brothers

and the places toward which each one looks from heaven’s citadel,

go on, reading the names written in tearful songs,

and, when you have read them, pour out prayers to the Lord.

May the merciful Almighty defend their souls from the enemy,

granting a blessed day of peace in heaven’s citadel.

And when you come to these verses of mine, I ask,

say in supplication: “God, now have mercy on wretched Paul!”

And Martin, glory of the world, our excellent Father,

[Col. 0800D] assist with your prayers, I beg you, and with prayers.

[Col. 0801A] I was always devoted to you while alive through love,

and my sacred hope was in God through Christ.

I was called Paul, servant of gracious Martin [Note: Edition reads “with fringes.”],

and my time in the world passed by briefly.

Fortunate Burgundy first saw me

poured forth in my mother’s womb and watered with tears.

Soon the illustrious author Martin, my beloved,

after my tender years, took me as his servant.

Through his revered servants and teachers

he imbued me with Scripture and sacred learning.

As a new guest in the world, I lived through seven decades,

always joined to them in brotherly love.

I was weak and ill, until I paid my debt,

and my soul itself left its limbs.

I was soon buried here by brotherly hands;

[Col. 0801B] this is my perpetual home and rest.

May the Almighty command souls to return eventually

to their ashes; then I shall be Paul again.

Now, brothers, commend my soul to Christ in your prayers,

and you, my brothers, farewell always and everywhere in God.

### CCLXIX. Epitaph of a certain person.

I ask you, traveler, pause here briefly as you come,

and examine my words with your heart.

So that from my image you may recognize your own fate:

see how my appearance is changed, and so will yours be.

What you are now, I once was—a traveler famous in the world;

and what I now am, you too will be.

I pursued the world’s delights with empty love;

now I am ash and dust, food for worms.

Therefore remember to care for your soul

rather than your flesh, since this remains and that perishes.

Why prepare fields for yourself, when you see me sleeping

in a small chamber? Such will your rest be.

Why clothe your body in Tyrian purple [Note: Perhaps “allow”],

when soon a hungry worm will feed on it in the dust?

Look: I who once shone with gems and gold

lie here in the tomb, dirtier than filth.

As flowers perish when threatening wind comes,

so all the glory of your flesh was like this [Note: Perhaps “has fled.”].

Reader, I ask you to return this poem’s favor to me,

and say: “Christ, grant pardon to your wretched one!”

### CCLXX. [Note: Compare this poem with chapters 24, 33, and 34 of the metrical *Life of Saint Willibrord* above, cols. 720 and 722, from which this has been pieced together.] On a bishop once of great merit.

This noble priest was of a great family,

but far nobler in his great merits.

He was a man called among the people by the name … [Note: Ms. reads “by the name Wilbrord.”]

A man outstanding in character … [Note: Ms. reads “outstanding among the people.”] and exceedingly beloved by all.

This man of God was patient, moderate, honorable,

outstanding in character and energetic in every action;

devout in heart, humble, gentle, and stern toward the proud,

[Col. 0802A] a comforter to the afflicted, poor for himself, rich toward the needy.

After, perfected by the merits of his life, he had completed

sixteen five-year periods as a priest,

and twelve months; when November was already near, on the eighth day before the Ides he migrated

to heaven’s hall, joined to angelic companies,

praising Christ with heavenly hymns, blessed forever without end.

As he grew great in merits and honorable,

he was an excellent teacher and distinguished bishop,

shining in our midst as a new morning star.

And the peoples whom blind darkness had previously held

he illumined with the light from the highest heaven.

This man of God was patient, moderate, honorable,

outstanding in character, gentle, and devout in speech.

After he had earned many gifts by perfected labor,

with Christ bringing them to completion for him,

then, filled with merits, years, and complete piety,

he rested in great peace, rejoicing.

His spirit happily migrated to heaven’s hall,

holding joys with the saints forever.

## EPIGRAMS AND RIDDLES

### 237. CCLXXI. A living poet after death.

Do you wish to know, traveler, how a poet lives after death?

Behold, I speak what you read; your voice is indeed mine.

### CCLXXII. A bath of hot water.

Let the guest be naked, if he wishes to play with me [Note: Edition reads “may the game be removed”],

and warm his body in my spring.

He who was once a fish, born in cold waters,

will now perhaps be a hot servant to man.

He who once carried wood now travels by wood,

running through meadows, but standing idle in houses.

When the devout guest comes naked into the hot hall,

so that here he may wash his limbs in my springs,

I beg him not to look, but to turn away his eyes;

for the guilty right hand of the first father covered it.

Nature teaches this, and propriety has also persuaded us:

let your face always be modest, boy.

### CCLXXIII. Riddles.

I was the cause of death, yet now I am called nothing [Note: *Malum*, “evil,” “sin.”].

Whoever reads me in the proper order will eat me [Note: *Malum*, “fruit.”].

He may ride upon me who reads me with his mouth turned across [Note: *Mulam*, “mule,” the animal.].

I have six little letters and an excellent power [Note: *Virtus*, “virtue,” “power.”].

Break my name completely in the middle of its course:

one part worships God [Note: *Tus* or *Thus*, “incense”],

the other signifies a man [Note: *Vir*, “man.”].

Let the fourth letter be removed; it will immediately make poison [Note: *Virus*, “poison.”].

There is now a sound man, entirely white-haired [Note: *Sanus*, “sound,” “healthy.”],

formed when the first maternal figure perishes [Note: *Anus*, “old woman.”].

When the two letters after the first perish, there will be a hideous sow [Note: *Sus*, “sow.”].

### CCLXXIV. Another riddle.

A presbyter celebrated Mass with the complete name [Note: *Magnus*, “great.”].

Remove one letter: he provides the feasts of Easter [Note: *Agnus*, “lamb.”].

And he will be a servant if the third is removed, at the table [Note: *Manus*, “hand.”].

And if the fourth is removed, he mixes evil words with poisons [Note: *Magus*, “magician.”].

He will be a thief if the first of the final two is added [Note: *Mus*, “mouse.”].

When the third letter is removed together with the first, strange!

a decrepit old woman runs through the house, leaning on a pickaxe [Note: Edition reads “a decrepit old woman”; F. reads “with a pickaxe.”].

### CCLXXV. Another riddle [Note: We leave its solution to others.].

You who travel the road through the sacred halls, reader,

say: what two monosyllables move entire disputes?

Say: what two pronouns break holy peace?

Say: what two pronouns make all things nouns?

Tell everything that belongs to the verb—which syllable will fashion it?

How does one who never existed speak with you?

Read these things and solve them quickly, or pay a bull to the poet [Note: Edition reads “to the gate.”].

### CCLXXVI. On the nightingale.

O nightingale, what hand has taken you from the thorn bushes [Note: Ms. reads “what right hand has snatched you from me.”],

she was envious of my joy.

You filled my breast with sweet-speaking Muses,

and my grieving spirit with honey-flowing song.

Therefore let flocks of birds come together from everywhere,

to mourn you with me in Pierian song.

Though despised in color, you were not despised in singing;

your broad voice sounded from a narrow breast [Note: Ms. reads “narrow throat.”].

Repeating sweet melody in the Muses’ varied modulation,

you always sang the Creator with your mouth.

Through dark nights your revered voice never ceased

from sacred songs—O glory and adornment!

What wonder if cherubim and seraphim praise the Thunderer

with perpetual voice, since your voice could do so?

O exceedingly blessed is the one who sings the Lord

with such devotion always, night and day!

Neither food nor drink—nor sleep [Note: The word “sleep” is redundant.]—

was sweeter to you than songs,

nor the companionship of another bird.

Nature gave you this, and the merciful Creator of nature,

whom you praised with unceasing voices,

so that you might teach us, buried in wine and sleep,

to break the sleep-bringing sluggishness of the mind.

You did this, unaware of reason and understanding,

by an index of nature noble enough;

all who possess understanding and great reason

would have done this for some time with their mouths!

The greatest reward for the one who praises will remain through the ages,

the eternal King in heaven’s everlasting citadel.

### CCLXXVII. [Note: Mabillon extracted these verses from a manuscript at Elnon in Belgium and published them in the *Analecta*, p. 409 of the new edition, where he noted: “Cuckoo, Menalcas, Daphnin, or Daphnis are assumed names in place of the real ones, as Alcuin customarily uses them; so too Bishop Theodulf of Orléans, who praises the poet Menalcas in book III, poem 3, and suggests in poem 1 that he presided over the royal table. Daphnis was a disciple of Alcuin, the one to whom he dedicated his exposition on the verse ‘Sixty queens,’ etc., in the Song of Songs.” About Cuckoo nothing else occurs to me, except that I think he is the prodigal son, whose intemperance and fall he also laments in Letters 73, 207, and 208.] On Cuckoo.

Let us mourn our sweetest Cuckoo, Daphnis,

whom the cruel stepmother suddenly snatched from her household.

Let us mourn him together with grieving voices;

begin, elder Menalcas, first, I ask you.

Alas, Cuckoo was accustomed to sing for us;

what wicked hour has now snatched you from your own?

Alas, Cuckoo, Cuckoo, in what region did I leave you?

That day was unfortunate for us:

though every human race mourns Cuckoo everywhere,

he is lost; alas, my Cuckoo is dying!

[Col. 0804B] Let Cuckoo not perish; he will come in springtime,

and, coming, will stir joyful songs for us.

Who knows whether he will come? I fear he has been submerged in the waves,

carried away by whirlpools and drowned in the waters.

Woe to me if Bacchus has plunged Cuckoo into the waves,

Bacchus who snatches young men into his deadly whirlpool.

### 238

If he lives, let him return and come back to the nourishing nests,

and let no raven tear Cuckoo apart with its savage claw.

Alas, who has snatched you, Cuckoo, from your father’s nest?

Alas, he has snatched you away—I do not know whether he will come.

If you care for songs, Cuckoo, while you are able to run,

your young Daphnis longs to have you.

The springtime is at hand, Cuckoo; now break your slumber.

Both the elder and Father Menalcas long for you.

At last, [Note: Perhaps, “while they pour forth.”] the young oxen of our book’s meadows,

[Col. 0804C] alone the cuckoo is absent; who, I ask, is feeding him?

Alas, wicked Bacchus, that impious one, feeds him badly,

who seeks to turn all hearts perversely beneath the whole sky.

Mourn the cuckoo now; mourn the cuckoo now, all of you:

he departed rejoicing; I think he returns in tears.

Yet I wish that we might have the cuckoo, tearful though he is,

and that we too might mourn together with the cuckoo.

Mourn your misfortunes, illustrious boy, mourn them with tears;

your whole heart mourns your misfortunes.

If hard flint did not give you birth, mourn, we beg you;

perhaps, remembering yourself, you are able to mourn.

The sweet love of a child compels a parent to weep,

when the child is suddenly snatched from his embrace.

When a brother loses his beloved blood-brother,

[Col. 0804D] what can he do now but himself continue to weep?

Once we were three, whom one spirit joined together;

now scarcely two remain together—the third has fled.

[Col. 0805A] Alas, he has fled, he has fled; therefore bitter lamentation

now remains for us, while the dear cuckoo departs.

Let us send songs after him, songs of mourning;

I think songs perhaps draw the cuckoo back.

May you always be happy, wherever you depart;

remember us, and always fare well everywhere!

## CCLXXVIII. [Note: Mabillon published this poem from the manuscript codex of St. Emmeram in *Veterum Analectorum*, new edition, p. 409.] The Fable of the Cock

The bird is called by its proper name “cock”;

it announces the light and strikes the shadows from the earth.

It distinguishes the hours, girds itself at the loins;

under its authority the flock of hens is governed.

Praising it, God says that it possesses understanding,

since it distinguishes the hours beneath the dark veil.

Alas! once, while hastening far away, the barriers of the paths

[Col. 0805B] hemmed it in as it sought food with its beak.

Thus, while wandering alone in search of nourishment,

alas, strutting boldly, excessively audacious and very proud,

it is caught by a lurking wolf. Pressed down by his weight,

it immediately found this means of escape:

“O most powerful wolf, your fame has often come to my ears,

and an unknown rumor has told me that your great

voice gives forth a mighty sound in clear harmonies.

Yet I do not grieve so much because I am devoured by your hated mouth

as because I am deprived of the opportunity to learn from you

whether what I was permitted to believe was true.”

The beast, credulous of the voice, and the wolf, swollen with delight

at the praise offered to him, opens his infernal throat

and spreads wide his greedy jaws, opening the innermost chamber

of his immense cavern.

[Col. 0805C] But the winged herald of the light swiftly snatches himself away,

leaps forth, flies, and quickly clings to a branch of a tree.

Soon, therefore, having gained sudden freedom

and sitting high above, he utters this song:

“Deservedly is deceived anyone who takes pride in vain,

and is caught without food by false praises,

while he attempts to scatter empty words before his meal.”

This concerns those who, although they themselves are a fable, having obtained the work of salvation by right, are deprived through dark deceits while heeding false, hollow airs of rumor.

## CCLXXIX. Recommendation for a Certain Brother

Whoever reads this, let him say: “Christ, I beg you, protect Alcuin.”

Beloved company, noble offspring of the father,

receive this brother, whom I have sent with kindly intention.

## CCLXXX. [Note: Alcuin wrote this poem, as is evident from its context, to Higbald, bishop, and the brothers of the church and monastery of Lindisfarne, on the occasion of the terrible disaster inflicted by the pagan Danes, who in the year 793 poured into Britain from the northern region of Germany. “For, running about here and there, they devastated, plundered, or burned everything, and, violating sacred places, slaughtered priests and clerics, and choirs of monks and nuns with savage cruelty. Then, having invaded the island of Lindisfarne, they attacked the church, trampled all the sacred things with polluted feet, [lacuna] dug up the altars, and seized and carried away everything precious.” Moreover, some of the brothers were killed, others drowned in the deep, and some were led away captive or thrown out naked.” Thus Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, book XXVI, p. 308, no. 26, from Turgot’s second book *On the History of Durham*. See also the notes to Letter 9 to the Lindisfarne community.] On the Mutability of Human Affairs and the Destruction of the Monastery of Lindisfarne

[Col. 0805D]

After the first man had left the gardens of Paradise

and, miserable, approached the wretched resources of the earth,

and with his offspring paid the penalty of grievous exile,

because treachery brings wicked thefts [F., “wicked fates”],

[Col. 0806A] mortal life ran through varied misfortunes,

and every human being experienced different days.

By the course of fate, sad things are mingled with joyful ones;

no one’s happiness has had a stable pattern.

No one will always possess happy days,

nor does anyone always hold secure joys for himself.

Nothing remains eternal beneath the lofty hinge of heaven;

everything is changed by varying times.

One day smiles, while another tomorrow will mourn its misfortunes;

a fortunate die-roll will make nothing fixed for you.

Wicked fortune always disturbs prosperity with sorrow,

as the sea’s wave returns in alternating turns.

Now the gracious day sparkles; the dark night will come with shadows.

Spring blooms with buds; winter strikes this beauty.

The starry vault is painted with kindly stars,

[Col. 0806B] which rain-bearing clouds suddenly snatch away.

Even the sun itself, blazing at midday, is withdrawn,

when the south wind thunders from the watery summit of heaven.

As lightning more often strikes lofty mountains,

and flames are accustomed to strike the highest parts of forests,

so very often a sudden ruin will come by evil chance

upon the greatest of great things.

The world itself, destined to perish, has given these examples everywhere,

the world that flourishes in riches and perishes in the sea.

Through the voice of the prophets, throughout the four quarters,

you now see kingdoms already overthrown, as foretold.

Babylon, noble city of the kingdom and foremost power of kings,

powerful Chaldea, has been destroyed.

Persia, distinguished in war and great triumphs,

alas, a single woman has overthrown you with her own arrows.

Behold, envious Fortune carried off Alexander, conqueror of the world, amid prosperity in the flower of India [Note: Perhaps, *invida* (“envious”), referring to Fortune.]

[Col. 0806C] Rome, head of the world, glory of the world, golden Rome—

now only a savage ruin remains to you.

The glory of Castrensis has remained equal to swords;

only a yellow fragment seems inert to the finger.

What should I sing of you, holy Jerusalem, illustrious city of King David,

matched by no place in the world?

In you were God’s temples, worship, praise, glory, and virtue;

in you the holy line of the Fathers remained in triumph.

239 But now, when anyone sees your final state, who can restrain his tears?

A people hostile to God already occupies your buildings.

Alas, Judaea, your inhabitant wanders through your cities;

rare is he, and all your ancient glory is perishing.

The noble temple, venerable throughout the whole world,

which Solomon built, is devoured by Chaldean fire.

Roman power again casts it down in war,

reducing its walls and long-standing buildings to ashes.

Behold, the abandoned house of Shiloh has remained through the ages,

in which the holy ark of the powerful God had been.

[Col. 0807A] Thus every glory that the hand of man has made flees,

and the glory of the ages flies away like a shadow.

As a thirsty man vainly dreams of clear waters for himself,

so a rich man in worldly treasures will be left destitute. [Variant: *dives* / *dites*, both meaning “rich.”]

Why should I unfold at such length the distant times of mourning,

and mourn in song the miserable days of the past?

While the present day suffers worse things throughout the world,

and the wretched world now grieves under domination,

broad Asia groans, pressed beneath pagan chains,

and a people hostile to God crushes and plunders it.

Africa, already the third part of the great world,

alas, is entirely subject to pestilential masters.

The people of the West, once a nation renowned in war,

now also serve hated scepters.

Whatever beauty they possessed, and the temples of the Lord’s splendor,

[Col. 0807B] the pagan hand has devastated and seized for itself.

May this general evil throughout the world lighten

what each person suffers alone, and may each bear it more lightly.

Now the gracious house of God, where Peter, the prince and first apostolic Father, rests in body,

is said to have been devastated by treacherous hands,

when an impious hand carried away the house’s treasures.

Italy had mourned, in the secure time of the Goths [F., “entirely”];

the enemy of God devastated the temples everywhere.

The blood of the saints poured out and now swims in the hall

where formerly the gracious honor of the Almighty had been.

All Gaul had experienced the swords of the Huns for three times three years,

stripped of its possessions.

Churches, cities, villages, castles, and sacred places,

together with their peoples, devouring fire seized.

[Col. 0807C] Why do you permit such things to happen in the world, Jesus?

By your hidden judgment, I cannot know.

Another life [*alia*; variant *altera*] is reserved for your people in the citadel of heaven,

where gracious peace flourishes and no battles occur.

Fire tests gold; temptation purifies the just,

so that the purified soul may seek the lofty stars.

This is the life of the just man: complete testing;

the sacred page has sung this into your ears.

The Father embraces every child born to him with pure love,

yet he will often give that child harsh scourges in sorrow.

Thus almighty God tested the saints through savage blows,

afterward giving them joyful rewards in heaven.

Let not instability, brothers, disturb you, holy men—

the instability of this world, indeed, with its varying whirlpools.

Such was and shall be the order of the changeable age;

no one can place certain trust in joy.

The one who lies in bed once contended in the fields

with stags, because weary old age is now present.

The man who once happily reclined on *Syrano* purple [materially uncertain; perhaps “Tyrian”]

can scarcely cover his chilled limbs with an old cloth.

Long life closes the eyes with dark blindness,

which is accustomed to count solitary atoms.

The right hand that once brandished swords and powerful weapons

now trembles and scarcely brings food to the mouth.

Behold, the once clearer voice suddenly sticks in the throat,

and, with ears inclined, it produces murmurs [Note: A German word: *Leife*, “faint murmurs.”].

[Col. 0808A] What more should I sing? All youth withers;

all bodily beauty now perishes and falls.

Only the empty skin scarcely clings to the bones,

and the old man does not recognize his own limbs.

What one person was, another will be; nor will he himself be what he is:

in changing times he will be his own thief.

Thus the coming day will change minds and limbs—

and would that it advance to something better in merits!

Therefore let us always love heavenly things instead,

and what will remain in heaven, rather than what will perish on earth.

Here time changes; you see that nothing is not mutable.

There one day will always be what it is.

To that place, I beg you, direct your mind, my reader;

there you will find what your heart desires.

There, as a stranger in the world, where your hope never deceives you,

you will behold the homeland that your love desires.

When you arrive there, you will find the good joys of everlasting life,

which you can always possess.

You will be joined forever as a joyful citizen to Christ;

he always remains, and you too will always be.

Why, grievously sad, do you mourn that you have lost gold?

It is better to gain God than gold. [Note: The edition reads *lucrifacere* (“to gain”), for *lucrificare*.]

Why do you pursue empty appearances with tearful complaints, my child?

Why do you desire these things, which are destined to perish?

The lover of the world, not of Christ, now mourns such things;

may it be Christ, I beg, not gold, who is your love.

To you, brothers, I now turn, my concern, my songs;

I shall address you in a few little verses.

You, royal in lineage, venerable offspring of holy parents,

who have already begotten you for God,

[Col. 0808C] now apply your thirsty ears to their heavenly merits [Note: Perhaps, “admonitions”],

with devout heart, mind, and hand.

So that he may always preserve through prayers the holy fold

which they established for God with united hearts.

Let not the dreadful temptation break your minds,

the impious temptation brought against you by an evil hand.

Rather, may it abound in the pursuit of a better life,

and always urge your minds to be present with God,

who raises the fallen, wounds, and heals;

who strikes and heals, crushes and lifts up.

By night and day alike persist in holy prayers,

so that merciful Jesus may preserve you everywhere.

And if there are things that please you, learn them with united heart,

and fulfill by hand what your devout mind desires.

[Col. 0808D] Thus at last a shield descends to you from on high,

and the Lord’s right hand will protect and govern you.

Remember your Fathers, to whom help always came from on high,

when the Thunderer granted his gracious aid.

Now Moses, by prayers more effectively than by the weapons of the army,

with outstretched hands directs the holy battles.

Many thousands of the pestilential people are laid low in death

for the tears of King Hezekiah.

To him also merciful God added fifteen years,

in response to the prayer which, dying, he poured from his mouth to God.

240 I shall sing to you, brothers, things known to you,

which the episcopal head of our church once accomplished:

[Col. 0809A] Long ago, far from the city of Bebba, the flame turned back at the prayers of the distinguished bishop Aidan.

[Note: The text reads *Ledani*. It should be read *Aidani*, or *Edani*, the bishop of Lindisfarne, by which name he is called in the next poem, verse 692. The Venerable Bede relates the same miracle concerning him in book III, chapter 16 of his *History*, as follows: “During his episcopate, the hostile army of the Mercians, under Penda, devastating the regions of the Northumbrians far and wide with impious destruction, reached the royal city, which was called after Queen Bebba, and attempted to consume it with flames. St. Aidan, seeing from the island of Farne the balls of fire and smoke being driven by raging winds above the city walls, is said to have raised his eyes and hands and said with tears: ‘See, Lord, how great evils Penda has done.’ When he had spoken, the winds immediately changed from the city toward those who had kindled them, and turned the fire back upon them, so that some were injured and all were terrified, and ceased attacking the city, since they recognized that it was being divinely aided.” Bebba is today Bamborough, in Latin *Camborra*, in Northumbria, situated opposite the island of Lindisfarne, which today bears the name Holyland, or Holy Island. See La Martinière, *Grand Dictionnaire*, entries “Bamborough” and “Lindisfarne.”]

Eadbert, your pious bishop and father, calmed by his prayers the blasts threatening death.

[Note: Eadbert became bishop of Lindisfarne in 688 and died on 6 May 698. The Venerable Bede discusses him in several places: *History of the English People*, IV.29; *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapters 11 and 12; and the other metrical Life, published by Canisius in Basnage’s edition of *Lectiones Antiquae*, II, p. 5 ff. Henschenius believed that the following verses of that poem refer to Saint Eadbert, *Acta Sanctorum*, II March, p. 108, Venetian edition, no. 40: “The taints of diseases flee; the impious rage of the dark demon ceases.” These words accord well with Alcuin’s present testimony. The Acts of Saint Eadbert are, however, lacking; Bede says that he once wrote them in verse, in the cited place: “[lacuna] I remember that I once recounted in verse the eminent deeds of that bishop.”]

That great father, bishop, shepherd, and priest, Cuthbert,

the glory now of your church,

accomplished many things through devout prayers, with the Lord granting them;

there is no need to recount them in our little verses,

since the renowned master Bede had already explained

the illustrious deeds of that father in heroic verse,

and all Britain celebrates him with frequent praises

and asks him in prayer to aid it devoutly.

These men and the others alike, if you keep their commands and are steadfast always to love God, may protect your fold through their prayers,

[Note: This verse is emended thus because Quercetanus’s edition erroneously read: *Illorum fixos est semper amore Dei*—“Of them is always fixed by the love of God.”]

driving out enemies and fostering your walls.

[Col. 0809B]

You have read, brothers, that what comes later is better than what came before;

so too will it be for you,

if you hope in the Lord with your heart, who afterward

is accustomed to give greater gifts after greater blows.

But you, bishop, successor of the saints [Note: “But you, bishop of the saints,” and so forth. He undoubtedly addresses Higbald, who governed the church of Lindisfarne at the time of that disaster, as is clear from Letter 9, written to him and the whole congregation of the church of Lindisfarne. See also Letter 11 to King Æthelred, and so forth.],

who feed the people and hold the holy places,

are, as I see, weighed down by a great burden of cares,

because such a dreadful blow occurred in your time.

With you I mourn your misfortunes, dearest brother;

my face streams with tears, and my sorrowful heart grieves.

Repeating it often, in such a murmur [Note: Read, “in silent murmuring.”] to myself,

I say to all how greatly that day must be mourned,

on which a pagan hand, coming from the ends of the earth,

suddenly approached our shores by ship,

[Col. 0809C] plundering the venerable tombs of two Fathers [Note: Perhaps, “of your Fathers”;]

and also defiling the temples dedicated to God.

And the purest vineyard of Christ God, Sorek,

suddenly became food for foxes’ teeth;

and the stones around the altars suddenly perished.

Therefore, behold, my lyre groans all the more.

The thing that used to offer gifts

was made a victim; I believe that it too was a devout offering.

That day was fortunate for them, if it made

our hearts sorrowful; thus they sought heaven,

and thus, through sacred blood, became companions of the saints—

they who submit themselves to the sword beneath Christ.

Therefore I think we ought not to mourn them,

whom a better life has snatched for itself into heaven.

Therefore cease, bishop, to mourn them with tears,

whom Christ now has as companions forever.

Rather make yourself ready with every virtue,

so that when you reach the place to which they have gone,

no sorrows may arise.

Illustrious patience grants everlasting life,

as the truthful voice of God itself had promised.

Bear patiently the sad burden of Christ, holy priest;

Job will provide an example, and he himself will be your guide.

[Col. 0810B] Paul too, the soldier of the Church, through a thousand triumphs,

who, strong in mind, did not grieve over his wounds.

What soldier can gain the palm without combat?

Abominable wars will give great rewards to their own.

Through swords, deaths, plagues, weapons, and fires,

the saints seek the blessed kingdoms through martyrdom.

He who conquers in battle now rejoices in the garland of war;

after the wars of earth, he reigns in heaven’s citadel.

If anything displeased Christ, who now sees all things,

correct it quickly in your ways.

So that the gracious shepherd may preserve his distinguished fold,

lest the wolf seize it through swift ambushes.

For God is not to be blamed for these punishments;

rather, our life must quickly be led toward what is better.

And his merciful clemency must be bent by our prayers,

so that he himself may remove the blows from us

and, in mercy, grant his servants consolations,

giving them times in which all things prosper.

Let us all sing joyful hymnic praises, with joyful mind,

always and everywhere together to the One enthroned on high.

To him be praise, worship, honor, virtue, blessing, and song;

always throughout eternity, great glory to God.

## CCLXXX bis. [Note: The poem was taken from the codex of St. Paul’s College; perhaps it is Alcuin’s, though it is burdened with many errors.—Transferred here from the *Addenda* in Frobenius, at the end of volume II. EDITOR.] On the Conversion of the Saxons

[Col. 0811A]

The fifth sad boundary of the world from its beginning [Note: Perhaps, “the fifth age.”]

had been completed, thoroughly corrupted by a harsh mass of disease [Note: Read *tabefactus acerbo* (“worn away by a harsh [mass]”).],

while the dreadful orbit had turned through four limits.

And while the revolving years returned in their daily course,

bringing to the Fathers the shining kingdoms that had been promised,

then the sixth, fortunate cycle began to turn [Text: *capit*; read *coepit*, “began.”],

which at last, after ancient and many ages,

was deemed worthy to receive the foretold coming of the lofty offspring.

The merciful Father, who from his throne looked down upon

the world adorned with pomp, lying beneath harsh death,

and, seeing the human race—which he had once made from clay—

plunged into the deep abyss of the pit,

then the almighty Father, most gracious author of all things,

[Col. 0811B] that pious sower who governs the heavenly sphere,

sent the holy offspring gently from the lofty citadel,

and at once golden light encircled the world.

He removed the dreadful crimes of shameful death,

washed away the world’s crime in the waters of the Jordan,

and marked the devout with the purple of precious blood.

Thus too he snatched the prey from the venom-spitting serpent’s jaws,

and despoiled the hot sands—*quoquidi* (so printed; meaning uncertain);

as a victorious conqueror he returned and went back to his native citadel.

About seven hundred and seventy years had now passed, if I am not mistaken,

as the reckoning, the index of the seven ancients, records;

such are the years now present in the passage of time.

In which year Charles happily reigns for the ninth year [Note: In the year 771 Charles assumed the kingdom alone; in the year 780 many Saxons were baptized, as the annalists report.]

[Col. 0811C] In that time a people sprung from the wicked blood of the Saxons

was deemed worthy to know the supreme King of heaven,

a people that formerly placed filthy, harsh images

in polluted shrines, and, feeding the pyre with swift flames

[Note: The text has *bustim*, in place of *ustim* (“pyre”); see Du Cange, entry “Bustus.”]

regularly slaughtered bloodstained bulls at the altars.

And by bowing their necks in worship of wicked demons,

reverently venerating their nobles and household gods,

while barbaric madness raged through their corrupted innermost being,

the pitiable people prayed according to the fortune of circumstances.

This was a people unlearned in serving Christ on high,

ignorant—for it refused to believe the Lord in its heart—

that he had come into the world for our salvation.

Prince Charles, bravely girded with shining weapons and sharp-crested helmets

[Note: The text has *adcinctos*; perhaps *accinctus*, “girded.”]

subdued this people with wondrous strength, aided by the eternal Judge

[Note: The text has *Arbitris*, in place of *Arbitri* (“Judge”); perhaps *juvatus*, “aided.”]

[Col. 0811D] through various disasters and a thousand triumphs,

through bloodstained shields and weapons of war,

through the power of valor and spears smeared with blood.

He crushed them and subjected them beneath his flashing sword;

he drew the forest bands toward the kingdoms of heaven,

and soon changed savage wolves into tender lambs.

The harsh-voiced crows, stained with dark blackness,

he suddenly transformed into bright white doves;

the winged griffins and flying harpies

he changed into peaceful birds,

and the fierce mastiffs he transformed into fallow deer

covered with soft wool.

The leaping tigers and lions with tawny necks,

just as one would tame a beast,

he enclosed within a more fitting fold.

Then, after sprinkling them with the dew of the saving bath,

under the name of the Father and the Begotten,

under the name of the holy gracious Spirit,

in whom the one hope of our life consists,

he sent these unskilled Christians toward the stars of heaven.

He anointed those washed in holy baptism with chrism,

so that they might now be able to pass beyond the smoking flames,

and he led the new offspring into Christ’s hall.

Moreover, when the Judge enthroned on high and Creator of Olympus

comes to condemn the world with avenging ashes,

and hurls the pestilential vessel, shattered by heavenly lightning

[Note: The text has *fractis*; perhaps *fractum*, “shattered.”]

[Col. 0812B] swiftly, bound, into the Stygian shadows,

and roasts the crafty serpent with a blazing sphere,

so that, suffering without end, it might wither in a pitch-black cauldron

[Note: The text has *marciscat*, for *marcescat*, “wither.”]

then, weighing the merits of all in a three-pound balance,

apportioning milky gifts to the good and sad things to the bitter,

may he meanwhile, in his mercy, grant, as so great a reward for the prince,

that he may possess the prizes of the starry kingdom;

may he taste the sweet pastures of the honey-flowing life—

pastures which our Redeemer long ago promised

from his own mouth to give to the heavenly beings.

## CCLXXXI. POEM ON THE BISHOPS AND SAINTS OF THE CHURCH OF YORK

From a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Thierry near Rheims.

[Col. 0812C]

### 241 PRELIMINARY NOTICE

The most celebrated Mabillon calls the author of this poem anonymous. With the assistance of D. Christopher Daubin, his colleague, he recovered it from a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Thierry, and inserted a fragment of it—omitting the portions borrowed from the Venerable Bede—in the *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, century III, part II, pp. 558 ff. For the poem’s heading in the aforesaid codex, omitting the author’s name, was as follows: “English History composed in heroic verse by a certain wise man.”

Mabillon later obtained the complete poem and, without doubting its author, published it under the name of Flaccus Alcuin in Thomas Gale’s *History of British, Saxon, and Anglo-Danish Writers*, Oxford, 1691, pp. 703 ff. “Although no mention is made by biographers either of this little work or of its author,” the cited editor says in his preface, “the author himself nevertheless did not wish to remain unknown; for, if verses 1515, 1530, and 1552 are carefully considered, you will infer that Alcuin was the father of this little book, without my needing to discuss at length its style, agreement of period, and other indications.”

[Col. 0813A] The very learned D. Rivet of the Congregation of St. Maur expresses almost the same opinion in volume IV of the *Literary History of France*, p. 333. There he solidly refutes the opinion of Oudin, who, in volume I of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 1923, makes Fridegod the author of this poem solely because the present poem seems to have been written in a harsher style than Alcuin’s other genuine works:

“The mere harshness of style,” he says, “is not enough for anyone to deny that this little book belongs to Alcuin, unless he wishes to deprive him of several poems much harsher still, which no one doubts are his. For some elegant passages occur in it which you would scarcely find in other poems of our poet. Nor does anything occur in this work concerning history that does not fit Alcuin’s age; indeed, the author relates many things that happened more than fifty years before that Fridegod, who first wrote after the middle of the following century, that is, the ninth, could have deserved the name of poet. This is easily demonstrated from what our author relates from verse [Col. 0813B] 1515 to verse 1595.” Thus D. Rivet argues soundly.

Certainly, after our poet had related that there were two disciples of Aelbert, bishop of York, who oversaw the building begun at his command—one Eanbald and the other Alcuin—he goes on to say that he entrusted the episcopal dignity to the former, Eanbald, but to the latter, Alcuin, the precious treasures above all else, namely the care of the library. He further indicates that he himself is the one who placed his own name, as the true author, at the head of this poem. Concerning the disciple to whom Aelbert had entrusted care of the books, he says in verse 1529:

“If you wish to know his proper name,

the present verses will immediately reveal it on their front.”

These points alone are so clear that, once carefully considered, they leave no room for doubt that this poem belongs to blessed Alcuin as its true author. Nevertheless, this may also be confirmed by reasoning drawn from other narratives in the poem, from Alcuin’s letters, and from his Life.

For the author of the poem declares that he was born, raised, and educated at York. Verses 16 ff.:

“. . . Since my mind hastens to sing the praises of my homeland

and to bring forth for a little while its ancient cradles,

in verses about the splendid city of York.”

Verses 1648 ff.:

“Here I, an unskilled sailor, having gathered these things in my little boats,

guiding them through the waves of the sea and across hidden shoals,

brought the merchandise lawfully back to the harbor of York,

since it was she who raised me as her own foster child

and, from my earliest years, however humbly instructed me,” and so forth.

Alcuin makes the same claim about himself in Letter 6, addressed to the brothers of the church of York, where he writes:

“You cherished the fragile years of my infancy with a mother’s affection; you endured the playful time of my childhood with devout patience; by the discipline of a father’s correction you taught me to reach the mature age of manhood; and you strengthened me through instruction in the sacred disciplines.”

242 Moreover, the author of the poem was a disciple of Aelbert, bishop of York, who entrusted to him, in verse 1525,

“. . . the precious treasures above all,

the books.”

And in verse 1532:

“To him he entrusted the display of wisdom, the study, the seat, and the books

which the illustrious teacher had previously collected from everywhere.”

Alcuin openly declares in Letter 56, addressed to Eanbald, that these treasures of books had been entrusted to him by the same Aelbert:

“Praise and glory be to the Lord God Almighty, who preserved my days in good prosperity, so that I might rejoice in the exaltation of my dearest son . . . who was deemed worthy to be the dispenser [Col. 0814A] of Christ’s mysteries, and to labor in my place in the church where I had been raised and educated, and to preside over the treasures of wisdom in which my beloved teacher, Archbishop Helbrechtus [Aelbert], left me as heir.”

The author of the Life relates the same thing in chapter 4, where he writes that after the death of Hechbertus or Egbertus, Alcuin received another father and teacher, Elcbertus or Aelbertus. Under him he advanced so greatly in learning that he surpassed the other disciples in wisdom and virtue; nevertheless, he so subdued the envy which this aroused against him through humility and gentleness that afterward they were even glad to regard him as second only to their teacher Aelbert.

From these arguments, therefore, it seems to me so clear that the present poem is an authentic work of Alcuin that I am confident no one will remain with doubts about the matter.

The most celebrated Mabillon thought this history of the bishops of York had been written around the year [Col. 0814B] 785. D. Rivet, however, in volume IV of the *Literary History of France*, p. 333, wishes to assign it to the year 796, when Eanbald, the bishop of York last treated here, died, and four years after Alcuin returned from England to Gaul in 792. The learned man seems to have been led to this by the following words, verses 1592 ff.:

“. . . while the year

is divided into four parts . . .”

But the excellent scholar is mistaken. Alcuin does not write there about Eanbald’s death, but only about the death and burial of his teacher Aelbert, whom he mourns and whose memory, he says, will never fade:

“While sun and night yield to each other; while the year

is divided into four parts; while the shoots grow in the earth,” and so forth.

## POEM

[Col. 0814C]

Christ God, power and wisdom of the supreme Father,

life, salvation, maker, renewer, and lover of humankind,

only Word of God, gracious giver of gifts,

give gifts to the mind and words to the fragile poet;

water my dull breast with a living stream,

so that my tongue may be able to speak of your gifts.

Without you no tongue can say anything worthy.

You also, citizens of Olympus, I entreat with supplication,
