O saints, mighty people, divine race of the Thunderer,

who carry victorious eagles into heaven’s citadel,

bringing royal gifts to the heavenly King—

he who for your sake willingly shed sacred blood on earth,

so that he might save you from the shadows

and lead you with himself into the hall of God the Father—

[Col. 0814D] bring your feet with me [Note: Perhaps, “prayers”] and join this poem

to your prayers; for my mind hastens to sing the praises of my homeland

and to bring forth for a little while its ancient cradles

in verses about the splendid city of York.

The Roman hand first founded this city high

with walls and towers, employing as companions

and fellow workers only the native British peoples.

(For fruitful Britain then rightly supported Roman kings,

who ruled the scepters of the world.)

It was to be a common marketplace of land and sea,

and to make the power of the kingdom secure for its leaders,

[Vers. 26.] a glory of empire and a terror to hostile arms;

[Col. 0815A] it was to be a hospitable harbor for ships coming from the farthest regions,

ships whose sailor, hastening across the ocean,

might bring his prow to rest after being wearied by the sea.

The fish-filled Ouse [English, Owse] washes it with its waters,

stretching flowering fields everywhere along its banks.

The land here and there is beautiful with hills and woods,

and its noble places have a lovely, healthy habitation,

destined by its fertility to possess many settlers.

For peoples chosen from various nations and kingdoms everywhere

come here, seeking through hope of profit, in a rich land,

wealth, a dwelling for themselves, gain, and a home.

Then, after the Roman hand withdrew, with scepters disturbed everywhere,

wishing to drive away savage enemies

and preserve the kingdom and seat of power in the West,

[Col. 0815B] a sluggish race of Britons held the city’s scepter.

Almost continually oppressed by battles with the Picts,

it finally, devastated, submitted to the burden of servitude;

nor was it able to defend its homeland with its own shields

or recover its ancestral freedom with swords.

There is an ancient people, powerful, distinguished in war and bodily strength,

between the peoples of Germany and the foreign kingdoms,

called by the name of Saxons because of their harshness.

The rulers of the kingdom decided to hire them with gifts,

so that they might be a help to the homeland and a terror to its enemies.

The fickle populace immediately applauds with clamorous voice,

and praises highly the decisions of its fathers.

The royal treasury chambers are broken open;

they prepare to send gifts to the unknown people,

so that the latter may agree more readily

to strike treaties of peace pleasing to themselves.

[Col. 0815C] But they regard such gifts as unworthy of so many vows.

They order ambassadors to depart and already plow the salty shoals

with swift ships; with sweet fear they repeat their vows

with tears, for the love of freedom and the hope

of recovering the homeland itself urged them on.

What more should I sing? Behold, the army came in haste,

carried across the waves of the watery sea,

bringing aid to its allies and driving out the wicked enemy;

it conquered through many battles and triumphs,

until the fierce Pict fled with his trembling host,

content to defend himself within his own shores.

Meanwhile this foreign soldier demands greater pay

for such services; this became the cause of war:

to turn the sword against the allied people

and drive the sluggish population from its ancestral kingdom.

This was seen as God’s doing, because the sinful people,

on account of their fathers’ sins on earth,

was destined to perish, while a happier people entered its cities—

a people that would preserve the Lord’s commands.

This was accomplished in abundance, through the gift of the Thunderer.

While the new scepters now grew strong through frequent triumphs,

and the people destined for God began to have powerful kings of its own,

[Vers. 78.] at that time the gracious bishop Gregory ruled,

venerable throughout the whole world,

and, as the greatest cultivator of the Roman Church’s fields,

devoted everywhere,

he scattered many seeds of everlasting life.

He had not only broken the Latin fields with the plowshare,

but, good and pious cultivator of a foreign field,

he plowed beyond the swelling waters of the ocean,

watering the Gentile hearts with the honey-flowing streams

of the divine word:

from these streams the Britons drank the draught of everlasting salvation,

by Christ’s gift.

Meanwhile Edwin [Note: Edwin, also called Edwinus, son of Alla, king of Northumbria. See Alford, year 617, no. 7 ff.],

sprung from the lineage of ancient kings,

born at York, destined to become lord over all,
Driven into exile [Note: [Col. 0815D] Driven into exile by King Æthelfrith. Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book II, chapter 12.] he fled the envious realms as a boy.

A vision [Note: [Col. 0816D] Ὅραμα, that is, “vision,” as in the *Life of Saint Willibrord*, chapter 2.] which he himself, while still a pagan, had seen from heaven,

[Col. 0816B] When night had fallen into sleep, alone, at a certain time,

Bearing an anxious heart burdened with cares, he went to a suitable place,

And silently sat beneath the dim light of the moon.

An unknown man stood before the young man’s eyes,

Suddenly appearing in dress and face, and addressed him in friendly words:

“What harsh anxiety, bravest of young men, is consuming you?

The eternal God-King, who made the stars of heaven,

Who gives you sure consolations through the beautiful stars that you behold.

Behold, he preserves your life from the enemy who seeks it;

Moreover, he sets the boundaries of a broad empire for you, extending to the sea.

May that God-King always be your God throughout all ages.”

And, placing his right hand upon the young man’s head as a pledge,

“He said: These shall be the tokens of our covenant with you.”

After saying this, the messenger suddenly departed from him.

Strength immediately coursed abundantly through all his veins,

And despair, driven far away, fled from his limbs and left him.

The outcome proved the words of the visitor:

The envious king, who sought both his empire and his life,

Immediately fell by an accursed sword.

Then the young man returned and entered the welcoming cities,

His ancestral cities, received with the favor of the people and nobles.

Soon receiving the honor of royal sovereignty,

He sought the welfare of his own people, generous toward all,

Not fierce through his scepter, but kind through his piety,

Becoming the people’s beloved, his country’s father, and the glory of the court.

By continual triumphs he overcame the hostile camps,

And added all the peoples to his dominion,

Across the borders and regions through which the island stretches far and wide.

Now the people of the Saxons, the Picts, the Scots, and the Britons

[Col. 0816D] were submitting to the king’s yoke with bowed necks.

Meanwhile, while the mighty king ruled his tribunal in the peaceful security of his kingdom,

With wars everywhere put to rest,

He restrained the peoples with the strong reins of justice.

Fury no longer snatched up weapons, pressed beneath the burden of the laws;

For each person feared the avenging swords of execution,

Unless he kept in his whole heart the prudent decrees

Which the ruler had established for his subject peoples to obey.

He took a faithful wife from the southern region [Note: [Col. 0816D] Æthelburh, daughter of King Æthelberht of Kent. Alford, year 616, no. 9 and elsewhere. Bede, Book II, chapter 9.],

[Verse 132.] Eminent in character and illustrious from the origin of her ancestors,

[Col. 0817A] And noble in all the virtues of the holy faith.

She was given an overseer of her honorable life,

Named Paulinus, a most distinguished citizen of the city

Of Rome, supported by the great honor of his merits.

He was truthful in speech and prudent in heart,

A worshiper of justice and a true lover of piety,

A Catholic teacher, dispensing heavenly gifts

To the peoples across the sea, just as the morning star

Precedes the sun’s rising and scatters the dark shadows of night,

Showing the world that the serene day has come.

So that pious father, through the divine light of the word,

Drove the grim shadows from human hearts.

One day, with steadfast courage, he approached the king

And recounted the sign which, as we said earlier [Note: [Col. 0817D] Above, verse 94 and following.],

The father had seen: that, beneath the dark night,

[Col. 0817B] He had seen the young man expelled from his ancestral lands, and had placed his hand upon his head.

The king, terrified and recognizing the signs of the salvation foretold,

Immediately descended humbly from his lofty throne,

And fell at the feet of the venerable bishop, saying:

“Now I shall do everything that I promised,

And, believing in the God of heaven, I shall worship him everywhere,

Who granted me life and the crown of kingship;

For he alone shall be my God throughout all ages.

But now tell us how he is to be worshiped.”

The bishop replied joyfully and readily:

“First, let the foul worship of the gods flee far away;

Let no blood of cattle smoke any longer upon false altars;

Let no soothsayer seek an omen in warm entrails;

Let no most foolish augur observe the songs of birds;

[Col. 0817C] Let all images of the gods be thrown down to the ground.”

Then the pious bishop began to testify openly and steadfastly

To everyone, in due order, concerning the mysteries of the faith,

Until the devout king conceived faith with his whole heart

And persuaded the people to believe in Christ.

Behold, at that time Coifi [Note: [Col. 0817D] In Bede he is called Coifi, in the same book, chapter 13.] was the chief of the priests

And the head of errors. The king said to him:

“Come, priest, take up weapons previously unfamiliar to you,

And be the first to defile the lofty shrine with a spear—

You who were once a teacher of crimes, now become one of salvation.”

The old man agreed to these words and replied briefly:

“Until now my life has hung by an uncertain thread,

And darkness has overwhelmed my mind with doubtful shadows.

From now on I shall follow what is certain, desiring to recognize the truth

And the eternal God; or else, if life ends,

[Col. 0817D] whether future torments await the wicked

Or rewards remain for the just.”

With these words he seized a spear in his threatening right hand,

And mounted a stallion, contrary to his usual custom.

Its mane flew about its neck, and its lofty neck swelled with pride;

Raising its breast, the swift hoof dug into the earth,

And impatient of delay, it shook the bit between its teeth,

Terrible as a Parthian becomes with his curved bow,

Or as one who whirls long spears lightly through the air.

So he himself directed his spear toward the heights of the shrine.

[Verse 186.] O exceedingly fortunate boldness in so great a deed!

[Col. 0818A] Before all others he defiled the altars which he himself had consecrated.

His complete faith became evident; though he had not yet been washed in the font,

He fulfilled the work of virtue through faithful devotion.

Immediately the entire crowd followed the bringer of salvation.

With united strength they demolished and destroyed the little shrine.

Then the structure of the profane temple collapsed,

And, utterly destroyed, crumbled into ashes.

Meanwhile the time of Easter came throughout the world,

When the king and his people resolved to undergo baptism,

Even beneath the lofty walls of the city of Eboracum.

There he quickly ordered a small church to be built,

So that within it he might receive the sacred water of baptism.

When the festival day of that blessed season dawned,

With his children, his leaders, and the people following,

In the eleventh year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0817D] In the eleventh year of his reign. Bede likewise says this in chapter 14, adding that the year was 627. Therefore he assumed the kingship in 616.]

[Col. 0818B] he was consecrated to Christ in the life-giving font

Within the walls of the aforementioned city.

From then on he raised its status higher

And established it as the metropolis of his kingdom.

Thus Bishop Gregory had once decreed,

When he sent the seeds of life from the Roman citadel

To the peoples of the English: he immediately ordered

That this city be regarded as the head of the churches

And the summit of honor, and that bishops and consecrated priests

Should receive their pallia and vestments there.

So the pious bishop Paulinus was the first to possess it,

Meditating on the law of the Lord night and day,

And diligently scattering the precepts of salvation among the peoples.

Therefore he converted many thousands to Christ.

Shining with the flames of faith and the fire of virtue,

He dispelled the northern cold for twice three years,

During which the excellent king Edwin likewise reigned

[Col. 0818C] and established his laws with just restraint,

Urging them to preserve the faith through gifts and threats [Note: [Col. 0818D] Perhaps, “inculcating.”],

And founded spacious churches in his cities.

Among them, the noble church at Eboracum,

Supported by solid columns, still remains,

Beautiful with lofty splendor.

There he was washed in the sacred water,

And for as long as he lived he kept the commandments of Christ.

Therefore God, in his mercy, was preparing to give him better kingdoms,

Joined to everlasting light.

For when the hour of his appointed death arrived,

The warrior suddenly fell in battle against his allies.

O, how utterly blind it is to trust in an earthly kingdom,

Which rushing Fortune turns and, through malign destinies,

Overthrows, and continually tosses about through changing hours!

Behold, after he had reigned for seventeen years,

[Col. 0818D] that most illustrious of kings, Edwin, fell [Note: [Col. 0818D] Edwin fell on the fourth day before the Ides of October, 633. Bede, in the work cited, chapter 20.].

After him, glorious Britain had no man such as he.

Yet the Almighty did not allow this to happen without vengeance,

But granted that Oswald, the king’s nephew [Note: [Col. 0818D] Bede, Book III, chapters 1 and following.], should reign.

Suddenly coming from foreign shores as an exile,

Firmly trusting in the armor of unconquered faith,

He led a small army in haste against the enemy,

Who was devastating his homeland, burning it with sword and fire,

[Verse 240.] With countless thousands, and excessively proud of his spoils.

[Col. 0819A] But pious Oswald, terrified by no numerical superiority,

Addressed his own troop with steadfast heart:

“O men whose courage in war is always vigorous,

Now, I beg you, take up unconquered strength in your hearts,

And seek God’s help, superior to every weapon,

With pious prayers. Bow your faces before the cross

Which I have raised here upon the mountain’s summit,

And which shines brightly with Christ’s trophy.

It too shall now grant us triumph over the enemy.”

Then the people’s prayerful cry was carried above the stars.

Thus before the cross, and before the Lord, the mighty God,

The whole army worshiped on bended knees.

After this was done, he boldly advanced against the enemy,

[Col. 0819B] Breaking into the hostile camp amid bloody slaughter.

As a cruel lion ravages sheepfolds with its cubs,

And the savage beast kills, devours, and drags away every sheep,

So King Oswald everywhere struck down the barbarian ranks,

Moving victoriously through weapons and enemies.

He cut them down and trampled them, crushing their fleeing wings.

Oswald’s army forestalled the enemy by laying them low,

Leaving streams of blood across the fields behind them,

Until the accursed Cadwallon himself fell,

Paying the penalty for his treachery in the slaughter of his own men.

The splendid victory yielded to the magnificent king.

When the enemies had been killed, the most holy Oswald entered the kingdom,

A hero worthy of his ancient ancestors.

A man powerful in virtue, protector of his homeland and its people,

[Col. 0819C] Outstanding in character, following Christ’s commandments,

Generous to the poor, sparing toward himself, rich toward everyone,

Truthful in judgment, kind through the piety of his heart,

Exalted in merits, yet humble in spirit,

Terrible to all enemies and pleasing to his friends,

As unconquered in war as he was faithful to his agreements in peace.

After he had grown strong through the scepter and height of kingship,

He built churches and adorned them with splendid gifts.

He supplied precious vessels for sacred services,

Clothed the altars with silver, gems, and gold,

And stretched silken hangings across the sacred walls,

Beautifully marked with golden coronets.

He hung sacred lamps throughout the various roofs,

So that the churches might present an image of the starry heavens.

Devoutly he led the flocks of Christ into them,

[Col. 0819D] so that they might sing praises to the Lord without end.

O piety, O lofty faith! For whatever he possessed,

He lavishly scattered in honor of the Lord’s treasures.

Therefore he became renowned for the titles of his virtues,

And was everywhere celebrated through the famous report of his miracles,

Which are now read throughout the world, inscribed in books.

Of these I now desire to touch upon a few with the poet’s lyre

And to recount portions of the song with my flowing pen.

[Verse 291.] For at a certain time the most holy bishop Aidan [Note: [Col. 0819D] Edan or Aidan, concerning whom see more in Bede, the work cited, chapters 5 and 6.]

[Col. 0820A] celebrated the Easter festival with the king and the people.

(The king followed his instructions in every action.)

At that time a great crowd of poor people lay in the streets,

Begging alms from the king with frequent cries.

As the king and the bishop entered and reclined together,

The king immediately sent a large silver dish, previously weighed with its substantial contents,

Together with the food, to the needy.

When the bishop saw this, he grasped the king’s right hand and said:

“May this hand, I pray, remain incorrupt forever.”

And so it happened. For after the holy king had been killed,

His right hand, cut from his body by a pagan sword,

Was hung from a stake.

Later, King Oswi [Note: [Col. 0819D] Oswi or Oswin, successor of Oswald. See the preceding poem concerning Lindisfarne. Bede, chapter 4.], heir of that king,

Brother of his brother and avenger of his blood,

Seized the hand and carried it to the city of Bebbanburg,

Placing the silver in a chest beneath the roof of the temple,

[Col. 0820B] which he himself had previously dedicated in the name of Peter.

To this day the sign remains: a growing fingernail,

A flexible tendon, living flesh, and a beautiful appearance.

How great his faith had been, or the power of his merits,

Shone forth more and more after his death through miracles everywhere.

For when he fell fighting for his homeland, killed by a pagan people,

Many healing miracles arose from the dust [Note: [Col. 0820D] Bede, chapter 9.].

Once, by chance, a traveler was making his way

Beside the field where the battle had been fought [Note: [Col. 0820D] *Scamma*. Greek σκάμμα, an arena where athletes wrestle. Isidore. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under this word.].

His horse suddenly began to grow weak in all its limbs,

Foaming bloodily at the mouth,

And, collapsing, rolled upon the field as though about to die.

When it reached the place where the pious King Oswald

Had once fallen, it immediately rose again with a healthy body

And eagerly began to crop the pleasant green grass.

The rider understood that something extraordinary was present in that place.

Marking it with a sign, he rode on from there

Toward the lodging to which he was heading.

Behold, a girl wasted by paralysis lay there,

Uttering repeated sighs, the last sounds of her wretched life.

While the household of her father’s niece lamented in confusion,

The host suggested that she be taken to the place where the horse

Had perhaps been healed.

The girl was placed upon a cart and carried there,

As the traveler directed, showing her the sacred places.

After her body had been laid upon the ground, she slept there for a short time.

When she awoke, she felt that her health had returned.

Then she asked for water, washed her face,

Arranged her hair, covered her head with a veil,

And afterward followed her guides cheerfully.

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Bede, chapter 10.] Another traveler, passing through the aforementioned places of battle,

[Col. 0820D] Beheld a stretch of ground more pleasant than any field

And more beautiful than the green grass.

He reflected to himself: “A holier man fell here.

I think that for this reason the earth is beneficial for healing.”

He tied some of the dust in a cloth and carried it with him.

Toward evening he arrived, weary, at a certain village

Where the inhabitants were feasting.

He entered one of the village cottages,

And, having been received, hung the cloth containing the dust

Upon a high post.

Suddenly it happened that a devouring fire, its flames flying upward,

Seized the high roof.

It could not be extinguished by any strength,

Until the fire had consumed the entire house.

Yet an exceedingly wondrous thing occurred:

The fiery heat feared to touch the post consecrated by the dust,

And it remained entirely untouched by the flames.

When everyone saw this power, great astonishment immediately overcame them.

Then they learned that the dust had been mixed with the sacred blood

Of King Oswald, who had been the cause of healing for many.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Bede, chapter 11.] After this place had become famous through the miracles accomplished there,

And peace had been restored joyfully to the churches of Christ,

The faithful queen Osthryth, wife of King Æthelred,

Who was the daughter of the holy Oswald’s brother,

Arranged for the relics of her uncle to be brought into the sacred building

[Col. 0821B] and deposited with fitting honor.

When the bones had been brought, the inhabitants of Lindsey

Were amazed by the widespread miracle.

They saw above the bones of the holy man a column

Shining all night upward toward the heights of heaven

With the light of an ethereal radiance.

The greater part of the relics was then covered by curtains.

At first, because of their ancient hatred, the inhabitants refused

To take up the bones and carry them to the monastery of the cruel man.

They left them outside overnight.

But when they saw the fire of the divine light,

They begged to retain with them what they had previously rejected.

In the morning, after washing the bones and placing them in a prepared sarcophagus,

They carried them beneath the great roof of the church with great honor,

[Col. 0821C] taking care to bury living treasures in the earth.

At that place, even to this day, many gifts of healing

Are granted to the sick through the merit of so great a patron,

If the power of holy faith accompanies them.

Of these it is enough to touch upon one with my hastening pen,

So that, devoted reader, you may believe the rest.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Bede, chapter 12.] A certain boy lay sick with fever for a long time,

Languishing in the monastery and soon destined to die there.

Behold, one day the wretched boy was carried to the sacred places of the tomb,

So that the bitter fever might not touch him through Oswald’s merits.

For faith commands whatever it asks.

As soon as the sick boy believed, he hurried back to his home,

Hastening with a healed body and joyful heart.

The diseased fever no longer dared to touch him.

Later, the fortunate King Offa adorned Oswald’s tomb

With silver, gems, gold, and great ornament,

So that the tomb’s glory and splendor might endure through the ages,

Receiving great rewards for a small labor.

The earth too shines, renowned for heavenly signs.

As I said, it had been washed by the body of the saint,

And it acquired the power to overcome the weapons of the wicked demon

And restore sound faculties to those whom he had afflicted.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Bede, chapter 11.] A certain abbess came to visit the sacred places

And to entrust herself to the saint’s merits.

When she was returning home, she carried with her some earth from the dust,

Having drawn from the bones a sacred water with which they had been washed.

After some time, a visitor came to her,

A man who had often been accustomed to be tormented by a demon at night.

[Verse 401.] Behold, suddenly he began, with dreadful cries,

To fill the wide spaces with his roaring,

And in his madness to tear himself with wicked bites.

When no one could bind him in chains

Or restrain the wretched man’s savage movements with lashes,

Someone hurried to tell the abbess.

When she saw the miserable movements and the madman’s cries,

She ordered a box containing the sacred dust to be brought.

As the virgin carrying it approached and entered the house’s vestibule,

The madman suddenly fell silent

And stilled all his movements, as though he had given his limbs to sleep.

Everyone standing there watched to see what the outcome would be.

After an hour had passed, the afflicted man himself sat up.

Breathing heavily, he said that he had been restored

To soundness of mind and that the wandering enemy had fled into the wandering air.

[Col. 0822B] Everyone marveled, speaking in astonishment,

Seeing him suddenly unharmed in his entire body,

Strong in bones and sinews, and likewise sound in mind.

They asked the cause of his sudden healing.

He replied joyfully:

“As the virgin came carrying the little box

And touched this vestibule with her feet, immediately

The demons that had been accustomed to torment me departed far away,

Just as darkness flees when light arrives.”

A portion of the blessed dust was given to him to carry with him.

After that, he was never again subjected to such torment.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Bede, Book III, chapter 2.] I shall sing of you also, holy cross,

Venerable and powerful through many miracles,

Although I cannot produce verses worthy of your praise.

You restored what had previously been lost.

Now once again through you victory yields to King Oswald,

As a few of my songs once sang.

[Col. 0822C] From then on your glory shone forth through wondrous signs.

All famous Britain runs to you in faith,

Seeking remedies for its various diseases.

Nor do you deceive those who come to you in hope;

For they often carry back the resources of healing.

I cannot run through everything with my rustic lyre

That is accomplished through you again and again—

For cattle and human beings, for young and old alike.

Indeed, fragments cut from you are carried everywhere,

And through them gracious gifts of healing are bestowed.

Of all these signs, it is enough to mention this one:

There was a certain brother whose arm had been shattered

By a grievous accident.

He groaned deeply in pain from his broken bones.

When excessive pain had increased and a burning swelling

Doubled the exhausted man’s tearful sighs,

Someone brought him, toward evening, old moss from the cross,

And the sick man placed it in his lap.

When he went to bed, he forgot to put the moss away

And, unaware, fell asleep with it still in his lap.

Awaking in the middle of the night while still ill,

He felt something cold against his side.

When he placed his hand there, he discovered that he had somehow become well,

And he felt nothing of the former fracture.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Bede, chapter 13.] The illustrious fame of the man not only rightly

[Verse 456.] Illuminates the peoples of Britain, but also beyond the waters of the sea

[Col. 0823A] spreads its rays, by which Germany too shone.

Some of populous Ireland also experienced them.

But among the many signs, I am pleased to relate this true one:

During the time of a terrible plague,

Which killed the peoples across the sea in a widespread disaster,

A learned scholar of the Scottish people, skilled in his art,

Had been struck by this disease in that homeland.

Educated through the study of books, but with no concern

For his future life, when the wretched man saw

That the day of death was approaching,

He began to tremble with great fear.

Because of the merits of his sins, he feared that when he died

He would be dragged to the dreadful realms of hell.

With a groaning voice he addressed his companion:

“Brother, the moment of bitter death is approaching for me,

And I shall soon be led to the realms of everlasting death,

Because for a long time now I have been serving my crimes completely.

Alas! Because of them I know that the deadly fires

Of Tartarus have been prepared for me.

Yet I sense with all my faculties that, if the Almighty should wish

To grant life to wretched me, I would strive with all my strength

To change my wicked character.

Nevertheless, I know that it is not solely through my merit

That I should live, unless the grace of compassionate Christ

Should grant me the gift of the beloved life

Through the merits of the saints.

Once I heard the praises of King Oswald

Celebrated far and wide for his great miracles.

Since you were born of Saxon stock, my companion,

Perhaps you now possess some relic of his?”

His companion immediately spoke faithfully into his ear:

[Col. 0823C] “I have with me a portion of the sacred wood

In which the head of that slain man had been fixed.

If you hold a firm heart of faith and believe,

Then, through the piety of so great a patron,

Divine mercy may grant you a long period of this life;

And perhaps, in addition, it will bestow the joys of eternity.”

There was no delay: he said that he believed with all his heart.

Then his companion blessed water,

And, placing in it a piece of the sacred wood,

Gave it to the sick man to drink.

He soon recovered and was rescued from death.

From then on he lived unharmed for a long time,

And turned his whole life toward the Lord.

Everywhere he rendered magnificent praises to God

And celebrated the Lord’s servant with great honor.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Bede, Book III, chapter 9.] After the holy Oswald had happily ruled

For three times three years the peoples [Col. 0823D] whom famous Britain contains,

With their divided languages and peoples named after their ancestors,

And after he had lived three times ten and eight years,

He devoted the sacred Nones of August to death.

He ascended through his shining merits to the heavenly kingdoms,

Leaving the earthly kingdom to his brother Oswi.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Bede, in the work cited, chapter 14.] Meanwhile Oswi, the new ruler of his own people,

Had acquired the scepters of power through much labor.

For he had often been attacked from different sides

By foreign plunderers ravaging the borders everywhere.

Moreover, he suffered wars from his own near relatives,

[Verse 512.] Who cruelly tore apart the entrails of the kingdom,

Filling their criminal right hands with kindred blood.

They did not fear to lead pagan armies through the ancestral cities,

Driven by savage envy,

Or, by such means, to attempt to overthrow the king through foreign strength.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Bede, in the work cited, chapter 24.] Among others, the hostile King Penda

Had been his enemy from his earliest years.

He was strong in courage and deceit,

A murderer of his brother and a fierce devastator of the kingdom.

He gathered thirty thousand men for war

And planned to lead an equal number of commanders with their troops,

All experienced in arms.

Coming with this force to ravage and overthrow the kingdom,

He destroyed its walls and killed its people with the sword.

As a torrent overflowing from high mountains

Lays fields flat, seizes crops, and cuts down forests,

So the fierce leader himself pressed upon everything as he devastated it,

Sending children, young men, and old men alike to destruction.

No sex or age moved him to an act of mercy,

For he spared no one under any law.

But the ruler, whose concern was to defend his people

And protect both himself and his subjects with Christ’s weapons,

Selected brave men and a great army of his own.

The king came prepared, with an unshaken heart,

Against the enemy, though with only a small force.

First, with steadfast heart, he sought the name of Olympus

With tears and prayers.

When he saw the hostile armies everywhere

Moving across the broad fields in countless ranks,

He set his small but eager troop against them,

Leading only three thousand men, but men ready for battle.

There was no delay: boldly he plunged into the midst of the enemy,

Driving back their lines, relying on the shield of Christ.

[Col. 0824C] Soon fear scattered the wings of the peoples who had been struck.

Forgetting the battle, they abandoned their weapons and missiles,

Sought safe places in flight, and tore down their own standards.

The victorious king everywhere struck down the ranks of the pale enemy [the reading *Pallantum* is uncertain],

Scolding the fleeing phalanxes with a terrible voice.

Weapons swam in blood; springs were changed by blood.

Penda himself fled as well, compelled by the magnitude of the disaster,

When he saw the slaughter and destruction of his men.

Yet he could not escape death by fleeing.

He too fell, killed by the victorious sword.

They rushed everywhere to seize the spoils,

And due praise was rendered to the Thunderer,

Who, in his mercy, always liberates all who hope in him

And saves them everywhere.

This war was also highly beneficial to many.

For the king rescued his people from their fierce enemies

And subjected the Mercians to the kindly scepter of the faith,

Having them washed in the consecrated stream of baptism.

Through him, by God’s gift, both peoples were enriched

With the magnificent gift of the heavenly people:

The one became heir to an earthly homeland,

The other a citizen of heaven.

Both peoples shone with a double triumph:

The one released from the yoke of the demon,

The other freed from an earthly enemy.

Afterward Oswi subdued many kingdoms through continuous triumphs

And nobly ruled the ancestral realms.

He subjected to himself the peoples across the sea in various directions,

[Verse 568.] Pressing some through terror and restraining others with the sword.

[Col. 0825A] Everywhere he carried victorious eagles through the kingdoms.

He was also most just in his equal laws,

Unconquered in wars and faithful in peace.

Generous in gifts to the distressed, pious, and equitable toward all.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Bede, Book IV, chapter 5.] Holding the empire for four times seven years,

He rested happily in peace after setting all things in order,

Handing the diadems to his own son Egfrid,

And, as he died, leaving the royal scepters to Egfrid.

At that time Bishop Wilfrid [Note: [Col. 0825D] Bishop Wilfrid. See his life in Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, third century, part I. See Bede, in the work cited, chapter 3.] shone forth,

Whom Almighty God infused with heavenly light

So that he might drive the grim shadows of error from the earth.

Therefore through many regions he scattered abundant lights of teaching

For the peoples and nations, bringing everlasting salvation.

Through his southern labors Saxony believed in Christ

And was drenched with the bright lamp of life.

[Col. 0825B] Nor did that bishop merely rescue the peoples’ souls

From wicked spiritual death through his blessed teachings;

He also saved those same people from present physical death.

For during three successive years at that time,

Neither dew nor rain watered the thirsty fields.

The parched earth withered beneath the fiery stars,

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Bede, Book IV, chapter 12.] And refused food alike to humans and beasts.

Famine was followed by a heap of deaths,

And many plunged headlong from high cliffs.

Others threw themselves beneath the rushing waves,

So that swift death might snatch them from prolonged torment.

But on the very day when that people,

Instructed in sacred teachings, received the water of baptism,

Rain descended, a serene breeze arose over the lands,

And the appearance of the earth returned to the green fields.

[Col. 0825C] The fields and mountains were adorned with flowering covering.

A fruitful year was given to rejoicing farmers.

In God, the living one, all flesh and hearts rejoiced,

As David had sung before,

Longing more surely in their hearts for eternal gifts,

Through whom they had previously received earthly benefits.

He too, compelled to travel to Rome,

Was first carried by the winds to the shores of the Frisians.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] Bede, Book V, chapter 20.] There he soon converted thousands of the people to Christ,

Showing them abundant gifts of everlasting salvation.

Wherever he moved his foot, he sowed pious seeds,

Watering their parched hearts with heavenly dew.

He filled their famous granaries with celestial fruit

And was praised with celebrated fame throughout the joyful world.

[Col. 0825D] While the pious priest desired to complete that journey,

Behold, he was suddenly struck by a grievous illness.

For many days, as the severe pain increased,

His body wasted away and reached its final end.

For four days he lay almost lifeless, deprived of all bodily awareness,

Without breath, without speech, his limbs numb.

Only in his chest did he scarcely draw cold breaths with a faint exhalation.

[Verse 621.] His companion disciples stood around him, groaning,

[Col. 0826A] Mourning the lamentable death of their father.

Behold, on the fifth day the father himself suddenly sat up,

Raised his eyes, looked at his companions, and said:

“What good is it to indulge in such terrible grief?

The Almighty Judge can soften whomever he wishes

And transform a final life into a new beginning.

For the merciful one sent his messenger from the stars,

Who stood before me, exceedingly splendid in a snow-white garment,

And with a fiery face foretold these things to me:

‘The Most High, enthroned on high, has sent me, Michael, from heaven

To say that you will now be strengthened against this illness,

Through the merits and prayers of holy Mother Mary.

She has heard with open ears from her heavenly throne

The groans, tears, and prayers of your companions,

And has asked for both life and health for you.

Nevertheless, be prepared when the fourth year arrives.

I myself shall then come again to visit you,

For you will die in peaceful times in your native land.’”

Life and health soon followed the angelic command.

After four full years had passed,

The foretold end of the excellent bishop followed.

Thus he was placed in the church which he had erected

In honor of Peter at Ripon, and was happily buried in peace.

In those times too there shone a holy man,

Cuthbert [Note: [Col. 0826D] Bishop Cuthbert. His life and miracles are drawn from the Venerable Bede, volume V of his works, volume XCIV of Migne’s *Patrologia*. Mabillon, second Benedictine century, part I.], who lived an angelic life in the body.

From childhood he had been distinguished by manifest signs,

And immediately grew in honorable character and merits.

Remaining a monk, renowned from his earliest years,

He became an apostolic teacher, and then a venerable priest.

He filled uncultivated places with fruitful green growth,

And watered thirsty meadows with everlasting springs.

Forming everyone through divine virtue into followers,

He scattered everywhere the rays of heavenly doctrine,

Dispelling the shadows of error with serene light.

There is a place in the ocean called Farne,

An island lacking springs and deprived of grain and trees.

The excellent warrior of Christ fearlessly sought it,

Desiring to gather contemplative flowers.

He strove to serve God alone, alone,

Lest worldly honor change his joyful mind.

Here the holy hermit lived for no short time,

Often enjoying the blessed companionship of angels,

And overcoming the poisonous weapons of the deadly dragon.

Nevertheless, withdrawn from there by the requests of many,

[Col. 0826D] At last he agreed to leave his secluded dwelling.

Compelled by the people and the king, and by their prayers,

He eventually accepted the rank of bishop.

He nobly and worthily ruled it for two years,

Gathering many gains of souls for the Thunderer,

And faithfully guarding the flock entrusted to him,

So that the lurking wolf would not gnaw Christ’s lambs.

But soon he rejected the height of worldly honor,

[Verse 674.] Seeking again the secrecy of his accustomed chamber.

[Col. 0827A] There he had foreseen the end of his present life,

And the island was consecrated by the death of God’s servant.

For that place continues to shine with radiant miracles,

Ever since, leaving the prison of his episcopal flesh,

His spirit, seeking the heights, ascended above the stars of heaven.

Miracles also occur through conspicuous events

At the place where his sacred body rests buried.

The whole of his life, until the day of his death,

Had been renowned for heavenly signs.

All these things the illustrious priest Bede

First wrote in prose as a learned master,

And afterward sang of his miracles in heroic verse [Note: [Col. 0827D] Venerable Bede, in the same work. Mabillon, second Benedictine century, part I.].

How healing followed the angelic command

When a burning swelling arose in his tender body.

Or how, when still a boy, he recalled five ships

Tossed upon the deep by the winds through his prayers.

Or how he saw the soul of Bishop Aidan

Carried above the stars while he was feeding tender lambs.

How, when he wished to nourish a heavenly being

With earthly bread, he deserved to receive heavenly food from him.

How beasts warmed him when chilled, with fur and breath,

And how he released from illness and guilt the brother who witnessed it.

And how, by praying, he took away hunger

From sailors cast upon the sea,

And foretold that calm weather was surely approaching.

Or how he foretold that a fish brought by an eagle

Would provide food for himself and his companion,

And so it happened.

[Col. 0827C] Or how he turned away the flames burning against the buildings,

When his prayers prevailed where the strength of young men could not.

And how a demon-possessed wife was healed by him

Before she entered the house of the petitioner.

Or how the holy man drove evil demons from Farne

When he was building a dwelling there for himself.

How from a dry turf he drew clear water,

Which, to the Father’s delight, provided a pleasant taste in the mouth.

How he sowed a crop for himself in a field

And drove the birds away from it by his word alone.

How the sea, together with its creatures, used to serve the saint.

He foretold many future things with truthful speech,

Concerning himself and others, which he had previously seen in foreknowledge.

How he restored health to the wife of a count,

To whom he had sent sacred water, driving away her disease.

How, having anointed a girl with chrism,

He healed her of an illness of the side and of pain in the head.

How, once again, bread blessed and sent by him,

When water was poured upon it, healed a certain sick man.

[Col. 0827D] How a traveler happened to find a young man about to die,

And restored his health through prayer.

How the pious Father, during a disease devastating the Britons,

Foretold health for a mother, her son, and the household.

How he saw the soul of a shepherd who had fallen from a tree

Carried by angelic hosts from heaven,

And how, while ill himself, he healed his servant,

Who had been weakened by a wasting intestinal disorder.

How, in the eleventh year after his death,

[Verse 729.] His body was found intact together with all his clothing.

[Col. 0828A] How a man possessed by a demon, over whom water was poured—

Water that had washed the Father’s sacred limbs—

Was healed.

How a certain man, drawing sick breaths, prayed

And was healed of his illness at the saint’s tomb.

And how a sick man, touching the cloths of the vessel with his eyes,
His pain and darkness departed from his sight.

Someone put on the Father’s shoes after his body had been loosened, and from that time went on with sound feet.

How the sick are healed by the covering beneath which the spirit of the saint, leaving earthly things, seeks the stars.

I have touched on these matters briefly, lest I seem entirely silent while lightly tracing in rustic song the famous deeds.

Since the illustrious master Bede once sang these things in full verse, with polished speech,

had he not himself anticipated our songs,

[Col. 0828B] I would begin to stretch out all my lyrical fibers.

I would not invoke Pan, nor Phoebus’ empty divinity,

but with all my heart I would pray for your aid,

that you, Christ, might grant me speech flowing like dew

for worthily recounting the praises of the holy Father.

After the warlike Egfrid had won triumphs here and there

and subdued fierce peoples beneath the sword,

he took as wife Adiltruda [Note: [Col. 0827D] Adiltruda, called Edildrida by Bede, chapter 19, book IV of the Ecclesiastical History.],

born of noble parents of royal stock,

but far nobler because she remained chaste in mind.

For although she had been joined to a proud marriage-bed,

and had already been the royal bride for twelve years,

she nevertheless remained an undefiled virgin throughout her life,

conquering the fires of the flesh amid the rights of marriage.

Blessed faith of the virgin, wondrous patience of the king!

[Col. 0828C] He is conquered here by her prayers, and she by love of the Thunderer;

both inwardly burning with the sacred fires of faith,

they remained chaste together, husband with wife.

And although she had lived as a virgin, wholly undefiled in body,

after her death the Lord disclosed it by evident signs;

for when her flesh had been buried for six decades,

it was found entirely incorrupt, together with all her clothing.

Her body was vigorous, and every limb remained supple,

and her holy face shone with radiant beauty.

And what is even more wondrous and truly amazing to tell:

a wound in her body, inflicted two days before her death

by a physician compelled by excessive fear,

appeared healed, with only the faintest scar

showing merely the traces of the former ulcer.

Likewise, the garment that had covered the virgin’s holy limbs

[Col. 0828D] often expelled the cruel serpent from those possessed.

Moreover, the earlier tomb that had received the holy limbs

of the blessed virgin in its sacred bosom beneath the earth

became for many the cause of the salvation they desired,

and itself provided healing to diseased eyes.

Therefore the aforesaid Bede composed a hymn in splendid verses

in praise of this holy maiden [Note: [Col. 0828D] “Hymn”: Bede, chapter 20, which Alcuin also mentions in letter 153.].

For this reason I have touched on these few matters in a brief little book,

as one recalling the proverb of old:

[Verse 784.] “Perhaps, traveler, you are carrying wood into the forest.”

[Col. 0829A] At that time also something memorable happened,

which, I think, may benefit many who read these things,

if anyone should consider them worthy of reading.

The king’s brother Aelfwine [Note: [Col. 0829D] Aelfwine: in Bede, book IV, chapter 22.] was killed in battle,

in which a certain soldier also, struck down in arms,

a nobleman [Note: [Col. 0829D] Named Imma. Bede, in the same passage.], fell, slain in a cruel massacre.

Lifeless, he passed the day and the following night;

yet, when his soul returned to his extinguished limbs,

he was restored to life, and, recovering strength,

he bound up his wounds, which were gaping open,

and began to depart with a vigorous stride. But he was captured by the enemy

and brought back by a diverted road to a certain count [Note: [Col. 0829D] To the count of King Æthelred. In Bede.].

The count ordered him to say who he was.

He nevertheless feared to confess that he had been born of illustrious stock,

saying: “I am a poor man and merely a peasant,

[Col. 0829B] and I lived bound by the law of marriage.”

The count took him and first tried to tend him;

but, lest he escape, he ordered him to be bound. Yet the man

could never be bound, for all the bonds

regularly came undone of their own accord in a wondrous manner.

When the enemies saw this, astonished in mind,

thinking that it resulted from magical arts or spells,

they repeatedly added new bonds to the old ones.

The count, amazed, summoned him privately

and asked him why he could not be bound,

whether he had perhaps previously learned magical arts.

He declared that he knew nothing of such practices.

250 “But I have a brother [Note: [Col. 0829D] His name was Tunna, a priest and abbot. Bede.],” he said,

“of a devout heart,

whom I know to sing the solemn Masses for me,

because he believes that I have been killed.

[Col. 0829C] And if my soul should now be held in another life,

I believe that, because of his prayers and frequent Masses,

it would be free and would escape every punishment.”

Then, having received these answers, the other recognized

that he was a leader born of a distinguished lineage.

And although he seemed to himself lawfully deserving death,

he rescued him from death, but sold him to another man,

who also tried to bind him with dreadful chains.

He could not do so, however, because, loosened in the manner already described,

he remained free in body from the bonds imposed upon him.

This happened repeatedly at the third hour of the day,

at which time his brother was accustomed

to offer the gifts of the Mass with a devout heart.

When the Lord saw such marvels,

he granted him the opportunity to ransom himself.

[Col. 0829D] He returned free, redeemed under the law of a price,

and, going home, told everything to his brother.

From his brother’s account he learned that the times

when he reported himself freed from his bonds

were precisely the times at which he remembered

that he had always celebrated the solemn Mass for God.

Egfrid [Note: [Col. 0829D] King Egfrid of Northumbria died in the year 685. Bede, book IV, chapter 26.] governed the kingdom successfully for fifteen years,

waging victorious wars,

until, sending armies with savage intent across the sea,

[Verse 837.] and ordering the innocent Scots, always friendly to the English,

to be devastated in bloody slaughter,

he himself, when the Picts fought against him,

fell defeated in a wretched destruction of his people,

leaving the rule of the kingdom to his brother Aldfrid [Note: [Col. 0830D] Aldfrid succeeded his brother Egfrid in 685.].

He had been instructed in sacred studies from his earliest years,

a sophist of powerful speech,

keen in intellect, and at once king and teacher.

The venerable priest Bosa [Note: [Col. 0830D] Bosa, bishop of York. See the histories collected by Matthew of Westminster concerning the bishops Wilfrid and Bosa. Venerable Bede, book IV of the Ecclesiastical History of the English, chapters 12 and 23.] presided over the Church,

at that time a man of high rank, worthy of his office by his merits,

a monk, bishop, teacher—moderate and honorable—

whom divine grace had adorned with sacred wreaths of virtues

and made shine with many gifts.

Therefore he amassed abundant profits for the Thunderer,

casting sacred nets through the worldly waters,

[Col. 0830B] and drew sea-born prey to Christ’s shores.

A good man without deceit, rich in heavenly piety,

he shone in the house of the Lord like a blazing morning star.

This Father adorned the worship of the Church,

and thoroughly separated it from the customs of the people;

he established that it should serve God alone at every hour,

so that the mystical lyre might continually resound beneath the plectrum,

singing the Lord’s heavenly hymns of praise.

Then the human voice would strike Olympus above,

while he arranged all the times in alternating order:

now there would be reading, now sacred prayer,

and everyone would offer God’s praises through bodily activity.

He ordered that the needs of the flesh be completed swiftly,

so that only a little sleep and food might be allotted to all.

No one was to claim as his own lands, provisions, houses,

money, or garments,

[Col. 0830C] nor anything else;

rather, everything was always to be shared by all.

Whoever seeks earthly things for himself, or, as an heir, the joys of +heaven;

+who would become common to all in the kingdom.

[The supplied syntax of these two lines is corrupt; the second line is translated literally, with its construction uncertain. The source places its critical signs before coelorum ("of heaven") and qui ("who").]

After this pious bishop had filled the time of his present life

with great virtues,

he happily passed into the heavenly court.

A memorable vision occurred in those same times,

which, I think, if it is written in our poem,

will benefit many who are to be called from death everlasting,

so that it may be able to heal souls destroyed by vices.

Behold, a certain man who had been dead for a long time rose again in body [Note: [Col. 0830D] Named Drithelm. Bede, book V, chapter 13.],

and brought back many things worthy of remembrance that he had seen.

Of these we shall add a few to our songs.

[Col. 0830D] He had been a married man of ordinary standing,

and had governed his life with just moderation.

Afterward he was afflicted with a severe bodily illness,

and for many days, as the powerful pain increased,

he lay sick and endured the extremity of danger.

At last he died at the beginning of the night;

but, drawing breath at the farthest edge of life,

he revived and, rising,

drove away all at once those who were carrying out

the funeral rites during that very night.

[Verse 890.] [Col. 0831A] His wife alone remained there, strengthened by greater love.

When her husband returned from death, he began to encourage her,

though she was exceedingly terrified and the others had fled:

“You alone,” he said, “remain faithful to me among them all.

I beg you, dearest wife, do not now fear me.

I am alive indeed; I have truly returned from death.

But another life must now be followed by me in a very different way,

and I must condemn myself for pleasures and luxury.”

Without delay, leaving all his riches,

he followed the rule of the monastery with a devoted heart.

There he subdued his body under such a severe burden

that all could easily recognize from his life

what sort of and how great a growth had previously arisen from his flesh.

He used to relate what he had seen in this manner:

“Brilliant was the one who led me out of the body.

We proceeded toward the rising of the summer sun,

until we came to a broad and deep valley,

whose lengthwise chasm extended without end.

One side of it burned with seething flames,

[Col. 0831B] while another was full of icy hail.

It was filled here and there with the souls of human beings.

When, excessively scorched, they could no longer endure the flames,

they leapt at once into the midst of the cold.

And when there too they could find no rest,

they were carried back and forth, weeping, into the fire-spewing flames.

Seeing this, I reflected to myself that perhaps this was

the infernal punishment of which I had often heard.

But while I was thinking such things, my guide said:

‘No; this is not hell, as you suppose.’

While I looked upon these things, he led me onward in fear.

Then suddenly I saw every place filled with darkness.

The image of thick night, entering with us,

settled around us, and I could see nothing

except the form of my guide and his shining garments.

Thus we entered beneath the solitary night through the shadows.

Behold, suddenly balls of exceedingly dreadful flame

rose as though from a well and then sank again.

Then my guide suddenly disappeared, and I remained alone,

placed trembling and stunned amid the darkness.

As the fiery spheres rose high

and in alternating movements returned to the depths of the abyss,

I saw all the heights of flame filled with the miserable spirits of human beings.

Like ashes, they rose and fell together with the flames,

[Col. 0831D] while an overpowering stench filled the whole region.

As I gazed farther on, terror stood around me on every side,

for I did not know what I should do,

where I could turn my steps,

or what end might await me in my misery.

Then suddenly I heard behind me the sound of groaning,

and also something like the laughter of a crowd rejoicing over a captured enemy.

When they came near, I recognized evil enemies

dragging five souls, howling, to their punishments;

with them they descended into the depths of the central abyss.

Then certain wicked demons rose from the fire-spewing well,

with flaming eyes.

They surrounded me, breathing foul fire from their nostrils

and flames from their mouths, and threatened to seize me with pincers.

Yet they could not touch me,

although they were capable of causing great terror.

[Verse 947.] [Col. 0832A] Then, enclosed in darkness and compelled by the enemy,

I looked around to see whether some aid might perhaps appear

by which I could now be saved from the bloodthirsty foe.

Then behind me there shone through the shadows something like a star.

Growing brighter and hastening forward, it drove away the enemies.

It was my guide, coming suddenly with light;

at his arrival the black demons fled.

From there he turned his path toward the winter rising of the sun,

and led me, rescued from night, into the shining air.

Before us a huge wall suddenly appeared,

which seemed so long and high that it had no end.

But when we came near it, I do not know by what manner or order,

we found ourselves standing on the top of the wall.

Behold, there was a great and most beautiful field.

Its fragrant radiance was so great

that it immediately drove away all the stench from me.

Such light poured over the sacred field on every side

that it surpassed the light of the sun and of day alike.

In those places I saw joyful companies of saints

dwelling and holding blessed seats.

As I looked upon these things, I wondered whether they were

the heavenly kingdoms promised to all the blessed.

While I was turning this over in my mind, my guide answered:

‘No; those are not the kingdoms of heaven, as you suppose.

Ahead shines a new and greater grace of light,

which surpasses the former light with overwhelming radiance.

For then that earlier light seemed truly very faint.

[Col. 0832C] There too resounds the sweetest voice of singers,

and with the light there was a wondrous fragrance,

so that, because of it, I considered the first place exceedingly small.

When I joyfully hoped that we would enter there,

my guide suddenly halted and turned back his steps.

He led me back by the road along which we had come,

and, when we had entered again the beautiful places of the earlier field,

he asked me whether I knew everything I had seen.

I said that I did not know, and immediately he added:

‘You saw the valley full of flames and cold,

in which souls are now being purged by bitter punishments

and return, once purified, to the rewards of life.

But the foul well that belches out fire

is the mouth of hell;

for whoever happens to fall into it

will never afterward be saved from it.

[Col. 0832D] That flower-bearing place, possessed by the white-clad youth,

is the rest in which those who have done good dwell

while awaiting the heavenly kingdoms.

They have done good, though in lesser measure than

holy faith requires.

For whoever is perfect in every respect

will enter the heavenly court immediately upon dying.

Near to it lies that radiant place,

full of excessive light and also of wondrous fragrance,

from which the sweetest voice of singers resounded.

Since you must now take up your body again

and live among human beings a life that will die,

correct, I beg you, your habits, words, and actions,

so that your holy dwelling may be counted among these companies.’

[Verse 1005.] When he said this, I do not know how,

[Col. 0833A] I suddenly saw myself clothed in my own body.”

Nor did this nation, mother of illustrious men,

keep those whom she had produced solely for herself,

as though enclosing them within the confines of her own kingdom.

Rather, she sent many of them far across the seas,

so that they might offer the seeds of life to other peoples.

Among these was the bishop called Saint

Egbert [Note: [Col. 0833D] Saint Egbert, bishop. Bede, book V, chapters 10 and 23. See also Mabillon, Acts of the Saints, century III, part I, pp. 487 ff. Alcuin also mentions Saint Egbert and Wigbert in Life of Saint Willibrord, chapter 4.],

who in the first years of his life

had left his homeland for love of the heavenly homeland.

Seeking a foreign land, he already gave the Scots

the greatest examples of life,

shining with the lamp of teaching,

instructing by his deeds and teaching all whom he addressed by his words,

generous to the poor, but always poor in his own regard.

Thus, a good man, he directed the governance of an excellent life,

shining with distinguished piety until the day of his death.

His companion, equal to him in merits and fitting in character,

was the illustrious Wibert [Note: [Col. 0833D] Wibert, perhaps Wicbert. See Bede, book V, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 10, and Mabillon, Life of Saint Wigbert, Acts, century III, [Col. 0834D] part I, p. 671. Preliminary observation no. 1.],

outstanding in every aspect of religious life.

But afterward separated from him,

he alone led a strict contemplative life.

From there he built an excellent fold for the monks of his people,

adorning it with the merits and practices of life,

zealous in feeding Christ’s sheep.

He himself led them by a narrow path along a straight road

to the pastures of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore he became renowned for miracles,

and, like a prophet, seeing many things yet to come,

remained distinguished everywhere.

Afterward he entered the joys of heavenly life.

But others, carried across the eastern sea in ships,

sought pagan soil, where they attempted to scatter

the words of salvation by sowing them in rustic hearts.

Such was the distinguished bishop Wilbrord [Note: [Col. 0834D] Bishop Wilbrord. Alcuin, in the Life mentioned above.],

who had won many thousands of the Frisian people for Christ

[Note: [Col. 0834D] Bede, book V, chapter 11.]

by heavenly admonitions,

and for many years adorned the dignity of a bishop,

building several churches there for God

and appointing priests and ministers of the word in them.

Having accomplished everything, he happily rested in peace.

Behold, two priests followed his example,

inflamed by an excessive fervor of faith;

both were called by the same name, Herwald [Note: [Col. 0834D] The two Herwalds, or Heuwalds, the White and the Black, martyrs. See Bede, book V, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 11.].

Their work was alike, and their end also the same.

One was white, the other black—the only difference was their hair;

but the Black had been more devoted to books than the White.

Thus these men entered the crossroads of the pagan Saxon people,

to see whether they could win anyone for Christ.

[Col. 0833D] But when the wretched people recognized the new customs

and practices of the faith,

they feared that the whole worship of the ancient gods

would quickly collapse.

They seized and killed them by a cruel death:

the White they immediately slaughtered with a bloody sword,

but against the Black they inflicted long tortures with harshness.

[Verse 1057.] Then they threw the bodies of the slain beneath the waters

of the Rhine.

[Col. 0834A] Yet the bodies were soon carried in a wondrous course

against the mighty blows of the river,

and swam through the waters all the way to their companions.

At whatever place the bodies arrived during the night,

a great ray of light shone from there above the stars.

Those who had previously killed the saints

saw this light shining every night.

One of the martyrs appeared by night to one of his companions and said:

“You can immediately find our bodies

where you see the light radiating from heaven.”

The vision did not deceive the companions.

For the bodies were found in those very places

and were buried with worthy honor for the pious martyrs.

Other ministers from that people also served as preachers

in those regions of the world.

[Col. 0834B] Among them the distinguished priests Suidbert and Vira

shone in their own times.

They were illustrious in the height of their virtues,

but I have not wished to touch upon all of them in my poem.

Now it is proper to bring the Muse back to the city of York,

from which she had withdrawn far away,

and to leave aside the succession of kings

who altered the periods of their rule after Aldfrid [Note: [Col. 0834D] See Alford, under the year 705, no. 5.],

who ruled for nineteen years

and afterward, when the time of peace had come,

was laid to rest among his fathers by the final lot.

Meanwhile, when Bosa sought the blessed kingdoms,

that most illustrious man, John,

received the governance of the Church.

He was a man distinguished in piety, faith, merits, and mind,

the summit of the episcopate and the pattern of the ancient Fathers,

pouring rivers of teaching from his pure heart,

with which he carefully watered the living meadows.

The honor of virtue accompanied him with evident signs,

a few of which it pleases us to recall in our songs.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] Bede, book V of the Ecclesiastical History of the English, chapter 2.]

While the pious Father himself was observing holy fasts,

he returned to a small enclosure accompanied by honorable men,

so that he might pluck heavenly flowers in his mind

and pay the Lord the tithes of his own life,

from which he might discover rich treasures in heaven.

Entering a place suited to strict observances,

he ordered the needy to be sought through the neighboring crossroads,

so that he himself might carry food to the poor.

Then a sick and mute young man was brought to him.

He could no longer utter words with any speech.

His head was covered with a horrible scab,

and instead of hair his skin remained marked with spots.

[Col. 0834D] The pious bishop gave this poor man a cloak

in which the miserable man might receive his customary alms.

After seven days had passed,

he ordered him to be brought back and to show his mute tongue.

He impressed upon it the sign of the holy cross,

and ordered the tongue that had long been silent to produce speech.

[Verse 1109.] He followed the Father’s command more quickly than words can say,

[Col. 0835A] breaking his silent silence by speaking with ready mouth,

and, completely mute before, he spoke in full utterance.

Throughout the entire day and the following night

he did not cease joyfully producing various words

and revealing the hidden thoughts of his mind.

Together with his voice, his skin also returned healthy;

new hairs grew back with curling locks.

The young man became handsome and ready in speech,

and thus, healed, went home rejoicing.

253 [Note: [Col. 0835D] The same, in the same place, chapter 3.]

Nor does it weary me to recall another praiseworthy sign,

while the shepherd watches over his folds with vigilant protection [Note: [Col. 0835D] “Folds,” that is, monasteries. See Du Cange.].

He came to visit the cell of the holy women.

Among them a certain young virgin was lying ill.

A vein in the middle of her arm had recently been cut,

and her hand had become stiff from an excessive swelling.

[Col. 0835B] The girl seemed likely to die very soon.

But the holy bishop restored her to health by the power of the Lord.

At her mother’s request, he entered the house where she lay,

greeted the maiden as usual,

and, offering prayers, blessed her sick hand.

The girl immediately grew stronger as the pain departed.

In a wondrous manner, when the bishop went out,

the disease withdrew from her whole body.

Immediately rescued by the Highest from great dangers,

the virgin sang praises and lived for many years.

[Note: [Col. 0835D] Bede, chapter 4.]

Another sign followed this one in similar fashion.

Behold, a certain count summoned the venerable John,

so that he might dedicate a church to the Lord.

His wife had been ill for many days,

lying for forty nights, overwhelmed by pain,

cold and unable to raise herself from her bed.

A livid pallor covered her face,

and a thin breath scarcely issued from her nostrils.

[Col. 0835C] The pious bishop sent her blessed water,

with which he had previously consecrated that church to the Lord,

so that she might drink it and anoint her suffering limbs.

When she had done this, healing spread through her body,

and the disease perished beneath the health-giving draught.

The power of the desired healing also arrived.

The woman immediately rose healthy from her bed

and, with renewed strength, carried cups to the kindly priest

and tirelessly served everyone.

Together with her husband, she gave thanks to God.

[Note: [Col. 0835D] The same, chapter 5.]

At another time a different count also summoned him

to dedicate a church to the Lord in the customary manner.

[Col. 0835D] His child had been overcome by a mortal disease

and lay dead in every part of his limbs,

except that his exhausted chest moved,

barely repeating faint sighs.

The count was then preparing the funeral rites for him,

and a coffin stood nearby in which his body

was soon to be buried, since no hope of life remained.

The leader himself, weeping, begged the bishop

[Verse 1163.] to deign to bless the boy immediately

[Col. 0836A] and offer prayers to the Lord for his life.

The pious and merciful man did not rightly refuse

what was asked with full faith.

He immediately visited the sick boy,

blessed him, and, returning as usual, greeted him:

“Recover, boy,” he said, “and regain your strength.”

Afterward, while the bishop and the leader were sitting down to dine,

the sick boy asked that cups be brought to him,

and the Lord, rejoicing that he was now able to drink,

sent him a cup of wine blessed by the bishop.

When he drank it, he immediately rose healthy and went away.

He entered the house where the leader and the bishop were dining.

When he declared that he wished to eat and drink with them,

he drank and ate while sitting joyfully among their joy.

After this he lived in good health for many years.

[Note: [Col. 0836D] The same, chapter 6.]

On another occasion the bishop was riding with his clergy

across a level plain suitable for riding.

Then the young men competed eagerly in a race with their horses.

But the pious bishop specifically forbade one of his companions

to take part in the idle game.

Nevertheless, against the prohibition, the reckless man

loosed the reins, trusting his horse,

and burst into the middle of the field.

As the fiery horse leapt over a certain hollow,

the young man fell with great force onto a stone

that happened to lie hidden beneath the turf,

level with the ground in the middle of the field.

No other stone was found in that field.

In his violent fall he struck his head and hand against it,

dislocated the joints of his skull,

and, with his brain shaken,

lay deprived of all his senses.

[Col. 0836C] He was dying, without any movement of his body.

It was then approximately the seventh hour of the day,

and his companions carried him home half-dead.

The priest remained awake through the night in prayer.

At first light he returned to the sick man,

laid his hand upon his head, and blessed him.

Calling him by his own name, he cried out to him.

Then, as though rising from a heavy sleep,

the man opened his eyes and answered his beloved Father.

He quickly recovered, his strength restored,

and on the following day rode joyfully,

proceeding on horseback with the bishop.

They say that John performed many other signs,

which I have not wished to recount here

because of the demands of brevity.

Here we have mentioned only those which the master Bede set down

with unquestioning faith,

weaving from the beginning a historical account

of the peoples and deeds of the English.

After that bishop had grown old,

while still living he yielded his seat of honor to another,

and with a devoted heart sought the monastery.

There he completed a life worthy of God.

At last, leaving behind the foreign laws of earth,

he was restored as a rightful heir to his heavenly homeland

[Note: [Col. 0836D] In the year 721.].

[Note: [Col. 0836D] Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English, chapter 3; Mabillon, book XX of the Annals, no. 22; and Benedictine Acts, century III, part II, p. 560. From this we learn that in the Church of York, besides the bishop, there was an abbot who presided over the monks occupying it. MABILLON.]

The distinguished priest Wilfrid succeeded John by right,

[Verse 1216.] a most worthy heir to the holy Father.

[Col. 0837A] He had previously been vice-lord and abbot of York.

Afterward, relying on the great height of his merits,

he assumed the honor worthy of the supreme bishop

and adorned his office with holy merits and character.

He added many beautiful ornaments to the titles of the holy church.

He rightly made silver vessels, radiant in beauty,

suitable for sacred services,

and covered the altar and crosses with sheets of gold.

Not wishing to conceal his treasures,

the prudent bishop spent them for the honor of God.

While the pious bishop was doing these things in the city of York,

he adorned other churches with rich gifts as well.

Nor did he care less, with a pious heart,

to multiply the flocks, following the Lord’s commandments

through the admonitions of teaching and shining examples.

[Col. 0837B] He fed some with nourishment of the mind,

but others with nourishment of the flesh.

He cherished these with heavenly things,

and increased those with bodily provisions.

With mouth and hand alike, generous in gifts to both,

he performed the work of piety under a twofold rule—

acceptable, venerable, honorable, and beloved by all.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Mabillon, book XXI of the Annals, no. 17.]

After that good shepherd had completed his works in the churches,

he sought a secluded enclosure

where he might now devote his whole mind to serving God.

Giving himself entirely to the contemplative life,

he abandoned the world’s various empty cares.

Although he remained on earth in body,

in his whole mind he nevertheless remained in heaven,

ever watchful and awaiting the rewards of heavenly life,

which at the appointed time, his earthly life completed,

he would receive, carried across the heavens in angelic arms.

[Col. 0837C] When he laid down the burdens of pastoral care,

he entrusted the rights of the venerable seat

to Ecgbert, whom he appointed as his successor and supreme bishop.

This Ecgbert was born of royal stock [Note: [Col. 0837D] This Ecgbert, brother of King Aedbert—called Eadbert by others—succeeded Wilfrid in the see of York when Wilfrid abdicated the dignity, in the year 732. Mabillon, Annals, book XXI, no. 17; Alford, under the year 738.],

of noble parental ancestry before the world,

but still more distinguished before the Lord by holy merits.

Rich in earthly wealth, which he scattered among the needy,

he became richer as he gathered it in heaven.

He was always devoted to caring for the needs of the poor,

granting treasures to the poor with a devout heart,

and, by losing them on earth, storing them for himself in heaven.

He was a most distinguished ruler of the Church

and an excellent teacher, venerable to all the people,

chosen for his character, approachable in justice,

fierce toward the wicked, yet at once gentle and severe.

[Col. 0837D] He divided nights and days among sacred duties,

unceasingly praying through the long nights,

[Verse 1264.] and celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass by day.

[Col. 0838A] In God’s houses he prepared many ornaments.

He clothed them in silver, gems, and gold,

hanging silk curtains with foreign designs.

He himself consecrated worthy ministers to the altars,

so that in various orders they might celebrate the feasts of the Thunderer.

He appointed others to sing with David’s harp,

so that they might cause hymns to resound to the Lord in measured turns.

His brother Aedbert, likewise nourished in Tyrian purple,

had taken up the royal scepters of the people.

He enlarged the boundaries of his kingdom,

often subduing hostile armies by terror.

Those were prosperous times for this people,

whom king and bishop ruled in harmonious authority:

the bishop governed the laws of the Church,

the king the affairs of the kingdom.

The bishop bore the pallia sent from apostolic shoulders;

[Col. 0838B] the king lifted the ancient diadems of his fathers onto his head.

The one was strong, the other pious;

the one energetic, the other kind.

They preserved in turn the rights of brotherly peace,

each fortunate in being aided by the other.

The bishop ruled the Church for thirty-four years [Note: [Col. 0837D] He died in the year 766. Mabillon, book XXIV of the Annals, no. 11.];

the king held the ancestral scepter for three times seven years.

Both, happy in merits, were buried in peace.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] In the year 735. Mabillon, book XXI of the Annals, no. 29, p. 99 at the end; and Benedictine Acts, century III, part II, p. 562.]

In the early years of this aforesaid bishop,

the outstanding priest Bede, distinguished for his merits,

sought the stars and closed the eyes of his present life.

From childhood he clung closely to books

and served sacred studies with all his heart.

For when he was seven years old,

his parents’ strict care caused him to enter

the enclosed monastery of Jarrow.

There the illustrious Ceolfrid [Note: [Col. 0838D] Bede, On the Six Ages of the World, under the year 4671: “In these times,” he says, “many nobles and commoners of the English people were accustomed to come from Britain to Rome. Among them was also my most reverend abbot Ceolfrid, seventy-four years old, who had been a priest for forty-seven years and an abbot for thirty-five. When he reached Lingon, he died there and was buried in the church of the blessed martyr twins.” See Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order, century II, part I, pp. 1009 ff.; Annals, book XX, no. 11.] was already abbot.

[Col. 0838C] Seeking foreign lands and led by love of Christ,

he died in exile within the territory of the city of Langres,

and there, happily, was buried with fitting honor.

After a long time his body was found

entirely intact and then brought back to its homeland.

Thus Bede, nurtured in that monastery,

adorned his youthful years with distinguished character.

For the eager young man constantly strove to learn and write,

working with a fervent, not sluggish, mind.

Thus, advancing, he rightly became a teacher.

Therefore the illustrious doctor produced many little works,

explaining the obscure books of sacred Scripture.

He also composed an art of meters,

and a remarkable volume on the Times,

which contains the courses, positions, periods, and laws of the stars.

[Col. 0838D] He also wrote historical booklets in distinguished prose,

and sang many poems with his metrical plectrum.

[Verse 1312.] In deed, mind, and faith,

throughout his life he always followed

the footsteps of the ancient Fathers along a straight path.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] Mabillon, cited work, p. 100.]
