What his life had been like before he became a teacher

was disclosed after his death by a clear sign of healing.

For while a certain sick man was girded with the relics

of the holy Father,

he was completely healed of his disease.

You also, Balthere [Note: [Col. 0839D] “During the seventeenth year of the episcopate of Cunewulf, bishop of Lindisfarne, and the twentieth year of the reign of Eadbert, king of the Northumbrians: ‘The man of God and priest Balther, who had led an anchoritic life at Tyningham, entered upon the way of the holy Fathers, departing to him who reformed him according to the image of his Son on the day before the Nones of March,’ says Turgot in his Book on the Church of Durham; and indeed in the year 756, according to Hoveden. He is commemorated in the Benedictine calendars on 27 November. His relics were transferred to Durham in the eleventh century. Read Bollandus under 6 March, where the site of the monastery or hermitage of Saint Balther in Scotland is located. MABILLON.], whom we touch with a Pierian plectrum,

and you, holy one, whose place we mark here in our verses,

255 keep us in your peaceful mind, we ask,

and now guide our little boat through the blue waters of the sea.

From there show us the sea’s monsters,

among craggy rocks and waves,

so that, carrying its burden, it may reach a safe harbor.

There is a place surrounded on every side by a wave-filled sea,

enclosed by dreadful cliffs and a precipitous shore.

There the mighty warrior Balthere, while still in an earthly body,

often conquered the aerial hosts,

[Col. 0839B] which varied their warfare against him in many forms.

Yet undaunted, he drove back the enemy camp,

always opposing the weapons of the wicked

with the blessed weapons of the cross,

the helmet and shield of faith.

That pious man, once when he was alone,

devoted himself to prayers,

meditating only on heavenly things.

Suddenly he heard a horrible noise and crashing,

as of a crowd bursting against an enemy.

Then the soul of someone from the heavenly clouds

fell before his feet,

shaken by overwhelming fear;

Soon afterward a threatening crowd followed in immense terror,

Wishing to torment the wretched woman with varied punishments.

But that pious Father seized her in his peaceful embrace,

Took her into his lap, and immediately asked her

[Col. 0839C] Who she was, why she was fleeing, and what evil she had done. Then she replied:

“I was a Levite, but with an evil mind

I embraced a woman’s breasts with my hands alone,

And, while living in the flesh, I was ashamed to confess my guilt.

Now for this reason fierce enemies follow me,

Tormenting me with harsh assaults for thirty days.

I was not seized, yet I did not remain safe.”

Then one of the enemies terrified him, crying out:

“Today you shall not escape, not even if you are held in the arms

Of Peter; you shall suffer the punishment you deserve, wretch.”

But the saint, angered by the insults against Peter,

Said: “Behold, I am a hundred times inferior to that

Apostolic prince in merits; but trusting in the mercy of the Thunderer,

I tell you, savage and cruel tyrant:

Today you shall not carry her with you beneath Tartarus.”

[Col. 0839D] Then the pious intercessor prostrated himself upon the ground

And with tears entreated the Lord on behalf of her guilt.

Nor did he cease pouring forth holy prayers

[Vers. 1360] Until he had seen with his own eyes the soul

[Col. 0840A] Borne aloft by angelic arms above the stars of heaven.

Christ’s mercy toward this pious Father also performed

A similar deed, and a sign equal to the former sign.

For just as Peter had walked upon the waves,

So it happened to this man: once, as he was walking

Along the precipitous edge of a lofty cliff, it happened by chance

That he fell; but, supported by the sea’s waves,

He walked with dry feet upon the waters.

And as though he were treading the fields of earth, so he walked upon the waves;

Indeed, the wave received him as he fell more gently

Than if hard fields had received a falling man.

As he fell, the wave flowed beneath him so that the fall would not injure him;

The ground remained beneath his steps so that the sea would not engulf him.

Thus he walked upon the solid strait as though along a road of earth,

Until he reached the ship that moved upon the waves;

[Col. 0840B] Then he climbed aboard on foot by a safe path.

There was no water on his clothing, no moisture clung to his shoes.

What nature forbids, your right hand grants, O Christ:

At your command the sea’s water becomes passable for the just;

But, by contrast, the earth becomes an avenging whirlpool for the wicked.

It bears the humble, while that other devours the proud.

But now we, your devoted servants, entreat you, holy Balthere,

That just as the wave carried your body from the sea,

Bringing you back unharmed to familiar shores,

So by your prayers you may make our souls escape

The world’s waves and enter the harbor of salvation.

In those same days the venerable Echa [Note: I have found no other information anywhere about this anchorite Echa. MABILL.] also shone forth,

A holy anchorite who pursued the solitudes of the wilderness,

Having already become chaste in body by fleeing earthly honors,

So that he might possess heavenly ones with God the King.

[Col. 0840C] Devotedly living an angelic life on earth,

He foretold many things to come with prophetic mind.

Of him the Muse forbids more to be told, as she returns

To the end of the poem and to the deeds of my own master;

He who, after Ecgbert, assumed the insignia of the venerable see,

The wise Aelbert, so named [Note: [Col. 0840D] Bishop Aelbert succeeded in 766; Hoveden, *Annals*, first part, p. 403. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXIV, nos. 11 and 12; he died in 780, idem, book XXV, no. 11. See also Alford under the years 766 and 767.].

A good and just man, generous, pious, and kind;

A supporter, teacher, and lover of the Catholic faith;

Ruler, teacher, defender, and foster-child of the Church;

Cultivator of justice, trumpet of the law, herald of salvation;

Hope of the poor, father to orphans, comforter of the needy.

Savage toward the harsh, gentle toward the good, and severe toward the proud;

Strong in adversity, and humble in prosperity.

Shrewd in mind, not talkative in speech, but vigorous in action.

As the summit of accumulated honor rose for him,

[Col. 0840D] So greatly did his mind submit itself in humble devotion.

I ask you, Euboric youth, to allow me to proceed

A little farther in verse concerning him.

[Vers. 1409] He who often drenched your senses with nectar,

[Col. 0841A] Pouring forth sweet juices from his honeyed breast,

Whom a most beautiful understanding seized from his earliest cradle

And carried to the citadel of the whole realm of knowledge,

Opening to him the secrets of the wisdom of learning.

He was born, then, of parents of considerable distinction.

From their care he was soon committed to nurturing studies,

And in boyhood was placed in a monastery,

So that his fragile age might grow mature in sacred learning.

Nor was the great hope of his parents placed in a boy in vain.

As the outstanding boy grew in bodily stature,

So he advanced in the understanding of books.

Thus, growing in merit with the years and with an alert mind,

He was made a holy Levite in the proper order.

When, as a fortunate young man, he had honorably discharged this office,

The worthy youth received the rights of the priesthood,

[Col. 0841B] So that he who had grown in noble merits might grow through the grades.

256 Then the pious and prudent teacher, at once doctor and priest,

Joined himself as companion to Bishop Ecgbert,

To whom he was already related by blood.

By him he was appointed defender of all the clergy,

And at the same time was placed as teacher in the city of Euborica.

When he watered the thirsty hearts of some with the flowing streams

Of learning and with the varied dew of study,

He diligently gave these the arts of grammatical reasoning,

And poured into those the streams of rhetorical speech;

He polished some on the whetstone of law,

And taught others to compose song in Aonian music;

Training others to make the Castalian reed resound,

And to traverse the ridges of Parnassus with lyric feet.

[Col. 0841C] But this same teacher made others understand

The harmony of heaven, the courses of the sun and moon,

The five zones of the sky, the seven wandering stars,

The laws of the constellations, their risings and settings;

The motions of the air and sea, and the trembling of the earth;

The natures of human beings, cattle, birds, and wild beasts;

The various kinds of number and their different figures.

He taught the fixed observance of the Paschal cycle,

Especially revealing the mysteries of sacred Scripture.

For he disclosed the depths of the unlearned and ancient Law.

Whenever he saw young men of outstanding character,

He joined them to himself, taught them, nurtured them, and loved them;

Therefore, throughout the sacred volumes, the teacher had many

Disciples enriched by diverse arts.

[Col. 0841D] More than once he traveled through foreign lands

Along distant roads, rejoicing, led by love of wisdom,

To see whether he might find there anything new in books or studies

That he could carry back with him to his own lands.

He also came devotedly to the Roman city,

[Vers. 1458] Rich in the love of God, visiting the holy places far and wide.

[Col. 0842A] Returning from there, he was received everywhere

With honor by kings and governors as a supreme teacher.

For great kings wished to retain a man

Who would water their lands with a flowing divine dew.

But hastening back to the task appointed for him,

By God’s dispensation he returned to benefit his homeland.

After he had been brought back to his native region,

He was soon compelled to assume pastoral care;

At the people’s request he was made supreme priest,

And adorned the office with his noble merits,

Found everywhere both a good officer and a good shepherd.

For cautiously he guarded the divine sheepfold,

So that no wolf might injure Christ’s lambs in any way—

The lambs for whom he provided the nourishment of the sacred word,

So that no bitter thirst or hunger might afflict them.

[Col. 0842B] He carried back upon his friendly shoulders

Those who had strayed from the flock through the trackless wastes of the wilderness

To the Lord’s fold;

Those unwilling to follow him when he called them in gentle speech

He pursued with the terrors and lashes of the law.

Nor did the just man spare an unjust king or ruler.

Yet, despite the burdens of his duties,

He did not lessen his fervent zeal for reading the ancient Scriptures;

He became both things together: a shrewd teacher and a pious priest,

Increasing the understanding of some and adorning others in their morals.

Nor, after the Father had attained such a height of honor,

Did he change his former way of life in clothing or food:

He avoided excessive delicacies, nor did he pursue things utterly mean,

But took delight in a moderate course.

Meanwhile, no less, filled with the fervor of faith,

He added varied ornaments of beauty to the churches.

[Col. 0842C] For when the mighty King Edvin [Note: King Edvin. Understand this as Edvin, king of the Northumbrians, concerning whom Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book II, chapter 14, relates: “King Eduinus was baptized at York on holy Easter Day, the day before the Ides of April (627), in the church of the holy apostle Peter, which he himself had quickly constructed there of wood while he was being catechized and instructed to receive baptism.” Bede’s account is difficult to reconcile with that of our poet unless, by transposing the words, one understands it as follows: King Edvin constructed a great wooden altar, which Bishop Aelbert, only after a full century, covered with silver, gold, and gems and, out of love for Saint Paul, changed its title from Saint Peter and dedicated it in Paul’s honor. See more about this king above, verses 194 and following.] received the water of baptism,

The bishop had built a great altar,

And covered it everywhere with silver, gems, and gold,

And dedicated it under the name of Saint Paul,

The teacher of the world, whom the teacher loved exceedingly.

He had suspended above the altar a lofty lamp [Note: *Farum*, that is, a candelabrum.],

Which holds three large vessels in each of nine rows;

He also raised a lofty banner of the cross above the altar,

And covered it entirely with precious metals.

All these objects, sufficiently grand, were constructed with beautiful workmanship,

And their great weights were matched by much refined silver.

He made another altar as well, and clothed it

With pure silver and precious stones;

He dedicated it alike to the martyrs and to the cross.

He ordered that a large ampulla of gold,

Of no small weight and refined purity,

[Col. 0842D] Should be made, from which the priest could pour wine

Into the chalice while celebrating the sacred rites.

In the days of this bishop the wondrous new structure of the basilica

Was begun, completed, and consecrated.

[Vers. 1580] This exceedingly lofty house, supported by solid columns,

[Col. 0843A] Which stand beneath curved arches,

Rises within with splendid ceilings and windows,

And shines beautifully, surrounded by many porticoes,

Containing numerous upper chambers beneath various roofs,

And holding thirty altars of varied adornment.

This temple was built by two disciples, Eanbald and Alcuin,

At the teacher’s command, both working together

With devoted minds upon the undertaking.

Yet the Father himself, together with his fellow bishop, [Note: Eanbald, who succeeded Aelbert while he was still living and after his resignation, at the beginning of September in 778. See below, verses 1564 and 1582.]

Had consecrated this temple

Ten days before he closed the final

Light of his present life, to holy wisdom.

Thus the most illustrious minister in sacred order,

A perfect bishop and full of merits and years,

Gladly handed over to Eanbald, his beloved pupil,

257 The episcopal dignity, and sought for himself a secluded enclosure

[Col. 0843B] Where he could now be free to serve God alone.

But to another [Note: Read *alii*, “to another,” namely Alcuin.] he handed over treasures dearer than all else:

Books, to a son who had always clung to his father

And was accustomed to drink thirstily from the streams of learning.

If you wish to know his proper name,

The present poem will immediately reveal it on its opening page [Note: The poet’s name does not appear in the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Thierry, says Mabillon; but that Alcuin’s name was prefixed to this poem can be sufficiently inferred from this passage alone.].

He divided his possessions among them in different allotments:

To one, the governance of the Church, treasures, lands, and talents;

To the other, the treasury of wisdom, study, the seat of learning, and books—

The books which the illustrious teacher had previously collected everywhere,

Gathering outstanding treasures beneath a single roof.

There you will find the traces of the ancient Fathers,

Whatever the Roman Latin world possesses on its own,

And whatever illustrious Greece has transmitted to the Latins;

Whatever the Hebrew people drank in a heavenly rain;

[Col. 0843C] And whatever Africa scattered in its light-giving radiance.

Whatever Father Jerome, whatever Hilary, Bishop Ambrose,

Augustine also, and holy Athanasius himself,

Whatever the ancestral Orosius published [Note: Some copies read *acutus*, “sharp-minded.”];

Whatever the supreme Gregory teaches, and Pope Leo;

Whatever Basil, and whatever Fulgentius, shine forth.

Likewise Cassiodorus, Chrysostom, and John.

Whatever Æthelhelm taught, whatever the teacher Bede;

Whatever Victorinus and Boethius wrote;

The ancient historians, Pompey and Pliny; Aristotle himself,

The keen philosopher; and the mighty orator Cicero.

Whatever Sedulius, or Juvencus himself, sings;

Alcuin [Note: Alcuin. From this Oudinus conjectures that Alcuin was not the author of this poem, since he surely would not have counted himself, while still alive, among the holy teachers. I, however, think that *Alcuinus* should be read *Alcimus* or *Alcinous*.] and Clement, Prosper, Paulinus, and Arator;

Whatever Fortunatus or Lactantius produce.

[Vers. 1553] Whatever Maro Virgil, Statius, Lucan, and the Author [wrote];

[Col. 0844A] Whatever the masters of grammatical art have written;

Whatever Probus, Phocas, Donatus, or Priscian;

Servius, Eutychius, Pompey, or Comminianus.

You will find many others there, reader,

Outstanding masters in learning, art, and language,

Who wrote many volumes with brilliant understanding.

But to write the names of all of them in the present poem

Seemed a longer task than the use of the lyre requires.

With these arrangements made, the supreme bishop completed his years,

Mature in every respect in merits and age.

After two years, together with as many months as years,

Had passed since the holy bishop sought his secluded enclosure,

He passed joyfully and successfully into the heavenly court,

Before his disciples, as shepherd, patriarch, and teacher.

But, mournful lyre of mine, leave this passage sooner,

[Col. 0844B] Lest you perish, submerged in a flood of tears,

While, with favorable sails, you have thus far hastened toward harbor.

Why do you strive to recall for us, in deepest sorrow, these fates,

When suddenly, before the eyes of us all,

Envious death closed in the final sleep

The eyes of the venerable supreme bishop, our father and teacher?

O grief for us! O black day! O bright day for him!

He left us orphaned, without a father,

Burdened with tears, harsh exile, and labor.

But he restored him to his homeland and to the heavenly Father,

Freed from tears, exile, and labor.

For now Christ is his love, his drink, his food—Christ is everything:

His life, faith, understanding, hope, light, way, glory, and strength.

[Col. 0844C] He slept in the fourteenth year of the supreme

Order he had received, beneath the sun on the eighth of November [Note: Hoveden, under the year 780, records the death in that year of Albert, or Aelbert, bishop of York; this is confirmed by the present passage. Above, at verse 1396, we noted from the same Hoveden, Mabillon, and Alford that Aelbert entered that episcopal see in 766. If fourteen years are added to that year—the length of time our poet says he survived after attaining the dignity—the year 780 results. Above also, at verses 1563 and following, it is said that blessed Aelbert lived two further years and the same number of months after leaving the episcopate, withdrawing into solitude, and handing the episcopal dignity to his disciple Eanbald. Hence you may conclude that Aelbert’s withdrawal and Eanbald’s ordination occurred in September 778. See Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXV, p. 255, no. 11.],

While that grievous day was shining in the sixth hour.

A great throng had gathered for his funeral,

With the bishop and clergy, people, young and old,

All honoring their father by laying his body to rest.

O Father, O shepherd, greatest hope of our life,

Without you we are driven across the troubled seas of the world;

Without you as our guide, we are enveloped by various waves,

Uncertain what harbor we may deserve to reach.

While day and night yield to each other,

While the year is divided into four seasons,

While shoots grow upon the earth,

While the stars shine and the wind drives the clouds,

[Vers. 1595] Your honor, your name, and your praises will always remain.

[Col. 0845A] As I wished, Thalia, to close you here

At a fixed ending, an event from our own days came before us.

Therefore, although weary, sing a few more verses,

And briefly take up the story of my boy,

Whose present witness I too happened to be.

There was, then, a certain young man brought up

In the city of Euborica, simple in mind but fervent in action.

He had guided the years of my childhood by his counsel,

And one night, as was his custom, alone

He persisted in prayer in the chapel of Christ’s Mother.

Then a holy light suddenly filled the house,

And with the light there came a man in white garments,

Radiant in appearance and noble in his dignified bearing.

With gentle words he raised the young man, who had fallen in great terror,

And showed him an open book.

[Col. 0845B] The young man read it through. Then, when he had closed the book,

The radiant man said to him: “You shall see greater things again.”

After saying this, the shining visitor suddenly disappeared.

258 Not long afterward, after several months,

The young man was struck throughout his limbs by a raging disease,

And, sick, lay for a long time near death,

Drawing the breath that was about to perish through his constricted nostrils.

As he lay in my arms, his spirit was suddenly snatched away,

And his body remained lifeless.

After some time he returned and again moved his limbs,

And told me that someone had led him

To exceedingly beautiful places, where he saw many people rejoicing,

Both unknown and known; but above all he recognized

The joyful pupils of that holy Church.

[Col. 0845C] They immediately received him in peaceful embraces

And wished to keep him with them forever.

But his guide quickly led him back along the path he had come,

To his own body, saying that at sunrise

He would already be in better health;

But that another of the brothers would die that day,

And that he had seen the place prepared for him.

The young man’s account was not false.

For he quickly recovered while the sun was glowing at its rising;

But before midday another had died.

Yet a short time later, in that same year,

The young man was struck by the ravaging plague of illness,

And immediately foretold to me what the disease would bring:

“I shall die of this sickness; soon I shall leave the prison of the flesh.”

And so it happened, since the great force of his illness

Increased and brought the young man to his final hour.

As he began to release his soul in a slender breath while dying,

One of the brothers was awake—a good and truthful man.

He saw a man descend from on high,

Radiant in face and clothing,

And immediately place his own mouth against the mouth of the dying man,

While gently embracing with his hands the limbs of the one lying there.

[Vers. 1646] Then, returning, he released the soul from the prison of the flesh

[Col. 0846A] And carried it, flying with him, above the stars of the heavens.

These things I, an unskilled sailor, gathered into frail vessels,

Steering through the waves of the sea and across its hidden shoals,

And by right brought the cargo back to the harbor of Euborica—

Since that city nourished me as its own pupil

And, in some measure, imbued me reverently from my earliest years.

For this reason I have written rustic songs for it about its own Fathers, kings, and saints.

Those saints alike, whom I have touched upon in these verses,

I entreat to steer our ship, through their merits and abundant prayers,

From the world’s whirlpool to the harbor of life.

## CCLXXXII. To Friducinus

[Note: See letter 224, to Friduinus; I do not think he is different from the person called Friducinus here.]

[Col. 0846B] Let this little letter, as it runs, bear my perpetual greeting to Friducinus [Note: [Col. 0845D; 0846D] This poem was copied from the Harleian manuscript codex, concerning which we have already said more; see vol. I, col. 137. From it we also extracted letter 224, to Friduin, abbot of Gerwice, who may seem to be the same as this Friducinus, except that the latter is called a faithful son while the former is revered as a Father.],

My son, in the peace upon your lips.

May you, the Father’s sweet love, always be well,

With sacred devotion and good prosperity.

Through the holy places of the saints, faithful son,

Always remember Albinus with lips of peace.

Be pious and gentle, proceeding with cautious moderation;

Wise in counsel and strong in devotion.

Truthful in speech and faithful in heart,

Praising Christ in the service of your mouth.

Diligent in prayers, especially in the temples of the saints;

May the aid of none of them pass you by.

Hold sober feasts with your righteous companions,

Generous to the poor as a father to the wretched.

Keep your own household from criminals and plunder,

Lest any of your people perhaps take something from another by force.

[Col. 0846C] The saint says: “Indeed, I have never seen the just man abandoned,

Nor his offspring begging for sacred bread.

The cry of the poor rises to the throne of Olympus,

And Christ himself will hear his prayers.

I beg that your table, or your house itself,

May not reek of theft or perhaps of plunder,

Nor of the spoils of the wretched.

May the priest of the Most High often be your guest,

And the servant of Christ, or the poor and homeless man,

Rather than a person accustomed to harmful, talkative chatter,

Who redoubles wicked words in your ears.”

## CCLXXXIII. To a Certain Person

May the flying Muse come to bring greetings to great Monus [Note: Perhaps Monna, to whom letter 183 is addressed.]

[Col. 0846D] To whom God grant eternal well-being through the ages;

And may the holy throng of saints throughout the world

Commend him continually to Christ in assiduous prayers, we pray.

May he, the son of Father Albinus, come safely,

When the appointed time arrives, gladly to the distinguished city

Where Saint Martin rests bodily.

This, I pray, may Christ’s gracious favor grant us.

But you, son, remember to serve God

With conduct pleasing to him, so that he may always protect you in gentleness;

May he lead you prosperously through unknown lands as you travel,

[Col. 0847A] And in his mercy bring you back to us again, rejoicing.

Watch carefully where you are going and what you are doing;

Remember also to preserve your own salvation.

Do not, I beg you, son, destroy yourself with too much wine,

Nor with food, since the world is sufficiently harmful in that respect.

Bitter illnesses arise from food and drink.

[Col. 0848A] A harmful fruit now hangs upon the tree,

By eating which the unwary will soon be weakened.

Let your tongue also be truthful and your speech wholesome;

Let food and drink be greatly moderated in your mouth.

Let your heart be watchful in prayer and your will pure,

In praises of the Lord throughout the places of the holy Fathers.

# THE SEVENTH PART OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, TEACHER OF CHARLEMAGNE

## DIDACTIC WORKS

[Col. 0847]

### 263 PREFATORY NOTICE

[Col. 0847] I think learned men will not be displeased that, among these genuine little works of blessed Alcuin, they do not find that incomplete book *On the Seven Arts* which the distinguished Quercetanus nevertheless attributed to our author on the authority of an old manuscript of Jacques Sirmond, and inserted into his edition beginning at page 1246. Indeed, it seems so clear to me that nothing in this book belongs to our Alcuin that, in the very Preface placed before it, the true author immediately reveals and identifies himself—namely, the very man who wrote the book *On Divine Institutions*:

“The preceding book,” he says, “completed by the Lord’s assistance, contains the Lessons of Divine Institutions; it is known to be comprised in thirty-three titles . . . . Now it is time that, in seven other titles of secular lessons, we should proceed through the text of the present book.”

Yet by the unanimous agreement of all learned men and the testimony of all manuscript codices, the true author of both *Divine Institutions* and the secular lessons arranged in seven titles—namely, on Grammar, Rhetoric, Dialectic, Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy—is Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator. This was demonstrated by many arguments by the most learned Maurist monk, D. Garetius, in his *Works of Aurelius Cassiodorus*, Preface, p. 10, Venice edition of 1729 [Note: *Patrologia*, volumes LXIX and LXX.].

Since, therefore, this book entitled *On the Seven Arts*—of which Quercetanus’s edition presents only the first two chapters, and those badly mutilated—is certainly falsely attributed to blessed Alcuin, while it exists complete under Cassiodorus and has been restored to its true parent, I think that we have rightly judged it should be severed from Alcuin’s genuine little works, without offending learned men.

We therefore begin this part with the *Dialogue on Grammatical Art*, which will be followed by a recently discovered little book *On Orthography*; this is followed by the *Dialogue on Rhetorical Art*, and another *On Dialectic*. To these is appended the *Disputation of Pippin with Albinus the Scholar*. Finally, we add certain studies and fragments on the Course and Leap of the Moon and on the Leap Year, which we have extracted from manuscript codices and, for the reasons to be set forth in the preliminary notices, attribute to Alcuin as their true author.

It is certainly regrettable that the remaining works which Alcuin unquestionably wrote on Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, the Metrical Art, and Astronomy have for the most part perished. Certainly the writer of his Life testifies that, at the request of Emperor Charles, Alcuin wrote not only on Grammar and Dialectic but also on Music. It also seems possible to infer from the beginning of the *Dialogue on Rhetoric* that he conveyed to the same emperor, not merely orally but in writing, instruction in the arts of Arithmetic and Astronomy. There Alcuin introduces Charles as saying:

“Since, by a few answers of yours, you opened for me the gates of rhetorical art and the barriers of dialectical subtlety, you have made me very attentive to their principles—especially because yesterday you skillfully led me into the storehouses of arithmetic and illuminated me with the splendor of astrology.”

These words plainly suggest that, before writing this *Dialogue on Rhetoric*, Alcuin had also composed similar works on Arithmetic and Astronomy. Finally, among Alcuin’s writings, Trithemius, in book II of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26, lists a book *On the Metrical Art*. Alcuin himself also promises his pupils Franco and Saxo that he will give them fuller instruction in metrics:

“More fully, with life as my companion, I shall show you these things, my sons, in the theory of meter.”

And a little later:

“You will understand these things more aptly in that subtlety of meters, because feet and accents cannot be understood except through short and long syllables.”

But either ravenous time has consumed all these works, or they perhaps still lie hidden in cabinets not yet searched, to be found one day by a more fortunate hand.

Meanwhile, from the materials we now bring to light from various manuscript codices, in forms much more accurately corrected than any in which they have ever appeared, the attentive reader will understand that Blessed Alcuin was thoroughly versed not only in exegetical and dogmatic sciences but also in secular letters and the liberal arts—indeed, that among the teachers of his age he was easily first:

“For he became all things to all,” says Canisius: “a theologian to theologians, a dialectician to dialecticians, a musician to musicians, a rhetorician to rhetoricians, a grammarian to grammarians, and even a boy to boys, so that he might win them all.”

He makes the same claim about himself in letter 43, to Charles, writing:

“I, your Flaccus . . . strive to serve some with the sacred honey of the Scriptures beneath the roofs of Saint Martin; I study to intoxicate others with the old unmixed wine of ancient disciplines; I shall begin to nourish others with the fruits of grammatical subtlety; I desire to illuminate some with the order of the stars, as though with the painted summit of a great house; becoming many things to many, so that I may instruct many for the advancement of God’s holy Church and for the adornment of your imperial kingdom.”

[Col. 0849]

## FIRST LITTLE WORK: GRAMMAR

### 265 PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0849A]

The present little work consists of two dialogues. The first is between the teacher and his pupils and serves as a preliminary instruction for acquiring true wisdom. The teacher teaches that one must ascend to it through Grammar, Rhetoric, Dialectic, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy, as though by steps. For that reason, in the manuscript codex of Freising, this first dialogue is prefaced by the following special title: *Disputation on True Philosophy*.

The second dialogue, which properly concerns the Art of Grammar, has three interlocutors: the teacher and two boys, one a Saxon and the other a Frank. How highly the celebrated Notker the Stammerer esteemed the grammar of blessed Alcuin may be judged from his words to his pupil Solomon, later bishop of the Church of Constance:

“Albinus,” he says, “composed such a grammar that Donatus, Nicomachus, Dositheus, and our Priscian seem to be nothing by comparison with it” [Note: Pezius, volume I of *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 8.].

But this praise is excessive. Nevertheless, it may be that this grammar surpasses many others in usefulness because of the method by which it is treated. That is the judgment of D. Rivet, *Literary History of France*, volume IV, p. 317, no. 21.

The distinguished D. Johann Wilhelm von Berger, public professor of eloquence, has commented fully and learnedly on this grammar, on the excellent learning found in it, and on the two boys Saxo and Franco, in two dissertations *On the Learning of the Carolingian Saxon*, delivered at Wittenberg in 1741. The celebrated and most distinguished D. Christoph Adolf Klotz, royal privy councillor to the king of Prussia, supplied me with a copy.

Canisius first brought this little work into public circulation, in volume V of *Ancient Readings*, pp. 988 and following, and it was also printed by Basnage, volume II, part I, p. 506. It was later inserted into Putsch’s *Collection of Ancient Grammarians*, published at Hanover in 1605.

[Col. 0849C] Here we present this grammar of blessed Alcuin, carefully corrected against the oldest and best manuscript codices, those of Freising and Saint Emmeram. We have removed numerous errors and supplied lacunae found in D. Quercetanus’s edition; in accordance with our practice, we indicate all such additions by enclosing them in these signs: [].

## THE PUPILS. THE TEACHER.

### THE PUPIL

We have often heard you, most learned teacher, saying that philosophy is the teacher of all virtues, and that it alone is what, among all the riches of the world, would never leave a person miserable who possessed it. By these words, as we freely admit, you have stirred us to seek such excellent happiness, since we wish to know what the substance of this instruction is and by what steps one can ascend to it.

[Col. 0849D] For [indeed (the edition reads: “therefore”)] our age is still tender, and without your extending a hand our weakness is scarcely sufficient to rise by itself. We understand, moreover, that the nature of the mind is in the heart, just as that of the eyes is in the head. Thus, if the eyes are struck by the sun’s radiance or by the presence of any other light, they can discern with the greatest clarity whatever comes before their gaze; but without the aid of light, it is well known that they remain in darkness.

So the vigor of the mind is receptive to wisdom if there is someone who begins to illuminate it.

### THE TEACHER

You have rightly brought forward the comparison between the eyes and the mind, my sons. But may he who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9) illuminate your minds, so that you may progress in that philosophy which, as you said, never abandons the person who possesses it.

### THE PUPILS

We know, teacher, we know with complete certainty that we must ask this of him who gives generously and reproaches no one. Nevertheless, we must be instructed gradually and, like the weak, led with a slower step until some strength increases in us.

A flint naturally contains fire within itself, which usually comes forth under a blow. So the light of knowledge is natural to human minds, but unless it is struck out by the teacher’s repeated attention, it lies hidden within, like a spark in a flint.

### THE TEACHER

It is easy enough to show you the way of wisdom, if you love it solely for God, [for knowledge of things], for the purity of the soul, for the discovery of truth, and also for its own sake—not for human praise, the honors of the world, or even the deceptive pleasures of riches. For the more these things are loved, the farther they cause those who seek them to stray from the true light of knowledge, just as a drunken man does not know by which road to return home.

### THE PUPILS

We admit that we have loved happiness; [Col. 0850C] but we do not know whether any happiness can exist in this world.

### THE TEACHER

The desire for the true good has been naturally implanted in human minds; but a wayward error leads many of them toward certain false goods. Some of these think that the greatest happiness consists in abundance of riches [credunt, “they think”; variant: credentes, “thinking”]; others rejoice in honors; others take pleasure in power; others delight in pleasures; others hunger for praise.

When these things are considered more carefully, they are found to be entangled in such great calamities that they scarcely seem to possess any happiness at all. Some people dream of these things and imagine that they will be true happiness; and although a natural inclination leads them toward the true good, manifold error nevertheless draws them away because of ignorance.

### THE PUPILS

What healthy-minded person does not know that these things are transient? Yet who does not know that an abundance of them assists the traveler through this life?

[Col. 0850D] ### THE TEACHER

Their moderate use assists; excess burdens. Hence the philosophical maxim is valid: “Nothing in excess.”

### THE PUPILS

It is well known that everything excessive is harmful. But to what limit should one seek an abundance of the things you listed shortly before?

### THE TEACHER

As much as the body’s necessity requires and as much as the pursuit of wisdom demands.

### THE PUPILS

We think it belongs to the perfect to restrain the course of their souls with the reins of such a principle.

### THE TEACHER

To this perfection, then, I exhort you, my sons, while your age is flourishing and your spirit is vigorous.

### THE PUPILS

Lead us, then, and guide us back through the paths of divine reason, and carry us to the summit of this perfection. For although our steps are unequal, we follow you as our guide.

### THE TEACHER

O human being, rational animal, immortal in your better part, image of your Creator: why do you destroy what is your own? Why do you seek what belongs to another? Why do you pursue what is low and abandon what is highest?

### THE PUPILS

What things are our own, and what things belong to others?

### THE TEACHER

Things sought outside are foreign, such as the gathering of riches; within lies the glory of wisdom. Therefore, O human being, if you are master of yourself, you will possess what you will never regret losing and what no fortune will be able to take away from you.

Why, then, O mortals, do you seek outside yourselves what you possess within?

DIS. We seek happiness.

MAG. You seek it rightly, if you seek what remains, and not what flees. You see with how many bitternesses earthly happiness is sprinkled: it comes wholly to no one, nor does it remain reliable for anyone, since nothing unchanging can be found in the present life. What is more beautiful than light? Yet it is darkened when darkness follows. What is more lovely than the flowers of summer? Yet they perish in winter’s cold. What is sweeter than bodily health? And who can be confident of possessing it perpetually? What is more delightful than tranquil peace? Yet it is often provoked by the bitter fuel of discord.

DIS. We do not doubt that all these things are as you say. But to what end do you say this?

MAG. So that you may recognize lesser things from greater ones.

DIS. How so?

MAG. If heaven and earth are always changed by their alternations, and the universal beauty and usefulness of all mortal things are likewise changed, how much more must the pleasure of any particular thing be transitory? And why should those things be loved that cannot endure? What do you human beings think about the praise of [a name (Edit., of a human being)], the dignity of honor, and the gathering of riches? You have read of Croesus’ wealth, Alexander’s fame, and Pompey’s honor. And what good will these things do those who are destined to perish? Each of them, through an untimely death, quickly lost the glory acquired with great labor, and in a certain sense diminished the integrity of his own knowledge [Ms., justice], since he sought praise for himself from the little speeches of others. Why do you labor to gather riches, which either abandon their possessors or are themselves abandoned? They enrich more by being spent than by being preserved [Ms., they strive]. For avarice makes people hated, while generosity makes them renowned. Their abundance is amassed only from the neediness [Ms., indulgence] of others. Why do you seek honors, the fuel of pride? Is there not one Father of all? And why do you wrong your Creator by loving worse things and losing better ones? He wished the human race to surpass all earthly things, but you thrust your dignity down beneath every lowly thing. How much better it is to be adorned inwardly than outwardly, and to polish the immortal soul with splendor.

267 DIS. What are the soul’s [perpetual] ornaments?

MAG. First of all, wisdom, which I urge you especially to pursue [Ms., recommend].

DIS. How do we know that wisdom is perpetual? And if all the things you listed earlier are transitory, why should knowledge of them not also pass away?

MAG. Do you think that the soul is perpetual?

DIS. We not only think so, but know it with complete certainty.

MAG. Is wisdom the soul’s adornment and dignity?

DIS. It truly is.

[Note: [Col. 0851D] These lines have been restored from the Frisingen manuscript.]

MAG. How could the soul be perpetually happy without wisdom, its adornment? [Col. 0852B] Is it not contrary to reason for the soul to be perpetual without its adornment and dignity? It follows, it seems, that both are perpetual: the soul, namely, and wisdom. Do you see that wealth very often abandons its possessor in every circumstance, and that all the honors of the world are repeatedly diminished?

DIS. We see, then, that not even royal power endures [Ms., as royal power endures].

MAG. What are riches without wisdom?

DIS. What the body is without the soul, as Solomon says: “What good are riches to a fool, when he cannot buy wisdom?” (Prov. XVII, 16).

MAG. Is this not what exalts the humble and raises the poor from the dungheap, so that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory?

[Col. 0852C] DIS. It is indeed; but it is as attractive to possess as it is laborious to acquire.

MAG. What soldier will be crowned without combat? What farmer abounds in bread without labor? Is it not an old proverb that the roots of learning are bitter, but its fruits sweet? Thus our orator also proves the same thing in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “No discipline, indeed, seems at the present time to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised by it.”

DIS. Lead us, then, wherever you wish; we follow willingly, because hope of reward usually lightens labor. For everyone who plows plows in hope of receiving the harvest. It is related that when that great philosopher Diogenes drove all his disciples away from him, saying, “Go, seek a master for yourselves; I have found one for myself,” Plato alone clung to him. One day, with muddy feet, Plato ran up and sat upon the master’s raised couch beside the teacher, whom Diogenes threatened to strike with his staff. The boy, bowing his head, replied: “No staff is so hard that it could separate me from your side.”

But if he, burning with love for secular wisdom, yet ignorant of the heavenly wisdom that leads to eternal life, persisted so ardently in following his master, how much more ought we to follow your footsteps, master, as you enter and leave—the footsteps of one who knows how to lead us not only along the literary road of the liberal studies, but who can also open for us the better paths of wisdom, which lead to eternal life [Col. 0853A] [open (supplied)]?

MAG. May divine grace go before us and lead us into the treasuries of spiritual wisdom, in which you may drink deeply from the fountain of divine abundance, so that within you there may be a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. But since, at the Apostle’s command, we read, “Let all your things be done decently and in order,” I think that you must be led through certain stages of learning from lower things to higher ones, until the wings of the virtues gradually grow, by which, flying toward the loftier sights of the pure ether, you may be able to say: “The king has brought us into his wine-cellars; we will exult and rejoice in them” (Song I, 3).

DIS. Give us your right hand, master, raise us from the ground of ignorance, and set us with you upon the steps of wisdom, on which we have often recognized you standing through the dignity of your conduct and the truth of your words. The beautiful order of things has led you to this point from your earliest age, as we have heard. And if it is permissible to lend our ears to poetic fables, it does not seem inappropriate to us that they assert that reasonings are the banquets of the gods.

MAG. More truly, my sons, you may say that reasonings are the food of angels and the adornment of souls, rather than the banquets of the gods.

DIS. However these things ought to be expressed, we beg that the first steps of wisdom be shown to us, so that, with God’s gift and your instruction, we may be able to advance from lower things to higher ones.

MAG. We read, as Solomon says, through whom Wisdom herself sang: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1). Although this statement pertains to divine wisdom, which built herself a house—that is, a body—in the Virgin’s womb and strengthened it with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or to the Church, which is the house of God, which she illuminated with those same gifts, nevertheless the wisdom of the liberal arts is strengthened by seven pillars; nor does it lead anyone to perfect knowledge in any other way than by raising him upon these seven pillars, or steps.

DIS. At last reveal what you promised, and, because of the frailty of our age, begin by nourishing us with softer food, so that, as our age increases, we may more easily reach what is solid.

MAG. With divine grace both going before and bringing the work to completion, I shall do what you have asked. I shall show you, for your contemplation, the seven steps of philosophy, and, with God’s gift and life as my companion, I shall lead you through them, according to the measure of our strength and the suitability of time and age, to the higher things of speculative knowledge.

DIS. Lead us, lead us still, and at last settle us from the nest of sloth among the branches of the wisdom given you by God, so that we may perceive some light of truth. Show us the seven steps of the theoretical discipline that you have so often promised us.

MAG. The steps you seek are these—and may you always be as eager to ascend [Edit., to learn] as you are now curious to see them: grammar, rhetoric [dialectic], arithmetic, [Col. 0854A] geometry, music, and astrology. Through these, philosophers have worn away both their leisure and their business. With these as their counsellors they became more illustrious, with these as their kings more celebrated, and, through these same disciplines, worthy of praise in eternal memory. Through these also the holy and catholic teachers and defenders of our faith have always proved superior to all heresiarchs in public controversies.

Through these paths, dearest sons, let your youth run each day, until a more mature age and a mind strengthened in understanding reach the heights of the Holy Scriptures. Thus may you become, armed on every side, altogether invincible defenders of the true faith and assertors of the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0853] In the Paris Royal manuscript, the following title is prefixed to the subsequent Dialogue: “Here happily begins Alcuin’s little work called the Handbook.”]

SAXO, FRANCO, THE STUDENTS; THE MASTER.

[Col. 0854B] There were two boys in the school of Master Albinus: one, Franco, the other, Saxo. They had very recently entered the thicket of grammatical intricacy. Therefore they decided, for the sake of memory, to extract a few rules of literary knowledge through questions and answers [Ms., a few little literary rules].

But the former of them, Franco, said to Saxo: “Come, Saxo, answer when I question you, because you are older. I am fourteen years old; you, I think, are fifteen.” To this Saxo replied: “I shall do so, provided that, if something more difficult is to be asked or something from philosophical learning is to be brought forward, we may question the master.”

Then the master said: “Your proposal pleases me, my sons, and I willingly approve your intelligence. First, tell me from what point you think your discussion ought most suitably to begin.”

DIS. From where, master, except from the letter?

MAG. You would be right, if you had not mentioned philosophy a little earlier [Ms., if we had not mentioned it]. Hence it is clear that the discussion should begin from the voice, for whose sake letters were invented; or rather, before everything else, we must ask in what ways a discussion is constituted.

DIS. We humbly ask you, master, to explain this to us. We confess that we do not know in what ways a discussion is constituted.

MAG. There are three things by which every conversation and discussion is completed: things, understanding, and voices. Things are what we perceive through the reasoning of the mind. Understandings are by which we learn the things themselves. Voices are by which we express the things we have understood; for this reason, as we have said, letters were invented.

DIS. But since you have spoken of the modes of discussion, we ask you to explain the differences of the voice.

MAG. There are four differences of voice: articulated and inarticulated; written and unwritten. An articulated voice is one that is uttered joined and bounded together with meaning, as in: “I sing of arms and the man . . .” An inarticulated voice proceeds from no meaning, such as a crack or a bellow. A written voice is one that can be written; an unwritten voice cannot be written.

DIS. From what is “voice” named?

MAG. From calling. There you have what you asked. Now begin with the letter, my sons.

FRANCO. You go first, Saxo: tell me from what “letter” is named.

SAXO. [Col. 0855A] As I think, a letter is, as it were, *legitera*, because it provides a path for readers.

269 FR. Give a definition as well.

SAXO. A letter is the smallest part of an articulated voice.

DIS. Does “letter” have another definition, master?

MAG. It does, but one that falls within the same meaning. A letter is indivisible, because we divide sentences into parts, parts into syllables, and syllables into letters. Letters themselves are indivisible.

DIS. Why are letters called elements?

MAG. Because just as elements, when joined together, complete a body, so these letters, glued together, compose a literary voice.

FR. Give us, colleague, the division of letters.

SAXO. They are either vowels or consonants. Consonants, in turn, are divided into semivowels and mutes.

[Col. 0855B] FR. State the reason for each division.

SAXO. Vowels can be pronounced by themselves and make a syllable by themselves. Consonants can neither be uttered by themselves nor make a syllable by themselves.

DIS. Do they have another reason for being divided, master?

MAG. They do. Vowels are like souls, consonants like bodies. The soul moves both itself and the body. But the body is motionless without the soul. So consonants are without vowels: they can be written by themselves, but they cannot be uttered or have force without vowels.

FR. Why are they called vowels and consonants?

SAXO. Vowels are so called because they fill out a voice by themselves, with no consonant attached. Consonants are so called because they do not sound by themselves but sound together with vowels.

FR. What is the difference between semivowels and mutes?

SAXO. To the extent that semivowels are surpassed by vowels, to that extent semivowels surpass mutes. They begin with vowels and end in themselves; they sound with greater euphony, and words more often end in semivowels than in mutes because of euphony—that is, sonority. Mutes, however, begin with themselves and end in vowels, and sound less pleasantly.

FR. As I think, we read in Donatus that three things befall letters: name, form, and power. There is no need to speak about names and forms, but I would like you to speak about power, first that of the vowels.

SAXO. Among the Latins there are five vowels. The Latins adopted the letter y as a sixth vowel because of Greek names, just as they adopted z as a consonant. Thus vowels, as has been said, make syllables by themselves; and when placed alone they also complete whole parts of speech: A, as in:

“Ah, may harsh ice not cut my tender soles!”

[Note: [Col. 0855D] Virgil, Eclogue X, 49: “Ah, may it not cut your tender soles,” etc.]

E, as in:

“. . . at the same time, thirsting, he drank up the stream.”

O, as in:

“O, if he had returned victorious over the Gauls to the city!”

I is also a verb:

“Go, glory, go; avail yourself of better fortunes!”

[Note: [Col. 0855D] Virgil, Aeneid VI, 546.]

But I and U pass into the power of consonants when, at the beginning of a syllable, they are joined to other vowels. For example: *janua*, *vates*, *jecur*, *veritas*, *Jonas*, *votum*. Or when they are placed before themselves, as in: *Juno*, *virgo*. These letters also become medial when they have the sound of the Greek vowel y [that is, i], when, after u, they are placed in the position of a consonant before a following d, m, r, t, or x: *video*, *vim*, *virtus*, *vitium*, *vix*. U likewise has the same sound—that is, the sound of y—when it occurs between q and another vowel, or after g and another vowel in the same syllable [is constituted], as in: *quisque*, *pingue*, *lingua*. There is also a case in which i stands for two consonants, when it occurs between two vowels, as in: *Troja*, *Maja*. U is likewise accepted in some places in the position of a double digamma, as in *cupii*, with a short i, and *Cupivi*, with a long i. And wherever v is placed in the position of a consonant, it must always be understood as a digamma.

FR. Do any of the consonants have particular powers?

SAXO. They do. First, each one has its own power, as it has its own name and form. Some of them are liquids, and thereby lose the force of consonants. Accents also often change in prose.

FR. Which are they?

SAXO. L, R, M, N. S also has a peculiar power. H is the sign of aspiration. X and Z, however, are double letters. But I think these matters belong to the subtleties of meter, in which we are not yet learned. Therefore do not question me further about them; let us hurry on to syllables.

## On the Syllable

[Col. 0856C] FR. What is a syllable?

SAXO. A literary voice uttered under one accent and one breath.

270 FR. With how many letters are syllables formed?

SAXO. Beginning with one and extending up to six: *a*, *ab*, *abs*, *Mars*, *stans*, *stirps*.

FR. Does a syllable have meaning by itself?

SAXO. It does not, unless a complete word consists of one syllable, as *ars*, *do*, *dic*, and others.

FR. How many properties does a syllable have [Al., how many accompany it]?

SAXO. Four: pitch, breath, duration, and number. The accent may be acute, grave, or circumflex; within a word it is fixed, outside a word it is uncertain, yet a syllable cannot exist without it. The breath may be rough or smooth. The duration is one or two [Ms., one or two]. The number is the number of letters.

FR. How does a syllable have one or two units of duration?

SAXO. [Col. 0856D] A short syllable has one; a long syllable has two.

FR. How do syllables become short or long?

SAXO. Short syllables are made by nature and by power [Note: [Col. 0856D] Manuscript: “Short syllables are made by the nature of the vowels”] [long syllables by nature and by position]. A syllable is naturally short when the vowel is pronounced quickly, as in *pater*. It is long when the voice lingers, as in *mater*. Or it is long when two vowels come together in a single syllable, which they call a diphthong. There are five such combinations: *ae*, *oe*, *au*, *eu*, *ei*.

FR. Why is it called a diphthong?

SAXO. As it were, a “double voice.” For whenever the sounds of two vowels come together in one syllable and one voice, it is called a diphthong.

FR. In how many ways do syllables become long by position?

SAXO. [Col. 0857A] Six. When a shortened vowel ends in two consonants, as in *ast*. Or in one double consonant, as in *dux*. Or when it ends in one consonant and is followed by another, as in *arca*. Or when it is followed by the double consonant x, as in *axis*. Or when j is placed in the position of a consonant, as in *Troja*. Or when it ends in a consonant and is followed by i or u placed in the position of a consonant, as in *advena*, *adjutor*.

FR. Is it [read: “if”] necessary for every syllable to be either long or short?

SAXO. There are syllables called common. At the poet’s discretion they can be either short or long. But since these matters belong to metrics, let us leave them aside.

FR. Let us ask the master further, so that we may not be ignorant of this rule as well.

DIS. Tell us, master, by what rule or in what ways can syllables be common?

MAG. Syllables become common in nine ways. They are common when a shortened vowel in the middle of a word is followed by two consonants, the first of which is any mute or the semivowel f and the second a liquid, as in *Tenebrae*, *pharetra*, *refluit*. Or when a shortened vowel ends in a consonant and is followed by h, as in *vir humilis*. Or when a syllable ends in a short vowel and is followed by two consonants, the first of which is s, as in *alba smaragdus*. Or when, after [any foot (Ms., two feet)], one short syllable remains at the end of a word, as in:

“Love conquers all things; let us too yield to Love.”

[Note: [Col. 0857D] Virgil, Eclogue X, 69.]

Or when some word ends in a diphthong and is followed by the vowel beginning the next word, as in: “*Insulae Ionio* . . .” Or when, in the same word, a long vowel is immediately followed by the vowel of another syllable, as in *fidei*. Or when a pronoun ending in the letter c is followed by the vowel beginning the next word, as in *hoc est*. Or when a shortened vowel in a word is followed by the double consonant z, as in *gaza*. Likewise, the final syllable in a meter is always indifferent and subject to the poet’s will. A syllable is also common when three consonants are involved, namely, when a syllable ends in a short vowel and is followed by s and then by a mute and a liquid, as in Horace:

“We leave, laughing at the rewards of the mad scribe.”

[Note: [Col. 0858D] Horace, Satires I, 5, 35.]

I shall show you these matters more fully, with life as our companion, in the study of meter, my sons.

[Col. 0857D] DIS. What do you wish, master? Shall we question you about feet and accents, following the order of the master Donatus?

MAG. You will understand these matters more suitably in the subtlety of meters. For feet and accents cannot be understood except from short and long syllables. Therefore turn your attention to the parts.

DIS. First, if it pleases you, master, explain to us from what “grammar” is named and what its function is.

MAG. Grammar is literary knowledge, and it is the guardian of correct speaking and writing. It is constituted by nature, reason, authority, and usage.

DIS. Into how many species is grammar divided?

MAG. Into twenty-six: voice, letters, syllables, parts, words, sentences, definitions, feet, accents, punctuation, marks, orthography [Ms., orthography . . . . .], analogy, etymology, glosses, differences, 271 barbarism, solecism, faults [Ms., fault], metaplasm, figures, tropes, prose, meters, fables, and histories.

DIS. Before we turn to a discussion of the parts, explain some knowledge of each of these to us, master, proceeding through them one by one.

MAG. You have already had voice, letter, and syllable in the preceding discussion. A word is the smallest part of a constructed voice and has a complete meaning. A sentence is an arrangement of words that displays a coherent and complete thought; and *oratio* (“sentence”) is so called as if from *oris ratio*, “the reason of the mouth.” A definition is a short statement enclosing each thing in its proper signification, as: “A human being is a mortal, rational animal, capable of laughter.” You must therefore know that definition pertains to all disciplines and things. A foot is a combination of syllables and a fixed measurement [Ms., enumeration] of durations. Feet are so called because meters walk by means of them [Ms., through them]. An accent is a fixed law and rule for raising and lowering a syllable. Punctuation marks are points for distinguishing meanings. Marks are certain figures either for abbreviating words or expressing meanings, or established for various reasons, as in Holy Scripture the obelus ÷ or the asterisk *. Orthography is correct writing: for example, the preposition *ad* takes d, while the conjunction *at* takes t. Analogy is the comparison of similar things, by which uncertain things are proved through certain ones. Etymology [Col. 0858C] is the origin and rationale of words, as in: *rex* (“king”) from *regere* (“to rule”), and *homo* (“human being”) from *humus* (“earth”). A gloss is the interpretation of one verb or noun, as in: *catus*, that is, “learned.” A difference is the distinction between two things together with an interpretation, as in: a king is so called because he is restrained; a tyrant, because he is cruel. A barbarism is one part of speech uttered incorrectly, as in the common proverb: “For a bad tree, a bad wedge must be sought at its knot.” A solecism is a sentence improperly constructed. Faults are things we must avoid in speech, and there are seven of them. Metaplasm is a rule of speech changed by metrical license or necessity. Figures are ornaments and forms of expression by which thoughts are clothed. A trope is a word transferred from its proper signification to an improper likeness, for the sake of ornament or necessity. [Col. 0858D] Prose is straightforward speech composed without meter and verse. Meters are so called because they are bounded by fixed measures of feet. Fables are invented accounts made for amusement or for conveying some meaning. History is a narration of an accomplished event. There you have brief definitions of each species. Now turn your attention to the parts.

DIS. We shall do as you command. Nevertheless, we ask you first to explain briefly the properties of the individual parts.

MAG. Your curiosity knows no limit. Thus you wish to exceed the bounds of a little handbook. The property of a noun is to signify substance, quality, or quantity; the property of a pronoun is to stand in place of a proper noun and signify definite persons. The property of a verb is to signify an action or a passion, or both, together with moods and tenses. The property of an adverb is to be placed with a verb and not to have a complete meaning without it, as in: “I read well.” The property of a participle is to have tense and case; for this reason some call it a “case-bearing verb.” The property of a conjunction is to be joined and to join the parts, sometimes placed before all the parts and sometimes after them. The property of a preposition is always to be placed separately before words in an oblique case.

## On the Noun

FR. Come, Saxo, let us enter into the discussion of the noun in order. First tell me: what is a noun?

SAXO. [Col. 0859B] According to the grammarians, a noun is a part of speech that assigns to every body or thing a common or proper quality. A noun is said as if from *notamen* (“a marker”), because by it we mark individual substances or things: common ones, such as *homo* (“human being”) and *disciplina* (“instruction”); or proper ones, such as *Virgilius* (“Virgil”) and *arithmetica* (“arithmetic”). Yet let us ask the master, Franco, for the philosophical definition of a noun.

MAG. A noun is a significant voice according to convention, without tense, signifying something definite in the nominative when “is” or “is not” is added, as in: “A human being is”; “A human being is not.” In [other] cases, although you may add “is” or “is not,” it signifies nothing definite unless you add what is or what is not. For example: “Of a human being is”; “Of a human being is not.” “According to convention”—that is, according to the arrangement of individual peoples—nouns are composed differently: what you call *aurum* in Latin is called χρυσός (*chrysos*) in Greek. The substance is one, but the names are different.

FR. How many properties befall a noun?

SAXO. Six, according to Donatus: quality, comparison, gender, number, form, and case. According to Priscian, there are five, because he combined quality and comparison and called them “species,” since all nouns are either of a proper species or appellative, principal or derivative. Proper, as *Julius*; appellative, as *mons* (“mountain”); principal, as *Julius*, *mons*; derivative, as *Julianus*, *montanus*. In these—that is, in the derivatives—he placed the comparisons of nouns.

FR. How many species of proper nouns are there?

SAXO. [Col. 0859D] Four: praenomen, nomen, cognomen, and agnomen. Praenomina are placed before proper names for the sake of dignity or distinction, as in *Anicius Boethius*: *Anicius* is said from the nobility and freedom of his lineage. For distinction, as in *Lucius Cornelius* and *Publius Cornelius*. Praenomina are indicated either by single, double, or triple letters. By a single letter: *M.*, *Marcus*. By two: *Cn.*, *Cneus*. By three: *Sex.*, *Sextus*. The *nomen* is each person’s proper name, as *Paulus*. The *cognomen* is a common name of kinship or family, as *Scipio*, for all that kinship was called by his name. The *agnomen* is a name derived from some event, as *Africanus*, because he was conquering Africa [F., had conquered it].

[Col. 0860A] FR. How many species of appellative nouns are there?

SAXO. There are many. Some are corporeal, such as *homo* (“human being”), *terra* (“earth”), and *mare* (“sea”). Others are incorporeal, such as *pietas* (“piety”), *dignitas* (“dignity”), and *justitia* (“justice”). Others are principal, such as *mons* (“mountain”) and *schola* (“school”). Others are derivative, such as *montanus* (“mountainous”) and *scholasticus* (“scholastic”). Others are comparative, such as *fortior* (“stronger”) and *fortissimus* (“strongest”). Others are denominative, such as *sanctus* (“holy”), *sanctitas* (“holiness”), *sapiens* (“wise”), and *sapientia* (“wisdom”). Others are diminutive, such as *rex* (“king”) and *regulus* (“little king”). Others are homonymous, such as *nepos* (“grandson/nephew”) and *acies* (“battle line/edge”). Others are synonymous, such as *gladius*, *ensis*, and *mucro*, all meaning “sword.” Others are adjectival and can be used in praise or blame, such as *justus homo* (“a just man”) and *injustus homo* (“an unjust man”). Others have an intermediate signification, such as *magnus* (“great”): we say *magnus imperator* (“a great commander”) and *magnus latro* (“a great robber”). These also often become accidental qualifiers, as in *niger corvus* (“a black raven”) and *altum mare* (“the deep sea”).

Others are relational, signifying something in relation to another, as in *filius* (“son”) and *servus* (“servant”). For by saying “son” and “servant,” we signify “father” and “master.” Others are quasi-relational, such as *dies* (“day”) and *nox* (“night”), *dextera* (“right hand”) and *sinistra* (“left hand”). For although one of these perishes, the other can nevertheless remain. This is not so with “son” and “servant.” Others signify a nation, such as *Graecus* (“Greek”) and *Hispanus* (“Spanish”); others a homeland, such as *Romanus* (“Roman”) and *Thebanus* (“Theban”). Others are interrogative, such as *qualis* (“of what kind?”), *quantus* (“how great?”), and *quot?* (“how many?”), when they retain their accents. Others are relative, such as *tantus* (“so great”), *talis* (“such”), and *tot* (“so many”). Others are collective, signifying many in the singular number, such as *populus* (“people”) and *plebs* (“common people”). Others are distributive, such as *bini* (“two each”), *terni* (“three each”), and *centeni* (“one hundred each”). Others are artificial, that is, made from a sound, such as *tintinnabulum* (“bell”), *turtur* (“turtledove”), and *clangor* (“clang”). Others are general, capable of being divided into different species, such as *animal* (“animal”) and *arbor* (“tree”). Others are specific, such as *homo* (“human being”) and *vitis* (“vine”). Others are ordinal, such as *primus* (“first”) and *secundus* (“second”). Others are numeral, such as *unum* (“one”), *duo* (“two”), and *tres* (“three”). Others are absolute, such as *Deus* (“God”) and *ratio* (“reason”). Others are temporal, such as *mensis* (“month”) and *annus* (“year”). Others are local, such as *propinquus* (“near”) and *longinquus* (“far”). Others are patronymic [Ms., patrimonial], such as *Scipiades*, from *Scipio*, and *Thesides*, from *Theseus*. These are often formed from grandfathers and founders, as *Iliades* from *Ilus* and *Aeneades* from *Aeneas*. There are also possessives, which signify something belonging to the things possessed, such as *Evandrius ensis* (“Evander’s sword”) and *regius honor* (“royal honor”). These are interpreted with the genitive of the principal noun [Ms., “These serve the principal genitive”], as *Evandri ensis* (“the sword of Evander”) and *regis honor* (“the honor of the king”). There are also other species that Donatus lists, but they are found among these, such as quality and quantity. In adjectives and accidental qualifiers one finds *bonus* (“good”) and *magnus* (“great”); these have a middling signification.

FR. From what do comparisons of nouns arise?

SAXO. From adjectival nouns and from accidental qualities of some substance that signify a quality or quantity of mind [Col. 0860D] or body, which can undergo increase or decrease. A human being or a stone is a substance. A human being is called wise and wiser; a stone is called great and greater. The comparative is always common in gender, as *hic et haec prudentior* (“this wiser [masculine and feminine]”). It makes the neuter in *-ius*, as *hoc prudentius* (“this more wisely/more prudent thing”). A comparative is also found used in place of a positive, as in Virgil (Aeneid V, 301):

“. . . the companions of aged Acestes,”

where *senioris* means “of the old man.” Sometimes it signifies less than the positive and is compared with no one, as in Virgil (Aeneid I, 322):

“Sadder, and her shining eyes drenched with tears.”

Here *tristior* signifies, in part, simply “sad.” Diminutives are also made from comparatives, such as *majusculus* (“rather large”) and *minusculus* (“rather small”); but, unlike other diminutives, they are not absolute [Ms., absolute], but refer to something, as in Terence (*Eunuchus* III, 3, 21):

“Thais is a little larger than I am.”

FR. Of what gender is the superlative formed?

SAXO. The superlative changes through all three genders: *prudentissimus, prudentissima, prudentissimum* (“wisest,” masculine, feminine, neuter).

FR. How many forms of superlatives are there?

SAXO. Eight: *-simus*, *-rimus*, into which most superlatives end; *-limus*, *-ximus*, *-timus*, *-tremus*, *-imus*, and *-nimus*, as in *sanctissimus* (“holiest”), *pulcherrimus* (“most beautiful”), *simillimus* (“most similar”), *maximus* (“greatest”), *ultimus* (“last”), *extremus* (“extreme”), *[primus]* (“first”), and *minimus* (“smallest”). The letter *e* is long, while the penultimate *i* is shortened everywhere except in *primus* [Col. 0861B] and *imus*.

FR. With which cases are the comparative and superlative joined?

SAXO. The comparative is joined with the ablative of either number, as: “Hector was stronger than Diomedes,” and “more daring than the Trojans.” The superlative is joined with the plural genitive, as: “Hector was the bravest of the Trojans.” It is also found joined with the singular genitive when the singular noun itself signifies a multitude, as: “Hector is the bravest of the Trojan nation.” Sometimes the superlative is placed by itself and compared with no one; then it must be understood as the adverb “very,” as: “Hercules was strongest,” that is, “very strong.”

FR. I remember, Saxo, that you said some appellative nouns were diminutives. Can diminutives be made from proper nouns?

SAXO. They can, as *Sergiolus* from *Sergius*, and *Antoniaster* from *Antonius*.

FR. In how many ways are diminutives formed?

SAXO. In three ways. Either for the sake of necessity, as *regulus* from *rex*, that is, “little king,” as in Sallust: “After the little kings gathered together.” Or for the sake of wit or courtesy, as in Juvenal (Satire 98):

“. . . I would rather be a little brother among giants.”

Or for the sake of flattery, as when *Sergiolus* is said of little boys [Edit., “little Sergiuses”].

FR. How many forms of diminutives are there?

SAXO. For the masculine gender, eleven: *-culus*, *-ulus* [Ms., *-illus*], *-olus*, *-ellus*, *-xillus*, *-illus*, *-ulus*, *-cio*, *-aster*, *-leus*, and *-tulus*. For example: *agniculus* (“little lamb”), *tantulus* (“so little”) [Ms., *tantillus*], *capreolus* (“little goat”), *agnellus* (“little lamb”), *pauxillus* (“very little”), *codicillus* (“little book”), *homulus* (“little man”), *homuncio* (“little human”), *parasitaster* (“little parasite”), *aculeus* (“little needle”), *nepotulus* (“little grandson/nephew”).

[Col. 0861D] For the feminine gender there are seven: *-cula*, *-ula*, *-ola*, *-ella*, *-xilla*, *-illa*, *-ulla*. For example: *agnicula* (“little ewe”), *sylvula* (“little wood”), *unciola* (“little ounce”), *capella* (“little she-goat”), *maxilla* (“little jaw”), *anguilla* (“little eel”), *ulla* (“little one”).

There are seven forms for the neuter: *-culum*, *-ulum*, *-olum*, *-ellum*, *-illum*, *-xillum*, *-ullum*. For example: *corpusculum* (“little body”), *capitulum* (“little head”), *laureolum* (“little laurel”), *lucellum* (“little light”), *villum* (“little villa”), *vexillum* (“little flag”), *ullum* (“little one”).

Diminutives of diminutives are also formed in the third and fourth degree, as: *Paulus*, *Paululus*; *pauxillus*, *pauxillulus*; *homo*, *homuncio*, *homunculus*, *homulus*, *homullulus*.

There, Franco, you have enough, as I think, about the species of appellatives, although no one could satisfy your greed.

[Col. 0862A] FR. I am not so greedy as you are envious, since you refuse to open anything unless compelled by questioning.

SAXO. Ask whatever you wish; I shall not be slow to answer.

## On Gender

FR. Now, as I judge, the order of the properties of the noun requires us to inquire about genders. First I would like to know from what genders are named.

SAXO. Genders are named from *generando* (“generating”). Therefore, strictly speaking, the genders are those that can generate: masculine and feminine. For the neuter and common genders are distinguished more by the quality of the voice than by nature. Epicene nouns are mixed and express masculine and feminine under one form.

FR. What is the difference between common and epicene?

SAXO. [Col. 0862B] A common noun is joined now with a masculine, now with a feminine article, as the construction of the sentence requires. An epicene noun is always expressed with one article and signifies animals of both natures with one word and one article.

FR. Are all nouns of a definite gender?

SAXO. By no means. [For many are of doubtful gender.]

FR. From what do nouns of doubtful gender arise? Perhaps for the sake of distinction?

SAXO. Not for the sake of distinction, nor for any necessity, but solely by the authority of the ancients, as: masculine and feminine *finis* (“end”), *cortex* (“bark”), *silex* (“flint”), *margo* (“edge”), *cardo* (“hinge”), *fornax* (“furnace”), [*cinis* (“ash”),] *frutex* (“shrub”), *frons* (“leaf/forehead”), *vesper* (“evening”), *humus* (“earth”), *artus* (“limb”), *limes* (“boundary”) [Edit., *arcus*, *limus*], and *latex* (“liquid”). *Sal* (“salt”) is masculine and neuter. Cato: “From the salt that is made among the Carthaginians.” Africanus: “Whatever he says is pure salt” [Ed., “true”].

274 FR. Which nouns are fixed?

SAXO. Those that cannot pass into another gender, such as *pater* (“father”) and *mater* (“mother”).

FR. Which are mobile?

SAXO. Those that can change and pass into another gender. Some come from proper nouns, such as *Marcius*, *Marcia*. Others from appellatives, such as *bonus, bona, bonum* (“good,” masculine, feminine, neuter).

FR. In how many letters do masculine nouns end?

SAXO. Seven: *a, o, l, n, r, s, x*; for example, *scriba* (“scribe”), *Cicero*, *sol* (“sun”), *flumen* (“river”) [Ms., *flamen*], *Caesar*, *bonus* (“good”), *rex* (“king”).

FR. How many letters do feminine nouns end in?

SAXO. The same, as *Roma*, *virgo* (“maiden”), *Tanaquil*, *Siren*, *mater*, *civitas* (“city”), *pax* (“peace”).

FR. How many letters do neuter nouns end in?

SAXO. Twelve: *a, e, i, u, l, m, n, r, s, c, t, d*; for example: *poema* (“poem”), *mare* (“sea”), *gummi* (“gum”), [Col. 0862D] *cornu* (“horn”), *mel* (“honey”), *regnum* (“kingdom”), *numen* (“divine power”), *tuber* (“swelling”), *sidus* (“star”), *lac* (“milk”), *caput* (“head”), *aliquid* (“something”).

[Common nouns, serving all three genders, end in *i, m, r, s, x*, such as *hic et haec et hoc frugi* (“thrifty”), *nequam* (“worthless”), *par* (“equal”), *prudens* (“wise”), and *audax* (“bold”).]

FR. How can I know of what gender any given noun is?

—SAXO. Each ending has rules laid down indicating how many genders may occur in it. But to state this would be lengthy and burdensome for our childish discussion.

FR. This is what I said earlier.

—SAXO. What do you mean?

FR. What else, except that you begrudge my expertise?

—SAXO. Not at all, brother; I merely wanted to set a limit to your greed.

[Col. 0863A] FR. You want to set a limit to my greed, not to your own obstinacy.

—SAXO. Come, continue; I shall follow wherever you wish.

FR. I shall continue by asking questions; you follow by answering. First tell me: where does the greatest difficulty in nouns lie?

—SAXO. In genders and declensions.

FR. How is declension recognized?

—SAXO. In the ending of the genitive case.

FR. How many are the endings of the genitive case?
