—SAXO. Five. Therefore there are five declensions of nouns.

FR. Name them individually.

—SAXO. The first ends in *ae*, as in *hic poeta, huius poetae* (“this poet, of this poet”). The second ends in *i*, as in *hic doctus, huius docti* (“this learned man, of this learned man”). The third ends in a shortened *is*, as in *hic pater, huius patris* (“this father, of this father”). The fourth ends in a lengthened *us*, as in *hic senatus, huius senatus* (“this senate, of this senate”). The fifth ends in divided *ei*, as in *hic dies, huius diei* (“this day, of this day”).

FR. Nouns ending in *a*: of what gender or declension are they?

—SAXO. All of them, if they are Latin, belong to the first declension and to the three genders: masculine, feminine, and common.

FR. Distinguish which belong to one gender and which to another.

—SAXO. Names of men ending in *a* are masculine, such as *Sylla* and *Seneca*. Proper names of other things, however, are feminine, such as *Roma*, *Ilia* [MS., *Italia*], and *curia*. All appellative nouns become feminine, such as *regina* (“queen”) and *iustitia* (“justice”), except those pertaining to the occupations of men, such as *lixa* (“sutler”), *scriba* (“scribe”), and *collega* (“colleague”); and those we have taken from the Greeks by changing an ending in *s* into *a*, as *poetes* and *citharistes*: we say *poeta* and *citharista*. Those compounded from verbs, or those that are derivative, are common, such as *hic et haec agricola* (“this male or female farmer”), *rurigena* (“country-born”), *advena* (“newcomer”), *patricida* (“patricide”), *conviva* (“guest”), and similar words.

FR. Continue with the rules for the other vowels.

—SAXO. I shall. All nouns ending in *e* are of the third declension and neuter gender, such as *hoc monile* (“this necklace”). Those ending in *i* are neuter: *hoc gummi* (“this gum”). All nouns ending in *o* are of the third declension, but of different genders. Proper masculine nouns with *e* before the *o* are *Labeo*, *ganeo*, and *aleo*. When *i* precedes the *o*, nouns that are verbal are feminine, such as *oratio* (“speech”), *actio* (“action”), and *coniugatio* (“conjugation”). When *g* or *d* precedes the *o*, if the *o* changes to *i* in the oblique cases, the nouns are feminine, such as *virgo*, *uligo*, *dulcedo*, and *cupido*, which is also masculine when it is a proper name. The exceptions are *hic ordo*, *cardo*, *mango*, *margo*, *praedo*, *cudo*, and *spado*; and common nouns such as *homo* and *latro*. Likewise *duo*, *ambo*, *octo*, and *pondo* are common. *Juno* and *caro* are feminine. All the others are masculine, such as *stellio*, *Cicero*, *carbo*, and *sermo*. Nouns ending in *u* are neuter and of the fourth declension, such as *cornu*, *genu*, and *gelu*. In the singular they are indeclinable.

FR. I approve what you say, although you say *III* [Al., *VI*, or *vi*, that is, “violently”]. But set out the rules for consonants yourself, while I remain silent and approve.

—SAXO. So be it. There are two neuters ending in *c*: *lac* and *alec*. Neuters ending in *d* include *quid*, *quod*, and *aliud*; reason proves in many ways that these are nouns. If they end in *al* and are Latin, they are neuter, such as *tribunal*, *vectigal*, and *sal*, which is found both masculine and neuter. If they are foreign, they are masculine, such as *Annibal*, and so forth. Those ending in *el* are neuter: *mel*, *fel*. In *il* there is one masculine, *pugil*; one feminine, *Tanaquil*; one common, *vigil*; and one indeclinable neuter, *nihil*. In *ol* there is one masculine, *sol*. Two masculine nouns end in *ul*: *consul* and *praesul*. One is common: *exsul*. In *am* there is one common noun, *hic et haec et hoc nequam*. All these are declined according to the third order [Al., “the third declension”]. All nouns ending in *um* are neuter and of the second declension, such as *templum, templi*. There are nine masculine nouns ending in *en*: *lien*, *rien*, *flamen*, *pecten*, *tibicen*, *fidicen*, *liticen*, *tubicen*, and *cornicen*. All the rest are neuter, such as *carmen* and *flumen*, and all are of the third declension. Nouns ending in *ar* are of the third declension and neuter, such as *torcular* and *pulvinar*. The exceptions are *hic Caesar*, *Jar*, and *Nar*, the name of a river; and common nouns such as *hic et haec et hoc par*, together with compounds derived from it: *impar*, *dispar*, and *compar*. Among nouns ending in *er*, except for *haec mater* and *haec mulier*, and these neuters—*Juber*, *papaver*, [*tuber*], *cadaver*, *laser*, *siler*, *iter*, *cicer*, and *siser*—and these common nouns, [*pauper* (Ed., *paucis*)], *uber*, *celer*, all the others are masculine. Some belong to the second declension, others to the third; their declension can easily be understood from the oblique cases. Therefore I think that one should not trouble oneself greatly over the diversity of declensions.

FR. Do as you please. For I can test the declensions myself, as you said.

—SAXO. Among nouns ending in *ir* there is one masculine, *hic vir*, and its compounds, such as *semivir*, *duumvir*, and *levir* [Al., *laevir*]. There is also one neuter, *hoc ir* (“half a palm”), indeclinable; and these are of the second declension. Nouns ending in *or* follow the form of the third declension and are masculine, whether proper or appellative, such as *Hector*, *orator*, *furor*, and *doctor*. The exceptions are the three feminines *soror*, *uxor*, and *arbor*; and these neuters: *ador*, *marmor*, *aequor*, *ebor*, *olor*, *femor*, and *cor*. Common nouns are *hic et haec auctor*, *discolor*, and *concolor*; also *hic et haec memor* and *immemor*. All comparatives ending in *or* are common, such as *hic et haec doctior* and *melior*, except one: *hic senior*. Among nouns ending in *ur*, one belongs to the second declension: *hic satur*, whose feminine is *satura*. The masculine nouns are *hic astur*, *turtur*, and *vultur*. Common nouns include *hic et haec augur* and *fur*. All the rest are neuter, such as *guttur*, *sulphur*, *murmur*, and *iecur*, and are of the third declension. Nouns ending in *as* are feminine, such as *haec dignitas* and *pietas*, except *hic as, assis*; *mas, maris*; *vas, vadis*; and *hoc vas, vasis*. Also neuter are *hoc fas*, *nefas*, and *nugas* of every gender [Al., *nugax*]; all are of the third declension. Proper names of the first declension are nevertheless found, such as *hic Aeneas* and *Lysias*. There are also names of countries of the third declension: *hic Mycenas*, *Capenas*, and *Arpinas*. Nouns ending in shortened *es*, if they can naturally signify either a male or a female, are made common, such as *hic et haec hebes*, that is, “slow.” The same applies to *teres*, *comes*, *dives*, *sospes*, *hospes*, *praeses*, *deses*, *obses*, *superstes*, *quadrupes*, and *sonipes*. All the others—those having no natural commonality with females [Al., “no common nature”]—are masculine, such as *stipes*, *limes*, *fomes*, and *cespes* [*meridies*]. The exceptions are those ending in the syllable *ges* and retaining *e* in the genitive, such as *haec seges, segetis*, *teges*, and *abies*; all are of the third declension. Other nouns ending in lengthened *es*, if proper names, are masculine, such as *Hercules* and *Ulixes*, as is the appellative *verres* when it means “boar”; common nouns include *haeres* and *locuples*. All the rest are feminine: some are of the third declension, such as *caedes*, *strages*, *vulpes*, and *apes*; others belong to the fifth, such as *facies*, *effigies*, *spes*, *res*, and *fides*. All nouns ending in pure *es* belong to the fifth declension, except *quies*, *abies*, and *paries*; and all those preceded by a consonant belong to the third declension, except *spes*, *fides*, and *res*. All nouns ending in *is* are of the third declension. But those ending in *is* which have *n* or *c* before the *is*, or which gain one syllable in the genitive, are all masculine, such as *hic panis* and *piscis*; *hic lapis, lapidis*. The exceptions are *haec bipennis*; *haec cuspis*; *cassis, cassidis*; and *hic et haec canis*. A few masculine nouns are also found that do not fall under these rules, such as *hic fustis*, *ensis*, *postis*, *anguis*, *unguis*, *collis*, *follis*, *corbis*, *vectis*, *mensis*, *torquis*, *axis*, and *orbis*. If they are adjectives, derivatives, or pertain only to human beings, they are always made common, such as *hic et haec fortis*, *suavis*, *dulcis*, *exsanguis*, *exanimis*, *civis*, *hostis*, and *aedilis*. All the others are feminine, such as *haec avis*, *classis*, and *cutis*; and all belong to the third order [that is, declension]. Among nouns ending in *os* there are three feminine: *cos*, *dos*, and *glos*. There are five common: *custos*, *sacerdos*, *bos*, *compos*, and *impos*. There are two neuters: *os, oris* (“mouth”) and *os, ossis* (“bone”). All the others are masculine: *mos*, *flos*, *ros*, *nepos*, and *lepos*; and all belong to the third declension. The ending *us* is so varied in genders and declensions that I cannot possibly set out its differences for you, France, within the narrow limits of our little exercise. It belongs to three declensions—the second, third, and fourth—and to the masculine, feminine, neuter, common, all-gender, and epicene categories.

FR. Nevertheless, set out some rules concerning it. For often, when we have no sun, we use lanterns to drive away the darkness of night.

—SAXO. Thus, proper or appellative nouns ending in *us*, whether movable or fixed, are of the second declension if they are masculine. Proper names include *Terentius, Terentii* and *Marcius, Marcii*. Movable nouns include *bonus, boni* and *sanctus, sancti*. Fixed nouns include *campus, campi*, *hortus, horti*, and *fumus, fumi*. There are also three feminine nouns: *haec colus*, *alvus*, and *humus*. Likewise, feminine names of trees belong to the second declension: *haec pirus*, *prunus*, *pinus*, *fagus, fagi*, and so forth. There are also three neuters: *hoc vulgus*, *virus*, and *pelagus*. All other neuters ending in *us* are of the third declension, such as *ius, iuris*, [*thus*], *munus*, *pondus*, *corpus*, and *pectus*. Feminines with lengthened *us* are all of the third declension and gain one syllable in the genitive, such as *salus, salutis* and *tellus, telluris*, with the *u* lengthened in the oblique cases, except *palus, paludis* and *Venus, Veneris*; and one of every gender, *hic et haec et hoc vetus, veteris*. A few are common, such as *hic et haec ligus, liguris*; *grus, gruis*; and *sus, suis*. There is an epicene noun, *mus, muris*, and one masculine, *lepus, leporis*. The following alone are feminine nouns of the fourth declension: *anus*, *manus*, *porticus*, *tribus*, *domus*, *nurus*, *socrus*, and *quercus*. Those derived from verbs or participial nouns [MS., “principal nouns”] are masculine and of the fourth declension, such as *hic status, huius status*, from *sto*; *hic ductus*, from *duco*; *consulatus*, from *consul*; and *tribunatus*, from *tribunus*. Likewise, nouns with *s* or *x* before *us* are masculine and of the fourth declension, such as *risus*, *metus*, and *sexus*. *Penus* and *specus* are found as masculine, feminine, and neuter, and occur in the second, third, and fourth declensions. It is also found in usage: *hic et haec acus* and *hoc acus, huius aceris*, “the chaff or refuse of grain.” *Pus* and *virus* are indeclinable.

All nouns ending in the letter *x*, whatever vowel or consonant precedes it, are of the third declension, but of different genders. To put it briefly, all nouns ending in *x* that signify accidental qualities are common, such as *hic et haec et hoc audax*, *aurifex*, and *velox*. Likewise, appellatives pertaining to human beings of either sex are common, such as *hic et haec coniux* and *dux*. Those pertaining only to males are masculine, such as *rex*; those pertaining only to females are feminine, such as *pellex*. Proper masculine names include *hic Ajax* and *Pollux*. Those that gain one syllable in the genitive are masculine, such as *hic vertex*, *apex*, [*varix*], *latex*, *cortex*, *codex*, *pollex*, *calix*, *fornix*, and the rest. The following are feminine: *haec fornax*, *silex*, *ilex*, *carex*, *salix*, *radix*, *cornix*, *filex*, *meretrix*, *cicatrix*, and *velox*. All verbal nouns are likewise feminine, such as *victrix*, *genitrix*, and *nutrix* [Al., *natrix*, which is also masculine]. All monosyllables are feminine, such as *pax*, *lex*, *pix*, *nox* [Al., *nux*], *lux*, *arx*, and *falx*, except *rex*, *hic grex*, and *hic et haec dux*. One neuter noun ending in *t* is found: *caput*; and its compounds *sinciput* and *occiput*.

Nouns ending in two consonants, if they signify accidental qualities [Al., “if they become accidental”], are all of the three genders, such as *hic et haec et hoc expers*, *prudens*, *inops*, *coelebs*, *princeps*, and *parens*. A few are masculine, such as *Mavors* and *Aruns*; a few feminine, such as *hiems*, *cohors*, and *adeps*. Monosyllables ending in two consonants are for the most part feminine, such as *ars*, *fors*, *gens*, *mors*, *lens*, *frons*, *pars*, *sors*, *scrobs*, *styps*, *trabs*, *urbs*, and *puls*. The exceptions are *hic mons*, *pons*, *fons*, *dens*, and *Mars*. Nouns ending in *aus* are feminine: *laus* and *fraus*. One ending in *aes* is masculine, *praes, praedis*; one is neuter, *aes, aeris*. At last, by this time, I was freeing myself from the heaviest debt of interest.

FR. But from a most welcome one. Therefore let us pass to number.

—SAXO. So be it.

## ON NUMBER

FR. What is number?

—SAXO. The form of a word, the distinguishing of quantity [Al., “the form of distinction, the quantity of distinction”].

FR. How many numbers do nouns have?

—SAXO. Two: singular, as *homo* (“man”); and plural, as *homines* (“men”). But the singular number is definite, while the plural is indefinite. When I say *homo*, it is certain that I have signified one person. [Col. 0867A] When I say *homines*, it is uncertain how many, unless I add *ten*, *one hundred*, *one thousand*, or any number; for the signification extends from two to innumerable persons.

FR. Which words have number?

—SAXO. Those that have persons—that is, nouns, pronouns, verbs, and participles. Thus, *vir, viri* (“man, men”); *ego lego, nos legimus* (“I read, we read”); *hic legens, hi legentes* (“this reader, these readers”). Infinitive and impersonal verbs therefore lack number, because they do not have persons.

FR. Do adverbs not have number?

—SAXO. They do, but number is not counted among the accidents of an adverb. The numbers of adverbs are indeclinable, and the same form is used with a singular and a plural word, as *ter feci* (“I did it three times”) and *ter fecimus* (“we did it three times”).

FR. What, then, is the difference between the indeclinable names of numbers and adverbs?

—SAXO. Adverbs are joined alike to singulars and plurals, as *millies dixi* (“I said it a thousand times”) and *millies diximus* (“we said it a thousand times”). Nouns, however, are joined only to plurals, as *mille homines diximus* (“we have said ‘a thousand men’”).

FR. Are there nouns which have both numbers in a single form?

—SAXO. There are. In the first declension, the singular genitive and dative are pronounced with the same form as the plural nominative and vocative: *huius* and *huic poetae*, as also *hi* and *o poetae*. You will very often find the same thing in all the declensions. In the second: *huius docti* and *hi docti*. In the third: *haec caedes* and *hae caedes*. In the fourth: *hic fluctus* and *huius fluctus*; and *hi*, *hos*, and *o fluctus*, with the *u* lengthened in all these cases. In the fifth: *haec res* and *o res*; and *hae*, *has*, and *o res*. You will also find forms common to the two numbers in pronouns and participles, such as *illi*, *isti*, and *ipsi*, which are both singular datives and plural nominatives. In participles, all movable forms have feminines in the singular nominative and neuters in the plural with the same form, as *haec victura femina* (“this woman who will conquer”) and *haec victura animalia* (“these animals that will conquer”). In verbs, however, no form can be the same in the singular and plural.

FR. Why are some nouns, as I read in Donatus, always singular, and others always plural?

—SAXO. By nature or by usage. By nature, as proper names, which are naturally individual, such as *Hector*, *Achilles*, *sol*, *luna*, *Italia*, and *Sicilia*. By usage, such as *sanguis*, *pulvis*, *lux*, and *vita*. Likewise, things pertaining to weight or measure are singular, such as *aurum*, *triticum*, and so forth. Similarly, some nouns are always plural by nature or by usage. By nature, such as *Gemini* and *pisces* in the heavens. By usage, such as *arma*, *moenia*, *nundinae*, and *Kalendae*. In every gender you will find some nouns always singular and some always plural; for the sake of brevity, I think they should be omitted here.

## ON FORMS

FR. Let it be as you wish; although unwillingly, I agree. But let us discuss forms. First tell me: what is the difference between formed words and derivative words?

—SAXO. Formed words are either simple, such as *magnus* (“great”), or compound, such as *magnanimus* (“great-souled”). Derivative words, however, are derived from a simple noun, such as *pietas* (“piety”) from *pius* (“pious”), or from a compound, such as *magnanimitas* (“great-souledness”) from *magnanimus*; these are called decomposed [secondary derivatives]. Compounds must always be intelligible and separable into complete words [Col. 0868A], whether they are composed from complete or corrupted forms: *respublica* (“republic”) is formed from complete words; *parricida* (“parricide”) from two corrupted forms, the noun *parens* (“parent”) and the verb *caedere* (“to kill”). If I say *magnanimitas* [Ed., *magnanimus*], it cannot be said to be compounded from *magnus* and *animitas*, because *animitas* [MS., *nimitas*] is not intelligible. Therefore *magnanimitas* must be derived from a compound, namely *magnanimus*.

FR. In how many ways are nouns compounded?

—SAXO. Four. From two complete forms, as *ius iurandum* (“oath”). From two corrupted forms, as *parricida*. From a complete and a corrupted form, as *inimicus* (“enemy”). From a corrupted and a complete form, as *efferus* (“wild”).

FR. With which parts of speech are nouns compounded?

—SAXO. With all except the interjection: with a noun [Ed., “nouns”], as *paterfamilias* (“father of a family”); with a pronoun, as *illiusmodi* (“of that sort”); 278 with a verb, as *Lucifer* (“light-bringer”); with an adverb, as *satisfactio* (“satisfaction”); with a participle, as *plebiscitum* (“plebiscite”); with a conjunction, as *uterque* (“each of the two”); and with a preposition, as *perfidus* (“faithless”).

FR. From how many words are nouns compounded?

—SAXO. From two, as *septentrio* (“north”). From three, as *inexpugnabilis* (“impregnable”). Or from several [MS., “from more numerous forms”], as *cuiuscunquemodi* (“of whatever kind”).

FR. How are compound nouns declined?

—SAXO. If they are compounded from a nominative and an oblique case, they are declined according to the part that is the nominative; the other case is not declined: *hic tribunusplebis, huius tribuniplebis, huic tribunoplebis* (“this tribune of the plebs, of this tribune of the plebs, to this tribune of the plebs”). If they are compounded from two nominatives, both parts are declined: *hoc iusiurandum, huius iuris iurandi, huic iuri iurando* (“this oath, of this oath, to this oath”). If they are compounded from two oblique cases, they remain indeclinable: *huiusmodi*, *istiusmodi*, *eiusmodi* (“of this sort,” “of that sort,” “of that sort”). Singulars are also compounded with plurals, as *orbis terrae* and *orbis terrarum* (“the world of the earth,” “the world of lands”). These same compounds can nevertheless also be separate words if you give them different accents, as *res publica* (“public matter,” “the state”), or if you insert a conjunction, as *tribunusque plebis* (“and the tribune of the plebs”).

FR. How are the accents of compounds formed?

—SAXO. In every case and in every compound they are always pronounced under one accent, as *iusiurandum*, *iuris iurandi*, and *cuiuscunquemodi*. Turn, France, to the cases, since you have what you asked concerning forms.

FR. I shall turn, and gladly turn, because you have set forth explanations about forms that please me.

## ON THE CASES

[Col. 0868D]

First explain to me why it is called a case.

—SAXO. *Casus* (“case”) is certainly so called from *cadere* (“to fall”), because one form falls from this sense into that one, or from this ending into that one.

FR. I know that there are six cases; but I want you, Saxo, to set out the meanings of each.

—SAXO. You desire this properly. The first is the nominative, because naming is performed through it. It is also called the “straight” case, because it is the first to arise by nature, and through its inflection the others arise. Next is the genitive, because through it we signify kind or lineage, as in *genus est Priami Hector* (“Hector is of the race of Priam”). It is also called the possessive, because we always signify possession through it, as *Priami regnum* (“Priam’s kingdom”). After this comes the dative, so called from *dare* (“to give”), signifying that we give something, as *do tibi illam rem* (“I give you that thing”). It is also called the mandative [MS., “commendative”], as *commendo homini illam rem* (“I commend that thing to the man”). In fourth place is the accusative, also called the causative, as *accuso hominem* (“I accuse the man”). Then comes the vocative, also called the salutative [MS., “salutatory”], as *o Aenea* and *salve Aenea* (“O Aeneas,” “hail, Aeneas!”). Finally comes the ablative, also called the comparative, signifying that something is removed or compared: *aufero ab Hectore gladium* (“I take the sword away from Hector”); and *fortior Hectore Achilles est* (“Achilles is stronger than Hector”).

FR. Also state the reason for the order in which they are placed.

—SAXO. The nominative takes the first place for itself because nature produced it first. The genitive takes the second because it possesses the natural bond of lineage and generates all the oblique cases. The dative takes the third because it is more appropriate to friends [Col. 0869B]. The accusative takes the fourth because it is more often used toward enemies. Then comes the vocative, because it is less complete in meaning than the others and belongs only to the second person, whereas the other cases are joined to all persons: *ego homo sum* (“I am a man”), *tu homo es* (“you are a man”), *ille homo est* (“he is a man”); *mei, tui, illius hominis est* (“it is mine, yours, his”); *mihi, tibi, illi homini da* (“give to me, to you, to that man”); *me, te, illum hominem accuso* (“I accuse me, you, that man”); *a me, a te, ab illo homine hoc protuli* (“I brought this forth from me, from you, from that man”). The vocative alone says: *o homo, veni* (“O man, come!”). But the ablative, which was discovered last, is placed last.

FR. Can all nouns be declined through every case?

—SAXO. They cannot, because there are nouns that have only the nominative and are called indeclinables, such as *fas*, *git*, *pus*, and *ir*. There are nouns that do not have a nominative, such as *Iovis, Iovi, Iovem, a Iove* (“Jupiter” in the genitive, dative, accusative, and ablative). There are others in which only three oblique cases are found: *frugi, frugem, a fruge*. Others have two, such as *vicem, a vice*. Others have one, such as *sponte* and *caepe*.

FR. How many case-forms are there?

—SAXO. There are six kinds. *Monoptota* are nouns that use one ending for every case, such as *gummi* and *nequam*. Under this rule also fall the names of letters and numbers from four up to one hundred. *Diptota* are those that have two different cases, such as *sors, a sorte*; or those in which all the cases are distinguished by only two differences, such as *cornu*, which has all its cases with a shortened [MS., “three with shortened *u* and three with lengthened *u*”]. Others are *triptota*, such as neuters of the second declension, which have three different case forms: *templum, templi, templo*; and all neuter plurals in every declension: *sidera, siderum, sideribus*. Others are *tetraptota*, such as all second-declension nouns ending in *r* [MS., *er*]: *puer, pueri, puero, puerum*. Others are *pentaptota*, such as masculine second-declension nouns ending in *us*: *doctus, docti, docto, doctum, docte*. *Hexaptota* are those that have six different cases, as *unus, unius, uni, unum, une, ab uno*.

FR. Do not find it burdensome to explain to me the endings of each case through all five declensions.

—SAXO. Your many questions are making me longer-winded.

FR. What if they make you more useful in necessary rules?

—SAXO. In the first declension, the genitive and dative end in the diphthong *ae*; the accusative in *am*. The vocative [like the nominative] and the ablative end in *a* [lengthened]. Thus: *hic poeta*; genitive, *huius poetae*; dative, *huic poetae*; *hunc poetam*; *o poeta*; *ab hoc poeta*. The plural nominative and vocative end in the diphthong *ae*. The genitive ends in *arum*, [the accusative in *as*]; the dative and ablative in *is*, unless distinction of gender requires otherwise, as in *deabus*, *filiabus*, *natabus*, and *equabus*: *hi poetae, horum poetarum, his poetis, hos poetas, o poetae, ab his poetis*.

The genitive of the second declension ends in *i*. The dative and ablative end in lengthened *o*. The accusative ends in *um*, unless the nouns are neuter, whose accusative everywhere follows their nominative, whether in the singular or plural. The vocative is like the nominative in all those [MS., “nouns”] that end in *m* or *r*. If proper nouns end in *ius*, the vocative ends in *i*, as *Virgilius, Virgili* [“Virgil”]. If the nominative ends in *us*, the vocative ends in *e*: *hic magnus, magni, magno, magnum, o magne, a magno* (“this great man,” etc.). The plural nominative and vocative end in *i*, except in the neuter. The genitive ends in *orum* [MS., *rum*]. The dative and ablative end in *is*, and the accusative in *os*: *hi magni, magnorum, magnis, magnos, o magni, a magnis*.

The genitive of the third declension ends in *is*. The dative ends in *i*. The accusative ends in *em*, but in a few nouns in *im*, such as *turrim*, *sitim* [*restim*, *puppim*]. The vocative is like the nominative. The ablative ends in shortened *e* in some nouns, as *a patre*; in others in *i*, as *Tiberi* [Ed., *Liberi*]; and in some in either *e* or *i*, as *a felice* and *a felici*. *Hic rex, regis, regi, regem, rex, a rege*. The plural nominative, accusative [and vocative] end in lengthened *es*. In a few, the accusative [F., nominative] ends in *is*, as *turris*. The genitive ends in *um*, and in some in *ium*, as *turrium*. The dative and ablative end in *bus*: *hi reges, regum, regibus, reges, o reges, a regibus*.

The singular genitive of the fourth declension ends in lengthened *us*. The dative ends in *ui*. The accusative ends in *um*. The vocative is like the nominative. The ablative ends in lengthened *u*: *hic senatus, huius senatus, huic senatui, hunc senatum, o senatus, ab hoc senatu*. The plural nominative, accusative, and vocative end in lengthened *us*. The genitive ends in *uum*. The dative and ablative end in *bus*: *hi senatus, horum senatuum, senatibus, senatus, o senatus, a senatibus*.

The singular genitive and dative of the fifth declension end in divided *ei*. The accusative ends in *em*. The vocative is like the nominative. The ablative is pronounced with *e* [MS., “with lengthened *e*”]: *haec res, huius rei, rei, rem, res, a re*. The plural nominative, accusative, and vocative end in *es*. The genitive ends in *um* [MS., *rum*]. The dative and ablative end in *bus*: *hae res, rerum, rebus, res, o res, a rebus*. Well, France, have you had enough about the noun?

FR. I would have had enough, Saxo, if the gnats in the master’s house had not filled my ears with their little questions. Nevertheless, if you please, let us pass to other matters. I shall also brush them away in a moment. You go wherever you wish; I shall follow where you go.

## ON THE PRONOUN

FR. What is a pronoun?

—SAXO. A part of speech placed with a case in the place of a noun, so that repeated use of the noun may not cause weariness to the listener or reader [MS., “might not cause”]; and it receives definite persons.

FR. How many accidents does a pronoun have [MS., “does it receive”]?

—SAXO. Six: kind, person, gender, number, form, and case.

FR. How many kinds of pronouns are there?

—SAXO. Two, because pronouns are either primitive or derivative.

FR. How many primitive pronouns are there?

—SAXO. Eight: *ego*, *tu*, *sui*, *ille*, *ipse*, *iste*, *hic*, and *is*.

FR. How many derivative pronouns are there?

—SAXO. Seven: *meus*, *tuus*, *suus*, *noster*, *vester*, *nostras*, and *vestras*.

FR. From what are these derived?

—SAXO. From the genitives of the primitive pronouns: *meus* from *mei*, *tuus* from *tui*, *suus* from *sui*, *noster* and *nostras* from *nostrum*, and *vester* and *vestras* from *vestrum*. These are the fifteen pronouns about which there is no doubt.

FR. How many persons do pronouns have?

—SAXO. Three. But the first and second persons each have only one form, because they are always present to one another: *ego*, *tu*. The third has six forms, because the varieties of third persons are numerous: *sui*, *ille*, *ipse*, *iste*, *hic*, and *is*. The third person is sometimes present, as *iste* (“this”), and sometimes absent, as *ille* (“that”).

## ON THE GENDERS OF PRONOUNS

FR. How many genders do pronouns have?

—SAXO. Five: masculine, as *hic*; feminine, as *haec*; neuter, as *hoc*; common, as *nostras* and *vestras*; and of all three genders, as *ego* and *tu*. Every pronoun must have three genders, either confused in one form, as *ego* and *tu*, or distinguished by different endings, as *meus, mea, meum*. For pronouns are accepted in place of the proper names of each thing.

## ON FORMS

FR. State the form of pronouns.

—SAXO. Some pronouns are simple, such as *iste* and *hic*. Some are compound, such as *istic*, which is compounded from *iste* and *hic*. *Idem* is compounded from the pronoun *is* and the adverb *demum*; it is common in number, as *idem vir* and *idem viri* (“the same man,” “the same men”): in the masculine the *i* is lengthened, in the neuter shortened; its feminine is *eadem*. Its composition is also doubled in the neuter, producing *idem idem* [MS., *identidem*], that is, “the same and the same.”

Pronouns are compounded with adverbs, as *eccum*, that is, *ecce eum* (“behold him!”), and *ellum*, *ecce illum* (“behold that man!”). They are compounded with a preposition, but through anastrophe, as *mecum*, *tecum*, and *secum* (“with me,” “with you,” “with himself”); and with a noun, as *huiusmodi* and *istiusmodi* (“of this sort,” “of that sort”).

FR. What is the formation of *egomet* and *huiusce*?

—SAXO. It is not composition but paragoge, that is, the addition of a syllable. There are four such additions: *met*, *ce*, *te*, and *pte*, as in *egomet*, *tute*, *meapte*, and *huiusce*. *Illice* is produced by apocope as *illic*, with the final [syllable] circumflexed.

## ON NUMBER

FR. How many numbers do pronouns have?

—SAXO. Two: singular, as *iste*; and plural, as *isti*.

Some are common in number, such as *sui*, *sibi*, *se*, and *a se*. These lack a nominative, because if there were *hi*, or a nominative, it would create confusion between *hi*, another pronoun, and *si*, the conjunction [Note: [Col. 0871D] The manuscript of St. Emmeram continues and concludes this section as follows: “For whenever this pronoun is used, it indicates a third person either acting and suffering simultaneously in relation to himself, as *poenitet illum sui* (‘he is sorry for himself’), *invidet sibi* (‘he envies himself’), *accusat se* (‘he accuses himself’); or acting himself while another acts upon him from outside, as *rogat ut sui causa facias* (‘he asks you to do it for his sake’), *petit ut sibi concedas* (‘he asks you to grant it to him’), *precatur ut se custodias* (‘he begs you to guard him’). When this occurs—that is, when the same person both acts and suffers, either from himself or from another—he does not need the nominative case, but rather the case with which the verb expressing the action is ordinarily joined, namely the genitive, dative, accusative, or ablative, all of which this pronoun has. For the verb itself has the nominative of the acting person. If I say, *Rogat te ut ad se venias* (‘He asks you to come to him’), you undoubtedly understand that in what I have said—*rogat*—the one who is the nominative is also included.”]. Or because transition or reciprocity of person cannot occur in a noun that always has *sui*: reciprocity, as *sui meminit* (“he remembers himself”); transition, as *suo servo loquitur* (“he speaks to his servant”).

## ON THE CASES

FR. State the cases of pronouns.

—SAXO. The cases of pronouns are like those of nouns, except that the first and third persons cannot have more than five cases, because the vocative cannot occur in them; it belongs exclusively to the second person. The exception is the possessive *meus* [MS., “possessive”], which forms the vocative *mi*, converting its two short *e*s into one long *i* for euphony. Its plural likewise has a vocative: *o noster* (“O our one”).

FR. How many case-forms occur in pronouns?

—SAXO. Some pronouns are *monoptota*, such as *eccum*, *ellum*, *mecum*, and *tecum*. Others are *triptota*, such as *sui, sibi, se*; *meum, tuum, suum* [Ed., *mecum, tecum, secum*]. Others are *tetraptota*: *tuus*, *suus*, *illud*, and *istud*. Others are *pentaptota*: *ille*, *ipse*, and *iste*. No pronouns are found that are *hexaptota*.

FR. Since pronouns have cases and numbers, they must also have declensions. I insist that you explain their rules.

—SAXO. You are an unscrupulous investigator.

FR. Rather, you are a grudging giver.

—SAXO. There are four declensions of pronouns. The first is seen in the three persons of the primitive pronouns. Their genitive and dative end in *i*, and their accusative and ablative in lengthened *e*: *ego, mei, mihi, me, a me*; *tu, tui, tibi, te, a te*; *sui, sibi, se, a se*. The plural first and second persons have the nominative and accusative in *os*, the genitive in *um* or *i*, and the dative and ablative in *is*: *nos, nostrum* or *nostri, nobis, nos, a nobis*. The same applies to *vos*. The third person has no nominative and is common in number throughout the remaining cases: *sui*.

FR. How are the persons of pronouns understood?

—SAXO. In the first syllables; the cases and numbers in the final ones. The second declension is found in the remaining five primitive pronouns. Their genitive ends in *ius*, and their dative in *i*, through all three genders, except *huic* alone, so that it may not be mistaken for the interjection *hui*. Their singular accusative and ablative, and all their plural cases in the masculine and neuter, preserve the endings of the second declension of nouns; in the feminine, those of the first. Thus: *ille, illius, illi, illum, ab illo*. In the plural: *illi, illorum, illis, illos, ab illis*. Feminine: *illa, illius, illi, illam, ab illa*. [And in the plural:] *illae, illarum, illis, illas, ab illis*. Neuter: *illud, illius, illi, illud, ab illo*. [And in the plural:] *illa, illorum, illis, illa, ab illis*. The other four are declined in the same way, except *hic et haec et hoc*, which takes *c* in every singular case except the genitive.

The third declension consists of the five derivative pronouns, which in both numbers are declined according to the rule for movable nouns: in the masculine and neuter according to the second declension, and in the feminine according to the first. They are *meus*, *tuus*, *suus*, *noster*, and *vester*.

The fourth declension consists of the common pronouns; they are declined like the two remaining ones, which follow the nouns of the third declension: *hic et haec nostras*, *vestras*, and *hoc nostrate*, *vestrate*; *nostratis*, *vestratis* [Note: [Col. 0873D] The manuscript reads: “The fourth declension is found in the two remaining pronouns, which follow and are declined like common nouns of the third declension: *hic et haec nostras*, and *hoc nostrate, nostratis*. Likewise *vestras*.”].

[(From a manuscript.) FR. Why are these pronouns not declined: *eccum, eccam; ellum, ellam*?

—SAXO. Because they are compounded from an oblique form and an indeclinable part.] There you have what you extorted by force.

FR. It is better to extort by force than not to have it. But tell me about *o*, which is joined to the vocative case in nouns, pronouns, and participles: is it a pronoun or not?

—SAXO. It is not a pronoun but an adverb of calling or wishing. It has the same meaning when you say *heus juvenis* and *o juvenis* (“hey, young man!” and “O young man!”). It can be joined to no other person except the second.

FR. Remember that you said there were fifteen pronouns. But what of the words that Donatus placed among pronouns: *quis*, *qualis*, *talis*, *quot*, *tot*, *quotus*, *totus*, [*quantus*, *tantus*]?

—SAXO. I remember saying that there were fifteen pronouns about which there was no doubt. Concerning those you mention, however, there is doubt whether they are pronouns or nouns. Priscian, the glory of Latin eloquence, calls them wholly interrogative, relative, or responsive nouns [MS., “nouns”], and denies that they can be pronouns, because they do not have definite persons, which is proper to a pronoun joined with a case. Likewise, through an error into which some have been led, certain other nine movable nouns are called pronouns because they have the declension of pronouns: *unus*, *ullus*, *nullus*, *solus*, *totus*, *alius*, *alter*, *uter*, and *neuter*. The reasoning supplied by extensive reading refutes them.

282. Whether *meus*, *tuus*, and *suus* ought to be called nouns, since in all their cases they follow the declension of nouns? To the extent that this seemed relevant to our childish discussion, you have enough concerning the pronoun. But now transfer your whole attention to the verb.

**FR.** I am satisfied with what I have, although I should have needed more. Nevertheless, as you advise, I shall transfer my entire attention to investigations of the verb. Prepare yourself to answer.

**SAXO.** I shall.

## On the Verb

**FR.** First of all, tell me the definition of a verb.

**SAXO.** Let us rather ask the teacher what the definition of a verb is according to philosophy.

**STUDENTS.** Master, according to philosophical reasoning, does this most fundamental part of speech have its own proper definition, just as the noun does?

**MASTER.** It has a subtle and noble definition, of the following kind: “A verb is a significant utterance according to convention, with time, signifying something determinate and accidental” [printed edition: “acceding”].

**STUDENTS.** Explain this definition to us, Father.

**MASTER.** When I say *lego* (“I read”), I signify the action of the reader; [Col. 0874B] the Greeks signify this action with another word. Therefore the verb is “according to convention,” and it draws time along with it. “Determinate,” that is, it signifies something definite; and “accidental”: for action or passion happens to a human being. But enter into your own discussion; we shall deal with these matters on another occasion.

**STUDENTS.** Let it be as you command.

**FR.** Saxo, state the property of the verb.

**SAXO.** A verb is a part of speech with tenses and moods, without case, signifying acting or being acted upon.

**FR.** If verbs signify action or passion, why are some called neuter?

**SAXO.** Not because they do not signify action or passion [printed edition: “lest they signify”], but because they signify one of these two. For active verbs signify the passion of another in relation to our action [and passive verbs likewise signify the action of another in relation to our passion]. When I say, “I love you,” you undergo my action, namely, that I love you. And when I say, “I am loved by you,” I undergo your action, namely, that you love me.

Neuter verbs, however, signify uniformly either the agent, as *ambulo* (“I walk”), *curro* (“I run”), *prandeo* (“I dine”), or the patient, as *ardeo* (“I burn”), *veneo* (“I am sold”), *vapulo* (“I am beaten”). They also do not require the cases that active and passive verbs require. Active verbs are joined with the accusative, as *amo te* (“I love you”); often with the genitive, as *memor sum tui* (“I am mindful of you”); and with the dative, as *dico tibi* (“I tell you”). Passive verbs are joined with the ablative, as *amor a te* (“I am loved by you”). Neuters are absolute and signify a complete sense by themselves, as *vivo* (“I live”), *spiro* (“I breathe”), *pergo* (“I proceed”).

**FR.** How many accidents does a verb have?

**SAXO.** Seven: signification, [Col. 0874D] which is also called gender; tense; mood; species; figure; person; and number.

The signification of verbs properly concerns action or passion. According to analogy, verbs end in two letters, *o* and *r*. Those ending in *o* are active and neuter; those ending in *r* are passive, deponent, and common. These are the five genders of verbs.

Active verbs are those that always signify action, as *amo te* (“I love you”). [Passive verbs are those that always signify passion, as *amor a te* (“I am loved by you”).] Nevertheless, if one considers the matter more deeply, one will find action in active verbs and passion in passive verbs, as we said above.

Neuter verbs [Col. 0875A] are always expressed uniformly: that is, they signify either action alone or passion alone. Action, as *manduco* (“I eat”), *curro* (“I run”) [manuscript: *ambulo*, “I walk”]; passion, as *vapulo a te* (“I am beaten by you”), [*veneo a te*, “I am sold by you”]. There are also neuters that contain passion intrinsically within themselves, and not from another external agent, as *rubeo* (“I grow red”), *ferveo* (“I boil”), *caleo* (“I am hot”), *aegroto* (“I am ill”), *ruo* (“I rush/fall”).

Deponent verbs likewise always have one signification, either active, as *sequor te* (“I follow you”), *praestolor te* (“I await you”), or without the addition of a case, as *luctor* (“I wrestle”), *loquor* (“I speak”); or passive, as *nascor a te* (“I am born from you”), *patior a te* (“I suffer at your hands”), *mereor a te* (“I am deserved by you”)”. Common verbs have, in one form, two significations, that of agent and patient, as *osculor te* (“I kiss you”), *osculor a te* (“I am kissed by you”).

**FR.** In how many ways are verbs declined?

**SAXO.** In two ways. Neuter verbs chiefly follow the rule of the active conjugation, while deponent and common verbs follow that of the passive conjugation. There are also passive neuters which, in the perfect and pluperfect tenses, have the passive declension. These alone are: *audeo, ausus sum* (“I dare, I have dared”); [*gaudeo, gavisus sum* (“I rejoice, I have rejoiced”); *soleo, solitus sum* (“I am accustomed, I have been accustomed”)]; *fido, fisus sum* (“I trust, I have trusted”); *fio, factus sum* (“I become, I have become”); and any compounds formed from these.

There are other passive neuters, contrary to those mentioned above: *comperior, mereor, divertor*; for they form their perfects as *comperii*, *merui*, *diverti*.

### 283

**FR.** Do verbs always have fixed significations?

**SAXO.** By no means do they always have fixed significations. Some, in one form or conjugation, have different meanings, as *colo*, which is understood as “I love,” “I inhabit,” and “I cultivate/plough.” *Committo* means “I trust” and “I entrust.” *Condo* means “I build” and “I conceal.” *Gratulor* is used for “I rejoice” and “I give thanks.”

There are others whose signification changes with the conjugation. This is distinguished in the second person: *mando, mandas*, from *mandare* (“I command, you command”); *mando, mandis*, from *manducare* (“I eat, you eat”) [manuscript: *mandendo*]; *fundo, fundas*, from *fundare* (“I found, you found”); *fundo, fundis*, from *fundere* (“I pour, you pour”); *volo, volas*, from *volare* (“I fly, you fly”); *volo, vis*, from *voluntas* (“I wish, you wish”) [manuscript: *volendo*].

*Sero, seras, seravi* (“I sow, you sow, I sowed”); *sero, seris, sevi* (“I join, you join, I joined”). *Lego, legas* (“I read, you read”); and *lego, legis* (“I gather, you gather”). *Dico, dicas*, with a short *i* (“I say, you say”); *dico, dicis*, with a long *i*. *Appello* and *compello*, *compellas*, mean “I call” and “you call out”; *appello, appellis* means “I bring near/apply.” *Repello, compello* means “I drive back, I compel.”

France, let what has been said about the varied signification of verbs suffice; now I proceed to the tenses [manuscript: “proceed!”].

**FR.** Let it be so. First tell me, whence is *tempus* (“tense/time”) derived?

**SAXO.** From *temperamentum* (“regulation, balance”), because all mortal things have time.

**FR.** How many tenses are there?

**SAXO.** Three according to nature: past, as *legi* (“I read”); present, as *lego* (“I read”); and future, as *legam* (“I shall read”). Yet by a certain necessity the past tense is divided into three intervals, because some things we say were completed long ago, as *legeram* (“I had read”); sometimes things were completed shortly before, as *legi heri* (“I read yesterday”); and sometimes things have begun but are not yet completed, as *legebam* (“I was reading”). Therefore we shall count five tenses in verbs.

**FR.** Which of these tenses holds the principal place among the others in verbs?

**SAXO.** The present, because we are in it while we speak about the past and the future. The past [Col. 0876A] and future are derived from the present. Although, therefore, the present tense naturally passes away in unstable motion, with one part of it already passing and another following, we nevertheless divide tenses for the ordering [printed edition: “ornamentation”] of different actions.

**FR.** Are all tenses found in all moods?

**SAXO.** By no means. The imperative, by natural necessity, has no past tense, because we command only what exists in the present or the future. The indicative and subjunctive, on the other hand, run through all tenses. The optative and infinitive also have all the tenses in certain cases, though with indistinct forms: *utinam legerem nunc et heri* (“would that I were reading now and yesterday”); *utinam legissem ante, ante, et ante quinquaginta annos* (“would that I had read before, before, and fifty years ago”). Likewise, *legere me volo et volebam* (“I wish and wished to read”), and *legisse me volui et volueram* (“I wished and had wished to have read”).

**FR.** Is this fivefold division of tenses found in all verbs?

**SAXO.** No. Some verbs do not preserve the system of tenses. Inchoative verbs, for example, are defective throughout the perfect and pluperfect. Likewise, all impersonal verbs that arise from themselves are defective in the future infinitive, as *poenitere, poenituisse* (“to repent, to have repented”); and most neuters are defective in the future infinitive, as *horreo, horrere, horruisse* (“I shudder, to shudder, to have shuddered”). For we do not say *poenitum ire*, and so forth.

There are also verbs that have no past tense except when it is taken from other verbs, as *percutio, percussi* (“I strike, I struck”); *ferio* has no past tense unless one says *percussi*. Likewise *statuo, statui* (“I establish, I established”); *sisto, statui* (“I stop, I stopped”); *sustollo, sustuli* (“I lift up, I lifted up”); *suffero, sustuli* (“I bear, I bore”); *tollo, tuli* (“I lift/remove, I lifted/removed”); and *fero, fers, fert*, whose perfect is *tuli*. *Insanio, insanivi* (“I am insane, I was insane”), and *fureo* also forms *insanivi*. *Cerno* means “I discern,” while *crevi* means “I grew”; *cresco* likewise forms *crevi*.

Inchoative and desiderative verbs are defective not only in the past but also in the future infinitive: *tepescere* (“to grow warm”), *parturire* (“to desire to give birth”). Verbs ending in *-or* lack the perfect and pluperfect tenses and the future subjunctive; these are declined through the past participle [and the substantive verb *sum*], as *amatus sum* (“I have been loved”), *amatus fueram* (“I had been loved”), *amatus ero* (“I shall have been loved”), and so forth.

## On the Moods of Verbs

**FR.** What and how many are the moods of verbs?

**SAXO.** Moods are the various inclinations [manuscript: “declensions”] [Col. 0876D] of the mind, displaying its various affections. There are five.

The indicative, also called the definitive, is the mood by which we indicate or define what is being done or suffered by us [Note: [Col. 0875D] “The solecism is to be excused for that age.” BASNAG.]. It is placed first because it is complete in persons and tenses, and the other moods take their rule from it. Alternatively, it is first because participles, nouns, and verbs are derived from it: from *duco* (“I lead”), *ducens* (“leading”); from *duxi* (“I led”), *ductus* (“led”) and *dux* (“leader”); from *ferveo* (“I boil”), *fervens* (“boiling”), *fervesco* (“I begin to boil”), and *fervor* (“heat”).

### 284

The imperative is the mood by which we command others to act or suffer. It is absolute in itself and does not need another part of speech to signify; for this reason it holds second place among the moods. We use it very frequently in prayers, as:

> “Muse, recall to me the causes . . .”

Next comes the optative, by which we express a wish. It is placed third in order because the one who wishes is lower than the one who commands. It requires an adverb of wishing to complete the sense, as *utinam legerem* (“would that I were reading”).

The subjunctive is placed fourth, and rightly so. To signify a complete sense it requires not only an adverb or conjunction but also another verb. Hence it is called “subjunctive,” as in Virgil (*Eclogue* 3.77):

> *Cum faciam vitula [manuscript: vitulam], pro frugibus ipse venito.*  
> “When I make an offering with a heifer, come yourself for the crops.”

It can be joined with all the other moods: *dum legerem, scripsi* (“while I was reading, I wrote”); *dum legam, scribe* (“while I read, write”); *dum legerem, utinam scriberem* (“while I was reading, would that I were writing”).

The infinitive is defective in persons and numbers and requires one of the four moods mentioned above to signify something complete: *legere propero* (“I hasten to read”); *legere propera* (“hasten to read”); *utinam legere properarem* (“would that I were hastening to read”); *cum legere properarem* (“when I was hastening to read”).

An impersonal verb arises from neuters of active signification or from active verbs, as *curritur* (“there is running”), *vivitur* (“there is living”), *legitur* (“there is reading”), *amatur* (“there is loving”). It is properly declined through all moods, persons, tenses, and numbers when pronouns are joined to it: *curritur a me, a te, ab illo* (“there is running by me, by you, by him”); *curritur a nobis, a vobis, ab illis* (“there is running by us, by you [plural], by them”). In the imperfect: *legebatur [a me]* (“there was reading [by me]”). In the perfect: *lectum est [vel lectum fuit a me]* (“there was reading [or: reading was done by me]”). In the pluperfect: *lectum erat* (“there had been reading”). In the future: *legetur [a me]* (“there will be reading [by me]”). The same applies through the other moods.

**FR.** What is the difference between an impersonal and an infinitive?

**SAXO.** Infinitives are joined to voluntary verbs, as *legere volo* (“I wish to read”); impersonals to pronouns, as *legitur a me* (“there is reading by me”).

**FR.** How many forms of impersonals are there?

**SAXO.** Four. They end either in *-tur*, *-at*, *-it*, or *-et*: *statur* (“one stands”), *restat* (“it remains”), *contingit* (“it happens”), *pudet* (“it shames”). Some ending in *-et* come from other verbs, as *miseret* (“it causes pity”). Others arise independently, as *pudet* (“it shames”), *poenitet* (“it causes repentance”), *decet* (“it is fitting”).

**FR.** What are the supines and participial forms?

**SAXO.** There are five such forms: *legendi, legendo, legendum, lectum, lectu*. Priscian insists that these are entirely nouns, because they lack tenses, do not distinguish persons, and are joined to separate prepositions: *ad legendum vado* (“I go to read”), or *legendo venio* (“I come by reading”).

**FR.** I am especially eager to hear about the system of species, because Donatus omitted this accident of the verb.

**SAXO.** He did not omit it, but touched upon it in the forms. There are two species of verbs. One is primary, which Donatus calls the perfect form, as *lego* (“I read”). The other is derivative, which he wished to call desiderative, frequentative, or [manuscript: “and”] inchoative: from *lego*, *lecturio* (“I desire to read”) and *lectito* (“I read frequently”); from *ferveo*, *fervesco* (“I begin to boil”).

These, namely the inchoatives, always end in *-sco* and belong to the third conjugation: *calesco, calescis* (“I grow warm, you grow warm”); *vesperasco, vesperascis* (“evening comes on, evening comes on for you”). They have neither a past tense nor future-tense participles.

Frequentatives belong to the first conjugation and end in *-tito*, *-to*, *-so*, or *-xo*: *lectito, lectitas* (“I read frequently, you read frequently”); *dicto, dictas* (“I say frequently”); *merso, mersas* (“I submerge repeatedly”); *nexo, nexas* (“I bind repeatedly”). They are always neuter [as are the inchoatives].

Desideratives end in *-urio* and belong only to the fourth conjugation: *lecturio, lecturis* (“I desire to read, you desire to read”); *esurio, esuris* (“I desire to eat, you desire to eat”), derived from *edo* (“I eat”).

There are also other species of derivative verbs: from *video* (“I see”), *viso* (“I desire to see”); from *facio* (“I make”), *facesso* (“I desire to make”); from *capio* (“I take”), *capesso* (“I desire to take”); from *lacero* (“I tear”), *lacesso* (“I provoke”); from *arceo* (“I ward off”), *arcesso* (“I summon”); from *acceo* (“I approach”), *accesso* (“I approach”). Their conjugation shows that they are not frequentatives.

There are also derivatives formed by diminution: from *sorbeo* (“I swallow”), *sorbillo* (“I sip”); from *garrio* (“I chatter”), *garrulo* (“I chatter lightly”); from *calvo* (“I make bald”), *calvillo* (“I make slightly bald”). Derivatives are also made from nouns: from *pater* (“father”), *patrisso* (“I behave like a father”); from *Graecus* (“Greek”), *graecisso* (“I behave like a Greek”).

Almost all impersonals are likewise derivatives from active [printed edition: adjectival] or neuter verbs: from *lego*, *legitur*; from *sto*, *statur*. Verbs are also found derived from adverbs: from *perendie* (“the day after tomorrow”), *perendino* (“I defer until the day after tomorrow”); from *cras* (“tomorrow”), *procrastino* (“I postpone”); from *intus* (“within”), *intro, intras, intravi* (“I enter, you enter, I entered”).

## 285. On the Figures of Verbs

**FR.** Please explain the figurative compositions of verbs.

**SAXO.** There are simple verbs, as *cupio* (“I desire”), *taceo* (“I am silent”); and compound verbs, as *concupio* (“I strongly desire”), *conticeo* (“I become silent”). There are also decomposed verbs, that is, derivatives from compounds, as *concupisco*, *conticesco*. Some are composed of three parts, as *perterrifico* (“I terrify greatly”).

Some change conjugation in composition: *do, das* (“I give, you give”), but *reddo, reddis* (“I return, you return”); *facio, facis* (“I make, you make”), but *amplifico, amplificas* (“I enlarge, you enlarge”). Some are compounds whose simple forms are not in use: *offendo* (“I offend”), *aspicio* (“I look at”), *aperio* (“I open”), *refragor* (“I oppose”). I have not found *fendo*, *spicio*, *perio*, or *fragor* in use.

Some change gender in composition: *sperno, spernis* (“I despise, you despise”), active; *aspernor, aspernaris* (“I despise, you despise”), deponent. [*Sentio*, neuter; *assentior*, deponent.] *Sedeo, sedes* (“I sit, you sit”), neuter; *insidior, insidiaris* (“I lie in wait, you lie in wait”), deponent; but *obsideo* (“I besiege”) and *adsideo* (“I sit beside”) are active.

*Eo* (“I go”) and *facio* (“I make”) are neuter; *adeo* (“I approach”), *subeo* (“I undergo”), *perficio* (“I complete”), *conficio* (“I accomplish”), and their compounds are active. They form *adeor, subeor, perficior, conficior*.

From the neuter *facio* arise the deponents *versificor, versificaris* (“I compose verse, you compose verse”) and *gratificor, gratificaris* (“I oblige, you oblige”). *Complecto* is active; *amplector* is deponent.

Verbs are compounded with nouns, as from *amplus* (“large”) and *facio* (“I make”), *amplifico* (“I enlarge”), from which comes the participle *amplificans* (“enlarging”); with another verb, as *calefacio*, that is, *calere facio* (“I make [something] hot”); with an adverb, as *benedico* (“I bless”); or with a preposition, as *indico* (“I point out”) and *subeo* (“I undergo”).

In composition, prepositions are always joined as though to the nominative case [printed edition: “case-form”], whose force verbs retain everywhere through all persons: *facio ego* (“I make”), *facis tu* (“you make”), *facit ille* (“he makes”), except that second-person imperatives take the vocative, as *scribe, Virgili* (“write, Virgil”); *lege, Terenti* (“read, Terence”).

## On the Conjugation of Verbs

**FR.** I have now learned about figures. But tell me the distinctions among the conjugations. First explain from where *conjugatio* (“conjugation”) is derived.

**SAXO.** *Conjugatio* is so called because many verbs are joined together under one system of declension.

**FR.** How many conjugations are there?

**SAXO.** Among the Greeks, ten [manuscript: “decim,” not incorrectly, but archaically; hence eleven]. Among the Latins, four.

Of verbs whose first person ends in *-o* and whose second ends in *-as*, as *amo, amas* (“I love, you love”), *sto, stas* (“I stand, you stand”), this is called the first conjugation. The second ends in *-es*, as *moneo, mones* (“I warn, you warn”). The third has a short *-is*, as *lego, legis* (“I read, you read”). The fourth has a long *-is*, as *munio, munis* (“I fortify, you fortify”).

Among verbs whose first person ends in *-or* and second in *-aris*, the first conjugation is *amor, amaris* (“I am loved, you are loved”), *criminor, criminaris* (“I accuse, you accuse”), *luctor, luctaris* (“I wrestle, you wrestle”). The second has a lengthened penultimate syllable in *-eris*: *doceor, doceris* (“I am taught, you are taught”), *reor, reris* (“I think, you think”). The third has a shortened penultimate syllable in *-eris*: *legor, legeris* (“I am read, you are read”), *sequor, sequeris* (“I follow, you follow”). The fourth has a lengthened penultimate syllable in *-iris*: *munior, muniris* (“I am fortified, you are fortified”), *molior, moliris* (“I undertake, you undertake”).

**FR.** Do individual verbs always have fixed conjugations?

**SAXO.** Some verbs are indistinguishable in the first person but are distinguished in the second by meaning and conjugation: *dico, dicis* (“I say, you say”) and *dico, dicas* (“I say, you say”); *volo, vis* (“I wish, you wish”) and *volo, volas* (“I fly, you fly”); *fundo, fundas* (“I found, you found”), *fundo, fundis* (“I pour, you pour”); *mando, mandas* (“I command, you command”), *mando, mandis* (“I eat, you eat”) [manuscript: *mundo, mundas, mundo, mundis*].

Conversely, some have one meaning but different conjugations: *denso, densas* and *denseo, denses* (“I make dense, you make dense”); *strideo, strides* and *strido, stridis* (“I hiss/screech, you hiss/screech”); *ferveo, ferves*—from which comes *fervesco, fervesci*—and *fervo, fervis* (“I boil, you boil”); *cieo, cies* and *cio, cis* (“I move, you move”); *dureo, dures*, from which come *duresco* and *duro, duras* (“I harden, you harden”); *tueor, tueris* and *tuor, tueris*, with a shortened penultimate syllable (“I protect, you protect”); *fulgeo, fulges* and *fulgo, fulgis* (“I shine, you shine”); *excelleo, excelles* and *excello, excellis* (“I excel, you excel”); *sono, sonas* and *sono, sonis* (“I sound, you sound”); *uno, unas* and *unio, unis* (“I unite, you unite”).

**FR.** In how many ways are verbs declined?

**SAXO.** Those whose first person reasonably ends in *-o* are declined in three ways, apart from the indicative perfect, the imperative, and the infinitive. According to the present tense, verbs of the three conjugations are ordinarily declined through all moods and tenses, except where stated otherwise.

The imperfect and pluperfect of the first conjugation, and likewise of the second and third, together with the optative, future, and present subjunctive of the fourth, are always declined in their final letters according to the present tense of the first conjugation:

*amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant* (“I love, you love, he/she loves, we love, you [plural] love, they love”);

*amabam, amabas, amabat, amabamus, amabatis, amabant* (“I was loving, you were loving, he/she was loving, we were loving, you were loving, they were loving”);

*amaveram, amaveras, amaverat, amaveramus, amaveratis, amaverant* (“I had loved, you had loved, he/she had loved, we had loved, you had loved, they had loved”).

Optative, future, and present subjunctive:

*doceam, doceas, doceat, doceamus, doceatis, doceant* (“may/will I teach, may/will you teach, may/will he teach, may/will we teach, may/will you [plural] teach, may/will they teach”).

According to the present tense of the second conjugation, the future indicative [printed edition: “according to the conjugation of the future indicative”] is formed.

In the third and fourth conjugations, the entire present and past of the optative, the imperfect subjunctive with a long penultimate syllable, and the pluperfect in every conjugation—including the optative, future, and present subjunctive of the first conjugation—are declined as follows. The parenthetical forms—*legam, leges, leget, emus, etis, ent* (“I shall read, you will read, he will read; we, you [plural], they will read”) and *doceo, ces, cet, cemus, cetis, cent* (“I teach, you teach, he teaches; we, you [plural], they teach”)—seem to pertain elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0879D] The material enclosed in parentheses appears to belong elsewhere.]: 

*amarem, amares, amaret, amaremus, amaretis, amarent* (“I might love, you might love, he/she might love, we might love, you [plural] might love, they might love”);

*amavissem, amavisses, amavisset, amavissemus, amavissetis, amavissent*, forms common to the subjunctive and optative.

Likewise, the present of the optative, future, and subjunctive:

*amem, ames, amet, amemus, ametis, ament* (“may I love, may you love, may he love, may we love, may you [plural] love, may they love”).

According to the present of the third conjugation and the future indicative of the first, second, and fourth conjugations ending in this manner, and according to the perfect and future subjunctive, except in the third-person plural, *u* changes to *i*:

*lego, legis, legit, legimus, legitis, legunt* (“I read, you read, he/she reads, we read, you [plural] read, they read”);

*amabo, amabis, amabit, amabimus, amabitis, amabunt* (“I shall love, you will love, he/she will love, we shall love, you [plural] will love, they will love”);

*docebo, docebis, docebit, docebimus, docebitis, docebunt* (“I shall teach, you will teach, he/she will teach, we shall teach, you [plural] will teach, they will teach”).

Perfect subjunctive:

*amaverim, amaveris, amaverit, amaverimus, amaveritis, amaverint* (“I may have loved, you may have loved, he/she may have loved, we may have loved, you [plural] may have loved, they may have loved”).

Likewise:

*amavero, amaveris, amaverit, amaverimus, amaveritis, amaverint* (“I shall have loved, you will have loved, he/she will have loved, we shall have loved, you [plural] will have loved, they will have loved”).

And in the fourth conjugation:

*ibo, ibis, ibit, ibimus, ibitis, ibunt* (“I shall go, you will go, he/she will go, we shall go, you [plural] will go, they will go”).

Of all these verbs, whose first and second persons are distinguished by two [manuscript: three] forms, the first person ends either in *-o*, *-am*, *-em*, or *-im*.

**FR.** How are the perfect and the imperative declined?

**SAXO.** Every perfect, when declined according to the rule, sends the first person into *-i*, the second into the syllable *-sti*, the third into *-it*, and the plural into *-imus*, *-istis*, and *-erunt* or *-ere*, with a long *e*.

**FR.** Give me the final letters of the imperative.

**SAXO.** Every singular imperative, because nature excludes it, has no first person and is joined to the vocative case, because in the second person it commands someone present. In the first conjugation it ends in long *a*, as *ama* (“love”); in the second, also in long *e*, as *ave* (“hail”) [manuscript: *habe*]; in the third, in short *e*, as *lege* (“read”); in the fourth, in long *i*, as *audi* (“hear”). Everywhere, whether in verbs or nouns, *i* placed at the end is lengthened.

The third person in the first conjugation ends in *-et*; in the other conjugations, in *-at*: *amet, habeat, legat, audiat* (“let him love, let him have, let him read, let him hear”).

The first person plural ends in *-mus*, the second in *-te*, and the third in *-ent* in the first conjugation, but in *-ant* in the others:

*amemus, amate, ament* (“let us love, love, let them love”);

*doceamus, docete, doceant* (“let us teach, teach, let them teach”), and so forth. Everywhere the penultimate syllable of the first and second persons is long, except for the second person of the third conjugation, as *legite* (“read”).

The future imperative has *-to* in the second person: *amato, habeto, legito, audito* (“you shall love/have/read/hear”), with a long penultimate syllable except in the third conjugation [manuscript: “except the third declension”].

The third person of the future is everywhere like the present; the third person and first person plural are likewise like the present plural. The second person plural ends in *-tote*: *amatote, habetote, legitote, auditote* (“you [plural] shall love, have, read, hear”). The third ends in *-nto*: *amanto, docento, legunto, audiunto* (“let them love, teach, read, hear”).

**FR.** Speak about the infinitives.

**SAXO.** Every present infinitive ends in *-re*, the past in *-sse*, and the future in *-ire* or *-esse* in every conjugation: *amare, amasse, amatum ire*, or *amaturum esse* (“to love, to have loved, to be going to love, to be going to love”).

**FR.** What should one think about the five gerund forms [manuscript: “gerundive forms”]?

**SAXO.** What else but what I said earlier: according to Priscian, they are entirely nouns. They take separate prepositions with accusative and ablative cases: *ad amandum* (“for loving/to love”), *in amando* (“in loving”), something that cannot happen to a verb.

**FR.** What, then, is the difference among *amandum*, *amando*, *amatum*, and *amatu*?

**SAXO.** *Amandum* signifies the necessity of love; *amatum*, the beginning of love. Similarly, *amando* refers to love itself; *amatu* is taken for *amatio* (“loving”), that is, for the thing itself.

**FR.** Explain the rules of the passive to me.

**SAXO.** I shall explain them briefly, lest I be more verbose than suits this childish game (thus the manuscripts). Every passive is formed everywhere from its active through all conjugations. In the present, imperfect, and future tenses, active forms ending in *-o* or *-m* take *-r* in the passive:

*amo, amor* (“I love, I am loved”);

*amabo, amabor* (“I shall love, I shall be loved”);

*amato, amator* (“you shall love, you shall be loved”);

*amanto, amantor* (“let them love, let them be loved”);

*amabam, amabar* (“I was loving, I was being loved”);

*amarem, amarer* (“I might love, I might be loved”);

*amem, amer* (“may I love, may I be loved”);

*legam, legar* (“I shall read, I shall be read”), and so forth.

The other persons are declined according to the rules already stated for the present tense of the three conjugations. The second person ends in *-ris* or *-re*, the third in *-tur*, the first plural in *-mur*, the second in *-mini*, and the third in *-ntur*.

The perfect and pluperfect of all moods, and the future subjunctive, are declined through the past participle and the auxiliary verb *sum*:

*amatus sum* or *amatus fui* (“I have been loved”);

*amatus eram* or *amatus fueram* (“I had been loved”).

Optative: *amatus essem* or *amatus fuissem* (“I might have been loved”).

Subjunctive: *amatus sim* or *amatus fuerim* (“may I have been loved”); *amatus essem* or *amatus fuissem* (“I might have been loved”).

Future: *amatus ero* or *amatus fuero* (“I shall have been loved”).

The second-person present passive imperative in every conjugation is like the active infinitive: *amare, docere, legere, audire* (“be loved, be taught, be read, be heard”), with a long penultimate syllable except in the third conjugation.

The third person ends in *-tur*, the first plural in *-mur*, the second in *-mini* [which is pronounced the same in the indicative and imperative in the first conjugation; printed edition: “the imperative and infinitive are pronounced alike”]. The third plural in the first conjugation ends in *-entur*, and in the others in *-antur*. The second person of the future ends in *-tor*, the third in *-tur*, the first plural in *-mur*, the second in *-minor*, and the third in *-ntor*:

*amare, ametur* (“be loved, let him be loved”);

*amemur, amaminor, amentor* (“let us be loved, be loved [plural], let them be loved”);

*ametor, ametur* (“you shall be loved, he shall be loved”);

*amemur, ameminor, amentor* (“let us be loved, be loved [plural], let them be loved”).

Passive infinitives always end in *-i* in the present: *amari, doceri, legi, audiri* (“to be loved, taught, read, heard”). The past is formed with the neuter participle and *esse* or *fuisse*: *doctum esse* or *doctum fuisse* (“to have been taught”). The future ends in *-iri*: *amatum iri* (“to be going to be loved”).

There you have, France, what you asked for; but your curiosity makes you destined not to be loved.

**FR.** Nor will your envy make you destined to be pleasing.

**SAXO.** Carefully! [Col. 0881D] lest the one who usually flogs hear us. But continue with the rest.

**FR.** As I think, the order of the accidents requires us to investigate the persons of verbs.

**SAXO.** There are three persons of verbs. The first is the one that speaks about itself and displays others. The second is the one to whom someone speaks. The third is the one about whom someone speaks. Unless there is a first person to utter speech, the others cannot exist.

The first and second persons of verbs are definite, for they display those who are present. The third is indefinite and therefore generally needs a pronoun to define it. The first person can join both the second and the third to itself: *ego et tu, et nos facimus* (“you and I, and we, do [it]”); *ego et ille facimus* (“he and I do [it]”). The second person, however, can join only the third to itself: *tu et ille facitis* (“you and he do [it]”). The third can join neither the first nor the second, but only another third: *iste et ille faciunt* (“this man and that man do [it]”).

In the singular imperative there cannot be a first person, because by nature the one who commands is separated from the one whom he commands. Infinitives and impersonals, as well as gerunds, naturally lack persons.

## On Number

**FR.** Explain number as an accident of verbs.

**SAXO.** Singular number, as *lego* (“I read”), and plural number, as *legimus* (“we read”), is added to a verb, just as to all the parts that have cases. But in a verb singular and plural number are never found under one form, as they are in other parts of speech: *dies, res* (“day, thing”), nominative singular and plural; *isti, illi* (“to this one, to those”), dative singular and nominative plural.

You should also know, France, that all verbs that are defective in persons are always defective in number as well, such as impersonals and infinitives. Therefore they assume persons and numbers when pronouns are added: *legitur a me, a nobis* (“there is reading by me, by us”); *legere te volo, et legere vos volo* (“I want you to read; I want you [plural] to read”).

**FR.** But since you have introduced defective verbs, I suddenly need you to explain defective forms under each individual accident, especially since our teacher Donatus touched upon these matters very obscurely and briefly.

**SAXO.** I am not your debtor for irrational things, but for rational ones and for those subject to rules. Nevertheless, so that you may know that I am not envious toward you, just as I understand that you are not tiresome toward me, I shall explain some of them.

Verbs, like the other parts of speech, become defective in three ways: through the necessity of nature, through an accident of circumstance, or for the sake of distinction.

Through the necessity of nature: if we wished to say the masculine of *nupta* (“married woman”), namely *nuptus* (“married man”), or the masculine of *puerpera* (“woman who has given birth”), namely *puerperus*, the very nature of the things prevents it. Or because of discordance of sound: if we wished to make the feminine *curstrix* from *cursor* (“runner”), as *victrix* from *victor*, it would be cacophonous.

Through an accident of circumstance, unusual and shameful forms are avoided, as are forms not used by authors. Thus, according to the rule, *do* could produce *dor*; but because it is not found in the authors, we refuse to say it.

For the sake of distinction, many forms are likewise avoided. Thus *fero, fers, fert* (“I carry, you carry, he carries”) is pronounced by syncope without the *i* in the second and third persons, so that if one said *feris, ferit*, it would be thought to come from *ferio* (“I strike”). Likewise *edo, es, est* (“I eat, you eat, he eats”) and *volo, vis, vult* (“I wish, you wish, he wishes”) have anomalous spelling for the sake of distinction.

*Volo* naturally lacks an imperative mood, because commands belong to necessity, not to will. Likewise, the authors preferred *fac, duc, dic, fer* (“do, lead, say, carry”) to be produced by apocope for the sake of distinction, so that if we said *face, duce, dice, fere*, we might think they signified something else.

Many other forms are not said because they are not found in the authors. Of these I shall explain some to your eager mind under the individual accidents.

*Quaeso* (“I ask” or “I beg”), introduced by *nam* (“for”), has no moods other than the indicative, a first person in both numbers, and the infinitive *quesere*. Likewise *ovat* (“he triumphs”) and *infit* (“he begins”) have only the third person; and *ovans* (“triumphant”) is their participle.

*Ausim*, that is, “may I have authority,” and *inquam* (“I say”), contrary to ordinary usage, are expressed in the first person.

*Salve* and *salvete* (“hail,” singular and plural) have only the second-person imperative. Likewise *cede* for *da* (“give”) [manuscript: *dic*, “say”]; *cete* for *date* (“give”) [manuscript: *cedite*, “withdraw”]. Terence: *Cete patri meo*, that is, “Give to my father.”

*Ave* (“hail”) is used for *gaude* (“rejoice”), and *avete* (“hail,” plural) for *gaudete* (“rejoice,” plural); these are second-person forms.

Likewise *faxo*, for *faciam* (“I shall do”), belongs only to the future indicative and is formed as follows: *faxo, faxis, faxit; faximus, faxitis, faxunt*, that is, “they will do.”

*Facesso*, *capesso*, and *viso* are desideratives, not frequentatives, because they do not belong to the first conjugation. *Facesso* means “I desire to do”; *capesso*, “I desire to take”; *viso*, “I desire to see.”

Likewise *sis*, that is, *si vis* (“if you wish”), and *sodes*, that is, *si audes* (“if you dare”), are second-person forms.

*Foret* is found for *esset* (“he/she might be”), *forent* for *essent* (“they might be”), and *fore* for *esse* (“to be”).

*Aio* (“I say”) and *meio* (“I urinate”) are defective in many forms. *Aio, ais, ait* (“I say, you say, he says”); *aitis, aiunt* (“you [plural] say, they say”); it lacks the first-person plural. *Ait* is its perfect. Likewise *meio* forms the infinitive *meiere* (“to urinate”).

Some verbs have the same present and imperfect [manuscript: perfect]. These alone are: *odi* (“I hate”), *novi* (“I know”), *memini* (“I remember”), *coepi* (“I began”), and *pepigi* (“I struck an agreement”). They are defective in the imperfect [alternate: imperative], except *memini*, which forms *memento* and *mementote* (“remember,” singular and plural). They are also defective in the future, infinitive, supines, and participles of both tenses [alternate: “of either tense”], except *odi*, which in a compound form makes two past participles: *exosus* (“hating”) and *perosus* (“hating thoroughly”).

There are also passive and deponent verbs that are defective in the past unless a past tense is taken from elsewhere to supplement their declension. Thus *feror* (“I am carried”), *ferior* (“I am struck”), *tollor* (“I am lifted”), *poscor* (“I am requested”), and *urgeor* (“I am pressed”) form their pasts from other verbs: *latus sum* (“I was carried”), *ictus sum* (“I was struck”), *sublatus sum* (“I was lifted”), *postulatus sum* (“I was requested”), *convictus sum* (“I was convicted”).

Likewise the deponents *vescor* (“I feed”), *fruor* (“I enjoy”), *medeor* (“I heal”), *liquor* (“I melt/flow”), and *reminiscor* [printed edition: *remuneror*] (“I remember”) form *pastus sum* (“I fed”), *potitus sum* (“I obtained”), *medicatus sum* (“I healed”), *liquefactus sum* (“I was melted”), and *recordatus sum* (“I remembered”).

The verb *sum* (“I am”), which has an irregular declension, is defective in the simple participle and in compounds of the present tense, except in two compounds formed from it, namely *absum* (“I am absent”) and *praesum* (“I am present/oversee”), which form *absens* (“absent”) and *praesens* (“present”).

*Possum, potes, potest* (“I can, you can, he can”) changes *s* into *t* for euphony. *Prosum, prodes, prodest* (“I benefit, you benefit, he benefits”) assumes *d* to avoid hiatus.

*Volo* (“I wish”), *malo* (“I prefer”), and the compound formed from it, *magis volo* (“I prefer,” literally “I wish more”), naturally lack the imperative, because commands belong to necessity, not to will. Yet another compound of *volo*, namely *nolo* (“I do not wish”), does have one: *noli* and *nolíte* (“do not wish,” singular and plural).

**FR.** I demand that you give me the fuller declension of these four verbs: *sum*, *fero*, *edo*, and *volo*.
