**SAXO.** Their declension is unusual in many places. Nevertheless, since their system is found in the examples of the teachers, I shall explain it.

The neuter verb *sum* is declined as follows:

**Present:** *sum, es, est* — “I am, you are, he/she is.”  
**Plural:** *sumus, estis, sunt* — “we are, you [plural] are, they are.”

**Imperfect:** *eram, eras, erat* — “I was, you were, he/she was.”  
**Plural:** *eramus, eratis, erant* — “we were, you [plural] were, they were.”

**Perfect:** *fui, fuisti, fuit* — “I was/have been, you were/have been, he/she was/has been.”  
**Plural:** *fuimus, fuistis, fuerunt* or *fuere* — “we were/have been, you [plural] were/have been, they were/have been.”

**Pluperfect:** *fueram, fueras, fuerat* — “I had been, you had been, he/she had been.”  
**Plural:** *fueramus, fueratis, fuerant* — “we had been, you [plural] had been, they had been.”

**Future:** *ero, eris, erit* — “I shall be, you will be, he/she will be.”  
**Plural:** *erimus, eritis, erunt* — “we shall be, you [plural] will be, they will be.”

**Present imperative:** second and third persons: *sis* or *es*, *sit* — “be,” “let him/her be.”  
**Plural:** *simus* [*estote* or] *sitis*, *sint* — “let us be,” “be,” “let them be”; also *sunto* and *suntote*.

**Present and imperfect optative:** *utinam essem, esses, esset* — “would that I were, you were, he/she were.”  
**Plural:** *essemus, essetis, essent* — “would that we were, you [plural] were, they were.”

**Perfect and pluperfect optative:** *fuissem, fuisses, fuisset* — “would that I had been, you had been, he/she had been.”  
**Plural:** *fuissemus, fuissetis, fuissent* — “would that we had been, you [plural] had been, they had been.”

**Future optative:** *sim, sis, sit* — “may I be, may you be, may he/she be.”  
**Plural:** *simus, sitis, sint* — “may we be, may you [plural] be, may they be.”

**Present subjunctive:** *cum sim, sis, sit* — “when I am, you are, he/she is.”  
**Plural:** *simus, sitis, sint* — “when we are, you [plural] are, they are.”

**Imperfect subjunctive:** *essem, esses, esset* — “I might be, you might be, he/she might be.”  
**Plural:** *essemus, essetis, essent* — “we might be, you [plural] might be, they might be.”

**Perfect subjunctive:** *cum fuerim, fueris, fuerit* — “when I have been, you have been, he/she has been.”  
**Plural:** *fuerimus, fueritis, fuerint* — “when we have been, you [plural] have been, they have been.”

**Pluperfect subjunctive:** *cum fuissem, fuisses, fuisset* — “when I had been, you had been, he/she had been.”  
**Plural:** *fuissemus, fuissetis, fuissent* — “when we had been, you [plural] had been, they had been.”

**Future subjunctive:** *cum fuero, fueris, fuerit* — “when I shall have been, you will have been, he/she will have been.”  
**Plural:** *fuerimus, fueritis, fuerint* — “when we shall have been, you [plural] will have been, they will have been.”

**Infinitive** (without number or persons): present, *esse* (“to be”); past, *fuisse* (“to have been”); future, *esse*, *ire*, and *fore* (“to be, to go, and to be about to be”).

### 289

Its present participle was formerly pronounced by the ancients as *ens*, from which *potens* (“powerful, able”) is formed. The future seems rather to arise from the verb *fio* (“I become”). Yet it can also be thought to derive from *fui* (“I was”). Its compounds are therefore declined as follows: *prosum, adsum, desum, obsum, intersum, praesum, supersum* (“I benefit, am present, am absent, am harmful, am involved, preside, survive”). Of these, only two have present participles: *praesens* (“present”) and *absens* (“absent”).

The verb *fero* (“I carry”) removes the *i* by syncope in the second and third persons for the sake of distinction, because of the verb *ferio* (“I strike”), which forms *ferio, feris, ferit* (“I strike, you strike, he strikes”).

**Present:** *fero, fers, fert* — “I carry, you carry, he/she carries.”  
**Plural:** *ferimus, fertis, ferunt* — “we carry, you [plural] carry, they carry.”

**Imperfect:** *ferebam, ferebas, ferebat* — “I was carrying, you were carrying, he/she was carrying.”  
**Plural:** *ferebamus, ferebatis, ferebant* — “we were carrying, you [plural] were carrying, they were carrying.”

**Perfect:** *tuli, tulisti, tulit* — “I carried, you carried, he/she carried.”  
**Plural:** *tulimus, tulistis, tulerunt* or *tulere* — “we carried, you [plural] carried, they carried.”

**Pluperfect:** *tuleram, tuleras, tulerat* — “I had carried, you had carried, he/she had carried.”  
**Plural:** *tuleramus, tuleratis, tulerant* — “we had carried, you [plural] had carried, they had carried.”

**Future:** *feram, feres, feret* — “I shall carry, you will carry, he/she will carry.”  
**Plural:** *feremus, feretis, ferent* — “we shall carry, you [plural] will carry, they will carry.”

**Present imperative:** *fer* [or *feras*], *ferat* — “carry,” “let him/her carry.”  
**Plural:** *feramus, ferte, ferant* — “let us carry, carry [plural], let them carry.”

**Future imperative:** *ferto* [or *feras*], *ferat* — “you shall carry,” “let him/her carry.”  
**Plural:** *feramus, fertote, ferant* — “let us carry, you [plural] shall carry, let them carry.”

**Optative:** [*utinam*] *ferrem, ferres, ferret* — “would that I carried, you carried, he/she carried.”  
**Plural:** *ferremus, ferretis, ferrent* — “would that we carried, you [plural] carried, they carried.”

**Pluperfect optative:** *tulissem, tulisses, tulisset* — “would that I had carried, you had carried, he/she had carried.”  
**Plural:** *tulissemus, tulissetis, tulissent* — “would that we had carried, you [plural] had carried, they had carried.”

**Future optative:** *feram, feras, ferat* — “may I carry, may you carry, may he/she carry.”  
**Plural:** *feramus, feratis, ferant* — “may we carry, may you [plural] carry, may they carry.”

**Present subjunctive:** [*cum*] *feram, feras, ferat* — “when I carry, you carry, he/she carries.”  
**Plural:** *feramus, feratis, ferant* — “when we carry, you [plural] carry, they carry.”

**Imperfect subjunctive:** *ferrem, ferres, ferret* — “I might carry, you might carry, he/she might carry.”  
**Plural:** *ferremus, ferretis, ferrent* — “we might carry, you [plural] might carry, they might carry.”

**Perfect subjunctive:** *tulerim, tuleris, tulerit* — “I may have carried, you may have carried, he/she may have carried.”  
**Plural:** *tulerimus, tuleritis, tulerint* — “we may have carried, you [plural] may have carried, they may have carried.”

**Pluperfect subjunctive:** *tulissem, tulisses, tulisset* — “I might have carried, you might have carried, he/she might have carried.”  
**Plural:** *tulissemus, tulissetis, tulissent* — “we might have carried, you [plural] might have carried, they might have carried.”

**Future subjunctive:** *tulero, tuleris, tulerit* — “I shall have carried, you will have carried, he/she will have carried.”  
**Plural:** *tulerimus, tuleritis, tulerint* — “we shall have carried, you [plural] will have carried, they will have carried.”

[Note: [Col. 0883D] The infinitive is missing.] **Edo** is an irregular verb, whose second and third persons, because of their difference, are pronounced by contraction. *Edo, es, est* (“I eat, you eat, he eats”). Plural: *edimus, estis, edunt*. Imperfect: *edebam, edebas, edebat*. Plural: *edebamus, edebatis, edebant*. Perfect: *edi, edisti, edit*. Plural: *edimus, edistis, ederunt* or *edere*. Pluperfect: *ederam, ederas, ederat*. Plural: *ederamus, ederatis, ederant*. Future: *edam, edes, edet*. Plural: *edemus, edetis, edent*. Imperative: *es, edat*. Plural: *edamus, este, edant*. Future: *esto, edat*. Plural: *edamus, estote, edant*, or *edunto, eduntote*.

Optative: *essem, esses, esset*. Plural: *essemus, essetis, essent*. [Perfect and pluperfect:] *edissem, edisses, edisset*. Plural: *edissemus, edissetis, edissent*. [Future:] *edam, edas, edat*. Plural: *edamus, edatis, edant*. In the subjunctive: *edam, edas, edat*. Plural: *edamus, edatis, edant*. *Essem, esses, esset*. Plural: *essemus, essetis, essent*. *Ederim, ederis, ederit*. Plural: *ederimus, [Col. 0885B] ederitis, ederint*. *Edissem, edisses, edisset*. Plural: *edissemus, edissetis, edissent*. *Edero, ederis, ederit*. Plural: *ederimus, ederitis, ederint*.

Present infinitive: *esse*. Likewise the past: *esse*. Future: *esum iri* or *esurum esse*. Impersonal: *estur* [Ms., *editur*]. Imperfect: *edebatur*. Perfect: *esum est* or *fuit*. Pluperfect: *esum erat* or *fuerat*. Future: *edetur*. Supines: *edendi, edendo, edendum*. *Esum, esu* [Al., *essum, essu*].

**Volo** (“I wish”) is likewise a neuter verb, pronounced by contraction in the second and third persons, and defective in the imperfect [Ms., imperative]. *Volo, vis, vult*. Plural: *volumus, vultis, volunt*. *Volebam, volebas, volebat*. Plural: *volebamus, volebatis, volebant*. *Volui, voluisti, [Col. 0885C] voluit*. Plural: *voluimus, voluistis, voluerunt* or *voluere*. *Volueram, volueras, voluerat*. Plural: *volueramus, volueratis, voluerant*. *Volam, voles, volet*. Plural: *volemus, voletis, volent*.

[Optative:] *Vellem, velles, vellet*. Plural: *vellemus, velletis, vellent*. *Voluissem, voluisses, voluisset*. Plural: *voluissemus, voluissetis, voluissent*. *Velim, velis, velit*. Plural: *velimus, velitis, velint*. *Vellem, velles, vellet*. Plural: *vellemus, velletis, vellent*. *Voluerim, volueris, voluerit*. Plural: *voluerimus, volueritis, voluerint*. *Voluissem, voluisses, voluisset*. Plural: *voluissemus, voluissetis, voluissent*. *Voluero, volueris, voluerit*. Plural: *voluerimus, volueritis, voluerint*. Infinitive, present: *velle*. Past: *voluisse*. Present participle: *volens* (“wishing”).

[Col. 0885D] Thus are the following declined: *nolo, non vis, non vult* (“I do not wish, you do not wish, he does not wish”), except that *nolo* has an imperative: *noli, nolite* (“do not wish”). *Malo, mavis, mavult* (“I prefer, you prefer, he prefers”), and the rest similarly.

You are harsh toward me, France. 290 Look! What a burden you have laid upon me, leading me through rough and thorny places. Let me at last breathe again.

**FRANCE.** I will let you go, and, in Virgil’s words (*Eclogue* IX, 65):

> … I shall lift this burden from you.

**SAXO.** Even if you lift this one, I fear you may place another upon me.

**FRANCE.** Do not be afraid:

> … Hard work conquers everything,

when it is persistent [Note: [Col. 0885D] Virgil, *Georgics* I, 145]. [Col. 0886A]

**SAXO.** It conquers; therefore let us go by the road that remains [Ms., “the road which”].

## On the Adverb

**FRANCE.** At last, Saxo, open your long-closed mouth and unfold for me the rules of adverbs, which have been shut away until now.

**SAXO.** I will, France. An adverb is an indeclinable part of speech, always attached to a verb. When added to verbs, it does what adjectives do when joined to common nouns. Thus, “a prudent man acts prudently”; “a fortunate man lives fortunately.”

**FRANCE.** How many properties does an adverb have?

**SAXO.** Three: kind, meaning, and form.

**FRANCE.** Explain its kind.

**SAXO.** Adverbs are either primitive or derivative. Primitive adverbs are those which arise from themselves, such as *non* (“not”), *ita* (“thus”), and *ceu* (“just as”). Derivative adverbs [Col. 0886B] arise from other adverbs, as *clanculum* (“secretly”) from *clam* (“secretly”), and *propius* (“nearer”) from *prope* (“near”).

They also arise from other parts of speech: from the noun *Latinus*, *Latine* (“in Latin”); from *Tullius*, *Tulliane* (“in the manner of Tullius”); from a verb, as *parcius* (“more sparingly”) from *parco* (“I spare”); from a noun and a verb, as *pedetentim* (“step by step”) from *pes* (“foot”) and *tento* (“I try”); from a pronoun, as *mecum* (“with me”) from *me* [Ms., *meatim*]; from *ille* and *hic*, *illic* (“there”); and from a preposition, as *extra* (“outside”) from *ex*.

**FRANCE.** Can an adverb, standing by itself, have a complete meaning?

**SAXO.** It cannot, unless it is joined to a verb or participle, as in *bene lego* (“I read well”), *bene legens* (“reading well”).

**FRANCE.** Can other parts of speech be used as adverbs?

**SAXO.** They can. Nouns are used as adverbs in various cases.

**FRANCE.** Give an example.

**SAXO.** The genitive is used as an adverb, as in *Romae*, “at Rome,” as in Cicero: *Romae ne sit* (“let him not be at Rome”). The dative is used in *vesperi* (“in the evening”) and *sorti* (“by lot”). Virgil (*Georgics* IV, 165):

> There are some for whom the watch at the gate [Al., “gates”] fell by lot.

The accusative is used in *Romam pergo* (“I proceed to Rome”) or *Athenas* (“to Athens”). Terence:

> Why do you go to Athens, you ignorant man?

The ablative is used, for example, by Virgil (*Eclogue* VII, 1):

> By chance Daphnis had sat beneath the spreading holm oak.

**FRANCE.** How can one distinguish whether such forms are nouns used in this way or adverbs?

**SAXO.** When nouns are taken in place of adverbs, they remain indeclinable, even though they are joined to different cases, as in *sublime volans, sublime volantis, sublime volanti*, and so on. If they are nouns, however, they are declined: *hoc sublime volans, hujus [Col. 0886D] sublimis volantis, huic sublimi volanti*, and so on.

**FRANCE.** Are any other parts of speech used as adverbs?

**SAXO.** They are. The conjunction *vel*, and the prepositions *per* and *ex*, are used with the meaning “very,” as in Cicero: *vel magnum bellum* (“a very great war”), meaning “very great.” *Excelsus* means “very high.”

## On the Forms of Adverbs

**FRANCE.** How many forms of adverbs are there?

**SAXO.** Three: simple, as *diu* (“for a long time”); compound, as *interdiu* (“during the day”); and derived from a compound, as *indocte* (“ignorantly”) from *indoctus* (“unlearned”), and *misericorditer* (“mercifully”) from *misericors* (“merciful”).

**FRANCE.** What is the meaning of adverbs [Ms., “how many kinds do they have”]?

**SAXO.** The meaning of adverbs has various kinds. Some are [Ed., “but are”] temporal, such as *pridem* (“formerly”), *nuper* (“recently”), and *nudiustertius* (“the day before yesterday”). Some signify only the present time, such as *nunc* (“now”) and *praesto* (“at hand”). Some signify the past, such as *heri* (“yesterday”) and *hesterno* (“on the previous day”). Some signify the future, such as *cras* (“tomorrow”) and *perendie* (“the day after tomorrow”).

Others are common to different times, such as *olim* (“once”), *dudum* (“a while ago”), and *quondam* (“formerly”). Of the past, Horace (*Satires* I.8):

> Once I was a fig-wood trunk, useless timber.

Of the present [Virgil, *Georgics* II, 403]:

> And now the vine has already put forth its late leaves.

Of the future, the same Virgil (*Aeneid* II, 207):

> Perhaps one day it will be pleasing to remember even these things.

*Dudum* is used of the past, as by Terence (*Andria* III.4.3):

> A little while ago I was somewhat afraid.

It is also used of the present, as by Virgil (*Aeneid* II, 103):

> It is enough even to hear this; now at last exact your penalties.

*Quondam* is used of the past:

> Once this virtue existed in this republic.

(Cicero, *First Speech against Catiline* 3.)

It is used of the present by Virgil (*Aeneid* II, 367):

> Even in the defeated, courage once more returns to their hearts.

Of the future:

> There will one day be a time.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Virgil, cited by Priscian.]

The compounds formed from these are similar: *aliquando* (“at some time”), *nequando* (“lest ever”), which have the accent on the penultimate syllable [Ms., antepenultimate] so that they are not thought to consist of two separate parts.

But *quando* (“when”), *quomodo* (“how”), *ubi* (“where”), *unde* (“whence”), *qua* (“by which way”), and *quo* (“where to”), when interrogative, have the acute accent; when relative, they have the grave accent through all their syllables. They have four distinctions: *quo*, toward a place; *ubi*, in a place; *unde*, from a place; *qua*, through or by a place.

*Quando* is also accepted as a causal conjunction. Virgil (*Aeneid* I, 265):

> For I shall speak, since this concern gnaws at you.

[Ms., “has gnawed at you.”] He used *quando* in the sense of *quoniam* (“since”).

There are also four other local distinctions. Toward a place: *huc, illuc* (“hither, thither”). In a place: *hic, illic* (“here, there”). From a place: *hinc, illinc, inde* (“from here, from there, thence”), together with compounds formed from *inde*: *subinde, perinde, exinde, proinde* (“immediately thereafter, likewise, thereafter, therefore”). All these have the accent on the penultimate syllable [Ms., antepenultimate]. Through or by a place: *hac, illac* (“by this way, by that way”).

There are also forms compounded with *versum* (“toward”) and a noun or pronoun [Ms., “there are certain forms having a single local meaning”]. Toward a place: *horsum* (“this way”), *deorsum* (“downward”), *sursum* (“upward”), *sinistrorsum* (“to the left”), *dextrorsum* (“to the right”), and *Italiam versum* (“toward Italy”). Also *quorsum*, that is, *quo versum* (“toward where”).

Some adverbs are dehortative, such as *ne* (“not,” “lest”), which is used for *neque* (“and not”), for *non* (“not”), and for *valde* (“very”). Cicero: *Ne dici quidem opus est* (“there is no need even to say it”), meaning *neque dici* (“nor is it necessary to say it”). Terence: *Ne dicam dolo* (“I will not say it deceitfully”), meaning *non dicam* (“I will not say it”). The same author: *Ne illa illum haud movit* (“very much she did not move him”), meaning *valde illa* [sc. *haud movit*].

Others are confirmative: *profecto* (“certainly”), *scilicet* (“of course”), *quippe* (“indeed”), *videlicet* (“plainly”), *nempe* (“surely”). Two parts of speech are sometimes used for these, such as *quidni* (“why not?”), *cur ne* (“why not?”), *sic est* (“so it is”), and *quid istic* (“what is that?”).

Others are oath-taking adverbs: *aedepol*, *aecastor*, *ercle*, *medius fidius*—all expressions meaning approximately “by Pollux,” “by Castor,” “by Hercules,” or “by my faith.” The preposition *per* is also used in this sense, as by Virgil (*Aeneid* X, 596):

> By you, and by the parents who begot you such as you are.

There is also a confirmative use of *per*. Terence: *Tu quoque perparce* (“you too, very sparingly”). In this way *sic* (“so”) is also oath-taking. Virgil (*Eclogue* IX, 30):

> So may the swarms too flee the yew trees of Cyrnos.

Others are optative: *utinam* (“would that”), which is compounded from *uti* and *enim* [Al., *nam*]. Also *o* (“O”) and *si* (“if”). Virgil:

> O, be present at last.

The same author (*Aeneid* VI, 187):

> If only that golden branch from the tree would now show itself to us.

Others are hortatory: *eia* and *aie* [Al., *age*] (“come on”). Others are gradual or mitigating: *pedetentim* (“step by step”), *paulatim* (“little by little”), *sensim* (“gradually”). Others are collective, common to place and time: *simul, una* (“together,” “at once”), meaning in the same place and at the same time.

Others are distributive or separating: *seorsum* (“apart”), *secus* (“otherwise”), *separatim* (“separately”), *secreto* (“secretly”), *utrinque* (“on both sides”), *divise* (“separately”), *singillatim* (“one by one”), *bifariam* (“in two ways”), and *omnifariam* (“in every way”).

Others indicate likeness: *ceu, quasi, velut, veluti, sic, sicuti, ut,* and *uti* (“as,” “just as,” “as if,” “in the manner that”). Others are ordinal: *deinde* (“then”), *continuo* (“immediately”), *protinus* (“straightaway”), *praeterea* (“besides”). Others are intensive: *valde* (“very”), *nimium* (“too much”), *prorsus* (“entirely”), *penitus* (“thoroughly”), *omnino* (“altogether”). Others are comparative: *magis* (“more”), *minus* (“less”), *ocius* (“more quickly”), which derives from the Greek ὠκύς (“swift”).

**FRANCE.** Do derivatives from other words retain the meaning or quality of their primitives?

**SAXO.** Certainly. Thus *Tulliane* (“in the manner of Tullius”) comes from *Tullius*; *corporaliter* (“bodily”) from *corpus* (“body”); *aliter* (“otherwise”) from *alius* (“other”); *graece* (“in Greek”) from *Graecus* (“Greek”); and *viriliter* (“manfully”) from *vir* (“man”).

**FRANCE.** Continue.

**SAXO.** Others are numerical: from *unus* (“one”), *semel* (“once”); from *duo* (“two”), *bis* (“twice”), and these alone are formed irregularly. The remaining numbers form adverbs from their own words: from *tres* (“three”), *ter* (“three times”); from *quatuor* (“four”), *quater* (“four times”); and so on through *decies* (“ten times”) and *millies* (“a thousand times”).

Others are demonstrative: *en, ecce* (“behold”). Others are interrogative: *cur* (“why”), *quare* (“for what reason”), *quamobrem* (“wherefore”). Others are negative: *non* (“not”), *haud* (“not”), *nunquam* (“never”), *minime* (“not at all”), when two parts are used for them, as *nullo modo* (“in no way”) and *nullatenus* (“in no respect”).

**FRANCE.** Can adverbs be synonymous or polysemous?

**SAXO.** They can. They are synonymous when many words signify one thing, as *en* and *ecce* (“behold”). This occurs in nearly all categories of meaning. They are polysemous when, for example, *ubi, quo, qua,* and *quomodo* are indefinite, interrogative, and relative. *O* also has different meanings. It is an adverb of calling. Virgil (*Aeneid* I, 528):

> O queen, for whom Jupiter is founding a new city.

It is an adverb of wonder. Juvenal (*Satires* X, 157):

> O, what a face …

It expresses indignation, as in:

> O the times! O the customs!

It also expresses wishing. Virgil:

> O, be present at last.

[Ms., *tantum*, “only.”]

In many other adverbs as well you will find several meanings in one and the same word. Conversely, one meaning may occur in different words, as, for example, in *aliquando, olim, dudum, cito, propere* [Ed., *prope*], *celeriter,* and *actutum*.

**FRANCE.** Are adverbs more suitably placed before or after?

**SAXO.** Clearly, they are more suitably placed before, like adjectives, as in: “a good man acts well”; “a brave commander fights bravely.” Nevertheless, many are found placed afterward, except monosyllables [Col. 0889A], such as *non, dum, en,* and *cur*. Demonstrative, interrogative, hortatory, similarity, vocative, and optative adverbs are also placed before: *en, ecce, cur, quare, eia, age, ceu, quasi, heus, utinam* (“behold,” “why,” “come,” “as,” “hey,” “would that”). There you have enough, France, about the adverb.

**FRANCE.** Not enough—but let us rest for an hour nonetheless.

**SAXO.** Let us rest.

## On the Participle

292 **FRANCE.** Rise, Saxo.

**SAXO.** What do you want, France?

**FRANCE.** I would like you to unfold the rules of participles for me.

**SAXO.** I will. But this part has rather little obscurity. Nevertheless, if you need anything, ask.

**FRANCE.** First, I think we should ask from what the participle received its name.

**SAXO.** It is called a participle because it possesses part of a noun and part of a verb, occupies a middle position between them, and is always derivative. No other part of speech has this property, since the other parts have primitive forms from which they are derived: from *rex* (“king”), *regalis* (“royal”); from *mei* (“of me”), *meus* (“my”); from *ferveo* (“I boil”), *fervesco* (“I begin to boil”); from *prope* (“near”), *propius* (“nearer”); from *ex* (“from”), *extra* (“outside”).

Participles, however, are always derived from verbs and cannot have comparison. If they are compared, they pass over into nouns. Thus *amans* (“loving”), coming from the verb *amo* (“I love”): if you make *amans, amantior, amantissimus* (“loving, more loving, most loving”), it is a noun, lacking tense.

**FRANCE.** But how can I recognize whether such a form is a noun or a participle?

**SAXO.** From the circumstances of its cases. A participle follows the case governed by its verb: *amo illum* (“I love him”), *amans illum* (“loving him”). A noun, however, follows the case of a verbal noun: *amator illius* (“lover of him”); thus we say *amans illius* (“loving him”). You see that the participle is joined to the accusative, while the noun is joined to the genitive. Participles also signify tense.

**FRANCE.** Do not some nouns also signify time, such as *annus* (“year”), *mensis* (“month”), *dies* (“day”), *hora* (“hour”), and many others?

**SAXO.** They do. But the difference is that those nouns signify nothing other than time itself. Participles, therefore, show that an action or experience is taking place at a particular time, not time itself. A participle also takes the cases taken by the verbs from which it is derived; it possesses the meanings of verbs and is used in place of a verb. Hence some call a participle a “casual verb,” because what the verb lacks by itself—namely, cases—it possesses in the participle.

[Col. 0889D] Therefore, in construction with oblique cases, where a verb cannot be joined, the participle takes the place of a verb, as follows:

- *Bonus [homo] loquebatur* — “the good man was speaking.”
- *Boni hominis loquentis orationem audivi* — “I heard the speech of the good man who was speaking.”
- *Bono homini loquenti respondi* — “I answered the good man who was speaking.”
- *Bonum hominem loquentem audivi* — “I heard the good man speaking.”
- *Tu bone homo loquere* — “you, good man, speak.”
- *A bono homine loquente didici* — “I learned from the good man who was speaking.”

Thus the nominative and vocative are called “straight” cases, because they can be joined directly to verbs.

**FRANCE.** What use does the participle have in the nominative and vocative, if it can be joined to oblique cases in place of a verb?

**SAXO.** It enables you to join verbs in the nominative and vocative without a conjunction. Different verbs cannot be joined without a conjunction: one must not say *lego, scribo* (“I read, I write”) or *doceo, discis* (“I teach, you learn”); rather, one says *lego et scribo* (“I read and write”) and *doceo et discis* (“I teach and you learn”).

If you put a participle in place of the first verb, it can properly be pronounced without a conjunction: *legens scribo* (“while reading, I write”), *docens discis* (“while teaching, you learn”). The participle was therefore devised so that in the nominative and vocative it could be used with another verb without a conjunction: *legens doceo* (“while reading, I teach”), in place of *lego et doceo* (“I read and teach”); and *legens fac* (“while reading, do it”), in place of *lege et fac* (“read and do it”). This construction is intransitive—that is, it shows that the person remains within the action itself.

The oblique cases of participles are useful because they are not only used without a conjunction, but can also pass over to other persons: *docentis potior* (“I prefer the one who teaches”), *docenti respondeo* (“I answer the one who teaches”), *docentem audio* (“I hear the one who teaches”), *illo docente didici* (“I learned while he was teaching”).

**FRANCE.** How many properties belong to a participle [Al., “belong to participles”]?

**SAXO.** Six: gender and case from the noun; meaning and tense from the verb; number and form from both.

**FRANCE.** How many genders does it have?

**SAXO.** Four: masculine, as *amatus* (“loved”); feminine, as *amata*; neuter, as *amatum*; and common to all genders, as *hic et haec et hoc amans* (“this male, female, or neuter person loving”).

Nature itself prevents a participle from having both the common gender of two genders and the epicene [Al., *epicenon*] category. Since the verbs from which participles arise are joined equally to all genders—*legit vir* (“the man reads”), *legit femina* (“the woman reads”), *legit mancipium* (“the slave reads”)—the participle derived from the verb is necessarily associated with the same genders.

Every participle ending in *-ans* or *-ens*, whether present or imperfect past, is of all three genders: *hic et haec et hoc laudans, docens, legens, audiens* (“this male, female, or neuter person praising, teaching, reading, hearing”). If they end in *-us*, whether past or future, they vary through the three genders: *amatus, amata, amatum* (“loved”); *amaturus, amatura, amaturum* (“about to love”).

**FRANCE.** Explain the cases of participles to me.

**SAXO.** There are six cases of participles, just as of nouns. No participles have been found defective in any case, just as no mobile nouns or nouns ending in two consonants are defective. Whatever forms are defective are fixed [the text here is uncertain: *fas [ditione] tabo*].

**FRANCE.** How are participles declined?

**SAXO.** In the manner of nouns ending in *-ens*, or of mobile nouns ending in *-us*.

**FRANCE.** How do the tenses of participles proceed?

**SAXO.** Participles have the same combined tenses as infinitive verbs: the present and the imperfect past. Likewise, they have the perfect and pluperfect past together, as in *legens scribo* (“while reading, I write”), *legens scribebam* (“while reading, I was writing”); *lectus fui* (“I was read”), *lectus fueram* (“I had been read”).

**FRANCE.** Are all tenses found in participles for every meaning of verbs?

**SAXO.** By no means. Since verbs have five meanings—active, passive, neuter, common, and deponent—participles from active and neuter verbs are found in the present and future: *amans, amaturus* (“loving, about to love”); *stans, staturus* (“standing, about to stand”).

But with the present participle and the substantive verb *sum* (“I am”), we express the perfect past: *amans fui, fuisti, fuit*, in place of *amavi, amavisti, amavit* (“I loved, you loved, he loved”); and similarly through all moods in the perfect and pluperfect past. Thus what is naturally absent from a simple word is supplied by the method of combination.

Nevertheless, past participles are found with certain neuter verbs: from *coeno* (“I dine”), *coenatus* (“having dined”); from *prandeo* (“I lunch”), *pransus* (“having lunched”); from *placeo* (“I please”), *placitus* (“pleased”); from *nubo* (“I marry”), *nupta* (“married”); from *pateo* (“I am open”), *passus* [textually difficult]. Virgil (*Aeneid* I, 484):

> The daughters of Ilium with their hair spread out,

that is, “scattered.”

A participle is also formed from *patior* (“I suffer”): *passus* (“having suffered”); from *juro* (“I swear”), *juratus* (“having sworn”); from *adsuesco* (“I grow accustomed”), *adsuetus* (“accustomed”); from *titubo* (“I stumble”), *titubatus* (“having stumbled”), and many others, such as *discessus* (“departed”), *interitus* (“perished”), *obitus* (“dead”), *occasus* (“fallen”), *potus* (“drunk”), *enectus* (“killed”) [Ed., *senectus*, “old age”].

There are also five neuter-passive verbs whose participles have three tenses: *gaudeo* (“I rejoice”), *gaudens, gavisus, gavisurus* (“rejoicing, having rejoiced, about to rejoice”); *audeo* (“I dare”), *audens, ausus, ausurus*; *soleo* (“I am accustomed”), *solens, solitus, soliturus*; *fio* (“I become”), *fiens, factus, futurus*.

The form *futurus* is used for the sake of distinction, lest, if *facturus* were said, it should be thought to come from *facio* (“I make”), which has active force and whose passive is *fio* (“I become”). *Fido* (“I trust”) likewise forms *fidens, fisus, fisurus* (“trusting, having trusted, about to trust”).

Two participles also come from the passive meaning: a past and a future, as *amatus, amandus* (“loved, to be loved”). In place of its present, authors are often found using the past for the sake of necessity.

Four participles arise from a common verb; and this is not surprising, since a common verb has both active and passive meaning. Therefore it has participles of both meanings: active, *criminans* (“accusing”) and *criminaturus* (“about to accuse”); passive, *criminatus* (“accused”) and *criminandus* (“to be accused”). *Criminatus* occurs with both meanings.

You should know, France, that all participles ending in *-dus* can also be nouns.

**FRANCE.** And how can I know, Saxo, whether they are nouns or participles?

**SAXO.** When they are nouns, they lose their tenses, as I told you earlier. Thus *docendus sum* (“I am to be taught”) is a participle; *ad docendam rhetoricam veni* (“I came for the teaching of rhetoric”) is a noun.

Three participles arise from a deponent verb: the present and imperfect past, *sequens* (“following”); the perfect and pluperfect past, *secutus* (“having followed”); and the future, *secuturus* (“about to follow”). Among the ancients, however, participles of the past tense with both active and passive meaning are found from such verbs, as *meditatus, auxiliatus, amplexatus, adminiculatus* (“having meditated, assisted, embraced, supported”); they can have either meaning.

**FRANCE.** Give me the numbers of participles.

**SAXO.** Participles have two numbers: singular, as *currens* (“running”); plural, as *currentes* (“running”). And just as you will find no participles defective in cases, so you will find none defective in number.

**FRANCE.** From where do the forms of participles come?

**SAXO.** Always from verbs: from *efficio* (“I accomplish”), *efficiens* (“accomplishing”); from *intelligo* (“I understand”), *intelligens* (“understanding”). A participle is never compounded by itself unless its verb has first been compounded. If participles are compounded independently, they pass into the force of nouns: *noceo* (“I harm”), *nocens* (“harming”); *innocens* (“innocent”) is a noun, as is *innocentior* (“more innocent”); *sapio* (“I am wise”), *sapiens* (“wise”); *insipiens* (“foolish”) [*insipientior*, “more foolish”] is a noun.

Their simple forms can be both nouns and participles; their compounds, however, are nouns only.

**FRANCE.** I remember that you said all participles are derivatives from verbs. I would like to know from which tenses or moods they are derived.

**SAXO.** Present participles are formed from the present tense of the indicative mood, and always end in *-ans* or *-ens*: from *amo, amas* (“I love, you love”), *amans* (“loving”); from *habeo, habes* (“I have, you have”), *habens* (“having”), with *n* inserted before the final letters of the second person.

In the third and fourth conjugations, the *o* is changed into *-ens* to form the participle: *lego, legens* (“I read, reading”); *audio, audiens* (“I hear, hearing”).

294 Past and future participles come from the supine ending in *-u*: *-s* is added for the past and *-rus* for the future: *amatu, amatus, amaturus* (“to love, loved, about to love”); *coenatu, coenatus, coenaturus*; *criminatu, criminatus, criminaturus*; *locutu, locutus, locuturus*. Only *mortuus* (“dead”) from *morior* (“I die”) has two *u*s.

Passive future participles come from the genitive of the present participle, with *-tis* changed to *-dus*: *amans, amantis, amandus* (“loving, of one loving, to be loved”).

**FRANCE.** If only you had wished to collect the more difficult verbs together with their perfect, supine, and participle! How necessary that would have been!

**SAXO.** It would indeed have been necessary, [Col. 0892B] but it would exceed the limits of our game.

**FRANCE.** Nevertheless, give me some difficult verbs; I can infer the rest more easily.

**SAXO.** I will. *Amo, amas, amavi, amatum, amatus* (“I love, you love, I loved, loved, having been loved”). *Necto, nectis, nexui, nexum, nexus* (“I bind, you bind, I bound, bound, having been bound”), and from it the frequentative *nexo* (“I bind repeatedly”). *Do, dedi, datum, daturus* (“I give, I gave, given, about to give”), with a short *a* everywhere. *Oro, oravi, oratum, oraturus* (“I pray, I prayed, prayed, about to pray”). *Seco, secui, sectum, secturus* (“I cut, I cut, cut, about to cut”). *Neco, necui, nectum, necturus* (“I kill, I killed, killed, about to kill”); *necatum* is also found from *neco*, but *necatus* means “killed by a sword,” whereas *nectus* means killed in any other way.

*Plico* and *plicavi* and *plicui* all occur. Hence both *plicatum* and *plicitum* are found; and likewise their compounds *explico, duplico,* and *implico* are pronounced in two ways.

For the sake of distinction, *lavi, cavi,* and *favi* change a long *a* into *au*: *lautu, lautus* (“washed”); *cautu, cautus* (“guarded”); *fautu, fautus* (“favored”), because *latum, catum,* and *fatum* have other meanings.

*Sto, stas, statum, staturum* (“I stand, you stand, stood, about to stand”): the long *a* is everywhere shortened in nouns derived from it, as *status* (“state”) and *stabilis* (“stable”), as Lucan writes (*Pharsalia* X, 240):

> … whose appointed times the blasts …

*Juvo, juvi, jutum* (“I help, I helped, helped”), with a long *u*; hence *adjutus* (“helped”). *Sterno, stravi, stratum, straturus* (“I spread, spread, spread out, about to spread”). *Edo, edi, esum, esurus* (“I eat, ate, eaten, about to eat”), from which comes *esurio* (“I am hungry”). *Eruo, eruis, erutum, eruturus* (“I uproot, uprooted, about to uproot”). *Cio, civi, citum, citurus* (“I summon, summoned, about to summon”). *Moveo, movi, motum, moturus* (“I move, moved, moved, about to move”). *Sedeo, sedi, sessum, sessurus* (“I sit, sat, sat, about to sit”), which doubles the *s* so that the two parts are not thought separate. *Foveo, fovi, fotum, foturus* (“I cherish, cherished, cherished, about to cherish”). *Facio, feci, factum, facturus* (“I make, made, made, about to make”).

You should also observe, France, that in almost all verbs which reduce the number of syllables in the perfect, the penultimate syllables are always lengthened, even if they were shortened in the present.

**FRANCE.** Why does this happen?

**SAXO.** So that they may compensate in their tenses for what is lacking in syllables: *sero, sevi, satum, saturus* (“I sow, sowed, sown, about to sow”), whence *sertus* (“woven”). *Sino, sivi, situm, siturus* (“I allow, allowed, allowed, about to allow”). *Pono, posui, positum, positurus* (“I place, placed, placed, about to place”). *Lino, livi, litum, liturus* (“I smear, smeared, smeared, about to smear”). *Eo, ivi, itum, iturus* (“I go, went, gone, about to go”). *Rideo, risi, risum, risurus* (“I laugh, laughed, laughed, about to laugh”). *Video, vidi, visum, visurus* (“I see, saw, seen, about to see”). *Ardeo, arsi, arsum, arsurus* (“I burn, burned, burned, about to burn”). *Mordeo, momordi, morsum, morsurus* (“I bite, bit, bitten, about to bite”). *Pendeo, pependi, pensum, [pensu] pensurus* (“I hang, hung, hung, about to hang”). *Tondeo, totondi, tonsum, [tonsu] tonsurus* (“I shear, sheared, shorn, about to shear”). *Spondeo, spopondi, sponsum, sponsurus* (“I promise, promised, promised, about to promise”), with the *s* lost in the second syllable.

*Candeo, studeo, frondeo* [Ed., *fundo*], and *splendeo* form supines: *canditum, studitum, fronditum, splenditum*, although supines or participles are very rarely found from neuter verbs of the second conjugation, such as *caleo* (“I am hot”), *tepeo* (“I am warm”), *horreo* (“I shudder”), *rubeo* (“I am red”), *palleo* (“I am pale”), and similar verbs.

But you do not need me to travel through every verb by a fourfold route. From the supines you will be able to understand the participles, or from the participles the supines.

**FRANCE.** Do so, nevertheless, to please me; always unfold the more obscure forms.

**SAXO.** From *pateo* (“I am open”), *patui, passum* is formed. *Meio, mixi, mictum* (“I urinate”) and *mingo, minxi, mictum* (“I urinate”), the latter losing its *n* for euphony; hence *micturus* (“about to urinate”). *Flecto* [Ms., *flexo*], *[flexis] flexi, flexus, flexurus* (“I bend, bent, bent, about to bend”). *Fluo, fluxi, [fluxum], fluxurus* (“I flow, flowed, flowed, about to flow”). *Obsoleo, obsolevi, obsoletum* (“I grow obsolete, grew obsolete, obsolete”), compounded from *obs* and *oleo*, not from *soleo*. From *careo* (“I lack”), *cassus* (“deprived”) and *cariturus* (“about to lack”) are found. *Habeo, [habui] habitum, habiturus* (“I have, had, had, about to have”). *Cado, cecidi, casum, casurus* (“I fall, fell, fallen, about to fall”). *Cedo, cessi, cessum, cessurus* (“I yield, yielded, yielded, about to yield”). *[Fodio] fodi, fossum [fossurus]* (“I dig, dug, dug, about to dig”).

[Col. 0893B] *Dedi, datum* (“I gave, given”); *credidi, creditum* (“I believed, believed”); *capio, cepi, captum* (“I take, took, taken”); *coepi, coeptum* (“I begin, began, begun”), whose present *caepio* is not in use; *sapivi, sapitum* (“I was wise, was wise”); *peperi, partum, pariturus* (“I bore, borne, about to bear”), and from it *parturio* (“I am in labor”). *Orior, ortus, orturus* [Al., *oriturus*] (“I arise, arisen, about to arise”); *morior, mortuus* (“I die, dead”), which alone is pronounced with two *u*s [*moriturus*, “about to die”].

*Quatior, quassum* (“I am shaken, shaken”), whence the frequentative *quasso, quassas* (“I shake repeatedly”). *Percutio, percussi, percussurus* (“I strike, struck, about to strike”), with two *s*s. *Uro, ussi, ussurus* (“I burn, burned, about to burn”); *farcio, farsi, farsum, farsurus* (“I stuff, stuffed, stuffed, about to stuff”); *sarcio, sarsi, sarsum, sarsurus* (“I mend, mended, mended, about to mend”); *potior, [potitus], potiturus* (“I obtain, obtained, about to obtain”); *[arguo] argui, argutum*, that is, “convicted,” *arguturus* (“about to accuse”). *Ruo, [ruis], ruitum* [Ms., *rutum*], *ruiturus* (“I rush, rushed, about to rush”); *loquor, locutum, locuturus* (“I speak, spoken, about to speak”). *Fruor, fructum* (“I enjoy, enjoyed”) is formed like *struo, structum, structurus* (“I build, built, about to build”).

*Caluo*, that is, “I deceive,” *calui, caluitum* [Ms., *calutum*], ought to be formed according to the rule; from it *calumnia* (“deceit”) is derived. *Neo, nevi, netum, neturus* [Al., *neutum, neuturus*] (“I spin, spun, spun, about to spin”).

You should also know that verbs which acquire the consonant *v* in the perfect often undergo contraction in the second and third persons: *neo, nevi, nevisti* or *nesti* (“I spin, I spun, you spun”); *amo, amavisti* or *amasti* (“I love, you loved”), and in the plural *amavistis* or *amastis*, *amaverunt* or *amarunt*.

Those which have the consonant *v* in the present cannot undergo contraction in the perfect: *lavo, lavasti* (“I wash, you washed”); no one says *lasti*, *lastis*, or *larunt*. *Ico, ici, ictum, icturus* (“I strike, struck, struck, about to strike”); the *i* is short in the present and perfect [or long: *quievi, quieturus*, “I rest, rested, about to rest”].

*[Linquo] liqui, lictu, licturus* (“I leave, left, about to leave”); from it, *reliqui, [relictum] relicturus* (“I leave behind, left behind, about to leave behind”). *Vinco, vici, victurus* (“I conquer, conquered, about to conquer”). *Cresco, crevi, cretum, creturus* (“I grow, grew, grown, about to grow”). *Scio, scivi, scitum, [Col. 0893D] sciturus* (“I know, knew, known, about to know”); from it *scisco* (“I inquire”). *Nosco, novi, notum, noturus* (“I learn, learned, known, about to know”). *Ignosco, ignoturus* (“I forgive, about to forgive”). *Pasco, pavi, pastum, pasturus* (“I feed, fed, fed, about to feed”). *Disco, discitum, disciturus* (“I learn, learned, about to learn”). *Parco, parsu, parsurus* (“I spare, spared, about to spare”). *Paciscor, pactum, pacturus* (“I agree, agreed, about to agree”). *Proficiscor, profectum, profecturus* (“I depart, departed, about to depart”). *Expergiscor*, in the perfect *experrectus* [Ed., *expergitus sum*], *experrectu, experrecturus* (“I awaken, awakened, about to awaken”). *Nanciscor, nactus sum, nactum, nacturus* (“I obtain, obtained, about to obtain”), without the *n* [in one form]. *Pangor, pactus, pacturus* (“I am fastened, fastened, about to be fastened”). *Fingor, fictus, ficturus* (“I am fashioned, fashioned, about to be fashioned”). *Tangor, tactus, tacturus* (“I am touched, touched, about to be touched”). *Jungor, junctus, juncturus* (“I am joined, joined, about to be joined”). *Fungor, functus, functurus* (“I perform, performed, about to perform”). *Plangor, planctus* (“I am beaten, beaten”). *Angor, anctus* (“I am strangled, strangled”); these form past participles.

Likewise *ulciscor, ultus* (“I avenge, avenged”); *irascor, iratus* (“I become angry, angered”); *defatiscor* [Ms., *deficiscor*], *defessus*, that is, “tired”; for from *deficio* (“I fail”) the participle *defectus* (“failed”) is formed. *Comminiscor, commentum* (“I devise, devised”); *adipiscor, adeptum* (“I obtain, obtained”). *Tundo, tutudi, tunsurus* (“I beat, beat, about to beat”). *Rado, rasi, [rasum] rasurus* (“I scrape, scraped, about to scrape”). *Credo, creditum, crediturus* (“I believe, believed, about to believe”). *Cado, casum*, with a long *a*.

In every supine and past participle, the *a* is lengthened in the penultimate syllable, except in *datum, statum,* and *satum*. *Findo, fidi, fissum, fissurus* (“I split, split, split, about to split”). From *comedo* (“I eat up”), both *comesum* and *comestum* are found. *Ostendo, ostentum* or *ostensum, ostensurus* (“I show, showed, shown, about to show”). *Mergo, mersi, mersum, mersurus* (“I plunge, plunged, plunged, about to plunge”). *Tergo, tersi, tersum, tersurus* (“I wipe, wiped, wiped, about to wipe”). *Pungo, pupugi* or *punxi, punctum* (“I prick, pricked, pricked”). *Ago, egi, actum, acturus* (“I do, did, done, about to do”). *Pango, pepigi, pactum* (“I fasten, fastened, fastened”); from it *impingo, [impegi]* (“I impress”). *Fingo, finxi, fictum* (“I shape, shaped, shaped”). *Stinguo, stinxi, stinctum* (“I extinguish, extinguished, extinguished”); from it *exstinguo* (“I extinguish”). *Ango, [anxi] anctum, anxurus* (“I distress, distressed, about to distress”). *Cogo, coegi, coactum* (“I compel, compelled, compelled”). *Veho, vexi, vectum* (“I carry, carried, carried”).

*Psallo, psalli* (“I sing to the lyre, to sing to the lyre”); I have found neither its supine nor its participle. *Vello, vulsi, vulsum* (“I tear, tore, torn”). *Pello, pepuli, pulsum* (“I drive, drove, driven”). *Alo, alui, alitus* or *altus* (“I nourish, nourished”). *Tollo, sustuli, sublatum, sublaturus* (“I lift, lifted, lifted, about to lift”). *Como, compsi, comptum, compturus* (“I adorn, adorned, about to adorn”). *Demo, dempsi, demptum* [*dempturus*] (“I remove, removed, about to remove”).

You should know that in forms of this kind the letter *p* must everywhere be placed between *m* and *-tum*.

*Vomo, vomui, vomitum* (“I vomit, vomited, vomited”). *Premo, pressi, pressum, pressurus* (“I press, pressed, pressed, about to press”). *Cano, cecini* (“I sing, sang”); from it *occino, occinui, occentum* (“I sing against, sang against, sung against”). *Succino, succentum* (“I sing in accompaniment, sung in accompaniment”). *Temno, tempsi, temptum* [Al., *contempno, contempsi, contemptum*] (“I despise, despised, despised”). *Creo, crevi, cretum* (“I create, created, created”); from it and the verb *do* (“I give”) *credo* (“I believe”) is compounded, as though meaning *certum do* (“I give certainty”).

*Lino, [lini et] livi* (“I smear, smeared”), or *linio, litum, liturus* (“I smear, smeared, about to smear”). You should know that both *litum* and *itum*, and their compounds *obitus* (“death”), *praeteritus* (“past”), and *situm* (“placed”), as well as *queo, quitum* (“I can, been able”), *cio, citum* (“I summon, summoned”), and *nequeo, nequitus* (“I cannot, unable”), shorten their penultimate syllables. This will not be found in other supines and participles derived from perfects ending in *-vi*: *amavi, amatus* (“I loved, loved”); *movi, motus* (“I moved, moved”); *cupivi, cupitum* (“I desired, desired”); *nevi, netum* (“I spun, spun”).

*Rumpo, rupi, ruptum* (“I break, broke, broken”). *Verro, [versi vel] verri, versum, versurus* (“I sweep, swept, swept, about to sweep”). *Quaero, quaesivi, quaesitum* (“I seek, sought, sought”). *Reor, ratus* (“I think, thought”). *Exsero, exserui, exsertum, exserturus* [Ms., *exero, exerui, exertum*, etc.] (“I thrust out, thrust out, thrust out, about to thrust out”). *Meto, messui, messum, messurus* (“I reap, reaped, reaped, about to reap”). *Mitto, misi, missum, missurus* (“I send, sent, sent, about to send”), with two *s*s, although *misi* should be written with one. *Peto, petivi, petitum* (“I seek, sought, sought”), with a long penultimate. *Texo, texui, textum* (“I weave, wove, woven”). *Nexo, nexui, nexum* (“I bind, bound, bound”). *Farcio, farsi, fartum* (“I stuff, stuffed, stuffed”), whence *fartores* (“stuffers”), just as from *sarcio, sarsi, sartum* come *sartores* (“menders”). *Sentio, sensi, sensum* (“I feel, felt, felt”). *Raucio, rausi, rausum* (“I make hoarse, made hoarse”). *Sepio, sepsi, septum* (“I fence in, fenced in, fenced in”). *Venio, veni, ventum, venturus* (“I come, came, come, about to come”). *Pario, peperi, partum, parturus* (“I bear, bore, borne, about to bear”). *Scio, scivi, scitum*, with the penultimate everywhere long, as in *auditus, munitus, arcessitus* (“heard, fortified, summoned”), except in the forms mentioned above [Ms., “previously noted”].

*Sepelio, sepelivi, sepultus, sepulturus* (“I bury, buried, buried, about to bury”). *Salio, salui* [Ms., *salivi*], *saltum* (“I leap, leaped, leaped”). *Salio* from *sal* (“salt”), *salivi, salsum, salsurus* (“I salt, salted, about to salt”); its past participle is also *salitus* and *salsus* [or *sallus*]. *Ambio, ambivi, ambitum* (“I go around, went around, gone around”); from it comes the noun *ambitus* (“circuit”), with a shortened penultimate syllable.

296 **FRANCE.** Why is that?

**SAXO.** Because *ambio* is compounded from that verb. Verbal nouns derived from the second conjugation have a short penultimate syllable: *habitus, monitus* (“state or condition,” “warning”).

You should also remember that impersonal verbs are defective in supines and participles, except in rare cases: from *poenitet* (“it repents”), *poenitens* (“repenting”), whence *poenitentia* (“repentance”); from *licet* (“it is permitted”), *licentia* (“permission”) and *licitus* (“permitted”); and from *libet* (“it pleases”), *libens* (“willing”).

## On the Conjunction

[Col. 0895A]

**FRANCE.** The order of the parts of speech now requires you to speak about the conjunction.

**SAXO.** A conjunction is an indeclinable part of speech, connective and meaningful [Ms., *consignificativa*, “co-signifying”], showing the force and arrangement of other parts of speech.

**FRANCE.** How does it show force and arrangement?

**SAXO.** It shows force when it signifies several things together, as in: “Aeneas was both pious and brave.” It shows arrangement when it indicates the consequence of things, as in: *si ambulat, movetur* (“if he walks, he moves”); for movement follows walking.

**FRANCE.** How many properties belong to a conjunction?

**SAXO.** Three: form, kind, and order. Its simple form is seen in *at, et,* and *sed* (“but,” “and,” “but”). Its compound form is seen in *atque, etenim,* and *sedenim* (“and,” “for indeed,” “but indeed”). These are recognized as compound from their accent.

**FRANCE.** Explain the kinds as well.

**SAXO.** According to Donatus, who calls them “powers,” there are five kinds: copulative, expletive, causal, disjunctive, and rational. According to Priscian, there are more. But these five are the principal kinds and contain the others within themselves.

**FRANCE.** Unfold examples of each kind.

**SAXO.** Copulative conjunctions join both words and meanings: *et, -que, at, atque, ac, ast* (“and,” “and,” “but,” “and,” “and,” “but”).

Disjunctive conjunctions join words but separate their meanings, signifying that one of two things is the case: *vel, ve, ne, nec, neque,* and *aut* (“or,” “or,” “whether,” “nor,” “or”).

Expletive conjunctions complete either a favorable or unfavorable meaning: *quidem, equidem, saltem* [Al., *saltim*], *videlicet, quanquam, quamvis, quoque, autem, porro, scilicet,* and *tamen* (“indeed,” “at least,” “namely,” “although,” “however,” “also,” “moreover,” “of course,” “nevertheless”).

Causal conjunctions signify an antecedent cause: *doctus sum, nam legi* (“I am learned, for I have read”); *si sol est, jam lucet* (“if the sun is out, it is already light”). The sun is the cause of the light. These include: *si* (“if”), *etsi* (“although”), *etiamsi* (“even if”), *siquidem* (“since indeed”), *quando* (“since”), *quandoquidem* (“since indeed”), *quinetiam* (“and indeed”), *quatenus* (“insofar as”), *sin* (“but if”), *seu* (“or whether”), *sive* (“or if”) [*neve*, “and not”], *namque* (“for indeed”), *ni* (“if not”), *nisi* (“unless”) [*nisi si*, “unless if”], *enim* (“for”), *etenim* (“for indeed”), *ne* (“lest”), *sedenim* (“but indeed”), *interea* (“meanwhile”), *quomobrem* (“wherefore”), *praesertim* (“especially”), *item* (“likewise”), *itemque* (“and likewise”), *ceterum* (“moreover”), *alioquin* (“otherwise”), and *praeterea* (“besides”).

Rational conjunctions give the reason for a matter: *ita* (“thus”), *itaque* (“and so”), *quoniam* (“since”), *enim* (“for”), *etenim* (“for indeed”), *enimvero* (“indeed”), *quia* (“because”), *quare* (“wherefore”), *quapropter* (“for which reason”), *quoniam* (“since”), *quidem* (“indeed”), *quippe* (“indeed”), *ergo* (“therefore”), *ideo* (“therefore”) [*igitur*, “therefore”], *scilicet* (“namely”), and *propterea* (“for that reason”) [*videlicet*, “namely”].

**FRANCE.** What is the order of conjunctions?

**SAXO.** [Col. 0895D] Some always come first: *at, ast, aut, ac, vel, nec, neque, si, quia, quatenus, sin, seu, sive, ni* [*nam*]. Others come after: *quidem, quoque,* and *autem*. Almost all the others can indifferently be placed either before or after, such as *ergo* and *igitur* (“therefore”).

Conjunctions are also often found passing into the force of other conjunctions. Thus the disjunctive conjunction *vel* is used in a copulative sense, as in Terence:

> … or even the king,

meaning “also the king.”

Other parts of speech are likewise used as conjunctions: nouns, as *qua causa? qua gratia? quam ob rem?* (“for what reason? for what purpose? why?”); verbs, as *quamvis* (“although”) and *licet* (“although”), used for *quanquam*. Virgil (*Aeneid* XI, 348):

> I shall indeed speak, although he threatens me with arms and death.

[Col. 0896A] There are also doubtful conjunctions: *ne, nec,* and *anne* (“whether,” “or whether”). Virgil (*Aeneid* III, 39; XI, 126):

> Shall I speak, or shall I be silent …?

> Shall I first admire the labors of justice, or those of war?

These are also interrogative, as in the same author (*Aeneid* X, 668):

> Did you deem me worthy of so great a crime?

They also become elective when something is chosen from different alternatives: *dives esse volo, quam pauper* (“I wish to be rich rather than poor”).

They also become adjunctive when they are joined to subjunctive verbs: *si, cum, ut, dum, quatenus* (“if,” “when,” “so that,” “while,” “insofar as”). For example, *si venias, facio* (“if you come, I will do it”):

> When I make offerings of a heifer for the crops, come yourself.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] Virgil, *Eclogue* III, 77.]

*Ut prosit tibi, facio* (“I do it so that it may benefit you”):

Having also suffered much in war while he founded the city [Note: [Col. 0896D] Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 9.]; [Col. 0896B] Insofar as I do this willingly. These same conjunctions can also be causal.

**FR.** But how shall I know to which category they belong?

**SAXO.** The adjunctive conjunctions are uttered with doubt; the causal ones with affirmation—for example: “You will be learned, if you read.” There are also conjunctions that signify diminution, as in (*Aeneid* IV, 327):

> At least, if some offspring born of you had been granted me.

They also become continuative, as in: “If he walks, he moves”; for movement continues the walking. These and other categories are found in Priscian, though they can nevertheless fall under the five categories mentioned above. But for now, let this suffice concerning conjunctions.

## ON THE PREPOSITION

**[Col. 0896C] FR.** What is a preposition?

**SAXO.** An indeclinable part of speech.

**FR.** What function does it have?

**SAXO.** That it be placed before other parts of speech, either by juxtaposition or by composition.

**FR.** How by juxtaposition?

**SAXO.** When it is placed outside the word; and this occurs with a noun or pronoun, with the accusative or ablative case: *ad hominem*, “to the man”; *ab homine*, “from the man”; *ad illum*, “to him”; *ab illo*, “from him.”

**FR.** How by composition?

**SAXO.** When it is joined with other parts [of speech] into a single word, as with a noun [Ms., *nomini*], through all the cases: *indoctus, indocti, indocto, indoctum, indocte, ab indocto*, “unlearned,” in its various forms. It is not compounded with a pronoun. It is compounded with a verb, as in *induco*, “I lead in,” and *expleo*, “I fill up.” With a participle it is joined through the derivation or consequence of compounded verbs [Col. 0896D], as in *inducens*, “leading in,” and *explens*, “filling up.” It is also joined to an adverb by composition, as in *perinde*, “just so”; *abhinc*, “from this point”; *deinceps*, “thereafter.” Indeed, it is compounded with itself, as in *imperitus* [Ms., *imperterritus*], “unskilled” [or “undaunted”]. It is also customarily taken in place of a causal conjunction, as in: *Per desidiam malitiae nascuntur*, “Evils arise through idleness,” that is, “because of idleness.” Likewise *propter* and *ob* can be used.

**FR.** Are prepositions ever placed after the word?

**SAXO.** Yes, but rarely. This happens for the sake of euphony, that is, good sound, as with pronouns: *mecum, tecum, secum, nobiscum, vobiscum*, “with me, with you, with him or her, with us, with you.” But poetic authority also allows you to find them placed afterward in verse [Col. 0897A], as in:

> *Maria omnia circum*,

“all around the seas.” Here the final syllable is given an acute accent, so that it will not be thought to be a noun.

**FR.** Do prepositions have accents in themselves?

**SAXO.** They have an acute accent at the end, both among the Greeks and among the Latins; nevertheless, this always turns into the grave accent, because a preposition everywhere attaches itself to the following word, whether by juxtaposition or composition, and is pronounced almost as one part with it. Prepositions are also found in the middle of a phrase, as in *qua de re*, “about which matter”; *quam ob rem*, “for what reason”; *qua in parte*, “in which part.”

**FR.** Are all prepositions compounded?

**SAXO.** Some are never compounded, such as *apud, erga, citra, circa, extra, infra, juxta, pene* [Al., *pone*], *prope, secundum, ultra, supra, circiter*. Some are never separated, such as *con, di, dis* [Col. 0897B], *re, se, an* [Ms., *am*]. Almost all the others are both compounded and separated. There are also some that suffer collision with a following vowel in composition, as in *coago, coarguo, coarto, coaequo*. Others take the consonant *d* before a following vowel, as in *emo, redimo*; *ago, redigo*; *prodes, prodest*. Some undergo syncope, as *supra* from *supera*, *extra* from *extera*, and *infra* from *infera*. Prepositions also corrupt other parts of speech in compositions in various ways, and are themselves corrupted; this occurs so frequently that examples are hardly needed.

**FR.** Can prepositions pass into other parts of speech?

**SAXO.** They can.

**FR.** Give examples.

**SAXO.** *Post* is a preposition. Virgil (*Georgics* III, 213):

> *Post montem oppositum*,

“behind the opposing mountain.” It passes into an adverb. The same author (*Aeneid* I, 140):

> *Post mihi non simili poena commissa luetis*,

“Afterward you shall pay me for the offense committed, with a punishment not the same.”

*Ante* is a preposition. Virgil (*Georgics* I, 125):

> *Ante Jovem nulli subigebant arva coloni*,

“Before Jupiter, no farmers tilled the fields.”

It passes into an adverb:

> *Ante, et Trinacria tentandus remus in unda*,

“Beforehand, and the oar must be tried upon the Trinacrian wave.”

Thus *supra, contra,* and *prope* also pass into adverbs.

**FR.** Can other parts of speech pass into prepositions?

**SAXO.** They can. For adverbs often pass into prepositions, as in *pridie Kalendas*, “the day before the Kalends.” Here *pridie* is a preposition. When certain nouns are deprived of their endings, they are also used in place of adverbs, as in *domo venio*, “I come from home,” instead of *a domo*. Likewise: *domum eo*, “I go home,” instead of *ad domum*.

**FR.** With which cases are separated prepositions joined?

**SAXO.** With the accusative and ablative.

### 298

**FR.** Which prepositions take the accusative?

**SAXO.** These monosyllables: *ad, ob, per, post, cis, trans*. The disyllables are: *apud, ante, citra, circa, erga, extra, inter, intra, juxta, prope, pone, praeter, propter, ultra, usque, penes*. The trisyllables are: *circiter, adversum, secundum*.

**FR.** Do they each have definite meanings?

**SAXO.** Not definite ones, but various meanings. It would take too long to explain their meanings.

**FR.** Explain them nevertheless, and gird yourself to do so as briefly as you can [Col. 0898A] [Al., *succingere*].

**SAXO.** I shall explain them.

*Ad* means “near” in composition or juxtaposition, as in *ad currum*, “near the chariot”; *ad Trojam*, “near Troy.” It also means “against”: *ad illum mihi pugna est*, “my fight is against him.” It is also taken to mean “up to”: *ad bellum Persicum*, “up to the Persian war.”

*Ob* means “for,” “against,” and “around.” Thus: *haudquaquam ob meritum*, “by no means according to merit,” that is, “for merit.” *Ob unius*, “against one”; *obambulo*, “I walk around”; *circumambulo*, “I walk around.”

*Per* is local, as in *per medium forum*, “through the middle of the forum.” It is temporal, as in *per medium diem*, “through the middle of the day.” It is also used in oaths:

> *Per te, per qui te talem genuere parentes* [Note: [Col. 0897D] Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 597.],

“By you, and by the parents who begot you such as you are.”

It also has the force of the adverb “very” [Ms., “contains”]. Terence: *perscitus puer*, “a very clever boy.” In composition it also signifies denial, as in *perfidus*, “faithless.”

*Post* is both compounded and separated, and signifies place. Virgil (*Georgics* III, 213): *post montem oppositum*, “behind the opposing mountain.” It also signifies time, as in *post multum tempus*, “after a long time.”

*Cis* has a local meaning, as in *cis Alpinam Galliam*, “on this side of Alpine Gaul.” It is also taken to mean “beyond,” as in *cis definitum tempus*, “beyond the appointed time.” From it comes *citra*.

*Cis* has a local meaning, as in *cis Alpinam Galliam*, “on this side of Alpine Gaul.” It is also taken to mean “beyond,” as in *cis definitum tempus*, “beyond the appointed time.” From it comes *citra*.

*Trans* is both compounded and separated, as in *transfero*, “I carry across,” and *trans Padum*, “across the Po.” In composition it often loses *n* and *s*, as in *traduco, trado, trano*. It is also used for “over,” as in *transgressus*, “having gone over,” that is, “having surpassed.”

*Apud* signifies place, as in *apud Numantiam*, “at Numantia.”

*Ante* signifies place and time, as in *ante januam*, “before the door,” and *ante annum*, “a year before.” From it are derived *antiquus* and *antiquarius*.

*Citra* has almost the same meaning as *cis*, except that *cis* is more often placed before proper names, and *citra* before common nouns: *cis Rhenum*, “on this side of the Rhine”; *cis Alpes*, “on this side of the Alps”; *citra forum*, “on this side of the forum.” From *cis* comes *citra*; from *citra*, *citer, citerior, citissimus*.

*Circa*, referring to place and time, is used for “near,” as in *circa templum*, “near the temple,” and *circa viginti annos*, “around twenty years.”

*Circum* is compounded and juxtaposed, as in *circumfero*, “I carry around,” and *circum mare*, “around the sea.”

*Circiter* pertains only to time, as in *circiter Kalendas Januarias*, “around the Kalends of January.”

*Erga* is not compounded and signifies disposition or feeling, as in *bonus est erga propinquos*, “he is good toward his relatives.”

*Contra* is both separated and compounded: *contra adulterium*, “against adultery,” and *contradico*, “I contradict.”

*Extra* is juxtaposed, as in *extra me*, “outside me.”

*Inter* governs both usages, as in *inter amicos*, “among friends”; *intervallum*, “interval”; *interpres*, “interpreter”—whose simple form is not in use. From *in* come *inter* and *intra*; from *sub*, *subter*; from *pro*, *propter*; from *cis*, *citra*; from *ex*, *extra*; from *prae*, *praeter*.

*Juxta* is used for *prope*, “near,” as in *juxta te*, “near you.”

*Secundum* has two meanings: proximity and imitation. *Secundum eum sedeo*, “I sit beside him”; *secundum mores ejus vivo*, “I live according to his customs.”

Let what has been said about the prepositions governing the accusative case—the more difficult ones—be sufficient for you.

**FR.** It is sufficient. But now turn yourself entirely to the ablative.

**SAXO.** The monosyllabic prepositions of the ablative are: *a, ab, abs, e, ex, de, pro, prae, cum*.

**FR.** Why did you not add *clam*?

**SAXO.** Because it is more properly an adverb, signifying manner, and it is diminished contrary to the nature of prepositions: *clam, clanculum*. It can also be uttered without a case, as in: “He does good openly, evil secretly.”

**[Col. 0899A FR.]** Continue with the others.

**SAXO.** The disyllables are: *coram, palam, sine, absque, tenus*.

**FR.** Explain the force of each.

**SAXO.** *A, ab, abs, e,* and *ex* have almost the same force of meaning. They are found alike in local, temporal, and ordinal uses: *est a domo*, “he is from home”; *a die*, “from the day”; *a te*, “from you”; and likewise the others. But *a* and *e* are more often placed before consonants, as in *a templo*, “from the temple,” and *e culmine*, “from the summit.” The others are joined to both vowels and consonants, by juxtaposition and composition, as in *abito, ab illo, abduco, ab hora*. Often *b* changes into another letter for the sake of euphony: into *r*, as in *arripio*; into *u*, as in *aufero*; into *s*, as in *asporto*.

*Ex* is also found used for *extra*, “outside,” as in *excludo*, for *extraccludo*: *exsul*, that is, “outside the soil.” Sometimes it means “very,” as an adverb: *excelsus*, “very high.” Sometimes it is privative, intensive, or completive, as in *exstirpo*, “I uproot”; *extendo*, “I stretch out”; *expleo*, “I fill up.”

In composition, *e* is privative or intensive, and is taken for “outside,” as in *enodes trunci*, “the knots removed from trunks”; *enarro*, “I explain”; *educo*, “I lead out.” It is derived from *abs*, *absque*.

For when *que* does not have the force or meaning of a conjunction, it is a syllable, not a part of speech, as in *ubique, undique, denique, itaque, utique, uterque, plerumque*; and therefore they do not change their accent. In *ce* and *met* attached to pronouns, as well as in *te*, the added syllable is not a conjunction.

*De* is memorial, intensive, and privative: *de homine*, “concerning a man”; *detraho*, “I draw away”; *desum*, “I am absent.”

*Pro* in juxtaposition and composition is local and temporal: *pro templo*, “in front of the temple”; *provideo*, “I foresee.” It is also used in place of *e*, “from,” and of *super*, “above,” or *ante*, “before,” or *ad*, “to,” or *in*, “in.” *Prominet* means “he projects,” for *eminet*, or “he projects above,” for *supereminet*.

*Pro curia signa sociis dare*, “to give signals to the allies in front of the senate-house,” that is, “before the senate-house.” Virgil (*Aeneid* V, 500):

> *Tum validis flexos incurvant viribus arcus*  
> *Pro se quisque viri*,

“Then the men bend their curved bows with all their strength, each according to his own strength.” *Pro testimonio*, “as testimony,” that is, “for a testimony.” It is also used as an interjection, as in *proh dolor*, “alas, what grief!” and it is circumflexed.

*Prae* is found in juxtaposition or composition and signifies “to,” “because of,” “above,” “very,” or “before.” Terence: *contempsi illum hic prae me*, “I despised him here in comparison with myself,” that is, “relative to myself.” Likewise: *fit misera prae amore*, “she becomes wretched because of love.” *Praesideo* means “I preside,” that is, “I stand above.” *Praevalidus* means “very strong.” *Praedico* means “I say beforehand.”

*Cum* is a copulative preposition, as in *cum ducibus vado*, “I go with the leaders.” It is never compounded, because *con* is placed in its position in composition, as in *concurro*, “I run together,” and *contraho*, “I draw together.” It should be understood that *con* and *in* change *n* into *m* when *b*, *m*, or *p* follows: *comburo, imbuo, comminus, immunis, compello, impello*. They change *n* into the following consonants when *l* or *r* follows: *collido, illido, corripio, irruo*.

For the sake of euphony, *cum* is also placed after certain pronouns: *mecum, tecum, secum, nobiscum, vobiscum*; in these the antepenultimate syllable is raised. When placed after other pronouns, it is given an acute accent: *quocum, quacum, quicum, quibuscum*.

*Coram* pertains to persons: *coram me, te, se*, “before me, you, him.” *Palam* is used with everything: *palam omnibus*, “openly before all.”

*Sine* [Col. 0900A] and *absque* are negative: *sine homine*, “without a man,” and *absque homine*, “without a man.” When *sine* precedes its noun, it is given the grave accent, as in *sine timore*, “without fear.” When it follows, it is given the acute accent. Virgil (*Aeneid* X, 31):

> *Si sine pace tua*,

“If without your peace.”

*Tenus* is placed after the word, as in *hactenus*, “thus far”; it is also joined with the genitive:

> *... Crurum tenus a mento palearia pendent* [Note: [Col. 0899D] Virgil, *Georgics* III, 53.],

“... the wattles hang from the chin down to the legs.”

There you have the prepositions.

**FR.** I have them, more or less; but I do not have the four prepositions common to both cases.

**SAXO.** What do you ask about them, beyond what Donatus said: that *in* and *sub* take the accusative when they signify going to a place, but the ablative when they signify being in a place? Thus: *in urbem vado*, “I go into the city”; *in urbe sum*, “I am in the city.” *Sub culmen eo*, “I go beneath the roof”; *sub culmine sum*, “I am beneath the roof.”

**FR.** That is satisfactory, but I ask for more.

**SAXO.** Why do you ask me, if Donatus is not sufficient for you?

**FR.** I would not have asked so much of you if Donatus had been sufficient for me [Ms., *sufficeret*].

**SAXO.** For *in*, when it means “against” or “to,” and *sub*, when it means “before” or “through,” are joined with the accusative. Thus *in hostem*, “against the enemy.” Also:

> *In puppim rediere rates*,

“the ships returned to the stern,” where it means “to the stern.”

> *Sub lucem exornant calathis* [Al., *exportans*] [Note: [Col. 0899D] The same source, 402.],

“they adorn [it] with baskets before dawn,” where it means “before dawn.”

And:

> *... Sub noctem cura recursat* [Note: [Col. 0899D] Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 666.],

“... toward night the care returns,” where it means “through the night.”

In composition, *in* is privative, as in *injustus*, “unjust,” and *improbus*, “wicked”; sometimes it is intensive, as in *imprimo*, “I press upon,” and *incuso*, “I accuse.”

*Sub* is also local, as in *subeo*, “I go beneath,” and *subpono*, “I place beneath.” It is also diminutive, as in *subrideo*, “I smile slightly,” and *subtristis*, “somewhat sad.” It changes its *b* into the following consonant when *c, f, g, m,* or *p* follows: *succumbo, suffero, suggero, submitto* [Perhaps *summitto*], *suppono*.

*Super*, when used for *supra*, governs the accusative:

> *Saeva sedens super arma* [Note: [Col. 0900D] Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 295.],

“sitting fiercely above the weapons,” that is, “above.”

When it means “concerning” or “in,” it governs the ablative:

> *Multa super Priamo rogitans* [Note: [Col. 0900D] The same source, 750.],

“asking many things concerning Priam.”

Likewise:

> *Fronde super viridi* [Note: [Col. 0900D] Virgil, *Eclogue* I, 81.],

“upon green foliage,” that is, “in the green.”

*Subter* governs the accusative, as in *subter terram*, “beneath the earth.” It also governs the ablative: *subter densa testudine*, “beneath the dense tortoise-formation.”

**FR.** Why are certain prepositions called “speech-prepositions”?

**SAXO.** Because they are always compounded in *loquelae*, that is, in words; and there are six: *di, dis, re, se, an* [Ms., *am*], and *con*. Thus: *diduco, distraho, recurro, recubo, amplector, congero* [Ms., *congredior*].

*Di* and *dis* are separative and have the same meaning as *ab* and *abs*: *divido*, “I divide”; *distraho*, “I draw apart.” *Dis* is compounded when *c, f, p, s, t,* or *i* functioning as a consonant follows: *discurro, differo, diffundo*, with *s* changed into *f* for euphony; *disputo, dissero, distraho, disjungo*. Before the other consonants, *di* is placed: *diduco, digero, diluo, dimitto, diruo*; and everywhere *di* is long, except in *dirimo* and *disertus*.

*Re* seems to have been formed from *retro* by apocope, as the meaning itself proves. What is *respicio* but *retro spicio*, “I look back”? What is *revertor* but *retro vertor*, “I turn back”?

*Se* is separative, as in *separo*, “I separate,” and *sejungo*, “I detach.” It is also privative, as in *secus*, “otherwise.” From *se* comes *seorsum*, “apart,” just as from *de* comes *deorsum*, and from *super* comes the adverb *sursum*, “upward.”

*Am* signifies “around” or “about,” as in *amplector*, “I embrace”; *amputo*, “I cut around”; *ambio*, “I go around.” In it, too, the consonant *b* is added because of *m*.

*Con* likewise signifies “together,” as in [*coneo*], and is used in place of the preposition *cum*, as in *concurro*, “I run together,” and *conjungo*, “I join together.”

There you have as much concerning the preposition as the brevity of our discussion allowed.

**FR.** I have what satisfies me. But let us complete the short stretch of road that remains [Al., *parum*; Ms., *pergamus*].

**SAXO.** Let us continue. And, following your custom, proceed by asking questions; I shall follow by answering.

## ON THE INTERJECTION

**FR.** What is an interjection?

**SAXO.** [It is a part of speech ...] Alas! Why do you ask me about an interjection? [Col. 0902A] How many such things did you hear me utter in an unformed voice while I lay at my teacher’s feet?

**FR.** I heard and feared them, and understood the movement of your spirit in the voice’s exclamation. Nevertheless, I think that interjections have different meanings, just as the movements of the spirit are different.

**SAXO.** They do, as you say. Some express joy, such as *evax*. Others laughter: *ha, ha, he*. Others rejection, such as *phy, ehoê*. Others encouragement, such as *eia*. Others mockery, such as *euge*. Others grief, such as *vae, heu, ei*. For example: *Hei mihi, qualis erat!*, “Alas for me, what sort of person he was!” Others express cursing, such as *ah!* Virgil (*Eclogue* I, 15):

> *... Ah silice in nuda connixa reliquit*,

“... ah, she left her leaning upon the bare flint.”

Others express fear, such as *at at*. Terence (*Eunuch* IV, 8, 18):

> *At at mihi homo formidolosus es*,

“Ah! Ah! You are a frightening man to me.”

Others express wonder, such as *papae* [Ms., *pape*]. Terence [Col. 0902B] (*Eunuch* II, 2, 48):

> *Papae! haec super ipsam Thaidem?*

“Good heavens! This, concerning Thais herself?”

**FR.** What do you say about their accents?

**SAXO.** What else but that they are uncertain, and are uttered in an unformed voice—longer or shorter, sharper or heavier—according to the quality of the emotion [Note: [Col. 0901B] Canisius and Quercetanus thought that a few remaining passages were missing from their manuscript and ought to be restored from other manuscripts. Yet both the Frisingensis and Saint-Emmeram manuscripts end in exactly the same way and with the same words as the codex I used [Col. 0902B].]

## [Col. 0901] SECOND OPUSCULUM: ON ORTHOGRAPHY

### 301. PRELIMINARY NOTICE

**[Col. 0901C]**

The author of his *Life* explicitly attests that the blessed Alcuin wrote *On Orthography*. Likewise Trithemius, in Book XI of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26, and the Englishman John Bale, in *British Writers*, century XI, list among Alcuin’s works one book *On Orthography*. Yet this work remained unknown, until the present time, even to the most diligent investigators of ancient libraries; no one knew or reported what its form, method, or condition was, so much so that the celebrated Cave did not hesitate to list it among the lost works.

When, while examining the very old manuscript codex of the library of the illustrious metropolitan chapter of Salzburg, marked with the number 71 and written around the beginning of the ninth century, we came upon an orthographical opusculum included among the genuine letters of Alcuin copied there, we began to suppose that this was the very opusculum of the blessed Alcuin that had hitherto been missing. Nor, as we trust, did this opinion deceive us [Col. 0901D]; for an opusculum written in an equally ancient hand, under the name of Master Albinus, was discovered by our friends and fellow members of San-Maur in the Royal Library of Paris, in a codex marked with the number 4841. There is plainly no cause or reason why it should not be trusted.

Indeed, since it is certain from the testimony of the nearly contemporary author of the *Life* that Alcuin wrote *On Orthography*, and since in the said royal manuscript, almost of the same age, there exists an opusculum *On Orthography* inscribed to Master Albinus, or Alcuin, who could hesitate even slightly before attributing it to this author as its true parent? Moreover, nothing is found in it that conflicts with Alcuin’s style or age; indeed, many statements are inserted here that Alcuin also affirmed elsewhere.

Thus, in his *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*, verse 147 (Volume I, column 615), he says: “*Immaturitas* is the nighttime, which is not mature—that is, suitable—for doing something while keeping watch; this is also commonly called an unsuitable hour.” These words are likewise found below under the letter I. Similarly, in his *Exposition of the Gradual Psalms*, verse 5 (column 620): “An *incola*, he says, is one who cultivates another’s land”; and below, under the same letter I, he explains the word in the same way: “An *indigena*, he says, is one born there; an *incola* is one who comes from elsewhere.”

Persuaded, therefore, by these reasons, we now publish this work *On Orthography* as a genuine offspring of Alcuin, from two manuscript codices: one royal Parisian codex, which is mutilated at the end, as we note below under the letter R; and the other Salzburg codex, with occasionally differing readings added.

Since the Venerable Bede likewise wrote a book *On Orthography*, in Volume I of his works, Basel edition [Patrologia, volume XC] [Col. 0902D], and since Alcuin borrowed some things from it, we shall not omit those passages belonging to the Venerable Bede, but shall distinguish them with these brackets: [].
