I believe that the book *On Orthography* preserved in England, at Cambridge, in Corpus Christi College, reported by Thomas Tanner in *Bibliotheca Britannico-Hibernica*, page 21, is none other than the one we publish here, since it has the same beginning as ours, namely: “*Aeternus, aetas* are written with the diphthong *ae*,” and so forth. But we have had no opportunity to see it.

## LETTER A

> **Let whoever wishes to utter ancient speech read me;  
> whoever does not follow me wishes to speak without rule.**  
> [Note: [Col. 0901D] Royal Ms.:  
> “... Whoever desires to know speech,  
> despising me, soon speaks without the rule of the Fathers.”]

*Aeternus, aetas, aequitas, aevum,* and *aequus*—“eternal,” “age,” “equity,” “age/eternity,” and “equal,” that is, “just”—are written with the *ae* diphthong; *aequus* has two *u*’s [Col. 0903A]. *Equus*, when it signifies an animal, must be written with a simple *e*.

[*Aula* in Latin is a royal house and is written with *a*. *Aule*, with a simple *e*, means in Greek an atrium. Therefore, in the psalm where we read, “Worship the Lord in his holy *aula*” (Psalm XXVIII, 2), *aula* should not be understood as “palace,” but in the Greek sense as “atrium.”]

*Aulea*, with *e*, means curtains or tents. Hence also in Isaiah, according to the Septuagint interpreters: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and fasten your *auleae*,” that is, your curtains.

*Actuarii*, with *u*, are those occupied with various activities. *Actarii* are called writers of records [Royal Ms., “*actuarius* ... is called”].

### 302

[*Ante*, the preposition, has many meanings. It signifies time when it is said: “Before the feast of Passover” (John XIII, 1). It signifies presence, as in: “Before the eyes of the nations he revealed his righteousness” (Psalm XCVII, 2), that is, “in the presence of the nations.” It signifies rank or precedence, as in: “He placed Ephraim before Manasseh” (Genesis XLVIII, 20). And: “He who comes after me was made before me” (John XV, 27), that is, “was preferred to me.”]

*Arguo, argui,* and *argutum*, “convicted,” produce *arguturus*. *Amo, amavi, amasti* form their usual derivatives. Often those verbs that take the consonant *v* in the perfect tense undergo syncope in the second and third persons, as *neo, nevi, nevisti* or *nesti*. But those that have the consonant *v* in the present cannot undergo syncope in the perfect: *lavo, lavasti* [Royal Ms., *lavisti*]. No one says *lasti* for *lavasti*.

*Adipiscor* forms *adeptus sum*. *Accusso* must be written with two *c*’s and two *s*’s [Col. 0903C]. *Accedo* has two *c*’s. Often, for the sake of euphony, we change *ab* into the following consonant, as in *afficio, affluo, allido, ammoneo, annuo, appono, arripio, assumo*. *Alligo* has two *l*’s. *Annuo* has two *n*’s. *Apparo* [Royal Ms., *appareo*] has two *p*’s. *Attuli* must be written with two *t*’s.

But *at*, when it is a conjunction, is written with *t*; when it is a preposition, with *d*. Likewise, the compound conjunction *atque* is written with *t*. The preposition *apud* ends in *d*.

From *artus*, “limb,” comes *artubus*; from *ars*, “art,” *artibus*. Similarly, from *arcus*, “bow,” *arcubus*; from *arx*, “citadel,” *arcibus*. [*Aeger animo*, “sick in mind”; *aegrotus corpore*, “sick in body”: both are written with the diphthong.]

*Alibi* means “in another place.” *Alias* means “at another time.” *Aer* is disyllabic and has no plural, except *aera*. *Aes* is monosyllabic. *Aufero* means *abfero*, with *b* changed into *u*.

The preposition *ad* is corrupted when the following verb begins with a consonant, as in *apponit* and *amittit*. *Allium* and *dolium* are written with *i*, as in Virgil (*Eclogue* II, 11):

> *Allia serpellumque*,

“garlic and creeping thyme.”

*Acer* forms the plural *acria* [Royal Ms., *acri*]. *Acris* forms the plural *acres*.

[*Audacter* is Latin, but *audaciter* is better, because nouns ending in the letter *x* take *r* and *i* in their adverbs: *atrox, atrociter*; *ferox, ferociter*. *Accersit* means “he summons.” *Arcessit* means “he accuses.”]

*Acervus*, with *u*, is a heap of any thing, perhaps stones or crops. *Acerbus*, with *b*, means unripe or harsh.

There are words written with two *u*’s, and their number of syllables consequently increases. For when one vowel is joined to another, not only do they fail to coalesce, but they also increase the number of syllables, as in *ingenuus, arduus, exiguus,* and *vacuus*, which must be written with *c*, not *q*. The same division occurs in verbs: *metuunt, statuunt, tribuunt, acuunt*, which likewise must be written with *c*, not *q*.

*Aspiro* and *aspicio* are written without *d*, with a single *s* [Royal Ms., *asspiro, asspicio*, with double *s*], although they are compounds with the preposition *ad*, because the *d* disappears there.

*Apparet*, “it appears,” is written with *p*. *Adparet*, “it obeys,” is written with *d*, not because of a rule but for the sake of distinction.

*Arbor* means every kind of wood or tree. *Arbusta* refers only to fruit-bearing trees.

*Avena*, when it refers to a sprout, is written without *h*, with *v*. [Col. 0904B] *Habena*, when it refers to the reins of animals, is written with *h* and *b*.

[*Advocatur* means “he is summoned to give legal assistance.” *Evocatur* means “he is summoned to offer service.” *Invocatur* means “he is called upon to provide help.” *Adportare* means “to bring something to.” *Asportare* means “to carry something away.” *Comportare* means “to carry together into one place.” *Deportare* means “to set down or carry away.” *Exportare* means “to remove.”]

*Album* is produced by nature; *candidum* by care.

[*Armarium* is where instruments of every kind of art are stored. *Armamentarium* is where only weapons of war are kept. *Accedit*, with *e*, comes from *ambulando*, “walking toward.” *Accidit*, with *i*, comes from an event.]

The preposition *ante* sometimes remains intact, as in *antecedit* and *antevenit*. Sometimes it is corrupted by changing *e* into *i*, as in *anticipat*.

The prepositions *a, ab,* and *abs* have one meaning: *a me*, “from me”; *ab homine*, “from a man”; *abstuli*, “I took away.” But *ab* is very frequently written when the following verb begins with a vowel, so that the word will not be burdened with many consonants, as in *ab uno*, “from one.” If the part of speech begins with a consonant, only *a* should be used, as in *a fratre*, “from a brother.”

Nevertheless, *abs* more often remains intact in composition for the sake of euphony: *abs te*, “from you,” and *abscondo*, “I hide,” sound better than *ab te* or *abcondo*, just as *ab urbe*, “from the city,” sounds better than *abs urbe*.

### 303

*Avunculus* is written with two *u*’s, because it is a diminutive of *avus*, “grandfather,” the syllable *uo* having been changed into *uun*. *Alvus*, when it means “belly,” is written with the digamma *u*; when it means a color [Royal Ms. adds: “which is *albus*, white”], it is written with *b*.

*Ara*, when it means an altar, is written without aspirated *h*; when it means a pigsty, it is written with aspiration. *Aemulus, aedituus,* and *aerumna* are all written with the diphthong. *Aequimanus* is likewise written with *ae*: it means “ambidextrous,” one who uses either hand as the right hand.

*Avarus*, when it signifies the vice, is written with *u*. If it refers to the people [Royal Ms. adds: “that is, the Abari”], it is written with *b*.

*Acclamo*, with two *c*’s, means “I falsely accuse someone.” *Reclamo* means “I call someone who is going away.” *Inclamo* and *succlamo* refer to murmuring. *Perclamo* [Ms., *proclamat*] signifies an elevation of the voice in praise or supplication. *Declamo* [Royal Ms., *proclamo*] means “I declaim rhetorically.” *Exclamo* is used when I raise my voice with all my strength.

*Alea*, if it signifies the game, is written with *e*; if it comes from *alius, alia*, “another,” it is read with *i*.

*Amittit*, with one *m*, means “he leaves.” *Ammittit*, with two *m*’s, means “he takes in.” Therefore one should say *inmissa*, “sent in,” and *ammitte te* or *admitte* [Royal Ms., “we say *inmissa*, *ammiti*, as *admitte*”].

*Affatim*, with two *f*’s, means “immediately” or “enough.” *Agger* is written with two *g*’s when it signifies a raised road or embankment; but if it means a field where something can be sown, it is written with one *g*.

*Accentus*, with two *c*’s, is where the voice is raised in a word [Royal Ms., “raised”]. *Angor*, “I suffer distress,” must be written with *n* and *g*. *Aeripedem*, “swift,” must be pronounced with *a* and *e* divided. *Allecti*, with two *l*’s, means “chosen,” and from it comes *allegit*. *Allicit*, “he invites,” is written similarly. *Altilia*, as though from *alatilia*, means “fattened birds.” *Attonitus*, with two *t*’s, means “intent” or “spread through with astonishment.” *Attingit* must be written with two *t*’s.

## LETTER B

*Benedictio* and *oratio* must have *t* in the penultimate syllable [Col. 0905B], not *c*, as do similar words. *B* changes into *s* before following *t* and *c*, as in *sustulit* and *suscipit*.

*Benificus*, compounded from the adverb *bene*, “well,” must be written with *b*. *Veneficus*, “poisonous” or “poisoner,” from *venenum*, “poison,” is written with *u*. *Bis*, the adverb “twice,” is written with *b*; *vis*, the noun “force,” with *u* [Royal Ms., “it is written thus: *haec vis, hujus vis, huic vi*”].

*Bile*, if it signifies gall, is written with *b*; if it refers to something rejected or worthless, from *vilis*, “cheap,” it is written with *u*.

*Berna*, if it signifies one born at home—that is, Greek **οἰκογενής** (*oikogenēs*, “home-born”)—is written with *b*. If it signifies a season, as in *verna tempora*, “spring seasons,” the authorities have chosen to write it with *u*. Both syllables of *berbena* begin with *b*.

[*Belzebub*, not *Belzebul*. *Belial*, not *Beliar*, should be said. *Baptismus, baptismi*, is found as a masculine noun; *baptisma, baptismatis*; and *baptismum, baptismi* [Salzburg Ms., *baptismus, baptisma*, and so forth].]

**[Col. 0905C]** The letter *b* does not retain its sound before *f*, but passes into it in composition: *offui*, not *obfui*; *suffero*, for *subfero*. In many places *b* likewise tends to pass into *s*, as in *sustuli, suscipio, susteneo, suspendo*, for *subtuli, subcipio, subteneo, subpendo*.

*Bes* or *bisse*, signifying eight ounces, must be written with *b*. *Bimus*, as though from *bihiemis*, and from which *bimatus* is derived, begins with *b*; likewise *biennis*, “lasting two years.”

*Benivolus, benignus,* and *benificus*, although compounded from the adverb *bene*, are nevertheless written with *i*, not *e*, in the second syllable. The same applies to *malivolus* and *malificus*, just as *pacificus* comes from *pax*.

*Bibo*, “I drink,” from *potus*, is written with two *b*’s and forms the perfect *bibi*. *Vivo*, “I live,” from *vita*, is written with two *v*’s—both consonants—and forms the perfect *vixi*.

*Bivium*, “a double road,” begins with *b* in the first syllable and with consonantal *u* in the second.

*Brevis*, “short,” has *v* in its second syllable, and from it comes *breviter*. *Balteum*, “belt,” is written with *e*.

*Beo, beas*, and from this *beatus*, “blessed”; likewise *meo, meas*, and from this *meatus*, “passage”; and *creo, creas*, and from this *creatus*, “created.”

## LETTER C

*Causa* is written with one *s*. [Note: [Col. 0905D] See the grammar concerning prepositions.]

The preposition *circum* loses its *m* in some places, as in *circuire*; in others it retains it, as in *circumvenit*; in others it is placed after the word, as in Virgil:

> *Maria omnia circum*,

“all around the seas.”

*Caverna* is written with *u*; *taberna* with *b*.

*Cana*, if it signifies a place, is written with one *n*; if it signifies a sprout—that is, *canna*—with two *n*’s.

*Cynomia*, if written with *y*, signifies a dog-fly. *Cynos* in Greek means “dog.”

*Coenomia*, with the diphthong *oe*, signifies the common fly, that is, a fly of every kind, because *coenon* in Greek means “common.” From this *coenobium*, “a common dwelling,” is named [Salzburg Ms., *coenubium*].

*Carduus* has three syllables, like *arduus, fatuus,* and *mortuus*. *Cuspis, cuspidis*, not *cuspēs*. *Commodamus*, “we lend what we receive,” is written with two *m*’s. *Mutuamus* is used when we receive equal things in return.

*Comminus* has two *m*’s; *eminus* one. We fight *comminus* with swords, “at close quarters”; *eminus* with spears, “from a distance,” because the former does not depart from the hand, whereas the latter is sent from the hands.

*Collocat* is written with two *l*’s.

### 304

*Cerno, cresco,* and *glisco* share one perfect tense, namely *crevi*. *Cupio* forms *cupivi* and *cupii*. *Casses*, “nets,” is written with two *s*’s.

*Comedia*, “comedy,” refers to songs sung at banquets and is written with a simple *e*.

*Comburo, comparo,* and *compono* are written with *m*, not *n*. The same applies to *complaceo, commoratus, comprehendo, commodat, computrescit, commendat, commune, complures*, and similar words [Royal Ms. adds: “they must be written with *m*”].

*Camelus* has one *l*. *Celo, celas*, “I hide,” is written with a simple *e*.

[*Caelo, caelas*, when it signifies a painting, must be written with the diphthong *ae*. From this it is better understood that *caelum*, “sky,” derives from the painting of the stars rather than from the idea that it conceals the secrets of mortals.

*Circa* pertains to visible matter or place. *Erga* concerns the mind, especially when it generates a more favorable affection toward relatives. *Circum* refers to time.]

**[Col. 0906C]** *Cis* has a local meaning, as in *cis Alpinam Galliam*, “on this side of Alpine Gaul”; and it is taken for “beyond,” as in *cis praefinitum tempus*, “beyond the appointed time.” From it comes *citra*.

*Citra* has almost the same meaning as *cis*, except that *cis* is more often placed before proper names, while *citra* is placed before common nouns: *cis Rhenum*, “on this side of the Rhine”; *cis Alpes*, “on this side of the Alps”; *citra forum*, “on this side of the forum.” From *cis* comes *citra*; from *citra*, *citer, citerior, citissimus*.

*Circiter* pertains only to number, as in *circiter tria millia*, “about three thousand,” or *circiter horarum decem*, “about ten hours.”

*Carcer* is where people are shut up. *Carceres* are the starting-gates from which chariots emerge.

*Cepit*, with a simple *e*, comes from *capio*, “to take.” *Coepit*, with the diphthong *oe*, comes from *incipio*, “to begin.” *Coepta*, with the diphthong *oe*; *incepta*, with a simple *e*.

If the preposition *con* is joined to verbs beginning with vowels, it loses its consonant *n*: *aequo, coaequo*; *eo, coeo*, and the rest. But if it is joined to verbs beginning with the digamma, it does not lose the letter *n*: *volo, convolo*; *vinco, convinco*.

*Coquus, coqui*: the first syllable is written with *c*, the second with *q*. For we do not say *quoquere*, but *coquere*. *Conjunx* [Royal Ms., *conjux*] should according to analogy be written with *n*, as *conjunx*; but for the sake of euphony the *n* is removed, and we say *conjux*.

When *c* follows, no vowel is aspirated: *acies, ecce, oculus*.

*Caelebs*, “celibate,” one who makes his way to heaven; *caelebs*, one who leads the life of heavenly beings; and *coelicola*, one who worships heaven, such as an angel—these are written with the diphthong *ae*.

*Coaetaneus*, “of the same age,” as though “equal in age,” is likewise written with the diphthong *ae*.

*Cado, cecidi*, from *cadere*, “to fall”; *caedo, caecidi*, from striking, is written with the diphthong *ae*. *Cedo, cessi*, from withdrawing, is written with *e*. *Caluo*, “I deceive,” is written with *u*. According to the rule it should form *calui*, and from it *calumnia* is derived.

## LETTER D

*Dilectum*, from choosing, is written with *di*. For *diligi* concerns affection, and from it come *dilectio* and *diligo* [Royal Ms.: “*diligi* concerns affection; *deligi* concerns judgment”]. *Deligi* is written with *de*; *deligi* concerns judgment.

*Delictum*, “sin,” is written with *e* in the first syllable and *i* in the second. *Dilectus*, “beloved,” with the order changed, should have *i* in the first syllable and *e* in the second.

*Delectatio, delector*, and the forms declined from them are written with *e* in both the first and second syllables.

*Deus* is written with a single *e*. *Daemon* is written with the diphthong *ae*.

*Decus* concerns honor; *decor*, appearance. *Descendo* is pronounced with *e*. *Desperatus* with *e*. *Dispersus* with *i*. *Deficiscor* forms *defectus sum*.

*De* is memorial, intensive, and privative: *de homine*, “concerning a man”; *detraho*, “I draw away”; *desum*, “I am absent.”

The preposition *de* is either placed in full in compounds, as in *deducere, demonstrare, detrudere*, or is corrupted by shortening the letter *e*, as in *deorsum*. For when the letter *e* changes into *i*, as in:

> *Aera dimovit tenebrosum et dispulit umbras*  
> [Note: [Col. 0907D] Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 839.],

“he moved away the dark air and scattered the shadows,” the word does not come from the preposition *de*, but from *dis*, as in *distraho*, “I draw apart,” and *disperio* [Royal Ms., *dispertior*].

Dissertus, that is, eloquent, is written with *di*. *Desertus*, that is, abandoned, with *de*. *Delator*, one who reports someone for accusation, with the preposition *de*. *Dilator*, when it means “to delay,” is written with the preposition *di*. *Deluit*, that is, “he cleansed,” with *de*. *Diluit*, that is, “he commands,” with *di*. *Deduco*, of bringing out a friend, with *de*. *Diduco*, however, that is, “I draw apart,” with *di*. *Didymus* has *i* in its first syllable and *y* in its second. *Discedo* must be written with *i*.

[Col. 0907C]

Indeed, *di* and *dis* are separative and have the same meaning, just as *ab* and *abs* do; for example, *divido*, “I divide,” and *distraho*, “I draw apart.” *Dis* is compounded when *c, f, p, s, t*, or *i* used as a consonant follows it: *discutio*, “I shake apart”; *differo*, “I carry apart”; *diffundo*, “I pour apart,” with *s* changed into *f* for the sake of euphony; *disputo*, “I argue”; *disspero* [Ms. Reg., *dissero*]; *distraho*, “I draw apart”; *disjungo*, “I separate.” Before the other consonants, *di* is prefixed: *diduco*, “I draw apart”; *digero*, “I distribute”; *diluo*, “I dissolve”; *dimitto*, “I release”; *diruo*, “I destroy.” Everywhere *di* is long, except in *dirimo*, “I separate,” and *disertus*, “eloquent.”

305. LETTER E

[Col. 0907D]

In composition, *e* is privative or intensive, as in *enodes trunci*, “trunks without knots,” and *enarro*, “I narrate.” *Ecquid* is written with *c* in the first syllable, since it means *enquid*, with *n* changed into *c*. *Edo*, from “to eat,” makes *es*, “you eat,” and *est*, “he eats.” *Esto*, “let it be”; *ecce*, “behold”; *consentio*, “I agree.” *Expergiscor* and *experior* form the perfect *expertus sum*. *Exsilium* must have *s*. Likewise, *x* changes into the letter *f*: *effluo*, “I flow out”; *effodio*, “I dig out”; *effero*, “I carry out”; *efficio*, “I accomplish.” *Exuviae* is written with *u*. *Excubiae* must be written with *b*. *Exsequi* must be written with *q*. *Emporium*, without *h*, is interpreted in Latin as “marketplace.” *Emolamentum* [Ms. Reg., *emolumentum*] is written with *e*. *Aemulatio* must be written with the diphthong *ae*. *Exsul* must be written with the added *s*, because it means “outside the soil” [*extra solum*]. *Exultat* is better written without *s*, because *x* consists of *c* and *s*. *Aequor, aequora* must be written with the diphthong *ae*, because the word was formed from *aqua*, “water.”

[*Exprobrat*, “he reproaches,” is used of one who recalls the benefits that he bestows. *Obprobrat*, “he reproaches,” is used of one who casts an insult [*obprobrium*] in someone’s face—that is, a fault; Ms. Reg., *opprobrat, opprobrium*.] *Exspectat* must be written with *s*. *Exspectatur*, that is, “he is expected to come”; *spectatur*, “he is looked at” or “approved” [with *s*]. [*Exercitus*, “worn out by labors”; *exercitatus*, “trained in studies” [without *s*]. *Exstruere* means “to build upward” [Ms. Reg., “*exstruere* means ‘to establish as understood,’” corrupt]; *instruere*, “to draw up a battle line” or “to arrange an action”; *adstruere*, “to affirm”; *construere*, “to join together in building”; *substruere*, “to build underneath something placed above.” *Eorundem* and *earundem* must be written with *n*, not *m*, for the sake of euphony.] The preposition *ex* is changed before the letter *f*: *effluo*, *effodio*, *efficio*, and the rest; these must therefore be written with double *f*. Before *b, d, g, l, m, n*, and *u* or *i* used as consonants, the preposition *ex* loses its *x*: *ebibit*, “he drank up”; *edidit*, “he brought forth”; *egessit*, “he carried out”; *elusit*, “he evaded”; *emicuit*, “he shone forth”; *enervavit*, “he weakened.” When *f* follows, however, it changes into the same letter: *effundo*, “I pour out.” *Expecto*, meaning “I comb,” must be written without *s*. *Exire*, “to go out,” is without *s*, since *ire*, “to go,” is simple; and so are all forms derived from it, such as *exitus*, “departure,” *exitium*, “destruction,” and *exitiale*, “destructive.” *Exscindo*, “I cut out”; *exsculpo*, “I carve out”; *exstruo*, “I build up,” must be written with *s*. Likewise *exsisto*, “I arise”: for we say *sistere* with *s*. *Examen*, “examination,” is without *s*. *Exiguae*, “small,” is likewise written without *s*. *Ex* is sometimes used for *extra*, “outside,” as in *excludo*, “I shut out,” and *extracludo*. *Exsul*, “exile,” means “outside the soil.” *Modo*, meaning “very,” as in *excelsus*, “very high.” *Modo* may be privative, intensive, or completive, as in *exstirpo*, “I uproot”; *extendo*, “I stretch out”; *expleo*, “I fill up.”

LETTER F

[Col. 0908C]

*Formosus* must be written without *n* in the second syllable, as are *harenosus*, “sandy”; *frondosus*, “leafy”; *aquosus*, “watery”; and *herbosus*, “grassy.” Participles, however, have *n*: *tonsus*, “shorn”; *tunsus*, “beaten”; *pransus*, “having eaten”; *pensus*, “weighed.” *Feriae* must also be written, not *fereae*. *Flavus*, “yellow,” begins with *f* in its first syllable, while the following syllable begins with *u*. *Fides, fidei*, “faith,” has a short first syllable. *Fides, fidis*, “string,” has both syllables long. [*Fidus* is used of a friend; *fidelis*, of a servant. *Fidus, fidissimus* has no comparative; instead one must say *magis fidus*, “more faithful,” and *minus fidus*, “less faithful.” *Fastus*, meaning arrogance, has the plural genitive *fastuum*. *Fastus*, referring to the books of the *Fasti*, is another word. *Fungi* means “to perform”; *defungi*, “to complete.” *Fremor* is the murmur of human beings; *fremitus* is the sound of beasts. We call something black *furvum*. [Col. 0908D] Something reddish is called *flavum*. *Fulvum* properly describes gold to which some blackish element has been added to enhance its brilliance [Ms. Reg., “is added”]. *Foros*, masculine, is the ship’s flooring where the rowers sit, and is always plural.] *Fedus*, meaning ugly, is written with simple *e*. *Foedus*, meaning a pact, with the diphthong *oe*. *Falso* is the ablative form of a noun, a first-conjugation verb, and an adverb. [*Flagitia* are sins we commit against God; *facinora*, crimes against a human being. *Fimus* and *fumus*, “manure” and “smoke”; *fames* and *fenum*, “hunger” and “hay”; and *fel*, “gall,” have no plural.]

*Fulcio*, “I support,” and *fulgeo*, “I shine,” have the same perfect, *fulsi*. The letter *F* was shaped after a certain letter called *digamma*, because it appears to have two strokes from the letter *gamma*. Because of the similarity of this sound, our people have placed the consonant *v* in its place, as in *votum*, “vow,” and *virgo*, “maiden,” instead of *fotum* and *firgo*.

Say *festuca*, “straw,” not *fistuca*. According to its etymology, if *forfices*, “shears,” derives from *filum*, “thread,” it is written with *f*, as are the shears of tailors. If it derives from *pilus*, “hair,” it is written with *p*: *forpices*, the shears of barbers. If from “taking,” it is written with *c*: *forcipes*, because they grasp hot metal, and these are the tools of smiths. For the ancients called *formum* “hot”; hence also *formosus*, “beautiful” [Ms. Reg., “*calidum*, hot”; *Faris, fatur*, from *fando*, “speaking”; it has no first person]. *Filex* is said of one who grants happiness. *Felix*, of one who receives happiness. *Filex* is that through which happiness is given. *Fingo, finxi, fictum, ficturus* forms its principal parts. *Findo, fidi, fissurus* forms them. *Figo* has *fixi*. 306. *Fundo, fundas*, “I found,” derives from *fundare*, “to found.” *Fundo, fundis*, “I pour,” derives from *fundere*, “to pour.” *Ferio*, “I strike,” and *percutio*, “I strike,” have one perfect, namely *percussi*, written with double *s*, just as *uro*, “I burn,” has *ussi*. *Fero, fers, fert* is used in the second and third persons for the sake of distinction, so that if one said *feris, ferit*, they would not be thought to derive from *ferio, feris, ferit*. *Fero* and *tollo* have the perfect *tuli*. *Furio* and *insanio* have one perfect, *insanivi*. *Facio* forms the imperative *fac*, “do,” for the sake of distinction, so that if one said *face*, it would not be thought to come from the noun *fax*, “torch.” Likewise *dic, duc,* and *fer* are produced by apocope [for the sake of distinction]; for if we said *dice, duce, fere*, we would be thought to mean something else.

LETTER G

[*Gaudium* is joy of the mind; *laetitia* is gladness; *exultatio* also applies to words and limbs.] *Gnatus* must be written with *g* and *n*, as must *gnavus*, because it retains the *g* in composition as well [Ms. Reg., “the *g* itself is retained,”] as in *agnatus*, “related by birth,” and *ignavus*, “sluggish.” [*Gremium* is the inner part; *sinus*, the outer. *Gith* is indeclinable and has no plural; it is neuter and is declined through all cases.] *Gnarus*, that is, learned, accomplished, knowledgeable. *Gnavus*, strong, active. *Garrit*, “he mutters subtly.” *Garrulus*, talkative, loquacious. *Gestit*, “he wishes, desires, longs for, hopes for.” *Gestat*, that is, “he carries.” *Gloriosus* derives from a multitude of brightness; the letter *c* has been changed into *g*. *Grandaevus*, as if “great in age,” is therefore written with double *u*. *Gratulor* means “I rejoice,” and “I give thanks.”

LETTER H

*Habeo*, “I have,” is written with aspiration, from *teneo*, “I hold.” *Abeo*, “I depart,” is without aspiration and is compounded from the two complete words *ab* and *eo*. *Hiatus* is an opening of the mouth, with aspiration. *Chiatus*, with *c* and *h*, signifies a vessel. *Hymnus* must be written with *h*. [The pronouns *hi* and *his* are written with a single *i*.] *Haud*, an adverb of negation, ends in *d* and is aspirated at the beginning. When it is a disjunctive conjunction meaning “or,” it is written *aut*, with *t* and without aspiration. *Hujusce* must be written with the letter *c*; for the ancients added *ce* to pronouns, as in *hicce, illicce, isticce*. When that final syllable *ce* was removed, *hic, illic, istic* remained. The accent, however, remains on the final syllable. *Hiems* must be written without *p*, although *sumpsi* is written with *p* because of the Greek letter *psi*, whose force in Latin is represented by *p* and *s*.

*Haurit*, “he draws up,” must be written with *h*; *audit*, “he hears,” without *h*. [*Herbescit ager*, “the field grows grassy,” when it produces grass, just as *adolescit*, “he grows up,” and *pubescit*, “he reaches puberty,” when it approaches the ear of grain [Ms. Reg., “when the ears approach”]. Aspiration may be placed before all vowels; after consonants it is used only with four letters: *c, t, p, r*, as in *habeo, heres, hiems, homo, humus, Chremens* [Ms. Reg., *Chremes*], *Tharso, Philippus, Rhodus*. *H* is therefore written externally beside vowels, so that they sound less strongly; with consonants it is written internally, so that they sound more strongly. *Habena*, “rein,” which governs, is written with *b* and aspiration; *avena*, “reed” or “straw,” with *v* and without aspiration. *Hiscit*, that is, “he opens his mouth.” *Hippocrita* is Greek; in Latin, *simulator*, “pretender.” For *hippo* in Greek means “false,” and *chrisis* means “judgment.”

LETTER I

*Inclytus* is a Greek word; for what the Greeks call *clyton*, the Latins call *gloriosum*, “glorious.” *Idiota* is Greek; in Latin, *imperitus*, “unskilled.” *Intervallum* is written with double *l*. *Interpretor* is written with simple *e*, as are all words derived from it. The preposition *inter*, in a word where *lego* follows, changes into *l*, as in *intellego*; in other words it remains intact, as in *interitus*, “death.” The pronoun *id*, from *is, ea, id*, is written with *d*. *It*, from *eo, is, it*, “he goes,” is written with *t*. *Jacet* is used of one who lies down. *Jecit* is used of one who throws any missile. *Impar* must be written with *m*. *Impleo* with *m*, not *n*. *Ipsum* must be neuter, not *ipsud*, like *illud* and *istud*; for the ancients used *ipsus*, not *ipsud*, as the masculine nominative. Hence in the Gospel: “All things were made through him” (*Omnia per ipsum facta sunt*), that is, through the Word. *Identidem* must be written with *n* in the first position, although it is compounded from *idem* and *itidem*.

*Inlexit*, with *e*, means “he seduced”; with *u*, “he enlightened.” *Incestum* must be written thus, although it comes from *incastus*. *Innixus*, “leaning upon” or “reclining.” *Innexus*, “bound.” *Indigena*, “born there”; *incola*, “coming from elsewhere.” The ancients called *intempestivum* “inopportune”; *tempestivum*, “opportune”; *oportunum* derives from *tempus*, “time.”

307. Thus *inmaturitas* is the nocturnal time that is not mature—that is, not suitable—for anything to be done while keeping watch; this is also commonly called *hora inportuna*, “an unsuitable hour.” [Note: The words enclosed in asterisks are found above, vol. I, in the *Exposition of Psalm 118*, verse 147, col. 615.]

*Juvenis, juvenior* has no superlative, like *senex, senior*. *Juvenis* and *senior* are commonly used of one another as *major* and *minor*, “greater/older” and “lesser/younger.” *Inpingo* forms the perfect *inpinxi* and *inpegi*. *Ira* arises from a sudden movement of the mind. *Iracundia* is a persistent vice. *Invidus* is one who envies. *Invidiosus* is one who suffers envy. When the preposition *in* is compounded and *p, b,* or *m* follows, it changes *n* into *m*: *improbus*, “wicked”; *imbuit*, “he drenched”; *immut at* [read *immut at*], “he changes”; *impius*, “ungodly.” Whenever *g* follows, however, it loses the *m*: *ignarus*, “unaware”; *ignotus*, “unknown,” since *gnarus* and *notus* are the simple forms.

LETTER K

[Col. 0911A]

*Kartago* and *Kalendae* must be written with *k*. Other words are better written with *c*.

LETTER L

*Liber*, whether it means a book, freedom, or bark, is written with *b* in every case. *Largitas* is generosity of character; *largitio*, lavishness or ambition. *Libidinosus* derives from *libido*, with *b*. *Lividus* derives from *livor* and must be written with *v*. [*Lepus* is the animal; *lepos*, the pleasantness of pleasure. Hence we call something agreeable *lepidum*.] *Limen* is the threshold of a house; *limes*, the boundary of a region. *Loqui* is proper to a human being; *obloqui*, to a detractor, just as *objecit*, “he opposed,” and *obponit*, “he sets against” [Ms. Reg., *obic it, opponit*]. *Adloqui* [Ms. Reg., *alloqui*] belongs to one who persuades, encourages, or commands. *Eloqui* belongs to an orator.

[Col. 0911B] *Laurentius* and other names whose singular nominative ends in *-ius* have the singular genitive and plural nominative in double *ii*. Their singular vocative ends in simple *i* or *ie*: *hic impius, hujus impii, o impie*, “this impious man, of this impious man, O impious one.” *Luceo* and *lugeo* have one perfect, *luxi*. *Lino* forms the perfect *linui* and *linivi*. *Laetus* is written with the diphthong *ae*, because *laetitia*, “gladness,” is said to derive from *latitudo*, “breadth.” Lepers are so called from the excessive itching of the scab itself; therefore the word must be written with *p*. *Lego, legas* derives from *eligere*, “to choose.” *Lego, legis* derives from *legere*, “to read.” *Loquor, loqueris, loquitur* must be written with *q*; *locutus*, however, is written with *c* and simple *u* for the sake of euphony.

LETTER M

*Munimentum* derives from *munire*, “to fortify”; *monumentum* pertains to a tomb. *Mille* is written with double *l*, although *milia* is written with one. If *malum* means fruit, pronounce the *a* long [Ms. Reg., “*malum* has a long *a*”]; if it means wickedness, pronounce it short. *Malus*, meaning the mast of a ship, likewise has a long *a*. *Malus*, “bad,” must have a short *a* [Ms. Reg., “has a short *a*”]. *Machina* must be written with *c* and *h*, meaning a device or contrivance. *Macte*, that is, “more greatly increased.” *Mollis*, if derived from *mollitia*, is written with double *l*. *Molis* [Ms. Reg., *moles*], if referring to weight, is written with one *l*. *Mane* refers to the gods of the underworld. *Mane*, without *s*, means the beginning of the day. *Marsuppium* must be written with double *p*. *Mas* is primitive; *mares* [Ms. Reg., *masculinum*; perhaps *masculus*] is diminutive. *Machaera* must be written with *c* and *h*, meaning “sword.” *Maceria*, “wall,” is written with simple *c*. *Mando, mandas* derives from *mandare*, “to entrust.” *Mando, mandis* derives from *manducare*, “to eat.” [Col. 0911D] *Metalla* is written with double *l*. *Mulceo* and *mulgeo* have one perfect, *mulsi*. *Menda* means deception or fraud; hence *mendax*, “lying,” and *mendacium*, “falsehood.”

*Mars* and *Mavors* are one and the same; hence some wish *Mavortia* to be used. *Manuviae*, “spoils”; *oblivium*, “forgetfulness”; *diluvium*, “flood”; *suavium*, “kiss”; *lividum*, “leaden-colored”; *flavius* [the text reads *favius*]; *avidus*, “greedy”; *fluvius*, “river”; *civitas*, “city”; and *exuviae*, “clothing stripped off,” are pronounced with consonantal *v* and short *i*. *Mattheus* and *Matthias* have double *t*, which the Greeks write with *τ* and *θ*. *Malo*, “I prefer,” means *magis volo*, “I want more”; *nolo*, “I do not wish,” means *ne volo*, “I do not wish,” and both are written with one *l*. *Malle*, “to prefer,” *velle*, “to wish,” and *nolle*, “not to wish,” are written with double *l*. *Mitto* is written with double *t*, and therefore its perfect is written with double *s*: *missi*. *Magnus*: the *g* is joined to the following syllable [Ms. Reg., “is joined to the following syllable”]. *Magister* means “greater in position”; for in Greek *isteron* means “station.”

LETTER N

*Nobilis, mobilis, debilis,* and *habilis* must be written with *b*. *Nanctus*, that is, “found” or “obtained,” must be written with *n* and *c*. *Nacturus*, the future participle, with *c* alone. Both *navita* and *nauta* are correct. *Nummularius* [Ms. Reg., *nummolarius*] is written with double *m*, since it means “one who distributes money.” *Nummisma* likewise has double *m*, since it is the impression or coinage of money. *Navus*, meaning diligent or effective, must be written with double *u*. 308 [*Nimis* is used of anything that is more than is proper. For that which is less than necessary is *parvum*, “little.” Between these lies the measure called *satis*, “enough.” Sometimes, however, the Latin language abuses this word and uses *nimis* for “very,” as we find it used in sacred writings. Thus in the Psalm: “You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly” (*Tu praecepisti mandata custodiri nimis*, Psalm 118:4), that is, “very greatly.”]

[*Nullus* is used both of a thing and of a person. *Nemo* is used of a person, as if *ne homo*, “not a human being” [Ms. Reg., “as *nemo homo*”]. *Novi* is declined like *odi* and *memini*. [A woman *nubit* to a man; a man *ducit uxorem*, “takes a wife.” A woman *nubit* because she covers her head and cheeks with a cloak.] In *nubo*, when a vowel follows, there must be *b*; before a consonant, *p*, as in *nupsi*. [*Nihil* is an adverb; *nihili* is a noun. A person of no importance is called *nihili*.] *Navigium* refers to every expedition of a fleet. *Nauta* is anyone who performs the work of sailing. *Navis* has its ablative ending in both *-i* and *-e* [Ms. Reg., “has its ablative ending in *-i* and *-e*.”] *Nequam* does not mean “bad,” but “useless.” *Neglegens* must be written with *g*, as if from *nec legens*, “not reading,” with *c* changed into *g*. *Narro, narratio* are written with double *r*. Both *nihil* and *nil* may be used.

LETTER O

[*Olea* is the tree itself; *oliva*, the fruit; *oleum*, the juice.] *Obaudiens* derives from *auris*, “ear,” because it hears one who commands; therefore it must be written with *au*. The preposition *ob* is sometimes placed in its full form, as in *obire*, “to meet” or “die,” and *oberr are*, “to wander about.” Sometimes it changes into the same letter with which the following word begins: *offulsit*, “it shone upon”; *ommutuit*, “he fell silent”; *opposuit*, “he opposed.” When *v* used as a consonant follows, it remains intact: *obversus*, “turned toward”; *obvius*, “encountering.” If *onus* derives from *onus, oneris*, “burden,” it is written with *o* alone; if from *honor*, “honor,” it is written with *h*. *Oblatrat* must be written with *b*. *Obstat* with *b*; *optat* with *p*. In *obstupui, obstupeo, obsum,* and *obstrepo*, *b* belongs to the preceding syllable and *s* to the second. The noun *obitus*, “death,” and the adverbs *subito*, “suddenly,” and *obiter*, “by the way,” begin from the prepositions *ob* and *sub*. *Obsolevit* does have *s*, but it belongs not to the verb itself but to the preposition *obs*, just as in *ab* and *abs*. *Obsolevit*, that is, “it grew old.” *Obnixus*, that is, “striving,” is written with *i*. *Obnexus*, that is, “bound,” must be written with *e*. *Occasus* has double *c* and one *s*.

LETTER P

*Pascha* and *Phase* are one and the same. *Parascheve* must be written with *u* in the final syllable. *Patriarcha* must have *h*, meaning “chief of the fathers.” [*Patrium* derives from *patria*, “fatherland”; *paternum* from *pater*, “father.” *Papaver* must be written with *v*.] *Pandectes*, “containing everything.” Therefore, when the Old and New Testaments are written together, they are jointly called a *Pandecten*. *Pangor* forms the perfect *pactus sum*. *Parumper*, that is, *parum* with the preposition *per* placed in reverse order; likewise *pubetenus*, with *s* removed by apocope. *Pario, peperi, partum* forms the supine, hence *pariturus*, “about to give birth.” *Parco* forms the perfect *parsi* [and *peperci*]. “I am patient under labor.” “I am full of good things” and “full of good people.” *Pavidus* and *avidus* must be written with *v*. *Pavus, pavi*, “peacock,” and *pavo, pavonis*, “peacock.” [“I regret the gift” (*Poenitet me muneris*). “I am displeased by perfection” (*Piget me perfectionis*). “I am ashamed of love” (*Pudet me amoris*). *Pecto* means “I comb the head,” not *pectino*. *Pexum*, not *pectinatum*.] *Pene*, “almost,” is a preposition; *penes*, “in the possession of,” an adverb; both are written with simple *e*. *Pennas* are the feathers of birds. *Pinnas* are the battlements of walls. *Peto* and *expeto* must be written without *s*. *Petredium* is said, with *h* removed in composition, from seeking inheritances. [*Pertinacia* is used of an evil matter, and *constantia* of a good one.]

*Percussum* refers to the body; *perculsum* to the mind. *Percutio, percussi* is written with double *s*, hence *percussurus*. *Perjurus* is one who swears falsely. *Pejurus*, as if “he swears worse,” has no *r* in the verb [Ms. Reg., “the verb *pejuro* must not have *r*, for it is as if *pejus juro*, ‘I swear worse’”]. *Phoebus*, that is, Apollo, is written so that *h* follows *p*. *Phoebus* means the sun; *Phoebe* or *Phoeba*, the moon; both are written with *p* and *h*. *Pignora* are pledges concerning sons and affections. *Pignera* are pledges concerning things. *Plagiarius*, “seducer.” *Plaustrum, capistrum, claustrum, vestrum, rastrum,* and similar words join three consonants, when followed by a vowel, into one syllable. We say *pluris* of something assessed at a greater sum; *plures* of a multitude. [Col. 0913C] *Plures* is the comparative degree, whose positive is *multi*. *Poderis*, with *o* and *e*, is a long tunic worn by priests in the Old Law. *Poena*, meaning punishment, is written with *o* and *e*. [*Pono* means “I establish something simply.” *Dispono* means “I am going to undertake something requiring greater effort or deliberation.” It also means “to arrange a treaty to be entered into.”] *Potior, potitus sum*, and *perfruor, perfructus sum*. *Potius* must be written with *o*, not *u*, because it derives from *potes* [Ms. Reg., *potis*]. [Among the ancients, *potior* is used with both *fructus* and *fructu* (genitive and ablative forms of “fruit”): *potior hanc rem*, “I obtain this thing”; *potior, potissimus* forms its degrees. *Potamus eum*, “we give drink to the one to whom we offer a drink” [Ms. Reg., *porrigimus*, “we offer”]. We call the places where apples grow *pometa*; where they are stored, *pomaria*. Something is *postulatur*, “requested,” honorably; *poscitur*, “demanded,” improperly. *Postumus*, with *h* removed [Ms. Reg., *posthumus*, with *h* removed; another reading: with *h* added] in composition, means one born after his father was buried, that is, after his father’s death.

In the tenses of verbs, *p* changes into *b*: *scribo, scripsi*; *labo, lapsi*; *nubo, nupsi*. *Praeeo*: “I go before him and others.” *Praedico*: “I say beforehand.” *Prae* occurs in juxtaposition or composition and means “to,” “against,” “above,” “very,” or “before.” Terence: “I despised him here *prae me*,” that is, “in comparison with myself.” Likewise: “She becomes wretched *prae amore*,” that is, “because of love.” *Praesideo*: “I preside over,” or “I sit above.” *Praevalidus*: “very strong.” The preposition *prae* and *praeterea*, “besides,” must be written with the diphthong *ae*. *Presto* must be written with *o*, not *u*; hence we say *prestolari*, not *prestulari*. Both *prehendo* and *prendo* may be used. *Pretium* has simple *e*. *Precari* means “to be asked” [Ms. Reg., “to ask”]; *deprecari*, “to excuse” or “to cleanse away”; both have simple *e*, as Virgil says (*Aeneid* 12.931):

> “Indeed, I have deserved it, nor do I seek to avert it,” he said.

*Praemium* has the diphthong *ae*. Otherwise *prooemium*, with *oe*, means a preface. When writing *praegnantem*, attach the *g* to the second syllable, or divide it in writing, as in *magnus, dignus, pignus* and similar words. *Primitiae* is plural only, although it is sometimes understood in the singular. *Privignus* may be pronounced with the *e* removed; for I judge its full form to be *privigenus*.

The verb *probo* has two meanings. We *probamus* what we have chosen, that is, we approve it. [Col. 0914B] We *probamus* what we test to determine its quality, as in “Test me, O God” (*Proba me Deus*). The preposition *pro*, although naturally long, is sometimes shortened in composition: partly by shortening, as in *proavus*, “great-grandfather”; partly by taking the letter *d*, as in *prodest*, “it benefits”; *proditus*, “betrayed”; *prodigus*, “wasteful.” Sometimes it remains intact and is itself the component joined to the word, as in *procuro*, “I administer.” Before *i* and *v* used as consonants it never loses or changes its letter, but sometimes takes one or is shortened, as in *providens*, “foreseeing,” and *projectus*, “thrown forward.” *Protinus*, with temporal *i*, means “immediately”:

> “Immediately Aeneas began to compete with his swift arrow.”  
> [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.485.]

*Protenus*, with *e*, is a local adverb, meaning “forward as far as,” as in:

> “When both lands were one continuously.”

*Pro* in juxtaposition or composition may be local or temporal [Ms. Reg., “local or temporal”]. *Pro templo*, “before the temple”; *provideo*, “I foresee”; and it may be understood as “above,” “before,” “toward,” or “in,” as in *prominet*, “it projects,” that is, “it rises above.” *Pro curia sociis signa dare*, “to give the signal to one’s companions before the senate house,” that is, before the senate house. Virgil (*Aeneid* 5.500):

> “With all their strength they bend their bows,  
> each man for himself,”

that is, “according to his own strength.” *Pro testimonio*, “for testimony,” that is, “in testimony.” It is also used as an interjection, as in *Pro dolor!*, “Alas!” and is circumflexed. *Pulmentum* and *pulmentarium* are both used. *Pudoris* must be written with *u* and *o*: [*Poderis*, with *o* and *e*, means a long tunic worn by priests in the Old Law.]

LETTER Q

*Quaestor*, from *quaerere*, “to seek,” as if *quaesitor*, “inquirer,” must be written with the diphthong *ae*. *Quaestus*, “profit,” likewise has the diphthong *ae*. *Questus*, “lamentation,” has *e* [Ms. Reg., *querimonia*, “complaint”]. *Quanquam* must have *n* in its first syllable, not *m*. *Quantus* and *tantus* have *n* for the sake of euphony; they derive from *quamtus* and *tamtus*. *Quantus* means “how great.” *Querela* is written with one *l*, like *suadela, tutela,* and *candela*. *Quatenus*, a local adverb meaning “how far,” is written with *e*. [*Quatinus*, a causal conjunction meaning “so that,” must be written with *i*. *Quaeritur*, “it is sought,” has the diphthong *ae*. *Queritur*, “he laments,” has *e*. *Queremonia* has double *e*. *Queror de te*, “I complain about you”; *queror tibi de illo*, “I complain to you about him.” Likewise *conqueror*, “I complain.”]

The syllable *qui* is written with *q, u,* and *i*. If it is divided, it must be written with *c, u,* and *i*. [Col. 0915A] The pronoun *quid* must be written with *d*. [*Quicquam* and *quicquid* are written with *c*, not *d*, in the middle.] In composition, *d* is generally changed into *c* [Ms. Reg., “changed into *c*”], as in the prepositions *accedo*, “I approach,” and *accumulo*, “I heap up.” The verb *quit*, from *queo, quis, quit*, is written with *t*. *Quot*, when it is a number, is written with *t*; when it is a pronoun, with *d*. [*Quoties* and *toties* must be written without *n*. *Quorundam*, like *eorundem*, is written with *n*, not *m*. *Quo vadis* means “to what place are you going?” *Qua vadis* means “by what road are you going?” *Quo* is sometimes used for *ubi*, “where.” Augustine: “You find a famous house *quo boni habitant*,” that is, “where good people live.” *Quotus* means “of what age,” hence we say *quota luna*, “what day of the moon.” Augustine: “Who in this life can exist who is not convicted of being a sinner?” That is, “at what age, or in what number of days or years.”] *Quotidie*, the adverb of number, must be written with *q* and *u*, not *c*, as if *quot diebus*, “on so many days.” *Cotidie*, the adverb of continuance, is written with *c* and simple *o*, not *q*, because it derives not from *quota die*, “on what day,” but from “the continuous day.” The letter *q* is correctly used when *u* immediately follows it and one or more other vowels are joined to it so as to form one syllable. Other words are written with *c*.

LETTER R

[*Radius* is masculine, not neuter *radium*. *Regium*, “what belonged to the king.” *Regale*, “what is worthy of a king” [Bed., “of a ruler”]. We say *recens feci*, “I recently did,” not *recenter*, using a noun as an adverb.] The preposition *re* is not only prefixed in its full form to certain parts of speech, as in *removet*, “he removes”; *refricat*, “he refreshes”; *respirat*, “he breathes again”; it also takes the letter *d*, as in *redolere*, “to smell sweet,” and *redire*, “to return.” Sometimes *d* is doubled, whenever the following syllable begins with it and one part of speech is completed: thus we say *reddere*, “to give back,” with double *d*; but *reducere*, “to lead back,” with one. *Redoleo* refers to perfume or ointment. The preposition *re* often doubles the consonants to which it is joined, as is common among the ancients: *cado, reccido*; *tuli, rettuli*; *pello, repello*; *do, reddo*; *lego, rellego*. *Reliquiae* must be written with *q* and one *l*, although Virgil, with poetic license, wrote (*Aeneid* 1.34): *Relliquiae Danaum*, “the remnants of the Danaans.”

The preposition *re* receives the letter *d* externally when it is joined to a verb beginning with a vowel; it does not receive *d* when joined to *u* used as a consonant: *ulcero, redulcero*; *ago, redigo*; *eo, redeo*; *voco, revoco*; *vinco, revinco*. [*Robor* is a tree; *robur*, strength. *Rubor*, color.] *Roseum*, “rosy,” has *e*. *Roseaceum*, “rose-colored,” is a mixture. *R* before *a, u,* and vowels is not aspirated: *arcus, urtica, urna*. In the marked words it is aspirated: *hara, harena, harundo*. When *e* follows *r*, it is pronounced lightly: *erus, eruum, ergon*. If *b, n,* or *s*, or a long *e*, follows *r*, it is pronounced heavily: *herba, herbidus, herbilis, herbosus*; the proper name *Hernia*, whence:

> “The Hernican rocks are inhabited,”  
> [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.684.]

*Hersilia, heredes, heredium*, the proper name *Herenius*, and *Hercules*.

[Col. 0916A] When *i* follows *r*, it is always aspirated: *hircus*, “goat”; *hirquittallus*; *hirpinus*; *hirsutus*, “shaggy”; *hirtus*, “rough”; *hirtuleius*; and the proper name *Hirrus* [Note: [Col. 0916D] Here the Paris manuscript Regius ends. The remainder is missing there], unless the word is monosyllabic, as *ir*; or comes from a verb’s movement, as *eo, is, irem*; or unless *a* follows *r*, in which case it is not aspirated: *ira, iratus, iracundus, irascor*, and everything derived from them. When *o* follows *r*, it is not aspirated: *orbus*. But if another *r* or *t* follows, it is aspirated: *horreo, horror, hortus, holerum, Hortentius*. *Hordeum*, “barley,” is marked with aspiration. *Rhythmus* is Greek; in Latin it is called *modulatio*, “rhythm” or “measured cadence.”

LETTER S

[*Salutare* is a recommendation or counsel; *salubre* is something harmless, which does not cause injury; *salutare* is something beneficial. *Salubre* refers to a place and to food. *Saevus, saevio, saevi, saevisti* are written with the diphthong *ae*. *Sagena*, with *e*, means a net. *Sagina*, with *i*, means fodder or fattening.] *Sal* may be masculine or neuter. *Sartrix* or *sertrix* means one who mends. *Sarcinator* is one who keeps packs. *Sat* is written with *t*, since it is formed by apocope from *satisfit*. *Saturitas* is used of food; in other matters, *satietas*. [*Sanguis* is used while blood is flowing; once poured out, it is called *cruor*.] *Scio, scivi, scitum, sciturus* forms its principal parts, and from it comes *scisco*. *Scribo* is written with *b*. *Scripsi* must be written with *p*, because *b* changes into *p* in the past tense. [*Secturus*, not *sectaturus* [L., *secaturus*], derives from *seco*.] The ancients said *sedum*; therefore *sed* must be written with *d*. *Sedeo, sedi*, hence *sessurus*, with double *s*. [*Segnities* is a vice; *segnitia*, coldness.] *Sensus* is a noun of the fourth declension and a past participle from the passive verb *sentior*, whose perfect is also *sensus sum, sensus es, sensus est*, not *sentitus*.]

Often *b* in the preposition *sub* changes into the following consonant for the sake of euphony: *suffero*, “I endure”; *suggero*, “I offer”; *summitto*, “I send under”; *suppono*, “I place beneath.” Often it remains intact when the following syllable begins with a vowel: *subaudio*, “I hear secretly”; *subesse*, “to be under”; *subire*, “to undergo”; *subsistere*, “to stand beneath”; *subala*, “armpit.” *Sanies*, “corruption”; *soccordia*, “sluggishness”; *sitis*, “thirst”; and, in the neuter, *sulphur*, “sulfur”; *scrupulum*, “scruple”; *sinape*, “mustard”; and *siler*, “osier,” occur only in the singular. But Virgil wrote (*Georgics* 3.449): *Sulphura viva*, “living sulfur”; and Terence used the masculine *scrupulus*. 311 *Sero, seras, seravi* derives from closing, and these forms come from *sera*, “evening.” Since in the evening the gates of cities are closed, *sera* also means the bars by which the gates or entrances of cities are secured, as in the Psalm: “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (*Quoniam confortavit seras portarum tuarum*, Psalm 147:13).

*Sero, seris, sevi* derives from sowing. *Sero rumores*, “I spread rumors,” that is, “I make them public.” *Servile, civile,* and *olive* must be written with *v*, with a long *i* before *l*. *Servus* and *saevus* have double *u*, the first being a digamma and the second a vowel. Likewise *parvus, pravus,* and *corvus*. [*Servitium* is a multitude of slaves. *Servitus* is the condition of servitude. The ancients, however, used *servitium* indifferently for serving. *Similis sum tui moribus*, “I am like you in character.” *Similis sum tibi facie*, “I resemble you in appearance.”] *Sicut* means “as” or “just as.” *Primus* is first among many; *prior*, first of two. Likewise *postremus* is last among many; *posterior*, later of two. *Solemn e*, “customary,” because it is customary annually, is written with one *l*. But according to Priscian, the *m* should be joined to the following syllable. [*Sol* is declined in both numbers; in the singular it denotes the sun itself, but *soles* denotes the individual days on which the sun illuminates the sky. Some ancient writers, however, called the individual periods of time *soles*, as Horace began: “I commend my suns to your whole church.” And Maro (*Eclogue* 9.52):

> “Often I remember, while singing,  
> that as a boy I brought long days to an end.”

*Solium* properly means a royal seat; hence in Greek it is called *basilicos thronus*, “the royal throne.” *Somnio*, not *somnior*; *somniavi*, not *somniatus sum*.

[*Sors, sortis*, “lot”; and *sors, sordis*, “dirt,” are also used. Hence Ambrose: “Let him cleanse the vessels, lest any dirt disfigure the grace of the wine.” [Col. 0917B] Some deny, however, that *sordes* has a singular nominative.] *Spondeo, spopondi* loses the *s* in the second syllable, as Priscian holds. [Say *sterceratos agros*, not *stercoratos*, of fields to which manure is brought for fertilization.] *Studio tibi feci*, “I did it for you while I was eager to help you.” *Studio tuo feci id*, “I did it while you were eager.” [*Sumimus* is used when we ourselves receive something from another. Thus, when we give, we should say *accipe*, “receive”; when we allow someone to take it, we should say *sume*, “take.”] *Sumpsi* must be written with *p*; likewise *sumpturus*. *Supervus* is one who wishes to appear greater than he is. *Supter* is written with *p*, not *b*. [*Supter* is what is pressed by something above it. *Suptus* is what has been lowered and is not touched by anything higher. *Super* is what projects above; *supra*, what has something beneath it.] *Supplico divinae pietati*, “I supplicate divine mercy,” with double *p*. *Suppellex* is written with double *p*. *Syria, Syracusae,* and *symbolum*, as in the ancient books and in our own, ought to be written with *y*.

LETTER T

*Totidem* is written with *t*, because it derives from the numeral *tot*, “so many,” used adverbially. The preposition *trans* is sometimes full, as in *transtulit*, “he transferred”; *transeo*, “I cross”; *transactum*, “completed.” In some words it admits *n* and *s*: *traducit*, “he leads across”; *traicit*, “he throws across.” *Tabula* and *fabula* must be written with *b*. [*Testor* is used when confirming something by a statement. *Contestor* means affirming with a certain authority. *Protestor* means announcing openly what must be avoided. *Obtestor* means compelling someone to swear. *Attestor* means calling someone to testify who is distinguished by dignity or authority [L., “who is eminent”]. *Detestor* means rejecting something accursed. One *triumphat hostem*, “triumphs over an enemy,” when one conquers him. God *triumphat nos*, “triumphs over us,” when he grants aid to conquer enemies.]

The verb *transmigro* has two meanings. *Transmigro* is used when I travel from one place to another. It is also used with an accusative when I transfer someone from one place to another, as in: “Nebuchadnezzar transferred the Jews from Jerusalem to Babylon.” The participle *transmigrans* likewise has two meanings: someone passing from one place to another, and someone transferring another from one place to another.] *Tunc* is an adverb of time; *tum*, of sequence. [*Terga* are used only of human beings, with *tergum* in the singular. *Tergus* is used of quadrupeds and forms the plural *tergora*, “hides.”] Therefore, in the example given by the grammarian, the construction is faulty:

> “And with our spear we tire the turned backs of the young bulls.”

For he applied to animals what belonged to human beings; this is a *cacosyntheton*, an ill-constructed expression.

One must say *tinguere*, not *tingere*. *Temeritas* is rashness without deliberation; *audacia*, boldness after deliberation. *Temperantia* concerns dispositions; *temperatio*, things; *temperies*, the condition of the air. If *turbo* is a proper name, it forms *turbonis*; if a common noun, *turbinis*. For whether it means a wind or the toy with which boys play, it is *turbo*. Virgil (*Aeneid* 7.379):

> “The spinning top beneath the twisted lash.”

312 *Teloneum*, not *theloneum*, that is, with simple *t* and without added aspiration. In Greek it is *telon*; in Latin, *vectigal*, “tax” or “toll.” *Traho* and *veho* change aspiration into *x* in the perfect: *traxi, vexi*. Other words discard aspiration: we say *prehendo* and *prendo*; *vehemens* and *vemens*; *nihil, nil,* and *nihili*. [Col. 0918B] *Hercule!* and *ercle!* are adverbs of swearing.

LETTER V

*Vinea*, if it means a tree, has *i* in the first syllable and *e* in the second; if it concerns indulgence, the first syllable has *e* and the second *i*, as in *venia*, “indulgence” or “forgiveness.” We must say *urgere*, not *urguere*. Virgil: “They are pressed by punishments.” Likewise: “To wield weapons with the hand.” *Vaccas*, if it means animals, is written with *v*; if it means laurel flowers, that is, *baccas*, with *b*. *Vallis* and *vallum* must be written with *v*. *Ballistra* and *ballena* with *b*. *Valva*, meaning a door, with *v*. *Balba* is a movable noun: *balbus, balba, balbum*. What means slow-speaking is written with *b*. *Valde*, an adverb deriving from the noun *validus*, “strong,” and corruptly formed from it, must be written with *v*.

[Col. 0918C] *Vellus*, if it signifies wool, is written with *v*; if *bellus*, that is, beautiful, with *b*. *Ver* and *vir* are to be written with *v*. *Vel*, if it is a conjunction, with *v*; if it signifies moisture, with *f*; if it signifies an idol, with *b*. In *verbera*, the first syllable begins with *v*, the second with *b*. *Ulciscor* has *ultus sum* as its perfect form. *Volo, volas* derives from *volando* (“flying”). *Volo, vis* derives from volition; it naturally has no imperative, because commands belong to necessity, not to the will.

[*Vis* has a double meaning: that of strength, namely what in Greek is called ΔΥΝΑΜΙΣ (*dýnamis*), and that of violence, which in Greek is called ΒΙΑ (*bía*). *Verbex vobis* must begin with *v*, and its genitive is *verbeces*, with a long *e* in the second syllable. But *vertex*, *cordex*, and *codex* have a short *i* in their oblique cases, as in *verticis*, [Col. 0918D] *corticis*, *codicis*, and other such forms.]

[*Ulterior* and *ultimus* have no positive degree.] *Veniunt* means “those who sell”; *veneunt*, “those who are sold.” *Velocitas* applies to feet and bodies; *celeritas* to minds and actions. *Ulcus* is something that arises. [*Vulnus* is something inflicted by another. *Urgeo*, not *urguo*. Virgil: “By which they are pressed by punishments.” *Ungo, unxi*, just as *pingo, pinxi*, both without *u*; nevertheless, in the derived noun it adds it, as in *pinguis, unguine*.] *Vulva*, *malva*, and *stiva* are written with *v* in the place of a consonant. *Valde* is formed by removing the letter *i*, as though it were *valide*. For *valide* is the complete form. *Villus* is a garment; *villa* is an estate.

[*Vas, vadis*, “a surety in respect of a loan,” is masculine; *vas, vassis*, “a vessel,” is neuter. Both are written with *v*; *fas*, “what is divinely permitted,” with *f*.] [Col. 0919A] It is indeclinable; hence *fasti* are the days on which the law is proclaimed. *Vesper* has uncertain gender, as Priscian holds; [Col. 0920A] therefore the evangelist said: “In the evening, which dawns on the first day of the week.”

[Note: [Col. 0919D] [[Col. 0919] This note appears at the foot of columns 919 and 920, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text.] The manuscript codices have this title: “A Discussion of Rhetoric and of the Virtues of the Most Wise King Charles and of Albinus the Teacher.” The same codices preface it with a poem beginning: “Who, I ask, wishes to know civic customs,” omitting the verses added here by Quercetanus from a certain manuscript, which concern the categories and which we present below [Col. 0920D] in the Preliminary Notice to Alcuin’s *Dialectic*.]

[Col. 0919]

## THIRD OPUSCULUM. DIALOGUE ON RHETORIC AND THE VIRTUES

### 313. PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0919B]

The dialogue, or discussion, between Charles the Great and Albinus concerning rhetoric and the virtues first appeared, so far as we know, at Haguenau, together with another dialogue between the same men concerning dialectic, through the work of Menrad Molther, printed by Johann Secer in 1529, in octavo. I obtained this little book from the Hanover library through the generosity—also after his death—of that distinguished and eminent man among scholars, D. Ludovicus Scheid; the celebrated Baluzius once used it, as can be gathered from these words written in his own hand on the first page: “Stephanus Baluzius Tutelensis.” In the Thuana Library, volume II, page 255, another edition of the year 1565 is listed, in quarto, published at Douai by Matthaeus Gallenius under the title *Rhetorical Institutions*. Moreover, Cave and the great *Ecclesiastical Library*, under the entry “Alcuin,” cite another Parisian edition of 1549. Subsequently the same little work was inserted into the *Collection of Ancient Rhetoricians*, printed in Paris by Drouart and Perier, [Col. 0920B] in quarto; we have not, however, seen that collection. The distinguished Quercetanus collated his text with one manuscript codex and with these editions, but nevertheless left many errors, which we have removed with the aid of better manuscripts from the libraries of Saint Emmeram, Freising, the gymnasium of the city of Regensburg, and others. On the authority of these manuscripts we have also restored the poems appended to the work to their proper order.

In this little book Alcuin has one purpose above all: to transmit rules for conducting civil cases in a contentious court. Thus we learn what sort of art it was in which the most wise ruler of so many peoples, Charles the Great, wished above all to be instructed by his teacher Alcuin: namely, the art of settling correctly and justly the various cases of litigating parties, and of administering justice to all according to the utmost requirements of the laws. Near the end he treats of the virtues—very briefly, indeed, but vigorously—showing that secular studies ought to be directed toward the pursuit of virtue and ought not to impede it.

[Col. 0919]

Who, I ask, wishes to know civic customs,  
Let him read the precepts contained in this book.

King Charles wrote these amid the cares of the court,  
And Albinus likewise; the one gave them, the other approved them.

One work belongs to both, though the purpose of the two differs:  
The one is the father of the world, the other its poor inhabitant.

Do not despise the book, reader, for its small body;  
Within a very small body the bee carries honey for you. [Manuscript: *apes*, “bees.”]

### KING CHARLES AND THE TEACHER ALBINUS

[Col. 0919C]

**CHARLES.** Since God has brought you and brought you back [Note: [Col. 0920D] “Brought you and brought you back.” Namely, from England, around the year 781, after the Roman embassy, and after the pallium brought back from there for Eanbald the archbishop. It was then that he began teaching these arts at the court of Charles the Great.], venerable teacher Albinus, I ask that I may question you briefly about the precepts of rhetorical reasoning. For I remember that you once said that the whole force of this art is concerned with civil questions. But, as you know very well, because of the affairs of the kingdom and the cares of the palace we customarily engage constantly in such questions, and it seems ridiculous not to know the precepts of an art whose practical demands necessarily involve us every day. Indeed, since you opened for me, by a few answers of yours [Edition: *paucissimis*, “by very few answers,”] some of the doors of rhetorical art and the barriers of dialectical subtlety, [Col. 0919D] you have made me very intent upon these disciplines; especially because yesterday you skillfully led me into the storehouses of arithmetic, or illuminated me with the splendor of astronomy.

### 314. **ALBINUS.** 

God has illuminated you, my lord King Charles, with every light of wisdom and adorned you with the brilliance of knowledge, so that you can not only readily follow the minds of teachers but also quickly outstrip them in many respects. And although the spark of my little intellect can add nothing to the flame-bearing light of your wisdom, nevertheless, lest anyone mark me as disobedient, I shall readily answer your questions [Edition: *promptis*, “with ready answers”]; and may I do so as shrewdly as obediently.

**CHARLES.** First, teacher, explain to me the beginning of this art [or discipline].

**ALBINUS.** I shall explain it according to the authority of the ancients. For, as the story goes, there was once a time when human beings wandered everywhere through the fields like beasts, managing most things by bodily strength and not by any reasoning of the mind. Divine religion was not yet honored, nor was the order of human duty; but blind and rash desire, in order to satisfy itself, abused bodily strength. At that time a certain great and wise man recognized what material and how great an opportunity for the greatest undertakings lay within human minds, if someone could draw it out and improve it through instruction. By a certain method he compelled the people scattered through the fields and hidden in woodland shelters to come together in one place, gathering them into a community and introducing a kind of peace that was useful and honorable. At first they protested because of their insolence; then, because of reason and speech, they listened more attentively. He transformed them from wild and savage beings into gentle and civilized people. And it seems to me, my lord king, that this could not have been accomplished by a silent or impoverished eloquence, so as suddenly to turn people away from their accustomed way of life and lead them into different modes of living.

## WHAT RHETORIC IS

**CHARLES.** From what is *rhetoric* derived?

**ALBINUS.** From the Greek expression ἈΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΡΗΤΟΡΕΥΩ, which means “I declaim, plead, speak” [Manuscripts: “that is, abundance of expression”].

**CHARLES.** What end does it pursue?

**ALBINUS.** The science of speaking well.

**CHARLES.** With what matters is it concerned?

**ALBINUS.** With civil questions [that is, learned questions] which can be conceived by the natural power of the mind. For just as it is natural for everyone to defend himself and strike another, even if he has not learned this through weapons and training, so it is almost natural for everyone to accuse others and clear himself, even if he has not learned this through practice. But those who are instructed by disciplines and trained by use employ speech more effectively and readily. For speaking is natural to everyone; nevertheless, the person who speaks through grammar greatly excels others.

**CHARLES.** You speak well, teacher. Our whole life, too, advances through disciplines and gains strength through practice. Therefore explain to us the rules of this rhetorical discipline. The daily necessity of our duties compels us to exercise ourselves in them. And first, tell me what [Manuscripts: “how many”] the parts of this art are.

## ON ITS PARTS

[Col. 0921D] **ALBINUS.** There are five parts of the rhetorical art: invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery. Invention is the devising of true or plausible matters that make a case credible. Arrangement is the distribution of the matters discovered into an ordered structure. Expression is the adaptation of suitable words to the invention. Memory is the firm apprehension by the mind of the matters and words belonging to the invention. Delivery is the regulation of voice and body according to the dignity of the matters and words.

First one must discover what one is to say; next arrange what one has discovered; then explain in words what one has arranged; fourth, grasp in memory what one has discovered and arranged and clothed in speech; [Col. 0922A] finally and above all, deliver what one has grasped in memory.

**CHARLES.** If rhetoric is concerned with civil cases and questions, it seems necessary to me that the cases themselves have certain kinds, which I should like to know and have demonstrated to me by examples.

**ALBINUS.** The rhetorical art is concerned with three kinds, namely the demonstrative, the deliberative, and the judicial. The demonstrative kind is that which assigns praise or blame to a particular person, as we read in Genesis about Abel and Cain: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings; but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look.” The deliberative kind consists in persuasion and dissuasion, 315 as we read in the Second Book of Kings how Ahithophel persuaded Absalom to destroy his father David, and how Hushai dissuaded him [from that plan] in order to save the king. The judicial kind is that in which accusation and defense occur, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles how the Jews, together with a certain orator named Tertullus, accused Paul before the governor Felix, and how Paul defended himself before that same [governor]. For in judicial proceedings the question is more often what is equitable; in demonstrative discourse, what is honorable is understood; in deliberation, what is honorable and useful is considered.

## ON THE CIRCUMSTANCES

**CHARLES.** How many circumstances does a case have?

**ALBINUS.** A complete case has seven circumstances, namely person, act, time, place, manner, occasion, and ability. In the person, the question is who acted; in the act, what he did; in time, when he did it; in place, where the act occurred; in manner, how it could have been done; in occasion, why he wished to do it; in ability, whether he possessed the power to do it. Through these circumstances a case can be both confirmed and weakened. For it is useless to ask in a dispute what happened if the person who acted is absent. Conversely, it is useless to establish the person if the act is not connected with that person. Likewise, such an event could not have occurred at such a place [or at such a time]; [nor could it have occurred in the manner asserted]; nor did he wish to do it for that reason; nor did such a person possess the power to have done it.

**CHARLES.** How many are the places of disputes?

**ALBINUS.** The places of disputes, which rhetors call the constitutions of cases—that is, the points at which the question rests and on which the parties first fail to agree—are rational or legal.

**CHARLES.** How many rational constitutions are there?

**ALBINUS.** Four: of fact, of name, of quality, and of transference.

**CHARLES.** Give examples of each.

**ALBINUS.** The first is a dispute about the fact itself, as in: “You did it.” “I did not.” This first dispute, which rests on the fact, is called the conjectural constitution, because the matter must be investigated through conjectures as to whether he did it or did not.

But when the litigants agree about the fact, they often introduce a dispute about the name, because the accuser tries to increase the charge through the name, while the defender tries to lessen it. For example, if someone has stolen a sacred object from a private place, should he be called a thief or a sacrilegious person? The defender says that he is a thief, because a thief pays four times the value; the accuser says that he is sacrilegious, because a sacrilegious person is punished by death. This is called the definitive constitution, because what a thief is and what a sacrilegious person is must be defined by reasoning, and it must be determined under which definition the person falls who stole a sacred object from a private place.

But if the accuser and defender agree about both the fact and the name of the fact, then the evaluation of the fact must be sought—that is, what kind of fact it is, whether just or unjust, useful or useless. This is called the general constitution. The following is an example: A certain Roman commander, when surrounded by enemies and unable to escape in any way, made an agreement with the enemy that he would surrender his arms. [Col. 0923B] After surrendering the arms, however, he brought his army out safely. Some accuse him of treason. Here both parties agree about the fact and about the name of the fact; but what kind of act it was is questioned in this way: “Was it better to lose the soldiers or to accept this most disgraceful condition?” This constitution has several parts, which we shall discuss below.

In the fourth constitution, which we call transference [Manuscript: “translative”], the question is whether the person who did the act ought to have done it, or whether he ought to have done it at that time, in that manner, in that place, or with those people with whom he did it. For example, if Orestes is accused of having killed his mother Clytemnestra [Manuscript: “Clemestra”]: it was not right for a son to kill his mother, although she had killed Agamemnon, his father and king of the Greeks. Here it must be asked through transference whether he acted rightly [Col. 0923C] [Manuscript: “whether he would have acted rightly”] or not.

**CHARLES.** Once the constitution of the case has been found, how is the constitution itself then to be considered?

**ALBINUS.** Once the constitution of the case has been discovered, it is immediately appropriate to consider whether the question of the case is simple or compound. A simple question contains only one question, as in: “Shall I declare war on the Corinthians or not?” [Manuscript: “Shall we declare war?”] A compound question consists of several questions, as in: “Should Carthage be destroyed, restored to the Carthaginians, or settled with a colony?”

### 316. **CHARLES.** 

But now confirm the legal constitutions with examples.

**ALBINUS.** It must be considered [as I have already said] whether the dispute is based on reasoning or on a written text. A dispute based on a written text arises from a written law, as follows:

**LAW:** “Let those who abandon a ship in a storm lose everything, and let the cargo and ship belong to those who remain aboard.”

Two men were sailing on the open sea, one owning the ship and the other its cargo. Moved by compassion, they took on board a certain shipwrecked man who was swimming. Later, when the storm began to toss them about even more violently, to such a degree that the owner of the ship, who was also the pilot, climbed into a skiff [Manuscript: “fled into”] that was attached to the ship by a rope, he did what he could from there to assist the ship. The man whose goods they were, however, lay upon his sword there in the ship [Manuscript: “would lie upon it”]; but the shipwrecked man went to the helm and steered the ship. When the storm had subsided, the ship reached the harbor [Manuscript: “is brought into harbor”]. The man who had lain upon the sword, having been only lightly wounded, recovered from his injury. Each of these three claimed the ship and its cargo for himself according to the written law. Here a question arises from the text: whose is the ship? Definitions must be supplied of what it means to abandon a ship and what it means to remain in a ship.

Ambiguity in a written law also often produces a question, as follows:

“Let a prostitute have no crown; if she has one, let it be confiscated.”

Here the ambiguity in the wording is whether the prostitute or the crown is to be confiscated.

A question also often arises from conflicting laws, when one law provides one thing about a matter and another provides something different.

**LAW:** “Whoever kills a tyrant may ask the magistrate for whatever thing he wishes as a reward, and shall receive it.”

**ANOTHER LAW:** “Once the tyrant has been killed, his nearest relatives by blood shall also be killed.”

Thebe, the wife of Alexander, who had seized tyranny in Thessaly, killed him at night. She demanded as her reward the son whom she had by the tyrant. Some say that, under the law, the boy ought to be killed; others say that he ought to be returned to his mother as her reward. The matter is before the court. Here it must be considered which law concerns the greater public benefit, which was written first, and what lawmakers each law had.

A controversy between the written text and its meaning arises when one party uses the very words that are written, while the other adds an entire argument directed toward what he says the writer intended [Manuscript: “will intend”]. Thus there is a law that forbids the gates to be opened at night. Someone opens them and admits friends into the town, lest they be overwhelmed by the enemy [Col. 0924C] if they remained outside. The accuser attends only to the letter; the defender to the meaning: he says that the writer of the law ordered the gates of the town to be closed against enemies, not against friends. Questions arise from the written text through reasoning or through definition of the law, when one party tries to interpret the text in one way and the other in another, or when they try to define the writer’s meaning differently. Such questions, as I have said, arise from the written text.

**CHARLES.** Once the place of the dispute has been understood, according to what you have said—whether it is based on reasoning or on a written text—where should the mind then be directed?

**ALBINUS.** It must be determined what the question, the reasoning, the judgment, and the support of the case are.

**CHARLES.** Speak about each separately.

**ALBINUS.** The question is the constitution on which the dispute of the case rests, as in: “You acted unjustly.” “I acted justly.” The reasoning is what the defendant uses to explain why he acted justly.
