Thus Orestes, if accused of matricide, has no defense unless he says: “I acted justly, for she had killed my father.” The judgment is derived from the reasoning. Its general form is: “Was it right for Orestes to have his mother killed, since she had killed Orestes’ father?” The support is the defender’s strongest argument—for example, if Orestes wishes to say that his mother’s attitude toward his father, toward himself, toward the kingdom, and toward her entire family was such that her children ought above all to have exacted punishment from her.

**CHARLES.** You said earlier that the general constitution had several parts [Edition: “which consists of several parts”]. I ask you, teacher, to explain them to me and confirm them by examples one by one, while I remain silent and approve.

**ALBINUS.** [I shall do so.] The controversy that demonstrates what kind of act the defendant is charged with is called the general constitution, and it has two parts: judicial and practical. The practical part is concerned with considering what the law requires according to civil custom and equity. The judges are responsible for this careful inquiry, and it contains an involved controversy concerning civil law, as follows:

A certain man, while he had no son, made an orphan his heir; but the orphan died before the inheritance had come into his power. A controversy arises from the father’s secondary heirs: “The possession is ours.” The claim of the orphan’s relatives is: “The money is ours, since our relative made no testament concerning it.” The rebuttal is: “On the contrary, it is ours, since we are the heirs named in the father’s will.” The question is the basis of the argument [Manuscript: “of the reasoning”]: “For the father wrote a will for the orphan; therefore what belongs to him must necessarily become ours.” The refutation of the argument is: “On the contrary, the father named a secondary heir for himself, not for the orphan; therefore the inheritance cannot become yours through that man’s will.” The judgment is: “Can anyone make a testament concerning the property of an orphan son [Edition: ‘make a re-testament concerning the sons of an orphan’], or are the father’s secondary heirs heirs of the head of the household himself but not also heirs of his orphan son?”

The judicial part is that in which the question concerns what is equitable and inequitable, and the basis of reward or punishment. It has two parts: absolute and assumptive. The absolute part contains within itself a question of right and wrong, as follows:

[Col. 0925C] When the Thebans had defeated the Lacedaemonians in war—and it is almost the custom of the Greeks, whenever they have waged war among themselves, for the victors to set up some trophy within their borders as a temporary declaration of victory [Manuscripts: “as a declaration of victory”], not so that the memory of the war might remain forever—they set up a bronze trophy. They are accused before the common council of Greece. The claim is: “It was not permitted.” The rebuttal is: “It was permitted.” The question is: “Was it permitted?” The reasoning is: “For by our valor we won such glory from the war that its eternal insignia should be left to our descendants; we set up the trophy.” The refutation is: “Nevertheless, it is not right for Greeks to set up against Greeks an eternal monument of hostility.” The judgment is: “When the Greeks set up against Greeks an eternal monument of hostility in order to celebrate supreme valor, did they act rightly or not?”

The assumptive part occurs when the act itself cannot be justified, but is defended by an argument assumed from elsewhere. It has four parts: comparison, transfer of guilt, removal of guilt, and concession [Manuscripts: “confession”].

Comparison occurs when some other act is shown [Manuscripts: “asserted”] to have been right or useful, and the act of which the defendant is accused is said to have been committed so that the other act could be performed, as in the example given shortly before [Manuscripts: “which we gave”]. When a Roman commander was surrounded by enemies and could not escape by any means except by making peace with the enemy and surrendering his arms, he preserved his soldiers by surrendering the arms; [Col. 0926A] but [afterward] he was accused of treason. The claim is: “It was not permitted to surrender the arms.” The rebuttal is: “It was permitted.” The question is: “Was it permitted?” The reasoning is: “For all the soldiers would have perished if I had not done this.” The refutation is: “That is not why you did it.” From these comes the judgment: “Would they have perished? And did you do it for that reason?” The comparison is: “Was it better to accept this most disgraceful condition or for the soldiers to perish?”

Transfer of guilt occurs when the defendant, having admitted the act of which he is accused, demonstrates that he acted justly because another person led him into the offense. It is as follows:

After Horatius had killed the three Curiatii [Manuscripts: “Curiatii” in another spelling] and lost two brothers, he returned home victorious. He noticed that his sister did not grieve over the death of her brothers [Manuscripts: “was not troubled by it”], but repeatedly called upon the name of her fiancé, one of the Curiatii, with groaning and lamentation. Unable to bear this, he killed the girl [Edition: “seeing this and being indignant, he killed the girl”]. He is accused. The claim is: “You unjustly killed your sister.” The rebuttal is: “I killed her justly.” The question is: “Did he kill her justly?” The reasoning is: “For she mourned the death of the enemy, neglected that of her brothers, and took the victory of myself and the Roman people badly.” The refutation is: “Nevertheless, a sister should not have been killed by her brother without trial.” The resulting judgment is: “When Horatia neglected the death of her brothers, mourned that of the enemy, and did not rejoice in the victory of her brother and the state, was it right for her to be killed without trial by her brother?”

Removal of guilt occurs when the claim concerning the act brought by the opponent is shifted to another person or another matter. This happens in two ways [Manuscripts: “in two parts”], for both the cause and the act itself are shifted.

Let this be an example of the removal of the cause: The Rhodians sent certain men as envoys to Athens. The officials had not provided the envoys with the expenses that ought to have been supplied, and the envoys did not depart. They are accused. The claim is: “They ought to have departed.” The rebuttal is: “They ought not to have departed.” The question is: “Should they have departed?” The reasoning is: “For the expenses customarily supplied from public funds were not given to them by the official.” The refutation is: “Nevertheless, you ought to have completed the public business entrusted to you.” The judgment is: “When the expenses owed from public funds were not given to those who were envoys, should they nevertheless have completed the business of their embassy?”

The act itself is shifted when the defendant denies that what is charged as a crime concerned either himself or his office, and says that even if there was some offense in it, it ought not to be attributed to him. The case is as follows:

Under a treaty once made with the Samnites, a certain noble young man held a pig at the commander’s order. When the treaty was rejected in the senate and the commander was handed over to the Samnites, someone in the senate said that the man who had held the pig ought also to be handed over. The claim is: “He ought to be handed over.” The rebuttal is: “He ought not to be.” The question is: “Should he be?” The reasoning is: “For it was neither my office nor my power to decide this, since I was not of the requisite age, was a private citizen, and the commander, possessing the highest authority and power, gave the order and saw to it that a sufficiently honorable treaty was concluded.” The refutation is: “Since you became a participant in a most disgraceful treaty, it is right that you be handed over as a matter of the highest religious obligation.” The judgment is: “When a man who possessed no power took part in a treaty and in so solemn a religious obligation at the commander’s order, ought he to be handed over to the enemy [or not]?”

This kind of case differs from the preceding one in that in the former the defendant admits that he ought to have done what the accuser says ought to have been done, but attributes the cause to some matter or person that prevented him from acting according to his will. In this case, however, he must not accuse another or transfer blame to someone else; he must show that the matter had nothing to do with him, with his power, or with his office.

Concession is the form by which the defendant does not justify the act itself but asks that he be forgiven. It has [two] parts: purification and supplication.

[Col. 0927B] Purification is the defense not of the act itself of the accused person but of his intention. It has three parts: ignorance, accident, and necessity.

Ignorance occurs when the accused denies that he knew something. For example: Among certain people there was a law that no one should sacrifice a calf to Diana. Some sailors, while being tossed about on the open sea by a contrary storm, vowed that if they reached the harbor they saw, they would sacrifice a calf to the god who was there. By chance there was in that harbor a shrine of Diana, to whom it was not permitted to sacrifice a calf. Unaware of the law, they disembarked and sacrificed the calf. They are accused. The claim is: “You sacrificed a calf to that goddess to whom it was not permitted.” The rebuttal consists in concession. The reasoning is: “I did not know that it was forbidden.” The refutation is: “Nevertheless, because you did what the law forbade, you deserve punishment.” The judgment is: “When someone has done what he ought not to have done, but did not know that it ought not to be done, is he deserving of punishment?”

Accident is introduced into a concession when it is shown that some force of fortune [Edition: “the force of his fortune”] stood in the way of the person’s will, as in this case:

Among the Lacedaemonians there was a law that, unless a contractor had supplied victims for a certain sacrifice, the penalty was death. When the day of the sacrifice approached, the man who had undertaken the contract began to drive the victims from the countryside into the city. Suddenly, however, the river Eurotas, which flows past Lacedaemon, was swollen and made violent by great storms, so that the victims could in no way be brought across it. To demonstrate his good will, the contractor placed all the victims on the riverbank, so that those on the opposite side of the river could see them. Although everyone recognized that the sudden swelling of the river had been the impediment [to his efforts], some nevertheless condemned him to death [Manuscripts: “summoned him to trial”]. The claim is: “The victims that you ought to have brought for the sacrifice were not present.” The rebuttal is: concession. The reasoning is: “For the river suddenly rose, and for that reason they could not be brought across.” The refutation is: “Nevertheless, because what the law commands was not done, you deserve punishment.” The judgment is: “When, in a matter where the contractor acted contrary to the law, the sudden swelling of the river opposed his efforts, is he deserving of punishment?”

Necessity is introduced when the defendant is defended on the ground that he acted under some force, as follows:

The Rhodians have a law that if a ship equipped with a ram is found in the harbor, it is to be confiscated. When there was a great storm on the open sea, the force of the winds drove a ship into the harbor of the Rhodians against the will of the sailors. The official says that the ship belongs to the state [Manuscripts: “calls it the people’s ship”]. The owner of the ship denies that it ought to be confiscated. The claim is: “A ship equipped with a ram was found in the harbor.” The rebuttal is: concession. The reasoning is: “We were driven into the harbor by force and necessity.” 319 The refutation is: “Nevertheless, under the law the ship ought to belong to the state” [Manuscripts: “ought”]. The judgment is: “When the law confiscates a ship equipped with a ram found in the harbor, and this ship was driven into the harbor by the force of the storm against the will of the sailors, should it be confiscated?”

Supplication occurs when the defendant confesses both that he committed the offense and that he committed it deliberately, yet asks that he be forgiven. This kind of case can occur very rarely, since it contains not a defense of the act but a request for pardon. This kind of case can scarcely be approved in court. Therefore, once the offense has been admitted, it is difficult to obtain forgiveness from the person who ought to be the avenger of offenses.

There you have the places of questions, the constitutions of cases, and the parts of the constitutions—matters that, as nature reveals them, you recognize through daily practice.

**CHARLES.** I shall recognize them if the Creator of natures helps me [Edition: “may he help me”]. Nevertheless, I still have something to ask you.

**ALBINUS.** Ask whatever you wish; I shall proceed wherever you lead me.

## ON THE PERSONS

**CHARLES.** How many persons are ordinarily involved in judicial proceedings?

**ALBINUS.** Four: the accuser in the case, the defender of the case, the witnesses [Edition: “the witness”], and the judge.

[Col. 0928C] **CHARLES.** What office does each perform?

**ALBINUS.** The judge uses equity, the witness truth, the accuser a claim intended to enlarge the case, and the defender a reduction intended to diminish it—unless the case happens to concern praise or a petition for reward. Then the order is reversed: the accuser must use reduction and the defender amplification.

**CHARLES.** In how many ways are amplification and reduction of a case achieved?

**ALBINUS.** In two ways: through impulse or through reasoning. Impulse is what urges someone to do something without reflection, through a certain emotion of the mind, such as love, anger, grief, drunkenness, and, in general, every state in which the mind seems to have been affected in such a way that it could not examine the matter with deliberation and care, but did what it did through a kind of emotional impulse rather than through reflection. Reasoning, on the other hand, is the careful and considered devising of a reason for doing or not doing something. It is said to have been present when the mind appears to have avoided or pursued something for a definite reason: if an act is said to have been done for the sake of friendship; to avenge an enemy; from fear; for glory; for money; or, to embrace everything generally, to retain, increase, or acquire some advantage—or, conversely, to reject, diminish, or avoid some disadvantage.

**CHARLES.** How should the accuser or defender use impulse or reasoning?

**ALBINUS.** When the accuser says that something was done under impulse, he must amplify in words and arguments that impulse, agitation, and emotion of the mind, and show how great is the force of love, how great a disturbance of the mind arises from anger, or from any of the causes that he says produced the impulse to do the act, so that it does not seem surprising if a mind stirred by such an agitation proceeded to some crime. He should confirm this with examples of people who previously committed similar acts under a similar impulse.

But when he says that someone committed an act not through impulse but through reasoning, he will show what advantage the person pursued or what disadvantage he sought to avoid, and he will magnify it as much as possible. Thus, if the act was done for the sake of glory, he should show how much glory the person thought he would gain. Likewise, if it was for domination, money, friendship, enmity, [Col. 0929B] or anything else that he says benefits the case, he must amplify it to the greatest extent.

The defender, on the contrary, will proceed in the opposite way. First, he will say that there was no impulse; or, if he admits that there was one, he will diminish it and show that it was very slight; or he will teach that acts of this kind do not ordinarily arise from such an impulse. He will weaken the suspicions of reasoning by saying either that there was no advantage, or only a small one, or that it belonged more to others, or that it belonged no more to the defendant than to others [Manuscripts: “more to him”]; or that the disadvantage to him was greater than the advantage, so that the magnitude of the alleged advantage could in no way have been sufficient; or that it could not be compared with the disadvantage that occurred or the danger that was incurred. All these same arguments will likewise be handled in relation to the avoidance of disadvantage.

## 320. ON THE DUTY OF THE PERSONS

[Col. 0929C]

**CHARLES.** Since you have spoken of the persons in a case, tell me, I ask, the places of the individual persons.

**ALBINUS.** I shall do so, although this belongs not so much to the precepts of the art [Edition: “these matters belong …”] as to the proper conduct of office. The judge is on the tribunal, with the case placed before him in the middle, for praise or punishment—for example, a defense or betrayal of the fatherland. The accuser is on the left. The defender of the case is on the right. The witnesses are behind [Edition: “also behind”].

**CHARLES.** Do they each have their own insignia?

**ALBINUS.** They do. The judge must be armed with the scepter of equity, the accuser with the dagger of malice, the defender with the shield of piety, and the witnesses with the trumpet of truth.

## ON THE PARTS OF SPEECH

[Col. 0929D] **CHARLES.** Even after all these circumstances adjoining the case have been found, what must then be sought, teacher?

**ALBINUS.** What else but the individual parts of the whole case?

CAR. I desire to hear what those parts are, and how many.

ALB. There are six [for there are six] parts by which a speech must be arranged by an orator: the opening of the case, the narration, the confirmation, the partition, the refutation, and the conclusion.

CAR. What is the opening?

ALB. A speech that suitably prepares the listener’s mind for the rest of the discourse.

CAR. How is this accomplished?

ALB. First, by making the listener well-disposed, attentive, and receptive.

CAR. As I see it, this must be attended to above all: that the listener be made well-disposed, attentive, and receptive. [Col. 0930A] But I should like to know how this can be done.

ALB. Goodwill is secured from four sources: from ourselves, from our opponents, from the person of the judges, and from the case itself.

From ourselves: if we speak without arrogance about our own deeds and services; if we dispel charges brought against us and certain less honorable suspicions cast upon us; if we bring forward the disadvantages that have occurred or the difficulties that threaten; and if we use humble and suppliant prayer and entreaty.

From the person of our opponents: if we bring them into hatred, envy, or contempt. We bring them into hatred if something they have done shamefully, arrogantly, cruelly, or maliciously is reported [the manuscripts read “they will be brought”]. We bring them into envy if their force, power, money, wealth, or kinship is brought forward, [Col. 0930B] together with their arrogant and intolerable use of these things, and the fact that they seem to place greater confidence in these matters than in their own case. They are brought into contempt if their inactivity, negligence, cowardice, lazy diligence, and luxurious leisure are displayed.

Goodwill will be won from the person of the listeners if deeds performed by them courageously, gently, and wisely are brought forward. This must by no means appear to be flattery: rather, one should show how honorable their reputation is considered to be, and how great is the expectation placed upon their judgment and authority.

From the circumstances of the case: if we raise our own case by praising it and lower the case of the others through contempt.

We shall make the listeners attentive if we demonstrate that what we are about to say is important, new, and incredible; or that it concerns everyone, or those who will hear it, or certain distinguished persons, [Col. 0930C] or the immortal gods, or the highest interests of the commonwealth; and if we promise that we shall shortly demonstrate our case and set out the point or points for judgment, if there are several.

We shall make the listeners receptive if we explain the substance of the case openly and briefly—that is, what the dispute consists in. But whoever wishes to make a good opening must first carefully recognize the type of his case.

CAR. How many types of cases are there?

ALB. Five: honorable, astonishing, low, doubtful, and obscure. An honorable type of case is one to which the listener’s mind immediately gives its support, without any speech of ours. An astonishing type is one from which the minds of those who are going to listen are alienated. [Col. 0930D] A low type is one that the listener disregards and does not seem worth much attention. A doubtful type is one in which either the judgment is uncertain, or the case shares both honor and disgrace, so as to produce goodwill and offense. An obscure type is one in which either the listeners are slow, or the case is entangled in matters difficult to understand.

### 321

CAR. Must an orator always begin plainly?

ALB. Sometimes plainly, sometimes indirectly. A plain speech is one to which the listener’s mind immediately gives its support, as occurs in an honorable type of case [the edition reads “case”]. But one that proceeds indirectly steals secretly into the listener’s mind, [Col. 0931A] as must be done in a low, doubtful, or obscure type of case.

This also must be understood: the opening ought to contain a very large measure of force and gravity, and, in general, everything pertaining to dignity; but very little display and polish [the manuscript reads “polishedness”]. For from these arises a certain suspicion of artificial diligence, which chiefly deprives the speech of credibility and the orator of authority.

CAR. Now I understand how a case ought to begin. Explain the structure of the narration.

ALB. Narration is an account of things done [or: of things as though done]. It ought to have three qualities: it must be brief, clear, and credible.

It will be brief if it begins where it must, rather than repeating matters from the very end; and if, when it is enough to state the substance of something, its parts are not also narrated. [Col. 0931B] For it is often enough to say what happened without narrating how it happened; and if the narration does not proceed farther than necessary; and if the speech does not pass over to some other matter; and if it is expressed so that sometimes what has not been said may be understood from what has been said; and if not only what is harmful but also what is neither harmful nor helpful is omitted; and if one refrains no less from an abundance of unnecessary matters than from an abundance of unnecessary words.

The narration can be clear if whatever happened first is explained first [the manuscript reads “whatever will be”], and the order of matters and times is preserved, so that things are narrated as they happened [the manuscript reads “as they will be”], or as they seemed capable of happening. Here care must be taken that nothing be stated in a confused or distorted manner, and that it not pass into [any] other matter. [Col. 0931C]

The narration will be credible if it appears to contain what normally appears in reality; if the dignities of the persons are preserved; if the causes of their actions are evident; if the opportunities for carrying them out seem to have existed [the manuscript reads “for doing”]; if the time was suitable; if there was enough space; and if the place is shown to have been appropriate for the same matter about which the narration is given [the manuscript reads “will be narrated”]. The matter must also be adapted both to the nature of those who acted, to popular report, and to the opinion of those who listen [the manuscript reads “who will listen”].

CAR. The order of things requires you to speak about the partition.

ALB. I shall do so. Partition is the division of matters relevant to the case itself. When properly made, it renders the whole speech clear and distinct. It has [Col. 0931D] two parts.

One part shows what is agreed with the opponents and what remains in dispute. Through it, something definite is assigned to the listener, upon which his mind ought to remain occupied.

The other part briefly sets out and distributes the matters about which we are going to speak [the text supplies “are”]. Through it the listener is enabled to hold definite matters in his mind. This part too ought to possess brevity, completeness, and limitation.

Brevity exists when no word is introduced unless it is necessary. Completeness is the quality by which we embrace in the partition all the classes of matters arising in the case about which we must speak. Limitation is the quality by which the partition includes only those matters that must again be discussed; and we must not say that we shall demonstrate more than is sufficient. [Col. 0932A]

In this way I shall show that the opponents could have done, wished to do, and did what we charge them with, although it is enough to show that they did it [the manuscript reads “could have done”].

CAR. Now turn to the rules of confirmation, master. I think these are especially necessary for everyone, so that each person may know how to confirm his own case; and although someone may act voluntarily, he cannot act with sufficient propriety without rules and practice.

ALB. It is as you say, my lord king. For all argumentation tends toward the methods of confirmation. But the forest of arguments is so vast that scarcely anything can be disclosed within the brevity of this dialogue of ours.

CAR. Nevertheless, compress many things into a few. Often one key opens many treasures in a treasury. [Col. 0932B]

ALB. I shall do what I can [the manuscript reads “as I can”]. Confirmation is argumentation by which you acquire credibility and authority for your case. It is accomplished in two ways: either from persons or from matters.

From persons, we consider these attributes: name, nature, way of life, fortune, condition, result [the manuscript reads “affection”], pursuits, plans, deeds, accidents, and speeches. For arguments can be drawn from each of these, according as the convenience of the case presents itself [the manuscript reads “offers itself”].

### 322

CAR. Although you are aiming at brevity, I nevertheless want a full account of this.

ALB. An argument is drawn from a name in the following way: for example, if we say that someone is called “cunning” because he acts with rash and sudden deliberation. Let us also use an example from Sacred Scripture: Esau says of his brother [Jacob], “Rightly is his name called Jacob”—that is, “supplanter”—“for a second time he has supplanted me.” [Col. 0932C]

In nature, sex, nation, fatherland, kinship, and age are considered. In sex: is the person a man or a woman? In nation: Greek or barbarian? In fatherland: Athenian or Roman? In kinship: from what ancestors and what blood-relations was he born? In age: a boy or an adolescent; older or an old man?

Likewise, an inference must often be drawn from the advantages or disadvantages of nature, as follows: strong or weak, tall or short, handsome or ugly, swift or slow, sharp or dull; retentive or forgetful, deceitful or simple.

Many suspicions are also drawn from a person’s associations and upbringing [the manuscript reads “way of life”], when it is asked how, among whom, and by whom he was raised and instructed; [Col. 0932D] with whom he associates; what his manner of life is; and what his domestic custom is [the text supplies “he lives”].

Argumentation more often arises from fortune when it is considered whether someone is a slave or free, wealthy or poor, noble or ignoble, fortunate or unfortunate, a private person or under another’s authority, or whether he was, is, or will be so; or, finally, when something is sought among the attributes understood to belong to fortune.

Condition consists in some complete and stable development of the mind or body. In this category are virtue, knowledge, and their opposites. The matter itself and the case will show what is relevant, and what this source of suspicion also reveals. [Col. 0933A]

For the nature of affection commonly presents a clear inference—for example, love, anger, or distress—because both their force is understood and the things that follow from each of them are easy to recognize.

A pursuit is a persistent and intense occupation, undertaken with great pleasure and directed toward some matter. Argumentation is readily drawn from it, according as the case itself requires [the edition reads “will be required”]. Something suspicious is likewise inferred from a plan; for a plan is a devised method of doing or not doing something [the manuscript reads “of doing”].

Deeds, accidents, and speeches are considered in relation to three times: what he did, what happened to him, or what he said; [Col. 0933B] what he is doing, what is happening to him, or what he is saying; or what he is going to do, what is going to happen to him, and what speech he is going to use. From these it will easily be seen what they contribute to confirming an inference of suspicion.

CAR. Are these sources common to the accuser and the defender?

ALB. They are employed according to the advantage of each side’s case.

CAR. How?

ALB. The accuser must condemn the life previously lived by the person whom he accuses, or his insolent nature; his malicious pursuits, wicked character, or bloody deeds. He must show, if he can, whether the man has previously been convicted of a similar offense [the manuscript reads “of some comparable offense”], and how disgraceful, greedy, insolent, or bloodthirsty he was, so that it should not be surprising that such a man rushed into such a crime. [Col. 0933C]

For to the extent that something is taken away from the honor and authority of the accused, to that extent the power of his entire defense is diminished. If the accused cannot be disgraced by any previous offense, the judges should be urged not to judge the man’s old reputation but the man’s new crime [the manuscript reads “that it must be judged”]. Previously, what he was had been concealed; now it is manifest. Therefore this matter should not be judged from his earlier life; rather, his earlier life should be condemned on account of this disgrace [the manuscript reads “the earlier life ought to be considered … condemned”].

CAR. If the accuser thrusts all these things upon the accused, what place of defense remains for him?

ALB. A suitable place of defense remains. Often, when one shield protects him, many harmful darts are repelled. [Col. 0933D]

First, the defender ought, if he can, to demonstrate that the accused’s life was most honorable and trustworthy, whether toward the commonwealth, his parents, his relatives, or his friends. His good deeds, if there are any [the manuscript reads “whatever there may be”], must be brought forward faithfully and courageously. It should be shown to be pitiable that such distinguished virtues should be obscured by so small an offense.

He should also show that he committed this very act not from any desire, malice, or disloyalty, but by accident, ignorance, or the suggestion of another; and that no one can wish to strive for the advancement of his fatherland, filial devotion toward his parents, or dignity of character [the edition reads “for devotion … for dignity”], if earlier good deeds are to be annulled by any minor [or trivial] offense. Moreover, it is harmful to the best men if any malicious person dares to bring accusations against the good.

### 323

[Col. 0934A] If there are also some disgraceful elements in his earlier life, it must be said that he committed them [the text has “him”] through imprudence [or “necessity”], or at the prompting of youth; or that they were fabricated by the envy of certain persons, or brought against him through a false opinion.

But if the disgrace or infamy of his life cannot in any way be softened by speech, one must deny that inquiry should be made into his life or character [the manuscript reads “to inquire”], and insist that the question concerns only the single crime of which he is accused. Therefore, leaving aside his past, one must deal with what is immediately at issue.

CAR. You said that some arguments come from persons and others from matters. What you have just described comes from persons. It remains for you to discuss those that come from matters. First, tell me what you call a matter [the manuscript reads “what you call matters”].

ALB. A matter is the deed itself over which there is a dispute between the accuser and the defender. [Col. 0934B]

When arguments are to be drawn from matters, three things must be considered. First, what came before the deed, what occurred in the deed, and what came after it. For example, in the case of the innkeeper [the edition reads “the case: you place”]:

Before the deed: the two men were traveling together as friends; they turned aside together to an inn; they dined together.

In the deed: night, sleep [the edition reads “dream”], and the killing.

After the deed: that he went away alone; that he abandoned his companion; that he possessed a bloody sword.

There is also a fourth point relating to the matter: what law applies to the deed; who its authorities are; or by what name the act that was done ought to be called.

Before the deed, the cause of the act must be considered: did he kill the man in hope of gain, out of enmity, from fear, or for the sake of a friend [the edition reads “friendship”]? [Col. 0934C] For it is incredible that anyone should wish to kill a man without reason.

In the performance of the deed, place, time, opportunity, method, and ability are usually considered: that is, it must be asked in what place, at what time, by what method, on what occasion, or by what means he killed the man.

After the deed has been carried out, certain signs of the deed will be considered: blood is a sign of killing, and flight is often a sign of guilt.

CAR. Now that the sources of arguments and confirmations have been recalled, argumentation itself, as I think, cannot possibly be uniform.

ALB. It is not uniform. But every argumentation constructed from the sources we have recalled must be either probable or necessary. [Col. 0934D]

Necessary argumentation is that which cannot happen otherwise, as in: “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man.” Such arguments are formed either by dilemma, by enumeration, or by simple conclusion.

By dilemma: in it, whichever alternative you concede is turned against you, in this manner: “If he is wicked, why do you defend him? If he is good, why do you accuse him?”

By enumeration: several possibilities are introduced, from which one conclusion necessarily follows, as follows: “It is necessary that this man was killed by him either out of enmity, or fear, or hope of gain, or for the sake of some friend. If none of these motives exists, it follows that this man was not killed by him; for a man cannot be killed without reason.”

By simple conclusion, in this way: “If you say that I did that at that time, I was crossing the sea at that time [the edition reads ‘then’]. [Col. 0935A] Therefore I not only did not do what you say, but could not even have done it [the manuscript reads ‘could not have done it’].”

CAR. As I understand, these arguments are altogether necessary. But, as I also see, one must carefully consider how this type of argumentation might be refuted.

ALB. It is as you understand, Charles [the manuscript omits the vocative “Charles”].

CAR. The arguments you described are necessary. Now describe the probable ones also [the manuscript reads “describe”].

ALB. Probable arguments are those that ordinarily happen truly, as in: “If she is a mother, she loves her son”; “If he is greedy, he disregards his oath.”

CAR. Are probable arguments always true?

ALB. Some are true in opinion; [Col. 0935B] others in resemblance.

In opinion: “The underworld is beneath the earth.” Resemblance is observed in opposites and in equals.

CAR. How in opposites and in equals?

ALB. In opposites, as follows: “If it is fitting to pardon those who have harmed us unintentionally, ought gratitude not to be shown to those who have benefited us necessarily?”

From an equal comparison [sic]: “As a harborless place cannot be safe for ships, so a mind without trust cannot be stable for friends.”

### 324

CAR. Is every argumentation confirmed, adorned, and examined only from these sources?

ALB. There are also arguments handled through induction or reasoning, but these belong more properly to philosophers. [Col. 0935C]

CAR. Nevertheless, speak about them.

ALB. Induction is a speech that proves something uncertain through certain matters and leads an unwilling person to assent.

CAR. This seems strange, if it can make someone consent against his will.

ALB. You will hear an example and perhaps believe it because of it.

A certain philosopher once entered into a discussion with Xenophon and his wife [the edition reads “after a discussion had begun”]. First he began a conversation with Xenophon’s wife:

“Tell me, please, wife of Xenophon: if your neighbor possessed more gold than you possess, would you prefer that gold or your own?”

“That,” she replied.

“What if she possessed clothing and other feminine adornments of greater value than those you possess? Would you prefer yours or hers?”

She replied, “Hers.”

“Come now,” he said, “what if she had a better husband than you have? Would you prefer your husband or hers?”

‘His,’ she replied. [Col. 0935D]

At this the woman blushed.

The philosopher then began a conversation with Xenophon.

“Please tell me, Xenophon: if your neighbor had a better horse than yours, would you prefer your horse or his?”

“His,” he replied.

“What if he possessed a better estate than you possess? Would you prefer yours or the better one?”

“The better one,” he replied [the manuscript reads: “Which estate, then, would you prefer to have?” “That one—the better one, of course,” he replied].

“What if he had a better wife than you have? Would you not also prefer her?” [The manuscript reads: “Which wife would you prefer?”]

At this point Xenophon too fell silent.

Then the philosopher said: “Since neither of you has answered me the one thing I alone wished to hear, [Col. 0936A] I myself shall say what each of you is thinking. You, woman, wish to have the best husband; and you, Xenophon, wish above all to have the finest wife [the manuscript reads “most excellent wife”]. Therefore, unless you bring it about that there is on earth neither a better husband nor a more excellent woman, you will certainly seek most eagerly what you will always think best: that you, as husband, should be married to the best woman, and that she should be married to the best possible husband [the manuscript reads ‘man’].”

Here he proved doubtful matters through matters that were not doubtful, by means of an inductive comparison. If someone had asked the question separately, perhaps the answer would not have been conceded.

CAR. That philosopher was not an Evangelical.

ALB. He was not [an Evangelical], but a rhetorician.

CAR. Why do we believe him?

ALB. He followed his own art. [Col. 0936B]

CAR. What does that have to do with this? Let us follow our own.

ALB. Follow whatever you wish; I shall follow you as you follow.

CAR. What should that induction be like?

ALB. It must always be similar to the matter for whose sake it is introduced.

CAR. Should it be clear or obscure?

ALB. One must take the greatest care that the opponent does not understand where those preliminary inductions are directed and at what conclusion they will arrive. For whoever sees this prevents the questioning from proceeding farther, either by keeping silent or by denying [the manuscript reads “who sees”].

CAR. What if he denies?

ALB. The similarity of the matters previously conceded must be demonstrated.

CAR. What if he is silent?

ALB. Then his response must be drawn out; or, since silence imitates confession, the argumentation must be brought to its conclusion, just as it is with matters conceded.

CAR. How is argumentation confirmed through reasoning? [Col. 0936C]

ALB. It is made through proposition, proof, assumption, and conclusion [the text also has “or” before “assumption”].

CAR. Make these clearer by any example.

ALB. The proposition is: “Things conducted with deliberation are managed better than things administered without deliberation.”

The proof is: “A household governed by reason and deliberation is better equipped in every respect than one administered without deliberation and reason.”

The assumption is as follows: “Nothing among all things is administered better than the universe” [another reading: “Nothing in all things…”].

Here another proof is introduced: “For the risings and settings of the stars, and the annual changes of crops, seasons, and days, are arranged in a sufficiently wondrous order and a fixed succession. These are signs that the universe is governed by great deliberation. [Col. 0936D]”

Then the awaited conclusion must be brought forward in this way: “If things conducted with deliberation are managed better than those conducted without deliberation, and nothing among all things is administered better than the whole universe [the text supplies this clause], then the universe is administered by deliberation” [another reading: “The universe is therefore governed most excellently”].

This argument is valid against those who say that the universe is moved by chance and not governed by deliberation.

CAR. What is more foolish than to think this?

ALB. A fool judges foolish things. Yet, according to Solomon, one must answer him, lest he seem wise to himself.

CAR. I remember, master, that among the parts of speech you named refutation. But I have heard such a long sequence of confirmations that scarcely any place seems to remain for the refuter by which he could weaken a case confirmed by these arguments. [Col. 0937A]

ALB. A place for weakening remains to him; but we need not concern ourselves with it. Nearly every case contains within itself both sources of confirmation and sources of refutation.

CAR. Nevertheless, I am left wondering what you intend to say about it.

ALB. I shall speak, and I shall speak briefly. Refutation is the process by which, through argument, the opponents’ confirmation is either weakened or removed.

It is drawn from the same sources as confirmation, because almost everything from which a matter can be confirmed can also be weakened. This occurs if what the confirmation is composed of is false, as in: “A wise man cannot be one who has neglected money”; “Many wise men have neglected money.”

Or if it is common, so that the opponents can say the same thing no less well, [Col. 0937B] as in: “Judges, it is because I had a true case that I pleaded briefly.”

Or if it is weak: “If it had not occurred to him, he would not have committed it.”

Or if it begins from something remote and farther removed than necessary: “If Scipio had not given his daughter Cornelia to Tiberius Gracchus, this sedition would not have arisen among their sons; therefore this evil must be attributed to Scipio” [the manuscript reads “assigned to Scipio”].

Or if it is offensive—that is, if it harms the will of those who listen—as when one happens to accuse love of money before a miser.

Or if it is adverse—that is, if it damages your own case—as when you ought to encourage your soldiers but praise the enemy’s forces and courage.

A dilemma is also refuted if it can be reversed, as follows: “If he is afraid, he must not be accused, because he is honest; but if he is not afraid, he knows himself to be innocent, and therefore must not be accused.” [Col. 0937C]

Here, whether you say that he is afraid or that he is not afraid, this is taken as conceded so that you may deny that he should be accused [the manuscript reads “so that you deny that he should be accused”]. It is refuted by reversal in this way: “On the contrary, he must be accused. If he is afraid, he testifies that he is not innocent; but if he is not afraid, he is not honest, and therefore must be accused.”

Enumeration is also refuted if something is omitted from the enumeration, as follows: “Since you possess that horse, you either bought it, received it by inheritance, were given it as a gift, or it was born at home. If none of these is true, you must have stolen it.” This is refuted if it can be said that the horse was captured from the enemy.

Arguments can be refuted in these and many other ways. The orator must guard against them with the greatest care—more carefully than I can explain to you, because of the brevity of my exposition.

[Col. 0937D]

CAR. Only the conclusion remains, which you placed last among the six parts of speech. The order requires you to speak about it.

ALB. The conclusion is the outcome and determination of the whole case.

CAR. How many parts does it have?

ALB. Three: enumeration, indignation, and lamentation.

CAR. What is the enumeration of the conclusion?

ALB. It is the process by which matters scattered throughout the speech are gathered into one place and, for the sake of recollection, are simultaneously brought before the eyes in a single view, as follows: “What more do you desire, judges, when I have told you this and this, and made this and this clear?”

CAR. What does indignation accomplish?

ALB. Hatred toward the opponent and [the manuscripts read “or”] offense toward his case. [Col. 0938A]

CAR. I especially wish to know how this can be accomplished.

ALB. Its rules are very numerous.

One method is to show that the matter defended by the opponent appears unworthy of the immortal gods, of the wisest men, of the senate, and of the entire people.

Another is to show that the opponent has committed other cruel, unjust, greedy, dishonorable, or defiant acts.

Another is to condemn his past life and character.

Another is to show what evil will occur if he is not punished.

Another is to show that forgiveness ought not to be granted for a voluntary crime or for one of an extraordinary kind [another reading: “that forgiveness ought not to be granted”].

Another is to display his pride or arrogance.

Another is to have the judge reflect upon himself, or upon his loved ones, if something of this kind had happened to them.

Another is to show that many eager persons are awaiting the decision in this matter, [Col. 0938B] so that from what is granted to this man they may understand what they too might be permitted to do in a similar matter.

We express indignation that a foul, cruel, impious, tyrannical crime should go unpunished; that an act so removed from every law and every principle of justice should not be avenged.

We speak of cruel acts committed against those who could neither injure others nor defend themselves, such as children, women, old men, and the weak.

We speak of atrocious deeds committed against foreigners, guests, neighbors, and friends.

We make the judge imagine that he himself was present and saw the deed with his own eyes.

We show, if it can be shown, that the act was committed by one from whom it was least appropriate, and by one who ought to have prevented it if someone else had committed it.

In these and many other ways, according as the case, the place, the time, and the persons present themselves, you must stir indignation or offense against the opponent. [Col. 0938C]

### 326

CAR. I understand well that the minds of the listeners can be provoked to indignation by such a speech.

ALB. For, as I said, amplifications and indignations can arise from those arguments that proceed from persons and matters.

CAR. They can, as I am certain. But tell me what lamentation is, what it accomplishes, and how it must be carried out.

ALB. Lamentation is a speech that seeks to win the pity of the listeners.

In it, one must first render the listener’s mind gentle and compassionate. This is accomplished in many ways: by showing what benefits the person has lost and in what hardships he now is—for example, in the death of a son, love, hope, comfort, and upbringing.

Also, by showing how many good things he had done for the one who inflicted such great evils upon him [the manuscripts read “would have done”]. [Col. 0938D]

Also, by showing what shameful and ignoble things the opponent brings forward.

Also, by showing how pitiable the situation would seem to you, judges, if you had been present.

Also: “While I hoped for good things, evils came upon me.”

Also, by lamenting poverty, weakness, and misfortune [the manuscripts read “the misfortune of weakness”].

Also, by lamenting separation from a parent, child, friend, brother, wife, or other beloved persons.

Also, by showing that the person is badly treated by those by whom this ought not to happen—friends or servants.

Also, by showing how compassionate I was toward him.

For the gravity and authority of speech often arouse pity more effectively [the manuscripts read “are more effective”] than humility and entreaty.

But now you have an account of the first and greatest part of rhetorical art, namely invention. Let us now pass to the other parts.

CAR. Let us pass on. But first tell me what sophistical speech is. [Col. 0939A]

ALB. If someone else had asked me from the school of your palace, perhaps I would have explained it to him [the manuscripts read “perhaps”].

CAR. Why to another and not to me? Are you envious that I should know this [the manuscripts read “are you envious of my knowing”]?

ALB. I am not envious; I am sparing you and honoring you.

CAR. I do not see that I am being honored when you refuse what I ask.

ALB. May I question you?

CAR. Why not? For to question wisely is to teach; and even if one person is the questioner and another the teacher, the thought of both nevertheless proceeds from one—that is, from the fountain of wisdom.

ALB. It does indeed proceed. And if one is the questioner and another the respondent [the manuscripts read “responds”], then you are not the same person who questions as I am who answers.

CAR. Certainly not the same.

ALB. What are you?

CAR. A human being.

ALB. Do you see how you can draw a conclusion against me?

CAR. How?

ALB. If you say, “I and you are not the same,” and I am a human being, it follows that you are not a human being. [Col. 0939B]

CAR. It follows.

ALB. But how many syllables does *homo*—“human being”—have?

CAR. Two.

ALB. Are you those two syllables?

CAR. Certainly not. But where is this leading?

ALB. So that you may understand sophistical cunning and see how you can be brought to a conclusion [another reading: “how it can be concluded”].

CAR. I see and understand. From the premises previously conceded, since I conceded both that I was a human being and that “human being” consists of two syllables, I can be brought to the conclusion that I am those two syllables. And I marvel at how secretly you first led me to conclude against you that you were not a human being, and then against myself that I was two syllables. [Col. 0939C]

## On Arrangement

I remember, master, that after invention you placed arrangement, in which you instructed [the edition reads “it is instructed”] the orator to distribute the matters he had discovered in an orderly fashion. If this part too has any rules of its own [the manuscripts read “some rules”], disclose them.

ALB. This part has few rules belonging to it by itself [the text supplies “alone”] that are not found among the rules of invention or expression. For arrangement is especially useful both to matters and to words; it gives ornament and credibility to arguments; and it bestows praise upon the speech, since everything must be distributed and composed not only in order but also with a certain sense of proportion and judgment, according as the present consideration of usefulness, propriety, or necessity requires.

As for the arrangement of words, it will be taught sufficiently fully when expression is discussed [the manuscript reads “is being discussed”]. The arrangement of matters, however, has been taught, part by part, in the rules of invention. [Col. 0939D]

## On Expression

CAR. The order of our discussion has now led us to an inquiry into expression, which brings great beauty to a case and dignity to a rhetorician. Nor can you excuse yourself from answering this as easily as you extricated yourself by means of the rules of arrangement [the edition reads “which you extricated yourself from”].

ALB. I am not excusing myself, but I shall follow your questions, my lord king, with a slow step but not a slow will.

CAR. First, explain what expression ought to be like.

ALB. It ought to be eloquent and clear.

CAR. How clear? [Col. 0940A]

ALB. It will be clear if you use significant and proper words, familiar words without ambiguity, with translations [metaphors] that are not drawn from too far away, and without an inserted hyperbaton [the manuscripts read “hyperbaton”].

CAR. How eloquent?

ALB. It will be eloquent if it observes the rules of grammar and is supported by the authority of the ancients.

CAR. How can our speech attain the authority of the ancients?

ALB. The books of the authors must be read, and their good expressions entrusted to memory [“so that those who have become accustomed to their manner of speaking will not be able to speak otherwise than eloquently, even when they wish to do so”]. Nevertheless, one should not use ancient words that our present usage no longer employs, except rarely, for the sake of ornament and sparingly. Yet eloquence is adorned more by familiar words.

CAR. Is eloquence more adorned in individual words or in the joining of words? [Col. 0940B]

ALB. In both. For the beauty of speech consists both in individual words and in the joining of words.

CAR. If it consists in both, speak about both.

ALB. In individual words there are two things that illuminate speech: either the word is proper, or it is transferred [metaphorical].

In proper words, the praise lies in avoiding what is vulgar and unfamiliar, and using words that are chosen and distinguished, in which something full and harmonious seems to reside. Here too habitual good usage has very great force.

In transferred words, the ornament is evident. Necessity produced them, compelled by poverty and constraint; afterward pleasure and delight celebrated them. Just as clothing was first discovered for the purpose of warding off cold, [Col. 0940C] and later was compelled to serve also for the adornment and dignity of the body, so transferred words were first established because of poverty of expression, and afterward were employed more frequently for pleasure and ornament [another reading: “because of poverty,” or “because of poverty and ornament”].

For even country people say, “The vines gem,” “the harvest luxuriates,” and “the grain billows.” What can scarcely be expressed by a proper word is made vivid by a transferred one.

Nevertheless, one ought to transfer those expressions that make the matter clearer, as in: “The sea bristles” [and “the sea boils with heat”]. Sometimes brevity is also achieved through a metaphor, as in: “The weapon fled from his hand.” For the imprudence involved in throwing the weapon could not be expressed more briefly in proper words. Since this is the highest praise of transferred words—that they reveal the meaning [the manuscripts read “of a transferred word … reveals”—the supplied source ends incompletely].

CAR. Is it permissible to derive a metaphor from any source whatsoever?

ALB. By no means, but only from honorable things. [Col. 0940D] For every obscenity in those things toward which the minds of the hearers will be drawn by the comparison must be avoided with the greatest care; as in the saying: “By the death of Africanus the republic was castrated,” and “the dung of the senate-house.” In both cases the thought suggested by the comparison is deformed. Likewise, the metaphor should not be greater than the matter requires, as in: “the storm of litigation.” Nor, conversely, should it be smaller, as in: “[the air thunders],” as though a sleeping man were snoring with his nostrils opened. There is also a beautiful metaphor by metonymy, when a thing is signified through the author of that thing, as Mars for war and Ceres for crops. Or when we name virtues and vices for the things in which they reside, as: “Into what house luxury has burst,” or “avarice has penetrated.” There is also a beautiful synecdochic metaphor, when we signify the whole from a part or a part from the whole, [Col. 0941A] as when we say “the roof” for the whole house, or “the sea” for the waves.

CAR. What ought the joining of words to be like?

ALB. Proper, well-composed, and compact: it should not gape with vowels, as in “Placida aura adest” (“A calm breeze is present”); nor be harsh with consonants, as in “Multum ille luget” (“He greatly mourns”). Nor should the following word begin with the final syllable of the preceding word, as in “Prima mater.” Nor should the first word, joined with the last, produce an obscenity, as in “Numerum nunquam intellexi” (“I have never understood the number”). One must also take care that empty words are not uttered merely to fill out the structure, rather than to express the matter itself [Mss., “to be done”]. And, to come to the highest point: just as wisdom is the foundation of all other things, so it is also in eloquence. For, as in life, so in speech, nothing is clearer [is] than that everything should be done wisely. Therefore the orator must foresee with the greatest care what is fitting for him and suitable to his case, not only in his arguments but also in his words. For not every circumstance, not every honor, not every authority, not every age—and indeed not every place, [or] time, or hearer—is to be treated in the same manner, either in choice of words or in arguments; and in every part of a speech, as in life, one must consider what is fitting.

## 328. ON MEMORY

CAR. What do you say about memory, that most noble part of rhetoric, as I believe?

ALB. What else but what Marcus Tullius says: memory is the treasury of all things. Unless [Mss., “unless”] it is employed as the guardian of thoughts, discoveries, and words [Al., “were employed”], we understand that everything—even if it has been excellent—will perish in the orator. [Col. 0941C]

CAR. Are there any rules concerning how it should either be employed or increased?

ALB. We have no other rules for it than practice in speaking [Ms., “learning”], the habit of writing, and devotion to thought; and drunkenness must be avoided, since it is especially harmful to every good study. It not only takes away the body’s health but also removes the mind’s integrity [Ms., “from the mind”].

CAR. These rules are sufficient if someone is capable of carrying them out. For, as I see, they are as difficult in substance as they are rare in words.

ALB. They are both difficult and useful.

## ON DELIVERY

CAR. But the order of my questions requires that your answer proceed to delivery, which I remember you said at the beginning of our discussion, master, was the fifth part of the rhetorical art. [Col. 0941D]

ALB. Delivery is the dignity of words, the adaptation [Al., “adapted”] of the voice to the meaning, and the regulation of the body. It excels to such a degree that, according to the judgment of the great Tullius, even an unlearned speech may [nevertheless] win praise if it is delivered excellently [Mss., “spoken excellently”]. However polished it may be, if it is delivered improperly it deserves contempt and ridicule—unless, my lord king, you happen to think otherwise.

CAR. I certainly do not think otherwise. But I would like you to point out the rules of this part as well, and the faults that must be avoided [Mss., “tell me”].

ALB. First, the regulation of the voice and breath, and the movement of the body and tongue, must be practiced; these depend less on theory than on labor. Any faults, if any [Mss., *qua* for *quae*], in the mouth must likewise be corrected with diligent care. Words should not be swollen, breathless, or growling in the throat; they should not resound through an empty mouth, nor be uttered harshly through grating teeth or gaping lips. Rather, they should be pronounced distinctly, evenly [Ms., *aequaliter*], gently, and clearly, so that each letter is articulated with its proper sound and every word is adorned with its legitimate accent. One should not shout with uncontrolled loudness, nor break the speech for purposes of display; instead, it must be apportioned according to places, matters, persons, cases, and times. Some things must be narrated simply, others urged with authority, others brought forth with indignation, and others softened with compassion, so that the voice and the speech always suit the case. These rules lead you to excellence in delivery and secure for you dignity and credibility for your case [Ms., “will secure”]. [Col. 0942B]

CAR. What is this regulation of the body that you said shortly before must be observed?

ALB. I said that it must necessarily be observed that the face be upright: the lips must not be twisted, an excessive opening must not stretch the mouth, the face must not be thrown backward, the eyes must not be cast down to the ground, the neck must not be inclined, and the eyebrows must not be raised or lowered. For these matters too have immense importance, because nothing that is unfitting can please. As Marcus Tullius says: “The chief principle of the art is that what you do should be fitting.” To lick or bite the lips is unbecoming, since even in forming words their movement should be moderate. One should speak with the mouth rather than merely with the lips.

[Col. 0942C] CAR. Venerable master, I admit that these things are pleasant and honorable, and greatly pleasing to me. But, as I see and understand, they demand constant practice and daily use; and they cannot reach complete perfection without continual meditation and assiduous practice, without which I think no discipline can be distinguished.

ALB. It is as you say, my lord king. For practice often overcomes talent and nature, and use surpasses the instruction of all teachers. Therefore invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery grow strong through sharp use and the most intense practice [Al., “growing strong”]. Habit almost takes the place of nature. For in every art, practiced habit produces confidence and steadfastness, without which no art makes progress. What good are weapons to the timid? Let a young man love praise and know that it is a great thing to be heard alone while many are silent. For although ambition itself is a vice, it is nevertheless often the cause of virtues. From adolescence he should learn not to fear speaking before many people, so that neither fear [may break] him nor excessive reverence hold him back, and so that, when equipped with all the resources of an orator, he may also possess excellence of spirit and confidence in speech.

CAR. Therefore, as it seems to me, those who are judged likely to take part in civil cases and worldly affairs should acquire the practice of speaking with great diligence from childhood. The voice [and words] too should be practiced, so that from an early age one may become accustomed to confidence of voice, abundance of words, and becoming bodily movement, and may perform without fear in public debates what he has done through habit in private. [Col. 0943A]

ALB. You understand truly and express the matter very well. For just as a soldier is trained in the camp, so an orator must be trained at home, so that he will not [Mss., *non* for *ne*] fear doing among many what he had practiced alone.

CAR. I now also see that domestic practice must begin to avoid what a public gathering could take away. For someone who wishes to speak honorably among strangers ought not to use dishonorable words among his own people. Since propriety is absolutely necessary in every part of life, it is especially necessary in speech, because speech generally reveals each person’s character—unless you, master, think otherwise.

ALB. I can think of nothing else concerning this matter. Therefore, in habitual conversation, words should be chosen that are refined, honorable, clear, and simple, uttered with an open mouth, a calm expression, and a composed face, without uncontrolled laughter and without shouting. For there is a good manner in speaking, as in walking: to proceed gently, without leaping and without lingering, so that everything shines with the moderation of a middle course. This is one of the four virtues, from which the other virtues proceed as from roots, and in which reside nobility of soul, dignity of life, moral propriety, and the praise of discipline. [Col. 0943B]

CAR. I understand that comic [Mss., “philosophical”] proverb to be necessary not only in conduct but also in speech.

ALB. Which one?

CAR. “Nothing in excess.”

## ON THE VIRTUES

[Col. 0943C] ALB. It is—and truly is—necessary in everything, because whatever exceeds the proper measure is a fault. Therefore the virtues are placed in the middle. I could say more about them to your venerable authority if our discussion were not hastening toward its end, and if it did not seem superfluous to discuss virtues with you, whose excellence is adorned not only by knowledge of the virtues but also by their effective practice.

CAR. Nevertheless, master, I will not allow you to close the pen of your answers before you explain to me the names and parts of the four virtues that you said are the roots of the other virtues. Shortly before, we agreed among ourselves that practice in conversation is necessary. In what could the study of speech be better placed than in the excellence of the virtues, which can be of great benefit both to writers and to readers? [Col. 0943D]

ALB. It is beneficial, as you say, my lord king, but I am constrained between the two. Concise brevity demands little, while a difficult subject requires more.

CAR. Keep yourself between the two, lest verbosity produce weariness or brevity produce ignorance.

ALB. First, one must know that some things are so clear and noble that they are not to be sought for any other benefit, but are to be loved and pursued solely for their own dignity.

CAR. I very much wish to recognize these things [Mss., “know”].

ALB. They are virtue, knowledge, truth, and good love.

CAR. Does not the Christian religion especially praise these?

ALB. It praises and venerates them.

CAR. What have philosophers to do with them?

ALB. They understood them in human nature and venerated them with the greatest zeal.

CAR. What, then, distinguishes such a philosopher from a Christian?

ALB. Faith and baptism.

CAR. Nevertheless, continue with the philosophical definitions of the virtues; and first say what virtue itself is.

ALB. Virtue is a disposition of the soul, the adornment of nature, the rule of life, and nobility of character.

CAR. How many parts does it have?

ALB. Four: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

CAR. What is prudence?

ALB. Knowledge of things and natures.

CAR. How many parts does it have?

ALB. Three: memory, understanding, and foresight.

CAR. Give the definitions of these as well.

ALB. Memory is that by which the soul recalls things that have been. Understanding is that by which it perceives things that are. Foresight is that by which something future is foreseen before it happens. [Col. 0944B]

## 330

CAR. Explain the nature of justice.

ALB. Justice is a disposition of the soul that assigns to each thing its proper dignity. In it the worship of divinity, the rights of humanity, and the equity of the whole of life are preserved.

CAR. Reveal its parts as well.

ALB. Partly it comes from the law of nature and partly from customary practice.

CAR. How does it come from the law of nature?

ALB. Because nature implants certain parts of it, such as religion, filial devotion [grace], vindication, respect, and truth.

CAR. Explain each of these more clearly.

ALB. Religion is that which brings care and ceremonies concerning a certain higher nature, which they call divine. Filial devotion is that by which duty and diligent reverence are rendered to those joined to us by blood and to those benevolent toward the fatherland. Grace contains remembrance of friendships and services, and the willingness to repay them [Mss., “enmities”]. Vindication is that by which a right or wrong, and altogether anything that will cause harm, is warded off by defense or vengeance. Respect is the esteem by which we honor people who surpass us in some dignity. Truth is that by which things that are, things that have been, or things that will be are reported [Ms., “spoken”].

CAR. How is justice preserved through customary practice?

ALB. Through pact, equality, judgment, and law.

CAR. I ask for more about these as well.

ALB. A pact is what is agreed upon among some people. Equality is that which is even toward all. A judgment is what has been established by the opinion of some great man or of several people. Law is written right for an entire people, prescribing what it must avoid or observe. [Col. 0944D]

CAR. Now I urgently ask you to set forth fortitude with its parts.

ALB. Fortitude is the magnanimous endurance of dangers and labors. Its parts are magnificence, confidence, patience, and perseverance.

CAR. Make their meanings clear.

ALB. Magnificence is the conception and administration of great and lofty things, with a certain broad and splendid purpose of mind [Edit., “an invitation of the mind”]. Confidence is that by which the mind places great trust in itself, with assured hope, in great and honorable matters. Patience is the voluntary and prolonged endurance of arduous or difficult things for the sake of honor or usefulness. Perseverance is stable and perpetual persistence in a course that has been carefully considered. [Col. 0945A]

CAR. It remains for you to speak about temperance, from which our inquiry concerning the virtues arose. I expect to hear its nature and that of its parts.

ALB. Temperance is the rational [Mss., “reasonable”] mastery of desire and of other improper impulses [“firm and moderate”] of the soul [Edit., “moderation of impulses”]. Its parts are self-control, clemency, and moderation. Self-control is that by which every evil desire is governed and restrained by the strong direction of judgment. Clemency is that by which injury and hatred are held back with a mild spirit. Moderation is that by which concern for the proper measure of the whole of life—whether in the movements of the soul or of the body [Edit., “customs”]—is everywhere preserved. [Col. 0945B]

CAR. Great honor before human beings and praise before the Lord [Mss., “God”] belong to the person who preserves this. But I am astonished that we Christians, if [those] philosophers preserved these virtues solely for their dignity or the praise they brought to life, should depart from them in so many ways through deviant error, since the Truth himself, Christ Jesus, promises the rewards of eternal glory to those who now preserve them in faith and charity [Mss., “observe them”].

ALB. We are more to be pitied than wondered at, because there are very many among our people whom neither fear of punishments nor the glory of rewards calls back to the dignity of the virtues.

CAR. I recognize this, and I cannot say without tears that there are many such people. Nevertheless, I ask you to explain, as briefly as you can, how these excellent virtues are to be understood and observed in our Christian religion. [Col. 0945C]

ALB. Does it not seem to you that wisdom is the understanding and fear of God according to the measure of the human mind, together with belief in his future judgment?

CAR. I understand [and agree] that nothing is more excellent than this wisdom [Mss., *huic sapientiae* for *hac sapientia*]. And I recall that it is written in Job: “Behold, the wisdom of man is piety.” [And what is piety except the worship of God, which] in Greek is called θεοσέβεια (“the worship of God”) [Mss., theosebion].

ALB. You understand well and truly. But what do you think justice is, except love of God and observance of his commandments?

CAR. I recognize this as well. Nothing is more just than this justice; indeed, there is no other justice except this.

ALB. Do you not see that fortitude is that by which the ancient enemy is conquered and the adversities of the world are endured courageously?

[Col. 0945D] 331 CAR. I certainly see it, and I consider nothing more praiseworthy than this victory.

ALB. Is temperance not that which restrains lust, represses avarice, and calms and moderates all the impulses of the soul?

CAR. It is, and truly [is, and] very necessary for every human being. But I still ask: toward what end is the observance of these virtues directed? [Col. 0946A]

ALB. So that God and one’s neighbor may be loved. Do you judge otherwise?

CAR. I judge nothing else. But brief as this is to hear, it is difficult and arduous to do.

ALB. What is easier than to love beautiful appearances, sweet flavors, pleasant sounds, fragrant odors, agreeable touches, honors, and the prosperity of the world? Is it easy for the soul to love these things, which withdraw like a fleeting shadow, and not to love God, who is eternal beauty, eternal sweetness, eternal delight, eternal fragrance, eternal pleasure, everlasting honor, and unfailing happiness? Especially since the divine Scriptures demand nothing else of us than that we love God and our Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves. For we have a promise from the one who does not know how to deceive: “My yoke is easy,” he says, “and my burden is light.” The love of this world is more laborious than the love of Christ. For what the soul seeks in it, it does not find—that is, happiness and eternity—since this lowest beauty passes and departs; either it abandons the lover or is abandoned by the lover. Let the soul therefore keep its proper order.

CAR. What is the soul’s order?

ALB. That it love what is above, namely God; rule what is below, namely the body; and nourish and cherish associated souls with love. Purified and relieved by these sacrifices, the soul will fly away from this laborious and wretched life [to rest] and will enter into the joy of its Lord [Al., “will depart”]. [Col. 0946C]

CAR. You praise a great and truly blessed man, master.

ALB. May God make you great and truly blessed, my lord king, and grant you, in the four-horse chariot of the virtues about which we spoke shortly before, to fly across this wicked world to the citadel of the heavenly kingdom on the twin wings of love.

CAR. May it be so, may it be so, by the gift of divine grace.

ALB. May this speech of ours, which began from the shifting character [Al., “genius”] of civil questions, have the end of eternal stability, lest someone claim that we have traveled so far in discussion for nothing.

CAR. Who would dare say that we have conversed in vain, if he is either an [inquisitive] investigator of honorable [worldly] arts or a follower of excellent virtues? As for me, I confess that the love of knowledge led me to these inquiries, and I thank you for not refusing the matters I asked about. Therefore I approve this benevolence in your answers and judge that it will benefit the diligent—provided that the stain of envy does not corrupt the reader.

Furthermore, the ancient philosophers called wisdom “philosophy,” that is, knowledge of all human and divine things. The ancients said that this philosophy has three parts: physics, ethics, and logic.

Mechanics is knowledge of craftsmanship in metals, wood, and stones. Medicine is the science of treatments discovered for the balance and health of the body [“and of places”]. O young men, for whom the age is suited to speaking,

Learn: the years depart like flowing water.

And, teachable ones, do not waste your days on empty pursuits.

The flowing wave does not return, nor does the rushing hour return.

May first youth flourish in the studies of virtues,

So that old age may shine with the great honor of praise.

Whoever you are who read this book, use the book happily through your years [Mss., “this”],

And, mindful of the author [Mss., “the authors”], say: “Have mercy, O God.”

If, reader, you seek to remove our mote,

First remove the beams from your own eye.

Learn, young man, how eloquence may conduct your cases,

So that you may be defender, care, and salvation to your people.

Learn, I beg you, young man, graceful gestures and manners,

So that your name may be praised throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0949A] Quercetanus assigned these verses to the *Dialectic*, but incorrectly. For the verses “Learn, young man, how eloquence…” clearly show that this poem is an exhortation to learn rhetoric and cultivate the virtues; and all the manuscripts we consulted support this. Canisius too found them at the end of the *Rhetoric* in the manuscript of St. Gall, with the letters L and K added, which he interprets as referring to Charles and Alcuin. Yet I do not know whether that most celebrated man read them correctly; for I suspect that the same marks occur there as those I saw in the manuscripts mentioned above, in the form in which they are presented here with the verses.]

[Col. 0949]

# FOURTH OPUSCULUM. ON DIALECTIC

## 334. PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0949B]

We mentioned above that Alcuin’s *Dialectic*, together with the *Rhetoric*, had already appeared in print at Hagenau in 1529 through Menrad Molther. The distinguished author of the *History of French Literature* did not notice this; in volume IV, page 317, no. 23, he attributed its first edition to Canisius. In the *Great Ecclesiastical Library* a similar edition of both little works is listed as having been produced at Ingolstadt in 1604, in quarto; it is the same as the Canisian edition. Separately, and without the *Rhetoric*, this same *Dialectic* of Alcuin was printed from a certain manuscript at Salzburg in 1629, under the care of the distinguished man Father Matthaeus Weiss, doctor of sacred theology and rector of the university, together with an *Introduction to Logic, or the Organon of Aristotle*, from the printing house of Christoph Kazenberger. At the end, Father Weiss added the following judgment: [Col. 0951A]

> “You observe, I believe, reader, that Alcuin generally employs enumeration, definitions, and examples, because he undertook not so much to write a subtle and precise *Dialectic*—by which name, outside the Lyceum, everything relating to the method of discussion is understood—an art or method, as rather to hand down some sort of knowledge of the elements of that same *Dialectic*.”
