So much for him. I have no doubt that this *Dialectic* of Alcuin, although it may perhaps seem less subtle than the ordinary Peripatetic logic of the more recent period, is nevertheless much more useful than that logic.

We present it here with many passages corrected from the manuscripts of Vienna, Freising, and St. Emmeram. As is our custom, we have placed variant readings and supplements within brackets in the text.

It is useful to transcribe here what the distinguished Basnage noted concerning this book in volume II of his *Lectures on Antiquity*, page 488, note:

> “There is another dialectic,” he says, “or another book on the Categories translated from Aristotle by Albinus [Col. 0951B] [Note: Translated by Alcuin. The learned man is mistaken through inattention. He ought to have said: ‘translated by Augustine, whom Alcuin inscribes to Charlemagne…’], in a manuscript I possess, which he inscribes to Charlemagne under this title and with this poem:”

Alcuin the master, arriving from the regions of Scythia, sent these Categories, composed by Aristotle in the language of the Greeks and later elucidated in Latin letters by Augustine, to Charles, king of the Franks, together with these verses:

This little book contains the ten words of nature,

Words which now contain, in wondrous reasoning,

Everything that can pass into our understanding.

Whoever reads it, let him praise the marvelous genius of the ancients,

And strive to exercise his own mind in such labor,

Adorning the years granted to life with honorable titles.

Augustine the master was pleased to translate this

From the treasures of the ancients with a Latin key—

And I send it now to you, great king,

Follower and lover of wisdom, who rejoice in such a gift,

To be read by you. [Col. 0951C]

[lacuna]

> “But those ten Categories ought not to be attributed to Augustine. Indeed, in the outstanding edition undertaken by the Benedictines, who possess the keenest judgment in distinguishing Augustine’s genuine works, they not only denied Augustine the *Dialectic* and the *Categories* drawn from Aristotle, but also the *Grammar* and the *Rhetoric*, and relegated them to the appendix of volume I together with the other spurious works.”

Nor is it entirely certain that Alcuin is the author of the verses transcribed here, although a very old manuscript of Saint-Germain bears his name at the head in these words: “Alcuin’s prologue to Charles Augustus concerning the Categories of Saint Augustine.” See the appendices to the works of Saint Augustine.

## 335. VERSES

Read me, you who desire to know the thoughts of the ancients;

Whoever grasps me is free from rusticity.

[Col. 0951D] I do not want my reader to be sluggish; I do not want him to be proud.

I inhabit the chambers of a devoted and humble heart.

I ask that the lover of wisdom not despise these riches,

Which the sailor carries from his own world across the sea.

# CHAPTER ONE. ON PHILOSOPHY AND ITS PARTS

**Charles.** Since we mentioned philosophy in the preceding conversation of our discussion [Molther’s edition: “since in the preceding discussion we mentioned philosophy in our conversation”], it seems fitting, master, that we begin to discuss it through somewhat broader inquiry.

**Albinus.** Let us do so, as seems fitting to your wisdom [Ms., “may seem fitting”].

**C.** [Col. 0952A] First of all, tell me from what philosophy derives its name.

**A.** From the love of wisdom. [For philosophy is the love of wisdom.] The Greeks call love *philon* (φίλον) and wisdom *sophian* (σοφίαν).

**C.** Give its definition as well.

**A.** Philosophy is inquiry into natures and knowledge of human and divine things, insofar as it is possible for a human being to judge. Philosophy is also uprightness of life, the study of living well, meditation on death, and contempt for the world. This latter meaning is more appropriate to Christians, who, having trampled worldly ambition underfoot, live in disciplined likeness of the future homeland.

**C.** Of what material does it consist?

**A.** Of knowledge and opinion [Mss., *opinatione*; and below, *opinatio*].

**C.** What is knowledge?

**A.** Knowledge is when something is perceived by a certain reasoning, as in the case of a solar eclipse: it is caused by the interposition of the moon’s body. [Col. 0952B]

**C.** What is opinion?

**A.** Opinion is when an uncertain matter remains concealed and cannot be defined by any firm reasoning, as with the magnitude of the heavens or the depth of the earth.

**C.** Into how many parts is philosophy divided? [Ms., “into what parts”]

**A.** Into three: physics, ethics, and logic.

**C.** Express these in Latin terms as well.

**A.** Physics is natural philosophy, ethics is moral philosophy, and logic is rational philosophy.

**C.** Explain the functions of each kind.

**A.** In physics, the cause of inquiry is pursued; in ethics, the order of living; in logic, the method of understanding.

**C.** Into how many kinds is physics divided?

**A.** Into four: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.

**C.** Into how many parts is ethics divided?

**A.** Also into four: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

**C.** Into how many kinds is logic divided?

**A.** Into two: dialectic and rhetoric. For the divine utterances too consist in these three branches of philosophy.

**C.** How so?

**A.** For they usually discuss either nature, as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes; or morals, as in Proverbs and throughout the books generally; or logic, for which our people claim the name theology, as in the Song of Songs and the holy Gospel.

**C.** What is theology?

**A.** Theology is what is called “contemplative” in Latin: having surpassed visible things, we contemplate something divine and heavenly with the mind alone. For true philosophy is also divided into these two parts, namely contemplative and practical. [Col. 0952D]

**C.** What is practical philosophy?

**A.** Practical philosophy consists in the activities necessary for this mortal life. Through it, therefore, an honorable manner of living is sought and institutions directed toward the virtues are practiced; through contemplative philosophy, God is loved and worshiped in hope and faith.

**C.** Who would dare disparage philosophy? [Edit., “philosophy” as object]

**A.** No wise person.

**C.** Truly, no wise person. But let us proceed to investigate the art of dialectic [Al., “the question of dialectic”]. First tell me, what is dialectic?

**A.** Dialectic is the rational discipline of inquiry, definition, and discussion, also capable of distinguishing the true from the false. [Col. 0953A]

**C.** From where does the word “dialectic” derive?

**A.** It is called dialectic because in it one argues about utterances. For *lexis* (λέξις) means “utterance.”

### 336

**C.** What is the difference between dialectic and rhetoric?

**A.** Dialectic and rhetoric are like the clenched fist and the open palm [edition: “extended”] in a man’s hand. The former concludes arguments in brief speech [another reading: “and by an argument”]; the latter ranges through the fields of eloquence in expansive discourse. The former contracts words; the latter extends them. Dialectic is sharper for discovering things, while rhetoric is more eloquent in expressing what has been discovered. The former requires a few serious students; the latter frequently proceeds before crowds.

**C.** How many species of dialectic are there?

**A.** Five principal ones: the Isagoge, the Categories, the forms and definitions of syllogisms, Topics, and Perihermeneia.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE ISAGOGE

**C.** What is the Isagoge?

**A.** *Isagoge* is called in Latin “introduction.”

**C.** What does “introduction” signify?

**A.** An introduction is that which leads our understanding, through various divisions of common things, toward the particular nature of each thing.

**C.** What are its parts?

**A.** Five, namely: genus, species, difference, accident, and property.

**C.** What is genus?

**A.** Genus is properly that which is distinguished through species; by a common name it shows what the substance about which you are asking is—for example, “animal.” For across its individual species, that is, human being, horse, ox, lion, and the rest, the genus is “animal,” and it is predicated equally of them all.

**C.** What is species?

**A.** Species is that which is predicated of several things differing in number but not in species, in answer to the question “what is it?” For “human being” is predicated equally of Socrates, Plato, and Cicero. There is one species of human beings according to nature, but many according to number.

**C.** What is difference?

**A.** Difference is that which shows what sort of animal this or that is. If it is asked what sort of thing a human being is, we say: “a rational and mortal animal.” For by these two characteristics the human being is distinguished from all other living creatures. By the term “rational,” the human being is separated from all creatures that do not use reason. When “mortal” is said, the human being is distinguished from angels. Angels are rational and immortal; other animals are mortal but not rational. Human beings alone consist of both: they share one characteristic with angels and the other with the remaining living creatures. O wondrous animal—celestial in one part and earthly in the other!

**C.** What is property?

**A.** Property exists when any species can naturally be designated by some definite additional characteristic and separated from the commonality of all other species. Thus it is the property of the human being alone to be capable of laughter [*risibilis*; possibly *risibilem*, “capable of laughing”; another reading: “property is laughter”].

It must also be understood that a singular property necessarily can always be converted, for example: “Whatever is a human being is capable of laughter,” and “Whatever is capable of laughter is a human being.” This is called necessary conversion. “Rational,” however, cannot be converted in this way. We may say, “Whatever is a human being is rational,” but not, in the reverse order, “Whatever is rational is a human being,” because angels are rational but are not human beings.

**C.** What is an accident?

**A.** An accident is anything that occurs or departs without destruction of the substance—for example, for a color, to remain white or black; for a body, to stand or lie down; to be hungry or satisfied; and other such things. There are also accidents that occur in such a way that they do not entirely depart, such as height or shortness in the body, and other features that sometimes occur inseparably in individual bodily members—for example, the curvature of the nose [manuscripts: “nostril”], the breadth or narrowness of the mouth, the roundness [edition: “pleasantness”] of the eyes, the evenness of the eyebrows, and many other things.

**C.** Join these five parts together in a single example.

**A.** Genus is “animal,” for it is a general term common to all things possessing a soul. Species is “human being,” for by a certain species it is separated from the other living creatures. Genus is the whole: for example, we call all living things “animals”; species is a part, as the human being is a certain part of animals. Difference is “rational, mortal”; by these two, as we said above, the human being differs from the other living creatures. Property is [“to laugh”], because, apart from the human being, laughter does not naturally belong to any animal [another reading: “no animal can laugh”]. Accident is, for example, color in the body and learning in the mind. These both occur and change with the variation of time.

### 337

**C.** How should a complete-sense sentence be formed from these five parts?

**A.** In this way: “The human being is a rational, mortal, laughter-capable animal, capable of good and evil.” Likewise, in every substantial statement we must continue introducing species and differences until, with everything that could be identical excluded, we arrive at what is being sought and the definite property of the substance whose definition we began to formulate is securely held.

What has been said in this commentary-style [manuscript: *commentitio*; another reading: *commentatitio*] discussion of Porphyry’s *Isagoge* is sufficient. The order now requires us to pass to Aristotle’s Categories.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE CATEGORIES

**C.** Let us follow the order, and first explain to us the etymology of that name.

**A.** *Categoriae* is Greek; in Latin they are called “predicaments.”

**C.** What do you mean when you say “predicaments”?

**A.** Whenever I speak about any thing, I predicate something of it, as the philosophers intended the matter to be understood.

**C.** In how many ways does that predication occur? We may, as it seems to me, call it a form of speech.

**A.** Your judgment is correct. Our speech occurs in two ways: either about substance or about accidents.

**C.** Why is it called substance?

**A.** It is called substance because it subsists, just as each nature exists in its own property.

**C.** How many accidents are there?

**A.** Nine for corporeal natures.

**C.** Which are they?

**A.** Quantity, relation, quality, doing, undergoing, position, where, when, and having [another reading: habit]. When these nine are joined to substance, which the Greeks call *ousia*, there are ten categories. Whatever a human being says is inevitably found among these ten words. But before we begin to discuss each of them individually, let us examine the rule of homonyms, which are instruments of the categories.

**C.** Let it be done! First explain the meanings of the names of the three species that we read about in grammar: homonyms, synonyms, and polyonyms.

**A.** In Latin, homonyms may be called equivocal terms, synonyms univocal terms, and polyonyms plurivocal terms.

**C.** I also await an explanation of their difference.

**A.** Homonyms occur when two things receive a common name but are separated by the interpretation of the thing itself; for example, a painted human being and a real human being. In these cases there is one name, but the account or interpretation is different. When you say that a real human being is an animal that moves, takes nourishment, and is endowed with reason, while you can say none of these things about a painted human being, they must necessarily be regarded as unlike.

Synonyms, however, are terms joined both in name and in their interpretation. For example, an animal is something that takes nourishment, breathes, moves, and is mortal. All these things can be said equally of a human being, a horse, and an ox.

Polyon yms occur when many names signify one thing, and no difference or account is given to explain why so many names signify one thing—for example, *ensis*, “sword”; *mucro*, “blade”; *gladius*, “sword.”

To these are also joined heteronyms [another reading: homonyms], which signify individual things by equally numerous names, but in which the account distinguishes the difference among the names—for example, “human being,” “mortal,” and “earthly.” “Human being” is derived from humanity; “mortal,” from the necessity of death; “earthly,” from earth, from which all things are generated [or: “is so called”].

**C.** To which species do proper names belong?

**A.** We must regularly understand that all proper names can become common and be called homonyms. Thus there is not one Cicero but several. They must, however, be distinguished by signs and by some particular characteristic, so that we can tell which Cicero is which, and which is another or a third—for example, by calling one fat and another thin; one tall and another short; one fair in color and another dark.

**C.** In how many ways do homonyms arise?

**A.** In two ways. They arise either accidentally or by human intention.

**C.** How accidentally?

**A.** When, by some chance, someone receives a name similar to another’s.

**C.** How by intention?

**A.** When the similarity of the name is attached deliberately by the person who imposes it [another reading: “is fashioned”].

**C.** Can these divisions themselves be further divided?

**A.** Of those that arise deliberately or by intention, there are four kinds: *Icon*, *kata analogian*, *aph’ henos*, and *pros hen* [Εἰκὼν, κατ’ ἀναλογίαν, ἀφ’ ἑνός, πρὸς ἕν].

### 338

**C.** Explain these in Latin.

**A.** Similarity, proportionality, derivation from one source, and reference to one thing.

**C.** Confirm this with examples.

**A.** “Similarity”: a painted human being and a real human being are joined only by similarity. “Proportionality”: just as we call the heart the beginning of an animal, so we call a spring the beginning of water; in a certain respect, a similarity of name appears to have been attached to both things.

“From one”: we speak of a medicinal iron instrument, a medicinal prescription, medicinal knowledge, and medicinal use; all these descend from one source.

“Toward one”: this potion is health-giving, that physician is health-giving, and that herb is health-giving. All these things seem to touch upon one thing, namely health.

**C.** Since you have explained the variety of names to me clearly, it remains for you to set out the principle of questions, which, I think, can consist only of names and verbs. Nature therefore teaches us that these are the two principal parts. A noun shows substance; a verb shows what someone does or what he undergoes.

**A.** All questions flow from three sources: either from things that exist, or from things that are perceived, or concerning things that are spoken.

The first concerns substances, because all the things that nature has produced exist. The second concerns the senses, because only those things that exist can be perceived by the senses, and we form and store their images in the mind. The third concerns expressions, because what someone conceives in the mind is displayed by the tongue as it gives expression to it.

Therefore, although these three are named separately, we must understand the discussion as a mixture of all three. For the person who speaks about things perceived also derives their origin from things and calls upon the resources of speech. Thus there are things that we either perceive through the senses of the body or gather through the mind and thought.

We grasp through the senses what we perceive by seeing, touching, hearing, tasting, or smelling. We know through the mind when we understand that any body—for example, a human being or an animal—consists of many parts; that it can grow or grow old; that at one time it may be troubled by cares and at another rest with a secure heart; that at one time it enjoys health and at another suffers pains; and that the unskilled can become skilled and the unlearned learned.

**C.** Perhaps wise men wished to distinguish these things by their proper names?

**A.** Indeed. For they ordered that what is distinguished by bodily sense should be called *ousia*, that is, substance. But what is gathered solely through the mind’s activity, or frequently changes, they preferred to call *symbebekos*, that is, accident [manuscript: *ac*; manuscripts: “to name”].

They also wished *ousia* to be called *hypokeimenon*, that is, “the underlying subject.” Those things that occur in it they called *en hypokeimeno*, that is, “in the underlying subject” [“accidents”]. Accidents must necessarily exist in some substance. Therefore the former is called the underlying substance, while the latter are accidents in the underlying substance—for example, learning in the mind, color in the body, or any of the nine accidents mentioned above.

**C.** Must we say that the accidents themselves exist either within *ousia* or outside *ousia*?

**A.** Some are within it and others outside it. Within *ousia* are quality, quantity, and position, for these cannot exist without it. As soon as you mention a human being or a horse, you must understand it to be two-footed or four-footed, white or black, standing or lying down.

Outside *ousia* are place, time, and habit. To be in a place or time, to be clothed or armed, is separate from substance. Other things are common, that is, both within and outside *ousia*, such as relation, doing, and undergoing.

The greater and the lesser have one aspect within themselves and another outside themselves. Likewise with doing: it is both external and internal, for no one can be said to cut unless he cuts another. The same applies to undergoing: no one can be cut or burned unless he undergoes this from another [manuscript: “will undergo it”].

**C.** Is there another difference among these accidents?

**A.** There is. Those things that exist in each individual must be either in one alone and in all; in one alone and not in all; in all and not in one alone; or neither in one alone nor in all. The Greeks call these four species *Enmocepanti*, *enmonoceupanti*, *expanti*, and *enmono ceute*, *enmono utipanti* [the manuscripts give variant forms: *Enmonocepanti … enpanti, ceunomo*].

**C.** I would like you to make these clearer with examples.

**A.** Suppose that someone wishing to define a human being says that the human being is capable of laughter. This exists in one alone and in all: only the human being laughs, and it is natural for all human beings to laugh.

“In one alone and not in all” would be the case if someone defining a human being said that the human being is capable of learning. This can be found in the human being alone, but not in every human being, for not everyone has learned some disciplines.

“In all and not in one alone” would be the case if someone defining a human being said that a human being is something that breathes and takes nourishment. This exists in every human being, but not in the human being alone, since cattle also take nourishment and wild animals breathe.

“Neither in one alone nor in all” would be the case if someone said in a definition of the human being that a human being is something white. This exists neither in the human being alone nor in every human being. A human being is not the only creature that is white, since an ox or a horse may also be white; nor is every human being white.

**C.** Which of these species make the more certain definition of *ousia*?

**A.** Two: “in one alone and in all,” and “in one alone but not in all”—for example, that the human being is capable of laughter and capable of learning. These two species show the way to investigate the *ousia* about which you are asking. The other two cannot signify anything certain.

## CHAPTER IV. ON QUANTITY

**C.** Having briefly traversed the parts by which *ousia* can be understood, it remains now to inquire into each of the accidents of *ousia*. Explain first the quantity that you placed first [another reading: “placed as primary”].

**A.** It was not placed first without reason. For when we have seen some body, we can estimate how great it is.

**C.** How is quantity usually estimated?

**A.** By the measurement of length, breadth, and height, since every body must possess these three. Each of these has two corresponding aspects: length has front and back; breadth has right and left; height has above and below. Every body is bounded by these six parts.

**C.** What if someone measures length alone?

**A.** Length measured without breadth is called *gramme*, that is, linear measurement.

**C.** What if someone adds breadth to length by measuring it?

**A.** When breadth has been measured together with length, it is called *epiphaneia*, that is, superficial measurement.

**C.** What if he adds height to these two?

**A.** When all three are joined in measurement, they complete a solid body with its six prescribed aspects. According to position [of place], they are also described as near or far. One thing that is to my right or left, in front or behind, is near; another is far. For example: this wall is near, while that mountain or that other mountain is far away.

**C.** Can the same be understood of below and above?

**A.** It can. But it must be understood that one thing is natural above and below, and another is what is around us.

**C.** What is natural above and below, and what is above and below in relation to us?

**A.** Naturally, heaven is always above and earth below, and this cannot be changed by our movement [edition: “marked”; manuscripts: “movement … to alter”]. But what is above and below in relation to us changes with our movement. Thus someone may ascend from a lower place to a higher one, or descend from a higher place to a lower one.

**C.** Are all things belonging to quantity included within these six aspects?

**A.** Not all of them have these arrangements. Time, number, and speech belong to quantity, but they are not subject to these boundaries. When we say “one,” “ten,” or “one hundred,” merely naming the number and not counting something corporeally, we find in them neither right nor left. The same is true of time and speech, especially since these pass with great speed.

Time always runs on in unstable motion, so much so that, for those who consider it carefully, almost nothing appears to be present. Speech is the same: before it has been spoken, it does not appear. It is therefore clear that these three do not possess a position composed of distinct parts.

**C.** Can quantity possess what the Greeks call *mallon* and *elatton* [more and less; manuscripts: *ceuton*, *cecoton*]?

**A.** It cannot. One cannot say “more two-footed” or “less two-footed,” nor is it permissible to say “more three” or “less three.” Likewise, time and speech do not possess more and less. Rather, all things belonging to quantity are to be called even or odd.

**C.** What if we say “more long” or “less long”?

**A.** Then it will be the category of relation. For we are accustomed to say “more similar” and “less similar”; and what is similar is similar to something similar.

### 340

## CHAPTER V. ON RELATION

**C.** Since you have mentioned the category of relation, explain its properties.

**A.** I shall do so, although it is out of order [another reading: “outside the order”], since quality was placed after quantity. We call something the category of relation when what it is is spoken of from another, without whose association it cannot exist, and whose entire force proceeds from conjunction with another—for example, “double” is called double in relation to “single,” “greater” is greater in relation to “less,” and “similar” is similar in relation to something similar.

**C.** It is clear that relation exists not by its own power but through conjunction with another. But if it can be defined in another way, state that definition.

**A.** Relation is then truly and properly so called when, under one origin and one ending, both what is joined and that to which it is joined are found—for example, slave and master: both either exist together or do not exist together. For when you have said “master,” the slave necessarily exists; but when you remove the master, the slave does not appear.

The same applies to double and single: they either destroy or reveal one another. When the double appears, the single arises; when the double perishes, the single cannot remain [edition: “half”]. Likewise, if the single does not exist, neither does the double. But if the single exists, the double necessarily appears.

**C.** In what number or cases do these conjunctions of names usually occur?

**A.** Most often in the singular number—for example, “the single of the double,” “the father of the son.” Some are joined with the genitive case, others with the dative, and many with the ablative.

With the genitive: “the slave of the master,” “the double of the single.”

With the dative: “similar to the similar,” “equal to the equal.”

With the ablative: “perceptible by sense.”

**C.** Can reciprocal conversion occur in this category?

**A.** Yes. Both expressions can reasonably be used: “the slave of the master” and “the master of the slave”; “the single of the double” and “the double of the single.”

It must be understood that relatives must always either arise together or perish together. When the slave is removed, there is no master; when the master is removed, the slave does not appear. The same applies to father and son.

Therefore, according to this rule of the category, the foolish blindness of Arius—or rather, one should say, his pitiable blindness—and that of his associates is astonishing: they asserted that the Son is later than the Father in time, although it is entirely established according to dialectic that the Son is coeternal with the Father [manuscripts: “the Son is coeternal to the Father.”] And if God the Father is eternal—which even their impiety did not dare to deny—then the Son is certainly eternal as well, by the necessity of dialectical reasoning.

## CHAPTER VI. ON QUALITY

**C.** Now explain the nature of quality, and first say what difference there is between quality and “what sort.”

**A.** We call sweetness, austerity, whiteness, and blackness “qualities.” “What sort” is understood whenever we say that something is white, sweet, or austere.

**C.** Quality seems to have a great deal in common with the other categories.

**A.** It enters into all the others, and is therefore more difficult. It is found in substance when we say “a learned human being”; in quantity, “a white or black surface”; in relation, “a prudent father” or “an excellent son”; in doing, “he dances vigorously”; in undergoing, “he bears wounds bravely”; in place, “a dark place”; in time, “a hot or cold month”; in lying, “he lies face down or on his back”; in having, “he is suitably armed.”

**C.** How many species does this category have?

**A.** Four, which Aristotle calls genera. The first genus is habit and disposition; the second, natural capacity; the third, passive qualities or passions; the fourth, forms and figures.

**C.** What is habit or disposition?

**A.** Habit is what the mind possesses for a long time, such as virtue and learning. Disposition is a changeable impulse of the mind, such as sudden desire or anger.

**C.** What is the difference between virtue and learning?

**A.** The difference is certainly that learning is confined to that part of the soul called rational. Virtue, however, embraces all the parts of the soul and governs and rules the entire soul under its command. Thus it subdues anger and removes desires, something that learning cannot do.

**C.** How many parts of the soul are there?

**A.** Three: rational, spirited, and appetitive. But that belongs elsewhere. Let us now continue the journey we began [another reading: “let us proceed”].

**C.** What is natural capacity?

**A.** Whenever someone appears by nature to be capable or incapable of doing something—for example, when we see the bodies of boys and say that in the future they will be runners or boxers [another reading: pugilists]. This is not because they already possess the skill, but because they appear capable of possessing it through natural power. Similarly, physicians often predict health or illness from the condition of the body.

**C.** What are passive qualities or passions?

**A.** Passive qualities are whiteness, blackness, and their intermediate shades, redness and pallor. These arise only through an affection of either soul or body. For something to become black is an affection of the body; for it to become pale or red is an affection of the soul.

When the soul is unable to bear the shame of disgrace, it pours an abundance of blood into the outer parts of the body, as if in self-defense. Hence we become red from excessive shame. Pallor likewise results from a similar affection of the soul: when it is struck by great fear, it flees toward the innermost parts of the heart, and the blood follows it, so that the body visible to us, deserted by blood, becomes pale.

If these qualities persist for a long time [in the body], they should be called passive qualities. If they last only briefly and soon depart, we call them passions instead.

**C.** Now explain the fourth species, and first clarify the difference between forms and figures.

**A.** Figures are attributed to inanimate things, such as a triangle or a quadrilateral. Forms, however, are attributed to living beings, when we assert that some are handsome or deformed [another reading: “some beautiful or deformed things”]. In this same genus of quality are found curvature and straightness, roughness and smoothness, rarity and density.

**C.** Does quality admit contrariety?

**A.** Some qualities do and some do not. Who doubts that illness is contrary to health, injustice to justice, and evil to good? On the other hand, nothing is contrary to dark or pale, triangular or quadrilateral.

**C.** Does it admit more and less?

**A.** It does entirely, but not in every case. We can say “whiter” or “blacker,” but we cannot say “more triangular” or “more quadrilateral” [manuscripts: “or less triangular”].

**C.** If each of these four categories mentioned above has some property of its own, would you explain it?

**A.** They do. It is proper to *ousia* that it be singular and one in number and that it receive contraries within itself. For example, an individual human being is a singular *ousia*, one in number, and capable of receiving contraries. Thus he can receive health at one time and illness at another.

The property of quantity is that all its instances are called even or odd—for example, this human being is equal or unequal in size to that human being.

Relation has the property that its terms are mutually convertible, as in “the slave of the master” and “the master of the slave.”

The distinctive feature of quality is that all things belonging to it are named similar or dissimilar according to quality: sweet is called similar or dissimilar to sweet, white to white, and hot to hot.

## CHAPTER VII. ON DOING AND UNDERGOING

### [Col. 0961B]

**C.** It remains for you to speak about doing and undergoing, in which the nature of verbs is especially evident; since they must exist together, answer correspondingly.

**A.** These two seem to descend from the source of quality. For what makes something hot must itself be hot, and we know what sort of thing hot is. Likewise, what becomes hot receives heat through an affection of quality. And the person who teaches is a teacher when he teaches, and makes the other a student. Both teacher and student, however, have some quality, and so forth in similar cases.

**C.** Are contraries found in these categories?

**A.** Things belonging to the same genus are usually similar but contrary in quality. For hot, which imparts its heat to cold [another reading: “which opposes cold by the power of its heat”], belongs to the same genus. Likewise, what is sweet does not make something sweet unless that thing was not sweet. If what undergoes the action were sweet by its own nature, it would not receive another sweetness. Therefore what undergoes the action must not be sweet, so that it may receive an external sweetness; and sweet and bitter are contraries in quality.

**C.** What do you mean by saying that they are similar in genus?

**A.** Fire cannot receive sweetness from honey, but water can, because they possess a certain similarity in genus.

**C.** Do they admit more and less?

**A.** They do. For we can say that a teacher teaches more or less, and that a student is more or less learned.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON LYING DOWN

**C.** What are we to understand by “lying down”?

**A.** What else but the situation and position of a body—whether someone lies down, stands, or sits? Every body, being enclosed within the six parts mentioned above, must be in some place and in some condition within that place: it may be extended in length, spread out in breadth, or raised in height. All these things concern the position of the body, and the position itself must be local [possibly: “the situation … local”].

## CHAPTER IX. ON WHERE AND WHEN

**C.** What do you have to say about “where” and “when”?

**A.** What else but that “where” signifies place and “when” signifies time? Every body must occupy some place at some time—for example, “I was in Rome, in the senate, before the third hour, after the month of March.” These expressions must be understood as existing in place and time, not as being place and time themselves.

## CHAPTER X. ON HAVING

**C.** It remains for you to begin speaking about “having,” and to explain in how many ways we are said to have something.

**A.** There are eight species of having.

The first occurs whenever we have something in the mind, such as justice, disciplines, virtues, or vices.

The second occurs whenever we are said to have something in the body, such as whiteness, blackness, variety, or other things that exist in the body through quality [edition: “settle upon the body”].

The third derives from quantity, whenever we are said to have a length of four or five feet [another reading: “whenever something is said to have …”].

The fourth occurs when we are affirmed to have something not in the whole body but in a part of the body, such as a ring on a finger or shoes or boots on a foot.

The fifth species occurs when we are said to have something not in the body but around the body, such as clothing and all garments.

The sixth occurs whenever we are said to have the very parts of the body, such as hands, feet, the head, or the other members that belong to the structure of the limbs.

The seventh place concerns what is said to have something as a container, whenever flour or wine is said to have a vessel [another reading: “the seventh belongs to place”].

The eighth degree of having is that which appears to show our possession or ownership, as when someone is said to have a house or estate [another reading: “the eighth species”].

**C.** Is it not permissible for us to say that a woman has a husband, or that a man has a wife, a father a son, and a son a parent?

**A.** Learned teachers rightly reject such expressions and affirm that they are improperly stated [edition: “improperly applied”]. They maintain that one cannot have what itself has the one who has it. They therefore judge it more correct to say that a woman has a husband in the sense that a husband exists for a woman; that a wife exists for a man; that a father exists for a son; and that a master exists for servants. They insist that the force of this verb lies in the fact that it cannot signify both that someone possesses another and that he is possessed.

**C.** Join these ten predicaments into a single sentence for me.

**A.** A complete [another reading: perfect] sentence can be formed from them in this way: “Augustine, a great orator, the son of that man, standing in the temple, today wears a fillet and is wearied by disputing.”

“Augustine” is substance; “great,” quantity; “orator,” quality; “the son of that man,” relation; “standing,” position; “in the temple,” place; “today,” time; “wearing a fillet” [manuscripts: *infulatus*], having; “by disputing,” doing; “is wearied,” undergoing.

### 343

**C.** Is substance the first thing underlying these nine accidents?

**A.** It is necessary for magnitude or quality to be found in every body; for father and son to exist between two substances; likewise, for every body to exist in place and time; to be clothed and to stand; and who does not recognize that doing or undergoing something must be considered in every body? These accidents are found only in some underlying substance.

## CHAPTER XI. ON CONTRARIES OR OPPOSITES

**C.** Since you have often introduced contraries in our discussion, I would like you to explain the nature of contraries, or opposites.

**A.** There are four genera of contraries, which Aristotle calls *antikeimena* [ἀντικείμενα], that is, opposites.

The first genus is called “different,” such as wisdom and folly. This genus is divided into three species.

Some of these have an intermediate term, such as white and black, which have pale and dark as intermediate colors.

Some have no intermediate term, such as health and illness. Nothing lies between them, because one of the two must necessarily be present in the body.

Some have an intermediate state, but its middle has no name unless a name is formed for it by negating the opposites. Thus just and unjust have something intermediate, such as spitting out phlegm and cleaning the ears. These have no name unless we call them “neither just nor unjust.”

The second genus of contrariety consists of relatives, which are opposed to one another in such a way that they are compared with one another, such as double and single, greater and less. This is the only genus of opposites that is mutually compared.

The third genus consists of things produced through habit and privation. In these cases it must be observed that both terms are found in the same matter, in the same place, and at an appropriate time. Blindness and sight belong to the same matter, for they consist in seeing and not seeing. They are in the same place, for both blindness and sight have their place in the eyes.

They belong to an appropriate time, as in the case of calling someone bald only when, at the time when he ought to have hair, he does not possess it. To have hair and not to have hair are opposites.

The fourth genus of contrariety arises from affirmation and negation: “Homer is debating”; “Homer is not debating”; “Macharius is running”; “Macharius is not running.” Among dialecticians this kind usually generates almost all questions.

**C.** Are evils sometimes opposed to evils?

**A.** Yes, according to the philosophers, who said that virtues are always intermediate and have vices on either side. I think that the Apostle signified this when he said that we must walk by the royal road, turning neither to the right nor to the left—that is, toward the “more just” or the “less just.”

**C.** How can there be excessive justice?

**A.** Excessive justice is severity; deficient justice is flattery [manuscripts: “more just” and “less just”]. Between these two evils they placed justice as the mean.

Likewise, between cunning and dullness they placed prudence; between lust and insensibility they established temperance; and between cowardice and rashness courage reigns.

C. In how many ways do we say “prior”?—A. There are five ways in which one thing is said to be prior to another. The first is when we say that someone is earlier in time, that is, older. The second way is by number, when we say that one is prior to two, because two arise from one, not one from two; and when one perishes, two cannot exist, whereas when two perish, one nevertheless remains. The third way is by order, as in the disciplines: first one must learn the forms and names of individual letters; next, one must learn the combinations of syllables; then acquire knowledge of words; finally, the use of speech [Edit., “reason”] must be undertaken by us, for the sake of which we first learn all the preceding members, as it were. The fourth way is when the more fortunate and better people are usually called “prior” by the common people. The fifth kind is when that is prior which makes another thing from itself, as, for example, if a human being exists, we rightly call him a rational, mortal animal capable of laughter.

[Col. 0964B] But this kind of priority can be converted upon itself.—C. How so?—A. For whatever is a human being is a mortal, rational animal capable of laughter; likewise, whatever is a mortal, rational animal capable of laughter must be a human being. Nevertheless, it is necessary that the human being exist first; and only thus, finally, can this definition, or conversion, be true.

C. I should also have wished to hear the ways in which we say that things exist simultaneously.—A. We say that things exist simultaneously in three ways: either in time, by nature, or by genus.—C. Give examples.—A. In time, as when we say that two human beings exist together at the same time—for example, Albinus and Homer. By nature, as the single and the double. By genus, as animals distinguished by species: one terrestrial, another flying, another aquatic; for all of them the genus “animal” is equally applicable.

C. In how many ways does difference arise?—A. By material, by workmanship, or by both.—C. Give an example.—A. By material, if there are two similar rings, one golden and the other silver. By workmanship, if dissimilar rings are fashioned from gold. By both, as when a ring is golden and a stylus silver.

## CHAPTER XII. ON ARGUMENTS

C. I should like you to explain to me the nature and diversity of arguments, and first of all I ask you to say what an argument is.—A. An argument is an assertion concerning a doubtful matter. And it consists of an announcement [perhaps, “enunciation”].—C. What is an announcement?—A. A sentence signifying what is true or false, in the nominative case with the addition of *is* and *is not* [that is, with *est* and *non est*], as: “A human being exists”; “A human being does not exist.”

C. What about the other cases?—A. Nothing signifies something true when *is* or *is not* is added, unless other parts are added, as: “It belongs to a human being,” so that he is mortal and rational. Likewise: “Laughter is a proper accidental attribute of a human being.” The same applies in the remaining cases.

C. I know that when I say, “A human being exists,” or “A human being does not exist,” it is true or false. But when I say, “Human being” or “non-human being”—for *human being* is a name—I should like you to say what “non-human being” is.—A. “Human being” is a name, as you say; “non-human being” is an indefinite name: you deny that it is a human being, but you do not show what it is.

C. Continue the account of arguments [Al., “enumeration of arguments”], and explain how they are set forth.—A. [Col. 0965A] Some propositions of arguments are universal; others particular; others singular; others indefinite.—C. Give examples of each of these.—A. Universal propositions are: “Every human being is just,” or “Every human being is unjust.” Particular propositions are: “Some human being is just,” or “Some human being is unjust.” Singular propositions are: “Homer is just,” or “Homer is unjust.” Indefinite propositions are: “A human being is just,” or “A human being is unjust.”

C. Why are these called propositions of arguments?—A. For these are simple propositions, and they are called categorical, that is, predicative.—C. Why are they called predicative?—A. Because “human being” is a substance, while “justice” is an accident; and justice is predicated of a human being.—C. What is the relation between “human being” and “just”? [Col. 0965B] Are they not two names [and two terms]?—A. They are indeed two names and two terms; and the major term is predicated of the minor term.—C. How so?—A. Justice is predicated of a human being, and “human being” is the minor term. For justice is predicated not only of a human being, but also of God and the angels; therefore “justice” is a greater term than “human being,” because it extends more widely [Mss., “goes”]. The human being is subject to justice, and the minor term is called the subject; the major term, because it extends more widely [Ms., “which goes”], is called the predicate.

C. I am surprised how an accident can be greater than a substance.—A. What is greater or better, a candle or the light that shines forth from a candle?—C. Certainly, the light.—A. Is not light an accident of the candle, while the candle is a substance?—C. It is, and I recognize from this that an accident can be better and greater than a substance. But continue with the rest.

A. There are also other propositions of arguments that are hypothetical, that is, conditional.—C. How are they conditional?—A. They are propositions in which some condition is presupposed; and they are of two kinds, as follows: “Every human being, if he is good, is just”; thus a human being is just if he possesses goodness. Likewise: “The heaven, if it is round, is revolving”; thus the heaven is revolving if it is round.

C. Is it necessary, then, as you said earlier, that one term be major and the other minor?—A. No, because terms are often equal, as in: “A human being is capable of laughter.” For no other nature is capable of laughter except a human being; and “capable of laughter” does not extend more widely [Col. 0965D] than to the human being alone.

C. How can we distinguish which terms are equal and which unequal?—A. Equal terms can be mutually converted in equal fashion, as follows: “Whatever is a human being is capable of laughter”; and “Whatever is capable of laughter is a human being.” Unequal terms cannot be converted in this way, as: “Whatever is a human being is just”; or “Whatever is just is a human being.”

C. How can any matter be confirmed or refuted by these arguments?—A. In this way: “If speaking correctly is good for every human being, then grammar is good.” No one doubts that speaking correctly is good; therefore grammar is good, because correct speech cannot exist without grammar. Likewise: “If rusticity is bad, then not studying grammar is bad,” because every human being without grammar is rustic. Likewise: “If all wisdom is good, then philosophy is good,” because philosophy is the highest wisdom. These are conditional syllogisms.

C. And which are predicative syllogisms?—A. Those that proceed simply [Al., “stand”], as follows: “Everything just is honorable; everything honorable is good; therefore everything just is good.” These are called universal affirmations, because the conclusion is universal: everything just is good. Likewise: “Everything just is honorable; nothing honorable is disgraceful; therefore nothing just is disgraceful.” Here one proceeds from a universal affirmation to a universal negation and confirms that nothing just is disgraceful. Likewise: “Some just thing is honorable; everything honorable is useful; therefore some just thing is useful.” Here it is affirmed particularly that some just thing is useful. Likewise: “Some just thing is honorable; nothing honorable is disgraceful; therefore some just thing is not disgraceful.” Here too, through negation, it is affirmed particularly that some just thing is not disgraceful. There are many kinds of these syllogisms. But these examples are sufficient for the present to understand universal and particular conclusions in affirmation and negation.

C. How should a syllogism be constructed?—A. Most often from three members, so that the third, the conclusion, is formed from the first two propositions. Thus, if it is asked whether chastity is useful, we say: “Every virtue is useful; chastity, however, is a virtue; therefore chastity is useful.” From usefulness and virtue, then, a certain third thing is gathered and necessarily concluded: that chastity is useful.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE KINDS OF DEFINITIONS

C. I should now like you to explain to me the kinds and divisions of definitions. First tell me what a definition is.—A. A definition is a brief and lucid sentence that concludes, through its proper signification, the nature of the thing in question as distinguished from other things.—C. How should it begin or end [Edit., “be defined”]?—A. It must first extend outward to what is immense, beginning with the genus; then, proceeding gradually through its parts, it must arrive at that in which alone the thing defined exists. Thus those who fashion statues first choose for themselves an immense stone; then, gradually reducing it and cutting away what is superfluous, they arrive at the formation of faces and limbs. So a definition, beginning with the genus, gradually casts off the generality of its words and strives to approach the proper dwelling-place of the thing to be demonstrated.

C. Give an example.—A. “A human being is an animate, rational, mortal substance capable of laughter.” This definition begins with the breadth of substance, because whatever has a nature can be called a substance. Then it calls a human being an animate substance; by saying “animate,” it separates the human being from those that do not possess a soul, that is, life. By saying “rational,” it separates the human being from all beings that lack reason. [Col. 0967A] By saying “mortal,” it separates the human being from the angels, who do not die. Thus it arrives at the property of the human being, namely, being capable of laughter, which belongs to the human being alone.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE SPECIES OF DEFINITIONS

C. How many species of definitions are there?—A. Fifteen. Some of these belong to dialecticians, others to rhetoricians.—C. I especially wish to hear those that belong more particularly to dialecticians.—A. There is a principal definition, which properly demonstrates the substance of any nature; philosophers chiefly use this kind, as in: “A human being is an animal that is rational, mortal, and capable of sense-perception and learning.” For this definition descends through species and differences until it reaches what is proper, and it most fully designates what a human being is.

There is also a species of definition called one “from knowledge,” which signifies a thing through an act, not through its substance, as: “A human being is a rational being that, by natural conception and exercise, presides over all animals.” Here it signifies the act of the human being, not the substance. Likewise in the Psalms: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.” Here what the blessed man does is signified through an act.

There is also a species of definition called qualitative, which designates any person by a quality. Thus, if it is asked what kind of person a human being is, the answer is: “A human being is one who is strong in talent, distinguished in the arts, and capable of distinguishing between good and evil.” Likewise, in the Psalms [Col. 0967C] the prophet shows what kind of person Christ is when he says: “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips.”

There is also a definition by difference, as when it is asked what difference there is between a king and a tyrant. By adding the difference, what each of them is is defined in this way: “A king is pious and moderate; a tyrant, however, is impious and savage.” And in the Psalm: “The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous shows mercy and gives.”

There is also a definition by privation [Al., “privation”]. Thus, if it is asked what substance is, it may be said that it is neither quality, nor quantity, nor any accident. Through this kind of definition even God can, to some extent, be understood. For although we can in no way comprehend what God is—namely, no one can express his nature as it is—nevertheless, according to the philosophers, he must be defined by what he is not. Thus we may say: “God is neither a body, nor an animal, nor any element, nor our sense, nor our intellect, nor anything that can be grasped through these.”

There is also a definition through the lack of a complete member within the same genus. Thus, if it is asked what a quadrant is, the answer is: “That which lacks a dodrans in order to be a whole unit.”

There is also a definition through praise, as: “A leader is the mind, [counsel,] and discipline of the state” [Mss., “The law is the counsel of the mind”]. And in the Psalm: “The law of the Lord is blameless, restoring souls; the testimony of the Lord is trustworthy, granting wisdom to the simple.”

[Col. 0968A] There is also a definition that is, as it were, according to reason, that is, when a lesser thing is shown under the name of a greater thing, as: “A human being is a lesser world”; and: “An edict is an annual law” [Al., “a law of the mind”].

C. To which part of the art of dialectic should these definitions chiefly be assigned?—A. To the Topics.

## CHAPTER XV. ON THE TOPICS

C. What are the Topics?—A. The seats of arguments, the sources of meanings, and the origins of expressions.—C. Into how many species are topical arguments divided?—A. The argumentation of the Topics, that is, of the places, is threefold, because arguments are either found in the matter itself under discussion; or arise when drawn from other things; or are taken from outside.

C. Explain the first species.—A. According to the dialecticians, arguments are taken from the matter itself in three ways: from the whole, from the parts, and from the end.—C. Confirm this with examples.—A. “The whole” is usually understood in two ways: either from the genus, as when it is asked whether justice is useful and a syllogism of this kind is made: “Every virtue is useful; justice, however, is a virtue; therefore justice is useful.” Here justice is proved useful from the whole—that is, from the genus, namely virtue, which is the genus of justice.

The whole is also that which is composed as an integral thing from many parts; thus the integrity of the world is composed of many parts, one of which is human beings. But if it is asked whether human affairs are governed by divine providence, a syllogism of this kind is made: “If the world is governed by God’s providence, and human beings are a part of the world, then human affairs are governed by divine providence.” Here it is necessary to understand that what belongs to the whole also belongs to the part [Edit., “what happens to the whole”].

Arguments are likewise drawn from the parts, as when the question is whether medicine is useful: “If driving away diseases, preserving health, and treating wounds are useful—these being parts of medicine—then medicine is useful.” An argument is also made from the end, which some call the mark. Thus, if it is asked whether justice is good, a syllogism of this kind is made: “If being blessed is good, then justice is good.” For this is the end of justice: that whoever lives according to justice may attain blessedness; and it is necessary that a thing whose end is good be itself good.

[Col. 0968D] C. How many species do those arguments have that are drawn from elsewhere?—A. Thirteen. Some are made from conjugates, some from the genus, some from the species, some from similarity, some from difference, some from contraries, some from what follows, some from antecedents, some from adjuncts, some from things that conflict, some from causes, some from effects, and some from comparison.—C. Explain this also more clearly with examples.—A. I shall do so.

### From conjugates

An argument is first drawn from conjugates when an inference is made from the derivation of a noun or verb, as: “If he has written, he is a writer”; “if a field is common-pasture land, there is a right to pasture it in common.” For *compascuus* and *compascere* are joined to one another.

Terence also says: “I am a human being; I consider nothing human alien to me.” And Cicero: “He said that Verres had swept away [Ms., ‘overthrown’] the province.”

### From the genus

An argument is from the genus when one descends from a general matter to some species, as: “The race of women is greedy; for Eurypila sold the life of her husband for gold” [Mss., “Erypila”; Al., “Eriphyle betrayed him”]. Likewise: “If he is lustful, he is also an adulterer; if he is greedy, he is also a thief.”

### From the species

An argument is from the species when, for example, we wish to prove someone cruel and show that certain acts were cruelly performed by him. Likewise, Virgil:

> But was it not thus that the Phrygian shepherd entered Lacedaemon  
> and carried Leda’s Helen to the Trojan cities?

(Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.363.)

[Col. 0969B] For “Phrygian shepherd” is a species; and if that one man did this, then other Trojans in general can do it also. For the species is always subordinate to the genus, as a human being is subordinate to animal. Therefore the genus is called the whole, and the species a part; thus desire is the genus of all lusts. A certain part, or species, of desire is greed.

### From similarity

An argument is from similarity when similar examples are presented, so that from what has certainly occurred in a similar matter, what is doubtful and under inquiry may also be confirmed. Similarity is often considered in contraries, as: “If it is fitting to forgive those who have inflicted harm through ignorance, then it is not necessary to show gratitude to those who have done good by necessity.” Here the contraries are doing good and doing harm. The similarity, however, lies in the dispositions: neither one wished to harm, nor did the other wish to benefit.

Similarity is also made through equals, when we draw a probable argument not from contrary things but from things very similar in nature. For example: “Just as a place in the sea without a harbor is unsafe for ships, so a mind without faith cannot be a harbor for friends.”

It is also made in matters that fall under the same principle, when the principle of one matter confirms the principle of another; for example: “The one who sold his son acted unjustly, and the one who bought him also acted unjustly” [Mss., “acted”].

### From difference

An argument is made from difference when things are separated by a difference, as Virgil says:

> You see neither the horses of Diomedes nor the chariot of Achilles.

(Virgil, *Aeneid* X.581.)

[Col. 0969D] Difference also occurs when, within the same genus, one species is distinguished from another, as Marcus Tullius says: “As Verres was in his urban province, so he was in his provincial one.”

### From contraries

An argument is taken from contraries when things differing from one another are set in opposition, as Virgil:

> O mother, to what destinies do you call me, or what do you seek by these things?  
> Shall ships made by mortal hands have the right  
> to be immortal, and shall Aeneas traverse  
> sure dangers amid uncertainty?

Virgil says that Jupiter spoke these words to Berecynthia.

Likewise: “If one who avoids and flees an enemy must be called a deserter, then certainly one who neither avoided nor fled him, but attacked him voluntarily [Ms., ‘attacked’], cannot in any way be called a deserter.” And: “If something is honorable, it is not disgraceful.” And: “If something was done lawfully, it cannot be prosecuted as an injury.”

### From what follows

An argument is from what follows when something inevitably follows from a given matter, as Virgil:

> We have not come either to ravage the Libyan household gods with the sword  
> or to carry stolen spoils back to the shores;  
> such is not the purpose of our heart.

And the rest.

Likewise: “If a woman has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man.” She has given birth; therefore it necessarily follows that she has had intercourse with a man.

### From antecedents

An argument is from antecedents when what follows is proved from what has previously taken place. Thus Marcus Tullius, speaking for Milo: “Since Clodius had foretold three days before that Milo would perish, and since he had not hesitated to reveal what he intended to do, can you doubt what he did?” The prediction preceded, and the deed followed. And the rest.

### From adjuncts

The credibility of an argument is taken from adjuncts when it is shown with probability what is going to result from any matter, as Virgil:

> [lacuna] If they drive us out, they believe that nothing will prevent them  
> from bringing all Hesperia completely beneath their yoke.

(Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.147.)

For every matter has something preceding, something simultaneous, and something following; and therefore we gather arguments from all these. In adjuncts also, as Cicero wished, one chiefly investigates what occurred before the matter, with the matter, and after the matter; this place pertains especially to conjecture. Before the matter: preparations and conversations. In the matter: the sound of footsteps. After the matter: pallor, blushing, and anything similar.

The place from antecedents, consequences, and things that conflict differs from conjoined or adjunct matters in this respect: conjoined matters do not always occur, whereas consequences always do. Those things, therefore, are consequences that necessarily follow a matter, as: “If it is day, it is light.” The same applies to antecedents and things that conflict: whatever follows any matter is necessarily connected with it [and whatever precedes it necessarily draws the consequence after it]; and whatever conflicts with it is of such a kind that it can never be connected with it.

### From things that conflict

An argument is from things that conflict when what is brought against the defendant is destroyed by some contradiction. Thus Cicero says: “This man, then, who is accused of wishing to kill you in his own house, was not only freed from danger by you but also enriched with the highest honor.” Likewise: “If on the day this murder was committed at Rome I was at Athens, I could not have taken part in the murder.”

### From causes

An argument is drawn from causes when it is proved from common custom that the matter under discussion could have occurred. Thus Terence:

> I was not without some fear, just now, of warning you to beware lest you do  
> what the common crowd of slaves disturbs [Al., “usually disturbs”] by tricks, so that you might deceive me.

(Terence, *Andria* III.4.3.)

[Col. 0971A] An argument is also made from a cause in this way: when we say that lust is the cause of adultery, or greed the cause of parricide. But then the force of the cause—that is, of greed or lust—must be discussed at greater length: insofar as the cause appears disgraceful, the deed too appears dishonorable. Thus: “Whoever enters a temple for the sake of making a profit is sacrilegious.” For it is not the deed itself that makes the wrongdoing, but the cause of doing it; and misdeeds are judged not by their outcome but by the attempt.

### From effects

An argument is from effects when something is proved from what has been done, as Virgil:

> Fear exposes degenerate spirits.

(Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.13.)

For fear is the cause of a spirit’s being degenerate; degeneracy is an effect of fear.

Efficient causes are those that accomplish something either through their own force, as fire produces burning, or without which something cannot be accomplished, as ships cannot exist without beams. Some efficient causes are necessary, others are not.

Joined to this place of efficient causes is the place of effects from causes, that is, of outcomes. For just as a cause indicates what has been effected, so an effect demonstrates what the cause was, as smoke demonstrates fire. Therefore Cicero placed efficient causation under the place of causes [Edit., “placed it under the place of efficiency”], but the outcome under the place of effects. Thus, if you have proved someone insolent, you may say that he will also be arrogant. Through the outcome—that is, the effect of insolence—you prove arrogance; and the cause of arrogance, that is, its efficient cause, is insolence [Al., “the cause of arrogance is insolence”].

### From comparison

An argument is drawn from comparison when the force of a judgment is confirmed by comparing persons or causes. Comparison always aims at magnifying the matter, and it occurs in three ways: from the greater, from the lesser, and from equals.

From the greater, as Virgil:

> You can arm brothers of one mind for battle.

(Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.335.)

Therefore, if you can do this with brothers, how much more can you do it with others? Likewise, from the greater: “If it is permitted to kill an adulterer, it is also permitted to beat him with whips.”

[Col. 0971D] From comparison with lesser things: “If it is permitted to kill a nocturnal thief, why not a brigand?” [Al., “why?”] Likewise, from the lesser: “If he will not hesitate to sin for the sake of a small sum of money, what will he do when a greater profit is set before him? Certainly he did not abstain” [Al., “he would not abstain”].

From comparison with equals, as Virgil:

> You can snatch Aeneas from the hands of the Greeks;  
> is it impious for us to have helped the Rutulians in some way?

(Virgil, *Aeneid* X.81–82.)

Likewise, from equals: “If someone denies that he committed a murder on the grounds that he himself did not strike the blow, it is said to him that it makes no difference whether he was the author of the murder or whether he himself struck the blow, because through either route the crime came to the same outcome.”

C. Do the evangelical parables belong to these species, where you said that arguments are drawn either from similarity or from contrariness?—A. They certainly do.—C. In what way?—A. Some parables are called “from equals,” others “from contraries.” Those from equals can be joined with these words: “As this is, so also is that.” Thus, concerning the servant who, after being released by his master, strangled his fellow servant, it may be said: “As the master dealt with this wicked servant who did not forgive his fellow servant, so also your heavenly Father will deal with you.” And the rest.

Likewise, concerning the moneylender who, after forgiving two debtors what they owed, was loved more by the one to whom he forgave more. And concerning the man who had two sons, the elder near him in the field and the younger living riotously in a distant land, and innumerable examples of this kind. For from the degree to which these things are similar, an understanding is drawn of the matter to which they are applied for the purpose of making it known.

Those that are from contraries can be joined with these words: “If this is so, how much more is that so?” Thus, a man who was awakened—not out of friendship but to escape annoyance—while already asleep, so that he might lend three loaves to his friend. “If that man, compelled by annoyance, gave, how much more will God, who loves his servants and urges us to ask [Al., ‘them to ask,’] give good things to those who ask him?”

Likewise, concerning the steward of iniquity, who, by falsifying documents, provided for himself and was praised by his master, the argument should be concluded in this way: if the man who practiced fraud could be praised by his master, how much more pleasing to the Lord God are those who faithfully perform [and] observe his commands and institutions [Al., “observe”]!

A comparison was likewise drawn from the unjust judge who was importuned by a widow to the judge God, with whom the unjust judge cannot be compared in any respect.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON THE *PERI HERMENEIAS*

C. I desire to hear from you the subtleties of the *Peri Hermeneias*, concerning which it has been said that Aristotle dipped his pen in the mind while writing them.—A. Their subtlety is immense; but the narrow scope of our discussion permits us to touch upon only a few matters, and it seems that we need explain only what they are concerned with [Al., “what they are”].

C. First explain the interpretation of that name.—A. They are called *Perihermeniae*, as though “concerning interpretation.”—C. How “concerning interpretation”?—A. Every thing that is one and can be signified by one expression is demonstrated either by a noun or by a verb.

C. How is this or that demonstrated?—A. Through a noun, the substance of every thing is signified, as “human being.” Through a verb, the action or passion of any thing is shown, as “the human being runs”; “the human being is burned.” These two parts of speech interpret the whole of whatever the mind has conceived for expression [Mss., “for speaking”].

C. What does “has conceived” mean?—A. “Has conceived” means “has understood.” For every expression is an interpreter of the mind, because expression interprets what the mind understands through *cataphasis* or *apophasis*.

C. Pronounce these two names in Latin.—A. *Cataphasis* [κατάφασις] is affirmation, as: “The human being runs.” [Col. 0973A] *Apophasis* [ἀπόφασις] is negation, as: “The human being does not run.”

C. How many species of the *Perihermeniae* are there?—A. The philosopher mentioned above [Al., “Aristotle himself”] divides them into seven species: noun, verb, sentence, enunciation, affirmation, negation, and contradiction.—C. Do you intend to lead me through grammar once again?—A. I do, but at a higher level. And if you ask questions, you will see how far the subtlety of dialectic differs from the simplicity of grammar.

### Definition of the noun

C. What is a noun?—A. A significant vocal expression established by convention, without time, signifying something defined, in the nominative case with *is* and *is not*, and in the oblique cases signifying nothing; no part of it is significant when separated. For example: “Socrates.”

C. Explain this philosophical definition more clearly.—A. A noun is a significant vocal expression. For every noun signifies something, whether visible or invisible, substantial or accidental.—C. [How can it be substantial or accidental?]—A. Every nature that can be called a substance, as “human being.” And something accidental belongs to every nature except God alone, as heat belongs to the human being in the body and learning in the mind.

C. Does goodness, justice, and the other virtues not belong accidentally to God?—A. Goodness and justice do not belong accidentally to him; rather, he himself is goodness and justice. The same must be understood of the other virtues.

C. What does “established by convention” mean?—A. It means “according to the linguistic composition of individual peoples.” The things themselves are the same among all peoples, but the names are different and are formed according to the convention of those who impose them. Thus the nature of gold is the same among Greeks and Latins, while the Greeks call it *chryson* (χρυσόν, “gold”) and the Latins *aurum*.

C. What does “without time” mean?—A. Because a noun does not bring time along with it, as verbs do.

C. What does “signifying something defined” mean?—A. Every noun in the nominative case, when joined with the substantive verb *sum*, signifies something definite in affirmation or negation, as: “I am a human being”; “you are a human being”; “he is a human being.” “I am not a tree”; “you are not a tree”; “he is not a tree.” In the oblique cases, however, it signifies nothing definite unless other parts are added to complete the signification, as: “This book belongs to this human being”; “Give this book to this human being”; “Make this human being read this book”; “I learned this book from this human being.”

C. What does “no part of it is significant when separated” mean?—A. “Socrates” is a three-syllable name; but when its individual syllables are separated, none signifies anything by itself, neither *So*, nor *cra*, nor *tes*.

C. Does not *domus*, if it is divided into two syllables, namely *do* and *mus*, nevertheless signify something? And there are countless examples of this kind.—A. It does signify something, but the signification of the second name has no connection with the signification of the earlier name. For *mus* is an animal in itself, and *do* is a verb signifying some action; but the signification of the two has no bearing on signifying a house.

C. In the case of compound nouns, such as *hircocervus*, which is called *tragelaphus* in Greek, does *hircocervus* not appear to be so called because it has some likeness to a deer and some likeness to a goat?—A. It may perhaps be so called for that reason. But if I name a *hircocervus*, what animal do you understand me to signify: a goat or a deer [Mss., “goats or deer”]?—C. Neither a goat nor a deer, but that animal which is customarily signified by this name.—A. Therefore that name signifies nothing separated that pertains to the first nature which it initially began to signify.

### Definition of the verb

C. What is a verb?—A. A significant vocal expression established by convention, signifying something defined together with time, and an accident.

C. From the interpretation of the preceding definition I understand what “significant vocal expression” and “established by convention” mean. And perhaps I see what “together with time” means, because a verb usually brings time along with it. But explain what “signifying something defined” and “an accident” mean.—A. Every verb signifies a definite action or passion, as “I see” or “I am seen.” And that action or passion ordinarily happens to some substance, as seeing or being seen happens, for example, to a human being.

C. If all verbs signify an action [Ms., “an act”] or passion, why are some called neuter?—A. Not because they lack one of these significations, but because they are always expressed uniformly: either as an action alone, as *manduco* (“I eat”) and *curro* (“I run”), or as a passion, as *vapulo* (“I am beaten”) and *veneo* (“I am sold”). But that belongs elsewhere.

### Definition of the sentence

[Col. 0974C]

C. What is a sentence?—A. An appropriate arrangement of parts, expressing a complete thought, some part of which is significant when separated.—C. What does “significant when separated” mean?—A. A complete sentence is: “Virgil sang of the descendants of Aeneas.” “Virgil,” “the descendants of Aeneas,” and “sang”—these three, when separated, each signify something by itself: “Virgil” signifies a human being, “the descendants of Aeneas” a people, and “sang” [an action].

### Definition of the enunciation

C. What is an enunciation?—A. An enunciation is a sentence signifying what is true or false.—C. How does it signify what is true or false?—A. According to the dialecticians, the principal species of sentence are five; but only this one, namely the enunciative sentence, signifies something true or false, as: “A human being exists,” or “A human being does not exist”; “Socrates is disputing,” “Socrates is not disputing.” Of these one must necessarily be true: either that Socrates is disputing or that Socrates is not disputing. And in this species alone philosophers who have disputed the truth or falsity of things have placed all their controversies.

C. Do the other four species not also belong to dialecticians?—A. They do not belong to dialecticians, but to grammarians.

C. Nevertheless, name them with examples.

### Interrogative

A. There is a species of sentence that is interrogative, as:

> Where are you going on foot, Moeris? Or by what road [Ms., “and by what road”] does it lead into the city?

[Note: Virgil, *Eclogues* IX.1.]

### Imperative

There is also a species of sentence that is imperative:

> Come now, go, my son; summon the West Winds and glide upon your wings.

[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.223.]

### Deprecative

There is also a species of sentence that is deprecative, as:

> Jupiter, be merciful, if you can be moved by any prayers.

[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* II.]

### Vocative

There is also a species of sentence that is vocative, as:

> Come here, O Meliboeus.

But none of these species can signify anything true or false [Col. 0975B]; only the enunciative species displays something as true or false.

### Definition of affirmation

[Col. 0976A]

C. What is affirmation?—A. Affirmation is an enunciation of something about something, as: “Socrates exists”; or of something about some thing, as: “The heaven is revolving.”

### Definition of contradiction and negation [Schema]

C. What is negation?—A. Negation is an enunciation of something away from something, as: “Socrates does not exist”; or of something about some thing, as: “The heaven is not revolving.”—C. What is contradiction?—A. Contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation, as: “Socrates is disputing”; “Socrates is not disputing.”
