[Note: [Col. 0975] Double-click the ornament icon that follows to view the structure of the schema whose contents are keyed below.]

Philosophy

Physics

Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, Astronomy

Ethics

Prudence, Justice [Col. 0976B], Fortitude, Temperance

Logic

Dialectic, Rhetoric [Note: [Col. 0976B] In the Viennese manuscript codex is added: “The discussion of Dialectic and its virtues by King Charles and Albinus ends.”]

## FIFTH OPUSCULUM. THE DISCUSSION OF PIPPIN, ROYAL AND MOST NOBLE YOUNG MAN, WITH ALBINUS THE SCHOLAR

### Preliminary Notice

[Col. 0975C]

Cl. Quercetanus published the following Discussion according to the copy printed at Hamburg in the year 1615. The same Discussion is found in the 900-year-old Salzburg manuscript, placed among the letters and poems of Alcuin, though without the author’s name; from it we have recorded variant readings.

Pippin: What is a letter?—Albinus: The guardian of history.

P: What is a word?—A: The betrayer of the mind.

P: Who generates the word?—A: The tongue.

P: What is the tongue?—A: The whip of the air.

P: What is air?—A: The guardian of life.

P: What is life?—A: The joy of the blessed, the sorrow of the wretched, the expectation of death.

P: What is death?—A: An unavoidable event, an uncertain pilgrimage, the tears of the living, the confirmation of a testament, the robber of a human being.

P: What is a human being?—A: Death’s chattel, a passing traveler, a guest of a place.

P: To what is a human being like?—A: To an apple.

P: How is a human being placed?—A: Like a lamp in the wind.

P: Where is he placed?—A: Within six walls.

P: Which?—A: Above, below; in front, behind; on the right and on the left.

353 P: In how many ways is he changeable?—A: Six.

P: Which?—A: Hunger and fullness; rest and labor; wakefulness and sleep.

[Col. 0976C] P: What is sleep?—A: An image of death.

P: What is human freedom?—A: Innocence.

P: What is the head?—A: The summit of the body.

P: What is the body?—A: The dwelling of the soul.

P: What is the hair?—A: The clothing of the head.

P: What is the beard?—A: The distinction of sex, the honor of age.

P: What is the brain?—A: The preserver of memory.

P: What are the eyes?—A: Guides of the body, vessels of light, indicators of the mind.

P: What are the nostrils?—A: The conveyance of odors.

P: What are the ears?—A: Collectors of sounds.

P: What is the forehead?—A: The image of the mind.

P: What is the mouth?—A: The nourisher of the body.

P: What are the teeth?—A: The millstone of bites [Ms., “millstones of bites”].

P: What are the lips?—A: The doors of the mouth.

P: What is the throat?—A: The devourer of food.

P: What are the hands?—A: The laborers of the body.

P: What are the fingers?—A: The plectrums of strings.

P: What is the lung?—A: The preserver of air.

P: What is the heart?—A: The receptacle of life.

P: What is the liver?—A: The guardian of heat.

P: What is bile?—A: The stirring up of anger.

P: What is the spleen?—A: Capable of laughter and joy.

P: What is the stomach?—A: The cooker of foods [Ms., “the cook of foods”].

P: What is the belly?—A: The guardian of fragile things.

[Col. 0977A] P: What are the bones?—A: The strength of the body.

P: What are the hips?—A: The architraves of columns.

P: What are the legs?—A: The columns of the body.

P: What are the feet?—A: A mobile foundation.

P: What is blood?—A: The moisture of the veins, the nourishment of life.

P: What are the veins?—A: The springs of the flesh.

P: What is heaven?—A: A revolving sphere, [an immense summit].

P: What is light?—A: The face of all things.

P: What is day?—A: The stimulus to labor.

P: What is the sun?—A: The splendor of the world, the beauty of heaven, the grace of nature, the honor of day, the distributor of the hours.

P: What is the moon?—A: The eye of night, generous with dew, [Col. 0977B] a foreseer of storms.

P: What are the stars?—A: The painting of the summit, the guides of sailors, the adornment of night.

P: What is rain?—A: The conception of earth, the mother of crops.

P: What is mist?—A: Night in the day, the labor of the eyes.

P: What is wind?—A: The disturbance of the air, the movement of waters, the dryness of the earth.

P: What is earth?—A: The mother of growing things, the nurse of the living, the granary of life, the devourer of all things.

P: What is the sea?—A: The road of boldness [Ms., “the road of life”], the boundary of earth, the divider of regions, the lodging of rivers, the source of rains, a refuge in dangers, a delight in pleasures.

[Col. 0977C] P: What are rivers?—A: An unceasing course, the restoration of the sun, the irrigation of the earth.

P: What is water?—A: The support of life, the washing away of filth.

P: What is fire?—A: Excessive heat, the nourishment of things being born, the ripening of crops.

P: What is cold?—A: A feverish condition of the limbs.

P: What is frost?—A: A persecution of grasses, the destruction [Ms., “persecutor … destroyer”] of leaves, the bond of the earth, the source of waters.

P: What is snow?—A: Dry water.

P: What is winter?—A: An exile of summer.

P: What is spring?—A: The painter of the earth.

P: What is summer?—A: The clothing of the earth, the ripening of crops.

P: What is autumn?—A: The granary of the year.

P: What is a year?—A: The chariot of the world.

P: Who drives it?—A: Night and day, cold and heat.

P: Who is its charioteer?—A: The sun and the moon.

P: How many palaces does it have?—A: Twelve.

P: Who are the governors of the palaces?—A: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, the Archer [Ms., Sagittarius], Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces.

P: How many days does it dwell in each palace?—A: The sun, thirty [days and ten and a half] hours [Note: [Col. 0977D] See Alcuin’s letter 83]. [Col. 0978A] The moon, two days and eight hours, and a bisse of one hour.

P: Master, I am afraid to go up so high.—A: Who brought you up?

P: Curiosity.—A: If you are afraid, I shall descend [Ms., “we shall descend”]. I shall follow wherever you go.

P: If I knew what a ship was, I would prepare one for you, so that you could come to me.—A: A ship is a wandering house, lodging anywhere, a traveler without footprints, near to the sand [Ms., “near to the sandy place”].

P: What is sand?—A: A wall of earth.

P: What is grass?—A: The clothing of the earth.

P: What are vegetables?—A: Friends of physicians, the praise of cooks.

P: What is it that makes bitter things sweet?—A: Hunger.

[Col. 0978B] P: What is it that does not make a person tired?—A: Profit.

354 P: What is sleep to a person who is awake?—A: Hope.

P: What is hope?—A: Relief from labor, [an uncertain outcome].

P: What is friendship?—A: Equality of friends [Ms., “of minds”].

P: What is faith?—A: Certainty concerning an unknown and wondrous thing.

P: What is a wonder?—A: Recently I saw a standing man, a dead man walking [Ms., “a dead man laboring and walking”], who never existed.

P: How can that be? Explain it to me.—A: An image in water.

[Col. 0978C] P: Why did I not understand this by myself, although I saw [this very man] so many times?—A: Because you are a young man of good character and natural intelligence, I shall propose some other wonders to you; try to determine whether you can work them out by yourself.

P: I shall do so [Ms., “we shall do so”]; nevertheless, if I say something contrary to the truth, correct me.—A: I shall do as you wish. An unknown man spoke with me without tongue or voice; he never existed before and never will exist afterward; I could not hear him, and I did not know him.

P: Perhaps a dream has wearied you, master?—A: Yes, my son. Hear another: I saw the dead begetting the living, and the dead were consumed by the breath of the living.

P: Fire was born from the rubbing of trees, consuming [the trees].—A: That is true. I heard the dead speaking many things.

P: Never properly, unless they are hung in the air.—A: Indeed. I saw an unquenchable fire resting in water.

P: You mean a flint [in water, I suppose].—A: It is as you suppose. I saw a dead man sitting upon a living man, and, in the laughter of the dead man, the living man died [Ms., “the living man dies”].

P: Our cooks know this [Ms., “Our cooks know”].—A: [They know]. But put your finger over your mouth, so that the boys may not hear what it is. I went hunting with others; in that hunt, if we caught anything, we carried nothing away with us; but what we could not catch, we carried home with us.

[Col. 0979A] P: This is a peasants’ hunt.—A: It is. I saw someone born before he was conceived.

P: You saw him, and perhaps you ate him.—A: I ate him. What is it that does not exist, yet has a name and gives an answer to one who makes a sound?

P: Ask “Biblos” in the forest [Ms., “Bilos in the woods”].—A: I saw a guest running with his house; he was silent, but his house made a sound.

P: Prepare a net for me, and I shall explain it to you.—A: Who is the one whom you cannot see [who … can], except with your eyes closed?

P: The one who snores shows him to you.—A: I saw a man holding eight in his hand, and suddenly he snatched seven from the eight, and six remained.

P: The boys know this in the schools.—A: Who is the one [Col. 0979B] who, if you remove his head, rises higher?

P: Go [Ms., “See”] to your bed, and there you will find him.—A: There were three: one was never born and died once. [The second was born once and never died.] The third was born once and died twice [Note: [Col. 0979] Compare Symphosius, Riddle 94, and Bonaventura Vulcanius, p. 294.]

P: The first is homonymous with the earth [Ms., “with mine”]; the second with my God; the third with a poor man.—A: Nevertheless, tell me the first letters [of the names].

P: I. V. [Ms., IIII,] 12 XXX.—A: I saw a flying woman with an iron beak, a wooden body, and a feathered tail, carrying death.

P: An ally of soldiers.—A: What is a soldier?

P: The wall of the empire, the fear of enemies, glorious service.—A: What is that which is and is not?

P: Nothing.—A: How can it be and not be [Ms., “be”]?

P: It exists in name, but does not exist in reality.—A: What is [Ms., “Who is”] the silent messenger?

[Col. 0980B] P: The one I hold in my hand.—A: What do you hold in your hand?

P: My letter [Ms., “your letter”].—A: Read happily, my son.

[Col. 0979]

## SIXTH OPUSCULUM. ON THE COURSE AND LEAP OF THE MOON AND THE BISSEXTILE (C, G)*

355 ### Preliminary Notice

[Col. 0979B]

Cl. Quercetanus included among Alcuin’s letters, under numbers 25 and 26, two sheets which, since they had nothing in the form of letters, it seemed appropriate to remove from there, transfer to this place, and append to those little works that had a similar subject—namely, astronomy. Alcuin appears to be referring to these sheets in letter 85 to Charles, where he writes: “As for the divisions of the signs by hours, and how nine lunar hours correspond to five solar days, I remember that I sent this to you in another letter.”

Alcuin also wrote several things to the same most wise king in which he attempted, according to the capacity of his age, to explain astronomical science. Most of these writings, as we noted above [Col. 847], have perished through the passage of time and the loss of men. Two little works, however, on the Leap of the Moon and on the Bissextile escaped this loss. Together with the short Calculation for finding the paschal moon, they still survive and are preserved in the Vatican library. I received them from the very learned man whom I have already praised elsewhere, Don Pietro Francesco Foggini, the most diligent custodian of that exceedingly rich library. These little works are found there among the Swedish Royal manuscripts, no. 226, fol. 18, and in the Palatine manuscript codex, no. 1449, fol. 11 verso.

Nor do I in any way doubt that these same little works truly belong to Alcuin, both because they are attributed to him in those very ancient codices and because Alcuin himself appears to identify them as products of his own labor in letters 82 and 100. In the former he says:

“To answer the questions in your little sheet … I shall undertake to add a few things about the various reckoning of the leap. First I shall set down what I have learned in the books of learned men. Second, what I have been able to investigate by the persuasion of reason. Third, what I have been able to remember from the mathematical discipline once heard.”

A little farther on he says:

“These calculations of the lunar leap, some of which I have set out distinctly on the pages of another little sheet, as I said above, I wrote from reading the interpretations of the fathers; others I investigated by conjecture of reason; others I gathered from various calculations of mathematicians.”

[Col. 0980B] Alcuin likewise testifies in letter 100 that he had once begun to treat the Bissextile briefly with a few little calculations. There he also declares that he had received from that most wise king “calculation sheets concerning the preparation of the lunar or bissextile reckoning,” in which, he says, “I found calculations most diligently sought out, most keenly discovered, and most nobly presented; and what my former devotion had begun concerning the Bissextile with a few little calculations, your most sagacious investigation has completed abundantly.” We are all the less doubtful that these few calculations are contained in the treatise which we publish here from the Vatican manuscript and at the end of it, since they are entirely consistent with Alcuin’s style and agree exceptionally well with the method of computation that he used elsewhere.

I think that the learned reader will not dislike what one of our colleagues observed while commenting on both of Alcuin’s brief treatises, On the Leap of the Moon and On the Bissextile, and added for the explanation and correction of each:

“An attentive reader,” he says, “will generally observe that all Alcuin’s calculations concerning the Leap of the Moon can be reduced to this sort of problem: namely, how, given the daily, monthly, or yearly lunar increment, one can calculate and extract the complete day called the leap after the nineteen-year cycle has elapsed—or conversely. Alcuin solves this in different hypotheses, sometimes taking the monthly increment to be four moments and a twelfth part of a moment, together with a five-hundred-and-sixty-fourth part of a moment, that is, an atom; sometimes four moments and forty-eight atoms, and so forth; sometimes supposing the increments to be given in units of time, sometimes in divisions of the ecliptic. He should be understood to have done this either to vary the calculation or—what seems more agreeable—as an aid to teaching. For just as it is certain that he taught astronomy in the palace school, so he was compelled to use different approaches according to the different capacities of his pupils.

“He treats the Bissextile with no less clarity, and the problem, as Alcuin presents it there, is extremely easy to understand. But he reserved the more difficult thorns of calculation in this matter for his David, as can be seen in letter 83, where—as he himself writes in letter 82—he also often entered the smoky kitchens of the mathematicians [Col. 0981A], and this can be gathered from the letters cited in the preface. Although in the former treatise he treats not so much calculations as the opinions of many people on this subject, many of which are well worth reading. These manuscripts are indeed corrupt and filled with errors through the scribes’ carelessness, but this very matter is what Alcuin, while still alive, complained about in his letter 84 to Charles.

“Moreover, although we possess few calculations under Alcuin’s name, I can scarcely doubt that many more have already been published under another name [Note: [Col. 0981D] This is also the case among the works of the Venerable Bede]. Certainly the three treatises that Bridefertus, Bede’s commentator, appended to chapter 40 of On the Reckoning of Time resemble Alcuin both in their style of writing and in their method of calculation. Someone could be led to a similar suspicion if he compared what is found in the Gloss on the Venerable Bede, vol. II, p. 83, with what Alcuin wrote to Charles in letter 83, and what appears in Bede, the cited volume, p. 89 [Patrologia, vol. XC], with what Alcuin wrote On the Reckoning of the Moon, and much else.”

Finally, in another Vatican manuscript codex, no. 1449, a Calculation is attributed to the master Albinus: how one may discover on what day of the month, or on which weekday, the fourteenth day of the paschal moon occurs over the course of nineteen years. As the verses added at the end testify, it was written to a certain count, of whose rank Alcuin had several friends and whom he often honored in his letters.

The same Calculation does indeed appear among the works of the Venerable Bede, vol. I, p. 195, in the Basel edition of 1563, inserted in the little work On the Arguments of the Moon; and again in vol. II, p. 345 [Patrologia, vol. XC], sewn onto the letter to Wicrhed, the presbyter, concerning the equinox according to Anatolius. But the most acute critics—Mabillon, François Chifflet, Pagi, Don Ceillier, and others—recognize and attest that this Appendix to the letter is spurious and absent from the better manuscript codices. The little work On the Arguments of the Moon is also rightly doubted to belong to the Venerable Bede, since it is not listed in the catalogue that the holy man compiled of his own works toward the end of his life. Therefore, on the authority of the manuscript codex, we attribute this Calculation to our Alcuin rather than to the Venerable Bede, since it was written in the year 777, as the text states—at a time when the Venerable Bede had long since ceased to live.

And thus, at last, the genuine little works of blessed Flaccus Alcuin come to an end—all that we have been able to find. Some were first collected by the distinguished man Andrea Quercetanus; some were discovered and published after him by other learned men; and some were obtained by us from the most celebrated libraries of Italy, Gaul, Germany, and England.

## THE RECKONING OF THE MOON XV

[Note: [Col. 0982D] Letter 25 of the Quercetanus edition.]

For example, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April the moon enters Aries at the first hour of the night; on the fourteenth day before the Kalends it remains in Aries, and for six hours of the thirteenth day before the Kalends, together with a bisse—that is, two-thirds of an hour. At the sixth hour of that thirteenth night it leaves Aries, and the total is fifty-four hours and a bisse (two-thirds of an hour), the length of time it remained in Aries. Always use this number of hours for each sign.

Then it enters Taurus at the third part of the seventh hour of the night—that is, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. From that point, count fifty-four hours for Taurus together with its bisse. There remain of the same night in which it entered Taurus a third of an hour and five hours, and twelve hours of the following day. Add to these the twenty-four hours of the twelfth day before the Kalends of April: the total is forty-one. To these add the hours of the night of the eleventh day before the Kalends—twelve hours—and the first hour of the following day, together with another third of the second hour of the day, so that Taurus may have its full bisse from the third of an hour at which the moon entered it and from that at which it left Taurus.

It enters Gemini at the second hour of the day, the bisse of that hour beginning; twelve hours of the day of the eleventh day before the Kalends remain there [perhaps ten, namely, a rounded number]. Add to these the twenty-four hours of the tenth day before the Kalends, making thirty-four hours. Add to these twenty hours from the ninth day before the Kalends, so that you may reach fifty-four hours. You will reach the eighth full hour of that day, when it leaves Gemini. These three signs have 163 hours [perhaps 162], together with the other two hours that have been added from the bisses of the three signs. The total for the three signs is 154 hours [perhaps 164].

On the ninth day before the Kalends, at the twenty-first hour, it enters Cancer, and you will have four hours of that day. Add these to the eighth day and the seventh day before the Kalends, and you will have fifty-two hours. To these add two hours from the beginning of the night of the sixth day before the Kalends, and the bisse of the third hour. In these nine days the moon traverses four signs, with two hours and the bisse of the third hour added from the tenth day.

It enters Leo at the third part of the third hour of the night of the sixth day before the Kalends of April, and you will have the twenty-first hour of that day [perhaps, “hours”]. Add to these the twenty-four hours of the fifth day before the Kalends, making forty-five hours. Add also nine hours from the day of the fourth day before the Kalends, making fifty-four hours. Add to these the third of the tenth hour, and it enters Virgo as the bisse of the tenth hour of the night begins; fourteen hours remain from the fourth day before the Kalends. Add these to the third day before the Kalends, and together they make thirty-eight. Add to these sixteen hours from the day before the Kalends—that is, the complete fourth hour of the day [perhaps, “one complete hour of the day” or “four complete hours of the day”]. These six signs comprise thirteen days and sixteen hours of the fourteenth day; the total number of hours is 328.

[Col. 0982C] The moon enters the sign of Libra at the fifth hour on the fourteenth day, which is the day before the Kalends of April. From that day eight hours remain. Add these eight to the hours of the day of the Kalends of April, and there will be thirty-two. Add to these twenty-two hours from the fourth day before the Nones, making fifty-four hours.

To these add the bisse of the twenty-third hour of that same day, when it leaves Libra and enters Scorpio, the third of the twenty-fourth hour beginning. One hour remains there from the day of the fourth day before the Nones. Add this hour to the third day before the Nones and the day before the Nones, and there will be forty-nine hours. From the day of the Nones retain five hours of that night, and you will have fifty-four hours in Scorpio and the third of the sixth hour of the night.

Then it enters Sagittarius as the bisse of that same sixth hour of the night begins; eighteen hours remain from the Nones of April. Add these to the eighth day before the Ides, and there will be forty-two hours. Add twelve hours from the seventh day before the Ides, and you will have fifty-four hours during which the moon remains in Sagittarius [perhaps “in Sagittarius”].

It enters Capricorn at the first hour of the day, and twelve hours of that day, the seventh day before the Ides, remain there. Add these to the sixth day before the Ides, and you will have thirty-six hours. Add to these eighteen hours from the fifth day before the Ides, which is the sixth hour of that day. Add also the bisse of the seventh hour; when this is complete, it will leave Capricorn and enter Aquarius as the third of the seventh hour begins, and five hours of that day remain.

Add these to the fourth and third days before the Ides, and you will have fifty-three hours. Add to these one hour from the day before the Ides and the third of the second hour of the night. When it leaves Aquarius, it enters Pisces as the bisse of the second hour of the night begins, on the day before the Ides of April; twenty-two hours remain from the day before the Ides of April. Add these to the Ides, and there will be forty-six hours. Add to these eight hours from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, and you will have fifty-four hours.

Once these calculations have been made, you will find that from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, from which we constructed the threshold of this calculation, there are twenty-seven days up to the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May; on the night of that day eight hours elapse. In these twenty-seven days and eight hours the moon traverses the twelve signs; the twenty-seven days amount to 656 hours, with eight additional hours.

If you wish to reach the thirteenth sign in the lunar course, count from the ninth hour of the night of the eighteenth day before the Kalends, the hour at which the twelve signs were completed. From that point count fifty-four hours and a bisse (two-thirds of an hour); of these, you have sixteen hours on the eighteenth day before the Kalends. Add the hours of the following day, that is, the seventeenth day before the Kalends, and they make forty hours; and you will have twenty-nine days of the seventeenth day before the Kalends [perhaps, “and you will have twenty-nine days: the seventeenth day before the Kalends”]. Add to these twelve hours of the thirtieth night, which reaches the sixteenth day before the Kalends, and you will have the complete hours of the thirteenth sign. At that hour, the complete twelfth hour of the night reaches conjunction with the sun, in which it remains, as is estimated, for two hours.

You will see that another burning [or illumination] will always occur after twelve hours. For the first rule of this calculation began at the evening hour in Aries, whereas now, with Aries completed and Taurus beginning, it reaches the morning hour of the day for the second time.

Pliny says that nine hours are reckoned for the moon against five days: that is, the moon travels in nine hours as much distance as the sun travels in five days. Each sign has thirty degrees; in each sign the moon remains for fifty-four hours and its bisse. Divide fifty-four hours by nine, and you will find six, nine times.

Likewise, the sun remains in each sign for thirty days and ten and a half hours. Divide thirty by five, and you will find six, five times in thirty; and the sun traverses one-sixth of each sign in five days, while the moon traverses one-sixth of a sign in nine hours. In nine days it traverses 120 degrees; likewise 120 degrees in another nine days, and again 120 degrees in another nine days. This makes twenty-seven days, through twenty-four hours, and 360 degrees.

It must be considered how the eight hours that remain in the moon correspond to the five days that remain in the sun, so that one may arrive at the days of the entire year; for the sun does not travel through those five days without the zodiacal circle. Should something be added in heaven to the 360 degrees? Or should the five days be divided among the individual degrees? Those five days contain 120 hours. Should one-third of an hour—that is, one trien—be assigned to each degree? For the eight hours of the lunar course are not empty, since, when it has been reckoned as twenty-seven days, the legitimate number of degrees can be completed if one adds to each day one-third of the fourteenth [perhaps twenty-fourth] degree, so as to reach 360 degrees, just as we found should be done in your most acute and carefully worked-out calculation.

[Note: [Col. 0983D] This appears to be part of the preceding writing. Quercetanus edition, letter 26. See letter 100.]

## ON THE COURSE OF THE MOON

[Col. 0984A] The moon, by the speed of its course, traverses each sign in two days, six hours, and a bisse (two-thirds of an hour). Each sign has thirty degrees. If, therefore, you wish to know how much time the moon spends in any one of the thirty degrees, take the hours of two days, which are forty-eight. Add to these six hours and a bisse; the total is fifty-four hours, the time the moon spends in each sign.

Distribute these fifty-four hours among the individual degrees in equal portions, assigning one hour to each degree; twenty-four hours will remain. Multiply these by points according to the rule that an hour contains five points, and the total is 120 points. Divide these by thirty; you will find four. Give each degree four points, and a bisse will remain.

Divide this by forty marks, because a complete hour has fifty marks [perhaps sixty], and a bisse consists of two parts of an hour; therefore, as I said, forty marks make a bisse of an hour. Give one mark to each degree, and ten marks remain. Multiply these by three, and the total is thirty.

You will see that in the space of one hour, four points, one mark, and one-third of a mark, the moon travels as far as the sun does in twenty-four hours and thirty-one marks [perhaps twenty-one marks].

[Note: [Col. 0983D] From the Swedish Royal manuscript, no. 226, fol. 18.]

## ON THE LEAP OF THE MOON: FIRST PROBLEM

Let us say a few things about the Leap of the Moon. First, concerning this lunar leap, one must ask where it is mentioned in Scripture; or why it is called a leap; and in what place, and on what day of the dates in the year, it ought to occur; and over how many years the lunar leap is prepared. One must also investigate more carefully how it increases, and how great it is in each year and in each month, and prove it by examples.

Dionysius mentions the lunar leap, saying [Note: [Col. 0984D] Dionysius Exiguus, letter to Boniface and Bonus, Patrologia, vol. LXVII, col. 23]:

“The last year of the nineteen-year cycle retains eighteen epacts, that is, lunar additions [Ms., ‘epacts, as always’]; then, in the first year, it accommodates not eleven days, as is customary in the other years, but twelve days. And because the cycle turns at the completion of thirty days, no epact is placed at the beginning of that cycle [Al., ‘no epacts … are placed’].”

That twelfth day, therefore, which Dionysius adds beyond the eleventh epact, without doubt indicates the day of the leap. For this reason it is said that in that year there are no epacts: they are not appropriate, but excessive. For through eighteen years eleven epacts always seem to be added; but in the year in which the leap is inserted, twelve rather than eleven epacts are found. For example, at the end of the nineteen-year cycle, the epacts do not rise from eighteen to twenty-nine, but to thirty.

Who, then, first discovered and added this day of the leap? Without doubt, the Egyptians. Hence Dionysius says: “From the first year, which has no lunar epacts—that is, no epacts appropriate to it—because, although the numbers of the tenth [read: nineteenth] preceding year are eighteen epacts, when one day has also been added by the Egyptians, they become thirty, that is, a complete lunar month.”

The one day, therefore, which Dionysius says was added by the Egyptians undoubtedly indicates the day of the leap. This lunar leap is therefore called a lunar increment or increase, because over eighteen years one day increases in the moon. Victor also speaks of this increase, that is, of the day of the leap, saying [Note: [Col. 0985D] Victor in the Preface to the Paschal Feast, in Petavius, vol. II, p. 504]:

“After nineteen years, when the sequence has been continued according to the custom of the Egyptians, this lunar increase grows.”

It must therefore be asked where this leap is placed according to the Latins. Without doubt, on 15 December [read: the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December].

Next, we must understand how this leap is shown according to the Latins in the epacts that run on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, and in which year of the cycle it is found. It is found, namely, in the sixteenth year according to the Latins.

For example, in that year, according to the Greeks, there are fifteen epacts on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. If it happens that the lunar epact fifteen falls on a Sunday on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April according to the reckoning of the Greeks, then, according to the tradition of the holy Council of Nicaea, Easter is celebrated. According to the Latins, however, Easter is not celebrated on the fifteenth moon, but on the sixteenth. Thus, in that year, their epacts run from the fourth moon to the sixteenth, as is found in Victor, because of the leap; for the Latins did not wish to celebrate Easter on that lunar epact on which Christ suffered, that is, on the fifteenth moon. [Note: [Col. 0985D] Victor, in the cited passage, records this concerning Latin custom: “But if it should happen that the full moon falls on Saturday and the fifteenth moon is found on the following Sunday, the Latins said that, that week having passed, it ought to be transferred to the next Sunday, that is, to the twenty-second moon.” This does not accord with Alcuin’s account. Note, however, that Alcuin here speaks of the sixteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which he says that the Latins place the leap; Victor is silent about this, unless this exception to the general rule has been omitted from the printed texts.]

359 How, then, is the leap demonstrated according to the Greeks, and on what day of the dates is it found? It is on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. According to Dionysius it is demonstrated as follows. For when Dionysius said [Note: [Col. 0986D] In letter II, Patrologia, vol. LXVII]:

“In the first year of the nineteen-year lunar cycle, [there are] seventeen [epacts]; from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to the Nones of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days,”

he placed the day of the leap at that place and on that day—that is, beginning from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0986D] Petavius, however, vol. I, p. 310, asserts that Dionysius fixed the lunar leap on 30 July and thus transferred it to the Roman calendar].

For Dionysius always counts from the fifteenth moon of the lunar year, whether common or embolismic, to the fourteenth paschal moon of the following year. Thus Dionysius placed the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, according to the tradition of the angel who revealed it by divine revelation to the monk Pachomius [Note: [Col. 0986D] Letter of blessed Cyril, in Petavius, vol. II, p. 503], as the paschal limit, with the fourteenth moon at the end of the entire cycle on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. Nevertheless, according to the reckoning of nature, the fifteenth moon is found [Correction: the fourteenth, for according to the epacts the moon is the fourteenth, but through the Dionysian leap the moon becomes the fifteenth].

For this reason Dionysius, according to the reckoning of the leap, begins the first year of the nineteen-year cycle with the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, that is, with the fifteenth moon; and according to the tradition of the angel he placed the limit on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, with the end of the entire cycle on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, at the fourteenth moon.

Likewise, according to the Greeks, the day of the leap is demonstrated in the epacts on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, because in that year, at the beginning of the cycle, no epacts are said to exist: they are not appropriate, since they are excessive. At that time twelve epacts are found added, from eighteen to thirty-two [read: thirty; in the last year of the cycle the epacts are eighteen, and in the following first year they are thirty, or rather none], with one day also added by the Egyptians to their eleven epacts.

How, then, is this day of the leap demonstrated in the moon, and how does it increase in each lunar month? It increases by four moments in every month. This must be observed with care and diligence.

It is demonstrated as follows. When the moon is said to contain twenty-nine [Ms., “nineteen”] and a half days, that is, twelve hours, it is by nature somewhat younger than it is thought to be; and therefore the moon’s renewal comes sooner, before the full twenty-nine and a half days—that is, twelve hours—have been completed.

For according to nature, the moon’s waning and renewal are faster by definite moments than they are said or thought to be according to the art of calculation. The lunar increase grows at the end of each lunar month by four moments and a twelfth part of a moment, together with a five-hundred-and-fifty-fourth part of a moment—that is, an atom—before the twelfth hour of the half-day that follows the twenty-nine days has been completed.

Thus over nineteen years—that is, twelve common years and seven embolismic years, containing 235 lunar months—that single day of twenty-four hours called the leap gradually increases, until the first moon becomes complete at the hour in which the moon is thought to wane or renew. Or the fifteenth moon is found on that day according to nature, when according to the art and reckoning of the epacts it is called the fourteenth moon, as we said concerning the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, on which day it is called both the fourteenth and the fifteenth moon.

If, then, you wish to know how much of this lunar increase grows in each year over nineteen years, and how much in each lunar month over 235 months, observe more carefully that in every common year one hour and eight moments are added. For ten months make one hour: for if you multiply ten four times, or four ten times, there are forty moments, that is, one hour; and two months produce eight moments, for twice four are eight moments. Thus, in a common year, which has twelve lunar months, one hour and eight moments are added toward the preparation of the saltus.

Thus, over nineteen years, as though all had been common years—leaving the seven embolismic years aside for the moment, about which we shall speak later—there accrue over nineteen years nineteen hours, that is, one hour for each year. Likewise, eight moments for each year: thus over nineteen years 152 moments are produced, that is, three hours and thirty-two moments. Together, therefore, there are twenty-two hours and thirty-two moments.

Let us therefore collect the moments from the seven embolismic years that we set aside separately: four moments for each embolismic month. Thus, from seven months, that is, from the seven embolisms, twenty-eight [Ms., twenty-four] moments are collected; for seven times four, or four times seven, are twenty-eight moments. Add these together with the thirty-two moments that you had previously; together they make sixty moments, that is, one and a half hours.

Add these sixty moments to the number of hours that you had previously, namely twenty-two: together they make twenty-three and a half hours, that is, twenty moments in addition to the twenty-three hours. If, therefore, over nineteen years you multiply 235 by four, collecting four moments for each month—or if four is multiplied by 235—you obtain 940 moments. For if you multiply 200 by four, you get 800; likewise, thirty times four is 120, and together these are 920; again, five times four is twenty, making 940 moments in all.

If you wish to divide these by groups of forty, that is, by complete hours, since forty moments make one hour, you must divide as follows. From 900 subtract nine times twenty; there remain nine groups of eighty, that is, eighteen groups of forty, which contain eighteen hours. Likewise, nine groups of twenty, in which twice eighty [Ms., “in twice eighty-three,” erroneously], are 160, that is, four groups of forty [Ms., forty-three, again erroneously], which contain four hours. Add these eighteen hours: they make twenty-two. There remain twenty [Ms., 120] [moments].

Add those together with the forty moments that you previously had in excess of 900: they make sixty moments. Set aside forty, that is, one hour; add it to the twenty-two, making twenty-three [hours], with twenty moments remaining, that is, half an hour. Thus, over nineteen years, as we said above, there accrue twenty-three and a half hours. There remains half an hour, that is, twenty moments, which is produced and completed from the twelfth part of a moment belonging to each of the 235 months.

And so, in twelve months, that is, in one common year, one moment is collected; and in nineteen years, as though all had been common years, leaving the seven embolisms aside, nineteen moments are collected. One moment remains, which is collected from the seven embolisms and from the atom of each month.

For from the six embolismic months half a moment is collected, namely 282 [Supplement: atoms]. Likewise, from the seventh embolismic month a twelfth part of a moment is collected, namely forty-seven atoms. For if you divide a moment into twelve parts, forty-seven multiplied by twelve gives 564 atoms.

Keep, therefore, the forty-seven atoms that we mentioned from the seventh embolism, that is, from one-twelfth of a moment; and collect one atom from each of the 235 months. You collect that many atoms, namely 235. Add them together with the forty-seven: they make 282, that is, half a moment.

Collect also the other half moment that you obtained from the six embolismic months, namely 282. Together there are 564 atoms, which make one moment. Add this one moment to the nineteen moments that you previously had from the twelfth part of a moment belonging to each month: thus they make twenty moments, that is, half an hour.

Add this half hour to the other half hour that you had in addition to the twenty-three hours: they make twenty-four hours, that is, one lunar day, which is called the *saltus*, or increase or augmentation.

If, therefore, you wish to know how much of this lunar augmentation grows in each month, it is four moments and a twelfth part of a moment, together with one forty-seventh of a twelfth part of a moment—that is, one atom—growing in each month.

It must therefore be asked: when the moon is said to be kindled after twenty-nine and a half days, that is, at the twelfth hour—but before the whole of the twelfth hour has ended, since the kindling occurs four moments before the end of the twelfth hour, which produces the *saltus*—how is that kindling of the day to be understood? Is the moon kindled during the day or during the night? At what hour, or at what point—or rather, at what moment—is the moon said to be kindled? And is it a sub-kindling, a middle kindling, or a super-kindling? [Note: [Col. 0987] On *sub-incensio*, and so forth, see Bridefertus, Bede’s scholiast, *Opera*, vol. II, p. 108.]

According to the reckoning of the Hebrews, the moon is said to be kindled after midday, that is, after six hours and a half-hour of the seventh hour. Consequently, the Hebrews take the beginning of the day from midday, because they reckon according to the moon, and at midday the moon’s age changes.

For this reason Anatolius of Alexandria says:

> Every day in the reckoning of the moon does not end in the evening with the same number with which it begins in the morning; for the day that begins in the morning is counted as thirteen until the sixth hour and a half, while by evening that same day is found to be fourteen. [Ms., “in the computation of the moon.”]

In this example Anatolius shows that the moon’s age changes every day after the sixth hour, during the half-hour of the seventh hour; and thus the moon is also thought to be kindled at that hour. Nevertheless, it must be investigated how this calculation can be proved according to the truth of nature.

361. For if the moon had always consisted of thirty days, or even twenty-nine, it could have happened that, after the thirtieth or even the twenty-ninth day had ended, it would always have been kindled at one hour and at the same point and moment, at the same time of day at which the moon had first been made. But since the moon is shown to contain twenty-nine and a half days, that is, twelve hours, that half-day makes the moon’s kindling variable. Therefore, if the moon’s kindling is said to occur at midday, count twenty-nine days from midday at the moon’s kindling to midday on the twenty-ninth day. Add twelve hours, from midday to midnight; then the moon is kindled at midnight.

The moon’s kindling, therefore, does not occur at one and the same temporal interval or under one and the same climatic region of the sky. Rather, naturally, the moon is kindled in every hour and at every moment, and in every part of the sky, above the earth and beneath the earth, through its annual revolution and indeed through its monthly cycle.

It must therefore be asked how many names this *saltus* has. There are five. It is called the lunar increase; it is also called the lunar augmentation; it is called the lunar change; it is also called one moon growing through all the years; and it is called the *saltus*.

And this *saltus*, as we said, is placed in four locations. According to Victorius and the Latins, it is placed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. According to the Greeks, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the moon—which at that point ought to have become twenty-nine days old—becomes thirty days old because of the *saltus*. According to the Egyptians, it is placed on the sixth day before the Kalends of October. According to Dionysius, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. On that day the moon is called both the fourteenth and the fifteenth because of the *saltus*.

Thus far concerning the moon’s *saltus*.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Bridefertus, Bede’s scholiast, published this work without the author’s name, *Opera*, vol. II, p. 145; from it we corrected the Vatican manuscript. It agrees with what is found above, cols. 987–988.]

# Treatise on the Moon’s *Saltus*. Problem Two

If you wish to know how the lunar day called the *saltus* is prepared and grows over nineteen years, and how much of this lunar augmentation occurs in each lunation—that is, in each lunar month—over 235 [months] (for that many lunar months there are in the nineteen-year cycle), multiply 235 by four, or four times 235. For four moments grow in each month; therefore all 235 months are multiplied by four. The result is 940 moments.

If you divide this whole number by forty, the result is twenty-three groups of forty and twenty moments, that is, twenty-three and a half hours. If you wish to know how the other half hour, which appears to be lacking, is collected and grows, it is without doubt understood as follows: not only do four moments of this lunar augmentation grow in each month, but also a twelfth part of a moment; moreover, an atom, that is, a five-hundred-and-sixty-fourth part of a moment, grows in every lunar month. Thus one moment is collected in twelve months.

For the moment, leaving aside those atoms about which we shall speak later, over nineteen years, as though all the years had been common years, while leaving the seven embolisms aside, nineteen moments accrue. The one moment that appears to be lacking is collected from the seven embolismic months [and the atom] of each month.

For from the six embolismic months half a moment is collected, containing 282 atoms; and another half moment is collected from the seventh embolismic month [Ms., “of the embolism,”], namely a twelfth part of a moment, containing forty-seven atoms. Collect, therefore, the atoms of each month, which are 235. Add them to the forty-seven: they make 282, that is, the other half moment.

Add 200 and 200: they make 400. Likewise, eighty and eighty make 160; and two and two make four. Thus, together there are 564 atoms, that is, one moment. Added to the nineteen, this produces twenty moments, that is, the other half hour. Add it to the twenty-three and a half hours: they make twenty-four hours, that is, one natural day called the *saltus*.

362. # Also on the Moon’s *Saltus*. Problem Three

If you wish to know how much of the moon’s *saltus* accrues in each day and in each lunar month, or in one common year, or in the nineteen-year cycle containing nineteen years, observe carefully that seventy-six [Ms., seventy-seven] atoms accrue in one day.

For example, if you wish to know how the seventy-six atoms are collected, take four moments and forty-eight atoms, since that much grows in each lunar month, as there are 235 lunar months in the nineteen-year cycle. Thus those four moments and forty-eight [atoms] are collected; together they are [II].304 [atoms]. [Note: [Col. 0990B] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]

Divide these into thirty parts, so that you may know how much grows in one day. Without doubt you will find seventy-six atoms in each part, with twenty-four remaining, which are not collected in that portion which . . . . . on the fifth [day]. [Note: [Col. 0989D] Read perhaps: “are collected in that portion.” The portions that remain ought to be placed on the fifth day. Alcuin evidently adds these four atoms, which would otherwise produce a fraction of 4/5 each day, after every five days; for every five days they would produce 20/5, that is, four atoms.]

For if you collect the twenty-four over five days [perhaps, “five times”], you will find 120 atoms. Divide them again into thirty parts, and in each part you will find four atoms, so that you can state fully how much has grown on the fifth day.

For example, the moon’s *saltus* ought to be placed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, according to the Greeks . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0990D] Perhaps read: “the moon’s *saltus* ought to be placed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April according to the Greeks [on which day one day is added to the epacts],” etc. That Alcuin here speaks of epacts is inferred from his saying: “One day more than in other years.” For this can be said and understood only of epacts, since the *saltus* rather removes one day from the year; but because of the *saltus*, twelve rather than eleven days are customarily assigned to the epacts, as Dionysius says above, col. 984.] one day of twenty-four hours, more than you find in other years. Thus, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, that is, at the beginning of the embolism, the efforts [perhaps, “the cause”] of the *saltus* grow by seventy-six atoms and . . . . . [perhaps, supplied: “four portions”].

On the second day, 152; on the third, 228; on the fourth, 304; and thus on the fifth, 384 atoms. Those four atoms come from the portion of the aforesaid remainder, and in ten days 763 [perhaps, 768] atoms are collected. In twenty days, [I]536 [atoms] [Note: [Col. 0990C] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.], which make two moments and 408 atoms, which make one moment and 213 atoms [read: “which make half a moment and 126 atoms”].

In thirty days 2,304 atoms are collected, which make four moments and forty-eight atoms, with the remainder carried forward. Thus in five months twenty moments are collected, that is, half an hour; in ten months one hour is collected; in one hundred months ten hours; in 200 months twenty hours; and in thirty-five months three and a half hours. Together, therefore, there are twenty-three and a half hours.

If you wish to know how the half hour that appears to be lacking is collected over nineteen years, calculate forty-eight over 235 months, for that many months there are in the nineteen-year cycle. If you multiply forty-eight by 235, together they make 11,280 atoms, which make twenty moments, that is, half an hour. Add this half hour to the twenty-three and a half: they make twenty-four hours, that is, one natural day called the *saltus*.

[Therefore, in the nineteen-year cycle there are days, namely [VI]936 [Note: [Col. 0991A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.], and hours [CLX]464 [Note: [Col. 0991A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.].] [Note: [Col. 0991D] These final words, enclosed in brackets, appear to have been added, since what is inferred here does not at all follow from what precedes, as will be clear to anyone who attempts the calculation.]

363. [Note: [Col. 0991D] The Venerable Bede teaches: “An hour contains four points, ten minutes, fifteen parts, forty moments, and in some lunar computations five points.” In these divisions of time, therefore, our Alcuin follows the course of the moon in preparing for the *saltus*, according to the knowledge of his age and, perhaps, the capacity of his students. For the calculations that now follow concerning the moon’s *saltus* by parts, minutes, moments, and atoms had to be made accessible to people of that age both because of their difficulty and because of their brevity. From this we may also infer why the ancients wished the hour to be divided into parts, minutes, moments, and atoms: namely, so that all their calculations, especially those concerning the moon, might be free of any fractional remainder.]

# Concerning the Moon’s *Saltus*. Problem Four

If you wish to understand the moon’s *saltus*, multiply 235 by four: they make 940 moments, that is, twenty-three and a half hours. If you wish to understand the half hour that appears to be lacking, [multiply] forty-eight atoms by 235 months: together they make [XI]280 [Note: [Col. 0991A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.], which make twenty moments, that is, half an hour. Add this to the aforesaid number of hours: they make twenty-four hours.

Thus far concerning the *saltus*.

# Concerning the Moon’s *Saltus* by Parts. Problem Five

If you wish to know how the *saltus* grows by parts, you must first understand that fifteen parts make one hour. Multiply fifteen by twenty-four: they make 360. Divide these by nineteen: the result is 342, which is eighteen times nineteen, with eighteen remaining.

Give each year of the nineteen-year cycle fifteen parts, that is, one hour, and each year you will have three parts remaining from those eighteen parts. Multiply these by nineteen: nineteen times three makes 57, with eighteen parts remaining. Add these to the 57: together they make 75. Divide by fifteen, since fifteen parts make one hour, and in 75 you will find fifteen five times, that is, five hours. Add these to the nineteen: they make twenty-four hours, and there is one complete day over nineteen years, which is called the *saltus*.

# Concerning the Moon’s *Saltus* by Minutes. Problem Six

If you wish to know how the *saltus* grows by minutes, you must know that ten minutes make one hour. Multiply ten by twenty-four: they make 240. Divide by nineteen. Twelve times ten and nineteen [or, twelve times nineteen] make 228, with twelve remaining.

[Next, you must know that one minute makes four moments. [Note: [Col. 0992D] The words enclosed in brackets appear to be interpolated; the discussion is not about finding the *saltus* by moments. Nor do they belong to the following problem, where an hour is taken as equal to forty moments.]]

Give each year ten minutes, that is, one complete hour, and you will have thirty-eight minutes remaining. Add to these the twelve minutes that remained from the previous calculation: they make fifty minutes. Divide by ten, since ten minutes make one hour, and fifty minutes make five hours. Add these to the eighteen, and you will have twenty-four hours, that is, one natural day called the *saltus*.

# Concerning the Moon’s *Saltus* by Moments. Problem Seven

[Col. 0992A]

If you wish to know how the day of the *saltus* grows in moments over nineteen years, calculate the moments of one hour, namely forty. Multiply forty by twenty-four, and they make 960. [Divide] by nineteen, and in 960 you will find nineteen fifty times, with ten remaining.

Keep fifty moments for each year, and you will have one hour and ten moments [or give each year of the nineteen years forty moments, that is, one hour]; ten moments remain for each year of the nineteen-year cycle. Multiply these by nineteen. Nineteen times ten makes 190. Add the ten moments that remained in the previous calculation: they make 200.

Divide these by forty-four: twice eighty makes 160, which is four hours. Twenty and twenty, which remain, make [Col. 0992B] forty. That is one hour. Add these five hours to the nineteen hours: they make twenty-four hours, and there is one complete day, which increases by moments over nineteen years.

364. # Also on the Moon’s *Saltus*. Problem Eight

[Note: [Col. 0992D] The calculation in the present problem is more subtle than the preceding ones and perhaps also more obscure, and it departs somewhat from Alcuin’s usual style. Perhaps it belongs to another author, whom he nevertheless wished to send along with the others to Charles. This author says that the measure of one day can be expressed not only in divisions of time but also, and even more so, in divisions of the zodiac and of the ecliptic—though he appears to confuse the two. Since the *saltus* is a day to be omitted when the moon’s ages are counted, he attempts to express it by divisions of the ecliptic, using the following analogy: through the complete number of months or weeks or days, and even hours, of the entire nineteen-year cycle, the interval required for the preparation of the *saltus* is traversed, an interval equal to the distance the sun itself describes in one day. Therefore, what part of this interval is traversed in one month, one week, one day, or even one hour? From this he reaches exceedingly small divisions of the ecliptic, which he calls mathematical constellations, and says that they are false because they were discovered by calculation, namely, as Bede says, for investigating human births.]

If you wish to arrive at the proper understanding of the lunar *saltus*, so that, according to the mathematicians, you may understand by what circle [F., “by what calculation or computation”] one day is subtracted from the moon’s course over nineteen years, you must pay more attention to the signs of the sky and to the divisions of each sign than to the hour of any particular day, as follows.

Thus, a day is what the sun travels through . . . . . in one day [perhaps supply: “completes”]. [The divisions traversed in one day, etc.] [Col. 0992C] In the zodiacal circle these are called divisions in the division of the stars, just as we call days divisions in the reckoning of years. For the lunar course of one day, consisting of twenty-four hours, is one day of the year, and is one division of the sky being traversed [F., “to be traversed” or “of traversing”]; and over nineteen years one such division will accrue toward the diminution of the course.

And if you wish to ask how or in what manner that diminution of one division is distributed through the individual solar courses [F., “through the individual solar courses”] among the divisions of the sky, the sun has 228 months in its course over nineteen years. Divide that one division of the solar course by 228 months, and one 228th of one division is traversed.

And if you wish to reach weeks, count the weeks of nineteen years; for there are fifty-two in one year. Multiply fifty by nineteen: they make 950, with two weeks remaining, which remain each year from the fifty. Multiply these by nineteen years: they make thirty-eight weeks. Add these to 950: they make 988, and there still remain nineteen days, which make two weeks, with five days remaining.

Add these two weeks to the preceding calculation [Note: [Col. 0994D] Something is missing; it may perhaps be supplied as follows: “they make 990 weeks; add also four leap days and eighteen hours, and they make,” etc.]. They make 991 weeks, with two days and eighteen hours remaining. One week accrues toward the diminution of the *saltus* as the 991st part of one division of the solar course, together with one three-hundred-and-ninety-first part of that 991st part.

But if you wish to reach days and desire to know how great the ratio of this diminution is for each day, count the days of nineteen years, which are [VI]937 [Note: [Col. 0993A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.], and [the corresponding part] of this number of days in the nineteen-year cycle accrues each day toward the diminution of that one division.

And if anyone wishes to reach the mathematicians’ constellation, let him calculate the hours of nineteen years and, according to the number of hours, divide that one division of the solar course in one day. Then there will be a false mathematical constellation, since it was discovered by calculation but investigated through careful inquiry. Nevertheless, as I said, the diminution of that one division is found in the number of hours contained in nineteen years. [Note: [Col. 0994D] The passage is corrupt.] For nineteen years contain [CLXVIII] [Note: [Col. 0993B] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] and forty-five times [hours]. A fourth part of 354,168. A thousandth part of one division of the solar course is subtracted in that one solar division, and the course through the zodiacal circle, as we have often said, tends to leap over one additional day every nineteen years in the moon’s course—a day which calculators have wished to call the *saltus*.

[Col. 0993C] And lest it seem false to anyone that one division of the zodiac can be split into so many divisions, let him consider the size of the sun, since, as they say, it is larger than the earth. From the sun’s magnitude let him form a conjecture about the breadth of each division through the individual stars; and, returning to himself, let him marvel more at the work of God than rely upon his own judgment.

365. # Here Begins the Discussion of the Leap Day

[Note: [Col. 0994D] The subject of this treatise is clear from its opening; its method is the same as that which Alcuin follows above concerning the moon’s *saltus*.]

Regarding the leap day, we must first ask why it is called *bissextus*, what produces the *bissextus*, from what material it is made, and from where it first began; how much of it grows in each year, and how much in each day and in each month; at what point and on which day of the calendar this *bissextus* is placed; and who first discovered the *bissextus*.

It is therefore called *bissextus* because of the expression “twice sixth Kalends.” Thus one says “the sixth day before the Kalends” today and “the sixth day before the Kalends” tomorrow. Or it is called this because *bis sextas sexies*—“twice six, six times”—is involved; and *sextas* signifies two hours. Thus twice two hours are four; likewise, four multiplied by six are twenty-four hours. Therefore it is called *bissextus*, because of *bis sextas sexies*. It is called *sextas* because [F., “because”] it is the sixth part of an *as*, that is, two ounces, if interpreted in terms of weights; alternatively, it signifies two hours.

What, then, produces the *bissextus*? It is the slowing of the sun’s course. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 0994D] More properly, Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*.] says:

> In a shorter and more ordinary account, the leap day is generated by the sun’s delay: it does not return fully in 365 days to the same line of the sky from which it departed. For example, at the vernal equinox, which according to the Egyptians occurs on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, when the rising sun reaches the middle of the east, if you observe carefully, you will find that in the following year, on the same day, it rises somewhat lower, unless you add the quarter, making the equinox fall on the eleventh [supply: “day before the Kalends of”] April. It maintains the same delay in the remaining years as well.

From what, then, is the *bissextus* produced? Without doubt, from four quarters, as it is read [Note: [Col. 0994D] In Bede, in the same passage.]:

> The *bissextus* is completed from the reckoning of the quarter over four years, when the sun returns late to the sign from which it departed, after 365 days with a quarter of a day added.

How many hours, then, does this leap day contain? Is it present only in the day, or in the night, or does it contain both day and night? And is the quarter from which this leap day arises artificial or natural?

Some think that this leap day contained twelve hours, while the other days were artificial [F., perhaps read: “that the other days were artificial”]. Hence it is read [Note: [Col. 0994D] In Bede, *On the Arguments of the Moon*, earlier in the work]:

> The *bissextus* is one day added every four years; for each year a quarter of an *as* grows, and when it has completed an *as* in the fourth year, it makes a leap year. It is called *bissextus* because twice six multiplied six times makes an *as*, which is one day. When, therefore, he said that a quarter of an *as* grows each year, he indicated three hours. For we know that an *as* has twelve ounces, which signify twelve hours; a quarter of twelve hours is three hours. Thus the leap day is made artificially from the three hours of each year over four years: three multiplied by four make twelve hours. They wish to prove this also by dividing the hours of the whole year into seven parts, and they say that what remains is the quarter that produces the leap day; they say that this follows from the reckoning of the Greeks.

Let us therefore divide the hours of the whole year, so that we may know what remains beyond the seven parts. We know that in the whole year there are [VIII]760 hours [Note: [Col. 0995A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]. Divide these by seven parts, as by the number of the seven days multiplied through the whole year—that is, fifty-two weeks and one day. Set aside seven, because there are seven parts, that is, seven times one thousand; in [I]760 [read: [I]760] [Note: [Col. 0995A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] there remain 760. Set aside 700, because there are seven parts—that is, seven times one hundred—and sixty remain. Set aside 600 [L., “there remain 1,060; set aside 700”], as we said above; 360 remain. Set aside 280, because twice seven times twenty are 280; eighty remain. Set aside 63, because nine times seven are 63; seventeen remain. Set aside fourteen, because twice seven are fourteen; three remain.

Those three hours that remain beyond the divisions of the hours of the whole year are said to be the artificial quarter. Thus, from four quarters over four years, there is one leap day containing twelve hours; for three multiplied by four make twelve hours.

Nevertheless, the above calculation is rejected by the authorities. They do not say that the quarter consists of three hours, but of six, and they do not say that the leap day consists of twelve hours, but of twenty-four. How, then, could that leap day have been twenty-four hours without a night? Therefore Augustine (*On Time*, no. 8) says of this quarter and of that leap day:

> Four quarters make one day, which must be intercalated into the course of four years so that the order of time may not be disturbed; this day they call the leap day. The quarter itself has six hours, for the whole day [Augustine adds: “that is,”] together with its night consists of twenty-four hours, of which the fourth part, the quarter of a day, is found to be six hours.

The question must therefore be asked where this quarter first came from and from where it derives its authority. This quarter existed from the beginning of the world, from the time when creatures were made. Jerome explained it in his treatise on the first testimony of Genesis, where it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). Jerome therefore said . . . [Note: [Col. 0995D] The passage is corrupt.]

Many have discussed this beginning, but I suppose that this beginning is the one about which Andromachus, the Jewish historiographer, wrote with great vigilance to others: that quarter lying in the middle of the night on the eleventh [day], because the world was made at midnight and will again be destroyed at midnight.

How, then, is this quarter to be recognized? The question must be asked whether it belongs to the day or to the night, or whether it is variable and extends through both day and night. [Note: [Col. 0995D] Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 36.]

> For the sun does not complete its course around the circuit of the sky through the twelve signs of the zodiac in 365 days, but is known to complete its course when six hours are added. Hence, if, for example, on the night of the equinox [Bede: “now the equinoctial”] the rising sun enters the place of the sky in the morning . . . [Note: [Col. 0996D] The wording differs somewhat in Bede.]

At the beginning of the year, in the following year it does not end that year at the same equinoctial place with the sun rising in the morning, but at midday; thus the second year will end in the evening. In the third year, however, it will end at midnight; and in the fourth year the sun will again appear at the beginning of the day in the same place and under the same sign.

Thus, at the beginning of the world, that quarter extended from the equinoctial midnight to morning. The three following days, namely the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the tenth day before the Kalends of April, and the ninth day before the Kalends of April, are said to have been equal, but without a reckoning of the hours between the days and nights—as though there had been [F., “three”] equinoctial days before the sun had been created. Before the creation of the sun, the original light moved in a circuit, as the sun now does.

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 4.]

> For the preceding three days, as it seemed to everyone, without any measurement of hours—for the stars had not yet been made—light spread day and darkness in equal balance [Bede: “it spread light and darkness in equal balance”].

This calculation is confirmed by the authority of the Greeks. For it is read in a letter of Maurinus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning these three days at the beginning of the world, before the luminaries existed. He himself said that the same length was established by God’s power during the first three days, made at the beginning of the world; but the sun added the course of the days when it shone upon the world. On the fourth day, conversely, the moon diminished the course of the nights.

Thus the authorities hand down—and Genesis likewise records—that the sun and moon were made on the fourth day, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the sun rose in the middle of the east. That year, therefore, from sunrise to sunrise, did not complete its full course until the added six hours, that is, one quarter, had been included; and then that first year ended at midday. In the following year, with six hours added, that is, the second quarter, it ended in the evening; then, in the third year, at midnight, with another six hours added, that is, the third quarter; and in the fourth year, with another six hours added, that is, with the fourth quarter, it completed its course from sunrise.

Thus it proceeds through all time: sometimes the whole year ends at midday, sometimes in the evening, sometimes at midnight, and sometimes at sunrise.

If, however, you wish to know at what point this quarter falls in the present year, determine how many years there have been since the beginning of the world—for example, 6,023. Divide these by four, because after four years this natural quarter always returns to the position in which it was at the beginning, namely, midday. Therefore set aside [4] [Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.], since the four parts are equal; [2]023 remain [Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]. Set aside [1]600 [Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.], since there are sixteen hundreds; 423 remain. Set aside 390 [L. 320], since there are four eighties; 103 remain. Set aside 80, since there are twenty fours; 23 remain. Set aside 20, since [Suppl. “five times”] there are four fives; 3 remain. Then that year ends at midnight.

### 367

At what point in the year, and on what day of the month, is this quarter of which we have spoken found? We ought to know that, according to the Greeks, it is at the vernal equinox, that is, on 12 Kalends of April, but it is said to be positioned at the end of that day. But how was it positioned at the beginning, when they say that, in that quarter of the night [Note: Something appears to be missing.], when the world was first made, the quarter from which the leap day arises ought for that reason naturally to be placed at the end of the year?

Accordingly, according to the Greeks, the beginning of the year is 11 Kalends of April, while the end is 12 Kalends of April. According to Anatolius, bishop of Alexandria and Laodicea [F. Laodicea], this quarter is found positioned on 8 Kalends of April, because on that day, as the authorities relate, the sun and moon—the two luminaries—were made. For that reason, according to Anatolius, 8 Kalends of April is called the beginning of the year and the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle [Note: See the words of Anatolius in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 32, p. 369, Cambridge edition, 1720.]:

> Thus, in the first year, the beginning of the first month—which is the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle—is, according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-sixth day of the month Phamenoth; according to the Macedonians, however, on the twenty-fifth day, that is, 8 Kalends of April [Note: Venerable Bede maintains that 11 Kalends of April should be read. See Petavius, vol. I, book VI, *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 11.]. On that day the sun is found not only to have ascended through the first part, but also to possess a quarter in it—that is, in the first part of the twelve parts. This first fraction of the twelve parts is the vernal equinox; it is itself the beginning of the months and the head of the cycle, as well as the completion of the course of the stars called planets, that is, “wandering” stars, and the end of the twelfth fraction and the limit of the entire cycle.

Thus Anatolius clearly demonstrates that this quarter is at the vernal equinox, which according to the Latins is 8 Kalends of April; nevertheless, it must occur at the end of 9 Kalends of April, that is, at the end of the year according to the Latins. For this reason the Latins make the beginning of the year 9 Kalends of April, because on that day the luminaries, the sun and the moon, were made; and so the end of the year is 9 Kalends of April. For this reason the solar concurrent and the leap day are found positioned on 9 Kalends of April.

We must therefore ask at how many points of the year the quarter from which the leap year arises is said to be positioned. At five points: according to the Greeks, at the equinox, that is, on 12 Kalends of April; according to Anatolius, on 9 Kalends of April—but at the end of that day, that is, between 9 and 8 Kalends of April, as we have said. According to Isidore, the leap day is said to occur on the sixth day before the Nones of March, so that it is called *bissextus*, as though “twice the sixth day before the Nones”: the sixth day before the Nones today, and the sixth day before the Nones tomorrow.

Hence Isidore says [Note: Isidore’s wording differs in the edition of D. du Breul, where *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 6, p. 248, reads as follows: “The leap day is inserted into the course of the moon from the sixth day before the Kalends of March up to the day before the Kalends of June.”]:

> The leap day is inserted into the lunar cycle from the sixth day before the Nones of March up to the day before the Kalends of January [Bede: “is inserted in the course of the moon”].

According to the Egyptians, however, the leap day is always positioned on 4 Kalends of [September], that is, at the end of the year according to the Egyptians. For the Egyptians have the beginning of their year on 3 Kalends of September. According to the Romans, however, and according to the authority of Julius Caesar, the leap day is placed on 6 Kalends of March. Thus we read in Macrobius [Note: In Bede]:

> Julius Caesar decreed that every fourth year the priests who were responsible for the months and days should insert one day, in that month and at that point in which days had also been intercalated among the ancients [Bede: “in which the month was intercalated”], namely, before the last [Bede: “before the five last”] days of the month of February; and he judged that this should be called the leap day.

This example shows that Julius Caesar was the first to name the leap day. For this reason, according to the Romans, the leap day is placed on 6 Kalends of March: the ancient Romans had the beginning of the year in the month of March, while the end of the year was in the month of February, that is, on 6 Kalends of March. Those five days that remain were intercalary days among the ancients, just as now among the Egyptians they are from 9 Kalends of September to 4 Kalends of September.

Concerning this leap day also, Chorus [F. Horus] of the Egyptians handed down the following statement:

> This day must be inserted before the fifth year begins.

From this example it is plainly inferred that the leap day ought to be placed at the end of the year, since he said, “before the fifth begins.”

Next we must know how much of this quarter increases on each day throughout the entire year, and how much increases in each month. On each day two *momentum*-parts increase; thus in three days two moments increase, in six days four moments, in twelve days eight moments, in fourteen [F. twenty-four] days sixteen moments. In thirty days and ten hours, twenty moments increase, that is, half an hour. Thus in three thirty-day months—that is, in ninety days, one day, and six hours—one and a half hours increase.

In six thirty-day months—that is, in two periods of ninety days—plus two days and twelve hours, three hours increase. Likewise in the other thirty-day months, as though there had been that many thirty-day periods together with two days and twelve hours, another three hours increase. Thus six hours of the quarter increase: that is, one-quarter of a natural day increases over twelve months, or one year of the four-year cycle. When four years have been completed and the four quarters have been gathered together at the end of the fourth year, before the fifth begins, the leap day arrives.

Thus far concerning the leap year.

## ANOTHER ARGUMENT CONCERNING THE LEAP YEAR
