If you wish to know how that natural quarter of six hours, which increases throughout the whole year, is understood to increase first on each day and then in each month, you must observe and investigate the matter carefully as follows. For if the matter is stated [F. “For thus it is stated”] and investigated, two-thirds of a moment are gathered on every day; thus in three days two moments, in six days four, in twelve days eight, in twenty-four days sixteen, and in thirty days and ten hours twenty moments are gathered, that is, half an hour.

Thus in three thirty-day months, one day, and six hours, one and a half hours are gathered, that is, sixty moments. In six months, two days, and eleven hours [F. twelve hours], 120 moments are gathered, that is, three hours in the increase and growth of the light, over 182 days and twelve hours. In the same way, by the same calculation and investigation, another three hours—from which [F. supply: “whence”] the natural quarter is made—are gathered in the increase and growth of the night and darkness from the summer solstice to the winter solstice over half the year, that is, six months—as though all the months had been equal thirty-day months—plus two days and twelve hours.

Thus on each day two-thirds of a moment are gathered; in thirty days and ten hours, twenty moments. In 110 [Read: 90] days, one day, and six hours, sixty moments are gathered, that is, one and a half hours. Thus in 180 days, two days, and twelve hours, another three hours are gathered in the increase of the night. Consequently, throughout the whole year the natural quarter appears to increase by six hours: three hours in the increase of the light from the winter solstice to the summer solstice, and another three hours in the increase of the night from the summer solstice to the winter solstice.

Thus six hours are produced—the hours that remain in the sun’s course until it returns to the same line and to the same place in the sky from which it departed, completing the circuit of the zodiacal circle in 365 days and six hours. Thus far we have said a little concerning the leap year.

[Note: From Vatican Palatine manuscript no. 1449, folio 11 verso. It appears in Bede, vol. I of the works, p. 195, Basel edition of 1563, inserted in the short work *On the Arguments of the Moon* and appended to the letter *On the Celebration of Easter*, addressed to the presbyter Wichred, vol. II, p. 345 (Patrologia, vol. XC, columns 605 and 710).]

## CALCULATION OF ALBINUS THE MASTER

How to determine on what day of the month, or on what weekday, the fourteenth day of the Paschal moon occurs over nineteen years.

March has regulars 36, and at the end 9 [Bede: “and the lesser 4”]. April has regulars 35, and at the end 7 [Bede: “and the lesser 7”].

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is at 30 on 11 Kalends of April; in that same year the fourteenth day of the moon falls on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on the Nones of April. Add 5 to 30 and use the result as the regulars of April for the year in which the fourteenth moon falls in April. In the year in which the fourteenth moon falls in March, assign to March the regulars 36.

You can easily recognize from the epacts whether the fourteenth moon falls in March or in April. If you have more than 15 or fewer than 5 epacts, the fourteenth moon is calculated in April [Bede: “in April”]; but if you have more than 5 and fewer than 15 epacts, the fourteenth moon is assigned to March.

Therefore retain 35 as the regulars for April, and always subtract the epacts of that year; what remains is the day of the fourteenth moon. For example: in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle there will be 12 epacts. Subtract 22 from 35, and 13 remain. On the thirteenth day of April, that is, on the Ides of April, the fourteenth moon occurs.

If you seek the weekday of the fourteenth moon, add the concurrent of that year to the number that remains—for example, to this 13, which applies at present. In April there are also 7 regulars. Add all these together, and then divide by seven; what remains is the weekday of the fourteenth moon, and thus you will reach the Sunday very easily.

In March, retain 36 as the regulars and subtract the epacts of that year. For example, in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle there are 11 epacts, making 25. On the twenty-fifth day of that month the fourteenth moon will occur, that is, on 8 Kalends of April.

If you seek the weekday of that day, add to the stated number the concurrent of that year and the 4 regulars in March. When these have been added together and divided by seven, what remains is the weekday of the fourteenth moon; if nothing remains, it is the seventh weekday.

Therefore, if after the epacts have been subtracted 30 remain, whatever remains is the day of the month on which you will find the fourteenth moon. Thus, in the year in which there are 4 epacts, subtract 4 from 35, and 31 remain; remove 30, and 1 remains. The fourteenth moon occurs on the first day of the month, that is, on the Kalends of April.

If, after the subtraction, only 30 remain, the fourteenth moon falls on the thirtieth day of the month. This occurs once within the nineteen years, when 6 epacts are assigned, and the fourteenth moon occurs on 3 Kalends of April.

To instruct you by examples in finding the weekday on which the fourteenth moon occurs, take the present year of the Lord’s incarnation, 776 [Note: The same appears in Bede, although he had died long before this year.]. Take the epacts of this year, 26, and subtract them from the 35 regulars; 9 remain. Behold, the fourteenth moon will be on the ninth day of the month, that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of April. Add also the concurrent of the present year, namely 1, to 9, making 10. Add 7 to this, making 17. Divide these by 7: twice 7 makes 14, and 3 remain. The fourteenth moon will therefore be on the third weekday; the fifteenth on the fourth; the sixteenth on the fifth; the seventeenth on the sixth; the eighteenth on the seventh; the nineteenth on the first—the day of Easter, namely, the fourteenth moon [Bede: “the fifth day before the Ides of April”]. The fourth day before the Ides is the fifteenth; the third day before the Ides is the sixteenth; the second day before the Ides is the seventeenth; the Ides is the eighteenth [Bede: “the fifteenth”]; the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May is the nineteenth.

In the second year after this one, there are 7 [Supply: “epacts”]. Since this is more than 5 and less than 15, the fourteenth moon belongs to March, and you will find it as follows: take the regulars of March, 36, and subtract 7 from them. Twenty-nine remain. On the twenty-ninth day of March, that is, on 4 Kalends of April, the fourteenth moon occurs.

To find the weekday, take the same 29 and add the concurrent of that year, namely 2, making 31. Add to this the 4 regulars, and the total will be 35. Divide by 7: five times 7 makes 35, and nothing remains, because the fourteenth moon will be on the seventh weekday, 4 Kalends of April. The fifth weekday, 3 Kalends of April, is itself Easter Sunday.

In this way, throughout each year of the nineteen-year cycle, by subtracting the annual epacts from these regulars and from the days, you will find the fourteenth moon without error. By adding the concurrent number prescribed to those regulars, you will also determine without difficulty the weekday of the fourteenth moon. After calculating the weekdays that remain in that week, assign the increasing age of the moon to each successive day; then you will very quickly find both the moon’s position and its age.

> These arguments, dear companion, I have written for you  
> By labor of my own; now tell me with what gift  
> You would compete with me today, while I, weary, offer you such things.

# THE EIGHTH PART OF THE BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, MASTER OF CHARLES THE GREAT—DUBIOUS WORKS

### 369. PRELIMINARY NOTICE

Besides the works that we have so far presented as being asserted, on certain grounds, to belong to the blessed Alcuin as genuine products of his mind, several others are circulated, some already printed and others still contained in manuscript codices. These indeed seem, not without reason, to have the same blessed man as their author; yet the reasons by which they are customarily or possibly claimed for him are not so clear that they leave no room for more rigorous critics to doubt the true author.

Certainly nothing is easier than to be mistaken or misled in judging the author of a book from a remote age that lacks the characteristic marks of its genuine parent. There are also works long believed to belong to Alcuin that were later discovered to be the products of others, or to have been falsely attributed to Alcuin.

Therefore, since truth requires that the genuine works of famous writers be separated from doubtful and spurious ones, we have considered it improper to confuse and mix them together. In this section, therefore, we shall present the doubtful minor works of the blessed Alcuin; in the following section we shall send the spurious works elsewhere, while preserving the same order of subjects that we used in the genuine works.

Among the doubtful works, then, we first list the *Confession of Faith*, edited under Alcuin’s name from an ancient manuscript by the most distinguished D. Peter Francis Chifflet, S.J. We preface it with the highly learned investigation of our great Mabillon concerning its antiquity and author, which we defend in the appended notes against the very slight criticisms of D. Jacques Basnage.

Second, we list a disputation of boys, consisting of questions and answers on various subjects—for example, the work of the six days, the names of God, the six ages of the world, and so forth—copied from a very ancient manuscript of the distinguished cathedral chapter of Salzburg. In the preliminary notice we give reasons why the same short work may belong to Alcuin.

Third, we list the *Propositions for Sharpening the Minds of the Young*, on the authority of a manuscript of the distinguished monastery of Einsiedeln. Finally, we add certain verses or poems from various editions and several manuscripts.

Learned men may perhaps have expected that, if not among the genuine works, at least among the doubtful ones, we would present the *Brief Statement of Faith against the Arians*. Jacob Sirmond first published it without the author’s name; it appears in volume I of the *Miscellaneous Works*, p. 224. Later, the distinguished D. Chifflet, S.J., discovered it under the name of Alcuin the deacon in a very ancient codex of the Carthusian monastery of Portes.

Certainly there are some celebrated writers who believe that such an ancient codex should not be denied credibility [Note: See *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 326.]. Nevertheless, the editors of volume I of the works of Saint Leo I, pope, p. 285, warn that this short work cannot be assigned to Alcuin: first, because it is entirely foreign to his style; and second, because the rebaptism practiced by the Arians does not fit Alcuin’s age, just as the old interpretation of several passages of Sacred Scripture employed in the same short work does not fit it.

There is also another reason, which almost compels us not to decide in favor of our Alcuin; and we are surprised that none of the learned have hitherto noticed it. The entire text of this *Brief Statement* is inserted in a letter of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, to his son Guarnarius, to whom he sends this short work under the title: *A Cloud [or Little Cloud] of Testimonies of Catholic Faith concerning the Incarnation of the Lord and the Holy and Undivided Trinity, and concerning the Avoidance of Repeated Baptism*.

The celebrated Baluze published this from codex 4310 of the Colbert Library [Col. 1002C], in book V of the *Miscellanies*, p. 1, and elsewhere. Either, therefore, this *Brief Statement* belongs to the blessed Benedict of Aniane—although the reasons given above from the observations of the editors of Saint Leo’s works oppose that attribution equally—or it certainly cannot be attributed to Alcuin, with whom Benedict enjoyed close personal friendship and whose author he could not have failed to know, but would have named honorably.

It seems to us that this *Brief Statement*, or *Little Cloud of Testimonies*, belongs to some earlier author and was sent by the blessed Benedict to his disciple Guarnarius in order to fortify him against the errors that had then arisen or were spreading in Spain.

Finally, we also remove from this section the little work *On the Parts of Speech*, which we have under the name of Albinus from Vatican Library manuscript 1491 and which we once wished to assign among Alcuin’s doubtful works. The aforementioned codex, however, was taught us to bear a false author’s name by the rare *Collection of Ancient Grammarians* by Putschius, recently placed in our hands, published at Hanover in 1605, where the same writing appears on p. 1838 under the name of Sergius commenting on the second edition of Donatus.

In the first place, therefore, we present the solid and learned *Investigation* of Mabillon, which appears among his earlier *Analecta*, edition of 1723, p. 490. In it this most learned man did two things. First, he demonstrated that the manuscript codex containing that *Confession of Faith* under the name of Albinus is so ancient that it reaches very nearly to the age of Charlemagne. Second, he showed that the *Confession* belongs more probably to Alcuin—whose name it also bears—than to any other writer of that age, and that no reason or argument can be produced for denying credence to the ancient codex’s writer, who names Albinus or Alcuin as the author.

Mabillon weighed these two points with such force of argument [Col. 1003D] and testimony that it is astonishing that D. Basnage, otherwise a learned and educated man, could have been so carried away by partisan zeal as to try to diminish them in volume II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, book XV, chapter 7, with responses that are certainly slight and weak. We shall dissolve those responses in their proper places.

## ON THE CONFESSION OF FAITH, THAT IS, ON ITS ANTIQUITY AND AUTHOR

### An Investigation by Jean Mabillon

[Note: Frobenius’s notes to this *Investigation* were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 1025–1027. Each letter in this text of the *Investigation* refers to the corresponding letter of the note in that separate document.]

In the year 1656, Peter Francis Chifflet, S.J., a learned man, printed at Dijon five short works by ancient writers on the Catholic faith. The first place among them is occupied by Alcuin’s *Confession of His Faith*. In this work the author commits to writing what he believes concerning the one and triune God, the Incarnation, the sacraments, and the other principles of our religion, especially concerning the Eucharist, where he explains the faith of the Catholic Church with the greatest clarity.

From this work, the person who composed the office of the Most Holy Sacrament in 1659 excerpted a passage concerning the Eucharist and prefixed Alcuin’s name to it. Nevertheless, in his notes he advanced various conjectures by which he sincerely acknowledges that he was moved not to attribute the work firmly to Alcuin.

The Calvinists accepted this doubt as a true and certain judgment. Among them, Jean Daille attempted in a separate dissertation to prove that this *Confession* was not Alcuin’s but belonged to another author later than Saint Anselm. That posthumous dissertation was published at Rouen in this very year.

After reading the arguments advanced on this matter both in the notes mentioned above and in Daille’s dissertation, it seemed to me that all of them could easily be dissolved and refuted simply by examining the ancient codex that Chifflet had used—provided that it is established that the codex was written in Alcuin’s age, as Chifflet himself judges, and that it was originally marked with Alcuin’s own name.

Therefore, since this *Confession* is of great importance for illuminating the controversies concerning the Eucharist, I took pains to obtain and inspect the aforementioned codex. At last, through the diligence of R. P. Lord Claude Bretagne, prior of the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, it was found in the distinguished library of the most illustrious Boerius, president of the supreme senate of Dijon, who generously lent us this splendid ancient treasure, *κειμήλιον*.

### 371

Having received this exemplar and carefully examined it, I noticed four matters that were entirely clear and established to me.

First, the title or inscription of the work, both on the first blank folio and at the beginning of the book, reads: *Confession of Faith of Albinus*.

Second, this title had been substituted by a later hand and in later ink for another title that had been written in red pigment, as the traces left behind testify.

Third, the writing of this codex approaches the age of Charlemagne and does not appear later than the ninth century; moreover, it is uniform throughout the work, except for the final twelve verses, which were written in lighter ink.

Fourth, Chifflet’s edition agrees excellently with the exemplar, apart from a few minor errors of the sort that necessarily occur in typographical work.

Here it will be enough for me to deal with the title and the antiquity of the work, the two matters chiefly placed in controversy. I shall first dispose of the question of antiquity, speaking of the author’s name afterward.

### I

The antiquity is first demonstrated by the elegance of the letter-forms, such as was customary in the age of Charlemagne; then by the form of the script and the manner of writing, both of which suggest the ninth century (a) [Note: These annotation marks refer the reader to Frobenius’s *Observations against the Censures of Basnage*, which we present at the end of this *Investigation*. Editor.].

Although this argument alone is sufficient to demonstrate the antiquity of the work, it has the disadvantage that it does not move everyone equally. Since it depends not on common sense or reasoning but on the judgment of the eyes and on experience and knowledge of ancient books, it happens that belief in it is difficult for antiquarians who have not seen the codex, as well as for those who are not versed in such matters even if they have seen it.

To remedy this double disadvantage, I offer the Boerian codex, which is now in our possession, for the former group to inspect and examine. To the latter I offer the testimony of learned men [Col. 1004D] who have expressed their judgment concerning the antiquity of the codex: let the former trust their own eyes, and let the latter yield to the authority of the most serious scholars. Fair-minded judges of affairs will readily grant that each person should be believed in his own field of expertise; it is to such people alone that I write these things.

In addition, I set before both groups here certain conjectures and probable arguments by which the antiquity of the same work may be made clearer.

The writer of this little work lived long before the age of the scholastics, as certain of his statements prove—statements not sufficiently precise for the scholastics’ understanding. For example, in chapter 2 of the first part he says:

> I beseech the Father through the Son, I beseech the Son through the Father, I beseech the Holy Spirit through the Father and the Son.

No scholastic of that age would have spoken in this way. Moreover, he translates *ὁμοούσιος* as “of the same essence” (*coessentialis*); the scholastics would have said “consubstantial.”

Next, if the author had lived after the emergence of the heresy of Berengarius, he would undoubtedly have avoided the errors defended by the Berengarians. Some of them asserted that part of the bread and wine was transformed into the flesh and blood of the Lord for the worthy, while another part remained unchanged for the unworthy, as Guitmund testifies in book III *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, and Alger in book I, chapter 21.

Since the author of the *Confession*—as the Calvinists themselves acknowledge—professed concerning the Eucharist the faith that we Catholics follow today, he would have been very far from the doctrine condemned in certain Berengarians. Consequently, he would have moderated these words found in part IV, chapter 7, of the *Confession*:

> So great is the power of this sacrifice that for the just alone, [not] for sinners, it is the body and blood of Christ.

These words suggest that the author flourished before the errors of Berengarius, although elsewhere he correctly explains his meaning.

Furthermore, John the abbot, in a little book of prayers that he composed for Agnes Augusta while Berengarius was still alive and compiled from the opinions of the Fathers, cites several fragments consisting of many verses from Chifflet’s *Confession*. I presented one of them above from that little book: John extracted the fragment from the end of the first and the beginning of the second part of this *Confession*, as I shall explain more fully below.

The author of the *Confession*, however, did not borrow these words from John; John borrowed them from the *Confession*. This is so because John derives all the statements of his little book from the Fathers, as he himself declares, and because the Boerian codex is older than John’s time by well over two hundred years.

Finally, the antiquity of the *Confession* mentioned above is established by certain statements or doctrines that were debated only in the ninth century (c). The author holds, in part III, chapter 28, that catechumens who die before baptism do not attain eternal life. The words of Chifflet’s *Confession* are:

> We say that no catechumen, even one who has died in good works, possesses eternal life, except through martyrdom, where the whole sacrament of baptism is completed. For confessors are baptized by blood, or by fire, or by other punishments.

Rabanus likewise asserted the same opinion in precisely the same words in book IV *On the Universe*, chapter 10; it may reasonably appear that he received it from his teacher Alcuin.

Likewise belonging to the age of Charlemagne is the controversy concerning a double predestination: one to glory and the other to punishment. From this doctrine its opponents claimed that it followed that human beings were predestined by God to evil or sin (d).

The *Confession* of Chifflet seems to indicate the emergence of this error in the passage just cited, where it says:

> I not only do not believe that some are predestined to evil by divine power; if there are people who wish to believe so great an evil, I pronounce an anathema upon them with complete abhorrence.

A certain Mingentius first stirred up the tinder of this controversy in Spain; then Egila, his disciple, during the reign of Charlemagne and while Alcuin was still alive. Pope Adrian is a witness to this in two letters: one addressed “to Egila the bishop, or to John the presbyter,” and the other addressed “to all orthodox bishops residing throughout Spain.”

In the first of these letters we read:

> But as for what some of them say—that predestination to life or to death is in God’s power—others say: Why do we ask God not to be overcome by temptation, since this is in our power, as though by freedom of the will?

The same words occur in the later letter, but with this addition:

> As for what some of them say—that predestination to life or to death is in God’s power and not in ours—they say: Why do we strive to live, since it is in God’s power? Others again say: Why do we ask God not to be overcome by temptation, since this is in our power, as though by freedom of the will?

From this it is clear that there were then two factions among the Spaniards: some asserting a double predestination, others denying it; and likewise some placing good and evil conduct within human freedom apart from God’s help, while others placed it not in our power but in the power of God who predestines—or whether some actually thought this way or were believed to think so.

Certainly, it is established from the foregoing words, and also from the antidote that Pope Adrian offers by adducing the authority of Saint Fulgentius, that Adrian was convinced that there were people who said that human beings were predestined by God to evil. He writes:

> Consider by what bonds of impiety they bind themselves: if I have been predestined to good, it will not be necessary for me to resist evil; but if I have been born for evil, exercising goodness will profit me nothing.

Almost the same controversy flared up again fifty years later on the occasion of Gottschalk; but from that time onward it was completely extinguished.

Therefore, the writer of Chifflet’s *Confession* lived either in the time of Pope Adrian or certainly in that of Gottschalk—much rather in Adrian’s time, since the Boerian codex, although it is not an autograph, comes very close to the age of Charlemagne.

What I have said thus far, unless I am mistaken, plainly demonstrates the antiquity of this work. It now remains to discuss the title.

### II

The Boerian codex gives the author’s name in this form: *Confession of Faith of Albinus*. This title appears both at the beginning of the codex, on a blank folio, and at the head of the work. I shall discuss only the latter, since the former appears to have been written before the other, while the latter seems to have been formed in imitation of and on the basis of the former.

This title at the beginning of the work was, as I have already said, substituted in a later hand and ink for another title written in red pigment. But who did this, and at what time, is not easy to determine.

When I questioned Chifflet about this matter by letter—he had used this exemplar for his edition—he replied that he had acquired the codex fifty years earlier from a bookseller in Lyon and had faithfully transferred to the printed books both the title and the text of the work exactly as they appeared in that codex.

Certainly every suspicion of deceit or fraud should be removed from a religious man who had rendered such excellent service to the republic of letters. For the fact that he substituted *Alcuini* for *Albini* makes no difference to the person, who had two names. His native name was Alchwinus, while his Latin and adopted name was Albinus Flaccus.

Indeed, this fact removes suspicion. If the editor had fabricated the title, he would have fabricated the same inscription in both places. Let us therefore suppose that someone else, at an uncertain but later date, affixed the newer title to the old book. It is reasonable to think that this was done not dishonestly but in accordance with equity and good faith. No reason can be imagined why anyone would have lied in this matter.

Therefore, whoever he was, he appears to have done this on the authority of some old codex, or perhaps of the very exemplar itself, whose fading letters he restored with new ink. But whether the matter was done in this way or in another—something I certainly wish had not happened—there are many things in that *Confession* that lead one to attribute the work to Alcuin.

Let us suppose that no title had been prefixed to the work. Once its antiquity has been established, I find no author of the time of Charlemagne to whom this *Confession* can reasonably be attributed except Alcuin. All the indications concerning the author that appear in the *Confession* itself fit him extremely well.

1. First, the author asks God that he may never be exalted by “the necessary services of those who serve, and the reverence offered by the brothers.” This fits Alcuin particularly well, since Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, reproached him for having twenty thousand servants (e); nor does Alcuin himself deny this in his response to Elipandus.

2. Next, on page 130, he laments that he had lost “the place of beloved solitude, the friend of sorrow, quiet, and repentance,” which he had always loved from his earliest years. “Therefore,” he says, “my soul, placed in distress and great sorrow, is ignorant of your judgment concerning it, because I have not been able to find again the secret retreat of accustomed quiet and the suitable leisure for you, which, once heedlessly lost, I could not recover. Yet this I still desire, sigh for, and seek; but, hindered by my sins, I cannot find it (f).” Alcuin expresses the same agitation of spirit in several passages, but especially in Letter 129 [Col. 1007D], where he writes:

“Nearly five years ago, God is my witness, I considered withdrawing from these occupations, not with a feigned heart; but, by the counsel of your pious foresight, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin, a service which, by God’s gift, is beneficial to the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical order. Yet the affection of my former intention has not departed from my heart, as I already declared to your piety last year.”

This he wrote to Charles, to whom he also sent another letter, namely Letter 132, on the same subject. Having obtained what he desired, he sent another letter to the brothers serving God in the regions of Gothia (Letter 133):

“But I,” he says, “tossed about by the storms of the world, have labored and toiled in vain in many places; but now, by God’s mercy, I have been cast like a shipwrecked man into the harbor of quiet.”

3. Finally, throughout this Confession one finds the same ideas and the same words as in Alcuin’s authentic book *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity* (g). The author of the disputed Confession begins [373] with these words:

“Be present to me, true light, God the almighty Father; be present to me, true light from light, etc.”

Alcuin uses precisely the same words in his invocation of the most holy Trinity, in column 756 of his works (*Patrologia Latina*, vol. CI, col. 54). I omit many other examples of the same kind.

Add to this the antiquity of the work established above: since it was composed in the time of Charlemagne, it can be assigned to no one more suitably than Alcuin, as I have already said. [Col. 1008B] This will become still clearer from the refutation of the arguments brought forward both against the antiquity of the work and against its attribution to Alcuin.

III.

The first argument is proposed in the *Notes on the Office of the Most Holy Sacrament*, no. 70, approximately as follows:

“This Confession is for the most part taken from Pelagius’s *Confession of Faith* and from Gennadius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, although those passages which show Pelagian or Semipelagian doctrine are found to have been corrected. Furthermore, the first two parts are excellent and pious, whereas the third part does not cohere with the first two, from which it repeats much word for word—something no author would have done in one and the same work.”

Such, roughly, are the conjectures of that anonymous writer [Col. 1008C], who nevertheless admits that the style of this Confession approaches Alcuin’s style, and that its author lived before the age of the scholastics; consequently, he acknowledges that nothing certain can be established from these conjectures.

Although this Anonymous Confession is almost sufficient to resolve the conjectures he has advanced, it is nevertheless useful to add a few observations in order to confirm the truth more fully.

1. No one should be troubled by the fact that the author of the Confession used Pelagius’s Confession (h). In Alcuin’s time it was recognized as a genuine work of Saint Jerome. This is clear both from Book III, chapter 1 of the *Caroline Books*, where this Confession is cited under Jerome’s name, and from a manuscript of the Caesarean Library. That codex, containing psalms, canticles, and various confessions, was written by the notary Dagulf at Charlemagne’s command and presented to Pope Hadrian. As Lambecius testifies in volume II of the *Caesarean Library*, it contains, among other works, Pelagius’s very Confession, under this title: *Confession of the Catholic Faith of Saint Jerome*. The Confession then follows in these words:

“We believe in God the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible, etc.”

This is Pelagius’s Confession itself [Note: [Col. 1007] See Part III, no. 32; these passages are certainly neither Pelagian nor Semipelagian.]. No one, therefore, should find it surprising that Alcuin transcribed Pelagius’s Confession into his own work, since he regarded it as Jerome’s—a writer whom he habitually transcribes throughout his works.

Nor is it surprising that he also used the testimony of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* [Col. 1009A], which scholars now recognize as the work of Gennadius of Marseilles, a Semipelagian. The reason is, first, that this book was formerly attributed to Saint Augustine and was subsequently included by later writers in the appendix to Augustine’s works; and, second, that eight hundred years ago it was praised, with an honorable preface concerning its author, even by those who recognized Gennadius as its actual author.

Pope Hadrian I, Alcuin’s contemporary, is a clear witness to this in his letter to Charlemagne concerning the veneration of sacred images. In support of his position, among other patristic authorities, he cites Gennadius in these words:

“In the sacred councils mentioned above, the following testimonies of my most holy predecessors, the pontiffs, were presented: namely, that of Saint Gennadius, bishop of Marseilles, concerning the manner in which the bodies or relics of the saints ought to be venerated, chapter 40:

‘The bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of the blessed martyrs, are to be honored with the utmost sincerity, as though they were the members of Christ,’ etc.”

These words of Gennadius are found in chapter 73 of his commonly circulated book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. Here one sees that Hadrian praised not only Gennadius but also his book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. It is therefore not surprising that Alcuin likewise praised both the book and its author in his Confession; nor can this be used as an argument for taking the Confession away from Alcuin. On the contrary, it supports its attribution to him.

For it was only after the controversies occasioned by Gottschalk that this little book of Gennadius was finally regarded as suspect and infected with the Semipelagian error, as is evident from the writings of Florus and of the Church of Lyons concerning predestination. Since, then, the author of the Chiffletian Confession greatly esteemed both Gennadius’s book and Gennadius himself, it follows that he lived before the controversies concerning Gottschalk.

Nor is there any obstacle in the claim that the third part of this Confession does not sufficiently cohere with the first two and repeats certain passages from them. In the Boerian manuscript, the two later parts were copied by the same hand as the first two; and this repetition is nothing other than a recapitulation of what preceded.

2. The second objection, which is the first of those drawn from Dallaeus, is based on the fact that the Chiffletian Confession contains many passages copied word for word both from the treatise *On the Mirror*, which is listed among Augustine’s spurious works, and from the book *Meditations*, falsely attributed to Augustine. Dallaeus maintains that both works belong to a later period. He argues that the treatise *On the Mirror* is later than the *Meditations*, and that the book of *Meditations* was compiled after Saint Anselm, from whose various minor works it was for the most part assembled.

I grant that these two books, *On the Mirror* and the *Meditations*, are later than Saint Anselm. But from this the Chiffletian Confession derives an advantage in antiquity, since the Boerian manuscript was written at least two hundred years before Anselm, as I demonstrated above (i). It has also just been established that the book of *Meditations* consists almost entirely of excerpts from the writings of John the Abbot.

As for the *Mirror*, anyone who considers the matter more closely will undoubtedly see that it was taken from the Chiffletian Confession. Since this treatise promises to be a specimen of Christian confession and contains only the Faith concerning the Trinity, it is plainly an incomplete work if it is separated from the second part of the Confession, which deals with the Incarnation. It follows, therefore, that the *Mirror* should rather be regarded as derived from the Confession—as an incomplete work from a complete one—than the Confession from the *Mirror*.

Moreover, John the Abbot begins his little book of prayers with two fragments. One is found at the end of the first part of the Confession, and likewise at the end of the Augustinian *Mirror*; the other occurs at the beginning of the second part [Col. 1010A] and again, at greater length, in chapter 10 of the fourth part. He took the later fragment from the Confession, and therefore the earlier one not from the [Col. 1010B] *Mirror*. Finally, all the surviving manuscript copies of the *Mirror* treatise are later. This is unsurprising, since the treatise itself was published separately after Anselm, as Dallaeus himself admits. But the Boerian exemplar of the Confession, written on parchment in Charlemagne’s time, points to the source from which the *Mirror* flowed like a stream.

3. Dallaeus raises another objection: the published catalogues of Alcuin’s works make no mention of the Chiffletian Confession. The catalogues which Chifflet adduces, he says, must be understood as referring to another Confession of Alcuin’s, one that begins with the same words as the Chiffletian Confession (k).

Let this be so. But who does not know how incomplete and mutilated the catalogues of ancient writers are, even when arranged by authors who were their contemporaries? Possidius catalogued the works of Saint Augustine; Eadmer those of Anselm; Gaufridus those of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux—all of them by authors contemporary with the writers concerned. Nevertheless, scholars have long been convinced of how deficient these catalogues are in many respects.

4. “But,” says Dallaeus, “the Chiffletian writer repeatedly plunders Alcuin, something Alcuin himself would not have done. Florilegists, or excerptors, do not ordinarily extract from their own books what they commit to writing, but from the books of others.”

On the contrary, this most strongly proves that the author was none other than Alcuin, since he adheres so closely to his own words and ideas. If Dallaeus’s argument were valid, the book *Against the Nations* would have to be denied to Tertullian [Col. 1010D], since it consists entirely of the words and arguments of his *Apology*—if indeed the latter is by another author. The same could be said of certain works of Augustine and of other writers.

But I see that Dallaeus insists on calling him a florilegist or excerptor. I deny that the Confessor—if I may use that term—is merely a florilegist or excerptor, since he intersperses his own words and ideas at length among those taken from others. He calls his work a *Little Collection of Excerpts*; but he used this term out of modesty, considering not so much the authors from whom he selected as the subject matter which he sampled. This manner of speaking has long been familiar in precisely this sense.

5. What Dallaeus adds is of lesser importance, as he himself admits: namely, that what the published Confession contains in Part IV, chapter 7, at the beginning, concerning the offering of bread and the chalice, was taken from the book *On Divine Offices*, wrongly attributed to Alcuin. No plausible reason can be given why the author of the Confession should be said to have taken this passage from the aforementioned book rather than that the compiler of that book took it from the Confession.

6. The disputant further attacks the aforementioned Confession with the argument that the Chiffletian Alcuin contains certain statements that diverge from the opinions of the genuine Alcuin. For example, when he discusses that heaven which Moses says was created by God in the beginning together with the earth (Confession, Part III, no. 37 and following), he advances two opinions, both of which the genuine Alcuin likewise presents (*Questions on Genesis*, no. 28). But he prefers the opinion which Alcuin himself mentioned only in second place, and then only briefly, while explaining the other at greater length.

Yet this too is an argument that the two are one and the same author, since both report the same opinions. As for the fact that the author of the Confession prefers one opinion to the other, whereas Alcuin left both undecided, this is something we frequently see happening to other authors when they reconsider an argument. After wavering between different positions before carefully examining the subject, they may later, once the matter has been more fully considered, embrace one opinion rather than another—or even an opposite one. Now Alcuin only lightly resolves the difficulties proposed in his questions on Genesis, and in particular this one, which the author of the Confession examines more carefully.

7. The following objection contains a commonplace repeated a hundred times by Calvinists. Dallaeus admits that the words of the published Confession, where it treats of the Eucharist, approach Catholic faith very closely; indeed, he says—and these are Dallaeus’s own words—that they can scarcely be explained truly and sincerely in any other way than according to that faith. Yet he thinks he can derive a powerful argument from this for maintaining that the Chiffletian writer is entirely different from the genuine Alcuin, who denies that Christ’s body is present on earth throughout the whole of the present age.

For this purpose he twists against it Alcuin’s words from his Commentary on John, Book V, chapter 28. There, explaining the words, “You have the poor with you always, but you will not always have me,” Alcuin shows that those who ministered of their resources to Christ while he conversed among men were not to be blamed:

“Since he himself would remain bodily with the Church for so short a time, while the poor, to whom alms could be given, were to be found there always.”

Dallaeus places great weight on the word “bodily,” which he prints in larger letters. As though we Catholics did not all openly profess precisely this same thing, confessing that Christ the Lord ceased, according to his external appearance and earthly manner of life, to be present on earth, while nevertheless believing that he truly remains in the Eucharist under the appearance of bread and wine.

What Dallaeus adds concerning accidents—namely, that according to the mind of the genuine Alcuin they are necessary in every substance—is not worth refuting, since Alcuin is speaking there of the natural state of things, whereas everything in the Eucharist is supernatural.

8. Dallaeus also heaps up a number of minor points. In particular, he objects that the author of the Confession calls Ambrose “Father Ambrose” and Gregory “Father Gregory,” whereas Alcuin calls them saints or blessed men, following the usage of the ancients. There are several other matters of this sort, on which I would be excessive if I lingered.

I am surprised that a learned man should derive an argument from so slight a cause. If, because the author of the Confession calls Ambrose “Father Ambrose” and Gregory “Father Gregory,” he must be judged different from Alcuin, who calls them blessed, then it must also be concluded that the author is different from himself, since at the beginning of Part IV he refers to “blessed Gregory.” But these arguments are meager and empty. Let us examine what Dallaeus regards as much more serious.

9. He objects that the aforementioned Confession contains certain statements foreign to Alcuin’s age. One example is the author’s mournful complaint about his own time, as though it were utterly wretched, and his almost tragic exclamation (Part III, no. 36):

“O unhappy age of ours,” he says, “which neither fears God nor respects the authority of the sacred canons! No one now prevents a sacrilegious or criminal man from approaching the ministry of sacred orders.” Then shortly afterward: “Alas, miserable me! What times I have been compelled to see!”

“These words,” says Dallaeus, “are incompatible with the prosperity of the Carolingian age. I do not doubt that Alcuin congratulated himself on having been born in that age, rather than, as an ungrateful man, ever staining his writings with words so envious of so excellent a prince and patron.”

There indeed is the most serious argument, crushed by whose weight Alcuin must rightly fall—if we believe Dallaeus. But anyone who considers the corrupted condition of human nature will readily admit that this is a very weak argument. However golden the age of Charlemagne may have been, how many vices nevertheless flourished that could provide a pious person with grounds for righteous grief? For what age ever had a more virtuous moral condition than the primitive Church? Yet how many crimes did Paul condemn among those first Christians? How many did other writers of that age condemn?

Let us see, then, whether the genuine Alcuin believed in his authentic writings that Charles’s age was free from every stain. On the contrary, he teaches precisely the opposite in Letter 162, written to Charles himself:

“We have seen,” he says, “in certain places the altars of God without a roof, defiled by the droppings of birds or by the urine of dogs. Your revered devotion to God can easily correct this through the bishops, so that the Lord’s table may remain in its place with due honor, or be carried into the larger church, according to the holy foresight of God’s priests. And let the altar of Christ, or the consecration of his body and blood, be treated honorably; let the sacrament that is the chief instrument of our salvation be consecrated, held, and guarded with every form of reverence.”

What do you say, Dallaeus? Will you deny that these words were spoken by the genuine Alcuin? You are not so disposed that you would commit such an act. Or do you think these matters insignificant? That thought will not occur to you. For although you do not hold a Catholic view of the Eucharist, you will nevertheless readily admit that altars and churches must be treated reverently; and anyone who went so far as to leave them exposed to rain, not to mention bird droppings or the urine of dogs, would be guilty of violating religion. Yet this was being perpetrated with impunity in more than one place during that golden age, namely under the reign of Charlemagne.

But lest you perhaps reply that this was the only matter Alcuin criticized, hear not one but many things which he indicates to the same emperor required correction in that golden age, in poem 232, addressing Charles as follows:

“For many things throughout the world must be corrected by you,

O king! O ruler! O glory of the Church!

The plague of simony is indeed spreading disastrously throughout the world;

The sacred gifts of God are bestowed for money.

Those things which the eternal God had commanded all to give freely,

The giver himself now receives for payment.

Judgment in a case also stands under the influence of the giver’s gift;

A gratuity turns justice in the mouth of the old man.

And after gifts have been given, witnesses come to the cups,

And then impious drunkenness acquits the guilty.

The savage power of certain men oppresses the wretched,

So that the rich may fill their own sacks.

Robbers committing theft roam about with impunity;

The accomplices are also the avengers of crimes.

May your revered power, O king, restrain such things;

God appointed you ruler of the kingdom.”

Go on, then, and maintain, if you can, that Alcuin was ungrateful—if he was not afraid to utter such envious words against his excellent prince and patron, much less to stain his writings with them. Or, if you do not dare to do that, finally admit that what the author of the aforementioned Confession says in condemnation of the vices of his age is not foreign to the genuine Alcuin. On this subject, read more in Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in his *Admonition to the Judges*.

10. Dallaeus raises another objection from the published Confession, which he claims is incompatible with Alcuin’s age: namely, the passage concerning the Jews in Part II, chapter 3:

“To them not even as strangers is permission granted to greet their native land, at least by setting foot upon it.”

Dallaeus comments on these words as follows:

“If he lived in the time of Hadrian, or of Constantine and the Christian emperors who succeeded him in the East for three or four centuries, or finally in the time of the Latins, who for a while held Judaea, acquired by arms in the year 1100, this statement has the appearance of truth. But it is foreign to Alcuin’s age, when the Saracens ruled throughout Judaea.”

I do not understand what Dallaeus intends by this comment. If the Confession had introduced these words as a reproach and correction, Dallaeus’s argument would have some appearance of validity. But since this passage concerns punishments divinely inflicted upon the Jews, it contains nothing that we cannot say in our own time, when unbelievers likewise dominate sacred places.

11. Related to this argument is the objection which the disputant draws from Part IV, chapter 4 of the Confession, where it says:

“The truth of the Eucharistic mystery—that is, the real presence of the Lord’s body—has sometimes been manifested to certain persons by divine revelation.”

Dallaeus understands this to mean that some people were divinely granted the ability to see with bodily eyes flesh and blood in place of bread and wine in the Eucharist. He asserts that this did not happen either in earlier times or in Alcuin’s time, but that prodigies of this kind only began to be disseminated in the fully developed ninth century, supposedly to support Paschasius’s error.

If I wished to seek an opportunity for dispute, I could object here that it is not clear whether the author of the Confession is speaking of a visible apparition of Christ’s body in the Eucharist or of some spiritual revelation by which Christ’s true presence in the sacrament was confirmed. It would not be difficult to cite revelations of this kind from authors earlier than Alcuin. I readily accept Dallaeus’s interpretation; but, with due respect to him, such prodigies were read of long before Paschasius’s time. One is the event concerning Plegislo, a religious priest, which Paschasius himself records. Certainly this pious man did not invent it, but received it from an ancient author.

Another event was committed to writing in Alcuin’s time by Paul the Deacon, a monk of Monte Cassino, in his *Life of Gregory the Great*: the event that occurred in the case of a Roman matron. But even before this there was another such account in the *Life of Saint Basil*, bishop of Caesarea, attributed to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium. It tells of a certain Hebrew to whom, while Christians were receiving communion, a little child appeared to be cut into pieces in Basil’s hands. These accounts, I say, were read before Alcuin’s time and could therefore have been before his eyes when he wrote the Confession.

“You say,” you reply, “that Basil’s Life was unknown to Latin ears before the pontificate of Nicholas I, when it was translated into Latin by Ursus, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.” On the contrary, before Ursus’s translation another version was already read, one published among the *Lives of the Fathers* and rendered in a more polished style by Surius. I draw the clearest proof of this from the book of Aeneas, bishop of Paris, *Against the Greeks*, Question 2, where he praises the *Life of Saint Basil*, translated word for word from Greek into Latin by a certain Greek named Eveimius. Therefore, under Charles the Bald—that is, in the middle of the ninth century—this Life was circulating among the Franks, and Alcuin could have read it.

Moreover, Alcuin had at hand a notable example recorded in Book V of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 18. There we read a saying of Arsenius concerning a certain old man living in Scetis, as the Corbie manuscript has it. The old man held an opinion about Christ’s body in the Eucharist contrary to the teaching of the Catholic Church: he believed that it was not Christ’s natural body but merely its figure. Three Fathers were summoned for this reason, and they prayed for the old man’s conversion. After the sacred rite had been performed, he was finally brought back to the true faith:

“For when the loaves had been placed upon the altar, it appeared only to those three as though a little child were lying upon the altar. And when the priest extended his hand to break the bread, an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, holding a knife in his hand, and cut the child into pieces; his blood he caught in the chalice.”

Then, when the old man approached “to receive Holy Communion, flesh covered with blood was given to him alone. When he saw this, he was terrified and cried out, saying: ‘I believe, Lord, that the bread placed upon the altar is your body, and that the chalice is your blood.’ Immediately that flesh in his hand became bread according to the mystery, and he received it, giving thanks to God with reverence.”

Alcuin could have read this remarkable passage either in a Greek manuscript of the kind praised by Photius or in the translation of Pelagius, a deacon of the Holy Roman Church, who rendered this fifth book into Latin.

12. But now, after the Confession has been attacked by various devices and arguments, let us come at last to the principal argument by which Dallaeus thought he had completely undermined its antiquity: namely, “that the same author of the Confession speaks of those who deny the real presence of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist only as adherents of a doctrine condemned by the public judgment of the Church and numbered among the heresies, and deals with them as with sectarians and heretics.”

To prove this, he adduces the following passage from Part IV, chapter 5 of the Confession:

“Now at last take heed, perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, and do not pass over with a deaf ear and an uncircumcised heart what is said: ‘Whoever eats me’—that is, his own flesh, not another’s, as he clearly demonstrates.”

Shortly afterward:

“But because the truth of so great a mystery is altogether different from what you suppose, deceived by a heretical spirit, it is rightly called the mystery of faith,” etc.

“By these words,” says Dallaeus, “he most clearly indicates that, at the time when he was writing, there were people who taught concerning the Eucharist a doctrine different from his own, and who had been condemned as heretics for that reason.” Dallaeus denies that any such people existed before the time of Berengarius.

This argument has more appearance than the others Dallaeus has advanced. But if its disguise is removed, it will prove just as empty as the rest. To see this, it is necessary to examine the matter more closely and to demonstrate that long before Berengarius was condemned, those who held an opinion about the Eucharist contrary to the teaching now received by the Catholic Church were regarded and designated as heretics.

For this purpose, one witness is sufficient: Deoduinus, or Theoduinus, bishop of Liège (m). In a letter to Philip, king of the Franks, written against the error of Berengarius when it had first begun to arise, he judged that Berengarius and his followers ought not to be heard, and that a council should be convened not so much to deliberate on their behalf as to determine their punishment. His reason was that their errors had been proscribed and condemned by the most numerous councils of the holy Fathers and by the clearest pronouncements of venerable teachers.

Therefore, before the error later condemned in Berengarius, numerous councils had defined the Catholic faith concerning the Eucharist and had decreed that those who held an opposing view were to be regarded as heretics, as Deoduinus judges and testifies. Although he cites one council of Toledo, he plainly asserts that many other councils had also assembled to address the Eucharistic question.

Indeed, during the reign of Robert among the Franks—that is, in the year 1025, indiction 8—Gerard, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, established the Catholic faith concerning the Eucharist against certain heretics who rejected the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. This is recorded in the synod held against them at Arras, which our Acherius will shortly publish in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*.

When that same bishop was treating ecclesiastical matters in that city during the days of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord, “it was reported to him that certain men had arrived there from the regions of Italy. Introducing a certain sect of a new heresy, they were attempting to overturn the discipline of evangelical and apostolic authority; and, putting forward a certain form of justice, they asserted that people could be purified by this alone, and that there was no other sacrament in the holy Church by which they could attain salvation.”

When brought before the bishop, they “reported that they were hearers of a certain Gandulf, a man from the regions of Italy, and that they had been instructed by him in the evangelical commandments and apostolic teaching; and that they accepted no Scripture apart from this one, but upheld it in word and deed.”

When questioned more closely, they denied the mystery of holy Baptism and likewise the sacraments of the Eucharist, Penance, and Matrimony. Gerard composed a separate chapter against each error: the first concerning Baptism, the second concerning the Lord’s body and blood. In the latter he addressed the heretics in these words:

“Now, having passed over these matters, let us proceed to that sacred and immutable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, which you are attempting, to your own confusion, to overthrow by attacking it against divine and apostolic tradition, unless you repent.”

Then, explaining the nature of the sacrament itself, he adds, among other things:

“When this sacrifice is consecrated upon the altar from bread and wine mixed with water, by an ineffable sanctification, through his cross and words; and when the saving remembrance of his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven is celebrated there, it becomes the true and proper body of the Lord Jesus Christ, and his true and proper blood, although it appears to be something else. For it appears to be natural bread, but it most truly becomes the body of Christ, as we have learned from the testimony of that same Truth.”

From this we understand that the truth of the Eucharist was affirmed at the Synod of Arras more than twenty-five years before Berengarius was condemned. I have quoted this passage at somewhat greater length because, unless I am mistaken, this synod was previously unknown, and because it contributes greatly to illuminating the events that follow.

At approximately the same time, namely in the year 1017, as Rodulfus Glaber testifies in *History*, Book III, chapter 8, the proponents of this same heresy were burned at Orléans. Their principal leaders were Herbert and Lisoius. Arefastus exposed their errors, which had been concealed under a pretense of false holiness. In the presence of King Robert, as the acts of the synod prove in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, he declared, among other things, that he had learned from them that the bread and wine which, through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the hands of priests, appeared to become a sacrament upon the altar could not be converted into Christ’s body and blood.

When they confessed this and could not be recalled from that error [Col. 1017A] or from their other errors, they were burned outside the city at the king’s command. No canon or decree is recorded as having been enacted here, but only the punishment inflicted upon heretics—namely, because their error, which denied the truth of the Lord’s body and blood in the Eucharist, had been proscribed by the common judgment of the Catholic Church, and people of this sort had been assigned to the class of heretics.

Moved by this conviction, the heretics mentioned above did not dare to entrust their error to public preaching; instead, through hidden passages and secret conversations, they instilled it into the minds of certain faithful and trusted persons. So powerful among them was the preconceived condemnation of their own error.

Saint Odo, bishop of Canterbury, dealt more mildly with other men of the same sort around the year 950. At that time, “certain clerics, led astray by a wicked error, attempted to assert that the bread and wine placed upon the altar remained, after consecration, in their former substance, and were merely a figure of Christ’s body and blood, not the true body and blood of Christ.

“Desiring to destroy their monstrous unbelief, blessed Odo, while one day he was devoutly attending the solemn rites of Mass in the presence of the entire people, asked, with visible tears, that the mercy of almighty God be present in his ministry and, in order to dispel human errors, reveal the substantial reality of the divine mysteries. When the breaking of the life-giving bread had been reached, immediately, between the hands of the bishop as he held the fragments of Christ’s body, blood began to flow drop by drop.”

Struck by the sight, everyone, and especially the sectarian clerics, immediately abandoned their error. The bishop himself and his attendants rejoiced in great thanksgiving, “because every error concerning the Lord’s body had been erased from the hearts of his people, and they would no longer doubt that the bread placed upon the altar was the true body of Christ, since they had seen true blood flow from it.”

These are the words of a very ancient author who composed an as-yet-unpublished little book on Odo’s life. William, monk of Malmesbury, summarized the passage. Therefore, at that time—that is, in the middle of the tenth century—it was regarded as monstrous unbelief and error for anyone to doubt the truth of the body of the Lord Christ in the Eucharist.

In the preceding century the Catholic position was the same: Catholics called the adherents of such an error heretics. The principal witness is Paschasius Radbertus, in Book 21 of *On the Sacrament of the Altar*:

“But we, seeking the Lord’s own meaning in a Catholic manner, should not follow the empty songs of heretics, but him who says: ‘Take and eat of it, all of you.’”

But was Paschasius an innovator? Certainly not; he was an advocate of the Catholic faith. This is clear both because the Catholic Church has always honored him by this title and because innovators do not usually call those who disagree with them heretics, but rather call heretics the corrupters of the ancient faith.

Here, however, we are not concerned with the matter itself but with the designation “heretic,” which Paschasius expressly applied to those who denied Eucharistic truth before the condemnation of Berengarius.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, agrees with Paschasius in chapter 31 of his earlier treatise *On Predestination*, where he speaks as follows:

“There are also others who, delighting in novel expressions from which they procure empty rumors for themselves, speak against the truth of the Catholic faith, saying namely: that the Godhead is threefold; that the sacrament of the altar is not the true body and true blood of the Lord, but only a memorial of his true body and blood.”

Thus Hincmar judged that such people were fighting against the truth of the Catholic faith and consequently were heretics.

The very same error (as I may observe in passing) seems to have been noted by Anastasius the Librarian when he says that Pope Nicholas I caused crosses of the purest silver to be made in the Basilica of the Savior, called Caesarea, “which hang before the image, or—as it is read in Baronius under the year 858—before the sacrament of the substance of that same Lord Jesus Christ.” It is as though he were saying “before the substantial image of the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ,” in the same way that Christ is called in the Epistle to the Hebrews the “image of the substance of the Father”; Anastasius seems to have alluded here to that passage. But if one follows Baronius’s reading—which I consider preferable—it is no less, and indeed very suitably, favorable to the Catholic faith. For why, I ask, did he add the word “substance,” unless he intended to oppose it to the word “image,” which the heretics of that time were abusing? Clearly, the words “the sacrament of the substance of Christ’s flesh” are opposed to these words: “the sacrament of the image of Christ’s flesh”; and they mean as much as if Anastasius had said, “the sacrament containing the substance of Christ’s flesh, not an image.” Otherwise, such a doubling of terms would be empty and absurd.

From all this it is plainly established that in the time of Hincmar and Paschasius Radbertus—that is, shortly after Alcuin’s death—those who doubted the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist were called heretics. Accordingly, John Dallaeus is wrong to attribute the Chiffletian Confession to Alcuin on the grounds that it calls people of this kind “deceived by a heretical spirit.”

I believe that the ancients called them heretics for two reasons: namely, because they considered those worthy of that name who departed from the received faith of Catholics, and because they were believed to have been condemned by the decrees of the ancient Fathers. In particular, this was the conviction of certain ancient Catholics: that our faith concerning the Eucharist had been sanctioned at the Council of Ephesus (n), and that those who followed the contrary doctrine had been consigned to condemnation.

Lanfranc held this view, as is clear from the *Dialogue against Berengar*, where he observes that two heresies had arisen in ancient times, although everyone at that time agreed “that the bread and wine were changed into the true flesh of the Son of Man and his true blood”; the dispute was over who that Son of Man was, different parties contending with one another. “For some,” he says, “thought that this ought to be understood as any human being, whether just or sinful. [Col. 1019A] Others held that he was not at that time any ordinary person from the crowd, but a just and sanctified man, separated from the common life of human beings by the loftiness of his life.”

Lanfranc then adds that at that synod “both these deadly plagues” were condemned, and that a decree was sent to Nestorius in these words:

> We approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not as though we were receiving ordinary flesh, God forbid, nor as though we were receiving a sanctified man joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as though we were receiving one who possesses a divine indwelling; but truly the life-giving flesh, made the very flesh of the Word himself.

Lanfranc then adds the canon of the council anathematizing those who thought otherwise. From this no one should doubt that Lanfranc was convinced that the Fathers at Ephesus had established the Eucharistic faith against the Novatians, and had regarded as heretics those who departed from that definition.

I do not now inquire whether Lanfranc understood the council’s meaning correctly. Certainly, in this passage the Fathers of Ephesus either define the true presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist or, at the very least, plainly presuppose it. I readily concede that Lanfranc was mistaken in explaining the council’s decree, and attributed more to it than its words convey. Here I am considering only what he thought the council intended: he was undoubtedly convinced that the error of the Sacramentarians had been condemned by its decree.

The abbot Heriger of Lobbes held the same conviction in his treatise on the Eucharist, which was published anonymously by Cellot in the appendix to the history of Gottschalk. In due course, God willing, I shall demonstrate by 379 further documents that the author of this treatise was Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, who died in 1007.

Among the arguments he adduces to prove the Eucharistic faith, he also cites the passage reported by Lanfranc from the Council of Ephesus under the name of Cyril, namely Cyril of Alexandria. The latter’s letter to Nestorius, from which Heriger draws his testimony, is included among the acts of the Council of Ephesus.

What if the author of the Chiffletian Confession, influenced by the same prejudice, interpreted the decree of the Council of Ephesus in the same way, and for that reason called those “deceived by a heretical spirit” who doubted the truth of this sacrament? Certainly, he appears plainly to allude to this passage in these words (Part IV, no. 5):

> Observe at last, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, and do not pass by with a deaf ear and an uncircumcised heart what is said: “Whoever eats me”—that is, he demonstrates that it is his own flesh, and not another’s.

Why did he say “his own flesh, and not another’s,” unless he intended to exclude that error which he thought had been condemned by the Fathers of Ephesus? This, then, is why he calls the adherents of such an error “deceived by a heretical spirit.”

But suppose that the author of the Chiffletian Confession was not referring to the Council of Ephesus or to any other council. Why could he not have called heretics those (o) who denied the true presence of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist contrary to the clear assertion of Holy Scripture or of Christ the Lord, contrary to the tradition of the ancestors, and finally contrary to the received faith of his own time?

Certainly, the Gallic authors of the ninth century who wrote against Claudius, bishop of Turin, regarding the veneration of sacred images call him a heretic, although no synod had at that time established such veneration. For the Gallican Church then rejected as profane the Second Council of Nicaea, which had been held on this matter.

Thus Ratramnus repeatedly reproaches those who denied that Christ the Lord had emerged from the most blessed Virgin’s womb by the ordinary human way as the authors of a new and unheard-of heresy, although no conciliar decree supported him. He did so because he believed that the opinion of his opponents departed from the authority of Holy Scripture and the Fathers.

Why, then, should the Chiffletian Confession not with even greater right have called heretics those who had departed from the true faith concerning the Eucharist, in opposition not only to Holy Scripture and the tradition of the Fathers but also to the common consensus of Catholics?

Add to this that in the Confession such people are not called heretics, but merely “deceived by a heretical spirit,” that is, deceived through the prompting of the devil, the author of heresies. By this expression the author seems to designate not actual heretics who spread their error among the people, but certain Catholics of doubtful faith who, excessively attached to human arguments and the senses, held an incorrect view of this divine sacrament.

Let this, then, be the substance of our reply: before Berengar was condemned, the opponents of what we call the real presence in the Eucharist had been branded with the mark and penalties of heresy at the Councils of Cambrai and Orléans; in the tenth century they were regarded as heretics by Odo of Canterbury; and in the ninth century by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, by Paschasius Radbertus, and by others. Furthermore, Lanfranc, Heriger, and the author of the Chiffletian Confession appear to have believed that these people had likewise been consigned to condemnation at the Council of Ephesus. Finally, it was rightly said in that Confession that they were “deceived by a heretical spirit,” since they departed in their Eucharistic faith from the authority of Holy Scripture and the Fathers, and even from the confession then received among all Catholics.

### 13

“But surely,” you object, “no author of earlier times—and not even anyone in Alcuin’s time—held or taught this faith concerning the truth of the Eucharist, such as the Confession itself professes.”

Paul the Deacon in his *Life of Gregory the Great* plainly refutes this objection. He sets forth the Catholic truth so explicitly that no one could explain it more clearly. On the occasion of an act committed by a Roman matron against the Eucharist, Paul introduces Gregory as speaking in this way:

> Learn, I say, from the Truth, which now bears witness: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh, and my blood is truly drink.” But our Creator, foreknowing our weakness, by the power through which he made all things from nothing, and by which he fashioned for himself a body from the flesh of the ever-virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit, converts bread and wine mixed with water into his flesh and blood, while their proper appearance remains, through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit in response to the Catholic prayer, for our restoration.

Paul then adds:

> Accordingly, he ordered everyone to pray for the divine power, so that it might restore the most holy mystery to its former appearance, making it possible for the woman to consume it. This was done. Thereupon the woman mentioned above, advancing greatly in holy religion and faith, was consecrated through participation in the Lord’s sacrament, and all who had witnessed the event grew in divine love and orthodox belief.

Thus far Paul in the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, which was printed in the first Benedictine century. Gerard cited this passage at the aforementioned Council of Cambrai. From it we understand that the faith then received concerning the Eucharist was that the bread and wine, while their proper appearance remained, were changed into the Lord’s flesh and blood, and that orthodox belief consisted in this conviction.

Bishop Haymo of Halberstadt, a contemporary of Paul and Alcuin, asserts the same doctrine in his *Treatise on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, recently published by our Acherius in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*. There he explains his own faith—and indeed that of all Catholics of his time—in these words:

> We therefore believe, faithfully confess, and hold that that substance—namely, of bread and wine—through the operation of divine power, as has already been said, that is, the nature of bread and wine, is substantially changed into another substance, namely, into flesh and blood.

And below:

> The invisible priest therefore changes his visible creatures into the substance of his flesh and blood by a hidden power. In the body and blood of Christ, because of the horror felt by those who receive them, the taste and appearance of bread and wine remain, while the nature of the substances has been wholly changed into the body and blood of Christ. But the senses of the flesh report one thing, and the faith of the mind reports another.

And so forth.

I omit many other testimonies of this kind concerning the matter, which outstanding defenders of the continuous faith concerning the Eucharist have already produced. I have thought it worthwhile to append here this remarkable passage of Haymo, since no one has hitherto brought it forward; nothing clearer could rightly be found to prove the faith of the Church.

I found the aforementioned treatise of Haymo in a six-hundred-year-old parchment manuscript in our library of Saint-Germain. It contains Haymo’s exposition of the Epistles read at Mass throughout the year. This treatise is inserted in the manuscript after the exposition of the Epistle for the Lord’s Supper, an Epistle devoted entirely to the mystery of the Eucharist. The exposition of that Epistle is followed by this treatise under the title:

> Here begins the treatise of Aimo on the body and blood of the Lord.

The author begins the treatise by continuing from the exposition of the aforementioned Epistle, as follows:

> But since the occasion offered by this Epistle permits something more extensive to be said about so great a sacrament, etc.

I have thought it worthwhile to mention this here. Thus, as I was saying, in Alcuin’s time the faith concerning the Eucharist that we profess was already received, precisely the faith that Alcuin himself professed in the disputed Confession.

### 14

“Why, then,” you ask, “did Paschasius, in the testimonies of the Fathers that he adduces to establish his position, omit Alcuin, unmentioned and unpraised, if this Confession was in fact Alcuin’s work?”

The reason is that Paschasius draws his authority solely from the ancient Fathers. When Paschasius composed his book, Alcuin had died only a few years earlier. Moreover, Paschasius omitted many other testimonies of the ancients that can easily be recovered from their genuine works. Dallaeus could deny those works on the same grounds if his argument proved anything. Finally, Paschasius omitted Alcuin’s Confession perhaps because it had not come to his attention, given the scarcity of books and the difficulty of communication at that time.

These are more or less the arguments that Dallaeus gathers against the author and antiquity of the Confession, apart from a few minor points that I have deliberately omitted. Among them are his arguments concerning the difference of style between the Confession and Alcuin’s genuine works, although other learned men recognize a uniformity of expression both in the Confession itself and in Alcuin’s authentic writings.

These points, I say, seemed minor and insufficiently certain even to Dallaeus himself. I have prudently passed over them, lest our disputes proceed at excessive length.

Let this suffice, according to my ability, concerning the author and antiquity of this work. I undertook to defend one of these points in such a way that I hope the other can be demonstrated as virtually certain. If I have not entirely succeeded, it will nevertheless be enough fruit for me that I have opened this field to scholars by discovering a manuscript whose mere inspection can persuade one of the work’s antiquity.

I appeal here to the eyes and judgment of all learned men who can inspect the Boerian manuscript, either at the monastery of Saint-Germain, as long as it remains in our possession, or at Dijon in the Boerian Library, to which it will shortly be returned.

If the arguments I have produced concerning the author do not establish the matter completely, they at least make it highly probable. If anyone wishes to refute them, let him not deal with me as though I were making the identity of the author the central point of the controversy; let him attack the antiquity of the Confession, which is what I chiefly defend.

Certainly, it matters little to the Christian commonwealth who the author of this work was—Alcuin or someone else—provided that everyone acknowledges him as a contemporary of Alcuin. I do not, however, intend to abandon Alcuin’s defense; I merely wish to define the proper limits of the controversy.
