In addition, since I had undertaken to do so, I thought I should insert here the testimony of expert men concerning the antiquity of the Boerian manuscript, so that those unable to see the manuscript may defer to the authority of men illustrious in the republic of letters.

### TESTIMONY  
### Concerning the antiquity of the Boerian manuscript

We, the undersigned, make known to all whom it may concern that we have seen and carefully examined a very old parchment manuscript, whose title has been substituted by a more recent hand in the place of the original title:

> CONFESSION OF FAITH OF ALBINUS.

This is the very Confession printed under Alcuin’s name by the Reverend Father Pierre-François Chifflet. We testify that the script of this manuscript approaches very closely to the time of Charlemagne and does not appear later than the ninth century. In witness whereof we have signed this document on the Ides of December, in the year of our Lord 1674.

The following signed the original:

A. Faure, Doctor and Sorbonnic associate.  
Joannes Garnier, priest of the Society of Jesus and professor of theology.  
Carolus Le Cointe, priest of the Oratory.  
De Vyon d’Herouval, auditor of the Chamber of Accounts.  
Du Fresne du Cange, treasurer of Amiens.  
[Col. 1023B] Hadrianus Valesius, royal historiographer.  
Stephanus Baluze, prefect of the Colbert Library.  
Cotelier, of the Sorbonne.  
De Launay, advocate in the supreme Parisian senate.

## 381. Remarks on the censures of the celebrated Basnagius

These censures were directed against the preceding investigation of D. Mabillon, published in volume II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 7, page 899 and following.

D. Basnagius understood how damaging it would be to the arguments of the Calvinist sect if it could be shown, from an ancient and genuine writing by a distinguished doctor—such as he himself considers Alcuin to have been—that the same faith concerning the Eucharist which the Catholic Church now professes had already prevailed in the eighth century.

Accordingly, after briefly recounting the various opinions long debated concerning the Confession of Faith edited by the Reverend Father Chifflet under Alcuin’s name, he concludes:

> A dispute so prolonged concerning a work in which the Church’s tradition concerning the Eucharist is so plainly established deserves at least a moment of attention to its examination.

He then continues:

> We may be permitted to assert that among the arguments Mabillon has brought forward there is not even one that proves the Confession to be Alcuin’s.

Let us examine how the learned man proves this assertion. We shall cite the passages of Mabillon’s *Investigation* that D. Basnagius attempted to refute; we shall then report his replies and finally briefly rebut them.

### (a) “It has the character of the ninth century.”

Basnagius replies:

> The authority of a single manuscript is not so great as to prove anything, since some monk might have imitated the script; and nothing is easier than to err in judging the antiquity of manuscripts.

In truth, only despair concerning his own case could have prompted D. Basnagius to make this accusation against monks. If such reasoning is allowed, many monuments of antiquity could easily be overthrown, although only a single copy of each remains.

D. Basnagius should therefore have produced solid reasons for his suspicion before censuring some monk or other. For that monk either wrote this Confession for his private use and devotion—in which case why would he imitate characters earlier than his own age?—or he wrote it to deceive people of his own time. Who would believe that he was thinking about those who would live several centuries later? Yet people of his own time would easily have detected the fraud from the more recent parchment and handwriting.

It is certainly easy for modern people to err in judging the antiquity of manuscripts—people, I mean, who are less practiced in handling them, less trained in the critical art of distinguishing spurious writings from genuine ones, and less cautious in forming judgments. But no one, not even D. Basnagius himself, would say this of the great master of that art, Mabillon, or of Charles Comte, Du Fresne, Valesius, Baluze, Cotelier, and the others whom Basnagius himself cites as witnesses.

“But,” Basnagius replies, “M. Dallaeus, experienced in judging the style of ancient authors and highly skilled at distinguishing genuine works from false ones, detected that this Confession was spurious and supported his conclusion with arguments.”

Yet Mabillon refuted those arguments and appealed to the antiquity of the manuscript, which, after inspecting it, men highly skilled in diplomatic science confirmed. Dallaeus, perhaps without having seen the manuscript, attacked it on the basis of a slight suspicion: that a monk might have imitated the appearance of ancient characters.

Which of these men deserves greater credence, let the learned decide. Certainly D. Ceillier, in his *History of Sacred Authors*, volume XVIII, chapter 21, no. 18, page 342, testifies that in the course of his history he discovered that Dallaeus had often been deceived in judging the genuine works of the ancient Fathers. No one will easily discover this in Mabillon.

### (b) “Because of the worthy men.”

Basnagius says:

> The author of the Confession does not agree with those Berengarians who said that part of the bread and wine was changed and part was not changed.

Let it be so. Nevertheless, if this Confessor, who was truly Catholic, had written after Berengar, he would have moderated the words cited by Mabillon, lest he appear to be suspected of the Berengarian error. Therefore he is earlier than Berengar, as Mabillon maintains.

### (c) “It was debated only in the ninth century.”

Basnagius replies:

> This doctrine also continued into the following centuries.

Let it be so. But Mabillon is not speaking of the doctrine; he is speaking of the debate concerning that doctrine, and he asserts that the debate did not extend beyond the ninth century.

### (d) “So that human beings might be predestined by God to evil or sin.”

“On the contrary,” says Basnagius, “this passage alone is sufficient to show that the author of the Confession could not have written in Alcuin’s time. For, first, the controversy being debated in Spain in the year 790 did not concern predestination to evil.”

Yet it did concern this, as Mabillon proves here, and Basnagius offers no reply to that point.

Second, Basnagius says:

> This opinion concerning predestination to evil did not penetrate into Gaul, where at that time there had been no controversy concerning grace; rather, this question first began to be debated there forty or fifty years after Alcuin’s death.

But this reply is very weak. Let us grant that while Alcuin was alive the controversy concerning predestination to evil was not debated in Gaul. Why, nevertheless, could knowledge of that error not have penetrated from Spain into neighboring Gaul, reaching people concerned with the purity of doctrine—an error that Alcuin would condemn in his Confession?

Furthermore, Mabillon says that when this controversy was debated in Gaul fifty years later, it was then decided and completely extinguished. From this he infers that the author of the Chiffletian Confession lived either in the time of Pope Adrian I or certainly in the time of Gottschalk—indeed, more probably in Adrian’s time, since the Boerian manuscript, which is not an autograph, approaches very closely to the time of Charlemagne.

Why did D. Basnagius pass over this so lightly?

### (e) “That he had twenty thousand servants.”

“As though,” says Basnagius, “no one could become proud even on account of a smaller number of servants.”

That can certainly happen. But Mabillon asks for nothing more than that this prayer be especially appropriate to Alcuin, and not easily attributable to another writer of that period in which, as has been demonstrated, the little book was composed.

### (f) “I cannot find.”

“Was Alcuin, then,” Basnagius replies, “the author of this Confession, since he raised similar complaints?”

But do such complaints really call Alcuin to mind? Mabillon’s point is that they can be attributed no less to Alcuin than to another writer of that age.

### (g) “In the book on the Faith of the Holy Trinity.”

“This argument,” says D. Basnagius, “does not support Alcuin at all; rather, it serves Dallaeus, who infers from the fact that the author of the Confession frequently cites certain statements from Alcuin that Alcuin is not the true parent of this offspring.”

But Mabillon has already sufficiently refuted this argument of Dallaeus above, at the fourth point.

### (h) “No one should be moved by the fact that the author of the Confession used Pelagius’s Confession,” and so forth.

D. Basnagius replies to this argument of Mabillon:

> Does the name of Augustine or Jerome prefixed to a confession of faith make it orthodox?

Certainly not. Yet such great names, if proper attention is lacking—as can happen to human beings—can easily lead someone into deception.

Although the author of the Confession did not adopt the errors of Pelagius or Cassian, he plainly contradicted them, as becomes evident to readers. Basnagius continues:

> We know that Alcuin was a defender of grace and a disciple of Saint Augustine. This alone is sufficient to judge that this Confession is not his, since a Pelagian Confession has been inserted into it. Indeed, the author of the Confession uses Pelagius’s Confession in order more easily to disseminate the errors of the Semipelagians; but this cannot at all be attributed to Alcuin.

The learned man is mistaken. This writer did not insert Pelagius’s errors into his own Confession, nor did he adopt what is less orthodox in that work. He holds an entirely Catholic view of grace in Part III, no. 31, and in many other places.

Accordingly, D. Basnagius slanders this writer, whom everyone judges to be truly Catholic, when he writes without offering any reason that the author used that Pelagian Confession in order more easily to disseminate the errors of the Semipelagians, which he himself contradicts in many ways.

Nor should it be considered surprising if a Confession of Pelagius, falsely marked with the name of Augustine or Jerome, deceived Alcuin. Pelagius knew how to conceal his error so skillfully that when his Confession was publicly read at Rome, all those present, together with Pope Zosimus, judged it to be orthodox—as those familiar with the history of Pelagianism know.

### (i) “As I demonstrated above.”

“On the contrary,” Basnagius says, “from the fact that many passages have been excerpted from the *Speculum* and the *Book of Meditations*, it is clear that the Boerian manuscript is not as old as Mabillon wishes to make it appear, but does not go beyond the eleventh century.”

What an astonishing reply! Mabillon denies that anything was excerpted from the *Speculum* and the *Book of Meditations*, and proves that the passages found both in the *Speculum* and the *Book of Meditations* and in the Confession were derived from the Confession into those little books rather than from those books into the Confession.

D. Basnagius does not prove the contrary with a single word. Yet he assumes the contrary as though it were admitted, and, without opposing any of Mabillon’s arguments, dares to infer that the Boerian manuscript is more recent than the *Speculum* and the *Book of Meditations*. No one would have expected this from a man of such reputation.

### (k)

To the third argument of Dallaeus, which Mabillon refutes, D. Basnagius adds:

> If the Confession were genuinely Alcuin’s, those writers who so diligently searched for ancient testimonies in favor of the real presence would have cited it in support of their position. Paschasius certainly would have used it as a shield against his opponents and ought not, as he did, to have forgotten this support.

Mabillon himself has already answered this argument above, in no. 14. For that reason D. Basnagius should not have repeated it while passing over Mabillon’s solution.

### 383. (l) “The book *Ad Nationes* must be denied to Tertullian.”

“Tertullian’s example,” says Basnagius, “does not fit. For the book *Ad Nationes* is the same as the *Apology*, differing only in edition, one being more polished and fuller than the other. It cannot be compared with the Chiffletian Confession, which is merely sprinkled with certain fragments of Alcuin.”

But it has not yet been established that the book *Ad Nationes* is identical with Tertullian’s *Apology*. See D. Remigius Ceillier, *General History of the Sacred Authors*, and so forth, volume II, page 408, no. 3.

In the meantime, Mabillon himself acknowledged that the two might be identical when he said: “if, nevertheless, it is another…”

### [Col. 1026A] (m) “Theoduinus of Liège.”

To this and the subsequent testimonies D. Basnagius replies that “the facts which D. Mabillon recounts with great fidelity are true; nevertheless, he considers them incapable of proving anything, because none of them is less than 150 years later than Alcuin. From these very facts,” he says, “we are persuaded that not even one heretic can be found in this matter before the tenth century … and that those who opposed Paschasius Radbertus and publicly defended their opinion were not regarded as heretics.”

But did D. Basnagius really not know that Paschasius Radbertus, Hincmar, Haymo of Halberstadt, and Anastasius—whose testimonies Mabillon cites—lived before the tenth century? Paschasius in particular lived almost at the same time as Alcuin and had as his teacher the blessed Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, who had been trained in Alcuin’s school. Moreover, Paschasius’s book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, in which those who denied the real presence are called followers of the heretics, was first published by Paschasius in the year 831.

Therefore, before the tenth century, and in Alcuin’s own time, those who contradicted that dogma were considered heretics; for that reason Alcuin himself could also have called them “deceived by a heretical spirit.”

The reason why Paschasius’s opponents were not regarded as formal heretics, as is claimed, is that they did not err concerning the substance of the dogma, or concerning the real presence itself of Christ’s body in the Eucharist. They merely criticized the unusual manner in which Paschasius explained that presence, when he said that Christ’s body in the Eucharist was the same body that was born from the Virgin Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the dead.

There is no need to discuss this matter at greater length here, since Mabillon himself treated it fully in the preface to volume IV of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines*, chapter 1, § 4.

### [Col. 1026C] (n) “At the Council of Ephesus.”

Basnagius replies:

> Mabillon, sensing the weakness of his earlier arguments and wishing to restore their force, has recourse to the Council of Ephesus, which had established the real presence and condemned the contrary error. At least Lanfranc and Cellot’s anonymous author believed this, says Mabillon. But he acknowledges that these men were deceived. These two men, Basnagius continues, were born after transubstantiation had been established and, eager to find some proof in their favor, sought something favorable to themselves in the Council of Ephesus. Yet, as Mabillon does not deny, they were deceived. Can Alcuin’s authorship of the Confession be inferred from such suppositions, in which those who denied the real presence are treated as heretics?

The learned man is mistaken. Mabillon does not use this argument, drawn from the Council of Ephesus, to prove that Alcuin was the author of the Chiffletian Confession. He uses it to weaken Dallaeus’s argument, by which Dallaeus denies the Confession to Alcuin on the grounds that it calls those who denied the real presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist “deceived by a heretical spirit.”

Mabillon gives the reason why not only those who openly opposed the dogma received by the Church at that time, but also certain Catholics of doubtful faith who, excessively attached to human arguments and the senses, held an incorrect view of this divine sacrament, could be called heretics—or at least, in the language of the author of the Chiffletian Confession, “deceived by a heretical spirit.”

The reason, he says, is that certain ancients—Lanfranc and Cellot’s anonymous author—were convinced that our faith concerning the Eucharist had been sanctioned at the Council of Ephesus and that those who followed the contrary doctrine had been consigned to condemnation.

“But these men were deceived,” you say. Let it be so. Let us nevertheless grant that learned men of the age of Charlemagne, including Alcuin, were subject to the same prejudice. No reason can be given why this could not have happened. Dallaeus therefore has a reason why those who denied the real presence could have been called heretics, or “deceived by a heretical spirit,” by Alcuin himself.

D. Basnagius’s criticism is therefore empty. If you wish, also read what Mabillon says concerning this definition of the Council of Ephesus—which, if it did not define the true presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, at least plainly presupposes it—in *Acts of the Saints*, volume IV, preface, chapter 1, § 2, page 13.

### [Col. 1027A] (o) “Why could he not have called them heretics?” and so forth.

D. Basnagius acknowledges that Alcuin could have denounced an error concerning the real presence in the Eucharist as heretical, even if it had never before been condemned by any council.

“But,” he says, “it must first be shown that there were heretics in Alcuin’s time who denied this. For the very existence of such heretics at that time is denied, and with the greatest justification, because it was not even possible: no one at that time dreamed of the real presence of Christ’s body in the sacrament.”

Should I believe that D. Basnagius either read or considered Mabillon’s arguments, by which, in no. 13, 384 he proves conclusively from Paul the Deacon and Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, that in Alcuin’s time the faith professed by the author of the disputed Confession was received?

If he did not read them, that was negligence. If he did read them, why did he not refute the testimonies brought forward by Mabillon before declaring that in Alcuin’s time no one dreamed of the real presence of Christ’s body in the sacrament?

You see, learned reader, how inept and weak are the replies by which D. Basnagius attempted to undermine D. Mabillon’s arguments concerning the antiquity and authorship of the Chiffletian Confession, and how little fidelity he displayed in reporting them.

The critique of the aforementioned D. Basnagius is of the same character; he appended it to epistle 87 of the Canisian edition (now 90), addressed to the people of Lyons, in order to draw Alcuin over to the Calvinist side. Among his notes he writes:

> Alcuin says: “The sanctification of this mystery likewise signifies the effect of our salvation: in the water the people of believers are understood; in the grains of wheat, from which flour is made so that bread may be produced, the union of the whole Church is signified. By the fire of the Holy Spirit it is cooked into one body, so that the members may be joined to their head. Likewise, in the waters which are mixed with wine, the figure of the gentiles is signified, as we have said; in the wine, however, the blood of the Lord’s Passion is displayed. Thus, when in the sacraments water is mixed with wheat or wine, the faithful people are joined to Christ as members of his body.”

“All these things,” Basnagius says, “take place mystically.” Why, however, did this learned man not review those words of Alcuin which are quoted a little earlier in the same place, and from which Alcuin’s faith concerning transubstantiation is sufficiently clear?

> “Thus also the bread which is consecrated into the body of Christ ought to be most pure, without the contamination of any other leaven.”

And again:

> “From water and flour bread is made, which is consecrated into the body of Christ; water and wine shall be consecrated into the blood of Christ.”

Let us grant Basnagius that, according to Alcuin’s mind in the words previously cited by Basnagius himself, the water and the bread employed in the sacrifice signify only mystically the unity of the Church; and that the unconsecrated wine, likewise prepared for the sacrifice, signifies the blood of the Lord’s Passion; and that the faithful people, through the water mixed with wheat and wine, are incorporated into Christ. Nevertheless, the words quoted by us a little earlier do not at all admit this interpretation. For no one who believes that nothing but a figure of Christ’s body and blood is displayed in the consecrated bread and wine would speak in that way.

Raise up the bronze serpent as a figure of the crucified Christ: who would say that this serpent had been consecrated into the body of the crucified Christ? Nonsense!

But so that no doubt may remain concerning Alcuin’s view of the real presence of Christ’s body and blood, or of the true transubstantiation of the bread and wine, it is useful to cite his words in epistle 41 to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, which ought to be inscribed in letters of gold:

> “I beg you,” he says, “do not forget the name of your friend Albinus in your holy prayers; but store it away in some treasury of memory, and bring it forth at the appropriate time, when you have consecrated the bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood.”

Whoever, in the face of words so clear, impugns the faith is—let me say with Mabillon, *On Gallican Liturgy*, book I, chapter 9, no. 25, at the end—not a lover of truth, but of controversy, error, and schism.

Mabillon’s arguments, therefore, in favor of the antiquity of the Chiffletian Confession remain unshaken; and this constitutes the principal point of the celebrated scholar’s *Disquisition*. The highest probability concerning the author of the aforesaid work likewise remains firm—namely, that it was Alcuin. This is sufficient for us to assign the aforementioned Confession a place among Alcuin’s doubtful works.

[Col. 1027]

## 385. ALBINUS’S CONFESSION OF FAITH, WHICH P. F. CHIFFLET, S.J.,

transcribed from the Lyon manuscript, whose hand is so ancient that it appears either contemporary with Alcuin himself or at least nearly so, and which both gives the title of the little work and identifies its author; he published it first among five little works of the ancient writers *On the Catholic Faith*, at Dijon in the year 1656. [Note: [Col. 1027] See the same editor in the two prefaces prefixed to this little work.] (G)*

## PART I. ON THE ONE AND TRIUNE GOD

### I.

[Col. 1027D] Be present to me, true Light, God the almighty Father. Be present to me, true Light from Light, the Word, Son of God, almighty God. Be present to me, true illumination, Holy Spirit, unity of the Father and the Son, holiness and love, almighty God. Be present to me, O Trinity and triune Unity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one almighty God.

My faith invokes you, Lord, the faith which you gave me for my salvation because of your goodness. My chaste knowledge and the sweet love of my faith invoke you, my God: you led that faith, after dispersing the darkness of my ignorance, to an understanding of the truth; after removing the bitterness of the world and applying the sweetness of your charity, you made it savory and honey-sweet for me.

The blessed Trinity invokes you through the clear voice and sincere cry of my faith. Nourishing me from my very cradle, you continually illumined this faith through the inspiration of your grace, and, increasing it, you confirmed it in me through the ministry of the preaching of Mother Church.

How sweet it has become in the mouth of my heart! How pleasantly it tastes upon the very palate of my soul’s joys! How powerfully and how frequently it strikes my mind, moving and admonishing all the senses of my spirit so that it delights in praising you! For you made us to praise you; yet our mind is restless until it rests in you. Rebuking my sluggishness and gathering me from the dispersion by which I am torn into fragments, while turning away from you, the One, I dissipate myself among many things: let me return into myself, rise above myself, and, passing beyond all things, reach you, so that I may exult in you with the heart’s rejoicing and bring forth praises through the service of my mouth.

May my heart grow warm in meditation upon the confession of your glory; may my spirit long for you and my mind burn with love for you, forgetful of vanity and misery, while it attends to you alone and, astonished and awestruck, clings to the unchangeability of your glory. May the eyes of faith behold you, the sun of righteousness, as it is written: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. VI).

### II.

I shall therefore flee, Lord, and gladly flee the clamorous tumult of all vanities. But where shall I flee, so as to avoid them, trample them beneath my feet, and drive them far from the serenity of a joyful contemplation? To you, who alone are the refuge and the single hope of the wretched. To you, my glory, and you who exalt my head.

To you I shall rise from the pit of misery and from the mire of filth; let me cling to you, as you yourself grant, honey-sweetness, so that you may become sweet to me, unfailing sweetness, blessed and secure sweetness.

I shall therefore seek you, Lord, while invoking you; and I shall invoke you while believing in you, so that, seeking you, I may find you, and, finding you, may bless you—you who have blessed us with every blessing.

My God, my one hope, hear me, lest, wearied, I should be unwilling to seek you; rather, may I seek your face continually and ardently. Give strength for seeking, you who have made it possible to find you and have granted ever greater hope of finding you.

Illumine, Lord, the eye of my heart with the transparent light of inward vision. For it is veiled and blinded by the dreadful darkness of sins and ignorance. Illumine it with the light of your grace, so that with the sincere eyes of faith and the pure light of my heart I may contemplate the mysteries of your kingdom.

But since “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner,” and faith without worthy works is not praised, I beseech the Father through the Son; I beseech the Son through the Father; I beseech the Holy Spirit through the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 1029D] These words suggest a style older than the age of scholastic theology], that all vices may be removed from me and all holy virtues planted in me, so that the sacrifice of praise offered by my faith, my God, may be acceptable to you and ascend to you as a pleasing fragrance.

### III.

I beseech you and humbly implore your mercy, O God, source and origin of all things, giver and preserver of the virtues. Increase faith in me continually: holy, upright, and undefiled faith; learned, catholic, and most prudent faith; fervent, unconquerable, and orthodox faith. May it work in me everything that pleases you through love and humility, and may it not be overcome amid the words of disputation in a time of persecution or on the day of necessity.

O God who searches hearts and kidneys, my health and my weakness are before you: I beg you to preserve the former and heal the latter. My knowledge and my ignorance are before you. Where you have opened to me, receive me as I enter; where you have closed, open to me as I knock, so that, hearing, I may understand you; understanding, love you; loving, praise you; and with my whole heart always desire the vision of your beauty.

I hear what your Scripture, which you sanctified and sent into the world, wishes to declare to us. I hear it and believe it, for it says: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must believe and worship in spirit and truth” (John IV, 24).

But the spirit is incomprehensible and incorporeal, unchangeable and uncircumscribed, wholly everywhere, divided nowhere, according to the truthful testimony of Scripture itself. In this way, indeed, the Creator is distinguished from the creature, among whom there are those who are also called spirits.

### IV.

[Col. 1030D] If this is so—or rather, because this is so [Note: [Col. 1030D] From Augustine, *Confessions*, book I, chapter 2]—

> “How shall I invoke my God, my God and my Lord? For surely I shall invoke him within myself when I call upon him. And what place is there in me into which my God may come, the God who made heaven and earth? Can anything in me, Lord my God, contain you? Or do heaven and earth, which you made and in which you made me, contain you? Or, because without you nothing would exist, does it follow that whatever exists contains you? Why then do I ask you to come into me, when I would not exist unless you were in me? For I am not now in hell, and yet you are there also. For even if I descend into hell, you are present. I would not exist, my God—I would not exist at all—unless you were in me. Or rather, I would not exist unless I were in you, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things. Even so, Lord, even so. Where, then, do I invoke you when I am in you? Or from where will you come into me? Where indeed can I withdraw? Where can I go? Perhaps outside heaven and earth, so that from there my God may come into me, the one who said: ‘I fill heaven and earth’ (Jer. XXIII, 24)? Do heaven and earth, then, contain you because you fill them? Or do you fill them and something remains because they do not contain you? And where do you pour out whatever of you remains after heaven and earth have been filled? Or do you need no one to contain you, since you contain all things? For you fill the things you fill by containing them. Vessels full of you do not make you stable; for even if they are broken, you are not poured out. And when you are poured out upon us, you do not fall, but you raise us up; nor are you scattered, but you gather us.

“Yet you who fill all things fill all things with your whole self. Or, because all things cannot contain you wholly, do they contain a part of you? And do all things simultaneously contain the same part? Or do individual things contain individual parts, the greater contain greater parts and the lesser lesser parts? Is one part of you therefore greater and another lesser? Or are you wholly everywhere, and no thing contains you wholly?”

### V.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] Augustine, cited passage, chapter 4]

“What, then, are you, Lord my God—what, I ask, except the Lord God? For who is God besides the Lord? Or who is God besides our God?” (Ps. XVII, 32)

No one at all, no one. There is no other God besides you, triune and one, one and triune, neither in heaven above nor on earth below. Who is like you? Who is glorious in holiness, awesome and praiseworthy in every virtue, like you, our God, who do great and wondrous things, things that cannot be searched out and whose number has no end?

All things magnify you; every spirit praises you. All those hosts of blessed spirits and heavenly citizens worship and bless you. To you Mother Church throughout the whole world offers prayers and continually gives praise.

I, the least of your servants, praise and bless you. My mind rejoices to you; all my bones cry out to you: “Who is like you, Lord?” And rightly all that you have made obeys, serves, and trembles at your command, you its Creator. You do whatever you will.

For you alone are truly Lord, the invisible, immeasurable, uncircumscribed, without location, immense, and incomprehensible God; wholly everywhere, present everywhere, penetrating all things ineffably, containing all things, knowing all things, seeing all things, all-powerful, and governing the universe. Wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly also everywhere; and there is no other God besides you, our God, in whom Mother Church, apostolic and universal, believes and whom she worships.

You rightly ought to be worshiped and venerated, feared and loved, always with every devotion, Lord our God. When we did not exist, you powerfully made us; and when we had been lost through our own fault, by your mercy and goodness you wonderfully restored us.

Therefore I confess to you, King of heaven and earth, and honor you with the sacrifice of praise. Since external gifts are lacking, with all the marrow of my heart, with everything that is in me, I render vows of praise to you.

### VI.

But since nothing can be offered to you that is acceptable except what comes from you, O God, in whose light we see light, I beg you: give light to my heart, give a word to my mouth, grant my mind to ascend to the heavenly dwelling, grant it to behold the fountain of goodness, and, having received the light, to fix the eyes of my soul upon you, who are visible to the inner vision.

And since we are partly of heaven and partly of earth, so that the corruptible body weighs down the soul and an earthly dwelling depresses the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wis. IX, 15), scatter the clouds and burdens of earthly mass, and, I beg you, illumine with your splendor the dark face of the inner man.

Halt wandering minds rushing through many byways. Subject the flesh to the spirit, appetite to reason, vices to virtues, the body to the soul; subject me inwardly and outwardly in all things to your will. Thus, when everything has been well ordered in its proper arrangement by your grace, may I deserve both to love you perfectly and to praise you worthily, crying out to you with lips and heart and with every virtue of which I am capable, and saying:

“Most high, almighty, most merciful, most just, most hidden, most present, most beautiful, most powerful, most gentle, unconquerable Lord our God: you are stable and incomprehensible, unchangeable while changing all things, invisible while seeing all things, immortal, without location, boundless, uncircumscribed, nowhere limited, ineffable, immeasurable, unspeakable, inscrutable, unmoved, touching all things, investigable, fearful and awesome, to be honored and revered” [Note: [Col. 1032D] Augustine, cited passage, chapter 7]:

> “Never new, never old, renewing all things and bringing the proud into old age—and they do not know it. Always active, always at rest; gathering and lacking nothing; carrying all things without burden; filling all things without being enclosed; creating and protecting all things; nourishing and perfecting them; seeking, although nothing is lacking to you; loving without becoming heated; jealous and secure; repenting and not grieving; becoming angry and remaining tranquil; changing works but never counsel; receiving what you find and never having lost it; never needy and rejoicing in gains; never greedy and demanding interest:

> “It is overpaid to you that you should owe; and who possesses anything that is not yours?

### VII.

“You repay debts while owing nothing; you give what is owed while losing nothing”—

you alone give life to all things; you created all things; you are everywhere and wholly everywhere; you can be felt but cannot be seen; you are absent nowhere, and yet you are far from the thoughts of the wicked. You are not absent even where you are far away, because where you are not present by grace, you are present by vengeance.

You touch all things, yet you do not touch all things equally. For some things you touch so that they may exist, but not so that they may live and perceive; some so that they may exist, live, and perceive, but not so that they may discern; some so that they may exist, live, perceive, and discern. Although you are never unlike yourself, you touch unlike things in unlike ways.

You are present everywhere and can scarcely be found. We follow you while you stand, yet we cannot grasp you. You hold all things, fill all things, encompass all things, surpass all things, sustain all things. You do not sustain from one side while surpassing from another; nor do you fill from one side while encompassing from another. Rather, by encompassing you fill, and by filling you encompass; by sustaining you surpass, and by surpassing you sustain.

You teach the hearts of the faithful without the noise of words. You reach powerfully from end to end and order all things sweetly (Wis. VIII, 1). You are not spread out through places, nor varied by times; you have neither comings nor goings. You dwell in inaccessible light (1 Tim. VI, 16), which no human being has seen, nor can see.

Remaining at rest in yourself, you traverse the whole everywhere. You cannot be cut or divided, because you are truly one. You are not made into parts; rather, wholly you hold the whole, fill the whole, illumine the whole, and possess the whole.

The human mind cannot conceive this mystery, nor can an eloquent tongue recount it, nor can the volumes of libraries, with all their extended discourse, explain it. Even if books filled the entire world, your ineffable knowledge could not be narrated. For you are truly unspeakable; in no way can you be written down or enclosed—you who are the source of divine light and the sun of eternal brightness.

### VIII.

For you are great without quantity and therefore immense; good without quality and therefore truly and supremely good. No one is good except you alone, whose will is your work, to whom willing is being able, who by your sole will made all things that you created from nothing, who possess your whole creation without any need, govern it without labor, and rule it without weariness. Nothing disturbs the order of your command, either in the highest or in the lowest things.

You are regarded as being in all places without being located; you contain all things without bodily form; you are present everywhere without position or movement. You are not the author of evil—which you cannot do—you for whom nothing is impossible. You never regretted having made anything, nor are you disturbed by the storm of such a movement of mind; nor is your kingdom merely a portion of the whole earth.

You neither approve nor command wickedness or crime. You never lie, because you are eternal truth. By your goodness alone we were made; by your justice we endure punishment; by your mercy we are freed.

For nothing heavenly, nothing fiery, nothing earthly, and nothing touched by bodily sense is to be worshiped in your place. You truly are what you are, and you do not change. To you above all and in a special way belongs what the Greeks say, **ὢν**, and the Latins say, **est**—“being”—because you are always the same, and your years shall not fail (Ps. XC, 28).

From this it is plainly understood that you, our God whom we worship, are without doubt the true and almighty God: invisible, although you may be seen by a devout understanding; incomprehensible, although you may be represented through grace; immeasurable, although you may be piously believed and holily contemplated by human senses; ineffable, although you may in some manner be called by the customary words of human speech, used figuratively. Therefore you are true and so great.

Whatever can be known, understood, conceived, or said about you is less than you are. But what is incomprehensible and immense, unspeakable and infinite, is known only to you. For this is what surpasses all understanding.

### IX.

This too is what causes you to be esteemed and certainly believed to be God: you cannot be found completely, and you cannot be wholly understood or contained. Thus the force of your greatness presents you to us as both known and unknown.

And this is the height of the guilt of those who despise you: they refuse to know you and to serve you, their Creator. They have what they may venerate knowingly; they have what they may admire in ignorance; they have what they may fear; they have what they may love.

For if you were wholly open to our knowledge, you could scarcely be believed to be the living and true God. Therefore those who were thought to be gods were found to be false, because they could be known in every respect—what they were and what kind they were.

But you, our wondrous and powerful God, who by the word with which you commanded, by the reason with which you ordered, and by the power with which you were able, brought forth from nothing the entire mass of this world together with all the equipment of the elements, bodies, and spirits, as an ornament of your majesty and glory.

You command time to proceed from that very beginning of the age, while remaining stable and giving all things to move. You adorned the earth with the manifold growth of fruits and heaven with the beautiful splendor of the stars, whose names, signs, powers, courses, and seasons you alone know.

You are gentle and kind, a strong Zealot and unconquerable Sabaoth, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, and showing mercy to thousands upon thousands of those who love you and fear your name.

If your works are so great and inscrutable, beautiful and astonishing, let those who wish say how you, their most beautiful Creator, can be contained. For it is certain that the maker of all things exists in a far different manner from the things he wished to be made by him. Yet from the beauty of circumscribed nature and the wondrous appearance of worldly things, your beauty—which you yourself are, because you are simple—can to some extent be understood through the excellence of your glory, which cannot be circumscribed.

Although no sense can reach the infinite and incomprehensible greatness of your divinity—not even the senses of those heavenly citizens—your essence is nevertheless known in a marvelous way when it is believed to exist.

### X.

Whenever I recall or hear the two short syllables and four letters with which “God” is written—for this name, almighty God, is rightly owed to you alone—and whenever I behold the great works of your power and contemplate the beauty of your wondrous creation, while silently considering within myself your mercies, which are from age to age—for let those who wish marvel at your power, but I marvel still more when I observe your mercies—then, in these four letters and two short syllables, I contemplate with the mind’s vision and the sincere eyes of faith something infinite and incomprehensible, immense and ineffable, as far as I am able to know and apprehend it, which you deign to grant to me, so small a being.

Are you, then, our God, merely two short syllables? Do we worship two short syllables, or desire to reach two short syllables, which almost cease to sound before they have begun, and in which the second has no place unless the first has already passed?

For there remains something great, truly supreme, incomparable and pre-eminent above all, utterly unlike everything else, which is called “God,” although the sound does not remain when “God” is said.

But because flesh does not know spirit, and invisible things are not seen by visible things—for “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. V, 7)—you, our God, exceedingly good and merciful, taking account of human weakness, deign to make yourself known to us not through your own proper nature, but through a certain other likeness.

Hence you are also described as possessing the qualities of our bodily members. You wish unworthy descriptions of passions to be applied to yourself for this purpose: since in our present misery we cannot know you as you are, you draw us from our things toward yours, so that, while you condescend to us, we may more easily rise to you.

In many ways, therefore, to signify you to human beings, you take images from lower things and apply them to yourself, although it is established that according to your proper nature you are invisible, incorporeal, incomprehensible, and uncircumscribed. Accordingly, you have never appeared to anyone according to your own essence, but in the ways you wished, through an assumed form of creatures, for the accomplishment of causes.

### XI.

The followers of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites are therefore mistaken. When they read that humanity was made in the image and likeness of God, they assert with foolish presumption that you possess human form. Yet in that passage it is believed that you created the mind, not the flesh, in your image.

Indeed, human speech says nothing worthy of you, because nothing can be worthily said of you according to quality or quantity, position or bodily form, or movement. Yet breadth, length, height, and depth are nevertheless read as belonging to you in some manner.

Breadth is the charity by which you gather us from error and hold us in the truth. Length is the patience with which you bear with us, the wicked, until, when we have been corrected, you restore us to our future homeland. Height is the way in which, through the immensity of your knowledge, you surpass every understanding of humans and angels. Depth is the way in which you arrange those who are to be condemned below, and, as a just Judge, ordain them according to righteous judgment.

Let anyone who wishes to taste something beforehand of your proper nature, O supreme goodness of God, go beyond every creature and direct the contemplation of his mind beyond all things.

For a person, placed far from vanity, is held more fully in the truth when, after everything else has been removed peacefully from his contemplation, whatever is God is both piously believed and holily contemplated in his heart.

Although no one in this valley of tears can effectively comprehend or define you, it has nevertheless been granted to our age to know something great and exceedingly wondrous about you, the supreme Good, since your grace has revealed it to us.

### XII.

Who before us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, could hear or know such things, and such clear things, concerning the Trinity and Unity, concerning persons and substance?

Concerning you, God the Father: that you are from no one and are therefore called unbegotten. Concerning your Son: that he is begotten and is from you, not from himself. Concerning the Holy Spirit: that he proceeds and is not from himself, but from you and the Son, whose Spirit he is.

Thus, just as you, Father, cannot be called either begotten or proceeding, so the Son ought to be called neither unbegotten nor proceeding; and likewise the Holy Spirit ought to be called neither unbegotten nor begotten. In this way the property of the persons plainly reveals to us one Father together with one Son and one Holy Spirit.

Who in earlier ages understood so wisely, professed so openly, and truly knew that you are one God and triune, neither separating the substance nor confusing the persons?

Your Son, sent forth from your bosom into our public sphere, revealed this rule of right faith more clearly to this final age. Before you displayed the Creator to creation, you, God, were known only in Judea, and in Israel the fame and worship of your great name were heard. But was it then understood so clearly or to such an extent as among us, who have been placed under grace?

Concerning the undivided Trinity, very few people at that time had any understanding. The sons of the lawgivers, struck by a fitting blindness, still do not know what they ought to know concerning the one Trinity or the triune Unity. Miserably unwilling to confess anything beyond the one God, they chatter evil words against us whenever it is said that you have a Son.

But the hearts of us who have come from the gentiles, which believe, and the mouths which confess, prove how many true things it has been granted us to understand concerning the triune and one God. The very scourges and death inflicted on account of this confession prove it as well. For it is written: “I have understood more than the elders” (Ps. CXVIII, 100).

### XIII.

Lord our God, living and true God, unless you were triune, the voice of Truth would not have said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). For we would not be commanded, Lord God, to be baptized in the name of one who was not the Lord God.

And again, unless you, the Trinity, were unquestionably one God, your voice would never have said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4).

Therefore, unless you, God the Father, were yourself God, and your Word, the Son, Jesus Christ, were himself God, and your gift, the Holy Spirit, were himself God, we would not read in the writings of truth: “God sent his Son” (Gal. IV, 4).

Nor would you, Only-begotten, have said concerning the Holy Spirit: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV, 26); and, “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John XV, 26); and elsewhere: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also: I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 9); and, “The Father, remaining in me, himself performs the works” (John V, 10).

For what else do these words teach us to believe except the triune and one God—you, Teacher of truth, in whose breast are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge?

You also say: “My teaching is not mine” (John VII, 16); and, “The word which you have heard is not mine” (John XIV, 24).

A wondrous thing! Speak, I beg you, Word of the Father. Answer, I beseech you, power and wisdom of the supreme Principle—but yourself the Principle from the Principle; not two Principles, but certainly one Principle.

Speak, Word who always remains; teach the servant who humbly asks. For what is as truly yours as you yourself are? Yet you are your own and not your own, because you are not from yourself, as you often testify in many passages, but from the Father, whose Word you are—not a sound that can be uttered in syllables and carried away, but eternally existing, living, and remaining.

Therefore you are the Word—not one that ceases when uttered, but one that remains when begotten; not transitory, but eternal; not made, but begotten; not merely begotten, but only-begotten. Reason is present for the one who orders, and power is at hand for the one who accomplishes, since you are truly God and supreme Lord.

### XIV.

[Col. 1036D] The Father begot you, the Only-begotten Word, from himself, through whom he created all things from nothing. Therefore we believe without doubt that, unless you, the all-knowing and all-powerful Word, were God, all things could in no way have been made through you.

How can a creature create anything? Certainly only God can create, he who was not created. For nothing except God is uncreated.

Far be it from our understanding to confess that anything comes from the Father except the Son. Therefore only God could be born from God.

Hence, when I wish to contemplate you as the Word of the Father, no words suffice by which I might explain you. When will I ever be able to speak adequately or worthily? Who can speak? About whom? A human being about God; a work about its maker; a mortal about the immortal; a creature about the Creator; a small being about the immense; a temporal being about the eternal—whose venerable omnipotence made us through gratuitous goodness, and whose ineffable grace, no less, saved us through all-powerful mercy.

You freely made the work of creative omnipotence, and omnipotently completed the work of saving grace. You possess perpetual power both to create what did not exist and to restore what was lost.

Therefore that foremost of theologians, contemplating more deeply than others with eagle-like eyes, would not have written:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1),

unless you, God the Word, were always with the Father, always together with the Father, always from the Father, and always in the Father—not as a vessel is in a vessel or a city beside a city, but as wisdom is in the wise, truth in the truthful, goodness in the good, and eternity in the eternal.

For nothing other than God—equal and coeternal with him from whom you were begotten—can exist in the substance of the Father.

Let every heretical perversity, therefore, fall silent and perish together with its authors. It is always hostile in controversy: now dividing the substance, now confusing the persons.

May Mother Church, instructed in heavenly disciplines, increase in faith and be ever more richly made fruitful in devout works. She judges it profane and exceedingly impious to worship three gods or to fail to distinguish the Trinity in its persons.

Finally, she has learned through heavenly instruction; she believes, confesses, and teaches that there is unquestionably one substance and three persons, knowing all things that pertain to the rule of faith.

### XV

Taught from childhood by this divinely inspired instruction and teaching, I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that you, O supreme Trinity, are one power and undivided majesty. I confess you as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: three in persons, one true and almighty God in substance, creator of things visible and invisible [Col. 1037C]. You are not a body, nor placed in a body, nor compounded from diverse kinds, nor fashioned by the joints of limbs, but are of one simple and incorporeal, invisible and uncircumscribed nature.

I believe and confess you, true Father, principle of supreme goodness and of the whole Godhead, God of uncircumscribed and unbegotten majesty, deriving your beginning from no one but giving beginning to all. You beget the Son, not by bodily generation, nor from outside yourself, nor by necessity or will, but by nature.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] In Pelagius, at the beginning of his Confession.]

I also confess you, true Son, ineffably born from the Father without beginning, true and only-begotten God, through whom all things were made, and the true Word of the Father—not made, not created, not adopted, [Col. 1037D] but begotten and of one substance with the Father, and in every respect so equal to God the Father that you cannot be inferior to him in time, rank, or power. I confess you, who were begotten, to be as great as he who begot you.

When I say that the Son was begotten by the Father, I do not assign any time to that divine and ineffable generation. Nor do I say that the Father once began to exist, or that you, his Son, once began to exist. For we cannot otherwise confess an eternal Father unless we also confess you as the coeternal Son. The Father is named from the Son, and there is no doubt that he who was always Father always possessed a Son.

I also believe you, Holy Spirit, true God, neither made, nor [Col. 1038A] created, nor begotten, nor unbegotten, but ineffably proceeding from the Father and the Son, and substantially abiding in the Father and likewise in the Son. Thus in every respect you are equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with God the Father and the Son, so that you cannot differ from them or precede them in will, power, eternity, or substance, since you proceed from them.

Thus: the eternal Father without birth; the eternal Son with birth; the eternal Holy Spirit with procession, without birth. The whole Father in the Son and Holy Spirit; the whole Son in the Father and Holy Spirit; the whole Holy Spirit abiding in the Father and Son. I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one almighty God, reigning everywhere with one power and one kingdom, one majesty and one eternity, from then and now and forever [Col. 1038B].

### XVI

Directing my intention toward this rule of faith, and seeking you, my God, as far as you enabled me, I desired in understanding to see what I had believed. For this reason I entered the apothecary-shop of the many delights by which Mother Church is nourished. There I considered many things and began to examine each one.

As I anxiously and eagerly hurried here and there, you, being good and wishing to aid the desire that you had given me, extended the hand of your mercy and loosened the knot of my uncertainty. Therefore I am now greatly delighted to think about you, to speak about you, and to bring forth your praises with a desiring heart, according to the measure of my smallness, so that in the present misery I may be held by the body alone, but by my mind [Col. 1038C] and with every eagerness may be held with you.

My Lord, triune and one God, kindle in me the light of knowledge by which I may be worthy to understand you as three and one God, just as you are three and one God. Remove from me more and more, as you have begun to do, the darkness of ignorance, so that I may see spiritual things spiritually, insofar as human frailty permits.

On this road along which I walk with you as my guide, give me understanding; inspire me and continually teach me by your grace how one ought irreproachably to believe in you, so that I may apprehend you as one God essentially and grasp you, incomprehensibly, as three personally: the unbegotten Father, the only-begotten Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both and remaining in both.

Let no moment of priority or posteriority intervene among the three, nor let there be an undivided [Col. 1038D] dominion. In creating, no counsel; in governing and perfecting creatures, no assistance or divine labor. 390 Whatever there is there that is natural is undivided; whatever is personal is unconfused. O ineffable mystery, and more difficult than all others to understand!

### XVII

The other sacraments held in your Church, Lord, are astonishing and venerable; but this sacrament of yours surpasses them all. For this is the mystery of your undivided Trinity, and that is the sacrament of the heavenly table, which feeds the faithful and devout souls with flesh and gives them drink with blood, so that they may neither hunger nor thirst forever.

My God, make me, with a pure and simple conscience, especially among all other things, perceive and believe, receive and retain these mysteries [Col. 1039A]. Do not permit my faith in them to waver in any way, I ask, Lord; but in your mercy grant me always to believe and understand them as their truth requires.

May your grace enter my heart, sounding without sound and speaking without noise the whole truth of such great mysteries. May that teacher of virtues and revealer of all truths flood my soul within and without everywhere with light and sweetness. Thus, illuminating and giving it taste, may she establish and confirm it in the very center of truth, so that I may neither wish nor be able to think otherwise about such great mysteries than is proper and fitting.

It is wonderful that I desire to speak, but my tongue cannot express what my mind longs for. Almighty Goodness, whose ears of mercy are open to the very desires of your poor [Col. 1039B], understand the cry of your servant’s heart and favor my prayers. Grant, Lord, that with the palate of my mind itself I may feel, taste, and savor these ineffable mysteries.

For they are great and exceedingly wondrous, while I am a little one and fail in contemplating them whenever I raise the eyes of faith to behold them. But since both are necessary for us in one way for salvation, God, creator of all, invisible Creator, who are one divinity in substance and true and perfect Trinity in persons, I implore you as God the Father, from whom are all things, and your Son, through whom are all things, together with the Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.

I humbly beseech you, my Lord, whom I confess as one true God in the Trinity, by whom we were created, redeemed, and enlightened—being desirous of such great mysteries [Col. 1039C]—feed me with milk, nourish me, and extend my smallness to the measure of a mature man, so that I may be able to receive this solid food of the perfect. For my eyes see my imperfection (Psalm 138:16).

### XVIII

God the Father, giver of all good things, to whom no one ever prays without hope of mercy, together with your Son and the Holy Spirit, give what my soul desires and asks of you. For those whose substance is one have also one gift; and their operation, gift, and power are so one that even in the distinctiveness of the persons, according to a deeper understanding, a certain unity is perceived.

The unity of your inseparable nature cannot have separable persons, because just as you are Trinity in unity and unity [Col. 1039D] in Trinity, so you cannot have separation among the persons. Those persons are sometimes named individually; but you, God the Trinity, wished to show yourself inseparable in the persons in such a way that no name occurring in any one person is not related, according to the rule of relation, to another person: for example, the Father to the Son, and the Son to the Father, or the Holy Spirit most truly to the Father and the Son.

Those names, however, that signify your substance, power, or essence, or whatever is properly said of God, belong equally to all the persons: great, good, eternal, almighty God, and everything that is naturally said of you as God. Therefore there is no name of nature that can belong to you, God the Father [Col. 1040A], in such a way that it cannot belong also to your Son or to the Holy Spirit.

We say that you, God the Father, are naturally God; but the Son is also naturally God, and the Holy Spirit is naturally God. Yet there are not three Gods, but one God naturally: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Therefore you, holy Trinity, are inseparable God, to be understood as such in the persons, although in speech you have names that are separable, because you admit no plural number in the names of nature. This shows that the persons cannot be divided in the holy Trinity, which you are, one true God, because the name of each person always looks toward another person.

If I say “Father,” I indicate the Son; if I name the Son, I proclaim the Father; if I call upon the Holy Spirit, it must be understood that he is the Spirit of someone—that is, of the Father and the Son [Col. 1040B].

### XIX

You, unity of the Godhead, manifold through the plurality of persons, are numerically innumerable, and therefore measurably immeasurable and weighably weightless. We do not profess the origin of the supreme goodness—which you yourself are—from which all things are, through which all things are, and in which all things are; rather, we say that all good things are so by participation in it.

For your divine substance has always lacked, and lacks, matter, although it does not lack form. By impressing that form upon individual things like a seal, you undoubtedly make them differ from you without any alteration through your increase or diminution.

Whatever exists in the nature of creatures is your creature, O triune Unity and one Trinity, God, whose omnipotence governs, rules, and fills all that it has created. We do not say that you fill all things [Col. 1040C] so that they contain you, but rather so that they themselves are contained by you.

Nor do you fill all things part by part. It must not be thought that each thing receives you according to the size of its portion—that the greatest receives more and the smallest less—since you yourself are rather in all things, or all things are in you. Your omnipotence encloses all things, and no one will be able to find an avenue by which to escape your power.

For whoever does not have you appeased will by no means escape you when angry. The immensity of your divine greatness is such that we understand you to be within all things but not enclosed, outside all things but not excluded.

Therefore you are interior, so that you may contain all things; you are exterior, so that by the immensity of your uncircumscribed greatness you may enclose all things. By being exterior, you are shown to be the Creator [Col. 1040D]; by being interior, you are shown to govern and rule all things.

And lest created things exist without you, you are within all things. But lest they exist outside you, you are exterior, so that all things may be enclosed by you—not by local magnitude, but by the power of your might—because you are present everywhere, and all things are present to you, although some understand this and others do not.

### XX

These and many other things holy Mother Church, universal and orthodox, taught me. By your grace you willed me to become her member, and through the constant illumination of your inspiration you graciously made me so certain and secure in all things through her heavenly teaching, Lord, as though I were beholding face to face, rather than through a mirror, many things that lie hidden, closed within mysteries [Col. 1041A].

She taught, therefore, that you alone are the living and true God, neither corporeal nor passible nor tangible; that no part of you can be perceived by bodily eyes; and that nothing of your substance or nature can in any way be violated, compounded, or fabricated.

You possess nothing greater or lesser in yourself, but are in every way and on every side perfect, without deformity; great without quantity; good without quality; everlasting without time; life without death; strong without weakness; truth without falsehood; wholly everywhere without place; present everywhere without position; filling all things without extension; present everywhere without contraction; transcending all things without movement; remaining within all things without fixed position; creating all things without need; ruling all things without labor; giving beginning to all things without having a beginning yourself; making all mutable things without undergoing change yourself; and always and everywhere reigning without end [Col. 1041B].

### XXI

Lord, one God, Trinity, incomprehensibly surpassing all things, you are so ineffable, infinite, and incomprehensible that everything that can be said about you is exceedingly small. We say many things, but cannot fully say what you are, because you yourself are the consummation of all speech.

When, therefore, we have reached you, many of these things that we say will undoubtedly cease, and you will remain one, all in all. Without end we shall say one thing, praising you as one, and, having been made one in you, we too shall be one [Col. 1041C].

We shall continually behold, without end, the incorruptible, supremely inseparable, and truly immutable Trinity; knowing all things in you and possessing in you perpetual joy, healed from every sickness and transformed into that glory of immortality. When this vision comes—the vision promised to be given face to face—when everything concerning the mysteries is openly announced to us, and the appearance of faith and the reality of hope take their place, then, knowing more clearly and certainly, we shall behold that in you, one Trinity, there is nothing created or servile.

There is nothing unequal, nothing equal merely by grace, nothing earlier or later, or lesser; nothing foreign or official in relation to another; nothing inserted by invasion or stealth; nothing differing in character or will; nothing singular in office or incommunicable to another [Col. 1041D]; nothing confused. Rather, everything is perfect, because everything is from one and is one—not solitary, however—since you, holy Father, are the supreme Good, supreme Wisdom, and supreme Goodness, the source of all things; and your Truth, through which we understand you, is in no respect unlike you.

That Truth is the form of all things and alone fills what all things desire. It is also the gift of both, by which all things that are blessed in you are blessed. Thus we worship and adore one immutable Trinity.

### XXII

When what is one is repeated three times, number is not accumulated, but that one thing is affirmed to exist. Begetting, begotten, and proceeding are indeed three persons [Col. 1042A], but one substance, just as fire, brightness, and heat are three names but one thing; just as memory, understanding, and will are shown separately but operate inseparably.

If this is found in creatures, what must be understood concerning you, the Creator? The nature of your supreme divinity is immobile in every way and immutable. The persons, however, are mutable according to relation, not according to property; and therefore there is Trinity in the relation of the persons, but unity in the substance of the nature.

There is unity because of the inseparable essence of the Godhead, but Trinity because of the distinctness of the names. We confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, ὑποστάσεις (*hypostaseis*), that is, subsistences. Yet we say these things about you, our God, insofar as human understanding can grasp them [Col. 1042B].

But who, living in this life, even with a crystal-clear breast, could penetrate the inner mysteries of your Trinity? How are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three persons and one nature? How are you, Father, called unbegotten; the Son, begotten; and the Holy Spirit called neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding? How is the Son born from you, the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from you and from the Son? How does the Son, by being born, not proceed, while the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, is not born? How is the Son not from himself but from you, and yet not later than you, from whom he is? How does the Holy Spirit proceed from you and from the Son, and yet is not preceded by you and the Son, from whom he proceeds? How are you three as one and one as three [Col. 1042C]? How are you three relatively and one essentially? How are you, triune and one God, not locally but everywhere, and not everywhere in part, but wholly everywhere, present everywhere, without position, place, or movement?

### XXIII

Who, I ask, could contemplate these things? Who could comprehend them, however endowed with virtue or knowledge? Yet this has been placed within the hope of the promise, because we shall see you, Lord. Each person will see more perceptively in proportion as he has lived more purely here, for, as Scripture testifies, the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8).

Then it will be plainly seen, once all the mind’s darkness has been removed, how the Son, who exists by arising, is not subsequent to you, Father, from whom he arises; and how the Spirit of both, who is produced by procession, is not preceded by you who produce him. For the splendor seen, seizing and lifting the pure gaze of the loving mind into the manifestation of your majesty opened before us, will raise it up [Col. 1042D]. Yet that glory is nature, and that nature is glory.

This vision is now begun in faith, but then it will be perfected in appearance, when we shall drink at the very source the coeternal Wisdom that we now receive through the mouths of teachers. Then all the sacraments and all the hidden things will be revealed to us. We shall not need the words of teachers there, nor any mysteries. We shall see you face to face, but, unless I am mistaken, from the place from which the angels see you.

What could then remain hidden from us, when you, our God, life of the living, cause of causes, form of forms, most beautiful form, 392 formless form, will make yourself known to us in clear vision [Col. 1043A]? It is not unworthy of you when we call you “form,” for your essence can be called appearance and form. It is not without reason that “most splendid” and “most beautiful” are included among your praises.

But this is a form without matter, movement, time, or place, and therefore it is one and is what it is. Other things, however, are not what they are. This alone can most truly say: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). It is so great and of such a nature that in this life the human mind dares not claim for itself anything from the vision of its beauty. That vision you reserve as the reward for your elect in the recompense to come.

### XXIV

When, therefore, we have reached you, fountain [Col. 1043B] of life, eternal light, and most sweet beauty, our thirst will be delightfully impressed upon us by the vision of you, together with satisfaction. Yet need will be far from thirst, and disgust far from satisfaction, because we shall be satisfied while thirsting, and shall thirst while satisfied.

You will finally be eternal life, joy, and crown for us. Your blessed vision will be the reward of our labor, so that, after the darkness of this mortality, when the light of your glory has drawn near, we may rejoice.

We shall behold the immutability of your essence, so that through it we too may become immutable—but not as you see yourself. In us, whatever we shall be, we shall be able to know; but in you, who cannot be comprehended, how can we know whatever you are? And if we shall be able, we cannot yet; and yet, when we shall be able, will we be able to know you as you, God, know yourself [Col. 1043C]?

Even rational and elect creation will not possess the vision of you equally. Each will receive according to the reward of its labor. Yet what is given to each will be fully sufficient to behold.

“How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord! Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Psalm 30:20; 33:5)! Fortunate are those who have already crossed the sea of this mortality and have deserved to reach the harbor of perpetual security.

Unfortunate are we, who are still tossed about on the salt sea of this life by storms blowing around us, and who, amid many dangers and varied mishaps, labor uncertainly to drag our ship onward. Lord, with you as our helmsman and guide, grant us to keep our course between Scylla and Charybdis in such a way that, with the ship intact and the cargo safe, we may reach you, the safest harbor.

### XXV

[Col. 1043D] Blessed is the soul that, released from its earthly prison, seeks heaven freely; that, joined to the blessed spirits, stands before your majesty; that sees you, uncircumscribed light; that is affected by no assault of either death or enemy; that rejoices in the gift of perpetual incorruption.

O vital life, sweet and lovable life, where there is no enemy attacking, no enticement of sin, but supreme and certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil joy, joyful happiness, happy eternity, eternal blessedness, and blessed vision and praise of you, God, without end!

Would that these things might come, and that this mortal body might be clothed with immortality! Would that this life, which ought to be called death rather than life, might cease and soon come to an end: this uncertain, blind, and miserable life, which swollen humors inflate; pains weaken; fevers dry up; air sickens; foods bloat; fasts waste; jests enervate; sorrows consume; anxiety constricts; security dulls; riches toss about; poverty casts down; youth exalts; old age bends; weakness breaks; grief depresses; and after all these things death destroys, putting an end to every joy, so that when they have ceased to exist, they seem not even to have existed [Col. 1044A].

Now, now may that kingdom come, Lord—come, I beseech you—that is without death and free from ending, to which no periods of time succeed throughout eternity; where continuous day without night knows no time; where are those hymn-singing choirs of angels and the fellowship of the citizens above; where is the sweet solemnity of those returning from the labor of pilgrimage; where are the watchful choirs of prophets, the ordered number of apostles, and the victorious army of innumerable martyrs, together with the steadfastness of confessors, comforted by receiving their reward [Col. 1044B];

where are faithful men whom the pleasure of this age could not soften from the strength of their manhood, and likewise holy women who, together with the world, conquered their sex; where are children who, while still in the flesh, surpassed their years in character; and old men whom age rendered weak but did not deprive of the virtue of their works.

### XXVI

Make me, my God, strive with all my heart toward the holy assembly of all these and toward the joy that will remain forever in beholding your beauty; make me run courageously and arrive happily.

Meanwhile, while I remain in this body, O instiller of good things, continually exercise my mind in these meditations [Col. 1044C]. Cleanse, I ask, the gaze of my heart; sharpen the understanding of my mind; kindle my spirit with heavenly fire, so that I may think of you alone, love you alone, and have you alone in heart and mouth—you who will be our reward without end.

And so that I may bear the burden of my mortality more lightly, give light to my heart and a word to my mouth. Open the secrets and deep mysteries of the sacred Scriptures concerning your kingdom. Give me tears born of love for you; give me the wings of faith and virtues, clothed in which I may fly upward to you and, despising earth, seek heaven.

This faith concerning you, through you, and in you I confess, O blessed, holy, and glorious Trinity; O true, supreme, and everlasting unity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit! God, Lord, Paraclete, charity, grace, communion [Col. 1044D].

True light, true light from light, true illumination. Living life, life from the living one, vivifier of the living. Fountain, river, irrigation.

One from himself, one from both. From one are all things, through one are all things, in one are all things: that is, the Father from himself, the Son from the other, the Holy Spirit from both, from the Father and the Son.

Ὢν (*ōn*, “being”) from himself, ὢν (*ōn*, “being”) from the other, ὢν (*ōn*, “being”) from both; but every ὢν (“being”) is always in the three, and every ὢν (“being”) is equally in each.

Truthful begetter, truth begotten, truth also proceeding. One power, equal majesty, equal glory, one and the same essence.

### XXVII

Triune and one God, almighty God, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by alteration (James 1:17), and therefore with you the course of time [Col. 1045A] is in no way varied by the alternation of day and night.

God, true light, who without approach illuminate what you choose, and without withdrawal abandon what you reject; therefore no defect arising from change comes upon you.

God, who, remaining immutable in yourself, created things that pass away in such a way that with you they cannot pass away; therefore in your sight time does not flow away, although outwardly it runs on among us.

God, in whose eternity those things remain fixed that outwardly flow forth unfixed through the turning of the ages; therefore your eternity is one day, which is closed by no end and opened by no beginning.

God, who without change simultaneously behold all things and comprehend them without extension: the good things you aid, the evil things you judge, those whom you reward when aiding them, and those whom you condemn when judging them. In these things, which you arrange in different order, you are not different [Col. 1045B].

God, who encompass your works from without and fill them within, cover them above and sustain them below: although you are superior in power, inferior in support; exterior in greatness, interior in subtlety, you are nevertheless superior and inferior without place, vast without breadth, subtle without attenuation.

Therefore, by the mass of a body you are nowhere; but by the uncircumscribed substance and immensity of your immutable nature you are absent nowhere. Yet because you, Creator, are far removed from creation, who can think how you are in a place when no place can contain you?
