You cannot be in a place at all, because you are everywhere but not in a place. You are believed to be your own non-local place, a circumscribed Spirit [F., “uncircumscribed”]. Hence it is difficult to discover where you are, but much more difficult where you are not [Col. 1045C].

Who can subsist or exist without you? And yet not everyone can be with you. For all things are from you and subsist through you.

### XXVIII

God, true and infinite blessedness, from whom, through whom, and in whom are blessed all things that are truly blessed.

God, true and supreme life, from whom, through whom, and in whom live all things that truly and supremely live.

God, good and beautiful, from whom, through whom, and in whom are good and beautiful all things that are truly good and beautiful.

God, above whom there is nothing, outside whom there is nothing, without whom there is nothing.

God, beneath whom is everything, with whom is everything, in whom is everything.

God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

God, whose faith arouses us, whose hope lifts us up, whose charity joins us.

God, who commands us to ask, causes us to find, and opens to those who knock [Col. 1045D].

God, to turn away from whom is to fall; to turn toward whom is to rise again; to remain in whom is to stand firm.

God, not to know whom is to die; to know whom is to live; to despise whom is to perish; to serve whom is to reign.

God, through whose merciful help the subordinate serves well and the superior rules well; therefore neither of them proceeds in the right order without you.

Invisible and immeasurable God, ineffable and eternal, incomprehensible and incorporeal, immortal and perpetual, immutable and uncircumscribed, wondrous and blessed; for you, being and living, being wise and understanding, knowing and being able, becoming beautiful and shining, are one and the same. You are simple and cannot be divided.

### XXIX

You are my living and true God, my gracious Lord, my great King [Col. 1046A]. I worship you as one God, the one principle of all natures, from whom the universe both begins and is perfected and contained.

One God, from whom we are, through whom we are, in whom we are; from whom we departed and became unlike him; the principle to which we return, the form that we follow, and the grace by which we are reconciled.

One God, by whose authorship we were created; the likeness through which we are restored to unity; and the peace by which we cling to unity.

One God, by whose creative power we live; through whom, restored, we live wisely; whom we love and in whom we rejoice, living blessedly.

I praise, bless, and adore you, and I give thanks to your clemency and goodness for all your gifts and bestowals, and for all the benefits of your mercy that you lavish upon my soul [Col. 1046B] and body, and have always lavished from my childhood and from my cradle, for your sake and for the sake of your holy name.

Thus, through experience, I have learned that you, our God, are the God of infinite mercy and boundless compassion, who wondrously guide and preserve your servants amid adversity and prosperity. You so govern their life in both conditions that adversity follows prosperity, and prosperity follows adversity.

Therefore let all your works confess to you, Lord, and let your holy ones bless you (Psalm 144:10); and, so that by confessing they may recover their senses, let even sinners not cease from your praises.

I am one of them. Although inclined more readily toward sins, with a desiring heart I nevertheless sing your praises—not with the dignity with which I ought, but with the ability I possess. Look, I ask, with a serene countenance upon this service of my smallness [Col. 1046C], and with favorable condescension accept this tiny sacrifice of my confession of faith, so that what came from you may return to you.

Look not so much at what I devoutly offer as at what I most devoutly wished and wish to say. Whatever is disgraceful or offends you, my soul abhors.

Would that I could offer such things as those hymn-singing choirs of angels offer! How gladly I would pour myself out entirely in your praises and tirelessly proclaim the song of your glory brilliantly in the midst of the Church!

But because I cannot do as they do, shall I therefore remain completely silent? Woe, Lord, to those who are silent about you, who loosen the mouths of the mute and make the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21)! Since it is permitted even to little ones to stammer out your praises, receive, I pray, the sacrifice from the hand of my tongue, from the love of my heart [Col. 1046D].

### XXX

But forgive, I ask, Lord, your most unworthy and unhappy servant, who speaks with you at length about you. Forgive me mercifully, because I devoted myself to this little florilegium not through presumptuous boldness, but through eagerness for my desire for you, so that I might always have with me a brief and handy word about you. Whenever I grow lukewarm through reading it, I may be rekindled in your love.

For we are placed in the midst of snares, and therefore easily grow cold toward heavenly desire. Hence we need a continual reminder by which, when awakened, we may return to you, our true and supreme good, whenever we drift away.

There are, indeed, many contemplations by which the soul devoted to you is afflicted and advances; but none delights me and occupies my mind as much as that which concerns your own nature [Col. 1047A].

For this reason I judged it necessary to set apart this little discourse solely for myself [F., “to pluck”], in which, concerning the omnipotence of your majesty, I confess with my mouth for salvation what I believe in my heart for righteousness: you, God the unbegotten Father; you, the only-begotten Son; you, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete; the holy and undivided Trinity, one God, infinite in greatness, almighty in power, supreme in goodness, beyond estimation in wisdom, fearsome in counsels, just in judgments, most secret in thoughts, truthful in words, holy in works, abundant in mercies, most patient toward offenders, and gracious toward penitents.

Always the same, eternal and everlasting, immortal and immutable, whom neither expanses enlarge nor the narrowness of places constricts; whom no receptacles confine; whom will does not vary; whom necessity does not corrupt; whom sorrows do not disturb and joys do not delight; whom forgetfulness does not remove and memory does not restore; for whom past things do not pass away and future things do not succeed; to whom origin gives no beginning, times no increase, and chance no end.

Rather, before the ages, in the ages, and through the ages you live forever. To you belong perpetual praise and eternal glory, supreme power and singular honor, perpetual kingdom and dominion without end, throughout the endless, tireless, and immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## PART II. ON THE INCARNATE WORD

[Col. 1047]

[Col. 1047B] **I.** In the preceding brief statement of my confession of faith, I confessed, O almighty Trinity, one God, examiner and searcher of my heart, the omnipotence of your majesty and the majesty of your omnipotence. Now, however, I confess with a pure heart and Catholic mouth how you deigned to come to the aid of the human race at the end of the ages.

For you alone, almighty Father, are nowhere read of as having been sent. Concerning your Only-Begotten, however, the Apostle writes: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4). When he says, “God sent his Son, made of a woman,” he clearly shows that he came as one sent into this world, when, born of Mary ever-virgin, he appeared on earth as true and perfect man. What, then, does the Evangelist mean when he says of him, “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:10)? He was sent there through his humanity where he had always been through his divinity.

I believe in my heart that this mission was the work of the Holy Trinity for our justification, and I confess it with my mouth for our salvation. Yet, because the Son willed to become man, we do not believe that either substance was changed into the other, that a fourth person was added to the mystery of the Trinity, or that the substance of the divine Word and of man was confused. Rather, what had been assumed from us might come to God, while that which had never not existed remained always what it had been.

For he who was not made fashioned for himself, in a wondrous and inexplicable manner, a dwelling: new in time, though not by deliberation, henceforth abiding in him and never to be brought to an end by any time. This mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus—but the one man without sin—alone made your name known to human beings, especially to those whom you gave him from the world. He announced everything to them, and knew it all the more truly and effectively than others.

For these are those who were appointed rulers over the whole earth, whose trumpet of preaching reached the ears of the entire world. Since they had seen these things from the beginning and had been ministers of the word, they handed down to us through the succession of the Fathers many mysteries of your kingdom, never before discovered, which first began to be proclaimed through the Lord—you, of course, making their words credible by signs, wonders, various powers, and marvelous distributions of the Holy Spirit according to your will.

**II.** This indeed is the reason why, relying upon it, we receive without any hesitation whatever the universal and apostolic Church, our mother, teaches. So firmly are we established by your grace in certain faith for the affirmation of such great testimonies that we do not fear to die by every kind of torture, knowing with certainty that a glorious life remains for us after death.

Strengthened by this security, we sing, chant, and write, cheerful and eager, sometimes word for word, sometimes sense for sense, according to apostolic tradition, concerning the marvelous work of our salvation—that is, the mystery of piety which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory (1 Tim. 3:6).

Yet, as I consider these things, I cannot cease to wonder with myself at the impiety of the Jews, who did not fear to lay hands upon Christ the Lord, thundering forth heavenly words and flashing with so many miracles. O hearts harder than stones and more foolish than brute beasts! Where, I ask, was the understanding and reason of those wretched people when they saw the heavenly physician freely heal an infinite multitude of sick people—that is, cast out demons, give sight to the blind, cleanse lepers, restore the paralyzed, return corpses to life—and perform these and many other things by the power of his word alone and without delay?

What were the blind people thinking when they saw even the elements serve him, so that, entering the sea, he commanded the winds and stilled the storms, showing by evident signs that he was your Son, O God the Father, and the one whom you had formerly promised in many ways through the prophets for our salvation?

At last, the envy of the faithless nation, long driven on by dreadful counsels, extorted by many cries that Christ be handed over to them for crucifixion. He himself had foretold that they would do these things; and, if that were not enough, so had the prophets of old. Yet, fastened to the cross, he willingly gave up the Spirit with a word, the executioner’s task having been forestalled.

**III.** At that very moment, the sun concealed itself and midday was changed into night. Then the Jews surrounded the one taken down from the cross and placed in the tomb with great vigilance, including a military guard, lest, since he had foretold that he would rise on the third day, the disciples secretly remove the body and deceive the suspicious.

But at the third dawn, when the earth was suddenly shaken, the stone that had blocked the tomb was rolled away, and the guard was driven off in terror, no disciples appearing and nothing being found in the place where he had been laid except the burial wrappings.

Nevertheless, the leaders of the Jews, not ceasing from the perfidy they had begun, bribed those who were telling the truth, so that they might more confidently spread the claim that he had been stolen by his disciples.

This was by your just judgment, Lord, as the sacred prophecy bears witness: first they were deprived of the understanding of their eyes and of the fruitfulness of their ears; afterward, as we see, they were cast out from their own seat. Now they wander dispersed and homeless throughout the world, deprived of their own heaven and soil, without law, without king, without priest, and without offering. They are not even permitted, under the right of resident foreigners, to greet their native land with so much as a footprint.

They deservedly suffer such things, since through envy rather than anything else they crucified the Lord of glory. Therefore Christ truly rose again, but not alone. He did not wish [395] to display himself publicly, perhaps lest the impious be freed from their error; but, more credibly, so that faith, destined for no ordinary reward, might be established through difficulty. He spent forty days with the disciples, appointed witnesses, teaching them what they were to teach.

Then, when all had been completed, he ascended into heaven before his own disciples on the mountain, surrounded by a cloud. Just as we await him as he ascended, so we await him as he will come, on the testimony of angels.

For two advents have been foretold: the first, which has already been completed, in the humility of human condition; the second, which threatens at the close of the age, in the majesty of divine power. When the time of this age has run its course, he will come to judge the righteous for eternal life, and the impious and sinners—who have stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath—for eternal punishment. All who have died from the beginning will be raised, restored, and summoned to judgment according to the fulfillment of each person’s merit.

**IV.** Lest my many sins, which are now hidden, appear before the angels and all the saints, give me, Lord, I ask, a place, a period, and the fruits of worthy repentance. Give me a contrite and humbled heart; give me the grace of tears; give light to my heart; give strength to my body, so that I may see what must be done and, for carrying out what you grant me to see, may grow strong in courage.

Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy, lest you destroy me, I beg you, together with my sins, vices, faults, and negligences. For your name’s sake, you who justify the ungodly and give life to the dead, and who make many sinners no longer sinners, give me your grace and amend my life. Improve my actions; order my habits. Take away from me what displeases you and harms me, and grant, according to your goodness, what you know can please you and benefit me.

Make me, I pray, through your grace, merciful, you to whom all things are possible and nothing is difficult, so that I may be able to please you truly before your eyes. I do not shrink from your kindly medicine, for I am very sick. In whatever order pleases you, heal my many illnesses and refine the dross of my sins to purity, before I depart, in whatever ways seem good to you.

But I have asked for your mercy, Lord, and I do not cease asking, because I desire this exceedingly. Soften my hard and stony heart with your wondrous and powerful anointing. Soften it, I pray, and by the fire of remorse make me daily become a living sacrifice before you.

Look upon me, Lord, and have mercy on me. Grant me the fulfillment of my petition and desire. Give abundant water to my head, and pour into my eyes a true fountain of tears, continually flowing, so that I may weep unceasingly, day and night, over the wounds of my soul, until the acceptable time, until the days of salvation, until there is still opportunity to mourn the evils I have done and continue to do daily.

May I, through the labors of repentance, enjoy eternal life with the good, and, at the last, at least with that venerable thief who, by a single word, became an heir of paradise at the very moment of death, because of your great mercy and goodness.

**V.** Hear, gracious Lord, hear the prayers of your servant. Remember your mercies, by which the human race has wondrously been helped through your goodness. How could you not love us, good Shepherd, who did not spare your own Son but handed him over for us ungodly people?

He was obedient to you even unto the death of the cross, that one free among the dead, having authority to lay down his life and to take it up again. For us he was victor and victim before you—and therefore victor because victim. For us he was priest and sacrifice before you—and therefore priest because sacrifice.

I rightly have a strong hope in him, that he will heal all my illnesses through the one who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us. I certainly could have despaired unless your Word had become flesh and dwelt among us. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to you through the death of your Son, how much more shall we now be saved from wrath through him?

I give you thanks, most merciful Father, for the holy incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son. With all my inmost being I bless your name for that most sacred shedding of blood by which we have been redeemed, imploring your ineffable goodness not to permit us to be ungrateful for such benefits or unworthy of so many mercies.

For we are no insignificant part of your work, whom you were pleased to redeem for yourself at so great a price. Who could, with due wonder, penetrate the immeasurable ocean of that supreme plan by which that man, the Lord’s man, was united with God and assumed into God—not by a confusion of substance but by a unity of person?

For Christ Jesus, mediator of God and human beings, our Lord, almighty God, is by no means one in his humanity and another in his divinity, but in both natures he is one and the same God-man, man-God.

Therefore he was neither conceived as a mere man nor afterward received divinity in order to become God. Rather, your Son himself, while his unchangeable essence—which is coeternal with you and with the Holy Spirit—remained unchanged, assumed flesh for our salvation, in which he could be shown to be eternal before the ages.

Thus, although one thing is from you and another from his mother, he is not one and another, so that—God forbid—two Sons should be spoken of. Rather, he himself is eternal from you, God the Father; he himself is temporal from his virgin mother. He himself is the one who made, and he himself is the one who was made, remaining from both and in both natures one: neither confused by the union of the natures nor divided into two by the distinction of the natures.

**VI.** Who is sufficient to contemplate, with the very gaze of the mind, the wondrous work of such mercy? Who would not marvel? Who would not revere it? What voice or tongue could render the praises that are owed?

O easy and immeasurable compassion! O kindness of divine reconciliation, ever marvelous and always to be marveled at! I marvel and am astonished, yet I rejoice and give many thanks.

We were children of wrath and destruction, and behold, we have been adopted as children of God. “Heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ,” says the Apostle (Rom. 8:7). Christ is the head of the Church, and the Church is Christ’s body; therefore we are Christ’s members. Whence has this come to us, and what are we that we should receive such things? Happy the soul that, surrounded in all things by divine assistance, has deserved to obtain the dignity of so great a glory through the uprightness of its life and conduct.

Ineffable God, of uncircumscribed nature, creator of all things, and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: you sent that same beloved Son from your bosom into the public arena of our life, to assume our life so that he might give us his, and so that he might be perfect God from you the Father and perfect man from his mother: wholly God and wholly man [396], one and the same Christ, eternal and temporal, immortal and destined to die, Creator and created, strong and weak, nourisher and nourished, shepherd and sheep, temporally dead yet living eternally with you.

He promised and gave the citizenship of life to those who love him, and said to us: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 15:16).

**VII.** Therefore I beseech you, Lord, and earnestly entreat you, most gracious, in the name of that same beloved Son of yours, to grant me to bless and glorify you in all things together with your Son. For those whose substance is one also have one gift.

Grant me also through him and with him the forgiveness of all sins and the keeping of your commandments, love of you and brotherly love; strong weapons of humility against the devil and perfect charity toward the brethren; moderation in food, drink, and sleep, and restraint from every lust and vain desire; chaste hearing and a simple gaze; purity of heart and cleanliness of body; a clean thought and watchfulness over mouth and heart, so that my heart may neither conceive wickedness within nor my tongue give birth to it outwardly; so that I may neither speak falsehood nor be silent about truth, neither hide what brings salvation nor utter what brings death.

I also pray that you grant me constancy in prayer, strength for fasting, and frequent reading, so that I may read your commands tirelessly, love them insatiably, fulfill them effectively, and correct by your grace whatever I discover to be corrupt in myself; so that I may hold fast what is straight, set in order what is deformed, cultivate what is beautiful, preserve what is sound, strengthen what is weak, and perseveringly guard everything that pleases you.

Grant me moreover to despise temporal things and to love eternal things with all my strength, so that I may reckon the world dead to me, neither rejoicing nor mourning over temporal matters; so that I may neither fear anything temporal nor love it. Let me not be corrupted by flatteries or shaken by adversities.

I ask your clemency, holy Father, in the name of your own Son: circumcise from me every vice of heart and body, and grant me increase and perfection of the virtues. Enlighten my understanding and my soul, so that I may ask of you what delights you to hear. Teach me what I ought to think, do, say, and keep silent about.

Give me prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Give me discernment in all things, to distinguish between the right and the left. Give me also an alert sense and provident understanding, so that I may distinguish between good and evil.

Take from my heart the sense of estrangement; heal in me the dullness of mind; uproot from my entrails counsels of wickedness; eradicate from my tongue the habit of slander, the readiness to lie, the vulgarity of speech, and all the acts of my vanity. Heal them by the art of your medicine.

**VIII.** Grant me continual progress in purified conduct. Hold me by the strength of your omnipotence, and do not permit me to wander according to the will of my own free choice. In accordance with your providence, order my entire life according to your will.

Do not permit this sinful soul, for which Christ died, to perish. Put your bridle in my jaws, and, like a tamed animal, draw me after you. For you know everything that is advantageous for me.

Let neither the devil, nor I, nor the world, nor anyone else be permitted to overturn your gifts, since everything that attempts to oppose you is utterly fragile. You have shown me great mercy from my childhood. Complete what you began.

Always and everywhere grant me, against the most savage enemy, the gracious aid of your protection, so that, just as he does not cease unwillingly to attack my frailty, he may likewise be compelled, confounded by your strength, to depart.

Grant that I may be little in my own eyes, so that I may find grace before you. Grant and ever increase in me firm faith, unshaken hope, perfect charity, profound humility, unconquerable patience, and perpetual chastity of body and soul.

Give contrition of heart and a fountain of tears. Give simplicity, innocence, and purity of heart; stability, constancy, and integrity of mind. Give unconquerable strength, so that I may be victorious over myself in all things.

Let reason rule the flesh, and your grace rule reason, so that I may not live like a beast, carried away by the impulse of the flesh, but that my conduct may be honorable and rational. Make me provident in everything and discerning in all things.

Grant me not to provide anyone an occasion for scandal, to love simplicity and truth, and earnestly to pursue the things that belong to peace and charity. Keep every hypocrisy and every pretense far from me, and make me serve you in truth.

**IX.** Grant me, I ask, with a good spirit, for your sake, to submit to the authority of my superiors and with a cheerful heart to hasten without delay to obedience, compassion, and concord.

Stir up my sluggishness with your goads, and make me persevere vigorously in your commandments and praises, night and day. Give me humble knowledge that builds up, and an educated and eloquent tongue, so that I may be able both to exhort the good to better things and to recall the wicked to the line of your righteousness.

Pour into my heart, I ask, through your Son, and grant me with him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety. Fill me with holy fear and love of you.

Give upper and lower irrigation. Grant me blessing from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth. Grant that my soul may burn with the fire of your love. Make me utterly extinguished to the world.

Grant me to possess before you a contrite and humbled heart. By your grace make me weep over all my sins before I die. Grant me to seek your face always with my whole soul and all my strength.

Pour your love into my breast, and write the sweet memory of you upon the tablets of my heart. Enlighten me with the light of heavenly prudence. Do not allow your image in me to be obscured; if it is defended by your aid, it is always noble.

May the gracious and faithful protection of the blessed angels be with me everywhere and always, I ask. Grant that, before you, the hosts of all the saints may intercede for me, wretched as I am, so that through their prayers and merits, by your mercy, I may be made worthy of the promises of your Son.

Grant me, most frail as I am, to imitate the footsteps of my blessed monastic fathers. Give me their gentleness, modesty, endurance, kindness, poverty, and long-suffering; contrition of heart and a fountain of tears; abstinence from food and drink; purity of heart and lips; spiritual joy; and perfect contempt for the world.

[397] Above all, Lord, I earnestly beg from you charity; I seek humility; I request patience, inseparable companions of my faith; and likewise true chastity of soul and body, as you gave these to them.

**X.** I pray you through your Son: look upon me and have mercy on me. Hear my prayer and grant me your grace because of the abundance of your goodness, which, continually remaining with me, may teach me to walk before you according to your will all the days of my life.

I ask for this; grant it to me: may it make me peaceful with my friends and tranquil with my enemies; may it restrain me from harsh speech and curb me from idle talk; may it compel me always to think of God or of the things that belong to God, and turn my eyes away from this vain world; may it place death before my eyes at every hour and forbid me to rejoice here; may it make me consider and mourn the beam and burden of my sins, and not allow me to scrutinize the offenses of others as though they were the lightest speck.

Finally, may it teach me and make me able to regard all the things of the world as nothing and to thirst for you alone, our God, with all my inmost being, even to the end. And just as by your most merciful compassion you gave me the will to come to you through it, so may you deign to grant wisdom and understanding, strength and ability of body and soul, to serve you always with the utmost devotion in all things, through that same gracious and instructive grace of yours, without which we are able neither to think nor to speak nor to do anything good.

And because your Only-Begotten himself said, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44), and, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6), I beseech you, holy Father, and humbly entreat you, my God: draw me to him, and may he himself lead me to you, there where he sits at your right hand; where there is everlasting life, eternally blessed and eternal security, secure tranquility, happy eternity, eternal happiness; where there is perfect love and no fear; where there is an everlasting day and one Spirit of all; where you, together with him, and he with you, live and reign eternally and forever in communion with the Holy Spirit, O God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

**PART III. AGAIN, ON THE TRIUNE AND ONE GOD, ON CHRIST, AND ON MANY OTHER ECCLESIASTICAL DOCTRINES**

[Col. 1053]

[Col. 1053D] **I.** With my heart I believe for justification, and with my mouth I confess for salvation, the holy and undivided Trinity, one power and undivided majesty: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one almighty God, maker of heaven and earth, creator of visible and invisible things, three in persons and one in substance.

The true Father is the source of supreme goodness and of the whole Godhead, God of uncircumscribed and unbegotten majesty, deriving his beginning from no one but giving beginning to all things, the highest good and creator of all things very good, begetting the Son not by bodily generation, nor from outside himself, nor by necessity or will, but by nature.

The true Son, ineffably born from the Father without beginning, [Col. 1054D] “true God, the Only-Begotten, and true Word of God, not made, not created, not adopted, but begotten and of one substance with the Father. And thus in all things equal to God the Father that he can be inferior neither in time, rank, nor power. We confess him who was begotten to be as great as he who begot him. Yet, when we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not assign any time to that divine and ineffable generation. Nor do we say that the Father ever began, or the Son. For we cannot otherwise confess the eternal Father unless we also confess the coeternal Son. The Father is called Father because of the Son, and he who is always Father has always had a Son.”

[Note: [Col. 1053D] Pelagius. See the Appendix to the works of St. Augustine.]

The true Holy Spirit also, true God, not made, not created, neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding ineffably from the Father and the Son together, and substantially abiding in the Father and the Son. Thus he is in all things equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with God the Father and the Son, so that he cannot differ from them, or precede them, in will, power, substance, or eternity—those from whom he proceeds.

The Father is eternal without birth; the Son is eternal with birth; and the Holy Spirit is eternal with procession, without birth. The whole Father abides in the Son and the Holy Spirit; the whole Son in the Father and the Holy Spirit; the whole Holy Spirit in the Father and the Son: namely, the holy and undivided Trinity, one almighty God, reigning from then and always and everywhere with one power, one kingdom, one majesty, and one eternity.

**II.** [Note: [Col. 1055D] Pelagius.] “Therefore there is no rank in this Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher. Rather, we say that the whole Godhead is equal in its perfection, so that, except for the names that indicate the distinct properties of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most properly be understood of all three.

“Accordingly, while condemning Arius, we say that the substance of the Trinity is one and the same, and we confess one God in three persons. At the same time, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons clearly according to their properties. We do not say that the Father is himself the Son, that the Son is himself the Father, or that the Holy Spirit is himself either; rather, the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

“For we confess not merely names but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons, which the Greeks call ὑποστάσεις (*hypostaseis*), that is, substances or subsistences. Nor does the Father ever exclude the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. Nor, conversely, has the Son or the Holy Spirit taken upon himself the name and person of the Father. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit.”

Therefore the Son most certainly is not the same person as the Father, although according to divinity he is the same as the Father. For we do not say that the Father [398] is from the Son as the Son is from the Father. The Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father. Therefore the Son is called God from God, light from light—not two lights or two gods, but one God and one light.

Again, the Father is the same as the Son, but not the same [F. lacking: “who is the Son”], because the person of the Father is most fittingly referred to the Son. The Holy Spirit, without doubt, is the same as the Father and the Son, but not the same [F. lacking: “who is the Father and the Son”]. For just as the Father is the Father of the Son and the Son is the Son of the Father, so also the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the holy Trinity, is the Spirit of none other than the Father and the Son.

Consequently, the Father and the Son are one, because whatever the Father has, the Son unquestionably has as well. For a single substantial reality could not proceed from two persons and exist in both at the same time unless the Father and the Son were one, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds equally.

**III.** Indeed, the Holy Spirit is truly the unity, holiness, and love of the Father and the Son, because what is said of him alone relatively, these two are naturally together. For it is written, “The Spirit is God” (John 14:24). From this it is plainly evident that the Holy Trinity, which is one true God, is naturally and according to essence Spirit.

Therefore God the Father is Spirit and is holy; God the Son is Spirit and is holy; and the Holy Spirit is no more Spirit than are the Father and the Son. Each of these individually is Spirit, and all together are one Spirit, just as they are one God.

Concerning the Father, because he is God, the Apostle proves it by saying: “One God and Father of all, from whom are all things” (Eph. 4:6; 1 Cor. 8:6). Concerning the Son, because he is God, the chief of the Evangelists bears witness, saying: “And the Word was God” (John 1:1). Concerning the Holy Spirit, because he is God, Paul again speaks, proving it in this way: “There are varieties of operations, but it is the same God” (1 Cor. 12:6).

Behold: the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. Yet one must not believe that there is a threefold number of deities in the holy Trinity, so that any believer would dare to say that there are three gods, just as God himself testifies of himself in a certain passage, saying: “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. 32:39).

For when something is repeated three times, a number is not accumulated; rather, the fact that it is one is expressly asserted. Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in substance, but are distinguished in persons and names.

The nature of the highest divinity is altogether immovable and unchangeable. The persons, however, are mutable according to relation, though not according to their properties. Thus, in the relation of the persons there is Trinity; in the substance of the nature, unity. There is unity because of the inseparable essence of the Godhead, but Trinity because of the diversity of the persons, each of whom has a certain property that cannot be transferred from one to another.

There is the begetter, the begotten, and the proceeding one: three persons, but one substance, one power, and one omnipotence.

**IV.** Thus far I have confessed what I think and spoken what I believe concerning the highest divinity, in which I believe with my heart and confess with my mouth the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the triune and one God—not a body, nor placed in a body, nor compounded from diverse forms, nor fashioned from joints of limbs, but of one simple, incorporeal, invisible, and uncircumscribed nature.

[Note: [Col. 1056D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 14.]

“For nothing created or servile is to be believed to exist in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, wishes; nothing unequal, as Eunomius; nothing equal by grace, as Aetius; nothing earlier or later, or less, as Arius; nothing foreign or official to another, as Macedonius; nothing inserted by persuasion [variant: by intrusion], as Manichaeus; nothing bodily, as Melito and Tertullian; nothing given bodily form, as the Anthropomorphite says; nothing invisible to itself, as Origen; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus; nothing different in conduct and will, as Marcion; nothing brought down from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian; nothing singular in office or incommunicable to another, as Origen; nothing confused, as Sabellius. Rather, everything is perfect, because everything is from one and is one, though not solitary, as Silvanus and Praxeas presume. The Pentapolitan doctrine is condemnable.”

**V.** Thus far concerning the one Trinity. Concerning the grace by which we have been redeemed, I shall now begin to confess, according to the tradition of Mother Church, what I believe.

For to believe rightly and think truly concerning the mediator of God and human beings, the true and perfect man, Christ Jesus, the Lord, God, and our Savior, unquestionably pertains to eternal salvation.

Although, therefore, as believers we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one God—namely, the almighty, eternal, unbegotten Father; the Son, begotten from the substance or nature of that same Father before absolutely every beginning, whether of time or of anything else, almighty, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Begetter; and the Holy Spirit, likewise almighty, equal to both, namely the Father and the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with them—that is, three persons or subsistences of one essence or nature, one power, operation, blessedness, and authority, so that there is a triune Unity and one Trinity, according to the truth of the Lord’s words:

“Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:11).

He says “in the name,” not “in the names,” both to show one God through the undivided name of the divine substance and to teach the distinction of the persons demonstrated by their properties. For since there is one name of the Godhead for three persons, the equality of the persons is shown, and nothing foreign or accidental is permitted to be understood in them. Thus each one of them is true and perfect God, so that from the fullness of divinity nothing less is understood in each individual and nothing more in the three.

**VI.** Since the truth is thus constituted, and Mother Church believes, confesses, and teaches without any ambiguity:

[Note: [Col. 1057D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 1.]

“that there is one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the Father because he has a Son; the Son because he has a Father; and the Holy Spirit because he is from the Father and the Son.

“The Father is therefore the principle of the Godhead. Just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit proceeds, not being born because he is not the Son, nor unbegotten because he is not the Father, nor made [399] because he is not from nothing, but proceeding from God the Father and God the Son.

“The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father. [The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son.]

“The Trinity is not confused into one person, nor is the divinity separated or diverse in nature. Rather, the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person; yet in the holy Trinity the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in nature.”

[Note: [Col. 1057D] Gennadius, same work, chapter 2.]

“Since this is so, nevertheless neither did the Father assume flesh nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone. Thus the one who was God’s Son in divinity himself became the Son of man in humanity, lest the name ‘Son’ pass to another who was not by birth the Son of God.

“Therefore the Son of God became the son of man, born according to the truth of nature: from God, the Son of God, born according to the truth of nature; from man, the Son of man, so that the name ‘Son’ might belong to him by birth—not by adoption or appellation—in both births, and so that he might be true God and true man, one Son.

“For we confess not two Christs or two Sons, but one Son who is God and man. For this reason we also call him Only-Begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of his nature has conferred upon him—not with the natures confused or mixed, as certain heretics [Gennadius: as the Timothians] wish, but united by fellowship.”

### VII

God, then, assumed a human being, and the human being passed into God—not through changeability of nature [Gennadius adds: “as the Apollinarians say”], but through God’s condescension—so that neither was God changed into human substance by assuming a human being, nor was the human being changed into divine substance by being glorified in God [Gennadius: “into God”]. For a change or convertibility of nature produces confusion, diminution, and abolition of substance.

The Son of God was therefore born from a human being, not through a human being—that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Hebion says—but from a Virgin, drawing flesh from the Virgin’s body and not bringing it with him from heaven, as Marcion [Gennadius adds: “Origen”] and Eutyches assert. He was not born in appearance—that is, without flesh—as Valentinus claims, nor in a merely imaginary likeness, but with a true body. Nor was it a true body in such a way that it was nevertheless not flesh from flesh, as Marcianus says. Rather, one Son was true God from divinity and true human being from flesh: in divinity, the Father’s Word and God; in humanity, soul and flesh.

The soul was not without perception and reason, as Apollinaris teaches, nor the flesh without a soul, as the Anomoean [Gennadius: “Eunomius”] teaches; rather, there were both a soul with its reason and flesh with its senses. Through these true senses he endured the pains of his flesh in the Passion and before the Passion. [Note: [Col. 1058D] Gennadius, same work, chapter 3.]

Nor was he born from the Virgin in such a way that, by being born as a human being, he received the beginning of divinity—as though, before he was born from the Virgin, he had not been God—as certain heretics [Gennadius: “Artemon, Berillus, and Marcellus”] taught. Rather, the eternal God and the human being born from the Virgin were one. [Col. 1058D]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] Gennadius, same work, chapter 5.]

The Son is therefore *homoousios*—that is, coessential—with the Father in divinity; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son; and the Son is *homoousios* with God and the human being. God remains in his human being in the glory of the Father [he is seen and desired to be seen by the angels and is adored by every creature (Gennadius: “the one desired to be seen by the angels”; [Col. 1059A] “just as the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is adored by the angels and by every creature”)]. He is not a human being for God, or Christ with God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but the human being is in God, and God is in the human being.

### VIII

For without any doubt the blessed Mary, mother of this Lord Jesus Christ, both gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin after childbirth. Nor should we assent to the blasphemy of Helvidius, who says: “A virgin before childbirth, not a virgin after childbirth.” Rather, with complete faith we must believe that the integrity of so great a virginity always remained inviolate.

Remaining a virgin, she gave birth to him just as she conceived him as a virgin. It was fitting—indeed, exceedingly fitting—that this one woman alone should be virgin before childbirth, virgin in childbirth, and virgin after childbirth: she who bore the incarnate Word of God, that is, true God and true human being. For this reason we confess that this same blessed Virgin is *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), that is, “Mother of God.”

From her was born one and the same Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and that same true Son of man. He is consubstantial and equal with the Father according to divinity, but in that respect inferior to the Father in which he is consubstantial with us, because in every respect he is like us except for sin.

Although, therefore, neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was born from the Virgin, but the Son alone, nevertheless the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together brought about this birth of the Son from the Virgin, as well as his Passion, resurrection, and all the other things pertaining to his humanity.

### IX

Let us therefore see whether perhaps in creation we can find something in which we may prove that certain three things are demonstrated separately and operate inseparably. For “his invisible attributes are perceived by the understanding from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (Rom. I, 20).

Although the lowest things are far removed from the highest, changeable things from the immutable, created things from the Creator, and human things from divine things, nevertheless even in creation itself, which is lowly and changeable, there are certain things that can both be demonstrated separately and operate inseparably, such as memory, understanding, and will.

By memory we retain what we hear; by understanding we recognize what we hold; by will we bring forth what we recognize. Although these three are named separately, nevertheless the name of one of them is produced by all three.

One cannot speak of memory alone unless will, understanding, and memory are operating. One cannot speak of understanding alone unless memory, will, and understanding are operating. One cannot speak of will alone unless memory, understanding, and will are operating.

Three have produced one of these names, but that one thing which the three have produced does not pertain to the three; it pertains to one. Three have produced the name “memory,” but this pertains only to memory itself. Three have produced the name “understanding,” but it pertains only to understanding itself. Three have produced the name “will,” but it pertains only to will itself.

Thus the Trinity made Christ’s flesh, but it pertains only to Christ. Three made the dove from heaven, but it pertains only to the Holy Spirit. Three made the voice from heaven, but that voice pertains only to the Father.

If, therefore, we find in ourselves three things demonstrated separately and operating inseparably, and if each of the three names is made by three while nevertheless pertaining not to the three but to one of them, let us believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can, through certain visible signs and through certain forms of assumed creation, be demonstrated separately and operate inseparably.

In ourselves we can know what exists; but in God, who made us, how can we know what he is—whatever he is? Even if we shall be able to know, we cannot yet do so; and when we shall be able, shall we be able to know God in the way God knows himself? Let us already believe there what we cannot see and cannot here fully comprehend.

The sun, although it is one, has heat and brightness; by heat it dries, and by brightness it illuminates. If in created things these and many other examples are found from which divine realities may, in some measure and with greater discernment, be perceived, it is foolish to doubt the Creator, since he was able to make such creatures.

### X

Created things are also found to be coeval, and they are found to be equal, but not both simultaneously. In God both are simultaneous.

There is one God and Father of all: the primary name of divinity, believed in itself, and called “Father”—God without beginning and without time. From himself he begot the Son, and from his own power brought forth the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the Son is from the Father, not from himself, but is the Father’s Son. The Father is God and the Son is God, but the Father is not the same person as the Son, although he is the same as the Son in nature.

The Holy Spirit is not unbegotten like the Father, but is the Spirit of the Father who is unbegotten. The begotten Son is not the Spirit’s Son; he is the Son himself, upon whom the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father.

Since the Father is unbegotten, and the Spirit belongs to him, some carelessly call the Holy Spirit unbegotten. The Holy Spirit is God from the Father and the Son, not from himself, lest believers should suppose there are two unbegotten beings or two Fathers.

The Son of the Father, begotten without beginning from the Father, cannot have another begotten companion, so that he may be believed to be the only-begotten and there may not be said to be two begotten beings.

For there is one unbegotten Father, one begotten Son, and one Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, coeternal with both. He is one Spirit. For there is one work, and the operation of the will is united in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding. The one is born, the other proceeds, as it is read in the Gospel of blessed John: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, he will announce all things to you” (John XV, 26; XIV, 26).

Therefore the Holy Spirit should not be considered unbegotten as the Father is, nor begotten as the Son is. For he received from the Son. No one receives from himself except the Father. Through the Son the Spirit who proceeds from the Father is sent.

For he who proceeds is another, but what proceeds is not other than that from which it proceeds. If the person is asked about, he is God, because whatever is in God or from God is also God. Thus the true confession of faith excludes union in the persons, while in the distinction of the persons it maintains unity.

### XI

The Father, God from himself, therefore ineffably and without beginning begot the Son, as has already been said in many ways, and brought forth the Holy Spirit from his own power: the Son, through whom he would create all things; the Spirit, through whom he would give life to all.

The Son, begotten from the Father, created all things that were made. The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, gave life to all things that were created.

Yet the Son also gives life, and the Holy Spirit also creates, because just as we believe that the most blessed Trinity is one in divinity, one in power, and one in substance, so also it is one in operation. No diversity should be perceived between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, except that the one is Father, the other Son, and the other Holy Spirit.

The Trinity is in the subsisting persons, but unity is in the nature. Therefore there is one God, whom we divide in the holy Trinity in the same way that we say that one human being possesses intelligence, memory, and understanding.

By intelligence we discover what we have learned; by memory we retain what we are taught; by understanding we attend to whatever we happen to see or hear.

What shall we do now? Does one wisdom in a human being not possess these three things? If, then, a human being possesses a threefold name in one wisdom, how does almighty God not possess the majesty of the Trinity in his one divinity?

If the transitory word of our mouth, when we speak, reaches everyone in its entirety and reaches each person in its entirety—if everyone possesses it, and possesses it wholly; if it proceeds to each of the hearers without departing from the speaker; if the others possess it while the speaker loses nothing; if the speaker is a creature and the hearers are creatures, and so great a marvel is produced from a human word in heart, mouth, and voice, in ears and perception—who is so foolish that, when he hears that God is everywhere and wholly everywhere, he would prefer to deny it?

### XII

In this life faith is of the greatest importance for such mysteries. For, as it is written, “The righteous person lives by faith,” and “faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Hebr. X, 28). In things that are seen, however, faith should not be called faith but knowledge.

As eternity relates to what has come into being, so truth relates to faith. Those two are above: eternity and truth. These two are below: what has come into being and faith. Therefore, in order that we may be recalled from the lowest things to the highest, and that what has come into being may receive eternity, we must come to truth through faith.

To teach us to advance through faith toward vision, the mediator of God and human beings came, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. He himself is the Wisdom of God, through whom all things were created.

Since no rational minds, whether of angels or human beings, become wise except by participation in him—and since we cling to him through the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts—this Trinity, which is one God, in divine providence provided for mortals, whose temporal life was occupied with things that arise and pass away.

The very Wisdom of God therefore assumed a human being into the unity of his person, in whom he would be born, live, die, and rise again in time. By words and deeds appropriate to our salvation, by suffering and endurance, he became below an example to human beings of returning, while above he is an example to angels of remaining.

Thus, while the truth of those who contemplate enjoys eternal things, and faith is owed to those who believe in things that have arisen, the human being is purified through faith in temporal things so that he may receive the truth of eternal things.

### XIII

For teaching these things, who else is so suitable? Our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and Wisdom of God, was born from the Father before the ages—indeed, he has always been born, because he neither began to be born nor ceases to be born.

Yet we cannot say that he is “always being born,” lest he appear imperfect. But so that he may be designated eternal and perfect, let us say both “always” and “born”: “born,” so that it pertains to perfection, and “always,” so that it pertains to eternity. In this way, an essence without time may somehow be designated in temporal speech.

Even in calling him “perfect” we fall far short of expressing that truth, because what has not been made cannot be called perfect. Yet the Lord, accommodating himself to the weakness of our language, says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V, 48).

In that divine birth he could not be known by the human race; therefore he came in humility so that he might be seen. He wished to be seen so that he might be imitated.

This birth in the flesh appeared contemptible to the wise of the world. They despised the weakness of his humanity, judging such things unworthy of God. Yet by this very fact the human being became all the more indebted to him, the more God accepted what was unworthy for the human being’s sake.

“Because the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (I Cor. I, 21). It is as though he said: since the world could not discover God, who is wisdom, through its own wisdom, it pleased God that the world should recognize God made human through the foolishness of humanity, so that his wisdom might descend to our foolish things and our blindness might see the light of heavenly prudence, illuminated by the mud of his flesh.

Born from the Father without time, he deigned to be born from his mother in time, so that, by enclosing his origin between a beginning and an end, he might reveal to the eyes of the human mind an origin that has neither beginning nor end.

His divine origin has neither a before nor an after. Since it always exists through eternity and encompasses everything that passes away, it encloses the course of time within itself. His human origin, however, because it both began and ended, received from time a before and an after.

### XIV

[Note: [Col. 1061D] Pelagius.]

“Therefore, at the end of the ages, he assumed from Mary, ever-virgin, a complete human being of our nature, and the Word became flesh by assuming a human being, not by changing his divinity,” when the Holy Spirit came upon the blessed Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her.

“We do not say, as certain most wicked people suppose, that the Holy Spirit served as seed, but that he acted through the power and might of the Creator.”

It is written: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX, 1), that is, it created flesh in the Virgin’s womb, animated by a rational soul.

Accordingly, it is rightly asked: since the works of the entire Trinity are inseparable, why is the creation of the flesh said to have been performed by the Holy Spirit alone? Because sanctification occurs through the Spirit, and the same Spirit is God in such a way that he is also the gift of God, the Holy Spirit is therefore said to have created Christ’s flesh in the Virgin’s womb.

We should understand that it was created through the sanctification of divine grace by the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that it was both a divine work and was assumed into the unity of the person of the only-begotten Son of God without any stain of original sin. Sanctified from the very conception and substantially united to the Word of God, it could thereafter receive no sin.

It was sanctified, and became divine flesh, to such an extent that not only could he himself have no sin, but he could also most effectively cleanse sins in others. Other human beings are sanctified so that they may be free from sins. That lordly human being, however, was sanctified so that, receiving no sin in himself in any way, he might justify sinners by the power of his divinity.

He was born from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary. Yet he was not born from the Holy Spirit as though he had the Spirit as his father; from the Virgin Mary he was born in such a way that he had her as his mother.

According to his humanity he was born from the Holy Spirit in such a way that he did not receive substance from the Holy Spirit. But, born from his mother, he received the substance of flesh from her substance—that is, he drew his own body from the Virgin’s body—so that, just as in divinity he was consubstantial with the Father, in humanity he might become consubstantial with his Mother, and the incomprehensible and invisible one might have that in which he could be seen and comprehended.

### XV

[Note: [Col. 1063D] Pelagius. These statements seem to some to be partly directed against the Nestorians and partly against the Eutychians, and therefore to have been added to his Confession after Pelagius. [Col. 1064D]]

“For this reason we confess that in Christ there is one person of the Son, while we say that there are two perfect and integral substances, namely, divinity and humanity, which consists of soul and body.

“Just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses only a solitary and bare human being in Christ, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less from human nature, or that the human being assumed in flesh, soul, or perception was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. Apart from the sole stain of sin, which is not natural, we confess that he was like us.

“Likewise, the blasphemy of those who attempt, with a novel meaning, to assert that from the time when he assumed flesh everything belonging to divinity migrated into the human being, and again that everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God, is to be abhorred. Through this confusion, both substances—divinity and humanity—would appear to have been emptied and changed from their proper state into something else, so that those who confess both an imperfect God in the Son and an imperfect human being would be judged to possess neither true God nor true human being.

“We, however, say that the Son of God assumed our passible nature in such a way that the impassible nature of God nevertheless remained. The Son of God suffered, not figuratively but truly, all that Scripture attests: hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind.

“He suffered according to that which could suffer—that is, not according to the substance that assumed, but according to the substance that was assumed. For the Son of God himself, according to his divinity, was impassible like the Father, invisible like the Father, and unchangeable like the Father.

“Although the Son’s own person, that is, the Word of God, assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, by his indwelling, the divinity of the Word according to its substance suffered nothing, so that the entire Trinity must be confessed to be impassible.

“The Son of God died according to the Scriptures, in accordance with that which could die. He rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, while the nature of the flesh in which he was born and suffered remained—the same flesh in which he also rose.

“For the substance of humanity was not emptied in him but glorified, and it will remain eternally with divinity.”

### XVI

“Having therefore received from the Father all power over the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, rewarding the righteous and punishing sinners.” [Col. 1064B]

The mysteries of his incarnation, cross, death, burial, resurrection, and ascension into heaven are so inexplicable that they cannot be adequately explained by the praises of any tongue—or even by the understanding of anyone.

In contemplating the cross, it is enough for us to consider this: the Lord chose suspension on wood above all other forms of death in order, through it, to abolish the first transgression involving wood. Just as in Adam there was a fall through the delight of the fruit, so in Christ there might be an erection through the harshness of the wood.

Many useful things pertaining to edification are also said about the construction of that same cross. The Apostle’s words—“rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. III, 17–18)—fit the construction of the cross wonderfully and truly.

The breadth of the cross is the transverse wood, where the hands are fastened. Through it joy and gladness of mind are signified, just as working is signified through the hands.

The length is the straight wood on which the whole body is extended. Through it patience and endurance are understood, by which we persevere in good works to the end.

The height is what rises above the transverse wood, to which the head is attached. Through it is signified the expectation of reward from the lofty justice of God, who will repay each person according to his works.

The depth is the part of the wood fixed into the earth. It prefigures the secret of the mystery and pertains to hidden grace, through which we act invisibly.

Therefore, when someone takes up Christ’s cross in order to follow him, let him hold fast to the breadth of love and the length of perseverance. Let him also possess the height, so that he may refer what he does to God and do it for God, patiently and cheerfully awaiting what God has promised those who love him.

Let him also hold fast to the depth, so that he may know that everything he rightly does, God does through him and in him by hidden grace.

Many other teachers understood this from the Apostle’s words, but Father Ambrose wished to understand something more excellent, saying of God that he surrounds his works externally, fills them internally, covers them above, and bears them below.

The position of the cross signifies the universality of Christ’s power: its head holds heaven, its feet the underworld, and its right and left sides the whole world.

If, however, one holds it not upright but flat and balanced evenly, it seems to display the four regions of the world, because Christ governs all things: as though those for whom the world has been crucified, and who have been crucified to the world, might be chosen and called by God from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea, and all might be saved through the cross.

### XVII

Christ was therefore born from a Virgin so that we might be reborn from the womb of the virgin Church.

He was circumcised so that we might be circumcised from the vices of flesh and spirit, in the stripping away of the old human being.

He was presented in the temple so that through it we might be reconciled to God.

He was baptized so that our sins might be washed away.

He was tempted so that he might free us from the devil’s temptation.

He was seized so that we might be released from subjection to demonic slavery.

He was sold so that he might redeem us with his blood.

He was bound so that he might release us from the knot of the curse.

He was mocked so that he might remove us from the mockery of demons.

He was humbled so that he might exalt us.

He was lifted up on the cross so that he might draw us to himself.

He was captured so that he might carry us away as captives from the hand of the devil.

He was stripped so that he might clothe the nakedness of our mortality with blessed immortality.

He was crowned with thorns so that he might pull out from us the thorns and thistles of the first curse.

He was given gall and vinegar to drink so that he might cause us to enter a land flowing with milk and honey.

Finally, he was sacrificed on the altar of the cross so that he might erase the sins of the whole world.

He died so that he might take captive the dominion of death.

He was buried so that he might bless the tombs of the saints.

He rose so that he might restore life to the dead and give his own people the hope of resurrection.

He ascended into heaven so that he might restore to humanity not only the paradise it had lost but also open the gate of heaven.

He now sits at the right hand of the Father so that he may grant the prayers of believers.

He will come to judge the living and the dead, repaying the good with good and the wicked with punishment without end.

Thus the devil’s stratagem failed. He set a calf against a calf and a goat against a goat, but he could not find an immaculate lamb. Therefore the wretched one lies defeated, and at the sight of the sign of Christ’s victory he grows pale, trembles, and flees.

### XVIII

But let no one say within himself, as though complaining against God: “Because our first parents sinned and, admitting the guilt of disobedience, fell into death, what guilt should have been assigned to all the rest, so that all alike should be held under the power of the devil because of one person’s sin? He alone should have suffered and felt the deserved anger of his presumption.”

Or: “Why was it necessary for God to become human? Could he not have saved us in another way?”

Certainly, as God and as almighty, he could have redeemed us without assuming a human being. But he did not wish to, because it was fitting to divine justice that he should recover the deceived and lost, wretched human beings not by strength and omnipotence, but by counsel and wisdom.

Children born from a male slave and a female slave can be nothing other than what their parents are. It has been decreed by both divine and human law that those born from slaves remain in slavery.

Therefore infants are held under original sin from the moment they are born, unless they are freed by the grace of baptism.

This is the reason why the devil, tripping us up in that root of our first parent, held the human being under his captivity as though justly: the human being had been created with free will, yet had consented to the devil’s unjust persuasion.

Created for life and for the freedom of his own will, he voluntarily made himself liable to death.

Such guilt therefore had to be destroyed, but it could not be destroyed except through sacrifice. A sacrifice had to be sought; but what kind of sacrifice could be found for the acquittal of human beings?

It was not just that victims of brute animals should be slaughtered for a rational human being. Thus the Apostle says: “It is necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be purified by these things, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these” (Hebr. IX, 23).

Therefore, if brute animals were not worthy victims for a rational creature—that is, for a human being—a human being had to be sought who could be offered for human beings, so that a rational victim might be slaughtered for a rational sinner.

### XIX

But what of the fact that a human being without sin could not be found? When would a victim offered for us be able to cleanse us from sin if it were not free from the contagion of sin itself? An unclean victim could not cleanse the unclean.

Therefore, to be a rational victim, a human being had to be offered; but to cleanse human beings from sins, that human being had to be without sin.

Yet who would be a human being without sin if he descended from the commixture of sin?

Accordingly, for our sake the Son of God came into the Virgin’s womb; there he became human for us. He assumed a nature, not guilt. He made his body a sacrifice for us and presented for sinners a victim without sin, one able both to die in humanity and to cleanse through righteousness.

When the ancient enemy saw him after his baptism, he immediately attacked him with temptations. Attempting to creep into his interior by various approaches, he was defeated and struck down by the very unconquerable integrity of Christ’s mind.

Since he could not prevail against his interior, he turned to his exterior, so that, having been defeated by the strength of his mind, he might at least seem to overcome by the death of his flesh the one whom he had been unable to deceive through temptation.

He was permitted to act against that which the mediator had received from us mortals. But where he was able to do something, there he was defeated in every respect. From the very fact that he received external power to kill the Lord’s flesh, his interior power—the power by which he held us—was killed.

He was defeated within precisely when he seemed to prevail externally. He who had held us as debtors by right of death lost the right of death over us, because through his agents he sought to destroy the flesh of one in whom he found nothing belonging to the debt of guilt.

Our Lord therefore paid for us a death that was not owed, so that the death owed to us might not harm us.

Although, with respect to the simple nature of divinity, being and the wisdom that is the essence of divinity are not different, nevertheless, as far as the outward appearance is concerned, he conquered the devil not by force but by reason.

The ancient enemy, through the excess of his presumption, lost even the one whom he had possessed under the law of an evil persuasion. By boldly attacking one in whom he had found nothing belonging to himself, he justly lost the one whom he had held as though justly.

He was therefore defeated by prudence and counsel, not by power and violence. When he was released to tempt him, he was excluded from possessing the human being, so that he might lose the one who was subject to him precisely where he had dared to engage the one who is above him.

It is therefore established that the sinful human being was freed through the human being who is God, in whom there could be no stain of sin. Thus almighty God, who is just and whose judgments are all just, did nothing against his own justice when he freed the deceived human being from the devil’s power through a human being.

The order of our salvation therefore required that one stratagem should outwit another, and that the deceiver should himself be deceived.

### XX

With these matters set forth beforehand, as though certain witnesses presented in support of my confession of faith, just as I cry out with a great cry before God with my whole heart, so, through the service of pen and mouth, I desire to say and proclaim in the ears of the Church:

“Before God we believe thus; before human beings we confess thus. For ‘with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’” (Rom. X, 10), as the Apostle says.

I believe that God exists; I believe God; I believe in God. I hold this in my heart, confess it with my mouth, and attest and confirm it in writing.

I believe that God exists because I see creation and understand the Creator. “He himself made us, and not we ourselves.”

I believe God because I have absolutely no doubt about the testimony of sacred Scripture, which he himself sanctified and sent into the world. I do not distrust any of his holy promises, which are held in hope. Nor do I disdain his sacred mysteries, which are hidden from me, as though I were contemptuous; rather, I venerate them devoutly, humbly awaiting their partial revelation even here, or their full revelation in the future.

I believe in God—as a creature in the Creator, a servant in the Lord, and a human being in God—because he alone is to be worshiped and adored: he who is God by nature and almighty, who made what was unformed and governs what has been made.

For it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV, 10). And the angel said to John: “See that you do not do this; worship God” (Rev. XIX, 10).

This worship, service, and honor are owed neither to blessed spirits nor to holy human beings, but only to the one Lord God.

How I believe that God is from God has been sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated in the preceding words. Now I desire to state with Catholic mouth how I believe in God.

It is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13).

I believe in almighty God, the unbegotten God, who arose from no one and began from no one; the invisible God, whom no one is able to see with the eyes of flesh; the incomprehensible God, who comprehends all things; the immutable God, who is not changed by times and does not grow old with age, but is always the same; who did not begin to live in time, but, always living, suffers no successor; the good and just God, Creator of heaven and earth.

I confess this God, and I confess him as Father, the Father of the Son. No one is a father without a son. The Father is therefore Father through the Son, possessing a son of whom he is father.

I call him the Father of the living Word, of his own power and Wisdom, whom he ineffably begot from himself before all ages—indeed, without beginning: Spirit from Spirit, God from God. In him all things were created, both the things in heaven and the things on earth, visible and invisible, as Paul teaches and John confirms.

“All things,” he says, “were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3).

I therefore confess this one God, the almighty Father. In him I believe; him I honor and praise with lips, heart, and every power available to me; I bless and adore him.

### XXI.

I also believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made. For us human beings and for our salvation he assumed flesh of human nature and a true soul, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. In that flesh, I both believe and confess that he suffered, was buried, and rose from the dead [Col. 1068C]; and that in the same flesh in which he lay in the tomb, after the resurrection he appeared to the disciples and taught them what had to be taught; and that before them and many others he ascended into heaven and now sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, reigns in eternal blessedness—from where we await him coming to judge the living and the dead.⁴⁰⁴

This is Christ Jesus our Lord, God and man, maker and made. With the eyes of faith I see the maker: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God, and God was the Word; all things were made through him” (John 1:1). And I see the one who was made: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., v. 14).

I believe and confess him to be true God and perfect man, existing from two natures and subsisting in both in the unity of one person. In this Creator and our Redeemer, who made us when we did not exist and redeemed us with his own blood when we had been lost, I believe. To him I bend my knees and bow my neck; him I worship, praise, and adore, with unfeigned faith and a pure conscience. I love him and desire him with my whole heart; I wish to please him alone; I desire and pray with all my inmost being to become his member through right faith and good works, if he himself deigns to grant it.

Yet when I confess that I believe in the Father and in the Son, with an intervening distinction, I do not—God forbid—divide the substance, but distinguish the persons, because the person of the Father is one and that of the Son another. Nevertheless, my mind’s belief is one and undivided, although I say separately, “I believe” and “I believe,” because the divinity of the Father and the Son is undivided and inseparable [Col. 1069A].

Therefore, although Christ alone was sent, he did not alone accomplish the salvation of the world. His sending is personal, but his operation is substantial; and, as has already been said, what is personal is not shared with another person, whereas what is substantial is undivided and common to the whole Trinity.

The title “Christ” is not shared with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but is proper and particular to the Son alone, and this on account of the flesh. For it is interpreted as “anointed,” but he was anointed in the assumed flesh, not in the divinity of the Word who assumed it.
