Nevertheless, because the flesh and the Word are one person, Christ is Christ according to the flesh, Christ according to the soul, and Christ according to the divinity. Thus we say that Christ descended into hell and that Christ lay in the tomb. The Apostle also says: “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them did” (1 Cor. 10:19), when they were led out through Moses, at a time when Christ did not yet exist except according to his everlasting divinity.

“I therefore anathematize and utterly reject those who say, ‘There was a time when he was not,’ and ‘Before he was born, he did not exist’; who say that he was made from things that did not subsist, or from another substance or essence; or who say that the Son of God is changeable and mutable. The Catholic and apostolic Church condemns such people and separates them from its fellowship.”

### XXII.

I believe in the Holy Spirit in the same way as in the Father and the Son, because the Holy Spirit is God [Col. 1069C], as are the Father and the Son. We ought to believe in no one else except God. For just as the one who begets cannot be one thing and the one begotten another, but what is begotten is God, just as the begetter is God, so what proceeds as Spirit cannot be one thing and the one from whom it proceeds another. Rather, what he himself is, that also proceeds from him: that is, God is born from God, and God proceeds from God.

Therefore, not with another or different faith, but with one and the same faith, I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son; who is worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son; who spoke through the prophets; who descended upon the Lord Jesus Christ in the form of a dove; who appeared to the disciples in fire, granting them the gifts of graces and knowledge of all languages.

He gives life to all things; he alone searches out the mysteries and the depths of God [Col. 1069D]; at the time of baptism he sanctifies the souls and bodies of believers. He is one, but manifold in his operations. He distributes the gifts of grace to each person as he wills. Without him the heart is dull and foolish; without his power no creature can attain eternity. By his majesty he also sanctifies all the powers of heaven.

He is a wondrous teacher and powerful craftsman, who in making things causes no delay; who softens hearts and brings forth tears in those who repent; who grants forgiveness of sins; against whom, if anyone blasphemes, he has no forgiveness, according to the Lord’s saying.

This Holy Spirit is called love, just as the one Word of God is called wisdom, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may all be called wisdom and love [Col. 1070A]. Truly, he is the love, holiness, and unity of the Father and the Son; and therefore he is properly named with the title “love.”

In this Holy Spirit, true God, I believe. Him I praise, bless, worship, and adore: the true light and sanctification of souls, who is the pledge of our inheritance. May he always enlighten our minds, lead us into all truth, make us cling to heavenly things, and prepare a worthy dwelling for God in our hearts, as the Lord Jesus Christ our Redeemer promised concerning that holy Paraclete.

### XXIII.

Therefore, with all my heart and with the sweetest love by which my soul has been refreshed through the integrity of faith, by God’s grace I believe, with all the darkness of error driven far away, and I confess that I will always believe [Col. 1070B].

I certainly believe in one God the almighty Father; in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, almighty God; and in one Holy Paraclete, the gift and Spirit of them both, almighty God.

In this holy and undivided Trinity, which is one power and an undivided Majesty, I believe earnestly and eagerly. I confess it with my lips; with all the strength I possess I worship, praise, magnify, invoke, bless, pray to, and adore it. To it I keep faith; to it I commit myself with complete devotion; to the living, true, and almighty God I entrust my life.

For when I say “God,” I confess the name of essence, because it is the name of the essence—that is, of the nature of the whole Trinity, not of one person alone. But when I add either “Father,” “Son,” or “Holy Spirit,” I declare the particular person of each [Col. 1070C]. For when we speak of God, those names that pertain to his substance are equal and common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Those, however, that designate the persons are called relative and indicate only the distinctive properties of the persons.

Moreover, I confess this faith to be true and catholic. This is my faith, for which I am prepared to die. The Apostles received this rule of faith from the Lord, so that they might baptize believers in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Through this faith, we who were children of death and of the devil have become children of God, of light, and of resurrection. Through this faith we are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love.

In the profession and power of this faith I desire to advance from day to day, asking the Lord with the Apostles: “Increase my faith” (Luke 17:5) [Col. 1070D].

The authority of the New and Old Testaments unfolds this Christian faith. Although the Old Testament itself contained the name of Christ and always indicated that he would come—the one whom we believe has now come through the Virgin’s childbirth—it is nevertheless shown to have spread throughout the world from the wondrous advent of our Savior himself.

### XXIV.

Our religion, which is called Christian and catholic, rests principally upon these foundations, with Christ, as we believe, revealing them: it asserts that the divine substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has existed from eternity; that the Father is from no one, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Yet we cannot explain clearly the manner of this procession, any more than the human mind can comprehend the generation of the Son [Col. 1071A]. The Old and New Testaments instruct us to believe these things. From this, as from the citadel of our religion, many have spoken contrary opinions, thinking in a human and, so to speak, carnal manner. Consequently, some of them accept neither the Old Testament nor the New in its entirety.

The Christian faith accepts both, believing in one nature and three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but one God and one principle; and in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is true God and perfect man, two substances and one person.

Therefore the divine nature, existing from eternity and enduring forever without any change, with no will but its own, freely wished to fashion the world and made it exist when it did not exist at all [Col. 1071B]. It did not bring it forth from its own substance, lest it be thought divine by nature; rather, it is said first to have created the angelic nature and formless matter, as it is written in the Book of Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). Thus God’s goodness would not be idle, but would have things in which to display its goodness over many ages beforehand.

For it must not be thought that he fashioned these things from elsewhere, as though something had existed whose existence, belonging to its own nature, assisted his will; or as though something existed that had not been made by him and nevertheless existed—an idea far from the understanding of the faithful and one God forbid.

### XXV.

From those things that were created—that is, from that formless matter—this visible world, together with all that is in it, is believed to have been both made and adorned [Col. 1071C]. By his word he brought forth the heavens and created all things, arranging heavenly things with the heavens and earthly things with the earth, assigning to each what belonged to it.

The angels, however, were created in such a condition that, if they wished, they could remain in blessedness; but if they did not wish to, they could also fall. Thus Satan fell with his legions of followers. The angelic powers that remained steadfast, fixed in divine love, received this reward for the fallen and proud angels: that they would neither wish nor be able to fall at all, possessing from God the power of immutability.

The devil, therefore, was not made so that he would be the devil, because God did not make evil. Rather, when he had been made by God as a good angel, through the vice of pride he made himself the devil. With his accomplices he wanders through this air, plotting against the salvation of the faithful.

I do not think that he knows the inner thoughts of the soul, except insofar as he detects them through certain external indications, especially from the very dispositions of souls that appear in the conduct of individuals. God alone knows the secrets of the heart.

We say that evil thoughts are not always aroused by his prompting, but sometimes arise from the movement of our own will; good thoughts, however, always come from God. The devil is a suggester of evil, not its instigator. We do not believe that he enters the soul substantially, but that he is united to it by approach and oppression. For only the Creator, subsisting by nature and incorporeal, is capable of his creation.

That renegade, then, was once surrounded by the glory and honor of the Creator’s presence; but as soon as he became proud, his fall became evident. He is not to be restored again to that angelic dignity, as Origen raves, but after the judgment he is to be cast down with his whole body into everlasting fire, where, living wickedly forever, he will die without end [Col. 1072A].

Accordingly, apart from the Trinity alone, which alone I confess and believe to be the one principle, I declare that everything existing, acting, or moving in heaven, on earth, and in the sea is a creature.

I therefore believe that evil, or wickedness, was not created by God but invented by the devil. I confess that the substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, is good, and that evil has no nature. Through the author of evil, wickedness enters into the rest.

Nothing by nature is immutable except God alone. He cannot be anything other than good, and as the creator of the universe he made nothing that was not good. Our flesh, therefore, is good, since it was created by the good and only God [Col. 1072B]. It is not evil, nor the cause of evil, nor composed of good and evil; rather, although good by creation, it is made good or evil by the soul’s will. It is this flesh that will stand before the tribunal of Christ.

### XXVI.

I believe in the holy, apostolic, universal, and orthodox Church, which has taught us this sound doctrine. I do not believe in it as though it were God; rather, I confess that it is in God and that God is in it—not as though it contained God, but rather as being contained by God.

This is the house of God; this is the bride of Christ. I call it the assembly of all the saints. In it are contained all the righteous—those who are, those who have been, and those who will be.

I say even more: all the orders of blessed spirits are also united in this one Church, as the Apostle teaches: “Because in Christ all things have been reconciled, not only those on earth but also those in heaven” (Col. 1:20) [Col. 1072C].

This entire sacred unity is called the city of God. This is the place where gold is smelted.

I believe that this one catholic Church, spread everywhere above and below, will be gathered into one blessedness: that is, that the whole Church together will reign in heaven with Christ, who is its head, because it is his body.

By God’s grace I have become a member of this body, although a small and weak one. I greatly desire and ask from God, the giver of all good things, to retain fellowship with it firmly in faith and action until the end.

Therefore, in this one holy Church, our catholic mother, which praises God throughout the entire world, I believe that I shall attain the communion of the saints [Col. 1072D], trusting not in my own merits but in the blood of Christ and in the prayers and merits of this mother Church.

There are also other pseudo-churches, deceived by demonic doctrines and not following Christ. I am ashamed and reluctant to mention their crimes and names amid the sacred words of my confession of faith. I have nothing in common with them; I pronounce an anathema upon them all. May I never have even a peaceful conversation with them.

If place and time require me to pursue them, I shall never cease to attack them as enemies of Christ, according to the knowledge and ability God has given and gives me. For they are divided from the body of Christ.

Those churches, darkened by the night of error, are dragged by the devil, their teacher, farther above and below than is fitting [Col. 1073A]. But the mother Church holds the middle position, which is proper to true virtue.

### XXVII.

This mother Church, called catholic, spread throughout the world in one and the same faith, is shown to exist in three ways. Whatever is held within it is either the authority of the Scriptures, universal tradition, or certainly a particular and local instruction.

It is wholly bound by authority, and likewise wholly by the universal tradition of the ancestors. But through private constitutions and particular instructions each church exists and is governed according to the diversity of places or as seemed best to each. Customs are indeed diverse, but the integrity of orthodox faith within it is one and the same.

Within this holy Church, where one God is rightly worshiped and there is one faith [Col. 1073B]:

“Holding to one baptism, I confess and affirm that it is to be celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as for adults” [Note: [Col. 1073D] From Pelagius’s Confession.], and by saying this I confirm it.

I assert that only those have been baptized who were immersed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, according to the rule established by the Lord. In this regeneration I believe that the forgiveness of all sins—both original and actual—is granted, and that the souls and bodies of the baptized are simultaneously sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

From that moment we receive him as the pledge of our inheritance, and through him the love of God is poured into our hearts. God consecrates the water and baptizes; he performs these things in us, although human rites appear outwardly [Col. 1073C].

We certainly do not say that those who have been baptized should be rebaptized if they fall after receiving the grace of baptism, lest the invocation or confession of the holy Trinity be nullified. Rather, we believe that they can be saved through repentance, which is practiced in many ways in the mother Church, which is the house of God.

Outside it, it is not lawful to believe that there is any forgiveness or any righteousness, since for those placed outside it neither the ecclesiastical sacraments nor anything good that can be done leads to salvation, but rather to destruction. Outside it, a person may die by various bodily deaths, but cannot be acceptable to God. For this is the place where gold is smelted.

### XXVIII.

I also hold, according to the catholic faith, that all who have been truly baptized can and ought, with God’s help and cooperation, to fulfill whatever pertains to the salvation of the soul, if they are willing to labor faithfully [Col. 1073D].

I not only do not believe that some people have been predestined by divine power for evil, but if there are people who wish to believe such an evil thing, I pronounce an anathema upon them with complete abhorrence. For God is good, merciful, and almighty.

Therefore, if we are evil, the fault is not his but ours and the devil’s, whose wicked counsels we obey.

Moreover, I call that true repentance which mourns what has been committed and thereafter does not commit either those sins or anything like them for which the person is repenting. Few are found who strive to repent in this manner.

Yet I do not doubt that those who repent well will enter the company of those who, with the Lord’s protection, preserved their lives free from every capital crime [Col. 1074A]. I say even more: they can become more excellent than those people in glory.

Concerning the healthy, this is indeed my view. Concerning the infirm, however, I hold the following, trusting in God’s most just mercy: if one of them repents of his sins in the final breath of life and, through a public act of satisfaction and lamentation, confesses his sins before all who are present there, his repentance is undoubtedly accepted by him who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50:19) and who does not desire the death of sinners (Ezek. 3:11), even if he immediately departs from life [F.: even if].

For God’s purpose, by which he decreed to save what had been lost, remains immovable.

But if anyone is troubled by what is written—that God permits no crime or sin to go unpunished [F.: “unpunished” is absent] [Col. 1074B]—we answer that there is a purifying fire in which they can be cleansed, and, once purified, they will be joined to those who will be placed at the right hand.

The quality and quantity of the punishments corresponding to the repentance that should have been undertaken in life lie within God’s judgment; he has accepted the tears flowing from a contrite heart.

Therefore, we say that the way of salvation is open to baptized people who act well. But we say that no catechumen, even one who has died while performing good works, possesses eternal life—except through martyrdom, in which all the sacraments of baptism are completed. Confessors are baptized by blood, fire, or other sufferings.

### XXIX.

I believe in the resurrection of the flesh, not of the soul. Although the soul may be abandoned by its life, which is God—that is its death—it can rise again from this death through repentance; nevertheless, it lives substantially and never dies. Therefore it does not need the resurrection of its substance.

Thus I believe that I shall rise in the flesh alone, in which I shall certainly die. The flesh will indeed rise, but so immortal and spiritual that thereafter it cannot die. It will be of the same nature but of another quality, because “the natural body is sown; the spiritual body will rise” (1 Cor. 15:44) [Col. 1074C].

[Note: [Col. 1074D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 6.] I confess the resurrection of all human beings, as I do my own, but one resurrection and once only: we shall all rise together—not a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of the wicked, but one resurrection of all.

No new body will rise in place of this flesh, but this very flesh will rise, with no member amputated from it and no part of the body lacking.

“The flesh of both the righteous and the unrighteous will rise incorruptible [Col. 1074D], so that it may either suffer punishments for sins or remain in eternal glory according to merits.”

I believe that the form of either sex will not be changed: a man will rise in the form of a man and a woman in the form of a woman. Social condition will cease, but not natural appearance, as it is written: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matt. 22:30). For the resurrection would not be genuine if what had fallen did not rise again.

“What we say in the Creed, that at the Lord’s coming the living and the dead will be judged, does not mean, as some wish, the righteous and sinners; rather, I think it more likely signifies those who will be found alive in the flesh—those who are believed to be going to die for this purpose, so that, raised immediately, they may be judged together with those who died earlier” [Col. 1075A].

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Gennadius, same work, chapter 8: “What we say—that the living and the dead will be judged—does not signify only the righteous and sinners, as Diodorus thinks. Rather, we believe that it also signifies those who will be found alive in the flesh, who are still believed to be going to die; or, as others hold, they will be changed, so that, raised or transformed, they may be judged together with those who died earlier.”]

There were some Catholics who believed that those whose souls remained in their bodies would be changed into incorruption, and that their laying aside mortality through transformation rather than death would be reckoned for them as resurrection from the dead. We, however, believe that all who live in the flesh will undoubtedly die.

For no human being, from the first age until this age in which we live, has been granted exemption from death. The death of Enoch and Elijah is delayed, but not removed. We say that the same thing will happen to them: the death given in Adam will rule over all his children.

Therefore I believe that all will die and all will rise again, so that I may say that we shall be restored in the same reality of our members in which we now exist; and whatever form we shall have once attained after the resurrection, in that form we shall remain forever [Col. 1075B].

While the body is decaying in the earth, however, I do not doubt that the soul is meanwhile kept either in a place of light or in a place of darkness, and that it immediately returns to the resurrected body, so that together we may enjoy either punishment or glory.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Gennadius, chapter 9, with a difference.] As for the resurrection and judgment, may I never say, as fools do, that wicked people, after being purified by punishments through the judge’s mercy and the prayers of the saints, will be joined to eternal glory. Rather, I believe the truth that says: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment” (Matt. 25:46).

### XXX.

We say that intellectual natures, which lack flesh, are immortal.

“[Note: [Col. 1076D] Pelagius.] I believe that souls are given by God, and I do not doubt that they were made by him. I anathematize those who say that the soul, as though it were a part of God, belongs to the divine substance.”

For God is impassible [Col. 1075C], whereas the soul is subject to various passions, as the daily outcome of things demonstrates.

“[Note: [Col. 1076D] Pelagius.] I also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies.”

If it is asked from what, or when, or how the soul was made, I confess that I do not know. Yet I do not say that it was made from any creature, lest I make it inferior to the other creatures over which it was established as mistress. I confess only that the body is generated through marital union.

The creation of the soul, however, is known only to the Creator of all things, who is its maker and giver. His power does not require matter from which to make what he wishes; rather, his will itself is the matter of those things that he commands to come into being or to exist.

“[Note: [Col. 1076D] Gennadius, chapter 15.] Nor do I believe that there are two souls in one human being, one animal soul by which the body is animated and another spiritual soul that supplies reason, as some have wished. Rather, I say that there is one and the same soul in the substance of a human being, which both gives life to the body through its association with it and orders itself through its own reason” [Col. 1075D].

Although it is one, this soul is called spirit, mind, intellect, reason, understanding, memory, and sense.

Although the question of the soul’s origin is exceedingly perplexing and obscure, and no one is read to have settled it as it ought to be settled, we can nevertheless freely confess that it was created in the image of God: the image is found in eternity, and the likeness in moral character [Col. 1076A].

It is enough for the Church to believe that the soul is both created by God and given by him. But who else forms the body in the mother’s womb and arranges it limb by limb? Blessed Job explains this sufficiently when he says: “Did you not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese, with skin and flesh?” (Job 10:10), and so forth.

“[Note: [Col. 1076D] Gennadius, chapter 16.] We say that only the human being has a substantial soul, which lives when separated from the body and retains its senses and faculties more vividly after death.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] The same, chapter 17.] The souls of animals, however, are not substantial, because they die with the flesh. Nor are they governed by reason, as some have thought; rather, they are driven toward everything by the impulse of nature” [Col. 1076B].

A human being, therefore, consists of two substances: a small world, possessing a soul and a body. The body indeed has its own senses, but it does not move them without the soul, because the soul is the life of the body, and God is the life of the soul.

### XXXI.

The soul is strengthened by reason and possesses within itself freedom of will to choose what it wishes. But free will was corrupted by Adam’s transgression and so weakened that it cannot be restored except through Christ’s grace.

For even if human nature had remained in the integrity in which it was created, it could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. How, then, can it recover without God what it lost?

That transgression of Adam weakened and cast down the free will both of Adam and of all his descendants [Col. 1076C]. I believe and confess that through one human being not only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, but also sin itself, which is the death of the soul, passed into the entire human race, as the Apostle says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all human beings sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

Because of this rule of faith, I believe and affirm with the mother Church that even infants, who could not themselves have committed any sins, are baptized for the forgiveness of sins, so that what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed through regeneration.

Therefore I do not wish to contemplate without attention the fact that those who are to be baptized, whatever their age, do not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them through the exorcisms and breathings of the clergy [Col. 1076D]. Then it becomes clear how the strong man is first bound, and afterward his goods are carried away and transferred to the victor, who leads captivity captive.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] Pelagius.] “Thus we confess free will, saying that we always need God’s help [Pelagius: ‘saying that we do not always need God’s help’]; and that those who, with Manichaeus, say that a human being cannot avoid sin are in error, just as those who, with Jovinianus, assert that a human being cannot sin. Each removes freedom of will. We, however, say that a human being is always able both to sin and not to sin, so that we continue to confess ourselves free in will.”

Nevertheless, I believe that God works in this way: holy thought, devout counsel, and every movement of good will come from him who is supremely good, without whom we can do nothing good. No one uses free will well except through Christ. No one is good by himself, unless he is granted participation in the one who alone is good.

### XXXII.

It must be believed with the greatest firmness that, through Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural capacity and innocence [Col. 1077B].

Therefore, although in accordance with right faith we profess God to be the author not only of all good affections, works, studies, and virtues by which one strives toward God from the beginning of faith, and although all human merits are preceded by his grace, and through him everything good begins both to be desired and to be done, we must also not doubt that the beginning of faith itself, and the very movement of belief by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and come to baptism, takes place through his inspiration, by which our will is changed from unbelief to faith.

Nevertheless, we do not remove free will; rather, we assert that it is freed by such great divine aid and grace that what was dark becomes luminous, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was imprudent becomes wise and provident.

For if there were no freedom of will, there would be neither laws nor punishments, nor would the admonitions of Scripture and the exhortations of the saints be given [Col. 1077C]. Again, if God’s grace did not work every good thing in human hearts and in free will itself, why would prayers to God be necessary?

Is it not the case that on Good Friday, throughout the whole world, the priests of the Lord in every catholic Church, with the peoples praying alongside them, ask God—as was handed down by the Apostles themselves—to grant faith to unbelievers? To let the light of truth appear to the Jews once the veil of their hearts has been removed? To bring heretics and schismatics back to the mother Church through faith and love?

And for the faithful, God is prayed to not only on that day but at all times, so that he himself may free us from evil and preserve us in what is good.

Therefore it must be believed most truly that God begins in us, without us, what is good; but he wishes to work it in us together with us, requiring from us a ready will, fervent zeal, and daily labors, so that we too may be fellow workers with God’s grace [Col. 1077D].

For he wishes to give his rewards to those who labor. Yet his goodness is so great that he wishes our merits to be his gifts. We must therefore return to him if we see anything in us growing weak through our own negligence, since he can heal our weaknesses.

### XXXIII.

Yet it must not be left unsaid that, if the will is ready, zeal burns, and labor and strength are vigorous, all these things are accomplished through the Lord’s mercy. The person who asserts or even thinks that anything pertaining to true salvation can be done without God through the power of nature is sufficiently foolish and proud [Col. 1078A].

I affirm that all the merits of the saints, all their zeal and good works, thoughts and words, must be referred to God’s glory and praise. With the Apostle I say concerning each of the saints: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). No one can please him for any reason other than what he himself has granted.

Nevertheless, all may possess his grace who are willing to practice what they believe.

We who are children of the mother Church firmly believe that, if Adam had not sinned, he would not have died, but would have been transferred, without bodily death, with all his children, to the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

Because he did not stand according to the Lord’s command, he did not rise above himself as an obedient person, but fell beneath himself as disobedient, and dragged all his descendants with him into death and into the many miseries that we suffer daily in mind and body [Col. 1078B].

Christ’s redemption, baptism, and the other sacraments maintained in the Church pertain not to the present age but to the age to come, and therefore they do not free us from this punishment of sin. While we are in the body, we groan within ourselves and endure harsh servitude; but we have a sure hope that we shall be transferred into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

For Christ’s blood has opened for us the door of eternal life. Before the Lord’s ascension, all the souls of the saints were held in hell, although in a peaceful bosom. After his ascension, when they leave the body, they go to Christ and are with him in glory, because that bond has now been erased by the Lord [Col. 1078C], and we have been freed from servile condition.

### XXXIV.

The Fathers of the Old Testament were saved through faith not by the good of nature that had previously been given in Adam, but by God’s grace. This grace makes us Christians, and, once faith has been received, makes us turn away from evil and do good, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17).

Christ bestowed certain medicinal sacraments, so that we might recognize that one thing is owed to us through the merit of nature and another through the gift of grace: that nature subjected us to nothing except punishment, whereas grace—which is attributed to no merits, since it would not be called grace if it were given on the basis of merits—brings everything that belongs to salvation.

No holy or just person living in mortal flesh is without sin. Therefore I firmly believe that the words of the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), are truly spoken in this life by all the saints, because they genuinely have something to mourn. Yet they do not thereby cease to be righteous, since they retain holiness in their intention.

They are freed from the law of sin and justified by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Certainly, no one acquires holiness through the powers of nature, but through the help of an upright purpose and by God’s grace.

Woe, therefore, to the wretched who presume upon their own righteousness and are not subject to the righteousness of God.

We learn from the Truth itself that signs can also be performed by wicked people in the Lord’s name. But I do not doubt that a person can become holy, just, and a person of God without the power of signs, if he conducts himself with disciplined and peaceful character [Col. 1079A].

[Note: [Col. 1079D] The following passages agree in sense, though not in wording, with Gennadius, chapters 30, 31, and 32.]

I call good the marriages granted by God their author for the sake of children, condemning those “who condemn either first marriages with Mani, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians.” But I assert that continence is better than these, if it is chosen for the sake of devoting oneself to God, with all pleasures rejected. I praise humble virginity and bodily and spiritual chastity, filled with labors for the Lord, and prefer them to both those goods, as an excellent offspring.

### XXXV.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] Gennadius, chapter 22, in different words.]

I confess that every creature of God, which the Creator granted for the use of food, is good, just as it was made. I declare that abstaining from these things for a time is useful—not out of religious superstition or abhorrence of God’s creation, but for the sake of bodily self-restraint. I say that using them when one wishes, and abstaining when one takes pleasure in abstinence, lies within human power. To regulate their use according to necessity and time is properly Christian, especially for those who delight in the good of virginity, so that they may more easily overcome both the nature of the body through integrity and the struggle for chastity through peace.

I accept penance with complete faith and honor it.

I affirm that it is good for possessions to be distributed to the poor according to an arrangement, but better for them to be given away all at once, so that one may thus become needy with Christ.

I testify and commend that the bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of martyrs, are to be honored, and that the basilicas called by their names are to be frequented with faithful devotion, as though they were members and places of Christ.

Although many things in this world seem confused and disordered, I confess that it is not driven by random movements but governed by divine providence. Nothing happens on earth without a reason. Only the pure in heart understand that God rules all things. I hear that even of the smallest things the Lord said: “Not one of the sparrows falls to the ground without your Father” (Matt. 10:29).

I believe in one principle and one supreme good, from which all good things proceed, anathematizing those who either introduce two principles unknown to themselves, as Cerdo and Marcion did; or two contrary principles, as Mani did; or three, as Theodotus did; or many, as Valentinus did.

“[Note: [Col. 1080D] Pelagius.] I also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for human beings, and that God’s commandments can be kept not by individuals but collectively by everyone.”

“[Note: [Col. 1080D] Pelagius.] I also reject and condemn those who say that the Son of God lied by necessity of the flesh, and that, because he assumed a human being, he was unable to do everything he wished. I likewise abhor the heresy of those who assert that there will be no distinction among merits in the future, and that there we shall possess the virtues which we neglected here.”

### XXXVI.

“[Note: [Col. 1080D] Pelagius.] I accept the New and Old Testament in the number of books handed down by the authority of the holy Catholic Church. Without nullifying faith in the historical account, I believe that everything written actually happened, but, in accordance with apostolic teaching, I desire to understand in them a spiritual meaning. For every divine authority appears to consist in these modes: either the historical mode, which announces nothing other than events that happened; or the allegorical mode, in which the order of the historical account cannot stand; or, certainly, a mode composed of both, so that it appears to remain both according to history and according to allegory. Sometimes a moral meaning is also drawn from the divine Scriptures; since this is the finest form of teaching, it greatly benefits the correction of life and the formation of character. These things shine forth sufficiently and abundantly for those who approach them humbly and understand them piously, holding them with a truthful heart. This heavenly teaching both shapes the present life through good works and promises eternal glory after life’s end.

“Moreover, I gladly read all those treatises, sermons, and commentaries which I know to have been composed by highly Catholic and distinguished authors. In them I perceive, with the astonishment of the heart’s ear, the Holy Spirit speaking, and from their marvelous knowledge I discern more clearly how great my own ignorance is. I also venerate the decrees of the pontiffs and those councils which the Roman Church accepts and praises, because they are the teaching and protection of the universal Church; and, to the best of my knowledge and ability, I defend them against their enemies.

“Therefore I declare that a man who has married two matrons after baptism is not to be ordained a cleric; nor is one who had one woman as a concubine rather than as a matron; nor one who took a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute in marriage; nor one who offers money through ambition, in imitation of Simon Magus. O unhappy times of ours, which neither fear God nor revere the force of the sacred canons! Nowadays no sacrilegious or criminal person is restrained from approaching the office of the sacred order. If clerical status is forbidden to a man who has had two wives, with what face does one who has been driven by the fury of lust through the pollutions of various kinds dare to become deacon, priest, or bishop? If a usurer is not to be ordained, and one who has mutilated a member of his own body for any reason is to be removed in accordance with the decrees of the councils, what should be done with a simoniac and a man of every kind of depravity? Alas, unhappy me! What times I have been made to see! Things necessary for bodily use are now treated more carefully than the sacred mysteries. That saying may rightly be applied to us: ‘You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves’ (John 6:26).”

### XXXVII.

Therefore, receiving with complete purity the holy Scriptures that we have mentioned, we do not readily give credence to tales about the contents of the Scriptures told by foreigners and strangers. May that teaching which pleases itself only in secret and is ashamed to come into public never enter the recesses of our ears. We not only flee from such teaching, but also pronounce anathema upon it, unwilling either to hear or to see the opinions of all heretics. Every teaching that does not accord with or conform to the ecclesiastical canon we not only do not accept, but condemn as alien to the truth of the faith.

I am not ashamed to confess my ignorance. In the divine books, especially the Old Testament, many things remain hidden from me; very few are those which I think are clear to me. Blessed Moses, to whom God wished to make known both the origin of the world and the constitution of the human race, spoke very briefly and obscurely, especially about those things that were made by God from nothing. Hence it happened that many people explained many things differently. Having read some of their writings, I confess that it is not sufficiently clear to me what was first made by God. For that reason I do not state definitively—as I have done up to now concerning the other matters that pertain to ecclesiastical doctrines—but I set forth both the interpretations and opinions of our predecessors.

There are those who believe that formless matter was made first, and afterward the angelic nature. One of them, as I think a man great in age and wisdom, left this written without hesitation:

> “In the beginning God created heaven, earth, and water from nothing; and while darkness still concealed the water itself, and water hid the earth, angels and all the heavenly powers were made.”

[Note: [Col. 1081D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 10.]

Would that Moses had described this without ambiguity, so that no one were permitted to doubt his assertion. Yet I greatly wonder with myself why that great man, when he could, as I think, have spoken plainly above all human beings, preferred to remain silent about such lofty matters. Father Gregory recalls this definition in a certain passage, though he presents it without affirming it, saying:

> “For the first nature of rational spirits is believed to have been created in time. If this is so, while the earth was invisible and unformed, while darkness was over the abyss, they anticipated through their existence, by the light of wisdom, the coming day of the age to follow.”

[Note: [Col. 1082D] Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVIII, chapter 14.]

### XXXVIII.

There are also others who judge that the angelic nature, being the more worthy and eminent creature, was first in the order of creation. Their interpretation appears to be supported by what the Lord said about Lucifer: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). For what are the ways of God except his actions, of which it is said through the prophet: “For my ways are not like your ways” (Isa. 55:8)? Behemoth is called the beginning of the ways because, in the nature of things, the Creator made him first in substance when creating him.

He held the primacy among the angels, with whom he had been created at the same time, as the prophet says: “The cedars were not taller than he” (Ezek. 31:8). Because he sinned, he was condemned without pardon, for he had been created great beyond comparison. Again, the same one says above: “You are the seal of likeness” (Ezek. 28:12). For what good did he not possess, if he was the seal of God’s likeness?

“As Father Gregory also says, it should be noted that when Behemoth is called the beginning of God’s ways, Arius’s mad doctrine is overthrown by clear reasoning. For Arius confesses that the Son is God’s creature. And behold, Behemoth is shown to have been created first in the making of things. It remains, therefore, either that Arius proclaim the Son uncreated, or that, in his folly, he suppose that the Son was created after Behemoth.”

[Note: [Col. 1082D] Gregory, same work, chapter 24.]

Perhaps the fact that the angels were created in the beginning is also demonstrated by what is said to blessed Job: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” and shortly afterward: “When the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:4, 7).

### XXXIX.

Moreover, men of respectable learning are found who prefer neither of these views, but say that both were created by God simultaneously, so that each may be called the beginning. This reasoning appears more probable, if they define the matter in this way:

Before any day of this age, God created both the higher and spiritual world with its inhabitants and the formless matter of this entire world, in accordance with what is written: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1).

For this is what Moses says according to the historical account: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Moses mentioned the higher world so briefly because he had resolved to write about this world in which the human being was made. He thought it sufficient to include the entire state and adornment of spiritual and invisible creation under the single name of “heaven,” which he said was made in the beginning; but he described the bodily, visible, and corruptible creation more extensively and in order. That is, while leaving unspoken the things that are too lofty to seek and too difficult to investigate, he set before us for consideration those things that were commanded or promised by God to everyone.

For this reason he also deliberately kept entirely silent about the fall of the transgressing angel and his companions, judging that this pertained to the state of the invisible and spiritual creature. In the beginning he says that only earth was made with heaven, although there are four elements. Why, unless because he was hastening toward matters that were more necessary? For it is not permissible to believe that the waters were not made by God together with heaven and earth. Even if he does not state this openly, he nevertheless signifies it openly when he indicates that they were illuminated by God and ordered at his command.

The other two elements also—that is, fire and air—although they are not mentioned, are certainly included by him in those things, namely earth and water, in which they were implanted. Fire embedded in the interior of the earth is revealed by the hot springs of the waters. It is also found in iron and stones, which, already created at that time, lay hidden in the bowels of the earth. Air, too, is known to be mixed into the earth itself from the fact that, when it has been moistened and receives the warmth of the sun, it immediately exhales abundant vapors.

Thus he indicates what sort of heaven was made in the beginning with the earth when he says: “But the earth was formless and empty” (Gen. 1:2). Why did he introduce these words about the earth, passing over heaven, unless he wished nothing of this kind to be understood about heaven? For this is the higher heaven, which, separated from every revolving condition of this world, always remains at rest in the glory of the divine presence; in it all things had always been perfectly ordered.

As for our heaven, in which the luminaries necessary for this age were placed, the legislator himself explains in what manner and at what time it was made in what follows. Therefore it is not to be believed that the higher heaven, inaccessible to the sight of all mortals, was created formless and empty like the earth, which at that time was such as part of it still remains beneath the deepest depths of the sea. Indeed, waters covered its entire surface to such a height that they reached even those places where they still remain in part above the firmament.

But [with] its inhabitants it was immediately created—that is, it was filled with the most blessed hosts of angels. The Creator himself testifies that they were created in the beginning together with heaven and earth, and that shortly afterward they related both their own creation and the beginning of all creation to the praise of the Creator. Speaking to Job, he said: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4); and shortly afterward: “When all the sons of God praised me” (ibid., v. 5).

Rightly, therefore, the heaven of heaven is said not to have been made formless or empty; nor is any place in it said to have remained for darkness or the abyss. The Lord God himself has illuminated it from the very beginning—he who is the true light and dwells in inaccessible light. By his most blessed vision, the angels created in the heavens of heavens had already begun to rejoice; and in that realm, where all things were soon perfectly ordered, the Holy Spirit brought illumination—not intending to bring them to perfection as in the lower regions, as it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2)—that is, by his own power, holding them in his own control as Creator, determining when he would gather them into one place so that dry land might appear.

He is said to have been borne over them not by spatial position, but by excelling in his will over the creatures to be arranged—like a craftsman whose intention is accustomed to govern the materials that are to be fashioned.

Saint Basil also refers to that higher and invisible creation in the second book of the *Hexaemeron*, saying:

> “For we believe that, if anything existed before the establishment of this sensible and corruptible world, it was certainly in light. For neither the dignity of the angels, nor all the heavenly host, nor whatever is named or capable of being addressed, nor any rational power or ministering spirit could dwell in darkness; rather, it possessed in light and joy the fitting condition proper to it.”

[Note: [Col. 1083] Basil, Homily 2 on the *Hexaemeron*, shortly after the middle; volume I of the works, p. 17.]

Well, therefore, is it said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). This clearly allows us to understand that both were made by him simultaneously, although it is not possible for human beings to speak of both simultaneously. The psalmist says: “In the beginning, you, Lord, founded the earth” (Ps. 101:26). Moses, however, says: “In the beginning God made heaven.” From this it is plainly gathered that the making of both was completed together—and with such speed through the power of God that the first moment of the world’s birth had not yet passed.

### XL.

Having heard these things, may I be kept from wishing to suspect anything sinister in the words of teachers who speak about such lofty matters, especially since Moses, with whom God spoke, left these matters almost untouched. For I see fulfilled the promise of God who says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

Therefore I praise modern teachers and gladly read their writings. While they turn over the statements of the ancients, they discover, by searching through the reading of many authors, the root of truth. The younger they are, the more perceptive they are, and the more their intelligence flourishes because they have drawn from many springs.

Of the three views that we have set forth, I neither investigate nor define which is truer, since I am a little man of very small understanding; rather, I leave the matter to the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the saying: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. 12:10). For God is invisible and incorporeal fire, who will reveal to us in that light of true knowledge all hidden things.

Not only the causes of created things, but also—and this is more excellent—the Creator himself will there be announced openly to us. For when our Creator is already shown to us face to face, the words of teachers will be set aside. The life-giving power itself, which forms the spirits of angels, will disclose how God presides over the chosen spirits.

How could anything remain hidden from us when God, the cause of causes, the life of the living, and the reason of rational beings, reveals himself to us in clear vision, with the darkness of our mind now completely wiped away? This is what the Truth says: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce to you openly” (John 16:25).

He asserts that he will announce the Father openly when, through the manifestation of his majesty, he shows both how he is not unequal to the one who begets him and how the Spirit of both proceeds, coeternal with each of them. Then we shall clearly see how that which exists by being born does not come after the one from whom it is born; how he who is produced by procession is not preceded by those who produce him. Then we shall clearly see how the one is, divisibly, three, and how the three are, indivisibly, one.

Then the tongue of the God who declares is the visible brightness of the one who raises us. Therefore those who say that God can indeed be seen in his brightness even in that region of blessedness, but cannot be seen in his nature, have been deceived by an inadequate subtlety of inquiry. Such people do not even suppose that the angels see God.

For in that simple and unchangeable essence, brightness is not one thing and nature another; rather, by its very nature it is brightness, and brightness is its nature, as the Truth promises: “I will manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). It is as though he openly said: “You who see me in your own nature, it remains for you to see me in my nature.”

### XLI.

Therefore, when we come to the very source of life, thirst and satiety will be delightfully impressed upon us. Yet necessity will be far from thirst, and disgust far from satiety, because those who thirst will be satisfied, and those who are satisfied will thirst.

We shall therefore see God, and he himself will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice in the light we have entered. Yet we shall not see him as he sees himself, because we are circumscribed by the very limitation by which we are creatures. This vision is now begun in faith, but then it is perfected in manifestation, when we shall drink at its very source the coeternal wisdom of God, which we now receive through the mouths of teachers.

In those invisible things created by God, which cannot be comprehended, we are able to learn with what humility we should venerate the Creator of all things, so that in this life the human mind may dare to claim nothing for itself from the appearance of almighty God—an appearance that he reserves solely as the reward of his chosen in the recompense to come.

This is undoubtedly that life called eternal, which we believe, hope for, await, and desire to reach, because while we are in the body we are away from the Lord. In the divine promises, therefore, we await nothing earthly or transitory: not marital union, not anything belonging to food or drink, not a future kingdom of Christ on earth, nor anything else perishable and common to this vain age, as many heretics have taught. Rather, we hold the kingdom of heaven as the promise, because after the resurrection, having received perfect blessedness and been made equal to the angels, we shall reign with God in heaven without end.

Truly, those who have lived according to God’s commandments and righteous acts in this world will live with Christ in heaven. This king, the son of a virgin, will be our perpetual contemplation; and therefore he himself will be our delight, our food, our perpetual praise, and our exultation that will endure without end. We shall see him as he is, but only with as much contemplation as is possible for one creature with respect to another. Then God will be all in all.

Then that heavenly city will be made one from angels and human beings, possessing an everlasting reward of blessedness: the sole union with the Creator and an indescribable vision of him. This is that eternal and blessed life which Mother Church believes in and patiently awaits, while she still walks here by faith. This is the fruit of all faith and good conduct. This is the hope for which we are born, believe, and are reborn. For its sake the saints of God endured such great labors. For love of it, martyrs remained steadfast amid torments and received death with joy. The prospect of this life makes God’s servants patient and long-suffering.

### XLII.

Neither the pagan nor the unbelieving Jew will possess this life, nor will the Christian who serves vices and crimes, because it has been prepared only for the faithful and for those who live chastely and piously. But they themselves, having become the body of the devil through evil action, will possess the eternal death that will belong to the devil and his angels.

If there are those who wish to understand this eternal life, which we believe in, as immortality and perpetual unchangeability, I do not wish to argue with them. Nevertheless, I take greater pleasure in believing that God is this life, and that whatever good we shall be comes to us from contemplation of and fellowship with him. For that happiness of always living would undoubtedly be the highest unhappiness if it lacked the glory of the divine vision.

Therefore the sole manifest vision of God will be the reward of all blessedness for us. From it come complete security, secure tranquility, tranquil joy, joyful happiness, happy eternity, and eternal unchangeability, so that we neither wish nor are able to be anything other than good and blessed.

Just as I believe and confess one Trinity, one faith, one baptism, one Church as mother, and one resurrection of the flesh, so also I believe that there is one life of the saints, because that ineffable Trinity, one power and undivided majesty, will be seen by all the saints.

Yet I say that the rewards will differ according to labor, because some will see God more and others less. Each person will behold him all the more deeply according to how purely he lived here or how greatly he struggled. But through love, which will there be perfected, all the saints will possess all good things together.

Conversely, we also say that punishments differ according to the measure of offenses. There is one fire of Gehenna, but it will torture those placed in it in different ways—some more, others less—each according to the merit for which punishment is due.

What wonder, then, if different people see the one God differently, each of the saints according to the reward of his own labor? Nevertheless, what each person has will fully suffice; no one will be able or wish to desire anything more. That one denarius which was ordered to be given to all who labored in the vineyard signifies this one life of the saints, which we call the vision of the one God, to be given to all the saints according to their merits.

[Note: [Col. 1085D] Transition to the following section.]

To this secure and everlasting life, among the other sacraments of the Church, there especially pertains that heavenly and life-giving mystery which our Lord Jesus Christ instituted and commanded to be offered in remembrance of himself for our salvation. Indeed, I think that the sacrament itself may be called eternal life, which begins here and is perfected there. Here we eat God; there we shall see him face to face. Concerning this mystery, I must not remain silent about what my faith is.

## PART IV. ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD, AND ON PERSONAL SINS

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085D] I. I have set forth the remaining matters above according to the correct rule of ecclesiastical doctrine. Now, in the final part of these matters, I wish to confess what I think about this, so that this little work of the confession of my faith may be brought to an end by this conclusion.

But who am I, or how great am I, that I should speak about the depth of so great and ineffable a mystery? It is enough for me if I can express in words, however inadequately, the faith that I hold in my heart, so that the confession itself may contribute to the salvation of my soul. This mystery is more to be venerated and feared than examined. Certainly no one is sufficient to comprehend it; no one speaks worthily about it. It must be grasped by faith, not sought out or discovered by reasoning.

Blessed Gregory, however, a suitable interpreter of so great a sacrament, speaks of it in a certain passage almost ineffably, as of an ineffable matter:

> “For which believer,” he says, “could doubt that at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that in the mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest things are joined to the lowest; that earthly things are united to heavenly things; and that one thing is made from visible and invisible realities?”

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 58.]

Therefore, although it is offered by a human being, this sacrament is nevertheless a divine reality. And if it is a divine reality—or rather, because it is so—far be it from us to understand anything there in any way except divinely and spiritually.

Thus, although with bodily eyes I see at the Lord’s altar a priest offering bread and wine, nevertheless, with the gaze of faith and the pure light of the heart, I behold that supreme priest and true pontiff, the Lord Jesus Christ, offering himself. From his flesh and blood we are nourished and given drink; washed and satisfied and sanctified, we are made participants in the one supreme divinity.

### II.

He is certainly himself the priest and himself the sacrifice. Therefore this saving victim is never and nowhere diminished or increased, impaired or changed, whether a righteous or criminal priest approaches the altar outwardly. This sacrament always and everywhere remains the same and identical.

For by Christ’s power and words that bread and cup were consecrated from the beginning. By Christ’s power and words they are always consecrated, and will be consecrated. He himself speaks daily through his priests. It is his word that sanctifies the heavenly sacraments. The priests perform the office, but Christ acts through the majesty of his divine power.

For he is that true Melchizedek who fulfills, through the offering of his body and blood, the holy sacrifices that Melchizedek then prefigured in mystery, and who has fulfilled them continually from the very beginning when he instituted them. Through the power of the Paraclete Spirit and heavenly blessing, he makes the holy body and blood his own.

In this most holy offering of the Lord’s body and blood, common service is rendered to God both by the priests and by the entire household of God. This is the service of God, which is owed to no other—not to the holy angels, nor to holy souls—but to the one living and true God alone.

Therefore those established in the heavenly dwellings do not wish us to sacrifice to them, but to God alone, whose creatures both they and we are. With them we are one city of God, part of which is on pilgrimage in us, while part of it assists us in them.

I do not doubt that this part—namely, the citizens above—takes part in this mystery, so that through angelic ministries and supplications it may be offered, as though from a lofty altar, before the sight of the divine majesty. For if in that house there is an everlasting sacrifice of praise and an everlasting priest, there is also an everlasting altar in heaven—not bodily, but rational and intelligible—to which this offering is conveyed.

Therefore, at the very hour of the offering, Christ is to be believed present with the heavenly ministers who attend him, consecrating what has been set before him.

Father Ambrose says concerning this:

> “Do not doubt that an angel is present when Christ is present, when Christ is sacrificed.”

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Ambrose, on chapter 1 of Luke, no. 28.]

For this is the true offering, in which the Son is offered and the Father is reconciled. This is the true and eternal victim, because its power for him is true and eternal, and through it salvation is truly and eternally accomplished. This is the saving victim, full of reason and full of mystery, celebrated spiritually and presented in the purity of faith. For the hearts of the faithful had to be cleansed by a rational offering so that they might become heavenly.

### III.

Through this mystery, by participating in Christ, we are all one in him: “There is neither male nor female, neither slave nor free.” We receive this unity especially through communion in this sacrament, because “we, though many, are one bread and one body,” and all partake of the one bread.

For the unity of the Church in Christ is so great that, just as there is one faith, one baptism, and one altar, so everywhere there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood.

The statement that is read, “Christ through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God” (Heb. 9:14), and also, “Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Eph. 5:2), is daily renewed for us to the Father in this sacrament of the body and blood of the Son of God.

This body and this blood are not gathered from ears of grain and grapevines; rather, through a definite consecration they become mystical for us. They do not come into being when the creation of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his flesh and blood through the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit.

Everything, therefore, that is done in this offering is a mystery, which must be grasped by the purity of simple faith and cannot be comprehended by the subtlety of reason. One thing is seen, another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual, namely divine, fruit.

Christ fills the altar and prepares himself as food. He is slain but not killed; he is eaten but not diminished; he restores but is not exhausted; eaten, he lives, because he rose from the dead.

O wondrous and ineffable reality! O mystery of faith! All eat from him, yet each person eats him whole. He is divided into parts, yet he is whole in each part. Eaten by the whole people, he remains sound and entire. Entire in heaven, entire in the hearts of the faithful, he is eaten as life; he cleanses sins, gives life to the dead, strengthens the weak, and preserves the healthy.

### IV.

For this unique victim saves the soul from eternal destruction; through the mystery it represents to us that death of the Only-Begotten, who, although he lives in himself immortally and incorruptibly after rising from the dead, is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering.

His body is received there, his flesh is divided for the salvation of the people, and his blood is drunk by the faithful. But who can comprehend how this happens, or unfold the deep mysteries of this sacrifice, which continually imitates the passion of the Only-Begotten Son for our absolution?

Just as the sacrament of the Holy Trinity, so also the mystery of the Lord’s passion and death, which is repeatedly enacted in this offering, is equally necessary for salvation and is equally to be received and retained with a pure conscience.

No believer ought to doubt the truth of so great a mystery, which has been proved by so many testimonies and has sometimes been revealed to certain people by divine revelation.

But I, the least of all the faithful, doubt nothing about it in any respect—thanks be to God. With my whole heart I believe, and with the firm confession of my mouth I acknowledge, that this sacrament of divine and life-giving power is the true flesh of Christ, from which we are nourished, and his true blood, from which we are given drink.

For this victim is the body and blood of Christ, as blessed Peter says: “Of the undefiled and immaculate Lamb, Christ” (1 Pet. 1:19). That bread is the bread of life and eternal life; and that cup is the cup of perpetual salvation.

By these divine mysteries we are cleansed and sanctified, and we become participants in the one divinity, because God remains in us and we in God.

I hear what the Truth itself says about these matters, and without doubt I believe him, since he cannot lie. He answered the disputing Jews, who did not understand the bread of concord and said, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:53 ff.). To them he said in his own person:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats this bread will live forever.”

V. Now at last take heed, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved peoples, and do not pass by with deaf ear and uncircumcised heart what is said: “Whoever eats me”—clearly he indicates his own flesh, and not another’s. For if this were not so, that mystery could by no means be called so wondrous, ineffable, and incomprehensible. Whoever believes God to be omnipotent certainly believes that He can easily make of anything whatever He wills. If this were so, it could surely be grasped by the senses and expressed in words. But since the truth of so great a mystery is far otherwise than you, deceived by a heretical spirit, suppose, it is rightly called “the mystery of faith.” It cannot be comprehended by human understanding or weighed by subtle reasoning, but is apprehended by the most devout purity of simple faith.

Thus, speaking of this sacrament to certain disciples who did not believe, the Lord said: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life; but there are some among you who do not believe” (John 6:64–65). He showed that He had spoken of a great mystery when He said, “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” But when He added, “Yet there are some among you who do not believe,” He showed that this mystery belongs only to faith and to the faithful, who receive those words faithfully. Therefore they are spirit and life to them, because they give them spiritual life through spiritual understanding.

Faith has no merit when human reason supplies the proof. Faith is better than reason, because full perfection is attained only through faith, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9 according to the Septuagint), and elsewhere: “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Hebrews 10:38). For there are few who can firmly uphold what they believe. Hence many of those who thought themselves capable of doing so have shamefully gone astray, when, abandoning the humility of faith, they presumed to climb above themselves by reason.

Since it is certain that Christ lives immortally and incorruptibly in Himself, who can grasp by reason how He gives us His flesh to eat? This wondrous sacrifice shows us Christ not as one who is to be given, but as one already given; not as one to be slain, but as one already slain; and shows us not as those who are to be redeemed, but as those already redeemed—in truth, just as the sacrifices of the ancient Law foretold all these things that were to come. But He who was able to introduce His true body, which He raised from the tomb, to His disciples through closed doors, without corruption or any injury to Himself, can certainly give us His flesh to eat without injury or loss to Himself.

VI. This is He who entered the world without opening the virgin’s womb; who walked upon the sea with a real body; who caused a few perishable and visible morsels of food to increase beneath the teeth of those who ate them. Why, then, do you doubt, when He Himself says to you: “Whoever eats me, he too will live because of me” (John 6)? It is God who does great and wondrous things, unsearchable, whose number cannot be counted. Do not, I beg you, seek to investigate this by reason. The matter is above you; it greatly exceeds your powers. No one can know the mysteries of Christ’s body and blood, because of the majesty of the matter. Let wonders give faith to wonders, and incomprehensible things to incomprehensible things. If divine operation can be comprehended by reason, it is not so very wondrous.

Cease questioning. Believe with me only this: Christ is ministered to us every day. Christ is the food and drink of the Church: flesh, food; blood, drink. Whose? Christ’s. Hear Him Himself saying: “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26), and, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:48). “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Thus He commended that this should be done and repeated in the Church until the end of the age, when there will be rest for the saints—not still in the sacrament by which the Church is joined together in this present time, so long as what flowed from Christ’s side is being drunk, but in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that in the clear contemplation of unchanging truth we may need no mysteries.

Therefore do not doubt or deny when you see the creature of bread and wine taken from the simple produce of the earth. Behold the omnipotence of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, who by a mere command makes His body and blood from them, without any delay. But you should not believe that it is done without reason when you see wine mixed with water being offered. For from the side of Christ, who is the true vine, when it was pierced by the lance, water came forth together with blood. That blood was poured out for the remission of sins. That water tempers the saving cup. It both provides the bath and the drink. These are the sacraments of the Church, without which one does not enter into true life, because they must be performed and received with exceeding devotion, love, and great fear.

Approach these things faithfully, investigating nothing, because it is the mystery of faith. Approach peacefully, because it is the sacrament of unity: by faith and by works you are united to the mother Church. This is signified by bread made from many grains and wine made from many grapes. Approach with thanksgiving, because it is the mystery of charity.

VII. The offering of that bread and cup is the commemoration and proclamation of Christ’s death. It is performed not so much through words as through the mysteries themselves, by which that precious death is commended more deeply and powerfully to our minds. For this reason He entrusted this sacrament to His disciples at the end, so that the memory of such great love—with which He loved us and saved us in this way—might be impressed more deeply upon their minds and ours.

Approach with a chaste and pure heart. If you have fallen grievously, if you still have a desire to sin, produce fruits worthy of repentance. First cleanse your conscience. If you approach unclean, you may be burdened rather than lifted up. So great is the power of this sacrifice that the body and blood of Christ belong only to the righteous [not to sinners]. It cleanses sins, without which this life cannot be lived.

O sacrament of piety! Because Christ foresaw that we would sin after that salvation by which He redeemed us, this ineffable sacrament was instituted, so that by its sanctification we might be cleansed continually. Therefore, for some it brings remission of sins and an increase of virtues; for others, the weight of judgment and the greatest destruction.

Approach reverently and with great trembling, because it is not something else but Christ who is given to be eaten. Do not fear when you eat God. He Himself commanded it. When Christ is eaten, what else is eaten but life? If life is eaten, then what does not die is undoubtedly eaten.

Approach believing and clean. Eat life; drink life. Then the body and blood of Christ will be life for each person—that is, when what is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually eaten and spiritually drunk in the very truth. What is that drinking except living? What is that eating except being refreshed? But you are refreshed in such a way that what refreshes you does not fail. For you will have life, and life is complete.

Receive the Lord Jesus into the hospitality of your mind. Where His body is, there Christ truly is. At this, one filled with wonder and love for so great a mystery composed these verses:

> O thing exceedingly wondrous! Who could behold  
> The innermost depths of the mystery that Jesus instituted?  
>   
> Here the sacred Lamb, worthy of honor, is slain upon the altar;  
> He is cut into parts, yet He is wholly present in every part.  
>   
> His life-giving flesh is eaten, and His sacred blood is drunk;  
> Yet He Himself remains whole, living and abiding everywhere.

VIII. This, then, is my faith and hope, which is in me by the gift of God’s mercy. For this faith the blessed Peter commands that we should be especially prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason. This is certainly the faith that I hold in my heart and profess with my mouth; with it I desire to live and with it to stand before the tribunal of Christ. Through it I believe that I shall be absolved from my sins.

I earnestly desire and implore the Lord’s mercy that this faith may always work in me what is good, through humility and love, even to the end. This faith is the staff of my defense, with which I may strike the crafty and deceitful liars in speech who lie in wait for us as we pass along the road of this age. It is my shield, by which I may repel venomous animals and deadly little creatures bursting from their caves, and avoid allowing the sword of the enemy, which is destined for slaughter, to find any exposed limb in me, stripped of the protection of faith.

This is our little book; this is the treasure of my faith, which I found in the well-cultivated field of the Catholic Church. This is the faith that Christ’s grace taught me in the bosom of mother Church, and which from the time of my baptism He has always deigned to increase in me. Thus we believe before God, and thus we confess with our lips before human beings, so that our knowledge may make faith known to human beings, and His image may bear witness before God.

Protect and guard this faith, O my Christ, my one hope and the strength of my salvation, as the law established within me, lest that most pitiless robber and king of confusion ever steal it from my heart.

IX. In this little work of my faith, which I offer to your piety, if anything has been set down with insufficient skill or caution, I beg you, Inspector of hearts, to look not so much at what I have said as at what I intended to say. You know, Lord, from whom nothing is hidden, how purely and faithfully I desire with all my heart both to believe before you and to confess before your holy Church everything that belongs to the most upright standard of orthodox faith.

If what I have set forth concerning my faith is correct, I give thanks to you, to whom thanks are due. For if nothing good comes from us, we ought to claim no praise from our good works. But if all good things come from you, who alone are good, then certainly every good thing that can exist must be referred to you. If, however, what I have written should in any respect depart from the rule of faith, I am ready to be corrected by your servants, my masters. I am not so self-loving that I would insist on preferring what I have said to a better judgment.

No one is a heretic unless he becomes a heretic through contention. But whoever is not ashamed to be reproved and does not disdain correction cannot in any way be called a heretic.
