Yet I ask you, O Lord, teacher of teachers, that if anything in my heart or in my statements concerning my faith displeases you, you above all correct me and teach me, O Power and Wisdom of the Father. Lead me, according to your promise, into all truth through your Holy Spirit, who teaches your servants without the tumult of words.

You know, O merciful One, that just as truth stands in your eyes—which cannot be deceived in contemplating what is true and right—so I desire to believe and confess concerning all things. And even this seems insufficient to me, because I desire not only to believe rightly but also to live well. The one depends upon the other, and one without the other can in no way please you. O how beautiful is the joining together, if both exist at once!

For although I am a sinner, nevertheless, because of those thirty golden shields [Note: Rather, three hundred, from 1 Kings 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 9:16], I do not wish to make bronze ones. The person who substitutes bronze for gold is the one who produces the jingle of words without the effect of works; and though he appears devout in number, he is found guilty when the value of the weight is considered. For the shield is a form of faith, according to the Apostle (Ephesians 6:16).

Therefore I implore your mercy: circumcise from me all the vices of heart and body. Grant me an increase and perfection of virtues. Grant me to live well and to know many things. By your grace make me always steadfast in faith and effective in works, so that the faith my tongue speaks and my hand bears witness to in writing may be confessed by my life through pious actions and good conduct, here and everywhere, now and always, for ever and ever. Amen.

X. Thus far, O omnipotent God, Trinity, Inspector and Searcher of my heart, I have confessed the omnipotence of your majesty and the majesty of your omnipotence, the essence of your glory and the glory of your essence. Now, however, I confess with my mouth before you, for salvation, how you deigned to aid the human race at the end of time, just as I believe it in my heart for righteousness, so that the light of your countenance, marked upon us, may render to you the testimony of my faith.

You, God the Father, are nowhere read to have been sent. Concerning your Son, however, the Apostle writes: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son” (Galatians 4:4). When he says “sent,” he clearly shows that He came into this world having been sent. But what does the chief of the evangelists say concerning Him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through Him” (John 1:10)? He was therefore sent there through humanity, where He had always been through divinity.

I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that this mission of the Son, pregnant with many great mysteries, is the work of the whole Holy Trinity. Who, then, can say how and how greatly you loved us, merciful Father, who, because of your love for us, did not spare even your own Son, but delivered Him up for us impious ones?

Subject to you even unto the death of the cross, He was given for us as victor and victim—and therefore victor because victim. For us He became before you priest and sacrifice—and therefore priest because sacrifice. I rightly have a firm hope in Him that you will heal all my sicknesses through Him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us.

I could certainly have despaired if your Word, O God, had not become flesh and dwelt among us. But now I do not dare to despair, because, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to you through His death; how much more, having now been justified, shall we be saved from wrath through Him?

In His name I ask your mercy: make me through your Holy Spirit steadfast in faith and perseveringly effective in works, so that the faith which my tongue speaks and my hand bears witness to in writing may also be confessed in every way and in all things by my life and conduct, as long as I remain in these frail limbs.

XI. Most merciful and most kind God, lover of humankind, who through your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, wondrously restored us by your piety and goodness when we had been lost through our own fault: I give you thanks, and render abundant thanks from the depths of my heart, because you sent that same Son from your bosom into our public life, to save us sinners, who were then children of wrath and destruction.

I give you thanks for His holy incarnation and birth, and for His glorious mother, my lady, from whom He deigned to assume flesh for our salvation. I give you thanks for all His works and teachings, by whose example we are instructed and formed to lead a good life. I give you thanks for His passion and cross, for His insults and scourging, for His spitting and blows, for His death and resurrection, for His ascension into heaven, and for His seat of majesty at your right hand.

I give you thanks for the most sacred outpouring of His precious blood, by which we have been redeemed, and for the most holy and life-giving mystery of His body and blood, by which we are daily fed and given drink, washed and sanctified in your holy Church, and made participants in your one supreme divinity.

I render you thanks, most merciful One, for all your mercies, by which you deigned wondrously to aid us who were lost through that same Son of yours, our Savior and Restorer, who died because of our sins and rose again for our vivification, and now sits at your right hand and intercedes for us. He has compassion together with you, because He is God from you, the Father, coeternal and consubstantial with you; therefore He is able to save us forever.

But also according to that in which He is human, you have given Him all power in heaven and on earth, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in your glory, O God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).

Therefore I bless your holy name and glorify you with all my heart for that wondrous and unspeakable union of divinity and humanity in the unity of the person: not one God and another man, but one and the same God and man, man and God, your one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, existing from two substances and always subsisting in both without confusion.

XII. O wondrous mystery! O unspeakable exchange! O marvelous and ever-to-be-marveled-at kindness of divine propitiation! We were not worthy servants, and behold, we have become sons of God! Indeed, heirs of God, and co-heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). Whence is this granted to us, and what are we in relation to such things?

But I ask you, most merciful God the Father, through that supreme priest and true pontiff who offered Himself to you as a sacrifice, laying down His life for His flock—I ask you through Him not to permit us to be ungrateful for such great benefits or unworthy of so many mercies.

Pour your Holy Spirit from heaven into our hearts, and make us both understand and reverence so great a mystery as is fitting and proper. Make us attain the height of so great a dignity through pious actions and good conduct. Grant us persevering service in your will, and grant us at last the good things you have prepared for those who love you.

Ineffable God, of uncircumscribed nature, founder of all things and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who sent that same beloved Son from your bosom into our public life, to assume our life so that He might give us His, and that He might be perfect God from the Father and perfect man from His mother—wholly God and wholly man, one and the same Christ, eternal and temporal, immortal and destined to die, creator and created, strong and weak, nourisher and nourished, shepherd and sheep, dead in time but living with you forever—who gave the citizenship of life to those who love Him and promised it to them, and said to us: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you” (John 15:16):

I therefore beseech you, Lord, in the name of that beloved Son of yours, give me wisdom and understanding, so that I may know you, one God, essentially with that same Son of yours and the Holy Spirit, and apprehend you as three in person. Whatever is natural is undivided; whatever is personal is unconfused. Your Word willed to become the Son of Man, yet neither substance was changed into the other. Let no fourth person be added to the mystery of the Trinity. Let the substance of God and man be united, not confused.

XIII. Grant, Lord, through Him and with Him, your Son, because where there is one substance there is also one gift. Grant me, I beg, not to desire to know more or less than is fitting; not to mock the ignorant, nor envy the more learned; to return your gifts to you and sorrowfully rebuke my own errors; to hate what you hate and always love with my whole heart what you love; to fulfill works commanded by faith, but not to prefer works to faith.

Grant me patience, but not hardness concealed beneath the appearance of patience; to exercise strength temperately, not cruelly; to be shrewd, but not to become deceitful; to be obedient, not to wish to command; to apply my mind to simplicity, not dullness; never to yield to the proud, but for your sake to agree with the humble; to become innocent, not foolish; to be pious, not unjust; never to love my own evil, nor arrogantly condemn another’s; to despise myself more in my sins than my neighbor; to care for my own wounds, not wickedly to pry into those of others.

Grant that I judge no one by suspicions but by facts; that I preserve sincere peace with the peaceful and never feign peace with the wicked; that I hate not people but evil; that I do not wish people to perish, but resist the killers of souls and cut off the root of every evil; that when you inflict a scourge I do not recoil; that I do not grieve over the retribution of justice but over the cause of the offense; that I sympathize with those who suffer and rejoice with those who do good; that I weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice; that I entrust the necessities of life to your judgment; that I neither rejoice nor grieve over temporal things; and that I place my hope in you alone.

XIV. Make me, my God, I beg, always steadfast in faith and effective in works; persevering in good things, but not unalterably fixed in sins. Make me truthful without arrogance, humble without pretense, cheerful without frivolity, sad without dejection, just without error, firm without impiety, strict without cruelty, good without dullness, merciful without excess, gentle without boastfulness, peaceful without hostility, watchful without madness, fasting without weakness, constant without obstinacy, obedient without fear, fervent without intemperance, acting without rashness, solicitous without restlessness, free without insolence, gentle without sluggishness, quiet without laziness, silent without indignation, generous without grasping, cautious without craftiness, holy without pretense, and always devoted to your service without manifest vices or feigned virtues.

Make me provident in all things and discerning in everything. Grant me to live well and to know many things; make me learned through study, but not desirous of appearing arrogant. In your goodness, make me teachable in matters pertaining to knowledge. Grant sharpness of understanding, ease in learning, and steadfastness in retaining. Grant an educated tongue and eloquence of speech together with such great and profound humility that no place for accursed pride may appear in me.

Grant that I may grasp the twofold instrument of your Law and faithfully fulfill the two commandments; that the Law may agree with the Gospels, and the Gospels with the Law and the Prophets, without any disagreement, but teach that you have supplied things fitting to their times.

XV. Grant, Lord, a disposition and action like those pleasing to you, and an irrevocable determination to persevere in you; let me have no portion with unbelievers. Let me set forth you as the true God, to be feared, worshiped, and loved above all things that you have made and even above ourselves; let me recognize that you did not need any of the things you made, but have always been Lord even of things yet to come.

Let me not provoke you to anger by murmuring; let me please you and those of yours in whom you are well pleased; and where there is no fear because of your name, let me not be afraid. In praising beautiful things, let me admire you as the creator of all good things, yet never become entangled in such things through love of them.

Let me despise all mutable present things as though they were perishing, and tirelessly long for the everlasting goods of future blessedness. Let these be granted to the predestined by undeserved mercy, but denied to the obstinate by incomprehensible and irreproachable justice. Let me understand that no one can be saved without the faith in which we live within mother Church, but that the sons of perdition ought not to be saved.

Let me increase in spiritual knowledge without becoming inflated. Let my soul wish to die healthfully to myself and to live for you; let me effectively practice repentance for the sins committed, with great contrition of heart and a fountain of tears. Let me neither seek nor desire fugitive honors and perishing riches, but always love usefulness and final necessity.

Let me never be puffed up by the necessary services of those who serve or by the respect shown by my brothers; let me accomplish everything in charity, and attribute all that is accomplished to you, Lord, the worker of every good, without whom we can do nothing good.

XVI. Since, after receiving the grace of baptism and after the faith that I promised you—or rather, what is worse, after receiving this monastic habit—I have committed many things in heart, word, and deed, and have perpetrated innumerable evils through pride and desire, through anger and impatience, through fraud and sloth, through swelling and arrogance, I humbly implore your mercy, God the Father.

In the name of your beloved Son, be merciful to me, the most wretched sinner, who day and night, at every hour and moment, sin greatly before you, adding sins to sins without number, and lying shamefully in them, through my own fault.

Through that supreme priest and true pontiff who offered Himself to you as a living, pure, and spotless victim upon the altar of the cross for us wretched sinners—your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ—I ask you, most kindly lover of humankind, to have mercy on me, your most wretched and unworthy servant.

For I am not like the countless and manifold servants of yours who served you with the utmost devotion from their very cradles, turning neither to the right nor to the left. I am not like those who, after public sins, deserved through repentance to become devoted to you. I am not like certain Christian women, joined to husbands, who nevertheless serve you with the utmost devotion according to their knowledge. Nor am I like many of those who appear evil and perverse in the eyes of human beings.

Alas for me, unhappy man! How, walking with my neck held high, have almost all the days of my life been consumed in vanity! How have I passed my time in earthly and useless thoughts! What useful thing have I done throughout my life? Wretched me! Woe to me, most miserable, who bear the false name of monk while doing nothing worthy of this name and habit.

XVII. Nevertheless, Lord, if perhaps I do or shall do anything good through your freely given grace, I do not know with what purpose I do it or by what strict measure it is weighed by you. You know, from whom nothing is hidden, what has happened to me because of my sins: how, on the road by which I was walking, my enemies hid a snare for me.

When they were lying in wait for me, as I think, through a human being, alas, I lost the place of my beloved solitude, the friend of sorrow, quiet, and repentance, which I had always loved from my earliest age. Therefore my soul has been placed in great distress and sorrow, ignorant of your judgment concerning it, because I have not been able to find again the secret of my accustomed quiet and the opportunity for withdrawal to you, which once, through carelessness, I lost.

Even now I desire, sigh for, and seek this; but because my sins impede me, I cannot find it. Therefore, O terrifying God in your counsels concerning the sons of humankind, I humbly and trembling greatly implore your holy and boundless clemency, in the name of that same beloved Son of yours: you who do not wish anyone to perish but desire to save all, do not abandon me to the hand of my own counsel, or to the judgment of my own will, or to the power or temptation of demons, or to the mistaken judgment or harmful counsel of human beings.

But in accordance with your piety and goodness, and according to your most kind providence, which cannot be deceived in its ordering, dispose the days of my life here and everywhere, now and always, according to your good pleasure. Direct my heart, tongue, and actions continually through your Holy Spirit according to your will and in your mercy, so that, with you as my ruler and guide, inspiring and assisting me, beginning and perfecting, from whom all good things proceed and through whom they are brought to completion, I may always strive to think, speak, and do what pleases you in truth and finally leads me to eternal life.

Have mercy and grant this through that same Jesus, your Son, our Savior and Restorer, who died for our sins and rose again for our vivification.

XVIII. Through that supreme priest and true pontiff who offered Himself to you as a sacrifice, I ask you: look upon me and have mercy on me; hear my prayer and grant me your grace because of the abundance of your goodness. Grant me forgiveness for my past evils, amendment concerning my present ones, and continual protection and caution against future faults.

Grant me place and time, and fruits worthy of repentance. Grant me a contrite and humbled heart; grant the grace of tears; grant light in my heart and strength in my body. Grant that fire which you sent when you came upon the earth and which you desire to burn. Grant me to burn with the fire of charity, to shine with the splendor of obedience, to glow with love’s ardor, not to perish amid dangers, to emerge safely from dangers, to hasten toward your sweetness, to come peacefully to the vision of you, to be satisfied forever with the manifestation of your vision, and to praise you without end throughout the eternity of ages.

Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me, enlightening my eyes so that I may see by what path I may reach you; strengthening my steps in you, so that I may not transgress the way; opening my mouth so that I may be able to speak about you, who gave me the desire to speak of your things, however much I have been able.

And because love of neighbor is joined to love of you, grant me to exercise that service which may bring about his salvation and attain to the praise and glory of your name. Amen.

[Col. 1097]

# DISPUTATION OF BOYS BY QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS

## 418. PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 1097D]

This work, which we present second among the doubtful writings of the blessed Alcuin, we discovered in a very ancient manuscript codex from Salzburg, nine hundred years old, marked number 67. Since no author’s name had been prefixed there, we hesitated for some time whether it should be attributed to the blessed Alcuin or to another writer of that age. Nor do we yet dare to pronounce anything with certainty about it, although there are weighty arguments in favor of Alcuin, which we submit for learned judgment.

First, the same codex contains other unquestionably authentic works of Alcuin; and after the present treatise there is found, written in the same hand, his Commentary on the Penitential Psalms, etc., together with a letter to Archbishop Arno.

Second, the style and method of this treatise are so similar to Alcuin’s style and method—like an egg to an egg, as I think no one who has worked through the writings of that celebrated man will deny—that no other writer of the age in which we have said this little work was composed, nor any earlier writer, can be identified whose style and method correspond more closely to it.

Moreover, this writing contains, in dialogue form, that brief Commentary on the words of Genesis, “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness,” which the learned Quercetanus published, removing the dialogue form, after his exposition of Genesis from a manuscript of Sirmondus, where it stood under the name of Alcuin [Note: See volume I of this edition, column 565].

It seems probable to us that this very little commentary was extracted by someone for his own particular use from this Dialogue, with the title prefixed: “Sayings of the blessed Albinus the Levite on the words of Genesis,” etc. I suspect that the same happened with other writings inserted here—for example, “On the Properties of the Names Attributed to God in the Scriptures,” which Trithemius lists among Alcuin’s writings in Book II of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26; and the Explanations of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer, which Yepes attributes to Alcuin in volume III, page 426, of his *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*.

It may, however, seem strange to someone that no one should have remembered this little work, which nevertheless, because of the excellence and selection of the subjects it treats, could and ought to have been of great use in Alcuin’s age and thereafter. But I attribute this to the negligence of those scribes who, when listing the little works of the blessed man, supplied bare titles, without mentioning the beginning or end of the contents or their method.

Possevinus and others count among Alcuin’s writings: “One book of Dialogues for his disciples”; “A Little Mirror of Ecclesiastical Doctrine”; “One book On Ecclesiastical Doctrines”; and “One book of Sentences.”

In the Laurentian Medicean Library, shelf 12, number 22, according to Montefaucon, *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, page 270, after the three books of Alcuin the Levite to Emperor Charles on the Trinity, there is a work entitled *Recapitulation of the Catholic Faith through Questions and Answers*. Under these titles, or under one of them, our little work—or *Disputation of Boys by Questions and Answers*—could easily be concealed.

And perhaps this treatise is that *Book of Sentences* which Trithemius, Possevinus, Helinandus, and others list among Alcuin’s writings. For the title of this treatise is: “Here begins the First Sentence on the Works of the Six Days.”

From these considerations, I think learned men will judge that the present little work could rightly be counted, if not among Alcuin’s certainly genuine works, at least among his doubtful works. From its beginning it is not obscure that a prologue or dedicatory letter, certainly prefixed in the autograph, is missing.

Almost the whole little work, moreover, is compiled—a form of writing familiar to our Alcuin—from the books of *Origins*, or *Etymologies*, and other treatises of Saint Isidore of Seville. We have carefully indicated these sources and have sometimes corrected passages that had been corrupted in the manuscript.

## 419. CHAPTER ONE

### IN THE DIVINE NAME OF THE TRINITY, THE FIRST SENTENCE ON THE WORKS OF THE SIX DAYS BEGINS, WITH ITS QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS FOR BOYS

**Questioner.** Since human frailty neither dares nor can begin the course of reasoning elsewhere than from the beginning of the Creator’s work, therefore, if it pleases your lordship to listen, we wish, insofar as it is granted by Him who created all things, to set forth before you something concerning the distinctions of the works of the six days.

Come, fellow student: since, as I have said—and you yourself know—we can neither dare nor manage to extend the beginning of our disputation higher, if it seems good to you, let us begin from that same beginning and, as the Lord deigns to grant, discuss the distinctions of those aforesaid six days and their works.

**Answerer.** I think that nowhere could we better begin our disputation than with the first creation itself and with the prescribed sacred and perfect number, as you asserted, which is perfect in every respect.

**Questioner.** Since you have judged thus, let it be so. But first I ask you to say how it is established that it is perfect.

**Answerer.** It is called perfect because it is completed by its parts.

What is the reason? **Answer:** It has one, which is its sixth part; two, which is its third; three, which is its half. Thus one, two, and three make six, whose perfection is thereby complete.

**Question:** Since you have judged that our discussion should begin from that beginning, tell me in which beginning almighty God established creation itself: in the beginning of time, or in the beginning of the Word of God, which is the only-begotten Son of God?

**Answer:** Not in the beginning of time, but in the beginning of the Word of God, concerning which the blessed evangelist John also says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1). Hence the Lord himself, when those asking “Who are you?” questioned him, replied: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25). In this beginning, therefore, almighty God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them.

**Question:** Now I want you to explain to me in order all the distinctions among the individual works of the aforementioned days.

**Answer:** On the first day, light was made from nothing; on the second, the firmament in the midst of the waters; on the third, the forms of the sea and the earth, together with those things that are rooted in the earth; on the fourth, the lights of heaven, from the light made on the first day; on the fifth, aquatic creatures and birds; and on the sixth, the remaining animals from the earth. Man, however, consists in the flesh of earth, but in the soul of nothing—concerning whom, when he was about to be created, God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

## CHAPTER II. ON THE NATURE OF MAN

**Question:** Since the Creator of all things deigned to create man in his own image and likeness, let us inquire carefully how and in what manner man is said to have been created in his image.

**Answer:** Let us do as you say, since it is necessary for us to know, insofar as he grants it, how we were created by him, so that we may be better able to praise his mercy. For, so to speak, if all our members could have been turned into tongues, we would in no way have been able to offer him worthy praises for the mere creation by which he deigned to create us.

**Question:** I agree entirely with what you say, but I humbly ask that you not refuse to indicate to me, insofar as you are able, how and in what manner we should confess that we were created by him.

**Answer:** According to what I have read, I shall do what you have asked. [Note: These are Alcuin’s *Dicta* on the passage of Genesis, “Let us make man,” etc., vol. I, col. 565, with the dialogue form omitted.]

The dignity of the human condition is recognized as so great that man was created not merely by the spoken command of the one commanding, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the holy Trinity and by the work of divine Majesty. Concerning this he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). The Creator granted this to man so that man might love him more ardently, the more wonderfully he understood himself to have been created by him. Nor did he grant him only this—that he fashioned him by the counsel of the holy Trinity—but also that he created him in his own image and likeness, a gift he granted to no other creature [Latin printed *alio*; read *alii*].

**Question:** It is true, as you assert; but I beg you to explain to me how he created man in his image.

**Answer:** First, he created him in his image—a matter that we must consider in the nobility of the inner man. Just as God, one and always wholly present everywhere, gives life to, moves, and governs all things, as the Apostle confirms: “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28), so the soul is wholly active throughout its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it.

**Question:** Tell me whether the same soul, which you have called the inner man, is greater in certain larger members of its body and smaller in the smaller members; or whether it occupies some particular place in that body.

**Answer:** It occupies no particular place there, nor is it greater in the larger members and smaller in the smaller ones; rather, it is wholly present in the smallest and wholly present in the largest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God that the soul possesses in itself.

**Question:** Can the same soul also possess an image of the Trinity?

**Answer:** Certainly it can.

**Question:** How?

**Answer:** Just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, in its own manner, is, lives, and knows.

**Question:** Can it have another corresponding structure in this respect?

**Answer:** It can.

**Question:** How?

**Answer:** There is another trinity in it, by which it was created in the image of its Creator, the perfect and supreme Trinity that exists in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Although the soul is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses three dignities within itself.

**Question:** What are these?

**Answer:** Understanding, will, and memory. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”—that is, with all your understanding, all your will, and all your memory.

**Question:** In what way do these correspond to one another?

**Answer:** Just as the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so will is begotten from understanding, and from both of these memory likewise proceeds. This can easily be understood, because without these three the soul cannot be perfect; nor can any one of these three, insofar as its blessedness is concerned, be complete without the other two.

**Question:** I still desire to hear from you about the same subject.

**Answer:** I shall continue to tell you what I know. Just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God possessing three persons, so the soul is understanding, the soul is will, and the soul is memory—not, however, three souls in one body, but one soul possessing three dignities. In these three our inner man wonderfully bears the image of God in its nature. From these, as from the soul’s more excellent dignities, we are commanded to love the Creator, so that insofar as he is understood, he may be loved, and insofar as he is loved, he may always be held in memory. Understanding of him alone is not sufficient unless the will is made active in his love; nor are these two sufficient unless memory is added, by which God may always remain in the mind of the one who understands and loves him. And just as there can be no moment in which man does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy, so there ought to be no moment in which memory does not possess him as present.

**Question:** What you have said about the image is sufficient for this occasion; but explain how we were created in the likeness of God.

**Answer:** I shall do so insofar as I am able by the Creator’s generosity. Just as God the Creator, who created us in his likeness, is love, is good, just and patient, gentle and pure, and merciful, together with the other marks of holy virtues that are read of him, so man was created to possess love, to be good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful. The more abundantly we possess these virtues, the closer we are to God and the greater the likeness of our Creator that we bear.

**Question:** But if—which God forbid—one of us wanders astray through the byways of vices and the divisions caused by crimes, degenerating from this most noble likeness of his Creator, what do you assert will happen to him?

**Answer:** May this never happen! For if it should perhaps occur, what else could happen except that what is written in us should be fulfilled: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). What greater honor could man have had than to be created in the likeness of his Maker and adorned with the same garments of virtue with which the Creator also is adorned? Of him it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed with beauty” (Ps. 92:1)—that is, he is adorned with the splendor of every virtue and the beauty of complete goodness. Conversely, what greater disgrace or more unhappy misery could there be for him than, having lost the glory of the likeness of his Creator, to descend into the likeness of shapeless and irrational beasts?

Therefore, dearest brother, consider more carefully the excellence of our first creation, recognize the venerable image of the holy Trinity, and strive to possess the honor of the divine likeness in which you were created, nobility of character, the practice of virtue, and the dignity of good conduct and merits. Thus, when he appears as he is, you may then appear like him who wonderfully created you in his likeness in the first Adam and restored you even more wonderfully in the second. [Note: Here Alcuin’s *Dicta* end in his works, at the place cited.]

Let this suffice concerning the image and likeness.

**Question:** Having completed the account of the image and likeness of the inner man—which, as you have explained thus far, takes precedence over all creatures—carefully explain what his nature is according to the account of the outer man, and what is meant by the nature itself.

**Answer:** [Note: From Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XI, chapter 1.] “Nature” is so called because it makes something be born; for it has the power of generating and making. Some [Latin *quidam*; manuscript *quaedam*] have said that nature is God, from whom all things were created and exist.

**Question:** What is a genus?

**Answer:** “Genus” is derived from *gignere*, “to beget”; its derivative name comes from the earth, from which [Latin *ex qua*; manuscript *ex quo*] all things are begotten.

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** For *gē* in Greek means “earth.”

**Question:** From where is “life” derived?

**Answer:** “Life” is so called because of vigor, or because it possesses the power of being born and growing. Hence trees are also said to have life, because they are born and grow.

**Question:** From where is “man” derived?

**Answer:** Man is so called because he was made from *humus*, earth, just as it is said in Genesis: “And God created man from the earth’s soil” (Gen. 2:7). [Another reading: “from clay.”] In an extended usage, the whole man is spoken of as consisting of both substances—that is, of the union of soul and body—for properly speaking, “man” is derived from *humus*.

**Question:** What is man called in Greek?

**Answer:** The Greeks called man *anthrōpos*, because, raised up from the earth, he looks upward toward the contemplation of his Maker. The poet Obidius [read *Ovidius*, Ovid] indicates this when he says (*Metamorphoses* I.84):

> While the other animals look down upon the earth,
>
> He gave man a face raised high,
>
> And commanded him to look upon heaven
>
> And lift his upright countenance toward the stars.

**Question:** Why is man said to look toward heaven?

**Answer:** He looks toward heaven with an erect posture so that he may seek God, not so that he may direct his attention toward the earth like cattle, which nature fashioned bent forward and obedient to the belly.

**Question:** Is man simple or twofold?

**Answer:** Man is twofold: inner and outer.

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** The inner man is the soul, and the outer man is the body.

**Question:** From where did the soul receive its name?

**Answer:** The soul received its name from the pagans [Isidore: “from the winds”], because it is wind; hence wind is called *anemos* in Greek. Since we draw air in through the mouth, we seem to live [manuscript: “to see”]. But this is plainly false.

**Question:** For what reason?

**Answer:** Because the soul is generated long before air can be drawn in [editorially supplied: “through the mouth”], since it already lives in the mother’s womb. Therefore the soul is not air, as some have thought, because [Latin *quia*; manuscript *quae*] they were unable to conceive of its incorporeal nature.

**Question:** Tell me whether spirit is the same as soul.

**Answer:** The evangelist declares that spirit is the same as soul when he says: “I have power to lay down my soul, and again I have power to take it up” (John 10:18). Concerning this same soul of the Lord, at the time of his Passion, the evangelist likewise said: “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). Therefore “to give up the spirit” means nothing other than “to lay down the soul.”

**Question:** Why is it called “soul”?

**Answer:** It is called soul because it lives.

**Question:** Why is it called “spirit”?

**Answer:** It is called spirit either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes into the body.

**Question:** What is the difference between *animus* and *anima*?

**Answer:** *Animus* is the same as *anima*, but *anima* is associated with life, while *animus* is associated with deliberation. Hence philosophers say that life can remain even without *animus*, and that the soul can endure without mind, which is why there are the mindless. For [editorially supplied: “they wish”] “mind” to be called so that one may know, and “soul” so that one may will.

**Question:** From where is “mind” derived?

**Answer:** Mind is so called because it stands out in the soul, or because it remembers. Hence those who forget are called mindless. Therefore it is not the soul itself, but what excels in the soul, that is called mind, as though it were its head or eye. Hence man himself is called the image of God according to the mind. All these aspects are so joined to the soul that they are one thing; for the soul has received different names according to the effects of its functions. Memory, too, is mind, which is why those who forget are called mindless.

**Question:** For what reason?

**Answer:** When it gives life to the body, it is soul; when it wills, it is *animus*; when it knows, it is mind; when it recalls, it is memory; when it judges what is right, it is reason; when it breathes, it is spirit; when it perceives something, it is sense. For this reason *animus* is also called sense, with reference to the things it perceives, and from this *sententia*—judgment or opinion—takes its name.

**Question:** From where is “body” derived?

**Answer:** It is called body because, once corrupted, it perishes; for it is dissoluble and mortal, and must eventually be dissolved.

**Question:** From where is “flesh” derived?

**Answer:** Flesh is called so from *creare*, “to create.”

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** The seed is the male’s generative material, from which the bodies of animals and human beings are conceived; hence parents are also called creators.

**Question:** Of what causes does flesh consist?

**Answer:** Flesh is composed of the four elements.

**Question:** Which ones?

**Answer:** Earth is in the flesh, air in the breath, moisture in the blood, and fire in the vital heat. The elements each possess their own portion in us, and when the structure is dissolved, each receives what is owed to it. [Isidore: “by which the structure is dissolved.”]

**Question:** What is the difference between flesh and body?

**Answer:** “Flesh” and “body” signify different things.

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** There is always body in flesh, but there is not always flesh in body.

**Question:** For what reason?

**Answer:** Flesh is what lives, and is therefore also body; body that does not live is not flesh. [Isidore: “is both body and flesh.”]

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** “Body” is said either of what is dead after life, or of what has been formed without life. Sometimes there is also body without flesh even when it has life, as in the case of grass and wood.

**Question:** How many bodily senses are there?

**Answer:** Five.

**Question:** What are they called?

**Answer:** Sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

**Question:** Which of these are opened and closed, and which remain open?

**Answer:** The eyes and mouth are opened and closed; the ears and nostrils remain open.

**Question:** Why are they called senses?

**Answer:** They are called senses because through them the soul, with the utmost subtlety, moves the whole body by the power of perception. Hence they are also called “present things,” because they are before the senses, just as things that are before the eyes are present to the eyes.

**Question:** What is sight?

**Answer:** Sight is what philosophers call the vitreous humor.

**Question:** From what does sight arise?

**Answer:** Some assert that sight is produced either by the outermost heavenly light or by an inner luminous spirit coming from the brain through narrow passages, emerging into the air after penetrating the membranes, and then producing sight through the commingling of similar matter.

**Question:** From where is “sight” derived?

**Answer:** Sight is so called because it is more lively, superior, and faster than the other senses, and because it has greater vigor—just as memory is more powerful among the other functions of the mind. For sight is closer to the brain, from which everything flows. Consequently, we say that we “see” things that belong to the other senses as well, as when we say, “See how it sounds,” or “See how it tastes,” and similarly in other cases.

**Question:** Why is hearing so called?

**Answer:** Hearing is so called because it draws in voices—that is, because it receives sounds when the air is struck.

**Question:** Why is smell so called?

**Answer:** It is called smell as though it were the touch of the odor of the air [Isidore: “the drawing-in (*attractus*) of the odor of the air”]. For odor is perceived when the air is touched; similarly, *olfactus* means that one is affected by odors.

**Question:** From where is taste derived?

**Answer:** Taste is so called from the throat.

**Question:** Why is touch so called?

**Answer:** Touch is so called because it handles and touches, and spreads the power of sensation through all the limbs. For by touch we test whatever we cannot judge by the other senses.

**Question:** How many kinds of touch are said to exist?

**Answer:** Two.

**Question:** What are they?

**Answer:** Either something comes from outside and strikes us, or it arises within the body itself so that it may be perceived.

**Question:** Does each sense possess its own nature, or not?

**Answer:** It certainly does.

**Question:** For what reason?

**Answer:** What is to be seen is grasped by the eyes; what is to be heard, by the ears; what is soft and hard is assessed by touch; flavor by taste; and odor is drawn in through the nostrils.

**Question:** What is the first part of man?

**Answer:** The first part of the body is the head.

**Question:** Why is it so called?

**Answer:** This name was given to it because all the senses and nerves take their beginning from it, and from it arises the whole source of vitality. All the senses appear there; hence it somehow represents the person of the soul itself, which governs the body.

**Question:** What is the crown of the head? [So in the manuscript.]

**Answer:** It is the part where the hair of the head is gathered and in which the hair is turned; hence it is so called.

**Question:** What is the skull?

**Answer:** The skull is so called from the bare bones, through a process of loss or stripping; the word is pronounced in the neuter gender.

**Question:** What is the back of the head?

**Answer:** The occiput is the rear part of the head, as though it were opposite the front of the head, or because it is the head turned backward.

**Question:** From where are “hairs” derived?

**Answer:** Hair is so called as though it were “the hairs of the head.” It was made both to provide beauty and to protect the brain against cold and defend it from the sun.

**Question:** Why are hairs called *pili*?

**Answer:** They are called *pili* from the skin from which they emerge, just as *pilum* is named from *pila*, where pigment is pounded.

**Question:** From where is *caesaries* derived?

**Answer:** *Caesaries* is so called from cutting, and therefore belongs only to men.

**Question:** Why to men and not to women?

**Answer:** Because it is fitting for a man to be shorn, but not fitting for a woman.

**Question:** What is *comae*?

**Answer:** Properly speaking, *comae* are uncut hair, and the word is Greek.

**Question:** For what reason?

**Answer:** The Greeks call hair *kaimoi*—perhaps **κόμαι**, from **κόπτω**, “I cut”—from cutting. Hence they also say *keirein* (**κείρειν**), “to shear.” From this come the words *cirri* and what those same Greeks call *mallon*—perhaps from **μαλλός**, “long wool.”

**Question:** From where are *crines* derived?

**Answer:** *Crines* properly belong to women. They are so called because they are divided by ribbons; hence the ribbons are called *discriminalia*, from which the divided locks are tied back.

**Question:** What are the temples? [So in the manuscript; correctly, *tempora*.]

**Answer:** The temples are the parts lying beneath the skull on the right and left.

**Question:** Why are they so called?

**Answer:** They are so named because they move, and by that mobility seem to change like periods of time separated by intervals.

**Question:** Why is the face so called?

**Answer:** *Facies* is derived from *effigies*, “image,” for in it the whole figure of a human being is found, as well as the recognition of each individual person. [Perhaps: “for there the whole figure of the human being is made.”]

**Question:** Why is the countenance so called?

**Answer:** The countenance is so called because through it the will of the mind is displayed.

**Question:** In what way?

**Answer:** According to the will, it changes into various movements, and thus the two differ from one another. For “face” is understood simply of each person’s natural appearance, whereas “countenance” signifies the quality of the emotions.

**Question:** From where did the forehead receive its name?

**Answer:** The forehead is named from the openings of the eyes. By its appearance it expresses a certain image of the mind and the movement of the intellect, whether it is joyful or sad.

Let this suffice for you, my brother, for this occasion concerning the account of human nature. [Thus far from Isidore.]

## CHAPTER III. ON SPIRITS

**Question:** This is sufficient for me. But if you please, let us return to the account of spirit, about which you said something a little earlier, and investigate, insofar as we are able with God’s permission, how many [manuscript: *quod*, for expected *quot*] spirits the same Creator of all things created.

**Answer:** It is a difficult matter to investigate, but let us nevertheless do as you say.

**Question:** Tell me, then, how many vital spirits are believed to exist.

**Answer:** According to what I have read, almighty God created three vital spirits.

**Question:** What are they?

**Answer:** One is not covered with flesh; another is covered with flesh but does not die with the flesh; the third is covered with flesh and dies with the flesh.

**Question:** Now explain to me which of these is not covered with flesh; which is covered with flesh but does not die with the flesh; and which is covered with flesh and dies with the flesh. Also, to which creature does each belong?

**Answer:** The spirit that is not covered with flesh belongs to the angels; the spirit that is covered with flesh but does not die with the flesh belongs to human beings; and the spirit that is covered with flesh and dies with the flesh belongs to beasts and all irrational animals.

**Question:** Are there more spirits, or not?

**Answer:** There certainly are.

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** A part of the soul is also called spirit—namely, the rational mind, which is the eye of the soul. It is capable of gifts of spirits [Latin *spirituum*; perhaps *spiritualium*, “spiritual gifts”] and receives the grace of divine indwelling by sharing in it, as the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23). And again: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Gal. 5:25). And likewise: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:9).

**Question:** Is there anything further for inquiry?

**Answer:** Yes.

**Question:** What?

**Answer:** The whole soul is also generally called spirit, as it is written of the Lord in the Gospel: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). And in the Psalm concerning human beings: “Their spirit went out” (Ps. 14:4). And Ecclesiastes says: “Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of Adam ascends upward?” (Eccl. 3:21). As I said above, the souls of all animals are called spirits, concerning which the same Ecclesiastes says: “Who knows whether the spirit of beasts descends downward?” At the end of the Psalms, as has already been said: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150:6). For in Hebrew it reads: “Let everything that breathes praise the Lord.” And in Genesis: “All flesh that has the spirit of life” (Gen. 7:15). The audible breath in man is also called spirit, as the Apostle says: “For if I pray with the tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit” (1 Cor. 14:14).

**Question:** I would still like to hear from you about the nature of spirits.

**Answer:** I shall continue to tell you what I know. The breath of the winds is also called spirit, as it is written: “The spirit of storms” (Ps. 10:7; Ps. 148:8). And elsewhere: “With a mighty spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. 47:8). The Lord also brought a spirit over the earth, and the waters were diminished (Gen. 8:1). Hostile powers are also called spirits, as it is written: “An evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Sam. 18:10). And again: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a man” (Matt. 12:43). The movement of the mind, whether toward excitation or toward submission, is also called spirit.

**Question:** How does it refer to excitation?

**Answer:** To excitation, as we have said [perhaps: “as we say”], when we speak of a man swollen with spirit; or as when we speak of the spirit of pride and the spirit of vainglory.

**Question:** How does it refer to submission?

**Answer:** Also to submission, in a positive sense, as in: “In a spirit of humility,” and “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). The Apostle says of the word of God that it reaches “to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4:12). In keeping with this usage, divine admonition is also called spirit, as it is written: “Behold, I will pour out my spirit upon you and make my words known to you” (Prov. 1:23). Again, the wicked are said to have perished when God breathed upon them and to have been consumed by the spirit of his anger. This is not said properly of God, however, but metaphorically, transferred to God from human emotions.

**Question:** Are other spirits also found?

**Answer:** It is also written concerning the sun: “The spirit goes, going round and round.” Or, as another translation has it: “The spirit, surveying all things in its circuit, proceeds” (Eccl. 1:6). The truth of the foregoing usages, in which things are called spirits, is evident; but concerning the statement that the sun is called spirit, it does not explain why it is so called, as the blessed Augustine testifies when he says: “Let those who can, say,” and so forth.

**Question:** Since these matters have been completed, I ask your charity to explain truthfully whether I may venture to investigate several spirits in the holy Scriptures.

**Answer:** Certainly.

**Question:** For what reason?

**Answer:** The supreme Creator and life-giver, almighty God, is called Spirit because of his spiritual and incorporeal nature, as the Truth says in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). The gifts of grace are also called spirits, as the evangelist testifies in reporting the Lord’s words: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly”; he adds: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:38). In this sense the Holy Spirit is said to dwell in minds, as the Apostle says: “Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit.” And shortly afterward: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20). And elsewhere: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Let this suffice concerning spirits.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE TEN NAMES OF GOD

[Note: Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Book II, chapter 26, lists among Alcuin’s writings one book, *On the Proper Names Attributed to God in the Scriptures*.]

**Question:** Having set forth the account of spirits, I now want you to tell me by what names God is called in the sacred Scriptures . . . [Supplement: “God is called.”]

**Answer:** God is read to have ten names.

**Question:** What are they?

**Answer:** The first name of God among the Hebrews is called *El*; the second, *Eloi*; the third, *Eloe*; the fourth, *Sabaoth*; the fifth, *Elion*; the sixth, *Eiei*; the seventh, *Adonai*; the eighth, *Ja*; the ninth, the tetragrammaton, which is *Jode Jode*; and the tenth, *Sadai*.

**Question:** Now I ask you to explain to me the meaning and interpretation of all those names you have mentioned—why they are so called.

**Answer:** According to what I have read, I shall do what you ask. [Note: From Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VII, chapter 1.]

The first name of God among the Hebrews, as I said, is *El*. Some have interpreted it as “God,” while others, expressing its etymology, have interpreted it as *Chyros* [perhaps Greek **ἰσχυρός**, “strong”], because he is not overcome by any weakness but is strong and sufficient to accomplish everything.

The second name is *Eloi*, and the third *Eloe*; both are translated into Latin as “God.” The name itself has been transferred into Latin from a Greek designation, for God is called *Theos* in Greek, meaning “fear.” Hence the name “God” was derived, because he is feared by those who worship him. Properly speaking, “God” is the name of the Trinity, referring to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The other names placed below also refer to this Trinity.

The fourth name of God is *Sabaoth*, which is translated into Latin as “of armies” or “of powers.” Concerning this, the angels say in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of powers” (Ps. 23:8). There are many powers in this ordering, such as angels, archangels, principalities, and powers, together with all the orders of the heavenly host; yet he is Lord of them all. For they are all beneath him and subject to his dominion.

The fifth is *Elion*, which is translated into Latin as “Most High,” who is above the heavens, as it is written of him: “The Lord is Most High; his glory is above the heavens” (Ps. 112:4). He is called “Most High” because he is exceedingly high; for *ex* is used to mean “very,” as in “eminent,” that is, “very exalted.”

The sixth is *Eiei*, that is, “He who is.” For God alone, who is eternal, truly possesses the name of being, since he alone has no beginning of existence. This name was conveyed to holy Moses through an angel. When Moses asked what the name of the one who commanded him to go to the people to free them from Egypt was, he answered: “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). In comparison with the one who truly is, because he is unchangeable, things that have been made and are changeable are as though they were not. What is said to have been is no longer; what is said “will be” is not yet. God, however, knows only being; he does not know having been or being in the future. The Father alone, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, truly is. Compared with his being, our being is non-being. Hence in conversation we say, “God lives,” because the essence that is life lives, and death does not possess it.

The seventh is *Adonai*, generally translated “Lord,” because he rules over every creature, or because every creature serves his dominion. Thus he is Lord and God, either because he rules over all things or because he is feared by all.

The eighth is *Ja*, which is used only of God and is also heard as the final syllable of *Alleluia*.

The ninth is the tetragrammaton, that is, “of four letters,” which is used properly among the Hebrews of God: *Jode*, that is, two *Ja*’s, which, doubled, form that ineffable and glorious name of God. It is called ineffable not because it cannot be pronounced, but because it cannot in any way be delimited by human sense and understanding. Since nothing worthy can be said about him, he is ineffable.

The tenth is *Sadai*, that is, “almighty.” He is called almighty because he can do all things—not because he can suffer what he does not will, but because he can do what he wills. If the former were possible, he would by no means be almighty. He does whatever he wills, and for this reason he is almighty. He is also almighty because all things that exist everywhere belong to him; for he alone possesses dominion over the whole world.

**Question:** Is it permissible to investigate more names of God, or not?

**Answer:** It is certainly permissible.

**Question:** How so?

**Answer:** Certain other names are also applied substantially to God, such as immortal, incorruptible, unchangeable, and eternal; hence he is rightly placed above every creature. He is also called invisible, impassible, simple, incorporeal, immeasurable, and perfect.

**Question:** Why is he called immortal?

**Answer:** He is called immortal, as it is written of him: “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Tim. 6:16), because there is no change in his nature. For every mutability may properly be called mortality. Accordingly, the soul too is said to die—not because it is changed and turned into a body or into some other substance, but because, within its own substance, whatever is now or was in another condition is found to be mortal insofar as it has ceased to be what it was. Thus God alone is called immortal, because he alone is unchangeable.

**Question:** Why is he called incorruptible?

**Answer:** He is called incorruptible because he cannot be corrupted, dissolved, or divided. Whatever can be divided can also perish; he can neither be divided nor destroyed, and therefore he is incorruptible.

**Question:** From where is he called unchangeable?

**Answer:** He is unchangeable because he always remains and does not know how to change. He does not increase, because he is perfect, nor diminish, because he is eternal.

**Question:** In what way is he eternal?

**Answer:** Because he is without time; he has neither beginning nor end. Hence he is also everlasting, since he is eternally eternal.

**Question:** From where is he called eternal?

**Answer:** Some believe that *aeternus* is derived from *aether*, because heaven is regarded as his dwelling. Hence the statement: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 113:16), and so forth.

**Question:** Why is he called invisible?

**Answer:** Because the Trinity has never appeared to mortal eyes in its own substance, except through the appearance of a subordinate, bodily creature [Latin *eamdemque*; Isidore *ejusdemque*]. For no one can see the manifestation of God’s essence and live, as was also said to Moses. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). He is an invisible reality and therefore must be sought not with the eye but with the heart.

**Question:** How is he impassible?

**Answer:** Because he is affected by none of the disturbances to which human frailty is subject. No passions touch him, such as lust, anger, desire, fear [Isidore: “pain”], grief, envy, and the rest by which the human mind is troubled. When God is said to become angry, to be jealous, or to grieve, this is said according to our customary usage. There is no disturbance in God; with him there is perfect tranquility.

**Question:** Why is he called simple?

**Answer:** He is called simple either because he does not lose what he possesses, or because he himself is not one thing and what is in him another. In a human being, being is one thing and knowing another: a person can exist without being wise. God, however, possesses essence and wisdom, but what he possesses, that he is. Everything is one in him, and therefore he is simple, because nothing accidental exists in him; what he is and what is in him are essentially the same, except insofar as something is related to a particular person. He is the supreme good because he is unchangeable. A creature is good, but not the supreme good, because it is changeable; although it is indeed good, it cannot also be supreme.

**Question:** Why is he called incorporeal?

**Answer:** God is called incorporeal, or non-corporeal, so that he may be believed or understood to be spirit and not body. For when he is called spirit, his substance is signified.

**Question:** Why is he called immeasurable?

**Answer:** Because he encompasses all things and is encompassed by no one; rather, all things are confined within his power.

Inter. Why is he called perfect? Resp. Because nothing can be added to him. Nevertheless, perfection is spoken of with reference to the completion of some deed. Inter. But God, who was not made, how can he be perfect? Resp. This word has been taken from our own usage because of human inadequacy, just as have the other words [insofar as what is ineffable may somehow be spoken (from Isidore)].

Inter. Why is he likewise called Creator? Resp. He is called Creator because all the things of the whole world were created by him; for nothing exists that has not derived its origin from God. He is also one, because he cannot be divided, or because nothing else can exist that possesses an equal measure of power.

Thus, all that has so far been said about God pertains to the whole Trinity, because of the one and coeternal substance—whether in the Father, or in his only-begotten Son in the form of God, or in the Holy Spirit, because there is one Spirit of God the Father and of his only-begotten Son.

Inter. Now I should like to know whether I might dare to investigate further concerning the names of God. Resp. Certainly you may. Inter. By what reasoning? Resp. There are also certain terms taken from our own usage and applied to God, derived from our bodily members or from things below. And because he is invisible and incorporeal in his proper nature, the forms of things are nevertheless ascribed to him according to the effects of his operations, so that he may more easily make himself known in accordance with our manner of speaking.

Inter. So that I may understand this, I beg you not to refuse to explain it to me. [Col. 1111D] Resp. Because he sees all things rightly, he is called an eye; because he hears all things rightly, he is called an ear; because he turns away, he walks; because he waits, he stands. Thus, in the other similar expressions, a likeness is transferred to God from human movements [Isidore: minds], as when he is said to forget and to remember. Hence the Prophet also says: “The Lord of hosts has sworn by his soul” (Jeremiah 51:14).

Inter. How is he said to have sworn by his soul, when God does not have a soul? Resp. This is stated according to the effect produced in our experience. Likewise, the face of God in the holy Scriptures is understood not as flesh but as divine knowledge, for the same reason that a person is known by seeing his face. Thus it is said to God in prayer: “Show us your face” [Col. 1112A]—as if it were said, “Grant us your knowledge.”

God’s footprints are spoken of in the same way, because now God is known through a mirror; but in perfection the Almighty will be found when, in the future, he is presented face to face to each of the elect, so that they may contemplate the very form whose footprints they now strive to grasp—that is, the one whom they are said to see through a mirror.

Position, condition, place, and time are likewise attributed to God metaphorically, not properly. For he is said to sit upon the Cherubim, which refers to position; and, “You clothed yourself with the abyss as with a garment” (Psalm 103:6), which refers to condition; and, “Your years will not fail” (Psalm 101:28), which refers to time; and, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm 138:8), which refers to place. [Col. 1112B] In the Prophet, too, the appearance of a cart carrying hay is attributed to God. All these expressions are figurative, because none of them properly belongs to the nature of his substance. Let what has been said to you thus far about the names of God suffice.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE SIX AGES OF THE WORLD, NAMELY, OF THE GREATER AND THE LESSER WORLD

Inter. This is sufficient for me. But since our discussion began with the number six, let us inquire in part into the rationale of the six ages of the world: what their order is, and how many generations or years are contained in each of them. I beg you to explain this briefly to me. Resp. As far as the Lord grants me ability, I shall discuss their generations; but as for the years, as you know, different people hold different opinions. Nevertheless, according to what I have been able to discover from the sources themselves, I shall answer your fraternity.

The first age was, unless I am mistaken, from Adam to Noah. It contained ten generations and, according to the Hebrews, [I] 656 years (1,656 years). [Note: [Col. 1112C] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they are to be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] According to the Seventy interpreters, [II] 242 years (2,242 years). [Note: [Col. 1112C] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they are to be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]

The second age extended from Noah to Abraham and likewise contained ten generations: 242 years according to the Hebrews, but 272 according to the Seventy.

The third extended from Abraham to David: fourteen generations and, according to the Hebrews, 942 years.

The fourth extended from David to the Babylonian captivity: fourteen generations and, according to the Hebrews, 474 years.

The fifth extended finally to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh: fourteen generations and, according to the Hebrews, 589 years.

The sixth, which is now in progress, has no fixed succession of generations or times, but is like an age in decrepitude, destined to end with the death of the whole world.

There you have, in brief, what you asked about the ages of the greater world.

Inter. I accept this, provided you would also say how many ages there are of the lesser world. Resp. They are, I think, just as many as those of the greater world.

Inter. And if there are just as many, how are they named, what is their order, and how many years do they contain? Resp. The first of them is infancy, the stage of a child being born into the light; it contains seven years. A human being is called an infant in the first age because he is still unable to utter words—that is, to speak.

The second is childhood, pure and not yet fit for generation, extending to fourteen years.

The third is adolescence, mature for procreation, extending to twenty-seven years.

The fourth is youth, the strongest of all the ages, ending in the fiftieth year.

The fifth age is the gravity of an older person, a decline from youth toward old age—still not old age, but no longer youth. This age begins at fifty and ends at seventy.

The sixth age is old age. It ends at no fixed number of years; rather, after the five preceding ages, however much life remains is assigned to old age.

Inter. What are we to understand by what is read in the Psalm: “And even to old age and senility” (Psalm 70:18)? Resp. Senility is the final part of old age, so called because it is the boundary of the sixth age. Let this suffice concerning the ages.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE MEASURE OF TIMES

[Col. 1113B]

Lord, since all ages and all periods of the world, as you know very well, pass and run their course through different spans of time, if it pleases you, with the Lord’s help we wish to discuss something about those times, insofar as we understand them in your presence.

Inter. Tell me, dearest brother: under how many headings is the account of these times contained, insofar as it concerns our present discussion? Resp. Unless I am mistaken, it appears to consist of ten headings.

Inter. What are they? Resp. The first heading concerns the word “chronicle”; the second, moments and hours; the third, days; the fourth, night; the fifth, weeks; the sixth, months; the seventh, solstices and equinoxes; the eighth, the seasons of the year; the ninth, years; and the tenth, Olympiads, lustrums, and jubilees.

Inter. You have given the number and names of the headings. Now I ask you not to refuse to explain to me in what language “chronicle” is called. Resp. Certainly, brother. Since you have humbly asked about what you wish to know, I gladly wish to explain what I understand to you. [Note: [Col. 1113D] From Isidore, *Book V of the Etymologies*, chapter 18 and following.] “Chronicle” is said in Greek; in Latin it is called a sequence of times.

426 Inter. Who composed it? Resp. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, published it among the Greeks, but Father Jerome translated it into Latin. For *chronos* [χρόνος] in Greek is interpreted in Latin as “time.”

Inter. Into how many parts are times divided? Resp. Into six.

Inter. What are they? Resp. Moments, hours, days, months, years, and lustrums.

Inter. What is a moment? Resp. A moment is the smallest and narrowest span of time, named from the movement of the heavenly bodies. It is the extremity of an hour in brief intervals, when one thing gives way to and succeeds another.

Inter. In what language is “hour” spoken? Resp. “Hour” is a Greek word, though it sounds Latin.

Inter. What is an hour? Resp. It is the end of a period, just as an [Col. 1114A] *ora* [“shore”; thus in the manuscript; read *ora*] is the end of the sea, rivers, and garments.

Inter. What is a day? Resp. A day is the presence of the sun, or the sun above the earth, just as night is the sun beneath the earth.

Inter. How so? Resp. The cause of there being day or night is that the sun is either above the earth or beneath the earth.

Inter. How many hours does a day have? Resp. A complete day has twenty-four hours, until day and night, through the span of their course from the east to another eastern rising, are completed by the revolving movement of the heavens. In ordinary usage, however, a single day is the interval from the rising of the sun to its setting.

Inter. How many divisions does a day have? Resp. Two.

Inter. Which? Resp. The daytime and the nighttime. The day indeed consists of twenty-four hours, but each span consists of twelve hours.

Inter. From where is the word “day” derived? Resp. It was named from the better part; hence it is customary to state a number of days without mentioning the night, just as it is written in the divine law: “There was evening and morning, one day.”

Inter. Tell me: according to the custom of each people, at what hours does the day begin? Resp. According to the Egyptians, it begins at sunset; according to the Persians, at sunrise; according to the Athenians, at the sixth hour of the day; but according to the Romans, at midnight. Hence the cockcrow occurs then, whose voice announces the coming of the day, when the midnight breath also blows.

Inter. From where are the days said to have derived their names? Resp. The days were named from the gods, whose names the Romans consecrated to certain heavenly bodies.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. They named the first day after the sun, which is chief among all the heavenly bodies, [Col. 1114C] just as that day is the head of all days. They named the second after the moon, which is nearest to the sun in brightness and size and borrows its light from it. The third was named after the star of Mars, which is called Vesper. The fourth was named after the star of Mercury, which some call the white circle. The fifth was named after the star of Jupiter, which they call Phaethon [Isidore: Phaethontem]. The sixth was named after the star of Venus, which they call Lucifer; among all the stars it has the greatest light. The seventh was named after the star of Saturn, which, placed in the sixth heaven, is said to complete its course in twenty years [Isidore: thirty].

Inter. Why were the days named after these seven stars? Resp. The pagans gave the days their names from these seven stars because they believed that something was produced for them through those stars. They said that from the sun they received spirit, from the moon [Col. 1114D] body, from Mercury intelligence and speech, from Venus pleasure, from Mars blood, from Jupiter self-control, and from Saturn moisture. Such was the folly of the pagans, who invented such ridiculous fantasies for themselves.

Inter. What is the day called among the Hebrews? Resp. Among the Hebrews, the first day is called “one of the Sabbath,” which among us is the Lord’s Day.

Inter. Why is it called the second of the Sabbath? Resp. The second of the Sabbath is the second weekday, which secular people call the day of the moon.

Inter. What is the third? Resp. The third of the Sabbath is the third weekday, which they call the day of Mars.

Inter. What is the fourth? Resp. The fourth of the Sabbath is the fourth weekday, which pagans call the day of Mercury.

Inter. What is the fifth? Resp. The fifth of the Sabbath is the fifth weekday—that is, the fifth from the Lord’s Day—which pagans call the day of Jupiter.

Inter. What is the sixth? Resp. The sixth of the Sabbath is called the sixth weekday, which those same pagans call the day of Venus.

Inter. What is the Sabbath? Resp. The Sabbath is either the seventh day from the Lord’s Day, which the pagans dedicated to Saturn, or it was named after Saturn [Isidore: Saturni].

Inter. What does “Sabbath” mean? Resp. “Sabbath” is translated from Hebrew into Latin as “rest,” because on that day God rested from all his works.

It is better, however, for Christian speech in the names of the days to proceed according to ecclesiastical usage. Nevertheless, if habit should perhaps lead someone to utter what he disapproves in his heart, let him understand that all those after whom these days were named were human beings. Because of certain mortal benefits [Isidore: and because they had benefited others], since they had achieved great power and distinction in this world, divine honors were bestowed upon them by their admirers, both in the names of days and in those of stars. But first the stars were named after human beings, and from the stars the days received their names.

Inter. From where are weekdays called *feriae*? Resp. *Feriae* are so called from *fari*, “to speak,” because they are a time for us to speak—that is, to speak in divine or human service. But from these feast days, days of rest were established for the sake of human beings and for divine rites [Isidore: But feast days were established from these for the sake of human beings, and days of rest for the sake of divine rites].

[Col. 1115C] Inter. How many divisions does the day have? Resp. Three.

Inter. What are they? Resp. Morning, midday, and the final part of the day.

Inter. What is morning? Resp. Morning is mature and full light, no longer twilight.

Inter. Why is it called “morning”? Resp. *Mane* is derived from *manus*.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. The ancients called *manus* “good” [Note: [Col. 1115D] “They called it good.” *Mana dies* was a familiar expression among the ancient Gauls, says Valesius in *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 562, used by those greeting one another in the morning, by which they wished their friends a good and auspicious day. See Du Cange, s.v. *Mana*.]; for what is better than light? Others think that *mane* is derived from souls, whose dwelling is from the moon to the earth [Isidore: from the *manes*, that is, the gods, whose…]. Others think it is derived from the air, because *manus* means bright and transparent…

Inter. Why is it called midday? Resp. *Meridies* is formed as if from *medidies*, that is, “middle-day,” or because the day is then purer. *Merum* means pure; for throughout the whole day nothing is brighter than midday, when the sun glows in the middle of heaven and illuminates the entire world with equal brightness.

Inter. What is the final part of the day? Resp. It is the last portion of the day, when the sun turns its course toward setting. It is called *suprema* because it is what remains toward the final part of the day.

Inter. Why is evening called *serum*? Resp. It is called *serum* from closed bolts, when night has already arrived, so that each person may become safer in sleep.

Inter. Why is it called “today”? [Note: [Col. 1116D] This agrees with the short treatise *On Orthography*.] Resp. *Hodie* means, as it were, “on this day.” Likewise, *quottidie*, not *cotidie*, means “on each of the days.” [Col. 1116A] In some places it is read differently: *cotidie* is said not from *quota die*, “on what day,” but from a continuous day.

Inter. Why is tomorrow called *cras*? Resp. *Cras* means “afterward.” “Yesterday” is *hesternum*, meaning “the previous day”; it is called *hesternum* because that day has already become foreign to us and, by passing away, alien.

Inter. From where is *pridie* derived? Resp. *Pridie* is formed as if from *priori die*, “on the earlier day.” *Perendie* means “through the day before,” or “in advance,” that is, earlier.

Inter. From where is night named? Resp. Night (*nox*) is named from harming (*nocere*), because it harms the eyes. For this reason it has the light of the moon and stars, so that it might not be unsightly, so that all who work at night might be comforted, and so that it might provide sufficient light for certain living creatures that cannot endure the sun’s light.

[Col. 1116B] Inter. Why was the alternation of day and night established? Resp. The alternation of night and day was established for the alternation of sleeping and keeping watch, and so that the rest of night might temper the labor of daytime work.

Inter. Why was night made? Resp. Either because the sun becomes weary from its long journey and, when it reaches the furthest extent of heaven, grows weak and, exhausted, breathes out its fires; or because it is forced beneath the earth by the same force with which it carried [perhaps “brought forth”] its light above the earth. Thus the earth’s shadow produces night. Hence Virgil says (*Aeneid* 2.250):

> Night rushes from Ocean,
>
> enveloping earth and sky in great shadow.
