Inter. How many divisions does the night have? Resp. Seven.

Inter. What are they? Resp. Evening, twilight, the hour of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn.

[Col. 1116C] Inter. What is evening? Resp. *Vesper* is named from the western star, which follows the setting sun and precedes the darkness that follows. Virgil says of it (*Aeneid* 1.378):

> Before day, Vesper settles the sun beneath the closed Olympus.

Inter. From where is the word “darkness” derived? Resp. Because it holds shadows.

Inter. What is twilight? Resp. Twilight is uncertain light. For *creperum* means “uncertain,” that is, between light and darkness.

Inter. What is the hour of silence? Resp. It is when everyone is silent; for *conticescere* means “to be silent.”

Inter. What is the dead of night? Resp. It is the middle and inactive period, the time when nothing can be done and everything is quiet in sleep. Time is not understood in itself except through human actions. The middle of the night lacks activity; therefore it is an inactive period [Isidore: *intempesta*, inactive], as if without time—that is, without the activity by which time is recognized. Hence the expression, “You have come at an inopportune time.” Thus it is called *tempesta* because it lacks times, that is, activities [Isidore reads: “Therefore it is called *intempesta*, because it lacks time, that is, activity”].

Inter. What is cockcrow? Resp. It is called *gallicinium* because of the roosters, as the announcement of light [Isidore: the announcer of light].

[Col. 1117A] Inter. What is morning? Resp. Morning is the period between the departure of darkness and the arrival of dawn. It is called *matutinum* because this period begins with morning.

Inter. What is dawn? Resp. Dawn is, as it were, the small light of day beginning. It is also the aurora that precedes the sun. Aurora is the beginning of the day becoming bright and the first radiance of the air; in Greek it is called *Eos* [ἠώς]. We call it *aurora* by derivation, as it were *Eorora* [Isidore: *Eorora*]. Hence the verse:

> Bright Eous shines from the author’s summit.

Inter. Why is a week called *ebdomada*? Resp. It is called *ebdomada* from the number of seven days, by the repetition of which months, years, and the age of the world are completed.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. The Greeks call seven *epta* [ἑπτά]; we call it *septimana*, as it were “seven lights.” For morning is light.

Inter. From where is the eighth day named? Resp. The eighth day is the first day to which one returns, and from which the sequence of weeks begins again.

Inter. From where is a month named? Resp. The name “month” is Greek, derived from the name of the moon.

Inter. How so? Resp. The moon is called *mene* [μήνη] in Greek. Hence among the Hebrews the legitimate months are counted not according to the sun’s circuit but according to the moon’s course, from one new moon to the next. The Egyptians, however, were the first, because of the moon’s swifter course and to prevent an error in reckoning from resulting from its speed, [Col. 1117C] to establish the month’s day according to the sun’s course, since the sun’s slower movement could be grasped more easily.

Inter. Why is January so called? Resp. The month of January was named after Janus, who was consecrated to it by the pagans—or because it is the boundary and gate of the year. Hence the same Janus is depicted with two faces, to show the entrance and exit of the year.

Inter. From where is February named? Resp. It is called February from *Februa* [*Februo*], that is, Pluto, to whom sacrifices were offered in that month. For the Romans consecrated January to the heavenly gods and February to the gods below, the *Manes*. Therefore February is named from *Februa*, that is, Pluto, not from fever, which is an illness.

Inter. From where is March named? Resp. March was named after Mars, the founder of the Roman people; or because at that time all living creatures are driven toward the male and toward the pleasure of intercourse.

Inter. By what other name is it called? Resp. It is also called the “month of new things,” because March is the first month of the year. It is also called November, evidently from the signs of new shoots, because in it, when new fruits become green, the passing of what has gone before is demonstrated.

Inter. From where is April named? Resp. *Aprelis* is said in place of Venus, as if from *afrondis* [Isidore: *Aphrodis*].

Inter. How so? Resp. In Greek Venus is called *Afrondis* [Isidore: Ἀφροδίτη]; or because in this month everything opens into flower, as if it were *aperilis*.

Inter. From where is May named? Resp. May was named after Maia, the mother of Mercury; or after the elders, who were the leaders of the state. For the Romans consecrated this month to the elders and the following one to the younger men, [Col. 1118A] from which it is also called June. Formerly the people were divided into centuries of elders and younger men.

428 Inter. From where are July and August named? Resp. July and August were named from the honors bestowed upon the men Julius Caesar and Augustus Caesar.

Inter. What were they called previously? Resp. Previously they were called Quintilis and Sextilis.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. Quintilis was so called because it was fifth from March, which the Romans testify was the first month of the year; Sextilis was similarly so called because it was sixth.

Inter. From where did September receive its name? Resp. September derives its name from number and rain, because it is seventh from March and has rains. Thus October, November, and December likewise received their names from number and rains. December brings the sequence of numbers to an end because the number ten closes the preceding numbers.

Inter. Why are the Kalends, Nones, and Ides so called? Resp. The Romans established the Kalends, Nones, and Ides either because of feast days or because of the duties of magistrates.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. On those days they assembled in the cities.

Inter. Why were they given these particular names? Resp. Some think that the Kalends are named from *colere*, “to honor.” Among the ancients, the beginnings of all months were honored, as among the Hebrews. Most Latins think that the Ides were named from *edere*, “to eat,” because among the ancients those days were devoted to feasting. The Nones were named from *nundinae*. The *nundinae* are public assemblies or markets.

Inter. Why is the solstice so called? Resp. *Solstitium* means, as it were, “the sun’s standing,” because when the sun stands still, the days or nights grow longer.

Inter. Why is it called the equinox? Resp. It is called the equinox because at that time day and night remain equal in the number of their hours.

Inter. How many solstices are there? Resp. Two.

Inter. Which? Resp. One is the summer solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, from which time the sun begins to return toward the lower circles. The other is the winter solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when the sun begins to seek the higher circles. Hence the day of the winter solstice is found to be the shortest, just as that of the summer solstice is the longest.

Inter. How many equinoxes are there? Resp. Two.

Inter. Which? Resp. One is the spring equinox and the other the autumn equinox, which the Greeks call *isēmĕrĭai* [ἰσημερίας].

Inter. At what times do these equinoxes occur? Resp. One occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; the other on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, because formerly the year was divided into only two parts, namely summer and winter, and the solstice into two hemispheres.

Inter. How many seasons of the year are there? Resp. Four.

Inter. Which? Resp. The first is spring, the second summer, the third autumn, and the fourth winter.

Inter. From where are they called seasons? Resp. They are called seasons from the tempering of their elements, because they temper one another through moisture, dryness, heat, and cold.

Inter. By what other name are they called? Resp. They are called courses because they do not stand still but run.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. After the world was made, the seasons were divided according to the character of the sun’s course into three-month periods. The ancients make the following distinction among those periods: the first month of spring is called new, the second mature, and the third declining. Summer likewise has its new, mature, and declining months. So also winter has its new, mature, and declining—or final—months. Hence the verse: “Winter at its extreme decline” [Isidore: “At the extreme falling of winter”].

Inter. From where is spring named? Resp. Spring is so called because the earth becomes green. For then, after winter, the earth is clothed with grasses, and everything bursts into flower.

Inter. From where is summer named? Resp. Summer is called *aestas* from heat, and *aestas* is as if from *usta*, that is, scorched and dry. For heat is dry.

Inter. From where is autumn named? Resp. Autumn is named from a period of weather, when the leaves of the trees fall and everything ripens.

Inter. Why is winter so called? Resp. Winter is the name given to the arrangement of the hemisphere [Isidore: “Winter was named according to a condition…”].

Inter. How so? Resp. Because then it revolves through a shorter circle [Isidore: “it turns through a shorter circle”]. Hence this season is also called *bruma*, as if from *brachin* [Isidore: Βραχεῖα ἡμέρα], that is, “short”; or from food, because at that time the appetite for eating is greater.

Inter. On what basis? Resp. In Greek, voracious eating is called *bruma*. Hence those who have an aversion to food are called *inbrumati*.

Inter. Why is *hibernus* so called? Resp. *Hibernus* is between winter and spring, as if *hivernus* [Isidore: *hyevernus*], though it often signifies the whole of winter by reference to one part.

Inter. To what are these seasons assigned? Resp. They are assigned to the several regions of the heavens.

Inter. How so? Resp. Spring is assigned to the east, because at that time everything rises from the earth. Summer is assigned to the south, because that region is more intensely aflame with heat. Winter is assigned to the north, because it lies numb under cold and perpetual frost. Autumn is assigned to the west, because it has severe diseases. Hence at that time all the leaves of the trees fall. The fact that autumn abounds in diseases is caused by this boundary between cold and heat and by the conflict within it of opposing airs.

Inter. What is a year? Resp. A year is the sun’s circuit, when, after completing 365 days, it returns to the same places among the stars.

Inter. From where is the word “year” derived? Resp. A year is so called because it turns as the months recur within it. Hence also *annulus*, “ring,” as if *annuus*, “annual,” that is, a circle, because it returns upon itself. Hence Virgil says (*Georgics* 2.402):

> And the year turns back upon itself along its own tracks.

Among the Egyptians this was represented before the invention of letters by a painted dragon biting its own tail, because it returns upon itself. Others say that a year is called *apotilanistai* [ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνανεούσθαι], that is, from renewal, because it is always renewed.

Inter. In what other ways are years divided? Resp. There are three kinds of years.

Inter. What are they? Resp. There is either a lunar year, which contains thirty days; or a solar year, which contains twelve months; or a great year, when all the planets return to the same place, which occurs after very many solar years.

Inter. What is an era, or who established it? Resp. The era of individual years was established by Caesar Augustus, when, after first conducting a census [Isidore: “when he conducted the census and”], he surveyed the Roman world.

Inter. From where is the word “era” derived? Resp. It was called *aera* because the whole world professed that it owed bronze—that is, money—to the state.

429 Inter. From where is an Olympiad named? Resp. Among the Greeks, an Olympiad was established at Elis, a city of Greece, when the Eleans held a contest and a quinquennial competition, with four intervening years free from such events. For this reason they called the period of the Elean contest an Olympiad, reckoning four years in one Olympiad.

Inter. What is a lustrum? Resp. A lustrum is *pentetēsis*, that is, a five-year period, which the Romans said was completed in the fifth year on account of the Olympiads. At that time there were still consuls; the era did not yet exist. It is a five-year period.

Inter. Why is it so called? Resp. It is called so because, after the census had been completed over five years in the state, the city of Rome was purified.

Inter. What does “jubilee” mean? Resp. It means “the year of remission.” It is both a Hebrew expression and a Hebrew number, formed by seven weeks of years—that is, forty-nine years. In those years trumpets were sounded, the ancient possession returned to everyone, debts were released, and freedoms were confirmed. We also celebrate this number in the days of Pentecost after the Lord’s resurrection: our guilt remitted and the written document of the whole debt canceled, we are freed from every bond and receive the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon us. Let these few things that have been presented to you concerning the reckoning of times suffice until greater matters are brought forward.

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE OLD TESTAMENT

Since all things accomplished and written down through the various successions of time from the beginning of creation are narrated and read chiefly in the Old Testament, let us, if you wish, discuss among ourselves, as the matter now presents itself, what diversity and multiplicity are found in that Testament.

Inter. Since these things are so, tell me why it is called the Old Testament. Resp. It is called the Old Testament because it ceased when the New came, as the Apostle says: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Inter. Into how many books is the Old Testament counted? Resp. Into forty-five.

Inter. What are their names? Resp. Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, four Books of Kings, Chronicles, Job, the Psalter, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, sixteen Books of the Prophets, Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Maccabees.

Inter. Now that you have given their number, I beg you to explain to me briefly what is principally contained in each of them. Resp. As far as the Lord grants me ability, I shall do so.

Inter. Tell me, then, what is contained in Genesis. Resp. [Note: [Col. 1121D] Isidore, *Book of the Prefaces*, from which this differs in many respects.] It contains the making of the world, the creation of the human being, the Flood, the division of the earth, the confusion of languages, and the deeds of all the patriarchs up to Israel’s entry into Egypt.

Inter. What is contained in Exodus? Resp. The servitude of the Hebrews, the plague of Egypt, the people’s departure, the protection of the cloud, the crossing of the Red Sea, Pharaoh’s drowning, the glory of the song of praise [Isidore: the singing of glory], the arrival in the wilderness, the food of manna, the waters changed into sweetness, the battle with Amalek, the commandments of the Decalogue, the ark of the covenant, and the dedication of the tabernacle and of the offering.

[Col. 1121B] Inter. What is contained in Leviticus? Resp. The law of sacrifices, the variety of offerings, the vestments of the high priests, the ministries of the Levites, the distinction of foods, the diversity of peoples, and the purifications of offerings [Isidore: “and of the offering”].

Inter. What is contained in Numbers? Resp. The departure of the tribes from Egypt and the mysteries of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness.

Inter. What is contained in Deuteronomy? Resp. A recapitulation of the law, and all that Moses gave [Isidore: commanded] and promised to the people between Paran, Oboth, and Laban, and Hazeroth, up to Kadesh-barnea; the curses of sinners and the promises of blessedness. There Moses sings a song; there he gives a blessing to the children of Israel; there, after seeing the promised land, he dies [Col. 1121C] and is buried.

Inter. What is contained in Joshua? Resp. The crossing of the Jordan by the children of Israel, the second circumcision, the overthrow of the Canaanites, the division of their land, and also the inheritance received by lot.

Inter. What is contained in the Book of Judges? Resp. The sins and servitude of Israel, the people’s cries, and God’s mercies toward them.

Inter. What is contained in Ruth? Resp. The history of the Moabite woman, from whose lineage David descended.

Inter. What is contained in the Books of Kings? Resp. The transfer of the Lord’s ark from the Jews to the Gentiles, the priesthood of Eli, and the reign of King Saul leading to David; the deeds of the kings of Judah and Israel; the migration of peoples, moreover, from the error of Israel’s idolatry into Assyria; and the arrival of Nebuchadnezzar in Jerusalem, together with the captivity of the rulers and the people and the overthrow of the city and the Temple.

Inter. What is contained in Chronicles? Resp. The order of generations and times, and instruction in the holy Scriptures. Also, whatever was omitted in the history of the Old Testament or perhaps not fully arranged is explained there in summary and briefly.

Inter. What is contained in Job? Resp. The losses, funerals, and scourges of that holy man, and the insulting words of his would-be comforters; also his laments, in which he mourns the misery of the whole world; God’s consolation to him from the whirlwind; and his twofold reward at the end.

Inter. What is contained in the Book of Psalms? Resp. It contains, allegorically and typologically, marked-out mysteries; but specifically, the birth, passion, and resurrection of Christ.

Inter. What is contained in the books of Solomon? Resp. In Proverbs, teaching moral matters through a common manner of speech, he set forth a higher understanding and fitted the observance of the commandments and instruction in heavenly teaching into brief sayings. In Ecclesiastes, examining the nature of things, he censures everything in the world as fleeting and vain and, having recognized the frailty of all things, admonishes us to renounce the world. In the Song of Songs, he declares under the figure of bridegroom and bride the heavenly or divine realities, the unity of Christ and the Church; and, stirring the soul to love heavenly things, he urges it to attain fellowship with God.

Inter. What is contained in the Prophets? Resp. Although many obscure things are read in them, I shall not refuse to present some of them to you.

Inter. Tell me, then, what should I understand in Isaiah? Resp. The concealment of the wings of the two Seraphim seated upon the throne of God; and, after the vision of Judah and Jerusalem, he turns his prophetic discourse against the other nations that are around it. According to the character of the places and the diversity of their way of life, he announces the evils that were to come upon them, and after the captivity he threatens the ruin of Babylon. Then he speaks of the slaughter of the Philistines, [Col. 1122C] the devastation of Moab, the destruction of Damascus, the disturbance of Egypt, the desolation of the desert sea, the siege of Edom, the flight and destruction of Arabia, the ruin of the valley of Zion, and also the overthrow of Tyre.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Jeremiah?

**Response:** His expression is simple, his meaning readily understood, and his bodily imitation and sufferings portray an image of the Redeemer: the destruction of the devil’s kingdom and the establishment of the dominion of justice, or faith.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Ezekiel?

**Response:** In him are described the mysteries of the whole Church, which was formed from Christ’s side.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Daniel?

**Response:** In him is read not only a prophecy of things to come, but also a determination of the time of the Incarnation or Passion from the succession of kings, or the number of years; likewise the kingdom of Antichrist, the day of judgment, and the kingdom of the saints; and at the end of his prophecy, the story of Susanna [Supplement: story].

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Hosea?

**Response:** Historically, the final faith of the Jews in Christ and the day of the Lord’s entire Resurrection are read there.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Joel?

**Response:** He alone, bringing an oracle against Judah and Jerusalem, after luxurious banquets summons Jerusalem to mourning, declares its destruction, and announces the calling of the nations.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Amos?

**Response:** Describing four crimes of the nations under the figure of the whole world, he announces Christ’s coming to all.

[Col. 1123A]

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Obadiah?

**Response:** A mystical rebuke of Edom’s pride—that is, of the former people’s audacity, because it killed Christ—and the future salvation of the Lord.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Jonah?

**Response:** He bears the figure of Christ’s Passion, death, and Resurrection in his shipwreck and being cast from the ship into the sea; likewise in his being swallowed by the sea-monster for three days and nights, and in his having proclaimed repentance to the world at Nineveh.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Micah?

**Response:** He threatens Samaria with the Lord’s anger because of its idols; announces the destruction that will come upon the people of Israel; and points out the place in which Christ would be born.

[Col. 1123B]

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Nahum?

**Response:** He declares that the idols of the nations must be destroyed, as well as Jerusalem, the city of blood. After its destruction, announcing feet that proclaim peace—that is, the coming of Christ the Savior—he cries out.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Habakkuk?

**Response:** At the beginning of his book he describes the devil with his members and ways; at the end he announces the coming and Passion of the Savior.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Zephaniah?

**Response:** He proclaims the crushing of Mount Zion, which is the hill of Jerusalem, as well as the overthrow of the other nations; he thunders the terror of the day of judgment; prophesies the third day of Christ’s Resurrection; and announces that, at Christ’s coming, the whole world will serve the Lord under one yoke.

[Col. 1123C]

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Haggai?

**Response:** The restoration of the Lord’s temple; the crushing of the nations or the shaking of the whole world; the coming of Christ; and the captivity of the people.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Zechariah?

**Response:** Various visions are read in him, too many to enumerate; in them, as is recognized, various mysteries are also to be understood.

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Malachi?

**Response:** At the beginning of his book he shows the Jews’ hatred of Esau and their love for the lesser people in Jacob. In what follows he rejects the sacrifices of Judea [Isidore: the former sacrifices of the Jews] and announces that the sacrifice will be transferred. At the end he announces the Lord’s coming and the day of judgment, the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of the wicked; and he announces the first coming of John and the second of Elijah.

[Col. 1123D]

**Interlocutor:** What is said in Ezra?

**Response:** The renewal of the walls of Jerusalem and of the temple, or altar; likewise the restoration of priestly law, or the summit of holy religion, adorned with many resources from the gifts of the nations and of the Persian princes.

**Interlocutor:** What is to be understood in the Books of the Maccabees?

**Response:** They foreshadow the battles between the Hebrew commanders and the Persian nations, the battles of the Sabbaths, and the noble triumphs of the Maccabees; also treaties of friendship with Roman commanders and the embassies that were carried out.

**Interlocutor:** The books about which you have so far given an account—into how many divisions are they divided according to the Hebrews?

**Response:** Into three.

**Interlocutor:** How?

**Response:** Into the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa.

[Col. 1124A]

**Interlocutor:** How is the first division, that of the Law, to be understood?

**Response:** The first division of the Law consists of five books.

**Interlocutor:** Which are they?

**Response:** The first is *Bresith*, which is Genesis; the second *Elesmod*, which is Exodus; the third *Vaiecra*, which is Leviticus; the fourth *Vagedaber*, which is Numbers; the fifth *Heliadabarim*, which is Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call *Thorat* and the Latins call the Law. This is properly called “the Law,” which was given through Moses.

**Interlocutor:** What is the second division?

**Response:** The second division is that of the Prophets, containing eight books.

[Col. 1124B]

**Interlocutor:** What are their names?

**Response:** The first is *Josue Bennon*, called in Latin *Jesus Nave*. The second is *Sopthim*, which is Judges. The third is Samuel, which is the First Book of Kings. The fourth is *Malachim*, which is the Second Book of Kings. The fifth is Isaiah. The sixth is Jeremiah. The seventh is Ezekiel. The eighth is *Tharesra*, called the Twelve Prophets; these books, because they are joined together for the sake of brevity, are counted as one.

**Interlocutor:** What is the third division?

**Response:** The third division is that of the Hagiographa, that is, the sayings of those who write sacred things; there are nine books.

**Interlocutor:** What are they called?

**Response:** The first is called Job. The second is the Psalter. The third is *Masloth*, which is the Proverbs of Solomon. The fourth is *Caeleth*, which is Ecclesiastes. The fifth is *Syrasirim*, which is the Song of Songs. The sixth is Daniel.

[Col. 1124C] 431

The seventh is *Dabreiamin*, which is “Words of Days,” that is, Chronicles. The eighth is Ezra. The ninth is Esther. Together these five, eight, and nine make twenty-two, as was stated above.

**Interlocutor:** Are there more books of the Old Testament, or not?

**Response:** There certainly are.

**Interlocutor:** Which are they?

**Response:** Some add Ruth and *Cynoth*, which in Latin is called the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa, making twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, corresponding to the twenty-four elders who stand before the Lord’s presence.

**Interlocutor:** Are any further books of the Old Testament found?

**Response:** Yes.

**Interlocutor:** How?

**Response:** There is also a fourth division of those books that are not in the Hebrew canon.

**Interlocutor:** What are they called?

[Col. 1124D]

**Response:** The first is the Book of Wisdom. The second is Ecclesiasticus. The third is Tobit. The fourth is Judith. The fifth and sixth are the Books of the Maccabees. Although the Jews separate them among the apocrypha, the Church of Christ honors and proclaims them among the divine books.

[Note: [Col. 1123] See what we noted concerning Book I against Elipandus in this volume, col. 254.]

**Interlocutor:** Now that you have gone through the names and divisions, and also indicated in part what is contained in these books, I ask you to explain to me who their authors were, and also why each of them is so called.

**Response:** Truly, brother, you ask a great and difficult matter of me. Nevertheless, insofar as I am able, with the Lord’s will, I shall explain it to you.

**Interlocutor:** Tell me, then, who were the authors of the books of the Old Testament?

[Col. 1125A]

**Response:** [Note: [Col. 1125D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 2.]

According to Hebrew tradition, the following are held to be the authors of the Old Testament. First, Moses produced the *cosmographicon*—the account of divine history—in five volumes, which is called the Pentateuch.

**Interlocutor:** Why is it called that?

**Response:** *Pentateuch* is so called from its five volumes.

**Interlocutor:** For what reason?

**Response:** *Penta* means “five” in Greek, while *teuchos* means “volume”; Genesis is also called the first [of these].

**Interlocutor:** Why is it called Genesis?

**Response:** The book is called Genesis because it contains the beginning of the world and the generation of the age.

**Interlocutor:** From where did Exodus receive its name?

**Response:** Exodus recounts the departure from Egypt, or the going out of the people of Israel, and received its name from this.

**Interlocutor:** Why is it called Leviticus?

**Response:** It is called Leviticus because it sets forth the ministries of the Levites and the variety of sacrifices, and because the entire Levitical order is altered in it [Isidore: is noted in it].

[Col. 1125B]

**Interlocutor:** Why is the book called Numbers? [Reading: *Numerorum*, “of Numbers.”]

**Response:** The book is called Numbers because the tribes that went out from Egypt are counted in it, and it contains a description of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness.

**Interlocutor:** Why is it called Deuteronomy?

**Response:** *Deuteronomy* is a Greek expression translated into Latin as “second law,” that is, “repetition,” and “prefiguration of the evangelical law.” It contains the earlier matters in such a way that everything repeated in it is nevertheless new.

**Interlocutor:** From whom did Joshua receive its name?

[Col. 1125C]

**Response:** The book of Joshua received its name from Jesus, son of Nun, whose history it contains. The Hebrews assert that Joshua himself was its author. In its text, after the crossing of the Jordan, the kingdoms of the enemies are overthrown, the land is divided among the people, and through the individual cities, villages, mountains, and borders the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem are prefigured.

**Interlocutor:** From where is Judges named?

**Response:** It is named from the leaders of the people who governed Israel after Moses and Joshua, before David and the other kings existed. Samuel is believed to have published this book.

**Interlocutor:** Why is the Book of Samuel so called?

**Response:** The Book of Samuel describes Samuel’s birth, priesthood, and deeds; therefore it received its name from him. Although this book contains the history of Saul and David, both are nevertheless referred to Samuel, because he anointed Saul as king and David as the future king. Samuel himself wrote the first part of the book; David wrote what follows, up to the end.

[Col. 1125D]

**Interlocutor:** Why is it called *Malachim* [Isidore: *Melachim*]?

**Response:** The book is called *Malachim* because it sets forth in chronological order the kings of Judah and of the Israelite nation, together with their deeds. *Malachim* in Hebrew is translated into Latin as “of kings.” Jeremiah first gathered this book into a single volume, for previously it had been scattered among the histories of the individual kings.

[Col. 1126A]

**Interlocutor:** In what language is Chronicles called?

**Response:** It is called *Paralipomenon* in Greek, which we may render as “things passed over” or “things left over,” because matters that were omitted or not fully reported in the Law and in the Books of Kings are explained here summarily and briefly.

**Interlocutor:** Who was the author of the Book of Job?

**Response:** Some think that Moses wrote the Book of Job; others think it was one of the prophets; still others judge that Job himself was its author after the affliction of his suffering, reasoning that the one who endured the struggles of spiritual combat should himself narrate the victories he achieved. Among the Hebrews, the beginning and end of the Book of Job are composed in prose; its middle section, from the passage that says, “Let the day perish on which I was born,” up to the passage, “Therefore I reproach myself and repent” (Job 3:3 and following), proceeds entirely in heroic meter.

[Col. 1126B]

**Interlocutor:** In what language is the Book of Psalms called?

**Response:** The Book of Psalms is called *Psalterium* in Greek, *Nabla* in Hebrew, and *organum* in Latin. It is called the Book of Psalms because, when one prophet sang to the psaltery, a chorus answered in harmony. The title in the Hebrew Psalms is *Hyspysta* [Isidore: *Thehilim*], which is interpreted as “volume of hymns.” The authors of the psalms, who are named in their titles, are Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Jeduthun, the sons of Korah, Heman [Ezrahites (omitted by Isidore)], and others, whom Ezra gathered into one volume. All the psalms among the Hebrews are composed in metrical verse. For, following the practice of the Roman Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, some proceed in iambics, others resound in the Alcaic [Isidore: elegiac] meter, while others shine in the Sapphic, proceeding in three- or four-foot measures.

[Col. 1126C]

**Interlocutor:** In what way are the books of Solomon arranged?

**Response:** Solomon, son of David and king of Israel, produced three volumes according to the number of his names. The first is *Masloth* [Isidore: *Misse*], which the Greeks call *Parabolas* and the Latins call Proverbs, because in it he displays, through comparative likeness, figures of speech and images of truth, while reserving the truth itself for readers to understand. He called the second book *Coeleth*, which is called *Ecclesiastes* in Greek and “Preacher” in Latin, because its discourse is directed not specifically to one person, as in Proverbs, but generally to everyone, teaching that everything we see in the world is transitory and brief and therefore not at all to be desired. He titled the third book *Syrasyrin* [Isidore: *sir hysirim*], which is rendered in Latin as the Song of Songs; there, in an epithalamial poem, it mystically sings of the union of Christ and the Church.

[Col. 1126D]

**Interlocutor:** Why is it called the Song of Songs?

**Response:** It is called the Song of Songs because it is placed above all the songs found in the sacred Scriptures, just as certain things in the Law are called “holy,” while others are greater and are called “Holy of Holies.” The poems of these three books are said to have been composed among their own people in hexameter and pentameter verses, as Josephus and Jerome write.

[Col. 1127A]

**Interlocutor:** Who composed the Book of Isaiah?

**Response:** Isaiah, more an evangelist than a prophet, published his book. Its entire text proceeds in eloquent prose, but the song proceeds in hexameter and pentameter rhythm [Isidore: verse].

**Interlocutor:** Who composed Jeremiah?

**Response:** Jeremiah likewise published his book together with his Lamentations, which we call *Laments* because they are used in times of sorrow and at funerals. In them he composed an alphabetic poem in four different meters. The first two are written almost in the Sapphic meter, because three little verses linked together and beginning with only one letter conclude a heroic phrase. The third alphabetic poem is written in trimeter, and its verses begin with three letters, that is, three verses at a time [Isidore: the same verses]. The fourth alphabetic poem is considered similar to the first and second.

[Col. 1127B]

**Interlocutor:** Who composed Ezekiel and Daniel?

**Response:** Ezekiel and Daniel are said to have been written by certain wise men. Ezekiel’s beginnings and endings are wrapped in many obscurities. Daniel, however, proclaims the kingdoms of the world in clear speech and marks the time of Christ’s coming with the most explicit prophecy. These are the four prophets who are called “greater,” because they produced lengthy volumes.

**Interlocutor:** Who were the authors of the Books of the Twelve Prophets?

**Response:** The Books of the Twelve Prophets are titled with the names of their authors. They are called “minor” because their discourses are brief. Hence they are joined together and contained in one volume. Their names are: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

[Col. 1127C]

**Interlocutor:** Who was the author of the Books of Ezra?

**Response:** The Book of Ezra is titled with the name of its author; in its text the discourses of Ezra and Nehemiah are contained together. No one should be troubled that it is called one Book of Ezra, because the second, third, and fourth are not found among the Hebrews but are counted among the apocrypha.

**Interlocutor:** Who wrote the Book of Esther?

**Response:** Esther herself is believed to have written the book. In it the same queen, under the figure of the Church, is said to have rescued God’s people from slavery and death; and after the enemy Haman, whose name is interpreted as “iniquity,” was killed, a day of celebration is handed down to posterity.

[Col. 1127D]

**Interlocutor:** Who are said to have written the Books of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and the Maccabees?

**Response:** The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews; hence its very title has more the flavor of Greek eloquence. The Jews assert that it belongs to Philo. It is called Wisdom because in it Christ’s coming—he who is the Father’s wisdom—and his Passion are clearly expressed. The Book of Ecclesiasticus was certainly composed by Jesus son of Sirach, a Jerusalemite, grandson [the manuscript reads this way] of Jesus the high priest, whom Zechariah mentions.

[Col. 1128A]

[Note: [Col. 1127D] “Because of the similarity of expression.” Compare verses 6 of the poem, col. 734.

These two books are joined by way of example:

“For their first is rightly called nurturing Wisdom.

The latter is marked by the name of Jesus.”]

Among the Latins, because of the similarity of its expression, this book is titled with Solomon’s name. It is called Ecclesiasticus because it was produced with great care and deliberation for the discipline of the whole Church and for religious conduct. It is also found among the Hebrews, but is counted among the apocrypha. It is not at all certain by which authors the books of Judith, Tobit, or the Maccabees were written. They bear the names of those whose deeds they record.

This brief account of the Old Testament may suffice for you on this occasion.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE NEW TESTAMENT

**Interlocutor:** What you have said about it is sufficient; but I ask you to explain why it is called the New Testament.

[Col. 1128B]

**Response:** It is called the New Testament because it makes new. For no one learns it except people renewed from their old state by grace and already belonging to the new covenant, which is the kingdom of heaven.

**Interlocutor:** What are the divisions of the books of the New Testament?

**Response:** Two.

**Interlocutor:** Which?

**Response:** The first is evangelical, containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second is apostolic, containing Paul in fourteen Epistles; Peter in two; John in three; James and Jude in one each; the Acts of the Apostles; and the Apocalypse.

**Interlocutor:** Who were the authors of this New Testament?

**Response:** The four books of the Gospels were written individually by the four men named above.

[Col. 1128C]

**Interlocutor:** Now I ask you to explain which of them wrote the Gospel first, in what language, and where and from what point he composed it. Do not refuse to do the same concerning the second, third, and fourth.

**Response:** [Note: [Col. 1128D] Isidore, cited above.]

First, Matthew wrote his Gospel in Hebrew letters and language. In Judea he began his evangelizing with Christ’s human birth, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). He thereby signifies that Christ descended bodily from the seed of the patriarchs, as had been promised by the prophets through the Holy Spirit.

Second, Mark, filled with the Holy Spirit, wrote Christ’s Gospel in Greek speech in Italy, following Peter as a disciple. He began with the prophetic spirit, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Mark 1:3), [Col. 1128D] to show that, after assuming flesh, Christ preached the Gospel to the world. For Christ himself was also called a prophet, as it is written: “And I have appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5).

Third, Luke, the most learned in Greek speech among all the evangelists—especially as a physician—wrote the Gospel in Greece for the bishop Theophilus. He began with the priestly spirit, saying: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah” (Luke 1:5). He thereby revealed that, after his bodily birth and the preaching of the Gospel, Christ became a sacrifice for the salvation of the world. For he is the priest of whom it is said in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4). When Christ came, the priesthood of the Jews fell silent, and the Law and prophecy ceased.

[Col. 1129A]

Fourth, John wrote the Gospel last, in Asia. He began with the Word, to show that the same Savior who graciously consented to be born and suffer for us was the Word of God before the ages; that he came from heaven; and that after death he returned again to heaven.

**Interlocutor:** Now I want you to explain why there are four who wrote these deeds, and also who the four are who, as the Prophet announces, were marked by the divine Spirit.

**Response:** The writers of the Gospel narratives are therefore said to be four because, as the Prophet says, four living creatures were shown: the first bearing the likeness of a man, the second of a lion, the third of a calf, and the fourth of an eagle. There is no doubt that these four creatures, bearing these figures, are the evangelists.

[Col. 1129B]

**Interlocutor:** Why were these evangelists compared with four living creatures?

**Response:** Because through the four parts of the world the faith of the Christian religion was spread by their preaching.

**Interlocutor:** Why are they called living creatures?

**Response:** Because the Gospel of Christ is preached for the sake of the human soul. They were also full of eyes within and without, because the Gospels foresee the things spoken by the prophets and the things promised in the earlier covenant. Their legs were straight because nothing crooked is found in the Gospels. They had six wings covering their legs and faces, for the things that had been hidden were revealed at Christ’s coming.

[Col. 1129C]

**Interlocutor:** Tell me why the evangelist placed the order backward in Christ’s genealogy, naming David first and Abraham afterward.

**Response:** The order was necessarily changed in this place. For if he had placed Abraham first and David afterward, he would have had to mention Abraham again in order to weave together the sequence of Christ’s genealogy.

**Interlocutor:** Why, passing over the others, did he call him the son of these men?

**Response:** He called him the son of these men because the promise is read as having been made only to them.

**Interlocutor:** How was the promise made to Abraham, and how to David?

**Response:** It was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18)—that seed is Christ. But to David: “I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb” (Psalm 131:11).

[Col. 1129D]

**Interlocutor:** Having completed the first division of the New Testament, tell me who were the authors of the second division that follows.

**Response:** I shall say what I understand.

**Interlocutor:** Tell me, then, who wrote Paul’s Epistles; how many there are; and where each was written.

**Response:** [Note: [Col. 1129D] Isidore, cited above.]

The apostle Paul wrote fourteen Epistles. Of these, he wrote nine to seven churches; the others he wrote to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. Concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, most Latins are uncertain that it is his, because of the difference in style. Some think that Barnabas wrote it; others suspect that it was written by Clement.

[Col. 1130A]

**Interlocutor:** Who wrote Peter’s Epistles, how many are there, and what are they called?

**Response:** Peter wrote two Epistles bearing his name. They are called catholic because they were written not merely to one people or city but generally to all nations.

**Interlocutor:** Who wrote those of James, John, and Jude?

**Response:** James, John, and Jude wrote their own Epistles.

**Interlocutor:** Who was the author of the Acts of the Apostles?

**Response:** The Acts of the Apostles sets forth the beginnings of the Christian faith among the nations and the history of the Church at its birth. It is clear that Luke the evangelist was the author of the Acts of the Apostles. In this work the infancy of the newly born Church is woven together, and the history of the apostles is preserved. Hence it is called the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 1130B]

**Interlocutor:** Who wrote the Apocalypse, at what time, and where?

**Response:** John the evangelist wrote the Book of the Apocalypse at the time when, because of preaching the Gospel, he is said to have been confined in the island of Patmos [reading: banished].

**Interlocutor:** In what language is *Apocalypse* said, and what does it mean?

**Response:** *Apocalypse* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “revelation.”

**Interlocutor:** What is revelation?

**Response:** Revelation is the disclosure of things that had been hidden, in accordance with what John himself says: “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known openly to his servants” (Revelation 1:1).

These writers, and the others whom we enumerated a little earlier in the Old Testament, are the writers of the sacred books. Speaking through the Holy Spirit for our instruction, they composed precepts for living and the rule of belief.

[Col. 1130C]

Apart from these, other volumes are called apocryphal.

**Interlocutor:** Why are they called apocryphal?

**Response:** They are called apocryphal—that is, “secret”—because they are doubtful. Their origin is hidden, and it is not evident to the Fathers, from whom the authority of the true Scriptures has come down to us through a most certain and well-known succession. Although some truth is found in these apocryphal books, nevertheless, because of the many falsehoods in them, they possess no canonical authority. The wise rightly judge that the works attributed to the persons named as their authors are not to be believed. For heretics produce many works under the names of prophets and more recent works under the names of apostles; all these have been removed from canonical authority through careful examination under the designation “apocryphal.”

[Col. 1130D]

434 **Interlocutor:** Behold, you have presented, in part, interpretations [manuscript: temptations], numbers, divisions, and authors, as well as the names of the books of the New Testament. Now I ask you to run through each of them and explain briefly whatever they contain.

**Response:** By the Lord’s will, I shall not grow weary of this.

**Interlocutor:** Tell me, then, what is principally contained in the books of the New Testament?

**Response:** As far as he permits who is the source of both the Old and the New Testament, I shall speak as the present inquiry requires.

[Col. 1131A]

**Interlocutor:** Since the books of the Gospels have rightly been placed at the beginning of them, tell me what they contain.

**Response:** I shall tell you briefly, insofar as I am able. They contain preaching, which nevertheless is understood to be one preaching because it proceeded from one and the same mouth of divinity. These are the four rivers flowing from the one spring of Paradise, which provide heavenly preaching throughout the whole world and pour the freshness of grace and faith from their stream.

**Interlocutor:** What is contained in Paul’s Epistles?

**Response:** In the one he wrote to the Romans, he praises the faith of the Roman people. In those to the Corinthians, he corrects a twofold doctrine. To the Galatians, through the grace of faith, he excludes the works of the Law. To the Ephesians, he magnifies them for the faith they have received. To the Colossians, he praises them because they have persevered in faith.

[Col. 1131B]

To the Philippians, he rejoices that they have kept the Gospel. To the Thessalonians, he boasts that they believed in faith [perhaps: by faith] and works and endured persecutions. To Timothy and Titus, he gives instruction concerning the churches. To Philemon, he makes a request concerning Onesimus, the reformed slave. In the last Epistle, which he wrote to the Hebrews, he strengthens those who had believed in Christ but afterward, frightened by Jewish persecutions, had withdrawn from the faith, and he recalls them to the grace of the Gospel.

**Interlocutor:** What is contained in Peter’s Epistles?

**Response:** There is depth of meaning in them, because they are filled with insights, so that through them the meaning of divine knowledge may be searched out.

**Interlocutor:** What is contained in James?

[Note: [Col. 1131] Here there is a defect and an omitted question concerning the Epistles of Saint John, to which the response here belongs.]

**Response:** The building up of the Church and the pouring out of charity in love of God and brotherly affection. In the second [Epistle of John], he urges devotion to love. In the third, he praises Gaius for his devotion to truth and is concerned with works of mercy.

[Col. 1131C]

**Interlocutor:** What is contained in Jude?

**Response:** A rebuke of those who blaspheme against Christ.

**Interlocutor:** What is contained in the Acts of the Apostles?

**Response:** The history of the Church at its birth and a description of the work of faith.

**Interlocutor:** What is contained in the Apocalypse?

**Response:** Many things, difficult indeed, are read in it, but I shall briefly present some of them to you. It contains the throne of the Son of Man and the twenty-four elders; likewise the four living creatures standing before the throne. It marks the end of the world, Michael’s battle with the dragon, the destruction of Antichrist, the punishment of the devil, and finally the resurrection of the dead, the renewal of heaven and earth, and other things.

[Col. 1131D]

Brother, gladly accept this brief account of the New Testament for the present, until, God willing, I bring forth greater matters from it for you.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE RANKS OF THE DIGNITY OF THE WHOLE CHURCH

**Interlocutor:** Tell me, then, brother, how many are the ecclesiastical ranks?

**Response:** Of those that, by God’s will, can presently concern us, there are eight.

**Interlocutor:** What are their names?

**Response:** The first is the doorkeeper, the second the psalmist, the third the lector, the fourth the exorcist, the fifth the acolyte, the sixth the subdeacon, the seventh the deacon, and the eighth the presbyter.

[Col. 1132A]

**Interlocutor:** Now I want you to tell me why he is called a doorkeeper.

**Response:** As I have read, I shall explain. They are called doorkeepers because they preside over the doors of the temple, so that they may know how to admit the faithful and reject the unfaithful. Hence the Lord also graciously became a doorkeeper when he opened the gates of hell, removed his elect from there, and left the reprobate behind.

**Interlocutor:** From where is the psalmist named?

**Response:** From singing psalms. They sing in order to arouse the souls of their hearers to compunction.

**Interlocutor:** Why are they called lectors?

**Response:** They are called lectors from reading. They proclaim to the peoples what they should follow. Hence the Lord is also called a lector when the Lord opened the book of the prophet Isaiah and read in the midst of the people, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18).

[Col. 1132B]

**Interlocutor:** Why is he called an exorcist?

**Response:** Exorcists are called from the Greek into Latin “those who adjure” or “those who rebuke.” Hence the Lord was also an exorcist when he cast seven demons out of Mary Magdalene.

**Interlocutor:** From where is the acolyte named, or what ministry does he have?

**Response:** Acolytes are called in Greek, but in Latin they are called *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” from carrying candles when the Gospel is to be read and the sacrifice offered.

**Interlocutor:** Why is he called a subdeacon?

**Response:** They are called subdeacons because they are subject to the commands and duties of the Levites. For they ought to [lacuna] keep the altar in honorable condition and prepare water for the service of the altar. Hence the Lord was also called a subdeacon, because at Cana of Galilee he changed water into wine.

[Col. 1132C]

**Interlocutor:** In what language is “deacon” said, or from where is the deacon so called?

**Response:** *Deacon* in Greek is called *minister* in Latin, because just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of ministry belongs to the deacon. Hence the Lord was called a deacon when he washed the feet of his disciples.

**Interlocutor:** Why is the same deacon called a Levite?

**Response:** The Levites are named from their ancestor. For the Levites arose from Levi.

**Interlocutor:** Since you have already spoken of deacons and Levites, whose proper ministry it is to read the Gospel [Supplement: you said, or something similar], the matter now requires me to ask you to say what the Gospel is, from where it derives, and whose words are set down in it.

[Col. 1132D]

**Response:** The Gospel properly means “good announcement,” and this announcement is certainly that of our Lord Jesus Christ; it announces life after death. The Gospel derives from the one who announces and shows that he who spoke through his prophets has come in the flesh, as it is written: “I who was speaking—behold, I am here” (Isaiah 52:6).

435

**Interlocutor:** You have explained what the Gospel is and from where it comes. Now I ask you to explain why there are four who wrote these deeds, and who these four are who were marked by one Spirit, as the Prophet announces.

[Col. 1133A]

**Response:** The writers of the Gospel narrative are therefore said to be four because, as the Prophet says, four living creatures were shown: the first bearing the likeness of a man, the second of a lion, the third of a calf, and the fourth of an eagle. There is no doubt that these four, bearing these figures, are the evangelists.

**Interlocutor:** Behold, you have stated the number and the figures of each. Now I want you to tell me all their names, and also for what reason each appears to bear these figures.

**Response:** Their names are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. But, with the Lord’s mercy, I shall explain why they bear these figures.

**Interlocutor:** Do so.

**Response:** Matthew bears the figure of a man because at the beginning of his Gospel he recounts the generation and birth of the Savior. For he begins this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1), and so forth.

[Col. 1133B]

Mark bears the figure of a lion because he begins in the wilderness, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Mark 1:3).

Luke bears the appearance of a calf, in whose likeness our Savior was sacrificed. Luke is therefore compared with a calf because its two horns signify the two Testaments and the four-hoofed feet signify the four Gospels, and because calves were offered in sacrifice at that time. Thus he begins with the priests: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron; her name was Elizabeth” (Luke 1:5).

[Col. 1133C]

John bears the likeness of an eagle because he sought lofty things. For he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; he was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1). And David says concerning Christ’s person: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 102:5), that is, the youth of Christ Jesus our Lord, because, rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven.

**Interlocutor:** Brother, insofar as I could, I have resolved your question for you. If it pleases you, I ask you to tell me why the evangelist placed the order backward in Christ’s genealogy, naming David first and Abraham afterward.

**Response:** Truly, according to what I have learned by reading, I shall relate it. The order was necessarily changed in this place. For if he had placed Abraham first and David afterward, he would again have had to mention Abraham in order to weave together the sequence of the genealogy.

**Interlocutor:** Why, passing over the others, did they call him the son of these men?

[Col. 1133D]

**Response:** They called him the son of these men because the promise is read as having been made only to them.

**Questioner:** How was the promise made to Abraham, and how to David?

**Answerer:** Abraham was told: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18)—which is Christ. But to David: “I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb” (Ps. CXXXI, 11). These few remarks concerning the account of the Gospels and their written records, on account of the shortness of the day, may suffice for this occasion, if it pleases your lordship [Cod.: *may suffice*].

**Questioner:** Now let us proceed to the other matters.

**Answerer:** Let it be done, as you say.

[Col. 1134A]

**Questioner:** Tell me, presbyter: in what language is the word called, and from where is it derived?

**Answerer:** *Presbyter* is Greek; in Latin it means “elder.” Yet they are not so called because of age or decrepit old age, but because of the honor and dignity which they have received.

**Questioner:** Why is the same person called a priest?

**Answerer:** The word *sacerdos* (“priest”) is compounded from Greek and Latin, as though meaning “one who gives what is sacred.” For just as a king is so called from *ruling*, so a priest is named from *sanctifying*. He consecrates and sanctifies.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE MASS

**Questioner:** Behold, my brother, concerning the order of the ranks about which you asked, I have briefly set forth an explanation for you. Now I ask you to explain to me the account of the Mass celebrated by them, [Col. 1134B] and why it is called by that name.

**Answerer:** Certainly, brother; you ask of me a difficult matter. Nevertheless, insofar as the present discussion requires and according to what I know, I will not refuse to answer you.

**Questioner:** From where is *missa* (“Mass”) derived?

**Answerer:** From *emitting* or *sending out*.

**Questioner:** In what way?

**Answerer:** The Mass takes its name from the time of the sacrifice, when the catechumens were sent outside, the levite proclaiming: “If any catechumen remains, let him be sent out,” because those who are known not yet to have been regenerated cannot be present at the sacrament [Cod.: *sacraments*] of the altar.

**Questioner:** Why is this sacrifice, of which you spoke, so called?

**Answerer:** It is called *sacrifice* because it is a sacred act, since it is consecrated for us by a mystical prayer in memory of the Lord’s Passion. Hence, at his command, we also call this the body and blood of Christ: so that, sanctified from the fruits of the earth, it becomes a sacrament through the invisible working of the Spirit of God. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup *Eucharistia* [Εὐχαριστία], which in Latin means “good grace.”

**Questioner:** From where is *offertory* derived?

**Answerer:** It is called an *offering* because it is carried to the altars and sanctified by the priests.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 19.]

**Questioner:** What is the difference between *gifts* and *offerings*?

**Answerer:** Gifts are properly said to be God’s [Cod.: *divine*]; offerings belong to human beings.

**Questioner:** In what way?

**Answerer:** Offerings are called acts of service, which the poor pay to the rich in place of gifts; but a gift is what is given to God. Hence in temples we also speak of *donaria*, votive gifts.

[Col. 1134D]

**Questioner:** From where are *offerings* called by that name?

**Answerer:** They are called *munera* because they are either received or given by hand.

**Questioner:** How many kinds are there of things that are offered?

**Answerer:** Two.

**Questioner:** Which?

**Answerer:** A gift and a sacrifice.

**Questioner:** What is a gift?

**Answerer:** A gift is anything fashioned from gold, silver, or any other material.

**Questioner:** What is a sacrifice?

**Answerer:** A sacrifice is a victim and whatever is burned or placed upon an altar. 436 For everything that is given to God is either spoken of as being given or is consecrated.

**Questioner:** In what way?

**Answerer:** Whatever is “spoken of as given” is given by the act of speaking, and from this it receives its name. Hence those who think that *consecration* signifies *dedication* are mistaken.

**Questioner:** From where is *immolation* derived?

[Col. 1135A]

**Answerer:** Among the ancients it was called *immolation* because victims were slaughtered upon the *mola* [Isidore: *mole*] of the altar. Hence also comes the term *slaughter* after immolation. Now, however, the term *immolation* is appropriately applied to the bread and cup.

**Questioner:** What is a libation?

**Answerer:** A libation is solely the offering of the cup. Hence it is said: “And he poured out a libation from the blood of the grape” (Ecclus. L, 16); for *to libate* means “to pour out.”

**Questioner:** From where are victims called *hostiae*?

**Answerer:** Among the ancients, *hostiae* were called sacrifices made before they went forth against an enemy.

**Questioner:** What are *victims*, and why are they so called?

**Answerer:** *Victims* are sacrifices which they immolated after victory, when the enemies had been defeated. Victims were greater sacrifices than *hostiae*. Others have thought that a victim was so called because it fell when struck by a blow, or because it was led bound to the altars.

[Col. 1135B]

**Questioner:** From where is *holocaust* derived?

**Answerer:** A holocaust is an offering in which everything is consumed by fire. For *holo* [ὅλον] in Greek means “the whole,” and *kausis* [καῦσις] means “burning”; hence *holocaust*, “entirely burned.”

**Questioner:** What are ceremonies?

**Answerer:** Among the Latins, *ceremonies* are called all sacred rites which among the Greeks are called *orgia* [ὄργια]. Properly, however, the teachers have thought that *caeremonia* derives from *carere*, “to lack,” as though *carimonia*, because in sacred rites people lacked for their own use the things offered there. Others believe that *ceremonies* properly concern the observances of the Jews—namely, abstinence from certain foods according to the old law—because those who observe them lack the things from which they abstain.

[Col. 1135C]

**Questioner:** From which pontiff did the Mass itself take its beginning?

**Answerer:** [Note: [Col. 1135D] Isidore, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15, with considerable difference.] The order of the Mass, or of the prayers by which the sacrifices offered to God are consecrated, was first instituted by Saint Peter, and the whole world performs its celebration under one and the same name.

**Questioner:** I humbly beseech you not to disdain opening to me what the same Mass contains.

**Answerer:** I shall speak according to my understanding. The order of the entire Mass contains seven prayers.

**Questioner:** What are they?

**Answerer:** The first of these prayers, where it says, “The Lord be with you,” or “Let us pray,” is an admonition directed to the people, so that they may be stirred up to worship God. The second is the collect that follows: an invocation of God, asking him mercifully to receive the prayers of the faithful and their offerings. The third is the prayer poured out for those who offer, or for faithful departed, in the collect said after the reception of the sacrifice, so that through that same sacrifice they may deserve to obtain forgiveness. The fourth, which follows, is for the kiss of peace and the charity of reconciliation, from “Lift up your hearts” through “through Christ our Lord.” The fifth is then the *inlatio* [Isidore: *illatio*], the prayer of offering in the sanctification of the oblation, from the place where it says, “Through whom the angels praise your majesty,” [Col. 1136A] up to the place where “Hosanna in the highest” is sung. In it, the whole company of earthly creatures and heavenly powers is also summoned to praise. Then the sixth follows: “Therefore, most merciful Father,” which is the confirmation of the sacrament, so that the offering, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, may be conformed [Note: [Col. 1135D] It is beyond doubt that the particle *in* must be supplied here, expressing that the sanctified offering is conformed or transformed *into* the body and blood of Christ—nothing other than transubstantiation.] to the body and blood [Note: [Col. 1136D] In Isidore, at the cited passage: “may be confirmed to the body and blood of Christ,” which makes no sense.]. The seventh prayer is the one which our Lord taught his disciples to pray, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

**Questioner:** How many petitions are contained in this prayer?

**Answerer:** I have answered you briefly, as far as I know, concerning the order of the Mass.

**Questioner:** Now I ask you likewise not to refuse to tell me, according to your understanding, what this prayer contains.

**Answerer:** I shall do so according to my understanding. [Col. 1136B] Seven petitions are contained in this prayer.

**Questioner:** What are they?

**Answerer:** The first is: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.” The second: “Your kingdom come.” The third: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” The fourth: “Give us this day our daily bread.” The fifth: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” The sixth: “And lead us not into temptation.” The seventh: “But deliver us from evil.”

**Questioner:** Now I ask you to tell me what is contained in these petitions.

**Answerer:** [Note: [Col. 1136D] Isidore, at the cited passage.] In the first three, eternal things are requested; in the following four, temporal things, which nevertheless are requested in order to attain eternal things.

**Questioner:** How so?

**Answerer:** For when we say, “Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. [Col. 1136C] Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth,” these three things indeed begin here, but are hoped for in that life where the sanctification of God, his will, and his kingdom will remain immortal in his saints. But daily bread, which is given either to the soul or to the flesh, is requested here. [[Note: [Col. 1136D] The words enclosed in brackets have been supplied from Isidore.] Here, after the provision of food, forgiveness is requested according to the example of fraternal pardon; here we ask that we not fall into the temptation of sin.] Here, finally, we implore God’s help so that we may be delivered from evils. But in the three mentioned above none of these temporal matters is present. Thus the Savior taught this prayer to his disciples; it contains the hope of the faithful and the confession of sins.

## CHAPTER XI. BEGINNING OF THE DISCUSSION OF FAITH

[Col. 1136D]

**Questioner:** I accept this. But since, as you know, we believe that all are saved through faith, I ask you to tell me how you understand your faith, or in whom you believe.

**Answerer:** I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.

**Questioner:** Why is he called almighty, and why creator?

**Answerer:** He is called almighty because he can do all things; creator because he created everything—heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them.

[Col. 1137A]

**Questioner:** Do you believe in Jesus Christ?

**Answerer:** Certainly. 437 I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who is true God and true man.

**Questioner:** In what way is he God, and in what way is he truly man?

**Answerer:** He is true God because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit. He is true man because he was born of the Virgin Mary.

**Questioner:** Behold him born. What happened afterward?

**Answerer:** After his holy birth, he grew in age and wisdom and completed thirty years. At that age he also deigned to be baptized by John the Baptist; after his baptism he taught and preached for three and a half years everything pertaining to eternal life.

**Questioner:** What happened after this preaching?

**Answerer:** During that very preaching he was seized by wicked and faithless Jews, from whom, because of their envy and because of our sins, he endured many blasphemies and many sufferings under Pontius Pilate, who was judge in Judea at that time.

[Col. 1137B]

**Questioner:** From where is the name Pontius derived?

**Answerer:** He received this name from the place where he was born.

**Questioner:** What happened after these things?

**Answerer:** Under that ruler he was crucified and died on the same cross. Then he was buried, and, while his body remained in the tomb, his soul descended to the underworld. From that underworld he mercifully freed the holy patriarchs—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and the holy prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the rest, together with all the others whom he had chosen; and, victorious, he rose from the dead on the third day.

**Questioner:** After he rose, what did he do?

**Answerer:** [Col. 1137C] After his most glorious and holy resurrection, he remained with his disciples for forty days and forty nights and ate with them, teaching and speaking many things about the kingdom of God.

**Questioner:** What happened afterward?

**Answerer:** After these things, while they watched, he ascended into heaven, where he sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, in whatever manner and fashion he wills.

**Questioner:** What will he do afterward?

**Answerer:** When the end of the world has come, he will come in the same body with which he ascended into heaven to judge the living and the dead.

**Questioner:** Who are the living, and who are the dead?

**Answerer:** The living are the righteous; the dead are sinners.

**Questioner:** Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?

**Answerer:** Without doubt I believe in the Holy Spirit, who is the same God [Col. 1137D] and the third person in the Trinity. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. In this Trinity I wholly believe and confess that there is one God.

**Questioner:** Do you believe in the holy catholic Church and in the communion of saints?

**Answerer:** I believe that the holy Church exists, but I do not believe in it, because it is not God but a convocation or congregation of Christians [the verb *est*, “is,” is supplied], as I said above [Note: [Col. 1137D] Rather, below, near the end].

**Questioner:** What does *catholic* mean?

**Answerer:** Universal—that is, spread throughout the whole world. I believe that there is a communion of saints, that is, fellowship and communion with the saints, if I hold the faith firmly and preserve it in my works.

**Questioner:** In what language is *Church* said?

**Answerer:** In Greek.

[Col. 1138A]

**Questioner:** What does it mean in Latin?

**Answerer:** “Convocation” or “congregation of Christians,” as I said above.

**Questioner:** Do you believe in the remission of sins?

**Answerer:** No; but I believe that there is remission of sins. For this reason the Son of God deigned to assume flesh: so that we, who because of our sins could not be saved, might be saved by his mercy.

**Questioner:** Do you believe in the resurrection of the flesh?

**Answerer:** I do not believe in it, but I believe that the flesh which in this life we bear under mortal conditions will rise immortal and render an account in association with the soul. Let us believe without doubt that we shall attain eternal life if we hold firmly what we have set forth up to this point and faithfully fulfill it in our works.

[Col. 1138B]

If you desire to know the account of this same faith more fully, you will find it in the following order.

**Questioner:** Tell me: the creed in which this same faith is contained—in what language is its name called? At what time, and by which authors, was it composed? And those who composed it—whose example did they follow?

**Answerer:** Certainly, brother: although you know that I am small not only in body but also in understanding, you ask of me a very difficult account. Nevertheless, because of my love for this same faith, I will not refuse to disclose to you what the Lord deigns to provide me concerning it.

**Questioner:** If I did not know such love on your part, I should never have presumed to ask such things of you.

**Answerer:** The name *symbolum* is Greek; in Latin it means “a contribution of money.” The blessed apostles composed it as a sign of faith after receiving the Holy Spirit and before separating from one another. But whose example they imitated in this action I shall briefly show, according to what I have read.

Certain Israelite tribes were fighting a civil war against one another. Since, because of the [arms or something similar supplied] of one people [or their dress], no distinction could be made among the combatants, that tribe whose cause for fighting was more just and which believed it had obtained victory through God’s help established for itself a fixed sign in speech. Thus the sacrament of a more secret word distinguished those whom identical clothing and the similarity of their weapons had confused [Cod.: *confunderat*, “had confounded”].

The blessed apostles likewise, who armed the Church of God against the malice of diabolical fury and were destined to be its defenders [Col. 1138D] and champions, following this example, handed down the mystery of the creed. And because there was to be a diversity among believers under the one name of Christ, the sign of the creed would separate the faithful from the faithless, revealing who was faithful and who an enemy of the Church.

**Questioner:** I greatly approve what you say, if only you had wished to identify the names of those tribes and the name of the secret word of which you spoke.

**Answerer:** If I remember correctly, I shall do what you requested. When Jephthah, the leader of the tribe of Gilead whose cause was more just, learned that its enemies—namely, the tribe of Ephraim—had come against it, he immediately seized the fords of the Jordan by which they would have to return.

[Col. 1139A]

When they recognized that they had been defeated and, fleeing from the battle, wished to escape by crossing those same fords, they asked permission to pass and were questioned: “Where are you from?” They replied, “From Gilead.” Immediately they were told: “If you are from Gilead, then say *Seboleth*,” which means “ear of grain.” When they could not pronounce it, they were at once beheaded, so that the truth of the secret word might be established.

This, then, is the secret word which the Gileadites established for themselves as a sign. Unless I am mistaken, the blessed apostles composed the aforesaid creed in imitation of it, so that, as was said above, they might distinguish the truth of belief between the faithful and the faithless of the Church. The blessed Peter began it, saying: “I believe in God the Father almighty,” and so forth.

[Col. 1139B]

**Questioner:** What you say is very good. But I beseech you carefully to explain how, in what manner, and in whom I ought to believe.

**Answerer:** I shall do so according to my understanding. Without doubt, God the Father almighty is to be believed; his power is perceived in such a way that his magnitude and quality remain unknown. We attain knowledge of his being and power not by investigation but by believing.

But in whom we ought to believe, the authority of our Redeemer teaches us, saying: “He who believes in me and in him who sent me has eternal life” (John III, 15). And elsewhere: “Believe in God, and believe in me” (ibid., XIV, 1). For, brother, what we see with the eyes of faith is greater for me than what our bodily sense can perceive.

**Questioner:** I entirely believe as you say. But I ask you to tell me what I ought to understand by “God,” what by “Father,” and what by “almighty.”

**Answerer:** In “God,” the unbegotten nature is shown; in “Father,” the truth of the only-begotten Son; and in “almighty,” the fullness of power.

**Questioner:** How so?

**Answerer:** He is almighty through his innate divinity, and Father through his omnipotence. We ought not to inquire how he is Father, because how he is God or almighty cannot be grasped by human minds.

**Questioner:** The explanation you gave of the first verse can suffice for this occasion. But tell me who composed the second, and how I ought to understand it.

**Answerer:** Andrew composed the second verse, saying: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” For just as we must confess the Father as God of all things, so we must confess his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is his Word. His beginning is from him, because he is God the Word. But that he who was the Son was made Christ is the dispensation of human redemption. That he is Lord belongs to the property of his nature. He is proclaimed and believed to be “only” or “only-begotten,” because he alone was begotten in this manner and has no partner in unity. When you hear “Son,” do not suppose that he was produced through any sexual act; rather, believe that in incomprehensible majesty God came forth from God, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John XVI, 28).

**Questioner:** Who composed the third verse, and what is understood in it?

**Answerer:** James said: “Who was conceived [Col. 1140A] of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” The Savior himself taught us that the Spirit is God, saying in the Gospel: “For the Spirit is God” (John IV, 24). Therefore we confess that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. When you hear “Holy Spirit,” recognize that his birth was at once marvelous and blameless. For what the Spirit does is heavenly, and what the Holy One accomplishes is inviolate.

When the necessity of our redemption demanded that God’s only-begotten Son become man, he brought into his birth the privilege of his own divinity [Possibly: “by his own divinity”], so that he might be born of a virgin. For he who came to renew the human nature grown old through sins wished to have a new law of birth. Thus God’s only-begotten Son became the son of man, so that he who was the creator of the world [Col. 1140B] might also become its redeemer.

**Questioner:** Explain to me the composer of the fourth verse, or what it contains.
