**Answerer:** The blessed apostle John composed the fourth verse, saying: “He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.” This Pilate was judge in Judea at that time, appointed by Caesar Tiberius, under whom the Lord suffered. He is also called Pontius from the place where he was born.

We must confess this Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, to be perfect God and likewise perfect man. Let us have no shame concerning his cross, because through his Passion we possess victory. For just as the Son of God was born not for himself but for us, so the immaculate Lamb of God suffered not for himself but [Col. 1140C] for us.

Who would not recognize this as a wondrous mystery, in which he who is God is preached, and the Lord is announced as crucified? We bear upon our foreheads the cross on which he was fastened in the body. Therefore we ought not to lament with sighs the mockeries, insults, and death that he endured, but to celebrate them with continual praises. For the sudden darkness of the sun, the trembling of the earth, the splitting of the rocks, and the resurrection of the dead sufficiently and abundantly displayed the glory of his Passion.

He was buried because it followed that he who had died should receive burial. Thus the earth received the blessing of his body for the consolation of the buried, so that he who was seen to be truly dead might be believed truly to have returned from the dead.

[Col. 1140D]

**Questioner:** I desire to hear from you the composer of the fifth verse and its explanation.

**Answerer:** Philip explained the fifth verse, saying: “He descended to the underworld; on the third day he rose from the dead.” In this the mystery of the Trinity and the dissolution of the natural law are shown, so that he might raise the man placed in the underworld to heaven.

For it was fitting that death, which had entered through man, should be undone through man. And just as we believe what belongs to death, so surely let us believe what belongs to life. And just as in the Passion there is the mystery of piety, so in the resurrection there is the working of piety [Possibly: *power*], as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18).

What fool would not believe that he rose, at whose command Lazarus, who had been buried, emerged from the tomb?

[Col. 1141A]

**Questioner:** Who composed the sixth verse, or what is to be understood in it?

**Answerer:** Bartholomew composed the sixth verse in this manner, saying: “He ascended into heaven.” For he ascended to the place from which he had come—not at someone else’s command, but by his own will.

Such glory was fitting for the man who was born of a virgin. Nor was it impossible for him to ascend into heaven, for whom it was possible to triumph over the underworld. Therefore it was necessary that he who had come from the kingdom to death should, after death, return to the kingdom.

And just as the earth rejoiced that it had received the Son of God, so heaven should rejoice that it had received the Son of man, as the Prophet says: “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult” (Ps. XCV, 11).

[Col. 1141B]

**Questioner:** I beseech you to explain to me the author of the seventh verse and its meaning.

**Answerer:** Thomas was the author of the seventh verse, saying: “He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.” That he sits is the gift of Christ’s victory; that he sits at the right hand of the Father is the privilege and participation of divinity in undivided love. This was to show the place reserved for the righteous and to point out the left hand for sinners. He is rightly proclaimed to sit at the Father’s right hand, in whom the devil, who is entirely left-handed, found nothing belonging to his own will.

**Questioner:** Who composed the eighth verse, or what does it contain?

**Answerer:** Matthew, composing the eighth verse, said: “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” The Lord will come to judgment in the very body in which he ascended into heaven.

It is necessary that he who created the human race should examine it, and that he who redeemed it should himself judge it. For it is just that the almighty Lord should distinguish his mortals—whom he formed by the power of his divinity and saved through the Father’s mercy—by the examination of judgment, so that he may hand the wicked over to the fire of Gehenna, but receive the pious into the fellowship of eternity.

What could be more just before God than that, since their lives were different in this world, their merits should be distinguished after this world? Where judgment is said to concern “the living” and the dead, let it be believed that God has care for all human beings.

[Col. 1141C]

**Questioner:** Who composed the ninth verse, or how is it to be understood?

**Answerer:** Again James added the ninth verse, saying: “I believe in the Holy Spirit.” This belongs to the form of faith: just as we believe in the Father and the Son, so also we must believe in the Holy Spirit without any doubt, so that those whose name is one may not have different confessions. And those who are one with themselves in heaven should not be separated by us on earth.

For just as nothing created can be made equal to divinity, so the nature of divinity excludes every division and inequality. Therefore, according to evangelical truth, just as the Son came forth from the Father, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. And just as the only-begotten Son is God, so the Holy Spirit is God.

And just as the Father has mercy on whomever he wills, and the Son reveals the Father to whomever he wills, so the Spirit is also read to inspire as he wills and to distribute the gifts of heavenly graces as he wills. Since these things are so, how could the Spirit not be believed to be one with the Father and the Son, when the ability to do what he wills belongs equally to him?

[Col. 1142A]

**Questioner:** It must certainly be believed as you assert. But I ask you to explain to me the author of the tenth verse and its meaning.

**Answerer:** Simon was the author of the tenth verse, saying: “The holy catholic Church, and so forth.” The holy Church exists, but we ought not to believe in it, because it is not God but the people and house of God. Through it sanctification has been given to mortals, and, as the number of believers increases, the increasingly holy world exults in God’s praises in almost every language.

The Church, cleansed through the sacrament of baptism from the contamination of sins, also transports the inhabitants of the earth to heaven. It is called catholic, that is, spread throughout the whole world.

The communion of saints, which follows, means that we should believe that we possess fellowship and communion of hope with those saints who, in the faith we have received, have migrated from the present world to God—provided that we hold that faith by living rightly and fulfill it in our works.

[Col. 1142B]

**Questioner:** Who composed the eleventh verse, or what should I understand in it?

**Answerer:** Thaddeus, composing the eleventh verse, said: “The remission of sins.” The remission of sins must certainly be believed, because this is the one remedy that absolves the human race from the sentence of everlasting death.

For this reason the only-begotten Son of the Most High deigned both to assume flesh and to undergo the cross, so that we, who because of crimes and sins could not escape, might by his indulgence be made innocent. Therefore the immaculate [Col. 1142C] Lamb was slain, so that the stains of the human race might be wiped away by his blood.

Behold the depth of the mystery! Behold the height of the sacrament! Here death gives back life, and the filth of sinners is cleansed by the blood of the innocent.

This remission does not nourish us toward sin, but warns us to fear sin now, since we understand that we cannot be saved without forgiveness. For the goodness of God, through the gift of his indulgence, does not arm us for guilt but acquits us for glory.

**Questioner:** Since the other verses have been explained, I humbly ask you to disclose who composed the twelfth, and what miracle it contains.

**Answerer:** Certainly, brother. As with the others, so also in this matter I shall kindly comply with your request, according to my understanding. Matthias, who was chosen by lot by the apostles after Judas, [Col. 1142D] added the twelfth verse, saying: “The resurrection of the flesh and eternal life.”

Let us believe that the flesh which in this life we bear under mortal conditions will rise immortal and render an account in association with the soul. For who, believing in God, could doubt the resurrection, when it is clear that this alone was the reason for Christ’s birth?

What benefit was there in his deigning to assume flesh perpetually, unless he was to give flesh perpetual life? What glory would there be in the Son of God’s not shrinking from the cross, desiring death, and enduring burial, unless by granting resurrection he bestowed life upon mortals?

Divinity makes this possible; faith holds that for it everything that it wills is possible. Finally, so that we may take examples of resurrection beyond doubt, the world itself, losing and recovering the beauty of its appearance, both dies and rises again.

We receive a demonstration of the future resurrection when grain entrusted to the furrows returns to its own stalk, and woods stripped by frost grow green again with renewed leaves. Everything that the earth produces is likewise multiplied and restored either from seed or from root.

What hardness of heart is it not to believe that man can be restored, when everything that has been made is repaired? As for eternal life, which follows, let us believe without any doubt that we shall attain it if we hold firmly what I have explained to you up to this point and faithfully preserve it in good works. For, as you know, faith without works is dead. This is evident to all.

[Col. 1143B]

This is the creed, my brother, which you asked me to explain to you. By its sign, as has been said, the faithful are separated from the faithless at the beginning. This is the creed whose truth makes every believer a Christian. This is the creed which sanctifies the living and restores the dead to life—to that life may he deign to lead us who, three and one, lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

440

## CHAPTER XII. BEGINNING OF THE DISCUSSION OF THE LORD’S PRAYER

**Questioner:** Having explained the faith to you as best I could, I now ask you to tell me, if you know it, the Lord’s Prayer, which our Lord Jesus Christ taught his disciples to pray.

**Answerer:** I know it.

**Questioner:** I humbly ask you to recite it to me.

**Answerer:** As I am able, through the mercy of that same Lord who taught it, I shall do so: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” and so forth.

[Col. 1143C]

**Questioner:** How many petitions are found in this prayer?

**Answerer:** Seven.

**Questioner:** What is the first?

**Answerer:** “Hallowed be your name.”

**Questioner:** How is what you said at the beginning—“Our Father, who are in heaven”—to be understood?

**Answerer:** It is an invocation of dignity, since we profess that we have God as our Father, because we are all brothers and have God as our Father in heaven.

**Questioner:** In the first petition, which you mentioned above, [Col. 1144A] what is to be understood?

**Answerer:** The Christian derives his name from Christ. Therefore, while we are called Christians, we bear Christ’s name, and we pray that we may be able to perform Christ’s works and that his name may be sanctified in us through our good works.

**Questioner:** What is the second petition?

**Answerer:** “Your kingdom come.”

**Questioner:** What is to be understood there?

**Answerer:** We pray that Christ may reign in us and not the devil; that the Church of Christ may always grow, in which God reigns; and that the day of judgment may come, because then the devil will cease to reign in the world and Christ will reign eternally with his saints.

**Questioner:** What is the third?

**Answerer:** “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.”

**Questioner:** How is it to be understood?

**Answerer:** Just as the angels in heaven obey your will, so may the righteous on earth do so. And just as your will is fulfilled in the saints, so may it also be fulfilled in sinners.

[Col. 1144B]

**Questioner:** What is the fourth?

**Answerer:** “Give us this day our daily bread.”

**Questioner:** What is understood in it?

**Answerer:** Here bread is understood in place of all food, by which we must live each day. We also pray for the reception of Christ’s body. Finally, we ask that he give himself to us, for he is the living bread.

**Questioner:** What is the fifth?

**Answerer:** “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

**Questioner:** What should be understood in it?

**Answerer:** We pray that he may forgive our sins in the same way that we also forgive our debtors.

**Questioner:** What is the sixth?

**Answerer:** “And lead us not into [Col. 1144C] temptation.”

**Questioner:** How is this understood?

**Answerer:** We do not ask that we not be tempted, because one who has not been tempted has not been tested. But we pray that he not lead us into a temptation which we cannot endure.

**Questioner:** What is the seventh?

**Answerer:** “But deliver us from evil.”

**Questioner:** How is it to be understood?

**Answerer:** That is, from the devil, from sin, and from every evil temptation.

**Questioner:** How is “Amen,” which is at the end, to be understood, and in what language is it said?

**Answerer:** *Amen* is Hebrew; in Latin it means “truly” and “faithfully.”

[Col. 1143]

# PROPOSITIONS OF ALCUIN, TEACHER OF THE EMPEROR CHARLES THE GREAT, FOR SHARPENING YOUNG PEOPLE

[Note: [Col. 1143D] This is the title in the manuscript codex of the monastery of Reichenau.]

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 1143D]

The following propositions are for the most part extant among the works of the Venerable Bede, volume I of the Basel edition of 1563, page 135 and following (Patrologia, volume XC, column 667). Learned scholars nevertheless consider that little work, along with several others in the same volume, to have been falsely attributed to Bede, because he made no mention of it in the catalogue of his works, which he himself composed.

It is, however, extant under the name of Alcuin in a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Reichenau, from which it came to us in transcription. Perhaps Alcuin should be understood as referring to this work when he writes to Charlemagne in Letter 101:

“I have sent to Your Excellence certain forms of expressions confirmed by examples and verses of the venerable Father, and some figures of arithmetical subtlety, for the sake of joy,” and so forth.

Here, then, is the reason which led us to assign this writing a place among Alcuin’s doubtful works. We compared it with the aforesaid edition of the Venerable Bede and corrected scribal errors in several places.

I admit that these propositions are of limited usefulness, and that they could be solved much more easily and clearly by the arithmetic cultivated today. Nevertheless, there may perhaps be readers who, attentive to every remnant of antiquity, will assign value to these as well and extract from them certain information contributing to knowledge of the calculations, measurements, and weights of the ancients. Some passages missing from the manuscript have been supplied from the Venerable Bede and are enclosed in these [ ] signs.

441

## I. PROPOSITION ABOUT THE SNAIL
The snail was invited by the swallow [manuscript: reed] to dinner within one league. But in one day it could not walk more than one ounce of a foot. Let whoever wishes say in how many [years or] days the snail reached that same dinner.

### Solution concerning the snail

In one league there are 1,500 paces: 7,000 feet, [90,000] ounces. *[Editorial note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000; in Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]* As many ounces as there are, so many days were required; these amount to 246 years and 210 days.

### II. Proposition concerning a man walking on the road

*[Editorial note: In Bede: “Concerning a man meeting other men on the road.”]*

A certain man walking along a road saw other men coming toward him and said to them: “I wish that you were as many again as you are, and half of that half, and half of this number [and again half of the half]; then, together with me, you would amount to 100.” Let whoever wishes say how many there were whom he first saw.

#### Solution to the same proposition

Those whom he first saw numbered 36. As many again would be 72. Half of half is 18. Half of this number is 9. Thus say: 72 and 18 make 90. Add 9, making 99. Add the speaker, and you will have 100.

### III. Proposition concerning two travelers

*[Editorial note: In Bede there is added: “Having seen storks.”]*

Two men traveling along a road, seeing storks, said to one another: “How many are there?” When they had calculated the number, they said: “If there were as many more; and three times as many again, and half of the third number, with two added, there would be 100.” Let whoever can say how many there were whom they first saw.

#### Solution concerning the storks

Twenty-eight and eighteen, and the third number in this way, make 84. Half of the third makes 14. Altogether there are 98. With two added, they appear as 100.

### IV. Proposition concerning a man and horses

*[Editorial note: In Bede there is added: “Grazing in a field.”]*

*[Col. 1145D]*

A certain man saw horses grazing in a field and expressed the wish: “Would that you were mine, and that there were as many more, and half of half as many; then surely I would boast of 100 horses.” Let whoever wishes determine how many horses that man first saw grazing.

#### Solution concerning the horses

There were 40 horses grazing. As many again make 80. Half of half of this, namely 20, when added, makes 100.

### V. Proposition concerning a purchaser of denarii

*[Editorial note: In Bede: “Concerning a merchant with 100 denarii.”]*

A certain purchaser [Bede: merchant] said: “I want to buy 100 pigs with 100 denarii, but on these terms: that a boar be bought for 10 denarii, a sow for 5 denarii, and two piglets for 1 denarius. Let whoever understands say how many boars, how many sows, and how many piglets there must be, so that in neither respect is the number exceeded or diminished.”

#### Solution concerning the purchaser

Make 9 sows and 1 boar for 55 denarii, and 80 piglets for 40. Here are 90 pigs. With the remaining 5 denarii, make 10 piglets, and you will have the number 100 in both respects.

### VI. Proposition concerning two merchants possessing 100 solidi

There were two merchants who jointly possessed 100 solidi, with which they bought pigs. They bought five pigs for two solidi, intending to fatten them and sell them again at a profit. When they saw that it was not the season for fattening pigs, and that they themselves were unable to feed them during the winter, they tried by selling them to make a profit, if they could; but they could not, because they were unable to sell them for more than they had paid, namely, to receive two solidi for five pigs. When they saw this, they said to one another: “Let us divide them.” By dividing and selling them at the price at which they had bought them, they made a profit. Let whoever is able say how many pigs there were at first; and let him divide and sell them and make the profit which he could not make by selling them all together.

#### Solution concerning the pigs

At first there were 250 pigs, bought for 100 solidi, as stated above, at five pigs for two solidi; for whether you say fifty times five or five times fifty, you will count 250. When these had been divided, one took 125 and the other likewise. One sold the inferior pigs, always three for a solidus; the other sold the better pigs, two for a solidus. Thus the one who sold the inferior pigs obtained 40 solidi from 120 pigs. The one who sold the better pigs obtained 60 solidi, because the inferior pigs were sold at thirty for ten solidi, while the better ones were sold at twenty for ten solidi. Five pigs remained for each of them; from these they were able to make a profit of four solidi and two denarii.

### VII. Proposition concerning a disk weighing 30 pounds

*[Col. 1146D]*

There is a disk weighing 30 pounds, or 600 solidi, containing gold, silver, brass, and tin. As much gold as it contains, it contains three times as much silver. As much silver as it contains, it contains three times as much brass. As much brass as it contains, it contains three times as much tin. Let whoever can say how much it weighs in each material.

#### Solution

The gold weighs 9 ounces; the silver, three times 9 ounces, that is, 2 pounds and 3 ounces. The brass weighs three times 2 pounds and [three times] 3 ounces, that is, 6 pounds and 9 ounces. The tin weighs three times 6 pounds and three times 9 ounces, that is, 20 pounds and 3 ounces. Nine ounces, together with 2 pounds and 3 ounces, 6 pounds and 9 ounces, and 20 pounds and 3 ounces, when added, make 30 pounds.

Again, alternatively, in solidi: the gold weighs 15 silver solidi. The silver weighs three times 15, that is, 45. The brass weighs three times 45, that is, 135. The tin weighs three times 135, that is, 405. Add 405, 135, 45, and 15, and you will find 600, which are 30 pounds.

### 442 VIII. Proposition concerning a vat

There is a vat filled by 100 measures, each containing three modii, and it has three pipes. Through one pipe a third part of the number of modii plus 6 runs; through the second, a third part alone; through the third, only a sixth. Let whoever wishes now say how many sextarii ran through each pipe.

#### Solution

Through the first pipe, [3] 600 sextarii ran. Through the second, [2] 400. Through the third, [1] 200.

*[Editorial note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]*

### IX. Proposition concerning a cloak

I have a cloak 100 cubits long and 80 wide. I want to make smaller cloaks from it in pieces, so that each piece is 5 cubits long and 4 cubits wide. Tell me, wise man, how many smaller cloaks can be made from it.

#### Solution

The eightieth part of 400 is 5, and the hundredth part is 4. Thus, whether you multiply 80 by 5 or 100 by 4, you will always find 400. That many cloaks there will be.

### X. Proposition concerning linen

I have one linen cloth 60 cubits long and 40 cubits wide. I want to make pieces from it, so that each piece is 6 cubits long and 4 cubits wide, sufficient for sewing a tunic. Let whoever wishes say how many tunics can be made from it.

#### Solution

A tenth of 60 is 6, while a tenth of 40 is 4. Thus, whether you multiply a tenth of 60 or a tenth of 40 ten times, you will find 100 pieces 6 cubits long and 4 cubits wide.

### XI. Proposition concerning two men taking one another’s sisters

*[Editorial note: In Bede: “Concerning two men each taking the other’s sister.”]*

If two men marry one another’s sisters, tell me, I ask, in what degree of relationship their children belong to one another.

#### Solution to the same proposition

For example, if I take my companion’s sister and he takes mine, and children are born to us, I am the paternal uncle of my sister’s son, and she is the paternal aunt of my son. In that relationship they belong to one another.

*[Editorial note: This solution is omitted in Bede.]*

### XII. Proposition concerning a certain head of a household and his three sons

A certain head of a household, dying, left to his three sons an inheritance of 30 glass vessels, of which 10 were full of oil, another 10 half-full, and the remaining 10 empty. Let whoever can divide the oil and the vessels so that each of the three sons receives an equal share both of the glass and of the oil.

#### Solution

There are therefore three sons and 30 vessels. Of the vessels, 10 are full, 10 half-full, and 10 empty. Multiply three by ten: the result is 30. Each son receives 10 vessels as his portion. Divide them into thirds: give the first son 10 half-full vessels, and then give the second 5 full and 5 empty vessels. You will give the same to the third, and there will be an equal division among the three brothers, both in oil and in glass.

### XIII. Proposition concerning a king

A certain king ordered his servant to gather an army from 30 villages, in such a way that from each village he took as many men as he had brought there. He himself came alone to the first village; to the second with one other; and already three men came to the third. Let whoever can say how many men had been gathered from the 30 villages.

#### Solution

At the first station there were 2; at the second, 4; at the third, 8; at the fourth, 16; at the fifth, 32; at the sixth, 64; at the seventh, 128; at the eighth, 256; at the ninth, 512; at the tenth, 1,024; at the eleventh, 2,048; at the twelfth, 4,096; at the fourteenth, 16,384; at the fifteenth, 32,768, and so forth.

*[Editorial note: The remaining numbers, in which the manuscript codex is repeatedly erroneous, I judged should be omitted; anyone can easily supply them, if desired, by continually doubling the last number.]*

### XIV. Proposition concerning an ox

How many footprints does an ox that plows all day make in the last furrow?

*[Editorial note: “Furrow” means the same as “plow-line.”]*

#### Solution

The ox makes no footprint at all in the last furrow, because it goes before the plow, and the plow follows it. For as many footprints as it makes by going first in cultivated soil, so many the plow following it erases by cultivating. Therefore no footprint of it is found in the last furrow.

### XV. Proposition concerning a man

I ask you to tell me how many furrows a man has made in his field when he has made three plowings from each end of the field.

#### Solution

From one end of the field, 3; from the other, 3; these make 6 furrows or plowings [Bede: 7].

### XVI. Proposition concerning two men leading oxen

*[Col. 1149A]*

Two men were leading oxen along a road. One said to the other: “Give me two oxen, and I will have as many oxen as you have.” But the other said: “You give me two oxen, and I will have twice as many as you have.” Let whoever wishes say how many oxen there were and how many each one had.

#### Solution

The first man, who asked that two be given to him, had 4 oxen. The one who was asked had 8. The man who was asked gave two to the petitioner, and each then had 6. The one who had first received the two returned them to the first giver, who had 6, and then had 8, which is twice 4; while the other had 4 remaining, which is half of 8.

### 443 XVII. Proposition concerning three brothers, each having a sister

There were three brothers, each of whom had a sister, and they had to cross a river—for each of them desired the sister of one of the others. When they came to the river, they found only a small boat in which no more than two of them could cross. Let whoever can say how they crossed the river without any one of the women being dishonored by one of them.

#### Solution

First of all, my sister and I would enter the boat and cross to the other side. After crossing the river, I would leave my sister out of the boat and bring the boat back to the bank. Then the sisters of the two men who had remained on the shore would enter. After those women had left the boat, my sister [who had crossed first] would enter and bring the boat back to us. When she had come out, the two brothers would enter the boat and cross to the other side. Then one of them, together with his sister, would enter the boat and cross to us. But I and the one who had navigated, with my sister remaining outside, would cross to the other side. After we had been carried to the bank, either one of those two women would bring the boat back to the other side, take my sister aboard, and return with her to us. Then the man whose sister had remained on the other side would enter the boat and bring her back with him. Thus the crossing would be completed without any defiling contact.

*[Editorial note: In Bede: “Thus, by such careful and diligent navigation, the crossing was completed without the stain of defilement.”]*

### XVIII. Proposition concerning a man, a goat, and a wolf

A certain man had to carry a wolf, a goat, and a bundle of cabbage across a river. He could find no other boat except one capable of carrying only two of them. He had therefore been instructed to carry all these things across entirely unharmed. Let whoever can say how he could cross with them unharmed.

#### Solution

In the same manner, I would first take the goat across and leave the wolf and the cabbage outside. Then I would return and carry across the wolf. After putting the wolf ashore, I would take the goat back in the boat and return with it. Having put the goat ashore, I would carry the cabbage across; then I would row back again, take up the goat, and bring it across. By doing this, the crossing would be safely completed, without the gulf of destruction.

### XIX. Proposition concerning a man and a woman weighing [the weight of a loaded cart]

A man and a woman, each of whom carried the weight of a loaded cart, together had two children whose combined weight was equal to that of a cart. They had to cross a river. They found a boat that could carry no more than one cartload. Let whoever thinks he can do so arrange their crossing without sinking the boat.

#### Solution

In the same order as above: first the two children would enter and cross, and one of them would bring the boat back. Then the mother would enter the boat and cross. Her son would next bring the boat back. After she had crossed, her brother would enter the boat, and both would cross to the other side. Again, one of them would bring the boat back to the father. Once it had been brought back, with the son standing outside, the father would cross. Again, the son who had crossed earlier would enter the boat and bring it back to his brother. Once it had been brought back, both would enter and cross. By such ingenious rowing the passage would perhaps be completed without shipwreck.

### XX. Proposition concerning hedgehogs

*[Bede: “Concerning hedgehogs.”]*

Concerning a male and female hedgehog, having two offspring who together weigh one pound, and wishing to cross a river.

#### Solution

Similarly, as above, the two young ones would cross first, and one of them would bring the boat back. The father would enter it and cross to the other side. Then the young one who had first crossed with its brother would bring the boat back to the bank. Its brother would enter it again, and both would cross. One of them would then go ashore, and the other would bring the boat back to the mother. The mother would enter it and cross. When she had gone ashore, her son, who had earlier crossed with his father, would enter the boat again and bring it back to his brother. Both would enter it and cross to the other side, and the crossing would be completed without anyone fearing shipwreck.

### XXI. Proposition concerning a field and sheep to be placed in it

There is a field 200 feet long and 100 feet wide. I want to put sheep in it, but in such a way that each sheep has 5 feet lengthwise and 4 feet widthwise. Tell me, I ask, whoever is able, how many sheep can be placed there.

#### Solution

The field itself is 200 feet long and 100 feet wide. Divide 200 by five [editorial note: namely, by dividing by 5], making 40. Then divide 100 by 4. The fourth part of 100 is 25. Thus, whether 40 is multiplied by 25 or 25 by 40, the number 1,000 is completed. Therefore that many sheep can be placed there.

### XXII. Proposition concerning a sloping field

There is a sloping field that has 100 perches on one side, 100 perches on the other side, 50 perches at the front, 60 perches in the middle, and 50 perches at the other front. Let whoever can say how many aripennes it should contain.

*[Editorial note: Bede has aripennos. See Du Cange, under “Arapennis,” and elsewhere.]*

#### Solution

The length of this field is 100 perches, and the width of each of the two fronts is 50; the middle measurement, however, is 60. Add the number of both fronts to the middle, making 160. Take a third of this, namely 53, and multiply by 100, making [5] 300. Divide into 12 equal parts, and 441 are found [Bede: 341]. Again divide the same into 12 parts, and 37 are found. So many aripennes there are in this field.

### 444 XXIII. Proposition concerning a quadrangular field

There is a quadrangular field that has 30 perches on one side, 32 perches on another, 34 perches at the front, and 32 at the other front. Let whoever can say how many aripennes should be enclosed in it.

#### Solution

The two lengths of this field make 62. Take half of 62, making 31. The two widths of the same field, when added, make 66. Take half of 66, making 33. Multiply three times once [Bede: thirty times], making 1,020. Divide by one-twelfth twice as above; that is, take 1,020 and divide by 12, making 85; then divide 85 again by 12, making 7. Therefore the number of aripennes in this field is seven.

### XXIV. Proposition concerning a triangular field

There is a triangular field that has 30 perches on one side, 30 perches on another, and 18 perches at the front. Let whoever can say how many aripennes it should contain.

#### Solution

Add the two lengths of this field, making 60. Take half of 60, making 30; and because it has 18 perches at the front, take half of 18, making 9. Multiply 9 by 30, making 270. From this make two twelfths, that is, divide 270 by one-twelfth, making 22½; and then divide 22½ again by one-twelfth [lacuna]—one aripennis and 10½ perches.

*[Editorial note: In Bede this gap is supplied as follows: “And they make 2, with 3 remaining, which is three parts of 12. Therefore there are in this number 2 aripennes and three parts of an aripennis.”]*

### XXV. Proposition concerning a round field

There is a round field whose circumference is 400 perches. Say how many aripennes it should contain.

#### Solution

The fourth part of this field, enclosed by 400 perches, is 100. If you multiply these by themselves, that is, if you multiply 100 by 100, the result is 10,000. You must divide this into 12 parts; for one-twelfth of 10,000 is 833⅓, and when you divide this again by 12, you will find 69⅓. For that many aripennes this kind of field is enclosed.

### XXVI. Proposition concerning the course of a dog and the flight of a hare

*[Printed heading: “Concerning the course of CBNKS. BC. FVGB. LFPPRKS.”]*

*[Editorial note: It should be read: “Concerning the course of a dog and the flight of a hare,” replacing certain consonants with the vowels immediately preceding them. This occurs frequently in manuscript codices.]*

There is a field 150 feet long. At one end stood a dog, and at the other stood a hare. The dog advanced after it—that is, he began to run after the hare. But whenever the dog made 9 feet in one leap, the hare covered 7. Let whoever wishes say how many feet and how many leaps the dog, in pursuing, and the hare, in fleeing, made until it was caught.

*[Bede: “until they had completed.”]*

#### Solution

The length of this field is 150 feet. Take half of 150, making 75. Since the dog covered 9 feet in one leap, multiplying 75 by 9 gives 675 feet: so many feet the dog ran in pursuing the hare until he caught it with a tenacious bite. But since the hare covered 7 feet in one leap, multiply the same 75 by 7. So many feet the hare completed in fleeing until it was overtaken.

### XXVII. Proposition concerning a quadrangular city

There is a quadrangular city that has 1,100 feet on one side, 1,000 feet on another, 600 feet at the front, and 600 feet at the other side. I want to place the roofs of houses there, in such a way that each house is 40 feet long and 30 feet wide. Let whoever wishes say how many houses it should contain.

#### Solution

If the two lengths of this city are added, they make 2,200. Likewise, if the two widths are added, they make 1,200. Therefore take half of 1,200, making 600; and again take half of 2,200, making 1,100. Since each house is 40 feet long and 30 feet wide, take a fortieth of 1,100, making 26; and again take a thirtieth of 600, making 20. Thus 20 multiplied by 26 makes 520. So many houses are to be accommodated.

### XXVIII. Proposition concerning a triangular city

*[Col. 1152D]*

There is a triangular city that has 100 feet on one side, 100 feet on another, and 90 feet at the front. I want to construct houses there, but in such a way that each house is 20 feet long and 10 feet wide. Let whoever can say how many houses it should contain.

#### Solution

The two sides of this city, when added, make 200; take half of 200, making 100. But because it has 90 feet at the front, take half of 90, making 45. Since the length of each house is 20 feet and its width 10 feet, take a twentieth of 100, making 5. A tenth of 40 is 4. Multiply 5 by 4, making 20. The city will contain 20 houses of this kind.

### XXIX. Proposition concerning a round city

There is a round city whose circuit measures 8,000 feet. Let whoever can say how many houses it should contain, so that each is 30 feet long and 20 feet wide.

#### Solution

In the circuit of this city 8,000 feet are counted; these are divided in the ratio of three to two into [3] 800 and [3] 200. The length of the houses is represented by the former, and their width by the latter. Therefore subtract half from each total, and from the larger 2,400 remain; from the smaller, [1] 600. Divide this [1] 600 by 20, and you will find eighty times twenty; and divide the larger total, namely [2] 400, by 30, and you will count eighty times thirty. Multiply eighty by eighty, making 6,400. So many houses of the kind described above can be built in this city.

### XXX. Proposition concerning a basilica

There is a basilica 240 feet long and 120 feet wide. Of its paving bricks, each brick is 23 ounces long, that is, 1 foot and 11 ounces, and 12 ounces wide, that is, 1 foot. Let whoever wishes say how many bricks should fill it.

#### Solution

The 140 feet of length accommodate 126 bricks, and the 120 feet of width accommodate 120 bricks, because each brick has the measure of one foot in width. Therefore multiply 100 by 126, and the total comes to [15] 120. So many bricks can cover the pavement of such a basilica.

### XXXI. Proposition concerning a wine cellar

*[Editorial note: Bede has cavana, a wine-storage chamber.]*

There is a wine cellar 100 feet long and 64 feet wide. Let whoever can say how many vats it should hold, but in such a way that each vat is 7 feet long and 4 feet wide—that is, in the middle—and that one passageway is 4 feet wide.

*[Editorial note: A passageway: a space between vats or wine vessels.]*

#### Solution

Within 100 there are fourteen sevens, while within 64 there are sixteen fours; of these, 4 are assigned to the passageway, which is included in the length of the cellar. Since therefore there are fifteen fours in 60, and fourteen sevens in 100, multiply 15 by 14, making 210. So many vats of the dimensions stated above can be contained in such a wine cellar.

### XXXII. Proposition concerning a certain head of a household

*[Col. 1154A]*

A certain head of a household had 20 dependents. He ordered that 20 modii of grain be given to them, with this arrangement: the men were to receive 3 modii each, the women 2 each, and the children half a modius each. Let whoever can say how many men, women, and children there ought to be.

#### Solution

Multiply 1 by 3, making 3; that is, one man received 3 modii. Likewise, multiply 5 by 2, making 10; that is, five women received 10 modii. Then multiply 7 by 2, making 14; that is, 14 children received 7 modii. Add 1, 5, and 14, making 20. These are the 20 members of the household. Then add 3, 7, and 10, making 20; these are the 20 modii. Thus altogether there are 20 members of the household and 20 modii.

### XXXIII. Proposition concerning another head of a household distributing grain to his household

A certain head of a household had 30 dependents, and ordered that 30 modii of grain be given to them. He ordered it in this way: the men were to receive 3 modii each, the women 2 each, and the children half a modius each. Let whoever can solve it say how many men, women, and children there were.

#### Solution

If you multiply 3 by 3, the result is 9. If you multiply 5 by 2, the result is 10. Then multiply 22 by ½, making 11. That is: 3 men received 9 modii, 5 women received 10, and 22 children received 11 modii. Added together, 3, 5, and 22 make 30 members of the household. Again, 9, 11, and 10, added together, make 30 modii. Thus there are altogether 30 members of the household and 30 modii.

### XXXIV. Another proposition concerning a head of a household dividing grain among his household

A certain head of a household had 100 dependents, and ordered that 100 modii of grain be given to them, with this arrangement: the men were to receive 3 modii each, the women 2 each, and the children half a modius each. Let whoever is able say how many men, women, and children there were.

#### Solution

Eleven threes make 33. Fifteen multiplied by 2 make 30; that is, 11 men received 33 modii, and 15 women received 30, while 74 children received 37 modii. Added together—that is, 11, 15, and 74—they make 100, which are the members of the household. Likewise, add 33, 30, and 37: they make 100, which are the modii. Thus, when these are added together, there are 100 members of the household and 100 modii.

### XXXV. Proposition concerning the death of a certain head of a household

A certain head of a household, dying, left children and property amounting to 960 solidi [Bede: 860], as well as a pregnant wife. He ordered that if a male child were born to her, it should receive three-quarters of the whole estate, namely 9 ounces, and its mother should receive one-quarter, namely 3 ounces. But if a daughter were born, she should receive seven-twelfths, namely 7 ounces [Bede: 5], and her mother should receive five-twelfths, namely 5 ounces. It happened, however, that she gave birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Let whoever can solve it say how much the mother received, how much the son, and how much the daughter.

#### Solution

Add 9 and 3, making 12, for 12 ounces make a pound. Again add 7 and 5 in the same way, making 12. Therefore twice 12 makes 24; 24 make two pounds, that is, 40 solidi.

*[Editorial note: Up to this point the solutions are found in Bede’s works, although the propositions there continue without solutions. What follows comes from the manuscript codex.]*

Then divide 960 solidi by 24; the twenty-fourth part of it is 40. Then, because three-quarters—or three-fourths—is indicated, multiply 40 by nine: the son received nine times 40, that is, 18 pounds, which make 360 solidi. Since the mother received one-third in relation to the son and one-fifth in relation to the daughter, 3 and 5 make 8. Therefore, because it is stated that she receives twice, or two times, 40 in an eighth part, multiply 40 by 8: the mother received eight times 40, that is, 16 pounds, which make 320 solidi. Then, because it is stated that the daughter receives seven-twelfths, take 40 in seven parts; then multiply 40 by 7, making 14 pounds, which make 280 solidi. This is what the daughter received. Add 360, 320, and 280: they make 960 solidi and 48 pounds.

### 446 XXXVI. Proposition concerning an old man’s greeting to a boy

A certain old man greeted a boy and said to him: “May you live, my son; live,” he said, “as many years as you have lived, and as many more, and three times as many. And may God add one of my years to you, and may you complete 100 years.” Let whoever can solve it say how old the boy was at that time.

#### Solution

When he said, “May you live as many years as you have lived,” the boy had already lived 8 years and 3 months. That much again makes 16 years and 6 months; and another such amount makes 33 years, which, multiplied by three, makes 99 years. One added to these makes 100.

### XXXVII. Proposition concerning a certain man wishing to build a house

A certain man, wishing to build a house, hired six craftsmen, five of whom were master builders and one an apprentice. An agreement was made between the man who wished to build and the craftsmen that 25 denarii would be given to them in wages for each day, but in such a way that the apprentice would receive half of what one of the masters received. Let whoever can say how much each of them received per day.

#### Solution
Take the first 22 denarii and divide them into 6 parts. Thus, for each of the masters—of whom there are five—4 denarii, since five times four makes 20. Take the two that remain, which are half of one, and give them to the apprentice; there are still 3 denarii left, which you shall distribute as follows. Make 11 parts from each denarius: three times eleven makes 33. Take those 30 parts and divide them among the five masters. Five times six makes 30. Thus each master receives 6 parts. Take the three parts that remain beyond the 30, which is half of six, and give them to the apprentice.

### XXXVIII. PROPOSITION ABOUT A CERTAIN BUYER OF ONE HUNDRED ANIMALS

A certain man wished to buy 100 assorted animals for 100 solidi, so that a horse would be bought for 3 solidi, an ox for 1 solidus, and 24 sheep for 1 solidus. Let whoever is able say how many horses, how many oxen, and how many sheep there were.

**Solution.**

Multiply three times twenty-three [that is, three times 23] by 1; the result is 69. And multiply twice twenty-four [that is, twice 24]; the result is 48. Therefore there are 23 horses, costing 69 solidi; 48 sheep, costing 2 solidi; and 29 oxen, costing 29 solidi. Add 23, 48, and 29: the result is 100 animals. Then add 69, 2, and 29: the result is 100 solidi. Thus, taken together, there are 100 animals and 100 solidi.

### XXXIX. PROPOSITION ABOUT A CERTAIN BUYER IN THE EAST

A certain man wished to buy 100 assorted animals in the East for 100 solidi. He ordered his servant to buy a camel for 5 solidi, a donkey for 1 solidus, and 20 sheep for 1 solidus. Let whoever wishes say how many camels, donkeys, or sheep there were in the transaction costing 100 solidi.

**Solution.**

If you multiply 10 nine times, [and] 5, the result is 95; that is, 19 camels were bought for 95 solidi. Add one to these—that is, one donkey for 1 solidus—and the result is 96. Then multiply twenty-four by 4; the result is 80, that is, 80 sheep for 4 solidi. Add 19, 1, and 80: the result is 100. These are the animals. Then add 95, 1, and 4: the result is 100 solidi. Thus, taken together, they make 100 animals and 100 solidi.

### XL. PROPOSITION ABOUT A MAN AND SHEEP GRAZING ON A MOUNTAIN

A certain man saw sheep grazing on a mountain and said: “Would that I had as many, and as many again, and half of half as many, and another half of that half, and that I, together with them, might enter my house as the hundredth.” Let whoever can solve it say how many sheep he saw grazing there.

**Solution.**

By “I would have as many,” he first meant 36 sheep. As many again makes 72; and half of this—namely, half of 36—makes 18. Again, half of this second half, that is, half of 18, makes 9. Add 36 and 36: the result is 72. Add 18: the result is 90. Add 9 to 90: the result is 99. The man himself, added to them, will be the hundredth.

### XLI. PROPOSITION ABOUT A SODE AND A SOW

**[Note: “Sode” means a pigsty or enclosure for pigs. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, under “Sudis.”]**

A certain householder established a new square enclosure, in which he placed a sow. She gave birth to 7 piglets in the middle of the enclosure; together with their mother, who is the eighth [another reading: “they are eight”], they then gave birth, each one, in every corner, to 7. She herself, again in the middle of the enclosure, together with all the offspring, gave birth to 7. Let whoever wishes say how many pigs there were, together with the mothers.

**Solution.**

In the first birth, which took place in the middle of the enclosure, there were 7 piglets, and their mother made the eighth. Thus eight multiplied by eight makes 64. That many piglets, together with their mothers, were in the first corner. Then 64 multiplied by 8 makes 512. That many piglets, together with their mothers, were in the second corner. Again, 512 multiplied by 8 makes [4]96 [i.e. 4,096]. That many were in the third corner, together with their mothers. If these are multiplied by 8, the result is 32,788, that many being in the fourth corner together with their mothers. Multiply 32,788 also by 8: the result is [200][62] and 304 [i.e. 262,304]. For that many grew when, finally, they gave birth in the middle of the enclosure.

**[Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they are to be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]**

### XLII. PROPOSITION ABOUT A LADDER HAVING ONE HUNDRED STEPS

There is a ladder having 100 steps. On the first step sat one dove; on the second, two; on the third, three; on the fourth, four; on the fifth, five—and so on at every step up to the hundredth. Let whoever can say how many doves there were altogether.

**Solution.**

The number is reckoned as follows. From the first step, on which one dove sits, take that one and add it to the 99 that stand on the ninety-ninth step, and there will be 100. Likewise pair the second with the ninety-eighth, and similarly you will find 100. Pair one from the higher steps with one from the lower steps in this order, and you will always find 100 in each pair of steps. The fiftieth step alone remains separate, having no counterpart; likewise the hundredth remains alone. Add them all, and you will find 5,050 doves.

**[Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they are to be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]**

### XLIII. PROPOSITION ABOUT PIGS

A certain man had 300 pigs and ordered that so many pigs, in an odd number, should be killed over three days. The same question applies to 30. Let whoever can say how many pigs, in odd numbers—whether out of 300 or out of 30—are to be killed over three days. This problem was composed as an insoluble one for the purpose of rebuking.

**Solution.**

Behold a fable! No one can solve it so that 300 pigs, or thirty, are killed over three days in odd numbers. This fable is only for rebuking children.

### XLIV. PROPOSITION ABOUT A BOY’S GREETING TO HIS FATHER

A certain boy greeted his father: “Hail, father!” he said. His father replied: “May you prosper, son! May you live as many years as you have lived, with those years doubled and tripled [another reading: “which you will double and triple”]; and take one of my years, and you will have 100 years. Let whoever can say how old the boy was at that time.”

**Solution.**

The boy was 16 years and 6 months old. Doubled, together with the months, this makes 33 years; tripled, it makes 99. When one year of the father is added, 100 appears.

### XLV. PROPOSITION

A dove sitting in a tree saw others flying and said to them: “Would that you were as many again and three times as many; then, together with me, you would be 100.” Let whoever can say how many doves were flying at first.

**Solution.**

There were 33 doves whom it first saw flying. As many again makes 66; and three times as many makes 99. Add the one sitting there, and there will be 100.

### XLVI. PROPOSITION ABOUT A PURSE FOUND BY A MAN

A certain man walking along a road found a purse containing two talents. Others who saw this also said to him: “Brother, give us an equal share of the find” [another reading: “of your find”]. He refused and did not wish to give them anything. But they attacked him, seized the purse, and each took 50 solidi for himself. When he saw that he could not resist, he put in his hand and seized 50 solidi. Let whoever wishes say how many men there were.

**Solution.**

Among certain people a talent contains 72 [another reading: 75] pounds or librae. A libra contains 72 gold solidi. Sixty-five times 72 makes [5]400 [i.e. 5,400]; doubled, this makes 10,800. In 10,800 there are 216 groups of fifty. Therefore there were that many men.

### XLVII. PROPOSITION ABOUT A BISHOP WHO ORDERED TWELVE LOAVES TO BE DIVIDED

A certain bishop ordered 12 loaves to be divided among the clergy. He prescribed that each priest should receive two loaves, a deacon half a loaf, and a reader a quarter of a loaf, with this condition: the number of clerics and the number of loaves should be the same. Let whoever wishes say how many priests, deacons, and readers there ought to be.

**Solution.**

Five times two makes 10: that is, five priests received ten loaves; one deacon received half a loaf; and six readers together received one and a half loaves. Add 5, 1, and 6: the result is 12. Again, add 10 and a half, 1, and one and a half: the result is 12. These are the 12 loaves; taken together, they make 12 people and 12 loaves. Thus the number of clerics and loaves is the same.

### XLVIII. PROPOSITION ABOUT A MAN WHO MET SCHOOLBOYS

A certain man met some schoolboys and said to them: “How many are you in the school?” One of them answered: “I do not wish to tell you. You count us twice, multiply the result by three, and then divide it into four parts. If you add me to the fourth part of the number, the total will be 100. Let whoever can say how many there were who previously met the traveler walking along the road.”

**Solution.**

Thirty-three twice [that is, twice 33] make 66: that many were those who previously met the traveler. This number, doubled, gives 132. Multiply it by three: the result is 396. Its fourth part is 99. Add the boy who answered, and you will find 100.

### XLIX. PROPOSITION ABOUT CARPENTERS

Seven carpenters made seven wheels each. Let whoever can say how many carts they made [another reading: “how many carts the wheels made”].

**Solution.**

Multiply seven by seven: the result is 49; that many wheels they made. But 12 multiplied by 4 gives 48. Of the 49 wheels, 12 carts were constructed, and one wheel remained over.

### L. PROPOSITION ABOUT WINE IN VESSELS

I ask whoever wishes to say how many sextarii 100 *metra* of wine contain; or, likewise, how many *meri* the 100 *metra* contain.

**Solution.**

One *metrum* holds 48 sextarii. Multiply 48 by 100: the result is 4,800. That many sextarii there are. Likewise, one *metrum* contains 289 *meri*. Multiply 289 by 100: the result is [28]900 [i.e. 28,900]. That many *meri* there are.

### LI. PROPOSITION ABOUT THE DIVISION OF WINE IN VESSELS BY A CERTAIN FATHER

A certain householder, when he was dying, left four vessels of wine to his four sons. In the first vessel were 40 *modii*, in the second 30, in the third 20, and in the fourth 10. Calling the steward of his household, he said: “Divide these four vessels, with the wine remaining inside them, among my four sons, but in such a way that each of them has one share both in the wine and in the vessels. Let whoever understands say how it must be divided so that all may receive an equal share.”

**Solution.**

In the first vessel there were 40 *modii*, in the second 30, in the third 20, and in the fourth 10. Add 40, 30, 20, and 10: the result is 100. Then divide the total of 100 by four. The fourth part of 100 is found to be 25; this number, doubled, produces 50. Thus each son receives 25 *modii* as his share, and two together receive 50. The 40 *modii* in the first vessel and the 10 in the fourth, joined together, make 50; you shall give this between two. Likewise join the 30 and 20 *modii* that were in the second and third vessels; they make 50, and this too, in the same way as above, you shall give between two. Each will then have 25 *modii*, and by doing this the division among the sons will be equal, both in the wine and in the vessels.

### LII. PROPOSITION ABOUT A HOUSEHOLDER

A certain householder ordered 90 *modii* of grain to be carried from one of his houses to another, which was 30 leagues away. The arrangement was that one camel should carry all the grain in three journeys, carrying 30 *modii* on each journey; the camel was also to eat one *modius* on every league. Let whoever wishes say how many *modii* would remain.

**Solution.**

On the first journey the camel carried 30 *modii* over 10 leagues. It ate one *modius* on each league—that is, it ate 20 *modii*, and 10 remained. On the second journey it likewise carried 30 *modii*, ate 20 of them, and 10 remained. On the third journey it did the same: it carried 30 *modii*, ate 20 of them, and 10 remained. Thus 30 *modii* remained from these loads, and 10 leagues of the journey remained. It carried those 30 *modii* home on a fourth journey, ate 10 of them on the way, and only 20 *modii* remained from the whole amount.

### LIII. PROPOSITION ABOUT THE HOUSEHOLDER OF A MONASTERY OF TWELVE MONKS

A certain father of a monastery had 12 monks. Calling the steward of his household, he gave him 204 eggs and ordered him to give each an equal share of them. He prescribed, however, that 85 eggs should be given among five priests [and 68 among four deacons, and 51 among three readers]. Let whoever is able, I ask, say how many eggs fell to each of them as his share, so that the number should neither exceed nor fall short anywhere, but each, as we have said above, should receive an equal share in everything.

**Solution.**

Divide 204 by 12. For its twelfth part is resolved into the seventeenth part, because whether you multiply 12 by 17 or 17 by 12, you will find 204. Just as the number 85, divided five ways, yields 17, so 68 divided four ways and 51 divided three ways do likewise. Add 5, 4, and 3: the result is 12. These are the 12 men. Again, add 85, 68, and 51: the result is 204. These are the 204 eggs. Thus each receives 17 eggs as his twelfth share. When 17 is divided equally, the result is . . . .

[Col. 1161]

## Several Other Writings, Somewhat Doubtfully Attributed to Blessed Alcuin

### I. [Note: A fragment of this letter, beginning with the words “to fix upon the pavement,” etc., was published by the distinguished P. Bernardus Pez after other letters of Alcuin, from a manuscript of Benedictbeuern, in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, p. 10. Yet that fragment does not cohere with its own beginning, which reads: “I am very pleased with the harmony between my son,” etc. That beginning belongs to another letter to Arn, now numbered 69 among the Alcuinian letters. We have copied here the complete letter, although it is very corrupt, from an excellent ninth-century Salzburg manuscript containing various other letter-formulas, similar to the formulas of Marculf and worthy of publication. From it, however, it is clear that this letter was not written to Arn, as the distinguished Pez believed and the distinguished Hansiz considered beyond doubt in *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 114, no. 25, but to Leo III, supreme pontiff. Whether it was written by Alcuin is another matter. This is certainly plausible; but the corrupt and truncated text prevents any firm conclusion.]**

## LETTER TO POPE LEO III

To the eminent and orthodox great man, crowned by God, Leo, jewel of priests, bishop of the highest and golden Roman See, happily ruling with glory and every honor: from that most worthless of all God’s servants, we ask health and glory for your unfadingly glorious crown of blessedness. We humbly desire your glory and favor, as though prostrate before your most holy feet, and we earnestly request your most holy service, because, insofar as the chosen Son of God has deigned to grant us strength, we desire to remain in your service, as is fitting and just for such a true angelic man and servant of God.

For we, your most humble little servants, have arranged, with the Lord’s help, to travel to Rome for the sake of prayer, to greet its holy shrines with pious kisses, to press warm kisses with our lips upon the pavement before Saint Peter, and to ask pardon and forgiveness for past sins. But now your graciousness knows that, because of the length of our land and the obstruction caused by the pagans, we have been quite unable to come here on the day appointed, as the great necessity of our weakness required [the Salzburg manuscript reads: “requires”]. Therefore we ask your holy clemency to be willing to ask pardon for us at his most blessed confession [the Salzburg manuscript reads: “to ask for pardon for sins”], so that through your intercession the merciful Lord may deign to grant us some release from the bonds of our sins.

We are not worthy to perform any service for you. We know that from God and Saint Peter you will obtain reward, recompense, and glory both in this world and in the world to come.

May the gracious Trinity and inseparable Unity preserve Lord Leo, supreme priest, now and always and forever, happily in the glory of God.

**[Note: “From God and Saint Peter,” etc. The distinguished Hansiz believed that these words clearly hinted at Arn’s archiepiscopal dignity, which had been intended for him by the supreme See. But this opinion is overturned by the fact that the letter was addressed not to Arn but to the supreme pontiff himself.]**

### II. An Anonymous Poem for the Poet’s Friends

**[Note: This poem was published by the illustrious abbot Le Beuf in his *Dissertations*, vol. I, p. 423, and seems attributable to Alcuin, both because it appears to disclose its author under the name Publius Albinus and because it accords with Alcuin’s character, age, and other circumstances of his time, as appears from these notes. We suspect that it was written after Alcuin’s return from Rome to Britain in 780, during which journey he became acquainted with the illustrious men whom he names here.]**

Castula, go quickly across the sea’s expanse [perhaps *chartula*, “little letter,” as in Ovid: “Little book, I do not envy you; without me you will go into the city”];

Seek the strong mouths of fish-filled Rhine, driven by the winds,

Entering the sea where it rolls with rushing waves.

Then let your prow be drawn by a long towline,

And let your stern not quickly be swept backward by the current.

If my Albricus [**Note:** Albricus, bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine, who died in 784. See Mabillon, *Annales*, book XXV, no. 44; *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. V, preface, p. XI.] should come to meet you on the river,

Say, as you hurry to the bishop powerful through his cattle-rich land [**Note:** Because of the region’s pastures.], “Hail!”

For prior Hadda supplies you, for no more than one night [possibly “one day and night”],

With honey, curds, and butter at the crossing,

Since Frisia produces neither oil nor wine.

From there raise your sails, leaving Dorsdrada [**Note:** It is better left to those who live nearer the mouths of the Rhine to discover what place this is; perhaps Dordrecht. In a diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, dated 779, the monastery’s abbot is granted exemption from tolls at Utrecht and Dorsdrada.],

Perhaps black Hrotberct [**Note:** Hrotberct is, I think, the same as Hrobertus, abbot of Saint-Germain, who soon afterward obtained the cited precept of Charlemagne. That document says that he maintained merchants and himself also practiced trade; Alcuin therefore names him here as a greedy merchant. Bouquet reproduces the diploma from the original, vol. V of the *Scriptores*, p. 742 (in *Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 963).] prepare hospitable roofs for you;

For, behold, the greedy merchant does not love your song.

But turn toward the shore of my poet Jonah;

There is a sure rest there for the weary who arrive:

Here vegetables abound for guests, here fish, here bread.

The city of Agrippina kindly opens its roofs to you.

Here greet Father Ricuulfus [**Note:** Ricuulfus may be the man who later, in 786, succeeded Lullus in the bishopric of Mainz.] in a humble voice;

Say: “Your praise, beloved, will always remain with me.”

From there you will seek Castella [**Note:** Castella, situated above the confluence of the Moselle and Rhine, is mentioned by Wandelbert, a monk of Prüm, in *On the Miracles of Saint Goar*.], sailing along the waves,

Until you reach the waters of the desired Moselle.

When you have plowed a stretch of the river Remigius [reading uncertain],

Then halt your raft; let the stern possess the sand,

And go on foot to the holy places of Father Wilbrord [**Note:** The holy places of Wilbrord, where his body rests, namely in the monastery of Echternach. See Mabillon, *Annales*, book XXI, no. 64, p. 115.];

Seek also the dwelling of the priest Samuel [**Note:** Mabillon, *Annales*, book XXVII, p. 360, no. 13, counts Samuel, later bishop of Worms, among Alcuin’s disciples at the school of Tours. But in 780, the year in which we believe this poem was written, Alcuin would not have honored him with the title “Father”; moreover, Alcuin opened the school at Tours later. We therefore think that this Samuel was either the abbot of Echternach, or the bishop of another place near Echternach, or some distinguished man and personal friend concealed under the assumed name Samuel.],

Remember to strike the doors with your Castalian plectrum,

And say with a Pythian voice to the boy who serves:

“Publius Albinus sent me from the British world

To carry sweet greetings to his very sweet Father.”

If you are granted an opportunity to speak in person,

Prostrate upon the ground, kiss the consecrated feet,

And say: “Farewell, Father Samuel”; say: “Live, priest.”

Now uncover your bosom and bring forth the honorable fathers,

Priscian and Phocas [**Note:** The grammarian Phocas.];

he rejoices in such a gift,

Unless Neptune has sunk them beneath the sea.

If he should wish to lead you to the king’s court [**Note:** Perhaps Aachen, or Ingelheim, or Worms, where the king may have been staying. In that year King Charles was on the Rhine.],

Go through the nobles, fathers, and brothers there, and greet them.

Before the king’s feet unfold all your songs,

Say repeatedly: “Hail, best of kings, hail!

Be my protector, guardian, and defender,

So that no envious tongue may harmfully attack me.

Let Paulinus, Peter, Albricus, Samuel, and Jonah [**Note:** It can be inferred from this that all of these men were then in Charlemagne’s court.],

Or whoever wishes to gnaw at my vitals with his bite,

Flee far away, terrified by you, and depart empty-handed.”

Murmur quietly: “Farewell, teacher Peter;

That savage man strikes with a club of Hercules—beware.”

Embrace joyfully the gifts of Master Paulinus,

And kiss him ten times upon his honey-bearing, gentle lips.

Greet Ricuulfus, Raefgot, and Radon properly,

And touch their ears gently while singing.

Say: “Companions, brothers, rejoice; hail and farewell.”

Perhaps you will come to the noble city of Mainz,

And say an everlasting farewell to Doctor Lullus [**Note:** Lullus, then archbishop of Mainz, or, in the ancient designation, of the city of Mainz.],

Who is regarded as the Church’s exemplar and the splendor of wisdom,

And in conduct and life is worthy of so great an honor.

O Bassinus [**Note:** Bassinus was bishop of Speyer. Together with Archbishop Lullus and Bishop Megingod of Würzburg, he was sent by Charles in 768 to consecrate the church of Saint Goar, built by Abbot Assuerus. See Mabillon, *Annales*, book XXIV, p. 216, no. 21.],

Glory of the good people of Speyer,

Please commend me, gracious Father, to Paul, my patron,

Whose gracious household made us both brothers.

Who, pious Fulcrade [**Note:** Perhaps Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis, who died in 784 and received an epitaph from Alcuin; see the genuine poems above, no. 266. See also Mabillon, vol. II of the *Annales*, passim.],

Would dare to touch you with the lyric plectrum?

You surpass the songs of the Muses in merit.

Yet now, Supreme Father, permit this ivy to creep about your temples [another reading: “sacred”],

by your customary goodness,

Or at least allow me once to say “hail” to you.

Come now, little letter, quickly board the prepared ship;

Let the hooked keel sail beneath you over the Rhine’s ocean.

May the golden substance of gold not delay you,

Which the weary inhabitant brings forth from the earth’s womb:

Let neither castles, houses, cities, nor flowering fields

Detain your sluggishness for even a single hour.

But flee, break your delays, hasten, hurry by flying,

And—would that you might find them safe, healthy, joyful, and vigorous—

Greet our friends gladly.

May almighty God grant them health through the ages,

And afterward lead them joyfully into the heavenly court.

When all this is done, return confidently to your homeland,

And remember to tell what each person says to you.

And when red buds . . . burst from their bark in spring,

May they see you playing beneath our roofs,

And bringing us new songs once again.

Then I shall fashion for you golden garlands from fresh flowers,

And you shall rest with me among pleasant meadows.

### III. Poem about Charlemagne and Pope Leo’s Arrival to Him

You may find this poem among the appendices to the works of Charlemagne, in volume XCVIII of this *Patrology*, column 1433.

### IV. 456 Verses about the Cell of Cormaric

**[Note: In Quercetanus this poem is joined to no. 222, now no. 229, but we have separated it because of the difference in subject. Mabillon, in *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 176, thinks that it is not by Alcuin because of these verses, in which it is said that the nourishing voice of a former teacher once sounded there and that he dictated wisdom with sacred lips. He nevertheless understands the passage as referring to the cell of Cormaric, as does the other poem, 106, formerly 198. The distinguished man adds there, p. 177, that the poem may also be understood of the cell of Saint Judoc. Later, in book XXVI of the *Annales*, p. 346, he judged that these verses should rather be attributed to the cell of Cormaric than to that of Judoc, because the pleasantness of the sky and soil suits the former more than the latter.]**

O my cell, my sweet and beloved dwelling,

Forever and ever, O my cell, farewell!

On every side a tree surrounds you with resounding branches,

A little grove always heavy with flowering foliage.

All your meadows will bloom with healing flowers and herbs,

Which the physician’s hand seeks by the aid of healing [another reading: “mouth”].

Rivers surround you, with flowering banks everywhere,

Where the fisherman joyfully stretches his nets.

Your enclosures among the gardens breathe fragrance from fruit-bearing branches,

With lilies mingled, white among red roses.

Every kind of bird resounds with morning songs,

And praises God the Creator with its voice.

In you once sounded the nourishing voice of a teacher,

Who handed down books of wisdom with sacred lips.

In you, at appointed times, the holy praise of the Thunderer

Sounded with peaceful voices and hearts.

Now, my cell, I lament you with tearful songs,

And, groaning, I lament your misfortunes from my heart.

For you have suddenly fled the songs of poets [another reading: “by fate”],

And now an unknown hand wholly possesses you [**Note:** “An unknown hand now wholly possesses you.” Perhaps these verses were written after the death of Flaccus—that is, Alcuin—and Homer—that is, Angilbert—by Fridugisus, abbot of Saint Martin of Tours and Alcuin’s successor. Seeing Cormaric already enjoying its own abbot, namely Jacob, he may have regarded the cell as having been taken away from him. If one prefers to interpret this epigram as referring to the cell of Saint Judoc, the occasion for complaint may have been that after Alcuin’s death its possession was transferred to the monastery of Ferrières and then into the hands of Count Odulf. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, often complained about this.].**

Neither Flaccus nor Homer, the poet [another reading: “fates”], will possess you now,

Nor will boys sing of the Muses beneath your roofs.

So all the glory of the age suddenly changes;

Everything is altered in various orders.

Nothing remains eternal; truly nothing is unchanging;

Dark night obscures the sacred day.

Cold winter suddenly strikes down the beautiful flowers,

And a sadder breeze disturbs the calm sea.

The sacred youth who used to drive stags across the fields

Now leans, an old man, weary upon his staff.

Wretched are we! Why do we love you, world, as a fugitive?

You flee from us, always rushing everywhere.

While you flee, may you flee on; let us always love Christ,

May the love of God always hold our hearts.

May that pious servant [another reading: “pious servants”] defend from the dreadful enemy,

Drawing our hearts—his own—to heaven;

Let us praise and love him with our whole heart;

He is our glory, life, and salvation.

### V. Verses of Alcuin

**[Note: The distinguished Baluzius published these verses under Alcuin’s name from manuscript 4167 of the Colbert Library, in book IV of his *Miscellanea*, p. 550. Their attribution to Alcuin is doubtful because the same verses, with several changes, occur in the Golden Gospel manuscript preserved in the church of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, written not under Charlemagne but under Charles the Bald. Nevertheless, it is possible that the scribes of that manuscript copied Alcuin’s verses from an older exemplar, altering some things according to the circumstances.]**

These verses are to be written at the front of the codex, where an image of Christ and images of the four evangelists and four prophets are included.

In a square arrangement, depicted in various figures,

The ranks of the saints behold great joys.

Among them Isaiah, trusting in exalted doctrine,

And Jeremiah likewise sing the wonders of the Lord;

Ezekiel describes the seat of God and these things,

And Daniel tells of Christ cut from the mountain.

Matthew describes the human birth of Christ;

Mark roars in the manner of a growling lion.

Luke bellows with loving devotion in Christ’s song.

By writing, you, John, penetrate heaven with your mind.

**[Note: The following four verses, omitted by Baluzius, are supplied here from the aforementioned Golden Gospel manuscript.]**

These are on the other page, where the Lamb is painted, together with the 24 elders, the earth, and the sea.

All that the present earth produces for nourishment,

And all that this appearance of the sea surrounds with its broad rim:

They always worship you, God the Lamb, upon the lofty throne,

Who, by your shed blood, wiped away the sins of the age,

And on the cross, may you wipe away the wounds of King Charles.

**[Note: The following five verses are again added from the same manuscript.]**

The renowned white assembly of prophets and venerable order,

The apostolic company intent upon heavenly garlands,

Praises, adores, and fears you with devoted heart.

And Prince Charles gazes upon you with open face,

Praying that he may live with you for a long age, forever.

In another place, where the Lamb alone is painted:

Moses showed this Lamb, destined in the Law,

To bear the wounds of death on behalf of all peoples.

Where the right hand of Christ is painted:

The right hand that governs the world under the Father’s dominion,

And carried its own-born Son across the heavens above.

At the end of the Gospel of John:

And Prince Charles, who is benevolent in holy manner—

Through whose help this codex displays his deeds.

At the end of the book, the scribes speak:

Thus far, cutting our way across the sacred sea,

Our keel has come to the end of the shore.

### VI. To Candidus Departing for Rome

**[Note: I copied this hitherto unpublished poem from an old Salzburg manuscript, no. 71, where it follows three letters of Angilbert, which we shall publish in the Appendix. It is not entirely clear whether it belongs to him or to Alcuin. I am inclined to pronounce it Alcuin’s because Candidus, whom the poem calls “born son” and “son,” was his beloved disciple.]**

My mind follows you, dearest Candidus, in sorrow;

I beg that your mind may carry me with it everywhere.

May the grace of Christ our God accompany you as you go

Through every place, sweet son, from the citadel of heaven.

And through lands, forests, rivers, and mountains,

May it grant you a straight road along a fortunate path,

So that the desired day may already see you within the walls

Of the splendid City, where are the thresholds of Saint Peter,

Who may carry your prayers to Christ above the lofty

Summits of heaven, as the merciful first Father of the world.

May those prayers flow from your heart’s mouth, with tears and body

Prostrate upon the earth before God’s altar.

From there, rushing toward the airy walls that are about to fall,

Come to the sacred dwelling of pious Paul.

Stretch yourself out in the form of a cross, with groaning heart,

And mourn there together the sins of father and son.

Then run, devout traveler, through the churches

Of the saints, always praising God with your voice,

Who granted the world such patrons,

Standing before the throne of the Father in the citadel of heaven,

Who conquered kingdoms throughout the world with rosy blood,

Carrying Christ’s cross upon their holy necks.

Ask these saints again and again, with devoted heart,

Always mercifully to be present to your prayers.

May the signs of your tears always stand before their pious ashes

Upon the sacred stones.

I also ask you, with diligent mind, to be present throughout the city

At sacred orders and festivals.

Observe what is suitable for each person and time,

So that you may be able to report everything accurately to the Father;

And through your counsel and gracious conduct may you be of benefit to your companions,

So that through you God’s holy Church may flourish.

If the gracious favor of Christ should bring you first

Before the sacred eyes of the apostolic Father,

Ask for the ashes, garments, or perhaps hairs of the Fathers,

Or the great joys of the sacred cross.

That it may be a support for our life throughout the ages,

and likewise ever and everywhere for our own people, in holiness.

When all these things have been duly accomplished, Christ showing mercy,

returning safely to the Father, proceed quickly.

[Col. 1167C] Let Phoebus no longer see you resting in the Palace,

but rise with Lucifer, rejoicing traveler.

Let neither the flame-bearing sun, nor wind, nor cold, nor rain-clouds

delay the journey of one now hastening to the Father.

Love conquers all, swifter than the east wind:

hasten, go, run, fly, hurry.

So that happy Jacob may see Joseph with his own eyes,

before the day of cruel death, in his own city.

What more should I sing to you? Go happily and prosperously along every road,

my son, now, with God showing mercy.

May the Creator of the world grant you every prosperity.

Farewell, dear son, beloved by your father.

## VII. [Note: [Col. 1167D] From Vatican manuscript codex 3850, eleventh century, folio 43 verso.] PRAYERS OF ALBINUS TO GOD AND THE APOSTLES

[Col. 1167D]

We beseech the aid of the supreme Author of the world,

who, while dwelling in glory, took flesh from Mary;
