who, descending from heaven, the living giver of life,

suffered the cross for all and gave gifts to humanity,

the most generous Lawgiver, God and Son of God.

After completing his holy triumphs, he ascended victorious

and sent into the world ten radiant Apostles,

whose immeasurable glory will shine throughout the ages.

Blessed first heir and vicar of Christ,

holy Peter the apostle, foremost of the holy flock.

[Col. 1168A] Bar-Jonah, lofty pillar, climbing the heights of heaven;

Peter, from the solid rock, following in Christ’s footsteps.

With pure and perfect labor, without fatal sorrow,

he rests honorably at Rome, having suffered the cross under Nero.

The radiant miracles of his virtues shone forth.

An outstanding preacher, he became renowned among all peoples;

he shone brightly for those who could not see, like the radiance of Phoebus;

holy Paul, an apostle chosen not by men,

filled with the worthy fruits of the Holy Spirit.

Caught up to the third heaven, he became the teacher of the nations,

establisher of the feeble, consoler of the grieving.

Tested by various fire, [lacuna] in triumph.

The ages proclaim his wisdom, which cannot be explained.

Very worthy and radiant, a teacher who instructed the nations,

holy Andrew, excellent apostle of Christ the King.

[Col. 1168B] Organ of the Holy Spirit, adorned with spiritual gifts;

brother of the apostle Peter, expounder of the Lord’s law.

With a lordly mind and countenance, an ornament in manly stature;

preaching in Achaea, he suffered the cross under Aegeas.

Now he reigns in glory, an Elias fit for the kingdom.

Him God restored from the labors of life to flowers.

458 Chosen at the summit of apostolic honor,

he shone with the clear light of evangelical doctrine:

James, highest climber of Christ’s glory,

excellent fulfiller of the supreme King’s victory.

Brother of John—*Agiae*, a reading of uncertain construction—and of illustrious memory,

beheaded by the sword, crowned by martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1167D] End in the manuscript codex.]

## VIII. [Note: [Col. 1168D] See Mabillon, *Acta sanctorum*, second century, part I, pp. 199–200; d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, new edition, vol. II, p. 307.] EPITAPH OF SAINT RICHARIUS, ABBOT, OR METRICAL VERSES COMMISSIONED BY CHARLEMAGNE, ENGRAVED IN GOLDEN LETTERS ON THE SAME GOLDEN COFFIN IN WHICH THE BODY OF SAINT RICHARIUS WAS PLACED

[Col. 1168C]

### On the front of the tomb

A golden urn covers the heavenly treasure,

Richarius, the worshiper of the Lord by name,

whom this Centula brought forth from a most noble lineage,

and who flourished as an outstanding shepherd of the place.

### On the right side

Setting aside the great worldly honor in which he shone,

he scorned abundant riches for the love of God.

Here, breaking his own body in hard struggle,

the pious and great man always shone throughout the world.

### At the top of the chest above

Here he restored life to the dead and light to the blind,

[Col. 1168D] and, through his care, salvation returned to lepers.

Full of apostolic virtues and words,

he always held heavenly banquets in his mouth.

### On the left side

For him Prince Charles, with benevolent intent, completed a fitting church and built a tomb,

after approximately one hundred and sixty years,

while the servant of the Lord still remains whole.

### At the foot end

So that, through his merits, he may gain the heavenly kingdoms

and peacefully govern the kingdoms of the Franks.

## IX. ALBINUS ON THE SEVEN SEALS [Note: [Col. 1169] From Vatican manuscript codex 5096, eleventh century, folio 3 verso.]

[Col. 1169A]

The first seal is the nativity; the second, baptism; the third, the cross; the fourth, the tomb; the fifth, the resurrection; the sixth, the ascension; the seventh, the judgment. These are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The first was wisdom, so that Christ might be born from the Virgin without human seed. The second was the spirit of understanding, so that in baptism sins might be remitted through those three waters, as it is said: “Stripping off the old man and putting on the new” (Col. III, 9). The third was counsel, so that Caiaphas might say: “It is better that one man should die than that the whole nation should perish” (John XI, 50). The fourth was the spirit of fortitude, because the body was in the tomb, and [Col. 1169B] Christ bound the devil in hell and led back to the kingdom those souls who were being unjustly detained there; and the Lord bit hell. The fifth was the spirit of knowledge, because, when he had risen from the dead, he caused us to believe and to rise, since we shall all rise, as it is said: “Arise, Lord, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Psalm CXXXI, 8). The sixth was the spirit of piety, because, when Christ ascended into heaven, the souls of the righteous also ascend to him, as Paul says: “I long [Col. 1170A] to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). The seventh was the spirit of fear, because, when Christ comes to judgment to reward the righteous, there will be great fear for sinners, as it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). And so forth.

These seven gifts of the Holy Spirit were present in the seven patriarchs.

Wisdom was in Adam, because he assigned names to all the wild animals and beasts, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea; and he was the first prophet, as he said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II, 23).

Understanding was in Noah, who built and steered the ark during the Flood.

Counsel was in Abraham, as it is said: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII, 1).

Fortitude was in Isaac, [Col. 1170B] because he loved his enemies.

Knowledge was in Jacob, because the angel of the Lord blessed him and said to him: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. XXXII, 28).

Piety was in Moses, because he said: “Blot me out of the book of the living” (Exod. XXXII, 32), in which you have written me.

Fear was in David, because he feared God when Saul entered the cave to relieve himself, and he said: “Far be it from me to lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed” (I Kings XXVI, 11).

# PART NINE OF THE BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, OR ALCUIN, MASTER OF CHARLEMAGNE — WORKS ATTRIBUTED TO HIM

[Col. 1169]

[Col. 1169]

459 PREFACE

[Col. 1169C]

We do not intend to include here all those little works that certain writers, sometimes on the basis of slight conjectures, have attributed to the blessed Alcuin as their author; nor those which, in certain manuscript codices, whether through the ignorance or the hasty judgment of scribes, were marked with his name but are now, by the common judgment of scholars, shown to belong to other writers.

Among these we first reckon the *Homiliary*, published many times in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. For it is clear from a letter of Charlemagne and from Paul’s own verses prefixed to the Cologne edition of 1557 (in volume XCV of the *Patrologia*) that it was first compiled by Paul the deacon and monk of Monte Cassino. The *Homiliary* which the writer of Alcuin’s Life mentions as having likewise been compiled by the blessed Alcuin in two volumes from the writings of the Fathers either still lies hidden on library shelves, has entirely perished, or—as, without impugning the reliability of the aforesaid writer, we believe—never occupied the pen of the blessed Alcuin. “Certainly,” says D. Rivet, volume IV of the *Literary History of France*, p. 337, “that undertaking, after the Collection of Paul the Deacon, who [Col. 1170C] was Alcuin’s contemporary, would have been wholly superfluous.”

Nor is there any similar commission from Charlemagne to Alcuin such as there is to Paul; Mabillon published a fragment of the latter from a very ancient codex of Reichenau in book XXVI of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 62. It may have happened that Paul’s Collection was later revised by Alcuin, or sent to some friends with a letter of his added; and that this subsequently gave the writer of the Life occasion to assign it, on premature judgment, to Alcuin as its first compiler. Whatever the truth may be, we do not think it worthwhile to mix into these Works of the blessed Alcuin writings that owe him nothing more than some form of arrangement.

The same must be said of the book called the *Comes*, containing the Epistles and Gospels distributed among the individual days of the year. It is indeed stated in the Chartres codex, cited by Mabillon in book XXVI of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 61, that this book was corrected by the blessed Alcuin at Charlemagne’s command, not that it was first composed by him.

We likewise judge that the work known as [Col. 1171A] the *Carolingian Books* should be omitted from this edition. [Note: [Col. 1171] See these books among the Works of the Blessed Charlemagne in our edition. EDITOR.] It first became known in print in the sixteenth century, published in 1549 without indication of place or printer by a pseudonymous author who prefixed to the preface addressed “To the Christian Reader” the name “Eli. Phili.” Scholars now agree that this name conceals John Tilius, first bishop of Briocense in Brittany and later bishop of Meaux; concerning the riddle of this name and its solution, consult André du Chesne, volume II of *French Affairs*, p. 352.

There are, to be sure, not a few learned men, chiefly from the Protestant camp, who try to persuade us that the author of those books was our blessed Alcuin. The following considerations, however, prevent us from giving them our assent.

First, the writer of the Life of the blessed Alcuin makes no mention of this work among the other writings he lists as Alcuin’s. He certainly ought not to have omitted it, since he composed that Life at a time when the controversy over the veneration of images among the Gauls and Germans [Col. 1171B] had not yet cooled down, and when the work’s author—or his Alcuin—could thereby have gained great renown among them.

Second, no trace of this controversy between the Gauls and Germans and the Greeks is found either in Alcuin’s letters or in his other dogmatic writings regarded as genuine productions. Thus one must conclude not only that the blessed man wrote nothing against the veneration of images, but also that it is completely uncertain whether he ever involved himself in that dispute by consenting to or contradicting either side.

Third, the style used by the author of the *Carolingian Books* plainly appears different from the style of the blessed Alcuin. No one who has studied those Works and compared the two styles will deny this. The Carolingian author, in the judgment of Fleury, volume IX, p. 511 of the Brussels edition of 1721, often creates great difficulties concerning trivial matters; he frequently employs arguments that are inept and irrelevant; and at times he treats [Col. 1171C] the bishops of the Council of Nicaea with excessively harsh language. Such a practice is foreign to the style of the blessed Alcuin, as is shown by what he wrote against Felix and Elipandus. Rather than drive them to despair and contempt for the truth by reproaching their errors more severely, he judged it better to recall them from error through letters and admonitions full of charity.

Nor can those expressions be Alcuin’s: *haeresei*, *haereseorum*, instead of *haeretici*, *haereticorum*. And, to pass over many other points, when did Alcuin ever call the apostle Paul “the evangelical innkeeper,” in a wholly unusual and tasteless form of address, as the Carolingian author does in book II, chapter 25, no. 228?

“But,” says D. Christian August Heumannus, in the preface to those same *Carolingian Books*, reprinted under his care at Hanover in 1731, p. 54, “Cassander noticed an agreement of style in his letter to Molinaeus”; and he claims to have discovered an entire chapter, in exactly the same words, in Alcuin’s commentaries on John. [Col. 1171D] But let the learned men Cassander and Heumannus take responsibility for the fact that we cannot put faith in them here, since they did not identify that chapter. Certainly, that very chapter has so far escaped both our eyes and our diligence.

D. Heumannus goes on to say that he well remembers that, when comparing Alcuin’s style in his books on the Trinity with the Carolingian work, he “came upon several passages which seemed to make it clear to him that both works had the same author.” Heumannus speaks cautiously enough here. The circumspect man evidently understood that one cannot conclude from a few passages or sentences agreeing in style with a particular writer that an extensive and complete work should be assigned to that same writer.

For our part, we frankly admit that the style of the books on the Trinity appears to us plainly different from the style of the *Carolingian Books*. [Col. 1172A] Here we appeal, as we should, to the judgment of learned men.

D. Heumannus believes a clearer argument for Alcuin can be drawn from the testimony of Hoveden in the *Annals* under the year 792 and of the Westminster chronicler under the year 793. There it is related that Albinus or Alcuin, against the synodal book sent from Constantinople and dispatched by Charlemagne to Britain, “wrote a letter wonderfully supported by the authority of the divine Scriptures, and brought it, together with that same book, from the person of the bishops and princes of England to the king of the Franks.” Heumannus says that Vossius has already observed that these words expressly represent Alcuin as the author of the Carolingian work.

We, however, find nothing in this testimony from which we can acknowledge that what Vossius observed is expressly stated. Even if we grant that Alcuin once wrote a letter against the veneration of the saints affirmed by the Council of Nicaea, we nevertheless believe that this letter cannot be considered the very [Col. 1172B] work that became known under the title of the *Carolingian Books*.

First, that work was written before the blessed Alcuin returned from England to Francia, around the beginning of the year 793. For in the preface Charlemagne—the name under which those books are marked—writes in book I, p. 8 of Heumannus’s edition, that the Second Council of Nicaea had taken place almost three years earlier. It is universally agreed that this council was held at Nicaea in 787. The *Carolingian Books*, therefore, cannot be dated later than three years after that year, or later than 791. Thus they were written before Alcuin’s return; and consequently he could not have brought those same books with him from Britain to Charlemagne after the books had already been composed in Francia two years earlier.

Second, the letter remembered by the English writers cited was written in Britain and, according to their account, was brought from there by Alcuin to Charlemagne in the name and on behalf of the bishops and princes of England. The Carolingian work, however, is said to have been [Col. 1172C] written in the name and on behalf of Charles, king of the Franks. The two works therefore cannot be identical.

Indeed, to state what we think, the silence of the writer of Alcuin’s Life, as well as of Alcuin himself, makes us suspicious of this account by Hoveden, the Westminster chronicler, and other writers who lived long after Alcuin. From that silence we believe a strong argument can be drawn that the blessed Alcuin never disputed or wrote anything about this doctrine. We indicated this opinion somewhat earlier.

We must add what D. Mabillon observed concerning the same testimony of the English writers in book XXVI of the *Annals*, no. 19: namely, that Alcuin himself testifies in book I against Elipandus that “at Charles’s command he came to Francia at that time, after the sect of the Adoptionists had been debated at Regensburg in 792, to attack that sect, not the Council of Nicaea.” Therefore he did not come to Francia again after that assembly in the name and at the command of the bishops or princes of Britain, but at the command of King Charles, since at that king’s command he had returned to Britain. [Col. 1172D] The credibility of Hoveden and the others is therefore shaken.

But this is sufficient to demonstrate that the blessed Alcuin was not the author of the Carolingian work and that it is therefore rightly removed from his Works. For this reason we properly disregard the remaining arguments that D. Heumannus attempted to produce in support of his opinion, since they are of exceedingly little weight and can easily be refuted by anyone who considers our arguments.

Finally, at this point we leave aside the *Life of Saint Judoc*, published by Mabillon in *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume II, pp. 566 and following. It was never published under Alcuin’s name; some nevertheless attributed it to him solely because he held a cell dedicated to Saint Judoc. The very learned D. Rivet, volume IV of the *Scriptorial History of France*, p. 79, has shown that its author was [Col. 1173A] an anonymous writer older than Alcuin and that his style differs entirely from Alcuin’s customary style. We add our own judgment to his.

Here, then, among the spurious little works of Alcuin, we chiefly present those which the distinguished Quercetanus inserted in various places in the first edition of the Works of the blessed Alcuin and which learned men might also miss in this edition. The first will be the book on the divine Offices; the second, a letter on the ceremonies of Baptism [Col. 1174A] to the emperor Charlemagne, together with certain related pieces newly discovered; the third, the *Life of Antichrist*; the fourth, homilies on the nativity of the Lord, on the purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, on her nativity, and on all the saints; the fifth, certain poems which, wherever possible, are referred to their proper authors.

To each of these little works we shall add, in our customary manner, notices serving either the instruction of scholars or the elucidation of the works. Let us therefore begin with the first.

[Col. 1173]

## BOOK ON THE DIVINE OFFICES (C, G)*

[Col. 1173]

461 PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 1173B]

[Col. 1173B]

This book on the divine Offices was first published under Alcuin’s name, among other writings of the same kind, at Cologne in 1568 under the care of Melchior Hittorp. D. Quercetanus later copied it from that edition and inserted it into his collected Works of the blessed Alcuin, adding several corrections and twelve complete chapters on the authority of an ancient manuscript codex.

The distinguished editor nevertheless admits in his preface, no. 17 near the end, that he has certain conjectures troubling him and that this book may never have been written by Alcuin: “For its author,” he says, “whoever he may be, declares himself to be an inhabitant of Gallia Braccata [Bracate Gaul] (chapter 38), and he attributes the question concerning the festivals of the saints in chapter 18 to Helpericus the monk, who, according to Trithemius, flourished in the year 1040. Finally, in chapter 32 he mentions the institution of the feast of All Saints on the Kalends of November, although from Sigebert and others we learn [Col. 1173C] that this feast began to be celebrated in Gaul and Germany long after Alcuin’s death, namely in the year 835.”

But this last argument is weak, as we noted in our remarks on letter 91, to Arno.

Scholars now agree that this book on the divine Offices is not Alcuin’s, partly because it contains much that is unworthy of Alcuin and partly because writings by authors of a later age have been inserted into it.

“This treatise,” according to D. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part I, in the *Eulogy of the Blessed Alcuin*, no. 16, p. 185, “is therefore a patchwork collected from various writings of Alcuin himself and of other, later authors. For chapter 40 is a treatise by Remigius of Auxerre, a monk, on the exposition of the Mass; and chapter 18 contains a letter by the monk Helpericus, who appears to be Hilpericus, a monk of Saint Gall in the eleventh century, as Quercetanus has already noted.

“Moreover, that treatise contains certain foolish and erroneous statements unworthy of Alcuin. One such statement is found in chapter 1, where it says that the Lord Christ was born under the consulship of Sulpicius and Camerinus, which is false. [Col. 1173D] It also says that he was baptized in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, under the consulship of Valerianus and Asiaticus, whereas it should have said Valerius Asiaticus and Messala, who nevertheless were not consuls in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. In addition, this writer says that *Pascha* is a Greek word, contrary to Alcuin’s explicit statement in book VI on John, chapter 32, where he says: ‘Pascha, brothers, is not, as some think, a Greek name, but Hebrew,’ and so forth.”

The whole work is therefore rightly rejected among the spurious writings.

## 462 CHAPTER I. WHY THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD IS CELEBRATED

The nativity of this most sacred day is so called because on it Christ was born: according to the Hebrew truth, in the year 3,952 from the creation of the world; according [Col. 1174B] to others, in the year 5,199, which was the forty-second year of the reign of Octavian Caesar Augustus. In that year, when the disturbances of all the nations throughout the world had been subdued and God the Father had established the firmest peace, Jesus Christ consecrated the sixth age of the world by his coming.

It was therefore fitting that peace should have been established throughout the world and that rebellious men should cease from wars and enmities. Public roads were also then ordered to be made safe, because the truest Way was about to be born; and, so that he might be recognized by all, he deigned to become man. For in order to address them, the Word became flesh.

Before he was born of the Virgin, however, portents and signs appeared in heaven and on earth. On a certain day, when Caesar Augustus was entering the city of Rome, at approximately the third hour of the day, [Col. 1174C] beneath a clear and serene sky, an arc-like ring resembling a rainbow was suddenly seen to surround the disk of the sun. This foretold the one who had both made and governed the sun itself and the entire world.

At that time he returned thirty thousand slaves to their masters. He also crucified three thousand whose masters could not be found. Then, entering the city in triumph, he remitted all the debts of the Roman people, canceling the records.

At about the same time, a most abundant spring of oil flowed throughout the entire day from the “Meritorious Tavern,” clearly signifying that Christ’s grace would proceed from that same tavern—that is, from the broad and generous Church—and that new peoples would come forth from the nations.

Indeed, Christ’s coming was signified in many signs associated with Augustus Caesar. Thus *Caesar* is interpreted as “principal possession,” while *Augustus* means “standing solemnly.” More fully, this expresses Christ, [Col. 1174D] who solemnly possesses all things and powerfully holds every principality.

The governor Cyrinus, whose name is interpreted as “heir,” signifies Peter, to whom the Lord granted the inheritance of the Church. Accordingly, when an edict had gone out from the aforesaid Caesar that the whole world should be registered, the aforementioned Cyrinus was sent to Judaea to register the people and their possessions.

In this registration, 4,100,000 Roman citizens were found, and sixty-four thousand colonies were established.

For earlier the same Caesar had forbidden everyone to dare to call him “lord,” because, while he was ruling, that most true Lord and emperor was destined to be born.

He is said to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. From that date 276 days are counted—that is, [Col. 1175A] nine months and seven days—up to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when he is believed to have been born under the consulship of Sulpicius and Camerinus. [Note: [Col. 1175D] See the preliminary notice.]

It was most fitting that he should be conceived at the time when the world was made through him and when the fruits of the earth are signified, and born at the time when the length of day increases and the darkness of night diminishes.

But one must ask: since he is said to have been born at night, why did the angel evangelize the shepherds, saying, “Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke II, 11)? By “today” he meant the day of the New Testament, when he brought the darkness of ignorance to an end and established the beginning of the light of knowledge.

It was also fitting that he should be born around the hour of night at which he rose from the dead. Hence Solomon says: “While all things were held in the midst of silence,” and so forth (Wis. VIII, 14).

[Col. 1175B] One must also ask why this feast does not have the same variability as Easter and Pentecost—namely, why it is not moved so that the days of the week defiled by Adam’s sin might be cleansed.

Augustine therefore says [Note: [Col. 1176D] Augustine, letter 55, no. 2]:

“We ought to know that the Lord’s birthday is not celebrated as a sacrament, but only to recall that he was born; and for that reason it was necessary only that the recurring day of the year on which the event itself occurred should be marked with festive devotion. At Easter and Pentecost, however, we recall not only what happened—that he died and rose again—but also understand, for the sacramental significance, those events that are testified to have taken place around him.”

[Col. 1175C] The vigils kept by the shepherds on this night are divided into four, signifying the four laws: the first natural, the second Mosaic, the third prophetic, and the fourth the New Testament, in which he appeared to the shepherds—that is, to the teachers of the Church.

We too must keep vigil with the shepherds, so that we may deserve to hear that most sweet harmony which was first sung on this night: “Glory to God in the highest,” and so forth.

For this reason Saint Telesphorus, the pope, wishing us to be especially watchful, arranged for Masses to be celebrated—perhaps three Masses [Note: *Forte leg.*, “perhaps read: three Masses”]: one in memory of Christ’s nativity, or of the angelic chorus; another Mass, which follows, signifying the new light of the Gospel with which we are illumined through the mystery of the incarnate Word; or on account of the shepherds’ visit to the Lord’s manger, where they found the living bread that is eaten daily by the faithful.

[Col. 1175D] The Romans celebrate this night as follows. On the preceding day, that is, on the vigil of the Lord’s birthday, at the ninth hour they sing Mass at Saint Mary’s. When it is finished, they sing the evening synaxis. Then they go to eat.

At twilight the apostolicus enters the aforesaid church for the vigil. They do not, however, sing the Introit there; rather, after completing the vigils and Matins, as they are contained in the Antiphonary, they sing the first Mass there during the night. When it is finished, they go to Saint Anastasia to sing another Mass during the night.

[Col. 1176A] Then they proceed to Saint Peter to celebrate the vigils there, beginning at the place where they find those who are keeping watch and singing psalms. For they themselves enter for the vigils at the customary time during the course of the night, sing the invitatory, and continue the order of the Antiphonary. Hence double offices are also described for this night in the Roman Antiphonaries.

## 463 CHAPTER II. ON CIRCUMCISION

This circumcision is nothing other than the cutting away in the flesh of the foreskin, which was commanded only to the Jews. It therefore began with Abraham, to whom the Lord gave this command: “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and an infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you” (Gen. XVII, 10, 12), so that it might be a sign of the covenant between God and faithful human beings.

In order that they might be cleansed from every impurity of flesh and spirit, the flesh was commanded to be circumcised. What Christ’s baptism is for us today in faith, circumcision provided for them on the eighth day, [Col. 1176B], the day on which he rose from the dead—except that the entrance into the kingdom of heaven was not yet open to those who had been circumcised.

But one may ask: since the Lord commanded circumcision in the Old Testament and was himself circumcised in the New, why did circumcision subsequently cease? He had not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, nor to appear unlike the holy fathers and prophets from whose lineage, according to the flesh, he deigned to be born.

For this reason he wished to be circumcised, either to remove from the Jews the excuse for saying, “You are unlike the fathers; therefore we do not wish to believe in you,” or because the old things have passed away and, behold, all things have become new. We ought to be circumcised not in the flesh but in the spirit.

For just as Christ accepted death for us, so he did not reject circumcision, so that we might be circumcised in spirit, since he delights in circumcision of the [Col. 1176C] heart, as the Prophet confirms: “In the last days the Lord will circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies.”

This is true circumcision of the heart: that we lay aside the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who has been created according to God (Col. III, 9–10).

## CHAPTER III. ON THE LORD’S OCTAVE

On this eighth day he was circumcised. This eighth day contains within itself complete fullness and is the perfect number. It is the Lord’s day and the day of the Lord’s resurrection.

The book of Leviticus reveals where its beginning came from: “The eighth day shall be most celebrated and most holy” (Lev. XXIII, 36). And in Chronicles: “Moreover, Mattithiah with the Levites on harps [Col. 1176D] sang *epinicion* for the eighth,” which *epinicion* signifies the Lord’s triumph (I Chron. XV, 21). The titles of the sixth and eleventh psalms are inscribed “for the eighth.”

This eighth day pertains to eternal rest. Hence we receive it in the singular number, since it is not changed by the succession of another day. The present world [perhaps, “number”], however, does not receive this eighth day, which is singular, but those days that we call octaves, because, once the seventh has ended, they always return to the first.

Some think that through this octave the Lord’s second coming is signified. Hence the prophet Amos says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; for it is a day of darkness and not of light” (Amos V, 18). And Zephaniah: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter and harsh; the strong man shall be troubled there” (Zeph. I, 14).

[Col. 1177A] Those who think that this day will come after six thousand years from the creation of the world, because the Lord is read to have ceased from his work on the seventh day, counting a thousand years as each day—since it is written, “A thousand years in his sight are like one day”—do not pay sufficient attention to the Lord’s testimony in the Gospel that the Son of Man does not know this day. It is therefore exceedingly presumptuous to inquire diligently into what divine providence did not wish to reveal to us.

Certainly, we ought to love and hope for that great and singular day which the prophet David, thirsting for it, called “one day,” saying: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm LXXXIII, 11).

[Col. 1177B] The octaves that we celebrate today are reverently observed because they coincide with the first days, just as one Lord’s day follows another and is celebrated with the same rite. Today we celebrate the coming of human beings to Christ, and in his nativity, his coming to human beings.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE KALENDS OF JANUARY

According to the folly of the pagans, these Kalends should rather be called things to be avoided than Kalends. At that time—when judges ruled over the children of Israel, that is, before Samson—there was a certain pagan prince in Italy named Janus, after whom the month of January was later named.

Ignorant people who did not know God feared this Janus as though he were a king and began to worship him as a god. They fashioned two faces for him, on account of the east and the west, and also called him four-faced, that is, Janus the double, on account of the four directions, or the four elements and the four seasons.

[Col. 1177C] But in doing this they fashioned a monster rather than a god. Therefore Numa, after Romulus, wished this to be the first month of the year, as the month of the two-headed god, looking back upon the end of the past year and forward to the beginning of the future; and it was called January because it is the boundary and door of the year. [Note: [Col. 1177] See Martène, *On the Ancient Discipline of the Church*, chapter 13, no. 15, p. 103.]

Thus ignorant people, worshiping it as though it were a god, consecrated the day itself with many obscenities. Some transformed themselves into monstrous shapes and assumed the appearance of beasts. Others, adopting feminine gestures, feminized their masculine faces; and rightly enough, those who passed into women’s attire lacked masculine strength.

[Col. 1177D] Some were polluted by fanatical omens; they made a din by dancing with their feet and leaping with applause. Others observed omens so carefully that they would not give anyone who asked either fire from their house or any other benefit.

They also received diabolical New Year’s gifts from others and handed them on to others themselves. They even kept little tables prepared throughout the night, full of food, believing that the Kalends of January could provide these things for the whole year.

Because the whole world was filled with these and other miseries, the universal Church established a public fast on this day, so that the Author of life might bring these calamities to an end.

[Col. 1178A] But since, by the Lord’s generosity, the faithful regard these things as worthless, even though some slight likenesses of them—God forbid—may still lurk among savage peoples, they must nevertheless be prohibited and driven away with every effort. Nothing new should be presumed for these Kalends beyond what is observed on the Kalends of the other months, except that the Lord’s octaves are celebrated with exceptional devotion, as stated above.

Nor should this be left unmentioned: when these diabolical superstitions were once being practiced at Rome, a certain holy man named Almachius said, “Today are the octaves of the Lord’s day. Cease these superstitions of idols and polluted sacrifices.” At the command of Alypius, prefect of the city, he was killed for this reason.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE LORD’S THEOPHANY OR EPIPHANY
[Col. 1178B] This most sacred solemnity, which is called by the Greeks *Theophany* or *Epiphany*, but in Latin is interpreted as “appearance,” “showing,” or “manifestation,” contains within itself mysteries of many kinds. When Christ had recently emerged from the Virgin’s womb, the Chaldean Magi, seeing in the East a star shining with such extraordinary brilliance that it surpassed the sun in light, recognized—having been instructed in the course of the stars—that this was the star which Balaam the Midianite, whose tradition they followed, had long ago foretold would appear, saying: “A star shall rise out of Jacob” (Num. XIV, 17), and so forth. For the heavenly body could be seen by day.

The first of these Magi was King Zoroaster, from whom they are said to have derived their origin. They shook the elements and disturbed the minds of men. From their number, once in Egypt, some resisted Moses, turning rods into dragons and water into blood. These men were called astrologers, and also *genethliaci*, because of their consideration of births. For they described the destinies of human beings according to the twelve signs of heaven. From the course of the stars under which people were born, they foretold their character and future events: that is, under what sign each person had been born and what effect it would have on the life of the one who was born. They were commonly called mathematicians; this kind of superstition they called in Latin *constellationes*, that is, “markings of the stars,” describing how the stars stood when someone was born. They were likewise called interpreters of the stars, as were those who, according to the Gospel, announced the birth of Christ; afterward, however, they were called mathematicians in name only.

[Col. 1178D] Knowledge of this art was permitted up to the Gospel, so that after Christ had been born no one would thereafter interpret anyone’s birth from heaven. Therefore, immediately disturbed and terrified by the sight of the star, and having taken gifts, they reached Christ’s cradle in Bethlehem on the thirteenth day—the day that is celebrated today—with the star leading them. Worshiping him with their tiara-covered heads, the keen curiosity of the Chaldeans rejoiced, because they saw born on earth the one whom they had recognized in heaven as foretold by the torches of the stars. They also offered him gifts, namely gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Because they came from far away, they foretold that the peoples of the nations would come to know the light of faith. By gold the king is shown; in frankincense God is recognized; through myrrh, the man who suffered and was buried.

[Col. 1179A] The priest Juvencus wonderfully expressed these gifts [in meter]:

> They bring gold, frankincense, and myrrh  
> For the king, for God, and for man.

On this day we omit one of the things that we celebrate at the Lord’s Nativity, namely the invitatory [Note: [Col. 1179D] See Martene, cited above, chapter 14, no. 6, p. 110.]. The institutor of the offices, insofar as he was able, wished the action of that time—when the events we commemorate took place—to be recalled to us in the customary office. Specifically, because he wished in this way to distinguish our good invitation, by which the faithful are invited and stirred to pray to God, from the invitation of Herod, who gathered the scribes and leaders of the Jews in order to learn where Christ would be born, intending to kill him, he omitted the invitatory of the present [Col. 1179B] office.

The Psalm “Our God is refuge and strength” (Ps. XLV, 2) is sung in an inverted order, because the Lord was worshiped by the Magi before he was baptized by John. Perhaps the institutor of this office wished rather to imitate the order in which the faithful come to baptism than to follow the order of the psalms. Past events, then, are properly recalled to memory when their explanations correspond to reason.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE BAPTISM OF THE LORD

When nearly thirty years of Christ’s life had been completed, he came to the Jordan to be baptized by John, namely in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, under the consulship of Valerian and Asiaticus [Note: [Col. 1179D] In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. More correctly, under the consulship of Valerius Asiaticus and Messala, although these men were not consuls in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, as we noted above in the Preliminary Notice.], and while four tetrarchs ruled in Judea, namely Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, the sons of Herod the Great; or, with Pilate as Roman governor and Annas and Caiaphas exercising the high priesthood.

For from the beginning of the world, according to the Hebrew text, 4,982 years had passed [Read: 3,982, as above in chapter 1], with the observation that the sixteenth year of Tiberius was the beginning of the eighty-first jubilee. According to the edition of the Seventy interpreters, however, the number of years is 5,229.

The Lord was baptized for three reasons. First, because he was human, in order to fulfill all the righteousness of the Law. Second, in order to confirm John’s baptism by his own baptism. Third, by sanctifying the waters of the Jordan, to show, through the descent of the dove, the coming of the Holy Spirit in the baptismal washing of believers. Immediately after his baptism he was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil, and he began to fast for us for forty days and forty nights.

According to this reckoning, the fast began with the Lord’s baptism and ended on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, when the devil, confounded, withdrew from him. From that time Jesus Christ also announced the way of salvation to the peoples, proving by signs and mighty works that what he said was true. He also began to perform the miracles written in the Gospel.

Thus the first miracle was that, after the annual manifestation, when he was invited to a wedding, he changed water into wine; this occurred on the third day after the calling of the disciples. We understand this wine made from water as the purest divine commands, or the holy Scriptures, containing the vigor of heavenly wisdom. This wedding signifies the joys of human salvation. The six water jars designate the six ages of the world, through which the righteous prefigured the Lord. By the master of the feast we understand the most powerful preacher, Paul.

He also performed a great miracle today, when he fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. The five thousand men who were fed with five loaves and two fish are the peoples of the Church, who, after the five bodily senses, are refreshed by Christ with the spiritual nourishment of the Law and satisfied by the two fish, as though by the twin Testaments.

Nor should it be passed over that this second birth of Christ, illuminated by so many mysteries, is more honorable than the first. Then he was merely born, and an angel addressed the shepherds. Today he was worshiped by the Magi with gifts. Today, when he was immersed in the waters of the Jordan, he was called the beloved Son by the Father from heaven, and the Holy Spirit was seen above him in the form of a dove. Today, after the sacrament of baptism, the head of the dragon was crushed. Today water was made wine, and the Church was joined to the same heavenly Bridegroom. Moreover, five thousand men were refreshed by him. For this reason it is interpreted as “manifestation,” because in these things he deigned to manifest himself to human beings.

That no one should presume to baptize on this feast, Pope Leo prohibits in the Decretals, as follows [Note: [Col. 1180D] Saint Pope Leo, Letter 16, to all the bishops of Sicily, chapter 6.]:

> “If anyone thinks that the feast of the Epiphany, which ought to be venerated with its proper honor, thereby possesses the privilege of baptism, let him know that the grace and purpose of that baptism were different, and that it did not possess the power by which they are reborn through the Holy Spirit. The Lord, who had no need of the remission of sin or of the remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as he also wished to be circumcised. But he established the power of regeneration when blood for redemption and the water of baptism flowed from his side. Therefore, for the baptism of the elect—who, according to apostolic practice, must be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching—only two times are to be observed, namely Easter and Pentecost, except in the danger of death, in the distress of persecution, and in fear of shipwreck [Note: [Col. 1180D] The same, chapters 3 and 5.]. For it is most fitting that, in the death of the crucified one and the resurrection of the dead one, the repentance of baptism should create a new nature from the old, so that Christ’s resurrection and death may work in those who are reborn, as the Apostle says: ‘Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?’ (Rom. VI, 3). The triple immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the lifting up from the waters is an image of his rising from the tomb.”

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY

Concerning this feast and the other feasts of Saint Mary, it is read in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs* [Note: [Col. 1181D] *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of Sergius. See Martene, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book I, chapter 15.] that Pope Sergius ordered litanies to be performed on the day of the Lord’s presentation in the temple. For it is written:

> “That on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Dormition and Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Simeon—which in Greek is called ὑπαπανθὴ (*Hypapante*, “Meeting”)—they should go out from Saint Hadrian with litanies, and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.”

Therefore, on that day, at dawn, all the clergy or people proceed with litanies and antiphons to the church of Saint Hadrian, awaiting [Col. 1181B] the pontiff. When the pontiff enters the sacristy, he puts on black vestments, and the clergy do likewise. After this, all receive individual candles from the hand of the pontiff. Then, at the pontiff’s command, the schola begins the antiphon: “Arise, O Lord,” and the Psalm “God, with our ears.” The pontiff leaves the sacristy with the ministers, first signaling to the schola that they should say the *Gloria*. Then he goes to the altar and prays until the *Gloria* is completed.

After kissing the altar, and the deacon likewise on either side, he says, and the schola sings, the verse: “The work that you have done,” without “Kyrie eleison.” When the antiphon is completed, the pontiff, standing before the altar, says: “The Lord be with you,” and “Let us pray.” The deacon says: “Let us bend the knee,” if the day has fallen within Septuagesima. The prayer follows: “Hear, we beseech you, O Lord, your people.”

When this has been completed, the schola begins, with one antiphon: “Adorn the bridal chamber.” Then: “Hail, full of grace.” Then: “Simeon received the answer.” When they have approached the courtyard of the church of Saint Mary, the litanies are to be performed. After these have been completed before the altar, and the pontiff has entered the sacristy, the schola begins at the entrance the antiphon: “We have received, O God.”

On that day, “Glory to God in the highest” is not sung if the feast has fallen within Septuagesima. Thereafter the Mass is celebrated in its proper order.

Concerning this feast, Bede, that distinguished priest and teacher, also says in his book *On the Times* [Note: [Col. 1181D] Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 10.]:

> “Numa dedicated the second month to Februus, that is, to Pluto, who was believed to have power over purifications; and it was necessary for the city to be purified in that month, in which he decreed that sacrifices should be offered to the Manes gods. [Col. 1181D] But Christian religion rightly changed this custom of purification, since in the same month, on the day of Saint Mary, the entire people, together with priests and ministers, proceeds through the churches and suitable places of the city while singing hymns with devotion, carrying in their hands the burning candles given by the pontiff. As this good custom grew, they learned to do the same on the feasts of the other celebrations of that blessed and perpetual Virgin—not, indeed, for the five-year purification of an earthly empire, but in perpetual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom. For, according to the parable [Col. 1182A] of the wise virgins, all the elect, coming with the shining lamps of good works to meet their Bridegroom and King, will immediately enter with him into the wedding feast of the heavenly city.”

## CHAPTER VIII. [Note: [Col. 1181D] The same arrangement is found in Amalarius, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 1, with which it also agrees in certain other matters.] ON SEPTUAGESIMA, SEXAGESIMA, QUINQUAGESIMA, AND QUADRAGESIMA

Septuagesima is reckoned, according to the headings of the Sacramentary and Antiphonary, nine weeks before Easter, on the seventh day of the week. The people of God were held captive in Babylon for seventy years. When these had been completed, they returned to Jerusalem. The number seventy recalls to our memory the whole period of the present age, during which we are strangers to the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore the author of our office placed Septuagesima in our offices, so that by abstaining from pleasures during this time we might show in our manner of life how those ought to live throughout the whole age who, after baptism, estrange themselves from the heavenly Jerusalem through sins.

For when the people return from captivity after seventy years, who does not see that, after the periods have elapsed which pass according to the sevenfold number of days, we too—that is, the Church of God—must return from the pilgrimage of this age to that heavenly Jerusalem? For this reason we do not sing Alleluia at that time, nor “Glory to God in the highest,” which are heavenly songs. The Psalm says: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI, 4).

There are some who pass the first week of Septuagesima without any observance of a new manner of life [Col. 1182C], except for changing Alleluia, for the use of dalmatics in certain places, and for omitting “Glory to God in the highest.” The Greeks sanctify the following week, namely Sexagesima, by their fast. Our clergy, following Pope Telesphorus, sanctify the next, namely Quinquagesima; he established a fast of seven weeks before Easter.

The teacher of our office, however, requires a more extensive change than we practice, in accordance with the constitution of his office. For he indicated the fast itself in the first prayer of the Mass, saying: “That we who are justly afflicted for our sins”—for here the word signifies affliction. In the Introit also he says: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell surrounded me.” Because of these pains we cannot be joyful and secure, but must prepare ourselves for battle, as the Apostle says: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (I Cor. IX, 25).

Ambrose says:

> “From everything that the same discipline teaches must be avoided: if they know that one person is to be crowned, how much more ought those things to be observed by whom salvation has been promised in its entirety?”

The Apostle teaches from what we who are about to fight must abstain, saying: “Fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be named among you” (Eph. V, 3).

Pope Telesphorus, ninth after the blessed Apostle, established in the Roman See that they should observe abstinence for seven weeks [Col. 1183A], as many still do. This period was then called Quinquagesima for two reasons: either because, in sequence, the number fifty is established after forty; or because from that point there are fifty days to the holy Resurrection.

Later Pope Melchiades, an African by birth and thirty-fourth after Saint Peter, established that no one should presume to fast on the first or fifth day of the week: on the first, because of the Lord’s resurrection; on the fifth, because on that day the Lord dined with his disciples and on that day ascended into heaven.

Then the faithful decided to devote eight weeks to fasting and to call the first Sunday “Sexagesima”—not because of a number of sixty days, but because of the usage of our language, by which, just as fifty is fitted to forty, so sixty is fitted to fifty, and seventy to sixty.

From Sexagesima to Easter there are eight weeks. If from each of them one subtracts the first and fifth days of the week from abstinence, as Melchiades established, and also the holy day of Easter itself, only forty days of abstinence remain, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Septuagesima is said to be celebrated by the faithful so that they may both return tithes of their days to God and nevertheless be able to relax the first and fifth days of the week and the Sabbath from fasting. From Septuagesima to Easter there are nine weeks, making sixty-four days. If from each week one subtracts the three aforementioned days, together with the sacred day of Easter, thirty-six days remain in the tenth part of the year for fasting.

The one who established the Sabbath as worthy of honor did not do so because of legal commandments, but because the Lord rested in the tomb on that day.

Augustine, book XV of *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 1183D] Rather book XVI, no. 3.]:

> “Not everything that is narrated as having happened should be thought to signify something, but for the sake of those things that signify something, those things that signify nothing are also attached. A field is not plowed only with the share; rather, for this to be done, the other parts of the plow are also necessary. Nor are only the strings of harps fitted for song; rather, so that they may be fitted, the other parts are also present.”

Again, in another form:

> Why is it called Septuagesima, when from that day until Easter there are no more than sixty-four days? It is the custom of the divine Scriptures that whenever a number has passed beyond any decade, so that it falls under the third units (*tertiis monadiis*; read *tertius*; the wording is uncertain), that number is not counted with the preceding decade but with the one toward which it tends. Read the book of Genesis in the genealogy of the sons of Noah.

Again, in another form:

> Why is it called Septuagesima, when from that day until Easter there are not seventy days? Septuagesima extends to the Sabbath before the octave of Easter. They are baptized, lay aside their white garments, and then ought to be confirmed by the bishop and receive the Holy Spirit through the imposition of hands. And because seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are described, those who are to receive him rightly celebrate Septuagesima beforehand.

For what the number seven signifies by itself, the same thing it signifies when multiplied by ten. Sexagesima extends to the middle of Easter, that is, to Wednesday of Easter week. Quinquagesima extends to Easter Day itself. Quadragesima extends to the day of the Lord’s Supper.

Count, therefore, the number of days that are in abstinence from Septuagesima to Quadragesima: you will find three times six, that is, eighteen days, excluding Sundays. If you divide this number according to a double proportion, you will find six in one part and twelve in the other. Six is to twelve in a simple proportion; twelve is to six in a double proportion.

Again, between the Lord’s Supper and Easter Day there are two days, and between Easter and the middle of Easter, which is Wednesday, there are two days, to which Sexagesima extends. From that day to the Sabbath to which Septuagesima reaches there are likewise two, making six altogether. Four is double two, just as two is simple.

The preceding numbers, therefore, which occur in abstinence, signify that our double death was destroyed by Christ’s single death. We were subject to death in soul and body, whereas Christ, through his bodily death, excluded death from both soul and body.

These days, which we celebrate with joy and gladness in the Lord’s resurrection, signify the resurrection which Christ bestowed in a double form through his single resurrection. For just as he died only in the body, so he rose only in the body. We, however, are first raised in soul when he forgives our sins, and in the future he will also raise our bodies.

## CHAPTER IX. [Note: [Col. 1183D] Some manuscripts place the chapters that follow on Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Quadragesima at the end of the book. We have judged that they should be left in the same order in which they were previously printed. Quercet.] ALSO ON SEPTUAGESIMA

Those who read the books of the sacred Law, namely the history of the Old Testament, readily know that the Israelite people often sinned against God. Although frequently admonished through the prophets, they refused to repent. Therefore, as is read in the Book of Kings and in the prophecy of blessed Ezekiel, after many corrections, while they remained, as we have said, in shamelessness, God handed them over to the hands of plunderers.

First the ten tribes were led into captivity by the Assyrians and their king. The tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, which had remained in Jerusalem, were repeatedly admonished by blessed Jeremiah and the other prophets to come to their senses and cease from evil deeds, lest they suffer the same things as those who had already been deported to Babylon. But they refused to listen and obstinately remained in the hardness and perversity of their hearts, in idolatry, and in their other offenses.

Therefore the Assyrian king Nebuchadnezzar returned with an army, devastated their regions, surrounded the city of Jerusalem with fortifications, and besieged it until, when the food supplies had failed, all were defeated and surrendered, and King Zedekiah fled from the abandoned city with his sons and the few who had remained with him.

After the city had been captured, the Assyrian people pursued and seized him and brought him before their king Nebuchadnezzar, together with his sons and the leaders of the Jewish people who were left. King Nebuchadnezzar pronounced judgments against King Zedekiah, as is read in the Book of Jeremiah, and ordered his sons and all the leaders of the Jews who remained to be killed in the presence of King Zedekiah. He ordered Zedekiah’s eyes to be torn out and led him bound in chains to Babylon.

He sent Nabuzardam, the commander of the army, to destroy the walls of Jerusalem. Thus, as it is written there, Nabuzardam, commander of the cooks, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem. And so they were all led into captivity in Babylonia, with only a few of the poor of the people left behind, those who were farmers and vine-growers.

In that captivity they remained in great affliction, want, and servitude for seventy years. Later, through the mercy of divine clemency, under Cyrus, king of the Persians, a large part of them—nearly fifty thousand people—returned to Jerusalem.

In the time of King Darius, the entire Jewish people returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, with Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, and Ezra the scribe. They built its walls and temple and dwelt in it. At that time their prophets Haggai and Zechariah greatly encouraged them to build the temple and the city.

The holy Church therefore recalls and celebrates this captivity of the Jewish people, which prefigured our pilgrimage, every year when it celebrates [Col. 1185C] Septuagesima. Just as that people, although unwillingly, was held in captivity and exile for seventy years, so we, the Christian people, voluntarily recalling our seventy-day pilgrimage and the distress of the present life, should strive with every eagerness to return to our homeland, which is the Jerusalem above, devoting ourselves to good works—namely vigils, fasts, and prayers.

Septuagesima begins on the day on which the Church customarily sings “They surrounded me,” and continues until the Sabbath of Easter week, when we sing “The Lord brought out.” For if all the days are counted, seventy are found there.

The number seventy recalls to our memory the whole period of the present age, during which we are strangers to the heavenly Jerusalem, because, as the Apostle says: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V, 6).

The prophet David understood this pilgrimage, having been anticipated by the Holy Spirit, and said in a psalm: “Do not be silent, for I am a sojourner with you,” and so forth (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). Again, in another psalm: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged,” and so forth (Ps. CXIX, 5).

The holy Church, also considering this pilgrimage, cries out on the first day of Septuagesima, surrounded by hardships and afflictions: “The groans surrounded me.” This voice clearly reveals the affliction and tribulation of the present age.

The prayer of that day also agrees with this affliction, in which [Col. 1186A] we say: “Hear mercifully, we beseech you, O Lord, the prayers of your people,” and so forth.

On that same day blessed Paul the Apostle also urges us toward the course of good works, saying: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX, 24). The Responsory sung on that day also corresponds well: “Helper.” So too does the Tract: “Out of the depths.”

For on these days, because of humility, we do not sing the angelic hymn, “Glory to God in the highest,” nor Alleluia, which is a song of joy and exultation. Instead of Alleluia we sing the humbler chant, namely the Tract, which is called *tractus* from *trahere*, “to draw,” because it is sung slowly and continuously; it signifies the groaning of holy Mother Church.

In the Gospel (Matt. XX), which is read on that day, the householder also invites us to work in the vineyard, so that by laboring faithfully we may deserve to receive the denarius of reward.

After the Gospel the Offertory is sung: “It is good to give thanks,” and the Communion antiphon: “Make your face shine.” When all these things are carefully examined, they breathe forth the great mysteries of the sacraments, indicate the groaning of the Church invoking God’s help amid tribulation, and instruct the hearer sufficiently in the teaching of spiritual understanding.

During these days also, as we have already said, we omit the angelic hymn and Alleluia, which is Hebrew. Instead of Alleluia, we use a humbler—that is, Latin—language, saying in psalms, hymns, and songs: “Praise to you, O Lord, King of eternal glory.”

For in the person of those who are held in captivity it is said in the psalm: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI, 4). Scripture says again: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccli. XV, 9).

Therefore, whoever during these days of Septuagesima, established most beneficially, rightly directs his course—that is, the state of this present life—so that, laying aside all foolish joy and vanity, he constantly devotes himself to fasts, vigils, prayers, almsgiving, and other good works, and continually remembers his pilgrimage, will celebrate holy Easter happily. He will also sing without end the song of joy, Alleluia, which is the praise of the Lord.

For *Pascha* is Greek [Note: [Col. 1185] “Pascha” in Greek. Incorrectly, unless this is a scribal error. See the Preliminary Notice.]; in Latin it is called *transitus*, “passage.” If we wish to celebrate holy Easter, let us pass over from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly things, and let us strive to migrate from transitory things to those that remain forever and eternally. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” and so forth (I Cor. V, 7).

The observance of Septuagesima ends on the Sabbath before the octave of Easter, when, as we have already said above, the holy Church customarily sings: “The Lord brought out.”

It fittingly corresponds to the Church’s mysteries that Septuagesima ends on the Sabbath. Because of our sins, we came into captivity and pilgrimage; but through the Lord’s grace and mercy we are brought back to rest, which is signified by the Sabbath. For *Sabbath* is interpreted as “rest.”

On that day two Alleluias are also sung, signifying the double joy of the saints. The Alleluia sung on the Sabbath, namely “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever,” signifies the joy which all who faithfully come to their end now receive in their souls, and in which all the saints who are in heavenly glory will rejoice forever.

The other two, which are sung on the following Sabbath, that is, at the end of Septuagesima, signify the double exultation of all the saints, when, as is read in the Apocalypse, after judgment has been completed, each of them will be given two robes: immortality and the blessedness of souls and bodies. Thus those who now rejoice only in the immortality of their individual souls will then enjoy the blessed immortality of both souls and bodies, together with the glory of everlasting blessedness.

May the good Lord, through his gratuitous mercy, deign to lead us to that glory of blessedness, to whom belong honor, praise, and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER X. [Note: [Col. 1187D] Many things again are found in Amalarius, book I, chapter 2.] ON SEXAGESIMA
Sexagesima begins on the Sunday following Septuagesima and ends on the Wednesday of Easter week. For during the preceding week, namely Septuagesima, the Church cries out that she is surrounded by sorrows and tribulations, and so constricted by afflictions and tribulations that she can scarcely breathe and no avenue of escape appears. Hence she says: “They surrounded me.” But in this period, that is, Sexagesima, she now invokes with something like renewed confidence and, as though imploring the clemency of almighty God, says: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” As though she were saying: Although you do not sleep, nor slumber—you who guard Israel—nevertheless, because you do not come quickly to our aid, you seem to sleep. “Why do you turn your face away?” Although our sins separate us from you, do not forget our condition, but look favorably upon the work of your creation: “Arise, and do not reject us forever, but see our tribulation.” “For our belly has clung to the earth,” that is, the inward sense of our heart has consented to the wickedness of this dust and frailty.

And again she cries out and, as though insistently seeking help, says: “Arise, O Lord; help us and redeem us”—that is, since we are not worthy to be redeemed, redeem us for the sake of your name, that is, freely and not according to our merit. The first prayer of that day says the same thing, in which it is said: “O Lord, who see that we place our confidence in none of our actions”—that is, that we have confidence in none of our good works—“but hope to be saved by your mercy alone.”

In the Epistle, the good athlete and teacher of the nations, Paul, is set before us, so that we may imitate his wisdom and courage. The Responsory is: “Let the nations know that the Lord is your name”—that is, let those who afflict and persecute us recognize that they are not true lords, nor does the name of lords belong to them, but to you alone, who created us and alone rule justly, “the Most High over all the earth.”

The Tract follows: “You have moved your land, O Lord, and troubled it.” By “you have moved the land,” he means that the conscience of sinners has been stirred to repentance. For the earth is moved when the sinner’s heart is roused to repentance and tears. After the earth has been moved, seed is introduced, because after the hearts of penitents have been stirred to tears, the seed of the word of God is received more eagerly, grows, and multiplies, producing more abundant fruit. Accordingly, the Gospel follows appropriately, in which much is told concerning the rocky and thorny soil, and concerning the good soil that produces fruit through perseverance.

In Septuagesima we were rebuked because we had stood idle, and we were invited to cultivate the vineyard. Now, in Sexagesima, the seed of the word of God is cast into our hearts as into good soil, so that it may grow and bear fruit, and so that through perseverance we may produce an abundant harvest.

The Offertory follows: “Make my steps firm.” The Church beseeches that her steps may be made firm, that is, that her journeys may be directed by the Lord along the paths of God’s ways, because human steps are directed by God, not by the human being himself. No one can be upright by himself unless aided by God, as the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing.” Therefore, what the Church understands that she cannot accomplish by herself, she asks the Lord with all her desires to fulfill.

She also says in the Communion: “I will go in to the altar of God.” Now the holy mother Church, trusting in the mercy of almighty God, presumes to say: “I will go in to the altar of God,” that is, “I will appear in his presence, and I will be glorified by his mercy.”

We have said that Sexagesima continues until the Wednesday of Easter week because sixty days are counted from the present day, on which we sing at the Introit, “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” up to the aforesaid day, on which we sing, “Come, you blessed of my Father.” This is not without a great mystery. For the number six is perfect and is completed by its parts. Its sixth part is one, its second part three, and its third part two. Thus one, two, and three make six. The number neither falls short nor exceeds. This is rarely found in any other number.

Ten times six, or six times ten, makes sixty. Therefore the sixtieth number, like the number six, signifies the perfection of good work. For there are six days in which one ought to work, and in six days we complete the whole course of our good activity. In six days God completed his works; and in the sixth age he deigned to visit the world in person and to redeem, by his own blood, the human being who had fallen from the delight of paradise and been deceived by the devil’s fraud.

Speaking of this number six and its perfection, blessed Augustine says in a certain passage:

> “The number six is not perfect because God completed all his works in it; rather, because the number six was perfect, God deigned to complete his works in it.”

[Note: [Col. 1188D] Saint Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IV, chapter 7, no. 14.]

Therefore it is necessary that during this Sexagesima we devote ourselves to good works and, with God’s help, strive to work out our salvation through vigils, fasts, prayers, and other good works. For those who pass through the course of the present life through six days of good activity, labor faithfully in righteous work, and persevere to the end in the good works they have begun, will receive the sixtieth fruit of their labor and the reward of eternal blessedness, hearing that desirable voice of his which is sung in the holy Church on that day: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). May almighty God grant that we hear this voice and receive that kingdom—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XI. ON QUINQUAGESIMA

[Note: [Col. 1189D] Compare Amalarius, cited work, chapter 3.]

Quinquagesima begins in the week following Sexagesima, when “Be to me a God of protection” is sung, and ends on the holy Sunday of Easter.

In Septuagesima we were surrounded by tribulations and distress; in Sexagesima we invoked the Lord and, as though he were sleeping, awakened him. In Quinquagesima, as though he were now nearer, we invoke him more boldly and readily, saying: “Be to me a God of protection.” In the first prayer of the Mass we say: “Hear our prayers mercifully, we beseech you, O Lord, and, having freed us from the bonds of sins, protect us from every adversity.”

These words already seem to possess great security, in which we say that we have been freed from all enemies and sins and ask to be defended by the Lord’s protection. In the Epistle, blessed Paul the Apostle also speaks, showing us the better spiritual gifts: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels,” and so forth, up to “a sounding cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1). At the end of this reading he shows by what defenses we ought to remain and be fortified in God’s protection, saying: “Now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13).

The Responsory follows: “You are the Lord who alone performs wonders.” It is as though he were saying: There is no other Lord besides you, O Lord. The images of the nations are not gods, but the works of human hands. You, however, truly are God, who save those who hope in you. “You have made your power known among the nations,” redeeming and freeing us from their hands. Again, in the verse, he says: “By your arm you have redeemed your people.”

The Tract also commands us to serve the Lord, who made us, and not the one to whom we live by sinning [Amalarius: “sold ourselves”].

In Septuagesima the soil of our heart was, as it were, plowed and cultivated by tribulations. In Sexagesima we received and sowed the seeds of the word of God. In Quinquagesima we gather the fruit of the seed and of good work. Hence the Gospel introduces a blind man, who signifies us: he seeks neither gold nor riches, but light, which he deserved to receive. We ought to seek that light more attentively, so that we may deserve to receive it as eternal and true.

The Offertory follows, having the same form—that is, remaining in thanksgiving—as it says: “Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes.”

The Communion recalls the ancient people who ate manna in the desert and were not deprived of their desire. It suggests by these words that if we remain in a good and holy desire, we will not be deprived of it, but will be granted eternal satisfaction, when what the Psalmist says elsewhere is fulfilled in us: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15).

Quinquagesima extends to the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. For from the day on which we sing, “Be to me a God of protection,” until the holy day of Easter, there are fifty days. This number pertains to the five bodily senses, namely hearing, sight, taste, smell, and touch. Just as the number six demonstrates the perfection of works, so the number five signifies all good works that are accomplished through the five bodily senses.

Five times ten makes fifty. Therefore, if someone fulfills the ten words of the Law through the five bodily senses—that is, through outward conduct—he will undoubtedly attain fellowship with the blessed resurrection celebrated at Easter.

There is another mystery in this number of fifty days. In the Old Testament the fiftieth year was called the Jubilee and the year of remission. In that year every possession returned to its rightful owner, and every owner, however he had been separated from it, returned freely to his own possession.

We, too, who in our first parent lost the inheritance of immortality that properly belonged to us, can, if we live well and justly during this time signified by the number fifty, return to our inheritance: that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem and the city of the saints, where there is true resurrection and blessed immortality, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whose resurrection our true resurrection and the remission of all sins are found.

## CHAPTER XII. ON QUADRAGESIMA

[Note: [Col. 1189D] Amalarius, chapter 4.]

Quadragesima begins on the Sunday following Quinquagesima and ends on the Wednesday [Amalarius: Thursday] before the Lord’s Pasch, when we sing: “In the name of the Lord every knee shall bow.”

In Quadragesima some part of our struggle has already been completed. The one whom we invoked as protector in Quinquagesima says in the Introit, as though offering consolation: “He called upon me,” and so forth. In the Epistle blessed Paul says: “At an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you.”

In the Responsory it is sung in the person of a righteous man or of the holy Church: “He has commanded his angels concerning you.” In the Tract the shield of divine protection is promised. In the Gospel the triumph of the Lord’s victory is set before us, namely, that by his example we may learn to fight against the devil and overcome him.

Concerning this number forty and the observance of the present time, we have nothing else to say except what blessed Gregory explains at the end of his exposition of the Gospel read on that day. He says:

[Note: [Col. 1190D] Saint Gregory, *Homily 16 on the Gospels*, nos. 5–6.]

> “But because the Gospel reading is appropriate to these days—for we have heard of the abstinence of our Redeemer for forty days—we begin the season of Forty Days. We must consider why this abstinence is observed according to the number forty days.
>
> “Moses fasted for forty days a second time in order to receive the Law. Elijah abstained for forty days in the desert. The very author of human beings, when he came to human beings, took no food whatsoever for forty days. Let us also, insofar as we can, strive during the annual season of Quadragesima to afflict our flesh through abstinence.
>
> “When, therefore, the number forty is observed in abstinence, what does this signify except that the power of the Decalogue is fulfilled through the four books of the holy Gospel? For ten multiplied by four rises to forty, because we fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue when we faithfully observe the four books of the holy Gospel.
>
> “From this another meaning can also be perceived. In this mortal body we exist from four elements, and through the pleasures of that same body we transgress the Lord’s commandments. The Lord’s commandments, however, were given through the Decalogue. Therefore, since through the desires of the flesh we have despised the commandments of the Decalogue, it is fitting that we afflict that same flesh four times ten.
>
> “There is, however, another interpretation that may be understood concerning this season of Quadragesima. From the present day until the joys of the Paschal solemnity there are six weeks, whose days number forty-two. When the six Sundays are subtracted from the abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. Since the year is reckoned as three hundred and sixty [five] days, and we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give, as it were, the tithes of our year to God, so that we who have lived for ourselves throughout the year we received may mortify ourselves through abstinence in the tithes belonging to our Creator.
>
> “But, dearly beloved brothers, just as you are commanded in the Law to offer tithes of your goods, so strive to offer tithes of your days to God. Let each person, according to the strength available to him, mortify his flesh, afflict its desires, kill shameful lusts, and, in Paul’s words, become a living sacrifice. A sacrifice is both offered and alive when a person does not depart from this life, yet kills himself with respect to carnal desires.
>
> “The joyful flesh drew us into guilt; when afflicted, let it lead us back to forgiveness. For the author of our death transgressed the commandment of life through the fruit of the forbidden tree. Therefore, since we fell from the joys of paradise through food, let us rise again to them, insofar as we can, through abstinence.
>
> “But let no one believe that this abstinence alone can suffice, since the Lord says through the prophet: ‘Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen?’ (Isa. 58:6). He adds: ‘Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh’ (ibid., v. 7).
>
> “The Lord therefore approves that fast which raises the hands of almsgiving to his eyes, which is practiced with love of neighbor, and which is prepared by compassion. Therefore give to another what you take away from yourself; and from what afflicts your flesh, let the flesh of your needy neighbor be restored.
>
> “For this reason the Lord says through the prophet: ‘When you fasted and mourned, did you truly fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?’ (Zech. 7:5–6). The one who receives bodily nourishment, which is a common gift of the Creator, without sharing it with the needy, eats and drinks for himself.
