And a person fasts for himself if he does not give to the poor what he temporarily takes away from himself, but keeps it to offer afterward to his belly.
>
> “Hence Joel says: ‘Sanctify a fast’ (Joel 1:14). To sanctify a fast is to show, together with other good works, a bodily abstinence worthy of God.
>
> “Let anger cease; let quarrels be put to sleep. For the flesh is worn down to no purpose if the spirit is not restrained from its evil pleasures, since the Lord says through the prophet: ‘Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and disputes, and you strike wickedly with your fist, and you demand all your debts’ (Isa. 58:3–4).
>
> “The person who demands back from his debtor what he gave does not do anything unjust; but it is fitting that whoever mortifies himself in penitence should forbid himself even what is justly his. Thus, thus, what we have done unjustly is forgiven by God when we penitents and afflicted persons, for love of him, relinquish even what is justly ours.”

## CHAPTER XIII. THE ORDER FOR IMPOSING PENITENCE ON WEDNESDAY, WHICH IS THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

First of all, the priest must admonish all Christians, on the basis of the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, to hasten to true confession and true penitence on the beginning of the fast—that is, today.

Concerning this Jerome says:

> “Would that sinners turn to penitence as quickly as the Lord is prepared even to change a sentence already determined. For God does not require a length of time, but measures the fullness of sincere devotion.”

Gregory says:

> “A person who waits for old age in order to undertake penitence is far removed from faith. For one must fear that, while hoping for mercy, he may fall under judgment.”

Again:

> “If someone corrected you for an external sin, then confess your inward sins, which he does not know.”

Finally, they must be admonished to return to reconciliation on the Lord’s Supper, as will be said below. But if someone is prevented by a journey, by some other occupation, or is perhaps so dull that the priest cannot persuade him of this, the priest should impose upon him both Lenten and annual penance and reconcile him immediately.

Priests, however, must strive with the greatest care to understand and teach the eight capital vices, together with their consequences and the testimonies of Scripture by which people are to be restrained and advanced toward better things, as they are set out here at the beginning. These eight vices are, first, pride, vainglory, envy, anger, avarice, sadness, gluttony of the belly, and lust.

### On pride

From pride, which is the head of all vices, the seven capital vices listed above arise. *Superbia*—“pride”—is said as though it meant “overstepping the mind,” concerning what is not. Hence a proud person is like someone walking outside the road. Scripture says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15).

It is therefore called the beginning of every sin because it preceded sin in the devil. It is not merely itself a sin; no sin could have been, can be, or will be committed without it. Moreover, desire and pride are so much one evil that desire cannot be found without pride. The first human being would not have eaten from the forbidden tree unless he had desired it; nor would he have been abandoned by the Lord unless he had first abandoned the Lord.

Augustine says concerning pride:

> “We must avoid pride, which knows how to deceive angels and destroy human beings.”

Jerome says:

> “The proud man will not be honored, nor will he accomplish his will.”

Ambrose says:

> “Pride made demons from angels, but humility makes human beings like the holy angels.”

### On vainglory

From vainglory—that is, vanity, which in Greek is called *κενοδοξία* (*kenodoxia*)—arise disobedience, hypocrisy, contentions, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations.

Vanity is an inflated desire for honors, sweet to the wretched and bitter to the perfected. The puffed-up serve it, and the exalted lie beneath it. The ardor of human praise inflames them so greatly that they undertake and willingly perform laborious works which the people may admire and through which their reputation may spread, without considering the burden involved.

Thus they fast, abstain, keep vigils, attend church, or sing psalms—although they do not perform any of these things without effort, they do them even with pleasure—so that they may be seen by human beings, whom they desire to please, rather than by God. Hence Truth says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

### On envy

From envy, or the envious person—so called from envying another’s happiness—arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in one’s neighbor’s adversity, and distress at his prosperity.

Concerning this the Apostle threatens, saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer; and whoever envies is in darkness and walks in darkness” (1 John 3:15; 2:11).

Nothing can be more unhappy than the envious person, who is tormented by another’s good. Envy bites the senses, burns the breast, and afflicts the mind. Whoever envies is like the devil, who through envy expelled the human being from paradise.

### On prolonged anger

From prolonged anger, which is called from indignation, and from which *iracundia*—irascibility—is also derived, because a person is driven into fury when his blood is inflamed, arise quarrels, swelling of the mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

Scripture says concerning it: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. 7:10). Elsewhere: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). In the Psalm concerning daily anger: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). The Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26), and elsewhere: “That anger is evil which disturbs the mind so that it loses sound judgment.”

### On sadness

From sadness, which arises from anger, arise malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness regarding the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things.

It should be understood that there is a distinction between *tristitia* and *moestitia*: *moestitia* belongs to the heart, whereas *tristitia* belongs to the face. For we call the mind mournful (*moestus*) or sluggish; a person is recognized as sad (*tristis*) by the face—his countenance cast down, his appearance pale, his eyes troubled, and his face disturbed.

The Apostle says of this sadness: “The sadness that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, but the sadness of the world produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Elsewhere: “Do not give sadness to your soul.” Isidore says:

> “Do you wish never to be sad? Live well. A secret conscience bears sadness gently.”

### On avarice

Avarice—which in Greek is called *philargyria*, that is, “love of money,” derived from greed, whence *avarus*, “avaricious,” as though “greedy for gold,” since the avaricious person is never satisfied with riches—produces betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and the hardening of the heart against mercy.

The Apostle says concerning it: “Neither the avaricious nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Solomon says: “The avaricious will not be satisfied with money” (Eccl. 5:9). The same writer says: “There is nothing more wicked than the avaricious person, and nothing more unjust than loving money” (Ecclus. 10:9). Again: “When a human being dies, he will inherit serpents and beasts and worms” (ibid., v. 13).

This vice is overcome by generosity toward the poor, visiting the sick, clothing the naked, returning what has been unjustly taken, and by weeping and tears with contrition of heart, as the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21).

### On gluttony of the belly

From gluttony of the belly, which in Greek is called *gastrimargia*, that is, dreadful greed and gluttony—so called from the throat—arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, foolish speech, excessive speech, and dullness of understanding; it is a spiritual vice.

It is written concerning this: “Whoever restrains his belly diminishes vices, but abundance of food nourishes evil desires. Many foods nourish the belly of fornication.” The Apostle says: “Not in reveling and drunkenness” (Rom. 13:13).

Because the first human being fell through the vice of gluttony, it is necessary that we rise again through abstinence. Joyful flesh drew us into sin; when afflicted, let it lead us back to forgiveness.

### On lust

From lust, which takes its name from luxury and is bodily uncleanness—hence *luxuriosus*, “lustful,” as though meaning “loosed” and “corrupting”—arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, instability, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, the influence of the present age, and dread or despair of future things.

It is a bodily vice. The Apostle says concerning it: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18). Again: “The Lord will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4).

Jerome says:

> “Woe to the one whose lust ends only when life ends.”

Through pride and fornication the devil rules over the whole human race. Fornication is greater than all sins; it is better to die than to fornicate; lust plunges a person into hell.

It should be understood that fornicators, lustful persons, Sodomites, adulterers, incestuous persons, defilers, rapists, effeminate persons, male-bedfellows, unclean persons, polluters, and immodest persons are all generally called lustful.

Fornication is therefore called love released from legitimate marriage and the unrestrained license to pursue and satisfy lust. Concerning it Scripture says: “Whoever fornicates sins against his own body”; and it is a greater crime because he takes away the members of Christ and makes them members of the devil (1 Cor. 6:18).

Lustful persons are those who do what they please; for they are desirous of pleasure. Sodomites are interpreted as “those who exclude themselves.” Adulterers are so called because they violate or pollute another’s marriage bed.

Incest is called as though it meant “unchaste,” because of unlawful intercourse: that is, whenever anyone presumes to fornicate with his own parent, sister, widow, stepmother, daughter, relative, or a woman consecrated to the Lord.

Defilers are called those who corrupt virgins. Rapists are named from *rapere*, “to seize,” because they enjoy violation through seizure.

The distinction between violation, adultery, and incest is as follows: violation concerns a virgin, adultery a married woman, and incest relatives.

“Effeminate” persons are those who are womanish, or who have no beards, or who tolerate another’s fornication. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Neither the effeminate nor male-bedfellows shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). They are companions of fornicators, unclean, polluted, defiled, associates of the lustful, polluters, deformed, and stained—or those who soil themselves with their own hands.

The immodest are said to be named from *podex*, “buttocks,” for we call stench and foulness *putor*; or an immodest person is one who brings shame upon himself through disgraceful conduct.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] “The immodest are named from *podex*.” Entirely inept.]

### Other vices

There are also other vices which, although they arise from the preceding ones, are classified elsewhere, such as sacrilege, which Augustine counts among the seven vices.

Sacrilege is the theft of sacred things, which afterward become objects of idol worship. Hence a sacrilegious person is so called because he selects and steals sacred things contrary to the laws; or a sacrilegious person is one who violates sacred places. The plunderers of churches do this.

Thieves are called from *furvus*, “dark,” because they approach at night. The distinction between a thief and a robber is this: whoever secretly removes another’s property is a thief; whoever steals and kills is a robber, called *latro* from *latere*, “to hide.”

Perjurers are those who swear wrongly, that is, badly. False-speakers are those who say something other than the truth.

A drunk person is one who drinks for a time; a drunkard is one who does so continually. Scripture says concerning him: “The drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

An *acedia*-stricken person is one who suffers anxiety or weariness of heart from *acedia*. Such a person is also called unstable or wandering; some count this among the eight vices.

There is this distinction between *patricide* and *parricide*: a patricide is one who kills a parent; a parricide, one who kills an equal or companion. A fratricide is one who kills a brother.

“Homicide” is composed from *homo*, “human being,” and *caedes*, “slaughter,” whence also “homicide.”

A foolish speaker is one who tells shameful or laughable stories. Hence foolish speech contains nothing wise in itself.

Buffoonery and jesting, which arise from some kind of cleverness, provoke laughter in those who hear them, although such people ought rather to mourn.

Shamefulness occurs when our senses are inflamed toward lust and the titillation of the flesh. The soul is set on fire and nothing restrains it through fear of God.

An idolater is one who serves idols. In the prophet we often find idolatry called fornication. Whoever loves money more than God worships the image of money and venerates the idols engraved upon it.

A whisperer is named from the sound of speech—that is, one who willingly listens to useless things. Hence Scripture says: “Do not be a whisperer” (Ecclus. 5:16).

Sorcerers and poisoners are those who prepare poison for the purpose of causing death and skillfully devise many evils.

Slanderers, long-tongued persons, or quarrelsome persons; lot-casters; and diviners or fanatical prognosticators are those who, under the name of a false religion, claim to practice divination and knowledge through certain practices—which they call “the lots of the saints.”

Soothsayers or haruspices properly are those who utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols.

Augurs are those who pay attention to omens, the flight, and the cries of birds. For auspices come voluntarily.

A fool is one who does not understand what he says or what others say; hence he is called senseless. Concerning him the Gospel says: “Whoever says, ‘You fool’” (Matt. 5:22). For this is a form of insult.

“Racha” means empty and vacuous, or without a brain. It is a form of contempt or anger. Hence the Gospel says: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Racha’” (Matt. 5:22). This is a provincial proverb.

Behold, the vices through which the human race is daily attacked by the devil have been briefly set forth.

For the rest, let the priests of Christ know that whenever Christians approach penitence, they must first fast with them for their errors, so that what the Lord said to the scribes of the Jews may not be said to them: “Woe to you lawyers, because you load people with burdens difficult to bear, while you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers” (Luke 11:46).

No one can lift up a person lying beneath a burden unless he bends down and extends his hand to him. Nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he shares in their stench. In the same way, a priest or bishop cannot heal wounds without attentive care and prayer.

Whenever you give counsel to a sinner, give him penitence at once as well: tell him how long he must fast and how he must redeem his sins, lest you forget how long he ought to abstain. For you will need to ask him about his sins again, because he may be ashamed to confess them a second time.

Not every cleric, nor any layperson, should presume to use or read this writing, except those who need to do so—namely, bishops or presbyters, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted. No one else should presume to exercise these judgments.

But if necessity arises and no presbyter is present, a deacon may receive the penitent and give him holy Communion.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] “A deacon.” See Martène, book I, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 6, article 6, no. 7.]

[Note: [Col. 1196D] Ibid., article 3.]

Finally, a priest instructed or moved by this authority, when receiving a penitent, should lay aside his staff if the penitent is a layperson. Whoever he may be—layperson, cleric, or monk—should humbly bow before the priest.

Then the priest says this prayer:

> “Lord almighty God, be gracious to me, a sinner, so that I may be able worthily to give you thanks,”

and the rest.

Next, the priest should command him to sit opposite and converse with him concerning the vices mentioned above and divine exhortations, lest, through shame, laziness, or forgetfulness, something rotten remain in his heart by which the devil may again lead him back to the vomit of sin.

The priest should also consider sex, age, condition, status, and person, and according to his judgment distinguish each case: requiring some to abstain from food, others to give alms, some to bend their knees more frequently, or to stand in the form of a cross, or to do something else of this kind that contributes to the salvation of the soul.

The same discernment must not be applied equally to everyone: it must distinguish among the rich and the poor, the free and the slave, the infant and the child, the young man and the adolescent, the aged, the dull and the foolish, the learned and the ignorant, the layperson and the cleric, the monk and the bishop, the presbyter and the deacon, the subdeacon and the lector; among those in orders, those married and unmarried, a virgin and a woman, a canoness and a nun, the weak and the infirm, the healthy and the sick.

He must also distinguish the character of people’s sins: between the continent and the incontinent; whether the sin was committed voluntarily, by accident, or in secret; with what kind of contrition it should be corrected; and necessity and free choice. He should distinguish places and times.

The priest should also take care that everyone be saved and that no one lose heart, because “the powerful will suffer powerful torments.” Jesus, son of Sirach, likewise says: “In judging, be merciful, like a father to orphans and like a husband to their mother” (Ecclus. 4:10). James says: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13). But mercy triumphs over judgment, so that he may attain the same end as Saint Benedict.

Those who perform true penitence should practice it in fasting and weeping, in almsgiving and prayers, and should not do again what they have perpetrated. If they do repeat it, they should nevertheless not persevere in it, because the Lord said:

> “You conceived evil; I forgave you. You spoke evil; I forgave you. You did evil; I forgave you. I do not forgive perseverance in evil.”

Therefore, he will not forgive those who persevere in evil. Judge righteous judgment according to the canons, so that others may have fear.

Nor should this be omitted: because of these sins we are afflicted with temporal scourges. Hence arise wars, raids by pagans, captivities, pestilences, famines, illnesses, deaths of human beings and animals, diseases, hardships, droughts, floods, storms of rain, harmful thunder and lightning, the severity of cold, the violence of heat, unjust kings, powerful men or very wicked judges, harmful beasts, and things of this kind. For the correction of these things also, laws are promulgated, just judgments are decreed, punishments, chains, tortures, scourges, exiles, amputations of limbs, losses of property, and deaths of various kinds are prescribed; and these evils cannot be removed from the world. Ecclesiastical discipline likewise comes into operation: correction, excommunication, exclusion from the church, penitential laws, and anathematization. Judges are appointed, officials apply themselves, and avengers are sent, so that these things may be corrected; yet they cannot be removed from the Church.

While these sins remain, alas, woe, how confidently we proceed toward the outer darkness—as though bedrooms were being built for us there, pleasures prepared, servants procured, treasures amassed, and ornaments multiplied—although Scripture says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Eccles. IX, 10). Against all these things war must be undertaken and fought fiercely, lest we be led into damnable sins.

After all these matters have been examined and the penitent strengthened, the priest asks him, saying: “Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?” Let the penitent answer: “I believe.”

“Do you believe that these three persons whom I have just named—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are one God?” Let him answer: “I believe.”

“Do you believe that in this very flesh in which you now exist you must rise again and receive either good or evil, according to what you have done?”

“I believe.”

“Do you wish to forgive all those who have sinned against you, so that God also may forgive your sins, since he himself says: ‘If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins’ (Matt. VI, 15)?”

If he wishes to forgive, receive his confession and prescribe penance for him; if he does not wish to do so, do not receive his confession. If he wishes to forgive all those who have sinned against him, let him confess all the sins that he can remember. The priest must nevertheless take care concerning the vices mentioned above, so that, for the sake of exhortation, he may bring them back to his memory and nothing remain hidden through the opposition of the devil.

When this has been done, let him kneel with his knees fixed on the ground and, leaning upon them, stand with his hands extended in supplication. Looking toward the priest with a gentle and tearful countenance, let him say these words:

“Indeed, many other sins, innumerable in number, are mine, which I cannot remember, in deeds, words, and thoughts. For all of them my wretched mind is pierced with remorse and is sometimes tormented by severe repentance. Therefore, I humbly beseech you for your counsel—or rather, your judgment—you who have been appointed mediator and intermediary between God and sinful humanity; and I humbly ask that you stand as intercessor for me concerning these same sins.”

When he has said this, let him prostrate his whole body upon the ground and produce groans, sighs, or tears from the depths of his heart, as God grants. The priest should allow him to lie prostrate for a little while, according to the extent to which he sees him pierced by divine inspiration. Then the priest should order him to rise. When he has stood upon his feet, let him await the priest’s judgment with trembling and humility. The priest should prescribe for him abstinence or a discipline, carefully weighing the quality of the person, the nature of the offense, the intention of the mind, and the health or weakness of the body.

After receiving the priest’s sentence, let him again prostrate himself at the priest’s feet, asking that prayer be made for him, so that divine visitation may suggest to him the strength to observe steadfastly what has been imposed upon him. Let him obey the priest’s judgment with such reverence as though he had received from the very mouth of divine majesty the remedies appropriate to his salvation.

Therefore one ought to approach penance with complete confidence and believe without hesitation, in faith, that sins can be abolished through penance—even if one repents at the final breath of life and one’s sins are disclosed through public lamentation—because God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that the sinner, saved by God’s mercy, may live. For we do not deny that mortal crimes may be absolved through private satisfaction. Daily and lesser sins, however, without which human life is not lived, are cleansed by the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.”

For almsgiving itself is to forgive a penitent person his offense. Hence the Lord says: “Give alms, and everything will be clean for you” (Luke XI, 41). The canons do not establish the duration of the time to be spent in penance for each individual crime with sufficient precision, but leave it rather to the judgment of the bishop, because with God the measure of time is not as valuable as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food as the mortification of vices.

This too must be understood: when male or female servants come to penance, do not compel them to fast as much as the wealthy, because they are not their own masters. Therefore impose upon them half the penance.

After this the priest should say these prayers over him:

“Hear, O Lord, our prayers, and spare the sins of those who confess to you.”

Another: “May your mercy, we beseech you, O Lord, go before this servant of yours.”

Another: “Be present, O Lord, at our supplications, and let it not be absent from this servant of yours.”

Another: “O Lord our God, whom our offense does not overcome.”

Another: “Be present, we beseech you, O Lord, to this servant of yours.”

Another: “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, to this servant of yours.”

Another: “I beseech the clemency of your majesty, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 1199D] This agrees with the *Liber Pontificalis* of Egbert of York, in Martène, cited work, chapter 7, p. 41.], “and the rest.”

After these have been said, let the priest order the penitent to rise from the ground. He himself should also rise from his seat. If the place and time are suitable, they should enter the church and, each leaning upon his knees or elbows, sing the psalms:

“O Lord, not in your anger,” II.  
“Bless the Lord, O my soul,” I.  
“Have mercy on me, O God.”  
“O God, in your name.”  
“Why do you boast?”  
Then: “Kyrie eleison.”  
“Our Father.”  
“Save your servant.”  
“Let your face shine.”  
“Send, O Lord.”  
Prayer: “O God, whose indulgence no one fails to need.”  
Mass.  
Antiphon: “Concerning necessities.”  
Prayer: “O God, who justify the ungodly.”  
Epistle: “Wash yourselves; be clean.”  
Gradual: “Save your servant.”  
Gospel: “Two men.”  
Offertory: “Have mercy on me, O Lord.”  
Prayer over the offerings: “By the power of this mystery, O Lord.”  
Communion: “God, be gracious.”  
At the conclusion: “Purify us, O Lord.”

On the same day a collect is held at Saint Anastasia.

Antiphon: “Hear us, O Lord, for your mercy is gracious.”  
Psalm: “Save me, O God.”

Meanwhile ashes are to be placed upon their heads, as the antiphon testifies.

Prayer: “Grant us, O Lord.”

Antiphon for the procession: “Beside the vestibule.”  
Also: “Let us be transformed.”  
Another: “Spare, O Lord.”

When these things have been completed, the litany follows. Then there is a station at Saint Sabina.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Amalarius, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 9. See Martène, *De antiqua Ecclesiae disciplina*, chapter 19, no. 27, p. 187.]

## Saturday before Palm Sunday

In the Sacramentary it is so entitled: “Saturday is vacant. The Lord Pope gives alms.”

One must consider how alms should especially be distributed on that day. Here it should be noted that what we celebrate concerning the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven, we perform in commemoration of those events that took place in their own time, as in the saying: “Whenever you do this,” and so forth. We have a preceding example of the almsgiving of the present Saturday, which we should imitate and recall to mind. For why should alms be given more specially by the apostolic authority on this day, when they ought to be given at all times?

The evangelist John says: “Six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany, to the house of Simon the leper, and there he raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb; and they made him a supper there. Mary therefore took a pound of ointment and anointed the Lord’s feet” (John XII). When Judas the traitor expressed indignation at this, Jesus answered in praise of the woman: “She has performed a good work upon me. For wherever this has been preached,” and so forth (Matt. XXVI, 10–13).

Whoever lives well anoints the Lord’s feet with ointment. That ointment was righteousness, and therefore it was a pound. Whoever gives his surplus to the poor wipes the Lord’s feet with his hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, and the world was filled with the woman’s good reputation.

Therefore, in memory of that most devoted woman, the apostolic man today does for Christ’s members what she did for the Head. For this reason there is no public station, though there is no cessation from the celebration of Mass, because he is occupied with this work.

Since no proper office is available for this weekday, it is repeated from the same weekdays, namely, from Wednesday:

Antiphon: “My deliverer.”

Reading from the prophet Zechariah: “Thus says the Lord: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your King will come to you, righteous and savior; he is poor and rides upon a donkey, upon a colt, the foal of a donkey,” and so forth.

Gospel according to Luke: “When Jesus had drawn near and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives.”

## CHAPTER XIV. PALM SUNDAY

Yesterday the Lord reclined at Bethany in the house of Simon—that is, six days before the Passion. Today, which is the fifth day before Passover, he went out from Bethany and sent two disciples into Jerusalem, saying to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and you will find a donkey and a colt; untie them and bring them to me.” They untied them and brought them to Jesus, placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them.

When the crowd that had come for the festival heard that Jesus was going to Jerusalem, they took palm branches, came out to meet him, and cried: “Hosanna; blessed is he who comes,” and so forth (Matt. XXI, 21 ff.).

It should be known that this day is distinguished by various names: Palm Sunday, or Sunday of flowers, or of branches; Hosanna; the Requested Passover, or the Passover of the Competentes; and the Sunday of those who wash their heads.

It is called Palm Sunday because on it the Lord, heading toward Jerusalem, was met by a very large crowd, which cried out on every side, “Hosanna,” a word interpreted as “save,” or “save us.” It is a Hebrew expression, which among them is called *Hosanna*.

The palm branches signify the victory by which the Lord was to overcome death by dying and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, through the trophy of the cross. The branches of the trees signify the sayings and examples of the Fathers. The great crowd signifies the innumerable army of martyrs who handed over their bodies for the Lord. The garments of the Apostles are works of righteousness. Hence in the psalm: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9).

The donkey upon which he sat indicated the simple hearts of the Gentiles, whom, by presiding over and governing them, he led to the vision of eternal peace.

It is called the Requested Passover, or the Passover of the Competentes, because today the Creed was handed over to the *competentes*, on account of the nearness of the solemnity of the Lord’s Passover, so that those who were already hastening to receive God’s grace might know the faith which they professed. They are called *competentes*, as if “those requesting together,” that is, those requesting Christ’s grace.

The common people call this day the Sunday of those who wash their heads because it is then customary to wash the heads of infants who are to be anointed on Holy Saturday, lest they should approach the anointing soiled by their observance of Lent.

How reverently this custom is cultivated by the most devout men may appropriately be inserted here for a little while. Today a certain very honorable portable shrine is prepared, into which the holy Gospel is placed, signifying Christ, and it is set up in the church before the altar from which the clergy are to proceed.

Then palms, flowers, and various kinds of foliage or olive branches are gathered together, over which the priest says this prayer:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who, before allowing your Son, our Lord, to suffer death for us …”

The blessing of the palms or branches follows:

“Almighty God, Christ …”

When these things have been completed, the palms are distributed by the custodians. As the people receive branches of trees, olives, or flowers, the antiphon is begun:

“Children of the Hebrews.”

Then the deacons take up the portable shrine mentioned above with the Gospel, carrying with great rejoicing the yoke of Christ, which is easy, and his burden, which is light. Holy water precedes them, together with candelabra, thuribles, and other ornaments. In addition, a laymen’s schola goes far ahead with banners and standards.

When the clergy and people leave the church, the antiphon is begun:

“When the Lord drew near.”

When it is finished, the schola begins the antiphon:

“They all began.”

Also: “When they had heard.”  
Also: “As he drew near.”

When they have entered the city or monastery, the responsory is said:

“As the Lord entered.”

Also: “The chief priests gathered together.”  
“One, however.”

When these things have been completed, the schola with the bearers and the remaining ornamentation stops at a suitable place before the church atrium. The clergy or people wait in the atrium, beginning the antiphon:

“They came out to meet him.”

The schola responds: “With angels and children.” When this is finished, two cantors begin certain verses:

“Israel, you are king.”

The choir responds, looking toward or bowing to the holy Gospel mentioned above:

“Glory, praise, and honor be to you” [Note: [Col. 1201D] This hymn is found among the works of Theodulf of Orléans, vol. II of Sirmond, p. 775. See also Martène, cited work, chapter 20, no. 13, p. 195, and Hugh Menard in the notes to the *Sacramentary of St. Gregory the Great*, note 234.].

Other verses follow in the same order. When they have been completed, the schola with the bearers begins the antiphon:

“Children of the Hebrews.”

Then all the people strew branches or flowers on both sides, singing the antiphon:

“Hosanna to the Son of David,”

and continue as far as the altar. Thus they enter for Mass. The ministers hold the palms in their hands until the completion of Mass.

Some omit the greeting during the Passion, namely, “The Lord be with you.” This is not read in the orders, but only on Good Friday, where the priestly office is omitted.

This week is called “great” either because the greatest moderation must be practiced in it, or because the greater office is commemorated in it.

## CHAPTER XV. WEDNESDAY OF HOLY WEEK

On Wednesday of Holy Week, at the third hour, the pope proceeds with all the clergy or people to the church and says the solemn prayers [Note: [Col. 1202D] “The solemn prayers.” See the cited *Sacramentary* for the same weekday, vol. III of the works of St. Gregory the Great, and the notes of Hugh Menard.], as on Good Friday.

When these have been completed and the altar has been kissed, he goes out. The priests of the churches, both urban and suburban, return to their own titular churches so that they may complete the same order on Friday. They should know this: what the bishop omits for himself, they commemorate there.

Afterward, at the eighth hour, they enter for Mass in the usual manner.

These prayers are celebrated today because on this Wednesday the Jews took counsel to kill the Lord. Therefore we ought to recall to mind the Jews’ cruel plan and Christ’s gentleness, so that against every injury we may arm ourselves with the weapons of prayer and patience, as he himself did, saying: “Father, forgive them” (Luke XXIII, 34).

A clear explanation follows of why the first responsory has one verse and the second five [Note: [Col. 1202D] Amalarius, cited work, chapter 11.].

The first man, Adam, suffered two deaths. In the first reading and first responsory, the death of the soul is signified; in the second reading and second responsory, the death of the body. For the Savior’s flesh was [given] for the salvation of the body, while his blood was poured out for our soul. Since every human being has one soul, the first responsory is therefore followed by one verse.

The second responsory, having five verses, signifies the five bodily senses that died in Adam, which Christ, by dying and rising again, restored to life and returned to their original condition.

The Passion that is read shows that the Jews’ plan prevailed for a time, and that Christ persevered in gentleness. The fact that it is pronounced without the greeting, and that the Sunday office is not performed on this day, signifies that the Jews’ wicked assembly conspired against Christ and that the disciples were silent because of the grief of his Passion, which continued until Friday. On that day the first man was created and redeemed.

During the three successive days that follow—Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—we celebrate the Lord’s three-day burial. Therefore, so that we may conform ourselves to the humility of his burial, we omit our exalted elements, namely, the *Gloria Patri* and the bells, that is, the signals.

## CHAPTERS XVI AND XVII. MAUNDY THURSDAY

[Col. 1203A]

On this sacred feast various events took place and continue to take place. One must rise for the vigils at the eighth hour of the night, and then the church is adorned with every light.

From this night until Holy Saturday, “O God, come to my assistance” is not said in the usual manner, nor is the *Gloria Patri* said in the psalms or responsories, or anywhere else. The cantor immediately begins the antiphon, as it is contained in the Antiphoner.

The lector should not ask for a blessing, nor should the reading be completed by the priest. Rather, he is ordered to bring it to an end from the words of the reading, or certainly to its termination.

The first readings are from the Lamentations of Jeremiah; the second, from the exposition of the psalm “Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead”; the third, from the Apostle: “When you come together as a community” [Col. 1203B]. On Good Friday and Holy Saturday, the readings are from the Lamentations mentioned above and Augustine’s exposition of the same psalm, and finally from Paul’s epistle: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest” [Note: [Col. 1203D] See Amalarius, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12, and Book IV, chapters 21 and 22.].

Through these nine readings—or psalms and responsories—which are recalled during these three nights, it is signified that the Lord, descending into hell, seized and carried from there three classes of human beings into the heavens, namely, to the fellowship of the nine orders of angels, as in the saying: “Two will be in one bed, two women will be grinding together, two will be in the field” (Luke XVII, 34).

Twenty-four lights are kindled on this night and extinguished one by one with each reading and responsory. These produce seventy-two illuminations and extinguishings, for the Lord lay in the tomb for that many hours. Light and song signify joy and gladness; the extinguishing of the lights signifies the falling away of the seventy-two disciples, or the sorrow of the Apostles, which they endured for seventy-two hours consecrated to Christ’s burial.

The lights are extinguished in this order during each night. At the beginning of the first psalm, a custodian stands ready with a reed on the right-hand side of the church. As soon as he hears the first antiphon, he extinguishes the first lamp. At the end of the following psalm, another is extinguished on the left side, and a third in the middle. The same order is followed for the others.

When all these have been extinguished, they are likewise extinguished during Matins, one with each antiphon. After the verse before the Gospel has been said, the central light is removed and kept until Holy Saturday.

When these things are finished, they go through the oratories, singing psalms with the antiphon. The *Gloria Patri* is also omitted, and so forth, because it recalls the glory of the Holy Trinity. Since the Son of God and the Son of Man, who came to suffer, are one person, Holy Church conforms herself to her Head and remains silent concerning his glorification until he is exalted through the triumph of victory.

Because the order of preachers was silent during the time of the Passion, the sound of signals and bells is omitted. Instead, a quieter sound of wood is used to assemble the people.

The kiss of peace is withheld without the greeting—not because it is evil when offered out of charity, but to avoid a deadly greeting such as the traitor Judas practiced, so that it may be shown what injury Christ suffered from his disciple and that we may likewise avoid doing injury to our brothers. The Lord was handed over by a deceitful sign.

The invitatory is not sung, so that we may know to avoid the wicked assembly such as that which took place among the Jews concerning Christ’s death.

The priestly office is not performed for God on these days, because the shepherd, who is Christ, was struck and the rams of the flock were scattered.

On this day the penitents return to the remission of sins, according to the decrees of Pope Innocent, who says: “Concerning penitents who, whether because of graver offenses or lighter ones, are doing penance, the custom of the Roman Church shows that, unless illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter.”

After this, the penitent leaves in the morning the place where he has performed penance and is presented in the bosom of the Church, with his whole body prostrate upon the ground. Then these psalms are sung:

“Have mercy on me, O God,” with the antiphon “A clean heart”; then “Kyrie eleison,” “Our Father,” the capitulum, and the prayers:

“Save your servant, O Lord.”  
“Turn again, O Lord.”  
“May the Lord send to you.”  
“Let your face shine.”  
“O Lord, behold my humiliation.”  
“Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is gracious.”

Prayer: “Be present, O Lord, at our supplications, and to me, who am the first also to need your mercy,” and the rest.

Another prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, to this servant of yours a worthy fruit of penance.”

Another: “O God, most kind creator of the human race and most merciful restorer.”

Another: “O God, beneath whose gaze every heart trembles and all consciences shudder,” and the rest.

After this the priest should admonish him not to repeat through renewed practice what he has washed away through repentance.

Mass, as above.

Antiphon: “But I have hoped in the Lord.”

“Almighty and everlasting God, to this servant who confesses …”

Epistle: “Seek the Lord while he may be found.”  
Gradual: “Concerning necessities.”  
Gospel: “Jesus lifted his eyes to heaven.”  
Offertory: “The Lord has become a firmament.”  
Secret: “God of the heavenly powers, from whose grace’s dew descends.”  
Collect: “Let your face shine.”  
Prayer at the conclusion: “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that the mystery of the new sacrament which we have received …”

On the same day the altars of the church, its walls, and its floors are washed, and the vessels consecrated to the Lord are purified [Note: [Col. 1204D] Amalarius, in the same place.].

Although their washing may be appropriate to ornamentation, nevertheless there is also a mystical meaning. The walls are called by the name “house of the church” because they contain the church, though they themselves are not the church. Since “church” means an assembly, human beings are the church, not the walls of the house.

Nevertheless, the walls are sanctified by the bishop for this reason: so that the coming of angels may be invited into them, and people entering there may know that they must restrain themselves from every filthy word, coarseness, and even frivolous thought, in order to hear what Moses heard when he wished to see the burning bush: “Remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5).

The sandals made from dead animals signify the sins of the old man. As we enter holy places where the Lord and his angels are, let us remove these sandals from ourselves and think upon the things that belong to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1205D] Amalarius, in the same place.]

The floor of the church signifies the hearers of teachers. The washing of the house, which is called “church” by designation, is a sign of the washing of the brothers’ feet. The washing of the brothers’ feet is a sign of the remission of sins, whether when they are forgiven by the Lord or when we forgive one another.

Today chrism is prepared or consecrated. Hence Christ—meaning “anointed”—is named from chrism. Moses first composed this ointment in Exodus at the Lord’s command; with it Aaron and his sons were first anointed as a testimony to their priesthood and holiness. Later kings too were consecrated with the same chrism. Hence they are also called “christs,” as in the saying: “Do not touch my christs” (Ps. CIV, 15).

At that time mystical anointing belonged only to kings and priests. But after our Lord, the true King and eternal Priest, had been smeared with this mystical ointment by God the heavenly Father, not only kings and bishops but the entire Church is now consecrated by anointing with chrism, because she is a member of the eternal King and Priest.

It is made from the purest and finest oil and balsam. Because we are a royal and priestly race, we are anointed after the washing, so that we may be reckoned by the name of Christ. The anointing with chrism sanctifies those who are now living from the dead.

It is therefore prepared on Thursday because Christ is said to have come to us in the fifth age of the world, or because, two days before Passover, Mary anointed the Lord’s head and feet.

The oil of the sick is blessed, because the Passion of Christ destroyed the author of death. His grace, signified by the anointing with oil, destroyed his weapons, which are daily sins, as James attests: “The prayer of faith will save the sick person, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James V, 15). The anointing with oil is its sign.

On the same day, at the ninth hour—that is, when the days are longer—or at the fifth hour, when they are shorter, fire is struck from a stone outside the basilica, and a candle is lit. From this new fire one lamp is lit by the church’s keeper and kept until Holy Saturday, to light the candle that is to be blessed on that same day. This will be discussed in the section on Holy Saturday.

The keeper places the lit candle at the top of a reed, facing the church into which they are about to enter, while the people follow him in complete silence and with bowed heads. The church itself remains without light. The custodians should have seven lamps prepared before the altar so that, without any hindrance or delay, they may be lit by the keeper’s hand with the same candle.

Afterward the church is adorned with every light by the custodians, and just as we have prescribed for this day, so also on Friday and Saturday. The order is that on Thursday the candle is carried by the keeper, on Friday by the archdeacon, and on Saturday by the junior bishop. In monasteries, on Thursday it is carried by the church’s custodian, on Friday by the superior, and on Saturday by the abbot.

After the church has been illuminated, the antiphon for Mass is begun:

“But we should glory.”

Meanwhile the bishop comes out of the sacristy with deacons wearing dalmatics and with seven candle-bearers before him, as on a solemn day, with all the appropriate ornamentation. As he passes through the middle of the schola, he nods to it so that it may sing the *Gloria*. Before he ascends to the altar, he gives the peace to the senior bishop and the senior priest, then to the deacons. Coming before the altar, he bows in prayer and lies prostrate upon the ground until the verse is repeated. When it is finished, “Kyrie eleison” is said. Then: “The Lord be with you,” and the Mass is performed.

On that day the chrism is prepared in this manner: near the end of Mass, before the words “Through whom you create all these good things, O Lord” are said, the oil is taken from the flasks offered by the people, and both the Lord Pope and all the priests bless it. Then follows the exorcism of the oil.

When these things have been completed, the Lord’s Prayer follows: “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord”; “The peace of the Lord”; and “Lamb of God.” The bishop alone receives Communion, returns to his seat, and then follows at the Communion:

“The Lord Jesus, after he had supped.”

Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled,” repeated as often as necessary. Meanwhile the clergy or the whole people receive Communion.

At Compline the prayer follows. When it has been completed, the deacon says: “Go; the dismissal is made.” Vespers follows this, as contained in the Antiphoner.

Concerning the same day, the orders state that the Lord’s Body is to be reserved for Communion on the following day [Note: [Col. 1205D] Amalarius, chapter 12.].

Augustine to Januarius: “There are some who wish to receive the Eucharist daily. Since the Lord’s Body is not consecrated on Good Friday, it is necessary that those who wish to communicate have a sacrifice from the preceding day, although the Romans do not do this. On this day the typological lamb is consumed, and the manner of communion [possibly: ‘communication’] is completed, as is that old sacrament through the cup which he extended to his disciples, giving thanks to God—[signifying?] that old things were to pass away and new ones come, which we must await until the Lord’s Resurrection. For the Lord said: ‘I will not drink from this fruit of the vine until that day’ (Mark XIV, 25),” and so forth.

## The Lord’s Supper

After this they proceed to the meal, from which the day is called the Lord’s Supper. It is called the Lord’s Supper because the Lord himself celebrated Passover with his disciples.

It took place in this manner. Toward evening the supper had been made—that is, prepared and brought as far as the diners’ table, but not yet consumed or finished. Jesus rose from the supper, laid aside his garments, and, taking a linen cloth, girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin. Coming first to Peter, he began to wash his feet and wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded, and likewise those of the disciples.

Peter said to him: “Lord, are you washing my feet?” And the Lord said: “What I am doing, you do not know now; but afterward you will understand,” and so forth (John XIII, 6).

After he had washed their feet, he reclined again [Note: [Col. 1206D] Amalarius, cited work.]. This should not be understood as though the supper had been consumed and completed. They were still dining when the Lord rose and washed their feet. For afterward he reclined again and later gave the morsel to his betrayer; it was already night, but the supper was certainly not yet finished—that is, bread was still on the table.

After a little while he said to the disciples: “If I have washed your feet, …”

Some religious men take a little food first, then wash the feet, and afterward dine. Instructed by this example, faithful Christians do not disdain to do for their fellow servants what Christ did for his disciples: to wash the feet of all, both the poor and strangers, and to give them something from their resources. Whoever cannot do this should release his neighbors from whatever they owe him, so that he may himself be forgiven in heaven.

For he himself washes our feet daily, since he intercedes for us. The washing of the church floors is itself a sign [perhaps: signifies] this.

During the washing of the feet these antiphons are sung:

“After the Lord had risen.”  
“If I, the Lord.”  
“The Lord Jesus gave a new commandment.”  
“By this everyone will know.”  
“Let us love one another.”  
“In those days.”  
“Before the feast of Passover.”  
“Charity.”

When these things have been completed, the altars are stripped around nightfall and remain so until Holy Saturday. The altar signifies Christ, who was then stripped of his garments—that is, of his disciples—when they all abandoned him and fled.

On this night Christ brings the old law to an end. It did not absolve sins but punished them. He gives the beginning of the New Testament, through which sins are absolved.

From this night until Saturday, some servants of God, imitating the Apostles, remain fasting. Others are content with bread alone and herbs, vegetables, or fermented drink [fragment ends].

## CHAPTER XVIII [Note: [Col. 1207D] Amalarius, chapter 13]. GOOD FRIDAY, WHICH IS PARASCEVE

[Col. 1207C]

*Parasceve* means “preparation”; it is also called the sixth day of the week. On this day the Jews prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, in accordance with the command concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much” (Exod. XVI, 5).

It is therefore held as a solemn day because on it Christ completed the mystery of the cross. For this reason he had come into the world: so that we who had been struck by the tree in Adam might again be healed through the mystery of the tree.

Because of this triumph, human ability offers Christ an annual celebration throughout the world, since he deigned to redeem the sin of the world by the blood of his Passion and, by conquering death through the cross, to set us free.

The threefold rationale of the Lord’s Passion is set forth. [Col. 1207D] First, so that Christ might be given as redemption for the guilt of the world, and the ancient enemy might be caught, as it were, by the hook of the cross—that is, so that he might vomit out those whom he had swallowed—not conquered by power, but by justice. The second reason is that he might provide a rule of life for those who would follow him as human beings; for this purpose he ascended the cross, so that he might offer us an example of suffering and resurrection. The third reason for undertaking the cross was that the pride of the world and its inflated wisdom might be humbled and collapse through the foolish preaching of the cross, as it is thought, so that it might become clear how much wiser than human beings is what is foolish in God.

But we must still consider why the Lord chose such a kind of death. For we read in the Gospel that the Pharisees wanted to hurl him down from the mountain: “But he, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4:30). Elsewhere too we read that the Jews picked up stones to throw at him: “But he hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8:59). Why did the Lord not wish to be thrown down, stoned, or cut down by the sword? Certainly he did this for the sake of our salvation. For Christ’s death is a sign of our salvation. Thus he did not wish to be stoned or cut down by the sword, since plainly we cannot always carry with us stones or iron by which we might defend ourselves. Rather, he chose the cross, which is expressed by a slight movement of the hand, and by which we are also protected against the enemy’s stratagems.

For by this sign of the cross the Lord’s body is consecrated, the baptismal font is sanctified, [Col. 1208B] priests and the other ecclesiastical orders are initiated, and everything whatsoever that is sanctified is consecrated by this sign of the Lord’s cross, together with the invocation of Christ’s name. For the cross itself contains a great mystery. Its position is such that its upper part reaches toward the heavens, while its lower part remains fixed in the earth and touches the depths of the underworld; its breadth, moreover, extends toward the regions of the world. For through the suffering of the cross Christ benefited the angels in heaven, whose number—diminished through the apostate angel—is daily restored from the souls of the faithful; and he benefited us, who are on earth, and those who, because of original sin, were being held in the underworld; and also those who dwelt in the various regions of the world. For he is the king of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms, so that every tongue may confess [Col. 1208C] “that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

When it lies horizontally, the cross extends toward the four regions of the world, namely east and west, north and south, because through his Passion Christ draws all nations to himself and has subjected all things to himself, in accordance with what he himself says after rising from the dead: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18).

[Note: [Col. 1207D] Annals, cited above, chapter 15. See Mabillon, *Commentary on the Roman Order*, p. LXXXIII, Paris edition, 1724.]

But why is Mass not sung today, nor on Holy Saturday, until the night vigils? Saint Pope Innocent says in the Decretals: “During these two days the sacraments are not celebrated at all, because the shepherd has been struck and the sheep of his flock have been scattered”; or else because we believe that the apostles, whom we ought to imitate, were in sadness and grief during these two days and remained fasting until the resurrection. On the day of Parasceve, therefore, Mass is not sung because on that day Jesus Christ offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for us, and that offering is sufficient for the salvation of believers.

On that day, at the fifth hour, the light is brought, as above, by the archdeacon or provost, and the seven lamps are lit; the pontiff, clergy, and people proceed to the church. Meanwhile the archdeacon goes out from the sacristy with the other deacons, dressed in dark chasubles; two candle-bearers go before them with lighted candles. They proceed silently to the altar, and, after the prayer has been completed [Col. 1209A] and the altar kissed, they go, as usual, to the pontiff’s seat. Then the archdeacon signals to the subdeacon that the first reading is to be read.

The responsory *Domine, audivi* (“Lord, I have heard”) follows. This responsory, with its four verses, signifies Christ, who assumed the four elements in the form of a human being. He hung upon the cross between two animals—that is, between two thieves. Another reading follows; then, according to Roman custom, the tract *Qui habitat* (“He who dwells”) follows. This tract draws us toward the length of eternal life, in which we shall see the salvation of God—that is, Christ, whom the most wicked Jews saw placed upon the cross today, and whom we believe we shall see face to face in his eternity. Here some sing a tract recently compiled: *Eripe me, Domine, ab homine*, “Deliver me, Lord, from man,” and so forth. It is followed, without a greeting, by the Passion of our Lord. [Col. 1209B]

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Amalarius, cited above.]

When this has been completed, two deacons immediately strip the altar of the linen cloth that had previously been placed beneath the Gospel, in the manner of a thief. Some, however, before the Passion is read, prepare two linen cloths loosely joined to one another; at the verse where it is read, “They divided my garments among themselves,” they tear the cloths apart here and there over the altar in the manner of a thief and carry them away with them.

Because the altar signifies Christ, and the apostles signify his garments, it is appropriate that something should lie beneath the Gospel for the sake of decency; when this has been removed, what was placed underneath is scraped away [Amalarius: “snatched away”], because when Christ was delivered into the hands of the wicked, the apostles fled. The linen cloth may signify John, who remained with the Lord until the cross and afterward concealed himself. The fact that the cloth is torn on that very day seems to signify that the painting expressed on the walls is intended to make us remember continually that the Lord suffered for us and that his garments were divided.

The darkness is represented by the extinguishing of the lights because then the true light of the world set, and darkness covered the whole world. It should be noted that in the Roman Church all the fire is extinguished on Friday and rekindled. In this act we imitate the principal fire, namely the corporeal sun, which hid itself from human eyes during the time of the Passion, from the sixth hour until the ninth, so that those who wickedly rejoiced at the dishonor of their Lord might not enjoy its light. For this reason it is extinguished on Friday at the sixth hour and renewed around the ninth hour; it is fitting that during these hours the events that took place at those hours should be recalled.

[Col. 1209D] Immediately the solemn prayers for Jerusalem follow. They are called solemn because they ought to be celebrated solemnly by everyone. In them mention is made of all the faithful and unfaithful. Nor is it inappropriate that, while the Lord was hanging on the cross and the Jews were insulting him, he prayed for them. From this we too should recall that whenever we suffer anything distressing or are persecuted by enemies, we ought immediately to flee to prayer.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Amalarius, cited above.]

For the dangers of this life, and for heretics and pagans, and in all the other prayers, we kneel, so that through this posture of the body we may attend to the humility of the mind [Amalarius: “show the humility of the mind”], except when we pray for the faithless Jews. For they knelt before the Lord while doing an evil deed, since they did this in mockery. To demonstrate that we ought to shun deeds performed under the guise of pretense, we avoid kneeling for the Jews.

Finally, the pontiff comes before the altar—or, as it is read in another order, passes to the right-hand part of the church beneath the throne—and says, “Let us pray”; and the deacon says, “Let us kneel.” Then the deacon says, “Rise,” and the pontiff gives the prayer, as it is contained in the Sacramentary. When these things have been finished, everyone goes outside. While the apostolic representative performs this, we begin at the ninth hour.

[Col. 1210B] [Note: [Col. 1209D] Amalarius, chapter 14.]

Toward evening, in all the churches of priests and bishops, and in monasteries, a cross is prepared before the altar and supported on either side by two acolytes. A cloth is placed before it. [Note: [Col. 1209D] *Orarium*. *Orarium* is used with various meanings; see Du Cange, under the word *Orarium*. Here it is an elongated cloth, like an orarium, spread beneath the cross for those who come to venerate it. It extends from the place where the cross is set to approximately the middle of the choir. This is still done in certain churches, including our church of Saint Emmeram. Hugo Menard, note 288.]

The pontiff comes alone and kisses the cross after venerating it. Then the priests and deacons and the others proceed in order, followed by the people. The pontiff sits in his chair until everyone has rendered homage.

[Note: [Col. 1210D] Amalarius, chapter 15.]

The first two priests, after venerating the cross, enter the sacristy and bring out the Lord’s body, which had remained from the previous day, placing it on a paten. A subdeacon holds before them a chalice with unconsecrated wine, and another subdeacon holds the paten with the aforesaid body of the Lord. The priests take the paten and chalice from them and place them upon the bare altar. The pontiff sits while the people venerate the cross.

While the pontiff or people first venerate it, the antiphon *Ecce lignum crucis* (“Behold the wood of the cross”) is sung, with Psalm *Beati immaculati* (“Blessed are the undefiled”). Then: *Crucem tuam adoramus*, “We adore your cross,” with Psalm *Deus misereatur* (“May God have mercy on us”). Another: *Dum fabricator*, “While the Maker….”

When we adore this cross, let our whole body cling to the earth, and let us behold in our mind the one whom we adore as hanging upon it; let us adore the power that it received from the Son of God. We prostrate ourselves bodily before the cross, and mentally before the Lord: we venerate the cross through which we have been redeemed, and we beseech the one who redeemed us.

[Note: [Col. 1210D] Amalarius, cited above.]

Those who cannot possess wood from the Lord’s cross rightly adore, without prejudice to faith, the cross that they do possess. Concerning the acts of veneration appropriate to each of the preceding prayers, blessed John Chrysostom says, among other things, as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1210D] Saint Chrysostom, *Homily on the Holy Cross*, spurious.]

“[Note: [Col. 1210D] Amalarius, cited above.] The cross is the foundation of the Church and the safeguard of the whole world. The cross is the proclamation of the apostles, the glory of martyrs, the hope of Christians. The cross is the joy of priests, the chastity of virgins, the abstinence of monks. The cross is the philosophy of emperors, the magnificence of kings, and the destruction of the proud. The cross is the physician of the sick, the guidance of those who sail, and the harbor of those in danger. The cross is the wisdom of the senseless and the freedom of slaves. The cross is a stumbling block to the Jews and the destruction of the impious. The cross is the destruction of temples and the expulsion of idols.”

When it has been venerated and returned to its place, the pontiff comes before the altar and says: “Instructed by saving commands…” *Our Father*. “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord.” When they have said “Amen,” he silently takes some of the consecrated bread and places it in the chalice. He does not say, “The peace of the Lord,” because the kisses of those standing around do not follow.

The unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the consecrated bread. [Note: [Col. 1211D] This should not be understood as though the unconsecrated wine becomes the blood of Christ through such an admixture, but rather that in such a mixture it receives a certain external sanctification. From this one should note the ancient custom, still in force, namely that the celebrant on Holy Friday communicates under only one species. Hugo Menard, note 293 on the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*.]

Then everyone communicates in silence, and all is completed. Whether this communion ought to take place has been related above.

Finally, when Joseph asked for the Lord’s body that day in the evening, and the women continued looking on until it was buried, they returned and bought spices and ointments; and on the following Sabbath they remained silent because of the commandment, but, having prepared the spices, they came in the morning to anoint the Lord’s body.

**Question:** Why is the Lord said to have been in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, when, as the Evangelist relates, he was crucified on Parasceve at the sixth hour, and around the ninth hour, after bowing his head, gave up his spirit; rested in the tomb on the Sabbath; and rose from the dead very early on the first day of the week?

This must be understood synecdochically, that is, the whole being taken from a part. For if you take part of Parasceve together with the preceding night, during which he was arrested, and likewise the Sabbath together with its night, and again the Lord’s night together with the day on which he rose as dawn was breaking, you will certainly find a complete three days and three nights.

It should also be understood that our death was twofold, namely in soul and in body. Christ’s death, however, was single, because he did not admit sin, which is the death of the soul; and his resurrection likewise was single. The Lord lay in the tomb for thirty-six hours, namely one day and two nights: twelve hours of the day correspond to the twenty-four hours of two nights, the single to the double. The twelve daylight hours correspond to the single death of our Redeemer; the twenty-four nighttime hours correspond to our double death. Thus, in a great mystery, he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. Coming to us, who were oppressed by death of the flesh, he brought his one death—that is, death of the flesh—and absolved our two deaths; he joined his single death to our double death and subdued our double death.

**Question:** Why do we celebrate the birthdays of the saints with joy, but Parasceve with sadness? Published by the monk Elpericus. [Note: [Col. 1212D] Elpericus the monk, who lived in the tenth century. See the preliminary notice; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XLVIII, no. 95; and *Analecta*, p. 431, Paris edition of 1723.] [Note: [Col. 1212D] This title is found in the manuscript. Quercetanus.]

The question proposed to me by your affection I undertake to clarify with all the greater difficulty because I have so far found it explained neither in the writings of the Fathers nor learned it through the tradition of teachers, nor have I heard that anyone asked about it. Therefore I delayed answering you, though you asked so many times, because I did not wish to say to you—or to anyone—anything that I could not prove by evident reasoning or the authority of Scripture. Whatever seemed to me to follow from this, I nevertheless tried to explain to you orally, so that I might free myself in this way from the difficulty. For when Solomon says, “Do not investigate matters higher than you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22), I fear attempting things to which the feebleness of my little intellect cannot rise. The lyric poet wisely admonishes us each to consider his own measure, saying:

“There is a certain point to which one may advance, if no further is granted.”

When, therefore, I had said that your hearing of the matter ought to suffice, you objected that human memory is fragile and cannot retain for long what it has heard, and that for this reason letters had been invented, so that what is forgotten through negligence may be recovered through diligence. You therefore pressed me more earnestly to commit these matters to writing for you in whatever style I could. If, then, anything inept has emerged, it will more justly be attributed not to my rashness but to your persistence. Yet I do not know whether I shall be able to express in words what I think.

You ask, therefore: since we solemnly celebrate with great rejoicing the days of the saints on which they departed from this world, so much so that on those days we relax somewhat the rigor of abstinence and live a little more freely, why are we commanded to celebrate the day of Christ’s Passion—on which he passed from this world through death, as the Gospel testifies—with great affliction, bodily mortification, and contrition of heart? As you say, ought we not to honor it all the more sublimely and festively, indeed more joyfully, insofar as Christ clearly surpasses the merit of all the saints?

This would, in my judgment, be rightly said, and that day would justly be regarded as more solemn than all festivals and celebrated with greater joy, if Christ, as a mere human being, had passed through temporal death to a glory that he had never previously possessed. We would rightly rejoice in that glory, knowing that he had attained it through death. But we know that Christ, the Son of God, has always existed gloriously before all ages, and that his glory can neither be diminished nor increased. Yet for our redemption he humbled himself so greatly that he not only deigned to assume the death of our flesh, but also, although immortal in his own nature, deigned to die in our nature. In this death he appears to have been more humbled than exalted. He endured it not from any necessity of his own, but by a kind and voluntary will; not for himself, since he owed nothing to death, but for us, who were subject to death.

It is therefore right that those for whom the impassible one suffered should sympathize with him throughout all the time of this world, and especially on the day of his Passion; that they should grieve with him who grieved for them, answer his sadness with sadness, and on this day above all mortify themselves with respect to every fleshly pleasure, out of love for the one who died for them.

For if, according to the Apostle, when one member suffers, the other members suffer with it, how much more ought those members that are ruled by the highest suffering member—that is, the head by which all the members are governed—to suffer with him? No believer is unaware that those who believe in Christ are Christ’s members and that he is the head of all who believe in him.

Conversely, the wicked are members of the devil; among them the chief place is held by the Jews who persecuted Christ, who clearly rejoiced enviously at Christ’s death. By contrast, the apostles, who are Christ’s chief members, were extraordinarily grieved at Christ’s unjust death.

If we confidently believe that we are numbered even among the least of Christ’s members, we ought to grieve with his more exalted members at the Passion of our head. Otherwise, if on this day we wish to devote ourselves to bodily joy, we may appear not to love Christ with the apostles but to insult his death with the Jews. Consequently—and may this not happen—we might rightly be counted not among Christ’s members, whom we do not wish to imitate, but among the devil’s members, with whom we seem to rejoice.

Let us therefore grieve over Christ’s death with the apostles, so that we may deserve to rejoice with them in his resurrection. Let us grieve while the wicked exult, so that afterward we may rejoice while they mourn. For the Jews, just as they rejoiced at his death, are shown to have been saddened by his resurrection.

Behold, as I was able, I have briefly explained why it is fitting to celebrate the day of Christ’s Passion in bodily affliction [Col. 1213C] and contrition of spirit, although I have lacked the words by which I might express what I am unable to convey.

It remains now to explain, as the eloquence of my tongue, by the Lord’s gift, shall suffice, likewise and briefly why we recall with the highest praises and great rejoicing the days of the saints on which they passed from this world.

First, I think it should be recalled that all Christians are brothers in Christ, as the Lord himself declares to all who believe in him: “Do not call anyone your father on earth. For you have one Father; you are all brothers” (Matthew 23:9). It is therefore truly established that all who have already departed from this world, whether those who still dwell in the world or those who will exist until the end of the age, if they believe in Christ, are brothers: they have been reborn in Christ through the one regeneration of baptism, nourished at the breasts of the one mother, the Church, joined by the bond of one faith as by the bond of the sweetest brotherhood, and called by gracious adoption by the same most merciful Father God to one and the same inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

We ought therefore to share with one another everything that happens to us with fraternal affection: to grieve together in adversity and to rejoice together in prosperity. Everyone who is truly a Christian knows that when the saints depart from this corruptible life, they migrate to a better life—that is, one incorruptible and imperishable: from darkness to perpetual light, from sorrow to everlasting joy, from labor to unending rest, [Col. 1214A] from prison to freedom, from servitude to a kingdom.

Hence ecclesiastical custom has prevailed in calling those days not funerary days but birthdays. For those who are sent forth from the pressures of this world, as from the narrowness of a very constricted womb, into the vast and radiant expanse of the heavenly dwelling are rightly said to be born.

If, then, we presume to be brothers of those whom we see glorified in this way, it is fitting that we congratulate their happiness, rejoice with their joy, share in the glory of our brothers, and honor with due praise and proper rejoicing their heavenly birthdays—their triumphs by which, through divine assistance, they conquered the devil and the world.

For if we pass them by mournfully or sadly, we will be convicted of a double error: either we seem not to believe that they have passed into glory and therefore mourn them as though they were dead; or, if we know that they have been granted happiness and do not rejoice with them, we are convicted of begrudging their glory.

And when we find that the ancients celebrated their own birthdays or those of their relatives—birthdays on which they had been poured into this miserable life—with such rejoicing that on those occasions they freely devoted themselves even to every bodily pleasure, how much more ought we to celebrate with spiritual gladness the birthdays of the holy Fathers, who were not born into miseries but passed from miseries into joys to be possessed without end—not dissolving ourselves in bodily allurements, as the pagans did, but exulting in Christ through spiritual songs and heavenly hymns, as Christians.

Nevertheless, we do not deny that we should live somewhat more freely in bodily terms than on other days, for the sake, as I think, of certain duller people who consider nothing festive unless they see it sweetened by bodily pleasure.

Since we know that these same saints attained the happiness we have described through temporal affliction, it is necessary that, just as we rejoice with their eternal joy, so we should also sympathize with their temporal distress, so that by following their footsteps in all things we may, through their intercession, deserve to reach the same joys.

To signify this, on the days preceding those birthdays, which we commonly call their vigils, we eat more sparingly than usual and devoutly anticipate the solemnities with the due observances of fasting and bodily mortification, so that, purified by the abstinence of the preceding day, we may celebrate more worthily [Col. 1214D] the joy of the following feast.

Accordingly, in the Mass of these vigils we omit the most festive alleluia melody, as on other days of fasting—unless, perhaps, the day should be Sunday, which the authority of the Lord’s resurrection compels us never to fast on, but always to keep festive.

The Lord figuratively signifies both things—the preceding compassion of the whole Church for the affliction of the saints and the rejoicing that follows from their glory—in the Gospel under the image of a woman, when he says that she is sorrowful while giving birth, but when she has given birth, she rejoices exceedingly (John 16:21).

Since we say that a woman is in labor when she is anxious before delivery, and that she gives birth when she brings forth the child, the woman through whom the holy Church is represented is rightly said to grieve when she is in labor. For when she sees that her children, whom she has conceived through faith, are hindered by various tribulations from the wicked before she gives birth to them in eternal life, she groans with great pains, distressed as though by the difficulty of childbirth. But when she has given birth to those whom she had labored to bring forth, from the narrowness of this world into the heavenly kingdom, it cannot be said how greatly she exults at the most blessed birth of her children.

The primitive Church enacted this historically during the time of persecution; but the Church that now exists, peace having already been restored by Christ, represents it spiritually through pious emulation.
