We therefore imitate the past pains of her labor in the vigils, fasts, and bodily affliction of the saints; but we emulate the subsequent joy of her who has already brought forth through the gladness of the feast itself.

To your persistence, dearest son, I have tried to give satisfaction as best I could, though not as I ought; yet, compelled by the difficulty of the question, I have perhaps become more verbose than I should.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON THE VIGIL OF HOLY SATURDAY OF EASTER

The observance of Easter Saturday is celebrated because on that day the Lord rested in the tomb. Hence, in Hebrew, it signifies “rest,” or because on that day, when the world had been completed, he rested. This day lies between Christ’s death and resurrection, signifying a certain rest of souls from all labor after death, through which there is a passage by the resurrection of the flesh to that life which Christ the Lord deigned to foreshadow by his resurrection.

And because all Christians honor it with such great reverence, or because the vigils extend until midnight, Saint Jerome teaches as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1215D] Amalarius, chapter 16.]

“It is a tradition of the apostles or of the Jews that Christ will come at midnight, in imitation of the time in Egypt when the Passover was celebrated. Hence I think that the apostolic tradition has continued, so that on the day of the Easter vigils it is not permitted to dismiss the people before midnight, as they await Christ’s coming. When that time has passed, they may confidently assume that it is time for everyone to keep the feast.”

The blessing of the candle also makes this clear: “This is the night”; and in the prayer of the Mass: “O God, who made this most sacred night…”

In the Roman Church within the city, early on the morning of the first day of the week, the archdeacon comes into the church, pours wax into a clean vessel, and mixes oil into it. He then blesses the wax and pours from it the shape of lambs. [Note: [Col. 1215D] See Hugo Menard, in the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*, note 300 at the end.] He keeps them in a clean place. On the octave of Easter, the archdeacon gives these lambs in the church, after Masses and communion, to the people; from them they cause incense to be lit in their homes and use it for fumigation in their houses whenever any need arises. Likewise, in the suburban cities they make them from oil.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] Amalarius, chapter 17.]

The lambs made by the Romans signify the immaculate Lamb made for us; for Christ must be brought back to our memory more frequently through all things. Saint Gregory instituted these with oil when he disclosed the mysteries of the Paschal Lamb.

[Note: [Col. 1216D] Amalarius, chapter 18.]

Pope Zosimus instituted the blessing of the candle among us. [Note: [Col. 1216D] Pope Zosimus. See Hugo Menard, note cited above.] It signifies the Lord, who went before the children of Israel in a pillar of fire. The wax signifies Christ’s humanity. For the honey in the wax is divinity in humanity.

This candle corresponds in its symbolism to the pillar of fire, which illuminated the people of Israel at night, as is expressed in the blessing itself: “But now we know the proclamation of its pillar.” That pillar signifies Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1216D] Amalarius, cited above.]

That pillar went before the children of Israel; our pillar, that is, the candle, goes before our catechumens. Its light signifies Christ, by whom both the present night is illuminated—namely, by the grace of the resurrection—and the catechumens who are to come to baptism.

The fact that it is blessed by the deacon follows Roman custom. For in that church the archdeacon prepares the lambs. For the seven days of the neophytes, this candle precedes the pontiff, who is the head of the people, because the pillar of fire went before the people until the promised land.

On that day, at the seventh hour, everyone proceeds to the church, and the light is carried by the bishop or abbot, with the people accompanying him as above; the seven lamps are lit. The candle that is to be blessed should already be prepared in the middle of the church, with all the clergy or people gathered on either side. Then the archdeacon comes, makes a cross upon it, lights it from the new fire, and completes the blessing of the candle.

The first part begins almost in the manner of a reading: “Let the angelic host of heaven now exult,” and so forth. The second is to be sung in the manner of a preface. Immediately after the candle has been blessed, two other candles, of human stature, are lit from it.

The candle that is lit from the new fire signifies the new teaching or grace of Christ in the New Testament, and the new grace by which the Lord’s night is illuminated. The two candles lit from it signify the teaching of the apostles, to whom it is said: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14).

The fact that they go before the catechumens to baptism signifies that the pillar of fire went before the children of Israel before they crossed the Red Sea. There too baptism figuratively took its beginning: “Moses baptized,” it says, “in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2). Thus the sea had the form of baptism, the cloud that of the Holy Spirit, and the manna that of the bread of life.

Then John baptized in repentance; after him Christ baptized with the perfect baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire. There are indeed three kinds of baptism. The first is that by which the filth of sins is washed away through the bath. The second is that by which someone is baptized in his own blood through martyrdom, by which Christ too deigned to be baptized. The third is that of tears, through which David and the Ninevites obtained mercy.

Finally, in baptism there are seven steps: three in the descent, because of the three things that we renounce; and three others in the ascent, because of the three things that we confess. The seventh, [Col. 1217A] which is the fourth, is like the Son of Man, extinguishing the furnace of fire. [Note: [Col. 1217D] The passage is corrupt.]

The four readings that follow before baptism, with their chants or prayers, pertain to the instruction of the catechumens and the newly baptized.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] Amalarius, chapter 21.]

The reason they are not announced at the beginning like the other readings—for example, “A reading from the Book of Genesis” or “from Exodus,” and the others in order—is this: the Apostle says, “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1:14). The catechumens are compared to the foolish; therefore the readings are announced to them in a different manner, so that the blindness of their hearts may be brought back to memory, since they do not yet know the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. An unknown author is proclaimed in vain to those for whom the most secure authority can become worthless through ignorance.

Before the readings are read, two notaries take the aforementioned lighted candles and hold them, one at the right horn of the altar and the other at the left, until the fonts. Then the reader ascends to read, without an announcement of the reading.

The first reading, from the Book of Genesis, begins as follows: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” and so forth.

Then follows, without a greeting: “O God, who wonderfully created the human being.”

The second reading, from the Book of Exodus: “It came to pass in the morning watch.”

Canticle: “Let us sing to the Lord.”

Prayer: “O God, whose ancient miracles…”

The third reading, from the prophet Isaiah: “Seven women shall take hold…”

Canticle: “A vineyard was made.”

“Let us pray. O God, who has brought us to celebrate the mystery of Easter…”

The fourth reading, from the prophet Isaiah: “This is the inheritance…”

Canticle: “Give ear, O heaven.”

“Let us pray. O God, [who] your Church…”

From Psalm 41, a canticle: “As the deer…”

Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you…”

Another prayer, from the same Psalm 41: “Almighty and everlasting God, look favorably upon the devotion of your people.”

Between these two canticles no reading is necessary, because, on account of the correspondence of the reading and the two psalms, they are suitably joined without another reading.

When the readings have been completed, they must descend to baptize.

At what hour baptism ought to be celebrated today, whether at Pentecost, and what priests preach to the neophytes, must briefly be explained here.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] See Alcuin, epistle 90, p. 109 near the end, and the epistle to Oudin, *On the Ceremonies of Baptism*, col. 611 of this volume.]

“First, when a pagan approaches baptism in order to become a catechumen, he renounces the evil spirit and all his destructive pomp. He is also exsufflated, so that, once the devil has been driven away, an entrance may be prepared for Christ the Lord. He is exorcised—that is, the evil spirit is adjured to depart and withdraw, giving place to the true Lord [Al.: the true God]. The catechumen who is listening, or the one who assists, receives salt, so that his rotten and fleeting sins may be cleansed by the divine gift of the salt of wisdom. Then the faith of the Apostles’ Creed is handed over to him, so that the empty house, abandoned by its former inhabitant, may be adorned with faith and a dwelling may be prepared for the Lord. Scrutinies are held, so that it may be examined repeatedly [Al.: the servant], whether, after the renunciation of Satan, the sacred words of the faith given to him have taken root firmly in his heart. His nostrils are also touched, so that, for as long as he draws breath through his nostrils, he may remain steadfast in the faith he has received. His breast likewise is anointed with the same oil [Al.: the same], so that the entrance to the devil may be closed by the sign of the holy cross. His shoulders are also signed, so that he may be protected on every side. Again, in the anointing of the breast [Al. adds: and shoulders], the firmness of faith and perseverance in good works are signified. Then he is baptized by a triple immersion in the name of the Holy Trinity. And rightly so: a human being, created in the image of the Holy Trinity, is restored to that same image through invocation of the Holy Trinity; and he who fell into death at the third stage of sin—that is, by consent—is raised from the font a third time, so that by grace he may rise to life. Then he is clothed in white garments because of the grace [Al.: joy] of regeneration, the purity of life, and the beauty of angelic splendor. At that point his head is anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he bears the diadem of royal and priestly dignity, according to the Apostle: ‘You are a chosen race, a royal, priestly people, offering yourselves to the living God as a holy sacrifice pleasing to God’ (1 Pet. II, 9). Thus he is strengthened with the body and blood of the Lord, so that he may be a member of that Head who suffered and rose again for him. Finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief priest, he receives the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, so that he may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others—the one who in baptism was given eternal life by grace.”

Today baptism is celebrated at the ninth hour, as at Pentecost, for this reason: the angel of the Lord came to Cornelius at the ninth hour (Acts X, 3ff.), announcing to him that his prayers and almsgiving had ascended into the presence of the Lord. He immediately sent for Peter and obtained the sacrament of baptism. It is also most fitting that, since at the ninth hour the author of life gave up his spirit, at that same ninth hour the holy Church should receive holy baptism.

That baptism may not generally be celebrated except today and at Pentecost is plainly denied by Saint Leo the pope, unless illness should intervene. Nor should this be omitted: the Romans celebrate six scrutinies during Lent, and the seventh today. In this number seven the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given in baptism are understood.

Finally, after the third hour on Saturday, those who are to be baptized prepare themselves for the church, together with their godfathers and godmothers, and are arranged by the acolyte: the males on the right and the females on the left. Then those who are able recite the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, or their godfathers and godmothers recite them on their behalf—the persons who are to receive them. Next the presbyter makes the sign of the cross on their foreheads with his thumb, saying: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” After this he lays his hands upon their heads and says the prayer for making a catechumen: “Almighty and everlasting God.”

Here, according to Saint Gregory, they recite the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or their godfathers recite them on their behalf. After this come the prayers on Holy Saturday for catechizing the infant. Then he touches their nostrils and ears with spittle and says into the right ear: “Ephata [Ephpheta],” that is, “Be opened”; at the nostrils: “For the fragrance of sweetness”; and at the left ear: “But you, depart, devil, for the judgment of God is approaching.”

Afterward he touches the child’s breast and the space between the shoulders with exorcized oil, making a cross with his thumb, and, calling the child by name, says: “Do you renounce Satan?” The child answers: “I renounce him.” “And all his works?” The child answers: “I renounce them.” “And all his pomps?” The child answers: “I renounce them.” The Creed follows. Here, according to Gregory, the readings and chants follow.

When these things have been completed, the pontiff proceeds with all due solemnity to bless the fonts, accompanied by the clergy or the people. The blessed candle also goes before him—or the two candles held by the notaries, having been lighted by the same pontiff—and the vessel containing oil and balsam is carried with great reverence. Those two candles likewise precede the pontiff everywhere until the octave of Easter.

As they go to the fonts, they sing the litanies, repeating them only three times. When these are finished before the fonts and silence has been made, while the priest stands, the blessing of the font follows: “Almighty and everlasting God,” and so forth. Then comes the consecration of the font, sung in the manner of a preface: “Eternal God, who by the invisible power of your sacraments…”

At the invocation of the Holy Spirit, which the priest proclaims in a loud voice—that is, with elevated devotion of mind—the blessed candle is lowered into the water, or the two candles that have been lighted from it, to demonstrate the presence of the Holy Spirit. The priest is already saying: “Let it descend into this fullness of the font.”

When the font has been blessed, the pontiff receives from the archdeacon the chrism mixed with oil in a vessel and sprinkles it across the middle of the font in the form of a cross. Then the pontiff sprinkles some of that water with his hand over the people. After this the people take some of the same water in small vessels to sprinkle in their houses or fields.

Then, while the godfather holds the infant whom he is to receive, the priest asks him as follows: “What is your name?” He answers. The priest continues: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” He answers: “I believe.” “And in Jesus Christ the Son, … ‘suffered’?” He answers: “I believe.” “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit and the holy Church?” He answers: “I believe.”

Then the priest baptizes him by three immersions, invoking the Holy Trinity only once, saying: “And I baptize you in the name of the Father”—and he immerses him once; “and of the Son”—and he immerses him again; “and of the Holy Spirit”—and he immerses him a third time.

When he has risen from the font, the presbyter makes the sign of the cross with chrism on his crown with his thumb, saying this prayer: “Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ…” Then he is received by the person who is to receive him; afterward the infant is clothed in his own garments.

If a bishop is present, he ought immediately to be confirmed with chrism and afterward to receive communion. If a bishop is absent, he is given communion by the presbyter, who says: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life. Amen.” The practice of certain godfathers drawing their godchildren out of the font is not found in the ritual books.

The Apostolic See treats this matter among the Romans as follows. [Note: [Col. 1219D] On this matter of the Apostolic See, see Menardus, note 334.] After the pontiff has baptized the infants, or after those whom he has ordered to do so have baptized them, they lift the infants in their arms and present them to one of the presbyters. He makes the sign of the cross with chrism on their crowns with his thumb, saying: “Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” as above.

When this has been completed, those who are to receive them stand ready with linen cloths in their hands. Then they receive the infants from the pontiff or from the deacons who baptized them. After they have been clothed, they are carried before the pontiff for confirmation. He gives each of them a white stole, a chrismal garment, and ten siliquae. [Note: [Cols. 1219D, 1220D] According to Isidore, *Origins*, book XVI, ch. 24, a *siliqua* is one twenty-fourth of a solidus, taking its name from a tree seed. CANGIUS.] Thus they are clothed.

After they have been dressed, the pontiff offers a prayer over them, laying his hand upon their heads and invoking the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. The prayer is: “Almighty and everlasting God, who causes regeneration…”

When this has been completed, he makes the sign of the cross with chrism on the forehead of each one with his thumb, saying: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you.” Let all answer: “And with your spirit.”

These words are a greeting to the new person who is being regenerated. Certainly, care must be taken that this not be neglected, because by this rite every legitimate baptism is confirmed in the name of Christianity.

It must also be ensured that they receive no food and are not nursed before they receive communion. Every day, until the octave, they should come to Mass and receive communion, while their parents make offerings on their behalf. The same things are to be done at Pentecost.

Regarding this confirmation, Saint Innocent the pope asserts that it may be performed by no one other than a bishop. Although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the fullness of the episcopate; therefore it belongs to bishops alone to sign with the chrism or to impart the Spirit, the Paraclete, just as the reading from the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates, which states that Peter and John were sent so that they might impart the Holy Spirit to the baptized.

Presbyters, whether without a bishop or in the presence of a bishop, may anoint the baptized with chrism when they baptize, but the chrism must have been consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs to bishops alone when they impart the Spirit, the Paraclete, to the baptized.

When a sick person comes to be baptized, do not perform the order written above. Instead, after “eternal and most just mercy,” add this prayer: “I beseech your healing, holy Lord and Father…” through “the grace of your baptism.” Through Christ.

When this has been completed, you say the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Then you catechize him with these words: “Nor are you unaware, Satan…” and so forth. Do not say the greater blessing over the fonts, but this lesser one for assistance: “Hear us, almighty God, and send the substance of this water…” through “may deserve eternal life.” Through Christ, and so forth.

After you have catechized him, bless the water with these words: “I exorcize you, creature of water, in the name of the Father, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, and of the Holy Spirit. If there is any phantom…” through “for the forgiveness of all sins, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and the world [the ending is abbreviated in the source].” Through Christ.

You baptize him and anoint him with chrism on the brain, saying to him: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Afterward you touch his head with chrism and say this prayer: “Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ…” You give him communion and confirm him as above.

When the baptism described above has also been completed on Holy Saturday, litanies are held by order of the pontiff before the altar. First, sevenfold, fivefold, and threefold litanies are made around the consecration of the baptistery, with the saints’ intercessions for those being reborn.

They begin as follows. One primicerius stands in the right choir and says with those beside him, “Kyrie eleison”; the secundicerius responds with the left choir, “Kyrie eleison,” up to four times. Then “Christe eleison,” up to three times. This is repeated seven times, and hence they are called “sevenfold.” The fivefold and threefold litanies are performed in the same order.

After this: “Christ, hear us,” up to seven times, and so in order, with an interval made. Fivefold litanies follow, repeated five times. When these have been completed, the bells are rung for the public Mass.

The ministers must be prepared before the door of the sacristy in such a way that, when the cantor says, “Light them,” they proceed without delay to the altar. Threefold litanies follow: “Kyrie eleison,” and so forth, through “Son of God, we beseech you.”

Then the pontiff emerges from the sacristy with great solemnity, with the aforementioned candle-bearers before him and with incense vessels. [p. 485] When the schola has sung “Agnus Dei,” the cantor says in a loud voice: “Light them.”

Then all the candles of the neophytes, which they hold in their hands, are lit first, demonstrating that through that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world each person ought to receive light.

The practice of extinguishing them through the consecration of the font, when the larger illuminated candles are lowered into it, has no authority. They remain without light until this hour, when the other candles of the church are lit, for this reason: they are first to receive the laying on of the bishop’s hand, and thus we are to believe that they are illuminated by the Holy Spirit. And just as the night in which we celebrate Mass has been brightened by the glory of the resurrection, so it too should be brightened by the light of the candles.

“Agnus Dei” follows. The things that follow are to be repeated slowly enough for the ministers to be able to proceed. “Christ, hear us”; “Kyrie eleison.” When these have been completed, the pontiff says: “Glory to God in the highest.”

We have said from the Decretals of Pope Innocent that Mass is not celebrated on Saturday. We have learned that this is so from the Office, which illuminates the whole coming night, as in the first prayer of the Mass: “God, who has made this most sacred night…”

Note the ministers’ chant addressed to the neophytes up to the Gospel, for example: “If you have risen with Christ.” “Alleluia” is sung first—Hebrew for “Praise the Lord”—because of the primacy of that language; then comes the Tractus in Latin.

The fact that before the Gospel nothing is carried except incense alone may be understood as referring to those spices which the women brought before dawn to anoint the Lord.

The fact that after the Gospel no Offertory is sung and the cantors remain silent during the sacrifice recalls the sacrifice, or silence, of the women. At that time they brought only the ointments.

“Holy, holy, holy,” which is the song of the angels, is sung because the angels did not remain silent about his resurrection. Again, in place of the women, the cantors keep silence at “Agnus Dei,” because when Mary asked the gardener, “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me” (John XX, 15), she believed rather that he had been carried off by theft than that he had taken away the sins of the world. Therefore she heard, when she wished to touch him: “Do not touch me.”

The priest, who is Christ’s vicar, fulfills his office. The prayer follows, to complete the service.

After all have received communion, the deacon says: “Go, the dismissal is made.” The response is: “Thanks be to God.”

On this night nothing is done among the Romans concerning the evening assembly, neither before Mass nor after Mass, because, according to Augustine and the other teachers, this Saturday has no evening office.

## CHAPTER XX. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

[Note: [Col. 1221D] Amalarius, ch. 34.]

On the holy day of Easter, at the entrance, Christ presents himself in the Church to his Father through the mouths of the prophets, saying: “I have risen.”

The first prayer shows that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom has been opened to us through the resurrection of our Head. The Epistle warns us to separate ourselves from the vices against which we struggled during the days of Lent. The Responsory shows how greatly those who are cleansed from vices ought to rejoice. In the Alleluia it is shown where the whole cause of joy lies. The Gospel explains more perfectly the cause of the entire joy.

On the same day at Vespers, the entire ecclesiastical order gathers early at Saint John’s in the principal church, in the place called the Crucifixion. There the schola begins “Kyrie eleison,” and with that chant they proceed as far as the altar.

After this “Alleluia” is begun for the psalm “The Lord said to my Lord.” Then “I will confess,” with “Alleluia”; and “Blessed is the man,” with “Alleluia.” When this is finished, “Alleluia” follows: “Our Passover,” with the verse “Let us feast.” Then the melody, then the Epistle according to the Romans.

Antiphon: “Go quickly.”  
Verse: “Behold, he will go before you.”  
Then another antiphon: “And looking back…”

In this week “Kyrie eleison” does not follow the Gospel. Instead, the priest says a prayer, and when it is finished they descend to the fonts with the antiphon “On the day of resurrection.”

The psalm follows: “Praise the Lord, children,” with “Alleluia.” Then “Alleluia: The Lord reigns.” Verse: “Your throne is prepared.” Another verse: “The rivers have lifted up.”

Then the melody, then the Gospel.

Antiphon: “Mary came.”  
The prayer follows.

Then they go to Saint John’s, to the Font or to the Vestment, with the antiphon “The stone.” The psalm follows, “When Israel went out,” with “Alleluia.” When it is finished, “Alleluia” follows: “Come, let us rejoice.” Verse: “Let us come before him.” Another verse: “Today, if you hear his voice…”

Then the melody. In the Gospel, the antiphon is: “Go, announce.” Verse: “There you will see him.” Another antiphon: “Do not be afraid.” The prayer follows.

When it is finished, they proceed to the cross with the antiphon “I saw water.” There they sing the psalm “When Israel went out” again, and “Alleluia: Come, let us rejoice,” as above.

Then the Gospel. Antiphon: “I will go before you.” The priest’s prayer follows.

When these things have been finished and the blessed offerings have been received, each person is sent back to his own titular church, so that he may celebrate Vespers there. They say only “Alleluia” over the psalm, and before the Gospel they say the Responsory “This is the day,” without a verse.

This arrangement is observed throughout the whole week up to the Sunday after the White-clad ones, with only the Alleluia and antiphons changed on each day; they sing the same psalms.

[Note: [Col. 1223D] The manuscript reads: “On the Saturday when they lay aside the white garments.” QUERCETAN.]

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE WHITE GARMENTS

[Note: [Col. 1223D] Amalarius, ch. 29.]

Today the White-clad ones, because they were baptized on Saturday, are stripped of their white garments. They are commonly called the White-clad ones because of their white clothing.[^c0117-6]

Just as seven days belong to the Old Testament because of the Sabbath, so eight days belong to the New Testament because of the eighth day of the resurrection. From Saturday to Saturday white garments are worn, which present us with an image of what we ought to be in the New Testament and of what sort of bodies we shall receive on the eighth day, on which we must be presented before the Lord with the pledge that we received in baptism.

The white garments of the White-clad ones are the works of the righteous, clean and bright at all times. The fact that they are stripped of these garments on Saturday signifies that the soul of every believer departing from the body will find the Sabbath—that is, rest—and will leave its garment here, namely, the body, in order to receive it again on the last day.

The eight days of the neophytes signify the course of the present life. Just as that Hebrew people, after crossing the Red Sea, with a column of fire leading them by night, entered the promised land in triumph over their enemies along the whole journey, so our baptized people, their past sins extinguished, are led daily to the Church, with the illuminated column of the candle preceding them.

From this it is understood that the candle ought not to be lit for any other use in any place except in remembrance of the light of the Holy Spirit while one is going to church.

The eight days of the neophytes are distinguished from the others—that is, the eighth day accords with the first. The eight offices that are performed in memory of the neophytes are distinguished from all the other offices that follow up to Pentecost.

The first has two praises, namely “Alleluia” and “Give thanks,” and the Tractus “Praise the Lord.” The eighth likewise has two: the two Alleluias “This is the day” and “Praise, children.” This is not done on any other Saturday until Pentecost.

The six middle offices contain a Responsory and an Alleluia. In memory of the first life that Adam had, “Alleluia” is sung first; and because it was not everlasting, the Tractus follows in a humbler manner, so that the humility of the later life may be remembered.

In remembrance of the supreme restoration—that is, of the final rest—which is restored on the seventh day and completed on the eighth day and in the eighth office, two Alleluias are sung: the first because life is restored, the second because it is everlasting. Likewise, on Sundays two Alleluias are concluded up to Pentecost.

There are two reasons why the soul praises the Lord on the seventh day—that is, in rest: one, for the glory already received; the other, for the resurrection still to be received. In the resurrection, however, the human being will consist of body and soul. And because the Lord’s resurrection preceded on the eighth day, what will take place in the resurrection is enacted through Sundays up to Pentecost: namely, that mind and body should praise the Lord.

Since in the meantime the soul praises the Lord without the body, one Alleluia is celebrated on each day. The six middle offices of Easter week, however, contain a Responsory and an Alleluia.

Just as the number seven signifies rest, so the number six signifies work. In this life we must devote ourselves to good works and must not cease praising God.

At the end of the verses of the Responsory “This is the day,” the order is reversed. “Blessed is he who comes” is placed before the verse “The stone which the builders rejected,” which is earlier in the order of the psalm. But it is sung on Friday because, among the other matters, it speaks especially of the Lord’s Passion, which took place on Friday. On that day the Jews rejected the Lord while building; on that day he was made the head of the corner.

The fact that baptism is performed only once signifies that Christ died for us only once. In this baptism there are unquestionably two covenants: first, to renounce the devil and his pomps; second, to believe in the mystery of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Infants are baptized when another person professes faith on their behalf because they are not yet able to speak or believe. If they should die before being regenerated, they unquestionably remain alienated from Christ’s kingdom.

Their godparents must therefore take care that, when the children reach the age of understanding, they instruct them in faith and good morals and earnestly teach them the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. If they neglect this, they should know that they will have to render an account before the Lord for those whose sponsors they became.

For as long as the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles is generally celebrated by the Church, the anointing with chrism ought likewise to be observed for everyone who receives the laying on of hands—and not without reason: for the Holy Spirit came to his guest in seven women, that is, in seven virtues.

On the Sunday after the White-clad ones—that is, on the octave of Easter—blessed wax is to be distributed after Mass, to be burned as incense in their houses or placed in their fields or vineyards, because of demonic illusions and against lightning and thunder.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE GREATER LITANY

[Note: [Col. 1224D] Amalarius, ch. 37, vol. XIV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 965. Some deficiencies are to be supplied from there. Add what he relates in book IV, ch. 24 and following.]

Roman custom inserts one day—namely, the seventh day before the Kalends of May—which it calls the day of the Greater Litany, not a day of fasting.

The Greek word λιτανεία (*litaneia*) means in Latin *deprecatio* or *rogatio*, “supplication” or “petition”; hence the term “Rogations.” A calm mind, free from an evil will, can pray to the Lord even while eating moderately.

At that time—that is, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May—enemies are accustomed to stir up war against neighboring kingdoms; hence I think that this provision was made prudently. Or perhaps it is because at that time everything is in a kind of growth: the crops sprout, the fruits of trees emerge from blossom, the vines and olive trees burst forth on their own trees, and the animals graze the fields.

Since these things are necessary for our use, we must ask that they be preserved by the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON THE DAYS OF THE ROGATIONS

[Alternative heading: “On the Rogations.”]

[Note: [Col. 1225D] Amalarius, ibid., p. 964.]

The three days of the Rogations, which are celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension, were established according to the custom of the Gallican Church by Saint Mamertus, [Note: [Col. 1225D] On St. Mamertus, see Hugo Menardus, notes on the sacramentary of St. Gregory, note 393; and Martene, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Discipline*, ch. 27, no. 2.] bishop of Vienne, on account of the attacks of harmful beasts, which at that time afflicted the people of God most grievously.

For when, because of the sins of Gaul, the peoples were being savagely killed by the madness of wolves, and no remedy for this scourge could be found, the bishops of Gaul are said to have assembled at Vienne, the chief city of Gaul. They jointly decreed that they should implore the Lord’s mercy by a three-day fast, following in the footsteps of the ancient Fathers.

When the eye of divine mercy looked favorably upon their prayers and mercifully removed the plague of this scourge, these days became an annual custom of celebration, to be observed throughout the provinces of Gaul before the day of the Ascension. This custom is still most devoutly observed among us on account of various calamities.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON THE LORD’S ASCENSION

The solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension is celebrated because on that same day, after his victory over the world and his return from hell, he is remembered as having ascended into heaven, as it is written: “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV, 8).

This feast is celebrated in the recurring cycle of the years so that the unity of the assumed flesh ascending to the right hand of the Father may be recalled. We believe that his body is in heaven just as it was when he ascended.

The angelic voice also testifies to this, saying: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11)—that is, in the same form and substance of flesh. To that flesh he certainly gave immortality; he did not remove its nature.

The right hand of the Father, at which the same Son is believed to sit, is not corporeal—for it is impious to think this about God. Rather, the right hand of the Father is the everlasting blessedness promised to the saints in the resurrection, namely, to the Church, which is Christ’s body. Likewise, his left hand is rightly understood as the misery and everlasting punishment that will be given to the ungodly.

## CHAPTER XXV. ON THE VIGIL

At the Vigil of Pentecost the service is conducted as on Holy Saturday of Easter.

Before descending to the fonts for baptism, the first reading is read: “God tested Abraham.” Prayer: “God, who made Abraham your servant…”

The second reading: “Moses wrote the song.” Chant: “Give ear, O heaven.” Prayer: “God, who through the sayings of the prophets…”

The third reading: “Seven women will take hold.” Chant: “A vineyard was made.” Prayer: “God, who caused us to celebrate…”

The fourth reading: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of life.” “Unchanging God.” Chant: “As a deer…” Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who have celebrated the Paschal feast…”

When the readings have been completed, they descend to the fonts with sacred chrism and candles, singing the litany with great reverence. When these things have been completed, baptism is performed as at the Vigil of Easter.

After ascending from the font, they must enter the public Mass at Saint John’s. First litanies are made, repeating the procession [the manuscript reads, “threefold, by asking”; perhaps it should be read, “repeating three times”]. When they have said “Agnus Dei,” it is to be said in a loud voice: “Light them.”

After all the lights have been lit, the pontiff proceeds with all his vestments to the altar and says: “Glory to God in the highest.” The Mass is then completed in its proper order.

## CHAPTER XXVI. ON PENTECOST

The beginning and cause of the feast of Pentecost must be recalled at somewhat greater length.

The day of Pentecost took its beginning when the voice of God was heard thundering from above on Mount Sinai and the Law was given to Moses. In the New Testament, Pentecost began when Christ displayed the coming of the Holy Spirit whom he had promised. He said that the Spirit would not come unless he himself ascended into heaven.

Finally, when Christ had entered the gate of heaven, after ten days had passed, the place suddenly trembled while the apostles were praying. As the Holy Spirit descended upon them, they were so inflamed that they spoke of God’s mighty works in the languages of all nations.

Thus the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, with grace poured out in the variety of languages, transmitted the solemnity to later generations. For this reason Pentecost is celebrated and the day itself is held to be especially distinguished.

This feast of the Gospel corresponds to the feast of the Law. There, after the lamb had been sacrificed and fifty days had passed, the Law of Moses was given, written by the finger of God. Here, after Christ had been killed—Christ who was led to sacrifice like a sheep—the true Passover is celebrated; and after fifty days have passed, the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, is given to the one hundred and twenty disciples, a number corresponding to the Mosaic age.

## CHAPTER XXVII. ON SUNDAY

The apostles established Sunday as a religious solemnity because on that day the Lord and our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is therefore called the Lord’s Day so that, abstaining on it from earthly works and the enticements of the world, we may devote ourselves solely to divine worship, giving this day honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection that we possess in it.

For just as the Lord Jesus Christ and our Savior rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too shall rise on the last day. Hence we also pray standing on Sunday, which is a sign of the future resurrection.

It is evident that this day is also solemn in the Holy Scriptures. It is the first day of the world; on it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created; on it Christ also rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles; and on the same day manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness.

For the Lord says: “For six days you shall gather it, but on the sixth day you shall gather twice as much” (Exod. XVI, 4–5). The sixth day is the Parasceve, which is placed before the Sabbath; the Sabbath is the seventh day, and it is followed by the Lord’s Day, on which manna first came from heaven.

From this the Jews may infer that even then our Lord’s Day was preferred to their Jewish Sabbath; even then it was shown that God’s grace did not descend to them from heaven, but did so on our holy Lord’s Day, on which the Lord first rained it down.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. ON THE FASTS OF THE FOUR SEASONS

There are four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These seasons commonly call us away from the love of charity through their pleasures. During them we ought to fast, even if the time should fall within Pentecost, when the feast of the sevenfold Spirit is celebrated, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. IX, 15).

Augustine says concerning these fasts: “Although ordination is not being performed, it is nevertheless necessary for our religion to celebrate the fasts of the four seasons.”

Pope Leo says of the same fast in his Homilies [Note: [Col. 1227D] These words seem to have been taken from epistle 9 of the new Venetian edition, ch. 1.]:  “For the fast to be celebrated at the conferral of the sacred orders, the custom of the primitive Church has prevailed, as when it is said: ‘As they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the work of the ministry,’ and so forth (Acts XIII, 2). Then, after fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away.”

On this day, namely Wednesday, two readings are read, because those who are entering the sacred order ought to be admonished to have knowledge of the Law and the Prophets. For the Law and the Prophets flourished in the fourth age; and in that same age David, the most warlike, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” struck down Goliath, that is, humility struck down pride.

Against this Goliath—that is, the devil—those who are promoted to sacred orders must fight in humility.

On Thursday there is no office and no Mass; therefore the service of Pentecost Sunday ought to be sung.

On Friday only one reading is read, because the Law and Prophecy are recapitulated in the one Gospel that is read in the sixth age of the world.

## CHAPTER XXIX. ON THE SATURDAY WITH TWELVE READINGS

The twelve readings are said because of the twelve readers, since among the ancient Romans they were read twice, namely in Greek and Latin—for there are only six, if I am not mistaken—for two reasons.

The first reason is that Greeks were present, to whom the Latin language was unknown, and Latins were present, to whom Greek was unfamiliar. The second reason was the unity of both peoples. This custom is still observed everywhere at Constantinople.

Nor is it without reason that in each fast there are three days, since each season has three months, and one day of fasting is consecrated for each month.

[Col. 1228B] And why this consecration is celebrated especially on Saturday, Augustine writes to Januarius as follows [Note: [Col. 1227D] St. Augustine, Book II, Letter 55, chapter 10]:

> “The Sabbath was commended to the former people to be celebrated in bodily rest, so that it might be a figure of sanctification in the repose of the Holy Spirit. For it is written: ‘God sanctified the seventh day’ (Gen. 2:3); and because ‘the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit’ (Rom. 5:5), sanctification is commemorated on the seventh day.”

The consecration of a bishop, however, who is the vicar of the apostles, indeed of Christ, takes place on Sunday, because on that same day he deigned to enlighten the hearts of the apostles through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, on Saturday four lessons are read when the blessing is given, because [Note: [Col. 1227D] Amalarius, cited above, chapter 3] there are four orders of those who bless the Lord, as in David’s words:

> “House of Israel, bless the Lord” (Ps. 134:19),

that is, the Israelite people;

> “House of Aaron,”

that is, the prelates;

> “House of Levi,”

that is, the ministers of God;

> “You who fear the Lord,”

that is, those from the other nations.

In these lessons those being ordained are instructed by the examples of the holy Fathers.

The next lesson of the ordination is read from the fiery furnace, because no one can rightly approach consecration unless he passes through the furnace and there blesses God, as in the saying:

> “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels,”

and so forth (Ecclus. 27:6).

Therefore they must pass through the furnace, which is signified by the fifth lesson, so that, having been tested, they may be able to approach the sacred mystery, as is read in the sixth lesson:

> “Knowing that tribulation produces patience,”

and so forth (Rom. 5:3).

Concerning the responsories, there is no need to say anything more than that a responsory answers each lesson. The tract shows the gravity which the consecrated person ought to preserve, lest, perhaps, raised up in pride, he fall into the devil’s snare; for the tract is always appointed in connection with humility. In each prayer we ought to display humility of mind by kneeling, except during the octave of Pentecost.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] What follows within brackets was inserted into the manuscript used by Quercetanus; it is omitted in Amalarius, where immediately after the preceding words “during Pentecost” there follows: “Only in the lesson from the fiery furnace,” etc., as below.]

[The year revolves through four seasons, and each season has three months. Individual days are devoted to fasting for each month. During each prayer in the twelve lessons we kneel, except in the eighth during Pentecost. Only during the prayer concerning the fiery furnace do we not kneel, 489 in all four Ember seasons. But if the week of Pentecost falls in the fourth month, let the fast be observed on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.

**Wednesday.** Antiphon: “O God, when you went forth.” Prayer without “Let us bend our knees”: “Grant, we beseech you, that the coming Spirit…” Reading from the Book of Wisdom: “In those days Solomon said to the children of Israel: Love righteousness,” up to “has knowledge of speech.”

**Thursday.** Antiphon: “Send forth your Spirit.” Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “Our minds.” Reading from the Acts of the Apostles: “In those days Peter, standing with the Twelve, raised his voice.” Alleluia: “Come, Holy Spirit.” Gospel according to John: [Col. 1229B] “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” Let us pray: “I will meditate.” Over the offering: “Receive, we beseech you, Lord, the offering presented.” Communion: “Your peace.” Post-communion: “Lord, Holy Spirit, sanctify our hearts.”

**Friday.** Antiphon: “Let my mouth be filled.” Verse: “In you, Lord, I have hoped,” and so forth. Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “Grant, we beseech you, merciful God, to your Church, that, gathered by the Holy Spirit…” Reading from the Acts of the Apostles: “In those days Peter opened his mouth and said: Men of Israel.” Alleluia: “The Spirit of the Lord.” Gospel according to Matthew: “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God,” up to “nor in the age to come.” Let us pray: “Praise the Lord, O my soul.” Secret: “Lord, the sacrifices offered before your sight…” [Col. 1229C] Communion: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” Post-communion: “Lord, Holy Spirit, sanctify our hearts.”

**Saturday.** Antiphon: “The charity of God.” Verse: “Lord God of my salvation.” Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “Kindly grant the Holy Spirit to our minds, we beseech you, Lord.” Reading from the prophet Joel: “Thus says the Lord God: I will pour out my Spirit.” Gradual: “Our protector.” Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “By that fire, O Lord, we beseech you…” Reading from the Book of Leviticus: “In those days the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel.” Gradual: “Be merciful.” Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “O God, who for the healing of souls…” Reading from the Book of Deuteronomy: “Moses said: Hear, O Israel, what I command you.” Gradual: “Turn, O Lord.” Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “Grant, almighty God, we beseech you, that, instructed by secular fasts…” Reading from the Book of Leviticus: [Col. 1229D] “In those days the Lord said to Moses: If you walk in my commandments.” Gradual: “Let my prayer be directed.” Let us pray, without “Let us bend our knees”: “Grant, almighty God, we beseech you, that we may abstain from bodily feasts in such a way…” Reading from the prophet Daniel: “In those days the angel of the Lord descended with Azariah.” “Blessed are you.”

This blessing is followed, without any collect inserted, by “Glory to God in the highest,” on account of the solemnity of Pentecost. Then it is said: “O God, who [did something] for the three children.” Reading from the Letter of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans: “Brothers, having been justified by faith…” Alleluia: “The Spirit, the Paraclete.” Gospel according to Luke: [Col. 1230A] “At that time Jesus, rising from the synagogue…” Let us pray: “Lord God of my salvation.” Secret: “That our fasts may be acceptable to you.” Communion: “I will not leave you.” Post-communion: “Lord, Holy Spirit, sanctify our hearts.”]

Only during the prayer concerning the fiery furnace [Note: [Col. 1229D] Amalarius, cited above, at the end] do we not kneel, when Nebuchadnezzar was compelling the people to worship the statue which he had made, so that our prayer to the one God might be separated from the error of the nations. There is no prayer after communion over the people, because this office is frequently performed toward Sunday night, when there is no kneeling at all.

## CHAPTER XXX. [Note: [Col. 1229D] Hugo Menard cites this chapter in full, note 418. See Amalarius, Book III, chapter 38.] ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

Three Masses are celebrated on the feast of Saint John because he shone forth with excellence through three distinguished triumphs. He came for this purpose: to prepare the way of the Lord by the example of his conduct; this triumph is celebrated at his vigil. Through the ministry of baptism he became renowned in signs; the triumph of this ministry is recalled in the first Mass. He remained a Nazirite from his mother’s womb; this gift is recalled on the day itself.

## CHAPTER XXXI. [Note: [Col. 1230D] See Menard, note 499.] ON THE NAMES OF THE FOUR CROWNED MARTYRS

The names of the Four Crowned Martyrs are these: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus. Their names and feast day, having been neglected through carelessness, could not be found at all. Therefore it was decreed that in their church the feast of five other saints who are recited in the Mass should be celebrated: Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, so that their memory too might be celebrated together with those five. Later, however, their names were revealed. Nevertheless, the solemnity, as it had been established, continued to be celebrated under the names of the other saints.

## CHAPTER XXXII. [Note: [Col. 1230D] See the same author, note 493, and Alcuin, Letter 91.] ON THE SOLEMNITY OF ALL SAINTS

It is written in the Pontifical Acts that Saint Boniface, pope, cleansed a certain Roman building called the Pantheon, which had been consecrated in honor of all demons, of all its impurities and consecrated it as a church in honor of the holy Mother of God and of all the Saints. Hence it was established that throughout the whole world, on the Kalends of November, just as on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, the entire people should strive to assemble in church for the solemn celebration of Mass in honor of all the Saints, attending to this: that whatever human frailty had performed less completely through ignorance or negligence during the solemnities of the saints might be made good in this holy observance.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. [Note: [Col. 1230D] Amalarius, Book III, chapter 39.] ON THE OFFERING, “There Was a Man”

The historical words are contained in the offertory; the words of the sick and grieving Job are contained in the verses. A sick man whose breathing is neither healthy nor strong is accustomed to repeat incomplete words again and again. The author of the Office, wishing to bring the sick Job affectingly back to our memory, repeatedly repeated the words in the manner of a sick man.

The offertory contains no repeated words, because the historian, writing the history, was not sick. In the verses of the aforesaid offertory, however, the words are doubled, tripled, and multiplied. Job was scourged wondrously, and wondrously and uniquely praised among the ancient Fathers for the victory of his patience. Therefore it is not contrary to truth if his words are composed differently in the verses in which he himself appears to speak than in the other verses.

Job was struck like a lyre: that is, through swift repetition, pain followed pain and wound followed wound. While one news-bearing messenger was present, another entered. As one messenger delivered his reproachful report, another immediately followed. His pain was manifold, and in proportion to the multitude of his pain his failing breath repeatedly made the same sounds.

The author of an antiphonary is accustomed, either by the distinction of the chant or by the distinction of its arrangement, to display the various emotions of the saints. Thus, concerning John Symmysta, he did so through a neuma with respect to the meaning of the words “wisdom and understanding” in the responsory “In the midst of the Church.” In this he imitates, in a certain way, the ineffable Word, of whom it was said: “In the beginning was the Word.”

He did likewise in the order of the Office sung for the Mass of the Innocents, in which “Glory to God in the highest” and “Alleluia” are omitted because of Rachel’s weeping, which prefigured our mother, holy Church; or because it was the time when those who had suffered were then descending to the gates of hell, while the ancient Fathers awaited Christ’s descent.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. ON THE DIGNITY OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL ORDER

[Col. 1231C]

The dignity of the ecclesiastical order derives its cause and origin from Aaron himself, the first priest. He is called the first with respect to ordination. For there were other priests before him, such as Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, who, offering bread and wine to God, signified the form and character of the new, that is, evangelical, sacrifice. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as well as many before them, such as Abel and Noah, are also said to have offered sacrifices to God. Yet none of them is found to have been ordained or consecrated to the priesthood, or to have been clothed in sacred and mystical garments, except Aaron, who was the first to be anointed with holy oil at the Lord’s command and adorned with priestly [Col. 1231D] vestments.

The Hebrews, however, relate that before Aaron the firstborn were priests. Indeed, they maintain that Melchizedek was Shem, Noah’s firstborn, the priest of God Most High. From all the tribes of Israel God chose the tribe of Levi, and from that tribe he chose Aaron as high priest; his sons, however, were of a lower rank or order, whom we call presbyters. The others in the same tribe they generally call Levites, assigned to different ranks and ministries.

Some of them were doorkeepers, and these were in the first and lowest rank; in the second were lectors; in the third, exorcists; in the fourth, acolytes; in the fifth, subdeacons; in the sixth, deacons; in the seventh, presbyters; and in the highest and more excellent rank were bishops, or pontiffs. These were the eight ranks of divine ministry, concerning which perhaps the prophet Ezekiel says in his mystical vision of the Temple:

> “And its ascent was by eight steps” (Ezek. 40:34, 37).

Now we must speak of each of them and briefly explain what office they held.

Doorkeepers were those who were also called custodians or gatekeepers. As it is read in the Book of Chronicles:

> “They were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of the Lord, and they dwelt round about in their watches” (1 Chron. 9:26–27),

guarding so that no unclean person might enter the temple of God.

The order of lectors received its form and beginning from the prophets. Lectors, therefore, are those who proclaim the word of God, to whom it is said:

> “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1).

[Col. 1232B] Exorcists were those who, by exorcisms—that is, adjurations composed by Solomon—drove demons from the possessed, such as the seven sons of Sceva are said to have been in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 19:13–14).

Acolytes were those who were responsible for lighting lamps in the tabernacle of God, according to what is read in Exodus:

> “Command the children of Israel to bring you purest oil from olive trees, crushed by the pestle,”

and so forth (Exod. 27:20).

They attended upon all the other, higher ranks. Hence they were called acolytes, that is, attendants; for ἀκολουθέω (*akoloutheō*) in Greek means *sequor*—“I follow”—in Latin. Now in the Church they are called candle-bearers, from carrying candles. At that time, however, they could not have been called by this name, since neither honey nor wax was brought into the Lord’s sacrifice. [Col. 1232C]

Subdeacons were those whom they called Nathinaeans. They were under the Levites, serving and assisting them. Hence they were called Nathinaeans, that is, humble ones, or those who serve in humility. Nathanael belonged to their number; he is praised by the Lord in the Gospel, for he confessed that he was the Son of God and the King of Israel (John 1:49).

### The Three Higher Ranks: Levites, Presbyters, and Bishops or Pontiffs

The order of Levites took its origin and name from the tribe of Levi itself. They are interpreted as “the taken,” because they were taken on behalf of all the tribes and assigned to the service of the Lord. Although the others of the lower order also belonged to the tribe of Levi, this order of Levites was specifically designated as being under the presbyters; they were consecrated through the ordination of Aaron and his sons and kept perpetual watch in the temple of God. They carried the ark and the tabernacle and offered the fat of the victims to the priests.

491 The seventh order was that of the priests or presbyters, namely, the sons of Aaron, to whom the sacrifices and burnt offerings and every worship of the temple of God had been entrusted and committed. It was their duty to distinguish between profane and holy, between unclean and clean. Whoever, according to the Law, was to be cleansed or adjudged unclean was declared clean or unclean by their judgment.

“Presbyter” is interpreted as “elder”; those who were chosen were perfected equally in age and gravity of conduct, because in ordaining God approves character and wisdom more than age. [Col. 1233A]

The eighth order followed these: that of the pontiffs, who were also called the leaders of the priests. One pontiff was appointed over all the priests or presbyters, superior to all the others and placed, as it were, at the summit of religion, so that the others might look to him and observe his judgment and decree.

It should be known that at first one pontiff was appointed at the Lord’s command. When he died, his son Eleazar assumed the priesthood; after Eleazar’s death, his son Phinehas succeeded him in the priesthood. Thus, until the time of David, the heirs of the pontificate succeeded one another, one after another.

When David had decided to build a temple for the Lord and wished to increase divine worship, he summoned the entire lineage of the sons of Aaron—both those descended from Eleazar and those descended from Ithamar—and divided them into twenty-four groups, choosing one pontiff from each. As for the others who belonged to the lower priestly groups, now called the presbyterate, he ordered them to exercise the office of presbyters. Each of these pontiffs, with the priests subject to him, ministered for eight days, that is, from Sabbath to Sabbath.

Although all were equal in priestly rank, one among them, who seemed more worthy, was distinguished by special reverence and bore the title of high priest. King David himself also first appointed those who would sing the psalms in the temple of the Lord with measured voice, delighting the minds of the people by the sublimity and sweetness of the voice with which they were sung and kindling them more ardently to love divine worship. [Col. 1233C]

We have spoken of the eight ranks which were most carefully observed in the time of the Old Law. The Church received them in the New Testament, in a manner both better and truer, because all those things happened to them in figure. Since these ranks are well known, and everyone knows through frequent practice what belongs to each and what is conferred upon them at their ordination, it is sufficient to recall them briefly a little further below.

## CHAPTER XXXV. [Note: [Col. 1233D] Hugo Menard, note 660.] ON THE TONSURE OF CLERICS

The tonsure of clerics is said to have taken its origin from the Nazirites. When someone bound himself by a vow to afflict himself through fasting and the observance of other practices, he abstained from everything that could intoxicate him or disturb the state of his mind and was always in the temple. Hence he was called a Nazirite, that is, holy and consecrated to the Lord.

When the days of his vow had been completed, he came to the temple of the Lord, offered for himself what the Law prescribed, shaved the hair of his head and beard, and burned part of the hair in the flame of the altar. Thus freed from his vow, he returned to his home.

It is said that blessed Peter was the first to make this kind of tonsure for himself, in the likeness of the Lord’s crown of thorns—or so that clerics might differ from laymen not only in dress but also in tonsure.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL RANKS

[Col. 1234A]

“Clergy” (*cleros*) in Greek means “lot,” or the inheritance of the Lord. Therefore whoever reaches the clerical order ought to be God’s inheritance, because he must always take care to possess the Lord and to be possessed by the Lord, so that he may say with the Psalmist:

> “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5).

We read in the Old Testament that the Lord said to Moses:

> “You shall give no inheritance to the sons of Levi, for I shall be their inheritance” (Deut. 10:9).

Hence they are called clerics, because they belong to the lot and inheritance of God, if they live according to the rule. If they do not live according to the rule—like those very great clerics who entirely imitate the dress of laymen, girding on weapons and doing the other things which the canonical order forbids—such men are not clerics.

What, then, are they? Acephali, that is, “headless,” without the head of religion. “Canon” in Greek means “rule” in Latin, because it leads a person by the straight path to the heavenly homeland; hence the term “canonical.” “Regular” means that one ought to live according to the rule, that is, rightly in the holy Church.

A doorkeeper is so called from the door of the Church, because he must take care that no pagan enter the church in any way, since by entering he pollutes it. He must also guard whatever is inside the church, so that it may remain safe, because the keys have been entrusted to him and the care of guarding the church has been committed to him.

A lector is so called from reading, because he has the ministry of reading in the church. The book of the divine writings has been entrusted to him, so that by pronouncing the divine lessons distinctly and intelligibly he may please the people. [Col. 1234C]

“Acolyte” in Greek, “candle-bearer” in Latin, means one who carries a candle. Their duty is to carry candles before the deacon when the Gospel is read in church—not to drive away darkness, especially when the sun is shining during the day, but to signify that we have come from the darkness of unbelief into the light of faith, and to serve as a sign of joy, so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be held in remembrance of which it is said:

> “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

“Exorcism” in Greek means in Latin a word of adjuration or rebuke; hence an exorcist is an adjurer. Their duty is to lay hands upon those possessed by demons [Col. 1234D] 492 and, by invoking the name of God, drive the demons from them, saying:

> “I adjure you, unclean spirit, by God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to depart from this servant of God.”

As the canons state, no one ought to usurp this ministry except those who hold the same office—whether a deacon, subdeacon, or exorcist.

A subdeacon is a subminister, because he is under the deacon, that is, under the minister. His ministry is to assist the deacon: he brings him the linen cloth upon which the body and blood of the Lord are to be consecrated. He brings him the paten with the offerings and the chalice containing wine and water, because blood and water came forth from the Lord’s side. After the sacrifice has been completed, he receives from the deacon the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood which remain, to collect or carry them away. [Col. 1235A]

“Deacon” in Greek, “Levite” in Hebrew, is interpreted in Latin as “the taken” or “minister.” “The taken,” because he is taken—that is, chosen—for service at the altar; “minister,” because he ministers to the presbyter. He places the linen cloth on the altar and sets down the bread and chalice; if a deacon is present, the presbyter has no authority either to place or remove them. Just as the office of consecrating belongs to the presbyter, so the office of ministering belongs to the deacon.

“Presbyter” in Greek means “elder” in Latin—not on account of old age, but on account of dignity, honor, and wisdom, because whoever is a presbyter ought to be wise, so that he may understand what he reads, understand the prayers he says both by day and by night, and understand what he sings in the Mass: “It is truly worthy and just,” “You, therefore,” “Our Father,” and so forth—that is, everything together with the Creed.

Adam lived 930 years, Noah 800, and none of them was called an old man. Abraham, however, who lived a very short time in comparison with them—namely, 165 years—was called an old man. Why? Because he was wiser than they.

“Priest” in Greek [Note: [Col. 1235D] “Priest” in Greek, etc.; indeed, the word itself is of Latin origin. Perhaps read: “Priest: in Greek *presbyter*, in Latin *sacerdos*, that is, one who gives what is sacred.”] is said in Latin to mean “one who gives what is sacred,” that is, one who offers a holy sacrifice to God.

Presbyters have the power to catechize, baptize, and anoint the sick with the ointment of blessed oil. They have also been granted the office of preaching in the church.

Above them are the bishops, conspicuous in place and dignity, and likewise in exceptional holiness and learning. To them alone belongs the power to prepare the sacred chrism, sign the foreheads of the baptized, and bestow the Holy Spirit upon them through the laying on of hands. They have the power to bind and loose. Through them also the public absolution of the people is solemnly carried out on the day of the Lord’s Supper.

It should be known, however, that in the earliest times of the Church presbyters were also called bishops. Later, as a useful provision, it was established that this name should be given only to pontiffs, so that the excellence of the higher rank might increase and the lower order might recognize the limit of its own measure. Thus there should be a difference in names, corresponding to the more exalted place of honor.

“Bishop” in Greek is said in Latin to mean “overseer”: ἐπί, “over,” and σκοπεῖν, “to look attentively.” Hence *episcopus*, “overseer,” that is, one who watches over, because he must watch over the life of his subjects: how they believe, how they live, and how they keep God’s commandments. [Col. 1235D]

In ancient times very high towers were constructed in each city. Every city had its own tower, in which a watchman stood constantly, so that from a distance he could see whether an army was approaching from any direction. If he saw an army coming, he immediately announced it to the king, and everyone prepared for war against that enemy.

The bishop now bears the likeness of that watchman. Just as the watchman stood at the height of a tower, so a bishop and presbyter ought to stand at the height of virtues. For just as that tower surpassed the other houses, so the life of bishops and presbyters ought to surpass the life of their subjects. And just as the watchman announced the enemy’s arrival so that the citizens might prepare themselves, so bishops and presbyters ought to announce to the peoples subject to them the coming of the most wicked enemy, the devil, so that they may guard themselves and not be captured in his snare.

God appointed bishops and presbyters as watchmen of souls, according to what he says to the prophet Ezekiel:

> “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman to the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17).

“Antistes” means, as it were, “standing before,” that is, before the altar. Hence some wish to explain *antistes* in this way. It is better, however, to derive it from the verb *antesto, antestas*, which means “I stand out” or “I excel,” because he surpasses the whole people in dignity and honor. [Col. 1236B]

“Pontiff” means, as it were, “one who makes a bridge,” because by word and example he ought to provide a bridge—that is, a way—for others, by which people may pass to the heavenly homeland. A bridge is a platform constructed over waters.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Note: [Col. 1235D] Roman Order VIII; Mabillon, chapter 2, *Musei Italici*, vol. II, p. 86; Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 1372.] HOW A BISHOP IS ORDAINED IN THE ROMAN CHURCH

When the bishop of a city has died, another is chosen by the clergy or the people. A decree is made by them, and they come to the apostolic see with their chosen man, bringing with them a petition—that is, letters of request—that he consecrate him as bishop.

Then the pontiff orders him to be examined concerning four canonical matters: concerning *arsanoquita* [Note: [Col. 1236D] *Arsanoquita*, from the Greek ἀρσενοκοίτης, “one who lies with males.” In Baluze, at the place cited: “Let him question him about four matters, that is, about *arsenoquita*, which means one who lies with a male, etc.”], concerning a woman consecrated to God, concerning quadrupeds, and whether he had a wife who had previously belonged to another man—the latter being called in Greek δευτερογαμία, “a second marriage.”

If he is found blameless in these matters, he swears before the archdeacon on the four Gospels; then he confirms over the body of blessed Peter that he will remain blameless in these matters. The same is done with presbyters and deacons.

After this, when the pontiff is seated and the entire clergy is standing by, he asks those who brought him about his conduct and how many years he served in each rank. Then he asks whether he belongs to that Church or to another. If he belongs to another, he asks whether he has a letter of release from his bishop. When it is produced, it is read publicly.

After this the pontiff adds:

> “What did you think of him?”

They answer:

> “Chastity, hospitality, kindness, and every good quality acceptable to God.”

And the pontiff says:

> “See to it, brothers, that he has not made you any promise. We know that this is simony and contrary to the canons.”

When they answer, “God forbid,” the chosen man is brought before the pontiff and prostrates himself on the ground. The apostolic then says to him:

> “May the Lord protect us.”

He then asks him about his orders, instructs him concerning canonical authority, and says:

> “Since these good qualities are found in you, you will abstain today—today you will abstain—and tomorrow, with God’s help, you will be consecrated.”

Then he goes outside.

On the following day, which is Sunday, the pontiff proceeds into the church in full vestments, while the entire clergy and people await him. Since he is ordained on Sunday, whereas the other ministers are ordained on Saturday, this has been explained above.

When the apostolic enters the sacristy, the schola begins at the entrance with the antiphon for the Ordination of a Pontiff. When the entrance rite is completed, the Kyrie eleison is not said; instead, the apostolic immediately says the prayer.

While the singers continue, the archdeacon comes out with the subdeacons and acolytes, clothes the chosen man in a dalmatic or chasuble, and introduces him. The pontiff says:

> “The entire clergy and the consenting people of the city and its surrounding districts have chosen this presbyter or deacon for themselves to be consecrated as their bishop. Let us therefore pray for this man, that our God and Lord may grant him the episcopal seat to govern his Church and the entire people.”

Then the schola begins the Kyrie eleison with the litany. The apostolic lord, together with the chosen man, the bishops, and the priests, lies prostrate on the ground before the altar. When the litanies have been completed, they rise, and he blesses him.

As for the practice in which two bishops hold the Gospel book over his head, while one pours the blessing over him and the other bishops who are present touch his head with their hands, it is found neither in ancient nor in modern authority, nor in Roman tradition.

It should also be known that the other ministers are ordained after the entrance antiphon and prayer, whereas bishops are ordained after the responsory has been sung. As for the practice of consecrating a bishop after the Gospel, no Order prescribes it.

When it is time to receive communion, the pontiff gives him a *formata* and consecrated offering. After receiving it, he communicates at the altar; he reserves the rest for himself, to communicate from it for forty days. Afterwards, at the command of the apostolic, he gives communion to the entire people.

What the consecration of bishops was like in ancient times is shown by Jerome in his letter to Evangelius [Note: [Col. 1237D] St. Jerome, Letter 146, addressed to Evangelus, not Evagrius]:

> “At Alexandria,” he says, “from the evangelist Mark down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always selected one of their own number and, placing him in a higher rank, called him bishop—just as if an army were to make its commander, and deacons were to choose from among themselves someone whom they knew to be capable and call him archdeacon.” [Col. 1237D]

The archdeacon undergoes the same consecration as the other deacons, but by the election of his brothers he is placed before them.

Likewise Jerome, commenting on the Letter to Titus [Note: [Col. 1237D] The same author, on chapter 1 of the Letter to Titus]:

> “Before schisms arose in religion, and people began to say, ‘I am of Paul,’ and so forth, the Church was governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each person began to claim as his own those whom he baptized, rather than claiming them for Christ, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, so that the entire care of the Church might belong to him and the seeds of schisms might be removed.” [Col. 1238A]

Why a bishop should be ordained by three or four bishops is taught by Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1238D] St. Gregory, Book II, Letter 31]:

> “Let such men assemble who may either rejoice in the advancement of the bishop being ordained or pour out prayers to almighty God for his protection.”

Why one man alone is forbidden to do this, Pope Innocent shows in the Decretals, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 1238D] In the Letter to Victricius, chapter 1]:

> “Let no one bishop presume to ordain a bishop, lest the benefice appear to have been conferred secretly.”

Augustine, in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul* [Note: [Col. 1238D] Augustine, chapter 16, vol. 1, p. 308], brought forward this verse of Horace concerning the wise man:

> “Strong, and wholly smooth and rounded in himself.”

He continues:

> “From this it follows, rightly: for neither in a good soul do you find anything that agrees with itself more completely on every side [than virtue], nor among plane figures anything more than the circle.” [Col. 1238B]

We renew the upper part of the head with the razor when, with resolute care, we cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind. On the lower part we wear a crown of hair when we harmoniously bring into accord, with reason, those things which must necessarily be governed according to the world.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. ON THE INDIVIDUAL GARMENTS WHICH PRIESTS AND THE OTHER ORDERS USED IN THE OLD TESTAMENT

Now we must speak of the individual garments which priests and the other orders used in the Old Testament. There were eight kinds of priestly garments: the close-fitting linen tunic, the hyacinth-colored tunic, the *superhumerale* (ephod), the *rationale* (breastpiece), the *cidaris* (turban), the belt, the golden plate on the forehead of the pontiff, and the linen undergarments.

The pontiff wore all these during the sacrifice. The priests of the lower ranks, however, were permitted to use only four: the close-fitting linen tunic, the *cidaris* (turban), the belt, and the linen undergarments. The remaining four belonged exclusively to the high priest. [Col. 1238C]

Let us now explain each of them.

The linen tunic was the innermost garment, which we call a shirt or undergarment. It is called close-fitting because it clung to the body, and its sleeves were so tight that it had no wrinkle at all. Soldiers commonly wear linen tunics fitted so closely to their limbs that they are unimpeded when directing a javelin, stretching out a shield, or brandishing a sword. Joab is also said to have worn such a tunic, fitted to the measure of his body. In its place priests or clerics now wear albs.

[Col. 1238D] 494 The tunic was entirely hyacinth-colored and admitted no other color. It descended to the feet, like the linen tunic; hence both were called in Greek *poderis*, that is, “reaching to the feet.” It had the appearance of golden pomegranates and golden bells.
