It had no sleeves, after the fashion of a *colobium*, and was therefore open where the arms emerged.

In place of the hyacinth-colored tunic, our pontiffs at first used *colobia*. A *colobium* is a garment without sleeves.

These two garments—the close-fitting linen tunic and the hyacinth-colored tunic—were fastened with a belt. This was a kind of girdle made of twisted byssus, hyacinth, purple, and scarlet, embroidered in the likeness of a serpent’s skin. It was four fingers wide. In place of this belt, the customary usage now employs the belts called Roman.

The shoulder-piece, called in Hebrew *ephod*, was so named because it covered the shoulders. Its fabric, made of all the colors, was a cubit in size—that is, it reached as far as the girdle—embracing the entire area of the chest, and was open on either side for the arms to be thrust out. In the middle of the chest a vacant space was left in this garment, a palm’s breadth in size, where the breastpiece was inserted, which in Hebrew is called *essin* and in Greek *logion*. The shoulder-piece had on each shoulder a single onyx stone, and on the stones were engraved the individual names of the twelve patriarchs. Even now the ministers of the Church of Christ have a shoulder-piece, which we call the *amict*, when they minister at the altar.

The breastpiece, made by variegated workmanship according to the fabric of the shoulder-piece—that is, made in the same colors—was square, measuring a palm in length and breadth. It had four rows of stones, three distributed in each row; the names of the twelve patriarchs were engraved upon them. There were also golden chains, golden hooks, and golden rings, both at the four corners of the breastpiece and at the corners of the shoulder-piece. The chains were inserted through these and joined the breastpiece and shoulder-piece above, while below they were fastened together by blue ribbons. In place of the breastpiece, the supreme pontiffs whom we call archbishops now use the pallium, which they receive from the holy Roman see when the pope presents it.

The tiara was a garment, namely a little round cap, divided as though it were half a sphere, so that one part was placed upon the head and extended beyond half the crown of the head. It had ribbons which, when wrapped around it, were fastened together repeatedly so that they would not easily slip loose. This belonged to the lesser priests. The supreme pontiff, however, in addition to the cap, had a golden and triple crown, above which, from the middle of the forehead, there rose something like a golden reed, resembling the plant called in Hebrew *acano* and in Greek *hios*, which among us in Latin is called *cidaris*.

[Note: [Col. 1239] “Resembling the plant . . . in Latin *cidaris*.” Nothing sound. Sirmond, in the manuscript.]

Around its circumference it had flowers resembling the flower of the plantain, extending from the back of the head to both temples. On the forehead there was an open space where a golden plate was inserted, bearing written upon it, in four letters, the name of God. Such a garment is not found in the Roman Church or in our regions. For it is not customary for those wearing caps to celebrate the divine mysteries. Among the Greeks, however, this is said of those who wear caps—*cuphias*—on their heads while they stand at the altars.

The golden plate on the pontiff’s forehead, upon which “Holy to the Lord,” or “the holiness of the Lord,” was engraved, was a more sacred ornament than the other vestments. “Holy to the Lord,” which was engraved there, was the holy and venerable name of God, written in four letters, namely, Jod, He, Vau, Heth: []. It was called ineffable—not because it cannot be pronounced, but because it can neither be defined nor grasped by the understanding of any creature, so that anything worthy of being said of God might be said. A blue ribbon was tied over the tiara, so that the name of God might crown and protect the whole beauty of the pontifical adornment. Nor did the Church of Christ receive this form of ornament from them.

The eighth, that is, the final ornament, was the linen undergarment, by which they covered the flesh of their shame, from the loins to the thighs, or, more commonly termed, the *femora*, when they approached the sacrifice. Such attire is so familiar in our regions that Gaul has thereby received the name “Braccata,” or “Trousered Gaul.”

Having briefly explained the garments with which the priests and ministers of the temple of God were adorned in the time of the Mosaic Law, garments which the Church received, once the grace of the Gospel had been revealed, in imitation of them, we must nevertheless point out—not word for word, but in summary—what those garments mystically signified and by what name they are now specially honored in the Church. There are, however, other things which they did not possess, such as the stole, sandals, and the handkerchief customarily carried in the hand for wiping away sweat, which we call by its common name the *fanon*.

Those garments which were to be worn in the sacred offices were types of holy virtues, and therefore they were also called holy. For making them, materials were chosen that were not merely varied but beautiful: gold, signifying the splendor of divine wisdom; with which was joined blue, the color of the air, signifying heavenly desire. Purple was added, imitating the color of blood, so that the elect might understand that they must exercise themselves in two kinds of martyrdom: namely, if necessary, they should not hesitate to die for Christ, and in time of peace they should kill their desires within themselves, putting to death their members with their vices and lusts. Scarlet dyed twice effectively indicates the love of God and neighbor, which must be firmly maintained. Byssus signifies a twofold chastity, of body and of soul; hence the Apostle says of a true widow: “That she may be holy both in body and in spirit” (I Cor. VII, 34). Christ’s pontiff ought to shine with these ornaments and be adorned with these colors.

The linen tunic and the tight-fitting byssus tunic signify the mortification of the flesh. For byssus or linen, worked through repeated beating and drawn out, woven, and refined by the subtlety of its nature, becomes a garment. Thus no one can be adorned for Christ unless all the passions of the flesh have been chastened and put to death. Hence it is rightly called tight-fitting; for we call a chaste person “restrained,” whereas, by contrast, we call the wanton “loose.”

The entirely blue tunic, which shone with an airy color, signifies a heavenly way of life. It was entirely blue because the priest ought to care for nothing earthly. For the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who approved him” (II Tim. II, 4).

The girdle, or belt, by which this tunic, together with the inner one—that is, the linen tunic—was bound, signifies continence, which is the mother and guardian of chastity, and with which it is especially fitting that pontiffs be adorned. Whoever is ungrateful to God loses it, as Job says of such men: “He loosens the belt of kings and binds their loins with a cord” (Job XII, 18). For he loosens—or permits to be loosened—the belt of kings, that is, of holy priests, namely, their chaste continence, when they begin to become elated over their virtues; and he binds their loins with the cord of severe repentance, so that those who ought to have aided the falls of others begin to lament their own failures.

The shoulder-piece, called *ephod* in Hebrew, signifies obedience to the commandments of God. The priest put it on so that he might remember that he ought vigorously to carry God’s precepts, as though a burden had been placed upon his shoulders. But because he carried the names of the patriarchs during the sacrifices, both on his shoulders and on his breast, the priest is thereby admonished to follow the faith and examples of the earlier Fathers, to remember in his prayers the faithful, who are the children of the apostles, and to set before them those same examples for imitation.

The breastpiece, which was on the pontiff’s forehead, signifies that the shepherd ought to be endowed with wisdom and instruction. It is also called the breastpiece of judgment because the ruler of the Church must always distinguish good from evil by careful examination and diligently consider what is appropriate, for whom, when, and in what manner. For this is what is said: “You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment instruction and truth” (Exod. XXVIII, 36), so that he may possess knowledge of the Scriptures by which he can teach others and rebuke those who contradict.

It was square because of the teaching of the four Gospels; double because of the firmness of knowledge and works. Its palm-sized measure, which is the extension of the fingers, signifies discernment in perseverance in good works. The four rows of stones, engraved with the names of the patriarchs, express the four principal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The three stones in each row demonstrate faith in the holy Trinity, or faith, hope, and charity. By the form of this ornament, the breastpiece, we are forewarned that all these things must necessarily be present in the pontiff’s heart.

The tiara, also called the *cidaris* and the mitre, both covered and adorned the pontiff’s head. It admonishes him that he ought to consecrate all the senses of his head to God, lest either his eyes be open to see vanity or the other senses active in the head consent to iniquity, and lest pleasure admitted through them stain the holiness of his mind.

The golden plate is a figure of divine majesty and power. It was carried on the pontiff’s forehead because the ineffable power of the Godhead rises above all that it has created. Therefore, as though sanctifying all things, it established for itself an eminent seat on the forehead—that is, in the ruling faculty of the mind. The four letters written on the plate are the four horns of the cross, which embraces the whole world; for the summit of all creation is granted to the cross of Christ, by which the foreheads of all the faithful are marked. The fact that the plate always appeared to be on the pontiff’s forehead shows that he must always exercise in his works the dignity which he displays in his attire, so that he may always possess what pleases the Lord and always be worthy to offer the petitions of his subjects to the Lord.

The undergarments by which the shameful parts of the body were covered signify continence from sexual intercourse, which is commanded to be observed with the greatest care by people of every rank. Hence it is said to be “for covering shame.” It is shameful for a priest to be disgraced by the reputation of a wanton youth; rather, he ought to be looked upon and honored by all as though in the citadel of chastity. But the fact that they put on the undergarments themselves, while Moses prescribes the rest, signifies that each person [perhaps: each one] ought to restrain himself from carnal desire; thereafter he should adorn those subject to him with virtues as with garments, just as Moses adorns the minister of the temple with vestments.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. WHAT THE GARMENTS OF THE CHURCH SIGNIFY

Sandals are so called from *soleae*. They are a kind of footwear worn by the ministers of the Church: below, the sole protects the feet from the earth, while above it has no covering and remains open. The Lord commanded the apostles to wear this kind of footwear. It signifies that the minister of the word of God ought not to devote himself to earthly things, but rather to yearn for heavenly things and conceal his preaching from no one.

After the sandals, among the garments of the Church, comes the shoulder-piece, which is made of the purest linen. By linen, which is taken from the earth and brought to whiteness through many labors, the human body is signified, since it consists of earth. Therefore, just as linen is brought to whiteness through many labors, so the human body, worn down by many calamities, ought to be white and pure from every stain of sins.

Next comes the *poderis*, commonly called the alba. It signifies perseverance in good action. Hence Joseph is described as having had a floor-length tunic among his brothers.

A tunic reaching to the ankle is a good work carried through to completion, for the ankle is the end of the body. Therefore, the person who carries the uprightness of a good work through to the end of the required action makes a good beginning. “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

Next comes the belt, called the girdle, by which the *poderis* is tightened so that it does not hang loosely around the feet. It signifies the discernment of all the virtues. For virtues without discernment are not virtues but vices; virtues are established in a certain middle point.

The orarium follows. It is called an orarium, that is, a stole, because it is granted to orators, that is, preachers. It admonishes the one who wears it to remember that he has been placed under the yoke of Christ, which is light and easy.

The dalmatic, which follows, is so called because it was discovered in Dalmatia. The use of dalmatics was instituted by blessed Pope Sylvester; previously they used colobia. A colobium is a garment without sleeves. Its being without sleeves signifies that every believer ought to be trained for the practice of good works. When, as we have said, the bareness of the arms was blamed, the use of dalmatics was discovered by blessed Sylvester. It is a garment in the form of a cross, admonishing the wearer that he ought to be crucified to the world, according to the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

It also has fringes on its left side. The left side signifies the present life, which abounds in various cares; these cares are signified by the fringes on the left side. The right side, which lacks fringes, expresses the future life, in which no cares trouble the souls of the saints. It is also seamless, because in the Church, or in the heart of each believer, there ought to be no division, but an undivided integrity of faith. The left side has fringes because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things; the right side does not, because the contemplative life contains nothing sinister within itself. The breadth of the sleeves signifies the generosity and cheerfulness of the giver. A deacon who is not wearing a dalmatic reads while girded with a *casula*, so that he may minister freely; or because it is his duty to go to the court on account of pressing necessities.

The *mappula*, carried on the left side, with which we wipe the discharge of the eyes and nose, signifies the present life, in which we suffer superfluous fluids. The *casula*, placed over all the garments, signifies charity, which surpasses the other virtues. Concerning it the Apostle says, after listing certain virtues: “But the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII, 13).

[Note: [Col. 1243D] Amalarius, Book II, chapter 23.]

The pallium of archbishops is over all the garments, like the plate on the pontiff’s forehead. The pallium is nothing other than the distinction between the archbishop and his suffragans. The pallium signifies the torque which those who competed lawfully used to receive. This too was that plate, as I have said, which the supreme pontiff wore around his temples, on which the name of God, the tetragrammaton—that is, the name of four letters—Jod, He, Vau, and Heth, was written.

Its interpretation is: Jod, “beginning”; He, “this one”; Vau, “life”; and Heth, “passion”—that is: “This is the beginning of the passion of life.” Many therefore suffered before Christ, but none of them brought life to human beings through his passion. Christ, however, whose blood was poured out on the cross for the redemption of the whole world, brought life to the human race.

According to another teacher, Jod means “beginning,” He “this one,” and Vau and Heth together are interpreted as “life.” This can be joined as follows: “This is Christ, the beginning and the life.”

This name was called “the holiness of the Lord,” as it is written: “They made the plate—that is, they consecrated it—and wrote upon it ‘Holy to the Lord’” (Exod. XXXIX, 29). This is interpreted as “ineffable,” not because it cannot be uttered, but because it cannot be defined, as it says, and in no way can be circumscribed.

Stephen, a Roman by nationality and the son of Jobius, as is recorded in the *Acts of the Pontiffs*, established that priests and Levites were not to use sacred garments in daily life except in the Church. Hence Jerome, in Book XIV on Ezekiel:

[Note: [Col. 1243D] St. Jerome, Book XIII on Ezekiel, chapter XLIV, verse 18.]

“Moreover, religion has one garment for ministry and another for ordinary use and common life.”

We customarily use the handkerchief to wipe the discharge of the eyes and nose and the excess saliva running over the lips. It signifies the diligence of worldly thought. It is carried in the left hand to show that in temporal life we suffer the weariness of superfluous fluid.

The variety of sandals signifies the variety of ministries.

[Note: [Col. 1243D] Amalarius, cited above, chapter 25.]

The office of bishop and priest is nearly the same. But because they are distinguished by name and honor, they are also distinguished by the variety of their sandals, so that error may be removed from our sight. A bishop has a fastening on his sandals which a priest does not have. It is the bishop’s duty to go here and there throughout the parish; therefore his sandals are tied so that they do not perhaps fall from his feet. The priest, who offers sacrifices at home, walks more loftily [Amalarius: more securely]. Since the deacon differs from the bishop in his office, it is not necessary for him to have different sandals; he too has a fastening, because it is his duty to go to the court. The subdeacon, who assists the deacon and is almost engaged in the same office, must have different sandals, lest he be mistaken for a deacon. Sandals signify that the preacher ought neither to conceal heavenly things nor to yearn for earthly things.

The use of signs was taken from the Old Testament. In the Book of Numbers the Lord said to Moses: “Make for yourself two trumpets of beaten silver, by which you may summon the assembly” (Num. X, 2).

[Note: [Col. 1243D] The material that follows this chapter in Quercetanus has been separated and placed under a new title because of the difference in subject matter.]

## Mystical Explanation of the Ceremonies of the Mass

[Note: [Col. 1244D] Amalarius, Book III, chapter 5.]

Pope Celestine added to the office of the Mass and established that the 150 psalms should be sung antiphonally by all before the sacrifice. Previously this was not done; only Paul’s Epistle and the holy Gospel were read, and then the Mass was celebrated. We understand this as meaning that he selected antiphons from all the psalms to be sung in the office of the Mass, for previously the Mass began with a reading. This custom is still retained at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.

The pontiff, proceeding in the person of Christ, brings with him the prophets, that is, the deacons, who announce from the Gospel the life to come; and the wise men, that is, the subdeacons, who know how to arrange the vessels of the Lord and what should be brought first and what later; and the scribes, that is, the acolytes, who kindle the hearts of the faithful from Scripture. Incense proceeds in the thurible, signifying a body filled with a good fragrance.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] Amalarius, in the same place.]

After he has been presented to the church, he stands bowed down as an example of Christ’s humility, in which he became obedient to the Father unto death. In that elevation [Amalarius: inclination] he gives peace to the ministers who are on his right and left. He himself is our peace, through whom we are reconciled to God. He offers the same peace to the singers who stand behind, in accordance with: “My peace I give you, my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). To those present he gives it; to those absent he leaves it. This is what we customarily say: The bishop signals to the cantor, who changes the praise from the old to the new and begins to praise the holy Trinity, saying, “Glory be to the Father,” and the deacons, as though a chorus of apostles, stand humbled with him and say: “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke XI, 1).

Then two deacons in turn go from opposite sides to kiss the sides of the altar. When it has been kissed [perhaps: by this kiss], the peace which the Lord commended to them is demonstrated, when he said: “Into whatever house you enter, say: Peace to this house” (Luke X, 5). The altar signifies the hearts of the elect.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Amalarius, in the same place.]

Then, in memory of Christ’s passion, the singers recite a verse from the Psalter. The lower part of the psaltery is struck, while the upper part resounds; Christ’s passion receives its striking from below, while from above comes the sweetness of the resurrection. Then he kisses the Gospel, in which the two peoples return to peace. After this he passes to the right side of the altar. It is clear to everyone that Christ always lived the right-hand life after he rose again. The deacons then stand in order, in accordance with: “If anyone wishes to come after me,” and so forth (Luke IX, 23).

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Amalarius, Book III, chapter 7.]

When the bishop ascends to the seat, the candle-stands are moved from their places into a single line extending to the altar. The candle-stands signify the gifts of grace, through which the Church is illuminated. Their arrangement in a single line signifies the unity of the Holy Spirit in the individual gifts. It may also be understood simply as the orderly arrangement of the candles for the unobstructed course of ministering around the altar.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Amalarius, in the same place, and Hugo Menard, note 7.]

Telesphorus, a Greek by nationality and formerly an anchorite, established that the angelic hymn should be sung before the sacrifice. Symmachus, the forty-fifth after Telesphorus, established that the same hymn should be sung every Sunday and on the birthdays of the martyrs.

We pray toward the east so that the mind may be admonished to turn toward the higher nature, that is, toward God.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Amalarius, cited above, chapter 10.]

After the labor and work of the ministry, the pontiff ascends the seat in memory of the Lord’s ascension, and those to whom he promised, “You shall sit upon twelve seats” (Matt. XIX, 28), sit with him. Those who sit signify the members of Christ resting in peace; those who stand signify those placed in combat. The cantor holds the tablets without any necessity, in accordance with: “Let them praise the name of the Lord in the choir,” and so forth. This jubilation, which they call a sequence, signifies the time when speech in words was not necessary, but the mind would show one mind to another by thought alone what it held within itself.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Amalarius, cited above, chapter 18.]

Pope Anastasius established that whenever the Gospel is read the priests should not sit, but should stand around it [Amalarius: stand bent over]. The deacon carries the Gospel on his left arm, signifying temporal life, in which it is necessary for the Gospel to be preached. The two candles carried before the Gospel signify that the Law and the Prophets preceded Christ’s coming; the thurible signifies the reputation for virtues proceeding from Christ.

The singers, after the manner of the Levites who provided everything necessary for the tabernacle, seek water at the fountain and keep it covered until the time of the sacrifice; thus they offer it clean.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Amalarius, cited above, chapter 21.]

Pope Sixtus established the addition to the original hymn, namely, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” and so forth.

Augustine, in Book VIII of *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 1245D] St. Augustine, Book X of *The City of God*, chapter 5.]:

“Therefore a visible sacrifice is the sacrament of an invisible sacrifice, that is, a sacred sign.”

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Amalarius, Book III, chapter 32, at the end.]

The kisses are exchanged in the Church by these persons, and they compel no one to arouse any titillation of lustful suggestion.

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Amalarius, cited above, chapter 33.]

Pope Sergius established that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body, “Lamb of God” should be sung by clergy and people.

The body of Christ is threefold, namely, that of those who have tasted death and are going to die. The first is the holy and spotless body which was taken from Mary. The second is that which walks upon the earth. The third is that which lies in the tombs. By the portion of the offering placed into the chalice is shown the body of Christ, which has already risen from the dead; by the portion eaten by the priest or people, the body still walking upon the earth; by the portion left on the altar until the end of the Mass, the body lying in the tombs until the end of the age.

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Mabillon and others attribute this to Remigius of Auxerre, volume V of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, p. 185.]

## CHAPTER XL. [Note: [Col. 1246D] Another version: “A brief explanation of the Mass.”] ON THE CELEBRATION OF THE MASS AND ITS SIGNIFICANCE

The celebration of the Mass is performed in commemoration of Christ’s passion. For he himself commanded the apostles to do this when he gave them his body and blood: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXI, 19), that is, in memory of my passion. As though he were saying: Recall to memory what I suffered for your salvation, and take care to offer the same for your salvation and that of your own.

The Apostle Peter is said to have celebrated this first of all at Antioch. At that time only three prayers were offered at the beginning of the faith, beginning at the place where it says: “Therefore this offering.” The Mass is called *missa*, as though “sent forth,” or as though “a sending,” because the faithful people, not presuming upon their own merits, send to almighty God through the ministry and prayer of the priest the prayers and offerings which they desire to offer to God. They recognize him as mediator between themselves and God, trusting that through his prayer and intercession they may be freed from all evils, reconciled to their Creator, and strengthened in all things.

Or, as Isidore says, it is called *missa* from “sending out.”

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Isidore, Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 10.]

For at the time when the priest begins to consecrate the Lord’s body, the deacon is to say after the Gospel: “If there is any catechumen, let him go outside.” Since the catechumens are then sent out of the church, they are not yet perfected and ought not to be present at the sacred mysteries.

Or in another way the Mass may be called *missa* because it sends us to God. It does not begin with the apostolic or Gospel reading, although that is plainly the greater thing, but rather with singing and psalmody, so that the sweetness of the melody may first soothe the hearts of the listeners. Then, after the modulation of the pleasant song, the people, inwardly attentive in spiritual matters through compunction of heart, may receive the saving words of the Gospel with ardent devotion.

The fact that the people gather in church on the Lord’s day or on feast days is believed to be done in imitation of the Israelite people, who gathered at the temple of the Lord at appointed times. They worked for six days and were commanded to rest on the seventh from every servile work, though not from meditation on the Law. Thus the Apostle says: “Moses has in every city those who preach him in the synagogues every Sabbath” (Acts XV, 21). Hence it has also become the custom of the Church to recite the song of Moses every Sabbath.

What they did on the Sabbath—which was regarded among them as the first day of the week, because on it God rested from his works—we undertake to do on the Lord’s day out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection. For it is necessary that on the day on which the Lord rose again, the people of God, abstaining from rural labors, should be instructed how to live spiritually for God throughout the whole week. The person who has unceasingly cared for the body destined to die throughout the week should on that day take care of the soul destined to live forever.

First of all, the antiphon for the entrance is sung. *Antiphon* is translated from Greek into Latin as “reciprocal voice,” whether two people sing psalms alternately, changing order, or one responds to one. The Greeks are said to have invented this kind of psalmody. It is called “for the entrance” because through it we enter into the divine office, just as through a doorway we enter into the hidden parts of a house.

Then is added: “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” Blessed Jerome composed these words, at the request of Pope Damasus, for the division of the psalms, which had previously been sung without distinction. But when this was by no means sufficient, at the further urging of the aforesaid pope he added: “As it was in the beginning,” and so forth. The cantor says this at the deacon’s signal, as he also says “Kyrie eleison,” because the cantor is admitted to the ministry so that the office may be performed completely. For a priest without a deacon has the name but not the office.

The deacon puts on the dalmatic in the form of a cross, so that, as a minister of Christ’s word recalling his passion to mind, he may not forget that just as Christ was crucified for the salvation of the world, so the minister of his word must crucify himself to vices and desires for love of the Redeemer. The whiteness of the same garment shows that the minister of Christ, who retains the authority to preach the Gospel in the Church, ought to possess the brightness of chastity in both mind and body. It also has scarlet stripes, signifying the blood of Christ poured out for the salvation of the world.

As the ministers proceed to the altar, the Gospel of Christ is carried in their midst, out of due honor, like the person of a mighty ruler proceeding in public amid ministers preceding and following him. The candles preceding the Gospel also show that through the grace of the Gospel the world, which had been in the darkness of sins, has been illuminated.

The fact that this same procession with the Gospel proceeds from the southern side toward the northern region declares that the Lord Jesus Christ, who brought the word of salvation to the world, arose from the southern side. For Jerusalem, in which the Lord Jesus Christ first proclaimed the word of salvation, has Bethlehem to its south; from that place the Savior himself came, as it is written: “God will come from the south” (Hab. III, 3).

When the cantor begins “Kyrie eleison,” the acolyte places the candles in order from the south toward the north, indicating by this action that the almighty Lord has had mercy on the world, both in the south and in the north.

The reason why Latins pronounce “Kyrie eleison” in Greek and Greeks pronounce it in Latin is that some expressions sound more fitting in Greek than in Latin, while some sound better in Latin than in Greek, and also so that we may show that we are one people and that both peoples believe in one God: “Kyrie, Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy,” that is, “You who are anointed—not with visible oil, but with the fullness of divinity—have mercy.” For *chrisma* means anointing.

Then the priest begins: “Glory to God in the highest,” the hymn sung by the angels at the Savior’s birth. Blessed Hilary of Poitiers later enlarged and completed it.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] Mabillon reads this way in *Gallican Liturgy*, volume I, chapter 4, p. 29. In Quercetanus it read *postea actum* instead of *auctum*. On the author of this hymn, see Tillemont, volume VII, p. 467, and Rivetus, *Gallia Litteraria*, volume I, part II, p. 180. See also Hugo Menard, note 7.]

This too is done in imitation of the angels, so that we may show that on earth we worship the same Lord whom the angels also venerate in heaven.

Afterward the priest says: “The Lord be with you,” greeting the people and praying that the Lord may be with them, just as he deigned to say through the Prophet: “I will dwell in them,” and so forth (II Cor. VI, 16); and as the Savior said to his disciples, and through them to all the faithful: “Behold, I am with you” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

This greeting is proved not to have been composed by human judgment but to have been taken from the authority of divine Scripture, where it is frequently found in both the singular and the plural. In the singular, as when the angel said to blessed Mary: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke I, 28); and as the angel similarly greeted Gideon: “The Lord is with you, mightiest of men” (Judg. VI, 12). In the plural, as in the Book of Ruth, where Boaz is recorded as having greeted his reapers by saying: “The Lord be with you” (Ruth II, 4); and as in Chronicles a prophet sent by God is found to have greeted Asa, king of Judah, and his army when they were returning victorious from battle: “The Lord be with you, because you have been with the Lord” (II Chron. XV, 2).

Therefore the Church, having received this salutary greeting from the priest, both prays by returning the greeting and returns the greeting by praying. It asks that, just as he desired the Lord to be with them, so the Lord may also be with him, saying: “And with your spirit”—that is, “May almighty God be with your soul, so that you may pray to him worthily for our salvation.” It does not say, “With you,” but “with your spirit,” so that the entire office which follows may be understood to be performed spiritually.

The Lord is rightly desired to be with the human spirit, because the human being was created in spirit and rational mind according to the image and likeness of God, and there the human being is capable of divine grace and illumination.

The episcopal greeting to the people, by which it is said, “Peace be with you,” or “Peace to you,” was likewise not invented by human judgment but taken from the authority of Holy Scripture. In the Old Testament, the angel is found to have said to the prophet Daniel: “Do not fear, man of desires; peace be with you; be strong and courageous” (Dan. X, 19). In the New Testament, that is, in the Gospel, the Lord is almost always read to have greeted the apostles by saying, “Peace to you.” He also commended this same form of greeting to those apostles, saying: “Into whatever city or house you enter, greet it, saying: Peace to this house” (Matt. X, 12).

Rightly, therefore, the successors of the apostles, that is, the rulers of the Churches, also use this greeting, saluting the house of God, where all ought to be children of peace, so that the greeting of peace resting upon them may be fruitful both to those who give the greeting and to those who receive it.

Then he says, “Let us pray,” inviting the people to pray together with him. Therefore the people ought to incline themselves until the priest begins to say, “Throughout all ages of ages.” The Collect follows. It is so called from *collection*, because the things read in the Church are collected from the authority of the divine Scriptures, [Col. 1249D] as is that concerning the three children; or because one prayer is gathered from many utterances; or it is called so from the gathering or assembly of the people, who then come together as one. In all the Collects, therefore, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.” is inserted, so that we may understand that everything given by the Father we receive through his Son, whose inheritance we are. Through him, therefore, we offer the sacrifice of praise and prayer, through whose death we have been reconciled when we were enemies.

When the priest says, “Who lives and reigns with you,” he admonishes the people to believe that the Son of God lives and reigns forever, without beginning or end, and that he possesses one and the same power equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as well as one substance. [Col. 1250A] “Amen” is the people’s confirmation of the prayer. For it is interpreted as “truly” or “faithfully,” as though the people were responding: “Truly, we faithfully believe as you say: namely, that the Son of God reigned with the Father and the Holy Spirit before all ages, reigns now, and will reign in the future, and that his kingdom and power are enclosed by no end.”

Next comes the apostolic reading before the Gospel, not because of rank, but according to the practice of the apostles, who went before the Lord, as the Gospel relates: the Lord sent them before him, two by two. The Epistle is called *supermissa*—“sent above”—because it is sent over the Old Testament and the Gospel, not because of rank, but so that whoever has entered the Gospel may find there the medicine of salvation.

When the subdeacon begins the apostolic reading, the candles are transferred in the opposite direction, from east to west, to signify that through the voice and preaching of the apostles the whole world has been illumined by the grace of faith—not only from south to north, but also from east to west. For by the names “east” and “west” all the regions of the world are comprehended, and the sun illumines them by its presence for so many days, as in the passage: “They will come from the east and the west” (Luke XIII, 29).

Afterward the responsory is sung. It is so called because it is repeated from the beginning. Then the *Alleluia* is sung. Translated from Hebrew into Latin, it sounds as “Praise God”; for *Alleluia* is said to mean “praise,” while *Iah* is the name of God, one of the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews. *Alleluia* was first added in the New Testament when John said: “I heard a voice in heaven saying, Alleluia” (Apoc. XIX, 6). Because we have learned that the angels praise God in heaven with this word, it has been believed that God delights in this form of praise. We also sing it for this reason: to show that we worship on earth the same God who is worshiped by the angels in heaven. The cantor inserts it before the Gospel reading so that all may praise him through whose grace all are saved, as though he were saying: “Since you are about to hear the words of the Gospel that confer salvation, praise the Lord, by whose favor you have deserved to receive this grace.”

The Gospel is carried to the lectern, with candles preceding it, to show that the grace of the Gospel has illumined the world. [Col. 1250D] The deacon who is about to proclaim the words of the Gospel turns his face toward the north, to show that the Word of God and the proclamation of the Holy Spirit are directed against him who always stands opposed to the Holy Spirit and shares nothing with him. For while the Holy Spirit, who is God, desires to gather people into faith, the devil strives to scatter them from the unity of the Church and the integrity of faith.

Just as the south, which is a warm wind that blows gently, signifies the Holy Spirit, who inflames the hearts he touches with the love of charity, so the north, which is harsh and cold, signifies the devil, who makes those whom he possesses sluggish and cold toward the love of charity and affection. That the devil is signified by the north is shown by the Prophet, who says: “O Lucifer, who used to say in your heart: ‘I will sit on the sides of the north,’” and so forth (Isa. XIV, 13).

The deacon makes the sign of the cross on his forehead, as he is about to announce the words of life, to show that he is a disciple of the one who endured the cross for the salvation of the whole world. Then he makes it on his breast, so that every vain and impure thought may be driven from his heart. He also greets the people, saying: “The Lord be with you,” so that the Lord may cleanse their hearts of worldly thoughts and deign to open them to receive the words of salvation. In response to this greeting, the people make the sign of the cross on their foreheads, so that he may cleanse their hearts of evil thoughts and so that they may remain pure for understanding the words of salvation.

The deacon says: “The continuation of the holy Gospel according to Matthew,” because what follows comes after the preceding portions of the Gospel. Thus, when the beginning of one of the evangelists is read, he does not say “The continuation,” but “The beginning.” “According to Matthew,” or Mark, or Luke, or John, is said so that it may be known according to which evangelist that reading is being given. It may also be understood in this way: he says “The continuation” because the things that follow the greeting are contained in that reading according to that evangelist.

The Gospel then follows. Translated from Greek into Latin, it means “good news.” And what is better news than this: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. III, 2)? The Gospel speaks of the incarnation of the Son of God, his miracles, preaching, resurrection, and ascension, as well as the glory of the elect and the condemnation of the reprobate. When the Gospel has been read, the people hasten once again to fortify themselves with the sign of the cross, so that what they have received for salvation from the divine utterances may remain sealed and protected by the seal of the cross, lest it be emptied from their minds through the devil’s deception.

After the Gospel has been recited, the priest again greets the people, praying that the words of salvation which they have received from the Lord may be confirmed in their hearts. He invites them to pray together with him, saying: “Let us pray.” Although among us the Collect is not then said between the Gospel and the Offertory, it is nevertheless said among the Greeks. According to what is done among us, this may be understood as an order that the whole people should devote themselves to the offering, while those who are about to offer present their intention, so that their offering may be acceptable to the Lord.

The Offertory follows. It receives this name because at that point the people offer their gifts. The Verses follow, so called from *turning*, because they return to the Offertory when the Offertory is repeated.

Meanwhile the priest receives the offerings from the people, so that he, who is mediator between God and the people, may offer their prayers and vows to the Lord. In this offering water is mixed with wine. Christ is signified by the wine, and the people by the water. If wine is offered without water, it seems to signify that Christ’s passion profited nothing for the human race; if water is offered without wine, it seems to signify that the people could have been saved without Christ’s passion. Both, therefore, are mixed together, so that it may be understood that the world was saved through Christ’s passion and could not have been saved without it.

The fact that, while the priest receives the offering, the clergy meanwhile offer praises to God was taken from the example of the people of Israel, who were accustomed to offer their offerings and vows to God with the melody of praise.

After the offering, incense is placed upon the altar, while the priest says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight,” and so forth. This means: “Just as incense is pleasing and acceptable in the sight of the people, so may my prayer become acceptable in your sight.”

When these things have been completed, the priest turns toward the people, asking them to join their prayers to his, so that he may deserve to be heard for their salvation. This is to be said by the priest in silence: “Pray for me, brothers, that my sacrifice and yours alike may be acceptable to the Lord.” The people, therefore, inclining themselves, ought to pray as follows: “May the Lord be in your heart and in your mouth, and may he receive from your mouth and your hands a sacrifice acceptable to him, for our salvation and that of all. Amen.” Or let everyone say: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” and so forth, “may it become rich.”

The corporal on which the Lord’s body is placed ought to be nothing other than linen, since we read that Joseph bought a clean linen cloth in which he wrapped the Lord’s body. Linen also is a pure growth of the earth; and the Lord had a pure and true body, not an illusory one. Just as linen reaches whiteness through much toil, so Jesus Christ, having endured many sufferings, departed from this world and was brought to the whiteness of resurrection and immortality. Therefore whoever desires to receive Christ’s body within himself must, through many labors of good works and through purity of mind and body, make himself clean and white.

It ought to be folded in such a way that neither its beginning nor its end is visible, just as the napkin was also found in the Lord’s tomb. The napkin is a binding for the head. By the head divinity is signified, because God is Christ’s head. The folding signifies that Christ, who in his humanity had a beginning by being born and an end by dying, had neither of these in his divinity, but has always existed.

[Col. 1252D] The priest says the Collect over the offerings, and at its conclusion, “Throughout all ages of ages,” as above. Up to this point there has been the Preface—that is, the preliminary address and the address to the people. From here the exhortation follows: “Lift up your hearts.” The priest exhorts the people, as though saying: “Now that you have been sufficiently instructed and strengthened by the apostolic and Gospel precepts, direct your hearts upward from earthly cares to the Lord, so that I may be able worthily to offer the sacrifice which you have offered to me to be offered to God.”

The people respond: “We have them with the Lord,” as though saying: “As you command, we have our hearts lifted toward the Lord, so that he may deign to receive our vow.” He exhorts them again: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God”—that is, both I and you, with “for all the good things bestowed by him” understood. The people respond and affirm this, [Col. 1253A] saying: “It is worthy and just that we give thanks to him, the Lord our God.”

This exhortation that follows is said to have been composed by Gelasius. The priest affirms the voice of the people and turns to God the Father, saying: “It is truly worthy and just”—that is, just as your people respond, it is worthy, just, and right to give thanks to you. “Salutary”—that is, full of salvation—because it pertains to the salvation of our body and soul, if we praise him worthily.

After the people have confessed that it is worthy and just to give thanks to God, the priest leaves aside the people to whom he was speaking and now turns toward God the Father, beginning to speak to him as one present: “For us to give you thanks,” and this not merely for an hour, but always—that is, at every time—in prosperity and adversity, everywhere, that is, in every place.

“Holy Lord,” who rules over all things that are in heaven and on earth, and who sanctifies all things through your holy blessing, so that they may be holy. The Greek *pater* is called *genitor* in Latin. For God ineffably begot the Son before all ages.

God is called omnipotent because he can do everything that befits him. He cannot lie, because he is truth; he cannot die, because he is immortal—indeed, because he is life; he cannot change, because he is immutable. He is called omnipotent in doing what he wills, not in suffering what he does not will.

God is eternal because he had no beginning and will have no end, because he neither began nor ceases. The thanks that we ought to offer must be offered through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is mediator between [Col. 1253C] God and us and who is the high priest of high priests.

*Christ* in Greek is called *unctus*—“anointed”—in Latin. The Son of God was anointed according to his humanity, not with visible oil, with which kings and priests were anointed as figures of our true King and Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, but with the fullness of divinity and the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized.

Christ, however, was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit when, after he had been baptized, the Spirit descended upon him like a dove. At that time he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, the Church, in which the baptized receive the Holy Spirit. Rather, he was anointed with a mystical anointing when, at the coming of [the angel] to the Virgin Mary, her womb was filled with the Holy Spirit: that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was so united to the true God in the Virgin’s womb that it became one person with him. Hence we also confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.

The anointing with oil signifies the fullness of the Holy Spirit, because just as a body saturated with the finest oil is refreshed and, in refreshing it, makes it more joyful, so the grace of the Holy Spirit, when it fills the heart, perfectly restores it in the love and affection of God, drives away from the mouth all the sorrow of fear which it had first acquired through sins, and, strengthening it in the perfection of charity, supplies the joyful exultation of hope for eternal life.

Through this Christ the angels praise your majesty, because through him they were created. And not only do the angels praise God the Father through him, but also those heavenly powers that possess dominion and authority over the others. These blessed and exalted spirits, therefore, praise the majesty of God through Christ, as they are addressed in the Psalm in a call to join in gladness: “Praise the Lord, all his powers” (Ps. CXLVIII, 2).

They also adore the same divine majesty, as it is said to the Lord in Ezra’s hymn of confession: “The armies of heaven adore you” (II Esdr. IX, 6). They tremble as well, as is said figuratively of them in the Book of Job: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his nod” (Job XXVI, 11). Yet, lest this trembling be punitive for them, it is not trembling of fear but of wonder.

Since, therefore, there is such devotion among those who praise in heaven, such veneration among those who adore, and such trembling among those who marvel, let human beings consider this—human beings to whom it was said: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Eccli. X, 9). Let them hear the Apostle admonishing: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. XI, 12).

The heavens also, which were made through Christ, praise God the Father when they stir us to praise him. The powers of heaven and the seraphim also concelebrate—that is, celebrate together—and praise him with united devotion and common joy. For *celebration* is an assembly of the people in praise, and we call things *celebrated* when they are done in a celebrated, that is, very numerous, assembly. It is said for this reason: they concelebrate his majesty with shared, that is, joined, exultation, because, praising without interruption, they rejoice in turn in him and in themselves through him.

The heavens therefore praise and concelebrate this creator and ruler of all, just as the sun and moon, the stars and the light, praise him. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Praise him, sun and moon,” and so forth, “waters that are above the heavens” (Ps. CXLVII, 3).

In the hymn of the three children, all the elements are likewise summoned to praise God—not because mute elements possess the capacity to praise, but because all things, when rightly contemplated, produce praise, and the heart is filled by consideration of creation so that it may pour forth a hymn to the Creator.

Because it would have been lengthy in this thanksgiving to name all the orders of angels, which are found to be nine in the Scriptures, “powers” are placed after “heavens.” By this name all heavenly spirits are generally called, as in the Psalm: “The Lord of powers himself is the King of glory” (Ps. [Col. 1254D] XXIII, 10). And again: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their powers” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

Finally the seraphim are placed there. They are the highest order of angelic spirits and truly blessed, burning with incomparable love because of their singular nearness to their Creator. Hence they are interpreted as “burning” or “kindling.”

It should be known that *cherubim* and *seraphim*, when pronounced with the letter *m*, according to the character of the Hebrew language, are masculine in gender and only plural in number. But if they are pronounced with the letter *n*, as they are placed in the Psalms and hymns and in the present thanksgiving, they change into the neuter gender according to Greek declension. Just as we say “bright stars,” “beautiful groves,” and “pleasant shores,” so let us understand blessed *seraphim* in the neuter gender [Col. 1255A] and plural number.

[Note: [Col. 1255] See Amalarius’s letter to Hetto the monk in d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 331.]

But so that the prayer might be directed to the Father alone, although the whole holy Trinity has one divinity and therefore equal honor and glorification, the apostles, with the Holy Spirit ordering them through this, decreed that those who were striving to uproot the errors of many gods by preaching one God should, under the mystery of the Trinity, determine that supplication in the rite of sacrifice be made to one person. They did this lest those who preached one God be accused of having fallen into a plurality of divinity.

Since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exist as one Godhead, one nature, one substance, and, finally, one power, one of the persons is invoked in the sacrifice for the preservation of the mystery of unity. No other person should be invoked except the one who is first, in whom the other two naturally remain [Col. 1255B] present.

“With whom also our voices,” and so forth. The voices of the angels are voices in praise of the Creator, namely, the innermost wonder of contemplation. What, then, ought our voices to be, which we ask to be admitted—that is, brought in—before God together with the angelic praises? Certainly such voices are not in the sound of the mouth but in the desire of the heart. For before the most secret ears of God, it is not our words but our desires that make voices.

Since the heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, the holy Church, which is to be joined to them in heaven and is to remain with them in the praises of God, rightly now praises God on earth with the very voices with which the holy angels praise him in heaven. It does this not through proud presumption but through humble confession, that is, humble praise, desiring to believe and confess the majesty of God in the world as it is seen and praised by the angels in heaven. For this confession is not confession of sin but of praise and thanksgiving.

Thus, by one confession—that is, praise and thanksgiving—human beings are already joined with the angels, praising him concerning heavenly and earthly things as the one who made heaven and earth, and saying: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; they are full” (Isa. VI, 3), and so forth. These are the voices of the angels praising in heaven.

Isaiah testifies that he heard this hymn of God’s glory, and John likewise heard it in the Apocalypse (Apoc. IV, 8). Therefore, not by human decision but by the combined authority of both Scriptures, we say “Holy” three times and “Lord” once, to show that the almighty God has a Trinity in persons and unity in substance.

*Sabaoth* is one of the ten names of God among the Hebrews, and it is interpreted as “of armies,” or “of powers,” or “of hosts.” “Lord of Sabaoth” means “Lord almighty,” because every army, host, and power of the angels serves him. We rightly call the angelic spirits a host, because we know that they fight against the aerial powers. Yet they carry out these battles not through labor but by command, because they can accomplish what they desire to do against unclean spirits through the help of the one who governs all things.

“Full of his glory,” that is, of his divinity, are heaven and earth, and he fills all things, according to what he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth” [Col. 1256A] (Jer. XXIII, 24).

To this hymn of the angels are added words taken from the Gospel, spoken by the crowds praising God and our King as he came to Jerusalem: “Hosanna in the highest” (Mark XI, 10), and so forth. Thus the full praise is completed from the prophetic and evangelical Scriptures, when, after praise and glory have been offered to the holy Trinity, thanksgiving is also added for the Savior’s coming. He is one of the Trinity who became human for our salvation and completed that salvation by dying and rising again.

Therefore, rightly giving him thanks, we say: “Hosanna,” that is, “salvation,” “in the highest.” Hence the Psalm says: “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. III, 9). It is also rightly added: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” according to what he himself says in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name” (John V, 43).

The crowds take the verse of praise from Psalm CXVII. It is clear that the Psalm was sung concerning the Lord, since what they say—“Hosanna”—is the same as what is said there: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity” (Ps. CXVII, 25). Immediately, in the same words, it adds: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

The addition “Hosanna,” that is, “salvation” or “save,” “in the highest,” clearly teaches that the Lord’s coming in the flesh is salvation not only for the human race on earth but also for the angels in heaven. For while we, the redeemed, are led to the heights, the number of the angels—which had been diminished when Satan fell—is filled up.

Therefore “Hosanna in the highest” is rightly sung in praise of the one for whom the entire dispensation of the Incarnation appeared, for the fulfillment of the glory of the heavenly homeland. Up to this point there have been the Preface and the exhortation; from here the supplication follows.

After these praises and thanksgivings for the great grace of our redemption, which is enacted and proclaimed in that divine mystery, the whole Church becomes silent. When all verbal noise has ceased, only intention directed toward God and the devotion of hearts remain, joined with the vows and desires of all. The priest begins to pour out the prayer by which the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is consecrated.

For at that hour of such a sacred and divine action, the whole Church, through God’s grace, ought to enter spiritually with the priest, and the priest with the Church, into God’s eternal and heavenly sanctuary, with the mind wholly separated from earthly thoughts. Since God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John IV, 24), the same Father God should be entreated in this manner: “Therefore, most merciful Father,” and so forth.

For this reason, it is said, the custom arose in the Church that this supplication and consecration should be sung silently by the priest, lest words so sacred and pertaining to so great a mystery should become cheapened when almost everyone, retaining them through habitual use, sang them in streets and squares and in other places where it was not fitting. It is also reported that, before this custom had become established, when shepherds sang these words in the fields, they were struck by divine power.

The priest therefore says: “We humbly ask and entreat”—and this through Jesus Christ, through whom every supplication and petition of ours ought to be directed to God, as through the true mediator and eternal priest, who sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us.

What he asks and petitions is then shown: namely, that he may regard the gifts, offerings, and holy sacrifices that are offered as accepted—that is, pleasing—and bless them. It is the priests’ role to offer and invoke the majesty of God; it is God’s role graciously to receive and bless what is offered. Thus he says: “That you may regard them as accepted and bless them,” as though he were humbly saying: “We ask that you sanctify these things by your Spirit and bless them with your mouth, so that what is performed through the ministry of our lowliness may be fulfilled through the effect of your power.”

When he adds: “These gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices,” he is not speaking of different things, but praising one thing by different names according to its greatness. For the things offered upon the divine altars are called offerings, as the Lord says: “If you offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23), and gifts or sacrifices, as the Apostle says concerning the high priest: “That he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Heb. V, 1). But, as has been said, the repetition of the words commends so great a sacrament and arouses pious devotion.

These are truly holy and undefiled—that is, inviolate and uncontaminated—sacrifices, which are offered in the ministry of the Lord’s body. Or they are called *illibata*, “untasted,” because they have not yet been sampled but remain whole. For *libare* can mean “to pour out” in one sense. Thus we read that David poured out water to the Lord which had been offered to him (II Kings XXIII, 16)—that is, he poured it out. In another sense *libare* means “to taste”; hence something is called *praelibata*, “pre-tasted,” when it has been tasted beforehand.

The priest gives the reason for which he offers these sacrifices. He says that he offers them first—that is, principally—for the Catholic Church, that is, the universal Church. It was fitting that the holy offering should begin for the Church of God spread throughout the whole world, which has been redeemed by the one blood of the Lord.

“Which you may deign to make peaceful”: so that it may have peace from heretics and pagans. “To unite”: since it has been scattered by the pagans and the doctrines of heretics. To unite seems to be the same as to make peaceful; to guard seems to be the same as to rule. By making peaceful, he unites it, joining the hearts of all the faithful in his peace and making the minds of all the faithful one in will through charity spread by the Holy Spirit. By guarding, he rules it, kindly governing and directing it amid all dangers.

After the general commemoration of the Church, the words “Together with your servant, our pope” are added. The unity of this ecclesiastical body is thereby commended more strongly, because the Lord established the worship of religion in such a way that he placed it principally in blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, and willed his gifts to flow from him, as from a kind of head, into the whole body.

Hence it is clear that those who are separated from the communion of the whole world are separated from it, as blessed Pelagius teaches: those who, because of some disagreement, do not regularly commemorate the apostolic pontiff during the sacred mysteries according to custom. According to some, *pope* means “wonderful” or “crowned”; but the better interpretation is “father of fathers,” that is, of bishops.

Then follows: “And our bishop.” Just as the commemoration of the universal Church is joined, for the sake of the unity of fellowship and peace, to the commemoration of the apostolic pontiff, so it is worthy and religious that individual Churches add the commemoration of their own bishops, thereby proving through that prayer that they preserve with them the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace.

The orthodox are called “those of right glory,” because, corrupted by no error, they glorify God by confessing the right faith. Thus the worshipers of the Catholic and apostolic faith are the same. They are Catholic—that is, universal—because the whole Church everywhere preserves it; and apostolic because the teaching of the apostles established it throughout the world.

“Through Christ our Lord” is added because neither the prayer of the Church nor an offering to God can be made except through the one mediator between God and human beings, as he himself commends this in the Gospel, saying: “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do” (John XIV, 14). The Church preserves this form of petition in all its prayers.

When it is said: “Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids,” and then “and all those standing around” is added, it is clear that this is as though a particular place were designated in which, after certain people have been named individually, the commemoration of the others who are present in the church is also added.

At this point the priest is free to name individually whomever he wishes and to commend them by name to God. Alternatively, it was certainly observed by the ancients that the names of those making offerings were recited there. The offerings must therefore first be commended, and then the names of those to whom they belong must be announced, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other things that precede.

“Whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is known”—that is, you alone see in the consciences of those who offer to you how rightly they believe and how devotedly they love. In these words it must faithfully be understood that the whole Church offers that sacrifice of praise to God, since it is said of the whole multitude of those standing around: “Who offer to you.” What is fulfilled specifically through the ministry of the priests is performed generally through the faith and devotion of all.

It is called a sacrifice of praise because it is offered in his praise. We do not give him what is ours; rather, we return what is his.

“For themselves and all their own”—that is, for those who belong to them by kinship, family relationship, or any other condition under the profession of the same faith, both living and dead. The reason for which they do this is then added: not for any earthly desire, not for temporal profit, but solely for the redemption of their souls, because in him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.

“For the hope of salvation”—that is, for eternal life, which is true salvation. “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. VIII, 24). And not only for eternal salvation, but also for temporal safety—that is, bodily health. *Incolumitas* means wholeness of health. Both kinds of health come from him, that of the soul and that of the body, concerning whom the Psalm sings: “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. III, 9). “They return their vows”—that is, sacrifices, or vows of faith and pious devotion.

“Being in communion,” and so forth, “up to ‘and all the saints.’” He says that the one who offers and all those standing around, who offer together, are in communion, and that they venerate the memory of the blessed Mother of God and of all the saints. For the sacrifice may be acceptable to God only when it is offered in the communion and fellowship of the saints and in the veneration of their memory, as though in the true temple of God, because the almighty God willed the foundation of his Church to consist in them.

We are therefore in communion with their memory as children with their fathers and as followers with those who preceded them. “Being in communion” means participating in their faith, because we have the same faith that they had. “Venerating their memory” means following their footsteps with piety and humility.

In this commemoration of the saints, the blessed Mother of God is placed first, through whom both they and we deserved to receive the author of life. The commemoration of the holy apostles and martyrs is then joined to hers—not only of those whose names are expressed here, but of all those whose number and names we cannot know. Nevertheless, if through faith we piously adhere to these chief saints, we are also joined to those others through communion with them.

“By whose merits,” and so forth. For on account of the merits and intercession of the righteous, the Lord has mercy, so that in all things, whether prosperous or adverse, we may be fortified by the help of his protection, through Christ our Lord.

Thus Moses, interceding for the sinful people, makes mention of the fathers. When Hezekiah sought help, he was told: “I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (IV Kings XX, 6). Nor should it be doubted that the petitions of the faithful are known by the spirits of the righteous. For those who see the glory of God within should not be thought to be ignorant of something that exists outside.

The Church therefore asks the aid of the martyrs, yet it does not sacrifice to the martyrs, but to the one God of the martyrs and of us. In this sacrifice they are named in their proper place as human beings of God who conquered the world in confessing him; they are not, however, invoked by the priest, because he is God’s priest, not theirs. The sacrifice itself is Christ’s body, which is not offered to them, because they themselves are not this body.

“Therefore this offering of our service”: for it is fitting that a servant should serve his Lord; “and of your whole household,” and so forth. In these words the unity of the Church is shown, when in that offering common service is rendered to God both by the priests and by the whole household of the house of God.

God is therefore prayed to accept graciously this offering, which the Church brings to him alone in due service, and to order our days—which we live amid various dangers—in his peace. When the course of this mortality has been completed, may he deign to rescue us from eternal condemnation and number us among the flock of his elect.

Gelasius principally composed this portion—namely, the exhortation, supplication, and consecration. But blessed Gregory added this verse: “And, rescued from eternal [Col. 1260A] condemnation,” up to “through Christ our Lord.”

Up to this point there has been the supplication; from here the consecration follows, beginning in this way: “Which offering,” and so forth.

God is prayed to accept the offering placed upon his altars and commended by such great prayers as a perfect Eucharist through the power of the Holy Spirit, so that it may be blessed in all things, *ascribed*—that is, received into the number of things pleasing to him—and *ratified*—that is, established with immovable and perpetual firmness. It is also to be *rational*, so that although it is taken from the simple fruits of the earth, through the power of the blessing it may become the body and blood of the Son of God. Thus, through this food and drink, what he himself promised may be fulfilled in us: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; and whoever eats me will himself live because of me” (John VI, 58).

This body and blood are not gathered in ears of grain but in the sacraments; through consecration they become mystical for us—they do not come into being by birth. That bread and that wine are indeed irrational in themselves. But the priest prays that, having been treated rationally and consecrated by almighty God, they may become rational by passing into the body of his Son, for us—that is, for our salvation.

What follows next—“Who, on the day before he suffered,” through “You shall do this in remembrance of me”—the apostles used after the Lord’s ascension. Therefore, since the Church celebrates the perpetual remembrance of her Redeemer, the Lord himself entrusted this practice to the apostles, and the apostles, in turn, to the whole Church, in these words. Without them no language, no region, no city—that is, no part of the Church—can consecrate this sacrament, as the Apostle declares: “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread,” and so forth (1 Cor. XII, 23). By Christ’s power and words, therefore, this bread and chalice were consecrated from the beginning, are always consecrated, and will be consecrated. For he himself, speaking through the priests, makes his holy body and blood perfect by heavenly blessing.

When he says, “Take this, all of you,” this commends unity, so that, sharing in Christ through this mystery, we may all be one in him, as the Apostle says: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Cor. X, 17). So great is the Church’s unity in Christ that everywhere there is one bread of Christ’s body [Col. 1260D] and one chalice of his blood: “Taking,” he says, “this glorious chalice.” He says “this one” because the chalice sacrificed by the Catholic priest is none other than the very one that the Lord handed on to the apostles. For just as the divinity of the Word of God is one, filling the whole world, so, although that body is consecrated in many places and on countless days, there are not many bodies of Christ, nor many chalices, but one body of Christ and one blood, together with what he received in the Virgin’s womb and gave to the apostles. The divinity of the Word fills what is everywhere and joins it together, making it so that, just as divinity itself is one, so it is joined to Christ’s body, and his body is truly one.

[Col. 1261A] It must therefore be observed that, whether someone receives more or less of it, all alike receive Christ’s body in its entirety—both the whole congregation generally and each individual particularly. Christ’s blood is the new testament because it is the new love with which he loved us to the point of death in the final ages of the world. It is therefore the blood of the new and eternal testament because it renews those whom it frees from the old condition and leads them to an eternal inheritance.

It is called “the mystery of faith” because we must believe that our salvation rests there. In his providence, he gave us this sacrament of salvation so that, since we sin daily and he can no longer die, through this sacrament of his body we may obtain forgiveness. For every day he is truly eaten and drunk, while he remains entire, living, and undefiled. It is a mystery because one thing appears and another is understood. What appears has bodily form; what is understood bears spiritual fruit.

But since it is a mystery, how is it called Christ’s body and blood? Almighty God, taking account of our weakness—we are not accustomed to eating raw flesh and drinking blood—causes those two gifts to remain in their former appearance, while they are truly Christ’s body and blood, as he himself says.

It must also be known that it is not lawful to offer the same chalice of the Lord’s blood unless it is mixed with water, because wine belonged to the mystery of our redemption, when he said: “I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine again,” and so forth (Matt. XXVI, 29). Water flowing from his side together with blood showed that wine had been pressed from the true vine of his flesh together with water. These are the Church’s sacraments, without which one does not enter into life.

The offering of that bread and chalice is a commemoration of Christ’s death. It is enacted not so much through words as through mysteries, by which that precious death is impressed more deeply upon our minds. For this reason, as he was going to his passion and departing from the world through the glory of his resurrection and ascension, he entrusted this final sacrament to his disciples, so that he might fix the memory of such great love more firmly in their minds.

Therefore, “we are mindful,” and so forth, has the same meaning as when he says: “Do this in remembrance of me.” What could be done more worthily and profitably than that, by frequently celebrating these mysteries, the Church should remember the blessed passion that wiped away the sins of the whole world? For he not only died for us because of our sins, but also rose for our justification; thus, by dying, he destroyed our death, and by rising, restored our life.

We are also mindful of his resurrection, by which he stripped hell; and, when he was taken up into heaven and opened for us the way of ascent, we are mindful also of his glorious ascension. We celebrate the price of our redemption through the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood so that we may always meditate joyfully upon what the Apostle says: “You were bought at a great price” (1 Cor. VI, 20).

Mindful, then, of these things, both the priest and the faithful people offer to God’s glorious, exalted, and majestic greatness—not from their own possessions but from his gifts and endowments—truly “a pure sacrifice, a holy sacrifice, an immaculate sacrifice.” This threefold repetition is praise of so great a mystery.

But what sacrifice does the Church offer? Is it not the one she received from God: the holy bread of eternal life and the chalice of everlasting salvation? Eternal life is in this bread, as the living bread itself says of itself: “I am the living bread; whoever eats this bread will live forever” (John VI, 51–52). He explains that this bread is his body: “And the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” And it is the chalice of everlasting salvation because that blood was poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

“Upon these,” it continues, “with a propitious and serene”—that is, favorable—“countenance, deign to look,” and so forth. This does not mean that God’s countenance ever changes; rather, he makes his countenance serene and illuminates it over us when he reveals his mercy to us. God is therefore asked, with a favorable and serene countenance—that is, with the declared presence of his goodness—to look upon the gifts of his Church and to regard them as accepted, that is, pleasing, just as he regarded the gifts of his righteous child Abel.

Abel’s faith, righteousness, and acceptance of his offering are commended both in the Law, in the Gospel, and in the Apostles’ Letters. He is called a child not on account of his age but on account of his purity and simplicity. “And,” it says, “as the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, which he offered in the sacrifice of his only son Isaac, offering him as a burnt offering”—Abraham being not only the patriarch of the Israelite people according to the flesh but also our patriarch according to faith.

It further adds: “And what your high priest Melchizedek offered to you.” His name is interpreted as “king of righteousness,” and his priesthood and sacrifice are so greatly magnified that the Apostle says of him: “Made like the Son of God in every respect, he remains a priest forever” (Heb. VII, 3).

What is added—“a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim”—has been inserted to complete the petition. All this is prayed because, in the ancient sacrifices—the sacrifice of Abel, which was from the firstborn of the sheep, and the sacrifice of Cain, which was from the fruits of the earth—the faith of the new testament was prefigured. That faith, praising the Lord through the grace of innocence, is placed above the earthly works of the Old Testament.

In the sacrifice of Abraham’s unique and beloved son, his sacrifice was prefigured, of whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17); and the Apostle says: “He did not spare his only Son,” and so forth (Rom. VIII, 32).
