Melchizedek’s sacrifice was also such a true sign of Christ’s sacrifice that this was foretold from it: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

“Beseeching you, almighty God, command these things to be carried,” and so forth. Who could comprehend words so profound? Who could speak worthily about them? They are more to be venerated than examined. Nevertheless, blessed Gregory, a capable interpreter of so great a sacrament, speaking of them in one place almost ineffably, as of an ineffable matter, says [Note: [Col. 1263D] Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 58]:

“Who among the faithful,” he says, “could doubt that, at the very hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and the lowest are joined, earthly things are united with heavenly things, and one reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

The same man says elsewhere: “At one and the same time and moment, the ministry of angels is snatched up on high to be joined to Christ’s body, and he is seen before the priest’s eyes upon the altar.”

Blessed Augustine likewise says of that same sublime altar in the sight of the divine majesty [Note: [Col. 1263D] The text is corrupt. In Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm XLII*, it reads: “For there is a certain sublime invisible altar, to which the unjust does not approach; only he approaches that altar who approaches this one securely. There he will find his life who, at this one, discerns his case.”]:

“There is a certain invisible altar of God, to which the one who approaches this altar securely does not approach. There he finds his life who at this one discerns his case.”

These statements are drawn from the Fathers’ words so that no one might think carnally that there is a bodily altar in heaven. Rather, we should understand the sublime altar of God, rational and intelligible, to exist in the chosen and rational creature—namely, the angelic and human creature. In the holy angels, from the time they were created, exalted in the contemplation of God and united to one another through Christ, it exists as the true and sublime altar of God. From it it receives the everlasting sacrifice of praise and the offering of rejoicing.

To this unity the whole multitude of the elect is joined now through faith and in the future through the vision of divine contemplation. Something ineffable therefore takes place in this offering also: through the ministry of angels, as though from a sublime altar, it is offered to the divine majesty, since Christ should be believed to be present with the heavenly ministers standing by, in order to consecrate what has been offered.

Hence blessed Ambrose says: “Do not doubt that an angel is present when Christ is present and Christ is sacrificed.” Through these mysteries he fills the hearts of the faithful with every heavenly blessing and grace, granting chastity to their bodies, faith to their minds, and purity to their thoughts.

“Remember also, Lord, your servants and handmaids,” and so forth. The devout mother Church also prays for her dead and commends them through the intercession of the sacred offering, firmly believing that the precious blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins benefits not only the salvation of the living but also that of the dead.

The faithful who depart from the body go before God, but they are not left behind by the Church. They go before with the sign of faith, because they were reborn through water and the Holy Spirit and marked with Christ’s cross. They sleep, as those who will truly be raised in the resurrection, in the sleep of peace, because they were not separated from the unity of Christ and the Church either by heresies or by mortal sins. Even if they had once been involved in such sins, they were healed through repentance, so that, through the prayer of the Church—to which it was said, “Whatever you loose shall be loosed” (Matt. XVI, 19)—they were reconciled and joined to the mystery of redemption. They died in peace through the mercy of him who does not desire the death of a sinner, and so forth.

For the souls of the pious dead are not separated from the Church. Otherwise their memory would not be made at the altar during the consecration of Christ’s body. After the words “in the sleep of peace,” therefore, the custom of the ancients was—and the Roman Church still does so today—that the names of the dead should immediately be read from the diptychs, that is, tablets. After the reading of the names, the following words were added:

“Grant to them”—namely, those whose names are remembered—“and to all who rest in Christ, a place of refreshment, where the heat of punishments is not felt; and of light,” of which the Psalmist says, “I shall be pleasing before God,” and so forth (Ps. LV, 13); “and of peace,” in which the souls of the saints rest, as it is written: “But they are in peace” (Wis. III, 3).

“And to us sinners, your servants,” and so forth. Although we ought always to acknowledge from the heart that we are sinners, we must confess this most especially when the sacred mystery is celebrated, together with the grace of forgiveness and the remission of sins. With humility and contrition of heart we must say to God: “And to us sinners,” hoping not in any merits of our own but in the abundance of his mercies, may he deign to grant some share and fellowship with his holy apostles, martyrs, and all the saints.

Thus, according to our measure, we who are now joined to them through the communion of faith, whose memory we venerate, and in whose communion and unity we celebrate these mysteries, may in the future receive with them a share in eternal blessedness. We ask that God’s goodness introduce us into their fellowship—not as one who assesses our merit but as the giver of forgiveness—so that, because we cannot be joined to the fellowship of the saints by merit, we may be joined to it through pardon.

At the end of the prayer, what we are to hope for and obtain is added through him, and immediately the conclusion of the entire consecration follows: “Through whom, Lord, you always create all these good things,” and so forth, through “Amen.”

Through Christ, God the Father created all these things not only at the beginning, by bringing them into being, but also continually creates them by propagating and restoring them. They are good because everything created by God is very good. He creates them and, when they have been offered in his sight, sanctifies them, so that what was simple creation may become sacrament. He gives them life, so that they may be mysteries of life, and blesses them with every heavenly blessing, enriching them with grace.

Through that same one, who sanctifies together with him and has given us such healthful nourishment from his body and blood; through him as the true mediator of God and human beings; with him as one equal to the Father; in him as one truly consubstantial with the Father—through him all honor and glory belong to God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son and possesses with the Father and the Son the unity of the Godhead.

Thus we are taught that in the Father there is authority, in the Son birth, in the Holy Spirit the communion of the Father and the Son, and in the three equality.

“For ever and ever.” They are called “ages of ages” as though they were ages remaining in the firm stability of God’s wisdom, producing the ages of those things that pass with time. Or “ages of ages” may simply be understood as what follows from what precedes, joined together in continuous connection, until the present age—which is woven from the various ages of time—comes to an end and the age to come succeeds it, an age without end, where God will be seen and praised without end.

“Amen,” which is answered by the whole Church, is interpreted as “true.” For the faithful answer this at the completion of so great a mystery, as they do in every lawful prayer, and by their response they seem to subscribe to it.

The priest then adds and says: “Let us pray.” The Church prays together with the priest, not with the voice but with the heart. There is silence, and the breast cries out to God in God’s ears: “Instructed by saving commandments.”

This is the saving commandment—that is, the commandment directed toward our salvation—by which the only-begotten Son taught us to speak. Through the washing of regeneration and the Spirit of adoption, he made us children of God and instructed us, not by human but by divine teaching, so that we might dare to say to God, “Our Father.” He taught us, saying: “Thus you shall pray: Our Father, who are in heaven,” and so forth (Matt. VI, 9).

Instructed, therefore, by divine teaching, not with the rashness of presumption but with the devotion of obedience, we dare to say to God the Father: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” and so forth. This petition is called the Lord’s Prayer because the Lord taught it; it is a prayer from the Lord.

The disciples asked the Lord to teach them how they ought to pray. The Lord said to them: “It is not necessary for you to speak at length in prayer, because the almighty One knows what is necessary before you ask him” (ibid., 7). Then he said to them: “When you pray, say: Our Father.”

“Father” is derived from *patrando*, that is, “bringing to completion.” Therefore, whoever invokes God as Father must prepare himself to be worthy to be called his son. If he calls him Father unjustly, he will receive judgment for that unjust invocation. For just as a son imitates a good father, as Isaac imitated Abraham and Jacob Isaac, so we who call God Father must imitate his holiness as good children, so that we may be holy and immaculate, according to what he himself says: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (1 Pet. I, 16).

At first the almighty Father was the Father of the Jews, according to what he himself says through the Prophet: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV, 22), and, “I nourished and exalted children, but they despised me” (Isa. I, 2). But what happened? Because of their unbelief he ceased to be their Father. Through his mercy he became our Father through faith and love, and to him we pray daily, saying, “Our Father.”

The almighty is called Father in two ways: either because he brought us into being—that is, created us—and formed us in our mothers’ wombs from flesh and soul, from the seed of man and woman, when we did not exist; or because he caused us to be reborn from water and the Holy Spirit when we were lost. The first birth made us children of transgression; the second, by forgiving all our sins, both original and actual, made us children of reconciliation.

Such is God, our Father.

“Who are in heaven.” The Psalmist says to God: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8). Even if it could happen that I had wings and flew to the farthest parts of the sea, there I would find you. And the Lord says through the Prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 24).

He is higher than heaven, deeper than the abyss, broader than earth, and longer than the sea. If he is everywhere through the fullness of his divinity and not through extension, why does he say specifically that he is in heaven? Because by “heaven” are understood the angels and righteous human beings, in whom God dwells most fully, according to what is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” “Our Father, who are in heaven” therefore means: You who dwell in the angels, whose dwelling is heaven, and in righteous human beings.

“Hallowed be your name.” God’s name is holy in itself. Why, then, do we say, “Hallowed be your name”? When we were reborn from water and the Holy Spirit at baptism, we were sanctified in the name of almighty God, when the priest said: “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” We therefore pray that the holiness then brought about in us at baptism through the invocation of God may remain in us forever, so that we may not pollute it but always remain holy. Just as we were then made holy, so may we remain holy perpetually.

Or, alternatively, “Hallowed be your name” may mean: May we understand how great the holiness of your name is; may it be held holy in all our works, so that, while we remember your holiness, we may fear to sin.

Or, alternatively: Suppose there is a good Christian who does good works. A pagan or a Jew sees this and says: “Blessed is the God who has such a servant.” God’s name is sanctified—that is, praised—through that good Christian. Conversely, an evil person is seen by a pagan doing evil, and the pagan says: “Look, there is a bad Christian; we are better than he.” Through that person the name is blasphemed, according to what Paul says: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. II, 24).

We therefore pray that God’s name may be sanctified—that is, praised and glorified—in our work. Whatever good we do is referred to his praise; whatever evil we do is referred to his dishonor.

“Your kingdom come.” Almighty God always reigns in heaven and on earth, but we do not now know how he reigns. Therefore we pray that his kingdom may come. What is this kingdom of God? Eternal blessedness, of which he will say to the elect: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matt. XXV, 34). We pray that this kingdom may come; the day of judgment must be prepared for with great care.

Or, alternatively: Almighty God reigns in his elect through hope, faith, love, and the other good things. Conversely, the devil reigns through lust, drunkenness, hatred, and other evils. We therefore pray the Lord to reign in us through righteousness, and not the devil through sin.

“Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” As in heaven—that is, in the angels who have never sinned—your good will exists and you regard their service as acceptable, so may your good will be done among human beings on earth, so that their service may please you.

Or, alternatively: By heaven is understood the Lord Jesus Christ, and by earth the holy Church. We know that just as a man comes from a woman, so heaven comes from earth [Note: [Col. 1267D] The passage is corrupt.]. From him it receives all its abundance. Likewise, whatever good the holy Church possesses, she receives from her husband Christ, according to what is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James I, 17).

“Let your will be done” is said to God the Father. As your will is in heaven—that is, in Christ—so may it be done on earth—that is, in the Church, which is his body.

Or: As your will is in heaven—that is, in righteous human beings—so may it be done on earth—that is, in sinners, so that through repentance they may become able to please you.

Or: “Your will be done, as in heaven”—that is, in our minds—“so on earth”—that is, in our bodies.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” *Pan* is Greek; in Latin it means “the whole” or “all”; from *pan* the word *panis*, “bread,” is derived. Therefore, by “bread” we can understand everything necessary, both food and drink, clothing, and every bodily support. It is called “daily bread” because it is necessary for us each day.

“Give us this day our daily bread” means: Grant us everything necessary for our sustenance and clothing—that is, everything necessary for our life—throughout the whole time of our life.

Or, alternatively: Here we can understand “bread” as the Lord’s body and blood, of which he says elsewhere: “Unless someone eats,” and so forth (John VI, 54). We pray that he may give us his flesh and blood to receive, so that through what we visibly receive we may be able to receive within us what we do not see, namely, almighty God, according to what he himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., 55).

The word “today” cannot generally be referred to the Lord’s body and blood, because there are people who cannot receive communion every day, either because they have been defiled by some discord with their neighbor or polluted by nocturnal emission. They are human beings and cannot always be prepared. Conversely, there are people who can receive communion every day. For them what the Lord said to Zacchaeus comes true: “Today I must remain in your house” (Luke XIX, 5). He received him joyfully into his house, because such people ought to receive the Lord’s body and blood with joy.

Those who cannot receive communion every day can say with the centurion: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof today” (Matt. VIII, 5)—you will enter on another day.

There are also people who do not wish to depart from their iniquity and abstain from the Lord’s body and blood under the pretext of humility. Blessed Augustine preached to such people: “Brothers, I am pleased with your humility, that you fear approaching the Lord’s body and blood; but it would be better for you to depart from your iniquities and, made clean through repentance, receive the Lord’s body and blood. As long as you do not approach, I am not pleased.”

Let us give another interpretation: “Our daily bread.” By “bread” we can understand the divine utterances, the knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, the Psalms, and the Gospel. “Give us this day our daily bread” means: Throughout the whole time of our life, refresh us with the teaching of the holy Scriptures. Just as the body is refreshed by bodily food, so the soul is refreshed by spiritual food toward love and knowledge of him.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Here “debts” means sins. We are debtors to God in two ways: either by doing what he forbade to be done or by failing to do what he commanded to be done.

He says in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII, 37). Do we not love God and our neighbor as he commands? We are debtors—that is, sinners.

He says: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth” (Matt. XV, 4). Do we not do this? We are debtors—that is, sinners.

These are the things the Lord commands to be done: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not swear falsely.” Do we not do the things the Lord forbade? We are debtors—that is, we sin by committing such great offenses against God’s commandments.

It is therefore necessary that, if we wish the Lord to forgive these things to us, we forgive from the heart a brother who sins against us or does us harm. Against him also we are sinners in two ways: either by doing what the Lord forbade—namely, if we unjustly scourge him or take away his property—or by failing to do what the Lord commanded, namely, if we do not love him and do not forgive what he commits against us.

If, then, we forgive him, we shall truly be able to say to God: “Forgive us our debts.” The meaning is: “Almighty God, as we forgive those who have sinned against us, so forgive us.” But if we do not forgive them, neither will he forgive us the sins we have committed against his commandments, because he himself said: “If you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI, 15).

“And do not lead us into temptation.” There is one temptation that concerns testing, of which Moses says to the Israelite people: “The Lord your God tests”—that is, proves—“you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII, 3). The Psalmist likewise says: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. XXV, 2). By this temptation God tested Abraham, and he was found faithful.

There is another temptation that concerns deception and destruction, of which the Apostle James says: “God tempts no one” (James I, 13)—namely, for the purpose of destroying him. The devil tempts by this temptation, in order to deceive and destroy. We pray that God may not allow us to be tempted beyond what our weakness can endure.

God is said to lead someone into temptation when he does not free him from temptation. Thus we read concerning Pharaoh: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. IX, 12). This means nothing other than that he did not soften his heart, which had become hardened.

“But deliver us from evil”—that is, from the devil, from the punishments of hell, and from every adversity of this age. “Amen” is the seal of this prayer, just as a seal confirms a document. It is as though the one who chants this prayer says to God: “Certainly, what I have said up to this point is true. If, then, I forgive the one who has sinned against me, you will forgive what I have done against your commandment; but if I do not forgive, neither will you forgive me.”

There are seven petitions in this prayer. The first three concern the soul and eternal life; [508] the final four concern the body and the present age. The sanctification of God’s name, his kingdom, and his good will will be perfected in the elect in the life to come.

But bread, forgiveness of sins, not being led into temptation, and deliverance from the devil and every adversity of this age are necessary for us in the present. In the future life there will be no hunger, but the elect will have eternal fullness from the contemplation of almighty God. In this life, however, bread is necessary, as is forgiveness, because here we sin; and here it is necessary for us to be delivered from the devil’s temptation and the tribulation of this age.

After the Lord’s Prayer, the whole Church pours out prayers to God for the completion of so great a mystery. At its conclusion the priest follows and says: “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord,” and so forth.

“Past evils” means sins already committed. Although the action has now ceased in us, guilt remains unless it is erased by God’s forgiveness. “Present evils” means daily sins in the soul, as well as the various illnesses and afflictions that often come upon the body, and the countless calamities that assail us from outside. Whenever we suffer these things, we ought to implore the help of him who alone, in his goodness, creates both souls and bodies.

“Future evils” means whatever may happen to us, whether through the devil’s temptations or through the miseries of the world. The Church therefore prays that what was said at the end of the prayer—“deliver us from evil”—may be granted to us through God’s mercy, so that we may be delivered from all evils that either happened to us in the past, are happening in the present, or are feared as possible in the future.

It follows: “and with the intercession on our behalf,” through “secure.” When the people of Israel were held in Babylonian captivity, the Lord commanded them to pray for the peace of that city: “In its peace,” he says, “shall be your peace.” The Apostle also urges that prayers be made for all people, for kings, and for those in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life.

Following this pattern, the faithful people, pilgrims in this age as though captives in Babylon and longing for their heavenly homeland, pray also for temporal peace, so that it may not obstruct spiritual peace. When all adversities have been removed through God’s goodness, the Church may lead a quiet and peaceful life.

She asks this by naming only a very few but highly eminent saints, so that, with the Mother of God interceding first—through whom salvation arose for us—and with the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, we may be found worthy to obtain it.

In this petition the other saints are not omitted; rather, by commemorating these, all their intercessions are sought. For all are so united with one another in God, and all desire and pray so earnestly for the salvation of human beings, that in the one all are regarded equally, and in the one all are equally disregarded.

When it says, “Graciously grant peace in our days,” it follows the example of Hezekiah. When he heard from the Prophet of the evils of the coming captivity, he replied: “Let there be peace and truth in my days” (2 Kings XX, 19), leaving the future to God’s judgment and praying concerning the present, which concerned his own salvation and that of the people.

Likewise, the Church prays for peace in our days. After us others, and after them still others, will pray in the same way until the end of the world. Why she asks for this peace she adds immediately: namely, “so that, aided by the help and protection of God’s mercy”—as far as the inward devotion of religion is concerned—we may always be free from sin, and—as far as outward peace is concerned—secure from every disturbance.

There follows what is customarily added in all ecclesiastical prayers: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth, as we have already said above.

When this prayer has been completed, the priest mingles the Lord’s offering, so that the Lord’s chalice may contain the sacrament in its entire fullness. As though by the joining together of the same mystery, he asks peace for the Church, saying: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.”

The Church likewise invokes this great good upon him, answering: “And with your spirit.” The Lord’s peace is Christ’s peace itself. It has no end and is the perfection of every devout action. True peace creates unity, since “whoever adheres to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. VI, 17).

After peace has been invoked, the whole Church, beginning with the priest, gives one another the kiss of peace, so that, when all are united in true peace, God may have a dwelling among them, as it is said: “God is in his holy place; God makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII, 7).

The Church preserves this practice from the apostles’ tradition. They frequently say to her: “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (1 Cor. XVI, 20)—that is, a peaceful, true, dove-like kiss, not feigned or deceitful, such as is used by those who “speak peace with their neighbor, while evil is in their hearts” (Ps. XXVII, 3).

Those, therefore, greet one another with a holy kiss who do not love in word or speech but in deed and truth (1 John III, 18).

During these rites all sing, and by singing they pray, saying: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world,” and so forth. No one takes away sins except the one for whom no human good is impossible and no evil incurable.

John demonstrates how he takes away the sins of the world in the Apocalypse, saying: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I, 5)—when he gave that blood for us on the cross, or when each of us, in the mystery of his sacred passion, was washed in the waters of baptism.

Indeed, every day he takes away the sins of the world and washes us from our daily sins in his blood, whenever the memory of that same blessed passion is recalled at the altar.

After this, the Eucharist having been received—that is, the good grace, for “by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone”—and thanksgiving having been celebrated, all respond, “Amen.” For this is the clear voice of Christ’s blood, which this blood expresses from the mouths of the faithful, who have been redeemed by that same blood.

When everything has been completed, absolution is given to the people standing by and observing, while the deacon proclaims: “Go, the dismissal has taken place.” Thus *missa* is understood as nothing other than dismissal, that is, absolution; after everything has been celebrated, the deacon declares it to have taken place when the people are dismissed from the solemn observance. Hence the canons also speak of the “Mass of the catechumens,” because after the reading of the Gospel the sacred mysteries begin to be celebrated, and no one except the baptized is permitted to be present at them. Then, when the deacon cried out, those same catechumens were sent outside. The Mass of the catechumens, therefore, took place before the celebration of the sacraments; the Mass of the faithful after the completion and participation in those same sacraments. Or *missa* means “sent forth,” that is, “directed”; or *missa* means “the offering and prayer made for us has been completed.”

## 509. CHAPTER XLI  
### ON THE CREED

[Note: The following six chapters were first restored by Quercetanus from a manuscript.]

*Symbolum* in Greek means in Latin “comparison,” or “sign,” or “indication.” It means “indication” because there the faith of the holy Trinity is indicated: how one ought to believe in the unbegotten Father, the begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both. It means “sign” because whoever utters these words shows that he belongs either to God or to the company of believers. It is called a “comparison” because it is a joining or bringing together of words into one.

Blessed Augustine and our predecessors transmit the tradition that, after the apostles received the Holy Spirit and were about to go forth into every land, they said that, since they believed in one God, it was good for them to preach one faith. There were twelve apostles; they composed twelve statements and declared that these were not to be written on little parchments but retained on the tablets of the heart: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

“I believe in God.” *Credo Deo*, *credo Deum*, and *credo in Deum* are different things. *Credo Deo* means: I believe that all things are in him; *credo Deum*: I believe that he speaks the truth; *credo in Deum*: that is, by believing, I love him.

“The almighty Father.” “Father” is a relational name derived from “son.” He is called Father because he has a son. For he cannot be called Father unless he has a son, nor son unless he has a father.

“Almighty.” He is called almighty because he can do all things. And why is he called almighty, when he cannot do everything? He cannot lie, because he is immutable. But one must understand that he can do whatever befits him.

“In Jesus Christ, his Son”—understand, “I believe.” “Jesus” is the name of the humanity assumed by the Word. The angel gave him this name when he came to the Virgin Mary, saying: “Behold, you will conceive and bear a son,” and so forth, “for he himself will save his people from their sins” (Luke 1:31). Jesus is called in Hebrew *Jesus*, in Greek *Soter* (“Savior”), and in Latin *Salvator* (“Savior”). “Christ” is *Christos* in Greek, *Messias* in Hebrew, and *Unctus* (“Anointed”) in Latin.

He was not anointed with visible oil, as were the patriarchs and prophets, who in ancient times were anointed with oil. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “Do not touch my anointed ones, etc.” (Psalm 104:15). Rather, he was anointed with invisible oil, that is, with the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

“Only-begotten.” He is called “only-begotten” because he is the only one belonging to God the Father. He is the only one belonging to God the Father because the Father had neither a Son before him nor afterward, nor did a mother likewise.

“Our Lord.” He is our Lord because he rules over us in all visible and invisible creatures.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit,” that is, through the work and ministry of the Holy Spirit. And if he was conceived by the Spirit, why is he not called the Son of the Holy Spirit? But one must understand that not everything born from something is called its son. For example, a hair grows from the head, but it is not called the son of the head. Similarly, a fingernail grows from the hand, but it is not called the son of the hand.

“Born of the Virgin Mary according to the flesh,” because blessed Mary was a virgin before the birth, during the birth, and after the birth. Blessed Augustine offers an analogy. There is a mirror in a house; someone enters it, and his shadow appears in the mirror as he enters and leaves, yet he does not break the mirror. In the same way, when the Lord went in and came forth, the virginal womb remained intact.

“Who suffered under Pontius Pilate” according to his humanity, because he was stoned, beaten with rods, spat upon, mocked, and afflicted with many blows; but his divinity remained incapable of suffering. Let us give an analogy for this. Someone cuts down a tree in which a ray of the sun is present. The tree is cut down, yet the sun’s ray suffers no harm. So the Lord Jesus suffered according to his humanity, but according to his divinity he remained incapable of suffering.

Pontius Pilate is the proper name of Pilate. He was ruler [perhaps: governor] in Judea under the emperor Tiberius. He was called Pontius either from the region of Pontus, or from the island of Pontus in which he was born, or from his family, as some think.

“Crucified,” that is, fastened to a cross with nails. Many say that the Lord suffered no injury there. For just as any man of thirty-three and a half years would suffer injury if he were crucified, so the Son of God suffered the punishment; for if he had not done so, it would not have been a true passion.

“Dead,” according to the flesh. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). The Lord therefore gave up his spirit at the ninth hour, because he had been crucified at the sixth hour. It was rightly ordered that at the same hour in which humanity had been expelled from paradise, it should there be restored.

“And buried.” He was buried by Joseph and Nicodemus, as we read, for he buried him in a new tomb that he had hewn in the rock.

“He descended into the underworld,” in the soul alone. Why? To free the elect who were being held there unjustly on account of original sin and to bring them back to heaven. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “I shall be your death, O Death” (Hosea 13:14). The Lord bit the underworld, because from it he took away one portion and left another.

“On the third day he rose again.” He was crucified on Friday, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose from the dead on Sunday, as he had foretold. Hence he says to the Father: “I will rise at dawn” (Psalm 56:9).

“He ascended into heaven” on the fortieth day after his resurrection. For he remained with his disciples for forty days and ate with them, as we read, a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb. He also drank with them, as Peter said: “We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:14). Why did he eat with them after the resurrection? Not because he needed bodily food, but to demonstrate that he had taken a true body from the tomb, not an artificial one. That food, however, so failed to remain through the power of his divinity that afterward it no longer existed—just as, for example, a drop of water disappears through the intense heat of fire.

“He sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.” He sits because he dwells happily in the greatness of the Father’s majesty.

“From there,” that is, from heaven, “he will come to judge the living and the dead.” The living are those who will then be found alive, because this world will be full of human beings. The dead are those who will be dead in body. Or the living are the righteous, and the dead are sinners.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” He says “holy” to distinguish him from the evil spirit, in whom no one ought to believe.

“The holy catholic Church”—understand, “I believe.” *Ecclesia* means in Greek, and in Latin “the congregation of the faithful.” There is this difference between a “congregation” and an “assembly”: an assembly is made up of the faithful, whereas a congregation may consist not only of the faithful but also of unbelievers, animals, and stones.

Καθολικός (*katholikos*) means in Greek “universal” in Latin, because the holy Church has been spread throughout the whole world.

“The communion of saints,” that is, fellowship, because they believe in one God, have been reborn through one baptism, strengthened by one Holy Spirit, and will deserve to pass into one eternal life.

“I believe that the forgiveness of sins is in the Church”: first through baptism, then through martyrdom, finally through almsgiving, afterward through prayer and other good works.

“I believe in the resurrection of the flesh,” because in this flesh in which we now exist we shall rise on the last day.

But what remains? “Eternal life,” that is, life without end. This is the difference between the eternal, the everlasting, and the temporal: the eternal is that which has neither had a beginning nor will have an end, as God; the everlasting is that which has a beginning but will not have an end, as human beings and angels—for although human beings die in the body, they will be immortal in soul; the temporal is that which has both a beginning and an end, as animals and beasts.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### ON THE OFFICES OF THE THIRD, SIXTH, AND NINTH HOURS

[Note: From Isidore, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book I, chapter 19.]

Daniel and the three youths devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplications; that is, they declared reverence for the Trinity through the three hours extending from the rising of day to the time of prayer. Likewise, from the third to the sixth, and from there to the ninth, the intervals of light, ended according to fixed measures, were arranged in equal divisions, so that the Trinity might be honored by being invoked three times a day.

This also serves as evidence of the venerable Trinity: the Holy Spirit descended to earth at the third hour—that is, in its proper place, number, and time—to fulfil the grace that Christ had promised. At the sixth hour Christ suffered, extending the torments of the cross until the ninth. Through such a sacrament, at the proper times appointed for prayer, the perfection of the Trinity is either praised in solemn celebrations or obtained through prayers offered in sets of three hours.

Even if the daily celebration is counted by fours until the evening office, that too is fitting: the numbers of four are signified because the world, divided into four parts, is saved in the Trinity. Likewise, at night the watches and military vigils are divided into four parts and separated by intervals of three hours, so that even in these nocturnal and worldly offices the mystery of the Trinity may be honored.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### ON THE EVENING HOURS

[Note: From the same author, the cited work, chapter 20.]

The evening office is the office at the end of the day and at the setting of the alternate light. Its solemn celebration comes from the Old Testament. In ancient times it was customary at this hour to offer sacrifices and to burn aromatics and incense upon the altar. The witness is that hymn-singer who had exercised royal and priestly office, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:2).

In the New Testament also, at the same hour, our Lord and Savior, while the apostles were dining, first handed on the mystery of his body and blood, so that that time might signify the evening of the world as the time of sacrifice. Therefore, in honor and remembrance of such great mysteries, it is fitting for us at these times to appear before God’s presence, to resound in his worship, offering him the sacrifice of our prayers and rejoicing together in his praises.

“Evening” (*vesperum*) is so called from the star called Vesper, which rises as the sun declines. Concerning it the Prophet says: “And he makes the evening arise over the children of human beings” (Job 38:32).

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### ON COMPLINE

[Note: From the same author, the cited work, chapter 21.]

Regarding the celebration of Compline, this too is found in the examples of the Fathers, as the prophet David says: “If I enter upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131:3ff.).

Who would not marvel at such devotion of spirit in the love of God, that he entirely forbade himself sleep—without which human bodies certainly fail—until the king and prophet found within his breast a place in which to build a temple for the Lord? This ought strongly to admonish us that, if we ourselves wish to be the Lord’s place and desire to be regarded as his dwelling or the temple of the Holy Spirit, we should imitate the examples of the saints as far as we can, lest what is written be said of us: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Psalm 75:6).

## 511. CHAPTER XLV  
### ON VIGILS

[Note: From Isidore, the cited work, chapter 22.]

The ancient devotion of vigils was a familiar good among all the saints. Thus the prophet Isaiah cries out to the Lord, saying: “My spirit watches for you by night, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isaiah 26:9). David likewise says: “At midnight I arose to confess to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118:62).

For at this time the destroying angel passed through and struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians. Therefore we ought to keep vigil, lest we be involved in the danger of the Egyptians. In the Gospel also, the Lord and Savior affirmed that he would come during these same hours. Thus, arousing his hearers to keep watch, he says: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching” (Luke 12:37). “And if he comes in the evening,” he says, “and if at midnight, and if at cockcrow, and finds them watching, they are blessed. Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Mark 13:35).

He taught vigils not only by words but also confirmed them by examples. For the Gospel testifies that “Jesus was spending the night in the prayers of God” (Luke 6:12). Paul and Silas are remembered as prisoners in the public jail, praying around midnight and singing a hymn, with all listening (Acts 16:25–26). Suddenly an earthquake occurred, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains were loosed.

Therefore at these hours we ought to maintain frequent psalmody and prayer in the holy offices and, even if our end should come, await it more securely in such an activity.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### ON MATINS

[Note: From the same author, the cited work, chapter 23.]

The same prophet David bears witness to the antiquity and authority of Matins, saying: “At matins I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper” (Psalm 62:7). And elsewhere: “My eyes went before the dawn toward you, that I might meditate on your words” (Psalm 118:148).

Cassian, however, says that the office of the morning solemnity was first instituted in the still-new age at the monastery in Bethlehem, where our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born from a virgin for the redemption of human salvation; and from that time the custom of celebrating it spread throughout the whole world.

At dawn, therefore, prayer is offered so that Christ’s resurrection may be celebrated. For in the morning light our Lord and Savior rose from the underworld, when the light that had set for sinners at Christ’s death began to rise for the faithful. At that same time, the hope of the future resurrection is held to belong to all, when the righteous and everyone else, rising from this temporal death as from the sleep of slumber, will awaken.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### ON THE ORDER FOR VISITING OR ANOINTING THE SICK, FROM THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA

[Note: From Pope Innocent’s letter to Bishop Decentius, chapter 8.]

“James the Apostle said: ‘Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him’ (James 5:14).

There is no doubt that this must be understood and received concerning sick believers, who may be anointed with holy oil prepared by the bishop. Not only priests but all Christians may use it for anointing in their own need or that of their relatives. It was granted to presbyters for this reason: bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot go to all the sick.

Moreover, if a bishop is able, or considers it appropriate, to visit, bless, and touch a sick person with chrism, he may do so without hesitation, since it is his office to prepare that chrism. Yet this chrism cannot be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. But to those from whom the other sacraments are denied, how can one kind be thought to be granted?”

After this authority had been promulgated, whenever a believer falls ill, the brothers enter the sick person’s presence with blessed water and with candles or incense before the holy oil, and they perform everything as it is contained in the Book of the Sacraments.

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### ON THE FACT THAT PENANCE MUST NOT BE DENIED AT THE POINT OF DEATH, FROM A DECREE OF POPE LEO

[Note: Pope Leo, Letter 18 [elsewhere 83] to Bishop Theodorus, chapter 5.]

Thus aid must be given to the needs of such people, so that neither the means of penance nor the grace of communion is denied them, if, even after losing the use of speech, they are shown by signs to be seeking it with an unimpaired mind. But if they have been so overwhelmed by illness that they cannot indicate, in the presence of the priest [an addition of the edition], what they had requested shortly before, testimony given on their behalf by the faithful ought to benefit them; nevertheless, they must receive both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation.

## 512. CHAPTER XLIX  
### ON THE COMMUNION THAT MUST NOT BE DENIED

[Note: Previously the title was “Concerning those who are at the point of death.” Quercetanus.]

Concerning those who are approaching death, the ancient and regular law must still be observed, so that if someone is departing from the body, he is not deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. But if someone who was considered hopeless and who received communion and became a participant in the offering should recover, let him be among those who receive only participation in prayer.

In general, whenever anyone is at the point of death and asks that the grace of communion be granted him, the bishop ought properly to give it from the offering. The case of those who have died without communion, however, must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the deaths of such people should be kept apart from the remedy of communion. We who did not give communion to them while they were alive cannot give communion to them after their death.

[Note: From Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, chapter 3.]

### How provision was formerly made for the dying

True conversion to the Lord among those at the end of life must be judged by the mind rather than by the time, because the Lord declares: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Ezekiel 18:33). Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the Judge to whom all hidden things are known to be revealed.

After these most sacred decrees, whenever a Christian senses that the moment of death is imminent, let him first renew his confession with purity and complete confidence. Then let him distribute everything he possesses. After this, let him forgive everyone who has sinned against him and be reconciled. Then let him ask for Masses and offerings, or holy communion.

After receiving it, even if he has eaten that very day, let him change his clothing to sackcloth and ashes or to a poorer garment. Then let the brothers enter with all solemnity, or the other faithful with blessed water and a cross, and with candles or incense, saying “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy,” repeating it three times.

After this the priest should say: “May the Lord raise him up to eternal life and have mercy on us.” Then the seven Penitential Psalms are to be sung with litanies, as time permits. Meanwhile, the accounts of the Lord’s Passion or other sacred Scriptures are to be read before him.

When these have been completed, the antiphon “Before I was born” follows. The psalm “The earth is the Lord’s” is sung with its repetition, and “Lord, have mercy” is said three times, as above. Then the priest says: “May the Lord place him in the bosom of Abraham and have mercy on us.” Prayers for commending the soul follow.

## CHAPTER L  
### ON THE FUNERAL RITES OF THE DEAD AND THEIR COMMEMORATION

[Note: In the manuscript the title is “The Order for the Dead.” Quercetanus.]

Augustine speaks as follows about these matters in his book *On Care for the Dead* and in the book *The City of God*:

“He who performs funeral rites for the dead does so out of love for the one who promised that bodies would rise again.”

“Nor are the bodies of the dead to be despised and cast aside, especially those of the faithful, whom the Holy Spirit used as instruments and vessels for every good work. Hence the funerals of the ancient faithful were cared for with dutiful piety, funeral rites were celebrated, and burials were provided. While they were still alive, they themselves entrusted to their sons the burial or transfer of their bodies; and Tobias is commended as having pleased God by burying the dead (Tobit 2:9; 12:12). The Lord himself, who was to rise on the third day, foretells that the good work of the glorious woman would be proclaimed, and Joseph, who buried him, is greatly praised.”

[Note: Saint Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 3; and Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 13.]

Therefore we ought to strive on behalf of our dead, so that they may be able to become participants in those whom Christ recalled from the confines of the underworld. In the same way we celebrate offices for them as are celebrated on those days when Christ descended into the underworld and is believed to have died.

Indeed, in some places prayer is offered generally for all the dead at all times in the evening office, except on Pentecost and feast days; in other places a Mass is celebrated for them every day. On the first days of the month and on anniversaries, offices are performed in the same manner with nine psalms, responsories, or readings.

Therefore, according to Augustine, “supplications for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. The Church has undertaken to offer them for all faithful Christians, even without mentioning their names, under a general commemoration, so that, for those who lack such prayers—parents, children, or whatever relatives or friends they may be—one common mother may provide them on their behalf. But if these supplications, which are performed with right and pious faith for the dead, were lacking, I think their spirits would receive no benefit if their lifeless bodies were placed in any holy place.”

[Note: Augustine, the same work, *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 4.]

Accordingly, those three days are rightly celebrated generally by everyone within the thirtieth day: the third, seventh, and thirtieth.

Concerning the third or seventh day, it is written in the Book of Numbers: “Whoever touches the corpse of a human being and becomes unclean on account of it shall be sprinkled with the water of purification for seven days, on the third and seventh day, and so he will be cleansed” (Numbers 19:11).

This uncleanness resulting from touching a corpse signifies the soul polluted by dead works. Because it has neglected the worship of God, we humbly confess this in thought, life, and understanding, and offer sacrifice to God on the third day, so that it may be cleansed from these sins. In the purification of the third day, on behalf of the deceased commended to God, we may also recall the third day of the Lord’s resurrection, on which supplication should be offered with greater devotion.

For the seventh day we have authority in the Book of Genesis. When Jacob died in Egypt and Joseph transferred him across the Jordan with a very great company, they celebrated his funeral rites there with great lamentation and kept seven days (Genesis 50). Elsewhere it is written: “The mourning of the dead lasts seven days, but the mourning of a fool lasts all the days of his life” (Sirach 22:13).

As for the fact that among some people the ninth day is celebrated and is called the novendial, Augustine condemns this in his *Book of Questions*, especially since no saint is shown to have done this and it is a custom of the pagans.

The seventh day certainly has authority in Scripture, because the number seven, on account of the mystery of the Sabbath, is above all an indication of rest. Hence it is rightly offered to the dead as to those who are resting.

Concerning the thirtieth day, it is written in the Book of Numbers: “When all the multitude saw that Aaron had died, they mourned over him for thirty days” (Numbers 20:30); and “the children of Israel mourned for Moses in the plains of Moab for thirty days” (Deuteronomy 34:8).

David and the children of Israel fasted for Saul and mourned him with the greatest lamentation. In the Book of Wisdom, concerning the third, seventh, and thirtieth days, it is said: “My son, pour out tears over the dead.” And shortly afterward: “Because of the bitter mourning, bear his lament.” Again: “Make mourning according to his merit, for one day or two, because of slander” (Sirach 38:16–18).

At first he said that mourning should last one day for the funeral procession, and afterward, because of detraction, he introduced one or two days—three days in all—into the mourning. Therefore we too ought to fast or give alms for those who were especially dear to us and weep inwardly for their sins, so that, with God’s help, we may at least complete for them what they ought to have done in life but did not do.

Meanwhile some ask whether it is lawful to celebrate Masses for all Christians. Augustine answers:

“Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living relatives when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they were alive, merited that they might afterward benefit from them.

There is a certain manner of life that is neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death. There is another that is so good that it does not require them; and again there is one so evil that, when it has departed from this life, it cannot be helped even by these things.

Therefore these things ought to be done for all who have been regenerated, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to come may be omitted.”

[Note: In the *Enchiridion*, chapter 110; and in the book *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 18.]

Especially noteworthy is the case of someone captured by enemies and bound in iron chains. A servant of God, namely his own brother, thought him dead and had Masses celebrated for him every day according to the custom for the dead. Very often his chains were loosened, and afterward he was freed from them.

It should also be noted that the fact that Masses for the dead are celebrated without the *Gloria* and *Alleluia*, and without the kiss of peace—which is an indication of joy—is done in imitation of the offices performed at the Lord’s death. This may be learned from Origen’s fifth homily on Leviticus, where he says:

“A sacrifice for sin is not made with oil, for he says: ‘He shall not put oil upon it,’ since it is already for sin. Therefore, upon what is for sin neither the oil of gladness nor the incense of sweetness is placed.”

For this reason it is celebrated without the *Gloria* and *Alleluia*. Without oil and incense, the Romans recite only three psalms in the evening offices, vigils, and morning offices of the dead, namely in remembrance of the Lord’s three-day burial.

[Note: Origen, Homily 5 on Leviticus, no. 6, p. 209, volume II of the Paris edition of his works, 1733.]

Those who commemorate the dead by the number nine, as on the days of the Kalends or anniversaries, represent the nocturnal offices that are rightly celebrated during the Lord’s Passion.

The anniversary day is repeated for the dead because we do not know what their condition is in the other life.

## CHAPTER LI  
### ON THE THIRD, SEVENTH, AND THIRTIETH DAYS FOR THE DEAD

[Note: This chapter is found separately in Vatican manuscript 3850, after Alcuin’s Prayers to God and the Apostles, which were given above in column 1027 among the doubtful works.]

The third day is celebrated especially for the absolution of the soul, because the soul is of a threefold nature: irascible, concupiscible, and rational; and because it is vigorous in ingenuity, understanding, and memory. Therefore the sacrifice is performed on the third day so that, if it has contracted anything wine-sodden through its dwelling with the flesh [Vatican manuscript: *cenulentum*, “muddy/foul”], it may be erased and the likeness of the Holy Trinity restored.

The seventh day is likewise assigned to the same offices so that the soul may be reconciled with its body. For the number seven consists of three and four: three is attributed to the soul, while four is assigned to the body on account of the four well-known humors of which it consists.

There is therefore a kind of quarrel between body and soul. The soul sinned because the flesh incited it and attracted it through its enticements. Therefore, so that the soul may be reconciled with its body, a holocaust is performed on the seventh day [manuscript: “of the seventh day”].

Perhaps this is related to what is said in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “The mourning of the dead lasts seven days, but the mourning of a fool lasts all the days of his life” (Sirach 22:13). We have said these things about the third and seventh days briefly and with authoritative support [manuscript: “some authoritative matters”].

As for the thirtieth day, we read in the books of the *Dialogues* that blessed Gregory commanded Masses and prayers to be celebrated for thirty continuous days for a certain monk named Justus [Vatican manuscript omits “Justus”], his necessary physician, whom he himself had condemned for the crime of possessing a private object. When these rites had been completed, it was revealed by God that he had received communion and the fellowship of the saints [manuscript: that fellowship had been restored].

[Note: Saint Gregory the Great, Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 55.]

Thus the salutary custom arose that the thirtieth day of the dead should be frequented with devout offices.

[Note: The words enclosed in brackets are omitted in the Vatican manuscript.]

[We may also bring forward here some authoritative evidence: the people are read to have mourned Aaron, the first of the priests, for thirty days (Numbers 20:30).]

There are those who say that this is done for the perfection of the number thirty, since the Lord was baptized at the age of thirty. David also was thirty years old when he assumed the government of the kingdom. Teachers further assert that the first human being was created at the age of thirty, and we believe and hope that our bodies will rise to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age. Many other mysteries of this matter also exist.

The thirtieth day is therefore celebrated so that the youth of incorruption may be renewed in the soul and the body that had been buried in humiliation may rise in glory, conformed to the body of Christ’s glory (Philippians 3:21).

## CHAPTER LII  
### ON THE MASS OF THE INNOCENTS

[Note: The following six chapters were also added from a manuscript by D. Quercetanus.]

Concerning the Mass of the Innocents, the Antiphoner says as follows: “Glory to God in the highest” is not sung, nor is the *Alleluia*, but that day is led along as though in sadness.

The composer of the present office of the Innocents says: “They wished and mourned.” Just as, by omitting kisses and the other customary rites, this separates us from the conduct of the wicked Jews on the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, or on Holy Saturday, so in the present festival it joins us to the grief of the devout women. Because of their sadness, we omit “Glory to God in the highest” and the *Alleluia*.

## CHAPTER LIII  
### WHY THE TEACHERS OF THE CHURCH ESTABLISHED THAT THE PERIOD OF LENT SHOULD BE OBSERVED BEFORE THE LORD’S PASSION

For a fitting reason the teachers of the Church established that the period of Lent should be observed before the Lord’s Passion, so that we may understand that the affliction of the present life produces future immortality.

To confirm this, the Lord himself fasted for forty days before his Passion and also remained with his disciples for forty days after the resurrection, completing both periods with the number forty, to show that the present life is a time of affliction and the future one of joy.

When he fasted for forty days before the Passion, he seemed to cry out: “Unless you repent, you will die in your sins” (John 8:24). And Peter says: “Abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Peter 2:11).

But when after the resurrection he remained with his disciples, making their hearts joyful, he seemed to promise that ineffable joy of which he says elsewhere: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22). And again: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

He fasted not only for forty days but also for forty nights, so that whether prosperity should flatter them—signified by days—or adversity should terrify them—signified by nights—the Christian mind might remain steadfast, as did the one who said: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report; as deceivers and truthful, as unknown and known” (2 Corinthians 6:7–8).

## CHAPTER LIV  
### PRAYERS OVER A PENITENT

Hear our prayers, Lord, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that those whom the guilt of conscience accuses may be absolved by the indulgence of your mercy. Through the Lord.

Another.

May your mercy, we ask, Lord, go before this servant of yours, and may all his iniquities be erased by swift forgiveness.

Another.

Be present, Lord, to our supplications, and may the compassion of your mercy not be far from this servant of yours. Heal his wounds and forgive his sins, so that, separated from you by no iniquities, he may always be able to cling to you, Lord. Through the Lord.

Another.

Lord our God, who are not overcome by our offense but are appeased by our satisfaction, look, we ask, upon this servant of yours, who confesses that he has sinned gravely against you. It is yours to grant absolution from crimes and forgiveness to sinners, for you have said that you prefer the repentance of sinners to their death. Grant, therefore, Lord, that he may celebrate the vigils of repentance for you and, when his conduct has been corrected, rejoice that eternal joys are bestowed upon him by you. Through the Lord.

Another.

I beseech, Lord, the mercy of your majesty and name: deign to grant pardon to this servant of yours, who confesses his sins and crimes, and to release him from the guilt of his past offenses—you who brought the lost sheep back to the fold upon your shoulders; you who were appeased by the prayers, or confession, of the publican. Be appeased also, Lord, by this servant of yours; graciously assist him in his prayers, so that, persevering in tearful confession, he may quickly obtain your mercy and, restored to the holy and sacred altars, may once again be renewed in the hope of eternal life and heavenly glory. Through the Lord.

Another.

Almighty, everlasting God, in your loving-kindness release the sins of this servant of yours who confesses them to you, so that the guilt of his conscience may not harm him more for punishment than the indulgence of your mercy benefits him for pardon. Through the Lord.

Another.

Almighty and merciful God, who have required the pardon of sins to be sought promptly in confession, come to the aid of those who have fallen and have mercy on those who confess, so that those whom the chain of offenses binds may be released by the greatness of your goodness. Through the Lord.

## 515. CHAPTER LV. [Note: From Isidore, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 16.] ON PENITENTS

Job first provided an example of repentance when, after his bereavements and afflictions, he nevertheless, in his own reproof, took up the mourning of repentance in sackcloth and ashes, saying: “Therefore I repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). After him David offered us instruction in repentance. Having fallen through a grave wound, when he heard his sin from the prophet, he immediately repented and healed his guilt through a confession of repentance (2 Samuel 12). Thus the Ninevites and many others confessed their sins and did penance. They were displeased with what they had been, and were pleased with what they became through God (Jonah 3:5).

Repentance is a remedy for a wound and a hope of salvation. Through it sinners are saved, and through it God is summoned to mercy. It is not measured by the passage of time, but by the depth of grief and tears. Repentance is not assessed by the course of months and seasons, but by the punishment with which the soul is afflicted and the flesh mortified. Those who do penance therefore grow their hair and beard, thereby displaying the abundance of the crimes with which the sinner’s head is burdened. Hair is understood as representing vices. “If a man grows his hair long,” says the Apostle, “it is a disgrace to him” (1 Corinthians 11:14). Penitents accept that very disgrace in proportion to their sins.

As for their prostration in sackcloth, sackcloth signifies remembrance of sins, because of the goats destined for the left hand. Therefore confessors prostrate themselves in sackcloth as though saying: “My sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5). They are sprinkled with ashes either so that they may remember that they are ash and dust, or because they have become dust—that is, impious. Thus the first human beings, those transgressors who departed from God and offended the Creator by their evil deeds, returned to the dust from which they had been made. The penitent therefore rightly laments his sin in sackcloth and ashes: in sackcloth, the harshness and compunction of sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead is displayed. For this reason we do penance in both, so that through the compunction of sackcloth we may recognize the vices we committed through guilt, and through the embers of ashes weigh the sentence of death to which we have come by sinning.

The catholic Church confidently binds people to undertake the remedy of repentance in the hope of pardon. After the one sacrament of baptism—which, commended by a unique tradition, it carefully forbids to be repeated—it supplies the aid of repentance as a medicinal remedy. By this remedy everyone ought to acknowledge that he has need because of the daily excesses of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life, provided only that honor and dignity are preserved. Thus, before God alone as witness, this is to be done by priests and deacons; by others, however, it is to be done with the priest solemnly attesting before God, so that fruitful confession may cover what reckless desire, or the mark of ignorance, seems to have contracted through negligence.

Just as we believe that all iniquities are forgiven in baptism, and that no sin is imputed through martyrdom, so we should acknowledge that sins are blotted out through the fruitful compunction of repentance. For the tears of penitents are reckoned by God in place of baptism. Therefore, however great and serious their offenses may be, God’s mercy must not be despaired of in them. In the practice of repentance, as stated above, the measure of time must not be considered so much as the measure of grief. “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm 50:19). Nevertheless, the more readily the intention of the mind was inclined toward evil in sinning, the more devoted must its affliction be in repentance.

Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through presumption he committed evil. But the person truly does penance who neither neglects to repent of what he has done nor continues to commit what he must yet repent of. Whoever continually pours out tears and nevertheless does not cease sinning has lamentation, but not cleansing.

If some are converted to repentance by God’s grace, they should not be disturbed if, after amendment and the abandonment of vice, their hearts are again troubled, so long as such a thought does not break out into consent or deed and cannot harm a good way of life. To bear thoughts of vice without carrying them through to completion is not for condemnation but for testing. It is not an occasion for undergoing danger, but rather for practicing virtue [Isidore: “for increasing perfection”]. Even if someone ceases to be wicked through repentance near the end of his life, he should not despair on that account because he is at the end of his final life. For God does not regard what we formerly were, but what we are found to be near the end. By one’s end he either justifies or condemns each person, as it is written: “He himself judges the ends of the earth” (1 Samuel 2:10). Elsewhere: “He himself considers the end of all things” (Job 28:3).

Accordingly, we do not doubt that a person may be justified near the end through repentance and compunction. But because this rarely happens, we must be afraid lest, while conversion is deferred until the end, uncertain death overtake us before repentance comes to our aid. For this reason, although conversion at the last moment is good, conversion undertaken long before the end is better, so that we may pass from this life more securely.

## CHAPTER LVI. [Note: From Isidore, cited work, book I, chapter 16.] ON THE NICENE CREED

The Creed that is proclaimed to the people at the time of the sacrifice was composed at the Council of Nicaea through the deliberation of 318 holy Fathers. Its rule of true faith surpasses such great mysteries of doctrine that it speaks about every aspect of faith; scarcely any heresy exists to which it does not respond through particular words or statements. It tramples upon every blasphemy of error, impiety, and treachery, and for this reason it is proclaimed by the people in every church with one and the same confession.

## CHAPTER LVII. [Note: From the same author, in the same place, book II, chapter 23.] ON THE RULE OF FAITH

This is, after the Apostles’ Creed, the most certain faith handed down by our teachers: that we confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be of one essence and of the same power and eternity. We confess one invisible God, while preserving in each person the property proper to that person, so that the Trinity is neither divided substantially nor altogether confused personally. We confess the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. The Son proceeds from the Father by being born; the Holy Spirit, however, proceeds without being born.

We confess that the Son himself assumed humanity from the Virgin without sin, so that the one whom he had created solely through goodness, when he freely fell, he might mercifully restore. We confess that he was truly crucified, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven in that same glorified flesh in which he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead.

We confess that one Christ, perfect in both substances, divine and human, bore them in one person: the integrity of both substances neither doubled the person, nor did the unity of the person confuse the two substances. One did not exclude the other, but preserved both unimpaired in their single right. The saving authority of the New and Old Testaments commends this: the former through prophecy, the latter through history truthfully fulfilled.

We must not agree with pagans or heretics about God or the world’s creation in those matters on which they dissent from the truth. Rather, we must believe only what the divine utterances testify in both Testaments: that God created neither humanity nor the universe out of necessity; that no visible or invisible substance exists except either that which is God or that which was created good by the good God; that God is supremely and unchangeably good, whereas creation is good in a lower and changeable way; and that the origin of souls is uncertain.

Nor is the nature of angels or of souls a part of the divine substance; rather, it is God’s creature, created from nothing. Therefore the incorporeal soul is plainly shown to be corporeal, since it can be apprehended and transferred by God and the angels. [Note: “Is plainly shown to be corporeal.” In my opinion the particle *non* is missing, and it should read “is plainly shown not to be corporeal,” etc., to avoid a contradiction and error. In Isidore, however, it reads: “But, being God’s creature, created from nothing, it is plainly shown to be in the body” (perhaps read “incorporeal”). “Since, therefore, it can be apprehended and transferred, it is nevertheless shown to be corporeal.” And below: “Without which the faith of divine worship grows sluggish in idle torpor, and with which the integrity of divine worship is perfected.”]

It was created in the image of God through piety of conduct, without which the faith of divine worship [does not] attain perfection. Each person should love God and his neighbor in God, advancing even to love of enemies, so that by progressing he may arrive at the goal.

Nor can one person be defiled by another’s sin where equal will and consent are absent. We must not believe that lawful marriages are condemned, although offspring born from them is also believed to be subject to original sin, and although the integrity of faithful virgins or those who practice continence is taught to be rightly preferred to them.

The one baptism of the Trinity, whose repetition is sacrilegious, must not be repeated; nor should it be thought that, because of the diversity of ministers who administer it, it is conferred differently upon different people. Rather, it is given by God’s singular power. Of this we read: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit; and I saw and bore witness that he is the Son of God” (John 1:33–34).

Nor should we think that we have no need of the remedies of repentance because of the daily excesses of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life. Rather, we should acknowledge that all sins are blotted out through fruitful repentance, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Psalm 31:1–2).

No one is joined to Christ the Head by his own powers, but through divine grace; and the perseverance of unbroken peace is strengthened in the unity of Christ’s Church. No good thing should be attributed to human will; rather, the entire number of the elect is acquired according to God’s purpose and will.

Temporal goods, common to the good and the wicked alike, are created by God and, by his dispensation, either granted or withheld from each person. In each of the faithful, it is not the possession of these goods but their use that must be judged either blameworthy or praiseworthy. It is certain and eternal goods alone that the good will be able to attain in the future. We believe that the Church, now formed by the pledge of those goods, is sustained; here it has the firstfruits of the Spirit, and in the future perfection; here it is sustained in hope, afterward nourished in reality; here it sees “through a mirror and in an enigma,” but in the future “face to face,” when faith has led it to vision. Then it will be perfected, so that we may enjoy the eternal goods of the Most High God and, by enjoying temporal things in God, do no harm either to God or to our neighbors.

We likewise have this hope of resurrection: in the same order and form in which the Lord himself rose from the dead, we too will rise in the same body in which we exist and live. We will not change our nature or sex, but will put off only fragility and vices. Satan himself, with his angels and worshipers, is to be condemned to eternal fire; nor is he, according to the sacrilegious argument of certain people, to be restored to his former, that is, angelic, dignity, from which he fell through his own wickedness.

This is the true integrity of the faith of catholic tradition. If any one element is rejected, the entire belief of faith is lost. See the thirty-seventh homily of Saint Augustine on the first part of the Evangelist John [Note: In printed editions, thirty-ninth, *Tracts on John*], whose beginning is: “The words of our Lord Jesus Christ which he spoke with the Jews, ordering his speech in such a way that the blind did not see,” and so forth.

## Letter of Amalarius, Archbishop of Trier, to the Emperor Charlemagne concerning the ceremonies of baptism

(See *Patrologia Latina*, volume XCIX, column 887.)

## 517. Maritime Verses of the Same Amalarius [Note: These verses are exceedingly corrupt in the manuscript. Perhaps they contain that account of the embassy whose existence Herman the Contracted attests for his own time and whose author D. Rivet believes to have been Amalarius, *History of France’s Literature*, volume IV, page 419.] Amalarius to the Venerable Abbot Peter

What, Father, are you retracing, you who know narrow stretches of time,

For you possess the quiet ones? Perhaps you are preparing to renew

Our sacks once more, or to break with your tooth

The crusts, and make all the crumbs fly through the air.

Agius, dwelling among leafy laurels, a most favorable lot,

Himself calls the brothers to the banquets of peace.

The slipping Arton shamefully separated those whom the South Wind

Had joined. Where do you hasten so, my abbot—where?

The Lord of the winds forbids you to proceed without a brother.

What wonder if Gregory lies there, weeping?

If it is not strange for Christ’s choir to tremble?

When the Lord touched the sea-shores, the disciples wept;

If Gregory did not endure the waves,

As evening was already approaching, he asked the storms to cease,

Storms which, the old man says, the greater Eurus raises.

The abbot orders the monk to lift his face upward,

To take at least a little from the brothers’ table.

Gregory said: “I will not rise from here unless this ship

Remains fixed; nor will I leave these planks.”

By night the watchful brother does not sleep, nor do the storms cease from continually troubling the salt waters with their waves.

And the high raft, plunging toward the deep, leaps far too quickly.

His head sorrowful, his mind distressed, he suffers grievously; at last,

When the darkness is overcome, he marvels at radiant Eous:

Terribly fearful winds were stirring the savage waters.

It recalls us to our course, to the hardest camp.

Perhaps the camp, brothers, the camp at Egin, delights,
