And it is enough to clap our hands for a long time,

Where Wippo weeps that he has seized the marked points with another’s hand.

With excessive sobbing he often disturbed our rest,

For whom the very sorrowful company lay grieving.

And remember the priest whom the stars raise up,

For the servant whom the end of his appointed course holds buried.

Pour forth prayers, venerable Father, together with the brothers.

Let us hurry first toward Constantinople;

Let us relax the frozen seasons for both of us in the Attic lands.

After we have toured the city of Constantinople,

And possessed this white stretch of nights twice four times ten,

The watchmen immediately stand, closing the entrances,

Lest perhaps a monk should pass through the city’s darkness,

But rather that he may sing the course of blessed Benedict.

Whether by chance or, rather, because they were unknown to us,

The unspeakable things of that city—which often blessed

So many men, such great servants, blessed through the ages—

Which we read once held the capital of the whole Eastern realm.

Then, returning late, Emperor Leo himself commands that

The brothers come to the king’s highest palace.

Here he speaks; here he prays for the life of Charles through the ages,

And, with kindly voice, remembers his acquaintances,

The whole sacred order, and the people of the Franks.

From there, released, the deep sea drew out its depths,

And the sea’s current and the raft, when a huge beast came.

Who can endure describing so many winds’ greedy wings

And not marvel at so many rattling thongs?

From one side the sea-waves return a terrible sound;

From the other savage forces shake the raft … [lacuna]

Of its belly. Greater still is the fear when the bitter death is near.

I am your prophet, holy Father: you will not escape from here

Unless you are drenched by waters and satisfied with rainstorms.

You may flee the Moors, but fear the Slavs and the Regids.

Heap up your weapons, so that you may slaughter the fearsome Moor,

Whom the ports show us, whom the rumors raise up.

Bend your bow until we cross the sea in our course.

Stand far from the land; leave the shores of the Slavs behind, and let them repel us.

After spring, though late, and after green Italy,

We rushed across it at speed, and with rapid flight,

Hastening through the woodland toward the worthy church of Saint Silvester.

The entire holy band of brothers stands before us,

All tearful; the excellent shepherd, himself weeping, receives the weeping;

Those who had been bereaved rejoice over the Father who has been saved.

Joy pours over the tears, because the company is glad;

They give tender kisses to their German monk Fathers.

We wish you to remain happily with the blessed brothers,

Among whom, Father, deign to remember your brother and your maritime companion,

Not now leaping away in sadness;

I am your brother also, since I gather no sad things.

Sad is the sky for a brother! For I am wearied by Charles’s death.

May God join us both together forever,

With Charles, once king, and with the blessed brothers.

## A Little Book on the Antichrist by Adso, Abbot of Dervensis

### 526. Preliminary Notice

The distinguished D. Andreas Quercetanus inserted this little book, from the manuscript of the illustrious man Jacques-Auguste de Thou, among the works of blessed Alcuin under the title *Life of the Antichrist to Charlemagne*, on page 1209, without hesitation declaring it to be the genuine work of our author. This opinion seems to be supported by the Royal Paris manuscript numbered 4411, which contains the same little book with this inscription: “Here begins the Life of the Antichrist to Charlemagne, edited by Alcuin,” as the celebrated editors of Saint Augustine’s works testify in the appendix to volume VI, page 722. It is also supported by the Englishman John Bale, who, in the second century of *British Writers*, lists among blessed Alcuin’s works “One book on the Antichrist to Charles,” whose beginning is: “First of all, that most especially.”

Yet scarcely any learned person now doubts that this treatise, just as it was formerly attributed through the carelessness and neglected criticism of scribes to Saint Augustine at the place cited above and to Rabanus Maurus in volume VI of the *Works*, page 177, was likewise falsely attributed to blessed Alcuin. Its true author is Adso, a monk and abbot of the monastery of Dervensis (Montier-en-Der).

The discovery and publication by du Chesne, in volume II of *Historical Writers of France*, page 844, of Adso’s dedicatory letter to Queen Gerberga, wife of Louis from Overseas, led scholars to this conclusion. The Maurists later published a fuller version of the letter in volume XI of Saint Augustine, among the additions and corrections. In that letter the celebrated abbot—famous for various other writings as well [see volume VI of *The Literary History of France*, pages 471 and following]—names himself as the author and professes to be answering Queen Gerberga’s questions about what should be believed concerning the Antichrist’s impiety, power, persecution, and origin.

He must therefore be trusted as a proven and pious man, and it must be believed that this little work did not yet exist before Adso laid his hand to it—that is, before the tenth century. The reason why the same book came to be attributed sometimes to Saint Augustine and sometimes to Rabanus Maurus requires little investigation. Scholars accustomed to examining and studying ancient manuscripts know that the little works of different writers are often mixed together in a single volume. Because of the principal work copied there, the volume bears the name of some celebrated writer, while the other works, deprived of their inscriptions, are added almost as an appendix. We could cite many examples of this, were it not exceedingly well known.

As for our blessed Alcuin, we think that a particular circumstance gave rise to the error and false attribution. The little book appears in Vatican manuscript 6444, a parchment quarto from the thirteenth century, and also in another manuscript, Palatine 345, a paper folio from the fifteenth century. In both it is attributed to Alcuin, yet it is addressed not to King Charles but to Heribert, Bishop of Cologne. It is likewise attributed to the same man under the name “Master Albinus” in two manuscripts of the Charterhouse of Axspach in Austria, from the fifteenth century, under this title: “Master Albinus to Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne, concerning the coming of the Antichrist.”

You can see how it could have happened that by ancient and careless copyists Albuinus was confused with Master Albinus, or Alcuin, because of the similarity of their names, although the former was much later and the latter much better known.

That Albuinus calls himself a hermit [Note: Sanderus, *Manuscript Library*, part I, page 156], or recluse of the once famous monastery of Gorze in the region of Metz. He also collected passages from Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers instructing people in the virtues, and dedicated that little work to the same Erimbert, Archbishop of Cologne. It still lies in the library of the canons regular of Tongeren. D. Martène published the letter prefixed to it in volume I of *Amplissima Collectio veterum Scriptorum*, page 360, where it may be read.

A second letter, in many respects similar to the first, is prefixed in the Vatican manuscripts to the little work on the Antichrist; it was plainly taken, together with the little work itself, from Adso’s treatise. It reads as follows:

“Albuinus, the least of all his servants, to Heribert, Bishop of Cologne: everlasting glory and peace. Since, Lord Father, I obtained the grace of your mercy, I have always been faithful to you in all things. Therefore, although my prayers are unworthy before God, I nevertheless always implore the mercy of our God for you, that he may make you reign happily with him after this life.

“Since you have a pious desire to hear the Scriptures and frequently to speak about our Redeemer, and also to know about the Antichrist’s impiety and persecution, as well as his power and origin, as you have deigned to command me, your servant, I wished to write something to you about the Antichrist and to make you partly certain of the matter, although you have among you very wise and highly necessary men for our times. Therefore, you who wish to know about the Antichrist will first note why he is so called,” and so forth.

The letter continues just as it is read in Adso, except for certain differences, which we note in their proper places.

To prevent anyone, after reading this letter, from wondering whether this book on the Antichrist should be attributed to Albuinus the hermit rather than to Adso, the dates of the two letters must be distinguished. Albuinus sent this book to Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne; therefore it was not written before the year 999, when Heribert was promoted to that archiepiscopal see [Note: Rupert of Deutz, *Life of Saint Heribert*, chapter 1, number 1; *Acta Sanctorum*, volume II of March, page 476].

Adso, however, sent it to Queen Gerberga while her elder, namely her husband Louis, was still alive. He professes that he continually implored divine mercy for Louis and his sons. Adso therefore wrote this treatise before the year 954, when Louis from Overseas died on the fourth day before the Ides of September [Note: Frodoard, *Chronicle*, under that year]. He wrote it while Rorico, Bishop of Laon, whom he praises at the end, was still alive. Rorico assumed that see in 949 and died in 976 [Note: D. Ceillier, *General History of the Sacred Authors*, volume XIX, page 700; authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume VI, page 43, number 58].

From these facts it is abundantly clear that Albuinus borrowed both the book and the letter itself from Adso, while nevertheless providing later writers with an occasion for error, so that they substituted Albinus or Alcuin for Albuinus. Later, when the little work mentioned a certain king of the Romans, tall in stature, handsome in appearance, splendid in countenance, and well-proportioned in every feature of his limbs, whose name began with the letter C, some perhaps interpreted this as Charles the Great and too confidently declared and wrote that the little work had been sent to him.

For the rest, this little book was compiled from passages of Saint Augustine, book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 11, and *Tractate 2 on chapter II of the Epistle of Saint John to the Parthians*; from Rabanus Maurus, book XXII on the Apostle, chapter 2; and from Alcuin’s own book III *On the Trinity*, chapter 29. If you wish, consult what D. Rivet writes in volume VI of *The Literary History of France*, pages 477 and following. Here we follow D. Quercetanus’s edition as the fuller one, and add from other editions and manuscript codices certain variant readings.

## The Little Book of Adso, Abbot of the Monastery of Dervensis, on the Antichrist, to Gerberga [Note: Adso the monk of Luxeuil later succeeded Alberic in the abbey of Dervensis because of his distinguished merits, around the year 968. He wrote this letter while not yet abbot, namely before the year 954, when Louis from Overseas died in October. See *Literary History of France*, volume V, page 471, and following.] Queen [Note: Gerberga, wife of Louis from Overseas and sister of Emperor Otto I. Frodoard.]

To the most excellent Queen Gerberga, endowed with royal dignity, beloved by God, worthy of praise among all the saints, mother of monks and leader of holy women, our lady Gerberga: Brother Adso, the least of all her servants, sends everlasting glory and peace.

Since, lady mother, I obtained the first fruit of your mercy, I have always been faithful to you in all things like your personal servant. Therefore, although my prayers are unworthy before the Lord, I nevertheless implore the mercy of our God for you and for your elder, your lord the king, and also for the safety of your sons, that in this life he may deign to preserve you and the empire for you, and after this life make you reign happily with him in heaven.

For if the Lord grants you prosperity and gives your sons a longer life, we know and believe without doubt that the Church of God will be exalted and that the order of our religion will multiply more and more. This is what I, your faithful servant, desire and greatly wish. If I could acquire the whole kingdom for you, I would gladly do so; but since I cannot accomplish that, I will pray to the Lord for your welfare and that of your sons, so that his grace may always go before you in your works, and his glory follow you piously and mercifully, so that, intent upon the divine commandments, you may fulfill the good things you desire, and thus receive the crown of the heavenly kingdom.

Since, then, you have a pious desire to hear the Scriptures and frequently to speak about our Redeemer, and also to know about the Antichrist’s impiety and persecution, as well as his power and origin, as you have deigned to command me, your servant, I wished to write something to you and to make you partly informed about the Antichrist, although you do not need to hear this from me, since you have among you a most wise shepherd, Lord Rorico [Note: Concerning Rorico, Bishop of Laon, see *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, Paris edition of 1751, page 521], a brilliant mirror of all wisdom and eloquence in this age of ours [perhaps add: “necessary”].

## 528

First of all, we must explain why he is called Antichrist. He is called this because he will be opposed to Christ in all things—that is, he will do what is contrary to Christ. [Note: Manuscript codices: “Therefore, those wishing to know about the Antichrist will first note why he is so called. Namely …” and so forth.]

Christ came in humility; he will come in pride. Christ came to raise up the humble and justify sinners; he, on the contrary, will cast down the humble, magnify sinners, exalt the impious, and always teach vices, which are contrary to virtues. He will destroy the evangelical law, restore the worship of demons to the world [Vatican Codex: “in the world”], seek his own glory, and call himself [God] the Almighty.

This Antichrist therefore has many ministers of his unbelief [same codex: “he will have many ministers of his wickedness”]. Many of them have already preceded him in the world, such as Nero, Antiochus, and Domitian. Even in our own time we know many Antichrists [to exist]: whoever—whether layman, canon, or monk—lives contrary to justice, attacks the rule of his order, and blasphemes what is good, is an Antichrist and a minister of Satan.

But let us now consider the Antichrist’s origin. I testify in Christ that I am not inventing what I am about to say from my own judgment [Note: Vatican Codex: “But I do not invent or devise from my own judgment what I say”]. Rather, by carefully rereading authentic books, I find all these things written there.

As our authorities say, the Antichrist will be born from the Jewish people, from the tribe of Dan, according to the prophecy that says: “Let Dan be a serpent on the road and a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hoof so that its rider falls backward” (Genesis 49:17). For like a serpent he will sit on the road and be on the path, so that he may strike those who walk along the path of justice [Vatican Codex: “along the paths … who walk”] and kill them with the poison of his wickedness.

He will be born from the union of father and mother, like other human beings—not, as some invent, from a virgin alone [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are omitted in the manuscript codices], [nor from a bishop and a nun, as others deliriously teach, but from a most filthy prostitute and a cruel scoundrel]. He will be conceived entirely in sin, begotten in sin, and born in sin. At the very beginning of his formation [same codex: “at the beginning of his conception”], the devil himself will enter his mother’s womb [Note: Vatican Codex: “he will enter his mother’s womb, and by the devil’s power he will be nourished and disturbed in his mother’s belly, and the devil’s power will always be with him.” The words enclosed in brackets are omitted]:

[the head of pride, the teacher of error, the fullness of wickedness. Once placed on high, as blessed Gregory says, he does not lose the nature of his power even when cast down. For this reason his power has not been displayed, nor is it now displayed: he is held bound by the strength of the divine dispensation. Then he will be released and will come forth, and through that vessel of his he will terribly deceive the nations.

This is the one of whom John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, holding in his hand a great chain and the key of the abyss; and he seized the dragon, who is the devil and Satan, and shut him up for a thousand years. After the thousand years he will be released and come forth, and deceive the nations” (Revelation 20:1 and following). He is the king over all the sons of pride, and his power will always be with him.]

Just as the Holy Spirit came upon the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, overshadowed her with his power, and filled her with divinity, so that she conceived from the Holy Spirit and what was born was divine and holy, so likewise the devil will descend upon the mother of the Antichrist, fill her entirely, surround her entirely, hold her entirely, and possess her completely within and without, so that, with the devil cooperating through the man, she may conceive, and what is born may be wholly iniquitous, wholly evil, and wholly lost.

Thus that man is called the son of perdition, because insofar as he is able he will destroy the human race, and in the end he himself will be destroyed.

Now that you have heard the manner of his birth, listen also to the place where he is to be born. Just as our Lord and Redeemer chose Bethlehem for himself, so that there he might deign to assume humanity for us and be born, so the devil knows a suitable place for that lost man called the Antichrist, from which the root of all evils is to arise: namely, the city of Babylon.

In this city [Note: Vatican Codex: “in the city of Babylon; namely, in this city”], which was once renowned and glorious [Note: Added from the Vatican Codex: “a city of the gentiles”] and the capital of the entire kingdom of the Persians, the Antichrist will be born. He is said to be raised and to dwell in the cities of Bethsaida and Chorazin [“and to conduct himself there”], cities which the Lord rebukes in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” (Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:13).

The Antichrist will have magicians, diviners, sorcerers, enchanters, and soothsayers, who, inspired by the devil, will nourish and instruct him and train him in every iniquity, falsehood, and wicked art. Evil spirits will always be his undivided guides, companions, and comrades [Vatican Codex: “fellow soldiers”].

Then, coming to Jerusalem, he will slaughter through various tortures all the Christians whom he cannot convert to himself, and he will establish his seat in the holy temple. He will also rebuild the destroyed temple that Solomon prepared for God, restore it to its former state, circumcise himself, and falsely claim to be the Son of the almighty God.

But first he will convert kings and princes to himself, and then through them the remaining peoples. The places through which the Lord Jesus Christ walked, he too will traverse; but first he will destroy what the Lord glorified. Then he will send his messengers and preachers throughout the whole world. His preaching and power will extend from sea to sea, from east to west, and from north to south. [Note: The words “to the west and from the north to” are added from Codex Vaticanus.] He will also perform many great and unheard-of signs and miracles. He will make terrifying fire descend from heaven; trees will suddenly blossom and grow [the same codex: “wither”]; the sea will be stirred up and suddenly become calm; the natures of things will also be changed into various forms; waters [the same codex: “the courses of the waters”] will be turned contrary to their courses and order; the air will be agitated by many winds and disturbances; and there will be other marvelous [the same codex: “innumerable”] and astonishing deeds—namely, the dead will be raised in the sight of men—so that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error (Matt. XXIV, 14).

529 [Note: The material enclosed in brackets is omitted in Codex Vaticanus.] There will also be falsehoods, alien to the truth, for by magic and illusion he will deceive men, just as Simon Magus also deceived the man who, thinking that he was killing him, killed a ram in his place.

When even those who are perfect and elect in God have seen signs so great and of such a kind, they will doubt whether he is the Christ who, according to the Scriptures, is to come at the end of the world, or not. [Note: From Codex Vaticanus.] All these miracles, however, will in every respect be false, produced through diabolical incantations; they will appear true to sinners and unbelievers.

He will raise persecution under the whole heaven against Christians and all the elect. Thus he will rise up against the faithful in three ways: by terror, by gifts, and by miracles. He will give those who believe in him abundant gold and silver [Note: Omitted in Codex Vaticanus; “for in his time all hidden treasures will be revealed”]. Those whom he cannot corrupt with gifts he will overcome by terror; those whom he cannot conquer by terror he will attempt to seduce with signs and miracles; and those whom he cannot deceive even with signs he will cruelly kill in the sight of all, after subjecting them to a wondrous death [Codex Vaticanus: “he will attempt to kill them by a pitiable death”].

Then there will be such tribulation as has never been upon the earth from the time when nations began to exist until that time. Then those who are in the field will flee to the mountains, saying, “Fall upon us”; and to the hills, “Cover us”; while the one who is upon the housetop will not descend into his house to take anything from it, but will throw himself headlong (Matt. XXIV, 16 ff.). Then every faithful Christian who is found will either deny God or, if he remains steadfast in the faith, will perish by the sword, by fire in a furnace, by serpents, by wild beasts, or by any other kind of torture whatsoever.

This exceedingly terrible and fearful tribulation will last three and a half years [Note: From Codex Vaticanus: “throughout the whole world”]. Then the days will be shortened for the sake of the elect (Matt. XXIV, 22); for unless the Lord had shortened the days, scarcely any flesh would be saved [Codex Vaticanus: “no flesh would have been saved”].

The time, namely, when Antichrist will come, or when the day of judgment will begin to appear, the Apostle Paul indicates in his Letter to the Thessalonians, saying: “Unless the falling away comes first, and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed, etc.” (II Thess. II, 3).

We know that after the kingdom of the Greeks, and likewise after the kingdom of the Persians—each of which flourished in its own time with great glory and power—finally, after the other kingdoms, the Roman kingdom also began [Royal Manuscript: “will begin”]. It was stronger than all the preceding kingdoms [Royal Manuscript: “will be”], and held all kingdoms under its dominion [the same manuscript: “will have”]. All the nations and peoples likewise were subject to Rome and served it under tribute [the same manuscript: “will be subject to and serve the Romans”].

Therefore the Apostle says that Antichrist will not come into the world beforehand, unless the falling away comes first—that is, unless all the kingdoms of the world have withdrawn from the Roman Empire, to which they were formerly subject. This time has not yet come. For although we see that the Roman kingdom has already been destroyed in large part, nevertheless, as long as the kings of the Franks endure, who are destined to hold the Roman Empire, the dignity of the Roman Empire will not perish altogether, because it will remain in its kings.

For our teachers relate [Note: D. Rivet calls this prophecy famous but insipid, *Hist. lit. Franciae*, vol. VI, p. 480. D. Le Beuf, *Recueil de divers écrits*, vol. II, p. 41 note, observes that it is not found in the copy preserved in the Abbey of Saint-Victor at Paris.] that one of the kings of the Franks will hold the Roman Empire in its entirety and will exist at the final time. He will be the greatest and the last of all kings. After governing his kingdom faithfully [Codex Vaticanus: “successfully,” or “happily”], he will finally come to Jerusalem and lay down his scepter and crown on the Mount of Olives.

This will be the end and completion of the empire of the Romans and of the Christians. According to the Apostle’s statement mentioned above, they say that Antichrist will immediately be present. Then that man of sin will be revealed—namely, Antichrist—who, although he is a man, will nevertheless be the source of all sins; and he will be the son of perdition, that is, the son of the devil [Note: Omitted in Augustine], not by nature but by imitation, because he will fulfill the devil’s will in every respect. The fullness of diabolical power and of every kind of wicked cunning will dwell in him [Another reading adds: “bodily”]; in him all the treasures of wickedness and iniquity will be hidden.

“He who opposes”—that is, he who is contrary to Christ God and to all his members. “And he is exalted”—that is, he is lifted up in pride—“above everything that is called God,” that is [Note: Omitted in Codex Vaticanus], above all the saints, who according to the Psalmist are called gods: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 6). Or [Note: The words “above all the gods of the nations” are omitted in Codex Vaticanus] above all the gods of the nations—namely, Hercules, Apollo, Jupiter, and Mercury, whom the pagans believe to be gods.

Antichrist will be exalted above all these gods, because he will make himself greater and stronger than them all. And not only above these, but also above everything that is worshiped—that is, above the Holy Trinity, which alone is to be worshiped and adored as Creator by all his creation. He will exalt himself so far that he will sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.

For, as we said above, born in the city of Babylon, he will come to Jerusalem, circumcise himself, and say to the Jews: “I am the Christ promised to you, who have come for your salvation, so that I may gather together and defend you who have been scattered.” Then [Note: From the Royal Manuscript and Augustine] all the Jews will hasten to him and, believing that they are receiving Christ, will receive the devil [Note: “They will receive the devil.” In Codex Vaticanus and in Rabanus the passage continues as follows: “Or Antichrist will sit in the temple of God, that is, in the holy Church, desiring to make all Christians martyrs; and he will be exalted and magnified, and in him will be the head of all evils, the devil, who is king over all the sons of pride. But lest Antichrist come suddenly and unexpectedly and deceive and destroy the whole human race all at once by his error, before his appearance two great prophets will be sent into the world.” Enoch and Elijah, etc., as below; the material cited here from the Sibylline verses is omitted.], according to what the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V, 43).

As we have it in the Sibylline verses, in the time of the aforesaid king—whose name will be C., king of the Romans and of the whole empire—he will be tall in stature, handsome in appearance, splendid in countenance, and well-proportioned in every feature of his limbs. There will be great riches, and the earth will yield its produce, so that a measure of wheat will be sold for one denarius, and wine and oil likewise.

Then the most filthy nations will rise from the north, whom King Alexander enclosed in Gog and Magog. These are twenty-two [Royal Manuscript: “twelve”] kingdoms, whose number is like the sand of the sea. When the Roman king hears of this, he will summon an army, wage war against them, and destroy them utterly.

He will always keep before his eyes the Scripture that says: “Let the king of the Romans claim for himself the whole kingdom of the earth.” Therefore he will devastate all the islands and cities, destroy all the temples of idols, and summon all pagans to baptism. The cross of Christ will be erected in every temple. The Jews too will then be converted to the Lord: “In those days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely” (Jer. XXIII, 16).

When the hundred and twelve years of his reign have been completed [Royal Manuscript: “twelve,” omitting “hundred”], he will come to Jerusalem and there, as stated, lay down his diadem and leave the kingdom of the Christians to God the Father and to his Son Christ Jesus. His tomb will be glorious.

Then two great prophets, Elijah and Enoch, will be sent into the world. They will fortify the faithful against Antichrist’s assault with divine weapons; they will instruct and encourage them, and prepare [Note: From Codex Vaticanus: “the elect”] them for battle.

[Note: In Codices Vaticanus and Augustinus the following is inserted: “Teaching and preaching for three and a half years; and they will convert to the grace of faith all the children of Israel whomsoever they find living at that time. These two great prophets and teachers will render them unconquerable among the elect against the oppression of so great a whirlwind. Then the Scripture will be fulfilled,” etc.]

Then the Scripture will be fulfilled which says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Rom. IX, 27).

[Col. 1296D] After they have completed their preaching, Antichrist will rise up against them and kill them [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “When, therefore, he has completed his preaching for three and a half years, Antichrist’s persecution will immediately begin to blaze up, and he will first take up his weapons against them and kill them,” etc.], as it is written in the Apocalypse: “And when they have finished their testimony,” he says, “the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them, and conquer them, and kill them,” etc. (Rev. XI, 7).

But after three days the Lord will raise these slain men. Then, pursuing the other faithful, he will either deliver them to the sword or make them apostates [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “After these two have been killed, he will pursue the others, make them glorious martyrs, or render them apostates.”]; and those who believe in him will receive the mark of his character on their foreheads.

But since we have spoken of his beginning and life, let us also say what end he will have. This Antichrist, the son of the devil and the worst artificer of every kind of wickedness, after troubling the whole world for three and a half years [with great persecution], torturing the people of God with various punishments, and crowning those who remain steadfast in the faith with martyrdom, will finally encounter God’s judgment against him, as the blessed Apostle Paul writes: “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (II Thess. II, 8).

[Note: Codex Vaticanus differs in what follows and continues: “With the spirit of his mouth; that is, whether the Lord Jesus kills him by the power of his command, or whether the archangel Michael kills him, he will be slain by the Lord’s power in Babylon, on his throne, in that place toward which the Lord will ascend to heaven.”]

For the splendor of Christ’s coming will be so overwhelming that, before the brilliance of the divine light, he will be entirely defiled by the foul matter discharged from his belly and will perish in fear.

The teachers also relate, as Pope Gregory says [Note: Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 15, no. 27: “For he will be crushed without a hand, since he will be struck with eternal death not by the warfare of angels or the contest of saints, but by the coming of the Judge, through the spirit of his mouth alone.” Saint Jerome, *Commentary on Daniel*, chapter XI, verse 45: “Then, he says, Antichrist will come to the summit of his mountain, that is, of the mountainous province—the summit of the Mount of Olives, which is called glorious because from it the Lord and Savior ascended to the Father—and no one will be able to aid Antichrist while the Lord rages against him. And they assert that Antichrist will perish there, from the place where the Lord ascended to heaven.”], that the archangel Michael will destroy him on the Mount of Olives, in his tent and on his throne, in the place from which the Lord ascended into heaven.

Both accounts can be true. For if Michael, going before the face of God who is coming for judgment, kills him, the power and command will belong not to Michael but to God.

We must also believe with the utmost firmness that, after Antichrist has been killed, the day of judgment will not immediately come [Note: From Codex Vaticanus: “nor will the Lord immediately come to judgment”]; rather, as we understand from the Book of Daniel, the Lord will grant forty days to those who have been bewitched and marked, so that they may repent [Note: Codices Vaticanus and Augustinus: “The Lord will grant forty days to the elect so that they may do penance.” Rabanus: “He will not immediately come to judgment, but the Lord will wait for certain people, as we understand from Daniel, who were led astray so that they might return to repentance. But after they have completed this repentance,” etc.], because they were deceived by Antichrist.

After they have completed this repentance, how much time will then pass, although I think that no one knows, remains in God’s dispensation. He will judge the world by fire at the hour that he appointed before the ages for judgment [Note: Here the text ends in Codex Vaticanus and in other manuscripts].

Nevertheless, Augustine, in his Letter beginning “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep,” explains many things about this with great clarity [Note: Saint Augustine, sermons 172 and 173, *On the Words of the Apostle*, concerning I Thess. IV, 12. In fact, however, there is nothing there on this subject]. And Jerome, in his exposition of the seven trumpets addressed to Evervinus [Note: Read “to Minervius and Alexander”; this is Letter 119 in the Verona edition], gives us there important lessons of knowledge.

[Note: This conclusion occurs in the manuscripts from which the editors of the works of Saint Augustine took the letter to Queen Gerberga.]

Behold, lady queen, I, your faithful servant, have faithfully fulfilled what you commanded. I am ready to obey whatever else you may be pleased to order.

[Col. 1297]

# FOUR HOMILIES ATTRIBUTED TO THE BLESSED ALCUIN

[Col. 1297]

## 531 PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 1297D]

The most distinguished D. Quercetanus, on page 1195, published three homilies under the name of blessed Alcuin, from the *Homiliary* and the *Sermons of the Fathers*, as he writes in the catalogue prefixed to the works he edited. He gives no other reason why they should be attributed to Alcuin.

The first concerns silence, in which the incarnate Word was sent. The second concerns the Nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary. The third was delivered on the feast of All Saints.

The second homily, on the Nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary, is nothing other than a literal, allegorical, and moral exposition of the names of the patriarchs and ancestors of Christ, cast by someone into the form of a homily. We published it, with variant readings, from the manuscript of Saint Emmeram among the genuine works of blessed Alcuin in volume I, part II, and explained the reason for doing so [Col. 1298D] there in the preliminary notice.

This homily is therefore omitted here. To the two remaining homilies we add two others: one on the same Nativity of the blessed Virgin, from the Paris Royal Manuscript no. 315, where it bears the name of blessed Alcuin; and another preached on the Hypapanti, or Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, from the *Miscellanies* of D. Baluzius, book I, pages 382–402, where it is likewise attributed to Master Alcuin and appears to have been delivered before the Emperor Charles by that most renowned man.

In truth, however, there is now no learned person who does not consider these homilies to be rejected as spurious.

The first general reason is this: although it is very likely that blessed Alcuin, as abbot of several monasteries, often encouraged the brothers entrusted to his care, on the occasion of the festivals that arose, through sermons to admire the most sublime mysteries of our religion, and exhorted them to cultivate truly Christian morals, to observe regular discipline, and to pursue perfection, and although, on the testimony of the ancients, it is credible that this same blessed man either collected or at least revised the homilies of the holy Fathers who preceded him, as we stated above in the preface to the spurious works, nevertheless no writer mentions any homilies that he himself delivered and at the same time committed to writing.

The second general reason is that none of those skilled in these sermons or homilies recognizes the style that blessed Alcuin used in his own writings—unless we say that in this genre of speaking and writing he borrowed a very large part from others, something he indeed does in some places, but never without identifying his sources.

The particular reason why the sermon on the Lord’s Hypapanti should be considered spurious is that it is attributed to blessed Alcuin neither in printed editions nor in any manuscript codices. To be sure, the most distinguished D. Stephanus Baluzius published that sermon under Alcuin’s name in the cited place of his *Miscellanies*, from an old manuscript of the Colbert Library—not because Alcuin’s name is prefixed there, but because it is presented among several other works of his and is said to have been delivered before Charlemagne, as appears from two places in the same copy.

But who does not know that in ancient manuscript codices the genuine writings of an author are often mixed with spurious ones? An attentive reader will also readily notice that the addresses to Charles Augustus, most glorious king, and so forth—which all the other printed copies and the manuscript lack—were inserted by some rash scribe, contrary to the connection of the discourse.

This sermon in fact belongs to Ambrose Autpertus, as the learned author of the *Literary History of France*, volume IV, pages 152–153 and 342, proves by solid arguments.

We therefore give here the homilies that have actually been published under Alcuin’s name: the first and third in Quercetanus, and the one on the Purification in Baluzius [Col. 1299C] B. V. To these we add another on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary from the Paris Royal Manuscript.

We have judged it necessary to omit the sermon on the Assumption of the same Blessed Virgin, or the response to questions concerning the temporal dissolution and everlasting assumption of the Virgin and Mother of the Lord, etc., which is found in volume VI of the works of Saint Augustine, page 729, among the spurious works, although the most renowned writer D. Petrus Lambecius attempts to assert it as Alcuin’s in the *Diary of the Sacred Journey to Zell*, Vienna edition, 1666, pages 121 ff.

For although the arguments by which he seeks to support his conjecture are not without some plausibility, we cannot agree with him so long as no ancient document or testimony is produced in favor of Alcuin rather than some other writer of that period. Nevertheless, for the benefit of readers, we have taken care to transcribe here in full D. Lambecius’s arguments from the cited booklet, so that each person may judge their value for himself.

> “I am thoroughly convinced,” he says, “that this treatise was written toward the end of the eighth century after Christ, namely at the same time when Charlemagne, not yet emperor, but only—as he himself likes to say—king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, first published his book of Capitularies, or ecclesiastical and civil laws. For Charlemagne himself indicates that at that time the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin had not yet been confirmed and sanctioned by public authority in Germany and Gaul, but was partly celebrated negligently and unevenly, and partly attacked impiously and maliciously by some people, when, after the other festivals of the year that he lists, he added this clause: ‘Concerning the Assumption of Saint Mary, we leave the matter to be investigated’ [Note: Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 158, in Baluzius, volume I, page 732].

> “It is therefore most probable that Charlemagne first proposed this question, privately and before all others, to his teacher Albinus Flaccus Alcuin; and that this treatise was composed by Alcuin as his answer. At its beginning, as though expressly referring and alluding to the words of Charlemagne just cited, it plainly testifies that he is not writing from his own initiative about what he understands concerning the temporal dissolution and everlasting assumption of the Virgin and Mother of the Lord, but is responding to questions.

> “This conjecture is confirmed by the words of Charlemagne cited above and by the opening of this treatise, which responds to Charlemagne’s words” [Note: “Which responds to the words of Charlemagne.” Yet this has not been established by any argument: it is not proved that this response is Alcuin’s answer to Charlemagne’s questions, since it could belong to another learned man of that time. Indeed, from the epilogue of the sermon or response itself it is clear that the author was responding not to Charlemagne’s questions but to questions from others joined to him by fraternal affection. For he says: “Let your fraternal charity therefore receive this understanding, according as the Spirit of Christ inspired it. The things that in this way urged me to speak have been shown in part.”]

> “The same conjecture is confirmed by Alcuin’s style” [Note: “Alcuin’s style confirms the same conjecture.” I myself do not detect it in that treatise; nor is the style as familiar as that which he uses in his other letters and responses to Charlemagne.] “and by the sacred questions that Charlemagne had previously proposed to him. It is confirmed by the assertion concerning the bodily assumption of the Blessed Virgin, which occurs elsewhere in Alcuin’s writings, and by the catalogue of Alcuin’s writings in Baleus, *Centuria II of the Writers of Britain*, where I believe that, under the book entitled *Responses to Questions* [Note: Baleus does not add what those questions were. Since Lambecius himself acknowledges that other sacred questions had also been proposed to Alcuin by Charlemagne, it remains uncertain which responses and which questions Baleus meant], this very treatise on the Assumption is signified.

> “Finally, this conjecture is confirmed by the Homiliary collected by Alcuin at Charlemagne’s command. Alcuin would certainly have inserted that treatise or sermon on the Assumption if it had been Saint Augustine’s and not his own. For the first person to enlarge Alcuin’s Homiliary with that sermon was Brother Laurentius Surius, the Carthusian, in the Cologne edition of 1576. It is not found in any of the older editions of the same Homiliary . . .”

Thus far Lambecius; we explain in the notes that follow what can and should be answered to him.

# FIRST HOMILY: ON SILENCE, IN WHICH THE INCARNATE WORD WAS SENT

[Col. 1300C]

See this homily among the works of Paul the Deacon, volume XCVI of this *Patrology*, column 1178.

# HOMILY II: THE SERMON OF MASTER ALCUIN TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES ON THE LORD’S HYPAPANTI

See the sermon now among the works of Saint Ambrose Autpertus, volume LXXXIX of the *Patrology*, column 1291.

## 540 HOMILY III: A SERMON OF ALCUIN ON THE NATIVITY OF THE PERPETUAL VIRGIN MARY

[Note: This is the title found in the cited manuscript codex.]

From Royal Manuscript no. 315.

The celebration of this day, beloved, admonishes us that we ought always to dwell upon the praise of the ever-virgin Mary. For today the blessed perpetual Virgin, Mary the Mother of God, was born from the seed of Abraham. Hence the archangels rightly rejoice and all the saints praise together with them. The whole world also rejoices with her, since through her it has received redemption [Note: Understand this soberly: it is through her that we received the Redeemer].

Therefore, as we celebrate the nativity of so exalted and glorious a Virgin, let us earnestly implore her protection with devout hearts. Her Lord, beholding in her true humility together with true virginity, revealed through the angel who announced salvation that she was to conceive the author of chastity, the lover of virginity, the friend of humility, and the Savior of the world, who before the beginning was ineffably begotten by God the Father himself.

If this beautiful woman, chosen by the Lord, sees with a devout heart that we celebrate her birth in holiness—provided that the smallness [or: wickedness] of our conscience does not accuse us of sins—we ought to believe and hope that she will not refuse to deign to intercede for us with the Lord our God. The intercession of that perpetual Virgin whose nativity we celebrate with solemn devotion will obtain forgiveness of sins.

O how blessed is the Virgin Mother of God, whose nativity announced joy throughout the whole world, and from whom Christ the Lord our God, the sun of justice, arose! He removed the curse of the ancient guilt and gave us blessing; he confounded death and granted us everlasting life.

Blessed, I say, is the Virgin Mary, who obtained the dignity of motherhood and did not lose her virginal chastity. O how glorious is the Virgin Mary! O how worthy of honor is her undefiled birth! O blessed is her virginity begun, her nativity, by which today, born from the illustrious lineage of King David, she herself caused the salvation of the world to appear to all believers.

O how blessed and venerable is the ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, whose birth today caused the true light to shine in the decaying darkness.

It is therefore altogether fitting, beloved, that we serve her with the greatest devotion, through whom the insignia of virginity have sprung forth for us. Nor should we be unaware that a book about her holy nativity is read by some [Note: The *Protevangelium of Saint James* and the *Apocryphal Gospel concerning the Nativity of Mary*, which is thought to have been committed to writing by Seleucus in the second century. See Saint Jerome, volume V of his works, page 441; Du Pin, preliminary dissertation, volume II, page 90, sections IV and V; Calmet, *Dissertation on the Apocryphal Gospels*, volume I, *Literal Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*, page CXIII, no. 6]. In it the merit of the father and mother of this Virgin, and the name of each—namely, Heli and Anna—are described.

That apocryphal work, as well as another concerning the passing of the same Virgin [Note: The *Gospel of the Passing of the Virgin*, listed among the apocrypha by Pope Gelasius, is found in certain libraries: Codex Labbe 453; Lambecius, book IV of the Vienna Library, manuscripts 232 and 244, and book V, page 24. In some places it is attributed to Saint James, the brother of the Lord; elsewhere to Saint John the Evangelist. It still lies unpublished, and it is not in the public interest that it should appear. Calmet, cited work, page CXXV, no. 25], should not be accepted by the Church, lest what is certain be received as uncertain, and what is doubtful as true.

It pleases me to pause briefly in the course of our sermon to praise her nativity today. This is held with the greatest firmness by the whole Catholic Church, because today she arose from royal descent—namely, from the lineage of the great King David. Truly, it is a great condescension that, on the day of the birth of so great a Mother, the tongue of flesh should not be silent in the praises of the Lord.

Let us see, then, brothers, who this Virgin is, so holy that the Holy Spirit deigned to come to her. Who is so beautiful that God chose her as his bride? Who is so chaste that she could remain a virgin after childbirth? She is the temple of God, that sealed fountain, and that closed gate in the house of the Lord.

Upon her, therefore, the Holy Spirit descended; over her the power of the Most High cast its shadow. From her Christ, powerful in virtues, came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber:

> “His going forth was from the summit of heaven, and he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVII, 6).

She is undefiled by intercourse, fruitful in childbirth, a virgin in chastity. She conceived as a virgin, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit. She gave birth not in sorrow but in joy. She nourished the food of angels and of men.

Truly blessed and worthy of every praise is she who, without human seed, brought forth heavenly bread for the world and gave birth to the Savior for the world. O how blessed is that mother, who conceived purity without any defilement and gave birth to healing without pain!

Blessed, I say, is the mother through whom the life of our race was restored; she received from heaven the offspring of God and gave birth to the world’s liberator, Redeemer, and Savior from sins and death. In a wondrous and ineffable manner she gave birth to both the Creator of all things and her own Creator.

She was chosen as an intact virgin, to whom the fruitfulness of motherhood would be granted; and she became a fruitful mother in whom the integrity of virginity would be preserved.

For if we contemplate a virgin who conceived flesh without carnal desire and gave birth to a man without a man, and if we wish to seek the reason for this deed, we collapse in the very act of our inquiry, since it is written: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8).

This saying, as we rightly understand it of Christ’s divine birth, may likewise be understood of his temporal birth from the Virgin. For John, the Lord’s forerunner and baptizer, was of such dignity, holiness, and merit that he saw the Holy Spirit resting upon Christ in the form of a dove. Yet he did not dare to speak, or even to think, of Christ’s temporal generation.

For he himself declares: “He must increase, but I must decrease; I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal” (John III, 30; I, 27).

What, then, is the strap of the sandal except the bond of the mystery of Christ’s incarnation from the immaculate Virgin? John therefore cannot untie the strap of the sandal, because even he, who recognized this incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

What, then, shall we, far inferior in merit, dare to inquire into—a mystery that not even the demons, nor the holy angels themselves, I will not say penetrate, but are in any way able to touch?

Let us believe only this: that she, a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a perpetual virgin after childbirth, conceived her Son through the power of the Holy Spirit, without corruption of the flesh, without the law of a man, and without human custom; and she gave birth with the enclosure of her womb closed. He was true man and true God, and he would die for us as man, while as God he would redeem and liberate us.

And what wonder is it, brothers, if God was born of a virgin? Who can doubt the power of so great a deed? No one can doubt that such a God is omnipotent. It is true, brothers, that God is omnipotent, and for that reason he can do all things.

How, then, will he be all-powerful if he could not do everything? But he can do everything. And how could he do everything if he could not be born of a virgin? Far be it from us, brothers, to yield to the unbelief of the Jews, who do not believe the prophets when they prophesy Christ’s incarnation through a virgin; or to be numbered among the heretics who deny this as well, thinking themselves wiser than God and blasphemously judging it unworthy of God to be born of a virgin [F.: “to believe this”].

For this holy Virgin of God, whose nativity we celebrate with solemn service, alone destroyed all heresies, since she believed the words of the archangel Gabriel. Therefore everything that was said to her by the Lord was fulfilled.

Mary herself, I say, the heavenly gate whose birthday we rejoice to celebrate, conceived nothing other than by believing.

O blessed Mary, worthy of every praise, who brought forth for us so great and such a Redeemer! O glorious Mother! O happy kisses impressed upon the lips of the nursing child! Amid the frequent signs of his infancy, when the crying and crawling child played with you, his mother, as a true son from you, while the true Lord from the Father commanded.

Born from you is he who made you. Born from you is he who brought forth water from the rock for the thirsty people. Born from you is he who appeared to Moses in the fire of the flame of the bush and gave him the law on Sinai. Born is he who caused Aaron’s staff to bud without water and brought forth fruit from it.

Born from you is he who walked upon the sea with his feet, rose from the tomb like a lion, and ascended victoriously into heaven. Born is he into whose face the angels long to look. Born from you is he who grants everlasting life to those who believe in him.

O blessed woman, a joy to the angels and desired by the saints! Your praise is less than your dignity deserves. Let your charity attend, beloved: this Mother of Christ is higher than heaven and deeper than the abyss. She is therefore rightly called the Lady of the angels, the terror of the underworld, and the mother of the nations.

Concerning her the Psalmist says:

> “In your beauty and your splendor, advance prosperously, go forth, and reign” (Ps. XLIV, 5).

And again:

> “The Queen stood at the right hand of God, clothed in a garment of gold” (ibid., 10).

Likewise:

> “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, for the King of glory has desired your beauty” (ibid., 11–12).

The King of glory so desired the beauty of the holy Virgin that he ineffably enclosed himself in her womb, having become man. He so desired her beauty that he assumed flesh from her—he who had created Adam.

And again, what can we fittingly say, or what can we relate, in praise of so glorious a Mother of God? Let the tongue of flesh now be silent, so that this same holy Mother of God may be honored with instruments. Let the timbrels clap, let the organs sound, let the ears of those who love her ring.

> “Clap your hands, all you nations; shout to God with a voice of rejoicing, for the Lord is most high, terrible, and a great King over all the heavens” (Ps. XLVI, 2–3),

and over the whole earth.

He deigned to be born of the Virgin Mary; and the Creator, clothed in royal flesh taken from a creature, deigned to visit the world from the Virgin’s palace.

O wondrous love of the almighty Father and of ineffable compassion toward us! Who could ever hope that God would be born of a woman? O immeasurable love of charity—that God should have permitted his own Son to suffer for the salvation of the human race, as the Apostle writes: “God did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). Who would not be astonished at the riches of such compassion? Who would not tremble before such ineffable charity? Who could ever conceive that the bearer of the world should be carried in a woman’s arms; that the bread of angels should be nourished; that the strength of heaven should be weakened; that the power of heaven should be humbled; that the Creator of angels should be placed in a manger; and that the life of all should die? For Christ died because of our sins and rose for our justification (Rom. 4:25).

O true charity and beloved eternity! O supreme love and supreme affection—that the servant might be redeemed, while the Son was not spared. I shall say it boldly, brothers: blessed and necessary was the fault of the first man, which deserved to have his own Lord as Redeemer. The envious serpent poured lethal venom in paradise; thus the gentle Lamb made medicine from poison, heaven from earth, the cross from the tree, life from the fruit, and the heavenly from the earthly. Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers out of envy, made glory from captivity and, though sold as a captive, became the prince who sold foreign peoples, so from a woman came a palace, from a wife his temple, and from Mary the heavenly entrance.

Let the rejoicing angels, the exultant archangels, cherubim and seraphim, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers, and the virtues of heaven now sing together; let them adore in glory and say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of glory. Hosanna in the highest.” You know, brothers, that *Sabaoth* means “of hosts”; *Hosanna* means “save” or “bring salvation.”

Finally, when the most blessed Virgin Mary, filled with the Holy Spirit, came into Elizabeth’s house, “the child leaped in her womb” (Luke 1:41). The Lord of hosts was therefore already displaying his army through its joy, driving away sadness and saving in the heights the world that had been lost on earth. Mary had to give birth to the great King who was to bring salvation [F.: “who brings salvation”], because he was already in her, purifying and sanctifying her; for after Elizabeth’s amazement, [supplement: “filled”] with the Holy Spirit, she said to Mary: “And from where does this come to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

Then the mother of Christ, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” [Col. 1304D] (ibid., 47). We must ask, brothers, what it means to magnify the Lord; for the Creator cannot be made great by the creature. It is said: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Eccl. 18:1); and the Psalmist says: “The founder of the rejoicing of the whole earth” [reading: “founded in rejoicing”] (Ps. 47:3); and elsewhere: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146:5).

But God is said to be magnified in two ways: either he is worshiped as God, or he is admired as great. God is magnified by us when he is magnified in us. Yet he is not magnified in us as he is magnified in Mary, from whom he assumed flesh. For from her the Son of God was born. God is uniquely magnified in Mary when she conceived the Son through the Word, gave birth without pain, and suckled the King and Savior of all ages.

The Lord, therefore, is magnified in Mary; let him also be magnified in us, if we admire him, rejoice, and give him thanks. Let us praise and adore him, who called us from darkness and the shadow of death to faith; from death to life; from corruption to incorruption; from exile to our homeland; from mourning to joy; and from earthly things back to heavenly things.

Let us imitate in some measure, brothers, the mother of the Lord, if we wish to become her children and sharers in the kingdom of our Lord. She became the mother of the Lord because she always delighted in heavenly things; and if we long for heavenly things, we do the will of God. If we do God’s will, we can be counted among the number and called by the name of mother—not naturally or properly, as she was. For the Son of the Virgin himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:50).

Let us therefore desire nothing earthly, nothing transitory, and let us regard what belongs to the present as something in which we should take no delight. Let us count all laughter as mourning, joy as sorrow, and the world as a prison. The mind that remains firmly established in Christ seeks no joy in this age. Hence Solomon says: “There is no joy except in the Lord”; and David says: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous” (Ps. 32:11). Again: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised, and my soul shall rejoice in the Lord” (Ps. 33:3). And: “My soul is like dry land before you” (Ps. 142:6). For how can one who rejoices so greatly in present things, who does not desire eternal things, who is elated when praised and driven by great goads of anger when blamed, possess the exultation of the elect?

The height of humility in which that blessed Virgin persevered is clearly shown by the fact that, when the messenger of Christ’s Incarnation had related to that holy mother all the things unheard of throughout the ages, she finally replied: “Behold,” she said, “the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:38).

O how great is the power of humility, upon whom the Lord deigns to come! “Upon whom,” says Scripture, “will the Lord rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at his words?” (Isa. 66:2). Hence humility is included among the other beatitudes, as the Savior testifies: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33:19). He did not say that he would save those humble in body, but those humble in spirit. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt us at the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5:6). And the Lord himself says to his disciples concerning himself: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

The Mother of God possessed the power of this holy humility, as she herself says: “The Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid; behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). And truly, brothers, the whole world through all generations calls her the mother of the Lord. Truly blessed is the humility that bore God for human beings and brought forth life for mortals. Truly blessed is the humility that announced the heavens, renewed them, purified the world, opened paradise, and freed the souls of the saints from the underworld.

Blessed indeed is the humility that is made the gate of paradise and established as the ladder of heaven. Mary became the heavenly ladder—the ladder, I say, by which God descended to earth. Mary became the palm of virgins, the glory of widows, the exultation of married women, the victory of Christians, and the joy of angels … [lacuna] of souls. Mary became the gate of heaven, the exaltation of the apostles, the praise of martyrs, the jubilation of confessors, the continence of virgins, the rule of monks, the standard of princes, and the justice of kings. She became the salvation of morals, the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, and the palm of victors.

Mary became exalted above the stars, holy [Col. 1306B] above all women; her illustrious life illumines all churches, heals the sick, restores the lost, and inspires hope in the despairing. This is the mother of Christ, who illumines peaceful minds: joyful in those who make progress, fruitful in penitents, glorious in those who persevere, and victorious in those who depart.

This, I say, this is the blessed Virgin who shows herself blessed by all generations, because God has regarded her humility.

Come, most blessed Mother of God; speak, so that your voice may resound throughout the whole world. Come, utter your words, because the Holy Spirit cries out in you, and in you the Church resounds daily. Say, therefore: “The Lord has done great things for me, because he is powerful” (Luke 1:49). What great things has he done? What is his name? “Powerful and holy is his name” [Col. 1306C]. What great things, then, has the Creator of the whole world done in you? From you, who were his creature, he deigned to be born.

Speak, therefore, glorious one; let your voice be heard in the heights: “When I was a humble girl, I pleased the King who is exalted above the stars; and when I was betrothed to a Jewish man, I pleased God.” I pleased him so that through me he might illumine the world.

O beloved ones, what praises can our frailty offer to this blessed Virgin? Through her the human race was restored; through her we found access to the heavenly kingdom. She is the one who, without human seed, brought forth the heavenly bread for the world; she is the one who obtained the dignity of motherhood and did not lose her virginal purity. From her arose Christ, our God, the sun of justice, who drove away the darkness of the world and illumined us with the radiance of faith.

Therefore, brothers, we humbly entreat the glorious Virgin: since we are unequal to the merits of the saints, may she excuse our sins by her prayers; may she admit our prayers into the sanctuary of hearing; and may she bring back the grace of reconciliation. Through her, may what we have done wrong be excused; may she receive what we offer; obtain what we ask; and excuse what we fear.

I dare to say, brothers, that among all the saints we find none so powerful in merits for calming the anger of the eternal Judge as she who deserved to become the mother of that same Redeemer and Judge. Therefore, may this blessed Virgin, herself a virgin above virgins, come to the aid of the wretched, help the fainthearted, comfort those who weep, pray for the people, intervene for the clergy, intercede for the choir of monks, and plead for the devout female sex.

Let us ask this; let us continually implore this; and may all who celebrate her solemn birthday experience her saving assistance.

Let us all say it; let us cry out with devoted hearts: O Virgin of virgins, may your holy compassion be holy toward us, toward the afflicted and grieving for whatever cause, and may your clemency extend over pilgrims. And when you see yourself exalted above the ethereal heavens, do not despise the prayers of our humility; but always free us from every danger, blessed Virgin.

If we are able, dear children, let us attempt, as best we can, to offer her praise, saying: O how undefiled is the virginity that surpasses all the angels in the heavenly realms and glorifies the virgin choirs! O how blessed is the mother who deserved to give birth to Christ the Lord, the holy King of glory! O how blessed are the feet that deserved to support Christ! O how fortunate are the breasts that suckled the Author and Redeemer of the world!

O ineffable Virgin! He who made you was carried by you; he who ruled the whole world was held in your lap; the Governor of the universe was supported by you. Therefore, exulting among the shining lilies of confessors and the budding roses of martyrs, you too reign in that most blessed kingdom of the blessed, because you follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

Amid the delights of paradise you walk with holy steps, and with a happy, unfading palm and a crown of glory you are glorified by your Son, your Lord, our Lord. Joined to the angelic choirs and associated with angelic companies, you remain in the chamber of the King, your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, adorned with gems and pearls [Col. 1307C] and decorated with necklaces.

A royal throne has been placed for you in the hall of the eternal King. The King himself of kings, loving his true mother and beautiful bride especially above all others, associates her with himself in an imperial embrace.

O how glorious is the holy Virgin Mary, who embraces the Lord in the heavenly kingdom—and rightly so, because he assumed flesh from you. Nor is it surprising that God rejoices with you in heaven, since you so often kissed him when he was born as a little child on earth [Note: In the manuscript those words are almost effaced and can scarcely be read; nevertheless, it is believed that they cannot be read otherwise.].

Possessing these blessings of yours, turn toward our perpetual salvation.

[Col. 1308A] In the midst of all this, therefore, brothers, let us entrust ourselves with the whole affection of our minds to the intercessions of that most blessed Virgin Mary; let us all implore her patronage. But what benefit is it for us to appeal with our voices unless we also hold fast to the examples of her humility? Let us therefore beseech so great a Queen that he who was born from her, who wondrously created humanity and redeemed it even more wondrously, may release the bonds of our sins and deign to introduce us into that region of perpetual security and peace.

Let us also take care, dearest brothers, that we who desire to attend the festival of this day appear clothed in the garments of humility and patience. Patience will then be true if it is righteous. Those possess righteous patience whose unconquered firmness of mind yields neither to pains nor to pleasures.

Let us not glory in our own righteousness, nor presume upon our own strength, but in him of whom the Prophet says: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Ps. 117:14). Therefore, let the Lord be our strength and praise; let God be for us complete praise, perfect glory, pure love, certain hope, firm security, sound ability, and incorrupt health; and let whatever pleases us in carnal things displease us.

Let temperance and abstinence with discretion be in us. Above all these things, let there be firm charity, which contains the whole law. Giving thanks to our Creator as far as we are able, let us joyfully celebrate the birthday of the most precious ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary, so that while we honor her frequently with humble service on earth, she may deign to commend us through constant prayer in heaven.

May this be accomplished by our Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to be born from her as God and man, and who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# POEMS ATTRIBUTED TO THE BLESSED ALCUIN

## 545 PRELIMINARY NOTICE

“In the poems as well,” says Mabillon in the *Elogium of Blessed Alcuin* [Note: See this *Elogium* below in the Appendix. EDITOR.], section 16, no. 82, “there are some spurious and illegitimate pieces: for example, the third poem, or epigram, about Bugga, which was written while Ina, king of the West Saxons, was reigning; he preceded Alcuin by nearly a century. The forty-eighth, about Æthelthryth, belongs to the venerable Bede. The one hundred and seventy-seventh belongs to Angilbert of Centula. Finally, if the one hundred and seventy-eighth is Alcuin’s, it must be said that the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome was despoiled before the year 840, when it is recorded that this was done by the Saracens. Indeed, since that poem concerns the pagans’ attack upon the island of Britain, I would readily believe it to be Alcuin’s, since in his time the Danes attacked that island. The moral verses which Lupus quotes from Alcuin in letter 20 are poem 179.”

We have, for our part, counted the poem otherwise numbered 178 among the genuine works under no. 280, believing, with Mabillon, that the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome might have been despoiled at some earlier time; especially since it is not asserted there with certainty that this happened, but only reported as follows:

“By the hands of the faithless it is said to have been laid waste,” etc.

No one else attributes those moral verses, which Servatus Lupus says Alcuin is reputed to have composed in the cited letter to Alcuin, to Alcuin; rather, they are thought to belong to Saint Columbanus.

We believe that several other pieces should be counted among these spurious works: namely, the verses to Pope Adrian, which Fabricius thinks flowed from Alcuin’s pen at the place cited in the note; poems 217 and 218 of the earlier edition, namely the epitaph of that same Pope Adrian; poem 185, which is Charles’s poem to Alcuin; poem 186, Charles’s poem to Paul, then a monk of Cassino, to which we add another of the same author to the same man from Fabricius; poem 177, which belongs to Angilbert, abbot of Centula, [Col. 1309A] to Saints Richarius and Elogius; poem 116, about the temple built by that same Angilbert; poem 117, about the temple built by Fardulf, abbot of Saint-Denis; the epitaphs of Hildegard and of Hildegard’s two daughters, Hildegard and Adelheid, which Quercetanus joined to the rest of Alcuin’s poems on page 1757; the acephalous poem in the same place; and finally the poem of Rabanus Maurus, in the same place, page 1756.

There also exist other poems or epigrams that someone might suppose to be Alcuin’s. Certain learned men wish all verses found somewhere under the name of Charlemagne, or written in that age with the author’s name suppressed, to be attributed to our Alcuin as the most celebrated poet of that time. But since we find them published nowhere under his name, and lack, as they say, positive grounds for attributing them to him, we rightly refrain from including them.

Of this kind are the verses about Charlemagne which, in the manuscript codex of the learned man Philippus Loyauté, advocate in the supreme court, are said to be “of the lord master in the palace,” and which are published in volume 2 of D. du Chesne’s *History of the Franks*, page 645. That very distinguished writer considers them to be either by Paul the Deacon or by Alcuin; but for precisely that reason we have no certainty that they are Alcuin’s.
