## 549 POEM III [Note: This third poem is among those published by Quercetanus, but is falsely attributed to Alcuin. Its true author testifies that he lived and wrote while Ina, or In, ruled the kingdom of the West Saxons; Ina is remembered as having abdicated the kingdom around the year 727. See Mabillon, volume 2 of the *Annals*, book 20, page 79, no. 79; Alford, *Anglo-Saxon Annals*, volume 2, under the year of Christ 725.] TO BUGGA’S TEMPLE [Note: *Bugga*. Mabillon thinks that this is the same woman whose letter to Boniface, while he was still a priest, appears among the Boniface letters as no. 35 (volume 89 of the Patrology, column 690, letter 3 in the new order). In that letter she congratulates him on his fortunate Roman journey; she says that she is not yet an abbess, but a lowly servant, although Saint Boniface honors her with the title of abbess in another letter to her. Mabillon, volume 2 of the *Annals*, book 19, page 13, and book 23, page 190, no. 42.]

This temple, built by Bugga with beautiful craftsmanship,

Was erected by the noble daughter of King Eutwin [Note: *Eutwin*. He was a prince of the West Saxons, perhaps one of the under-kings who, for about ten years after Cenwalch, held the divided kingdom of that people among themselves; perhaps no other than Esewin, concerning whom see William of Malmesbury. Mabillon, cited book 19, page 9, no. 16.],

He who first governed the empire of the Saxons rightly;

Despising the gifts and heights of the present kingdom,

He abandoned the riches of the world and the reins of worldly things,

Lavishly devoting resources to newly founded basilicas.

The country people now preserve the rights of the monasteries [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

Then she went forth to seek a consecrated life,

When she abandoned her own kingdom for the name of Christ.

Yet before that he had fought battles in three wars,

And likewise completed wars with three triumphs;

Or he ruled the kingdom happily for many years,

Until, converted, he withdrew into a blessed cell.

From there he sought the heights above, shining with merits,

Led by angelic hosts to the summits of heaven,

Joined to the citizens of heaven in a joyful … heavenly lot.

After him succeeded the king famous in war and arms,

Powerful Ceadualla [Note: *King Ceadualla*. He died at Rome after receiving baptism in the year 689, on 20 April. See Alford, *Ecclesiastical Anglo-Saxon Annals*, under the years 688 and 689.], possessor and heir of the kingdom;

But soon abandoning imperial power and the world’s scepter,

He plowed the swelling blue waters with curved ships,

And traversed the sea’s plains with the oar.

The icy waters rattled beneath the windy blasts,

Until the boat struck the shores with its rough prow.

Then he crossed the cloud-covered Alps on foot,

Enclosed by snowy ramparts and the mountain’s summit.

At his arrival Rome’s clemency rejoiced,

And at the same time the clergy of the Church throughout the world rejoiced,

While he, blessed, deserved to be plunged into the waters of baptism.

After the white garments [Note: *After the white garments*. That is, after baptism. “For when the king has been baptized,” says Alford at the cited place, page 397, no. 5, “he is clothed in a white garment, which he never afterward removes … for, since he had not yet laid aside the virginal garment, he is seized by illness, etc.” In his epitaph according to the Venerable Bede, book 5, chapter 7, we read:

“Whom the grace of Christ, cleansing in the font of rebirth,

Immediately made white and bore into the heavenly citadel.”]

he grew weak with illness,

Until he closed the channels of mortal life,

Seeking the lofty kingdoms of the heavenly spheres,

Ascending the bright summit of star-bearing Olympus.

But when these princes had penetrated the lofty heaven—

“Whose two names I have already described above” [Note: By this the poet seems to imply that he had written something else about Eutwin and Ceadualla, kings of the West Saxons.]—

A third received the scepter, a wealthy ruler,

Whom the peoples call Ina, with an uncertain surname [Note: *Ina*. King Ina, successor of Eadwala, who likewise abandoned his kingdom and went to Rome in the year 728. See Alford under the years 689 and following.],

Who now governs the Saxons’ empire by right.

While he ruled, a new chapel of lofty structure

The humble servant of Christ, Bugga, built,

Where the sacred altars shine under a name twice sixfold;

Moreover, an altar of the Virgin consecrates the apse.

Let us all, therefore, celebrate the present day with rejoicing,

And sing responsive songs to God and Christ.

## 550

The months roll on through eternal festivals,

And in their appointed cycles the years’ periods will revolve.

Let the antiphons strike the ears with sweet harmonies,

And let the hymn resound with twin choirs of psalms.

Let the articulated voice ring back in hymns and frequent song,

[Col. 1311A] and shake the lofty vault with a clamorous hymn.

Brothers, let us praise the Thunderer with a voice of praise,

And let the crowd of Sisters cry out with repeated songs.

Let us bring forth hymns, psalms, and responsories suitable to the festivals

Beneath the vaulted roof of the temple,

Speaking the melody of the psalter with frequent chanting.

Let us strive to stretch the lyre from its strings,

As the Psalmist commands, to stretch the strings twice fivefold.

Let each person adorn the new chapel with his voice,

And let the male or female reader unfold the sacred volumes.

This is the day on which the festivals of the temple shine;

The Virgin Mary sanctified it by her birth,

Which continually … the times of August [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

While the torrent of Sextilis is divided through the middle of its course,

It restores to us once more the joys of the mind,

As Mary’s solemn festivals return in their appointed cycles,

And the venerable altars stand furnished with pious gifts.

This house shines within with serene light,

Which the sun perhaps illuminates through glass windows,

Spreading clear rays through the square-shaped temple.

Many are the ornaments of the newly built basilica.

Golden hangings gleam with twisted threads,

Beautiful coverings for the sacred altar;

And a golden chalice, covered with gems, glitters,

As the sky glows with suitably arranged [F.: “open”] stars.

Thus the broad paten stands fashioned in silver,

Bearing the remedies of our divine life,

For we are nourished by the sacred body and blood of Christ.

Here a sheet of the cross shines in yellow gold,

And at the same time is adorned with gems and silver metal.

Here too a thurible, enclosed all around by little capitals,

Hangs from above, opening smoky apertures.

From them the Sabæan incense will breathe forth ambrosial fragrance

When the priests are commanded to offer Masses.

Now let clear glory be given to the Father, who is unbegotten;

Let no less glory be offered to the Son, who is begotten;

And let the Holy Spirit share in praise together with them.

## POEM VIII. ALCUIN TO THE SAME

Behold, Paul, may God increase your hours three times fivefold,

As he added three periods of five years to pious Hezekiah.

You desire that he add three times five years to my life

After its limits, in Pierian song.

What are you doing now as a soldier, you who were once ready,

Paul, to cut the necks of our enemies with a sword?

Now, an old man, your right hand has grown weak and exhausted by war;

Your left hand cannot raise your head aloft or lift shields.

What can you do now, a commoner in the city,

You who fear to see the camps of war crowned with laurel?

The blood grows sluggish in your aged body;

Your heart is colder and lacks love of praise.

## POEM X. ANGILBERT, ABBOT, TO SAINTS RICHARIUS AND ELOGIUS

See it among the works of Saint Angilbert, in volume 99 of the Patrology, column 849.

## 552 [Note: In Quercetanus this poem is number 116. It appears to have been composed after the death of Angilbert, abbot of Centula, which occurred in the year 814, because the poet wishes to pray for his everlasting rest. It was therefore falsely attributed to Alcuin, who died before Angilbert. See the Life of Saint Angilbert in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, fourth century, part 1, pages 91 ff.] POEM XI. TO THE TEMPLE BUILT BY ANGILBERT

Everything you see renewed with the highest beauty,

The sacred temple within and without,

Angilbert, rejoicing, has now made through fatherly love

For the saints and for the everlasting God alike,

Sparing none of his own resources. For whatever he possessed

He has already given to the Church with generous devotion.

And you, servant of God, who come … from elsewhere [F.: “from another place”], traveler,

Make your way through these beautiful precincts of the monastery.

With devout heart behold the churches of God and Christ,

The varied adornment wrought through pious labor.

Always speak great praises of Christ with your mouth,

Who willed your servant to be able to do such things.

And say: “Grant heavenly rest to your servant, O Christ,

Who made these beautiful things in your name.

And you, servants of God, intercede for him always,

That Christ may preserve his servant everywhere.

May he forgive his sins and grant eternal salvation.”

[Note: In Quercetanus, no. 117. Fardulf was abbot of Saint-Denis near Paris in the year 793, during the reign of Charlemagne, whom he accompanied on the expedition against the Saxons in 795. He died in the year 806 or the following year, that is, three years after Alcuin. It is therefore not Alcuin’s, on account of the verse “Grant him perpetual …,” which presupposes that Fardulf had already died.]

## POEM XII. TO THE TEMPLE BUILT BY FARDULF, THE ABBOT

Fardulf the abbot had made this excellent work.

Grant him perpetual reward, O Christ, we pray.

This is the gracious house, the place of pardon, the gracious place of salvation;

Here God dwells, granting the pious prayers of the one who asks,

Through the merits of the saints, whose sacred bodies rest here.

This ciborium too Fardulf the abbot had made.

## POEM XVI. ACEPHALOUS POEM

[Col. 1314A]

[long lacuna]

Albinus [Note: *Albinus*. Not the author of the poem, but an intercessor before God. Whether this name is to be understood of the deceased Alcuin, already received into heaven, or of another Albinus who lived in the time of the emperor Lothair and his wife Ermengard, around the year 824, is unknown. This would have to be determined from the beginning of the poem, if it should ever be discovered.] himself asks in his prayers,

That you may live happily amid the turmoil of the present world;

This little company of your servants asks God for this on your behalf.

When, after the times of the world, you have been placed in paradise,

May you receive the rewards that endure without end.

Together with this beloved wife, Ermengard [Note: *Ermengard*. Or Irmengard, who married Lothair, son of Emperor Louis the Pious, in the year 821, and bore three sons, Louis, Lothair, and Charles. She died in the year 951. *Annals of Metz*.],

May you be a powerful queen for all time.

May you live happily with him for very many years,

And may you be able to see offspring born from your offspring.

You, O glory of the kingdom, most faithful hope of the empire,

Fare well, Lothair, handsome young man, well enough.

May the love of Christ bind you and your brothers [Note: *May love bind you and your brothers*. For long-standing hostilities broke out among them, but peace was made in the year 849.],

So that no enemy may approach us.

Thus may you hold the kingdom of the world in the fields of the world,

So that after death the heavenly kingdoms may possess you.

# APPENDICES TO THE WORKS OF THE BLESSED ALCUIN

[Col. 1313]

## 555 PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 1313C] While we were occupied with collecting the works of Blessed Alcuin and preparing a new edition of them, certain letters, charters, and ancient records came to our attention, as well as some more recent observations by learned men. These materials concern the affairs and deeds of that blessed man and of his age, but could not conveniently be referred to the genuine, doubtful, or spurious works of the same author. It therefore seemed necessary that they should be presented at the end of the entire collection in three appendices [Note: We add a fourth, consisting of certain short works, namely the *Book of Prayers*, which we compiled from Martène, and the *Elogium of Alcuin*, which we excerpted from Mabillon. EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGY.] in the same order that we observed in the works themselves: namely, that the letters should appear first; second, the materials concerning doctrine, especially the doctrine of Christ’s adoption; and third, those concerning history.

The first appendix therefore contains those letters which the distinguished Quercetanus inserted among the Alcuinian letters, I think for no other reason than that he believed them to have flowed from the pen of Blessed Alcuin. But since this reason did not satisfy us at all, we judged that they should be removed from that order, though not entirely omitted, [Col. 1313D] lest learned men, if they are referred somewhere to the works of Alcuin on account of them, should look for them in vain in this new edition.

These are the following letters: among Quercetanus’s letters, no. 61, Charles to Athilhard, archbishop; no. 83, Charles to Homer; no. 84, Charles to Pope Leo; no. 85, Charles to King Offa; and no. 111, the same author to Nicephorus, emperor of Constantinople. To these we add another letter by the same author to Emperor Michael, which until now had remained unknown but was recently discovered in a manuscript of the Harleian Library among Alcuin’s unpublished letters.

We also thought that this would be an appropriate place for three unpublished letters of Angilbert, abbot of Centula, a close associate of Blessed Alcuin. We found them mixed among Alcuin’s letters in a very ancient manuscript from Salzburg, as we noted in the preliminary notice prefixed to the letters.

We further add a letter by an anonymous author concerning the seventieth, sixtieth, and fiftieth year, which in Quercetanus was number 109.

Finally, to all these we append three ordinances of Charlemagne for the monasteries of Cormaric and Saint Martin, to which it was sometimes necessary to refer the reader in the course of the work, and especially in the Life of Blessed Alcuin.

In the second appendix we have placed certain documents pertaining to a fuller history of Adoptionism, in which Alcuin’s labors occupy both sides of the controversy; some of these are unpublished, while others have been emended or elucidated from manuscript codices and other sources. Their order is as follows:

1. The letter of Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo—or rather, of all the bishops of Spain who agreed with him in his error—to Charlemagne. It was first published by the learned D. Henricus Florezius of the Order of St. Augustine in a book exceedingly rare in our country, entitled *España Sagrada*, vol. V, appendix X, p. 558. From there the learned D. Christ. Guil. Franc. Walchius transcribed it and inserted it in his *History of the Adoptionists*, p. 154.

2. The previously unpublished and long-desired letter of those same bishops to the bishops of Gaul, Germany, Aquitaine, and Austria, concerning the same doctrine of Christ’s adoption. Credit for obtaining it must be given to the distinguished and most ready helper of literary labors, D. Georgius Majansius, a noble Valencian, who, after finally overcoming the obstinacy of those in charge of the literary treasures, was able to extract it from a manuscript codex of the church of Toledo. I owe my acquaintance with and the goodwill of this man to the most courteous gentlemen who spontaneously offered their services in securing it for me: D. Christianus Fridericus Temler, secretary for ecclesiastical affairs to the most powerful king of Denmark; and D. Carolus Christophorus Pluer, then chaplain of the Danish royal embassy at the court of the Catholic king—two men born for the benefit of letters.

We shall later publish the letters of the distinguished D. Majansius to me and to D. Pluer concerning the fate of this letter and other writings of Elipandus, Etherius, and Beatus, so that nothing may be lacking that could bring light to an obscure matter or lend credibility to one in doubt. These are the two letters that the most Christian emperor Charlemagne and the bishops of his dominions, assembled with the papal legates at Frankfurt in the year 794, had before their eyes, examined carefully, and refuted with many arguments.

There still exist, moreover, letters replying to them, both those of Charlemagne and those of the bishops of Gaul, Germany, and Aquitaine. Although they have often been published in the acts of councils, we did not wish to omit them from this place, because of the connection between the two sets and for the convenience of readers.

Third, we include here the same refutations by Charlemagne and the bishops present at the council of Frankfurt of the earlier letters, collated with a notable and nearly contemporary manuscript codex of our library at St. Emmeram’s, from which we have drawn certain variant readings. We omit the remaining documents relating to that council, namely, the letter of Adrian I, supreme pontiff, and another of the bishops of Italy, or Paulinus of Aquileia’s *Sacrosyllabum*. For although the errors of Elipandus are also refuted in those documents, and although they were sent by Charlemagne to the bishops of Spain after the council had ended, they are not properly replies to all the arguments of the Spaniards. They can therefore easily be absent from this place without inconvenience.

Fourth, so that nothing relevant to the history of the proceedings and dispute concerning Christ’s adoption—in which blessed Alcuin became so illustrious—might be lacking in this new edition of his works, we have excerpted from the books written by Etherius and Beatus against Elipandus only those passages from which the disturbances stirred up by Elipandus in Spain may be understood—disturbances that had already been set in motion for some time before they reached Gaul or Germany.

From those books, therefore, we have transcribed here the passages that recount and report at the outset the dissension that arose in the churches of Spain, together with the confessions and creeds of both parties and their differences. To these we add the letter of Elipandus, bishop, to the abbot Fidelis, collated by the distinguished D. Majansius with Pellicer’s edition in the *Annals of Spain*, book IX, no. 18, p. 406.

The distinguished D. Catelinot, a member of the Benedictine Congregation of Saints Vanne and Hydulphe, had wished to append to the new edition of the works of blessed Alcuin that he was planning the complete books of Etherius and Beatus against Elipandus, as well as the writings of St. Benedict, abbot of Aniane, against the same error. I too had initially intended to follow his plan, as I indicated on p. 17 of the prospectus of the works of blessed Alcuin published some years ago. I changed my mind, however, lest the volume grow excessively through the addition of less necessary foreign treatises already available elsewhere. I was persuaded that learned men would not miss among these works everything that had been done or written against Elipandus and Felix at that time, but only those things capable of bringing light and historical credibility to Alcuin’s own works.

Nevertheless, I trust that for the same reason I shall win the gratitude of learned men if here I share with them the letters of the highly praised D. Majansius, written to me on the occasion of the discovery of the above-mentioned letter of the Spanish bishops, together with his distinguished discussion of the writings of Elipandus, Beatus, and Etherius.

Nor, I hope, will learned men—who know how to assign value to every remnant of antiquity—take it amiss if, fifth and finally, I append to this appendix, from two ancient manuscript codices, the Salzburg and Freising codices, a writing and a not inconsiderable discussion on the Image of God. I believe this work has hitherto remained unpublished; in the Freising codex it is attributed to Candidus, perhaps that Candidus whose services our Alcuin employed on many occasions.

This subject is one of those in which the men of that age, united in the work of restoring letters, exercised their abilities. Blessed Alcuin himself certainly published a similar discussion, which we have presented in Part II of Volume I.

In the third appendix we first present a work which, unless we are mistaken, is still unpublished. We discovered it in manuscript codex 71 of the Salzburg library, under the title: *Description of the Churches of the City of Rome*. It is placed there between Alcuin’s letter to Felix the heretic, first published by us in Volume I, p. 783 [Note: In the new edition of this work, Volume II, column 119. — Editor], and letter 55 of our edition, now numbered 69, to Arno.

Although we do not dare to conclude from this position that the work belongs to blessed Alcuin as its author, even though it is neither foreign to his pious curiosity nor inconsistent with his customary style, there will nevertheless, we believe, be some for whom this distinguished monument of antiquity will not be unwelcome.

The second place in this third appendix will be occupied by a work that might appear entirely foreign to our subject. Its title in an old codex is: *The Most Beautiful Exchange of Letters between Alexander, Great King of the Macedonians, and Dindimus, King of the Brahmans*. Nevertheless, we did not wish it to be absent from the works of blessed Alcuin, because he once sent this same exchange to Charlemagne as a gift, as the verses appended at the end testify.

This work, from an eleventh-century manuscript codex that formerly belonged to the celebrated Benedictine monastery of Millstatt in Carinthia, was transcribed with great industry, with certain corrections added, and communicated to me by the highly learned D. Matthias Rieberer, S.J., librarian and historian at the Jesuit Professors’ House in Vienna. From him the republic of letters eagerly awaits the continuation of *Germania Sacra*, which has thus far been delayed by the death of the celebrated P. Hansiz.

The aforementioned scholar believed that these letters might belong to Alcuin and that they had hitherto remained unpublished. As to the first point, although the arguments that the distinguished D. Rieberer adduces in favor of blessed Alcuin may seem to possess some plausibility, the contrary opinion appears more convincing to us: namely, that these letters are older than Alcuin and that in his age they were believed to contain the correspondence of Paul and Seneca. Alcuin may have found them elsewhere and wished to send them as a gift to Charlemagne, whom he knew to take pleasure in narratives that contributed to his learning. Nor were we able to detect in them the style otherwise familiar to blessed Alcuin; and, as we believe, neither will others detect it who are familiar with the reading of his works.

As for D. Rieberer’s other assertion, we are not surprised that it seemed to the learned man that these letters were still unpublished. They do, in fact, appear in a book exceedingly rare in our lands, namely, at the end of Palladius’ work *On the Peoples of India and the Brahmans*, London edition, 1668, edited by Edward Bisseus, with whose edition we collated this one, marking the variants.

For a long time we hesitated over what judgment should be formed concerning these letters and their authors. Since, among our other occupations, we had no opportunity to investigate at length and with laborious research a matter so obscure and so little relevant to our principal purpose, we consulted a man highly learned in Greek and Roman history, D. Georgius Henricus Martini, rector and public professor of the gymnasium of the city of Regensburg, asking him to shed light on the obscure matter. Kindly agreeing to our request, he set forth his opinion in a letter rich in varied learning, which we have decided to append at the end of the little work. We trust that it will not displease learned readers.

Moreover, we cannot persuade ourselves that those letters were fabricated with malicious intent and composed to deceive. I recall from Strabo and others that certain Brahmans conferred with Alexander of Macedon concerning their wisdom and customs. From this perhaps some ancient writer found occasion to compose these letters as a school exercise, or perhaps to translate genuine letters from Greek into Latin. But after the excellent effort of the most learned D. Martini, I should not wish to comment further on this matter.

[Col. 1317]

## THREE LETTERS OF ANGILBERT TO A CERTAIN BISHOP

### 562. PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 1317D]

I transcribed the following three letters from Salzburg manuscript codex 71, where they are appended to fifty-three letters of Alcuin to Arno. At the end the scribe added this note: “Up to this point, Albinus the teacher.” In the margin of the following letter the same scribe added another note: “Also Angilbert.” Because of this note, no one will doubt that the three immediately following letters are to be attributed to Angilbert, abbot of Centula. This is especially so because in the third letter the writer invites the bishop to the monastery of St. Richard, of which Angilbert was abbot.

That the letters were addressed to a certain bishop is clear from the text; but which see he governed is unknown. It may be conjectured that he was Arno of Salzburg, since they are preserved in a codex belonging to his church and are intermingled with Alcuinian letters addressed to him; especially because the first letter mentions the monastery and brothers of St. Amand, an abbey that Arno held in addition to the bishopric of Salzburg.

### LETTER I

To the most beloved Father, most faithful friend, and dearest brother, that bishop worthy of God whom I must name with the greatest love and honor. I, your humble and most faithful son in Christ, through these lines of my lowliness wish you, and all the sons of God’s holy Church subject to your sacred government [Read: government], health in the present life and the happiness of eternal glory.

Know, most beloved Father, that through God’s mercy, with the intercession of all the saints and your prayer assisting us, all is well with us, except that my illness—in which, according to the Apostle, I gladly glory—seems to be increasing more and more. For this reason also the lord king, in his almsgiving, allowed me to go to the monastery, so that, with the Lord’s protection, I might attend to my illness.

Eight days before the lord king set out for Saxony, Peter arrived with a letter from the apostolic lord. Among other things it stated that he had personally invested you, on behalf of the king, with the church of St. Paul and the monastery of St. Stephen [Note: We do not know which church of St. Paul or which monastery of St. Stephen is meant here, in which this bishop [Arno] was invested by the apostolic lord at the intercession of Pippin and by the command of King Charles; nor do we have any certain knowledge of the other circumstances touched upon in this letter.].

The lord king was therefore greatly pleased, and we, insofar as we were able, praising your goodness and fidelity, increased the king’s joy. For it is written: “There is no comparison with a faithful friend.” And again, according to the same Scripture: “If a friend remains firm, he will be to you as an equal, and he acts faithfully among your household.” And again: “A faithful friend is the medicine of life.” And again: “A faithful friend is a strong protection; whoever finds him has found a treasure” (Ecclesiasticus 6:15, 11, 16, 14). Yet according to the wise, such a friend is rarely found and difficult to preserve. For Pippin too promised us that he would intercede in this matter.

We ask that you deign to receive the present messengers with your customary kindness. The monastery of St. Amand is safe and well with its brothers; they pray together with us that he may deign to govern, protect, and preserve you, most beloved Father, for the advancement of his holy Church and for our joy, through many years.

With earnest prayers we beg you to hasten to make us more certain, through your sacred letters, of your arrival and of your desired prosperity and beloved happiness. For we do not expect to go to meet the lord king until after the middle of September.

[Col. 1319A]

What more shall I say? God is my witness: I desire faithfully to labor for your advancement, and, with the Lord’s help, I shall never cease from that labor throughout the days of my life. I commend myself entirely, most beloved Father and most faithful friend, to your sacred and God-worthy prayers.

### 563. LETTER II

To the most beloved Father, that bishop whom I must name with the greatest honor and love (Name). I, your most faithful son, through these lines wish your Paternity eternal salvation in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

With devoted mind we offer thanks to your goodness for all the kindness that your holiness continually deigns to bestow upon our lowliness, especially for your sacred prayers, which, as we trust, you do not disdain to pour out before the Lord for us.

We have received your honey-sweet and wholly honorable letters. When we read them through, they made us happy in part and sad in part, because from them we learned of your labor on account of the weakness of your body. But what is better than gladly glorifying, according to the Apostle, in our infirmities (2 Corinthians 12:9)? And elsewhere: “For whom the Lord loves, he reproves, and as a father he takes pleasure in his son” (Proverbs 3:12).

We have heard nothing certain concerning the lord king’s journey, nor do we expect that he will move so quickly toward those regions. As for your business, God willing, as we told you personally, we must strive for our common benefit in the Lord. I shall not forget you, most beloved Father, nor your advancement, insofar as, through the Lord’s mercy, I am able, throughout all the days of my life. Do not forget me, most holy Father and most faithful friend, for all time. May God be our helper both here and forever. Amen! Amen!

### LETTER III

[Col. 1319C]

Your faithful son (Name) sends greetings to the most holy Father, that bishop whom I must name with the greatest love and honor (Name).

On the fourth day before the Ides of August we returned immense thanks to almighty God, when your letter informed us of your desired good health and praiseworthy happiness. God is my witness how unceasingly I desire to hear and see you.

As for what you asked us to consider carefully—how you ought to proceed—I cannot write anything definite to you, because I am still uncertain about the lord king’s return [Note: This may refer to Charlemagne’s return from the Saxon expedition; Alcuin also wished to be informed about it in letter 67.].

Nevertheless, it does not seem necessary to us for you to go farther to meet him than the Rhine, unless his command has not reached you. As for our meeting, almighty God knows that I desire your presence with every desire, and I hope that it will benefit us both if we speak together before you come to the lord king.

But if this is to take place before the Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God, which is on the sixth day before the Ides of September, then it is necessary for your holiness to turn aside to us, so that you may both enjoy prayer in the Lord at the church of St. Richard, your intercessor, and fulfill brotherly charity toward us. For we greatly need to attend to some care of our body until the aforesaid day.

And if it should happen that you remain longer at that holy place [Perhaps St. Amand], then we can come to meet you wherever your command may be. Farewell, most holy Father, praying for us happily in the Lord, and fulfill my desire, so that the Lord may fulfill all your petitions and protect you from holy Zion.

## REPLY OF A CERTAIN PERSON [Note: Among the letters of the Quercetan edition of Alcuin, no. 109.] CONCERNING THE SEVENTIETH, SIXTIETH, AND FIFTIETH

To the blessed brothers living happily and advancing toward greater happiness, from that sinful and humble bishop.

I give worthy thanks to God, insofar as I am able, who supplies many good things through you to those whom he has taken for himself by working many good works in you. I ask his greatness not to cease, in his abundance, most mercifully increasing his grace in you until the end.

And although I consider myself unfit for this work, yet, with conscience biting me, I recognize that I am faithful. Therefore I earnestly and humbly ask that you, as fellow soldiers of Christ, obtain for me in every respect through your merits what you request, and take companions with you as your masters [The reading may be *athletas*, “athletes,” rather than *laetas*, “joyful ones.”].

Giving thanks to almighty God, who has deigned until now to protect you with his right hand, I would offer thanks for your blessed conduct of thanksgiving. If not worthy thanks, since I am not able to repay what I owe, nevertheless I shall not omit, insofar as I can, to offer very many thanks to your holiness for your most pious and God-worthy prayers.

I do not doubt that your religious excellence most piously knows the labor that they undertake: they pour out before the Lord not only their own sacred prayers, but also prayers for all others, so that they may likewise deserve to enjoy the fellowship of the saints. And although you have undertaken this labor on behalf of me, unworthy and lacking merit in return, nevertheless you shall have your work remaining in the reward of the just.

May Christ, the giver of blessing, deign to guide you to the very end of the course of this revolving world and also rescue you from unconquerable temptations.

### 564

Therefore pure charity compels me to offer your venerable fraternity the requested letter of reply, not with such estimation—or rather presumption—as though we claimed to teach your discernment anything through our ignorance, but lest you think that we refuse to serve your command by declining conversation with you.

As best we can, we shall disclose what you ask, gathered from the statements of others. We have indeed heard various opinions concerning the question you mention. But I confess that I read a letter composed about it in a remarkable manner. At present, so far as I know, it is not held in our monastery, and we are entirely ignorant of its author. But we have heard from those who say so that it belonged to Master Albinus [Note: See Charlemagne’s letter 81 to Alcuin, vol. C, col. 263.]. We neither wish to affirm nor deny this.

What we have committed to memory from it, although in different words, we shall endeavor to recount. First we ask your affection not to call me a compiler of ancient authors, and therefore to say that I did not wish to show the aforesaid letter but changed its words, while preserving its meaning, out of a desire for empty glory. For I openly admit to you that what I say belongs to another.

You know from canonical authority how and why the time of Lent was established. The holy and distinguished teacher Gregory clearly explained this in his homily on the Gospel: “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert.”

You proposed that we should ask why or for what reason Quinquagesima, or Sexagesima, or even Septuagesima is so called, and why it is celebrated throughout the holy Church [Note: See Alcuin’s letter that is numbered 80 in this edition, vol. C, col. 259. Yet it is not the letter imitated by this writer, but another in which Charlemagne wrote a reply to Alcuin on the same question, no. 81, as will be clear to anyone who compares the two.].

It is also clear that the six weeks during which the holy Church devoted itself to abstinence contain forty-two days. But when the six Sundays are subtracted from the abstinence, thirty-six days remain to be fasted, as though a tithe of the year. Although those weeks therefore contain, as we have said, forty-two days, the holy Fathers nevertheless decided to call them Lent.

Then Telesphorus, who was honored in the holy see of the Roman Church as the ninth after Peter, prince of the apostles, established for his dioceses that abstinence should be observed for seven weeks. We know that many still do this; these weeks likewise contain fifty days.

The faithful then chose to call that period Quinquagesima for two reasons: either because, in the order of speech, the number fifty is customarily counted after forty; or because from that point there are fifty days until the holy day of the Resurrection.

There you have the origin of the name Quinquagesima. But perhaps your diligence wonders why the aforementioned Father Telesphorus prescribed fifty days of abstinence. His words show that he wished, insofar as human frailty permits, to imitate the type of the Lord and Redeemer of the world, who, having assumed dense bodily nature, fasted from human food for forty continuous days.

From the fifty days mentioned, if you subtract eight Sundays from the abstinence, forty-two days are assigned to abstinence. But those two days that exceed the number forty contain a great sacrament in themselves. The first is called the Lord’s Supper, and the other Holy Saturday. Although the canons establish that they are days of abstinence, on account of their sacramental significance they are nevertheless much freer than the others.

Afterward the pontiff Melchiades, an African by birth and the thirty-fourth apostolic bishop after St. Peter in the Roman Church, established that no one should presume to fast on the first or fifth day of the week: on the first, because of the Lord’s Resurrection; on the fifth, because on that day the Lord supped with his disciples and was honored by his glorious Ascension.

Then the faithful decided to devote eight weeks to fasting and to call the first Sunday Sexagesima—not because of a number of sixty days, as we said above that Quinquagesima could be named from the number fifty days, but because of our customary manner of speaking: just as the fiftieth corresponds appropriately to the fortieth, so the sixtieth corresponds to the seventieth.

From Sexagesima until the second day of the Lord’s Resurrection there are, as we said, eight weeks. If from each of them you subtract the first and fifth days of the week, as the great pontiff Melchiades established, and also the holy Paschal day itself, forty days of abstinence nevertheless remain, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Septuagesima is said to be celebrated by the faithful so that they may return tithes of their days to God and nevertheless be able to relax the strictness of fasting on the first, fifth, and seventh days of the week. From Septuagesima to Easter there are nine weeks, making sixty-four days. If from each week you subtract the three days mentioned, and if you fast on the sacred Paschal day for thirty-three days as a tithe, as in Lent [Read: thirty-six days], you see that those who established six weeks of abstinence and those who established nine agree in returning tithes of their days to God in equal measure.

Those who prescribe fasting for seven weeks and those who prescribe it for eight appear equally, by abstaining for forty days, to follow in the Lord’s footsteps. But the one who established that Saturday should be honored did so not because of the legal commandments, which are a shadow of the truth, but because the Lord rested in the tomb on that day, and as evening approached the joy of the holy Resurrection is honorably celebrated.

We cannot name the author of this practice because fraudulent forgetfulness has entered within us. In calculating the number of the days mentioned above, employ careful reckoners; and if you find anything to criticize, let it be corrected when we are gathered together. May he assist us who said that, when two or three are gathered in his name [Read: honor], he stands in their midst.

## CERTAIN DECREES OF CHARLEMAGNE

### 565. I

He grants the monastery of Cormaric the right to establish monks of St. Benedict there and confirms the donation of that place made to the monastery of St. Martin of Tours.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 92.)

### II

He grants the same monastery freedom from toll exactions for ships transporting necessities to the monastery.

[Col. 1322C]

(See the same volume, col. 993.)

### 566. III

He grants and confirms to the monastery of St. Martin, and to its property and people, privileges of immunity from every judicial authority, including that of the royal treasury.

(See the same volume, col. 990.)

[Col. 1321]

## SECOND APPENDIX. DOGMATIC WRITINGS

### 567. LETTER OF THE BISHOPS OF SPAIN TO CHARLEMAGNE

Concerning the controversy over Christ’s adoption.

[Col. 1321D]

(See *Patrologia*, vol. XCVI, col. 867.)

### 568. LETTER OF THE BISHOPS OF SPAIN TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL, AQUITAINE, AND AUSTRIA

Concerning the same controversy.

(From a manuscript codex of the Toledo library.)

To all the lords and most reverend brothers in Christ, the priests of Gaul and Aquitaine [Thus the manuscript; read: Aquitaine] and Austria. We, the unworthy and insignificant bishops of Spain and the other faithful of Christ, wish eternal salvation in the Lord. Amen.

[Col. 1322D]

#### I

A mournful and disastrous opinion has reached our knowledge, an opinion that has utterly crushed us: namely, that the poisonous discourse and sulfurous stench of the pernicious doctrine of Beatus, the foul priest of Asturias, an antiphrastic, pseudo-Christ, and pseudo-prophet, has everywhere defiled the secret recesses of your hearts because he asserts that the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God did not exist at all according to the form of human servitude, and that he did not assume a true, visible form from the Virgin [Note: This is falsely attributed to Beatus.].

#### II

We, therefore, on the contrary, according to the doctrines of the holy and venerable Fathers Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine [Thus the manuscript; read: Augustine], Jerome, Fulgentius, Isidore, Eugenius, Ildephonsus, Julian, and the other orthodox and catholic teachers, confess and believe that God the Son of God was begotten before all times, without beginning, from the Father—coeternal, of like substance, and consubstantial—not by adoption but by generation, not by grace but by nature. The same Son himself bears witness to this: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), together with the other things that the same true God and true man spoke to us concerning his divinity.

For the salvation of the human race, however, at the end of time, proceeding from that intimate and ineffable substance of the Father without departing from the Father, seeking the lowest places of this world, appearing publicly for the human race, and assuming from the Virgin an invisible, visible body, ineffably born through the intact virginal womb of his mother, we confess and believe, according to the tradition of the Fathers, that he was made of a woman and made under the law; that he is the Son of God not by generation but by adoption [Manuscript: *adobtione*; so throughout]; not by nature but by grace. The same Lord bears witness to this when he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

And the Evangelist says of him: “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was in him” (Luke 1:80). And again: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

#### III

Concerning this adoption of the flesh, blessed Ambrose speaks in his *Book on the Trinity* [Note: St. Ambrose, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 8, no. 87], saying:

“How have you been turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God?” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). For those beings are falsely represented as gods, whereas by nature God is living and true. Indeed, by our very usage [Note: “By our very usage.” The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt say that the Spaniards cited this from St. Hilary; they omit, however, the following testimony, which the Spaniards also cite from St. Hilary.] there is both an adopted son and a true son. We do not say that the adopted son is a son by nature, who is the true son [Note: The passage is truncated. The complete text reads: “We do not say that the adopted son is a son by nature, but when we say ‘by nature,’ we mean the one who is the true son.”].

Again, after some intervening material [Note: St. Ambrose, the same work, chapter 9, no. 104]:

“For the Virgin’s childbirth did not change nature but renewed the manner of generation. In the end, flesh was born from flesh. The Virgin therefore had from herself what she could transmit. The mother did not give what was alien, but contributed what was her own from her entrails, in an unusual manner but with the customary gift. The Virgin therefore possessed flesh, which by the established law of nature she transferred into the fetus.

Accordingly, the nature of Mary, who generated according to the flesh, and of him who was generated, is the same, and he is not unlike his brothers, because Scripture says that he should become like his brothers in all things (Hebrews 11:17). The Son of God is indeed like us, not according to the fullness of divinity, but according to the rational soul and, to speak more explicitly, the truth of human [Ambrose: human] nature and of our body.”

### 569. IV

Likewise blessed Hilary of Poitiers says [Note: St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 27. See what blessed Alcuin answered concerning this passage on col. 206 of this volume. For the correct reading of this passage, consult our edition of Hilary’s works at the place cited there, *Patrologia*, vol. X.]:

“The Virgin gives birth, and birth is present; the infant cries, and the praising angels adore; the swaddling clothes are soiled, and God is adored. Thus the dignity of fatherhood [Hilary: power] is not lost while the lowliness of the flesh is adopted.”

### V

Likewise blessed Jerome, in his *Exposition of the Apocalypse*, says [Note: The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt read this passage differently, namely: “And I will give him a white stone, that is, the adoption of the sons of God.” This commentary of blessed Jerome is now found nowhere.]:

“A white stone, that is, a white gem: the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God” (Revelation 2:17).

Likewise, in his letter to Caesarius [Note: “To Caesarius.” The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt read “to Cerasia.” This letter too is unknown. See Alcuin, book II *Against Elipandus*, no. 10 and following]:

“It was not this Word, who must be believed to have been in the Father and with the Father, but the man whom God the Word had received in the grace of salvation, who heard: ‘Today I have begotten you’ (Psalm 2:7; Hebrews 5:5). This Son of Man, through the Son of God, is found worthy to be in the Son of God; adoption is not separated from nature, but nature is joined with adoption.”

### VI

Blessed Augustine too, in his *Exposition* [Thus the manuscript] of the Gospel according to John, speaking according to the form of divinity, says [Note: St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 25. The genuine text is: “Since he was the only Son of God, not by grace but by nature, so that he might also be full of grace, he was made the Son of man.”]:

“The Son of God is not so by adoption but by generation, not by grace but by nature.”

Likewise, in a homily speaking according to the form of human servitude, he says [Note: *Tractate* XXIX on John, no. 8, where the text reads: “You have been adopted, but not by your merits; seek the glory of him from whom you, an adopted man, have this grace—the glory sought by him who was born uniquely from him.” Marvel at the cunning of heretical men, who twist to Christ himself what is said concerning the adoption of redeemed human beings.]:

“Man is adopted, whose glory he sought who was uniquely born from him.”

Behold: the one whom Augustine says was adopted, the apostle John says is the one of whom we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who also intercedes for us (1 John 2:1).

Source/review notes: All 26 supplied editorial notes, exact variant forms, Augustinian interpolations, and the Isidore lacuna remain explicit.

### VII

Accordingly, blessed Isidore says in the *Book of Etymologies* [Note: [Col. 1324D] St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VII, chapter 2.]:

> “He is called *only-begotten* with respect to the excellence of his divinity, because he has no brothers; but *firstborn* with respect to his assumption of humanity, in which he deigned, through the adoption of grace, to have brothers, among whom he would be firstborn.”

### VIII

Likewise, our predecessors Eugenius, Ildephonsus, and Julian, bishops of the see of Toledo [Note: [Col. 1324D] These testimonies seem indeed to have been taken from the Mozarabic liturgy; nevertheless, below, in no. 13, the authors of each statement are named individually.], said the following in the Mass [printed Latin: *in missam*; read: *in missa*] of the Lord’s Supper:

> “Who, through the passion of adopted humanity [printed *passione*; read *passionem*], while he did not spare his own body, finally did not spare ours either—that is, he did not spare it again” [Note: [Col. 1324D] Alcuin says: “This statement makes no sense, nor is it sufficiently clear what its composer intended these words to signify in praying to God.” *Book II Against Elipandus*, no. 7.].

And elsewhere:

> “Who, through the passion of adopted humanity [printed *passione*; read *passionem*], as though he had not displayed certain spoils in the acquisition of the people now present, displayed them from his triumph; and although unchangeable divinity did not have a battle, the assumed frailty had a victory.”

Likewise, in the Mass of the Ascension of the Lord:

> “Today our Savior, after the adoption of flesh, returns to the seat of divinity.”

Likewise, in the Mass for the Dead:

> “Those whom you have made participants in adoption, command to be fellow heirs of your inheritance.”

Behold those whom he does not hesitate to call participants in adoption; he desires that they become fellow heirs in the inheritance.

### IX

E [Note: [Col. 1324D] This letter E, which in the Toledo manuscript is prefixed here to the confession of the Spanish bishops, perhaps denotes Elipandus, their principal leader.]

We therefore believe and confess that God the Son of God is light from light, true God from true God, begotten from the Father as only-begotten without adoption; but that at the end of time he became firstborn by assuming true humanity from the Virgin, in the adoption of flesh: only-begotten by nature, firstborn in adoption and grace. Concerning him the Apostle says:

> “For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

Brothers, namely, those of whom he says through the Psalmist:

> “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Psalm 21:23).

Where else could they be brothers than through the adoption of flesh alone, by which he deigned to have brothers? Concerning them the Holy Spirit spoke through David:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

His companions are those concerning whom the apostle John says:

> “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Like him, certainly, in the adoption of flesh; not like him in divinity.

We believe that that anointing of the Holy Spirit—by which, especially in the Son of God according to his humanity, it was accomplished more abundantly than in his elect, through the sevenfold charisms of spiritual graces [manuscript: *charismata*]—is the anointing of which Isaiah speaks, saying:

> “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:2–3).

We believe that this fullness of anointing exists in the adopted and firstborn Son of God alone; but in the other saints this kind of grace of anointing has been given according to measure.

Concerning the only-begotten Son, however, without adoption, there is the voice of the Father saying:

> “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:4).

And again through the Psalmist:

> “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44:2).

And again elsewhere:

> “The truth of righteousness shall go forth from my mouth” [Read: “the word of righteousness”] (Isaiah 45:23).

Likewise, the voice of the Son, without adoption, says:

> “Before every creature I proceeded from the mouth of the Most High; before the morning star arose, I existed; before you spread out the plains and raised up the mountains on high, I existed” (Sirach 24:5; Proverbs 8:25ff.).

The Father rejoiced with him daily, while he delighted in the perfected world. And again:

> “Before the hills I was brought forth. The earth did not yet exist; when he was preparing the heavens, I was present; when he enclosed the sea with boundaries and established a law for the waters, I existed” (ibid.).

Likewise, the voice of the Father concerning the firstborn and adopted Son says through Moses:

> “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you would me” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

And in the Gospel:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matthew 17:5).

And through David:

> “He shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’ And I will make him firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth. Forever I will preserve my mercy for him, and my covenant shall remain faithful to him. I will establish his seat forever and ever, and his throne shall be like the days of heaven” (Psalm 88:27ff.).

Again he says to him:

> “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

Again the Father says to him through Isaiah:

> “I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth.”

And again:

> “I will go before you, and I will make the mountains level; I will break the bars of iron, and I will give you hidden treasures, so that you may know that I am the Lord your God” (Isaiah 45:2–3).

And through Micah:

> “Shall I give my firstborn for my wickedness, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul?” (Micah 6:7).

By “firstborn” he meant according to humanity; by “fruit of my womb,” according to divinity.

And again he says to David concerning the firstborn Son:

> “When you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up one from your loins who shall sit upon the throne of Israel. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (2 Samuel 7:12).

And elsewhere, in the Book of Jesus son of Sirach:

> “Have mercy, Lord, upon your people, over whom your name has been invoked, and upon Israel, whom you have made equal with your firstborn” (Sirach 36:14).

The Apostle Paul, therefore, speaking of his divinity and humanity together, says:

> “In many ways and by many means God formerly spoke to our fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages. He is the radiance of his glory and the likeness of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power. Having made purification for sins, he sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again, when he brings him into the world, he says, ‘Let all his angels worship him’” (Hebrews 1:1ff.).

### X

Having prefaced these statements of the holy Fathers, by which our assertions are strengthened, we have jointly decreed that we shall in no way depart from their decrees or footsteps, but shall diligently obey their commands. Thus, in the one and same Son of God and man, in one person, there are two complete and perfect natures—of God and of man, of Lord and of servant, of the visible and the invisible—and also three substances, namely, of the Word, the soul, and the flesh. Thus it is to be believed that in the one and same person of God and man there is both a deified man and a humanized God, in accordance with the eloquence of blessed Augustine, who says:

> “For in the form of a servant he was crucified, and yet the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified. Such indeed was that assumption which made God man and man God.”

And after some intervening material:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6). What does “he did not regard it as something to be seized” mean? He did not usurp equality with God, but was in that equality in which he had been born. Receiving the form of a servant, he did not lose what he was, but received what he was not.”

The same author also says:

> “In the fact, too, that it is written of him that he received the promise of the Holy Spirit from God and poured it out, both natures are shown [printed *monstratus*; perhaps *monstrata*], namely, the human and the divine: he received as man, and poured out as God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore Christ himself, the Son of God, is both God and man” [“and as God he gave from heaven, and as man he received on earth”].

The same author also says:

> “The Son of God, immutably good, remaining himself what he was and receiving from us what he was not, deigned to enter into association with our nature without injury to his own.”

The same author further says:

> “All these things are referred to the Word in order to indicate one person of the Son of God, lest there appear to be two Christs, one God and another man. It was indeed done in such a way that not only the Word of God and the flesh of man, but also the rational soul of man, and this whole reality, should be called both God because of God and man because of man. Therefore there is one Christ, not by a confusion of substance but by the unity of person.” [Note: [Col. 1325D] St. Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, Book I, chapter 7.] [Note: [Col. 1325D] See what the bishops of Frankfurt reply concerning this and the following authorities, *Synodal Epistle*, no. 14.]

> “God the Father and man—namely, the handmaid and virgin Mary—are indeed different in substance” [Note: [Col. 1325D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Augustine, in the passage where he is treating this matter: “The substance of God the Father is indeed different, and that of the human mother.”]; “yet the substance of God the Father and of the Son is not different” [Augustine: “and of God the Son”], just as the substance of the human mother and the human son is not different. But hear what this Son says in the Prophets: “From the womb of my mother, you are my God” (Psalm 21:11), to show that the Father is his God because he became man. For man was born from his mother’s womb, and according to his humanity God was born from the Virgin, so that not only would the one who begot him from himself [that is, from his own substance] [Note: [Col. 1326D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Augustine.] be his Father, but would also be his God, and the one who created a man from his mother’s womb would be his God” [Note: [Col. 1326D] Augustine: “Who begot him from himself, and would also be his God, whom he created as man from his mother’s womb.” Up to this point the words are Augustine’s; what follows appears to have been appended and is extremely corrupt.].

When, therefore, we read, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), in the Word we understand the true Son of God; in the flesh we acknowledge the true son of man, joined to him by the indescribable abundance of grace. For this reason John also says of him:

> “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.”

And shortly afterward:

> “With complete integrity we confess both man in God, the Son of God, and God in man, the son of the Virgin. It is an entirely complete and faithful account that in the one and same Christ, in whom divinity and humanity are joined into unity of person in the virgin womb of the mother, just as God begot man, so also man is believed to have begotten God; so that the one who assumed and that which he assumed are one person in the Trinity. For the assumption of man did not produce a quaternity, but the Trinity remained, that ineffable assumption effecting the truth of one person in God and man.”

> [Note: [Col. 1327D] St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 35, volume VI of the Works.] [Note: [Col. 1327D] The additions enclosed in brackets are interpolations and are not found in Augustine.]

> “Accordingly, Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is both God and man. God before all ages; man in our age. He is God because he is the Word of God; but he is man because a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word in unity of person. Therefore, insofar as he is God, he and the Father are one; insofar as he is man, the Father is greater than he. For although he was the only-begotten Son of God, [not by adoption but by generation,] and not by grace but by nature, in order that he might also be made the son of man, full [in the form [read: form] of a servant by adoption and] of grace. The same one, from both, is one Christ, who [Augustine: ‘because’], although he was in the form of God, did not regard it as a seizure that he should be equal to God by nature” [Note: [Col. 1327D] Augustine continues as follows: “But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not losing or diminishing the form of God, and so forth.”] [Augustine: “which was natural to him, that is, to be equal to God”]. “And therefore he was made lower and remained equal; one and the same, both, as it is said: one thing because of the Word and another because of man” [Note: [Col. 1327D] Augustine adds: “Equal to the Father because of the Word, lower than the Father because of man. One Son of God and likewise son of man; one son of man and likewise Son of God,” and so forth.]. “And therefore one Son of God, not two sons” [Augustine: “not two sons of God”], “God and man, but one Son of God: God without beginning, man having received a beginning” [Augustine: “from a definite beginning”], “our Lord Jesus Christ.”

For God and man are not two, but one Christ. He is one, not through the conversion of divinity into flesh, but through the assumption of humanity into God. For just as in every human being there are indeed two substances but one person, soul and flesh, so also in our Lord and Savior, although each substance preserves its integrity—so that divinity is not congealed in flesh, nor humanity dissolved in divinity—both together are nevertheless one Christ, one Redeemer and Lord of the world. The explanation of this unity is so comprehensive that whatever things are human are attributed to God.

> “And therefore, when we call Christ the Son of God, we do not separate the man; nor, again, when we call the same Christ the son of man, do we separate God. According to his humanity he was on earth, not in heaven, where he now is, when he said: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven’” (John 3:13). [Note: [Col. 1328D] St. Augustine, *On the Presence of God to Dardanus*, or Letter 187, no. 9, volume II of the Works.]

And again the same author, after some intervening material:

> “A mediator appeared between God and human beings, joining both natures into unity of person, so that he might elevate the customary through the uncustomary and temper the uncustomary with the customary.”

### XI

For this reason, then, we have brought forward the statements of the teachers in our defense: so that we may believe that the only-begotten Son of God, begotten timelessly from the Father, is not so by adoption but by generation, and not by grace but by nature; but that at the end of time, for the salvation of the human race, by assuming flesh from the Virgin in the form of a servant, according to the Apostle, he became the firstborn among brothers (Romans 8:29), in the one and same person of God and man, not by generation but by adoption, and not by nature but by grace—in that form in which he is equal to his mother, not in that in which he is equal to the Father. For in the form of a servant he is a servant and therefore adopted; but in the form of the Lord, he is the Lord of the servant.

Concerning this form of servitude God the Father speaks through the Prophet, saying:

> “Behold, my servant shall understand” (Isaiah 52:13).

And again:

> “Behold, my servant; I will receive him. My chosen one; my soul has been pleased with him” (ibid., 1).

### XII

But why should anyone—whoever he may be—be reluctant to accept adoption according to humanity in the Son of God, when the Psalmist says of him:

> “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6)?

And he himself says of himself through the Psalmist:

> “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:7).

And the Prophet says of him:

> “We saw him, and he had no appearance; and we shall consider [read: ‘we considered’] him as though he were a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isaiah 53:2, 4).

[lacuna] … his humility, he was called in humility as though … the adoption of flesh in the Son of God … Whoever he may be, is it not more disgraceful and … to say adoption in the Son of God rather … [Perhaps: “than servitude”]?

Since the Apostle Paul also confirms his divinity, saying:

> “Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard it as a seizure to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6ff.).

Why should anyone—whoever he may be—be afraid to call adoptive the one whom prophetic speech does not fear to call a servant? Is the name “servant” more honorable than “adopted son”? For an adopted person is called an affiliated son; and you, whoever you are, are afraid to call him adopted?

The Prophet says:

> “And we considered him as though he were a leper.”

And you are afraid to call him adopted?

Why were these lesser things said of the Son of God? Let the Prophet answer:

> “He was humbled because of our iniquities, and he was crushed because of our crimes; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we were healed. The Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he delivered himself up” (Isaiah 53:5ff.).

[lacuna] … If by his will … he did not shrink from it, he who subjected his own body to the scourges of the impious and stretched out his own hands, innocent of wrongdoing, upon the cross, so that he might free us from the dominion of the ancient enemy by justice rather than by power.

### XIII

We therefore believe and confess that the only-begotten Son of God is timeless, incorporeal, ineffable, invisible, and without adoption. We believe that at the end of time he emerged ineffably and bodily from the womb of the Virgin Mary [printed *uterum*; read *utero*] as the firstborn, his divinity not diminished, in the adoption of flesh, according to David, who says:

> “He called upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’ And I will make him firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth” (Psalm 88:27–28).

According to Micah:

> “Shall I give my firstborn for my wickedness?” (Micah 6:7).

According to Jesus son of Sirach, who says:

> “Have mercy, Lord, upon your people, over whom your name has been invoked, and upon Israel, whom you have made equal with your firstborn” (Sirach 36:14).

Likewise, he became a companion of the human race, according to David, who says:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

According to the Apostle, he was conformed to the human race, as he himself says:

> “For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29),

according to the nature of adoption.

He says [Note: [Col. 1328D] Perhaps something should be added: “According to Ambrose, who says …,” whose testimony was cited above, no. 3.], in our customary usage, that he is an adopted son.

According to Augustine, who says (above, no. 6):

> “An adopted man, who was uniquely born from him.”

According to Jerome, who says (no. 5):

> “The white gem is the adoption of flesh in the Son of God.”

According to Isidore, who says (no. 7):

> “He is called firstborn with respect to his assumption of humanity, in which, through the adoption of grace, he deigned to have brothers, among whom he would be firstborn.”

Accordingly, following blessed Gregory, we call the Son of God firstborn without sin, and only-begotten without adoption.

According to Eugenius, who says (no. 8):

> “Who, through the passion of adopted humanity, while he did not spare [printed *indulxit*; variant *indulsit*] his own body, finally did not spare ours either.”

According to Ildephonsus, who says (no. 8):

> “Today, after the adoption of flesh, he returns to the seat of divinity.”

According to Julian, who says (ibid.):

> “Those whom you have made participants in adoption, command to be fellow heirs of your inheritance.”

### XIV

We also thought it worthwhile to connect with this work what the Apostle Paul writes to the Galatians, saying:

> “We have the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

Concerning this spirit the Psalmist also says:

> “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19).

Blessed Augustine also says concerning this in his *Dogmas* [Note: [Col. 1329D] These words do not occur in the *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which are wrongly attributed to Augustine, Appendix, volume VIII of the Works.]:

> “Before the Ascension, therefore, the Apostles received the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which they could forgive sins and baptize, and pour the spirit of adoption into believers. After the Ascension, however, they received a much greater grace of the Holy Spirit in the working of miracles, the grace of healings, and the reception of various languages.”

Likewise blessed Isidore says in the *Book of Differences* [Note: [Col. 1329D] Isidore, *On the Differences of the Spirit*, distinction 28, where it reads: “When the Gospel came, it removed the cruelty of the Law, sins,” and so forth.]:

> “When Jesus Christ came, [he removed] the cruelty [of the Law; lacuna in the printed quotation]. The sins that the Law punished through the spirit of servitude, he *sorte superavit*—‘overcame by lot/fate’—through the spirit of adoption [Isidore reads *laxavit*, ‘released’ or ‘relaxed,’ and omits *sorte*]. He made sons out of servants; he granted the love of fulfilling the Law [Isidore adds *omnibus*, ‘to all’]; and if thereafter they commit deeds deserving punishment, through that same spirit of adoption he forgave them [Isidore: *indulget*, ‘he forgives’]. He provided a form of right conduct and, so that what he taught might be done [Isidore: ‘so that the things he taught might be done’], infused the assisting Spirit.”

For in the exorcisms we also say against the enemy:

> “Depart from these servants, confounded and shut out by the spirit of adoption.”

Behold: if we do not fear calling the Holy Spirit [manuscript; read: “the adoptive Holy Spirit”], who is incorporeal, invisible, and ineffable, at one time a gift and at another time adoptive, why is it doubted that the Son of God, according to the form of a servant, with his divinity emptied, bodily, visible, and tangible, may be called adoptive?

### XV

Certainly, if, according to the Lord’s statement, every word stands upon the testimony of two or three witnesses (Matthew 18:16), how much more should you reckon [perhaps *reputetis*; printed *refutatis*] the truthful testimony of so many venerable Fathers concerning the adoption of flesh in the Son of God?

From these examples, written in an immense [Majansius perhaps: “treasury”] … according to the strength of our abilities [the same perhaps: “for firmness”] and the poverty of our understanding, we have gathered what we could and set it forth as … [perhaps: “a testimony of truth”], which must rightly be guarded …

It remains that whoever denies adoption … undoubtedly affirms that the true man … was in no way born …

Therefore, if any faithful soul in Christ, moved by … [Majansius perhaps: “zeal”] of charity, says that it is contrary or blasphemous to call the Son of God adoptive according to the form of a servant, then without doubt—and may it never be said—the following too will be blasphemous: that Christ, the Son of God, is at one time called a lion, at another a lion’s cub, at another a calf, at another a sheep or lamb, victim, offering, sacrifice, burnt offering; according to the variety of circumstances, prince and priest, man and prophet, rod and flower and root, judge and king, righteous one and righteousness, apostle and bishop, arm, servant, ointment, shepherd, child, firstborn, door, angel, arrow, eagle, vulture, cornerstone, rock, and other such names.

If these names, assumed by him for the salvation of the human race, as has been said, are all full of blasphemy, may such a thing be far from us. May it be far from the hearts of the faithful that they should fear to say what the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures do not fear to declare: that he is adoptive.

### XVI

To whom, then, should we compare Beatus in antiphrasis—that foul mouth stuffed with every impurity, from whose sides *autina* [uncertain] hangs—unless to Nabuzardan, the chief of the cooks [Note: [Col. 1329D] Nabuzardan was not chief of the cooks, but commander of the army. 2 Kings 25.], the destroyer of the walls of Jerusalem, that is, the transgressor of the Holy Scriptures?

Or to whom but Faustus the Manichaean, who asserted that the patriarchs were merchants? Concerning him blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1329D] St. Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book XIV, chapter 2, volume IV of the Works.]:

> “The pious man Faustus grieves that the Spirit” [Augustine: “Christ”] “was cursed by Moses,”

because Moses says:

> “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deuteronomy 21:23).

Faustus grieved that Christ was cursed; the impious Beatus grieves that someone should call Christ adoptive according to the form of a servant. He is contrary to the apostle John and the evangelist, who do not fear to call the Son of God, with his divinity emptied, an advocate, that is, adoptive and full of grace in the form of a servant.

He is also contrary to Ambrose, Hilary, Isidore, Jerome, and the other teachers, who proclaim to us that he is adoptive in his humanity, not in his divinity.

### XVII

And again, to whom should we compare Beatus in antiphrasis, unless to Migetius [Note: [Col. 1330D] Migetius. From him the heretics called Migetians took their name. They differed from the Catholics in the celebration of Easter and were therefore condemned at the Council of Seville, presided over by Elipandus. Basnage, *Thesaurus Monumentorum Canisii*, volume II, p. 311, among the notes. Elipandus boasts there of overturning this error in his letter to Fidelis.], the teacher of the Casianians and Salibanians [Majansius: “Sabellians,” as below], who arose in our time?

When his physician was cauterizing his head because of a type of madness, he considered himself like Christ and chose twelve apostles for himself. Seeing a certain little woman standing nearby and grieving over her, he is said to have told her:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise.”

This impious Beatus resembles Migetius in his example of madness. When he had sat down drunk with wine and was ordaining an abbot for brute animals, he is said to have considered himself to be Christ and to have said to one Rufinus—worthy in name and merit, as the same Rufinus himself attests with his own mouth—repeating the words three times:

> “Simon Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.”

For this reason we compare Migetius and Beatus: they were equal in honor and alike in virtue.

For that same Migetius predicted that he would rise again on the third day when he was dying. And Beatus, during the vigil of Easter, prophesied to Hordonius of Liébana [Note: [Col. 1330D] That is, from the town of Liébana. Majansius.] and our people that the end of the world had come. The people, terrified and crazed, are said to have fasted that night without taking any food, until the ninth hour of the Lord’s Day.

A certain Honorius [perhaps the same Hordonius] is said, when he realized that he was being afflicted by hunger, to have said to the people:

> “Let us eat and drink, and if we are going to die, at least let us die satisfied.”

The same person, however [Note: [Col. 1330D] Perhaps “Migetianus” is missing.] … pretending to be exhausted, rose again on the third day … alive in soul, but dead in body.

### XVIII

We anathematize Bonosus, who asserts that the Son of God was begotten without [Note: [Col. 1330D] Supply: “a mother,” as the argument of Elipandus’ letter to Fidelis requires.] … and was adoptive.

Likewise, we anathematize Sabellius, who deliriously asserts that he himself is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and not *ipsud* [uncertain corrupt reading].

We anathematize Arius, who considers the Son and the Holy Spirit to be creatures.

We anathematize Mani, who preaches that Christ was God alone and not man.

We anathematize Beatus, an antiphrasis devoted to the lust of the flesh, and Aetherius, a wild ass of a teacher of beasts, who preach that the Son of God, according to the form of human servitude, did not at all possess the adoption of flesh.

### XIX

Therefore we beseech you, venerable prelates of the Churches in Christ, by the coming of the Lord and the terrible judgment, to order that the things we have said above be [lacuna] and to present them with every readiness for selection to the glorious prince [Majansius: “Charles the Great”], knowing truly this:

> “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts; and then each one will receive praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Do not judge according to appearances, but judge with righteous judgment; with the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure by which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (John 7:24).

We ask your graciousness that, just as we have been marked beforehand by the standard of the one Christ, so we may preserve inviolate that peace which Christ commended to his disciples.
