If your prudence should think otherwise, may your returning word both dispel our negligence and illuminate the hidden recesses of our heart with the ray of the light of true doctrine, so that the love of Christ may rightly remain in us, and so that those whom the abundance of Christ makes fruitful may in no way be divided by the expanse of the earth.

[Note: [Col. 1331B] This letter is preserved in the archive of the Church of Toledo, from which it was faithfully copied.]

## Synodal Letter of the Council of Frankfurt, Sent to the Bishops of Spain

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Copied from the edition of the Councils by D. Mansi, with variant readings added from the contemporary manuscript of St. Emmeram and others.]

A refutation of the preceding letter of those same men.

The holy synod and venerable Fathers in Christ, together with all the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Aquitaine [manuscript: Equitania], and the entire clergy of Catholic peace, send to the bishops of Spain and to all the others there who bear the name of Christianity greeting of eternal blessedness in the Lord God, Jesus Christ, the true and proper Son of God.

### I

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said:

> “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20),

we, gathered together in an assembly of charity, under the command and presidency of our most devout and glorious lord, our king Charles [manuscript: “lord Charles”], to renew, with the counsel of peaceful unanimity, the state of the holy Church of God, and to proclaim the truth of the orthodox faith, in which, through the operation of divine grace, the beginning and end of our salvation exist—a faith to which nothing can be added or taken away, and which ought to be one for all Christians—say with the blessed Apostle:

> “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in us all” (Ephesians 4:5–6).

In this faith lies all holiness of life and all hope of eternal reward; without it there is nothing holy, nothing acceptable to God, nothing living.

> “The righteous person lives by faith.”

Whoever loses it through the devil’s deception is alive but dead; for just as righteousness is obtained through faith, so eternal life is obtained through true faith, as the Lord and Savior says:

> “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

### II

Among the other matters that we considered for the firmness of this faith, while our lord king presided and assisted with exceptional piety and praiseworthy wisdom, his glorious excellence suddenly ordered the document of your faith to be brought before us. When it had been read through to the end by a notary, with us listening attentively as he distinguished the statements and preserved their precise meanings, we heard that certain new assertions had been written in it. They agreed less with the ancient traditions of the holy teachers than they were somehow confirmed by your recent inventions.

But two difficult matters occurred to our minds in the document you sent.

The first is why what is found in the statements of the holy Fathers and confirmed by the universal custom of Catholic sanction should not suffice for us, when Scripture says:

> “Do not transgress the boundaries of your fathers” (Proverbs 22:28).

Are we more perceptive in discovering the way of truth than the apostolic teachers? And why should we dare to affirm anything that is not found in their writings?

The second matter is why any human being should dare to investigate the generation of the Son of God, whether his eternal generation from the Father or his temporal generation from his mother, when Scripture says:

> “Do not seek what is higher than you” (Sirach 3:22).

Therefore Saint Augustine says in his sermon on the Nativity of Christ [Note: [Col. 1331D] Perhaps from Sermon 196, volume V of the Works.]:

> “Rightly, beloved, the birth of our Savior is a matter for wonder—not only that divine birth concerning which it was said, ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ but also that human birth concerning which the same evangelist says, ‘The Word became flesh’” (John 1:6, 14).

Hence the Prophet also says:

> “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53:12).

For divine things are to be venerated more by faith than investigated by reasoning.

### III

But it is time for us to come to an examination of the meaning of your little treatise, in which we find testimonies of the holy Fathers set down in various places, but corrupted by the poison of evil perfidy [the manuscript: “bad”],and the teeth of your serpent-like error inserted among the most beautiful flowers of the Catholic faith. You suppressed the names of the books and the numbers of the chapters, so that your error might be investigated with greater difficulty. From this alone it is clear that you erred deliberately, while striving to stain the venerable meanings of the holy Fathers by omitting certain words. And we wonder—or rather, we grieve—why you should wish to do this; why you are not afraid to disturb, with a heretical foot, the purest fountains of the Catholic faith.

At the beginning of your little treatise we find written what you inserted:

> “We confess and believe that the Son of God was begotten before all ages, without beginning, from the Father, coeternal and consubstantial, not by adoption but by generation.”

[Note: Epistle of the Spanish bishops, no. 2; Col. 1331D.]

A little later, in the same place, one read:

> “We confess and believe that he was made from a woman, made under the law, and that he is not the Son of God by nature but by adoption; not by nature but by grace.”

Behold the serpent lurking among the fruit-bearing trees of paradise, so that it may deceive the unsuspecting. These testimonies were transferred from the sermons of Saint Augustine; but we find that heretical perversity added in the following sentence:

> “He is not the Son of God by nature but by adoption.”

We shall demonstrate this more fully, God willing, in what follows. For now, however, we have inserted it merely to point out to readers and to help them avoid the deadly juices of the poison.

As for the example that you quoted, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), he said this not on account of adoption, but on account of the form of a servant, in which he is less than the Father. In the same way, and on account of the form of a servant, it was said:

> “But the child grew and was strengthened in spirit” (Luke 2:40).

This statement of John, however—“We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14)—works against the adoption of the flesh. If he is the only-begotten, how then is he adopted? Or if he is not the proper Son, how then is he full of grace and truth?

### IV

Accordingly, in what follows in the epistle of your assertion, we find that Hilary is said to have written:

> “For in our own usage there is an adopted son and a true Son; we do not say that an adopted son is a son by nature, whereas the true one is Son.”

[Note: The Spanish bishops cite this from Ambrose, not Hilary, in their epistle, no. 3. The response to the passage from Saint Hilary, which they likewise quote there in no. 4, is absent both from the printed editions and from our manuscript.]

You see how a blind mind brings forward testimonies against its own position. Who would dare to say that Christ is not truly the Son of God, when John the Baptist bears witness that he saw the Spirit of God descending and remaining upon him:

> “And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:34)?

The Apostle also testifies concerning him:

> “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Romans 9:5).

And if he is true God, he is also the true Son; and if he is the true Son, he is certainly not adopted. For an adopted son, as the testimony of Saint Hilary—or, properly, Ambrose—states, is not truly a son by nature.

### V

Likewise, in the Treatise on the Apocalypse attributed to blessed Jerome, we find the following testimony in the aforesaid epistle:

> “The white stone, that is, a white gem: the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God.”

[Note: Spanish epistle, cited place, no. 5; Col. 1333D.]

But the same Treatise contains something quite different:

> “And I will give him,” he says, “a white stone, that is, the adoption of the children of God; for a stone is a precious gem.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Whether by the stone the body made white through baptism is signified, or whether by the name ‘stone’ the divine Word is signified.”

The epistle of blessed Jerome, which you say was written to Cerasia [the Spanish epistle has “to Caesarius,”] has so far been found neither among the Romans nor among us. Nor do we think that he ever wrote things contrary to himself. It is better to believe genuine copies than doubtful ones.

Behold a perversity worse than every form of evasion, which pours the poisons of its infidelity into the purest meanings of the holy Fathers.

### VI

The epistle continues:

> “Likewise, in a homily of Saint Augustine [read: ‘Saint Augustine says’], he speaks in this way according to the form of human servitude: ‘A man is adopted, whose glory he sought who was born uniquely from him.’ Behold, the one whom Augustine says was adopted, John says that we have as an advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1).

At this point we do not know what should be done first: whether the perversity should be rejected, or the ignorance removed [the manuscript: “ridiculed”].

In the twenty-sixth homily in his exposition of the statement in which the Lord said, “Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18), after an appropriate exposition he adds:

> “What ought you, a human being, to do? When you do something good, you seek your own glory; but when you do something evil, you devise accusations against God. Pay attention to yourself: you are a creature, acknowledge your Creator; you are a servant, do not despise your Lord; you have been adopted, but you have not earned it [the manuscript reads: ‘not by merits’]. Seek the glory of him from whom you have this grace. A man is adopted, whose glory he sought who was born uniquely from him.”

[Note: Treatise 29 on John, no. 8; Col. 1333D.]

He said of Christ, “the uniquely born”; but of us, “the adopted man.” The writer of the epistle, in a most perverse understanding, transferred this adoption to Christ’s humanity. In this perversion both the ignorance of the writer and his evil intention are evident and unmistakable.

The falsity of his evil intention appears immediately in the sentence that follows, where he said:

> “Behold, the one whom Augustine calls adopted, the apostle John calls an advocate.”

For it is certain that the apostle John calls Christ an advocate, as he himself testifies:

> “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Lord.”

It is equally clear that Saint Augustine is speaking of some human being adopted by grace, as can be known with complete certainty from the continuation of the passage.

### VII

The same little book of yours continues:

[Note: In the Spanish epistle, no. 8. The Frankfurters, however, give no response to the testimony of Saint Isidore which they cite in no. 7 of the epistle; Cols. 1333D–1334D.]

> “Likewise, our predecessors Eugene, Ildefonsus, and Julian, bishops of the see of Toledo, said the following in their doctrinal writings, in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper: ‘Who, through the passion of the adopted man, did not spare his own body.’ Likewise, in the Mass of the Ascension of the Lord: ‘Today our Savior, through the adoption of the flesh, returned to the seat of divinity,’”

and other statements that you have taken from the sayings of your fathers, so that it may be clear what kind of fathers you have, and so that all may know whence you have been delivered into the hands of unbelievers.

Because you denied that the man Christ is the true Son of God the Father, he did not wish to be your defender, but handed you over to the hands of his enemies, so that those who refused to receive him might rule over you; and while they openly disparage him, you secretly dishonor him.

Nor do you wish to believe the testimony of Christ himself concerning himself:

> “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1).

When he said, “your,” he showed his proper sonship, just as the Father also confirmed it by his testimony at the baptism:

> “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17).

He said, “my”; he also added, “beloved,” so that it might be understood that he is the proper Son, as the Apostle said:

> “He did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32).

It is better to believe the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son than that of your Ildefonsus, who composed for you such prayers in the solemn celebrations of the Mass as the universal and holy Church of God does not possess; nor do we think that you are heard in them.

And if your Ildefonsus called Christ “adopted” in his prayers, our Pope Gregory of the Roman see, the most illustrious teacher throughout the world, did not hesitate always to call him “the only-begotten” in his prayers.

In the prayer appointed for the Monday after Palm Sunday he wrote:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we who fail amid so many adversities because of our weakness may breathe again through the passion of your only-begotten Son.”

Likewise, on the Wednesday of that same week:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we who are constantly afflicted by our transgressions may be freed through the passion of your only-begotten Son.”

Likewise, in the Mass of the Ascension of the Lord:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we who believe that on this day your only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, ascended into heaven—”

Likewise, in the prayer of the holy cross:

> “O God, who in your goodness deigned to redeem the human race by the precious blood of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ—”

Behold: he called him “the only-begotten,” by whose blood we have been redeemed.

### VIII

As for what you say in your profession of faith:

> “The only-begotten from the Father without adoption; but the firstborn at the end of time, when he assumed a true man from the Virgin in the adoption of the flesh; the only-begotten in nature, the firstborn in adoption and grace.”

[Note: Same place, no. 9; Col. 1334D.]

We know that the Son of God is both only-begotten and firstborn according to both natures. He is only-begotten because he alone was begotten without beginning from God the Father, and he alone was born from his Virgin Mother at the beginning of time. Therefore he is only-begotten according to both natures.

He is also firstborn, because every only-begotten son is firstborn, although according to human generation not every firstborn is only-begotten. The same Son of God is, as you say, the firstborn of the Virgin; he is also the only-begotten, because he had no other carnal brothers born after him.

He is therefore also firstborn to God the Father, because he was begotten from God the Father before any creature existed or any time existed. The Apostle bears witness to this when he writes to the Colossians:

> “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light; who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. All things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him. He is also the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place in everything, because in him the whole fullness of divinity was pleased to dwell bodily” (Colossians 1:12–19).

Likewise Solomon says:

> “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning. I was established from eternity and from ancient times, before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist, and I had already been conceived; the springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet been established with their massive weight. Before the hills I was brought forth” (Proverbs 8:22–25).

Likewise, in the Book of Wisdom, Wisdom herself—that is, the Son of God—says:

> “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature. I caused unfailing light to rise in the heavens, and like a mist I covered the whole earth. I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclesiasticus 24:5–7).

Likewise blessed Jerome, in his Treatise on the Epistle to Titus, where the Apostle says, “Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us” (Titus 2:12), says:

> “Where is Arius, that serpent? Where is Eunomius, that snake? Jesus Christ the Savior is called the great God, not the firstborn of every creature; not the Word of God and Wisdom, which are names belonging to divine generation, but Jesus and Christ, names belonging to the man who was assumed. Nor do we say that there is one Jesus Christ and another Word, as the new heresy falsely accuses us; rather, we call the same one both before the ages [and after the ages], both before the world and after Mary—indeed, from Mary—the great God, our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us.”

### IX

We have set forth these testimonies so that you may recognize that God and our Lord Jesus Christ is, according to both natures, both only-begotten and firstborn—not adopted, but the great God.

Nor, as Helvidius blasphemes, are brothers called his brothers because he is firstborn, but because of the affection of paternal love. For we read that in the Holy Scriptures brothers are called by four modes, as blessed Jerome testifies in his little book against that same Helvidius: “by nature, by nation, by kinship, and by affection.”

> “By nature: Esau and Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Andrew and Peter, James and John. By nation: all Jews are called brothers among themselves, as in Deuteronomy: ‘If you buy your brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew woman, he shall serve you for six years, and in the seventh year you shall release him free from you’ (Deuteronomy 15:12). And in the same book: ‘You shall appoint over yourself as ruler the one whom the Lord your God chooses, one who is from among your brothers’ (Deuteronomy 17:15). And so forth.

> “By kinship, those who belong to one family are called brothers, as Lot is called Abraham’s brother, although he was the son of his brother Haran. Abraham said: ‘Let there be no quarrel between me and you, nor between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are all brothers’ (Genesis 13:8).”

[The manuscript of Saint-Emmeram reads “all men.”]

By this same rule, James, Judas, and Simon are called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospel.

> “By affection also people are called brothers, and this is divided into spiritual and common affection. Spiritually, all Christians are called brothers, as in the saying: ‘Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity’ (Psalm 132:1). And the Savior says: ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers’ (Psalm 22:22), and elsewhere: ‘Go, tell my brothers’ (John 20:17).

> “In the common sense, all human beings, born from one Father, are joined together by equal kinship.”

Thus [the manuscript: “here”] Jerome says that the Lord’s brothers are brothers by affection, not by adoption, where he says:

> “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”

And again:

> “Go, tell my brothers.”

### X

Your epistle continues:

> “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). “Like him, certainly, in the adoption of the flesh, but not like him in divinity.”

[Note: No. 9 cited; Col. 1335D.]

But Catholic Fathers have understood the meaning of this statement quite differently. Saint Augustine says in his Epistle to the Virgin Italica:

> “Therefore we shall see in proportion as we shall be like him, because even now we do not see in proportion as we are unlike him. From there, then, we shall see where [Augustine: “whence”] we shall be like him. But what person, utterly out of his mind, would say that we either are or shall be like God in body? This likeness, therefore, exists in the inner person, who is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the knowledge [Augustine: ‘image’] of him who created him. And the more we advance in recognition [Augustine: ‘knowledge’] and love of him, the more like him we become. For although our outer person is being corrupted, the inner person is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16). Even so, however great our progress may be in this life, it remains far from that perfection of likeness which will make us capable of seeing God.”

[Note: Volume II of the works, Letter 92, no. 3; Col. 1335D.]

What, then, do you suppose David said concerning adopted brothers:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:7)?

Blessed Jerome and the other interpreters of Holy Scripture did not wish this participation in anointing to be understood of adopted brothers, but of kings who were called “christs” and who are read to have been anointed with oil made by human composition. Blessed Jerome explained this in his Treatise on the same psalm:

> “With the oil of gladness above your companions. Other kings, who prefigured him and were called his companions because they reigned, were anointed with corruptible oil. But this one, the Son of God, was anointed by God the Father with the oil of exultation—that is, of resurrection, ascension, and dominion—for Christ was anointed by nature, whereas we are anointed by grace, because divinity was fully present in him.”

[Note: In the manuscript the word “ascension” is absent, although it appears in the Pseudo-Jerome text; Col. 1336D.]

### XI

Likewise, after many testimonies, all of which it would take too long to pursue, you finally stumbled upon the saying of Micah, in which the Prophet assumed in himself the person of a repentant people. There you also revealed the foolishness of your blasphemy when you said:

> “Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul?” (Micah 6:7).

[Note: No. 9 cited; Col. 1336D.]

You interpreted “my firstborn” according to humanity, and “the fruit of my womb” according to divinity. What Catholic ears would not recoil from hearing this interpretation? What faithful person would not reject it with a wrinkled nose? The exposition of this statement among you is so ridiculous and foolish that, out of regard for the holiness of the ears, we prefer to remain silent about what we think of your interpretation rather than explain it. We leave it to the reader’s judgment to decide what to think of you in this matter.

We shall say only what blessed Jerome understood from this statement. In his Treatise on the same Prophet he says:

> “God had summoned the people to judgment. Knowing its sin, the people does not wish to argue but to plead; yet it has no confidence even in its prayers. For nothing worthy can be offered to God for sin, and no humility can wash away the stains of offenses. It is impossible for the blood of bulls and calves, marrow-filled burnt offerings, the blood of rams, or the fat of fatted goats to wash away the filth of the soul. ‘Shall I,’ he says, ‘give my firstborn for my transgression,’ as the king of Moab is described as having done? Or ‘the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul,’ as Jephthah did when, rashly fulfilling his vow, he offered his daughter?”

The Saint-Emmeram manuscript reads: “with blood … through burnt offerings … with gore.”

He also explained the allegorical interpretation according to the Septuagint in this way:

> “If I give my firstborn for my impiety, and the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul, I shall indeed give whatever is first in me, but for my sin and impiety I shall offer God nothing worthy. Hence David also prays and says: ‘Wash me more and more [the manuscripts: “David also says: Wash me greatly”] from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin’” (Psalm 51:3).

### XII

Likewise, when you mention the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Hebrews, you do not understand that everything you have quoted stands against you, and that Christ the Lord is everywhere and always called the Son of God, not a servant and not an adopted son.

[Note: No. 9, at the end; Col. 1337D.] This is clear in the testimonies that you wished to quote from the beginning of that Epistle:

> “In many and various ways God formerly spoke to our fathers through the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. He is the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, and he upholds all things by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be his Father, and he will be my Son’? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘Let all the angels of God adore him’” (Hebrews 1:1–6).

These testimonies therefore call our Lord Jesus Christ neither a servant nor an adopted son, but the Son and heir of all things. In the continuation of the same Epistle we likewise read:

> “Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant; but Christ was faithful as a Son in his house” (Hebrews 3:5–6).

And shortly before:

> “For he has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses” (Hebrews 3:3).

How can he have greater glory if he is a servant like Moses, or adopted from a servant?

Blessed Augustine also wonderfully distinguished these two in the third homily on the holy Gospel according to John, saying:

> “Hold firmly, therefore, brothers, to this truth: ‘The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ’ (John 1:17). Through a servant the law was given and made people guilty; through the ruler forgiveness was given and freed the guilty. ‘The law was given through Moses.’ Let the servant claim no more for himself than what was accomplished through him. Chosen for a great ministry as a faithful man in the house, he was nevertheless a servant: he could act according to the law, but he could not release anyone from the guilt of the law.”

[Note: Saint Augustine, Treatise 3 on John, nos. 15–16; Col. 1337D.]

### XIII

What is read later in your epistle is this:

> “With these statements of the holy Fathers set forth above and our assertions strengthened by them, we have jointly decreed that we must in no way depart from their decrees or footsteps.”

[Note: Spanish epistle, no. 10; Col. 1337D.]

We desire, and we beseech the Lord, that what you say may indeed be entirely true. But so far we have not perceived that it is so. May divine mercy one day bring it about that you do not transgress the boundaries established by the holy Fathers.

### XIV

As for what you added later, we do not find it stated in the profession of the Nicene Creed that Christ has two natures and three substances, or that he is “a divinized man” and “a humanized God.”

[Note: No. 10 cited; Col. 1337D.]

What is human nature except soul and body? Or what is the distinction between nature and substance that makes it necessary for us to speak of three substances, rather than simply confess, as the holy Fathers did, our Lord Jesus Christ as true God and true man in one person?

The person of the Son remained in the Trinity, and to that person a human nature was added, so that there might be one person, God and man—not a divinized man and a humanized God, but God-man and man-God: because of the unity of person, one Son of God and the same one son of man, perfect God and perfect man.

A perfect man consists of nothing other than soul and body. Thus holy Pope Leo, in his fourth homily on the Nativity of the Lord, calls the same thing both nature and substance, saying:

> “He preserved both natures in so great a union that glorification did not consume the lower, nor assumption diminish the higher. Therefore, with the property of each substance preserved, and with both joined into one person, and so forth.”

[Note: Saint Pope Leo, Sermon 21; Col. 1337D.]

Nor do we deny that these three truly exist in Christ: namely, divinity, soul, and body. But because he is truly called God and man, in the name “God” everything that belongs to God is designated, and in the name “man” everything that belongs to man is understood. Therefore it is sufficient to confess in him one perfect substance of divinity and another perfect substance of humanity.

For it is one thing to contend against heretics, and another to confess the pure faith faithfully. In the former case the truth of Christ’s soul and flesh had to be demonstrated; in the latter, the perfect humanity in the same Christ must be confessed.

Thus Saint Augustine, in the book called the *Enchiridion*, explained the matter most clearly and in a Catholic manner in chapter eleven (chapter 36, no. 11):

> “From the moment he began to be man, man began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and this one uniquely; and because of God the Word, who, having assumed him, was made flesh, he was certainly God. Just as any human being is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, the Word and man.”

[Col. 1338B.]

### XV

Ecclesiastical usage customarily names two substances in Christ, namely God and man, as Cassiodorus also confirmed in his Treatise on the second psalm, strengthening it with a statement of Saint Augustine:

> “So that the Christian mind may not waver amid heretical disputes, although it ought to believe all things truly and firmly, we shall conclude the definition of the term itself with a brief explanation grounded in the authority of the Fathers. Let us therefore hear blessed [the manuscript: ‘most blessed’] and most learned Augustine speaking in his Exposition of the Evangelist John:

> “‘Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet both together are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. Accordingly, Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh. Once this truth has been recognized, we appropriately avoid deadly errors.’”

[Note: Saint Augustine, Treatise 78 on John; Col. 1337D.]

Likewise blessed Ambrose says in a hymn for the Nativity of the Lord:

> “A giant of twofold substance, eager to run his course.”

[Note: Saint Ambrose, Hymn 4, volume IV of the works; Col. 1338D.]

Likewise Saint Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter thirteen:

> “Accordingly, as we confess, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God from God and was born man from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, is, in both substances—namely divine and human—the only Son of God the almighty Father.”

[The manuscript reads: “our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God from God.”]

Likewise, in the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*:

> “Therefore there are not two Christs or two sons, but one Son, God and man [another reading: ‘the only Son’]. For this reason we call him only-begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of his nature has granted him.”

[Note: These words are found in the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, volume VIII of the works of Saint Augustine, Appendix; Col. 1338D.]

Isidore likewise says in Book VII of the *Etymologies*:

> “Human nature was joined to the Son of God in such a way that from two substances there came to be one person.”

[Note: Saint Isidore, Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2 at the end; Col. 1338D.]

### XVI

Likewise Paschasius, deacon of the holy Roman Church, in Book II of his most beautiful work composed on the Holy Spirit—an opuscle mentioned by blessed Pope Gregory of Rome in the *Books of Dialogues*—says in chapter four:

[Note: *Patrologia*, vol. 62, col. 29; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 40; Col. 1338D.]

> “Thus in God and man there is a twofold substance, but not a twofold person, because one person can consume another person, whereas one substance cannot consume another substance, since person belongs to the realm of law, while substance belongs to the realm of nature.

> “At this point it seems necessary for us to assert, by testimonies, one person and two substances in Christ the Lord, both God and man [Paschasius: ‘both God and man’s’]. Set forth one person of the Redeemer, God and man. The Apostle says: ‘If they had known the wisdom of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Corinthians 2:8).

> “If you ask how the inviolate one could suffer and the incomprehensible one be crucified, the unity of person makes it possible for what the man endured to be believed to have been endured by God.

> “Likewise, when the Evangelist says: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven’ (John 3:13), how could he say that the Son of man had descended from heaven before the day of his passion, resurrection, or ascension, and yet remained in the heavenly places, unless the reasoning of truth resolves this through the unity of person?

> “In another passage, the person of the head and the body is joined, when we read: ‘For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink’ (Matthew 25:35). What does the unity of person accomplish? The man is fed, and God is refreshed; the foot is comforted [Paschasius: ‘the foot is joined’], and the head testifies that it feels the soothing.

> “He therefore says: ‘They would never have crucified the Lord of glory’; and, conversely: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.’ See how, through the unity of person, human things are mingled with divine things and divine things with human things. God is crucified, and the man is remembered as descending from heaven and remaining in heaven.”

A little later in the same chapter he says:

> “The Apostle Paul also clearly set forth the two substances, removing the obscurity of the mystery, when he said: ‘Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever’” (Romans 9:5).

### XVII

Yet among the clearest and most Catholic statements of Saint Augustine, which you scattered and set down in disorder for the defense—as you say—of your position, but, as we understand it, for the accusation of your error, you did not hesitate to mix in adulterated ideas, pretending that he said what we do not find in his writings.

From this it is evident that you do not trust your own case, because you did not find your faith confirmed in the examples of the holy Fathers. Therefore you inserted adulterated ideas of perversity, asserting that they said what they did not say. This can be recognized with complete certainty in chapter eleven of the book of Saint Augustine called the *Enchiridion*, as we have already mentioned. We set down the text of that chapter so that your error may be more easily exposed and the ineptness of your malice may become known.

The aforesaid Father says:

> “Accordingly, Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is God and man: God before all ages, man in our age. He is God because he is the Word of God—for ‘the Word was God’; but he is man because, in the unity of person, rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word.

> “Therefore, insofar as he is God, he and the Father are one; but insofar as he is man, the Father is greater than he. Although he was the only Son of God, not by grace but by nature, so that he might also be full of grace, he became likewise the son of man, the same one, both things from both, one Christ.

> “For although he existed in the form of God, he did not regard as robbery what he was by nature, namely, being equal to God; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, without losing or diminishing the form of God. Thus he was made less and remained equal: one person in both, as has been said, but one thing because of the Word and another because of the man: because of the Word, equal to the Father; because of the man, less.

> “He is one Son of God and likewise the son of man; one son of man and likewise the Son of God. There are not two sons of God, God and man, but one Son of God: God without beginning, man from a definite beginning—our Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Note: Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 35; Col. 1339D.]

### XVIII

Thus you did not hesitate to mix the poisons of infidelity into these most truthful assertions of the Catholic faith.

Where he said:

> “Although he was the only Son of God, not by grace but by nature, so that he might also be full of grace, he became likewise the son of man, the same one, both things from both, one Christ,”

you inserted, to confirm your error, what he did not say, in this form:

[Note: Spanish epistle, no. 10; Col. 1339D.]

> “Although he was the only Son of God, not by adoption but by generation, and not by grace but by nature, so that he might also be full in the form of a servant, he became the son of man through adoption and grace, the same one, both things from both [the manuscript: ‘from both things’], one Christ.”

Let whoever reads this look and understand how great this perversity and evasion are. Why do you stain the meanings of the holy Fathers and mix the poison of error into Catholic honey? What do you mean when you say that God is by nature the Son of God and by birth the Son of God? What do you mean by joining adoption to grace, when in the same chapter, a little later, that remarkable teacher did not hesitate to call the one who is the son of man the only Son of God, saying, as we explained above:

> “From the moment he began to be man, man began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and this one uniquely; and because of the Word, who, having assumed him, was made flesh, he was certainly God. Just as any human being is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, the Word and man.”

[Note: Saint Augustine, cited place, chapter 36; Col. 1339D.]

Therefore, if he is the only one, how is he adopted, when there are many adopted sons? One cannot be called “the only one” among many.

Likewise, the unity of person that exists in the Son of God and the Son of the Virgin removes the insult of adoption. If, then, the one born from the Virgin is true God, how can he be adopted and a servant? For you would never dare to confess God as a servant or an adopted son.

And if the Prophet had called him a servant, this would nevertheless not have been because of the condition of servitude, but because of the obedience of humility by which he became obedient to the Father even unto death. Pope Leo says in his second homily on the Nativity of Christ:

> “The nature was taken from the Lord’s mother, not guilt; the form of a servant was created without the condition of servitude.”

[Note: Saint Pope Leo, Sermon 22, chapter 3; *Patrologia Latina*, volume 54, column 196; Col. 1340D.]

Likewise Saint Augustine says in his thirty-ninth homily [the manuscript: “the thirtieth”]:

> “Our Lord, even in the form of a servant, was not a servant, but even in the form of a servant he was Lord.”

Was not the blessed Virgin Mary descended, according to the nobility of this world, from a royal and free lineage? The Holy Spirit came upon this Virgin of royal dignity and caused a son to be begotten from her. It would be astonishing if the Holy Spirit could not make the man born from her perfect and freeborn.

### XIX

But we also wish to hear from you whether Adam, the first Father of the human race, who was created from virgin earth, was created free or a servant. If a servant, how then was he the image of God? If free, why then was Christ likewise not freeborn from the Virgin? Indeed, man was made from a better earth—one animated and immaculate—through the operation of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “The first man was made from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47). If we confess that the earthly man was created free, why do we not much more confess that the heavenly man was free?

From what cause, then, was Adam made a servant, unless from sin, as the Apostle Peter attests: “For whoever commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8:34). But Christ did not commit sin; therefore he is not the servant of sin, but rather its liberator and redeemer, of those who are servants of sin. He himself attests this: “If the Son makes you free, you shall be truly free” (ibid., 36).

But perhaps you say that he was the servant of man [Manuscript: “is”]. What does the Prophet say? “Give to the king your judgment, O God, and your justice to the king’s son. And all the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:1, 11). The Apostle likewise says: “He subjected all things beneath his feet” (1 Cor. 15:26). This is repeated [Manuscript: “is found”] more often than there is need to demonstrate by examples that he is Lord of all, not anyone’s servant.

Or do you wish to call him the servant of angels because it was said: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6)? Certainly he was made lower on account of the mortality of the flesh, not on account of servile condition; and therefore it immediately follows: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8:6ff.).

The Apostle likewise says to the Hebrews: “He was made so much better than the angels as he inherited a name more excellent than theirs.” And again: “When he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God adore him’” (Heb. 1:4, 6).

### XX

What do you say about God the Father, who at his baptism and also at the Transfiguration that took place on the mountain called him Son, not servant: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17; 17:5)?

On this statement blessed Hilary, in Book VI *On the Faith*, argued as follows [Note: St. Hilary, *Patrologia*, vol. X, col. 174, no. 23. Blessed Alcuin also brought this passage against Felix in his book against the same man, in this volume, col. 89.]:

> “If the statement ‘This is my Son’ expresses what is proper and unique, why do we bring against God the Father the calumny of attributing to him a sonship that he has declared to be proper? Does it seem to you that by saying this he means: ‘I have others surnamed as sons, but this one is my Son? I have bestowed the name of adoption on many, but this one is my Son. Do not seek another, and do not fail to believe that this is he.’ Thus, as though by a pointing finger and by the force of the words, I indicate him when I say that he is both mine and Son. This indeed [Manuscript: “therefore”] was the meaning of the Father’s voice—not that [Manuscript: “whereby”] he who was to be baptized in order to fulfill all righteousness was unknown, but that he who was seen as man for the sacrament of our salvation might be recognized by God’s voice as the Son of God.”

It remains, therefore, that he is King and Redeemer, God and Son of God. Concerning him the Apostle also says to the Romans: “He did not spare his own Son” (Rom. 8:32). He called him his own, not adopted.

On this statement the same blessed Hilary says in the aforementioned book [Note: Ibid., no. 45.]:

> “Will the designation of adoption still exist in him in whom this name expresses what is proper?”

A little later he says:

> “Consider the force of the statement, so that you may understand the greatness of the love. Examine what ‘proper’ means, lest you fail to recognize the truth. For now the Apostle says ‘his own Son,’ although in many other passages he had often said either ‘his son’ or ‘his.’ Although many books, through the translators’ straightforward understanding, have ‘his Son’ written in this passage instead of ‘his own Son,’ nevertheless the Greek language, in which the Apostle spoke, here uses ‘own’ rather than ‘his’ [Hilary: ‘uses’]. And although ordinary understanding (Latin: *sensus*; Hilary: *sensu*) does not sufficiently distinguish between ‘own’ and ‘his,’ the Apostle nevertheless, after mentioning ‘his Son’ in his other statements, says here: ‘He did not spare his own Son.’”

Likewise, in Book VIII (no. 28):

> “Do you perceive what is lacking in you when you deny Christ what belongs to him? If Christ is your Lord by the nature of God, you have the Holy Spirit. But if this Lord is Lord by an adopted name, then, lacking the Holy Spirit, you are animated by the spirit of error, because no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, in the *Dogma of the Catholic Faith* [Note: This passage occurs in the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, attributed to Gennadius, in vol. VIII of the Appendix to St. Augustine]:

> “Therefore the Son of God, having become man, was born a son according to the truth of nature: from God, the Son of God; and according to the truth of nature, from man, the son of man. Thus the truth of the Only-Begotten [Gennadius: ‘the truth of the begotten one’] would possess the name of Son by being born in both births—not by adoption or by designation—so that there might be one Son, true God and true man.”

Likewise, the holy evangelist John taught us to believe that he is truly the Son, saying: “We have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God” (1 John 4:14–15).

And shortly afterward:

> “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

### XXI

But you, whoever you are, who proclaim Christ to be adopted, I should like to know where this opinion of yours came from; show where you learned this name. The patriarchs did not know it, the prophets did not say it, the apostles did not preach it, the holy interpreters kept silent about it, and the teachers of our faith did not teach it.

Perhaps you were carried up into the third heaven and there heard secret words that would have remained unknown to the holy Church of God until now, had you not been carried up into the third heaven. Or perhaps you reclined upon the Lord’s breast and there heard what blessed John was not worthy to hear. Or perhaps the Lamb, leading you through the choirs of angels, showed you this name. Or perhaps the Lion from the tribe of Judah opened for you the book sealed with seven seals, so that you might understand these mysteries and utter names that would have remained unknown to the four living creatures, indeed unheard by the whole world, unless you, a new teacher, had come to disclose your name.

### XXII

For you will say: “Why are you afraid to call Christ the Lord adopted?” I tell you: neither did the apostles call him so, nor did the holy and catholic Church of God have the custom of naming him so. Rather, she did not even believe him to be adopted, but his own Son, in accordance with the preceding testimonies of the apostles and the doctrines of the holy teachers.

There are, indeed, many names in the holy Scriptures for our Lord Jesus Christ: lion, lamb, stone, worm, and many such names, all of which have definite and mystical explanations for why they are used. “Adopted,” however, has no other meaning than that Jesus Christ is not the proper Son of God, and that he was not begotten from the Virgin as a son, but adopted into sonship—I do not know from what servant—as you say.

We would give allegorical interpretations of these names if they were necessary to the present argument: lion, on account of royal dignity; lamb, on account of innocence; worm, on account of the humility of the Incarnation.

But when you say that he is called a leper [Note: Spanish epistle, no. 12], you seem not to have considered carefully how the prophet used this name: “We considered him as one stricken with leprosy, and struck by God, and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities” (Isa. 53:4ff.). He said “as one stricken with leprosy,” not “a leper.” Likewise, he said “we considered,” that is, as blessed Jerome explained in his treatise on this prophet [Note: St. Jerome, vol. IV of his works]:

> “We thought that he was bearing his own sins; but when we understood more truly, he was wounded for our iniquities.”

He was in no way struck by the disease of leprosy in his body, nor wounded by the leprosy of sin in his soul. As far as our memory recalls, we do not read in the holy Scriptures that he was called a wolf or a vulture, nor do we read that he was called adopted.

### XXIII

Was not this same heresy of yours once rejected and even condemned in Nestorius by the universal holy Church? Perhaps that is why you were unwilling to anathematize him, although in your letter (no. 18) you anathematized others—namely, Bonosus, Arius, Sabellius, and Manichaeus—who held perverse opinions concerning the Son of God.

Was he not condemned for this reason: that he believed blessed Mary, ever virgin, to be the mother not of God but only of a man? Concerning his heresy, the holy Cyril wrote to the presbyter Eulogius as follows [Note: St. Cyril, vol. V of his works, p. 134]:

> “Nestorius, therefore, in his expositions pretends to say that there is one Son and one Lord [Manuscript: ‘one God’], but he refers sonship to the Word of God alone.”

A little later:

> “For when he says that the Word of God is called Christ because he has a conjunction with Christ, how is it not evident that he is speaking of two Christs, if Christ has conjunction with Christ, as one with another?”

Nestorius seems to speak of conjunction where you speak of adoption. What is adoption except a conjunction of love, by which a father joins to himself through adoption a son whom he does not possess as his own? And it is entirely certain, as we have said above, that one is a proper son and another an adopted son.

Will there not then be two sons for God the Father, one proper and the other adopted? No Catholic dares to say this. What else is it to say that the same Virgin gave birth to an adopted son or a servant, except to deny that God was born from her?

If God was begotten, he is by no means adopted, but a son [Perhaps read: “but a proper Son”], because the person of a proper son is one thing, and the person of an adopted son or servant another [Manuscript: “or servant”].

And we know that there is one person in Christ, God and man, just as blessed Gregory wrote in a letter to Bishop Quirinus [Another reading: Quiricus]:

> “The flesh was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and the divinity afterward came into the flesh; rather, as soon as the Word came into the womb, the Word, while preserving the power proper to his own nature, became flesh. And the same perfect man—namely, in the truth of flesh and of a rational soul—was born through the Virgin’s womb, the Son of God” [Gregory adds: “the Only-Begotten”].

If, therefore, from the very time of conception the true God, the Son of God, was conceived, when was there a time when he was man without God, so that he might be adopted as a son?

For just as there was never a time when God the Father was without God the Son, of whom it was said, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), so there was never a time when the man Jesus was without God, of whom it was said, “The Word became flesh” (ibid., 14)—that is, God became man.

Just as Arius separated the Son from the Father by saying, “There was a time when the Son of God did not exist,” so by adoption you separate the man Christ from the Son of God.

### XXIV

And we are astonished that, while you produce so many testimonies of the holy Fathers, you do not understand that you set your own opinion against those same testimonies, understanding some perversely and interpreting others most wickedly, in accordance with the Apostle: “Not understanding either what they say or concerning what they make assertions” (1 Tim. 1:7).

We beseech you: let it be enough for you to say in the confession of the Catholic faith what the holy Fathers said, and thus to hold the creed of ecclesiastical profession as the most holy teachers expounded it. We are far inferior to them in devising words appropriate to the apostolic faith. Let us only firmly believe and hold what those who were filled with the Spirit of God and were given to us by God as teachers wrote.

What displeases you in our Lord [Manuscript omits “our”] Jesus Christ, that he should be truly the Son of God the Father, when he himself both called himself Son and called himself the Truth, saying: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). And again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Unless perhaps you wish to say with the Jews: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” He himself will immediately answer you on his own behalf [Manuscript: “answers”]:

> “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true.”

And shortly afterward:

> “In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true. I am the one who bear witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8:13–14, 17–18).

The Father thundered from heaven and called him his Son. Christ, from earth to heaven [Manuscript: “the heavens”], cried out and called himself Son; yet you, together with the Jews, remain unbelieving.

The thief called him Lord on the cross. The centurion, seeing him die, cried out: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54). The demons also, with their whole legion, proclaimed him truly the Son of the Most High God, as is read in the holy Gospels. Yet Elipandus, with his own legion, still denies that he is truly the Son of God [Manuscript: “Elefantus”].

When Christ asked the apostles, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?”—he asked about the Son of Man, and Peter answered concerning the Son of Man: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” For this praiseworthy confession he deserved to hear from God our Savior himself:

> “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:13, 16–17).

He called him his Father, the one who had revealed these things. The Father revealed mysteries concerning his Son, unheard of by worldly wisdom; and for this glorious confession he rewarded blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, with authority over heaven and earth, saying:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (ibid., 18–19).

Hear [Manuscript: “you have heard”] what this apostolic faith merited; see what your adoption merits.

Paul preached the same one who was crucified as the power of God and the wisdom of God, writing to the Corinthians:

> “But we preach Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness, but to believers the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24).

Behold what testimony these two lights of the world offer concerning Christ, the Son of God; yet you still wish to call him adopted, and to say that the Son of God received the spirit of adoption together with us.

Isaiah calls him Son [Manuscript adds “however”]:

> “A Son has been given to us, and the rule has been placed upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, God the Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isa. 9:6).

### XXV

Understand, brothers, what you read, and do not invent new and unknown names; hold instead to those found in holy Scripture. For those names found there concerning Christ God have honorable meanings suited to our salvation. Do not wander through human inventions, but strengthen yourselves upon the solidity of the holy Scriptures. Read them, teach them, for in them is eternal life.

You have repeatedly insisted and reiterated that you set forth testimonies consonant with the holy Fathers. But, as we have shown, you understand their statements very differently from those who themselves inserted these testimonies into their books. And we find—as we said above—that you have most certainly infected their holiest writings with the poison of heretical perversity and inserted words that we nowhere read in their books.

Unless perhaps your teachers [Note: Namely, Ildephonsus, Eugenius, and Julianus, Spanish writers who at that time were unknown to the bishops of Gaul, Germany, and Italy] held such opinions. Their names, we think, would have remained unknown to the holy and universal Church of God until now, had you not made the schism of this error known to the world.

Cease, brothers, from slandering your fathers through the ears of the Christian people, and from separating yourselves from the holy Church of God. Do not run through the byways of error or dig for yourselves cisterns shattered by heretical faith, which cannot hold the purest waters. Rather, hasten by the royal road to the clearest fountain of Catholic purity, and drink from it the spirit of charity and faith, so that from your belly may flow living waters leaping up into eternal life.

Keep yourselves within the boundaries of the holy Fathers, and do not turn over [Manuscript: “turn yourselves over to”] new little questions; for they are useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear them. It is enough for you to follow in the footsteps of the holy Fathers and to hold their words with firm faith.

For in our Lord they proved teachers in the faith and guides [Manuscript: “teachers”] to life. Their wisdom, full of the Spirit of God, is recorded in their books, and their life shines with miracles of merit and is most holy [Manuscript: “their most holy life shines”]. Their souls reign in heaven with God, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1345A], for their great labor of piety.

### XXVI

Follow these men, therefore, with all the strength of your soul and with the full affection of charity, so that, clinging to the unshaken firmness of their teachings, you may deserve, by the gift of the true and proper Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, to share fellowship with them in heavenly eternal blessedness.

Cease, brothers, from preaching as a servant the one whom we have as King and Redeemer, to whom all authority has been given in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18). Stop calling adopted the one who is true God and the true Son of God:

> “At whose name every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10–11).

Understand that in this profession of yours there lay hidden two forms of diabolical deception: namely, that you, who have been redeemed by the grace of baptism, might be separated from the unity of the Catholic Church and drawn back from the way of eternal salvation by the snare of schismatic error; and that you might bar the beginnings of the Christian faith from the nations among whom you live, while you preach as a servant and an adopted one our Lord Jesus Christ, whom we worship and adore as God.

These are the devil’s arguments: to overthrow you in the faith and to turn them away from the faith. Cease, brothers, cease from this wickedness, and become teachers of life to yourselves and guides to faith for your neighbors.

Consider what a scandal this is among pagan nations: that the God of the Christians should be said to be a servant or adopted. We are adopted through him [Manuscript: “adopted ones”]; he is not adopted together with us. Through him we have been freed from servitude; he is not a servant together with us.

Why should we call him a servant who preferred to call us friends rather than servants, saying:

> “I will no longer call you servants, but friends, because the servant does not know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

Consider with what charity he called us friends; with that charity let us call him God, the Son of God, and let us love him with our whole heart, because he first loved us and handed himself over for us, so that he might cleanse for himself a people acceptable to him and zealous for good works (Tit. 2:14).

Let us believe him to be Lord, not servant, since he himself says:

> “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13).

And let us confess him to be true God and the true Son of God in both natures, namely, the divine and the human.

Let us believe that he wills everything that is better and can do everything that he wills, as it is said:

> “All that the Lord willed he did, in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 113:3).

Who denies that proper sonship is better in the Son than adoption? And since the omnipotent Son of God wished to assume the nature of our weakness into the unity of his person, so that he might be the mediator between God and human beings, why should he not, from the better and much more excellent dignity of sons, associate our humanity with himself in the unity of his person, so that from his glorious and proper nobility he might redeem the ignobility of our servitude?

For medicine came to the sick, mercy to the wretched, the redeemer to the guilty, the free one to servants, as it is said:

> “The God of vengeance has acted freely” (Ps. 113:1).

And in the Gospel:

> “If the Son makes you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36).

Let us not be ungrateful for the Lord’s great benefits—our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we were created and by whom we were again redeemed and adopted into the glory of the children of God.

Let us preach him as true and living God and truly the Son of God, so that we may deserve to attain his most blessed vision, in which there is eternal blessedness and blessed eternity.

To him be praise and glory throughout all eternities. Amen.

# Letters of the Most Illustrious Don Gregorio Mayans, Nobleman of Valencia, Illuminating the Acts and Writings of Elipandus

## I

To the most illustrious lord Don Frobenius, abbot of Emmeram, most distinguished prince of the Holy Roman Empire: Gregorio Mayans, nobleman of Valencia, sends his greetings.

[Note: The following encomium of this most celebrated man was written to me by Don Charles Christopher Pluer, then residing at Portugo [perhaps Pórtugos], at the mineral springs in the mountains of Granada, in a preliminary notice praised by me, dated 10 June 1765:

> “There are certainly not lacking in Spain men distinguished by wisdom and learning; among them the celebrated Gregorio Mayans must undoubtedly be regarded as leader and standard-bearer. For this man, together with his most learned brother Antonio, devoted himself exclusively to letters. When Gregory was royal librarian, he voluntarily resigned that office in order to yield to envy. Yet this change of circumstances was far from turning the man away from his love of learning; rather, it seems to have given him an added spur. It is certainly true that, apart from Gregory, no one can be found in all Spain who combines an equal zeal for service with solid scholarly distinction.”]

Your humanity, most illustrious lord, is such that you would draw even me, unwilling, into your service; how much more will you lead one who is willing and eager?

Before you sent me any letters, I energetically urged my friends living at Toledo to undertake to read, with every diligence, the still-unpublished letter of Elipandus, despite the extreme difficulty [Note: Flores likewise complained of the difficulty of reading this manuscript, in vol. V of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 539, and in a letter he wrote to the superior general of his order. The latter, urged by the eminent Cardinal Passionei, who during his lifetime was most favorably disposed toward my studies, had instructed him to take every possible measure to have that letter of Elipandus to the bishops of Gaul, etc.—of which he had given only the beginning and end in his history—copied in full.] encountered in reading it, and to send me a copy.

So much effort have they devoted to the task that they no longer despair of achieving what will be most pleasing to me and highly acceptable to you. Their desire to satisfy your wishes has made it possible to hope that the letter—which previously seemed readable only in certain passages—may now be copied almost in its entirety.

It remains for the chapter of that church to permit the letter to be copied. This presents no slight difficulty, but the distinguished men who are strongly devoted to your service and eminent for their learning—Aurelius Beneito, dean of that church; Francisco Perez, treasurer; and Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, canon—are confident that they can overcome it.

[Col. 1346D] If they obtain that permission, they will also compare the books of Beatus and Etherius, edited by the distinguished Stevartius, with the Toledo manuscript from which they were copied, though not with sufficient accuracy [Note: See below, Mayans’s letter to Don Pluer, no. 12].

The remaining letters of Elipandus that you desire I have taken from volume V of *Hispania Sacra* by the hardworking Augustinian Recollect monk Enrique Flórez, together with his short history of Elipandus’s affairs, although it is of little importance, so that you may lack nothing.

### 589

Since, while reading these letters, certain matters occurred to me that make their reading and meaning easier, I thought it appropriate to note them in the margins for your benefit. Permit me, most illustrious lord, to show myself obedient to you in small matters, since I cannot do so in great ones.

You know perfectly well that in Elipandus’s time the Latin language had, in much of its structure, degenerated into the vernacular language that we Spaniards now use. Latin nouns, which had cases, were losing them; the cases that Latin requires we supply with articles, prepositions, and interjections. Thus, among us, a single noun ending—whether singular or plural—serves in place of all the cases required by Latin syntax.

For example, the usual basis of Spanish nouns is the Latin ablative. Thus *a mensa* becomes *mesa*; *a templo*, *templo*; *a sermone*, through apocope, *sermon*; and *a fructu* and *die*, with the final vowels altered, become *fruto* and *dia*.

With this understood, when Elipandus says in his letter to Felix, “Domino Felice,” the case that in uncorrupted Latin would be the sixth case is, in the corrupted language degenerating into Spanish, the fifth case, because of the absence of the interjection *o*, which is very frequently supplied in vocatives. From this single observation you will discover that many of the strange scribal forms occurring in Elipandus’s letters are Hispanisms.

I leave it for you and the illustrious C. F. Temler to consider whether it is appropriate to correct the writing of a barbarous age. For what principle forbids us to write *nolluit* instead of *noluit*, and six hundred such forms? Where the sense is obscure, let the monstrous reading be preserved, so that the truth may more easily be restored; but where the meaning is certain, what compels us to reproduce the copyists’ faults? You will judge these and other matters according to your supreme learning.

It remains, most illustrious lord abbot and prince, whom I venerate above all, for me to thank you because you have deigned to explain your wishes to me. I shall take care to carry them out with every zeal and diligence.

May Almighty God grant you a long and vigorous life, so that you may be able to promote the welfare of the Catholic Church.

Oliva, in the kingdom of Valencia, 30 July 1763.

## II

To the most illustrious lord Don Frobenius, prince of the Holy Roman Empire and abbot of St. Emmeram at Regensburg, etc.: Gregorio Mayans, nobleman of Valencia, sends his warmest greetings.

I do not wish to flatter you with smoke, most exalted prince, most deserving abbot, and most illustrious lord. But so that you may know how highly I value your authority, I inform you that, although I had already despaired of obtaining the letter of Elipandus—which learned men had desired for two hundred years and which you had sought so earnestly, and which is itself extremely difficult to read—I nevertheless applied the greatest diligence to the matter.

I persisted until I obtained it from the distinguished Aurelius Beneito, dean of the Church of Toledo [Col. 1347D], who, lest your hopes should prove vain, after the fruitless efforts of his chapter to obtain its consent, left nothing undone to ensure that your wish might be fulfilled.

Receive, therefore, a faithfully transcribed copy, with several lacunae that no mortal can fill because the letters have disappeared. Through you, let this singular monument come before the eyes of learned men.

You will also receive with this letter a copy of another letter of Elipandus to Fidelis, as it was published by the distinguished José Pellicer in *Annales Hispaniae*, Book IX, no. 18, p. 406. For Don Temler desires Pellicer’s notes.

The same distinguished man wishes to see the letters of Álvaro of Córdoba to John of Seville. So that he may read them, I ordered that they be extracted from Flórez’s *Hispania Sacra* and delivered to the illustrious Charles Christopher Pluer, through whom they will be forwarded to Don Temler [Note: These letters are contained in vol. XI of *Hispania Sacra*, which, together with vol. X, in which Elipandus’s affairs are treated, I received from the same Don Temler, who is highly favorable to my studies.]

What troubles me, however, is this: although the volume of the distinguished Petrus Stevartius containing the books of Etherius and Beatus is being sent to me at your command so that those books may be compared with the Toledo manuscripts from which they were formerly copied, I have nevertheless been informed that this comparison cannot in any way be carried out, because there is no hope that the chapter of that church will grant such permission.

In any other matters, most exalted prince, in which I may be able to offer my service, command me as you please. I shall in no way disappoint your opinion of me or your expectations.

Farewell, prince, etc., and count me among your dependents.

Oliva, 25 February 1765.

After writing this, I thought it appropriate to submit to your judgment certain conjectures by which I have attempted to fill some gaps in Elipandus’s unpublished letter. The remaining wounds seem to me incurable.

## III

To the most illustrious and most worthy lord Don Frobenius, abbot of the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg and prince of the Holy Roman Empire: Gregorio Mayans, nobleman of Valencia, sends his greetings.

There was no reason, most illustrious lord, for you to take so much trouble as to write and thank me for the letters of Elipandus sent to you. For whatever service I render you is owed to you by the fullest right.

The manuscript and unpublished letter of Elipandus that I sent you [590] was the first that he wrote, and the one condemned by the Council of Frankfurt and attacked by Saints Beatus and Etherius [Note: “Which Beatus and Etherius attacked.” I cannot agree here with Don Mayans; for it seems to me that Elipandus’s contest with Beatus and Etherius began long before the Council of Frankfurt and before Elipandus’s letter to the bishops of Gaul was written. See the reasons for my opinion in the *Historical Dissertation*, nos. 6 and 7.].

Therefore, in the Toledo codex 140, it is read first among three letters; it is followed by two others, which Enrique Flórez published after having them copied from the same codex at the command of the distinguished Juan Antonio de Las Infantas, dean of the Church of Toledo and, while he lived, my friend.

The *Apologeticus* of Beatus and Etherius against Elipandus is in codex 162, with which another work by Samson, abbot of Córdoba, forms a single body. The codex was written in ancient Lombard script. Because the copyist, through ignorance of the letters, inverted a quire when binding it, from chapter 15 of Book II through the end of the book, the same error was repeated in another, more recent codex, codex 163.

That codex was copied by the amanuensis of the most learned man Juan Bautista Pérez, bishop of Segorbe. Several notes and corrections by this incomparable man appear in the margin, making it likely that he compared the ancient exemplar with the recent one. Aurelius Beneito, the distinguished dean of the same church and my very dear friend, is a witness to these notes and corrections; he knows perfectly the handwriting both of Pérez and of his amanuensis.

I further observed that Juan Mariana, in his *History of the Affairs of Spain*, rendered by himself into Spanish and published at Toledo by Diego Rodríguez in 1623, used the papers—that is, the manuscripts—of Juan Bautista Pérez, bishop of Segorbe, as he himself admits at the end of the index of authors from whom he composed his history.

I therefore readily believe that Mariana, who did not frequent archives, did not read the original *Apologeticus* of Beatus and Etherius, but a recent copy of it, which he shared with Andreas Schottus, and Schottus with Petrus Stevartius.

I wished to inform you, most illustrious lord, about these matters, which may perhaps seem trifling, so that you might understand how greatly I desire to deserve well of you.

If I had that most ancient codex before my eyes, I might perhaps arrange its pages by observing with what words each folio begins and ends. If I can obtain knowledge of this matter, I shall inform you of it.

Farewell, most illustrious, most gracious, and most learned lord, abbot and prince.

Oliva, 3 May 1766.

## IV

To the most distinguished and learned man Charles Christopher Pluer: Gregorio Mayans, nobleman of Valencia, sends his greetings.

1. Among the greatest benefits that I derive from our literary correspondence, this is the most delightful to me: that through your friendship you make me agreeable to your friends, men of the highest distinction, by frequently providing me with opportunities to comply with their wishes. Although, therefore, I lack the abundance of books necessary to satisfy the desires of the most illustrious Abbot of Emmeram, whose scholarly plans the distinguished C. F. Temler wishes to bring to a successful conclusion [Col. 1349B], I shall briefly indicate what occurs to me, so that the most illustrious abbot may understand that it is not willingness but ability that I lack for carrying out his commands. Yet so eminent a man possesses the authority to accomplish many things that I can only point out.

2. The facts concerning Elipandus, a Goth by nation (as his name indicates), and metropolitan of Toledo, are so well known that it is better to say nothing about them than to say little. His error was this: that Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, was not the proper Son of God but an adopted son. That he was a follower of the bishop of Urgell, named Felix—truly an unfortunate man—is testified by Jonas of Orléans at the beginning of his books against Claudius of Turin. Yet both received their burning and smoking brand from the Bonosian heretics, against whom Justinian, bishop of the Church of Valencia, wrote expressly. As the blessed Isidore reports in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 33, Justinian flourished in Spain during the reign of Theudis, king of the Goths, that is, from the year 534. Theudis reigned for seventeen years.

[Col. 1349C] 3. Heretics commonly corrupt the uncorrupted testimonies of truth by their own interpretation and cover them with a fine exterior, so that they may more easily deceive others. It is therefore unsurprising that Elipandus wished to conceal his error not only by the authority of the divine Scriptures but also by that of the Mozarabic liturgy, in order to attract the minds of the Spaniards, as is clear from Elipandus’s own letter to Albinus, no. 11, in Henry Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. V, p. 568. But an examination of how absurdly he abused the Hispanic liturgy belongs to another man’s leisure rather than mine. Moreover, before this subject could be treated with the dignity it deserves, there ought to be an edition of the eleven volumes containing the Gothic and Mozarabic liturgy in the library of the Church of Toledo. Our friend Andrés Marcos Burriel, of the Society of Jesus, devoted outstanding labor to describing them; his exceptional efforts are evident in the Royal Library at Madrid.

4. Since Elipandus was metropolitan of the Church of Toledo, he took great pride in that title, as may be seen in his letter to Fidelis, written in the year 785. Since he possessed so eminent a dignity, he easily drew several men of Córdoba into his error, as Paul Alvarus of Córdoba testifies in his letter to Aurelius Flavius John of Seville, no. 27, in Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XI, p. 122. He also drew Ascaricus into the same error, a man distinguished by episcopal dignity, since Elipandus himself called him “Lord Bishop” at the beginning of his letter to Fidelis; Pope Adrian likewise mentions that bishop in Letter 3, otherwise 37. Neither of them, however, identified his see, although writers as flimsy as fig trees have made him bishop of Braga, as may be seen in the *Letters of the Bishops* which Jerome Higuera forged under their name and advertised as collected and annotated by Julian Peter, archpresbyter of Saint Justa. The illustrious [Col. 1350A] Laurentius Ramírez de Prado added his own notes to them and appended that utterly foolish supplement to the works of Liutprand that he published, so that like might rejoice in like. See pp. 515, 516, and 522.

To prevent Julian Peter’s manuscript notes from appearing to be by the same hand, Higuera altered the bishop’s name in his customary fashion, calling him Arcarius, in *Adversaria*, nos. 409 and 410. Whatever his see may have been, he consulted Elipandus, and Elipandus himself praised him for that reason, as is clear from the beginning of his letter to Fidelis.

Yet Elipandus himself was not so free from the prickings of conscience that he did not consult Felix, bishop of Urgell, by whom he had been perversely instructed, as Einhard testifies under the year 792; nevertheless, he obstinately persisted in his error. Therefore, to omit the condemnations of his error that are commonly known, he deserved to be struck by the ecclesiastical thunderbolt of Bishop Theudula, as Alvarus of Córdoba testifies in his letter to John of Seville, whose opening word is *Englogae* [Note: [Col. 1349] Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol.
