XI, no. 27, p. 123.]. Its words are these:

> “At the time when the plague of Elipandus was ravaging our province, and a deadly rhomphaia was violently rending our hearts, more cruel than a barbarian sword [otherwise, wrongly: “cruelly”], your bishop Theudula—now summoned [that is, already dead]—after many varied and venerable statements concerning the proper identity of Christ, composed the summary of his entire exposition with this conclusion, saying: ‘If anyone says that Christ’s flesh is adopted by the Father, let him be anathema. Amen.’”

Since this letter was sent to John of Seville, and in it Theudula is called “your bishop,” just as elsewhere Isidore is called “your” bishop, there can be no doubt that Theudula was bishop of Seville—namely, the same man who in the catalogue of the bishops of Seville found in the Gothic codex of Saint Emilianus, which I published in the *Life of Nicolás Antonio*, § 156, is called Meudula (which should be read thus). The reading should, however, be restored to Teudula, because of the easy interchange of the Gothic letter T with M, to which it is similar.

According to the aforementioned catalogue, Teudula was the forty-first bishop of that see, successor to Humilianus [Col. 1350C]; David followed him.

By way of incidental service to the truth, I shall here note the error of Johann Albert Fabricius in *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. II, book VI, p. 482: he believed that Abbot Fidelis held Jesus Christ to be the adopted Son of God. For although it is certain that Elipandus wrote to him as to a man infected with this error, as may be seen in Joseph Pellicer’s *Annals of Spain*, book IX, no. 18, p. 406, Etherius and Beatus nevertheless called him “brother,” in Sandoval’s *Notes*, p. 126, and he seems to have conducted himself faithfully, as may be observed in Morales, book XIII, chapter 16, fol. 43, p. 2, and in Vázquez, *First Dissertation on the Adoption of Christ*, chapter 1, p. 224. There Vázquez says that Fidelis showed only the letter to Beatus and Etherius, and therefore no blame should be attached to him.

5. Several Spaniards made the boldest attempt to absolve Elipandus from obstinacy. Among them Gabriel Vázquez stands out, in his two *Dissertations against the Errors of Felix and Elipandus*, published at Alcalá in 1594, as does Juan Eusebio Nieremberg in the letter published by the distinguished Laurentius Ramírez de Prado, that most diligent embellisher of flimsy fictions, in his notes to Liutprand, p. 518. It is therefore unsurprising that very many writers, following their authority, assert that Elipandus died in communion with the Catholic Church.

It is certainly clear from the letter that Elipandus sent in August of the year 799 to Felix, who was then an exile at Lyon, that he had already reached his eighty-second year. Since Felix at that time had either finally repented or was pretending to have repented, Elipandus bitterly rebuked him for writing to him about retracting his error. Nor should it seem strange that Elipandus was not deprived of his episcopal dignity on Felix’s example: that would have been difficult, since Elipandus was under [Col. 1351A] the authority of the king of Córdoba.

Paul Alvarus was therefore right, writing after his death, to call him a heretic in Letter 4 to John of Seville; Jonas of Orléans, who died in the year 842, did the same. The acts of Beatus that Juan Tamayo de Salazar brought to light from the darkness of his own brain on 19 February move me not at all, for they were copied from Mariana’s *History* and other recent writings, to whose fables he added his own [Note: [Col. 1351D] See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, fourth century, p. 733.].

6. But let us now discuss Elipandus’s writings, of which only his letters survive. Of these, those found among the works of Alcuin and of the blessed Etherius were commonly circulated. The codex of the Church of Toledo, however, preserved three letters, two of which have already been published, while the third has not yet seen the light of day.

The first letter is entitled: “Letter addressed to Migetius the heretic.” From him, the heretics called Migetians and the heresy Migetian are named in Elipandus’s letter to Fidelis. In some handwritten books this Migetius is called Igetius; he is likewise named so in the newest catalogue of the manuscripts of the library of the Church of Toledo, codex 140. That catalogue was compiled in 1727 by Diego Mecolaeta and Martín Sarmiento, Benedictine monks.

In Pope Adrian’s Letter 3, otherwise 99, he is called Mingentius; by the distinguished Joseph Pellicer, in his learned *Annals of Spain*, book VIII, nos. 13 and 14, and by Juan Gómez Bravo, in *Bishops of Córdoba*, p. 106, he is called Migentius. Hence the heretics are called Migentians in the reply of Bishop Saul addressed to Alvarus, in Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XI, p. 165.

This letter of Elipandus was published from the manuscript codex of the Church of Toledo by Henry Flórez in volume V of *España Sagrada*, p. 543. From it Migetius’s heresy is better understood than before, and light is also shed on the matters that Elipandus himself proudly indicated in his letter to Fidelis and that Pope Adrian wrote against it.

7. Elipandus’s second letter was sent to Charlemagne. Henry Flórez published it from the aforementioned Toledo codex in volume V of *España Sagrada*, p. [Col. 1351C] 558. In former times Ambrosius Morales, book XIII, chapter 25, fol. 44, letter B, and Gabriel Vázquez, in his first dissertation against the errors of Felix and Elipandus, chapter 1, fol. 224, had wished for it; and it casts new light on Charlemagne’s letter to Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain, which is printed in volume IV, part III, of the *Councils of Spain* in the recent edition of Joseph Catalani, which I use.

592 8. The third letter of Elipandus, contained in the same Toledo codex, no. 140, is unpublished because that codex has been poorly preserved, as Flórez reports in volume V of *España Sagrada*, p. 557, where he makes light of the wretched condition of the codex. The inscription of the letter is as follows:

“To the most reverend lords and brothers in Christ, to all the priests of Gaul, Aquitaine, and Austria (for so that part of France lying between the Rhine and the Meuse was called at that time), we, the unworthy and insignificant bishops of Spain, and all the faithful, wish eternal salvation in the Lord. Amen.”

The bishops of the Elipandian faction wrote this letter to the bishops mentioned above so that they might reopen the examination of the case of Felix, bishop of Urgell, because at that time he was under the rule of Charlemagne, who occupied the district of Urgell. This letter is mentioned in the aforementioned letter sent to Charlemagne; it was therefore written before that one, and diligent effort ought to be made to transmit it and publish it.

But who will read it, since it was written in Gothic and the codex is in such poor condition? If I possessed the authority enjoyed by the most illustrious Abbot of Emmeram, the difficulty would be less. For the sake of so great a prince, however, I shall try to discover what I can obtain from my friends. This indication will suffice concerning the history of Elipandus.

9. Let us now discuss the writings of Beatus and Etherius. These two defenders of Christ’s glory fought together for the truth of the Catholic faith, and each deserves the palm of victory. Beatus was Etherius’s teacher, as Elipandus recorded in his letter to Abbot Fidelis, which the distinguished Joseph Pellicer published with several notes in his *Annals of Spain*, book IX, no. 18.

As the highly learned Gaspar Ibáñez de Segovia, Marquis of Mondéjar, observed in *The Preaching of Saint James in Spain*, chapter 22, fol. 128, Alvarus of Córdoba called Beatus “the priest of Liébana” in Letter 18 to Aurelius Flavius John, published by Flórez in *España Sagrada*, vol. XI, pp. 120 and 127—not a monk, nor an abbot.

Alcuin, in book I against Elipandus, honored him with the title “abbot,” but in the sense of “priest,” which is still used in Galicia to designate parish priests. In the kingdom of Valencia, *abadía*, that is, “abbey,” means the house of a parish priest.

Even if he had been a monk, he would not have belonged to the Benedictine community, which had not yet been introduced into Spain at that time, although an attempt is made to confirm this with numerous forged documents [Note: [Col. 1352D] Consult the distinguished Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, fourth century, p. 733.].

Etherius was bishop of Uxama; for that reason Beatus called him “Father” at the end of his *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, as may be seen in the Marquis of Mondéjar’s aforementioned book on *The Preaching of Saint James*, chapter 21, fol. 128, p. 1. For the same reason Elipandus, metropolitan of Toledo, called him “brother” in his letter to Fidelis.

Alvarus of Córdoba, in Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XI, Letter 1 to John, no. 7, p. 85, and Letter 4 to the same John, nos. 24 and 34, pp. 120 and 127, praised the work against Elipandus under the name of Beatus alone. Whether he wrote this by abbreviation may be questioned, and I believe that he did. For in Letter 1 to John, where Beatus is first mentioned, the copy of Nicolás Antonio from which I made my own reads:

> “Also from the book of Beatus Heterius against Elipandus.”

Nicolás Antonio correctly noted in the margin of his copy and in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book VI, chapter 2, no. 37, that it should read:

> “Of Beatus and Heterius.”

It should likewise be read that way in Flórez, volume XI, p. 84, no. 5, of Alvarus’s letter.

In any event, Beatus was the author of that work, and therefore he is cited before Etherius, who was associated with him to give the work greater authority, since he was a bishop. Because of that dignity, however, Etherius was placed before Beatus in the inscription or salutation of the letter, which was highly honorific toward Elipandus according to the custom of that time. As Prudentius Sandoval testifies in his notes to the *Chronicles of the Bishops*, p. 126, it reads:

> “To our most eminent and beloved of God, Elipandus, archbishop of the see of Toledo: Etherius and Beatus send greetings in the Lord.”

10. This work of Beatus and Etherius is still preserved in the library of the Church of Toledo, where two copies may be seen, one original and the other copied from it. The first is codex 162 of the latest catalogue; the second is codex 163. These seem to be the two copies mentioned by Nicolás Antonio in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book VI, chapter 2, no. 16.

Whether García Loaysa copied his own copy of this work from them or obtained it elsewhere is uncertain. He possessed one copy and mentioned it in the margin of his notes to the Decree of Gundemar, p. 280 of the *Collection of the Councils of Spain*. His words are:

> “I possess the book of Etherius, bishop of Uxama, and Beatus against Elipandus.”

11. The first person to mention the preceding codex of the Church of Toledo, written in ancient Gothic characters, was Ambrosius Morales. When he published books XI and XII of the *General Chronicle of Spain*, he prefixed a preface entitled: “Concerning the ancient books and certain other aids that I possessed for writing the many things that follow.” There, on folio 10, under the letter A, he wrote:

> “I also had another book from the holy church, in very ancient Gothic script, containing what Bishop Etherius of Osma and Beatus the priest wrote against Archbishop Elipandus, as well as the *Apologeticus* of Samson, abbot of Córdoba.”

Translated literally into Latin, these words read:

> “I also obtained from the holy church [of Toledo] another book written in very ancient Gothic letters, containing what Etherius, bishop of Uxama, and Beatus the priest wrote against Archbishop Elipandus, and the *Apologeticus* of Samson, abbot of Córdoba.”

Later, at the appropriate place—book XIII, chapter 26, fol. 43, letter F—Morales mentioned the same codex in these words:

> “This work is found written in very ancient Gothic script in the library of the holy church of Toledo, where I saw it and extracted much from the book.”

That is:

> “This work, written in very ancient Gothic letters, exists in the library of the holy Church of Toledo, where I saw it and extracted much from the book.”

[Col. 1353B] Gabriel Vázquez also mentioned this codex of the Church of Toledo, praising it in his first dissertation against the error of Felix and Elipandus concerning the servitude and adoption of Christ, chapter 1, fol. 224, p. 1, and chapter 6, fol. 229, p. 2.

The distinguished Mauro Castellá Ferrer, relying on Morales’s authority, likewise praised the same codex in his *History of Saint James*, book III, chapter 19, fol. 302, p. 2. Prudentius Sandoval did the same in his notes to the *Chronicles of the Bishops*, p. 126, where, citing the same codex, he says:

> “In this treatise, or reply, which is in the library of Toledo, everything that happened in this matter is described at great length, including how the archbishop [Elipandus], recognizing that he had erred, corrected himself.”

That is:

> “In this treatise or reply, preserved in the library of Toledo, everything that happened in this matter is recounted at length, including how the archbishop [Elipandus] retracted his error after recognizing that he had been wrong.”

But this last statement is not found in that book. Sandoval genuinely believed that an event had occurred which Morales, without any foundation, had merely conjectured in book XIII, chapter 26, fol. 44, letter E. Sandoval had Morales’s *Chronicle* before his eyes, as is clear from the following page of his notes, namely page 127.

On this same subject Juan Mariana wrote in book VII of *On the Affairs of Spain*, book VIII:

> “What happened to Elipandus is unknown; I would rather believe that he obeyed the judgment of the Fathers [of Frankfurt] and, abandoning his erroneous opinion, changed his mind.”

Later, in the same history, which he translated into Spanish in order to offer something to the ears of the common people, he asserted Elipandus’s repentance as certain in his own judgment. Since it is easy for great men to draw others into their errors, Vázquez, following Mariana, confirmed this fiction in his second dissertation against Felix and Elipandus, published at Alcalá in 1594, chapter 12, fol. 271, by means of the fabricated testimony of Eutrandius, which, as Vázquez himself reports, he received from his associate Jerome Higuera, the forger of the fictitious Eutrandius or Liutprand.

[Col. 1353D] Thus those who wish to deceive others fall into the snare themselves.

12. Subsequently, the two books of Etherius, bishop of Uxama, and Beatus, priest of Liébana, against Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, concerning the adoption of Christ the Son of God, were first brought to light from the Toledo library and published by Peter Stevartius in a separate volume of *Distinguished Greek and Latin Authors*, printed at Ingolstadt by Eder in 1616, in quarto.

Stevartius had received the work from Andreas Schottus. Although Schottus was a highly learned man, he was not experienced in reading Gothic letters. Consequently, that edition, which is defective in comparison with the Toledo manuscript, ought to be collated with it by someone skilled in the matter. As Stevartius received it, however, the work was often reprinted.

Aubertus Miraeus mentioned the same Toledo codex in his *Supplement to Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 224. In 1685 Cardinal Aguirre himself saw the codex in the Toledo library, as he reports in volume I of the *Councils of Spain*, Ecclesiastical Dissertation IX, excursus 3, § 34, p. 144. In the following year, when he published the *Catalogue of the Councils of Spain* at Salamanca, by Lucas Pérez, he mentioned the same codex, which he had seen, on p. 169.

Finally, to omit others, Juan Ferreras speaks of the same codex under the year of Christ 782, no. 2.

In addition to the aforementioned codex of the Church of Toledo, the distinguished García Loaysa, as I indicated above, possessed another copy, as he himself says in a marginal note to the Decree of Gundemar, p. 280 of the *Collection of the Councils of Spain*, later repeated and enlarged by Cardinal Aguirre and most recently by Joseph Catalani.

Loaysa bequeathed his library to his kinsman Pedro Carvajal, dean of the Church of Toledo and later bishop of Lauria. The latter left it to his relatives in the city of Plasencia. By them it was transferred to the monastery of Saint Vincent, belonging to the Order of Preachers in that city; in our own time it was transported from there to the Royal Library at Madrid.

13. Let us now speak of another distinguished work of Beatus, priest of Liébana, which is addressed to Etherius, bishop of Uxama—namely, the *Commentary on the Apocalypse*. Nicolás Antonio mentioned this work in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book VI, chapter 2, no. 40, and the Marquis of Mondéjar in *The Preaching of Saint James in Spain*, chapter 22, fol. 127, p. 2. Ambrosius Morales spoke of it in glowing terms in book XIII, chapter 27, fol. 46, letter C, in his manuscript *Sacred Journey* in the Royal Library at Madrid, from which I copied my own copy; Nicolás Antonio did the same in the place cited.

Since Apringius, bishop of Beja, interpreted the Apocalypse of Saint John, as the blessed Isidore testifies in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 30, some writers confused the work of this earlier Apringius with that of Beatus. But the Marquis of Mondéjar, carefully comparing the two works, recognized their difference and noted it in his book on *The Preaching of Saint James in Spain*, chapter 22, fol. 124 and following.

Ambrosius Morales, book XI, chapter 49; Luis de Alcázar, *Notes on the Apocalypse*, note 26, section 3; Philippe Labbe, *New Manuscript Library*, part I, p. 25; the Marquis of Mondéjar, *The Preaching of Saint James in Spain*, chapter 22; and Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book IV, chapter 2, are all well worth reading concerning the Commentary of the bishop of Beja and its copies.

In his *Manuscript Adversaria*, Nicolás Antonio asserts—as he does also in the *Bibliotheca*—that he copied this work from a copy of the codex of Luis de San Lorenzo, who had taken his copy from a Barcelona codex. That copy passed into the possession of the distinguished Manuel Sarmiento de Mendoza, magistral canon of the Church of Seville, from whom the highly learned Doctor Martín Vázquez Siruela obtained it. Later it came to the eminent Juan Lucas Cortés, who allowed Nicolás Antonio to copy it, as the Marquis of Mondéjar relates in *The Preaching of Saint James*, chapter 22, fol. 122, p. 2.

This codex is preserved in the Royal Library at Madrid. Juan Ferreras was planning to publish it with other writers, as he himself says in his first dissertation on the preaching of Saint James in Spain, p. 8. But let us now discuss Beatus’s *Commentary on the Apocalypse*.

14. According to the Marquis of Mondéjar in his book on the preaching of Saint James in Spain, chapter 22, fol. 130, p. 2, this work of Beatus is divided into twelve books. The first person to mention it was Ambrosius Morales, book XIII, chapter 27, where he wrote that he had seen four copies, though without the author’s name; nevertheless, he proved by sound conjectures that the author was Beatus.

This is clearly confirmed by other codices. The first copy Morales saw was on parchment and was kept in the Church of Vallis Cavata (Valcavado), a town situated near Saldaña. Nicolás Antonio mentions this codex in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book VI, chapter 2, no. 44. According to Morales, it was written in the Spanish era 1008 [Col. 1355A], that is, in the year 970.

From this date of its script it is clear that it was the codex which the highly learned Juan Bautista Pérez called “the Leonese” in a note to chapter 30 of Saint Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, and which he reports having seen. That distinguished man, a renowned restorer of Spanish ecclesiastical history, saw very many books relating to ecclesiastical history, drawn from the archives of Spanish churches through the authority and favor of Philip II.

I believe that Pérez was the private individual in whose possession Higuera says he saw the codex of the Church of Vallis Cavata, as Nicolás Antonio reports in the place cited. For Higuera counted the great Pérez among his friends.

Aubertus Miraeus was therefore wrong in his notes to Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 17, when he attributed that note by Pérez to García Loaysa. It is certain that the notes appended to Saint Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* belong to Juan Bautista Pérez, as the editor of Isidore’s works, Juan Grial, observed in his preface [Note: [Col. 1355D] The notes that immediately follow the text of the individual books of the *Sentences* are those of the Spanish Loaysa. Those placed after all the books of Saint Isidore in Brieul’s edition belong to other learned men; [Col. 1356D] Juan Grial collected and enlarged them. See the index of Saint Isidore’s books prefixed to his works, near the end, and p. 618 at the end.].

This was later confirmed by Nicolás Antonio in *Bibliotheca Hispana*, vol. I, p. 494; Joseph Rodríguez in *Bibliotheca Valentina*, p. 244; and Vicente Ximeno in *Valencian Writers*, vol. I, p. 203.

Loaysa, however, published in his *Collection of the Councils*, p. 788, a book of the blessed Isidore without notes, at Madrid, by Pedro Madrigal, in 1593. In the same year, at Turin, by Juan Bautista Bevilaqua, that same Loaysa published the three books of the *Sentences* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, corrected and annotated by himself. There, in the same year and by the same printer, he also published, in quarto, the *Chronicle of Don Isidore, archbishop of Seville*, likewise corrected and furnished with scholia by himself.

If Loaysa had possessed Beatus’s *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, he would certainly have said so, since in a marginal note to the Decree of Gundemar, p. 280, he informed his readers that he possessed the book of Etherius, bishop of Uxama, and Beatus against Elipandus.

15. The second copy, mentioned in Morales, book XIII, chapter 28, fol. 46, letter E, is described by him as follows:

> “Another book of these is in the distinguished library of the royal monastery of Saint Isidore of León. The book belonged, as I believe, to King Ferdinand the First, or he ordered it to be written, as is indicated in some way at the beginning. It certainly appears to be a royal treasure, because of the many large illuminations in gold and the paintings it contains, executed with some skill. Thus it does not appear to belong to such ancient times. At the end it is said that the writing was completed in the year 1047 of our Redeemer, which is the year 1085 of the era, and that is the date marked there.”

That is:

> “Another book among these is in the distinguished library of the monastery of Saint Isidore of León. The book belonged, as I believe, to King Ferdinand the First, or was one that he ordered to be written, as is indicated in some way at the beginning. It clearly appears to be a royal treasure because of the many large golden illuminations and paintings that it contains, executed with some skill. Therefore it does not seem to belong to those very ancient times [he had earlier mentioned a copy written in the year 1008 of the era]. At the end it is said that the writing was completed in the year 1047 of our Redeemer, which is the year 1085 of the era, the date marked there.”

This copy later belonged to the Marquis of Mondéjar, as he himself says in his book on *The Preaching of Saint James in Spain*, chapter 22, fol. 126, p. 1. Nicolás Antonio, in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book VI, chapter 2, no. 41, and Cardinal Aguirre, volume I of the *Councils*, Catalani’s edition, p. 143, report the same.

In 1706, however, certain books fell into the royal treasury because their owners had supported the Austrian cause. The distinguished Melchor Rafael Macanaz then took the opportunity to persuade Philip V to establish and furnish a library at Madrid. At that time the library of the Marquis of Mondéjar was transferred there. It had been seized by the Austrians in the town of Mondéjar, to which the marquis had withdrawn, and was being transported to Barcelona when Philip V’s soldiers recovered it. It was acquired by him, as its new owner, by right of war.

For this reason Andrés Durana—that is, Arnaud, with the letters reversed—asserted in his *Defense of the Arrival and Preaching of James the Greater in Spain*, p. 96, that this book of Beatus was preserved in the Royal Library. Arnaud had been the secretary of the Marquis of Mondéjar and later, when he testified to this, became royal librarian. Juan Ferreras, director of the same library, likewise testifies to it in his first dissertation on the arrival of James in Spain, p. 7. Manuel Caetano de Sousa agreed with him in *The Spanish Expedition of the Apostle Saint James the Greater*, vol. I, p. 644.

16. Morales himself, book XIII, chapter 27, fol. 46, letter F, mentions two further copies. He wrote:

> “I also know of another, older book, as I believe, of this Exposition, in the library of the holy Church of Oviedo, and another in the royal monastery of Our Lady of Guadalupe; I have seen them all. None of them bears Beatus’s name, which I believe he concealed out of humility.”

That is:

> “Another book, older in my opinion, of this Exposition is in the library of the holy Church of Oviedo, and another in the monastery of Our Lady of Guadalupe; I have seen all of them. None bears Beatus’s name, which I believe he concealed out of Christian humility.”

As for the first, the Oviedo codex, it seems not to have remained there long, as may be inferred from what Licentiate Espinosa—that is, a man designated as a doctor—wrote in a letter to Master Christopher de Valomares, preserved in Nicolás Antonio, book XII of the *Censorship of Fabulous Histories*, chapter 7, p. 531, col. 1. I shall translate and transcribe his memorable words here:

[Col. 1356C]

> “Since there was no one,” he says, “who knew how to read the Gothic characters, everyone laid sacrilegious hands upon that precious treasure of books, in order to make coverings for children’s primers from the parchments of Gothic books. When Ambrosius Morales arrived here, he wrote a memorandum-list of the books that were present. The noble Pedro Ponce of León then requested some of them from us [without doubt by royal authority], and the king [Philip II] removed others from Saint Isidore. Thus we were deprived of many books, and of nearly the best of them all; they all ended up in the monastery of El Escorial, where they have a perpetual prison.”

For this reason no later mention was made of this codex.

17. The other codex, belonging to the monastery of Guadalupe, is mentioned by Morales in his *Sacred Journey*, fol. 43, p. 2 of my copy. His words are:

> “An Exposition of the Apocalypse, which is like a golden chain, drawn from Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Fulgentius, Gregory, Tyconius, Irenaeus, Apringius, and Isidore—all of whom the preface names. It does not bear the name of the person who wrote it. But if I were in my study at Alcalá, I could easily investigate the matter by following the clues provided by what comes next. Valcavado is a small place in this bishopric of León, near Saldaña, and there they venerate a saint named San Bieco, whose arm they possess. They also have a book resembling the one I mentioned on the Apocalypse, and there they assert that this saint wrote it. In its preface this codex bears the name of the person to whom it is addressed—which the one of Saint Isidore does not—and that person is Etherius. From this alone the author might be traced, since I have seen and extracted something from a Gothic book possessed by the holy Church of Toledo. This book of Valcavado has now been brought here to León so that it might be compared with the other one of Saint Isidore, and I saw it there. In my poor judgment this work is excellent and fully deserving of being printed. I suspect that it is one of the works of which the Prior of El Escorial has knowledge, since there is another copy of it at Guadalupe. Both codices were written more than 550 years ago, as appears from what is said at the end.”

That is:

> “An Exposition of the Apocalypse, which is like a golden chain, drawn from Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Fulgentius, Gregory, Tyconius, Irenaeus, Apringius, and Isidore, all of whom the preface names, does not bear the name of its author. But if I were at Complutum in my museum, I would certainly discover the truth by following the traces of what follows. Vallis Cavata is a small town in this bishopric of León, near Saldaña, and there they venerate a saint named San Bieco, whose arm they possess. They also have a book resembling the one I mentioned on the Apocalypse, and there they assert that this saint wrote it. In the preface this codex bears the name of the person to whom it is addressed—which the codex of Saint Isidore does not—and that person is Etherius. From this alone it may be possible to investigate who the author is, since I have seen and extracted something from a Gothic book possessed by the holy Church of Toledo. This book of Vallis Cavata has now been brought here to León so that it might be compared with the other book of Saint Isidore, and I saw it there. In my very poor judgment this work is excellent and fully deserving of being circulated in print. I suspect that it is the same work of which the Prior of El Escorial—Ferdinand of Ciudad Real, a very learned man—has knowledge, because he possesses another copy of it at Guadalupe. Both codices were written more than five hundred and fifty years ago, as appears from what is said at the end.”

Morales wrote his account of his *Journey* by order of Philip II in the year 1572.

### 18

Morales mentioned all four of these examples in the aforementioned *Sacred Journey*, fols. 42 and 43, and likewise 79 and 159 of the manuscript described by me. He also mentioned another manuscript of the monastery of Spinensis, about which he wrote in the same *Sacred Journey*, fol. 150:

> “Exposition of the Apocalypse, without the author’s name. It could be that of Saint Beatus, of whom I have spoken in connection with other libraries.”

That is:

> “Exposition of the Apocalypse, without the author’s name. It may be that of Saint Beatus, about whom I spoke when discussing other libraries.”

But since Morales later nowhere mentioned this manuscript in his published *Chronicles*, perhaps the Spinensis copy was by Apringius and not by Beatus.

### 19

From the foregoing it may be concluded that Prudentius Sandovallius spoke carelessly in his *Annotations*, fols. 125 and 127, where he said that the manuscripts which had existed in the libraries of various churches in the time of Ambrosius Morales still existed there in his own time, although they had already been removed from those places and a considerable part of them had been transferred to the Escurial library.

### 20

Besides the manuscripts mentioned by Ambrosius Morales, there was another in the church of Toledo, as the same Morales reports in his *Sacred Journey*, fol. 79. His words are these:

> “Exposition of the Apocalypse. It is the same one that I have already indicated in the section on Saint Isidore of León; and with very good conjecture I understand that it was compiled a very few years after the destruction of Spain by a very learned cleric named Beatus, who also wrote another work against Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, together with Etherius, a bishop, apparently, of Osma. This book is in the principal church of Toledo, written in Gothic script.”

That is:

> “Exposition of the Apocalypse, which I have already indicated when discussing the church of Saint Isidore of León; and, on the basis of a very good conjecture, I understand that it was composed a few years after the ruin of Spain by a very learned cleric named Beatus. He also wrote another work against Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, together with Etherius, apparently bishop of Uxama. This book is preserved in the principal church of Toledo, in Gothic characters.”

Nicolaus Antonius mentions the same manuscript in book VI, chapter 2, no. 41, of his *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, and Joannes Ferrara mentions it in his first *Dissertation on the Preaching of the Gospel in Spain by the Apostle James the son of Zebedee*, published in 1711. But in 1727, when the most recent catalogue of the books of the church of Toledo was compiled, it no longer existed there, since it was not listed in that catalogue.

### 21

To these examples I shall add another, which Cardinal Antonius de Aragón possessed, as Nicolaus Antonius reports in book VI, chapter 2, no. 41, of his *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*. After his death, his library was transferred to his brother, Cardinal Paschasius de Aragón, as Doctor Franciscus Ignatius de Porres testifies in the preface which he placed before the *Republic of Letters* of the distinguished man Diego Saavedra, published at Alcalá by María Fernández in 1670.

### 22

Cardinal Aguirre, in volume I of the *Councils of Spain*, revised edition, p. 143, col. 2, says that the distinguished man Joannes Lucas Cortesius possessed another copy. It is strange that his closest friends, Nicolaus Antonius and the Marquis of Mondéjar, did not mention this. Perhaps the cardinal was deceived, confusing it with the idea of a copy of Apringius’s work which the Marquis of Mondéjar saw in Cortesius’s possession and which he himself mentions in *The Preaching of Blessed James in Spain*, chapter 22, fol. 124, p. 2.

In the same place Aguirre says that Morales possessed this work of Beatus, written in extremely ancient characters. In this too he was misled by opinion, for Morales, the most diligent narrator of ancient manuscripts, nowhere stated, either in his *Chronicles* or in his *Sacred Journey*, that he owned such a manuscript.

Joannes Ferreras, in his first *Dissertation on the Preaching of the Gospel in Spain by Saint James the son of Zebedee*, p. 7, says that another copy of Beatus’s *Exposition of the Apocalypse* exists in the library of the College of Saint Ambrose of the Society of Jesus at Valladolid.

So much for the works of Beatus. From his writings the history of Beatus and Etherius must be extracted.

### 23

It is fitting that we mention Basiliscus, who appears to have written against Elipandus, as may be gathered from the fourth letter of Paulus Alvarus of Córdoba to Aurelius Flavius Joannes, no. 28, p. 123, in Flórez’s *Sacred Spain*, volume XI. Alvarus’s somewhat obscure words are these:

> “Hear what Basiliscus says to Elipandus. ‘He adds,’ he says, ‘someone: God the Father did not beget flesh.’ I myself acknowledge that he did not beget flesh, but he begot the Son, whose flesh it is.”

I think that the text should read: “You add,” he says—that is, Basiliscus speaking to Elipandus—“God the Father,” and so forth.

Joannes Gómez Bravo, in *The Bishops of Córdoba*, chapter 2, p. 109, reads it as follows: “But he says,” he says, “someone.” If this reading is preferred, let it stand on my authority. Yet it would be better to read *dicet*, “he will say”; and that “someone” is a certain Bonosian.

On the following page Bravo suggested that this Basiliscus may perhaps have been one of the envoys of Alphonsus Lastus to Charlemagne in the year 798. That embassy is mentioned by the anonymous *Annals* from the Pithaean Library, p. 13, and by Ado under the same year, although he does not give Basiliscus’s name. But I do not dare either to affirm or deny Bravo’s conjecture. Nor is Basiliscus’s episcopal dignity proved in any way, although Bravo wishes him to have been a bishop.

As for the letter of Benedict of Aniane, the abbot, against Elipandus and Felix of Urgell, nothing memorable occurs to me.

### 24

You now understand, most learned sir, in which libraries the works are found that can assist the truly magnificent plan of the illustrious abbot of Emmeram: namely, in the royal libraries, those of the Escurial and Madrid, and in the church of Toledo.

In the latter I have excellent friends, from whose generosity I may hope for something, unless their own occupations stand in the way. In the former, however, we shall scarcely obtain anything without the king’s permission. You may therefore inform the distinguished Temler that nothing would be more expedient than for the illustrious abbot himself to write to the king. In that way he will obtain whatever he wishes.

I wish I were there, where I could show how eagerly I desire to obey the illustrious abbot’s commands and to satisfy, in a manner worthy of him, the wishes of the distinguished and most learned Temler. But you, most courteous sir, know very well that I lack the ability, not the will, to accomplish everything which I can imagine would be agreeable and pleasing to you.

Farewell, and love me.

Oliva, 21 November 1763.

# CANDIDUS, ON THE IMAGE OF GOD

[Note: See above the *Notice* prefixed to the Appendices, col. 1313.]

From a ninth-century manuscript of Salzburg.

It seems rightly said to me that the inner man is the image of God. For the soul is the name given to the whole inner man, by which that muddy mass, moistened with juices lest it dry out and dissolve, is given life, governed, and held together.

God is said to be that power ineffably great, innumerably wise, and incomparably sweet, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things that exist; by whom all things that exist are governed and in whom all things that exist are held together.

By “all things” I mean the whole universe itself, which is the totality of everything that is other than the one who made it and was not made. Yet he himself is the one from whom, and the one who is from him, and the one through whom the “that which” exists.

God himself, from whom he is, is called Father by us poor creatures in understanding and poorer still in words. That which is from him is called the Son. That through which he is is the Holy Spirit.

God is therefore called Father because he is himself the one from whom come both wisdom, by which all things are ordered, and love, by which all things wish to remain as they have been ordered. From whom I am, and who is from him, and through whom those two love one another: these are three. And those three are therefore one because those two are from one in such a way that they are nevertheless not separated from him; and he himself is what they themselves are, and they themselves are what he himself is; and he himself is what they are, and they are what he is, yet they are not he, and he is not they.

That power is God; and God himself is three; and each one of those three [Note: “three” is undoubtedly superfluous.] is God; and all three together are not gods but God.

The Creator therefore made the human soul in his own image. I call that soul “mind” as well [perhaps: *etiam*, “also”], though I call it “soul” for one reason and “mind” for another. For everything in a human being that lives is soul. But when the soul acts within itself, by itself and through itself alone, it is usually called mind; when it fills the functions assigned to it, it is more commonly called soul.

Mind therefore begets knowledge, and loves to know what it knows. I do not mean by “knowledge” that by which something is suddenly known which had previously been thought unknown. I mean that by which anything, and everything whatever that is known or unknown, can be known.

The mind begets that knowledge; and once it has been begotten, it can be called knowledge. There are therefore already two: the mind and what the mind itself knows.

A third remains, common to both. Every mind loves to know whatever it knows. Love is present no less between two: the one who loves and what is loved. There is therefore one love belonging to both, and it is the third.

It cannot be denied that this whole is one soul, and that one soul is these three. For just as these three are truly one soul, so this one, this other, and this third are no less truly one soul.

Let this exalted creature therefore compare itself with its Creator, who is exalted above it—except for that which is wholly removed far above it: the fact that every goodness, every good, and all the sweetness of goodness and good are from the Creator himself, whereas for the creature not only its existence but also its being of such a character comes from another and not from itself.

And he himself always is what he is. The soul too is in a certain manner unchangeable according to its own mode. For the soul is always soul, and it knows, and it wishes to know.

Let the soul therefore compare itself, as I have said, with its Creator in the manner in which it can. Let the mind be called father, because it begets knowledge. Let knowledge be called son, because it is from another and is nothing other than that very thing which he himself is, from whom it is.

Let love be called the Holy Spirit, because it belongs to both those who love one another. Hence in our Scriptures love—that is, charity—which is in God toward us and which is from us toward God, is very often itself called “spirit.”

# THIRD APPENDIX: HISTORICAL

## Notice of the Churches of the City of Rome

And from the Salzburg manuscript. (C)

First in the city of Rome, the bodies of the blessed martyrs John and Paul rest in a large and very beautiful basilica. Then proceed through the city toward the north until you reach the Flaminian Gate, where Saint Valentine the martyr rests on the Flaminian Way in a large basilica which Honorius restored; other martyrs are underground in the northern district.

Then go east until you come to the church of John the martyr on the Salarian Way [the manuscript: *ecclesia Johanni martir.*]. There the martyr Diogenes rests, and in another chamber Bonifacianus, and the martyr Sixtus underground; the martyr Blastus is underground. Then John the martyr; afterward Longinus the martyr.

Then go southward along the Salarian Way until you reach Saint Hermes. There Bassilissa, a virgin and martyr, rests first; in another chamber are Maximus the martyr and Saint Hermes the martyr, far underground; in another cavern are the martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus, and then Victor the martyr.

Afterward, by the same road, you reach Saint Pamphilus the martyr, twenty-four steps underground.

Then you come to Saint Felicitas by another road, also called the Salarian Way. There she rests in a church above ground, and Pope Boniface the martyr in another place, while her sons are below, underground.

Then by the same road you reach the church of Saint Saturninus, pope and martyr. In another church the virgin and martyr Daria rests, and the martyr Chrysanthus. Afterward, by the same road, you reach the cavern where Saint Hilaria the martyr is.

Then by the same road you go to Saint Alexander the martyr. There Theodulus and Eventus rest, and far within the cavern Alexander the martyr rests.

Afterward, ascending by the same road, you reach the church of Saint Sylvester. There a multitude of saints rests: first Saint Sylvester, pope and confessor; at his feet Saint Siricius, pope; on the right side Pope Celestine and Bishop Marcellus; the martyrs Philip and Felix and a multitude of saints beneath the main altar; in one cavern the martyr Crescentius; in another Saint Prisca the martyr; and Fimitis rests in a chamber as you leave. In another are Saint Potentiana the martyr and Praxedis.

Afterward go east until you reach Saint Emerentiana the martyr, who rests in a church above ground; and two martyrs, Victor and Alexander, are in a cavern below.

Then by the Nomentan Way you reach the church of Saint Agnes, which is beautiful. She alone rests there, and Bishop Honorius restored it with marvelous workmanship.

Afterward you leave that road and reach Saint Hippolytus the martyr, who rests underground in a chamber; his wife, Concordia the martyr, is before the entrance. In another chamber are Saint Tryphonia, queen and martyr, and her daughter Cyrilla, virgin and martyr, whom Meditus [read: Messius] Decius killed, his wife and daughter; and Saint Genesius the martyr.

Afterward you reach the church of Saint Lawrence. There are two great basilicas in …, and he rests there. Outside the church there is a small chamber on the western side [the manuscript reads *in hoc occidentur* incorrectly; perhaps *in occidente*]. Saint Abundius and Herenius the martyrs rest there.

On the Tiburtine Way there is also the stone which many people lift with one finger, not knowing what they are doing. In another church above ground many martyrs rest: the first is Saint Cyriaca, widow and martyr; in another place Saint Justin; beside him Saint Crescentius the martyr and a multitude of saints. Far underground in a cavern rests the martyr Romanus.

Afterward you ascend to the church of Saint Agapitus the martyr and deacon of Saint Sixtus the pope.

At Saint Helena, on the Campanian Way, many martyrs rest. On the northern side of Helena’s church is first Tiburtius the martyr. Then you enter a cavern, where the holy martyrs Peter, presbyter, and Marcellinus rest. Farther within the cave are Gorgonius the martyr and many others. In one place within the cavern are forty martyrs, and in another thirty martyrs; in a third are the Four Crowned Martyrs, and Saint Helena in her rotunda.

Then you reach Saint Gordianus the martyr, whose body rests beneath the great altar in the church of Saint Epimachus. The martyrs Quintus and Quartus rest beside the church in a chamber, and far within the cavern is Trophimus the martyr.

Then by the same road you reach a cavern. Here, by the same road, Saint Eugenia, virgin and martyr, rests in a chamber of the church; in another place is Emisseus the martyr.

Afterward you reach Saint Sebastian the martyr by the Appian Way. His body lies in the lower place, and there are the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul, in which they rested for forty years. On the western side of the church you descend by steps [the manuscript reads *discendis*, as it does throughout], where Pope Cyrinus, martyr, rests. By the same road, toward the north, you reach the holy martyrs Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus.

There you enter a large cavern and find Saint Urban, bishop and confessor; in another place the martyrs Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons of Sixtus; in a third place Cyrinus the martyr; in a fourth Januarius the martyr. In a third church, again, the martyr Synon rests.

By the same road you reach Saint Cecilia. There is an innumerable multitude of martyrs: first Pope Sixtus the martyr, Pope Dionysius the martyr, Pope Julian the martyr, Flavianus the martyr, and Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr. Eighty martyrs rest there below. Pope Zephyrinus, confessor, rests above. Pope Eusebius, martyr, rests far within a cavern. Pope Cornelius, martyr, rests far within another cavern.

Afterward you reach Saint Soter, virgin and martyr. By the same road you come to a small church where Saint Xystus was beheaded with his deacons. His body lies toward the north.

Then leave the Appian Way and reach Pope Mark, martyr. Afterward, by the Ardeatine Way, go to Pope Damasus, martyr. In another church you will find the two deacons and martyrs Mark and Marcellianus, brothers by birth; their body rests above beneath the great altar.

Then descend by steps to the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus. Proceed westward and you will find Felix, bishop and martyr; descend by steps to his body. Then go to Saint Paul on the Ostian Way.

On the southern side, observe the church of Saint Thecla, situated upon a hill; her body rests in a cavern on the northern side. On the western side of the Tiber is the church of the blessed Felix the martyr, in which his body rests, along with that of Alexander the martyr and Saint Sabina the martyr.

Then, on the northern side of the church of Saint Paul, the church of Saint Aristus, Saint Christina, and Saint Victoria appears, where they rest. Then descend toward the north and find the church of Saint Candida, virgin and martyr, whose body rests there.

Descend into the cavern and find an innumerable multitude of martyrs. The martyr Pumenius rests there, and the martyr Milix in another place; the entire cavern is filled with the bones of martyrs.

Then ascend and reach Pope Anastasius, martyr; in another place the martyr Polion rests. Then enter a large church, where the holy martyrs Abdo and Sennes rest. Then leave and enter the place where Pope Innocent, martyr, rests.

Then walk to Saint Pancratius, whose body rests in a beautiful church on the Aurelian Way, which Pope Honorius built for the most part. In that church enter far underground, where you will find Arthemius the martyr; in another place Saint Paulinus the martyr; and in another cavern Saint Sophia the martyr and her two daughters, Agape and Pistis, martyrs.

Then ascend and reach the church. There Saint Processus and Saint Martinianus rest underground, and Saint Lucina, virgin and martyr, rests above. Then by the same road you reach the two holy pontiffs and martyrs named Felix.

Afterward, by the same road, you reach a church where you will find Pope Callistus, martyr, and, in another place in the upper house, Pope Julius, martyr.

Then enter by the Vatican Way until you reach the basilica of blessed Peter, which the Emperor Constantine founded, distinguished and beautiful above all the churches of the whole world. The blessed body of Peter rests in its western district.

There is also another place near the city of Milan, opposite the eastern district outside the city. There is the church of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and Saint Victor the martyr. In another church are Saint Maforius and Felix the martyr. In one corner is Saint Simplicianus, confessor. In a church on the right side Saint Valeria, mother of the saints Gervasius and Protasius, rests there; Saint Dionysius the martyr, Saint Aurelius the martyr, and Saint Nazarius the martyr rest in his own church. In one corner is Saint Morimonianus, confessor; in another church are Saint Celsus the martyr and Saint Maternus, bishop and confessor. Saint Storius, confessor, and Saint Magnus, confessor, and Saint Eugenia, confessor.

As you enter the portico of Saint Andrew [the manuscript: *sanctae*], an altar of Saint Lawrence meets you on the left; then one of Saint Vitus; then one of Saint Cassianus; then, in the middle of the rotunda, one of Andrew himself; then one of Saint Thomas; then one of Saint Apollinaris; finally one of Saint Sixtus.

As you leave, Saint Martin will receive you and lead you to Saint Petronilla. There the Savior of the world will first receive you and assign you to Saint Anastasia; she will assign you to the most holy Mother of God, who commends you to Saint Petronilla, so that she may lead you to her son, the Savior of the world.

He sends you through the blessed Theodore to Saint Michael the archangel, so that by his intercession you may again be led to his most holy Mother; she will return you to the twelve apostles, who through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, send you again to Saint Mary.

From her left side Pope Leo will receive you and return you again to that same Mother of God. With her help you will finally proceed through the crypt to the head of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. From there you will reach the main altar and his *confessio* [perhaps, “confession-shrine”].

After pouring out tears of penitence, you go to the place where that most blessed apostle appeared to one of his attendants. Then proceed to the altar of that same holy apostle which is called the altar of the Shepherd; there, they say, the attendant was protected from a fall by the apostle Peter.

You must then go to the portico where the banner of the life-giving cross is kept. As you enter toward the fountain, there is an altar set into the wall of Saint George the martyr. Then go to Saint John the Evangelist. After greeting him, you will reach Saint John the Baptist. Under his guidance run to the manger of Saint Mary. After kissing it, proceed to the portico of Petronilla.

Rejoicing, ascend to the *lectur* of Saint Gregory the holy Father [as the manuscript reads], in which he gave back his spirit to God the giver, a worthy offering. There you have eleven altars.

From there descend and hasten to the prayer [read: *orationem*] of Saint Mary called the Ancient. Then go to the purple stones lying in the middle of the pavement, arranged in the form of a cross. From there you must go to the body of Saint Gregory the Father, and from that place to Saint Mary called the New.

## The holy places of the martyrs outside the city of Rome

First, Peter rests bodily in the western part of the city, beside the Cornelian Way at the first milestone. Almost the entire pontifical order, except for a small number, rests in the same place in their own tombs [perhaps: *tumbis*]. There too, beside the same road, are the seats [read: *sedes*] of the apostles; their marble table and couch are still visible today [read: *hodie*]. The table which Peter made with his own hands, now serving as an altar, is also there.

Beside the same road lie Saint Rufina, Saint Secunda, Saint Mary, Saint Marius, Saint Ambacus, Saint Audifax, and very many other saints.

Not far from there, on the left, beside the Aurelian Way, lie buried Saint Processus, Saint Martianis, Saint Pancrantius [as the manuscript reads], Saint Paulinus, Saint Arthemius, Saint Felix, Saint Callistus, Saint Calopus, and many others.

Beside the Portuensian Way, which is also on the western side of the city, Saint Abdo and Saint Sennes, Saint Milex and Saint Vincentius, Saint Polion, Saint Julius, Saint Pymenius, Saint Felix, Saint Simplicius, Saint Faustinus, and Beatricis [perhaps: Saint Beatrix] sleep.

In the southern part of this city, beside the Ostian Way, the apostle Paul rests bodily. There also sleeps Timothy, bishop and martyr, whom the book of Sylvester mentions. Before the façade of the same basilica is an oratory of Stephen the martyr. The stone with which Stephen was stoned has been placed upon the altar there.

Not far from there, toward the south, is the monastery of Aquae Salviae, where the head of Saint Anastasius is kept and the place where Paul was beheaded.

Near the basilica of Paul is the church of Saint Thecla, where she lies bodily; and not far from there is the church of Saint Felix, where he sleeps. When he departed to heaven, Adauctus was hastening there with him, and both rest in one place. Nemesius the martyr also lies there with very many others.

Beside the Ardeatine Way is the church of Saint Petronilla; Saint Nereus and Saint Achilleus are also there, as is Petronilla herself, buried.

Near the same road Pope Damasus was laid to rest, together with his sister Martha. In another basilica not far away, Mark and Marcellianus are honored; and in yet another church another Mark is honored together with Marcellinus.

Beside the Appian Way, on the eastern side of the city, is the church of Saint Soteris the martyr, where she lies with many martyrs. Beside the same road is the church of Pope Sixtus, where he sleeps. Cecilia the virgin also rests there; Saint Tarsitius and Saint Zephyrinus lie there in one tomb; Saint Eusebius, Saint Colocerus, and Saint Parthenius lie there separately, each in his own place; and eight hundred martyrs rest there.

Not far from there, in the cemetery of Callistus, Cornelius and Cyprian sleep in a church; in another cavern is Saint Colocerus the deacon.

Beside the same road is also a church of many saints: Januarius, the eldest of the seven sons of Felicitas; Urbanus; Agapitus; Felicissimus; Cyrinus; Zeno, the brother of Valentinus; Tiburtius; Valerianus; and Maximus. Many martyrs rest there.

Beside the same road is the church of Saint Sebastian the martyr, where he sleeps. The burial places of the apostles are there too, in which they rested for forty years. Cyrinus the martyr is also buried there.

By the same road one reaches the city of Alba, and through that city the church of Saint Senator, where Perpetua lies bodily, together with innumerable saints. Great marvels occur there.

Beside the Latin Way is the church of Saint Gordianus, where he lies in one tomb with his brother Epimachus. Quartus and Quintus are also there. Sulpitius and Servilianus, Saint Solia, and Trophimus sleep there buried with many martyrs.

Beside the same road is the basilica of Tertullianus, where he lies with many martyrs. The church of Saint Eugenia is also beside that road, where she lies in one tomb with her mother.

There Pope Stephen sleeps with his entire clergy, numbering twenty-eight martyrs. There are buried Saint Nemesius, Saint Olympius, Saint Sympronius, Saint Theodulus, Saint Superius, Saint Obloteris, and Saint Tiburticanus, martyrs. On the same road is the church of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.

Beside the Lavican Way is the church of Saint Helena, where she lies bodily. These saints sleep there: Peter, Marcellinus, Tiburtius, the thirty holy soldiers, Gorgonius, Genuinus, Maximus, and the Four Crowned Martyrs—Claudius, Nicostratus, Simpronianus, and Castorius.

In underground crypts an innumerable multitude of martyrs lies buried. Simplicius.

Beside the Penestrinam Way [as the manuscript reads; i.e. Praenestine], near the aqueduct, is the church of Saint Stratonicus, bishop and martyr, and of Saint Castolus; their bodies are buried far underground.

Beside the Tiburtine Way, near the city wall, is the church of Saint Januarius, bishop and martyr. On the same road is the church of Saint Agapitus, greatly honored for the bodies of martyrs.

Near the same road is the church of Saint Lawrence the Major, in which his body had first been buried. There is also a new basilica of marvelous beauty, where he now rests.

Under the same altar Abundus has also been laid to rest. Outside, in the portico, is the stone which once hung from Abundus’s neck and was thrown into a well. Hereneus, Julianus, Primitivus, Tacteus, Nemesius, Eugenius, Justi, Crescentianus, and Romanus are buried there. Saint Cyriaca, Saint Simferosanus [as the manuscript reads], and Justina are also martyrs there, together with many others.

From there, northward and upward on the hill, is the basilica of Saint Hippolytus, where he lies with his entire household of nineteen martyrs. There is a prison in which Lawrence was confined. There are also Tryphonia, the wife of Caesar Decius, and her daughter Cyrilla; between them are Concordia, Saint Genesius, and many martyrs.

Beside the Nomentan Way is Saint Nicomedes, and beside the same road is the basilica of Saint Agnes, of marvelous beauty, where she lies bodily. Nearby her sister Emerentiana sleeps in another basilica. In a separate church Constantia, the daughter of Constantine, rests.

Saint Alexander, Saint Felicis [as the manuscript reads], Saint Papia, Saint Victor, and many others sleep there.

Beside the Salarian Way is the church of Saint Felicitas, where she lies bodily. Her son Sillanus, one of the seven, is also buried there, and Pope Boniface sleeps there with many saints.

Beside the same road Pope Saturninus sleeps with many martyrs. In another church are Saint Chrysanthus, the virgin Daria, and sixty-two martyrs.

Nearby lie Saint Alexander, Saint Vitalis, and Saint Martial, three of the seven sons of Felicitas, with many martyrs. In the inner cavern are Saint Theodulus and Eventus. There also rest the seven virgins: Saint Saturnina, Saint Hilaria, Saint Dominanda, Saint Serotina, Saint Paulina, Saint Donata, and Saint Rogantina.

Beside the same Salarian Way Saint Sylvester rests, with Pope Siricius at his feet, together with very many others: Pope Celestine; Saint Potentiana; Saint Praxedis; Bishop Marcellus; Saint Crescentianus; Saint Maurus; Saint Marcellinus; Saint Prisca; Saint Fimitis; Saint Paul; Saint Felix, one of the seven; Saint Philip, one of the seven; Saint Semetrius; and, in one tomb beneath the main altar, three hundred and sixty-five martyrs.

By the same road one also comes to the church of Saint Michael, seven miles from the city.

Not far from there, westward along the same road, in underground crypts eighty steps below ground, Saint Pamphilus, Saint Candidus, and Saint Cyrinus lie with many martyrs.

From there, as one proceeds westward, the basilica of Saint Hermes appears, where the martyr himself lies far underground. Saint Crispus, Saint Herculanus, Saint Maximilianus, and Saint Basilissa are there.

In another cavern are buried Saint Hyacinthus and Saint Protus, Saint Victor, and Saint Leopardus, with many martyrs.

Not far from there in the west is the church of Saint John the martyr. His head is placed beneath the altar in one place and his body in another. Saint Diogenes, Saint Sixtus, Saint Liberatus, Saint Blastus, Saint Maurus, and Saint Longina, John’s mother, are buried there, together with another 1,222 martyrs.

Then, near the Flaminian Way, the magnificently decorated church of Saint Valentine the martyr appears, where he lies bodily. Many saints are buried there in the northern district.

These are the churches found inside Rome.

The Constantinian Basilica, also called the Basilica of the Savior and likewise called the Basilica of Saint John.

The basilica called Saint Mary Major.

The basilica called Saint Anastasia, where the crosses carried in the processions are kept.

The basilica called Saint Mary the Ancient.

The basilica called Saint Mary the Rotunda.

The basilica called Saint Mary across the Tiber. There is an image of Saint Mary which was made by itself.

The basilica called that of the Apostles James and Philip.

The basilica called that of John and Paul, where both lie in one tomb.

The basilica called that of Cosmas and Damian.

The basilica called that of Saint Lawrence, where the gridiron of that same Lawrence is kept.

The basilica called Saint Peter in Chains, where the chain with which Peter was bound is kept.

The basilica called Saint Hadrian.

The basilica called Saint Chrysogonus.

The basilica called Saint George.

The basilica called Saint Clement.

The basilica called Saint Agatha.

The basilica called Saint Stephen.

The basilica called Saint Mark.

The basilica called Saint Marcellinus.

The basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel.

The basilica of Saint Boniface the martyr, where he sleeps.

In all these basilicas a public station is held at appointed times.

# THE MOST BEAUTIFUL EXCHANGE OF LETTERS BETWEEN ALEXANDER, GREAT KING OF THE MACEDONIANS, AND DINDYMUS, KING OF THE BRAHMANS, BEGINS

[Note: In the edition, the title reads: “The exchange of letters on philosophy between Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians, and Dindymus, king of the Brahmans.”]

From the Millstatt manuscript and Palladius’s edition. (C)

It has often come to my ears by report that your manner of life differs from the common way of human beings wherever they are [Edit.: “from that of ordinary men, who are everywhere”]; for they report that you use neither the resources of the land nor those of the sea. This matter, marvelous because of its novelty, seems unbelievable amid the license of rumor; and rightly I have hastened to consult you through these letters, Dindymus, so that, if what we hear [Edit.: “have heard”] is true, and if you do this for the sake of philosophy, you may explain it without delay. Once I have become more certain, I too shall, if possible, become a follower of this discipline. From my earliest youth I have always devoted myself to the pursuit of the virtues, and I have preserved, not carelessly, as I think, the precepts of innocence handed down to me by wise men. Through them we are so instructed for living well that we do not altogether lose the causes and remedies of living well. But since your outstanding diligence introduces, in addition to those philosophical principles and customary teachings of the philosophers, a certain mode of uniquely rigorous observance [Note: At Col. 1365D the edition reads: “But since your outstanding diligence is offered,” etc.; Bissaeus thinks *fertur* (“is borne”) should be read, and below substitutes *inducere* for *inducit*. But, omitting *offertur*, as in the manuscript, no other correction is needed.], I ask you to disclose it without delay; for no loss will result to you from this, while we perhaps shall gain some advantage. Community is a free thing [Edit.: “it is a thing to be shared”], and, when communicated to another, it passes on without suffering any diminution. Just as, from a single torch [Edit.: “from a single lamp”], if you kindle many lights, you cause no loss to the original material—for indeed you acquire the capacity to gain more whenever you acquire the means to bestow more. Therefore I beg you to provide answers to what I have asked.

[Note: In the edition the title is: “The First Response of King Dindymus against King Alexander the Great of the Macedonians.”]

## THE RESPONSE OF KING DINDYMUS (C)

Alexander, we gladly commend your wish to know what perfect wisdom is, although you profess that you are not ignorant of it [Edit.: “although I commend you for professing that you are not ignorant of it”]; for you have preferred to attain the one thing that is superior to every kingdom. Indeed, a commander without philosophy is believed not merely to rule, but to serve many [Edit.: “a commander who is outside philosophy is believed not merely to rule, but to serve very many.”] Nevertheless, since it seems sufficiently difficult and almost impossible for you now to be brought over to our institutions, seeing that you have been imbued with disciplines and customs far different from those required by our practice, I had resolved to remain silent, to grant you pardon for the matters about which you ask, and to beg your indulgence—especially since I have no abundant eloquence at my disposal and you, occupied with military necessities, have little time for reading. But lest you say that I am abandoning you out of envy, I shall explain, as best I can, what you seek. You rightly rejected the reports about us that had earlier been brought to you, being, as you were, distrustful of rumor [Possibly *autem* (“however”) for *enim*]; for people commonly delight in fabrications. Now, content to learn the truth of matters without uncertainty, recognize what practices we possess for living happily [Possible supplement: “what laws, or a similar word, we possess”] [Note: The edition reads: “Now learn from me without uncertainty, content with the truth of the matter, recognizing what sort of people we are for living happily.”] Let it be for your judgment whether you think what we shall set forth ought to be followed or rejected.

[Col. 1367A] The nation of the Bragmans therefore lives a pure and simple life. It is captured by no allurements of possessions; it desires nothing beyond what the law of nature demands; it suffers and endures everything, considering necessary whatever it knows is not superfluous. Our nourishment is always readily available—not what the ingenuity of luxury, searching through all the elements, seeks out, but what the earth, untouched by iron [Manuscript: “wrapped,” evidently erroneous], produces. We load our table with harmless feasts [Note: The edition reads: “But what the earth, untouched by iron, produces, we load our table with feasts.”]

This is why we count neither kinds nor names of diseases, but enjoy the long-lasting joys of unimpaired health [Note: The edition reads: “But we enjoy the long-lasting joys of unimpaired health.”] Accordingly, among us there is no use of herbs for healing bodies, nor do we seek assistance for harming others [Edit. adds: “when established”]. One person does not beg another for help where people live among equals; there is no place for envy where no one is superior. Equality in poverty makes everyone rich. We have no courts, because we do not commit acts requiring correction; we hold no laws of the sort by which crimes are prosecuted among you. For while severe enactments often prohibit unknown crimes, they have taught people about them [Edit.: “while severe fears prohibit unknown crimes, they have taught them.”]

There is one law for the nation: not to go against the right of nature [Note: This reflects the teaching of the Stoics. Thus Cleanthes said that the highest end of human beings is “to live in agreement with nature” (ὁμολογουμένως τῇ φύσει ζῆν), or “to live in harmony with nature” (συμφώνως τῇ φύσει ζῆν). Others expressed it as living within the limit of nature, or following nature. See Buddeus, *History of Philosophy*, chapter 4, p. 261. Martini.]

We show mercy to no one, because we ourselves commit nothing deserving pity. By forgiving the sins of others, we do not wash away our own faults; nor do we redeem accumulated crimes by scattering wealth. For what benefit does generosity expended on a neighbor’s offense provide, when what is bestowed resembles its author [Edit.: “resembles avarice, what is bestowed”]? And perhaps the person with whom the morally guilty man shares what he has hastily acquired is more corrupt, so that the recipient is regarded as equal to the giver in vice [Edit.: “removed from vice”]. For depravity makes equal those whom it touches.

We do not engage in labor that nourishes avarice; we avoid shameful idleness [Edit.: “shameful leisure”]; we do not surrender our limbs to lust, to be weakened; we do not use the night to preserve our wickedness; we do nothing that the law [P. Rieberer: perhaps “light”] would punish [Edit.: “that would be punished”].

Among us it is forbidden to wound the mountain ridges with teeth [Edit.: “to be wounded”], or to furrow the beauty of the fields with plowshares [Edit.: “to water”], or to yoke creaking carts to groaning bulls. We do not torment our stomachs with bloody banquets; for the sake of eating, we do not search out the hidden places of the shore with ritual devices [Note: The edition reads: “For the sake of eating, we do not search out cut-off parts of the shore with nets.”]. We do not deceive creatures of the sea by secret hunting [Edit.: “by cut-off parts”], nor do we strike at the freedom of the air by capturing birds; we do not lay waste to the inhabitants of the forests by tracking them, nor do we bring the spoils of wild beasts home.

We possess everything that we do not desire. Desire is indeed the most savage plague, which, when it seizes the needy, commonly makes them needy, because it never finds an end to seeking. The more it has been enriched, the more it begs for the use of indulgence [Edit. better: “for the use of lust”].

We do not raise towered summits; nor do we artificially temper the healthy air; nor do we confine the cold courses of waters in a station of boiling [Edit.: “fermenting”] substance. Why should we ask for baths, when our bodies do not become dirty through unclean contractions [Edit.: “contact”]? We grow warm in the sun, are moistened by dew, quench our thirst from a stream [Edit.: “streams”], and the earth provides our bed. Anxiety does not break our sleep; thought does not weary our minds. We do not stir up dominion over people like ourselves through arrogance [Edit.: “we do not exercise arrogant authority”]; nor do we force anyone into even the least servitude. We judge that only the body ought to serve the mind [Note: P. Rieberer thought the text should read: “Nor do we force anything into the least servitude—the body, which alone, etc.” But the reading in the edition may perhaps be better: “Nor do we afflict anyone with even the least servitude, except the body, which alone we judge ought to serve the mind.”]

Otherwise it is cruelty to compel into obedience those whom the same nature has brought forth as our brothers, and to whom inheritance of common goods is promised by one God the Father.

In building houses we do not loosen stones with fire; nor do we remake clay, kneaded back into stones, in furnaces [Edit.: “in the manner of a furnace”]; nor do we make harder cement by mixing in wind-borne dust [Note: This seems to refer to volcanic earth from Puteoli, customarily carried by ships in every direction. P. Rieberer]. We do not lay foundations in the deep; nor, by our power, mutilate the ancient possession of the ocean, so that we may have sunny rooms where once there was stormy navigation, while we strive somehow to enlarge the narrower spaces of the earth [Col. 1368B] and provide, as it were, additions to the Creator’s deficiency [Note: The edition reads: “So that none of ours may be deprived of the ancient possession of the ocean: there let us have sunny rooms where once there had been stormy navigation, while we somehow enlarge the narrower constructions of the earth and provide, as it were, additions to the Creator’s deficiency.” I scarcely think this reading preferable to that of the manuscript. Martini.]

Rather, we live spaciously in excavated caves of the earth or in the hollow hiding places of mountains. There we fear neither the roar of winds nor the whirlwinds of any storm. A cave protects us from rain more safely than a roof tile [Note: The edition reads: “The use of this dwelling is twofold for us: while we live, it benefits life; when we die, burial . . . . . No garment is woven in dyed color. P. Rieberer thinks the text should read: ‘The cave protects us more safely than a roof tile, whose use, etc.’”]. Its use is twofold: while we live, it serves as a dwelling; when we die, as a burial place.

Among us there is no costly garment, and no clothing is woven in a dark-dyed color. Our limbs are covered with the protection of papyrus—or, more truly, with modesty.

Our women do not adorn themselves in order to please. They regard the cultivation of adornment as more of a burden than a decoration [Edit.: “honor”]. For they do not know how, in increasing their beauty, to desire more than they have received from nature. Who can improve the work of nature? Once it has been made, such an attempt is either fruitless, because it is defeated, or criminal, because it is presumptuous.

Among us no incest, adultery, or corruption is named. Lust does not summon us to intercourse, but love of offspring; we know no love except dutiful love [Edit.: “pure love”]. We do not prevent pregnant offspring from proceeding by abortive acts [Edit.: “we do not know how to proceed by abortive acts”], nor do we search for the death of another within a living body [Note: The edition reads: “Nor do we bring death upon another living body in anger.”]. In observing human beings [P. Rieberer: perhaps “in conceiving human beings”], we do not deprive God of his rightful claim on account of sterility [Id.: perhaps “under the pretext of sterility”] [Note: The edition reads: “In conceiving human beings, we do not deprive God of his rightful claim on account of sterility.”] Nor, in snatching away the lives of survivors, do we press with swords the lingering threads of the Fates.

We do not take up weapons or wage wars. We establish peace by our morals, not by our strength. Fortune alone is the adversary against whom we often fight and always win; having tested its recklessness against us, it laments. We make no complaint about the fates, because by acting rightly we do not grant them power against us.

We do not suffer death except the death brought by an enfeebled old age. Finally, no parent accompanies the funeral of a child. We do not construct tombs resembling temples for the dead, nor do we store cremated corpses in jewel-encrusted urns [Edit.: “nor carry them in”]. I would regard this not as an honor but rather as a punishment [Edit.: “I would call it not an honor but rather a punishment”]. For what is more pitiable than these bones, which are burned so that the mother earth may receive them into her embrace?

## Apostrophe to Wealth

But these are your arguments, Wealth: you have granted neither satiety to the living nor final rest to the dead. As I see, your madness has found something to torment human beings even after death. You do not allow the earth to warm in its bosom the ashes of those whom it produced; under the attractive appearance of service, you rob the wretched of a joyous burial. Let human beings learn what sort of return you offer your lovers [Edit.: “what return you offer your lovers”].

You are the cause of every evil among mortals [Edit.: “among mortal beings”]. You affirm that Asia and Libya can be confined within narrow boundaries. You make the sun’s course tremble while Alexander searches out its limits with weapons. You suggested that the guardian of Tartarus could be lulled to sleep by a payment. You consume everything, yet always wear a hungry face. You have stained the pious right hands of fathers with the throats of their children [Edit.: “with the throats of their children”]. You led modest young men into intercourse with their mothers, while desire itself stood stupefied [Edit.: “while desire itself stood stupefied,” feminine]. You have driven the gentlest kings into arrogance, persuading them that the spaces of the earth are not enough and urging them to seek seats in the heavens.

Nor have you left even your gods free from disease [A word may be missing: “from this disease”], for through them too you commit unspeakable acts [Edit.: “you committed them”]. Jupiter and Proserpina are witnesses: Jupiter, because he deceived a chaste woman in the form of gold; Proserpina, because she receives a living body into Tartarus only when gold has been offered [Note: Horace, Book III, Ode 16, line 8; Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI, line 140; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XIV, lines 112 and following].

You deprive free people of honor and bestow nobility on slaves. You exalt captives in triumphs. You make kings unable to do what they wish. You strip judges of integrity. You possess everything, and rule over all who possess you. Only the wisdom of the Bragmans surpasses you, by refusing to love you. But enough of this; now let us go through the remaining matters [Note: This word is absent from the manuscript].”

We Bragmans do not suffer pestilence, for we do not pollute the air of heaven with foul acts. Nature always maintains harmony with the seasons among us, and the elements, undisturbed, preserve their proper cycles [Note: The edition reads: “We Bragmans do not suffer pestilence; for we are not polluted by foul acts. Heaven always maintains a temperate climate among us; nature agrees with the seasons, so that the elements, undisturbed, preserve their cycles.”]

Our remedy for illness is frugality. It can not only cure diseases that have already entered the body, but also prevent them from coming. We do not seek theatrical entertainments [The manuscript reads “ludicra exspectacula,” apparently in place of “spectacula”], horse races, or stage obscenities. We do not regard the arena as a pleasure [The manuscript reads “harenam,” apparently in place of “arenam”]. We recoil from streams of flowing blood. For what would a mime do here, where he could find no trick that he might display for our ridicule? What would a tragic actor do, finding nothing to mourn with shouting [Note: The edition reads: “For what would a mime do here, where he could find no trace that he might display for our ridicule? What would a tragedian do, finding nothing with shouting?”]?
