Why should young men be exposed to savage beasts, when no one considers such a punishment to be deserved by any offense [Edit.: “when no one’s offense is considered worthy of such punishment”]?

When we wish to attend a theater, we reread the memorials of your deeds. Although they are most deserving of laughter, we weep over them.

The structure of the world offers us other spectacles and different pleasures. In it we see the heaven beautifully formed, shining with the diversity of the constellations and the brilliance of the stars. We see the sun borne on crimson yokes, spreading its locks, rooted throughout the circle of the world; the returning year, resting upon its twelve months, follows its course from there. The seasons, beautiful in appearance and accompanied everywhere by garlands of vine leaves, attend it [Note: The manuscript reads this corruptly. The edition has: “Enclosed by seasons and encircled with vine-leaf garlands they attend.” Eduard Bissaeus thinks this should be corrected to: “Enclosed by the seasons and encircled by vine leaves.” The distinguished P. Rieberer corrects the manuscript as follows: “The beautiful seasons, encircled by vine leaves,” etc.]. The rolling days and still more swiftly rolling hours precede it.

We also behold the sea adorned with a purple hue [Edit.: “we strive to make . . . beautiful”], stirred always by calm and friendly waves [Edit.: “which is always stirred”]. It is thought not to strike its sister earth but to embrace it. Its many-shaped fish and wandering dolphins perform innocent leaps across the wet and billowing waters [Note: The edition reads: “And wandering dolphins innocently perform the moist waves and leaps of the sea.”]

We likewise delight in the cheerful appearance of green fields [Edit.: “seasons”]. From them a most pleasing fragrance exhales flowers [Edit.: “a flower”] of sweetness, feeding both the eyes and the mind. The shaded loveliness of groves and springs also delights us; there various birds, ringing out in musical harmonies, compose sweet melodies [So in both manuscript and edition]. These are the spectacles of nature, which are difficult to imitate and blameworthy to reject.

We do not plow the sea with fleets for the sake of trade, nor, lying beneath another sun, seek foreign provinces out of disdain for our own land. The sea is accustomed to provide both savage dangers to travelers and great marvels to those who arrive [Note: The edition reads: “Which provides such savage dangers to travelers.”]. Never has a foreign appearance inflamed us with the heat of its beauty, since we believe nothing more fitting than the sight of what belongs to us. Nor will material bound by many circumstances of wealth make us its servants, when unrestrained poverty has produced us free.

We do not learn the art of speaking well, nor do we devote ourselves to the eloquence of rhetoricians and orators. Its function is to fabricate lies with ornamented speech, to lend credibility to crimes, and to declare the most innocent people guilty of parricide. While they think they have seized the fruit [Edit.: “the deed”] of another’s praise through an unjust victory, they do not know that they have lost the fortress of their own conscience.

Among us speech is simple [Edit.: “eloquence”] and shared equally with everyone, prescribing only this: not to lie [Words omitted in the edition]. We do not attend the schools of the philosophers, whose conflicting teaching defines nothing stable or certain, always splitting apart the earlier propositions among those who follow their doctrines [Edit.: “always rescinding them”]. One faction places the good in moral excellence, another in pleasure; and they cannot demonstrate how they themselves could know what they assert, but dare to establish unverified matters through ambiguous opinions.

Our philosophy is straightforward. It knows how to help only justly, and does not know how to harm, not even justly [Edit.: “nor is it just to harm”]. Nor does it think it right to inflict upon others what causes us sorrow when it is inflicted [Note: The edition reads: “Nor is it sweet to inflict upon others what causes us sorrow when it is inflicted.”]

In honor of the divine we do not slaughter harmless animals; we do not build shrines encrusted with silver metals; we do not dedicate altars shining with gold and gems. If you offer these things to a god who does not possess them, you assert yourself superior; if you offer them to one who possesses them, you assert yourself his equal. Whichever you do, it is an insult. For whoever invites heavenly beings with prices offends them [The manuscript erroneously reads: “defends”].

God does not accept bloody sacrifices; he loves worship without blood. He rejects deadly offerings. He is appeased by the word of those who pray [Edit.: “by those who pray”], and this alone is his commerce with humanity [The edition omits “commerce”]. He takes immense pleasure in his own likeness. FOR GOD IS THE WORD. By this he created the world; by this he governs and nourishes all things. We venerate this, we love this, and from this we draw breath, since GOD HIMSELF IS SPIRIT AND MIND. Therefore he is not appeased by earthly riches or by the lavishness of gifts, but by religious works and thanksgiving.

For this reason we judge you exceedingly witless and pitiable, because you do not accept [Possible reading: “suspect”] that your origin is heavenly and that you possess a great kinship with God. Instead, you obscure the splendor of your lineage with the most worthless things, since your greatest pleasure lies in the flesh. You cherish it, worship it, and love it, although both the touch of the living flesh is horrifying and the contact of the dead is impure [Edit.: “the handling of the living”]. In its uses, the elements are troubled [Edit.: “benefits are troubled”], and the world labors to provide its services.

What is more outrageous, you even dare to appease God with slaughtered flesh, and you discharge the worship of religion not to the one who alone exists, but to many who do not exist—and in this, plainly, you have been deceived by the flesh.

For you say that the human being is a small world [Edit.: “you say that the human being is pure”]. And just as many limbs are arranged within it, so you imagine various gods established in heaven [Note: The edition reads: “And so, since its limbs are arranged in multiplicity, you imagine other gods established in heaven.”]. You assign to each of them separate parts of your body, sacrifice victims familiar to each, and give them carefully selected names. You assert that Minerva holds the citadel of the head, namely wisdom; that Juno, mistress of anger [Edit.: “presiding over anger”], possesses the heart; that Mars, leader of wars [Edit.: “presiding over wars”], marks the chest, suited to wounds; that Mercury, discoverer of eloquence, guards the gates of the tongue [Edit.: “crouches beneath them”]; that Hercules has claimed the arms for himself, as befits a fighter; that Cupid controls the liver as its secret keeper [Manuscript: “restrains”]; that Bacchus, author of drunkenness, occupies the storerooms of the throat [Manuscript: “possesses”]; that Ceres, giver of grain, inhabits the granaries of the belly; that Venus, mother of lust, has occupied the chambers of the thighs; that Jupiter, as an aerial spirit, has his tribunal [Edit.: “court”] in the nostrils; and that Apollo, teacher of medicine and music, possesses the dwelling places of the palms.

By handing over the entire structure of the human being to the gods you name, you have reserved no part of the bodily dwelling for your own seats [Note: The edition reads: “And by handing over such a great structure of the human being to the gods whom you name as your masters, you leave no part of the bodily dwelling reserved for your own seats.”]. Yet they do not return the favor owed to us as free guests, but impose upon us, as dependent tenants, a tribute to be paid, exacting different tributes from different people [Edit.: “one demands one thing, another another”; P. Rieberer: “they appease one with one thing and another with another”].

Thus a boar is assigned to Mars; a he-goat is dedicated to Bacchus; a peacock is slaughtered for Juno; a bull is led to Jupiter [Edit.: “is dedicated”]; a swan is offered to Apollo; a dove is assigned to Venus; an owl is consecrated to Minerva; meal is offered to Ceres; honey is spread before Mercury; a poplar crown surrounds the altars of Hercules; and rose garlands adorn the shrine of Cupid [Edit.: “decorate it”]. They do not allow the same common couch to be offered to them [Possible reading: “to the same gods”], even if necessity requires it [The manuscript reads “when it demanded it”; Edit.: “if it demands it”]. Instead, each god obtains his own priests and the gift assigned to him by lot—if indeed they are to be called gods, since no power has been given them except over the particular animals offered to them.

You offer vows worthy of your errors—or rather, worthy of torture. In truth, you invoke not helpful gods but the most dreadful executioners, who tear apart your entrails with a variety of punishments. For there must be as many punishments established in your body as there are gods, since each compels you to serve his own mockeries.

One draws you to war; another leads the same person to luxury. One urges you to seek opportunities for gain [Edit.: “an opportunity for gain”]; another implants the desire to feast. All command, demand, and press you. None grants time for rest. Thus, while your senses are lulled by hidden seduction, your wretched body, burdened [Edit.: “bound”] with numerous duties, wastes away. And so it happens that, because through dullness you are unable to cast away the seeds of your evils, you worship them as divine powers.

Indeed, I marvel at you. Since you are greedy for wealth and devoted to avarice, you are lavish toward so many gods in vain, especially since they command everything execrable. If they hear you when you sacrifice, you incur losses to your conscience [Edit.: “you draw them along”]; if they do not hear you, you incur losses to your resources. Therefore, whether they are angry or favorable, they always do harm.

These are the Furies that avenge crimes; these are the torments of Tartarus celebrated in the songs of your poets [Note: The edition reads: “These are those Tartarean torments celebrated in song, which,” etc.]. They torture you as though you were already dead, because of your impious and profane superstition and your contempt for true religion.

For if you wish to look more intently upon your miseries, you find that nothing has been reported idly about the underworld [Edit.: “you will find”]. Whatever images are imagined to exist there—you are they.

Thus the Eumenides are the foulest thoughts; Persephone [in the edition: Tisiphone] is a depraved conscience; the bloodless shadow feeds upon your bodies, which lack soundness of mind [The word “feeds” is redundant in the manuscript]. The infernal punishments are the sleepless vigils caused by the continual persistence of wrongdoing. Tartarus [Edit.: “Tantalus”] is the insatiable and ever-thirsty greed of desire. Cerberus is the evil greed of the belly, which, because one mouth is not enough for it, has been given three mouths [Manuscript: “hours”]. The Hydra [Manuscript: “Ydra”] is the foulness of vices that grow again after satiety [Edit.: “the Hydra is the foulnesses”]. The viper’s crown is the dreadful squalor of filthy deeds. Pluto is the sluggish mind that rules the human body; because it has been deprived of heavenly goods, it has rightly been condemned to the seats of hell. The pallid gods [Edit.: “wandering”; perhaps “deceitful”] are the gods whom you worship without reason.

O most fortunate people, whose religion is a crime and whose life is a punishment!

## THE RESPONSE OF ALEXANDER (C)

If these things are as you claim, Dindymus, then, as far as I can see, only the Bragmans are counted among the number of human beings, and only they are believed to be exempt from bodily substance. They are said to be free from all vices; they do not enjoy the pleasures granted by nature; they regard as a crime the fact that we are born; they consider everything we do to be forbidden; they judge the benefits of advantages expended upon mortals to be burdensome instead of necessary [Note: That is, “burdensome rather than necessary.” P. Rieberer]; they declare the service of various arts to be criminal [Edit.: “criminal services”]; and they altogether destroy the laws of living. Either they profess themselves to be gods [Edit.: “do not profess themselves to be gods”], or they envy God, whose most beautiful creation they condemn. In my judgment these things ought to be counted as madness rather than philosophy.

## THE RESPONSE OF DINDYMUS (C)

“We,” said Dindymus, “are not inhabitants of this world but newcomers. We did not come into the world in order to be pleased to remain in it, but to pass through it. For we hasten toward our ancestral home [Manuscript: “our ancestral country”], unburdened by the weight of any crimes, lingering in no dwelling places of allurements, and bound to no taverns of disgrace. We scarcely touch anything dishonorable [Edit.: “we have scarcely touched anything of theirs”]; we hide no thefts of desire among our gains [Edit.: “for our supports”], since we proceed with the face of our conscience uncovered, so that, unencumbered and unimpeded, we may traverse the appointed stretch of our journey [Edit.: “and, unencumbered, we traverse the appointed journey.”]

“We do not say that we are gods [Edit.: “that we are not gods”], nor do we, as you accuse us, maliciously disparage the immensity of the heavenly work [Edit.: “with envy”]. Rather, we assert that you misuse God’s goodness. We do not know that everything is permitted, but we affirm that everything ought to be fitting. Yet we often ask to relinquish, in accordance with moral excellence, those things that the will claims for itself.

“God, the creator of all things, formed various species in the world, since it could in no way exist without their diversity [Omitted in the edition]. He permitted their use to be discerned by human judgment. Whoever, therefore, abandons inferior things and pursues better ones is not himself a god, but becomes God’s friend.

“But why, I ask, did it seem right to you to say that we, living temperately and piously, are gods [Edit.: “gods,” dative], or at least that we envy God? This suspicion falls more justly upon you. When the swelling of excessive prosperity has inflated your arrogance, you forget that you are human beings and maintain that God does not care for mortals. You build temples for yourselves, raise altars, and rejoice that you are invoked through the sacrifices of animals. This is certainly done for your father, for your grandfather, and for all your ancestors; perhaps the construction of pyramids promises the same to you [Edit.: “the instruction of pyramids”].

Therefore I would more truly call you mad, because you do not understand what you are doing. Or, if you knowingly despise God, you are held guilty of sacrilege [Edit.: “may be held guilty”]. Why, then, do you attach the darkness of your blindness to those who see correctly and wound our minds with such an affliction [Note: The edition reads: “Since, then, you attach the darkness of your blindness to those who see clearly and wound your mind with such an insult, why do you not allow us,” etc. Neither the manuscript nor the printed editions yields a grammatical reading through the division of the sentences. Perhaps it should be written: “Why, then, attaching the darkness of your blindness to those who see correctly, and wounding your own mind with such an affliction, do you not allow us at least to pay tears for your miseries, which is the final duty of the dying?” Martini]? Why do you not allow us at least to pay tears for your miseries, which is the final duty of those who are perishing [Edit.: “to pay”]?

“You are very much to be lamented, since punishments are prepared for you that cannot be expiated for the injury done to divinity [Edit.: “for the injury done to the divine nature”; the editor favors the printed reading]. The clearest proof of this is the just condemnation of Salmoneus. He imitated the flash of the heavenly light and experienced what he was imitating. Or consider the burial of Enceladus, who, when he tried with violent efforts to attack heaven, was crushed beneath the tomb of a burning mountain. Such honors are bestowed upon those who do not recognize themselves as mortal [Edit.: “who do not recognize that they are mortal].”

## THE RESPONSE OF ALEXANDER (C)

“You now call yourself blessed, Dindymus, because nature established your dwelling in that part of the world where neither entry is open to newcomers nor departure to natives. Surrounded by guards of opposing difficulty, since you cannot avoid your homeland, you praise it; and what you suffer as the cause of your condemnation, you boast that you have earned through devotion to continence.

“According to your judgment, then, those too must be called blessed who, bound in perpetual chains and wasting away in prolonged squalor, drag out a penal life that grows old with them. For your philosophy does not differ from theirs. The forbidden use of goods is, for you, a useful torment. What the laws among us have decreed for criminals, the law of nature has imposed upon you; and the commands that necessity has given to your continence, prison has established for them. Thus those whom you call philosophers are pronounced guilty by us [Edit.: “are pronounced guilty”].

“And surely it is more fitting for us to mourn your miseries and to draw deep sighs over such great evils. For what is more afflicted, what more wretched, than a human being who has been denied the power to live freely?

“In the meantime, it is clear what God, the author and judge, has thought about your customs [Note: The edition reads: “The author God, I say, will be present as judge concerning your customs”]. He did not wish to reserve you for Tartarean punishments after death, but decided that while alive you should endure the poverty of the dead. You decorate it with the false name of philosophy [Edit.: “you decorate it”], yet no fruit of praise is thereby gained for you. For there is no merit in virtue in obtaining what you cannot change [Edit.: “what you cannot change”]. But that should be called glory which each person has bestowed upon himself [Note: The edition reads: “Nor should that be called glory which each person has not bestowed upon himself.”]

“More truly, therefore, I affirm that what you are living is not blessedness but chastisement. And, if you agree, let us go through the individual parts of your institutions.”

The Brāhmans do not have the practice of sowing seeds in the earth [Edit., committing seeds to the soil]; of adorning trees with vines; of clothing the bareness of the fields with plantations of trees [Col. 1374B]; or of constructing beautiful buildings. The obvious reason for all these things is that nature’s displeasure has not supplied you with the metal iron [Edit., iron and metal], by which everything we have enumerated is cultivated and made; nor can you obtain it from elsewhere through maritime trade. Thus you must necessarily spend a horrible life, grazing upon herbs and vine-shoots like cattle. Or do not wolves do the same, when prey supplies them with no meat and they are compelled to satisfy the madness of hunger with food from the earth?

But if you were permitted to migrate into our lands, the philosophy of your poverty would certainly not be required; it would remain deserted within its own boundaries. Or if we could cross over into your settlements, we would become impoverished in wisdom [Edit., we would make the wise impoverished]. What exile is not immediately accompanied by self-restraint? When it comes voluntarily, it is virtue; when it comes by command, it is punishment. Therefore it is not life lived amid narrow circumstances and poverty, but life lived temperately amid abundance, that deserves praise [Edit., temperately]. Otherwise blindness and poverty alone would receive the glory of virtues: the one because it has nothing to enjoy, the other because it does not see what it might desire [Note: [Col. 1374D] In Edit.: The one because it does not see, the other because it has nothing to desire.].

Thus, as you assert, the appearance of none of your women is enhanced by ornaments [Edit., none of your women]; I agree [Edit., I agree with you], since neither craftsmanship nor any material is available. No one among you is inflamed by the heat of incest or adultery. It would indeed be a marvelous work of God [Edit., a marvelous thing], if you lived according to your own judgment rather than necessity; if contemplation of chastity, not the sight of deformity, kept your mind from illicit loves; if chastity, rather than fasts imposed by compulsion [Edit., not by compelled fasts, but by fasts prescribed], elicited a testimony of the will. For no fiercer plague can befall mortals than this condition, which does not ordinarily remove the desires of lust from human feelings [Edit., such desires] [Col. 1374D], but the act itself; that is, it does not restrain the mind from crime, but the body from action; it does not repress the command of the one giving orders, but removes the obedience of the one serving.

The cause of sin therefore remains, when, even with it at hand, he would not submit to it even if he could [reading materially uncertain; the text is mutilated] [Note: [Col. 1374D] R. P. Rieberer considers this text mutilated [Col. 1375D] and restores it conjecturally as follows: “The cause of sin remains as long as the desire for wrongdoing is present; only the person who, even if he could, would not commit it escapes it.” The printed editions, however, agree with the manuscript.].

You say that you have neither laws nor judgments; that you do not study letters [Col. 1375A]; that you neither ask for mercy nor grant it. It is clear that all these things you share with beasts, which, just as they lack the capacity for sensation [Edit., for eating; Bisaeus: perhaps “for taking in”], have also been deprived of the will to enjoy. To us rational beings—that is, to human beings endowed with reason—whom no law of hunger constrains, who are prompted to live well by free choice, so that voluntary self-restraint may receive a worthy reward, nature has given many blandishments, which stronger virtue usually restrains. For it is impossible that the governance of so great a world should not have made joyful things succeed sorrowful ones [Edit., should not govern and make joyful things succeed sorrowful ones], through the regulation of some form of balance; since human will and the mind of mortals vary according to different circumstances [Edit., are changed], and are adapted to the movements of causes as the seasons alternate.

Indeed, the forms of our minds change with the alteration of the heavens [Col. 1375B]; they shine brightly on a clear day but, when a cloud is forced upon them, grow dim. The condition of the senses themselves also appears no less unstable than varied, and changes not only with the qualities of things but also with the stages of life [Note: [Col. 1376D] In Edit.: “And it changes not only with things but also with the stages of life.”]. Hence infancy rejoices in simplicity, youth exults in rashness, and old age is slowed by weakness. Who would demand either cunning from a child, constancy from a young man, or mobility from an old man?

Many things are delightful to our sight, others to our hearing, and some to our sense of smell, touch, or taste. Through them the harshness of the hardships we incur through labor is softened. Thus at one time we are entertained by dances, at another by songs; sometimes we are refreshed by the sweetness of a scent, the taste of something sweet, or the gentle softness of contact [Edit., touch]. All these things derive their material from the elements, which are also believed to be the principles of our life; through the intermingling of these contraries a structure of the human race is formed [Col. 1375C], so that each thing, satisfying its own parts, supplies us under providential ordering with a familiar support by which the bodily mass, wisely constructed, endures.

Thus the fruits of seeds are supplied to us from the earth [Edit., are shown to us]; an abundance of fish is brought forth from the sea [Edit., is carried out]; flocks of birds are bestowed from the air. If, by using these things, you wish to abstain from them [Edit., by rejecting them], you will either be branded with pride, because you reject gifts that have been given, or with envy, because it is supplied by one who is better [Edit., what they supply].

The Brāhman people indeed, distinguished by wondrous customs,

Here it is read; reader, let the mind behold faith.

Here the answers of Paul and Seneca are briefly contained [Note: [Col. 1376D] Rather “are read,” which cannot be discerned from the manuscript because of an erasure. Rieberer.]

Whatever I have noted, each under its own name,

These gifts, great one, glory of the world and most illustrious Caesar,

Your Albinus, your servant, sent to you.

## Critical Observations on the Preceding Letters

[Col. 1375D]

To the most illustrious and most reverend lord, Lord Frobenius Forster, prince of the Holy Roman Empire and abbot of St. Emmeram, most distinguished in piety, learning, and merits, a splendid and distinguished patron of the best arts, Georgius Henricus Martini, master of Leipzig and professor and rector of the Regensburg Gymnasium, sends respectful greetings.

Most illustrious, most reverend, and most gracious prince and abbot, when you had undertaken the plan of bringing together all the books of Alcuin, however many were written—or are believed to have been written—by him into something like a single corpus, and of publishing them together, a task that no one before you had accomplished, you took care, at considerable expense but with a zeal and prudence all the more deserving of praise, to have copies made and sent to you from Denmark, Britain, Spain, and other provinces where it seemed likely that anything written by this outstanding man might be found. Thus whatever of his works lay hidden in the libraries established there, and whatever you judged necessary for completing the comprehensive edition you had long been preparing, you might have at hand for its preparation and refinement [p. 607] [Col. 1376A].

Your undertaking—an enterprise supremely suited to your incomparable learning and prudence, and greater and more excellent than all my praise—will be raised up with such commendations and received with such applause by men knowledgeable in these matters that, in my judgment, it will also be commended to others who publish the books of any author whatever as a model for imitation. Crowned by this praise, as by the desired and most welcome fruit of your labors and vigils, you will certainly have reason to rejoice and to congratulate yourself [Col. 1376B]; and I earnestly wish that you may be able to rejoice and congratulate yourself for as long as possible.

Meanwhile, when you were reviewing the books you had received from so many distant provinces and comparing them with the greatest care, it seemed appropriate to you to entrust to me for examination a little work extracted from and transmitted through several manuscript books of Alcuin. With that singular and almost incredible indulgence which you show toward me, you requested whatever opinion I might have concerning it, and generously indicated that some critical and philological observations of mine would be especially acceptable and suited to your purpose, so that you might scatter them, wherever they seemed necessary, through the places in the little work that was to be published.

Although I have not yet been able to comply with this wish of yours—more difficult to carry out, almost beyond the small powers of my intellect, yet also agreeable and highly honorable to me—because of the regular duties of my office, I shall now obey it as far as I can. I shall communicate to you whatever opinion I may have concerning this little work, together with some observations [Col. 1376C], subject, however, to this condition: if you find my reflections worthy of both our persons, append them to your fuller edition as an everlasting memorial both of your singular kindness toward me and of my just devotion and obedience toward you, and hand them down to posterity; but if not, suppress and eradicate them in whatever manner you wish.

For I am neither so perverse nor so vain an admirer of my own things as to believe that others see nothing while I see everything, or to pronounce my own writings perfect and complete in every respect while declaring those of others slight, full of errors, and inelegant. Such is the rashness of many who, pleased with themselves, immediately disparage whatever they see or hear written by others, look down upon it with an elevated brow, and judge it unworthy of reading, although they themselves have never published anything committed to writing and do not dare to publish anything [Col. 1376D].

Far removed from the arrogance of such men—αὐθάδεια, “self-will,” the ridiculous daughter of detestable φιλαυτία, “self-love”—and always devoted to modesty, I readily admit that I may have slipped even in what I am submitting to you. If, through the acuteness of your intellect, you should see that this has happened to me, I earnestly beg and beseech you to prefer concealing my error to publishing it.

When you have granted this request, most reverend prince and abbot, I shall count this proof of your generous and noble spirit among the other benefits with which you have so often honored me, and I publicly promise that their memory will never die within me. With these remarks, let us proceed, if you please, to the matter itself.

Most indulgent patron, you could understand from the few remarks that I remember discussing with you, when I last attended upon you to pay my respects, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, “in passing,” what my general opinion was concerning the little work in question, which is entitled *A Most Elegant Exchange of Letters between Alexander, Great King of the Macedonians, and Dindymus, King of the Brāhmans*. Although you did not deny that my opinion was highly plausible, indeed probably correct, you nevertheless wished me to set it down in writing more fully explained and supported by necessary arguments. I shall therefore do what I have been ordered to do and undertake to explain the matter in the proper order.

You are not unaware, especially from the history of earlier times and most particularly from literary history, that people were once too ready in praising and accepting books which the cunning, pious fraud, or sordid pursuit of profit of certain persons brought into the light adorned with the names of men once exceedingly famous. They did not investigate their γνησιότης, “authenticity,” before approving them and using them as reliable and authoritative witnesses for confirming some matter. Through this credulity—or, to say nothing more serious, through this practice—it happened that such books, suspected under the name of νοθεία, “spuriousness,” and therefore properly to be rejected, became as if fountains from which countless and extremely serious errors, harmful to nearly every discipline, began to flow [Col. 1377B].

To restrain this evil, learned and ingenious men discovered and refined the discipline called criticism. In other matters it proposes and teaches laws and precepts which anyone investigating the γνησιότης, “authenticity,” of a book must keep before his eyes and follow with the greatest care, lest he slip in such an undertaking.

Its first and principal rule commands us to see whether any writers, especially writers worthy of confidence, testify that the little work in question was actually written by the author to whom it is attributed. Their testimony in some measure confirms and establishes its γνησιότης; their silence, on the contrary, greatly weakens the case and makes it doubtful, indeed may make it possible for us properly to doubt—or even altogether deny—that the work proceeded from him [Col. 1377C]. This is all the more so when such trustworthy writers have diligently investigated and described the deeds of the person who is said to have composed the little work.

This, then, is the position of the little work I have been ordered to examine. No ancient author known to me, whether contemporary with Alexander the Great or living for some time afterward, testifies that it was written by him. In his history of Alexander, Quintus Curtius Rufus is so far from testifying that Alexander sent letters to the king of the Brāhmans and received letters from him that he does not mention the Brāhmans, the king, or even the king’s prefect by a single word.

Arrian, an author as trustworthy as any, who in describing the military expedition of Alexander the Great followed the authority and memoirs of Ptolemy son of Lagus, a man who had taken part in most of Alexander’s deeds, does indeed state in Book VI, on page 409 of my edition, that Alexander, after capturing a certain town by force, killed τῶν Βραχμάνων, ὅσοι αἴτιοι τῆς ἀποστάσεως ἐγένοντο—that is, “those of the Brāhmans who were known to have been responsible for the revolt.” Shortly afterward he adds:

καὶ τοῦτον (that is, Musicanus) [p. 608] κρεμᾶσαι Ἀλέξανδρος κελεύει ἐν τῇ αὐτοῦ γῇ, καὶ τῶν Βραχμάνων ὅσοι αἴτιοι τῆς ἀποστάσεως κατέστησαν—

that is, “Alexander orders this man to be hanged in his own land, together with all those Brāhmans who had become responsible for the revolt.” The author glosses this as: “he orders him to be crucified in his own land.”

But when Arrian adds the words οἱ δὴ σοφισταὶ τοῖς Ἰνδοῖς εἰσίν, “who are indeed sophists, or wise men, among the Indians,” he seems sufficiently to show that they possessed neither some distinct and proper territory in which they dwelt nor a king whom they obeyed, but lived instead in the provinces of other kings, such as Sambus or Sabbus, Musicanus, and others. It is therefore certain that no letters could exist either to or from such a king.

Plutarch, in his *Life of Alexander*, on page 239 of my edition, does report that Alexander wished ten gymnosophists—the name by which the Brāhmans are included—to come into his presence for a meeting and conversation, and he also records the more difficult questions that Alexander proposed for them to solve. He likewise records whatever other writings, letters, and similar works the Macedonian committed to writing. But concerning a monarchy of the gymnosophists, a king administering their affairs, or literary correspondence between this king and the king of the Macedonians, he says absolutely nothing. From his silence it may rightly be inferred that whatever is said or circulated about such a king of philosophers and about letters written both to him and by him must be counted among fables and mere inventions.

If we may rely upon the authority of Arrian and Plutarch—and certainly we may—I cannot avoid declaring the letters in question false and fabricated on this ground alone [Col. 1378A].

A second reason that compels me to this judgment is the language used by the authors in composing the letters under discussion. They survive written, as we see, in Latin, a language that it is hardly plausible either Alexander or the Brāhmans knew or employed in writing. Where would men born and living in provinces so far removed from Latium have learned it? Would anyone suppose that they maintained teachers of Latin, as we maintain teachers of French or German, or sent their young men to Latium, as our people send theirs to France, so that, imbued with the ability, elegance, and charm of the Latin language, they might recommend, introduce, and establish its use among their fellow citizens?

Who, I ask, would believe that men afflicted by poverty, living so far from Latium, so stubbornly hostile to foreign customs, and so pleased with themselves had done any of these things? Everything that trustworthy authors report about the customs and institutions of the Brāhmans, and everything found written in these very letters, utterly refutes such a view and prevents us from accepting it.

Anyone who has even slightly investigated and considered the character of these men, and especially of Alexander, will understand that it is wholly contrary to the truth to suppose that either party learned a language not yet sufficiently cultivated and polished, and ordinarily used in only a small part of Italy by a people that was still almost obscure and not yet flourishing in the glory of successful and prosperous achievements [Col. 1378C].

What advantages or benefits could Alexander have gained from it? In his military expedition, the study of the languages spoken by the peoples who looked toward the rising sun promised and offered him far greater advantages than the cultivation of Latin. What could the Brāhmans—sophists or philosophers living among the peoples of India—have gained from it, when they would never transmit their doctrines of wisdom to Latins and could not obtain them from Latin books, since at that time there were none? Both parties would certainly have wasted their labor if they had applied themselves to a language utterly useless and unprofitable to them.

But suppose that, nevertheless, they did learn it and employ it in composing these letters. Even then, considering the period in which they lived, their style could not help but have a more ancient Latin flavor than the style in which the letters under discussion have been written. The latter, like a shrew-mouse, betrays itself through the signs and filth of a barbarous Iron Age, whereas letters written in Latin by Alexander ought to display something like the infancy of the Latin language and the character of the Twelve Tables [Col. 1378D].

Since this is so, I seem justified in affirming that the letters in question are false and fabricated for this reason also.

But it might be possible, someone may say, that they were first written in another language and that someone—whether Alcuin or another learned man—translated them into Latin during what is called the Middle Ages and published them. I hear the objection. Yet even so the difficulty is not sufficiently removed; rather, it is increased.

For on this assumption you must produce witnesses by whom you establish not one point but two: first, in what language they were originally written by the alleged authors; and second, by whom, and at what time and place, they were afterward translated into Latin. Until, therefore, you bring forward trustworthy authors as witnesses who clearly and plainly establish both points, I may continue to regard them as suspect under the charge of νοθεία, “spuriousness” [Col. 1379A].

Lest I seem to do this rashly, I shall illuminate the matter by the example of a book especially relevant here. You know that there exists, and is in the hands of learned men, a book entitled *A Specimen of the Wisdom of the Ancient Indians*, which is said to contain the moral doctrines of the Brāhmans. They claim that it was written more than two thousand years ago in the ancient language of the Indians, and that it was afterward translated into Persian, Syriac, and Arabic. In Arabic it is entitled *Kalīla and Dimna*, or *Kulila and Dimna*, as some prefer, until Simeon Seth, around the year 1100, rendered it from Arabic into Greek.

Sebastian Gottfried Stark published this Greek translation from the Holstenian manuscript, together with a new Latin translation, under the title *A Specimen of the Wisdom of the Ancient Indians, that is, A Very Ancient Ethical-Political Book*, Berlin, 1697. Anyone wishing to learn more about it must consult Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, Book V, chapter 5, page 460, and Petrus Daniel Huet, *On the Origin of Roman Fables*, page 21 and following. The latter author also testifies, in the same place I have indicated, that another book exists, composed in French and adorned with the name of Pilpay, who is fancifully represented as having been one of the Brāhmans, and that it does not differ greatly from the former.

We shall not touch upon that book here; I shall say a few things about the other. In it we have a book which is certainly known to have been translated into Latin by Stark and published together with the Greek text. It is said to have been made in Greek from Arabic by Simeon Seth; while the Arabic, Syriac, and Persian versions, along with several others [p. 609], are said to have flowed from the ancient language of the Indians in which the book was first written. The book contains and transmits to posterity a dialogue between Absolon, king of the Indians, and a certain gymnosophist, who reveals his thoughts to him through cleverly devised fables and shapes his character.

On what authors, on what wealthy and trustworthy witnesses, is this last claim believed? On none. From this it follows—as I shall cut the matter short—that the book itself, even if we know who translated it from Greek into Latin, must rightly and deservedly be counted among spurious and fabricated works [Col. 1379C].

If learned men therefore judge in this way of a book to which not a few features lend the appearance of γνησιότης, “authenticity,” how much more must such a judgment be passed upon letters whose authors and origins are wholly unknown and which rest upon the authority and testimony of no writer? Let them remain hidden, then—let them remain hidden forever. At least, let them deceive no one any longer.

Learned men and experts in criticism also instruct us, when we wish to investigate the γνησιότης of a book, to examine and observe whether any rites or institutions of the author, observed by him while writing or employed as arguments for confirming some proposition, offer any assistance toward properly resolving the question and completely settling the dispute that has begun concerning it.

For if the rites and institutions under consideration were customary in the age in which the author lived, among the people to whom he is attributed, and in the provinces about which he speaks, they say that the matter is sound and that the book displays a sufficiently strong sign of γνησιότης. If, on the contrary, the institutions mentioned there were not customary or appropriate to the age, people, or provinces under discussion, the author’s credibility and concern for truth are seriously weakened, and his book cannot avoid being regarded as suspect under the charge of νοθεία, “spuriousness.”

Applying this rule and precept of the most distinguished critics to the reading and examination of the letters in question, I noticed in them many institutions described as those of the king of the Brāhmans and reproached to Alexander—institutions that neither he could have known, given the period in which he lived, the distance of the places, and the absence of mutual intercourse, nor could he properly have reproached Alexander and the Greeks with. They were institutions customary not so much among the Greeks as among the Romans, and among the Romans only toward the end of the free republic and under emperors administering the state [Col. 1380A].

It follows that the author of the letters cannot have been the king to whom they are attributed, unless you maintain that he was a prophet who anticipated in his mind, long before they were enacted and established, the customs and institutions of the future. Since no prudent person would wish to affirm or defend this, it will easily be understood that the authors of the letters in question were not the kings of the Brāhmans and Macedonians, but a man living many centuries after Alexander the Great, and a thoroughly inept, inelegant, and foolish man—one who could so seriously err and stumble, and mix round things with square ones, as the saying goes.

Lest my opinion seem false and rash to anyone, it must be confirmed by several examples. In the very first letter Dindymus, king of the Brāhmans, writes boastfully of himself and his fellow citizens:

“We do not lay foundations in the deep; nor is the ancient possession of the ocean mutilated by our force, so that we may have sunny chambers where once there was stormy navigation, while we strive somehow to enlarge the narrow confines of the earth and provide, as it were, certain supplements to the Creator’s deficiency.”

In boasting that these things were far removed from himself and his people, and reproaching Alexander and the Greeks with them, that imaginary king was astonishingly deluded and showed himself wholly ignorant of Greek affairs. For I think no one will be able to prove with reliable evidence that the Greeks laid foundations of massive structures in the sea and built villas, gardens, and baths upon them for the sake of pleasure.

Suppose, indeed, that some of them advanced to that degree of luxury. Even so, it scarcely seems likely that they did so before the time of Alexander the Great, during a period when they were engaged almost continually in wars. They were rather devoted to their appetites and bellies, pursuing lavish banquets and the pleasures of drinking parties, and for this reason were very frequently and very vehemently rebuked by comic poets. Compare Homer, *Odyssey*, Book II, verses 55 and following; and Horace, *Epistles*, Book I, 2, verses 27 and following:

“We are a mere number, born to consume the fruits,

the suitors of Penelope, good-for-nothings, and the youth of Alcinoüs,

who spent more than was fitting in caring for his skin;

to whom it was beautiful to sleep until midday

and to drive away care through idleness

to the sound of the lyre.”

Thus, by a reproach that did not touch the Greeks in the slightest, that spurious Dindymus unquestionably disgraced himself.

Moreover, these words seem to me certainly to allude to passages repeatedly used by Horace, such as *Odes*, Book II, Ode 12, from the beginning:

“Soon only a few acres will leave the royal plow;

everywhere the broad ponds of Lake Lucrinus

will be seen spreading farther and farther,” etc.

Likewise, Ode 15, verses 17 and following:

“You arrange for marble to be cut

at the very moment of death; and, forgetful of the tomb,

you build houses;

and beside the sea that roars at Baiae

you press to move back the shore,

where the confined bank is too poor for you.”

And also *Odes*, Book III, Ode 1, verses 33 and following:

“The contracted waters feel the fish.

With massive structures cast into the deep, the contractor

frequently drops cement here

with his servants, while the disdainful

master of the land—”

But the poet of Venusia in these passages criticized not so much the custom of the Greeks as the mad behavior of his own fellow citizens. Nor was it an ancient practice customary among their ancestors [p. 610],

“not thus prescribed by Romulus

under the auspices of unshorn Cato

and the standard of the ancient men” (*Odes*, Book II, Ode 12, verses 11 and following),

but a recent practice that had spread more widely from the final period of the free republic and was corrupting the minds of his fellow citizens.

Many Roman authors state that Lucius Lucullus was the first to begin it. Cicero criticizes the magnificence of the villas built by him and the evil that flowed from his example in *On Duties* I.39, in these words:

“Who would question the virtue of Lucius Lucullus, a most distinguished man? Yet how many have imitated the magnificence of his villas?”

Horace alludes to the number of cloaks purchased by him in *Epistles* I.6, verses 40 and following:

“Lucullus, they say, had cloaks enough

to supply a hundred actors if asked for them.

‘How could I possess so many?’ he says.

‘Yet I shall seek them, and whatever I have

I shall send.’”

A little later he writes that Lucullus had five thousand cloaks at home, enough to supply part or all of them. In this, however, the poet seems to have exaggerated the matter beyond the truth. For Plutarch, in the *Life of Lucullus*, on page 177 of my edition, writes:

“Once, when a general requested purple cloaks, he replied, after considering whether he had any, that he would give them. Then, the next day, he asked him how many he needed. When the man said that one hundred would suffice, he ordered him to take twice that number.”

This same Plutarch, shortly before, reports much more about his luxury, including the following relevant details:

“The gardens of Lucullus are counted among the most luxurious of royal gardens. His works along the coast and around Naples—where he hung hills over great excavations, surrounded his residences with sea-wheels and fish-breeding channels, and built marine dwellings—when the Stoic Tubero saw them, he called him ‘Xerxes in a toga.’ Around Tusculum he also had country residences, observation points commanding the surrounding landscape, and structures consisting of open halls and promenades, and so forth.”

M. Varro confirms the same in *On Agriculture*, chapter 17. He says that, opposite Naples, Lucius Lucullus, after cutting through a mountain and admitting seawater into fishponds in which the water flowed back and forth, would not yield even to Neptune in fishing. Compare Pliny, *Natural History*, Book VIII, chapter 54.

Thus Velleius Paterculus rightly writes of him in *Roman History* II.33:

“Lucullus, otherwise a most distinguished man, was the first author of this extravagant luxury in buildings, banquets, and furnishings. Because of the massive structures he cast into the sea and the sea that he brought inland by cutting through mountains, Pompey the Great was accustomed, not without wit, to call him ‘Xerxes in a toga.’”

Since Lucius Lucullus was elected consul in the year 679 from the founding of the City and sent out from Rome to conduct the Mithridatic War, in which he acquired such vast and immense wealth, and since after his return he became the principal originator of such massive structures and villas, how could Dindymus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great and therefore alive around the year 430 from the founding of the City, reproach the Greeks for this kind of luxury—more than two hundred and fifty years before any Roman had indulged in it?

I see no way in which anyone could defend an error so serious and conspicuous—an ἀναχρονισμός, “anachronism”—or give it even the appearance of truth, let alone excuse it or make it seem less significant. It is so absurd that it plainly reveals the ignorance and stupidity of the man who fabricated these letters and proves that the letters themselves are spurious and fabricated [Col. 1381D].

With nearly the same prophetic ability, or rather with the same cunning or stupidity in deception, that fictitious king of the Brāhmans anticipated other Roman institutions by more than two hundred years and either reproached them to the Greeks or denied that he and his people followed them.

Among these are what he says about mimes, who formed a particular class of actors among the Romans but not among the Greeks; about tragic actors and their method of lamenting with much shouting; and about the abominable practice of exposing human beings to savage beasts. This is known to have been customary only among the Roman people, especially under emperors administering the state, and among other peoples seeking the favor of the Romans.

Most of these practices are more recent than the age of Alexander the Great. Thus the real Dindymus, if he had ever existed, could not have mentioned them in his letters, reproached anyone with them, or boasted that they were foreign to himself and his people, since they would have been entirely unknown to him.

He also discusses sacred rites and victims slaughtered in honor of the gods with excessive cleverness and almost in accordance with the opinions of philosophers who followed the discipline of Pythagoras. Concerning the gods of the Greeks and Romans, he argues many points with insufficient accuracy and makes several false assertions.

The author of the letters was no less seriously mistaken in attributing the construction of the pyramids to Alexander. These Egyptian monuments, which Pliny records among the wonders of the world, are far older and were built, at great expense and not without considerable skill, at least 1,900 years before Alexander took possession of Egypt. This error, too, whoever the man may have been, sufficiently exposes his ignorance and greatly diminishes his credibility.

I shall now pass over in silence several other matters that are either entirely false or at least doubtful, such as his account of the use of papyrus for covering the body. I consider what I have brought forward sufficient to establish how ignorant of affairs and how stupid the man must have been who, having fabricated the letters in question, could attribute them to Alexander and Dindymus—even if Dindymus ever lived and was in fact king of the Brāhmans.

Moreover, as I was reading the letters themselves, various expressions in their style raised a new difficulty for me, all the greater because they seem to savor of the Latin version of the Sacred Code, or at least to agree very closely with some of its expressions. To ensure that I am not thought to be making an unsupported claim, I shall immediately provide examples.

Elsewhere one reads: “By the Word he is propitiated by those praying . . . and he delights exceedingly in his own likeness; for the Word is God.” Elsewhere: “God himself is spirit and mind.” In another place: “From the one God, the Father of common blessings, an inheritance is promised.” Elsewhere: “to cherish the flesh, to honor the flesh, to love the flesh, to be deceived by the flesh,” and so forth.

I shall refrain from identifying here the passages of Sacred Scripture that I believe were present to the mind of the author who wrote these words, because I suppose that no one who reads this little essay can be ignorant of them.

If I am not greatly mistaken and deceived in this matter, but rather rightly suspect that these expressions were drawn from the Latin version of the Sacred Code, how could a man who was without the true religion have used them in his letters and yet have flourished in the reputation of wisdom long before that Latin version had been completed and published? From what other source he could have drawn them—if not all, certainly some of them—I at least cannot see [p. 611] [Col. 1382C].

Their use readily persuades me to believe that the authors of the letters themselves were not Alexander and Dindymus, but some later impostor, or at least a man learned in the literature of his own age, who composed them either to entertain the mind or to cultivate his style.

Let whoever wishes think otherwise; he is free to do so as far as I am concerned. I shall remain steadfast in my opinion, and I shall never believe that they were written by the kings whose names adorn them.

The entire style of expression employed in composing these letters seems wholly to confirm my opinion, whatever it may be. It is so constituted that a man well and properly versed in reading the classical authors of Latium, and accustomed to their elegance, symmetry, dignity, and clarity, cannot endure the style of these letters; for it is neither pure, nor elegant, nor even, but at one moment humble [Col. 1382D] and frigid, at another resembling poetry and inflated. It betrays some kind of sophistic artifice and is often filled with inept witticisms, as they are commonly called, antitheses, and plays upon words and ingenuity; it plainly abounds in the vilest solecisms and barbarisms.

To substantiate each of the points I have mentioned, I would have to transcribe entire letters. That would be burdensome both for me, who am writing this, and for anyone reading it. I shall therefore append only a few passages full of solecisms and barbarisms. What person sufficiently acquainted with Latin, I ask, would ever have said: “The matter … seems incredible through the license of rumors”; “you will generate no harm to the principal material”; “may you provide answers to the questions”; likewise: “But enough of these things; now let us run through the rest”; “let us run through the individual parts of your institutions”; or: “to care for illnesses that have slipped in”?

Who would have written *exspectacula*, which occurs frequently; or, “when we wish to await the theater”; likewise: “to exercise innocent [creatures] in dances across wet and wave-filled waters”; “various birds, sounding sweet melodies with musical harmonies” [Col. 1383A]; “whose office it is to fabricate lies with ornamented speeches”; “always splitting apart the earlier resolutions by those who follow”; “to prolong for himself a punitive life growing old with him”; and other passages of the same kind.

It is troublesome to transcribe more such flowers of rhetoric. No one could have patched them together and imposed them on others except a person utterly ignorant and utterly witless. It is impossible to say how absurd, how cold, and how barren is the apostrophe to riches contained in the first letter of Dindymus. It has the unmistakable flavor of a mere sophist wishing to deceive by the allurements of words.

But, in truth, to what end are all these observations, which you discuss so copiously, and almost more copiously than is proper? Clearly, so that it may be understood that these letters are beyond doubt spurious and fictitious, and that no reader of them may allow himself to be deceived by such things. Rather, let him cast off that credulity—if he happens to possess it—which led our forefathers to accept and defend writings adorned with the name of any sort of man, whatever famous name he once bore. [Col. 1383B] How much harm that credulity in many minds has done to good literature—let me say nothing more serious—is known to all who have investigated its history with somewhat greater care.

If I possessed such credulity, or if I did not hesitate to impose upon others, I could at this very moment publish from some manuscript two poems, one adorned with the name of Virgil [Col. 1384A], the other with that of Naso, and, after publishing them, seek praise over a *mustaceum* cake [Latin: *laudem in mustaceo*], as the saying goes. But my zeal for discovering and disseminating the truth makes me neither believe that those to whom they are attributed are their authors nor wish to persuade others of it.

Moved by the same consideration, I have composed this work which you now have in your hands, most distinguished prince and most reverend abbot, so that others too may clearly see what you yourself believe, and may not suppose that the letters which you have decided to submit once more to the press were actually written by Alexander the Great and Dindymus, whose names they bear.

If I come to understand that in this matter I have satisfied your desire and expectation, I shall count it among the great blessings of my life. If not, I earnestly beg you to think that what you perceive as deceiving your opinion has arisen not so much from any lack of the just and proper devotion and reverence I owe you as from a deficiency in sufficiently ready and refined learning. For the rest, expect from me at all times every form of the highest zeal [Col. 1384B] and service toward you. I shall certainly attend with the greatest eagerness and diligence to everything I understand to concern you, and I shall preserve the memory of your astonishing kindness and indulgence toward me. Farewell, and favor my affairs.

Given from my study on the Kalends of June, in the year 1770.

[Col. 1383]

## FOURTH APPENDIX. LITURGICAL AND HISTORICAL MATERIAL

### A Booklet of Sacred Prayers

From the Floriac manuscript, approximately 900 years old, in Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*.

[Col. 1383C]

## IN THE NAME OF CHRIST BEGIN THE PRAYERS WHICH THE BLESSED FATHERS CUSTOMARILY SANG DAILY, PRAISING GOD AND ENTREATING HIS MERCY.

### Prayer of Saint Hilary, which he appended to the twelve books he composed on the Holy Trinity

Holy Trinity, I beg you to preserve this undefiled religious faith of mine, and grant me, until the departure of my spirit, this confession of my conscience: that I may always hold what I professed when I was baptized in the symbol of my regeneration—in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—namely, that I may worship you as our Father, your Son together with you, and that I may be found worthy of your Holy Spirit, who proceeds from you through the Only-Begotten. For he is a trustworthy witness to the faith for me when he says: “Father, all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine.” My God Jesus Christ, remaining in you, and from you and with you always God, who are blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

### Prayer of Saint John the Evangelist

[Col. 1383D]

Lord Jesus Christ, I beseech you by your mercy and kindness to grant me forgiveness of my sins. Open to me, as I knock, the door of life, and let the prince of darkness not confront me. Let the foot of pride not come against me, and let a hostile hand not touch me; but receive me according to your word and lead me to the banquet of your feasts, where all your friends feast with you. For you are Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.

### Prayer of Saint Martin

God of glory, God who are the one and true God, who alone are just, God in whom all things, under whom all things, and through whom all things were made: hear me as I pray, as you heard the three boys from the furnace of burning fire; hear me as I pray, as you heard Jonah from the belly of the whale [Col. 1384C]; hear me as I pray, as you heard Susanna and freed her from the hand of wicked witnesses; hear me as I pray, as you heard Peter at sea and Paul in chains. Spare my soul, spare my deeds, spare all my crimes—you who with the Father, and so forth.

### Prayer of Saint Ambrose

Grant me, Lord, holy and loving Father, understanding that understands you, perception that perceives you, a mind that savors you, diligence that seeks you, wisdom that both finds you, a soul that recognizes you, eyes of the heart that see you, a manner of life that pleases you, perseverance that awaits you, a perfect end, your presence, a holy resurrection, a good recompense, and eternal life—you who reign for ever and ever. Amen.

### Prayer of Saint Augustine

God of justice, I beseech you; God of mercy [Col. 1384D], invisible God, incomprehensible God, unspeakable God, eternal God, everlasting God, blessed God, God of whom all things are, in whom all things are, under whom all things are, and through whom all things exist. Spare my soul, spare my evils, spare my sins, spare my crimes. Visit the sick, tend the suffering, heal the languishing. Give me a heart that fears you, understanding that comprehends you, ears that hear your voice, eyes of the heart that see you.

Give me a spark of your wisdom, which may show me the path of your ordinances and teach me to turn away from the jaws of the enemy. Have mercy on me, God; spare me, because I have sinned against you. Forgive me, because I have sinned against you, and through the hardness of my heart I rush onward into the very death of my sins.

I, in mouth; I, in heart; I, in deed—in every vice and every crime I am polluted and covered. I ask forgiveness because I acknowledge my crimes; I confess my wicked deeds, which, even if I did not confess them, could not be hidden from you. For you are the searcher of heart and kidneys: hidden things are revealed to you [Col. 1385A], and crimes are exposed. Have mercy on me, God.

Lord, do not allow me to perish; do not let me be consumed by everlasting darkness and perpetual death. Take away from my heart an estranged understanding. Heal in me the dullness of mind; root out from my inward parts counsels of wickedness; erase from my tongue the habit of slander, deceitfulness in lying, buffoonery, and all the acts of my vanity. Heal them by the art of your medicine, and circumcise in me the vices of heart and body.

Have mercy on me, God, because you know my deeds and my transgressions. If you had wished to pursue and punish me in judgment, the earth would long ago have swallowed me alive. But your kindness is so great that you do not allow anyone to perish; rather, you await all, that they may return to the place of repentance.

Since, therefore, you grant time for repentance, grant also the ability to act, so that this time of your forgiveness, which in your goodness you deign to bestow on us, may not be empty. Have mercy on me, Lord God. Do not despise me, nor turn your face away from me. I do not ask your mercy on account of my justice, but because of your great kindness [Col. 1385B]. Look upon me, Lord, from the holy seat of your majesty, and illuminate the darkness of my heart with the ray of your splendor.

Protect me, Lord, with the shield of the truth of your faith, so that the fiery darts of the devil may not pierce me. For whatever it is that my misery asks of you, or does not receive, or dares not ask, or does not understand—grant this through your power; and through your majesty and compassion bestow what saves the soul from death. As I depart from this chaos of darkness, extend your hand to me and show me the light.

Have mercy on me, Lord God. Restore what is broken, heal what is corrupted, cleanse what is defiled, forgive what I have done, and grant that I may not do it again, O Savior of the world, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God for ever and ever. Amen.

### Here begins the prayer of the blessed presbyter Jerome

When I rise in the morning, attend to me, Lord [Col. 1385C], and govern all my acts, my words, and my thoughts, so that I may spend the whole day according to your will. Grant me, Lord, your fear, contrition of heart, humility of mind, purity of conscience, so that I may despise the earth, look toward heaven, fear hell, hate sins, and love justice.

Cut away from me, Lord, the appetite of gluttony, the desire for fornication, the love of money, the plague of anger, the justice of the world, weariness of mind, empty joy, and the tyranny of pride. Plant in me, Lord, the virtue of abstinence, continence of the flesh, purity of mind, voluntary poverty, true patience, spiritual joy, steadiness of soul, contrition of heart, unfeigned humility, and brotherly love.

Guard my mouth, so that I may not speak empty words, chatter about worldly things, slander those who are absent, curse those who are present, or return a curse for a curse. Instead, may I bless the Lord at all times; may his praise always be in my mouth [Col. 1385D].

Guard my eyes, so that they may not look upon a woman in order to desire her, nor desire my neighbor’s property or the delights of this world. Rather, may I say with David’s spirit: “My eyes are always toward the Lord,” and the rest. And again: “To you I have lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven.”

Guard my ears, so that they may not hear a slanderous tongue, hear a lie, or hear an idle word; but may they be open every day to hear the word of God.

Guard my feet, so that they may not go around idle houses, but may stand firmly and motionless in the prayer of God.

Guard my hands, so that they may not often be extended to receive gifts, but rather may be raised each day in the Lord’s prayers, clean and pure, without anger and disputation, so that I may say that prophetic utterance: “The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”

Guard, Lord, our departure, as we set out in your name, and may your holy heavenly angel accompany us, able to lead us to the appointed place and direct our feet in the way of peace [Col. 1386A] and truth.

Guard, Lord, our thoughts, words, and deeds, so that we may fulfill your will in your sight and walk in your way throughout all the days of our life, through the Redeemer of our souls, our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever.

### Prayer of Saint Ephrem the Deacon

Lord God and my Savior, why have you forsaken me? Have mercy on me, for you alone are the lover of all. Save me, a sinner, for you alone are without sin. Rescue me from the filth of my iniquities, so that I may not be stuck there forever.

Deliver me from the mouth of my enemy; for behold, like a roaring lion he desires to devour me. Stir up your power and come, that you may save me. Send forth your flashes of lightning and scatter all the strength of the enemy, O lover of humankind, most kind God.

I adjure you by your mercies: do not place me with the goats at your left hand, with those who have provoked you. Do not say to me, “I do not know you”; but grant me, because of your great mercy [Col. 1386B], unceasing contrition and weeping of heart, and sanctify me so that I may become a temple of your grace. You who live …

### Prayer of the blessed Gregory, in which he gives due thanks to almighty God

I praise you and give thanks to you, my God of mercy, who have deigned to lead me to knowledge of you and, through the cleansing of holy baptism, to gather me among the children of your adoption.

I praise you and give thanks to you, who from the very beginnings of infancy until this hour have patiently awaited my amendment, although I have been flowing away through many vices, because of your boundless goodness.

I praise and glorify you, who have very often delivered me from many tribulations, anxieties, calamities, and miseries, and who have until now exempted me from eternal punishments and the torments of this body.

I praise and glorify you, who have deigned, by the grace of your compassion, to bestow on me health of limbs, tranquility of times, honor, affection, and charity, if indeed such gifts are in me.

I ask you, Lord [Col. 1386C] God, by the immeasurable kindness of your sweetness, to perfect the good things begun in me; repel whatever in me displeases you; rescue me from all the tribulations, iniquities, and various evils that remain; direct my thoughts, words, and deeds alike according to your will; and do not take my soul from this world before it has sought amendment.

Guard me always and everywhere, walking according to your will amid adversity and prosperity, and at last lead me to the desired joys of the vision of you.

### Prayer of Saint Ambrose, in which he asks forgiveness for his sins

Compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful, great and terrible God, I confess to you my sins, my crimes, my misdeeds; I disclose to you my offenses, my wounds, my wicked deeds. Because of your ineffable goodness, bestow medicine upon me, wretched as I am.

For in your exceeding gentleness you have deigned to say [Col. 1386D]: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

I confess that I have acted wickedly; my way is perverse in your sight. My life has fallen into the pit of misery. My soul has been extinguished by my iniquities. Pride, lust, anger, impatience, malice, envy, gluttony, drunkenness, desire, robbery, lying, perjury, buffoonery, foolish speech, ignorance, negligence, and other plagues have killed my soul.

My heart and my lips are polluted; my sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are polluted; and in every way—in thought, speech, and action—I am ruined.

I ask you, Lord God, whose mercy has no end: draw me after you, as you drew the sinful woman. Give me contrition of mind and body and abundant fountains of tears, as you granted her not to cease kissing your feet, wetting them with tears, and wiping them with her hair. Grant that, in proportion to the greatness of my iniquities, my love for you may be great, so that because of the immensity of your compassion [Col. 1387A] you may forgive me all my sins.

Grant me forgiveness for the past, continence regarding present evils, and caution regarding the future. Make me obtain your mercy in its fullness before I die; and do not allow my days to end before you forgive my sins. But, as you will and know, have mercy on me.

### Also, of the blessed Pope Gregory, concerning confession of sins and the asking of forgiveness for them

Give me, Lord, a confession that is pleasing to you. May unspeakable groans be brought forth in my heart and embrace your profound goodness in humility of heart. Give me the very thing to ask for which you delight to hear. Plant that very thing in my soul, so that you yourself may continually be my delight.

Give me tears born of affection for you, which may dissolve the bonds of my sins. Hear, my God; hear, light of my eyes; hear what I ask, and grant me what I should ask, so that you may hear.

If you look away, I perish; if you look upon me, I live. If you do not regard my justice, I stink; if you regard your mercy [Col. 1387B], you raise the stinking one from the tomb.

What evil do I, a corruptible creature, not possess? And what good do you, the Creator and most powerful renewer of the creature, not possess? Through my vice I fell from your hand; you are a powerful craftsman, able to fashion me again into something pleasing to you.

Correct me in your mercy; do not correct me in anger. Take far from me what you hate in me; implant in me the spirit of chastity and continence; put every vice to death in me, and make my soul alive in you.

Grant me to ask for this, so that in asking you I may not offend you. Grant what you yourself may always preserve. Take away from me what harms me; grant the very thing that benefits me.

I lay my wounds open before you; do not deny me your medicine. Care for what you receive, and do not cease continually to care for what you heal, O my hope, my strength, my mercy, my everlasting compassion, who are, and who were, and who remain for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1387C]

### Also, a prayer of Isidore concerning the same matter

I beseech your mercy, Lord; I implore your mercy; I implore your compassion; I seek your kindness. Blot out my sins, wash away my crimes, cleanse the stains of my sins, purge the blemish of my crimes, wipe away the filth of my offenses, wash away the filth of my iniquities; do not delay my cleansing.

God, I offer my entire self to you to be healed. May my soul receive salvation; give salvation to my wound. God, grant a remedy for my illnesses; through the treatment of wounds restore me to health.

I am wounded; I seek a remedy. I am sick; I ask for medicine. My flesh has been consumed; my appearance has wasted away; my bones have dried up; my limbs have withered. I have drawn near to corruption; the shadow of death has seized me; darkness has covered me; the gloom of hell has enveloped me; the horror of darkness has oppressed me.

Teach me to do your will, because you are my God. To you belong honor and glory, power and dominion, for ever and ever. Amen.

### Also, a prayer of Isidore for all Christians

[Col. 1387D]

Kind and hearable Lord, our God Jesus Christ, we earnestly ask your kindness, so that through the intervention and merit of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary and of all the holy angels, archangels, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, virgins, confessors, monks, and all the citizens of heaven, you may increase the faith of your holy Catholic Church; grant peace; grant indulgence and forgiveness of sins to our rulers and to us; grant health to the sick, restoration to the fallen, favorable weather, and to faithful travelers by sea and land a prosperous journey and a harbor of salvation; joy to those in tribulation; relief to the oppressed; to captives, prisoners, and exiles, release, cleansing, and return to their homeland; mutual charity to those who are divided by discord; true faith to unbelievers; and perpetual rest to faithful departed.

In your mercy, deign to give us here and everywhere your holy angel as guardian and defender [Col. 1388A], you who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God for ever and ever. Amen.

### Hymn of the blessed Ambrose for the sick

Christ, heavenly medicine of the Father,

true physician of human salvation,

powerfully reveal your favor

to the provident people through their prayers.

Behold, we beseech you for the sick,

whom the harmful plague of illness shakes;

as a merciful one, relieve the disease

with which those lying here are shaken.

You who, manifest in power,

immediately save Peter’s mother-in-law

lying with fever, the child of the royal official,

and the boy of the centurion.

Give strength to the weary, languishing people.

Let abundant health flow among the people,

restoring the sick to their former strength

as is your accustomed way.

[Col. 1388B]

Heal the diseases of bodies and souls;

apply a remedy to the causes of wounds,

lest suffering burn our bodies

without bearing fruit.

Let every assault that destroys withdraw;

let every torturing attack melt away;

let the strength of desired health

cherish the limbs of the suffering.

Now, God, have mercy on our tears;

heal those for whom we now ask you,

so that every sick person lying down

may feel your healing.

So that, while they are worn down by the evils inflicted,

they may enter the kingdoms of heaven,

made participants in a fitting rank

by the fruit that accompanies them.

[The syntax of the printed lines *Eruditorem numero decori / Compotes* is uncertain.]

Glory to the Father and to the Begotten Son,

and to you, life-giving Spirit,

ever equal to both,

one God throughout every age [Col. 1388C].

Let the choir sing and echo glory;

let it speak, sing, and repeat glory:

life-giving Spirit, one God,

throughout every age.

### Hymn of Fortunatus the presbyter on the Passion and cross of our Savior Jesus Christ

Sing, tongue, of the glorious

battle of the contest,

and upon the trophy of the cross

proclaim the noble triumph:

how the Redeemer of the world,

sacrificed, conquered.

Grieving over the deception

of the first-formed parent,

when, by the bite of the deadly fruit,

he fell to death,

he himself then marked the wood [Col. 1388D]

to undo the losses caused by the wood.

The order of our salvation

demanded this work:

that by the art of the many-formed destroyer

he might outwit the art,

and bring healing from the place

where the enemy had wounded.

When, therefore, the fullness

of the appointed time came,

the Maker of the world was born,

sent from the Father’s citadel,

and, having come forth in flesh

from a virgin womb,

the infant wails, enclosed

in the narrow manger;

the virgin mother binds

his limbs in swaddling clothes,

and the tight bandage joins together

his feet, hands, and legs. [Col. 1389A]

When six periods of five years

had now been completed,

and, fulfilling the appointed bodily time,

he willingly gave himself

over to the Passion for this purpose;

the Lamb was lifted upon the cross,

to be sacrificed upon the wood.

Here vinegar, gall, reed,

spittle, nails, and spear

pierce the gentle body;

blood pours forth in a stream—

earth, sea, stars, and world,

by which stream they are healed.

Faithful cross, noblest

of all, the one tree:

no forest produces

a flower, leaf, or bud like you.

Sweet wood and sweet nail,

sustaining a sweet burden.

Bend your branches, lofty tree;

relax your stretched fibers [Col. 1389B],

and let that rigidity slacken

which your nature gave you,

so that you may extend upon gentle wood

the limbs of the heavenly King.

You alone were worthy

to bear the price of the world *(alternative: age)*,

and to prepare a harbor
