### On faith

“I confess that I believe in the Lord the Father, who created all things; and in the Lord the Son, who was begotten by him before the ages; and in the Lord the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both—that is, the holy Trinity, naturally one true Lord, not three gods, but three persons in one substance, divinity, and majesty, existing always without beginning. I confess also the same Son, who was always with the Father, [Col. 1412A] born of the Virgin Mary through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, true God and true man in two natures, namely divine and human, but in one person; that he suffered in the flesh, died, was buried, descended to hell not in body but in soul, without losing his divinity, and on the third day rose again in the same flesh in which he died; that he ascended into heaven, will come again with glory, will judge, and will render to each according to his works. I confess that I believe in the holy Catholic Church and in the forgiveness of sins, whether through baptism or through repentance, and that I shall rise again in the same flesh in which I now live, unto eternal life. This is the true faith, known to the faithful in a few words, so that, subdued by believing, they may live rightly; by living rightly, cleanse the heart; with a cleansed heart, understand what they believe; and possess eternal life.”

## Memorandum concerning the order of daily prayer

[Col. 1412B] Venerable Father, let this be the first word to proceed from your mouth when you rise from sleep: “Lord, open my lips,” and the rest. Then: “Give ear to my words, Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God, for to you I shall pray. Lord, in the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I shall stand before you and shall see you, Lord.”

Afterward: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will. We praise you, we bless you, we adore you, we glorify you, we give you thanks because of your great glory, Lord God, heavenly king, God the almighty Father; Lord, only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ; Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father; you who take away the sins of the world, receive our supplication; you who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us. For you alone are holy, you alone are Lord, you alone are most high, Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen. Deign, Lord, to keep us from sin on this day.”

And then: “God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me,” with the knees bent three times and the Gloria said the third time. Then the Lord’s Prayer. Then, after signing the forehead and eyes, and all the limbs with the sign of the cross, take the Gospel in the hand, turn the face toward the east, and say: “Matthew and Isaiah, intercede for me.” Then turn the face toward the south and say: “Mark and Jeremiah, intercede for me.” Then turn the face toward the west and say: “Luke and Ezekiel, defend me.” Then turn the face to the left and say: “John and Daniel, guard me.”

Afterward say: “The cross is my refuge, the cross is my certain salvation, the Lord’s cross is with me; the cross is what I always adore.”

Then the Lord’s Prayer. Afterward say: “Give us, Lord, understanding, that we may know your testimonies. Open for us the senses and eyes of the heart, as you opened the senses of the apostles, so that we may be able to understand the holy Scriptures.”

With the Gospel opened, read one or two pages of it with attentive mind, so that what has been said may be fulfilled: “His will is in the law of the Lord”; and, “In his law he will meditate day and night.” And again: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him.”

Afterward let one page of Paul’s epistles also be read, so that each person may know, according to the evangelical and apostolic rule, what he ought to do in God’s service or what he ought to preach to others.

Then: “Christ, hear us,” and the rest that follows in the litany. Then the Lord’s Prayer.

Then, in private prayers, the sixteen psalms, namely:

1. “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.”
2. “How long, Lord?”
3. “The Lord rules me.”
4. “The Lord is my illumination.”
5. “Have mercy on me, God, according to…”
6. “God, in your name…”
7. “May God have mercy on us.”
8. “God, attend to my help.”
9. “You have blessed, Lord.”
10. “Incline your ear, Lord.”
11. “To you I have lifted my eyes.”
12. “Out of the depths.”
13. “Lord, you have searched me and known me.”
14. “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man.”
15. “Lord, hear me.”
16. Then: “Praise the Lord in his holy places.”

[Col. 1413A] Afterward: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to others.”

Then say: “But I direct my prayer to you, Lord; it is a time of favor, God. In the abundance of your mercy hear me, in the truth of your salvation. Deliver me from the mire, that I may not sink; free me from those who hate me, and from the depths of waters. Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor the pit close its mouth over me. Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your mercies look upon me, and do not turn your face away from your servant, for I am afflicted; quickly hear me. Attend to my soul and deliver it; because of my enemies rescue me, Lord.”

Afterward, “Christ, hear us,” three times, and the rest that follows, as before. Then the Lord’s Prayer and “I believe in God.”

All these things are to be done in private prayers at the first hour of the day; afterward let the particular prayers and the litany be completed in full.—Each Christian must carefully weigh and earnestly consider that he may venerate within himself the holy image of the divine Trinity with fitting honor. This image exists in the human soul, which is the inner human being, the spirit of the human being. For just as the one God is always wholly and fully present everywhere, giving life to, moving, and governing all things—as the Apostle says, “In him we live and move and are”—so the human soul is everywhere wholly alive within its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. It is not greater in the body’s larger members and smaller in its smaller members, but wholly in the smallest and wholly in the greatest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God, which the soul possesses within itself as a great and noble nature.

Perhaps someone says: “If, then, it is the image of one God, how is it the image of the holy Trinity?” The answer is this: first, just as God exists, lives, and knows. Further, although the holy Trinity is of one nature, it nevertheless has within itself three dignities, namely understanding, will, and memory. Similarly, the human soul is one mind, one life, one substance, just as God is one in three persons but one in substance. These three things that the soul possesses within itself are not three lives, just as there are not three gods, but one life, just as there is one God; nor are there three minds, but one mind; consequently, not three substances, but one substance. Therefore these three are one: one life, one mind, one substance of the human soul, just as there is one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For the soul also possesses three other things within itself, namely understanding, will, and memory. Yet these three are one soul, because understanding does not exist without will, just as the Father never existed without the Son; nor does will exist without understanding, just as the Son does not exist without the Father; neither understanding nor will exists without memory, just as neither the Father nor the Son exists without the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both. So memory also proceeds from understanding and will, because if understanding did not exist, will certainly would not exist; and if understanding and will did not exist, whose memory would there be? Yet these three are one soul. Thus there is one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is well demonstrated in the Gospel when it says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart”—that is, with all your understanding—“and with all your soul”—that is, with all your will—“and with all your mind”—that is, with all your memory.

The soul does not exist without these three; rather, the soul is understanding, the soul is will, the soul is memory—not three souls, but one soul possessing these three dignities within itself, in which it bears the image of God. Therefore each person must carefully consider and recognize in himself the excellence of his original condition and the venerable image of the holy Trinity within himself, and strive with the greatest devotion to venerate the God for whom he was created through nobility of conduct, the practice of good works, and the dignity of his merits, so that he may deserve to attain eternal glory and blessedness before God.

## The faith of Aurelius Augustine concerning the Son of God

[Col. 1414A]

This is the faith which is given in a few words to newly converted Christians to be held in the Creed. These few words are known to the faithful, so that, subdued by believing, they may live rightly; by living rightly, cleanse the heart; and with a cleansed heart understand what they believe.

One God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, invisible, incomprehensible, inviolable, undefiled, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light. He himself is true light, life and truth, good and supreme, and whatever human speech can declare concerning him. Yet these things are given by him so that they may in some manner be spoken. From him are all things, through him are all things, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and all things created through him and in him, as is revealed in both Testaments to the humble and those who seek devoutly. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

“God, attend to my help,” three times [Col. 1414B] with the Gloria and “Lord, have mercy.” The Lord’s Prayer and prayers. “And lead us not…” “I said, Lord, have mercy on me.” “Turn, Lord; how long?” “The eyes of the Lord.” “Let them confess to you, Lord.” “Do not forsake me, Lord.” “Attend to my help, Lord, God of my salvation.” “May it please you, Lord.” “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults.” “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth.” “Do not incline my heart.” “Do not enter into judgment.” “Let my mouth be filled with praise.” “Yet, O Lord, save me; look upon your servants, and let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us; direct hearts today, Lord.” Afterward: “The Lord be with you.”

## Another prayer

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who are the teacher of the saints and direct the paths of the saints, direct an angel of peace with us, who may lead us to the appointed places. Let our company be joyful, so that no enemy may waylay us on our journey. Let the approach of the wicked be far from us, and may the holy one always deign to be our companion. Through the Lord.

## Prayer for travelers

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, deign to be favorable toward our supplications, and send your holy angel with us, who may protect us from every adversity and guard us everywhere in the service of your holy name, so that no enemy may deceive us on our way, but that we may deserve triumph over every foe and the constant assistance of your mercy; so that, fulfilling your commands, we may return safely to our own homes, through you, Christ Jesus, who live with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Almighty and merciful God, we suppliantly invoke your name over us, that, by your merciful generosity, we may walk well in prosperity, and that your name may always be in our thoughts, words, and deeds. May your holy angels accompany us; may the prayers of the archangels, patriarchs, prophets, [Col. 1414D] apostles, martyrs, confessors, and all your saints assist us. Send over us, Lord, the spirit of chastity, kindness, and truth, of mercy and generosity, and of your perpetual charity, light, and peace; may it rule us, protect us, and defend us from every evil, so that by level and straight roads, with complete confidence and without hindrance, we may reach the desired places, and in your holy name return in health and joy to our own dwellings. Through our Lord Jesus.

Lord Jesus Christ, most gentle God, who said that you prefer the repentance of sinners to their death, I humbly beseech your immeasurable mercy concerning all my capital and lesser sins and offenses, by whatever manner I may have been defiled by any of them, or may still be so, or may stand guilty before you, whether in thought, word, or deed, knowingly or unknowingly, willingly or unwillingly, asleep or awake: grant me to make a pure confession before you and before your holy angels, and to undertake true and fruitful repentance and fitting amendment before the day of my departure—whether my sin lies in pride, the mother of all vices; in sacrilege of any kind; in bodily or spiritual homicide; in adultery and every uncleanness of heart and body; or even in love of pleasure; in false testimony, a lying word, or even an idle word; in perjury or an oath; in some theft; in plunder or fraud; in hatred or envy toward any neighbor; or in meditation upon deceit; in evil zeal; in detraction or murmuring; in ill will or unjust or immoderate anger; whether in avarice, the root of all evils; in gluttony or drunkenness and every evil desire and grasping; in boasting or desire for empty glory and every hypocrisy; in acedia or torpor and every laziness and negligence [Col. 1415B] in God’s work; whether in a brother’s supplication or in contempt for him; in unjust judgment or the condemnation of the innocent; or in having allowed my body more labor than I ought, in every transgression of the Lord’s commandments.

Then also concerning my lesser sins, whatever their number or kind, as far as I perceive and understand them, or as many as I am able to enumerate: whenever, prompted by gluttony, I took more food or drink than necessity required; whenever I slept more than I ought; whenever I spoke more, or kept silent more, than was just; whenever I made more disturbance than circumstances required; whenever in any way I consented to iniquity and did not rebuke those committing offenses; whenever I was not afraid to anger the poor who cried out to me, neither heard their groaning nor consoled the sorrowful person according to my strength, ability, and knowledge; whenever I neglected to assist those in need and the less powerful, and practiced almsgiving less or more sparingly than I ought; whenever I did not fast when I was able or ought to have done so; whenever I rose late for prayers and vigils, later than my need required; whenever in the holy church, or in any place or time of prayer, I occupied myself with idle and wicked conversations, and was unstable and wandering in my mind when I ought to have been praying or praising God; whenever I did not minister to those placed in bonds, tribulations, or sickness, nor visit them; whenever I did not recall the quarrelsome and dissenting to harmony; whenever I exasperated my elders, brethren, or any persons more than was proper for me; whenever I ensnared someone with unjust flatteries; whenever I was not afraid to curse others or to blaspheme against others; whenever I was disobedient to God’s commands, or despised the admonitions of a person directing me toward justice or of others who were good; whenever I presumed too much, or remained longer than I ought in unjust contention or obstinacy; whenever I occupied myself with foolish merriment, buffoonery, laughter, and empty joking; whenever I was not afraid to speak insulting words to others or despise others; whenever I repaid, or considered repaying, injuries or insulting words directed against me with vengeance, and retained unjust bitterness in my heart; whenever I loved this world more than God—concerning these things also, and all other evils, greater or lesser, whether I remember them or do not remember them, in whatever things or in whatever manner I have sinned or offended, I confess all alike to you, most merciful Lord God.

You, Lord, through your ineffable mercy, grant me in this present life to make a pure confession of all these things, and true and fruitful repentance, and by your mercy to merit forgiveness here with fitting amendment; and through the intercessions and merits of your saints grant me to attain eternal blessedness—you who remain and live, God reigning forever and ever. Amen.

## Historical Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*)

### Chapter One. The four Albins; Alcuin’s various names, homeland, and parents

[Col. 1415D]

1. At the outset the four Albins must be distinguished, lest anyone fall into error with certain learned men. The first was Albinus, abbot of the monastery of Canterbury, praised in the preface to the *History* of the venerable Bede, and in book V, chapter 21, to whom a letter of Bede is extant. The second was Albinus or Alcuin, with whom we are concerned here, much younger than that first Albinus, who had already departed this life at the time when Bede undertook to write his *History*, as is sufficiently clear from Bede’s words, since Alcuin had not yet been born. Nevertheless, the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius thought them one and the same person, and his authority drew several others into error. The third was Albinus, chamberlain of Pope Leo III, according to Einhard’s *Annals* under the year [Col. 1417A] 799. I add a fourth, Albuinus, a monk of Hersfeld in the eleventh century, whom Christopher Brower confuses with our Albinus or Alcuin, as we shall say below, no. 77.

2. Alcuin had various names. At first, I think, he was called Alcwin, a Saxon designation; afterward, by the softer and Latin name, Albinus, to which the forename Flaccus was added. Thus he not infrequently signs his letters “Flaccus Albinus”; elsewhere he is Alcuinus, and in epigrams Alcuin. It is therefore worthwhile to know what Jacobus Sirmondus astutely observed in his notes on Apollinaris Sidonius: among people of the Middle Ages it became customary for noble or distinguished persons to use several names, while each nevertheless had one proper name, which they always placed last. In this respect the later age departed from the practice and custom of the ancient Romans. For the Romans, while the Republic endured, the proper name was the first one, that is, the forename. Accordingly, Albinus was Alcuin’s proper name and Flaccus his common name; [Col. 1417B] therefore he should not be called Albinus Flaccus, as most write, but Flaccus Albinus. Alcuin himself preserves this order in some of his letters. The same should be observed with Paschasius Radbertus, Servatus Lupus, and other people of the Middle Ages. They are mistaken, then, whether those who assign Paschasius as Radbertus’s proper name, or those who call Lupus Servatus with the order reversed.

3. Alcuin was born in the province of York, “of a noble stock of the English people,” as the author of his Life says. The names of both parents are unknown. He is said to have possessed a large inheritance in his homeland, according to Life, no. 12. He had a brother, Aquila, bishop of Salzburg, or of Juvavum, as is clear from letter 66 (now 102), addressed “To my dearest brother Aquila, bishop”; two other letters of Alcuin, 78 and 104 (now 92 and 36), are likewise extant to him. But who this Aquila finally was—for that name is not found in the catalogues of the archbishops of Salzburg—was shown above under the year 809, where the elevation of Saint Amandus was discussed: namely, that Aquila was Arno, not John, contrary to Brower’s opinion.

### Chapter Two. His education in the monastery of York, his teachers, and the school

4. From childhood Alcuin was educated at York in the monastery attached to the principal basilica. He himself acknowledges this in a letter to the brothers of the church of York in these words: “You cherished the fragile years of my infancy with maternal affection, and with devout patience endured the unruly period of my childhood; by the disciplines of paternal correction you taught me to reach the complete age of manhood, and strengthened me through instruction in the sacred disciplines.”

5. His teachers were not Bede—who perhaps had died before he was born—but Egbert and Aelbert, successive bishops of York. The author of the Life bears witness concerning both. The matter is clear concerning Egbert from the letter to Eanbald, a fragment of which the monk William of Malmesbury reports in book I, chapter 3, of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, and from a fragment of another letter to Charles, where Alcuin calls Egbert his teacher. The former fragment is this: “Praise and glory to God, who has preserved my days in good prosperity, so that I might rejoice in the elevation of my dearest son, who would labor in my place in the church where I had been nurtured and educated, and preside over the treasures of wisdom in which my beloved teacher, Archbishop Egbert, left me an heir.” Thus Alcuin congratulates his pupil Eanbald on his promotion to the see of York.

The fact concerning Aelbert is also established by an anonymous little poem on the bishops of York, which survives in the Appendix of the third century, in which Alcuin is remembered as Aelbert’s pupil. Under these teachers he learned not only the Latin language but also acquired some knowledge of Greek and Hebrew, as appears from his writings, especially letter 27.

[Col. 1418A] 6. In the year 765, when Egbert was near death, he entrusted the library of the church of York to Alcuin, “so that he might preside over the treasures of wisdom,” as is read in the aforementioned letter to Eanbald. Under Bishop Aelbert, who succeeded Egbert, Alcuin became head of the school at York, where he had Ludger, Fridugis, the younger Eanbald, and very many other pupils, as I shall say below. Moreover, he himself, together with the elder Eanbald, advanced the construction of a new building for that church, undertaken by Bishop Aelbert, as the anonymous poet already cited testifies, whose verses are these:

> These two disciples built this temple at their teacher’s command,  
> Eanbald and Alcuin, both  
> Devoting themselves with faithful mind to the work in harmony.

At that time he also presided over a cell situated on the seacoast at the promontories of the Ocean among the Northumbrians. He mentions it in the prologue to the Life of Saint Willibrord and in the poem on Saint Wilgis, in the first part of the third century.

### Chapter Three. Alcuin’s monastic profession is established

[Col. 1418B]

7. Before we follow Alcuin as he came from Britain into Gaul, we must investigate what kind of profession the devout man had: monastic or canonical. Trithemius, Paulus Langius, Wion, and other members of our order count him among our monks; but it must further be seen whether their opinion can be established by the testimony of the ancients, since some more recent writers oppose it. I shall honestly bring forward the foundations of both sides—not those that have so far been advanced, for I have not found the argument yet treated with precision, but those that can be advanced.

8. The arguments that support Alcuin’s monastic profession are of such a kind that they seem to remove every doubt raised against it.

### 9. ARGUMENT I

It is clear from the foregoing [Col. 1418C] that Alcuin was brought up in the household of the principal church of York. No one who has read the letters he wrote to the brothers of York will deny that he was formally attached and bound to that same church. First, the heading of Letter 50 (now 6) must be considered:

“To the brothers of the most holy congregation and sweetest charity of the church of York, Alcuin the deacon, son of that devout mother, etc.”

He was therefore a son of that church, not merely by reason of education or subjection—for in that sense all Christians of any diocese may be called sons of the Mother Church—but by reason of adoption, which he had merited in that household or congregation. For he explains the matter in this way in the body of the letter:

“Let us follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers who begot us in Christ, gathered us into this most sacred fold, and nourished us with the paternal milk of devotion.”

And below:

“Let us always possess fraternal and peaceful charity, so that, as Christ’s sheep, we may feast on the pastures of the same life, remain within the wall of one fold, and call upon God’s mercy for ourselves in one house of prayer.” [Col. 1418D]

And at the end:

“I, your devoted son, never forget you, my fathers.”

From these words it is understood that he belonged to the same fold, household, and family. Indeed, we are compelled to admit this by his long residence in that household, by the custody of the library entrusted to him by Egbert, and by the direction of the school committed to him. Such an office is usually entrusted to outsiders more rarely, especially among monks, and particularly when suitable members of the household are available.

Finally, after the bishop of his church had died, while Alcuin was staying in Gaul, he was summoned to his own church for the election of a new bishop, as appears from Letter 88 (now 54). This proves that he was a cardinal deacon of that same church—that is, a member of its household and intimate circle.

### 10. 

At that time the monastic institution was flourishing in the church of York. Bede calls it a monastery in his letter to Egbert, bishop of that church:

“I remember,” he says, “that last year, when I was staying with you for several days in your monastery for the sake of reading,” [Col. 1419A] etc.

At that time, I do not know whether the name “monastery” had not yet been extended to signify also the residences of canons, as it was in the age of Charlemagne.

Furthermore, the discipline of regular life was preserved in that church, as Alcuin himself testifies in his letter to the brothers of York:

“Be of one mind in every good counsel, united in every discipline of regular life.”

By these words he means monastic discipline. For this reason, in that letter he urges them to humility and obedience, virtues that he repeatedly commends to monks, and he calls the brothers of York servants of God, a designation by which monks are commonly described by those ancient authors:

“It is better,” he says, “for the servants of God to adorn the soul with ecclesiastical morals than to clothe the body with the pompous vanity of lay custom.”

That “regular life” signifies monastic discipline in Alcuin is clear from Letter 89 (now 198), in which he advises Hundruda, a devout Englishwoman, that in the king’s palace the devotion of regular life should be seen in her conduct; and from Letter 99 (now 111), in which he advises the monks of Gothia to be content with the precepts of regular life and never to alter the observance of regular life.

Finally, [Col. 1419B] a poet of uncertain name, Alcuin’s contemporary and fellow student, says in his poem on the bishops of York that the younger Wilfrid was vicedominus and abbot of York.

A vicedominus or vicedomnus was the name of an office in the bishop’s household. Wilfrid was vicedominus and abbot of that same church. I say “abbot” of monks: for in cathedral churches of monks, besides the bishop there was also an abbot, who was chiefly responsible for the care of regular discipline, as is established by clear examples, which I shall cite elsewhere.

What is more, Aelbert, who succeeded Wilfrid after Egbert, is said to have lived as a monk in the monastery of York, taught the liberal arts there, and, after ten years in the episcopate, returned to the same monastery precincts, where he spent the rest of his life. This passage does not seem capable of being understood of any monastery other than that of York. [Col. 1419C]

Finally, Saint Ludger, who had Alcuin as his teacher in that place for three years, is recorded as having been educated in a monastery of monks at York, in the anonymous and nearly contemporary little book On the Life of Ludger.

All this proves abundantly that in Alcuin’s time monks lived in the church of York, and that he himself was enrolled among them—certainly none other than Benedictines. For at that time, as John the deacon of that period testifies in Book IV, chapter 82, of his Life of Gregory the Great, “hardly any monk could be found in those regions who did not observe the rule of Benedict, both in his profession and in his habit.”

And indeed, if Alcuin was a monk, he belonged to no institution other than ours, as the following arguments drawn from his own writings clearly prove. They show that he observed our rule and was especially devoted to it.

### 11. ARGUMENT II

The second argument is that Charlemagne chose him as abbot to correct the morals of the monks of Tours, as we shall say later. Although, during Charlemagne’s reign, secular abbots occupied not a few monasteries, nowhere, if I remember correctly, was the task of restoring monastic discipline entrusted to a secular abbot. On the contrary, it was always the universal opinion that the life of monks could not be reformed except by regular abbots. This is admirably demonstrated by Pope Nicholas I in the privilege granted to the monks of Corbie and by the Fathers of the Council of Trosly in chapter 3.

### 12. ARGUMENT III

The third argument is drawn from the zeal and concern Alcuin displayed in promoting monastic discipline, as is shown by various letters he wrote to monks of different monasteries. Such are Letter 31 (now 29) to the Martinian monks, written before he was abbot; Letter 49 (now 14) to the monks of Wir; Letter 64 (now 52) to the monks of Saint Liudger; Letter 69 (now 90) to the brothers of Lyon—that is, to the monks of the island monastery of Barbara; Letters 71 and 99 (now 111 and 112) to the brothers in the province of the Goths; Letter 78 (now 113) to the brothers of Juvavum, or Salzburg; and Letter 79 (now 20) to the monks of Saint Salvator. [Col. 1420A]

In all these letters he exhorts them to humility, obedience, charity, and the other monastic virtues. Moreover, these letters show that he was very intimate with the monks, whom he habitually calls his brothers. This is especially clear in the case of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, whom he is said to have held as his very dear friend, as well as Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, whom he calls “Antony” in Letter 107 (now 189).

All those whom I have just mentioned professed the rule of Saint Benedict.

### 13. ARGUMENT IV

The fourth argument is closely related and connected with the preceding one: Alcuin reveals a distinctly filial affection for Saint Benedict the Father in more than one place, especially in Epigrams 112 and 171 (now 196 and 254). In the former we read this distich on Saint Benedict:

[Col. 1420B]

> The holy throng of monks throughout the world celebrates you,  
> Whose life was written by your inspiration.

And in the latter:

> Farewell, O Benedict, greatest shepherd of monks.  
> Rule by your prayers those whom you beget by your words.

And below:

> Therefore, aid your own everywhere with your prayers.  
> May your flock grow in number, beloved shepherd.

> Now, as the flock increases in number, the shepherd’s glory grows:  
> Behold, preserve your servants by your merits.

And in the epigram to Maurus, or Rabanus, 178 (now 280):

> While you pour out tears to the Lord in Benedict’s hall,  
> Remember Albinus, your sweet friend.

A disciple of Saint Benedict could scarcely have a different disposition: he would naturally desire the increase of his father’s flock and seek to win the favor and assistance of that same father.

### 14. ARGUMENT V

The fifth argument is drawn from the prayers and confession that Alcuin composed. In the first part of his little book On the Use of the Psalms, shortly before the middle, he says:

“Grant me to follow [Col. 1420C] and imitate the footsteps of your beloved Father, my Benedict.”

And in the second part, when describing the prayer of monks, he goes through all the degrees of humility established by Saint Benedict.

In the first part mentioned above, where he treats of confession, he has these words:

“I continually despise your commandments; at every moment I violate my promises, by which I vowed that I would observe the holy rule.”

And in the second part:

“I sought a monastery and undertook the monastic life; but wretched that I am, I am always entangled in various forms of frivolity.”

### 15. 

“But,” you object, “Alcuin says these things in the person of the monks of Tours, for whose benefit he was dictating them.”

Let it be so: then at least he presided over monks who followed the rule of Saint Benedict, among whom he himself lived no differently from one of them.

### 16. 

[Col. 1420D]

But in another confession, or profession of faith, in which Alcuin speaks in his own person, he expressly professes himself to be a monk. The learned Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius of the Society of Jesus published this Confession, divided into four parts. In part II, chapter 9, of that Confession he prays:

“Grant me, most frail as I am, to imitate the footsteps of the blessed monks, my fathers.”

And in part IV, chapter 16:

“After putting on this monastic garment, I committed many things in heart, word, and deed.”

And below:

“Woe to me, most wretched, who bear the false name of monk, doing nothing worthy of this name and habit.”

From these words it is clear that Alcuin wore the garment and habit of a monk together with the name.

In part IV, chapter 15, he prays that he may never be exalted by the necessary services of attendants or by the respect shown him by his brothers. This corresponds to the objection made by Elipandus against Alcuin, namely, that he had “twenty thousand servants.”

And in chapter 17:

“I have lost,” he says, “the place of beloved solitude, the companion of sorrow, quiet, and penitence, which I have always loved from my earliest age. Therefore my soul is placed in great anguish and sorrow, ignorant of your judgment concerning it, because I have not been able to find again the secret of my accustomed quiet and the fitting leisure for turning toward you—what I once lost through carelessness. Yet this I still desire, sigh for, and seek; but because of my sins I cannot find it.” [Col. 1421A]

These words plainly show that the author was a certain monk who was an abbot and father of monks, surrounded by a great multitude of servants, repeatedly dragged from the monastery into the turbulent affairs of the world, and longing to be enclosed again in the solitude of the monastery, free from secular business. All this applies to Alcuin, whose Letter 23 (now 129) contains precisely the same sentiments.

Moreover, in part IV, chapter 15, of this Confession, Alcuin asks God to grant him the grace to fulfill what our rule commands, namely, “always to love lowliness and the lowest condition.” These words correspond exactly to the words of the Benedictine Rule, chapter 7, sixth degree of humility: that the monk should be content with every low and inferior condition.

That this Confession was made by Alcuin in his own person is proved by the testimonies just cited and by what the author says of himself in part I, chapter 30, where he writes:

“I considered it necessary to address this little discourse to myself alone,” etc.

Read the beginning of part IV. I know that some doubt whether this Confession is Alcuin’s; we shall refute their reasons for doubting below.

[Note: [Col. 1421D] See Mabillon’s Dissertation on Alcuin’s Confession of Faith, above, col. 1004. EDIT.]

### 17. 

These are the principal arguments by which Alcuin’s monastic profession can be established. Nothing is opposed to them by the fact that in his letters Alcuin does not style himself a monk, but a levite or deacon. For if this consideration proved anything, it would equally prove that he was not an abbot, since, unless I am mistaken, he nowhere prefixes that title to his letters.

The custom of those times was, as I have often said, that each person was called by the designation of the rank in which he was enrolled, while the title of monk or abbot was often omitted. This is why Alcuin is always called a levite by the ancients, sometimes an abbot, and more rarely a monk.

I find no one older who gives him the name of monk than Hariulf, the monk of Centula, who, toward the end of the eleventh century, calls Alcuin an abbot, levite, and monk in Book II, chapter 11, of the Chronicle of Centula. [Col. 1421C]

### 18. 

Some objections of greater weight may be drawn from the Life prefixed above.

[Note: [Col. 1422D] Volume I of our edition. EDIT.]

### 19. OBJECTION I

The first objection is that, in his prologue, the author proposes the life of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, for imitation by monks, and the life of Alcuin for imitation by canons, in these words:

“Let us follow the footsteps of those who, as they themselves proved with absolute certainty, lived together with them in their own time and evidently pleased Christ—namely, Benedict, worthy of imitation in all things by monks, and Alcuin by canons.”

### 20. 

These words certainly prove that Alcuin’s life was more common and more suited to canons than Benedict’s, if by “canons” the author means secular canons.

But perhaps he called monks of a milder and less strict way of life “canons,” such as the monks of Tours and Saint-Denis, some of whom called themselves monks and others canons. Hence [Col. 1421D] Charlemagne writes in a letter to the Martinian monks:

“Whether you are called canons or monks,” etc.

Ardo describes these monks of a less strict way of life in his book On the Life of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane. Louis Augustus appointed Benedict “over all the monasteries in his kingdom, so that he might display the salutary norm to everyone.” Ardo says:

“For there were certain monasteries observing canonical institutions but ignorant of the precepts of the rule. Obedient to the emperor’s command, he visited the monasteries of each one, not once or twice but many times, displaying the teachings of the rule, examining it with them point by point, confirming what was known and explaining what was unknown. Thus, by God’s providence, almost all the monasteries situated in Aquitaine received the regular form.”

These words plainly show that at that time there were monks of a looser way of life who observed canonical institutions—that is, those of canons—and neglected the monastic rule. Alcuin is proposed as an example for them, while Benedict is proposed for monks of a stricter way of life.

The Fathers of the Council of Tours, held in 813, compel these abbots and monks of a looser way of life, in chapter 25, “to return to their former state,” especially those abbots who “seemed to conduct themselves among their own more canonically than monastically.” [Col. 1422A]

While Alcuin was compelled to remain at the king’s court, his life was indeed more canonical than monastic. Later, when he was restored to himself and Charlemagne granted him permission to withdraw to the monastery of Tours, he returned again to the laws of a stricter monastic rule. Hence, in number 14 of the preceding book, it is said that his subsequent life was not inferior to the monastic life.

It may also be answered that by “canons” the author means monks of cathedral churches, such as existed in England, Germany, and even Rome. The commonly circulated Anastasius calls these “canonical monks” in his account of Pope Gregory IV.

The old translator of Hugo of Reutlingen, cited by Goldast in his notes on chapter 4 of Ekkehard the Younger, says:

“In the course of time certain Alemanni, and especially canons of the Order of Saint Benedict, who [Col. 1422B] [practiced] musical chant,” etc.

Perhaps, therefore, Alcuin is proposed as an example to monks of this kind. As I have said, his life was not so severe and rigid as Benedict’s, although both were monastic.

### 21. OBJECTION II

The second objection is found in these words, with which the author, praising Alcuin in chapter 3 of the Life for his religiously ordered life, then exclaims:

“O truly a monk, a monk without a vow!”

### 22. 

I answer that there really were at that time monks without a monk’s vow, although they wore the monastic habit. Thus Ludger—if, indeed, his case can be taken as an example—after having worn the monastic habit for at least twenty years, later became a bishop and “ceased to wear the cowl, because he had not made the promise to observe the rule of monks.”

Or certainly Alcuin may be called “a monk without a monk’s vow” because he had not embraced that stricter form of monastic life, but a softer and more moderate one.

Finally—and this interpretation seems preferable to me—Alcuin is not absolutely called “a monk without a monk’s vow,” [Col. 1422C] but is so called with reference to the time when he was still a boy, as is clear to anyone who reads the entire passage: that is, the time when his age did not yet permit him to profess monastic vows.

You will reply that Sigulf and Fridugis, Alcuin’s disciples, who were educated in the school of the church of York, wore the canonical habit.

Let it be so; but it is not established that they were formally attached to the principal church of York. Sigulf is certainly said to have been guardian of the church of the city of York; by this title I think the rector of one of the city’s churches is meant.

Perhaps the congregation in the church of York was mixed, consisting of both monks and canons, as was also the case in certain monasteries. Unless you prefer to say that in that church what Adam writes concerning Bremen took place: clerics [Col. 1422D] wore the canonical habit but lived according to a monastic rule.

### 23. OBJECTION III

[Col. 1422D]

The third objection may be drawn from chapter 8, where the author says that Alcuin wished “to leave the world,” having requested from Charlemagne permission “to lead a monastic life” in the monastery of Fulda “according to the rule of Saint Benedict.” But he was compelled to remain among the Martinian monks, where “his life was not inferior to the monastic life.”

“Therefore,” you say, “he was not truly a monk, but only in aspiration, affection, and conduct.”

### 24. 

There is some truth in these statements, but some points are obscure and require explanation. What the author says—that Alcuin wished “to leave the world”—is obscure, since by “world” he must have meant secular occupations, not the world itself, to which Alcuin had renounced his allegiance from childhood.

This explanation is suggested by Letter 23 (now [Col. 1423A] 131) to Charlemagne, which contains these words:

“For nearly five years now, I call God to witness, I have considered withdrawing from secular occupations with a sincere heart; but, by the counsel of your pious foresight, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin, God granting that this might benefit the Catholic faith and the ecclesiastical order. Yet the desire of my former intention has not departed from my heart, as I already declared to your piety last year.”

And below:

“I desire, without any doubt, to live or rest among the brothers faithfully serving God in the church of Saint Martin.”

Two things must be observed here. First, Alcuin had considered withdrawing from the secular occupations in which he was entangled at court. Second, he wished to spend the remainder of his life in quiet—not at Fulda, but among the brothers of the church of Saint Martin.

This he eventually obtained, fulfilling his desire, as we shall say later.

The substance of the answer is this: repeatedly distracted by the affairs of the court, Alcuin longed for withdrawal—not in order to leave the world, but to leave secular occupations; not in order to assume the name of monastic life for the first time, but to resume his former way of life in its entirety, freed from the business of the world. [Col. 1423B]

### 25. 

These are the observations I have been able to make in support of Alcuin’s monastic profession. If they seem too lengthy to some, they may freely pass them over as they wish. The fame of the man and the necessity of my office certainly required this diligence of me.

## CHAPTER IV. Alcuin’s Arrival in Gaul and His Achievements

### 26. 

Learned men have hitherto admitted only one arrival of Alcuin in Gaul; it is necessary to distinguish two or three.

If that Albinus, the favorite of King Charles, whom the commonly circulated Anastasius says was sent with Abbot Wulfard to Pope Hadrian in the eleventh indiction—that is, in the year 773—is the same person as Alcuin, then it must be said that Alcuin came to Gaul and attached himself to Charles before that year.

Certainly Sigebert testifies in his Chronicle [Col. 1423C] and in his book On Illustrious Men that Alcuin was called the emperor’s favorite. If this is established, three arrivals of Alcuin in Gaul must be admitted.

### 27. 

For in the year 780, when he was returning from Rome after being sent there to obtain the pallium for Eanbald, his successor as bishop of York after Aelbert’s death, he met Charlemagne at Parma. Charlemagne invited him into Francia, as we understand from the earlier Life.

Letter 23 (now 131) seems to belong here. In it he praises Charles for having endeavored to summon “lovers of wisdom from different parts of the world”:

“Among whom,” he says, “you took care to summon even me, the least servant of that same holy wisdom, from the farthest ends of Britain.”

Unless perhaps this should be referred to Alcuin’s final journey to Gaul, which he undertook at divine prompting—though I do not know whether also at Charles’s urging.

In the earlier arrival, however, which we are discussing here, I think the event mentioned by Alcuin in Letter 15 (now 101) occurred: [Col. 1423D]

“When I went to Rome as a young man, and stayed for several days in Pavia, the royal city, a certain Jew named Julius held a disputation with Master Peter”—namely Peter of Pisa, Charlemagne’s teacher of grammar.

Alcuin, detained in Gaul in this way, remained for some time at the palace. Then it happened that King Charles, who, as Einhard testifies, “had listened to the aged deacon Peter of Pisa in learning grammar,” had as his teacher in the other disciplines “Albinus, surnamed Alcuin, likewise a deacon from Britain, a man of Saxon origin and learned in every field, from whom he devoted much time and labor especially to learning rhetoric, dialectic, and above all astronomy.”

Thus Charles not undeservedly calls him “my most beloved teacher in Christ” in a fragment of a letter quoted in Alcuin’s Letter 6 (now 162), whatever Baronius may say to the contrary.

The verses of Epigram 199 (now 115), addressed to the brothers of York and urging them to compose verses, refer to this: [Col. 1424A]

> For such gifts please your Father,  
> Who now makes the noble arts resound in royal ears  
> And leads one who follows through the meadows of the Fathers,  
> Reigning beneath the splendid bough of lofty wisdom.

At that time Alcuin formed a friendship with Homer, or Angilbert, and wrote Letter 42 (now 26) to him when he was already primicerius of the palace of Pippin, king of Italy, around the year 783.

At approximately the same time he wrote Letter 93 (now 44) to Damoetas, or Ricolf, who had set out with King Charles on the Saxon expedition, before Ricolf succeeded Lull to the see of Mainz in 787.

He is also said to have written a letter to Ludger, who was then staying at Monte Cassino, at Charlemagne’s command, to recall him to Francia, according to Book I, chapter 14, of the second Life of Saint Liudger. If this is true, Alcuin was in Gaul in the year 786.

### 28. 

After spending some time at the palace, Alcuin returned to his homeland, [Col. 1424B] as appears from number 13 of the Life. This seems to have occurred in the year 790, when the letter to Colcu, a lector in Scotland, was written, as I shall prove later in number 87.

Returning from Gaul, he distributed various gifts to churches and monasteries, both on his own behalf and on behalf of King Charles, whom he had recently left. He indicates that disagreement had arisen between Kings Charles and Offa, “so that navigation between the two sides was forbidden.” Then he adds:

“There are those who say that we are to be sent to those regions for the sake of peace.”

We learn the cause of this quarrel from chapter 15 of the published edition of the Chronicle of Fontenelle. There it is said that Charlemagne “requested in marriage” for his namesake son the daughter of King Offa. But when Offa refused unless Berta, daughter of Charlemagne, were given in marriage to his son, Charles, angered by this, ordered “that no one from the island and people of Britain should reach the coast of the Ocean Sea in Gaul for the sake of trade. But this was prevented by the admonition and supplication of Abbot Gervold.”

### 29. 

[Col. 1424C] After three years, having obtained permission from his bishop, Alcuin returned to Francia by divine prompting, to oppose the error of Elipandus and Felix, which was spreading within the Church.

Thus he relates the matter himself in the preface to his books Against Elipandus:

“By divine dispensation, as I believe, commanding it, I came when summoned to Charles, the glorious ruler and king of this realm, worthy to be named with every honor, just as a certain most holy man, endowed with the spirit of prophecy, had foretold in my homeland that this was God’s will. Moreover, my venerable and wholly God-devoted teacher had given me this command: if anywhere I heard new sects arise contrary to apostolic teachings, I should immediately devote my entire self to the defense of the Catholic faith.”

This teacher of Alcuin was Aelbert, as appears from number 11 of the Life.

### 30. 

Alcuin himself indicates the time of this second arrival in Francia in Book I Against Elipandus: [Col. 1424D]

“Before I had come to Francia at the command of that most wise king Charles, this same sect of your error, while that glorious prince presided, was debated in the presence of Felix, whom you are accustomed to praise greatly, then the defender of your party, in the most celebrated place called Regensburg.”

But according to the Annals of an unknown author, to which the monk of Angoulême bears witness in his Life of Charles, “in the year 792 the Felician heresy was first condemned at Regensburg, although its author himself denied it.”

Therefore, since Alcuin took part in the Council of Frankfurt, assembled against the same heresy in the year 794, it must be said that he returned to Francia toward the end of 792 or in the following year.

### 31. 

Speaking of this journey, Roger of Hoveden writes:

“In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 792, Charles, king of the Franks, sent to Britain a synodal book sent to him from Constantinople. In that book, alas, what grief! many incongruous things and things contrary to the true faith were found, especially the assertion, [Col. 1425A] confirmed unanimously by nearly all the Eastern teachers, no fewer than three hundred bishops or more, that images ought to be adored—a practice which the Church of God utterly abhors. Against this Albinus wrote a letter wonderfully supported by the authority of the divine Scriptures, and brought it, together with the same book, to the king of the Franks on behalf of our bishops and princes.”

## CHAPTER V. Alcuin’s Presence at Two Councils

### 32. 

After returning to Francia, the devout man attended the Council of Frankfurt in 794. His work there had such influence that the Fathers admitted him to share in their votes and issued a decree, the last of the council, [Col. 1425B] in these words:

“Charles also urged that the holy synod should deign to receive Alcuin into its fellowship and prayers, since he was a man learned in ecclesiastical doctrine. Accordingly, the entire synod agreed to the lord king’s admonition and received him into their fellowship and prayers.”

### 33. 

How much labor he undertook to destroy the heresy concerning Christ’s adoption taught by the bishops Elipandus and Felix is shown by the seven books he published Against Felix. It is also shown by the four books published Against Elipandus, which, as he himself says in Book I Against Elipandus, “were read and approved in the presence of the lord king and his priests.”

### 34. 

He then mentions the Council of Aachen, convened in 799 after the Council of Urgel:

“But Felix himself,” he says, “in the thirty-second year of the aforesaid glorious ruler, having been summoned, came of his own will to the palace at Aachen. There, in the presence of the lord king and his nobles and the priests of God, he was rationally heard and truly convicted; and, giving glory to God and confessing the true faith, he returned with his disciples who were present there at that time to the peace of Catholic unanimity.”

This occurred through the work and disputation of Alcuin, who convicted Felix at that assembly, [Col. 1425C] as appears from chapter 7 of the Life, although he modestly concealed the fact.

## CHAPTER VI. His Administration of Various Monasteries, Properly Undertaken

### 35. 

[Col. 1425D] Charles placed him in charge of various monasteries in order to retain him in Gaul by this kind of bond. For shortly after his last arrival in Francia, “Charles gave him two monasteries: Bethlehem, also called Ferrières, and Saint-Loup near Troyes,” as stated in chapter 6 of the Life.

He also added the cell of Saint Judoc and the monastery of Saint Martin. The time at which Alcuin took charge of the latter, and what he accomplished there, must be explained.

### 36. 

Alcuin speaks of the administration of the Martinian monastery entrusted to him in Letter 23 (now 129):

“For nearly five years now, I call God to witness, I have considered withdrawing from secular occupations with a sincere heart; but, by the counsel of your pious foresight, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin.”

This letter was written when Charlemagne was returning from Italy. In it Alcuin says that he had been anxious about Charles’s return from Italy and that, at last, although late, he heard the desired cry of those hastening toward him:

“He is coming now, now he has crossed the Alps.”

This must be assigned to the year 801, when Charles, having been called emperor, returned from Rome to this region.

It cannot be referred to his penultimate journey across the Alps, which occurred in 786, since Alcuin was not placed over the abbey of Saint Martin until after the Council of Frankfurt. Since the event therefore occurred five years before 801, it must be said to have taken place in 796.

### 37. 

The Sainte-Marthes make Alcuin the successor of Garulf as abbot of the Martinian monastery. [Col. 1426A] Yet it is established that he succeeded not Garulf but Itherius.

In the diploma that Charles granted Alcuin for the monastery of Cormaric, Charles calls Itherius the former abbot of that monastery, as we shall see later in number 56.

The same is proved by a diploma granted by Pippin, king of Aquitaine, to Abbot Fridugis, preserved by Labbe in his Curious Miscellanies. In it, “Itherius, formerly abbot,” is said to have given the estate of Marciac in precarious tenure to Erlald, steward of Louis Augustus; and afterward “the lord Alcuin [in the printed editions, incorrectly, Alcrinus], successor and rector of that same monastery,” is said to have confirmed it to the aforesaid Erlald at the request of Louis.

This is the Itherius to whom Alcuin, when he lay dying, addressed Letter 75 (now 32), headed “To Itherius, my most beloved Father,” in which he consoles and encourages him in that final struggle.

### 38. 

In this office the blameless man accomplished many admirable things. He recalled the monks—some of whom called themselves canons and others monks—from a looser way of life to religious discipline. He introduced a community of monks into the monastery of Cormaric, whose construction had been begun by Abbot Itherius. He established a hospice for travelers in the district of Troyes, and an oratory [Col. 1426B] at Tours. Finally, he opened public schools in that city.

All these matters must be discussed individually.

## CHAPTER VII. The Condition of the Monastery of Saint Martin under Alcuin

### 39. 

It is established from a letter of Ibbô, bishop of Tours, granting the privilege of immunity to the brothers of that place, “where the monks appear to live according to the rule of Saint Benedict,” that the monastery distinguished by the name and tomb of Saint Martin was subject to Benedictine monks in the seventh century.

In the little book On the Life of Saint Pardulf, abbot of Waractum, written in the time of Charles, surnamed Martel, mention is made of Abbot Audeland and the monks of that same place. Likewise, in chapter 9 of the published edition of the Chronicle of Fontenelle, [Col. 1426C] “Teutsind, Father of the monastery of Saint Martin,” is praised. The same work, under the year 834, says of him:

“He used to say to the brothers of the church of Tours: ‘Unless you correct your life and morals, I shall bring my provost Erinharius from Fontenelle here, and he will teach you to plow your furrows straight.’”

Whether Teutsind carried this out is uncertain. But it is clear that even under Charlemagne the discipline of regular life there had become so lax that some called themselves canons and others monks, as is evident from a manuscript letter of Charles written to them on behalf of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, who was reclaiming a certain accused man who had taken refuge at the tomb of Saint Martin.

From this we understand that what the letters of Louis Augustus attest concerning the monastery of Saint-Denis had also occurred in this monastery: some monks, forgetful of their profession—or at least repentant of it—preferred to call themselves canons, while others called themselves monks, adopting different kinds of clothing and ways of life according to the inclination of each one.

This was the principal reason that moved Charlemagne, after the death of Abbot Itherius, to send Alcuin there to correct their morals. Before this time Alcuin had already written Letter 31 (now 23) to them, exhorting them to charity, obedience, and humility:

“These three,” he says, “will open the gates of heaven to monks.”

He had prefaced this by saying that “it is not praiseworthy to imitate the habit of the Fathers in clothing without observing the commandments they established for those serving God.” [Col. 1426D]

Then he asks them not to consider him “presumptuous” for writing these things to them:

“Charity,” he says, “compelled me to burst forth in this letter.”

These words sufficiently indicate that he wrote the letter before he obtained the administration of the place.

After he had acquired that office, he addressed to them a letter On the Confession of Sins, headed:

“To the most beloved sons in Christ and youths of good hope who appear to serve the Lord Jesus in the church of the supreme pontiff and great protector, blessed Martin, and who are instructed by ecclesiastical teachers in the Lord God.”

He judged—and rightly—that this was the first path of return to God.

Nor was his labor fruitless, as is proved by Letter 23 (now 129) to Charles, which contains these words:

“I desire without any doubt, God in his mercy permitting it, to live or rest among the brothers faithfully serving God in the church of Saint Martin.”

Source/review notes: Documentary lacunae, conjectures, variant forms, and the esophica/theosophica uncertainty remain explicit.

[Col. 1427A] **40.** I believe I have discovered convincing evidence that monks remained in that place while Alcuin was alive. Itherius, abbot of Martinianus, subscribed, together with several monks of his monastery, to the principal document concerning the condition of the monastery of Cormaricus in the twenty-third year of King Charles. Of these, those who were priests or deacons, omitting—as was then customary—the title “monk,” appended their respective orders, “priest” or “deacon”; those below these ranks subscribed as “monks.”

After Itherius’s death, Alcuin introduced monks into the monastery of Cormaricus, having obtained Charles’s privilege “that that place should not be removed from the authority of Saint Martin, but that monks dwelling there should live fully under the rule of Saint Benedict and receive protection and assistance from the abbots of the monastery of Saint Martin,” by whom they were to be governed. The charter was issued in the twenty-second year of Charles’s reign, that is, in the year 800.

Yet it was far removed from the religion both of that excellent prince and of Alcuin, as well as from the customs of that age, that monasteries of monks should from the outset be subjected to canons. Add that, shortly before he was placed in charge of the monastery of Tours, Alcuin called the Martinian monks “monks” in the letter already cited in no. 39.

Finally, Alcuin’s successor and disciple Fridugisus is listed among the enrolled brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall, not with the canons but with his monks, in the following manner: “Names of the brothers from Tours: Fridegisus, abbot; Flodomarus, monk; Gisledramnus, monk; Ansegarius, monk; Adilleodus, monk; Helmoinus,” and so forth, in Goldast. It is therefore clear that, under the abbot Fridugisus or Fridegisus, monks continued for some time in that place.

Consequently, the statement in the Tours chronicle is false: “In the year 796 King Charles, by the authority of Pope Hadrian, established canons in the church of blessed Martin and appointed Alcuin, his teacher, over them.” Certainly Alcuin was placed in charge of that monastery in that very year, not to govern canons substituted for monks, but to lead the monks, who were too lax, back to a proper manner of life. [Col. 1427C] At the time when Charles wrote to them on behalf of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, some of them presented themselves as monks and others as canons; at that time the venerable Alcuin was in charge of the place.

**41.** Nevertheless, I believe that canons were substituted for the monks under the governance of Abbot Fridulgisus. Certainly, before the middle of the ninth century there were already canons in the church of Saint Martin. This is clear from the testament of Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, who in the year 835 “bequeathed one pound to the Martinian canons,” and from the history of the translation of Saint Martin, written by Saint Odo, in which the canons of Saint Martin are said to have carried the sacred body out of the city of Tours in 853. Audradus Modicus calls them “the clerics of Lord Martin,” and in a charter granted by Charles the Bald to Abbot Hugh in the thirtieth year of his reign, A.D. 860, they are called “the venerable canons of the aforesaid monastery,” as recorded by Labbe in *Curious Miscellanies*.

From this I conclude that the canons succeeded the monks in that place under Abbot Fridugisus; but how this happened remains to be investigated.

[Col. 1427D] **42.** Saint Odo the abbot relates the matter as follows, in John the monk’s third book of his *Life*, chapter 1:

“Some years ago, while a monastic community still remained at the church of blessed Martin, which is at Tours, they began to abandon their proper manner and customs and to corrupt their way of life and profession according to their own wills. For, abandoning their native and customary garments, they began to wear brightly colored and flowing cucullae and tunics adorned with cloaks. The shoes with which they clothed their feet were also so shell-shaped and polished that they seemed to have taken on the appearance of glass. For the nocturnal praises, lest they should strike their foot against anything, they rose with the light of day. They did many things of this kind, and many others like them, against the rights of the rule.

When God had determined to put an end to these things, one night, while all were sleeping and one of them remained awake during that same hour, he saw two men enter the dormitory. One of them was holding a sword in his hand, while the other commanded him, pointing them out one by one with these words: ‘Strike this one, and strike that one.’ When he wished to attack the man who was watching these things, the latter cried out and adjured him, saying: ‘I adjure you by the living God: do not kill me.’ Immediately the executioner withdrew his sword, and he alone escaped from them all.”

**43.** This is Saint Odo’s account, which the monk John received from his own mouth. It ought certainly to possess great authority, both because of the gravity of the holy man and because he was nearly contemporary with the event.

**44.** Ademar, a monk of Ecolisma, explains the matter somewhat differently in his *Chronicle*, where he speaks of Charles the Bald and of the monks’ entrance into the monastery of Saint Martial:

“At that time,” he says, “the monks of Saint Martin at Tours, compelled by no one, before the body of that same saint, cast aside the monastic habit and put on the canonical habit, confirming this with solemn oaths over the body of blessed Martin. After they had been refreshed with meat, they were immediately struck by a plague, and when morning came they were found dead in their beds, all of them, from the greatest to the least; and from then on the place itself was inhabited by canons.” [Col. 1428B]

A most violent plague afflicted Gaul in the years 819 and 823, according to Einhard. Perhaps this disaster occurred in one or the other of those years.

**45.** I infer that Fridugisus readily assisted this change from a similar act that he perpetrated in the monastery of Sithiu, over which he was also in charge. For when he became abbot of the churches of Saint Bertin and Saint Omer in 820,

“seeing that the whole abbey had been assigned to the use of so many monks—namely, one hundred and thirty monks dwelling between the two monasteries—and that nothing had been set apart for his own pleasures, blinded by the dart of avarice, at the principal establishment of Saint Bertin, where eighty-three monks served the Lord, he retained sixty rather for human praise than for the love of God; the rest, men of stricter life, whom he thought would not consent to his perversity, he expelled from the monastery. In the monastery of Saint Omer also, where forty monks lived according to the rule, he appointed thirty canons. And because he was a canon, he lived secularly with the canons in the monastery of Saint Omer.”

This is taken from the anonymous author of Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Bertin*, chapter 6. In the following chapter the author says that Fridugisus died “in the fourteenth year of his administration,” namely, in 834. From this it is probable that Fridugisus was, if not the author, at least the supporter and approver of this kind of change in the monastery of Saint Martin.

**46.** How the monastery was organized after that change is reported by Philip, dean; Rainaldus, treasurer; and the entire chapter of Saint Martin of Tours, in a letter written to Philip, archbishop of Cologne, concerning the life of Saint Martin and some of his miracles:

“After many years had passed, the church of Saint Martin underwent a change both of order and of custom. Since the monks, either through sloth or because of the disturbance caused by those who frequented the church, did not continue their duties fully, canons were substituted by the princes of the land. The three hundred prebends that then existed were reduced to one hundred and fifty. And to moderate that tedious and intolerable labor, those continuous and interminable alternations of the singers were divided into fixed and orderly hours, as is done in other churches.

As for the revenues and treasures of the church itself, a very large portion was cut off from it. With this portion three communities were built and dedicated, to serve at the discretion of the canons. All these things still endure today in the name of Christ.”

They wrote this approximately in the year 1145. I found this letter, however, in a manuscript among other letters of Wibert, abbot of Gembloux, who was flourishing at that time.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Schools at Tours and Elsewhere; Other Actions of Alcuin at Tours

**47.** Alcuin not only corrected the conduct of the monks of Tours, but also opened public schools there, which people flocked to from every direction.

“I, your Flaccus,” he says in his first letter (now 43) to Charles, “in accordance with your exhortation and good will, strive to serve some the sacred honey of the Scriptures beneath the roofs of Saint Martin; I endeavor to intoxicate others with the ancient wine of the old disciplines; I shall begin to nourish others with the fruits of grammatical subtlety; I desire to illuminate some with the order of the stars, like the painted roof of a great house; becoming many things to many people, so that I may educate the greatest number for the advancement of the holy Church of God and for the adornment of your imperial kingdom.”

Alcuin addresses these words to David, the name by which he usually called Charlemagne.

**48.** Alcuin is also said to have maintained schools elsewhere, namely at Rome and in the monasteries of Fulda, Saint Gall, and Saint Medard, if we believe Trithemius and several others. Altfrid, in Book I of *The Life of Saint Liudger*, no. 9, praises Alcuin, “who in the time of the younger Charles exercised the office of teacher at Tours and in Francia.” These words sufficiently show that he taught somewhere besides Tours, though the places are not so certain.

**49.** I am certain that he taught letters neither at Rome nor at Fulda nor in the monastery of Saint Gall. How incompatible a Roman residence would have been with his wishes is shown by his thirteenth letter (now 109) to Charles, who, when he was about to travel to Rome in 800, had tried to drag him along with him.

“But concerning this also,” he says, “which you wished to reproach me for—that I prefer the smoke-blackened roofs of Tours to the gilded arches of Rome—I know that your prudence has read: ‘It is better to sit in the corner of a roof than in a common house with a quarrelsome woman.’ And, to speak peaceably, iron harms the eyes more than smoke. For, content with the smoky roofs of Tours, through the providence of your goodness I remain in peace by God’s gift; but Rome, which began in fraternal discord, has not ceased to retain its implanted poison of dissension to this day.” [Col. 1429C]

Those who thought that he had taught at Rome seem to have been misled by Rabanus Maurus’s poem prefixed to his books *On the Cross*. The poem is entitled *Albinus’s Intercession for Maurus*. Since the poem is dedicated to Saint Martin, they referred it to the Roman pontiff.

This was Trithemius’s opportunity for error in Book I of *The Life of Rabanus*. There he praises Alcuin:

“who was the first among the Gauls and Italians, having presided over public monastic schools at Rome, Paris, and Soissons, to write many works for the common benefit and to train many highly learned students in every branch of knowledge. To this venerable man, who at that time was guardian and minister of the Lateran church in the city of Rome and presided over public monastic schools, Abbot Ratgar of Fulda sent Rabanus.”

In writing this, Trithemius undoubtedly had in mind the following verses of the aforementioned poem:

> Holy bishop of God, living through your merits forever,  
> Receive with pious mind the cause that we bring.  
> For when I was the humble guardian and minister  
> Of this church, reading its sacred teachings,  
> I taught this boy with the divine nourishment of the Word,  
> With ethical admonitions and studies of wisdom.

These verses, which Rabanus dedicated in Alcuin’s person to Saint Martin—whose church Alcuin, that is, the abbot, was guardian and minister—Trithemius referred to the Roman pontiff and the Lateran church.

**50.** Although Alcuin maintained schools most diligently at Caesarodunum of Tours, he nevertheless came repeatedly to the court with his pupils when invited by Charlemagne. Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, refers to this in Book III, poem 3, addressed to Angilbert, where he speaks of the members of the court:

> The aged Flaccus leaves the city, accompanied by boys;  
> When the full light returns, then he himself returns home.

[Col. 1430A] And at the end:

> When Flaccus comes, accompanied by boys and by songs,  
> Then you may hope for better things.

Since this stay at court was burdensome to the holy man, he often asked Charles to release him from it. At last he obtained this, as we shall later relate. Moreover, after his earlier arrival in Gaul, he was constantly at the palace in order to instruct Charles in various disciplines; see above, no. 27.

**51.** This was the reason why the origin of the University of Paris was attributed to Alcuin. Since the court was frequently at Paris, where Alcuin taught letters, he came to be called the founder of the University of Paris, because he had been placed in charge of the palace schools. Certainly he encouraged Charles—if he was not himself the originator—to complete a new Athens in Francia, in Letter 10; by both his words and his writings he kindled the minds of the Franks toward literary studies.

**52.** On another occasion he spent time with his pupils in a little cell in the wilderness. This cell seems to me to have been none other than the monastery of Cormaricus, of which I shall speak later. He also performed a particularly useful service for the learned at Charles’s court: he caused writers thereafter to observe commas and points, which had long been neglected. This is clear from Letter 15 (now 101) and Poem 126 (now 67).

**53.** Finally, it is evident from Epigrams 219 and 221 that he restored the sacred buildings at the monastery of Tours. The latter reads as follows:

> Albinus came from the far-off land of the poet,  
> Sent to these regions by illustrious Britain.  
> Charles, renowned king of this world, received him,  
> Both because of his devotion to sacred wisdom  
> And because of his affection.  
> He ordered the long-ruined roofs of the chambers,  
> As you see, reader, to be wholly renewed throughout the court;  
> Establishing these places as most suitable for sacred relics,  
> So that the resting places of the saints might possess fitting honors—  
> As it is right on earth to venerate the holy men  
> Whom God has willed to reign forever in heaven.

## CHAPTER IX. The Introduction of Monks into the Monastery of Cormaricus

[Col. 1430C]

**54.** After Alcuin had restored monastic discipline, as best he could, in the monastery of Tours and had established literary studies there, he also thought it his responsibility to introduce monks observing our rule into the monastery of Cormaricus (Cormeri), begun by his predecessor Itherius. Such a thought would scarcely have occurred to a man who preferred the canonical life to the monastic.

**55.** Itherius, in his document concerning the condition of this monastery, drawn up in the twenty-third year of Charles’s reign, on the seventh day before the Ides of February—that is, in the year 791—says that he had built a church in which he constructed three altars:

“where,” he says, “we placed relics of the holy apostles: on the senior altar, that is, the principal altar, those of Saint Paul; on another, those of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles; and on the third, those of Saint Martin.”

He also says that, at the dedication of the aforementioned basilica, he transferred certain estates “to the aforesaid holy place, which is called the Cell of Saint Paul, and which from ancient times until now has been called Cormaricus.”

From these and other documents, Joachim Perionius, the singular ornament of that place, rightly refutes the fiction of those who claim that Cormaricus was so named from *cor moerens*, “a grieving heart.” They say that this phrase was used by the monk who alone is said to have escaped the slaughter carried out by an angel in the monastery of Tours, and who, withdrawing into that wilderness, gave rise to the monastery of Cormaricus. When asked who he was, he supposedly gave only this answer: “A grieving heart.” Hence the name Cormeriacus was left to the place.

How fictional this story is is shown by the fact that in 791, before that disaster of the monks of Tours had occurred, the monastery of Cormaricus—incorrectly called Cormeriacum—began to be founded in a place that, according to Itherius, had been called Cormaricus from ancient times.

[Col. 1431A] **56.** After Itherius’s death, Alcuin obtained a document from Charlemagne “that he might lawfully establish monks in the cell of Saint Paul, which by the rustic name is called Cormaricus, who would live there according to the rule and statutes of Saint Benedict; a place that his predecessor, Abbot Itherius, had acquired by purchase.” The charter was issued at Tours, in the monastery of Saint Martin, on the third day before the Nones of June, in the thirty-second and thirty-seventh years of Charles’s reign—that is, in the year 800. In that year Charles, after celebrating Easter at Centula, went to the tomb of Saint Martin.

Twenty monks were brought into Cormaricus. Benedict, abbot of Aniane, is recorded by Ardo in his life as having supplied them to Alcuin. They were ordered to be subject to the abbot of Saint Martin.

**57.** This monastery remained under the governance of the abbot of Saint Martin until the seventh year of the empire of Louis Augustus. In that year the emperor granted “that the monks of that place might lawfully elect an abbot from the same Cormarican community according to the rule of Saint Benedict, though with the consent of the abbot and community of Saint Martin; and that the Cormarican community should contain at least fifty monks.”

Perhaps someone will think that the Cormaricans were granted the power to elect their own abbot from among themselves because of the change from monks to canons in the Tours monastery of Saint Martin.

The first proper abbot elected at Cormaricus was Jacob, praised in the book on the restoration of the monastery of Glanfeuil. He was succeeded by Odacer, a kinsman of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, as appears from Lupus’s Letter 86. Letter 90 was also written to him. Odacer enriched the neighboring monastery of Villaloup, or Villeloin, with the property of his own monastery, secured it with a privilege from Louis, king of Germany, and arranged for the church of the place to be dedicated by Herard, bishop of Tours, in the year 859.

Finally, in 1096, Pope Urban II ordered at the Council of Tours “by perpetual decree” that the abbot of Cormaricus “shall take the staff from the tomb of blessed Martin when he is elected; likewise, whenever an abbot dies, the staff shall always be returned to that same place, so that over those most holy limbs of the apostolic confessor that sign of pastoral rule may always be received by order of the dean and chapter together.” This is recorded in the papal letters in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*.

The monastery of Cormaricus, situated on the Anger River—the Indre—in the region of Tours, under the Benedictine congregation of Saint Maur, continues to exist to this day, as does Villaloup.
