**58.** I believe that two of Alcuin’s epigrams refer to Cormaricus, namely Epigrams 198 and 222 (now 221 and 229), concerning a cell in the wilderness where literary studies are said at some time to have been cultivated by Alcuin and Homer—that is, Angilbert, abbot of Centula.

The following verses are found in the former:

> This is the more noble little rustic cell  
> You see built beneath a woodland roof in the wilderness.  
> Here it flourishes in sacred studies; it reads through  
> The laws of *esophia* [Note: [Col. 1431D] Perhaps *theosophia*, “divine wisdom.”]  
> And handles the secret sayings of the elders.

And in Epigram 222:

> O my cell, my sweet dwelling, dearly loved,  
> Farewell, my cell, forever and ever.  
> On every side a tree surrounds you with resonant branches,  
> A little wood always heavy with flowering foliage.  
> All the meadows will bloom with health-giving flowers and herbs,  
> Which the physician seeks with the healing aid of his right hand.  
> Rivers surround you everywhere with flowering banks,  
> Where the fisherman joyfully spreads his nets in the Betia.  
> Your enclosures breathe the fragrance of fruit-bearing orchards,  
> With white lilies mingled with little red roses.  
> Every kind of bird sings its morning songs  
> And praises God the Creator with its voice.  
> Once within you the nourishing voice of the master resounded,  
> Who with sacred lips entrusted books of wisdom.  
> At appointed times within you sacred praise of the Thunderer  
> Sounded with peaceful voices and peaceful hearts.  
> Now, my cell, I lament you with tearful songs,  
> And groaning in my heart I lament your misfortunes.  
> For suddenly, by fate [F., *fato*], you have fled from the poems,  
> And now an unknown hand wholly possesses you.  
> Now neither Flaccus nor Homer, by fate [F., “by speech”], will possess you;  
> Nor will the boys sing of the Muses beneath your roof.

This poem does not seem to be by Alcuin, because of the verses in which it is said that the nourishing voice of the master once resounded in that place and that he taught wisdom with sacred lips. Perhaps the transfer of governance from Fridugisus to Jacob, the proper abbot of that place, is signified; previously Jacob had been subject to the abbot of Saint Martin.

Unless one prefers to interpret this epigram as referring to the cell of Saint Judoc, possession of which after Alcuin’s death was transferred to the monastery of Ferrières and then into the hands of Count Odulfus. Abbot Lupus of Ferrières repeatedly complains about this matter. Louis the Pious had assigned this cell to him, whereas Charlemagne had previously granted it to Alcuin “for the provision of alms to pilgrims,” as Lupus writes in Letter 11.

Alcuin speaks of this cell in Letter 93 (now 44): [Col. 1432B] “Martin,” he says, “remained sick in the villages near Saint Judoc.”

**59.** In addition, Alcuin built and endowed a hospice at a place called the Twelve Bridges, in the district of Troyes on the Seine, for the benefit of the poor, and especially of pilgrims. It will not be burdensome to reproduce here the document drawn up by Alcuin concerning this matter:

“In the name of the Lord who reigns forever. I, Alcuin, although unworthy, rector and governor of the monastery and possessions of Saint Martin, the most illustrious confessor of Christ, dictated this document by the command and decree of Lord Charles, most serene emperor, so that hereafter no disturbance might be caused by my successors or by any person whatsoever concerning the matters written below.

I have determined, under the inspiration of Christ God and with the favor of Lord Charles, to build, at the celebrated place called the Twelve Bridges, a hospice for receiving pilgrims, as an act of almsgiving on behalf of the aforesaid lord emperor, his offspring, and his entire family, and for the stability of the Frankish army. I have done so, receiving from my lord a small portion of land between two bridges and the two waters of the Seine, as is contained below within its boundaries. There I built an oratory of the most blessed mother of God, Mary, and hospitable buildings for the perpetual reception of pilgrims, as we have said.

My lord also added, with a written record and instrument of documents and by the authority of his holy name, ten holdings of land in the Champagne of Rheims, at a place called Marmorico-villa, Marmeriville. Leotard, a nobleman, also gave from his own property, as perpetual alms, land and possessions in two places, namely Ferroco and Marniaco. Frambert, a priest, also gave something at a place called Brituaria.

His nephew, named Marato, also gave, under the title of sale, land at a place called Mariniaco, for which I gave him four pounds of silver. Then, by the authority of the lord emperor, we transferred to the same place the properties at a place called Patiaco, and the villages of Dofio and Muerneto, as the deed of donation sets forth; and elsewhere, at a place called Patiaco on the Igrua, as well as at Curcella and in the village of Cavanno, which Sigbert and his parents assigned to Saint Martin.

Also in the village of Collorio and in the Flaviacian valley and at Muilliare, which Adalbert, son of Beringarius, assigned on behalf of his brother Ermenfred to the interests of the same saint, as is contained in the individual legal donations, everything belonging or pertaining to those places in every respect.

Other free men dwelling in those regions also gave small portions of land in various places in perpetual right, as at Mount Gratianus, and so forth. All these properties, lawfully possessed and held, belonging to the aforesaid church of blessed Mary, by the arrangement written below, I therefore transfer in perpetual right, as alms for our lord and for myself, to Jesus Christ and Saint Martin, for the perpetual reception of the poor, so that travelers may there receive assistance continually, according to the possibility and blessing of the Lord, which I believe he will grant that place and its possessions through the intercession of blessed Mary and Saint Martin, as alms from my lord King Charles, from his perpetual offspring and the kings of the Franks, for the remedy of my soul, for the prosperity of my successors, and for the salvation of the holy family of Saint Martin.

I beseech, by the name and majesty of the holy Trinity, by the blood of our redemption, and by the terrible judgment in which each person will render an account of his faith and all his works, that this gift of my lord, my donation, and the reception of pilgrims there may remain eternally firm and inviolable in perpetual right, under the protection and administration of the abbots of Saint Martin; that it not be granted as a benefice to anyone, but be assigned for service under the governance of faithful men who fear God.

I especially adjure him, by the fellowship of the holy cross and the holy Trinity, to see faithfully to it and cause to be distributed to the poor whatever the blessing of God makes fruitful in those portions of land. I also adjure all present and future princes and those exercising authority, so that, after hearing the authority of our most beloved lord emperor and my own, they may ensure without disturbance that our decreed will remain firm. Thus he himself may deserve to become a participant forever in this blessing, believing with us what is believed and consenting to this declaration, so that by God’s mercy it may benefit him equally as alms, just as it benefits me, who, with God’s help, first of all arranged for these things to be done.

Great and most gracious is the goodness of the Lord and our Redeeming God, who will repay each person of good will and sound faith with an eternal reward.

This single charter can suffice in every place and court for ecclesiastical donations, transfers, leases, and claims, even if it is read in the presence of faithful men and worshipers of God. I adjure them by the name of the eternal God, by the authority of his redemption, and by the grace of baptism, which they were privileged to receive from their very cradles, that whoever hears this document grant assent, according to the possibility or authority bestowed upon him, to this donation of ours. Otherwise, if he does not do so, when he must render an account with holy Mary and Saint Martin accusing me—but in place of the poor and pilgrims—he will receive the account of his own condemnation at the future judgment, when Christ comes in his majesty to judge all human actions.

May this charter [lacuna], with its small possessions, remain free from every obstruction, burden, and liability imposed by counts, vicars, judges, or any authority whatsoever. And so that it may be believed more firmly, my lord has deigned to confirm it below with his own hand, and more securely with the wax of his ring, so that no sacrilegious or reckless person may presume to invalidate anything contained in it.”

[Col. 1433D] No date is found on the parchment from which this copy was transcribed. Later, Ingelwinus, abbot of Saint Martin, assigned this hospice to the monastery of Cormaricus, “so that the monks of that monastery might restore it and the place itself to its former condition, and that the poor there, according to the previously established number—namely, twenty—might always be supported in food and all other necessities, and might have there a refuge for their safety because of the pursuit of the pagans.” This is recorded in a charter of Charles the Bald, issued at Vermeria on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction and the twenty-fifth year of his reign.

The place is now called Pontes, or Ponts, and contains a priory subject to the abbey of Cormaricus.

## CHAPTER X. Alcuin’s Withdrawal to the Monastery of Saint Martin and His Resignation of the Office of Superior

**60.** Although Alcuin was in charge of the monastery of Tours and frequently stayed there, he was nevertheless repeatedly summoned to the court by Charles, who enjoyed his company and conversation. This was extremely burdensome to Alcuin, who ardently longed for solitude and withdrawal. Several letters bear witness to this.

In Letter 17 (now 132), he asks Charles not to take offense that, though invited by him to the palace, he does not come:

“Behold your Flaccus,” he says, “his body worn out and the belt of military labor laid aside, has chosen with his whole desire, in accordance with the most pious counsel of his lord David, to serve God alone in quiet peace. Because [conjecture: *quando*, “when”] he is forced to fight again and sweat beneath the burden of arms, the weakness of his body denies him the strength to lift even what lies upon the ground. . . . And, to speak plainly, which I must plainly beg: I beseech you, let not the holy mind of my lord grow angry at my delay, because I am not now able to come. I shall come again, if it pleases God, at a suitable time. Nor do I think that my devotion can benefit your excellence in any way more than through continual prayers before Saint Martin.” [Col. 1434B]

And in Letter 19 (now 134):

“I beseech the mercy of your unconquered goodness, that the holy mind and kindly will which are in you should in no way grow angry at my weakness, but, with pious compassion, allow one who is weary to rest, to persist in prayers for you, and to go before the face of the eternal Judge in confession and tears.”

He expresses the same desire in Letter 92 (now 25) to Homer:

“With you gone,” he says, “I often attempted to reach the harbor of stability; but the Ruler of affairs and dispenser of souls has not yet granted me the ability to do what he once granted me the will to do.”

There are several other letters on the same subject.

**61.** At last the venerable abbot obtained what he had desired, in the year, as I believe, 804, when he appears to have relinquished the governance of the abbey. Certainly in 801, when he wrote Letter 23 (now 129), he had not yet obtained this, as his own words prove:

“Nearly five years ago, I call God to witness, I resolved with no false heart to withdraw from secular occupations. But, by the counsel of your pious providence, I was transferred into the service of Saint Martin, becoming, by God’s gift, useful to the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical order. Yet the affection of my former intention has not departed from my heart, as I already told your piety after the passing of a year.” [Col. 1434C]

The place he desired for his withdrawal is indicated by these words:

“I desire, without any doubt, to live or rest among the brothers faithfully serving God in the church of Saint Martin, if God in his mercy permits it.”

Hence I find doubtful what the author of the *Life* writes in chapter 8: namely, that Alcuin contemplated withdrawing to the monastery of Fulda, repeatedly requested this from Charles, and did not obtain it. Whatever the case, he obtained his withdrawal in the monastery of Tours, as Letter 99 (now 133) to the brothers serving God in the regions of Gothia sufficiently suggests:

“As for me,” he says, “troubled by the storms of the world, I have labored in vain and wearied myself in many places; but now, like a shipwrecked man, I have been cast by God’s mercy into the harbor of rest. In it I lie weary and wounded, and I beseech your unanimity to assist me by the constancy of your holy prayers.”

I interpret Charlemagne’s poem concerning this withdrawal; it stands among Alcuin’s epigrams as no. 185 (*Patrologia*, vol. 98, col. 1352), as follows:

> King Charles, rejoicing in you . . . father . . . teacher,  
> With these few verses [I ask for] eternal salvation in Christ [perhaps: “eternal salvation”].  
> My mind, I confess, rejoices with honey-sweet affection,  
> Beloved teacher of yours. Therefore I wished in songs,  
> O venerable one, to comfort your old age with the Muses.

And below:

> Now you hold the better paths of holy life,  
> Until you come to the heights of the heavenly kingdom,  
> Rejoicing with the saints, joined to Christ forever.  
> And, teacher, I beg you, carry me with you in your prayers  
> To the gracious heights of the compassionate King  
> Toward which you are striving.

**62.** As I have already said, I assign this withdrawal to the year 804, the year in which Alcuin was hitherto believed to have died, because in that year he divided the governance of his monasteries among his disciples: the Martinian monastery to Fridugisus and the monastery of Ferrières to Sigulfus. The writer of the *Life* noted this division in chapter 8, where Alcuin is said to have “divided the monasteries entrusted to him among his disciples.”

Certainly Louis, son of Charlemagne and then king of Aquitaine, granted a privilege for Cormaricus “to Abbot Fridegisus from the monastery of Saint Martin” in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, which fell in the year 807.

It is surprising that he entrusted both monasteries to two canons, for Fridugisus and Sigulfus were canons—although Sigulfus later exchanged the canonical habit for the monastic, as Lupus writes in Letter 29.

## CHAPTER XI. Alcuin’s Disciples

**63.** Alcuin had many disciples at York, in Charles’s palace, at Caesarodunum of Tours, and perhaps also at Cormaricus.

[Col. 1435B] **64.** At York, under his instruction, were Eanbald the Younger, later bishop of York after the elder; the aforementioned Fridugisus, at whose request he wrote the books *On the Trinity*; Joseppus or Josephus, of whom I shall speak later; Liudger, later bishop of Mimigardeford; Putul, praised by Altfrid in Liudger’s *Life*; and many others.

**65.** At the palace he had as disciples Charles the Great, who at one time gloried in having him as his teacher; Homer or Angilbert, Charlemagne’s son-in-law and later the holy abbot of Centula, whom I said above sometimes cultivated the Muses with Alcuin at Cormaricus; Charlemagne’s daughters Gisela and Rictrude, to whom he dedicated commentaries on John; and Damoetas or Ricolfus, together with Mopsus and the others mentioned in Letter 93 (now 44).

66. In the monastery at Tours he had as students Onias, Candidus, and Nathanael, to whom the book on Ecclesiastes is inscribed; Oduin, to whom he writes concerning the ceremonies of baptism; Daphnis, for whose benefit he explains a verse from the Song of Songs; Maurus, or Rabanus, later archbishop of Mainz; Simeon, later bishop of Worms, praised in Letter 101 (now 73); Withso, Raganard, Waldram, Adalbert, and Osulf, concerning whom see chapter 8 of the *Life*. Add to these Siguifus, for whom this *Life* was written and to whom the book on Questions of Genesis was dedicated, and Amalarius, as Amalarius himself attests in book 1, chapter 58, of *On the Order of the Antiphoner*. Finally, during Alcuin’s lifetime Paul the monk lived in the monastery of Saint Martin; his epitaph is preserved in Alcuin and is epigram 267 (now 268).

67. I have noticed several things about Josepphus, or Joseph, in published and manuscript books, which I think it worthwhile to bring together here. Alcuin says that Joseph was in good health in his letter to Colcu, preserved by Ussher among the Irish letters; but in Letter 67 (now 173), addressed to his beloved son Joseph, he expresses sorrow over Joseph’s ill health. In Letter 74 (now 174), he begs Remigius, the bishop, to pray for the soul of Joseph, his pupil. Joseph therefore died before his teacher.

I once doubted whether he was the same Joseph whom Charlemagne wished to place over a certain monastery, as we read in a letter from Theodemar, abbot, to King Charles; or whether he was Josue, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Volturno, of whom I shall speak below under the year 818. But I have no doubt that he is the Joseph who, at Alcuin’s command, abridged Jerome’s commentaries on the prophet Isaiah. We possess Joseph’s epitome in our manuscript codex no. 585, at whose beginning these verses are read:

> Who can unfold, reader, in brief words,  
> The mysteries of Isaiah, handling and turning over all things?  
> Saint Jerome, employing lengthy treatises,  
> Wisely explained him through great intricacies.  
> From his immense books I shall attempt to excerpt  
> What may briefly disclose the prophet’s meaning.  
> Thus it pleases Albinus that we undertake such labor.

The epitome itself begins: “All the holy prophets, as Jerome confirms with many examples, etc.” At the end of the epitome are the following verses:

> Jerome instructed me, at the beginning of this final little book,  
> That, for anyone to whom the text of the books on Isaiah  
> Should itself seem too long, I should excerpt them all  
> And compress their vast meanings into brief words.  
> Therefore, obeying your commands, dearest one,  
> I have dedicated these things, briefly gathered, to you, Albinus.  
> Would that these might often repay you with remembrance of us.  
> As you read them, kindly Father, pray diligently for us,  
> And say more than once: “May the Lord preserve Joseph.”  
> These words also I return to you from my whole heart.  
> Dear master, hail; may the Lord preserve you everywhere.

“I have devoutly excerpted these things, as briefly as I could, from Jerome’s diffuse treatise on Isaiah, just as you, most beloved master Albinus, commanded. For you instructed me to follow throughout only what was absolutely necessary for the meaning and the course of the Hebrew truth, and to avoid the uncertain and confused tracks both of “ba . . .” [reading uncertain] and of the other interpreters and treatises. I believe that you wished this to be done for two reasons: either that the labor of reading long books might be lightened for readers who are fastidious and lukewarm, or that for men of intelligence and ardent spirit a readier and shorter path to the truth might be provided. But if anyone despises these things as being shorter and therefore more obscure—for brevity is often accompanied by obscurity—let him run with uplifted head to the source from which we drew them; and if this little stream is not enough for him, he may be satisfied from above, where the river overflows its banks. [lacuna]

But you, beloved master, in return for our labor, share with us the grace of your blessing and prayer, so that, as we knock upon the mercy of our Redeemer, he may not despise us but, in view of his great mercy toward many, may also regard in us the work of his hands; and, after we have overcome the waves of this world’s temptations and broken through the nets of our [sins], may the merciful Lord Jesus lead us to the harbor of an undisturbed life.”

Thus far concerning Joseph’s previously unknown work. He is called “Joseph abbot” at the beginning by the person who supplied the title of the book. I shall speak elsewhere, in their proper places, of the holy men Angilbert, Liudger, and Rabanus.

## CHAPTER XII. Zeal for the integrity of faith and morals; modesty

68. How earnestly Alcuin was devoted to the Christian cause is attested by several books written by him, both against Felix, bishop of Urgel, and against Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, who held unsound views concerning Christ’s dignity as Son. It is also attested by several letters that he wrote to preserve and restore the integrity of the faith, such as Letter 69 (now 90) to the brothers of Lyons, or to the monks of the Island of Barbe, against those who mixed salt into the Eucharistic bread and those who wished a single immersion to be used in baptism; and Letter 71 (now 134) to the brothers in the province of the Goths, or to the monks of Septimania, concerning the necessity of confession; as well as several others.

69. He commended integrity of morals with no less zeal in letters written both to bishops and to monks, so that they might reform religious conduct in themselves and in others. Particularly notable on this subject is Letter 6 (now 162) to King Charles, in which he chiefly censures two things in the clergy.

First:

> “I hear,” he says, “that throughout the churches of Christ there is a certain practice that is not sufficiently praiseworthy, which your most prudent authority could easily correct, if the report is true and is not rather a false excuse—namely, that priests lay upon their bishops what they themselves do not wish to do. For they say that bishops have forbidden priests and deacons to preach in the churches.”

He argues at length against this prohibition.

Second:

> “We have also seen,” he says, “in some places the altars of God without a roof, defiled by the droppings of birds or by the urine of dogs. Your reverend will in God can easily correct this through the bishops, so that the Lord’s table may remain in its place with fitting honor, or be carried into the principal church, according to the holy prudence of God’s priests. And let it be treated honorably, whether it is Christ’s altar or the consecration of his body and blood; and let the principal sacrament of our salvation be consecrated, held, and guarded with every form of reverence.”

What the pious man thought about remitting the tithes that Charles wished to exact from the newly Christianized people of Saxony is shown by Letters 7 and 11 (now 33 and 95). He attacks the simoniacs in Letter 88 (now 54) and in epigram 271 (now 232). In Letter 107 (now 189), he asks Antonius, or Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, to recall Homer—another name for Angilbert—from theatrical spectacles, just as he himself had attempted to do in a letter to Angilbert on spectacles and the devil’s fabrications, all of which Holy Scripture forbids.

70. How modestly he either corrected his writings or submitted them to the judgment of others is shown especially by Letter 9 (now 82) to Charles:

> “As for what you took care to admonish me at the end of your letter—that if anything needs humble correction it should be corrected—I have never, by God’s gift, been obstinate in my error, nor confident in my own opinions, nor so disposed that I could not readily accept a better judgment.”

And in Letter 15 (now 101) to the same man:

> “We give thanks to your revered piety because, in accordance with your command, you had the little book addressed to you recited to the ears of your wisdom; and because you ordered its errors to be marked and sent it back for correction, although you could have corrected it better yourself—for another person’s judgment in any work very often has greater force than that of the author himself.”

This is sufficient as an example of his other virtues.

## CHAPTER XIII. His death, tomb, epitaph, memory, and praises

71. The author of the *Life* reports that Alcuin died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June in the year 804, and later writers have followed him. The day must clearly be retained; three arguments seem to show that the year must be corrected.

72. The first argument is drawn from poem 54 (now 29), which Alcuin wrote concerning the elevation—as it is called—of the body of Saint Amandus, not before the year 809, when that elevation took place. I do not see how this argument can be evaded. For it cannot be said that this poem, or epigram, is not Alcuin’s, since his name appears in it. Nor can the error be attributed to Milo, who assigned the time of the elevation, or to a copyist, since the year 809 is expressed both in the printed books and in manuscripts in Milo’s sermon on this elevation, and is confirmed by the metrical *Life* written by him and by other authors, as was shown above under the year in which this elevation was discussed. Milo certainly received that year from eyewitnesses. Moreover, Alcuin sometimes visited the monastery of Saint Amandus, as appears from Letter 66 (now 102).

73. The second point is that Alcuin is said to have been at Aachen with Charlemagne when Saint Liudger departed to heaven—that is, in the very year 809, in which Liudger’s death is beyond dispute. I know that Altfrid, bishop, kept silent about this in the *Life of Saint Liudger*: namely, that when Liudger was dying, Alcuin, observing the stars with Charles, divined Liudger’s death. Yet another anonymous author of the same *Life* certainly committed this to posterity. He recorded it nearly fifty years after the event.

74. The third argument also proves that Alcuin’s life must be extended beyond the year 809. It is drawn from the fact that Alcuin urged his pupil Rabanus to write two books on the Cross, which Rabanus dedicated to Saint Martin in Alcuin’s name, undoubtedly while Alcuin was still alive.

A letter of Alcuin, Letter 55 (now 150), addressed to blessed Maurus, the son of Saint Benedict—that is, to Rabanus—survives concerning the completion of this work. In the printed editions it is falsely said to have been written to Benedict. In it Alcuin addresses Maurus as follows:

> “I ask that you make firm the promise you made to write the little book at my request, and that my joy may be fulfilled.”

These words must be understood of the work on the Cross, which is known to have been Rabanus’s first work. After completing it, Rabanus later dedicated the work to Saint Martin in a poem published under Alcuin’s name, in which Alcuin offers it. This kind of commendation is ordinarily written only in the person of a living man. The poem begins in this way, preceded by the title “Albinus’s Intercession for Maurus”:

> Holy bishop of God, living forever through your merits,  
> Receive with pious mind the cause that we bring.  
> For when I was the humble guardian and minister  
> Of this church, reading the sacred teachings,  
> I taught this boy by the divine inspiration of the word, etc.

Someone may perhaps force an interpretation upon the words “when I was the humble guardian and minister of this church,” as though they applied not to a living but to a dead man. In fact, however, they indicate only that at that time Alcuin was no longer rector or abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, as was proved above.

Now Rabanus composed this work after completing six lustra of life, as is clear from the same poem—namely, in the very year in which he was ordained priest by Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, who did not assume the see before the year 815. Therefore Alcuin was still alive in that year, since this dedicatory poem was written while he lived.

If anyone nevertheless insists more stubbornly that Rabanus adapted this poem for Alcuin after Alcuin’s death, he must at least concede that Alcuin had encouraged him to complete the work at the time when Rabanus was in charge of the schools at Fulda. For at the end of the aforementioned Letter 55 (now 150), Alcuin bids farewell to Maurus and his pupils. It must be proved below, in its proper place in Rabanus’s *Eulogy*, that Rabanus was not placed in charge of the schools at Fulda until the year 810. Consequently, Alcuin lived beyond that year.

75. Three further conjectures of no little weight support this conclusion. One is that Alcuin corrected the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments at Charlemagne’s command, as he himself testifies in the letter prefixed to book 6 of his commentary on John. He presented these corrected books to Charles together with Letter 20 (now 131).

Thegan, however, reports that Charles devoted himself to correcting the sacred books shortly before his death:

> “For in the final period before the day of his death he had the four Gospels of Christ most carefully corrected with the Greeks and Syrians.”

It is highly probable that at that time he summoned Alcuin to collaborate with him.

This is strongly confirmed by another conjecture: namely, that in his commentary on John—which he had undertaken at the request of Gisela and Rictrude, or Rotrude, the religious daughters of Charles—he inscribes and dedicates the first five books to Gisela and Rictrude, but the remaining two to Gisela’s sister Columba, who was dedicated to God, omitting Rictrude. This indicates that Rictrude had already died. Her death occurred in the year 810, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, as is clear from the Frankish annals.

For it is not plausible that Alcuin would have dedicated the two later books to anyone other than Rictrude, who had urged him to compose the work, if she had still been alive.

The third conjecture is that Alcuin sent three books on the Faith of the Holy Trinity to Emperor Charles “at the time of the most celebrated assembly, when the priests of God and the preachers of the Christian people had gathered together by imperial command.” This seems to be understood of the synods that Charles ordered to be convened throughout his kingdom in the year 813.

It might also be added that Alcuin wrote a book on the *Life of Charlemagne*, who died in 814. But since it is uncertain whether that book embraced the whole of Charles’s life, and since some think it was nothing other than the little poem whose fragment Canisius published, and after him Chesnius, ending with Charles’s arrival in Rome before Pope Leo, it must be admitted that it could have been written before Charles’s death.

76. The arguments I have presented clearly prove, unless I am mistaken, that Alcuin lived until the year 815 or at least beyond the year 810. The author of the *Life*, therefore, and the later writers who followed him must be corrected, since they assigned Alcuin’s death to the year 804.

Certainly, although the authority of this writer—nearly Alcuin’s contemporary—must be highly valued, he nevertheless committed certain other errors, which prove that he should not be followed in everything. I do not know whether Harpesfeld, a man of keen judgment, sensed this, since he placed Alcuin’s death in the year 809.

77. Alcuin’s body was buried in the church of Saint Martin, as the author of the *Life* testifies—not in the monastery of Cormaric, as William of Malmesbury thought in book 1, chapter 3, of *The Kings of the English*; nor at Hersfeld, as Brower supposed in book 1, chapter 10, of *The Antiquities of Fulda*.

Brower was led into error by an epitaph of a certain Albinus that recently stood in the church at Hersfeld. This epitaph, which Brower reported and Chesnius after him placed after Alcuin’s *Life*, is neither of great importance nor to be attributed to Alcuin. It perhaps belonged to Albinus, or Albuinus, a monk of Hersfeld, concerning whom the following is read in the Hildesheim chronicle under the year 1034:

> “Bruno was succeeded at Nienburg by Albwinus, most learned in the philosophical arts, provost of Hersfeld, who had previously been a most renowned schoolmaster.”

Later it may have happened that, having received from their elders the tradition that Albuinus was buried in their church, the monks of Hersfeld, through confusion of names, thought that he was the great Albinus, or Alcuin, and composed this crude epitaph for him.

78. Writers who lived nearer to Alcuin’s own time proclaim his memory and holiness. While he was still alive, Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, calls him powerful in work and speech in book 3, poem 1; and Jonas, Theodulf’s successor, calls him “the venerable master Alcuin” in book 3, chapter 6, of *On the Instruction of the Laity*.

Rabanus, his pupil, enrolled him in the sacred calendar on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June with these words: “The deposition of Lord Alcuin.” In the letter prefixed to his commentaries on the Books of Kings, he calls his teacher Albinus “of blessed memory.”

Hincmar, in a letter to Rabanus, praises “blessed Alcuin”; and in his letter *On the Non-Trinal Deity* he praises Alcuin as holy and venerable. In Letter 1 to Charles, against Gottschalk, he mentions “Alcuin, a religious and learned man,” and lists him among those Fathers whose faith and teaching the Roman See not only accepted most favorably but also extolled with many praises.

Ardo, in his book on the *Life of Benedict, abbot of Aniane*, calls Alcuin illustrious in wisdom and venerable for the merit of his holiness.

Finally, in the *Annals of Fulda* under the year 794 he is commended with this eulogy:

> “At this time Alcuin, also called Albinus—that is, by another name—is regarded as distinguished for holiness and learning.”

And in the brief chronicle of Tours:

> “In the year 804 Saint Alcuin died,”

namely, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, as is established by the *Life*, by Rabanus, and by Hariulf, a monk of Centula.

Yet, so far as I know, the Church nowhere celebrated Alcuin’s feast day—not even the Church of Tours.

79. Some may perhaps blame Alcuin for having held several abbacies and for having had many servants—that is, if we believe Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, twenty thousand servants.

It is true that he held several abbacies in Gaul: Ferrières with the cell of Saint Judoc, Troyes of Saint Lupus, and Tours of Saint Martin with the cell of Cormaric. But he held them not to grow richer through them, but to correct monks who had fallen into a looser way of life.

Nor, I think, did he have any servants other than those attached to his monasteries. At that time very many servants belonged to monks.

It is better, however, to listen to Alcuin himself responding to both objections in the letter prefixed to his books against Elipandus:

> “It is one thing to possess the world, and another to be possessed by the world. One man possesses riches and does not possess them; another does not possess them and possesses them. I have never acquired a human being for my own service. Rather, desiring in devoted charity to serve all the servants of Christ my God, I came, by divine dispensation—as I believe, at God’s command—when I was summoned to Charles, the glorious ruler and king of this kingdom, whose name must be mentioned with every honor, so that I might have the means of performing that service.”

Alcuin’s abundance of wealth can therefore be excused, both because his mind was free from desire for it and because he rightly distributed it for the use of the monks over whom he presided.

Certainly Letter 37 (now 184) to the priest Ead shows how far he was from desiring riches:

> “By the prayers of your devotion, lead us into that same degree of poverty in which, with God bringing it about, you safely remain. You hold in your hands what we once thought of holding; but the waves of the world have carried our little boat, in stormy winds, into the whirlpool of riches. I beg you to strive, by the pious prayers of your devotion, to call me back to the harbor of rest. I desire it, but I do not do it.”

The pious man wrote this and much else to Ead, who was evidently a monk. Moreover, Alcuin clearly indicates here that he had once remained in the harbor of rest—that is, in a monastery—and had lived there free from riches, in monastic simplicity. He desired to be called back to that harbor, as I noted above in section 60.

## CHAPTER XIV. Judgment on Alcuin’s writings

80. Finally, as regards Alcuin’s writings, almost all were published by André Chesne in Paris in the year 1617, with the exception of several works that I shall mention below.

81. In that edition, learned men regard the book *On the Divine Offices* as spurious, first because it is a miscellany collected from various writings of Alcuin himself and of other, later authors. Chapter 40 is a treatise by Remigius of Auxerre, a monk, *On the Explanation of the Mass*; and chapter 18 cites a letter by the monk Helpricus, who seems to have been Hilperic, a monk of Saint Gall, in the eleventh century.

They also reject it because it contains certain absurdities and errors unworthy of Alcuin. For example, in chapter 1 it says that the Lord Christ was born under the consulship of Sulpicius and Camerinus, which is false. It likewise says that he was baptized in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, under the consulship of Valerianus and Asiaticus, whereas it should have said “under the consulship of Valerius Asiaticus and Messala,” although these men were not consuls in the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

It also says that *Pascha* is a Greek word, contrary to Alcuin’s explicit statement in book 6, chapter 32, of his commentary on John:

> “Passover, brothers, is not, as certain people think, a Greek name, but a Hebrew one.”

Finally, in chapter 13 it derives *impudicus* (“shameless”) from *podex* (“buttocks”); in chapter 36 it says that *sacerdos* (“priest”) is a Greek word; and in chapter 38 it writes foolishly about the *cidaris*.

82. Some poems are also spurious and falsely attributed to him. Such is poem, or epigram, 3, concerning Bugga, which was written under Ina, king of the West Saxons, who preceded Alcuin by nearly a century; poem 48, concerning Ethildritha, which belongs to Bede the Venerable; and poem 177, which belongs to Angilbert, abbot of Centula.

Finally, if poem 178 is Alcuin’s, it must be said that the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome was stripped before the year 840, when it is recorded that this was done by the Saracens. Since the poem concerns the attack of pagans upon the island of Britain, I could easily believe that it is Alcuin’s, for in his time the Danes invaded that island.

The moral verses that Lupus cites from Alcuin in Letter 20 are poem 179.

83. The Chesne edition omits the commentaries on four of Paul’s Epistles—namely, Ephesians, Titus, Philemon, and Hebrews. It also omits the preface to the penitential psalms addressed to Arno, bishop of Salzburg, which appears in volume 9 of the *Spicilegium*; three letters published in volume 7 of the same work; and the letter to Candidus and Nathanael, of which a fragment is given below.

Two volumes of homilies are also missing, as are the commentaries on Proverbs and the Song of Songs, which are mentioned in chapter 12 of the *Life*. To these must be added the *Confession of Faith*, consisting of four parts, and the book on the *Life of Charlemagne*. A few observations must be made concerning both works.

84. This *Confession* was first printed at Dijon in 1656 by the learned priest Pierre-François Chifflet of the Society of Jesus, from a very old Lyon manuscript that bears the author’s name.

Some learned men doubt whether this *Confession* is genuinely Alcuin’s work. Their principal arguments can be seen in the historical index appended to the *Office of the Most Holy Sacrament*. The substance of the criticism is as follows.

The first two parts are excellent and devout, but are drawn largely from other works of Alcuin, especially from his prayers. The third part does not cohere with the first two, from which it repeats much word for word—something no author would have done in one and the same work. Moreover, this part is taken from the *Confession of Pelagius* and from the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, although those passages that suggest the Pelagian heresy have been corrected.

The fourth part ends at chapter 9, for what follows is a miscellany of various prayers that are poorly joined together.

The style approaches Alcuin’s style—not perfectly polished and corrected, but vigorous and burning with devotion. The author lived before the age of the scholastics and used certain words that the scholastic age would scarcely have admitted.

Finally, the author of the index admits that nothing certain can be determined from these conjectures.

Some add another reason for doubt: that the *Confession* contains several excerpts from the *Meditations* of Saint Anselm. But who knows whether Anselm borrowed them from Alcuin?

It is not surprising if Alcuin used the *Confession of Pelagius*, which was then believed to be Jerome’s, as is evident from book 3, chapter 10, of the Carolingian work against images.

The fact that some passages do not cohere sufficiently and that certain things are repeated may result either from the *Confession* being composed of various sayings of the Fathers that amount to the same thing, or from the movement of an ardent mind, which in such agitations is carried in various directions without order.

In chapter 15 of part 4, the author asks God that he may “never be exalted by the necessary services of those who serve him or by the reverence shown him by his brothers.” These words clearly suggest that the author was an abbot, surrounded by a large number and retinue of servants and monks. This fits Alcuin exactly, since he is said to have had twenty thousand servants, as I noted above.

The author of the *Confession* adds in chapter 17 of the same part:

> “I have lost the place of my beloved solitude, the friend of sorrow, rest, and repentance, which I have always loved from my earliest age. Therefore my soul has been placed in great distress and sorrow, ignorant of your judgment concerning it: for I have not been able to find again the secret of my accustomed quiet and the suitable leisure for turning to you, which once, through my carelessness, I lost. Yet I still desire, sigh for, and seek it; but because my sins hinder me, I cannot find it.”

Alcuin describes the same agitation of spirit above, in sections 60 and 61. From these and other considerations it may be concluded that he himself was the author of this *Confession*.

85. That the *Life of Charlemagne* was written by the same author is shown especially by the subscription to Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, appended in the Thuane manuscript and published by Chesne in volume 2 in the following form:

> “The remaining deeds of his actions, and also those things commonly sung about him in poems, are not fully described here; but seek them in the *Life* that Alcuin writes about him.”

Baleus also lists the *Life of Charlemagne* among Alcuin’s works.

Moved by this testimony, Henricus Canisius attributed to Alcuin the poem on Charles’s arrival before Pope Leo at Rome. André Chesne appears to have approved Canisius’s conjecture in his edition of Alcuin’s works.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, cites in part 8 of the *Panormia* a fragment from the deeds of Charlemagne according to Alcuin, in these words:

> “King Charles, entreated by the request and prayers of Adrian, bishop of the city of Rome, undertook war against the Lombards. This war had previously been undertaken by his father, though only after great difficulty and at the pope’s entreaty.”

But exactly the same words occur in Einhard’s book *On the Life of Charlemagne*, which is known to be Einhard’s work.

86. In volume 4 of the *Spicilegium*, page 485, where there is a description of the treasury of Centula made in the year 831 at the command of Louis Augustus, the following are mentioned:

> “A Gregorian and Gelasian Missal, arranged in modern times by Albinus, and a complete Lectionary arranged by the aforementioned Albinus.”

By the latter I understand a book of Epistles and Gospels, on the basis of the words inserted there.

Finally, Alcuin is said above, in section 31, to have written a book on images, although I do not know whether this is sufficiently established. It is certain, however, that at Charles’s command he corrected the books of the Old and New Testaments, as noted above in section 75.

87. Before I finish my observations on Alcuin’s writings, it may not be out of place to set out here a sequence of some of his letters according to the chronological order in which they were written, as it occurred to me while reading through them.

In the year 790, a letter to Colcu was written in England, namely, in the year after Charles had defeated the Slavs. In it Alcuin says that he ought to be sent to arrange peace between Charles and King Offa. This is recorded in the letter, which Ussher published in full among the Irish letters. He incorrectly assigns it to the year 795, as I noted above in section 28.

In the year 794, he wrote Letter 63 (now 18) to Pope Hadrian through Angilbert, who carried the acts of the Council of Frankfurt to Rome. He also wrote another letter concerning the murder of King Æthelred, a fragment of which William of Malmesbury, the monk, reports in book 1, chapter 3, of *The Kings of the English*.

In the year 796, he wrote Letter 72 (now 24) to Pope Leo through Angilbert. Charles’s Letters 83 and 84, among Alcuin’s letters (*Patrologia Latina* 98, col. 907), also concern this journey. He sent Letter 75 (now 32) to Itherius, abbot of Saint Martin, who was close to death. He wrote Letter 92 (now 25) to Homer, or Angilbert, who was staying in Rome. In Letter 90 (now 37), he expresses sympathy with the sick Charles and requests that captives be released because of the subjugation of the Huns. Letter 91 (now 38) to Pippin concerns the same matter.

In the year 797, Letter 88 (now 54) concerned the election of the younger Eanbald as bishop of York; Letter 3 (now 76) concerned the leap of the moon in the final year of the nineteen-year cycle. In Letter 112 (now 39) to Paulinus, he mentions the embassy sent by the Avars to Charles in that year.

In the year 799, he sent what he calls a little book against the heresy of adoptionism, together with Letter 15 (now 101). He discusses the mutilation of Pope Leo in Letters 12 and 13 (now 96 and 109).

In the year 800, he mourned the death of Queen Liutgard in Letters 21 and 22 (now 106 and 107). In Letters 13, 17, and 19 (now 107, 132, and 134), he refused to go to Rome. At Centula he was asked to write the *Life of Saint Richarius*.

In the year 801, he congratulated Charles on his return from Italy in Letter 23 (now 129). In Letter 24 (now 133), he dissuaded him from the expedition to Benevento.

88. These are the observations I have been able to make concerning Alcuin’s writings. It remains for me to present a fragment of his letter to Candidus and Nathanael from our notes, as I promised. (See among Alcuin’s letters, volume C, column 408.)

# INDEX OF THE SUBJECTS AND STATEMENTS CONTAINED IN THE WORKS OF BLESSED ALCUIN

In this index, the Roman numerals I and II signify the first or second volume, according to the division of Frobenius’s edition; the Arabic numerals indicate the page.

[Note: [Col. 1443] In this index, Roman numerals I and II refer to PL 100 and 101. Arabic numbers refer to column numbers printed in the text in bold type.]

[Col. 1443] A
Aaron, why he is called the first priest, II, 490. Type of Christ, I, 388. Abgarus, a pagan king. Christ wrote him a letter, II, 222. The abbot’s duty toward the monks, II, 163. Secular honor may advance spiritual glory, ibid. Prayer for an abbot or congregation, 41. Abel, why he is called righteous, I, 306. Why “righteous boy” occurs in the canon of the Mass, II, 504.—Abel’s sacrifice, why it was accepted and Cain’s rejected, I, 306. His murder, a type of Christ’s Passion, 483. Abijah, what it signifies, I, 450, 451, 454. Why Abimelech was not killed when God told him that he would die, I, 324. Abita, a religious woman, II, 170, 171. Abiud, what it signifies, I, 450, 452, 455. In what year weaning took place among the Hebrews, I, 324. Abraham, what it signifies, I, 320, 350, 351, 353. Which letter was added to his name, 320.—Abraham recognized the Creator through astrology, I, 94. How he uniquely addressed the Lord when three men appeared to him, 321. Why he called himself dust and ashes, 322. Why he held a feast at Isaac’s weaning, 324. He rejected the idols of the Chaldeans, 317. Why he was commanded to leave his land, ibid. The greatness of the promises made to him, 318. Why he concealed that Sarah was his wife, ibid. How he is excused from adultery, 320. Why he received circumcision, 321.—Why Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son, 325. His faith and trust in God, ibid. His twofold seed, ibid. Who are to be blessed in his seed, 318. Who his sons are, 553. Where his sons by Keturah settled, 327.—Verses on Abraham’s sacrifice, II, 208.

Abstinence practiced for bodily continence is useful, II, 408. The allegories of the abyss in Holy Scripture, I, 181. Accent, what it is, II, 271. Accident, what it is, II, 336.—How many and what kinds of accidents belong to corporeal natures, II, 337. The diversity of accidents, 338. How accusation occurs in court, II, 319, 322. Acedia, what it is and what its effects are, II, 143. It drives monks from their cells into the world, ibid. How it is overcome, ibid.—Who is acedious and whence the term is derived, II, 472. Ahaz, what it signifies, I, 450, 452, 454. Achim, what it signifies, I, 450, 452, 455. Acolytes: who they are and whence they are called so, II, 434. The duty of acolytes under the old law, 490. The author of the Acts of the Apostles, II, 433. What the Acts contain, 434. The Alps of Acunumbiae (Agauniae), II, 194.

Adalbert, Alcuin’s disciple and abbot of Ferrières, I, 72. His surname was Magus, 112, 130. Adalbert of the monastery of Saint Martin, I, 171. Adalhard, whose assumed name was Antonius, abbot of Corbie, I, 206. He lived with Angilbert at the court of King Pippin, ibid. and 206. His brothers and sisters were sent into exile, ibid. His parents, ibid. Adalwin, bishop, a very faithful man and devoted to holy religion, I, 164. He came to Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, ibid. Bishop of Regensburg, Simpert’s successor, 165, note. He carried Arno’s letters to Alcuin, 164, 166.

Adam signifies the four quarters of the world, I, 489. Why he received the law although he was lord of the world, I, 305. How he consented to Eve, 309. Why he shifted the sin onto her, 310. How Adam’s sin harmed his descendants, II, 402.—Why Adam and Eve were not ashamed while naked, I, 309. Why they hid themselves after midday, 310.—Adam would not have died if he had not sinned, II, 408.

[Col. 1444]

The nature of the diamond, I, 906. Epitaph of Adeleidis, daughter of King Charles, II, 554. Adhelric (Aldric), a levite, I, 130. Later abbot of Ferrières, ibid. See Aldric. Adiltrude, betrothed of King Ecgfrith, II, 249. See Edildrydis.

How adolescents in monasteries should conduct themselves toward the elderly, I, 30. In what matters they should be instructed and admonished, 205. The name Adonai, what it signifies as a name of God, II, 423. Adonnanus (Saint), II, 219.

The obstinacy of the Adoptionists, I, 42. The heresy whispers secretly in corners, 534. Its novelty, 562. Condemned in Nestorius, II, 580. Originating from the Bonosian heresy, 590. See the Historical Dissertation at the end of volume I (in the new edition, volume II, col. 303).—The error of adoption is similar to that of Nestorius, I, 794. See the Dogmatic Dissertation at the end of volume I (new edition, volume II, col. 337).—Adoption is wrongly attributed to Christ, I, 107. It is improperly confused with assumption, 639, 780. And with grace, ibid. and 781, 816, 817, 864.—The term “adoption” is unheard of in the Church, I, 905; II, 580. It is never applied to Christ in Scripture, I, 784, 790, 791, 802.—The new terms “adoption” and “naming” are detestable when applied to Christ, I, 140.—The Fathers’ testimonies concerning adoption in the Son of God, corrupted by heretics, I, 870; II, 568 ff. They are refuted, I, 886 ff.—An adoptive son is a false son, not a true son, I, 784.

Pope Adrian, vicar of Saint Peter, I, 25. When he began his pontificate, 26. He condemned Felix, bishop of Urgel, 882. When he died, I, 26. His epitaph, II, 550. Adso, abbot of the monastery of Der, II, 527, note. He wrote a booklet on the Antichrist, 526. Adulators must be avoided, I, 76. Adulterers, who they are, II, 472.

The Lord’s two advents: one of mercy, the other of judgment, I, 541. Adverb, what it is, II, 290. Its distinctive property, 271. Its species, 290. Its figures, ibid. Its meaning, ibid. How adversities should be endured, I, 234 ff. How one who is God is an advocate, I, 834.

Aidan, a most holy prelate, II, 245. See Aidanus. Eadbert, king of the Northumbrians, II, 254, note. Brother of Ecgberht, archbishop of York, ibid. He died after twenty-one years of prosperous rule.

Æthelberht, I, 70. Who he was, 72, note.—Æthelberht, bishop of Hexham, I, 196. Tilli’s successor, 197.—Æthelberht, surnamed Pren, king of Kent, captured by the Mercians, I, 79. He succeeded Alric, 81. He harassed Bishop Aedilbardus, ibid.

Æthelhard, archbishop of Canterbury, I, 13; also called Aedelhard, Etilhard, Aethelred, Adelard, Athilhard, and Athelhardus, 16, 60, 79, 83. A venerable and prudent man, 79. He temporarily abandoned his see, 79. He convened a synod, 84. He held a meeting with Eanbald of York for the reform of the clergy, 148. He traveled to Rome twice, 84, 85. Through his efforts metropolitan dignity and peace among the bishops were restored, ibid. On his way to Rome he was commended to King Charles, 85. On his way to Rome, he met Alcuin’s messenger at Saint-Judoc, 148. His companions on the journey, ibid. Alcuin sent his saddle and horse to meet him, ibid. He also advised him, after completing his embassy, to return to his sheep, ibid. Charlemagne wrote to him, II, 557.

Æthelred (Edilrad), king of the Northumbrians, I, 17. Driven from the kingdom, restored, and finally killed, 19, note, 20. See Ethelredus. Æthelthryth, a servant of God and formerly a queen, I, 210. Insufficiently known, 211.

How Egypt provides pasture despite the failure of rains there, I, 333. Egyptians introduced into the palace school, I, 90. Who they were, 93, note. Their computation is disapproved, 91, 98. Aelbert, Alcuin’s teacher, traveled for the sake of learning, with Alcuin accompanying him, I, 62. He succeeded Ecgberht in the episcopate, II, 255, verse 1395. At what time, ibid., note. His praises and virtues, verse 1400. Related by blood to his predecessor Ecgberht, 556. Appointed master of the school at York, verse 1430. What disciplines he taught, verses 1433 ff. He traveled to foreign lands and also to Rome, verse 1453. The reason for his journey, verse 1455. Kings wished to retain him as their teacher, verse 1461. Returning from his journey, he became a bishop, verse 1465. His care in the episcopate, verses 1470 ff. He adorned churches, verse 1487. He covered an altar in honor of Saint Paul and another in honor of the holy martyrs and the holy cross with precious metals, verses 1490 and 1500. He built a new basilica, verses 1505 ff. He consecrated it with his fellow bishop ten days before his death, verse 1517. He bestowed pontifical dignity upon Eanbald, verse 1522. He handed over his treasures of books to Alcuin, 257, verse 1525. He assembled a library, verse 1533. Its contents are described, verses 1535 ff. The number of years he ruled, verse 1585 and note. His death, verses 1565 and 1582. His funeral, verses 1585 ff. Alcuin mourns his death, verses 1568 ff.

Aelim, a bishop. See Alimus. Various riddles, II, 231, 237, 354. Aenon, the place where John baptized, I, 494. The equinoxes: whence they are named and when they occur, II, 428. Air, what it is, II, 352. An era, what it is and who established it, II, 428. Eardwulfus [also Eardulfus], king, I, 67. Successor of Æthelred in the kingdom of Northumbria, 67. Recalled from exile to the throne, ibid. He mobilized an army against King Cenwulf of Mercia, 148.

Aericus, duke of Friuli (also called Henry, Eric, and Erich), I, 4. A venerable man, 46. Through him Alcuin sent a letter to Paulinus, ibid. Summer, what it is, II, 353. Whence it is named, 428. The ages of man, I, 500; II, 425. The ages of the world, what they are and how many, ibid.

Æthelred, bishop of Canterbury, I, 66. What “eternal” signifies, I, 178. Whether it is the same as “everlasting,” ibid. How it differs from “immortal,” ibid. “From perpetuity,” II, 510. It is understood in Scripture in three ways, I, 179. What Ethiopia signifies in Scripture, I, 766. How aeon and world-age are distinguished, I, 178. Affirmation, what it is, II, 352.

Africa, whence its name is derived, I, 327. It serves pestilential masters, II, 239. Hagar and Ishmael signify the carnal people of the Old Testament, I, 326. The Hagarenes, also called Saracens, I, 6. They rule in Africa and Asia, ibid. The punishment of Saint Agatha, II, 548. Her altar, 210, 212, 213. Aginnum, chief city of the Nitiobriges, I, 36. Aginus, to whom Alcuin wrote: a bishop of Bergamo or of Verona, I, 36, 46, note. The altar of Saint Agnes, II, 220. The source of a cognomen, II, 270. How the Paschal Lamb is to be eaten, I, 815. The use of lambs cast from blessed wax on Holy Saturday, 482.—Who instituted the singing of the Agnus Dei at Mass, II, 497. Why it is sung, 508.

Saint Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne, averted the flames from the city by his prayers, II, 240, note. He was King Oswald’s companion at table, 245. He blessed the king because of his generosity toward the needy, ibid. Saint Cuthbert saw his soul carried into heaven, 248. The priestly alb, and its significance, II, 495. Alberic, abbot of Der, II, 527, note. Albert, abbot and successor of Saint Willibrord, II, 193. Why the baptized are clothed in white garments, I, 110; II, 127, 483, 523. Albric, bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine, II, 449, note. When he died, ibid. Albuin the hermit: what he wrote, II, 526. He is not the author of the booklet on the Antichrist, ibid. King Alcfrith founded the monastery of Ripon, II, 184.

Alchard, bishop, I, 270. Whether he is the same as Alcheard or Elehard of Elmham, 271. He subscribed the Council of Clofesho, ibid. Alcuin now calls himself Flaccus, now Flaccus Albinus, now simply Albinus; in various places and letters he is written Alchuinus, Alquinus, and so forth. See the Historical Preface, volume I. He calls himself a levite, or deacon, I, 13, 17, 114, 130, and elsewhere; a veteran soldier, 96, 99, 137; an overseas swan, 129; Christ’s household servant, 143; a household servant of the holy Church of God, 154; a matricularius, 150, 260, 206; a matricularius of Saint Martin, 159.

Alcuin was born of noble lineage. See the Preface on his Life. He had brothers and sisters in England, I, 152, 153, note. He calls Aquila his brother, 114. In what sense, 111, 113, note, [Col. 1446] 135. He was educated and instructed in letters in the Church of York, I, 8, 64; II, 258. He later became a member of that Church, I, 9, 10. He was a pupil of Ecgberht, archbishop of York, I, 53, 54, note. He also had Aelbert, archbishop, as teacher, I, 64; II, 256. He accompanied him on a scholarly journey, I, 62. From him he received responsibility for the school and library, II, 257. He was heir to the treasures of his wisdom, I, 64.

As a young man he went to Rome and spent several days at Pavia, I, 126, note. There he listened to certain teachers, 86. He became master of the brothers of York, I, 8. Second after Aelbert, II, 242. He taught in Britain while learning flourished with the passage of time, I, 53. Whether at the academy of Cambridge, 56, note. By lawful succession he presided over the maritime cell where the body of Saint Wilgisi lay, II, 183, 184. He was entrusted with governing the congregation of Saint John the Baptist, I, 288. Which congregation this was, 289, note. He was learned in Hebrew and Greek. See the Preface on his Life.

A poet: what his poetry was, II, 201, 202. Whether he wrote on the art of meter, ibid. He wished his disciples to follow not his habits but his exhortations, I, 204. As a young man he wrote a letter to Daphnis, I, 408. He was summoned from the farthest boundaries of Britain to Charles, king of the Franks, I, 150. To defend the Catholic faith, I, 861, 882. To teach true wisdom in Francia, I, 150; II, 217. Coming from Britain, he was received by Charles, II, 217. He departed from Gaul for Britain, I, 7. There he was detained because of the novelty of the kingdom, 5. He returned to Gaul, 882.

He had outstanding friends and assistants throughout the whole island of Britain, 13, 17, 85. He wrote to Felix of Urgel with the pen of charity, I, 7, 757, 783, 789. He received Felix’s book addressed to him, I, 95. He labored to refute it, 96, 97, 124, 139. He sent to Lyons to recover another writing of Felix, I, 125. He informed the Irish that new sects had arisen in Spain, I, 285. He announced Felix’s errors to the abbots and monks of Gothia and refuted them, I, 760 ff. He attacked the same errors in seven other books, I, 783 ff. He had those books with him in the disputation at Aachen against Felix, 787 ff. He handed them over to Laidrad and his companions as assistance when they departed for Spain, 148. He submitted them to the judgment of King Charles, I, 124, 125, 787 ff. He excused any errors that might have crept in, 125.

The king summoned him to the palace to contend with Felix, I, 112, 113. He had a major dispute with him in the presence of the king and the holy Fathers, 148—namely, at the Council of Aachen, ibid. There he made Felix Catholic, 862, 878, 880, 882. He never disputed with Felix face to face except at the Council of Aachen, 788. His seven books against Felix were approved in the presence of the king and Christ’s priests, 882.

He urged Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, to abandon his errors, I, 860, 863 ff. Elipandus attacked him with insults and abuse, 860, 861, 868 ff. Alcuin cleared himself of Elipandus’s false accusation, 879, 881. He composed four books against him, 876 ff.; he sent and dedicated them to Laidrad and his companions as assistance, 860 ff., 862.

Alcuin was called “teacher” by many, I, 704. He was also called “preceptor” by King Charles, I, 180, 184, note; II, 234. What sciences he taught him, I, 704; II, 313. At what time, ibid., note. He was also a teacher of morals and piety, II, 2. He was always devoted to the Roman See, I, 30. He longed for the harbor of stability, I, 31. He left the royal palace, 67, 91. King Charles transferred him to the service of Saint Martin, I, 151. He desired to live and rest among the brothers of Saint Martin, 151. With his whole desire he chose to serve God alone at Saint Martin, ibid., 154. When he became abbot of Tours, ibid., 918. At Tours he taught various disciplines, 53. Already an old man, ibid. and 138. He wished a new Athens to be perfected in Francia, 102. He taught neither at Paris nor at Fulda, 54. Every day he struggled against the rusticity of Tours, 126. He strove to restore the distinctions of points, commas, and so forth, which had then been neglected, 126, 127. He desired the books he had left in his homeland, 53. He read the extensive and voluminous works and countless letters of the holy Fathers Jerome and Augustine, 893.

He obtained the cell of Saint Paul (Cormaricus) from Charles for the monastery of Saint Martin, II, 565. He introduced monks of Saint Benedict into it, ibid. and 135, 137. He built an oratory, 217. He ordered a small house to be prepared for the safekeeping of holy relics, II, 217. He restored sacred buildings, 217. His humble confession concerning himself, I, 48. His pure confession of sins, II, 63. His prayer concerning the knowledge of God, 78. His prayer at night, 126. While resting at Tours, he received a poem from Charles, 551. He gave thanks for the many benefits he had received from Charles from the time of his first arrival in Francia, I, 157. He complained about the scarcity of lovers of philosophy and arithmetic, I, 94.

He was intimate with Benedict of Aniane, I, 272, 273. He wrote several letters to him, ibid. His generosity toward guests, I, 67. He sent two table vessels to Arno, 168. Other gifts to the same man, 148. Others to Simeon, 67. He refused to arrange a new missal booklet, ibid. He was joined by intimate love to Paulinus of Aquileia, II, 230. He defended the brothers of Saint Martin against the violence of the bishop of Orléans, I, 169, 260. He cleared himself of slander, 261. He was received into the fellowship of the household of Saint Peter of Corbie, 206. He sent a storax-colored cloak and a missal sheet to the people of Fulda, I, 157. He did not write it at the request of Saint Boniface or for priests newly converted to the faith, ibid. He formed a friendship with the abbot and brothers of Mont-Olivier, I, 288. He received gifts from Arno, 129, 161, 257. He desired holy relics to be brought to him from Rome, II, 456.

He was to be sent to Offa of Mercia for the sake of peace, I, 6. Why he thought it better to remain on his pilgrimage, 57. He declares that he had never been unfaithful to Offa or to the English people, 11. He sent his dearest son to Offa to be taught the sciences, 57. He was summoned to the election of the archbishop of York, 62. But he was prevented from coming, 63. He instructed the elected Eanbald in the episcopal office, ibid. He visited the monastery of Centula with King Charles, II, 175.

His journey to Saint-Amand, Baralla, and other places, I, 67. To Gysla, Saint-Loup, and Ferrières, 68. To Saint Martin and elsewhere, 69, 70. Again to Saint-Amand, 127. From the palace to Baralla, 148. He traveled through the breadth of Belgica, 102, 103. He awaited Arno at the house of Saint Martin, 159.

Alcuin praised Charles for his concern to spread the faith and offered excellent advice for this purpose, I, 37. He received gifts from him, 93. Invited to appear before the king, he excused himself, I, 92, 154. He was informed of Pope Leo’s arrival in Francia, 119. He urged Charles to avenge the crime committed against the pope, 117, 119. He refused to go to Rome, 120. He was prevented by ill health, 134. He replied to Charles when the latter reproached him for this, 138. He sent his own boys instead, ibid.

He urged Charles to remove the vices increasing in the kingdom and Church, II, 229. Summoned to the palace, he could not come because of illness, I, 154, 158, 160, 247. He accompanied Charles, who was going to Spain, with prayers and verses, II, 229. With him he traveled from Tours to Aachen, I, 239. He consoled Charles over the death of Queen Liudgard, I, 132. He eagerly awaited Charles’s return from Italy, 150. He sent the boy Candidus with little gifts to meet him, 151. He dedicated his services during the holidays to Charles’s honor, II, 4.

He wrote on arithmetic, astronomy, music, the art of meter, and almost all the sciences, II, 264. On orthography, 301 ff. The book On the Seven Liberal Arts is not his, II, 263. His grammar is praised, 265. He wrote the Breviary, or prayers for the hours, at Charles’s request, 52. Many letters, many of which are still missing, I, 2, 273, 274. He committed to the fire Arno’s letter concerning the conduct of the apostolic man, Pope Leo. Why he did so, I, 135. At the command of King Charles he corrected the divine books and brought them together into one body, 59! He offered them to the king through Nathanael, 154, 248.

He dedicated the Questions on Genesis to his companion Sigulf, 305. He wrote on the blessing of the patriarchs under the name of Samuel and his fellow student, 304. He dedicated the Enchiridion on the Psalms to Arno, 342. Whether he was the author of the Hymn on the Fifteen Psalms of Ascents, 389. He sent a Commentary on Ecclesiastes to Arno for copying, 161, 162. Whether he was the author of the Commentary on the Song of Songs, 391 ff. He wrote on the genealogy of Christ’s humanity, 447. Whether he also wrote a Commentary on the whole Gospel of Saint Matthew, ibid. He wrote commentaries on John while at Tours, 461. At what time he completed them, 457, 460. As Easter approached, he initially sent the last two books to Gysla and Columba, 591. From which teachers he compiled those commentaries, 464. A passage there was corrupted by heretics, 528. Whether he wrote on all the evangelists, 458.

He wrote commentaries on some, not all, of Saint Paul’s Epistles, 649. He promised Arno that he would treat the basis of the Catholic faith, 161. He wrote books on the Trinity, where and when, 168, note, 702. He sent them to Arno, 168. Whether he wrote on the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, 743. He dedicated the book On the Virtues to Count Guido, II, 128 ff. When he wrote the booklet On the Reason of the Soul for Eulalia, 151. He wrote, abridged, or corrected the Lives of certain saints, II, 156. Antiphons, responsories, and hymns concerning Saint Richarius that have perished, 158. Whether he was the author of Saint Richarius’s epitaph, ibid.; for the text, see II, 458. He wrote the Life of Saint Willibrord in Francia, 191, note. In what year, 158.

He sent to Arno a letter on confession written for the brothers of Saint Martin, I, 168, 169. Through Fredegis he directed to the same man a handbook containing many things: Expositions on the Psalms, Bede’s Short Psalter, and so forth, I, 169. He was the author of the poem on the Bishops and Saints of the Church of York, II, 241 ff. Whether he was the author of the confession of faith published by D. Chifflet, 369, 370. The Breviary of Faith against the Arians is not his, ibid. Nor is the booklet on the parts of speech, 370. Whether he was the author of the disputation of boys through questions and answers, 418. Whether he was the author of the poem on the cell of Cormaricus, 456, note, or of another poem on Aristotle’s Categories, 334. Whether he wrote any homilies, 531. He is not the author of the commonly circulated Homiliary, 459. Nor of the book called the Comes, ibid. Nor of the Caroline Books, ibid. He refutes Heumann’s contrary opinion, 460. He did not write the Life of Saint Judoc, ibid. Nor the booklet on the Antichrist, 526.

After laying aside the occupations of the world, he desired to serve God alone, I, 228. Cast down into the harbor of rest, [Col. 1448] I, 142. Freed from the noise of the world, 159, 163. He sat quietly at Saint Martin’s, having laid down the burden of pastoral care, 148. With the king’s consent he chose assistants from among his disciples, ibid. He freed himself from the turmoil of this age, 162.—He suffered from headaches, I, 125. He was feverish, 63, 96, 124, 134, 148, 206, 280. Illness prevented him from meeting the king returning from Italy, 151. And from coming to the king and his daughter Gysla, 149. He was somewhat better after his illness, 67, 157. His illnesses increased daily, 157. As the disease worsened, he desired to remain at Saint Martin’s, 157. In his bent old age he was beset by continual fever, 162. Broken by years and illnesses, 228. After much scourging he was brought to despair of life, 157.—For more on Alcuin, see his Life, prefixed to these works, and the testimonies of the ancients, where the material is presented more fully and in better order.

Aldric, Alcuin’s disciple and later abbot of Ferrières, I, 130. Sent to Elnon to strengthen discipline, ibid. Aldulf (Aduulf), bishop of Lichfield, invested with the pallium, I, 81. The correspondence between Alexander, king of the Macedonians, and Dindimus, king of the Brahmans, in letters, II, 600 ff. Alfleda. See Elfleda. Alfordus is corrected, I, 67. Alfrida, I, 211. Alfrida, sister of Alfleda and daughter of King Offa, also called Etheldritha, 67. Alfwin, brother of King Ecgfrith, killed in battle, II, 249. Alimus, bishop of Savona, I, 112, 113, 136.

The category “relation,” and its properties, II, 340. Alleluia: what it is, whence the word comes, and why it is sung at Mass, II, 499. Why it is not sung from Septuagesima until Easter, 466, 468. Almachius, martyr, II, 464. Alric, king of Kent, I, 81. Christ’s altar must be treated honorably, I, 184.—Altars neglected in some places because they are without a roof, ibid. Altars adorned as in ancient times, II, 550.—What the stripping of the altars on Thursday of Holy Week signifies, II, 478.

Altfrid succeeded his brother Ecgfrith in the kingdom of Northumbria, II, 250, verse 842. Learned in sacred and secular studies, verse 843. He died, verse 1079. Althelmus, bishop of the West Saxons, II, 546, note. Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, wrote a letter on the ceremonies of baptism to Charlemagne, II, 517. Maritime verses, 520. Amalgar, a vassal of Saint Martin sent by Alcuin to calm the disturbance that had arisen there over the case of the cleric of Orléans, I, 162.

Amandus, Saint, I, 71. His death and virtues, II, 209.—The church and tomb of Saint Amandus, II, 208, 209. Altar, 211, 213. Monastery, I, 67; II, 562. Prayer to him, II, 208. Verses about him, ibid. Although ambition is a vice, it is nevertheless frequently the cause of virtue, II, 328.

Ambrose, Saint, a most courageous fighter against heretical depravity, I, 901. His sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, cited by Alcuin, is unknown, 777. His prayer for forgiveness of sins, II, 79. Another, 81. Hymn for the sick, 86. “Amen”: what it is and its interpretation, I, 551; II, 499, 506, 507. Friendship, what it is, II, 354. Friend, who he is and whence the word comes, I, 97. Who is a true friend, 203. The faithful friend is commended, II, 145.—There are many friends in prosperity, few in adversity, I, 224.

The vestment called the amict of the priests of the old and new law, II, 493, 494. Amminadab, what it signifies, I, 450, 451, 453. Ammon, what it signifies, I, 450, 452, 454. How the almond, locust, and caper suit an old man, I, 444. Analogy, what it is, II, 271. Saint Benedict raised the monastery of Aniane at his own expense, I, 273. Anastasius, martyr, II, 218.—Pope Anastasius, II, 497.—What Anastasius the Librarian thinks about those who err concerning the truth of the Eucharist, II, 378. What Anatolius of Alexandria thinks about the change in the moon’s age, II, 360. What he thinks about the first month of the first year, 367.

The congregation of Saint Andrew, I, 196. Oratory, II, 184. Church, 214. Altar, 211, 217.—Verses about Saint Andrew, II, 209, 221. Andromachus, Jewish historiographer, II, 366. The *Stromata* of Angelomus, abbot of Luxeuil, on the Song of Songs, I, 392. “Angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature, I, 667.—Why Moses passed over the creation and fall of the angels in silence, II, 410.—Whether the angelic nature was created at the same time as unformed matter, II, 409, 410. What Saint Jerome thought about their creation before the formation of this visible world, I, 651.—The angelic nature fell into sin, I, 724; II, 405.—Why the sin of the angels is passed over in silence in Genesis, I, 305.—Why it is incurable, ibid.—The good angels are made unchangeable in goodness by God’s power, II, 405.—The fall of the angels was pride, I, 107.—“Angel” used of Christ in Scripture, I, 325.—Angels, when appearing to human beings, assume a body, I, 321. Through them God speaks to human beings, 722. They visit the canonical hours and brotherly congregations, 282, 283. They fight against the aerial powers, not by labor but by command, II, 501.

Angilbert, I, 36. His assumed name was Homer, 31, 32. Also Flaccus Homer, 33. See Homer. First secretary of King Pippin’s palace, I, 32. Secretary of royal power, 26. A poet, II, 552, note. He married Berta, daughter of Charlemagne, I, 32, note. He withdrew to the monastery of Centula, ibid. He went to Rome, 35. Abbot of Saint Richarius, II, 175. Sent by King Charles to Pope Adrian, I, 25, 26, note. He brought Felix of Urgel to Rome, 32, note. He carried the acts of the Council of Frankfurt there, ibid. Sent to Pope Leo, 31. Alcuin requested holy relics from him, I, 32. He built the roof of Saint Richarius, II, 552. He gave everything he had to the church, ibid. His prayer-poem to Saints Richarius and Eligius, ibid. His three letters to a certain bishop, II, 562. His death, I, 32, note.

Angilram, archbishop, I, 27. First officer of the Holy Chapel, ibid. Bishop of Metz, 28, note. He began to adorn the tomb of Saint Nabor, II, 215. His death, I, 28, note; II, 215, note.

England devastated by pagans and stained with the blood of its lords and princes, I, 57. The peoples and nation of the English, I, II, 59.—The English and Saxons came to Britain: in what year, I, 16, note.—The ancient lineage of the kings of the English failed, I, 78. Their kings are now of uncertain origin, ibid.

Anianus, bishop of Orléans, II, 218.—The altar of Saint Anianus, II, 224. The monastery of Aniane, chief of the others in Septimania, I, 141.

The soul, whence it is named, II, 421. Whether it is the same as spirit, ibid., 149. How it can be defined, ibid. What its nature is, 407. Whether there are two souls in one person, ibid. The origin of souls, whence it comes, 150, 407. Whether they are propagated with bodies, I, 332, 445. Whether they exist before a human being is born, 422.—The soul is not corporeal, II, 149, 150. It is not part of the divine nature, ibid. and 407. It is wholly active throughout the body, 419, 420. It governs the body through the five senses, 149. It is swift in forming ideas, 148. From known species it forms unknown ones, ibid. It does not think of several things at one moment, ibid. It shares in the body’s pains, I, 854. The only noble soul is the one that loves God, II, 146. It is signified by the Samaritan woman, I, 501, 502.

The nature of the soul is threefold, II, 146. Its four superior virtues, ibid. Its perpetual ornaments, 267. The order of things to be done, 331. Its beauty is virtue; its deformity, vice, 149, 150. What its life and death are, II, 148. What its blessedness is, 149. Few know its nature, 146.—The soul is ennobled by the image and likeness of its Creator, II, 147. It is glorified by its Creator with two dignities, 148. It bears the image of the Holy Trinity within itself, and what that image is, I, 139; II, 147, 420. It becomes vile and deformed by withdrawing from God, 147. It can lose blessedness, but not eternity, 149. It did not sin before union with the body, 407.

Whether Christ’s soul has full knowledge of his divinity, I, 719. And how he is said not to know the day of judgment, ibid. It was never separated from the Word from the moment the Word became flesh, I, 884.—By what wings souls are carried to heavenly blessedness, I, 47.—Some doubted whether the souls of the saints are received into heaven before the day of judgment, I, 147. Where they were kept before Christ’s Ascension, II, 408.

How all the animals entered the ark, I, 313. They prefigured the Church, 633. What should be thought about their nourishment, 314.
