Why land animals have more of the curse than aquatic animals, ibid.—The souls of animals, what they are, II, 407. Concerning the animals signifying the four evangelists, II, 204. Whether mind and soul are the same, II, 421.—The nature of the mind in the heart, as that of the eyes in the head, II, 265.

Anniversary days customarily celebrated for the dead, II, 512, 513. A year, what it is, II, 353. And whence it is named, 428. The lunar, solar, and great year, ibid.—How many seasons the year has, ibid. Its guides and palaces, 353.—From which month the lawful year should begin, I, 90, 91.

The conjectures of an anonymous author against Alcuin’s confession of faith are refuted, II, 373 ff. Ansfrid, bishop, II, 218.

[Col. 1450]

The Anthropomorphite heretics are mistaken, II, 388. Why the Antichrist is so called, II, 528. From what people and from whom, and how, he will be born, I, 338; II, 528. Where he will be nourished, ibid. He is signified by the horned serpent, I, 338. What ministers he will have, II, 528. When he will be revealed, 529. He will be attacked by Elijah and Enoch, I, 734; II, 530. What end he will have, ibid., note. Antiphon, what it is and by whom it was invented, II, 498. Antistes, what it is and whence the word comes, II, 492.

Antonius, I, 296.—Antonius, the assumed name of Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, I, 205, 206, note. Alcuin sent him a letter through Homer, 35. See Adalhard. Aper, abbot of Nobiliacum, and his tomb, II, 214, note. The Apocalypse: by whom, when, and where it was written, II, 433. What it contains, 434.—Alcuin wrote a commentary on the Apocalypse, II, 612. To whom verses were formerly attributed, ibid. The Apocrypha, what writings are so called, II, 434. The error of Apollinaris condemned, II, 401. Apollinaris, Saint, a teacher, II, 219. Apollos, the person about whom Paul writes, who he was, I, 660.

The Apostles are Christ’s eyes, I, 337; hunters, 338; stones of good pleasure, 356; roads by which one comes to life, 362; the twelve hours of the day, 573; arrows, 383. According to the canons, the Apostolic See is judicial, not subject to judgment, I, 134. Its exalted dignity, 117. Appia, whom Paul calls his dearest sister, I, 661, 662. Apringius, bishop of Beja, wrote a commentary on the Apocalypse, II, 593. The origin and remarkable nature of bees, I, 814.

Water, what it is, II, 353.—The movement of the water in the pool, what it means, I, 508.—Living water in the Gospel, what it means, I, 501.—Why water is mixed with wine at Mass, I, 107, 108; II, 500.—Where the waters returned after the Flood, I, 315.—Whether and how fresh waters flowing into the sea are consumed, I, 414.—The power of water blessed by Saint Willibrord, II, 191.

Aquila went from Rome to Saxony to see Leo, I, 123 and note.—Aquila, a bishop. See Arno. What the north wind signifies, II, 499. The basilica at Aachen, magnificently built by Charlemagne, I, 99.—The public assembly at Aachen, I, 162, note. Aquitaine, a province of Charlemagne’s kingdom, II, 566. Aram, what it signifies, I, 450, 451, 453. Arborius, a prefect, II, 160. Noah’s ark, I, 312. What mystery its dimensions contain, 313.

Archanbald, archbishop and Alcuin’s fellow student, I, 40, 41, note. See Eanbald. The altar of the holy archangels, II, 224. An archdeacon is ordained as a deacon, II, 493. Who the chief steward at the wedding in Cana of Galilee was, I, 483. Who is to be understood by him, II, 465. Archippus, whom Paul calls his fellow soldier, who he was, I, 661. Why the rainbow was placed in the sky as a sign of security, and why it has different colors, I, 315.

Ardbert, an illustrious man, I, 271. Whether he is the same as Heardbert, the duke, 272, note. Alcuin commends the venerable abbot Lui to him, ibid. Aredius, Saint, I, 265. Sand, what it is, II, 353. Whom it signifies, I, 318, 415. Argubium, what place it is and where it is situated, II, 158. Argument and the species and variety of arguments, II, 323, 344, 347. The ram, what it signifies in Scripture, I, 319. From Isaac…
sacrificed, where it comes from, 325. Arigius, duke of Benevento, I, 156. Aristarchus, co-worker of Saint Paul, I, 664. The notable saying of Aristippus the philosopher when shipwrecked, I, 185. Aristotle is said, while writing the books *On Interpretation*, to have dipped his pen in his mind, I, 47, 350. What arithmetic is, II, 232. Its usefulness, I, 87. Necessary for understanding the divine Scriptures, 94. —Arithmetical propositions for sharpening the minds of young men, II, 441. How perversely Arius thinks about the Son of God, I, 562; II, 573. He stained East and West with his poison, I, 870. He perished by an impious death, 894. —The Arian heresy, I, 571, 881, 888, 894. Golden bracelets sent by Luidgarda to Paulinus the patriarch, I, 35, 36, note.

Arno, bishop of Salzburg, I, 5, 134. He is called archbishop, Letter 105, 141, 143, 144, 145, 146. “Supreme watcher,” Letter 87. “Chief priest,” Letter 155. “Chief watcher,” Letter 161. Supreme priest, I, 342. Alcuin’s father in merit, brother in affection, son in age, [Col. 1451] I, 111, 240, 253. His brother in affection, 127. Alcuin’s disciple, II, 232. Educated from childhood in the canonical life and regular discipline, I, 161. Alcuin loves him above all the bishops, 160, 161. He was deeply attached to him, 167. He writes many letters to Alcuin, 104, 105, 113, 128, 134, 152, and elsewhere. He writes one to him concerning the conduct of an apostolic man; Alcuin burned it, 135. He asked Alcuin to instruct him concerning the canonical life, regular discipline, and secular judgment, 161. Abbot of the brothers of Juvavum, 116. Abbot of Elnon, II, 208, note. He renews the church of Saint Michael, ibid., and the tomb of Saint Amandus, 209; and dedicates the cemetery of the brothers at Elnon, 217. Bishop of Salzburg, he travels to Rome to settle disputes, I, 68, note. There he wishes to secure metropolitan rank, ibid. He returns from Italy, 70, note. He was chosen among the royal emissaries, 164, note. He expresses to Alcuin his anguish of mind over secular service, 148. He goes as a preacher into Hunnia, accompanied by the army, 104. He receives from King Charles a third part of the fruits of his labors, ibid. He visits Alcuin, I, 130. Alcuin awaits him in the house of Saint Martin, 159. He was frequently in Rome, 148, note. He receives the pallium from the Apostolic See, 112, 121. He is asked to reconcile the dissenting ecclesiastical persons at Rome, 153. As he returns from Italy, Alcuin sends him two letters, 161. Two others to the palace, ibid. Whether he accompanied Pope Leo from Rome to Saxony, 126, note. He is praised for the fervor of his faith and his gifts of charity, 342. Alcuin dedicates to him the *Enchiridion on the Psalms*, ibid. He sends Alcuin a chasuble for the solemn celebration of Masses, 167, 168. He receives two table vessels from Alcuin, ibid. He sends gifts to Alcuin, 148. Likewise, he receives from Alcuin a little cloak, a tent, and a cup, 157.

Arnold, abbot, I, 290. Who he was and of which monastery is unknown, 291, note. Arnonus (Arnobius), a man of keen intellect, I, 845. Arnulf, abbot of the monastery of Glons, successor of Albaldus and disciple of Benedict of Aniane, I, 291, note. Arnulf, brother, II, 213. What *Arsanoquita* is, II, 492, note. Who the haruspices were, II, 472. Whether Ascaricus was bishop of Braga, 590, 591. The solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension, II, 487. Asia oppressed by pagans, II, 239. What the she-ass and her colt mystically signify, I, 582. The Assumption is not the same as adoption, I, 864. What the asterisk is as a sign, II, 271. Who the astrologers were, II, 464. —What astrology is, II, 332. —Astrological prediction formerly prohibited to Christians, II, 464. What astronomy is, II, 332. The right of asylum of holy places is defended, I, 170 ff. The monks of Athanacum, I, 111. Athanasius, a devoted soldier of the Church, II, 218. Always devoted to his teacher, Bishop Alexander, I, 750. The symbol *Quicumque* is attributed to him, ibid., 756, as is also his disputation with Arius, 755. —Whether a letter of Athanasius to Potamius, cited by Alcuin, still exists, 778, note. Athelard, archbishop. See Aedilhard. Athelred (Edelred), son of Athelwold, emerged from prison to take the throne, I, 5. Athelwold (Ethelwold, Adelwald), father of Athelred, king of the Northumbrians, I, 5, note. A new and more excellent Athens is to arise in Francia, I, 102. Ato, abbot of the monastery of Nobiliacum, II, 212, note; 213, 214. Successor of Aper, 214. He built the church of Saint Lambert, 212, note. He erected an altar at the graves of the dead, so that sacrifice might be celebrated for them, 214, note. The city of Arras, II, 168. It was plundered by the Huns, ibid. Fortified by the protection of Saint Vedastus, 172. —Saint Vedastus, bishop of Arras, II, 168. Gerard, 377. —The Synod of Arras against certain Italians erring in the faith, II, 377. —Inscriptions of the church of Arras, II, 209. What an atrium is, I, 389. Attila, king of the Huns, plundered Arras, II, 168. Ava, sister, is commended to Gisla’s prayers, I, 149. She orders a sacred book to be written, II, 205. What avarice is and what its offspring are, II, 142, 472. How it is conquered and healed, ibid. Description of the Avar, I, 425. His misery, 426, 427; II, 138. —The frauds of the Avars are condemned, II, 138. The Avars (Huns) defeated and scattered in Italy and Bavaria, I, 6. They promise the faith of Christianity, 45. Their envoys are sent to Charlemagne concerning peace and submission, ibid. —What happened in Avaria, Alcuin investigates from Arno, I, 39. And he is informed by the same man, 40. Hearing, a sense: why it is so called, II, 421. Altar of Saint Audoin, II, 210. Audomarus, bishop of Thérouanne, II, 171. [Col. 1452] The monastery of Saint Augendus (Saint Eugendus), I, 345. Its abbot, Manno, ibid. Who the augurs were, II, 472. Auguries, sneezing, and similar practices are to be prohibited, I, 198. The book of Saint Augustine on catechizing the unlearned is commended, I, 38. Sermons on the Gospel of Saint John read by women, 461. His letter to Hilary and Prosper is unknown, I, 797, note; 798, note. Certain other books of his that are cited and unknown, 806, note. Saint Augustine of Canterbury introduced the education of boys into England, I, 66. The first preacher there, 79. Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, I, 170. —What the canons of the Synods of Orléans decree concerning fugitives to the church, I, 172. What the ear cut off from Malchus signifies, I, 623. —What the ears are, II, 353. —Why the ears of the baptized are touched, II, 522. What the dawn of day is, II, 233. Gold benefits the giver, not the possessor, I, 127. Ausonia, I, 146. What the south wind signifies, II, 499. Austria, “the kingdom of kingdoms,” I, 870. Saint Autbert, bishop of Arras, transfers Saint Vedastus, II, 171. He wrote a homily on the Lord’s Presentation, 539. What autumn is, II, 353. From where it gets its name, 428. Why it abounds in diseases, ibid. Auxentius the heretic, II, 159. The river Axona (Aisne), II, 166. What Aza signifies, I, 450, 451, 454. What Azor is, I, 450, 452, 455. What the days of Unleavened Bread are, I, 625.

## B

The city and tower of Babylon: whether they were one and the same work, I, 317. Bavaria, I, 41. See Baugaria.

Bala the maidservant: whether she should be called a wife or a concubine, I, 328.

Description of the baths at Aachen constructed by Charlemagne, I, 248. — Description of a hot bath, II, 237.

What the belt is, II, 494. Its mystical interpretation, 495.

Balther, priest and hermit, II, 254, verse 1318 and note. Where his desert or monastery was situated, 255, note. He fights against demonic assaults, verse 1325. His visions and miracles, verse 1332. When he lived, 254, note.

The time for baptizing in antiquity, II, 483. — Why no one ought to be baptized on the feast of Epiphany, II, 465.

How a person to be baptized in adulthood ought to be instructed, I, 38, 42, 50. — Even one baptized by a heretic ought not to be rebaptized, I, 490.

Why the baptized person is clothed in white garments, I, 110, 127; II, 123. Why he is confirmed with the body and blood of the Lord, ibid. He ought immediately to be confirmed by the bishop who is present, II, 484. — Why the head of the baptized person is anointed with chrism, I, 110, 127; II, 523.

There is one baptism, I, 109; II, 486. It must not be repeated, I, 490; II, 406, 516. It is to be administered not in the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but in one name, I, 109. — How many kinds and degrees of baptism there are, II, 482. The ceremonies and order are explained, I, 109; II, 127, 483, 484, 520 and following. Sponsors, 483. — Alcuin argues that a triple immersion should be performed in baptism, I, 108, 147. Nevertheless, a triple invocation of the Holy Trinity should not be made, ibid. and II, 484. — In the sacrament of baptism there are three visible and three invisible things, I, 42, 604. — How the baptism of newly converted peoples ought to be performed, I, 38. — Baptism of infants, I, 38, 42, 659. Of little children who cannot speak, 547; II, 523. It is necessary, II, 407. Those who have not been baptized are alienated from the kingdom of Christ after death, 486. — Baptism reforms us according to the image of the Creator, II, 520. — In baptism the Word cleanses the water, I, 603. What agreements are made, II, 486. — Through baptism both original and actual sins are forgiven, II, 406.

The baptism of Christ, I, 733; II, 464. In what it differs from the baptism of John, I, 733, 810, 865.

Baralla, a village: where it was situated, I, 67, 148. A small dwelling of Saint Martin, ibid., note.

What the beard is, II, 353.

What barbarism is, II, 271.

Baronius corrected, I, 26.

The altar of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, II, 219. A poem concerning it, 222.

Who Basiliscus, Elipandus’s opponent, was, II, 596.

Basnage’s criticisms against Mabillon are censured, II, 381. His criticisms against Canisius are examined, 450.

The body of Saint Bathildis is transferred to a new basilica built by Gisla in the monastery at Chelles, I, 148.

Baturicus, bishop of Regensburg, a contemporary of Alcuin, I, 457.

At Bangaria the Avars or Huns were defeated and scattered, I, 6.

Baugulf, abbot of Fulda. See Bonulfus.

The altar of Saint Bavo, II, 216.

[Column 1453]

What true blessedness consists in, I, 383; II, 266. — The summit of blessedness is to see God, I, 158, 237. — No one can attain true blessedness except through the Catholic faith, I, 706, 707. — The doubt of certain people concerning the blessedness of the saints before the day of judgment is refuted, I, 147.

Beatus, abbot, I, 793. Whether he was a Benedictine monk, II, 592. Teacher of Bishop Etherius, II, 592. He is attacked by Elipandus, I, 868, 869, 870. What other writings he left, II, 592. He wrote on the Apocalypse, 593. Whether he alone is the author of the work against Elipandus, 592. Where that work is still preserved, ibid. What the condition of its manuscript is, 590. It is stubbornly guarded by the people of Toledo, 589. — Beatus’s commentary on the Apocalypse, II, 593. It must not be confused with the similar commentary of Apringius, bishop of Beja, ibid. Its manuscript copies are catalogued, ibid. and following. — The Acts of Beatus: from where they were transcribed, II, 591.

Bebban, a city in Northumbria, II, 240, note. There, in the church of Saint Peter, the incorrupt right hand of Saint Oswald is buried, 245, verse 305.

Bede, the teacher, I, 100; II, 254, verse 1304. Alcuin of his own time calls him “teacher,” 22, 23, note. He also calls him his own teacher, 282. A monk under the discipline of Benedict and Ceolfrith, 23, note. At the age of seven he was entrusted to the monastery of Jarrow, II, 254, verse 1292.

He wrote the Life of Saint Cuthbert in prose and in heroic verse, II, 240, 248, verse 684, 249, verse 743; a history of the English from the nation’s earliest origin, II, 253, verse 1207; a hymn in praise of Æthelthryth, 249, verse 780; a short Psalter, I, 169; II, 96 and following; a treatise on the Apostolic Epistles, I, 205. Alcuin sent that treatise to his sister and daughter, 251. His other works are catalogued, II, 254, verse 1305.

Whether the commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, included among his works, belongs to him, I, 458. What he thought about the daily creation of souls, I, 510. A saying of his concerning the presence of angels at the canonical hours is reported, 282. Through his relics a sick man was delivered from the plague, II, 254, verse 1316. When he died, ibid., verse 1287 and following. See our historical Preface.

Begnod, a friend of Alcuin, appointed together with Sacen to instruct a certain household, I, 200.

Bezalel, learned in the waters of Helias, II, 228.

The dry fields of Belgium, I, 102. There was the village or cell of Saint Josse, 103.

The blessing of canons, II, 20. — Various blessings, II, 18. — How the blessings of the patriarch Jacob are to be understood, I, 334.

Saint Benedict, a great shepherd and outstanding father, II, 551. — The Rule of Saint Benedict is to be explained in the community’s own language, I, 22. His reply is cited from the Rule, 130. His prayer, II, 84. Altar, 210, 218. Church, 225. — The office of Saint Benedict, II, 525. — A poem addressed to Saint Benedict, II, 233.

Benedict Biscop built the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow, I, 23, note.

Benedict and Ceolfrith, 21, 23, note, 283.

Benedict, abbot, established regular monastic life in the monastery at Aniane in Gothia, I, 135, 273. Reformer of monasteries, especially in Aquitaine, 268. Alcuin received brothers from him for the monastery at Cormaric, 135. He sent twenty monks for the monastery of the Barbarian Island, 272. He frequently visited the palace and Alcuin himself, 268, note. He was sent with Leidrad and Nefridius to Spain, 148, 268. Alcuin dismissed him from his presence with tears, 267. Through him Alcuin sent the monks of Gothia a booklet against the errors of the Adoptionists, 139. He was also commended by him to Bishop Nifridus, 267. Alcuin wrote many letters to him, 272, 273.

Beneito, Aurelius, dean of the Church of Toledo, II, 588.

The Beneventan homeland or land, I, 155. A hostile expedition against it, ibid. and 156, note. Count Chrodgarius was sent with Pippin to devastate it, 157 and note. Alcuin interceded for it, 155. — The Beneventan controversy, I, 157. — The Beneventan monastery of Saint Peter, called *Ad Corpus*, I, 156, note. — The Beneventan dukes Arichis, Grimoald, and Romuald, I, 156. Arichis and Romuald were removed after only a brief interval, ibid., note.

From what places the goodwill of the audience is won, II, 320.

Beornradus (Beornredus, Berneradus), from abbot of Echternach to archbishop of Sens, II, 158, 183, note. He wrote letters to Alcuin, ibid. At his request Alcuin wrote the Life of Saint Willibrord, ibid. When he lived, ibid., note.

Beornwinus, an English priest, a man of great authority, I, 11, note.

The monks of Berg are commended to Bishop Macarius, II, 232.

[Column 1454]

Berger, Johann Wilhelm’s dissertation on the learning of Carolingian Saxony is mentioned, II, 265.

Bernarius, brother of Adalhard, a monk of Lérins, I, 206, note. He was summoned with his abbot to the palace, ibid. He was transferred to Corbie, ibid., note. By the emperor Louis he was driven into exile with his brothers and his sister Gundrada and sent back to Lérins, ibid. He is numbered among the saints of Lérins, ibid.

Bertus, a distinguished bishop, II, 218.

Bezalel, an intimate of Charles and a familiar helper of Alcuin, I, 126. Eginhard is called by this name, 127, note.

Bethany, a city on the slope of the Mount of Olives; it is interpreted as “house of obedience,” I, 475. It signifies the Church, 579.

What Bathsheba signifies, I, 450, 451, 453.

Bethsaida, “house of winds,” I, 479.

Description of the old library of York, II, 257, verse 1535 and following.

Where the leap year is so called and where it originates, II, 365 and following, 367. — Certain matters concerning the leap year, I, 124.

Temporal goods were created by God, II, 516. — In temporal goods, it is not possession but use that should be considered, ibid. — The vanity of the goods of this age, II, 266.

The brothers of Saint Boniface at Fulda, I, 254. See the brothers of Fulda. The tomb, 255. Alcuin sent a storax-colored pallium to cover his body, ibid. — Alcuin sent the Mass of Saint Boniface to the men of Fulda, I, 157. — Verses on Saint Boniface and his companions, II, 220.

In what Bonosus was mistaken, I, 573.

Bonulfus (Baugulfus), abbot of Fulda and a friend of Alcuin, I, 157. A letter of Charles to him is catalogued, ibid., note.

What Boaz signifies, I, 450, 451, 454.

Why the ox is better than the lion, I, 315.

Bosa, a bishop, presided over the Church of York, II, 250, verse 846 and note. A monk, ibid., verse 848. He established the common life, verse 865 and following. He died joyfully, verse 874.

The arm of the Lord is called the Son of God: how, I, 587.

Brequigny, a member of the Royal Academy of Paris, communicated letters discovered in England, I, column 138. His letters concerning this matter, ibid.

The Bretons. See Britons, Britanni.

The Breviary of the Psalter: whether Saint Jerome was its author, I, 798.

The altar of Saint Briccius, II, 219.

Saint Brigid of Scotland, II, 219.

The causes of the calamities of the islands of Britain, I, 15. The death and destruction of its kings, 20, note, 74. Its shores devastated by pagans, 78. — The island of Britain, once celebrated for its multitude of teachers, now has few laborers in the Lord’s harvest, I, 269. From there many depart to preach the Gospel to foreign peoples, II, 251, verse 1007.

The Britons on this side of the sea were subdued by Charles, I, 139, note.

The nation of the Britons is sluggish, II, 240. It is harassed by the Picts and summons the Saxons to its aid, ibid.

“Bruma,” in Greek, means “gluttony,” II, 428.

Bugga, daughter of King Eadwulf, II, 549. She built a church with beautiful workmanship, ibid. Whether she is the same woman whose letter to Saint Boniface survives, ibid., note.

Buitta, the faithful messenger of the priest Cudrad, I, 224.

Burgundy, a province of Charlemagne, II, 566.

Wine vessels of the Butrists (Buttists), II, 215, note.

What byssus signifies, II, 494.

## C
Cadaloc was killed together with Goteram at the fortress of Guntion, I, 165, note. Cadwala, attacked by Saint Oswald, fell, II, 244, verse 262. The man blind from birth signifies the human race, I, 557. — The healing of the blind man through spittle is explained mystically, I, 158. The suffering of Saint Cecilia the virgin, II, 548. Her altar, II, 210, 212. What ceremonies are, II, 436. From where the term *caesaries* is derived, II, 422. Caidoc, an Irish priest distinguished for holiness, II, 176. He came with his companion Frichorius to the regions of Pontiva, ibid. Angilbert wrote the epitaph of him and his companion, ibid. Abbot Gervinus raised the bodies of both from the earth, ibid.

Why Cain’s sacrifice was rejected, I, 306, 311. Josephus writes that Caiaphas had bought back from Herod the priesthood, which he held for only one year, I, 623. What the woman’s heel is, I, 310. A chalice made of gold and silver for the service of the altar, I, 915. — A golden chalice covered with gems for celebrating Mass, II, 550. What Calvary is, II, 422. Calwinus, I, 75, 148. An English presbyter in the church at York, [Col. 1455] 76. Whether he was a monk, 77. He presided over the cell of Saint Stephen, 75.

Why the use of bells ceases on the Lord’s Supper, II, 476. The whole of Champagne venerates Saint Remigius, II, 194. Campolus, a religious man, II, 559. Who he was, 560, note. What Cana of Galilee signifies, I, 482. Candidus, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 24, 69, 169. By another name Witto, 70; and Witzo, 174, note. Whether he is the same as Candidus of Fulda, 151, note. He withdrew to Britain, 55, note. From there Alcuin wishes him to return to him, 13. Having been brought out with Nathanael from the nest of paternal instruction, he lives at court, 169, 170. Alcuin instructs him concerning the dispute with the bishop of Orléans, ibid. A witness to Arno’s religious life, 112. Alcuin praises him highly, 148. He carries two little documents of his to Alcuin, 159. He is sent with small gifts to meet the king returning from Italy, 151. Returning from Rome, he reports good news about the king, 24, and about all the faithful, 157. He carries Alcuin’s letter to the king, 178, and certain petitions, 155. He praises Theodulf, archbishop, to Alcuin, 162. He carries Alcuin’s books against Felix to Charles, 788, 921, note. — Verses addressed to Candidus as he was going to Rome, II, 457. Who composed them, ibid., note. — Candidus’s work *On the Image of God*, II, 596. Candidus, a little boy, I, 54, note. Candidus the presbyter, I, 410.

Canisius corrected, I, 67, 111, 120, 146. Why the canon of the Mass is said in silence, II, 502. — Interpretation of the canon of the Mass, ibid. following. From where canons are so called, II, 491. Let none of the brothers separate himself from the canonical hours, I, 10. Kent, or Cantium, I, 78. There the most illustrious lights of Britain rest, ibid. The faith and nobility of the men of Canterbury are praised, ibid. Why the *Song of Songs* is so called, II, 432. In what style it was written, ibid. Ministers of the royal chapel, II, 320. Capernaum, a type of this world, I, 486. From where *capilli* and *pilli* are derived, II, 422. A cloak given to Alcuin by Gisla, I, 149. What the goat signifies in Scripture, I, 319. What the head is, and why it is so called, II, 353, 422. — What the serpent’s head signifies, I, 310. Washing of the head on Holy Saturday, II, 475. In what way flesh and body have different meanings, II, 421. — Flesh signifies the frailty of human nature, I, 312. How the eating of meat during the days of Lent is censured, II, 557.

Charles, duke of the Franks, defeats the Frisians and their king Radbod, II, 188, 197, chapter 9. He appoints Saint Willibrord bishop at Utrecht, 188, note. Charles, king of Germany, Gaul, and Italy, I, 37. Most august and most Christian emperor, 703. Alcuin almost always calls him David, 24, 44, 52, 81, and in nearly all the letters. Why, 24, 120. He had Peter of Pisa as his teacher in grammar, I, 126. He learned rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, and astronomy from Alcuin, 704, II, 313. At what time, ibid., note. Together with Alcuin he composes the art of rhetoric, approving it, 313. Amid the responsibilities of ruling, he strives to learn the secrets of the philosophers, II, 152. Skilled in astrology, I, 98, 101. He summons Alcuin from the farthest regions of Britain because of his zeal for wisdom, 150; II, 217, 234. He attracts lovers of wisdom with rewards and honors, I, 150. He summons them from different parts of the world, ibid. What studies flourish at his court, II, 228.

— Charles summons Alcuin to himself so that he may assist him in the Catholic faith, I, 861, 882. He arranges for the condemnation of Felix of Urgell, ibid. He took care that a reply be made to Felix’s little book, 97. He receives a letter from Elipandus and other bishops of Spain, II, 567. Alcuin rouses him to avenge the crime of the Romans, I, 117, 119. He announces a journey to Italy at Mainz, 139. He hastens to set out for Rome from Germany in order to restrain the destruction caused by criminals, 138. After the coronation he returns from Rome to Gaul, 150, 151, note. Charles celebrates Easter at Aachen, I, 116. He enters Saxony, ibid. He remains in Saxony, I, 63 and note, and reaches its farthest borders, 69. He labors to convert the Saxons from idolatry to the true God, 37. He subjects the Huns to himself and converts them, I, 37, 44, note. He completed that war through his son Pippin, 139, note. To Arno, who was going to preach among the Huns, he grants a third part of his labors, 104, 105, note. At his insistence the ancient Saxons and the peoples of the Frisians were converted to the faith, 6. He converts very many peoples to the love and praise of Christ, 51. He takes a large part of Spain from the Saracens, 6. He subdued the Britons on this side of the sea, 139, note, and acted successfully against the Saracens, ibid. He prepares a fleet against the Normans, 137, note.

— Through envoys sent to Scotland and returning, Charles receives news of the nation’s unbelief and the king’s death, I, 57, [Col. 1456] note. He is at odds with King Offa, 6. What caused the disagreement, 7. He sends gifts to him, I, 57. Likewise to King Æthelred and to the episcopal sees, ibid. He sent a large sum of money to Jerusalem, to be distributed among the holy places and the poor, 246, note. He ordered that the altar of Saint Peter at Cologne be adorned with metalwork, 216. He visits the monastery of Centula, II, 175. He is expected to come to the patronage of Saint Martin, I, 128. He comes there, ibid., note. He transfers Alcuin into the service of Saint Martin, 151, note. He often sets him questions from the Gospels to explain, 184. He sends him gifts, 93. How much he bestowed upon him, 157. He also sends poems to Paul of Cassino, ibid. Charles wrote about the meaning of Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima, I, 88, 89. He sends Pope Adrian a Psalter written in gold letters, II, 550, note. He wrote Adrian’s epitaph, ibid. Whether he himself composed some verses, ibid., note.

— He is called the unconquered and most wise ruler, I, 704. The best ruler, greatest victor, 178. Patron of Rome, 229. Catholic in faith, king in power, pontiff in preaching, judge in equity, philosopher in liberal studies, renowned in character, and outstanding in every virtue, I, 882. Surpassing all in the splendor of wisdom and the fervor of holy religion, I, 123. In wisdom another Solomon, 88, 92; II, 152. Learned and devout, ibid. Pious and just defender of the Christian people, I, 52. Ruler of the Christian people, 117. Always steadfast and firm in mind, 97. Glory of the Christian people, defense of the churches, consolation of the present life, 119. Prosperity of the kingdom, safety of the people, glory of the Church, protection of all the faithful of Christ, 156. Ruler and defender of the Church, II, 228. Avenger of crimes, ruler of those who err, consoler of the sorrowful, exalter of the good, 117. Enriched by command of earthly happiness and the breadth of spiritual wisdom, 138. Armed with two swords by divine authority, 124. Raised through every office to the highest honor of secular power, 155. He quiets the errors of schisms, 123. He purifies Christ’s churches from the doctrines of the faithless, 124. He does not cease to fortify the Catholic faith against sects of perverse doctrine, 24. He is held by illness, I, 44. Poems addressed to him, II, 228.

Charles, son of Charles the Great, an illustrious man and young king, I, 148. He negotiates peace with the Saxons, 119. He received the royal name and crown from the apostolic bishop, 148. He is crowned at Rome together with his father, ibid., note. When he was born and died, ibid. Alcuin calls him his son, ibid. He is praised for mercy and humility, ibid.

Cassian departs from the faith in certain matters, I, 789. His book against the sect of heretical depravity is unknown, 821. Cassiodorus, an outstanding interpreter of the Psalms, I, 188. — Cassiodorus’s books of the *Institutions* attributed to Alcuin, II, 264. What sort of place a fortress is, II, 449, note. The fortress of Guntion, I, 165, note.

Chastity is commended, II, 137. How it is to be preserved, ibid. It is especially necessary for ministers of the altar, ibid. It is of no value without the integrity of the Catholic faith, I, 495. The camps of God that Jacob saw on his journey: what they are, I, 329. What the *casula* signifies, II, 496. — Alcuin sends Arno a *casula* for the solemn celebrations of Mass, I, 167. From where the cases of nouns are named, II, 278. How many there are and what they are, ibid.

Even if catechumens die in good works, they will not have eternal life, 406. — Communion of the body and blood of Christ is not given to catechumens, I, 490. What the categories are and how many there are, II, 337. By whom Aristotle’s categories were translated into Latin, 334. What their use is, I, 704. Verses *On the Chains*, or bonds, of Saint Peter, II, 223. A *caucellus*, a small vessel, I, 67. The monastery of Causiacum, or Choisy, I, 67, 68, note.

King Ceadvala of the Saxons abandoned the scepter, II, 549. His journey to Rome, ibid. There he was baptized and died, ibid. and note. Cedar is interpreted as “darkness”; it signifies sinners, I, 377, 393. The scent of cedars drives away serpents, I, 395. *Cedron* is the Greek plural genitive, in Latin *cedrorum*, I, 621. Ceilmundus, minister of Offa, king of the Mercians, I, 85. See Ceommundus.

Two coastal cells over which Alcuin presided, II, 183, note. — A coastal cell in the province of Northumbria, I, 289, note. Saint Wiligisius was buried there, II, 183, note. Whether it was formerly dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, ibid. Whether it is the same one over which Alcuin presided by legitimate succession, ibid., note. A wine-cellar church, I, 395. *Cenodoxia*, II, 143. See Vainglory. Ecclesiastical censures, II, 473. The monastery of Centula, or Saint-Riquier, II, 175, 176. Its abbot was Angilbert, ibid. Where it was situated, 176, note, 182.

[Col. 1457] Ceolfrid, first abbot of the monastery of Jarrow, I, 23, 283. In his time the Venerable Bede entered the monastery, II, 254, verse 1294. Seeking a foreign land, he died and was buried at Langres, verse 1295, note. His body was found intact and brought back to his homeland, verse 1298. Ceommundus, companion of Æthelhard on his journey to Rome, I, 148. Minister of Offa, king of the Mercians, ibid., note. See Ceilmundus.

The use of blessed wax against demonic illusions, lightning, and thunder, II, 486. What the brain is, II, 353. The blessing of candles on Holy Saturday, II, 482. — Why two candles are carried before the Gospel, II, 497, 499. The lighting of candles after baptism, II, 485. The origin of candles at the feast of the Purification, II, 466. What *cereostrata* signify, II, 497. From whom Cethura descended and what she signifies, I, 326.

The Chaldeans regarded fire as a god, I, 94, 317. Why Ham was cursed in his descendants, I, 316. Whether the Canaanite woman was a widow, I, 31, note. Charity is twofold, I, 29. It is the foundation of every good work, 605, 606. It is the unity of souls, 191. It holds first place among the divine commandments, and what its perfection is, II, 129. In what it must especially be shown, I, 210. — Mutual charity is the sign of Christ’s discipleship, I, 163. It is recognized as existing in the true Church alone, 858. It can be divided neither by distance between lands nor destroyed by forgetfulness, 123. It does not tolerate forgetfulness, 269. — Commendation of charity in the members of Christ, I, 388. — Charity moves the foot toward progress, pride toward falling, I, 377. Whoever sins against charity is a transgressor of the whole law, 858. Nothing is good that is not done through charity, 698. Without charity no commandment is acceptable to God, I, 605. Without it there is no virtue, 148. Without it nothing pleases God, nor is any gift acceptable at the altar, 267. Without it the soul is dead, 268.

Chlodwig, or Louis, brother of the younger King Charles, repeatedly asks for and receives admonitory letters from Alcuin, I, 148. Chlotar, the brother to whom Alcuin entrusted a letter to be delivered to Arno, I, 113. The preparation of chrism on the day of the Lord’s Supper, II, 477. Its mystery, ibid. — Why the head of the baptized person is anointed with chrism, I, 110; II, 127, 523. Christian, a presbyter from the monastery of Saint Benedict, I, 171, note. The altar of Saint Christopher, II, 219.

What Christ signifies, I, 450, 452; II, 509. From where he is so called, I, 762; II, 500. He was true God as soon as conceived in the womb, I, 471, 825, 827, 366, 893; II, 580. He was not first conceived and born as a human being and afterward made the Son of God, 766, 780, 781, 839. His generation is ineffable, I, 814. What signs preceded his birth, II, 462. Why his conception and birth are celebrated, ibid. Why he was born at night, II, 462. Why he wished to be circumcised, 463. When he was brought to the temple and legal offerings were presented for him, I, 484.

— Christ is the proper Son of God, not an adoptive son; true God, not merely titular God, I, 139, 534, 761 and following, 795, 820 and following; II, 574 and following. God by nature, not merely by name, I, 883. According to both natures, he is the son of Mary and, according to both, also the Son of God, I, 140, 847. He cannot be called the adoptive Son of the blessed Virgin according to his divinity, 796. One Son of God, not two, 729, 845.

— In Christ there is one person, I, 140, 530, and a twofold substance, 602; II, 577, 578. What distinction exists between the two natures, I, 730. What their union is, II, 398. The natures in him are not confused but joined in one person, I, 819, 837; II, 395. What belongs to each nature, I, 731. The Word, flesh, and soul are one Christ, 768. The unity of person removes the insult of adoption, II, 579.

— Christ is the Word and man, I, 568. He has two births and two natures, 794, 837. Only-begotten and firstborn in both natures, 822, 885; II, 575. Only-begotten and only Son, I, 797, and frequently elsewhere. Entirely the Son of God and entirely the Son of man, I, 803, 890. How he can be called David and the Son of God, 812. He is to be adored in the flesh, I, 818. How he is called a servant, I, 816, 826, 839; II, 578, 579. He ought not to be called a debtor, I, 839, nor a God-bearing man (*deifer homo*), 844, nor a captive, 887. How he is subject to the Father, 841. Christ had no need of regeneration or baptism, I, 140, 810, 812. Why he wished to be baptized, I, 495, 733, 865; II, 464, 465. Where, when, and by whom he was baptized, II, 464. How he was anointed, I, 811, 812; II, 509. He baptizes not with the baptism with which he himself was baptized, I, 494.

— Christ was in the world through his divinity; he came into the world through the incarnation, I, 469. He himself existed before the world; before Christ there was nothing, 547. How he is both vine and cultivator, 603. How he is called a lamb, stone, worm, and leper, II, 580. Shepherd, door, doorkeeper, and sheep, I, 564. How he is our advocate, 834. In Scripture some things are said of him literally and some figuratively, [Col. 1458] 826, 868. His mission was personal, his operation substantial, II, 404.

— Christ is prophet and priest, II, 433. According to the order of Melchizedek, I, 685. King, and what his kingdom is, 521. King of Israel, in what sense, 582. A poor and wise king, 423. King of the Jews and of the nations, 630. How he is called the arm of the Lord, I, 587. He is compared with King David, 359. The true Solomon, the peaceful king, 382. He bore in himself the office of all the prophets, I, 451. Good by nature, 837. He suffered the weaknesses of the flesh not by necessity but voluntarily, 841. Everything he did was done for our salvation, 733. His praises, I, 914.

— How Christ is like and unlike us, I, 797. How he who was conceived of the Holy Spirit is not the son of this Spirit, 726, 742; II, 509. How he did not receive the Spirit by measure, I, 719. How he exercised the ecclesiastical orders, II, 434. Whether and how he prayed for himself and for us, I, 857. Whether he was ignorant of the day of judgment, 719, 835. Whether Christ’s soul possessed full knowledge of his divinity, 719. Letter to Abagar, a pagan king, 276. Why Christ chose no other kind of death than the cross, II, 478. At what hour he was crucified, I, 629, 630. He gave up his spirit not by necessity but by his own will, 187, 188. Alone among the dead, free, 840. He truly, not merely apparently, suffered, II, 401. How his divinity remained incapable of suffering during the Passion, 509. How he is said to have been in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, 480. According to the flesh alone he lay in the tomb; according to the soul alone he descended into hell, I, 732. How many times he appeared after the resurrection, 643. According to his entire humanity he ascended into heaven, 188. How he was glorified and is to be glorified, 585, 616. How he is called predestined, ibid. The error of certain persons concerning the glory of Christ’s flesh, 24. He is truly eaten and drunk in the Eucharist, II, 504.

— Through Christ alone and his sacrifice could the world be freed from sins, II, 402. — Faith in Christ and confession of his mysteries, II, 394, 398, 401. Who Christians were before Christ’s coming, I, 563. — How dangerous it is to deny oneself to be a Christian, I, 624. — What the life of Christians ought to be, I, 286.

Chrodgarius, a count, I, 157. He commends a little boy and his brother to Alcuin for instruction, ibid. He was sent with Pippin to devastate the territory of Benevento, ibid., note. Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, not a Roman, I, 767. From where *chronica* is derived, II, 425. Who its author was, 426. Bishop Chumberctus signed the council of Chelsea, I, 270. What the *cidaris* is, II, 495. What the penitential haircloth signifies, II, 515. Cinebrilitus, bishop of the West Saxons, companion of Æthelhard on his journey to Rome, I, 148. What being sprinkled with ashes in penance signifies, II, 515.

What circumcision signified, I, 536. Why it was commanded to Abraham, 321. Why it ceased in the New Testament, II, 463. — The feast of Christ’s circumcision, and its cause and origin, II, 463. Clement, successor of Saint Peter, II, 210. Clement, also called Willibrord. See Willibrord. Clement the Scot, I, 93, note. What clemency, a part of the virtue of temperance, is, II, 330. Who clerics are and from where they are called, II, 491. At the beginning of the Church they were all preachers, I, 183. Bigamists and incontinent men are not to be ordained, II, 409. Clerics accompanying a bishop who is going to the king are not to wear silk garments, I, 234.

— The office and conduct of clerics, II, 163, 164. From where the tonsure originated, 491. What it should be like, 493. — The life of clerics in England was for a long time corrupt and degraded, I, 233.

Clovis, king of the Franks, makes war on the Alemanni and defeats them, II, 164, 165. He vows that he will be a Christian, ibid. He is instructed in the faith by Saint Vedast, ibid. He is baptized by Saint Remigius, ibid. On the day of Christ’s Nativity, 166. King Chlotar, son of Clovis, summoned by Ocino to dinner, I, 169. Clotildis, wife of Clovis, a religious queen initiated into the sacraments of baptism, II, 165. What twice-dyed scarlet signifies, II, 494.

Coifi, or Coivi, a pagan priest in Britain, destroys a shrine with the people and embraces the faith, II, 241, verse 175. What Pope Celestine established concerning the Mass, II, 497. What heaven is, II, 353. Of what nature it is, 306. — What is signified at the beginning of Genesis by the name “heaven and earth,” I, 307. What the joys of heaven are for the perfect and imperfect, II, 251, verse 964 and following.

The mysteries of the Lord’s Supper on Thursday of Holy Week, I, 89. Its celebration and ceremonies, II, 476. Its etymology, 478. — How Christ celebrated the Supper with his disciples, II, 478. Coenwulf, or Kenulf, king of the Mercians, I, 67. He was raised to the throne not by title of blood but by merit of virtues, I, 67, note. Successor of Ecgfrith, ibid. His lineage, ibid. He wages war with Eardwulf, king of Northumbria, 236, note. From where a cognomen is derived, II, 272. The cell of Saint Stephen at Coisaca, or Choisy, I, 128, note. Colcus, a lector in Scotland, I, 6. Alcuin’s letter to him concerning the departure of the Saracens is lacking, ibid. What a collect is and from where it is named, II, 499. A collect to be said concerning judgment, 18. The *colobium*, a sleeveless garment, II, 494. What it signifies, 496.

Why the dove carried an olive branch, I, 315. A type of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 476, 484, 487. Columba, I, 149, 459. A female disciple of Alcuin, 591. He calls her his daughter, 157, 591. See Richtrudis. Crowned doves flying through the chambers of the palace, I, 249. The altar of Saint Columba, virgin and martyr, II, 213. Saint Columbanus, or Columba, a Scot, II, 219. Columbanus’s *Monostichon*, 546. His prayer, 121. His altar, 218, note.

What hair is, II, 422. Counts, and what their office is, I, 213. Communion of the body and blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ is to be received after confession, I, 145. It is not to be denied at the point of death, II, 512. The cases of the dead are to be left to God’s judgment when they die without communion, ibid. — Who can or cannot communicate daily, II, 507. The hour of Compline and its celebration, II, 510. Contrition of heart arises from humility, II, 133. What its effects and qualities are, ibid.

Councils received by the Roman Church as universal are the documents and protection of the Church, II, 409. What a true preacher ought to be, I, 412. What the conclusion of a speech is, and its parts, II, 325. For what purpose concupiscence was given to man, II, 147. Condatensis, a village of the diocese of Tours, II, 162.

The confession of faith, II, 46, 385 and following. Of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 28. And the praise of the Most Holy Trinity, 35. Of majesty and the request for pardon, 42. Confession of sins exists in the Church after baptism, I, 116, 144. It is to be made by laypeople to priests, 143. What it accomplishes for penitents, I, 155. The confession of the sick, 295. What the confession of a dying person ought to be like, II, 512. He should disclose to the priest every tiny defilement of words, thoughts, and deeds, 295. It should be made of all those things that they can remember, II, 473. In Scripture it does not always signify repentance, I, 144.

— Alcuin’s pure confession of sins, II, 63. For monks, 24, 25, 44, 45, 46, 84. — The form and manner of confession, II, 44, 45. Its usefulness and necessity, I, 286, 347, 249; II, 154 and following. — The antiquity of auricular confession, II, 5. — The remedy of confession is to be applied frequently, II, 133. — Through confession sins are washed away, I, 347. The sinner is freed from a threefold death, 145. — An error concerning the confession of sins is refuted, I, 143. — All hope of pardon rests upon confession, II, 134. — How a person who conceals a sin in confession is punished after death, II, 255, verse 1343.

What a confessor must observe concerning the different conditions of penitents, II, 473. How he ought to question a penitent, ibid. He must judge according to the canons, ibid. He is a mediator between God and the sinner, 474. — Prayers of the confessor, II, 474. — How the person confessing his sins ought to conduct himself, II, 474.

What confirmation is in rhetorical speech, II, 321. By what arguments it is made, ibid. and 322. The confirmation of a baptized person must be performed by a bishop, II, 484. Not by presbyters, ibid. Its rite, ibid. Its antiquity, ibid. Saint Congallus, a Scot, II, 219.

What conjunction is in grammar, II, 296. Its proper characteristic, 271. Its figure, species, and order, 296. Whom should be chosen as the kings’ counselors, I, 241, 242. What consonant letters are and from where they are named, II, 269. Constantinople is called a second Rome, I, 118, note. The emperor Constantine, son of Irene, is deposed after his eyes are put out, I, 40, 118. Constantine’s constitution concerning fugitives who seek refuge in churches, I, 172.

A prayer “for contemplation and love of the heavenly homeland,” II, 27. What continence, a part of the virtue of temperance, is, II, 330. It is better than marriage when chosen for the purpose of serving God, 408. How many kinds of opposites there are, II, 343. How many kinds of controversy there are, II, 316. The places of controversies, 315. Conversion to God should not be postponed, II, 134. The immoderate use of banquets must be prohibited to priests, I, 80. — At banquets and in merriment we lose compunction of heart, I, 428.

[Col. 1460] What the twelve baskets of fragments signify, I, 520. What the heart is, II, 353. What it means for the heart to be contrite, I, 354. The monastery of Corbie is called the household of Saint Peter, 206 and note. Its abbot was Antonius, ibid. — The brothers of Corbie, I, 62 and note. Cordova, or Córdoba, a city, I, 862. The origin of the Adoptian heresy was there, 916. Some people of Córdoba were led into error by Elipandus, II, 590. The monastery of Cormaric, dedicated to Saint Paul, I, 40, 67, 68. There Alcuin established a new community from brothers of Gothia, 135, 137, note. — The distinction of the cell at Cormaric, II, 215. A poem about it, 456. The altar of Saint Cornelius the martyr, II, 219. What are the names of the four crowned saints, II, 489.

Why the corporal at Mass is linen, and its folding, II, 500. What the body is, II, 353. From where the word is derived, 421. How it consists of the four elements, ibid. In how many days it is formed, I, 489. From what things a solid body is composed, II, 339. — The qualities of bodies at the resurrection, I, 735. — What the threefold body of Christ is, II, 497. It is one, although it is consecrated many times and in many places, II, 504. The consecration of Christ’s body and blood is the principal sacrament of our salvation, I, 184. Through the power of the blessing, bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, II, 503. Christ himself perfects his body and blood in the Mass, 504.

— The real presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist was revealed to certain people in ancient times, II, 376, 413. Whether those who denied that presence before Berengar can be called heretics, 377 and following. The truth of that presence is shown by a miracle, ibid., 378. — Those once baptized were strengthened with the Lord’s body and blood, I, 110; II, 127, 523.

Fraternal correction is commended, I, 488. What Christ’s shoelaces signify, I, 474; II, 540. Where the raven sent out from the ark rested, I, 314. Corydon the schoolmaster; a poem addressed to him, II, 235. The altar of Saints Cosmas and Damian, II, 210, 214. How *cotidie* and *quotidie* differ, II, 310, 427. What the hips are, II, 353.

Why the Creator cursed the earth and not the waters, I, 306. — The wondrous union of the Creator with the creature, I, 718. How creatures existed in God before they were made, I, 468. — How many rational creatures God created, I, 305, 724. Which things he made from nothing, 306. To believe comes before understanding, I, 532, 535, 911. No one believes by necessity but by will, 527. — “To believe God,” “to believe God as an object,” and “to believe in God” differ, II, 509. — To believe Christ is different from believing in Christ, I, 535. Credulus, a friend of Alcuin, I, 148. The little river Criento, or Chrincon, II, 171. Crimes are to be believed slowly, but, once known, punished more quickly, I, 322. From where hair is called *crines*, II, 422. The forest of Crisciacum; where it is situated, II, 280. The altar of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, II, 210. The monastery of Crowland, I, 67.

How great a good the cross is, and its mystical explanation, I, 631. It contains a great mystery within itself, II, 478. A cross erected by King Saint Oswald on the summit of a mountain is worshiped by the entire army, 244, verse 252. — Why and how the sign of the cross is used by the Church, I, 681; II, 499. Why, and by whom, the baptized are signed with the sign of the cross, II, 521. — The adoration of the cross on Good Friday, II, 479. Its praises, ibid. and 480. Its relics are sought, I, 49. — The altar of the Holy Cross, II, 210, 219. — Poems concerning the Holy Cross, II, 223, 230. What the legs are, II, 353.

Alcuin sends Cuculus to Simeon, archbishop of York, I, 67, 148. — A lament for the lost Cuculus, II, 237. Who he was, ibid., note. Saint Cuthbert, or Cudberctus, a bishop, I, 12, 224. The great Father, shepherd, and glory of the Church of Lindisfarne, II, 240. Remaining a monk, he becomes an apostolic teacher, 248, verse 676. He lives as a solitary on the island of Farne, ibid., verse 656. He saw the soul of Saint Aidan carried above the stars, verse 692. He died, verse 676. He is renowned for miracles, 248, verse 677 and following. His body was found intact with its clothing in the eleventh year after his death, 249, verse 728. His church was devastated by pagans, I, 11, 12, 19, 22. We must place our confidence in his intercession, I, 224. — Bede wrote the life of Saint Cuthbert in prose and in heroic verse, II, 240, 248, verse 684 and following, 249, verse 743.

Cudradus, a presbyter of Lindisfarne, was preserved by God amid the hands of the pagans, I, 8. What the stone knife with which circumcision was performed signifies, I, 536. Bishop Cuniberctus in Britain—whether he was Kinebertus, I, 269, note. He attended the synodal assembly, ibid. See Chumbertus. — Cunibertus was sent to adjudicate the case of Pope Leo, I, 269, note. Curia, a city, I, 266. Remedius, bishop of Chur, ibid. and 136. — Monasteries in the extent of the diocese of Chur, 266. What the cypress signifies, I, 395. The prayer of Saint Cyprian the martyr, II, 94. — His altar, 219. Saint Cyriacus, a boy, with his mother Julitta, II, 218. Saint Cyril, the most powerful destroyer of the Nestorian sect, I, 901. Cyrinus, a governor, is interpreted as “heir,” II, 462. How he signifies Peter, ibid.

D
## D

Dagobertus, distinguished by secular power and noble in religion, II, 176. He is salutarily chastised by Saint Richarius, 179. He invites him to his table, 180. To him he grants revenues and lights, ibid. He also gives him land called Campania, ibid.

Dallaeus attacks Alcuin’s confession of faith, II, 370. Refuted by Mabillon, 373.

The use, name, and interpretation of the dalmatic, II, 496, 498.

Damoetas: whether a secular man, I, 54, 55, note. He is called a great fisherman, 148. Chief priest, ibid. The surname of Riculfus, archbishop of Mainz, 55, 148 and note. See Riculfus.

Why Dan is called a serpent, I, 338.

The Danes ravage the shores of Britain, I, 79. A most savage people, II, 187. They resist the preaching of Saint Willibrord, ibid. Their king is Ungendus, ibid. The children of the Danes are carried off to Francia, ibid.

Who wrote Daniel’s prophecies, II, 432.

Daphnus, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 408 ff.; II, 237.

Dares, a young man, II, 229.

David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable,” I, 386, 450, 451, 453. He signifies Christ, 386, 793. An example of repentance, II, 515. He wrote the second part of the Book of Samuel, 431.

David, Emperor Charlemagne. See Carolus.

David, bishop of Seville, successor of Theudula, II, 591.

How the prepositions *de*, *dis*, and *des* are to be used, I, 34.

In the Lord’s Prayer, “debts” means sins, I, 839; II, 507. Who are called debtors in Scripture, I, 839. We are debtors of God in two ways, II, 507.

How the first three commandments of the Decalogue pertain to love of the Trinity, I, 340.

Whether the yoke of tithes should be imposed on uncultivated peoples at the beginning of the faith, I, 38, 117. Their collection is thought to have hindered the conversion of the Saxons, 51, 104.

The threefold dedication of Solomon’s Temple and its commemoration, I, 569.

How defense is made in judgment, II, 322.

What a definition is, II, 271, 345. Allegorical definitions of names, II, 352 ff. Modes of definition, II, 345. Their types, 346.

The names of the dead customarily recited at Mass, II, 505. Funerals and anniversaries are celebrated, 512. To pray, fast, give alms, and celebrate Masses for the faithful departed is good and beneficial for them, I, 131, 212; II, 37, 512, 513. Why the third, seventh, and thirtieth days are celebrated, 512, 513.

Delia, daughter, II, 230.

Some interpret *delictum* as a light sin, I, 347; and when it is against us, 352.

Demas, Paul’s assistant, I, 664.

What teeth are, II, 353. The functions of the teeth, I, 444.

Deoduinus (Theoduinus), bishop of Liège: what he thought about Berengar’s errors before Berengar’s condemnation, II, 377.

A slanderer is like a serpent, I, 439.

God first created the angelic nature and formless matter, II, 405. How many rational creatures he created, I, 305. Why he created the world in the six-day number, 306. In what sense he is to be understood as having rested from every work on the seventh day, I, 305. Why he permitted man to be tempted although he foresaw that man would consent, 309. Why he questioned Adam as though ignorant of where he was, 310. In what sense he is said not to know certain things, 719. He is the cause of all things that exist, so that they may exist, 714. How he hardens the heart without being the cause of sin, 588.

God is above all things, I, 714. There are two kinds, the true and the titular, 823. Why he did not give the law at the beginning, 306. He is wholly everywhere, 715, 717; II, 148. He is present in the saints in one way and presides over sinners in another, 717. How he can be seen, 721, 722, 741. He is not encompassed by place, II, 393. Why he is said to dwell more in heaven than on earth, I, 715, 742; II, 506. Why he wished to atone for sin by himself rather than through an angel, I, 306. In what sense he is said to have sworn by his soul, II, 425. How he is truly unity and truly Trinity, I, 707, 739. See Trinity.

The names and perfections of God are described and explained, II, 386, 424. What God’s kingdom in us is, II, 506. His will was not changed by creation, I, 468. In what sense human beings are like God, II, 576. To love God is natural to every human being, II, 146. If he is not loved here, he will not be seen there, I, 237. Nothing is predicated of God according to accident, I, 710, 713; II, 350. There is no change in him, although Scripture speaks of him in human fashion, I, 716. Whether being, living, understanding, and being able differ at all, 720, 741. It is better to say that things are equal to God than similar to him, I, 715. Some things are predicated substantially, others relatively, 708. This distinction must necessarily be made, 709. What is said substantially, II, 424.

The banquets of the gods are rational principles, II, 267.

The monastery of Dervense: its abbots Albericus and Adso, II, 527, note.

Why Deuteronomy is so called, II, 431.

The Devil, in Latin “accuser,” I, 657. Why he is called a murderer, 554. In what sense he is called “the prince of this world,” 602. He is a wolf in the Church, 564. A liar and the father of lies, 554. He was not made by God so as to be the Devil, II, 405. He once stood in God’s presence, ibid. He will never be restored to angelic dignity, ibid. A foolish king, I, 423. How he reigns in us, II, 506. A serpent, I, 439. Why he is so hostile to human salvation, 306. He rarely fights the servants of God openly, but under the appearance of piety, 140. Sometimes he receives from God the power to tempt the elect, II, 30. He roams through this air, plotting against the salvation of the faithful, 405. He is kept chained by the power of God’s might, 528. From where the Devil’s first evil will arose, I, 311.

The name and office of deacons, II, 434, 492. Why they are called Levites, ibid.

What dialectic is and from where it is named, II, 335. How it differs from rhetoric, 336. What its kinds are and how many, ibid.

What diction is, II, 271. How figurative and derivative expressions differ, 277.

Dido, bishop of Laon, almost contemporary with Alcuin, I, 743.

What a day is and its parts, II, 426. How the days of the week are named by the Romans, ibid.; by the Hebrews, ibid. The days of labor are few, those of reward many, I, 105.

What difference is, II, 271, 336.

What fingers are, II, 353.

What the three highest dignities in the world are, I, 117.

What perfect love of God is, I, 643. It distinguishes the saints from the world, 601. It consists in observance of the commandments, II, 129. Love of neighbor, commended by Christ, gathers the new people, I, 596. How necessary the commandment of love is to all, II, 163. To love Christ is to keep his commandments, I, 600, 605.

What the time of dawn indicates, I, 541.

Verses on the Flood of Noah, II, 207.

Dinah, Jacob’s only daughter, I, 332.

Dindimus, king of the Brahmans, and his letters to Alexander, II, 600 ff.

Diogenes, the great philosopher, II, 267.

What Dionysius the Little established concerning the leap of the moon, II, 358, 359, and elsewhere.

The altar of Saint Dionysius, II, 210, 212, 224; and that of his companions, poem 192. His cult, 194.

From where *diphthong* is named, II, 270.

Discretion among monks is the mother of virtues, I, 77.

What *dispositio*, a part of rhetorical discourse, is, II, 314, 326.

The Disputation with Felicianus the Arian: whether it is by Saint Augustine, I, 842, note.

Whether the divinity of Christ was conceived, born, and suffered together with the flesh, I, 742. It cannot be called adoptive with respect to the Blessed Virgin, 881. He never abandoned the man whom he assumed, I, 732, 742.

The substance of the divinity is wholly invisible and incomprehensible to creatures in its own nature, I, 721.

The description of the rich man, I, 426.

Riches are to be despised, II, 226. They are not to be cared for, 266. What true riches are, I, 55, 56. Unjust riches are not to be loved, 18. They are given for distribution, not possession, 388. The vanity of riches, I, 410. One person’s abundance is another’s poverty, ibid.

Some teachers of the Church are compared with queens, others with concubines, I, 403, 409.

Pain is often healed by time when it could not be healed by reason, I, 131.

The institution and solemnity of the Lord’s Day, II, 487, 488. On that day the people abstain from agricultural labor. Why, 498.

Why “The Lord be with you” is sung at Mass, II, 498, 499.

The gifts of the faithful are diverse, yet each is given to each by the one and the same Spirit, I, 724.

Dorsdrada: what place it is, II, 449, note.

Dragitus, king of the Slavs, submitted to Charlemagne, I, 7, note. Drago, king of the Wends, likewise, ibid.

Drances, II, 228.

Drida. See Zuendrida.

Drithelm comes back to life from the dead, II, 250, verse 879. He relates marvelous things about purgatory, heaven, and hell, verse 905, 1006.

Dungal, bishop, I, 284. Who he was and of what see is unknown, 286, note. Dungal the Irishman, a pilgrim in Francia, ibid. A recluse of Saint-Denis, he writes in defense of the cult of holy images, ibid.

Dungal, abbot: seven unpublished letters of his are preserved in the Harleian Library in England, I, 2.

The number twelve, consecrated to the Apostles, I, 532. The mysteries of the number twelve, I, 520.

## E

Eada, priest, I, 201. Whether he was a monk, 202, note.

Eadbaldus, abbot of Gerwic, I, 23, note; 284, note.

Eadbertus, king of Northumbria. See Aedbertus.

Eadbertus, bishop of Lindisfarne, calms the blasts of death by his prayers, II, 240. When he lived and died, ibid., note. His deeds, written by Bede, have been lost, ibid.

Eanbaldus, priest, I, 9, 10, note.

Eanbaldus the Elder, archbishop of York, I, 28, note. A fellow student of Alcuin, 40, 41, note; II, 256, verse 1515. While alive, Aelbertus handed over the episcopal office to him, verse 1522. With him he consecrated a new basilica, verse 1517. When he died, I, 41, note; 62, note; 66, note.

Eanbaldus the Younger, surnamed Simeon, I, 148 and note. He is elected archbishop of York, I, 62, 66, note. An industrious disciple of Alcuin, ibid. Alcuin teaches him about the episcopal office, 63. He held a conversation with Aedilhard of Canterbury, 148. See Simeon.

Eantbaldus, prelate, sends gifts to Pope Leo, II, 228.

Eanulfus, priest, I, 291. Whether he was an Englishman and a monk, 292, note.

Eardulfus, king of Northumbria. See Aerduulfus.

Why Ebdamada is so called, II, 427.

Eberhardus, count, founder of the monastery of Morbac, I, 62, note. A relative of Saint Leodegarius, ibid.

Ebila, what region it is and from where it is named, I, 327.

York, a city and the capital of the whole kingdom, I, 20. Alcuin completed his studies there, 54. There a rain of blood was seen to fall, 20. See the city of Euborica.

The Church of York is vacant, I, 62. The election of a new bishop is under discussion, ibid., 63. The brothers of the Church of York and the letters to them, I, 8, 9, 28, note; 62. They professed the Benedictine rule, 9, note. Besides a bishop, they had an abbot who was in charge of the monks, II, 253, note. Their teacher was Alcuin, I, 8. He commends to them concord with Archbishop Eanbald, 28. A vision of their future eternal blessedness, 9. A poem addressed to them, II, 234.

A poem about the bishops and saints of the Church of York, II, 242 ff. Its author was Alcuin, 241.

A description of the library of the Church of York, II, 257, verses 1535 ff.

In Scripture, drunkenness is taken for satiety, I, 332. How great an evil it is, 323. Who are drunk and habitually drunken, II, 472.

What the Church is, II, 510. Why it is called Catholic, II, 439, 510. It is composed of three orders of the faithful, I, 485. Zion, 354, 356, 381, 385. The city of God, II, 405. The house of God, ibid. The moon, I, 378. Christ’s wife, 384. Bride and virgin, 495. A woman giving birth in sorrow, 613. Like a woman in labor, II, 481, 482. A widow despised by the world but betrothed to Christ, I, 388. Christ’s ark, I, 387. Aaron’s garment, 388. A locked garden, 400. David’s tower, 399. The proper sheepfold of the faithful, 119. The city and house of obedience, 579. Troubled by the wickedness of evil people, 117. Besieged by the Devil and freed by Christ, 437. Always attacked from the beginning, 384. It advances amid temptations, 522. Black in afflictions, beautiful in virtues, 393. A vineyard abounding in the fruit of faith, 407. It speaks in the languages of all nations, 540. It exists and is governed in three ways, II, 406. Before Christ’s ascension it existed only in Judea; afterward throughout the whole world, I, 406. How firm it is through the gathering together of its children, II, 582. Salvation exists in the universal Church alone, ibid. In it all the orders of the blessed are joined together, 405.

The authority of the Church concerning the number of books and the meaning of Sacred Scripture, II, 409. The negligence and luxury of ministers are censured, I, 440.

The Roman Church is the head of the others, I, 792. Its authority must be followed, 110, 857.

How churches are to be governed, I, 199.

The canons threaten violators of churches with a terrible anathema, I, 63. Those who flee to churches for refuge are not to be forcibly removed, 172.

Information about the churches of the cities of Rome and Milan, II, 597 ff.

Who Ecclesiastes was and why he was so called, I, 411, 412. The Book of Ecclesiastes was composed by Solomon in repentance, and how it is to be understood, 412. Why it was placed in the catalogue of the divine books, 446.

From where the book Ecclesiasticus is named and who wrote it, II, 432. Among the Hebrews it is regarded as apocryphal, ibid.

The dignity and ranks of the ecclesiastical order, II, 490, 491.

Ecgfridus (Egfertus), king of the Mercians, the most noble son of Offa and Zuendrida, I, 59, note; 225, note. Crowned king while his father was still alive, 74, note. He succeeded his father and died prematurely, ibid. The cause of his premature death, 229, note. Alcuin calls him his son, 209.

Echa, an anchorite who led an angelic life, II, 255, verse 1387. Endowed with the gift of prophecy, verse 1392. At what time he flourished, verse 1387.

Edelburga, daughter of Ethelbert, king of Kent, and wife of King Edwin, II, 243, verse 131 and note.

Edelhardus, metropolitan of the Church of Dorchester, I, 85. See Aedilhardus.

Edelredus, king, II, 245, verse 358. His wife was Osthfrida, ibid.

Edilthida [also Adiltruda, Edildrida, Aetheldrytha], born of royal stock, II, 249, verse 753, note. Wife first of Tombert, prince of the Gyrvii, and after his death of King Egfrid of Northumbria, 249, verse 752. She remained a virgin in marriage, verses 757 and 758. Her body was found incorrupt with its clothing after almost ten years, 249, verse 765. Bede wrote a hymn about her, I, 169; II, 249, verse 780. Alcuin sent it to Arno, I, 169.

Edilburga, I, 67. A nun and abbess of the monastery of Crowland, ibid., note. Her parentage is unknown, ibid. Whether she was a sister of Alfleda, ibid. Her sister was deprived of her husband’s bed, ibid. Alcuin sent her a flask and paten for offering an oblation to God; Luidgarda sent her a pallium, ibid.

Edilthruda, I, 212. Whether she is the same as Edilthida, 213, note.

Edwin, king of Northumbria, son of Alla, II, 243, verse 90, note. As a boy he was driven into exile by King Ethelfrid, verse 92 and note. His vision in sleep, verse 93 ff. He received the kingdom after Ethelfrid was killed, verse 113 ff. He subjected the peoples of the whole island to himself, verse 120 ff. His wife, verse 131, note. He was baptized with his children, nobles, and people, 244, verse 194 ff. and note. After Pope Gregory’s decree, he elevated the city of York into a metropolitan see, verse 203 ff. He founded large churches in the cities, verse 219. When he fell, verse 231 and note.

Effrata is interpreted as “mirror,” I, 387. There Jacob buried his wife Rachel, 330. It is the same as Bethlehem, ibid.

The prayers of Saint Ephrem the deacon, II, 123.

Saint Egbert, prelate, II, 252, verse 1013. Seeking foreign lands, he teaches the Scots, verse 1015. See the Egberts.

Egbert, called a saint, devotes himself to a holier life in Ireland, II, 185. Whether he was a bishop or archbishop, ibid., note. He is not to be confused with Egbert of York, ibid.

Egbert (Ecgbert), archbishop of York and successor of Wilfrid, II, 254, verse 1248. Brother of Eadbert, king of the Northumbrians, verse 1250 and note; verse 1270. His virtues and care of the Church, verse 1252 ff. He received the pallium from the Apostolic See, verse 1279. He governed the Church for thirty-four years, verse 1284, note. He is not to be confused with Aelbert, I, 66, note.

Egfred, son of Oswin, king of the Mercians, succeeds his father, II, 247, verse 575. His charters for the monastery of Saint Alban are mentioned, I, 272, note.

Egfrid, king of Northumbria, famous for his triumphs, took Adiltruda as his bride, II, 249, verse 750. He lived chastely in marriage, verse 762. He ravaged the harmless Scots, 250, verse 837. He was slain by the Picts, verse 840. When he died, ibid., note.

Egila, disciple of Mingentius, II, 371.

The fortress of Egin, II, 525.

Eginhard, Charlemagne’s steward, called Bezalel, I, 127.

Eiei, a name of God, II, 423.

El, a name of God, ibid.

Elcbertus. See Egbertus.

What Eleazar signifies, I, 450, 452, 455.

All the elect are members of Christ, I, 492.

The election of bishops should be free, I, 63. It should not be simoniacal, 62.

Almsgiving is twofold, I, 65. It is commended to everyone, ibid. and 209. It must be given to everyone who asks, without discrimination, 441. It is given by people possessing earthly goods, II, 136. A prayer for those who give alms, II, 42. Alms given by the pope on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, II, 474. The fruits of almsgiving, II, 136. Three kinds, 137.

The number and nature of the elements, I, 306.

Elfleda (Alfleda), daughter of Offa, king of the Mercians, widow of Ethelred, I, 67.

What Eliachim signifies, I, 450, 452, 255.

Elijah and Enoch will come before the Judgment, I, 734.

The church of Saint Elidius, bishop of Pictavia, II, 213.

Eliezer is said to have founded Damascus, I, 319.

Elion, a name of God, II, 423.

Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, a Goth by nationality, II, 590. Famous for many years because of his advanced age and religious life, I, 860. A decrepit old man of eighty-two years, 916. He is admonished to persevere in the Catholic faith, ibid., 860, 863. He wrote against Alcuin in favor of Christ’s adoption, 868. But he is refuted in four books, 876 ff. He wrote to Felix of Urgel, formerly a defender of his sect but now converted, I, 862, 915. He was the first in the regions of Spain to spread the evil of unbelief, 860. Those whom he drew with him into error, II, 590. He answered Alcuin with words of cursing, I, 860. He reproached him for his wealth and multitude of servants, 869. He slandered the blessed abbot, I, 869, 870. He was sternly rebuked by Alcuin, 906. He attempted to distort the opinions of the Fathers, 889 ff., 893 ff. Persistent in heresy, 136. Corrupted by the Spanish error, 879. Paul Alvarus calls him a heretic, II, 591. He sent Felix’s letter to the people of Córdoba, I, 916. Whether he ever repented, II, 591, 593.

Elipandus’s doctrine is close to the impiety of the Arian and Nestorian heresies, I, 881, 894, 908; II, 588. Where his letters were found and published, 591.

What Eliud signifies, I, 450, 452, 455.

The inscriptions of the monastery of Elnon, II, 108, 217. Its abbot was Aquila, or Arno, ibid., note. The brothers’ cemetery, ibid.

What *elocutio*, a part of discourse, is, II, 314. What it ought to be like, 327.

Elpericus, a monk, II, 480. When he lived, ibid., note.

Emanus, priest of Urgel, I, 917.

Emmanuel consists of two things, divinity and humanity, I, 764.

Enbaldus, priest. See Eanbaldus.

What the *Encaenia* are among the Jews, I, 569.

Engaddi, “fountain of the kid,” signifies baptism, I, 394.

Engilpertus. See Angilbertus.

Why Enoch was preserved from death, I, 306. He will come with Elijah, 734.

Enolfus (Joannes), dean of Saint Cyriacus at Worms, I, 304.

What a grammatical enunciation is, II, 344. What it is in dialectic, 351.

Who Epaphras, Saint Paul’s fellow prisoner, was, I, 664.

What the Council of Ephesus decreed concerning the faith of the Eucharist, II, 378.

What kind of garment the ephod was, II, 494. Its mystical meaning, 495.

What Epicurus’s doctrine was, I, 435.

Epimenides, Cretan poet, I, 655.

The Epiphany of the Lord and its feast, II, 464. What feasts are commemorated together with it, 465. Why no one should be baptized on that day, 465, 493.

How a bishop was formerly elected and ordained, II, 492, 493. He was consecrated on Sunday, 488. He ought not to abandon his see, I, 79. He should recognize himself as a minister, not a master, 121. The accusation and correction of bad bishops are difficult, I, 433.

From where bishops are named and what their office is, I, 13, 14, 19, 63, 73, 80, 197; II, 652. Whether they surpass presbyters in dignity, ibid. They are compared with watchmen, II, 492. With what virtues they should shine, I, 73, 198, 199, 243, 269. They are exalted angels of God, I, 14. Lights of the Church, ibid. Salt of the earth, lights of the world, and so forth, 16. What sort of clerics they should have in their households, 17. Whether they can demand provisions from monasteries contrary to custom, 265, 266.

The power of bishops, II, 492.

From where *epistola* is named, I, 205. For what purpose letters are written, I, 43, 127. Who wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews and the other Catholic Epistles, II, 433. What the Mass Epistle is and from where it originated, II, 499.

The monastery of Echternach (Esternaco), II, 188. The body of Saint Willibrord rests there, 190.

Ericus (Hericus), duke of Friuli, overcome by treachery, I, 123, note; 165, note.

Ermedeus, servant of Felix of Urgel, I, 916.

Ermegildus, priest of Urgel, 917.

Ermengardis, queen and wife of King Lothair, II, 554.

How necessary the effectiveness of learning is in every dignity, I, 53.

Esau, dwelling on Mount Seir after his father’s death, I, 331. There he propagated the nation of the Idumeans, ibid.

Who wrote the books of Ezra, II, 432.

The word “essence” is properly said of God, I, 177.

Esternaco. See the monastery of Echternach.

Esther, a figure of the Church, II, 432. Who wrote the Book of Esther, ibid.

Ethelardus, archbishop, I, 83, 84. See Aedilhardus.

Queen Etheldritha gives Hexham to Wilfrid by exchange, I, 197, note.

Etheldrita, married to King Ethelwald, 211, note.

Ethelfrid drives the boy Edwin from the kingdom, II, 243, verse 92. He fell by a wicked sword, ibid., verse 111.

Ethelredus, king of the Northumbrians, to whom Charlemagne sent gifts, I, 57. He was killed by his own people, ibid., note; 85, note; 228, note.

Ethelredus, heir to the kingdom of the East Angles, beheaded, I, 211, note; 67, note.

Etherius, bishop. See Hiterius.

Ethics and its parts, II, 335.

What etymology is, II, 271.

Euborica, the city of York, I, 54; II, 234. First founded by the Romans, 242, verse 19. It is described, ibid., verses 20 ff. It is elevated into the metropolitan see of the kingdom, verses 203 ff. The bishops of the city of Euborica, ibid., verses 1077 ff.

The Eucharist. See the Body of Christ.

The mystery of the Eucharist is not to be investigated by reason, II, 412, 413, 414. In this mystery Christ, by a mere act of will, makes his body and blood from bread and wine, II, 414. In it Christ himself is truly eaten and drunk, 504. How one should approach this sacrament, 414. What Alcuin’s opinion is concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, 381. This was corrupted by a certain malicious person, I, 528.

The reservation of the Eucharist on Maundy Thursday, II, 477.

The monastery of Saint Eugendus. See Augendus.

Eugenia, an English virgin, I, 207, 208, note.

The metrical prayer of Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, II, 103. His testimony was cited by the Adoptionists, 569. It is rejected, 575.

Eulalia, whose true name was Gundrada, I, 148. Praised for chastity, ibid., note. She lived in the royal palace, II, 150, 152. Devoted to the best studies, 151. She wished to be instructed by Alcuin about the nature of the soul, 146 ff. A poem addressed to her, 151, 152. See Gundrada.

Eulogies sent as a reproach, I, 262.

Eutwinus, king of the West Saxons, II, 549, note. How many wars he fought and how many good deeds he performed, ibid.

The error of Eutyches, I, 794, 819.

Eve was punished with three evils, I, 846. See Woman. Verses on her fall, II, 707.

Why there are four Evangelists and why they are compared with four living creatures, II, 433, 435.

What the Gospel is and from where the name comes, II, 434, 499. In what language, where, and from what source the Gospels were written, II, 432, 433 ff. Why the Gospel is carried before the preceding candles at Mass, II, 497, 499.

From where Exodus received its name, II, 431.

Who exorcists are and from where they are named, II, 434, 491. Their office under the old law, 490. In the Church, 491, 492.

Exorcism in baptism, II, 522.

The exordium of a speech, II, 320. What must be attended to in it, ibid. and 321.

Who the *expediti vernaculi* are, I, 318.

How ancient funeral rites are and how they should be arranged, II, 512. To attend funerals is more useful than banquets, I, 428.

Exsuperius, priest of Urgel, I, 917.

What Hezekiah signifies, I, 450, 452, 454. What he obtained by prayer, II, 239.

Who wrote Ezekiel’s prophecies, II, 432.

## F

What a fable and history are, II, 271.

Why the face is so called, II, 422.

Fardulfus, abbot of Saint-Denis: when he lived and died, II, 552, note.

Moroaldus, abbot of the monastery of Farfa, I, 207.

The island of Farne, barren, II, 248, verse 656. It is cleansed of demons through the prayers of Saint Cuthbert, 249, verse 705.
