Who a fool is and from where the word comes, II, 472.

What the honeycomb signifies, I, 641.

What bile is, II, 355.

Felicianus, Arian bishop, I, 842.

What happiness is to be sought, II, 266.

The altar of Saint Felix the priest, II, 219.

Felix, bishop of Urgel, I, 7. Alcuin commends himself to his intercessions, ibid. and 8, note. He is condemned at Regensburg and Rome because of the novelty of his doctrine, 882, 918. Having renounced his error, he returned to his vomit, ibid. Alcuin warns him to abandon the novelty of his doctrine, 783 ff. How he answered Alcuin, 789, 882. His booklet was brought to Alcuin, I, 95. His opinion concerning the unity of the Church, I, 791. He feared openly to confess two persons in one Christ; how, 823. He makes Christ a solitary man, 832. He holds that Christ needed baptism, 140. He agrees with Nestorius, 854. He asserts that Christ is called God because he is joined and attached to God, 856. He perversely expounds Sacred Scripture, 832. He unfaithfully reports the texts of the holy Fathers, 842, 849 ff. In the testimonies produced on his behalf, he proves himself now ignorant, now unlearned, now malicious, 849. His errors, 789, 869. They are refuted by Alcuin, ibid. and following. The summary of his errors, 827. Some praise his writings, 784. He writes certain things in a Catholic manner, but whether sincerely, 830.

Felix is summoned to King Charles to give an account of his faith, I, 112. He is brought before King Charles, 917. He is granted the power to defend his opinion, ibid. At Aachen he is convicted by rational disputation and freed from error, 880, 882. At first he was to be handed over to Riculfus, archbishop of Trier, to be chastised and guarded, 148. Later, after confessing and renouncing his error, he was handed over to Laidradus of Lyon for examination, ibid. He was made a Catholic by Alcuin, 878. He was reconciled in friendship with him at Saint Martin’s, 141, note. An advocate, not the author, of the novelty, I, 798.

Felix’s conversion to the Catholic faith, I, 862, 878, 880, 882, 888, 892, 908. His confession of faith was sent to the priests and faithful of the parish of Urgel, 917 ff. Elipandus, unaware that Felix had already converted, wrote to him about this matter, 862.

Felix’s disputation with a Saracen, I, 125.

The Felician heresy was put to rest, I, 123, 125.

The linen undergarments of the priests under the old law, II, 494. What they signify, 495.

From where the word *feriae* is named, II, 426.

Wednesday, which is the beginning of the fast: how penance is to be administered, II, 471 ff.

The ceremonies of Wednesday in Holy Week, II, 475.

The celebration of Maundy Thursday, II, 476 ff., and its mysteries, I, 89. There is no fast on that day, ibid.

Good Friday and its solemnity, II, 478.

The monastery of Saint Peter at Ferrières was entrusted to Alcuin’s care, I, 68, 69, note.

Festal days are celebrated more leniently in monasteries, with the strictness relaxed, II, 194.

What the fig tree signifies in Scripture, I, 481.

Fidelis, abbot, II, 585. Elipandus wrote to him, II, 587. Whether he was infected by Elipandus’s error, 591.

What confidence, a part of the virtue of fortitude, is, II, 330.

What faith is, II, 354. It is believing what you do not see, I, 551. Its virtue and merit, 470. It is the life of the soul, 575. The beginning of our salvation, II, 582. Better than reason, 413. Necessary where reason fails, I, 193. Faith in Catholic peace is necessary for salvation, 707; II, 129. There must be one faith among all Christians, II, 583. Orthodox faith is preserved by the universal Church, 582. It is voluntary, and no one can be compelled to it, I, 42, 50. Faith working through love is the grace of God, 472.

The creed issued at Nicaea, II, 117.

The perfection of the Catholic faith, I, 129. What its rule is, II, 516.

Whether Lot’s daughters can be absolved from incest, I, 323.

Saint Filibert built the monasteries of Gemeticum and Herense, II, 212, note. His altar, ibid.

In what sense the Son of God is called the beginning, I, 468. Coeternal and coequal with the Father, not by growing but by being begotten, 570, 590. The only-begotten, 712. The only one incarnate, 729, 742. How he is to be understood as sent by the Father, 726. Why he is called now equal to and now less than the Father, 727. According to the form of a servant, less than the Father, less than himself, and less than the Holy Spirit, 728. He will judge the world in the form in which he was judged, 512, 513, 514. He is to be honored with the same honor as the Father, 512. Whether he can be called “omnipotent from the Omnipotent,” just as “God from God” is said, 741. Why, although conceived from the Holy Spirit, he is not called the Son of the Holy Spirit, 726, 742. According to his humanity he is not an adoptive son but a proper son, 729.

A son cannot be both the natural and adoptive son of the same father, I, 813. A proper and adoptive son cannot be one person, 107, 140, 763, 770, 808, 854, 886; II, 580. An adoptive son is not truly a son by nature, II, 574. The Only-Begotten cannot be or be called adoptive, I, 822, 907; II, 574. How the same person can have two fathers, 812.

Who are proper and adoptive sons, I, 842, 877. Who are the sons of God and the daughters of men, I, 311, 312.

“End” has various meanings in Scripture, I, 179.

Flavius Damoeta, I, 54, 56. A very distinguished man, ibid. He went to Saxony and was placed in charge of administering justice, 55, 56, note. Whether he was a bishop, ibid., note. The surname of Riculfus, archbishop of Mainz, 55, 243. See Damoeta and Riculfus.

The abbots of the monastery of Fleury: Magnulfus, Fulradus, and Theodulfus, II, 215, note.

The cult of Saint Florian, II, 218.

Fogginius, custodian of the Vatican Library, is praised, I, 757. His preface to Alcuin’s booklet sent to the abbots and monks of Gothia, 759.

The blessing of baptismal fonts, II, 483, 484.

Fordradus, priest, I, 33, 220, 221, note.

Fordredus, abbot, came to Rome on account of his monastery, I, 221, note.

The monastery of Forest-Montier was founded, II, 180 and note.

The furnace: inscriptions addressed to it, II, 227.

What fornication is and what its effects are, II, 472. Remedies for it, 142.

When *forsitan* is a word of doubt, I, 545.

What fortitude is, II, 145, 330. Its parts, ibid. What true fortitude is, 146.

The inconstancy of Fortune, II, 239.

Fortunatus’s hymn, “Pange lingua,” II, 90. The epitaph of a Christian poet, 214.

Fosites, an image of a god, II, 187.

Where the island of Fositesland is situated, II, 187. It is the same as the island of Farria, ibid., note.

The letter of the Council of Frankfurt against the bishops of Spain, II, 573 ff.

The Dialogue of Franco and Saxo on Grammar, II, 208 ff.

The future king of the Franks will be the greatest and last in the time of Antichrist, II, 529. This prophecy is judged foolish, ibid., note.

The greatness of the Frankish kingdom, I, 117.

The clothing of the ancient Franks, I, 203.

Who the brothers of the Lord are in Scripture, I, 486. They were not born from but were blood relatives of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 533. In Scripture, “brothers” is used for “sons,” I, 327. They are also called by that name in four other ways, II, 576.

Who a fratricide is, II, 472.

Fraud must be avoided, II, 138.

Fredegisus, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 148, 149, 739. Also called Fridugisus and Fridugilsus, 215, 216. He carried Charlemagne’s gifts to Alcuin, I, 93. He also carried Alcuin’s handbook, containing many things, to Arno, 169.

Frisia produces neither oil nor wine, II, 449.

Frichorius, an Irish priest flourishing in holiness, II, 176. Saint Angilbert wrote his epitaph and that of Caidocus, ibid., note. Abbot Gervinus raised the bodies of both from the earth, ibid.

Whether Fridegodus was the author of the poem on the bishops of York, II, 241.

Friducinus wrote a poem to him, II, 258. Whether he is the same as Friduinus, ibid., note.

Friduinus, a friend of Alcuin, I, 283. Abbot of Giro and Wir, successor of Eadbald, 284, note.

What cold is, II, 353.

Frisia. See Fresia.

The Frisians were defiled by pagan rites, II, 185. They were conquered by Charles, duke of the Franks, I, 188, 197. With King Charles pressing them, they were converted, 6. They were baptized by Saint Willibrord, II, 187, 188, 197. The king of the Frisians was Radbod, II, 185.

What the forehead is, II, 353. From where it receives its name, 422.

Fulda, where Saint Boniface’s tomb is, I, 255. Whether Alcuin taught letters there, 54, note; 256.

The brothers of Fulda; a letter to them, I, 157. Alcuin sent them a storax-colored pallium and a Mass booklet, ibid. The abbots of Fulda: Sturmio, Baugulfus, and Ratgarius, I, 256, note.

Saint Fulgentius, a teacher of brilliant speech and approved faith, I, 901, 907.

Saint Fulgentius’s booklet on the Holy Spirit, I, 754 and note.

Fulradus (Fulcradus), abbot of Saint-Denis and chaplain of King Pippin, II, 235, note. When he died, II, 440, note. His tomb and epitaph, 235.

How funerals are to be arranged, II, 512.

What the cords with which the wicked were driven from the Temple signify, I, 488.

From where thieves are named and how they differ from robbers, II, 472.

How rage differs from anger, I, 346, 349. The wrath of God is purgatorial fire, ibid.

## G
Gabriel (Saint): altar, II, 224.

Gale (Chelle): monastery of Gisla, sister of King Charles, I, 128, note. A new basilica was built there, into which the body of Saint Bathildis was transferred, 148, note.

Galilee: what it signifies, I, 479.

All Gaul stripped by the Huns, II, 239.

—Gaul Bracata: whence so called, II, 494.

—The peoples of Gaul afflicted by wolves, II, 486. By what remedy they were freed, ibid. and 487.

Gallicellula, I, 214. An assumed name of one of Alcuin’s disciples, 215, note.

[Col. 1469]

The monastic cock, which usually rouses the brothers for vigils, I, 123.

—The cock deceiving the wolf: a fable, II, 238.

Gandolfovilla, I, 159. Where it is situated, 160, note.

Gandulfus, whose disciples were condemned for heretical opinions at the synod of Arras, II, 377.

Gluttony of the belly (*gastrimargia*): in Latin, *ventris ingluvies*, II, 472. What vices it produces, ibid.

The joy of Christ in us, and our joy in Christ: in what it consists, I, 603.

—Full joy: the blessedness of eternal peace, 614.

Treasury: what it is, I, 546.

Gelasius, prelate, II, 213.

Pope Gelasius’s prayer for the Church, II, 89. He is the author of the Preface in the Mass, 500.

Ice: what it is, II, 353.

The two genealogies of Christ wrongly explained, I, 811. Correctly explained, 812.

—The genealogy of Christ’s humanity explained according to a threefold sense, I, 450ff.

The generation, or birth, of Christ is indescribable, I, 814.

The book of Genesis: whence it derives its name, II, 431.

The *genethliaci*, and why and from where they are so called, II, 464.

The authority of Gennadius of Marseille formerly commended, II, 373.

Genovefa (Saint), virgin: altar, II, 211.

The nations divided and dispersed by languages, I, 316.

Why genuflection is not made during the prayer for the Jews on Good Friday, II, 479.

Genus: what it properly is, II, 336. Whence the term derives, 420.

—How many genera there are, II, 273.

Geometry: what it is, II, 332.

George (Saint), the victor: altar, II, 210.

George, patriarch of the city of Jerusalem, I, 148. Elsewhere called Gregory and Sergius, ibid., note.

Gerard, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, reproved certain men concerning the Eucharist and condemned them at a synod before Berengar, II, 377.

Gerberga, queen and wife of Louis the Transmarine, II, 527, note. To her Abbot Adso dedicated a little book on the Antichrist, 526, 527.

Gerfridus, bishop of Münster and abbot of Werden, successor of Saint Liudger, II, 204, note. He had a copy of Sacred Scripture written, ibid. He restored churches, ibid.

Germanus (Saint), prelate: altar, II, 211. His cult at Paris, 194.

The customs of the Germans are touched upon in their drinking from a full cup, I, 62.

Geroldus, prefect of Bavaria, killed, I, 123, note; 165, note.

Gervasius and Protasius (Saints), martyrs: altar, II, 214.

Gervinus, abbot of Centula, raised the bodies of Saints Caidocus and Frichorius from the earth, II, 176, note.

The origin of giants, I, 312.

Gildas, the wisest of the Britons, I, 15. Elsewhere called Gilbus, 78, 79, note. He wrote a letter on the destruction of Britain, 16, note. When he lived and died, ibid.

Gisla (Gysla), the king’s sister, I, 128, 148, note. She had the additional name Lucia, 458. Alcuin calls her his sister, 148, 250, 251, 591. Abbess of the monastery of Chelles, 148, note. She built a new church in honor of the holy Mother of God, ibid. She sent messengers to Alcuin, 68. He visited her, 119, 120. She wrote a letter from Paris to Alcuin at Tours, 460. He sent her and Columba his Commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, 459, 462ff., 591. She gave Alcuin a cross for the basilica at Troyes and a cope, 148, 149. She possessed certain treatises of Bede, sent by Alcuin, 205, 251.

—Gisla, the third daughter of Charles by Hildegard, I, 149, 150, note. She attended the hunting at Aachen in splendid attire, II, 453.

—Gisla, sister or daughter of Charlemagne? A nun admonished by Alcuin to virtue and to the reading of Sacred Scripture, I, 293.

Gislebertus, abbot of Elnone and bishop of Tournai, II, 235, note. His epitaph, ibid.

Gislemarus, a distinguished man of the region of Ponthieu, II, 179, 180. He provided Saint Richarius with a place in the forest of Troncq, ibid.

The flaming and revolving sword: what it is, I, 310, 311.

—The sword is understood in many ways in Scripture, I, 181.

—The two swords mentioned in the Gospel: what they signify, I, 180, 182.

The inequality of the terrestrial globe is noted, I, 99.

Vain glory: what it is, II, 143, 471. What vices arise from it, 144. What remedies exist against it, ibid.

Why “Glory be to the Father” is sung in the Church, and who instituted it, II, 498. Why it is omitted in the Office of the Lord’s Supper, 476.

Who instituted the singing of “Glory in the highest” at Mass, II, 497, 298.

Gloss: what it is, II, 271.

The dedication of the church at Gorze by Grodegandus, bishop of Metz, II, 225.

[Col. 1470]

Goteramus, the first count of the frontier district, killed at the castle of Guntionis, I, 165.

Gothia, otherwise Septimania, I, 141.

—The abbots and monks of Gothia, I, 139, 141. Alcuin sent them a little book against Felix, 139, 141, note; 760ff. He instructed them in excellent teachings, 141.

The Goths or Huns, I, 12.

—The Goths ravage the churches of Italy in Italy, II, 239.

—An exhortatory poem to the Gothic people, II, 234.

The ecclesiastical orders: what and how many they are, II, 434, 491. They are to be conferred without remuneration, 488, 652.

The Greeks came to Italy with a fleet, I, 6. They were defeated by the commanders of King Charles, ibid.

Grammar: what it is and what its kinds are, II, 270.

—A dialogue between teacher and pupils on grammar, II, 265ff.

Gratitude, as a part of the virtue of justice: what it is, II, 330.

—The necessity of Christ’s grace, II, 407. Also necessary for the beginning of faith, 408. It does not remove free will, ibid. It precedes the work of faith, I, 598. Signified by visible anointing in baptism, 811.

—May grace precede, and obedience follow, I, 383.

—The grace of God by which God became man: what it is, I, 725.

—The fullness of grace in Christ, I, 471, 725.

—Without the grace of the Holy Spirit, human intelligence accomplishes nothing, I, 285.

—Without God’s grace, not even a good will can exist in a human being, I, 436, 717.

—The various gifts of grace in the Church, I, 724.

Gravenek, prince and abbot of Kempten, II, 3.

Gregory (Saint), martyr, II, 219.

Gregory (Saint), pope, Father of the Church, II, 210. A man of the purest faith, I, 901, 906. He offers the word of God to the pagan Britons, II, 243, lines 78ff. He composed the prayers of the Mass, I, 892.

—Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule* is commended, I, 43, 73, 74, 76, 204. Likewise his *Dialogues*, 253.

—Saint Gregory’s *Sacramentary*, I, 144, 146. A prayer in honor of all the saints, II, 107. Another, 110, 118. His letter to Leander, about which Alcuin is uncertain, I, 110.

Grimoaldus, duke of Benevento, I, 156.

Grodegandus, bishop of Metz, II, 225, note. See Hrogandus.

Gudbertus (Saint). See Cudbertus.

William, duke of Bavaria: for whose use the prayer book of Charles the Bald was published, II, 4.

Gluttony: what it is and what kind of sin it is, II, 142. Its effects, ibid.

Gluttony: whence the term derives, and what vices arise from it, II, 472.

Gundrada, a virgin surnamed Eulalia, I, 148. She lived at court with other virgins, ibid. She is praised for chastity, ibid. She was the sister of Abbot Adalhard of Corbie, ibid., note. She was sent into exile with her brothers by Louis Augustus, 206, note. See Eulalia.

Gundefredus, priest of Urgell, I, 917.

Gundun restored the church of Saint Martin, II, 213.

Guntarius, Arno’s footman, I, 130.

The castle of Guntionis, I, 165, note.

Gunvinus, a priest, restored a ruined church, II, 214.

Taste: whence it is so called, II, 421.

The brothers and monastery of the Church of Jarrow (Gyrvensis, Gyroensis), I, 21, 23. Founded by King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, 23, note. Its abbots were Ceolfrith, ibid.; Eadbaldus, ibid., note; and Friduinus, 283, 284, note.

Gysla. See Gisla.

H

To have: its category and kinds, II, 342.

Habit, a species of quality: what it is, II, 740.

Who is a legitimate heir, I, 190.

Heresy: in Greek, it is named from “choice,” I, 660. How it differs from schism, ibid.

The causes of heretical depravity, I, 790.

—Heretics who seek to gather the Church without the Lord labor in vain, 382. They are compared with fools, 439. They do not enter the sheepfold through the door but climb in from elsewhere, 562.

—The pride of heretics, I, 386. Their rashness in interpreting Scripture, 905.

The church of Hexham was granted by Ethelthryth to Saint Wilfrid, I, 197, note. Its magnificence, ibid.

What Haimo of Halberstadt thought about the truth of the Eucharist, II, 379, 380.

Hansiz’s conjectures are mistaken, I, 40, 69, 122, 127, 165; II, 448, note.

Heardbertus, duke, signs a double charter of King Ecgfrith of Mercia, I, 272.

Why the city of Hebron was called by three names, I, 326.

Hechstanus, a priest surnamed Altapetra, I, 199, 200, note.

King Ethelred, I, 85, note. See Aedilredus, Ethelredus.

[Col. 1471]

Helbrechtus, Alcuin’s teacher, I, 64, 66, note. See Aelbertus.

Helena, discoverer of the holy Cross, II, 219.

Alsace (*l’Alsace*), I, 41.

Helpericus. See Elpericus.

The blasphemy of the heretic Helvidius, II, 399.

Grass: what it is, II, 353.

Herbertus and Lisoius burned at Orléans on account of heresy, II, 377.

Heribertus, archbishop of Cologne: when he lived, II, 527.

Herigerus, abbot of Lobbes, uses the Council of Ephesus to prove the faith concerning the Eucharist, II, 378.

Hermon: what it signifies, I, 389.

Herwaldus, abbot, and Niger, priests and followers of Saint Willibrord, II, 252, lines 1045ff. They preach to the Saxons, line 1049. They are killed, line 1054, and drowned in the Rhine, line 1057. They are miraculously rescued from it and honorably buried, line 1070.

The people of Hesperia serve under hated scepters, II, 239.

Heteronyms: what they are, II, 337.

Ireland is populous, II, 246, line 458. It once flourished in scholastic learning, 185.

—The most learned teachers of Ireland once produced much advancement throughout the churches of Britain, Gaul, and Italy, I, 285.

—The brothers of Ireland are praised for their religious way of life and pursuit of wisdom, I, 284, 286, note. Alcuin announced to them the new sects that had arisen in Spain, 285. They professed the same Rule of Saint Benedict as the English monks, 286, note.

Winter: whence the term derives, II, 428.

Jerome (Saint), teacher of the Church, II, 210, 225. A most renowned teacher of Sacred Scripture, I, 461, 901.

—Saint Jerome’s statement that might seem to favor the Pelagians is qualified, I, 418. His opinion concerning the creation of the angels before this visible world, 651. Whether he was the author of the *Breviary on the Psalter*, 798. A treatise on the Psalter under his name exists in manuscript in the library of Saint Emmeram, 814, note. His treatise *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* is unknown, 775. His Commentary on the Apocalypse is likewise unknown, II, 569, note. His Letter to Caesarius is also unknown, ibid., note. The book *On the Birthdays of the Saints throughout the Year*: whether it is a martyrology, 111.

—Saint Jerome’s prayers, II, 39, 120, 121.

—Saint Jerome: altar, II, 225.

Jerusalem: what it signifies, I, 354.

The distinguished praise of Hilary (Saint), I, 827, 901. The preface cited by Alcuin is missing, ibid., note. Whether the text was corrupted by Felix, 842; II, 569, note.

—Saint Hilary’s prayer, II, 117. Altar, 209. The cult of his relics at Poitiers, 194.

Hildebald, archbishop of Cologne, built an altar to Saint Peter at Charlemagne’s command, 216. He adorned another with metalwork, 225.

Hildegarius, a relative of Arno, I, 112. He carried books from the library of Saint Martin with him, ibid. and 114.

Hildrud, a virgin, daughter of Charlemagne by Fastrada, II, 453, note. She attended the hunting at Aachen, ibid.

The brothers of the island of Lérins came to Alcuin, I, 206.

—The brothers of Lérins, I, 278. See Lérins.

Hinchaldus, bishop of Lindisfarne. See Hugibaldus.

Hincmar of Rheims considers the heretics mistaken concerning the truth of the Eucharist, II, 378.

It is called a fish-filled river, 123, note. Which were the smoothed timbers of Noah’s ark, I, 312. Why the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge were created, I, 305, 308.

The calamity of Lindisfarne caused by pagans, I, 11, 12. — An exhortation to the brothers of Lindisfarne, II, 239. The city of Lindissa, II, 245, verse 363 and following. What the tongue is, II, 352. What a deceitful tongue is, I, 376. — The primordial language in which the family remained, I, 317. — From where the diversity of languages arose, ibid. — The three languages distinguished above the others, I, 630. — The degeneration of the Latin language into the Spanish vernacular, II, 589. The word *liniare*, in what passage it occurs, I, 848. Liobradus, or Liodradus, bishop of Lyon, I, 106, note. See Laidradus.

The brothers of the island of Lérins question Alcuin, I, 110. They come to Alcuin, 275, note, and also to Saint Martin’s frequently, ibid. and 279, note, 280. The founder of that monastery was Saint Honoratus, bishop of Arles, 279, note. They secretly confess their disobedience and negligence to Alcuin, 280. He intercedes for them, ibid. Lisojus, a heretic. See Herbertus.

The litany, or prayer to Christ, II, 153. — From where the word *litania* is derived, II, 486. — Why and when the greater litany is celebrated, ibid. — How the litanies are recited on Holy Saturday, 484. — Litanies of the saints, 66. Those concerning all the saints, to be recited on the four weekdays, collected from Saint Jerome, 111 and following. To be recited on each weekday, 62, 111, 112 and following.

What a letter is, II, 269, 352. From where it is called so, 268. Why letters are called elements, 269. — The division and accidents of letters, ibid. The Gothic and Mozarabic liturgy is preserved in an eleven-volume manuscript in the library at Toledo, II, 590.

Liudgarda, a most devout woman in God, I, 27. A noblewoman, 67. A religious woman, 263. Wife of Charlemagne, 28, note, 36, note. She fosters more refined literature, ibid. Alcuin calls her his daughter, 55, note. She recovered from a dangerous illness, ibid. She was to celebrate the Mass of Saint Mary with the infants at Nivelles, 67, 68, note. She sent two golden bracelets to Paulinus the patriarch, 36. A pallium [sent] to Abbess Æthelburh, 67, note. She sent a silver bowl and storax to Peter, archbishop of Milan, 192. Her goodwill toward the servants of God and the churches, ibid. Her epitaph, I, 131, 132, note. Liudgarius, Saint. See Leodegarius. Liudgerus, bishop of Mimigardeford, I, 158, note. Verses on the church built by him, II, 220, note. Liuphrammus, archbishop of Salzburg, had Alcuin’s poems collected, I, col. 1087, note. When he presided over that Church, ibid.

How many the topics of controversies are, II, 315. Logic and its parts, II, 332, 335. Lorenzana, Francisco Antonio, canon of the Church of Toledo, II, 589. Why Lot fled to Segor and from there to the mountain, I, 322. Why his wife was turned into a pillar of salt, 323. Whether he was guilty of incest, ibid. See Lot’s daughters. [Col. 1478] Lothair II, 554. Son of Louis the Pious, husband of Ermengardis, ibid., note.

The washing of feet on Maundy Thursday, II, 478. Formerly customary among pilgrims, 213. Whether Saint Luke was ignorant of the Hebrew letters, I, 333. Paul’s assistant, 664. Why he bears the form of a calf, II, 435. Whom the lamps signify in Scripture, I, 516, 543. The Lucernarium, a part of the divine office, I, 375. Lucia, a virgin, II, 234. — The Lucia whom Alcuin calls his sister, I, 157 and note. Her proper name was Gisla, 458. See Sister Gisla. The altar of Saint Lucia the virgin, II, 210. Louis, the brother of Charles the Younger, I, 148, note. See Chlodwig. Louis the Transmarine: in what year he died, II, 527. The brothers of Lyon, I, 106, 111, note. Luitgardis. See Liutgarda. Lullo, or Lulla, abbot, I, 271, note. He subscribes the decree of Archbishop Æthelard at the Council of Clovesho, ibid. He is commended to Ardbertus, an illustrious man, 272, note. Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, II, 449, note.

What the lighting and extinguishing of lamps on Maundy Thursday signify, II, 476. What the moon is, II, 353. Whether it is of a cold nature, I, 98. It is a type of the Church, 378. — How the fourteenth moon is found, II, 368. — What the reckoning of the fifteenth moon is, II, 356. — The reckoning of the paschal moon ought to remain unchangeable, I, 83, 103. — The lunar leap: by what other names it is called, II, 361. In what places it occurs, ibid. It is explained, I, 81. When it occurred, I, 104. Its calculations are sent to Charlemagne, 92, 124. And they are defended against the Egyptian boys, 98. Eight problems concerning the lunar leap, II, 358 and following. The moon’s course through the individual signs, I, 100 and following; II, 357. Its various calculations, I, 102. Some of these Alcuin sends to Charlemagne, 124. The causes of lunar diminution, I, 102.

The monastery of Saint Lupus, I, 67. Entrusted to Alcuin’s care, 68, note. The basilica at Troyes, 149, note. — The intercessions of Saint Lupus, 148. Who the wolves in the Church are, I, 564. Lupicinus, honored according to worldly standards, II, 160. The nightingale. A poem about it, II, 236. What a lustrum is and from where the word comes, II, 429. What light is, II, 353. Why it was created on the first day, I, 307. From where luxury is called by that name, and what vices arise from it, II, 472.

## M

Mabillon’s investigation concerning the author of the confession of faith attributed to Alcuin, II, 370 and following. It is defended against the criticisms of D. Basnage, 381 and following. His conjectures sometimes fail, I, 136, note, 137, note, 158, note, 165, note. What a wall means in Scripture, I, 396. The author of the books of the Maccabees is considered uncertain, II, 432. Macharius, bishop of Trier, I, 192, 193, 194. See Rigbodus. Madrisius, praised as editor of the works of Saint Paulinus the patriarch, I, 35, note. He is corrected in some places, 48, note, 136, note, 137, note; II, 231, note.

Maganfredus, a faithful man of Charlemagne, I, 97, 99, note. Alcuin’s dearest friend, 155. He died in his homeland of Benevento, ibid. See Megenfridus. Magenharius, count of the city of Sens, I, 213, note. See Meginharius. Who the Chaldean Magi were and what their study was, II, 464. — The journey of the Magi to Christ and their gifts, II, 464. Maginarius, abbot of Saint-Denis, successor of Fulrad, II, 236. His epitaph, ibid. What it means to magnify the Lord, II, 541. What magnificence is, II, 330. Magnulfus, or Magulfus, abbot of Fleury; verses about him, II, 215, note. Magus, a disciple of Alcuin, commended to Arno, I, 112, 113, note. A good brother, 114. The same as Adalbertus, 130, note, 168, note.

Certain letters of the noble Valentinian Majansius, II, 588 and following. Past, present, and future evils from which the priest asks to be freed in the Mass, II, 508. Why the book Malachi is so called, II, 431. Who arranged it in its order, ibid. What Malchus means in Latin and what the cutting off of his ear signifies, I, 182, 623. The monk Malchus mourned a monk in the desert whom he had lost in the monastery, I, 140. [Col. 1479] Who the slanderers are, II, 472. Who the sorcerers are, ibid. *Mallum* and *mallus* mean the same as judgment and assembly, I, 200, note. What evil is, I, 311. One evil man mixed among the good corrupts very many, I, 437. Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, instituted the Rogation Days, II, 486. The hymn of Mamertus Claudianus, II, 90. Mammon is called the unjust riches of the world, I, 410. What Manasseh means, I, 450, 452, 454. The commandments of God can be observed by all and by each individual, II, 409. *Mandrae* means the same as monasteries, II, 253, note. The error of the Manichaeans, II, 573. What manna signifies, I, 528. Manno, provost of the monastery of Saint Eugendus, I, 345.

The many dwelling places in the kingdom of God signify different ranks of merits, I, 597. What the hands are, II, 353. — The hand of the Lord signifies God’s power, I, 368; the Savior, 376. — Why hands are imposed on the baptized, II, 127. — In Scripture, hands are understood as works, I, 422. What the *mappula* is, II, 496. The altar of Saint Marcellus, II, 219. Mark, Paul’s assistant, I, 664. Why Saint Mark the evangelist bears the form of a lion, II, 435. What the sea is, II, 353. It signifies the present age, I, 518, 640. — What the Sea of Tiberias is and its mystical interpretation, I, 518.

What Mary signifies, I, 450, 452, 456. — The Blessed Virgin Mary came from a royal and free lineage, II, 579. Without violation of her bodily integrity she conceived and gave birth to the Word of God, I, 731; II, 509. She remained a virgin after childbirth, I, 725; II, 399, 533, 541. How she subjected herself to the law of purification, 533. Why she was called “woman” by Christ, I, 482. She became Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”) and Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer”), 731, 845; II, 399. She is to be believed and confessed as Mother of God, I, 471. She is not to be called a conditional handmaid, I, 839. Nor a titular or merely nominal Mother of God, 847. She was honored with three gifts: the angelic salutation, divine blessing, and the fullness of grace, 846. Mother of believers, II, 536. — The singular praises of Blessed Mary, II, 542. Altar, 217, 223, 225. How effective her intercession is, 542. — How the Lord was magnified in Blessed Mary, II, 542. — Verses on Blessed Mary the virgin, II, 213, 218, 219. Whether Mary of Clopas was truly the sister of the Blessed Virgin, II, 221, note.

Maro, II, 228. Verses concerning Saint Martha, II, 207. Georg Heinrich Martini, rector of the city gymnasium at Regensburg, is praised, II, 556. His learned commentary on the letters of Alexander the Great and Dindimus, king of the Brahmans, 606. Saint Martin, bishop of Tours: his homeland, parents, and status, II, 159. He resisted Arian perfidy, ibid. He regenerated his mother in Christ, ibid. Driven into Gaul, he joined Saint Hilary, ibid. He built a cell for himself near Poitiers, 160. A great intercessor with God, I, 29. Always honored by the kings and kingdom of the Franks, 262. — The virtues of Saint Martin, II, 160, 161. Miracles, ibid. and 162. His death and burial, 161, 162. Patronage and cult, 194. Church, 209, 213. Chapel, 224. Altar, 210, 223, 224. Prayer, 121.

A small dwelling not far from Saint-Amand, Baralla, I, 148. The immunity of his churches, I, 265. — The boys of Saint Martin, II, 154. A great multitude of sons, I, 168. — The brothers of Saint Martin, I, 29. At times they said they were monks, at times canons, and at times neither, 175. They accept Alcuin as master and rector from the king, ibid. They are accused before the king by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, 174. They are summoned to the royal assembly, 175. They are defended by Alcuin, 169. And praised for the propriety of monastic life, ibid. — The priests of Saint Martin serving in the churches are harassed by the bishop with new exactions, I, 265. Martin, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 55. Martin the priest is commended to the intercession of George, patriarch of Jerusalem, I, 148.

The star of Mars, long hidden, suddenly shone forth, I, 97, 98, 101. The cause of its concealment, ibid. In martyrdom the sacraments of baptism are completed, II, 406. What Mathan means, I, 450, 452, 455. Who mathematicians are and from where they are called so, II, 464. Saint Matthias the apostle; verses about him, II, 223. Why Saint Matthew the evangelist is represented by the form of a man, II, 435. — The altar of Saint Matthew, II, 210. A poem about him, 222. The antiquity of Matins, II, 511.

The church and altar of Saint Maurice, II, 218, 224. What Bishop Maurinus of Alexandria established concerning the three days at the beginning of the world, II, 366. Saint Maurontus was baptized by Saint Richarius, II, 179, note. His mother was Richtrudis, ibid. Maurontus, guardian of royal lands and forests, II, 160. After laying aside secular dress, he became a monk, ibid. He founded the monastery of Forest, ibid., note. Maurus, the boy of Saint Benedict, I, 162, note; II, 233, note. A disciple of Alcuin, II, 162, note. See Rhabanus. The altar of Saint Maximilian the confessor, II, 218. The emperor Maximus: Saint Martin foretold to him victory in Italy and his death at Aquileia, II, 161. What mechanics is, II, 332. The church and altar of Saint Medard, II, 219, 224, 225.

The mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, I, 604, 605, 730. What the science of medicine is, II, 332. The studies of physicians at Charlemagne’s court, II, 228. Milan, a city stained by Arian perfidy, II, 159. Formerly an imperial city, 194. What churches, altars, and bodies of saints were formerly there, II, 598. Megenfredus, treasurer of the royal palace, I, 50. Almost an intimate counselor, 52, note. Commander of the Saxon army in the expedition against the Huns, ibid. Meginarius, a wise and energetic man, I, 213, note. Whether he is the same as Maginharius and Meginherus, ibid. See Maginharius.

Pope Melchiades, successor of Sylvester, I, 89. He decreed that no one should fast on Monday or Thursday, ibid., and II, 466. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest: who he is, without father and mother, I, 319, 685, 686. Whether he is the same as Shem, II, 490. He is interpreted as “king of righteousness,” I, 686. A type of Christ, ibid. and 687. What memory is as a part of oratory, and what its aids are, II, 314, 328. — What memory is as a part of the virtue of prudence, II, 329. Menalca, master of the cooks, II, 228. Menalca the elder, II, 237. From where the mind is so called, II, 421. It is the spirit and eye of the soul, 422. Christ’s table is Sacred Scripture, I, 384. — The blessing of the table in verse, II, 213.

From where the month is named and what its parts are, II, 427. From where Quintilis and Sextilis received their names, 428. Who the hireling in the Church is, I, 564. Merula, an assumed name of an unknown man, I, 123. What metaplasm is, II, 271. What meters are called, ibid. Saint Michael the archangel brings Bishop Saint Wilfrid a message of restored health and of the time of his death, II, 248. — The intercession of Saint Michael, II, 225. Church, 223. Altar, 209, 211, 212. — Verses on Saint Michael, II, 208.

The Migetian heretics, II, 572, note. Who Migetius was, or Mingentius, II, 572, 573, 591. What he thought concerning predestination to evil, 371. More about him in the Dissertation on the Heresy of the Adoptianists, vol. II, col. 303. Militane, a follower of Elipandus, I, 915. Common soldiers, that is, men of low birth, I, 148. — Why the excessive number of soldiers accompanying a bishop is criticized, ibid. The mystical significance of the number one thousand, I, 520. Who the ministers of Christ are and what it means to minister to Christ, I, 584.

The miracle concerning the coming Christ that Caesar Augustus saw, II, 462. — Miracles are testimonies of holiness, II, 182. Unwise mercy is that which benefits a few and harms many, I, 148. It is to be exercised toward those who sin against us, II, 131. How great a good it is, ibid. — How great the mercy of God toward human beings is, I, 351. Its time is now, ibid. and 355. — The mercy of a judge without discipline creates security for sinning, II, 131.

What the Mass is, II, 508. From where it is called by that name, 435. Why it is called a sacrifice, ibid. From where it took its beginning, 436. It was first celebrated by Saint Peter at Antioch, 497. What the ancient form was like, 496. Its contents, ibid. Its celebration, 497. Its ceremonies explained mystically, 496, 497. How precious the vestments formerly used for it were, 550. — It is believed that the dead are freed from punishments by the sacrifice of the Mass, II, 250, verse 815. Its wondrous power, ibid. — The Mass of the catechumens, II, 508. Of the Innocents, 514. Of the Holy Trinity, 6. For asking the grace of the Holy Spirit, 7. For sins, 8. For requesting tears, ibid. For requesting the angels’ help, 9. Against temptations of thought, ibid. Of holy wisdom, 10. For requesting humility, 10. Of charity, 11. Against temptations of the flesh, [Col. 1481] 12. Of the Holy Cross, 12. Of tribulation and necessity, 13. Of Saint Mary, ibid. In commemoration of Saint Mary, 14. Of one apostle, ibid. Of several apostles, 15. Of one martyr, ibid. Of several martyrs, 16. In a church of Holy Martyrs, ibid. Of sacred relics, 17. Daily Mass of the saints, ibid. For enemies, ibid. For one confessing his sins, 18. For the salvation of the living and the repose of the dead, ibid. — The Mass of Saint Augustine, II, 7, 9–14. — Three Masses on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, II, 462. Likewise three on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, 469. — Why Masses for the dead are celebrated without the Gloria and Alleluia, II, 513. Whether it is permissible to celebrate them for all deceased Christians, ibid.

A small missal sent by Alcuin to the monks of Vedast, I, 59, 60. Also to the monks of Fulda, 256. — The Gregorian and Gelasian missal books arranged by Alcuin, II, 3. The royal envoys are not poor persons, but archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts, I, 152, 153, note. How the sending of the Son by the Father is to be understood, I, 726. — The mission of Christ is the Incarnation, I, 515, 516, 542, 550. — What the mission of the Holy Spirit is, I, 726.

What modesty is as a part of the virtue of temperance, II, 330. How sadness differs from grief, II, 471. What a moment of time is, II, 426. A monk must not possess even a single coin without the abbot’s permission, I, 291. — Monks must avoid stolen meals and excessive attention to clothing, I, 22, 23. — Charity, obedience, and stability are commended to monks, I, 140. The way to God is the unity of charity and humble obedience, 60. There should always be either work or a little book in their hands, ibid. The study of Sacred Scripture is commended to them because of the spreading heresies, 115. — The happy life of monks, I, 114. The primitive Church initiated it, ibid. — The whole life of monks consists in charity, humility, and obedience, I, 107, 289. Their virtues and studies, 115. Not only their secular possessions but also the affection of their will should be held in common, 114. What the mutual duties of seniors and juniors are, 289 and following. — An exhortation to monks to sing nocturnal praises, II, 226.

Moni, a disciple of Alcuin, II, 258. An exhortatory poem addressed to him as he was traveling through unknown lands, ibid. Whether he is the same as Monna, ibid. Monna, a priest, Greek *anthropos*, “man,” I, 200, 201, note. Mount Zion signifies Christ, I, 381. The mountains around Zion are the angels, prophets, and preachers, I, 381. The monastery of Mount Olivet, Montoliou, I, 289, note. Its first founder and rector was Olumundus, ibid. Mopsus, a disciple of Alcuin, ill at Saint Martin’s, I, 55. The monks of Morbach, I, 62, note. — By whom the monastery of Morbach was founded and established, I, 62, note. Those who die in works of charity live to God, I, 132. How provision was formerly made for the dying, II, 512. Moroaldus, abbot of the congregation of Saint Mary of Farfa, I, 206, 207.

What death is, II, 352. It is called sleep, I, 574. Man’s death is twofold, 308, 734. Death was put to death by the death of Christ, 132. — When grace arrived, the kingdom of death was destroyed, I, 187. — The devil and sin also come under the name of death, I, 186. — Death must be remembered amid joys, II, 226. Whether it is better to await death in a canonical office or in monastic holiness, I, 296. What the four-day-dead man signifies, I, 574. — The dead are to be accompanied with compassion, not mourning, I, 132 and 133. How they are happier than the living, 422. — The funeral rites and commemoration of the dead, II, 512. The banks of the Meuse, I, 39. Moses’ prayer is more powerful than an army, II, 148.

From where woman is called by that name and what she signifies mystically, I, 431. Why she was built from the side of the sleeping man, 309. Whether before sin she was under the authority of man, 310. How she is the source of all evils, 431. In giving birth amid sorrow she is a type of the Church, 613. Of how many elements the world consists, I, 306. Why it is perfect in the number six, ibid. It began in springtime, 414. It is governed not by rash movements but by providence, II, 409. How the Holy Spirit reproves the world, I, 610. — People deceived by love of the world are called worldly, I, 469, 586, 599. — How many and what the ages of the world are, II, 425. — By the name “this world,” the Church is often understood, I, 607. The evil of murmuring is censured in monks, I, 114. A poem to the Muses for the benefit of a royal youth, II, 230. What music is, II, 332.

## N

What Naasson means, I, 450, 451, 455. From where the Nabataean region received its name and where it is situated, I, 327. [Col. 1482] The inscriptions of the monastery of Saint Nabor, II, 215. Verses on the tomb of the holy martyr, ibid. What the nostrils are, II, 353. Why they are touched in baptism, I, 109, 110, 127; II, 522. What rhetorical narration is and what it ought to be like, II, 321. Why the feast of the Nativity of the Lord is not movable, II, 462. — Verses on the Nativity of the Lord, II, 207. The birthdays of the saints are called the days of their departure from the world, I, 613. Why they are celebrated with joy, II, 480, 481. What Nathanael means, I, 481. — Nathanael, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 169, 174, note, 157, note, 410. He is surnamed Fridugis, 174, note. He is called a deacon, 410. An archdeacon, 148. He is commended to the prayers of George, patriarch of Jerusalem, ibid. Present with the king in the bath, 157. The virgins Lucia and Columba are entrusted to his care, ibid. He carries Alcuin’s letter to Charlemagne together with the most holy gift of Sacred Scripture, 157, note. Who the Nathinaeans are, II, 490.

Why the Nativity of the Lord is celebrated, and what portents and signs preceded it, II, 462. — The birthdays of Pharaoh and Herod were formerly festive in honor of them, I, 332. From where nature is named, II, 420. The term is rightly applied to God, I, 177. — The two natures in Christ, proper and perfect, I, 793, 794, 819, 879, 898. Which properties belong to each, 731, 732. What the ship is, II, 353. Who the Nazarenes are, II, 491. What Nazareth means, I, 479. Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans, formerly called Sychar, I, 334. What the cloud is, II, 353. Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne, I, 267, 268. See Nifridius. He is sent to Spain with Laidradus and Benedict, I, 148, 268. He was also abbot of Urbion, 148, note. Indeed, he was its first abbot and founder, 268, note.

What a matter is and what arguments are to be drawn from it in controversies, II, 323. Nemias, cupbearer of Charlemagne’s court, II, 228. How Nimrod was a giant and a mighty hunter, I, 316. He was the first to strive to rule over human beings, ibid. Nestorius did not openly say that there were two persons in Christ, I, 854, 879, 881. He pretended to say that there was one Son, II, 550. — The heresy of Nestorius, I, 794, 795, 814, 831, 881, 888, 894, 908, 919. His creed, 919. Neustria, a part of Charlemagne’s kingdom, II, 566. Why Nicodemus came to Christ by night, I, 490, 540. From where Nicopolis received its name, I, 660. Nifridius, a bishop, I, 267. See Nefridius. Saint Ninia the bishop was renowned for many virtues, I, 297. The apostle of the Picts, ibid., note. His church and monastery, called Candida Casa, ibid. and note. Alcuin’s letter to his brothers, ibid. Nineveh and Robooth are not two cities, I, 316. The monastery of Nivelles, or Nivigella, I, 67. Built at the urging of Itta and Saint Amandus, 68, note.

What snow is, II, 353. The monastery of Nobiliacum, distinguished by the name of Saint Vedast, II, 172, note. Its abbots were Aper and Ato, 214. Its inscriptions, 212. Nobiliacus, a place near Arras: why it was so called, II, 172. How Noah was a perfect man, I, 312. How he became drunk after the Flood, 316. What a noun is grammatically and philosophically, II, 271, 350. Its proper meaning, 271. — The accidents, species, and genera of nouns, 272, 273. Number and figures, 275. Cases, 276. And declensions, 277. — The name of God is holy, II, 506. Why we ask that it be hallowed, ibid. How it is ineffable although written with four Hebrew letters, 494. It is hung on the forehead of the pontiff, ibid. — What the proper and significant names in Christ are, I, 868. — The names of the Fathers of the Old Testament and their allegories, I, 450, 451 and following. — A good name is better than precious ointments, I, 428.

From where the Nones are called by that name, II, 428. — From where the office of the ninth hour comes, II, 510. Noroberet, or Norbert, a traveling priest, is commended to friends, I, 221. For what sins the kings of Northumbria were punished, I, 227. What the signs obelus and asterisk are, II, 271. Noviantus, or Novientus, Alcuin’s small estate, I, 128. Where it is situated, 129, note. From where night is called by that name, II, 427. What its parts are, ibid. What it signifies in Sacred Scripture, I, 389; II, 553. Clouds signify prophets and teachers, I, 441. Numa established January as the first month, II, 463. What the number of nouns is, II, 277. The mystical interpretation of the 153 fish in the Gospel, I, 41, 244, 641. — The mystical significance of the number fifteen, I, 376, 389. [Col. 1483] The division and variety of numbers, I, 408. Their typological interpretation, 87. Their great importance in Sacred Scripture, 344. — A comparison of the numbers in the Old and New Testaments, I, 214. — From where the Book of Numbers is named, II, 431. The function of money-changers, I, 487. Lawful marriages are not to be condemned, II, 516. Nevertheless, the continence of virgins is to be preferred to them, ibid. The first and second marriages are to be called good, 408. — What the wedding at Cana of Galilee signifies, II, 465. The night raven, a type of repentance, I, 355.

## O
Obedience: how meritorious is the virtue, I, 484. — Through obedience a person reaches hidden wisdom, I, 370. Obelus: what kind of sign, II, 271. Obeth: what it signifies, I, 450, 451, 453. The *oblati*, or those offered or donated to monasteries, are not included under the name “monks,” II, 172. The daily offerings of rulers at Mass, I, 67. Observance, as a part of the virtue of justice: what it is, II, 330. Occiput: what it is, II, 422. Ocialdus, abbot of Centula and successor of Saint Richarius, II, 180, note, 181. A man of proven and perfect holiness, ibid. He transfers the body of Saint Richarius, ibid. Ocinus, a noble Frank, II, 169. Why the octave of the Nativity of the Lord is celebrated, II, 463. How the number eighty is attributed to the concubines in the *Song of Songs*, I, 409. Eyes: what they are, II, 353. — Why the eyes of Adam and Eve were opened, I, 309. — The eyes of Jesus mystically signify the gifts of his Spirit, I, 519. — The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, I, 337. Odilleoz, a faithful brother, I, 61. Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, brought those who were mistaken concerning the Eucharist to the truth by a miracle, II, 377, 378. Why something is called “odorous,” II, 421. Oduinus, a priest, II, 127. Odultus, a friend of Arno and Alcuin, I, 164. To be instructed by Arno concerning his office, 165. He is listed among the royal envoys, ibid., note.

Offa, king of the Mercians, I, 11, 57, 58; II, 557. He is also called Offanus, 58, note, 67, 85. The glory of Britain, 58. His daughters were Elfleda and Alfrida, 226, note. He disagreed with Charlemagne, I, 6. The cause of that disagreement, 7, note. Charlemagne sends him gifts, I, 57. He promotes learning in his kingdom, 58. He removes the Mercian churches from the metropolitan see of Canterbury, I, 67, note, 81, note. He adorned the tomb of Saint Oswald the king, II, 246, verse 388. He did many things well and many things cruelly, I, 67. His coin recently discovered, 58. Offertory in the Mass: what it is, II, 435. Concerning the offertory: “There was a man in the land,” II, 490. The parts of the divine office among monks, I, 375. What care should be taken concerning it in monasteries, II, 163. — Offices for each weekday, II, 52 ff. Oil signifies good works, I, 435, and the grace of heavenly mercy, 541. — The blessing of the oil of the sick on Maundy Thursday, II, 477. What the Mount of Olives mystically signifies, I, 541. Olomundus, connected with Alcuin by friendship, I, 288. The first founder and superior of the monastery of Mount Olivet, 289, note. When he died, ibid., note. Olympias: what it is and where the name comes from, II, 429. Omerus, I, 126. See Homerus. The immensity of God’s omnipotence, I, 715. Onias, a priest and disciple of Alcuin, I, 292, note, 410. He is commended to the prayers of George, patriarch of Jerusalem, 148. What the evil works are that lead to hell, and the good works that raise one to heaven, I, 17, 18. — Dead works are sins, I, 693. Good works cannot exist without faith, 524. How the works of believers will be greater than Christ’s works, 598. Opinion: what it is, II, 335.

One should pray daily with tears for the various afflictions that we suffer, II, 35; by all and for all, 36; before sleep in the dormitory cell, 38. Orarium: what it is and what it signifies, II, 477, note, 495. A grammatical sentence: what it is, II, 271. — How many parts a rhetorical speech has, II, 320. Division and confirmation, 321. How it is embellished, 327. — A dialectical sentence: what it is, II, 351. — Prayer: what it is, I, 354. It is commended alternately with the reading of Sacred Scripture, 157. — How effective is the prayer of the saints, II, 239. — Abbreviation of the secret prayer, II, 22. Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, 436, 440, 506. Its seven petitions, 507. — What should be requested in prayer, I, 598. What should be observed, 354. — Prayer for obtaining the virtues, etc., II, 25; to the Father in the name of the Son, 26; for contemplation, 27; for preserving humility, 28; in temptations from unclean spirits, 30; in various tribulations, 32, 69; at the very beginning of the day, 33; for preserving discretion in silence and speech, I, 39. — Prayer for singing psalms for oneself and others, II, 40; for father, mother, and the whole family, 41; for the abbot and the congregation, ibid.; for relatives and all those commended to us, ibid.; for our relatives and all the faithful departed, 82; for those who give alms, 42; for the faithful departed, 37; for knowledge of God and the forgiveness of sins, 43; for peace, II, 508; for a prosperous journey and voyage, 123. — The prayer of monks, II, 47. Another prayer for all kinds of people, 48. Prayers of Saint Augustine, 77, 103, 117, 124; of Aurelius Prudentius in verse, 77; of Saint Ambrose, 79, 81; of Saint Benedict, 84; of Saint Cyprian the martyr, 94; of Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, 103; of Saint Gregory the pope, 107, 110, 118, 120; of Saint Jerome, 39, 120, 121; of Saint Hilary, 117; of Saint Isidore, 86, 106, 121, 122; of Saint Martin, 121; of Saint Columbanus, ibid.; of Saint Ephrem the deacon, 123; of Alcuin, at night, 126; of the same, on knowledge of God and forgiveness of sins, 78; of the same, to Christ, 225; of Solomon, at the dedication of the Temple, I, 447; of the poet, to the twelve apostles, II, 223. — A prayer formerly said after the Litany of the Saints, II, 116; over those serving for a week, 20; to God and the apostles, 457. — Why prayers for the dead are offered by the Church, II, 505. — Prayers over a penitent, II, 514. Prayers for the canonical hours, 19, 50; concerning the Holy Cross, 19, 50; concerning Saint Mary, 20; at the *Mandatum*, ibid.; before and after Communion, 51; solemn prayers on Good Friday, 479.

What an orator should be, II, 331. He should use the ideas of ancient authors, not ancient words, 327. The monastery of Orbionense (Urbionense) of the Blessed Virgin: where its name comes from, I, 268, note. It is also called the Blessed Virgin’s monastery of Novalia and of Crassa, ibid. Its first founder and abbot was Nifridius, ibid. The world: how it was divided among the sons and grandsons of Noah, I, 316. — Alcuin recognized only three parts of the world, I, 215. The Roman Order is commended in ecclesiastical worship, I, 65. Its antiquity, 66. — The rite for imposing penance at the beginning of the fast, II, 471 ff. — How many ecclesiastical orders there are and what they are, II, 434. Origen deviates from the faith in certain matters, I, 789. The orthodox: who they are, II, 502. Orthography: what it is, II, 271. Alcuin’s writing on it, 301 ff. Mouth: what it is, II, 353. Hosanna: where the word comes from, I, 581; II, 475. Why it is sung in the preface of the Mass, 502. Osbald, patrician of Northumbria, I, 17. Suspected of regicide and the shedding of much blood, 67, note. Osbert, duke of Northumbria, I, 17, 20, note. Whether he was a patrician of the Mercians, ibid. Bones: what they are, II, 353. Osthfrida, wife of King Æthelred, II, 245, verse 358. Niece of Saint Oswald the king, ibid., verse 359. She honorably buries her uncle’s relics, ibid., verse 360. Ostiarius: who he is, I, 564. — The office of doorkeepers under the old law, II, 490; under the new law, 491, 434. What the door in the side of the ark prefigured, I, 633. The door is Christ, I, 565. What it means to go out and come in through this door, ibid. and 567. Osulf, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 218, note, 220, note. He is rebuked for his perverse conduct, 218. — Osulf, servant of Charles the Younger, I, 241.

Oswald (Saint), nephew and successor of King Edwin, II, 244, verse 235 ff. He fights bravely against the enemy, ibid. He encourages his men to battle, verse 242. As victor, he governs the kingdom in holiness, verse 265 ff. He builds and adorns churches, verse 275 ff. His right hand is generous and incorruptible toward the poor, verse 291 ff. He is killed in battle against the pagans, verse 312. — Miracles of Saint Oswald after his death, II, 245, verse 314. Dust mixed with his blood becomes a cause of salvation for many, verse 354. The power and efficacy of his relics, verses 213 ff., verses 460 ff. His fame and patronage among foreigners, 246, verse 455. His death, 247, verse 499 ff. Oswi (Oswin), brother and successor of Saint Oswald, II, 245, verse 304; 247, verse 505. He is attacked in many wars, verses 509 and 517. He emerges victorious, verse 540 ff. He leads the Mercians to baptism, verse 559. He reigns happily, verse 560 ff. His death, verse 573. Who are called the sheep of Christ, I, 570. Who they were before his coming, 563. Ozias: what he signifies, I, 450, 452, 454.

## P

Saint Pachomius: an angel appeared to him, II, 359. The pacts and treaties of the Western and Eastern emperors, confirmed by the signatures of priests and nobles, II, 561. Pagans did much harm throughout the islands of the Ocean in the regions of Aquitaine, I, 135. They ravage the Gallic and German coast, 137, note. — The good works of pagans are empty, I, 561. The critique of Pagi on Letter 80 is examined, I, 118. Palatiolum, formerly a monastery of virgins, now a collegiate church, II, 190. What the archiepiscopal pallium signifies, I, 121; II, 496. The *superhumerale* is called “holiness” and the “pallium of holiness,” I, 121, and also the priestly diadem, 162. It is marked with a cross in front and behind, 121. What it admonishes those who wear it, 162. Archbishops receive it from the chief see, II, 494. It must never be used without the ministry of deacons, I, 65. Palm Sunday and its celebration, II, 475 ff. — What the palms customarily carried in the hands signify, II, 153. Altar of Saint Pancratius, II, 219. *Pandecten*: the Old and New Testament written together, II, 308. Where the word “bread” is derived from, II, 507. What “daily” means, ibid. What the bread should be like over which Christ’s body is consecrated, I, 107. The body of Christ is one everywhere, II, 504. — The offering of bread and the chalice is a commemoration of Christ’s death, II, 504. — The bread from heaven signified by manna, I, 525, 528. — The bread of life and observance of the commandments, I, 355. — What the five loaves in the Gospel mystically signify, I, 519. Pannonia, the native region of Saint Martin, II, 159. The Pantheon, a temple consecrated in honor of all the saints, II, 489. What “pope” signifies, II, 502. Pavia, a royal city, I, 126. Paradise is interpreted as “garden of delights,” I, 622. It is our homeland, II, 545. *Paralipomenon*: in what language the name is used, II, 431. Good Friday: what it is, II, 478. Why it is celebrated in sadness, 480, 481. Its solemnity, 478, 479 ff. Its ceremonies, ibid. and 480. On that day the priest communicates under one species, ibid., note.

Parents must be honored, I, 341. The suburbs of the city of Paris rejoice in the assistance of Saints Dionysius and Germanus, II, 194. Whether Alcuin established a school at Paris, I, 54, note. “Parishioners” means parish priests or curates, I, 116, note. Their conduct and duties, ibid. How parricide and patricide differ, II, 472. Participle: what it is and where the term comes from, II, 292. Its difference from a noun and its accidents, ibid. and 239. Its proper characteristic, 271. — From where participles are derived, II, 293 ff. A nursing infant is carried to the Church lest it die without baptism, I, 547. — How infants who do not speak become believers through baptism, II, 523. Those baptized and dying before the use of reason are freed from damnation, ibid. and 524. “Pascha” is a Hebrew name, in Latin *transitus*, “passing over,” I, 591. *Petitum* or *competentium*: what it is, II, 475. When it is celebrated by Latins and Greeks, 358. Whether and how it differs from the days of unleavened bread, I, 625. The Passover of the Jews was in shadow; ours is in the light, 578. The solemnity and ceremonies of Easter Day, II, 485. Paschasius Radbertus judges heretics who are mistaken concerning the truth of the Eucharist, II, 378. How pastures are found in Egypt when the rains fail, I, 333. — What the pastures of Christ’s sheep are, I, 565. The sparrow: what kind of bird it is and whom it denotes, I, 355. Rescued from a snare, it denotes Christ, 380. — “Sparrow” as an assumed name for an unknown man, I, 232. Cardinal Passioneus illuminates Alcuin’s Letter 56 with notes, I, 66 ff. He is praised, 392. The threefold cause of the Lord’s Passion, II, 478. Who the true shepherd is, I, 564.

“Father” is said to derive from *patrando*, that is, “completing,” II, 506. — God the Father is called omnipotent in two ways, ibid. How he continues to work even now, I, 510. He is wholly in the Son, and the Son wholly in the Father, 620. Why he alone is named in the preface of the Mass, II, 501. He begot the Son neither by necessity nor by will, but by nature, I, 177. Just as the Father is life, so the Son is life, 721. He is not from anyone, 598. Why he alone is not said to have been sent, 727. How he was not incarnated, I, 729, 742. He performs some works through the Son in the form of God, and others through the same Son in the form of a servant, 733. — To speak of the Father and the Son does not imply difference of substance, I, 711. — What should be said of the Father and the Son according to substance, and what according to relation, I, 709. — The statement, “Who alone does great wonders,” must not be understood of the Father alone, I, 722, 741. — Prayer to God the Father in the name of the Son, II, 26, 27.

To suffer, a category, II, 341. Patience: what it is, II, 330. What true patience is, 123. It makes martyrs without sword or flame, ibid. How necessary it is in this world for those serving God, I, 165, 166. What it should be like in superiors toward their subjects, 280. — Praise and commendation of patience, II, 132. Images of the patriarchs Adam, Noah, and Abraham, II, 225. — Why the first patriarchs were shepherds of sheep, I, 315, 333. — Archbishops are sometimes called patriarchs, I, 194, note. Godfathers and godmothers, II, 483. What their office is, 486. Saint Patrick, the glory of the Scots, II, 219. Propagator of the faith and monastic life in Ireland, I, 286, note. The names of the fathers of the Old Testament and the allegories of their names, I, 450. — The writings of the holy Fathers are read with gratitude, II, 409.

Saint Paulinus, first archbishop of York, I, 20; II, 244, verse 210. A citizen of the city of Rome, 243, verse 135. He preaches the faith to the Britons, verse 139 ff. He teaches King Edwin the true religion, verses 145 ff. He converts the king and people to Christ, 244, verses 165 and 213 ff. Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, I, 35, 45, 46, 49, 69, 146. An outstanding teacher and devout instructor in heavenly life, 4. His life is illuminated by Madrisius, ibid., note, 35, note. Alcuin appeals to him for the defense of the Catholic faith, 97, 146, and 147. Alcuin desires that he come to the king at Aachen in the matter of Felix, 113. He sent the king a little book on the Catholic faith, 136, 137. His little book, or confession of faith, is praised, 146, 147, note. Alcuin commends himself to his memory in the Mass, 49. Poems and praises addressed to him, II, 230. Paulinus of Nola, bishop, is healed by Saint Martin of eye pain and blindness, II, 160.

What epistles and how many Saint Paul wrote, II, 433. What they contain, 434. Whether his severed head flowed with blood, 221, note. — Altar of Saint Paul the apostle, II, 211, 218. Church, 562. Intercession, 223. Verses concerning him, 217, 220. — The cell of Saint Paul, called Cormaricus, is subject to the monastery of Saint Martin, II, 565. — The case of Saint Paul’s monastery of Cormaricus argued at Rome, I, 67, 68, 70. Paulus, a monk of Monte Cassino, II, 551. Previously he had followed the military camp, ibid., note. He wrote epitaphs for Queen Hildegard and her daughters, 553. What he thought concerning the truth of the Eucharist, 379. Poems of Charlemagne addressed to him, 551. Paulus, a monk of Saint Martin, and his encomium or epitaph, II, 236. Who the poor of Christ are, I, 388. — The poor man’s hand is Christ’s treasury, I, 127. Poverty should be loved, II, 226. Poverty is tranquil when governed by the rudder of humility, I, 202.

Peace should be maintained with all people, I, 659. It should be preserved with the good, but not with criminals, II, 130. It is the mother of love, ibid. — The peace that Christ gives is described, I, 601, 615. — “Peace be with you”: why it is sung at Mass, II, 498. — Why the kiss of peace is not given on Maundy Thursday, II, 476. — Those who divide the Church hate peace, I, 377. A living sinner compared with a dog, I, 435. How he can be called better than a righteous person who has died, ibid. He ought to pray with confidence, 359. If he ceases to be wicked near the end of life, he should not despair, II, 515. — Sinners are not to be excluded from the Church, I, 171. They are not to be condemned by a person before the proper time, ibid. — The punishment of sinners after the resurrection, I, 735.

Every sin is committed by thought, speech, or deed, I, 109. Original and actual sin, ibid. The ways in which they are committed, ibid. Why it was expiated by the Creator himself and not by an angel, 306. — The guilt of sin remains after the act, II, 508. — Why the angelic sin is passed over in silence in Genesis, I, 305. Why it is incurable, ibid. — The sin of unbelief among the Jews cannot be excused, I, 608. — How sins are said to be covered in the Psalms, I, 347. Dead works are sins, 693. They are signified by the corpses of the dead, 333. What evils they cause among the people, II, 473. By what means they are forgiven in the Church, 510. How daily sins are forgiven, 474. A comb described humorously in the form of an animal, I, 56, 57, note. Why the breast of the baptized is anointed, I, 110, 127; II, 522. The form established for ecclesiastical funds, I, 594. Pelagius said that Christ was a solitary man, I, 814. His confession was formerly attributed to Saint Jerome, II, 373. — By what argument the Pelagian sect is refuted, I, 436. The Egyptian bird pelican signifies hermits, I, 355. Penda, a strong and cruel king, II, 247, verses 518 ff. He is defeated in war against Oswin, verse 544, and himself is killed, verse 552. The Pentateuch: where the name comes from and who its author is, II, 431. The vigil of Pentecost, II, 487. The origin of the feast, ibid.

A purse in Scripture signifies the public substance of riches; a pouch signifies what is hidden, I, 182. Pilgrims traveling to the thresholds of the holy apostles are to be assisted by kings, I, 32. They are to be received as guests, 221. Perez (Francis), treasurer of the Church of Toledo, II, 588. Perez (John Baptist), bishop of Segorbe, is praised, II, 590. John Mariana made use of his papers, ibid. *Perihermeniae*: what they are, II, 350. *Periochae*: what they are, II, 315. Perjurers: who they are, II, 472. The perpetual: what it is and where the term comes from, I, 178. How it differs from the eternal and the temporal, II, 510. Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, built a church in honor of Saint Martin, II, 161, 162. Perseverance: what it is, II, 330. It is commended in good works, 141. There is one person in Christ, God and man, not two, I, 530, 895, 896 ff. — All the persons of the Holy Trinity together are not something greater than any one of them, I, 710. What is proper to each, 711, 712, 739, 740. The metrical foot: what it is and where the term comes from, II, 271. — Feet: what they are, II, 353. — It was formerly customary to wash the feet of guests, II, 213. *Peteredium*: the term is derived from seeking an inheritance, II, 308. Saint Petronilla, daughter of Saint Peter, II, 218. Why Saint Peter the apostle is called Simon of John, I, 644. Why he was asked three times whether he loved the Lord, ibid. His entering the tomb signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles, 634. How many epistles he wrote, II, 433, 434. He opens the gates that the cherubim closed, I, 132. He was appointed by Christ as head of the Church, 65. — Why Saint Peter’s threefold denial was permitted by God, I, 624, 625. It is undone by a threefold confession, ibid. and 644.

The church of Saint Peter the apostle, II, 210, 213, 220. Oratory, 209. Altar, 211, 216. — A poem concerning Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, II, 220. Concerning his chains, 223. Concerning his vision at Joppa, 207. — The brothers of Saint Peter, the church at Benevento and the cells belonging to it, I, 155. Alcuin intercedes for them, ibid., 156. — The brothers of Saint Peter at Wearmouth, I, 282, 283, note. Their dwellings and manner of life are praised, 282. — The church of Saint Peter built by Saint Hrodbert, II, 217. — The church of Saint Peter restored by Abbot Rado, II, 211. — The brothers of Saint Peter at Salzburg, I, 116, note.

Peter, archbishop of Milan, I, 191. Also called Oldradus, 192, note. He wrote to Charlemagne concerning the translation of Saint Augustine, ibid. Favorably disposed toward Alcuin, 192. He receives gifts as alms from Queen Liutgard, ibid., note. Peter, master at Charlemagne’s palace, teaches grammar, I, 126. Phanuel is interpreted as “the face of God,” I, 538. Phares: where the name comes from, I, 332. What it signifies, 450, 451, 453. Philemon, to whom Paul writes: who he was, I, 661. A poem concerning Philip the apostle, II, 222. Philosophers are the discoverers of the arts, I, 94. Philosophy: what it is and where the term comes from, II, 335. The teacher of all virtues, 265. Its sublimity and usefulness, 268. Its divisions, 332, 335. The error of the heretic Photinus, I, 562. He is condemned, II, 401. Physics: what it is and what its parts are, II, 335. Poitiers, rich in the relics of blessed Hilary, II, 194. The Picts attack the Britons, II, 242, verse 42. They are driven out by the Saxons, 243, verse 65. Victorious against King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, 250, verse 840. Piety, as a part of the virtue of justice: what it is, II, 330. — What the exercises of piety should be, I, 211.

Pilate was a Roman citizen, of Pontius origin, I, 626; II, 437, 509. He was appointed judge in Judea by Tiberius, 438. Pippin, son of Charles the Duke, father of Charlemagne, honorably receives Saint Willibrord, II, 185. By whom he is baptized, 191, 199. He grants the monastery of Saint Martin a charter of immunity, 566. His death, 188. Pippin, son of Charlemagne and Hildegard, received his name from his grandfather. Previously called Carloman, he was king of Italy, I, 32, 33, note, 44, 45, note. His wife was an unnamed woman, ibid., note. He returned to his father from the expedition against the Huns, ibid., note. He undertook a hostile expedition against the people of Benevento, 156, note. Because of that expedition, while Charlemagne returned to Francia, he remained in Italy, 157, note. His dispute with Albinus, II, 352 ff.

The fishing expeditions before and after the resurrection: what they signify, I, 640. The Pool of Bethesda: its mystical meaning, I, 507 ff. — The Pool of Siloam, a type of baptism, I, 558 ff. A roasted fish: what it signifies, I, 641. — Whether there were fish in the ark, I, 313. — What the two fish by which the multitude was fed signified, I, 519. — Allegorical exposition of the 153 fish in the Gospel, I, 41, 244, 245, 641, 642. Why planets are called wandering stars, I, 97. Plato did not allow himself to be separated from Diogenes, II, 267. Altar of Saint Platon the martyr, II, 210. Pliny the Younger, a most devoted investigator of natural things, I, 100. Alcuin requests his little books on the varied courses of the stars, ibid. Pluer (Dr. Charles Christopher), ecclesiastic of the Danish embassy at the court of the Catholic king, II, 555. A letter of Dr. Gregory Majansius to him, 590 ff. Rain: what it is, II, 353. — A rain of blood at the city of York, I, 20. — Whether there was rain before the Flood, I, 315. *Poderis*, in Latin *talaris*, II, 494. What garment it was in the Old Testament, 308; what it was in the New Testament, 495.

A penitent ought to disclose his sins through confession, II, 154. — Penitents, customarily surrounded by iron rings, used to come to the church, II, 192. How they are to be instructed at the beginning of the fast, 473. — What the weeping and mourning of penitents should be like, II, 515. — Three kinds of penitents, I, 355. Examples, 351; II, 515. Penance: what it is and how it should be performed, II, 154 ff. What true and perfect penance is, I, 351, 373; II, 134, 406. It is measured not by time but by mourning and tears, 515. How long it should be performed, 474. It is scarcely fruitful without confession, 156. Late penance is dangerous, 471. It must not be postponed, I, 355; II, 515. How it is to be imposed on Christians, 471, 473; on priests and Levites, 515. It must not be denied to those at the point of death, 511. The penance of the sick is also accepted by divine mercy, 406. — Penance to be imposed at the beginning of the fast, II, 471 ff. — Works of penance, II, 156. Their fruits, 134, 154 ff. Incentives to perform them, ibid. and 155, 156. — How one should approach penance, II, 474. — The groans of public penitents, II, 24. What poetry was like in Alcuin’s time, II, 202. *Polonyma*: what they are, II, 337. *Polyandrum*, a cemetery, II, 217. What *pometa* and *pomeria* are called, II, 309. Pontiff: where the term comes from, II, 492. What his office is, I, 678. — The Roman pontiff is the vicar of Saint Peter and heir of his power, I, 25. Chosen by God, vicar of the apostles, prince of the Church, heir of the Fathers, 30. — What succession and order the pontiffs had under the old law, II, 491. What garments they wore, 493. The province of Pontiva (Ponthieu), II, 176, note. How a newly established people should be taught and directed, I, 42. Pauses in a rhetorical speech: what they are, II, 271. Natural power, dialectically: what it is, II, 341. Secular and spiritual power: what the office of each is, I, 15.

God’s commandments are many in their diversity of operation, but one at the root of charity, I, 606. They are not to be debated but fulfilled with a devout mind, 432. Christ’s predestination, I, 616. It is not believed that some are predestined to evil, II, 406. When this controversy concerning predestination to evil began, 371. The categories or predicaments: what they are, II, 337. How they are to be understood of God, I, 713. The preaching of God’s word is to be carried out in monastic churches on feast days, II, 163. — As wickedness increases, preaching must not be broken off but increased, I, 556. — What order should be observed in preaching, I, 42, 50. From the beginning of the Church, preachers were appointed from every order of clerics, I, 183. What kind of preachers should be appointed for newly converted peoples, 37, 51. They are compared with angels, 481. No power or vanity of the world should hinder their voice, 269. What they must observe and what they must avoid, 51, 182.

Exposition of the preface of the Mass, II, 500. The patience of superiors must be the salvation of their subjects, I, 280. What their virtues are, 283. The Church and its ornaments should be their treasure, not a private chest, 284. Preposition: what it is, II, 297. Its property, 271. How the prepositions *de*, *dis*, and *des* are used, I, 34. — Prepositions used in speech, II, 299. Signs concerning Christ at Rome, II, 462. God’s foreknowledge does not compel anyone to sin, I, 587. Whether Pilate’s praetorium was in the house of Caiaphas, I, 625.

“Priest” is called *senior* in Latin, I, 199; II, 435, 491. Whether, according to Saint Jerome, a priest is the same as a bishop, I, 653. Without a deacon he has the name but not the office, II, 498. — Who priests are and where the name comes from, II, 492. In the earliest times of the Church bishops were called by this name, ibid. How they ought to conduct themselves, I, 75. They should be elders in conduct, 199. — The power and office of priests, II, 492. Their conduct, I, 65, 199. — Whether preaching should be forbidden to priests by bishops who are present, I, 183.

What the firstborn sold by Esau were, I, 327. — Before Aaron, the firstborn exercised the priesthood, ibid. How the prince of this world, the devil, is cast out, I, 585. How he was judged, 611. — Opposing leaders of the Church perished, I, 148. — The duty of the princes of this world, I, 18. How they are to be obeyed, 166. How the Son of God is called “Beginning,” I, 548. How this is said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 468, 548. Priscian, the glory of Latin eloquence, II, 281. In how many ways “prior” is said, II, 313. Exactions imposed by a bishop contrary to custom are censured, I, 265. Alcuin’s prodigal son, and a very useful admonition addressed to him, I, 218. Pronoun: what it is, II, 279. Its property, 271. Its species, genders, figures, number, and cases, 279 ff. Delivery, a part of rhetorical speech: what it is, II, 314, 328. Prophets were sowers, not reapers, I, 504. Why they are called “lesser,” II, 432. The spirit of prophecy is not always present to the minds of the prophets, II, 21. The kinds of propositions, II, 344. The proper: what it is, II, 336. — Things proper are spoken of in various ways, I, 921. Prose: what it is, II, 271. What sense Solomon’s Proverbs have, I, 445. Providence, as a part of the virtue of prudence: what it is, II, 329. A province, a part of Charlemagne’s kingdom, II, 566. Who our neighbor is, II, 129. Prudence: what it is and what its parts are, II, 144, 329.

What it means to sing psalms with the spirit and with the mind, II, 149. — Examples of singing psalms while riding, I, 66. The mysteries of Psalm 118, I, 343, and its excellence, II, 34. — Psalms and hymns for praising God on each day, 23. — Psalms to be said on various occasions, II, 21. To be sung for every tribulation, 79. — In what language the Book of Psalms is named, II, 431. Who its authors are and what its style is, ibid. — The usefulness and efficacy of the Psalms, II, 21. What the number of the penitential and gradual psalms signifies, I, 343, 344. — A psalm on the Incarnation, II, 91; on the Passion, 92; on the Resurrection, 93; on the Ascension, ibid.; in honor of Saint Mary, 108; of the apostles, ibid.; of the martyrs, 109; of the confessors, 110. Why the psalmist is so called, II, 434. Psalmody is to be performed with delight, I, 366. The Psalter collected by the Venerable Bede in sweet verses, I, 169; II, 96 ff. The boy in the Gospel who had five loaves: who he mystically was, I, 519. — The boys of Saint Martin, II, 154. — When the school of boys and clerics was established, I, 65, 66. What they should be instructed in, 198. What the foal of a she-ass signifies in Scripture, I, 582. Lung: what it is, II, 353. Points for distinguishing meanings are called pauses, II, 271. Alcuin attempts to restore their distinctions, previously neglected, I, 126, 127. Purgatorial fire, 346, 349, 735, 736. The faithful can be cleansed in it, II, 406. — Description of the souls in purgatory, II, 250, verses 905 ff. The Purification of the Blessed Virgin and a homily on it, II, 533. Ceremonies on its feast, 465. Purple, wool mixed with the blood of the murex: what it signifies, I, 845. Why it was added to priestly garments, II, 494. What a well signifies in Scripture, I, 500. Pythagoras teaches geometry by questioning, I, 184.

The number forty, a type of penance, I, 87, 315. It is taken for the perfection of a rightly ordered life, 508. When Lent begins and ends, II, 470, 564. Where the name comes from, I, 87; II, 470.
