The question of cause in a trial: what it is and what its types are, II, 316, 317. It flows from three sources, 338. Quality: what it is and what its types are, II, 340 and 341. “When,” as a category: what it is, II, 342. How quantity should be estimated and what its measures are, II, 339. The four-day-old dead man: what he signifies, I, 574. Why and when the Ember Days were instituted, II, 488. The office of those days during the week of Pentecost, 489. Quintilian’s judgment in defense of the woman who gave birth to an Ethiopian, I, 328. Altar of Saint Quintinus the martyr, II, 211, 212, 224. How *quotidie* and *cotidie* differ, II, 310, 427.

## R

**Racha**, what it is, II, 472, 473. **Radbod**, pagan king of the Frisians, II, 185, 187. He plotted against the life of Saint Willibrord, ibid. Nevertheless, overcome by the saint’s steadfastness, he sent the holy man back to Pippin, ibid. and 188. He was defeated by Charles, duke of the Franks, ibid. **Rado**, abbot of Saint Vedast, I, 60, note. In what year he became abbot, II, 163, note, 207, note. He restored the Sacred Codex after it had been consumed by flames, 207. His death, 163, note.

**Raganbert** (Ragerbert), bishop of an unknown see, I, 265, 266, note. He harassed the churches and priests of Saint Martin with new exactions, ibid.

**Rahab**, what she signifies, I, 450, 451, 453.

**Raiginis-Burg**, I, 882. See **Ratisbon**.

**Ramesse**, what land it is, I, 333.

**Palm branches**, what they signify, I, 581; II, 475. —The feast of branches, or of palms, and its origin, II, 474.

**Altar of Saint Raphael**, II, 224.

**Robbers**, who they are and why they are so called, II, 472.

**Ratbert**, I, 14, note. See **Rupert**.

**Reason**, for what purpose it was given to human beings, II, 147.

**Reasoning**, what it is, II, 319. And what use it has in rhetoric, 324.

**The breastpiece of the priests**, what it was in the Old Testament, II, 494, 495.

**Adalwin**, bishop of Ratisbon, I, 164, 165, note, 166. The synod at which Felix’s error was condemned, 115, note, 882.

**Razim** is interpreted as “giants,” I, 318.

**The redemption of the world**, how it was accomplished, I, 187.

**The refectory of the brothers**, inscriptions in it, II, 213, 214, 226.

**Regenberctus**, a teacher, II, 230, note.

**Regium** and **regale**, how they differ, II, 310.

**The happiness of a kingdom**, whence it comes, I, 120. —Happy kingdoms, if philosophers ruled and kings devoted themselves to philosophy, I, 150.

**The kingdom of God**, what it is in us, II, 506. What Christ’s kingdom is, I, 627.

**Regular clerics**, why so called, II, 491.

**Reguliaca**, where the estate was situated, II, 166. It is a village called Rilly, ibid., note.

**Relatives**, what they are, II, 343.

**Religion**, as a part of the virtue of justice, what it is, II, 330.

**The relics of the saints** are to be honored, II, 225, 409. Their power and efficacy against demons, 246, verse 392 ff. —Alcuin asks for the protection of the relics of the holy cross and of others, I, 49.

**Remedius (Saint) (Remigius)**, bishop of Reims, teacher of the Franks, and his altar, II, 210, 219, 225. He baptized Clovis, II, 165, 166. He is honored throughout Campania, 194.

**Remedius**, bishop of Chur, a friend of Alcuin, I, 195. He sent gifts to Alcuin, ibid. He collected ecclesiastical canons, ibid., note. He wrote letters to Alcuin, 195. Alcuin exhorted him to perform the episcopal office well, ibid.

**Remedius, decurio**, I, 136. In place of *decurio*, read “of Chur,” 195.

**Remigius**, bishop of Strasbourg, I, 195, note.

**Remigius**. See **Remedius of Chur**.

**The remission of sins**, by what means it takes place in the Church, II, 510.

**The rebuke of an adversary in court**, II, 325.

**The three rests** mentioned by the apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, I, 674.

**The origin and etymology of the responsories** in the ecclesiastical office, II, 499.

**The resurrection**, twofold: of bodies and of souls, I, 514, 734. Of bodies on the last day, 735; II, 406. —The resurrection preceded in the Head what is to follow in the members, I, 387.

**King** is derived from “to rule,” I, 18. —How kings ought to live, I, 20, 59, 242. Their duty, 18. —Those are kings who rule themselves well, I, 356.

**Hrabanus**, surnamed Maurus, I, 162, note. Fellow student of Samuel, archbishop of Worms, 205, note. More about him in the Preface. —Verses on Hrabanus Maurus, II, 233.

**The city of Reims** rejoices in the protection of Saint Remigius, II, 194.

**Rhaetia**, I, 39.

**Rhetoric**, what it is, and its origin and force, II, 314. Its parts and kinds, ibid., 331.

**Ricbodus (Ricbodo)**. See **Rigbodus**.

**Richarius (Saint)**, where he was born, II, 176. Whether he came from a distinguished lineage, 158, 176, note. He received two Irish priests and protected them against the insolence of the people, ibid. He was moved to repentance and assumed the religious habit, 177. He became a priest and preached the word of God, ibid. He went to Britain and freed the slaves whom he had left in Gaul, 178. He returned to Gaul, ibid. He visited Richtrude, a devout woman, and baptized her son Maurontus after saving him from danger, 179, note. He gave King Dagobert salutary counsels, ibid. He founded a church at Centula, 180. He built a monastery near Argubium, 158. His death, burial, and translation, 181. His epitaph, whose author may have been Alcuin, 156. He appeared gloriously to Sigobard, ibid. His miracles, 182. His book of miracles was lost, 158. —Writers of the Life of Saint Richarius, II, 158. His altar, 210. The church constructed by Angilbert, 552.

**Richbodus** (Richbodus), I, 97. See **Rigbodus**.

**Rictruda**, or **Rictrudis**, a disciple of Alcuin, I, 157, note, 430, 462. With the additional name Columba, 458, 459. See **Columba**.

**Rictrudis**, a devout woman visited by Saint Richarius, II, 179. Whether she was the same as Rictrude, abbess of Marchiennes, ibid., note.

**Riculfus**, surnamed Damoetas, archbishop of Mainz, I, 55, 56, note, 148 and note. He succeeded Lullus in the archbishopric, II, 419, note. Felix of Urgell was first entrusted to his custody, I, 148. He labored for the peace of the Church, ibid. He accompanied Pope Leo, together with others, when Leo was returning from France to Rome, ibid., note.

**Rigbodus** (Richbodus, Richbonus), surnamed Macharius, I, 192, 193, 194. Archbishop of Trier, 193, note, 194. Previously a monk and abbot of Mettlach, 193, note. A disciple of Alcuin, but a lover of Virgil Maro, ibid. Alcuin challenged him to defend the Catholic faith, 97. Alcuin asked him for a homily of Pope Leo and Bede’s treatise on Tobit, 194. Letter 108 was not written to him but to Arno, 136, note. He recovered from illness, 194. A poem about him, II, 230. A poem addressed to him, 232.

**Rinacurura**, a city of Egypt, I, 320.

**The brothers of the Ripensian Church**, II, 184. See **Willibrord**.

**The laughter of Abraham and Sarah**, what it signifies, I, 321.

**Rehoboam**, what he signifies, I, 450, 451, 453, 454.

**To ask** signifies not only “to request” but also “to inquire,” I, 613.

**The institution of the feast of Rogations**, where and when it took place, II, 468.

**Rome**, having begun in fraternal discord, nourishes the poison of dissension, I, 138. It was devastated by the hands of treachery, II, 239. —The great assembly at Rome concerning Pope Leo, II, 253, 254. The Roman synod against Felix of Urgell, I, 918.

**The schism of the Roman Church** must be repaired not by a new addition but according to the ancient order, I, 148. —An account of the Roman churches, II, 597 ff. Which saints’ bodies are found there, ibid. —How many Roman citizens were found in the census of Augustus, II, 462. —Whether the Roman Empire, the strongest of all kingdoms, still continues, and how long it will last, II, 529.

**Romuald**, duke of Benevento, son of Arichis and brother of Grimoald, I, 156, note.

**Rorico of Laon**, in what year he became bishop and in what year he died, II, 527.

**The dew of Hermon** is the grace of Christ, I, 389.

**The bramble**, to what kind it belongs, I, 33.

**Rupert (Saint)** built the church of Saint Peter at Salzburg, II, 217. —The monastery of Saint Rupert, I, 70. Its sons, 114, note.

**Ruth**, what she signifies, I, 450, 451, 453.

## S

**Sabaoth**, what it signifies, II, 423, 501.

**Sabaria**, a town of Pannonia and the birthplace of Saint Martin, II, 159.

**Sabbath**, what it is interpreted to mean, II, 426. It is spiritual: to have no sin, I, 509, 559. —The Sabbath before Palm Sunday, II, 474. Why the pope gives alms on this day, ibid. —How the Sabbath before the day of the Resurrection is to be observed, I, 110. On it some break their fast, 89. —The veneration of Holy Saturday, II, 482. Its sacred rites, 483. —The solemnity and etymology of the Sabbath in White Week, II, 485, 486. —Why and from what it is called the Sabbath of the twelve readings, II, 488. —Why the Sabbath day is blessed and sanctified, I, 341.

**Sabellius**, his error, I, 562, 571; II, 573.

**The purse** in Scripture signifies the hidden substance of riches, I, 182.

**Sacen**, a friend of Alcuin, I, 200.

**Priest**, why so called, II, 435. —The priest’s tongue should be the key of the heavenly kingdom and his throat the trumpet of the eternal King, I, 72. —It belongs to the priest to bless; it belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing, I, 328. —Who the priests of the Old Testament were, and what their office was, II, 491. —The priests of the Church and their office, I, 78; II, 292. They are God’s angels, the lights of the Church, and teachers of Christ’s flock, I, 14. What care they should exercise in teaching, I, 344. How they ought to deal with penitents and confessors, II, 473. What they ought to admonish kings about, 285. —**Commendatory priests**, who seek honors and avoid ministry, I, 51, 52, note. They are often chosen through favor, not merit, 438.

**The excellence of the priesthood**, I, 686. The difference between the Old and New Testaments, 687, 688.

**Sacrifice**, what it is, II, 435. In every sacrifice four things must be considered: to whom, by whom, what, and for whom it is offered, I, 188. —Why Christ’s sacrifice is not many sacrifices but one, I, 695. —Christ himself accomplishes the sacrifice of the Eucharist, II, 412. He always remains the same, whatever the condition of the priests, ibid. The heavenly citizens take part in it, ibid. It is not offered to the saints, 503. It is the body of Christ, ibid. —In the sacrifice of Christ’s body, bread, wine, and water—not salt—are to be used, I, 107. The bread is consecrated into the body, and the water and wine into Christ’s blood, ibid. What bread, wine, and water signify mystically, 108. —The sacrifice of righteousness is Christ’s Passion, I, 354. —Comparison of the sacrifices of Christ and Melchizedek, I, 679. —What sacrifices God requires, I, 353.

**Sacrilege**, what it is, II, 472. Why “sacrilegious” is so called, ibid.

**Sadai**, a name of God, II, 424.

**Zadok**, what he signifies, I, 450, 452, 455.

**The age (saeculum)**, what it is and how it differs from an aeon (*aevum*), II, 178, 179. —The three periods of the age: those of the patriarchs, prophets, and evangelists, I, 482.

**The net of heretics**, what it is, I, 436.

**Arrows in the hand of the mighty**, the apostles, I, 383. They are also the words of God’s teaching, 349, 377.

**Salt** is not to be put into the sacrifice of Christ’s body, I, 107. Why it was used for victims under the old law, ibid. Why it is used in baptism, 109.

**Salathiel**, what he signifies, I, 450, 452, 455.

**Salem**, whether it is the same as Jerusalem, I, 319, 685.

**The inscriptions of the Salzburg monastery**, II, 217. The church of Saint Peter constructed by Saint Rupert, ibid. The cathedral basilica erected by Saint Virgil, 218, note.

**Solomon**, called by three names, I, 411. “Pacific” is the interpretation, ibid. and 450, 451, 453. He produced three books: which they are and what their connection is, I, 411; II, 431, 432.

**Salpinx**, that is, “trumpet,” II, 221, note.

**The congregation of the Holy Savior** and its abbot Usuald, I, 27, 28, note.

**Saint Salvus**, martyr, II, 216, 224.

**Samaria**, an image of idolatry, I, 500.

**Samaritan**, interpreted as “guardian,” I, 555. —The Samaritans were devoted to images of mute animals, I, 500. —The dispute between the Samaritans and the Jews, I, 503.

**The altar of Saint Samson**, II, 219.

**Samuel** is believed to be the author of the Book of Judges, II, 431. —Who the authors of the Books of Samuel were, ibid.

**Samuel**, a disciple of Alcuin and fellow student of Hrabanus Maurus, I, 205, note. Whether he was bishop of Worms, ibid.

**Samuel the priest**, who he was, II, 449, note.

**The saints** enjoy unequal glory because of the diversity of their merits, I, 9, 10, 736, 741. They will be endowed with such blessedness that none greater can exist, I, 614. They are our powerful intercessors, 113. Through their prayers we trust that sins are forgiven in the Church, 171. —The intercession and invocation of the saints, II, 503. Their blessedness, 544. Their communion, what it is, 439. Why the days of their death are celebrated with joy, 481. Why they are called “birthdays,” I, 613; II, 481. How great the concourse to their relics, II, 194. —The feasts of the saints are to be honored with praise of God and almsgiving, I, 211. How vigils are to be observed, II, 481. —The feast of All Saints, I, 112. It is to be prepared for by a three-day fast, 113. When and by whom it was instituted, II, 489. When its celebration began in Gaul and Germany, I, 113, note. A homily on it, II, 543. —Which saints’ bodies are found at Rome, II, 597 ff.

**Holy**, why it is said three times in the Mass, II, 501.

**The sandals of bishops**, what they are like and what they signify, II, 495, 496.

**Blood**, what it is, II, 353.

**Nothing should be done by a wise man without reason**, I, 429. What difference there is between the wise and the foolish, 417. —The multitude of the wise is the health of the world, I, 67. Labor is exposed to the disputes of fools, 417. Wise sayings do not flatter but prick, 445.

**Wisdom**, what it is, I, 186. What true wisdom is, 169, 439; II, 129, 151. How much it accomplishes, I, 150. It is better than strength, 437. In what respect it is better than riches, 429; II, 267. Its first quality is freedom from folly, I, 415. —Wisdom rests on the seven columns of the liberal arts, II, 268. By what method it is to be acquired, 265. As laborious to acquire as it is splendid to possess, 267. In acquiring it, it should not be hard to give the weight of gold, I, 67. Its flowers never wither, 157. —The wisdom from above is peaceable, not contentious, I, 792. —The commendation of wisdom and learning, I, 53, 150, 169; II, 267. —The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews, II, 432.

**Saracens**, also called **Hagarenes**, plundered by the commanders of King Charles, I, 6. They rule in Asia and Africa, ibid. In Septimania they fought with the Franks and returned victorious, 143, note.

**Sarah**, seized by Pharaoh: how she was not violated, I, 318. Why God rebuked her for laughing, 321. What letter was added to her name, ibid. And what interpretation is given to her name, ibid. Her remarkable beauty, 323.

**Satan** is never to be restored to his former dignity, II, 516.

**Saxons**, or **Saxi**, why they are so called, II, 242, verse 48. They were summoned by the Britons to aid them against the Picts, ibid., verse 46. They drove out the Picts, verse 62 ff. They expelled the Britons themselves from the kingdom, verse 67 ff. —The ancient Saxons and Frisians, converted to the faith under King Charles, I, 6, 7, note. A wicked people, 118, note, 120. A cursed and God-despised generation, I, 135. They repeatedly abandoned the sacrament of baptism, 42. They were not to be harassed by the imposition of tithes and the severity of punishments, 51. —The harshness of the Saxons softened, I, 37. Peace was negotiated with them, 119. —A dialogue on grammar between Saxon and Frankish boys and their teacher, II, 268. —The education of a Carolingian Saxon, and a dissertation on it, II, 265. —The end of the Saxon war, I, 702, 703. Charlemagne’s Saxon expedition, I, 69, note, 72, note.

**Scamma**, the arena of wrestling, II, 247, note.

**The shoulders of the baptized**, why they are marked with oil, I, 110, 127; II, 522.

**The Scarpus**, a river near the monastery of Elnon, II, 208, note.

**Scenopegia**, what it is, I, 532, 533, 539.

**Figures of speech** are ornaments of eloquence, II, 271.

**Schism**, how it differs from heresy, I, 660. —The errors of schisms brought to rest, I, 123. See **Felician heresy**.

**The Egyptian school** operates in the palace of King Charles, I, 90. —The schools of boys and clerics should be separated, I, 65.

**The altar of Saint Scholastica**, virgin, II, 210.

**Knowledge**, what it is, II, 335. What knowledge of piety is, I, 650. Secular letters are to be commended to the young as the foundation of evangelical wisdom, 285. —The riches of the sciences are never exhausted, I, 157.

**Slavs**, otherwise called **Vionudi**, subjected by King Charles to his rule, I, 6, 7, note. —The Slavic kings Dragitus and his son, ibid.

**Scopilio**, archpriest of Saint Vedast, II, 170. He buried Saint Vedast, 171.

**A certain Scot**, learned but impious, II, 246, verse 462. Through the help of Saint Oswald he was healed and converted, 247, verses 494 and 496. —The Scottish people are always friendly to the English, II, 250, verse 839.

**Sacred Scripture** is Christ’s table, I, 384. It speaks of Christ in three ways, 855. Its individual sentences have multiple meanings, 400. The allegorical and historical senses, 334. And the moral sense, II, 409. —Summaries of the books of the Old Testament, II, 429 and 430. They are divided into three orders: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, 430. Other books absent from the Hebrew canon are nevertheless received by the Church, 431. —How delightful and useful the reading and knowledge of Holy Scripture are, I, 460; II, 130. **Scrutinies**, why they are performed in baptism, I, 109; II, 127, 521. Seven Romans celebrate them before baptism, II, 483.

**Zedekiah** is captured and deprived of his eyes, II, 467.

**A hymn of Bishop Sedulius**, I, 125.

**Segor**, first called Bale and later Salissa, I, 322. Frequently undermined by earthquakes, ibid.

**The seed of Abraham**, twofold: carnal and spiritual, I, 325.

**Everlasting**, why so called, I, 178.

**The number six**, a perfect number, I, 87, 95, 307, 358, 522, 579; II, 419, 468. —The mysteries of the number six, I, 579.

**A vision of Seneca’s boy** in the Church of York, I, 9.

**The inconveniences of old age**, I, 444.

**Elders**, how they ought to behave toward young men, I, 255.

**Old age**, its final stage, II, 425.

**The bodily senses**, how many there are and why they are so called, II, 421. They are represented by the five husbands of the Samaritan woman, I, 501.

**The number seven** has great perfection in Scripture, I, 343. Its mysteries, 642.

**The seventh day**, why it is celebrated for the dead, II, 513.

**Septimania**. Felix of Urgell spread heresy there, I, 141. There the Saracens fought with the Franks, 143.

**Septuagesima**, why so called, I, 86, 89; II, 466. When it begins and ends, 467. —Its origin, I, 89; II, 466. Why it is celebrated by the faithful, I, 89; II, 467, 564. Its etymology and its celebration among various peoples, I, 86, 89; II, 466.

**The ornamentation of tombs** is vain, I, 211.

**The burial of the dead** signifies the remission of sins, I, 333.

**The sequence** in the Mass is the same as the jubilus, II, 497. —Why it is called the sequence of the Gospel, II, 499.

**Seraphim**, why they are so called, II, 501. Pronounced with *m*, they are masculine; with *n*, neuter, ibid.

**Pope Sergius**, II, 497. He ordained Willibrord archbishop, 186, 197.

**The serpent**, why it is called more crafty than all living creatures, I, 309. Why it was not asked why it had done this, 310. —The elevation of the bronze serpent, a type of Christ’s Passion, I, 492, 293.

**The monastery of Saint Servatius** at Maastricht, I, 40, note. Its brothers, 128, 129, note.

**Slavery**, twofold: voluntary and conditional, I, 840. The slavery of sin, 551, 552.

**Servant**, why so called, I, 333. —Either iniquity or adversity makes people servants, ibid.

**Sitting**, how it is to be understood in Scripture, I, 383. —The Lord’s sitting, the humility of the Incarnation, I, 541.

**The number sixty** is applied to queens in the Song of Songs, I, 409.

**Sexagesima**, why so called, and why and how it is celebrated, I, 86, 89; II, 468, 564. When it begins and ends, 468.

**The celebration of the sixth hour** in the divine office, whence it comes, II, 510.

**Sychar, Shechem, and Sichima**, I, 334.

**A brief exposition of the seven seals** in the Apocalypse, II, 458.

**To seal or mark something**, what it is, I, 524, 768, 851, 904.

**Sigobard**, the noble companion-in-arms of blessed Richarius, II, 180. He fitted a wooden sarcophagus for Saint Richarius’s burial, 181.

**Sigonius**, a priest of Urgell, I, 917.

**Signulfus**, Alcuin’s inseparable companion, I, 405. Extremely devoted to sacred reading, ibid.

**On Silence**, a homily on the silence into which the incarnate Word was sent, II, 532.

**The pool of Siloam**, a type of baptism, I, 558.

**Pope Saint Sylvester** instituted the use of the dalmatics, II, 496. His canons, I, 134, 137, 172. —The church and brothers of Saint Sylvester, II, 525.

The name is an assumed name of Eanbald the Younger, archbishop of York, 67, note, 148, note. Alcuin raised him and brought him to mature perfection, 76. He suffered troubles and tribulation, 75. **The likeness of God in human beings**, how it ought to be understood, I, 339 ff.

**Simon** is interpreted as “obedient,” I, 121. —Simon Zelotes. Taking its root from the judges of the world, it crept even into the apostolic see, 168. —The Simonian plague sprouts throughout the world, II, 229.

**To be together**, in how many ways the expression is used, II, 344.

**The bosom of God the Father**, how it is to be understood, I, 473.

**Captive Zion**, whence it comes and what it signifies, I, 181. In angels it is eternal; in human beings it is captive, ibid. —Zion, the Church, I, 354, 356, 381, 385, 387.

**Sizimarius**, a brother, I, 280. Sent by Alcuin with words of greeting to Theotgarius, ibid.

**The Slavs** are subdued by King Charles, I, 6.

**The Sodomites**, who they were, II, 472. Why their sin was punished by fire, I, 323. Why the infants too were burned with their parents, 322.

**The sun**, what it is, II, 353. By its rising and setting it signifies the destruction of the world, I, 413. Why it is called spirit, 414. —The course of the sun through the several signs, I, 93. Alcuin sent some calculations concerning it to Charlemagne, 124.

**Solaria**, what they are and why so called, II, 211.

**Solecism**, what it is, II, 271.

**The solstices**, why they are so called, how many there are, and on what days they occur, II, 428.

**Sleep**, what it is, II, 353. It must be shaken off by the young, 212, 226. Dreams are not to be believed, I, 425.

**Sophistical speech**, what it is, II, 326.

**The lot of the righteous**, what it is, I, 381.

**Soothsayers**, who they are, II, 472.

**Species**, what it is, II, 336.

**Spectacles**, disapproved, I, 206.

**Speratus**, a bishop, I, 72, 270. Whether he was an Englishman, 74, note. Alcuin’s letters to him, ibid.

**Hope**, what it is, II, 354. It is necessary for the soul, 130. —Hope of reward produces love of the commandment, I, 375. —Our hope rests more on God’s mercies than on our own merits, I, 385.

**Spirit**, used to mean anger, I, 312. —The spirit of a human being is the soul, I, 539. —How many spirits, and which, are named in Scripture, II, 422, 423. —How the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, I, 307. —The Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, I, 535, 540, 609, 713, 744 ff. He is also sent, 726, 754. He should be called neither unbegotten nor begotten, 712, 740. Whether he is spoken of relatively or substantially, 708, 740. Why he does not have a relation corresponding equally to that of the Father and the Son, ibid. He is the common Spirit of the Father and the Son, 638, 709, 753. Why he is nowhere read to be less than the Father, 728. How his being sent is to be understood, 726. How he was not incarnate, 729. How he is called the gift of God, ibid. and 723. When the controversy over the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son arose, 743. —Why the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in the form of a dove, I, 470. In Christ alone he remains perpetually in truth, ibid. —The Holy Spirit is compared with ointment, I, 388, 393. Why he is called the Paraclete, 599, 723. Why and how he appeared in the form of a dove, fire, and tongues, 277, 728. Why he was given twice by Christ, 638, 724. Whether he was given in the baptism of the disciples before the Lord’s Ascension, 499. How he came to the ancient saints before his coming at Pentecost, 539, 585, 599. —The unity of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, I, 723. —How charity is attributed to the Holy Spirit, I, 742. —The confession of faith in the Holy Spirit, II, 404.

**The spleen**, what it is, II, 353.

**The stars**, what they are, II, 353. The wandering stars: which they are and why so called, I, 97, 100.

**Pope Stephen**, II, 496. Pope Stephen IV granted the pallium to Theodulf of Orléans, I, 174, note.

**The altar of Saint Stephen**, the protomartyr, II, 208, 214. His church, 216. His monastery, 562. His cell, I, 75, 77, note. —The discovery of Saint Stephen’s body, I, 634. —Verses about Saint Stephen, II, 208.

**Sneezings**. See **Omens**.

**The priestly stole**, what it is, II, 495.

**The stomach**, what it is, II, 353.

**The *storacium***, a cloak, whence the name is derived, I, 157, note, 192, note.

**Stratocles**, a friend and son, or disciple, of Alcuin, I, 200.

**Fools** are compared with sand, I, 415.

**A foolish talker**, who he is, II, 472.

**Fornication**, how it differs from adultery and incest, II, 472.

**Subdeacons** and their office under the old law, II, 490. Under the new law, or in the Church, 434, 492.

**The three subsistences**, whether they are correctly predicated of God, I, 177.

**Substance**, what it is and why so called, II, 337. Whether and how it differs from essence and nature, I, 176. Whether and how it is said of God, 177.

**Succinctum**: a letter is so called, II, 232, note.

**The sudarium**, what it signifies, II, 496.

**Suestra**, a cell, now the monastery of Susteren, II, 189, note.

**The suffrages of the living**, what benefit they bring to the dead, I, 196.

**Suidbert**, with the priest Vira, preaches the word of God in Saxony, II, 252, verse 1073 ff.

**The altar of Saint Sulpitius**, bishop of Bourges, II, 213, 218.

**Sulpitius**, a reader teaching young men in the palace school so that they would not err in accents, II, 228.

**The proud** are persecutors of the humble, I, 366.

**Pride**, the cause of all diseases, cured by Christ’s humility, I, 525. Pride does its own will; humility does the will of God, ibid. What a sin it is, and how grave, II, 140, 142, 471. It vanishes when death comes, I, 355. It often arises from good works, II, 141, 142. —Pride scatters what fasts and almsgiving gather, II, 133. —The pride of human beings divided their tongues; the humility of Christ gathered them together, I, 316.

**The superhumeral** in the Old Testament: what garment it was, II, 494. Its mystical interpretation, 495. —The superhumeral in the Church: what it is and what it signifies, II, 495. —The holiness of the superhumeral, I, 121. See **Pallium**.

**The duty of superiors**, how it is to be performed toward their subjects, I, 210.

**Suspicion** is the greatest vice of human nature, I, 365.

**A whisperer**, who he is, II, 472.

**A syllable**, what it is, II, 269. And what features belong to it, 270.

**A syllogism**, how it is formed and how many kinds there are, II, 345.

**The creed**, what it is and why so called, II, 437. When and for what purpose it was composed by the apostles, ibid. It is compared with the sign or symbol of the Gileadites, ibid. Its exposition, 436 ff., 509, 522. —The Nicene Creed opposes all heresies, II, 515. It is also the rule of faith, 516. —The creed of faith in the Holy Trinity, I, 738. —The creed *Quicumque*, attributed to Saint Athanasius, I, 750, 756. —No new names are to be inserted into the creed of faith, I, 107.

**Pope Symmachus**, II, 497.

**The synagogue**, mother of the primitive Church, I, 394. She came first to the tomb but did not enter, 635.

**The synod of Ratisbon**, against Felix, in the year 792, I, 115, 882. The synod of Aachen, 702. The Roman synod of the year 799, 918. The synod of Sinuessa concerning Pope Marcellus, 134, 137. The synod of England for the reform of the clergy, 233.

**Synonyms**, what they are, II, 337.

## T
Description of the mystical meaning of Moses’ tabernacle, I, 691. Why it is called “touch,” and how many kinds of it there are, II, 421. Tapeta and sagellum, gifts sent to a friend, I, 68. Pope Telesphorus, ninth after St. Peter, I, 89; II, 466, 497. He instituted seven weeks of abstinence, I, 89. He decreed that Masses be celebrated at the Nativity of the Lord, II, 462. Tollhouse in mountain monasteries, I, 195. Temler of Copenhagen, secretary to the king of the Danes, is praised, I, 391. What temperance is and how noble a virtue it is, II, 145, 330, 331. It is the royal road of our whole life, I, 77. It is perfected through the love of God, II, 146. Its parts, 330, 333. Temples. What honor is owed them, I, 487.—The two constructions of the Temple of Jerusalem, I, 489. What the temples of the head are and why they are so called, II, 422. The difference between time and eternity, I, 178. Some philosophers think that the present does not exist, 651. Into how many and what parts time is divided, II, 426. Temptation, either for testing or for deception, II, 507. In how many ways it occurs in Scripture, I, 324.—Prayer during temptations from unclean spirits, II, 31. Teotgarius, abbot, perhaps of Lérins, I, 280, 281, note. What earth is, II, 353. How it was invisible and unformed, I, 307. Why it brought forth thorns and thistles after the curse, 310. Why it alone, and not the waters also, was cursed, 306.—The land of the South, where Isaac lived, what it is, I, 326.—Earth signifies sinners, I, 356; human nature, 369; the Church, II, 507.—The earth’s strength diminished after the Flood, I, 312. Why the thirtieth day is celebrated for the dead, II, 512.—Why the third day is celebrated for the dead, II, 512.—The origin of celebrating the third hour in the divine office, II, 510. A testament obtains validity through the testator’s death, I, 190. He is unworthy of it who proves ungrateful to the testator, ibid.—Why the Old Testament is so called, how many books it contains, and which they are, with a synopsis of them, II, 429. Why the New Testament is so called, the order of its books, and their authors, 432, 433 ff.—The Old Testament is signified by the number seven, the New by the number eight, I, 441. The difference between the two, 697. A witness who conceals the truth is equally guilty with one who tells a lie, II, 139.—False witnesses are answerable to God, to the judge, and to the innocent party, II, 139. How the testimony of two or three is true, I, 542, 543.—What the testimonies of God are, I, 374. Tetradius, a proconsular man; his conversion, II, 160. What the Tetragrammaton is, II, 424. Its interpretation, 496. Bishop Theuduinus of Orléans is sought as an associate in defense of the Catholic faith against Felix’s tract, I, 97, 99, note. See Theudulphus. What Thamar signifies, I, 450, 451, 453. Terah departed from the fire of the Chaldeans with his sons, I, 317. Theoduinus. See Deoduinus. [Col. 1497] Archbishop Theodulphus, I, 170, no. 1. See Theudulphus. What theology is, II, 335. Theophany. See Epiphany. Theophilus, a disciple of the twofold evangelical truth, I, 26. Whether he is the same as Theophylact, 27, note. Theophylact, teacher of wisdom, II, 231. Notary of the Apostolic See, ibid., note. Two men of this name flourished in Alcuin’s time, ibid. Theothertus, royal envoy, investigates the case of the cleric of Orléans at St. Martin’s, I, 162. What the theristrum, with which Rebecca covered herself, was, I, 326. Theudula, bishop of Seville, condemned Elipandus’s errors, II, 591. Who his predecessor and successor were, ibid. Bishop Theudulphus (of Orléans) disputes with the brothers of St. Martin, I, 170. He brings a complaint against them before the emperor, 174. And he became greatly inflamed against them, I, 176. Alcuin wrote to him when he was in the prime of life, 157. When he received the pallium and became bishop, 162, note. He is called archbishop, 170, nos. 1 and 2, 157. Not by the dignity of his see, but personally, ibid. He attended the Council of Aachen in 802, ibid. and note. An embassy and prefecture in the province of Narbonne were entrusted to him, ibid. Alcuin calls him “great pontiff” and “father of the vineyards,” ibid. His wisdom and virtues are praised, ibid. Thiel (Pancratius), scholasticus of St. Cyriacus at Worms, I, 304. How much the unbelief of St. Thomas the Apostle benefited us, I, 638. A poem about him, II, 221. What the thurible signifies at Mass, II, 496. Thyrsis and Menalcas, II, 228. What the tiara of the priests of the Old Testament is and what it signifies, II, 494, 495. Tiberias, a city healthy because of its warm waters, I, 518. Ticinum, a city of Italy; St. Martin was raised there, II, 159. Bishop Tifredus, I, 270. Whether he is the same as Bishop Tidfrith of the city of Damaca, who subscribed the Council of Clovesho, 271, note. Bishop Tilherus of Hexham, whom Æthelbert succeeded, I, 197, note. Filial fear of the Lord is commended, II, 135. The Timothians and their error, I, 796. The author of the books of Tobit is uncertain, II, 432. The origin of the clerical tonsure, II, 491. What it is like, 493. What the precious stone topaz signifies, I, 766. It contains within itself the beauty of all gems, 372. What topics are and their kinds, II, 346 ff. Toretmund, Aedilhard’s companion on the journey to Rome, I, 148. See Torhemundus. Torhemundus, the faithful servant of King Æthelred of Northumbria, I, 85. He vigorously avenged his lord’s blood, ibid. A torrent signifies the enormity of persecution, I, 380.—“Torrents” are called winter rivers, I, 382. In how many ways “whole” is said, II, 346, 347. Trajectum, a fortress and episcopal see, II, 185, 188, 197. Its bishop was St. Willibrord, ibid. An illustrious testimony to the dogma of transubstantiation, I, 49, note. Description of the city of Trier, II, 199. The chapel of St. Lupus in the city of Troyes, I, 148, note. The triclinium, that is, three rows of reclining diners, signifies the three orders of the faithful, I, 485. Why the thirtieth day is celebrated for the dead, II, 513, 514. The Trinity must not be said to be separable either in nature or in persons, I, 712, 740.—The works of the Holy Trinity are inseparable, I, 740. Yet some works properly belong to particular persons, 711. What is proper to each person, 739. What is personal in it is not common, but what is substantial is, II, 404. Whether it is permissible to say that the Holy Trinity is a nature, I, 176, 177. In the Holy Trinity there is distinction of persons, not of nature, 534, 730. It is better to say that there are three persons in God than three subsistences, 177. Those who err against the faith of the Trinity, II, 398.—Confession of the Holy Trinity, I, 738; II, 388, 389, 397. Invocation of the same, I, 737.—How the mystery of the Trinity was known before Christ, II, 388. Whether the three and the one are found in created things, II, 399. The forest of Tristiacum, II, 180, note. See Crisciacum. The origin of sadness and the vices it produces, II, 471. One kind is salutary, another destructive, 143. Its harmful effects and how it is overcome, ibid. What a trope is, II, 271. Tullum, a town, II, 165. An episcopal city on the Moselle, ibid., note. Tulpiacum, commonly Zullich; whether a battle with the Alemanni was fought there, II, 164, note. [Col. 1498] What Christ’s seamless tunic signifies, I, 631.—What the close-fitting linen tunic was as a garment in the Old Testament, II, 493. What it signifies, 494.—What the hyacinth-colored tunic was as a garment, II, 494. What it designated in the priest, 495.—Why leather tunics were made for man, I, 310. Tunna, priest and abbot, brother of the noble Imma, II, 250, note. He helped his slain brother through the sacrifice of the Mass, ibid., lines 812 ff. Tours, the city where St. Martin rests, II, 209. A small city in walls, but great through the patronage of St. Martin, 194. There was a shortage of grain and wine there, 71. The school of Tours was governed by Alcuin, I, 126. The bishop of Tours, I, 170, 174, note. Alcuin preferred smoke-blackened roofs to the gilded Roman palaces, 138. Inscriptions of the monastery of Tours, II, 211. Whether the tower and city of Babylon were one work or two, I, 317.—The Tower of the Flock, beside which Jacob lived, where it was situated, I, 330.

## U

When U changes into the power of a consonant, II, 269. “Ubi,” a category, II, 342. Umbrinsgstam, a noble Englishman, II, 557. By whom the anointing of the sick is to be performed, II, 510. The king of the Danes, a cruel man, to be anointed, II, 187. Ointment on the head signifies the Holy Spirit, I, 388, 393.—What the ointment made from genuine nard was, I, 580. The unity of the Church, spread throughout the whole world, I, 791.—The faith concerning the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity, I, 707. Ur, the fire among the Chaldeans, I, 317. What Uriah signifies, I, 450, 453. The Usa (Owse), the river that flows through York, II, 242, line 30. Usualdus, abbot of the monastery of St. Saviour, I, 27, 28, note. How a wineskin in frost signifies the mortal body, I, 369.

## V

What a cow signifies in Scripture, I, 319. The heretic Valentinus maintained that there are two baptisms, I, 109. Whatever is changeable is vanity, I, 413. Vasco, a Levite, completed the adornment of St. Vedast’s tomb, II, 215. A poem addressed to him, 105, ibid. St. Vedast, an outstanding preacher, II, 164. He instructed King Clovis in the faith and accompanied him to Reims to be baptized by St. Remigius, 165. At Tullum he devoted himself to the contemplative life, ibid. He restored sight to a blind man in the king’s presence, 166. Clovis commended him to St. Remigius, 167. He obtained wine from God through prayer, ibid. He ordered Urso to depart and forbade his return, 168. St. Remigius ordained him bishop of Arras, 165, 168. He built churches at Arras, ibid. and 169. He healed a blind man and a lame man, 168. King Chlothar, son of Clovis, summoned him to an estate, 169. He poured forth the word of God among the banqueters, ibid. He broke vessels infected by magic with the sign of the cross, ibid. How many years he governed the Church, 169. When he died, 172. His death was foretold by a luminous column, 170. His burial, ibid. and 171. His translation, ibid. He is renowned for miracles, 172. The writers of his life, 158.—The church of St. Vedast restored by Abbot Rado, II, 209. Verses at his tomb, 210. Alcuin wrote a Mass and a homiliary admonition about him, I, 60, note; II, 172.—A hymn about St. Vedast, II, 174.—The monks of St. Vedast, I, 59. Alcuin sent them metrical inscriptions, a missal, and other things, ibid. and 60.—Inscriptions of the monastery of St. Vedast, II, 209. What those who sell oxen, sheep, and doves signify, I, 487, 488. Who sorcerers are, II, 472. Venerius, priest of Elipandus, epistle I, 916. What the belly is, 353.—What the inner belly of the human being is, I, 539.—Gluttony of the belly, or gastrimargia, II, 472. What wind is, II, 353. What spring is, II, 353. From where it receives its name, 428. The Word of God was conceived in the Virgin’s womb through the conception of his flesh, I, 730. Whether and how it can be said to dwell in Christ, 848.—Through the Word, who is God, we were created; through the Word made flesh, we were recreated, I, 360. What a word is grammatically, II, 282, 351. Its proper characteristic, 271.—The moods of verbs, II, 281. Their accidents, 282. Their figures and conjugations, 285. Their number, 287.—Words are signs of the things we conceive in the mind, I, 179. What truth, as a part of the virtue of justice, is, II, 330. It is natural to every human being, I, 179. The lover of truth need fear no reprover, I, 790. From where verses derive their name, II, 500. What the crown of the head is, II, 422. Celebration of the evening hours, II, 510. Sacred vestments are to be used only in the Church, II, 496. Priestly vestments in the Old Testament and in the Church, 493, 494, 495. [Col. 1499] What the division of Christ’s garments and the casting of lots for his tunic signify, I, 631.—The care of clothing is unbecoming in clerics, I, 9, 12, 17, 21, 23, 201. It is reprehensible in monks, 23. Christ is the way of the testimonies of God, I, 362.—The way of truth is likewise Christ, 364.—What it is to direct the way of the Lord, I, 473. What the changing fortunes of human affairs are, II, 238. From where victims derive their name, II, 436. Victor, bishop of Capua. A certain short work of his on the Epistle to the Romans is cited, I, 776. It is mentioned by no one, ibid., note. His Book of Betrothed Persons is likewise unknown, 833, note.—The altar of St. Victor, II, 209. Victorinus (Marius), an outstanding rhetorician who proceeded from Cicero’s school to the battles of the Church, I, 910, note. What Victorius determined concerning the day of the moon’s leap, II, 358. Vienne, a principal city of Gaul, where the Rogation rites were first instituted, II, 486, 487. The vigil of the shepherds: what it prefigured, II, 462.—How the vigil of Pentecost is observed, II, 487.—The vigils of the saints are to be celebrated with fasting, II, 481.—How ancient the devotion to vigils is, II, 511. At the festivals of the saints, the people were eager to attend the vigils, II, 195. What vengeance, a part of the virtue of justice, is, II, 330. The word vinula is a light, soft, and flexible word, II, 207, note. The wine at the wedding in Cana of Galilee was not made from nothing, I, 485. What it signifies, II, 465.—Why wine is mixed with water at Mass, II, 500.—Whether people used wine before the Flood, I, 316. The Vionudi are called Slavs, I, 6. By others they are called Winidi, Wilcii, Wilzi, and Wulzi, 7, note. From where “man” derives its name, I, 431.—Who are usually designated by the name “men” in Scripture, I, 501, 520. Vira, a priest, II, 252, line 1073. Virgilius, bishop of Salzburg, built the cathedral basilica, II, 218, note. How noble virgins ought to conduct themselves at court, I, 148, epistle 125. With what virtues they should shine, 293 ff.—The altar of the holy virgins, II, 214. Virginity should be fruitful through the abundance of almsgiving, I, 209.—Commendation of virginity, ibid., 208 ff. What virtue is, II, 144, 329. And how many parts it has, ibid.—What the principal virtues are, II, 144, 329.—Christian virtues are expounded, II, 330.—Charity is the perfection of the virtues, II, 146.—The powers of heaven are, generally speaking, all the heavenly spirits, II, 501. The vision of God is complete blessedness, I, 158. It reveals the mysteries that now exist, II, 91.—What happiness belongs to the blessed vision, II, 392, 411.—The marvelous vision of a young man of York, II, 257, lines 1601 ff.—The visions of the Old Testament occurred chiefly through angelic ministrations, I, 722.—There are three kinds of visions, I, 215, 216. What sight is and from where it derives its name, II, 421. What life is, II, 352. From where it derives its name, 420. The present life is full of miseries, 392. Everyone is judged at the end of life, I, 104. If it is long, let it be good; if it is short, let it also be good, II, 135.—The course of this life, what it is, II, 533. The eight criminal vices: what they are, II, 471.—How many vices of diction there are, II, 271. Vittildus, a priest of Orgellitanum, I, 917. A calf in the school of St. Martin, sent by Alcuin to Aquila, I, 176.—Which calves are understood in the psalm, I, 354. Pleasure compared with drunkenness, I, 416. What vices voracity produces, II, 472. From where the voice derives its name, and the differences among voices, II, 268. What an articulate voice is, ibid.—“The voice of the people, the voice of God”: a deceptive maxim, I, 191. What the vowel letters are and from where they derive their name, II, 269. How many there are among the Latins, ibid. Why the face is called vultus, II, 422. Vungise, a district commonly called Vouzy, II, 166, note.

## W

Walachrum, a village—or rather the island of Walacra or Walacria in Zeeland—II, 188, note. Waldo, son of Arichis, duke of Benevento, I, 156, note. Wicbertus, a priest in Ireland, devoted himself to holiness of life, II, 185. Companion of St. Egbert, 252, line 1021; he founded a monastery for the monks of his own people, ibid., line 1025. Famous for signs and prophecy, lines 1030 ff. Wicus, the cell of St. Judoc, I, 55, 119, 120, note; 148, note; 206. See Judoc. Wido, a faithful count and royal envoy, I, 162. He governed the maritime March of Brittany, ibid., note. He was prefect of St. Martin’s possessions, [Col. 1500] I, 276, 277, note. He was called as a witness to the innocence of the brothers of St. Martin, 162. Occupied with military affairs, II, 128. Alcuin dedicated to him a book on virtues and vices, ibid. St. Wilfrid, bishop of York, illumined southern Saxony with the light of faith, II, 247, line 582. He freed a people oppressed by famine after they received baptism, 248, lines 595 ff. On his way to Rome he preached Christ to the Frisians with great success, lines 605 ff. He was rescued from a dangerous illness through the merits and prayers of the blessed Virgin Mary, ibid., line 633. From Queen Æthelthryth he obtained, by exchange, the place of Hexham, belonging to the royal fisc, I, 197, note. His death and burial, II, 248, lines 640 ff. Wilfrid II, bishop of York, succeeded John, II, 253, line 1215. Previously steward and abbot at York, ibid., line 1217. He adorned churches with sacred silver and gold vessels, lines 1222 ff. His virtues, lines 1230 ff. He lived as a solitary, lines 1237 ff. And after entrusting the pastoral care to Egbert, he died holy, lines 1245 ff. Wilgisus, a Saxon by birth, in the province of Northumbria, II, 183, 200, chap. 33. Father of St. Willibrord, 183, 184, 193, 200, chap. 33. He first embraced monastic life and afterward the solitary life, 184, 200, chap. 34. He gathered a small community, ibid. His piety and death, ibid. His anniversary is celebrated with wine multiplied from heaven, 194. St. Willibrord, a Briton by nation, son of St. Wilgisus, I, 184. His marvelous birth, ibid. and 200, chap. 34. He was sent to study at the monastery of Ripon, ibid. There he became a cleric and monk, ibid. With the consent of his abbot he departed for Ireland, 185. He reached Trajectum with twelve companions, ibid. At the urging of King Pippin he set out for Rome, 186, 197, chap. 3. He traveled to Rome twice, 186, note. There Pope Sergius ordained him archbishop, 186, note. And he was called Clement, ibid. He returned to Francia, 186, 197, chap. 6. He attempted to preach the word of God to the Frisians and Danes, 187, 197, chap. 7. He brought thirty catechized and baptized boys to Francia, 187. He won many thousands of Frisians for Christ, 252, line 1036. On the island of Fositesland he baptized three men, 187. In Francia he preached the Gospel, built churches, appointed priests in them, and so forth, 188. He attempted to overthrow the idol on the island of Walacra, ibid., 198, chap. 14. He built and dedicated the monastery of Echternach, 192, 199, chap. 27. He carried a golden cross with him on his journey, 193. Among the Frisians he built churches, 252, line 1040. He was established as bishop at Trajectum, 188, note; 177, chap. 11. He baptized Pippin, son of Duke Charles and father of Charlemagne, 191, 199, chap. 23. His gentleness, 188, 189. His natural gifts and virtues of character, 191. He performed various miracles during his life, 189 ff., 198, chap. 15 ff., and after his death, 192, 199, chap. 28 ff. His death, 192, 199, chap. 24. Where he was buried, 192, 199, chap. 27.—St. Willibrord’s well, 189, note. A homily for his feast, 194 ff. The kings of the Winidi, Witsan and Drago, I, 7. The brothers of the Church of Wir, I, 21, 283. See the brothers of St. Peter. They lived by the sea, 22.—The monastery of Wir in England, I, 23, note. Built by Bishop Benedict, ibid., note. Dedicated to the apostle St. Peter, 283, note. Witiricus, a cleric of Orgellitanum, I, 917. Witsan, king of the Winidi, I, 7. Witto, I, 70. Perhaps Candidus, 72, note. Wulframnus, companion of St. Willibrord in preaching, II, 187.

## Y

The letter Y, the sixth vowel adopted from the Greeks, II, 269.

## Z

Zebulun and his blessing are expounded, I, 337. Zacharias, palace priest, was sent by Charlemagne to Jerusalem with a large sum of money, I, 148, note. He came to Rome with two monks sent by the patriarch of Jerusalem, bringing the keys of the Holy Sepulchre, 457. Verses about Zacchaeus, II, 207. From where Zara received its name, I, 332. It is interpreted as “east,” ibid. What it signifies, 450, 451, 455. Zilpah, a handmaid; whether she should be called a wife or a concubine, I, 328. Zeal is good if tempered by gentleness, I, 172. Zenan, mentioned by Paul: who he was, I, 660. The distinguished work of Zenocrates the architect, I, 185. What the priestly girdle signifies, II, 495. Zoroaster, king and first of the Magi, II, 464. What Zerubbabel signifies, I, 450, 452, 453. Zuendrida, also called Drida, wife of King Offa and mother of Ecgfrith, I, 59, note. Whether she was related to Charlemagne, ibid. Her piety was characteristic of her sex, ibid. Zullich. See Tulpiacum.

# INDEX OF THE SUBJECTS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## FOURTH SHORT WORK.—TWO BOOKS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT WILLIBRORD, BISHOP OF UTRECHT. 693

Prologue. 693

### BOOK ONE. 693

### CHAPTER I.—Wilgisus first embraces the monastic life, then a solitary life. He is renowned for miracles. From gifts of kings and magnates he builds a church. Alcuin succeeds by lawful inheritance. 693

### CHAPTER II.—The wondrous conception of Saint Willibrord. A vision of his mother. Interpretation of the vision. 695

### CHAPTER III.—The birth and baptism of Saint Willibrord. He becomes a cleric and monk. 696

### CHAPTER IV.—He sets out for Ireland. 696

### CHAPTER V.—He burns with the desire to convert pagans. 697

### CHAPTER VI.—He comes to Utrecht with twelve companions. Departing thence, he seeks Francia and is honourably received by Pippin. At Pippin’s urging, he seeks Rome to be ordained bishop. 697

### CHAPTER VII.—Angelic vision. He is ordained archbishop and called Clement. 698

### CHAPTER VIII.—He returns to Francia and devotes himself to the work of the Gospel with very great fruit. 699

### CHAPTER IX.—He preaches Christ in Frisia, likewise in Denmark; from there he leads thirty boys into Francia. 699

### CHAPTER X.—He despises the superstition of a barbarous people. One of his companions is slain and becomes a martyr. With great confidence he announces Christ to the king. The king sends him back to Pippin. 700

### CHAPTER XI.—In Francia he preaches the Gospel more ardently. From the gifts offered, after appointing priests everywhere, he builds churches. 701

### CHAPTER XII.—Charles Martel conquers many peoples. Saint Willibrord becomes bishop of Utrecht. 701

### CHAPTER XIII.—He smashes an idol. Struck with a sword, he suffers no injury. Divine vengeance upon the assailant. 702
